一.etymology: Cardinal number 'one', written since oracle-bone antiquity with a single horizontal stroke. In spoken Mandarin, 一 undergoes regular tone sandhi: yī in counting and ordinals (第一), rising yí before a fourth tone (一个 yí gè), and falling yì before tones 1, 2, and 3 (一杯 yì bēi).

history.meaning: numeral one; single; whole

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 一 (via 萌典)

一下.etymology: Verbal classifier phrase combining 一 ('one') + 下 ('downward stroke or beat; single occurrence of an action'). Placed after a verb (看一下, 等一下), it softens commands and marks a brief, casual, or single-attempt action.

history.meaning: one stroke/time -> brief verbal measure ('for a moment, once')

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 一下 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: all at once; in a single stroke

一下子.etymology: A vernacular numeral-classifier-suffix formation combining 一 (yī, 'one; single'), the verbal action classifier 下 (xià, originally 'below; to descend', grammaticalized in Tang–Song vernacular into a measure for brief actions or strokes), and the nominalizing diminutive suffix 子 (zi). From the literal sense 'one stroke' or 'one beat of time', it lexicalized into a punctual adverbial meaning 'in a single instant' or 'all of a sudden'.

history.meaning: one stroke, one time, or a brief action (early vernacular Chinese)
in one go; all at once; suddenly

morphemes.meaning: stroke; brief occurrence of an action

一下子.notes: Pronounced yíxiàzi with tone sandhi on 一 before fourth-tone 下; ubiquitous in spoken dialogue to mark abrupt transitions or sudden realizations.

rootFamily.gloss: a bit; once; for a moment
three strokes and five divisions—neatly and quickly

一丝丝.etymology: Reduplicated numeral-classifier phrase from 一 ('one') + 丝丝 ('fine threads; wisps'), where 丝 (simplified from 絲, two silk cocoons 糸 side by side) originally denoted raw silk filaments spun by silkworms. Because a single silk filament was the traditional Chinese unit of minimal thickness and weight (one hundred-thousandth of a liang), reduplicating 丝 into 一丝丝 vividly expresses delicate wisps of aroma, breeze, or faint emotion.

history.meaning: a single filament of raw silk; a tiny fraction
fine wisps of; a faint trace of

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 一丝丝

一个.etymology: Compound numeral-classifier phrase joining 一 ('one', spoken rising yí before fourth tone) + 个 (default general classifier, originally 箇/個 'bamboo stalk, single unit'). Serves both to count single items and, in colloquial Mandarin, like an indefinite article ('a, a certain').

history.meaning: one unit; a single (item or person)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 一个 (via 萌典)

一个月.etymology: A numeral-classifier-noun phrase structured as modifier-head: 一 (yī, 'one') + general classifier 个 (gè, simplified from 個/箇, originally a measure word for bamboo stalks in Classical Chinese) + 月 (yuè, 'moon; month', from an oracle-bone crescent pictograph). In Classical Chinese, 'one month' was expressed directly as 一月 without a classifier; in Mandarin, 一月 shifted to mean 'January', making the classifier 个 obligatory to denote the duration 'one month'.

history.meaning: one month or the first lunar month (without classifier)
duration of one month (distinguished from calendar month)
one month (simplified script standard)

一个月.notes: Never omit 个 when expressing duration: 一个月 means 'one month', whereas 一月 strictly means 'January'.

rootFamily.gloss: month end; end of the month

一些.etymology: A numeral-classifier compound formed from 一 (yī, 'one; a') and the plural/indefinite measure morpheme 些 (xiē). In Classical Chinese (notably *Chu Ci*), 些 functioned as a verse-final modal particle (pronounced suò); during the Six Dynasties and Tang vernacular period, 些 grammaticalized into an indefinite quantifier meaning 'a small amount; several', pairing with 一 to form a determiner for unspecified small quantities or pluralities.

history.meaning: sentence-final exclamatory particle in southern Chu poetry
a little bit; a small quantity (Tang–Song vernacular)
some; a few; a certain amount

一些.notes: Pronounced yìxiē (tone sandhi before first-tone 些); modifies both countable nouns (一些人, 'some people') and mass/abstract nouns (一些时间, 'some time').

cognates.meaning: one item; one case or matter

一件.etymology: A numeral-classifier construction pairing 一 (yī, 'one') with 件 (jiàn, 'item; discrete matter'). Phono-semantically composed of 人 ('person') and 牛 ('ox'), 件 originally meant 'to divide; to butcher and apportion cattle' as glossed in *Shuowen Jiezi* (分也). By Tang–Song vernacular Chinese, the sense of an apportioned share evolved into a bound classifier for discrete affairs, garments, documents, and luggage.

history.meaning: to divide, separate, or itemize
one discrete item, garment, or affair

morphemes.meaning: classifier for matters, clothing, documents, or items

一件.notes: Pronounced yíjiàn; in TV production and workplace dialogue, 一件事 ('one matter/issue') and 一件案子 ('one case') are staple collocations.

一份.etymology: A numeral-classifier compound joining 一 (yī, 'one') with 份 (fèn, 'portion; allotted share; copy'). Morphologically derived from 分 (fēn, 'to divide') with the person radical 亻 added to distinguish the noun 'allotted share or role' (also written 分 in Classical Chinese, as in 名分). From 'one divided portion', 一份 extended in modern administrative and media usage to count duplicated documents, contracts, proposals, meals, and jobs.

history.meaning: one tenth; one allotted portion or share
one share, portion, copy, or job position

morphemes.meaning: portion; share; copy of a document or newspaper

一份.notes: Pronounced yífèn; essential in office and media settings for proposals (一份策划案), contracts (一份合同), and roles/jobs (一份工作).

一会儿.etymology: A northern Mandarin rhotacized numeral-noun compound consisting of 一 (yī, 'one'), 会 (huì, traditional 會, originally 'to meet; to converge'), and the diminutive retroflex suffix 儿 (-r, 兒). In Literary and early vernacular Chinese, 会 developed the temporal sense 'conjuncture; brief interval where events meet'. Adding rhotacization (儿化) in Beijing-based Mandarin yielded 一会儿 ('a brief moment' or 'in a short while').

history.meaning: one gathering; a brief juncture or interval of time
a little while; in a moment (rhotacized colloquial form)

一会儿.notes: Pronounced yíhuìr; functions both as a duration complement (等一会儿, 'wait a while') and as a temporal adverb before a verb (一会儿见, 'see you in a bit').

一共.etymology: Adverb meaning 'altogether, in total', formed from 一 ('one single whole') + 共 ('together, shared', attested from oracle-bone and bronze inscriptions showing two hands holding an object together).

history.meaning: all together; in total

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 一共 (via 萌典)

一分不差.etymology: Four-character idiom built from 一 ('one') + 分 ('minute; one-tenth unit of measure', knife radical 刀 splitting 八 'apart') + 不 ('not') + 差 ('err; fall short; deviate'). Originally applied to exact weights, silver measures, and sundial or water-clock timekeeping, it became the standard modern phrase for punctuality down to the exact minute.

morphemes.meaning: does not deviate or fall short

history.meaning: not off by a single fraction in weight or measure
not a minute off; right on the dot

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 一分不差

一切.etymology: A Literary Chinese modifier-head / verbal-summary compound of 一 (yī, 'one; single stroke') and 切 (qiè, here reflecting the Middle Chinese reading *tshet, 'to cut evenly across', distinct from qiē 'to slice'). Originating in Han administrative prose (e.g., *Book of Han*, meaning 'by a single sweeping cut; uniformly across the board'), 一切 was adopted by Six Dynasties Buddhist translators such as Kumarajiva to render Sanskrit *sarva* ('all; the entirety of phenomena'), cementing its modern pronoun and determiner sense.

history.meaning: with one uniform cut; across the board; provisionally
all dharmas; the totality of things (calquing Sanskrit sarva)
everything; all; every

morphemes.meaning: to cut across evenly; encompassing all together

一切.notes: Always pronounced yíqiè (fourth tone on 切), never *yīqiē; commonly modifies nouns without 的 (一切问题, 'all problems') or stands alone as a pronoun (这一切, 'all of this').

一刻.etymology: Time expression combining 一 ('one') + 刻 ('carved notch on a clepsydra water clock', knife radical 刂 + phonetic 亥 hài). Under the traditional 96-notch daily water-clock system refactored in the early Qing dynasty, one 刻 equaled 15 minutes ('a quarter of an hour'); also used for 'a brief moment'.

history.meaning: one notch-interval on a water clock
quarter of an hour (15 minutes); a short moment

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 一刻 (via 萌典)

一千七百.etymology: A regular decimal additive-multiplicative numeral phrase composed of two coordinative place-value constituents: 一千 (yīqiān, '1 × 1000') + 七百 (qībǎi, '7 × 100'). All four sinographs trace directly to Shang oracle-bone numerals: 一 (single horizontal tally stroke), 千 (person 人 modified with a stroke for 'thousand'), 七 (cross-cut tally for 'seven'), and 百 (phonetic 白 with numeral stroke 一 for 'hundred'). Already structured identically in late Shang and Western Zhou inscriptions without needing an intervening conjunction when adjacent decimal places are filled.

history.meaning: one thousand and seven hundred (additive decimal compound)
one thousand seven hundred (1,700)

一千七百.notes: Pronounced yìqiān qībǎi; in colloquial speech when no smaller digits follow, 百 is optionally omitted (一千七, 'seventeen hundred').

一半.etymology: Numeral compound of 一 ('one') + 半 ('half', originally an ideogram in bronze and seal script showing an ox 牛 split in two by 八 'divide').

history.meaning: one half

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 一半 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: one phrase; a single word or line of verse

一句.etymology: A numeral-classifier compound combining 一 (yī, 'one') and 句 (jù, 'clause; sentence; poetic line'). In Old Chinese, 句 (related to 勾 gōu, 'hook; curved') referred to a hooked pause-mark used by scribes to segment text, and hence the clause bounded by that pause. Paired with 一, it counts spoken remarks, lines of script dialogue, or verses of poetry.

history.meaning: textual pause-hook; syntactic clause or verse line
one sentence, one line of verse, or a single remark

morphemes.meaning: classifier for sentences, spoken remarks, or lines of dialogue

一句.notes: Pronounced yíjù; in colloquial Mandarin, 说一句 ('let me say one thing') or 一句话 ('in a word / one sentence') often compresses an entire argument into a punchy takeaway.

rootFamily.gloss: line of dialogue in a play or script

一号机.etymology: A modern technical modifier-head compound built from the ordinal designation 一号 (yīhào, 'Number One', from 一 'one' + 号/號 hào 'designation, code number') modifying 机 (jī, simplified from 機, originally 'crossbow trigger mechanism; loom', modernized across East Asia—reinforced by Japanese 機 *-ki* compounds—to mean 'machine, aircraft, or camera'). In broadcast television and live-studio directing, 一号机 is the clipped professional term for 一号摄像机 ('Camera 1', typically the wide master-shot camera).

history.meaning: trigger mechanism, loom, or pivotal device
Unit No. 1; Aircraft No. 1; Camera One in broadcast studio jargon

morphemes.meaning: machine; camera unit (clipped from 摄像机)

一号机.notes: Pronounced yīhàojī (note that 一 stays first tone yī when used as an ordinal/serial number rather than a quantity!); control-room directors call 切一号机 ('cut to Camera One').

cognates.meaning: completely; (with negative) not at all; heading in one direction

一向.etymology: A Literary and vernacular modifier-head compound uniting 一 (yī, 'one; single; unbroken') and 向 (xiàng, originally an oracle-bone pictograph of a north-facing window, extended to 'direction; orientation; hitherto/past period'). In Tang–Song poetry and prose, 一向 meant both 'facing one continuous direction' and 'for a continuous stretch of recent time'; in Modern Mandarin it stabilized as a temporal-aspectual adverb meaning 'consistently from the past up to now; all along'.

history.meaning: in a single direction; for a recent stretch of time (Tang–Song usage)
all along; consistently; always (with habitual states or dispositions)

一向.notes: Pronounced yíxiàng; pairs with stative verbs, adjectives, or habitual attitudes (他一向很严谨, 'he has always been rigorous'), never with future or single-event actions.

cognates.meaning: one round; one lap; one week

一周.etymology: A numeral-classifier/noun compound combining 一 (yī, 'one') and 周 (zhōu, 'complete circuit; cycle; revolution', written 週 in traditional script when denoting cycles or weeks). In Classical Chinese, 一周 meant 'one full revolution' or 'one full year-cycle'. During late Qing modernization—reinforced by Meiji Japanese 週 (*shū*) for the seven-day Western week alongside 星期—一周 became the concise formal-neutral Mandarin term for 'one week'.

history.meaning: one full circuit, lap, or annual cycle
one seven-day week; one complete lap

一周.notes: Pronounced yìzhōu; takes no intervening classifier (*一个周 is non-standard in formal writing, unlike 一个星期 or 一个礼拜), and is standard in broadcast schedules (一周播两集, 'airing two episodes a week').

cognates.meaning: one ingredient; a comrade of the same group/cabal

一味.etymology: Originally a Classical Chinese numeral-noun / classifier phrase from 一 (yī, 'one; single') + 味 (wèi, 'taste, flavor; medicinal ingredient'). In traditional Chinese pharmacology, 一味药 meant 'a single medicinal herb', while in Chan/Buddhist texts 一味 signified 'of one uniform essence/flavor' (Sanskrit *ekarasa*). By Ming–Qing vernacular prose, clinging to 'just one flavor/method' without variation grammaticalized into a mildly critical adverb meaning 'blindly, stubbornly, or invariably'.

history.meaning: one flavor; a single medicinal ingredient; uniform Buddhist essence
single-mindedly; stubbornly; blindly doing one thing without adapting

一味.notes: Pronounced yíwèi; carries a negative or cautionary connotation in modern Mandarin (e.g., 不能一味妥协, 'cannot blindly compromise'), unlike neutral 一直 ('continuously').

cognates.meaning: number-one male star; top brother/leader in a field

一哥.etymology: A modern Cantonese entertainment and media coinage borrowed into Mainland Mandarin, built as an ordinal modifier-head compound from 一 (yī, clipped from 第一 dì-yī, 'number one; top-ranked') + 哥 (gē, 'elder brother', an early medieval loan into Chinese—often linked to Altaic *aka*—widely used in southern Chinese and Hong Kong showbiz as an honorific for male stars and senior figures). Popularized in late-20th-century Hong Kong TV (TVB) journalism to crown a network's undisputed leading male star or anchor.

history.meaning: top-ranked male actor/singer at a Hong Kong broadcaster or label; Police Commissioner nickname
leading man; number-one male star or top industry figure in Mainland media slang

morphemes.meaning: elder brother; respected male figure or star

一哥.notes: Pronounced yīgē (keeping level first tone on 一 because it stands for ordinal 第一, 'No. 1', though casual speakers occasionally apply sandhi); paired symmetrically with 一姐 ('top female star').

rootFamily.gloss: top female star; leading lady of a network

一块.etymology: A numeral-classifier compound formed from 一 (yī, 'one; single') and 块 (kuài, traditional 塊, composed of 土 'earth' + 鬼 phonetic, originally meaning 'clod of earth' in Classical Chinese, e.g., *Zuo Zhuan*). As 块 evolved into a classifier for chunks, plots of land, and currency units, 'in one single piece/plot of ground' (一块地) grammaticalized in northern Mandarin into an adverb and spatial noun meaning 'in the same place' or 'together'.

history.meaning: clod or lump of earth
one lump/piece; one plot of ground; one yuan currency unit
together; in the same place (adverbial extension alongside 'one piece')

morphemes.meaning: lump; piece; shared patch of space

一块.notes: Pronounced yíkuài; serves both as the non-rhotacized written/southern equivalent of 一块儿 ('together') and literally as 'one piece' or 'one yuan/kuai'.

一块儿.etymology: The rhotacized (儿化 érhuà) Beijing and northern Mandarin lexicalization of 一块 (yī 'one' + 块 kuài 'clod, piece, patch of ground') plus the diminutive suffix 儿 (-r, 兒). Here rhotacization performs a crucial morphological disambiguation: non-rhotacized 一块 often retains its literal numeral-classifier sense ('one piece' or 'one yuan'), whereas 一块儿 (yíkuàir) obligatorily marks the spatial-comitative sense 'in the same place' or 'together'.

history.meaning: one piece or one shared patch of ground
together; at the same location (rhotacized comitative adverb/place word)

一块儿.notes: Pronounced yíkuàir; interchangeable with 一起 in everyday northern speech (咱们一块儿去, 'let's go together') and also acts as a spatial object after 到 or 在 (凑到一块儿, 'gather together').

cognates.meaning: one sound; a cry or shout

一声.etymology: A numeral-classifier compound joining 一 (yī, 'one; single') and 声 (shēng, traditional 聲, originally depicting a hand striking a hanging stone chime 磬 above an ear 耳). In Classical Chinese, 声 denoted pitched acoustic sound or vocal utterance; paired with 一 as a verbal/vocal classifier, 一声 counts a single cry, shout, knock, or brief verbal notice (as in 说一声, 'give a quick word').

history.meaning: one musical note, chime stroke, or vocal sound
a single sound, cry, or brief verbal heads-up; First Tone in Mandarin phonetics

一声.notes: Pronounced yìshēng when meaning 'a sound / a quick word' (告诉我一声, 'let me know'), but yīshēng (level first tone) when naming Mandarin's 'First Tone'!

rootFamily.gloss: without uttering a single sound; silently
at a single word of command

一声令下.etymology: A four-character idiomatic subject-predicate clause (chengyu-style narrative phrase) structured internally as [modifier + subject + predicate]: 一声 (yìshēng, 'a single vocal utterance') modifies 令 (lìng, 'command, order', originally an oracle-bone graph of a kneeling figure receiving instructions from an authority symbol 亼), followed by the directional-verbal predicate 下 (xià, 'descends / is handed down from above'). Drawn from military and imperial administrative imagery where an order descends from the commander's dais, triggering instant collective action.

history.meaning: an official or military order is issued downward
the instant a single word of command is given (prompting immediate action)

morphemes.meaning: to descend; to be issued downward

一声令下.notes: Pronounced yìshēng lìng xià; vivid in film/TV production sets when a director or producer gives the cue (导演一声令下, 全组开拍, 'at the director's word, the whole crew started rolling').

一夜之间.etymology: A Literary-structured four-character temporal modifier-head phrase modeled on Classical Chinese `X + 之 + 间`: 一夜 (yíyè, 'one single night', from 一 'one' + 夜 yè 'night') + the Classical genitive subordinator 之 (zhī, 'of') + the spatial-temporal localizer 间 (jiān, traditional 間, originally 'moonlight seen through a doorway gap 門+月', hence 'interval, space between'). Literally 'within the span of a single night', it lexicalized to describe sudden, dramatic transformations occurring 'overnight'.

history.form: 一夜之間 / 一夜之间
history.meaning: within the interval of one night; overnight (sudden rise, fame, or reversal)

一夜之间.notes: Pronounced yíyè zhījiān; a signature showbiz and media collocation for viral stardom or sudden crisis (一夜之间爆红, 'shot to fame overnight').

rootFamily.gloss: instantaneous; in the blink of an eye

cognates.meaning: a big pile of; tons of

一大堆.etymology: An expanded numeral-adjective-classifier construction joining 一 (yī, 'one; a'), the intensifying dimensional adjective 大 (dà, 'big; huge'), and the collective mass classifier 堆 (duī, composed of 土 'earth' + 隹 phonetic, originally 'mound of heaped earth' in Classical Chinese, e.g., *Shi Ji*). Inserting 大 directly before a collective or container classifier (like 一大群, 一大碗) is a productive Mandarin pattern; 一大堆 metaphorically extends 'a huge mound' to 'tons of' problems, tasks, documents, or people.

history.meaning: mound or heap of earth
one pile or heap (classifier phrase)
a huge pile of; tons of; a slew of (concrete or abstract items)

一大堆.notes: Pronounced yídàduī; colloquial and expressive for overwhelming workloads (一大堆烂摊子, 'a huge pile of messes'; 一大堆事儿, 'tons of things to handle'), so avoid it in stiff official prose.

cognates.meaning: bright and early in the morning

一大早.etymology: An emphatic vernacular temporal noun phrase built from 一 (yī, here marking immediacy/completeness right from the outset, as in 一清早) + the colloquial degree intensifier 大 (dà, 'full, right in the thick of', as in 大白天 'broad daylight' or 大半夜 'dead of night') + 早 (zǎo, 'early morning', originally depicting the sun 日 rising above grass/plants 十). Together, 一大早 vividly emphasizes 'first thing bright and early in the morning'.

history.meaning: very early in the morning (vernacular intensifier + temporal root)
bright and early; at the crack of dawn

一大早.notes: Pronounced yídàzǎo; often carries mild surprise or complaint about how early something happened (一大早就来敲门, 'came knocking first thing in the morning').

一天.etymology: A numeral-noun / quasi-classifier compound combining 一 (yī, 'one; whole') and 天 (tiān, originally an anthropomorphic Shang-Zhou graph of the 'head/crown' above a standing figure 大, hence 'sky, heaven, Supreme Deity'). In Classical Chinese, 'one day' was 一日 (yīrì), while 一天 meant 'one expanse of sky/heaven'. During the Tang–Song vernacular shift, 天 ('sky/daylight cycle') supplanted 日 as the spoken word for 'day', giving 一天 the senses 'one day', 'one fine day (in the past/future)', and 'all day long'.

history.meaning: the single overarching sky or firmament (whereas 'one day' was 一日)
one twenty-four-hour day; a certain day; the whole day

一天.notes: Pronounced yìtiān; like 年 and 周, 天 is a self-classifying temporal noun—never say *一个天! Pre-verbally with 都 (一天都在忙), 一天 means 'the entire day'.

cognates.meaning: all day long; from morning till night
cognates.word: 一天到晚 (jat1 tin1 dou3 maan5)

一天到晚.etymology: A colloquial four-character temporal-extent phrase combining 一天 (yìtiān, 'throughout the whole day, starting from morning') with the directional verb-object span 到晚 (dàowǎn, 'reaching until evening/night', from 到 dào 'arrive at, up to' + 晚 wǎn 'evening, dusk'). Blending 'one whole day' with 'from [morning] till night' (cf. 从早到晚), it grammaticalized in Mandarin into an emphatic adverbial meaning 'all day long' or 'constantly'.

history.meaning: from morning until evening
all day long; incessantly; round the clock

一天到晚.notes: Pronounced yìtiān dàowǎn; very frequently conveys exasperation or hyperbole when describing someone's non-stop habit (一天到晚就知道工作, 'all you ever do from morning till night is work').

一套.etymology: A numeral-classifier phrase turned idiomatic noun, formed from 一 (yī, 'one') + 套 (tào, composed of 大 'large' + 長/镸 'long', originally 'outer wrap, slipcover, or harness loop' in Middle and vernacular Chinese). From counting matched sets of books, garments, or martial-arts routines (套路), 一套 lexicalized into a standalone noun meaning 'a complete repertoire/knack' (when praised, as in 有一套) or 'a stale routine/gimmick' (when dismissed, as in 少来这一套).

history.meaning: outer casing, slipcover, or overlapping layer; matched suite of songs in Yuan drama
one complete set; an effective knack/system or a contrived routine/act

morphemes.meaning: set; suite; system of methods or routines

一套.notes: Pronounced yítào; watch the sharp polarity shift by frame: 他真有一套! praises real skill ('he really knows his stuff!'), whereas 别耍这一套! rejects manipulation ('cut that act!').

一如既往.etymology: A Literary Chinese-styled four-character verb-object idiom (chengyu) structured as adverbial 一 (yī, 'entirely; uniformly', a classic literary adverbial function distinct from the numeral 'one') + transitive verb 如 (rú, 'to be like; to accord with') + nominalized object 既往 (jìwǎng, 'that which has already passed; the past', attested in Confucius's *Analects* 3.21: 既往不咎, 'let bygones be bygones', from perfective 既 'already' + 往 'gone'). Literally 'entirely resembling what has gone before', i.e., 'just as in the past; consistently as always'.

history.meaning: that which is already past and gone (*Analects*)
entirely as in the past; unswervingly as always

morphemes.meaning: to resemble; to be just like

一如既往.notes: Pronounced yìrú jìwǎng; polished formal register favored in speeches, press releases, and professional acknowledgments (一如既往地支持, 'support us as always').

cognates.meaning: number-one female star; top sister/diva of a company

一姐.etymology: A modern Hong Kong Cantonese media and showbiz compound borrowed into Mainland Mandarin alongside 一哥, built as an ordinal modifier-head noun from 一 (yī, clipped from 第一 dì-yī, 'number one; premier') + 姐 (jiě, 'elder sister', in *Shuowen Jiezi* originally the蜀 dialect word for 'mother', later shifting across Chinese to 'elder sister' and respectful/familiar address for senior women in a profession). Coined in TVB entertainment reporting to designate a television network's, record label's, or agency's top-billed female star or anchorwoman.

history.meaning: top-ranked female actress, diva, or anchor at a Hong Kong network or label
top female star, leading lady, or queen of a broadcast platform in Mainland showbiz

morphemes.meaning: elder sister; respected leading woman in a field

一姐.notes: Pronounced yījiě (preserving level first tone on ordinal 一 in standard broadcast speech, e.g., 卫视一姐, 'the satellite network's top female host/star').

一字不差.etymology: Four-character idiom composed of 一 ('one') + 字 ('written character; word', roof 宀 over child 子) + 不 ('not') + 差 ('err; deviate; fall short'). Modelled on classical scribal and printing collocations requiring copyists to reproduce texts without a single erroneous or missing character, it is the standard idiom for verbatim recitation or copying.

history.meaning: copied or recited without a single character differing
word for word; verbatim

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 一字不差

一季.etymology: A numeral-noun / classifier compound combining 一 (yī, 'one') and 季 (jì, composed of 禾 'young grain' + 子 'child'). In Classical Chinese seniority order (伯仲叔季), 季 meant 'youngest of brothers' and hence the 'last/third month of a three-month season' (e.g., 季春, 'late spring'), before broadening to mean an entire three-month 'season' or 'quarter'. In contemporary Chinese television and streaming media (calquing English TV 'season'), 一季 also functions as the standard classifier phrase for 'one season' of a series or reality show.

history.meaning: youngest brother; the final month of a three-month season
one meteorological/agricultural season or fiscal quarter
one calendar season; one broadcast season of a TV/variety show

morphemes.meaning: three-month season; fiscal quarter; broadcast season of a show

一季.notes: Pronounced yíjì with tone sandhi when counting ('one season', 拍了一季), but dì-yī jì (level first tone) in ordinal 第一季 ('Season 1' of a show).

一定.etymology: Adverb and adjective meaning 'settled, fixed; certainly, without fail', from 一 ('unified, single') + 定 ('settle, fix', roof 宀 + 正 'upright/foot settled inside a house'). In Classical texts (such as Hanfeizi), 一定 meant 'once fixed or unified'; in Mandarin it grammaticalized into a strong modal adverb ('definitely, must').

history.meaning: once settled; fixed as one
certainly; definitely; fixed

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 一定 (via 萌典)

一宿.etymology: A northern colloquial numeral-classifier compound pairing 一 (yī, 'one; one whole') with 宿 (xiǔ, traditional/standard character 宿, an oracle-bone pictograph of a person 人 lying on a woven sleeping mat 百/𠀠 beneath a roof 宀, originally 'to lodge for the night'). Chinese preserves a classic three-way literary/colloquial reading split on 宿: literary sù ('lodge; stay overnight'), astronomical xiù ('lunar mansion/constellation'), and colloquial northern vernacular xiǔ ('a night's span' when preceded by numerals, as in 一宿 or 两宿).

history.meaning: one overnight lodging or halt on a journey
one whole night (colloquial northern Mandarin measure of night duration)

一宿.notes: Crucial polyphone trap: read yìxiǔ (third tone on 宿, NOT *yísù!) when meaning 'one whole night' in spoken Mandarin (熬了一宿, 'pulled an all-nighter'), whereas 住宿 ('lodging') is read zhùsù.

rootFamily.gloss: all night long; whole night (read xiǔ)

cognates.meaning: one session, term, or graduating class

一届.etymology: A numeral-classifier compound joining 一 (yī, 'one') and 届 (jiè, variant/simplified from 屆, composed of 尸 'body' + 凷/由, glossed in *Shuowen* and Classical texts as 'to reach, arrive at an extremity or appointed time', e.g., *Book of Documents* 无远弗届). From 'arriving at a scheduled recurrence', 届 grammaticalized in modern institutional Chinese into the specialized classifier for periodic conferences, graduating classes, terms of office, film festivals, and seasonal competition editions.

history.meaning: to reach; to arrive at a limit or appointed time
one scheduled session, edition, cohort, or term (conferences, awards, festivals, graduates)

morphemes.meaning: classifier for regularly recurring sessions, editions, classes, or terms

一届.notes: Pronounced yíjiè; only counts events or cohorts that recur on a regular cycle—awards shows (新一届电影节), talent competitions, parliaments, or graduating classes—never ad-hoc meetings (use 次 or 场 instead).

rootFamily.gloss: current year's graduating cohort or current edition

一干二净.etymology: Four-character idiom built on the numeral frame 一…二… ('first… second… / thoroughly') splitting the compound 干净 ('clean', 干/乾 'dry' + 净 'clean, pure'). Describes something wiped, forgotten, or used up 'completely and utterly clean, without a trace left'.

history.form: 一乾二淨 / 一干二净
history.meaning: thoroughly clean; completely gone without a trace

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 一干二净 (via 萌典)

一年.etymology: A numeral-noun / self-classifying temporal compound combining 一 (yī, 'one; one whole') and 年 (nián, Shang oracle-bone graph 秊 depicting a person 人 carrying ripe grain 禾 on their back). In early Zhou bronze inscriptions and Classical texts, 年 originally meant 'grain harvest'; because northern millet yielded one main harvest per solar cycle, 年 became the standard word for 'year' (supplanting Shang 祀 'ritual cycle' and coexisting with 岁 suì 'Jupiter cycle / year of age').

history.meaning: one annual harvest cycle; one calendar year
one year; throughout a whole year

一年.notes: Pronounced yìnián; like 天 and 周, 年 is an autonomous measure noun that never takes 个 (*一个年 is ungrammatical; compare 一个月, which requires 个).

rootFamily.gloss: four seasons of a year; all year round
year end; Lunar New Year's Eve period

一年一度.etymology: A four-character symmetrical numeral-classifier expression (一 A 一 B pattern) combining 一年 (yī nián, 'one year', where 年 originally depicted a person carrying harvested grain, hence an annual harvest cycle) and 一度 (yī dù, 'one occurrence/pass', from 度 'to measure, pass through'). Attested in Tang-Song poetry (e.g., Du Mu and Song lyrics describing annual festivals like Qixi or Mid-Autumn), it functions as an attributive modifier marking ceremonial or recurring yearly events.

history.meaning: harvest cycle (年) and measured interval or passage (度) in Old Chinese
occurring once each year, originally of seasonal winds and annual festivals
annual, once-a-year (used attributively before galas, awards, and ceremonies)

一年一度.notes: Usually followed by 的 (de) before nouns for major recurring events, especially in entertainment media: 一年一度的盛典 ('annual grand gala/awards ceremony').

一年年.etymology: Reduplicated temporal phrase of 一 ('one') + 年 ('year, harvest cycle', originally showing a person carrying grain禾) + 年, expressing 'year after year, with each passing year'.

history.meaning: year after year; year by year

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 一年年 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: once, one time; at one point

一度.etymology: A numeral-classifier compound pairing 一 (yī, 'one') with 度 (dù, Middle Chinese *duH, originally 'linear measure, standard' and verbally *dak 'to cross, pass over'). In Literary Chinese, 一度 literally denoted 'one crossing' or 'one occasion/turn'. By Modern Mandarin, alongside its literal count sense in set phrases, it grammaticalized into a temporal adverb meaning 'for a period in the past' or 'at one point (before circumstances changed)'.

history.meaning: one time, one occasion, or a single crossing/passage
at one point, once (temporarily in the past, implying subsequent change)

一度.notes: Frequently used in news and showbiz narration to highlight a dramatic peak or crisis that later shifted, e.g., 收视率一度破二 ('ratings at one point broke 2%') or 场面一度失控 ('the scene briefly spiraled out of control').

一律.etymology: A modifier-head compound formed from 一 (yī, 'one, single, same') + 律 (lǜ, Middle Chinese *lwit, 'statute, pitch-pipe standard, regulation'). Originally a noun phrase in Han–Tang legal and poetic prose meaning 'a single legal statute' or 'one uniform poetic meter/pitch', it underwent adverbialization in late imperial administrative Chinese to mean 'without exception, uniformly, across the board'.

history.meaning: a single statute, standard pitch, or uniform poetic meter
according to the same rule; uniformly (in Qing administrative edicts)
uniformly, all without exception (adverbial before predicates)

一律.notes: Carries a firm, authoritative or bureaucratic tone in rules and notices (e.g., 违者一律严惩 'violators will uniformly be strictly punished'; 后台一律凭工作证入内 'all backstage entry strictly requires a staff pass').

rootFamily.gloss: stereotyped, all following the same rigid pattern

一手.etymology: A numeral-noun / modifier-head compound combining 一 (yī, 'one, single') and 手 (shǒu, 'hand; skill; agent'). In Classical and Middle Chinese, 一手 literally meant 'one hand', then extended metonymically to 'a single person's effort/control' as well as 'a trick/skill' (as in board games and martial arts). Used adverbially before transitive creation or management verbs, it means 'single-handedly, personally from scratch'.

history.meaning: one physical hand (e.g., using a single hand)
a specialized skill/move; by one's sole agency or effort
single-handedly (adverb); firsthand (adjective, e.g., 一手资料)

一手.notes: Ubiquitous in entertainment industry contexts with verbs of talent/show creation: 一手捧红 ('single-handedly make [a star] famous'), 一手打造 ('build/produce from the ground up'), 一手包办 ('handle everything oneself').

cognates.meaning: to cover the sky with one hand, monopolize power

一手遮天.etymology: A four-character idiomatic verb phrase (chengyu) structured as adverbial instrument 一手 (yī shǒu, 'with a single hand') + verb-object 遮天 (zhē tiān, 'to blot out / screen the heavens'). Derived from Tang poet Cao Tang's line 手遮日曜 ('screening the sun's brilliance with one's hand') and popularized in Ming–Qing vernacular fiction describing corrupt court ministers who hoodwink the emperor (天 'Heaven') and monopolize power.

history.meaning: attempting with one hand to cover the eyes of everyone in the realm (Tang proverb)
deceiving the sovereign and monopolizing unchecked authority
to wield absolute, manipulative control behind the scenes; to cover up the truth single-handedly

morphemes.meaning: sky, heaven (metaphor for public view or higher authority)

一手遮天.notes: Strongly pejorative; frequently used in media dramas when accusing a powerful executive, tycoon, or PR boss of suppressing scandals or rigging outcomes (你以为在圈里能一手遮天吗？).

一批.etymology: A numeral-classifier compound combining 一 (yī, 'one') + 批 (pī, Middle Chinese *phej, originally 'to strike/slap with the hand', later 'to write an official rescript/endorsement on a memorial'). Because goods, documents, and personnel were approved and dispatched together under a single official endorsement (批文), 批 grammaticalized in Ming–Qing commercial and bureaucratic Chinese into a collective classifier for 'a batch, shipment, or cohort'.

history.meaning: to strike with the hand; to pare or slice
an official endorsement on documents; a consignment/batch cleared together
a batch, group, or wave of people or things

一批.notes: Applies equally to commodities and people without disrespect when referring to cohorts: 一批新人 ('a new cohort of rookies/trainees'), 一批设备 ('a batch of equipment').

一把.etymology: A numeral-classifier compound joining 一 (yī, 'one') with 把 (bǎ, Middle Chinese *paeX, originally a verb 'to grasp, hold in the hand' with the hand radical 扌). From 'that which fills one grasp', 把 developed into a nominal classifier for handled objects (knives, chairs), handfuls (tears, sweat, rice), and—by verbal extension in vernacular Mandarin—a verbal classifier for 'one round, go, or vigorous attempt' (as in gambling, gaming, or pitching in to help).

history.meaning: to grasp or hold in a single hand
a handful; a single handled implement (classifier)
a handful/handle; colloquially 'one round, one go, a burst of effort' after verbs

一把.notes: Extremely idiomatic after verbs to express 'giving something a real go' or 'lending a hand': 帮我一把 ('give me a hand'), 拼一把 / 赌一把 ('go all out / take a gamble on it'), 体验一把 ('have a taste/go of it').

一整天.etymology: A numeral-modifier-noun temporal phrase composed of 一 (yī, 'one') + 整 (zhěng, 'whole, complete, neat', phono-semantic compound of 敕 'to put in order' + 正 'upright/exact') + 天 (tiān, 'sky, heaven; calendar day'). While Classical Chinese expressed 'all day' with 终日 (zhōngrì), vernacular Mandarin replaced 日 with 天 and inserted 整 between the numeral and quasi-classifier noun to emphasize unbroken, exhausting duration ('one entire day').

history.meaning: from morning till night, throughout the day (Classical equivalents)
the entire day uninterruptedly (vernacular replacement using 天 'day')

一整天.notes: Compare 整天 (often pre-verbal, carrying complaint: 'all the time / constantly', e.g., 他整天抱怨) vs. 一整天 (quantifies a concrete single full day, often post-verbal duration: 录了一整天节目 'recorded the show for one whole day').

一旦.etymology: A Classical modifier-head compound of 一 (yī, 'one, a single') + 旦 (dàn, Old Chinese *taːns, an ideograph showing the sun 日 rising above the horizon line 一, hence 'dawn, morning, day'). Originally meaning 'in a single morning' (i.e., 'overnight, suddenly, in one brief moment', attested in *Zuo Zhuan* and *Shiji*), its suddenness in conditional contexts grammaticalized into the conjunction/adverb 'once, should it happen that'.

history.meaning: one morning; in a single day, suddenly, abruptly
if one day, in the event that (transitional conditional temporal adverb)
once (a condition is triggered), in case

一旦.notes: Watch out for the Japanese/Korean false friend: Japanese 一旦 (ittan) and Korean 일단 (ildan) commonly mean 'first / for now', whereas Mandarin 一旦 strictly introduces a critical conditional trigger ('once X happens, Y inevitably follows', e.g., 一旦播出 'once it airs').

rootFamily.gloss: ruined in a single morning / overnight
between morning and evening; any moment

一条.etymology: A numeral-classifier compound pairing 一 (yī, 'one') with 条 (tiáo, Traditional 條, Middle Chinese *dew, originally 'a slender tree twig or branch'). Through visual metaphor of long, narrow, or linear shape, 条 became one of Mandarin's core sortal classifiers during the Six Dynasties and Tang period—covering ropes, roads, rivers, fish, dogs, trousers, legal clauses, and in modern media, news items, text messages, and hot-search entries.

history.meaning: slender branch, shoot, or twig; orderly division/clause
classifier phrase for slender objects, roads, rivers, and written clauses
one item/piece (of news, messages, rules, paths, or long flexible things)

morphemes.meaning: strip, slender object, clause, item (of news/messages)

一条.notes: Essential in modern digital and broadcast media as the standard classifier for feeds and notices: 一条热搜 ('a trending topic entry'), 一条微信/短信 ('a WeChat/text message'), 一条新闻 ('a piece of news'), 一条线索 ('a lead/clue').

cognates.meaning: one cup/glass; full to the brim

一杯.etymology: A numeral-classifier/measure phrase joining 一 (yī, 'one') + 杯 (bēi, variant 盃, Middle Chinese *pwoj, phono-semantic with 木 'wood' or 皿 'vessel' + 不 phonetic). In Warring States and Han texts, 杯 denoted a small wooden or lacquered bowl used for wine, soup, or food (e.g., 一杯羹 'a cup of broth' in *Shiji*). It subsequently specialized into a container measure word for 'one cup, mug, or glass' of any beverage.

history.meaning: one wooden/lacquered drinking or soup cupful (e.g., 一杯水, 一杯羹)
one cup of wine or tea (central trope in Tang banqueting poetry, e.g., Wang Wei, Li Bai)
one cup, glass, or mug (of coffee, tea, alcohol, water)

一杯.notes: Used elliptically without a noun (喝一杯 'grab a drink together', 敬你一杯 'toast a glass to you') and in the idiom 分一杯羹 ('get a share of the spoils/profits', literally 'share a cup of broth').

一样.etymology: Adjective and equative marker meaning 'the same, alike', combining 一 ('one and the same') + 样 (樣, 'wooden pattern, model, appearance', tree 木 + 羕).

history.meaning: of one pattern; identical; the same

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 一样 (via 萌典)

一楼.etymology: A numeral-head compound combining 一 (yī, 'one, first') + 楼 (lóu, Traditional 樓, Middle Chinese *luw, phono-semantic from 木 'wood' + 婁 phonetic, originally denoting a multi-story timber tower or upper gallery). With modern multi-story architecture, 楼 shifted from 'whole storied building' to 'individual story/floor', adopting ordinal numbering starting from ground level (一楼 = street/ground floor in Mainland China and Taiwan).

history.meaning: multi-story wooden watchtower, pavilion, or upper story
an entire storied pavilion ('one tower'); later, the ground/first level of a building

一楼.notes: Regional & digital usage: In Mainland China and Taiwan, 一楼 is the street-level ground floor (American 'first floor', British 'ground floor'), whereas Hong Kong Cantonese often calls street level 地下 (G/F) and the floor above 一樓. Online, 一楼 also means the first comment/reply in a forum thread!

一模一样.etymology: Four-character emphatic idiom meaning 'completely identical, cast from the very same mold', pairing 一模 ('one mold/matrix', 模 mú 'wooden or clay casting mold') with 一样 ('one pattern/appearance').

history.form: 一模一樣 / 一模一样
history.meaning: from the same mold and pattern -> exactly alike

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 一模一样 (via 萌典)

一次.etymology: A numeral-classifier compound joining 一 (yī, 'one') + 次 (cì, Middle Chinese *tshijH, originally 'to halt/camp in sequence on a march', hence 'order, rank, turn'). From 'one ordered turn or stop', 次 grammaticalized from the Six Dynasties through Song vernacular into the most general verbal/event classifier in Mandarin ('time, occurrence'), replacing earlier Classical verbal counts that placed pure numerals directly before verbs.

history.meaning: halting place on a march; sequence, rank, next in order
one turn in sequence; one occasion or occurrence
once, one time (default event/verbal classifier phrase)

一次.notes: Contrast 一次 (neutral count of occurrences: 去过一次 'went once') with 一遍 (emphasizes completing an entire process from start to finish: 剧本看了一遍 'read the script all the way through once').

rootFamily.gloss: again and again, time after time

一次次.etymology: A reduplicated numeral-classifier adverbial formed by contracting 一次又一次 or 一次一次 into the ABB pattern 一次次 (yī cì cì, 'one time [after] time'). In Mandarin morphosyntax, reduplicating a classifier after 一 (compare 一个个, 一幕幕, 一遍遍) shifts reference from a single bounded instance to an iterative, vivid sequence of repeated occurrences, lending heightened emotional or narrative cadence.

history.meaning: a single turn or occurrence
time after time, repeatedly in succession (contracted ABB iterative pattern)

一次次.notes: More literary and emotionally charged than 多次 ('many times'); heavily favored in drama monologues, lyrics, and trailers (一次次跌倒，又一次次站起来 'falling time after time, and rising again time after time').

一流.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 一 (yī, 'one, first, same') + 流 (liú, 'water current, stream; social/intellectual school, rank, or tier'). In Six Dynasties aristocratic ranking (*Shishuo Xinyu*) and Tang prose, 第一流 ('the very first stream/grade') designated scholars and statesmen of supreme caliber, alongside 一流 meaning 'people of the same class'. Reinforced in modern East Asia alongside Japanese *ichiryū*, 一流 became a non-predicative/predicative adjective meaning 'first-rate, world-class'.

history.meaning: the foremost rank of literati; people belonging to the same stream/category
first-rate, top-tier, highest caliber (of talent, institutions, craftsmanship)

一流.notes: Describes enduring quality, skill, or institutional prestige (一流的制作团队 'a first-rate production team'; 演技一流 'top-notch acting'), whereas 一线 ('A-list / tier-1') specifically measures current market/commercial ranking.

一点.etymology: Quantifier phrase meaning 'a little bit, a touch' (and 'one o'clock'), from 一 ('one') + 点 (點, 'tiny black dot or speck', 黑 'black' + phonetic 占 zhàn).

morphemes.meaning: dot; tiny amount; hour on the clock

history.meaning: one dot/speck -> a little bit; one o'clock

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 一点 (via 萌典)

一点儿.etymology: Erhua diminutive form of 一点 ('a little bit; a dot'), combining 一 ('one') + 点 (simplified from 點, black 黑 + phonetic 占 'speck; dot') + retroflex diminutive suffix 儿 (from 兒 'child'). In Northern Mandarin, adding 儿 distinguishes the quantifier 'a little bit' (一点儿, yìdiǎnr) from the clock time 'one o'clock' (一点, yīdiǎn).

history.meaning: a tiny speck; a small amount
a little bit; slightly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 一点儿

一点半.etymology: A colloquial clock-time compound built from 一 (yī, 'one') + 点 (diǎn, Traditional 點, originally 'black speck/dot', which in Tang–Qing night-watch timekeeping meant striking the bronze gong/bell to mark subdivisions of a watch, later reanalyzed with mechanical clocks as 'o'clock' where the hour hand points) + 半 (bàn, 'half', ideograph dividing an ox 牛 with 八). Shortened from 一点钟半 ('one o'clock and a half'), meaning '1:30'.

history.meaning: subdivisions ('strokes/dots') of the five night watches marked by striking a gong or clepsydra
half past one on a mechanical 12/24-hour clock ('one o'clock plus half an hour')

一点半.notes: Ambiguous between 1:30 AM and 1:30 PM unless preceded by 凌晨 ('wee hours', 凌晨一点半 = 1:30 AM) or 下午 ('afternoon', 下午一点半 = 1:30 PM); in tight TV production schedules, 凌晨一点半收工 ('wrapping at 1:30 AM') is a classic trope.

rootFamily.gloss: half a day; a very long time (colloquial)

一点点.etymology: Diminutive reduplication of 一点 ('a little bit'), doubling 点 ('dot, speck') to emphasize minute quantity: 'just a tiny bit, ever so slightly'.

history.meaning: a tiny little bit

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 一点点 (via 萌典)

一片真心.etymology: A four-character nominal phrase pairing the poetic numeral-classifier 一片 (yī piàn, literally 'one flat slice/expanse', used since Tang poetry—e.g., Wang Changling's 一片冰心在玉壶 'a pure expanse of ice-clear heart in a jade pot'—to quantify undivided, boundless feelings or scenery) with the modifier-head noun 真心 (zhēnxīn, 'true/genuine heart', from Daoist-Buddhist discourse on authentic mind-heart). Together it denotes 'unalloyed, wholehearted sincerity'.

history.meaning: an undivided, pure expanse of heart/feeling (Tang poetic collocation)
wholehearted, undivided sincerity and devotion (in Yuan–Ming drama and vernacular fiction)
wholehearted sincerity, genuine devotion or affection

一片真心.notes: Common in emotional dialogue and romantic or mentorship arcs, often paired with 辜负 ('to betray/let down': 别辜负人家的一片真心 'don't let down their wholehearted sincerity') or 付出 ('pour out devotion').

一百.etymology: A multiplicative numeral compound of 一 (yī, Old Chinese *qjit, 'one') + 百 (bǎi, Old Chinese *pˤrak, 'hundred', attested on Shang oracle bones as a compound of 一 atop 白 phonetic, sharing Sino-Tibetan root *p-rja with Tibetan *brgya*). While Old Chinese regularly used bare 百 for '100' (and figuratively 'all, myriad'), Mandarin obligatorily prefixes explicit coefficient 一 when counting exact hundreds ('100').

history.meaning: one hundred (oracle bone and bronze inscriptions); figuratively 'all, numerous'
exact cardinal numeral 'one hundred' (mandatory explicit 'one' before 百 in counting)

一百.notes: Unlike 十 ('10', where bare 十十四 vs. 一十四 differs: 10-19 at word start drops 一, e.g., 十五 '15'), 百 NEVER drops 一 for 100–199 in Mandarin: you must say 一百 ('100'), never bare *百块. Figuratively used in 一百个放心 ('100% reassured').

一百三十.etymology: A decimal additive-multiplicative cardinal numeral structured as (一 × 百) + (三 × 十): 一百 (yībǎi, 'one hundred', OC *qjit pˤrak) + 三十 (sānshí, 'thirty', OC *s.rum gip). Chinese decimal place-value composition dates back directly to Shang dynasty oracle bone inscriptions (which joined hundreds and tens originally with ㄓ/又 'and', later juxtaposed directly without a conjunction by the Han period).

history.meaning: one hundred and thirty (oracle bone / Classical Chinese decimal compounding)
one hundred thirty (explicitly retaining coefficient 一 before 百 and final unit 十 before classifiers)

一百三十.notes: When followed by a classifier or noun, the final 十 MUST be kept (一百三十个人 '130 people', 一百三十万 '1.3 million'); only when standing alone without a following noun/classifier can colloquial speech shorten it to 一百三.

一百四.etymology: An apocopated colloquial decimal numeral representing 一百四十 (yībǎi sìshí, 'one hundred forty'), formed from 一百 ('one hundred') + 四 ('four [tens]', Old Chinese *s.lijs), with the trailing lower-order unit 十 ('ten') elided by Mandarin's rule of neighboring place-value implication. In spoken Mandarin, after an explicit higher unit (百, 千, 万), a single bare digit immediately occupies the next lower decimal slot unless零 (líng, 'zero') intervenes.

history.meaning: one hundred forty in Classical Chinese decimal notation
colloquial place-value ellipsis of final 十 ('140', contrasting with 一百零四 '104')

一百四.notes: Crucial learner trap: 一百四 ALWAYS means 140, NEVER 104 (which requires zero-placeholder 零: 一百零四)! Also, you cannot place a classifier directly after 一百四 (*一百四个人 is ungrammatical; restore 十 → 一百四十个人, though currency/metrics allow implicit sub-units like 一百四[十块]).

一百次.etymology: A numeral-classifier frequency phrase combining cardinal numeral 一百 (yībǎi, 'one hundred') with verbal event classifier 次 (cì, 'time, occurrence', from Classical 'halting place / sequence'). Inheriting Classical Chinese's hyperbolic use of 百 ('hundred' = countless, complete), 一百次 functions both literally ('100 occurrences') and rhetorically in spoken Mandarin ('a hundred times over / countless times').

history.form: 百遍 / 百回 / 百次
history.meaning: a hundred times (often rhetorical for 'countless times' in Tang–Song poetry and vernacular)
a hundred times (literal count or emphatic hyperbole in speech)

一百次.notes: Often used hyperbolically in exasperated or emphatic speech on set and in daily life: 我跟你说过一百次了！ ('I've told you a hundred times already!'). Note tone sandhi: 一 (yī) becomes fourth tone (yìbǎi cì) before third-tone 百.

rootFamily.gloss: a hundredfold, a hundred times as much

一直.etymology: Adverb meaning 'straight ahead; continuously; all along', combining 一 ('unbroken, single') + 直 ('straight, unbent', an eye 目 looking straight along a plumb line).

history.meaning: in one straight line; continuously; all along

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 一直 (via 萌典)

一瞬间.etymology: Temporal noun meaning 'an instant, the blink of an eye', combining 一 ('one') + 瞬 ('blink, wink of the eye', eye radical 目 + 舜 shùn, from Buddhist translations of Sanskrit kṣaṇa 'instant') + 间 ('interval of space or time').

history.meaning: the space of a single blink -> an instant

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 一瞬间 (via 萌典)

一笔.etymology: A numeral-classifier compound joining 一 (yī, 'one') + 笔 (bǐ, Traditional 筆, Old Chinese *p.[r]ut, from 竹 'bamboo' + 聿 'writing brush held by a hand'). Because financial accounts, debts, and commercial transactions in Song–Ming merchant ledgers were entered with a single brush-entry, 笔 extended metonymically from 'writing brush / calligraphic stroke' to a classifier for sums of money, deals, debts, and artistic works.

history.meaning: bamboo writing/painting brush; written prose
a single brushstroke; a single ledger entry of debt or silver (e.g., 一笔账)
a sum of (money/funding), a deal/transaction, or a stroke of writing/art

morphemes.meaning: sum (of money), financial entry/deal; brush, stroke

一笔.notes: The go-to classifier in business and film/TV production financing: 一笔投资 ('a sum of investment'), 一笔巨款 ('a huge sum of money'), 一笔交易 ('a business deal'), and the idiom 一笔勾销 ('write off completely with one stroke of the brush').

rootFamily.gloss: write off at one stroke, cancel completely

一笔一画.etymology: A symmetric four-character coordinative idiom (一 A 一 B pattern) pairing 笔 (bǐ, Traditional 筆, 'brush movement / stroke') and 画 (huà, Traditional 畫, Middle Chinese *hweaH, originally an ideograph of a stylus/brush 聿 delineating field boundaries, hence 'delineated line, character stroke'). Referring literally to writing each calligraphic stroke in proper sequence without slurring, it metaphorically denotes meticulous, conscientious execution.

history.meaning: brushwork lines and structural strokes of Chinese characters (calligraphy treatises)
writing every single stroke carefully; doing things methodically and conscientiously

一笔一画.notes: Used both literally for neat handwriting (contrasting with 龙飞凤舞 'flamboyant/illegible scrawl') and figuratively for painstakingly crafting a script, contract, or career step by step.

一类.etymology: A numeral-classifier / modifier-head compound combining 一 (yī, 'one, a single, the same') + 类 (lèi, Traditional 類, Middle Chinese *lwijH, originally a sacrificial ritual term composed of 米 'rice', 犬 'dog', and 頁 'head', early attested in pre-Qin philosophical logic—Xunzi, Mozi—meaning 'kind, species, category sharing essential likeness'). Thus 一类 denotes either 'one category (of)' or 'the same kind/ilk'.

history.meaning: one logical/natural species or category; sharing the same kind (e.g., Xunzi, Han prose)
one category/tier (e.g., Grade-A); people or things of the same type ('such as X and the like')

一类.notes: Two common syntactic patterns: (1) before a noun: 这一类节目 ('this genre/type of show'); (2) after examples as a summarizer: 综艺、真人秀一类的节目 ('shows of the variety / reality-TV sort'), or predicatively 我们是一类人 ('we're the same kind of people').

cognates.meaning: system, lineage, series (source of 系列)

一系列.etymology: A modern quantifier phrase combining 一 (yī, 'one, a whole') with 系列 (xìliè, 'series, sequence'), itself a Sino-Japanese return loan (*wasei-kango* 系列 *keiretsu*, coined in Meiji-Taisho Japan to translate Western 'series / system / affiliation' from Classical Chinese 系 'linked thread, lineage' + 列 'ordered row, array'). Adopted into 20th-century Mandarin, 一系列 functions as a collective quantifier meaning 'a whole series/string of'.

history.meaning: separate Classical roots: 系 ('to tie, silken lineage') and 列 ('arranged rank, row')
series, interconnected system or sequence (Meiji–Showa Japanese Sino-compound)
a series of, a string/cascade of (abstract events, measures, or works)

一系列.notes: Functions grammatically like a collective numeral-classifier without needing 的 (though 的 is optional): 一系列问题 ('a string of problems'), 一系列宣传活动 ('a series of promotional campaigns'). Compare 一连串 (more vivid/rapid chain of events).

cognates.meaning: first line, frontline, top active tier

一线.etymology: A modifier-head compound of 一 (yī, 'one, first') + 线 (xiàn, Traditional 線/綫, from 糸 'silk' + 戔/泉 phonetic, originally 'fine thread, filament'). In Classical poetry, 一线 meant 'a slender sliver/thread' (e.g., 一线天 'a thread of sky through a gorge', 一线希望 'a glimmer of hope'). In the 20th century (abbreviated from 第一线, calquing military 'first line / frontline'), it came to mean 'frontline (fieldwork)', and later in Chinese urban economics and entertainment, 'Tier-1 / A-list'.

history.meaning: a single fine thread; a tiny sliver or glimmer (e.g., of sky, life, or hope)
the military or industrial frontline; hands-on operational level
frontline; Tier-1 (cities like Beijing/Shanghai) and A-list / top-tier (celebrities, satellite networks)

一线.notes: Signature entertainment & media buzzword in *Behind the Scenes*: 一线明星 ('A-list star'), 一线卫视 ('top-tier satellite TV network'), 一线城市 ('Tier-1 metropolis'), alongside 一线员工 ('frontline production crew').

一经.etymology: A formal conditional/temporal adverb compounding adverbial 一 (yī, here functioning not as cardinal 'one' but as an aspectual trigger 'as soon as, once', attested since Classical Chinese 一見 'upon first seeing') + 经 (jīng, Traditional 經, originally 'warp threads of a loom', hence 'to pass through, undergo'). Crystallized in Ming–Qing legal and bureaucratic prose (一经查实 'as soon as investigated and verified'), it introduces a formal passive-like trigger before a two-syllable verb.

history.meaning: warp threads; to pass through, experience, or undergo
once having undergone / as soon as [action occurs] (administrative and legal documentary formula)
as soon as, once (formal register adverb followed by disyllabic verb + 便/就/即)

morphemes.meaning: to pass through, undergo, be subjected to

一经.notes: High-register written expression common in contracts, broadcasting announcements, and PR statements: 节目一经播出，便引发热议 ('as soon as the show aired, it sparked heated discussion'); 商品一经售出 ('once goods are sold').

一脸.etymology: A totalizing quantifier-body-part compound formed from 一 (yī, here carrying its holistic 'all over, completely' sense, parallel to 一身 'all over the body' and 一地 'all over the floor') + 脸 (liǎn, Middle Chinese *kjaemX, originally 'upper cheek / area beneath the eyes' in Six Dynasties–Tang cosmetics poetry, before replacing Classical 面 *miàn* as the everyday vernacular word for 'face' in Yuan–Ming Mandarin). Literally 'a whole face full of'.

history.meaning: cheeks (especially rouged cheeks in Tang–Song lyric poetry)
covering one's entire face (sweat, dust, or an unmistakable facial expression)
all over one's face, wearing a face full of (an emotion, look, or substance)

一脸.notes: Exceptionally productive in vivid storytelling and internet slang right before emotion/state words without needing a verb: 一脸懵 / 一脸茫然 ('a totally blank/bewildered look on one's face'), 一脸严肃 ('deadly serious all over one's face'), 一脸嫌弃 ('a look of pure disdain').

rootFamily.gloss: facial expression, look on one's face; mood

一致.etymology: A Classical modifier-head philosophical compound from *Yijing* (*Xici II*: 天下同归而殊途，一致而百虑 'the world reaches the same destination by different paths, and shares one ultimate aim amidst a hundred deliberations'), combining 一 (yī, 'one, identical') + 致 (zhì, Old Chinese *tids, 'to arrive at, bring to an ultimate end, culmination'). Re-energized across modern East Asia via Meiji Japanese *itchi* to translate 'unanimity / consistency', it functions in Mandarin as both an adjective ('consistent, identical') and an adverb ('unanimously').

history.meaning: one and the same ultimate principle, aim, or culmination (*Book of Changes*)
agreement, correspondence, unanimity (expanded in modern Sino-Japanese and Mandarin legal/political usage)
unanimously (adverb: 一致通过 'pass unanimously'); consistent, identical (adjective: 意见一致)

morphemes.meaning: ultimate aim, attainment, direction, bring about

一致.notes: Works smoothly both as a pre-verbal adverb (评委一致认为 'the judges unanimously agreed'; 一致好评 'unanimous rave reviews') and as a predicate adjective (言行一致 'words and deeds match').

一般.etymology: Originally a vernacular Buddhist and Tang–Song poetic compound of 一 (yī, 'one, same') + 般 (bān, Middle Chinese *pan, originally 'to transport/turn around', borrowed phonetically in Tang–Song vernacular for 'sort, kind, manner'). In Chan Buddhist texts and Song lyrics, 一般 meant 'the exact same kind, alike'. In Meiji Japan, 一般 (*ippan*) was repurposed to translate German *allgemein* / English *general, universal* (opposed to 特殊 'special'), returning to modern Mandarin as 'ordinary, average' (adj.) and 'generally, usually' (adv.).

history.meaning: of the exact same sort or appearance; alike (Tang–Song Chan texts and poetry)
general, universal, ordinary (Meiji Japanese philosophical/scientific semantic shift)
generally, usually (adverb); ordinary, so-so (adjective); 'just like' (postposition: 像做梦一般)

一般.notes: Watch three distinct modern uses: (1) adverb 'usually': 我一般不熬夜 ('I usually don't stay up late'); (2) understated critique 'mediocre / so-so': 这个方案很一般 ('this proposal is pretty average'); (3) literary simile particle 'like': 奇迹一般 ('like a miracle')—preserving its old Tang–Song sense 'the same sort'!

cognates.meaning: same level of understanding; stoop to someone's level

一般见识.etymology: A four-character modifier-head idiom combining 一般 (yībān, 'the same kind or level', from 一 'one/same' + 般 'sort, class') with the coordinative noun compound 见识 (jiànshi, 'experience and judgment', literally 见 'see' + 识 'know/discern'). Attested in Ming–Qing vernacular fiction such as Journey to the West and Dream of the Red Chamber, it originally meant 'sharing the exact same (low) level of discernment' and grammaticalized in negative frames with 跟/和...一般见识 to mean lowering oneself to argue with someone petty or ignorant.

history.meaning: of the same sort + perception and knowledge (separate Middle Chinese collocations)
possessing the same shallow level of discernment; stooping to quarrel with an inferior
stoop to someone's level; take petty offense

一般见识.notes: Almost exclusively used in the negative or劝阻 (persuasive) pattern 别跟他一般见识 ('don't stoop to his level'), a staple phrase in workplace dramas for defusing ego clashes.

rootFamily.gloss: knowledge and experience; broaden one's horizons

cognates.meaning: a single word; brief remark (cognate Sino-Xenic compound base)

一言为定.etymology: A Classical-style subject-predicate / pivotal four-character idiom (chengyu): 一言 (yīyán, modifier-head 'one word / a single spoken pledge') + 为 (wéi, copular/transformative verb 'to serve as / constitute') + 定 (dìng, stative/resultative 'settled, fixed'). Echoing Classical Chinese maxims on verbal trustworthiness (such as Analects 一言兴邦 and Yuan–Ming drama dialogue 一言既出), the phrase crystallized in Yuan zaju and Ming vernacular tales as a performative formula sealing an oral contract.

history.meaning: a single word/maxim + to make settled/fixed
settled by a single spoken word; a binding verbal promise
it's a deal; settled once and for all

一言为定.notes: Used standalone as a brisk conversational clincher ('It's a deal!') after pitching or negotiating terms, carrying slightly firmer solemnity than 说定了.

rootFamily.gloss: once a word leaves one's lips (even a team of four horses cannot overtake it)
to reach a final decision; finalize

一起.etymology: Adverb meaning 'together, in the same place, at once', from 一 ('one') + 起 ('rise, start, batch/group',走 + 己).

history.meaning: in one group/batch -> together; at the same time

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 一起 (via 萌典)

一趟一趟.etymology: A reduplicated numeral-classifier adverbial phrase (一 A 一 A pattern) built from 一 (yī, 'one') and the verbal/nominal classifier 趟 (tàng, 'a trip, journey, or pass'). The character 趟 (earlier also written  or  in vernacular texts) combines the 'walk/run' radical 走 with the phonetic 尚 (shàng/tāng) and emerged in Song–Yuan–Ming northern vernacular as a measure word for round-trip errands; full phrase reduplication expresses distributive iteration ('trip after wearying trip').

history.meaning: one row, track, or journey back and forth
trip after trip; repeatedly going back and forth

一趟一趟.notes: Conveys physical effort or persistence (e.g., 一趟一趟地跑 'running back and forth repeatedly' to deliver scripts or secure approvals), often followed by the adverbial marker 地.

rootFamily.gloss: one trip; once back and forth
to wade through; tread a path

一路.etymology: Compound of 一 ('one, the whole') + 路 ('road, journey', foot 足 + phonetic 各 gè), meaning 'all the way along the journey' or 'taking the same route' (as in 一路平安 'have a safe trip all the way').

history.meaning: the whole road/journey; along the way; of the same sort

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 一路 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: peace and tranquility; safe and sound

一路平安.etymology: A four-character subject-predicate benediction combining 一路 (yīlù, modifier-head 'the entire road / all along the journey', where 一 means 'whole, throughout') and 平安 (píng'ān, coordinative stative compound from 平 'level, calm, unperturbed' + 安 'secure, peaceful'). While 平安 dates back to Classical and Han texts as a general term for safety and well-being, pairing it with 一路 became the standard Early Mandarin farewell blessing for travelers facing hazardous overland or river routes.

history.meaning: level and secure; free from danger or illness
safe and peaceful along the whole road/voyage
safe travels; bon voyage

一路平安.notes: Standard warm send-off for overland or general travel; speakers often switch to 一路顺风 ('fair winds all the way') except before flights, where 一路平安 is preferred to avoid mentioning 'wind'.

rootFamily.gloss: smooth sailing all the way; bon voyage
all the way; the whole journey

一转眼.etymology: Formed from the quantifier/temporal prefix 一 (yī, 'once, a single') modifying the verb-object compound 转眼 (zhuǎnyǎn, 'to turn or roll the eye', from 转 'turn, revolve' + 眼 'eye'). Modeled on older Buddhist Chinese calques for a 'ksana' (instant) such as 转瞬 (zhuǎnshùn) and 弹指 (tánzhǐ, 'snap of the fingers'), 一转眼 arose in Tang–Song–Ming vernacular to vividify the fleeting passage of time through the brief physical motion of shifting one's gaze.

history.meaning: to turn one's eyes; shift one's gaze; in an instant
in the single turn of an eye; before one knows it
in the blink of an eye; in a flash

一转眼.notes: Used both for sudden disappearance ('vanished in a flash') and nostalgic leaps of years ('in the blink of an eye, ten years have passed'), frequently paired with 工夫 or 之间.

rootFamily.gloss: in the twinkling of an eye (literary)
in the blink of an eye

cognates.meaning: fellows; peer group; generation (from same Sino-Xenic root 輩)

一辈子.etymology: A modifier-head colloquial nominal combining 一 (yī, 'one, an entire') with 辈子 (bèizi, 'generation; lifetime'), itself formed from Classical 辈 (bèi, originally 'rows of war chariots dispatched in batches', combining 车 'chariot' + 非 phonetic/aligned wings, extended to 'peer rank, generation') plus the Mandarin nominalizing suffix 子 (-zi). From 'one generational span', 一辈子 shifted in Qing northern Mandarin to denote the entirety of an individual's mortal life.

history.meaning: batch of chariots; rank; peer group; generation
a generational rank; an entire human lifespan
all one's life; a lifetime

一辈子.notes: Warm, colloquial counterpart to formal 一生 (yīshēng); in TV drama dialogue it carries strong emotional weight in vows or career devotion (e.g., 做一辈子幕后 'work behind the scenes all one's life').

rootFamily.gloss: senior generation; veteran in an industry

一边.etymology: Spatial noun ('one side') and correlative conjunction ('at the same time, while…', often paired as 一边…一边…), combining 一 ('one') + 边 (邊, 'edge, margin, side').

history.meaning: one side; simultaneously

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 一边 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to advance; enter (Sino-Xenic cognate of 進)

一进.etymology: A grammaticalized temporal-adverbial construction combining adverbial 一 (yī, 'once, the very moment that') with the directional verb 进 (jìn, simplified from 進, ideogrammic compound of 辶 'walk' + 隹 'short-tailed bird', originally 'to advance forward' since birds hop forward without stepping backward, later replacing Classical 入 'to enter' in Mandarin). In the correlative frame 一进 [place] 就..., 一 marks immediate sequentiality upon crossing a threshold.

history.meaning: to advance forward; approach; present at court
to enter an enclosed space or institution
as soon as one enters; upon stepping into

一进.notes: Typically takes a spatial or institutional object (一进门 'the moment one walks in the door', 一进公司 'right after joining the company') and pairs with 就 in the main clause.

rootFamily.gloss: to walk in the door; get started in a trade

一遍.etymology: A numeral-classifier compound of 一 (yī, 'one') + 遍 (biàn, also written 徧 in Classical texts, combining 辶 'walk' or 彳 'step' + 扁 phonetic, originally 'all around, everywhere, universally'). During the Six Dynasties and Tang period, 遍 grammaticalized from 'to traverse completely' into a verbal action classifier counting complete start-to-finish cycles of reading, reciting, rehearsing, or inspecting.

history.meaning: everywhere; to go all the way around; pervade
one complete recitation, traversal, or performance
one time through (from beginning to end)

一遍.notes: Crucial learner distinction from 一次 (yīcì): 一次 counts raw occurrences, whereas 一遍 emphasizes completing the entire process from start to finish (e.g., 顺一遍台词 'run through the lines once', 看一遍片子 'screen the cut all the way through').

rootFamily.gloss: to cover every corner; all over

一针见血.etymology: A compressed serial-verb / conditional-resultative four-character idiom: 一针 (yīzhēn, 'with a single needle prick', from 针, bronze/seal 金 'metal' + 十/箴 'needle') + 见血 (jiànxiě, verb-object 'to see/draw blood'). Drawn from traditional Chinese acupuncture and bloodletting therapy (刺络放血) and attested metaphorically in Southern Song Neo-Confucian dialogues and Ming–Qing criticism, it likens trenchant critique to a physician hitting a vessel on the very first prick.

history.meaning: acupuncture needle + drawing blood upon pricking a vessel
cutting straight to the core truth or flaw in a single remark
hit the nail on the head; incisive and to the point

一针见血.notes: High-frequency praise (or wincing acknowledgment) in media/editorial meetings for a producer's or critic's razor-sharp diagnosis: 一针见血地指出问题 ('incisively pinpoint the flaw'). Note pronunciation: 血 is literary xuè here, not colloquial xiě.

rootFamily.gloss: lifeblood; painstaking effort poured into a work

一阵子.etymology: Formed from 一 (yī, 'one, a') + 阵 (zhèn, originally 陣/陳, 'battle formation, ranks of troops', later extended to sudden bursts or spells of wind, rain, or emotion) + the diminutive/nominalizing Mandarin suffix 子 (-zi). As 阵 shifted from spatial military alignment in Classical Chinese to a temporal classifier for passing waves of phenomena in Tang–Song vernacular, suffixing -子 created an indefinite duration noun meaning 'a spell or stretch of time'.

history.meaning: military battle array; troop formation
a burst, gust, or passing spell (of wind, rain, or activity)
a period of time; a while; a spell

一阵子.notes: Commonly combines with demonstratives to frame recent work cycles: 这阵子 ('lately / this past stretch'), 前一阵子 ('a little while ago'), or 忙一阵子 ('be busy for a spell').

rootFamily.gloss: battle array; lineup (e.g., 明星阵容 'star-studded cast/lineup')
a gust/burst (e.g., 一阵掌声 'a burst of applause')

cognates.meaning: one face/side; the whole surface; on the other hand
one side; page one; one aspect

一面.etymology: A numeral-classifier / modifier-head compound of 一 (yī, 'one') + 面 (miàn, oracle bone pictograph of a human face enclosed in a frame around an eye 目). In Classical and Middle Chinese, 面 meant 'face', 'to face directly', and 'surface/side', yielding polysemous uses of 一面: (1) verbal classifier for a face-to-face meeting (见一面, 'meet once in person'), (2) 'one side/aspect' of an issue or character, and (3) correlative 'simultaneously' (一面...一面...).

history.meaning: human countenance; to face in person; one side or direction
one face-to-face meeting; simultaneously doing two actions
once in person (after 见); one side/aspect; at the same time

一面.notes: In interpersonal contexts like 见一面 ('meet up once in person'), 一面 functions as a post-verbal complement of encounter; in HR/production contexts, Watch out for the homographic clip 一面 meaning 'first-round interview' (第一轮面试)!

cognates.meaning: karma; destined connection (Sino-Xenic cognate of 縁)

一面之缘.etymology: A Literary Chinese modifier-head noun phrase structured around the subordinating particle 之 (zhī, 'of'): 一面 (yīmiàn, 'a single face-to-face meeting') + 之 + 缘 (yuán, originally 'hem or ornamental border of a silk garment', from 糸 'silk' + 彖 phonetic, which in Chinese Buddhism translated Sanskrit pratyaya 'conditioning cause / karmic affinity'). Attested from Tang–Song letters and Yuan–Ming vernacular, it frames even a fleeting one-time meeting as a thread of predestined affinity.

history.meaning: hem of a robe; karmic condition or destined connection
history.stage: Classical to Six Dynasties Buddhist Chinese

history.meaning: the destined affinity of having met once face-to-face
a brief single encounter; having met only once

一面之缘.notes: Usually governed by 有 ('to have'): 有一面之缘 ('to have met once briefly'), polite and refined for networking or recalling a passing industry acquaintance without overstating intimacy.

rootFamily.gloss: destined affinity; fate that brings people together
unrelated; having no destined luck with something
a single-word relationship (e.g., mentor of one crucial word)

一首.etymology: A numeral-classifier phrase of 一 (yī, 'one') + 首 (shǒu, oracle bone pictograph of a horned or haired head with prominent hair tufts and eye). Because Classical Chinese poems and musical lyrics were titled or indexed by their opening ('head') line or heading, 首 grammaticalized during the Han–Six Dynasties era from 'head / beginning' into the canonical classifier for poems, hymns, and songs.

history.meaning: human or animal head; chief; beginning section
one complete poem or lyric piece
one (classifier for songs, melodies, and poems)

morphemes.meaning: measure word for songs and poems (lit. 'head')

一首.notes: Essential music-production and variety-show vocabulary (一首歌 'a song', 主打歌一首 'one lead single'); note tone sandhi: 一 (yī) shifts to rising second tone (yí shǒu) before third-tone 首.

rootFamily.gloss: first; premier; chief (e.g., 首席 'chief officer / first chair')

丁.etymology: Originally an oracle-bone and bronze-script pictograph of a square-headed nail or peg seen from above (Middle Chinese *teng*). In culinary usage since the Song and Yuan dynasties, its compact four-sided head inspired the metaphorical sense of small, even cubes of diced meat or vegetables (菜丁, 胡萝卜丁).

morphemes.meaning: nail head; fourth heavenly stem; small diced cube

history.meaning: nail or peg head; fourth cyclical stem
finely diced cube of meat or vegetable
diced cube of food

七.etymology: Cardinal numeral 'seven'. In Shang oracle-bone and Zhou bronze inscriptions, 七 was written as a cross (+), originally representing a cut (later written 切 qiē) and borrowed phonetically from antiquity for the number seven.

history.meaning: cross-shaped graph borrowed for numeral seven

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 七 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: seven + ten (cognate Sino-Tibetan roots bdun + bcu)

七十.etymology: A multiplicative decimal numeral compound combining 七 (qī, Old Chinese *s.n̥iːt, 'seven', originally an oracle bone cross-cut mark '+' representing 'to slice/cut' 切, borrowed rebus-wise for 'seven') and 十 (shí, Old Chinese *g.[d]əp, 'ten', originally a vertical needle/tally stroke evolving into a cross). Already attested in Shang oracle bone inscriptions (often written as a ligature) and immortalized in Confucius's Analects (七十而从心所欲) as a milestone of elder mastery.

history.meaning: seven tens; seventy (attested in Shang oracle bone tallies)
seventy; 'rare since antiquity' (from Du Fu's 人生七十古来稀)
seventy

七十.notes: Transparent decimal multiplication (7 × 10); in cultural contexts, turning 70 is classically honored as 古稀之年 ('the age rare since antiquity', from Du Fu).

rootFamily.gloss: at odds; chaotic; all sorts of (lit. 'seven-eight')

万.etymology: Simplified from traditional 萬 (wàn, Old Chinese *C.maːns), which in Shang oracle bone script was a vivid pictograph of a scorpion with pincers and a segmented, curving stinger tail; meanwhile the simplified form 万 (originally 卍/万, a distinct ancient graph) served as a popular cursive shorthand since the Han–Six Dynasties period before official adoption. Borrowed early by phonetic rebus for the numeral 'ten thousand' (the primary East Asian myriad grouping unit) and figuratively 'countless, absolute'.

history.meaning: scorpion (borrowed rebus-wise for ten thousand / myriad)
ten thousand; myriad; utterly/by all means
ten thousand (base-10,000 unit); countless

万.notes: East Asian numbers group by four digits (万 = 10⁴, 亿 = 10⁸) rather than Western thousands (10³): mentally anchor 1万 = 10k, 10万 = 100k, and 100万 = 1 million when reading budgets or streaming view counts!

rootFamily.gloss: just in case; one in ten thousand contingency
tens of thousands; millions upon millions

万物.etymology: A Classical Chinese modifier-head philosophical compound: 万 (wàn, 'ten thousand, myriad, all') + 物 (wù, from 牛 'ox' + 勿 phonetic/variegated hide, originally 'multicolored sacrificial ox', generalized in Zhou philosophy to 'living creature, physical thing, phenomenon'). Central to Daoist and Confucian cosmology—most famously Laozi's Dao De Jing (万物作焉, 天地万物)—it denotes the totality of phenomenal beings in the cosmos.

history.meaning: the myriad creatures and phenomena between heaven and earth
all things in creation; the natural universe

万物.notes: Elevated literary/philosophical register (e.g., 万物复苏 'all nature awakens in spring'), yet playfully revived in modern media catchphrases like 万物皆可综艺 ('anything can be turned into a variety show').

rootFamily.gloss: myriad phenomena; every kind of spectacle

三.etymology: Cardinal numeral 'three', an ancient indicative graph (指事字) written since Shang oracle bones with three parallel horizontal strokes.

history.meaning: three horizontal strokes = numeral three; repeatedly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 三 (via 萌典)

三个.etymology: A numeral-classifier phrase combining 三 (sān, Old Chinese *s.rum, an ancient indicant graph of three horizontal tally strokes) and the general Mandarin classifier 个 (gè, simplified from 個/箇, originally 'single stalk of bamboo' with 竹 radical). During the Six Dynasties through Song period, 箇/個 bleached from counting bamboo culms and arrows into the default universal classifier for people, abstract units, and unclassified objects.

history.meaning: three stalks of bamboo or arrow shafts
three individual items or persons (generalized classifier)
three (general count form before nouns or standalone)

三个.notes: In everyday Mandarin,個/个 is pronounced unstressed ge (sān ge); remember the proverb 三个臭皮匠，顶个诸葛亮 ('three humble cobblers equal one Zhuge Liang'—teamwork beats lone genius).

三倍.etymology: A numeral-measure compound of 三 (sān, 'three') + 倍 (bèi, phono-semantic character of 人 'person' + 咅 phonetic, originally 'to turn one's back on / rebel' [later written 背] and in Classical arithmetic 'to double / fold over in equal measure').
