Already attested in the Book of Poetry (贾用三倍, 'merchants make threefold profit') and Mencius, 倍 grammaticalized as the standard multiplicative suffix '-fold / times as much'.

history.meaning: threefold profit or quantity (attested in Shijing & Mencius)
three times as much; triple

三倍.notes: Watch out for a notorious translation trap with verbs of increase: 是原来的三倍 unambiguously means '3x the original', whereas 增加了三倍 ('increased BY three times') mathematically equals 4x the original!

rootFamily.gloss: to double (e.g., 翻倍 'double in value/ratings')
playback speed (e.g., 二倍速 '2x speed viewing')
redoubled; doubly (e.g., 事半功倍 'half the effort, twice the result')

三十.etymology: Multiplicative decimal numeral combining 三 ('three') + 十 ('ten') for 'thirty' (historically also contracted into the single graph 卅 sà).

history.meaning: three tens = thirty

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 三十 (via 萌典)

三十七条.etymology: A composite numeral-classifier phrase built from multiplicative-additive 三十七 (sānshíqī, 'thirty-seven': 三 'three' × 十 'ten' + 七 'seven') plus the classifier 条 (tiáo, simplified from 條, phono-semantic with 木 'tree/wood' + 攸 phonetic, originally 'slender branch or twig' in the Book of Poetry). Because Classical statutes, contract clauses, and bamboo slips were arranged in long narrow strips, 条 evolved into the classifier for elongated objects as well as clauses, messages, news items, and guidelines.

history.meaning: slender tree branch or shoot; orderly strip
thirty-seven articles, clauses, or itemized regulations
history.stage: Middle Chinese / Imperial Legal & Administrative Prose

history.meaning: thirty-seven items, clauses, messages, or long objects

morphemes.meaning: classifier for clauses, messages, rules, or long narrow items

三十七条.notes: In modern workplace and media dialogue, 条 counts contract clauses (合同条款), regulatory rules, text/WeChat messages (三十七条未读消息), hot-search entries (热搜), and video clips.

三天.etymology: A numeral-measure temporal noun combining 三 (sān, 'three') with 天 (tiān, oracle bone pictograph of a standing figure 大 with an emphasized head or overhead sky, 'heaven, sky'). In Classical Chinese, 'day' was expressed by 日 (rì, 'sun'), while 天 meant 'sky/Heaven'; during the Six Dynasties through Tang–Song vernacular shift, 天 metonymically extended from 'the sky's daily cycle (daylight)' to become Mandarin's primary spoken measure word for calendar days, requiring no intervening 个.

history.meaning: three days (Classical 日) vs. sky/celestial deity (天)
three days (vernacular replacement of 三日)
three days

三天.notes: Like 年 (year) and 周 (week), 天 is an autonomous measure noun and NEVER takes 个 (*三个天 is ungrammatical); also idiomatic in 三天两头 ('every other day / constantly').

三次.etymology: A numeral-classifier compound of 三 (sān, 'three') + 次 (cì, oracle bone/seal graph of 二 'two/sequence' + 欠 'person yawning/halting breath', originally 'to camp in sequence / encampment' and hence 'order, rank, next in turn'). From 'sequential turn or station' in Classical Chinese, 次 grammaticalized into the general verbal classifier for discrete occurrences or iterations ('three times').

history.meaning: military halting station; sequential order; halting three times
three occurrences or times
three times

三次.notes: Neutral, all-purpose frequency count ('three times'); compare 三遍 ('three full passes from start to finish') and 三趟 ('three round trips').

cognates.meaning: three-shift system (parallel modern Sino-compound 三交代制)

三班制.etymology: A modern institutional modifier-head compound structured as [三班 (sānbān, 'three shifts/squads') + 制 (zhì, suffix '-system')]. 班 originally depicted dividing jade (珏, two pieces of jade split by 刀 'knife') to distribute tokens of rank to court officials standing in ordered rows, evolving to mean 'scheduled duty roster / work shift'; 制 (from 刀 'knife' + 未 'tree with branches', 'to cut/fashion rules') became a productive 19th–20th century Sino-Japanese/Mandarin affix for administrative systems, yielding 三班制 for 24-hour three-shift rotation.

history.meaning: ordered rank/court duty roster + institutional regulation
twenty-four-hour industrial or broadcast three-shift work system

三班制.notes: Closely linked to the colloquial phrase 三班倒 (sānbāndǎo, 'rotating three shifts around the clock'), frequently invoked in TV post-production and broadcast control rooms working 24/7 before air dates.

rootFamily.gloss: rotating three shifts around the clock
producer system (central to TV/film management in 幕后之王)

三百万.etymology: A hierarchical multiplicative numeral compound structured as [三百 (sānbǎi, 'three hundred', from 三 'three' × 百 Old Chinese *pˤrak 'hundred') × 万 (wàn, 'ten thousand')]. Because Chinese numeration since the Zhou–Han 'mid-scale' (下数/万进) standardization groups powers of ten by myriads (10⁴) rather than thousands (10³), 'three million' (3 × 10⁶) is analyzed compositionally as 'three hundred ten-thousands' (300 × 10,000).

history.meaning: three hundred myriads (3,000,000 in myriad-scale reckoning)
three million

三百万.notes: Remember that 百万 (bǎiwàn, 'hundred ten-thousands') is the exact Chinese equivalent of 'million'—hence 百万粉丝 ('a million followers') and 三百万预算 ('a 3-million budget').

rootFamily.gloss: tens of millions; by all means

三百六.etymology: An elliptical colloquial numeral construction standing for 三百六十 (sānbǎi liùshí, 'three hundred sixty'), formed from 三百 ('three hundred') + 六 ('six [tens]'). By regular Mandarin numeral apocope, when a multi-digit number ends in a single non-zero sub-unit directly below the preceding place value and no classifier immediately follows, the final unit (here 十 'ten') drops—hence 360 becomes 三百六, echoing traditional Chinese circular/calendrical 360-degree and 360-trade (三百六十行) symbolism.

history.meaning: three hundred and sixty (days of the lunar-solar schematic year / degrees)
three hundred sixty (colloquial apocopated numeral; also 3.6M/360 yuan in context)

morphemes.meaning: six (elliptical for sixty, i.e., six tens)

三百六.notes: Crucial Mandarin numeral rule: 三百六 ALWAYS means 360 (never 306, which must insert 零: 三百零六!), UNLESS a classifier immediately follows—you must restore 十 before a classifier (三百六十度 '360 degrees', never *三百六度).

rootFamily.gloss: all walks of life; every trade and profession (lit. '360 trades')
two hundred fifty (idiomatic slang for ' knucklehead / fool')

cognates.meaning: bout; round; inning (borrowed from Chinese vernacular martial novels)

三百回合.etymology: A numeral-classifier martial idiom combining hyperbolic 三百 (sānbǎi, 'three hundred') with 回合 (huíhé, coordinative compound of 回 'turn back, wheel around' + 合 'clash, come together'). Originating in Song–Yuan storytelling and Ming historical romances like Romance of the Three Kingdoms and Water Margin, one 回合 denoted a single mounted pass in which two cavalry generals charged, clashed weapons (合), and wheeled their horses back around (回) for the next pass; fighting 'three hundred bouts' meant a grueling marathon duel between evenly matched titans.

history.meaning: one clash and wheeling turn of mounted warriors in combat
wage an epic marathon duel of three hundred passes without a victor
three hundred rounds/bouts (humorous or dramatic idiom for an epic showdown)

三百回合.notes: Almost always collocated with 大战 ('wage a great battle'): 大战三百回合, used playfully in modern workplace and showbiz banter for marathon pitch debates, bidding wars, or drinking/negotiation showdowns.

rootFamily.gloss: bout; round (of boxing, debate, negotiation, or gaming)
to cross swords; engage in a contest of wits or skill

cognates.meaning: worldview (source of 観 suffix via 世界観 translating German Weltanschauung)

三观.etymology: A 21st-century Mainland Mandarin abbreviatory compound (缩略语) condensing 世界观 (shìjièguān, 'worldview'), 人生观 (rénshēngguān, 'outlook on life'), and 价值观 (jiàzhíguān, 'system of values') into 三 ('three') + 观 (guān, Classical 'to observe contemplatively / Daoist-Buddhist meditative insight', repurposed in Meiji Japan via 世界観 to translate German Weltanschauung). First formalized in mid-2000s Chinese civic discourse, 三观 exploded into everyday pop-culture and media critique in the 2010s.

history.meaning: watchtower; careful observation; philosophical/meditative insight

history.form: 世界觀 / 人生觀 / 價值觀
history.meaning: worldview, life outlook, and value system (via Japanese calques of German philosophy)
core values and moral/intellectual outlook (literally 'the Three Views')

morphemes.meaning: three (standing for world, life, and values)

三观.notes: Ubiquitous in Chinese TV/film criticism and dating/workplace talk: 三观很正 ('wholesome/sound core values'), 三观合 ('compatible values'), and 毁三观 ('shatter one's moral/common-sense worldview').

rootFamily.gloss: worldview (calque of German Weltanschauung via Japanese)

上.etymology: Indicative character (指事字) written in oracle-bone script as a short mark above a horizontal baseline, denoting 'above, top, upper' and verbally 'ascend, go up, board, attend, serve'.

history.meaning: above; top; ascend; go up

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 上 (via 萌典)

上一场.etymology: A spatial-to-temporal demonstrative-numeral-classifier phrase: 上 (shàng, originally an Old Chinese indicant stroke above a baseline meaning 'above / upper', metaphorically mapped onto 'earlier / preceding' because Chinese text and genealogical scrolls read vertically from top to bottom) + 一 (yī, 'one') + 场 (chǎng, simplified from 場, from 土 'levelled earth' + 易 phonetic, originally 'cleared altar ground or threshing floor', extended in Song–Yuan theater to a stage performance, match, or session).

history.meaning: levelled earthen altar ground or threshing floor
one theatrical performance, examination session, or bout
the previous round, scene, match, or performance session

上一场.notes: Core live-production and competition vocabulary (上一场比赛 'the previous competition round', 上一场戏 'the previous scene shot'); 一 is often dropped in rapid speech (上场戏), though watch out for the verb-object homograph 上场 (shàngchǎng, 'to step onto the stage/court')!

rootFamily.gloss: the next round, match, or show
live scene; on-site set or studio floor

cognates.meaning: top and bottom; superiors and subordinates; approximately (Sino-Japanese)
top and bottom; superiors and inferiors

上下.etymology: An antonymic coordinative compound (反义并列复合词) pairing the two foundational Old Chinese spatial indicants 上 (shàng, 'above, high, superior') and 下 (xià, 'below, low, subordinate'). Attested from the Book of Documents and Analects onward, its polarity naturally projected from physical verticality ('top and bottom') onto institutional hierarchy ('rulers and subjects; management and staff, i.e., everyone throughout an organization') as well as numerical approximation ('more or less').

history.meaning: heaven above and earth below; sovereigns/superiors and subjects/subordinates
approximately; give or take (alongside hierarchical 'from top to bottom')
from top to bottom (everyone in a group); superiors and subordinates; roughly

上下.notes: In corporate and showbiz dramas, 全公司上下 ('everyone in the company from top to bottom') and 打点上下 ('smooth things over up and down the hierarchy') are idiomatic staples.

rootFamily.gloss: context (in a text or script, lit. 'upper and lower text')
equally matched; hard to tell who is better
higher-ups and subordinates; chain of command

上个月.etymology: A temporal modifier-classifier-head phrase combining deictic 上 (shàng, 'preceding, previous', via Chinese vertical-timeline metaphor where earlier events sit 'above') + the general classifier 个 (gè) + 月 (yuè, oracle bone crescent-moon pictograph meaning 'moon; lunar/calendar month'). Unlike 天 ('day') and 年 ('year'), which reject 个, 月 ('month') requires 个 when counting or specifying relative months in Mandarin, distinguishing 上个月 ('last month') from Classical 上月.

history.meaning: the preceding lunar month (without classifier)
last month (with obligatory Mandarin classifier 個)
last month

上个月.notes: Keep the classifier contrast sharp: 上个月 ('last month') vs. 上月 (terse written/news style), and NEVER confuse with 一月 ('January') vs. 一个月 ('one month's duration')!

rootFamily.gloss: end of the month (key KPI/broadcast deadline)

上会.etymology: A compact verb-object institutional compound pairing transitive/directional 上 (shàng, 'to ascend to, submit up to, go before a higher body') with 会 (huì, simplified from 會, originally depicting fitting a lid over a cooking vessel to bring ingredients together, hence 'assembly, meeting, council'). Modeled on bureaucratic expressions like 上报 ('report upward') and 上朝 ('attend imperial court'), 上会 arose in modern Chinese government, corporate, and media-platform jargon to mean 'putting a proposal or project onto the formal agenda of an executive review committee'.

history.meaning: to assemble; meet together; official gathering
attend a temple fair or join a rotating credit society
submit a proposal/project to a review or decision-making committee meeting

morphemes.meaning: to go up to; submit before; enter onto the agenda of

上会.notes: High-frequency insider buzzword in Chinese TV networks, streaming platforms, and VC/corporate offices (e.g., 这个项目下周上会 'this show proposal goes before the greenlight committee next week'); behaves as a separable VO verb (上不了会 'can't make it to the review meeting').

rootFamily.gloss: pass the committee review / get greenlit at the meeting
to hold or attend a meeting

cognates.meaning: upload (alternative to アップロード)
cognates.word: アップロード / 上伝 (rare)

上传.etymology: A late twentieth-century computing calque of English 'upload', structured as an adverbial-verb (modifier-head) compound: 上 (shàng, 'upward; toward a higher node or server', Old Chinese *djaŋs) modifies 传 / 傳 (chuán, 'to transmit, relay by post', originally denoting courier relay stations in Classical Chinese). Modelled in direct antonymy with 下载 (xiàzài, 'download') and competing regionally with 上载 (shàngzài).

history.meaning: to relay messages or goods via courier stations
to transmit data from a local client upward to a remote server

上传.notes: In television and digital media production (as in 幕后之王), 上传 pairs routinely with 素材 ('raw footage') or 成片 ('final cut') and is far more common in Mainland Mandarin than 上载.

上午.etymology: A modifier-head temporal compound combining 上 (shàng, 'earlier, preceding, upper', reflecting the vertical metaphor of time flowing downward in Chinese) with 午 (wǔ, the seventh Earthly Branch 午时 corresponding to 11:00–13:00 and hence 'solar noon'). Literally 'the earlier part leading up to noon', attested in vernacular and administrative Chinese from the Song–Yuan period onward to contrast with 下午 ('afternoon') and 正午 ('high noon').

history.meaning: seventh Earthly Branch; midday period (11 a.m. to 1 p.m.)
the first half of the daytime before noon; forenoon
morning (typically ~8:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m., after 早晨)

上午.notes: Unlike English 'morning', 上午 refers specifically to the working forenoon (roughly 8 or 9 a.m. until noon), whereas early morning upon waking is 早上 or 早晨.

上半截.etymology: The term '上半截' (shàngbànjié, upper half) is formed by '上' (upper), '半' (half), and the classifier '截' (section, piece). '截' originally referred to cutting or severing, containing the '戈' (halberd) radical, indicating an action involving a weapon. By the Tang and Song dynasties, '截' transitioned into a classifier for distinct segments of long objects, such as logs or roads. '上半截' emerged in vernacular contexts to describe the top portion of a vertically oriented object. Today, it is commonly applied to physical objects, clothing, or metaphorical structures.

history.meaning: upper half

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 上半截

上去.etymology: Directional verb compound combining 上 ('ascend, move upward') + 去 ('go away from the speaker'), used both as an independent verb ('go up') and as a directional complement after action verbs (走上去 'walk up there').

history.meaning: go upward (away from speaker)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 上去 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to go onstage; to assume office (Sino-Japanese jōdai)
to mount a platform or stage

上台.etymology: A separable verb-object (动宾) compound formed from 上 (shàng, 'to ascend, mount') and 台 (tái, simplified merging of 臺 'raised earthen terrace, viewing platform, stage'). Originally describing literal ascent onto a ceremonial terrace or traditional opera pavilion (戏台), it extended both to theatrical/broadcast performance ('go onstage') and metaphorically to political life ('come to power, assume office').

history.meaning: to ascend a raised terrace or ceremonial platform
to step onto a theatrical opera stage to perform
to go onstage (showbiz) or assume political power

morphemes.meaning: to ascend, mount, go up onto

上台.notes: As a separable VO verb, aspect particles and complements insert between the characters (e.g., 上不了台 'unable to go onstage / unpresentable', 上过一次台 'have been onstage once').

rootFamily.gloss: to step down from the stage or from office

上周.etymology: Temporal compound of 上 ('previous, preceding', treating time as flowing downward from earlier/above to later/below) + 周 ('week, cycle of seven days').

history.meaning: last week; the previous week

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 上周 (via 萌典)

上回.etymology: A modifier-classifier nominal compound combining spatial-temporal 上 (shàng, 'previous, preceding') with 回 (huí, originally 'to revolve, turn around', grammaticalized in Song–Yuan storytelling vernacular 话本 as a chapter and event classifier meaning 'episode, bout, time'). Literally 'the previous turn/episode', preserving the narrative flavour of traditional chapter-divided fiction (章回小说).

history.meaning: to turn back, revolve, eddy
the preceding chapter or storytelling session; last time
last time, on the previous occasion (colloquial)

上回.notes: More colloquial and conversational than 上次, with strong northern Mandarin and storytelling resonance (famous from the cliffhanger formula 上回书说到 'as told in the last episode').

上天.etymology: An ancient modifier-head compound attested already in the Book of Odes (诗经·小雅: 上天同云) and Book of Documents (尚书), combining 上 (shàng, 'supreme, lofty, on high') with 天 (tiān, Old Chinese *l'iːn, originally an anthropomorphic depiction of the great sky/deity overhead). In Zhou dynasty cosmology it denoted both the physical vault of the sky and anthropomorphic Providence governing human destiny.

history.meaning: Sovereign Heaven on high; supreme cosmic deity and firmament
providence, fate, heaven (as noun); also VO 'ascend to the sky'

上天.notes: Watch the syntax and stress: as a noun meaning 'Heaven / Providence' (上天的安排 'fate's arrangement'), it is modifier-head; in colloquial speech it can also function as a VO verb meaning 'go up into the sky / space' (上天入地).

cognates.meaning: bringing seasonal produce to market; compare 上場 (jōjō) for IPO
to enter the market / go public

上市.etymology: A verb-object (动宾) compound formed from 上 (shàng, 'to enter upon, appear on') and 市 (shì, 'walled marketplace, trade fair'). In Ming–Qing commercial vernacular it described fresh seasonal crops or wares arriving at market stalls; in twentieth-century financial Chinese, 市 narrowed metonymically to 股市 ('stock market'), yielding the modern corporate sense 'to launch an IPO / go public'.

history.meaning: (of seasonal goods or produce) to appear for sale in the marketplace
to launch a product commercially; to list shares publicly on a stock exchange

morphemes.meaning: to enter, appear on, go onto

上市.notes: In media-industry dramas like 幕后之王, 上市公司 ('publicly listed company') is central to valuation and M&A plotlines; note that consumer products also 上市 ('hit the shelves / launch').

rootFamily.gloss: to delist (from a stock exchange) or go off-season

上心.etymology: Originally a vernacular verb-object (动宾) compound combining 上 (shàng, 'to lodge upon, rise into') and 心 (xīn, 'heart-mind', the seat of both cognition and emotion in Classical Chinese philosophy). Attested in Qing vernacular novels such as Dream of the Red Chamber (红楼梦), 'taking something into one's heart-mind' lexicalized into a gradable stative adjective meaning 'attentive, mindful, emotionally invested' (e.g., 很上心).

history.meaning: to take to heart, keep in mind, pay heed to
attentive, conscientious, emotionally invested (accepts degree adverbs)

上心.notes: Typically takes 对 to mark the target of care (他对这个项目很上心 'he is deeply invested in this project'); unlike 用心 ('diligent/focused'), 上心 emphasizes personal care and emotional attentiveness.

上方.etymology: Spatial compound of 上 ('upper, above') + 方 ('direction, region, quarter'), referring to the space or area directly above.

history.meaning: the upper region; space above

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 上方 (via 萌典)

上来.etymology: A compound directional verb (复合趋向动词) pairing the path verb 上 (shàng, 'to move upward, ascend') with the deictic venitive verb 来 / 來 (lái, 'to come toward the speaker's vantage point', originally depicting wheat 麥 before phonetic loan in Old Chinese *m·rˤə). Emerging during the Late Medieval Chinese grammaticalization of serial verb constructions, it encodes upward motion anchored toward the speaker or metaphorical progression into view.

history.meaning: serial verbs: ascend and come hither
to come up; also compound directional/inchoative complement after main verbs

上来.notes: Beyond physical movement ('come upstairs/onstage'), 上来 functions idiomatic-grammatically in 一上来 ('right from the get-go') and as a resultative complement of recall or ability (答不上来 'unable to come up with the answer').

上桌.etymology: Verb-object compound of 上 ('ascend, be brought up onto') + 桌 ('table', 卓 + 木), meaning either 'serve food onto the dining table' or 'take one's seat at the table for a meal'.

history.meaning: be served onto the table; sit down at the table

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 上桌 (via 萌典)

上楼.etymology: Verb-object compound of 上 ('go up, ascend') + 楼 (樓, 'multi-story building, upper floor', wood 木 + phonetic 婁 lóu), meaning 'go upstairs'.

history.meaning: ascend a tower -> go upstairs

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 上楼 (via 萌典)

上次.etymology: A modifier-classifier temporal noun combining 上 (shàng, 'preceding, previous') with 次 (cì, Old Chinese *s-nhits, originally 'halting place in sequence, camp order', grammaticalized in Medieval Chinese into the general verbal classifier for occurrences and iterations). Literally 'the preceding sequence/occurrence', forming a symmetrical paradigm with 这次 ('this time') and 下次 ('next time').

history.meaning: pitched camp in sequence; ordered rank or turn
the previous time or occasion

上次.notes: Register-neutral and usable across formal broadcasting, business meetings, and casual conversation alike, whereas 上回 is decidedly informal.

上班.etymology: Verb-object compound of 上 ('go to, enter upon') + 班 ('ordered rank, duty shift', originally two pieces of jade 王 separated by a knife 刀, hence 'distribute ranks, standing duty line'). Originally used for court officials or attendants taking their scheduled shift, now the everyday word for 'go to work, start work'.

history.meaning: report for one's scheduled duty shift
go to work; be on duty

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 上班 (via 萌典)

上瘾.etymology: A separable verb-object (动宾) compound uniting 上 (shàng, 'to contract, fall into, develop') with 瘾 / 癮 (yǐn, formed with the sickness radical 疒 and phonetic 隱 yǐn 'hidden, latent', originally denoting a chronic rash or deep-seated craving, publicized heavily during the Qing dynasty opium crisis). Literally 'to develop a craving/addiction', later bleached in everyday speech to mean getting hooked on hobbies, shows, or habits.

history.meaning: cutaneous eruption; latent chronic ailment or deep habitual craving
to become physiologically addicted (especially to opium or tobacco)
to become addicted; colloquially to get hooked on an activity or show

上瘾.notes: Separable VO verb (上了瘾 'got hooked'); in entertainment marketing, 让人上瘾 ('binge-worthy / addictive') is standard praise for hit variety shows and dramas, alongside slang 上头.

rootFamily.gloss: to satisfy a craving, have great fun
chronic addiction (e.g. 毒瘾, 网瘾)
to kick an addiction, quit a habit

上线.etymology: A verb-object (动宾) compound from 上 (shàng, 'to enter onto, connect to') and 线 / 線 (xiàn, 'silk thread, wire, line'). First used in twentieth-century industrial and telecommunications contexts ('enter the assembly line' or 'connect to a telephone/broadcast line'), it calqued English 'go online' in the internet era and expanded in Chinese media/tech jargon to mean 'officially launch or premiere on a streaming platform'.

history.meaning: to go onto a production line or connect to a telecommunications line
to log on / go online; (of an app, film, or show) to launch on digital platforms

morphemes.meaning: thread, wire, network line, platform stream (線)

上线.notes: In modern Chinese TV and streaming production (like 幕后之王), 节目上线 means a show premieres on streaming video platforms (contrasting with 开播 for traditional broadcast TV); note also the homographic noun 上线 meaning 'upper-level handler/contact'.

rootFamily.gloss: to go offline; be pulled from streaming

上网.etymology: A separable verb-object (动宾) neologism coined in the 1990s combining 上 (shàng, 'to get onto, access') with 网 / 網 (wǎng, Old Chinese *maŋʔ, originally 'knotted fishing or hunting net', semantically extended as a calque of English 'Net / Web' via 互联网 'Internet'). Literally 'to get onto the Net', mirroring physical access expressions like 上街 ('go out on the street') or 上车 ('board a vehicle').

history.meaning: knotted cord net for catching fish, birds, or game
to access the Internet, browse the Web (also in sports: approach the net)

上网.notes: Separable VO verb: duration and objects go in the middle (上了一晚上网 'surfed the net all night', 上不了网 'can't connect to the internet').

上课.etymology: Verb-object compound of 上 ('attend, go to') + 课 (課, 'assigned lesson, class', speech 言 + phonetic 果 guǒ, originally 'test, assess, assign quota'). Means both 'attend class' (for students) and 'teach/hold class' (for teachers).

history.meaning: begin or attend an assigned lesson/class

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 上课 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: boarding a vehicle (compare 乗車 jōsha)

上车.etymology: An ancient verb-object (动宾) phrase attested since Classical Chinese (e.g. Analects 论语 and Book of Rites 礼记, describing ritual deportment when mounting a horse-drawn chariot 車), formed from 上 (shàng, 'to ascend, mount') and 车 / 車 (chē / Classical jū, 'wheeled carriage, chariot'). With modern transport it generalizes to boarding any land vehicle (car, bus, train, subway), and in internet slang means 'join in on a group deal or trend'.

history.meaning: to mount a horse-drawn carriage or war chariot
to get into a car or board a bus/train; (slang) join a group buy or trend

上车.notes: Covers cars, buses, and trains (but planes and boats typically prefer 登机 and 上船); in contemporary youth and e-commerce slang, 上车! means 'hop on the deal / count me in!'.

rootFamily.gloss: to get out of a car / get off a train or bus
film crew / production team (originally chariot unit)

上面.etymology: Locative noun combining 上 ('top, above') + 面 ('face, surface'), meaning 'on top of, above, the upper surface' (and figuratively 'higher authorities').

history.meaning: upper surface; above; on top

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 上面 (via 萌典)

下.etymology: Indicative character (指事字) written in oracle-bone script as a short mark beneath a horizontal baseline, directly opposite 上: 'below, under, lower' and verbally 'descend, fall, get off, finish (duty/class)'.

history.meaning: below; under; descend

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 下 (via 萌典)

下一期.etymology: A three-morpheme demonstrative-numeral-classifier noun phrase: 下 (xià, 'subsequent, following', reflecting the downward flow of future time in Chinese spatial-temporal metaphor) + 一 (yī, 'one') + 期 (qī, Old Chinese *ɡə, 'appointed time, lunar cycle, scheduled installment'). In print journalism and television broadcasting, 期 became the dedicated classifier for periodic issues of magazines and non-narrative broadcast installments such as variety shows.

history.meaning: appointed date, stipulated cycle, full year (qīnián)
scheduled issue of a periodical or cohort of a training course
the next issue (of a magazine) or next episode (of a variety/talk show)

下一期.notes: Crucial media distinction in 幕后之王: variety shows, reality shows, and podcasts measure episodes in 期 (下一期节目), whereas scripted narrative dramas measure episodes in 集 (下一集).

rootFamily.gloss: previous episode (of a variety show) / last issue

下一步.etymology: A specifier-numeral-classifier phrase built from 下 (xià, 'following, subsequent'), 一 (yī, 'one'), and 步 (bù, oracle-bone script depicting a pair of left and right footprints 止 stepping forward in succession, Old Chinese *bˤas, 'pace, stride'). Extended metaphorically from physical walking and board-game moves (such as 棋步 in Go and Xiangqi) to strategic planning, denoting 'the next move or phase of action'.

history.meaning: a double pace (left and right foot); to walk on foot
the next physical step; metaphorically the next strategic phase or move

下一步.notes: Functions both as a noun phrase ('what is the next step?' 下一步是什么) and directly as a sentence-initial temporal/discourse adverbial ('next, we will...' 下一步我们要...).

下不起来.etymology: A four-syllable negative potential inchoative verb construction (V + 不 + 起来): meteorological 下 (xià, 'to fall from the sky', applied to rain/snow in Vernacular Mandarin replacing Classical 雨 yù / 降 jiàng) + negative potential interfix 不 (bù, 'cannot') + compound inchoative complement 起来 / 起來 (qǐlái, 'to rise up -> begin and build momentum'). Together it expresses that precipitation threatens to fall but fails to get properly underway or gather intensity.

history.meaning: to fall downward (replacing Classical verbal 降 for rain and snow)
negative potential inchoative construction: unable to initiate or build up V
unable to start falling in earnest or build into steady rain/snow

morphemes.meaning: to get started and gain momentum (起來)

下不起来.notes: In Mandarin aspectual grammar, -起来 marks the onset and upward buildup of an action; inserting 不 (下不起来) means the clouds may drizzle or threaten, yet a real downpour never materializes (relevant to outdoor location shoots!).

rootFamily.gloss: unable to recall / bring to mind

下个月.etymology: A deictic temporal phrase structured as specifier 下 (xià, 'next, following') + general classifier 个 / 個 (gè, simplified from bamboo tally 箇/個) + noun head 月 (yuè, oracle-bone crescent moon pictograph, Old Chinese *ŋʷat, 'moon, calendar month'). Notice how 個 intrudes obligatorily between 下 and 月 to mean 'next month', distinguishing the calendar noun phrase from the ungrammatical bare *下月 in casual spoken rhythm (though literary/terse 下月 exists in writing).

history.meaning: moon; lunar calendar month

history.form: 下個月 / 下个月 (xià ge yuè)
history.meaning: the coming calendar month; next month

下个月.notes: Learner trap: 'month' requires 个 in spoken temporal expressions (上个月, 这个月, 下个月), whereas 'year' and 'day' NEVER take 个 (*下个年 is wrong — say 明年; *下个天 is wrong — say 明天 or 第二天).

下午.etymology: Temporal noun combining 下 ('after, following') + 午 ('noon', the seventh Earthly Branch corresponding to 11 a.m.–1 p.m., midday): 'afternoon'.

morphemes.meaning: following; lower half of the day

history.meaning: the hours after midday; afternoon

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 下午 (via 萌典)

下厨房.etymology: A colloquial verb-object (动宾) phrase combining directional-locative 下 (xià, 'to go down into a workspace or service quarter') with 厨房 / 廚房 (chúfáng, modifier-head noun from 廚 'cookhouse, slaughter-and-prep room' + 房 'side room, chamber'). Historically, traditional courtyard residences situated kitchens in lower or rear subsidiary wings relative to elevated main halls (上房/堂屋), motivating 下 ('go down to') for entering workspaces like kitchens, workshops, or fields.

history.meaning: kitchen room or culinary outbuilding in an estate

history.form: 下廚房 / 下厨房 (xià chúfáng)
history.meaning: to go into the kitchen personally to prepare a meal

morphemes.meaning: to enter a workspace, go down into

下厨房.notes: Famously paired in the modern domestic proverb 上得厅堂，下得厨房 ('graceful in the drawing room, capable in the kitchen'), praising someone versatile both in public/professional life and at home; shortened form is 下厨.

下去.etymology: Directional verb compound of 下 ('descend, move down') + 去 ('go away from the speaker'). Used literally for 'go down' and as an aspectual complement after verbs meaning 'continue on doing' (说下去 'keep on speaking').

history.meaning: go down; continue on into the future

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 下去 (via 萌典)

下发.etymology: An administrative modifier-verb (偏正) compound combining directional 下 (xià, 'downward through an institutional hierarchy') with 发 / 發 (fā, Old Chinese *pjat, 'to shoot forth an arrow -> dispatch, issue, distribute'). Formed in bureaucratic and institutional Chinese to denote top-down dissemination of official documents, budgets, or regulatory notices from a higher governing body or headquarters to subordinate units.

history.meaning: to loose an arrow; to send forth, dispatch decrees or provisions
to issue or distribute (notices, documents, funds) downward to lower tiers

下发.notes: High-register bureaucratic/corporate verb common in Chinese media regulation (e.g. 广电总局下发通知 'the broadcast regulator issued a notice') and company headquarters directives; takes concrete or textual objects like 文件, 通知, or 补贴.

下周.etymology: Temporal compound of 下 ('next, following', viewing future time as flowing downward) + 周 ('week, seven-day cycle'): 'next week'.

history.meaning: next week

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 下周 (via 萌典)

下地.etymology: Separable verb-object compound combining 下 ('descend; step down', originally an indicator mark below a horizontal baseline) + 地 ('earth; ground; floor', earth radical 土 + phonetic 也 yě). Alongside its agricultural sense ('go out into the fields'), everyday Mandarin uses it for stepping out of bed onto the floor after illness or injury.

history.meaning: step down from a bed platform onto the floor
get out of bed; set foot on the ground

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 下地

下属.etymology: A modifier-head / nominalized compound attested in Imperial historiography (e.g. History of Song 宋史), uniting hierarchical 下 (xià, 'lower in rank, beneath') with 属 / 屬 (shǔ, originally 'to be attached to, affiliated under jurisdiction', from tail 尾 phonetic series). It denotes both individual employees reporting to a superior ('subordinate') and subsidiary institutions under a parent organization (e.g. 下属机构).

history.meaning: lower-ranking officials under a magistrate's or commander's jurisdiction
workplace subordinate, direct report; affiliated subsidiary unit

下属.notes: Polite, professional workplace term contrasting with 上司 or 上级 ('boss / superior'), far more respectful than 手下 ('underling / henchman', which sounds triad-like or authoritarian in modern offices).

下巴.etymology: Colloquial Mandarin body-part compound formed from 下 (xià, 'lower; underneath') and 巴 (ba, originally denoting the jaw/chin region or an clinging appendage, attested in early vernacular compounds such as 下巴颏儿). In Classical Chinese the chin and jaw were called 颏 (kē) or 颔 (hàn), whereas spoken Northern and Southwestern Mandarin generalized 下巴 with a neutral-toned second syllable. The word denotes both the point of the chin and the movable lower jaw.

history.meaning: lower jaw; chin (replacing literary 颔/颏)
chin; lower jaw

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 下巴

cognates.meaning: perpetrator; also 'unskilled' (heta) via native semantic shift
to strike a blow / take action (hạ thủ)

下手.etymology: A polysemous compound of 下 (xià, 'lower; to put down') and 手 (shǒu, 'hand; skilled person'). Pronunciation splits etymologically by structure: as a neutral-tone modifier-head noun 下手 (xiàshou, 'lower-ranking hand'), attested in Yuan–Ming vernacular, it means 'assistant, right-hand helper' (e.g. 打下手); as a full-tone VO verb 下手 (xiàshǒu, 'lay hands on'), attested since Tang Chan Buddhist texts, it means 'to put one's hand to a task or strike a blow'.

history.meaning: VO verb: to set one's hand to action, strike, or execute
modifier-head noun: lower seat at a table; assistant or apprentice helper

morphemes.meaning: subordinate, lower (noun); to apply, lay down (verb)

下手.notes: Mind the tone! With neutral tone (xiàshou), especially in 给……打下手 ('act as assistant to someone'), it means 'assistant/helping hand'; with third tone (xiàshǒu), it means 'start working on / strike against' (无从下手 'not know where to start').

rootFamily.gloss: to serve as an assistant, lend a hand

下文.etymology: A modifier-head literary compound pairing spatial-textual 下 (xià, 'below, subsequent — literally lower down on vertical bamboo slips or scroll columns') with 文 (wén, Old Chinese *mən, 'interwoven pattern -> written characters, prose passage'). Originally philological terminology for 'the passage following below', in Ming–Qing vernacular it acquired the metaphorical sense 'subsequent outcome, follow-up response, what happens next'.

history.meaning: the subsequent lines or passage lower down in a written text
textual continuation; metaphorically the sequel, follow-up, or later development of an affair

下文.notes: Very frequently used in the negative idiom 没有下文了 ('there was never any follow-up / the matter fizzled out without a word'), e.g. after a promising pitch meeting or audition.

下来.etymology: Directional verb compound of 下 ('descend, come down') + 来 ('come toward the speaker'). Used literally ('come down') and as a complement showing an action bringing something to a halt, detachment, or completion up to the present.

history.meaning: come down toward the speaker; settle down

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 下来 (via 萌典)

下楼.etymology: Verb-object compound of 下 ('descend, go down') + 楼 (樓, 'storied building, floor'): 'go downstairs'.

history.meaning: descend from an upper floor; go downstairs

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 下楼 (via 萌典)

下次.etymology: Temporal compound of 下 ('next, following') + 次 ('order, sequence, time/occurrence'): 'next time'.

history.meaning: the next occasion; next time

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 下次 (via 萌典)

下次见.etymology: A three-character conversational valediction structured as temporal adverbial 下次 (xiàcì, 'next time', from 下 'subsequent' + classifier 次 'sequence, occasion') modifying the verb 见 / 見 (jiàn, oracle-bone kneeling human figure topped by a prominent eye 目, Old Chinese *kˤens, 'to see, meet'). Parallel to 再见 ('see again') and 明天见 ('see you tomorrow'), omitting subject and object pronouns via standard Chinese topic-drop economy.

history.meaning: to perceive with the eyes; to meet in audience

history.form: 下次見 / 下次见 (xiàcì jiàn)
history.meaning: see you next time (parting greeting and broadcast sign-off)

下次见.notes: Warm, natural sign-off used both among friends/colleagues and by TV/podcast hosts wrapping up an episode (我们下次见! 'See you next time!').

cognates.meaning: launching a ship; (modern kōzui/gesui differs: 下水 gesui = sewage!)
cognates.word: 下水 (false friend in modern JP: sewage)

下水.etymology: A separable verb-object (动宾) compound from 下 (xià, 'to descend into, enter') and 水 (shuǐ, pictograph of flowing river currents, Old Chinese *s.turʔ, 'water'). Literally 'to go down into the water' (of swimmers, divers, or newly built vessels sliding down a slipway), it also developed rich figurative senses in twentieth-century Mandarin: 'venturing into private business' or 'being lured into corruption/compromised dealings' (拉人下水).

history.meaning: to descend into a river or pool; to launch a newly constructed boat into water
to enter water; (figurative) enter commercial waters or get dragged into shady dealings

下水.notes: Beware two tricky pitfalls: (1) Japanese 下水 (gesui) and Chinese 下水道 mean 'sewage/drain', whereas verb 下水 (xiàshuǐ) means 'enter the water'; (2) with neutral tone 下水 (xiàshui), it is a culinary noun meaning 'animal offal / giblets'!

rootFamily.gloss: to drag someone into trouble or shady dealings

下狠手.etymology: An expanded separable verb-object phrase derived by inserting the attributive adjective 狠 (hěn, originally 'ferocious snapping of dogs, ruthless, fierce', with dog radical 犭 + 艮) inside the VO compound 下手 (xiàshǒu, 'to lay hands on, strike a blow'). Literally 'to deal a ruthless blow', in contemporary business and media parlance it often softens hyperbolically to 'make a drastic, no-holds-barred move' (including against oneself or one's own budget/script).

history.meaning: fierce, intractable, ruthless (originally of fighting hounds)
to strike viciously or deal an unsparing blow
to act ruthlessly; (colloquial/business) take drastic, all-out measures

morphemes.meaning: to apply, strike with, lay down

下狠手.notes: Commonly paired with 对 (对竞争对手下狠手 'play hardball against rivals', or对自己下狠手 'push oneself ruthlessly / spare no effort in editing or training'); similar to 下狠心 ('steel one's resolve').

rootFamily.gloss: to steel one's heart, make a ruthless resolution
to strike a blow / start taking action

cognates.meaning: to finish a shift of duty (hạ ban)

下班.etymology: A separable verb-object (动宾) compound combining 下 (xià, 'to step down from, conclude') with 班 (bān, Old Chinese *pˤran, originally two jade pieces 珏 divided by a knife 刀 'to distribute jade insignia by rank', hence 'ordered court rank, imperial guard shift, scheduled duty roster'). First used for palace officials and theatrical troupes finishing their rostered shift in Late Imperial China, it generalized to modern industrial and office work hours.

history.meaning: to distribute jade tallies; ordered court rank or standing guard shift
to step down from one's rostered court duty or palace watch shift
to get off work, finish one's workday or shift

morphemes.meaning: duty shift, work roster, scheduled class/rank

下班.notes: Separable VO verb: never put an object after 下班 (*下班公司 is ungrammatical); aspect markers go inside (下了班去吃饭 'grab food after getting off work'), and in media crews 加班 ('work overtime') often eclipses 下班!

rootFamily.gloss: to go to work, start one's shift
on-duty shift, to be on duty

cognates.meaning: conveying a command from superior to inferior (Sino-Japanese katatsu)
handing down official orders or directives

下达.etymology: A Classical Chinese adverbial-verb compound attested already in the Analects (论语·宪问: 君子上达，小人下达, where it originally meant 'progressing downward toward mundane things'), later reanalyzed in imperial administrative prose (paired in 上情下达 'conditions above and below communicated') from 下 ('downward to subordinates') + 达 / 達 (dá, 'to reach, arrive, cause to reach'). In modern Mandarin it means 'to hand down or issue authoritative orders, quotas, or targets'.

history.meaning: to reach downward; to make higher decrees reach lower officials and populace
to officially issue or hand down (orders, directives, production targets)

下达.notes: Compare with 下发: 下达 collocates with abstract commands, tasks, and KPIs (下达命令 'issue an order', 下达指标 'hand down targets/quotas'), whereas 下发 collocates with concrete documents or funds (下发文件).

rootFamily.gloss: to convey, pass on (instructions or spirit of a meeting)
to reach, achieve (an agreement or goal)

下锅.etymology: A separable culinary verb-object (动宾) compound uniting 下 (xià, 'to drop into, put down into') with 锅 / 鍋 (guō, metal radical 金 + phonetic 咼 guō, arising in Medieval Chinese for round-bottomed metal cooking cauldrons and woks, replacing Classical 鼎/釜). Used both transitively ('put ingredients into the pot/wok') and ergatively/intransitively ('ingredients go into the boiling pot', e.g. 饺子下锅了).

history.meaning: metal cooking pot, cauldron, or wok
to put ingredients into the cooking pot, or (of food) go into the pot

morphemes.meaning: to put down into, drop into

下锅.notes: Famous in the vivid idiom 等米下锅 ('waiting for rice to put in the pot' — desperately awaiting funds or raw materials to keep operating); also watch modern slang 背锅 ('take the blame / carry the can').

rootFamily.gloss: to come out of the wok / be freshly released (of food or new episodes)
to take the blame as a scapegoat (slang)

下雨.etymology: Verb-object weather construction of 下 ('fall from above, descend') + 雨 ('rain', a pictograph of raindrops falling from the sky vault): literally 'fall rain' = 'it rains / to rain'.

history.meaning: rain falls; to rain

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 下雨 (via 萌典)

下面.etymology: Locative noun combining 下 ('below, under') + 面 ('face, surface, side'): 'below, underneath, the lower part, next/following'.

history.meaning: underside; below; following

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 下面 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: dismounting; dropping out of an election race

下马.etymology: An ancient verb-object (动宾) compound from 下 (xià, 'to dismount, descend from') and 马 / 馬 (mǎ, oracle-bone pictograph of a maned horse, Old Chinese *mˤraʔ). In Classical and Imperial China it meant dismounting from horseback (as before sacred temples marked by 下马碑 'dismounting steles') or unhorsing a rival general in combat; in twentieth-century Mandarin, contrasting with 上马 ('mount up -> launch a major project'), it came to mean 'cancel, scrap, or axe a project'.

history.meaning: to dismount from a horse (out of respect or after battle)
(of a major engineering or media project) be cancelled/axed; (of an official) be toppled for corruption

下马.notes: Essential TV/business vocabulary: 节目上马 means greenlighting and launching production on a show, while 节目下马 means the project gets axed/shelved mid-development; in anti-corruption news, 官员下马 means an official falls from power.

rootFamily.gloss: to mount a horse; to launch a major project
initial show of strength / intimidating opening blow

不.etymology: General negation adverb ('not, no') for present, future, habitual, and stative predicates, attested from Shang oracle bones through every stage of Chinese. Spoken bù shifts automatically to rising second tone bú immediately before another fourth-tone syllable (不是 bú shì).

history.meaning: negative particle 'not'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 不 (via 萌典)

不一样.etymology: A negated stative phrase composed of negative adverb 不 (bù, Old Chinese *pə, 'not') + numeral 一 (yī, 'one, identical, same') + noun/classifier 样 / 樣 (yàng, originally 'acorn of the Daimyo oak 橡', borrowed phonetically in Tang–Song vernacular for 'wooden pattern, mould, appearance, kind'). Since 一样 literally means 'of one pattern / identical', 不一样 means 'not of the same mould -> different, distinct, unconventional', frequently nominalized in media slogans (e.g. 看见不一样 'see the extraordinary / difference').

history.meaning: acorn; borrowed in Tang administrative and vernacular Chinese for 'model, pattern, sample'

history.form: 不一樣 / 不一样 (bù yīyàng)
history.meaning: not of the same kind or appearance; different, distinct, out of the ordinary

不一样.notes: Spoken with tone sandhi on both characters: bù yīyàng -> bú yíyàng; used predicatively (跟以前不一样 'different from before'), attributively (不一样的烟火 'a different kind of fireworks'), and nominalized ('something unique / the difference').

rootFamily.gloss: likewise, equally, in the same way

cognates.meaning: unable to reach or match (verbal complement)

不上.etymology: A negated directional and potential verb complement formed from the negative adverb 不 (bù, 'not') and 上 (shàng, 'to ascend; to reach; to attach'). In Early Mandarin vernacular, V-不上 emerged as the negative counterpart of V-得上, grammaticalizing spatial upward movement ('failing to climb onto') into an abstract marker of inability to reach a standard, match a rival, or connect with a target.

history.meaning: to not ascend; to fail to go up or present to a superior
unable to reach, attach to, or measure up to (negated potential complement)
unable to match, reach, or catch up with (post-verbal potential complement)

morphemes.meaning: to ascend; to reach or attain a level

不上.notes: Strictly bound as a post-verbal potential complement in high-frequency frames like 比不上 ('cannot compare to'), 赶不上 ('cannot catch up with'), and 谈不上 ('cannot be called / out of the question').

rootFamily.gloss: cannot compare to, no match for
cannot catch up with, miss (a train/deadline)
out of the question, cannot even speak of

cognates.word: 過言ではない (kagon de wa nai)

不为过.etymology: A Literary Chinese negative-copular predicate phrase (modifier-verb-object structure) composed of 不 (bù, 'not'), 为 (wéi, 'to constitute; to be deemed as'), and 过 (guò, Traditional 過, originally 'to pass beyond a boundary', hence 'excess, transgression, overstatement'). Literally meaning 'does not constitute going too far', it survived from classical argumentative prose into modern formal Mandarin as a rhetorical hedge validating strong praise or criticism.

history.meaning: does not count as a transgression or going beyond proper bounds
not an exaggeration; not going too far to say

morphemes.meaning: to be, to constitute, to count as

不为过.notes: Typically concludes a clause introduced by 毫不夸张地说 ('without exaggeration') or 说是…也不为过 ('even calling it X would not be an overstatement'), common in media reviews and industry commentary.

rootFamily.gloss: not to be considered as, not to count as

cognates.meaning: unable to finish or accomplish (potential complement)

不了.etymology: A negated potential complement combining the negative adverb 不 (bù, 'not') with 了 (liǎo, Middle Chinese *lewuX, 'to finish, complete, bring to conclusion'). During the Tang–Song vernacular transition, post-verbal 了 bifurcated into the unstressed perfective aspect marker le and the stressed resultative/potential verb liǎo ('to finish/manage'); V-不了 grammaticalized from 'cannot finish V-ing' into a general potential marker meaning 'incapable of V-ing'.

history.meaning: unfinished, not brought to completion; unclear
cannot finish; unable to accomplish (post-verbal potential complement)
unable to, cannot (potential complement); endless (in idioms)

morphemes.meaning: to finish, complete, manage to do

不了.notes: Always pronounced bùliǎo (never *bùle) when functioning as a potential complement after a verb (e.g., 走不了 'cannot leave', 解决不了 'cannot solve'); also appears in the idiom 不了了之 ('settle a matter by leaving it unsettled').

rootFamily.gloss: to settle a matter by leaving it unresolved
to understand clearly; to bring to an end

不二.etymology: A Classical Chinese negative-numeral compound from 不 (bù, 'not') and 二 (èr, 'two; divided; dual'). Originally used in pre-Qin political philosophy (such as the *Xunzi* and *Zuo Zhuan*) to mean 'undivided loyalty' or 'admitting no rival', it gained profound philosophical weight in Chinese Mahayana Buddhism (especially the *Vimalakīrti Nirdeśa Sūtra*'s 不二法门, modeling Sanskrit *advaita*, 'non-duality') before secularizing into 'peerless, one and only'.

history.meaning: not two; undivided in loyalty; uniform in price
non-duality (translating Sanskrit advaita in Buddhist texts)
one and only, unique, unmatched

不二.notes: Used almost exclusively as an attributive modifier before nouns in elevated or commercial prose, especially in 不二法门 ('the single best method') and 不二人选 ('the undisputed choice').

rootFamily.gloss: the one and only way, sovereign method (orig. Buddhist non-duality)
uniform price, no bargaining (lit. not two prices)

不二人选.etymology: A four-character modifier-head nominal phrase built by combining the classical attribute 不二 (bù'èr, 'not two; admitting no second; unique') with the noun compound 人选 (rénxuǎn, 'person selected; candidate', attested since the *Book of Sui* / *History of the Northern Dynasties*). The resulting expression literally denotes 'the candidate to whom there is no second alternative'.

history.meaning: separate classical items: 'unique/non-dual' + 'chosen candidate for office'
the undisputed first choice; the only person for a role or post

不二人选.notes: Ubiquitous in entertainment, casting, and corporate HR discourse (e.g., 担任总制片人的不二人选 'the undisputed choice for executive producer').

rootFamily.gloss: candidate, person selected for a role

不仅.etymology: A negated restrictive adverbial conjunction composed of 不 (bù, 'not') and 仅 (jǐn, Traditional 僅, Middle Chinese *gjinH, originally 'barely, scarcely reaching a limit' in Classical Chinese, later shifting to 'merely, only'). By negating the restrictive particle ('not merely'), it forms a correlative conjunction introducing the baseline clause before an additive clause marked by 而且, 还, or 也.

history.meaning: not barely; not restricted to a small amount
not only, not merely (correlative conjunction)

不仅.notes: Slightly more formal than 不但 and much more formal than 不光; pairs with 而且 ('moreover'), 还 ('also'), or 甚至 ('even') in the second clause.

rootFamily.gloss: not only does it take... (emphatic pattern)

cognates.meaning: will not; do not know how to
cognates.word: 唔識 (m4 sik1) / 唔會 (m4 wui5)

不会.etymology: A negated modal auxiliary formed from 不 (bù, 'not') and 会 (huì, Traditional 會, originally 'to assemble, meet, converge', which evolved in Tang–Song vernacular to mean 'to mentally grasp, understand how to' and subsequently grammaticalized into an epistemic/future modal 'to be likely to; will'). Thus 不会 carries both dynamic modality ('do not know how to') and epistemic/predictive modality ('unlikely to; will not').

history.meaning: do not meet or assemble; fail to coincide or understand
do not know how to (lack an acquired skill)
will not, unlikely to; unable to (learned skill)

morphemes.meaning: to know how to; to be likely to, will (modal auxiliary)

不会.notes: In spoken Mandarin, 不会吧？ ('No way! / You can't be serious!') is a ubiquitous expression of disbelief, whereas 不会 at the end of a response politely deflects thanks or apologies ('Not at all / No problem').

rootFamily.gloss: to master, understand thoroughly Through learning

不但.etymology: A negated restrictive conjunction formed from 不 (bù, 'not') and 但 (dàn, Middle Chinese *danH, 'merely, only, solely', which grammaticalized in Han–Six Dynasties vernacular from the verb 袒 'to strip bare, expose the upper body' -> 'bare, nothing but'). Negating 'merely' yields 'not only', attested across medieval vernacular texts as the standard correlative opener paired with 而且 or 并且.

history.meaning: not merely, not solely (adverbial phrase in Han–Tang texts)
not only (correlative conjunction paired with 而且/也)

不但.notes: Note the fossilized classical meaning of 但 ('only/merely') inside 不但: while standalone 但 means 'but/however' in modern Mandarin, inside 不但 (and 但愿 'if only') it preserves its medieval sense 'only'.

rootFamily.gloss: if only, I only wish that...
no harm in doing, might as well

不住.etymology: A negated resultative/potential verb complement combining 不 (bù, 'not') with 住 (zhù, 'to halt, stay, hold fast in place'). In medieval vernacular Chinese, post-verbal 住 grammaticalized from a full verb meaning 'to stop or reside' into a phase/resultative complement indicating firm fixation or containment (e.g., 抓住 'grasp firmly', 忍住 'hold back'). Negating it as V-不住 expresses inability to hold steady, restrain, or withstand an action or emotion.

history.meaning: do not stop or halt; incessantly, without pausing
unable to hold back, secure, or withstand (post-verbal complement); continuously (adverbial)

morphemes.meaning: to stay firm, hold in place, restrain

不住.notes: Highly productive after psychological or physical control verbs: 忍不住 ('cannot help / cannot hold back'), 撑不住 ('cannot hold out'), 靠不住 ('unreliable'), and 对不住 ('sorry / have let someone down').

rootFamily.gloss: cannot help (doing), unable to restrain oneself
unable to hold on or endure under pressure

不佳.etymology: A Literary Chinese negated stative verb compound consisting of 不 (bù, 'not') and 佳 (jiā, Old Chinese *kˤre, 'fine, comely, auspicious, excellent', written with 人 'person' and phonetic 圭 guī 'jade tablet'). Used since Han and Six Dynasties prose as a polite, elevated euphemism for unfavorable conditions, poor health, or disappointing performance.

history.meaning: not fine, inauspicious, unwell in spirit or health
unsatisfactory, subpar, poor (formal register)

不佳.notes: Strictly书面语 (written/formal register); usually follows a two-syllable abstract noun as a predicate in news or industry reports, such as 状态不佳 ('out of form'), 收视不佳 ('poor viewership ratings'), or 心情不佳 ('in a bad mood').

rootFamily.gloss: masterpiece, fine work (of art or media)

不便.etymology: A Classical Chinese negated adjectival/nominal compound formed from 不 (bù, 'not') and 便 (biàn, Middle Chinese *bjenH, 'advantageous, expedient, convenient, smooth'). Attested in the *Records of the Grand Historian* (*Shiji*) and Han administrative memorials for policies or terrains that are 'inexpedient' or 'unsuitable', it now functions both as a formal noun ('inconvenience') and an elliptical predicate meaning 'inopportune / not at liberty to'.

history.meaning: inexpedient, disadvantageous, unsuitable for action
inconvenience (noun); inappropriate or not at liberty to do something (verb/adj)

不便.notes: Serves two distinct grammatical roles: as a noun in polite apologies (给您带来不便 'cause you inconvenience') and as a modal-like predicate before a verb (不便透露 'not at liberty to disclose').

cognates.word: 唔停 (m4 ting4) / 不停 (bat1 ting4)

不停.etymology: A negated verbal/adverbial compound composed of 不 (bù, 'not') and 停 (tíng, Middle Chinese *deng, 'to halt, pause, lodge at a post station'). As 停 replaced classical 止 in vernacular Chinese for stopping motion or activity, 不停 developed into both a pre-verbal manner adverb (不停地 V, 'incessantly V-ing') and a post-verbal complement (V个不停, 'V without stopping').

history.meaning: without halting or lodging; unceasingly
nonstop, incessantly, continuously

不停.notes: Very common in the colloquial construction V + 个 + 不停 (e.g., 笑个不停 'laugh nonstop', 响个不停 'ring incessantly'), where 个 acts as a grammaticalized ligature before the complement.

rootFamily.gloss: to pause, suspend temporarily (e.g., media playback)
to stay, linger, remain at a stage

不光.etymology: A colloquial Mandarin negated restrictive adverbial/conjunction formed from 不 (bù, 'not') and 光 (guāng, originally 'light, radiance', which underwent semantic bleaching in Northern Mandarin via 'smooth, bare, stripped naked' -> 'nothing left but, merely, only'). Negating this restrictive sense of 光 ('only') produces 不光 ('not only, not just').

history.meaning: bare, naked; merely, solely (Northern vernacular semantic shift)
not only, not just (colloquial correlative adverb/conjunction)

不光.notes: Conversational equivalent of 不仅 and 不但; can be followed directly by a copula (不光是… 'not only is it...') or a noun/verb phrase, paired with 还 or 连…也 in the second clause.

rootFamily.gloss: relying solely on, just by virtue of
merely speaking without acting, all talk

不光彩.etymology: A negated adjectival compound formed by prefixing 不 (bù, 'not, un-') to the coordinative compound 光彩 (guāngcǎi, 'luster, radiance, brilliance' -> 'honor, prestige, glory', composed of 光 'light' + 彩 'colored sheen/splendor'). Literally meaning 'lacking luster or moral radiance', it denotes conduct or origins that are dishonorable, shady, or embarrassing to expose in public.

history.meaning: bright luster and color; honorable distinction, social radiance
dishonorable, disgraceful, underhanded, shady

不光彩.notes: Frequently modifies 手段 ('underhanded tactics'), 过去 ('a shady past'), or 角色 ('an inglorious role'), serving as a slightly euphemistic way to call something unethical or scandalous.

cognates.meaning: to have nothing to do with

不关.etymology: A negated relational verb formed from 不 (bù, 'not') and 关 (guān, Traditional 關, originally 'wooden crossbar of a gate; frontier pass', hence 'to interlock, connect, implicate, concern'). In vernacular Chinese from the Song–Yuan period onward, 不关 replaced or existed alongside 不干 in the frame 不关…的事 ('does not implicate/concern someone's affair').

history.meaning: does not bolt/interlock; does not pass through or pertain to
to have nothing to do with, to not concern (someone)

morphemes.meaning: to concern, involve, be connected to (orig. gate crossbar)

不关.notes: Almost always occurs in the fixed frame 不关 + [Person] + 的事 (e.g., 不关你的事 'none of your business / it has nothing to do with you'); compare the formal synonym 无关.

rootFamily.gloss: unrelated, having nothing to do with (formal)
to care about, be concerned with

cognates.meaning: never again, no second time (in idioms like 不再帰)

不再.etymology: A negated temporal/repetitive adverb composed of 不 (bù, 'not') and 再 (zài, Old Chinese *tsˤəs, 'twice, a second time', later broadening in vernacular Mandarin to 'again, anymore, further'). In Classical Chinese 不再 meant 'not happening twice' (e.g., 时不再来 'time does not come a second time'); in modern Mandarin it functions as an aspectual adverb meaning 'no longer, no more'.

history.meaning: not twice; not occurring a second time
no longer, no more (cessation of a state or habitual action)

morphemes.meaning: again, a second time, any longer

不再.notes: Placed directly before verbs or adjectives to mark the termination of a previous state (e.g., 不再犹豫 'hesitate no longer', 不再年轻 'no longer young').

rootFamily.gloss: once more, a second time; never again (with negation)

不准.etymology: A negated compound formed from 不 (bù, 'not') and 准 (zhǔn, which merges two distinct characters in Simplified Chinese: 准 'to grant, approve, permit' in administrative/legal usage—originally a graphical variant of 準 used in bureaucratic endorsements—and 準 'water-level gauge; accurate, exact'). Consequently, 不准 means either 'to forbid, not permit' (pre-verbal deontic modal) or 'inaccurate' (stative predicate).

history.meaning: not approved by official decree (不准); not level or accurate (不準)
to forbid, prohibit, not allow; inaccurate, uncertain (in 说不准)

morphemes.meaning: to permit, allow (from official endorsement 准); accurate (from 準)

不准.notes: Carries an authoritative, imperative tone when used at the start of a clause ('You are not allowed to... / No V-ing!'), stronger and more direct than 不让; in 说不准 ('cannot say for sure'), 准 reflects 準 ('accurate').

不到.etymology: A negated directional/resultative verb and quantitative verb composed of 不 (bù, 'not') and 到 (dào, Old Chinese *tˤaw-s, 'to arrive at, reach a destination or limit'). Functions both as a standalone verb before quantities ('failing to reach [an amount]', i.e., 'less than, under') and as a post-verbal potential/resultative complement (V-不到, 'unable to reach, find, or achieve by V-ing').

history.meaning: to fail to arrive at a place or attain a standard
less than (before numbers); unable to reach or achieve (post-verbal complement)

不到.notes: Watch the position: before a number/measure phrase, 不到 means 'less than / under' (不到三天 'less than three days'); after a verb, it is a potential complement meaning 'cannot succeed in V-ing' (找不到 'cannot find', 想不到 'unexpected').

rootFamily.gloss: unable to accomplish or manage to do

不到位.etymology: A negated verb-object/resultative adjectival compound formed from 不 (bù, 'not') and 到位 (dàowèi, 'to reach the designated position or proper level', from 到 'reach' + 位 'position, seat, standard'). Originally referring to funds, personnel, or stage/field positions arriving at their assigned spot, 到位 metaphorized in late 20th-century Mandarin into 'thorough, on point, up to standard', making 不到位 'falling short, inadequate, not thorough enough'.

history.meaning: to arrive at one's appointed seat or post; (of funds/gear) to be in place
inadequate, falling short of the mark, not thorough or nuanced enough

morphemes.meaning: designated position, proper standard or mark

不到位.notes: A favorite critique word among directors, producers, and managers: 沟通不到位 ('communication fell short'), 表演不到位 ('the acting didn't quite hit the mark'), 宣传不到位 ('promotion was inadequate').

rootFamily.gloss: in place, on point, thorough and up to standard
all in one step, accomplished thoroughly at once

不可.etymology: A foundational Classical Chinese negated modal compound from 不 (bù, 'not') and 可 (kě, Old Chinese *kʰˤajʔ, 'may, can, permissible, acceptable, fitting'). In pre-Qin texts (*Analects*, *Mencius*), 不可 stood alone as a complete predicate meaning 'that will not do / it is impermissible'. In modern Mandarin, it survives in elevated modal constructions, double-negative emphatic frames (非…不可), and four-character idioms.

history.meaning: it is impermissible; one must not; cannot be approved
cannot, must not (formal); essential part of 非…不可 ('must') and 不可+V idioms

不可.notes: Rarely used alone before casual verbs in speech (where 不能 or 不可以 is preferred), but ubiquitous in the emphatic frame 非…不可 ('absolutely must...') and after adjectives as an intensifier (急得不可开交, 高兴得非同小可).

rootFamily.gloss: cannot help but, have no choice but to

不可能.etymology: Formed by negating 可能 (kěnéng, 'possible, feasible; possibility') with 不 (bù, 'not'). While 不可 and 能 co-occurred sequentially in Classical Chinese ('cannot be capable of'), the fused lexicalized concept 不可能 ('impossible; impossibility') crystallized during the Meiji-era Sino-Japanese translation of Western philosophical and scientific terms (Japanese 不可能 *fukanō* rendering English/French *impossible*) and re-entered modern Mandarin as a core modal adjective, noun, and adverb.

history.meaning: cannot be capable of (two separate modal elements: 不可 + 能)
impossible, impossibility (modern lexicalized compound via Meiji Japanese)
impossible, cannot possibly, no way

不可能.notes: Functions flexibly as a pre-verbal modal ('cannot possibly V'), a predicative adjective ('is impossible'), or an attributive modifier (不可能的任务 'Mission: Impossible').

不可限量.etymology: A four-character Literary Chinese modal-passive idiom composed of 不可 (bùkě, 'cannot be') and the coordinative verb compound 限量 (xiànliáng, 'to bound and measure; to set a limit or quota on', from 限 'boundary, threshold' + 量 'to measure with a vessel'). Originally popularized in Chinese Buddhist translations (such as the *Lotus Sutra*, describing immeasurable merit) and Tang–Song historical prose, it denotes potential or prospects that cannot be circumscribed or measured.

history.meaning: cannot be measured or bounded (of Buddhist merit or vast quantities)
boundless, limitless, immeasurable (especially of someone's future prospects)

不可限量.notes: Note the pronunciation liáng (second tone, verbal 'to measure') or liàng (fourth tone, assimilated to modern 限量 'limited edition'); overwhelmingly collocates with 前途 ('future prospects') or 潜力 ('potential'), as in 前途不可限量 ('a boundless future').

不同.etymology: A Classical Chinese negated stative verb and nominal compound formed from 不 (bù, 'not') and 同 (tóng, Old Chinese *dˤoŋ, 'same, alike, together, in harmony'). Attested in the *Analects* (君子和而不同 'The noble person seeks harmony, not sameness') and throughout pre-Qin philosophy, it functions in modern Mandarin as an adjective ('different, distinct'), a stative predicate (与…不同 'differ from'), and an abstract noun ('difference').

history.meaning: not identical; to not conform or collude blindly; differing
different, distinct (adjective); difference (noun)

不同.notes: Unlike 不同的 + Noun (attributive), when used predicatively ('A is different from B') it takes the prepositional frame A跟B不同 (spoken) or A与B不同 (formal), never a direct object.

不在.etymology: A Classical Chinese negated existential/locative verb compound formed from 不 (bù, 'not') and 在 (zài, Old Chinese *dzˤəʔ, 'to be present at, exist, reside in, depend upon'). In Classical Chinese (e.g., *Analects* 父母在，不远游; 刘禹锡 山不在高), 不在 meant 'is not present', 'does not lie in / depend on', or euphemistically 'has passed away'. All three senses remain active in modern Mandarin.

history.meaning: to not be present; to not consist in/depend on; (euphemism) to be deceased
to be absent, away, no longer in a place or state; to not lie in

morphemes.meaning: to be located at, be present, exist in

不在.notes: Frequently appears in showbiz/workplace expressions like 心不在焉 ('absent-minded / distracted') and 状态不在 ('off one's game'); do not confuse with its homophone 不再 ('no longer').

rootFamily.gloss: absent-minded, distracted (lit. the mind is not in it)

不在乎.etymology: A vernacular Mandarin negated psychological verb formed by negating 在乎 (zàihu, 'to care about, mind, take to heart') with 不 (bù, 'not'). The verb 在乎 itself arose through the lexicalization of the Classical Chinese verb-preposition sequence 在乎 (zài hū, 'to lie in, depend upon, rest with', where 乎 is the classical locative/prepositional particle equivalent to 于). By the Qing dynasty, 'it rests upon X' had shifted in Beijing vernacular to 'to attach importance to / care about X'.

history.meaning: does not lie in or depend upon [something] (Classical verb 在 + preposition 乎)
to not care about, not mind, be indifferent to (lexicalized compound verb)
to not care about, pay no heed to; (in 满不在乎) utterly unconcerned

morphemes.meaning: to lie in, rest on, be concerned with
at, in, upon (classical preposition fused as unstressed verbal suffix -hu)

不在乎.notes: The final syllable 乎 is pronounced in the neutral tone (bù zàihu); compare 不在意 ('not mind / not take notice of'), which is slightly gentler and less defiant than 不在乎.

rootFamily.gloss: to mind, take to heart, pay attention to

不太.etymology: A negated degree adverb formed from 不 (bù, 'not') and 太 (tài, Old Chinese *tʰˤajs, 'excessively, extremely, very, too', graphical variant of 大 dà 'great'). While 太 alone often marks excess ('too much'), negating it as 不太 softens the negation of the following adjective or mental verb ('not very, not particularly, not so'), functioning as a pragmatic hedge in polite conversation.

history.meaning: not excessively, not overly
not very, not quite, not particularly (softened degree adverb)

不太.notes: Essential for diplomatic understatement in Chinese workplace and media settings: saying 不太好 ('not so good') or 不太合适 ('not quite appropriate') politely communicates rejection without harshness.

rootFamily.gloss: too much, excessive; over the top
not very good, rather poor (polite understatement)

cognates.meaning: without losing; not failing to be (in classical idioms)

不失.etymology: A Classical Chinese negated verb compound from 不 (bù, 'not') and 失 (shī, Old Chinese *l̥i[t], 'to let slip from the hand, lose, miss, err, fail in duty'). Attested in the *Classic of Changes* (*Yijing*), *Analects* (因不失其亲，亦可宗也), and *Daodejing* (不失其所者久), it survives in modern Mandarin primarily in two high-register patterns: 'without losing [a quality]' (不失风度 'without losing poise') and the copular frame 不失为 ('can still be counted as / is not a bad...').

history.meaning: to not lose, not let slip, not fail in propriety or timing
to still retain, not lose (a quality); in 不失为, 'may still be considered a good...'

morphemes.meaning: to lose, forfeit, miss, fail in

不失.notes: Most commonly encountered in formal reviews or commentary in the pattern 既…又不失… ('both X and yet retaining Y', e.g., 严谨而不失幽默 'rigorous yet not lacking in humor') and 不失为一个好办法 ('is after all a good solution').

rootFamily.gloss: can still be considered as, is after all a (good choice)
the time must not be lost, opportunity knocks but once

不好.etymology: A negated stative verb and pre-verbal modal compound formed from 不 (bù, 'not') and 好 (hǎo, Old Chinese *qʰˤuʔ, originally 'pleasing, comely, fine', broadened across Chinese history into the general positive evaluator 'good, well' and the pre-verbal marker 'easy to; convenient to; socially appropriate to'). Thus 不好 means not only 'bad' or 'unwell', but before a verb means 'hard to V' or 'embarrassing/inappropriate to V'.

history.meaning: not comely; (as bù hào) to not be fond of
bad, poor, unwell; difficult or awkward to do (before a verb)
bad, unwell; awkward/inconvenient to (+ verb); Oh no! (exclamation)

morphemes.meaning: good, well; easy or fitting to do

不好.notes: Before a verb, 不好 + V often expresses social delicacy rather than physical difficulty: 我不好意思拒绝 ('I feel awkward refusing') or 这事我不好插手 ('It's not my place / awkward for me to step into this matter').

rootFamily.gloss: embarrassed, shy; sorry to bother you
hard to say; awkward for me to say

不好受.etymology: A negated adverb-verb adjectival compound composed of 不 (bù, 'not'), 好 (hǎo, functioning as a pre-verbal modal prefix meaning 'easy to, pleasant to, comfortable to'), and 受 (shòu, Old Chinese *duʔ, 'to receive, accept, endure, bear'). Literally 'not easy or pleasant to endure', it parallels 难受 (nánshòu) and describes either physical discomfort or emotional distress and heartache.

history.meaning: easy/hard to endure or bear (vernacular adverbial-passive adjective)
uncomfortable, hard to bear, feeling awful (physically or emotionally)

不好受.notes: Frequently predicates 心里 ('in one's heart'), as in 心里很不好受 ('feeling awful inside'), or describes tough circumstances (日子不好受 'having a rough time of it'). Compare the synonymous 难受.

rootFamily.gloss: unable to bear or stand it anymore

不好意思.etymology: Colloquial polite formula combining 不好 ('not good, awkward') + 意思 ('thought, feeling, state of mind'), literally 'feel awkward in mind/face'. Originally describing shyness or embarrassment ('feel embarrassed to'), it became a standard everyday expression for 'excuse me, sorry to trouble you'.

history.stage: Qing vernacular (e.g., Hongloumeng) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: feel embarrassed/shy -> excuse me, sorry

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 不好意思 (via 萌典)

不如.etymology: Classical and modern comparative verb combining 不 ('not') + 如 ('be like, equal, match'), literally 'not match / not be as good as', and by extension 'it would be better to…'.

history.stage: Classical Chinese (Analects, Zuozhuan) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: not equal to; inferior to; better to

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 不如 (via 萌典)

不妥.etymology: A Literary and administrative Mandarin negated adjectival compound formed from 不 (bù, 'not') and 妥 (tuǒ, Old Chinese *n̥ˤojʔ, written with 爪 'hand' over 女 'woman', originally meaning 'tranquil, settled, secure, stable'). In Ming–Qing bureaucratic memorials and vernacular fiction, 妥 came to mean 'properly arranged, sound, appropriate', making 不妥 the standard diplomatic term for 'ill-advised, inappropriate, or not quite sound'.

history.meaning: unsettled, insecure, not yet peacefully arranged
improperly arranged, unsound (in Ming–Qing official memorials and vernacular)
inappropriate, unwise, improper, amiss

不妥.notes: A refined, diplomatic word favored in professional or leadership contexts to flag a problem or reject a proposal tactfully (e.g., 这样做恐有不妥 'doing it this way might be unwise', 言辞不妥 'inappropriate wording').

不妨.etymology: A modifier-head negated predicate formed from Classical Chinese 不 (bù, Middle Chinese *pjuw, general verbal negator) and 妨 (fáng, MC *phjang, 'to hinder, obstruct, harm'). Literally 'does not hinder' or 'causes no harm', it grammaticalized in Tang–Song vernacular prose from a literal clause ('it does not interfere') into a polite modal adverb inviting or suggesting a course of action ('one might as well').

history.meaning: does not hinder or injure
there is no harm in; might as well (modal adverb)
might as well, there is no harm in trying

不妨.notes: Polite, persuasive register; frequently paired with 试试 (shìshi, 'give it a try') in pitches and creative meetings to soften a bold proposal without sounding pushy.

不宜.etymology: A Classical Chinese negator-predicate compound joining 不 (bù, Middle Chinese *pjuw, 'not') with 宜 (yí, MC *ngje, originally depicting sacrificial meat on an altar block 俎, hence 'ritually fitting, proper, ought'). Attested since Old Chinese texts such as the Mencius and almanac prescriptions, the modifier-head structure denotes that an action or timing lacks propriety or practical suitability.

history.meaning: ritually improper; not fitting circumstances
inadvisable; traditional epistolary closing ('I shall say no more')
to be unsuitable for, inadvisable to

不宜.notes: Formal written and broadcast register; common in PR advisories, broadcast censorship notices (少儿不宜, 'unsuitable for minors'), and scheduling decisions (不宜公开, 'inadvisable to make public').

不容侵犯.etymology: A four-character Sino-compound combining the negated modal verb 不容 (bùróng, 'does not tolerate/allow', from 不 'not' + 容 MC *yowng 'to contain, permit') with the coordinative verb compound 侵犯 (qīnfàn, 'to encroach and violate', from 侵 MC *tshim 'to stealthily invade' + 犯 MC *bjamX 'to transgress, offend against'). Structurally a verb-object/modal-complement phrase ('brooks no encroachment'), it crystallized in modern legal, diplomatic, and rights discourse.

history.meaning: cannot contain; does not permit
to invade territory or transgress boundaries
inviolable, brooking no infringement (sovereignty, IP, or personal rights)

不容侵犯.notes: Solemn, emphatic four-character phrase; in media production and entertainment law it frequently defends intellectual property, creative版权 (copyright), or an artist's privacy rights.

不对.etymology: Negated stative compound from 不 ('not') + 对 (simplified from 對, originally depicting a ceremonial stand or matching tallies held in the hand 寸). From the sense of two halves of a tally failing to match up, 不对 developed the general meaning of 'incorrect, amiss, or out of order'.

history.meaning: not matching; failing to correspond
incorrect; wrong; something amiss

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 不对

不小心.etymology: Negated manner phrase of 不 ('not') + 小心 ('careful, cautious', literally 'make one's heart/mind small and attentive' in Classical Chinese): 'carelessly, accidentally, by mistake'.

history.meaning: not careful; accidentally

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 不小心 (via 萌典)

不少.etymology: Litotes compound of 不 ('not') + 少 ('few, little'), meaning 'not a few' -> 'quite a lot, many, plenty of'.

history.meaning: not few -> quite a lot, many

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 不少 (via 萌典)

不就好了.etymology: An idiomatic Modern Mandarin rhetorical frame built by stacking rhetorical negation 不 (bù, 'isn't it...') onto the consequent adverb 就 (jiù, 'then, simply'), the resultative predicate 好 (hǎo, 'fine, settled'), and the change-of-state particle 了 (le). Rather than negating the predicate, initial 不 functions interrogatively to present an obvious, effortless solution ('if X happens, isn't everything settled then?').

history.meaning: then it will be fine / settled
wouldn't that settle it? / isn't it fine just to... (rhetorical frame)

不就好了.notes: Colloquial, briskly pragmatic spoken construction (X + 不就好了(吗)); often carries a hint of impatience in fast-paced production rooms ('Why overcomplicate it—just cut that scene and we're done!').

不开.etymology: A negated potential directional/resultative complement combining the potential infixal negator 不 (bù, 'cannot, unable to') with 开 (kāi, Middle Chinese *khaj, 'to open, separate, part').
