As V + 开 evolved in Early Mandarin from literal spatial opening ('open apart') to figurative detachment and mental release, V + 不开 came to express an inability to separate from, shake off, or fit within a space.

history.meaning: to unbolt a door, open apart
unable to open, spread out, or detach from
unable to get away from, shake off, or let go mentally (potential complement)

不开.notes: Bound verbal complement never used standalone at the start of a clause; crucial in collocations like 离不开 ('cannot do without'), 走不开 ('tied up at work'),甩不开 ('can't shake off'), and 想不开 ('take things too hard').

rootFamily.gloss: unable to leave or do without
unable to get away from duties
to take to heart, be unable to get over

cognates.meaning: unavoidable, cannot help (in やむを得ず)

不得.etymology: Formed from 不 (bù, 'not') + 得 (dé, Middle Chinese *tok, 'to obtain, succeed, be permitted'). It followed a dual grammaticalization pathway: preverbally in Classical legal and administrative prose (不得 + V), it retained deontic prohibition ('must not, is forbidden to'); postverbally in Tang–Song vernacular (V + 不得), it became a potential/evaluative complement ('cannot be V-ed, ought not V').

history.meaning: to fail to obtain; unable to achieve
postverbal complement: cannot or must not be V-ed
must not (formal preverbal); cannot/unfit to (postverbal complement, e.g. 怪不得, 舍不得)

不得.notes: Watch syntax and pronunciation: preverbal 不得 (bùdé + V, 'shall not') belongs to stern contracts and broadcast regulations, whereas postverbal V + 不得 (bude, neutral tone, as in 舍不得 'hate to part with' or 怪不得 'no wonder') is everyday speech.

rootFamily.gloss: reluctant to part with or spend

不得不.etymology: A Classical Chinese double-negation modal construction combining 不得 (bùdé, 'cannot obtain / is not permitted to') with a second negator 不 (bù, 'not') preceding a main verb: literally 'cannot not [do]'. Already well attested in Warring States and Han prose, the logical cancellation of twin negations expresses external compulsion, situational necessity, or reluctant obligation ('have no alternative but to').

history.meaning: cannot fail to; compelled by circumstances to
have no choice but to, cannot help doing (fixed modal adverbial)

不得不.notes: Unlike 必须 (bìxū, objective duty), 不得不 highlights external pressure or reluctance—ubiquitous in showbiz crises ('不得不承认, I have to admit' or '不得不撤档, forced to pull the release').

不必.etymology: A modifier-head negated modal compound from 不 (bù, 'not') and 必 (bì, Old Chinese *pjit, Middle Chinese *pjit, originally depicting a handle or ladle divider, loaned early for 'certainly, inevitably, must'). Negating necessity rather than obligation ('not necessary' rather than 'must not'), 不必 shifted from Classical epistemic 'not necessarily' toward deontic 'need not, there is no need to'.

history.meaning: not necessarily; need not insist on
there is no need to, need not (modal adverb)

不必.notes: Classic learner trap: negating 必须 ('must') yields 不必 or 不用 ('need not'), never 必须不! Slightly more polished and composed than 不用, as in 大可不必 ('really quite unnecessary').

rootFamily.gloss: not necessarily, may not be so

不怕.etymology: A negated psych-verb phrase combining 不 (bù, 'not') with 怕 (pà, Middle Chinese *phaeh, semantic 忄 'heart' + phonetic 白 *baek, originally 'calm, unmoved' like 惔怕 before supplanting Classical 畏/恐 in Tang vernacular in the sense 'to fear, dread'). Alongside literal fearlessness ('not afraid of'), it developed a conditional-concessive rhetorical usage ('never mind even if; no worry about scarcity').

history.meaning: to fear, dread (supplanting 畏/恐 in vernacular)
not to fear; unafraid of (even if...)

不怕.notes: Appears in famous resilient proverbs quoted in high-stakes workplace dramas, such as 不怕一万，就怕万一 ('don't fear the ten thousand expected things, just guard against the one-in-ten-thousand mishap').

不怕死.etymology: A lexicalized negated verb-object (VO) phrase that functions adjectivally: 不 (bù, 'not') + 怕 (pà, 'to fear') + 死 (sǐ, Old Chinese *sijʔ, Middle Chinese *sijX, 'death, to die'). Modeled semantically on the Classical Chinese idiom 不畏死 (as in Laozi 74, 民不畏死 'when the people do not fear death'), the vernacular replacement with 怕 created a vivid colloquial descriptor for reckless grit or heroic audacity.

history.meaning: not fearing death (Classical precursor)
unafraid of dying; daredevil, fearless

不怕死.notes: In contemporary workplace and media banter, 不怕死 is constantly used hyperbolically for bold subordinates or investigative producers who dare challenge powerful executives or taboo topics (不怕死的敢说真话).

不想.etymology: A modifier-head negated volitional/cognitive verb phrase composed of 不 (bù, 'not') and 想 (xiǎng, Middle Chinese *sjangX, semantic 心 'heart-mind' + phonetic 相 *sjang, 'to picture mentally, long for, ponder'). In Early Mandarin, 想 grammaticalized into a volitional auxiliary ('to want to, feel like doing'), while an older Classical-derived homograph sense ('unexpectedly, little did one think', short for 不料想) survives in literary narrative.

history.meaning: not to visualize or dwell upon mentally
unexpectedly, little did one think (narrative conjunction); not want to
do not want to, not feel like doing

不想.notes: Softer and more subjective than 不愿意 ('unwilling') or 不肯 ('refuse'): saying 我不想去 expresses personal disinclination rather than stubborn defiance; in written prose, clause-initial 不想 can still mean 'unexpectedly'.

不愧.etymology: A Classical Chinese negated stative verb from 不 (bù, 'not') + 愧 (kuì, Middle Chinese *kjwijH, semantic 忄 'heart' + 鬼 'ghost/spirit', 'ashamed, conscience-stricken'). Attested in the Mengzi and Shijing (不愧于天, 'having nothing to be ashamed of before Heaven'), litotes ('need feel no shame toward [a title]') shifted it into an admiring evaluative adverbial ('fully lives up to, truly worthy of').

history.meaning: to have a clear conscience, feel no shame before
fully deserving of a reputation, truly worthy of being called

不愧.notes: Almost always appears in the praising frame 不愧是 + Noun ('truly lives up to being [a top producer / veteran star]!'), a staple compliment in studio and industry dialogue.

rootFamily.gloss: worthy of, with a clear conscience

不愿意.etymology: Formed by negating the disyllabic psych-modal compound 愿意 (yuànyì, 'willing, wishing') with 不 (bù, 'not'). Within 愿意, 愿 (Traditional 願, MC *ngjwonH, semantic 頁 'head' + 原, 'earnest wish, vow') pairs coordinatively/modifier-head with 意 (MC *ʔjijH, 'thought, intention'). Solidified in Early Mandarin, 不愿意 expresses inner emotional or volitional reluctance to consent.

history.meaning: heartfelt wish, earnest intention (often in Buddhist/vernacular vows)
unwilling, disinclined to agree or participate

不愿意.notes: Expresses inner attitude ('unwilling') rather than active confrontation; in northern colloquial speech, standalone 不愿意 can also mean 'to get sulky or displeased' when someone's pride is bruised.

rootFamily.gloss: voluntary, of one's own free will

不改则死.etymology: A terse four-character Classical-style conditional maxim structured as [negated protasis] + 则 (zé, 'then') + [apodosis]: 不 (bù, 'not') + 改 (gǎi, MC *kojX, semantic 攵 'strike/action' + 己, 'to alter, correct, reform') + 则 (zé, MC *tsok, Classical conditional connective 'then inevitably') + 死 (sǐ, 'to perish, die'). Echoing Warring States legalist and strategic aphorisms (compare 不进则退 'advance or fall back'), it frames institutional innovation as existential survival.

history.meaning: if not X, then inevitably Y (Classical conditional template)
innovate/reform or perish (corporate and media-industry slogan)

不改则死.notes: Punchy boardroom and TV-industry aphorism ('adapt or die'), frequently paired in legacy-media transformation debates with 改了找死，不改等死 ('reforming courts death; failing to reform awaits death').

rootFamily.gloss: to improve, revamp (e.g. a show format)

cognates.word: 不敢当 (ふかんとう, fukantō)

cognates.meaning: undeserving of praise, I dare not accept

不敢当.etymology: A Classical Chinese honorific self-deprecating formula: 不 (bù, 'not') + 敢 (gǎn, MC *kamX, 'to dare, presume') + 当 (Traditional 當, dāng, MC *tang, 'to match, bear, shoulder, deserve'). Attested in the Zuo Zhuan and Shiji (臣不敢当, 'your servant dares not presume to bear [this honor/office]'), it ritualized into the standard polite deflection of high praise or hospitality across the Sinosphere.

history.meaning: dare not presume to accept a rank, charge, or honor
you flatter me; I hardly deserve such praise (polite formula)

不敢当.notes: Courteous, slightly formal social deflection used at industry banquets and networking events when praised by peers or elders (often reduplicated warmly as 不敢当，不敢当).

不是.etymology: Negated copula combining 不 ('not', pronounced rising bú by tone sandhi before fourth-tone shì) + 是 ('be; right/this'). Functions as 'is not / no', in rhetorical tag questions, and as a noun meaning 'fault, blame' (赔不是 'apologize for a fault').

history.meaning: is not; no; fault/wrong

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 不是 (via 萌典)

不止.etymology: Composed of 不 (bù, 'not') + 止 (zhǐ, Old Chinese *təʔ, Middle Chinese *tsyiX, pictograph of a footprint趾 signifying 'to halt, stop at a limit'). In Classical Chinese it functioned both verbally ('without ceasing', postpositively as in 血流不止) and restrictively ('does not stop at [this amount/scope]'), whence its Modern Mandarin adverbial sense 'more than, not merely'.

history.meaning: not to halt; without ceasing; not stopping at a boundary
more than (with quantities); not merely; incessantly (postverbal)

morphemes.meaning: to stop, halt at a limit

不止.notes: Distinguish spelling carefully from 不只 (bùzhǐ, 'not only', strictly a conjunction paired with 而且/还): 不止 handles numerical excess (不止一次, 'more than once') and postverbal 'incessantly' (大笑不止).

不比.etymology: A negated comparative verb combining 不 (bù, 'not') with 比 (bǐ, Old Chinese *pijʔ, Middle Chinese *pjijX, depicting two figures standing side by side, hence 'to line up, match, compare'). In vernacular Chinese from the Song–Ming era onward, A 不比 B came to mean 'A cannot be equated with B' (i.e., circumstances have changed or A lacks B's advantages), rather than simple symmetric inequality.

history.meaning: not to form cliques; not comparable in rank or closeness
unlike, cannot be compared on equal footing with (e.g., 今不比昔)

morphemes.meaning: to compare, match, line up alongside

不比.notes: Subtle grammar point: standard comparative negation uses 不如 or 没有 ('A is not as good as B'), whereas A 不比 B means 'A isn't in the same situation/league as B' (现在不比以前了, 'things now aren't like the old days').

不满.etymology: A modifier-head compound of 不 (bù, 'not') + 满 (Traditional 滿, mǎn, Middle Chinese *mwanX, semantic 氵 'water' + phonetic 㒼, 'brimming over, full to capacity'). Originally spatial and quantitative in Classical Chinese ('not reaching full measure', e.g., 不满百人 'fewer than a hundred people'), its psychological sense ('emotionally unfulfilled, resentful, dissatisfied') expanded across both Ming–Qing vernacular and Meiji-era Japanese Sino-vocabulary (不満).

history.meaning: not full; falling short of a measure, quota, or age
dissatisfied, displeased, harboring grievance; also 'under [a number/age]'

不满.notes: Functions as adjective, transitive verb (不满他的做法), or noun (表达不满, 'voice discontent')—a staple of media headlines reporting fan backlash or investor grievances.

不然.etymology: Conjunction combining 不 ('not') + 然 ('so, thus'), literally 'if it is not so' -> 'otherwise, or else'. Attested since Classical Chinese (Mencius, Zuozhuan).

history.meaning: it is not so -> otherwise, if not

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 不然 (via 萌典)

不用.etymology: Formed from 不 (bù, 'not') + 用 (yòng, Old Chinese *loŋs, Middle Chinese *yowngH, 'to employ, make use of, need'). In Classical Chinese 不用 meant 'not to employ (talent or force)'; as 用 developed a nominal/modal sense 'usefulness, need' in Early Mandarin (compare 何用 'what need'), 不用 grammaticalized into the everyday spoken modal adverb 'need not, do not have to' (often contracted in Beijing speech to 甭 béng).

history.meaning: not to employ (officials, weapons, or rites)
there is no need to, do not bother to (modal adverb)
need not, do not need to (standard colloquial equivalent of 不必)

不用.notes: Everyday conversational workhorse: 不用谢 ('no need to thank me') and 不用说 ('needless to say'); in northern speech its rapid fusion produced the single character 甭 (béng).

不等.etymology: A homographic pair of modifier-head compounds combining 不 (bù, 'not') + 等 (děng, Middle Chinese *tongX, semantic 竹 'bamboo slips' + 寺 'court', originally 'neat alignment of bamboo tallies, rank, equal', which later developed the vernacular verbal sense 'to wait'). In vernacular syntax 不等 + NP/clause means 'not wait for' or 'before [someone finishes]', whereas Classical/technical 不等 retains 'unequal, varying'.

history.meaning: unequal in rank, measure, or kind
not to wait for; before [an action completes] (vernacular verb/preposition)

不等.notes: In dramatic storytelling and fast-moving broadcast schedules, 时间不等任何人 ('time waits for no one') and 不等他说完 ('before he even finished speaking') create immediate narrative urgency.

不算什么.etymology: An idiomatic Modern Mandarin verb-object predicate uniting 不算 (bùsuàn, 'does not count as', from 不 'not' + 算 MC *swanH, semantic 竹 'bamboo counting rods' + 具, 'to reckon, tally, count as') with the indefinite pronoun 什么 (shénme, 'what, anything of consequence', evolved from Tang–Song 甚么/拾没). In negative polarity contexts, 什么 loses its interrogative force and denotes 'anything remarkable or significant'.

history.meaning: not to tally; does not count as valid
counts for little, is nothing special or formidable

不算什么.notes: Used either modestly to downplay one's own effort or stoically to shrug off a setback ('这点挫折不算什么', 'this little setback is nothing').

不管.etymology: Formed from 不 (bù, 'not') + 管 (guǎn, Middle Chinese *kwanX, semantic 竹 'bamboo' + 官, originally 'bamboo pipe/flute' and 'key to a lock', whence 'to hold the key to, administer, take charge of, mind'). In Yuan–Ming vernacular, 不管 evolved from the literal verb phrase 'not take charge of / not care about' into an unconditional concessive conjunction ('regardless of, no matter') paired with 都 or 也.

history.meaning: bamboo pipe; lock-key; to govern or be in charge of
not to mind or interfere with; regardless of (concessive conjunction)
not care about / leave unattended (verb); no matter (conjunction)

morphemes.meaning: to manage, control, mind, care about

不管.notes: Dual-role powerhouse: as a verb, 坐视不管 means 'sit back and ignore'; as a conjunction, 不管 must introduce a choice or question word (不管谁 / 不管成不成) and pair with 都 or 也 in the main clause.

不管怎样.etymology: A fixed concessive discourse phrase combining the unconditional marker 不管 (bùguǎn, 'not minding, regardless of') with the interrogative manner/state pronoun 怎样 (zěnyàng, 'how, in what manner', from Early Mandarin 怎 'how', fused from 作甚 'doing what', + 样 'pattern, appearance, way'). Together they sweep aside all possible scenarios ('no matter how things stand, in any event').

history.meaning: in what manner, how (vernacular interrogative)
no matter what, in any case, regardless of how things turn out

不管怎样.notes: Slightly cleaner and less colloquial than 不管怎么说 ('no matter how you put it'), and more conversational than 无论如何; ideal for pivoting a tense meeting back to actionable next steps.

不经意.etymology: A Classical/Literary Chinese negated verb-object phrase: 不 (bù, 'not') + 经 (Traditional 經, jīng, MC *keng, originally 'warp threads of a loom', hence 'to pass through, apply methodically') + 意 (yì, MC *ʔjijH, 'mind, conscious thought, attention'). Literally 'not passing through conscious attention', it was prized in Tang–Song aesthetics and painting criticism (不经意处, effortless spontaneity) before becoming a general adverbial for casual or accidental action.

history.meaning: not paying deliberate heed; uncontrived, effortless (in poetry and brushwork)
inadvertently, casually, without noticing (often 不经意间)

不经意.notes: Frequently paired with 间 as 不经意间 ('in an unguarded/casual moment')—a favorite cinematic and screenwriting phrase for subtle glances or accidental revelations on camera.

cognates.meaning: refusal to consent (kanbun: 肯んぜず)

不肯.etymology: Composed of 不 (bù, 'not') + 肯 (kěn, Old Chinese *kʰˤəŋʔ, Middle Chinese *khongX, originally 肎 depicting flesh 肉 clinging to bone 冎, 'tendon-attached meat, crux', loaned by Han–Six Dynasties times for 'to consent, deign, be willing'). Unlike passive reluctance, 不肯 denotes active refusal to yield, consent, or budge on a point.

history.meaning: flesh attached to bone; loaned for 'to consent / refuse to deign'
stubbornly refuse to, will not consent to

morphemes.meaning: to consent, agree, be willing to

不肯.notes: Stronger and more resolute than 不愿意: 不愿意 is internal reluctance ('would rather not'), whereas 不肯 is active, firm refusal in negotiations ('死活不肯签字', 'flatly refuses to sign no matter what').

不能.etymology: Negated modal verb combining 不 ('not') + 能 ('be able, can, allowed to'), expressing inability or prohibition ('cannot, must not'). Attested throughout Classical and Modern Chinese.

history.meaning: be unable to; cannot; must not

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 不能 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: bad influence, adverse effect (parallel Sino-components 不良 + 影響)
cognates.word: 悪影響 / 不良 (ふりょう + えいきょう)

不良影响.etymology: A four-character modifier-head nominal phrase pairing 不良 (bùliáng, 'unwholesome, adverse, defective', from 不 'not' + 良 MC *ljang 'good, virtuous, sound') with 影响 (Traditional 影響, yǐngxiǎng, coordinative metaphor from 影 MC *ʔjangX 'shadow' + 響 MC *xjangX 'echo'). In Classical Chinese (Shangshu), 如影随形，如响应声 described how consequences follow actions like shadow and echo; Meiji Japanese (影響, eikyō) standardized its modern abstract sense 'influence, impact', which re-entered modern Chinese.

history.meaning: shadow and echo (metaphor for swift response); faint trace
abstract 'influence, effect, impact' (semantic shift popularized via Meiji Japanese)
adverse effect, negative social or reputational impact

不良影响.notes: Quintessential Chinese media-regulation, PR crisis, and apology-statement collocation: 造成不良影响 ('cause a negative public/social impact') appears in virtually every celebrity scandal notice or broadcast rectification order.

rootFamily.gloss: clout, sphere of influence (e.g. media reach)

不行.etymology: Formed from 不 (bù, 'not') + 行 (xíng, Old Chinese *gˤraŋ, Middle Chinese *haeng, pictograph of a four-way crossroads 彳+亍, 'to walk, proceed, be put into practice, work out'). From 'a road cannot be walked' and 'a policy does not go through' in Classical Chinese, 不行 generalized in Mandarin into an all-purpose evaluative and deontic predicate: 'won't do, not permitted, incompetent, on the brink of collapse'.

history.meaning: not to walk or advance; (of laws/dao) not put into practice
unworkable, won't do, out of the question; critically ill

morphemes.meaning: to go, work, be permissible or capable

不行.notes: Watch three distinct Mandarin uses: (1) standalone refusal ('No way / That won't work!'); (2) capability judgement (他能力不行, 'he's not up to standard'); and (3) degree complement Adj + 得不行 ('exhausted/thrilled beyond words', e.g. 累得不行).

不要.etymology: Composed of 不 (bù, 'not') + 要 (yào, Middle Chinese *ʔjiewH, originally pictograph of a person's waist 腰 held with two hands, loaned for 'to seek, demand, want, require'). As 要 grammaticalized in Early Mandarin into a volitional and future/deontic auxiliary, 不要 developed from transitive 'not want [something]' into the primary spoken prohibitive auxiliary 'do not!' (paralleled by its northern phonetic fusion 别 bié).

history.meaning: waist; to intercept, seek, demand
do not want; prohibitive auxiliary 'do not!'
do not (imperative); not want (transitive verb)

morphemes.meaning: to want, demand, be going to

不要.notes: More direct and forceful than 别 (bié, historically fused from 不要); also forms the trendy emphatic internet/youth frame 不要太 + Adj ('way too [good/cool]!', literally an ironic warning not to be excessively good).

cognates.meaning: missing, out of sight (e.g. 行方不明 / 不見)

不见.etymology: A Classical Chinese negated verb from 不 (bù, 'not') + 见 (Traditional 見, jiàn, Old Chinese *kˤens, Middle Chinese *kenH, pictograph of a prominent eye 目 atop a kneeling person 儿, 'to perceive visually, grant or have an audience with, meet'). Because 见 in courtly and social Chinese denoted formally receiving a visitor, 不见 carries both the perceptual/resultative sense 'out of sight, vanished' and the volitional social sense 'refuse to receive/meet'.

history.meaning: not to perceive; to decline to grant an audience to a visitor
refuse to meet (active verb, e.g. 闭门不见); disappear/go missing (with 了)

morphemes.meaning: to see, catch sight of, meet/receive

不见.notes: Context splits its two lively uses: without 了 before a person (谁也不见, 避而不见), it means 'refuse to see/meet anyone'—classic VIP or executive stonewalling; after an object with 了 (手机不见了), it means 'has gone missing'.

rootFamily.gloss: be there or be square ('not leave until we meet')

不许.etymology: Composed of 不 (bù, 'not') + 许 (Traditional 許, xǔ, Old Chinese *qʰˤaʔ, Middle Chinese *xjoX, semantic 言 'speech' + phonetic 午, 'to assent verbally, promise, grant permission'). Attested since Warring States narratives (where sovereigns or parents grant or withhold 许), 不许 grammaticalized into an authoritative spoken and written prohibitive verb ('forbid, not allow, you are not permitted to').

history.meaning: to refuse verbal consent, decline a request or treaty
not allowed, forbidden to (authoritative prohibition)

不许.notes: Carries personal authority—used by directors on set (不许笑场, 'no breaking character/laughing!'), bosses laying down ground rules, or playfully domineering partners (不许走, 'you're not allowed to leave'), whereas 不得 belongs to written regulations.

cognates.meaning: to bear; to owe; to fail

不负.etymology: A Classical Chinese negated verb phrase (bù fù, traditional 不負) formed from the negative adverb 不 (Middle Chinese *pjuw, 'not') modifying the transitive verb 負 (MC *bjuwX, originally depicting a person 人 bearing shells/cowries 貝 on their back, hence 'to carry on the back', extending to 'to turn one's back on, betray, fail to live up to'). Negating 'betray/fail' yields the litotes 'to not let down' or 'to prove worthy of'.

history.meaning: to carry on the back; to turn one's back on, betray, disappoint
to not betray a trust, promise, or expectation (e.g., 不負眾望)
to live up to, to do justice to (effort, youth, audience expectations)

morphemes.meaning: to turn one's back on; to betray or fail

不负.notes: Elevated, semi-literary register frequently used in media slogans, award speeches, and promotional copy, especially in four-character frames like 不负众望 ('live up to everyone's expectations') and 不负韶华 ('make the most of one's prime').

rootFamily.gloss: to let down, fail to live up to
to take responsibility, be in charge of

不走心.etymology: A modern colloquial Mandarin negated verb-object compound (bù zǒuxīn) combining the negator 不 ('not') with the verb-object compound 走心 (zǒuxīn, literally 'to pass through / engage the heart-mind'). In Classical and traditional medicine contexts, 心 (MC *sim) denoted both the physical heart and cognitive attention; in contemporary northern Mandarin and showbiz slang, 走心 came to mean investing genuine thought and emotion, so 不走心 describes perfunctory, mechanical execution.

history.meaning: to move/travel + heart-mind (seat of thought and feeling)
to take to heart; (later Beijing/northern vernacular) to be attentive and emotionally invested
half-hearted, perfunctory, phoning it in

不走心.notes: Ubiquitous in TV production and creative industries (e.g., 幕后之王) when directors or producers critique a sloppy script, distracted acting, or lazy stage design ('phoning it in'); contrasts directly with 走心 ('thoughtful, heartfelt').

不足.etymology: An ancient Classical Chinese negated stative verb compound (bùzú) composed of the negative adverb 不 (MC *pjuw, 'not') modifying 足 (MC *tsjowk, originally 'foot', extended early in Old Chinese *tsok to mean 'ample, sufficient, enough to stand on'). Attested already in pre-Qin classics such as the Analects and Laozi, the negated phrase lexicalized into both a predicate ('to be insufficient') and an abstract noun ('shortcoming, deficiency').

history.meaning: not enough, unworthy of, insufficient to (e.g., 不足為外人道)
deficiency, shortage, inadequacy
insufficient, lacking; shortcoming (noun)

不足.notes: Functions smoothly as an adjective (预算不足, 'budget is insufficient'), a noun (找出不足, 'identify shortcomings'), or before a verb in formal prose (不足为奇, 'hardly surprising').

不过.etymology: Originally a verb phrase of 不 ('not') + 过 (過, 'surpass, exceed'), meaning 'does not exceed / merely, only'. From late imperial vernacular onward, it also grammaticalized into a mild adversative conjunction ('however, but, though').

history.meaning: does not exceed; merely
only; however, but

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 不过 (via 萌典)

不还价.etymology: A vernacular Mandarin negated verb-object phrase (bù huánjià, traditional 不還價) built from 不 ('not') + 还 (huán, MC *hwaen, 'to return, give back, counter') + 价 (jià, traditional 價, MC *kaeH, 'price, value'). In traditional Chinese marketplace negotiation, the seller 'opens a price' (开价/要价) and the buyer 'returns/counters a price' (还价); negating the VO compound signals a fixed-price transaction where counter-offers are refused.

history.meaning: to make a counter-offer in commercial bargaining
no bargaining, firm price

不还价.notes: Often paired with its seller-side counterpart in the four-character retail idiom 不二价 ('one firm price') or contrasted with 讨价还价 ('haggle back and forth'); figuratively used in business negotiations for non-negotiable terms.

不错.etymology: Litotes adjective combining 不 ('not') + 错 (錯, 'wrong, mistaken, bad', originally gold/metal 钅 inlaid in cross-patterns, then 'staggered, mistaken'). Means both 'correct, quite right' and approvingly 'not bad, pretty good'.

history.meaning: not mistaken -> pretty good, quite nice

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 不错 (via 萌典)

不间断.etymology: A negated coordinative/resultative verb compound (bù jiànduàn, traditional 不間斷) formed from 不 ('not, without') and 间断 (jiànduàn). Inside 间断, 间 (Traditional 間, MC *kaenH in the verbal/intervening reading, 'to create a gap, interpose, separate') pairs coordinatively with 断 (Traditional 斷, MC *dwanH/*duanX, 'to sever, cut off, cease'). Negating 'gap and severing' yields 'uninterrupted, continuous, round-the-clock'.

history.meaning: to have intervals or breaks; to be interrupted
uninterrupted, non-stop, continuous

morphemes.meaning: to space apart, interpose a gap

不间断.notes: Note the fourth-tone pronunciation jiàn (not first-tone jiān) because 間 here means 'to leave a gap / alternate'; common in broadcast/streaming contexts such as 24小时不间断直播 ('24-hour non-stop livestream').

不难.etymology: A transparent Classical-to-Modern negated adjectival construction (bù nán, traditional 不難) combining the negator 不 (MC *pjuw, 'not') with the stative verb/adjective 难 (Traditional 難, MC *nan, 'difficult, arduous'; note the departing-tone noun reading nàn 'disaster'). Frequently used as a litotes ('not hard' = 'quite easy') before perception and cognition verbs in rhetorical exposition.

history.meaning: not difficult, easy to accomplish
not hard; easy (especially before verbs of seeing/imagining)

不难.notes: Especially idiomatic in analytical commentary right before 看出, 发现, or 想象 — e.g., 不难看出 ('it is not hard to see / one can easily tell').

不雅.etymology: A Literary Chinese negated stative compound (bùyǎ) combining 不 ('not, un-') with 雅 (MC *ngaeX, Old Chinese *N-qˤraʔ, originally associated with courtly standard speech and the Odes 雅 of the Shijing, hence 'courtly, refined, elegant, proper' as opposed to 俗 'vulgar'). Literally 'unrefined', it underwent euphemistic narrowing in modern media and legal Mandarin to mean 'indecent, unseemly, or lewd'.

history.meaning: unrefined, inelegant in literary style or deportment
improper, unseemly; (euphemistic) indecent, sexually explicit

不雅.notes: Standard media and legal euphemism in Mainland entertainment news: 不雅照 ('indecent/leaked explicit photos'), 不雅视频 ('explicit video'), and 不雅举动 ('unseemly behavior in public').

不靠谱.etymology: A northern Mandarin (originally Beijing dialect) negated verb-object compound (bù kàopǔ, traditional 不靠譜, often rhotacized as bù kàopǔr) formed from 不 ('not') + 靠 (kào, 'to lean on, stay close to, rely on') + 谱 (pǔ, traditional 譜, MC *phuX, 'register, manual, musical/operatic score, established standard'). In Peking opera and traditional craftsmanship, following the 谱 meant adhering to reliable rules; 'not leaning on the score/standard' evolved into 'unreliable, flaky, implausible'.

history.meaning: register, musical/opera score; established standard or plan
on the mark vs. off-base, unreliable (Beijing vernacular)
unreliable, flaky, sketchy (general Mandarin)

morphemes.meaning: to lean on, conform to, rely upon

不靠谱.notes: High-frequency conversational adjective applied equally to people ('flaky'), plans ('half-baked'), or rumors ('sketchy'); still slightly informal for stiff legal prose, where 不可靠 is preferred.

rootFamily.gloss: off the mark, outrageous, wildly implausible

cognates.meaning: to give, award, participate in (ataeru / yo)

与.etymology: Originally written 與 (simplified 与 from its ancient cursive/component form 𠔼), Old Chinese *laʔ (MC *yoX). In bone and bronze inscriptions it depicted two pairs of hands lifting or handing over an object together, expressing the verbal root 'to give, grant; to join with'. By classic grammaticalization in Old Chinese, the comitative verb 'to accompany / join with' bleached into a comitative preposition ('with') and nominal coordinating conjunction ('and').

history.meaning: to give, bestow; to ally or associate with
with (preposition); and (nominal conjunction)
with, and (formal/written register); to participate (yù, in 参与)

与.notes: Marks formal or written style in modern Mandarin where everyday speech uses 跟 or 和; note that like 和, 与 coordinates nouns or nominalized phrases rather than full clauses, and changes tone to yù in 参与 ('participate').

rootFamily.gloss: to get along with, interact with

与其.etymology: A Classical Chinese comparative-preferential conjunction (yǔqí, traditional 與其) fossilized from comitative/comparative 與 ('compared with, if one were to side with') plus the modal/pronominal demonstrative particle 其 (MC *gi, 'that, its; modal marker of a hypothetical alternative'). Attested in the Analects (e.g., 禮，與其奢也，寧儉 'In ritual, rather than extravagance, better frugality'), it introduces the dispreferred option before 宁可 or 不如.

history.meaning: compared with doing X [better to do Y]; rather than X…
rather than X, it is not as good as (= better to) Y
rather than (correlative conjunction paired with 不如 or 宁可)

与其.notes: Almost always requires a correlative partner in the second clause — typically 与其 A，不如 B ('rather than A, it's better to B') or 与其 A，宁可 B ('would rather B than A'); placing 与其 alone without a second clause is ungrammatical.

cognates.meaning: whether or not (yeobu, standard legal/formal term)

与否.etymology: A Literary Chinese enclitic disjunctive compound (yǔfǒu, traditional 與否) joining the conjunction 與 (MC *yoX, 'and, or') with the clausal negator 否 (MC *pjuwX, 'not so, to not be the case'). Placed immediately after a two-syllable verb or adjective (X與否, equivalent to Classical X與不X), it condenses a polar 'whether X or not' question into an abstract nominalized phrase.

history.meaning: whether [verb/adj] or not so
or not (post-verbal/post-adjectival bound marker of polar alternatives)

与否.notes: Strictly post-positional and formal/written: attach it after a disyllabic predicate like 成功与否 ('whether successful or not') or 同意与否 ('whether one agrees or not'), never at the start of a clause (unlike 是否, which precedes the verb).

专业.etymology: Compound of 专 (專, 'concentrated, specialized, exclusive') + 业 (業, 'occupation, field of study, enterprise'). Used in traditional prose for 'focusing on one's calling' and standardized in modern Chinese for an academic 'major', a specialized 'profession/trade', or the adjective 'professional'.

history.meaning: devote oneself to an occupation
academic major; specialty; professional

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 专业 (via 萌典)

专卖店.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-compound (zhuānmàidiàn, traditional 專賣店) formed from 专卖 (zhuānmài, 'exclusive/monopolized sale': adverbial 專 MC *tsywen 'exclusively, solely' + verb 賣 MC *maejH 'to sell') modifying the head noun 店 (diàn, MC *temH, 'inn, shop, retail store'). Historically, 專賣 referred to state salt/iron/tobacco monopolies (inspired by Classical 專利 and Meiji Japanese fiscal term 専売); in post-1980s commercial Mandarin, 专卖店 shifted to licensed single-brand boutiques.

history.meaning: exclusive or state-monopolized sale of regulated commodities
history.stage: Late Imperial / Early Modern Sinitic (cf. Japanese 専売)

history.meaning: authorized single-brand retail boutique or specialty shop

专卖店.notes: Refers specifically to an authorized mono-brand retail outlet (e.g., 苹果专卖店, luxury fashion boutiques) rather than a multi-brand hobby shop (which is often 专门店 or 精品店).

专家.etymology: A modifier-head compound (zhuānjiā, traditional 專家) combining 专 (Traditional 專, MC *tsywen, originally depicting a hand 寸 turning a spindle 叀, hence 'focused, concentrated, single-minded') and the agentive/school noun 家 (MC *kae, originally 'household, lineage', extended in Warring States–Han scholarship to 'master or school of learning', as in 儒家, 法家). Already attested in Han–Tang historiography for scholars mastering a single classic, it generalized in modern Mandarin to 'specialist, expert'.

history.meaning: a scholarly lineage or master specializing in a single classic or craft
professional expert, technical or academic specialist

专家.notes: Used seriously for domain authorities (行业专家, 'industry expert'), though in Mainland internet slang it is occasionally punned as 砖家 ('brick-thrower / armchair quack') to mock out-of-touch pundits.

专门.etymology: A Classical modifier-head compound (zhuānmén, traditional 專門) composed of 专 (Traditional 專, MC *tsywen, 'exclusive, single-minded') modifying 门 (Traditional 門, MC *mwon, literally 'two-leafed gate', extended in Han scholarship to 'master's gate, academic lineage, branch of learning'). In Han texts (e.g., Book of Han), 專門 meant studying under one scholarly lineage exclusively; in modern Mandarin (reinforced by Sino-Japanese 専門), it functions both as an attributive adjective ('specialized') and adverb ('specially, on purpose').

history.meaning: a single scholarly school or lineage of textual transmission
specialized, dedicated (adj.); specifically, expressly for a purpose (adv.)

专门.notes: Watch its dual syntax: before a noun (often with 的) it means 'dedicated/specialized' (专门的团队, 'a dedicated team'), while before a verb it acts as an adverb meaning 'specially / expressly' (我专门来找你, 'I came specially to see you').

世上.etymology: A noun-postposition locative compound (shìshàng) joining 世 (MC *syejH, Old Chinese *hljaps, originally 'thirty years / one generation', extended under Classical and Buddhist usage to 'the human realm, the mortal world', translating Sanskrit loka) with the localizer 上 (MC *dzyangX/*dzyangH, 'upon, in'). Together they mean 'upon the world / in human society'.

history.meaning: generation, human realm + upon/above
in the mortal world, among humankind (frequent in Tang poetry & Buddhist vernacular)
in the world, on earth

世上.notes: Unlike 世界 ('the geographical/global world'), 世上 is inherently locative and rhetorical — it needs no 在 or 里 after it and appears constantly in aphorisms like 世上无难事 ('nothing in the world is impossible').

rootFamily.gloss: human affairs, the ways of the world

世家.etymology: A Classical modifier-head compound (shìjiā) combining 世 (MC *syejH, 'generation; hereditary, from generation to generation') and 家 (MC *kae, 'clan, noble house, family'). Attested in Mencius (仲子，齊之世家也 'Zhongzi belongs to an old hereditary house of Qi') and immortalized by Sima Qian in the Shiji (史記) as the biographical category for feudal hereditary houses, it broadened to any family renowned across generations for a profession or art.

history.meaning: hereditary noble clan holding fiefs and office across generations; Shiji chronicle category
aristocratic lineage of old standing and scholarly prestige
prominent family; family renowned for a craft across generations (e.g., 音乐世家)

世家.notes: In contemporary Mandarin and entertainment bios, 世家 usually highlights multi-generational mastery of a field — e.g., 书香世家 ('scholarly family'), 音乐世家 ('family of musicians'), or 演艺世家 ('acting dynasty').

世界.etymology: Originally a Chinese Buddhist loan-translation (calque) of Sanskrit lokadhātu ('cosmos, realm of living beings'), coined during Six Dynasties sutra translations such as the Śūraṅgama Sūtra. In Buddhist cosmology, 世 (shì, 'generation, thirty-year span') denoted past, present, and future time, while 界 (jiè, 'boundary, cardinal direction') denoted east, west, north, south, above, and below—together uniting time and space into the 'universe'. By the Tang–Song period 世界 passed into everyday secular Chinese for the human world.

history.meaning: time (世) + space (界), calquing Sanskrit lokadhātu
the world; realm of human society

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 世界

业内.etymology: A modern Sino-compound locative noun (yènèi, traditional 業內) pairing 业 (Traditional 業, MC *ngjaep, originally the toothed crossboard of a bell/drum stand, extended to 'undertaking, occupation, industry' as short for 行业/产业) with the locative head 内 (Traditional 內, MC *nwojH, 'inside, within'). Modeled on compact bureaucratic and journalistic locatives, it denotes the insider sphere of a specific trade or profession.

history.meaning: occupation/undertaking + inside/within
within the industry, inside the trade/sector

morphemes.meaning: industry, profession, trade (short for 行业)

业内.notes: Staple term in media/entertainment drama dialogue (like 幕后之王): 业内人士 ('industry insiders') and 业内口碑 ('reputation within the industry'), contrasting neatly with 业外 or 圈外 ('outside the industry/circle').

业务.etymology: A coordinative Sino-compound (yèwù, traditional 業務) uniting 业 (Traditional 業, MC *ngjaep, 'occupation, enterprise, line of work') and 务 (Traditional 務, MC *mjuH, 'to devote effort to; affairs, duties, tasks'). While attested sparsely in pre-modern Chinese for scholarly or occupational pursuits, its modern corporate and institutional sense ('business operations, professional work, line of business') was standardized via Meiji Japanese 業務 (gyōmu) translating Western 'business / operational duties'.

history.meaning: occupational or scholarly affairs and duties
institutional/commercial business operations (Meiji Sino-Japanese standardization)
business operations, core services, professional competency (e.g., 业务能力)

业务.notes: False-friend alert: 业务 does NOT mean 'a company' (公司/企业); it means 'business operations, service lines, or professional skill' — in showbiz Mandarin, 业务能力强 ('strong professional chops') praises an idol's or producer's actual craft.

业绩.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-compound (yèjì, traditional 業績, variant 業蹟) combining 业 (Traditional 業, MC *ngjaep, 'undertaking, business, enterprise') with 绩 (Traditional 績, MC *tsek, originally depicting silk/hemp threads 糸 twisted together into a measurable skein, hence 'spun hemp' -> 'accumulated merit, accomplishment'). Popularized in modern East Asian corporate vocabulary alongside Japanese 業績 (gyōseki), it denotes quantifiable achievements or sales/revenue results.

history.meaning: undertaking/work + spun hemp -> accomplished merit
notable accomplishments; measurable corporate or scholarly performance results
history.stage: Early Modern East Asian / Meiji return influence

history.meaning: business performance, revenue/KPI track record, achievements

morphemes.meaning: achievement, merit, measurable result (lit. spun thread)

业绩.notes: Whereas 成绩 usually refers to school grades or general results, 业绩 specifically targets commercial KPIs, revenue targets, ratings, and career track records (冲业绩, 'push to hit sales/performance targets').

东.etymology: Simplified from 东/東 (dōng), one of the four primary cardinal directions attested since Shang-dynasty oracle-bone inscriptions. In early paleography 東 depicts a tied sack or bundle pierced by a wooden pole; the graph was borrowed very early (or reinterpreted through the rising sun behind a tree 木 + 日 in the Shuowen Jiezi tradition) to write the word for 'east', the direction of sunrise. Throughout traditional Chinese urban planning and courtyard architecture, east carries auspicious associations with spring and morning light.

history.meaning: tied bundle graph used for cardinal east
east; host (master of the eastern stair 東道主)
east (simplified form)

东方.etymology: An ancient Classical modifier-head directional compound (dōngfāng, traditional 東方) formed from 东 (Traditional 東, MC *tuwng, Old Chinese *tˤoŋ, originally a tied sack 束, borrowed phonetically or reinterpreted via the rising sun 日 behind trees 木 for 'east') modifying 方 (MC *pjang, 'direction, quarter, region'). Attested in oracle bone inscriptions and the Shijing for the eastern quarter, in modern Mandarin it also translates geopolitical/cultural 'the East / the Orient'.

history.meaning: the eastern cardinal direction or eastern borderlands
the East (directional); the Orient / Eastern civilization (contrasted with 西方)

东方.notes: Used for grand cultural, geopolitical, or brand names (东方文化 'Eastern culture', 东方卫视 'Dragon TV / Shanghai Oriental TV'), whereas everyday physical directions use 东边 or 东面 ('the east side').

东西.etymology: Everyday noun meaning 'thing, object, stuff', literally 'east and west' (东 'east' + 西 'west'). Emerged during the Tang–Song period—often linked to buying goods from the Eastern and Western Markets (东市, 西市) of imperial capitals like Chang'an, or as a directional merism encompassing 'everything from east to west'. Note that 西 moves to neutral tone (dōngxi) when meaning 'thing'.

history.meaning: commodities from east and west -> things, objects
thing; object; stuff

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 东西 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: the Chinese / land of silk (via Old Chinese *s-lə -> Seres)

丝.etymology: An ancient pictograph (sī, traditional 絲, MC *si, Old Chinese *s-lə — the ultimate etymon via Central Asian trade routes of Greek Σῆρες and English 'silk') depicting two twisted skeins of raw silk fibers (糸+糸) reeled from silkworm cocoons. Because a single raw silk filament is proverbially gossamer-thin (0.00001 chi in traditional metrology), 丝 grammaticalized into a classifier/minimizer meaning 'the tiniest shred, trace, or hint'.

history.meaning: raw reeled silk thread; stringed musical instruments
fine filament; decimal weight/length unit (one hundred-thousandth); tiny trace
silk thread, julienned strip; (classifier) the slightest trace/bit (e.g., 一丝希望)

morphemes.meaning: silk thread; fine strand; slightest trace

丝.notes: As a figurative measure word (一丝笑容 'a faint smile', 没有一丝犹豫 'without a shred of hesitation'), it lends crisp literary polish; in culinary names (土豆丝), it means 'finely julienned shreds'.

rootFamily.gloss: the slightest bit (usually in negative sentences)

丝带.etymology: Compound noun of 丝 (絲, 'silk thread', a pictograph of two twisted skeins of silk) + 带 (帶, 'belt, sash, ribbon', depicting a waistband with hanging cloths): 'silk ribbon, ribbon'.

history.meaning: silk sash or ribbon

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 丝带 (via 萌典)

丢.etymology: Colloquial verb meaning 'lose, misplace; throw, toss; leave behind'. Graphically an ideographic alteration of 去 ('go away, discard') with a top stroke, attested in medieval rhyme books and vernacular drama as a variant associated with 丟/去 ('cast away, lose').

history.meaning: toss away; lose; leave behind

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 丢 (via 萌典)

丢下.etymology: A vernacular Mandarin directional/resultative verb compound (diūxià) combining the action verb 丢 (diū, a graphic simplification/variant derived from 去 'to cast away, depart' with a top stroke 一, attested from Song–Yuan vernacular texts meaning 'to toss, drop, lose, leave') with the directional complement 下 (xià, MC *haeX, 'down; behind, remaining in place'). Together they express dropping an object or forsaking/leaving someone behind.

history.meaning: to cast aside, throw down, lose (vernacular Mandarin innovation)
to toss down; to leave behind, abandon (people or responsibilities)

丢下.notes: Commonly takes a human or duty object in emotional narratives — e.g., 丢下孩子不管 ('abandon the child and walk away') or 丢下手头的工作 ('drop the work at hand').

丢人.etymology: A colloquial northern Mandarin separable verb-object compound (diūrén, literally 'to lose [one's standing as a] person') pairing 丢 (diū, 'to lose, forfeit') with 人 (rén, MC *nyin, 'person; social personhood, public dignity'). Paralleling 丢脸 ('lose face'), it reflects traditional Chinese social ethics where public shame forfeits one's moral or social standing before peers.

history.meaning: to lose + personhood/social standing before others
to lose face, disgrace oneself; embarrassing, shameful

丢人.notes: Because 丢人 is an underlying VO (separable) compound, modifiers often split it (丢大人了 'massively embarrassed oneself', 丢死人了 'mortifying'), though it also takes degree adverbs like 真丢人 ('so embarrassing').

丢人现眼.etymology: A vivid four-character vernacular coordinative idiom (diūrén-xiànyǎn, traditional 丟人現眼) pairing two parallel verb-object clauses: 丢人 ('lose social dignity/face') + 现眼 (xiànyǎn, traditional 現眼: 現 MC *henH 'to expose, show openly' + 眼 MC *ngaenX 'eyes [of onlookers]', i.e. 'make an unsightly spectacle before people's eyes'). Attested in Qing vernacular fiction such as Dream of the Red Chamber (红楼梦), it intensifies 'lose face' into public humiliation.

history.form: 丟人現眼 / 现世报眼
history.meaning: to disgrace oneself and make an embarrassing spectacle before onlookers (Qing Beijing vernacular)
to make a fool/spectacle of oneself in public, bring utter embarrassment

丢人现眼.notes: Stronger and more scolding than 丢人 or 丢脸 alone — frequently heard in heated workplace or family arguments: 别在这儿丢人现眼了！ ('Stop making a fool of yourself right here!').

rootFamily.gloss: to make a fool of oneself (Beijing colloquial)
to make a fool of oneself in public (idiom)

丢掉.etymology: A resultative verb compound (diūdiào) formed from the vernacular verb 丢 (diū, 'to throw, lose') plus the phase/resultative complement 掉 (diào, MC *dewk, originally 'to shake, wag', shifting in Tang–Song vernacular to 'to fall off' and grammaticalizing into a productive completive/disposal marker 'away, off'). Depending on volition, it means either intentionally 'throwing away' or unintentionally 'losing/forfeiting'.

history.meaning: to cast/lose + to fall off / away (disposal complement)
to throw away, discard; to lose or forfeit (a job, life, opportunity)

丢掉.notes: Context disambiguates volition: 丢掉垃圾 means 'throw away trash' (intentional), whereas 丢掉工作 ('lose one's job') or 丢掉冠军 ('forfeit the championship') is involuntary loss.

两.etymology: Word for 'two' used before measure words and paired nouns (两个房间 'two rooms', 两把钥匙 'two keys'). In Classical Chinese, 兩 denoted a matched pair (such as two chariot wheels) and a unit of weight, explaining why Mandarin prefers 两 when counting concrete items with classifiers while keeping 二 for abstract counting and ordinals.

history.meaning: pair; both; two

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 兩 (via 萌典)

两个.etymology: A numeral-classifier phrase (liǎng gè, traditional 兩個) combining 两 (Traditional 兩, MC *ljangX, originally depicting a paired chariot yoke or balanced scale weights, hence 'a natural pair, both', which gradually supplanted 二 before classifiers in Middle-to-Early-Mandarin) and the general classifier 个 (Traditional 個/箇, MC *kaH, originally a single stalk of bamboo 竹, bleached into the default individualizing measure word).

history.meaning: a pair/couple + individual bamboo tally or item
two (general count before nouns or standalone pronominal 'two of them')
two (standard numeral + general classifier phrase)

两个.notes: Fundamental Mandarin rule: count abstract digits with 二 (一、二、三), but before 个 and almost all measure words use 两 (两个, never *二个 in standard Mandarin); in fast northern speech 两个 fuses into the single character 俩 (liǎ).

rootFamily.gloss: two (colloquial contraction of 两个, never followed by 个)

两千.etymology: A multiplicative-decimal numeral compound (liǎngqiān, traditional 兩千) combining 两 (Traditional 兩, MC *ljangX, 'two, pair') with the decimal base 千 (MC *tshen, Old Chinese *s.n̥ˤiŋ, an oracle-bone phonosemantic graph built on 人 'person' with a stroke 一 marking a thousand). Whereas Classical Chinese exclusively used 二千, Mandarin generalized 两 before large decimal bases (千, 万, 亿).

history.meaning: two thousand (standard Classical numeral compound)
two thousand (Mandarin numeral phrase alongside 二千)

两千.notes: In spoken Mandarin, 两千 is strongly preferred over 二千 when standing alone (e.g., 两千块钱 '2,000 yuan'), whereas 二 is required inside multi-digit sequences like 一万二千 ('12,000') in stricter normative usage (though 一万两千 is also widely heard).

rootFamily.gloss: by all means;千萬 + negator = never

两千多万.etymology: A complex Mandarin approximative numeral phrase (liǎngqiān duō wàn, traditional 兩千多萬) structured around the Sinitic myriad-based (10⁴) counting system: [两千 ('2,000') + 多 (MC *ta, 'more than, in excess of', approximative infix)] × 万 (Traditional 萬, MC *mjonH, originally a scorpion graph borrowed phonetically in Shang inscriptions for 'ten thousand / myriad'). Because Chinese groups large numbers in powers of 10,000 rather than 1,000, '2,000-plus myriads' equals 'over 20,000,000 (twenty million)'.

history.meaning: twenty million in the Sinitic myriad-based place system
over twenty million (approximative spoken/written Mandarin numeral)

两千多万.notes: Classic English-to-Chinese mental math trap: convert 'million' by shifting the comma one place — 1百万 = 1M, 1千万 = 10M, so 两千多万 is 'over 20 million' (common in TV production budgets, box office, and view counts), NOT 'two thousand and ten thousand'!

rootFamily.gloss: tens of millions; by all means

两口子.etymology: A colloquial northern Mandarin nominal compound (liǎngkǒuzi, traditional 兩口子, with neutral-tone 子 zi) formed from 两 ('two') + 口 (kǒu, MC *khuwX, literally 'mouth', used since Classical census records such as 戶口 and 人口 as a synecdochic classifier for 'mouths to feed / household members') + the diminutive nominalizing suffix 子 (-zi). Literally 'a household of two mouths', it lexicalized specifically into 'husband and wife, married couple'.

history.meaning: mouth -> individual household member to be fed (e.g., 百口之家)
a household of two; husband and wife (Ming–Qing northern vernacular)
married couple, husband and wife (warm, colloquial register)

两口子.notes: Warm, folksy conversational noun (e.g., 小两口 'the young married couple'); never use it for unmarried dating partners (情侣) or on formal legal forms (which use 夫妻).

两次.etymology: A numeral + verbal-classifier phrase (liǎng cì, traditional 兩次) combining 两 ('two') with 次 (cì, MC *tshijH, originally depicting halting and resting in camp order along a march, hence 'halting place -> sequence, rank, turn', which grammaticalized in Middle and Early Mandarin into the default verbal classifier for occurrences or occasions). Together they express 'two times, twice'.

history.meaning: encampment, halting station; sequential order, rank
time, occurrence, occasion (replacing or complementing 番/回/遍)
twice, on two occasions

两次.notes: Distinguish 两次 ('twice / two separate instances', e.g. 去了两次 'went twice') from 两遍 ('two complete run-throughs from start to finish', e.g. 剧本改了两遍 'revised the script all the way through twice').

rootFamily.gloss: repeatedly, time and again (idiomatic: 'one time, two times')
rootFamily.word: 三番两次 / 一次两次

两边.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正结构) formed from 两 (trad. 兩, Middle Chinese *ljangX*, originally a dual measure for paired chariot wheels or textiles, hence 'both, a pair') modifying 边 (trad. 邊, MC *pen*, 'margin, border, side'). Attested from Six Dynasties and Tang-Song vernacular literature onward, the spatial sense 'both sides of a boundary or road' broadened naturally into social and institutional 'both factions, the two opposing camps'.

history.meaning: both edges, banks, or physical sides of a space
both physical sides; both parties or camps in a dispute or negotiation

两边.notes: Unlike 双方 (shuāngfāng), which belongs to formal legal or diplomatic register, 两边 is conversational and versatile—equally natural for physical staging ('both sides of the studio') and rival teams or agencies ('appeasing both camps', 两边讨好).

rootFamily.gloss: one side; at the same time

严格.etymology: Originally a Literary Chinese modifier-head or coordinative compound combining 严 (trad. 嚴, MC *ngjaem*, 'stern, solemn,urgent') with 格 (MC *kaek*, 'wooden lattice, standard, rule, moral bearing'). While sporadically attested in late Imperial Chinese prose for austere deportment or strict regulations, its modern adjectival vitality as 'rigorous, strictly adhering to standards' was strongly reinforced in the late 19th century by Meiji Japanese 厳格 (*genkaku*), used to render European notions of methodological and institutional rigor.

history.meaning: austere demeanor; strict adherence to set rules or standards
strict, rigorous, exact (translating Western scientific and institutional rigor)
strict, rigorous, exacting (of rules, demands, or standards)

严格.notes: Carries a neutral-to-positive evaluation implying high standards and professionalism (e.g., 严格把关, 'strictly vet quality' in TV post-production), contrasting with 严苛, which implies excessive harshness.

严禁.etymology: Legal and administrative verb compound from 严 (simplified from 嚴, 'strict; stern; urgent') + 禁 ('forbid; prohibit; taboo', forest 林 over altar 示). Used in imperial edicts and magistrate proclamations since the Han and Tang dynasties, it remains the standard formal heading on public prohibition signs.

history.meaning: strictly prohibit by official decree
strictly forbid; strictly prohibited

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 严禁

严苛.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative compound (联合结构) pairing two near-synonymous adjectival roots: 严 (trad. 嚴, MC *ngjaem*, 'stern, severe, relentless') and 苛 (MC *kha*, originally 'tiny grass/weed' under the grass radical 艹, extended in Old Chinese to 'petty, nitpicking, oppressive, draconian', famously in *Liji*'s 苛政猛于虎 'oppressive governance is fiercer than a tiger'). Together they intensify the sense of unforgiving, nitpicking severity.

history.meaning: oppressive and draconian (especially of penal laws, taxation, or governance)
harsh, exacting, unforgivingly severe (of conditions, critiques, or bosses)

严苛.notes: Slightly more literary than 严格 and distinctly more critical in tone: calling a producer's standards 严苛 emphasizes how grueling, nitpicking, or nearly unreasonable they feel to subordinates.

rootFamily.gloss: demand excessively, ask too much of

严重.etymology: Compound adjective of 严 (嚴, 'strict, stern, urgent') + 重 ('heavy, weighty, grave'). In Classical Chinese (e.g., Shiji, Hanshu), 嚴重 described dignified, stern gravity or strict laws; in modern Mandarin it means 'serious, grave, severe, critical'.

history.meaning: stern and weighty; dignified
serious; severe; critical

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 严重 (via 萌典)

个.etymology: Mandarin's default general measure word (classifier) placed between a number or demonstrative and a noun (一个人, 这个房间). Originally counting stalks of bamboo (written 箇 with the bamboo radical 竹, or 個 with 亻 in Classical texts like Xunzi and Shiji), it broadened by the Six Dynasties and Tang period into a universal classifier.

morphemes.meaning: bamboo stalk / single unit -> general classifier

history.meaning: counter for bamboo shafts, arrows, individual items
general measure word

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 個 (via 萌典)

个人.etymology: Compound of 个 (個, 'single, individual') + 人 ('person'), meaning 'individual, personal' (as opposed to collective 集体 or public 公共). Widely popularized in late 19th- and early 20th-century modern prose alongside Japanese 個人 (kojin).

history.meaning: an individual person; personal

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 个人 (via 萌典)

个人简历.etymology: A modern four-character modifier-head nominal phrase (偏正短语) composed of 个人 (trad. 個人, 'individual', a Meiji Japanese *wasei-kango* return loan 個人 *kojin* translating English *individual*) modifying 简历 (trad. 簡歷, itself a modifier-head compound from 简 'bamboo slip; brief, concise' + 历 'to pass through, chronological experience', abridged from 履历 'biographical record'). Coined in 20th-century bureaucratic and HR Chinese for a concise biographical summary.

history.meaning: concise chronological summary of official posts and background

history.form: 个人简历 / 個人簡歷
history.meaning: personal résumé, curriculum vitae

个人简历.notes: In everyday office and entertainment-industry hiring, 简历 is usually sufficient on its own (投简历, 'submit a résumé'); adding 个人 appears on formal application headers, talent profiles, and press kits.

个子.etymology: Colloquial noun meaning 'height, stature, build of a person', formed from 个 (個, 'single unit, body frame') + nominal suffix 子 (neutral tone zi).

history.meaning: bodily stature; height

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 个子 (via 萌典)

个性.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-compound (偏正结构) combining 个 (trad. 個, MC *kaH*, originally a tally for bamboo stalks, hence 'single, individual') with 性 (MC *sjengH*, from 心 'heart-mind' + 生 'birth/growth', meaning 'inborn nature, disposition'). Coined in Meiji Japan as 個性 (*kosei*) by scholars such as Inoue Tetsujirō to translate Western philosophical and psychological *individuality*, then borrowed into late Qing and May Fourth Mandarin.

history.meaning: individuality, specific properties distinguishing an individual entity
individuality, distinctive personality, flair

个性.notes: Unlike 性格 (neutral 'personality/temperament'), 个性 highlights distinctiveness or edge: praising a singer or show with 很有个性 means 'has real attitude/distinctive style', though in workplace contexts it can euphemize stubbornness.

个案.etymology: A modern modifier-head nominal compound (偏正结构) joining 个 (trad. 個, 'single, individual, particular') with 案 (MC *'anH*, originally a short-legged wooden tray or magistrate's desk, metonymically extended in Han–Tang bureaucratic Chinese to the official dossier laid upon the desk, hence 'legal or administrative case'). Developed in modern legal, sociological, and managerial Mandarin to render 'individual case' or 'isolated incident'.

history.meaning: wooden writing desk; official dossier or legal case on the magistrate's desk
individual case (in social work/law); isolated incident, exception

个案.notes: In Mainland PR and corporate crisis management, 只是个案 ('merely an isolated case') is a classic damage-control formula used to deny systemic failure; in Taiwan and Hong Kong, 个案 also commonly translates 'case study' or 'client case'.

丫头.etymology: A vernacular metonymic compound (偏正/后缀结构) combining 丫 (MC *'ae*, pictographic of a fork or bifurcated branch, used for the twin forked hair-buns worn by unmarried girls in premodern China) + 头 (trad. 頭, MC *duw*, 'head', reduced in Mandarin to neutral-tone `-tou`). First attested in Tang poetry (e.g., Liu Yuxi referring to a young attendant's twin hair-coils), it shifted in Song–Qing vernacular to 'maidservant' and simultaneously to an affectionate address for a young girl.

history.meaning: fork-bunned head: a child or young girl wearing twin hair coils
female bondservant, household maidservant
girl, lass (affectionate, teasing, or mildly patronizing address by elders/seniors)

morphemes.meaning: forked shape; twin hair-buns of a girl
head (bleached to nominal suffix in neutral tone)

丫头.notes: Always pronounced with a neutral second syllable (yātou). In modern dramas, mentors, parents, or romantic leads use 小丫头 or 傻丫头 affectionately or teasingly; used by a stranger or peer in a professional setting, however, it can sound condescending.

中.etymology: Ancient graph attested on Shang oracle bones—showing a vertical flagpole or tally passing through the center of a drum or ring—meaning 'center, middle, inside, among; China (中国)' (read zhōng) and 'hit the target, be affected by' (read zhòng).

morphemes.meaning: pole through the center = middle, inside

history.meaning: center; middle; inside; hit the mark

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 中 (via 萌典)

中伤.etymology: A Classical Chinese resultative/serial-verb compound formed from 中 in its departing-tone verbal reading *zhòng* (MC *trjuwngH*, Old Chinese *truŋ-s*, 'to hit the target with an arrow, strike home') + 伤 (trad. 傷, MC *syang*, 'to wound, injure'). Attested in *Lüshi Chunqiu*, *Shiji*, and *Han Shu* originally for striking and wounding (or poisoning) a victim, and already in Han political prose metaphorized as 'striking covertly with slander to ruin someone's standing'.

history.meaning: to hit the mark and inflict a wound; to strike covertly with malicious slander
to slander, malign, defame maliciously behind someone's back

中伤.notes: Watch the tone and homophone trap: 中伤 is zhòngshāng (4th tone on 中, 'malign/slander', often in 恶意中伤), whereas 重伤 is also zhòngshāng ('seriously wound/severe injury'). Never pronounce it *zhōngshāng.

中午.etymology: Temporal noun combining 中 ('middle, exact center') + 午 ('noon, the midday Earthly Branch 11 a.m.–1 p.m.'): 'midday, noon'.

history.meaning: high noon; midday

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 中午 (via 萌典)

中央.etymology: Compound noun of 中 ('center, middle') + 央 ('center, midpoint', showing a person 大 standing in the middle of a frame 冂). Attested in the Shijing (Book of Odes: 宛在水中央 'right in the middle of the water') for the physical center, and used in modern Chinese both spatially ('center') and politically ('central authorities').

history.meaning: the very center; middle
center; central leadership

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 中央 (via 萌典)

中心.etymology: A Classical Chinese modifier-head compound (偏正结构) combining level-tone 中 (*zhōng*, MC *trjuwng*, pictograph of a banner-pole piercing the middle of a drum or target ring, 'middle, interior') + 心 (MC *sim*, 'heart, mind, core'). In Warring States texts (*Zhuangzi*, *Xunzi*, *Classic of Poetry* commentary) 中心 meant 'deep within one's heart/mind'; later spatialized—and reinforced by modern scientific/urban Japanese 中心 (*chūshin*)—to mean geometric, institutional, or thematic 'center, hub'.

history.meaning: the inner heart; deep within one's mind or feelings
spatial, geometric, institutional, or thematic center / hub

中心.notes: Distinguish 中心 ('center/hub', e.g., 制作中心 'production center', 以观众为中心 'audience-centric') from exact homophone 重心 (zhòngxīn, 'center of gravity, strategic priority') and 衷心 (zhōngxīn, 'wholehearted, sincere').

中控室.etymology: A 20th-century technical acronymic modifier-head compound (缩略偏正词) compressed from 中央控制室 ('central control room'): 中 ('central, master', from 中央) + 控 (MC *khuwngH*, originally 'to draw a bow or pull reins to check a horse', modernized in 控制 'to control, regulate') + head noun 室 (MC *syit*, 'chamber, room'). Standard engineering and broadcast-television terminology for a TV network's master control room (MCR).

history.meaning: central control room (industrial, military, and broadcast engineering)
master control room (MCR) in broadcasting, stage tech, or building security

中控室.notes: In Chinese TV production (as seen in *Behind the Scenes*), distinguish 中控室 (MCR, which routes final network feeds on-air) from 导播室 / 导播间 (the studio/gallery control room where the technical director switches live cameras).

cognates.meaning: advertisement, public notice (shared root of 广告)

中插广告.etymology: A contemporary Chinese broadcast and streaming-media compound (偏正结构) pairing the modifier 中插 ('inserted midway', itself adverbial modifier 中 'mid-program, in the middle' + verb 插 MC *tshreap* 'to pierce, insert, interpose') with head noun 广告 (trad. 廣告, 'advertisement', popularized via Meiji Japanese 広告 *kōkoku* from 广 'wide, broad' + 告 'announce, proclaim'). Coined in the 2010s Chinese online-video boom for mid-roll or native cast-acted mini-commercials embedded inside drama episodes.

history.meaning: interstitial commercial break slotted into radio or television programming

history.form: 中插广告 / 中插廣告
history.meaning: mid-roll embedded commercial or native mini-skit ad mid-episode

中插广告.notes: Industry jargon often shortened to 中插: in Chinese web dramas and variety shows, Creative Mid-Rolls (创意中插) feature supporting actors staying in-costume for a 30-second comedic ad mid-episode, commanding higher ad rates than standard pre-roll贴片广告.

中文.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正结构) abbreviated from 中国文字 / 中国语文, combining 中 ('China / Central States', from 中国) with 文 (MC *mjun*, originally an oracle-bone pictograph of a standing figure with chest markings/tattoos, evolving through 'pattern, ornament' to 'written graphs, literary text, language'). Consolidated in late Qing and 20th-century international contact to name Chinese in parallel with 英文, 法文, etc.

history.meaning: written script, literary Chinese text (contrasted with non-Sinitic scripts)
written and spoken Chinese language as a whole

中文.notes: While strict linguists sometimes distinguish 中文 (originally skewing toward written Chinese) from 汉语 (spoken Sinitic/Mandarin), in everyday usage 中文 seamlessly covers both reading/writing and speaking ('Do you speak Chinese?' = 你会说中文吗？).

中毒.etymology: A Classical Chinese verb-object compound (动宾结构) formed from departing-tone 中 (*zhòng*, MC *trjuwngH*, 'to be struck by, contract, suffer an affliction') + 毒 (MC *dowk*, 'poison, venom, noxious substance'). Attested in early philosophical and medical texts (*Lunheng*, *Zhouhou Beiji Fang*) for ingesting or being struck by poison; in contemporary internet and showbiz slang (reinforced by Japanese 中毒 *chūdoku* 'addiction'), figuratively extended to 'hopelessly hooked on a show, song, or idol'.

history.meaning: to be struck or afflicted by poison or venomous miasma
medical poisoning; (slang) to be addicted to or obsessed with media/trends

中毒.notes: Pronounced zhòngdú (4th tone on 中), and grammatically a separable verb-object word (离合词): 'deeply poisoned / obsessed' inserts modifiers inside, e.g., 中了这部剧的毒 or 中毒太深 ('hooked way too deep').

中英文.etymology: A coordinate-modifier + head compound (联合定语偏正词) compressed from 中文与英文: 中 ('Chinese', clipping of 中国) + 英 ('English/British', clipped phonetic loan from 英吉利 *Yīngjílì* 'England', originally written to transcribe *Eng-g-li*) + shared head 文 ('written script, language'). Standard modern shorthand in bilingual contracts, subtitles, and international media production.

history.meaning: English script and language (late Qing treaty-port usage)
Chinese and English languages; bilingual Chinese-English text or speech

中英文.notes: Very common in media localization and entertainment contracts: 中英文字幕 ('bilingual Chinese-English subtitles') and 中英文双语主持 ('bilingual Mandarin-English emceeing').

中间.etymology: Spatial and relational noun combining 中 ('middle, center') + 间 (間, 'space between, interval', originally moonlight 月 shining through double doors 門): 'in the middle, between, among'.

history.meaning: the space in the middle; between

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 中间 (via 萌典)

丰富.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative compound (联合结构) uniting two synonymous morphemes of ritual and material plenty: 丰 (trad. 豐, MC *phjuwng*, oracle-bone pictograph of luxuriant grain or jade offerings heaped inside a ritual vessel 豆, hence 'lush, bumper, bountiful') + 富 (MC *pjuwH*, roof 宀 over a full wine-jar 畐, 'wealthy, amply stocked'). Attested together since the Han dynasty (*Lunheng*, *Sanguozhi*) for material abundance, and used both adjectivally ('rich, varied') and causatively ('to enrich').

history.meaning: materially plentiful, bountiful in harvests or wealth
rich, abundant, varied (of content/experience); transitive: to enrich

morphemes.meaning: bountiful, lush (trad. 豐, full ritual vessel)
wealthy, abundant (full jar under a roof)

丰富.notes: Note that simplified 丰 merges two distinct historical characters: 丰 ('graceful, lush vegetation') and 豐 ('abundant ritual vessel'—the etymon here). 丰富 describes intangible richness (经验丰富 'rich experience', 内容丰富 'rich content'), never personal financial wealth (use 富有 or 有钱).

丰盛.etymology: Coordinative adjective compound of 丰 (豐, 'abundant, lush', originally a ceremonial vessel 豆 heaped full of jade or grain 丰) + 盛 ('full, flourishing, plentiful', grain mounded in a dish 皿). Describes a lavish, sumptuous meal or rich abundance.

history.meaning: abundant and full; lavish, sumptuous (especially of food)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 丰盛 (via 萌典)

串.etymology: An iconic pictographic character (象形/指事字; MC *tsyhwenH*, Old Chinese *kʰˤron-s*, closely related to 贯 *kˤron-s* 'pierce through cowries') depicting two rectangular objects—originally cowrie shells, jade plaques, or pieces of meat—impaled on a single vertical rod or cord. From its primary verbal sense 'to skewer, string together in sequence', it grammaticalized in medieval vernacular Chinese into a measure word (classifier) for anything clustered, strung, or cascading in a row.

history.meaning: to pierce through and string objects together; habitual familiarity
classifier for strung items (beads, coins, keys, grapes) and sequential clusters

morphemes.meaning: skewer, string together; classifier for strung or clustered items

串.notes: As a classifier, 一串 covers physical clusters (一串钥匙 'a bunch of keys', 一串葡萄 'a cluster of grapes') and abstract sequences (一串数字 'a string of numbers', 一连串问题 'a cascade of problems'); in showbiz, 串场 means 'linking segments onstage as an emcee' and 客串 means 'make a cameo appearance'.

串通.etymology: A verbal compound combining 串 (MC *tsyhwenH*, 'to string together, link up across boundaries') with resultative/coordinative 通 (MC *thuwng*, 'to pass all the way through, communicate covertly'). Crystallized in Yuan–Ming legal memorials and vernacular fiction (*Water Margin*, *Jin Ping Mei*) to describe clerks, witnesses, or bandits secretly linking their stories or plots behind closed doors—hence 'to collude, conspire'.

history.meaning: to connect covertly across parties (esp. corrupt officials, litigants, or bandits)
to collude, conspire, act in secret cahoots

串通.notes: Strongly derogatory—never use 串通 for legitimate teamwork or coordination (use 沟通 or 配合). Frequently appears in the four-character idiom 串通一气 ('collude as one clique / be in cahoots') in corporate intrigue dramas.

为.etymology: Ancient character (為) whose oracle-bone graph showed a hand leading an elephant (象) to perform work, yielding 'do, make, act as, become' (read wéi) and the benefactive/purposive preposition 'for, for the sake of, because of' (read wèi).

history.meaning: do, make, act as (wéi); for the sake of, because of (wèi)
for; to; act as

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 为 (via 萌典)

为了.etymology: Purposive preposition meaning 'in order to, for the sake of', formed in vernacular Mandarin by reinforcing the preposition 为 (wèi, 'for') with the completive/emplacing suffix 了 (le).

history.meaning: for the purpose of; in order to

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 为了 (via 萌典)

为什么.etymology: Interrogative adverb meaning 'why?, for what reason?', combining 为 (wèi, 'for, on account of') + 什么 ('what?').

history.meaning: for what -> why

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 为什么 (via 萌典)

为此.etymology: A lexicalized Classical Chinese prepositional phrase (介宾结构) joining departing-tone 为 (trad. 為, *wèi*, MC *hjweH*, 'on behalf of, for the sake of, because of'—derived by tonal derivation from level-tone *wéi* 'do, act') with the proximal demonstrative pronoun 此 (MC *tshjeX*, 'this, this matter'). Used continuously from Pre-Qin prose into modern formal Mandarin as a discourse connector meaning 'for this purpose' or 'on account of this'.

history.meaning: for this reason; for the sake of this matter (preposition + demonstrative)
to this end, for this reason, over this (clause-initial or pre-verbal adverbial)

morphemes.meaning: for the sake of, because of (wèi)

为此.notes: Always read wèicǐ (4th tone on 为). A crisp formal cohesive device in news scripts, press releases, and polished dialogue (e.g., 他为此付出了很多, 'He paid a heavy price for this'), replacing wordier spoken phrases like 为了这件事.

rootFamily.gloss: in order to, for the sake of

cognates.meaning: feel awkward; make things hard for

为难.etymology: Originated in Classical Chinese as a copular-predicate sequence (动宾/系表结构): level-tone 为 (trad. 為, *wéi*, MC *hjwe*, originally an oracle-bone graph of a hand leading an elephant, 'to do, make, constitute, deem') + 难 (trad. 難, MC *nan*, 'difficult, arduous'), literally 'to be difficult' (e.g., *Mencius*, *Analects* 为之难). By Tang–Song vernacular, it split into two enduring senses: psych-adjective 'feeling put in an awkward bind' and causative verb 'deliberately making things hard for someone'.

history.meaning: to constitute a difficulty; to be hard to accomplish
to feel caught in a dilemma; to give someone a hard time
feel embarrassed/put on the spot; make things difficult for someone

为难.notes: Always read wéinán (both 2nd tone). Notice its dual syntax: 让我很为难 ('puts me in a really tight spot', stative) vs. 别为难实习生 ('don't give the intern a hard time', transitive verb)—a staple line in workplace dramas.

rootFamily.gloss: put someone on the spot / harass
dilemma, caught between two hard choices
feel embarrassed / sorry to trouble you

为首.etymology: A Classical Chinese copular verb-object compound (动宾结构) pairing level-tone 为 (trad. 為, *wéi*, MC *hjwe*, 'to act as, serve as, stand as') with 首 (MC *syuwX*, oracle-bone pictograph of a horned/haired head, hence 'head, chief, ringleader'). Attested across early historiography (*Zuo Zhuan*, *Shiji*) in constructions naming the foremost figure of an alliance, faction, or rebellion.

history.meaning: to stand at the head; to serve as chief or ringleader
headed by, led by (almost always framed as 以…为首)

为首.notes: Pronounced wéishǒu (2nd tone on 为). In modern Mandarin it rarely stands alone as a bare predicate; learn the fixed frame 以 [person/entity] 为首的 [group] ('the group/clique headed by X'), neutral for teams/delegations or critical for rival cliques.

主业.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正结构) combining 主 (MC *tsyuX*, originally a pictograph of a lamp stand with a burning wick flame—later written 炷—extended in Old Chinese to 'host, master, principal, primary') with 业 (trad. 業, MC *ngjaep*, originally the notched horizontal crossbar of a bell/drum rack, extended to 'patrimony, enterprise, profession'). Reinforced in modern East Asian economics alongside Japanese 主業 (*shugyō*) in opposition to 副业 ('side business').

history.meaning: ancestral estate, primary livelihood (traditionally agriculture in Imperial China)
core business (of a company); primary profession or day job (of an individual)

主业.notes: Used both at corporate scale (聚焦主业, 'refocus on core business' when a media group trims side ventures) and jokingly about multi-hyphenate celebrities or staff (主业是歌手，副业是段子手, 'singer by main trade, comedian on the side').

主人.etymology: Compound of 主 ('host, master, owner', originally a lamp wick flame 丶 rising above a stand 王) + 人 ('person'). Attested in Classical Chinese (Zuozhuan, Mencius) for a host receiving guests or a household head; today means 'host, owner, master'.

history.meaning: host (vis-à-vis guest); household master; owner

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 主人 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: person in charge, chief, senior supervisor

主任.etymology: A compound of 主 ('preside over, principal') + 任 (MC *nyimH*, 'burden carried on a shoulder-pole; official charge, post, responsibility'). In Classical Chinese (*Hanfeizi*, *Hanshu*), 主任 appeared verbally/nominally as 'bearing principal responsibility' or 'chief duty'; during Meiji administrative modernization, Japanese institutionalized 主任 (*shunin*) as a bureaucratic rank, which late Qing and Republican reforms re-adopted across Chinese government, schools, hospitals, and broadcast bureaus as 'director / department head'.

history.meaning: to hold principal responsibility; chief official trust
designated official in charge of an administrative section
director, head of a department, office, or homeroom (title and form of address)

主任.notes: Spanning huge prestige differences depending on the institution—from a school homeroom teacher (班主任) or TV programming office head (编播部主任) all the way up to ministerial-level commission chairs—and routinely used directly after a surname as polite address (王主任).

rootFamily.gloss: serve as, hold the post of

cognates.meaning: venue, assembly hall (shared sub-compound 会場)

主会场.etymology: A three-morpheme modifier-head compound (偏正结构) prefixing 主 ('main, primary') onto 会场 (trad. 會場, 'assembly or event venue', itself a modern Sino-Japanese reinforced compound 会場 *kaijō* from 会 'gather, assembly' + 场 'leveled open ground, stage, arena'). Developed in 20th-century conference organization and popularized nationwide by multi-city live television galas such as the CCTV Spring Festival Gala.

history.meaning: meeting hall, convention site, event venue
main venue or flagship stage (contrasted with satellite sub-venues)

主会场.notes: Essential live-event and broadcast production vocabulary: major televised concerts, New Year countdowns, and award shows link a flagship 主会场 with regional satellite stages called 分会场 (fēnhuìchǎng).

主动.etymology: A modifier-head / verb-compound Sino-Japanese return loan (和制汉语回归词): coined in Meiji Japan as 主動 (*shudō*) from 主 ('self-governing, principal, agent') + 动 (trad. 動, MC *duwngX*, 'move, act') to translate Western mechanical ('driving gear'), grammatical ('active voice'), and philosophical ('autonomous agency') *active*, symmetrically paired with 受動/被動 (*passive*). Borrowed into early 20th-century Mandarin and deeply popularized through modern strategic and everyday speech.

history.meaning: active, self-moving, driving (vs. passive/driven in philosophy, grammar, mechanics)
proactive, on one's own initiative (adj./adv.); the upper hand or initiative (noun)

主动.notes: Works effortlessly as an adjective (他很主动, 'he's very proactive/makes the first move'), an adverb directly before verbs (主动承认, 'voluntarily admit'; 主动联系, 'reach out first'), and a noun in 掌握主动权 ('hold the initiative'). Its exact antonym is 被动 ('passive / backed into a corner').

rootFamily.gloss: passive; forced onto the back foot

cognates.meaning: sortie, sally forth to attack (shared sub-compound 出撃)
sortie, launch an attack (shared sub-compound 출격)
