主动出击.etymology: A modern four-character adverbial-head verbal phrase (偏正四字格) pairing 主动 (trad. 主動, 'on one's own initiative, proactively') with the serial-verb military compound 出击 (trad. 出擊, from 出 'go out from fortifications, sally forth' + 击 MC *kek* 'strike, attack', attested in classical warfare and reinforced by modern military 出撃). Metaphorized across business competition, PR, and romance for seizing the offensive rather than waiting passively.

history.meaning: to sally forth from defensive positions and strike the enemy

history.form: 主动出击 / 主動出擊
history.meaning: to take the offensive; proactively make one's move in business, PR, or negotiation

主动出击.notes: A favorite boardroom, talent-management, and PR crisis phrase contrasting with 坐以待毙 ('sit waiting for doom') or 被动挨打 ('passively take hits'): e.g., pitching a bold new show format before rivals corner the market.

主厨.etymology: Modern culinary compound of 主 ('host; master; chief', originally a lamp wick flame above a stand) + 厨 ('kitchen; cook', shelter radical 广 + phonetic 尌 shù). Modeled on traditional kitchen brigade titles, it designates the head or executive chef directing a restaurant or bakery kitchen.

history.meaning: kitchen; cookhouse
head chef; executive chef

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 主厨

主张.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative compound (联合结构) uniting 主 ('preside over, direct, hold fast') + 张 (trad. 張, MC *trjang*, 'draw a bowstring taut, stretch out, deploy, set forth'). First famously attested in *Zhuangzi* (〈天运〉: 孰主张是, 'Who directs and stretches forth these cosmic motions?'), it shifted in Song–Ming vernacular to 'make the decision / back someone up' (做主), and in late Qing–modern Mandarin—reshaped by Meiji Japanese 主張 (*shuchō*)—acquired its modern legal and discursive sense 'to advocate, assert, claim (a right)'.

history.meaning: to govern, direct, and set in motion (of cosmic or political forces)
to decide a matter; fixed resolve or backing (cf. 自主张)
to advocate, maintain a position, assert/claim legal rights; a proposition or stance
history.stage: Modern Mandarin (reinforced via Meiji Japanese shuchō)

主张.notes: Note two distinct registers: in IP/entertainment law and formal debate, 主张权利 means 'assert/claim one's legal rights'; meanwhile, the older vernacular sense survives intact in 擅自做主张 or 自作主张 ('act presumptuously on one's own authority without asking the boss').

rootFamily.gloss: act on one's own authority without permission
take charge, make the call for someone

主意.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正结构) from 主 ('ruling, principal, settled') + 意 (MC *'iH*, from 音 'sound/voice' over 心 'heart', 'thought, intention, mind'). In Han–Tang prose (*Book of Later Han*, Tang memorials), *zhǔyì* (full fourth tone on 意) meant 'one's governing intention or settled resolve'. In Ming–Qing Northern Mandarin vernacular (*Dream of the Red Chamber*), the second syllable weakened to neutral tone (*zhǔyi*) as the meaning concretized to 'clever plan, idea, course of action'.

history.meaning: governing intention, inner resolve, fixed mind
plan, idea, brainstorm, counsel on what to do

主意.notes: Crucial pronunciation trap for learners: 主意 ('idea, plan') is zhǔyi (3rd tone + neutral tone), NEVER zhǔyì, which sounds like 主义 ('-ism, ideology', e.g., 现实主义). Classic collocations: 出主意 ('come up with ideas'), 拿主意 ('make up one's mind'), 打…的主意 ('have designs on / scheme to get').

cognates.meaning: abbot of a Buddhist temple; presiding over

主持.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative verbal compound (联合结构) pairing 主 ('preside over, take charge') + 持 (MC *drji*, from 手 'hand' + 寺 phonetic, 'grasp firmly, uphold, maintain'). Attested in *Shiji* and *Book of Jin* for managing state or household affairs, it was adopted in medieval Chinese Buddhism (interchanging with 住持) for the abbot who 'upholds the Dharma and presides over a monastery', and in 20th-century civic and broadcast Mandarin extended to chairing meetings, directing projects, and hosting radio/TV shows.

history.meaning: to take charge of and maintain state, military, or household affairs
abbot presiding over a Buddhist monastery and upholding the Dharma
to chair (a meeting), spearhead (overall operations), or host/anchor (a broadcast show)

主持.notes: Spans three vivid modern collocations: media hosting (主持节目, 'host a TV show'), formal governance/management (主持大局, 'take charge of the overall situation', 主持会议 'chair a meeting'), and moral arbitration (主持公道). Can also function colloquially as a noun ('who is tonight's host?').

主持人.etymology: A modern agentive nominal compound (偏正/后缀派生词) formed by attaching the productive human agentive head 人 (MC *nyin*, 'person') to the verbal compound 主持 ('to preside over, chair, host'). Standardized in late 20th-century Mainland and Taiwan radio/television broadcasting (notably from the early 1980s onward as conversational show hosts replaced stiff script-reading 播音员 'announcers') to render English *host*, *presenter*, *anchor*, or *moderator*.

history.meaning: radio/TV script announcer; ceremonial master of ceremonies (earlier terms)
television/radio program host, talk-show presenter, news anchor, or panel moderator

主持人.notes: In Mainland Chinese television, 主持人 implies personality, improvisation, and editorial presence onstage, contrasting with 播音员 (traditional news/voice announcer), 司仪 (wedding/ceremony emcee), and 制片人 / 制作人 (the behind-the-scenes producer running the show).

cognates.meaning: uphold justice, see fair play done
cognates.word: 主持公道 (zyu2 ci4 gung1 dou6)

主持公道.etymology: A four-character verb-object idiom (动宾四字格) combining 主持 ('to preside over, uphold, champion') with 公道 (itself a Classical Chinese modifier-head noun from 公 MC *kuwng* 'public, impartial, unselfish' + 道 MC *dawX* 'way, moral principle', attested since *Xunzi* and *Hanfeizi* for 'the impartial way / public justice'). Solidified in Ming–Qing vernacular courtroom and chivalric (*wuxia*) narratives where wronged parties appeal to a respected elder or magistrate to see fair play done.

history.meaning: impartial moral principle; public fairness opposed to private bias (私)
to adjudicate impartially; step forward to champion fairness for the wronged

主持公道.notes: Typically occurs in the frame 为/替 [someone] 主持公道 ('stand up for fairness on someone's behalf'), appealing to a senior boss, union/industry elder, or public opinion when someone has been bullied or framed.

主播.etymology: A 20th-century modifier-head Mandarin compound combining 主 (zhǔ, 'chief, host, principal'; originally a pictograph of a lampwick flame 炷, extended in Classical Chinese to 'master, host') and 播 (bō, 'sow, scatter, disseminate'; Old Chinese *pˤar-s, attested in the Shijing for sowing grain). Formed as a syllabic contraction of 主要播音员 (zhǔyào bōyīnyuán, 'lead broadcast announcer') with the rise of radio and television journalism, and extended in 21st-century Chinese digital culture to livestreaming hosts.

history.meaning: Classical Chinese roots: 'host/master' (主) and 'to sow seeds, scatter abroad' (播)
lead radio or television news anchor responsible for hosting a broadcast program
broadcast anchor or online livestream creator/host

主播.notes: Covers both prestige television news anchors (新闻主播) and e-commerce or entertainment livestreamers (带货主播, 网络主播); in TV production dramas like Behind the Scenes (幕后之王), it specifically denotes on-air hosts paired with off-camera producers (幕后制作人).

rootFamily.gloss: host a show; master of ceremonies

主流.etymology: A modifier-head compound composed of 主 (zhǔ, 'principal, main') and 流 (liú, 'flowing water, river current, stream'). In Literary Chinese geography and hydrography, 主流 denoted the trunk channel of a river system in contrast to 支流 (zhīliú, 'tributaries'). In late 19th- and 20th-century East Asian prose—strongly reinforced by Meiji–Taishō Japanese 主流 (shuryū) as a semantic match for English 'mainstream'—it acquired its dominant figurative sense of prevailing ideological, artistic, or commercial currents.

history.meaning: trunk channel or primary current of a river system (contrasted with 支流 'tributary')

history.form: 主流 (cf. Japanese 主流 shuryū)
history.meaning: dominant tendency, prevailing school of thought, cultural or media mainstream

主流.notes: Functions both as a noun (进入主流 'enter the mainstream') and as a non-gradable attributive modifier (主流媒体 'mainstream media', 主流音乐 'mainstream music'), frequently contrasted with 小众 (xiǎozhòng, 'niche/indie').

主管.etymology: Compound verb and noun combining 主 ('preside over, be in charge of') + 管 ('manage, control', originally a bamboo key or pipe): 'be in charge of; person in charge, supervisor, manager'. Attested since Tang–Song administrative usage.

history.meaning: have primary charge of an office
supervisor; manager; be in charge of

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 主管 (via 萌典)

主要.etymology: Adjective meaning 'main, principal, primary, chief', combining 主 ('chief, leading, host') + 要 ('essential, vital, waist/pivot').

history.meaning: chief and essential -> main, primary

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 主要 (via 萌典)

举.etymology: Simplified from 舉 (jǔ), whose traditional bronze and seal script depicts pairs of hands (與/廾) lifting an object aloft together. In Classical Chinese 舉 meant 'to raise with both hands, to hoist, to recommend for office, or to undertake an action', also developing the collective sense 'entire' (举世 'the whole world'). Modern Mandarin preserves its concrete physical core 'to lift up or hold aloft' (举手, 举杯) alongside formal compounds such as 举行 ('to hold an event').

morphemes.meaning: lift up with the hands; raise aloft (simplified from 舉)

history.meaning: lift with two hands; raise; nominate
hold up; raise aloft

举办.etymology: A coordinative transitive verb compound joining 举 (舉, jǔ, 'lift up, initiate, undertake'; Old Chinese *[k]ʷraʔ, depicting hands raising something aloft) and 办 (辦, bàn, 'manage, administer, transact'; differentiated in imperial orthography from 辨 'distinguish' by the radical 力/辛 for exertion in official business). Combining Classical 举 ('launch an undertaking, hold a rite') with Qing administrative 办 ('execute, handle'), 举办 crystallized in late Qing and Republican Mandarin for staging formal public events, exhibitions, or broadcasts.

history.meaning: Classical 'initiate, raise up' (舉) and late imperial administrative 'manage, execute official affairs' (辦)
to organize, stage, or host an institutional event, competition, or festival

举办.notes: Takes institutional or public event nouns as objects (举办晚会 'stage a gala', 举办比赛 'hold a competition'); unlike 举行 (jǔxíng, 'take place / hold'), 举办 foregrounds the organizer's behind-the-scenes planning, funding, and execution.

rootFamily.gloss: hold or stage (a ceremony, meeting, or contest)

举报.etymology: A coordinative legal-administrative verb compound of 举 (舉, jǔ, 'cite, bring forward, impeach', as in Classical 举发 'expose wrongdoing' and 检举 'inform against') and 报 (報, bào, 'report to a superior, requite, notify'; originally depicting a hand restraining a kneeling offender 幸 + 卩). Rooted in Ming–Qing bureaucratic memorials where officials reported malfeasance upward to court censors, 举报 specialized in modern Mandarin into reporting illegal, corrupt, or rule-breaking conduct to authorities or platform regulators.

history.meaning: submit an official memorial nominating or reporting a matter/offense to higher imperial authorities
report misconduct, inform against lawbreakers, blow the whistle to regulators

举报.notes: Always implies reporting wrongdoing to an authority or regulatory body (实名举报 'real-name whistleblowing', 恶意举报 'malicious reporting on social platforms'); never use it for neutral news reporting, which is 报道 (bàodào).

rootFamily.gloss: inform against, expose offences to authorities
sound an alarm, report an emergency to police

举起.etymology: Resultative directional compound of 举 ('lift with both hands', derived from 昇/與 depicting hands raising an object aloft) + 起 ('rise; upward', walk radical 走 + 己). The second morpheme marks the upward trajectory completed by the lifting action.

history.meaning: raise with both hands; elevate
raise; lift up

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 举起

久.etymology: Adjective meaning 'for a long time, long-lasting'. Shuowen Jiezi explains the small-seal graph as a person supported or cauterized with moxa from behind (related to 灸 jiǔ 'moxibustion' and 柩 jiù 'coffin kept for a long time'), borrowed since the earliest classics (Shijing, Laozi) for temporal duration.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Shijing, Laozi) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: long in time; enduring

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 久 (via 萌典)

义务.etymology: A Sino-Japanese graphic loan (wasei-kango) adopted from Meiji Japanese 義務 (gimu), coined in the 1860s–1870s by Japanese legal scholars (notably Nishi Amane and Mitsukuri Rinshō) using Classical Chinese morphemes in a modifier-head structure: 义 (義, yì, 'righteousness, moral principle, what is fitting') + 务 (務, wù, 'imperative task, affair to attend to'). Borrowed into late Qing Chinese alongside 权利 (quánlì, 'rights') to translate Western jurisprudential 'obligation/duty', and secondarily extended in 20th-century Mandarin to mean 'voluntary, pro bono, unpaid'.

history.meaning: Classical Chinese morphemes: 'moral righteousness/duty' (義) and 'earnestly pursued affair/task' (務)

history.form: 義務 (Meiji Japanese gimu → Late Qing Chinese yìwù)
history.meaning: legal, civic, or moral obligation paired with 權利 (rights)
legal/moral duty; attributively, unpaid voluntary service or compulsory public schooling

义务.notes: Watch the two distinct attributive senses in Mandarin: 义务教育 means 'compulsory education' (from legal duty), whereas 义务演出 means 'charity/unpaid performance' (acting solely out of public spirit without remuneration).

rootFamily.gloss: public or official affairs; civil service

cognates.meaning: of, this (read no or kore in kanbun kundoku)

之.etymology: One of the core grammatical morphemes of Sinitic, Old Chinese *tə (Middle Chinese tsyi). In Shang oracle bone script (止 atop a horizontal baseline 一), 之 is an ideograph depicting a foot stepping out from a starting point, originally a full verb meaning 'to go to, proceed toward'. Already in Western Zhou bronze inscriptions and the Shijing, phonetic loan and grammaticalization yielded a distal/anaphoric demonstrative ('this/that'), a post-verbal third-person object pronoun ('him, her, it, them'), and the canonical Literary Chinese attributive/genitive subordinator ('of, 's') preserved in elevated modern Mandarin.

history.meaning: to go toward, arrive at; demonstrative 'this, that'
subordinating genitive linker ('of'), clausal nominalizer, and 3rd-person object pronoun ('it/him/her/them')
high-register attributive particle ('of') in titles, idioms, and formal/literary constructions

之.notes: Replaced by 的 (de) in everyday spoken Mandarin, 之 imparts formal weight, dramatic grandeur, or fixed idiomatic rhythm—hence showbiz titles like 幕后之王 ('King Behind the Scenes') rather than the prosaic 幕后的王.

rootFamily.gloss: in a word, all in all (lit. 'summing it up')

cognates.meaning: one of (calqued in modern Vietnamese as một trong...)

之一.etymology: A Classical Chinese partitive phrase combining the genitive/attributive particle 之 (zhī, 'of, among') with the cardinal numeral 一 (yī, 'one'; Old Chinese *ʔi[t]). Placed immediately after a plural or collective noun phrase (NP + 之一, 'one belonging to [NP]'), the construction appears sporadically in Classical historiography (such as Shiji and Hanshu) and expanded dramatically in 20th-century Standardized Written Mandarin through Europeanized prose translating English 'one of the [superlative/plural noun]'.

history.meaning: one part or one member belonging to a preceding group or whole
one of (post-nominal partitive marker following a plural group, often paired with 最 'most')

之一.notes: Unlike English 'one of the best producers', Mandarin strictly places 之一 at the very end of the noun phrase (最优秀的制作人之一), and contemporary internet/showbiz slang playfully negates it as 没有之一 ('bar none, period—not merely one of them!').

之下.etymology: A Literary Chinese postpositional locative phrase composed of the genitive linker 之 (zhī, 'of') and the spatial relational noun 下 (xià, 'underside, space below'; Old Chinese *gˤraʔ, an ancient indicative symbol marking position beneath a reference line). In Classical texts such as the Shijing (普天之下 'beneath all heaven'), 之下 marked concrete physical space under a canopy or sovereign; in modern Mandarin it grammaticalized into an abstract circumposition (在……之下) framing conditions, emotions, comparisons, or authority.

history.meaning: physical space directly beneath an object, sky, or seat of power
under specified circumstances, pressure, leadership, or emotional impulse

之下.notes: Requires a disyllabic or complex noun phrase before it—often paired with 在 (在重压之下 'under heavy pressure', 在聚光灯之下 'under the spotlight') or sudden emotional states (一怒之下 'in a fit of anger', 情急之下 'in desperation').

之内.etymology: Postpositional phrase combining the Classical attributive particle 之 ('of, ’s') + 内 ('inside, within'): 'within, inside of' (used for both spatial bounds and time limits, e.g. 三天之内 'within three days').

history.meaning: the interior of -> within, inside

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 之内 (via 萌典)

之前.etymology: Temporal and spatial postposition combining 之 (Classical attributive linker) + 前 ('front, before'): 'before, prior to, ago'.

history.meaning: before; prior to

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 之前 (via 萌典)

之后.etymology: Temporal and spatial postposition combining 之 (Classical attributive linker) + 后 (後, 'behind, after, later'): 'after, afterwards, later on'.

history.meaning: after; behind; subsequently

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 之后 (via 萌典)

之外.etymology: A Literary Chinese locative and exclusionary phrase joining the genitive particle 之 (zhī, 'of') with the spatial noun 外 (wài, 'outside, exterior, beyond'; Old Chinese *[ŋ]ʷˤat-s, combining 夕 'evening/crescent' and 卜 'divination crack'). In Classical prose (e.g., Zhuangzi's 游乎方之外 'roaming beyond the bounds of worldly convention' and 度外 'outside one's calculations'), 之外 marked physical or conceptual exteriors, evolving in modern Mandarin into the standard postposition for 'beyond, outside of' and the exclusionary frame 除(了)……之外 ('apart from, besides').

history.meaning: physical space outside a boundary, wall, or realm
beyond expectations or scope; apart from, in addition to, with the exception of

之外.notes: In `除了 X 之外`, look at the following adverb to tell inclusion from exclusion: followed by 还/也 ('also') it means 'in addition to X', whereas followed by 都/全 ('all') it means 'except for X'. Frequent in set phrases like 意料之外 ('beyond expectations') and 镜头之外 ('off camera').

rootFamily.gloss: within, inside a limit or timeframe

之夜.etymology: Literary-styled noun phrase frame combining 之 ('of') + 夜 ('night'), used in titles and event names (e.g., 音乐之夜 'night of music') to mean 'the night of…'.

history.meaning: the night of (something)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 之夜 (via 萌典)

之子.etymology: A Literary Chinese modifier-head genitive phrase formed from the possessive particle 之 (zhī, 'of, 's') and 子 (zǐ, 'offspring, son, child'; Old Chinese *tsəʔ, oracle bone pictograph of a swaddled infant with outstretched arms). Philologically, this post-nominal genitive (`NP + 之子`, 'son/child of NP', as in 天之子 'Son of Heaven' or 将门之子 'son of a general's house') is distinct from the archaic Shijing sequence 之子于归 (*Tao Yao*), where initial 之 functioned as a demonstrative ('this young bride'); only the genitive construction survives in modern elevated Mandarin.

history.meaning: this young person / this bride (archaic Shijing usage with demonstrative 之)

history.form: X 之子 (genitive linker + head noun)
history.meaning: son, child, or lineal scion of X
formal/dramatic 'son of X' or metaphorical 'child/favorite of X' in titles and epithets

之子.notes: Strictly literary and title-register in modern Mandarin (e.g., 天选之子 'the chosen one', 天之骄子 'heaven's favored scion'); in ordinary conversation one always says `X 的儿子` rather than `X 之子`.

之所以.etymology: A lexicalized Classical Chinese syntactic sequence uniting three grammatical words: 之 (zhī, functioning here as the Classical clausal nominalizer inserted between a subject and predicate to turn a clause into a noun phrase), 所 (suǒ, relative object nominalizer, 'that which'), and 以 (yǐ, instrumental/causal preposition, 'by means of, on account of'). In Classical prose (`NP + 之 + 所以 + VP + 者`), the constituent boundary fell between 之 and 所以, literally 'NP's [that-by-which it VPs]'; reanalysis in modern Mandarin fused 之所以 into a single result-first causal conjunction ('the reason why...').

history.meaning: that by means of which / the reason on account of which [Subject] acts (Classical nominalized clause)
fused causal conjunction: 'the reason why [outcome happens] (is because...)'

morphemes.meaning: clausal nominalizing linker between subject and predicate

之所以.notes: Reverses normal Chinese cause-before-effect order (因为……所以……) by spotlighting a known result first and then revealing its hidden motive (`他之所以退赛，是因为……` 'The reason he withdrew from the show is because...'). Avoid omitting 是因为 in the second clause.

rootFamily.gloss: therefore, so (causal conjunction from Classical 'that by which')

cognates.meaning: between (rendered no aida in kanbun kundoku)

之间.etymology: A Literary Chinese relational locative phrase formed from the genitive linker 之 (zhī, 'of') and 间 (間, variant 閒, jiān, 'crevice, gap, interval'; Old Chinese *kˤre[n], originally depicting moonlight 月 glimpsed through the crack of double doors 門). Attested throughout Classical literature for spatial, temporal, and interpersonal intervals (such as 天地之间 'between heaven and earth' in Laozi and Zhuangzi), 之间 remains the core postposition in modern Mandarin for expressing mutual relations or intervals between two or more entities.

history.meaning: spatial gap, temporal moment, or interval between two boundaries

history.form: (在) A 和/与 B 之间
history.meaning: between A and B (spatially, temporally, or in interpersonal/institutional relations)

之间.notes: Normally pairs with a coordinate phrase (`在台前与幕后之间` 'between onstage and backstage') or a plural noun (`同事之间` 'among colleagues'); never place 之间 before the noun like English 'between'.

rootFamily.gloss: instantly, in the blink of an eye

乌烟瘴气.etymology: A four-character coordinative idiom (chéngyǔ) juxtaposing two parallel modifier-head noun phrases: 乌烟 (烏煙, wūyān, 'black smoke', where 乌 is originally a pictograph of a crow, hence 'jet-black') and 瘴气 (瘴氣, zhàngqì, 'pestilential miasma', referring to humid, malaria-inducing vapors historically dreaded by northern officials posted to tropical Lingnan and southwestern China). Coalescing in late Qing and 20th-century polemical prose (famously used by Mao Zedong in political essays), it shifted from noxious air to a metaphor for a foul, corrupt, scandal-plagued social milieu.

history.meaning: literal 'black soot/smoke' and 'subtropical malarial miasma' in traditional medical and geographical writing
foul, chaotic, corrupt, or toxic atmosphere in an organization or public sphere

乌烟瘴气.notes: Commonly used with 搞得 or 弄得 (`把整个圈子搞得乌烟瘴气` 'turn the whole entertainment circle into a toxic mess') when criticizing cutthroat PR smear campaigns, cyberbullying, or corrupt workplace politics.

乐坛.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-compound combining 乐 (樂, yuè, 'music'; Old Chinese *[ŋ]ˤrawk, oracle bone pictograph of silk strings stretched over a wooden frame) and 坛 (壇, tán, 'raised earthen sacrificial altar, ceremonial platform'). By the Tang–Song era, 坛 had extended metaphorically from ritual altars (祭坛) and lecture platforms (杏坛) to prestigious literary circles (文坛, 诗坛); in modern East Asian journalism (alongside Japanese 楽壇 gakudan), 乐坛 became the standard term for the professional music industry and its artistic community.

history.meaning: Classical 'ritual/court music' (樂) and 'raised earthen altar or ceremonial dais' (壇)
the music world, professional music industry or pop/classical scene

乐坛.notes: Be careful to pronounce 乐 as yuè ('music'), never lè ('happy')! Often modified by regional/language labels in entertainment media, such as 华语乐坛 ('the Mandopop/Chinese-language music scene') or 歌坛 ('the singing/pop world').

乐意.etymology: Formed from 乐 (樂, lè, 'joy, delight, take pleasure in'; Old Chinese *[r]ˤawk, etymologically derived from the same graph as 樂 yuè 'music' via the joy of musical performance) and 意 (yì, 'thought, mind, intention, inclination'; heart 心 discerning sound/words 音). In Han–Tang poetic prose (such as Li Bai's 乐意相关禽对语), 乐意 was a modifier-head noun phrase meaning 'joyful mood, cheerful spirit'; in Ming–Qing vernacular Mandarin it reanalyzed into a psychological stative verb/adjective meaning 'pleased in mind to do something, willing, glad to'.

history.meaning: cheerful mood, joyous feeling or congenial spirit (noun phrase)
willing, happy to, gladly consenting (adjective and modal-like psych verb)

乐意.notes: Unlike 愿意 (yuànyì, neutral willingness or volition even for solemn sacrifices), 乐意 carries genuine warmth and cheerful enthusiasm (`我很乐意帮忙` 'I'd be delighted to help'); negated as 不乐意 in colloquial speech, it often means 'displeased, grumpy, reluctant'.

乐谱.etymology: Compound of 乐 (yuè, 'music', originally depicting strings mounted on a wooden stand 木) + 谱 (pǔ, 'register, chart, notation book', 言 speech/record + 普 'universal/ordered').

history.meaning: tablature and musical notation books
sheet music; musical score

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 乐谱 (via 萌典)

乐队.etymology: A modifier-head compound of 乐 (樂, yuè, 'music, musical performance') and 队 (隊, duì, 'troop, file, organized detachment'; originally 'fall from a height' from 阜 'mound', borrowed early in Classical military usage for a squad of soldiers). Although 乐队 already appeared in Tang–Song court records (such as Songshi and Menglianglu) denoting uniformed processional troupes of court musicians, its modern meaning ('Western orchestra, live studio house band, rock/pop band') was revitalized in late Qing–Republican China alongside Meiji Japanese 楽隊 (gakutai).

history.meaning: imperial court or ritual procession troupe of musicians and dancers

history.form: 樂隊 / 乐队 (cf. Japanese 楽隊 gakutai)
history.meaning: marching band, symphony orchestra (管弦乐队), live TV studio band, or rock/pop band (摇滚乐队)

乐队.notes: Covers the full spectrum from 交响乐队 ('symphony orchestra') and 现场乐队 ('live house band' on music competition shows) to 摇滚乐队 ('rock band'); in Taiwan and Hong Kong entertainment Mandarin, pop/rock bands are also commonly called 乐团 (yuètuán).

九.etymology: Cardinal numeral 'nine'. In Shang oracle-bone script, 九 depicted a bent arm or elbow (later written 肘 zhǒu with the flesh radical), borrowed phonetically since the earliest inscriptions for the number nine and symbolically associated in Chinese tradition with ultimate yang and longevity (homophonous with 久 'long-lasting').

history.meaning: bent-arm graph borrowed for numeral nine

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 九 (via 萌典)

九年.etymology: A numeral-measure temporal compound of 九 (jiǔ, 'nine'; Old Chinese *[k]uʔ, genetically cognate with Written Tibetan dgu and Written Burmese kuih; oracle bone graph depicts a bent elbow/arm) and 年 (nián, 'year'; Old Chinese *C.nˤi[ŋ], originally written 秊 depicting a person 人 carrying ripened grain 禾, meaning 'annual harvest' before generalizing to a calendar year). Beyond literal counting since Western Zhou inscriptions, 九—as the highest single yang digit—imbued 九年 in Classical lore with the sense of a long cycle of testing or devotion (e.g., Bodhidharma's 面壁九年).

history.meaning: nine annual harvests; a span of nine calendar years
nine years (both literal duration and culturally resonant span, e.g., 九年义务教育)

九年.notes: Notice that 年 (nián, 'year') and 天 (tiān, 'day') are autonomous temporal measure nouns in Mandarin and never take 个 (*九个年 is ungrammatical; compare 九个月 'nine months').

九零后.etymology: A 21st-century generational compound formed by affixing the temporal/cohort noun 后 (後, hòu, 'after, post-, generation born after') to 九零 (jiǔlíng, digit-by-digit shorthand for 1990s, from 九 'nine' + 零 'zero'; 零 originally meant 'light steady rain' and then 'fractional remainder' in traditional mathematics before denoting 0). Modeled directly on 八零后 (bālíng-hòu, coined in late-1990s literary criticism for authors born in the 1980s), 九零后 entered mass PRC media around 2008 to label digital-native youth born between 1990 and 1999.

history.meaning: constituent morphemes: 'nine', 'fractional remainder / zero', and 'after / posterity'
the post-1990s generation (cohort born between 1990 and 1999)

morphemes.meaning: after; demographic cohort born in/after a decade

九零后.notes: Frequently written numerically as 90后 in media headlines; productive across every decade (80后, 95后, 00后 'post-2000s Gen Z') to contrast workplace attitudes and media consumption habits in contemporary Chinese dramas.

也.etymology: In Classical Chinese, 也 was the quintessential sentence-final particle of judgment, identification, and pause ('A, B 也' = 'A is B'). From the Tang–Song vernacular onward, it shifted to a pre-verbal adverb meaning 'also, too, as well, even'.

history.meaning: clause-final copular and modal particle
pre-verbal adverb 'also, too, even'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 也 (via 萌典)

也好.etymology: A lexicalized vernacular Mandarin evaluative and concessive expression combining the adverb 也 (yě, 'also, even'; originally a Classical clause-final particle of judgment or pause, which grammaticalized in Tang–Song vernacular bianwen and Chan dialogues into the additive/concessive adverb 'also, even if') and the stative verb 好 (hǎo, 'good, fine, acceptable'; Old Chinese *qʰˤuʔ). Used alone as a predicate, it means 'would also be good / might as well'; reduplicated across parallel clauses (`A 也好，B 也好`), it grammaticalized into a correlative concessive particle meaning 'whether A or B'.

history.meaning: that too is fine; might as well be good
clause-final 'might as well / fine too'; correlative particle 'whether ... or ... (either way)'

也好.notes: When paired in `台前也好，幕后也好，都要靠实力` ('Whether onstage or behind the scenes, you have to rely on real skill'), it is almostalways followed in the main clause by 都 (dōu) or 也 (yě) to underscore that the conclusion holds regardless of the choice.

rootFamily.gloss: may as well drop it; whether ... or ... (synonymous concessive particle)

也许.etymology: Modal adverb meaning 'perhaps, maybe, probablemente', formed in vernacular Mandarin from 也 ('also, even') + 许 (許, 'allow, grant, perhaps/approximate').

history.meaning: perhaps; maybe

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 也许 (via 萌典)

习惯.etymology: Compound verb and noun of 习 (習, 'practice repeatedly', originally showing young birds 羽 practicing flight under the sun/white 白) + 惯 (慣, 'be accustomed to, habit', heart 忄 + 貫 'pierce/string through'). Means 'habit, custom' and 'get used to'.

history.meaning: grow accustomed through repeated practice
habit; custom; be used to

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 习惯 (via 萌典)

书.etymology: Originally a verb meaning 'write with a brush' (書, showing a hand holding a writing brush 聿 above 曰/者), then 'written document, letter' in Classical Chinese, and from the Han–Six Dynasties onward the general word for 'book'.

history.meaning: write; calligraphy; written document or letter
book; letter

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 书 (via 萌典)

书店.etymology: Determinative compound of 书 ('book; written volume', brush radical 聿 + 曰) + 店 ('shop; commercial establishment', shelter radical 广 + 占 zhān). Replacing older terms such as 书肆 and 书坊 during the late Qing and Republican eras, it is the universal modern word for a bookstore.

history.meaning: bookstall and woodblock-printing bookshop
bookshop; bookstore

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 书店

书房.etymology: Compound noun of 书 (書, 'books, writing') + 房 ('side room, chamber', door 户 + phonetic 方 fāng), naming a private study or reading room in a house.

history.meaning: study; reading and writing room

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 书房 (via 萌典)

书架.etymology: Compound noun of 书 (書, 'books') + 架 ('wooden frame, rack, shelf', 加 + 木): 'bookshelf, bookcase'.

history.meaning: wooden rack for holding books -> bookshelf

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 书架 (via 萌典)

书桌.etymology: Compound noun of 书 (書, 'books, writing') + 桌 ('table'): 'writing desk, study desk'.

history.meaning: writing desk; study table

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 书桌 (via 萌典)

书脊.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 书脊. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 书脊 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 书脊 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 书脊 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 书脊. The etymology of 书脊 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 书脊
middle form of 书脊
modern form of 书脊

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 书脊

买.etymology: Verb meaning 'buy, purchase' (traditional 買, combining a net 罒/网 over cowrie shells 貝 'ancient shell currency', literally 'net/acquire goods with shell money'). Contrast 卖 (賣 = 出 + 買, 'put out for sale, sell').

history.meaning: purchase with shell currency
buy; purchase

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 买 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: settle/close the bill, tally the check (etymological source)

买单.etymology: A late 20th-century verb-object borrowing into Mandarin from Cantonese 埋單 (Jyutping maai4 daan1, 'tally/settle the restaurant check'), composed in Cantonese of 埋 (maai4, 'bring together, close up, settle') + 單 (daan1, 'bill, slip, itemized list'). Because Cantonese maai4 sounds close to Mandarin mǎi (買/买, 'to buy') and 'buying the bill' offered a transparent folk-etymological reanalysis, northern speakers respelled 埋单 as 买单 as Guangdong–Hong Kong dining culture spread nationwide in the 1980s–1990s.

history.meaning: add up and settle a dining or commercial bill ('close the slip')

history.form: 买单 (also written 埋单 in Mandarin)
history.meaning: pay the restaurant check; figuratively, foot the bill or bear the cost of someone's mistake

morphemes.meaning: pay/buy (Mandarin phonetic-semantic adaptation of Cantonese 埋 'settle, close')

买单.notes: Because 买单 is already a verb-object compound, never put an object right after it (*买单这顿饭); use 为……买单 instead—especially in its ubiquitous media/business metaphor `为错误的决定买单` ('pay the price for a bad decision').

rootFamily.gloss: settle the bill (etymological spelling retained in print)
settle accounts, check out, pay the bill

买家.etymology: Compound noun of 买 ('buy') + 家 ('household, specialist/party in a transaction', as in 卖家 'seller', 东家 'proprietor'): 'buyer, purchaser'.

morphemes.meaning: party or person engaged in an activity

history.stage: Song–Ming commercial vernacular to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: purchasing party; buyer

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 买家 (via 萌典)

乱.etymology: Inherited from Old Chinese *[r]ˤon-s (Middle Chinese lwanH), simplified 乱 from traditional 亂. In Shang oracle bone and Western Zhou bronze scripts, 𤔔 depicts two hands (爪 above and 又 below) working on tangled silk threads wound on a frame, with 乚 added as a movement/unraveling stroke. This concrete textile image produced a celebrated Classical Chinese auto-antonym (enantiosemy): in early Shangshu chapters 亂 could mean 'to untangle, put in order, govern', while its enduring primary sense across Classical and modern Mandarin is 'tangled, chaotic, disorderly, in turmoil', as well as the adverb 'indiscriminately, wildly'.

history.meaning: tangled silk threads; by extension both 'untangle/govern' (archaic) and 'disordered, in rebellion'
messy, chaotic, confused (adj.); throw into confusion (verb); recklessly, at random (adverb before verbs)

乱.notes: Placed directly before a monosyllabic verb, 乱 acts as a vivid colloquial adverb meaning 'recklessly / without rhyme or reason': 乱说 ('talk nonsense'), 乱改剧本 ('butcher/randomly rewrite a script'), 乱带节奏 ('stir up toxic online narratives').

rootFamily.gloss: flustered and busy, in a frantic rush

乱子.etymology: A vernacular Mandarin derived noun formed by attaching the neutral-tone nominalizing suffix 子 (-zi, grammaticalized during the Medieval to Early Mandarin transition from Classical 子 'child, seed, small object') to the adjectival/verbal root 乱 (亂, luàn, 'disorder, turmoil, disturbance'). Attested in Qing Beijing-dialect novels such as Hongloumeng and Ernü Yingxiong Zhuan, 乱子 scaled down Classical 乱 ('rebellion, state upheaval') into an everyday countable noun for an unexpected mishap, scandal, or operational crisis.

history.meaning: local disturbance, troublesome incident, unexpected blunder
trouble, mess, crisis, unforeseen hitch

乱子.notes: Almost always appears in punchy colloquial verb-object collocations—especially 出乱子 ('something goes wrong / a crisis breaks out' during a live broadcast), 捅乱子 ('poke a hornet's nest / cause a mess'), and 惹乱子 ('invite trouble').

rootFamily.gloss: cause serious trouble, stir up a disaster

了.etymology: Neutral-tone aspect and sentence particle le marking a completed action (after a verb) or a newly changed situation (at the end of a sentence). Grammaticalized during the Tang and Song dynasties from the full verb 了 (liǎo, 'finish, complete'), which is already illustrated in its particle sense in Su Shi's Song lyrics.

history.meaning: finish; bring to completion
completed-action particle

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 了 (via 萌典)

了不起.etymology: A lexicalized negative potential complement phrase built from the verb 了 (liǎo, 'finish, settle, bring to a conclusion, cope with'; Old Chinese *[r]ˤiwʔ), the negative potential infix 不 (bu, 'cannot'), and the resultative/directional complement 起 (qǐ, 'lift up, sustain, bear the weight of'). Arising in Ming–Qing vernacular fiction, 了不起 literally meant 'so grave or overwhelming that one cannot bear or contain it' (compare 不得了), before pragmatic hyperbole shifted its primary modern meaning to strong admiration: 'extraordinary, remarkable, amazing'.

history.meaning: overwhelmingly serious, beyond one's ability to handle or contain
extraordinary, amazing, formidable (often used ironically in rhetorical questions: 有什么了不起？)

了不起.notes: Don't confuse 了不起 ('amazing, remarkable' for people or achievements) with its mirror twin 不得了 (bùdéliǎo, 'terrible, dire' or post-adjectival intensifier `高兴得不得了` 'thrilled beyond words'); in arguments, `有什么了不起？` means 'What's the big deal? / Who do they think they are?'.

rootFamily.gloss: look down upon (negative potential with -不起)

cognates.meaning: understand as clearly as pointing to one's palm (literary Sino-Korean)

了如指掌.etymology: A four-character Classical Chinese predicate-complement idiom (chéngyǔ) ultimately derived from Lunyu (Analects 3.11, Ba Yi): asked about the grand ancestral dì sacrifice, Confucius said that anyone who truly grasped its meaning could govern the realm 'as effortlessly as this' while pointing to his palm (指其掌). Han commentator He Yan glossed this as 言其明且易也 ('meaning it is lucid and easy'), and Tang–Song writers condensed the image with 了 (originally often written 瞭, liǎo, 'clear-sighted, thoroughly understood') + 如 (rú, 'like, just as') + 指掌 ('pointing to one's own palm').

history.form: 指其掌 (Lunyu 3.11) → 瞭如指掌 / 了如指掌
history.meaning: as plain and effortless as pointing at the palm of one's own hand
know every detail inside and out, know like the back of one's hand

morphemes.meaning: clear, thoroughly understood (read liǎo; traditional variant 瞭)

了如指掌.notes: Note the amusing anatomical mirror between English and Chinese: English knows something 'like the back of one's hand', whereas Chinese looks at the lines on one's open palm (指掌). Typically takes 对 to introduce the topic (`对节目流程了如指掌` 'know the show's rundown inside out').

rootFamily.gloss: control, have firmly in hand (lit. 'grasp in the palm')

了解.etymology: A coordinative verb compound pairing 了 (liǎo, 'comprehend thoroughly, bring to clarity'; simplified Chinese also merges 瞭 'clear-sighted' into 了, so traditional scripts write either 了解 or 瞭姐/瞭解, with 了解 being the older medieval form) and 解 (jiě, 'untie, dissect, analyze, understand'; originally depicting a knife 刀 separating an ox's horn 角 from the animal). Attested in Six Dynasties Buddhist translations and Song Neo-Confucian dialogues (such as Zhuzi Yulei) for 'fathom clearly', it broadened in modern Mandarin to cover both deep comprehension and active fact-finding.

history.form: 了解 (Medieval Buddhist & Song Neo-Confucian prose)
history.meaning: fathom thoroughly, penetrate the meaning of a doctrine or principle
understand (a person, situation, or field); find out about, investigate

了解.notes: Watch two nuances: first, unlike Japanese 了解 (ryōkai, 'Roger that / understood!'), Mandarin uses 收到 or 明白 to acknowledge instructions; second, `我去了解一下` is an active verb meaning 'Let me go check / find out about the situation', not static 'understanding'.

rootFamily.gloss: clear, plain to understand (with 了 liǎo)

cognates.meaning: bestow, give (literary kanbun verb yo / ataeru)

予.etymology: Inherited from Old Chinese *laʔ (Middle Chinese yoX, modern Mandarin yǔ 'give, grant'), etymologically distinct from its homographic reading yú (Old Chinese *la, archaic first-person pronoun 'I, me') and allofamically related to 与 (與, yǔ, 'give'). In seal script, Xu Shen's Shuowen Jiezi analyzes 予 as depicting one hand/shuttle passing an object forward to another (推予也，象相予之形). Retaining its Classical transitive sense, 予 functions in modern Mandarin as an elevated formal verb and bound stem in legal, institutional, and broadcast announcements.

history.meaning: hand over, bestow, confer upon (alongside homograph *la > yú 'I, me')
formal/official verb 'grant, accord, impose' (especially before disyllabic verbal nouns or in 予以)

予.notes: High-register institutional word seen in official notices, contracts, and disciplinary statements (e.g., `不予录用` 'decline to hire', `予以支持` 'accord support', `免予处罚` 'exempt from penalty'); everyday speech always uses 给 (gěi).

rootFamily.gloss: give, accord, mete out (formal light verb before 2-syllable nouns)
confer, award (a prize, title, or honor)
give, render, extend (support, attention, or help)

争分夺秒.etymology: A modern four-character parallel verb-object idiom (chéngyǔ) pairing 争分 (爭分, zhēng fēn, 'contend for every minute') with 夺秒 (奪秒, duó miǎo, 'wrest every second'). Built on the Classical template of 寸阴必争 ('vie for every inch of shadow on the sundial', Jinshu), it substitutes modern horological units adopted during late Ming–Qing calendrical science: 分 (fēn, 'division, one-sixtieth of an hour, minute') and 秒 (miǎo, originally the delicate 'beard/awn on a grain husk' under 禾, extended in traditional metrology to minute fractions and then 'second').

history.form: 寸陰必爭 / 分秒必爭
history.meaning: earlier Literary & early modern precursors: 'contend for every inch of sundial shadow / every minute and second'
race against the clock, seize every minute and second without wasting an instant

争分夺秒.notes: Functions vividly as an adverbial modifier with 地 (`导演组正在争分夺秒地抢修播出带` 'The directing team is racing against the clock to fix the broadcast tape') in live-television countdowns, emergency rescues, and deadline crunches.

rootFamily.gloss: every single minute and second counts (close synonym)
vie to seize, compete fiercely for

cognates.meaning: strive to win/obtain, secure through struggle
strive for, make use of time/opportunity (Hán-Việt)

争取.etymology: A verb-resultative / coordinative compound uniting 争 (爭, zhēng, 'contend, vie, struggle for'; Old Chinese *[ts]ˤreŋ, bronze script depicting two hands pulling an object in opposite directions) and 取 (qǔ, 'take, seize, obtain'; Old Chinese *tsʰˤoʔ, originally depicting a hand 又 cutting off a left ear 耳 as a battlefield tally). Used in Classical and Medieval histories (e.g., Sanguozhi, Zizhi Tongjian) for contending to capture strategic territory or advantage, 争取 developed in modern Mandarin into striving actively to win an opportunity, budget, audience, or goal.

history.meaning: contend with rivals in order to seize territory, profit, or strategic advantage
strive for, campaign to win over (people or resources), do one's utmost to achieve

争取.notes: Versatile across three object types: abstract opportunities (`争取机会` 'fight for a chance'), people (`争取观众支持` 'win over audience support'), and verbal clauses (`争取按时开播` 'strive to go on air on schedule').

争吵.etymology: Coordinative compound verb and noun of 争 (爭, 'contend, strive', originally two hands pulling on an object in opposite directions) + 吵 ('make a racket, quarrel', mouth 口 + 少): 'quarrel, argue noisily, bicker'.

history.meaning: quarrel; wrangle; noisy argument

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 争吵 (via 萌典)

争得过.etymology: A colloquial Mandarin affirmative potential complement construction built on the verb 争 (爭, zhēng, 'compete, contend, argue'), the potential modal infix 得 (de, grammaticalized in Medieval–Early Mandarin from Classical 得 'obtain, succeed, be able'), and the comparative/surpassing complement 过 (過, guò, 'pass beyond, surpass, prevail over'). Paired systematically with its negative counterpart 争不过 (zhēngbuguò, 'unable to outcompete'), the `V + 得过` pattern crystallized in vernacular Mandarin to express having the clout, resources, or stamina to beat an opponent.

history.form: 爭 + 得 + 過 (Early Mandarin potential construction)
history.meaning: succeed in surpassing an opponent in contention or argument
able to outcompete, able to win out over or prevail against a rival

争得过.notes: In natural speech, affirmative 争得过 appears overwhelmingly in rhetorical questions expressing skepticism (`咱们小团队哪儿争得过卫视巨头？` 'How could our small team possibly outcompete a satellite-TV giant?'), while plain negative statements use 争不过.

rootFamily.gloss: unable to outcompete or win an argument against (negative counterpart)
able to defeat in a fight or competition (parallel -得过 pattern)
able to talk down or out-argue someone

争执.etymology: A coordinative compound combining 争 (爭, zhēng, 'contend, argue, dispute') and 执 (執, zhí, 'grasp firmly, cling stubbornly to'; Old Chinese *təp, oracle bone script depicting a kneeling figure with wrists locked in wooden manacles 幸 + 丮, originally 'apprehend, hold fast', extended in Classical prose to 'hold rigidly to a view', as in 固执). Attested in Tang–Song historical chronicles (such as Jiu Tangshu and Songshi) for officials clashing while refusing to yield their positions, 争执 serves in modern Mandarin as both verb and noun for a heated clash of views.

history.meaning: contend verbally while each party clings unyieldingly to its own stance
dispute, altercation, deadlock of opinions (noun); argue stubbornly (verb)

morphemes.meaning: hold fast, cling stubbornly to an opinion

争执.notes: More formal than 吵架 (chǎojià, 'quarrel/row') and highlights stubbornness over creative or practical disagreements—most often used nominally in `发生争执` ('get into an altercation/dispute') or the four-character phrase `争执不下` ('locked in a heated stalemate with neither side backing down').

争论.etymology: Coordinative Sino-compound (并列结构) uniting 争 (trad. 爭, Middle Chinese *tsrɛng*, depicting two hands pulling fiercely at an object, hence 'to contend, vie') and 论 (trad. 論, MC *lwən*, from 言 'speech' + 侖 'ordered bamboo slips', hence 'to discourse systematically, reason'). Attested in Warring States and Han prose (such as Xunzi and Shiji) for verbal disputation over policy or doctrine, it passed seamlessly into modern Mandarin as both a verb and noun for 'debate'.

history.meaning: to contend verbally over principle or policy; disputation
debate, controversy; to argue a point

争论.notes: Focuses on clash of viewpoints (e.g., 引发争论 'spark a debate' over a show's creative direction), whereas 辩论 implies a more formal, structured debate and 争吵 implies an emotional quarrel.

事.etymology: Noun meaning 'matter, affair, work, job, incident'. In Shang oracle-bone and Zhou bronze inscriptions, 事 (closely related to 史 'scribe/chronicle' and 吏 'official') showed a hand holding a hunting or writing implement/banner at court, denoting 'official duty, service, affair'.

morphemes.meaning: hand holding court standard/implement = affair, business, matter

history.meaning: court service; official affair; matter; serve
matter; affair; thing to do; trouble

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 事 (via 萌典)

事业.etymology: Coordinative compound (并列结构) pairing 事 (MC *dzriH*, 'affair, official service, undertaking') with 业 (trad. 業, MC *ngjæp*, originally depicting the carved toothed crossboard of a ritual bell-stand, extended to 'great estate, patrimony, profession'). First canonized in the Yijing (Xici I: 舉而措之天下之民，謂之事業, 'applying it to the people of the world is called a great undertaking'), and modernized in late 19th-century East Asia (alongside Japanese jigyō) to denote a lifelong career, public welfare institution, or major enterprise.

history.meaning: great public accomplishment or state undertaking
patrimony, scholarly or official accomplishment
career, vocation, public enterprise

事业.notes: Carries loftier, long-term vocational weight than 工作 ('job'); in entertainment dramas, 搞事业 ('focusing on one's career' over romance) is a ubiquitous catchphrase.

事业心.etymology: Modifier-head compound (偏正结构) built from 事业 (trad. 事業, 'career, lifelong undertaking') modifying the nominal head 心 (MC *sim*, 'heart-mind, disposition, inner drive'). Formed productively in 20th-century Mandarin on the psychological `[noun/verb] + 心` template (parallel to 责任心 'sense of responsibility' and 上进心 'drive to improve') to lexicalize inner commitment to professional achievement.

history.meaning: great undertaking + heart-mind (separate classical lexemes)
career ambition, dedication to one's profession

事业心.notes: Almost always collocates with 强 ('strong') or 重 ('heavy'), as in 事业心很强 ('very career-driven'), carrying positive connotations unlike 野心 ('unbridled ambition').

事件.etymology: Compound of 事 (MC *dzriH*, 'affair, matter') + 件 (MC *gjænX*, 'item, discrete case, document', originally 人 + 牛 suggesting partitioning cattle). In Song–Ming administrative vernacular, 事件 meant 'itemized matters or bureaucratic files' (a noun-plus-classifier/collective formation). In the Meiji era, Japanese repurposed 事件 (*jiken*) for legal cases and major public incidents; this journalistic and legal sense was re-imported into modern Chinese as an orthographic return loan.

history.meaning: itemized matters, administrative particulars
notable incident, legal case, public affair
major incident, news event, public controversy

事件.notes: In PR and media production, 事件 denotes a bounded, newsworthy incident or scandal (e.g., 公关事件 'PR crisis incident'), never a celebratory party or routine event (活动).

事儿.etymology: Rhotacized (儿化 *érhuà*) Northern Mandarin noun formed from 事 (MC *dzriH*, Old Chinese *\*[m-s-]rəʔ-s*, 'affair, service, business', originally depicting a hand holding a court tally or brush) plus the nonsyllabic retroflex suffix -儿 (trad. 兒, MC *nye*, originally 'child', grammaticalized from Tang–Yuan northern vernacular into a diminutive and nominalizing coda, yielding `shìr`).

history.meaning: ritual/official service, affair, occupation
colloquial matter, errand, trouble, or business
matter, affair, gig, or fuss (colloquial)

事儿.notes: Quintessential Beijing/Northern spoken register in showbiz dialogue: 没事儿 ('it's fine'), 有事儿说事儿 ('get straight to the point'), and 事儿多 ('fussy, high-maintenance').

rootFamily.gloss: to get into trouble, have an accident

事关.etymology: Subject-predicate lexicalized verbal frame (主谓结构 functioning transitively) from Literary Chinese: 事 (MC *dzriH*, 'the matter at hand') + 关 (trad. 關, MC *kwæn*, originally depicting wooden crossbars bolting double gate-leaves 門, metaphorically extended by Han–Tang times to 'pivotal nexus' and 'to hinge upon, implicate, concern'). Retained in elevated modern prose to introduce high-stakes consequences.

history.meaning: the affair hinges upon or implicates [a larger sphere]
to concern, touch upon, have a bearing on

morphemes.meaning: to bolt; to hinge upon, concern

事关.notes: Formal bound-style verb that always takes an abstract, weighty object directly without prepositions—such as 事关生死 ('a matter of life and death') or 事关公司声誉 ('concerns company reputation').

rootFamily.gloss: be a matter of grave importance

事关重大.etymology: Four-character Literary Chinese clause (主谓宾/补结构) combining 事关 (trad. 事關, subject-verb 'the matter hinges upon / concerns') with the coordinative adjectival-nominal complement 重大 ('weighty and great', from 重 MC *drjungX* 'heavy, grave' + 大 MC *dajH* 'great'). Originating in Ming–Qing memorials and official dispatches, it crystallized into a standard set phrase stressing high stakes.

history.meaning: the matter implicates grave state or administrative consequences
to be a matter of grave importance

事关重大.notes: Used as a standalone predicate in crisis meetings or boardroom scenes (e.g., 这件事事关重大，不能外传 'this matter is of grave importance and cannot leak').

事实.etymology: Modifier-head / coordinative compound joining 事 (MC *dzriH*, 'affair, deed') and 实 (trad. 實, MC *zyit*, originally 宀 'roof' over 貫 'strings of cowries/goods', hence 'full, substantial, true reality'). Attested in Han–Six Dynasties historiography (e.g., Hou Hanshu: 事寔/事實) for 'the actual substance of events', and standardized across modern East Asia via Meiji Japanese *jijitsu* (事実) as the exact equivalent of Western 'fact'.

history.meaning: actual particulars and true substance of an affair
objective fact (as opposed to opinion or fiction)
fact, reality

事实.notes: Frequently appears in media/legal collocations like 摆事实 ('lay out the facts'), 既成事实 ('fait accompli'), and adverbial 事实上 ('in fact, actually').

事态.etymology: Modifier-head compound (偏正结构) of 事 (MC *dzriH*, 'affair, unfolding event') modifying 态 (trad. 態, MC *thojH*, from 能 phonetic/semantic 'bear/capability' + 心 'disposition', meaning 'posture, bearing, state'). While 態 denoted personal bearing in Classical prose, the compound 事態 gained modern currency through Sino-Japanese journalism (*jitai*) to describe the dynamic posture or trajectory of an unfolding situation.

history.meaning: bodily bearing, demeanor, configuration
evolving state of affairs, critical situation
course of events, (usually serious) situation

事态.notes: Almost exclusively used for tense, deteriorating, or crisis situations (e.g., 控制事态 'contain the situation', 事态严重 'the situation is grave'), unlike neutral 情况.

事情.etymology: Originally a modifier-head compound (偏正结构) of 事 ('affair') + 情 (MC *dzjeng*, which in Old and Classical Chinese meant 'genuine reality, actual circumstances' before narrowing to 'emotion'). In Xunzi and Zhuangzi, 事情 meant 'the true reality of things'; in Tang–Song vernacular Mandarin, the compound generalized to 'matter, business' with tonal neutralization on the second syllable (`shìqing`).

history.meaning: the genuine nature and actual circumstances of affairs
affair, incident, piece of business
matter, affair, thing, situation

事情.notes: Watch for the Sino-Japanese false friend: Mandarin 事情 (`shìqing`, neutral second tone) means any general 'matter/thing to do', whereas Japanese 事情 (*jijō*) means 'underlying circumstances/reasons' (Mandarin 情况/内情).

rootFamily.gloss: truth, actual facts of a case

事故.etymology: Coordinative compound (并列结构) of 事 (MC *dzriH*, 'affair, untoward event') + 故 (MC *kuH*, 'cause, precedent, unforeseen mishap or calamity', cf. 变故 'sudden misfortune'). In Zhouli commentaries and Ming–Qing vernacular, 事故 ranged broadly from 'reason/excuse' to 'unexpected trouble'; in modern Chinese (reinforced by Japanese *jiko* 事故) it specialized to 'operational or traffic accident'.

history.meaning: cause, affair, or unforeseen mishap/calamity
accident, operational failure, mishap

事故.notes: In live television and stage production (*幕后之王*), 播出事故 ('broadcasting accident / on-air fiasco') and 舞台事故 ('stage mishap') are high-stakes industry terms.

二.etymology: Cardinal numeral 'two', written since oracle-bone inscriptions with two parallel horizontal strokes. Used in counting ('one, two, three'), ordinals (第二 'second'), floor/room numbers (二楼 'second floor'), and multi-digit numbers (十二 'twelve', 二十 'twenty').

history.meaning: numeral two; second

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 二 (via 萌典)

二人世界.etymology: Modern four-character modifier-head phrase (偏正结构) combining 二人 ('two persons, a couple') with 世界 ('world, private realm'). 世界 itself entered Medieval Chinese as a Buddhist Sanskrit calque of *lokadhātu*: 世 (MC *syejH*, 'generation, temporal flujo') + 界 (MC *kɛjH*, 'spatial boundary'). Coined in late 20th-century Cantonese/Taiwanese urban pop culture and absorbed across Mandarin to mean a romantic couple's uninterrupted private life.

history.meaning: spatiotemporal cosmos (calque of Sanskrit lokadhātu)
a romantic couple's private time/world apart from family or work

二人世界.notes: Commonly paired with verbs like 过 ('spend/enjoy', 过二人世界) or 打扰 ('intrude upon', 别打扰他们的二人世界) when busy professionals carve out date time.

rootFamily.gloss: solo/monopoly show; traditional duet folk opera

二位.etymology: Numeral-classifier pronominal compound (数量结构 used referentially) formed from 二 (OC *\*ni[j]-s*, MC *nyijH*, 'two') + 位 (MC *hjwijH*, originally ideogrammatic 人 'person' + 立 'standing at an assigned court rank'). From Tang–Song vernacular onward, 位 grammaticalized from 'seat of honor' into an honorific human classifier; using 二 (rather than colloquial 两) before 位 preserves a crisp, deferential formula of direct address.

history.meaning: assigned standing place at court; official rank or throne
you two honored guests/gentlefolk (deferential address)
the two of you, both of you (polite)

二位.notes: Exception to the usual rule requiring 两 before classifiers: 二位 sounds polished and deferential in hospitality or VIP reception ('the two of you'), whereas 两位 is the neutral polite count ('two people').

二十.etymology: Multiplicative decimal numeral compound (偏正/相乘数词结构) combining 二 (Old Chinese *\*ni[j]-s*, MC *nyijH*, 'two', depicted as two parallel horizontal tally strokes) and 十 (OC *\*t.[g]əp*, MC *dzyip*, 'ten', originally a vertical stroke representing a completed tenfold count). Inherited from Proto-Sino-Tibetan decimal morphology and attested since Shang oracle bone inscriptions (where it also appeared as the graphic ligature 廿 *niàn*).

history.meaning: two tens, twenty
twenty

二十.notes: In formal dates or literary titles you may still encounter the single-character ligature 廿 (*niàn*, 'twenty'), though spoken Mandarin universally uses 二十.

二十二.etymology: Multiplicative-additive decimal numeral compound (`[2 × 10] + 2`) composed of 二十 ('twenty', 二 'two' × 十 'ten') followed by the unit 二 ('two'). In Archaic Chinese inscriptions and classical prose, tens and units were often linked by 又 (*yòu*, 'and further', e.g., 二十又二); from Han times onward the conjunction dropped out, leaving transparent juxtapositional place-value syntax.

history.meaning: twenty and two
twenty-two

二十二.notes: Even when counting nouns with classifiers (where standalone '2' must become 两), numbers above ten strictly retain 二 in the units slot: 二十二个人 ('twenty-two people'), never *二十两个人.

二十八.etymology: Compound numeral of 二 ('two') + 十 ('ten') + 八 ('eight') = 'twenty-eight' (in traditional astronomy, also the number of lunar mansions 二十八宿).

history.meaning: two tens and eight = twenty-eight

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 二十八 (via 萌典)

二十号.etymology: Modifier-head nominal compound (偏正/序数结构) pairing the numeral 二十 ('twenty') with 号 (trad. 號, MC *hawH*, 'identifying mark, title, designation, number', from 号 'shout/call' + 虎 'tiger'). In late Qing treaty-port and Republican usage, 号 was adopted for numbered days of the Western/civil calendar month as the spoken counterpart to Literary Chinese 日 (*rì*).

history.meaning: name, command, identifying mark or shop sign
number twenty; the twentieth day of the month
the twentieth (of the month); No. 20

二十号.notes: Standard in spoken scheduling (e.g., 二十号录制 'taping on the 20th'), whereas written contracts, press releases, and broadcast graphics use 二十日 (`èrshí rì`).

二十四.etymology: Compound numeral of 二 ('two') + 十 ('ten') + 四 ('four') = 'twenty-four' (culturally familiar from the 24 hours of a day and the 24 solar terms 二十四节气 of the traditional lunisolar calendar).

history.meaning: two tens and four = twenty-four

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 二十四 (via 萌典)

二十年.etymology: Numeral-measure temporal phrase combining 二十 ('twenty') with 年 (OC *\*C.nˤi[ŋ]*, MC *nen*, archaic form 秊 depicting a person 人 bearing harvested grain 禾 on the back). Originally meaning 'grain harvest' in Shang oracle bones, 年 shifted by Western Zhou to 'annual cycle / year' and functions as an autonomous measure noun that takes numerals directly without an intervening classifier.

history.meaning: twenty ritual/harvest cycles (twenty years)
a span of twenty years

二十年.notes: Because 年 is already a self-contained temporal measure word, never insert 个 (*二十个年 is ungrammatical; compare 二十年 vs. 二十个月 'twenty months').

二号机.etymology: Modifier-head technical compound (偏正结构) built from 二号 (trad. 二號, 'number two, unit #2') modifying 机 (trad. 機, MC *kj+j*, originally the wooden trigger mechanism of a crossbow or weaving loom, broadened in modern Chinese and Sino-Japanese *nigōki* 二号機 to 'machine, apparatus, aircraft, or camera'). In television studio production, it arose as concise control-room ellipsis for 二号摄像机 ('Camera 2').

history.meaning: crossbow trigger, loom mechanism, pivotal device
Machine/Aircraft Unit No. 2 (industrial/aviation nomenclature)
Camera Two (in TV/film studios); Unit 2

二号机.notes: Core control-room jargon in *Behind the Scenes* (*幕后之王*): directors call 切二号机 ('cut to Camera 2!') alongside 机位 ('camera position/angle') and 主机 ('main A-camera').

sources.title: Wiktionary: 号机 / 號機 components

二手.etymology: '二手' (èrshǒu, secondhand) literally means 'second hand', tracing back to ancient concepts of intermediaries. In early texts, '手' (hand) often represented a person involved in an action or trade, such as a craftsman. The concept of something passing through a 'second hand' developed fully in pre-modern commerce to describe goods that were not bought directly from the producer but rather resold. By the 20th century, influenced partially by the English 'secondhand', it became the standard term for used goods in modern Chinese. It is now ubiquitous in contexts like cars, houses, and clothing.

history.meaning: firsthand

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 二手

二重唱.etymology: Modifier-head musical compound (偏正结构): 二 ('two') + 重 (MC *drjung*, read *chóng*, 'layered, doubled, -fold') + 唱 (MC *tshjangH*, 'to sing, lead in song'). Coined in Meiji Japan (*nijūshō* 二重唱) to translate European conservatory terminology (*duetto* / vocal duet) where two independent vocal lines unfold simultaneously, and adopted into modern Chinese musicological and stage vocabulary.

history.meaning: two-part vocal duet (calque of Italian duetto)
vocal duet (with two independent vocal parts)

二重唱.notes: In music shows, distinguish 二重唱 (formal two-part harmony duet), 对唱 (antiphonal call-and-response pop duet), and 二重奏 (instrumental duet).

二重奏.etymology: Modern musical compound of 二重 ('twofold, double', read èrchóng) + 奏 ('perform music, play an instrument', originally presenting something with both hands at court): 'instrumental duet'.

history.meaning: two-part instrumental performance; duet

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 二重奏 (via 萌典)

于.etymology: Allative/locative preposition (介词). In Shang oracle bones and Western Zhou bronzes, 于 (OC *\*ɢʷ(r)a*, MC *hju*, originally depicting a breath/wind instrument or phonetic loan) was the primary preposition meaning 'at, in, to, toward'. Warring States texts largely supplanted it with 於 (OC *\*ʔ(r)a*, originally a crow pictogram borrowed phonetically). Mainland Chinese script simplification merged functional 於 back into archaic 于.

history.meaning: to go to; at, in, toward, by (primary locative/allative coverb)
at, in, with respect to, than (literary preposition)
at, in, on, regarding (formal preposition and post-verbal complement)

于.notes: Marks formal or written register in modern Mandarin, appearing either in literary idioms (于公于私) or fused onto disyllabic verbs as a bound preposition (属于 'belong to', 取决于 'depend on', 善于 'excel at').

于公于私.etymology: Symmetric four-character Literary Chinese adverbial idiom (并列介宾结构) pairing two parallel prepositional phrases: 于公 (trad. 於公, 'in respect of public/official duty', 公 originally depicting dividing 八 shared goods openly 厶) and 于私 (trad. 於私, 'in respect of private/personal sentiment', 私 originally 'personally tended grain 禾'). Built on the classical 公/私 ('public impartiality vs. private interest') dichotomy central to Chinese statecraft.

history.meaning: whether judged by official duty or private obligation
both professionally and personally; from both business and personal standpoints

morphemes.meaning: in respect of, from the standpoint of
in respect of, from the standpoint of

于公于私.notes: A favorite workplace drama rhetorical opener: used when persuading a colleague or talent that a decision makes sense both for company business (公) and personal loyalty (私).

云海.etymology: Modifier-head poetic compound (偏正结构) in which 云 (trad. 雲, MC *hjun*, archaic 云 depicting curling vapor, later augmented with 雨 'rain') modifies 海 (MC *xojX*, 'sea, boundless expanse'), literally 'sea of clouds'. Celebrated in Tang–Song landscape poetry for mountain-top cloud vistas (such as Mount Huangshan), it is repurposed in *Behind the Scenes* (*幕后之王*) as a prestigious proper name (e.g., Yunhai Satellite TV 云海卫视 / Yunhai city).

history.meaning: boundless expanse of clouds viewed from high peaks or celestial realms
sea of clouds; Yunhai (fictional metropolis/broadcaster name)

云海.notes: Chinese provincial satellite networks (卫视) often bear poetic geographic names; fictional 云海 ('Sea of Clouds') evokes lofty stature and sweeping broadcast reach.

rootFamily.gloss: crowd of people ('people mountain, people sea')

互相.etymology: Coordinative adverbial compound (并列结构) uniting two synonymous reciprocity morphemes: 互 (MC *huH*, originally depicting a bamboo cord-winding reel with interlocking crosspieces, hence 'interlocking, reciprocally') and 相 (MC *sjang*, originally 目 'eye' + 木 'tree' = 'inspect', grammaticalized in Old Chinese into a reciprocal adverb 'each other'). Attested together from Six Dynasties and Tang prose as a reinforced disyllabic adverb.

history.meaning: mutually, each other (monosyllabic preverbal adverbs)
reciprocally, toward one another
mutually, each other (preverbal adverb)

互相.notes: Grammar trap: 互相 is strictly an adverb placed before verbs (互相帮助 'help each other'), whereas 相互 can also modify nouns (相互关系 'mutual relationship') and 彼此 can act as a pronoun ('each other').

五.etymology: Cardinal numeral 'five'. In Shang oracle-bone and Zhou bronze scripts, 五 was written as an X-shaped hourglass between two horizontal strokes (𠄡), representing the crossing of yin and yang or counting marks between heaven and earth.

history.meaning: crossing graph between two strokes = numeral five

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 五 (via 萌典)

五位.etymology: Numeral-classifier honorific phrase (数量结构) combining 五 (OC *\*C.ŋˤaʔ*, MC *nguX*, 'five', originally an intersecting X-shaped tally mark framed between heaven and earth lines 二) with 位 (MC *hjwijH*, 'court rank/seat', grammaticalized since Tang–Song vernacular as a deferential human classifier). Note that in Classical cosmology 五位 denoted the 'five elemental positions' or 'five noble ranks', whereas modern usage is transparently honorific counting.

history.meaning: five court ranks or five directional/elemental positions
five honored persons (polite numeral + classifier)

五位.notes: Standard stage-host and panel-show phrasing (e.g., 五位评委老师 'the five esteemed judges'); never combine 位 with self-referential nouns (*我们五位自己 sounds presumptuous—use 我们五个人).

rootFamily.gloss: seat, place (on a panel or venue)
guest of honor, panelist (often counted with 位)

五十.etymology: Multiplicative decimal numeral compound (相乘数词结构) composed of 五 (OC *\*C.ŋˤaʔ*, MC *nguX*, 'five') multiplying 十 (OC *\*t.[g]əp*, MC *dzyip*, 'ten'), literally 'five tens'. Attested in Shang oracle bone inscriptions (often written as a vertical ligature stacking 五 and 十) and preserved unchanged across three millennia of Chinese and Sino-Tibetan decimal counting.

history.meaning: five tens, fifty (including Confucius's 'at fifty I knew Heaven's mandate' 五十而知天命)
fifty

五十.notes: Culturally echoed in the idiom 五十步笑百步 ('retreating fifty paces and mocking one who retreated a hundred'—the pot calling the kettle black, from Mencius).

五十七.etymology: Multiplicative-additive decimal numeral compound (`[5 × 10] + 7`) joining 五十 ('fifty', 五 'five' × 十 'ten') with 七 (OC *\*[tsʰ]i[t]*, MC *tshit*, 'seven', originally a crosswise incision/tally mark +, later bent at the bottom hook to differentiate it graphically from 十 'ten'). Follows regular Sino-Tibetan decimal juxtaposition.

history.meaning: fifty and seven
fifty-seven

五十七.notes: In noisy studio intercoms or radio callouts, 七 (`qī`) is sometimes pronounced `guǎi` ('bent hook') in military/technical telecom code to avoid confusion with 一 (`yī`, pronounced `yāo`), though standard speech uses `wǔshíqī`.

rootFamily.gloss: Chinese Valentine's Day (7th night of 7th moon)

五千个.etymology: Numeral-classifier phrase (数量结构) combining 五千 ('five thousand', from 五 'five' × 千 OC *\*s.n̥ˤi[ŋ]*, MC *tshen* 'thousand', graphically 人 + stroke) with the universal classifier 个 (trad. 個/箇, MC *kaH*, originally denoting a single 'bamboo stalk' before bleaching in Tang–Song vernacular into the default general classifier for discrete entities).

history.meaning: five thousand (modifying nouns directly without classifier)
five thousand [items/units/people]

morphemes.meaning: general classifier for discrete items or people

五千个.notes: Unlike 2 (`两千`) where 二 switches to 两 before 千, 5 remains 五千; adding 个 (`gè`, neutral tone) either precedes a countable noun (五千个座位 '5,000 seats') or stands pronominally ('five thousand of them').

rootFamily.gloss: by all means;千萬 (ten million -> earnestly)

五千言.etymology: Modifier-head classical bibliographic compound (偏正结构) pairing 五千 ('five thousand') with 言 (MC *ngjon*, 'spoken word, saying, written character'). In Han and Six Dynasties philology, 言 regularly counted characters per line or text (e.g., 五言诗 'five-character-regulated verse'); 老子五千言 ('Laozi's Five-Thousand-Character Classic') became the canonical metonym for the *Daodejing*, later generalized to any pithy foundational canon.

history.meaning: Laozi's Daodejing (comprising roughly 5,000 characters)
the Daodejing; by extension, a concise, authoritative 5,000-character treatise or classic

五千言.notes: Alludes directly to Laozi's *Daodejing*—invoking 五千言 in modern dialogue lends philosophical gravitas, implying distilled wisdom packed into minimal words.

五折.etymology: Commercial discount term combining 五 ('five') + 折 ('fold, tenth part retained of the original price'). In Chinese retail pricing, 'N 折' means paying N/10 of the full price—so 五折 means '50% of the price = 50% off, half price'.

history.stage: Late Imperial to Modern commercial Mandarin
history.meaning: five-tenths of the original price = 50% off

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 五折 (via 萌典)

五星级.etymology: Compound modifier of 五 ('five') + 星 ('star') + 级 (級, 'grade, rank, tier', silk 纟 + 及): 'five-star rating/grade' (especially of luxury hotels or service standards).

history.meaning: five-star grade/level

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 五星级 (via 萌典)

五月.etymology: Calendar compound of 五 ('five, fifth') + 月 ('month, moon'): 'May' in the modern Gregorian calendar (and historically the fifth lunar month, home to the Dragon Boat Festival 端午节).

history.meaning: the fifth month; May

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 五月 (via 萌典)

五金.etymology: Compound of 五 ('five') + 金 ('metal'). In Classical Chinese (Wuyue Chunqiu, Hanshu), 五金 denoted the five traditional metals—gold, silver, copper, iron, and tin (金、银、铜、铁、锡); in modern commerce it refers collectively to 'hardware, metal fittings, and tools'.

history.meaning: the five metals (gold, silver, copper, iron, tin)
metal hardware and tools

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 五金 (via 萌典)

五金店.etymology: Compound noun combining 五金 ('hardware, metal tools and fittings') + 店 ('shop, store', shelter 广 + 占): 'hardware store'.

history.meaning: hardware store

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 五金店 (via 萌典)

亚麻.etymology: Botanical compound of 亚 (used in modern botanical nomenclature for *Linum usitatissimum*, true flax, distinguishing it from native ramie 苎麻 and hemp 大麻) + 麻 ('bast fiber plant; hemp/linen', pictograph of fiber bundles drying under a shed 广). It denotes both the flax plant and cool, breathable woven linen fabric.

history.meaning: hemp and bast textile fibers
flax; linen fabric

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 亚麻

些.etymology: Indefinite paucal quantifier and pluralizing classifier/particle. Graphically phono-semantic (此 *cǐ* phonetic + 二). First attested in the Warring States Chuci (*Zhaohun* 招魂) as a verse-final rhythmic particle read *suò*; in Late Medieval and Tang–Song vernacular (*bianwen* and Chan *yulu*), 些 (MC *sja* / *se*) emerged as an indefinite quantifier meaning 'a small amount, some, slightly'.

history.meaning: sentence-final rhythmic/modal incantation particle
a small quantity, a little bit, somewhat (cf. 些子, 些少)
some, a few (indefinite plural classifier); slightly (comparative suffix)

些.notes: Extremely versatile grammatical workhorse: attaches to demonstratives for plurals (这些 'these', 那些 'those'), follows 一 for 'some' (一些), and follows adjectives for mild comparatives (好些 'somewhat better').

rootFamily.gloss: some, a number of, a little

交.etymology: Pictograph in oracle-bone and bronze script of a standing person with crossed legs, yielding the core sense 'cross, intersect', and by extension 'exchange, hand over, deliver, pay, make friends with'.

morphemes.meaning: figure with crossed legs = intersect, hand over, exchange

history.meaning: cross; intersect; exchange; associate with
hand over; submit; pay; intersect

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 交 (via 萌典)

交代.etymology: Coordinative / serial-verb compound (并列/连动结构) uniting 交 (MC *kæw*, 'to cross, hand over, transfer', originally depicting a figure with crossed legs) and 代 (MC *dojH*, 'to replace, succeed in turn'). In Song–Qing officialdom, 交代 meant 'to hand over seals, ledgers, and unfinished business to an incoming successor'. Because an outgoing magistrate had to brief his successor and clear accounts, the word evolved into 'to instruct/brief', 'to give an accounting/closure', and 'to confess'.

history.meaning: to transfer official post, seals, and accounts to a successor
to brief/instruct; to account for or give closure; to confess

交代.notes: Rich drama polysemy: as a verb, 交代工作 ('brief/hand off tasks') or 交代清楚 ('explain/confess everything'); as a noun, 给观众一个交代 ('give the audience a satisfactory explanation/resolution'). Watch Japanese false friend 交代 (*kōtai*), which kept only the literal 'shift change/replacement' sense.

rootFamily.gloss: to hand over, transfer (work or custody)

cognates.meaning: to report completion of an errand

交差.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound originating in Ming–Qing bureaucratic vernacular: 交 (jiāo, Old Chinese *kraw, 'to cross, hand over, submit') + 差 (chāi, Middle Chinese tsrhje, 'official errand, corvée commission', elliptical for 差事 chāishi). Junior runners and magistrates' clerks literally 'handed back their commission' to a superior upon completing an assigned dispatch; in modern Mandarin it generalized to accounting for any delegated duty or meeting expectations.

history.meaning: to dispatch an envoy; an official corvée or errand
to report back to a magistrate upon completing an official commission
to report completion of a task; to fulfill an assignment satisfactorily

交差.notes: Note the reading chāi (not chā or chà), preserved in role/errand words like 出差 ('go on a business trip') and 差事; in workplace and TV production contexts, 不好交差 means 'hard to explain oneself to the boss'.

交换.etymology: A coordinative compound (trad. 交換, jiāohuàn) uniting 交 ('to cross, transfer reciprocally') and 换/換 ('to swap, trade, change hands', phono-semantic with 扌 'hand' + 奐). Attested as a verb in Tang–Song Literary Chinese for mutual bartering of goods or posts, it was standardized as both noun and verb in late-19th-century East Asian modernity alongside Meiji Japanese 交換 (kōkan) to render Western economic and institutional 'exchange'.

history.meaning: to trade or barter items reciprocally
economic, diplomatic, or technical exchange (Meiji lexical standardization)
exchange, trade, swap (of goods, opinions, or data)

交换.notes: Requires mutual reciprocity between two parties (e.g., 交换意见 'exchange views', 交换条件 'quid pro quo'), unlike 更换 which means unilateral replacement.

交接.etymology: A coordinative verb compound of 交 (jiāo, 'to cross, meet, hand over') and 接 (jiē, 'to join, connect, receive'). In Classical Chinese (e.g., Liji and dynastic histories), 交接 meant 'to border upon, join together, or associate socially'. In administrative Mandarin, its two constituents polarized into complementary roles of a single transfer event: the outgoing person hands over (交) and the incoming successor receives (接) responsibilities or assets.

history.meaning: to come into contact, connect, or associate socially
to transfer and receive official seals and post duties
to hand over work, shifts, or institutional authority

交接.notes: Standard corporate and production-team term for onboarding/offboarding handovers (工作交接 'work handover', 交接班 'shift handover').

rootFamily.gloss: take over duties or a role
take over a shift or position
hand over, brief someone on duties

交朋友.etymology: A separable verb-object (VO) phrase built from 交 (jiāo, 'to associate reciprocally, befriend', originally an oracle-bone pictograph of a person with crossed legs signifying intersection) and the disyllabic noun 朋友 (péngyou, 'friend'). 朋友 is itself an archaic pre-Qin coordinative compound pairing 朋 ('fellow student or peer cohort', originally strings of cowrie shells) with 友 ('comrade, ally', oracle-bone graph of two right hands acting in concert).

history.meaning: to cultivate friendships with peers
to make friends, enter into friendship
