交朋友.notes: As a separable VO construction, modifiers and aspect markers insert between 交 and 朋友 (e.g., 交了几个好朋友 'made several good friends', 交个朋友 'let's become friends').

交流.etymology: Originally a modifier-head verbal compound in Classical Chinese: 交 (jiāo, 'mutually, crisscrossing') + 流 (liú, 'to flow'), describing converging rivers or streams flowing across one another. During the Meiji era in Japan, 交流 (kōryū) was adapted first in physics for 'alternating current' (AC) and then figuratively for two-way intellectual and cultural interaction, re-entering 20th-century Mandarin as a graphic return loan for interpersonal communication.

history.meaning: waters or streams flowing together in crisscrossing channels
alternating electric current; reciprocal cultural exchange
to exchange ideas, communicate, interact across groups

交流.notes: Implies two-way, egalitarian sharing of ideas or creative insights (深入交流 'in-depth exchange'), whereas 沟通 emphasizes bridging a gap or resolving misunderstandings.

交给.etymology: A verb-complement compound (trad. 交給, jiāogěi) formed in Mandarin vernacular from 交 (jiāo, 'to hand over, deliver, entrust') + 给/給 (gěi, originally 'to supply amply' in Classical Chinese, grammaticalized in Mandarin into the primary dative/recipient verb-complement 'to'). Together they form a transitive predicate requiring an indirect object recipient right after 给, marking transfer of custody or responsibility.

history.meaning: to hand over, consign to someone
to hand over to, entrust a task or item to (a recipient)

交给.notes: Must be followed immediately by the recipient (e.g., 把这个项目交给你 'entrust this project to you'); use the disposal marker 把 when placing the transferred object before the verb.

交还.etymology: Compound verb of 交 ('hand over, deliver') + 还 (還, read huán, 'return, give back'): 'hand back, return (something borrowed or held) to its owner'.

history.meaning: hand over and return; give back

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 交还 (via 萌典)

产业.etymology: A coordinative compound (trad. 產業, chǎnyè) combining 产/產 ('to give birth, produce, property') and 业/業 ('patrimony, occupation, estate', originally depicting a wooden rack supporting ritual bells). In Han-dynasty histories such as Shiji and Hanshu, 產業 denoted private family real estate and livelihood. In Meiji Japan, 産業 (sangyō) was semantically repurposed to translate macroeconomic 'industry', returning to modern Mandarin for entire commercial sectors.

history.meaning: family estate, household property, and livelihood
economic sector, productive industry
economic industry or commercial sector (e.g., cultural/media industry)

产业.notes: Refers to macro-level economic sectors including service and entertainment fields (文化产业 'cultural industry', 影视产业 'film & TV industry'), whereas 工业 specifically means manufacturing/heavy industry.

产出.etymology: A verb-directional/resultative compound (trad. 產出, chǎnchū) composed of 产/產 ('to give birth to, breed, generate') + 出 ('to emerge, come forth'). Literally 'to bring forth by producing', it underwent nominalization in 20th-century economic and industrial Mandarin—calquing the conceptual pairing of English 'input and output' (投入产出)—to denote measurable yield, creative deliverables, or economic output.

history.meaning: to bear forth, yield natural products
economic or creative output, production yield

产出.notes: Heavily used in media production and business analytics both as a noun ('yield/deliverables', 高产出 'high output') and a verb ('to churn out content'), often paired with 投入 ('input/investment').

产品.etymology: A modifier-head compound (trad. 產品, chǎnpǐn) formed from 产/產 ('produced, yielded') modifying 品 ('article, grade, commodity', originally three mouths 吅+口 representing a multitude of vessels or items classified into grades). Coined in modern Chinese commercial and industrial vocabulary during the late 19th to early 20th centuries to designate standardized goods, creative works, or software offerings.

history.meaning: classified articles; regional natural produce
manufactured commodity, commercial or creative product

产品.notes: In modern Chinese tech and entertainment industries, 产品 extends beyond physical goods to shows, apps, and formats (综艺产品 'variety-show product', 产品经理 'product manager').

产权.etymology: Legal and economic compound of 产 (產, 'property, estate, production') + 权 (權, 'right, legal title, authority', originally a sliding scale weight): 'property rights, ownership title'.

history.meaning: property ownership; title to real estate or assets

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 产权 (via 萌典)

产生.etymology: A coordinative verb compound (trad. 產生, chǎnshēng) uniting two near-synonymous Classical Chinese verbs of biological nativity: 产/產 ('to give birth, breed') and 生 ('to sprout, bear, live', depicting a plant shoot emerging from soil). Attested in Warring States and Han prose (such as Xunzi and Shiji) for natural generation of living creatures and resources, it broadened in modern Mandarin to abstract causation ('to give rise to, engender').

history.meaning: to give birth to offspring; natural generation of flora, fauna, or minerals
to produce, engender, give rise to (effects, ideas, conflicts, or feelings)

产生.notes: Takes abstract objects (产生影响 'produce an impact', 产生分歧 'give rise to disagreements'), never concrete manufactured goods—use 生产 for factory or studio production.

享受.etymology: A coordinative verb compound pairing 享 (xiǎng, originally an oracle-bone pictograph 亯 of an ancestral temple pavilion where sacrificial food was presented and partaken of) with 受 (shòu, 'to receive, accept', showing two hands passing a boat/vessel). In Literary Chinese, 享受 meant 'to receive and partake of imperial rank, tribute, or Heaven-sent blessings'; in modern Mandarin it secularized into savoring comfort, leisure, or aesthetic pleasure.

history.meaning: to receive sacrificial offerings, official emoluments, or karmic blessings
to enjoy comforts, savor life, or experience pleasure (verb and noun)

morphemes.meaning: to partake of offerings or blessings

享受.notes: Functions as both a transitive verb (享受生活 'savor life', 享受过程 'enjoy the process') and a noun ('a treat/luxury', 视觉享受 'a visual treat'); contrast 享有 which is strictly 'to hold/enjoy rights or prestige'.

cognates.meaning: to consume, enjoy the use of

享用.etymology: A coordinative/serial-verb compound combining 享 (xiǎng, 'to partake of sacrificial banquets or blessings') and 用 (yòng, 'to use, consume, partake of food/drink'). Emerging in Song–Ming vernacular literature (such as Journey to the West and Water Margin), it initially referred deferentially to deities, monarchs, or honored guests partaking of banquets and tribute, retaining an elevated, courteous register in modern hospitality.

history.meaning: (of gods, rulers, or elders) to partake of tribute or banquet dishes
to enjoy food, drink, or fine facilities (polite register)

享用.notes: Polite hospitality verb typically reserved for meals, beverages, or VIP amenities (请慢用 / 请享用美食 'please enjoy your meal'), whereas 享受 covers emotional and experiential enjoyment.

亮.etymology: Adjective and verb meaning 'bright, shining, clear; resonant (of voice); become light'. Evolved in Han–Medieval script as a graphic variant related to 諒/明 (combining 高 'high' top + 儿/几 'human legs' standing in an open, elevated, well-lit place).

history.meaning: bright; clear; shine; resonant

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 亮 (via 萌典)

亮堂堂.etymology: An expressive ABB-pattern state adjective built from 亮 (liàng, 'bright, clear, luminous') and the reduplicated suffixal vividizer 堂堂 (tángtáng, evoking the spaciousness and open light of a main hall 堂). Mandarin productively attaches reduplicated disyllabic endings to single-syllable adjectives to convey sensory warmth and immediacy (compare 暖洋洋 'toasty warm', 香喷喷 'fragrantly steaming'). Here 亮堂堂 specifically pictures a room or courtyard flooded with open, cheerful light.

morphemes.meaning: reduplicated vivid suffix evoking an open, sunlit hall

history.meaning: bright and spacious (of rooms or courtyards)
brightly lit; cheerful and airy

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 亮堂堂

亮点.etymology: A modifier-head noun compound (trad. 亮點, liàngdiǎn) formed from 亮 ('bright, luminous, shining') + 点/點 ('spot, speck, point', originally 黑 'black' + phonetic 占 'speck of ink'). Used literally in 20th-century optics, photography, and cathode-ray displays for a 'luminous spot', it expanded metaphorically in 1990s Chinese media, TV production, and business journalism—paralleling English 'highlight' or 'bright spot'—for a standout attraction or selling point.

history.meaning: spot of light in optics, astronomy, or display screens
standout highlight, selling point, or memorable moment in a show or plan

亮点.notes: Ubiquitous pitch-room buzzword in Chinese television and marketing (节目最大的亮点 'the show's biggest highlight/hook'), paired alongside痛点 ('pain point') and 卖点 ('selling point').

亮相.etymology: A separable verb-object (VO) compound originating in Beijing Opera (京剧 Jīngjù) stagecraft: 亮 (liàng, 'to flash, display clearly in the light') + 相 (xiàng, 'stage posture, facial expression, outward form'). When a principal character enters the stage or finishes an acrobatic sequence, they freeze sharply to 'display their pose' to rhythmic percussion. From mid-20th-century theater jargon it generalized to any public debut, red-carpet appearance, or product unveiling.

history.meaning: actor freezing in a dramatic sculptural pose on stage upon entrance or climax
to make a public debut, appear before media, or unveil one's stance

亮相.notes: Note the fourth-tone reading xiàng ('appearance/pose', as in 照相 'take a photo'); widely used in entertainment journalism for stars, shows, or new products debuting publicly (首次亮相 'make a debut appearance').

rootFamily.gloss: show one's trump card or true stance
reveal one's face, appear in public

亲.etymology: Monosyllabic root (trad. 親, qīn) from Old Chinese *tsʰin, descending from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *tsjən ~ *ŋjən ('kinsman, close relative'). The traditional graph 親 is a phono-semantic compound combining 見 ('to see face-to-face') with phonetic 亲/榛 (*tsʰin); Simplified Chinese retains the left component 亲 alone. From its core noun sense of 'parents / blood kin', it developed attributive senses of 'one's own by blood', 'intimate/dear', and adverbial 'in person'.

history.meaning: parents, blood kin; to keep close, cherish affectionately
one's own, close, dear; to kiss; e-commerce term of endearment ('dear')

morphemes.meaning: blood kin, one's own, close, dear (trad. 親)

亲.notes: Besides 'one's own' (亲妹妹 'biological younger sister') and 'close', 亲 is also read qìng in 亲家 ('in-laws') and became famous in modern Chinese internet culture via Taobao customer service addressing buyers as 亲 ('dear!').

cognates.meaning: speaking directly with one's own mouth (literary)

亲口.etymology: A modifier-head adverbial compound (trad. 親口, qīnkǒu) combining 亲/親 ('one's own, in person') + 口 ('mouth', pictograph of an open mouth). Attested from Tang–Song vernacular narratives and legal/historical records to underscore firsthand oral testimony—that a statement, confession, or promise came directly 'from someone's own lips' rather than through hearsay or intermediaries.

history.meaning: with one's own mouth (in direct speech or imperial decree)
personally, with one's own lips (modifying verbs of speaking or promising)

亲口.notes: Used exclusively before speech-act verbs such as 说 ('say'), 承认 ('admit'), 答应 ('promise'), or 告诉 ('tell') to stress undeniable firsthand confirmation (他亲口答应的 'he promised it with his own lips').

亲密.etymology: A coordinative adjective compound (trad. 親密, qīnmì) pairing 亲/親 ('close as kin, affectionate') with 密 ('dense, tight, leaving no gap', originally a roof 宀 over phonetic 必 over 山 'hidden mountain recess'). Attested since Ban Gu's Hanshu (Book of Han) to describe trusted courtiers or companions whose bond is so close that nothing can come between them.

history.meaning: closely trusted, without distance between ruler and minister or kin
intimate, close (of friendships, romantic relationships, or alliances)

亲密.notes: Describes emotional or relational closeness between people or groups (关系亲密 'close relationship', 亲密无间 'inseparably close'); for physical closeness or close monitoring of events, use 密切 instead.

亲手.etymology: Adverbial compound of 亲 (親, 'in person, oneself, close') + 手 ('hand'): 'with one's own hands, personally'. Attested from Tang–Song poetry and prose.

history.meaning: with one's own hands; personally

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 亲手 (via 萌典)

亲爱.etymology: A coordinative compound (trad. 親愛, qīn'ài) uniting 亲/親 ('to treat with familial closeness') and 爱/愛 ('to cherish, hold dear', traditional graph depicting a heart 心 inside a figure looking back reluctantly 夊). In pre-Qin philosophy (Mozi, Xunzi), 親愛 functioned as a transitive verb 'to love and cherish affectionately'. In modern Chinese, reinforced by translation of European letter salutations ('Dear...'), it became the standard attributive adjective 'dear, beloved' (亲爱的).

history.meaning: to feel familial affection for and cherish (one's kin or subjects)
dear, beloved (epistolary salutation, public address, and romantic vocative)

亲爱.notes: Almost always appears with structural particle 的 (亲爱的观众朋友们 'Dear viewers!'); used standalone as a noun phrase, 亲爱的 serves as the romantic vocative 'honey / darling'.

亲笔.etymology: A modifier-head compound (trad. 親筆, qīnbǐ) formed from 亲/親 ('in person, one's own') + 笔/筆 ('writing brush, pen; handwriting', from 竹 'bamboo shaft' + 聿 'hand holding a stylus'). Established in Tang–Song imperial administration and literati culture to certify edicts, letters, or inscriptions drafted in the author's own calligraphy rather than drafted by a secretariat scribe (代筆).

history.meaning: written with the emperor's or official's own brush; holographic manuscript
in one's own handwriting; personally signed or written

亲笔.notes: Used both adverbially before writing verbs (亲笔写信 'write a letter in one's own hand') and attributively in showbiz/collectibles (亲笔签名 'hand-signed autograph').

rootFamily.gloss: write as a ghostwriter or proxy

亲自.etymology: A coordinative reflexive adverb (trad. 親自, qīnzì) pairing 亲/親 ('personally, firsthand') with 自 ('oneself', originally an oracle-bone pictograph of a human nose—speakers in antiquity pointed to their nose to indicate 'self'). Attested since Warring States and Han historical prose (Zhanguoce, Shiji) to highlight that a ruler, general, or senior figure undertakes an action in person rather than delegating it to subordinates.

history.meaning: (of a sovereign or commander) in person, by oneself
in person, personally (adverb preceding action verbs)

亲自.notes: Carries pragmatic prestige: it normally implies someone of status, authority, or busyness taking the trouble to do something themselves (总监亲自审片 'the chief director reviewed the cut in person').

亲自出马.etymology: A four-character adverbial-predicate phrase (trad. 親自出馬, qīnzì chūmǎ) combining the reflexive adverb 亲自 ('in person') with the vernacular military VO compound 出马/出馬 (chū 'to ride forth' + mǎ 'warhorse'). In Yuan–Ming military romances such as Romance of the Three Kingdoms, 出馬 meant a veteran general mounting his steed to enter combat; paired with 親自, it idiomatically portrays a boss, master, or heavyweight stepping directly into the fray.

history.meaning: to mount one's warhorse and ride forth into battle

history.form: 親自出馬 / 亲自出马
history.meaning: for a senior figure or expert to step in and handle a matter personally

亲自出马.notes: Lively, slightly dramatic idiom used when junior staff cannot resolve a high-stakes negotiation or crisis and a top producer, executive, or mentor takes charge personally.

rootFamily.gloss: take the stage, step forward to handle something
go into battle, take the field
at the very start of taking action (lit. 'as soon as the horse goes out')

人.etymology: Foundational pictograph (象形字) attested from Shang oracle bones onward, showing the side profile of a standing human figure with arm and leg: 'person, human being, people, someone else'.

history.meaning: side profile of a standing human = person, people

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 人 (via 萌典)

人事.etymology: A modifier-head noun compound combining 人 (rén, 'human') and 事 (shì, 'affairs, service, official business'). In Classical Chinese (Mengzi, Shiji), 人事 contrasted 'human effort and social affairs' against Heaven's decree (天命), and also meant worldly consciousness (不省人事 'unconscious'). In Meiji Japan (人事 jinji) and 20th-century Chinese institutional administration, it specialized to organizational staffing, appointments, and 'personnel / HR'.

history.meaning: human affairs and effort (contrasted with Heaven); social etiquette and consciousness
organizational appointments, dismissals, and personnel administration
human resources (HR department or staff), personnel matters

人事.notes: In everyday office Mandarin, 人事 refers both to HR matters (人事变动 'personnel shake-up', 人事部 'HR department') and colloquially to an HR specialist, while preserving older idioms like 不省人事 ('unconscious') and 尽人事 ('do everything humanly possible').

rootFamily.gloss: party involved in an affair or case

人人.etymology: Distributive nominal reduplication of 人 (rén, Old Chinese *njin, 'person, human being', originally an oracle-bone profile of a standing human figure). Reduplicating a monosyllabic count noun to express universal quantification ('every single X') is a foundational Sinitic morphological rule attested continuously since the Shijing (Book of Odes) and Mengzi (人人親其親 'everyone cherishes their own kin').

history.meaning: every person, each individual universally
everyone, everybody (typically in subject position)

人人.notes: Grammatically restricted chiefly to subject or topic position, often paired with 都 or 有责 (人人皆知 'known to everyone', 人人平等 'everyone is equal'); it cannot stand as a post-verbal object (use 每个人 instead).

人力资源.etymology: A four-character modern compound (trad. 人力資源, rénlì zīyuán) nested from two modifier-head compounds: 人力 ('human labor/strength', attested since Classical Chinese: 人 'human' + 力 'sinew/strength') modifying 资源/資源 ('resources', Meiji/modern Sino-compound from 資 'capital, material endowment' + 源 'water springhead, source'). Coined in late-20th-century Chinese management discourse as a precise lexical calque of English 'human resources' (HR).

history.meaning: human physical strength or labor power
natural or economic source capital ('resources')
human resources (workforce talent capital and corporate HR management)

人力资源.notes: More formal and strategic than 人事: corporate titles favor 人力资源部 ('Human Resources Department', often abbreviated 人资 or English 'HR') to emphasize talent development over mere administrative record-keeping.

人员.etymology: A collective noun compound (trad. 人員, rényuán) combining 人 ('person') and 员/員 ('round ding-cauldron -> count/quota -> official on a roster'). Beginning in Tang–Song civil service administration, 員 served as the classifier and noun for appointed officials within a fixed quota (員額). By the late Qing and Meiji eras, 人員 solidified as an institutional collective noun for 'staff members, personnel' assigned to a role or unit.

history.meaning: appointed officials; allotted staffing quota
personnel, staff members, crew attached to a function or organization

morphemes.meaning: member of a roster, official, quota unit (trad. 員)

人员.notes: Functions as a collective/non-count-style noun modified by role nouns rather than individual numerals (工作人员 'working staff/crew', 演职人员 'cast and crew'—say 一名工作人员, never *一个人员).

人家.etymology: Originally a transparent modifier-head noun phrase in Classical Chinese: 人 (rén, 'people') + 家 (jiā, 'household, family, dwelling', showing a pig 豕 under a roof 宀), meaning 'human dwellings or someone's family' (read rénjiā). In Tang–Song vernacular poetry and storytelling, unstressed 人家 (rénjia) underwent pronominalization: first referring to 'other people / someone else', then to a specific third party ('him/her/them'), and finally by pragmatic self-distancing to the speaker ('me').

history.meaning: human households, families, inhabited dwellings
other people, someone else (indefinite third-person pronoun)
others; he/she/they (anaphoric); 'me' (colloquial/affective first-person)

人家.notes: Pronounced with neutral tone rénjia as a pronoun ('others / him / her / me', e.g., 别笑话人家 'don't laugh at them/me'), vs. full tone rénjiā when meaning 'household' or 'a woman's prospective husband's family'.

人尽其用.etymology: A four-character Literary Chinese clause-idiom (trad. 人盡其用, rén jìn qí yòng) condensed by blending two parallel maxims from Sun Yat-sen's famous 1894 reformist memorial to Li Hongzhang (上李鴻章書): 人能盡其才 ('people can exhaust their talent') and 物能盡其用 ('things can exhaust their utility'). Structurally topic-comment: 人 ('each person') + 尽/盡 ('exhausts, fulfills to the utmost', originally a hand brushing an empty vessel clean) + 其 ('their') + 用 ('practical function/use').

history.form: 人能盡其才，物能盡其用
history.meaning: people fulfill their talents to the utmost, and materials fulfill their utility to the utmost
to deploy every person so their abilities are put to optimal use

morphemes.meaning: to exhaust, bring to the fullest (trad. 盡)

人尽其用.notes: Popular in HR and producer-team leadership talk; purist editors traditionally prefer 人尽其才 ('let people fulfill their talent', paired with 物尽其用 for objects), though 人尽其用 is now thoroughly established in workplace Mandarin.

rootFamily.gloss: put everyone's talent to full use (canonical form)
make the best use of everything

cognates.meaning: sign of people, human figure or silhouette
human shadow or trace of a person

人影.etymology: A modifier-head noun compound pairing 人 (rén, 'person') with 影 (yǐng, 'shadow, silhouette, reflection', formed in early medieval script by adding 彡 'light rays/pattern' to classical 景 *krang 'sunlight/shadow'). Celebrated in Tang poetry (e.g., Wang Wei's 空山不見人 'in empty hills no one is seen' alongside衣香人影 'fragrant robes and human silhouettes'), it came to denote not just a literal shadow, but the faintest visible trace of a person's presence.

history.meaning: a person's cast shadow or fleeting silhouette
human figure; the slightest visible sign or trace of someone

人影.notes: Frequently appears in emphatic negative constructions (连个人影都没看见 'didn't see so much as a soul/shadow', 不见人影 'nowhere to be seen') when someone vanishes or fails to show up on set.

rootFamily.gloss: figure viewed from behind or afar

cognates.meaning: people's hearts, public sentiment, human nature

人心.etymology: A modifier-head compound of 人 (rén, 'people, human beings') + 心 (xīn, 'heart-mind', ancient pictograph of the cardiac organ, regarded in Chinese antiquity as the seat of both emotion and cognition). A cornerstone of pre-Qin political philosophy in the Shangshu and Mengzi, where winning or losing 人心 ('the collective allegiance and morale of the populace') determines the Mandate of Heaven, alongside individual human conscience and hidden motives.

history.meaning: popular allegiance, collective morale, or unpredictable human desires (contrasted with 道心)
public sentiment, team morale, or someone's inner feelings and loyalty

人心.notes: Key leadership collocations include 得人心 ('win people's hearts/loyalty'), 收买人心 ('buy off loyalties'), and 深入人心 ('resonate deeply with the public').

人情.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 人 (rén, 'human') and 情 (qíng, 'innate emotional disposition, genuine feeling', phono-semantic with 心 'heart' + phonetic 青). In the Liji (Book of Rites), 人情 denoted the seven natural human emotions common to all mortals. Over imperial social history, it evolved into a foundational Chinese sociological concept governing reciprocal interpersonal warmth, social tact, gift-giving etiquette, and transferable 'personal favors'.

history.meaning: universal innate human emotions, desires, and sensibilities
social reciprocity, ceremonial gift obligations, and interpersonal goodwill
personal favor, social credit/debt, human warmth or sensibility

人情.notes: Treated almost like a social currency in Chinese professional and media networks: you can 'owe a favor' (欠人情), 'do someone a favor' (卖/做个人情), 'repay a favor' (还人情), or call someone 'warm/humane' (有人情味).

人情味.etymology: A three-character modifier-head compound built on Classical Chinese 人情 (rénqíng, 'human feelings, social reciprocity'; attested in the Book of Rites / 礼记) suffixed with 味 (wèi, 'taste, flavour, aesthetic quality'). Literally 'the flavour of human sentiment', its modern lexicalized compound form was popularized alongside Meiji–Taishō Japanese 人情味 (ninjōmi) and adopted widely into modern Mandarin to denote genuine interpersonal warmth as opposed to cold bureaucratic procedure.

history.meaning: natural human emotions and desires (Book of Rites)
social obligation, personal favour, worldly reciprocity
human warmth, empathetic touch, personal kindness

人情味.notes: Frequently paired with 有 or 充满 (有人情味, 'humane/warm-hearted') or 缺乏/没 (没人情味, 'cold and impersonal'), especially in workplace and TV production critiques.

人手.etymology: A modifier-head synecdochic compound combining 人 (rén, 'person') + 手 (shǒu, 'hand'). In Literary Chinese, 人手 originally meant either 'a human hand' or 'into everyone's hands' (e.g., 人手一册, 'a copy in every person's hand'). By vernacular Tang–Song and Ming–Qing Mandarin, 'hands of people' underwent metonymic shift—parallel to English 'all hands on deck'—to denote available workers or staffing capacity on a job.

history.meaning: a person's physical hand; each person's hand
available workers, staffing, manpower

人手.notes: Commonly used in production crew logistics with 不足 or 不够 (人手不够, 'short-handed') and 调配 (调配人手, 'deploy crew/staff'); note that in 人手一份 it retains the older distributive sense 'one copy per person'.

人才.etymology: A modifier-head compound from Classical Chinese 人 (rén, 'person') + 才 (cái, 'natural endowment, timber, capability'; historically interchangeable with 材, 'fine timber'). Attested in the Book of Poetry (诗经) commentaries and Mencius-era discourse on statecraft, where cultivating capable individuals was likened to nurturing straight timber for palace beams; it shifted from 'human ability' in the abstract to countable 'talented individuals, skilled professionals'.

history.meaning: human endowment, moral and practical calibre (also Handsome bearing in vernacular fiction)
talented person, skilled specialist or creative professional

人才.notes: In media and corporate Mandarin, 挖人才 ('poach talent') and 留住人才 ('retain talent') are staple collocations; spoken ironically (真是个“人才”), it mocks someone's bizarre antics.

人气.etymology: An orthographic return loan (graphic reborrowing) in its showbiz sense from Japanese 人気 (ninki, 'public favour, popularity'), superimposed onto native Chinese 人气 (rénqì, simplified from 人氣). In Classical and vernacular Chinese, 人气 meant 'human breath, scent, or presence of living people' (modifier-head: 人 'human' + 气 'vital vapour/aura'). In Edo–Meiji Japan, 人気 came to mean the collective mood and favour of theatre/sumo audiences; this entertainment sense entered Taiwan and Hong Kong media in the late 20th century before sweeping Mainland showbiz Mandarin.

history.meaning: human breath, bodily aura, or lively presence of inhabitants
public sentiment, box-office appeal, popularity
celebrity popularity, fan following, buzz

人气.notes: Essential entertainment-industry jargon (攒人气 'build buzz', 人气偶像 'popular idol', 超高人气 'sky-high popularity'); in real estate or restaurant contexts, 有人气 still echoes the older sense of 'bustling foot traffic'.

人物.etymology: Originally a coordinative compound in Classical Chinese combining 人 (rén, 'humans') + 物 (wù, 'living beings, myriad things'), meaning 'humans and other creatures' (attested in Histories of the Han and Three Kingdoms). During the Wei–Jin 'pure conversation' (清谈) tradition of character appraisal (e.g., Liu Shao's 人物志, Treatise on Human Abilities), the compound narrowed via hendiadys to 'notable human figures and their qualities', later extending in drama and fiction criticism to 'fictional character' as well as 'VIP / big shot'.

history.meaning: humans and myriad creatures alike
notable personage; human character and bearing (Wei–Jin period)
public figure, VIP; dramatic or fictional character

人物.notes: Carries two key media senses: a prominent player (大人物 'big shot', 领军人物 'leading figure') and a scripted persona or show guest profile (人物设定 / 人设 'character persona').

rootFamily.gloss: character persona (abbr. of 人物设定)

人生.etymology: Compound of 人 ('human being') + 生 ('life, lifetime, living'): 'human life, one's lifetime and experience'. Attested since Classical philosophy and Han poetry (e.g., 人生天地间 'human life between heaven and earth').

history.stage: Classical & Han Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: human life; one's lifetime

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 人生 (via 萌典)

cognates.word: 人生大事 (jan4 sang1 daai6 si6)

人生大事.etymology: A four-character modifier-head phrase composed of 人生 (rénshēng, 'human life', itself subject-predicate 'a person lives') modifying 大事 (dàshì, 'great affair, momentous matter', attested in Zuo Zhuan: 国之大事 'the great affairs of state'). In vernacular Chinese family discourse from the late imperial era onward, 'the great affair of human life' became an idiomatic euphemism specifically for marriage and settling down, alongside broader milestones of birth, career, and death.

history.meaning: momentous affairs of state—specifically sacrifice and warfare (Zuo Zhuan)
pivotal milestone of a person's life, euphemistically matrimony

人生大事.notes: When parents or colleagues ask when someone will 解决人生大事 ('settle their major life matter'), they almost always mean getting married rather than career achievements.

人类.etymology: A modifier-head compound of 人 (rén, 'human') + 类 (lèi, simplified from 類, 'kind, category, species'). Although attested sporadically in Literary Chinese texts (such as Han–Tang prose contrasting 'the category of humans' with beasts or spirits), its modern scientific and philosophical sense—translating English 'humankind / humanity' and taxonomic Homo—was standardized via Meiji Japanese 人類 (jinrui) and disseminated across late Qing Mandarin intellectual writing.

history.meaning: the class or kind of human beings (as opposed to birds and beasts)
humanity, humankind as a biological and universal collective

人类.notes: Refers to the human species collectively (全人类 'all humankind'); in colloquial banter, 反人类 ('anti-human / inhumane') is playfully used for awful designs or gruelling work schedules.

rootFamily.gloss: peer, one of the same kind

人行道.etymology: Three-character municipal compound of 人 ('person; pedestrian') + 行 ('walk; travel', originally a four-way street crossroads pictograph) + 道 ('road; path; way', movement radical 辶 + 首 'head'). Coined in modern urban planning to distinguish raised pedestrian sidewalks from vehicle lanes (车道).

history.meaning: pedestrian sidewalk
pavement; sidewalk

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 人行道

人身攻击.etymology: A four-character modifier-head legal and rhetorical calque combining 人身 (rénshēn, coordinative/modifier-head 'a person's own body and persona') + 攻击 (gōngjī, coordinative verb-noun 'assault and strike', simplified from 攻擊). Shaped in modern East Asian public discourse alongside Meiji–Taishō Japanese 人身攻撃 (jinshin kōgeki) to translate Latin argumentum ad hominem and Western English 'personal attack'—criticizing an opponent's private character or appearance rather than their work or argument.

history.meaning: the human body/person; military assault (attested separately in Classical histories)
ad hominem attack, character assassination in debate or media

人身攻击.notes: Widely used in online fandom wars, press conferences, and talent-show judging (进行人身攻击 'launch a personal attack'); contrast with 对事不对人 ('address the issue, not the person').

人选.etymology: A compound of 人 (rén, 'person') + 选 (xuǎn, simplified from 選, 'select, choose'). Structurally an object-preposed / modifier-head nominalization ('selection of personnel' -> 'the person selected'), attested in Tang–Song bureaucratic prose regarding civil-service appointments and reinforced in modern Mandarin administrative and casting usage to mean a candidate or nominee under consideration for a specific role.

history.meaning: selection and appointment of officials; distinguished appointees
candidate, prospective choice for a post or role

人选.notes: Unlike 候选人 (a formal election or award 'nominee'), 人选 refers to whoever is suitable for a slot in casting or staffing (最佳人选 'the ideal choice/candidate', 物色人选 'scout candidates').

什么.etymology: Everyday question word 'what?' (shén me), descended from Tang–Song vernacular 拾沒 / 什麼 ('what thing?'). Used standalone (什么？ 'What?') or directly before a noun (什么茶？ 'What kind of tea?').

history.meaning: interrogative 'what?'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 什麼 (via 萌典)

什么样.etymology: Avernacular interrogative modifier-head construction uniting 什么 (shénme, 'what') + 样 (yàng, simplified from 樣, 'pattern, appearance, kind'). Interrogative 什么 evolved in Tang–Song vernacular from 拾没 / 甚么 (shènme), ultimately contracting Middle Chinese 是物 (dzyeX mjut, literally 'this thing -> what thing?'). Combined with 样 (originally a wooden pattern/mould, 橡/樣), it asks 'of what pattern or sort?'.

history.form: 是物 -> 甚摩 / 甚么
history.meaning: what thing? what? (Tang–Song vernacular contraction)
what kind of, what sort of appearance or nature

什么样.notes: Modifies nouns with or without 的 (什么样的人 / 什么样儿 'what kind of person / what it looks like'), and pairs in correlative clauses like 你是什么样的人，就会遇到什么样的人.

仇.etymology: A phono-semantic character combining semantic 亻 (rén, 'person') + phonetic 九 (jiǔ; Old Chinese *gʷru). In Old Chinese, 仇 (*gʷru, Middle Chinese gjuw) originally denoted a 'pair, mate, counterpart' (as in 诗经: 君子好逑/仇, 'a fine match for the lord'). Because a direct counterpart in battle or rivalry is also an adversary, it underwent semantic polarization to 'rival, foe', and further merged with 讐/雠 (chóu, 'respond, exact retribution') under PRC simplification to mean 'feud, hatred, enmity'.

history.meaning: companion, mate, match; rival counterpart (Book of Odes)
personal enemy, blood feud, vengeance
enmity, grievance, hatred, foe (merging 仇 and 雠)

仇.notes: Read chóu for 'enmity/grudge' (报仇 'avenge', 记仇 'hold a grudge', 结仇 'make an enemy'), but retains the older reading qiú as a Chinese surname and in 伉俪/好仇 ('matched spouse').

仇人.etymology: A modifier-head compound joining 仇 (chóu, 'enmity, vendetta, blood grievance', historically written 讎人 or 仇人) + 人 (rén, 'person'). Attested since Han and Six Dynasties historical narratives to distinguish a personal adversary bound by a specific feud or grievance from a military enemy of the state (敌人, dírén).

history.meaning: person against whom one bears a blood debt or vendetta
personal enemy, bitter rival, foe

仇人.notes: Stronger and more personal than 对手 ('competitor/rival'); famous in the proverb 仇人见面，分外眼红 ('when enemies meet, their eyes blaze with fury').

今儿.etymology: A Northern Mandarin/Beijing colloquialism formed via erhua (儿化) suffixation of 今 (jīn, 'present, now, today'; Old Chinese *krəm) + diminutive nominal suffix -儿 (-r, reduced from 儿 ér, 'child/small thing'). In Classical Chinese, single-character 今 could stand alone for 'now / today'; Qing-era Beijing speech attached the retroflex coda -r (often expanded as 今儿个 jīnrge) to create a brisk spoken time noun contrasting with 明儿 (míngr, 'tomorrow') and 昨儿 (zuór, 'yesterday').

history.meaning: now, the present moment or day
today (colloquial Northern Mandarin with erhua suffix)

今儿.notes: Pronounced as a single retroflex syllable jīnr (never two syllables *jīn-ér!); adds warm, informal Northern conversational flavour in dialogue compared to neutral 今天.

今天.etymology: Noun meaning 'today', combining 今 ('now, present', attested on Shang oracle bones and in the Shijing) with 天 ('day'). Parallels 昨天 ('yesterday') and 明天 ('tomorrow'), and sits before or right after the subject without any preposition.

history.meaning: today
today

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 今天 (via 萌典)

今年.etymology: A modifier-head temporal compound combining demonstrative-temporal 今 (jīn, 'present, current'; Old Chinese *krəm) + 年 (nián, 'harvest cycle, year'; Old Chinese *nˤiŋ, originally depicting a person carrying ripened grain 禾). Attested continuously since Classical Chinese (e.g., Zuo Zhuan and Mencius) to denote the current calendar or agricultural year, outlasting Literary Chinese 今岁 (jīnsuì) in everyday speech.

history.meaning: the current harvest cycle or reigning year (Zuo Zhuan)
this calendar year

今年.notes: Remember the asymmetry in Mandarin temporal compounds: 今天/今年 use 今 ('present'), whereas 'this week/month' use 这个星期 / 这个月 (never *今月 in standard Mandarin, unlike Japanese 今月).

今晚.etymology: Temporal compound of 今 ('present, current, today') + 晚 ('evening, night'): 'this evening, tonight'.

history.meaning: this evening; tonight

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 今晚 (via 萌典)

介入.etymology: A verb-complement / directional compound formed from 介 (jiè, 'lie between, interpose, act as intermediary'; originally depicting protective armour plates between a person's body and the outside) + 入 (rù, 'enter into'). Popularized in modern East Asian legal, diplomatic, and media prose alongside Japanese 介入 (kainyū) to express a third party 'stepping in between' an ongoing dispute, investigation, or relationship.

history.meaning: wear armour; lie between two sides, mediate (Classical texts)
intervene, step into a dispute or ongoing process

介入.notes: Used both neutrally for official involvement (警方介入调查 'police step in to investigate') and negatively for intruding into a couple's relationship or another department's turf.

rootFamily.gloss: mind, take offence (let something lodge between)

介意.etymology: Verb-object compound of 介 ('lodge between, let something stick like a thorn or armor plate') + 意 ('mind, thought'): 'take offense, mind, let something bother one' (most often negated: 不介意 'don't mind').

history.stage: Han–Six Dynasties Classical Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: harbor a matter in one's mind -> mind, take offense

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 介意 (via 萌典)

介绍.etymology: A coordinative compound from Classical Chinese ritual terminology combining 介 (jiè, 'intermediary attendant assisting a guest') + 绍 (shào, simplified from 紹, 'continue in succession, connect threads', from 纟 'silk' + 召 phonetic). In the Records of the Grand Historian (史记·鲁仲连邹阳列传) and Rites of Zhou, ceremonial hosts and guests communicated through relays of attendants (介 and 绍) who passed messages in sequence; this ritual mediation generalized to 'introduce people to one another' and 'present/brief information'.

history.meaning: act as ritual intermediary relaying word between host and guest (Shiji)
act as go-between, recommend or broker an acquaintance
introduce (a person), present or brief on (a topic/project)

介绍.notes: Note the reversed character order in Japanese 紹介 (shōkai) and Korean 소개 (sogae); in Mandarin, avoid redundant *介绍给…认识 when 介绍 alone suffices (我来介绍一下 'let me make an introduction').

仍.etymology: A phono-semantic character composed of semantic 亻 (rén, 'person') + phonetic 乃 (nǎi; Old Chinese *nˤə -> 仍 *nəŋ, Middle Chinese nyɨng). In Old Chinese (Analects, Laozi), 仍 functioned as a transitive verb meaning 'follow along old lines, repeat successively, draw near' (e.g., 仍旧贯 'follow the old practice'). From 'continuing along the prior state', it grammaticalized in Literary Chinese into a temporal-aspectual adverb meaning 'still, yet, as before'.

history.meaning: follow precedent, repeat successively, conform to (Analects)
still, nonetheless, remaining as before

仍.notes: Monosyllabic 仍 has a crisp, slightly formal/written tone common in news, scripts, and captions; in casual conversation, disyllabic 仍然 or 还是 is generally preferred.

从.etymology: Ideographic character (会意字) showing one person (人) walking directly behind another (人), originally written 从 in oracle-bone script before later adding 彳/止 to form 從 (and simplified back to the ancient form 从). Means 'follow, comply with' and the preposition 'from, since, through'.

morphemes.meaning: one person following another = follow; from

history.meaning: one person following another -> follow; from

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 从 (via 萌典)

从不.etymology: A disyllabic negative temporal adverb condensed from 从来不 (cónglái bù, 'from the past until now, never'). Here 从 (cóng, 'from, starting from; ever') marks an unbroken span of time or habitual principle, while 不 (bù, 'not') negates habitual or volitional action (contrast 从没 cóngméi, which negates past experiential events). Because 从不 is crisp and rhythmic, spoken and written Mandarin favor it before disyllabic verbs to state firm personal habits.

history.meaning: from past to present, never
never (as a rule or habit)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 从不

cognates.word: 從今以後 (cung4 gam1 ji5 hau6)

从今以后.etymology: A four-character prepositional-temporal phrase structured as 从今 (cóng jīn, prepositional phrase 'starting from the present', with 从 simplified from 從, originally two people walking one behind another 彳+从) + 以后 (yǐhòu, 'thereafter, onward', from Classical 以 'taking as boundary' + 后/後 'after, behind'). Attested in vernacular Buddhist transformation texts (变文) of the Tang dynasty and Song–Ming storytelling as an emphatic vow or turning-point marker.

history.form: 從今已後 / 從今以後
history.meaning: from this present moment afterward (Tang–Song vernacular prose)
from today onward, henceforth

从今以后.notes: More solemn and emotionally resolute than plain 以后 ('later / in the future'); often used in dramatic pledges, breakups, or new beginnings (从今以后，我们两清了 'from today onward, we are even').

从头到尾.etymology: Four-character idiom built on the spatial metaphor of an animal's body: 从 ('from') + 头 (simplified from 頭, 'head') + 到 ('to; until') + 尾 ('tail', corpse/body 尸 with hair 毛 at the rear). Attested in Song-dynasty Chan Buddhist recorded sayings (語錄) and vernacular fiction, it means 'from beginning to end; from start to finish'.

history.meaning: from head to tail; from beginning to end
from start to finish; thoroughly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 从头到尾

从容.etymology: Alliterative binome (双声联绵词, read cóngróng) attested since the Classic of Documents (Shangshu) and Chuci, describing bearing and movement that is 'unhurried, calm, composed, poised, with ample leeway'.

history.meaning: natural, unhurried, and composed in bearing
calm; unhurried; poised

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 从容 (via 萌典)

cognates.word: 從小到大 (cung4 siu2 dou3 daai6)

从小到大.etymology: A four-character correlative prepositional frame 从…到… (cóng... dào..., 'from... all the way to...') spanning antonymic life-stage adjectives 小 (xiǎo, 'small, young in age') and 大 (dà, 'big, grown-up'). Built through transparent vernacular Mandarin pattern productivity, it traces an unbroken biographical span from early childhood up to one's current adult self.

history.meaning: since childhood, from a young age
from childhood to adulthood, one's whole life growing up

从小到大.notes: Typically followed by 都 or 就 to underscore lifelong consistency (我从小到大都没见过这种事 'in my whole life growing up, I have never seen anything like this').

从来.etymology: Temporal adverb combining 从 ('from') + 来 ('coming up to the present, hitherto'): 'all along, from the beginning, (with negation) never'. Attested from Tang–Song poetry and vernacular.

history.meaning: from past to present; always; (with 不/没) never

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 从来 (via 萌典)

从来不.etymology: An emphatic negative adverbial phrase combining 从来 (cónglái, 'all along, from past until now'—from 从 'from the origin' + directional/temporal 来 'coming hitherto', attested in Tang poetry and Song vernacular) + habitual/volitional negator 不 (bù, 'not'). Together they negate a habit, trait, or principle across all time ('never as a rule'), contrasting with 从来没(有), which negates experiential events ('have never once happened to').

history.meaning: from the beginning up to the present, all along (Tang–Song poetry)
never (habitually or by principle)

morphemes.meaning: coming up to the present, hitherto

从来不.notes: Crucial grammar distinction: use 从来不 for habits, rules, or personality (他从来不迟到 'he is never late'), and 从来没(有)…过 for past life experiences (他从来没迟到过 'he has never been late before').

仔仔细细.etymology: An AABB vivid reduplication of the disyllabic adjective 仔细 (zǐxì, 'careful, meticulous, attentive'). In Tang–Song Literary and vernacular Chinese, the word was originally written 子细 (zǐxì)—pairing 子 ('tiny seed/offspring, minute detail') + 细 (simplified from 細, 'fine silk thread, minute') as a coordinative synonym compound meaning 'minute and fine-grained'. Later, semantic 亻 was added to yield 仔, and Mandarin AABB reduplication intensified its descriptive force into an adverbial/adjectival 'thoroughly and painstakingly'.

history.meaning: minute, fine-grained; attentive in detail (Book of Northern History / Tang poetry)
careful, cautious, frugal or meticulous
very carefully, thoroughly, down to the finest detail

仔仔细细.notes: Usually followed by 地 before an action verb (仔仔细细地检查了一遍 'inspected it thoroughly from top to bottom'); conveys hands-on patience rather than mere caution.

仔细.etymology: Adjective and adverb meaning 'careful, attentive, meticulous, frugal'. Originally written 子細 in Han–Tang texts (e.g., History of the Northern Dynasties, Du Fu's poetry) with the literal sense 'small and fine-grained', later written 仔細 with the person radical 亻.

history.meaning: fine-grained; detailed; careful
careful; attentive; thorough

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 仔细 (via 萌典)

他.etymology: Third-person singular masculine or general pronoun ('he, him'), formed from 亻 ('person') and 也. In Classical Chinese (Mencius, Zhuangzi), 他 (also written 它 or 佗) meant 'other, another person'; during the Tang dynasty it grammaticalized into the general third-person pronoun.

history.meaning: another; other person
third-person singular pronoun

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 他 (via 萌典)

他们.etymology: Third-person plural pronoun ('they, them'), formed from 他 ('he / person') plus the plural marker 们 (men). Used for male or mixed groups of people without any subject-versus-object case change.

history.meaning: third-person plural 'they, them'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 他們 (via 萌典)

他俩.etymology: A Northern Mandarin pronominal compound uniting third-person pronoun 他 (tā, 'he/she/other'; evolved in Tang–Song vernacular from Classical Chinese demonstrative 佗/他 *lˤaj, 'other, another') + fusion numeral-classifier 俩 (liǎ, 'two of'). Phonologically and historically, 俩 (liǎ) is a colloquial contraction (合音) of 两个 (liǎng gè, 'two [classifier]'), attested in Ming–Qing Beijing vernacular and written with semantic 亻 ('person') + 两 ('two').

history.meaning: other, another (Classical Chinese demonstrative)
third-person singular pronoun 'he/she' (Tang–Song vernacular)
the two of them (contraction of 他们两个)

morphemes.meaning: two of (fused numeral + classifier 两个)

他俩.notes: Because 俩 already incorporates the classifier 个, NEVER add 个 or another measure word after it (*他俩个人 is ungrammatical; say 他俩 or 他们两个).

rootFamily.gloss: trick, clever skill (written with same character, read liǎng!)

他家.etymology: A modifier-head possessive phrase without overt particle 的, combining third-person pronoun 他 (tā, 'he, his'; from Classical Chinese 佗/他 'another') + kinship/spatial noun 家 (jiā, 'home, household, clan'; Old Chinese *kˤra, oracle-bone graph depicting a pig 豕 beneath a roof 宀). In Mandarin grammar, close inalienable relationships involving homes, kin, and collectives regularly omit 的, yielding tight disyllabic units like 我家, 你家, and 他家.

history.meaning: ancestral household, noble clan estate; home
another family / someone else (Tang–Song); his home or household (Mandarin)

他家.notes: Beyond literally meaning 'his home/family', in contemporary entertainment and e-commerce slang 他家 also means 'that idol's fandom/agency' or 'that shop/brand' (e.g., 他家的艺人 'artists signed to their agency').

仗义.etymology: Originally a verb-object compound from Literary and vernacular Chinese combining 仗 (zhàng, 'lean upon, rely on, uphold'; originally a long-handled weapon held in hand, hence 'wield or rely upon') + 义 (yì, simplified from 義, 'righteousness, code of honour, sworn loyalty'). Famous in Yuan–Ming heroic vernacular fiction such as Water Margin (水浒传) in four-character idioms like 仗义疏财 ('uphold righteousness and disperse wealth to help others') and 仗义执言 ('speak up out of righteousness'), it lexicalized as a colloquial adjective describing a stand-up, fiercely loyal friend.

history.meaning: uphold moral righteousness or chivalric duty (Tang–Song histories & Water Margin)
loyal to friends, chivalrous, generous and stand-up

morphemes.meaning: righteousness, personal loyalty, code of honour

仗义.notes: High-praise colloquial compliment in Northern Chinese social life (这人特别仗义 'this guy is a total stand-up friend' / 不够仗义 'not being a loyal pal'), rooted in traditional jiānghú brotherhood ethics.

付.etymology: Ideogram (会意字) attested in oracle-bone and seal script showing a person (亻) and a hand (寸) handing something over: 'hand over, deliver, entrust; pay'.

history.meaning: hand over; entrust to
pay (money); hand over

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 付 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: put in effort, sacrifice, pay out

付出.etymology: A verb-directional / resultative compound formed from 付 (fù, 'hand over, entrust, pay'; ideogrammic compound of 亻 'person' + 寸 'hand', depicting one person handing an item to another) + directional complement 出 (chū, 'go out, put forth'). Originally concrete ('disburse or pay out money'), in modern Mandarin it underwent metaphorical extension to investing intangible effort, emotion, sweat, or personal sacrifice into a project or relationship, and also nominalized ('effort/sacrifice invested').

history.meaning: hand over, entrust, deliver to another person (Classical prose)
pay out (funds); invest effort, time, or personal sacrifice

付出.notes: Equally common with concrete/figurative objects (付出努力 'put in effort', 付出代价 'pay a price') and as an intransitive verb or noun in emotional/work contexts (默默付出 'quietly give one's all').

付给.etymology: A verb-complement / dative compound joining transitive verb 付 (fù, 'hand over, pay', from 亻 'person' + 寸 'hand') + recipient-marking complement 给 (gěi, simplified from 給, originally 'supply amply' in Classical Chinese, grammaticalized in Qing–modern Mandarin into 'give / to'). The resulting V-给 dative construction explicitly introduces the recipient of a monetary payment or handover immediately after the verb.

history.meaning: hand over (付); supply provisions amply (給) (separate Classical verbs)
pay (money, fees, royalties) over to a recipient

付给.notes: Must be followed directly by the recipient noun/pronoun before any sum of money (付给他一笔违约金 'pay him a contract-breach fee', never *付一笔钱给他 with 付给 kept together).

付钱.etymology: Verb-object compound of 付 ('hand over, pay') + 钱 (錢, 'coin, money', metal 钅 + 戋): 'pay money, settle the bill'.

history.stage: Song–Ming commercial vernacular to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: pay money

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 付钱 (via 萌典)

代价.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 代 (dài, 'substitute, stand in for, exchange') + 价 (jià, simplified from 價, 'value, market price'). Standardized as an economic and legal Sino-Japanese compound 代価 (daika, 'equivalent monetary value given in exchange for goods or labour') in Meiji Japan and adopted into late Qing–Republican Chinese; in modern Mandarin, while 价格/价钱 cover literal price tags, 代价 specialized almost exclusively into the figurative cost, toll, or sacrifice exacted for an outcome.

history.meaning: monetary equivalent or compensation paid in exchange for goods
figurative price, toll, or sacrifice paid to achieve a goal

代价.notes: False-friend trap for learners: never ask a shopkeeper *这个代价多少 for a store price (use 价格 or 多少钱); 代价 is for sacrifices and consequences (不惜一切代价 'at all costs', 惨重的代价 'a heavy price').

cognates.meaning: algebraic substitution; emotional projection (感情移入)

代入感.etymology: A modern Chinese media, gaming, and literary-criticism neologism formed as a modifier-head derivative: 代入 (dàirù, verb-complement 'substitute into') + nominalizing suffix -感 (-gǎn, 'sense, feeling'). 代入 itself entered modern Chinese from Meiji Japanese mathematical terminology 代入 (dainyū, 'substituting a value for a variable in an equation'). Late-20th-century ACGN (anime/gaming/web-novel) and TV critics metaphorized 'plugging oneself into the variable' to describe an audience's visceral self-projection and immersion in a character or storyline.

history.meaning: algebraic substitution of a number or expression for a variable
audience immersion, emotional projection, relatability of a story or performance

代入感.notes: Signature TV-production and viewer buzzword (代入感很强 'super immersive/relatable', 毫无代入感 'impossible to get into'); often contrasted with 出戏 ('breaking immersion / pulling the viewer out of the scene').

rootFamily.gloss: sense of體驗 / user experience feel

cognates.meaning: proxy, agency, acting on behalf of

代理.etymology: An adverbial-head verbal/nominal compound combining 代 (dài, 'in place of, on behalf of') + 理 (lǐ, 'manage, administer, put in order'; originally 'dress and polish jade along its veins', from 玉 + 里). While phrases like 代为料理 ('manage affairs on someone's behalf') existed in Literary Chinese, modern legal and commercial 代理 ('legal proxy, commercial agent, acting official') was codified alongside Meiji Japanese civil-law terminology 代理 (dairi, translating German Stellvertretung / English 'agency').

history.meaning: administer affairs temporarily in place of another official
act as legal proxy, commercial distributor, or acting officeholder

morphemes.meaning: in place of, on behalf of

代理.notes: Functions as a verb (代理版权 'represent/distribute copyright'), an institutional modifier (代理制作人 'acting producer', 总代理 'sole distributor'), and a noun via 代理人 ('agent/proxy').

代表.etymology: A compound uniting 代 (dài, 'substitute for, act in place of') + 表 (biǎo, 'outer garment, display outwardly, stand as visible emblem'). Coined in Meiji Japan as 代表 (daihyō) to translate Western political and legal 'representation / representative' (standing visibly on behalf of a constituency or group) and rapidly borrowed into late-19th-century Chinese constitutional and journalistic prose; in spoken Mandarin it further extended from 'speak/stand for a group' to semantic 'signify, mean, indicate'.

history.meaning: political delegate or legal representative (Meiji neologism)
delegate, representative; act on behalf of an institution or group
represent; exemplify; mean, signify (in everyday reasoning)

morphemes.meaning: stand in for, on behalf of

代表.notes: Spans three everyday uses: noun ('delegate/rep'), institutional verb (我代表节目组 'on behalf of the show crew'), and logical verb 'mean/imply' especially in negation (沉默不代表同意 'silence doesn't mean consent').

代表作.etymology: A three-morpheme modifier-head Sino-Japanese return loan (wasei-kango) modeled on Meiji–Taishō Japanese 代表作 (daihyōsaku), combining 代表 (dàibiǎo, 'to stand as an outward sign for, represent') with the nominal head 作 (zuò, 'creative work, opus'). While 代 ('substitute, act in place of') and 表 ('outer marker, display') existed separately in Classical Chinese, their fusion with 作 created modern East Asian arts and media terminology for an artist's defining work.

history.meaning: Classical roots: 'substitute', 'manifest outwardly', and 'make / literary composition'
an author's or artist's defining creative work
signature work, career-defining hit film, album, or book

代表作.notes: In entertainment and showbiz Mandarin (such as 幕后之王), having or lacking a 代表作 is the ultimate benchmark separating durable A-list talent from fleeting traffic stars (流量明星).

代言.etymology: An adverbial-verb compound formed from 代 (dài, 'in place of, on behalf of') modifying 言 (yán, 'to speak, utter words'). In Song–Ming Literary Chinese, 代言 denoted drafting imperial edicts on the sovereign's behalf or writing in character for dramatic personae; in contemporary commercial Mandarin, it underwent semantic specialization to mean endorsing a brand as its public face.

history.meaning: to speak on another's behalf; to draft decrees or dramatic lines in persona
to serve as spokesperson; to endorse a commercial brand or product

morphemes.meaning: in place of, on behalf of

代言.notes: Used both transitively with a brand object (代言某品牌 'endorse a brand') and in the frame 为…代言 ('speak for / be the face of...').

代言人.etymology: A modifier-head agentive noun combining 代言 (dàiyán, 'speak on someone's behalf') with the human head noun 人 (rén, 'person'). Reinforced in late 19th- and early 20th-century East Asia via Meiji Japanese 代言人 (daigennin, initially designating a legal advocate before shifting to 'spokesperson'), it entered Chinese political prose as 'mouthpiece/representative' and later showbiz marketing as 'celebrity brand ambassador'.

history.meaning: legal proxy or advocate speaking for a litigant (1870s–1890s)
political or institutional spokesperson, mouthpiece
celebrity brand ambassador or commercial face of a label

代言人.notes: Distinguish commercial 代言人 ('brand ambassador / celebrity endorser') from official institutional 发言人 (fāyánrén, 'press spokesperson' for a ministry or company).

rootFamily.gloss: to endorse a brand; speak for

代购.etymology: A modifier-verb compound pairing 代 (dài, 'acting as proxy, on someone's behalf') with 购 (gòu, traditional 購, phono-semantic character from 貝 'cowrie/money' + 冓 phonetic, originally 'seek to buy with a reward, purchase'). Used in 20th-century administrative Chinese for institutional procurement agencies, 代购 exploded in 2000s Mainland internet culture to denote cross-border personal shoppers buying overseas tax-free or luxury goods for domestic clients.

history.meaning: offer a bounty for; purchase with money
commission purchasing on behalf of another party or institution
buy overseas goods on someone's behalf; cross-border personal shopper

代购.notes: Functions seamlessly as both a verb ('to buy overseas for clients', 做代购) and an informal noun referring to the personal shopper themselves (找个代购).

令人.etymology: A lexicalized pivotal causative sequence derived directly from Classical Chinese syntax: 令 (lìng, Old Chinese *riŋs, 'to command, cause, bring about') followed by the generic human pivot 人 (rén, 'people, one'). In Literary Chinese, 令人 introduced an experiential predicate ('causes a person to...'), and in Modern Mandarin it survives productively as a semi-formal prefixoid forming two-syllable emotive adjectives and verbs.

history.meaning: command someone to...; cause people to experience (a state)
make one feel... (productive causative-experiential frame before disyllabic states)

令人.notes: More written and elevated than colloquial 让人 (ràng rén) or 叫人 (jiào rén); overwhelmingly pairs with disyllabic psychological verbs like 令人期待 ('exciting to anticipate') or 令人失望 ('disappointing').

cognates.meaning: by means of, with (kanbun particle motte)

以.etymology: One of Classical Chinese's foundational function words (Old Chinese *ləʔ, Middle Chinese yijX). Early bronze and bamboo forms (㠯) depict an object or plowshare carried by hand, originally a full verb meaning 'to take, lift, employ, lead'. Through serial-verb grammaticalization in pre-Qin Chinese, 'take X [and] do Y' evolved into the primary instrumental coverb ('with, using'), causal marker ('because of'), and purposive linker ('in order to').

history.meaning: to take, wield, employ; to lead (troops)
with, by means of; on account of; in order to
using, taking as (in formal frames like 以…为主) and bound stem in spatial/conjunctive compounds

以.notes: In modern speech, standalone 以 belongs to formal or written registers (often paired with 为 in 以…为… 'take X as Y'), whereas everyday conversation uses 用 (yòng, 'use') or 拿 (ná, 'take').

cognates.meaning: or more; the above; that is all

以上.etymology: A Classical Chinese delimitative compound combining 以 (yǐ, 'taking [a reference point] as boundary') with 上 (shàng, 'upward, higher, preceding in text'). Attested in Confucius's Analects (雍也: 中人以上, 'those above mediocrity'), it originally marked an upward rank or threshold; because traditional Chinese scrolls unrolled vertically from top to bottom, 'above' naturally referred to previously written content ('the above'), and modern workplace usage also absorbed the Japanese closing formula 以上 (ijō, 'that concludes my remarks').

history.meaning: from a given rank or level upward (inclusive boundary)
the preceding text written higher up on the page/scroll
more than / and above (postposition); the above-mentioned; 'that's all' (presentation sign-off)

以上.notes: In contracts, age rules, and statistics, X以上 normally includes X itself ('X or above'); in corporate meetings and media pitches, ending an email or slide deck with 以上 signals 'that's everything from me'.

以为.etymology: Classical construction 以…為… ('take [something] to be…, regard as…') contracted when the object is omitted or understood into the disyllabic verb 以为 ('think, suppose, assume—often mistakenly').

history.meaning: take to be; consider; deem
think/assume (often wrongly)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 以为 (via 萌典)

以免.etymology: A negative-purposive conjunction coalesced from the Classical Chinese purposive marker 以 (yǐ, 'in order to, thereby') plus the verb 免 (miǎn, Old Chinese *mronʔ, 'escape, avert, be spared from'). Frequently appearing in Han and medieval administrative memorials (e.g., 以免后患 'so as to avert future trouble'), the two syllables fused into a single clause-introducing conjunction meaning 'lest, so as to avoid'.

history.meaning: thereby to escape or be spared from (punishment or calamity)
lest, in order to avoid (conjunction introducing an undesirable consequence)

以免.notes: Always introduces the unwanted outcome to be prevented after the main preventative action, never at the start of the whole sentence—slightly more compact and formal than 免得 (miǎnde) or 省得 (shěngde).

以前.etymology: Temporal noun and postposition combining 以 (linker marking a boundary in time or space) + 前 ('before, front, earlier'): 'before, previously, in the past'.

history.meaning: prior to a point in time; before; formerly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 以前 (via 萌典)

以及.etymology: A coordinative conjunction formed by fusing Classical Chinese 以 (yǐ, functioning as a connective particle) with 及 (jí, Old Chinese *ɡrɯb, originally depicting a hand catching up to a person, 'reach to, extend to, and'). Used in Literary Chinese to link primary items with supplementary ones, 以及 entered Modern Standard Mandarin as a formal coordinator capable of joining noun phrases, verb phrases, or clauses where simple 和 cannot.

history.meaning: catch up to, reach; and (asymmetric Classical coordinator)
extending down to; and also, as well as
as well as, along with (formal multi-level coordinator)

以及.notes: Ideal for layered lists: use顿号 (、) or 和 inside tight sub-groups and 以及 before the final, broader, or longer item (e.g., 导演、编剧以及全体幕后人员).

以后.etymology: Temporal noun and postposition combining 以 (boundary linker) + 后 (後, 'after, behind, later'): 'after, afterwards, in the future, later on'.

history.meaning: after a point in time; later; in the future

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 以后 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: except for, outside of, other than

以外.etymology: A Classical Chinese spatial-delimitative compound uniting 以 (yǐ, 'taking [a boundary] as reference') and 外 (wài, 'outside, exterior, beyond'). In Warring States and Han prose (such as 九州以外 'beyond the Nine Provinces'), it marked geographical space outside a border; through conceptual metaphor, exterior space grammaticalized into set exclusion ('other than, apart from').

history.meaning: physically outside a frontier or boundary
beyond (a limit); apart from, except for (often paired with 除了)

以外.notes: Most frequently appears in the circumposition 除了…以外 ('apart from / besides...'), where the following clause takes 都 ('except for X, all...') for exclusion or 还/也 ('in addition to X, also...') for inclusion.

以来.etymology: A Classical temporal postposition composed of 以 (yǐ, 'from [a starting point]') and 来 (lái, traditional 來, 'come [hither toward the speaker's present]'). Already idiomatic in Mencius (自生民以来 'ever since living folk first existed'), it conceptualizes time as moving forward from a past anchor up to the present moment of speaking.

history.meaning: coming forward in time from a specified past event or era
since (postposition after a past point or duration, often with 自/从)

morphemes.meaning: come hither toward the present (trad. 來)

以来.notes: Unlike English 'since', 以来 goes AFTER the time phrase (出道以来 'since debuting', 三年以来 'for the past three years') and can attach to either a past point in time or a duration extending to now.

以茶代酒.etymology: A four-character Classical-pattern serial-verb phrase: 以 (yǐ, 'use, take') + 茶 (chá, 'tea') + 代 (dài, 'substitute for') + 酒 (jiǔ, 'fermented grain liquor, wine'). The locus classicus goes back to Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms (三国志·吴书·韦曜传), where Emperor Sun Hao of Eastern Wu secretly granted the scholar Wei Yao—who could hold barely two升 of wine—tea in place of liquor at court banquets (密赐茶荈以当酒 / 以茶代酒).

history.meaning: secretly grant tea leaves to stand in for wine at imperial banquets
polite dining formula: toast with tea in place of alcohol

以茶代酒.notes: Essential Chinese banquet etiquette: when abstaining due to driving, health, or work, saying 我以茶代酒敬您一杯 ('I toast you a cup using tea in place of wine') preserves full respect at business dinners.

以身相许.etymology: A four-character literary idiom (chéngyǔ) built on Classical serial-verb syntax: 以 (yǐ, 'with, taking') + 身 (shēn, 'one's own person/body') + 相 (xiāng, asymmetrical directional adverb 'to him/the other party', not reciprocal 'each other') + 许 (xǔ, traditional 許, 'promise in marriage, betroth'). Crystallized in Ming–Qing vernacular novellas and chuanqi romances, where a rescued maiden vows to marry her benefactor in lifelong gratitude.

history.meaning: pledge one's life to the state; promise in marriage
(of a woman) vow to marry a hero to repay a life-saving debt
pledge oneself in marriage; (jocular) offer oneself in exaggerated thanks

以身相许.notes: Today almost always used humorously or ironically among friends and in rom-coms ('You saved my project—guess I'll have to 以身相许!'), playing on classic wuxia/costume-drama tropes (救命之恩，以身相许).

rootFamily.gloss: devote one's life to; sacrifice oneself
test the law on one's own person (defy the law)

以防万一.etymology: Four-character idiom built from classical purpose marker 以 ('in order to') + 防 ('guard against; dike', mound radical 阜 + phonetic 方) + 万一 ('one in ten thousand', i.e., a rare, unexpected contingency). Attested in Song–Ming administrative and vernacular prose, it remains the standard everyday phrase for taking a sensible precaution 'just in case'.

morphemes.meaning: one chance in ten thousand; an unexpected event

history.meaning: take precautions against an unlikely mishap
just in case

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 以防万一

仨.etymology: A Northern Mandarin fusion word (合音字 héyīnzì) and compound ideograph combining 亻 (rén, 'person') with 三 (sān, 'three') to represent the rapid colloquial contraction of 三个 (sān ge, 'three [items/people]') into a single open syllable sā. Parallel to 俩 (liǎ < 两个 'two'), it became well attested in Qing-dynasty Beijing speech records and Republican vernacular fiction.

history.meaning: three (numeral + general classifier)
the three of (us/them), three (fused numeral-classifier)

仨.notes: Because 仨 already incorporates the classifier 个 inside its pronunciation, NEVER add 个 or another measure word after it—say 我们仨 ('the three of us') or 仨人, never *仨个人.

rootFamily.gloss: several times over; three or four

仪式.etymology: A coordinative noun compound uniting 仪 (yí, traditional 儀, 'proper bearing, deportment, ritual model') and 式 (shì, 'norm, pattern, liturgical rule'). Already attested in Ban Gu's Book of Han (汉书) for exemplary norms and court protocol, 仪式 was revitalized and standardized across modern East Asia alongside Meiji Japanese 儀式 (gishiki) to denote public ceremonies, launches, and rites.

history.meaning: exemplary deportment, statutory rules, and court ritual norms
formal public ceremony, rite, or commemorative event

仪式.notes: In contemporary media and lifestyle Mandarin, 仪式感 (yíshìgǎn, 'a sense of ritual/occasion') is a ubiquitous buzzword for making everyday moments or showbiz launches feel special.

们.etymology: Plural suffix (們, neutral tone men) attached to personal pronouns (我们, 你们, 他们) and human nouns (朋友们, 孩子们). Emerged in Tang–Song northern vernacular under various phonetic spellings (such as 弭, 伟, 懣, 門) before standardizing on 們 (person 亻 + phonetic 門 mén).

history.meaning: collective plural marker for pronouns and people
plural suffix for pronouns and human nouns

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 们 (via 萌典)

仰慕.etymology: A modifier-verb / coordinative psychological compound joining 仰 (yǎng, 'tilt the head upward, look up toward') with 慕 (mù, phono-semantic from 心 'heart' + 莫 phonetic, 'yearn after, cherish, admire'). Attested since Eastern Han and Three Kingdoms prose (including Cao Zhi's memorials and Book of the Later Han), it projects physical upward gaze onto heartfelt veneration for someone of higher talent or virtue.

history.meaning: look up to with heartfelt yearning and reverence for virtue or renown
admire deeply, revere from afar (often of mentors, seniors, or romantic ideals)

morphemes.meaning: raise the head, look up to

仰慕.notes: A staple of polite first-meeting flattery in professional circles: 久仰 / 仰慕已久 ('I have admired your work for a long time'), and with -者 (仰慕者) it means 'secret admirer / devoted fan'.

rootFamily.gloss: faith, belief (look up to and trust)
long have I admired your name (polite greeting)

仰望.etymology: A modifier-verb compound pairing 仰 (yǎng, Old Chinese *ŋaŋʔ, 'lift the face skyward', the antonym of 俯 fǔ 'bow down') with 望 (wàng, 'gaze afar; look toward in hope'). Present in Warring States classics such as Zhuangzi and Xunzi, it retains both its concrete bodily sense ('tilt one's head to gaze at the stars or peaks') and its figurative extension ('look up to an exalted figure or rely hopingly upon').

history.meaning: lift one's head to gaze upward; look expectantly toward a superior for sustenance or guidance
gaze upward at (sky, heights); look up to someone far above one's station

morphemes.meaning: gaze into the distance, look toward

仰望.notes: Compared with 仰慕 (warm personal admiration), 仰望 highlights vertical distance and awe—either literal (仰望星空 'gazing up at the starry sky') or status-based (looking up to an untouchable industry titan).

rootFamily.gloss: look down from a height, overlook

件.etymology: Versatile measure word counting upper-body clothing (一件外套 'a coat'), pieces of luggage (一件行李), and matters or affairs (一件事). Combining 亻 ('person') and 牛 ('ox'), Shuo Wen Jie Zi defines 件 as 'divide, distinguish into distinct items'.

history.meaning: distinguish; individual item
classifier for garments, luggage, matters

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 件 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: price, cost; bean sprouts (unrelated homograph) / giá cả

价.etymology: Traditional 價 (jià, Old Chinese *kraːs, Middle Chinese kæH) is a phono-semantic derivative combining 亻 ('person') with 賈 (gǔ, Old Chinese *klaːʔ, 'stationary merchant; to trade'); the Old Chinese *-s suffix derived the noun 'commercial worth, asking price' from 'to trade'. Simplified Chinese 价 repurposes an archaic homophonous-looking graph 价 (jiè, 'attendant; good') to replace 價.

history.meaning: merchant; by *-s derivation, commercial price or worth
monetary price, market rate; reputation/worth
price, rate, cost; chemical valence (modern scientific loan extension)

价.notes: In spoken Mandarin, standalone 价 usually takes retroflex 价儿 (jiàr) in phrases like 讲价 / 砍价 ('haggle over the price'), while disyllabic 价格 (jiàgé) or 价钱 (jiàqian) serves as the standalone noun.

价值.etymology: A coordinative/predicate compound joining 价 (jià, trad. 價, 'price') and 值 (zhí, 'meet, be equivalent to, be worth'). In Song–Qing vernacular Chinese, 价值 originally meant concrete monetary equivalence ('the price it commands'); during the Meiji era, Japanese scholars selected 価値 (kachi) to translate German Wert and English value in philosophy and Marxian/classical economics, re-exporting abstract axiological senses into modern Chinese.

history.meaning: monetary price or market worth of an object
philosophical, aesthetic, and economic 'value' (calquing German Wert / English value)
economic value, commercial worth, and abstract significance/merit

价值.notes: Functions primarily as a noun ('commercial value' 商业价值, 'have value' 有价值), though in elevated written prose it can still act transitively before a sum ('valued at ten million' 价值千万).

价值不菲.etymology: A four-character subject-predicate idiom pairing the noun 价值 (jiàzhí, 'monetary worth') with the Classical litotes predicate 不菲 (bùfěi, 'not meager, not inconsiderable'). 菲 (fěi, Old Chinese *pʰɯjʔ) originally named a turnip/radish-like edible plant (艹 + 非) and in Confucius's Analects (泰伯: 菲饮食 'meager food and drink') meant 'thin, frugal, slight'; negating it with 不 yields elegant understatement for 'commanding a steep price'.

history.meaning: radish-like plant; thin, meager, slight (of offerings or diet)
not slight, considerable (of gifts, expenses, or achievements)
worth a small fortune, carrying a hefty price tag

价值不菲.notes: Watch the tone of 菲: in this sense ('meager, humble', also seen in 妄自菲薄 'unduly belittle oneself') it is third tone fěi, NOT first tone fēi (which means 'fragrant, luxuriant' as in 芳菲 or phonetic transliterations).

价值观.etymology: A three-morpheme modifier-head philosophical compound attaching the conceptual suffixoid -观 (guān, traditional 觀, 'contemplative view, outlook') to 价值 (jiàzhí, 'value'). Modeled alongside Japanese 価値観 (kachikan) on early 20th-century Neo-Kantian German compounds in -anschauung (such as Weltanschauung → 世界观 and Wertanschauung → 价值观), it denotes an individual's or society's core hierarchy of moral and life priorities.

history.meaning: observe closely, contemplate; Daoist/Buddhist meditative insight
philosophical conception of values (calquing German Wert- / -anschauung models)

价值观.notes: In modern Chinese pop culture and media reviews, 世界观 ('worldview'), 人生观 ('outlook on life'), and 价值观 ('values') are collectively nicknamed 三观 (sānguān—e.g., 三观很正 'having wholesome, grounded values').

价钱.etymology: Compound noun of 价 (價, 'value, price', person 亻 + 賈 gǔ 'merchant') + 钱 (錢, 'money, copper cash'): 'price (of goods)'.

history.stage: Tang–Song commercial vernacular to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: monetary price

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 价钱 (via 萌典)

任何.etymology: Universal/free-choice determiner meaning 'any, whatever', combining 任 ('allow, let, no matter how') + 何 ('what, which').

history.meaning: no matter which -> any, whatever

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 任何 (via 萌典)

任何人.etymology: A universal-indefinite pronominal compound formed from the determiner 任何 (rènhé, 'any whatsoever'—itself built from permissive 任 'allow without restriction, no matter' + interrogative 何 'what, which') modifying 人 (rén, 'person'). Consolidated during the May Fourth vernacular movement and early 20th-century legal/translation Mandarin to render English 'anyone / anybody' with emphatic totality.

history.meaning: no matter what / whichever (permissive verb + Classical interrogative)
anyone at all, anybody whatsoever (emphatic universal/negative-polarity pronoun)

任何人.notes: Nearly always paired with 都 ('anyone at all [can/must]...') in affirmative statements or 也不/都不 ('not... anyone at all') in negations to satisfy Mandarin's quantification harmony.

任务.etymology: A coordinative noun compound combining 任 (rèn, Old Chinese *njɯms, originally 'carry a burden on a shoulder pole', hence 'official charge, responsibility') and 务 (wù, traditional 務, 'devote effort to; urgent affair, duty'). Attested in Tang–Song administrative prose for state responsibilities (公务职责) and reinforced in modern military, organizational, and gaming Mandarin alongside Japanese 任務 (ninmu) to mean 'assigned mission, task, or quest'.

history.meaning: shoulder a charge / official post + urgent state affair or duty
official responsibilities and administrative duties entrusted to an official
assigned mission, project task, or quest objective

任务.notes: Pronounced with a neutral second syllable in everyday Beijing speech (rènwu) or fourth tone in formal broadcasts; standard verb collocations are 完成任务 ('accomplish a mission') and 接任务 ('take on an assignment').

rootFamily.gloss: appoint to an office; assume a post

任意.etymology: Originally a verb-object phrase pairing 任 (rèn, 'give free rein to, indulge, follow without restraint') with 意 (yì, 'one's mind, inclination, wish'). Attested in Ban Gu's Book of Han and medieval Buddhist translations for acting purely according to personal whim, 任意 later also absorbed the Sino-Japanese technical sense (任意 nin'i) of 'arbitrary, any chosen at random' in mathematics, law, and computing.

history.meaning: follow one's own inclinations without restraint; act willfully
freely, willfully (adverb); arbitrary, any chosen at will (attributive modifier)

任意.notes: Carries two distinct register flavors: before misconduct verbs (任意妄为, 任意篡改) it criticizes willful recklessness, whereas before nouns in rules, promos, or math (任意挑选, 任意三角形) it neutrally means 'any... of your choice'.

rootFamily.gloss: headstrong, willful (often of a spoiled person)

任由.etymology: A coordinative permissive verb compounded from two near-synonymous Classical roots: 任 (rèn, 'leave unchecked, entrust, allow') and 由 (yóu, 'follow from, leave up to, let'). Formed in late imperial and modern vernacular Mandarin on the pattern of 任凭 (rènpíng) and 由得 (yóude), it governs a pivotal clause ('leave X free to do Y without intervention').

history.meaning: separate Classical verbs meaning 'entrust / leave to' and 'proceed from / depend upon'
let someone or something act entirely as they please without stopping them

任由.notes: Usually implies passive non-interference—letting rumors spread (任由谣言发酵) or letting someone have their way when one could have stepped in—similar in structure and tone to 任凭 (rènpíng) and 听任 (tīngrèn).

rootFamily.gloss: no matter how; let someone do as they please
