份.etymology: Measure word and noun meaning 'portion, share, copy (of a newspaper, contract, or meal)'. Graphically combines person (亻) + 分 ('divide, allot'), created to distinguish the noun/classifier 份 (fèn, 'allotted share') from the verb 分 (fēn, 'divide').

history.meaning: allotted share; portion
classifier for portions, copies, jobs, gifts

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 份 (via 萌典)

仿.etymology: A phono-semantic character (Old Chinese *pʰaŋʔ, Middle Chinese phjangX) composed of semantic 亻 ('person') and phonetic 方 (fāng, *paŋ, 'side by side, compare'). In Classical Chinese, 仿 originally meant 'dimly resemble, seem parallel to' (preserved in 仿佛 fǎngfú, 'as if'), while the active transitive sense 'copy, model after' was frequently written with the graphic variant 倣 (亻 + 放); modern standard orthography merged 倣 into 仿.

history.meaning: resemble closely, seem as though (especially in binome 仿佛)
imitate, copy, model after an exemplar (calligraphy, craft, or policy)
imitate, emulate; imitation / knock-off (as in 高仿 'high-grade replica')

仿.notes: Productive in media, fashion, and manufacturing compounds: 模仿 ('imitate'), 仿照 ('model on'), 仿古 ('antique-style'), and colloquial 高仿 ('high-end counterfeit/replica').

企业.etymology: A Meiji Japanese Sino-compound return loan (企業 kigyō, coined to translate English enterprise and German Unternehmung), built from Classical roots 企 (qǐ, Old Chinese *kʰjeʔ, originally a person standing with raised heel 止, 'stand on tiptoe in expectation, plan ambitiously') and 业 (yè, traditional 業, 'undertaking, trade, estate'). Borrowed into late Qing and Republican Chinese, it became the standard formal term for a commercial firm or industrial corporation.

history.meaning: Classical roots: 'stand on tiptoe / plan eagerly' and 'occupation / ancestral undertaking'
commercial or industrial enterprise (Meiji economic neologism)
business enterprise, company, corporate entity

企业.notes: Mainland pronunciation is third tone qǐyè (Taiwan standard allows fourth tone qìyè); more institutional and macro-economic than 公司 (gōngsī, a specific registered company), appearing in 企业家 ('entrepreneur') and 国有企业 ('state-owned enterprise').

cognates.word: 伏線 (fukusen, parallel metaphor) / 伏筆 (fukuhitsu)

伏笔.etymology: A modifier-head term from indigenous Ming–Qing Chinese fiction and drama narratology, combining 伏 (fú, originally a person 亻 crouching beside a dog 犬, 'lie prostrate, hide in ambush, conceal') with 笔 (bǐ, traditional 筆, 'writing brush; a narrative stroke'). Popularized by 17th-century literary critics Jin Shengtan (金圣叹) and Mao Zonggang (毛宗岗) in their interlinear commentaries on Water Margin and Romance of the Three Kingdoms, it likens an early narrative clue to troops lying in ambush (埋伏) for a later plot reveal.

history.meaning: a 'concealed brush-stroke' planted early in a novel or play to prepare a later plot turn
narrative foreshadowing in scripts/novels; quiet strategic groundwork laid for later use

morphemes.meaning: writing brush; stroke of composition (trad. 筆)

伏笔.notes: In screenwriting and TV production talk, standard collocations follow the military 'ambush' metaphor: 埋下伏笔 ('plant foreshadowing') or 打下伏笔 ('lay quiet groundwork').

rootFamily.gloss: literary style, touch with the brush

休假.etymology: A verb-object (and nominalized) compound formed from 休 (xiū, compound ideograph of a person 亻 leaning against a tree 木, 'cease labor, rest in shade') and 假 (jià, Middle Chinese kæH, distinct in tone and sense from jiǎ 'false/borrow', meaning 'official furlough, statutory leave of absence'). Attested in Six Dynasties and Tang bureaucratic histories (such as Book of Jin 晋书) for court officials taking scheduled rest leave, it remains the standard Mandarin term for workplace vacation.

history.meaning: (of imperial officials) take statutory rest furlough from court duties
take leave from work, go on vacation (separable VO verb and noun)

休假.notes: Behaves as a separable verb-object word (离合词): to specify duration or frequency, insert it between 休 and 假—e.g., 休了一个星期的年假 ('took a week of annual leave').

休息.etymology: Coordinative verb compound of 休 ('rest, cease', an ideogram of a person 亻 leaning against a tree 木 in the shade) + 息 ('breathe, rest, cease', nose 自 'self/nose' above heart 心). Attested since the Shijing and Zuozhuan.

morphemes.meaning: person resting by a tree = rest

history.meaning: stop in the shade and catch one's breath; rest
rest; take a break

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 休息 (via 萌典)

cognates.word: 休憩室 (kyūkeishitsu, parallel formation) / 休息室 (kyūsokushitsu)

休息室.etymology: A three-morpheme modifier-head architectural compound combining 休息 (xiūxi, an ancient coordinative verb already attested in the Classic of Poetry 诗经·周南·汉广: 休 'lean against a tree to rest' + 息 'draw breath, cease exertion') with the locative head noun 室 (shì, 'inner chamber, room'). Coined in modern institutional Chinese to designate dedicated lounges in studios, theaters, airports, and offices.

history.meaning: pause beneath shade and catch one's breath; cease labor
lounge, staff break room, VIP waiting room, or backstage green room

休息室.notes: In TV production and live events, 休息室 (or 艺人休息室 / 贵宾休息室) is the exact equivalent of English 'green room' or 'VIP backstage lounge' where guests wait before going on air.

休息间.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining the coordinative disyllabic verb 休息 (xiūxi, 'to rest, cease and breathe', from 休 'to lean against a tree and rest' + 息 'to breathe, cease') with the spatial head noun 间 (traditional 間, jiān, 'room, space between'). In modern television and studio production environments, it designates a dedicated lounge or backstage dressing room for performers and crew.

history.meaning: to cease activity and catch one's breath; to rest (Classical Chinese)
crevice, interval, partitioned room or bay between pillars
lounge, waiting room, backstage dressing room

休息间.notes: Slightly more compact and studio-oriented than 休息室 (xiūxishì); in broadcast production, 艺人休息间 specifically refers to a celebrity's private green room or dressing room.

rootFamily.gloss: private room or booth (in a restaurant/club)

众星.etymology: A modifier-head compound formed from 众 (traditional 眾, zhòng, 'multitude, crowd, all', originally an ideogram of three people working under an eye or sun) modifying 星 (xīng, 'star, celestial body'). Attested in Classical Chinese cosmology—famously in the Analects (论语·为政) phrase 众星共之 ('all the stars bow toward the North Star')—before undergoing metaphorical extension in modern entertainment journalism to mean an assembly of celebrities.

history.meaning: the multitude of stars in the night sky (Analects)
a galaxy of celebrities, all the assembled stars

众星.notes: High-frequency headline word in entertainment media, especially in four-character idioms like 众星云集 ('stars gather like clouds') and 众星捧月 ('a crowd of stars surrounding the moon').

众筹.etymology: A 21st-century neologism coined as a semantic calque of English 'crowdfunding', structured with a subject/instrument modifier and verbal head: 众 (traditional 眾, zhòng, 'the crowd, multitude, public') + 筹 (traditional 籌, chóu, originally 'bamboo tally stick used for counting', hence 'to plan, calculate, raise funds', truncated from 筹资 chóuzī 'to raise capital' or 筹款 chóukuǎn 'to raise money').

history.meaning: bamboo counting tally; to plan, calculate, or levy
to raise funds or capital for a venture
to crowdfund; crowdfunding (calque of English crowdfunding)

众筹.notes: Used as both a verb and a noun in startup, film production, and fan-support contexts (e.g., 发起众筹 'launch a crowdfunding campaign').

rootFamily.gloss: to prepare, plan and arrange in advance

优先.etymology: An adverbial and verbal compound pairing 优 (traditional 優, yōu, originally 'actor/entertainer', extended in Classical Chinese to 'abundant, superior, preferential') with 先 (xiān, 'first, in front, ahead'). Popularized in modern East Asian legal and administrative vocabulary alongside Japanese 優先 (yūsen) to render Western legal concepts of priority and right of precedence.

history.meaning: abundant, generous, superior, preferential treatment
taking precedence, having priority over others

优先.notes: Commonly modifies verbs directly as an adverbial (e.g., 优先考虑 'give priority consideration to', 优先录用 'hire with priority') or forms nouns like 优先权 ('right of priority').

优势.etymology: A modifier-head compound consisting of 优 (traditional 優, yōu, 'superior, surpassing, abundant') and 势 (traditional 勢, shì, 'strategic configuration, momentum, power, positional force'). While both roots are deeply rooted in Classical Chinese statecraft (such as Sunzi's concept of 势), the disyllabic compound crystallized in modern Sino-Japanese and Mandarin discourse to denote strategic or competitive superiority.

history.meaning: strategic advantage, positional momentum, power (Art of War)
dominant position, competitive edge, advantage

优势.notes: Its direct antonym is 劣势 (lièshì, 'disadvantage, inferior position'); frequent collocations in business and media include 占据优势 ('hold the upper hand') and 核心优势 ('core strength').

优秀.etymology: A coordinative adjectival compound joining 优 (traditional 優, yōu, 'abundant, superior, refined') and 秀 (xiù, originally 'grain coming into ear and flowering', hence 'flourishing, elegant, outstanding'). Both morphemes appear paired in imperial evaluation and literary criticism before standardizing in modern Mandarin and Sino-Japanese (優秀) as the standard grade and descriptor for 'excellent, outstanding'.

history.meaning: grain flowering into ear; flourishing, outstanding talent
outstanding, excellent in character or performance

优秀.notes: Used both for high-level praise of professionals (优秀的制作人 'an outstanding producer') and in contemporary colloquial irony (你真优秀 'well aren't you something').

会.etymology: Polysemous verb and noun (會, originally depicting a covered vessel with a lid coming together): 'meet, assemble, meeting' and as a modal verb 'know how to (a learned skill); be likely to, will'.

morphemes.meaning: come together -> meet; master a skill; will

history.meaning: come together; meet; understand; happen to
can (learned skill); will/likely to; meeting

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 会 (via 萌典)

会上.etymology: A locative noun phrase formed by attaching the postpositional localizer 上 (shàng, 'on, upon, within the sphere of') to the bound noun 会 (traditional 會, huì, 'assembly, meeting, conference', abbreviated from 会议 huìyì). In Mandarin spatial-temporal metaphor, events and organizations take 上 to mark active participation or occurrence within the bounds of the gathering.

history.meaning: to assemble, come together; an assembly or gathering
at the meeting, during the conference session

会上.notes: Functions syntactically as a time/place nominal at the start of a clause or after 在 (e.g., 在会上宣布 'announce at the meeting'), contrasting with 会前 ('before the meeting') and 会后 ('after the meeting').

会儿.etymology: An erhua (儿化) diminutive nominal derived from 会 (traditional 會, huì, 'junction, convergence of time, brief moment') suffixed with the retroflex diminutive 儿 (ér, originally 'child', grammaticalized in Northern Mandarin into a phonological rhotic coda marking smallness or brevity). Already in Tang–Song vernacular, 会 (and 会子 huìzi) denoted a brief interval of time.

history.meaning: a juncture of time, a brief moment or spell
a little while, a brief moment (with northern rhotic suffix)

会儿.notes: Almost always bound to a determiner or numeral in speech: 一会儿 ('a little while / in a moment'), 这会儿 ('right now'), 那会儿 ('back then'), or 多大会儿 ('how long').

rootFamily.gloss: a little while; in a moment

会前.etymology: A temporal-locative compound combining 会 (traditional 會, huì, 'meeting, conference', shortened from 会议 huìyì) with the temporal postposition 前 (qián, 'before, in front of, prior to', originally 'to advance without walking' on a boat, written 歬). It follows the productive Chinese pattern where monosyllabic event nouns take 前/中/后 to denote phases of an event.

history.meaning: in front, ahead, prior in time or space
prior to the meeting, pre-conference

会前.notes: Frequently used directly as a temporal adverbial or attributive modifier without 的 (e.g., 会前准备 'pre-meeting preparation', 会前沟通 'aligning before the meeting').

会场.etymology: A modifier-head compound joining 会 (traditional 會, huì, 'assembly, gathering, conference') and 场 (traditional 場, chǎng, originally 'leveled earthen altar or threshing ground', generalized to 'open site, arena, venue'). Shared across the Sinosphere (Japanese 会場 kaijō), it designates the physical hall or auditorium where a formal conference, ceremony, or live broadcast takes place.

history.meaning: leveled ceremonial ground, arena, gathering place
conference hall, assembly venue, event site

会场.notes: In live television and galas, studios distinguish between 主会场 ('main venue') and 分会场 ('sub-venue / satellite venue').

rootFamily.gloss: venue,場地, space for an event

会客厅.etymology: A three-character modifier-head compound where the verb-object compound 会客 (traditional 會客, huìkè, 'to meet/receive guests', from 会 'to meet' + 客 'guest, visitor') modifies the architectural head noun 厅 (traditional 廳, tīng, 'central hall, government reception hall, large room'). It denotes a formal parlor or executive reception room used for receiving visitors.

history.meaning: to meet and receive guests or visitors
large hall for official business or receiving guests
reception hall, drawing room, VIP lounge

会客厅.notes: More formal and institutional than 客厅 (kètīng, which usually means a home 'living room'); companies, television networks, and government offices have a 会客厅 for VIP guests.

cognates.meaning: meeting place, assembly office, club house

会所.etymology: A modifier-head compound formed from 会 (traditional 會, huì, 'association, guild, gathering') and 所 (suǒ, 'place, building, institution'). In Ming–Qing China and Edo Japan (会所 kaisho), it referred to guildhalls and civic assembly offices; in late-20th-century Hong Kong Cantonese, it was revitalized to translate British 'clubhouse', subsequently spreading into Mainland Mandarin for upscale private clubs.

history.meaning: place of assembly; merchant guildhall or civic office
private members' club, luxury clubhouse, spa/leisure club

会所.notes: In contemporary Mainland usage, 私人会所 ('private club') carries strong connotations of high-end, exclusive business networking or luxury leisure behind closed doors.

会议.etymology: A coordinative compound combining 会 (traditional 會, huì, 'to assemble, come together') and 议 (traditional 議, yì, 'to deliberate, discuss, debate matters of state'). Already attested as a verbal expression ('to assemble and deliberate') in Han dynasty histories such as the Shiji (史记), it was later reinforced via Meiji Japanese 会議 (kaigi) as the standard modern noun for a formal conference or meeting.

history.meaning: to assemble at court and deliberate on state policy (Shiji)
formal meeting, conference, parliamentary or corporate session

会议.notes: The standard formal noun corresponding to the colloquial verb-object phrase 开会 (kāihuì, 'to hold/attend a meeting'); common collocations include 召开会议 ('convene a conference') and 主持会议 ('chair a meeting').

rootFamily.gloss: to hold or attend a meeting

会议室.etymology: A modifier-head compound appending the architectural head noun 室 (shì, 'inner room, chamber') to the disyllabic noun 会议 (traditional 會議, huìyì, 'meeting, conference'). Built on the productive East Asian institutional naming pattern `[activity/function] + 室` (cf. 办公室 'office', 休息室 'lounge'), shared directly with Japanese 会議室 (kaigishitsu).

history.meaning: inner chamber of a building, room
conference room, boardroom

会议室.notes: In corporate and media production settings, 会议室 is the everyday term for any office meeting room or boardroom (e.g., 大会议室 'main boardroom').

cognates.meaning: minutes of a meeting, proceedings record

会议记录.etymology: A four-character modifier-head compound joining 会议 (traditional 會議, huìyì, 'meeting, conference') with 记录 (traditional 記錄, jìlù, 'written record, minutes', itself a coordinative compound of 记 'to write down, remember' and 录 'to copy, inscribe on metal/bamboo'). It denotes the official written transcript or minutes of a meeting.

history.meaning: to inscribe and record events or documents

history.form: 會議記錄 / 会议记录
history.meaning: meeting minutes, official record of proceedings

会议记录.notes: Doing the minutes is expressed as 做会议记录; for a more concise, action-item-oriented summary distributed after a meeting, corporate Mandarin also uses 会议纪要 (huìyì jìyào).

rootFamily.gloss: summary of meeting minutes, memorandum of proceedings
documentary film; to record and document

cognates.meaning: president of a society/club; chairman of the board
chairman of a conglomerate (chaebol); club president

会长.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 会 (traditional 會, huì, 'association, society, club, guild') with 长 (traditional 長, zhǎng, 'elder, chief, head, leader', Old Chinese *tjaŋʔ). Used historically for leaders of religious or mutual-aid societies, and reinforced in modern times by Japanese 会長 (kaichō) to designate the president of a club, student council, fan club, or trade association.

history.meaning: senior, elder, chief of a group or office
president or head of an association, society, or club

会长.notes: Note the pronunciation zhǎng (third tone, 'chief/head'), not cháng ('long'). In Mandarin, 会长 usually leads an association (协会), fan club (后援会), or chamber of commerce (商会), whereas a corporate board chair is 董事长 (dǒngshìzhǎng).

rootFamily.gloss: chairman of the board of directors

传.etymology: Phono-semantic character (傳, person 亻 + phonetic 專 zhuān): read chuán as a verb meaning 'pass on, transmit, hand down, spread, summon', and read zhuàn as a noun meaning 'commentary, biography, historical record'.

history.meaning: relay by post-station; pass down; transmit (chuán); commentary/biography (zhuàn)
pass; transmit; spread

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 传 (via 萌典)

传出.etymology: A verb-directional (resultative) compound pairing the root verb 传 (traditional 傳, chuán, 'to pass on, transmit, relay from station to station') with the directional complement 出 (chū, 'to go out, emerge, come forth'). It depicts news, sound, or rumors radiating outward from an enclosed or private source into public awareness.

history.meaning: to relay by post-horse; to hand down, transmit, circulate
to emanate, leak out, spread outward (of news, sound, or rumor)

传出.notes: Very common in entertainment journalism for news or gossip leaking out (e.g., 传出消息 'word got out', 传出绯闻 'rumors of a romance broke out').

rootFamily.gloss: to come in, be introduced from abroad (of news/sounds/ideas)

cognates.meaning: bill, invoice, chit (false friend in modern business)

传单.etymology: A modifier-head or verb-object nominal compound combining 传 (traditional 傳, chuán, 'to circulate, pass around, propagate') with 单 (traditional 單, dān, 'single sheet of paper, printed slip, list'). Originally referring to a circulating notice slip in late imperial administration, it became the standard modern word for a printed handbill, promotional flyer, or leaflet.

history.meaning: circulating official notice slip or dispatch sheet
printed handbill, promotional flyer, propaganda leaflet

传单.notes: Takes the verb 发 (fā) or 派发 (pàifā) for 'handing out flyers' (发传单) and the measure word 张 (zhāng, 'sheet') or 份 (fèn, 'copy').

传媒.etymology: A late-20th-century syllabic portmanteau contraction of 传播媒介 (traditional 傳播媒介, chuánbō méijiè, 'medium of communication / mass media'), pairing 传 (traditional 傳, chuán, 'to transmit, disseminate') with 媒 (méi, originally 'marriage go-between, matchmaker', hence 'intermediary, medium'). Coined in Hong Kong media discourse before becoming ubiquitous across Mainland China for the media industry.

history.meaning: marriage go-between, intermediary (Book of Odes)
communications medium, mass media
the media, media industry (contraction of 传播媒介)

传媒.notes: Slightly more institutional and industry-oriented than 媒体 (méitǐ); entertainment and broadcasting companies routinely name themselves XX文化传媒有限公司 ('XX Culture & Media Co., Ltd.').

传播.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound uniting 传 (traditional 傳, chuán, 'to pass down, relay, transmit') and 播 (bō, originally 'to sow seeds by hand', hence 'to scatter, broadcast, spread far and wide'). Attested in Northern and Southern Dynasties and Tang literary texts (such as the Beishi 北史), and later adopted in modern media studies to translate English 'communication', 'dissemination', and 'propagation'.

history.meaning: to pass on and scatter widely (of fame, teachings, or edicts)
to disseminate, propagate, broadcast; mass communication

传播.notes: Both a core everyday verb ('spread news/culture/viruses') and the formal academic term for 'communication studies' (传播学 chuánbōxué, 大众传播 'mass communication').

rootFamily.gloss: to broadcast, air (a show or video)

传票.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 传 (traditional 傳, chuán, in its legal/official sense 'to summon, call before a magistrate', short for 传唤 chuánhuàn) and 票 (piào, 'printed slip, warrant, ticket'). Originating in Ming–Qing yamen administration for a magistrate's warrant summoning a party to court, it remains the standard Chinese legal term for a subpoena or court summons.

history.meaning: magistrate's warrant slip summoning a person to the yamen court
court summons, subpoena

morphemes.meaning: to summon to court, call forward (cf. 传唤)

传票.notes: Major false friend with Japanese 伝票 (denpyō) and Korean 전표 (jeonpyo), which mean a harmless commercial 'invoice/voucher/receipt slip', whereas Mandarin 法院传票 is a 'court subpoena/summons'.

rootFamily.gloss: to summon to court or police questioning
to summon for interrogation (of a suspect)

传说.etymology: A compound of 传 (traditional 傳, chuán, 'to hand down, pass on orally from person to person') and 说 (traditional 說, shuō, 'to speak, narrate; narrative account, theory'). Attested in Tang–Song literature for oral accounts passed down through generations, it functions both as a coordinative verb ('it is rumored / people say') and as a noun ('legend, folk tale, rumor').

history.meaning: to pass on by word of mouth; an orally transmitted account
legend, folklore; rumor; it is said that...

传说.notes: Can mean an ancient folk legend (民间传说) or, in everyday workplace/showbiz speech, an unverified rumor or hearsay ('they say that...'). Avoid confusing with the ancient Shang dynasty prime minister Fu Yue, whose name is written 傅說 (Fù Yuè).

rootFamily.gloss: hearsay, rumor, what is heard around
biography (read zhuàn); or to pass down (chuán)

传说中.etymology: A locative-attributive phrase composed of the noun 传说 (traditional 傳說, chuánshuō, 'legend, rumor, oral tradition') followed by the postposition 中 (zhōng, 'inside, within, among'). Literally meaning 'within legend' or 'in the rumors', it grammaticalized in modern vernacular and internet Mandarin into an idiomatic pre-nominal modifier meaning 'fabled, legendary, much-talked-about'.

history.meaning: in legends, according to folklore or oral tradition
the fabled, much-hyped, oft-rumored (person or thing)

传说中.notes: Extremely common in conversational and showbiz banter before 的 + noun: e.g., 你就是传说中的魔鬼制作人 ('So you are the fabled demon producer everyone talks about!').

传遍.etymology: A verb-resultative compound combining the action verb 传 (traditional 傳, chuán, 'to transmit, spread, circulate') with the resultative complement 遍 (biàn, traditional 遍/遍, 'all over, everywhere, throughout', originally 'to go all the way around'). The second morpheme specifies that the transmission has reached every corner of a given domain.

history.meaning: to make a complete circuit; all over, everywhere, universal
to spread all over, circulate throughout (a city, industry, or country)

传遍.notes: Takes a place or group directly as its object without needing a preposition: e.g., 消息很快就传遍了整个公司 ('The news quickly spread throughout the entire company').

rootFamily.gloss: all over the world; or everywhere in the sky/land

传闻.etymology: A Classical Chinese compound pairing 传 (traditional 傳, chuán, 'to pass on, relay at secondhand') with 闻 (traditional 聞, wén, originally 'to hear with the ears', later 'what is heard, news, report'). Famously contrasted with direct observation in the Gongyang Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals (公羊传), which distinguished 所见 ('what was witnessed'), 所闻 ('what was heard'), and 所传闻 ('what was heard at secondhand').

history.meaning: to hear through secondhand transmission (Gongyang Zhuan)
rumor, hearsay, unverified media report

传闻.notes: More formal and journalistic than 八卦 ('gossip'); entertainment PR statements frequently address 坊间传闻 ('street rumors') or 不实传闻 ('untrue rumors').

伤.etymology: Verb and noun meaning 'injure, wound, hurt, harm' (傷, person 亻 + 𠂉/昜 yáng phonetic, from 創/𥏼 'arrow/blade wound').

history.meaning: wound; injure; grieve
injure; hurt; wound

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 伤 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: bodily injury, assault and battery, harm

cognates.word: thương hại (note: shifted to 'to pity' in modern Vietnamese!)

伤害.etymology: A coordinative verb-and-noun compound joining 伤 (traditional 傷, shāng, 'to wound with a weapon, injure, grieve') and 害 (hài, 'to harm, damage, impair, destroy'). Attested since the Warring States period (e.g., Mencius and Xunzi) for inflicting physical or moral harm, it functions in modern Mandarin as both a transitive verb ('to hurt/harm') and an abstract noun ('harm, trauma, injury').

history.meaning: to wound, injure, or do harm to life or virtue (Mencius)
to harm, hurt (emotionally or physically); injury, harm, damage

伤害.notes: Covers both physical injury (人身伤害 'personal bodily injury') and emotional or reputational hurt (造成伤害 'cause harm/hurt', 伤害感情 'hurt someone's feelings'). Note the striking Vietnamese false friend thương hại, which evolved semantically to mean 'to pity/feel sorry for'.

rootFamily.gloss: to sustain an injury, get hurt/wounded

伪热度.etymology: A contemporary Chinese media and internet compound formed by prefixing the classical negative/evaluative morpheme 伪 (traditional 偽, wěi, 'false, counterfeit, man-made, bogus', composed of 人 'person' + 为 'to make/contrive') to the modifier-head noun 热度 (rèdù, 'degree of heat', metaphorically 'media buzz, trending popularity', from 热 'hot' + 度 'degree/measure'). It denotes artificially manufactured online traffic or fake buzz.

history.meaning: human artifice; false, counterfeit, spurious (Xunzi)
temperature, degree of heat; popular enthusiasm or media buzz
fake buzz, astroturfed or artificially inflated popularity

伪热度.notes: A key critical term in contemporary Chinese entertainment and marketing for popularity inflated via bots (水军 'water army'), bought trending topics (买热搜), or click farms rather than genuine audience engagement.

rootFamily.gloss: degree of heat; media buzz, trending popularity
fake fan (e.g., bandwagon fan); or hypocrisy (伪善)

估值.etymology: A concise financial compound formed from 估 (gū, 'to estimate, appraise market price, evaluate', originally a vernacular/mercantile character related to 贾 gǔ 'merchant/trade') and 值 (zhí, 'price, monetary worth, value', originally 'to hold upright / meet equivalently'). Coined as a compact modern economic term—also functioning as an abbreviation of 评估价值 ('appraised value')—for asset or company valuation.

history.meaning: to appraise, estimate the market price or tax value of goods
appraised value, financial valuation (of a startup or company)

估值.notes: Ubiquitous in venture capital, film/TV production financing, and tech startup discussions (e.g., 公司估值十亿 'the company is valued at one billion').

rootFamily.gloss: value, worth; or market capitalization (市值)

估计.etymology: A coordinative verb-and-noun compound combining 估 (gū, 'to appraise, gauge, estimate a price or quantity') with 计 (traditional 計, jì, 'to calculate, count, reckon', from 言 'speech/words' + 十 'ten', i.e., counting up to ten). Emerging in Ming–Qing vernacular and mercantile usage, it broadened from calculating approximate financial costs to general epistemic estimation ('to reckon, suppose').

history.meaning: to count, calculate, tally up accounts; plan or calculation
to appraise and calculate approximately; to estimate, reckon, guess

估计.notes: Functions both as a transitive verb of quantitative estimation (估计成本 'estimate the cost') and as a conversational epistemic adverbial meaning 'probably / I reckon' (他估计不来了 'He probably isn't coming').

rootFamily.gloss: to appraise price; or to weigh/gauge (估量)
to expect, forecast, project in advance

伴侣.etymology: A coordinative nominal compound uniting two near-synonymous roots with the 'person' radical (亻): 伴 (bàn, 'companion, associate; to accompany', from 人 + 半 'half', i.e., one's other half or mate in a pair) and 侣 (traditional 侶, lǚ, 'traveling companion, fellow, mate', related to 旅 'troop/travel together'). Attested in Tang–Song poetry for a fellow traveler or literary companion, it now primarily denotes a romantic life partner or spouse.

history.meaning: fellow traveler, companion on a journey or in seclusion (Tang–Song poetry)
life companion, romantic partner, spouse

伴侣.notes: More formal, inclusive, and poetic than 男/女朋友 or 老公/老婆; used for 'life partner' (终身伴侣), 'soulmate' (灵魂伴侣), and inclusive legal/social contexts ('domestic partner').

rootFamily.gloss: partner, buddy, fellow member of a group

伴奏.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-compound combining 伴 (bàn, Middle Chinese *bwanH*, 'companion; to accompany') and 奏 (zòu, Middle Chinese *tsuwH*, 'to present to the throne; to perform music on instruments'). Coined as a Meiji-era Japanese wasei-kango (伴奏, bansō) to render European musical 'accompaniment' and borrowed into late-Qing and Republican Mandarin; in contemporary television and studio production it further denotes a pre-recorded instrumental backing track (as opposed to a vocal master).

history.meaning: to perform ritual court music or present memorials to the sovereign
instrumental or vocal accompaniment supporting a principal melody
musical accompaniment; pre-recorded instrumental backing track in broadcast and karaoke production

伴奏.notes: In live TV variety shows and recording studios (such as in 幕后之王), 伴奏帯 or 伴奏 specifically refers to the instrumental backing track without lead vocals (contrasted with 原唱, 'original vocal track', or 清唱, 'a cappella').

rootFamily.gloss: backup dancing; to dance as accompaniment
to perform on a musical instrument

cognates.meaning: to stretch, extend, grow (kun'yomi reading applied to kanji)

伸.etymology: A phono-semantic graph combining the semantic classifier 亻 ('person') with the phonetic-semantic stem 申 (shēn, Old Chinese *l̥iŋ, Middle Chinese *syin, originally a pictograph of forked lightning stretching across the sky). In early Classical manuscripts, 申 and 信 were often used interchangeably for 'to unbend, stretch out' (contrasted with 屈, 'to bend, contract') before 伸 stabilized as the dedicated somatic and spatial verb for extending a limb or object.

history.meaning: to extend, unbend, straighten out (antonym of 屈)
to stretch the body or limbs; to redress a grievance
to stretch out, extend, reach forth

伸.notes: Core Classical antonym pair 屈伸 ('bending and stretching') survives in idioms like 能屈能伸 ('able to bow down or stand tall as circumstances demand'); in everyday Mandarin 伸 typically takes body parts as objects (伸手, 伸腿, 伸懒腰).

rootFamily.gloss: able to yield and assert oneself flexibly

cognates.meaning: to reach out one's hand; to ask for money or help

伸手.etymology: A transparent verb-object (动宾) compound uniting 伸 (shēn, 'to stretch forth, extend') and 手 (shǒu, Old Chinese *n̥juʔ, Middle Chinese *syuwX, 'hand'). Attested across medieval and early vernacular narratives in its literal somatic sense ('to reach out one's hand', e.g., 伸手不见五指, 'so dark one cannot see the five fingers on an outstretched hand'), it later developed two prominent figurative extensions: soliciting handouts and encroaching on someone else's domain.

history.meaning: to extend one's hand physically
to reach out a hand; to beg or ask for favors/money without effort
to reach out one's hand; to ask for handouts or meddle in outside turf

伸手.notes: Functioning as a separable verb-object compound (离合词, e.g., 伸出手来), 伸手 in workplace and media dramas often carries a sharp figurative edge: 向家里伸手 ('ask one's family for money') or 手伸得太长 ('overstepping boundaries / meddling in another team's project').

rootFamily.gloss: so pitch-dark you cannot see your own fingers
chronic freeloader who expects everything handed to them
to step in, intervene, take action

cognates.meaning: visiting to inquire after someone's health or pay respects

伺候.etymology: A coordinative verb compound pairing 伺 (Middle Chinese *tsiH*, 'to peer at, observe closely, attend upon') and 候 (Middle Chinese *huwH*, 'to watch for signs, await, wait upon'). In Han through Tang Literary Chinese (pronounced sìhòu), it meant 'to reconnoiter, spy out, or watch attentively for'. During the Yuan, Ming, and Qing dynasties, northern vernacular speech shifted the initial vowel and reduced the second syllable to neutral tone (cìhou), specializing its sense to 'waiting hand and foot upon superiors or finicky charges'.

history.meaning: to watch closely for signs, reconnoiter, or await orders
to wait upon masters, elders, or officials in domestic/court service
to wait upon, tend to, or cater to demanding people (often ironic)

伺候.notes: Pronounced cìhou (with cì-, NOT sì-, and a neutral second syllable) in colloquial speech; in modern workplaces and entertainment crews, 难伺候 ('hard to please / high-maintenance') is the classic complaint about diva celebrities or demanding clients.

rootFamily.gloss: to spy on, watch for an opportunity
to wait in line or in a waiting room

似的.etymology: An enclitic similative particle grammaticalized in northern vernacular Mandarin from 似 (Middle Chinese *ziX*, 'to resemble, be like', preserving a specialized colloquial reading shì distinct from literary sì) fused with the adverbial/attributive marker 的 (de, written 底 or 地 in Song–Yuan texts). Frequently paired as the closing bracket of discontinuous comparative frames such as 像…似的 or 跟…似的 ('just as though…'), it softens or dramatizes figurative comparisons.

history.meaning: appearing thus; in a manner resembling
just like, as if (enclitic similative marker in northern Mandarin)
as if, just like (postpositional particle of comparison)

似的.notes: Watch the mandatory polyphone (多音字): 似 is pronounced sì everywhere else (似乎 sìhū, 相似 xiāngsì), and is read shì ONLY in 似的 (shìde); pair it naturally with 跟 or 像, as in 跟疯了似的 ('like crazy').

cognates.meaning: however, provided that (in 但し tadashi)

但.etymology: A phono-semantic character formed from 亻 ('person') and phonetic 旦 (dàn, Old Chinese *daːns, Middle Chinese *danH). Etymologically cognate with 袒 ('to strip bare to the waist'), the graph was loaned in Qin–Han Chinese for a restrictive adverb meaning 'only, merely, solely' (as in 但见, 'one only sees'). In conversational and narrative contexts, 'merely [note that X]' pragmatically invited contrast with a preceding clause, grammaticalizing 但 into a core adversative conjunction ('but, yet').

history.meaning: bare-chested, stripped to the waist (cognate with 袒); loaned for 'only, merely'
only; so long as; however, yet
but, yet (concise adversative conjunction); merely (in fixed idioms)

但.notes: Monosyllabic 但 feels punchier and slightly tighter in register than disyllabic 但是, while its older Classical sense 'only / merely' remains alive in everyday idioms like 不求有功，但求无过 ('seeking no merit, asking only to avoid blame') and 但愿 ('if only / I only wish').

rootFamily.gloss: if only, I only hope that
might as well, there is no harm in speaking frankly

但凡.etymology: A coordinative conditional-universal conjunctional compound fusing 但 (dàn, in its Six Dynasties–Tang conditional sense 'so long as, whenever') with 凡 (fán, Old Chinese *bom, Middle Chinese *bjon, 'all, every, whatsoever'). Lexicalized in Tang transformation texts (变文), Song Neo-Confucian dialogues, and Ming–Qing vernacular fiction, 但凡 unites universal quantification with minimal threshold conditionality ('in every case where; so long as there is even a bit of').

history.meaning: in all cases whatever; whenever anyone
whoever, whenever, so long as (often introducing universal rules or counterfactuals)
as long as there is any (even slightly); whenever

但凡.notes: In contemporary spoken Mandarin and drama dialogue, 但凡 ('as long as there were even a shred of...') very frequently sets up exasperated counterfactuals: 但凡你用点心 ('If you had put in even an ounce of effort...').

cognates.word: 但係 / 但是 (daan6 hai6 / daan6 si6)

但是.etymology: A disyllabic conjunction formed through the boundary reanalysis of restrictive/adversative 但 (dàn, 'only, however') followed by demonstrative-turned-copula 是 (shì, Middle Chinese *dzyeX*, 'this; is'). In Han through Tang texts, 但是 was originally an inclusive conditional sequence meaning 'so long as it is / whatever is' (parallel to modern 只要是), before re-grammaticalizing in Song–Yuan–Ming vernacular into the primary Mandarin adversative conjunction 'but, however'.

history.meaning: only this; whatever is / so long as it is
however, yet, but (adversative clause connector)
but, however (standard disyllabic adversative conjunction)

但是.notes: Pairs canonically with 虽然 ('although... yet...') in Mandarin's concessive-adversative frame 虽然…但是… (remember that English forbids 'although... but...', whereas Mandarin strongly prefers keeping 但是 or 可是 in the main clause!).

rootFamily.gloss: nevertheless, could it be, or rather

位.etymology: Polite measure word for people—especially guests, teachers, and elders (一位客人 'a guest', 一位老师 'a teacher'). Combining 亻 ('person') and 立 ('stand'), 位 in Classical court texts named a person's proper standing place or seat of honor, naturally becoming a respectful counter.

history.meaning: standing place; seat; rank

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 位 (via 萌典)

位置.etymology: Compound noun of 位 ('standing place at court, seat, position', person 亻 + 立 'stand') + 置 ('set up, place, position', net 罒 + 直): 'position, location, seat, place'.

history.meaning: assigned rank/seat -> spatial position, location

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 位置 (via 萌典)

低.etymology: Adjective and verb meaning 'low (in height, level, pitch, or voice); bow/hang down', formed from person (亻) + 氐 (dī, 'base, bottom, root touching the ground').

history.meaning: low; beneath; droop or bow down

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 低 (via 萌典)

低头.etymology: Verb-object compound of 低 ('lower, bow down') + 头 (頭, 'head'): 'lower one's head, look down' (famously in Li Bai's 举头望明月，低头思故乡) and figuratively 'yield, submit'.

history.meaning: bow/lower one's head; yield

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 低头 (via 萌典)

低沉.etymology: The word '低沉' (dīchén, low and deep) pairs '低' (low) and '沉' (heavy, sink). '沉' historically features the water radical, originally describing objects submerging in a river. In classical poetry, these two concepts were often linked to describe atmospheric phenomena, such as heavy, looming clouds. Later, the term metaphorically extended to describe sounds that are deep in pitch or quiet in volume. By the modern era, it broadened further to include emotional states, depicting a gloomy or depressed mood.

history.meaning: low

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 低沉

cognates.meaning: lower-order animal (in taxonomy: 下等動物; kanji cognate components 低級 + 動物)

低级动物.etymology: A four-character modifier-head nominal phrase built from two disyllabic modifier-head Sino-compounds: 低级 (dījí: 低 'low' + 级 'step, rank, taxonomic grade') modifying 动物 (dòngwù: 动 'moving, animate' + 物 'creature, thing', attested in the Classical Rites of Zhou 周礼 in contrast to 植物 and standardized in modern East Asian biology via Meiji Japanese 動物 dōbutsu). From evolutionary taxonomy ('lower-order / primitive animal'), colloquial Mandarin extended it figuratively to people ruled by raw impulse or base appetites.

history.meaning: animate, mobile creatures (contrasted with stationary plants 植物 in Zhouli)
lower invertebrate or evolutionary primitive organism in modern zoology
primitive creature; figurative slur or self-reproach for someone driven by base instincts

低级动物.notes: Used outside biology as either stinging sarcasm or wry self-deprecation (e.g., admitting one is slaves to hunger, exhaustion, or impulse—contrast with 高级动物, 'higher-order beings / humans').

rootFamily.gloss: higher animal (often referring ironically to humans)

低调.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 低 (dī, Middle Chinese *tej*, 'low, bowed') and 调 (diào, traditional 調, Middle Chinese *dewH*, 'musical pitch, mode, tonal register'). Initially a technical term in acoustics, musicology ('low pitch/register'), and photography/cinematography ('low-key lighting', calquing English low-key), it gained widespread metaphorical currency in late 20th-century Hong Kong, Taiwanese, and Mainland media discourse for 'keeping a low public profile, understated, discreet'.

history.meaning: low musical register; low-key tonal value in visual arts and photography
understated, discreet, avoiding publicity or ostentation (calquing English 'low-key')

低调.notes: Ubiquitous in entertainment PR and celebrity gossip—e.g., 低调处理 ('handle discreetly out of the press'), 低调奢华 ('understated luxury'), and its direct antonym 高调 ('high-profile, flashy, flamboyant').

住.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining person (亻) + 主 (zhǔ, originally a stationary lamp post). Originally meant 'stop, halt, stay in place', which evolved into both the main verb 'live, reside, stay (at a hotel or home)' and the resultative complement '-zhù' ('hold fast, stop firm', as in 卡住, 记住).

history.meaning: halt; stay; dwell
live/reside; stay; resultative complement 'firmly/to a stop'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 住 (via 萌典)

住处.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound formed from 住 (zhù, Middle Chinese *drjuH*, 'to halt, dwell, reside') modifying 处 (chù, traditional 處, Middle Chinese *tsyhoH*, 'dwelling spot, locus, place', distinguished by departing tone from verbal chǔ 'to dwell, handle'). Emerging in Six Dynasties Buddhist translations and Tang–Song vernacular prose as 住 became the primary verb for 'reside' (displacing Classical 居), 住处 denotes a concrete place of lodging or residence.

history.meaning: monastic lodging, abode, or resting place (also a Buddhist term for mental abiding)
dwelling place, quarters, home address
residence, living quarters, place to stay

住处.notes: Slightly less bureaucratic than 住址 ('registered residential address') and less permanent-sounding than 住宅 ('residential property'); 找个住处 simply means finding a place to live/stay. Always pronounce 处 in fourth tone (zhùchù) when it means 'place'.

住满.etymology: Resultative verb compound combining 住 ('live, stay, occupy') + 满 (滿, 'full, filled to capacity'): 'be fully occupied, booked solid, filled with residents/guests'.

history.meaning: filled to capacity with occupants/guests

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 住满 (via 萌典)

住院.etymology: A modern verb-object (动宾) separable compound combining 住 (zhù, 'to stay, reside temporarily') with 院 (yuàn, Middle Chinese *hjwænH*, originally a walled courtyard in Tang official and monastic architecture, here clipped from 医院 yīyuàn, 'hospital'). Formed in 19th–20th century Mandarin alongside modern clinical medicine, 住院 specifically designates inpatient admission (as opposed to outpatient visits 门诊 and discharge 出院).

history.meaning: walled courtyard compound; Tang–Song state bureau, academy, or hospice (e.g., 安济坊 / 病坊)
to be admitted to and stay in a hospital as an inpatient

morphemes.meaning: hospital (clipped from 医院, originally 'walled courtyard institution')

住院.notes: 住院 is a classic separable verb (离合词): 'hospitalized for a week' is 住了一个星期的院 (never *住院了一个星期), and its direct opposite is 出院 ('to be discharged from the hospital').

rootFamily.gloss: to be discharged from the hospital

体力活儿.etymology: A three-morpheme colloquial northern Mandarin compound consisting of modifier 体力 (tǐlì, traditional 體力, modifier-head: 体 'body' + 力 'strength, physical power'), head noun 活 (huó, clipped from 活计 or 生活 in Ming–Qing vernacular to mean 'work, job, manual task'), and the rhotic diminutive/nominalizing suffix 儿 (-r, 儿化). Contrasted directly with 脑力活儿 ('mental/desk work'), it refers to grueling physical labor or exhausting legwork.

history.meaning: bodily vigor and physical stamina
livelihood, manual craft, chore, or piece of work
heavy manual labor; physically exhausting task

体力活儿.notes: Notice how the 儿化 suffix (-r) distinguishes noun 活儿 (huór, 'work, job, gig') from adjective/verb 活 (huó, 'alive; to live'); in TV production crews, white-collar staff jokingly call marathon shoots, hauling gear, or late-night editing 体力活儿 ('sheer physical grunt work').

rootFamily.gloss: to work, do manual labor or chores

cognates.meaning: embodiment, personification, giving concrete form to

体现.etymology: A compound verb uniting 体 (tǐ, traditional 體, Middle Chinese *thejX*, 'body, inner substance; to embody') and 现 (xiàn, traditional 現, Middle Chinese *henH*, 'to become visible, manifest', originally the sheen of polished jade and the verbal counterpart of 见). Drawing on Song–Ming Neo-Confucian metaphysics where invisible substance (体) manifests in phenomena (现) and reinforced by Meiji-era Sino-Japanese 体現 (taigen), it means giving concrete, observable expression to an abstract quality, value, or intent.

history.meaning: essential substance (体) versus outward manifestation (现) in Buddhist and Neo-Confucian philosophy
to embody, manifest concretely, reflect an underlying principle or quality

体现.notes: Takes abstract nouns as objects—体现价值 ('embody value'), 体现诚意 ('demonstrate sincerity'), 体现了细节 ('reflects attention to detail')—whereas 表现 focuses more on outward behavioral performance ('how someone performs/acts').

rootFamily.gloss: to experience personally, appreciate through lived insight

cognates.meaning: system, organized theoretical or institutional structure

体系.etymology: A modifier-head / coordinative Sino-compound of 体 (tǐ, traditional 體, 'organic body, whole structure') and 系 (xì, traditional 系, Middle Chinese *hejH*, 'linked silken thread, lineage, interconnected series'). Coined as a Meiji Japanese scholarly compound (体系, taikei) to translate German System and English system in philosophy and science, it entered early 20th-century Mandarin to denote a macro-level, logically or institutionally integrated framework.

history.meaning: systematic philosophical, legal, or scientific body of knowledge (translating European 'System')
overarching organizational, industrial, or theoretical system/framework

体系.notes: Compare 体系 with 系统 (xìtǒng): 体系 always refers to a grand, abstract institutional or conceptual architecture (工业体系 'industrial ecosystem', 评估体系 'evaluation framework'), never a concrete computer OS or plumbing system (which must be 系统).

rootFamily.gloss: connection, contact; to get in touch

体育.etymology: A Sino-compound combining 体 (tǐ, traditional 體, 'physical body') and 育 (yù, Old Chinese *luɡ, Middle Chinese *yuwk*, 'to give birth to, rear, cultivate, educate'). Modeled in 1870s Meiji Japan as 体育 (taiiku) to render French éducation physique and English physical education alongside 徳育 ('moral education') and 知育 ('intellectual education'), it was adopted into late-Qing educational reform (and Mao Zedong's famous 1917 essay 体育之研究) and broadened in Mainland Mandarin to encompass competitive sports generally.

history.meaning: physical education and bodily cultivation in modern schooling
physical education; bodily training and calisthenics
physical education (PE) as well as competitive sports and athletics industry

体育.notes: In Mainland Mandarin, 体育 covers both school PE class (体育课) and the entire sports broadcast/entertainment sector (体育频道 'sports channel', 体育馆 'indoor stadium/arena'), whereas Japanese 体育 stayed narrower ('PE class', using スポーツ for sports).

体谅.etymology: Compound verb of 体 (體, 'put oneself in another's body/shoes, empathize with') + 谅 (諒, 'forgive, understand, trust', speech 讠 + 京): 'make allowances for, show understanding and empathy toward'.

history.meaning: empathize with and make allowances for; understand

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 体谅 (via 萌典)

体面.etymology: A coordinative compound uniting 体 (tǐ, traditional 體, 'bodily bearing, proper institutional decorum', as in 体统) and 面 (miàn, Middle Chinese *mjenH*, 'face, outward front, social standing'). Attested in Song–Yuan–Ming vernacular texts (such as 朱子语类, 水浒传, and 红楼梦) as a noun meaning 'dignified bearing and social face', it shifted syntactically into a stative verb/adjective meaning 'dignified, respectable, civil, graceful without losing face'.

history.meaning: proper bodily form, social prestige, and outward dignity
prestigious, handsome, respectable, preserving social face (noun and adjective)
dignified, decent, civil, respectable; social dignity

体面.notes: Carries enormous cultural weight in modern urban dramas and pop songs (like Yu Wenwen's hit 体面): 体面地离开 or 给彼此留点体面 means parting ways or handling a crisis with grace, mutual dignity, and no ugly public fallout.

何地.etymology: A Classical Chinese modifier-head interrogative pronoun formed from 何 (hé, Old Chinese *ɡaːl, Middle Chinese *ha*, 'what, which') modifying 地 (dì, Middle Chinese *dijH*, 'earth, territory, locality, place'). Standard in Literary Chinese historical and philosophical prose for asking 'what place; where', it survives in modern Mandarin in elevated, journalistic, or rhetorical frames (such as 身在何地 or 流落何地).

history.meaning: what territory, what place, where
where, what location (formal, written, and four-character idiomatic register)

何地.notes: High-register literary equivalent of colloquial 什么地方 / 哪里; in spoken Mandarin it rarely stands alone as a casual question, appearing instead in rhetorical formulas like 置我于何地 ('what position does that put me in?') or 何时何地.

cognates.meaning: where, what place (read izuko / doko via kun'yomi)

何处.etymology: A Classical modifier-head interrogative compound pairing 何 (hé, 'what, which') with 处 (chù, traditional 處, Middle Chinese *tsyhoH*, 'resting spot, locus, place', whose Old Chinese form combined 虍 tiger-stripes phonetic with 几 'small bench where one stops to rest'). Immortalized in Han–Tang lyric poetry (e.g., 人生何处不相逢, 'where in life do people not meet again?'), it remains productive in poised or poetic modern Mandarin for 'where, whither'.

history.meaning: at what spot, where, whither (especially in Han–Tang verse and prose)
where, from/to what place (poetic, rhetorical, and formal Mandarin)

何处.notes: More lyrical than 何地 and far more formal than 哪儿 / 哪里; common in set expressions like 从何处说起 ('where should one even begin to tell it?'), 何处安身 ('where to find shelter'), and 无处不在 ('omnipresent').

cognates.meaning: why of all things / why must (cf. 하필 hapil)

何必.etymology: A Classical Chinese rhetorical adverbial compound combining interrogative adverb 何 (hé, 'why, to what end') with modal adverb 必 (bì, Old Chinese *piɡ, Middle Chinese *pjit*, 'necessarily, must'). Attested since the Warring States period in the Analects (论语: 何必改作, 'why must it be rebuilt?') and Mencius (孟子: 王何必曰利, 'why must Your Majesty speak of profit?'), it crystallized as a single lexicalized adverbial expressing gentle dissuasion or pointed reproach ('why must one; what need is there to').

history.meaning: for what reason must one... (transparent two-word sequence in Warring States prose)
why bother, there is no need to (lexicalized rhetorical adverb)
why must, why go to the trouble of (often closed with 呢)

何必.notes: Unlike 何地 or 何处, 何必 is completely natural in everyday spoken Mandarin! Frequently paired with 呢—as in 何必呢？ ('Why put yourself/us through this?') or 早知今日，何必当初 ('Had you known today would come, why act like that back then?').

cognates.meaning: when and where (itsu doko; Sino-Japanese kanji parallel 何時何処)

何时何地.etymology: A symmetrical four-character parallel coordinative phrase (ABAC pattern) yoking 何时 (héshí, traditional 何時: 何 'what' + 时 'time, season') and 何地 (hédì: 何 'what' + 地 'place, ground'). Built on Classical Chinese parallelism pairing time (时) and space (地), it functions in modern Mandarin both as a formal compound interrogative ('when and where') and—preceded by 无论 or 不管—as an emphatic universal expression ('whenever and wherever').

history.form: 何时 / 何地 (何時 / 何地)
history.meaning: what season/hour and what territory/place in Classical prose and verse
when and where; (with 无论/不管) at any time and in any place whatsoever

何时何地.notes: Most often heard in motivational speeches, oaths, and drama lines inside the frame 无论何时何地 ('no matter when or where'); its positive colloquial counterpart is 随时随地 ('at any time and any place, on the fly').

rootFamily.gloss: at any time and any place, anytime anywhere
time and location, venue and schedule

何止.etymology: Rhetorical adverbial compound of 何 ('how, what') + 止 ('stop at, merely, only'): literally 'how does it stop at…?' -> 'far more than, not merely, by no means limited to'. Attested since Classical prose.

history.meaning: how could it stop at -> far more than, not just

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 何止 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: spare energy, remaining capacity or margin

余力.etymology: A Classical modifier-head compound uniting 余 (yú, simplified from 餘, Middle Chinese *yo*, 'surplus, leftover, remaining abundance', distinct in Traditional script from first-person pronoun 余) and 力 (lì, Old Chinese *rɯɡ, Middle Chinese *lik*, 'muscular strength, effort, capability'). Attested in Confucius's Analects (论语·学而: 行有余力，则以学文, 'when after practicing moral duties one has spare strength, use it to study literature') and the Warring States Stratagems (不遗余力, 'leaving no spare strength behind').

history.meaning: leftover physical strength or resources after fulfilling primary duties (Analects, Han Feizi)
spare capacity, reserve energy, financial or mental margin

余力.notes: Note that simplified 余 merges two distinct Traditional characters—餘 ('surplus', as here in 余力 and 多余) and archaic pronoun 余 ('I, me'); in modern speech 余力 often pairs with 心无余力 or the idiom 不遗余力 ('sparing no effort').

rootFamily.gloss: to spare no effort, go all out

作.etymology: Ancient character attested on oracle bones (originally 乍, showing cuts or work on material, later adding person 亻): 'make, compose, write, act as, regard as, rise'.

history.meaning: rise; make; create; act as
write/compose; act as; do (in compounds)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 作 (via 萌典)

作为.etymology: Classical and modern compound of 作 ('act as, make') + 为 (為, 'be, do, serve as'). Functions both as a preposition/verb meaning 'as, in the capacity of, serve as' and as a noun meaning 'conduct, accomplishment, deed'.

history.meaning: actions; deeds; create
as / in the role of; accomplishment

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 作为 (via 萌典)

作息.etymology: An antonymous coordinative compound (反义并列) compressing 作 (zuò, Old Chinese *tsaːɡ, Middle Chinese *tsak*, 'to rise up, stir into action, labor') and 息 (xī, Old Chinese *sɯɡ, Middle Chinese *sik*, 'to draw breath, cease toil, rest'). Directly distilled from the ancient agrarian proverb 日出而作，日入而息 ('when the sun rises, work; when the sun sets, rest', recorded in the Jirang Ge 击壤歌), it shifted in modern Mandarin from a verbal pair into a noun denoting one's daily sleep-and-work schedule.

history.meaning: rising at dawn to till the fields and ceasing at dusk to rest
alternation of labor and rest; activity and repose
daily routine of work and sleep; daily timetable (作息时间)

作息.notes: A staple of discussions around burnout and media production life: 规律作息 means 'a regular sleep/work schedule', while 倒时差 or 昼夜颠倒的作息 describes the upside-down nocturnal hours of TV directors and editors.

rootFamily.gloss: daily timetable of work and rest hours

作曲家.etymology: Three-morpheme compound of 作 ('create, compose') + 曲 ('melody, musical piece') + specialist suffix 家 ('recognized master or practitioner of an art', originally 'household/school of thought').

history.meaning: musical composer

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 作曲家

作秀.etymology: A hybrid verb-object (动宾) Sino-English blend combining the native Chinese verb 作 (zuò, 'to make, stage, put on', alternatively written 做) with the phonetic loanword 秀 (xiù, Middle Chinese *sjuwH*, originally 'ear of grain coming into flower; elegant, outstanding', adopted in 20th-century Taiwanese and Hong Kong entertainment Mandarin to transliterate English show). Coined in 1970s–1980s Taiwan for variety-stage performances (作秀, 'doing a stage/cabaret gig'), it entered Mainland Mandarin in the 1990s primarily in the pejorative sense of staging a publicity stunt or grandstanding for cameras.

history.meaning: phonetic-semantic rendering of English 'show' (live stage, fashion, or variety performance)
to perform commercial cabaret or variety-show bookings (Taiwan entertainment industry)
to put on a show, stage a PR stunt, grandstand insincerely for public attention

作秀.notes: Central showbiz and PR vocabulary: while 秀 alone is neutral/hip (脱口秀 'talk show', 真人秀 'reality show', 走秀 'catwalk modeling'), 作秀 in Mainland Mandarin almost always implies performative insincerity ('putting on an act / PR stunt').

rootFamily.gloss: to walk the runway, model on a catwalk

cognates.meaning: creator, author of a literary or artistic work

作者.etymology: An agentive nominalization formed in Classical Chinese from 作 (zuò, 'to originate, create, compose') plus the nominalizing enclitic pronoun 者 (zhě, Middle Chinese *tsyaeX*, 'one who'). In the Analects (作者七人矣) and the Record of Music in the Book of Rites (礼记·乐记: 作者之谓圣，述者之谓明, 'he who originates [rites and music] is called a sage; he who transmits them is called wise'), 作者 designated a cultural founder or innovator before narrowing in medieval and modern usage to the writer or creator of a text or artwork.

history.meaning: sage originator of institutions, rites, or canonical texts (contrasted with 述者 'transmitter')
composer of prose, poetry, painting, or drama
author, writer, original creator of a written or creative work

作者.notes: Distinguish 作者 ('the author of a specific book, script, or post', e.g., 原作作者 'author of the original IP') from 作家 (zuòjiā, 'a professional novelist/literary writer by vocation').

rootFamily.gloss: to create, produce an original artistic work

作证.etymology: A verb-object (动宾) compound uniting 作 (zuò, 'to act as, serve as, make') with 证 (zhèng, traditional 證, Middle Chinese *tsyingH*, from 言 'speech' + phonetic 登, 'verbal testimony, remonstrance, verification'; note that simplified 证 merged 證 'testify/proof' with 症/證 'symptom'). Used in Classical and vernacular legal narratives for serving as a witness or supplying proof, it functions in modern Mandarin as a separable verb meaning 'to testify, bear witness'.

history.meaning: to serve as a witness or furnish corroborating testimony in disputes or trials
to testify in court, vouch for someone, bear witness

morphemes.meaning: to serve as, make, act as

作证.notes: Commonly framed with 为 or 给 to mark the beneficiary: 我可以为你作证 ('I can vouch/testify for you') or 出庭作证 ('appear in court to testify').

cognates.meaning: literary or artistic style of an author/artist

作风.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 作 (zuò, 'creating, acting, working') with 风 (fēng, traditional 風, Old Chinese *plum, Middle Chinese *pjuwng*, 'wind', extended since the Classic of Poetry 诗经·国风 to mean 'prevailing air, custom, ethos, manner'). First popularized in early 20th-century literary criticism (parallel to Japanese 作風 sakufū, 'an author's artistic style'), it was broadened in 1930s–1940s Chinese organizational and political prose into 'one's characteristic way of working, institutional ethos, or personal conduct'.

history.meaning: distinctive creative or literary style of a writer or painter
institutional work ethos, operational manner, or moral conduct (工作作风, 生活作风)

作风.notes: Watch out for false friends with Japanese 作風 (which still means 'artistic style', Mandarin 风格): in Mandarin, 作风 refers to how a person or team operates and behaves—e.g., 雷厉风行的作风 ('a brisk, decisive working style') or 生活作风问题 (a classic euphemism for personal/romantic indiscretions).

你.etymology: Everyday singular second-person pronoun ('you'), combining the person classifier 亻 with 尔 (ěr), which itself served as a second-person pronoun in Classical Chinese. Attested in Northern Dynasties and Tang vernacular texts such as the Book of Zhou (Zhou Shu), 你 gradually replaced 尔 and 汝 as the standard spoken Mandarin pronoun among peers and colleagues.

history.meaning: second-person pronoun 'thou, you'
singular 'you'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 你 (via 萌典)

你们.etymology: Second-person plural pronoun ('you all'), combining 你 ('you') with the human plural marker 们 (men). Unlike French vous, Mandarin 你们 always addresses two or more people; polite singular respect uses 您 instead.

history.meaning: plural 'you'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 你們 (via 萌典)

你好.etymology: Universal Mandarin greeting ('hello'), built from 你 ('you') + 好 ('good, well'—originally a short wish '[may] you [be] well'). Because two third-tone syllables meet (nǐ + hǎo), the first naturally lifts to second tone in speech: ní hǎo.

history.meaning: everyday greeting 'hello'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 你好 (via 萌典)

你家.etymology: A colloquial modifier-head possessive nominal/pronominal phrase pairing the second-person singular pronoun 你 (nǐ, graphical specialization of Tang–Song vernacular 伱/尔 from Classical 爾, Middle Chinese *nriX*) directly with 家 (jiā, Old Chinese *kraː, Middle Chinese *kae*, originally a roof 宀 over a pig 豕, 'household, family, clan'). Because Mandarin allows kinship and household nouns to drop possessive 的 after personal pronouns, 你家 developed from 'your family/home' into an intimate, teasing, or partisan possessive determiner ('your [partner/boss/idol]').

history.meaning: your household, your clan or residence
your family, your home; polite or colloquial possessive marker before kin/associates
your family's; affectionate, fan-culture, or sarcastic possessive ('that X of yours')

morphemes.meaning: family, household, home; in-group possessive marker

你家.notes: In entertainment fandom and workplace banter, 你家 (and 我家) marks affectionate or teasing affiliation—e.g., 你家艺人 ('that artist of yours'), 你家那位 ('your significant other'), or sarcastic disbelief: 你家电视台这么开啊？ ('Is that how YOUR TV station runs things?!').

佩服.etymology: A coordinative metaphorical compound uniting 佩 (pèi, Middle Chinese *bwojH*, 'to wear ornamental jade pendants at the waist-girdle') and 服 (fú, Old Chinese *bɯɡ, Middle Chinese *bjuwk*, 'to wear garments next to the body; to keep close to heart; to submit willingly'). Originally evoking the Classical image of wearing a mentor's precepts like jade pendants at one's waist and robes on one's chest so as never to forget them, it lexicalized in Tang–Song–Ming prose into 'to admire wholeheartedly, take one's hat off to'.

history.meaning: to wear jade pendants at the belt (佩) and garments on the body (服); metaphorically to cherish teachings close to one's person
to treasure instructions respectfully in one's heart and submit with admiration
to admire genuinely, be deeply impressed by someone's skill or courage

morphemes.meaning: to wear at the waist; to cherish respectfully
to wear on the body; to be convinced and won over

佩服.notes: Expresses heartfelt (or playfully exaggerated) respect for someone's competence, grit, or nerve—compare 羡慕 ('envy what someone has') with 佩服 ('admire what someone can do'); doubling it as 佩服，佩服！ or 佩服得五体投地 ('prostrate in utter admiration') is classic idiomatic praise.

rootFamily.gloss: to be unconvinced, refuse to concede defeat

cognates.meaning: to send, cause, use (cf. 唔使 m4 sai2 'no need')

使.etymology: A monosyllabic verb combining 亻 ('person') with 吏 ('official, emissary'), belonging to an Old Chinese root family (*s-rɯʔ, Middle Chinese *sriX* for the verb and *sriH* for noun 'envoy') shared with 事 ('affair, service') and 吏 ('magistrate'). In Bronze Inscriptions and Classical Chinese, 使 meant 'to dispatch on a mission' and causatively 'to command or cause someone to act'; in Tang–Song–Yuan northern vernacular, dispatching an agent broadened into wielding an instrument, yielding modern colloquial 'to use, exert, pull (a move or trick)'.

history.meaning: to dispatch an envoy; to command or cause someone to do something (causative pivot verb)
to employ, wield, apply a tool, strength, or stratagem
formal causative ('make/cause'); colloquial transitive verb ('use, exert, pull a trick/look')

morphemes.meaning: to dispatch, cause to; to use, deploy, exert

使.notes: 使 lives a fascinating double life in modern Mandarin: as a causative verb ('make/cause', 使人感动) it sounds formal and written, whereas as a transitive verb meaning 'use / pull off' it is earthy northern colloquialism—使劲 ('exert strength'), 好使 ('works great / handy'), 使眼色 ('shoot a meaningful wink/look'), and 使手段 ('pull underhanded tricks').

rootFamily.gloss: to exert all one's strength, strain

使劲.etymology: A Northern Mandarin verb-object (VO) compound formed from 使 (shǐ, 'dispatch, employ, apply', Old Chinese *s-rəʔ) and 勁 (trad. 勁, colloquial reading jìn vs. literary jìng, 'muscular strength, taut vigor', OC *kˤeŋ-s). Structurally 'exert strength', it lexicalized in Ming–Qing vernacular Mandarin and frequently takes rhotacization (使勁兒 shǐjìnr) when used adverbially before action verbs to mean 'with all one's might'.

history.meaning: taut, unyielding strength of a bow or sinew
exert physical effort; strain one's muscles
with all one's might; vigorously (physical or figurative)

使劲.notes: As a separable VO compound (离合词), aspect markers and complements split it apart (e.g., 使了半天劲 'exerted effort for ages'); in Northern speech it almost always carries erhua as 使劲儿.

使用权.etymology: A three-character modifier-head legal compound combining the coordinative disyllabic verb 使用 (shǐyòng, 'employ and utilize', from 使 'employ' + 用 'use') with the head noun 權 (trad. 權 quán, originally 'steelyard sliding weight', extended in Classical Chinese to 'leverage, authority'). Standardized in modern East Asian civil law via Meiji Japanese 使用権 (shiyōken, translating Roman/Germanic civil law usus / Nutzungsrecht) to denote licensed usage rights distinct from ownership.

history.meaning: steelyard weight; tactical leverage and authority
civil-law right to use property without owning title
usage rights over land, music, formats, or intellectual property

使用权.notes: Crucial in TV and music production (such as licensing show formats or soundtrack cues): contrast 使用权 ('usage rights') with 所有权 ('ownership') and 版权 ('copyright').

使绊子.etymology: A colloquial Northern Mandarin verb-object (VO) idiom composed of 使 (shǐ, 'deploy, apply a move') + 絆子 (trad. 絆子 bànzi, from 絆 'hobble a horse's legs with a tether, trip' + nominalizing suffix 子). Originating as technical jargon in Chinese wrestling (摔跤 shuāijiāo) for a covert leg-sweep or foot-hook used to throw an opponent off balance, it shifted metaphorically into workplace and political slang for secretly sabotaging a rival behind the scenes.

history.meaning: rope tether used to hobble a horse's feet; entangle
execute a leg-trip throw in wrestling
secretly obstruct or trip someone up behind the scenes

使绊子.notes: Typically takes the target with 给: 暗中给人使绊子 ('trip someone up behind their back'), a staple expression for office and entertainment-industry intrigue.

供应.etymology: A coordinative compound uniting 供 (gōng, 'present offerings, furnish provisions', Old Chinese *koŋ) and 應 (trad. 應 yìng, 'respond to, meet a demand', OC *ʔəŋ-s). First attested in Tang–Song Buddhist monastic regulations and imperial fiscal administration for furnishing food and requisites in response to official or ritual need, it generalized in modern Chinese economics to denote commercial and logistical 'supply'.

history.meaning: present ritual offerings (供) and answer needs (應)
furnish provisions and hospitality to officials, troops, or monks
supply goods, resources, or content to meet demand

供应.notes: Note the fourth tone on 应 (gōngyìng, 'meet a demand'), never first tone; pairs frequently with 链 in 供应链 ('supply chain') or 商 in 供应商 ('supplier/vendor').

依.etymology: An ideophonetic character combining semantic 亻 ('person') with phonetic 衣 (yī, Old Chinese *ʔəj, 'garment', also contributing the semantic notion of clinging closely like clothing). In the Shijing (Book of Odes) it functioned as a full verb meaning 'lean upon, shelter beside'; across Han and Six Dynasties prose it grammaticalized along a classic body-posture pathway ('lean on' > 'follow closely' > 'in accordance with') into a coverb/preposition.

history.meaning: lean physically against; cleave closely to for shelter
comply with; act in accordance with a precedent or rule
according to, going by (preposition); comply with (in set phrases)

依.notes: Slightly more literary or idiomatic than 按/按照 for standards (依法 'according to law'), yet completely colloquial when introducing personal judgment (依我看, 依你说).

依我看.etymology: A fixed clausal stance marker built around the coverb 依 (yī, 'going by, judging according to') taking the embedded subject-verb clause 我看 (wǒ kàn, 'I look at / view [the matter]'). Emerging in Ming–Qing vernacular fiction (such as Hongloumeng and Rulin Waishi) alongside variants like 依我說, it frames the speaker's upcoming assessment as a reasoned personal perspective rather than an objective decree.

history.meaning: judging by my humble observation
going by how I see things; in my judgment
the way I see it, in my view (conversational discourse marker)

依我看.notes: Placed sentence-initially before a comma to offer candid advice or pushback in meetings and pitches; slightly warmer and more conversational than the formal 在我看来.

rootFamily.gloss: view, opinion, take on a matter

依然.etymology: A Classical Chinese stative-adverbial derivative joining 依 (yī, 'adhere to the prior state, remain leaning as before') with the suffix 然 (rán, 'thus, in such a manner', Old Chinese *njan). Popularized in Tang poetry and prose (e.g., scenery or feelings remaining unchanged despite elapsed years or turmoil), it survived intact into Modern Mandarin as an elevated synonym of 仍然 ('still, as ever').

history.meaning: clinging as before; unchanged in appearance or state
still, just as before despite intervening change

morphemes.meaning: remain adhering to the prior state

依然.notes: Carries a more literary, poignant, or emphatic register than 还是 or 仍然—favored in voiceovers, scripts, and headlines (e.g., 收视率依然稳居第一 'ratings still hold first place').

rootFamily.gloss: just as in the past, unchanged

依赖.etymology: A coordinative verb compound pairing 依 (yī, 'lean against, take shelter with') and 賴 (trad. 賴 lài, 'rely upon for support, draw benefit from', Old Chinese *rˤat-s). Attested since the Sanguozhi (Records of the Three Kingdoms) and Jinshu for political factions or states depending on a patron for survival, it expresses deep structural, psychological, or economic dependence where the subject cannot easily stand alone.

history.meaning: depend on a powerful patron or ally for survival
rely heavily on; be psychologically or structurally dependent on

morphemes.meaning: rely upon, depend on for gain or support

依赖.notes: Beware the Japanese false friend 依頼 (irai, usually 'commission/request a task'); in Mandarin 依赖 implies unilateral dependence (often excessive, as in 过度依赖流量明星 'over-relying on traffic stars').

依靠.etymology: A coordinative compound combining classical 依 (yī, 'lean upon') with vernacular 靠 (kào, 'lean one's back against', originally glossed in the Shuowen Jiezi as 相違 'turn backs against one another', which shifted in Tang–Song vernacular to 'rest one's weight against a solid backing'). Functioning both as a transitive verb ('rely on') and a concrete noun ('backing, pillar of support'), it carries a more neutral or positive agency than 依赖.

history.meaning: lean against a physical support (replacing classical 倚)
lean on for backing; someone or something to fall back on

morphemes.meaning: rest one's back against, rely on

依靠.notes: Unlike 依赖 (which often suggests passive dependency), 依靠 can highlight active strategic reliance (依靠团队实力 'relying on the team's strength') and also acts as a noun meaning 'pillar of support' (失去了依靠).

rootFamily.gloss: backing, powerful patron behind the scenes

侥幸.etymology: Originally written 徼幸 in the Liji (Book of Rites, Zhongyong) and Zuo Zhuan, later graphicized with semantic 亻 and 彳/亻 radicals as 僥倖 (simplified 侥幸): a verb-object/coordinative fusion of 徼/僥 (jiǎo, 'seek, angle for, intercept beyond one's station') and 幸 (xìng, 'undeserved good fortune, imperial favor'). From 'presumptuously angling for undeserved luck', it broadened to any fluke escape or windfall.

history.meaning: covet or seek undeserved fortune contrary to moral principle
escape disaster or succeed unexpectedly by sheer fluke
by a stroke of luck; wishful gamble on getting away with something

morphemes.meaning: angle for, seek beyond one's deserts

侥幸.notes: Most common in the warning phrase 抱有侥幸心理 ('harbor a wishful "maybe I'll get away with it" mentality'), e.g., when cutting corners on broadcast compliance or copyright clearance.

侵权.etymology: A modern verb-object (VO) legal compound condensed from 侵犯權利 ('encroach upon legal rights'), combining 侵 (qīn, 'advance stealthily or gradually across another's bounds', Old Chinese *tsʰim; in the Mencius and Zuo Zhuan, raiding without drums or bells) and 權 (trad. 權 quán, 'legal right, entitlement'). In modern civil code (侵权责任 'tort liability') and media law, it denotes tortious infringement—above all copyright or portrait-right infringement.

history.meaning: incursion across borders without formal declaration of war
usurp administrative authority or encroach upon civil rights
history.stage: Late Imperial to Republican legal prose

history.meaning: commit tortious infringement, especially IP/copyright infringement

侵权.notes: In media and entertainment contexts, 侵权 defaults to IP/copyright or likeness infringement unless specified otherwise; legally, 侵权法 is 'tort law' broadly.

侵犯.etymology: A coordinative transitive verb uniting two complementary Classical verbs of transgression: 侵 (qīn, 'encroach stealthily or incrementally', Old Chinese *tsʰim) and 犯 (fàn, 'charge head-on against a barrier, offend authority', OC *bomʔ, with semantic 犭 'hound lunging'). Attested in Han dynasty historiography (Shiji, Hanshu) for military border violations and lese-majeste, it now takes abstract legal objects like rights, sovereignty, and privacy.

history.meaning: raid frontiers or transgress against imperial authority
violate or infringe upon rights, sovereignty, bodily integrity, or copyright

morphemes.meaning: transgress, offend, charge across a boundary

侵犯.notes: Whereas 侵权 is an intransitive/separable VO verb ('commit infringement'), 侵犯 is strictly transitive and requires an explicit object: 侵犯版权 ('infringe copyright'), 侵犯隐私 ('invade privacy').

侵的权.etymology: An inflected separable-verb (離合詞 líhécí) expansion of the verb-object compound 侵權 (trad. 侵權 qīnquán, 'encroach + rights'). Because Mandarin VO compounds preserve internal syntactic transparency, inserting the attributive/cleft particle 的 (de) between the verb 侵 ('encroach upon') and object 權 ('rights') forms a relative or pseudo-cleft construction highlighting who committed the infringement or whose rights were violated.

history.meaning: encroach upon legal or intellectual property rights (VO compound)
split-verb cleft/relative form focusing the agent or circumstances of infringement

morphemes.meaning: attributive / past-focus cleft marker splitting a VO verb

侵的权.notes: Used in sharp dialogue to pin down responsibility—e.g., 是他们先侵的权 ('It was they who infringed copyright first!') or 侵的谁的权？ ('Whose rights did they infringe?'). Never say *侵权的 in this cleft slot.

rootFamily.gloss: defend one's legal rights (parallel VO verb)
grant authorization / license rights (parallel VO verb)

便宜.etymology: A coordinative compound of 便 (biàn/pián, 'convenient, advantageous, at ease', Old Chinese *ben-s) and 宜 (yí, 'fitting, opportune, proper', OC *ŋ(r)aj). In Han administrative prose (Shiji, Hanshu: 便宜行事 'act at one's discretion as circumstances suit'), it was read biànyí ('expedient advantage'). In Yuan–Ming vernacular Mandarin, a colloquial doublet piányi arose for 'advantageous deal > inexpensive bargain' and 'petty/unfair advantage'.

history.meaning: expedient measures suited to the occasion; discretionary advantage
advantageous bargain; low in price; unearned gain at another's expense
piányi: cheap / unfair advantage (noun); biànyí: convenient (literary)

便宜.notes: Pronounced piányi both as an adjective ('cheap') and as a noun ('unfair advantage', especially in 占便宜 'take advantage of someone' and 讨便宜); read biànyí only in literary phrases like 便宜行事.

rootFamily.gloss: take unfair advantage of; score a petty gain

俗.etymology: An ideophonetic graph combining semantic 亻 ('person, human community') with phonetic 谷 (gǔ/yù, Old Chinese *s-ɡok > Middle Chinese zjowk). In pre-Qin ritual classics (Zhouli, Liji), 俗 neutrally denoted local folkways and popular customs shaped by terrain and habit, contrasted with courtly norm 雅 (yǎ, 'elegance'). Chinese Buddhism adopted it for Sanskrit laukika/gṛhastha ('secular/lay'), while literati aesthetics extended it to 'unrefined, philistine, cliché, tacky'.

history.meaning: local customs and folkways of the populace
the lay, secular world (vs. monastic); unrefined or commonplace taste
tacky, kitschy, cliché, conventional (adj.); custom (bound root)

俗.notes: In creative critiques (scripts, stage design, styling), calling an idea 太俗了 means 'too corny/cliché/tacky', whereas 通俗 ('accessible/popular') is neutral-to-positive and 低俗 ('lowbrow/vulgar') is strongly pejorative.

俗事.etymology: A modifier-head noun compound pairing 俗 (sú, 'worldly, secular, mundane') with 事 (shì, 'affairs, obligations, daily business', Old Chinese *m-s-rəʔ-s). Coined in Six Dynasties and Tang recluse poetry and Buddhist-Daoist discourse (e.g., Bai Juyi and Wang Wei), it contrasts the dusty entanglements of career, money, and social etiquette against spiritual cultivation or pure artistic creation.

history.meaning: secular obligations contrasted with monastic retreat or eremitic leisure
mundane chores, worldly entanglements, everyday administrative trivia

俗事.notes: Slightly literary or wry in tone—often used by artists, writers, or executives lamenting paperwork, budgets, and social obligations (俗事缠身 'bogged down by worldly chores').

rootFamily.gloss: the mortal/secular world; cynical wisdom of the world

保.etymology: Ancient ideogram (会意字) attested on Shang oracle bones showing an adult person (亻) carrying and sheltering a child (子, with swaddling marks in bronze script) on their back: 'protect, guard, keep safe, guarantee'.
