history.meaning: adult holding a child -> protect, nurture, keep safe
protect; keep; guarantee

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 保 (via 萌典)

保住.etymology: A verb-resultative (動補 dòngbǔ) compound uniting 保 (bǎo, Old Chinese *pˤuʔ; oracle-bone graph depicts an adult cradling a swaddled child 子 on the back, hence 'shield, nurture, protect') with the resultative complement 住 (zhù, grammaticalized in Tang–Song vernacular from 'halt, dwell firmly' into a marker of secure fixation). Literally 'protect so that it stays put', i.e., manage to save or hold on to something imperiled.

history.meaning: cradle and protect an infant; guard a stronghold
resultative pattern marking firm retention against loss or motion
successfully save, preserve, or hang on to (a job, life, ranking, or secret)

morphemes.meaning: hold fast, stay firmly in place

保住.notes: Supports potential infixes 得/不 freely: 保得住饭碗 ('can keep one's job') vs. 保不住秘密 ('cannot keep a secret under wraps')—always implies an active threat of loss.

保养.etymology: Coordinative compound verb and noun of 保 ('protect, preserve') + 养 (養, 'nourish, maintain, care for'): originally 'nurture and care for health/people' in Classical Chinese, extended in modern Mandarin to 'maintain, service (machinery, vehicles, or skin)'.

history.meaning: nurture and care for
maintain; service; take care of one's health

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 保养 (via 萌典)

保守.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative verb formed from 保 (bǎo, 'protect, hold secure') and 守 (shǒu, 'guard a territory, stand watch', Old Chinese *s-tuʔ). In the Mencius and Guoyu it meant 'defend and preserve ancestral territory or state institutions'; in the late 19th century, Meiji Japanese 保守 (hoshu) repurposed the classical compound to translate English conservative, whence it re-entered modern Mandarin as an adjective ('conservative, cautious') alongside native VO 保守秘密 ('keep a secret').

history.meaning: guard and hold fast to territory, patrimony, or moral integrity
politically or culturally conservative (translating English 'conservative')
conservative, risk-averse, cautious (adj.); guard closely (in 保守秘密)

morphemes.meaning: guard, hold a post, keep watch over

保守.notes: Dual-function word: as an adjective it means 'conservative/cautious' (保守估计 'a conservative estimate', 思想保守), while as a transitive verb it survives in 保守秘密 ('keep a secret'). Japanese 保守 also means technical 'maintenance' (Chinese 维护).

保安.etymology: Originally a Classical Chinese verb-object/coordinative phrase combining 保 (bǎo, 'protect, safeguard') and 安 (ān, 'peace, domestic tranquility', depicting a woman 女 beneath a roof 宀). Used in Tang–Song statecraft (and echoed in the Song 保甲 mutual-security system and place names like Bao'an) for 'preserving local peace', it became a modern institutional noun for 'public/industrial security' and, in post-1980s Mainland Mandarin, metonymically shifted to the person: 'security guard'.

history.meaning: preserve peace and shelter the populace from unrest
public peace maintenance; civil security corps
building/event security guard; studio or campus security staff

保安.notes: In Mainland China 保安 primarily refers to a uniformed 'security guard' at gates, studios, or offices (whereas Taiwan prefers 保全 bǎoquán); 'public security' as a police bureau is 公安, and 'security check' is 安检.

保密.etymology: Verb-object compound of 保 ('keep, guard') + 密 ('secret, confidential, dense/closed'): 'keep a secret, maintain confidentiality'.

history.meaning: keep secret; maintain confidentiality

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 保密 (via 萌典)

保护.etymology: Coordinative verb compound of 保 ('protect, shelter') + 护 (護, 'guard, defend, shield'). Attested since Han texts and Buddhist translations.

history.meaning: protect; guard; safeguard

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 保护 (via 萌典)

保护办.etymology: Abbreviated institutional compound combining 保护 ('protection, conservation', e.g., historic building or environmental protection) + 办 (short for 办公室 'office'): 'Protection/Conservation Office'.

history.meaning: Protection/Conservation Office (short for 保护办公室)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 保护办 (via 萌典)

保持.etymology: Coordinative verb compound of 保 ('preserve, keep') + 持 ('hold, maintain, grasp in hand', hand 扌 + 寺): 'keep, maintain, preserve (a state, level, or contact)'.

history.meaning: hold and preserve; maintain; keep

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 保持 (via 萌典)

保暖.etymology: Verb-object compound of 保 ('keep, retain') + 暖 ('warmth, warm', sun 日 + 爰): 'keep warm, retain body or room heat'.

history.meaning: retain warmth; keep warm

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 保暖 (via 萌典)

保温.etymology: Verb-object compound of 保 ('preserve, retain') + 温 ('temperature, warmth'): 'retain heat, keep warm, thermal insulation'.

history.meaning: keep warm; thermal insulation

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 保温 (via 萌典)

保留.etymology: A coordinative transitive verb uniting 保 (bǎo, 'keep safe, preserve') and 留 (liú, 'detain, hold back, cause to remain', Old Chinese *C-ru). While attested sporadically in late imperial vernacular for keeping an item behind, its modern legal, parliamentary, and administrative range ('retain rights/seats; reserve judgment; preserve heritage') was reinforced by Meiji Japanese 保留 (horyū, translating diplomatic and legal reservation).

history.meaning: guard intact (保) and hold back from departure (留)
withhold final decision; formally reserve legal or diplomatic rights
retain, keep (footage/slots/traditions); hold back (reservations)

保留.notes: Covers both keeping something valuable in an edit or lineup (保留这个镜头 'keep this shot') and holding back opinions or effort (持保留态度 'maintain reservations', 毫无保留 'holding nothing back').

rootFamily.gloss: repertoire piece, signature act kept on the program

保管.etymology: Compound verb and noun of 保 ('safeguard, keep safe') + 管 ('manage, have custody of'): 'take care of, keep in safe custody, storehouse keeper' (and colloquially 'guarantee, for sure').

history.meaning: keep in safe custody; look after; certainly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 保管 (via 萌典)

保证.etymology: Compound verb and noun of 保 ('vouch for, guarantee') + 证 (證, 'testify, verify, proof'): 'guarantee, pledge, assure'.

history.stage: Tang–Song legal/administrative Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: stand surety for; guarantee; pledge

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 保证 (via 萌典)

保重.etymology: A Classical epistolary compound combining 保 (bǎo, 'protect, nurture') and 重 (zhòng, 'weighty > treat as precious, cherish one's body', Old Chinese *N-toŋʔ). Crystallized in Tang–Song letters and parting poems (frequently 善自保重 or 保重千金之軀, 'cherish your thousand-gold frame'), it survived into modern spoken and written Mandarin as the standard heartfelt farewell urging someone facing travel, stress, or illness to look after themselves.

history.meaning: cherish and guard well your own precious person (letter closing)
take good care of your health (parting salutation or verb)

morphemes.meaning: value highly, treat as weighty and precious

保重.notes: Used at serious or affectionate partings (多保重！ 'Take good care of yourself!' or 保重身体), carrying more emotional weight than a casual 慢走 or 再见.

rootFamily.gloss: cherish and value (often parting Literary phrase 珍重)

保险丝.etymology: Modern technical word for an electrical 'fuse': 保险 ('safe, secure', literally 'guard against danger', also 'insurance') + 丝 ('thread, fine wire'). The name describes the device by its job and its form: a thin wire that melts to keep the rest of the circuit safe. A more technical synonym is 熔丝 ('melting wire').

history.meaning: secure against danger
electrical fuse

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 保险丝 (via 萌典)

保障.etymology: A coordinative compound from 保 (bǎo, 'defensive fort, protect') and 障 (zhàng, 'earthen dike, screen, defensive barrier', Old Chinese *taŋ-s, with semantic 阝 'mound/wall'). In the Zuo Zhuan (Duke Ding, Year 12: 且成，孟氏之保障也), 保障 referred literally to a strategic frontier stronghold shielding a state's heartland; over time this concrete bulwark metaphorized into an institutional, material, or legal 'safeguard' and the verb 'ensure/safeguard'.

history.meaning: defensive garrison town or earthen bulwark shielding a territory
institutional shield, legal guarantee, or logistical safeguard (noun & verb)

保障.notes: Distinguish 保障 from 保证 (bǎozhèng): 保证 is a personal promise or pledge ('I guarantee...'), whereas 保障 is a structural, systemic, or logistical safeguard (社会保障 'social security', 后勤保障 'logistical support', 权益有保障).

信.etymology: Ideogram (会意字) of person (亻) + speech/word (言): originally 'trustworthy speech, truthfulness, believe, trust' in Classical Chinese, then 'envoy/messenger and their token', and from the Six Dynasties–Tang onward the standard noun for 'letter, mail, message'.

history.meaning: truthful; trust; believe; envoy's token
letter; mail; believe; trust

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 信 (via 萌典)

信任.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative verb/noun compound uniting 信 (xìn, 'deem truthful, place faith in', ideogrammatic compound of 亻 'person' + 言 'speech', Old Chinese *s-niŋ-s) and 任 (rèn, 'shoulder a burden > entrust with official responsibility', OC *njəm-s). Prominent in Han–Three Kingdoms political memorials (Shiji, Hanshu) for a sovereign trusting and empowering an official, it generalized in modern Mandarin to interpersonal and professional trust.

history.meaning: trust a minister and delegate official responsibility to him
trust, have confidence in someone's integrity and competence (verb & noun)

信任.notes: Retains subtle undertones of delegating responsibility (赢得客户的信任 'win the client's trust', 不信任案 'motion of no confidence'); more everyday and personal than the elevated 信赖.

信号.etymology: A modifier-head noun compound formed from 信 (xìn, 'agreed tally, message, authenticating token') and 號 (trad. 號 hào, 'command call, distinguishing mark, emblem'). Pre-modern military texts used 信號/號信 for prearranged smoke beacons, flags, or gongs conveying battlefield orders; in the late 19th century (alongside Meiji Japanese 信号 shingō), it expanded to telegraphy, radio broadcasting, traffic lights (信号灯), and figurative cues.

history.meaning: authenticating tally/message (信) and command call/emblem (號)
telegraphic, maritime, railway, and broadcast transmission signal
cell/Wi-Fi/broadcast signal; figurative cue or market indicator

信号.notes: Essential in live TV/streaming production (切信号 'switch the broadcast feed', 信号中断 'signal dropout'), cell reception (没信号 'no bars'), and figurative analysis (释放出危险信号 'send out a warning signal').

信封.etymology: Compound noun of 信 ('letter') + 封 ('seal, envelope, sealed wrapper', originally planting trees on an earthen mound to mark a boundary, then sealing an official dispatch): 'envelope'.

history.meaning: sealed wrapper for a letter; envelope

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 信封 (via 萌典)

信心.etymology: A modifier-head compound joining 信 (xìn, 'faith, conviction') and 心 (xīn, 'heart-mind', Old Chinese *səm). Coined in Six Dynasties Chinese Buddhist scripture translations (e.g., Kumārajīva and Buddhabhadra rendering Sanskrit śraddhācitta, 'a mind of serene religious faith', immortalized in Sengcan's Chan poem 信心銘 Xīnxīnmíng), it underwent complete secularization in 20th-century Mandarin to mean psychological 'confidence' in oneself or a venture.

history.meaning: unwavering mind of religious faith in the Dharma (translating śraddhācitta)
confidence in achieving a goal, recovery, or market success

信心.notes: Cross-linguistic trap: Japanese 信心 (shinjin) still means devout 'religious faith', whereas Mandarin 信心 is secular 'confidence' (对节目充满信心 'full of confidence in the show'; compare 自信 'self-confidence').

信息.etymology: A coordinative noun compound pairing 信 (xìn, 'envoy's report, letter, tidings') and 息 (xī, originally 'breath' from 自 'nose' + 心 'heart', extended in Han–Tang Chinese to 'stirrings, news, tidings', cf. 消息 xiāoxī). First attested in Southern Tang poet Li Zhong's verse (夢斷巫山信息稀, 'dreams broken on Mt. Wu, tidings from afar are scarce'), it was revived in mid-20th-century Mainland scientific Mandarin to translate cybernetic and Shannon-Weaver 'information'.

history.meaning: news, word, or letters from someone far away
history.stage: Five Dynasties & Song Literary Chinese (10th c.)

history.meaning: data/information (scientific & digital) as well as text messages and intel

信息.notes: In Mainland Mandarin 信息 means both technical/general 'information' (信息时代, 信息量很大 'a lot to unpack') and a mobile 'text/chat message' (发信息); Taiwan and Hong Kong distinguish 資訊 (zīxùn, 'information') from 訊息 (xùnxī, 'message').

信箱.etymology: Determinative compound of 信 ('letter; message; trustworthiness', person radical 亻 + 言 'speech') + 箱 ('box; chest; trunk', bamboo radical 竹 + phonetic 相 xiāng). Introduced with modern postal delivery in the late Qing era, it denotes both a household letterbox at the gate and a public postbox.

history.meaning: bamboo storage chest or carriage box
mailbox; letterbox

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 信箱

信誉.etymology: A coordinative noun compound uniting two classical Confucian virtues: 信 (xìn, 'keeping one's word, commercial and moral trustworthiness') and 譽 (trad. 譽 yù, 'public praise, acclaim, good name', Old Chinese *la-s, containing 言 'speech' + 與 phonetic). Synthesized in modern commercial and institutional Chinese, it specifically links outward renown (譽) to proven reliability in honoring commitments and debts (信).

history.meaning: trustworthiness in word (信) and public praise/renown (譽)
institutional prestige, commercial reputation, and creditworthiness

信誉.notes: Compare 声誉 ('prestige/fame' broadly) and 信用 ('credit/keeping promises'): 信誉 specifically denotes reputation built on reliability and honest dealing (商业信誉, 信誉扫地 'reputation utterly ruined').

俩.etymology: Colloquial fusion word (合音字, read liǎ) combining person (亻) + 两 (兩, 'two'). Represents a phonological contraction of 两个 (liǎng gè, 'two [people/units]'), so it is never followed by another classifier (我们俩 'the two of us', 兄弟俩 'the two brothers').

history.stage: Qing northern vernacular to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: contraction of 两个 = the two of (them/us); a couple

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 俩 (via 萌典)

修.etymology: Ancient character showing a feather/ornament (彡) and hand action (攵) washing or adorning a person (攸): originally 'adorn, cultivate, make long/orderly', and by extension 'repair, mend, fix, build (roads/bridges), study, trim'.

history.meaning: cultivate; put in order; repair; build
repair; fix; mend; build

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 修 (via 萌典)

修复.etymology: Coordinate-resultative compound of 修 ('repair; refurbish; embellish', phonetic 攸 yōu + 彡 'ornamental strokes') + 复 ('return to a former state; restore', depicting feet retracing a path). Attested in classical historiography for repairing city walls and temples, it is today the standard term for architectural and artistic restoration.

history.meaning: repair and restore dykes, walls, or halls
restore; repair (heritage buildings or instruments)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 修复

修改.etymology: A coordinative/sequential transitive verb joining 修 (xiū, 'put in order, trim, compile and repair', Old Chinese *s-liw, containing 彡 'decorative strokes/brushwork') and 改 (gǎi, 'alter, correct an error, replace', OC *kˤəʔ, showing 攵 'hand with rod' correcting 己). Attested in Song–Ming official historiography and legal drafting for amending statutes or manuscripts, it is today the standard verb for revising texts, scripts, designs, and code.

history.meaning: amend and redraft official statutes, chronicles, or literary manuscripts
revise, edit, or modify documents, scripts, contracts, settings, or laws

morphemes.meaning: put in order, trim, repair, compile

修改.notes: Every producer, screenwriter, and designer's daily word (修改方案 'revise the proposal', 反复修改剧本 'revise the script repeatedly'); less formal spoken shorthand is simply 改.

rootFamily.gloss: adapt, rewrite (a novel into a screenplay)

修炼.etymology: A coordinative verb rooted in Tang–Song Daoist internal and external alchemy, combining 修 (xiū, 'cultivate spiritual and moral practice') with 煉 (trad. 煉 liàn, 'smelt ore or refine cinnabar elixir in fire', semantic 火 'fire' + 柬, distinct from silk-degumming 練). Originally describing an adept refining vital essence, breath, and spirit (精氣神) toward immortality, it entered wuxia/xianxia lore and modern workplace idiom for painstakingly honing one's craft and inner poise.

history.meaning: cultivate Daoist asceticism and alchemically refine inner vital essence
practice martial/immortal arts; figuratively hone one's craft, temperament, or mastery

morphemes.meaning: smelt and purify with fire, refine alchemically

修炼.notes: Always spelled with the fire radical 炼 (smelting metal/elixir), unlike 熟练 or 训练 (silk radical 练); used playfully or admiringly in creative industries for years of behind-the-scenes mastery (修炼内功 'hone one's core craft').

rootFamily.gloss: temper and hone through hardship; condense prose

修饰.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative verb combining 修 (xiū, 'trim, put in order, cultivate') and 飾 (trad. 飾 shì, 'wipe clean with a cloth > adorn, ornament', Old Chinese *l̥ək, originally 食 phonetic + 巾 'cloth'). Attested in the Liji (Book of Rites) and Hanshu for grooming one's attire, comportment, and prose style, it later also absorbed the modern grammatical sense 'modify/qualify' (via Meiji Japanese 修飾 shūshoku) alongside visual and vocal retouching.

history.meaning: groom one's outward appearance, ritual demeanor, or literary phrasing
grammatical modification (modifier qualifying a head word)
polish wording; touch up makeup/photos/audio; grammatically modify

修饰.notes: Spans three domains: rhetoric (修饰词句 'polish phrasing', 不加修饰 'unvarnished/raw'), grooming & post-production (修饰脸型/声音 'contour the face / sweeten vocals'), and grammar (副词修饰动词 'adverbs modify verbs').

rootFamily.gloss: cover up, gloss over a flaw or mistake

倍.etymology: Classifier and verb meaning 'times, -fold (multiple of a quantity); double', formed from person (亻) + phonetic 咅 (pǒu/bèi). Attested since Mencius and Mozi for multiplying quantities.

history.meaning: twofold; -fold; times as much

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 倍 (via 萌典)

倒.etymology: Phono-semantic character of person (亻) + 到 (dào). Read dǎo: 'fall over, topple, collapse, change (trains/shifts)'; read dào: 'invert, turn upside down, pour (tea/water), back up (a vehicle), on the contrary'.

history.meaning: topple, fall (dǎo); invert, pour, move backward, contrarily (dào)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 倒 (via 萌典)

倒车.etymology: Homographic compound with two tonal readings: read dào chē (with 倒 dào 'move in reverse') it means 'back up / reverse a vehicle'; read dǎo chē (with 倒 dǎo 'shift, transfer') it means 'change buses or trains'.

history.meaning: reverse a vehicle (dàochē); transfer vehicles (dǎochē)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 倒车 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to suffer bad luck, be jinxed

倒霉.etymology: A verb-object compound (dǎoméi) originally written 倒楣 in Ming–Qing Jiangnan vernacular. According to late Ming scholar Gu Qiyuan's Kezuo Zhuiyu (客座贅語), examination candidates in Zhejiang hung a lintel banner (楣, méi) over their gate for good fortune and took it down (倒, dǎo) upon failing the imperial exam; by folk graphic assimilation to dampness and rot, 楣 was re-written as 霉 ('mold, mildew').

history.meaning: to take down the auspicious lintel banner after failing the civil service examination
to suffer a streak of bad luck or misfortune

morphemes.meaning: mold, mildew (graphic folk replacement for 楣 'door lintel')

倒霉.notes: Separable verb-object (离合词) in colloquial speech: you can insert aspect markers or modifiers between the two characters, as in 倒了大霉 ('suffered terrible bad luck').

倔.etymology: Adjective meaning 'stubborn, unyielding, blunt in temper' (read juè alone, or jué in 倔强 juéjiàng), formed from person (亻) + 屈 (qū, here paradoxically evoking stiff, unbending temperament).

history.stage: Han–Tang Chinese (倔強) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: stubborn; unbending; obstinate

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 倔 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to borrow, rent, lease (in compounds like 借用)

借.etymology: A phono-semantic compound (形聲) from Old Chinese *tsjak (Middle Chinese tsjak,tsjaeH), composed of semantic 亻 ('person', indicating interpersonal transaction) and phonetic 昔 (*sjak). Already attested in pre-Qin Classical Chinese with bidirectional valency covering both 'to lend out' and 'to borrow', as well as 'to make use of as a pretext'.

history.meaning: to lend or borrow; to rely upon or avail oneself of
to borrow, lend, or use as a pretext; if, supposing
to borrow; to lend; to use as an opportunity or excuse

morphemes.meaning: to borrow; to lend; to avail oneself of

借.notes: Because 借 means both 'borrow' and 'lend', Mandarin disambiguates direction with prepositions or directional complements: 向/跟人借 ('borrow from someone') versus 借给人 ('lend to someone').

rootFamily.gloss: to draw lessons from, use for reference

cognates.meaning: to make a gift using someone else's resources
cognates.word: 借花獻佛 (ze3 faa1 hin3 fat6)

借花献佛.etymology: A four-character serial verb idiom (成語, jièhuā-xiànfó) composed of two parallel verb-object clauses: 借花 ('borrow flowers') + 献佛 ('present to the Buddha'). It alludes to the Buddhist Past and Present Causes and Effects Sutra (過去現在因果經), in which the ascetic Sumati borrows seven lotus blossoms from a girl to offer to Dipankara Buddha; in Ming–Qing vernacular it generalized to offering hospitality or favors using another person's resources.

history.meaning: to borrow lotus flowers to present as an offering to the Buddha
to present someone else's items or setup to do a favor or show goodwill

借花献佛.notes: Often used self-deprecatingly by a host or producer when treating guests with food, drinks, or stage resources provided by a third party.

rootFamily.gloss: to kill someone with a borrowed knife (act through a proxy)
to offer sacrifices or tribute; to dedicate

cognates.meaning: to second or temporarily transfer personnel

借调.etymology: A coordinative-serial verb compound (jièdiào) combining 借 ('to borrow temporarily') and 调 (調, Middle Chinese dewH, 'to transfer, assign, deploy officially'). Originating in late imperial bureaucratic administration (where officials were temporarily requisitioned across provinces or ministries) and standardized in modern Chinese institutional and media production management for seconding staff across departments while keeping their original payroll/roster status.

history.meaning: to requisition officials or troops temporarily from another jurisdiction
to second or temporarily transfer an employee to another unit or project team

借调.notes: Common in corporate, government, and TV studio settings when a director or producer 'borrows' an editor or planner from another department for a specific project without changing their formal HR affiliation.

rootFamily.gloss: to deploy, allocate resources or staff

值得.etymology: Compound verb and adjective of 值 ('be worth, match in value', person 亻 + 直 'straight/equivalent') + 得 ('obtain, deserve, modal marker of worth'): 'be worth (doing or the price), deserve'.

history.meaning: be worth; merit

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 值得 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to be on duty, work a shift

值班.etymology: A verb-object compound (zhíbān) formed from 值 (Middle Chinese driH, 'to meet with, fall on one's turn, be on duty', originally written 直 in Classical Chinese) and 班 (Middle Chinese paen, 'ranked line of court officials, shift, scheduled group'). In Song–Qing court bureaucracy, officials took turns standing watch in their assigned court rank (直班/值班); in modern usage it denotes working a scheduled shift or standing duty watch.

history.meaning: to take one's scheduled turn attending court or guard duty
to be on duty, work a scheduled shift (especially at a studio, office, or hospital)

morphemes.meaning: to fall on one's turn, be on duty
shift, scheduled duty group, court rank

值班.notes: A separable verb-object compound (离合词): while 值班 refers specifically to scheduled duty or watch shifts (e.g., night control-room duty at a TV station), regular daily commuting is 上班.

rootFamily.gloss: to be on duty for the day (e.g., classroom or studio roster)
to work overtime, work an extra shift

cognates.meaning: hypothetical enemy, potential adversary in military exercises

假想敌.etymology: A three-character modifier-head noun compound (jiǎxiǎngdí) consisting of the verbal modifier 假想 ('to suppose, hypothesize', a modern Sino-Japanese compound 仮想 *kasō* formed from 假 'provisional, hypothetical' + 想 'conceive, imagine') modifying the head noun 敌 (敵, 'enemy, rival'). Originally coined in late 19th/early 20th-century military strategy (modeled on German/English 'hypothetical enemy' via Japanese 仮想敵) to designate a target adversary in war games, before expanding into business and media competition.

history.form: 假想敵 (after Japanese 仮想敵)
history.meaning: hypothetical enemy state or force designated for military planning and war games
imagined enemy, perceived rival or competitor in workplace or industry rivalry

假想敌.notes: In workplace dramas like *Behind the Scenes*, 把某人当成假想敌 ('to treat someone as an imaginary rival') describes projecting rivalry onto a colleague who may not even view you as an opponent.

假期.etymology: A modifier-head noun compound (jiàqī) formed from 假 (read in the departing tone, Middle Chinese kaeH, 'official leave of absence, furlough granted to officials', derived from the sense 'borrowed/granted time', often written 暇 in early texts) and 期 (Middle Chinese gij, 'appointed time, fixed period, duration'). In Han–Tang administrative usage, 假 denoted a statutory rest day (such as the five-day 休假 of Han officials), and 假期 specified the allotted duration of leave.

history.meaning: statutory leave of absence granted to imperial officials
allotted period of official leave; holiday, vacation period

假期.notes: Watch the tonal distinction on 假: fourth tone jià means 'holiday/leave' (假期, 请假, 放假), whereas third tone jiǎ means 'false, fake, provisional' (假的, 假装).

rootFamily.gloss: to go on vacation, take a holiday
scheduled broadcast slot or production schedule window

假的.etymology: A descriptive adjectival construction (jiǎde) combining the root 假 (Old Chinese *kraːʔ, Middle Chinese kaeX, originally 'borrowed, temporary, non-intrinsic', contrasted with 真 'authentic, Daoist true essence' from the Zhuangzi onward) and the nominalizing/attributive particle 的 (de, grammaticalized from Literary Chinese 之/底 in Tang–Song vernacular). The construction functions predicatively ('is fake') or nominally ('a fake one').

history.meaning: borrowed, provisional, artificial (contrasted with innate or genuine)
counterfeit, sham, false thing or statement

假的.notes: Non-gradable predicative adjective in Mandarin: instead of saying *很假 in formal prose, speakers typically use 是假的 ('it's fake') or the conversational disbelief tag 真的假的？ ('Really? No way!').

假装.etymology: A modifier-head or coordinative verbal compound (jiǎzhuāng) formed from 假 (Middle Chinese kaeX, 'false, feigned, simulated') and 装 (裝, Middle Chinese tsrjang, 'to attire, dress up, outfit, put on an act'). Originally referring to dressing up in theatrical costume or disguise in Song–Yuan drama and vernacular fiction, it broadened to mean feigning any attitude, emotion, or state of ignorance.

history.meaning: to dress in disguise, put on theatrical attire or a false persona
to pretend, feign, make believe

morphemes.meaning: to dress up, attire, act, feign

假装.notes: Takes a verbal or clausal complement directly without a preposition (e.g., 假装不知道 'pretend not to know', 假装没事 'pretend nothing happened').

rootFamily.gloss: to play dumb, act ignorant on purpose
to pose, put on airs, feign an attitude

偏偏.etymology: A reduplicated adverb (piānpiān) from the root 偏 (Old Chinese *pʰen, Middle Chinese phjen, 'inclined to one side, slanting, partial, non-centered'). In Classical Chinese, 偏 meant 'leaning to one side' (contrasted with 正 'upright, centered'); in Tang–Song poetry and Yuan–Ming vernacular, reduplicated 偏偏 developed a counter-expectational modal sense: reality 'tilts' perversely toward the very outcome least desired or expected.

history.meaning: tilted, leaning to one side, partial, biased
distinctly, singularly; by perverse coincidence, against expectations
ironically, of all things, deliberately contrary to expectations or wishes

morphemes.meaning: inclined, slanting, contrary to the norm

偏偏.notes: Expresses strong speaker frustration or irony: either fate perversely ruins a plan (偏偏这时候停电 'the power had to go out right at this moment') or an agent stubbornly does the opposite of advice.

rootFamily.gloss: to favor one side unfairly, play favorites

做.etymology: Everyday verb for 'do, make, produce, cook, act as'. Emerged in Tang–Song vernacular as a specialized graphic differentiation of 作 (zuò, adding person 亻 to 故 gù) to carry the colloquial spoken reading zuò ('make, do').

history.meaning: make; do; produce; act as

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 做 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to keep doing, carry on doing (colloquial 做落去)

做下去.etymology: A verb-directional complement construction (zuò xiàqù) composed of the action verb 做 ('to do, make, work on', a vernacular graphic differentiation of 作 emerging in Tang–Song texts) followed by the compound directional complement 下去 (literally 'downward and away from the speaker'). Through metaphorical mapping of time as downward/forward movement along a path, 下去 grammaticalized as a continuative aspect marker meaning 'to continue an already started action into the future'.

history.meaning: to carry an action downward and away; to continue performing an activity

morphemes.meaning: to do, make, engage in work
away from the present point into the future (continuative aspect)

做下去.notes: Frequently used in potential form with 得 or 不 inside the verb-complement cluster: 做得下去 ('able to keep doing it / stay in the industry') vs. 做不下去 ('unable to carry on').

rootFamily.gloss: to persist, hold out to the end

cognates.meaning: to work, handle matters (also 做嘢)

做事.etymology: A verb-object compound (zuòshì) formed from 做 ('to do, perform, make', vernacular derivative of Classical 作 *tsˤak) and 事 (Old Chinese *m-s-rəʔ-s, Middle Chinese dzriH, originally 'official duty, service at court, affair, business'). Attested since Song–Yuan vernacular as the everyday equivalent of Classical 作事 / 行事, denoting both 'handling practical affairs' and 'working in a job'.

history.meaning: to undertake affairs, perform official or practical business
to handle matters, conduct oneself in work, hold a job

做事.notes: In workplace evaluation (e.g., 先做人，后做事 'first learn how to be a person, then how to handle work'), 做事 emphasizes execution competence, reliability, and professional conduct.

rootFamily.gloss: to conduct oneself, behave with integrity
to handle official business or run errands

cognates.meaning: to handle matters, get work done

做事情.etymology: An expanded verb-object phrase (zuò shìqing) pairing the verb 做 ('to do, handle') with the disyllabic noun 事情 ('affair, matter, task'). The object 事情 itself is a coordinative-modifier compound from Classical 事 ('affair, undertaking') and 情 ('actual circumstances, reality of a situation', as in 事之情实), which fused in Tang–Song vernacular into a general disyllabic noun for 'matters, tasks, things to be done'.

history.meaning: the actual facts or circumstances of an affair
to handle practical tasks, get actual work done

morphemes.meaning: circumstance, situation (neutral tone in 事情)

做事情.notes: Compared to the tighter compound 做事, the three-syllable 做事情 sounds slightly more concrete and conversational, often contrasting real productive work with office politics (我是来做事情的 'I am here to get real work done').

rootFamily.gloss: truth, actual facts of a matter

cognates.meaning: to produce, make, arrive at (a decision or achievement)

做出.etymology: A verb-resultative/directional compound (zuòchū) combining 做 ('to make, do, produce', vernacular graph for 作) with the directional/resultative complement 出 (Old Chinese *t-kʰut, Middle Chinese tshwit, 'to emerge, come out into visibility'). In modern Mandarin formal and media prose, 出 marks the bringing into existence of an abstract result or public act, functioning as a light resultative verb before abstract nouns like 决定 ('decision'), 贡献 ('contribution'), or 调整 ('adjustment').

history.meaning: to craft or bring forth an object or action into view
to make, put forth, produce (especially an abstract decision, response, or achievement)

做出.notes: Functions as a formal 'support verb' (light verb) taking two-syllable abstract verbal nouns: 做出决定 ('make a decision'), 做出让步 ('make a concession'), 做出回应 ('issue a response'). Also written 作出 in formal documents.

rootFamily.gloss: to put forward, propose, raise (a question or plan)

cognates.meaning: to do well; to finish preparing

做好.etymology: A verb-resultative compound (zuòhǎo) formed from the verb 做 ('to do, make, prepare') and the resultative complement 好 (Old Chinese *qʰˤuʔ, Middle Chinese xawX, 'good, satisfactory, completed to a proper standard'). In Mandarin resultative syntax, post-verbal 好 carries dual semantics: qualitative perfection ('to do something well') and completive readiness ('to finish doing/preparing something properly').

history.meaning: to complete a task satisfactorily; to do something well or get ready in advance

做好.notes: Has two distinct readings depending on context: 'do a good job on X' (把节目做好 'make the show well') and 'finish preparing for X in advance' (做好心理准备 'be mentally prepared').

cognates.meaning: to visit as a guest, be a guest
to be a guest, visit someone's home

做客.etymology: A verb-object compound (zuòkè, also written 作客 in Literary Chinese) combining 做/作 ('to act as, serve as, be') and 客 (Old Chinese *kʰˤrak, Middle Chinese khaek, 'visitor, guest, traveler away from home'). In Tang poetry (e.g., Wang Wei's 獨在異鄉為異客 and Du Fu's 作客), 作客 meant 'to sojourn as a stranger in another land'; in Ming–Qing and modern Mandarin, 做客 narrowed to visiting someone's home or appearing as an invited guest on a talk show or broadcast program.

history.meaning: to sojourn away from home as a traveler or stranger
to visit as a guest at someone's home or appear as a guest on a broadcast show

morphemes.meaning: to act as, be in the role of

做客.notes: In modern media Mandarin, 做客 can take a studio, show, or platform directly as a locative object without 在/到: e.g., 做客直播间 ('appear as a guest in the livestream studio'). Some style guides distinguish 作客 ('sojourn away from home') from 做客 ('be a guest').

rootFamily.gloss: distinguished guest (especially on a TV or talk show)

cognates.meaning: to set up a scam or rigged game

做局.etymology: A verb-object compound (zuòjú) combining 做 ('to construct, set up, fabricate') and 局 (Old Chinese *N-kʰrok, Middle Chinese gjowk, originally 'chessboard layout, game of Go/liubo', by extension 'scheme, setup, trap'). Derived from late imperial gambling and Go terminology—where a 局 was a staged game or rigged betting configuration (such as 设局 or 骗局)—做局 means to orchestrate a covert setup or trap to manipulate a target into a predetermined outcome.

history.meaning: board-game position or match; structured arrangement
to stage a rigged gambling match or confidence trick; to orchestrate a trap or scheme
history.stage: Late Imperial Vernacular to Modern Mandarin

morphemes.meaning: board-game layout; staged scheme, trap, situation

做局.notes: Very frequent in corporate, PR, and entertainment-industry dramas: 给某人做局 ('set up a trap for someone') implies a calculated, multi-person scheme where the victim thinks events are unfolding naturally.

rootFamily.gloss: overall situation, big picture; strategic breadth of mind
to break out of a deadlock or rigged situation

cognates.meaning: to make an issue of, elaborate on a pretext

做文章.etymology: A three-character verb-object idiom (zuò wénzhāng) combining 做 ('to compose, write') and 文章 (Classical Chinese 'ornate pattern of colors/stripes', later 'literary composition, essay'). During the Ming and Qing dynasties, civil service candidates had to compose eight-legged essays (八股文) elaborating extensively on a fixed, often tiny snippet of the Four Books (做文章); by metaphor, 'writing an essay on X' came to mean seizing upon a pretext or angle to spin a narrative, stir up controversy, or exploit an issue.

history.meaning: interwoven colored patterns; literary composition or essay
to compose an examination essay on a set topic; figuratively, to make a big issue of or exploit a pretext

做文章.notes: Almost always preceded by a locative frame such as 在…上做文章 ('capitalize on / make an issue out of...') or 拿…做文章 ('use X as a pretext to stir things up'), especially in PR and media spin.

rootFamily.gloss: to insinuate, hint at something between the lines (literally 'write an essay inside the words')
rootFamily.word: 骨子里做文章 / 话里有文章

rootFamily.gloss: to make a mountain out of a molehill (literally 'make a big essay on a small topic')

做梦.etymology: Verb-object compound of 做 ('make, have') + 梦 (夢, 'dream', originally showing a person on a couch/bed 爿 with dim vision 苜 at night 夕): 'dream, have a dream' (and figuratively 'daydream, pipe dream').

history.meaning: have a dream; dream

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 做梦 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to start doing, work one's way up from

做起.etymology: A verb-directional complement compound (zuòqǐ) formed from 做 ('to do, work as, act') and the directional/aspectual complement 起 (Old Chinese *kʰəʔ, Middle Chinese khijX, 'to rise, get up, originate'). Through metaphorical extension from upward physical motion ('rising') to temporal inception, post-verbal 起 grammaticalized in Early Mandarin as an inchoative aspect marker meaning 'to begin doing' or 'to start from a foundational point'.

history.meaning: to rise into action; to begin doing or start out from a given level

morphemes.meaning: up; to begin, initiate (inchoative directional complement)

做起.notes: Used in two key patterns: (1) 从…做起 ('start from...', e.g., 从实习生做起 'work one's way up from an intern', 从小事做起 'start with small things'), and (2) 做起 + Noun + 来 ('begin doing Noun').

rootFamily.gloss: to start speaking; speaking of which
to initiate, launch (an event or campaign)

停.etymology: Phono-semantic character of person (亻) + 亭 (tíng, 'roadside pavilion where travelers halt and rest'): 'stop, halt, pause, park (a vehicle)'.

history.meaning: stop at a way-pavilion -> halt, cease, park

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 停 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to stop work, suspend operations or go on strike
suspension of construction or factory work

停工.etymology: A verb-object compound (tínggōng) combining 停 (Middle Chinese deng, 'to halt, rest at a wayside pavilion', originally derived from 亭 'roadside post pavilion where travelers stopped') and 工 (Old Chinese *kˤoŋ, Middle Chinese kuwng, 'craftsman's tool, artisan labor, construction or production work'). Attested in late imperial administrative records for suspending public works or workshops, and in modern usage for halting factory, construction, or film/TV studio production.

history.meaning: to suspend artisan labor or imperial construction projects
to stop work, suspend production or filming operations

停工.notes: Antonym of 开工 ('start work / begin filming or construction') and 复工 ('resume work'); in film and television production, 剧组停工 means a crew has halted shooting due to funding, weather, or regulatory issues.

rootFamily.gloss: to start work, commence production or filming
to resume work or production after a halt

cognates.meaning: to take off the air, suspend broadcasting

停播.etymology: A modern verb-object/verb-complement compound (tíngbō) formed from 停 ('to stop, suspend') and 播 (Old Chinese *pˤar-s, Middle Chinese paH, originally 'to sow seeds by scattering', extended in 20th-century media Chinese to 'broadcast, transmit signals widely' as an abbreviation of 广播 / 播出). Coined in the modern radio and television era to denote taking a program off the air or suspending its broadcast run.

history.meaning: to sow seeds; to spread or disseminate widely
to suspend or cancel the broadcast of a radio, TV, or streaming program

morphemes.meaning: to broadcast, air (short for 播出 / 广播)

停播.notes: Core television-industry term in *Behind the Scenes*: 节目停播 can refer to a temporary hiatus (e.g., for schedule adjustments or rectification 整改) or permanent cancellation of a show's broadcast.

停止.etymology: A coordinative synonymous verb compound (tíngzhǐ) uniting 停 (Middle Chinese deng, 'to halt, rest at a wayside station', from 亭 'post pavilion') and 止 (Old Chinese *təʔ, Middle Chinese tsyiX, originally an oracle-bone pictograph of a foot 趾 standing still, hence 'to come to a standstill, cease'). Already paired in Six Dynasties and Tang prose, the compound combines a vernacular/middle-register verb (停) with the core Classical verb for cessation (止).

history.meaning: foot; to stand still, halt, cease
to halt movement, linger, cease an activity
history.stage: Middle Chinese (Six Dynasties–Tang) to Modern Mandarin

morphemes.meaning: to halt, pause, stop (originally at a pavilion)

停止.notes: More formal and transitive than standalone 停: unlike 停, 停止 cannot take a directional complement (*停止下来 is ungrammatical; use 停下来), and it readily takes verbal or abstract noun objects (停止录影 'stop recording', 停止合作 'cease cooperation').

rootFamily.gloss: to prevent, stop someone from doing something
to suspend, call a timeout; pause button

停电.etymology: Verb-object compound of 停 ('stop, cut off') + 电 (電, 'electricity, power'): 'have a power outage, the electricity goes out'.

history.meaning: power outage; electricity cut

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 停电 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to suspend from official duty or office

停职.etymology: A verb-object compound (tíngzhí) combining 停 ('to halt, suspend') and 职 (職, Old Chinese *tək, Middle Chinese tsyik, 'official duty, post, bureaucratic office'). Used in Qing administrative law and modern civil-service/corporate HR regulations to denote temporarily stripping an official or employee of their duties and authority pending investigation or disciplinary review, without yet terminating their employment status.

history.meaning: to suspend an official from exercising the duties of office pending investigation or discipline
history.stage: Late Imperial Administrative Chinese to Modern Mandarin

停职.notes: Distinct from 撤职 ('dismiss from a post') and 开除 ('fire/expel'): 停职 is a temporary suspension (often in the phrase 停职反省 'suspended to reflect on one's mistakes' or 停职调查 'suspended pending investigation'). Also functions as a separable verb-object (被停了职).

rootFamily.gloss: to resign from one's job or post
to dismiss or remove from office

健全.etymology: A coordinative adjectival and causative-verbal compound (jiànquán) formed from 健 (Old Chinese *gans, Middle Chinese gjonH, 'strong, vigorous, unflagging', inspired by the Yijing hexagram Qian: 天行健 'Heaven's movement is ever-vigorous') and 全 (Old Chinese *dzˤon, Middle Chinese dzjwen, 'complete, intact, whole, flawless'). Reinforced in modern East Asian lexicon via Japanese 健全 (*kenzen*, used to translate English 'sound' as in 'a sound mind in a sound body' and 'sound institutions'), it describes both physical/mental wholeness and well-developed institutional systems.

history.meaning: vigorous in strength and intact/complete in form
physically and mentally sound; (of laws, systems, or mechanisms) well-developed and complete; to make sound
history.stage: Modern Mandarin (reinforced by Sino-Japanese 健全)

健全.notes: Functions both as an adjective (身心健全 'physically and mentally sound', 制度健全 'the system is well-established') and as a transitive verb in formal policy/corporate prose (健全管理机制 'to strengthen and perfect the management mechanism').

cognates.meaning: idol, statue, icon; object of worship or fandom

偶像.etymology: A modifier-head noun compound (ǒuxiàng) combining 偶 (Old Chinese *ŋˤoʔ, Middle Chinese nguwX, originally 'wooden or earthen human effigy/puppet made as a burial companion, pair, counterpart') and 像 (Old Chinese *s-ɢaŋʔ, Middle Chinese zjangX, 'likeness, sculpted image, figure'). Attested in Han–Tang texts (such as the Shiji and Hou Hanshu) for carved wooden or clay statues, it was adopted in 19th-century missionary Bible translations and Meiji Japanese (偶像 *gūzō*) to render Greek *eidōlon* / English 'idol', and later extended to pop-culture stars and admired role models.

history.meaning: carved wooden or clay human effigy, statue, or burial figure

history.form: 偶像 (cf. Japanese 偶像 gūzō)
history.meaning: religious idol or object of blind worship (translating English 'idol' / Greek eidōlon)
admired role model, pop star, or entertainment idol

偶像.notes: In Chinese entertainment terminology, 偶像剧 ('idol drama') and 偶像包袱 ('idol baggage' — a celebrity's fear of looking unglamorous in front of fans) are ubiquitous showbiz expressions.

偷.etymology: Phono-semantic character of person (亻) + 俞 (yú/tōu). In Classical Chinese (Zuozhuan, Analects), 偷 meant 'remiss, makeshift, snatch a moment'; from the Han–Six Dynasties onward it became the primary verb for 'steal' and adverbially 'secretly, stealthily'.

history.meaning: remiss;苟且; snatch time
steal; pilfer; secretly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 偷 (via 萌典)

偷偷.etymology: A reduplicated adverb (tōutōu) from the root 偷 (Old Chinese *tʰˤo, Middle Chinese thuw, originally 'negligent, frivolous, opportunistic, to steal a moment of ease', as in Classical 偷安, before shifting in Han–Six Dynasties vernacular to 'to steal, pilfer' and 'stealthily'). Reduplicating 偷 attenuates the criminal sense of theft into a pure manner adverb meaning 'furtively, covertly, without others noticing'.

history.meaning: to act opportunistically or negligently; to steal; stealthily
secretly, stealthily, quietly behind others' backs

morphemes.meaning: vivid manner-adverbial reduplication ('on the sly, furtively')

偷偷.notes: Often followed by the adverbial particle 地 (偷偷地) or expanded into the four-character colloquial idiom 偷偷摸摸 ('furtive, sneaking around'). Unlike 暗中 ('secretly/covertly' in formal or strategic contexts), 偷偷 is everyday conversational register.

cognates.meaning: to photograph secretly, take paparazzi or candid shots
voyeuristic or covert photography/filming (rendered 盗撮 tōsatsu)

偷拍.etymology: A modifier-head verb compound (tōupāi) in which the adverbial morpheme 偷 ('stealthily, without permission') modifies the verb 拍 (Middle Chinese phaek, originally 'to clap, pat, strike a musical beat', extended in 20th-century Mandarin via 拍照 / 拍摄 to 'take photographs or shoot film', originally from clapping the camera shutter or slate). Coined in modern media and journalism for covert photography, hidden-camera recording, or paparazzi shots.

history.meaning: to pat, clap, strike a musical beat
to take a photograph or shoot motion-picture film
to photograph or film covertly (paparazzi shots, candid/undercover recording, or illicit filming)

morphemes.meaning: to photograph, shoot film or video (short for 拍照/拍摄)

偷拍.notes: Covers a wide spectrum in entertainment and news contexts: celebrity paparazzi photography (狗仔队偷拍), undercover investigative journalism (暗访偷拍), and illegal hidden-camera voyeurism.

rootFamily.gloss: to shoot film, photograph, produce video

偷看.etymology: A subordinate-verb + head-verb compound combining 偷 (tōu, originally 'to steal, pilfer', grammaticalized preverbally as 'furtively, on the sly') and 看 (kàn, 'to look at, read, watch'). In Classical Chinese 偷 meant 'remiss, makeshift, or stolen', and from Tang–Song vernacular onward 偷 regularly preceded action verbs (偷听 'eavesdrop', 偷笑 'snicker secretly', 偷看 'peek') to express doing something without permission or notice.

history.meaning: steal a glance; look secretly
peek; sneak a look

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 偷看

cognates.meaning: to launch a sneak attack, ambush

偷袭.etymology: A modifier-head verb compound (tōuxí) formed from adverbial 偷 ('stealthily, by surprise') and the head verb 袭 (襲, Old Chinese *s-lap, Middle Chinese zjip, originally 'a double-layered robe for dressing the dead', extended in Classical military texts like the Zuo Zhuan and Sunzi's Art of War to 'march covertly with muffled drums to strike an unprepared enemy'). Because Classical 襲 already inherently meant 'surprise attack', prefixing 偷 in vernacular Chinese transparently reinforced its covert nature.

history.meaning: double garment; to launch a covert military raid without sounding war drums
to ambush, launch a surprise attack; figuratively, to catch someone off guard

morphemes.meaning: to raid, strike an unprepared enemy, attack by surprise

偷袭.notes: Used both literally in military/gaming contexts and playfully or metaphorically in everyday life (e.g., an unannounced inspection, a sudden kiss, or a rival dropping a surprise release to ambush ratings).

rootFamily.gloss: to raid, attack, hit (as a storm or assault)
to plagiarize, copy someone else's work covertly

傍晚.etymology: Temporal noun combining 傍 (bàng, 'draw near to, border on', person 亻 + 旁 'side/near') + 晚 ('evening'): 'toward evening, at dusk, nightfall'. Attested in Song poetry and prose.

history.meaning: approaching evening; dusk; nightfall

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 傍晚 (via 萌典)

储藏室.etymology: Three-character compound of 储 (儲, 'store up, save', person 亻 + 诸) + 藏 (cáng, 'store away, hide') + 室 ('room, chamber'): 'storage room, storeroom, pantry'.

history.meaning: storage room; storeroom

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 储藏室 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to hold an event, press, bring on (in 開催 kaisai, 催促 saisoku)

催.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形聲, cuī) from Old Chinese *tsʰˤuj (Middle Chinese tshwoj), composed of semantic 亻 ('person') and phonetic 崔 (*dzˤuj). Glossed in the Han-dynasty Shuowen Jiezi as 相擣也 ('to press upon one another'), it has continuously meant 'to urge, hasten, press someone to act quickly' from Classical poetry (e.g., Du Fu's 催租 'pressing for rent/taxes') through modern Mandarin.

history.meaning: to press upon, hasten, urge someone to act quickly
to urge, hurry, press for delivery, payment, or action

morphemes.meaning: to urge, hasten, press for; to accelerate or induce

催.notes: Extremely productive in workplace and media Mandarin as a monosyllabic verb taking concrete objects of what is being demanded: 催稿 ('chase down a script/manuscript'), 催款 ('press for payment'), 催更 ('pester a creator for the next episode/update').

rootFamily.gloss: to urge, press someone repeatedly to act
tear-jerking, moving an audience to tears (literally 'urging tears')

催吐.etymology: A causative verb-object compound (cuītù) formed from 催 (Middle Chinese tshwoj, here in its medical/physiological causative sense 'to induce, stimulate, hasten the onset of', parallel to 催眠 'induce sleep' and 催产 'induce labor') and 吐 (Old Chinese *tʰˤaʔ-s, Middle Chinese thuH in the departing tone, 'to vomit, disgorge'). Originally a traditional Chinese and modern pharmacological term (e.g., 催吐剂 'emetic agent'), it is also used for self-induced vomiting after poisoning, alcohol binging, or disordered eating.

history.meaning: to vomit, regurgitate, spit out
to induce vomiting (medically via emetics or physically via gag reflex)

morphemes.meaning: to induce, stimulate, hasten the onset of
to vomit, throw up (fourth tone tù)

催吐.notes: Note the tonal split on 吐: fourth tone tù means involuntary or forceful vomiting (催吐, 呕吐 'vomit', 吐血 'spit blood'), whereas third tone tǔ means voluntarily spitting out from the mouth or uttering (吐痰 'spit phlegm', 吐露 'confide').

rootFamily.gloss: to vomit, throw up; nausea and vomiting
to confide, reveal one's true feelings (tǔlù)

傻.etymology: A Middle Chinese phono-semantic compound (形聲, MC *ʂˠaX) combining the semantic person radical 亻 with 𡕢 (a graphic variant related to 俊/夋) as phonetic. First recorded in Song-dynasty rime dictionaries such as the Guangyun (廣韻) and Jiyun (集韻) with the sense "nimble, flighty, frivolous" (輕慧貌) or "unruly", it underwent pejorative semantic shift in Jin-Yuan northern vernacular drama (元曲) to mean "simple-minded, muddle-headed, foolish, or artlessly naive".

history.meaning: flighty, nimble, slightly eccentric or frivolous
simple-minded, muddle-headed, lacking street smarts
foolish, silly, endearingly naive; stunned motionless

傻.notes: In conversational Mandarin and TV dialogue, 傻 often carries affectionate teasing ("silly, sweet and naive", as in 傻瓜 or 傻白甜) rather than harsh insult, and before a verb or as a resultative complement (看傻了) it means "stunned silly".

傻子.etymology: A root-plus-suffix nominal derivation (附加式合成詞) formed in Early Mandarin by attaching the unstressed nominalizing suffix 子 (-zi, grammaticalized from Classical Chinese 子 *tsəʔ "child, master") to the vernacular adjectival root 傻 (shǎ, "foolish, simple-minded"). Widely attested in Ming–Qing vernacular fiction such as Dream of the Red Chamber (紅樓夢), where 子 turns a descriptive quality into a concrete human noun denoting a simpleton or gullible person.

history.meaning: foolish root + nominalizing diminutive suffix
simpleton, gullible person, village fool
fool, dupe; affectionately naive person

傻子.notes: Notice the neutral tone on 子 (shǎzi); depending on prosody and context in workplace dramas, it ranges from biting mockery ("sucker, idiot") to tender self-deprecation ("I was such a fool for believing them").

rootFamily.gloss: pretend to be naive, play dumb

像.etymology: Phono-semantic character of person (亻) + 象 (xiàng, originally the pictograph of an elephant, used in Classical Chinese for 'image, likeness, resemble'). 像 specifies 'portrait, figure, likeness' and the verb/preposition 'resemble, look like, be like, such as'.

history.meaning: likeness; image; resemble
resemble; look like; such as; portrait

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 像 (via 萌典)

像是.etymology: An Early Mandarin vernacular compound predicate combining 像 (xiàng, "resemble, likeness, image", differentiated graphically via the person radical 亻 from Classical 象 *s-ljaŋʔ "elephant > figure/semblance") with the copula 是 (shì, grammaticalized in Han–Six Dynasties Chinese from the Old Chinese proximal demonstrative *djeʔ "this"). Together they form an epistemicapproximative verb ("resemble being, look as though"), softening categorical assertions into visual or inferential impressions.

history.meaning: resemble + demonstrative/copula "to be"
seem like, appear to be; such as, for instance

像是.notes: Functions both before predicates/clauses to hedge an observation (他像是生气了, "he seems angry") and before noun phrases to introduce examples ("such as, like"), frequently paired with the clause-final particle 似的 or 一样.

像样.etymology: Verb-object compound used as an adjective, combining 像 ('resemble, look like') + 样 (樣, 'proper model, standard appearance'): 'up to standard, presentable, decent'.

history.meaning: look like a proper model -> presentable, decent

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 像样 (via 萌典)

僵.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形聲, OC *klaŋ, MC *kjaeng) composed of semantic 亻 (person) and phonetic 畺 (jiāng, "boundary fields"). In Classical Chinese (e.g., Shiji and Lunheng) 僵 meant "to fall flat on one's back, lie prostrate without rotting" and became interchangeable with 殭 ("rigor mortis, stiffened corpse or calcified silkworm", as in 白殭蠶). From corporeal rigor it extended metaphorically to limbs numb from cold, wooden facial expressions on camera, and deadlocked negotiations.

history.meaning: fall prostrate, topple flat on the ground
stiffened without decaying, rigor mortis, rigid
stiff, numb; wooden in expression; deadlocked, awkward

僵.notes: In showbiz and workplace dialogue, 僵 describes both camera-shy physical stiffness (表情很僵, "wooden expression") and strained interpersonal standoffs (把关系搞僵了, "pushed the relationship to an awkward impasse").

儿.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 儿. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 儿 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 儿 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 儿 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 儿. The etymology of 儿 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 儿
middle form of 儿
modern form of 儿

儿子.etymology: Originally a Classical Chinese coordinative noun phrase 兒子 combining 兒 (ér, OC *ŋe, pictograph of an infant with an unclosed fontanelle: "infant, boy, youth") and 子 (zǐ, OC *tsəʔ, "offspring, child, son"). In Warring States and Han texts (such as Mencius and Shiji), 兒子 meant "young children" or "boys" collectively with both syllables bearing full lexical tone; during the Tang–Song vernacular transition, 子 bleached into the neutral-tone nominal suffix -zi while narrowing semantically from "child" to specifically "male offspring, son".

history.meaning: infants, young children, boys
male child, one's own son
son (Simplified form merging 兒 into 儿)

儿子.notes: Unlike single-syllable 儿, which only survives as a bound morpheme (儿女, 女儿) or retroflex erhua suffix (-r), disyllabic 儿子 is the standard everyday word for "son" across registers.

允许.etymology: A coordinative (parallel) disyllabic verb compound (並列結構, Traditional 允許) pairing two ancient Classical Chinese verbs of assent: 允 (yǔn, OC *lunʔ, attested in the Shangshu with the senses "truly, sincere; to consent, ratify") and 許 (xǔ, OC *qʰˤraʔ, semantic 言 "speech" + phonetic 午, "to listen and accede, promise, grant"). Lexicalized together in imperial administrative prose for granting official sanction, it became the standard Modern Mandarin verb for permitting an action or state of affairs.

history.meaning: to ratify sincerely + to accede to a request
grant imperial or official consent, approve
permit, allow (by authority, rules, or circumstances)

允许.notes: Slightly more formal than 让 (ràng) or 准 (zhǔn); frequently takes impersonal subjects in media production contexts (时间不允许, "the schedule doesn't allow it"; 条件允许, "conditions permitting").

cognates.meaning: elder statesman, senior figure in a field

元老.etymology: A Classical Chinese modifier-head compound (偏正結構) composed of 元 (yuán, OC *ŋor, originally depicting a prominent human head: "head, primary, chief, grand") modifying 老 (lǎo, OC *rˤuʔ, "venerable elder, senior minister of state"). First attested in the Book of Odes (詩經·小雅·采芑: 方叔元老, 克壯其猶, "Fang Shu, the grand elder statesman, mighty in his counsels"), it was adopted in Meiji Japan as genrō for imperial elder advisers and returned into modern Chinese corporate and media usage for founding veterans of an institution.

history.meaning: chief elder minister of the royal court
venerable senior statesman serving across reigns
founding veteran, senior pillar of a party, company, or TV network

元老.notes: In corporate and TV-industry dramas like 幕后之王, 元老级人物 ("founding-veteran-tier figure") refers to long-serving executives or producers who helped build the network from day one and wield deep informal clout.

rootFamily.gloss: veteran, senior elder in a sect or firm

兄弟.etymology: Coordinative kinship compound of 兄 ('elder brother', mouth 口 atop a standing person 儿, the eldest who speaks/instructs) + 弟 ('younger brother', originally leather binding wrapped in sequence around a shaft). Means 'older and younger brothers; brothers; fraternal'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Shijing) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: elder and younger brothers; brothers

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 兄弟 (via 萌典)

兄弟们.etymology: A trimorphemic collective human noun formed by adding the Mandarin plural/collective suffix 们 (Traditional 們, -men, grammaticalized in Song–Yuan vernacular via variants 懣/每 from 門 "clan, household") onto the Classical Chinese coordinative dvandva compound 兄弟 (xiōngdì: 兄 OC *qʷʰraŋ "elder brother" + 弟 OC *lˤəjʔ "younger brother"). While Classical 兄弟 covered male siblings (and occasionally sisters), 兄弟们 crystallized in vernacular speech as a warm vocative rallying comrades, coworkers, or crewmates.

history.meaning: elder and younger brothers; male kinsmen
brothers, sworn comrades (early plural suffixation)
brothers; folks, crewmates, comrades-in-arms (vocative)

兄弟们.notes: Note the pronunciation contrast: literal "older and younger brothers" is full-toned xiōngdì, whereas colloquial "buddy/bro" is neutral-toned xiōngdi; in production-crew pep talks, 兄弟们 ("folks! team! guys!") rallies mixed-gender crews through camaraderie.

充分.etymology: Originally a verb-object compound (動賓結構) composed of 充 (chōng, OC *tʰjuŋ, "to fill up, stuff, satisfy") and 分 (fèn, OC *bəns, "allotted portion, proper measure, full quota"), literally "filling the full measure". Attested sporadically in Song–Ming vernacular and administrative prose, its modern adjectival and adverbial scope ("ample, thorough, to the fullest") was heavily reinforced in Late Qing and Republican Chinese by Meiji Japanese 充分 (jūbun, an orthographic variant of 十分 "ten tenths").

history.meaning: fill up one's allotted quota or full measure
sufficient, complete (reinforced via Sino-Japanese kango)
ample, full, thorough; fully (adverbial before disyllabic verbs)

充分.notes: Often paired in logic and formal prose with 必要 (充分必要条件, "necessary and sufficient condition") and frequently used adverbially before formal two-syllable verbs like 准备 ("fully prepare"), 利用 ("make full use of"), or 体现 ("fully embody").

cognates.meaning: be filled with, permeate, brim with
be filled to the brim, abound with

充满.etymology: A coordinative-resultative disyllabic verb compound (並列/動補結構, Traditional 充滿) joining 充 (chōng, OC *tʰjuŋ, "fill, pack solid, reach throughout") and 滿 (mǎn, OC *mˤonʔ, semantic 氵 "water" + phonetic 㒼, "fill a vessel to overflowing, brimful"). Attested from Eastern Han prose (such as Wang Chong's Lunheng 論衡) and Medieval Chinese Buddhist translations, the two near-synonymous roots reinforce complete spatial or emotional saturation.

history.meaning: fill a space or vessel to capacity; pervade (of qi or sound)
be full of, brim with (concrete objects or abstract emotions/energy)

充满.notes: Takes abstract nouns directly as objects without needing a preposition (充满信心 "brimming with confidence", 充满悬念 "packed with suspense"—a staple of showbiz pitch meetings).

充血.etymology: A verb-object Sinitic compound (動賓結構) composed of 充 (chōng, "fill, engorge") + 血 (xuè/xiě, OC *m̥ˤik, pictograph of sacrificial blood in a ritual chalice: "blood"). Coined as a Meiji-era Japanese medical *wasei-kango* (充血 jūketsu) to render German *Hyperämie* / English *hyperemia* (localized vascular engorgement with blood) and borrowed into Late Qing–Republican Chinese medical and everyday vocabulary.

history.meaning: localized engorgement of blood vessels (hyperemia)
flush with blood, become bloodshot or congested

充血.notes: Standard literary/medical reading is chōngxuè (though colloquial northern speech sometimes says chōngxiě); in TV production slang, 眼睛充血 ("bloodshot eyes") vividly evokes pulling consecutive all-nighters in the editing bay, while 大脑充血 means losing one's cool in a rush of blood to the head.

先.etymology: Ancient ideogram attested on Shang oracle bones showing a foot (止/之) advancing ahead of a person (儿): 'go first, earlier, before, first, ancestors/deceased'.

history.meaning: foot stepping ahead of a person = first, before, earlier
first; in advance; earlier

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 先 (via 萌典)

先生.etymology: Compound of 先 ('earlier, first') + 生 ('born'). In the Analects and Mencius, 先生 literally meant 'one born before me'—hence 'elder, teacher, master'. In modern Mandarin it remains a respectful title for a 'teacher/scholar' and is the standard polite word for 'Mr., gentleman, sir, husband'.

history.meaning: one born earlier -> elder, master, teacher
Mr.; sir; gentleman; husband; respected teacher

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 先生 (via 萌典)

光.etymology: Ancient ideogram attested on Shang oracle bones showing fire (火) blazing atop a kneeling human figure (儿): 'light, radiance, brightness, honor', and by extension 'bare, smooth, used up completely (吃光)' and adverbially 'only, merely'.

history.meaning: fire above a person = light, brightness, glory
light; ray; bare/empty; only/merely

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 光 (via 萌典)

光临.etymology: Polite honorific compound of 光 ('radiance, honor with your presence') + 临 (臨, 'look down upon, approach, arrive'). Literally 'your radiant presence descends here', standard in welcoming guests or customers (欢迎光临).

history.stage: Six Dynasties–Tang epistolary Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: honor us with your radiant arrival; welcome

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 光临 (via 萌典)

光是.etymology: A vernacular restrictive focus adverb formed in Ming–Qing Mandarin by combining 光 (guāng, OC *kʷˤaŋ, originally depicting fire above a kneeling person: "radiance, bright" > "smooth, bare, stripped naked" > semantically bleached to "merely, alone") with the focus particle 是 (shì, grammaticalized from the copula "to be"). Literally "barely/solely being X", it isolates one subset or cost to underscore that even that single item suffices to prove a larger point.

history.meaning: bright light, radiance > bare, stripped, uncovered
solely, merely, just considering X alone
merely, just, simply (paired with 就 in the following clause)

光是.notes: Almost always triggers the correlative adverb 就 (jiù) or 都 (dōu) in the main predicate: 光是场地费就要一百万 ("just the venue fee alone costs a million").

光滑.etymology: Coordinate descriptive compound of 光 ('bright; polished; sleek', fire 火 above a kneeling figure 儿) + 滑 ('smooth; slippery', water radical 氵 + phonetic 骨 gǔ). Together they describe a surface free of roughness, from kneaded bread dough to polished wood or glass.

history.meaning: sleek and smooth to the touch
smooth; glossy

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 光滑

光秃秃.etymology: ABB-pattern vivid descriptive adjective combining 光 ('bare, stripped smooth') + reduplicated 秃 (禿, 'bald, bare of hair or vegetation', showing grain 禾 over a person 儿 without cover): 'completely bare, bald, leafless, barren'.

history.meaning: completely bare, bald, or stripped

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 光秃秃 (via 萌典)

光线.etymology: Compound noun of 光 ('light') + 线 (線, 'thread, line, ray'): 'ray of light, lighting, illumination'.

history.meaning: light ray; lighting conditions

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 光线 (via 萌典)

克.etymology: Originally an ancient pictograph/ideograph 克 (kè, 'to shoulder a burden, overcome, prevail'), attested on Shang oracle bones. In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, when Chinese standardized metric units, 克 was selected as a phonetic-clipping abbreviation of 克兰姆 (kèlánmǔ), the transliteration of French/English gramme/gram. It now functions universally as the standard classifier for grams (千克 'kilogram', 毫克 'milligram') in kitchens, markets, and science.

morphemes.meaning: gram (abbreviated phonetic loan from 克兰姆 < French gramme)

history.meaning: bear; overcome; subdue
phonetic adaptation and single-character abbreviation for metric gram
gram (metric unit of mass)

免.etymology: An ancient compound ideograph (會意, OC *mranʔ, MC *mjenX; distinct from 兔 "rabbit", which has an extra final stroke) originally depicting a person removing ritual/armored headgear or slipping free from bodily constraint. In Warring States texts such as the Zuozhuan (左傳) and Liji (禮記), 免 meant both "to escape disaster, spare from punishment" and "to remove one's official cap (免冠), strip or relieve of office", giving rise to its dual modern poles of "exempt/waive" and "dismiss from a post".

history.meaning: remove headgear; escape peril; relieve an official of office
remit taxes/corvée, pardon, dismiss from bureaucratic rank
remove from office; exempt, waive, dispense with; avoid

免.notes: In corporate boardrooms and official notices, 任免 (rènmiǎn, "appointment and dismissal") pairs 免 directly as the antonym of 任 ("appoint"); in everyday speech, 免了! means "skip it / no need!".

免去.etymology: A verb-complement / directional-resultative compound (動補結構) combining 免 (miǎn, "relieve of, exempt, remove") with the ablative/directional verb 去 (qù, OC *kʰˤraʔs, "depart, cast away, eliminate"). Attested in Tang–Song Literary Chinese in the general sense "dispense with, spare from", 免去 crystallized in modern Chinese administrative and corporate governance prose as the transitive formal verb for stripping or relieving someone of a specific post (免去……职务) or waiving tedious procedures.

history.meaning: cast off, spare from, dispense with (hardship or ritual)
formally relieve of (an official post); save/eliminate (trouble)

免去.notes: Unlike intransitive/VO 免职 (which cannot take a direct title object), 免去 is transitive and takes the specific title or person+title directly: 免去其总监职务 ("relieve him/her of the post of director").

免得.etymology: A negative-purpose subordinating conjunction ("lest, so as not to") grammaticalized in Ming–Qing vernacular Mandarin (attested in Journey to the West 西遊記 and Dream of the Red Chamber 紅樓夢) from 免 (miǎn, "avoid, avert") plus the post-verbal modal/complement particle 得 (de, bleached from Classical 得 *tˤək "obtain, succeed in"). Parallel to Literary Chinese 以免 (yǐmiǎn) and colloquial 省得 (shěngde), it links a precautionary action to the undesirable outcome it prevents.

history.meaning: succeed in avoiding (verb + resultative particle)
lest, so as not to (conjunction introducing averted consequence)

免得.notes: Colloquial counterpart to written 以免 (yǐmiǎn): use 免得 in spoken dialogue (快存盘，免得死机, "save quickly so it doesn't crash") and 以免 in memos or contracts.

cognates.meaning: dismissal from office, removal from post
dismiss from office, relieve of post

免职.etymology: A verb-object administrative compound (動賓結構, Traditional 免職) combining 免 (miǎn, "relieve of, dismiss") with its object 職 (zhí, OC *tək, semantic 耳 "ear" + phonetic 音/戠, "official duty, bureaucratic post"). Modeled directly on Han-dynasty imperial terms such as 免官 ("remove from officialdom", Shiji 史記) and standardized across modern East Asian civil-service and corporate law (alongside Meiji Japanese 免職 menshoku) for formal removal from an appointed office.

history.meaning: relieve an imperial official of bureaucratic post
remove from office, dismiss from a managerial or public post

免职.notes: Because 免职 is already a separable verb-object (离合词) construction ("dismiss-from-post"), passivizing a person uses 被免职 ("was removed from office") rather than *免职他; also note it strips a managerial post without necessarily terminating employment (unlike 开除 "fire").

rootFamily.gloss: join a company, start a job

免费.etymology: Verb-object compound used as an adjective and adverb, combining 免 ('exempt, waive, excuse from') + 费 (費, 'fee, expense, cost'): 'waive the fee -> free of charge, complimentary'.

history.meaning: exempt from fees; free of charge

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 免费 (via 萌典)

兔子不吃窝边草.etymology: A traditional seven-character vernacular proverb (俗語, Traditional 兔子不吃窩邊草) attested in Ming–Qing vernacular fiction (with early variants like 兔兒不吃窠邊草 in Jin Ping Mei 金瓶梅 and Ernü Yingxiong Zhuan 兒女英雄傳). Structurally a full SVO clause—兔子 ("rabbit") + 不吃 ("does not eat") + 窝边草 ("grass beside its burrow")—it draws on folk zoology: a wise hare leaves the foliage around its den intact to preserve camouflage from predators, originally advising outlaws or neighbors not to prey on locals, before shifting in modern urban speech to discouraging workplace or friend-circle romance.

history.meaning: a hare leaves grass by its burrow untouched (do not rob or harm neighbors)

history.form: 兔子不吃窝边草 (tùzi bù chī wōbiāncǎo)
history.meaning: don't stir trouble near home; humorously: don't date coworkers or close friends

morphemes.meaning: rabbit, hare (兔 + nominal suffix 子)
does not eat (negator 不 + verb 吃)

兔子不吃窝边草.notes: In contemporary office and showbiz comedies, characters cite this proverb teasingly against office romance—and playful contrarians often retort 窝边草有啥不好吃 ("what's wrong with eating grass right outside the burrow?").

rootFamily.gloss: cunning hare has three burrows (have backup plans)
bird's nest; cozy home or den

cognates.meaning: check into a hotel, move into a property

入住.etymology: A serial/complement verb compound (連謂/動補結構) pairing 入 (rù, OC *njup, wedge-shaped pictograph meaning "enter, go inside") with 住 (zhù, MC *drjuH, semantic 亻 "person" + phonetic 主, "halt, dwell, reside"). While 入 and 住 co-occurred loosely in premodern vernacular, 入住 lexicalized as a crisp disyllabic register term in late 20th-century Hong Kong/Cantonese hospitality and real-estate Chinese before becoming standard across Mainland Mandarin for hotel check-ins and residential move-ins.

history.meaning: enter + halt/dwell (unfused serial verbs)
take up occupancy in a newly built property or check into lodging

入住.notes: Carefully distinguish homophonous 入住 (rùzhù, with 住 "live/stay": individuals checking into a hotel or moving into an apartment) from 入驻 (rùzhù, with 驻 "station/garrison": companies, studios, or creators officially setting up on a platform or business park).

cognates.meaning: entrance, admission to a hall or stadium

入场.etymology: A verb-object compound (動賓結構, Traditional 入場) combining 入 (rù, OC *njup, "enter") and 場 (chǎng, OC *lraŋ, semantic 土 "leveled earth" + phonetic 昜, "cleared sacrificial ground, threshing floor > examination compound, stage, arena"). In Tang–Song Literary Chinese 入場 specifically meant candidates entering the walled civil-service examination compound (科場); in the modern era (reinforced by Japanese 入場 nyūjō, as in 入場券 "admission ticket") it generalized to audiences entering a studio/venue, athletes marching in, or investors entering a market.

history.meaning: candidates entering the imperial civil-service examination hall
enter an auditorium, broadcast studio, stadium, or financial market

morphemes.meaning: leveled ground, stage, studio venue, market (Traditional 場)

入场.notes: In live TV taping, 观众入场 ("audience load-in / seating") marks the countdown before filming; in business strategy, 资本入场 means capital pouring into an industry sector.

rootFamily.gloss: exit the venue, leave the stage/market

入室弟子.etymology: A Classical four-character modifier-head expression (偏正結構) derived from Confucius's famous architectural metaphor of scholarship in Analects 11.15 (論語·先進: 由也升堂矣，未入於室也, "Zilu has ascended the main hall, yet has not entered the inner chamber"). In ancient residential layout, guests reached the outer hall (堂) while only trusted intimates entered the private rear chamber (室); combining VO 入室 ("enter the inner chamber", i.e., attain esoteric mastery) with 弟子 ("junior kinsman > disciple") yielded "inner-sanctum personal apprentice".

history.meaning: ascend the outer hall and enter the inner chamber (reach profound mastery)
personal disciple admitted to a master's private chamber and highest teachings
handpicked protégé or inner apprentice of a master artist, scholar, or senior producer

morphemes.meaning: inner chamber of a residence (symbolizing esoteric mastery)

入室弟子.notes: Carries high prestige in arts, media, and academia: calling a young producer a veteran's 入室弟子 implies personal mentorship and succession to their core craft (compare 关门弟子, "final apprentice taken before retirement").

rootFamily.gloss: advance from outer hall to inner chamber; master an art
a master's final, youngest personal apprentice

入组.etymology: A modern verb-object compound (動賓結構, Traditional 入組) combining 入 (rù, "enter, join") with 組 (zǔ, OC *tsˤaʔ, semantic 纟/糸 "silk" + phonetic 且, originally "woven silk ribbon/cord" > "bind together, organize" > clipped noun for 劇組 jùzǔ "film/television production crew" or 項目組 "project team"). Originally used in clinical trials ("enroll in a study cohort") and party/corporate administration, it became ubiquitous contemporary Mainland entertainment-industry jargon for cast or crew officially reporting to location to join a production unit.

history.meaning: woven silk cord or tassel; to braid together
join a working group or enroll in a clinical study group
report on set to officially join a film/TV production crew (剧组)

morphemes.meaning: production crew (clipped from 剧组) / organized group (Traditional 組)

入组.notes: Near-synonymous in showbiz talk with 进组 (jìnzǔ) and paired with its opposite 杀青 (shāqīng, "wrap filming") or 出组 ("leave the set"); a separable VO verb (入了组, "already joined the crew on set").

rootFamily.gloss: film, drama, or TV production crew
join the production crew on set (colloquial variant)

cognates.meaning: enter a profession or clerical ministry

入职.etymology: A verb-object administrative compound (動賓結構, Traditional 入職) built from 入 (rù, "enter, assume") and 職 (zhí, OC *tək, "official post, duty, employment"). Modeled on Classical Chinese bureaucratic VO compounds such as 入官 ("enter civil office") and 就職 ("assume high office"), 入職 gained widespread currency in late 20th-century Hong Kong/Cantonese human-resources terminology before becoming the universal Mainland corporate Mandarin term for employee onboarding.

history.meaning: enter upon bureaucratic duties or officialdom
onboard at a company, formally start employment

入职.notes: Covers ordinary staff onboarding (办理入职手续, "complete onboarding paperwork"; 新入职员工, "new hires"), whereas 就职 (jiùzhí) is reserved for high-ranking inauguration (such as presidents or CEOs taking office), and 离职 ("leave a company") is its direct HR antonym.

rootFamily.gloss: leave one's job, depart a company

cognates.meaning: be stationed in, move troops into

入驻.etymology: A serial/complement verb compound (連謂/動補結構, Traditional 入駐) combining 入 (rù, "enter") and 駐 (zhù, MC *trjuH, semantic 馬 "horse" + phonetic 主 "lampstand/stay still", originally "a horse halting carriage", hence "garrison troops, station envoys"). Historically restricted to military and diplomatic dispatches ("troops entering and garrisoning a city"), in 21st-century Mainland Chinese commerce and media it expanded metaphorically to brands, production studios, or celebrities officially opening an account or headquarters in an industrial park, mall, or digital platform.

history.meaning: halt horses and carriages; encamp, station troops
march into and garrison a territory; establish a diplomatic mission
officially set up shop, open an official presence (of studios, brands, or creators on platforms/parks)

morphemes.meaning: halt a horse > garrison, be officially stationed (Traditional 駐)
