入驻.notes: A classic spelling trap with homophone 入住: individual guests/residents 入住 a hotel or flat, whereas institutions, celebrity studios, or verified creators 入驻 a media park, shopping mall, or social platform (工作室正式入驻).

rootFamily.gloss: stationed at, accredited to (e.g., foreign correspondent 驻外记者)
check in, move into a residence (homophone contrast)

全.etymology: Adjective and adverb meaning 'whole, complete, entire; completely, all'. In small-seal script (Shuowen Jiezi), 全 combines 入 ('enter/gather') + 王 (玉 'jade'), denoting 'pure, intact, unblemished jade without flaw' -> 'complete, whole'.

history.meaning: intact unblemished jade -> whole, complete, keep safe
whole; entire; all; completely

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 全 (via 萌典)

全世界.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正結構) prefixing 全 (quán, OC *dzon, "intact, complete, entire", originally depicting flawless carved jade) to 世界 (shìjiè). Crucially, 世界 itself was coined in Six Dynasties Chinese Buddhist translations (such as the Śūraṅgama Sūtra 楞嚴經) to render Sanskrit *lokadhātu* by uniting temporal 世 (shì, "succession of thirty-year generations, past-present-future") with spatial 界 (jiè, "four cardinal boundaries"). Modern 全世界 denotes the entire globe across all nations.

history.meaning: Buddhist cosmos uniting time (世) and space (界), rendering Sanskrit lokadhātu
the entire geographic and human world across the globe

全世界.notes: Beyond literal global reach, colloquial Mandarin and romantic/workplace dramas constantly use 全世界 hyperbolically for "everyone around me" (全世界都知道了, רק你不知道, "the whole world knows except you!").

全会.etymology: A modern modifier-head syllabic abbreviation (縮略語, Traditional 全會) contracted from 全體會議 (quántǐ huìyì, "plenary conference/assembly"), combining 全 (quán, "all, entire, plenary") with 會 (huì, OC *gˤops, originally depicting a lidded cooking vessel coming together: "gather, assemble, meeting"). Coined in 20th-century Chinese political and organizational vocabulary to render Russian *plenum* / English *plenary session*, it denotes a formal assembly of every full and alternate member of a governing body or board.

history.meaning: plenary session of a political central committee or congress
plenary session (political or high-level corporate/network general assembly)

morphemes.meaning: all, entire, plenary (clipped from 全体)

全会.notes: Carries solemn institutional weight (famous from news headlines like 三中全会, "Third Plenary Session"); when used inside a TV network or corporation (台里开全会), it signals a high-stakes all-hands leadership assembly rather than a casual team huddle.

全副武装.etymology: A four-character modifier-head set phrase (偏正結構, Traditional 全副武裝) composed of 全副 ("complete set": 全 "entire" + classifier 副 fù "matched set of gear/armor/utensils") modifying 武裝 (wǔzhuāng: 武 "martial, military" + 裝 "attire, equipment", standardized in modern Chinese alongside Meiji Sino-Japanese 武裝 busō "armament"). Literally "outfitted in a complete set of combat gear", it expanded from military reporting into playful everyday and entertainment usage for dressing head-to-toe in protective or disguising layers.

history.meaning: outfitted with a complete set of military weapons and combat gear
in full combat gear; humorously bundled up head-to-toe (against cold, sun, rain, or paparazzi)

morphemes.meaning: complete set, suite (of gear, armor, or accessories)

全副武装.notes: A favorite humorous hyperbole in showbiz and daily life: a celebrity stepping into an airport in cap, sunglasses, mask, and long coat—or a crew member wrapped in parkas for a winter night shoot—is described as 全副武装.

全力.etymology: A Classical Chinese modifier-head compound (偏正結構) combining 全 (quán, OC *dzon, "whole, intact, unsparing") and 力 (lì, OC *k.rək, pictograph of a sinew or woodenard-plow: "muscular strength, power, effort"). Attested in Warring States and Han historical texts such as Zhanguoce (戰國策) and Hou Hanshu (後漢書) for committing an army's undivided strength, in Modern Mandarin it functions both nominally (尽全力, "exert full strength") and directly as a preverbal manner adverb ("all-out, whole-heartedly").

history.meaning: undivided military or physical strength
full strength (noun); with all one's might, all-out (adverbial)

全力.notes: As an adverb it modifies disyllabic action verbs directly without 地 (全力支持 "support wholeheartedly", 全力抢救 "make all-out efforts to rescue", 全力配合 "cooperate fully"), and anchors the classic idiom 全力以赴 ("go all out").

rootFamily.gloss: go all out, spare no effort
do one's utmost, try one's best

全台.etymology: A modern modifier-head compound (偏正結構, Traditional 全臺/全台) combining 全 (quán, "entire, whole") with 台 (tái, here the clipped institutional morpheme from 電視台 diànshìtái "television station/network" or 電台 diàntái "radio station"). Historically, 臺 (OC *lˤə) denoted a lofty stamped-earth viewing terrace and, from the Han dynasty onward, high central government secretariats (such as 御史臺), which yielded modern "broadcasting station/network"—making 全台 "the entire TV network".

history.meaning: raised earthen viewing terrace; high imperial secretariat or observatory

history.form: 電台 / 電視台 > 台
history.meaning: radio or television broadcasting station/network
the entire TV/radio station or network (also homographic abbreviation for 全台湾 "all of Taiwan")

morphemes.meaning: broadcasting station/network (clipped from 电视台; Traditional 臺)

全台.notes: Context disambiguates two common senses of 全台: inside a Mainland media drama like 幕后之王, 全台上下 means "everyone across the entire TV network" (alongside 台长 "network president" and 台里 "at the network"), whereas in Taiwanese news headlines 全台 abbreviates 全台湾 ("across all of Taiwan").

rootFamily.gloss: head/president of a TV or radio station

cognates.meaning: all members, the entire crew or cast

全员.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正結構, Traditional 全員) formed from 全 (quán, "all, entire") and 員 (yuán, OC *ɢʷren, originally a bronzeware graph of a round cauldron opening > "round, circumference" > extended in Warring States–Han bureaucracy to "quota/count of officials, personnel, member"). Standardized in modern institutional prose via shared Sino-Japanese 全員 (zen'in), it refers compactly to the entire staff, cast, or roster of a team.

history.meaning: roundness > numeric quota > official personnel, staff member
all personnel, every member of a unit or ship/crew
all staff, the entire production crew, full cast/roster

全员.notes: Ubiquitous in both corporate operations (全员大会 "all-hands meeting", 全员通知 "@channel/all-staff notice") and modern variety-show/pop-culture slang (e.g., 全员恶人 "every character in the cast is a villain", 全员晋级 "every contestant advances").

全员待命.etymology: A four-character subject-predicate institutional phrase (主謂結構, Traditional 全員待命) uniting the subject 全員 ("all personnel, entire crew") with the Classical Chinese verb-object predicate 待命 (dàimìng: 待 OC *dˤəʔ "await, stand ready for" + 命 OC *m-riŋs "imperial/military command, orders", attested in Warring States histories such as Guoyu 國語 and Zuozhuan 左傳). Originally a military readiness directive ("all troops stand by for orders"), it moved seamlessly into emergency response and live television control-room parlance for "all hands on standby".

history.meaning: await sovereign or military orders before acting
all personnel/crew remain on alert standby ready for immediate deployment

全员待命.notes: Wait! Notice the clean Chinese phrasing in notes: In live broadcasting, crisis PR, and tech launches, 全员待命 means nobody clocks out or turns off their phone—every department stays ready to jump into action the instant the director or executive gives the word.

rootFamily.gloss: stand by for orders, be on call

全国.etymology: Originally a Classical Chinese verb-object construction 全國 (quán guó, Middle Chinese *dzjwen kwok) attested in Warring States strategy texts such as Zhan Guo Ce ("to preserve the state intact"), combining 全 ("complete, whole; to keep intact") and 國 ("walled state, polity"). Reanalyzed into a modifier-head nominal compound meaning "the entire nation," reinforced in modern Mandarin alongside Meiji-era Sino-Japanese 全国 (zenkoku) in modern administrative and broadcast usage.

history.meaning: to keep the state whole and unharmed
the entire realm or dynastic state
the whole country, nationwide

全国.notes: Functions both as a noun and an attributive modifier without 的 in broadcast and media collocations like 全国首播 ("nationwide premiere") and 全国收视率 ("national ratings").

全城.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正结构) formed from 全 (quán, Middle Chinese *dzjwen, "whole, entire; to preserve intact") and 城 (chéng, Middle Chinese *dzyeng, originally "rammed-earth city wall," extended by metonymy to "walled city, municipality"). In Classical Chinese, 全城 occurred initially as a verb-object phrase ("to preserve a besieged city intact") before lexicalizing in medieval and modern vernacular Chinese into the nominal sense "the entire city."

history.meaning: to save or preserve a walled city intact
all inhabitants within a walled city
the entire city, citywide

全城.notes: Staple promotional buzzword in urban media and entertainment marketing, as in 全城热议 ("the talk of the whole town") or 全城直播 ("citywide livestream").

全才.etymology: A Literary Chinese modifier-head nominal compound pairing 全 (quán, Middle Chinese *dzjwen, "complete, lacking nothing") with 才 (cái, Middle Chinese *dzoj, originally sprouting timber, extended early to "natural endowment, capability, person of talent"). Attested in imperial historiography such as the Book of Jin (晋书) to praise officials possessing both civil and martial mastery, it survived directly into modern Mandarin to denote a versatile multi-hyphenate professional.

history.meaning: complete statecraft talent encompassing civil and military abilities
all-rounder, versatile multi-talented person

全才.notes: Contrasts directly with 专才 (zhuāncái, "specialist"); in television production, a 全才制作人 is a producer who can write, edit, pitch, and direct.

全新.etymology: Modifier-head adjective compound of 全 ('completely, wholly') + 新 ('new, fresh'): 'brand-new, completely new'.

history.meaning: brand-new; completely new

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 全新 (via 萌典)

全景.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound of 全 (quán, Middle Chinese *dzjwen, "entire, full") and 景 (jǐng, Middle Chinese *kjangX, originally "bright sunlight," extended in Six Dynasties landscape aesthetics to "scenery, vista, view"). Used in premodern landscape poetry and garden writing for an unobstructed vista, 全景 was adapted in modern photography, cinema, and television production (alongside Sino-Japanese 全景 zenkei) to translate "panorama" and the technical camera framing "full/wide shot."

history.meaning: unobstructed view of an entire landscape
panorama; wide shot or full shot in cinematography

全景.notes: In TV studio direction (*幕后之王* control-room jargon), 全景 specifically denotes a full/wide shot showing actors head-to-toe within the set, distinct from 远景 (extreme wide/long shot) and 特写 (close-up).

rootFamily.gloss: close-up or medium-close shot; nearby view

全案.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 全 (quán, "complete, end-to-end") and 案 (àn, Middle Chinese *'anH, originally a wooden tray or magistrate's desk, metonymically extended in imperial bureaucracy to "official dossier, legal case file, formal plan"). Originally denoting a complete archival dossier in Qing administrative prose, 全案 was revitalized in late-20th-century Taiwanese and mainland Chinese advertising, PR, and television production for a comprehensive, turnkey project proposal or full-service campaign deck.

history.meaning: complete official case dossier or archival record
comprehensive proposal, full-service project deck, turnkey plan

全案.notes: High-frequency agency and showbiz pitch noun: 全案策划 ("full-service campaign planning") means handling everything from concept and copywriting to execution, rather than a piecemeal deliverable.

全流程.etymology: A modern right-branching modifier-head nominal compound [全 + [流 + 程]] built by prefixing 全 (quán, "whole, end-to-end") to 流程 (liúchéng, "workflow, process sequence"). Within 流程, 流 (liú, Middle Chinese *ljuw, "to flow, current") modifies 程 (chéng, Middle Chinese *drjeng, originally a grain measure, then "stage of a journey, regulated procedure"). Coined in 20th-century industrial engineering and management Chinese, 全流程 entered television and media operations for an end-to-end production rundown.

history.meaning: flow path of water; industrial process sequence
entire end-to-end workflow or operational rundown

全流程.notes: In TV production rooms, 全流程彩排 ("full-rundown dress rehearsal") means running a live show from opening cue to closing credits without stopping.

rootFamily.gloss: the whole way through, full journey

全球.etymology: A modern modifier-head compound combining 全 (quán, "whole, entire") with 球 (qiú, Middle Chinese *gjuw, originally a fine jade chime or sphere, later "ball, globe"), formed by clipping 全地球 ("the entire terrestrial globe") after Jesuit cartographers introduced 地球 (dìqiú, "earth-sphere") in late Ming China. In the 20th century, 全球 became the standard Mandarin equivalent of English "global" and "worldwide."

history.meaning: terrestrial globe (Jesuit astronomical coinage)
the entire globe, worldwide, global

morphemes.meaning: globe, sphere (short for 地球, Earth)

全球.notes: Used directly before nouns or verbs without 的 in media phrases like 全球同步直播 ("global simulcast") and 全球化 ("globalization").

全程.etymology: A modifier-head compound joining 全 (quán, Middle Chinese *dzjwen, "whole, complete") and 程 (chéng, Middle Chinese *drjeng, "measured stage of travel, journey, course"). In Literary Chinese travel writing, 全程 referred literally to the full physical distance between two post stations; in modern Mandarin it grammaticalized by zero-derivation from a spatial/temporal noun ("the whole course") into a high-frequency adverbial modifier meaning "from start to finish, the whole way through."

history.meaning: full distance or complete itinerary of a journey
the entire course; (adverbially) the whole way through

全程.notes: Placed directly before the verb as an adverbial in media Chinese, e.g., 全程跟拍 ("follow with cameras the whole way") or internet slang 全程高能 ("nonstop thrills from start to finish").

全网.etymology: A contemporary modifier-head compound combining 全 (quán, "entire, across the board") with 网 (傳統字 網, wǎng, Middle Chinese *mjwangX, originally a knotted fishing or hunting net, calqued in late-20th-century computing for "network" and clipped from 互联网 "Internet"). First used in telecommunications for "entire physical network," 全网 exploded in post-2010 Chinese digital media to mean "across all online platforms, the entire internet."

history.meaning: an entire telecommunications or power network
the entire internet, across all digital platforms

morphemes.meaning: net, network, Internet (short for 互联网)

全网.notes: Ubiquitous in Chinese entertainment and PR: 全网独播 ("exclusive stream on a single platform across the web") vs. 全网封杀 ("blacklisted across every social and streaming platform").

rootFamily.gloss: official website or official social account

cognates.meaning: whole body and soul, complete devotion
cognates.word: 全身全霊 (ぜんしんぜんれい, zenshin-zenrei)

全身心.etymology: A three-character modifier-head structure [全 + [身 + 心]] in which 全 (quán, "whole, complete") scopes over the Classical Chinese coordinative compound 身心 (shēnxīn, "body and mind/heart," pairing 身 *syin "corporal self, body" with 心 *sim "heart-mind"). Rooted in Buddhist and Neo-Confucian self-cultivation discourse contrasting physical form and mental intent, 全身心 functions in modern Mandarin both nominally and adverbially ("body and soul, wholeheartedly").

history.meaning: physical body and heart-mind (in Buddhist and Confucian cultivation)
with one's whole body and mind, wholeheartedly

全身心.notes: Most naturally collocates with 投入 (tóurù, "to throw oneself into"), e.g., 全身心投入工作 ("throw oneself body and soul into one's work").

rootFamily.gloss: the whole body, from head to toe

全部.etymology: Compound noun and determiner of 全 ('whole, entire') + 部 ('part, section, division, totality'): 'the whole lot, all, entire, complete'.

history.meaning: all; the whole; entire part

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 全部 (via 萌典)

全都.etymology: A vernacular coordinative/reinforcing adverbial compound (同义复合词) uniting two universal quantifiers: 全 (quán, Middle Chinese *dzjwen, originally stative verb "complete, intact," grammaticalized in early Mandarin into the totality adverb "completely, all") and 都 (dōu, Middle Chinese *tuw, originally "imperial capital; to gather," grammaticalized since Tang–Song vernacular into the distributive universal adverb "all, without exception"). Stacking the two creates emphatic universal quantification ("every single one, all without exception").

history.meaning: to gather together; (Tang–Song vernacular) all, entirely
all without exception, every single one

全都.notes: Remember the pronunciation is quándōu (not dū!): like 都 alone, 全都 strictly quantifies elements that precede it in the clause (咱们全都知道, never *全都咱们知道).

全靠.etymology: An adverbial modifier-verb compound combining the totality adverb 全 (quán, Middle Chinese *dzjwen, "entirely, solely") with the verb 靠 (kào, Middle Chinese *khawH, originally "to lean against mutually; to oppose," shifting in Song–Yuan vernacular Chinese to "to lean on physically" and metaphorically "to rely or depend upon"). Together, 全靠 lexicalized in vernacular narrative and spoken Mandarin to express exclusive causal or personal reliance ("to depend entirely upon").

history.meaning: to lean against; to rely or depend on
to depend entirely on, owe everything to

全靠.notes: Warm and idiomatic in spoken teamwork praise—e.g., 这期节目能播全靠大家 ("Getting this episode on air is entirely thanks to everyone")—carrying stronger credit-giving force than 依靠.

全面.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-compound joining 全 (quán, Middle Chinese *dzjwen, "whole, complete") and 面 (miàn, Middle Chinese *mjienH, originally "human face," extended to "surface, side, aspect, dimension"). While literal spatial uses ("the entire surface/front") existed in Literary Chinese, its abstract adjectival and adverbial senses ("all-round, comprehensive, full-scale") expanded rapidly in late-19th and early-20th-century Mandarin via mutual reinforcement with Meiji Sino-Japanese 全面 (zenmen).

history.meaning: the whole face or entire physical surface
all-sided, comprehensive, full-scale (adjective & adverb)
history.stage: Modern Mandarin (20th c., reinforced by Japanese zenmen)

全面.notes: Pairs naturally as the antonym of 片面 (piànmiàn, "one-sided, partial") and acts either as an adjective (考虑得很全面, "thought through comprehensively") or pre-verbal adverb (全面升级, "upgrade across the board").

八.etymology: Cardinal numeral 'eight'. In Shang oracle-bone and Zhou bronze scripts, 八 is written with two diverging curved strokes (八) indicating 'part, divide in two' (the ancestor of 分 'divide', which adds a knife 刀), borrowed since earliest antiquity for the number eight.

history.meaning: two diverging strokes ('divide') borrowed for numeral eight

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 八 (via 萌典)

八九不离十.etymology: A vivid northern Mandarin vernacular numeric idiom (俗语) literally reading "eight or nine does not stray far from ten" (八 bā "eight" + 九 jiǔ "nine" + 不 bù "not" + 离/離 lí "to depart, be distant from" + 十 shí "ten"). Drawing on Chinese decimal reckoning where ten represents 100% completeness (as in 十全十美), hitting eight or nine out of ten parts became a colloquial metaphor attested in Qing–Republican vernacular fiction for an estimate, guess, or execution that is almost spot-on.

history.meaning: eight or nine out of ten—very close to complete accuracy
pretty close to the mark, mostly accurate, almost certain

morphemes.meaning: to stray or be distant from

八九不离十.notes: Colloquial predicate phrase used for shrewd guesses or near-final drafts—e.g., 猜得八九不离十 ("guessed pretty much on the money"); avoid in stiff legal or official bulletins.

rootFamily.gloss: eighty to ninety percent; most likely
perfect in every way (lit. ten-complete ten-beautiful)

八十.etymology: A multiplicative-decimal numeral compound attested continuously since Shang dynasty oracle bone inscriptions (甲骨文, written initially as a ligature or juxtaposition of 八 and 十), combining Old Chinese *pˤret > 八 (bā, "eight") with Old Chinese *g.[d]əp > 十 (shí, "ten"), both inherited from Proto-Sino-Tibetan (*b-r-gyat "eight" and *gip / *ts(y)i(p) "ten"). Its transparent [multiplier + base-10] syntax has remained unchanged for over three millennia.

history.meaning: eight tens, eighty (attested in Shang oracle bones and Zhou bronzes)
eighty

八十.notes: In media and cultural shorthand, 八十年代 ("the 1980s") and 八零后 ("post-80s generation") evoke distinct generational aesthetics in Chinese television storytelling.

八卦.etymology: Originally a Classical Chinese modifier-head noun 八卦 (bāguà, Middle Chinese *pɛt kwɛH, "the Eight Trigrams" of the Yijing / Book of Changes), combining 八 ("eight") and 卦 ("divinatory trigram"). Its modern entertainment sense ("celebrity gossip, tabloid chatter; nosy") arose as a mid-20th-century Hong Kong Cantonese semantic loan: Hong Kong magazines placed octagonal Eight-Trigram motifs on cover insets of entertainment pullouts (八卦杂志) or Riffed on Cantonese 𠵼詐/八婆 ("meddlesome"), exporting the slang across Mandarin media in the 1990s.

history.meaning: the Eight Trigrams used in Yijing cosmology and divination
entertainment magazine gossip section; nosy chatter
tabloid gossip, showbiz rumor; (adj./v.) nosy, to gossip

morphemes.meaning: divinatory trigram (extended via Cantonese media to gossip)

八卦.notes: Versatile across parts of speech in showbiz Mandarin: noun (娱乐八卦, "celeb gossip"), adjective (他很八卦, "he's super nosy"), and transitive/intransitive verb (八卦一下, "dish a little gossip").

八度.etymology: Musical compound of 八 ('eight') + 度 ('degree, scale step'): 'octave' (the interval spanning eight diatonic scale steps).

history.meaning: eight scale degrees = musical octave

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 八度 (via 萌典)

八角.etymology: A numeral-noun compound uniting 八 (bā, 'eight') and 角 (jiǎo, originally an animal 'horn', extended in antiquity to 'angle, corner, or pointed projection'). Literally 'eight-cornered' or 'eight-pointed', 八角 describes geometric octagons, eight-eaved pavilions (八角亭), and eight-pointed compass roses in cartography. Because the dried fruit pod of Illicium verum forms an eight-pointed star, 八角 also became the everyday Mandarin name for culinary star anise.

history.meaning: eight corners; octagonal shape
eight-pointed / octagonal; star anise (eight-pod spice)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 八角

cognates.word: 公 (こう, kō; おおやけ, ōyake)

公.etymology: Attested in Shang oracle bone and Western Zhou bronze inscriptions, 公 (gōng, Old Chinese *C.qˤoŋ, Middle Chinese *kuwng) depicts 八 ("to divide equally") above 厶/口 (a shared vessel or enclosure, contrasting with 私 sī, "private grain"), encoding "equal division, communal, impartial." In Zhou feudalism it denoted the ruler's palace, high noble rank ("duke"), and public governance, evolving into the foundational Chinese root for "official business, public interest, shared."

history.meaning: clan lord, duke; ruler's courtyard; impartial sharing
public realm, state administration, official duty (opposed to 私 private)
official business, public interest, collective property

公.notes: As a standalone noun in modern Mandarin, 公 mostly appears in crisp semi-classical idioms and workplace set phrases contrasting public duty with personal matters, such as 公私分明 ("keep official business and personal life strictly separate") and 因公出差 ("travel on company/official business").

rootFamily.gloss: to handle official business, work in an office
public and private; official vs. personal

公事.etymology: Compound noun of 公 ('public, official, shared', contrasting with 私 'private') + 事 ('business, affair'): 'official business, public duties'. Attested since the Zuozhuan and Analects.

history.meaning: official business; public affairs

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 公事 (via 萌典)

公交车.etymology: '公交车' (gōngjiāochē, bus) is an abbreviation of '公共交通汽车' (public transport automobile). The concept of '公共' (public) entered modern Chinese through late 19th-century translations of Western sociological texts, while '交通' (transportation) originally meant 'intersecting' in classical Chinese before taking on its modern logistical sense. As public motorized transport developed in Chinese cities during the 20th century, the full term was found too cumbersome for daily use. The abbreviation '公交车' became the dominant vernacular term in mainland China by the late 20th century.

history.meaning: station

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 公交车

公众.etymology: Compound noun of 公 ('public, general') + 众 (眾, 'multitude, crowd', originally three people 乑 under an eye/sun): 'the public, the general public'.

history.meaning: the general public

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 公众 (via 萌典)

公关.etymology: A 20th-century syllabic abbreviation (缩略语) of 公共关系 (gōnggòng guānxì), itself a semantic calque of English "public relations" combining 公共 ("public, communal," coordinative/modifier compound on 公) and 关系 ("relations, connections," originally "bolt and catch of a gate"). Condensed into the disyllabic compound 公关 by taking the first morpheme of each word (公 + 关), it subsequently developed verbal usage ("to do PR, manage a crisis") in contemporary Chinese media and corporate culture.

history.meaning: public relations (calque of English 'public relations')
public relations (PR); to conduct PR or crisis management

公关.notes: Central vocabulary in Chinese entertainment dramas (*幕后之王*): 危机公关 ("crisis PR") and 紧急公关 ("emergency spin control") are triggered whenever a celebrity scandal or broadcast mishap trends online.

公关部.etymology: A right-headed institutional modifier-head compound [公关 + 部] formed by suffixing 部 (bù, Middle Chinese *buwX, originally "military division, administrative category, ministry") to 公关 (gōngguān, clipped calque of 公共关系 "public relations"). Following the modern Sino-Japanese and Republican organizational pattern of naming corporate divisions with -部 (cf. 宣传部, 市场部), 公关部 designates an enterprise's or network's in-house public-relations department.

history.meaning: administrative division, government board or ministry
corporate or institutional public-relations department

公关部.notes: In Chinese media companies, 公关部 handles external press statements, brand image, and crisis mitigation, whereas 宣传部 / 宣发团队 focuses on show promotion and marketing rollouts.

公司.etymology: Compound of 公 ('public, joint') + 司 ('manage, department, office'). First used in Qing dynasty trade for the British East India Company (公班衙 / 公司) and overseas Chinese commercial associations, then standardized across modern Chinese for any 'company, corporation, firm'.

history.meaning: chartered trading company or guild
business company; firm; corporation

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 公司 (via 萌典)

公告.etymology: An adverbial-head / modifier-head Sino-compound pairing 公 (gōng, Middle Chinese *kuwng, "publicly, officially") with 告 (gào, Middle Chinese *kowk / *kawH, in Shang oracle bones depicting cattle 牛 offered before a ritual mouth 口 to "report to ancestors," hence "to proclaim, notify"). Used in Literary Chinese and codified across East Asian administrative law via Meiji Sino-Japanese 公告 (kōkoku), it denotes a formal written bulletin issued by a government body, listed company, or broadcaster.

history.meaning: to notify openly or proclaim to the public
formal statutory or corporate public notice, official bulletin
history.stage: Modern Mandarin (reinforced by Sino-Japanese legal terminology)

公告.notes: High-register written noun (and formal verb): TV networks and talent agencies 发布公告 ("issue an official bulletin") for schedule changes, contract terminations, or regulatory disclosures.

rootFamily.gloss: advance notice; show trailer or teaser

公园.etymology: The term '公园' (gōngyuán, public park) is a modern loanword, largely re-imported into Chinese via Japanese during the late Qing dynasty. It translates the Western concept of a 'public park'. Before this, Chinese gardens ('园林') were exclusively private, belonging to the imperial family or wealthy scholars. The compound combines '公' (public, shared) and '园' (garden, enclosure). The establishment of the first modern parks in treaty ports like Shanghai popularized the term, and it is now the standard word for municipal recreational spaces.

history.meaning: garden

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 公园

公安局.etymology: A three-character institutional compound [公安 + 局] built from 公安 (gōng'ān, "public peace and safety," combining 公 "public" + 安 *'an "peace, security," popularized in late-19th-century East Asian administrative prose alongside Japanese 公安 kōan) and the head noun 局 (jú, Middle Chinese *gjowk, originally "game board; compartmentalized office," hence "government bureau"). Adopted by the Chinese state in the mid-20th century as the official municipal and county police authority.

history.meaning: public peace and social safety
history.stage: Late Qing–Early Republican Chinese (via Sino-Japanese kōan)

history.meaning: Public Security Bureau, municipal/county police headquarters

公安局.notes: Mainland China's official municipal police bureau (colloquially shortened to 局里 in crime/workplace dramas), distinct from a neighborhood precinct station (派出所, pàichūsuǒ) and from Taiwan/Hong Kong 警察局 / 警署.

rootFamily.gloss: Administration of Radio and Television (media regulator)

公布.etymology: An adverbial-verb compound (偏正/状中结构) attested in Classical Chinese (e.g., Records of the Grand Historian / 史记), combining 公 (gōng, Middle Chinese *kuwng, "openly, to the public") with 布 (傳統字 佈/布, bù, Middle Chinese *puH, originally "hemp cloth," extended in Old Chinese to "to spread out, disseminate, promulgate"). Reinforced in modern East Asian legal vocabulary alongside Sino-Japanese 公布 (kōfu), in Mandarin it broadened beyond statutory promulgation to announcing results, lineups, or secrets publicly.

history.meaning: to spread abroad openly, make widely known
to promulgate laws; to announce results, lists, or news publicly

公布.notes: Takes concrete informational objects previously kept confidential or pending: 公布名单 ("announce the shortlist/cast list"), 公布结果 ("announce the results"), or 公布恋情 ("go public with a romance").

rootFamily.gloss: to release, publish, hold a press launch

公平.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative adjectival compound (联合结构) attested in Warring States philosophy (Xunzi / 荀子, Han Feizi / 韩非子), pairing 公 (gōng, Middle Chinese *kuwng, "impartial, unselfish, public-minded") with 平 (píng, Middle Chinese *bjaeng, "level, even, balanced like water or scales"). Originally praising an official or legal standard free from private favoritism (私) and tilt (偏), it remains the core East Asian adjective for "fair, equitable."

history.meaning: impartial and even-handed in governance and law
fair, equitable, unbiased

公平.notes: In competition reality shows, hosts routinely pledge 公平、公正、公开 ("fair, just, and transparent"): 公平 stresses equal rules for all contestants, while 公正 stresses upright, unbiased judging.

cognates.word: 公平競争 (こうへいきょうそう, kōhei kyōsō)

公平竞争.etymology: A four-character modifier-head phrase [公平 + 竞争] combining Classical Chinese 公平 (gōngpíng, "impartial and level, fair") with 竞争 (傳統字 競爭, jìngzhēng, "to vie and contend"). While 競 (*gjaengH, two figures vying side by side) and 爭 (*tsrɛng, two hands pulling at an object) occurred in Classical texts such as Zhuangzi, modern 竞争 crystallized as a standard term via late-19th-century Meiji translation (競争 kyōsō, popularized in Chinese by Yan Fu's 物竞天择) for market and Darwinian "competition."

history.meaning: to strive or contend against rivals
economic, athletic, or evolutionary competition (via Japanese kyōsō)
to compete fairly; fair competition / level playing field

公平竞争.notes: Functions smoothly as both a verbal predicate (大家公平竞争, "let's all compete fairly") and a nominalized concept in bidding pitches (公平竞争的环境, "a level playing field").

cognates.meaning: opening to the public, public release

公开.etymology: An adverbial-verb / modifier-head Sino-compound combining 公 (gōng, Middle Chinese *kuwng, "public, non-private") and 开 (傳統字 開, kāi, Middle Chinese *khoj, depicting two hands lifting a bar to open double gate doors, "to open, unseal"). Consolidated across modern East Asia through Meiji Sino-Japanese 公開 (kōkai, translating English "open to the public / public disclosure"), in Mandarin 公开 operates flexibly as an adjective ("open, public"), transitive verb ("to disclose"), and adverb ("publicly, openly").

history.meaning: to open an institution, court, or document to the general public
publicly, openly (adv.); public (adj.); to make public (v.)

公开.notes: Unlike 公布 (a pure verb taking informational nouns), 公开 works as an adverb directly before action verbs—e.g., 公开道歉 ("apologize publicly") or 公开招标 ("hold an open public tender").

公斤.etymology: Metric measure word combining 公 ('international/metric standard', short for 公制) + 斤 ('catty, traditional weight unit'): 'kilogram' (equal to two市斤 'market catties' of 500g each).

history.meaning: metric catty = kilogram (1,000 grams)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 公斤 (via 萌典)

公益.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-compound combining 公 (gōng, Middle Chinese *kuwng, "public, communal") with 益 (yì, Middle Chinese *'jiek, originally water overflowing a vessel 皿, hence "to increase, benefit, advantage"). Standardized in Meiji Japan as 公益 (kōeki) to render Western legal-philosophical "public interest / common good" (in contrast to 私益 shieki, "private gain") and adopted into late-Qing Chinese, in contemporary Mandarin it also encompasses non-profit charity and public-service initiatives.

history.meaning: the public good, general societal benefit (Meiji kōeki loan)
public welfare, non-profit philanthropy, public-service cause

公益.notes: Essential in Chinese broadcast and celebrity PR: 公益广告 translates "public service announcement (PSA)" (mandated on Chinese TV channels), and 做公益 means doing charitable/public-welfare work.

六.etymology: Cardinal numeral 'six'. In Shang oracle-bone script, 六 resembled a peaked roof or tent structure (介/六), borrowed phonetically since earliest antiquity for the number six.

history.meaning: numeral six

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 六 (via 萌典)

六七年.etymology: A numeral-measure temporal phrase [六七 + 年] illustrating the classic Sinitic approximative juxtaposition rule (相邻数字连用表概数), attested since Classical Chinese (e.g., Analects / 论语 "冠者五六人"): placing two adjacent cardinal numerals 六 (liù, Old Chinese *k.ruk, "six") and 七 (qī, Old Chinese *tsʰi[t], "seven") side by side without a conjunction expresses an approximate range ("six or seven"), modifying the unbound temporal classifier/noun 年 (nián, originally "grain harvest," hence "year").

history.meaning: a span of roughly six or seven years (Classical approximative syntax)
six or seven years

六七年.notes: Note two crucial grammar points: adjacent numbers 六七 never need 或 ("or") in idiomatic speech, and 年 is a self-classifying noun—so you say 六七年, never *六七个年 (though 六七年的时间 is fine).

rootFamily.gloss: three to five years, several years
over ten years, a dozen-plus years

cognates.meaning: joint undertaking, working together on a matter

共事.etymology: Attested in Han-dynasty historiography (Records of the Grand Historian / 史记 and Book of Han / 汉书), 共事 (gòngshì) joins 共 (gòng, Middle Chinese *gjowngH, in bronze script depicting two hands 廾 lifting an object together, hence "together, jointly") and 事 (shì, Middle Chinese *dzriH, "court affair, official service, work"). Originally a verb-object or adverbial-verbal phrase meaning "to serve the same lord or manage state affairs together," it narrowed in modern Mandarin to "to work together as colleagues."

history.meaning: to handle court affairs together or serve the same ruler
to work together as colleagues in the same workplace or team

morphemes.meaning: to serve, engage in official or professional work

共事.notes: Intransitive verb following the pattern 跟/与 + [person] + 共事 (e.g., 很高兴跟您共事, "It's been a pleasure working with you"); the noun for "colleague" flips the prefix to 同事 (tóngshì), never *共事 as a person noun.

cognates.word: 享有 / 共用 (cf. 共享 kyōkō)

共享.etymology: An adverbial-verb compound (状中结构) attested in Literary Chinese combining 共 (gòng, Middle Chinese *gjowngH, "together, in common") with 享 (xiǎng, Middle Chinese *xjangX, originally depicting an ancestral temple hall where sacrificial offerings are presented and partaken of, hence "to partake of, enjoy"). Historically used in formal blessings like 共享太平 ("partake together in great peace"), 共享 surged in late-20th and 21st-century Mandarin to translate digital "resource/file sharing" and the "sharing economy" (共享经济).

history.meaning: to partake jointly in blessings, offerings, or peace
to share pooled resources, data, rights, or public services

morphemes.meaning: to enjoy, partake of, have use of

共享.notes: Distinguish carefully from 分享 (fēnxiǎng): 共享 means pooling access to a shared resource or database (资源共享, 共享单车 "shared bikes"), whereas 分享 means sharing stories, feelings, links, or food with others.

rootFamily.gloss: to share (experiences, posts, food) with others

共同.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative compound (联合结构) attested since Han texts (e.g., Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian / 史记), uniting two near-synonymous morphemes: 共 (gòng, Middle Chinese *gjowngH, "together, shared by two hands") and 同 (tóng, Middle Chinese *duwng, "aligned as one, identical, together"). Reinforced in modern sociopolitical and legal usage alongside Meiji Sino-Japanese 共同 (kyōdō), it functions in Mandarin both as an adverb ("jointly, together") and a non-predicative adjective ("common, shared").

history.meaning: acting together in concert, shared in common
jointly, together (adv.); common, mutual (attributive adj.)

共同.notes: Higher-register than 一起: use 共同 before disyllabic formal verbs (共同出品 "co-produce," 共同努力 "strive together") and before abstract nouns (共同语言 "common ground/language").

cognates.meaning: common topic, shared subject of conversation

共同话题.etymology: A modifier-head nominal phrase combining 共同 (gòngtóng, "common, shared", a coordinative compound of 共 "together, share" + 同 "same, alike") with 话题 / 話題 (huàtí, "topic of conversation", a modifier-head compound of 话 / 話 "speech, talk" + 题 / 題 "forehead; inscription, heading, subject"). While 共同 and 題 are ancient Chinese items, 話題 was lexicalized in Meiji-era Japanese (wadai) for a conversational subject and re-entered modern Mandarin, yielding 共同话题 for interpersonal "common ground."

history.form: 共 / 同 / 話 / 題
history.meaning: to share together / same / speech / forehead or inscribed heading
subject or theme of conversation

history.form: 共同话题 / 共同話題 (gòngtóng huàtí)
history.meaning: shared topics of conversation, common ground between people

共同话题.notes: Commonly used with 有 ("have") or 没有 ("lack") when describing social compatibility, networking, or romantic chemistry (e.g., 我们很有共同话题, "we have a lot to talk about").

cognates.meaning: advancing and retreating; course of action, staying or resigning
advance and retreat, course of action

共进退.etymology: An adverbial-verb phrase formed from 共 (gòng, "together, jointly") modifying the classical antonymous coordinative compound 进退 / 進退 (jìntuì, literally "to advance and to retreat"). In Classical Chinese texts such as the Yijing and Liji, 進退 referred both to military movement and to courtly conduct or political career decisions; prefaced with 共 ("together"), it signifies binding one's fate to an ally or team to "advance and retreat together."

history.meaning: to advance and retreat; proper ceremonial movement or political course of action
to advance and retreat together in battle or political alliance
to stand or fall together, share the same fate as a team

共进退.notes: Frequently appears in the frame 与/跟……共进退 ("stand or fall together with...") in workplace dramas, corporate pledges, and team solidarity speeches.

rootFamily.gloss: in a dilemma, nowhere to advance or retreat
to share joys and sorrows together

关.etymology: Originally depicting a wooden crossbar or bolt drawn across double doors (關 = 門 'double doors' + 𢇇 'draw bolts/threads through'): 'bolt a door, close, shut, turn off (an appliance); mountain pass/customs barrier; concern/involve'.

history.meaning: door bolt; bar a gate; frontier pass; concern
close; shut; turn off; pass; concern

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 关 (via 萌典)

关上.etymology: A verb-resultative compound combining 关 / 關 (guān, "to draw a wooden crossbar across a gate, to close") with the directional/resultative complement 上 (shàng, "up; into contact or closed completion"). Paleographically, 關 depicts a latching crossbar mechanism inside a two-leaf gate (門); in vernacular Mandarin, post-verbal 上 grammaticalized from "ascend" into a resultative telic marker indicating that two surfaces or parts have come together and latched shut.

history.meaning: wooden crossbar of a gate; to bolt a door shut
to close or latch shut completely (a door, window, or lid)

morphemes.meaning: resultative marker of contact and closure

关上.notes: Unlike simple 关 ("close"), 关上 emphasizes the completed action of latching or sealing something shut; it readily takes the disposal marker 把 (e.g., 把门关上, "shut the door").

rootFamily.gloss: to close the door; to shut down business
to close or lock up inside; to shut off
to close together (e.g., a book or eyes)

cognates.word: に関して (ni kanshite) / 関於 (kan'o)

关于.etymology: A prepositional compound formed from 关 / 關 (guān, "to involve, interconnect, relate to") and the classical locative/relational preposition 于 / 於 (yú, "in, at, with respect to"). While 關 meant "to have bearing on" in Literary Chinese, the grammaticalized prepositional phrase 關於 ("regarding, concerning, as for") expanded rapidly in late 19th- and early 20th-century written Chinese under the influence of Meiji Japanese に関して (ni kanshite) and translations of European prepositions like "concerning" and "about."

history.meaning: to relate to / with respect to (separate verb and preposition)
regarding, concerning, about (compound preposition introducing a topic)

morphemes.meaning: to relate to, involve, touch upon

关于.notes: Introduces a broad topic rather than a direct target; placed either at the start of a sentence (关于这个问题，...) or directly before a noun as a modifier with 的 (关于幕后制作的书).

rootFamily.gloss: concerning, toward (a specific target or person)

cognates.meaning: to care about, be concerned with

关心.etymology: Originally a verb-object compound of 关 / 關 (guān, "to engage, touch upon, involve") + 心 (xīn, "heart, mind"), literally "to engage or touch one's heart-mind." Attested from the Tang and Song dynasties in the sense of "to weigh on the mind" or "to command one's attention," it shifted in vernacular Mandarin into an active transitive verb and adjective meaning to care solicitously about someone's well-being.

history.meaning: to engage the mind, weigh upon one's thoughts
to care about, show solicitous concern for someone or something

关心.notes: Watch out for the Sino-Japanese/Sino-Korean false friend: Japanese 関心 (kanshin) and Korean 관심 (gwansim) mean intellectual "interest," whereas Mandarin 关心 means emotional or personal "care and concern."

关机.etymology: A modern verb-object compound combining 关 / 關 (guān, "to shut, close, turn off") with 机 / 機 (jī, originally the trigger mechanism of a crossbow or a wooden loom, generalized in modern Chinese as a bound morpheme for "machine, engine, aircraft, or telephone"). Formed by analogy with earlier mechanical phrases like 停机 ("stop a loom/machine") and 开机 ("start up a machine/device"), 关机 denotes shutting down an electronic device or switching off a mobile phone.

history.meaning: gate-bolt (to shut) + crossbow trigger / loom mechanism
to shut down industrial machinery; to power off a phone or computer; to wrap filming on a movie/TV production

关机.notes: In film and television production (such as Behind the Scenes / 幕后之王), 关机 also has the specialized showbiz meaning "to wrap filming" (shutting down the cameras, paired with 开机 "start filming"), alongside everyday "turn off one's phone."

rootFamily.gloss: to power on a device; to start filming a production
to halt a machine; to have phone service suspended

关注.etymology: A coordinative verb compound pairing 关 / 關 (guān, "to involve, show concern for," as in 關心) with 注 (zhù, "to pour water into a vessel; metaphorically to fix one's gaze or concentration upon," as in 注意 or 注視). In Ming–Qing literary Chinese it meant to look after with close care; in contemporary Mandarin media and internet usage, it means both "to pay close attention to (an issue)" and "to follow/subscribe to (a social media account)."

history.meaning: to look upon with solicitous care and fixed attention
to pay close attention to a topic; to follow an account on social media

morphemes.meaning: to care about, involve, relate to
to pour into; to fix one's attention or gaze upon

关注.notes: The standard button label on Chinese social platforms (Weibo, Douyin, Bilibili) for "Follow" (点关注, "click follow"; 取消关注 / 取关, "unfollow").

rootFamily.gloss: to pay attention to, take note of
to focus exclusively on, be absorbed in

关注度.etymology: A three-character derived noun formed by attaching the productive Sino-Japanese/modern Chinese degree suffix -度 (dù, originally "linear measure, rule, degree of an arc") to the coordinative verb stem 关注 / 關注 (guānzhù, "to pay attention to, follow"). Patterned after media and statistical compounds like 知名度 ("fame/recognition index") and 热度 ("heat/popularity level"), it quantifies the intensity of public or media attention a topic or celebrity commands.

history.meaning: to pay attention + measure/degree
level of public attention, media buzz, or audience engagement

关注度.notes: A staple buzzword in television production, PR, and entertainment marketing (e.g., 提高节目关注度, "boost the show's public buzz").

关注量.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 关注 / 關注 (guānzhù, "following, subscription, attention") with 量 (liàng, originally "to measure grain with a vessel," whence "quantity, volume, numerical count"). Coined in the internet and social-media era alongside 点击量 ("click volume") and 播放量 ("playback count"), it refers to the measurable numerical count of followers or subscriptions an account or topic accumulates.

history.meaning: to pay attention + measured capacity or quantity
follower count, subscription volume, total number of follows
history.stage: Contemporary Mandarin (21st c. digital media coinage)

morphemes.meaning: to fix one's gaze or attention upon

关注量.notes: Contrast 关注度 (qualitative/relative intensity of public buzz) with 关注量 (the concrete numerical count of followers or subscriptions on a platform).

rootFamily.gloss: total playback or view count (of video/audio)

关照.etymology: A coordinative verb compound of 关 / 關 (guān, "to relate to, look after," originally alternating with 觀 "to observe, contemplate") and 照 (zhào, "to shine upon, illuminate; by extension, to look after, care for," as in 照顧). In Tang–Song Chan Buddhist texts (written 觀照 / 關照), it meant illuminating reality with mindful awareness; in Ming–Qing vernacular Mandarin and Wu dialects, it secularized into "to look out for someone, extend patronage, or give a verbal heads-up."

history.meaning: to illuminate and contemplate with mindful awareness (Buddhist)
to look after, show patronage to; to notify verbally
to look out for, take care of, extend favor to (often in workplace/social settings)

morphemes.meaning: to involve, look after, attend to
to shine upon; to look after, care for

关照.notes: Essential in polite workplace formulas such as 请多关照 ("please look out for me / I look forward to working with you," parallel to Japanese どうぞよろしく).

rootFamily.gloss: to take care of, look after, attend to
to take care of according to need, show consideration
to care about, be concerned with

关系.etymology: A coordinative compound uniting 关 / 關 (guān, "to bolt a gate, interconnect, involve") and 系 / 係 / 繫 (xì, "to tie, bind with a cord, link together"). Both morphemes express physical fastening—a wooden gate-bar and a tied rope—which metaphorically converged in Song–Yuan vernacular to mean "causal bearing, implication, or consequence" (e.g., 有关系, "it matters"). In the late 19th and 20th centuries, reinforced by Meiji Japanese 関係 (kankei), it broadened to cover abstract logical relations as well as interpersonal relationships and social networks (guanxi).

history.meaning: interconnection, causal bearing, critical consequence
relationship, connection, relevance; interpersonal network or pull (guanxi)

关系.notes: Covers everything from "it doesn't matter" (没关系) and romantic/interpersonal ties (人际关系) to the culturally central concept of backdoor social clout (拉关系 / 走关系, "pull strings").

rootFamily.gloss: to contact, get in touch; connection

关联.etymology: A coordinative compound of 关 / 關 (guān, "to bolt together, interconnect, involve") and 联 / 聯 (lián, "to join in a continuous sequence, link together"). In the Shuowen Jiezi, 聯 is analyzed as 耳 ("ear") + 絲 ("silk threads"), signifying continuous concatenation. Together, 關聯 ("interlocking and linking") denotes a structural, logical, or institutional connection between two entities, functioning as both a verb ("to be connected/affiliated") and a noun ("connection, correlation").

history.meaning: to interlock and string together; mutual connection or involvement
connection, correlation, affiliation (including corporate or data linkage)

关联.notes: More formal and analytical than 关系: 关联 refers to objective correlations, corporate affiliations (关联公司), or linked accounts/data, never to personal friendships or romantic ties.

rootFamily.gloss: to unite, join forces; alliance, union

关键.etymology: A classical coordinative noun compound of 关 / 關 (guān, "the wooden crossbar that bolts a double gate") and 键 / 鍵 (jiàn, "the metal bolt of a lock, or the metal linchpin that holds a chariot wheel on its axle"). Because removing either the wooden bar or the metal pin causes the entire gate or wheel assembly to fail, by the Southern Dynasties (attested in the Nan Shi / History of the Southern Dynasties) 關鍵 had already developed the metaphorical sense of "the decisive mechanism, crux, or key factor," later shifting to a high-frequency adjective ("crucial, pivotal").

history.meaning: wooden gate-bar and metal lock-bolt / axle linchpin
the decisive mechanism or crux of an affair or literary work
crux, key factor (noun); crucial, pivotal, key (adjective)

morphemes.meaning: metal lock-pin or axle linchpin; key (of a keyboard/instrument)

关键.notes: Notice how the exact same mechanical metaphor ("lock bolt / key") independently produced English "key (crucial)" and Chinese 关键; in modern tech, 键 also translates "button/key" on a keyboard (键盘).

关键点.etymology: A three-character modifier-head nominal compound formed from 关键 / 關鍵 (guānjiàn, "crucial, pivotal," originally "gate-bar and lock-pin") modifying 点 / 點 (diǎn, originally "a small black fleck or ink dot," from 黑 "black" + 占 phonetic, extended in modern Chinese to geometric, temporal, and analytical "points"). It designates the specific locus, juncture, or issue upon which the success of an entire plan or narrative hinges.

history.meaning: gate-bolt / crux + black dot or mark
key point, decisive crux, pivotal juncture in a project or plot

morphemes.meaning: dot, point, specific locus or juncture

关键点.notes: Common in business strategy, scriptwriting, and media production meetings (e.g., 抓住问题的关键点, "grasp the crux of the problem").

关门.etymology: A transparent verb-object compound combining 关 / 關 (guān, "to draw the crossbar, to shut") with its original etymological object 门 / 門 (mén, pictograph of a two-leaf swinging gate or door). Because 關 already incorporates the door radical 門 around a latching mechanism, 關門 literally re-expresses the ancient root phrase "to bolt a gate." Beyond physically shutting a door, it developed the idiomatic mercantile senses "to close up shop for the night" and "to go out of business permanently."

history.meaning: to bolt a city gate, frontier pass, or household door
to close the door; to close for the day; to shut down a business permanently

关门.notes: As a separable verb-object compound (离合词), aspect markers and complements go between the characters: 关了门 ("closed the door"), 关不上门 ("can't get the door shut").

rootFamily.gloss: to open the door; to open for business

兴奋.etymology: A coordinative compound of 兴 / 興 (xīng, "to rise up, rouse, lift together," depicting four hands lifting a vessel 昇/同) and 奋 / 奮 (fèn, "to spread wings and take flight from a field; to rouse oneself vigorously," combining 奞 "bird spreading wings" + 田 "field"). In Classical Chinese (e.g., Hou Hanshu and Song prose), 興奮 meant "to rouse oneself to vigorous effort or moral action." During the Meiji period, Japanese scholars adopted 興奮 (kōfun) to translate Western physiological and psychological "excitation / excitement," and this modern sense returned to Mandarin.

history.meaning: to rouse oneself to vigorous action, rise up with energy
physiological stimulation; emotional excitement or agitation
excited, thrilled, emotionally or physiologically stimulated

morphemes.meaning: to rise, rouse, flourish (read xīng in first tone here)
to spread wings; to rouse oneself, exert vigorously

兴奋.notes: Pronunciation trap for learners: 兴 is read first tone (xīng) in 兴奋 ("excited"), NOT fourth tone (xìng) as in 高兴 (gāoxìng, "happy") or 兴趣 (xìngqù, "interest").

rootFamily.gloss: to struggle, strive hard for a goal

兴许.etymology: A colloquial northern Mandarin modal adverb combining 兴 / 興 (xīng, from the vernacular modal sense "to permit, happen by chance, be possible," as seen in 不兴 "not allowed / not the custom" and 兴是 "perhaps") with 许 / 許 (xǔ, originally "to grant, allow," which grammaticalized in post-classical Chinese into an epistemic marker of approximation and possibility, as in 也许 and 或许). Lexicalized in Qing-dynasty northern vernacular (attested in Hongloumeng / Dream of the Red Chamber), it means "perhaps, maybe, by some chance."

history.meaning: to arise / allow + to grant / approximate possibility marker
perhaps, maybe, possibly (colloquial epistemic adverb)
history.stage: Qing Dynasty Northern Mandarin to Modern Mandarin

morphemes.meaning: to arise by chance, permit, be possible
to allow; modal marker of uncertainty or approximation

兴许.notes: Carries a warm, conversational, slightly northern Mandarin flavor compared to standard 也许 ("maybe") or slightly more formal 或许 ("perhaps").

rootFamily.gloss: not allowed, out of the question (colloquial)

其中.etymology: A fossilized Classical Chinese modifier-head locative phrase composed of 其 (qí, Old Chinese *gə, the third-person genitive and demonstrative pronoun "its, their, that") + 中 (zhōng, "interior, middle, midst," originally a banner pole through the center of a target or camp). Literally "in the midst of it/them," it has functioned continuously since pre-Qin prose (such as the Analects and Mencius) to pick out a subset or element from a previously mentioned group.

history.meaning: in the midst of it/them, therein (two-word syntactic phrase)
among them, in it, of which (lexicalized compound noun/pronoun)

其中.notes: Used both to narrow down a subset in statistics/narration (三个人，其中两个是导演, "three people, two of whom are directors") and in idioms like 乐在其中 ("find joy right in the midst of doing it").

其他.etymology: A determiner-pronoun compound formed from Classical Chinese 其 (qí, demonstrative/partitive pronoun "that, the") + 他 (tā, originally written 佗 or 它, meaning "other, another, different" long before it became the third-person singular pronoun "he/she" in Tang–Song vernacular). In Classical and Medieval Chinese (written 其佗 or 其他), it meant "those other things/people, the remaining ones," surviving into modern Mandarin as the standard determiner for "other, else."

history.meaning: that other, the remaining ones, things besides this
other, else (used before nouns or standalone for people and things)

morphemes.meaning: other, another, else (original sense of 他/佗)

其他.notes: In modern orthography, 其他 (with the person radical 亻) is the universal default for both people and things ("other people, other matters"), whereas 其它 (with the neuter/animal radical 它) is restricted strictly to non-human objects and is now less common.

其实.etymology: Disjunctive adverb combining 其 ('its', third-person possessive pronoun in Classical Chinese) + 实 (實, 'reality, substance, fruit/fact', cowrie wealth 貫 under a roof 宀). Literally 'its reality / in fact', used in Classical prose and grammaticalized in Mandarin as 'actually, in fact, as a matter of fact'.

history.meaning: its substance/reality; its fruit
in fact; actually

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 其实 (via 萌典)

典型.etymology: A coordinative compound of 典 (diǎn, "canon, authoritative statute, standard," paleographically depicting sacred bamboo tablets 冊 elevated on a ceremonial stand 丌) and 型 (xíng, "earthen mold used for casting bronze vessels," from 土 "earth/clay" + 刑 phonetic, whence "pattern, model, type"). In the Shijing and Han–Tang texts (often written 典刑), it meant "ancient statutes and exemplary models"; in modern Mandarin (reinforced by Japanese 典型 tenkei, used to translate Greek/European "type / archetype"), it serves as both a noun ("archetype, representative model") and an adjective ("typical, classic").

history.meaning: established statutes and laws; exemplary moral paragon or precedent
representative archetype or specimen (noun); typical, classic (adjective)

morphemes.meaning: clay casting mold; model, pattern, type

典型.notes: Frequently modifies nouns with 的 (典型的例子, "a textbook/classic example") or describes someone's personality (他就是典型的工作狂, "he is a textbook workaholic").

cognates.meaning: to nourish, rear, look after (Sino-Tibetan cognate)

养.etymology: A foundational monomorphemic verb (养 / 養, Old Chinese *[ɢ]ʷraŋʔ) whose traditional graph combines 羊 (yáng, "sheep," acting as both phonetic and pastoral semantic indicator) and 食 (shí, "food, to feed"); oracle bone forms also show a hand driving or tending a sheep. From its core meaning of herding livestock and providing nourishment to elders, it developed a rich polysemy across Chinese history: to feed and rear children or animals, to support financially, to cultivate moral character or habits, and to convalesce or restore health.

history.meaning: to herd and feed sheep; to provide food for parents and children; to nourish
to raise (children, pets, plants), support financially, cultivate (habits), recuperate (health)

morphemes.meaning: to feed, raise, nourish, cultivate, recuperate

养.notes: One of Mandarin's most versatile verbs: 养孩子 ("raise a child"), 养猫 ("keep a cat"), 养家 ("support a family"), 养神 ("rest one's mind"), and 养生 ("preserve health/wellness").

rootFamily.gloss: to maintain (a car/skin); to take care of one's health

cognates.meaning: training, cultivation, fostering (of personnel or habits)

养成.etymology: A verb-resultative compound combining 养 / 養 (yǎng, "to nourish, nurture, foster over time") with the resultative complement 成 (chéng, "to complete, accomplish, become"). Attested in classical prose (e.g., Xunzi and Han texts) for nurturing trees or talent until maturity, in modern Mandarin it specifically denotes cultivating a habit, disposition, or skill gradually until it becomes second nature.

history.meaning: to nurture living things or moral qualities until fully grown or accomplished
to cultivate, form, or develop (especially a lasting habit or trait)

养成.notes: The overwhelmingly most common collocation is 养成（好/坏）习惯 ("form a [good/bad] habit"); in pop culture and gaming, 养成系 ("cultivation/growth-type") refers to idols or characters fans watch grow from trainees to stars.

rootFamily.gloss: to foster, train, develop (people or feelings)

cognates.meaning: aquaculture, breeding, cultivation (e.g., pearls, oysters, fish)

养殖.etymology: A coordinative verb/noun compound uniting 养 / 養 (yǎng, "to feed, rear, tend") and 殖 (zhí, "to breed, multiply, propagate, increase livestock or wealth," attested in the Zuozhuan and Guoyu). Reinforced in modern agricultural and fishery terminology alongside Japanese 養殖 (yōshoku), it refers to the systematic human breeding and husbandry of aquatic organisms (fish, shrimp, pearls) or livestock and poultry.

history.meaning: to rear/feed + to propagate/multiply biologically
to breed, farm, or cultivate commercially (livestock, poultry, or aquatic species)

养殖.notes: Used exclusively for commercial or agricultural breeding (e.g., 水产养殖 "aquaculture", 养殖场 "breeding farm"), never for raising household pets or children (which use simple 养).

养活.etymology: A vernacular verb-resultative compound formed from 养 / 養 (yǎng, "to feed, provide sustenance for") and the resultative complement 活 (huó, originally "flowing water," early extended to "alive, to live"; pronounced in neutral tone huo in this compound). Literally "to feed so as to keep alive," it is attested from Yuan–Ming vernacular literature for supporting dependents (a family or oneself) financially and for keeping delicate plants or young animals alive.

history.meaning: to feed and keep alive; to provide livelihood for dependents
to support financially (oneself or a family); to keep a pet or plant alive

养活.notes: Because it is a verb-resultative compound, potential infixes go in the middle: 养得活 ("able to afford to support / keep alive") and 养不活 ("unable to support financially / keep alive").

养父母.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound in which 养 / 養 (yǎng, "rearing, adoptive," contrasting with 生 "birth/biological") modifies the classical coordinative compound 父母 (fùmǔ, "father and mother, parents," from 父 "father," originally a hand holding a ritual axe/rod of authority, + 母 "mother," a kneeling woman with prominent breasts nursing a child). Traditional Chinese family law distinguished 養父母 (adoptive parents who raise a child as their heir) from 生父母 (biological parents).

history.meaning: adoptive father and mother under clan and imperial family law
adoptive parents, foster parents

养父母.notes: Directly parallels 养父 ("adoptive father"), 养母 ("adoptive mother"), 养子 ("adopted son"), and 养女 ("adopted daughter"), contrasting with 亲生父母 ("biological parents").

养病.etymology: A verb-object compound of 养 / 養 (yǎng, "to nurse, restore, tend to one's vitality") + 病 (bìng, "illness, disease," a phono-semantic character combining the sickness radical 疒 depicting a person lying on a sickbed with 丙 phonetic). Syntactically, 养病 exemplifies Mandarin's oblique/causative VO pattern (like 救火 "fight a fire" or 治病 "treat an illness"): one does not nourish the disease itself, but rather nurses one's body on account of an illness in order to recuperate.

history.meaning: to withdraw from official duties or labor to nurse one's health during illness
to recuperate, rest up and convalesce from an illness

morphemes.meaning: to nurse, restore, care for one's health

养病.notes: Don't translate literally as "grow an illness"! Just as 救火 ("rescue-fire") means "put out a fire," 养病 ("nurse-illness") means "rest up to recover from an illness" (在家养病, "recuperating at home").

rootFamily.gloss: to recuperate, convalesce (often at a sanatorium or resort)
to rest and nurse a wound or injury
to rest and build up one's energy/strength

养胃粥.etymology: A three-character modifier-head compound consisting of the verb-object modifier 养胃 / 養胃 (yǎngwèi, "to nourish and soothe the stomach," from 养 "nourish, care for" + 胃 "stomach," whose ancient graph depicts a pouch filled with rice grains above flesh 月/肉) modifying the head noun 粥 (zhōu, "rice gruel, congee," whose graph depicts rice 米 simmering between two curls of rising steam 弓). Rooted in traditional Chinese dietary therapy (食疗), where warm, slow-cooked congee is prized for restoring digestive qi, it denotes a gentle stomach-soothing porridge.

history.meaning: to nourish the stomach (traditional medical concept) + boiled rice gruel
stomach-soothing congee or restorative rice porridge

养胃粥.notes: In Chinese drama tropes (including Behind the Scenes / 幕后之王), bringing someone 养胃粥 when they skip meals or suffer from stress-induced stomachaches (胃病) is a classic gesture of quiet care and romance.

rootFamily.gloss: stomachache, gastric ailment (common among overworked professionals)

兼.etymology: Ideographic character depicting a single hand (又) grasping two stalks of grain (秝) at once (Old Chinese *kˤem*, Middle Chinese *kem*). From 'hold two things simultaneously' it developed its classical and modern conjunctional sense 'and concurrently; combining two roles or functions'.

morphemes.meaning: hold two things at once; combine concurrently

history.meaning: grasp two grain stalks in one hand; combine
and concurrently; combined with

cognates.meaning: taking both into consideration, balancing two roles
to attend to both sides simultaneously

兼顾.etymology: An adverbial-verb compound combining 兼 (jiān, "simultaneously, holding two things at once," whose oracle bone and seal script graphs depict a single hand 又 grasping two stalks of grain 禾 together) with 顾 / 顧 (gù, "to turn the head 頁 to look back at a bird 雇; by extension, to attend to, look after, take into account"). Literally "to look after two things with one grasp," it denotes giving due consideration or care to multiple competing responsibilities at the same time.

history.meaning: to hold two stalks in one hand (simultaneously) + to look back / attend to
to attend to both or multiple things simultaneously, balance competing priorities

morphemes.meaning: simultaneously, holding two things at once
to look back, attend to, take into consideration

兼顾.notes: Frequently used when discussing work-life balance (兼顾工作和家庭, "juggle work and family") or in the four-character idiom 统筹兼顾 ("plan as a whole and give due consideration to all parties").

rootFamily.gloss: to hold a concurrent job; part-time job / side hustle
to take into consideration, care for

内.etymology: A core Sino-Tibetan spatial root (内 / 內, Old Chinese *nˤəp-s). In oracle bone and bronze inscriptions, the character is a compound ideograph showing 入 ("to enter") placed inside 冂 ("a roofed enclosure or boundary"). Originally it represented both the transitive verb "to bring inside, admit" (later written 納, OC *nˤəp) and its exoactive/locative noun derivative "the interior, inside, within" (OC *nˤəp-s), functioning in modern Mandarin as a postposition for spatial, institutional, or temporal boundaries.

history.meaning: to enter an enclosure; the interior, inner chambers, within
inside, within (a space, organization, or time period); internal

morphemes.meaning: inside, interior, within a boundary or period

内.notes: Placed after a noun or time phrase (often as ……之内 or ……以内) to mean "within": 三天内 ("within three days"), 行业内 / 圈内 ("inside the industry / showbiz circle").

rootFamily.gloss: within, inside of (spatial or temporal limit)

内容.etymology: A modifier-head compound of 内 / 內 (nèi, "inside, interior") + 容 (róng, "to contain, hold, accommodate," originally depicting a deep valley 谷 beneath a roof 宀 capable of holding vast volume). In Classical Chinese, 內容 referred literally to what could be contained inside a vessel or space (or to inner countenance). In the Meiji era, Japanese scholars repurposed 内容 (naiyō) to translate German Inhalt / English "content, substance" (in philosophical contrast to 形式 keishiki "form"), and this abstract sense was re-adopted into modern Mandarin.

history.meaning: what is held inside a space or vessel; inner capacity
substance or content of a text, speech, or concept (contrasted with form)
history.stage: Meiji Japanese semantic return loan (late 19th c.)

history.meaning: content, substance (of a book, conversation, contract, or digital media)

morphemes.meaning: to contain, hold; what is contained

内容.notes: In modern media and television production, 内容 translates both everyday "contents/details" (工作内容, "job duties") and industry "media content" (内容为王, "content is king").

rootFamily.gloss: capacity, volume (of a container or memory drive)

内幕.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 内 (nèi, 'inside, interior') and 幕 (mù, 'curtain, tent, stage'). Originally referring to the inner curtains of a stage or a general's command tent (幕府, mùfǔ), it underwent metaphorical extension from theatrical and military privacy to mean the undisclosed dealings or behind-the-scenes details of an event or organization, reinforced in modern Mandarin by shared Sino-Japanese journalistic usage (内幕, naimaku).

history.meaning: interior space and overhead tent or stage curtain
behind-the-scenes details, inside story, confidential dealings

内幕.notes: Frequently paired with verbs like 揭开 (jiēkāi, 'to uncover') or 曝光 (bàoguāng, 'to expose') in media and entertainment journalism, as well as in the compound 内幕交易 (insider trading).

rootFamily.gloss: to open a curtain; to inaugurate

内涵.etymology: A modifier-head compound formed from 内 (nèi, 'inside, within') and 涵 (hán, 'to soak, to contain, to encompass'). In Literary Chinese, 涵 denoted water submerging or a vessel holding liquid, later abstracting to intellectual or moral capacity (as in 涵养, hányǎng). In modern Mandarin, 内涵 functions both as a philosophical/logical term for 'intension/connotation' (contrasted with 外延, 'extension') and as a general noun for cultural depth, substance, or personal sophistication.

history.meaning: to hold or submerge within; internal capacity
logical intension; inner depth, substance, cultural richness

内涵.notes: In formal critique, 有内涵 praises a person or creative work for having deep substance; in contemporary internet slang, 内涵 is also used transitively as a verb meaning 'to subtly shade or insinuate against someone'.

rootFamily.gloss: to encompass, to cover, to include

内部.etymology: A modifier-head compound composed of 内 (nèi, 'inside, interior') and 部 (bù, 'section, division, part, ministry'). While both characters are ancient in Classical Chinese, their combination to denote the spatial or institutional 'interior' of a structure or organization was standardized across East Asia during the Meiji-era modernization of administrative and scientific lexicon (compare Japanese 内部, naibu), contrasting directly with 外部 (wàibù, 'external, outside').

history.meaning: inner quarters and administrative division or category
interior space; internal affairs or members of an organization

内部.notes: Often used attributively without 的 in corporate and media contexts, such as 内部消息 (insider tip), 内部矛盾 (internal conflict), or 内部认购 (internal subscription).

内鬼.etymology: A metaphorical modifier-head compound combining 内 (nèi, 'inside, internal') and 鬼 (guǐ, 'ghost, spirit, sly or treacherous person'). Drawing on the vernacular Chinese trope of 鬼 as a secretive, malevolent, or scheming agent (compare 捣鬼, dǎoguǐ, 'to play tricks'), 内鬼 emerged in modern vernacular and Hong Kong/Cantonese crime and espionage parlance before spreading throughout standard Mandarin to denote a mole, double agent, or corporate insider who leaks confidential information.

history.meaning: inside/interior and ghost or spirit of the dead
secretive insider traitor, mole, internal informant

内鬼.notes: Commonly collocated with 抓 (zhuā, 'to catch') or 揪出 (jiūchū, 'to ferrets out') in corporate thrillers and workplace dramas when hunting down who leaked a project proposal.

rootFamily.gloss: to play tricks, to sabotage secretly

再.etymology: Ancient graph showing a frame or structure duplicated/layered a second time: in Classical Chinese 'twice, a second time', and in modern Mandarin the primary adverb for 'again (in the future), once more, further, then'.

history.meaning: twice; a second time
again; once more; further; then

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 再 (via 萌典)

再战.etymology: An adverbial modifier-head verbal compound formed from 再 (zài, 'twice, a second time, again') and 战 (traditional 戰, zhàn, 'to fight, battle, war'). Attested in Classical Chinese military narratives (such as the *Zuo Zhuan* and historical chronicles) where 再 strictly meant 'a second time' before broadening in post-Classical Chinese to 'once more, again'. In contemporary Mandarin, it is widely used figuratively in sports, business, and entertainment competitions for staging a comeback or competing again.

history.meaning: to engage in battle a second time
to battle once again, to return to competition, to stage a rematch

morphemes.meaning: again, a second time, once more
to fight, to battle, to compete

再战.notes: Carries an energetic, heroic register; frequently appears in headlines and showbiz slogans like 再战江湖 ('to return to the arena/industry for another battle').

rootFamily.gloss: to make persistent efforts, to redouble efforts after a win/setback

再次.etymology: An adverbial compound combining 再 (zài, 'a second time, again') and 次 (cì, originally 'to halt in sequence, camping order', grammaticalized into the measure word for 'time, occurrence, sequence'). Modelled on earlier Literary Chinese expressions such as 再三 ('twice and three times, repeatedly') and 屡次 ('repeatedly'), 再次 solidified in modern Mandarin as the standard slightly formal adverb meaning 'once more' or 'for a second/subsequent time'.

history.meaning: twice/second time and sequential order or halting place
once again, a second time, once more

再次.notes: Unlike單-character 再 (which typically refers to future/unrealized repetition) or 又 (which typically refers to realized/past repetition), 再次 can modify both past and future verbs in formal and neutral registers.

再没.etymology: Emphatic negative phrase combining 再 ('again, ever again, any more') + 没 ('not have, did not'): 'never again, no longer, there is no… anymore'.

history.meaning: never again; no longer

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 再没 (via 萌典)

再现.etymology: An adverbial-head verbal compound of 再 (zài, 'again, once more') and 现 (traditional 現, xiàn, 'to appear, to manifest, to become visible', originally a graphic differentiation of 見 jiàn/xiàn 'to see / to appear'). While the literal sense 'to appear again' is transparent in Literary Chinese, its transitive aesthetic and media sense—'to recreate, to reproduce on screen or stage, to represent artistically'—was reinforced by Meiji-period Japanese 再現 (saigen), translating Western aesthetic terms like German *Darstellung* or English *reproduction*.

history.meaning: to appear or manifest a second time
to reappear; to recreate, reproduce, or bring back to life on stage/screen

morphemes.meaning: to appear, to manifest, to present

再现.notes: Used both intransitively (辉煌再现, 'glory reappears') and transitively in media production (再现经典场景, 'to recreate a classic scene').

rootFamily.gloss: to present, to display, to unfold

再见.etymology: Standard Mandarin farewell ('goodbye', literally 'again see / meet again'), pairing 再 ('once more, again') with 见 ('see, meet'). Mirrors friendly 'see you again' expressions worldwide without restricting the time of day.

history.meaning: modern greeting 'see you again; goodbye'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 再見 (via 萌典)

再说.etymology: Originally a transparent adverbial-head verbal phrase combining 再 (zài, 'again, later, further') and 说 (traditional 説/說, shuō, 'to speak, to discuss'), literally meaning 'to speak of it again (later)'—hence its verbal usage 'to put off discussion until later'. Through discourse grammaticalization in Early Mandarin and vernacular fiction (such as *Dream of the Red Chamber*), the phrase 'let us speak further' evolved into a sentence-initial or clause-linking conjunctive marker meaning 'besides, what is more, furthermore'.

history.meaning: to say again; to discuss at a later time
to talk about it later (verb); besides, moreover (conjunction)

morphemes.meaning: to speak, to say, to discuss

再说.notes: Pay attention to position and stress: at the end of a clause (以后再说吧), it is a verb phrase meaning 'let's talk about it later'; at the start of a clause (再说，现在也没时间), it is a conjunction meaning 'besides / what's more'.

冒失.etymology: A coordinative verbal-adjective compound combining 冒 (mào, originally 'to cover and press forward blindly', hence 'rashly, boldly, without heed') and 失 (shī, 'to lose, to err, to slip up, to miss the mark'). Attested in Ming and Qing vernacular literature (such as *Water Margin* and *Journey to the West*), the pairing of 'charging ahead blindly' (冒) and 'committing a slip/faux pas' (失) lexicalized with a neutral-tone second syllable (màoshi) to describe brash, tactless, or careless behavior.

history.meaning: to push ahead blindly and to lose control or commit an error
rash, tactless, abrupt, careless in speech or action

morphemes.meaning: to err, to slip, to lose propriety

冒失.notes: The second syllable is pronounced in the neutral tone (màoshi) in standard Mandarin; a reckless blunderer is colloquially called a 冒失鬼 (màoshiguǐ).

rootFamily.gloss: a slip, mistake, fault in duty

cognates.meaning: to violate, to desecrate, to offend
to offend, to affront, to violate

冒犯.etymology: A coordinative transitive verbal compound joining 冒 (mào, 'to push against, to brave, to encroach upon rashly') and 犯 (fàn, 'totransgress, to invade, to violate a boundary or superior'). Already combined in Han- and Tang-dynasty historical prose (such as the *Book of Han*), 冒犯 originally denoted physically braving hazards or encroaching upon imperial authority, later softening in social interaction to mean offending someone's dignity or overstepping social boundaries.

history.meaning: to encroach upon authority, to transgress or brave directly
to offend, to affront, to disrespect someone's feelings or dignity

morphemes.meaning: to encroach rashly, to infringe upon
to violate, to transgress, to offend

冒犯.notes: Frequently used in polite apologies such as 多有冒犯 ('I have offended you in many ways / pardon my presumption') when disagreeing with a senior colleague or client.

rootFamily.gloss: to take the liberty of, presumptuous
to infringe upon, to violate rights

冒险.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound composed of 冒 (mào, 'to brave, to face directly without flinching, to expose oneself to') and 险 (traditional 險, xiǎn, 'steep defile, precipice, danger, hazard'). Attested in Classical and Medieval Chinese military texts (e.g., 冒险进取, 'to brave rugged terrain and advance'), it functions in modern Mandarin both as a separable verb-object phrase ('to take a risk') and, reinforced by Sino-Japanese 冒険 (bōken), as a noun/adjective meaning 'adventure' or 'adventurous'.

history.meaning: to brave dangerous terrain or military peril
to take a risk, to venture; adventure; risky

morphemes.meaning: to brave, to face directly, to risk

冒险.notes: Because it has a verb-object internal structure, modifiers can be inserted between the two characters in speech: 冒了一个很大的险 ('took a huge risk').
