冒雨.etymology: Verb-object compound of 冒 ('push forward braving cover/obstacle', originally a cap/hood covering the eyes 目) + 雨 ('rain'): 'brave the rain, go out in spite of the rain'. Attested in Han–Tang historical prose and poetry.

history.meaning: go forward braving the rain

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 冒雨 (via 萌典)

写.etymology: Originally 寫 (roof 宀 + 舄 xì), meaning in Classical Chinese 'transfer items from one vessel/house to another, pour out, unburden (one's heart), copy a text or portrait'. From the Six Dynasties and Tang period onward, 寫 replaced 書 as the everyday verb for 'write, compose'.

history.meaning: transfer; pour out; copy out
write; compose

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 写 (via 萌典)

写到.etymology: A verb-complement (resultative/directional) construction formed from 写 (traditional 寫, xiě, originally 'to transfer, to pour out, to sketch', replacing 書 shū in vernacular Chinese as 'to write') and the resultative/prepositional complement 到 (dào, 'to arrive at, to reach, onto'). In Mandarin grammar, 到 attached to 写 marks either the spatial destination onto which text is written (写到黑板上, 'write onto the blackboard') or the topical/temporal point reached in a text or speech (写到这里, 'write up to this point / write about this').

history.meaning: to sketch/copy out and to arrive at a destination
to write onto (a surface); to reach a certain point or topic in writing

写到.notes: Carefully distinguish 写到 ('write onto [a place]' or 'write up to/about [a topic]') from its homophone 写道 (xiědào, 'wrote as follows: ...', used before a direct quotation).

rootFamily.gloss: to write as follows (introducing a quote)

写字板.etymology: Modern three-morpheme compound from 写 (simplified from 寫, 'write') + 字 ('character; script') + 板 ('board; plank; backing plate', wood 木 + phonetic 反). Coined in the twentieth century for a portable rigid board with a spring clip at the top used for writing while standing or walking.

history.meaning: clipboard; writing board

写完.etymology: Resultative verb compound of 写 ('write') + 完 ('finish, complete'): 'finish writing'.

history.meaning: finish writing

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 写完 (via 萌典)

军令.etymology: A modifier-head compound joining 军 (traditional 軍, jūn, 'army, military force, troops', originally depicting a war chariot surrounded by an encampment) and 令 (lìng, 'command, decree, order'). Attested in Classical Chinese military treatises such as *The Art of War* (孙子兵法) and the *Records of the Grand Historian* (史记), 军令 denoted binding martial decrees punishable by death if disobeyed; in modern workplace and media production culture, it is frequently used hyperbolically for an ironclad executive directive.

history.meaning: binding martial command issued by a general
military order; strict, non-negotiable directive in a team or company

军令.notes: In Chinese corporate and TV production culture, 立军令状 (lì jūnlìngzhuàng, 'to sign a martial pledge') means staking one's position or bonus on hitting a strict deadline or ratings target.

rootFamily.gloss: written pledge to fulfill a mission or face punishment

军规.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 军 (traditional 軍, jūn, 'army, military') and 规 (traditional 規, guī, originally 'carpenter's compass for drawing circles', extended in Classical Chinese to 'standard, rule, regulation'). Historically referring to standing codes of military conduct (contrasted with 军令, specific tactical orders), 军规 is frequently used metaphorically in modern Chinese corporate and production teams (e.g., 部门军规) for strict, non-negotiable team ground rules.

history.meaning: military forces and carpenter's compass or standard code
military regulations; strict team or corporate ground rules

军规.notes: Also famous in Chinese translation as the title of Joseph Heller's novel *Catch-22* (第二十二条军规, Dì-èrshí'èr tiáo jūnguī), which became a standard Mandarin idiom for a no-win paradoxical rule.

cognates.meaning: naming, crowning with a title sponsor name

冠名.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound composed of 冠 (guàn, verbal reading of guān 'hat, cap, crown', meaning 'to cap, to place at the head, to prefix') and 名 (míng, 'name, title'). In Literary Chinese, 冠 (guàn) referred to the coming-of-age capping ceremony and by extension placing a title or surname at the top. In contemporary Chinese media and broadcasting, 冠名 specializes to mean placing a sponsor's brand name at the very front of a television show, concert, or stadium title (title sponsorship).

history.meaning: to place a cap/crown at the head and a name or title
to prefix a name; to title-sponsor a program, event, or venue

morphemes.meaning: to cap, to crown, to place at the head

冠名.notes: Pronounced in the fourth tone guànmíng (not first tone guānmíng) because 冠 functions verbally ('to crown/cap with a name'), just as in 冠军 (guànjūn, 'champion').

冠名商.etymology: A three-character modifier-head compound built by attaching the agentive/commercial head noun 商 (shāng, originally the Shang dynasty, extended to 'itinerant merchant, trader, commercial firm') to the verb-object compound 冠名 (guànmíng, 'to crown with a name, to title-sponsor'). Coined in modern Chinese television and live-entertainment commerce, it designates the corporate brand that purchases naming rights (冠名权) to have its name announced before the program's title.

history.meaning: to prefix a title and merchant/commercial dealer
title sponsor, naming-rights corporate sponsor of a show or event

morphemes.meaning: to crown with a name, title-sponsor

冠名商.notes: In Chinese variety shows (*综艺节目*) and TV dramas, the 冠名商 is the highest-tier advertiser (often affectionately called 金主爸爸, 'sugar-daddy sponsor'), superior to regular 赞助商 (co-sponsors).

冬天.etymology: Compound noun of 冬 ('winter', the fourth and final season, originally knotted ends of a cord 夂 with ice 冫 below) + 天 ('sky, season, time of year'): 'winter'.

history.meaning: the winter season; winter

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 冬天 (via 萌典)

冰.etymology: Noun and verb meaning 'ice; freeze; chill on ice'. In Old Chinese, 'ice' was written 仌 (two chevron-like ice crystals, now the two-dot ice radical 冫), while 冰 (冫 + 水) was a variant of 凝 ('congeal, freeze') before becoming the standard character for 'ice'.

history.meaning: frozen water; ice; congeal
ice; ice-cold; chill

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 冰 (via 萌典)

冰凉.etymology: Modifier-head adjective compound of 冰 ('ice') + 凉 ('cool, cold'): 'ice-cold,freezing cold to the touch'.

history.meaning: cold as ice; ice-cold

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 冰凉 (via 萌典)

冰块.etymology: Nominal compound from 冰 ('ice', originally 仌, two chevron cracks in frozen water) + 块 (simplified from 塊, earth 土 + 鬼 'lump; chunk; block'). Historically referring to blocks of winter river ice cut and stored in underground ice cellars (冰窖), it now commonly denotes ice cubes used to chill beverages.

history.meaning: chunk or block of ice
ice cube; block of ice

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 冰块

冰箱.etymology: Compound noun of 冰 ('ice') + 箱 ('chest, box, cabinet', bamboo 竹 + 相). Originally named insulated wooden chests cooled with blocks of natural ice in Ming–Qing households (succeeding ancient bronze/wooden 冰鉴), and was retained in the 20th century for the electric 'refrigerator, fridge'.

history.meaning: insulated ice chest
electric refrigerator

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 冰箱 (via 萌典)

冰美式.etymology: A modern clipped modifier-head compound shortened from 冰美式咖啡 (bīng měishì kāfēi, 'iced American-style coffee'). It combines 冰 (bīng, 'ice, iced'), 美 (měi, short for 美国 Měiguó, 'United States of America', an phonetic-semantic abbreviation of 亚美利加), and 式 (shì, 'style, pattern, formula'), with the head noun 咖啡 (kāfēi, 'coffee') elided through everyday urban café ellipsis. It has become a cultural trope in contemporary Chinese workplace and entertainment dramas as the staple drink of sleep-deprived producers and actors.

history.meaning: iced American-style coffee (full phrase)
iced Americano (clipped noun)

morphemes.meaning: style, type, mode (with 咖啡 elided)

冰美式.notes: In Chinese showbiz and office culture, ordering a 冰美式 is associated with staying awake during grueling shoots (续命水, 'life-extending water') and reducing morning facial puffiness (消水肿) before going on camera.

冲.etymology: Merged simplified graph representing two historical characters: (1) 沖 (water 氵 + 中 zhōng, 'surge, pour boiling water over, rinse, infuse tea, rush toward', read chōng) and (2) 衝 (行 + 重, 'thoroughfare, charge ahead, dash; toward/facing [read chòng]').

history.meaning: rinse/infuse vs. rush/face toward
rinse; infuse; rush/dash (chōng); facing/forceful (chòng)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 冲 (via 萌典)

决定.etymology: Originally a resultative/coordinative verbal compound combining 决 (traditional 決, jué, 'to breach a dike, to cut through, to resolve decisively') and 定 (dìng, 'to settle, to fix firmly, to establish'). Attested in Classical and Medieval Chinese texts (such as the *Records of the Grand Historian* and Buddhist translations where it rendered Sanskrit *niścaya*, 'fixed certainty'), 决定 meant 'to settle conclusively' or 'certainly', and in modern Mandarin serves as both the core transitive verb 'to decide' and the noun 'decision'.

history.meaning: to breach a channel and fix a course; to settle conclusively; certainly
to decide, to determine; a decision or resolution

morphemes.meaning: to cut through, to resolve, to decide
to settle, to fix firmly, to establish

决定.notes: Functions effortlessly as both a verb (决定留下来, 'decide to stay') and a noun (做了一个决定, 'made a decision'), as well as in the attributive compound 决定性 ('decisive').

rootFamily.gloss: resolution, formal decision; to pass a resolution
to make up one's mind; determination
to make a strategic decision; policy decision

cognates.meaning: final match, finals (short for 決勝戦)

决赛.etymology: A modifier-head compound formed from 决 (traditional 決, jué, 'to decide, to determine victory or defeat', as in 决胜 juéshèng) and 赛 (traditional 賽, sài, originally 'to make a thank-offering to the gods in rivalry', hence 'to compete, contest, match'). Coined in modern Chinese sports and competition terminology, 决赛 designates the final decisive round of a tournament or talent competition that determines the champion.

history.meaning: to resolve decisively and ritual thank-offering or festival rivalry
final match, finals of a competition or tournament

决赛.notes: Forms a standard progression in Chinese singing shows and sports tournaments: 海选 (mass auditions) -> 初赛 (preliminaries) -> 复赛 (quarter/semi-qualifiers) -> 半决赛 (semifinals) -> 总决赛 (grand finals).

cognates.meaning: moreover, how much more so (literary reading: いわんや)

况且.etymology: A coordinative compound conjunction formed from two Classical Chinese particles: 况 (traditional 況/况, kuàng, originally 'cold water', borrowed for 'state/condition' and grammaticalized in Classical Chinese as 'how much more so, moreover') and 且 (qiě, 'moreover, furthermore, even'). Already combined in post-Classical and Tang-Song Literary Chinese, 况且 fused their additive and rhetorical senses into a single conjunction introducing an additional, corroborating reason ('besides, moreover, in addition').

history.meaning: how much more so (rhetorical particle) and furthermore/moreover
moreover, besides, furthermore (adding a supporting reason)

况且.notes: Slightly more formal and argumentative than 再说; compare 何况 (hékuàng, 'let alone / much less'), which shares 况 but carries a stronger rhetorical tone.

rootFamily.gloss: let alone, much less, how much more so

冷.etymology: Phono-semantic character of ice (冫) + 令 (lìng), attested since Han texts and Шуоwen Jiezi: 'cold, chilly' (and figuratively 'unpopular, deserted, cold in manner').

history.stage: Han Classical Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: cold; chilly; frosty

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 冷 (via 萌典)

冷水.etymology: Modifier-head noun compound of 冷 ('cold') + 水 ('water'): 'cold water, unboiled/unchilled or tap water' (also in 泼冷水 'pour cold water on enthusiasm').

history.meaning: cold water

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 冷水 (via 萌典)

冷清.etymology: A coordinative adjectival compound pairing 冷 (lěng, 'cold, chilly, frosty', containing the ice radical 冫) and 清 (qīng, 'clear, pure, quiet, austere', containing the water radical 氵). Attested in Tang- and Song-dynasty poetry (often in the inverted form 清冷 qīnglěng, 'chilly and clear') before stabilizing as 冷清 in Yuan drama and Ming vernacular fiction, it shifted from physical coolness and clarity to the social and emotional atmosphere of a place that is deserted, lonely, and lacking bustle (as opposed to 热闹, rènao).

history.meaning: chilly, clear, and austerely quiet (of weather or courtyard)
deserted, cheerless, quiet and lacking visitors or excitement

冷清.notes: Often pronounced with a neutral second syllable (lěngqing) in northern Mandarin and reduplicated as 冷冷清清; its direct antonym in Chinese cultural life is 热闹 (rènao, 'lively, bustling').

冷雨.etymology: Modifier-head noun phrase of 冷 ('cold, chilly') + 雨 ('rain'): 'cold rain, chilly rain'.

history.meaning: cold rain

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 冷雨 (via 萌典)

冷静.etymology: A coordinative compound combining 冷 (lěng, 'cold, cool') and 静 (traditional 靜, jìng, 'still, quiet, tranquil'). In Tang- and Song-dynasty poetry, 冷静 described a physically chilly and silent environment (nearly synonymous with 冷清). During the late 19th and early 20th centuries, strongly reinforced by Japanese 冷静 (reisei), its primary meaning shifted to psychological composure—being cool-headed, rational, and unswayed by panic or anger.

history.meaning: chilly and silent (of a night, hall, or landscape)
calm, cool-headed, composed (adjective); to calm down (verb)

冷静.notes: Functions both as an adjective (保持冷静, 'stay calm') and as an intransitive/causative verb (先冷静一下, 'calm down for a moment first'). Beware the Korean cognate 냉정 (naengjeong), which often means 'cold-hearted/callous' (= Chinese 冷酷).

rootFamily.gloss: calm, tranquil, peaceful; to calm down

cognates.meaning: freezing; freezing of assets or projects
to freeze, to congeal; to freeze assets

冻结.etymology: A coordinative/resultative verbal compound joining 冻 (traditional 凍, dòng, 'to freeze, ice', with the ice radical 冫) and 结 (traditional 結, jié, 'to tie a knot, to congeal, to solidify, to form'). Attested in Classical Chinese meteorological and medical texts (such as the *Liji* and *Huainanzi*) for water freezing solid into ice, in the 20th century it acquired the financial, legal, and institutional metaphor of 'freezing' funds, personnel hiring, or media projects (calquing English *freeze* via shared Sino-Japanese 凍結, tōketsu).

history.meaning: to freeze solid, to congeal into ice (of water or soil)
to freeze physically; to freeze bank accounts, budgets, or projects

morphemes.meaning: to congeal, to solidify, to bind fast

冻结.notes: Very common in business and television production contexts: 冻结资金 ('freeze funds'), 冻结账号 ('freeze an account'), or 冻结项目 ('put a project on ice').

rootFamily.gloss: to freeze, to ice over (of rivers or surfaces)
to unfreeze, to thaw; to lift a freeze on assets
to solidify, to congeal, to freeze in place

凄凉.etymology: A coordinative adjectival compound combining 凄 (traditional 淒/悽, qī, 'piercingly cold' with the ice/water radical, and 'sorrowful, grieved' with the heart radical 悽, merged in simplified script as 凄) and 凉 (traditional 涼, liáng, 'cool, chilly, bleak, thin'). Celebrated in Tang poetry (such as Bai Juyi and Li Shangyin), 凄凉 fuses physical autumn/winter chill with emotional grief and abandonment, describing a desolate, bleak, and mournful condition.

history.meaning: piercingly cold and mournfully desolate (of autumn wind or exile)
desolate, bleak, dreary, lonely and miserable

凄凉.notes: Stronger and more tragic in tone than 冷清: while 冷清 means a place lacks visitors or liveliness, 凄凉 implies bleakness, decline, or pathetic solitude (e.g., 晚景凄凉, 'desolate in one's declining years').

rootFamily.gloss: dreary and desolate, bleak (often of scenery or mood)
sorrowful and desolate, tragic and bleak
cold, dreary, and miserable (of wind, rain, or cries)

准.etymology: Simplified graph merging two Classical characters: (1) 準 (water 氵 + 隼 'falcon' + 十, originally a carpenter's water-level device used to check horizontal flatness, hence 'standard, accurate, exact, definitely', read zhǔn) and (2) 准 (ice 冫 + 隹, an administrative abbreviation of 準 used in official documents for 'approve, grant, allow').

history.form: 準 (water level, standard, accurate) / 准 (official approval)
history.meaning: accurate standard; permit
accurate; on target; allow/permit; definitely

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 准 (via 萌典)

准信.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound formed from 准 (traditional 準, zhǔn, originally 'water-level instrument', extended to 'standard, accurate, definite, certain') and 信 (xìn, originally 'trustworthy speech', extended in Classical and Medieval Chinese to 'messenger, letter, news, word'). Coined in northern colloquial Mandarin, 准信 literally means 'accurate/definite word'—a firm answer, reliable confirmation, or definite promise that one can count on.

history.meaning: water-level accuracy/certainty and letter, message, or tidings
definite word, firm answer, reliable confirmation (often with 儿: 准信儿)

准信.notes: In northern spoken Mandarin, it almost always takes erhua as 准信儿 (zhǔnxìnr), typically in the collocation 给个准信儿 ('give me a definite answer/confirmation').

准备.etymology: Coordinative verb and noun compound of 准 (準, 'reckon in advance, set as standard') + 备 (備, 'prepare, make ready, equip'): 'prepare, get ready, plan/intend to'. Attested from Song–Yuan administrative and vernacular texts.

history.meaning: make ready in advance; prepare; intend to

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 准备 (via 萌典)

准夫君.etymology: A prefixed modifier-head compound combining the prefixoid 准 (traditional 準, zhǔn, 'quasi-, para-, prospective, -to-be', an extension of 'approaching the standard', reinforced by Japanese 準 jun- calquing Latin *quasi-* / *sub-*) with the Classical Chinese honorific compound 夫君 (fūjūn, from 夫 fū 'adult man, husband' + 君 jūn 'lord, noble gentleman'). Playfully blending a modern prefixoid with an archaic literary term for 'husband', 准夫君 means 'husband-to-be' or 'fiancé'.

history.meaning: noble lord; respectful Literary Chinese term of address by a wife for her husband
husband-to-be, prospective husband (playful or literary register for fiancé)

准夫君.notes: Whereas 未婚夫 (wèihūnfū) is the neutral standard word for 'fiancé', 准夫君 (or colloquial 准老公) is used playfully by friends, media hosts, or romance characters to tease an engaged woman.

准时.etymology: Compound adjective and adverb of 准 (準, 'exact, accurate') + 时 (時, 'time'): 'on time, punctual'.

history.meaning: exact to the time = punctual, on time

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 准时 (via 萌典)

凉.etymology: Phono-semantic character of water/ice (氵/冫) + 京 (jīng/liáng): 'cool, pleasantly chilly; let something hot cool down; disappointed (心凉)'.

history.meaning: cool; chilly; thin
cool; cold; cool off

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 凉 (via 萌典)

凉水.etymology: Compound noun of 凉 ('cool, cold') + 水 ('water'): 'cool water, cold (often unboiled) water'.

history.meaning: cool or cold water

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 凉水 (via 萌典)

减肥餐.etymology: A three-character modifier-head compound composed of the verb-object compound 减肥 (jiǎnféi, 'to reduce fat, to lose weight', from 减 jiǎn 'to subtract, diminish' + 肥 féi 'fat, plump') modifying the head noun 餐 (cān, 'meal, food'). Coined in late 20th-century health, fitness, and entertainment culture, 减肥餐 denotes a calorie-restricted, low-fat meal designed specifically for weight loss.

history.meaning: to diminish/reduce, rich/fat meat, and meal or to eat
weight-loss meal, diet meal, low-calorie meal

morphemes.meaning: to reduce fat, to lose weight

减肥餐.notes: In Chinese celebrity and fitness culture, 减肥餐 is closely associated with boiled chicken breast and broccoli (水煮鸡胸肉配西兰花) and is sometimes euphemized as 轻食 (qīngshí, 'light food') or 减脂餐 ('fat-loss meal').

rootFamily.gloss: to lose weight, to slim down
to diet, to restrict food intake

减薪.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound formed from 减 (traditional 減, jiǎn, 'to lessen, to subtract, to reduce') and 薪 (xīn, originally 'firewood, kindling', extended in Classical administrative usage via 薪水 xīnshuǐ 'firewood and water allowance' to mean 'official stipend, salary, wages'). In modern Mandarin corporate vocabulary, 减薪 means to cut salaries or take a pay cut.

history.meaning: to reduce/diminish and firewood allowance or official stipend
to cut salary, to take a pay cut

morphemes.meaning: to reduce, to cut, to subtract

减薪.notes: Its direct antonym is 加薪 (jiāxīn, 'to raise salary / get a pay raise'); often paired with 裁员 (cáiyuán, 'layoffs') in corporate restructuring news (裁员减薪).

凑钱.etymology: A separable verb-object (VO) compound combining 凑 (traditional 湊, còu, originally 'of streams converging on a hub', extended in vernacular Chinese to 'to gather together from various sources, to pool, to scrape together') and 钱 (traditional 錢, qián, originally 'agricultural spade tool', then 'bronze coin', and finally 'money' in general). Common since Early Mandarin vernacular fiction, 凑钱 describes multiple people chipping in funds or an individual scraping money together from multiple sources to meet an urgent expense.

history.meaning: to converge like streams / gather together and bronze coins or money
to pool money together, to scrape together funds

morphemes.meaning: to gather together, to pool, to scrape together

凑钱.notes: As a separable verb-object phrase (离合词), aspect markers and complements go between the characters: 凑够了钱 ('scraped together enough money') or 大家凑点儿钱 ('everyone chip in some money').

rootFamily.gloss: to pool together, to piece together, to assemble
to make up the numbers, to join in the fun

凝乳.etymology: Compound noun from 凝 ('congeal; curdle; freeze', ice 冫 + phonetic 疑) + 乳 ('milk; breast', depicting a mother cradling a child 子 under a claw/hand 爫). Already used in medieval Chinese medical and culinary treatises for soured or rennet-set milk curds, it was also adopted in modern culinary Mandarin to translate Western fruit curds such as lemon curd (柠檬凝乳).

history.meaning: coagulated milk curds
curd; fruit curd (e.g., lemon curd)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 凝乳

cognates.meaning: to solidify, to coagulate, to congeal

凝固.etymology: A coordinative/resultative verbal compound joining 凝 (níng, 'to congeal, to freeze, to coalesce', containing the ice radical 冫) and 固 (gù, 'firm, solid, hard, fixed'). Attested in Classical Chinese philosophical and poetic texts (such as the *Yijing* commentaries and Han prose) for liquids congealing into a solid state, in modern usage it serves both as a scientific term for 'solidification/coagulation' and as a vivid literary metaphor for an atmosphere, smile, or expression freezing in place.

history.meaning: to congeal and become firm or solid (of ice, earth, or vital qi)
to solidify or coagulate (physics/chemistry); to freeze in place (of expressions, time, or atmosphere)

morphemes.meaning: to congeal, to condense, to freeze

凝固.notes: Frequently used in narrative prose and screenplays to describe sudden awkwardness or shock: 空气仿佛凝固了 ('the air seemed to freeze solid') or 笑容凝固在脸上 ('the smile froze on their face').

rootFamily.gloss: to condense, to coalesce; cohesion (凝聚力)
to gaze fixedly, to stare intently

凝聚力.etymology: A three-character modifier-head compound built from the coordinative disyllabic verb 凝聚 (níngjù, 'to condense, to coalesce') plus the nominal head 力 (lì, 'force, power'). 凝 (níng, Old Chinese *ŋrəŋ) originally denoted water freezing into ice (written with the ice radical 冫) and by extension any congealing or concentration, while 聚 (jù) meant 'to gather together in a crowd'. Originally coined as a modern scientific calque for physical 'cohesive force' (intermolecular attraction), it expanded metaphorically in twentieth-century sociological and organizational Mandarin to denote group solidarity and team cohesion.

history.meaning: to freeze/congeal and to gather together (separate verbs)
to condense, coalesce, or concentrate into one mass
physical cohesive force; figuratively, team solidarity and social cohesion

凝聚力.notes: In media production and corporate contexts, 凝聚力 frequently collocates with 团队 (tuánduì, 'team') and 增强 (zēngqiáng, 'to strengthen') to describe how a producer or director keeps a crew united under pressure.

rootFamily.gloss: to gaze fixedly, fix one's eyes on

几.etymology: Simplified character merging two ancient graphs: (1) 幾 (two skeins of silk 丝 guarded by a halberd 戍, 'subtle, nearly, how many?, a few', read jǐ), the source of the interrogative/indefinite numeral 'how many?; several, a few'; and (2) 几 (jī, pictograph of a low small table).

morphemes.meaning: how many; a few (jǐ); small table (jī)

history.meaning: subtle sign; nearly; how many?
how many?; several, a few

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 几 (via 萌典)

几个.etymology: A quantifier-classifier compound formed from 几 (jǐ, Traditional 幾, 'how many; a few') and the general classifier 个 (gè, Traditional 個/箇, originally denoting a single bamboo stalk before grammaticalizing into a universal individual classifier). In Classical Chinese, 幾 meant 'subtle sign, nearness' and functioned interrogatively as 'how many?'; by Late Imperial vernacular Mandarin, combining 幾 with 個 yielded both the interrogative 'how many?' (for small expected numbers) and the indefinite 'several, a few'.

history.meaning: subtle omen; nearly; how many?
how many (items/people)?; a few, several
several, a few; how many (with rising question intonation)

morphemes.meaning: how many; a few, several (small number)
general classifier for individuals or units

几个.notes: With neutral tone on 个 (jǐge) in a declarative sentence it means 'several' (usually 2 to 9); in an interrogative clause it asks 'how many?' when the speaker expects a single-digit answer.

cognates.meaning: a few days, how many days

几天.etymology: A quantifier-head temporal compound combining the indeterminate numeral 几 (jǐ, Traditional 幾, 'how many; a few') directly with the temporal noun/measure word 天 (tiān, 'sky, heaven; day'). Notice that like other core temporal units in Chinese (天, 年, 周), 天 functions as its own measure word and does not take an intervening classifier like 个. As 天 displaced Classical 日 (rì) in vernacular northern Chinese for counting days, 几天 became the standard spoken form for 'a few days' or 'how many days?'.

history.meaning: how many days?; a few days
a few days; how many days?

几天.notes: Often paired with demonstrative modifiers such as 这几天 (zhè jǐ tiān, 'these past few days / the next few days') or 过几天 (guò jǐ tiān, 'in a few days').

几年.etymology: A quantifier-head temporal compound composed of 几 (jǐ, Traditional 幾, 'how many; a few') and 年 (nián, Old Chinese *C.nˤi[ŋ], originally the harvest of grain crops, which came to denote the agricultural cycle of a year). Because 年 is an autonomous temporal measure noun, 几 modifies it directly without a classifier. The phrase has been attested since Classical and Medieval Chinese poetry (where 幾年 asked 'how many years?' or lamented the fleeting passage of several years) and remains unchanged in Modern Mandarin.

history.meaning: how many years?; several years
a few years, several years; how many years?

几年.notes: Like 几天, 年 never takes 个 (*几个年 is ungrammatical); common conversational frames include 这几年 ('in recent years') and 好几年 ('quite a few years').

几点钟.etymology: A three-character interrogative temporal compound combining 几 (jǐ, 'what number, how many'), 点 (diǎn, Traditional 點, originally 'black speck, dot, drop of water in a clepsydra, or strike on a night-watch gong/bell'), and 钟 (zhōng, Traditional 鐘, 'bell, clock'). In imperial China, night watches were marked by striking a bronze bell or drum (打更點鐘); when Western mechanical chiming clocks were introduced in the late Ming and Qing dynasties, 点钟 came to mean 'stroke of the clock, o'clock' (and also 'hour' after numerals).

history.meaning: to strike a bell to mark the time; hour on a mechanical clock
what time (o'clock) is it?

morphemes.meaning: dot, stroke on a timekeeping bell, o'clock

几点钟.notes: Adding 钟 to 几点 makes the question slightly more specific or emphatic in spoken Mandarin; note the contrast between 三点钟 ('three o'clock') and 三个钟头 ('three hours').

rootFamily.gloss: on the dot, on time; o'clock

凡.etymology: A single-character morpheme 凡 (fán, Old Chinese *[b]rom), originally an oracle-bone pictograph of a flat wooden tray, pan, or mold frame. From the concrete notion of a standard mold or frame that encompasses everything cast within it, 凡 developed two closely linked extensions in Classical Chinese: (1) a distributive adverb/pronoun meaning 'all, in general, whatsoever', and (2) an adjective meaning 'ordinary, commonplace, earthly/mortal' (in contrast to sacred or transcendent). As a personal given name (as in the drama's protagonist 淳于乔 or characters named 凡), it evokes unpretentious groundedness or the aspiration to transcend the ordinary (不凡, 超凡).

history.meaning: wooden tray/frame (oracle bone); in general, all, every; ordinary, commonplace
the mortal world, secular realm (Buddhist and Daoist usage)
ordinary, mundane; all/every (in 凡是); popular given-name character

morphemes.meaning: ordinary, mortal; all, every; Fan (given name)

凡.notes: In Chinese naming culture, 凡 is prized for its philosophical modesty ('staying grounded in the ordinary') while echoing compounds like 非凡 (fēifán, 'extraordinary') and 超凡 (chāofán, 'transcendent').

cognates.meaning: to rely on, possess (as a spirit)
to lean on, rely on (as in 빙자)

凭.etymology: Represented in Simplified Chinese by 凭 (píng), which merges Classical 凭 ('to lean against a low table 几', composed of 任 phonetic and 几 'small table' semantic) and 憑 ('to lean upon, rely on, take as evidence', composed of 馮 phonetic and 心 semantic). In Classical Chinese, 憑/凭 meant physically leaning one's body on a railing or armrest; through regular grammaticalization across Medieval and Early Mandarin, the verb 'to lean on, rely on' evolved into a preposition meaning 'on the basis of, relying on, judging by'.

history.meaning: to lean physically upon a table or railing; to rely upon for support
to rely on; documentary proof or credential (as in 文憑, 憑據)
on the basis of, relying on, judging by, no matter (prep.)

morphemes.meaning: to lean on, rely on; on the basis of, by virtue of

凭.notes: Very frequent in rhetorical challenges such as 凭什么？ (píng shénme?, 'on what grounds? / why should you have the right to...?'), a staple of workplace and drama dialogue.

rootFamily.gloss: to rely on, by virtue of (formal)

凭着.etymology: A compound preposition formed from the verb/preposition 凭 (píng, Traditional 憑, 'to lean on, rely on') plus the imperfective/durative aspect suffix 着 (zhe, Traditional 著, which grammaticalized from the Middle Chinese verb 著 'to attach, adhere, remain in contact'). Adding 着 preserves the continuous state of 'holding onto or leaning upon' a resource, quality, or credential while carrying out the main clause's action ('relying on X, [subject does Y]').

history.meaning: to lean/rely upon + to adhere/continue (verb + complement)
relying on, by virtue of, on the strength of (prepositional compound)

morphemes.meaning: to lean on, rely on, base on
durative/continuous aspect marker, maintaining a state

凭着.notes: 凭着 is slightly more vivid and conversational than bare 凭 or formal 凭借, typically introducing an inner quality, skill, or passion (e.g., 凭着一腔热血, 'by virtue of sheer passion') that drives someone's success.

rootFamily.gloss: on the basis of, relying on
to rely on, by virtue of (formal disyllabic)

凶.etymology: In Simplified Chinese, 凶 (xiōng, Old Chinese *qʰ(r)oŋ) merges two etymologically related Classical characters: (1) 凶, an ideograph depicting a deep pit (凵) containing crossed hazards or someone falling in (乂), originally meaning 'inauspicious, calamitous, crop failure' (the antonym of 吉 jí, 'auspicious'); and (2) 兇, formed by adding the 'person' legs component (儿) to 凶, meaning 'terrifying, violent, ferocious, murderous'. In colloquial Modern Mandarin, 凶 shifted further to describe a person's temper ('fierce, harsh, bossy') or the intensity of an action ('intense, severe').

history.meaning: inauspicious, calamitous (凶); terrified, violent, murderous (兇)
ferocious, fierce, cruel, sinister
fierce, ferocious; harsh/strict in demeanor; intense; or (transitively in slang) to snap at someone

凶.notes: In everyday workplace and relationship talk, 凶 often means 'strict, intimidating, or sharp-tongued' (e.g., 老板很凶, 'the boss is fierce') or even functions transitively in colloquial speech (别凶我, 'don't snap at me').

rootFamily.gloss: auspicious or inauspicious, good or ill fortune

出.etymology: Ancient ideogram attested on Shang oracle bones showing a foot (止/屮) stepping out of a cave or enclosure (凵): 'go out, come out, exit, produce, issue, happen, exceed'.

history.meaning: foot stepping out of an enclosure = go out, come out, produce
go/come out; issue; occur; directional complement 'out'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 出 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to have an accident, for something bad to happen

出事.etymology: A separable verb-object (VO) compound formed from the existential/directional verb 出 (chū, 'to emerge, come out, occur') and the nominal object 事 (shì, 'matter, affair, incident, trouble'). While 事 is neutral on its own, in existential VO phrases like 出事 and 有事, semantic narrowing (pejoration by euphemistic understatement) restricts 事 to an untoward incident, accident, or crisis ('for trouble or an accident to happen').

history.meaning: to go out to serve in affairs / for an affair to arise
to meet with an accident, for something bad or a crisis to occur

出事.notes: Because 出事 is a separable verb-object (离合词 líhécí), modifiers and aspect markers are inserted between the two characters: 出大事了 ('something huge/terrible happened') or 出了事 ('an accident happened').

rootFamily.gloss: to stir up trouble, cause an accident

cognates.meaning: going out to take up an official post

出任.etymology: A formal disyllabic verb compound combining 出 (chū, 'to step forth, come out into public view, go out to a post') and 任 (rèn, 'to bear a burden, hold office, be appointed to a post'). In Classical Chinese bureaucratic usage, 出 specifically contrasted with 入 (serving inside the central imperial court) to mean 'going out to take a provincial or external appointment', or more broadly 'stepping forth to assume an official duty'. In Modern Mandarin it functions as a transitive formal verb taking a high-ranking title as its object.

history.meaning: to leave the capital to assume a regional office; to step forth and take up an official post
to take up the post of, assume the position of (a senior executive, producer, or official)

morphemes.meaning: to step forth, come out into public service
to assume office, serve as, bear responsibility

出任.notes: Belongs to formal journalistic and corporate register; it is reserved for high-status roles (e.g., 出任总制片人 'take up the post of chief producer', 出任CEO) and never used for entry-level jobs.

rootFamily.gloss: to serve as, hold the post of
to appoint to an office or position
to take office, assume a post

出卖.etymology: A directional/coordinative verb compound formed from 出 (chū, 'outward, to part with, hand over') and 卖 (mài, Traditional 賣, 'to sell', originally derived from 出 over 買 'buy'). Literally meaning 'to sell off or offer for sale', it underwent powerful metaphorical pejoration in Mandarin: just as one parts with goods for personal profit, to 'sell out' (出卖) a friend, ally, secret, or one's own integrity for gain came to mean 'to betray, sell out'.

history.meaning: to put up for sale, sell off goods or property
to betray, sell out (a friend, organization, secret, or conscience); (rarely) to sell off

出卖.notes: In modern Mandarin, the literal commercial sense 'to sell goods' has been almost completely taken over by 出售 (chūshòu), leaving 出卖 exclusively negative ('to betray / sell out', e.g., 出卖朋友, 出卖商业机密).

rootFamily.gloss: to sell, offer for sale (formal commercial)

出去.etymology: Directional verb compound of 出 ('exit, move out') + 去 ('go away from the speaker'): 'go out' (and as a directional complement after verbs: 走出去 'walk out').

history.meaning: go out (away from speaker)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 出去 (via 萌典)

出发.etymology: A coordinative verb compound combining 出 (chū, 'to go out, exit, step forth') and 发 (fā, Traditional 發, 'to shoot an arrow, send forth, set out on a journey'). Attested in Classical and Medieval Chinese texts for troops or travelers setting forth on an expedition, the compound was also reinforced in modern pan-East Asian usage alongside Japanese 出発 (shuppatsu). In Modern Mandarin it means both 'to depart on a journey' and figuratively 'to start from (a premise or consideration)' in the frame 从……出发.

history.meaning: to send forth; to set out on a march or journey
to set out, depart; to proceed from a standpoint or consideration (从…出发)

出发.notes: Beyond physical travel, pay close attention to the high-frequency argumentative pattern 从……出发 (cóng ... chūfā, 'proceeding from / taking ... as the starting point'), e.g., 从观众的需求出发 ('starting from the audience's needs').

rootFamily.gloss: starting point, motive, point of departure
to initiate, launch, sponsor (an event or project)
to set off, start a journey (literary/formal)

出售.etymology: Verb compound of 出 ('put out, offer') + 售 ('sell', originally a bird/goods leaving the seller's hand through speech 口): 'offer for sale, sell'.

history.stage: Song–Ming commercial Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: put out for sale; sell

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 出售 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: departure from a country, going abroad
to leave the country, go abroad

出国.etymology: A separable verb-object (VO) compound composed of 出 (chū, 'to exit, go outside of') and 国 (guó, Traditional 國, 'walled state, country, nation'). In Classical Chinese, 出國 meant leaving the capital city or leaving one's feudal state (for diplomacy, exile, or war). With the rise of modern nation-states, it specialized to mean crossing national borders to go abroad for study, work, or travel.

history.meaning: to leave the capital city or depart one's feudal state
to go abroad, leave one's home country

出国.notes: Like other VO directional compounds (出事, 出差), 出国 is separable (e.g., 出过两次国, 'have been abroad twice') and pairs directly with purpose verbs such as 出国留学 ('go abroad to study') or 出国深造 ('go abroad for advanced training').

rootFamily.gloss: to return to one's home country

cognates.meaning: participation in a contest, appearing onstage/in an arena

出场.etymology: A separable verb-object (VO) compound combining 出 (chū, 'to come out, step forth') and 场 (chǎng, Traditional 場, originally 'leveled earth altar or threshing ground', later 'stage, arena, performance venue'). Originating in traditional Chinese theater (戏曲 xìqǔ) and examination arenas, 出场 denoted an actor stepping out from backstage (幕后 mùhòu) onto the visible stage, and later broadened to athletes entering a playing field or a key figure making their entrance in a story or crisis.

history.meaning: to exit the imperial examination hall; for an opera performer to step onto the stage
to come onstage, enter the arena, make an appearance (in a show, competition, or narrative)

出场.notes: Central to live television and showbiz vocabulary (e.g., 出场顺序 'order of appearance onstage', 出场费 'appearance fee' paid to celebrity guests).

rootFamily.gloss: appearance fee (for a performer or guest)
on the spot, live at the venue/set
opening act, to start a show

cognates.meaning: to make a sound, speak up

出声.etymology: A separable verb-object (VO) compound formed from 出 (chū, 'to emit, let out, produce') and 声 (shēng, Traditional 聲, originally depicting a hand striking a suspended stone chime 磬 and an ear 耳, meaning 'sound, voice, tone'). In both literal acoustics and interpersonal interaction, 出声 means to emit a vocal sound or break silence by speaking up.

history.meaning: to emit a sound, utter a voice or cry
to make a sound, utter a word, speak up (often in negation: 不出声)

出声.notes: Most frequently encountered in negative or resultative constructions such as 一声不出 / 不出声 ('not making a peep / keeping silent') or 笑出声来 ('to laugh out loud').

rootFamily.gloss: to speak out, make an official statement or voice support
to utter a sound or word (colloquial synonym)

cognates.meaning: to rise above others, stand up for someone; slightly over (a number)

出头.etymology: A separable verb-object (VO) compound combining 出 (chū, 'to stick out, emerge above') and 头 (tóu, Traditional 頭, 'head, top'). In Song-dynasty poetry and vernacular prose, 出頭 originally described bamboo shoots or plants pushing their heads up above the soil or above surrounding vegetation. From this vivid image of 'raising one's head above the surface', it developed three metaphorical branches: (1) rising out of poverty or obscurity ('getting ahead'), (2) sticking one's neck out to take the lead or stand up for someone in a dispute (替人出头), and (3) exceeding a round number by a small amount (三十出头, 'just over thirty').

history.meaning: (of plants/shoots) to emerge above the ground or rise above others; to free oneself from hardship
to rise from obscurity; to stand up for someone / take the lead in a conflict; slightly over a round number

morphemes.meaning: to emerge, stick out, rise above

出头.notes: Notice the proverb 枪打出头鸟 (qiāng dǎ chūtóuniǎo, 'the gun shoots the bird that sticks its head out'), which captures traditional caution toward standing out, contrasted with 替……出头 ('standing up to defend someone').

rootFamily.gloss: to show one's face in public, come forward
person who sticks their neck out (literally 'bird that pokes its head out')
take the lead, be the first to act

cognates.meaning: the day one finally succeeds or breaks through
cognates.word: 出頭之日 (ceot1 tau4 zi1 jat6)

出头之日.etymology: A four-character semi-literary nominal phrase structured as [modifier + 之 + head]: 出头 (chūtóu, 'lifting one's head out of oppression, obscurity, or hardship') + the Classical attributive particle 之 (zhī, functioning like modern 的) + 日 (rì, 'day, time'). Retaining Classical syntax gives this phrase solemn emotional weight: it denotes the long-awaited 'day of breakthrough' when an unappreciated talent or struggling worker finally steps into recognition.

history.form: 出頭之日 / 出头之日
history.meaning: the day of emerging from hardship or obscurity into recognition and success

morphemes.meaning: to emerge, rise above hardship or obscurity

出头之日.notes: Almost always used with verbs of long endurance and anticipation such as 熬到出头之日 ('to tough it out until the day of breakthrough') or 永无出头之日 ('never to have a chance to shine').

rootFamily.gloss: to rise from obscurity; stand up for someone
to stand out conspicuously among one's peers (idiom)
days to come, in the future (literary)

出奇.etymology: Originally a classical military verb-object phrase from Sunzi and historical chronicles—出奇制胜 ('to deploy unexpected maneuvers to win victory')—combining 出 (chū, 'to bring forth, exceed') and 奇 (qí, 'unusual, extraordinary, marvellous'). Over time 'bringing forth the extraordinary' shifted from strategic surprise into a general descriptive expression meaning 'surpassing ordinary expectations', commonly used with 地 before adjectives (出奇地轻 'surprisingly light').

history.meaning: launch an unexpected stratagem (as in 出奇制胜)
remarkably; surprisingly; beyond expectation

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 出奇

cognates.meaning: to go on a business trip

出差.etymology: A separable verb-object (VO) compound composed of 出 (chū, 'to go out, leave one's home station') and 差 (chāi, Old Chinese *tsʰrˤaj, originally 'to select and dispatch someone on an official errand', written with the heteronym reading chāi as in 差遣 chāiqiǎn and 钦差 qīnchāi, distinct from chà 'lack/bad' and chā 'difference'). In Ming and Qing administrative language, 出差 meant being dispatched away from one's yamen or garrison on official government duty; in Modern Mandarin it broadened to any out-of-town business trip.

history.meaning: to be dispatched out of the yamen/office on an official government errand or corvée duty
to go on a business trip away from one's regular workplace

morphemes.meaning: to go out, travel away from base

出差.notes: Watch the pronunciation: 差 has four readings in Mandarin, and whenever it means 'errand, dispatch, or courier' (出差, 差事, 邮差), it is always read first tone chāi, never chà.

rootFamily.gloss: to send on an errand, dispatch

cognates.meaning: attendance, presence at a meeting or ceremony

出席.etymology: A verb-object compound formed from 出 (chū, 'to come out, appear at') and 席 (xí, originally 'woven straw mat' on which people sat in ancient China before chairs were adopted, hence 'seat, banquet place, parliamentary seat'). While 席 meant 'seat at a gathering' since Classical Chinese, the compound 出席 (contrasted with 缺席 quēxí, 'to be absent from one's seat') was standardized in Meiji-era Japan (shusseki) for parliamentary, academic, and diplomatic attendance and entered modern standard Chinese as a formal transitive verb.

history.meaning: woven sitting mat; seat at a banquet, lecture, or council
to take one's seat at an assembly, attend formally (Meiji Japanese usage)
to attend, be present at (a formal meeting, ceremony, press conference, or summit)

morphemes.meaning: to appear at, come forth to
mat, seat, formal place at an assembly

出席.notes: Unlike 参加 (cānjiā, 'to participate in'), which works for any casual activity, 出席 is high-register and indicates dignified presence at a formal event (e.g., 出席发布会 'attend a press conference', 出席颁奖典礼 'attend an awards ceremony').

rootFamily.gloss: to be absent from a meeting or event
seat, place (at a venue or in a parliament)

出息.etymology: Originally an economic verb-object compound combining 出 (chū, 'to yield, produce') and 息 (xī, originally 'breath', extended in Classical Chinese to 'growth, offspring, and financial interest yielded by capital', as in 利息 lìxī). In Medieval and Early Mandarin, 出息 meant 'the profit, rent, or interest yielded by land or capital'. By metaphorically comparing a young person to an investment made by their family, colloquial Mandarin shifted 出息 (with neutral tone chūxi) to mean 'future promise, ambition, capability of amounting to something'.

history.meaning: to yield interest or profit; financial return or income from an asset or estate
promising future, ambition, personal prospects (especially in 有出息 / 没出息)

morphemes.meaning: breath; growth, interest, return on investment (neutral tone xi)

出息.notes: Always pronounced with a neutral tone on the second syllable (chūxi) and almost exclusively used in the evaluative frames 有出息 ('promising, bound to succeed') and 没出息 ('good-for-nothing, lacking ambition').

cognates.meaning: to take action, strike, spend money, or sell off

出手.etymology: A separable verb-object (VO) compound formed from 出 (chū, 'to put forth, extend') and 手 (shǒu, 'hand; skill'). Originating in martial arts and board games ('to thrust out one's hand to strike or make a move'), 出手 branched into three vivid everyday senses: (1) to step in and take decisive action (often rescuing a situation or showing one's skill), (2) the manner in which one parts with money (e.g., 出手大方 'generous in spending'), and (3) to let go of goods from one's hands, i.e., to sell off.

history.meaning: to extend the hand; to strike a blow in combat or make a move in a game; to display one's craftsmanship
to make a move, intervene decisively; to spend money (generously/stingily); to sell off an item

morphemes.meaning: to put forth, extend, release from

出手.notes: In workplace and showbiz dramas, 大佬出手 ('a big shot steps in and makes a move') or 该出手时就出手 ('make your move when the time is right') highlights decisive, high-skill intervention.

rootFamily.gloss: to start, put one's hand to a task; to strike first
to pull back one's hand, stop doing something bad

出来.etymology: Directional verb compound of 出 ('exit, emerge') + 来 ('come toward the speaker'). Used literally ('come out') and as a resultative/directional complement showing emergence, completion, or recognition (看出来 'make out by looking', 想出来 'think up').

history.meaning: come out; emerge; figure out

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 出来 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: out of line, exceeding proper bounds; extraordinary

出格.etymology: Originally a verb-object compound combining 出 (chū, 'to step outside of, exceed') and 格 (gé, originally 'tree branches', extended in Classical Chinese to 'wooden lattice/grid, standard rule, moral or legal framework', and specifically the ruled grid squares of calligraphy paper). Just as a brush stroke that strays outside the ruled square (格子) violates calligraphic form, behavior or speech that steps outside accepted norms is described as 出格 ('out of line, over the top, improper').

history.meaning: to surpass ordinary standards (originally often positive: 'extraordinary, above standard'); to exceed established rules
out of line, overstepping bounds, improper or excessive (of words or behavior)

morphemes.meaning: to step outside of, exceed, cross beyond

出格.notes: In Tang-Song literature 出格 could praise someone as 'extraordinary', whereas in Modern Mandarin it is almost always critical or cautionary (e.g., 做出格的事 'do something out of line', 说话太出格 'speak way out of bounds').

rootFamily.gloss: up to standard, qualified, passing grade
to cross the line, overstep one's authority or bounds

cognates.meaning: to vent anger; to breathe/emit air

出气.etymology: A separable verb-object (VO) compound formed from 出 (chū, 'to let out, release, vent') and 气 (qì, Traditional 氣, 'breath, air, vital energy; pent-up anger or grievance'). In traditional Chinese physiology and emotion metaphors, anger and humiliation are conceptualized as hot, pressurized 气 trapped in the chest (受气 shòuqì, 生气 shēngqì). Releasing that pent-up pressure is 出气 ('to vent one's anger/spleen'), and doing so on behalf of someone wronged (替人出气) means 'to avenge a slight or stand up for someone'.

history.meaning: to exhale breath, emit vapor; to vent pent-up resentment or anger
to vent one's anger/frustration; to get back at someone or stand up for someone who was wronged

morphemes.meaning: air, breath; pent-up anger or grievance

出气.notes: Note the colloquial noun derivative 出气筒 (chūqìtǒng, literally 'air-venting tube' -> 'punching bag / scapegoat someone vents their anger on').

rootFamily.gloss: to suffer bullying or mistreatment without being able to fight back
emotional punching bag, person one vents anger on

cognates.meaning: appearance in a show, film, or broadcast

出演.etymology: A disyllabic verb compound combining 出 (chū, 'to come forth in public, appear onstage') and 演 (yǎn, originally 'flowing water extending far', later 'to practice, elaborate, perform drama'). Patterned in modern East Asian theater and broadcasting vocabulary as a Sino-Japanese compound (Japanese 出演 shutsuen, 'appearing in a performance') and adopted into Modern Mandarin, 出演 functions as a transitive verb taking either a production title or a character role as its object ('to appear in / play the role of').

history.meaning: to appear before an audience and perform in a play or program (modern Japanese theatrical/broadcast coinage)
to appear in, perform in, or play a role in (a film, TV drama, or stage production)

morphemes.meaning: to come forth, appear publicly on screen or stage

出演.notes: A staple of entertainment press releases: unlike 表演 ('to perform' in general), 出演 is transitive and takes either the show or the role directly, e.g., 出演男主角 ('star as the male lead') or 友情出演 ('make a special guest appearance').

rootFamily.gloss: to play the role of, portray (a specific character)
to star in as the lead actor; lead actor/actress

出炉.etymology: Verb-object compound of 出 ('come out of') + 炉 (爐, 'oven, furnace, stove'): literally 'come fresh out of the oven/kiln' (of bread, pastries, or metal/porcelain), and figuratively 'be newly released or published (of a report, plan, or list)'.

history.meaning: come fresh out of the furnace/oven; be newly released

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 出炉 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: publishing house (calque with native head nhà + xuất bản)

出版社.etymology: A three-character modifier-head noun compound formed from the verb-object compound 出版 (chūbǎn, 'to publish', literally 'to put out printing blocks/editions', where 版 originally denoted wooden planks used for woodblock printing) plus the institutional head noun 社 (shè, originally the 'altar of the god of the soil' around which a village community gathered, later 'association, society, agency, press'). Coined in Meiji Japan as 出版社 (shuppansha) during the rise of modern print capitalism, it became the standard word for 'publishing house' across East Asia.

history.meaning: woodblock printing edition + community association/society
commercial or institutional publishing company (Meiji Japanese coinage)
publishing house, press, book publisher

出版社.notes: Notice how the suffix 社 (shè) marks media, literary, and travel institutions in Mandarin: 出版社 ('publishing house'), 报社 ('newspaper office'), 通讯社 ('news agency'), and 旅行社 ('travel agency').

rootFamily.gloss: to publish, come off the press

cognates.meaning: appearance, emergence, arrival on the scene

出现.etymology: A coordinative/resultative verb compound combining 出 (chū, 'to come out, emerge from concealment') and 现 (xiàn, Traditional 現, 'to become visible, manifest', originally written 見 xiàn in Classical Chinese before receiving the jade radical 王/玉 to distinguish the intransitive 'appear/manifest' reading from transitive jiàn 'see'). Already attested in Medieval Buddhist translations for the manifestation of Buddhas or phenomena in the world, it is the core Mandarin verb for 'to appear, emerge, arise'.

history.meaning: to come forth and become visible; to manifest in the world (especially in Buddhist texts)
to appear, emerge, arise, show up (of people, phenomena, or problems)

出现.notes: Syntactically, 出现 often functions as an existential/presentative verb whose logical subject follows it when introducing new information: 节目组出现了问题 ('A problem arose in the production crew').

rootFamily.gloss: to manifest, display, show off; performance/behavior

出租车.etymology: Three-character compound of 出租 ('rent out, lease for hire', 出 'put out' + 租 'rent/tax grain') + 车 ('vehicle, car'): 'taxicab, taxi'.

history.meaning: car for hire; taxi

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 出租车 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: doctor's visit, seeing patients at a clinic or on call

出诊.etymology: A verb-object medical compound formed from 出 (chū, 'to go out from one's residence or inner office') and 诊 (zhěn, Traditional 診, 'to examine a patient, take the pulse, diagnose', composed of speech 言 and phonetic 㐱). Originally meaning 'for a physician to leave the clinic and visit a patient at home (make a house call)', in contemporary Mainland Chinese hospital administration 出诊 also denotes a specialist physician coming out to hold scheduled outpatient clinic hours (门诊 ménzhěn).

history.meaning: for a physician to travel out to a patient's home to examine and treat them (make a house call); in modern hospitals, also to hold scheduled outpatient consultations

morphemes.meaning: to go out (on a call or to the clinic floor)

出诊.notes: In modern Mainland hospitals, 专家出诊时间 means 'specialist outpatient consultation hours', whereas in everyday residential contexts 医生上门出诊 means 'a doctor making a home house call'.

rootFamily.gloss: outpatient clinic service; to see patients at a clinic

出路.etymology: A modifier-head noun compound combining 出 (chū, 'exiting, leading out') and 路 (lù, 'road, path, way'). Literally denoting a physical 'exit route' from an enclosure or military encirclement in Classical and Medieval texts, it underwent a natural metaphorical extension in Modern Mandarin to mean a 'way out of a predicament', an 'economic outlet for goods', or a 'viable future career path'.

history.meaning: physical road leading out; escape route for troops
way out of a crisis; career prospects or viable future path (for a person, industry, or media format)

出路.notes: In physical buildings, 'exit' is always 出口 (chūkǒu); 出路 is used almost exclusively in the figurative sense of 'a way out of a dilemma' or 'a viable career/industry future' (e.g., 传统媒体的出路, 'the future path for traditional media').

rootFamily.gloss: dead end, road to ruin, no way out
line of thought, train of thinking, approach

cognates.meaning: to derail; to have an extramarital or romantic affair

出轨.etymology: A separable verb-object (VO) compound formed from 出 (chū, 'to leave, deviate from') and 轨 (guǐ, Traditional 軌, originally 'the axle-width gauge between two chariot wheel ruts', which guaranteed that all carriages rode in the same tracks after Qin Shi Huang standardized axle widths: 车同轨). In Classical Chinese, 出軌 meant 'stepping outside established laws or planetary orbits'; in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries it acquired the literal sense of a train 'derailing from its tracks', and in contemporary Mandarin it became the standard metaphor for 'straying from marital or romantic fidelity (cheating / having an affair)'.

history.meaning: to deviate from chariot wheel ruts; figuratively, to transgress established laws, norms, or celestial orbits
(of a train or tram) to derail from the tracks; figuratively, to deviate from proper conduct
to have a romantic or marital affair, cheat on one's partner (also literal train derailment)

morphemes.meaning: to leave, stray outside of, jump off
wheel rut, railway track, proper orbit/norm

出轨.notes: In celebrity gossip and modern relationship dramas, 出轨 almost always means 'cheating on a partner / having an affair' (often subdivided into 精神出轨 'emotional infidelity' and 肉体出轨 'physical infidelity'), while literal train derailment is now more often called 脱轨 (tuōguǐ).

rootFamily.gloss: track, rail, planetary orbit; proper course
the right track, normal institutionalized course (as in 步入正轨)
to derail (literal train or figurative plan)

出远门.etymology: Colloquial separable verb-object phrase combining 出 ('go out; exit') + 远 ('distant; far', walk radical 辶 + phonetic 袁 yuán) + 门 ('gate; household door'). Literally 'to step out through the gate on a distant journey', it is the warm traditional expression for traveling far from home.

history.meaning: leave home on a long journey
travel far from home; go on a long trip

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 出远门

cognates.meaning: leaving home to become a monk; entering a profession; making a debut
setting out on a path; entering the world

出道.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound formed from 出 (chū, 'to go out, emerge') and 道 (dào, 'way, path, guild, or spiritual/professional calling'). In Medieval and Early Modern Chinese, 出道 referred to a Buddhist or Daoist novice completing monastic training to preach in the world, or an apprentice finishing training to practice a trade independently; in modern East Asian entertainment, it narrowed to an artist's official professional debut.

history.meaning: to attain the Way and go forth to preach, or to complete an apprenticeship and enter a trade
to make one's official professional debut in the entertainment industry

morphemes.meaning: to go out, emerge, step forth
path, way, profession, sphere of practice

出道.notes: A separable verb-object (离合词) in showbiz Mandarin; modifiers can be inserted or attached via prepositions, as in 正式出道 ('officially debut') or 出道十年 ('ten years since debuting').

rootFamily.gloss: to appear on stage, enter the scene
peer or fellow practitioner in the same trade
to gain prominence, rise to fame

cognates.meaning: to make an error, go wrong

出错.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound combining 出 (chū, 'to produce, give rise to, manifest') and 错 (cuò, Traditional 錯, originally 'to inlay metal with gold or silver; grindstone; intersecting', which evolved in Classical Chinese to mean 'crossed, disordered, mistaken'). Literally 'to produce an error' or 'for a mistake to emerge', it functions as an intransitive separable verb phrase indicating that a process or person has gone awry.

history.meaning: to inlay metal; to cross or disorder; by extension, error or mistake
to yield an error, go wrong, make a mistake

morphemes.meaning: error, fault, mistake (originally cross-grinding or disorder)

出错.notes: Often takes the retroflex suffix -兒 (出错儿, chūcuòr) in northern spoken Mandarin and behaves as a separable VO compound (e.g., 出了一点错, 'made a slight mistake').

rootFamily.gloss: to have an accident or problem occur

出镜率.etymology: A three-character modifier-head derivative built by suffixing 率 (lǜ, 'rate, ratio, proportion') to the verb-object compound 出镜 (chūjìng, Traditional 出鏡, 'to appear before the camera lens'). Here 镜 (originally 'bronze mirror' in Classical Chinese, later extended to optical lenses and cameras) serves as the object of 出 ('to appear in'), originating in Cantonese and Hong Kong film/television jargon before spreading across Mandarin broadcast media.

history.meaning: to appear on camera or in the frame (originally Hong Kong film/TV industry coinage)
frequency or rate of on-screen appearances; media exposure rate

morphemes.meaning: to appear, step out, show up

出镜率.notes: Standard television and entertainment industry metric; also used figuratively in everyday speech for clothing or props that appear repeatedly in someone's photos.

rootFamily.gloss: camera lens; shot or take in filming

出门.etymology: Verb-object compound of 出 ('go out of') + 门 (門, 'door, gate, home'): 'go out the door, leave home, travel away from home'. Attested since the Shijing and Classics.

history.stage: Old & Classical Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: step out the gate; leave home

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 出门 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: leaving a monastic sub-temple; being discharged from the hospital
cognates.word: 出院 (shutsuin, matches 退院 taiin in modern medical use)

出院.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound of 出 (chū, 'to exit, leave') and 院 (yuàn, 'courtyard, walled compound, institution'). In Tang–Song Literary Chinese, 院 denoted a government bureau, academy, or Buddhist cloister, so 出院 meant leaving a monastery or courtyard; in modern Chinese, 院 clips 医院 (yīyuàn, 'hospital'), yielding the standard medical verb 'to be discharged from the hospital'.

history.meaning: to step out of a courtyard, academy, or monastic compound
to be discharged from a hospital after inpatient treatment

morphemes.meaning: to leave, exit, be discharged from
hospital (clipping of 医院; originally walled courtyard or institution)

出院.notes: Pairs directly with its antonym 住院 (zhùyuàn, 'to be hospitalized / admitted to hospital') and functions as a separable verb-object compound (e.g., 办出院手续, 'handle discharge procedures').

rootFamily.gloss: to be admitted to hospital, be hospitalized

cognates.meaning: appearing in person, showing one's face
to appear in person, come forward

出面.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound combining 出 (chū, 'to put forth, show, come out') and 面 (miàn, 'face, surface, personal presence'). In Literary Chinese, 出面 literally meant 'to show one's face' or 'to appear in public'; through metonymy in vernacular and modern Chinese, 'face' came to represent personal prestige, authority, and direct intervention, giving the sense 'to step forward personally (to mediate, negotiate, or take responsibility)'.

history.meaning: to show one's face, appear in public view
to step forward in person or act in an official/authoritative capacity to resolve a matter

morphemes.meaning: to put forth, come forward, appear

出面.notes: Frequently precedes another verb in serial verb constructions (e.g., 出面解决 'step in to resolve', 出面澄清 'come forward to clarify a rumor in PR crises').

rootFamily.gloss: to appear on the scene in person (often of a VIP)

分.etymology: Ancient ideogram (会意字) combining 八 ('part, divide in two') + 刀 ('knife'): 'cut apart, divide, distribute, separate, distinguish' (read fēn), and as a unit 'minute (1/60 of an hour or degree); cent (1/100 of a yuan); point/score; one-tenth'. Read fèn, it means 'allotted share, component, duty'.

history.meaning: knife dividing in two = divide, separate (fēn); allotted share (fèn)
divide; minute; point; cent

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 分 (via 萌典)

cognates.word: 分唔清楚 (fan1 m4 cing1 co2)

分不清楚.etymology: A negative potential resultative verb construction composed of the verb root 分 (fēn, 'to divide, distinguish, tell apart'), the negative potential infix 不 (bù, 'cannot'), and the disyllabic resultative complement 清楚 (qīngchu, 'clear and distinct', originally a Classical Chinese coordinative compound of 清 'limpid water' and 楚 'neatly arranged', from the phrase 清清楚楚 / 衣冠楚楚). Literally 'by dividing, unable to make clear and distinct'.

history.meaning: 分 'to cleave/distinguish' + 清楚 'clear and orderly' as independent items
cannot tell apart, unable to distinguish clearly (negative potential resultative)

morphemes.meaning: negative potential marker ('cannot achieve the result')

分不清楚.notes: Its affirmative potential counterpart is 分得清楚 ('able to tell apart'); in brisk speech, the final syllable is often dropped to form the three-character variant 分不清 (fēnbuqīng).

分享.etymology: A subordinative/serial verb compound uniting 分 (fēn, 'to divide, apportion, distribute', depicting a knife 刀 cleaving something 八) and 享 (xiǎng, originally 'to present sacrificial offerings at an ancestral temple', later 'to receive and enjoy a benefit or feast'). Originally meaning 'to apportion and partake of a reward or blessing together' in Literary Chinese, in modern Mandarin it broadened to sharing experiences, ideas, or digital media content.

history.meaning: to apportion and partake in sacrificial blessings, rewards, or privileges together
to share (joy, experiences, resources, or digital posts) with others

morphemes.meaning: to enjoy, partake of, benefit from

分享.notes: Unlike 分担 (fēndān, 'to share a burden, cost, or responsibility'), 分享 is reserved for positive or neutral things—joy, stories, files, or social media posts.

rootFamily.gloss: to share a burden or responsibility

分别.etymology: A coordinative compound of two synonymous verbs of cleaving: 分 (fēn, 'to divide in two with a knife 刀') and 别 (bié, Traditional 別, 'to cut apart bone and flesh with a knife 刂; to separate, distinguish'). In Classical and Buddhist Chinese, 分别 meant 'to distinguish, discriminate, or part ways'; through grammaticalization in pre-modern and modern Mandarin, it also developed the adverbial function 'separately, respectively'.

history.meaning: to cleave apart, distinguish, discriminate; to part ways with someone
separately, respectively (adverb); to part ways (verb); difference (noun)

分别.notes: As an adverb ('respectively'), it is always pronounced fēnbié; in older or literary usage meaning 'to discern/discriminate', it was sometimes read fēnbiè.

cognates.meaning: one-tenth of an inch; degree, measure, social station
a tiny measure; degree, sense of propriety

分寸.etymology: A coordinative compound of two small traditional Chinese units of length: 分 (fēn, one-tenth of a 寸) and 寸 (cùn, the 'Chinese inch', approximately 3.3 cm, originally depicting a hand 又 with a mark 一 at the pulse point). In Classical Chinese (e.g., *Hanfeizi*), juxtaposing 'tenths of an inch and inches' denoted exact measurement or a tiny extent; by metonymy, knowing the exact measure became 'sense of proportion, tact, and proper bounds in speech or behavior'.

history.meaning: tenths of an inch and inches; minute linear measurements or tiny amount
proper measure, sense of proportion, tact, and appropriateness in conduct

morphemes.meaning: one-tenth of a Chinese inch; small unit of measure or degree

分寸.notes: Most commonly used in the collocations 有分寸 ('tactful, knowing where to draw the line'), 把握分寸 ('gauge the proper bounds'), and 没分寸 ('lacking tact, crossing the line').

rootFamily.gloss: sense of propriety; proper degree of measurement
square inch; figuratively, the heart or mind

分成.etymology: Resultative verb compound of 分 ('divide, split') + 成 ('become, form into'): 'divide into (parts/groups)' (and as a noun/verb phrase, 'share profits by percentage').

history.meaning: divide into; split by percentage

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 分成 (via 萌典)

分手.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound formed from 分 (fēn, 'to separate, part') and 手 (shǒu, 'hand'). Attested in Six Dynasties and Tang poetry (literally 'to unclasp hands when parting'), 分手 originally meant bidding farewell to a friend or colleague as each went their own way; in 20th-century vernacular Mandarin, it specialized primarily into ending a romantic relationship ('to break up').

history.meaning: to unclasp hands at parting; to bid farewell and go separate ways
to break up (of romantic partners); to part company

morphemes.meaning: hand (metonymic for clasping hands in companionship)

分手.notes: A separable verb-object compound (e.g., 分了手 'broke up', 和他分手 'break up with him'); its antonym in romantic contexts is 复合 (fùhé, 'get back together') or 牵手 (qiānshǒu, 'hold hands / pair up').

rootFamily.gloss: to hold hands; to join forces or enter a relationship
to let go, release one's grip or let someone go

分散.etymology: A coordinative compound joining 分 (fēn, 'to divide, split apart') and 散 (sàn / sǎn, 'to scatter, disperse, break up', originally depicting beating肉/bamboo to separate fibers). Attested in Classical Chinese texts such as *Xunzi* and *Hanshu* for scattering troops, populations, or resources, it functions in modern Mandarin both as a transitive/intransitive verb ('to disperse, divert') and as a stative adjective ('scattered, decentralized, unfocused').

history.meaning: to divide and scatter (people, troops, or family members)
scattered, dispersed, decentralized (adj.); to divert or distribute (verb)

分散.notes: Commonly collocates with 注意力 (分散注意力, 'to distract / divert attention') and 风险 (分散风险, 'to diversify risk'), and contrasts with 集中 (jízhōng, 'concentrated, centralized').

分析师.etymology: A three-character agentive compound formed by adding the occupational suffix 师 (shī, Traditional 師, 'master, specialist, teacher') to 分析 (fēnxī, 'to analyze'). 分析 itself is a Classical Chinese coordinative compound of 分 ('to cleave with a knife') and 析 ('to split wood 木 with an axe 斤'), which was revitalized in late 19th-century Meiji Japan (bunseki) and Chinese scientific translation to render European 'analysis'.

history.meaning: to cleave and split apart; to divide an argument or territory into parts
scientific, logical, or quantitative analysis (calque of European 'analysis')
professional analyst (in finance, data, media ratings, or industry research)

morphemes.meaning: to split wood with an axe; to dissect, resolve into elements

分析师.notes: The suffix 师 denotes a skilled technical or certified professional (compare 设计师 'designer', 工程师 'engineer', 剪辑师 'film editor').

分歧.etymology: A verb-complement or coordinative compound combining 分 (fēn, 'to divide, branch apart') and 歧 (qí, 'forked road, diverging path', derived from 止 'foot/step' + 支 'branch'). Literally denoting a road splitting into diverging branches in Literary Chinese (compare 岐路 'forked road'), it metaphorically came to denote a divergence of opinions, creative vision, or policy—a rift or disagreement.

history.meaning: to branch off into a forked road; diverging paths
divergence of opinion, ideological rift, discrepancy

分歧.notes: Standard formal noun for disagreements in negotiations or creative teams; typically paired with 产生分歧 ('develop a rift'), 存在分歧 ('have differences'), or 消除分歧 ('bridge differences').

rootFamily.gloss: ambiguity, divergent interpretations of a text or phrase
discrimination, prejudice (literally 'viewing with a skewed/divergent eye')

分神.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound of 分 (fēn, 'to divide, divert') and 神 (shén, 'spirit, vital mind, mental focus', originally 'deity/lightning spirit' in Old Chinese, then 'spirit/consciousness' in Daoist and medical thought as in 精神). In pre-modern vernacular, 分神 could mean either 'to spare a bit of your mental energy (to help me)' or 'to have one's mental focus split'; in modern Mandarin it primarily means 'to get distracted'.

history.meaning: to divide one's spirit/mental attention; (polite) to trouble someone to pay heed
to get distracted, lose concentration, have one's attention divided

分神.notes: Often takes the retroflex suffix -兒 (分神儿, fēnshénr) in spoken Mandarin and is synonymous with 分心 (fēnxīn) and 走神 (zǒushén, 'for one's mind to wander').

rootFamily.gloss: for the mind to wander, zone out
to focus one's mind, concentrate intently

分贝.etymology: Hybrid calque-phonetic compound coined for the acoustic unit 'decibel' (dB): 分 ('one-tenth, deci-') + 贝 ('bel', phonetic rendering of Alexander Graham Bell's surname, 贝尔).

history.meaning: one-tenth of a bel = decibel (dB)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 分贝 (via 萌典)

分钟.etymology: Compound time unit of 分 ('minute, 1/60th division') + 钟 (鐘, 'clock, bell'). Added 钟 to disambiguate a 'minute of time' (一分钟) from money cents or test points.

history.meaning: minute (on a clock)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 分钟 (via 萌典)

切.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 七 (qī, originally the graph for cutting) + 刀 ('knife'): read qiē 'cut, slice, chop with a knife (and in geometry, tangent)'; read qiè 'press close together (as in taking the pulse 切脉), urgent, eager, by all means'.

history.meaning: cut/carve with a blade (qiē); press close, earnest, urgent (qiè)
cut; slice (qiē); close/eager (qiè)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 切 (via 萌典)

切实.etymology: A coordinative compound of 切 (qiè, originally 'to cut closely with a knife', extended in Classical Chinese to 'close to the mark, pressing, earnest', from taking the pulse closely by pressing the artery) and 实 (shí, Traditional 實, 'full of wealth/grain under a roof 宀; solid, real, substantial'). Together they mean 'closely matching reality and solid'—hence concrete, practical, and feasible.

history.meaning: closely matching the facts, earnest, substantial and true to reality
concrete, practical, realistic, earnest (as an adjective or adverbial modifier)

morphemes.meaning: close to reality, pressing, earnest (originally 'to cut/press closely')

切实.notes: Frequently used in official, business, and production management registers in four-character collocations like 切实可行 ('concrete and feasible') or as an adverbial before action verbs (切实保障, 'concretely safeguard').

列.etymology: Ideographic/phono-semantic character of 歹/歺 ('broken bone/fragments') + 刀 (刂, 'knife'): originally 'split apart, arrange in order', hence 'line up, arrange in a row, list' and the measure word for 'a row, a train of cars (一列火车)'.

history.meaning: divide and arrange in order; rank; row
arrange; list; row; classifier for trains

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 列 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to list in a table; list

列表.etymology: Formed from 列 (liè, 'to arrange in a row, line up, array') and 表 (biǎo, originally 'outer fur garment', extended in Han historiography to 'display externally' and thus 'chronological chart, table, or schedule', as in Sima Qian's *Shiji* tables). Originally a verb-object phrase meaning 'to set out in a chart or table', in modern Mandarin and computing it lexicalized as a noun meaning 'list, schedule, or playlist'.

history.meaning: to arrange items in a tabular chart or memorial list (verb-object)
list, tabular schedule, playlist, or UI list view (noun)

morphemes.meaning: to arrange in a row, line up, enumerate
table, chart, schedule (originally outer garment / outward display)

列表.notes: Ubiquitous in media production and software interfaces (e.g., 播放列表 'playlist', 节目列表 'program schedule', 下拉列表 'drop-down list').

刘.etymology: Simplified from 劉 (liú), a phono-semantic/compound ideograph combining 卯 (or 丣 yǒu, phonetic), 金 ('metal'), and 刀 ('knife/axe'). In Old Chinese (e.g., *Shujing*), 劉 denoted a battle-axe and the verb 'to slay, vanquish'; it became a prominent toponymic and noble lineage surname during the Zhou dynasty and rose to imperial prestige as the ruling surname of the Han dynasty founded by Liu Bang (Emperor Gaozu).

history.meaning: battle-axe; to slay or vanquish; ancient fief and lineage name
imperial house surname of the Han dynasty; one of the most common Chinese surnames

刘.notes: One of China's top five most populous surnames; in workplace and production-team speech, it combines with prefixes or titles like 老刘 ('Old Liu'), 小刘 ('Young Liu'), or 刘总 ('Director/CEO Liu').

rootFamily.gloss: bangs, fringe of hair across the forehead (folk-etymologized with Daoist immortal Liu Hai)
a deeply discerning talent scout (alluding to Tang critic Liu Fen 刘蕡)

刚.etymology: Phono-semantic character (剛) of 冈 (岡, gāng phonetic) + 刀 (刂, 'knife/blade'): originally 'hard, strong, unyielding (of metal or character)' in Classical Chinese. From Tang–Song vernacular onward, it developed the temporal adverb sense 'just, barely, just a moment ago'.

history.meaning: hard; firm; unyielding
just; barely; just now

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 刚 (via 萌典)

刚刚.etymology: Reduplication of the adverb 刚 ('just'): used both as a temporal adverb ('just now, a moment ago') and to mean 'barely, just enough'.

history.meaning: just a moment ago; barely

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 刚刚 (via 萌典)

刚好.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining the degree/temporal adverb 刚 (gāng, Traditional 剛, originally 'hard, unyielding steel/blade', grammaticalized in Vernacular Chinese since the Tang–Song period to mean 'just at the exact point, barely, just now') with 好 (hǎo, 'good, fitting, proper'). Literally 'exact-to-the-point and fitting', it expresses either spatial/quantitative exactness ('just right') or temporal coincidence ('happen to, by coincidence').

history.meaning: hard, unyielding, firm (of metal or character)
just right in degree; by coincidence, happen to, just now

刚好.notes: Near-synonymous with 正好 (zhènghǎo) and 恰巧 (qiàqiǎo); can function both as a predicate ('That amount is just right': 数量刚好) and as a pre-verbal adverb ('I happened to see him': 我刚好看见他).

rootFamily.gloss: just now, a moment ago (temporal adverb)

刚才.etymology: Temporal noun combining 刚 ('just') + 才 ('just now, only then'): 'just now, a moment ago' (syntactically a time noun that can precede or follow the subject, unlike the pure adverb 刚).

history.meaning: the moment just past; just now

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 刚才 (via 萌典)
