创伤.etymology: A coordinative compound of two synonymous Classical Chinese nouns/verbs for bodily injury: 创 (chuāng, Traditional 創, originally written 刅, depicting a knife blade 刀 inflicting a cut—its primary sense in Old Chinese before being borrowed for chuàng 'to initiate') and 伤 (shāng, Traditional 傷, 'wound, injury, to hurt'). Attested in the *Liji* (Book of Rites) for physical lacerations, in modern Mandarin it also translates psychological 'trauma'.

history.meaning: blade wounds and lacerations; physical injury from weapons
physical wound or severe psychological/emotional trauma (心灵创伤)

morphemes.meaning: cut, blade wound, sore (read chuāng in this sense)

创伤.notes: Watch the tone of 创: in the original sense of 'wound/trauma' (创伤, 重创), standard Mainland Mandarin prescribes first tone chuāngshāng, whereas in senses of 'create/initiate' (创意, 创造, 创新) it is fourth tone chuàng.

rootFamily.gloss: to inflict heavy losses or a severe blow; heavy wound
to injure, harm, hurt someone's feelings

创意.etymology: Formed from 创 (chuàng, Traditional 創, 'to initiate, pioneer, originate'—derived from 'first cut of the blade in clearing land or timber') and 意 (yì, 'thought, idea, conception', composed of 音 'sound/words' over 心 'heart-mind'). Attested in Literary Chinese (e.g., Du Fu's poetry) as a verb-object phrase meaning 'to originate a new poetic conception', it lexicalized in modern Chinese and Sino-Japanese into a noun meaning 'creative concept, originality, or pitch'.

history.meaning: to originate a fresh thought or literary conception (verb-object)
creative concept, originality, creative pitch in media/advertising (noun/adj.)

创意.notes: A core keyword in *Behind the Scenes* (*幕后之王*) and media production: 创意总监 ('creative director'), 节目创意 ('show concept/format pitch'), and 有创意 ('creative, original').

rootFamily.gloss: to create, produce (a work of art, script, or literature)
to found, establish; to start a business/venture
originality, original work (not adapted or plagiarized)

cognates.word: 刷新 / 革新 (compare 創新 sōshin)

创新.etymology: A verb-complement / verb-object compound combining 创 (chuàng, Traditional 創, 'to initiate, pioneer, establish for the first time') and 新 (xīn, 'new, fresh'). While Literary Chinese used 创新 occasionally for 'founding something anew', the word rose to prominence in 20th-century Mandarin to translate Economist Joseph Schumpeter's concept of 'innovation'—bringing forth novel methods, technologies, or creative formats by discarding old conventions.

history.meaning: to initiate or establish something new
to innovate; innovation (in technology, business, or artistic formats)

创新.notes: Functions seamlessly as both a verb (勇于创新 'dare to innovate', 创新节目模式 'innovate the show format') and a noun (自主创新 'independent innovation').

rootFamily.gloss: to reform, innovate (often institutional or technological)
to pioneer, blaze a new trail

cognates.meaning: creation, making for the first time

创造.etymology: A coordinative verb compound pairing 创 (chuàng, Traditional 創, 'to initiate, begin, carve out for the first time') and 造 (zào, 'to build, construct, make, bring into being'). Attested in Classical and Han texts such as the *Shiji* and *Hanshu* for founding dynasties, laws, or edifices, it later also absorbed the philosophical and Western sense of 'creation' ex nihilo and achieving unprecedented records.

history.meaning: to initiate and construct; to found an institution, edifice, or system for the first time
to create, bring into being, produce; to set or achieve (a record, miracle, or value)

创造.notes: Compare 创造 ('to create something new or achieve a record/value', e.g., 创造收视纪录 'set a ratings record') with 制造 (zhìzào, 'to manufacture physical goods or fabricate trouble/rumors').

rootFamily.gloss: to build, craft, fashion (a brand or hit show)

初次.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 初 (chū, 'beginning, first, initial', an ideogrammatic compound of 衣 'garment' and 刀 'knife'—cutting cloth with a knife is the very first step in tailoring clothes) and 次 (cì, originally 'camping order of troops in sequence', grammaticalized into the measure word for 'time, occasion, occurrence'). Together they mean 'on the first occasion, for the first time'.

history.meaning: 初 'first cut of cloth; beginning' + 次 'order of encampment; sequence'
the first time, for the first time (modifier or adverbial)

morphemes.meaning: first, initial, beginning (originally cutting cloth with a knife)

初次.notes: Slightly more formal than 第一次 (dì-yī cì); enshrined in the polite greeting 初次见面，请多关照 ('Nice to meet you for the first time, thank you for your guidance') and collocations like 初次登台 ('first time on stage').

rootFamily.gloss: initial, at the very beginning, original
original intention or aspiration (originally a Buddhist term)

初稿.etymology: A modifier-head noun compound formed from 初 (chū, 'first, initial', from cutting cloth 刀 + 衣) and 稿 (gǎo, variant 藁, composed of 禾 'grain stalk' and 高 phonetic, originally meaning 'straw or dried grain stalks', which in Literary Chinese came by metaphor to mean a 'rough, unpolished literary draft'—just as English 'draft' or 'straw man' evokes raw material). Together they denote the initial rough draft of a text, script, or proposal.

history.meaning: dried grain stalks, straw; by extension, an unpolished literary draft
first draft, preliminary manuscript of a document, script, or plan

morphemes.meaning: draft, manuscript, sketch (originally grain stalk / straw)

初稿.notes: In media, publishing, and scriptwriting workflows, 初稿 ('first draft') progresses through 改稿 ('revising the draft') and 审稿 ('reviewing the draft') to 定稿 (dìnggǎo, 'finalized draft') or 终稿 (zhōnggǎo, 'final version').

rootFamily.gloss: to finalize a manuscript or script; final draft
manuscript, article, script, or press release

初级.etymology: A modifier-head compound joining 初 (chū, 'first, initial, elementary') and 级 (jí, Traditional 級, composed of 糸 'silk thread' and 及 phonetic, originally 'order of silk threads', then under the Qin legal code 'severed enemy heads awarded one rank of nobility each', and hence 'step, grade, rank, or tier'). Together they mean 'initial rank or tier'—hence junior, elementary, or entry-level.

history.meaning: order of silk threads; grade of nobility earned in battle; stone steps
elementary level, primary stage, junior or entry-level rank

morphemes.meaning: grade, rank, level, step (originally silk-thread order / rank)

初级.notes: Forms a standard three-tier hierarchy across Chinese workplaces, exams, and proficiency scales: 初级 ('junior / elementary'), 中级 (zhōngjí, 'intermediate / mid-level'), and 高级 (gāojí, 'senior / advanced').

初选.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining the temporal/ordinal modifier 初 (chū, 'first, initial, preliminary') and the verb/noun 选 (xuǎn, Traditional 選, 'to choose, select, elect'). Originating in imperial bureaucratic and literary selection terminology and modernized in 20th-century electoral and competition contexts, it denotes a preliminary screening, first-round audition, or political primary election.

history.meaning: first-round screening or preliminary election/audition (in politics, contests, or talent casting)

morphemes.meaning: initially, in the first round, preliminarily

初选.notes: In talent shows and television production (*幕后之王*), contestants must pass 初选 ('first-round selection / preliminary screening') or 海选 ('open mass auditions') before entering 复选 ('second-round callbacks') and 决赛 ('finals').

rootFamily.gloss: open mass audition or preliminary screening
to be selected, make the shortlist or final roster
to select and appoint; talent selection competition

cognates.meaning: to strike out, delete, expunge (in compounds like 削除 sakujo)

删.etymology: An ideogrammatic compound (会意) combining 册 (cè, Traditional 冊, depicting bamboo or wooden slips bound together with cords, the writing medium of antiquity) and 刀 (刂, dāo, 'knife'). Before paper, scribes erased errors on bamboo slips by scraping off the inked surface layer with a small bronze or iron書刀 ('book-knife'); thus 删 literally meant 'to pare a bamboo slip with a knife to expunge text', evolving into 'to delete, edit out, or strike out'.

history.meaning: to scrape written characters off bamboo slips with a scribe's knife; to abridge or expunge text (as in Confucius's 刪詩 'editing the Odes')
to delete, strike out, edit out, remove (text, scenes, or digital files)

morphemes.meaning: to delete, erase, expunge (originally scraping bamboo slips 册 with a knife 刂)

删.notes: Used alone as a monosyllabic verb mainly in spoken or informal Mandarin (e.g., 把这段删了 'delete this part', 删好友 'unfriend / delete a contact'); in formal writing, disyllabic 删除 or 删减 is preferred.

rootFamily.gloss: to abridge, cut down, edit out (scenes or word count)
to revise and edit text by cutting and changing

cognates.meaning: to delete footage or cut film scenes

删片.etymology: A contemporary verb-object (VO) compound formed from 删 (shān, 'to delete, cut, expunge') and 片 (piàn, originally a pictograph of half a split tree trunk 爿 'flat wood chip/slice', extended in modern Chinese to photographic film strips 胶片 and video files/episodes 节目片源). In television and film production, 删片 means deleting master video files or cutting footage from a film/show.

history.meaning: 刪 'to scrape text off bamboo slips' + 片 'flat slice of wood'
to delete video master files or cut footage from a broadcast program or film

morphemes.meaning: film, video footage, episode master file (clipping of 片子 / 成片)

删片.notes: A separable VO verb in post-production and broadcast jargon; in northern speech 片 often takes the retroflex suffix and high-level colloquial tone (删片儿, shānpiānr) when referring to film/video clips.

rootFamily.gloss: finished film or final edited video master
film, movie, video clip, or television episode

删除.etymology: A coordinative / verb-resultative compound uniting 删 (shān, Traditional 刪, 'to scrape off bamboo slips with a knife; to expunge') and 除 (chú, originally 'steps to a palace hall', extended in Classical Chinese to 'sweep away, clear out, remove'). Attested in Han dynasty histories (e.g., *Hanshu*) for expunging superfluous laws or passages from texts, it is today the standard formal and computing term for 'delete'.

history.meaning: to pare away and remove superfluous passages, statutes, or records
to delete, erase, remove (text, scenes, or digital data)

morphemes.meaning: to scrape off, expunge, strike out

删除.notes: The standard disyllabic verb on Chinese software buttons and formal editing instructions ('Delete'); unlike 删, 删除 is never split as a separable verb.

判断.etymology: A coordinative compound of two Classical Chinese verbs of cutting that evolved into legal and cognitive terms: 判 (pàn, composed of 半 'half' and 刀 'knife', literally 'to cleave in half', hence a magistrate splitting tally credentials or handing down a verdict) and 断 (duàn, Traditional 斷, 'to sever silk threads with an axe 斤; to decide conclusively'). From 'adjudicating a legal case' in Tang–Song Chinese, it broadened in modern Sino-Japanese and Mandarin to cognitive 'judgment, assessment, and determination'.

history.meaning: to cleave and sever; to hear and adjudicate a legal suit or official petition
to judge, assess, determine; logical or practical judgment (verb and noun)

morphemes.meaning: to cleave in half with a knife; to distinguish, adjudicate, judge
to sever, cut off; to decide, determine conclusively

判断.notes: Used both as a transitive verb (判断市场趋势 'assess market trends') and as a noun (做出判断 'make a judgment'), and forms the compound 判断力 (pànduànlì, 'good judgment, discernment').

rootFamily.gloss: court verdict, judicial ruling; to sentence

cognates.meaning: sharp weapon; effective tool; high capability

利器.etymology: Modifier-head (偏正) compound formed from 利 (lì, "sharp, keen, cutting", an ancient ideogrammic compound of 禾 grain and 刀 knife depicting harvesting with a sharp blade) + 器 (qì, "vessel, implement, weapon"). Famously attested in Classical Chinese philosophical texts—including the Dao De Jing (Ch. 36: 国之利器不可以示人, "the sharp weapons of the state must not be displayed to others") and the Analects (Wei Ling Gong: 工欲善其事，必先利其器, "a craftsman who wishes to do his work well must first sharpen his tools")—the term evolved from literal bladed weaponry and artisan tools into a figurative designation for a trump card, powerhouse asset, or "secret weapon" in business and media competition.

history.meaning: sharp military weapon; keen-edged artisan tool or state instrument
effective instrument; decisive tool or talent
powerful tool; secret weapon; killer app or decisive asset

利器.notes: Frequently used in media, tech, and corporate strategy in the pattern X是...的利器 ("X is a secret weapon / killer tool for...").

利润.etymology: Coordinative (并列) compound uniting 利 (lì, "benefit, material gain, interest") and 润 (rùn, "moisture, enrichment, financial margin"). Originally attested in Early Middle Chinese historical prose (such as the Records of the Three Kingdoms / Sanguozhi) with the general sense of material enrichment or benefit, the compound was adopted by Meiji-era Japanese scholars as 利潤 (rijun) to render Western political-economy "profit" (surplus value over cost of production) and subsequently re-entered modern Mandarin as a foundational financial and corporate noun.

history.meaning: enrichment, material benefit, nourishing gain
economic profit, surplus return on capital
financial profit, net or gross margin in commerce

利润.notes: Refers specifically to monetary/accounting profit (as in 利润率 "profit margin" or 净利润 "net profit"), unlike broader好处 ("benefit").

rootFamily.gloss: moist, sleek; to lubricate or remunerate
remuneration for writing or artwork (lit. moistening the brush)

利用.etymology: Classical Chinese compound originating in the Book of Changes (Yijing, Qian hexagram: 利用宾于王, and Xici commentary: 利用安身, "benefiting usage so as to secure one's person"), combining 利 (lì, "to make advantageous, benefit, sharpen") and 用 (yòng, "to use, employ; utility"). In Classical texts it functioned as a verb-object or coordinative phrase meaning "to make advantageous use of"; in the modern era (reinforced via Japanese 利用 riyō), it grammaticalized into a transitive verb spanning neutral "to utilize/employ (resources, time)" and pejorative "to exploit/manipulate (a person) for selfish ends."

history.meaning: to benefit utility; advantageous application of tools or conduct
to utilize, make use of (resources); to exploit or use (someone)

利用.notes: Neutral when the object is a thing or opportunity (利用时间 "make use of time"), but strongly pejorative when the object is a person (你别利用我 "don't use/manipulate me").

利索.etymology: Colloquial Northern Mandarin adjective formed from 利 (lì, "sharp, smooth, unhindered, nimble") + 索 (suo, originally "twine, rope" or "to search", here functioning as a vernacular prosodic suffixoid with neutral tone that reinforces smoothness and completion, cf. 罗嗦 / 利利索索). Attested in Qing-dynasty Beijing vernacular fiction such as Dream of the Red Chamber (Hongloumeng), the word extended the metaphor of a clean, unentangled blade or cord to describe agile physical movement, fluent speech, neatness, or having a messy affair completely sorted out.

history.meaning: nimble, unencumbered, brisk and tidy in speech or action
clean and tidy, brisk, efficient, completely sorted out

morphemes.meaning: vernacular descriptive element denoting smoothness or completion (neutral tone)

利索.notes: Spoken Northern Mandarin register (second syllable always neutral tone lìsuo); often reduplicated as 利利索索 for vivid emphasis ("neat and brisk").

利落.etymology: Vernacular Mandarin compound attested from Song–Yuan baihua literature through Ming–Qing novels (such as Water Margin and Dream of the Red Chamber), combining 利 (lì, "sharp, nimble, smooth") and 落 (luò, read with neutral tone luo, "to fall into place, settle, conclude cleanly"). Structurally a coordinative/complementary compound, it pairs the keenness of a sharp edge (利) with a clean, decisive landing (落) to portray actions, speech, or layouts that are crisp, efficient, and free of sloppy loose ends.

history.meaning: agile, brisk, settled cleanly without dragging on
crisp, neat and efficient; completely settled or finished

morphemes.meaning: settle, fall into place, finish cleanly (neutral tone in compound)

利落.notes: Frequently pairs with 干净 in the four-character idiom 干净利落 ("clean and crisp; neat and efficient without any fuss").

别.etymology: Ideogram (別) showing a knife (刂/刀) separating bone from bone/flesh (咼): 'separate, part, distinguish, other/another (别人); fasten with a pin'. In modern northern Mandarin, 别 (bié) also serves as the prohibitive adverb 'don't!' (widely analyzed as a phonetic fusion of 不要 bú yào).

history.meaning: cut apart; separate; distinguish; another
prohibitive 'don't!' (fusion of 不要); other; leave

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 别 (via 萌典)

别人.etymology: Compound pronoun of 别 ('other, another, separate') + 人 ('person, people'): 'other people, others, someone else'.

history.meaning: another person; other people; others

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 别人 (via 萌典)

别去.etymology: Colloquial Mandarin negative imperative verb phrase composed of 别 (bié, prohibitive adverb "do not!", widely explained by historical linguists as a late-imperial Northern Mandarin phonological fusion/contraction of 不要 bùyào, reinforced by the ancient sense of 别 "to turn away, separate") + 去 (qù, "to go, depart from the speaker's location", originally meaning "to leave" in Classical Chinese). It functions as a direct spoken command or earnest piece of advice telling the addressee not to go somewhere.

history.meaning: do not go; refrain from departing
don't go (colloquial prohibitive phrase)

别去.notes: In spoken Mandarin, 别去 is softer and more conversational than the formal prohibitive 请勿前往 ("please do not proceed there"). Note that in classical poetry 别去 could mean "to part and leave," a sense obsolete in casual speech.

rootFamily.gloss: don't mention it; not to speak of

别扭.etymology: Vernacular Northern Mandarin coordinative compound combining 别 (read biè in the fourth tone: "stubborn, perverse, contrary, unable to turn smoothly", related to 别劲) and 扭 (niǔ, read with neutral tone niu: "to twist, wrench, turn awkwardly", an ideogrammic/phono-semantic character of 手 hand + 丑 twisting claw). Literally describing two mechanical parts or limbs twisted out of alignment so they jam against each other, it evolved in Qing and modern Beijing vernacular to express psychological discomfort, awkwardness in style or speech, and interpersonal friction.

history.meaning: twisted, jammed, refractory, at odds
awkward, unnatural, uncomfortable; difficult or stubborn in temperament

morphemes.meaning: contrary, stubborn, jammed (pronounced biè in 4th tone)
twist, wrench, turn awkwardly (neutral tone in compound)

别扭.notes: Watch the tone: 别 is pronounced biè (4th tone, traditionally written 彆) here, not bié (2nd tone). Can be used as an adjective (说话很别扭 "speaking unnaturally") or in the VO phrase 闹别扭 ("to have a spat / be at odds").

别查.etymology: Colloquial Mandarin negative imperative verb-object/adverb-verb phrase formed from 别 (bié, prohibitive adverb "do not, stop", derived from the vernacular contraction of 不要 bùyào in Northern Mandarin) + 查 (chá, "to investigate, inspect, audit, look up", originally a graph for a wooden raft 楂 that was borrowed in Middle Chinese for 察/稽查 "to examine closely"). Used in spoken drama and workplace dialogue to instruct someone to call off an investigation or stop checking records.

history.meaning: do not investigate; stop checking or auditing

别查.notes: Often followed by 了 (别查了 "stop investigating / drop the inquiry") when telling someone to halt an ongoing search or audit.

别的.etymology: Vernacular Mandarin determiner/pronoun construction consisting of 别 (bié, "to divide, distinguish, separate; other, another", originally an oracle-bone and bronze script ideogram of a knife 刀 cutting bone 冎 apart, whence "distinct, other") + 的 (de, subordinating and nominalizing structural particle, which evolved from Tang–Song vernacular 底 and functionally replaced Classical Chinese 之/者). Crystallized in early baihua Mandarin, 别的 functions both as an attributive determiner ("other X") and as a standalone pronominal ("something/someone else").

history.meaning: to divide, separate; distinct, another (as in 别国, 别人)
other, another, anything else (attributive and pronominal)

别的.notes: Unlike 别人 ("other people"), 别的 can modify any noun (别的事 "other matters", 别的节目 "other shows") or stand alone as a pronoun (还要别的吗？ "Do you want anything else?").

刮.etymology: Written 刮 (guā), combining 舌 ('tongue', here remnant of an older phonetic/graphic component 𠯑) with the knife radical 刂 (刀, 'blade'), attested in Classical Chinese with the core sense 'to scrape, pare, or shave clean with a blade'. Under simplified orthography, 刮 also merged the distinct storm-wind character 颳 (composed of 風 'wind' + phonetic 𠯑, meaning 'of wind, to blow'). Consequently modern 刮 covers both surface scraping (刮响, 刮胡子) and gusts of wind (刮风).

morphemes.meaning: scrape with an edge (刀); also merged simplified form of 颳 'wind blows'

history.meaning: scrape, plane, or rub off a surface
scrape, scratch; blow (of wind)

刮痕.etymology: A modifier-head compound joining 刮 (guā, 'to scrape, scratch against a hard surface') and 痕 (hén, 'scar, trace, mark', formed with the sickness/blemish radical 疒 and phonetic 艮). Whereas 伤痕 refers to a bodily scar and 折痕 to a paper fold, 刮痕 specifically denotes a linear scratch or scuff left on wood, metal, paint, or stone by friction.

history.meaning: scar or physical trace (痕迹)
surface scratch or scrape mark

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 刮痕

到.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining 至 ('arrive, reach a destination', showing an arrow hitting the ground) + 刀 (刂, phonetic dào): 'arrive at, reach, go to; up until; thoughtful/thorough (周到)'.

history.meaning: arrive; reach
arrive; reach; to/until; resultative complement of attainment

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 到 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: arriving at one's post, assuming office
arrival at a newly appointed post

到任.etymology: Verb-object (动宾) compound formed from 到 (dào, "to arrive at, reach", a phono-semantic compound of 至 "arrive" and phonetic 刀) + 任 (rèn, "official post, appointed office, duty", originally "to carry a load or entrust"). Originating in imperial Chinese bureaucratic terminology (attested across Tang, Song, and Ming–Qing administrative records) to denote a newly commissioned magistrate or governor arriving at their jurisdiction to take up the seal of office, it remains standard in modern corporate and institutional contexts for an executive assuming a new post.

history.meaning: (of an imperial official) to arrive at one's jurisdiction and assume office
to take up a post, assume office (of diplomats, executives, or officials)

到任.notes: Slightly formal and institutional in register; frequently used in corporate announcements when a new director, CEO, or department head officially starts work (新总监今天到任).

rootFamily.gloss: assume office, take up a post
appoint to an official or corporate position
leave office, step down from a post

到位.etymology: Verb-object (动宾) compound combining 到 (dào, "to arrive at, reach") + 位 (wèi, "seat, rank, designated position", an ideogrammic compound of 人 "person" standing at 立 "a court station"). In Classical ritual texts (such as the Book of Rites), 到位 literally meant stepping into one's assigned ceremonial station. In modern Mandarin, it underwent rich metaphorical expansion: first to personnel, equipment, or capital "getting into position / being in place," and subsequently to an adjectival predicate meaning "spot-on, thorough, up to standard, or well-executed" (e.g., 表演很到位).

history.meaning: to arrive at one's ceremonial rank or assigned seat
to get into position (of crew, funds, gear); spot-on, thorough, up to the mark (of execution)

morphemes.meaning: position, place, designated spot or standard

到位.notes: In TV/film production, used both literally as a stage call (灯光摄像到位 "lighting and cameras in position!") and evaluatively as an adjective with 很/非常 (细节处理得很到位 "the details were handled spot-on").

rootFamily.gloss: be in one's post or seat; on the job

到处.etymology: Spatial adverb combining 到 ('reach, go to') + 处 (處, 'place'): 'everyplace one reaches -> everywhere, all over'. Attested frequently from Tang–Song poetry (e.g., 春眠不觉晓，处处闻啼鸟 / 到处).

history.meaning: everywhere; in all places

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 到处 (via 萌典)

到头.etymology: Verb-object (动宾) compound formed from 到 (dào, "to reach, arrive at") + 头 (tóu, "head; extremity, terminus, end point"). Beginning in Tang and Song vernacular poetry and Chan (Zen) Buddhist recorded sayings (yulu), 头 grammaticalized and extended from anatomical "head" to the spatial or temporal "end/limit" of a road, thread, or lifespan. 到头 thus came to mean reaching the very end of a path or process, coming to a close, or hitting an ultimate limit.

history.meaning: to reach the extremity or end of a road, cycle, or process
to reach the end, come to a close, hit a limit

到头.notes: Often used with 了 (走到了尽头 / 日子到头了 "the days have come to an end") or extended into 到头来 ("in the end, after all is said and done").

rootFamily.gloss: in the end, finally, when all is said and done

到底.etymology: Verb-object phrase of 到 ('reach') + 底 ('bottom, end'). Means literally 'to the very bottom / to the very end' (坚持到底), and as a modal adverb in questions or realizations: 'after all, in the end, on earth (what/why on earth…?)'.

history.meaning: to the very bottom/end; after all; on earth (in questions)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 到底 (via 萌典)

到手.etymology: Verb-object (动宾) compound uniting 到 (dào, "to arrive at, reach") and 手 (shǒu, "hand, personal grasp", a pictograph of a five-fingered hand). Attested in Tang–Song poetry and vernacular prose, it literally depicts a coveted object, letter, or prize arriving directly in one's hand, from which it idiomatized into "to obtain, secure in one's possession, clinch (a contract or rights), or receive (take-home pay)."

history.meaning: to arrive in one's hands; to come into one's grasp
to obtain, secure in one's possession, have in hand (of contracts, money, prizes)

到手.notes: Very common in business and workplace speech for both clinching a deal (版权终于到手了 "we finally got the copyright in hand") and net take-home pay (到手工资 "after-tax take-home salary").

rootFamily.gloss: begin, set one's hand to, get started
put one's hand to; start a task

到时候.etymology: Vernacular Mandarin verb-object temporal phrase that lexicalized into a sentence-level temporal adverbial: 到 (dào, "to reach, arrive at [a point in time]") + 时候 (shíhou, "time, juncture, moment", itself a disyllabic compound of 时 "season, time" and 候 "five-day phenological period, watch, juncture"). Emerging in Ming–Qing baihua fiction, 到时候 projects the speaker and listener forward to an anticipated future moment ("when that time arrives, when the time comes").

history.meaning: when the appointed moment or juncture arrives
when the time comes, at that future juncture

morphemes.meaning: time, moment, juncture (neutral tone on 候)

到时候.notes: In rapid Northern speech, often contracted via erhua to 到时候儿 or paired with 再说 (到时候再说吧 "let's cross that bridge when we come to it").

到齐.etymology: Resultative verb compound (动补结构) composed of 到 (dào, "to arrive, be present") + 齐 (qí, "even, uniform, complete, all together", originally an oracle-bone pictograph of three grain heads standing at equal height in a field). In this construction, 到 expresses the action of arriving while 齐 serves as the resultative complement indicating that every member of an expected group or set of items is now present without omission.

history.meaning: to arrive in full number; all present and accounted for
to all arrive, be all present (of meeting attendees, cast, or materials)

到齐.notes: Supports potential infixes: 到得齐 ("able to all arrive") and 到不齐 ("unable to get everyone present at once"). Essential before starting a meeting or shoot (人到齐了，我们开会 "Everyone's here, let's start the meeting").

cognates.meaning: production (of film, TV, art), creation, manufacture

制作.etymology: Coordinative (并列) compound formed from 制 (zhì, representing traditional 製 "to cut cloth, fashion, manufacture" merged with 制 "to regulate, establish") + 作 (zuò, "to make, create, compose"). Attested in Classical Chinese ritual and historical texts (such as the Rites of Zhou, Book of Rites, and Shiji) for crafting ceremonial vessels, music, or institutions. In the 20th century, reinforced by Japanese 制作/製作 (seisaku), it became the standard professional term across East Asia for film, television, music, and stage production.

history.meaning: to fashion ritual implements, compose music, or establish institutions; literary creation
production; to produce, make, or craft (especially TV shows, films, music, and digital media)

morphemes.meaning: fashion, cut and make, manufacture (trad. 製/制)

制作.notes: Whereas 制造 (zhìzào) refers to industrial/factory manufacturing, 制作 (zhìzuò) is used for creative, artistic, broadcast, or culinary production (节目制作 "show production", 后期制作 "post-production").

rootFamily.gloss: work of art, literary or media work

制作人.etymology: Modifier-head (偏正) occupational noun formed from 制作 (zhìzuò, "media/artistic production; to produce") + 人 (rén, "person, specialist", functioning as an agentive suffix equivalent to English "-er"). Coined in the modern Chinese television, radio, and recording industries as a calque of English "producer," it specifically designates the creative and operational mastermind who helms a variety show, television program, or music album from concept to broadcast.

history.meaning: producer (of television programs, variety shows, or music albums)
history.stage: Modern Mandarin (20th–21st c. broadcast & music industry)

制作人.notes: Industry nuance in *Behind the Scenes* (幕后之王): 制作人 (producer/showrunner) is the standard title in variety shows (综艺) and music for the creative head, whereas 制片人 is preferred in narrative film and scripted TV dramas for the financial/administrative producer.

rootFamily.gloss: film/TV producer (especially scripted drama and cinema)

制作会.etymology: Modifier-head (偏正) compound combining 制作 (zhìzuò, "broadcast/media production") + 会 (huì, "meeting, assembly, conference", clipped from 会议 huìyì, originally meaning "to assemble, come together" beneath a lid 亼). Formed in modern Chinese television and film studio jargon, it denotes a production meeting where producers, directors, writers, and technical heads align on rundown schedules, scripts, staging, and budgets.

history.meaning: production meeting (in television, film, or stage production)

制作会.notes: Takes the verb 开 (开制作会 "to hold a production meeting"), a staple workplace collocation in broadcast television dramas.

cognates.meaning: production department (in broadcasting, publishing, or studios)

制作部.etymology: Modifier-head (偏正) institutional compound composed of 制作 (zhìzuò, "production of media/creative works") + 部 (bù, "department, division, ministry", originally denoting a territorial or administrative section with the mound/city radical 阝). Modeled on modern East Asian corporate and bureaucratic nomenclature (parallel to Japanese 制作部 seisakubu), it names the "Production Department" within a television network, studio, or media agency responsible for creating and executing programs.

history.meaning: production department or division in a broadcast network, studio, or publisher

制作部.notes: In a media company hierarchy, 制作部 contrasts with 宣传部 / 宣发部 (PR & Marketing Department), 广告部 (Advertising Department), and 行政部 (Administration Department).

制图员.etymology: Occupational compound formed from 制图 ('drafting; cartography', from 制 'make; fashion; regulate' + 图 'map; diagram; chart') + agentive suffix 员 ('member; technical specialist', originally a round bronze cauldron ding 鼎 with a circle above its rim).

history.meaning: cartographer; architectural or engineering drafter

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 制图员

cognates.meaning: system, institution, established regime or rules

制度.etymology: Coordinative (并列) compound uniting 制 (zhì, "decree, regulation, cut pattern") and 度 (dù, "linear measure, standard, law", originally a hand 又 measuring a span). Attested in the Book of Changes (Yijing, Jie hexagram: 节以制度，不伤财，不害民, "regulating by means of standards and rules so as neither to waste wealth nor harm the people") and the Book of Rites. In Meiji Japan, 制度 (seido) was used to translate Western political and sociological "system / institution," returning to modern Mandarin to denote both macro-level socio-political systems and micro-level corporate rules and bylaws.

history.meaning: ritual standards, statutory measurements, imperial decrees and regulations
political, legal, or social institution/system (translating English "system / institution")
institutional system; corporate rules, policies, and regulations

制度.notes: False-friend alert for learners: 制度 refers to an institutional or regulatory system (公司制度 "company rules/policies", 政治制度 "political system"), NEVER a computer or technical system (which is 系统 xìtǒng).

rootFamily.gloss: establish, formulate, draw up (laws or rules)

cognates.meaning: restraint, stopping by force or authority, control

制止.etymology: Coordinative and resultative (并列/动补) verb compound combining 制 (zhì, "to restrain, overpower, govern, curb") + 止 (zhǐ, "to stop, halt, cease", originally an oracle-bone pictograph of a human foot). Attested in Classical and Early Middle Chinese historiography (including the Book of the Later Han / Hou Hanshu and Zizhi Tongjian), it denotes exercising authority, pressure, or physical intervention to bring an ongoing or incipient harmful action to a halt.

history.meaning: to restrain and halt by imperial authority or force
to stop, curb, prevent, or put an end to (unruly or improper behavior)

制止.notes: Unlike 停止 ("to stop doing something oneself"), 制止 is strictly transitive and means stopping *someone else's* undesirable action or a bad situation (及时制止 "to step in and stop it in time").

制片.etymology: Verb-object (动宾) compound formed from 制 (zhì, representing 製作/制造 "to manufacture, produce") + 片 (piàn, "flat slice, celluloid film strip, motion picture", clipped from 影片 yǐngpiàn). Coined in early 20th-century Shanghai cinema studios to mean "producing motion pictures" (as in 制片厂 "film studio"), it underwent metonymic shift in film and television industry parlance to serve as conversational shorthand for the producer or production manager on set (制片主任 / 制片人).

history.meaning: film production; manufacturing motion pictures (as in 制片厂)
film/TV production; shorthand for producer or line/unit production manager

morphemes.meaning: film, motion picture (clipped from 影片)

制片.notes: On a Chinese film or TV set, calling someone 制片 often refers either to the executive producer (制片人) or to the hands-on line/unit production manager (现场制片 / 制片主任) who handles logistics, budgets, and locations.

制片人.etymology: Modifier-head (偏正) occupational compound consisting of 制片 (zhìpiàn, "film/drama production; to produce a film") + 人 (rén, "person, specialist", acting as an agentive suffix). Developed in modern Chinese cinema and television terminology as the standard title for a film or drama "producer"—the executive responsible for project development, financing, budgeting, hiring key talent, and overseeing the business and logistical lifecycle of a production.

history.meaning: film or television drama producer (overseeing financing, management, and production)
history.stage: Modern Mandarin (20th–21st c. cinema and TV)

制片人.notes: Distinguished from 导演 (director, who leads creative filming on set) and 出品人 (presenter/studio financier); the 制片人 bridges capital and creative execution.

rootFamily.gloss: presenter, executive financier of a film/show

制衡.etymology: Modern literary and political compound formed by blending 制 (zhì, "to restrain, check, control", clipped from 制约 zhìyuē) + 衡 (héng, "steelyard balance beam, equilibrium, to weigh and counterbalance", clipped from 平衡 pínghéng). Structurally a coordinative/causal verb compound ("to check and thereby balance"), it was coined in modern Chinese political science to translate the Western constitutional doctrine of "checks and balances" (权力制衡) and rapidly entered corporate boardroom and media strategy discourse.

history.meaning: to check and balance; to counterbalance rival powers or factions in politics or corporate governance

morphemes.meaning: restrain, check, keep under control (from 制约)
weigh, balance, maintain equilibrium (from 平衡)

制衡.notes: High-register strategic verb favored in boardroom dramas and political analysis (相互制衡 "mutually check and balance each other").

rootFamily.gloss: weigh, measure, evaluate pros and cons

刷.etymology: Character combining 尸/巾 ('cloth/body') + 刀 (刂, 'blade/scraper'): originally 'scrape, wipe clean, brush'. Used in Mandarin as a noun ('brush') and verb ('brush, scrub, paint/coat with a brush, swipe a card'), and read shuā as an onomatopoeia for a swift swishing sound.

history.meaning: scrape; wipe clean; brush
brush; scrub; paint; swipe (a card)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 刷 (via 萌典)

刷卡.etymology: Modern verb-object (动宾) compound uniting 刷 (shuā, "to brush, sweep rapidly across a surface", originally an ideogrammic compound with 刀 knife and 巾/尸 cloth for scraping and brushing clean) + 卡 (kǎ, "card", a 20th-century phonetic loan and clipping of English "card" via 卡片 kǎpiàn). Coined in late 20th-century Mandarin with the proliferation of magnetic-stripe credit cards, transit cards, and RFID office badges, it extended the physical sweeping motion of brushing (刷) to swiping or tapping a card at a reader.

history.meaning: to swipe or tap a bank card, transit card, or employee security badge

morphemes.meaning: brush, swipe rapidly across a reader
card, keycard, bank card (loan from English "card")

刷卡.notes: As a separable verb-object (离合词), aspect markers and modifiers go in the middle: 刷了卡 ("swiped the card"), 刷一下卡 ("give the card/badge a quick swipe"). Covers both magnetic swiping and contactless RFID tapping.

rootFamily.gloss: card (credit card, ID card, greeting card)
flood the screen; go viral across feeds
punch in/out at work; visit a trendy landmark

刷子.etymology: Derived noun from 刷 ('scrape; brush; wipe clean', knife 刂 beside a cloth napkin 巾 beneath a body 尸) + nominal suffix 子. Brushes made of hog bristles or horsehair bound into wood or bamboo handles have been used in China since antiquity for cleaning utensils, applying ink to stone inscriptions, and coating wood with oil or lacquer.

history.meaning: bristle brush for scrubbing or coating
brush (paintbrush, pastry brush, scrubbing brush)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 刷子

刷屏.etymology: Contemporary Chinese internet and media verb-object (动宾) neologism combining 刷 (shuā, "to brush, sweep over, refresh rapidly") + 屏 (píng, "screen, display monitor", clipped from 屏幕 píngmù; in Classical Chinese 屏 originally meant a decorative folding screen or partition wall that shields view). Originating in late-1990s BBS forums and chatrooms for spamming repetitive text so rapidly that it wipes/fills the entire monitor, it broadened in the social-media and television era to mean a viral topic, show, or celebrity dominating everyone's feeds and live bullet-comment screens (弹幕).

history.meaning: to spam a chatroom or forum with repetitive posts that fill the display
to flood the screen (with bullet comments); to go viral and dominate social media feeds

morphemes.meaning: screen, monitor, social feed (clipped from 屏幕)

刷屏.notes: In media and showbiz (like *Behind the Scenes*), 刷屏 is a coveted metric of viral success: 被某节目刷屏了 means "my entire social feed is flooded with posts about that show."

rootFamily.gloss: dominated the screen (of an actor appearing in every show on air)

cognates.meaning: reform, renovation, complete renewal; breaking a record

刷新.etymology: Resultative verb compound (动补结构) formed from 刷 (shuā, "to scrub, brush, wipe clean") + 新 (xīn, "new, fresh"). Literally "to scrub away the old until brand new" (attested in late imperial vernacular Chinese and popularized across East Asia via Japanese 刷新 sasshin for institutional reform and record-breaking), it developed two primary modern senses: figuratively surpassing and setting a new high (刷新纪录 "to break/reset a record" or 刷新认知 "to reshape one's understanding"), and digitally "refreshing" a webpage or data feed.

history.meaning: to scrub clean and make brand new; to renovate or reform thoroughly
to break/reset (a record or perception); to refresh (a computer screen or webpage)

刷新.notes: Highly versatile across media ratings (刷新收视纪录 "break viewership records"), computing (刷新页面 "refresh the page"), and slang (刷新三观 "completely blow/reshape one's worldview").

rootFamily.gloss: update, renew, replace the old with new
innovate, bring forth new ideas; innovation

刷漆.etymology: Verb-object compound of 刷 ('brush on, apply with a brush') + 漆 ('lacquer, paint', originally sap dripping from a lacquer tree 桼): 'apply paint, brush on paint or lacquer'.

history.meaning: paint with a brush; apply coat of paint

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 刷漆 (via 萌典)

刻.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 亥 (hài/kè phonetic) + 刀 (刂, 'knife, engraving blade'): 'carve, engrave, cut notches; water-clock notch (quarter-hour); moment; harsh/cutting (刻薄)'.

history.meaning: carve with a blade; notch on a water clock
carve; engrave; quarter of an hour; moment

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 刻 (via 萌典)

刻度.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 刻度. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 刻度 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 刻度 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 刻度 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 刻度. The etymology of 刻度 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 刻度
middle form of 刻度
modern form of 刻度

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 刻度

前.etymology: Originally written 歬 (a foot 止 standing on a boat 舟 moving forward without paddling), later adding a knife 刀 to form 前 (which originally meant 'trim/cut'—subsequently re-written 剪 with a second刀—while 前 took over 'move forward, front, before, ago, former').

morphemes.meaning: foot on a boat advancing forward

history.meaning: advance forward; front; before; earlier
front; forward; before; ago; former

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 前 (via 萌典)

前两天.etymology: Modifier-head (偏正) temporal noun phrase composed of 前 (qián, "front, before, prior, ago", originally written 歬 depicting a foot 止 atop a boat 舟 moving forward) + 两 (liǎng, "two, a pair", functioning in colloquial Mandarin temporal phrases as an approximate paucal quantifier meaning "a couple of, a few") + 天 (tiān, "sky, Heaven; twenty-four-hour day"). Because 两 is idiomatic and non-exact here, 前两天 means "the past couple of days" or "a few days ago" rather than strictly "48 hours ago."

history.meaning: the past couple of days, a few days ago (vernacular temporal expression)

morphemes.meaning: two; idiomatically a couple of, a few

前两天.notes: Crucial learner distinction: "two days ago" (the day before yesterday) is 前天 (qiántiān); 前两天 (qiánliǎngtiān) is approximate and means "a couple of days ago / the other day" (virtually synonymous with 前几天).

rootFamily.gloss: a few days ago, the other day
in a couple of days (in the near future)

前几天.etymology: Modifier-head (偏正) temporal noun phrase uniting 前 (qián, "before, prior, ago") + 几 (jǐ, originally a small low table 幾 or "how many?", used in affirmative declarative clauses as an indefinite paucal quantifier meaning "several, a few, a small number of") + 天 (tiān, "day"). Formed in vernacular Mandarin as the standard spoken way to anchor an event in the recent, unspecified past ("a few days ago, the other day").

history.meaning: a few days ago, several days ago, the other day

前几天.notes: Placed either before or right after the subject to set the time frame (我前几天见过他 or 前几天我见过他 "I saw him a few days ago")—never at the end of a Chinese sentence like English "ago".

rootFamily.gloss: the past couple of days, a few days ago
the past few days, these last few days

前半段.etymology: Three-morpheme structural noun of 前 ('front; first; earlier') + 半 ('half', depicting an ox 牛 divided by八) + 段 ('section; segment; passage'). Paired symmetrically with 后半段 ('second half'), it designates the opening half of a musical piece, story, or journey.

history.meaning: first half of a passage, piece, or route

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 前半段

前台.etymology: Compound noun of 前 ('front') + 台 ('stage, counter, desk'): originally 'the front of the theater stage' (as opposed to 后台 'backstage'), and in modern hotels, offices, and companies 'the front desk, reception desk'.

history.meaning: front of the stage -> reception desk, front desk

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 前台 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: the other day, a few days ago (cognate characters, slightly broader sense)
cognates.word: 先日 (senjitsu) / 前日 (zenjitsu - previous day)

前天.etymology: Modifier-head (偏正) deictic temporal compound formed from 前 (qián, "ahead, prior to the preceding one") + 天 (tiān, "sky, day", which systematically replaced Classical Chinese 日 rì in Northern vernacular time nouns during the Tang–Yuan transition, cf. 今日 → 今天, 昨日 → 昨天). Derived from Literary Chinese 前日 (qiánrì), where 前 designates one step further back in the past than 昨 ("yesterday"), it fixes the exact calendar reference "the day before yesterday."

history.meaning: the day before yesterday; formerly, in days past
the day before yesterday (two days prior to today)

morphemes.meaning: before, prior (one step further back than yesterday)

前天.notes: Part of Mandarin's symmetrical 5-day deictic system around 今天 (today): 大前天 (3 days ago) → 前天 (day before yesterday) → 昨天 (yesterday) → 今天 (today) → 明天 (tomorrow) → 后天 (day after tomorrow) → 大后天 (3 days from now).

rootFamily.gloss: three days ago (the day before the day before yesterday)

前女友.etymology: A modern Mandarin modifier-head compound prefixing the temporal-spatial attributive 前 (qián, 'former, previous', originally 'to advance' in Oracle Bone and Bronze inscriptions, showing a foot 止 atop a boat 舟) to 女友 (nǚyǒu, 'girlfriend', itself a 20th-century modifier-head coinage from 女 'female' + 友 'friend'). The prefixal use of 前 to mark a former role or relationship ('ex-') expanded from imperial and bureaucratic titles (such as 前任 'former incumbent') into modern interpersonal vocabulary under the influence of English 'ex-girlfriend'.

history.meaning: before, prior, former (spatial and temporal anteriority)
female friend; romantic girlfriend
ex-girlfriend, former female romantic partner

前女友.notes: Frequently contrasted with 现女友 (xiànnǚyǒu, 'current girlfriend') and shortened colloquially to 前任 (qiánrèn, 'ex'); a staple trope in urban romance dramas.

前嫌.etymology: A Literary Chinese modifier-head compound combining 前 (qián, 'prior, former, past') with 嫌 (xián, 'suspicion, resentment, ill will', formed with the semantic woman radical 女 and phonetic 兼 jiān 'simultaneous', originally denoting an unsettled or suspicious mind). Attested in Tang and Song dynasty historical prose, it denotes lingering grievances or old animosities between rivals before reconciliation.

history.meaning: suspicion, doubt, resentment, aversion
prior resentment, old grudge or suspicion
past grudge, previous ill will (chiefly in set idioms)

前嫌.notes: Almost always bound in the four-character idiom 尽释前嫌 (jìnshì qiánxián) or 不计前嫌 (bùjì qiánxián, 'to let bygones be bygones / set aside old grudges'), common when rival executives or artists team up.

rootFamily.gloss: to set aside past grudges, let bygones be bygones

cognates.word: 前代未聞 (zendai mimon, structural parallel)

前所未有.etymology: A four-character Literary Chinese fixed idiom (chengyu) built with classical nominalization syntax: 前 (qián, 'in the past, previously') + 所 (suǒ, relative object nominalizer 'that which') + 未 (wèi, aspectual negator 'not yet, never up to now') + 有 (yǒu, 'to have, to exist'). Literally 'that which the past has never yet had', it is attested in Song dynasty philosophical and historical texts (such as the Xu Zizhi Tongjian Changbian) to describe events without historical precedent.

history.form: 前所未有 (qián suǒ wèi yǒu)
history.meaning: that which has never existed in previous times
unprecedented, never before seen or experienced

前所未有.notes: Frequently used as an attributive modifier with 的 (前所未有的挑战, 'an unprecedented challenge') in media pitches, PR statements, and crisis scenes.

前所未见.etymology: A four-character Literary Chinese idiom (chengyu) patterned directly on the classical relative construction 前 (qián, 'previously, in times past') + 所 (suǒ, passive/object nominalizing particle 'that which') + 未 (wèi, 'not yet, never') + 见 (jiàn, Traditional 見, 'to see, to witness', depicting an eye 目 atop a standing person 儿). Literally 'that which was never witnessed before', it shifts the existential focus of 前所未有 to visual and experiential novelty.

history.form: 前所未見 (qián suǒ wèi jiàn)
history.meaning: that which has never been witnessed in the past
never seen before, visually or experientially unprecedented

前所未见.notes: Preferred over 前所未有 when emphasizing visual spectacle, stage design, or a show format that audiences have literally never laid eyes on before.

前排.etymology: A modifier-head spatial compound uniting 前 (qián, 'front, forward') and 排 (pái, originally a verb 'to push, to arrange in order' with the hand radical 扌 and phonetic 非 fēi, which evolved into a noun and classifier for a 'row, line, or tier of seats/people'). Literally 'front row', it refers to the foremost seating tier in theaters, auditoriums, or studios, as well as a vanguard position.

history.meaning: to push open; to arrange in a row or line
front row (of soldiers, seats, or spectators)

前排.notes: In live television recordings, award galas, and press conferences, 前排 seating signals VIP status; in internet slang, 前排 means 'grabbing a front-row seat' early in a trending comment thread.

rootFamily.gloss: to line up, queue; to arrange in order

前提.etymology: A Sino-Japanese philosophical coinage (*wasei-kango*, Japanese 前提 *zentei*) borrowed into modern Mandarin in the late 19th and early 20th centuries to translate Western logical 'premise' (Latin *praemissa*, literally 'things sent before'). It combines 前 (qián, 'before, prior, in advance') with 提 (tí, 'to raise, to put forward, to posit'). From formal logic (major and minor premises in a syllogism), it generalized in Mandarin to mean any essential precondition or prerequisite for a negotiation or plan.

history.meaning: logical premise (translating Latin praemissa / English premise)
logical premise; prerequisite, precondition for action or agreement

morphemes.meaning: to put forward, to posit, to raise

前提.notes: Commonly framed in business negotiations as 在……的前提下 (zài ... de qiántí xià, 'on the premise/condition that...') or 前提是…… ('the precondition is...').

rootFamily.gloss: to bring up, to mention; to advance (a schedule)

前朝旧事.etymology: A four-character modifier-head literary phrase composed of two parallel disyllabic units: 前朝 (qiáncháo, 'the former dynasty or previous court/administration', from 前 'previous' + 朝 cháo 'imperial court, dynasty', originally 'morning audience with the sovereign') modifying 旧事 (jiùshì, Traditional 舊事, 'old affairs, bygone events', from 旧 'old, past' + 事 'matter, affair'). In historical writing and poetic nostalgia, it referred to the politics and anecdotes of a fallen dynasty; in modern corporate and media speech, it is used metaphorically for the politics or disputes of a previous leadership regime.

history.meaning: events and court affairs of the preceding imperial dynasty
bygone affairs of a former era or previous corporate administration

前朝旧事.notes: Used with ironic or humorous gravitas in Chinese workplace dramas (often alongside 一朝天子一朝臣, 'a new emperor brings a new court') to refer to projects or rivalries left over from a previous CEO or department head.

rootFamily.gloss: courtiers/veterans left over from the former dynasty/administration

cognates.meaning: first period, early stage, first half-year

前期.etymology: A modifier-head temporal compound uniting 前 (qián, 'front, early, prior') with 期 (qī, 'appointed time, period, phase, cycle', written with phonetic 其 qí and semantic 月 'moon/month', originally denoting an agreed-upon date or lunar cycle). Reinforced in modern bureaucratic and industrial terminology by Sino-Japanese 前期 (*zenki*, 'first term / early phase'), it designates the initial phase of a historical era, illness, or project. In film and television production, it specifically translates 'pre-production' (and principal photography prior to post-production).

history.meaning: appointed time, stipulated period, full cycle
earlier period, initial phase; pre-production stage in media

前期.notes: In film/TV industry jargon (*Behind the Scenes*), 前期 (pre-production/shooting phase, e.g. 前期筹备 'upfront preparation', 前期拍摄 'principal photography') contrasts directly with 后期 (hòuqī, 'post-production / editing & VFX').

前站.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 前 (qián, 'forward, advance, ahead') with 站 (zhàn, 'relay station, halting post', originally 'to stand erect' from 立 'stand' + phonetic 占 zhān, which came to denote post-road relay stations 驿站 in Yuan and Ming administrative Chinese under Mongolic *jam* influence). Originally denoting the next relay station ahead on an imperial courier route, it evolved in military and logistical usage into an 'advance post' or 'vanguard party', especially in the verb-object phrase 打前站 ('to go ahead as an advance scouting/prep team').

history.meaning: to stand upright; imperial courier relay station (Yuan–Ming)
the relay station ahead; advance post or scouting party

前站.notes: Most commonly heard in the collocation 打前站 (dǎ qiánzhàn, 'to act as an advance party / scout locations and arrange logistics ahead of the main crew'), essential in on-location TV production.

rootFamily.gloss: to go ahead as an advance party, do advance logistics

前行.etymology: A Literary Chinese adverbial-head verbal compound joining 前 (qián, functioning adverbially as 'forward, ahead', which was in fact the primary verbal sense of 前 in Classical Chinese: 'to step forward') with 行 (xíng, 'to walk, to travel, to move, to proceed', whose Oracle Bone glyph depicts a four-way crossroads). Attested in Han and Six Dynasties prose and poetry, it retains an elevated, literary register in modern Mandarin meaning 'to journey onward' or 'to forge ahead despite obstacles'.

history.meaning: to walk forward, to advance along a road
to move forward, to press ahead (often figuratively in life or career)

morphemes.meaning: to walk, to go, to proceed

前行.notes: More poetic and inspirational than 往前走 (wǎng qián zǒu) or 前进 (qiánjìn); frequently appears in slogans and speeches such as 负重前行 ('forging ahead while bearing heavy burdens') or 一路前行.

rootFamily.gloss: traveler, pedestrian; person on a journey

前途.etymology: A Literary Chinese modifier-head compound combining 前 (qián, 'ahead, in front, future') with 途 (tú, 'road, way, path, journey', formed with the walking radical 辶 and phonetic 余 yú). Originally referring literally to the physical road stretching ahead of a traveler in Tang dynasty poetry and prose, it underwent metaphorical extension to denote one's 'journey ahead in life'—specifically career prospects, future promise, and professional destiny.

history.meaning: the road ahead on a physical journey
future path in life, career prospects, outlook

前途.notes: Very common in predicate and attributive phrases like 有前途 (yǒu qiántú, 'promising / having a bright future'), 前途无量 ('boundless prospects'), and 赌上自己的前途 ('to stake one's career future').

rootFamily.gloss: halfway, midway through a task or journey

前门.etymology: Compound noun from 前 ('front; forward', originally 歬, a foot 止 advancing on a boat 舟) + 门 (simplified from 門, pictograph of double swinging gate leaves). Used both for the front entrance of any building or courtyard and as the proper name of the great southern gate (正陽門) of Ming-Qing Beijing.

history.meaning: front gate of a palace or residence
front door; main entrance

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 前门

前面.etymology: Locative noun combining 前 ('front, ahead') + 面 ('face, surface, side'): 'in front, ahead, the front side, preceding'.

history.meaning: in front; ahead; the forepart

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 前面 (via 萌典)

剑.etymology: A phono-semantic character (Simplified 剑, Traditional 劍, Old Chinese *kram-s) composed of the phonetic component 佥 (qiān, Traditional 僉, *skʰram, 'all together / sharp') and the semantic 'knife/blade' radical 刂 (刀 dāo). In Classical Chinese weapon terminology, 剑 specifically denoted a straight, double-edged thrusting and slashing sword worn by aristocrats and scholars, strictly distinguished from 刀 (dāo, a single-edged saber or blade).

history.meaning: straight double-edged bronze or iron sword
double-edged sword; metaphorical sharpness or leverage (as in 尚方宝剑 / 双刃剑)

剑.notes: In modern corporate and media dialogues, 剑 appears constantly in idioms like 双刃剑 (shuāngrènjiàn, 'double-edged sword'), 亮剑 ('to draw one's sword / show one's hand'), and 剑走偏锋 ('to take an unorthodox, risky approach').

rootFamily.gloss: to win by an unorthodox move, take a bold unconventional path

剧.etymology: A phono-semantic character (Simplified 剧, Traditional 劇) formed with the semantic 'knife/blade' radical 刂 (刀) and phonetic 豦 (jù, depicting a fierce struggle between a tiger 虍 and a wild boar 豕). Its primary Classical Chinese sense was 'severe, intense, arduous, or fast-moving' (as in 剧烈 'intense'). In Tang and Song vernacular, via compounds like 杂剧 (zájù, 'variety plays'), it developed the sense of 'theatrical play, stage performance', and in modern usage serves as the core bound and free noun for 'drama, play, or television series'.

history.meaning: severe, intense, acute; burdensome administrative toil
theatrical performance, stage play, comedic or dramatic spectacle
drama, play, TV series, scripted show; intense (in compounds)

剧.notes: In entertainment industry Mandarin, 剧 alone commonly means a scripted TV/web drama series (e.g., 追剧 'binge/follow a series', 拍剧 'shoot a drama', 大剧 'blockbuster series'), distinct from 综艺 (zōngyì, 'variety show').

rootFamily.gloss: film/TV production crew, cast and crew on set
plot, storyline of a play or show

剩.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 乘 (chéng/shèng phonetic) + 刀 (刂, 'knife dividing'): 'be left over, remain, surplus'. Attested from Tang–Song poetry and vernacular prose (alongside earlier 賸).

history.meaning: be left over; remain as surplus

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 剩 (via 萌典)

剩下.etymology: A verb-complement compound combining 剩 (shèng, 'to remain, to be left over, surplus', written with the 'knife' radical 刂 and phonetic 乘 chéng, originally meaning 'to have a surplus after division or cutting') with the directional/resultative complement 下 (xià, 'down, remaining behind in place'). While 剩 alone carried the classical and medieval meaning of 'surplus/remnant', attaching 下 in vernacular Mandarin grammaticalized the sense of items, time, or people remaining behind after the rest have been consumed, eliminated, or removed.

history.meaning: to have a surplus, to remain over and above
to be left over, to remain behind after subtraction or departure

morphemes.meaning: to remain, to be left over, surplus

剩下.notes: Can function transitively with the remaining quantity as post-verbal object (只剩下三天, 'only three days remain') or nominalized with 的 as 剩下的 ('the remainder / the rest').

剪.etymology: Ideographic/phono-semantic character combining 前 (qián/jiǎn, which already contained a knife 刂 and meant 'trim') + an additional 刀 ('knife/blade') at the bottom: 'cut with scissors, clip, shear, trim; scissors (剪刀)'.

history.meaning: cut even; clip; shear
cut with scissors; trim; clip

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 剪 (via 萌典)

剪掉.etymology: A verb-resultative compound uniting the action verb 剪 (jiǎn, 'to cut with scissors or shears, to clip, to trim', composed of phonetic 前 qián and the semantic 'knife' radical 刀 at the bottom) with the phase/resultative complement 掉 (diào, originally 'to shake, to fall', grammaticalized in Mandarin as a completive marker meaning 'off, away, completely disposed of'). Together they mean 'to snip off, cut away, or edit out completely'.

history.meaning: to clip with shears, to trim feathers or cloth, to sever
to cut off with scissors; to edit or splice out (film/audio footage)

morphemes.meaning: to cut with scissors, to clip, to edit film

剪掉.notes: In television and film production (*Behind the Scenes*), 剪掉 specifically means 'to cut/edit out a scene or line in the editing room' (e.g., 把这段戏剪掉, 'cut this scene out').

rootFamily.gloss: film/video editing, montage; to edit footage
to cut out, delete, expunge (text or scenes)

副.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 畐 (fù/pì phonetic) + 刀 (刂, 'knife splitting'): originally 'split in two, matching counterpart', hence 'assistant, deputy, vice-, secondary' and the measure word for 'a matched pair (glasses, gloves), a set, or a facial expression (一副笑脸)'.

history.meaning: split; matching counterpart; deputy/assistant
deputy/vice-; classifier for pairs, sets, and expressions

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 副 (via 萌典)

副总裁.etymology: A three-character modifier-head title prefixing 副 (fù, 'deputy, assistant, secondary, vice-', originally 'to split or second' with the knife radical 刂) to 总裁 (zǒngcái, Traditional 總裁, 'president, director-general, chief executive'). 总裁 originated in Ming and Qing imperial bureaucracy as the title of the 'Director-General' overseeing grand state compilation projects (from 总 'to gather/oversee overall' + 裁 'to cut cloth, judge, decide'), was adopted in Meiji Japan (*sōsai*) for party and bank presidents, and returned to modern Chinese corporate usage for 'company president / CEO', making 副总裁 'corporate vice president (VP)'.

history.meaning: Director-General / Deputy Director-General of imperial historiography commissions
vice president (VP) of a corporation, media conglomerate, or financial institution

副总裁.notes: In Chinese corporate hierarchy, 副总裁 (often abbreviated in speech to 副总 fùzǒng, and addressed as X总) ranks below the 总裁 (President/CEO) and 董事长 (Chairman of the Board).

rootFamily.gloss: deputy general manager; colloquial short form for VP
to cut staff, downsize; to make a ruling/arbitrate

力推.etymology: A concise adverbial-head verbal compound modeled on Classical Chinese noun-as-adverb syntax: 力 (lì, 'strength, power, effort', functioning adverbially as 'with all one's strength, vigorously', originally a pictograph of a sinew or wooden plow) modifies 推 (tuī, 'to push forward, to promote, to recommend, to champion', from hand radical 扌 + phonetic 隹 zhuī). Literally 'to push forward with full force', it evolved from literary usage ('to esteem or recommend highly') into a high-frequency media and commercial verb meaning 'to champion, heavily promote, or throw full company backing behind'.

history.meaning: to push with full physical strength; to esteem or recommend earnestly
to strongly champion, heavily promote (an artist, project, or policy)

morphemes.meaning: to push, to promote, to recommend, to champion

力推.notes: A signature media/entertainment industry verb: when a studio or executive 力推 a newcomer, show, or project (e.g., 公司力推的新人, 'a new artist heavily pushed by the agency'), they allocate top resources and publicity to them.

rootFamily.gloss: to promote, popularize, market (a product or program)
to strive with all one's might, spare no effort

力气.etymology: Compound noun of 力 ('muscular strength, sinew/plow', neutral tone li in this word) + 气 (氣, 'vital breath, energy'): 'physical strength, effort, might'.

history.meaning: physical strength; muscular effort

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 力气 (via 萌典)

力量.etymology: A compound of 力 (lì, 'physical strength, muscle power, force') and 量 (liàng, originally 'to measure grain by volume' and by extension 'capacity, measure, magnitude'). Attested in Six Dynasties and Tang Buddhist translations and secular prose, 力量 originally meant 'the measure or capacity of one's strength'. In modern Mandarin, it denotes both physical/abstract 'power, strength, impact' and collective human resources ('workforce, personnel force', as in 师资力量 or 骨干力量).

history.meaning: capacity of physical strength; spiritual or political capability
physical strength; abstract power/influence; institutional workforce or personnel force

力量.notes: Pronounced with a neutral tone on the second syllable (lìliang) in standard Mainland speech; in organizational contexts (e.g., 中坚力量 'core backbone workforce'), it translates naturally as 'workforce, talent pool, or institutional muscle'.

劝.etymology: A phono-semantic character (Simplified 劝, Traditional 勸, Old Chinese *kʰʷan-s) composed of the semantic 'strength/effort' radical 力 (lì, replaced on the left by 又 in simplified script) and the phonetic 雚 (guàn, 'heron'). In Classical Chinese (as in Xunzi's famous treatise 劝学 *Quànxué*, 'An Exhortation to Learning'), 劝 meant exclusively 'to encourage, exhort, urge forward to positive action'. Over time, through pairing with 谏 (jiàn, 'remonstrate') and 阻 (zǔ, 'dissuade'), it broadened in Mandarin to mean 'to advise, urge, try to persuade, or talk someone into/out of something'.

history.meaning: to exhort, encourage, stimulate to effort or virtue
to advise, urge, try to persuade or soothe; to counsel against rash action

morphemes.meaning: to advise, urge, exhort, try to persuade

劝.notes: Crucial learner distinction: 劝 (quàn) means 'to try to persuade / advise' (attempt), whereas 劝服 (quànfú) or 说服 (shuōfú) means 'to succeed in persuading' (result); hence 我劝了他半天，他还是不听 ('I tried to talk sense into him for ages, but he still wouldn't listen').

rootFamily.gloss: to advise and dissuade, talk someone out of doing something
to step in to break up a fight or argument
to urge someone to drink alcohol at a banquet

劝架.etymology: A vernacular Mandarin verb-object compound combining 劝 (quàn, 'to advise, urge, pacify, talk down') with 架 (jià, originally a 'wooden frame or rack' from 枷/加 + 木, which in early modern vernacular verb-object phrases like 打架 dǎjià 'to fight/brawl' and 吵架 chǎojià 'to quarrel' came to mean 'a brawl, altercation, or heated dispute'). Because it is a separable verb-object construction (离合词), aspect markers and modifiers can be inserted between the two syllables (e.g., 劝了半天架).

history.meaning: to engage in a brawl or heated quarrel (vernacular nominal sense of 架)
to mediate an altercation, step in to calm down and separate people fighting or arguing

劝架.notes: A classic separable verb (离合词): say 去劝个架 ('go break up the fight') or 帮着劝劝架, never *劝架他们 (instead use 给他们劝架, 'mediate between them').

rootFamily.gloss: to fight, brawl, come to blows
to quarrel, have a verbal row
to try to persuade, counsel, talk round

办.etymology: A character from the 辡 (biàn, 'two criminals/parties contending against each other in law') phonetic-semantic series: Traditional 辦 places 力 (lì, 'effort, strength, labor') between the two 辛 components of 辡, literally 'to exert effort to resolve or manage a matter' (Simplified 办 derives from its cursive shorthand, combining 力 with two flanking strokes). Emerging in Song and Yuan administrative vernacular as a specialization of 辨 (biàn, 'to distinguish/manage'), 办 became the core Mandarin transitive verb meaning 'to handle, manage, set up, run, or get done'.

history.meaning: to exert effort in managing official duties, procuring supplies, or settling cases
to do, handle, manage, run (an enterprise/event), process, or punish by law

morphemes.meaning: to handle, manage, do, run, set up

办.notes: Unlike 做 (zuò, general 'make/do') or 干 (gàn, 'work/do'), 办 implies handling something that requires organization, authority, procedures, or problem-solving (办节目 'produce/run a show', 办公司 'set up a company', 怎么办 'what to do / how to handle it').

rootFamily.gloss: to handle affairs, get things done

办事.etymology: A verb-object compound (separable verb 离合词) joining 办 (bàn, 'to handle, manage, execute') with 事 (shì, 'affair, matter, business, official duty', whose Oracle Bone form depicts a hand holding a hunting or writing implement for court service). Attested from Song and Qing administrative and vernacular texts, it means 'to handle practical affairs, attend to business, or get things done efficiently'.

history.meaning: to manage official duties or execute assigned commissions
to handle affairs, run errands/business, get things done

办事.notes: Frequently used to evaluate competence and reliability in workplace settings: 办事牢靠 ('reliable at getting things done'), 办事效率高 ('high efficiency in handling matters'), or 按规矩办事 ('do things by the book').

rootFamily.gloss: liaison office, representative agency (e.g. 驻京办事处)
to work in an office, handle official business
to handle matters, conduct oneself in the world

办事员.etymology: Three-character occupational noun combining 办事 ('handle affairs/official tasks', 办 'manage/do' + 事 'affair') + 员 ('staff member, personnel'): 'office clerk, administrative staff member'.

history.meaning: office clerk; administrative worker

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 办事员 (via 萌典)

办公.etymology: A verb-object compound uniting 办 (bàn, 'to handle, administer, transact') with 公 (gōng, 'public affairs, official business, state or organizational duty', originally contrasting with 私 sī 'private/personal'). Originating in Qing dynasty administrative terminology (办公事, 'to transact official government business'), it broadened in modern Mandarin to mean 'to work at a desk/office' or 'to conduct institutional/corporate work'.

history.meaning: to transact public or imperial government business
to work in an office, handle administrative or corporate business

办公.notes: Serves both as an intransitive verb phrase (在家办公 'work from home', 现场办公 'work on-site') and as the modifier in compounds like 办公室 (bàngōngshì, 'office') and 办公桌 ('office desk').

rootFamily.gloss: official business, public duty; on business
to handle affairs, get things done

办公室.etymology: Three-character compound of 办公 ('handle official/company business', 办 'manage' + 公 'public/official affairs') + 室 ('room'): 'office'.

history.meaning: office room; office

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 办公室 (via 萌典)

办公楼.etymology: Three-character compound of 办公 ('do office work, handle official business') + 楼 (樓, 'multi-story building'): 'office building'.

history.meaning: office building

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 办公楼 (via 萌典)

cognates.word: 手続き (tetsuzuki, source of 手续)

办手续.etymology: A verb-object collocation pairing the native Mandarin verb 办 (bàn, 'to handle, process, go through') with the noun object 手续 (shǒuxù, Traditional 手續, 'procedures, formalities, paperwork'). 手续 is a late-19th/early-20th-century graphic loan from Japanese 手続き (*tetsuzuki*, 'procedure, sequence of steps', from 手 *te* 'hand/means' + 続き *tsuzuki* 'continuation, sequence'). Together, 办手续 means 'to go through official formalities or complete required paperwork'.

history.meaning: sequence of operational steps, legal or administrative formalities
history.stage: Meiji Japanese loan into Early Modern Chinese

history.meaning: to complete paperwork, go through official or administrative formalities

办手续.notes: Used across HR, legal, and travel contexts: 办入职手续 ('complete onboarding paperwork'), 办离职手续 ('process resignation formalities'), and 办签证手续 ('process visa paperwork').

rootFamily.gloss: to handle, process (formally, e.g. 办理手续)

办法.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound uniting 办 (bàn, 'to handle, manage, resolve') with 法 (fǎ, 'law, rule, method, way', whose ancient form 灋 combined 水 'water, level as a standard' and 廌 'a mythical unicorn-like beast that butts the guilty'). Emerging in Qing dynasty vernacular and official correspondence (meaning 'the method of handling a matter'), 办法 became the standard everyday Mandarin noun for 'way, method, solution, or course of action'.

history.meaning: method of handling an official matter; administrative regulation or measure
way, method, means, solution to a problem; administrative measure (in legal titles)

办法.notes: While 方法 (fāngfǎ) denotes a systematic or technical 'method/approach', 办法 focuses on a practical 'way out / solution to get something done' (想办法 'think of a way', 没办法 'no way / can't be helped'). In formal law, 办法 also means 'administrative measures/regulations' (管理办法).

rootFamily.gloss: to handle affairs, get things done

办过.etymology: A verb-aspect construction combining the transitive verb 办 (bàn, 'to handle, organize, host, run, or process', Traditional 辦) with the experiential aspectual suffix 过 (guò, Traditional 過, grammaticalized from the full verb 'to pass through, to cross over' into an unstressed aspect marker denoting 'to have had the experience of doing something at least once in the past'). In media and event contexts, 办过 commonly means 'to have previously held, hosted, or produced (an event, concert, or show)' or 'to have processed'.

history.meaning: to pass by, cross over (spatial motion verb)
experiential aspect marker indicating a past event or prior experience
to have held, hosted, organized, or handled before

办过.notes: Contrasts with 办了 (bànle, completive aspect: 'held/did it') by emphasizing prior track record or experience (e.g., 他以前办过大型晚会, 'He has experience hosting/producing large-scale gala shows before').

rootFamily.gloss: to hold, host, stage (an event, exhibition, or festival)
to undertake, be the organizer/host of an event
to found, establish (a school, enterprise, or publication)

功劳.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative compound uniting two near-synonymous nouns of achievement: 功 (gōng, 'meritorious achievement, result of work', formed from 工 gōng 'carpenter's square / skillful work' + 力 lì 'strength') and 劳 (láo, Traditional 勞, 'toil, exertion, service rendered through hard labor', originally depicting fire 爫/火 burning over a dwelling 冖 with 力 'strength' below). In the *Rites of Zhou* (*Zhouli*) and Han histories, 功 denoted state-building achievement while 劳 denoted diligent toil on campaign; fused together as 功劳, it means 'meritorious service, contribution, or credit for an accomplishment'.

history.meaning: meritorious state service and military toil deserving imperial reward
credit, contribution, meritorious effort in achieving a result

功劳.notes: Often appears in the workplace proverb 没有功劳也有苦劳 (méiyǒu gōngláo yě yǒu kǔláo, 'even if one didn't achieve the big breakthrough/credit, one still put in hard toil') and 抢功劳 ('to steal credit').

rootFamily.gloss: to claim credit for oneself, take the credit
hard toil without glamorous results (contrasted with 功劳)

cognates.meaning: Chinese martial arts; supreme skill from hard practice
devising a scheme, ingenuity, effort; martial arts

功夫.etymology: A compound originating in Six Dynasties and Tang-Song Chinese (historically written interchangeably as 工夫 and 功夫), combining 功/工 (gōng, 'work, skillful achievement, effort') with 夫 (fū, 'adult man, laborer, corvée worker'). Initially referring to manual laborers on state construction projects and the 'man-hours or labor-time' they expended, it evolved in Song Neo-Confucianism and Chan Buddhism to mean 'dedicated practice, self-cultivation, and deep skill acquired through sustained effort', and in modern Mandarin denotes 'time, effort, workmanship, or mastery (including martial arts)'.

history.meaning: corvée laborers; labor-time and effort expended on a task
disciplined practice, scholarly/spiritual cultivation, mastery of a craft or martial art
effort, time, and skill invested; accomplished craftsmanship or martial arts mastery

morphemes.meaning: man, laborer (representing man-hours and human exertion)

功夫.notes: In modern Mainland orthography, 功夫 (gōngfu) is preferred for 'skill, mastery, effort invested' (e.g., 下功夫 'put in serious effort/time', 真功夫 'real skill'), while 工夫 is often preferred for 'free time / span of time' (没工夫 'have no time'), though the two remain closely intertwined.

rootFamily.gloss: to put in serious time and effort, apply oneself deeply
foundational skill, solid grounding in a craft
skill, art, workmanship; level of mastery

功底.etymology: A modifier-head compound joining 功 (gōng, 'skill, training, accomplished mastery achieved through disciplined practice', as in 功夫 and 基本功) with 底 (dǐ, 'bottom, base, foundation, underlying groundwork', originally the bottom or foundation of a building with the shelter radical 广 and phonetic 氐 dī). Originating in traditional Chinese theater (戏曲), calligraphy, and martial arts terminology, it denotes the 'underlying foundation of technical skill' upon which an artist's or professional's performance rests.

history.meaning: trained skill + foundational base/groundwork
foundational training and solid technical grounding in performing arts, writing, or a profession

功底.notes: Highly prized in entertainment and media critiques: 台词功底 ('solid grounding in line delivery/voice work'), 舞蹈功底 ('dance foundation'), or 文字功底深厚 ('deep foundational skill in writing').

rootFamily.gloss: basic skills, fundamentals (in arts, sports, or work)

加.etymology: Ideogram (会意字) combining 力 ('strength/plow') + 口 ('mouth/call'): Shuowen Jiezi explains it as adding words or effort one atop another, hence 'add, increase, plus, put in'.

history.meaning: place on top of; add; increase
add; plus; increase

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 加 (via 萌典)

加上.etymology: A verb-complement compound that grammaticalized into a coordinating/additive conjunction: 加 (jiā, 'to add, increase, place atop', composed of 力 'strength' + 口 'mouth', originally 'to add words or effort') combined with the directional/resultative complement 上 (shàng, 'up, onto, in addition'). Used verbally as 'to add onto (a list, total, or calculation)', it grammaticalized at the clause and phrase boundary to mean 'plus, on top of that, coupled with, counting in'.

history.meaning: to add, augment, place upon
to add onto (verbal); plus, in addition to, coupled with (conjunctive)

加上.notes: Functions seamlessly both as a literal verb (加上这笔费用, 'counting in / adding this expense') and as a discourse connector introducing an additional reason or factor (再加上时间紧迫, 'and on top of that, time is tight').

rootFamily.gloss: moreover, in addition, on top of that (slightly more formal)
to join, become a member of, add into
