加倍.etymology: Verb-object compound of 加 ('add, increase') + 倍 ('fold, double'): 'double, redouble, twice as much'. Attested since Han texts.

history.stage: Han Classical Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: double; increase twofold; redouble

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 加倍 (via 萌典)

加入.etymology: A coordinative-resultative verb compound formed from 加 (jiā, 'to add, append, increase'; Old Chinese *kˤra, originalmente depicting strength 力 applied to speech 口 or tools) and 入 (rù, 'to enter, go into'; Old Chinese *njup). While both characters appear adjacent in Literary Chinese in the literal sense of 'to add into', the modern institutional sense 'to join an organization, treaty, or group' was reinforced in late 19th-century Meiji Japanese legal and diplomatic usage as 加入 (kanyū) before standardizing across modern Mandarin.

history.meaning: to add and enter; to append into a collection or count
accession to a treaty; joining an association or society
to join (a group, team, organization) or add into (a mix)

加入.notes: Takes either an organization/group as object (加入团队 'join the team') or a substance/element added to a mix (加入调味料 'add seasoning'); more general and less commercially formal than 加盟.

rootFamily.gloss: to join an alliance or franchise; to sign on with a project

加把劲.etymology: A colloquial northern Mandarin verb-object phrase built on the verb 加 (jiā, 'to add, apply more'), the verbal classifier 把 (bǎ, originally 'to grasp in the hand', here functioning as an indefinite measure word meaning 'a handful or burst of'), and the head noun 劲 (jìn, traditional 勁, 'muscular strength, vigor, effort'). As a separable verb (离合词), it literally pictures 'putting in one more grip of strength' to push a task over the finish line. Often pronounced with erhua in spoken Beijing and northern Mandarin as 加把劲儿 (jiā bǎ jìnr).

history.meaning: vigor, forceful strength, sinewy power
to apply an extra burst of physical or mental effort
to put in extra effort, push harder toward a goal

morphemes.meaning: to add, increase, put in more
a grasp, burst, or measure of (effort)

加把劲.notes: Very common in team pep talks on production sets and workplaces (e.g., 大家再加把劲 'everyone push a bit harder'); often takes the diminutive rhotic suffix 儿 (加把劲儿) in spoken Mandarin.

cognates.meaning: add oil! cheer on, keep going!

加油.etymology: A verb-object compound from 加 (jiā, 'to add, replenish') and 油 (yóu, 'oil, lamp oil, fuel, lubricant'). Literally 'to add oil (to a lamp or machine)' or 'to refuel (an engine)', its figurative shift to 'make an extra effort; cheer on!' is associated both with Qing-era traditions—such as a magistrate in Guizhou (Zhang瑛, father of Zhang Zhidong) having runners pour lamp oil into scholars' study lamps at midnight to encourage their studies—and with 20th-century automotive/Macau Grand Prix racing imagery ('step on the gas / give it more fuel'), popularized across the Sinosphere via Hong Kong Cantonese (gaa1 jau4) and Taiwan Mandarin.

history.meaning: to replenish lamp oil or apply lubricating oil
to refuel a vehicle; to step on the accelerator
to cheer on, root for; 'go for it! keep fighting!'

加油.notes: A separable verb (离合词): when cheering someone specifically, use 给 + person + 加油 (e.g., 给你加油 'rooting for you'), never *加油你. Formally entered the Oxford English Dictionary in 2018 as 'add oil'.

rootFamily.gloss: greasy; slick and unctuous in manner

cognates.meaning: to work overtime; to add scheduled flights/runs

加班.etymology: A verb-object compound uniting 加 (jiā, 'to add, append') and 班 (bān, 'shift, scheduled duty, rank, class'; Old Chinese *pˤran, originally depicting a knife 刀 dividing jade 珏 to distribute rank tokens among officials, hence 'ordered file, duty roster, work shift'). Originally denoting the addition of an extra work shift or an extra scheduled run of a train, ship, or theatrical troupe, it became the standard workplace verb for working overtime beyond regular hours.

history.meaning: ordered rank of court officials; rotating duty roster
to add an extra scheduled run or performance shift
to work overtime; to put in extra hours at work

加班.notes: A separable verb (离合词): durations or modifiers go between the characters, e.g., 加了三个小时的班 ('worked three hours of overtime') or 加夜班 ('work a night overtime shift'). Ubiquitous in media production and corporate culture (often intensified as 加班加点).

rootFamily.gloss: to start work, go on duty
to finish work, get off duty
to be on duty, work a scheduled shift

cognates.meaning: affiliation, joining a league or federation, franchising
affiliation, joining a league, franchise membership

加盟.etymology: A verb-object compound composed of 加 (jiā, 'to add, join') and 盟 (méng, 'solemn covenant, blood oath, alliance'; Old Chinese *mraŋ, graphically a sacrificial vessel 皿 beneath bright light 明, representing a ritual treaty sealed over sacrificial blood in Spring and Autumn interstate diplomacy). Reinforced via Meiji Japanese 加盟 (kamei) for acceding to international leagues or commercial federations, it later expanded in contemporary Chinese business and entertainment media to mean 'to franchise' or '(of a high-profile star, director, or investor) to sign on and join a major production'.

history.meaning: to swear a blood covenant between feudal states; alliance
to accede to a treaty, league, or federation
to join an alliance, become a commercial franchisee, or (of stars/talent) join a cast or show

加盟.notes: In entertainment and TV production (*幕后之王*), 加盟 is the preferred elevated verb for announcing that a celebrity, director, or studio is joining a show or lineup (e.g., 实力派歌手倾情加盟), signaling prestige and partnership rather than mere employment.

务实性.etymology: A trimorphemic abstract noun built from the Classical verb-object compound 务实 (wùshí, 'to devote oneself to concrete realities') plus the productive abstract nominalizing suffix -性 (-xìng, 'nature, quality, -ness, -ity'). Within 务实, 务 (wù, traditional 務; Old Chinese *moks) means 'to strive after, apply oneself to, attend to', and 实 (shí, traditional 實; Old Chinese *mə-lit, strings of cowries 貫 under a roof 宀) means 'full, substantial, actual fact' (as opposed to 务虚 wùxū, 'discussing abstract theory or ideology'). The suffix -性 was popularized in modern Chinese through Meiji Japanese translations of European -ity/-ness philosophical and administrative terms.

history.meaning: to pursue substantial realities rather than empty reputation (attested in Han Yu & Song prose)
pragmatic, dealing with concrete matters
practicality, pragmatic character or orientation

morphemes.meaning: to devote oneself to, engage in, pursue

务实性.notes: Used in formal briefings, executive proposals, and media critiques (e.g., 方案的务实性 'the practicality of the proposal'); for describing a person directly, use the adjective 务实 ('pragmatic') rather than 务实性.

rootFamily.gloss: to discuss abstract principles, strategy, or ideology

动.etymology: Phono-semantic character (traditional 動, combining 重 zhòng 'heavy/move' + 力 'strength'; simplified 动 uses 云 yún + 力): 'move, stir, act, touch, arouse (feelings), change'.

history.meaning: exert strength to move -> move, stir, act
move; stir; touch; act

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 动 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: motive power, kinetic power, dynamic force; motivation

动力.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-Japanese compound combining 动 (dòng, traditional 動, 'to move, stir, set in motion'; Old Chinese *Cə-[d]ˤoŋʔ, composed of 重 phonetic and 力 semantic 'strength') and 力 (lì, 'physical force, power, strength'; Old Chinese *k.rək, pictograph of a sinew or plowshare). Standardized in Meiji Japan as 動力 (dōryoku) to translate Western physics and engineering 'motive power' or 'kinetic power' (as in steam or electrical engines), it was borrowed into turn-of-the-20th-century Mandarin and swiftly acquired the psychological and organizational sense of 'motivation, impetus, driving force'.

history.meaning: motive power, mechanical force driving machinery
mechanical motive power; psychological motivation or driving impetus

动力.notes: Functions both in technical contexts (动力系统 'powertrain/propulsion system') and everyday psychology/workplace speech (工作的动力 'motivation to work', 化压力为动力 'turn pressure into motivation').

动动.etymology: Tentative verb reduplication (VV pattern) of 动 (simplified from 動, heavy 重 + strength 力 'move; stir; act'). In Mandarin grammar, reduplicating a monosyllabic action verb softens the command or describes a brief, casual, or testing movement such as wiggling one's toes or stretching one's limbs.

history.meaning: move a little; give a wiggle
move a bit; wiggle; flex

动员.etymology: A verb-object Sino-Japanese return loan from 动 (dòng, traditional 動, 'to move, put into action') and 员 (yuán, traditional 員, 'personnel, member, staff'; Old Chinese *ɢʷren, originally a round cauldron 鼎 with a rim ○, extended to 'headcount, roster of officials'). Coined in Meiji Japan as 動員 (dōin) to translate German *Mobilmachung* / French *mobilisation* (putting armed forces personnel on active war footing), it entered modern Chinese military vocabulary and subsequently broadened into civilian, corporate, and production contexts meaning 'to rally personnel, muster resources, or persuade someone into action'.

history.meaning: military mobilization of troops and reserves for war
to mobilize the masses or armed forces; to rally a team or persuade someone to participate

morphemes.meaning: to set in motion, activate, stir

动员.notes: Used both for large-scale rallying (总动员 'general mobilization; all hands on deck', 动员大会 'pep-rally / kickoff assembly') and interpersonal persuasion (做他的动员工作 'talk him into joining/cooperating').

rootFamily.gloss: to mobilize, draw upon, put into use (resources/funds)

cognates.meaning: dynamic feel, sense of movement, energetic vibe

动感.etymology: A modern modifier-head compound pairing 动 (dòng, traditional 動, 'movement, motion, dynamic energy') with 感 (gǎn, 'feeling, sensation, aesthetic impression'; Old Chinese *kˤəmʔ, composed of 咸 phonetic 'all/penetrating' and 心 'heart-mind'). Formed on the model of aesthetic compounds in `-感` (such as 美感 'sense of beauty' and 节奏感 'sense of rhythm'), it denotes the vivid impression of kinetic energy, rhythm, and vitality conveyed by music, stage choreography, camera work, or visual design.

history.meaning: to be moved in the heart; sensation, perceptual response
sense of motion; kinetic, rhythmic energy in performance, music, or design

动感.notes: Functions as both a noun (充满动感 'full of kinetic energy') and an attributive modifier in entertainment and lifestyle contexts (动感音乐 'upbeat dynamic music', 动感单车 'indoor spinning bike').

动手.etymology: A verb-object compound formed from 动 (dòng, traditional 動, 'to move, set in motion, use') and 手 (shǒu, 'hand'; Old Chinese *n̥uʔ). Literally 'to move one's hand(s)', it developed two distinct idiomatic branches in vernacular Chinese from the Song–Yuan period onward: (1) to put one's hands to a task ('to start work, get cracking, do it oneself') and (2) to raise a hand against someone ('to get physical, strike first in a fight').

history.meaning: to move one's hands; to begin executing a task or to strike a blow
to start work / DIY; to resort to physical force or blows

动手.notes: Context disambiguates its two core senses: 自己动手 ('do it yourself / get hands-on') vs. 君子动口不动手 ('a gentleman uses his mouth/words, not his fists'). Also a separable verb (动起手来).

rootFamily.gloss: to tamper secretly, play underhanded tricks
to put one's hand to a task, set about (doing something)

动手脚.etymology: An idiomatic verb-object phrase built from 动 (dòng, traditional 動, 'to move, manipulate') and the coordinative compound 手脚 (shǒujiǎo, 'hands and feet', hence 'secret bodily motions, sleight of hand, covert manipulation'). Already attested in Yuan–Ming vernacular fiction (such as *Water Margin* and *Jin Ping Mei*), 'moving one's hands and feet' stealthily behind the scenes evolved into the figurative sense of tampering with equipment, doctoring accounts or contracts, or pulling underhanded tricks.

history.meaning: hands and feet; bodily movements or secret maneuvers
to make covert gestures; to tamper with something or play tricks behind someone's back
to tamper secretly (with data, gear, contracts) or play underhanded tricks

动手脚.notes: Typically used with prepositional phrases in `-上` or `-里` to indicate what was tampered with: 在合同上动手脚 ('tamper with the contract') or 在音响设备上动了手脚 ('sabotaged the audio gear').

rootFamily.gloss: to get physical; to start work with one's hands
to act stealthily, do things behind someone's back
flustered, in a frantic rush ('hands busy, feet chaotic')

动用.etymology: A coordinative/serial verb compound uniting 动 (dòng, traditional 動, 'to stir, move from storage, activate') and 用 (yòng, 'to use, employ, expend'; Old Chinese *loŋs). Historically used in Ming–Qing administrative prose for disturbing and expending reserved state treasury funds, granary stores, or military troops that are normally kept in reserve, it retains the nuance in modern Mandarin of drawing upon significant or special resources (capital, connections, emergency equipment, executive authority).

history.meaning: to draw upon reserved treasury silver, grain stores, or garrison troops
to mobilize, draw upon, or deploy (funds, connections, equipment, authority)

morphemes.meaning: to activate, move from reserve, stir

动用.notes: Unlike ordinary 用 ('use'), 动用 implies tapping into substantial, reserved, or weighty resources—such as 动用人脉 ('pull strings / tap into one's network'), 动用公款 ('dip into public/company funds'), or 动用武力 ('resort to force').

rootFamily.gloss: to utilize, make use of, take advantage of
to apply, put to practical use

动词.etymology: A modifier-head grammatical compound formed from 动 (dòng, traditional 動, 'action, motion, dynamic') and 词 (cí, traditional 詞, 'word, expression, part of speech'; Old Chinese *sə.lə, composed of 言 'speech' and 司 phonetic). While traditional Chinese philology classified content words into 实字 ('full words'), 活字 ('living words', i.e. verbs), and 死字 ('static words', i.e. nouns), the exact term 動詞 (dōshi) was coined in Edo–Meiji Japan (building on *Rangaku* Dutch grammar studies by scholars like Ōtsuki Fumihiko) to translate Latin *verbum* / Dutch *werkwoord* ('action-word'), and was adopted into modern Chinese linguistics at the turn of the 20th century.

history.meaning: 'living/dynamic character' (traditional Chinese & Ma Jianzhong's 1898 term for verb)
verb (calqued on Dutch werkwoord 'action-word')
verb (part of speech)

morphemes.meaning: word, lexical item, part of speech

动词.notes: In Ma Jianzhong's pioneering 1898 Chinese grammar *Mashi Wentong* (马氏文通), verbs were called 动字 (dòngzì); the Japanese-derived 动词 soon replaced it alongside 名词 ('noun') and 形容词 ('adjective').

动静.etymology: An antonymic coordinative compound (偏义复词 / *piānyì fùcí*, an asymmetric compound where only one constituent's meaning remains active) uniting 动 (dòng, traditional 動, 'movement, activity') and 静 (jìng, 'stillness, quiet, rest'; Old Chinese *dzengʔ). In Classical Chinese philosophical prose (such as the *Yijing* and Daoist texts), 动静 meant symmetrically 'movement and stillness; action and rest'. By the Tang–Song vernacular era, when used in contexts of listening or watching out for something, the semantic weight shifted entirely onto 动, yielding the modern sense 'sound of movement, stir, sign of activity or development' (usually with neutral tone on the second syllable: dòngjing).

history.meaning: movement and stillness; activity and rest; deportment
slightest sound or stir of movement; news or sign of activity
movement, noise, stir, or sign of development/happening

动静.notes: Pronounced with a neutral second syllable (dòngjing); although 静 means 'quiet', 有动静 means 'there is noise/movement/news', while 没动静 means 'all is quiet / no word or progress yet'. A classic linguistic example of an asymmetric compound (偏义复词).

cognates.meaning: supporting performance, assisting in a show or play

助演.etymology: A modifier-head theatrical and broadcasting compound formed from 助 (zhù, 'to assist, aid, support'; Old Chinese *dzra-s, composed of 且 phonetic and 力 'strength') and 演 (yǎn, 'to perform, act, stage, evolve'; Old Chinese *N-q(r)anʔ, originally 'flowing water extending far', later 'to expound, practice, perform on stage'). Popularized across East Asian stage, film, and variety television terminology (cf. Japanese 助演 joen and Korean 조연 joyeon), it functions in Mandarin both as a verb ('to perform in support of a main contestant or lead act') and as a noun ('supporting performer, backing act').

history.meaning: to assist + to expound or perform a martial/theatrical art
supporting performance or supporting role in theater and film
to perform as a supporting act; supporting performer in a variety show or concert

morphemes.meaning: to perform, act, put on a show

助演.notes: In Chinese variety and music competition shows (like those produced in *幕后之王*), 助演 specifically refers to a guest artist or fellow performer who joins a contestant's stage number to boost their performance, distinct from a dramatic film's 配角 ('supporting role/character').

rootFamily.gloss: lead actor, starring performer; to star in
director (of a film, drama, or TV show)

助演嘉宾.etymology: A four-character modifier-head television and live-entertainment compound combining 助演 (zhùyǎn, 'supporting performance / backing act', from 助 'assist' + 演 'perform') with 嘉宾 (jiābīn, 'honored guest, esteemed visitor'). The second element 嘉宾 is a direct survivor from Archaic Chinese court poetry—famously opening the *Classic of Poetry* (*Shijing*, 'Luming': 我有嘉宾，鼓瑟吹笙 'I have honored guests; we play the se-zither and blow the mouth-organ')—composed of 嘉 (jiā, 'auspicious, fine, praiseworthy') and 宾 (bīn, traditional 賓, 'guest of honor', with 貝 cowrie shell indicating ceremonial gifts). In modern broadcasting, 嘉宾 denotes a celebrity guest on a show.

history.meaning: esteemed and auspicious court guest (*Shijing*, c. 9th–8th c. BCE)
invited celebrity guest or panelist on a broadcast program
special guest artist invited to perform alongside a contestant or headliner

助演嘉宾.notes: A staple term in Chinese music reality shows (such as *Singer* / *歌手*) and variety finals, where securing a top-tier 助演嘉宾 ('special guest performer') is a major behind-the-scenes producer triumph.

rootFamily.gloss: supporting performer; to perform in support
honored guest; celebrity guest on a TV show
special invited guest (for a concert or talk show)

助理.etymology: Originally a Literary Chinese verb-object/coordinative compound from 助 (zhù, 'to assist, aid') and 理 (lǐ, 'to dress jade; to put in order, govern, manage, administer'; Old Chinese *rəʔ). In imperial histories (such as the *Book of Han*), 助理 was a verb phrase meaning 'to assist in governing the realm or managing affairs'. In the 20th century, it was nominalized to translate English 'assistant' as a professional job title—ranging from executive assistants (总裁助理) and production assistants (制作助理) to celebrity personal assistants (艺人助理).

history.meaning: to assist in governing the state or administering affairs (*Book of Han*)
assistant, aide (professional title and occupational role)

morphemes.meaning: to manage, administer, put in order

助理.notes: Distinguish 助理 from 助手 (zhùshǒu): 助理 is an official job title or workplace position (e.g., 制作人助理 'producer's assistant', 总经理助理 'assistant to the GM'), whereas 助手 is a general, descriptive word for a helper or right-hand person (得力助手 'capable right-hand helper').

rootFamily.gloss: to manage, handle, process; to tidy up

助阵.etymology: A verb-object military compound composed of 助 (zhù, 'to assist, bolster, reinforce') and 阵 (zhèn, traditional 陣, earlier written 陳; Old Chinese *d-rəns, 'battle array, tactical formation, frontline ranks'). In Tang–Ming military narratives and martial romances (such as *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*), 助阵 meant deploying allied troops or beating war drums to bolster a battle formation during combat (e.g., 擂鼓助阵 'beat the war drums to boost the battle line'). In modern Mandarin, it metaphorically describes friends, fans, or celebrity guests turning out in person to cheer on or lend star power to an event, premiere, or competition.

history.meaning: to reinforce a battle formation or beat drums to boost troop morale in combat
to turn out to cheer, lend moral support, or lend star power to an event or performance

助阵.notes: Very frequent in entertainment journalism and showbiz PR (e.g., 好友亲临现场助阵 'good friends came to the venue in person to lend support'), retaining a vivid, energetic sense of 'rallying to someone's corner'. Also a separable verb (助个阵).

rootFamily.gloss: lineup, cast, roster of performers or players
to go into battle; to step onto the stage/field to compete

cognates.meaning: effort, exertion, endeavor; to work hard
to strive, make great effort; endeavor

努力.etymology: A Classical Chinese verb-object compound formed from 努 (nǔ, 'to exert oneself, strain every sinew'; Old Chinese *nˤaʔ, composed of 奴 phonetic and 力 'strength') and 力 (lì, 'physical strength, effort'). First attested in Han dynasty prose and yuefu poetry—most famously the closing exhortation of the Han ballad *Changge Xing* (长歌行): 少壮不努力，老大徒伤悲 ('If in youth and prime one does not exert one's strength, in old age one will grieve in vain')—where it literally meant 'to exert one's strength'. In modern Mandarin it functions as an adjective ('hardworking, diligent'), a verb ('to strive'), and a noun ('effort').

history.meaning: to exert one's physical or moral strength; to strive earnestly (Han dynasty *Yuefu*)
hardworking, diligent (adj.); to strive, work hard (v.); effort (n.)

努力.notes: Unlike 勤劳 (which describes an enduring character virtue of industriousness, often of laborers or a people), 努力 focuses on active, goal-directed effort and can modify verbs directly (努力工作 'work hard', 努力学习 'study hard').

rootFamily.gloss: to protrude or pout (the lips) with effort; to strain
to spare no effort, do one's utmost
physical strength, stamina; capability, real strength

劫持.etymology: A coordinative verb compound pairing 劫 (jié, 'to rob by force, coerce, plunder'; Old Chinese *krep, originally written 劦 'combined strength' + 去/刀, signifying taking away by threat of force) and 持 (chí, 'to grasp, hold fast, control'; Old Chinese *drə, from 手 'hand' + 寺 phonetic). Attested in Han and Three Kingdoms historical chronicles (such as *Records of the Grand Historian* and *Book of the Later Han*) for seizing a ruler or hostage at swordpoint to compel obedience, it became the standard modern legal and media term for hijacking an aircraft/vehicle or holding hostages by force.

history.meaning: to seize and hold a person (such as a sovereign or official) by armed coercion (*Hou Hanshu*)
to hijack (a plane, ship, vehicle), take hostage, or figuratively hijack (emotions, public opinion, web browsers)

morphemes.meaning: to rob by force, coerce, abduct

劫持.notes: Beyond literal hostage-taking (劫持人质) or plane hijacking (劫机), contemporary media and PR discourse frequently uses it metaphorically: 道德劫持 ('moral hijacking/guilt-tripping'), 情感劫持 ('emotional blackmail/hijacking'), or 流量劫持 ('traffic hijacking').

rootFamily.gloss: to coerce, hold under duress, blackmail into compliance

劲爆.etymology: A modern vernacular compound borrowed into general Mandarin from Hong Kong Cantonese media and pop-culture slang (勁爆 ging6 baau3). In Cantonese, 勁 (ging6, Mandarin jìn/jìng, 'strong, powerful') functions both as an adjective ('awesome, intense, fierce') and as an intensifying adverb ('super, extremely'), while 爆 (baau3, Mandarin bào, 'to crackle in fire, explode, burst') denotes something 'explosive, sensational, or off-the-charts'. Together, 劲爆 describes news, stage performances, music beats, or gossip that is electrifying, sensational, and hard-hitting.

history.meaning: intensely explosive; sensational, red-hot (Hong Kong entertainment press & Cantopop slang)
explosive, sensational (news/gossip); electrifying, high-energy (music/stage show)

劲爆.notes: Note the pronunciation: although 劲 is pronounced jìn ('strength/effort') in 加把劲, in the compound 劲爆 it is most commonly pronounced jìnbào in Mainland media speech (though jìngbào, following the literary reading of 劲 'strong', is also widely heard). Staple showbiz buzzword for 劲爆消息 ('bombshell news') and 劲爆舞曲 ('hard-hitting dance track').

rootFamily.gloss: vitality, vigor, forceful strength; strong, sturdy
to break news/gossip; a bombshell revelation in media

劳逸结合.etymology: A four-character subject-predicate idiom formed from the antonymic coordinate pair 劳逸 (láoyì, 'toil and ease, labor and rest') and the compound verb 结合 (jiéhé, 'to bind together, integrate, combine'). 劳 (láo, traditional 勞; Old Chinese *rˤaw, originally two fires 炏 over a roof 冖 with 力 'strength', depicting exhausting labor by lamplight) and 逸 (yì; Old Chinese *litlek, a hare 兔 escaping 辶, hence 'unfettered ease, leisure') have been paired as philosophical opposites since Classical texts like the *Zuo Zhuan* and *Xunzi* (劳逸之势). In 20th-century Mandarin, 劳逸结合 crystallized as a standard four-character phrase advocating a healthy balance between work and rest.

history.meaning: toil and ease; exhaustion and rest (paired in Classical military and political texts)
to combine work with adequate rest; to maintain work-life balance

劳逸结合.notes: The go-to idiomatic equivalent for 'work-life balance' or 'pacing oneself' when advising overworked colleagues or production crews (e.g., 注意劳逸结合，别累垮了身体 'remember to balance work and rest, don't burn out your health').

rootFamily.gloss: to wait at ease for an exhausted enemy (classic stratagem)

勇气.etymology: A modifier-head compound from 勇 (yǒng, 'brave, valiant, bold'; Old Chinese *loŋʔ, composed of 甬 phonetic 'welling/surging up' and 力 'strength') and 气 (qì, traditional 氣, 'vital breath, spirit, moral energy, mettle'; Old Chinese *C.qʰəp-s). Attested in Classical Chinese military and historical texts—such as the *Zuo Zhuan* (曹刿论战: 一鼓作气 'the first drumbeat rouses their martial spirit/courage') and *Records of the Grand Historian*—where 勇气 literally denoted the surging vital breath (*qì*) that empowers a warrior to face danger without flinching. In modern Mandarin it is the standard word for moral or physical courage.

history.meaning: martial spirit, valorous vital breath in battle (*Zuo Zhuan*, *Shiji*)
courage, bravery, nerve (both physical and moral/emotional)

勇气.notes: Collocates characteristically with verbs of 'mustering' or 'gathering up' spirit: 鼓起勇气 ('muster up the courage [to confess/speak]') and 拿出勇气 ('show some courage/nerve'). Note that 勇气的气 retains its full fourth tone (yǒngqì), unlike 客气 (kèqi) or 力气 (lìqi).

rootFamily.gloss: boldness,魄力;氣魄 imposing spirit or daring vision

cognates.meaning: working hard, studying diligently; giving a discount (semantic shift in Japanese)

勉强.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative compound uniting two near-synonymous verbs of exertion: 勉 (miǎn, 'to exert oneself, strive, encourage'; Old Chinese *mranʔ) and 强 (qiǎng, traditional 強/彊, here in its third-tone verbal reading *N-kaŋʔ, 'to force oneself, compel, make an effort against resistance', distinct from second-tone qiáng 'strong'). In Pre-Qin and Han texts (such as the *Liji* and *Xunzi*), 勉强 meant positively 'to exert oneself earnestly despite difficulty'. Over time, the sense of 'forcing action against resistance' split into three modern Mandarin senses: (1) verb: 'to force or compel someone against their will', (2) adverb: 'reluctantly, grudgingly, with difficulty', and (3) adjective: 'barely adequate, far-fetched, strained'.

history.meaning: to exert oneself earnestly; to strive with determination (*Liji*, *Dong Zhongshu*)
to force oneself or another; to manage with difficulty; strained or reluctant
(v.) to force/compel; (adv.) reluctantly, barely; (adj.) strained, unconvincing, barely passable

morphemes.meaning: to force, compel, strain against resistance (qiǎng)

勉强.notes: A notorious false friend with Japanese! Japanese 勉強 (benkyō) preserved the Classical Chinese sense 'to exert oneself diligently' and shifted to mean 'to study' (or 'for a merchant to try hard to lower the price'), whereas Mandarin 勉强 evolved to mean 'to force someone' (别勉强自己 'don't force yourself'), 'barely' (勉强及格 'barely pass'), or 'strained/far-fetched' (理由很勉强). Always pronounced miǎnqiǎng (3rd + 3rd tone -> 2nd + 3rd in sandhi).

rootFamily.gloss: to force, compel, coerce (stronger than 勉强)
to encourage, urge on; mutual encouragement
to do one's utmost, exert all one's strength

勒索.etymology: A coordinative/serial verb compound formed from 勒 (lè, 'to bridle a horse, rein in, compel by force'; Old Chinese *rˤək, depicting a leather bridle 革 with a bit in the mouth, governed by strength 力) and 索 (suǒ, 'to twist thick rope; to search out, demand, exact'; Old Chinese *sˤak). Literally 'to rein in (a victim) with a bridle and demand payment with a rope', the compound emerged in Song–Yuan–Ming legal and vernacular usage to describe corrupt officials, bandits, or blackmailers coercively extracting money or valuables through threats or leverage.

history.meaning: to bridle/compel by force + to demand or exact tribute
to extort money or goods by coercion or abuse of power (Yuan–Ming vernacular & legal codes)
to blackmail, extort, hold for ransom (including cyber ransomware 勒索软件)

morphemes.meaning: to bridle, restrain, compel by force or threat
to demand, exact, ask for payment

勒索.notes: Frequently paired in legal and media contexts as the four-character phrase 敲诈勒索 (qiāozhà lèsuǒ, 'extortion and blackmail'), and used in tech/cybersecurity for ransomware (勒索软件 / 勒索病毒). Note the pronunciation lèsuǒ (not lēisuǒ; lēi is the colloquial spoken reading for 'tie tightly').

rootFamily.gloss: to demand payment, claim compensation or damages
to rein in one's horse at the edge of a precipice (idiom: pull back from disaster in time)

cognates.word: 募金 (ぼきん, bokin - parallel compound with 募)

募捐.etymology: A coordinative/serial verb compound uniting 募 (mù, 'to summon widely, recruit, canvass for support'; Old Chinese *mˤaks, from 莫 phonetic and 力 'strength/effort') and 捐 (juān, 'to cast aside, relinquish; to contribute money for public relief or official rank'; Old Chinese *kʷen, from 手 'hand' and 肙 phonetic). In Classical Chinese, 募 meant calling for volunteers or supplies by public notice, while 捐 evolved during the Han–Qing dynasties from 'relinquishing personal wealth' to 'donating funds for famine relief or public works'. Combined as 募捐, it specifically means 'to solicit and collect charitable donations; to fundraise'.

history.meaning: to canvass publicly for volunteers/supplies + to relinquish wealth for public relief
to solicit charitable contributions; to organize a fundraising drive or benefit

morphemes.meaning: to canvass, solicit publicly, raise, recruit

募捐.notes: Crucial distinction for learners: 募捐 means 'to solicit/raise donations' (organizers, charities, or telethon producers do 募捐), whereas 'to make a donation / donate money' as an individual giver is 捐款 (juānkuǎn) or 捐赠 (juānzèng). In media (*幕后之王*), charity galas are 慈善募捐晚会.

rootFamily.gloss: to donate money, contribute funds (as a donor)
to raise funds, collect capital; to recruit talent/troops

cognates.meaning: hard work, labor, service; working diligently

勤劳.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative compound uniting two near-synonymous morphemes of toil: 勤 (qín, 'unstinting, diligent, frequent in service'; Old Chinese *gər, composed of 堇 phonetic 'clay/scarce' and 力 'strength') and 劳 (láo, traditional 勞, 'toil, exertion, physical labor'; Old Chinese *rˤaw). Attested together as early as the *Classic of Poetry* (*Shijing*, 'Hongyan' preface and 'FaMu') and the *Book of Han*, where 勤劳 meant 'toiling unstintingly and enduring hardship in service'. In modern Mandarin it is an elevated, admiring adjective meaning 'industrious, hardworking, diligent'.

history.meaning: to toil unstintingly; physical hardship and devoted labor (*Shijing* commentaries, *Hanshu*)
industrious, hardworking, diligent (as an enduring character trait or cultural virtue)

勤劳.notes: Register nuance: 勤劳 praises a deep-seated character virtue of industriousness (often used for parents, farmers, working people, or bees: 勤劳的双手 'hardworking hands', 勤劳致富 'prosper through hard work'). For everyday school or office effort ('work/study hard'), use 努力 or 勤奋 instead.

rootFamily.gloss: diligent, assiduous (especially in study or career)
labor, physical work; Labor Day (劳动节)
hardworking and thrifty, industrious and frugal

勺.etymology: Pictograph (象形字) attested from Shang oracle bones and Zhou bronzes showing a curved ladle with a small dot inside representing liquid or food being scooped: 'spoon, ladle' and a traditional small volume measure (1/100 of a 升 liter).

morphemes.meaning: curved bowl and handle of a ladle

history.meaning: ladle with liquid inside = scoop, ladle, spoon
spoon; ladle; classifier for spoonfuls

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 勺 (via 萌典)

勺子.etymology: Colloquial noun meaning 'spoon, ladle, scoop', formed from the pictographic root 勺 ('ladle') + nominal suffix 子 (neutral tone zi).

history.meaning: spoon; ladle

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 勺子 (via 萌典)

匀.etymology: Originally an oracle-bone and bronze-script character 勻 composed of wrapping 勹 around 二 ('two; equal division'), representing an even, balanced portion (Middle Chinese *ywin*). Used both as an adjective ('even; uniform') and as a transitive verb meaning to spread, divide, or coat something evenly.

history.meaning: equal weight; even division
even; uniform; spread or stir evenly

包.etymology: Ancient pictograph/ideogram showing a fetus (巳) enclosed inside a curved womb/wrapping (勹): 'wrap, bundle, pack, surround, include, undertake/guarantee, bag, bun'.

history.meaning: enclose; wrap up; contain
wrap; bag/pack; bun; guarantee; classifier for packs

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 包 (via 萌典)

包在我身上.etymology: A vivid colloquial Mandarin idiom meaning 'leave it to me / I guarantee it'. Its core verb is 包 (bāo; Old Chinese *pˤru, originally a pictograph of a fetus 巳 enclosed within a womb 勹, meaning 'to wrap up, encompass'). In Song–Ming commercial and vernacular Chinese, 'wrapping up the whole bundle' (包揽) developed the legal and social sense of 'to undertake full responsibility for a task, to underwrite or vouch for an outcome'. Paired with the locative phrase 在我身上 ('upon my own body/shoulders'), it literally means 'the entire responsibility is wrapped and placed squarely on my shoulders'. Often preceded by the topic-subject 这事 ('this matter').

history.meaning: to take full charge of, contract for, or guarantee an outcome

history.form: 包在我身上 (bāo zài wǒ shēnshang)
history.meaning: 'consider it placed on my shoulders' — leave it to me, I've got it covered!

morphemes.meaning: to undertake fully, guarantee, take complete charge of

包在我身上.notes: A warm, confident conversational reassurance used when taking ownership of a tough problem for a colleague, boss, or friend (e.g., 这事儿包在我身上！ 'Leave this matter to me!'). Closely related to 打包票 ('give a 100% guarantee').

rootFamily.gloss: to take full charge of, monopolize or undertake everything
to vouch for, give a firm guarantee ('issue a guarantee ticket')
to contract for a project; outsourcing (外包)

包括.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative verb compound formed from 包 (bāo, 'to wrap, enfold, contain'; Old Chinese *pˤru, womb/enclosure pictograph) and 括 (kuò, 'to tie up the mouth of a sack, bind together, gather in'; Old Chinese *kˤot, from 手 'hand' and 舌 phonetic, cf. *Yijing* 括囊 'tying up a sack'). Literally 'to wrap around and tie together in one bundle', it is attested from the Han dynasty onward (e.g., Ban Gu's *Han Shu* and *Xijing Fu*: 包括于其中 'encompassing everything within it') and serves in modern Mandarin as the standard verb and prepositional marker for 'to include, comprise, encompass'.

history.meaning: to wrap up and bind together; to encompass and take in the whole (*Hanshu*)
to include, comprise, consist of (often with ...在内)

morphemes.meaning: to tie together, gather in, encompass

包括.notes: Often frames an illustrative item with the circumposition 包括...在内 ('including X within it', e.g., 包括导演在内的所有工作人员 'all staff members, including the director'). Distinguish from 包含 (bāohán, 'to contain/embody an inner quality, emotion, or abstract meaning').

rootFamily.gloss: to contain, embody, hold within (often abstract qualities or feelings)

cognates.meaning: to excuse, forgive, bear with (polite formula)

包涵.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative compound uniting 包 (bāo, 'to wrap, embrace, hold within') and 涵 (hán, 'to submerge, soak, contain like a deep pool of water'; Old Chinese *gˤom, from 水 'water' and 函 'to hold inside'). Originally a vivid hydrological and moral metaphor in Tang–Song literary prose (such as Su Shi and Zhu Xi) picturing an ocean or deep basin vast enough to 'enfold and submerge' all streams and impurities—hence 'broad-minded magnanimity and tolerance'. In Ming–Qing vernacular and modern Mandarin, it specialized into a polite, deferential verb meaning 'to bear with, make allowances for, forgive (a shortcoming or offense)'.

history.meaning: to encompass like deep water; magnanimous capacity to tolerate faults (Song dynasty Neo-Confucian prose)
to forgive, bear with, make allowances for (courteous conversational formula)

morphemes.meaning: to hold like deep water, submerge, tolerate magnanimously

包涵.notes: Homophonous with 包含 (bāohán, 'to contain/include'), which is a frequent spelling trap! 包涵 with the water radical (氵) is used almost exclusively in polite apologies and hospitality formulas asking others for patience: 请多包涵 or 多多包涵 ('please bear with me / please excuse any shortcomings').

rootFamily.gloss: self-restraint, poise, cultural refinement and tolerance ('deep-water cultivation')
to forgive, tolerate, be understanding and magnanimous
to contain, embody (homophone written with 含 'hold in the mouth')

包装.etymology: Coordinative verb and noun compound of 包 ('wrap') + 装 (裝, 'pack, load, outfit'): 'pack, package, wrap; packaging'.

history.meaning: package; wrap up; packaging

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 包装 (via 萌典)

包裹.etymology: A synonym-compound uniting two classical wrapping verbs: 包 (bāo, originally a pictograph of an embryo enclosed in the womb, hence 'to wrap, enfold') and 裹 (guǒ, 'to bind around with cloth', formed from 衣 'garment' enclosing 果 as phonetic). Used first in Han–Tang prose as a transitive verb 'to swathe or bundle up', 包裹 nominalized into 'a cloth-wrapped travel bundle' and in modern postal usage 'a mailed parcel or package'.

history.meaning: wrap and bind securely in cloth (verb)
cloth-tied travel bundle carried over the shoulder
parcel; postal package; bundle

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 包裹

匆忙.etymology: A coordinative (parallel) compound (并列结构) combining 匆 (cōng, variants 悤/怱, Middle Chinese *tshuwng, originally depicting a chimney vent 囱 over a heart 心 to evoke agitation and breathlessness) and 忙 (máng, MC *mang, phono-semantic compound with 忄 'heart' and phonetic 亡 *mjang, meaning 'anxious, hurried, pressed for time'). The pairing reinforces the sense of hasty, flustered movement under time pressure.

history.meaning: agitated in mind; hurried and anxious (attested separately in Han–Tang texts)
hasty, rushed, pressed for time
hurried, rushed, hasty

匆忙.notes: Frequently reduplicated as 匆匆忙忙 (cōngcōng-mángmáng) for vivid adverbial emphasis; contrasts with 急忙 (jímáng), which stresses urgency and sudden reaction rather than general haste.

化友.etymology: A compact verb-object / resultative construction (动宾/结果结构) distilled from the classical four-character idiom 化敌为友 (huà dí wéi yǒu, 'to transform an enemy into a friend'). It combines 化 (huà, Old Chinese *qʰʷˤraj-s, originally depicting one upright person 人 beside an inverted person 匕, signifying 'to transform, convert, melt') with 友 (yǒu, OC *ɢʷəʔ, originally two right hands 又 joined in mutual assistance, meaning 'friend, companion').

history.meaning: to transform an enemy into an ally or friend
to turn (rivals) into friends; to become friends after hostility

化友.notes: Usually encountered in parallel four-character phrasing such as 化敌为友 or in conversational/subtitle compression where rivals reconcile into allies.

化妆.etymology: Historically a verb-object or coordinative compound combining 化 (huà, 'to transform, embellish, fashion') and 妆 (zhuāng, traditional 妝/粧, Middle Chinese *tsrjang, composed of 爿 'bed/frame' and 女 'woman', meaning 'female adornment, facial grooming, cosmetic attire'). Attested in medieval Chinese poetry (originally often written 化装/化妆 interchangeably) and reinforced in modern Mandarin alongside Japanese 化粧 (keshō), it became strictly differentiated in modern orthography from 化装 (theatrical disguise/costuming).

history.meaning: to adorn oneself, apply facial cosmetics and hair ornaments
to apply rouge and powder; cosmetic adornment
to put on makeup (separable verb-object compound)

化妆.notes: Functions as a separable verb (离合词), e.g., 化了个淡妆 ('put on light makeup'); in film and television production, 化妆 refers to beauty/character makeup, whereas 化装 refers to disguise or full costume impersonation.

化妆间.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正结构) formed by attaching the spatial noun suffix 间 (jiān, traditional 間, originally depicting moonlight 月 shining through the crevice of a double door 門, evolving from 'crevice, interval' to 'partitioned room, chamber') to the verbal-nominal stem 化妆 (huàzhuāng, 'applying makeup'). It supplanted older literary terms like 妆阁 (zhuānggé, 'lady's boudoir') in modern theater, broadcasting, and studio architecture.

history.meaning: lady's dressing chamber or boudoir
backstage dressing room for performers; powder room

化妆间.notes: In Chinese television and live-show production (*幕后之王*), 化妆间 is the backstage dressing and makeup room for hosts and guests; note that in Taiwan and Hong Kong, 化妆室/化妆间 in public venues can also euphemistically mean 'restroom/lavatory'.

化解.etymology: A coordinative/resultative verbal compound (并列/动补结构) combining 化 (huà, Old Chinese *qʰʷˤraj-s, 'to melt, dissolve, transform') and 解 (jiě, OC *kˤreʔ, originally depicting two hands 廾 separating a cow's 牛 horn 角 with a knife 刀, hence 'to untie, dissect, loosen, dispel'). Literally 'to melt away and untie', it shifted from physical dissolution and Daoist/medical dispersion of stagnation to the metaphorical defusing of crises, hostility, and awkwardness.

history.meaning: to melt and loosen; to disperse (stagnation, illness, or misfortune)
to defuse, resolve, or neutralize (a crisis, conflict, or embarrassment)

化解.notes: A high-frequency verb in PR and crisis management contexts, typically collocating with abstract negative objects such as 化解危机 (defuse a crisis), 化解矛盾 (resolve a conflict), or 化解尴尬 (smooth over awkwardness).

北.etymology: In Shang oracle-bone script, 北 depicts two human figures standing back to back (Middle Chinese *pok*), originally writing the word 'back; turn one's back' (later written 背 bèi with the flesh radical 月). Because traditional Chinese houses and palaces faced south toward the sun, one's back faced north, so 北 became the cardinal direction 'north'.

morphemes.meaning: north (originally two figures standing back to back)

history.meaning: two people back to back -> back; north
north; northern
north

cognates.meaning: to match, pair as spouses (Sino-Vietnamese cognate)

匹配.etymology: A classical coordinative compound (并列结构) uniting 匹 (pǐ, Old Chinese *pʰi[t], originally a measure for bolts of cloth and paired horses, hence 'mate, equal, counterpart') and 配 (pèi, OC *pʰˤə[t]-s, composed of 酉 'fermented wine vessel' and 己 'kneeling person', originally meaning wine color and early extended to 'to pair as spouse, to match in rank or proportion'). Attested in Classical Chinese for marital pairing and equal standing, it expanded in modern Mandarin to technical, data, and professional compatibility.

history.meaning: to join in marriage; a worthy mate or counterpart
to match in status, marry; to pair harmoniously
to match, be commensurate with, pair up (resources, data, or partners)

匹配.notes: Used both in formal business/production contexts (e.g., 资源与定位相匹配, 'resources match the positioning') and in gaming/dating algorithms ('matchmaking').

rootFamily.gloss: to pair up, coordinate, match (clothing or roles)
to be a match for, rival, equal

区.etymology: Originally 區, showing three mouths/vessels (品) stored inside a curved enclosure (匚): 'store, divide into compartments, distinguish, area, district, region, zone'.

history.meaning: subdivided storage -> distinguish; small area; region
district; area; zone; distinguish

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 区 (via 萌典)

区分.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound (并列结构) joining 区 (qū, traditional 區, Old Chinese *kʰˤ(r)o, depicting three vessels 品 concealed inside an enclosure 匚, meaning 'to store separately, categorize, area/division') and 分 (fēn, OC *pə[n], depicting a knife 刀 cleaving something in two 八, meaning 'to divide, cleave, distinguish'). Already attested in Classical Chinese (*Lunyu* commentaries and histories) in the sense of dividing into distinct categories, and reinforced in modern taxonomy and administration alongside Japanese 区分 (kubun).

history.meaning: to divide into separate sections or classes; to set apart
to distinguish, differentiate, demarcate

区分.notes: Often takes the resultative complement 开来 (区分开来, 'to tell apart clearly'); slightly more analytical and boundary-focused than 分别 (fēnbié) or 辨别 (biànbié).

rootFamily.gloss: to divide up, demarcate (zones or spheres)

医治.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound (并列结构) combining 医 (yī, traditional 醫, Old Chinese *ʔə, originally a complex character combining 匚 'quiver/case', 矢 'arrow', 殳 'hand with instrument/lance', and 酉 'medicinal elixir/fermented spirits', meaning 'healer, medical craft, to treat illness') and 治 (zhì, OC *C.lrə, originally the name of a river, extended to 'to regulate water, put in order, heal'). Both morphemes independently mean 'to treat or cure an illness' in Classical Chinese.

history.meaning: to practice healing; to regulate and cure disease (used singly or in parallel in pre-Qin and Han medical texts)
to provide medical treatment, cure an illness or wound
to treat medically, cure, heal

morphemes.meaning: regulate, put in order, cure, heal

医治.notes: Slightly more formal or literary than simple 治病 (zhìbìng); frequently used in hospital bulletins (e.g., 医治无效, 'medical treatment proved unavailing') as well as metaphorically for healing emotional trauma.

rootFamily.gloss: to treat, cure; therapy, medical treatment

医生.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正结构) combining 医 (yī, traditional 醫, 'medicine, healing art') with the personal/scholarly suffix 生 (shēng, Old Chinese *sreŋ, originally depicting grass sprouting from the earth, extended in Tang–Song administration to 'student, scholar, practitioner', as in 先生 and 书生). First coined in the Tang dynasty (*Tang Liudian*) as an official title for trainees in the Imperial Medical Office (太医署), it generalized in vernacular Mandarin to mean any licensed physician.

history.meaning: medical trainee or scholar in the Imperial Medical Academy (Tang–Song official title)
practicing physician, healer
doctor, medical physician

医生.notes: The standard pan-Chinese word for 'doctor' (used both as a common noun and a polite title after a surname, e.g., 王医生); in northern China, colloquial speech also frequently uses 大夫 (dàifu).

医疗.etymology: A coordinative compound (并列结构) pairing 医 (yī, traditional 醫, 'to treat illness, medical art') with 疗 (liáo, traditional 療, Middle Chinese *ljew, phono-semantic compound with 疒 'sickness radical' and phonetic  *ljew, meaning 'to cure, heal, recuperate'). While both roots are classical, the compound 医疗 gained high institutional currency in the 20th century (reinforced by Sino-Japanese 医療 *iryō*) to denote organized healthcare and clinical treatment systems.

history.meaning: to heal with medicine; to treat and nurse an illness
medical treatment; institutional healthcare and clinical therapy

医疗.notes: Primarily used as a noun or attributive modifier in institutional and policy collocations such as 医疗保险 (health insurance), 医疗器械 (medical equipment), and 医疗团队 (medical team).

医药单.etymology: A three-character modifier-head nominal compound (偏正结构) built from the coordinative compound 医药 (yīyào, traditional 醫藥, 'medicine and drugs; medical care and pharmaceuticals', where 药 *yào* combines 艹 'plant/herb' and phonetic 乐/樂 *lạc*) modifying the head noun 单 (dān, traditional 單, originally meaning 'single, unlined', which in Song–Qing commercial vernacular developed the sense of 'a single sheet of paper recording an itemized list, bill, invoice, or prescription').

history.meaning: physicians and herbal medicines; medical remedies (attested since Han texts)
written prescription slip or itemized bill of charges
itemized medical and pharmaceutical bill or hospital receipt

医药单.notes: In hospital and workplace drama plots, 医药单 refers to the itemized hospital/pharmacy receipt required for 报销 (expense reimbursement) of 医药费 (medical expenses).

cognates.meaning: medical clinic, doctor's office; historically hospital (Sino-Japanese cognate)

医院.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正结构) combining 医 (yī, traditional 醫, 'medicine, healing') with 院 (yuàn, Middle Chinese *hjwænH, composed of 阝 'mound/wall' and 完 'complete enclosure', originally meaning a walled courtyard or mansion and since the Tang dynasty denoting an official bureau, academy, or public institution, as in 书院 and 翰林院). Adopted in the 19th century by missionary and modernizing physicians to translate Western 'hospital'.

history.meaning: imperial medical bureau; public charity infirmary (Tang–Song precursors)
modern medical institution for inpatient and outpatient care (19th-century missionary/modern coinage)
hospital

morphemes.meaning: walled courtyard; public institution or establishment

医院.notes: False friend alert across East Asia: in Mainland China, 医院 is a full-scale 'hospital', whereas in Japan (医院 *iin*) and Korea (의원 *uiwon*) it denotes a smaller private clinic (while 'hospital' there is 病院 *byōin* / 병원 *byeongwon*).

rootFamily.gloss: to be admitted to the hospital, be hospitalized
to be discharged from the hospital
dean or director of a hospital/institute

十.etymology: Cardinal numeral 'ten'. In Shang oracle-bone script, 十 was written as a single vertical stroke (|), to which Zhou bronze script added a central dot that thickened into a horizontal cross-stroke (十), symbolizing completeness across all four directions.

history.meaning: vertical/crossed tally = numeral ten; complete

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 十 (via 萌典)

十一.etymology: An additive decimal numeral compound combining 十 (shí, Old Chinese *g.[d]əp, originally a vertical tally stroke ｜ on oracle bones later crossed with a horizontal stroke or dot, inheriting Proto-Sino-Tibetan *g-jip 'ten') and 一 (yī, OC *ʔi[t], a single horizontal tally stroke representing 'one', from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *ʔit). In earliest oracle bone inscriptions, 'eleven' was sometimes written with the conjunctive 十又一 ('ten and one') before stabilizing as 十一.

history.meaning: ten plus one; eleven (oracle bone and bronze inscriptions)
the cardinal number eleven; also 'one tenth' in classical fraction syntax
eleven; also shorthand (shí-yī) for October 1st (National Day holiday)

十一.notes: Besides the number 11, 十一 (pronounced shí-yī, digit by digit) is universal mainland shorthand for October 1st (10月1日, China's National Day Golden Week), and 双十一 ('Double Eleven', Nov 11) is the massive e-commerce shopping festival.

十二.etymology: Additive decimal numeral combining 十 ('ten') + 二 ('two') = 'twelve' (culturally central as the number of Earthly Branches 十二地支, zodiac animals 十二生肖, and months of the year).

history.meaning: ten plus two = twelve

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 十二 (via 萌典)

十二歌王.etymology: A proper-name modifier-head title (偏正专名) coined for the television drama *Behind the Scenes* (*幕后之王*), combining the numeral 十二 (shí'èr, 'twelve', evoking a full annual cycle or zodiacal roster of twelve) with 歌王 (gēwáng, a modifier-head compound of 歌 *gē* 'song, singing, vocalist' + 王 *wáng* 'king, champion, reigning monarch'). The compound 歌王 has been used in Chinese pop culture since the mid-20th century (especially in Hong Kong and Taiwan music awards and reality singing shows like *我是歌手*) to crown the top vocalist of a competition.

history.meaning: to sing / sovereign king (classical roots)
'King of Song', title for a reigning male vocalist or grand champion of a singing contest
Twelve Singers / Twelve Kings of Song (flagship singing competition show in *Behind the Scenes*)

morphemes.meaning: king, champion, supreme master of a field

十二歌王.notes: In Chinese entertainment television, productive suffixes like -王 (歌王 'King of Song', 舞王 'King of Dance', 喜剧之王 'King of Comedy') and -后 (歌后 'Queen of Song', 影后 'Best Actress') are standard showbiz titles for competition champions and award winners.

rootFamily.gloss: King of Song; singing competition grand champion
Queen of Song; premier female vocalist

十五.etymology: An additive decimal numeral compound combining 十 (shí, Old Chinese *g.[d]əp, 'ten') and 五 (wǔ, OC *C.ŋˤaʔ, originally written in oracle bone and bronze script as an X-shaped crisscross 乂 between two horizontal bars 二 symbolizing the intersection of yin and yang between heaven and earth, inheriting Proto-Sino-Tibetan *l-ŋa 'five'). Culturally, the 15th day of the lunar month (朔望月之望) marks the full moon.

history.meaning: ten plus five; fifteen (attested in Shang oracle bones and *Analects* '吾十有五而志于学')
fifteen; also the fifteenth day of a lunar month (full moon night)

十五.notes: In cultural and idiomatic usage, 十五 by itself often refers to the 15th day of the lunar month (especially 正月十五, the Lantern Festival), as in the proverb 躲得过初一，躲不过十五 ('You may dodge the 1st of the month, but you can't dodge the 15th').

rootFamily.gloss: full moon of the 15th lunar night
in perfect detail (lit. from five to ten, counting in fives)

十六.etymology: Additive decimal numeral combining 十 ('ten') + 六 ('six') = 'sixteen' (also the number of liǎng 两 in a traditional Chinese catty 斤, preserved in the idiom 半斤八两 'six of one, half a dozen of the other').

history.meaning: ten plus six = sixteen

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 十六 (via 萌典)

十分.etymology: Degree adverb meaning 'very, extremely, completely, 100%', literally 'ten tenths / ten parts out of ten' (十 'ten' + 分 'tenth part'). Originated in Tang–Song expressions measuring fullness or purity (such as gold fineness or fullness of blossom) on a ten-part scale.

history.meaning: ten parts out of ten (full measure)
very; extremely; completely

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 十分 (via 萌典)

十月.etymology: A modifier-head calendrical compound (偏正结构) combining the numeral 十 (shí, Old Chinese *g.[d]əp, 'ten, tenth') with 月 (yuè, OC *ŋʷat, pictograph of a crescent moon 🌙, meaning 'moon, month'). Attested as early as the *Book of Odes* (*Shijing*: 「十月之交」 and 「十月获稻」) for the tenth month of the traditional lunisolar calendar, and mapped onto October when China adopted the Gregorian calendar (公历) in 1912.

history.meaning: the tenth month of the traditional Chinese lunisolar calendar (early winter)
October in the Gregorian calendar (or tenth lunar month when specified as 农历十月); also 'ten lunar months' of pregnancy (十月怀胎)

十月.notes: Chinese month names are completely regular number + 月 compounds (一月 through 十二月); note that in idioms like 十月怀胎 ('ten months of pregnancy'), 十月 means a duration of ten lunar months (~280 days), whereas in modern dates 十月 means October (and takes no 个: 十月 = October vs. 十个月 = ten months).

十有八九.etymology: A four-character idiomatic proportional phrase (成语/熟语) literally meaning 'out of ten (cases), there are eight or nine'. It derives from Classical Chinese fractional expressions such as 十之八九 (shí zhī bā jiǔ) and 十常八九 ('in ten, it is biasanya eight or nine times'), replacing the classical genitive particle 之 with the existential verb 有 (yǒu, 'to have, there are') in vernacular Mandarin to express an overwhelming probability (80–90% certainty).

history.form: 十之八九 / 十常八九
history.meaning: eight or nine parts out of ten (attested in Han–Jin histories such as *Jin Shu*)
in eight or nine cases out of ten; in all likelihood (Ming–Qing vernacular novels)
nine times out of ten; most likely, almost certainly

十有八九.notes: Functions adverbially before a verb or predicate clause to express strong speaker deduction (e.g., 他十有八九不会来, 'Nine times out of ten he won't come'); synonymous with the more colloquial 八成 (bāchéng, '80%, most likely').

rootFamily.gloss: eight or nine out of ten (slightly more literary variant)
pretty much certain, almost done (lit. eight or nine does not depart from ten)

十足.etymology: Compound adjective/adverb from 十 ('ten; complete perfection') + 足 ('foot; sufficient; full to the brim'). Originating in Song- and Ming-dynasty bullion terminology where 'ten-parts pure silver' (十足紋銀) denoted 100% fineness, it generalized to mean 'full of; one hundred percent; through and through'.

history.meaning: one hundred percent pure (of silver); fully sufficient
full of; thoroughgoing; 100%

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 十足

千.etymology: A single-morpheme phono-semantic character (形声字) dating back to Shang oracle bone inscriptions (甲骨文), originally formed from 人 (rén, Old Chinese *ni[ŋ], 'person', providing the phonetic core) with a horizontal tally stroke 一 across the lower stem to signify the number 'one thousand' (OC *s.n̥ˤi[ŋ], Middle Chinese *tshen). In anti-fraud financial writing (大写), it is written as 仟.

history.meaning: one thousand (attested in Shang oracle bones for troop and sacrifice counts)
one thousand; figuratively 'countless, myriad, in every way' (paired with 万/萬)
thousand; also emphatic adverbial prefix in 千万 ('by all means')

千.notes: When counting an exact thousand in Mandarin, 一千 (yīqiān) is required (unlike English where 'a thousand' or 'thousand' may vary, bare 千 only appears after another digit like 两千 or in four-character idioms like 千方百计 and 千千万万).

rootFamily.gloss: ten thousand; tens of thousands; by all means,千萬 (emphatic adverb)
by every possible means, by hook or by crook

千万.etymology: Compound of 千 ('thousand') + 万 (萬, 'ten thousand'): literally 'ten million, countless thousands'. In Tang–Song vernacular it grammaticalized in imperatives and exhortations into an emphatic adverb meaning 'by all means, whatever you do (be sure to / never…)'.

history.meaning: ten million; countless
by all means; be sure to

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 千万 (via 萌典)

升.etymology: Pictograph of a scooping ladle holding grain or liquid: originally a dry/liquid volume measure ('liter / pint', about 1 liter in modern metric use), and since the Shijing and Yijing a verb meaning 'rise, ascend, go up, promote in rank'.

history.meaning: grain measure (liter); rise, ascend, promote
rise; ascend; promote; liter

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 升 (via 萌典)

升任.etymology: A serial/resultative verbal compound (连动/动补结构) combining 升 (shēng, traditional 昇/陞 in the sense of 'ascend, rise in rank', Old Chinese *s-təŋ, originally a ladle measure that came to mean 'to rise, mount upward') and 任 (rèn, OC *nə[m]-s, 'to bear a burden, hold office, assume a post'). Literally 'to ascend and assume the post of', it continues classical bureaucratic terminology (such as 陞任 in Ming–Qing official gazettes).

history.meaning: to be promoted and appointed to an official government post (Ming–Qing bureaucratic prose)
to be promoted to (a specific executive, official, or managerial title)

morphemes.meaning: assume office, take up a post or responsibility

升任.notes: A formal transitive verb that must be followed immediately by the specific title or role assumed (e.g., 升任总监, 'be promoted to Chief Director'); for intransitive 'get promoted', use 升职 (shēngzhí) or 晋升 (jìnshēng).

rootFamily.gloss: to get a job promotion (intransitive VO)
to serve as, hold the post of
to appoint to an official or corporate post

cognates.meaning: promotion in grade or rank (Sino-Japanese cognate)
to advance in rank, upgrade (Sino-Vietnamese cognate)

升级.etymology: A verb-object compound (动宾结构) combining 升 (shēng, 'to rise, ascend, advance') and 级 (jí, traditional 級, Old Chinese *krəp, composed of 纟 'silk thread' and phonetic 及 *gəp, originally meaning the ordered quality grades of silk threads and steps of a staircase, and since Qin legal law denoting 'ranks of merit/decapitated enemy heads' and later 'official grades or school levels'). In late 20th-century Mandarin, it expanded via calquing of English 'upgrade' and 'escalate'.

history.meaning: to advance a step in official rank or civil ladder
to move up a grade in school or rank; to escalate (a conflict)
to upgrade (software, equipment, consumption, or show format), level up, or escalate

升级.notes: Extremely versatile in modern Chinese: covers school promotion (move up a grade), conflict escalation (矛盾升级), gaming ('level up'), software/hardware ('upgrade'), and TV show revamps (赛制全面升级, 'competition format fully upgraded').

升职.etymology: Verb-object compound of 升 ('rise, promote') + 职 (職, 'official post, job position'): 'be promoted to a higher job position, get a promotion'.

history.meaning: be promoted in post/rank

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 升职 (via 萌典)

午休.etymology: A modifier-head verbal/nominal compound (偏正结构) combining 午 (wǔ, Old Chinese *[m].qʰˤaʔ, the seventh Earthly Branch 地支 corresponding to 11:00 a.m.–1:00 p.m., hence 'noon, midday') and 休 (xiū, OC *qʰ(r)u, an associative compound 会意字 depicting a person 人 leaning against a tree 木 to rest in its shade, meaning 'to rest, cease work'). Literally 'to rest at midday'.

history.meaning: to sleep during the daytime or at noon (attested in Classical & Tang poetry)
to take a midday break or nap between morning and afternoon work shifts

morphemes.meaning: rest, take a break, cease work

午休.notes: Broader than 午睡 (wǔshuì, 'afternoon nap/siesta'): 午休 covers the entire midday break period at school or work (午休时间, 'lunch break hours'), during which Chinese office workers and film crews often take a short nap.

rootFamily.gloss: to take leave, be on vacation

午餐.etymology: Compound noun of 午 ('noon, midday') + 餐 ('meal, eat'): 'lunch, midday meal' (slightly more formal than 午饭).

history.meaning: midday meal; lunch

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 午餐 (via 萌典)

午饭.etymology: Everyday compound noun of 午 ('noon, midday') + 饭 (飯, 'cooked grain, meal'): 'lunch'.

history.meaning: midday meal; lunch

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 午饭 (via 萌典)

半.etymology: Ancient ideogram (会意字) showing 八 ('part, divide in two') above 牛 ('ox'): literally 'split an ox in half', hence 'half, semi-, mid-, incomplete'.

history.meaning: ox divided in two = half; in the middle of
half; semi-

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 半 (via 萌典)

半价.etymology: Modifier-head noun compound of 半 ('half') + 价 (價, 'price'): 'half price (50% off)'.

history.stage: Song–Ming commercial Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: half price

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 半价 (via 萌典)

cognates.word: bán kết (short for bán quyết tái)

半决赛.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正结构) formed as a morphological calque of English *semi-final(s)*: 半 (bàn, Old Chinese *pˤan-s, depicting an ox 牛 split in two by八, meaning 'half, semi-') + 决赛 (juésài, traditional 決賽, 'final match/championship round', from 决 'to decide conclusively' + 赛 'competition, originally a thanksgiving sacrifice 賽 after harvest that evolved into competing in splendor').

history.meaning: final decisive match of a sporting or artistic competition (early 20th-century athletic vocabulary)
semi-final round preceding the grand final (calqued from English *semi-final*)

半决赛.notes: Standard in Mainland China for sports tournaments and reality competition shows (*幕后之王*); in Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Japan/Korea, the synonym 准决赛 (zhǔnjuésài, 'quasi-final / pre-final') is also widely used.

半周.etymology: A quantifier-noun compound (数量结构) combining 半 (bàn, Old Chinese *pˤan-s, originally an ox 牛 divided in two 八, meaning 'half') and 周 (zhōu, traditional 週 in the sense of 'cycle, week', OC *tiw, originally meaning 'densely planted field' or 'to encircle, complete a full circuit/revolution'). In modern Chinese, 周 serves as a classifierless temporal measure noun for a seven-day week (adapted from the seven-day planetary cycle 七曜).

history.meaning: half a circumference or half a revolution/cycle (classical astronomical and geometric sense)
half a week (three to four days); also half a lap/cycle

半周.notes: Like 天 (day) and 年 (year), 周 ('week') is a quasi-classifier temporal noun and takes no 个: say 半周 ('half a week'), contrasting with 半个星期 (bàn ge xīngqī) and 半个礼拜 (bàn ge lǐbài) which require 个.

半壁江山.etymology: A four-character modifier-head idiom (偏正成语) combining 半壁 (bànbì, 'half of a cliff/wall, a fractured half of a realm', from 半 'half' + 壁 *bì* 'defensive wall, precipice') with 江山 (jiāngshān, 'rivers and mountains', the classic metonymy for 'the state's territory, sovereign realm, or an entire industry domain', literally Yangtze River 江 + mountains 山). Historically popularized in Southern Song and Ming–Qing patriotic poetry and drama (referring to the Southern Song holding onto half of China south of the Huai/Yangtze after losing the north to the Jurchen Jin), it evolved in modern Mandarin to mean 'half of an entire industry, market, or field'.

history.meaning: rivers and mountains (sovereign territory); half of a defensive wall or realm (attested in Tang–Song poetry and Southern Song laments)
half of a country's territory preserved or remaining after invasion (Ming–Qing historical drama & prose)
half the country; figuratively half of an entire industry, market share, or professional field

morphemes.meaning: half of a wall/realm, a truncated half
rivers (Yangtze) and mountains; sovereign realm or industry domain

半壁江山.notes: A staple expression in Chinese media and entertainment journalism: e.g., 撑起华语乐坛的半壁江山 ('holding up half the sky/field of the Mandopop music industry') or 占领综艺市场的半壁江山 ('occupying half the variety-show market').

rootFamily.gloss: rivers and mountains; country, state power, industry throne
half the sky (famous Mao-era phrase for women's contribution)
one's own turf, hard-won territory or career domain

半夜.etymology: Temporal compound of 半 ('half, middle of') + 夜 ('night'): 'midnight, the middle of the night'. Attested since Classical prose and Tang poetry.

history.stage: Classical & Tang Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: middle of the night; midnight

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 半夜 (via 萌典)

半天.etymology: A modifier-head temporal compound (偏正结构) combining 半 (bàn, Old Chinese *pˤan-s, 'half') and 天 (tiān, OC *l̥ˤin, originally an anthropomorphic front-view drawing of a standing figure with a prominent head, meaning 'sky, heaven' and extended in vernacular Chinese to 'day, daytime'). In colloquial Mandarin since the Ming–Qing period, 半天 underwent hyperbolic semantic extension from 'half a day' to 'a very long time, ages' when waiting or struggling.

history.meaning: half a day (classical literary equivalent, as in Tang poetry '偷得浮生半日闲')
half of the sky (mid-air); half a day; figuratively a long while (Ming–Qing vernacular fiction such as *Hongloumeng*)
half a day; colloquially 'for ages, a long time' (after verbs or before 才)

半天.notes: In everyday speech, 半天 after a verb (e.g., 等了半天 'waited for ages', 找了半天 'looked everywhere for a long time') or before 才 almost always means 'a long time' (often just 10–30 frustrating minutes) rather than a literal 12 hours! Also used as a discourse marker 搞了半天 ('after all that, it turns out...').

rootFamily.gloss: half a day (literary); half a day's leisure (偷得浮生半日闲)
the whole day, all day long
after all that fuss, it turns out that... (colloquial idiom)

cognates.meaning: half a year, six months (Sino-Japanese cognate)

半年.etymology: A quantifier-noun temporal compound (偏正/数量结构) combining 半 (bàn, Old Chinese *pˤan-s, 'half') and 年 (nián, OC *C.nˤi[ŋ], originally written 秊 in oracle bone script as a person 人 carrying a ripe grain stalk 禾 on their back, meaning 'harvest' and by extension 'a full agricultural year' since only one main crop cycle occurred annually in northern China).Attested from Han-Tang prose onward for a six-month period.

history.meaning: half an agricultural or calendar year; six months (attested in Six Dynasties & Tang texts)
half a year, six months

半年.notes: Because 年 functions directly as a measure word, it never takes 个 (*半个年 is ungrammatical; compare 六个月 'six months'). Divided in corporate and television scheduling into 上半年 (first half of the year, H1) and 下半年 (second half of the year, H2).

rootFamily.gloss: a year and a half (used figuratively for roughly a year)

半级.etymology: A quantifier-noun compound (数量结构) combining 半 (bàn, Old Chinese *pˤan-s, 'half') with 级 (jí, traditional 級, OC *krəp, originally 'grades of silk thread' and 'steps of a stairway', extended to administrative ranks, civil service tiers, and technical levels). In bureaucratic and corporate hierarchies, 半级 denotes a half-step rank difference (such as between a deputy post and a full post, or a sub-tier promotion/demotion).

history.meaning: step of a stair; grade in the imperial nine-rank civil service (九品官人法)
half a rank, half a bureaucratic or technical grade/level

半级.notes: In Chinese organizational culture (civil service, state media, and corporate hierarchies), expressions like 高半级 ('half a rank higher') or 官大一级压死人，大出半级也管人 describe subtle status differences between nominally peer roles (such as an executive with a concurrent leadership seat).

rootFamily.gloss: to upgrade, be promoted a level, escalate

半辈子.etymology: A modifier-head colloquial nominal compound (偏正结构) combining 半 (bàn, 'half') with 辈子 (bèizi, 'lifetime, generation'). Here 辈 (bèi, Old Chinese *pˤə[t]-s, composed of 非 'lined up in two wings' over 车 'chariots', originally meaning 'a contingent of a hundred war chariots dispatched together', then 'a cohort, generation of people', and in Mandarin vernacular suffixed with 子 to mean 'the span of one's whole life'). Literally 'half a lifetime'.

history.meaning: a cohort of war chariots; a generation or peer class of people (Classical Chinese)
half of a person's lifespan (vernacular equivalent of literary 半生 in Ming–Qing fiction)
half a lifetime; decades of one's life spent in a career or marriage

半辈子.notes: Colloquial, emotionally resonant counterpart to literary 半生 (bànshēng); often divided into 上半辈子 (the first half of one's life) and 下半辈子 (the rest of one's life), or used hyperbolically (我干了半辈子电视, 'I've worked in television for half a lifetime').

rootFamily.gloss: all one's life, a whole lifetime
the rest/second half of one's life
half a lifetime (literary register, e.g., 出走半生)

cognates.meaning: ethnic Chinese person, Hoa people (Sino-Vietnamese cognate)

华人.etymology: A modifier-head ethnonymic compound (偏正结构) combining 华 (huá, traditional 華, Old Chinese *N-qʷʰˤra, originally a blossom/flower 𠌶 symbolizing magnificent cultural efflorescence and the sacred Mount Hua 华山 in the Central Plains heartland, serving since the pre-Qin compound 华夏 *Huáxià* as the self-designation of Chinese civilization) and 人 (rén, OC *ni[ŋ], 'person, people'). Already used in Tang–Song texts to contrast Chinese people with foreign peoples (胡人/夷人), in modern usage it specifically denotes people of ethnic Chinese descent worldwide regardless of citizenship.

history.meaning: people of the Huaxia civilization (contrasted with frontier peoples in Six Dynasties & Tang texts)
person of ethnic Chinese heritage worldwide (especially overseas ethnic Chinese regardless of nationality)

华人.notes: Crucial distinction in modern usage: 中国人 (Zhōngguórén) denotes a citizen/national of China, 华侨 (huáqiáo) denotes a Chinese citizen residing abroad, while 华人 (huárén) is an inclusive cultural/ethnic term covering ethnic Chinese globally (e.g., 美籍华人 'Chinese American', 全球华人 'global Chinese community').

rootFamily.gloss: Chinese citizen living abroad, overseas Chinese national
the Chinese language (especially in Southeast Asia & global media)

协调.etymology: A coordinative verbal/adjectival compound (并列结构) uniting 协 (xié, traditional 協, Old Chinese *ɦlˤep, composed of 十 'ten/multitude' and 劦 'three plows/strengths 力 joined together', meaning 'to unite strength, harmonize, cooperate') and 调 (tiáo, traditional 調, OC *lˤiw, composed of 言 'speech' and 周 'all-round/complete', originally meaning 'to tune musical instruments or blend flavors into harmony'). Classical Chinese used 协调 for musical and cosmic harmony; modern Mandarin extended it (reinforced by Japanese 協調 *kyōchō*) to organizational and interpersonal coordination.

history.meaning: harmonious in tone or proportion; to bring music or elements into accord (attested in Six Dynasties & Tang texts)
to coordinate (departments, schedules, stakeholders); well-proportioned and harmonious

协调.notes: Functions both as a transitive verb meaning 'to coordinate/mediate between parties' (e.g., 协调各部门档期, 'coordinate schedules across departments' — a core producer duty in *幕后之王*) and as an adjective meaning 'well-coordinated, proportional' (动作很协调).

rootFamily.gloss: to adjust, regulate, restructure (schedules or lineup)

单.etymology: Written 單 in traditional script; oracle bone forms depict a forked hunting weapon, net, or flat shield-like implement. In Old Chinese (*tˁar), the graph came to denote 'single, unlined (of garments), solitary' as opposed to 複 ('double, lined'). From its adjectival sense of 'single, alone', it grammaticalized in Literary and early Vernacular Chinese into a restrictive adverb meaning 'solely, specifically, separately, or merely'.

history.meaning: forked hunting implement; single, unlined garment; solitary
single, alone; only, merely, separately
separately, specially, alone, solely

单.notes: As an adverb before a verb (e.g., 单看 'looking solely at', 单说 'speaking specifically of'), 单 emphasizes singling out one item or angle from a broader group.

单凭.etymology: A modifier-head prepositional/verbal compound (单凭, trad. 單憑) formed from the restrictive adverb 单 (dān, 'solely, merely, alone') modifying the verb/preposition 凭 (píng, trad. 憑, 'to lean upon, rely on, take as basis'). Literally 'leaning solely upon', it crystallized in vernacular Chinese to introduce a single, often insufficient condition or piece of evidence.

history.meaning: to lean against; to rely upon, depend on
relying solely upon, merely on the basis of
relying solely on, merely by virtue of

morphemes.meaning: to lean on, rely on, base on

单凭.notes: Frequently paired with a rhetorical negative or concessive clause in the second half of a sentence (e.g., 单凭这一点还不够 'relying solely on this one point is still not enough').

单子.etymology: Colloquial noun meaning 'printed form, list, bill, slip, receipt; bedsheet', formed from 单 (單, 'single sheet, list, bill') + nominal suffix 子 (-zi).

history.meaning: written list, slip, bill, or sheet

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 单子 (via 萌典)

单独.etymology: A coordinative (synonymic) compound (单独, trad. 單獨) combining 单 (dān, 'single, uncoupled') and 独 (dú, trad. 獨, 'solitary, alone', originally depicting a flock-guarding dog known for fighting alone). Already attested in Classical and Literary Chinese for 'solitary, by oneself', its modern adverbial and attributive usage ('independently, on one's own') was further reinforced across East Asia by Meiji Japanese 単独 (tandoku).

history.meaning: solitary, unassisted, standing alone
independently, alone, on one's own, separately

单独.notes: In workplace and production dramas, 单独行动 ('act on one's own without team clearance') and 单独谈谈 ('speak privately one-on-one') are high-frequency collocations.

单身.etymology: A modifier-head compound (单身, trad. 單身) composed of 单 (dān, 'single, solitary') + 身 (shēn, 'body, person, self'), literally 'a single body/person'. In Tang–Song literary and vernacular texts (such as Bai Juyi's poetry and Dunhuang bianwen), it meant 'all alone, unaccompanied' or 'an unattached individual', later specializing in modern social usage to mean 'unmarried, single'.

history.meaning: a solitary person; alone, unaccompanied by family or retinue
single, unmarried, unattached

单身.notes: Gives rise to popular modern slang like 单身贵族 ('single aristocrat / happily single professional') and 单身狗 ('single dog', humorous self-deprecating slang for an unmarried person).

卖.etymology: Ideographic compound (traditional 賣) placing 出 ('put out, send forth', simplified to 十 at the top) above 買 (买, 'buy, trade with shell money'): literally 'put goods out for purchase' = 'sell' (and by extension 'betray [卖国] or show off').

history.meaning: put out to trade = sell
sell

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 卖 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to keep listeners in suspense; to be coy with details

卖关子.etymology: A verb-object idiomatic phrase (卖关子, trad. 賣關子) originating in Song–Yuan–Ming oral storytelling (说书 shuōshū): 卖 (mài, 'to sell, show off, ply') + 关子 (guānzi, from 关节 guānjié 'pivotal joint, critical juncture, plot climax' + nominal suffix 子). Street storytellers would deliberately halt their narrative at the most gripping cliffhanger to collect money or ensure the audience returned for the next session.

history.meaning: pivotal juncture or climax in a dramatic plot or oral tale
to pause at a story's climax to entice payment; to leave listeners hanging
to keep listeners in suspense, withhold the punchline or key detail

morphemes.meaning: to sell, display, ply as a trick

卖关子.notes: A separable verb-object phrase (离合词): most commonly heard in the negative imperative 别卖关子了！ ('Stop keeping us in suspense! / Spit it out!'). In TV production, cutting to a commercial right before a reveal is a visual form of 卖关子.

rootFamily.gloss: to show off one's cleverness or skill

卖钱.etymology: A verb-object purposive compound (卖钱, trad. 賣錢) combining 卖 (mài, trad. 賣, derived from 出 'send out' over 買 'trade', hence 'to sell') and 钱 (qián, trad. 錢, originally an agricultural spade or weeding hoe in Old Chinese *dzan, which became a bronze spade-coin and later 'copper cash, money' in general). The object 钱 specifies the proceeds or purpose of the sale ('to sell in exchange for money').

history.meaning: to sell goods; bronze coin, money
to sell things for money, monetize by selling

morphemes.meaning: to sell, part with for a price

卖钱.notes: Functions as a separable verb-object compound (e.g., 卖不了多少钱 'cannot sell for much money') and often contrasts commercial monetization with artistic or sentimental value.

南.etymology: The character '南' (nán, south) is an ancient oracle bone script graph. Its earliest forms depict a bell or a hanging musical instrument, which was possibly a phonetic loan for the direction 'south'.
