The ancient Chinese oriented their maps and buildings facing south to capture sunlight and avoid harsh northern winds, cementing '南' as a culturally significant direction associated with warmth and the ruler's perspective. It has retained its primary directional meaning continuously for over three millennia. In modern usage, it is a foundational morpheme in geography.

history.meaning: north

南方.etymology: Compound directional noun of 南 ('south', an ancient bronze bell/hanging instrument graph borrowed since Shang oracle bones for 'south') + 方 ('direction, region'): 'the south, southern region'. Attested since the Shijing and Mencius.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Shijing, Mencius) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: the southern direction; the south

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 南方 (via 萌典)

博.etymology: In Old Chinese (*pˁak) and Classical Chinese, 博 carried two intertwined senses: 'broad, extensive, abundant' (cognate with 溥/敷 'spread wide') and 'to play the ancient board game liubo (六博), to gamble or contend for stakes'. From 'contending for stakes in a game', it developed the transitive verbal sense 'to vie for, win, court, or garner' (attention, sympathy, or applause).

history.meaning: broad, extensive; to play the board game liubo, contend for stakes
extensive, erudite; to gamble; to trade for or win (favor/praise)
to win, court, grab, curry (sympathy, eyeballs, laughter)

morphemes.meaning: broad, extensive; to contend for, win, court

博.notes: Heavily used in media and entertainment discourse for publicity-seeking tactics: 博眼球 ('grab eyeballs/attention'), 博同情 ('court sympathy'), 博关注 ('fish for attention'), and 博一笑 ('win a laugh').

rootFamily.gloss: to try to win, court, curry (favor/sympathy)

占.etymology: Ancient ideogram (会意字) attested on Shang oracle bones combining 卜 ('divination crack on turtle shell or bone') + 口 ('mouth interpreting the omen'): originally read zhān ('divine, foretell'), and read zhàn (historically also written 佔) for 'occupy, take up (space or time), account for, seize'.

history.meaning: read oracle cracks (zhān); take possession of, occupy (zhàn)
occupy; take up; constitute (zhàn); divine (zhān)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 占 (via 萌典)

卡.etymology: Compound ideogram combining 上 ('up') and 下 ('down') sharing a middle horizontal stroke—literally 'stuck neither able to go up nor down'. Read qiǎ, it means 'wedge, jam, get stuck, checkpoint, clip'; read kǎ, it also serves since the 20th century as a phonetic loan for 'card, calorie, truck (卡车), cassette'.

history.meaning: guardhouse pass; wedge between up and down; get stuck
get stuck, clip (qiǎ); card, truck, calorie (kǎ)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 卡 (via 萌典)

卡住.etymology: Resultative verb compound of 卡 ('wedge, jam between') + 住 ('hold fast, come to a halt'): 'get stuck, jam fast, choke/block'.

history.meaning: get jammed; become stuck fast

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 卡住 (via 萌典)

卡扣.etymology: Compound noun of 卡 ('clip, wedge, catch') + 扣 ('buckle, button, fasten'): 'snap fastener, buckle clip, latch'.

history.meaning: snap-fit clip; buckle fastener

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 卡扣 (via 萌典)

卡片.etymology: A modern phono-semantic hybrid compound: 卡 (kǎ) is a phonetic loanword adopted in late Qing and Republican coastal cities (especially Shanghai) to transliterate English 'card', while 片 (piàn, 'thin, flat slice, slip, or sheet') serves as an indigenous Chinese morphological head/classifier denoting a flat rectangular piece of stiff paper or cardstock.

history.meaning: phonetic loan for a Western paper card or calling card
card, index card, cue card, greeting card

morphemes.meaning: flat, thin slice, sheet, or slip

卡片.notes: In television variety production, host cue cards are called 台词卡 or 手卡 (literally 'hand cards'), a specialization of 卡片.

卡车.etymology: Early-20th-century hybrid phono-semantic loan combining 卡 (kǎ, phonetic rendering of English 'car' / 'cart') + native head noun 车 ('wheeled vehicle', pictograph of a carriage seen from above).

history.meaning: motorized cargo truck
truck; lorry

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 卡车

卧室.etymology: A Classical modifier-head compound (卧室, trad. 臥室) formed from 卧 (wò, trad. 臥, 'to lie down, recline, sleep', depicting a subject 臣 bending down to rest) modifying 室 (shì, 'inner chamber, room', from 宀 'roof' over 至 'arrive/innermost recess'). Attested since the Han dynasty (e.g., Book of Han) for an inner sleeping chamber.

history.meaning: inner sleeping chamber, retiring room
bedchamber, private sleeping quarters
bedroom

卧室.notes: The standard written and spoken Mandarin term for 'bedroom' (e.g., 主卧 'master bedroom', 次卧 'secondary bedroom'), slightly more formal than colloquial 睡房 (used in southern dialects/Cantonese).

rootFamily.gloss: sleeping car / sleeper berth on a train
full of hidden talent (lit. crouching tiger, hidden dragon)

cognates.meaning: crouching tiger, hidden dragon; hidden talents
crouching tiger, hidden dragon; hidden masters
crouching tiger, hidden dragon; undiscovered talent

卧虎藏龙.etymology: A symmetrical four-character idiom (卧虎藏龙, trad. 臥虎藏龍) built from two parallel phrases: 卧虎 ('reclining/crouching tiger') and 藏龙 ('hidden/concealed dragon'). It derives from the Northern Zhou poet Yu Xin's (庾信, 513–581) rhapsody '暗石疑藏虎，盘根似卧龙' ('Dark rocks seem to conceal tigers; coiled roots resemble reclining dragons'), originally describing awe-inspiring terrain and later metaphorically denoting a place brimming with unnoticed masters or hidden talent.

history.form: 暗石疑藏虎，盤根似臥龍
history.meaning: dark rocks seem to hide tigers, coiled roots resemble reclining dragons (awe-inspiring landscape)

history.form: 臥虎藏龍 / 藏龍臥虎
history.meaning: a place or circle full of concealed heroes and extraordinary unpretentious talent
full of hidden talent, teeming with undiscovered masters

morphemes.meaning: to hide, conceal, lie in store

卧虎藏龙.notes: Also reversible as 藏龙卧虎; made globally famous by Ang Lee's 2000 martial arts film 'Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon' (based on Wang Dulu's 1941 novel). Often used as a predicate after a place or organization: 这家公司真是卧虎藏龙.

rootFamily.gloss: to work undercover as a mole/informant
to hide, conceal, go into hiding

cognates.word: 衛星チャンネル / 衛星頻道

卫星频道.etymology: A modern four-character modifier-head compound (卫星频道, trad. 衛星頻道) joining two technical compounds: 卫星 (wèixīng, literally 'guarding/escorting star', coined in modern astronomy as a calque for 'planetary/artificial satellite' after French/English 'satellite' from Latin satelles 'bodyguard, attendant') + 频道 (píndào, from 频 'frequency' + 道 'channel, pathway', calquing radio-frequency 'channel').

history.meaning: attendant star; natural moon or artificial orbital satellite (calque of Latin satelles)
satellite television channel

卫星频道.notes: In China's broadcasting system, provincial flagship channels broadcast nationwide via satellite (卫星频道, abbreviated 卫视), competing fiercely for prime-time drama and variety show ratings against streaming platforms.

卫视.etymology: A modern disyllabic portmanteau/abbreviation (卫视, trad. 衛視) formed by extracting the first character of 卫星 (wèixīng, 'satellite', where 卫 means 'to guard, escort') and the second character of 电视 (diànshì, 'television', literally 'electric vision', where 视 means 'to view, look at'). Popularized in the 1990s with the launch of Star TV (星空卫视) and provincial satellite networks in mainland China.

history.meaning: satellite television broadcasting
satellite TV network or flagship provincial satellite channel

morphemes.meaning: television / vision (short for 电视 'electric vision')

卫视.notes: In Chinese media industry parlance, 卫视 refers specifically to major provincial satellite networks (such as 湖南卫视, 东方卫视, 浙江卫视) and contrasts with 网播 ('online streaming broadcast') or 地面频道 ('local terrestrial channels').

印.etymology: In oracle bone and bronze inscriptions, 印 depicts a descending hand/claw (爪) pressing down firmly upon a kneeling figure or tally (卩). In Old Chinese (*[ʔ]i[n]-s), it originally denoted an official seal of authority and the act of pressing a seal into clay (封泥), later generalizing with the Tang–Song invention of woodblock and movable-type printing to mean 'to print, engrave, or leave an impression'.

history.meaning: official seal or tally; to press down, stamp into clay
official seal, stamp, mark; to imprint, print from woodblocks
to print, engrave, stamp; seal, mark, impression

morphemes.meaning: seal, stamp; to press, imprint, print

印.notes: Used both literally for printing physical materials (印名片 'print business cards', 印刷 'printing press') and figuratively for etching memories into the mind (印在脑海里 'imprinted in one's mind').

印章.etymology: Coordinative noun compound of 印 ('official seal, stamp', originally a hand 爪 pressing down a kneeling figure 卩) + 章 ('insignia, emblem, seal'): 'seal, signet, stamp'. Attested since Han historical texts.

history.stage: Han Classical Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: engraved seal or stamp

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 印章 (via 萌典)

危机.etymology: A modifier-head compound (危机, trad. 危機) combining 危 (wēi, 'precipitous, perilous, danger', depicting a person on a cliff) and 机 (jī, trad. 機, 'crossbow trigger mechanism; incipient turning point or critical juncture'). Attested in Six Dynasties and Tang Literary Chinese (e.g., Lu Ji's Wen Fu and Zhao Lin's Yinhualu) meaning 'latent peril / trigger of danger', it was adopted in Meiji Japan (危機 kiki) to translate English 'crisis' (from Greek krisis 'turning point, decision') and returned to modern Chinese with that modern socio-political sense.

history.meaning: hidden trigger of danger, perilous juncture or trap
crisis, critical turning point (translation of English crisis)
crisis, critical predicament or emergency

morphemes.meaning: crossbow trigger, pivotal mechanism, critical juncture

危机.notes: Despite the famous Western motivational trope that 危机 means 'danger + opportunity', philologically 机 here means 'incipient trigger / critical juncture' (as in 枢机), not 机会 ('opportunity')—though Chinese speakers themselves occasionally play on the pun in business rhetoric.

rootFamily.gloss: turning point, favorable shift in a crisis

cognates.word: 危機公關 (ngai4 gei1 gung1 gwaan1)

危机公关.etymology: A contemporary four-character modifier-head compound (危机公关, trad. 危機公關) combining 危机 (wēijī, 'crisis') with 公关 (gōngguān, the syllabic abbreviation of 公共关系 gōnggòng guānxì, itself a 20th-century calque of English 'public relations'). The whole compound calques English 'crisis public relations / crisis management PR'.

history.meaning: public relations (calque and syllabic contraction of English public relations)
crisis public relations, emergency reputation management

危机公关.notes: A signature buzzword in Chinese entertainment and corporate workplace dramas (*幕后之王*), used both as a noun ('emergency PR strategy') and verbally (做危机公关 'to run crisis PR / damage control' after a celebrity scandal or broadcast mishap).

rootFamily.gloss: to pass a test or survive a crisis

即使.etymology: A compound hypothetical-concessive conjunction formed from 即 (jí, originally depicting a person kneeling beside a vessel of food 皀 to eat, hence 'to approach, right then, granted that') and 使 (shǐ, 'to send, cause, suppose, let it be that'). Each character independently functioned in Classical Chinese as a hypothetical marker ('even if / suppose that'); their combination into the disyllabic reinforcing compound 即使 is attested from the Han and Six Dynasties onward.

history.meaning: to approach / granted that + to cause / suppose that
even supposing that, even if
even if, even though (concessive conjunction)

morphemes.meaning: granted that, even at the moment of
to cause, suppose, let it be that

即使.notes: Almost always correlates with 也 (yě) or 还是 (háishi) in the main clause: 即使……也…… ('Even if [X], still [Y]'). Slightly more formal in register than 就算 (jiùsuàn) or 哪怕 (nǎpà).

即兴.etymology: A verb-object / relational compound (即兴, trad. 即興) composed of 即 (jí, 'to approach, right at the present moment/scene') + 兴 (xìng, trad. 興, read in the departing/fourth tone, meaning 'poetic inspiration, stirred mood, creative impulse', from the Classical poetic principle of 赋比兴). Originating in Tang–Song poetics for composing verse inspired on the spot, it was also adopted in Japanese (即興 sokkyō) to render Western musical/theatrical 'improvisation'.

history.meaning: stirred to poetic inspiration by the immediate scene or moment
improvised, impromptu, off-the-cuff, ad-libbed

morphemes.meaning: right upon the moment, approaching the scene

即兴.notes: Note the fourth-tone pronunciation xìng ('mood, inspiration', as in 兴趣, 尽兴), never first-tone xīng. Common in stage and broadcast contexts: 即兴表演 ('improv performance'), 即兴发挥 ('ad-lib / improvise on the spot').

rootFamily.gloss: to enjoy oneself to the fullest, high spirits

即将.etymology: A coordinative temporal-aspectual adverb compound (即将, trad. 即將) formed by combining two Classical Chinese immediacy/futurity markers: 即 (jí, 'presently, immediately, right away') and 将 (jiāng, trad. 將, originally 'to lead, bring forward', grammaticalized since Old Chinese as a prospective aspect adverb meaning 'about to, going to'). Together they reinforce imminent future action.

history.meaning: presently, right away + about to, going to
on the verge of, about to happen presently
about to, very soon, on the point of

morphemes.meaning: about to, going to, in the near future

即将.notes: Belongs to formal and broadcast register (e.g., 节目即将开始 'The program is about to begin', 即将上映 'coming soon to theaters'); unlike 快要, 即将 cannot take a sentence-final 了 (*即将开始了 is generally avoided in strict style in favor of 即将开始).

rootFamily.gloss: right away, immediately, on the spot
about to, on the verge of (literary)

cognates.word: 即日生效 (zik1 jat6 sang1 haau6)

即日生效.etymology: A four-character administrative and legal phrase (即日生效, trad. 即日生效) structured as a temporal adverbial modifier followed by a verb-object predicate: 即日 (jírì, a Classical compound meaning 'this very day, the same day', from 即 'this very' + 日 'day') + 生效 (shēngxiào, 'to generate legal or practical effect', from 生 'to produce, give birth to' + 效 'efficacy, result').

history.meaning: on that very day, this very day
effective immediately, takes legal or administrative effect today

morphemes.meaning: to produce, generate, come into being

即日生效.notes: Standard formula at the end of corporate notices, personnel appointments, and contracts (e.g., 本任命即日生效 'This appointment takes effect immediately'), or expanded as 自即日起生效.

rootFamily.gloss: to lose effect, expire, become invalid

却.etymology: Originally written 卻 (combining 谷 'valley/palate' + 卩 'kneeling person'), meaning 'step back, retreat, decline/refuse (推却)'. In Tang–Song poetry and vernacular Mandarin, it grammaticalized into a pre-verbal adversative adverb meaning 'yet, however, but, unexpectedly'.

history.meaning: step back; repel; decline
yet; however; contrarily (pre-verbal adverb)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 却 (via 萌典)

卷.etymology: Merged simplified graph representing: (1) 捲 (read juǎn, 'roll up, sweep along, rolled-up item') and 卷 (read juǎn as a classifier for rolls of film, tape, or paper; read juàn as a noun meaning 'scroll, book volume, examination paper', originally from curving the knees 卩).

history.meaning: bend/roll up (juǎn); rolled scroll, volume (juàn)
roll up; classifier for rolls (juǎn); volume, exam paper (juàn)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 卷 (via 萌典)

卷尺.etymology: Compound noun of 卷 (捲, read juǎn, 'roll up, coil') + 尺 ('Chinese foot; ruler/measuring rule'): 'tape measure, retractable measuring tape'.

history.meaning: roll-up measuring rule; tape measure

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 卷尺 (via 萌典)

卷帘门.etymology: Three-character compound of 卷帘 ('roll-up curtain/shutter', 卷 'roll up' + 帘 'hanging screen/curtain') + 门 ('door'): 'roller shutter door, rolling security gate'.

history.meaning: rolling shutter door

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 卷帘门 (via 萌典)

卸.etymology: Ideographic/phono-semantic character combining 午/缹 ('pestle/horse') + 止 ('stop') + 卩 ('kneeling person'): originally 'unharness horses from a chariot and take off armor', hence 'unload (cargo), dismantle/detach (parts), lay down (a burden or office)'.

history.meaning: unharness a chariot; lay off armor
unload; remove; disassemble

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 卸 (via 萌典)

历史.etymology: Compound of 历 (歷, 'pass through in succession, experience, past ages') + 史 ('court chronicler, historical record'). Used in Classical Chinese for chronicles of past dynasties and standardized in the late 19th century (alongside Japanese 歴史 rekishi) for the modern academic discipline and concept of 'history'.

history.meaning: annals of successive dynasties
history; past course of events

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 历史 (via 萌典)

历史纪录.etymology: A four-character modifier-head nominal phrase (历史纪录, trad. 歷史紀錄) combining 历史 (lìshǐ, 'history', composed of 历 'past succession, chronicle' + 史 'court scribe, annals', popularized across East Asia via Meiji Japanese 歴史 rekishi) and 纪录 (jìlù, 'record, best achieved performance mark', from 纪 'to thread, chronicle' + 录 'to inscribe, register'). Literally 'a record across all of history', hence 'all-time record'.

history.meaning: chronological history + written chronicle or performance benchmark
all-time record, historical high/low benchmark

morphemes.meaning: to chronicle, record (typically as a noun/benchmark)

历史纪录.notes: In careful Mainland usage, 纪录 (with 纟) refers to a noun benchmark or documentary (破历史纪录 'break an all-time record', 纪录片 'documentary'), whereas 记录 (with 讠) is preferred for the verb 'to take notes/record' or written minutes. Common collocations: 创下/打破/刷新历史纪录.

cognates.meaning: advantages and disadvantages, pros and cons, stakes
pros and cons; formidable, fierce, awesome

厉害.etymology: Originally an antonymic coordinative compound written 利害 (lìhài) in Classical Chinese (e.g., Zhuangzi, Shiji), combining 利 ('sharp; benefit, advantage') and 害 ('harm, injury, disadvantage') to mean 'gains and losses, what is at stake'. In Yuan–Ming–Qing vernacular Chinese, focus shifted from 'pros and cons' to 'vital stakes / severe consequences', and the first character was re-written with homophonous 厉 (lì, trad. 厲, 'whetstone; fierce, stern, severe'), yielding 厉害 (lìhai, neutral tone on second syllable) meaning 'fierce, terrible, formidable, awesome'.

history.meaning: benefit and harm; advantages and disadvantages; vital stakes
crucial stakes; severe, fierce, hard to deal with
fierce, severe, formidable, amazing, awesome

morphemes.meaning: whetstone; stern, fierce, severe (replacing earlier 利 'sharp/benefit')
harm, injury, severity (neutral tone in colloquial usage)

厉害.notes: Pronounced lìhai (with a neutral tone on 害) when meaning 'formidable, amazing, intense', contrasting with the literary spelling 利害 (lìhài, full fourth tone on both syllables), which retains the ancient meaning 'pros and cons / conflict of interest' (as in 利害关系).

rootFamily.gloss: gains and losses, stakes, conflict of interest
Afraid of, fearful; to harm, injure

压.etymology: Simplified from 壓 (yā), a phono-semantic character with the earth radical 土 ('soil, ground weight') and phonetic 厭 (yàn, 'press down, satiate'). In Classical Chinese 壓 meant 'to crush beneath fallen earth or stone, to weigh down from above', extending naturally to holding light objects flat (压纸 'weight down paper') and figuratively to calming or suppressing pressure.

morphemes.meaning: press down from above; weight down (simplified from 壓, earth 土 radical)

history.meaning: crush; press down with weight
press; weigh down; pin underneath

压力.etymology: Compound noun of 压 (壓, 'press down, crush, weigh upon') + 力 ('force'). Coined in modern physics for mechanical/fluid 'pressure' and extended across everyday Mandarin to psychological, work, or social 'stress, pressure'.

history.meaning: physical pressure; mental or social stress

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 压力 (via 萌典)

压力山大.etymology: A playful early-21st-century Chinese internet neologism (emerging around 2010 on Baidu Tieba and Weibo) structured as a topic-comment four-character phrase: 压力 (yālì, 'pressure, stress') + 山大 (shāndà, 'as huge as a mountain', compressed from 压力大得像山一样). Crucially, the entire four-syllable string 压力山大 (yālì shāndà) is a quasi-homophonic pun on 亚历山大 (Yàlìshāndà), the standard Mandarin transliteration of the Western name 'Alexander'.

history.meaning: Mandarin transliteration of the given name Alexander
under mountain-sized pressure, super stressed (humorous internet idiom)

压力山大.notes: Used predicatively (我最近压力山大 'I've been under mountain-sized stress lately') to express heavy workplace or academic pressure with a light, self-deprecating tone.

rootFamily.gloss: tall, rich, and handsome / upscale and impressive (slang)

厘米.etymology: Modern metric measure word combining 厘 (traditional 釐, traditional Chinese decimal fraction equal to one-hundredth of a unit) + 米 ('meter', phonetic loan via French *mètre* / English *meter*). Standardized in the twentieth century as the official Chinese term for 'centimeter' (1/100 of a meter).

history.meaning: centimeter (cm)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 厘米

厚.etymology: Adjective meaning 'thick (opposite of 薄 báo 'thin'); deep, generous, rich (of flavor or kindness)'. In oracle-bone and bronze scripts, 厚 combined 厂 ('cliff overhang') + 石/日 + 子, evoking the massive thickness of earth and rock.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: thick; substantial; generous; deep

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 厚 (via 萌典)

厚厚.etymology: Vivid AA-reduplication of the adjective 厚 ('thick'): 'thick, nice and thick, in a thick layer' (e.g., 厚厚的一本书 'a hefty thick book').

history.meaning: very thick; in a thick layer

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 厚厚 (via 萌典)

原位.etymology: A concise determinative compound joining 原 (yuán, originally 'mountain springhead 源', hence 'source, original, former') and 位 (wèi, 'standing place, assigned seat or position', depicting a person 亻 standing 立 at court). Literally 'original position', 原位 is used throughout everyday Mandarin when returning tools, furniture, or flagstones cleanly to the exact spot where they stood.

history.meaning: origin/former + standing position
original place; exact former position

rootFamily.gloss: polite measure word for people; seat

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 原位

cognates.meaning: original author, creator of an adapted work

原作者.etymology: A three-character modifier-head agentive compound formed from 原 (yuán, 'original, source, firsthand') + 作者 (zuòzhě, 'author, creator', itself composed of Classical 作 'to make, compose' + agentive nominalizer 者 'the one who'), or analyzed as 原作 ('original work') + 者 ('-er'). Standardized in modern publishing and media law alongside Japanese 原作者 (gensakusha).

history.meaning: one who creates, founder, literary author or composer
original author or creator (especially of an adapted work)

原作者.notes: Essential in IP (intellectual property) and television adaptation discussions (e.g., 尊重原作者 'respect the original author') when turning a web novel or foreign format into a script.

原则.etymology: A modifier-head compound (原则, trad. 原則) combining 原 (yuán, 'fountainhead, origin, fundamental') and 则 (zé, trad. 則, 'rule, law, pattern, standard', originally depicting cauldron inscriptions 鼎 cut with a knife 刀 as binding laws). While attested sporadically in Tang poetry (e.g., Du Fu), its modern sense as an abstract guiding rule or 'principle' was crystallized in Meiji Japan (原則 gensoku) to translate Western philosophical and legal 'principle' (Latin principium) and re-imported into modern Chinese.

history.meaning: original standard or pattern
principle, fundamental rule (translation of English/French principle)
principle, fundamental rule or moral baseline

原则.notes: Frequently used with 上 to mean 'in principle' (原则上同意 'agree in principle') or to describe personal integrity (有原则 'principled', 原则问题 'a matter of principle').

cognates.meaning: original, self-created, not adapted or plagiarized

原创.etymology: A modifier-head compound (原创, trad. 原創) composed of 原 (yuán, 'source, original, firsthand') and 创 (chuàng, trad. 創/剏, originally 'knife wound / to cut open', extended in Classical Chinese to 'to initiate, pioneer, create for the first time'). Literally 'created at the source / firsthand creation', distinguishing independent creative works from adaptations, remakes, or licensed imports.

history.meaning: fountainhead, origin + to initiate, pioneer, found
original, self-created, non-adapted creative work

原创.notes: A central thematic keyword in *幕后之王* (*Behind the Scenes*): Chinese television producers debate developing本土原创节目 ('homegrown original variety shows') versus buying foreign format rights (引进版权/买模式).

rootFamily.gloss: original creative power / capacity for originality

cognates.meaning: original creative power, capacity for originality

原创力.etymology: A three-character modifier-head compound (原创力, trad. 原創力) formed by attaching the productive abstract-noun suffix 力 (lì, 'strength, power, capacity, faculty', originally depicting a sinew or plowshare) to 原创 (yuánchuàng, 'original creation, originality'). Modeled on modern capacity compounds such as 创造力 ('creativity') and 想象力 ('imagination').

history.meaning: original creation + power, capacity, faculty
original creative power, capacity for independent innovation

原创力.notes: Frequently used in cultural policy, media industry summits, and creative-industry critiques to denote an organization's or nation's core ability to generate original IP rather than imitate.

原因.etymology: A coordinative (synonymic) noun compound combining 原 (yuán, originally 厵/源, 'water spring emerging from beneath a cliff 厂, fountainhead, source') and 因 (yīn, originally depicting a person 大 resting on a mat 囗, hence 'basis, that upon which something relies, cause'). Used in pre-modern Chinese historical and Buddhist causality texts and reinforced in modern philosophical and everyday usage alongside Meiji Japanese 原因 (gen'in).

history.meaning: fountainhead, source + basis, underlying cause
underlying origin and cause of an event
reason, cause, underlying factor

原因.notes: Often pairs with 结果 ('result, outcome') in cause-and-effect discussions; unlike 理由 ('justification, stated excuse/argument'), 原因 refers to the objective or actual underlying cause.

原地.etymology: A modifier-head spatial noun compound composed of 原 (yuán, 'original, former, unchanged') and 地 (dì, 'earth, ground, spot, location'). Literally 'the original ground/spot', it denotes either the exact physical spot where someone or something was already standing, or figuratively a state of zero forward progress.

history.meaning: original, former + ground, place, locality
the exact spot, original place, in place (without moving)

原地.notes: Functions directly as a pre-verbal adverbial without 在 in many set expressions: 原地踏步 ('mark time in place / stagnate without making progress'), 原地待命 ('stand by on the spot'), and internet slang 原地出道 ('debut right on the spot').

rootFamily.gloss: original site or location (of a building/institution)
intact, in its original state without being moved

原封不动.etymology: Four-character idiom from 原 ('original') + 封 ('paper seal; sealed strip on a letter, door, or jar') + 不 ('not') + 动 (simplified from 動, 'move; disturb'). Literally describing a parcel, wine jar, or silver packet whose original wax or paper seal has not been broken or tampered with, it means 'left completely intact and untouched'.

history.meaning: with the original seal unbroken
left completely intact; untouched in its original state

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 原封不动

cognates.meaning: original text, source text (in original language)

原文.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 原 (yuán, 'original, source, unaltered') and 文 (wén, originally a pictograph of a standing figure with chest markings/tattoos, evolving to mean 'pattern, written graph, literary text, passage'). Developed in Classical Chinese philology and exegesis to distinguish the unglossed, untranslated, or unedited primary text from commentaries (注文) or translations (译文).

history.meaning: the primary, unglossed source text of a classic or document
original text, verbatim wording, or original social media post

原文.notes: In traditional publishing and scholarship, 原文 contrasts with 译文 ('translated text'); on Chinese social media (Weibo/WeChat), 查看原文 or 原文已删除 refers to the 'original post' in a repost chain.

cognates.meaning: original copy, script/novel on which a film is based; originally (motomoto)

原本.etymology: A coordinative compound formed from 原 (yuán, 'fountainhead, source, origin') and 本 (běn, depicting a stroke at the base of a tree 木 to signify 'root, foundation, origin', and by extension a 'bound volume or manuscript edition'). In Classical Chinese (e.g., Hanshu), 原本 was a noun meaning 'fundamental root/source' or 'master manuscript copy'; in vernacular Mandarin it grammaticalized into a high-frequency temporal/modal adverb meaning 'originally, at first, formerly'.

history.meaning: root source, fundamental origin; to trace to the root
original master copy or manuscript edition; fundamental origin
originally, formerly, at first (adverb); master copy (noun)

morphemes.meaning: tree root, foundation, original state or edition

原本.notes: As an adverb ('originally, at first'), 原本 is slightly more formal and literary than 原来 (yuánlái) or 本来 (běnlái), and unlike 原来, 原本 cannot mean 'it turns out that / I just realized that!' upon discovering a new fact.

rootFamily.gloss: originally, formerly; as it turns out

原来.etymology: Compound of 原 ('source, origin, original', originally a spring 泉 emerging beneath a cliff 厂) + 来 ('come'). Functions both as an adjective ('original, former') and as an adverb of sudden realization ('so it turns out that…, all along').

history.meaning: originally; former; as it turns out

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 原来 (via 萌典)

原版.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) compound combining 原 (yuán, 'source, origin, original'; originally written 厵 in seal script, depicting a spring flowing out from beneath a cliff 厂) and 版 (bǎn, 'wooden printing block, edition, version', from 片 'split wood plank' + phonetic 反 fǎn). Originally referring to woodblock-printed master editions as opposed to reprints or pirated copies, it expanded in modern media and television production to mean the original, unadapted format or master recording of a show or song.

history.meaning: mountain spring (origin) + wooden plank for writing or block printing
original woodblock or movable-type printing edition
original version, master edition, or unadapted format of a publication, song, or broadcast program

原版.notes: In entertainment and television production, 原版 frequently contrasts with 翻拍版 (remake) or 改编版 (adapted version), and can also function attributively (e.g., 原版节目 'the original format of the show').

原计划.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) nominal phrase formed by prefixing the attributive modifier 原 (yuán, 'original, former, initial') to the disyllabic noun 计划 (jìhuà, Traditional 計劃, 'plan, project'). 计划 itself is a coordinative compound pairing 计 (jì, 'calculate, reckon, devise') and 划 (huà, 'delineate, mark off boundaries, lay out'), popularized in its modern administrative sense alongside Meiji-era Japanese 計画 (keikaku).

history.meaning: to reckon/calculate + to draw boundaries or chart a strategy
systematic plan, schedule, or project
original plan, initial schedule prior to revision

原计划.notes: Commonly used in production scheduling with prepositions like 按 (àn, 'according to'): 按原计划进行 ('proceed according to the original plan').

rootFamily.gloss: planning and production (of a show or event)

原谅.etymology: A coordinative (联合) verbal compound uniting 原 (yuán, here in its extended Classical verbal sense 'to trace to the source, examine the underlying motives, pardon') and 谅 (liàng, Traditional 諒, 'to trust, understand empathetically, excuse', from 言 'speech/words' + phonetic 京 jīng). In Literary Chinese, tracing a person's error back to its original intent (推原其情) naturally developed into pardoning and showing understanding.

history.meaning: to trace to the root cause (原) and trust/empathize with sincerity (諒)
to understand someone's circumstances and pardon a fault
to forgive, pardon, excuse

morphemes.meaning: trace to the origin, pardon, excuse

原谅.notes: Unlike 宽恕 (kuānshù, solemn or lofty forgiveness), 原谅 is the everyday word across spoken and written registers for forgiving personal mistakes or professional missteps.

rootFamily.gloss: to understand and forgive, make allowances for

厨房.etymology: Compound noun of 厨 (廚, 'kitchen, cookhouse') + 房 ('room, building'): 'kitchen'. Attested since the Six Dynasties and Tang period.

history.meaning: kitchen

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 厨房 (via 萌典)

厨艺.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) compound combining 厨 (chú, Traditional 廚, 'kitchen, cookhouse', from 广 'shelter' + 尌 'stand upright/arrange') and 艺 (yì, Traditional 藝, originally 埶, depicting a person 丮 planting a seedling 艸 in soil, 'cultivation, skill, craft, art'). Together they denote the cultivated craft of cooking.

history.meaning: kitchen/cookhouse (廚) + planting skill or accomplished craft (藝)
culinary skill, craftsmanship in cooking

厨艺.notes: Frequently appears in lifestyle and variety-show contexts with verbs like 展示厨艺 ('show off one's cooking skills') or 苦练厨艺 ('practice one's culinary craft').

去.etymology: Ancient graph attested on Shang oracle bones showing a person (大) stepping away from an enclosure or cave (口/凵). In Classical Chinese, 去 meant 'leave, depart from (a place)'; from the Han–Tang period onward, it shifted to the deictic opposite of 来 ('come'): 'go (there), go to; remove/get rid of; past (去年)'.

history.meaning: depart from; leave; remove
go (away from speaker); go to; remove

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 去 (via 萌典)

去世.etymology: Euphemistic verb-object compound of 去 ('depart from, leave', preserving the Classical sense of 去) + 世 ('the world, human life'): 'depart from the world -> pass away, die'. Attested since the Jin and Tang dynasties.

history.meaning: leave the world; pass away

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 去世 (via 萌典)

去年.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) temporal compound composed of 去 (qù, 'departed, gone by, past') modifying 年 (nián, originally 秊 in oracle bone script, depicting a person carrying harvested grain 禾, hence 'harvest cycle, year'). Attested since Han and Six Dynasties literature for the year that has just departed.

history.meaning: to depart/leave behind (去) + annual grain harvest cycle (年)
the bygone year, last year
last year

去年.notes: Forms a temporal triad with 今年 (this year) and 明年 (next year); note that 'last month' and 'last week' use 上 (上个月, 上周) rather than 去.

rootFamily.gloss: the past, bygone times; to go over to

去掉.etymology: A verb-resultative (动补 / 述补) compound formed by the action verb 去 (qù, here retaining its Classical transitive sense 'to remove, get rid of, cast off', Old Chinese *kh(r)aʔ-s) followed by the phase/resultative complement 掉 (diào, 'to fall, drop away, dispose of completely'). In vernacular Mandarin, 掉 grammaticalized from 'fall/drop' into a productive resultative marker of elimination or removal.

history.meaning: to remove, discard, drive away (transitive reading)
to remove completely, drop out, eliminate

morphemes.meaning: fall off, away, completely disposed of

去掉.notes: In audio-visual editing and post-production, 去掉 is standardly used for cutting out unwanted segments, noise, or credits (e.g., 把杂音去掉 'remove the background noise').

rootFamily.gloss: to delete, cut out (text or footage)

参与.etymology: A coordinative/serial verbal compound (联合) combining 参 (cān, Traditional 參, 'to join in as a third party, intervene, counsel', related to 三 'three') and 与 (yù, Traditional 與, here in its fourth-tone verbal reading *yù* < Middle Chinese *joH*, 'to take part in, be party to, share in', derived from 'give/accompany'). Attested in Classical historiography (such as the *Book of Han*) for taking part in state affairs or deliberations.

history.meaning: to join in alongside others (參) and share/take part in deliberations (與)
to participate in, be involved in a process, project, or decision

morphemes.meaning: take part in, be party to (traditionally read yù)

参与.notes: Whereas 参加 (cānjiā) emphasizes formally joining an organization or attending an event, 参与 (cānyù) emphasizes active involvement in a process or creative work (e.g., 参与制作 'participate in the production'). Although prescriptive dictionaries historically gave 与 the reading yù here, yǔ is now standard in mainland Mandarin.

rootFamily.gloss: to join, attend, take part in

参与者.etymology: A derived agentive noun formed by suffixing the Classical nominalizer and agent marker 者 (zhě, 'one who, that which') to the disyllabic verbal stem 参与 (cānyù, Traditional 參與, 'to participate in, be involved in'). In modern Mandarin, -者 productively translates English agentive '-er/-ant' nouns across formal, legal, and media registers.

history.meaning: one who takes part in affairs or counsels (參與 + nominalizer 者)
participant, stakeholder or active contributor in an activity or program

参与者.notes: Used in formal, broadcast, and legal contexts for anyone actively involved in a project, game, or production; more formal than 参加的人.

rootFamily.gloss: to participate in, be involved in

参加.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound (联合) combining 参 (cān, Traditional 參, 'to enter among, join in as a peer') and 加 (jiā, 'to add, append, join to', from 力 'strength' + 口). While attested in Classical Chinese for adding or cross-checking, its modern sense of joining an organization, competition, or event was reinforced and popularized through Meiji-era Japanese 参加 (sanka).

history.meaning: to intermix/join in (參) + to add/increase (加)
to join a group, attend a meeting, or enter a competition
to join, attend, take part in (an event, contest, or organization)

参加.notes: Takes concrete events, competitions, meetings, or organizations as its direct object (e.g., 参加比赛 'enter a competition', 参加节目 'appear on a show').

rootFamily.gloss: to participate in, be involved in (a process)
to compete in a tournament or contest (short for 参加比赛)
to join, become a member of

又.etymology: Pictograph (象形字) in Shang oracle-bone script of a right hand with three fingers shown. Borrowed from the earliest inscriptions for the adverb 'again, once more (especially of realized or recurring actions), also, both… and…, moreover'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: right-hand graph borrowed for 'again, also, moreover'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 又 (via 萌典)

叉子.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 叉子. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 叉子 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 叉子 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 叉子 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 叉子. The etymology of 叉子 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 叉子
middle form of 叉子
modern form of 叉子

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 叉子

cognates.meaning: to reach, amount to; and, as well as (および oyobi)
to reach, extend to; and, as well as

及.etymology: In oracle bone and bronze inscriptions, 及 (jí, Old Chinese *\*[m-k-]rəp*, Middle Chinese *gip*) is an ideogram depicting a hand (又) grabbing onto the back of a person (人) ahead—literally 'to catch up with, overtake, reach'. From 'reaching to / extending to', it grammaticalized already in Shang and Zhou inscriptions into a coordinating conjunction meaning 'and, along with, as well as'.

history.form: 及 (Oracle Bone & Bronze Script: 人 + 又)
history.meaning: to overtake from behind, catch up with, reach
to reach, attain; (conjunction) and, together with, as well as
and, as well as (formal coordinating conjunction joining noun phrases)

morphemes.meaning: reach, attain; and, as well as

及.notes: In modern Mandarin, 及 as a conjunction belongs to formal, written, legal, and broadcast registers (e.g., 出品人及总制片人 'executive producer and general producer'), connecting nominal elements where the first item is often primary and the following items supplementary.

rootFamily.gloss: as well as, and, along with
to involve, touch upon, relate to

及时.etymology: A verb-object (动宾) compound formed from 及 (jí, in its primary verbal sense 'to catch up with, reach, arrive at') and 时 (shí, Traditional 時, 'season, time, right moment', from 日 'sun' + 寺). Attested in the *Book of Odes* (*Shijing*) and *Mengzi* with the literal meaning 'to catch the right season / while there is still time', evolving into an adjective and adverb meaning 'timely, promptly, without delay'.

history.meaning: to catch the proper season; while time still permits
at the right moment, seasonably, without losing time
in time, promptly, timely (adjective and adverb)

及时.notes: Functions both as an adverb before a verb (及时处理 'handle promptly', 及时沟通 'communicate in time') and as a stative verb/adjective (来得很及时 'arrived right on time').

rootFamily.gloss: there is still time, able to make it in time
too late, unable to make it in time

双.etymology: Measure word for things that come in natural matched pairs (一双皮鞋 'a pair of leather shoes', 一双手 'a pair of hands'). The traditional graph 雙 shows two birds (隹 + 隹) held in one hand (又)—literally 'a matched pair held together'.

history.meaning: pair of birds; matched pair

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 雙 (via 萌典)

双倍.etymology: Quantitative compound of 双 ('pair; two; double', originally two birds 隹 held in one hand 又) + 倍 ('times; fold; double', person radical 亻 + phonetic 咅 pǒu). Used in everyday commerce and recipes for a twofold quantity.

history.meaning: twofold; double quantity
double; twice as much

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 双倍

双方.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) compound combining 双 (shuāng, Traditional 雙, depicting a hand 又 holding two birds 隹隹, hence 'a pair, both, two') and 方 (fāng, 'direction, side, party'). Together they denote 'both sides' or 'the two parties' in an interaction, negotiation, contract, or competition.

history.meaning: a pair of birds held in hand (雙) + direction/side (方)
both sides, the two parties (in diplomacy, law, or competition)

双方.notes: Essential in contract law, media negotiations, and competitive broadcasts (e.g., 合同双方 'both parties to the contract', 双方选手 'contestants on both sides'); compare 单方 (unilateral) and 多方 (multilateral).

rootFamily.gloss: party A and party B (client and contractor in media/contracts)

cognates.meaning: master's degree (修士 shūshi; archaic 碩士 sekishi)

双硕士.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) compound formed by prefixing 双 (shuāng, Traditional 雙, 'pair, double, dual') to 硕士 (shuòshì, Traditional 碩士, 'master's degree'). In Classical Chinese, 碩士 (composed of 碩 'great, eminent, large-headed' + 士 'scholar') denoted a scholar of great virtue and erudition; in modern Chinese academic terminology, it was repurposed to translate the Western academic 'Master's degree' (ranked between 学士 Bachelor and 博士 Doctor).

history.meaning: eminent scholar of great learning and virtue
Master's degree holder or degree (modern academic calque)
dual master's degrees, holder of two master's degrees

双硕士.notes: Often highlighted in media biographies and workplace dramas as a mark of elite educational credentials (e.g., 拥有双硕士学位 'holds dual master's degrees'); parallel to 双学位 (double bachelor's degree).

双胞胎.etymology: Three-character compound of 双 (雙, 'pair, two', originally two birds 隹 held in one hand 又) + 胞 ('womb, placenta, born of the same parents', flesh 月 + 包 'wrap') + 胎 ('fetus, birth'): 'twins'.

history.meaning: twins born from the same womb/pregnancy

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 双胞胎 (via 萌典)

双败淘汰制.etymology: A complex multi-layered modifier-head (偏正) compound calquing English 'double-elimination system': 双败 (shuāngbài, 'two defeats / double loss') modifies 淘汰 (táotài, a coordinative compound of two water-radical verbs 淘 'to wash grain or pan for gold in water, rinse away impurities' and 汰 'to wash out excess, sift out'), which in turn modifies the head suffix 制 (zhì, 'system, institutional format'). Literally, 'a system of sifting out after two defeats'.

history.meaning: to wash away sand/chaff in water and sift out impurities
elimination tournament system (modern sports and competition term)
double-elimination tournament format (requiring two losses for elimination)

双败淘汰制.notes: Widely used in esports, sports tournaments, and competitive reality/singing shows (such as those produced in *Behind the Scenes*) where contestants drop from a winners' bracket (胜者组) to a losers' bracket (败者组) after one loss and are only eliminated after a second loss.

rootFamily.gloss: to eliminate, wash out, phase out

反响.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) compound combining 反 (fǎn, 'to turn back, return, reflect') and 响 (xiǎng, Traditional 響, 'echo, reverberating sound', from 音 'sound' + 鄉 xiāng 'facing/direction'). Originally denoting a physical acoustic echo bouncing back off a valley or wall, it shifted metaphorically in modern Sino-Japanese and Mandarin usage to denote the public response, critical reception, or buzz generated by a broadcast, artwork, or policy.

history.meaning: returned sound, acoustic echo reverberating back
echo; public reaction, audience response, social repercussions

反响.notes: A staple of media and entertainment discourse; typical collocations include 引起强烈反响 ('spark a strong public response') and 节目播出后反响热烈 ('the show received an enthusiastic reception after airing').

rootFamily.gloss: to respond, answer a call; response

反对.etymology: A coordinative/modifier-head compound combining 反 (fǎn, depicts a hand 又 turning an object over under a cliff 厂, 'to turn over, reverse, go against') and 对 (duì, Traditional 對, 'to face, confront, stand opposite'). Attested in Classical texts for standing in mutual opposition or contrast, it gained its modern political and interpersonal verbal sense 'to oppose, object to' in synergy with Meiji-era Japanese 反対 (hantai).

history.meaning: to stand in reverse or opposite correspondence; contrasting counterparts
to oppose, object to, take a stand against
to oppose, object to, disagree with

反对.notes: The direct antonym of 赞成 (zànchéng, 'approve/support') or 同意 (tóngyì, 'agree'); in boardroom or production meetings, 投反对票 means 'to cast a dissenting/nay vote'.

rootFamily.gloss: opposite, contrary, on the other hand
objection, dissenting opinion (e.g., 提出反对意见)

反应.etymology: Compound verb and noun of 反 ('turn back, return') + 应 (應, 'respond, answer, echo'): 'react, respond; chemical or physiological reaction; response'.

history.meaning: respond back; reaction; response

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 反应 (via 萌典)

反映.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) verbal compound combining 反 (fǎn, 'back, in return, reverse') and 映 (yìng, 'to shine upon, cast light or an image, mirror', from 日 'sun' + phonetic 央 yāng). Literally 'to cast light/images back' (optical reflection), it extended metaphorically to mirroring social realities in art, and in modern Mandarin further developed the administrative and workplace sense of 'reporting feedback or problems upward to a person in authority'.

history.meaning: to turn back (反) + to shine light or cast a visual image (映)
optical reflection; to mirror or embody conditions, realities, or sentiments
to reflect, mirror; to report feedback, voice a concern or complaint to superiors

morphemes.meaning: shine upon, mirror, project an image

反映.notes: Crucial homophone distinction in Mandarin: 反映 (fǎnyìng, 'to reflect a situation; to report feedback upward', e.g., 向导演反映问题 'report an issue to the director') vs. 反应 (fǎnyìng, 'chemical, physiological, or emotional reaction/response').

rootFamily.gloss: to release/screen a movie in theaters
reflection (of light, sound, or neural reflex)

cognates.meaning: return to the right way, rebellion; counter-argument (はんせい hansei)

反正.etymology: Originally a Classical Chinese verb-object compound (动宾) found in the *Gongyang Commentary* on the *Spring and Autumn Annals* (*拨乱反正*, 'to quell chaos and return [反] to the right/upright [正]'). In vernacular Mandarin from the Ming and Qing dynasties onward, it underwent a reanalysis as an antonymic coordinate pair—'whether upside-down (反, reverse) or right-side-up (正, obverse)'—grammaticalizing into a modal adverb meaning 'either way, in any case, anyhow'.

history.meaning: to return (反) to what is upright and orthodox (正)
whether reverse side or right side; either way, under any circumstances
anyway, in any case, anyhow (conversational discourse adverb)

反正.notes: Very frequent in spoken dialogue to dismiss a complication or state an unchanging conclusion ('Anyway / No matter which way you look at it...'); compare its formal historical preservation in the idiom 拨乱反正 ('bring order out of chaos').

rootFamily.gloss: positive and negative, obverse and reverse sides
negative side, reverse side (of an issue or coin)

反而.etymology: A compound conjunctive adverb formed in Literary and early Vernacular Chinese by combining the adverbial use of 反 (fǎn, 'conversely, on the contrary, turning back against expectations') with the Classical connective particle 而 (ér, originally a pictograph of facial whiskers, grammaticalized as an adverbial-to-verb linker). Over time, 反 + 而 lexicalized into a single disyllabic adverb marking counter-expectation ('instead, on the contrary').

history.meaning: turning conversely (反) + adverbial connective particle (而)
on the contrary, instead (contrary to what one would expect)

morphemes.meaning: and yet, linking adverbial to predicate

反而.notes: Often paired with 不但... ('not only...') or 没有... ('did not...') to express an unexpected reversal: e.g., 收视率不但没降，反而升了 ('Not only did the ratings not drop, on the contrary they rose'). Never placed before the subject unless a comma intervenes.

rootFamily.gloss: conversely, instead (literary equivalent of 反而)

cognates.meaning: to turn one's back, betray, rebel

反背.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound (联合) combining 反 (fǎn, 'to turn over, reverse, rebel against') and 背 (bèi, 'the back [of the body], to turn one's back on, go against', from 北 'two people standing back-to-back' + 肉 'flesh'). Physically, it describes turning something to its reverse side or clasping one's hands behind one's back; figuratively in Literary and Vernacular Chinese, it means 'to turn against, reverse allegiance, betray'.

history.meaning: to turn over/against (反) and turn one's back upon (背)
to turn one's back on an ally, betray; to clasp hands behind the back or turn opposite

morphemes.meaning: back, turn one's back on, go against

反背.notes: Can be used physically (反背着手 'with hands clasped behind one's back') or figuratively for reversing direction or turning against a former agreement or partner.

rootFamily.gloss: to violate, go against (principles or agreements)
the back side, reverse, behind the scenes

反诉.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) legal compound combining 反 (fǎn, 'in return, counter-, reverse') and 诉 (sù, Traditional 訴, 'to accuse, lodge a complaint, sue', from 言 'speech' + 斥 'drive away/reproach'). While attested in traditional Chinese legal texts for counter-accusations, its precise modern procedural meaning ('to file a counterclaim/countersuit against the plaintiff in an ongoing civil action') was standardized via modern Continental/Sino-Japanese jurisprudence (反訴 hanso).

history.meaning: to lodge a counter-accusation against one's accuser
to countersue, file a formal counterclaim in court

反诉.notes: In media contract disputes and intellectual property battles (frequent plot points in *Behind the Scenes*), 提起反诉 means 'to file a countersuit' against the original plaintiff (原告).

rootFamily.gloss: to sue, bring a lawsuit against
to appeal a court verdict to a higher court

反过来.etymology: A verb-directional (动趋) construction formed from the action verb 反 (fǎn, 'to turn over, invert, reverse') followed by the compound directional complement 过来 (guòlái, Traditional 過來, 'across/over + hither toward the speaker or normal reference point'). Literally 'having turned over so as to face this way', it lexicalized in spoken and written Mandarin as a discourse adverbial meaning 'conversely, the other way around, backwards'.

history.meaning: to turn around or flip over toward the speaker's side (literal directional phrase)
to turn around/invert; (adverbial) conversely, the other way around, in turn

morphemes.meaning: cross over, pass across (change of orientation)

反过来.notes: Frequently followed by verbs of speech or thought—such as 反过来说 ('to put it the other way around') or 反过来想 ('if you think about it from the opposite angle')—to pivot perspective in a discussion.

rootFamily.gloss: to turn back around (away from reference point)

cognates.meaning: to shoot, emit, send forth, issue
to emit, send out, issue, broadcast

发.etymology: Representing Traditional 發 (fā, Old Chinese *\*pjat*, Middle Chinese *pjwat*; distinct from 髮 'hair', though merged in Simplified Chinese as 发), the character combines 癶 ('two feet planted apart pushing forward') with 弓 ('bow') and 殳 ('hand wielding a weapon/striker'). Its primary sense in Oracle Bone and Classical texts is 'to shoot an arrow from a bow, launch forth'. From 'shoot forth', it broadened to 'dispatch, issue, release, manifest', and in contemporary digital and broadcast Chinese to 'post online, send (a message), release (content)'.

history.meaning: to shoot an arrow from a bow; to set forth, launch
to dispatch, deliver, issue, distribute, manifest
to send (messages/emails), post (on social media), release or broadcast (episodes/songs)

morphemes.meaning: shoot forth, send, issue, release, post

发.notes: One of the most versatile verbs in modern media and everyday digital life: 发消息 ('send a message'), 发微博 ('post on Weibo'), 发片 ('release an album/film'), 发通稿 ('send out a press release'). Note that Simplified 发 merges Traditional 發 (fā, 'send/emit') and 髮 (fà, 'head hair', as in 发型).

发个.etymology: A colloquial Mandarin verb–classifier contraction formed by the transitive verb 发 (fā, Traditional 發, 'to send, post, issue') followed by the general classifier 个 (ge, Traditional 個, reduced from 一 + 个 'one [item] of'). In spoken Mandarin, when the numeral 一 (yī, 'one') occurs in post-verbal object position before a classifier, it is routinely elided, leaving the bound rhythm unit [Verb + 个] + Noun (e.g., 发个消息 'send a message', 发个定位 'send a location pin').

history.meaning: to send or issue one [item] (full verb + numeral + classifier construction)
send a... / post a quick... (spoken contraction with elided numeral 一)

morphemes.meaning: a, an (general individual classifier, Trad. 個)

发个.notes: Dropping 一 in 发个... softens the tone and makes the action sound casual, quick, and low-effort in workplace or casual chat (e.g., 给我发个邮件 'shoot me an email', 发个朋友圈 'make a quick WeChat Moments post').

rootFamily.gloss: to send a red envelope (cash gift/bonus)

发光.etymology: A verb-object (动宾) compound uniting 发 (fā, Traditional 發, 'to emit, radiate, send forth') and 光 (guāng, in Oracle Bone script depicting fire 火 above a kneeling person 儿, 'light, radiance, brightness'). Literally 'to emit light', it describes both physical luminescence and, figuratively in showbiz and career contexts, a person's talent shining brightly on stage or behind the scenes.

history.meaning: to emit or radiate light, shine forth
to shine, glow, luminesce; (figuratively) to stand out brilliantly, shine in one's role

发光.notes: In entertainment and motivational contexts, 闪闪发光 ('shining brightly') and 发光发热 ('emit light and heat'—i.e., contribute one's full talent and energy in a role, even behind the scenes) are iconic expressions.

rootFamily.gloss: to shine and generate heat; make a passionate contribution

发呆.etymology: A verb-object / inchoative state compound combining 发 (fā, Traditional 發, here functioning as an inchoative prefixal verb meaning 'to manifest, break out into, fall into a state of', as in 发愁, 发怒) and 呆 (dāi, originally an variant of 保 or 某 depicting a swaddled child or a person with an open mouth 口 over trees 木, meaning 'slow-witted, wooden, stupor, daze'). Together they mean 'to slip into a daze, stare blankly, zone out'.

history.meaning: to fall into a stupor or dazed, motionless state
to stare blankly, daydream, zone out, be lost in thought

morphemes.meaning: manifest, enter into a state of (Trad. 發)
dazed, wooden, blank, stupor (also trad. 獃)

发呆.notes: A separable verb (离合词), so duration and aspect markers go between the two characters: e.g., 发了一会儿呆 ('zoned out for a little while'), 别光坐着发呆 ('don't just sit there staring into space').

rootFamily.gloss: to freeze in shock, be stunned or dumbfounded

发型.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) compound combining 发 (fà, here representing Traditional 髮, 'head hair', composed of semantic 髟 'long flowing hair' + phonetic 犮 bá; note that in Old Chinese 髮 *\*pjat* and 發 *\*pjat* were homophonous and etymologically related as hair 'sprouting/shooting forth' from the scalp) and 型 (xíng, 'earthen mold for casting metal, model, style, shape'). Reinforced by modern Japanese 髪型 (kamigata), it means 'hairstyle, hairdo'.

history.meaning: head hair (髮) + clay casting mold or form (型)
hairstyle, hairdo, styling of the hair

发型.notes: Crucial pronunciation and character note: in 发型, 发 represents Traditional 髮 ('hair') and is pronounced in the fourth tone (fàxíng) in mainland standard Mandarin (fǎxíng in Taiwan), whereas in 发光, 发展, and 发布, 发 represents Traditional 發 ('emit') and is pronounced in the first tone (fā).

rootFamily.gloss: styling, visual design, make-up and wardrobe造型

发展.etymology: A coordinative / serial verbal compound (联合) combining 发 (fā, Traditional 發, 'to shoot forth, open up, initiate') and 展 (zhǎn, 'to unroll, unfold, extend, spread out', from 尸 'body' + 㠯). While both characters co-occurred in Literary Chinese for 'unfolding and extending', the compound was popularized in late 19th- and early 20th-century Sino-Japanese (発展 hatten) and Mandarin as the standard equivalent of English 'develop / development'.

history.meaning: to send forth/open up (發) and unroll/extend outward (展)
to expand, evolve, progress (adopted for modern social, economic, and career 'development')
history.stage: Late Qing / Early Modern Sino-Japanese & Mandarin

history.meaning: to develop, grow, expand; development, career progression

morphemes.meaning: send forth, open up, initiate (Trad. 發)

发展.notes: In the entertainment industry, 发展 often refers specifically to an artist's or producer's career trajectory or market focus (e.g., 回国发展 'return to China to build one's career', 往幕后发展 'pivot toward behind-the-scenes work').

rootFamily.gloss: to unfold, launch, carry out (a plot or campaign)
progress, headway (in a project or negotiation)
to expand, broaden (a market or business scope)

cognates.meaning: presentation event, recital, launch press conference

发布会.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) compound formed from the disyllabic verbal noun 发布 (fābù, Traditional 發布/發佈, a coordinative compound of 發 'issue, send forth' + 布 'spread out like cloth, proclaim publicly to all') modifying the head noun 会 (huì, Traditional 會, 'gathering, assembly, conference'). Literally 'an assembly for public proclamation/release', it serves in modern media as the standard term for a press conference or product/program launch event.

history.meaning: to issue and spread abroad an official proclamation or edict
press conference, official launch event (for a film, television show, product, or news announcement)

发布会.notes: A central ritual of the film, television, and tech industries: 新闻发布会 ('news press conference'), 新片发布会 ('new film launch press conference'), and 开机发布会 ('production kickoff press conference').

发帖.etymology: A verb-object (动宾) compound combining 发 (fā, Traditional 發, 'to send out, issue, post') and 帖 (tiě, 'written slip of silk or paper, invitation card, placard, notice', from 巾 'cloth/silk strip' + phonetic 占 zhān). Historically, 发帖 meant dispatching written invitation cards (请帖) or posting public notices (字帖/告示); in the late 1990s Chinese internet BBS era, 帖 was repurposed to translate an online forum 'post' or 'thread', making 发帖 the universal verb for posting a thread online.

history.meaning: to send out written invitation cards or post public notices on silk/paper slips
to post a message or start a thread on an online forum, BBS, or social media platform

morphemes.meaning: written slip, card, notice; online forum post/thread

发帖.notes: Note the three-tone differentiation of 帖 in Mandarin: tiě for 'card/forum post' (发帖 fātiě, 帖子 tiězi, 请帖 qǐngtiě), tiè for 'calligraphy model book' (字帖 zìtiè), and tiē for 'submissive/fitting snugly' (服帖 fútiē). In PR and entertainment marketing, 删帖 ('delete a post') and 回帖 ('reply to a thread') are key companion terms.

rootFamily.gloss: online forum post, thread; card, invitation
to reply to an online forum thread
to delete an online post or thread (often in PR crisis management)

发抖.etymology: Verb-object/inchoative compound of 发 (發, 'break out into, manifest a bodily state') + 抖 ('tremble, shiver, shake'): 'tremble, shiver, shake (from cold, fear, or anger)'.

history.meaning: shiver; tremble; shake

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 发抖 (via 萌典)

发油.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正結構) formed from 髮 (fà, Middle Chinese *pjwot, Old Chinese *pjat, 'head hair', merged into simplified 发) and 油 (yóu, MC *yuw, 'plant or animal oil, grease'). Unlike most words beginning with simplified 发 (which represent 發 'to emit'), 发油 preserves the distinct etymon 髮 ('cranial hair') modifying 油 ('conditioning oil').

history.meaning: head hair and natural plant or animal grease used for anointing hair in pre-modern grooming
perfumed hair oil, pomade, or styling grease used in modern grooming and backstage makeup

发油.notes: In Mainland Mandarin this is pronounced fàyóu (fourth tone on 发 because it derives from 髮 'hair', not 發 'issue'), though fāyóu is commonly heard colloquially; in film and television production it refers to styling pomade used by wardrobe and makeup crews.

发火.etymology: Metaphorical verb-object compound of 发 (發, 'emit, flare up') + 火 ('fire, internal heat/anger' in traditional Chinese medicine and everyday metaphor): 'flare up in anger, lose one's temper; catch fire/ignite'.

history.meaning: flare up; lose one's temper; ignite

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 发火 (via 萌典)

发现.etymology: Compound verb and noun of 发 (發, 'open up, uncover, bring forth') + 现 (現, 'appear, become visible, manifest'): 'discover, find, notice, realize; discovery'.

history.meaning: cause to appear / notice what was hidden -> discover, find

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 发现 (via 萌典)

发生.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound (聯合結構) joining 發 (fā, MC *pjwot, 'to shoot forth, sprout, manifest') and 生 (shēng, MC *sraeng, 'to germinate, be born, come into being'). Attested in Literary Chinese for the sprouting of vegetation or emergence of phenomena, it was revitalized in the late nineteenth century via Meiji Japanese 発生 (hassei) to render European concepts of 'occurrence', 'genesis', and 'eventuation'.

history.meaning: to sprout forth, germinate, or bring living things into being (of seasonal nature)
to originate, develop, or occur as a natural, medical, or social phenomenon
to happen, occur, take place (of events, accidents, or changes)

morphemes.meaning: to shoot forth, emit, arise (traditional 發)
to grow, be born, come into existence

发生.notes: An intransitive or non-agentive verb that never takes a person as its subject; in newsrooms and production scripts it typically introduces unplanned incidents (发生意外, 发生冲突).

发疯.etymology: A verb-object compound (動賓結構) composed of 發 (fā, 'to break out, manifest an acute condition') and 瘋 (fēng, MC *pjuwng, 'neurological disorder, leprosy, insanity', derived from 風 'wind' with the illness radical 疒, reflecting the traditional Chinese medical belief that pathogenic wind invading the body causes madness and convulsions).

history.meaning: wind-induced ailment, paralysis, or mental derangement in traditional Chinese medicine
to suffer an onset of madness; by extension, to act frantic, unhinged, or wildly obsessed

morphemes.meaning: to break out, manifest, suffer an onset of (traditional 發)

发疯.notes: Separable verb (VO): aspect markers and complements insert between the characters (e.g., 发了疯, 发什么疯). In showbiz dialogue, often used hyperbolically for working mania or emotional meltdowns.

rootFamily.gloss: to go into a frenzy, go berserk

发病.etymology: A verb-object medical compound (動賓結構) combining 發 (fā, MC *pjwot, 'to erupt, break out, become manifest') with 病 (bìng, MC *bjaengH, 'severe illness, disease, malady'). In classical medical treatises such as the *Shanghan Lun*, 發病 denotes the clinical onset when latent pathogenic factors manifest as overt symptoms.

history.meaning: clinical eruption or acute onset of a latent illness or febrile disorder
to have an acute flare-up of a chronic condition, or for a disease to break out

morphemes.meaning: to break out, erupt, manifest (traditional 發)

发病.notes: Unlike 生病 (general 'getting sick'), 发病 specifically emphasizes the acute onset of symptoms or a sudden flare-up of an underlying physical or psychiatric condition (e.g., 心脏病发病).

rootFamily.gloss: to break out, flare up (of an condition)

发票.etymology: Originally a verb-object compound (動賓結構) meaning 'to issue a slip/voucher', lexicalized during the Ming–Qing commercial expansion into a noun denoting the itemized dispatch manifest accompanying wholesale goods, formed from 發 (fā, 'to issue, dispatch') and 票 (piào, 'printed slip, warrant, ticket'). In modern PRC fiscal administration, it specifically denotes an official government-monitored tax receipt.

history.meaning: commercial dispatch bill or itemized manifest issued by a merchant house alongside shipped goods
official tax-validated invoice or receipt required for business reimbursement and accounting

发票.notes: Crucial cultural distinction: in Mainland China, a 收据 (shōujù) or 小票 (xiǎopiào) is a simple cashier slip, whereas a 发票 (fāpiào) is an official tax-registered invoice needed to expense production or corporate costs (开发票).

cognates.meaning: to release a manuscript or news copy

发稿.etymology: A verb-object compound (動賓結構) formed from 發 (fā, 'to dispatch, transmit, release') and 稿 (gǎo, MC *kawX, originally 'cereal straw, stalks', extended by metaphor to 'rough draft, manuscript, news copy' because early drafts were considered raw and unfinished like straw). Coined in modern journalism and publishing for releasing copy to the press or wire services.

history.meaning: dried grain stalks; metaphorically a rough literary draft or preliminary sketch
to dispatch news copy to the printing press, wire service, or media outlets; a press release

morphemes.meaning: to send out, issue, release (traditional 發)

发稿.notes: A core media and PR term (separable VO, e.g., 发了一篇稿): journalists use it for filing a story before deadline, while PR teams in entertainment use it for pushing press releases to media portals.

rootFamily.gloss: to submit a manuscript for publication

发给.etymology: A verb-complement compound (動補結構) combining 發 (fā, MC *pjwot, 'to send out, issue, distribute') with the dative/recipient complement 給 (gěi, originally jǐ, MC *kijp, 'to supply, provide, grant', which grammaticalized in Mandarin into the standard recipient marker 'to'). It encodes both the transmission of an item or message and its arrival at a designated recipient.

history.meaning: to issue and supply provisions, stipends, or official credentials to subordinates
to send to (digitally or by post) or distribute/issue to (a recipient)

发给.notes: Must be followed immediately by the recipient noun/pronoun before the direct object (e.g., 发给我一份合同 'send me a contract'), or used with 把 (把通告发给大家).

rootFamily.gloss: to hand over to, entrust to

发脾气.etymology: A verb-object idiomatic phrase (動賓短語) uniting 發 (fā, 'to vent, let out, manifest') with 脾氣 (píqì, 'temperament, bad temper'). In Traditional Chinese Medicine, 脾氣 literally denoted the vital energy (氣, qì) of the spleen (脾, pí); because imbalances of organ qi were held to govern emotional volatility and irritability, 脾氣 shifted in Ming–Qing vernacular to mean one's disposition or outburst of anger.

history.meaning: the functional vital energy (qi) of the spleen digestive system in classical medical theory
to vent one's temper, flare up in anger, throw a tantrum

发脾气.notes: A separable verb-object construction: to specify whom one is angry at, use the preposition 冲 (chòng) or 对 (duì), or insert an adjective before 脾气 (e.g., 对导演发了一通大脾气).

rootFamily.gloss: to flare up in anger, lose one's cool

发表.etymology: Compound verb of 发 ('send forth; issue', originally drawing and releasing a bowstring 弓) + 表 ('outer garment; display outwardly; make public'). Adopted across East Asia in the late 19th century as the standard verb for publishing written or musical works and delivering formal statements.

history.meaning: manifest outwardly; bring to light
publish (a work); issue publicly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 发表

发誓.etymology: A verb-object compound (動賓結構) formed from 發 (fā, MC *pjwot, 'to utter, proclaim, put forth') and 誓 (shì, MC *dzyejH, Old Chinese *djed-s, 'solemn oath, covenant, military pledge', composed of 折 'to snap an arrow/branch in token of an oath' and 言 'speech'). Widely used in Buddhist vows (發誓願) and vernacular oaths since the medieval period.

history.meaning: to pronounce a solemn ritual or military pledge; in Buddhist texts, to make a bodhisattva vow
to swear an oath, vow solemnly

morphemes.meaning: to utter, declare, put forth (traditional 發)

发誓.notes: Often paired with的对天 ('to heaven') or followed by a clause stating the vow; as a separable VO verb, one can say 发毒誓 ('swear a blood/deadly oath') or 发过誓 ('have sworn before').

rootFamily.gloss: to vow solemnly, pledge one's life

发车.etymology: Verb-object compound of 发 (發, 'send forth, dispatch, set out') + 车 ('vehicle, train, bus'): '(of a train or bus) depart on schedule; dispatch a vehicle'.

history.meaning: dispatch war chariots or carriages
(of a train or bus) depart; dispatch a vehicle

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 发车 (via 萌典)

发软.etymology: Inchoative verb-complement compound of 发 (發, 'grow, turn, feel [of a bodily sensation]') + 软 (軟, 'soft, weak, limp'): 'go limp, feel weak at the knees or in the limbs'.

history.meaning: go limp; feel weak and soft (of legs/body)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 发软 (via 萌典)

发达.etymology: A coordinative compound (聯合結構) uniting 發 (fā, MC *pjwot, 'to rise up, expand, flourish') and 達 (dá, MC *dat, 'to break through, attain high rank, reach fulfillment'). In Literary Chinese it meant achieving official eminence and prosperity; in the late nineteenth century, Japanese 発達 (hattatsu) added the modern scientific and economic sense of 'well-developed' (of organs, industries, or nations).

history.meaning: to rise from obscurity to official distinction, wealth, and social prominence
structurally or economically advanced, highly developed (of anatomy, commerce, or nations)
history.stage: Late Qing / Meiji Sino-Japanese loan reinforcement

history.meaning: developed, thriving, well-developed (of economies, media networks, or muscles); colloquially, to strike it rich

morphemes.meaning: to reach, attain prominence, succeed (traditional 達)

发达.notes: Has two distinct registers: as a stative adjective it describes advanced systems or body parts (发达国家 'developed country', 传媒业很发达); colloquially with 了 (发达了!), it means 'struck it rich / made it big'.

发黏.etymology: Inchoative verb-adjective compound from 发 (simplified from 發, 'emit; become; turn') + 黏 ('sticky; glutinous; viscous', millet 黍 + phonetic 占). In Mandarin, prefixing 发 to a sensory adjective describes the onset of an undesirable or noticeable physical state, here becoming tacky or sticky to the touch.

history.meaning: become sticky; feel tacky

叔叔.etymology: Reduplicated kinship noun from 叔 (originally a hand 又 picking up beans/items 尗, used since the Shijing and尔雅 Erya for 'father's younger brother, the third of four brothers 伯仲叔季'). In Mandarin, 叔叔 means 'father's younger brother (uncle)' and is also used politely for any man of one's father's generation.

history.meaning: father's younger brother
uncle (father's younger brother); polite address for a man of father's generation

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 叔叔 (via 萌典)

取.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 取. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 取 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 取 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 取 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 取. The etymology of 取 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 取
middle form of 取
modern form of 取

取决于.etymology: A Literary Chinese verbal-prepositional construction (動介結構) formed from 取決 (qǔjué, 'to take a decision, obtain resolution', from 取 'to take, draw' + 決 'to breach a dike; to decide, settle') and the classical locative/ablative preposition 於 (yú, simplified 于, 'in, at, from, upon'). Attested in historical prose for drawing final judgment from an authority or decisive factor.

history.meaning: to seek or obtain a final ruling or adjudication from a sovereign or higher standard
to depend on, hinge upon, be determined by (factors, conditions, or choices)

取决于.notes: Belongs to formal and analytical register: the subject is the outcome in question, and the object of 取决于 is the decisive variable or person (e.g., 节目能不能播取决于审核结果).

取消.etymology: A graphic return loan from Japanese 取消 (torikeshi, nominalization of native Japanese verb 取り消す torikesu, 'to take back and erase, revoke, cancel'), repurposed into Chinese using the Middle Chinese readings of 取 (qǔ, MC *tshjuX, 'to take, withdraw') and 消 (xiāo, MC *sjew, 'to melt away, dissolve, extinguish'). Adopted during the late Qing legal and administrative reforms.

history.meaning: to retract a statement or revoke an official permit or legal act in Edo–Meiji Japanese
to cancel, call off, abolish, or revoke (a schedule, qualification, or broadcast)

取消.notes: Takes abstract nouns of scheduled events, rights, or statuses as objects (取消航班, 取消资格, 取消录制); never used for deleting text or physical objects (use 删除 or 抹掉).

受.etymology: Ancient ideogram attested on Shang oracle bones showing one hand (爫/爪) above and another hand (又) below passing a boat-shaped tray or token (舟/冖) between them: 'receive, accept' (contrast 授 shòu 'hand over, give', which later added 扌), and in Mandarin also a passive/experiencer marker ('suffer, endure, be subjected to').

history.meaning: two hands passing an object = receive, accept, endure
receive; accept; suffer/endure; passive marker

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 受 (via 萌典)

受不了.etymology: A negative potential verb-complement construction (可能補語結構) composed of 受 (shòu, MC *dzyuwX, 'to receive, endure, bear'), the negative infix 不 (bù, 'not'), and 了 (liǎo, MC *lewx, 'to finish, complete', which grammaticalized in post-Tang vernacular into a potential complement marker denoting capability). Literally 'unable to finish enduring'.

history.meaning: unable to bear to completion; incapable of enduring a burden or ordeal
cannot stand, unable to bear or tolerate (physical pain, stress, or annoying behavior)

受不了.notes: Here 了 is always pronounced liǎo (third tone), never neutral tone le; its affirmative counterpart is 受得了 ('able to bear/handle'). Can be used intransitively or take a direct object (我受不了他这种脾气).

rootFamily.gloss: hard to bear, physically or emotionally uncomfortable

受到.etymology: A resultative verb-complement compound (動補結構) joining 受 (shòu, MC *dzyuwX, Old Chinese *duʔ, 'to receive, accept, undergo') with 到 (dào, MC *tawH, 'to arrive at, reach, attain'). The complement 到 marks the actualization and arrival of an external action upon the grammatical subject, functioning as a lexicalized passive-like marker in modern prose.

history.meaning: to receive in hand (depicting two hands passing a boat/vessel); to undergo an action
to receive, suffer, or be subjected to (abstract actions such as praise, criticism, impact, or harm)

morphemes.meaning: to receive, undergo, be subjected to
to arrive at, attain (marking completion of reception)

受到.notes: Takes two-syllable abstract verbal nouns as objects—both positive (受到欢迎 'be welcomed', 受到表扬 'receive praise') and negative (受到批评 'be criticized', 受到影响 'be affected'). Never used for concrete gifts (use 收到).

rootFamily.gloss: to receive (concrete items, messages, or payments)
to suffer, be subjected to (severe misfortune)

受困者.etymology: An agent/patient nominalization (偏正/附加式合成詞) built from the passive verb-object/complement compound 受困 (shòukùn, 'to suffer encirclement or distress', from 受 'to undergo' + 困 'hemmed in, stranded, exhausted', depicting a tree ⽊ enclosed within four walls 囗) plus the classical nominalizing suffix 者 (zhě, MC *tsyaeX, 'the one who...').

history.meaning: to be hemmed in, besieged militarily, or trapped in dire straits
stranded person, trapped individual (in disasters, accidents, or emergencies)

受困者.notes: Standard journalistic and broadcast news register (used frequently in live disaster reporting and rescue coverage); the suffix 者 marks a formal category of people in news copy.

受害人.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正結構) formed from the verb-object compound 受害 (shòuhài, 'to suffer injury, harm, or murder', from 受 'to undergo' + 害 'harm, calamity, damage') modifying the head noun 人 (rén, 'person, legal party'). Standardized in modern legal and journalistic Mandarin to designate the injured party in a crime, tort, or scandal.

history.meaning: to suffer harm, political persecution, or fatal injury
victim, injured party (in legal proceedings, criminal cases, or public scandals)

受害人.notes: Slightly more legal and procedural than 受害者 (shòuhàizhě): statutory law and police reports prefer 受害人 ('injured party') by analogy with 当事人 ('party to a case') and 嫌疑人 ('suspect').

rootFamily.gloss: party directly involved in a legal case or incident

受潮.etymology: Verb-object compound of 受 ('be affected by, suffer') + 潮 ('moisture, dampness', originally the rising sea tide): 'become damp, be affected by moisture or humidity'.
