history.meaning: absorb moisture; get damp

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 受潮 (via 萌典)

受益方.etymology: A three-morpheme legal-commercial compound (偏正結構) combining the verb-object root 受益 (shòuyì, 'to receive benefit or profit', attested since the *Shangshu* and *Mencius*, from 受 'to receive' + 益 'increase, benefit', originally depicting water overflowing a vessel 皿) with the head noun 方 (fāng, MC *pjang, 'direction, side, contractual party').

history.meaning: to receive moral, intellectual, or material benefit (as in 謙受益 'humility receives benefit')
beneficiary, the party or entity that reaps the benefit in a contract, transaction, or media event

morphemes.meaning: side, party (in a contract or dispute)

受益方.notes: While 受益人 refers specifically to an individual beneficiary (e.g., on an insurance policy), 受益方 uses 方 ('side/party') to include corporations, platforms, or factions that profit from a deal or controversy.

rootFamily.gloss: individual beneficiary (e.g., of a trust or insurance)

受罚.etymology: A verb-object compound (動賓結構) composed of 受 (shòu, MC *dzyuwX, 'to receive, undergo, submit to') and 罰 (fá, MC *bjwot, 'punishment, fine, penalty', an ideogrammic compound of 罒 'net' + 言 'speech/berating' + 刀 'knife'). Attested in Classical Chinese legal and historical texts for undergoing state or disciplinary punishment.

history.meaning: to undergo legal chastisement, corporal penalty, or official fine under state law
to be punished, take a penalty (in law, workplace discipline, school, or game shows)

受罚.notes: A separable VO verb (e.g., 受了重罚 'received a heavy penalty'); in variety shows and corporate media settings it covers everything from regulatory fines to playful game-show forfeits.

rootFamily.gloss: to impose a fine; fine, penalty fee

受苦.etymology: A verb-object compound (動賓結構) formed from 受 (shòu, 'to endure, undergo, receive') and 苦 (kǔ, MC *khuX, originally 'bitter sow-thistle', extended to 'bitter taste' and metaphorically to 'pain, hardship, existential suffering'). Deeply reinforced in medieval Chinese through Buddhist translations rendering Sanskrit *duḥkha* ('suffering') in contrast to 享樂 ('enjoying pleasure').

history.meaning: to endure karmic suffering (*duḥkha*), physical torment, or privation in medieval Buddhist and secular texts
to suffer hardship, go through rough times, endure privation

受苦.notes: Separable verb-object compound (e.g., 受了不少苦 'suffered quite a lot of hardship'). Compare 吃苦 (chīkǔ), which praises someone's active grit and willingness to endure tough work, whereas 受苦 focuses on the pain or mistreatment endured.

rootFamily.gloss: to bear hardships willingly, have grit

受邀人.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正結構) formed from the passive verb-object compound 受邀 (shòuyāo, 'to receive an invitation', from 受 'to receive' + 邀 yāo, MC *'jew, 'to intercept on the road; to invite, summon') modifying 人 (rén, 'person'). Characteristic of modern formal event management, media galas, and contractual terminology.

history.meaning: to invite a guest; to be honored with an invitation
invitee, invited guest or participant (on formal guest lists, tenders, or event rosters)

受邀人.notes: Used on formal guest lists, contracts, and event passes in television and gala production; in spoken conversation, 受邀嘉宾 ('invited VIP guest') is more common.

rootFamily.gloss: to be invited (to attend or speak)

变.etymology: Phono-semantic/ideographic character (traditional 變, combining 䜌 luán 'tangled silk threads/speech' + 攵 'hand action' -> 'rearrange threads, change, transform'): 'change, alter, become, turn into'.

history.meaning: alter; transform; change
change; become; turn into

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 变 (via 萌典)

变动.etymology: A coordinative compound (聯合結構) pairing 變 (biàn, MC *pjenH, 'to alter, change') with 動 (dòng, MC *duwngX, 'to move, stir, shift'). Used in classical philosophical and astronomical texts for the shifting movements of cosmos and human affairs, and standardized in modern administrative and economic usage for personnel, schedule, or market shifts.

history.meaning: cosmic or political stirrings, transformations, and movements (attested in the *Book of Changes* commentaries)
to shift, alter, or adjust; a change or adjustment (especially in personnel, schedules, or prices)

变动.notes: Functions as both a verb and a noun; compared to 变化 (general change), 变动 specifically refers to structural shifts in rosters, schedules, positions, or lineups (人事变动 'personnel shake-up', 节目时间有变动).

rootFamily.gloss: change, alteration (to a text or plan)

变化.etymology: A classic coordinative compound (聯合結構) joining 變 (biàn, MC *pjenH, 'gradual or abrupt alteration') and 化 (huà, MC *xwaeH, Old Chinese *qʰʷˤrar-s, depicting one person upright and one inverted 匕, 'complete metamorphosis or transmutation'). Central to pre-Qin cosmology in the *Yijing*, *Zhuangzi*, and *Xunzi*, where 變 denoted visible alteration and 化 denoted fundamental transformation.

history.meaning: cosmic alternation and metamorphosis of yin and yang, seasons, and living beings in pre-Qin philosophy
change, variation, or transformation (used as both a noun and an intransitive verb)

变化.notes: Unlike 改变 (which can take a direct object: 改变计划 'change the plan'), 变化 is primarily a noun (发生很大的变化) or an intransitive verb ('to vary/change').

变得.etymology: A verb-particle compound formed from the root verb 變 (biàn, MC *pjenH, 'to change, turn') followed by the structural complement marker 得 (de, grammaticalized in Tang–Song vernacular from the full verb 得 dé, MC *tok, 'to obtain, get, attain'). In Mandarin grammar, 变得 functions as a copular change-of-state verb introducing an adjectival or clausal state.

history.meaning: to change and attain a resulting quality or state in vernacular narrative prose
history.stage: Medieval to Early Modern Vernacular Chinese

history.meaning: to become, grow, turn (followed by an adjective or stative phrase)

morphemes.meaning: complement marker introducing resulting state or degree

变得.notes: Crucial grammar rule for learners: 变得 must be followed by an adjective or descriptive phrase (变得很成熟 'become very mature'), whereas 变成 is followed by a noun (变成明星 'become a star').

rootFamily.gloss: to turn into, become (followed by a noun)
to appear, seem, look (followed by an adjective)
to feel, think, find (followed by a clause/adj)

变成.etymology: A resultative verb-complement compound (動補結構) combining 變 (biàn, MC *pjenH, 'to alter, change') with the resultative verb 成 (chéng, MC *dzyeng, 'to complete, accomplish, form into'). The second morpheme 成 specifies that the process of change culminates in a new identity, entity, or completed form.

history.meaning: to transform and take shape as a new form or substance in medieval Buddhist and secular texts
to turn into, change into, become (followed by a noun phrase)

变成.notes: Takes a noun or nominal phrase as its object (把小说变成剧本 'turn a novel into a script', 变成好朋友); contrast with 变得, which takes adjectives.

rootFamily.gloss: to become, grow (followed by an adjective)
to become, come to be (formal, followed by a noun)
to cause, bring about, result in

变故.etymology: A coordinative nominal compound (聯合結構) composed of 變 (biàn, MC *pjenH, 'abrupt change, upheaval, calamity') and 故 (gù, MC *kuH, 'cause, incident, unforeseen mishap, death'). Attested since the *Zuo Zhuan* and *Zhouli* for sudden political coups, military emergencies, or family tragedies that disrupt the normal order.

history.meaning: sudden political upheaval, state emergency, or unforeseen calamity in classical historiography
unforeseen misfortune, sudden upheaval, or drastic turn of events (in a family, career, or project)

变故.notes: Always carries a serious, negative, or dramatic connotation (e.g., 遭遇家庭变故 'suffer a family tragedy', 发生重大变故); never used for neutral or positive changes.

变着法子.etymology: A colloquial northern Mandarin verb-object phrase (動賓短語) built from 變 (biàn, 'to vary, switch'), the durative/manner aspect particle 着 (zhe, 'while doing, by way of'), and 法子 (fǎzi, colloquial nominalization of 法 'method, law, way' + diminutive noun suffix 子 zi). Literally 'continually switching methods', it functions adverbially before a main verb to mean 'trying every conceivable angle or trick'.

history.form: 變着法兒 / 變着法子
history.meaning: switching methods one after another; devising clever or devious ways in Qing–modern Beijing vernacular
to try every clever, creative, or devious angle; to find new ways to do something

变着法子.notes: In northern speech, often pronounced with *erhua* as 变着法儿 (biànzhe fǎr). Used adverbially before another verb: can be affectionate (变着法子给他做菜 'finding new ways to cook for him') or critical (变着法子整人 'finding devious ways to make life hard for someone').

rootFamily.gloss: to think of a way, try every means

叠.etymology: Character (疊/迭) originally showing multiple sacrificial jade/meat vessels (晶/宜) piled atop one another: 'pile up in layers, repeat, fold (clothes, paper, or bedding)'.

history.meaning: pile up in layers; repeat; fold
fold; pile up; classifier for stacks

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 叠 (via 萌典)

口.etymology: Foundational pictograph (象形字) attested from Shang oracle bones depicting an open mouth: 'mouth, opening, entrance, doorway, spout, cut/nick' and a classifier for family members, wells, bites, or spoken words.

history.meaning: open mouth; opening; pass
mouth; opening; entrance; classifier for people/bites

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 口 (via 萌典)

口中.etymology: A noun-localizer phrase (方位短語) composed of 口 (kǒu, MC *khuwX, Old Chinese *kʰˤoʔ, pictograph of an open mouth, denoting both the anatomical organ and spoken utterance) and the postpositional localizer 中 (zhōng, MC *trjuwng, 'middle, interior, inside'). By metonymy from 'inside the mouth', it came in classical and vernacular Chinese to mean 'in someone's speech or account'.

history.meaning: literally inside the oral cavity; metonymically, in the words or testimony issuing from someone's mouth
in someone's words, talk, or narrative account (e.g., 别人眼中、口中的他)

口中.notes: When preceded by a person (e.g., 从他口中得知 'learn from his own lips', 外界口中的王牌制作人 'the ace producer in people's talk'), it belongs to a slightly literary or narrative register; for the physical mouth in daily conversation, 嘴里 (zuǐlǐ) is preferred.

rootFamily.gloss: tone of voice, manner of speaking

cognates.meaning: tone of voice; boastful talk; bad breath

口气.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正結構) formed from 口 (kǒu, 'mouth, speech') modifying 氣 (qì, MC *khjijH, 'breath, exhalation, vital energy, manner'). Originally referring to the physical breath exhaled from the mouth, it developed in Ming–Qing literary criticism and vernacular fiction to denote the 'breath/cadence of speech' (tone of voice, implied attitude) as well as 'a gulp of pent-up breath/frustration'.

history.meaning: physical breath exhaled from the mouth in medical and early ritual texts
manner or tone of speaking, implied attitude; also a breath of relief or pent-up resentment (as in 鬆一口氣, 咽下這口氣)

morphemes.meaning: breath, air, vital energy, aura/manner (traditional 氣)

口气.notes: Watch for two major senses in drama dialogue: (1) 'tone of voice / swagger' (口气不小 'talking big', 听他的口气 'judging by his tone'); and (2) 'a breath of emotion/pride' when preceded by 一 (松了一口气 'breathe a sigh of relief', 咽不下这口气 'cannot swallow this humiliation').

rootFamily.gloss: accent, regional pronunciation; tone of voice
to vent anger, get even, win respect

口袋.etymology: Compound noun of 口 ('opening, mouth of a bag') + 袋 ('bag, sack, pouch', 代 + 衣 'cloth'): 'bag, sack' and in modern Mandarin especially a garment 'pocket'.

history.meaning: cloth bag or sack; garment pocket

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 口袋 (via 萌典)

句.etymology: Ancient character combining 勹 ('curve, hook') + 口 ('mouth/speech'): originally 'curved/hooked' (later written 勾 gōu) and 'a pause or completed unit in speech/verse', hence 'sentence, clause, line of verse' and the classifier for spoken or written sentences (一句话).

history.meaning: pause marking a phrase; sentence; verse line
sentence; classifier for sentences or remarks

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 句 (via 萌典)

句子.etymology: Compound noun formed from 句 ('sentence, clause') + nominal suffix 子 (-zi): 'grammatical sentence'.

history.stage: Tang–Song literary criticism to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: a verse line or grammatical sentence

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 句子 (via 萌典)

另.etymology: A graphical and lexical derivative of 叧 (guǎ, 'to pare flesh from bone, separate', the top component of 剮 and original left side of 別 bié 'to divide, separate'). Emerging in medieval vulgar orthography by splitting or altering 別/叧 into 口 over 力, 另 (lìng) took on the sense 'separate, another, outside the current group, in addition'.

history.meaning: graphic variant arising in Tang–Song vernacular documents meaning 'separate, divided, another'
another, the other (determiner); separately, in addition, besides (adverb before monosyllabic or disyllabic verbs)

另.notes: As a determiner, 另 must be followed by a numeral + classifier (另一个人 'another person', 另一部戏 'another drama'); before verbs, it acts as a concise adverb meaning 'separately / anew' (另找工作 'find another job', 另作安排 'make separate arrangements').

rootFamily.gloss: be another matter altogether, count as an exception

另外.etymology: Compound pronoun, determiner, and conjunction of 另 ('separate, other, another', split from 別) + 外 ('outside, besides, beyond'): 'another, other; in addition, besides, furthermore'.

history.meaning: in addition; besides; another

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 另外 (via 萌典)

另当别论.etymology: A four-character idiomatic predicate phrase (四字格成語) structured as an interlocking parallel construction: 另 (lìng, 'separately, otherwise') + 當 (dāng, MC *tang, 'ought to, should') + 別 (bié, MC *bjet, 'differently, distinctly, in another category') + 論 (lùn, MC *lwijH / *lwon, 'to discuss, judge, evaluate'). Literally 'ought to be judged separately in a different category'.

history.meaning: ought to be evaluated separately as a distinct case outside the general rule in Qing–modern prose

另当别论.notes: Here 当 is pronounced dāng (first tone, 'ought to'), not dàng. Commonly used at the end of a conditional sentence (那是另当别论, or 如果...就另当别论了) to carve out an exception to a rule just stated.

rootFamily.gloss: cannot be mentioned in the same breath, not comparable
to treat everything the same, lump together
to judge something on its own merits, take a matter on its own terms

另有.etymology: A modifier-head verbal compound formed from 另 (lìng, 'separate, other, in addition', originally a variant split from 令 meaning 'divided/separate') modifying the existential and possessive verb 有 (yǒu, 'to have, there is'). In Literary and early Mandarin prose, it functions as a compact disyllabic predicate introducing an alternative or undisclosed possession, plan, or motive, before taking a two-syllable object (e.g., 另有隐情, 另有打算).

history.meaning: separate / other + to have, to exist
to have other (plans, uses, motives); there is separately

另有.notes: Typically takes disyllabic abstract objects or four-character idioms in formal or dramatic contexts, such as 另有打算 ('have other plans'), 另有企图 ('have ulterior motives'), or 另有安排 ('have other arrangements').

rootFamily.gloss: to have inside information or hidden details

只.etymology: Simplified graph merging two Classical characters: (1) 只/祇/只 (read zhǐ, originally a clause-final particle in the Shijing, then the restrictive adverb 'only, merely, just') and (2) 隻 (read zhī, showing one bird 隹 in a hand 又: 'single one of a pair' -> general classifier for animals, birds, boats, and one of a pair of hands/shoes).

history.form: 只 / 祇 (only, zhǐ) & 隻 (single bird in hand -> classifier, zhī)
history.meaning: restrictive adverb vs. unit classifier
only, just (zhǐ); classifier for animals/single items (zhī)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 只 (via 萌典)

只不过.etymology: A grammaticalized trisyliabic restrictive adverbial compound combining the restrictive particle 只 (zhǐ, 'only, merely') with 不过 (bùguò, 'not surpassing, no more than', itself a negated directional/comparative compound of 不 'not' + 过 'to pass, exceed'). Originating in Song–Yuan vernacular Chinese as a literal predicate ('it merely does not exceed...'), it grammaticalized into a discourse marker and adverb softening a contrast or downplaying a statement ('merely, it is only that').

history.meaning: does not exceed, no more than
merely not exceeding; nothing more than
merely, only that, just that (adversative or downplaying adverb)

只不过.notes: Frequently paired with 罢了 or 而已 at the end of a clause (只不过……罢了, 'it is merely... and nothing more') to downplay the severity of a situation or introduce a mild caveat.

rootFamily.gloss: only, merely (followed by a noun or verb)

只会.etymology: A modifier-head modal compound combining the restrictive adverb 只 (zhǐ, 'only, exclusively') with the modal auxiliary verb 会 (huì, originally 'to assemble, meet', later grammaticalized into a modal expressing acquired skill 'know how to' or epistemic/future likelihood 'will, be likely to'). Depending on context, 只会 either restricts ability ('only know how to do X') or restricts inevitable consequence ('will only result in X').

history.meaning: only + to be able to / to be likely to
will only (lead to); only know how to

morphemes.meaning: will, be likely to; know how to

只会.notes: Has two distinct senses in spoken dialogue: epistemic prediction ('Doing this will only make things worse', 这只会让事情更糟) and critical assessment of skill ('He only knows how to talk big', 他只会说大话).

rootFamily.gloss: can only, have no choice but to
to know how to; meeting; will

只是.etymology: Compound of 只 (zhǐ, 'only, merely') + 是 ('be; focus marker'): means both 'merely is, simply' and as a mild adversative conjunction 'only that, however, except that'.

history.meaning: merely; only; however, it's just that

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 只是 (via 萌典)

只有.etymology: Restrictive verb/conjunction compound of 只 (zhǐ, 'only') + 有 ('have, there is'): 'there is only…' and in correlative conditionals 'only if… (只有…才…)'.

history.meaning: only have; only if

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 只有 (via 萌典)

只能.etymology: A modifier-head modal verb compound composed of the restrictive adverb 只 (zhǐ, 'only, solely') and the modal auxiliary 能 (néng, originally a pictograph of a bear-like creature, loaned in Old Chinese for 'ability, capability' and later 'to be able to, can'). Together, the compound expresses deontic or circumstantial necessity: when all other options are excluded, the subject 'can only' or 'has no choice but to' act in a certain way.

history.meaning: only + to be capable of / permitted by circumstances
can only, have no choice but to

只能.notes: Close in meaning to 只好 ('have no choice but to'), but 只能 emphasizes objective constraints or rules ('Given the budget, we can only cut scenes'), whereas 只好 emphasizes reluctant personal compromise.

rootFamily.gloss: will only; only know how to

只要.etymology: Conditional conjunction combining 只 (zhǐ, 'only') + 要 ('need, require'): literally 'only need…' -> 'so long as, provided that' (typically paired with 就 in the main clause: 只要…就…).

history.meaning: only need -> as long as, provided that

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 只要 (via 萌典)

只闻其名.etymology: A four-character semi-literary idiom (成语/惯用语) structured as a restrictive verb-object clause: 只 (zhǐ, 'only') + 闻 (wén, 'to hear', Classical Chinese verb of auditory perception) + 其 (qí, Classical third-person genitive pronoun 'his/her/its') + 名 (míng, 'name, reputation'). It frequently pairs with 不见其人 ('without seeing the person') to describe a legendary or elusive figure known solely through fame or rumor.

history.meaning: to hear someone's name or reputation
to hear only their name without seeing the person in the flesh

history.form: 只闻其名 (zhǐ wén qí míng)
history.meaning: to know someone or something only by reputation

只闻其名.notes: Often used in media and industry circles when finally meeting a famous producer, writer, or executive behind the scenes: 久仰大名，以前一直只闻其名 ('Long admired your name; previously I knew you only by reputation').

rootFamily.gloss: to know someone only by reputation without having met them

叫.etymology: Phono-semantic character (historically also ) combining 口 ('mouth') + 丩 (jiū, 'intertwine/cry out'): 'cry out, shout, call; animal cry; be called/named (我叫…); ask/order someone to do; passive marker in spoken Mandarin'.

history.meaning: call out; cry aloud
shout; call; be named; make/let; passive marker

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 叫 (via 萌典)

叫好.etymology: A verb-object compound originating in traditional Chinese theater and opera culture, composed of 叫 (jiào, 'to shout, cry out, call') and 好 (hǎo, 'good!, bravo!', functioning as the quoted exclamation). Literally 'to shout bravo', it referred to audience members calling out praise during an opera or acrobatics performance, and later generalized to critical acclaim in film, television, and the arts.

history.meaning: to shout 'bravo!' at a theatrical or street performance
to applaud vocally; to win critical praise and audience acclaim

叫好.notes: A staple of entertainment industry jargon in the phrase 叫好又叫座 ('critically acclaimed and commercially successful' — literally 'wins bravos and fills seats') versus 叫好不叫座 ('critically acclaimed but a box-office flop').

rootFamily.gloss: to draw big audiences, be a box-office hit
to shout, to call; to order

叫醒.etymology: Resultative verb compound from 叫 ('call; shout') + 醒 ('sober up; wake from sleep', wine vessel 酉 + phonetic 星). First used in Tang-Song poetry and vernacular prose, it transparently combines the action of calling out with the resulting state of waking up.

history.meaning: call someone awake
wake someone up

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 叫醒

召回.etymology: A verb-resultative/directional compound formed from 召 (zhào, 'to summon by authority, issue an imperial call', written with 刀 over 口 representing a vocal command from above) and 回 (huí, 'to return, turn back'). Originally used in imperial administration for summoning an envoy or official back to court, in modern Mandarin it also translates English 'recall' in commercial law (product recall) and corporate or diplomatic contexts.

history.meaning: to summon an official or general back to the imperial court
to recall (an ambassador, personnel, or defective commercial products)

召回.notes: Used across high-register domains: diplomatic recalls (召回大使), corporate/studio personnel recalls, and consumer product recalls (产品召回). Do not confuse the character 召 (zhào) with 招 (zhāo, 'to beckon, recruit').

召开.etymology: A modern verb-resultative compound combining 召 (zhào, 'to summon, call together officially') with 开 (kāi, 'to open, hold, inaugurate [a meeting]'). Formed in 20th-century administrative Mandarin by blending the classical sense of 召 ('to summon participants') with 开会 ('to hold/open a meeting'), meaning 'to summon participants and open a formal conference or session'.

history.meaning: to summon officially + to open / initiate
to convene, to hold (a formal meeting, press conference, or congress)

召开.notes: Takes only formal meeting nouns as its object—such as 召开会议 ('convene a meeting') or 召开新闻发布会 ('hold a press conference')—never people (use 召集 for gathering people).

cognates.meaning: to convene, call together (e.g., the Diet or military reserves)

召集.etymology: A verb-resultative/coordinative compound attested in Classical Chinese histories (such as *Shiji* and *Hanshu*), formed from 召 (zhào, 'to summon by decree or authority') and 集 (jí, 'to gather, assemble', originally depicting birds perched together on a tree 雧). Literally 'to summon so as to assemble', it was reinforced in modern East Asian administrative vocabulary via shared Sino-Japanese usage (召集 shōshū).

history.meaning: to summon and assemble troops, officials, or retainers
to convene, muster, or gather people for a meeting or task

召集.notes: Unlike 召开 (which takes a meeting as its object, e.g., 召开会议), 召集 typically takes people or staff as its object (e.g., 召集大家 'gather everyone together', 召集主创人员 'assemble the creative team'), though 召集会议 is also occasionally used for smaller meetings.

rootFamily.gloss: convener, coordinator of a meeting or group

叮嘱.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound combining 叮 (dīng, originally an onomatopoeic/vocal character from 叮咛 dīngníng, 'to speak repeatedly and earnestly') and 嘱 (zhǔ, 'to enjoin, entrust, urge', from 嘱咐 zhǔfù). Each syllable carries the mouth radical 口, underscoring spoken exhortation. Formed in vernacular Mandarin as a blend of 叮咛 and 嘱咐, it denotes giving repeated, caring reminders or instructions.

history.meaning: to exhort repeatedly + to entrust, instruct
to urge repeatedly, remind with care and concern

morphemes.meaning: to enjoin, to instruct, to entrust (from 嘱咐)

叮嘱.notes: Carries a warm, attentive, or earnest tone—typically used when a parent, mentor, director, or doctor carefully reminds someone what to do or watch out for (再三叮嘱, 'to remind again and again').

rootFamily.gloss: to urge repeatedly, give earnest reminders
to enjoin, tell, instruct with care

可.etymology: Ancient character combining 口 ('mouth') + 丂 ('exhalation of breath'): originally 'sing/exhale smoothly -> approve, permit, may, can, worthy of (-able)', and in Mandarin also anadversative conjunction ('but, yet', short for 可是) and an emphatic adverb ('really, indeed; in questions: ever/at all?').

history.meaning: approve; permit; can; worthy of
can/may; but/yet; emphatic 'really'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 可 (via 萌典)

可不可行.etymology: An A-not-A (正反问) interrogative construction formed by reduplicating the first syllable of the disyllabic adjective 可行 (kěxíng, 'feasible, practicable, workable', composed of the potential prefix 可 'can be, worthy of being' + 行 'carried out, practiced, walked') around the negation particle 不 (bù, 'not'): 可 + 不 + 可行. This Mandarin morphosyntactic pattern turns a predicate into an embedded or direct yes-no question ('is it feasible or not?').

history.meaning: capable of being carried out or put into practice
whether or not (a plan or proposal) is feasible

morphemes.meaning: can be, feasible (first syllable of 可行)
to carry out, to work, to practice

可不可行.notes: Illustrates Mandarin's incomplete A-not-AB reduplication rule for two-syllable adjectives: instead of *可行不可行, speakers drop the second syllable in the first half to say 可不可行 ('feasible or not?'), common in pitch meetings when evaluating a script or proposal (这个方案可不可行).

rootFamily.gloss: can or cannot; whether it is permissible

可以.etymology: Compound modal verb originally formed from two Classical words: 可 ('permissible, possible') + 以 ('by means of, to'). Rebracketed from '可 [以 V]' ('possible [with which to V]') into the disyllabic modal verb 可以 meaning 'can, may, be permitted to; pretty good / passable'.

history.meaning: able/permissible therewith to…
can; may; be allowed to; not bad

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 可以 (via 萌典)

可怕.etymology: A derivative adjective formed from the passive-potential prefix 可 (kě, 'worthy of being, inducing, -able/-ible', from Old Chinese *kʰaːlʔ) attached to the psych-verb 怕 (pà, 'to fear, dread', with the heart radical 忄 + phonetic 白). Literally 'worthy of being feared' or 'fear-inducing', it evolved in vernacular Mandarin from literal terror ('frightening') to an evaluative intensifier ('formidable, tremendous, scary in scale or competence').

history.meaning: worthy of dread; inducing fear (vernacular replacement of Classical 可畏)
scary, frightening; formidable, awe-inspiringly intense

可怕.notes: In workplace and showbiz dialogue, 可怕 often means 'formidable' rather than 'spooky'—e.g., 真正可怕的对手 ('a truly formidable rival') or describing someone's work ethic as 努力得可怕 ('scarily hardworking').

可怜.etymology: Adjective and verb formed with the Classical prefix 可 ('worthy of, -able') + 怜 (憐, 'pity, feel tenderness or sympathy for', heart 忄 + 粦 lín). In Tang poetry 可怜 often meant 'lovable, endearing' as well as 'pitiful'; in modern Mandarin it means 'pitiful, poor, pathetic; have pity on'.

history.meaning: worthy of pity or affection; touching
pitiful; poor; take pity on

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 可怜 (via 萌典)

可惜.etymology: Adjective and verb formed from 可 ('worthy of') + 惜 ('regret, grudge, cherish, begrudge leaving'): 'regrettable, it is a pity, what a shame'. Attested since Han–Tang poetry and prose.

history.meaning: worthy of regret -> what a pity, regrettable

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 可惜 (via 萌典)

可是.etymology: Adversative conjunction combining 可 ('however, yet') + 是 (focus/copular formative): 'but, however, yet' (and when stressed as adverbs, 'indeed, really is').

history.meaning: but; however; indeed is

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 可是 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: cute, adorable (borrowed/adapted into ateji 可愛い kawaii)

可爱.etymology: A Classical Chinese adjective formed from the passive-potential prefix 可 (kě, 'worthy of being, -able') and the verb 爱 (ài, 'to love, cherish, hold dear'). Attested as early as the *Shujing* (Book of Documents) and * Mencius* in the high moral sense 'worthy of affection or esteem', it shifted in vernacular Mandarin and across East Asia (compare Japanese 可愛い *kawaii*) toward 'endearing, charming, cute'.

history.meaning: worthy of affection, esteem, or fondness
lovable, endearing, cute, charming

可爱.notes: While everyday speech uses 可爱 for 'cute' (children, pets, styling), high-register Mandarin still retains its older sense of 'endearing and admirable' (e.g., 最可爱的人, 'the most admirable/beloved people').

可算.etymology: '可算' (kěsuàn, finally) is an adverbial phrase composed of '可' (indeed, emphasizes) and '算' (to count as, to calculate). '算' originally referred to calculating with bamboo slips, as seen in its bamboo radical. In vernacular Chinese of the Ming and Qing dynasties, '算' developed a meaning of 'considering something to be the case'. When paired with '可', it expresses a sense of relief or emotional emphasis that an expected event has finally materialized. It is widely used in spoken Mandarin to convey a strong sense of 'at last'.

history.meaning: finally

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 可算

可能.etymology: A coordinative compound of two Classical Chinese modal verbs: 可 (kě, 'may, be permissible, be feasible') and 能 (néng, 'can, be capable of'). Although juxtaposed in Literary Chinese (e.g., 不可得而能), its modern usage as a unified adjective ('possible'), noun ('possibility'), and epistemic adverb ('maybe, perhaps') was heavily shaped by Meiji-era Japanese *wasei-kango* usage of 可能 (*kanō*) translating European 'possible', which re-entered Mandarin in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

history.meaning: permissible / feasible + capable of
possible, potential (translating English/German 'possible/möglich')
possible (adj.); maybe, perhaps (adv.); possibility (noun)

可能.notes: Unusually versatile in grammar: it functions as an epistemic adverb before a verb (他可能不来了, 'He might not come'), a predicative adjective (这完全可能, 'This is entirely possible'), and a noun after 有/没有 (还有一种可能, 'There is one more possibility').

rootFamily.gloss: as much as possible, to the utmost

可能性.etymology: A trimorphemic abstract noun formed by suffixing the nominalizer -性 (-xìng, originally 'innate nature, quality', grammaticalized in modern Sino-Japanese and Mandarin as an abstract noun suffix equivalent to English '-ity / -ness') to the compound 可能 (kěnéng, 'possible'). Adapted via Japanese 可能性 (*kanōsei*, translating German *Möglichkeit* and English *possibility*), it strictly nominalizes 'possible' into 'likelihood, degree of possibility, or potentiality'.

history.meaning: possibility, potentiality (philosophical and scientific calque of German Möglichkeit)
possibility, likelihood, probability; potential

可能性.notes: Unlike 可能 (which can be an adverb, adjective, or noun), 可能性 is strictly a noun and collocates with adjectives of size or probability: 可能性很大 ('the likelihood is very high'), 排除这种可能性 ('rule out this possibility').

cognates.meaning: platform, stand, stage; counter for machines and vehicles
platform, stage, stand; counter for vehicles/machines

台.etymology: In Simplified Chinese, 台 (tái) merges four historically distinct characters: (1) 臺 (tái, Old Chinese *dɯː, 'elevated earthen viewing terrace or platform'), (2) 台 (yí, 'I/me; joyful', later used as a vernacular shorthand for 臺), (3) 檯 (tái, 'table, desk, counter'), and (4) 颱 (tái, 'typhoon'). From 'elevated platform' (臺), its meaning extended to 'theatrical stage' (舞台), 'broadcasting station/network' (电视台, via 'signal/observation tower'), and a classifier for heavy or elevated apparatus, machines, and stage performances (一台机器, 一台戏).

history.meaning: high, flat-topped earthen terrace or lookout tower
theatrical stage; raised table or counter; classifier for theatrical shows
stage, platform; broadcasting station/network; classifier for machines, appliances, and shows

morphemes.meaning: elevated platform, stage, broadcasting station; classifier for machines and shows

台.notes: In television and media contexts (*幕后之王*), 台 simultaneously appears in the sense of 'stage' (上台, 舞台), 'TV station/network' (电视台, 台长, 台里), and 'classifier for a full stage show or piece of broadcasting equipment' (一台晚会, 一台摄像机).

rootFamily.gloss: stage lines, dialogue in a script

台上.etymology: A locative noun compound formed from 台 (tái, written 臺 in Traditional Chinese, 'elevated platform, theatrical stage, podium') followed by the postpositional locativeizer 上 (shàng, 'on, upon, above'). Originally denoting the top of a raised terrace or altar, in theatrical and public-speaking contexts it lexicalized into a place noun meaning 'onstage' or 'at the podium'.

history.meaning: upon the raised terrace or viewing platform
onstage, on the podium (in contrast to the audience or offstage preparation)

台上.notes: Frequently paired with 台下 in the classic performing-arts proverb 台上一分钟，台下十年功 ('One minute onstage takes ten years of hard practice offstage').

rootFamily.gloss: below the stage, in the audience; offstage
to go onstage, to appear before the audience; to come to power

cognates.meaning: beneath the platform/pedestal; form of address to royalty/cardinals

台下.etymology: A locative noun compound composed of 台 (tái / 臺, 'elevated terrace, theatrical stage, podium') and the locative postposition 下 (xià, 'under, below, beneath'). In Classical Chinese, 臺下 could mean 'beneath the terrace' or serve as a deferential epistolary address ('beneath your platform', akin to 阁下). In vernacular theater and modern Mandarin, it denotes the area below the stage—specifically the audience seating area ('in the audience/house') or life offstage.

history.meaning: at the foot of the raised terrace; deferential title ('beneath your seat')
below the stage, in the audience; offstage in private preparation or life

台下.notes: Depending on context, 台下 contrasts with 台上 in two ways: spatially during a show ('the audience below the stage', 台下掌声雷动) or temporally/professionally ('offstage in private life or rehearsal', 台上风光，台下辛酸).

rootFamily.gloss: to step down from the stage; to leave office; to get out of an awkward spot

台前幕后.etymology: A four-character coordinative phrase juxtaposing two parallel locative compounds from theatrical staging: 台前 (táiqián, 'in front of the stage / before the camera', from 台 'stage' + 前 'front') and 幕后 (mùhòu, 'behind the curtain / behind the scenes', from 幕 'stage curtain, canopy' + 后 'behind, back'). Together, they encompass the entirety of an entertainment production—both the visible performers in the spotlight and the unseen producers, directors, and crew behind the curtain.

history.meaning: in front of the theatrical stage + behind the stage curtain/tent
onstage and behind the scenes; both on-camera talent and off-camera production crew and stories

台前幕后.notes: Central thematic expression in media and entertainment (directly echoing the title *幕后之王* 'Behind the Scenes'): used both for the whole cast-and-crew team (台前幕后的工作人员) and for inside stories of a production (揭秘台前幕后的故事).

rootFamily.gloss: behind the scenes, backstage (also used for a mastermind)
onstage, in front of the audience or camera

台灯.etymology: Compound noun of 台 (臺, 'table, desk, platform') + 灯 (燈, 'lamp, light'): 'desk lamp, table lamp'.

history.meaning: desk lamp; table lamp

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 台灯 (via 萌典)

台网.etymology: A contemporary 21st-century Chinese media industry portmanteau (coordinate abbreviation, 缩略语) combining 台 (tái, clipped from 电视台 diànshìtái, 'television station/network') and 网 (wǎng, clipped from 网络视频平台 wǎngluò shìpín píngtái or 互联网 hùliánwǎng, 'online streaming platform / internet'). Coined in mainland Chinese broadcasting during the 2010s to describe the convergence and dual-distribution model of traditional satellite TV networks and online streaming platforms.

history.meaning: television broadcasting station + internet / online network
television network and online streaming platform (dual-broadcasting ecosystem)

morphemes.meaning: online platform / internet (from 网络/网站)

台网.notes: A key business term in modern Chinese television production (*幕后之王*), appearing in phrases like 台网联动 ('TV-and-online interactive synergy'), 台网同播 ('simultaneous broadcast on TV and streaming platforms'), and 先网后台 ('streaming-first, TV-second release').

台脚.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound composed of 台 (tái / 臺, 'stage, raised platform, table') and 脚 (jiǎo, 'foot, base, lower edge'). Originally referring literally to the base or front/outer edge of a theatrical stage or the leg of a table, in traditional Chinese opera and stagecraft it also developed specialized senses regarding a performer's footing and stage movement or the footlights/edge of the stage.

history.meaning: the base or lower edge of a raised platform or theatrical stage; stage footing in opera
edge or foot of the stage; supporting pillars or base of a stage/table

台脚.notes: In stage production and live event directing, 台脚 refers physically to the front/bottom edge of the stage (near the pit or first row); in southern dialects (such as Cantonese and Wu) and traditional opera, it can also refer to stage presence/footwork or a supporting cast member.

rootFamily.gloss: corner of the stage; corner of a table
steps leading up to a stage or platform; a way to save face
at the foot of a wall; foundation

台里.etymology: A locative institutional compound formed from 台 (tái, clipped from 电视台 diànshìtái 'television station' or 电台 diàntái 'radio station') plus the interior locative suffix 里 (lǐ, 'inside, within'). Paralleling organizational terms like 厂里 ('the factory/studio'), 局里 ('the bureau'), and 部里 ('the ministry'), appending 里 turns an institution noun into an insider's collective reference to 'the TV network / station management / headquarters'.

history.form: 電台 / 電視台 + 裏 (lǐ)
history.meaning: broadcasting station + inside / within
inside the TV/radio station; the network (as an institutional authority or workplace)

morphemes.meaning: broadcasting station, TV network (from 电视台/电台)

台里.notes: Frequently used as an animate institutional subject in media workplaces: 台里决定 ('The network has decided...'), 台里的领导 ('the executives at the station'). Pronounced with a neutral tone on 里 (táilǐ / táili) in natural speech.

rootFamily.gloss: head/director of a TV or radio station
inside the film studio / factory (institutional parallel)

台阶.etymology: Compound noun of 台 (臺, 'raised terrace, platform') + 阶 (階, 'steps, stairs leading up to a terrace', mound 阝 + 皆). Means literally 'flight of steps, stairs' and figuratively in 找台阶下 'a face-saving way out of an awkward situation'.

history.meaning: steps leading up a terrace; stairs; face-saving way out

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 台阶 (via 萌典)

台面.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound combining 台 (tái, historically written 檯 for 'table, counter, desk' or 臺 for 'stage, platform') and 面 (miàn, 'face, surface, top'). Literally 'the surface of a table, counter, or stage', it developed a vivid metaphorical extension in Mandarin politics, business, and media: 'the open table of public negotiation and polite scrutiny', contrasting with backroom or under-the-table dealings.

history.meaning: surface of a table, counter, or stage; visible display surface
tabletop, counter surface; open discussion, public view, presentable formality

台面.notes: Most often encountered in idiomatic collocations with 上 ('on') or 下 ('under'): 拿到台面上来说 ('bring it out onto the table for open discussion') and 上不了台面 ('unpresentable, too shady or crude to be shown in public').

rootFamily.gloss: in the open, aboveboard, on the table

史上.etymology: A compact two-character locative compound clipped from 历史上 (lìshǐ shàng, 'in history'), composed of 史 (shǐ, 'history, annals', originally an archaic pictograph of a hand holding a tally or record-keeping instrument in court) and the temporal-locative postposition 上 (shàng, 'in, on, within the domain of'). Popularized in modern journalistic and promotional Chinese (reinforced by Japanese 史上 *shijō*) as a punchy modifier before superlatives ('in all of history, ever').

history.meaning: court scribe / historical annals + upon / within
in the annals of history; (with superlatives) of all time, ever

史上.notes: A favorite buzzword in media marketing and entertainment headlines right before 最 ('most'): 史上最严 ('the strictest in history'), 史上最高收视率 ('the highest ratings ever').

右.etymology: Ancient graph attested on Shang oracle bones as 又 (pictograph of a right hand), to which 口 ('mouth', suggesting assistance/eating with the right hand) was later added to distinguish 'right (side/hand)' (右) from the adverb 'again' (又) and 'assist' (佑).

history.meaning: right hand; right side; honor/assist
right (opposite of left 左)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 右 (via 萌典)

右上角.etymology: A transparent three-morpheme spatial compound built from 右 (yòu, 'right-hand side'), 上 (shàng, 'upper, top'), and 角 (jiǎo, 'corner, angle'). Mandarin systematically names all four corners of a page, screen, or courtyard by pairing left/right (左/右) before upper/lower (上/下) plus 角—mirroring English 'upper-right corner' in the fixed order 'right-upper-corner'.

history.meaning: upper-right corner (of a page, map, or frame)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 右上角

右下角.etymology: Formed parallel to 右上角 from 右 (yòu, 'right-hand side'), 下 (xià, 'lower, bottom'), and 角 (jiǎo, 'corner, angle'), literally 'right-lower-corner'. In East Asian and Western book arts alike, 右下角 is a standard reference point for seals, colophons, compass roses, and artist signatures along the bottom margin.

history.meaning: lower-right corner; bottom-right corner

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 右下角

右手.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 右 ('right') + 手 ('hand'): 'right hand'. Attested since the Shijing and Classics.

history.stage: Old & Classical Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: right hand

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 右手 (via 萌典)

右脚.etymology: Compound noun from 右 ('right-hand side', hand 又 + mouth 口) + 脚 ('foot; leg', flesh 月 + phonetic 却). Contrasted with 左脚 ('left foot') in everyday anatomical and movement expressions.

history.meaning: right foot
right foot

右边.etymology: Locative compound noun of 右 ('right') + 边 (邊, 'side'): 'the right side, to the right'.

history.meaning: the right-hand side

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 右边 (via 萌典)

叶子.etymology: Built from 叶 (yè, simplified from 葉, depicting plant shoots 艹 atop a branching tree 木 with phonetic 枼 'thin flat plank') plus the neutral-toned Mandarin nominal suffix 子 (zi). In Old Chinese 葉 denoted thin, flat foliage as well as thin sheets of metal or book leaves. Adding 子 in vernacular Northern and Southwestern Mandarin distinguishes the concrete botanical leaf (叶子) from bound compounds like 茶叶 ('tea leaves') or 枫叶 ('maple leaf').

morphemes.meaning: botanical leaf; thin flat sheet (simplified from 葉)

history.meaning: foliage leaf; thin sheet
leaf of a tree, herb, or garden plant

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 叶子

号.etymology: Originally 號 (combining 号 háo 'cry out' + 虎 'tiger'): read háo 'roar, wail, cry aloud', and read hào 'call, command, name, alias/courtesy title, mark/signal, ordinal number/date of the month, size, brass horn/bugle'.

history.meaning: cry out (háo); command, designation, mark (hào)
number; date of month; size; mark; horn

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 号 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to call upon, appeal to, rally

号召.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound attested in Classical Chinese texts (such as *Zhuangzi* and *Hanshu*), formed from 号 (hào / 號, 'to cry out, proclaim, issue a command or signal') and 召 (zhào, 'to summon by authority'). Originally meaning 'to shout a summons' or 'to command and gather troops', in modern Mandarin it denotes issuing a public appeal to rally people behind a cause or initiative, and as a noun, 'a public call or appeal'.

history.meaning: to shout a summons; to call and muster by proclamation
to call upon, appeal to, rally (verb); a public appeal or rallying call (noun)

morphemes.meaning: to cry out, proclaim, issue an order (號)

号召.notes: In entertainment and media, the derived noun 号召力 ('rallying power / appeal / draw') is crucial for measuring a star's or director's box-office and ratings pull (票房号召力, 收视号召力).

rootFamily.gloss: rallying power, charismatic appeal, box-office draw

号码.etymology: Compound noun of 号 (號, 'identifying number, designation') + 码 (碼, 'counting tally, numeral symbol', originally agate pebbles used as gaming/counting counters): 'number (phone number, room number, license plate, or clothing size)'.

history.meaning: serial or identifying number; size

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 号码 (via 萌典)

司机.etymology: Verb-object compound used as an occupational noun, combining 司 ('take charge of, manage, operate') + 机 (機, 'machine, engine, locomotive'): originally coined in late Qing / early Republican railways for a 'locomotive engineer, engine operator', then generalized to any 'driver, chauffeur'.

history.meaning: person in charge of the engine -> train engineer, vehicle driver

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 司机 (via 萌典)

吃.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 口 ('mouth') + 乞 (qǐ). In Classical Chinese, 吃 (read jí) meant 'stammer, stutter' (as in 口吃), while 'eat' was 食 (shí) or 喫 (chī). From the Tang–Song vernacular onward, 吃 was borrowed to write 喫 (chī) and became the universal Mandarin verb for 'eat, take (medicine), absorb, suffer'.

history.meaning: eat was written 食 or 喫
eat; consume; suffer

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 吃 (via 萌典)

吃相.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound combining 吃 (chī, 'to eat') and 相 (xiàng, 'outward appearance, posture, deportment, physiognomy'). Originating in colloquial Mandarin and Wu/Jianghuai dialects for a person's physical posture and table manners while eating, in contemporary Mandarin it underwent a sharp metaphorical shift to describe how gracefully or greedily a person, company, or celebrity pursues profit, credit, or advantage.

history.meaning: one's posture, facial expression, and manners while eating food
history.stage: Early Modern Colloquial Mandarin & Wu Dialect

history.meaning: table manners; (figuratively) the manner in which one chases profit, fame, or advantage

吃相.notes: Almost always used figuratively in the critique 吃相太难看 ('their table manners are too ugly' = 'they are being shamelessly greedy/unscrupulous in grabbing money or credit', e.g., when a show inserts excessive ads or a competitor plays dirty).

rootFamily.gloss: embarrassed or pathetic look when losing composure

吃药.etymology: A verb-object compound composed of 吃 (chī, originally 'to stutter' in Classical Chinese, which replaced 食 shí and 喫 qī/chī in vernacular Mandarin as the general verb 'to eat, ingest orally') and 药 (yào / 藥, 'medicinal herb, medicine, drug', with the grass radical 艹 over 樂). In Mandarin, oral ingestion of solid or liquid medicine is conceptualized with the verb 吃 ('eat/take') or 服 (formal 'ingest').

history.form: 服藥 (fúyào) → 喫藥 / 吃藥 (chīyào)
history.meaning: to ingest medicinal herbs or decoctions orally (vernacular replacement of Classical 服藥)
to take medicine (literally); (colloquial slang) to get tricked or take a loss, or 'take your meds' in banter

morphemes.meaning: to eat, to ingest orally, to take

吃药.notes: Whereas English 'take medicine' uses 'take' and Japanese uses 飲む ('drink'), Mandarin uses 吃 ('eat') for pills, powders, and liquid decoctions alike; in formal medical contexts, 服药 is used instead. In slang banter, 忘了吃药 ('forgot to take one's meds') teases someone acting erratically.

吃饭.etymology: A prototypical separable verb-object compound (离合词) formed from 吃 (chī, vernacular Mandarin 'to eat', replacing Classical 食 shí and graphically merging with 喫) and 饭 (fàn / 飯, 'cooked grain/rice, meal'). Originally meaning 'to eat cooked grain/rice', by metonymy 饭 came to stand for any regular meal, and by further metaphorical extension in vernacular Mandarin, 'to make a living, earn one's bread'.

history.form: 食飯 (shífàn) → 喫飯 / 吃飯 (chīfàn)
history.meaning: to eat cooked grain or rice; to have a meal
to eat a meal, dine; (figuratively) to make a living, support oneself professionally

吃饭.notes: A separable verb (离合词)—aspect particles and modifiers go between the two characters (吃过饭, 吃了一顿饭). Also widely used in career contexts for 'making a living' (靠手艺吃饭, 'make a living by one's craft'; 靠脸吃饭, 'make a living off one's looks').

rootFamily.gloss: social dinner party or banquet (often for networking)
to suffer losses, bear a disadvantage

吃香.etymology: Originally a verb-object compound composed of 吃 (chī, 'to eat, absorb, partake of') and 香 (xiāng, 'fragrance, incense, savory food'). Derived either from Buddhist/popular temple imagery of spirits or deities 'partaking of burnt incense offerings' (享香火) or from 'eating fragrant, savory delicacies', it lexicalized in early modern vernacular Mandarin into an adjective meaning 'enjoying high favor, in high demand, very popular'.

history.meaning: to partake of incense offerings or savory food; hence to be favored and well-treated
in high demand, very popular, well-favored (of a profession, skill, or person)

morphemes.meaning: to eat, to partake of, to enjoy
fragrance, incense, savory food; favored status

吃香.notes: Although historically a verb-object compound, in modern Mandarin 吃香 functions as a gradable adjective modified by 很 or 最: 这种题材现在很吃香 ('This kind of genre is in high demand right now') or 幕后制作人才越来越吃香 ('Behind-the-scenes production talent is increasingly sought-after').

rootFamily.gloss: hot commodity, someone or something in high demand ('steamed bun')
capable of succeeding or thriving anywhere ('able to eat open a path')

cognates.meaning: each, every, plural marker for polite groups

各.etymology: An oracle-bone and bronze-inscription compound ideograph (各, Old Chinese *klaːɡ) depicting a downward-pointing foot (夊/夂, 'stepping, arriving') approaching a mouth or pit/dwelling entrance (口). Its original verbal meaning in archaic Chinese was 'to arrive, come' (later written 格), before being loaned in Pre-Qin Classical Chinese for the distributive pronoun/determiner 'each, every,各自的/differently' (originally glossed in *Shuowen Jiezi* as 異辭也, 'differing words/going one's own way').

history.meaning: to arrive, come to a place (ancestral graph of 格)
history.stage: Shang–Early Zhou Oracle Bone & Bronze Inscriptions

history.meaning: each, individually, respectively (distributive pronoun and adverb)
each, every, various (distributive determiner before classifiers or monosyllabic nouns)

各.notes: In modern Mandarin, 各 can directly precede monosyllabic nouns or classifiers without needing 个 (e.g., 各部门 'each department', 各位 'everyone [polite]', 各方 'all parties'), and frequently forms parallel four-character idioms like 各抒己见 ('each airs their own view') or 各司其职 ('each attends to their own duties').

rootFamily.gloss: everybody, ladies and gentlemen (polite form of address)

各个.etymology: A modifier-head distributive compound combining 各 (gè, Middle Chinese *kak, 'each, every', originally depicting a foot 夂 arriving at a cave or enclosure 口 to go one's own way) and 个 (traditional 個/箇, gè, originally a tally of bamboo stalks and later the general classifier for discrete entities). By pairing the distributive determiner with the universal classifier, Early Mandarin created an explicit pluralizable pronoun and determiner meaning 'each and every individual item or category'.

history.meaning: to arrive independently; each, apiece
each individual one; every single unit
each, every (typically modifying plural or collective nouns)

各个.notes: Unlike 每个 (měi gè), which focuses on a single representative unit and can take a classifier or singular noun, 各个 directly precedes a disyllabic category noun without an extra classifier (e.g., 各个部门 'every department', 各个环节 'every stage of production').

rootFamily.gloss: each person, everyone; each for oneself
all kinds of, every sort of

cognates.meaning: ladies and gentlemen, all of you

各位.etymology: A modifier-head honorific pronominal compound formed from 各 (gè, 'each, every') and 位 (wèi, Middle Chinese *hjwih, originally 'court standing position or rank' from 人 'person' next to 立 'stand'). In Literary Chinese, 位 denoted an official's seat or station at court; using a person's seat to refer to the person themselves followed classical metonymic deference (comparable to 陛下 'beneath the steps'). Combining 各 with 位 yielded an respectful collective address meaning 'each honoured person in their station'.

history.meaning: assigned standing place at court; official rank or seat
each person of rank; polite plural address for an assembly
everyone, ladies and gentlemen (polite vocative and pronoun)

morphemes.meaning: seat, rank; polite classifier for persons

各位.notes: The go-to polite opening in Chinese broadcasts, press conferences, and production meetings (e.g., 各位老师 'respected teachers/mentors', 各位观众 'dear viewers'); it can stand alone or directly precede a title without 们.

rootFamily.gloss: take your positions, on your marks
to be in position, up to standard, thorough

cognates.meaning: each family; each school of thought or household

各家.etymology: A modifier-head compound joining 各 (gè, 'each, every') and 家 (jiā, Middle Chinese *kæ, from 宀 'roof' over 豕 'pig', originally 'dwelling, household, aristocratic clan'). Already in Han-era historiography, 家 extended from a domestic household to a philosophical school (诸子百家 'the Hundred Schools of Thought') and later to commercial guilds, publishing houses, and media outlets. 各家 thus evolved from 'each household or school' to modern entertainment and journalism usage meaning 'every competing network, agency, or media outlet'.

history.meaning: each aristocratic clan; each philosophical school or scholarly lineage
every household, family, or guild establishment
every household; every competing firm, agency, or media outlet

morphemes.meaning: household, family; school of thought; commercial enterprise or outlet

各家.notes: In entertainment and media contexts (*Behind the Scenes*), 各家 frequently refers to rival satellite TV networks (各家卫视), talent agencies, or even rival celebrity fan clubs (各家粉丝).

rootFamily.gloss: the Hundred Schools of Thought; numerous schools/experts

cognates.meaning: take your positions; on your marks
cognates.word: 各就各位 (gok3 zau6 gok3 wai6-2)

各就各位.etymology: A four-character subject-predicate-object directive formula structured as 各 (gè, 'each person') + 就 (jiù, Middle Chinese *dzjuwH, 'to approach, move toward, take up') + 各位 (gèwèi, 'one's respective position/seat'). Rooted in Classical Chinese court and military ritual where officials 'approached their assigned stations' (就位), the reduplicated distributive pattern A-就-A-位 crystallized in modern athletics ('on your marks!') and studio stage management ('places, everyone!').

history.meaning: to approach and occupy one's ritual or official station at court

history.form: 各就各位 (gè jiù gè wèi)
history.meaning: each person takes their respective station; 'on your marks' (track and field) or 'places, everyone' (film/TV production)

各就各位.notes: On a television soundstage or live broadcast floor, floor directors call out 各就各位 just before rolling cameras or going live; in sports, it is the official starter's command for 'On your marks!' (followed by 预备 'Set!').

rootFamily.gloss: to take one's seat or assigned post
to be in position, properly executed

各方.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 各 (gè, 'each, every') and 方 (fāng, Middle Chinese *pjang, originally 'two boats lashed side by side' or 'plow blade', early on meaning 'square, compass direction, region, quarter'). In Classical Chinese, 各方 referred spatially to 'every direction or region of the realm'; in modern legal, diplomatic, and commercial Chinese, 方 denotes a contracting or interested 'party/side', making 各方 'all parties or stakeholders'.

history.meaning: every geographical direction, all regions of the empire
all sides, all stakeholders, every party involved in a negotiation or project

morphemes.meaning: direction, side, quarter; party or stakeholder

各方.notes: Extremely common in corporate and media negotiations (e.g., 协调各方利益 'coordinate the interests of all stakeholders', 各方代表 'representatives from all sides'). Compare 合作方 ('collaborating party') and 甲方/乙方 ('Party A / Party B').

cognates.meaning: each has its own merits and lasting value
cognates.word: 各有千秋 (gok3 jau5 cin1 cau1)

各有千秋.etymology: A four-character literary idiom (chengyu) structured as a subject-verb-object clause: 各 (gè, 'each') + 有 (yǒu, 'possesses') + 千秋 (qiānqiū, literally 'a thousand autumns', metonymic for 'a thousand years, enduring legacy through the ages'). Popularized by the Qing poet Zhao Yi (赵翼, 1727–1814) in his *Poems on Poetry* (*论诗*): '满眼生机转化钧，天工人巧日争新；预支五百年新意，到了千年又觉陈。李杜诗篇万口传，至今已觉不新鲜；江山代有才人出，各领风骚数百年' alongside the critical appraisal that rival masters 'each possess a thousand autumns of enduring fame' (各有千秋). From 'each having its own immortal historical stature', the idiom generalized to 'each has its own distinct merits and strengths'.

history.meaning: a thousand autumns; longevity, a millennium of posterity
each literary figure or work possesses its own enduring historical value across the ages
each has its own merits, strengths, and distinctive appeal

各有千秋.notes: A diplomatic, high-register compliment used by judges, producers, and critics when comparing two strong performers or proposals without declaring one inferior to the other.

rootFamily.gloss: each has its own strong points
Autumn and Spring; annals, age, prime of life

各种各样.etymology: A symmetric four-character coordinative compound built on the A-B-A-C distributive template, pairing 各种 (gèzhǒng, 'every seed/species/kind', from 种 zhǒng 'grain seed, category') with 各样 (gèyàng, 'every pattern/style/shape', from 样 yàng, originally a wooden model or acorn-oak pattern). By juxtaposing taxonomic 'species/type' (种) with visible 'form/appearance' (样), the quadrisyllabic expression intensifies the sense of diversity to mean 'all kinds and varieties of'.

history.meaning: seed/species (種) and wooden pattern/shape (樣)

history.form: 各種各樣 / 各种各样 (gèzhǒng gèyàng)
history.meaning: all kinds and sorts of, every conceivable variety of

各种各样.notes: Typically followed by 的 before a noun (e.g., 各种各样的问题 'all kinds of problems'); in fast speech or informal media talk, 各种 alone is sometimes used adverbially as slang ('all kinds of...'), whereas 各种各样 remains standard across all registers.

rootFamily.gloss: all kinds of, various types of
in the same way; identical, the same

合.etymology: Ancient ideogram attested on Shang oracle bones showing an inverted lid (亼) fitting snugly over the mouth of a vessel (口): 'close, shut, join together, combine, fit, suit, add up to'.

history.meaning: lid fitting a vessel mouth = close, join, match
close; combine; fit; suit; total

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 合 (via 萌典)

合不拢嘴.etymology: Four-character colloquial idiom from 合 ('close; shut') + 不拢 ('unable to bring together', simplified from 不攏) + 嘴 ('mouth; lips'). Literally 'unable to close one's mouth', it is commonly paired with 笑得 ('laugh/smile until...') to depict someone grinning from ear to ear with delight.

morphemes.meaning: unable to close or bring together

history.meaning: unable to shut one's mouth from laughing
grin from ear to ear; beam with joy

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 合不拢嘴

cognates.meaning: combination into a single body; mecha docking/combination; union

合体.etymology: Originally a Classical Chinese verb-object compound combining 合 (hé, Middle Chinese *hop, 'to join together, close, unite', depicting a lid fitting a vessel) and 体 (traditional 體, tǐ, Middle Chinese *thjejX, 'body, physical form, structural substance'). In classical texts and Chinese philology, 合体 denoted either two people becoming one flesh in marriage/alliance or a compound ideographic/phono-semantic character (合体字, as opposed to single-component 独体字). In late 20th-century Japanese pop culture (合体 *gattai*, used of giant robots docking into one), the term gained lively media currency, which reinforced its modern Chinese entertainment sense: former bandmates, co-stars, or a famous duo 'reuniting onstage or appearing together in public'.

history.meaning: to join into a single body or substance; compound Chinese character (vs. 獨體)
structural fusion or docking of separate units into one body (popularized in Japanese mecha/pop culture)
to combine into one; (showbiz) to reunite onstage or make a joint appearance as a full group/duo

合体.notes: In contemporary Chinese entertainment news and *Behind the Scenes*, 合体 is the signature buzzword for a long-awaited reunion performance or joint appearance by band members, celebrity couples, or iconic co-stars. Can take an object inside the split construction 合个体 or modify nouns (e.g., 合体演出 'reunion performance').

合作.etymology: A modifier-head verbal and nominal compound formed from 合 (hé, 'together, jointly, in union') and 作 (zuò, Middle Chinese *tsak, 'to make, do, create, work'). Attested in Literary Chinese for 'working or composing jointly' (such as multiple painters or poets creating a single work), it was reinforced in the late 19th and early 20th centuries—partly alongside Japanese 合作 (*gassaku*, 'joint artistic creation') and modern translations of Western economic 'cooperation' (e.g., 合作社 'cooperative society')—to become the universal Mandarin term for 'cooperation, collaboration, to work together'.

history.meaning: to compose, build, or labor jointly on a work
to cooperate, collaborate; cooperation, joint venture or artistic collaboration

合作.notes: Note that you cannot say *合作某人 ('collaborate someone'); always use the comitative preposition 跟/与/和 (e.g., 跟他们合作 'collaborate with them') or the celebratory four-character toast 合作愉快 ('Here's to a pleasant collaboration!').

cognates.word: 合作夥伴 (hap6 zok3 fo2 bun6)

合作伙伴.etymology: A four-character modifier-head nominal compound combining 合作 (hézuò, 'cooperation, collaboration') with 伙伴 (traditional 夥伴, huǒbàn, 'companion, comrade, partner'). 伙伴 itself has a vivid military and commercial history: 火 (later written 伙/夥) referred in the Northern and Southern Dynasties and Tang military system (府兵制) to a ten-man mess squad sharing a single cooking fire (同火), while 伴 (bàn, from 人 + 半 'half') meant 'one half of a pair, companion'. A 'messmate' (火伴) became a merchant shipping partner and, paired with 合作, now translates modern corporate 'business/strategic partner'.

history.meaning: messmate sharing the same cooking fire in a military squad (attested in the *Ballad of Mulan*: 火伴皆驚忙)
guild associate, commercial partner, or close companion
business partner, strategic partner, collaborating associate

morphemes.meaning: messmate, group, associate (originally sharing a cooking fire)
companion, mate, half of a pair

合作伙伴.notes: In media and corporate Chinese, 合作伙伴 refers to both individual collaborators and institutional sponsors/allies (e.g., 战略合作伙伴 'strategic partner', 独家合作伙伴 'exclusive partner').

合作方.etymology: A modifier-head institutional compound built from 合作 (hézuò, 'cooperation, collaboration') and the bound head noun 方 (fāng, 'side, quarter, contracting party'). Modeled on modern legal and administrative terminology where -方 productively marks institutional stakeholders (such as 甲方 'Party A', 主办方 'organizer', 投资方 'investor'), 合作方 designates an external firm, network, or agency engaged in a joint project.

history.meaning: direction, side, quarter
collaborating party, partner organization or stakeholder in a contract/project

合作方.notes: Whereas 合作伙伴 sounds warm and relationship-focused ('partner'), 合作方 is a neutral, contractual term referring to 'the partner side/company' in production deals (compare 品牌方 'the brand side', 节目方 'the show's producers').

合口.etymology: A verb-object compound (functioning adjectivally) composed of 合 (hé, 'to fit, match, suit, close together') and 口 (kǒu, Middle Chinese *khuwX, 'mouth, palate, opening'). In Classical and Literary Chinese, 合口 had several literal senses: closing the mouth, the healing together of a wound's edges, and in traditional Chinese phonology (等韵学), 'rounded-lip syllables' (合口呼, opposed to unrounded 开口呼). In vernacular Mandarin, the sense 'matching the mouth/palate' lexicalized as 'suiting one's culinary taste, palatable'.

history.meaning: to close the mouth; for a wound or gap to close together; unanimity of voices
labialized or rounded-lip rime category in traditional Chinese phonology
suiting one's taste, palatable (of food and drink)

morphemes.meaning: to fit, suit, match, close together

合口.notes: Often expanded in speech to 合口味 (hé kǒuwèi) or 合胃口 (hé wèikǒu, 'suit one's appetite/taste'); because it is an underlying VO compound, modifiers can be inserted between the characters (e.g., 合不合你的口 'does it suit your taste?').

合同.etymology: Compound of 合 ('join, match together') + 同 ('same, tallying'). In Tang–Song-Yuan commerce and administration, a 合同 was a two-part tally document stamped across the seam so the two halves could be matched together to verify authenticity; today it is the standard word for a legal 'contract, agreement'.

history.meaning: split-tally agreement matched along a seam
contract; agreement

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 合同 (via 萌典)

合奏.etymology: Musical compound of 合 ('join together; harmonize', depicting a lid meeting a vessel mouth) + 奏 ('present music; perform on instruments', originally hands offering a ceremonial branch upward). Attested in court and ritual music treatises since antiquity for multiple instruments playing in ensemble.

history.meaning: perform music together in ensemble
play music together; instrumental ensemble

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 合奏

合并.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound pairing two synonymous roots: 合 (hé, 'to join together, unite') and 并 (traditional 併/并, bìng, Middle Chinese *pjengH, originally depicting two people standing side by side 竝 or bound together, meaning 'to combine, annex, absorb into one'). Attested in Classical Chinese historiography for unifying territories or administrative units, it is now the standard corporate, legal, and technical term for merging companies, departments, or files.

history.meaning: to annex, unite territories, or combine administrative bodies into one
to merge, consolidate, amalgamate (companies, departments, data, or medical conditions)

morphemes.meaning: to combine, merge, annex side by side

合并.notes: In business and media drama contexts (*Behind the Scenes*), 合并 refers to corporate mergers (公司合并) or consolidating two production departments (部门合并); in M&A finance, it pairs with 收购 ('acquisition') to form 并购 (bìnggòu, 'mergers and acquisitions').

rootFamily.gloss: to annex, swallow up a rival firm or territory
to combine into one body, reunite onstage

cognates.meaning: to take a group photo; group photograph

合影.etymology: A compound combining 合 (hé, 'together, jointly') and 影 (yǐng, Middle Chinese *'jængX, 'shadow, reflection, image'). In Classical Chinese, 影 meant a cast shadow or a painted portrait (影像). When photography entered China in the 19th century, 影 was adopted for 'photographic image' (摄影 'to capture shadows/photograph'), and 合影 was coined on the model of literary compounds for 'jointly capturing images in one frame'—meaning both 'to pose for a photograph together' and 'a group photo'.

history.meaning: shadow, reflection; painted portrait likeness
to pose together for a photograph; a group or two-person photo

合影.notes: Frequently used in the 4-character set phrase 合影留念 ('take a group photo as a keepsake') at wrap parties, press events, and fan meet-and-greets. Spoken Mandarin also uses 合照 (hézhào) interchangeably.

rootFamily.gloss: group photo; to take a photo together

合成.etymology: A resultative verbal compound formed from 合 (hé, 'to combine, join together') and 成 (chéng, Middle Chinese *dzyeng, 'to become, complete, form into'). Attested in Classical and Literary Chinese in the literal transparent sense 'to combine so as to form (a whole)', the compound was repurposed in Meiji-era Japan (合成 *gōsei*) to translate Western scientific 'synthesis' (as in chemistry, 化学合成, and logic/grammar) and re-entered modern Mandarin, where it also covers audio synthesis (合成器 'synthesizer') and post-production digital compositing (特效合成).

history.meaning: to join components together to form a completed whole
chemical or scientific synthesis (calque of Greek/European 'synthesis')
to synthesize; (film/TV post-production) to digitally composite audio, video, or visual effects

合成.notes: In television and music production (*Behind the Scenes*), 合成 refers to audio mixing/stem bounce, electronic sound synthesis, or VFX video compositing (后期合成 'post-production compositing'), as well as fake/photoshopped images (合成照片).

cognates.meaning: passing an exam; meeting inspection standards, qualified
passing an exam; meeting standards, qualified
to meet standards, be qualified or eligible

合格.etymology: A verb-object compound (functioning as an adjective or intransitive verb) combining 合 (hé, 'to conform to, match, meet') and 格 (gé, Middle Chinese *kæk, originally 'tall tree branches' and by extension 'wooden lattice, rule, standard, grade, format'). In Imperial Chinese civil administration and poetry criticism, 合於格 or 合格 meant 'conforming to the prescribed legal code, bureaucratic regulation, or metrical standard'. Reinforced by modern Japanese 合格 (*gōkaku*, 'passing an examination or quality inspection'), in Mandarin it primarily means 'up to standard, qualified, meeting quality specs'.

history.meaning: conforming to official regulations, bureaucratic standards, or poetic meter
up to standard, qualified, passing quality inspection or professional requirements

合格.notes: Beware a major false friend with Japanese: in Japanese, 合格 (*gōkaku*) means 'passing a test/exam', whereas in Mandarin 'passing a test' is 及格 (jígé) or 考上, while 合格 means 'qualified / up to professional or quality standards' (e.g., 一个合格的制作人 'a qualified producer').

rootFamily.gloss: to pass an exam (reach the passing grade)

合理.etymology: A verb-object compound functioning adjectivally, formed from 合 (hé, 'to accord with, conform to') and 理 (lǐ, Middle Chinese *liX, originally 'to carve jade along its natural veins', from 玉 'jade' + 里 phonetic, and in classical philosophy 'inherent pattern, cosmic principle, reason'). In Classical and Neo-Confucian prose, 合乎理 or 合理 meant 'in accordance with moral or natural principle'. In modern East Asian usage, it also absorbed the sense of Western 'rational' and 'reasonable'.

history.meaning: veins in jade; natural order, underlying principle, reason
conforming to natural or moral principle; just and proper
reasonable, rational, equitable (of prices, schedules, demands, or logic)

合理.notes: Frequently paired with 合法 ('legal') in the four-character phrase 合情合理 ('fair and reasonable, satisfying both human sentiment 情 and reason 理').

rootFamily.gloss: rational, reasoned (as opposed to emotional 感性)

合约.etymology: A modifier-head or coordinative compound combining 合 (hé, 'jointly, mutually uniting') and 约 (traditional 約, yuē, Middle Chinese *'jak, originally 'to bind with silk cords', from 糸 'silk' + 勺 phonetic, extended to 'covenant, pact, treaty, agreement'). In Classical Chinese (e.g., during the Warring States period), 合约 meant 'to form a joint alliance or pact' (compare 合纵 'Vertical Alliance'). In modern Chinese—especially in Hong Kong, Taiwan, and the Mainland entertainment/sports industries—合约 is the standard term for an artist management or broadcast 'contract'.

history.meaning: to bind together in a covenant or alliance; a mutual pact
contract, binding legal agreement (especially talent agency, entertainment, or commercial contracts)

morphemes.meaning: to bind with cord; pact, covenant, contract

合约.notes: While 合同 (hétong) is the everyday Mainland legal word for general employment or lease contracts, 合约 (héyuē) is strongly favored in the entertainment industry for celebrity agency contracts (经纪合约), licensing deals, and contract renewals/terminations (续约 / 解约).

rootFamily.gloss: to terminate a contract; breach or dissolve an agreement

合适.etymology: Coordinative adjective compound of 合 ('fit, match, conform to') + 适 (適, 'suit, fit, comfortable'): 'suitable, fitting, appropriate, right'.

history.meaning: fitting and suitable; appropriate

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 合适 (via 萌典)

合页.etymology: Visual joinery metaphor combining 合 ('close together, bring two halves flush') + 页 ('flat leaf'), picturing the two flat metal leaves of a butt hinge folding together like the pages of a book around their central pin.

history.meaning: two-leaf metal door or shutter hinge
hinge

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 合页

吉总.etymology: A surname-plus-title vocative compound combining the Chinese surname 吉 (Jí, Middle Chinese *kjit, originally 'auspicious, fortunate', depicting a ritual weapon or jade tablet 士 placed in a vessel 口) with the clipped executive title 总 (traditional 總, zǒng, Middle Chinese *tsuwngX, originally 'to tie silk threads into a bundle', hence 'overall, chief'). In post-1980s Mainland corporate usage, 总 was clipped from executive titles such as 总经理 (zǒngjīnglǐ, 'general manager'), 总裁 (zǒngcái, 'president/CEO'), and 总监 (zǒngjiān, 'chief director') to form a productive post-nominal honorific attached directly after a surname.

history.meaning: auspicious / surname Jí (吉); to bind together, chief/general (總)

history.form: 总经理 / 总裁 / 总监
history.meaning: general manager, company president, chief director
President Ji / Director Ji / Boss Ji (addressing the character Ji Xiu or an executive surnamed Ji)

morphemes.meaning: chief executive, general manager, president, or director (clipped from 总经理/总裁/总监)

吉总.notes: In modern Chinese workplaces and media dramas like *Behind the Scenes*, [Surname] + 总 (e.g., 吉总, 淳于总, 郁总) is the universal polite address for any senior executive, producer, or client boss—often used generously as a flattering business honorific even for mid-level directors.

cognates.meaning: Jisoo (cognate Sino-Korean given name written with 吉秀 or 智秀)

吉秀.etymology: A two-character Chinese personal name (referring to a character in *Behind the Scenes* / *幕后之王*, also addressed professionally as 吉总) composed of the surname 吉 (Jí, Middle Chinese *kjit, 'auspicious, fortunate, propitious', an ancient surname traced in traditional genealogies to descendants of the Western Zhou court official Yin Jifu 尹吉甫) and the given name 秀 (xiù, Middle Chinese *sjuwH, originally depicting grain coming into ear and flowering 禾 + 乃, hence 'flowering, flourishing, elegant, outstanding'). Together the name evokes 'auspicious elegance and outstanding talent'.

history.meaning: auspicious, propitious (吉); grain flowering into ear, flourishing, outstanding (秀)
Ji Xiu (Chinese personal name combining surname 吉 and given name 秀)

吉秀.notes: Besides its classical sense of 'elegant/outstanding' in given names like 吉秀, the character 秀 (xiù) was phonetically borrowed in modern Mandarin from English *show* to mean a live or broadcast 'show' (e.g., 真人秀 'reality show', 脱口秀 'talk show', 走秀 'catwalk show').

rootFamily.gloss: President Ji, Director Ji (executive address for Ji Xiu)
talented, elegant and refined; talent show/draft in Imperial or modern media

同.etymology: Ancient ideogram showing a cover/frame (冂) fitting over a mouth/opening (口) with a unifying stroke (一): 'join together, share in common, the same, alike' and as a preposition 'with, together with'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: same; alike; together; with

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 同 (via 萌典)

同一.etymology: Compound determiner and adjective of 同 ('same') + 一 ('one'): 'the very same, one and the same, identical'.

history.meaning: one and the same; identical

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 同一 (via 萌典)

同事.etymology: Compound of 同 ('together, shared') + 事 ('serve, work on an affair/post'). In Classical Chinese (e.g., Shangshu, Hanfeizi), 同事 meant 'work together on the same official duty'; in modern Mandarin it is the standard noun for 'colleague, coworker'.

history.meaning: share the same official task
colleague; coworker

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 同事 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: equal benevolence; colleagues in the same profession

同仁.etymology: Originally a Classical Chinese philosophical phrase from Han Yu's (韩愈, 768–824) *Origin of the Way* (*原道*): 博爱之谓仁……圣人一视而同仁 ('Universal love is called benevolence... the sage looks upon all equally with the same benevolence', whence the idiom 一视同仁). Here 同 (tóng, 'same, shared') modified 仁 (rén, 'humaneness, benevolence'). In Late Imperial and Republican Chinese, because 仁 (rén) and 人 (rén, 'person') are homophonous, 同仁 became an elevated written graphic variant of 同人 (derived from the *I Ching* hexagram 同人 'Fellowship with Men'), shifting in meaning to 'fellow members of the same profession or institution, esteemed colleagues'.

history.meaning: to regard all people equally with the same Confucian benevolence (Han Yu, Tang dynasty)
fellows of the same aspiration or guild; colleagues sharing a calling
colleagues, fellow professionals across an organization or industry (formal/honorific collective noun)

morphemes.meaning: benevolence, humanity; (by homophonous association with 人) fellow person/colleague

同仁.notes: A formal, respectful collective noun used in speeches, open letters, and industry gatherings (e.g., 各位同仁 'dear colleagues', 业界同仁 'fellow professionals in the industry'); for an individual everyday coworker, use 同事 (tóngshì) instead.

rootFamily.gloss: to treat everyone equally without discrimination
peer in the same trade or industry
