cognates.meaning: to appear on the same stage; competing broadcast networks

同台.etymology: A modifier-head verbal and adverbial compound formed from 同 (tóng, Middle Chinese *duwng, 'same, together') and 台 (traditional 臺, tái, Middle Chinese *doj, originally 'raised earthen viewing platform or terrace', later 'theatrical stage' 舞台 and 'broadcasting station' 电视台). Originating in traditional Chinese opera where rival troupes or celebrated actors 'performed on the same raised stage' (同台演出), it remains a staple of contemporary television and concert production for 'sharing the stage' or 'competing head-to-head on the same platform'.

history.meaning: raised earthen terrace or viewing tower
to perform together on the same opera stage; (earlier also) colleagues in the same imperial bureau (省臺)
to share the same stage, appear onstage together (or belong to the same TV station)

同台.notes: Often precedes verbs of performance or competition in four-character collocations such as 同台演出 ('perform onstage together'), 同台飙戏 ('trade acting chops in the same scene'), and 同台竞技 ('compete on the same stage'). In TV workplace contexts, it can also mean 'working at the same TV network'.

rootFamily.gloss: to go onstage, appear in a show
backstage, behind the scenes;后台 support

cognates.meaning: in the same venue, session, or scene

同场.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 同 (tóng, 'same, shared') and 场 (traditional 場, chǎng, Middle Chinese *drjang, from 土 'earth' + 易 phonetic, originally 'cleared flat ground for ritual sacrifices or threshing grain', later 'arena, examination hall, theatrical scene, or scheduled screening/session'). In traditional drama and imperial examinations, 同场 meant 'in the same examination session or theatrical venue'; in modern film, concert, and broadcast usage, it means 'in the same venue, session, match, or scene'.

history.meaning: flat cleared earthen altar or threshing floor
taking the imperial examination in the same session; performing in the same arena
on the same stage/arena, in the same session, match, or scene (often used adverbially)

morphemes.meaning: venue, arena, stage; session, screening, or scene

同场.notes: Closely parallels 同台, as in 同场竞技 ('compete in the same arena/session') or 同场加映 ('bonus screening in the same session'); while 台 emphasizes the physical 'stage', 场 emphasizes the 'venue, match, live recording session, or scene'.

rootFamily.gloss: live site, filming set, on the scene
to make an entrance, come onstage/onscreen

cognates.meaning: studying the same field or under the same teacher; fellow student

同学.etymology: A modifier-head compound formed from 同 (tóng, 'together, same') and 学 (traditional 學, xué, Middle Chinese *hæwk, 'to study, learn; school'). First attested in Classical Chinese historical prose (such as the *Zuo Zhuan* and *Records of the Grand Historian*) as a verb phrase meaning 'to study together under the same master' and by nominalization 'a fellow disciple or schoolmate'. In 20th-century Mandarin, in addition to 'classmate/schoolmate', 同学 became the universal polite vocative for addressing any student on campus.

history.meaning: to study together under the same teacher; a fellow disciple or scholar
classmate, schoolmate, alumnus of the same school; polite form of address for a student

同学.notes: In modern China, teachers and campus staff address students directly as 同学 (e.g., 这位同学 'this student here', 同学们好 'hello, class/students'); in playful urban workplace slang, young professionals also call peers '[Name] 同学' for friendly rapport.

rootFamily.gloss: fellow apprentice or disciple under the same master/mentor

cognates.meaning: of the same age; the same year

同岁.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 同 (tóng, 'same') and 岁 (traditional 歲, suì, Middle Chinese *sjwejH, originally the planet Jupiter 岁星 whose twelve-year orbital cycle marked the calendar, written with 步 'step' and 戌 'halberd', and by the Warring States period 'year of age, harvest year'). Attested in medieval Chinese poetry and vernacular narrative for 'born in the same year, of the very same age'.

history.meaning: the planet Jupiter; annual cycle, year, year of a person's age
in the same calendar year; born in the same year, of the same age
of the same age (in years)

同岁.notes: Used predicatively with 跟/和 (e.g., 我跟他同岁 'I am the same age as him'); for a noun meaning 'peer of the same age or generation', use 同龄人 (tónglíngrén).

rootFamily.gloss: of the same age bracket; peer (同龄人)

同意.etymology: Verb-object/modifier-head compound of 同 ('share the same') + 意 ('thought, mind, opinion'): 'be of the same mind -> agree, consent, approve'. Attested since the Mozi and的后汉书 Book of the Later Han.

history.stage: Classical Chinese (Mozi, Hou Hanshu) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: be of one mind; agree; consent

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 同意 (via 萌典)

同时.etymology: Temporal noun, adverb, and conjunction combining 同 ('same') + 时 (時, 'time'): 'at the same time, simultaneously; moreover'. Attested since Classical prose.

history.meaning: at the same time; simultaneously; moreover

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 同时 (via 萌典)

同样.etymology: A modifier-head compound formed from 同 (tóng, 'same, identical') and 样 (traditional 樣, yàng, Middle Chinese *yangH, 'wooden pattern, model, shape, manner, appearance'). Emerging in Tang–Song vernacular Chinese when 样 became the primary noun and classifier for 'shape, style, or manner', 同样 lexicalized as 'of the same pattern/appearance' and developed into both an attributive adjective ('the same, identical') and a sentence-linking adverb ('likewise, equally').

history.meaning: of the same model, pattern, or appearance
the same, identical; likewise, equally, by the same token

同样.notes: Unlike 一样 (yíyàng), which is most often predicative (跟……一样 'the same as...'), 同样 excels at the start of a clause or before a verb/adjective to mean 'likewise / equally' (e.g., 同样重要 'equally important', 同样，我们也需要…… 'Likewise, we also need...').

rootFamily.gloss: all kinds of, every sort of

同步.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 同 (tóng, 'same, together') and 步 (bù, Middle Chinese *buH, oracle bone script depicting two feet 止 stepping one after another, meaning 'pace, stride, step'). In Classical Chinese, 同步 meant literally 'walking in step together' or 'measures of the same pace'. In the 20th century, it was adopted as the technical calque for Greek-derived *synchronous* / *synchronization* (in physics, telecommunications, film audio-video sync, and data syncing), whence its ubiquitous modern adverbial sense 'in sync, simultaneously'.

history.meaning: to walk in step together; of the same pace or stride measurement
synchronous (physics/engineering/film audio-video sync); in sync, simultaneously, in tandem

morphemes.meaning: step, pace, stride; stage of a process

同步.notes: Essential in broadcasting and digital media: 声画同步 ('audio-video in sync'), 同步直播 ('simulcast / simultaneous live broadcast'), and 同步更新 ('simultaneous update'); in office slang, 跟某人同步信息 is also used as a verb phrase meaning 'to sync up / bring someone up to speed on info'.

同质化.etymology: A three-morpheme modern academic and media compound formed from 同质 (tóngzhì, 'of the same quality, nature, or substance', from 同 'same' + 质 traditional 質 'substance, nature, quality', calquing Western *homogeneous*) plus the productive deadjectival/denominal suffix -化 (-huà, 'transformation into, -ization', popularized via Meiji Japanese translations of European *-fication / -ization*). Originally a term in sociology, economics, and chemistry for 'homogenization', 同质化 became a critical buzzword in contemporary Chinese television and tech commentary for 'unoriginal copycat sameness' across competing shows or products.

history.meaning: of the same intrinsic nature, substance, or quality; homogeneous
homogenization; (media/business criticism) lack of differentiation, copycat sameness across products or TV formats

同质化.notes: A quintessential industry critique in *Behind the Scenes*: when every network clones the same singing contest or reality show format, producers complain that 节目同质化太严重 ('program homogenization / copycat sameness is way too severe'), contrasting it with 差异化 (chāyìhuà, 'differentiation').

rootFamily.gloss: quality, intrinsic character; (physics/commerce) mass or quality
differentiation (the strategic opposite of 同质化)

cognates.meaning: name, reputation; counter for persons or rank

名.etymology: Inherited from Old Chinese *C.meŋ (Middle Chinese *mjieng), descending from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *r-miŋ ('name', cognate with Tibetan མིང *ming* and Burmese မည် *many*). The character 名 is a compound ideogram (会意) combining 夕 (xī, 'dusk, darkness') and 口 (kǒu, 'mouth'): as explained in Xu Shen's *Shuowen Jiezi* (100 CE), 'at dusk one cannot see another person in the dark, so one calls out with the mouth to identify oneself' (自命也，从口从夕；夕者，冥也，冥不相见，故以口自名). From 'personal name', it extended to 'title, fame, reputation', a classifier for ranked persons, and 'place/rank in a competition or chart' (第一名 'first place').

history.meaning: to call out one's name in the dark; personal name, appellation, philosophical term vs. reality (名實)
name, fame, renown; classifier for individuals on an official roster or exam ranking list
name; fame; classifier for people with a role/status; place or rank in a competition/chart (e.g. 第一名)

morphemes.meaning: name, reputation; classifier for persons; rank or place in a contest

名.notes: After ordinal numbers (第 + number + 名), 名 means 'place/rank' in ratings, charts, or contests (e.g., 收视率第一名 'number one in viewership ratings', 前三名 'the top three places'); after cardinal numbers before a noun, it acts as a formal classifier for people (e.g., 三名选手 'three contestants').

rootFamily.gloss: ranking, place in a competition or chart

名下.etymology: Locative/legal phrase combining 名 ('name') + 下 ('under'): 'under someone's name (of registered property, accounts, or ownership)'.

history.stage: Tang–Song legal & vernacular Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: under a person's registered name

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 名下 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: living up to one's reputation (literary Sino-Japanese)
well-deserved reputation, living up to one's fame

名不虚传.etymology: A four-character classical idiom (chengyu) structured as a topic-comment clause: 名 (míng, 'fame, reputation') + 不 (bù, 'not') + 虚 (xū, Middle Chinese *khjo, 'empty, hollow, unfounded, false') + 传 (traditional 傳, chuán, Middle Chinese *drjwen, 'to pass down, circulate, spread'). Attested in Sima Qian's *Records of the Grand Historian* (*Shiji*, c. 94 BCE, in the variant 然名不虚立 'yet a reputation is not established on emptiness') and in its exact modern wording in Song-dynasty texts such as Kou Zhun's biography and the *Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp* (*景德传灯录*), it literally means 'a reputation is not spread in vain / without basis'—hence 'to truly live up to one's reputation'.

history.form: 名不虛立 / 名下無虛士
history.meaning: a great reputation is never established without real substance; beneath a famous name there is no hollow scholar
one's fame is not circulated falsely; well-deserved renown (attested in Song-era chronicles and Chan records)

history.form: 名不虚传 (míng bù xū chuán)
history.meaning: to truly live up to one's reputation, have well-deserved fame

morphemes.meaning: emptily, falsely, without substance or basis

名不虚传.notes: Very often preceded by 果然 ('indeed, just as expected') or 真是 when experiencing someone's legendary skill firsthand (e.g., 魔鬼制作人果然名不虚传 'The "Demon Producer" truly lives up to his reputation!'). Its direct antonym is 徒有虚名 ('possessing only an empty name').

rootFamily.gloss: worthy of the name, living up to its title in reality
having an empty reputation without real merit (antonym)
word of mouth, legendary rumor or传闻

cognates.meaning: nominal title; in the name of

名义.etymology: A coordinative and modifier-head compound from Classical Chinese 名義 (míngyì), combining 名 (míng, 'name, title, designation') and 義 / 义 (yì, 'proper meaning, moral principle, rightful status'). In early Confucian and legal-philosophical texts (such as the Xunzi and Han commentaries on rectifying names, 正名), 名義 denoted the rightful ethical obligation or substantive principle inherent in a formal title; in modern Mandarin (reinforced by Japanese legal usage 名義 meigi) it shifted toward 'nominal capacity, formal title, or pretext under which an action is taken'.

history.meaning: the moral principle, duty, or proper meaning attached to a formal title
formal title, nominal capacity, or ostensible pretext (often in 以…的名义 'in the name of')

名义.notes: Most frequently used in the frame 以…的名义 (yǐ ... de míngyì, 'in the name of...') or the adjective 名义上 (míngyì shàng, 'nominal / on paper only'), contrasting formal title with actual backstage power.

名单.etymology: Compound noun of 名 ('name') + 单 (單, 'single sheet, list'): 'name list, roster, roll'.

history.meaning: list of names; roster

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 名单 (via 萌典)

名嘴.etymology: A modern Mandarin modifier-head compound combining 名 (míng, 'famous, celebrated, renowned') with 嘴 (zuǐ, 'mouth', used by metonymy for an articulate speaker, commentator, or talk-show host). Originally popularized in late 20th-century Taiwanese and Hong Kong broadcast media before spreading across Mainland entertainment television, it parallels formations like 名笔 ('celebrated writer') and 名角 ('famous opera/stage actor'), elevating colloquial 嘴 ('mouth/lip') into a badge of rapid-fire broadcast eloquence.

history.meaning: separate morphemes: 'famous/renowned' + 'beak, mouth, eloquent speaker'
celebrated talk-show host, pundit, or sharp-tongued broadcast commentator

morphemes.meaning: mouth; eloquent speaker or host (by metonymy)

名嘴.notes: A quintessential showbiz and broadcasting term for star MCs, talk-show hosts, and sharp-witted pundits whose primary asset is fast, persuasive verbal delivery.

名声.etymology: A coordinative compound from Classical Chinese 名聲 (míngshēng), pairing 名 (míng, 'name, renown') with 聲 / 声 (shēng, 'voice, sound, public report'). Attested already in the Mengzi and the Guanzi, the compound rests on the classical metaphor that a person's 'name' (名) travels outward like 'sound' (聲) carried on the wind; in modern Mandarin it serves as the everyday word for public reputation (good or bad), slightly more colloquial and neutral than 名誉 (míngyù).

history.meaning: public renown; the sound of one's name spreading abroad
social reputation or standing (either positive or negative)

名声.notes: Unlike 名誉 (which sounds formal, legal, or institutional), 名声 is everyday spoken Mandarin and can be modified as 好名声 ('good name') or 坏名声 / 名声不好 ('bad reputation').

名头.etymology: An early vernacular Mandarin suffixed noun formed from 名 (míng, 'name, title, fame') plus the nominalizing and substantive suffix 頭 / 头 (tóu, originally 'head', grammaticalized in Song–Yuan vernacular to mark a concrete handle, aspect, or quality). Attested in Yuan drama and Ming–Qing vernacular novels (such as Water Margin and Dream of the Red Chamber), 名頭 denotes either the impressive-sounding label attached to a person or project, or the clout and recognition that such a title commands.

history.meaning: name, title, or public clout in colloquial speech
grand-sounding designation, titular prestige, or public reputation

morphemes.meaning: nominal suffix indicating a tangible title, handle, or quality

名头.notes: Often carries a slightly pragmatic or skeptical undertone in showbiz and business (e.g., 名头很大 'has a very grand-sounding title/reputation'), emphasizing how impressive a title sounds from the outside.

名字.etymology: Compound noun originally pairing two distinct Classical naming customs: 名 ('personal given name' bestowed in infancy, from 夕 'dusk' + 口 'mouth calling out one's name in the dark') + 字 ('courtesy name / style name' taken at adulthood). By the Six Dynasties and Tang period, the pair fused into the general everyday word for 'name (of a person or thing)'.

morphemes.meaning: style name -> general word for name (neutral tone)

history.meaning: personal given name (名) and adult style name (字)
name (of a person or thing)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 名字 (via 萌典)

名片.etymology: A modifier-head compound from late imperial and early modern Mandarin combining 名 (míng, 'name') and 片 (piàn, 'flat thin slice, slip of paper, card'). In classical and imperial times, visiting cards were Bamboo/wood tablets (刺 cì or 謁 yè) and later red paper slips called 名帖 (míngtiě); in the late Qing and Republican eras, as smaller Western-style card-stock calling cards spread through treaty ports and commercial circles, 名片 ('name card/slip') became the standard term, also acquiring the figurative sense of a signature work or flagship emblem.

history.meaning: inscribed wooden tablet or paper visiting slip presented upon calling on a host
printed calling card or business card; (figuratively) a signature calling card or emblem

名片.notes: Takes the classifier 张 (zhāng); in media and entertainment, calling a hit show or star someone's 金字名片 or 招牌名片 means it serves as their 'calling card' to the industry.

名誉.etymology: A coordinative compound from Classical Chinese 名譽 (míngyù), uniting 名 (míng, 'name, standing') and 譽 / 誉 (yù, 'praise, eulogy, high esteem'). Attested in the Mozi, Xunzi, and Shiji, where it denoted public acclamation and honorable renown, the term was further reinforced in late 19th-century East Asian legal and institutional modernity (alongside Japanese 名誉 meiyo) to translate Western legal concepts of 'honor, good name, defamation of character (名誉侵权)', and 'honorary (emeritus) title'.

history.meaning: public praise, acclaimed name, and honorable renown
personal or institutional honor, legal reputation, or honorary status (e.g. 名誉主席)

名誉.notes: Higher-register and more positive than 名声: used in legal contexts (侵犯名誉权 'infringe on reputation rights') and institutional titles (名誉出品人 'honorary producer').

名额.etymology: A modifier-head administrative compound from late imperial Chinese 名額 (míng'é), composed of 名 (míng, 'named person on a roster, registered individual') and 額 / 额 (é, originally 'forehead', extended in Tang–Song bureaucratic usage to mean 'inscribed plaque' and hence a 'fixed numerical ceiling or quota'). Originally used in Qing civil-service examinations and military/official staffing for the fixed number of candidates or stipendiary posts permitted on an official roll, it now denotes any limited slot or quota in competitions, admissions, or broadcasts.

history.meaning: fixed quota of registered names on an imperial examination or civil/military roster
allotted spot, headcount quota, or entry slot in a competition or program

morphemes.meaning: registered name; individual person on a roll

名额.notes: In talent shows and TV production, 晋级名额 ('advancement slots') and 争夺名额 ('compete for a spot') are staple phrases for limited competition berths.

后.etymology: A polysemous character that in Simplified Chinese merges two originally distinct Classical Chinese graphs: (1) 後 (hòu, Old Chinese *ɢˤoʔ, combining 彳 'step/walk', 幺 'tiny/thread' suggesting trailing or tethered movement, and 夂 'lagging foot'), meaning 'to walk behind, come after, rear, later, descendants'; and (2) 后 (hòu, Old Chinese *ɢˤoʔ), originally meaning 'sovereign ruler' in Shang–Zhou texts and later 'empress, queen consort'. In almost all spatial and temporal senses ('behind, back, after, later'), 后 represents Classical 後.

history.meaning: to lag behind; rear in space; subsequent in time; posterity
behind, back, after, later (as well as empress/queen in court compounds)

后.notes: Productive both as a spatial/temporal localizer (之后 'after', 背后 'behind') and as a prefix in showbiz/production terms (幕后 'behind the scenes', 后期 'post-production').

后半段.etymology: Three-character compound of 后 (後, 'latter, back') + 半 ('half') + 段 ('section, segment, stretch'): 'the second half, the latter section (of a journey, performance, or text)'.

history.meaning: the latter half/section

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 后半段 (via 萌典)

后台.etymology: A modifier-head compound from 後臺 / 后台 (hòutái), joining 後 / 后 (hòu, 'rear, behind') and 臺 / 台 (tái, 'raised platform, theatrical stage'). Originating in traditional Chinese opera theaters (戏台) for the dressing and preparation area behind the curtain—as opposed to 前台 (qiántái, 'front of stage')—it subsequently expanded in modern Mandarin to two additional domains: figurative 'powerful behind-the-scenes patron or political/corporate backing' (有后台 'to have powerful connections') and computing 'back-end / background process'.

history.meaning: the rear dressing and waiting area behind a traditional opera stage
backstage area in theater/TV; behind-the-scenes powerful patron; software back-end

后台.notes: Has a crucial triple meaning in contemporary media dramas: literal studio backstage (去后台准备), a powerful backer/patron (后台很硬 'has rock-solid backing'), and website/app backend data (后台数据).

rootFamily.gloss: front of stage; reception desk; foreground

后备.etymology: A modifier-head (originally adverbial-verbal) Sino-compound 後備 / 后备 (hòubèi), combining 後 / 后 (hòu, 'in the rear, for later contingency') and 備 / 备 (bèi, 'to prepare, equip, hold in readiness'). While classical texts used 備 to mean military readiness, the compound 後備 crystallized in Meiji Japanese (後備 kōbi, translating European military 'second-line reserve forces' as in 後備軍) and was adopted into late Qing and modern Chinese military and organizational vocabulary, broadening into a general attributive modifier meaning 'backup, reserve, or standby'.

history.meaning: second-line military reserve forces held in readiness behind the active front line
backup, reserve, or standby (personnel, plans, resources, or talent pool)

morphemes.meaning: rear; subsequent; held behind for contingency (traditionally 後)

后备.notes: Functions primarily as an attributive modifier before nouns (后备力量 'reserve strength', 后备人才 'talent pipeline', 后备箱 'car trunk/boot') rather than as a standalone predicate.

rootFamily.gloss: to keep for backup; spare; alternative

后备团队.etymology: A four-character modifier-head nominal compound (後備團隊 / 后备团队, hòubèi tuánduì) combining the attributive noun 後備 / 后备 (hòubèi, 'backup, reserve') with the coordinative collective noun 團隊 / 团队 (tuánduì, 'team, crew, working group', from 團 'round body, group, regiment' + 隊 'squad, file of soldiers, team'). Typical of modern corporate and television production terminology, it designates a standby or second-tier crew ready to step in when the primary production team faces an emergency or capacity crunch.

history.meaning: military/organizational 'reserve' + collective 'regiment/team'
backup team, reserve production crew, or standby project unit

morphemes.meaning: backup; reserve; held in readiness (traditionally 後備)
team; crew; organized group (traditionally 團隊)

后备团队.notes: Common in live television and large project management where a shadow or standby crew (后备团队) is kept briefed in case the lead team encounters a crisis.

后备方案.etymology: A four-character modifier-head compound (後備方案 / 后备方案, hòubèi fāng'àn) pairing 後備 / 后备 (hòubèi, 'backup, contingency reserve') with 方案 (fāng'àn, 'plan, scheme, proposal', from 方 'method, prescription, direction' + 案 'official desk, dossier, drafted proposal'). In modern administrative, broadcast, and crisis-management Mandarin, it serves as the standard professional equivalent of English 'backup plan' or 'Plan B'.

history.meaning: 'reserve/standby' + 'drafted official proposal or operational scheme'
backup plan, contingency plan, or Plan B in project and broadcast management

后备方案.notes: In television production and corporate settings, 后备方案 (or 备选方案 / 预案) is the standard phrase for a contingency plan prepared before a live broadcast or pitch.

后头.etymology: An early vernacular Mandarin locative and temporal noun (後頭 / 后头, hòutou) formed from the spatial/temporal root 後 / 后 (hòu, 'behind, back, after') and the unstressed localizer suffix 頭 / 头 (-tou, grammaticalized from 'head' in Tang–Song vernacular to form location words alongside 前頭, 裏頭, 外頭). Attested from Song–Yuan vernacular texts onward, it denotes both spatial position ('at the back, behind') and temporal sequence ('later on, afterward, in the future').

history.meaning: in the rear; behind; subsequently (in Song–Ming vernacular narrative)
behind, in the back; later on, in the upcoming part (read with neutral tone hòutou)

morphemes.meaning: localizer suffix marking spatial or temporal position (neutral tone)

后头.notes: Colloquial and conversational (with neutral-tone -tou), often used metaphorically for what is still to come: 好戏还在后头 ('the best part of the show is still to come').

后悔.etymology: An adverbial-head verbal compound from Classical Chinese 後悔 (hòuhuǐ), combining 後 / 后 (hòu, 'afterward, belatedly, after the fact') with 悔 (huǐ, 'to repent, feel remorse', bearing the heart radical 忄/心 and phonetic 每 měi). Attested in Han-dynasty historical prose such as the Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian) and Hanshu, the compound literally captures the insight that remorse (悔) always arrives after (後) the deed is already done.

history.meaning: to feel remorse afterward; belated repentance over a past action
to regret; to feel remorseful about a choice or action

morphemes.meaning: afterward; belatedly; after the fact (traditionally 後)

后悔.notes: Colloquially paired in the humorous expression 后悔药 (hòuhuǐyào, 'medicine for regret', as in 世上没有后悔药 'there is no cure for regret once it is too late').

rootFamily.gloss: to repent and mend one's ways

后招.etymology: A modifier-head compound from martial arts, chess, and strategic parlance (後招 / 后招, hòuzhāo), combining 後 / 后 (hòu, 'subsequent, held back for later') with 招 (zhāo, originally 'to beckon with the hand', extended in vernacular Chinese to mean 'a martial-arts move, chess maneuver, trick, or tactical step'). Contrasting with 先招 ('opening gambit'), 后招 denotes a follow-up maneuver or hidden trump card kept in reserve to counter an opponent's response.

history.meaning: follow-up move or counter-maneuver held in reserve in martial arts or board games
backup move, hidden follow-up tactic, or ace up one's sleeve in negotiations and competition

morphemes.meaning: subsequent; held in reserve for later (traditionally 後)
move; maneuver; tactical trick or play

后招.notes: Frequently used in workplace and showbiz dramas in phrases like 留有后招 ('keep an ace up one's sleeve') or 还有后招 ('still have another move coming').

rootFamily.gloss: ultimate move; trump card; big move

cognates.meaning: supporters' association; fan club; political/sports booster club

后援会.etymology: A modern Sino-Japanese institutional compound (後援會 / 后援会, hòuyuánhuì), formed from 後援 / 后援 (hòuyuán, 'rear reinforcement, backing, support', from 後 'behind/rear' + 援 'to pull up by hand, aid, rescue') and the organizational suffix 會 / 会 (huì, 'association, society, club'). While 後援 appeared in classical Chinese military contexts for rear-echelon reinforcements, the three-character noun 後援會 was coined in modern Japan (後援会 kōenkai) for political, athletic, and entertainment booster clubs, and entered Mandarin via Taiwanese, Hong Kong, and Japanese pop-idol culture as the standard term for an organized celebrity fan club.

history.meaning: military reinforcements or backing from the rear
organized supporters' or patrons' association for a politician, athlete, or performer
organized celebrity fan club or official fan support association (e.g. 粉丝后援会)

morphemes.meaning: rear backing; support; reinforcement (traditionally 後援)

后援会.notes: In Chinese entertainment culture, an official 粉丝后援会 is a highly organized body that coordinates concert light-sticks, trending hashtags, box-office support, and charity drives for an idol.

rootFamily.gloss: to support; to aid; to assist

后期中心.etymology: A four-character modifier-head media-industry compound (後期中心 / 后期中心, hòuqī zhōngxīn), combining 後期 / 后期 (hòuqī, literally 'later period/stage', specialized in film and television via ellipsis of 后期制作 hòuqī zhìzuò for 'post-production') with 中心 (zhōngxīn, 'center, hub', literally 'middle heart/core'). In contemporary Chinese broadcasting networks and studio complexes, 后期中心 designates the dedicated division or facility responsible for editing, color grading, visual effects, sound mixing, and subtitling after principal photography wraps.

history.meaning: 'later stage / final phase' + 'central core / institutional hub'
post-production center or editing/VFX hub in a television network or film studio

morphemes.meaning: post-production; later stage (short for 后期制作, traditionally 後期)

后期中心.notes: In Chinese TV industry jargon, 后期 alone frequently stands for 'post-production' or even 'post-production editor' (e.g., 加鸡腿给后期 'give a bonus drumstick to the video editor').

后来.etymology: Temporal noun combining 后 (後, 'after, later') + 来 ('come'): in Classical Chinese 'those who come later (successors)', and from Tang–Song vernacular onward 'afterwards, later on (in the past)'.

history.meaning: those who come after; latecomers
afterwards; later on

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 后来 (via 萌典)

后爹.etymology: A colloquial modifier-head kinship compound (後爹 / 后爹, hòudiē), combining 後 / 后 (hòu, 'subsequent, later in sequence', used since Han–Tang times in kinship terms like 後母 'stepmother' and 後夫 'second husband' to mark a relation formed by remarriage) with the vernacular kinship noun 爹 (diē, 'dad, father', attested since the Six Dynasties in the Ballad of Mulan 阿爺/阿爹 with the father radical 父 and phonetic 多). It serves as the vivid spoken counterpart to formal 继父 (jìfù, 'stepfather').

history.meaning: stepmother / stepfather (parent by a subsequent marriage)
stepfather (colloquial); figuratively, someone who treats a person or project harshly like an unloved stepchild

后爹.notes: Colloquial and earthy compared to formal 继父 (jìfù); often used humorously in workplace complaints (像后爹养的 'treated like a stepchild' — given no budget or resources).

后边.etymology: A vernacular Mandarin spatial localizer compound (後邊 / 后边, hòubian), formed from 後 / 后 (hòu, 'behind, rear, back') and the localizer suffix 邊 / 边 (-bian, originally 'side, edge, border, margin', grammaticalized in Northern Mandarin into a directional/locative noun suffix alongside 前边, 左边, 里边). Pronounced with a neutral tone on the second syllable (hòubian, and often rhotacized in Beijing/Northern speech as 后边儿 hòubiār), it denotes the space behind an object or person, or a later point in a queue or sequence.

history.meaning: the rear side; the area behind (in Ming–Qing Northern vernacular)
behind, at the back, in the rear (usually neutral tone hòubian)

morphemes.meaning: side; locative suffix forming place words (traditionally 邊)

后边.notes: Slightly more conversational and northern-flavored than 后面 (hòumiàn), and slightly less folksy than 后头 (hòutou); all three translate 'behind / in the back'.

后门.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 后 (後, 'back, rear') + 门 (門, 'door, gate'): literally 'back door, rear entrance' and figuratively (as in 走后门) 'pulling strings, backdoor connections'.

history.meaning: back door; rear gate; backdoor influence

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 后门 (via 萌典)

后面.etymology: Locative compound noun of 后 (後, 'behind, back, rear') + 面 ('face, side, surface'): 'behind, at the back, the rear, later part'.

history.meaning: behind; at the back; the rear

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 后面 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to debunk, roast, or deflate a friend's boast; literally 'spit into the feeding trough/bowl'
the 'straight man' role in manzai comedy who butts in to point out absurdities

吐槽.etymology: A modern Mandarin verb-object compound (吐槽, tùcáo; literally 吐 tù 'to spit out, vomit' + 槽 cáo 'trough, manger, groove') with a double-layered cross-dialectal and translingual history. Originally written 吐嘈 or 黜臭 in Taiwanese Hokkien (thuh-chhàu, 'to expose someone's flaws, deflate a boast, or give someone a hard time'), the characters 吐槽 were adopted by Taiwanese translators in the 1990s–2000s to render Japanese manzai comedy term ツッコミ (tsukkomi, the sharp-tongued 'straight man' who interrupts to point out the funny man's absurdities). Via anime/manga subtitling and bullet-screen video sites (Bilibili, AcFun), 吐槽 swept Mainland Mandarin to mean 'to roast, riff sarcastically on flaws, or vent humorously'.

history.meaning: to expose someone's bluff or deflate a friend in banter (Taiwanese Hokkien)

history.form: 吐槽 (translating Japanese ツッコミ tsukkomi)
history.meaning: to interject with a deadpan comedic counterpoint to an absurd remark or plot hole
to roast, poke fun at plot holes/flaws, or vent/gripe humorously (often separable: 吐了个槽)

morphemes.meaning: to spit out; to vent; to utter
trough (reanalyzed as the noun object 'gripe / comedic roast')

吐槽.notes: Behaves as a separable verb-object (离合词) in Mandarin (e.g., 吐个槽 'have a quick gripe', 无力吐槽 'too absurd to even roast') and spawned the noun 槽点 (cáodiǎn, 'roast-worthy flaw').

rootFamily.gloss: roast-worthy flaw or plot hole in a show/plan
to confide; to pour out one's heart or grievances
to speak unpleasantly; sharp-tongued remark (idiom: 狗嘴里吐不出象牙)

向.etymology: Pictograph in Shang oracle-bone script of a house (宀) with a north-facing window opening (口): originally 'north window', then 'face toward, turn toward, direction, side with' and the preposition 'toward, to, from'.

history.meaning: north-facing window -> face toward, direction
toward; to; direction; always

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 向 (via 萌典)

向前.etymology: A preposition-object / verb-complement directional compound (向前, xiàngqián), combining 向 (xiàng, originally a 'north-facing window' in oracle bone script, extended in Classical Chinese to 'to face toward, turn toward, direction') with 前 (qián, 'front, ahead, forward'). Used both literally for physical movement ahead (向前走 'walk forward') and figuratively for progressive mindset or moving on from setbacks (向前看 'look ahead to the future').

history.meaning: facing the front; advancing forward in space (and occasionally 'previously' in Tang–Song vernacular)
forward, ahead, onward (in space, progress, or outlook)

morphemes.meaning: toward; facing; in the direction of

向前.notes: Common in motivational and workplace contexts: 向前看 ('look forward / move on') is also famously used in a witty homophonic pun 向钱看 ('look toward money!').

rootFamily.gloss: to advance; to move forward; progress

向来.etymology: Temporal adverb combining 向 ('in the past, heretofore') + 来 ('coming up to now'): 'all along, always (up to the present)'. Attested since Six Dynasties and Tang poetry.

history.meaning: heretofore; all along; always

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 向来 (via 萌典)

向死而生.etymology: A four-character philosophical and rhetorical phrase (向死而生, xiàng sǐ ér shēng) structured with classical Chinese grammar: 向 (xiàng, 'facing toward, oriented toward') + 死 (sǐ, 'death, perishing') + 而 (ér, classical conjunctive particle connecting manner/condition to action) + 生 (shēng, 'to live, come alive, survive'). While echoing classical Chinese military axioms such as Sunzi's 置之死地而后生 ('place troops on fatal ground and only then will they fight to live'), the exact four-character formulation 向死而生 was coined by Chinese philosophers (notably translating Martin Heidegger's Sein-zum-Tode 'Being-toward-death' in *Sein und Zeit* / 《存在与时间》) and subsequently entered popular media and business rhetoric to mean 'finding the courage to live or fight back to victory precisely by confronting total defeat or mortality'.

history.form: 置之死地而後生 (Sunzi, Art of War)
history.meaning: classical precursor: 'cast troops onto fatal ground and subsequently they will survive by fighting desperately'
'Being-toward-death': authentic existence awakened by confronting one's finitude and mortality
to fight back to life and breakthrough from the brink of elimination or ruin

morphemes.meaning: and thereby; and thus (classical connective particle)
to live; to be reborn; to survive and thrive

向死而生.notes: Bridges existential philosophy and high-stakes drama: used in *Behind the Scenes* (*幕后之王*) and competitive shows when a cornered team risks everything to stage a comeback.

rootFamily.gloss: to survive after being cast into fatal ground (classical idiom)
narrow escape from death; surviving a desperate crisis
starting anew from desperate straits; rebirth from ruin

向阳.etymology: Verb-object compound used as an adjective, combining 向 ('face toward') + 阳 (陽, 'the sun, sunny south side'): 'facing the sun, sunny, sunward' (famously in the Song verse 近水楼台先得月，向阳花木易为春).

history.stage: Song dynasty poetry to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: facing the sun; sunny

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 向阳 (via 萌典)

吓.etymology: Phono-semantic character (嚇) combining 口 ('mouth') + 赫 (hè, 'fiery red, awe-inspiring', simplified to 下 xià). Read hè in Classical Chinese (Zhuangzi) for an angry threatening shout (as in 恐吓 kǒnghè), and read xià in vernacular Mandarin for 'frighten, scare, startle'.

history.meaning: angry shout; threaten
scare; frighten; startle

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 吓 (via 萌典)

吓人.etymology: A verb-object compound lexicalized as an adjective (嚇人 / 吓人, xiàrén), composed of 嚇 / 吓 (xià, 'to frighten, startle, terrify') and its generic human object 人 (rén, 'person, people'). Originally a phono-semantic character 嚇 (with mouth 口 and doubled 赤 'fiery red', pronounced hè in Classical Chinese meaning 'tojeer/threaten angrily' as in the Zhuangzi), the character acquired the colloquial Northern Mandarin reading xià ('to scare') in Ming–Qing vernacular; combined with 人, 吓人 literally means 'scares people' and functions as the everyday adjective for 'scary, alarming, or shockingly intense'.

history.meaning: to hiss or roar threateningly; to intimidate (e.g. Zhuangzi 鴟得腐鼠…嚇)

history.form: 嚇人 / 吓人 (colloquial reading xiàrén)
history.meaning: frightening people; scary, alarming, or shockingly high/intense

morphemes.meaning: person; people (forming an adjectival VO compound)

吓人.notes: Besides literal fright, 吓人 is constantly used as a degree complement or predicate for shocking numbers or intensity: 贵得吓人 ('scarily expensive'), 收视率高得吓人 ('ratings are scary high').

rootFamily.gloss: to scare; to bluff; to intimidate (colloquial)
to threaten; to intimidate (formal, read kǒnghè)

吓唬.etymology: A colloquial Northern Mandarin disyllabic verb (嚇唬 / 吓唬, xiàhu), pairing 嚇 / 吓 (xià, 'to frighten, startle') with 唬 (hǔ, neutralized to -hu, with the mouth radical 口 and 虎 'tiger', originally an onomatopoeic character for a tiger's roar in Classical Chinese that developed the vernacular sense 'to bluff, hoax, or cow with bluster'). Attested in Qing vernacular novels like Dream of the Red Chamber (红楼梦), 吓唬 specifically emphasizes trying to intimidate or bluff someone with verbal threats or a fierce front.

history.meaning: roar of a tiger; later vernacular 'to bluff, cow, or deceive by bluster'
to scare, intimidate, or bluff someone (pronounced with neutral second syllable)

morphemes.meaning: to bluff; to roar at; to intimidate (neutral tone -hu)

吓唬.notes: Often implies empty bluster or playful intimidation rather than genuine mortal danger—hence the classic retort 你别吓唬我！ ('Don't try to scare/bluff me!').

rootFamily.gloss: to bluff; to fool people with bluster

吓怕.etymology: A resultative verb compound (嚇怕 / 吓怕, xiàpà), formed from the causative action verb 嚇 / 吓 (xià, 'to frighten, startle') followed by the psychological state verb 怕 (pà, 'to fear, dread, be afraid', from heart 忄 and phonetic 白 bái) serving as a resultative complement. Literally 'to frighten (someone) until they become afraid/timid', it expresses being so thoroughly rattled by a past shock or crisis that one becomes gun-shy or hesitant afterward.

history.meaning: causative verb 'frighten' + resultative state 'become fearful'
to scare off; to rattle thoroughly so that someone becomes gun-shy (often in 被吓怕了)

morphemes.meaning: into a state of fear or timidity (resultative complement)

吓怕.notes: Almost always appears with the completive particle 了 or in passive/potential constructions: 被吓怕了 ('was scared off / became gun-shy from the experience') or 吓不怕 ('cannot be intimidated').

rootFamily.gloss: to be afraid; to fear; to dread

吓我一跳.etymology: An idiomatic four-syllable colloquial verb-complement construction (嚇我一跳 / 吓我一跳, xià wǒ yī tiào), built from the verb 嚇 / 吓 (xià, 'to startle, frighten'), the indirect/affected pronoun object 我 (wǒ, 'me'), the numeral 一 (yī, 'one, a sudden'), and the verbal classifier/resultative noun 跳 (tiào, 'jump, leap, start'). Literally 'startled me [into] one jump', it depicts the involuntary physical jolt or heart-skip when someone is caught off guard by a sudden noise, appearance, or piece of news.

history.form: 驚了一跳 / 嚇了一跳
history.meaning: startled into a sudden physical jump or jolt of the heart (Ming–Qing vernacular fiction)
'You startled me!' / 'Gave me a fright!' (everyday spoken exclamation)

吓我一跳.notes: One of the most natural spoken exclamations in Mandarin when someone sneaks up on you or drops sudden dramatic news; can also take 了 (吓了我一跳).

rootFamily.gloss: to give someone a sudden fright (base idiom)
heartbeat; palpitation from excitement or shock

吓死.etymology: A hyperbolic resultative verb compound (嚇死 / 吓死, xiàsǐ), pairing the verb 嚇 / 吓 (xià, 'to frighten, startle') with 死 (sǐ, 'to die, to death') functioning as an extreme degree or resultative complement. While 吓死 can occasionally mean literally 'frightened to death', in everyday Mandarin (alongside 累死 'tired to death', 笑死 'laugh to death', 急死 'worried to death') 死 is grammaticalized into an expressive intensifier meaning 'scared half to death / terrified out of one's wits'.

history.meaning: to frighten to death (literally or hyperbolically in Ming–Qing vernacular)
to scare half to death; to terrify utterly (hyperbolic intensifier construction)

morphemes.meaning: to death; to an extreme degree (hyperbolic resultative complement)

吓死.notes: Extremely common in spoken exclamations such as 吓死我了！ ('You scared me to death!') or 吓死宝宝了 ('Scared the daylights out of me', playful internet slang).

吗.etymology: Sentence-final particle turning any declarative statement into a neutral yes/no question without changing word order. Grammaticalized in Song–Yuan–Ming vernacular from earlier negative finals (such as 无 wú / 么 me appended at the end of a statement to ask 'or not?'), with 口 added to show its purely spoken particle role.

history.meaning: sentence-final yes/no question particle

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 嗎 (via 萌典)

否则.etymology: A lexicalized Classical Chinese conditional conjunction (否則 / 否则, fǒuzé), formed by the fusion of two adjacent syntactic elements across a clause boundary: 否 (fǒu, 'not so; if it is not the case', standing as a pro-clause negator for an entire preceding proposition, attested in the Mengzi and Zuozhuan) and 則 / 则 (zé, 'then, in that case, consequently', the standard classical correlative conjunction). Literally 'if not so, then...', the two-character sequence fused into a single modern conjunction meaning 'otherwise, or else, failing which'.

history.meaning: 'if not so, then...' (two separate syntactic words across a conditional clause boundary)
otherwise; or else; if not (lexicalized disyllabic conjunction)

morphemes.meaning: not so; if it is not the case (clausal negator)
then; in that case; consequently (traditionally 則)

否则.notes: Slightly more formal and decisive than spoken 要不然 (yàobùrán); frequently paired with 除非 ('unless... otherwise 否则...').

吧.etymology: Sentence-final particle softening commands into warm invitations ('let's…', 'go ahead and…') or asking for gentle confirmation. Formed with 口 ('mouth') + 巴 (bā phonetic) and evolved from earlier imperative/concessive finals like 罢 (bà, 'finish, let it be') in Ming–Qing colloquial speech.

history.meaning: final particle softening suggestions and assumptions

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 吧 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to instruct; to order; to bid (written 分付 / 吩咐)

吩咐.etymology: A disyllabic verb (吩咐, fēnfù, read with a neutral tone on the second syllable fēnfu in standard Mandarin) that evolved from the Middle Chinese verb 分付 (fēnfù, literally 分 'to divide, allot, apportion' + 付 'to hand over, entrust'). In Tang–Song administrative and vernacular texts, 分付 shifted from 'to allot and hand over property or tasks' to 'to give verbal instructions or orders to a subordinate or younger person'; during the Yuan–Ming period, the mouth radical 口 was added to both characters (creating 吩咐) to mark the specifically oral act of issuing instructions or bidding someone to do something.

history.meaning: to apportion and hand over; to entrust a task with instructions

history.form: 吩咐 (with mouth radical 口 added)
history.meaning: to give verbal instructions, orders, or directions (typically from a superior or elder)
history.stage: Early Vernacular Mandarin (Yuan–Ming) to Modern Mandarin

morphemes.meaning: to instruct; to allot verbally (from 分 with 口 radical)
to entrust; to command verbally (from 付 with 口 radical, neutral tone -fu)

吩咐.notes: Carries a clear hierarchy of authority or polite deference: subordinates or service staff often ask 有什么吩咐？ ('What are your orders / How may I assist you?').

rootFamily.gloss: to exhort; to enjoin repeatedly with care
to entrust; to hand over for care or action
to assign; to distribute tasks or resources

听.etymology: Simplified form of 聽 (which combined 耳 'ear' + 壬 + 悳 'attentive heart/virtue': 'listen with ear and heart'). The character 听 originally existed in Classical dictionaries with a different reading (yǐn, 'laugh with open mouth') before being adopted from cursive/popular shorthand for 聽 ('listen, hear, obey, allow; tin can [loan from English tin]').

history.meaning: listen attentively with ear and mind; heed; allow
listen; hear; heed; can (of food/drink)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 听 (via 萌典)

听到.etymology: A verb-resultative compound (聽到 / 听到, tīngdào), combining the perception verb 聽 / 听 (tīng, 'to listen, hearken', traditionally written with ear 耳, 壬, and 悳 'virtue/attentive heart', simplified via the cursive/vulgar homophone 听 originally meaning 'to smile') with the resultative complement 到 (dào, 'to arrive, reach, succeed in attaining'). In Chinese grammar, bare 听 denotes the volitional act of 'listening', whereas adding the resultative 到 ('reach/perceive') converts it into an achievement verb meaning 'to actually hear (perceive the sound reaching the ear)'.

history.meaning: from monomorphemic 'to listen/hear and heed' to analytic resultative 'listen + perceive/reach'
to hear; to catch a sound or piece of news (action + successful perception)

morphemes.meaning: to listen; to attend with the ear (traditionally 聽)

听到.notes: Crucial Mandarin distinction: 我在听 ('I am listening' — process) vs. 我听到了 ('I heard it' — successful result); nearly synonymous with 听见 (tīngjiàn).

rootFamily.gloss: to hear; to perceive by ear (synonymous resultative)
to hear it said; hearsay; rumor has it
to see; to catch sight of (parallel visual resultative)

听听.etymology: Reduplicated verb from 听 ('listen'): 'listen a bit, have a listen, hear someone out' (verb reduplication in Mandarin marks a brief, tentative, or relaxed action).

history.meaning: listen for a moment; have a listen

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 听听 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to leave things to fate (calque/shared Sino-Japanese roots 天 and 命)
cognates.word: 天命に任せる (tenmei ni makaseru)

听天由命.etymology: A symmetric four-character chengyu (成语, idiomatic set phrase) formed from two parallel verb-object clauses: 听天 (tīngtiān, 'to obey/yield to Heaven', where 听/聽 carries its older Literary Chinese sense 'to allow, let, submit to' rather than merely 'to hear') and 由命 (yóumìng, 'to follow destiny/fate'). Attested in Qing-dynasty vernacular fiction such as Liu E's The Travels of Lao Can (老残游记), it evolved from classical Confucian fatalism ('Heaven's decree') into a colloquial expression of resigned acceptance when facing circumstances beyond one's control.

history.meaning: to submit to Heaven's will and follow one's allotted destiny
history.stage: Late Imperial Literary & Vernacular Chinese (Qing Dynasty)

history.meaning: to leave things to fate; to resign oneself to whatever happens

morphemes.meaning: to allow, submit to, obey (Classical sense of 聽)
to follow, abide by, leave to

听天由命.notes: Often used after exhausting all practical efforts (e.g., 尽人事，听天由命 'do one's utmost and leave the rest to fate'); in media production, used when a show's broadcast approval or ratings are out of the crew's hands.

rootFamily.gloss: Heaven's will, mandate of Heaven, destiny
to allow someone to do as they please, to let things slide
to believe rumors uncritically (lit. hear the road and follow the途)

sources.title: Wiktionary: 聽天由命 / 听天由命

听懂.etymology: A modern Mandarin verb-resultative compound (动补结构) combining the action verb 听 (tīng, simplified from 聽, 'to listen, hear') with the resultative complement 懂 (dǒng, 'to understand, comprehend'). While 聽 is ancient (attested since Oracle Bone and Bronze inscriptions), 懂 emerged as a vernacular verb of mental comprehension during the Song–Ming period and became highly productive as a resultative complement in Mandarin alongside 看懂 ('understand by reading/watching').

history.meaning: to hear, listen to, heed
to understand what one hears; to follow spoken language or music

morphemes.meaning: to listen, to hear (simplified from 聽)

听懂.notes: Regularly takes potential infixes: 听得懂 (tīngdedǒng, 'able to understand by listening') and 听不懂 (tīngbudǒng, 'unable to understand what is heard').

rootFamily.gloss: to understand by reading or watching
to understand, to make sense of

听见.etymology: Resultative verb compound combining the action verb 听 ('listen') + the perceptual resultative complement 见 (見, 'perceive, catch'): 'hear (actually perceive the sound)'.

history.meaning: listen and perceive = hear

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 听见 (via 萌典)

听说.etymology: Serial verb compound of 听 ('hear') + 说 (說, 'say, speak'): 'hear it said, hear tell, be told that'.

history.meaning: hear people say; hear that…

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 听说 (via 萌典)

听起来.etymology: Evaluative verb-complement construction combining 听 ('listen, hear') + 起来 (inchoative/evaluative directional complement 'when one starts to perceive/judge it'): 'sound (like / adj.), to the ear it seems…'.

history.meaning: sound (good, strange, like…)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 听起来 (via 萌典)

启动.etymology: A verb-complement / coordinative Sino-compound (啟動 / 启动, qǐdòng) combining 启 (qǐ, traditional 啟/啓, originally 'to open a door', extended to 'to initiate, open up, start') and 动 (dòng, traditional 動, 'to move, set in motion'). First attested in medieval Chinese prose in the literal sense of 'setting out on a journey or beginning movement', it was revitalized in the 20th century (reinforced by Japanese 起動 kidō in engineering and computing) to mean 'to start up an engine/system' and figuratively 'to launch a project, plan, or production'.

history.meaning: to begin moving; to set out or stir into motion
to start up (machinery/software); to launch or initiate (a project, program, or mechanism)

morphemes.meaning: to open, initiate, start (simplified from 啟)
to move, set in motion, activate (simplified from 動)

启动.notes: Ubiquitous in television, film, and corporate contexts for kicking off a major project (e.g., 启动项目 'launch a project', 启动仪式 'launch ceremony').

rootFamily.gloss: to set out on a journey, embark

启幕.etymology: A verb-object compound (啟幕 / 启幕, qǐmù) composed of 启 (qǐ, traditional 啟, 'to open, raise, initiate') and 幕 (mù, originally 'overhead canopy or tent curtain' in Classical Chinese, later specialized in modern theater as 'stage curtain'). Formed on the theatrical metaphor of parting or raising the stage curtain to begin a performance, it stands in direct opposition to 落幕 (luòmù, 'to lower the curtain; to conclude') and 闭幕 (bìmù, 'to close').

history.meaning: to open or raise the stage curtain at the start of a theatrical performance
to raise the curtain; to premiere or officially open (a festival, show, or major event)

morphemes.meaning: to open, part, initiate (simplified from 啟)
curtain, tent canopy, theatrical screen or act

启幕.notes: High-register, journalistic and showbiz verb favored in entertainment headlines (e.g., 盛大启幕 'grandly opens/premieres'); compare 开幕 (kāimù), which is more standard for formal conferences or ceremonies.

rootFamily.gloss: to open a ceremony or exhibition (lit. open the curtain)
to lower the curtain, come to a close

启用.etymology: A coordinative/serial verb compound (啟用 / 启用, qǐyòng) combining 启 (qǐ, traditional 啟, 'to open, initiate, commission') and 用 (yòng, 'to use, employ, put into service'). Historically in Literary Chinese, it overlapped with 起用 (qǐyòng, 'to recall or appoint an official to office'), before modern orthography largely differentiated 启用 ('to bring facilities, equipment, seals, or systems into service', though also increasingly used for deploying talent) from 起用 ('to appoint or cast personnel').

history.meaning: to commission into service; to appoint or recall a person to official duty
to start using, bring into service (facilities, logos, systems, or newly tapped talent)

morphemes.meaning: to open, initiate, unlock for service (simplified from 啟)

启用.notes: Prescriptive editors distinguish 启用 (for objects, systems, studios, or accounts) from 起用 (for appointing/casting people, e.g. 起用新人 'cast newcomers'), though in media scripts 启用 is frequently used for both.

rootFamily.gloss: to promote or appoint (personnel/actors) to a key role

吵.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 口 ('mouth/voice') + 少 (shǎo/chǎo phonetic): 'noisy, clamorous (of a place or sound); quarrel, argue loudly; disturb with noise'.

history.meaning: noisy; clamor; quarrel vocally

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 吵 (via 萌典)

吵架.etymology: A vernacular verb-object compound (吵架, chǎojià) formed from 吵 (chǎo, 'to make a racket, clamor, wrangle', a phono-semantic character with 口 'mouth' and 少 phonetic, attested from Song–Yuan vernacular onwards) and 架 (jià, originally 'wooden frame or rack', which in Ming–Qing vernacular developed the sense of 'a bout of fighting or mutual altercation', as also seen in 打架 dǎjià 'to brawl'). Because it is syntactically a separable verb-object construction (离合词), aspect markers and measure words insert between the two syllables (e.g., 吵了一架 'had a quarrel').

history.meaning: to engage in a noisy verbal altercation or row
to quarrel, argue, have a verbal fight

morphemes.meaning: to make noise, clamor, squabble verbally

吵架.notes: A classic separable verb (离合词): never say *吵架他; instead use preposition 跟/和 (跟他吵架 'quarrel with him') or insert complements inside (吵起架来, 吵了一架).

rootFamily.gloss: noisy, clamorous; to kick up a fuss
to bicker, squabble (lit. quarrel with mouths)

吵醒.etymology: Resultative verb compound of 吵 ('make noise, disturb with clamor') + 醒 ('wake up'): 'wake someone up by making noise'.

history.meaning: awaken by noise

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 吵醒 (via 萌典)

吸.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 吸. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 吸 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 吸 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 吸 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 吸. The etymology of 吸 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 吸
middle form of 吸
modern form of 吸

吹.etymology: Ancient ideogram attested on Shang oracle bones combining 口 ('mouth') + 欠 (pictograph of a kneeling person with mouth open exhaling breath): 'blow (with the breath or of the wind), play a wind instrument, boast/brag (吹牛), fall through/break up'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: exhale breath through the mouth = blow; play wind instruments; brag

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 吹 (via 萌典)

吹捧.etymology: A vivid coordinative verb compound (吹捧, chuīpěng) uniting two metaphorical actions: 吹 (chuī, literally 'to blow air or play a wind instrument', extended in vernacular Mandarin to 'boast, puff up, hype', as in 吹牛) and 捧 (pěng, literally 'to hold up or cradle in both hands', which in traditional Beijing opera and theater slang meant 'to boost or patrocinate an actor to stardom', as in 捧角儿 pěngjuér 'boost a performer'). Together they mean 'to flatter lavishly, tout, or hype someone up'.

history.meaning: to blow/puff up (吹) and to hold aloft in both hands / patronize an actor (捧)
history.stage: Late Imperial Vernacular & Beijing Opera Argot

history.meaning: to flatter, tout, lavishly praise or hype up (often excessively)

morphemes.meaning: to blow, puff up, boast, hype
to hold up in both hands; to exalt, boost, or flatter (a celebrity or superior)

吹捧.notes: Carries a distinctly pejorative nuance ('sycophantic flattery' or 'overhyping' in media PR); the phrase 互相吹捧 ('mutual flattery /商業互吹') is a staple of entertainment industry banter.

rootFamily.gloss: to groom and promote someone to stardom (showbiz term)
to flatter or hype someone to the skies (often setting them up to fail)

呀.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 口 ('mouth') + 牙 (yá phonetic). Used both as a sentence-initial interjection of surprise ('ah!, oh!') and as the regular phonetic fusion of the sentence-final particle 啊 (a) after a preceding vowel ending in -a, -e, -i, -o, or -ü.

history.meaning: interjection of surprise (yā); vowel-assimilated form of final particle 啊 (ya)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 呀 (via 萌典)

呈现.etymology: A coordinative/resultative literary compound (呈現 / 呈现, chéngxiàn) combining 呈 (chéng, 'to submit respectfully to a superior, to display, to show') and 现 (xiàn, traditional 現, originally 'the luster of jade', extended in Middle Chinese to 'to appear, become visible, manifest'). Used in Literary Chinese to describe how scenery, symptoms, or qualities 'manifest or display themselves', it is now also widely used transitively in media and arts for 'presenting or rendering' a work before an audience.

history.meaning: to manifest, appear, reveal a state or appearance before the eyes
to present, exhibit, take on (an appearance), or bring before viewers

morphemes.meaning: to appear, become visible, manifest (simplified from 現)

呈现.notes: A favorite verb in television/stage production (e.g., 舞台呈现 'stage presentation', 完美呈现给观众 'present完美ly to the audience'); can be both transitive ('present a show') and descriptive ('present a trend').

rootFamily.gloss: to submit or hand in respectfully (a petition or document)
to展现, display, unfold before viewers

cognates.meaning: to tell, inform, announce; accusation/notice in Sino-Japanese compounds

告.etymology: An ancient primary verb (告, gào; Old Chinese *kˤuk / *kˤuks) attested in Shang dynasty Oracle Bone inscriptions, where the graph depicts cattle (牛) over a mouth (口)—interpreted by paleographers since the Shuowen Jiezi as offering a sacrificial ox while praying/reporting to ancestral spirits. From 'ritually report to superiors/spirits', it branched in Classical Chinese into two core senses: (1) 'to inform, declare, tell' (preserved in 告诉, 告别, 广告) and (2) 'to report a grievance to a magistrate, to accuse or sue' (the primary standalone transitive verb meaning in spoken Mandarin today).

history.meaning: to report ritually to spirits or superiors; to announce, inform; to lodge an accusation
to sue in court, press charges against, or report on someone; (in compounds) to tell, announce

morphemes.meaning: to report, inform, announce; to accuse or sue at law

告.notes: As a standalone verb in modern spoken Mandarin, 告 almost always means 'to sue' or 'to tell on someone' (e.g., 我去法院告你 'I'll sue you in court'); for ordinary 'to tell', use the disyllabic 告诉 (gàosu).

告诉.etymology: Coordinative verb compound of 告 ('report, announce, declare') + 诉 (訴, 'recount, inform, appeal', neutral tone su in this word): 'tell, inform, let someone know'.

history.meaning: report an accusation or grievance
tell; inform

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 告诉 (via 萌典)

告辞.etymology: A Classical Chinese verb-object / coordinative compound (告辭 / 告辞, gàocí) combining 告 (gào, 'to inform respectfully, announce') and 辞 (cí, traditional 辭, 'speech, words; to decline; to take leave, depart'). Originally denoting the formal words spoken when taking leave of a host or resigning from an official post in pre-modern China, it grammaticalized into a polite, slightly formal intransitive verb meaning 'to bid farewell and depart'.

history.meaning: to state one's reasons for declining or departing; to formally announce one's departure from a host or office
to take leave; to say goodbye and depart (polite/formal)

morphemes.meaning: words of parting; to take leave, depart (simplified from 辭)

告辞.notes: Polite and slightly formal or literary (e.g., 先行告辞 'I shall take my leave first'); in casual internet and youth slang, 告辞 ('I'm outta here!') is often used humorously to exit an awkward situation.

rootFamily.gloss: to resign from a job (lit. take leave of an official post)
to decline politely, excuse oneself from

呗.etymology: A colloquial sentence-final modal particle (呗, bei, traditional 唄). The character 唄 was originally coined in medieval Buddhist translation texts as a phono-semantic transcription of Sanskrit pāṭha / bhasa ('Buddhist liturgical chanting', read bài, as in 梵呗 fànbài). In late imperial and modern Northern Mandarin, the character was borrowed phonetically (假借) to write a neutral-tone sentence-final particle (probably derived from a weakened fusion of 吧/罢 ba + 欸 ei) signaling either 'it's obvious, what else would you expect?' or reluctant acquiescence ('fine, might as well').

history.meaning: Buddhist hymn or liturgical chanting (loan from Prakrit/Sanskrit)
sentence-final modal particle marking obviousness ('obviously!') or reluctant resignation ('might as well')

morphemes.meaning: sentence-final modal particle indicating obviousness or resigned acceptance (traditional 唄)

呗.notes: Pronounced in the neutral tone (bei); marks casual spoken dialogue and conveys either 'duh, obviously' or 'well, if we have no choice, let's just do it'. Never use in formal writing.

rootFamily.gloss: modal particle for suggestions or assumptions (closely related in function)
sentence-final particle of obviousness (more formal/southern counterpart)

cognates.meaning: Sino-Vietnamese cognate roots (typically nhân viên is used for staff)

员工.etymology: A modern coordinative / modifier-head nominal compound (員工 / 员工, yuángōng) combining 员 (yuán, traditional 員, originally a bronze cauldron ding above a circle, meaning 'round, number/quota', which evolved in Tang–Song Chinese into a suffix for personnel or officials, e.g., 官员, 人员) and 工 (gōng, originally a carpenter's square, meaning 'artisan, worker, labor'). Emerging in 20th-century commercial and enterprise Chinese as an umbrella term encompassing both white-collar clerical personnel (职员 zhíyuán) and manual workers (工人 gōngrén), it became the standard modern corporate word for 'employee, staff member'.

history.meaning: personnel/officials on a roster (員) and artisans/laborers (工)
employees, staff members of a company or institution collectively and individually
history.stage: Modern Standard Mandarin (20th–21st century corporate usage)

morphemes.meaning: member of a staff or organization, personnel (simplified from 員)

员工.notes: The universal corporate term for 'employee/staff' in modern businesses (compare 职员 'office clerk/white-collar staff' and 人员 'personnel' in bureaucratic contexts).

rootFamily.gloss: personnel, staff (often used in categories like 工作人员 'working staff')

员工手册.etymology: A four-character modifier-head nominal compound (員工手冊 / 员工手册, yuángōng shǒucè) combining 员工 (yuángōng, 'employee, staff') and 手册 (shǒucè, 'handbook, manual', literally 'hand-volume'). Within 手册, 册 (cè, traditional 冊) is an ancient pictograph of bamboo slips bound together with leather thongs to form a book, while 手 ('hand') specifies a compact reference volume kept ready at hand. Together, the compound translates modern corporate HR terminology ('employee handbook').

history.meaning: a portable pocket book or manual kept at hand for reference
employee handbook; corporate manual detailing company rules, policies, and benefits

morphemes.meaning: employee, staff member (simplified from 員工)
hand; portable, held in the hand
booklet, bound volume, register (originally bound bamboo slips)

员工手册.notes: Standard HR document given during onboarding (入职培训); in workplace dramas like *Behind the Scenes*, citing the 员工手册 often signals bureaucratic rule-enforcing.

cognates.meaning: company cafeteria, employee canteen (sharing the Sino-Japanese head 食堂)

员工食堂.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (員工食堂 / 员工食堂, yuángōng shítáng) combining 员工 (yuángōng, 'employee, staff') and 食堂 (shítáng, 'dining hall, canteen, cafeteria', literally 'eating-hall'). The head word 食堂 originated in medieval Chinese Buddhist monasteries (and was borrowed into Japanese as shokudō) to denote the monastic refectory or communal dining hall where monks took meals, before generalizing in modern East Asia to institutional and corporate cafeterias.

history.meaning: communal dining hall or refectory in a Buddhist monastery or noble household
staff canteen, employee cafeteria in a company or institution

morphemes.meaning: employee, staff member (simplified from 員工)
hall, large room in a building complex

员工食堂.notes: In Chinese workplace culture and dramas, the quality of a company's 员工食堂 is a frequent topic of office gossip and a benchmark of corporate welfare (福利).

员工餐.etymology: A compact modifier-head compound (員工餐 / 员工餐, yuángōngcān) formed from 员工 (yuángōng, 'employee, staff') and the productive bound head 餐 (cān, 'meal, food', originally a Classical Chinese verb/noun meaning 'to eat, swallow; prepared meal'). Patterned on modern catering compounds with -餐 (such as 工作餐 'working meal', 快餐 'fast food', 自助餐 'buffet'), it refers to the meals provided to staff by a restaurant, film crew, or company.

history.meaning: to eat or swallow; a cooked meal or food ration
staff meal; meal provided for employees at a workplace or restaurant

员工餐.notes: In restaurants and hospitality, 员工餐 is the daily family meal cooked for staff before service; on film/TV sets, crew meals are more commonly called 盒饭 (héfàn, 'boxed meals') or 工作餐 (gōngzuòcān).

rootFamily.gloss: working meal, business lunch/box meal on duty

呢.etymology: Sentence-final particle used for bounce-back follow-up questions ('And what about X?' 你呢？) and for highlighting an ongoing state ('right now'). Written with 口 ('mouth') plus 尼 (ní phonetic), its conversational particle uses are richly attested in Qing vernacular novels such as Honglou Meng.

history.meaning: follow-up question and ongoing-state particle

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 呢 (via 萌典)

周.etymology: Ancient character attested on Shang oracle bones and Zhou bronzes (showing closely planted fields 田 with口, and also merging 週 'go around a full cycle'): 'all around, circumference, complete/thorough, cycle, week; the Zhou Dynasty (c. 1046–256 BCE) and common Chinese surname Zhou'.

history.meaning: closely tended field; Zhou state/dynasty; surname; all around
surname Zhou; week; circumference; thorough

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 周 (via 萌典)

周年.etymology: '周年' (zhōunián, anniversary) combines '周' (cycle, complete circuit) and '年' (year). In classical contexts, '周' often referred to a complete revolution, such as celestial movements. The term '周年' originally denoted a full year passing, often used in the context of mourning rituals in imperial China, such as the one-year anniversary of a parent's death. In modern times, its semantic scope expanded to cover any significant annual commemoration. It is now commonly used for celebrations of businesses, marriages, and historical events.

history.meaning: anniversary

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 周年

周期.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-compound (週期 / 周期, zhōuqī) combining 周 (zhōu, often written 週 in traditional script for this sense, meaning 'a full circuit, revolution, circumference, complete turn') and 期 (qī, 'appointed time, fixed interval, phase'). While both roots are ancient in Chinese calendrical astronomy (where 周天 meant a full celestial revolution), 周期 was standardized in Meiji-era Japan (周期 shūki) to translate Western scientific 'period/cycle' (in physics, chemistry's 周期表 'periodic table', and economics) and re-entered modern Mandarin, where it extended to media/industrial 'production cycle or timeframe'.

history.meaning: a complete revolution or circuit (周/週) and a fixed calendrical interval (期)
recurring period or oscillation cycle in physics, astronomy, and chemistry
history.stage: Meiji Japanese Scientific Coinage & Return Loan (late 19th–early 20th c.)

history.meaning: cycle, period; production timeframe or project turnaround cycle

morphemes.meaning: complete circuit, revolution, full turn (traditional also 週)
fixed interval of time, phase, period

周期.notes: In film, TV, and business contexts, 制作周期 (zhìzuò zhōuqī) or 项目周期 frequently means 'production timeframe / turnaround schedule' rather than a strictly repeating loop.

rootFamily.gloss: to go round and begin again, move in endless cycles

周末.etymology: Temporal compound of 周 (週, 'week, seven-day cycle') + 末 ('tip of a tree -> end, final part'): 'weekend'.

history.meaning: end of the week; weekend

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 周末 (via 萌典)

味.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 味. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 味 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 味 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 味 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 味. The etymology of 味 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 味
middle form of 味
modern form of 味

cognates.meaning: taste, flavor, charm (sharing the root 味)

味儿.etymology: The rhotacized (儿化, érhuà) vernacular Northern Mandarin noun form of 味 (wèi, Old Chinese *mət-s, 'taste, flavor, smell', written with 口 'mouth' and phonetic 未 wèi) plus the diminutive nominal suffix 儿 (-r, written 兒 in traditional script, originally meaning 'child'). In Mandarin phonology, attaching -r causes the coda of wèi to drop and the nucleus to rhotacize into [wɚ˥˩] (wèir), converting the bound/literary root 味 into a free colloquial noun meaning 'taste, smell, odor, or distinctive vibe/flair'.

history.meaning: taste, flavor (one of the Five Flavors 五味); aesthetic relish or meaning in poetry
taste, smell, odor; distinctive style, atmosphere, or authentic feel
history.stage: Late Imperial Beijing & Modern Northern Mandarin

morphemes.meaning: rhotacized noun suffix (儿化韵, simplified from 兒)

味儿.notes: Pronounced as a single rhotacized syllable wèir (not two separate syllables *wèi-ér); besides literal food taste or bad smell (有味儿 'smelly'), it often means 'authentic stylistic vibe' (e.g., 有那味儿了 'now it's got that right vibe!').

rootFamily.gloss: enough, satisfying, up to the mark (lit.够味儿 'enough flavor')

味道.etymology: Compound noun of 味 ('taste, flavor, smell', mouth 口 + 未) + 道 ('way, quality', neutral tone dao in this word): 'taste, flavor (of food/drink); smell, odor, aroma; subtle feel or interest'.

history.meaning: the savor of the Way; flavor
taste; flavor; smell; odor

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 味道 (via 萌典)

呼.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 口 ('mouth') + 乎 (hū phonetic). Attested since Classical Chinese for 'breathe out, exhale' (opposite of 吸 'inhale'), 'call out, shout', and as a vivid interjection/onomatopoeia for sighing in relief ('phew!') or whistling wind.

history.meaning: exhale; call out; cry
exhale; call; interjection 'phew! / whoosh'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 呼 (via 萌典)

呼吁.etymology: A coordinative verb compound (呼籲 / 呼吁, hūyù) uniting 呼 (hū, 'to exhale, cry out, shout, call') and 吁 (yù, traditional 籲, a phono-semantic character with 竹/龠 'bamboo flute' and 頁 'head', meaning 'to implore, appeal to a higher authority, cry out in distress'). In Classical and Imperial Chinese (e.g., 呼吁无门 'nowhere to cry out for redress'), it meant crying out in anguish for help; in modern Mandarin it shifted into a public-sphere verb meaning 'to call upon the public or authorities, to issue an earnest appeal'.

history.meaning: to cry out in distress; to implore or appeal to Heaven or authorities for aid
to publicly appeal for, call upon (the public, industry, or government) to take action

morphemes.meaning: to call out, shout, cry aloud
to implore, appeal earnestly (traditional 籲; merged into 吁 in simplified script)

呼吁.notes: Watch the pronunciation and character merger: here 吁 represents traditional 籲 and is read yù (hūyù), whereas in 长吁短叹 ('sighing and groaning') 吁 is read xū. High-register verb common in media statements and charity campaigns.

rootFamily.gloss: to call out, shout, cheer aloud
to summon, call upon (a spiritual or poetic call)
public appeal or outcry, voice of the people (lit. sound of calling)

呼吸.etymology: Antonymic verb and noun compound pairing 呼 ('exhale, breathe out') + 吸 ('inhale, breathe in'): 'breathe, respiration, breath'. Attested since the Zhuangzi and Huangdi Neijing.

history.meaning: exhale and inhale = breathe, respiration

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 呼吸 (via 萌典)

呼喊.etymology: A synonymous coordinative verb compound (呼喊, hūhǎn) pairing the ancient root 呼 (hū, 'to breathe out, cry aloud, call out', attested since Old Chinese) with the vernacular vocal verb 喊 (hǎn, 'to shout, yell, holler at the top of one's voice', which rose to prominence in Tang–Song vernacular Chinese). The combination reinforces the physical act of projecting the voice loudly to call someone, cheer, or shout slogans.

history.meaning: to call aloud (呼) and to shout or yell (喊)
to shout, yell, call out, or cheer aloud (e.g. in a crowd or audience)

morphemes.meaning: to cry out, call aloud, shout

呼喊.notes: Describes physical shouting or crowd cheering (e.g., 观众大声呼喊 'the audience shouted/cheered loudly'); unlike 呼吁 (hūyù), which is an abstract public appeal, 呼喊 is literal vocal shouting.

rootFamily.gloss: to call out gently or emotionally, summon
to shout loudly, cry out (battle cry or rally)

命.etymology: Ancient character (in oracle-bone and early bronze script identical with 令 lìng, showing a kneeling figure 卩 beneath an assembly roof 亼 receiving a command, later adding 口 'mouth'): 'command, decree; heaven's mandate; life,vitality; fate, destiny'.

morphemes.meaning: command issued to a kneeling person

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: royal/heavenly decree; life; fate/destiny

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 命 (via 萌典)

命令.etymology: A classic synonymous coordinative compound (命令, mìnglìng) attested since Warring States Classical Chinese (such as Mencius and Xunzi). In early bronze inscriptions, 命 (mìng) and 令 (lìng) were originally graphical variants of the same word family (Old Chinese *m-riŋ-s vs. *riŋ-s, depicting a kneeling figure 卩 beneath a mouth 口 or canopy 亼 receiving a royal decree). Once differentiated into two characters—命 ('royal mandate, decree, fate') and 令 ('administrative order, command')—they were compounded together to mean an authoritative command or order.

history.meaning: sovereign decree, royal mandate, or official command issued by a ruler or superior
history.stage: Old Chinese (Warring States texts) & Literary Chinese

history.meaning: order, command, directive (noun); to order or command someone (verb)

morphemes.meaning: order, ordinance, command; to direct or cause

命令.notes: Functions seamlessly as both a noun (听从命令 'obey orders', 下达命令 'issue an order') and a transitive verb (命令他马上回来 'order him to return immediately').

和.etymology: Originally 龢 (a panpipe 龠 + grain 禾, 'musical harmony of tuned pipes'), written 和 (mouth 口 + phonetic 禾 hé): in Classical Chinese 'harmonious, gentle, peace', and from the Han–Tang vernacular onward grammaticalized into the primary coordinating conjunction and comitative preposition 'and; with' (also read huó 'knead flour with water', huò 'mix/blend').

history.meaning: musical harmony; peace; gentle; respond in song
and; together with; peace/harmony

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 和 (via 萌典)

和好.etymology: Coordinative verb compound of 和 ('harmonious, at peace') + 好 ('on good terms, friendly'): 'become reconciled, make up after a quarrel, restore good relations'. Attested since Classical histories (Shiji, Hanshu).

history.stage: Han Classical Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: reconcile; make peace; get back on good terms

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 和好 (via 萌典)

和弦.etymology: Musical compound of 和 ('harmonious; blend in tune', originally mouth 口 + panpipe 禾) + 弦 ('bowstring; musical string of a zither or lute', bow radical 弓 + 玄 xuán). Literally 'strings sounding in harmony', it is the standard modern Chinese term for a musical chord.

history.meaning: tune strings into harmony
musical chord

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 和弦

和稀泥.etymology: An idiomatic three-character verb-object phrase (和稀泥, huò xīní) where 和 is read in the fourth tone huò (originally a distinct verb meaning 'to mix, blend, or stir liquid into powder/earth', contrast hé 'peaceful' and huó 'to knead dough') and 稀泥 (xīní) means 'thin, watery mud or mortar'. Taken from bricklaying and plastering—where watery mud is smeared over cracks without structural support—it became a vivid Beijing/Northern colloquialism for mediating a dispute by papering over conflicts and compromising principles so as not to offend either side.

history.meaning: literally, to mix or stir thin, watery mud/mortar
history.stage: Late Imperial & Early Modern Northern Mandarin Vernacular

history.meaning: to smooth things over unprincipledly; to play peacemaker by glossing over right and wrong

morphemes.meaning: to mix, stir, blend (liquid and mud/powder; read huò in 4th tone)

和稀泥.notes: Crucial pronunciation alert: 和 here MUST be pronounced huò (4th tone), never hé! A person who habitually does this is called a 老好人 ('people-pleaser') or 和事佬 ('unprincipled peacemaker').

rootFamily.gloss: unprincipled peacemaker who smooths over disputes
to knead dough (here 和 is read huó in the 2nd tone)
thin mud; (figuratively) a helpless or spineless mess (e.g. 烂泥扶不上墙)
