和解.etymology: A Classical Chinese verb compound (和解, héjiě) combining 和 (hé, 'peaceful, harmonious; to make peace') and 解 (jiě, 'to untie a knot, loosen, resolve, dispel'). Attested as early as the Records of the Grand Historian (史记 Shǐjì) and Book of Han for resolving hostilities or untying political/personal feuds peaceably, it was also adopted in modern East Asian legal terminology (alongside Japanese 和解 wakai) for an out-of-court settlement or formal reconciliation.

history.meaning: to make peace and untie/resolve a feud or conflict
to reconcile, become reconciled; (law) to reach an amicable or out-of-court settlement

morphemes.meaning: to untie, resolve, settle (a dispute or knot)

和解.notes: Used across registers: from personal relationships and psychological healing (与自己和解 'reconcile with oneself') to legal/corporate disputes (庭外和解 'settle out of court').

rootFamily.gloss: to mediate, act as peacemaker in a dispute
to resolve, dissolve (a crisis, misunderstanding, or conflict)

cognates.word: hài hòa (reversed order 諧和) / hòa hài

和谐.etymology: An ancient synonymous coordinative compound (和諧 / 和谐, héxié) rooted in Classical Chinese musical acoustics. Both characters originally referred to musical consonance: 和 (hé, written as 龢 in early texts with the panpipe radical 龠) meant different musical notes blending in proportion, while 谐 (xié, traditional 諧, with 言 'speech/sound' and 皆 'all together') meant voices or instruments sounding in unison. Attested in the Book of Documents (尚书 Shàngshū: 八音克谐 'the eight musical timbres can be harmonized') and Zuo Zhuan, it generalized from musical concord to social, interpersonal, and aesthetic harmony.

history.meaning: musical consonance; instruments and voices blending in concord; cordial agreement
harmonious, getting along well, balanced and concordant (interpersonally, socially, or aesthetically)

morphemes.meaning: in unison, concordant, agreeing (simplified from 諧)

和谐.notes: Standard positive adjective for team dynamics, family relations, or visual design; colloquially on the Chinese internet, 被和谐 ('to get harmonized') is also used ironically as a euphemism for content censorship.

rootFamily.gloss: to reconcile, settle a dispute peaceably
concordant, harmonious (especially of music or married couples, e.g. 琴瑟和谐)

咔嗒.etymology: Disyllabic onomatopoeia (read kāda or kādā) written with the mouth radical 口 on both syllables to imitate a crisp mechanical clicking, snapping, or latching sound ('click, clack').

history.meaning: onomatopoeia for a sharp click, latch, or snap

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 咔嗒 (via 萌典)

咕嘟.etymology: Onomatopoeic disyllable formed with the mouth radical 口 on both characters (咕 gū + 嘟 dū) to imitate the low, rhythmic bubbling sound of thick soup, porridge, or tea simmering in a pot.

history.meaning: bubble and simmer softly in a pot
bubble; simmer softly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 咕嘟

咖啡.etymology: Phonetic loanword (transliteration) from European words for 'coffee' (French café / English coffee / Dutch koffie, ultimately from Arabic qahwa via Ottoman Turkish kahve), written with two mouth-radical characters 咖 (kā) + 啡 (fēi) and attested in Chinese since the early 19th century.

morphemes.meaning: transliteration of French café / English coffee

history.stage: 19th-century Qing port cities to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: phonetic borrowing for 'coffee'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 咖啡 (via 萌典)

咖啡厅.etymology: Hybrid compound combining the loanword 咖啡 ('coffee') + 厅 (廳, 'hall, lounge, parlor'): 'café, coffeehouse, coffee lounge'.

history.meaning: coffee lounge; café

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 咖啡厅 (via 萌典)

咖啡杯.etymology: Compound noun combining 咖啡 ('coffee') + 杯 ('cup', wood 木 + 不): 'coffee cup, coffee mug'.

history.meaning: coffee cup

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 咖啡杯 (via 萌典)

咖啡角.etymology: Modern lifestyle compound combining 咖啡 ('coffee', phonetic loan from French *café* / English *coffee* with mouth radical 口) + 角 ('corner; nook', originally a pictograph of an animal horn). Formed on the productive pattern `X + 角` for a dedicated corner area inside an inn, office, or bookstore.

history.meaning: coffee corner; coffee nook

咖啡馆.etymology: Compound noun combining 咖啡 ('coffee') + 馆 (館, 'public establishment, house, shop for food/lodging'): 'coffeehouse, café'.

history.meaning: coffeehouse; café

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 咖啡馆 (via 萌典)

咦.etymology: Exclamatory interjection (read yí with a rising second tone) combining 口 ('mouth') + 夷 (yí phonetic), expressing mild surprise, curiosity, or puzzlement ('eh?, oh?, huh?').

history.meaning: interjection of surprise or questioning ('eh?, huh?')

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 咦 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: consultation, inquiry by an official body or council

咨询.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative verb/noun compound (諮詢 / 咨询, zīxún) originating in the Book of Songs (诗经 Shījīng, poem *Huanghuang Zhe Hua*: 周爰咨询 'everywhere seeking counsel and making inquiries') and glossed in the Zuo Zhuan as 'to consult regarding affairs of state'. Both 咨 (zī, also written 諮 in traditional script with 言 'speech') and 询 (xún, traditional 詢) mean 'to inquire, seek advice, deliberate with others'. In modern Mandarin it denotes professional consultation, advisory services, or customer inquiries.

history.meaning: to seek counsel, inquire broadly, deliberate on affairs of state (attested in Shijing & Zuo Zhuan)
consultation, professional advisory service; to consult or inquire about information

morphemes.meaning: to consult, take counsel, inquire (traditional also 諮)
to ask, inquire into, seek advice (simplified from 詢)

咨询.notes: Do not confuse 咨询 (zīxún, 'consultation / to consult', with 言/口) with its exact homophone 资讯 (zīxùn, 'information / news media', with 讯 'message'). Widely used in 心理咨询 ('psychological counseling') and 管理咨询 ('management consulting').

rootFamily.gloss: information, news, data (related compound sharing 资)

咬.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 口 ('mouth') + 交 (jiāo/yǎo, 'interlock/cross', referring to upper and lower jaws closing together, replacing earlier Classical 齩 with the tooth radical 齒): 'bite, snap at, grip with the teeth; pronounce words; (of gears) mesh'.

history.stage: Han–Tang Chinese (齩 / 咬) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: bite with the teeth; grip; mesh

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 咬 (via 萌典)

咬合.etymology: Compound verb and noun of 咬 ('bite, grip with teeth') + 合 ('close together, fit snugly'): '(of upper and lower teeth, gears, or latch teeth) mesh, occlude, engage tightly'.

history.meaning: occlusion of teeth; meshing/engagement of gears or latches

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 咬合 (via 萌典)

咱.etymology: A colloquial Northern Mandarin first-person inclusive pronoun (咱, zán, also read zá in compounds like 咱家). Attested from Song, Jin, and Yuan dynasty vernacular texts (originally written phonetically as 昝, 喒, or 咱), historical linguists trace 咱 to a phonological contraction (合音 héyīn) of 自家 (zìjiā, 'one's own self/family', widely used in Tang–Song vernacular as a first-person pronoun) or 自己 (zìjǐ). In modern Mandarin, 咱 (and its pluralized form 咱们) is the hallmark Northern inclusive 'we/us' (including both speaker and listener) or an intimate substitute for 'I/me'.

history.form: 自家 → 昝 / 喒 / 咱 (zán / zá)
history.meaning: phonological contraction of 自家 ('oneself / our side') used as first-person pronoun in Song–Yuan vernacular drama and fiction
inclusive 'we, us, our' (including the addressee) or intimate colloquial 'I, me' in Northern Mandarin

morphemes.meaning: we/us (inclusive of listener) or colloquial I/me (contracted from Song–Yuan 自家)

咱.notes: Signals warmth, solidarity, and Northern colloquial rapport by pulling the listener into the same group ('you and I together'), contrasting with 我们 (wǒmen), which can exclude the listener. Often precedes nouns directly without 的 (e.g., 咱爸 'our dad', 咱公司 'our company').

rootFamily.gloss: the two of us (you and I)
I, myself (archaic Song–Ming vernacular pronoun read zájiā)

咱们.etymology: A compound personal pronoun (咱們 / 咱们, zánmen) formed by attaching the Mandarin human plural/collective suffix -们 (-men, traditional -們, which evolved in Song–Yuan vernacular from earlier 懣/每/辈) to the inclusive first-person pronoun root 咱 (zán, itself a Song–Yuan contraction of 自家 'one's own people'). Standard Mandarin grammar codifies a clusivity distinction inherited from Beijing speech: 咱们 is strictly inclusive ('we', including both the speaker and the person spoken to), whereas 我们 can be either exclusive ('we, not you') or general.

history.meaning: inclusive first-person plural pronoun ('we, you and I together') in Yuan–Qing northern vernacular literature (e.g. Dream of the Red Chamber)
we, us, our (inclusive of the listener; also used warmly to mean 'you' or 'I')

morphemes.meaning: inclusive first-person pronoun ('you and I / our side')
collective plural suffix for human pronouns and nouns (simplified from 們)

咱们.notes: Use 咱们 when inviting or including the listener (e.g., 咱们走吧 'let's go!'); NEVER use 咱们 when speaking to an outsider excluded from the action (you cannot say *咱们先走了，再见 to a host staying behind—use 我们 instead).

rootFamily.gloss: the two of us (you and I)
we, us (general or listener-excluding first-person plural)

咱俩.etymology: A colloquial Northern Mandarin dual pronoun compound (咱倆 / 咱俩, zánliǎ) combining the inclusive first-person pronoun 咱 (zán, 'we/us including you') with the fused dual numeral-classifier 俩 (liǎ, traditional 倆, a phonological fusion 合音 of 两个 liǎng gè, 'two + general classifier'). Because 俩 already incorporates the classifier 个 internally, 咱俩 means 'the two of us (you and I)' and never takes a following classifier (*咱俩个 is ungrammatical).

history.meaning: fusion of inclusive 咱 ('we') + 倆 ('two of', contracted from 兩個) in late imperial Beijing speech
history.stage: Late Imperial & Early Modern Beijing Mandarin

history.meaning: the two of us (specifically the speaker and the listener)

morphemes.meaning: two of (fused from 两个 liǎng gè; simplified from 倆)

咱俩.notes: Strictly includes the listener ('you and I'); if talking to a third party about yourself and someone else ('he/she and I, not you'), say 我们俩 (wǒmen liǎ). Remember never to add 个 after 俩!

咸.etymology: Merged simplified graph: in Classical Chinese, 咸 (xián, combining 戌 'axe' + 口 'mouth') meant 'all, completely, together'. Because 鹹 ('salty, salted, briny', combining 鹵 'rock/brine salt' + phonetic 咸 xián) shared the exact sound xián, 咸 was adopted as the simplified character for 'salty, savory'.

history.meaning: brine-salt radical 鹵 + phonetic 咸
salty; salted

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 咸 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: throat (咽 in); to swallow (嚥 en); to choke/sob (咽 etsu)
to swallow (嚥 yeon); throat (咽 in)

咽.etymology: A polysemous and heterophonic character (咽) representing both a native Old Chinese root and a simplified character merger. In Classical Chinese, 咽 had two cognate readings from the same Sino-Tibetan 'throat/swallow' root (*ʔˤin / *ʔˤins / *ʔˤet): (1) yān ('pharynx, throat', as in 咽喉 yānhóu) and (2) yè ('to choke, sob with a constricted throat', as in 呜咽 wūyè). For the verb 'to swallow, gulp down' (yàn), traditional Chinese orthography created the distinct character 嚥 (with 口 'mouth' and phonetic 燕 yàn, 'swallow bird'), which 20th-century simplified Chinese merged back into 咽.

history.meaning: throat/pharynx (yān); to swallow down food or saliva (yàn, later written 嚥); to choke or sob (yè)
to swallow, gulp down (food, saliva, or figuratively one's anger/grief)

morphemes.meaning: to swallow, gulp down (read yàn; corresponds to traditional 嚥)

咽.notes: A classic three-reading character (多音字): read yàn (4th tone) when it is the verb 'to swallow' (咽口水 'swallow saliva', 咽不下这口气 'can't swallow this insult'), yān (1st tone) for the anatomical noun 'throat' (咽喉), and yè (4th tone) in 呜咽 ('to sob/choke').

rootFamily.gloss: to swallow down, gulp down completely
to gobble up, wolf down without chewing (lit. swallow dates whole)
pharynx and larynx, throat; strategic choke point (here read yānhóu)

cognates.meaning: Sino-Vietnamese cognate roots 品 and 牌
cognates.word: phẩm bài (rare; thương hiệu 商標 is standard)

品牌.etymology: A modern modifier-head nominal compound (品牌, pǐnpái) combining 品 (pǐn, 'category, grade, quality, commercial product/commodity', as in 商品, 产品) and 牌 (pái, originally 'wooden signboard, placard, or tally' in Middle Chinese, which in Ming–Qing commerce came to mean a shop's signboard or trademark, as in 招牌 zhāopái and 牌子 páizi). Coined in 20th-century Chinese commercial discourse to translate English 'brand' (distinguishing the broader market identity and reputation of a product line from the strictly legal registration term 商标 shāngbiāo 'trademark'), it is now foundational in marketing and media.

history.meaning: wooden shop signboard or maker's plaque identifying a merchant's wares
commercial brand, make, or corporate/artistic brand identity
history.stage: Modern Standard Mandarin (20th–21st century marketing & commerce)

品牌.notes: In formal business and media contexts (e.g., 品牌方 'the brand/sponsor', 打造个人品牌 'build a personal brand'), always use 品牌; in casual speech for 'what brand/make is this?', 牌子 (páizi) is more conversational.

rootFamily.gloss: shop signboard; signature product or flagship specialty
quality (of a product or person's character)

cognates.meaning: brand value (sharing the Sino-Japanese head 価値 kachi)

品牌价值.etymology: A four-character modifier-head nominal compound (品牌價值 / 品牌价值, pǐnpái jiàzhí) combining 品牌 (pǐnpái, 'commercial brand') with 价值 (jiàzhí, 'value, worth'). While 价 (jià, traditional 價, 'monetary price') and 值 (zhí, 'to be worth, encounter, value') both existed in Literary Chinese, the compound 價值 was standardized in Meiji-era Japan (価値 kachi) as the philosophical and economic translation of Western 'value' (German *Wert* / English *value*) before returning to modern Chinese, where 品牌价值 translates marketing 'brand value / brand equity'.

history.meaning: economic and philosophical value or worth (Meiji translation loan into modern Chinese)
brand value, brand equity (the financial and reputational worth of a brand or IP)

品牌价值.notes: A staple term in media sponsorship, IP valuation, and entertainment management (e.g., 提升节目品牌价值 'elevate the show's brand value', 商业与品牌价值 'commercial and brand value').

rootFamily.gloss: system of values, worldview and outlook on value

品质.etymology: A coordinative compound of 品 (pǐn, "rank, grade, category, character") and 质 (zhì, Traditional 質, "substance, nature, disposition"). In Six Dynasties and Tang literary prose, 品質 denoted a person's innate character, literary cultivation, and court rank; in modern Chinese (reinforced by Japanese 品質 hinshitsu), it expanded to denote the intrinsic quality or calibre of both creative works/products and personal character.

history.meaning: personal disposition, moral and social calibre of an individual
intrinsic quality of goods, artistic productions, or personal character

品质.notes: Slightly more elevated and subjective than 质量 (zhìliàng, objective/technical quality); in media and television production (such as 幕后之王), 品质 often praises the artistic calibre of a show or a person's integrity.

哄.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 口 ('mouth') + 共 (gòng/hōng phonetic). Has three tonal readings in Mandarin: hōng ('roar of many voices/laughter', as in 哄堂大笑), hǒng ('coax, soothe a child, wheedle, trick with sweet words'), and hòng ('create an uproar, disperse in commotion').

history.meaning: roar of voices (hōng); coax, soothe, humor (hǒng); commotion (hòng)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 哄 (via 萌典)

哆音.etymology: Musical compound combining 哆 (duō, phonetic transcription of the solfège syllable 'do', the tonic first note of the scale) + 音 ('musical note, tone'): 'the note Do (or C)'.

history.meaning: the solfège note Do / C tone

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 哆音 (via 萌典)

哇.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 口 ('mouth') + 圭 (guī/wā phonetic). Used since Han–Medieval Chinese for the sound of crying or vomiting, and in modern Mandarin as the everyday interjection of amazement or admiration ('wow!, whoa!') and as the sentence-final particle assimilated from 啊 after -u or -ao.

history.meaning: sound of wailing or retching
interjection 'wow!' (wā); final particle after -u/-ao (wa)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 哇 (via 萌典)

哈.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 口 ('mouth') + 合 (hé/hā phonetic): 'breathe out with open mouth, yawn (打哈欠), bend over (哈腰)' and the universal onomatopoeia for laughter ('ha!').

history.meaning: exhale with open mouth; laugh 'ha!'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 哈 (via 萌典)

哈哈.etymology: Reduplicated onomatopoeia from 哈 ('ha'): imitates hearty open-mouthed laughter ('haha!') and functions as a colloquial noun in 打哈哈 ('joke around, laugh something off').

history.meaning: sound of hearty laughter 'haha!'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 哈哈 (via 萌典)

响.etymology: Phono-semantic character (traditional 響, combining 鄉 xiāng phonetic + 音 'sound'; simplified 响 uses 口 'mouth' + 向 xiàng phonetic): originally 'echo, reverberate' (as in Laozi's 音声相和 and 影响 'shadow and echo'), then 'make a sound, ring, loud, noisy, resonant'.

history.meaning: echo; reverberation; sound
make a sound; ring; loud; classifier for sounds

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 响 (via 萌典)

响声.etymology: Coordinative noun compound of 响 (響, 'reverberating sound, ring') + 声 (聲, 'sound, noise'): 'sound, noise, report'.

history.meaning: sound; noise

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 响声 (via 萌典)

哎呀.etymology: Compound interjection combining 哎 (āi) + 呀 (yā), expressing sudden surprise, dismay, pain, wonder, or impatience ('oh dear!, gosh!, oops!, my goodness!').

history.stage: Yuan–Ming drama & vernacular to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: exclamation of surprise, alarm, or dismay ('oh my!, oops!')

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 哎呀 (via 萌典)

哎哟.etymology: Compound interjection combining 哎 (āi) + 哟 (yō), expressing sudden physical pain, startlement, or teasing surprise ('ouch!, ow!, oh my!').

history.meaning: exclamation of pain or surprise ('ouch!, oh dear!')

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 哎哟 (via 萌典)

哥.etymology: Written with 哥 (gē), originally a phono-semantic graph (doubled 可 kě) used in Old Chinese as an ancient orthographic variant of 歌 (gē, "to sing"). During the Tang dynasty, under the influence of northern pastoralist languages (compare Old Turkic aqa / Mongolic aqa "elder brother, senior male"), 哥 was borrowed phonetically to write the vernacular kinship term for "elder brother" (and occasionally "father" in Tang royal usage), eventually displacing 兄 (xiōng) in spoken Mandarin.

history.meaning: to sing, song (graphic precursor of 歌)
elder brother; father (colloquial Tang kinship address)
elder brother; respectful or friendly address for a male peer or senior

哥.notes: In entertainment and production circles, attaching 哥 after a surname or given name (or calling someone 大哥) signals respect and camaraderie toward a male colleague, director, or senior crew member regardless of blood relation.

rootFamily.gloss: big brother; boss, senior male figure

哥们.etymology: Formed from the kinship root 哥 (gē, "elder brother") plus the collective human plural suffix 们 (men, Traditional 們, grammaticalized in Song–Yuan vernacular from 懣 or 門 "clan, group"). Originally meaning "brothers" (siblings of the same family) in Ming–Qing vernacular fiction, it underwent semantic broadening in northern Mandarin to mean "close male friends, buddies, bros" and can even refer to a single male pal in colloquial speech.

history.meaning: brothers of the same family; band of sworn brothers
buddies, bros; a close male friend

morphemes.meaning: collective human plural or group marker

哥们.notes: Although morphologically plural with 们, 哥们 is frequently used in the singular in colloquial speech (e.g., 他是我好哥们 "he is my good buddy") and in gender-neutral modern slang (女哥们 "female bro/platonic male-style friend").

哥们儿.etymology: The rhotacized (儿化 érhuà) form of 哥们 (gēmen), combining 哥 ("elder brother"), the collective suffix 们 ("group, plural"), and the diminutive/affectionate retroflex suffix 儿 (-r, reduced from 兒 "child, small thing"). In Beijing and northern Mandarin phonology, the suffix 儿 merges with the preceding syllable 们 to produce [kɤ˥.mər˧], imparting a warm, informal, and idiomatic northern register meaning "close buddy, pal, bro".

history.meaning: brothers; sworn buddies in Beijing vernacular
close pal, buddy, bro (colloquial northern Mandarin)

哥们儿.notes: In spoken Beijing and northern Chinese dialogue, 哥们儿 is strongly preferred over non-rhotacized 哥们, and often serves as a casual vocative ("Hey man / Hey bro!") to address a male stranger or coworker.

rootFamily.gloss: code of brotherhood, personal loyalty to friends

哥哥.etymology: Reduplicated kinship noun from 哥 (doubling 可 kě; originally meant 'sing/voice'—the ancestor of 歌 'song'). During the Tang dynasty, northern Chinese adopted 阿哥 / 哥哥 (possibly influenced by or converging with Inner Asian kinship terms like Old Turkic aqa) to replace Classical 兄 as the everyday word for 'elder brother'.

history.meaning: elder brother (replacing Classical 兄 in everyday speech)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 哥哥 (via 萌典)

哦.etymology: Phono-semantic interjection combining 口 ('mouth') + 我 (wǒ/ó/ò phonetic). Read ó (rising tone) for questioning surprise or dawning realization ('oh really?, is that so?'), and ò (falling tone) for acknowledgment and understanding ('oh, I see').

history.meaning: interjection of questioning surprise (ó) or realization (ò)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 哦 (via 萌典)

哪.etymology: Interrogative determiner ('which?'), written with 口 ('mouth') beside 那 to distinguish rising third-tone nǎ ('which?') from falling fourth-tone nà ('that'). Followed by a measure word (哪个 'which one?', 哪间房 'which room?') or 里/儿 (哪里 / 哪儿 'where?').

history.meaning: interrogative 'which?'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 哪 (via 萌典)

哪个.etymology: A determiner-classifier compound combining the interrogative stem 哪 (nǎ / něi, "which", differentiated graphically with 口 from the older demonstrative/interrogative 那 nà) and the general classifier 个 (gè, Traditional 個/箇, originally "bamboo stalk", later generalized as the default classifier for individuals and items). Notice that the spoken pronunciation něige arose as a phonological fusion of 哪 (nǎ) + 一 (yī, "one") + 个 (gè).

history.meaning: which one (written without the口 radical before modern orthographic differentiation)
which; which one; who (colloquial)

哪个.notes: Can be pronounced nǎge or (via fusion with 一) něige; in colloquial dialogue, 哪个 can also stand alone as "who?" (e.g., 哪个说的？ "Who said that?").

哪些.etymology: A determiner-classifier compound of the interrogative morpheme 哪 (nǎ, "which", derived from medieval interrogative 那) and the plural/indefinite quantifier 些 (xiē, "some, a few, a small amount", which grammaticalized from a clause-final particle in Chu dialect into a measure for small quantities or plural groupings by the Tang–Song period). Together they ask "which ones" when referring to multiple items or people.

history.meaning: which ones; those ones (written identically with 那 before modern orthographic split)
which ones (interrogative plural pronoun/determiner)

morphemes.meaning: plural or indefinite quantity marker (some, several)

哪些.notes: Unlike 哪个 (which asks about a single item or requires a noun), 哪些 inherently asks for a plural list or subset and cannot be followed by another classifier.

哪位.etymology: A determiner-classifier compound composed of the interrogative stem 哪 (nǎ, "which") and the honorific human classifier 位 (wèi, originally "court rank, official seat, standing place" in Old Chinese, depicting a person 人 standing 立 at their appointed station). Because addressing a person directly seemed overly blunt, referencing their "seat" or "station" (位) became a polite classifier for people in Tang–Song vernacular.

history.meaning: which gentleman/person (early vernacular prior to 哪/那 distinction)
which person, who (polite interrogative pronoun)

morphemes.meaning: polite classifier for people (lit. seat, position)

哪位.notes: Standard polite way to ask "Who is it?" on the phone or in professional workplace settings (e.g., 请问您是哪位？ "May I ask who is calling?"), contrasting with the blunter 谁 (shéi).

哪儿.etymology: Spoken northern Mandarin rhotacized (儿化 érhuà) form of 哪里 ('where?'), combining the interrogative root 哪 ('which?') + the retroflex locative suffix 儿 (-r, contracted from 里/儿): 'where?, wherever, anywhere'.

history.stage: Qing Beijing vernacular to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: where? (rhotacized spoken equivalent of 哪里)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 哪儿 (via 萌典)

哪回.etymology: A determiner-classifier compound formed from the interrogative root 哪 (nǎ, "which") and the verbal/temporal classifier 回 (huí, originally a spiral pictograph meaning "to revolve, to turn around, to return"). During the Tang and Song dynasties, 回 developed from "a cycle or turn" into a vernacular measure word for occurrences, episodes, or chapters (compare 章回小说), yielding 哪回 "which time, which occasion".

history.meaning: which occasion; that time (in Yuan–Ming vernacular storytelling)
which time, when (colloquial interrogative)

哪回.notes: More colloquial and conversational than 哪次 (nǎ cì); frequently used in rhetorical questions to mean "when have I ever not..." (e.g., 哪回不是我帮你善后？ "Which time wasn't it me cleaning up your mess?").

哪怕.etymology: A lexicalized rhetorical verb-object/adverb-verb construction from 哪 (nǎ, rhetorical interrogative "how, where, what") and 怕 (pà, "to fear, to dread"). Literally asking "what is there to fear (even if)?" or "how could one fear...", it grammaticalized in Song–Yuan vernacular into a concessive conjunction meaning "even if, even though, no matter how", introducing a hypothetical extreme case.

history.meaning: what is there to fear; even if (in Song–Yuan vernacular texts)
even if, even though (concessive conjunction)

morphemes.meaning: to fear, to be afraid of

哪怕.notes: Typically paired with 也 (yě), 都 (dōu), or 还 (hái) in the main clause (哪怕……也…… "even if X, still Y") to emphasize determination or an extreme concession.

rootFamily.gloss: for fear that, lest; I'm afraid that

哪敢.etymology: A modifier-head rhetorical compound of 哪 (nǎ, rhetorical interrogative adverb "how, where") and the modal verb 敢 (gǎn, "to dare, to have the audacity"). Literally meaning "how could [I/one] dare?", it functions both as an emphatic rhetorical denial in dialogue and as a polite self-deprecating formula similar to Classical 豈敢 (qǐgǎn) or colloquial 不敢当 (bùgǎndāng).

history.meaning: how could one dare (vernacular equivalent of Classical 豈敢)
how would I dare; I wouldn't dare (rhetorical/polite expression)

哪敢.notes: Frequently used in workplace banter—either earnestly to show deference to a boss or playfully/sarcastically ("Oh, how would I ever dare offend you!").

rootFamily.gloss: even if (lit. what is there to fear)
I don't deserve the compliment, you flatter me

哪边.etymology: A determiner-localizer compound combining the interrogative stem 哪 (nǎ, "which") and the spatial localizer 边 (biān, Traditional 邊, originally "cliff edge, border, margin" in Old Chinese, later bleached into a directional suffix meaning "side, direction, area"). Together they inquire about location, direction, or faction ("which side, which way, where").

history.meaning: which side; over there (prior to modern graphic split between 哪 and 那)
which side, which way, which faction

哪边.notes: Besides physical direction ("which way?"), 哪边 often asks about corporate or interpersonal allegiance in office drama (e.g., 你到底站哪边？ "Whose side are you on anyway?").

哪里.etymology: Standard question word meaning 'where?', combining 哪 ('which?') and 里 ('inside, place'). Stays in the exact sentence slot of the answer rather than moving to the front: 电脑在哪里？ ('The computer is where?').

history.meaning: where; what place

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 哪裡 (via 萌典)

哭.etymology: Ancient ideogram combining two mouths (吅, 'cry out loudly') above 犬 ('dog', originally depicting a hound howling or wailing at ritual mourning): 'weep aloud, cry, sob'. In Classical Chinese 哭 specifically meant 'weep with vocal sound' (as opposed to 泣 'shed silent tears'); in Mandarin it is the general verb for 'cry'.

history.meaning: wail aloud in grief
cry; weep

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 哭 (via 萌典)

哼.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 口 ('mouth') + 亨 (hēng phonetic). Read hēng as a verb ('hum a tune softly, groan, snort through the nose') and read哼 (hng) as an interjection of disdain, skepticism, or dissatisfaction ('hmph!,umph!').

history.meaning: hum, groan, snort (hēng); interjection 'hmph!' (hng)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 哼 (via 萌典)

唬.etymology: A phono-semantic compound combining the mouth radical 口 (kǒu, indicating vocal roaring or verbal speech) and the phonetic-semantic component 虎 (hǔ, "tiger", Old Chinese *qʰˤraʔ). Originally an onomatopoeic and descriptive verb in Classical texts meaning "to roar like a tiger" or the sound of a beast growling, by the Yuan and Ming dynasties it evolved in northern vernacular into "to scare, to intimidate, to bluff" through loud bluster or empty threats.

history.meaning: roar of a tiger; to roar or bellow
to startle, to intimidate, to bluff or hoodwink with bluster

morphemes.meaning: to bluff, to intimidate, to scare (lit. tiger's roar)

唬.notes: Very common in colloquial dialogue when calling someone's bluff: 你别唬我 ("Don't try to bluff/scare me!") or 唬人 ("to bluff people, to look intimidating on the surface").

rootFamily.gloss: to bluff or deceive people, to put on an intimidating front
to scare, to intimidate, to browbeat
to fool, to hoodwink, to bluff

唯一.etymology: A compound of the Classical Chinese restrictive copula/focus particle 唯 (wéi, "only, solely, none other than", also written 惟) and the numeral 一 (yī, "one, single, unified"). Attested in Classical texts (such as the Shangshu and Buddhist scriptures translating Sanskrit eka "one and only"), it literally meant "only one" before stabilizing as an attributive modifier meaning "sole, only, unique".

history.meaning: only one, unified and single-minded; the sole one
only, sole, unique (attributive modifier)

唯一.notes: Functions primarily as an adjective/modifier before nouns (often with 的, e.g., 唯一的选择 "the only choice"), whereas 唯独 (wéidú) is an adverbial focus marker meaning "only [X, to the exclusion of all others]".

rootFamily.gloss: aestheticism; idealistic pursuit of beauty alone
to be the only one in charge, arrogant and bossy

唯独.etymology: A coordinative emphatic compound combining two Classical Chinese restrictive adverbs: 唯 (wéi, "only, solely, exclusively") and 独 (dú, Traditional 獨, "alone, solitary, only"). By pairing two synonymous restrictive morphemes, Literary and early Vernacular Chinese created an emphatic focus adverb meaning "only, exclusively, singling out one exception in contrast to everything else".

history.meaning: only, alone, exclusively (emphatic restrictive adverb)
only, except for (highlighting a sole exception)

唯独.notes: Used to contrast a single exception against a universal rule (e.g., 大家都同意，唯独他反对 "Everyone agreed; only he objected"); never used directly before a noun with 的 like 唯一.

cognates.meaning: to chant, to recite, to advocate
to sing, to chant, to call out

唱.etymology: A phono-semantic compound combining the mouth radical 口 (kǒu, indicating vocalization) and the phonetic component 昌 (chāng, Old Chinese *tʰjaŋ, also carrying the semantic notion of "clear, resonant, flourishing"). In Old Chinese (originally often written 倡), 唱 meant "to lead a song, to intone first so others may follow in harmony" (as in 一唱三叹 and 唱和), before generalizing in Middle and Modern Chinese to "to sing" or "to call out loudly".

history.meaning: to lead in singing, to initiate a chant or melody
to sing, to chant; to call out loudly

morphemes.meaning: to sing, to chant; to call out

唱.notes: In music and showbiz terminology, 唱 forms the core of compounds like 主唱 ("lead vocalist"), 假唱 ("lip-syncing"), and 唱功 ("vocal technique/singing skill").

唱歌.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound uniting the verb 唱 (chàng, "to sing, to intone vocally") with its cognate object 歌 (gē, "song, melody", originally written 哥 in Old Chinese). Because Mandarin disprefers monosyllabic transitive verbs without an explicit object in neutral intransitive contexts, 歌 serves as a dummy or default object so 唱歌 functions as the citation verb "to sing".

history.meaning: to chant or sing a song
to sing (general intransitive verb-object compound)

唱歌.notes: As a separable verb-object (离合词 líhécí) compound, aspect particles, durations, and modifiers must be inserted between 唱 and 歌 (e.g., 唱了一首歌 "sang a song", 唱得好听的歌).

商业.etymology: Compound noun of 商 ('trade, commerce, merchant', from the Shang dynasty people who became famous across Zhou China as traveling traders) + 业 (業, 'occupation, industry, sector'): 'commerce, trade, business'.

history.meaning: the occupation of merchants
commerce; business; commercial

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 商业 (via 萌典)

商业利益.etymology: A four-character modifier-head nominal phrase composed of two disyllabic Sino-compounds: 商业 (shāngyè, Traditional 商業, from 商 "commerce, merchant, tracing to the traders of the Shang dynasty" + 業 "enterprise, profession, industry") modifying 利益 (lìyì, a coordinative compound of 利 "profit, benefit, sharp advantage" + 益 "increase, gain, benefit", originally depicting water overflowing a vessel 皿). Together they denote "commercial interests, financial profit".

history.meaning: mercantile trade (商業) and benefit/advantage (利益) as independent compounds
commercial interests, business profit motives

商业利益.notes: A central tension in media dramas like 幕后之王: creative producers frequently debate how to balance 艺术品质 ("artistic quality") against 商业利益 ("commercial profit/sponsor demands").

商业活动.etymology: A four-character modifier-head compound combining 商业 (shāngyè, Traditional 商業, "commerce, business", from 商 "trade, merchant" + 業 "industry, occupation") with 活动 (huódòng, Traditional 活動, "activity, event, movement", from 活 "alive, active" + 動 "to move, to act", reinforced in its modern sociological sense "organized event/activity" via Meiji Japanese 活動 katsudō). In modern Chinese entertainment, it specifically denotes paid promotional events or brand appearances.

history.meaning: commercial trade (商業) and dynamic movement/activity (活動)
commercial activity; paid brand promotion or celebrity endorsement event

商业活动.notes: In the Chinese entertainment industry, 接商业活动 (often abbreviated to 商演 shāngyǎn for commercial performances) refers to celebrities attending ribbon-cuttings, brand launches, or promotional gigs for pay.

商品.etymology: A modifier-head compound of 商 (shāng, "trade, commerce, merchant", historically derived from the people of the fallen Shang dynasty who became itinerant traders during the Zhou dynasty) and 品 (pǐn, "article, item, category of goods"). Attested in Song dynasty texts for "merchant wares" and later standardized across East Asia (alongside Japanese 商品 shōhin as the translation of English/Marxian "commodity") to mean "merchandise, commercial product".

history.meaning: wares or grades of goods traded by merchants
commodity, merchandise, commercial product (economics and retail)

商品.notes: Refers specifically to goods produced for exchange on the market ("commodities/merchandise"), whereas 产品 (chǎnpǐn) focuses on the production side ("manufactured or creative product").

cognates.meaning: to estimate, to deliberate, to weigh options
to negotiate, to discuss, to deliberate

商量.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound pairing 商 (shāng, "to deliberate, to reckon, to consult", related to assessing prices in trade and musical pitch calculation) and 量 (liáng, pronounced輕聲 liang in this word, originally "to measure volume with a vessel, to weigh, to estimate"). First attested in Six Dynasties and Tang texts with the sense "to weigh and estimate carefully", it evolved into the everyday Mandarin verb "to discuss, to talk over, to consult".

history.meaning: to measure, estimate, and deliberate carefully
to talk over, to discuss and reach mutual agreement (with neutral tone on 量)

morphemes.meaning: to consult, to deliberate, to discuss
to measure, to weigh, to estimate

商量.notes: More conversational and collaborative than 讨论 (tǎolùn, formal discussion) or 协商 (xiéshāng, official negotiation); common in phrases like 好商量 ("easy to talk over / negotiable") and 有事好商量.

rootFamily.gloss: to discuss and decide, to confer (more formal)
to discuss, to talk over (slightly more formal)

啊.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 口 ('mouth') + 阿 (ā phonetic). Serves both as a tone-bearing sentence-initial interjection ('ah!, oh!, what?, huh?') and, in neutral tone (a), as Mandarin's most common sentence-final modal particle softening statements, questions, reminders, and exclamations.

history.meaning: interjection (ā/á/ǎ/à) and sentence-final modal particle (a)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 啊 (via 萌典)

啥.etymology: Written with 口 (kǒu, colloquial speech marker) + 舍 (shě, phonetic), 啥 (shá) is a contraction and phonological descendant of the Middle Chinese interrogative pronoun 什摩 / 什麼 (shénme, early vernacular pronunciation *dʑiɪp-mwa > *ɕa-ma > shá), which itself derived from 什物 ("assorted things, what thing"). In northern, central, and southwestern Mandarin dialects, the disyllabic 什么 fused into the single syllable 啥 ("what").

history.meaning: what (disyllabic vernacular interrogative pronoun in Tang–Song texts)
what (monosyllabic colloquial contraction in northern and central Mandarin)

啥.notes: Highly colloquial and ubiquitous in spoken northern Chinese (e.g., 干啥？ "What are you doing?", 没啥 "It's nothing"), though avoided in formal written prose where 什么 is standard.

啦.etymology: Sentence-final fusion particle (合音字, read la) combining the perfective/change-of-state particle 了 (le) + the exclamatory/emphatic particle 啊 (a): 'le + a = la', adding lively finality, reassurance, or enumeration.

history.meaning: phonetic contraction of 了 (le) + 啊 (a)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 啦 (via 萌典)

啪.etymology: Phono-semantic onomatopoeia combining 口 ('mouth/sound') + 拍 (pāi, 'slap, clap'): imitates a sharp slapping, snapping, popping, or slamming sound ('smack!, snap!, bang!, pop!').

history.meaning: onomatopoeia for a sharp slap, bang, or snap

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 啪 (via 萌典)

喂.etymology: Written with 喂 (composed of 口 kǒu "mouth" + 畏 wèi phonetic), a character that serves two etymologically distinct roles in Modern Mandarin: (1) an exclamation/interjection (pronounced wéi when answering the telephone or seeking attention, and wèi when calling out "hey!"), which originated as a natural vocal call for attention and was standardized in the early 20th century as China's telephone greeting; and (2) the verb wèi ("to feed", historically written 餧 with the food radical 食).

history.meaning: to feed animals or children; also used for vocal exclamations of fear or calling out
hello (on the telephone, wéi); hey! (calling attention, wèi); to feed (wèi)

喂.notes: Pronounced in the rising 2nd tone (wéi) for polite telephone greetings ("Hello?"), but in the falling 4th tone (wèi) when shouting "Hey!" to get someone's attention or when used as the verb "to feed".

rootFamily.gloss: to feed and raise, to rear
to feed (food to a child, patient, or pet)

cognates.meaning: dealing with the aftermath, remedial measures
to remedy the aftermath, post-crisis settlement

善后.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound from Classical Chinese 善 (shàn, used here as a causative/putative verb "to make good, to handle well, to rectify") and 后 (hòu, Traditional 後, "what comes after, the aftermath, subsequent consequences"). First prominently attested in the Zuozhuan and later in Sunzi's Art of War commentary (善其後 "to make good its aftermath"), it means "to clean up the aftermath, to deal with problems left behind after a crisis".

history.meaning: to handle subsequent affairs well, to rehabilitate after war or disaster
to clean up the aftermath, to do damage control after a crisis or mistake

morphemes.meaning: to handle well, to make good, to mend

善后.notes: In media, PR, and crisis-management contexts (central to 幕后之王), 善后 refers to "damage control" or "cleaning up a mess" after a live-broadcast mishap or celebrity scandal.

rootFamily.gloss: to resolve or settle a matter properly

善良.etymology: A coordinative adjectival compound joining two synonymous Classical Chinese moral roots: 善 (shàn, "virtuous, good, auspicious", originally written 譱 with 羊 "sheep, auspiciousness" and 言 "speech") and 良 (liáng, "good, fine, upright, innately pure"). Attested since the Book of Han (漢書) and Three Kingdoms period, it describes a person's disposition as "kind-hearted, pure, benevolent, and free of malice".

history.meaning: virtuous, upright, and benevolent in moral character
kind-hearted, good and honest, gentle

善良.notes: Describes deep, innate moral goodness and kindness of heart (心地善良), rather than mere social politeness or friendliness (for which 友好 or 客气 is used).

rootFamily.gloss: to clean up the aftermath (lit. make good the aftermath)

喊.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 口 ('mouth') + 咸 (xián/hǎn phonetic): 'shout, cry out, yell, call someone'. Attested from Han–Tang vernacular and histories.

history.meaning: shout; call out loudly; yell

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 喊 (via 萌典)

喘.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 口 ('mouth/breath') + 耑 (duān/chuǎn phonetic): 'pant, gasp for breath, breathe heavily; asthma (哮喘)'. Attested since the Shijing and medical classics.

history.stage: Old & Classical Chinese (Shijing, Neijing) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: pant; gasp for breath; breathe rapidly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 喘 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: comedy (theatrical/cinematic genre, source of modern Chinese sense)

喜剧.etymology: A modifier-head compound of 喜 (xǐ, "joy, delight, happiness", originally depicting a drum 壴 and a smiling/singing mouth 口) and 剧 (jù, Traditional 劇, originally "intense, severe", later "theatrical play, drama"). Coined as a Meiji-era Japanese *wasei-kango* (喜劇 kigeki) to translate English "comedy" and French "comédie" in symmetrical opposition to 悲劇 (higeki / bēijù, "tragedy"), and rapidly borrowed into modern Chinese theatrical and film vocabulary.

history.meaning: comedy (Meiji Japanese translation of Western theatrical comedy)
comedy (in theater, film, television, and everyday situations)

喜剧.notes: Pairs directly with its antonym 悲剧 (bēijù, "tragedy"); in showbiz, a comedic actor is a 喜剧演员, and "stand-up comedy" is 脱口秀 or 单口喜剧.

喜欢.etymology: Coordinative psychological verb compound of 喜 ('rejoice, delight in', originally a drum 壴 + mouth 口 smiling/singing in celebration) + 欢 (歡, 'joyous, glad', neutral tone huan in this word). In Classical and Tang–Song texts it meant 'feel happy and joyful'; in Mandarin it is the primary transitive verb for 'like, be fond of, love'.

history.meaning: feel joyful and delighted
like; be fond of; feel happy

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 喜欢 (via 萌典)

喝.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 口 ('mouth') + 曷 (hé/hē phonetic). In Classical Chinese, 喝 meant 'shout loudly' (still read hè in 喝彩 'cheer') or 'hoarse voice', while 'drink' was 飲 (yǐn). In Ming–Qing vernacular, 喝 (read hē) replaced 飲 as the everyday Mandarin verb for 'drink (water, tea, soup, alcohol)'.

history.meaning: shout aloud; hoarse
drink (replacing Classical 飲 in spoken Mandarin)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 喝 (via 萌典)

喝不了.etymology: A potential resultative verb construction formed from the action verb 喝 (hē, "to drink", originally "to shout, to wheeze" in Classical Chinese before replacing 飲 yǐn in early Mandarin as the everyday word for drinking), the negative potential infix 不 (bù, "not, cannot"), and the phase/completion complement 了 (liǎo, from the verb 了 "to finish, to complete, to dispose of"). Together, 喝不了 means "unable to finish drinking" or "incapable of drinking".

history.meaning: cannot finish drinking; unable to drink (in Ming–Qing vernacular)
unable to drink; cannot finish drinking (negative potential complement)

morphemes.meaning: to finish, to be able to carry out (pronounced liǎo)

喝不了.notes: Here 了 must be pronounced liǎo (not neutral le); at Chinese business banquets (酒局), saying 我实在喝不了 ("I really can't drink / can't hold any more liquor") is a standard way to decline a toast.

rootFamily.gloss: able to drink, able to finish drinking (affirmative counterpart)
unable to eat or finish eating

喝大酒.etymology: A colloquial verb-object phrase combining 喝 (hē, "to drink") with the modified object 大酒 (dàjiǔ, literally "big alcohol/heavy liquor", from 大 "big, heavy, major" + 酒 "alcoholic beverage", whose graph combines water 氵 with the fermentation jar 酉). In northern Mandarin vernacular, inserting 大 before 酒 intensifies the event as a whole: "to drink heavily, to go out for a serious drinking session or boozy feast".

history.meaning: to drink heavily or attend a lavish drinking banquet (northern colloquialism)

morphemes.meaning: big, heavy, on a grand scale

喝大酒.notes: In northern Chinese slang, 喝大酒 implies not just a casual glass of wine, but a proper, boisterous session of heavy drinking—either to celebrate a major wrap/deal or to blow off steam with close friends.

rootFamily.gloss: to drink alone while brooding or depressed
to get blind drunk, to drink too much

喝茶.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound of 喝 (hē, "to drink", which superseded Literary Chinese 飲 yǐn and 吃 chī "to take tea" in northern Mandarin during the Ming–Qing period) and 茶 (chá, "tea", graphically differentiated during the Tang dynasty under Lu Yu's Classic of Tea 茶經 by removing one stroke from 荼 tú "bitter herb"). Beyond literal tea-drinking, 喝茶 acquired rich cultural extensions in Cantonese dim sum culture and modern bureaucratic slang.

history.meaning: to drink tea (pre-Qing and southern vernacular phrasing)
to drink tea; (figuratively) to chat over tea or be summoned for an official warning talk

喝茶.notes: Besides literally having tea or going for Cantonese dim sum, 请喝茶 ("to invite for tea") is a widespread modern euphemism for being called in for a stern talk or investigation by authorities or regulators.

喝酒.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound pairing the vernacular verb 喝 (hē, "to drink", originally "to wheeze or shout" in Old Chinese before semantically shifting to "to gulp down liquid" in Yuan–Ming Mandarin, replacing Classical 飲酒 yǐnjiǔ) with the default object 酒 (jiǔ, "alcoholic beverage, wine, spirits", composed of water 氵 and the narrow-necked fermentation vessel 酉). It serves as the standard Mandarin verb for drinking alcohol.

history.meaning: to drink fermented spirits or wine (Classical 飲酒; Song–Ming vernacular 吃酒)
to drink alcohol; to attend a drinking banquet

喝酒.notes: Like 唱歌, 喝酒 is a separable verb-object (离合词) compound: modifiers and complements go in between (e.g., 喝了三杯酒 "drank three glasses of alcohol", 喝不喝酒).

rootFamily.gloss: to go out for serious/heavy drinks
drinking party, business banquet involving alcohol

喝闷酒.etymology: A verb-object phrase combining 喝 (hē, "to drink") with 闷酒 (mènjiǔ, Traditional 悶酒, literally "gloomy/stifled alcohol", where 悶 mèn depicts a heart 心 shut inside a door 門, meaning "depressed, stifled,闷悶不樂, bottled-up"). By transferring the drinker's emotional state (闷 "brooding, sulking") onto the noun 酒 ("alcohol"), Chinese creates the vivid idiomatic expression 喝闷酒 "to drink sulkily (often alone) to drown one's sorrows".

history.meaning: to drink alcohol in gloomy silence while nursing grievances (Ming–Qing vernacular novels)
to drink alone while brooding, sulking, or drowning one's sorrows

喝闷酒.notes: Note that 闷 is pronounced in the 4th tone (mèn, "depressed, gloomy") here, not the 1st tone (mēn, "stuffy/airtight"); a classic TV drama trope where a stressed character drinks alone in silence at a bar.

rootFamily.gloss: to go out for heavy drinks

喷泉.etymology: Compound noun of 喷 (噴, 'spurt, gush, spray out', mouth 口 + 賁) + 泉 ('spring of water', originally a pictograph of water flowing out of a cave): 'fountain, gushing spring'.

history.stage: Tang–Song poetry (natural gushing springs) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: gushing spring; architectural fountain

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 喷泉 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: sentence-final modal particle indicating obviousness or completion

喽.etymology: A colloquial Mandarin sentence-final modal particle (喽, Traditional 嘍, lóu / lou), formed as a phono-semantic character with the mouth radical 口 (kǒu, indicating vocalization or speech) and the phonetic component 娄 (Traditional 婁, lóu). Historically attested in Yuan- and Ming-dynasty vernacular drama and fiction as a lively discourse marker, it likely arose through phonetic fusion of the perfective/change-of-state particle 了 (le) with an expressive vowel or final *u/o* coloring, signaling upbeat invitation, brisk completion, or light-hearted obviousness.

history.meaning: phonetic base originally meaning 'to trail, tether, or repeat frequently' in Classical Chinese
colloquial chatter, bird calls, or sentence-final modal particle in Yuan–Ming vernacular literature
upbeat sentence-final particle expressing brisk encouragement, reminders, or cheerful finality

morphemes.meaning: mouth; marks a spoken exclamation or modal particle
phonetic component supplying the lóu reading

喽.notes: Frequently used at the end of brisk imperatives or announcements on television sets and variety shows (e.g., 开工喽 kāigōng lou, 'let's get to work!') to project warmth and momentum without sounding bossy.

rootFamily.gloss: minions, rank-and-file underlings in a gang
mole cricket (colloquial insect name using the same phonetic graph)

嗓门.etymology: Colloquial compound noun from 嗓 ('throat; larynx; voice', mouth 口 + phonetic 桑) + 门 (simplified from 門, 'gate; opening; valve'). By comparing the throat and vocal cords to a gate through which sound issues, 嗓门 came to denote the volume and projection of a person's voice.

history.meaning: throat; vocal volume and projection
voice; volume of one's voice (especially loud)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 嗓门

嗡嗡.etymology: Reduplicated onomatopoeia from 嗡 (mouth 口 + 翁 wēng phonetic), imitating a low continuous droning, humming, or buzzing sound (of bees, insects, machinery, or ringing ears).

history.meaning: buzzing; humming; droning sound

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 嗡嗡 (via 萌典)

嗯.etymology: An onomatopoeic and paralinguistic interjection (嗯, ng / ńg / ňg / ǹg / ēn), graphically constructed with the mouth radical 口 (kǒu, marking a vocal sound) combined with 因 (yīn) as an approximate phonetic indicator. Rather than descending from a lexical Sino-Tibetan root, it directly transcribes a bilabial or velar nasal murmur ([m̩], [n̩], or [ŋ̍]) produced with a closed or nearly closed mouth, whose contour tone shifts its pragmatic force from questioning curiosity (rising ńg) to hesitant reflection (dipping ňg) or firm agreement (falling ǹg).

history.meaning: late vernacular phonetic character coined to transcribe nasal conversational grunts and murmurs
interjection of acknowledgment ('uh-huh, yes'), hesitation ('hmm'), or surprise ('huh?')

morphemes.meaning: mouth; indicates a vocalized sound or interjection
approximate phonetic element pointing to a front/central nasal rime

嗯.notes: Although dictionaries standardize the spelling pronunciation ēn, native speakers in natural dialogue almost universally pronounce it as a syllabic nasal (ǹg or m̀) with the lips closed; falling tone signals 'yes / got it', while rising tone means 'huh? / what did you say?'.

rootFamily.gloss: to groan; a nasal hum of hesitation or pain
informal 'uh-huh' acknowledging what someone just said

嘉宾.etymology: A classical modifier-head compound (偏正结构) composed of 嘉 (jiā, 'auspicious, admirable, fine, praiseworthy') and 宾 (Traditional 賓, bīn, 'guest, visitor', built with the cowrie/valuables component 贝 indicating gift-giving hospitality). Attested at the very dawn of the Chinese literary canon in the *Book of Odes* (*Shijing*, ode *Luming*: 我有嘉宾，鼓瑟吹笙 'I have honored guests; we strum the zither and blow the mouth-organ'), it originally denoted aristocratic guests at ritual banquets and was revitalized in modern broadcast media to designate featured celebrity guests or panelists on variety and talk shows.

history.meaning: noble, virtuous, and auspicious guests entertained at royal or aristocratic ritual banquets
distinguished guest at weddings, state banquets, or literary gatherings
honored guest; featured celebrity guest, panelist, or presenter on a television program or live event

morphemes.meaning: fine, auspicious, admirable, worthy of praise

嘉宾.notes: The standard showbiz and broadcasting term for a guest star or panelist on a variety show (特邀嘉宾 tèyāo jiābīn, 'special guest', or 飞行嘉宾 fēixíng jiābīn, 'flying/episodic guest' vs. 常驻嘉宾 chángzhù jiābīn, 'regular cast member').

rootFamily.gloss: words or deeds worthy of praise; to commend formally
guests and visitors collectively; hotel (宾馆)

嘛.etymology: Sentence-final modal particle (neutral tone ma) combining 口 ('mouth') + 麻 (má phonetic). Marks a point as obvious, reasonable, or something the listener should already know ('well, of course, after all'), or marks a topic pause.

history.meaning: modal particle indicating obviousness ('well, naturally') or topic pause

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 嘛 (via 萌典)

嘱咐.etymology: A coordinative disyllabic verb compound (联合结构) pairing two synonymous speech verbs: 嘱 (Traditional 囑, zhǔ, 'to enjoin, entrust, urge earnestly', formed from 口 'mouth' + 属 shǔ 'to attach/entrust') and 咐 (fù, 'to instruct, exhale/speak to', formed from 口 'mouth' + 付 fù 'to hand over, entrust'). In Classical Chinese the concept was written 属付 (zhǔfù, literally 'to attach and hand over a duty'); during the Tang–Song vernacular transition, the mouth radical 口 was added to both graphs to specify oral admonition and caring instruction passed from an elder, superior, or loved one.

history.meaning: to entrust a charge or responsibility to someone's care
to give earnest verbal instructions or parting admonitions
to instruct, remind caringly, or urge someone to be careful

morphemes.meaning: to enjoin, urge earnestly, entrust verbally
to instruct, hand over a verbal charge

嘱咐.notes: Carries a warm, protective, or earnest emotional coloring (unlike cold administrative 命令 'order'); often used when parents, mentors, or directors remind someone to take care of their health or remember crucial details (千叮咛万嘱咐 'reminding a thousand times').

rootFamily.gloss: last words or dying injunctions; medical orders (医嘱)
to entrust a task or care to someone reliable
to instruct a subordinate to carry something out

cognates.meaning: beak, bill of a bird (kuchibashi, using kanji 嘴)

嘴.etymology: Originally a phono-semantic character 觜 (zǐ / zuǐ) denoting the feather tufts or horns on an owl's head and by extension a bird's pointed beak, later augmented with the mouth radical 口 to form 嘴 (zuǐ). In Classical Chinese, 口 (kǒu) was the standard word for the human mouth while 嘴 meant 'bird's bill' or a projecting spout; during the Tang, Song, and Yuan vernacular shifts, 嘴 underwent semantic broadening from 'pointed beak/snout' to become the primary colloquial Mandarin noun for the human mouth and lips, largely displacing standalone 口 in everyday speech.

history.meaning: horn-like feather tufts on an owl; bird's bill; the Turtle Beak lunar mansion
bird's beak; projecting spout of a vessel; colloquially, the human mouth and lips
mouth, lips, spout, or anything shaped like a projecting mouth; speech habits

morphemes.meaning: mouth; semantic determinative for oral anatomy and speech
owl's horn-tuft or pointed beak (觜, supplying both the zuǐ sound and the core image of a protruding bill)

嘴.notes: In modern Mandarin, 嘴 is the everyday spoken word for 'mouth' (闭嘴 bìzuǐ 'shut up', 亲嘴 qīnzuǐ 'kiss on the lips'), whereas 口 (kǒu) survives mainly in formal idioms, classifiers (一口水 'a mouthful of water'), and written compounds (口腔 'oral cavity').

rootFamily.gloss: picky eater; finicky with food (literally 'beaky/choosy mouth')

嘴上.etymology: A noun-localizer compound (方位结构) formed by attaching the enclitic locative postposition 上 (shàng / shang, 'on, upon, on the surface of') to the somatic noun 嘴 (zuǐ, 'mouth, lips'). Literally 'upon the lips', it underwent a natural metonymic extension in vernacular Mandarin from the physical surface of the mouth to 'in one's outward speech' or 'what one says aloud', systematically contrasted in Chinese rhetoric with 心里 (xīnlǐ, 'in one's heart/mind') or 行动上 (xíngdòng shang, 'in actual deeds').

history.meaning: physically on the lips or around the mouth; figuratively, in outward verbal expression
on one's lips; in what one says aloud (often contrasted with inner feelings or real action)

morphemes.meaning: on, upon; in the domain or medium of

嘴上.notes: Almost always used to highlight a gap between outward talk and inner truth—for example, 嘴上说不要，心里很诚实 ('saying no with one's lips while being very honest in one's heart') or 嘴上功夫 ('mere lip service / fast talk').

rootFamily.gloss: in one's mouth; in one's speech
verbal skill, glib talk without action

嘴型.etymology: A modern modifier-head compound (偏正结构) combining 嘴 (zuǐ, 'mouth, lips') with 型 (xíng, originally 'clay mold for casting metal' from 刑 phonetic + 土 'earth', extended to 'shape, contour, model'). Coined in modern Chinese phonetics, vocal pedagogy, and film/broadcast production, it denotes the visible articulatory configuration and movement of a speaker's or singer's lips when forming vowels and consonants—crucial in television and film post-production for dubbing (配音) and lip-syncing (对嘴型).

history.meaning: articulatory lip shape in vocal training, acting, and phonological description
lip shape, contour of the mouth, or visible movement of the lips during speech or singing

嘴型.notes: In Chinese television and music production (central to *Behind the Scenes*), 对嘴型 (duì zuǐxíng, 'matching lip movements') refers both to singers lip-syncing on stage and to ADR voice actors matching dialogue to an actor's on-screen mouth movements.

rootFamily.gloss: to lip-sync; to match dubbing to on-screen lip movements
lip shape, mouth posture in phonetics (literary synonym)

嘴巴.etymology: A vernacular suffixed somatic noun (附加式合成词) consisting of the root noun 嘴 (zuǐ, 'mouth, beak') and the neutralized nominal suffix 巴 (ba, originally meaning 'something that clings or adheres', widely grammaticalized in Mandarin and southwestern dialects as a noun-forming suffix for body parts and physical appendages, cf. 尾巴 wěiba 'tail', 下巴 xiàba 'chin'). By adding 巴, Mandarin converts monosyllabic 嘴 into a prosodically balanced disyllabic trochee (zuǐba) referring to the fleshy mouth, cheeks, and lips.

history.meaning: the mouth and lower cheeks; in Yuan–Ming vernacular, also a slap across the face/mouth
mouth, lips (colloquial standard disyllabic noun)

morphemes.meaning: colloquial nominal suffix attached to body parts and appendages (neutral tone ba)

嘴巴.notes: Watch out for a classic Northern Mandarin idiom: with a classifier like 一个嘴巴 (yī ge zuǐba) or 抽嘴巴 (chōu zuǐba), it means 'a slap across the face/mouth', whereas without a slap verb it simply means 'mouth' (嘴巴很甜 'sweet-talking mouth').

rootFamily.gloss: chin, lower jaw (sharing the somatic suffix -ba)
a slap in the face (Northern colloquialism)

嘴皮子.etymology: A three-character colloquial northern Mandarin compound formed from the modifier-head base 嘴皮 (zuǐpí, literally 'mouth-skin', i.e., the outer skin of the lips) plus the diminutive nominal suffix 子 (zi). By metonymy from the thin, rapidly moving skin of the lips during speech, 嘴皮子 (zuǐpízi) came to denote a person's sheer verbal agility, glibness, or physical effort expended in persuading others (as in 磨破嘴皮子 'wearing out one's lips talking').

history.meaning: the lips; colloquial northern metonym for fast, glib, or tireless talking
lips; one's tongue or verbal facility in persuasion and banter (colloquial)

morphemes.meaning: skin, outer layer (together 嘴皮 = lips)

嘴皮子.notes: Commonly heard in vivid colloquial collocations such as 耍嘴皮子 (shuǎ zuǐpízi, 'to show off with slick talk / all talk and no action') and 磨破嘴皮子 (mópò zuǐpízi, 'to talk until one's lips are worn thin trying to convince someone').

rootFamily.gloss: to boast or brag with slick, empty words

嘴硬.etymology: Subject-predicate idiom used as an adjective/verb, combining 嘴 ('mouth, speech') + 硬 ('hard, stiff, unyielding'): 'stubborn in speech, refusing to admit fault or defeat verbally even when inwardly wrong or scared'.

history.meaning: talk tough; refuse to admit fault or weakness

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 嘴硬 (via 萌典)

嘴里.etymology: A noun-localizer compound (方位结构) combining the somatic noun 嘴 (zuǐ, 'mouth') with the interior locative suffix 里 (Traditional 裏/裡, lǐ / li, originally 'inside lining of a garment', grammaticalized as 'inside, within'). Literally denoting the physical interior of the oral cavity ('in the mouth'), it extends figuratively in everyday discourse to mean 'out of someone's mouth' or 'in the way someone talks about things' (e.g., 从他嘴里说出来 'coming out of his mouth').

history.meaning: inside the mouth; in the words spoken by someone
in or from someone's mouth; in someone's verbal remarks

嘴里.notes: Used both literally for food or objects in the mouth (嘴里嚼着东西 'chewing something in one's mouth') and figuratively for someone's reliability as a speaker (狗嘴里吐不出象牙 'a dog's mouth cannot spit out ivory' — a foul-mouthed person won't say anything nice).

rootFamily.gloss: on one's lips; in outward speech
in one's heart or mind (the standard rhetorical counterpart to 嘴里/嘴上)
in one's hands; under one's control

嘶.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining the mouth radical 口 with phonetic 斯 (*sī*), originally denoting the neighing of a horse or a raspy, hoarse voice in Classical Chinese (Middle Chinese *sje*). In modern Mandarin it also serves as an onomatopoeic interjection for a sharp hiss of indrawn breath when wincing from sudden pain.

morphemes.meaning: hiss; sharp intake of breath; neigh

history.meaning: neigh of a horse; hoarse cry
hiss; sharp intake of breath from pain

嘿.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 嘿. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 嘿 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 嘿 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 嘿 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 嘿. The etymology of 嘿 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 嘿
middle form of 嘿
modern form of 嘿

噪音.etymology: Compound noun of 噪 ('chirping of a flock of birds in a tree -> clamor, din, harsh noise', 口 + 喿) + 音 ('sound'): 'noise, unwanted or grating sound, acoustic noise'.

history.meaning: unwanted or harsh noise

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 噪音 (via 萌典)

嚣张气焰.etymology: A four-character modifier-head phrase (偏正四字格) uniting two vivid classical compounds: 嚣张 (Traditional 囂張, xiāozhāng, 'clamorous and overbearing', from 嚣 'din of many mouths around a head 页' + 张 'to stretch a bow, expand aggressively') and 气焰 (Traditional 氣焰, qìyàn, literally 'vapor and roaring flames', a metaphor attested since the Tang–Song era for someone's blazing, intimidating momentum or haughty demeanor). Together, 嚣张气焰 paints an opponent's arrogant bluster as a roaring fire that needs to be dampened or extinguished.

history.meaning: 囂張 ('clamorous expansion') and 氣焰 ('blazing vapor/flame of one's aura') attested separately in Medieval Chinese prose
arrogant bluster, aggressive momentum, or overbearing haughtiness of an adversary

morphemes.meaning: clamorous, noisy, insolently loud (嚣) + stretched out, blatantly expanding (张) → rampant, arrogant
vital breath/aura (气) + blazing flame (焰) → fiery momentum, haughty bluster

嚣张气焰.notes: Because 气焰 literally means 'fiery flames of aura', it collocates in Mandarin with fire-quenching verbs like 打击 (dǎjī, 'strike down') or 灭 (miè, 'extinguish'), as in 灭一灭他的嚣张气焰 ('take the wind out of his arrogant sails / quench his bluster').

四.etymology: Cardinal numeral 'four'. Originally written in early Shang oracle-bone script with four horizontal strokes (亖), then replaced by the borrowed graph 四 (originally a pictograph of the nose/nostrils exhaling breath, later written 泗 'nasal mucus' and 呬 'breathe').

history.meaning: four horizontal strokes replaced by borrowed graph 四 = numeral four

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 四 (via 萌典)

四十.etymology: Multiplicative decimal numeral of 四 ('four') + 十 ('ten') = 'forty' (historically also written with the single contracted character 卌 xì, and famous from Confucius's 吾十有五而志于学…四十而不惑 'at forty I had no doubts').

history.meaning: four tens = forty

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 四十 (via 萌典)

四十五.etymology: Decimal numeral compound of 四 ('four') + 十 ('ten') + 五 ('five'), literally 'four tens and five'. In clock time expressions, 五点四十五分 ('5:45') denotes a quarter to six.

history.meaning: forty-five
forty-five

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 四十五

四十好几.etymology: A colloquial approximative numeral phrase constructed by juxtaposition of the round decade 四十 (sìshí, 'forty', 4 × 10) with the vernacular excess modifier 好几 (Traditional 好幾, hǎojǐ, 'quite a few, a good several', where 好 functions as an intensifying adverb meaning 'a good deal, quite' before the indeterminate numeral 几 'how many / several'). In spoken Mandarin, appending 好几 to any round ten (二十好几, 四十好几) indicates that the count exceeds the decade by a substantial margin (typically 45–49), i.e., 'well past forty'.

history.meaning: forty plus a good several (colloquial northern Mandarin age/quantity approximation)
well over forty; in one's mid-to-late forties

morphemes.meaning: quite, a good deal (intensifying prefix before numerals/quantifiers)
several, a few (between three and nine)

四十好几.notes: Most often used in casual conversation to describe a person's age (他都四十好几的人了, 'he's already well past forty / pushing fifty'), implying they are old enough to know better or settle down.

rootFamily.gloss: quite a few, a good many
forty-something (neutral approximation, unlike 四十好几 which stresses the upper half of the decade)
well over thirty; in one's mid-to-late thirties

四周.etymology: A numeral-noun spatial compound uniting 四 (sì, 'four', standing for the four cardinal sides) and 周 (zhōu, 'perimeter, circuit, all around', attested on Shang bronzes as a finely gridded field enclosure). In Classical prose 四周 already meant 'the entire perimeter on all four sides' of a city wall, pit, or courtyard, and it remains standard in modern Mandarin for anything surrounding a central spot.

history.meaning: all four sides of an enclosure or boundary
all around; surrounding perimeter

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 四周

四月份.etymology: A modifier-head calendar compound consisting of 四月 (sìyuè, literally 'fourth moon/month', originally the fourth lunar month in Classical Chinese and repurposed in the 20th century for Gregorian 'April') plus the nominal suffix 份 (fèn, 'portion, allotted share, unit within a series', formed from 人 'person' + 分 fēn 'to divide'). Adding 份 to a month name (四月份) frames the month as a bounded time-slice or scheduling unit within the year's twelve divisions, a usage especially common in business, production schedules, and journalism.

history.meaning: the fourth month of the traditional Chinese lunisolar calendar (roughly May)
the month of April (Gregorian calendar) treated as a distinct period or scheduling block

morphemes.meaning: portion, allotted segment or time-block within a whole series

四月份.notes: While 四月 (sìyuè) is required when giving a specific date (四月十号 'April 10th'), 四月份 (sìyuèfèn) is preferred when referring to the month as a whole block of time or work cycle (四月份的档期 'the April production schedule').

rootFamily.gloss: month (as a category or scheduling unit, e.g., 按月份统计)
year (as a chronological unit or vintage, e.g., 年份酒)

四百.etymology: A multiplicative decimal numeral compound (偏正数词结构) inherited directly from Old Chinese (attested on Shang oracle bones and Zhou bronzes), combining the multiplier 四 (sì < Old Chinese *s.lijs, 'four') with the decimal base 百 (bǎi < Old Chinese *pˤrak, 'hundred', written with 一 'one' atop 白 bái as phonetic). In Chinese numeral syntax, placing a digit 1–9 before 百 multiplies the base (4 × 100 = 400), a transparent positional rule unchanged for over three millennia.

history.meaning: four hundred (attested in Shang bone inscriptions and Western Zhou bronze records of troops and tribute)
four hundred

四百.notes: In colloquial Mandarin, 'four hundred and fifty' can be shortened to 四百五 (sìbǎiwǔ), dropping the final 十, though learners should be aware that in some northern dialects 二百五 (èrbǎiwǔ, '250') is slang for a foolish or reckless person, whereas 四百 has no such stigma.

回.etymology: Ancient pictograph/ideogram attested in oracle-bone and bronze scripts as a spiral whirlpool or eddy (回): 'revolve, turn around -> return, go/come back, reply/answer, chapter/time (classifier for occurrences or chapters of vernacular novels)'.

morphemes.meaning: revolving spiral = turn back, return, reply

history.meaning: whirlpool spiral -> revolve, turn back
return; go back; reply; classifier for times/chapters

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 回 (via 萌典)

回事.etymology: A vernacular classifier-noun sequence that lexicalized into a compound noun (回事, huíshì, often with兒化 huíshìr in Beijing speech), composed of 回 (huí, originally a pictograph of a swirling whirlpool or spiral, extended to 'a turn, a cycle, an episode or chapter of a story') functioning as a measure word for events, followed by 事 (shì, 'matter, affair, business'). Because vernacular storytellers counted episodes and occurrences by the 回 ('turn/chapter'), 一回事 ('one episode-affair') and 怎么回事 ('what kind of turn-of-events') solidified as the core colloquial way to frame a situation or matter.

history.meaning: one affair / two separate matters (classifier 回 + noun 事 in Ming–Qing vernacular fiction)
matter, affair, situation (bound in constructions with 怎么, 一, 两, 当)

morphemes.meaning: turn, cycle, episode, instance (measure word for occurrences and affairs)

回事.notes: Never stands alone as a bare noun; it is always preceded by a question word or numeral/demonstrative in high-frequency frames: 怎么回事？ (zěnme huíshì, 'what's going on?'), 这是一码事/一回事 ('that's one and the same thing'), or 不当回事 ('not take it seriously').

rootFamily.gloss: what is going on? what's the matter?
a chapter-by-chapter vernacular novel (sharing the 'episode/turn' sense of 回)

回去.etymology: A directional verb compound (动趋结构) combining the motion verb 回 (huí, originally a spiral pictograph meaning 'to revolve, turn around, return to a starting point') with the deictic directional complement 去 (qù / qu, originally 'to leave, depart from a place', grammaticalized as a complement marking motion away from the speaker's current location). Contrasting systematically with 回来 (huílai, 'come back toward the speaker'), 回去 specifies heading back to one's home, office, or origin point away from where the speaker currently stands.

history.meaning: to turn back and depart; to return to a prior location away from the current scene (attested in Tang–Song vernacular and poetry)
to go back, head back, return (away from the speaker)

morphemes.meaning: to turn around, return to an earlier place or state
to go (motion away from the speaker's current position)

回去.notes: Besides physical motion ('go back home'), 回去 attaches after other verbs as a complex directional complement meaning 'back to where it came from' or 'suppressing back in', as in 把眼泪咽回去 ('swallow one's tears back down') or 怼回去 ('clap back / retort').

rootFamily.gloss: to come back (motion toward the speaker)
to go home, return to one's family

cognates.meaning: returning to one's home country or province (kikoku)
cognates.word: 帰国 (きこく) / 回国 (かいこく)

回国.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound (动宾结构) formed from the verb 回 (huí, 'to turn back, return') and the nominal object 国 (Traditional 國, guó, originally 'walled city-state or fiefdom defended by weapons 戈 within boundaries 口/囗', in modern usage 'nation, country, homeland'). In pre-modern texts 回国 could refer to a feudal lord or envoy returning to his state; in modern Mandarin it specifically denotes an expatriate, overseas student, diplomat, or traveler returning to their home country from abroad.

history.meaning: to return to one's feudal state, principality, or native kingdom
to return to one's home country from abroad; to repatriate

回国.notes: Because 回国 is an inseparable verb-object (VO) structure, it cannot take another direct object; duration or frequency complements must be inserted between the two characters (e.g., 回了一趟国 huíle yī tàng guó, 'went back to the home country for a trip').

rootFamily.gloss: to go abroad, leave one's country (the direct antonym VO compound)
returnee from overseas study or work ('sea turtle' pun on 海归)
to return home, go back to one's native place

回声.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 回 ('return, rebound') + 声 (聲, 'sound, voice'): 'reflected sound, echo'.

history.meaning: returning sound; echo

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 回声 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: recovery, restoration to a former state (kaifuku)

回复.etymology: A coordinative verb compound (联合结构) uniting two verbs of returning: 回 (huí, 'to turn around, revolve back') and 复 (Traditional 覆 or 復, fù; in Simplified Chinese 复 merges both 復 'to retrace one's steps, return to a prior state' and 覆 'to turn over, reply by letter'). Because of those two classical graphs, 回復/回覆 historically carried two distinct senses: (1) with 復, 'to restore or recover a prior state' (now usually written 恢复 huīfù in Mandarin, though preserved as 回復 kaifuku in Japanese), and (2) with 覆, 'to send back a reply to a message or letter', which is the dominant meaning of 回复 in contemporary Mandarin.

history.meaning: to return to an original state (復); to send back an official response or reply by letter (覆)
to reply, respond, or get back to someone (especially in messages, emails, and formal communication)

morphemes.meaning: to turn back, send back in return
to answer, reciprocate, return (merging Traditional 覆 'reply' and 復 'return')

回复.notes: The standard term for replying to texts, emails, comments, or work inquiries (收到请回复 'please reply upon receipt'); in Traditional Chinese (Taiwan/Hong Kong), the 'reply' sense is carefully distinguished as 回覆, while 回復 means 'to recover/restore'.

rootFamily.gloss: to give a formal reply or answer (synonymous compound with 复)
to recover, restore to an original state (the modern Mandarin cousin for the 'recovery' sense)
to write back a letter or message

回头.etymology: Verb-object compound of 回 ('turn back') + 头 (頭, 'head'). Means literally 'turn one's head around / look back', figuratively 'repent/turn back', and in colloquial northern Mandarin an adverb meaning 'in a little while, later on (回头见 see you later)'.

history.meaning: turn one's head back; later on / shortly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 回头 (via 萌典)

回头见.etymology: A colloquial three-character valediction phrase formed from 回头 (Traditional 回頭, huítóu, literally the verb-object phrase 'to turn one's head around', which grammaticalized in northern vernacular Mandarin into a temporal adverb meaning 'in a moment, shortly, later on') followed by the verb 见 (Traditional 見, jiàn, 'to see, meet'). Literally 'turn our heads and we'll see each other again', it reflects the casual everyday image of parting briefly and looking back to meet again soon.

history.meaning: literally 'to turn one's head back'; in Ming–Qing Beijing vernacular, 'after a short while, later on'
see you later! catch you soon! (casual parting greeting)

morphemes.meaning: literally 'turn the head' (回 + 头) → idiomatically 'in a little while, later on'

回头见.notes: One of the most natural, breezy ways to say 'see you later' among colleagues on a film set or in an office; similarly, 回头聊 (huítóu liáo) means 'let's chat later / catch up soon'.

rootFamily.gloss: to turn one's head; later on, in a little while
goodbye, see you again (standard polite farewell)

回家.etymology: Verb-object compound of 回 ('return, go back to') + 家 ('home, family'): 'return home, go home'.

history.meaning: go home; return home

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 回家 (via 萌典)

回形针.etymology: Three-character descriptive compound of 回形 ('shaped like the nested rectangular character 回') + 针 (針, 'pin, needle, wire clip'): 'paper clip' (named after the looped concentric rectangle shape of a Gem paper clip).

history.meaning: 回-shaped wire pin = paper clip

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 回形针 (via 萌典)

回忆.etymology: Compound verb and noun of 回 ('turn back toward the past') + 忆 (憶, 'remember, call to mind', heart 忄 + 意): 'recall, recollect, reminisce; memory, recollection'.

history.meaning: call past events back to mind; recollection; memory

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 回忆 (via 萌典)

回忆录.etymology: A three-character modifier-head nominal compound (偏正结构) built from the disyllabic verb-noun 回忆 (Traditional 回憶, huíyì, 'to recall, recollect, call back to mind', from 回 'turn back' + 忆 'remember, ponder in the heart 忄') modifying the head noun 录 (Traditional 錄, lù, originally 'metallic luster/inscribing on bronze', extended in Classical historiography to 'a written record, register, or chronicle'). Coined in modern literary Chinese to translate the Western genre of *memoirs*, it designates a first-person historical account written from personal recollection.

history.meaning: 回憶 ('recollecting the past') attested in Tang–Song poetry; 錄 ('chronicle/record') standard in imperial historiography
memoirs; an autobiographical book or essay chronicling past events from personal memory

morphemes.meaning: to turn back (回) + to remember in the heart (忆) → recollection, memory

回忆录.notes: Unlike 自传 (zìzhuàn, a comprehensive cradle-to-present 'autobiography'), 回忆录 focuses on specific periods, historic events, or famous colleagues the author personally witnessed.

cognates.meaning: to recover, reclaim, call back (hồi thu / thu hồi)
