回收.etymology: A directional-action verb compound combining 回 (huí, 'back, returning to origin') and 收 (shōu, 'to gather, collect, receive, take in', written with 纠 phonetic and 攵 'hand holding a stick to gather'). Popularized across East Asia in the late 19th and 20th centuries (reinforced by Japanese *wasei-kango* 回収 kaishū in economics and industry), it denotes taking back something previously issued, spent, or discarded—ranging from recouping financial investment (回收成本) and recalling defective products to recycling waste materials.

history.meaning: to withdraw currency from circulation, recoup capital, or call back issued documents
to collect back, recover, retrieve (funds, rights, or materials); to recycle

morphemes.meaning: to gather in, collect, take back

回收.notes: In media and business contexts, 回收 often means 'recouping costs/investment' (回收资金) or 'taking back rights/authority', while in everyday life 可回收垃圾 (kě huíshōu lājī) is the ubiquitous label on 'recyclable' bins.

rootFamily.gloss: to take back, revoke, withdraw (native Mandarin verb-complement counterpart)
recycling bin (on computers or for physical waste)
to acquire, buy up (a company or goods)

回来.etymology: Directional verb compound of 回 ('return') + 来 ('come toward the speaker'): 'come back, return here' (and as a directional complement after verbs: 拿回来 'bring back').

history.meaning: come back; return

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 回来 (via 萌典)

回答.etymology: A coordinative verb-noun compound (联合结构) pairing 回 (huí, 'to turn back, return a response') with 答 (dá, 'to answer, reciprocate', originally written with the bamboo radical 竹 and 合 hé 'to join/match', evoking matching bamboo tallies or reciprocating a call). Attested since the Song–Yuan period, it joins the directional notion of 'sending back' (回) with the communicative act of 'matching/answering a question' (答) to form the primary standard Mandarin word for answering a question orally or in writing.

history.meaning: to respond in return to a question or statement (attested in Song–Yuan vernacular texts and Zen dialogues)
to answer, reply; an answer or response

morphemes.meaning: to return, send back in response

回答.notes: Unlike 回复 (huífù), which takes a person or a message/email as its object, 回答 typically takes a question (回答问题 'answer a question') or a person directly in spoken Q&A contexts like press conferences and interviews.

rootFamily.gloss: answer, solution to a question or problem
to reply formally, give a definitive answer
to answer a call or roll; to respond to a question (inverted order)

cognates.meaning: retrospection, looking back on the past (kaiko)
to look back on the past (hồi cố)

回顾.etymology: A modifier-head or serial verb compound combining 回 (huí, 'to turn around, turn back') and 顾 (Traditional 顧, gù, formed from 雇 phonetic and 页 yè 'head', originally meaning 'to turn the head to look at'). In Classical and Medieval Chinese poetry (such as Bai Juyi's *Song of Everlasting Sorrow*: 回顾下望人寰处 'turning her head back to gaze down upon the mortal realm'), it meant literally turning one's head to look behind; in modern Mandarin it functions primarily figuratively as 'to look back on past events' or 'a retrospective/recap'.

history.meaning: literally to turn one's head around to gaze back at what lies behind
to look back on the past, review; a retrospective or recap (in broadcasting and journalism)

morphemes.meaning: to turn the head (页) and gaze at; to attend to

回顾.notes: In television production and live broadcasts, 精彩回顾 (jīngcǎi huígù) is the standard on-screen title for a 'highlight reel / recap of previous episodes', while 回顾展 (huígùzhǎn) means a 'retrospective exhibition'.

rootFamily.gloss: to look after, care for; to give consideration to
to look back cleanly without regret (idiom: 义无反顾 'press forward with no turning back')
customer, client (literally 'honored one who turns to visit')

回馈.etymology: A compound verb (动补/联合结构) uniting 回 (huí, 'to return, give back in reciprocation') with 馈 (Traditional 饋/餽, kuì, formed with the food radical 食/饣 and 贵 guì as phonetic, originally meaning 'to present food or gifts to a superior or guest' in Classical Chinese). Historically denoting a return gift of food or tribute, 回馈 was revitalized in late 20th-century Taiwan and Mainland Mandarin—Initially to translate cybernetic and engineering 'feedback' (alongside 反馈 fǎnkuì) and subsequently in commerce and media for 'giving back to, rewarding' loyal audiences, fans, or society.

history.meaning: to present a return gift or offering of food in reciprocation for hospitality
to give back to, reward (audiences, customers, or society); feedback (Especially in Taiwan Mandarin)

morphemes.meaning: in return, back toward the giver
to present food or gifts respectfully; to bestow

回馈.notes: A favorite word in entertainment marketing and corporate PR: 回馈粉丝 (huíkuì fěnsī, 'giving back to the fans') or 回馈社会 ('giving back to society'); note that for technical or editorial 'feedback' on Mainland China sets, 反馈 (fǎnkuì) is much more common.

rootFamily.gloss: to present as a gift, bestow generously (formal)
to repay kindness or trust (synonymous 'give back' verb)

因.etymology: Originally a pictographic or ideographic character (因, yīn < Old Chinese *ʔin) depicting a person (大) lying upon or conforming to a woven mat (囗), whence the earliest Classical Chinese verbal meanings 'to rely upon, follow along with, build upon what precedes'. From 'relying on a prior foundation', its sense evolved naturally in Warring States philosophical prose into 'the underlying basis or cause' (further reinforced by Buddhist translations using 因 for Sanskrit *hetu* 'primary cause'), and grammatically into the formal preposition and conjunction 'because of, owing to'.

history.meaning: woven mat; to rely on, follow along with, adapt to existing conditions; by means of
primary cause (Sanskrit hetu, paired with 果 guǒ 'effect/fruit'); because of, owing to
because of, owing to (formal/written preposition); cause, factor (bound in compounds)

morphemes.meaning: to rely on; underlying cause; because of, owing to

因.notes: Standalone 因 as a preposition ('because of') belongs to formal written Chinese, news tickers, and official notices (e.g., 因天气原因取消 'cancelled owing to weather reasons'); in everyday spoken conversation, always use the disyllabic 因为 (yīnwèi) instead.

rootFamily.gloss: because, owing to (standard spoken and written conjunction/preposition)

因为.etymology: Causal conjunction and preposition combining 因 ('rely on, follow upon, because of') + 为 (為, read wèi, 'for the sake of, because of'): 'because, on account of, owing to' (often paired with 所以 'therefore').

history.meaning: because; owing to

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 因为 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: because of this, therefore (classical kanbun reading inshi / kore ni yorite)

因此.etymology: A lexicalized preposition-pronoun compound (介宾结构凝结成连词) formed in Classical Chinese by combining the causal preposition 因 (yīn, 'relying on, because of') with the proximal demonstrative pronoun 此 (cǐ, 'this'). Literally meaning 'because of this / on account of this', it functioned as a two-word phrase in Warring States and Han texts (such as the *Records of the Grand Historian*) before coalescing into a single resultative conjunction meaning 'therefore, consequently, for this reason'.

history.meaning: by relying on this; on account of this specific fact or situation (two-word prepositional phrase)
therefore, consequently, because of this (cohesive conjunction introducing a result)

morphemes.meaning: by reason of, owing to, based on
this (proximal demonstrative referring to the preceding clause)

因此.notes: More formal and analytical than colloquial 所以 (suǒyǐ); because 因此 already contains 因 ('because of this'), it usually stands on its own at the start of the result clause rather than pairing closely with a preceding 因为 in the same short sentence.

rootFamily.gloss: because of, for the sake of (the causal counterpart to 因此)
for this reason, to this end (parallel classical preposition + 此 compound)
from this, hereby, thus (parallel classical preposition + 此 compound)

团.etymology: A phono-semantic character (团, Traditional 團, tuán < Old Chinese *C.tˤon) constructed with the enclosure radical 囗 (wéi, signifying a surrounding boundary or circle) and the phonetic 专 (Traditional 專, zhuān, replaced in Simplified Chinese by 才 cái as a cursive shorthand). Originally meaning 'round, circular, rolled into a ball' (as in classical poetry describing the round moon or a ball of露 dew), it developed the verbal sense 'to gather into a tight circle, coalesce' and subsequently the nominal sense of an organized human collective: a military regiment, artistic troupe, delegation, or youth league.

history.meaning: round, circular, spherical (like the full moon or a rolled ball of clay/dew)
to roll or gather into a lump; a local militia unit or guild organization (e.g., 團練)
group, artistic troupe, tour group, delegation, military regiment; classifier for round lumps or balls

morphemes.meaning: simplified cursive form replacing Traditional 專 (supplying the dento-alveolar -uán rime)

团.notes: In the entertainment industry, 团 commonly refers to an idol group, music band, or performing arts troupe (e.g., 男团 nántuán 'boy group', 女团 nǚtuán 'girl group', 成团 chéngtuán 'to debut as a group', 剧团 jùtuán 'theater troupe').

rootFamily.gloss: family reunion; round and complete (like the full moon)

cognates.meaning: leader of a delegation, troupe, or group (danchō)
head of a troupe, delegation, or corps (danjang)
head of a delegation or regiment (đoàn trưởng)

团长.etymology: A modifier-head institutional title (偏正结构) combining 团 (Traditional 團, tuán, 'regiment, troupe, delegation, club, group') with 长 (Traditional 長, read zhǎng in its verbal/titular sense 'elder, chief, head, leader', originally depicting a long-haired elder with a walking staff). Historically used for leaders of local militia corps (团练) and modernized in the early 20th century (alongside Japanese 団長 danchō) for the commander of a military regiment as well as the director or head of an orchestra, theater troupe, tour group, or campus club.

history.meaning: chief of a local defense militia or community association in late imperial China
regimental commander (military); director of a performing arts troupe, head of a delegation, or club/tour leader

morphemes.meaning: regiment, performing troupe, delegation, club, or group
chief, elder, leader, head (read zhǎng, not cháng)

团长.notes: Be sure to pronounce 长 as third-tone zhǎng ('chief/head'), never second-tone cháng ('long'); depending on context, 团长 can be a colonel commanding a military regiment, the artistic director of a symphony orchestra (交响乐团团长), or the playful leader of a reality-show travel cast.

rootFamily.gloss: team leader, captain (of a squad or sports team)
president or chairman of an association or club
director of a film or television drama (another key showbiz title)

团队.etymology: A coordinative nominal compound (联合结构) pairing two collective nouns of military and organizational origin: 团 (Traditional 團, tuán, 'coherent group, corps, regiment') and 队 (Traditional 隊, duì, originally 'to fall from a mound 阝', borrowed in Classical Chinese for 隧/队列 'a ranked file of soldiers, squad, column'). In the mid-20th century 团队 referred to military units (regiments and squads) or youth organizations, before being adopted in late 20th-century management, tech, and media production discourse to translate English *team*—emphasizing collaborative synergy toward a shared project goal.

history.meaning: military regiments and squads collectively; organized ranks or youth corps
team; a collaborative professional group working together on a project, show, or enterprise

morphemes.meaning: coherent group, corps, circle of people

团队.notes: The go-to word in modern Chinese workplaces and entertainment studios for a professional 'team' or 'crew' (制作团队 zhìzuò tuánduì 'production team', 团队精神 tuánduì jīngshén 'team spirit'), distinct from 队伍 (duìwu, a physical line/queue or large rank-and-file contingent).

cognates.meaning: garden and grove; classical landscape garden (wollim)
garden and forest; classical landscape garden (viên lâm)

园林.etymology: A coordinative compound (联合结构) uniting 园 (Traditional 園, yuán, 'walled orchard or cultivated garden', formed from the enclosure 囗 and phonetic 袁 yuán) with 林 (lín, 'woods, grove, forest', an ideograph of two trees 木 standing side by side). First celebrated in Six Dynasties landscape poetry and prose (such as Wang Xizhi and Xie Lingyun), the pairing 园林 captures the defining aesthetic ideal of classical Chinese landscape architecture: bringing the untamed natural beauty of mountain groves and water (林泉) inside the cultivated walls of an estate (园), creating a microcosm of nature in miniature.

history.meaning: walled gardens and natural groves; aristocratic country estates blending orchards and woodland (Six Dynasties–Tang poetry)
classical landscaped scholarly or imperial garden featuring pavilions, rockeries, ponds, and trees (Song–Qing)
classical Chinese garden; landscape architecture and urban greenery design

morphemes.meaning: walled orchard, enclosed garden, courtyard estate
grove of trees, woods, natural forest

园林.notes: Unlike 花园 (huāyuán, a residential or Western-style 'flower garden') or 公园 (gōngyuán, a modern 'public park'), 园林 evokes traditional Chinese landscape architecture (such as the Classical Gardens of Suzhou, 苏州园林) with rockeries, winding corridors, ponds, and pavilions, or the professional discipline of landscape architecture (风景园林).

rootFamily.gloss: forest, woods (three-tree 森 + two-tree 林)

cognates.meaning: to be troubled, distressed, at a loss

困.etymology: In Simplified Chinese, 困 (kùn) merges two historically related characters. The original graph 困 is an associative compound (会意) depicting a tree (木, mù) hemmed in on all four sides by an enclosure (囗, wéi), unable to grow freely; in the *Shuowen Jiezi* it glosses an abandoned or ruined dwelling, and in Classical Chinese it meant 'confined, besieged, hard-pressed, exhausted'. From the sense of physical exhaustion emerged the vernacular Mandarin sense 'sleepy, drowsy', for which a dedicated phono-semantic character 睏 (eye 目 + phonetic 困) was coined in late imperial vernacular before being merged back into 困 in 20th-century script simplification.

history.meaning: hemmed in, besieged, afflicted, exhausted
weary-eyed, sleepy, drowsy
sleepy, drowsy; trapped, distressed (merged simplified graph)

morphemes.meaning: tree (hemmed in inside an enclosure) / merged with 睏 (目 eye + 困)

困.notes: As a standalone adjective in everyday speech, 困 almost always means 'sleepy' (e.g., 我好困 'I'm so sleepy'), whereas in bound compounds like 困难 (difficulty) or 困境 (predicament) it retains its classical meaning of 'trapped, hard-pressed'.

困境.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) Sino-compound combining 困 (kùn, 'hemmed in, besieged, distressed') and 境 (jìng, 'boundary, territory, circumstances, state'). Literally 'a hemmed-in territory' or 'besieged circumstances', the compound arose in Literary Chinese to describe a spatial or existential state in which every avenue of advance feels blocked, evolving in modern Mandarin to denote an institutional, creative, or personal predicament, dilemma, or bottleneck.

history.meaning: hemmed-in state; border or territory under distress
predicament, dilemma, bottleneck, tight corner

困境.notes: Commonly collocates with 陷入 (xiànrù, 'fall into') and 走出/摆脱 (zǒuchū/bǎituō, 'step out of / break free from'); in media and business contexts, 行业困境 refers to an industry-wide bottleneck.

rootFamily.gloss: realm, state of mind or art

围.etymology: Originally 圍, showing an enclosure (囗) around 韋 (wéi, which in oracle-bone script depicted feet walking in a circle around a walled town): 'surround, enclose, encircle, gather around; circumference; scarf/apron'.

history.meaning: patrol around a walled town = surround, besiege, enclose
surround; enclose; wrap around

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 围 (via 萌典)

围绕.etymology: A coordinative (并列) verbal compound pairing two synonymous roots: 围 (Trad. 圍, wéi, 'to enclose, surround, besiege', from 囗 'enclosure' + phonetic 韋 'patrolling guards') and 绕 (Trad. 繞, rào, 'to wind silk around, coil, encircle', from 糸 'silk thread' + phonetic 堯). Attested in Han and Six Dynasties texts (and heavily used in Chinese Buddhist scriptures to translate Sanskrit *pradakṣiṇa*, 'circumambulating a stupa or Buddha in reverence'), it expanded from physical encirclement to abstractly centering a discussion, plot, or project around a core theme.

history.meaning: to encircle physically; to circumambulate in ritual reverence
to revolve around; to center on (a topic, theme, or core issue)

morphemes.meaning: to wind around, coil, loop around

围绕.notes: Frequently used in production and editorial meetings in the frame 围绕……展开 ('to unfold/develop around [a theme or core conflict]').

围裙.etymology: Compound of 围 ('encircle; wrap around', enclosure radical 囗 + phonetic 韦 wéi) + 裙 ('skirt; lower garment', clothing radical 衤 + phonetic 君 jūn). Literally 'a wrap-around skirt', it is the universal Mandarin word for a kitchen or workshop apron.

history.meaning: wrap-around protective apron
apron

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 围裙

固定.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 固定. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 固定 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 固定 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 固定 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 固定. The etymology of 固定 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 固定
middle form of 固定
modern form of 固定

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 固定

国.etymology: In bone and bronze inscriptions, the word was originally written 或 (huò, Old Chinese *ɡʷˤək), an associative graph combining 戈 (gē, 'dagger-axe/halberd') guarding 口 (kǒu, 'walled settlement/population') and 一 (yī, 'territorial boundary line'). When 或 was borrowed for the grammatical sense 'someone, perhaps', an outer enclosure 囗 (wéi, 'city wall / border') was added to form the traditional character 國 ('walled city-state, fiefdom, kingdom'). The simplified form 国 adopts a long-standing cursive and popular variant placing 玉 (yù, 'jade', symbolizing the sovereign's jade seal of state) inside 囗.

history.meaning: walled capital city; feudal city-state or fiefdom
dynastic empire, kingdom, principality
sovereign nation-state, country; national (as a prefix)

morphemes.meaning: jade (symbol of royal authority; replacing Trad. 或 'armed defense of a settlement')

国.notes: In Classical Chinese, 国 often meant just the walled capital city (as opposed to 野 yě, the rural hinterland), whereas in modern compounds (国剧, 国产, 国家) it means 'nation' or 'national'.

国内.etymology: A modifier-head locative compound of 国 (Trad. 國, guó, 'state, nation') and 内 (nèi, 'inside, interior'). In Classical texts such as the *Zuo Zhuan* and *Mengzi*, 國內 referred to the interior of a feudal state or within the walls of the royal capital. In modern Mandarin (paralleling Japanese 国内 *kokunai*), it designates the domestic sphere within a sovereign nation-state's borders, contrasting with 国外 (abroad) and 国际 (international).

history.meaning: within the feudal state or royal capital
domestic, inside the country, home market

国内.notes: Functions syntactically as a place word (can follow 在 or 去 directly, e.g., 在国内很火 'very popular domestically') and as an attributive modifier (国内市场 'the domestic market').

国外.etymology: A modifier-head locative compound formed from 国 (Trad. 國, guó, 'state, nation') and 外 (wài, 'outside, exterior, beyond'). In pre-imperial and imperial Chinese, 國外 denoted lands outside the capital walls or beyond a feudal state's borders; in modern Mandarin, it shifted with the modern nation-state concept to mean 'abroad, overseas, foreign countries'.

history.meaning: outside the capital city or beyond the borders of a feudal state
abroad, overseas, foreign countries

国外.notes: Like 国内, 国外 is a locative noun that takes prepositions or verbs of motion directly without needing a localizer like 里 (e.g., 去国外留学 'go abroad to study').

国际.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-compound of 国 (Trad. 國, guó, 'nation, state') and 际 (Trad. 際, jì, 'border, juncture, meeting point, intercourse between'). Originally coined in Meiji Japan as a *wasei-kango* (和製漢語) 国際 (*kokusai*, 'intercourse/juncture between nations') in the 1870s–1880s to translate English *international* (itself coined by Jeremy Bentham in 1780), and subsequently borrowed into late Qing Chinese where it became standard across modern diplomacy, law, and media.

history.meaning: intercourse between nations; international (translation of English 'international')
international, global, among nations
history.stage: Late Qing to Modern Standard Mandarin

国际.notes: In showbiz and branding, 走国际路线 ('pursuing an international track/image') and 国际化 ('internationalization') describe adapting domestic IP or talent for global audiences.

图.etymology: Originally 圖 (an enclosure 囗 containing 啚 bǐ, 'granary/village boundaries'): originally 'map out territory and granaries', hence 'drawing, map, chart, diagram, picture; plan, seek, scheme for'.

history.meaning: map; chart; drawing; plan/seek
picture; diagram; map; chart; seek

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 图 (via 萌典)

图书.etymology: Coordinative compound from 图 (simplified from 圖, 'map; chart; diagram') + 书 (simplified from 書, 'written book; document'). Attested as early as the *Classic of Changes* (易經: 河出圖，洛出書 'the Yellow River brought forth the chart and the Luo River brought forth the writing'), it now collectively refers to books and publications.

history.meaning: maps, charts, and books; imperial archives
books; library collection

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 图书

图书馆.etymology: Three-character compound of 图书 ('charts and books -> books and publications', recalling the Classical pair 河图洛书) + 馆 (館, 'public building, hall, institution'): 'library'.

history.meaning: public or institutional library

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 图书馆 (via 萌典)

图片.etymology: A modifier-head noun compound combining 图 (Trad. 圖, tú, 'diagram, map, drawing, chart') and 片 (piàn, colloquially piān in Northern Mandarin for media slices, 'flat thin slice, sheet, card, photographic plate'). Formed in modern Chinese alongside print journalism, photography, and later digital media to designate a standalone visual image, photograph, or graphic plate, contrasting with 图书 (books) and 文字 (text).

history.meaning: drawn diagram/chart + flat sheet or photographic plate
picture, photograph, visual image (print or digital)

morphemes.meaning: flat thin sheet, plate, print, card

图片.notes: 图片 is the standard term for static images in publishing, design, and digital interfaces (e.g., 发张图片 'send an image'), whereas 照片 specifically means a camera photograph and 画 means a painting/drawing.

图纸.etymology: Compound noun of 图 (圖, 'technical drawing, blueprint, plan') + 纸 (紙, 'paper'): 'architectural or engineering drawing, blueprint, plan'.

history.meaning: blueprint; technical drawing; design plan

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 图纸 (via 萌典)

圆.etymology: Phono-semantic character (圓) combining 囗 ('enclosure, circle') + 员 (員, yuán, originally depicting a round bronze cauldron mouth 口 above 鼎): 'round, circular, spherical; full (of the moon); make complete/plausible; unit of currency (yuan)'.

history.meaning: round cauldron rim -> circular, round, complete
round; circular; complete

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 圆 (via 萌典)

圆圆.etymology: Vivid AA-reduplication of the adjective 圆 ('round'): 'nice and round, perfectly round' (e.g., 圆圆的月亮 'the round full moon').

history.meaning: round; nicely circular

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 圆圆 (via 萌典)

圆润.etymology: Coordinative adjective compound from 圆 (simplified from 圓, 'round; full; circular') + 润 (simplified from 潤, water 氵 + phonetic 閏 'moist; glossy; smooth'). Originally used in classical criticism to praise pearls, jade, calligraphy strokes, and singing voices that are both well-rounded and smooth without harsh edges.

history.meaning: round and lustrous (of pearls or jade); mellow (of voice)
mellow and full (of sound); smooth and rounded

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 圆润

圆满.etymology: A coordinative adjectival compound of 圆 (Trad. 圓, yuán, 'round, spherical, complete without corners or gaps') and 满 (Trad. 滿, mǎn, 'full to the brim, abundant'). Originated in Six Dynasties and Tang Chinese Buddhist translations of Sanskrit *paripūrṇa* ('completely full, perfected, lacking nothing', evoking the waxing of the full moon as a metaphor for spiritual perfection and karmic completion, 功德圆满). It later entered general vernacular and formal usage to describe an event, life, or story ending that is wholly satisfactory and flawless.

history.meaning: spiritually perfected and lacking nothing (calque/translation of Sanskrit paripūrṇa)
complete, fulfilling, wholly satisfactory, without a hitch

圆满.notes: A favorite high-register word in broadcasting and event production: 演出取得圆满成功 ('the performance achieved a complete success') or 大团圆/圆满结局 ('a fulfilling/happy ending').

圆舞曲.etymology: Semantic calque coined for the European waltz: 圆 ('round/revolving') + 舞 ('dance') + 曲 ('musical piece'), literally 'revolving-dance music', capturing the whirling turns behind German Walzer (from walzen 'revolve').

history.meaning: waltz (alongside phonetic loan 华尔兹)

cognates.meaning: revolving ballroom dance in 3/4 time (semantic model)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 圆舞曲 (via 萌典)

圈.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 囗 ('enclosure') + 卷 (juàn/quān phonetic). Originally read juàn for an 'animal pen or fold'; read quān as a noun, classifier, and verb meaning 'circle, ring, loop; classifier for laps or rounds; enclose or mark with a circle'.

history.meaning: animal pen (juàn); curved bowl/circle (quān)
circle; ring; loop; classifier for laps or rounds

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 圈 (via 萌典)

圈子.etymology: A root-plus-suffix nominal derivation combining 圈 (quān, 'circle, ring, loop', originally juàn, 'livestock pen, enclosure', from 囗 'enclosure' + phonetic 卷 'roll/curve') and the diminutive/nominalizing suffix 子 (zi, neutral tone). Literally 'a small ring or loop', it extended metaphorically from physical circles (and Mahjong/social rounds) to closed social cliques, professional networks, and especially the entertainment or media industry (娱乐圈, 影视圈).

history.meaning: physical ring, circular enclosure, rim
social circle, professional community, industry clique (especially showbiz)

圈子.notes: In media and workplace drama, 混圈子 means 'to mingle/make one's way in an industry circle', and 兜圈子 means 'to beat around the bush (walk in circles)'.

rootFamily.gloss: to break out of a niche circle into mainstream popularity

圈里人.etymology: A trimorphemic modifier-head compound built from the locative phrase 圈里 (quānlǐ, 'inside the circle', from 圈 'ring, professional circle' + localizer 里 [Trad. 裡/裏] 'lining of a garment -> inside, within') modifying the head noun 人 (rén, 'person'). Coined in modern colloquial Mandarin to contrast insiders who know the unspoken rules and networks of a trade—especially entertainment, television, arts, or finance—with outsiders (圈外人 / 门外汉).

history.meaning: a person inside a professional or social circle; industry insider

圈里人.notes: In showbiz contexts (*幕后之王*), 圈里人 (or its slightly more formal variant 圈内人) refers specifically to fellow entertainment-industry professionals—producers, directors, agents, and performers—as opposed to 圈外人 (non-industry civilians).

cognates.meaning: the king's/emperor's sacred will; divine will

圣意.etymology: A modifier-head Literary Chinese compound of 圣 (Trad. 聖, shèng, 'sage, all-hearing/perceptive ruler, sacred, imperial', originally depicting a person with a prominent ear 耳 and mouth 口 who hears and understands all) and 意 (yì, 'thought, intention, will', from 音 'sound/voice' in the 心 'heart-mind'). In imperial court usage, 聖意 meant the sovereign's sacred intention or unspoken royal will; in modern Mandarin workplace and media banter, it is used ironically and humorously for the mysterious wishes of a top boss or executive.

history.meaning: the sacred intention or decree of a sage-king or emperor
imperial will (in costume dramas); what the top boss secretly wants (humorous workplace/showbiz slang)

圣意.notes: Almost always used today in the ironic idiom 揣摩圣意 (chuǎimó shèngyì, 'trying to divine the emperor's hidden mind') when subordinates try to guess what an inscrutable CEO or chief producer really wants.

在.etymology: Locative verb ('be at, in, on'), locative coverb ('at, in'), and progressive marker ('right in the middle of doing'). In Classical Chinese (Analects, Shijing), 在 already means 'reside in, be located at, exist'; modern Mandarin extends that 'being at a point' sense to ongoing actions before verbs.

history.meaning: be located at; exist; remain

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 在 (via 萌典)

在乎.etymology: Formed from the verb 在 (zài, 'to reside in, consist in, depend upon') plus the Classical Chinese prepositional/locative enclitic 乎 (hū, functionally equivalent to 於/于 'in, at, upon'). In Classical and Literary Chinese (e.g., Ouyang Xiu's *Zuiweng Ting Ji*: 醉翁之意不在酒，在乎山水之间也), 在乎 introduced a locative or causal complement meaning 'lies in, consists in'. During the Qing dynasty vernacular transition, when the following object was fronted or omitted, 在乎 lexicalized into a single psychological verb with a neutral second syllable (zàihu), shifting to mean 'to care about, take to heart, mind'.

history.meaning: to reside in, consist in, depend upon (verb + preposition)
to care about, mind, take to heart (often in negative 不在乎)
history.stage: Late Imperial Vernacular (Qing) to Modern Mandarin

morphemes.meaning: to reside in, be located at, hinge on
in, at, with regard to (neutralized to -hu)

在乎.notes: The second syllable 乎 must be pronounced in the neutral tone (zàihu); compare 在于 (zàiyú), which kept the classical meaning 'lie in, depend on', whereas 在乎 shifted to emotional caring ('care about').

rootFamily.gloss: to care about, mind, take notice of

在于.etymology: A verb-preposition compound combining 在 (zài, 'to exist at, reside in, hinge upon') with the classical locative preposition 于 (Trad. 於, yú, 'in, at, on'). Directly continuing the Classical Chinese construction 在於, it grammaticalized into a disyllabic transitive verb in modern standard Mandarin that links an abstract subject (such as a problem, key, or value) to its decisive locus or cause ('lies in, consists in, depends on').

history.meaning: is located in; resides or consists in
to lie in, consist in, depend on, be determined by

morphemes.meaning: to exist in, reside at, depend on

在于.notes: Typically takes abstract subjects like 关键 (key), 问题 (problem), or 区别 (difference), e.g., 问题的关键在于…… ('The crux of the problem lies in...').

rootFamily.gloss: to care about, mind (parallel formation with 乎)

在你看来.etymology: An idiomatic prepositional-verbal discourse frame composed of the locative preposition 在 (zài, 'at, in the standpoint of'), the second-person pronoun 你 (nǐ, 'you'), and the compound verb 看来 (kànlái, 'looking at it / as it comes into view', from 看 'to look, regard' + directional complement 来 'hither, toward the observer'). Literally 'as seen from your vantage point', it coalesced in modern Mandarin as a conversational stance marker meaning 'in your eyes, as you see it'.

history.meaning: looking at it from [person]'s standpoint; as it appears to [person]
in your eyes, in your view, from your perspective

morphemes.meaning: looking at it, judging from how it appears

在你看来.notes: Often used at the start of a question or challenge in dialogue to probe an interlocutor's subjective judgment (e.g., 在你看来，这个节目能火吗？ 'In your eyes, can this show become a hit?').

rootFamily.gloss: in my view, as I see it

在场.etymology: A verb-object (动宾) locative compound of 在 (zài, 'to be present at') and 场 (Trad. 場, chǎng, originally a leveled earthen area for sacrificial rituals or threshing grain, from 土 'earth' + phonetic 易, later extended to a stage, arena, or scene of action). Literally 'to be on the ground/stage', it denotes physical presence at the site where an event, broadcast shoot, or incident occurs.

history.meaning: present at the ritual altar, examination ground, or theatrical stage
to be present on the scene; in attendance (at an event, set, or incident)

morphemes.meaning: to be at, be present in

在场.notes: Used both predicatively (当时他也在场 'he was also present at the time') and attributively before nouns without 的 (所有在场人员 'all personnel present on the scene').

rootFamily.gloss: to appear on stage / enter the scene

cognates.meaning: keeping in mind, paying heed to
to keep in mind, pay attention to

在意.etymology: A verb-object (动宾) compound uniting 在 (zài, 'to reside in, keep in') and 意 (yì, 'mind, thought, attention'). Literally 'to keep [something] in one's mind/thoughts'. Attested since Six Dynasties and Tang–Song writings (frequently in negated phrases like 不足在意 'not worth keeping on one's mind' or 不甚在意 'not paying much heed'), it evolved into a common Mandarin verb meaning 'to care about, mind, take personally, or pay close attention to'.

history.meaning: to keep in one's thoughts; to take heed of (often negated as 不在意)
to care about, mind, take to heart

morphemes.meaning: to be in, keep in, hold at

在意.notes: Very close in meaning to 在乎, but 在意 sounds slightly gentler and more inward/emotional (keeping something on one's mind or feeling sensitive about a remark), whereas 在乎 can sound more defiant or outward (e.g., 我不在乎 'I don't care!').

rootFamily.gloss: deliberately, on purpose (or to mind, jíyì/zheyì)

在我看来.etymology: An idiomatic prepositional-verbal frame built from the locative preposition 在 (zài, 'at, in the locus of'), the first-person pronoun 我 (wǒ, 'I, me', originally an oracle-bone pictograph of a serrated polearm borrowed early for the first-person pronoun), and the directional compound 看来 (kànlái, 'looking at it / as it comes into view'). Literally 'looking at it from where I stand', it serves as a polite, reflective discourse marker meaning 'in my view, as I see it'.

history.meaning: judging from how it looks from my standpoint
in my view, as I see it, from my perspective

morphemes.meaning: looking at it, as it appears to the observer

在我看来.notes: Slightly more reflective and analytical than 我觉得 ('I feel/think'); ideal in meetings, critiques, or interviews when presenting a reasoned personal evaluation.

rootFamily.gloss: in your eyes, in your view

cognates.meaning: being enrolled at school, being on campus

在校.etymology: A verb-object (动宾) Sino-compound combining 在 (zài, 'to be present at, remain in') and 校 (xiào, 'school, academy', from 木 'wooden stocks/enclosure' + phonetic 交, attested since the *Mengzi* `夏曰校` as an ancient community school). Modernized during the late Qing and Meiji educational reforms (alongside Japanese 在校 *zaikō*) to denote the status of being currently enrolled as a student at a school or university, prior to graduation.

history.meaning: present at or enrolled in an educational institution
currently enrolled at school; on campus (often attributive, as in 在校生)

morphemes.meaning: to be at, be currently enrolled in

在校.notes: Most frequently used as a non-predicative adjective before nouns without 的, as in 在校生 / 在校大学生 ('currently enrolled college student', contrasting with 毕业生 'graduate' or 社会人 'working adult').

在线.etymology: A modern verb-object (动宾) compound of 在 (zài, 'to be on, remain connected to') and 线 (Trad. 線/綫, xiàn, 'silk thread -> wire, circuit, communication line'). Originally coined in late 20th-century telecommunications and computing as a morphological calque of English *on-line* ('connected to a telephone or computer network line'). In 2010s Mandarin internet and showbiz vernacular, it underwent a vivid metaphorical extension to mean 'actively functioning at peak level, on point, switched on' (e.g., 智商在线, 演技在线).

history.meaning: connected to a telecommunications or computer line (calque of English 'online')
be online, stay connected; (slang) on point, fully switched on and performing well

morphemes.meaning: to be on, stay connected at

在线.notes: Beyond literal internet status ('online'), showbiz critiques constantly use [noun] + 在线 to praise someone's skills or attributes being 'on point'—e.g., 演技在线 ('acting is on point'), 颜值在线 ('visuals are on point'), 智商在线 ('making smart choices').

rootFamily.gloss: launch online, go live (of a show or app)
go offline; be taken down (of a show)

地.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 土 ('earth, soil, ground') + 也 (yě/dì phonetic). Read dì as a noun meaning 'the earth (paired with 天 heaven), ground, land, floor, place, position'; read neutral-tone de in Mandarin as the structural particle turning an adjective or phrase into a pre-verbal adverbial modifier (慢慢地走).

history.meaning: earth; ground; land; region
ground, place (dì); adverbial particle (de)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 地 (via 萌典)

地上.etymology: Locative compound combining 地 ('ground, floor') + 上 ('on, surface'): 'on the ground, on the floor'.

history.meaning: on the ground; on the floor; on earth

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 地上 (via 萌典)

地下室.etymology: Three-character compound of 地下 ('underground, below ground level') + 室 ('room, chamber'): 'basement, cellar'.

history.meaning: room below ground level; basement; cellar

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 地下室 (via 萌典)

地位.etymology: A coordinative / modifier-head Sino-compound combining 地 (dì, 'earth, ground, place, rank') and 位 (wèi, 'standing place at court, seat of office, rank', graphically a person 亻 standing 立 at their assigned court post). Attested in medieval Chinese (*Nan Shi*, Tang poetry) for one's physical place or official station, and reinforced in modern East Asian sociopolitical discourse (alongside Japanese 地位 *chii*) to denote social, professional, or industry status and standing.

history.meaning: assigned court station, rank, or physical site
social, legal, or professional status, standing, prestige

地位.notes: In entertainment industry talk, 江湖地位 ('standing in the arena/industry') and 咖位 (kāwèi, 'star tier/billing status') are key measures of an artist's or producer's clout.

rootFamily.gloss: star billing tier, celebrity status (showbiz slang)

地图.etymology: Compound of 地 ('earth; land; territory', earth radical 土 + 也) + 图 ('drawing; chart; map', enclosure radical 囗 framing a territory plan). Attested as early as the *Zhan Guo Ce* (Warring States Strategies, 3rd century BCE), when rolled silk and wooden maps of terrain were presented at court.

history.stage: Warring States Classical Chinese (*Zhan Guo Ce*)
history.meaning: territorial map or chart
map

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 地图

地址.etymology: Compound noun of 地 ('land, place, location') + 址 ('foundation of a wall or building, site', earth 土 + 止 'foot/base'): originally 'land site, plot foundation' in Tang–Song texts, and in modern Mandarin the standard word for a mailing or street 'address'.

history.meaning: building site; plot of land
mailing or street address; location

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 地址 (via 萌典)

地方.etymology: Compound of 地 ('earth, land') + 方 ('square, region, quarter'). Originated in ancient Chinese cosmology (天圆地方 'heaven is round and earth is square/quartered'), evolved into 'local region/administration (di fang)' vs. the central court, and with neutral tone (dìfang) became the everyday noun for 'place, space, spot, part'.

history.meaning: earth's quarters; territory
place, spot, room (dìfang); local/regional (dìfāng)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 地方 (via 萌典)

地板.etymology: Compound noun of 地 ('ground, floor') + 板 ('wooden plank, board'): 'wooden floorboards, floor (of an indoor room)'.

history.meaning: wooden floorboards; indoor floor

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 地板 (via 萌典)

地标.etymology: A modern determinative compound combining 地 (dì, 'earth, ground, geographic locality') and 标 (biāo, simplified from 標, 'treetop marker, signpost, survey beacon'). Originally referring in surveying and navigation to a physical boundary stone or coastal beacon erected on land, 地标 expanded in twentieth-century urban geography—reinforced by English 'landmark'—to denote any distinctive tower, fountain, or building by which people orient themselves.

history.meaning: geodetic or boundary marker on the ground
architectural or neighborhood landmark

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 地标

地步.etymology: A compound of 地 (dì, 'ground, place, space') and 步 (bù, 'step, pace, stride', originally two feet 止 stepping one after another). Arising in Song and Yuan vernacular and administrative prose (e.g., Zhu Xi's *Zhuzi Yulei*), 地步 originally meant the physical ground under one's feet, room to step/maneuver (as in 留有地步 'leave room to maneuver'), or a point reached along a journey. From 'the point one's steps have reached', it evolved into 'degree, extent, stage, or plight'—especially an extreme or regrettable pass.

history.meaning: physical footing, room to maneuver, point reached along a path
degree, extent, stage, plight (usually an unfavorable or extreme state)

morphemes.meaning: step, pace, stage reached along a path

地步.notes: Almost always appears in the construction 到(了)……的地步 ('reach the point/plight of...'), typically describing a situation that has deteriorated or escalated to an extreme degree (e.g., 走到今天这个地步 'having come to this pass today').

rootFamily.gloss: room for maneuver, leeway (synonymous in 留余地)

地毯.etymology: Compound noun of 地 ('floor, ground') + 毯 ('woven woolen rug or blanket', hair/wool 毛 + 炎): 'carpet, rug'. Attested since Tang–Song accounts of Central Asian and domestic woven rugs.

history.meaning: floor rug; carpet

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 地毯 (via 萌典)

地球.etymology: A modifier-head astronomical neologism combining 地 (dì, 'earth, land') and 球 (qiú, originally a resonant jade sphere or chime, later any 'ball, globe, sphere'). Coined in late Ming China by the Jesuit missionary Matteo Ricci (利玛窦) and Chinese scholar-officials such as Li Zhizao and Xu Guangqi on the 1602 world map *Kunyu Wanguo Quantu* (坤舆万国全图) to translate the Western scientific concept of the *terrestrial globe* (Latin *globus terrae*), overturning the traditional Chinese cosmological dictum 天圆地方 ('heaven is round and earth is square'). Later borrowed from Chinese into Japanese, Korean, and Vietnamese.

history.form: 地球 (Late Ming Scientific Chinese, c. 1602)
history.meaning: the spherical Earth, terrestrial globe (coined by Matteo Ricci & Chinese collaborators)
planet Earth, the world/globe

地球.notes: A rare example of a modern scientific term coined first in Ming-dynasty Chinese and exported to Japan (*chikyū*) rather than the reverse; colloquially used in hyperbole like 地球人都知道 ('everyone on planet Earth knows').

地窖.etymology: Compound noun from 地 ('earth; ground') + 窖 ('underground cellar or storage pit', cave/hole radical 穴 over 告). Underground storage pits for grain, vegetables, wine, and winter ice have been excavated across northern China since Neolithic times to keep provisions cool in summer and frost-free in winter.

history.meaning: subterranean storage pit or vault
cellar; root cellar; basement vault

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 地窖

地道.etymology: A compound of 地 (dì, 'earth, locality, region') and 道 (dào, 'way, path, administrative circuit/province, standard'). With a neutral second tone (dìdao, 'authentic, genuine, idiomatic, thorough'), it arose by metathesis from 道地 (dàodì), a term originating in Song–Ming traditional Chinese pharmacology (道地药材) where 道 referred to historical Tang/Song administrative circuits (such as 川道 Sichuan, 怀道 Henan): herbs grown in their premier native circuit were praised as 道地 ('from the genuine region'). In Northern/Beijing Mandarin, 道地 inverted to 地道 (dìdao) and generalized to mean 'authentic, genuine, idiomatic'. (With a full fourth tone dìdào, it is a separate literal compound meaning 'underground tunnel'.)

history.meaning: genuinely sourced from the proper geographical circuit (of medicinal herbs)
authentic, genuine, idiomatic (of language, cuisine, or craftsmanship)
history.stage: Qing Beijing Mandarin to Modern Standard Mandarin

morphemes.meaning: circuit/region, standard, way (pronounced neutral tone -dao for 'authentic')

地道.notes: Pay attention to tone: dìdao (neutral second syllable) means 'authentic, idiomatic' (他的普通话很地道 'his Mandarin is very idiomatic'), whereas dìdào (falling fourth tone) means 'underground tunnel' (地道战 'tunnel warfare'). Bothの地道 and 道地 remain in active use today.

rootFamily.gloss: authentic, genuine (original un-inverted form, common in Southern/Taiwan Mandarin)
thickness/generosity of character; honest and kind (related Northern slang)

地铁.etymology: A disyllabic syllabic abbreviation (缩略语) of 地下铁道 (dìxià tiědào) or 地下铁路 (dìxià tiělù, 'underground railway'), combining 地 (dì, 'ground/earth', standing for 地下 'underground') and 铁 (Trad. 鐵, tiě, 'iron', standing for 铁道/铁路 'iron road, railway'). Modeled on the 20th-century Sino-Japanese compound 地下鐵道 (*chika tetsudō*, shortened in Japanese to three-character 地下鉄 *chikatetsu*, and further compressed in Mainland Mandarin to the two-character prosodic template 地铁).

history.form: 地下鐵道 / 地下鐵路 (Early 20th c.)
history.meaning: underground iron road / subterranean railway
subway, metro, underground rapid transit

地铁.notes: Mainland China uses 地铁 (dìtiě), whereas Hong Kong calls its system 港铁 (MTR) / 地铁 and Taiwan uses 捷运 (jiéyùn, 'rapid transit'). High-speed rail follows the exact same abbreviation pattern: 高速铁路 -> 高铁 (gāotiě).

rootFamily.gloss: high-speed rail (short for 高速铁路)

场.etymology: Phono-semantic character (traditional 場, earth 土 + 易 yáng): originally 'cleared, packed flat earth used for sacrifices or threshing grain', hence 'open ground, square, stage, field, scene' and a verbal/nominal classifier for 'a bout, session, show, match, or spell of rain (一场雨)'.

history.meaning: sacrificial or threshing ground; arena
site; field; venue; classifier for events, shows, or rain

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 场 (via 萌典)

场合.etymology: A Sino-Japanese return loan (*wasei-kango* 和製漢語) written 場合: originally a native Japanese compound *ba-ai* (combining *ba* 場 'place, scene, spot' + *ai* 合, the nominalized stem of *au* 'to meet, coincide, fit'), meaning 'the juncture where place and circumstance meet -> case, situation, occasion'. When borrowed into modern Chinese in the early 20th century and read with Sino-Chinese pronunciations as chǎnghé, it specialized to mean a 'social occasion, public setting, or specific situational context' rather than a purely grammatical 'in the case that' (which Japanese *baai* often expresses).

history.meaning: conjuncture of place and circumstance; case, occasion, situation
occasion, social setting, public or situational context

场合.notes: A classic false friend with Japanese: Japanese 場合 (*baai*) usually means 'in the case/event that (if...)', whereas Chinese 场合 strictly means a social setting or occasion (e.g., 公共场合 'public places/settings', 正式场合 'formal occasions', 注意说话的场合 'mind the setting when you speak').

场地.etymology: A modifier-head / coordinative noun compound of 场 (Trad. 場, chǎng, 'leveled earthen ground, arena, stage, activity ground') and 地 (dì, 'land, ground, physical space'). Attested in late imperial vernacular for a plot of open ground or threshing floor, it developed in modern Mandarin into the standard term for a physical venue, studio space, sports field, or event site.

history.meaning: leveled open ground, threshing floor, or courtyard plot
venue, site, studio or event space, sports ground

场地.notes: Unlike 场合 (which refers to the abstract social occasion or atmosphere), 场地 refers to the concrete physical space or real estate that must be booked, rented, or set up (e.g., 租场地 'rent a venue', 拍摄场地 'filming location/studio space').

坏.etymology: Phono-semantic character (traditional 壞, combining earth 土 + 褱 huái; simplified 坏 uses 土 + 不): in Classical Chinese 'crumble, collapse (of earthen walls or buildings), ruin, spoil', and in modern Mandarin the general adjective and complement for 'broken, out of order, spoiled, bad, wicked'.

history.meaning: (of walls/structures) collapse; ruin; decay
broken; spoiled; bad; wicked

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 坏 (via 萌典)

坏习惯.etymology: A modifier-head trimorphemic noun compound combining the adjective 坏 (Trad. 壞, huài, originally 'collapsed earthen wall, ruined, spoiled' from 土 'earth' + phonetic 懐/褱, later generalized to 'bad') with the disyllabic noun 习惯 (Trad. 習慣, xíguàn, 'habit, custom'). 习惯 itself is a classical coordinative compound of 习 (Trad. 習, xí, 'a young bird flapping its wings repeatedly -> to practice repeatedly') and 惯 (Trad. 慣, guàn, 'to be accustomed to, habitual', from 心 'heart-mind' + 貫 'pierce through/string together').

history.meaning: to practice repeatedly until accustomed (e.g.,賈誼: 少成若天性，習慣如自然)
bad habit, undesirable behavioral routine

morphemes.meaning: to practice repeatedly (习) + to be accustomed to (惯) -> habit

坏习惯.notes: Typically collocates with 养成 (yǎngchéng, 'develop/cultivate [a habit]') and 改掉 (gǎidiào, 'break/get rid of [a bad habit]'). In higher-register prose, a bad habit or vice is called 恶习 (èxí) or 陋习 (lòuxí).

坏了.etymology: Predicative and exclamatory phrase combining 坏 ('broken, spoiled, gone wrong') + change-of-state particle 了 (le): '(something) is broken / out of order / spoiled' and as an exclamation 'uh-oh!, oh no!'.

history.meaning: broken; out of order; 'oh no!'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 坏了 (via 萌典)

坏事.etymology: A structurally dual compound of 坏 (Trad. 壞, huài, originally 'to crumble, ruin, destroy', and adjectivally 'spoiled, bad, wicked') and 事 (shì, 'affair, matter, deed, enterprise'). Depending on how the two morphemes relate syntactically, 坏事 splits into two distinct lexical senses: (1) as a modifier-head (偏正) noun, 'a bad deed, wicked act, or unfortunate event'; (2) as a verb-object (动宾) compound retaining the ancient causative verb sense of 壞 ('to ruin/spoil'), meaning 'to ruin an affair, spoil a plan, or bungle things' (often 坏了事 or 坏事儿).

history.meaning: to ruin an affair or state enterprise (verb-object); a ruined or wicked matter (modifier-head)
bad thing, evil deed (noun); to ruin plans, mess things up (separable verb)

morphemes.meaning: bad, wicked (adj); to ruin, spoil, wreck (verb)

坏事.notes: Watch the syntax to tell the two meanings apart: 做坏事 means 'do bad things / commit misdeeds' (noun), whereas 一着急就容易坏事 or 坏了我的大事 means 'ruin the plan / mess things up' (verb-object). In spoken Beijing Mandarin, 坏菜 (huàicài) is a lively slang synonym for 'bungling a plan'.

坐.etymology: Ancient ideogram (会意字) showing two people (从) kneeling/sitting facing each other on the ground/earth (土): 'sit, take a seat; travel by (bus, train, plane, boat); (of buildings) face a direction; put a pot on the stove'.

history.meaning: two figures kneeling on the ground = sit
sit; ride/travel by vehicle

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 坐 (via 萌典)

坐下.etymology: A verb-directional (动趋) compound uniting 坐 (zuò, 'to sit', an associative graph 坐 depicting two people 人人 kneeling/sitting face-to-face upon the earth 土) with the directional complement 下 (xià, 'down, downward', originally an indicative sign with a short stroke below a baseline). While Classical Chinese used monosyllabic 坐 for taking a seat (originally kneeling with buttocks resting on one's heels on a floor mat, before high chairs became widespread in the Tang–Song transition), vernacular Mandarin paired it with directional 下 to express the completed downward motion of sitting down.

history.meaning: to kneel-sit on a floor mat (resting on one's heels)
to sit down (on a chair or seat); to settle into a seated position

坐下.notes: Often expanded with the complex directional complement 下来 (坐下来聊 'sit down and chat', emphasizing settling down into a state of conversation). For a polite one-word invitation to sit, 请坐 ('please have a seat') is preferred over 请坐下 (which can sound slightly like a command).

rootFamily.gloss: to take one's seat (formal, at a ceremony or meeting)

坐坐.etymology: A tentative verb reduplication (AA pattern) of 坐 (zuò, 'to sit'), an associogram (会意) depicting two people (二人) kneeling face-to-face upon the earth (土). In Mandarin grammar, reduplicating a monosyllabic action verb softens the imperative and denotes a brief, casual, or hospitable duration ('sit for a little while; come in and chat').

history.meaning: to kneel on both knees; to sit on a mat
to sit for a bit; to drop by for a casual visit and chat

morphemes.meaning: to sit; to take a seat
tentative aspect marker indicating brief, relaxed duration

坐坐.notes: Used constantly in hospitality and office etiquette (e.g., 来我办公室坐坐, 'drop by my office for a chat'), where the second syllable is pronounced in the neutral tone (zuòzuo).

rootFamily.gloss: to ride in a vehicle; to take a seat

cognates.meaning: to sit properly; to sit tight

坐好.etymology: A verb-complement (resultative) compound combining 坐 (zuò, 'to sit') with the resultative complement 好 (hǎo, 'properly, securely, to completion'). While 好 originally meant 'good' or 'fine' in Classical Chinese, by the Tang–Song vernacular period it grammaticalized after action verbs to indicate that an action is brought to a stable, satisfactory, or secure state.

history.meaning: to sit + good/well
to sit properly, securely, or in readiness

坐好.notes: Functions both literally ('sit up straight / hold on tight in a vehicle') and figuratively ('buckle up / get ready for a wild ride' in media and live broadcasts).

rootFamily.gloss: to stand firm; to stand properly
to prepare fully; to get ready

cognates.meaning: reaping profits without effort (playing the fisherman)

坐收.etymology: A modifier-head (adverbial-verb) compound from Literary Chinese: 坐 (zuò, used adverbially to mean 'while sitting idle; without lifting a finger') + 收 (shōu, 'to gather, harvest, reap'). It derives from classical idioms such as 坐收渔利 ('to sit back and reap the fisherman's profit', alluding to the Warring States fable of the snipe and the clam in *Zhan Guo Ce*).

history.meaning: to collect or harvest without expending effort
to sit back and reap (gains, royalties, or third-party benefits)

morphemes.meaning: sitting idle; effortlessly; without taking action
to harvest; to collect; to reap

坐收.notes: Frequently collocates with 渔翁之利 ('fisherman's profit' when two rivals exhaust each other) or 成果 ('fruits of labor') in business and media commentary.

rootFamily.gloss: to sit back and enjoy the fruits of others' labor

cognates.meaning: to garrison; to command in person

坐镇.etymology: A serial/coordinative verbal compound from medieval Literary Chinese military usage: 坐 (zuò, 'to be stationed at a seat of authority') + 镇 (傳統: 鎮, zhèn, 'to press down, pacify, garrison a strategic stronghold'). Originally describing a commander personally garrisoning a vital frontier post to deter unrest, it broadened in modern Mandarin to mean a senior executive, director, or star personally presiding over a project or studio to ensure success.

history.meaning: (of a general or governor) to personally garrison and pacify a region
to command in person; to hold the fort as the authoritative leader on site

morphemes.meaning: to be seated; to occupy a post
to garrison; to stabilize; to preside over with authority

坐镇.notes: Very common in showbiz and corporate contexts (e.g., 总导演亲自坐镇, 'the chief director is personally on set calling the shots') to convey reassuring authority.

rootFamily.gloss: to sit in command; to direct from the rear

坑.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 土 ('earth, ground') + 亢 (kāng, 'neck/high hollow'): 'pit, hole, hollow in the ground, depression, tunnel' (and colloquially 'entrap, cheat').

history.stage: Classical Chinese (originally 阬 / 坑) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: earthen pit; hollow; puddle/hole

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 坑 (via 萌典)

块.etymology: Phono-semantic character (traditional 塊, earth 土 + 鬼 guǐ; simplified 块 uses 土 + 夬 guài): originally 'clod or lump of earth' in Classical Chinese (Zhuangzi, Chuci). In Mandarin it became the standard classifier for 'a piece, lump, chunk, slice, plot of land' and for the basic unit of currency ('yuan, buck', 一块钱).

history.meaning: clod of earth; lump
classifier for pieces, chunks, and currency units (yuan)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 块 (via 萌典)

块钱.etymology: A classifier-noun compound formed from 块 (傳統: 塊, kuài, originally 'clod of earth', later classifier for solid pieces or silver dollars) + 钱 (傳統: 錢, qián, originally an ancient farming spade used as early bronze currency, hence 'money/coin'). In late Imperial and Republican China, silver dollars (银元) were counted in 'pieces' (一块银元,一块钱), cementing 块钱 as the standard spoken counterpart to formal 元 (yuán).

history.form: 塊 (kuài, clod) + 錢 (qián, bronze spade coin)
history.meaning: lump of earth; bronze coin
one piece of silver currency; one dollar/yuan
yuan; dollar (colloquial currency unit after numerals)

morphemes.meaning: piece; lump; spoken unit for basic currency (yuan/dollar)

块钱.notes: Strictly preceded by a number or quantifier in spoken Mandarin (e.g., 十块钱, 几块钱); in formal contracts or price tags, 元 (yuán) is written instead.

rootFamily.gloss: to make money; to earn a profit

坚信.etymology: A modifier-head (adverbial-verb) compound composed of 坚 (傳統: 堅, jiān, 'hard, solid, firm', containing 土 'earth' at the base) modifying 信 (xìn, 'to trust, believe; truthful word', an associogram of 人 'person' + 言 'speech'). Literally 'to firmly believe', it denotes unwavering conviction in a principle, plan, or outcome.

history.meaning: to hold fast to faith or trust; firm conviction
to firmly believe; to have unshakable faith that...

坚信.notes: Takes a clause or abstract noun as its object (e.g., 我坚信这档节目会成功, 'I firmly believe this show will succeed') and belongs to an earnest, inspirational register.

坚决.etymology: A coordinative compound combining 坚 (傳統: 堅, jiān, 'hard, solid, unyielding') and 决 (傳統: 決, jué, 'to breach a dike; to decide, resolve definitively'). In Classical Chinese, 決 denoted cutting open a water channel so the flow is irreversible; paired with 堅, it portrays an attitude or decision that is both rock-solid and decisively settled.

history.meaning: unyielding and decisive in temperament or action
resolute, firm, determined (attitude, stance, or refusal)

坚决.notes: Often functions adverbially before verbs of opposition or support (e.g., 坚决反对 'resolutely oppose', 态度坚决 'have an unyielding attitude').

坚强.etymology: A coordinative adjectival compound from Classical Chinese (attested in *Liji* and *Hanfeizi*) uniting 坚 (傳統: 堅, jiān, 'hard, solid, durable') and 强 (傳統: 強, qiáng, 'strong, powerful, resilient'). Originally describing the physical hardness and tensile strength of armor, timber, or military forces, it evolved in modern Mandarin to emphasize psychological resilience and inner fortitude in the face of adversity.

history.meaning: physically hard and strong; militarily formidable
emotionally strong, resilient, and staunch under hardship

坚强.notes: Unlike 强壮 (physically muscular/robust), 坚强 refers primarily to mental toughness, willpower, and emotional resilience (e.g., 内心坚强, 'inwardly strong').

垃圾桶.etymology: Three-character compound of 垃圾 ('rubbish, trash, garbage', originally a southern/Wu dialect compound 垃圾 lèsè adopted into standard Mandarin as lājī) + 桶 ('bucket, pail, bin', wood 木 + 甬): 'trash can, wastebin, garbage bin'.

history.meaning: trash can; wastebasket; garbage bin

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 垃圾桶 (via 萌典)

垫.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining 执 ('hold/set in place', phonetic and semantic) above earth radical 土, originally meaning to fill in low ground or place a support underneath. From this arose both the verbal sense 'prop up or cushion from below' and the nominal sense 'pad, mat, or cushion'.

morphemes.meaning: place underneath to support; pad; cushion

history.meaning: fill in or prop up from underneath
prop up; pad; cushion

垮.etymology: A phono-semantic compound (形声) combining the semantic radical 土 (tǔ, 'earth, soil, wall') with the phonetic component 夸 (kuā, Old Chinese *kʷʰˤra, which also carries the core phonesthemic sense of 'sagging, slumping, or spreading apart', cf. 跨 'to straddle' and 侉). Originally prominent in Southwestern Mandarin dialects for an earthen bank or wall caving in, it entered standard Mandarin for physical, physical-health, or organizational collapse.

history.meaning: (of an earthen embankment or wall) to cave in, collapse
to collapse, break down (of structures, health, regimes, or projects)

morphemes.meaning: to collapse; to cave in; to break down

垮.notes: Frequently serves as a resultative complement after verbs of exhaustion or defeat: 累垮 ('collapse from exhaustion'), 打垮 ('crush/bring down'), or 垮台 ('fall from power / go bust').

rootFamily.gloss: to fall from power; to collapse (of an enterprise or cabinet)
to collapse; to fall apart (of a face/expression or structure)
to boast; to exaggerate (sharing phonetic 夸)

cognates.word: 埋める (うめる, umeru) / 埋 (まい, mai)

埋.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形声) formed with semantic radical 土 (tǔ, 'earth, soil') and phonetic 里 (lǐ, Old Chinese *mə.rəʔ; compare 埋 Old Chinese *m.rˤə, 'to bury in the ground'). In Classical Chinese (written 薶 in the *Shuowen Jiezi*), it denoted burying sacrificial offerings in the earth to honor spirits of the land, before generalizing to burying anything underground or planting hidden traps/clues.

history.meaning: to bury sacrificial victims or jade in the earth; to inter
to bury in the ground; to cover up; to plant secretly (clues, mines, or personnel)

morphemes.meaning: to bury; to cover with earth; to conceal

埋.notes: Note the pronunciation split: pronounced mái in almost all senses ('bury, hide', e.g., 埋伏 'ambush', 埋头 'immerse oneself'), but read mán only in 埋怨 (mányuàn, 'to blame/grumble'). In scriptwriting and media, 埋梗 or 埋伏笔 means 'to plant an Easter egg or foreshadowing'.

rootFamily.gloss: to lie in ambush; to plant foreshadowing
to bury one's head in work; to immerse oneself

城区.etymology: Compound noun of 城 ('walled city, urban center') + 区 (區, 'district, area, zone'): 'urban area, city proper, city district'.

history.meaning: urban district; city proper

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 城区 (via 萌典)

城外.etymology: Locative compound of 城 ('city wall, city') + 外 ('outside'): 'outside the city walls, on the outskirts of town'. Attested throughout Classical and Tang–Song poetry.

history.stage: Classical & Tang–Song Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: outside the city; outskirts

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 城外 (via 萌典)

城市.etymology: Coordinative noun compound pairing the two defining institutions of traditional Chinese urban settlements: 城 ('rammed-earth defensive city wall and administrative seat', 土 + 成) + 市 ('enclosed marketplace for trade'). Together they form the modern word for 'city, town'.

history.meaning: city walls and marketplaces
city; urban center

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 城市 (via 萌典)

城里.etymology: Locative compound of 城 ('city') + 里 (裡, 'inside'): 'inside the city, in town, downtown'.

history.meaning: in the city; in town

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 城里 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to foster; to train; to cultivate

培养.etymology: A coordinative agricultural metaphor combining 培 (péi, 'to bank up loose earth around the roots of a plant', with radical 土 'earth') and 养 (傳統: 養, yǎng, 'to nourish, raise, rear', from 羊 'sheep' + 食 'food'). Just as a gardener mounds soil around young shoots and waters them, 培养 came to mean nurturing human talent, habits, or feelings over time. Was also reinforced in the 19th–20th centuries via Japanese *baiyō* for biological 'culture'.

history.meaning: to mound soil around plants and nourish their growth; to nurture vitality
to cultivate, mentor, and foster (talent, successors, habits); to culture (cells)

morphemes.meaning: to mound earth around roots; to foster
to nourish; to raise; to rear

培养.notes: Focuses on long-term, holistic mentorship and character/interest development (e.g., 培养新人 'mentor new talent', 培养感情 'build rapport'), whereas 培训 targets structured, short-term skill training.

rootFamily.gloss: to nurture; to breed; to foster

培训.etymology: A modern coordinative compound combining 培 (péi, 'to bank up earth around roots; to foster and develop', abstracted from 培养) and 训 (傳統: 訓, xùn, 'to instruct, drill, coach', from 言 'speech' + 川 'flowing stream', i.e., guiding someone smoothly with words, as in 训练). It was coined in 20th-century institutional Chinese to denote systematic vocational or professional training.

history.meaning: separate classical roots for nurturing and verbal instruction
to train professionally; structured corporate or vocational training program

morphemes.meaning: to instruct; to coach; to drill

培训.notes: Used as both a transitive verb and a noun in workplace and entertainment-industry settings (e.g., 练习生培训 'trainee bootcamp/coaching', 员工培训 'staff training').

rootFamily.gloss: to drill; physical or skill training
lesson; moral learned from a mistake

基本.etymology: A coordinative architectural-botanical compound combining 基 (jī, 'rammed-earth foundation of a wall or building', with semantic 土 'earth' at the base and phonetic 其) and 本 (běn, 'taproot of a tree', formed by adding a stroke at the base of 木 'tree'). Attested in Han-dynasty historical prose (*Hanshu*) for the 'foundation and root' of governance, it developed in modern Mandarin into an attributive adjective ('basic, fundamental') and adverb ('basically, on the whole').

history.meaning: foundation of a building and root of a tree; fundamental basis of the state
basic, fundamental (adj.); basically, in the main (adv.)

基本.notes: As an adverb, 基本 directly precedes verbs or adjectives (e.g., 基本完成 'basically completed', 基本一致 'basically consistent'); to modify an entire clause or stand before the subject, use 基本上.

基本上.etymology: Formed by suffixing the spatial-domain enclitic 上 (shàng, 'on the level/plane of; in terms of') to the coordinative noun/adjective 基本 (jīběn, 'foundation and root; fundamental basis'). In modern Mandarin grammar, -上 productively converts abstract nouns into sentence-level viewpoint or degree adverbs (cf. 事实上 'in fact', 原则上 'in principle'), yielding 'on a fundamental level; basically; for the most part'.

history.meaning: upon the fundamental basis
basically; on the whole; for all practical purposes

morphemes.meaning: on the plane of; in terms of (adverbializer)

基本上.notes: More flexible than bare 基本: 基本上 can appear either before the subject (基本上大家都同意) or between the subject and predicate (大家基本上都同意).

基金.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-Japanese compound (*wasei-kango* 基金 *kikin*) coined during the Meiji era to translate Western financial concepts of 'endowment' or 'capital fund', and subsequently borrowed back into Mandarin. It pairs 基 (jī, 'foundation, base') as a modifier with 金 (jīn, 'metal, gold, money, capital'), literally 'foundational capital' set aside for a dedicated purpose or investment pool.

history.meaning: foundational capital; endowment fund (Meiji-era translation of English 'fund')
financial fund (investment fund, venture fund, or charitable endowment)

基金.notes: Refers to the pool of capital itself (e.g., 买基金 'buy mutual funds', 影视投资基金 'film & TV investment fund'), whereas the organization managing a charitable or grant-making endowment is a 基金会.

cognates.word: 基金会 (ききんかい, kikinkai)

基金会.etymology: A three-character compound formed by adding the institutional suffix 会 (傳統: 會, huì, 'assembly, society, association, board') to 基金 (jījīn, 'endowment fund'). It designates the legal organization, board of trustees, or philanthropic institution that administers a dedicated fund (translating English 'foundation', e.g., charitable or cultural foundations).

history.meaning: institutional association administering an endowment or philanthropic fund

基金会.notes: Distinguish 基金 (the money or investment product) from 基金会 (the institution or charity, such as 慈善基金会 'charitable foundation').

堂堂.etymology: A full reduplication (AA stative ideophone) of 堂 (táng, 'elevated main hall of a palace or ancestral temple', built upon a high rammed-earth platform 土 with phonetic 尚 shàng 'lofty'). Attested in the *Analects* of Confucius (*Lunyu*: 堂堂乎张也, 'How imposing in bearing is Zizhang!'), the reduplication evokes the lofty, open, and awe-inspiring grandeur of a great hall, extending to a person's dignified bearing or illustrious status.

history.meaning: lofty and imposing like a great hall; stately and dignified in demeanor
dignified, illustrious, formidable; (before a title) a whole / a prestigious...

morphemes.meaning: intensifying reduplication denoting imposing grandeur or open dignity

堂堂.notes: Often used before a prestigious title to express rhetorical disbelief or irony when someone acts beneath their station: 堂堂总监，竟然做这种事 ('How could a whole chief director stoop to doing something like this!').

rootFamily.gloss: open and aboveboard; honorable and dignified
grand; magnificent; resplendent (of a building or speech)

cognates.meaning: to pile up; sedimentary (in 堆積)

堆.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形声, originally written 𠂤 in oracle bone script depicting a terraced mound of earth) combining the semantic radical 土 (tǔ, 'earth, soil') with the phonetic component 隹 (zhuī, Old Chinese *tur; compare 堆 Old Chinese *tˤuj). Originally a noun meaning an earthen mound or hillock, it developed by conversion into a transitive verb ('to heap up, stack up, pile together') and a measure word for heaps or crowds.

history.meaning: mound of earth; hillock; heap of stones
to stack up, pile up (verb); a pile, heap, crowd, or ton of (classifier/noun)

morphemes.meaning: to pile up; to stack; a heap or mound

堆.notes: Extremely versatile in spoken Mandarin: as a verb (桌上堆满了文件 'files are stacked all over the desk', 脸上堆笑 'pile on a forced smile') and as an informal quantifier 一大堆 ('a huge pile / a ton of troubles or tasks').

rootFamily.gloss: to pile up; to accumulate (goods, work, or clouds)
to stack; to pile neatly on top of one another
to gather in a crowd; to cluster together

堵.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 土 ('earth, rammed-earth wall') + 者 (zhě/dǔ phonetic). In Classical Chinese, 堵 meant 'a section of earthen wall (and classifier for walls: 一堵墙)'; from the medieval period onward it also became a verb meaning 'stop up, block, clog, feel stifled'.

history.meaning: rammed-earth wall; classifier for walls
block up; clog; congested; classifier for walls

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 堵 (via 萌典)

堵车.etymology: Verb-object compound of 堵 ('block, congest') + 车 ('vehicles, traffic'): 'have a traffic jam, be stuck in traffic'.

history.meaning: traffic jam; traffic congestion

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 堵车 (via 萌典)

塑封.etymology: Modern compound of 塑 ('mold clay; plastic', from 朔 shuò + 土 'earth', shortened from 塑料 'plastic') + 封 ('seal up; enclose in an envelope', originally planting a boundary tree on a mound). Literally 'to seal in plastic film', i.e., to laminate paper or cards against moisture.

history.meaning: heat-seal in plastic; laminate

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 塑封

塞.etymology: Ancient character showing two hands (廾) placing bricks/blocks (𡨄) in a gap with earth (土) at the bottom: read sāi in everyday Mandarin for 'stuff, cram, plug up, cork, stopper'; read sài for 'frontier pass/fortress (边塞)'; read sè in formal compounds like 堵塞 ('block, obstruct').

morphemes.meaning: hands packing blocks into a space

history.meaning: fill a gap; block up; frontier stronghold
stuff, plug, stopper (sāi); block (sè); frontier pass (sài)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 塞 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to fill a vacancy; to fill in the blanks

填空.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound composed of 填 (tián, 'to fill in an earthen pit or depression, to stuff full', with semantic 土 'earth' and phonetic 真 zhēn) + 空 (kòng, 'an empty space, vacancy, blank slot', fourth tone in the nominal/verbal sense 'gap/vacancy'). Originally referring to filling a physical cavity or an official job vacancy, it specialized in modern education for 'fill-in-the-blank' exam questions, and figuratively in drama/romance for acting as a stopgap or emotional stand-in.

history.meaning: to fill in a cavity or vacant official post
to fill in a blank (on a test or schedule); to step in as a substitute or emotional rebound

morphemes.meaning: to fill in; to stuff; to pad
blank space; vacancy; emotional or scheduling gap

填空.notes: Because it is a separable verb-object (离合词) where 空 is pronounced in the 4th tone (tiánkòng), modifiers can be inserted between the characters (e.g., 填这个空, 'fill this gap/slot'). In *Behind the Scenes*, it is used poignantly for treating someone as an emotional placeholder.

rootFamily.gloss: to fill out (a form or questionnaire)
to fill up a vacuum or gap (in an industry or market)

cognates.meaning: boundary; spiritual realm or state of mastery
realm; plane of spiritual or artistic attainment

境界.etymology: A coordinative compound from Classical Chinese uniting 境 (jìng, 'territorial border, frontier, enclosed region', with radical 土 'land') and 界 (jiè, 'boundary line between fields', from 田 'field' + 介 'to divide'). Originally meaning 'geographical border or territory', during the Six Dynasties and Tang period it was adopted by Chinese Buddhist translators (such as Xuanzang) to render Sanskrit *viṣaya* or *gocara* ('sphere of sensory perception or spiritual plane of consciousness'), whence aesthetic critic Wang Guowei popularized it for the supreme 'artistic/spiritual realm' or peak level of mastery.

history.meaning: geographical boundary; territorial frontier between states
sphere of cognition; spiritual plane attained through meditation
aesthetic, moral, or professional realm; peak level of mastery and vision

morphemes.meaning: territory; region; state of mind or environment

境界.notes: Praising someone's 境界高 ('high realm/plane') means their artistic vision, professional mastery, or philosophical outlook transcends petty concerns and ordinary technique.

rootFamily.gloss: circumstances; plight; situation one is in
artistic conception; poetic mood or atmosphere

墙.etymology: Phono-semantic character (traditional 牆, originally combining 爿 'planks/framing boards for rammed earth' + 嗇 sè/qiáng phonetic, later written with the earth radical 土): 'wall (of a room, house, or courtyard)'.

history.meaning: rammed-earth or brick wall
wall

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 墙 (via 萌典)

墙上.etymology: Locative compound combining 墙 ('wall') + 上 ('on, upon'): 'on the wall'.

history.meaning: on the wall

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 墙上 (via 萌典)

墙边.etymology: Locative compound combining 墙 ('wall') + 边 (邊, 'side, edge'): 'by the wall, alongside the wall'.

history.meaning: beside the wall; along the wall

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 墙边 (via 萌典)

增加.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound attested since the Han dynasty (*Liji*, *Lunheng*), combining 增 (zēng, 'to add layer upon layer, to pile up soil or silk', with radical 土 'earth' and phonetic 曾 céng 'layer/tier') and 加 (jiā, 'to add effort to speech; to augment, place on top', from 力 'strength' + 口 'mouth'). Both morphemes converge on the core meaning 'to augment in quantity, degree, or number'.

history.meaning: to add upon; to augment in number or bulk
to increase, boost, add (budget, ratings, personnel, or difficulty)

morphemes.meaning: to add layer by layer; to increase

增加.notes: Can be used both transitively (增加预算 'increase the budget') and intransitively (收视率增加了 'viewership ratings increased'); its direct antonym is 减少 (jiǎnshǎo, 'to decrease').

rootFamily.gloss: to strengthen; to enhance; to reinforce

墨水.etymology: Compound of 墨 ('black soot ink', combining 黑 'black' + 土 'earth', from pine-soot inksticks) + 水 ('water/liquid'), naming liquid pen ink in contrast to solid inksticks ground on an inkstone.

history.meaning: pine-soot inkstick
liquid fountain-pen ink

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 墨水 (via 萌典)

声.etymology: Ancient character (traditional 聲) showing a hand with a mallet (殳) striking a suspended L-shaped stone chime (聲/磬) and an ear (耳) listening below: 'sound, voice, tone (the four tones of Mandarin 四声); make a sound; reputation; classifier for utterances or sounds'.

morphemes.meaning: stone chime + mallet + ear = sound, voice

history.meaning: striking a stone chime heard by the ear = sound, voice, tone
sound; voice; tone; classifier for sounds

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 声 (via 萌典)

声学.etymology: Compound academic noun combining 声 (聲, 'sound') + 学 (學, 'study, science, -logy'): 'acoustics'.

history.meaning: the science of sound; acoustics

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 声学 (via 萌典)

声明.etymology: Originally a verb-object or coordinative compound in Classical Chinese (*Zuozhuan*) combining 声 (傳統: 聲, shēng, 'voice, sound, public proclamation', originally depicting striking a stone chime 磬 and hearing with the ear 耳) + 明 (míng, 'to make clear, illuminate, elucidate'). Literally 'to voice aloud and make clear', it later also translated Sanskrit *śabda-vidyā* (phonology/grammar) in medieval Buddhism before standardizing in modern diplomatic and media discourse for an official 'public statement' or 'to declare publicly'.

history.meaning: to proclaim aloud and make clear one's righteous cause or decree
official public statement, press release (noun); to state or declare publicly (verb)

声明.notes: In entertainment and PR crises, agencies routinely issue an official statement (发表声明 or 严正声明 'solemn statement') to clarify rumors or protect a celebrity's rights. Do not confuse with 说明 (to explain/instructions).

声誉.etymology: A coordinative nominal compound from Classical Chinese combining 声 (傳統: 聲, shēng, 'sound, voice, renown that travels far like sound') and 誉 (傳統: 譽, yù, 'praise, acclaim, good name', composed of 言 'speech/praise' and phonetic 與 yǔ). Because a person's reputation is carried on the voices and praises of others, 声誉 denotes high public esteem, institutional prestige, and moral/professional standing.

history.meaning: fame and public praise enjoyed by a scholar or official
reputation, prestige, good standing (of an individual, brand, or media network)

morphemes.meaning: praise; acclaim; honor and good name
