声誉.notes: A formal, positive-register noun (e.g., 享有很高的声誉 'enjoy high prestige', 损害公司声誉 'damage the company's reputation'); compare 名声, which is more colloquial and can be good or bad.

rootFamily.gloss: fame; reputation; moral standing (of a person or institution)

声音.etymology: Coordinative noun compound pairing two Classical acoustic terms: 声 (聲, 'general sound or vocal sound') + 音 ('articulated musical tone or speech sound'). In modern Mandarin they fuse into the everyday word for 'sound, voice'.

history.meaning: sounds and musical tones
sound; voice

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 声音 (via 萌典)

壳.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 壳. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 壳 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 壳 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 壳 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 壳. The etymology of 壳 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 壳
middle form of 壳
modern form of 壳

壶.etymology: Pictograph (traditional 壺) attested from Shang oracle bones and Zhou bronzes depicting a round-bellied bronze or ceramic vessel with a lid (士) on top and a ring foot at the bottom: 'pot, kettle, teapot, flask, jug' and classifier for pots of liquid.

morphemes.meaning: body and foot of a pot

history.meaning: lidded ritual wine or water vessel
kettle; teapot; flask; classifier for pots

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 壶 (via 萌典)

壶嘴.etymology: Compound noun of 壶 (壺, 'kettle, teapot') + 嘴 ('beak, mouth, spout'): 'spout of a kettle or teapot'.

history.meaning: spout of a teapot or kettle

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 壶嘴 (via 萌典)

cognates.word: 処 (しょ, sho / ところ, tokoro)

cognates.meaning: place; office; to deal with or get along

处.etymology: Originally written 処/處 in oracle bone and seal script, depicting a person resting by a small table or stool (几) with walking feet (夂) stopping, plus phonetic 虍 (hū, tiger stripes). This yielded two tonal derivations in Middle and Modern Chinese: the rising tone (chǔ, Old Chinese *t-qʰaʔ) for the verb 'to dwell, stay, be situated in, get along with, manage', and the departing tone (chù, Old Chinese *t-qʰas) for the derived noun 'dwelling place, location, administrative department/office'.

history.meaning: to stop and rest; to dwell (verb, chǔ); dwelling place, spot (noun, chù)
to get along with, be in, handle (chǔ); place, administrative department/bureau (chù)

morphemes.meaning: to dwell, get along, handle (chǔ); place, administrative department (chù)

处.notes: Master the tone split by part of speech: Verb = 3rd tone chǔ (相处 'get along', 处理 'handle', 处在 'be situated in'); Noun = 4th tone chù (秘书处 'secretariat department', 好处 'benefit', 到处 'everywhere'). In colloquial speech, 处对象 (chǔ duìxiàng) means 'to date someone'.

rootFamily.gloss: to get along with one another; interpersonal interaction

cognates.meaning: to be situated in (a state or position)

处在.etymology: A verb-preposition (verb-complement) compound combining 处 (傳統: 處, chǔ, 3rd tone, 'to dwell, reside, be situated') with the locative verb/preposition 在 (zài, 'at, in, existing at'). It serves as the slightly more conversational counterpart to Literary-flavored 处于 (chǔyú), describing a person, project, or organization being situated in a particular phase, predicament, or environment.

history.form: 處 (chǔ, to dwell/be situated) + 在 (zài, at/in)
history.meaning: to reside or be situated at a place or state
to be in (a certain stage, position, or set of circumstances)

morphemes.meaning: to be situated; to dwell; to find oneself
in; at; within (a state, stage, or environment)

处在.notes: Always followed by a locative phrase ending in 中, 当中, or 阶段 (e.g., 处在关键阶段 'be at a critical stage', 处在风口浪尖上 'be in the eye of the storm'). Pronounced chǔzài (3rd tone + 4th tone).

rootFamily.gloss: to be in (a state or position; slightly more formal than 处在)
to be located in; situated at (geographically)

处境.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound combining the verbal morpheme 处 (傳統: 處, chǔ, 3rd tone, 'that in which one dwells or finds oneself') modifying the head noun 境 (jìng, 'region, environment, circumstances'). Literally 'the environment in which one is situated', it almost always refers to unfavorable, awkward, or precarious circumstances ('plight, predicament').

history.meaning: the circumstances or environment in which a person finds themselves
circumstances, plight, predicament (especially difficult or awkward ones)

morphemes.meaning: where one is situated; dwelling in (chǔ)

处境.notes: Pronounced chǔjìng (3rd tone on 处). Frequently collocates with adjectives of difficulty or awkwardness: 处境尴尬 ('in an awkward position'), 处境艰难 ('in a tough plight'), or 处境危险 ('in a dangerous situation').

cognates.word: 処々 (しょしょ, shosho) / 所々 (ところどころ, tokorodokoro)

处处.etymology: A distributive reduplication (AA noun-to-adverb pattern) of the nominal reading 处 (傳統: 處, chù, 4th tone, 'place, point, aspect'). Just as 人人 means 'every person' and 天天 means 'every day', 处处 literally means 'in every place' and broadened in Literary and Modern Chinese to mean 'in every respect, at every turn, in every detail'.

history.meaning: in every place; everywhere throughout the land
history.stage: Middle Chinese (Tang Poetry, e.g., Meng Haoran's 處處聞啼鳥)

history.meaning: everywhere; in every respect; at every turn (in behavior or work)

morphemes.meaning: distributive reduplication meaning 'every single place or aspect'

处处.notes: Pronounced chùchù (4th tone on both syllables). While 到处 (dàochù) is strictly spatial ('all over the place'), 处处 is commonly abstract, describing how someone acts 'at every turn' (e.g., 处处为别人着想 'consider others in every respect', 处处针对我 'pick on me at every turn').

rootFamily.gloss: deep inside; depths (of a place or the heart)

cognates.meaning: to handle; to process; to resolve

处理.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound attested since the Six Dynasties and Tang period, pairing 处 (傳統: 處, chǔ, 3rd tone, 'to manage, arrange, decide upon') with 理 (lǐ, originally 'to carve and polish raw jade along its natural veins', from 玉 'jade' + phonetic 里, hence 'to put in order, regulate, administer'). Reinforced in modern times by Japanese *shori* (処理) for technical/data 'processing' and clearance disposal.

history.meaning: to administer, adjudicate, and put affairs in order
to handle, deal with (problems, crises, relationships); to process (data, audio/video); to sell off at a discount

morphemes.meaning: to manage; to settle; to dispose of (chǔ)
to dress jade along its veins; to put in order; to regulate

处理.notes: Pronounced chǔlǐ (often two 3rd tones sandbied to chúlǐ). Covers everything from crisis management (处理危机) and interpersonal tact (处理人际关系) to post-production editing (后期处理) and clearance sales (处理品).

rootFamily.gloss: to put in order; to sort out; to organize
to discipline; to punish; disciplinary action

cognates.meaning: to experience fully; to receive widely

备受.etymology: A modifier-head (adverbial-verb) compound from Literary Chinese: 备 (傳統: 備, bèi, originally 'to prepare arrows in a quiver', hence 'complete, exhaustive, fully, to the utmost degree') modifying 受 (shòu, 'to receive, undergo, be subjected to', originally depicting a boat 舟 passed from one hand 爪 to another 又). Literally 'to receive or undergo to the fullest extent', it is sometimes misspelled 倍受 ('doubly receive') in informal writing, though 备受 is the etymologically standard form.

history.meaning: to experience or endure thoroughly (hardships or favor)
to receive wide/intense (praise, attention, controversy, or torment); to be fully subjected to

morphemes.meaning: fully; thoroughly; exhaustively; to the utmost degree
to receive; to undergo; to be the object of

备受.notes: A high-frequency media and journalistic semi-prefix that must be followed by a two-character verb/noun of emotion, attention, or hardship: 备受关注 ('receive intense attention'), 备受好评 ('receive rave reviews'), 备受争议 ('be mired in controversy'), or 备受煎熬 ('suffer deep torment').

cognates.meaning: attention;聚焦 of public gaze (in 注目)
cognates.word: 嘱目 (しょくもく, shokumoku) / 注目 (ちゅうもく, chūmoku)

cognates.meaning: focusing attention; fixing one's eyes upon

备受瞩目.etymology: A four-character journalistic and literary phrase combining 备受 (bèishòu, 'to thoroughly/widely receive') with 瞩目 (傳統: 矚目, zhǔmù, 'to fix one's gaze upon', a verb-object or coordinative compound of 瞩 zhǔ 'to gaze intently', from 目 'eye' + 属 shǔ 'to attach/focus', and 目 mù 'eye'). Together, it literally means 'to be the object upon which all eyes are intently fixed'.

history.meaning: to fix one's eyes intently upon something
to attract intense public attention; to be in the spotlight and highly anticipated

morphemes.meaning: to gaze intently; to fix one's eyes upon

备受瞩目.notes: A staple expression in entertainment journalism and award-show narration (e.g., 这是一部备受瞩目的新剧, 'This is a highly anticipated new drama in the public spotlight').

cognates.meaning: prepared plan; filing for the record (archaic/Sino-Japanese)

备案.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound formed from 备 (bèi, traditional 備, Middle Chinese *bjojH*, 'to prepare, provide, keep in readiness') and 案 (àn, Middle Chinese *'anH*, originally 'wooden tray or official desk', extended to 'legal case, official dossier, record'). Originating in late imperial Ming and Qing bureaucratic administration (as a contraction of 存案备查 'to preserve in the files for future inspection'), it denotes submitting and registering documents on the official record so that authorities can review or verify them later.

history.meaning: to prepare in advance / an official's wooden desk or the legal dossier placed upon it
to archive an administrative report or legal case on file for future official inspection
to file for the record; to register a project, broadcast program, or website with regulatory authorities

morphemes.meaning: prepare, provide, keep ready for reference
desk; official file, record, legal dossier

备案.notes: In mainland Chinese television and film production (a central theme in *Behind the Scenes*), every drama script, variety show, or web domain must complete *bèi'àn* (regulatory filing with the NRTA or MIIT) before shooting or airing; unlike 审批 (*shěnpī*, full prior examination and approval), *bèi'àn* is nominally a record-filing procedure, though still mandatory.

rootFamily.gloss: keep on file for future reference

备注.etymology: Compound noun and verb of 备 (備, 'prepare for reference') + 注 ('explanatory note, annotation'): 'remark, note, comment field (on a form, order, or document)'.

history.meaning: explanatory note or remark for reference

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 备注 (via 萌典)

备用.etymology: Verb-object compound used as an adjective and verb, combining 备 (備, 'prepare in advance, keep in reserve') + 用 ('use'): 'keep in reserve for future or emergency use; spare, backup (e.g., 备用钥匙 spare key)'.

history.meaning: prepared for use; spare; backup

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 备用 (via 萌典)

备菜.etymology: Verb-object culinary compound of 备 ('prepare in advance; make ready', originally a quiver full of arrows ready for use) + 菜 ('vegetables; dishes', grass radical 艹 + phonetic 采 cǎi). In restaurant and home kitchens alike, it denotes washing, peeling, and cutting ingredients (*mise en place*) before cooking begins.

history.meaning: prepare ingredients ahead of cooking (mise en place)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 备菜

复仇.etymology: A classical verb-object (VO) compound uniting 复 (fù, traditional 復, Old Chinese *\*m-p(r)uk*, 'to return, turn back, repay, reciprocate') and 仇 (chóu, traditional 讎 or 仇, Old Chinese *\*[g]ʷru*, 'match, adversary, blood feud, enmity'). Attested in pre-Qin ritual and historical classics such as the *Zuo Zhuan* and *Book of Rites* (*Liji*), it literally means 'to repay an enmity in kind'—originally a solemn kinship obligation under the ancient code of blood vengeance, later generalized to any act of retaliation or avenging a wrong.

history.meaning: to reciprocate a blood feud; to fulfill the ritual duty of avenging slain kin
to take revenge, avenge a grievance or defeat

复仇.notes: More formal and dramatic than the everyday verb 报仇 (*bàochóu*); *fùchóu* is heavily favored in literary titles, film/TV genres (e.g., 复仇剧 *fùchóujù* 'revenge drama'), and nominalized compounds like 复仇者 (*fùchóuzhě* 'avenger').

复杂.etymology: A coordinative (parallel) compound of 复 (fù, traditional 複, written with the garment radical 衤, originally 'lined or double-layered garment', hence 'reduplicated, multi-layered, compound') and 杂 (zá, traditional 雜, originally 'garment woven of multiple colors', hence 'mixed, variegated, heterogeneous'). Notice that 复 here simplifies traditional 複 ('layered/double'), not 復 ('return'). While both morphemes co-occurred in literary Chinese to describe variegated or multi-layered things, the compound was popularized in its modern abstract sense via Meiji-era Japanese 複雑 (*fukuzatsu*), coined to translate European philosophical and scientific terms for 'complex' and 'complicated'.

history.meaning: lined double-layered garment / mixed of five colors, heterogeneous
composed of multiple interwoven elements; complex (translating English 'complex / complicated')
complicated, complex, intricate (of situations, emotions, or structures)

复杂.notes: The standard antonym of 简单 (*jiǎndān*, 'simple'); in workplace and showbiz dramas, *fùzá* often describes tangled interpersonal networks (关系复杂) or someone with shrewd, inscrutable motives (心思复杂).

cognates.meaning: repechage, consolation/revival round (lit. loser revival match)

复活赛.etymology: A three-character modifier-head compound built from 复活 (fùhuó, traditional 復活, 'to return to life, resurrect, revive'—itself composed of 復 'return/again' + 活 'live, survive') modifying the head noun 赛 (sài, traditional 賽, originally 'a ritual thanksgiving offering to repay the gods', later 'competition to surpass others, match, tournament'). *Fùhuó* is attested in Six Dynasties tales of the strange (*Soushen Ji*) for coming back from the dead; in modern sports and reality television competitions, suffixing *-sài* created *fùhuósài* to render French/English *repechage* ('revival round / wildcard comeback round').

history.meaning: to return to life from death; resurrection
ritual offering in repayment to deities; contest of superiority
revival round, repechage match in tournaments and televised talent shows

复活赛.notes: A staple term in Chinese reality competition and singing shows (such as those produced in *Behind the Scenes*), where previously eliminated contestants (*táotài xuǎnshǒu*) battle in a *fùhuósài* to win back a spot in the finals (*juezài*).

rootFamily.gloss: come back to life, resurrect, revive

夏天.etymology: Compound noun of 夏 ('summer', originally a grand human figure with head 页, hands, and feet 夊 in ceremonial dance, denoting the great flourishing season) + 天 ('season, sky, time of year'): 'summer'.

history.meaning: the summer season; summer

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 夏天 (via 萌典)

夏日.etymology: A classical seasonal compound pairing 夏 (xià, 'summer', originally depicting a ceremonial human figure in seal script) and 日 (rì, 'sun; day'). Attested in early poetry such as the Classic of Poetry (诗经, 夏日炎炎 'blazing summer days'), 夏日 meant both 'the summer sun' and 'summer days'. In contemporary Mandarin it carries a warm, literary or artisanal tone compared with everyday 夏天.

history.meaning: summer sun; long summer day
summer; summertime (literary and culinary register)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 夏日

外.etymology: Ideogram combining 夕 ('evening/crescent moon') + 卜 ('divination crack'): Shuowen Jiezi notes that divining was normally performed by day, so divining at night (夕) was 'outside the norm / beyond', yielding the core spatial sense 'outside, exterior, outer, foreign, other, maternal relatives'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: outside; exterior; beyond; foreign

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 外 (via 萌典)

外侧.etymology: Spatial compound from 外 ('outside; exterior') + 侧 (simplified from 側, person 亻 + phonetic 則 'side; flank'). Used in anatomy, architecture, and everyday description to specify the outer edge or lateral side of a foot, wall, or road.

history.meaning: outer side; exterior flank

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 外侧

cognates.meaning: takeout food, delivery (parallel Sino-compound 外賣)

外卖.etymology: Originally an adverbial-verb (modifier-head) compound composed of 外 (wài, 'outside, external, off-premises') modifying 卖 (mài, traditional 賣, originally 出 'go out' over 買 'buy', meaning 'to sell'). In early modern commerce it functioned verbally as 'to sell goods outside the shop or to external markets' (contrasted with 内销/堂食). In late 20th-century Hong Kong, Taiwan, and mainland urban usage, it underwent nominalization to denote cooked food sold for off-premise consumption ('takeout / takeaway') and, with mobile apps, on-demand food delivery.

history.meaning: to sell merchandise or provisions outside one's shop or household
takeout food, restaurant delivery order (and by extension the delivery industry)

外卖.notes: To 'order takeout/delivery' is 点外卖 (*diǎn wàimài*) or 叫外卖 (*jiào wàimài*), while the ubiquitous courier is called an 外卖员 (*wàimàiyuán*) or affectionately 外卖小哥 (*wàimài xiǎogē*).

rootFamily.gloss: to buy and sell; business, trade

外卡.etymology: A modern modifier-head half-calque (hybrid loan-translation) combining native 外 (wài, 'outside, extra-quota, outside regular qualification channels', rendering the tournament sense of English *wild*) with the phonetic-semantic loanword 卡 (kǎ, short for 卡片 *kǎpiàn*, borrowed from English *card*). Coined in late 20th-century Chinese sports journalism to translate English *wild card* (which passed from poker into international tennis and championship tournaments in the 1970s), it was subsequently adopted by television variety and talent shows for a special discretionary pass into a competition.

history.meaning: playing card of arbitrary value; discretionary tournament entry granted to a non-qualifier
wild card entry or pass in sports tournaments and televised competitions

外卡.notes: In sports and TV showbiz (such as singing competitions in *Behind the Scenes*), a contestant invited directly into the main draw without going through standard qualifying rounds is an 外卡选手 (*wàikǎ xuǎnshǒu*, 'wild-card contestant').

rootFamily.gloss: customs checkpoint; level in a game (native reading guānkǎ)

外号.etymology: A modifier-head compound of 外 (wài, 'outside, informal, extra-official') and 号 (hào, traditional 號, Old Chinese *\*[C.g]ˤaw-s*, 'to call out, cry; name, designation, literary style'). In pre-modern China, an educated person possessed a formal given name (名 *míng*), a courtesy name (字 *zì*), and a self-chosen literary title (號 *hào*); by the Yuan and Ming vernacular novels (notably *Water Margin* 水滸傳, where every outlaw bears a colorful epithet), *wàihào* ('outside designation') denoted an informal nickname bestowed by the public based on appearance, habits, or reputation.

history.meaning: an unofficial epithet or sobriquet bestowed by outsiders (contrasted with formal 名, 字, and 號)
nickname, moniker (often playful or teasing)

外号.notes: Unlike 昵称 (*nìchēng*, an affectionate pet name) or 小名 (*xiǎomíng*, a childhood milk name used by family), *wàihào* (like 绰号 *chuòhào*) is typically coined by peers or coworkers—to 'give someone a nickname' is 起外号 (*qǐ wàihào*).

外国.etymology: Compound of 外 ('outside; beyond; foreign') + 国 ('state; country; nation', enclosure 囗 around玉/或). In Classical texts 外国 denoted states outside one's own principality; in modern Mandarin it means any foreign country or 'abroad'.

history.meaning: external or neighboring states
foreign country; abroad

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 外国

外国人.etymology: A left-branching modifier-head compound formed from 外国 (wàiguó, traditional 外國, 'foreign country, outer state'—itself a modifier-head compound of 外 'outside, external' + 國 'walled polity, state, country') modifying the head noun 人 (rén, 'person, human being'). In Classical Chinese (*Zuo Zhuan*, *Shiji*), *wàiguó* meant vassal states outside the royal Zhou domain or lands beyond the Han frontiers; in the 19th century, as East Asian treaties codified Westphalian sovereignty, *wàiguórén* (alongside Japanese *gaikokujin*) became the standard neutral legal and everyday term for a foreign national.

history.meaning: a person from a state outside one's own feudatory or beyond the imperial borders
foreigner, foreign national, citizen of another country

外国人.notes: The polite, standard term for a foreigner (compare colloquial 老外 *lǎowài*, which is casual and friendly, or formal 外宾 *wàibīn* 'foreign guest', used in diplomatic and hospitality contexts).

sources.title: Wiktionary: 外國人 / 外国人

外头.etymology: Colloquial locative noun combining 外 ('outside') + nominal locative suffix 头 (頭, neutral tone tou, bleached from 'head/end'): 'outside, outdoors'.

history.meaning: outside; outdoors

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 外头 (via 萌典)

外套.etymology: Compound noun of 外 ('outer') + 套 ('outer case, cover, garment worn over others'): 'outer coat, jacket, overcoat'.

history.meaning: outer coat; jacket

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 外套 (via 萌典)

外景地.etymology: A left-branching modifier-head compound consisting of 外景 (wàijǐng, 'exterior scene, outdoor view, on-location filming'—from 外 'outside, exterior' + 景 'sunlit view, scenery, stage/film setting') plus the head noun 地 (dì, 'earth, place, site, location'). In traditional Chinese aesthetics and garden architecture, *wàijǐng* denoted natural scenery outside a pavilion or wall; in 20th-century cinema and television production, *wàijǐng* came to mean outdoor on-location shooting (as opposed to 内景 *nèijǐng* or 棚拍, indoor soundstage shooting), and suffixing *-dì* designated the physical outdoor filming site.

history.meaning: external landscape or natural vista visible beyond a building or courtyard
exterior scene; on-location outdoor filming outside a studio soundstage
outdoor filming location, on-location shoot site

外景地.notes: Essential film/TV crew jargon in *Behind the Scenes*: going out to shoot on location is 出外景 (*chū wàijǐng*) or 拍外景 (*pāi wàijǐng*), while scouting outdoor locations is 选外景地 (*xuǎn wàijǐngdì*).

外流.etymology: An adverbial-verb (modifier-head) compound in which 外 (wài, 'outward, to the outside, beyond borders') modifies the verb 流 (liú, Old Chinese *\*[r]u*, 'to flow, stream, circulate, drift'). Originally used in physical geography and imperial statecraft for rivers flowing to the outer sea or coinage/grain draining beyond state borders, it extended in modern economics to capital or talent flight (资金/人才外流) and in entertainment media to the unauthorized leaking of confidential scripts, demo tracks, or unedited footage outside a studio.

history.meaning: to flow outward (of rivers draining to the ocean or wealth draining abroad)
to drain or flow out (of capital/talent); to leak out to the public (of confidential media or data)

外流.notes: In media and showbiz contexts, *wàiliú* (alongside 外泄 *wàixiè*) frequently describes the accidental or malicious leaking of unreleased audio, scripts, or behind-the-scenes video (音源外流, 剧本外流).

cognates.meaning: the external world, the outside; objective world in philosophy

外界.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 外 (wài, 'outside, external') with 界 (jiè, Old Chinese *\*kˤr[e]ts*, originally a boundary line between ploughed fields 田, hence 'border, realm, sphere, world'). First shaped by medieval Chinese Buddhist epistemology—where *wàijiè* denoted the external phenomenal realm (*bāhyārtha* / *dhātu*) as opposed to internal consciousness—and later reinforced by Meiji Japanese philosophical usage (外界 *gaikai*, 'the external/objective world'), it broadened in modern journalism to mean 'the public at large; people and media outside a given organization or circle'.

history.meaning: the external sphere of sensory objects outside the mind or monastery
the objective external world (in philosophy and psychology)
the outside world; the general public, media, and observers outside an organization

外界.notes: Very common in PR and entertainment journalism (e.g., 外界猜测 'outside speculation', 向外界公布 'announce to the public'), where *wàijiè* contrasts everyone outside a company or production crew with 内部 (*nèibù*, insiders).

外皮.etymology: Compound noun of 外 ('outer, exterior') + 皮 ('skin, peel, bark, rind, cover'): 'outer skin, peel, rind, outer casing or wrapper'.

history.meaning: outer skin, bark, peel, or cover

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 外皮 (via 萌典)

外籍.etymology: A modifier-head compound formed from 外 (wài, 'outside, non-local, foreign') and 籍 (jí, Old Chinese *\*[dz]Ak*, written with the bamboo radical 竹, originally 'bamboo tablet register of population and land', hence 'household registration, native county domicile, citizenship'). Under the imperial household-registry system (*hùjí* 戶籍), *wàijí* referred to an official or resident registered in a different province or prefecture; in the modern nation-state era, as 籍 came to signify national citizenship (国籍 *guójí*), *wàijí* shifted to mean 'of foreign nationality, holding a foreign passport'.

history.meaning: registered in an outside prefecture or province; an external administrative roll
foreign-national, holding foreign citizenship (e.g.,外籍华人, 外籍演员)

morphemes.meaning: bamboo census tablet; household register; nationality

外籍.notes: A formal, non-inflecting attributive adjective used before nouns (e.g., 外籍艺人 'foreign-national artist/entertainer', 外籍员工 'expat/foreign employee'); ethnic Chinese who hold foreign citizenship are specifically termed 外籍华人 (*wàijí huárén*).

rootFamily.gloss: ancestral home, native place of family register

外边.etymology: A root-plus-localizer compound uniting the directional root 外 (wài, 'outside, exterior') with the spatial suffix 边 (biān, traditional 邊, Old Chinese *\*pˤe[n]*, originally 'cliff edge, margin, frontier borderland'). During the Tang, Song, and Yuan vernacular transition, *biān* underwent semantic bleaching from 'border/edge' into a general locative noun suffix (pronounced with a neutral tone *-bian* in Northern Mandarin) attached to monosyllabic spatial roots (里边, 外边, 上边, 下边) to create disyllabic place words.

history.meaning: outer frontier or borderland / outer edge or side
the outside, exterior space (colloquial locative noun with neutral-tone suffix)

morphemes.meaning: side, edge; spatial noun marker (trad. 邊)

外边.notes: *Wàibian* (often rhotacized in Beijing speech as 外边儿 *wàibianr*) is slightly more colloquial and northern in flavor than 外面 (*wàimiàn*), though the two are interchangeable in everyday dialogue for 'outside'.

外部.etymology: A modifier-head compound of 外 (wài, 'outside, external') and 部 (bù, Old Chinese *\*[b]ˤoʔ*, originally an administrative division, military command, or classification section, hence 'part, section, sector, department'). In historical Chinese texts, *wàibù* denoted outer frontier divisions or external tribal groups; reinforced in the late 19th and early 20th centuries by Meiji Japanese 外部 (*gaibu*), it became the standard formal term for the 'external part/surface' of an object or the 'external environment/actors' outside an institution.

history.meaning: outer frontier divisions or external administrative jurisdictions
exterior part, external sector or environment (contrasted with 内部)

外部.notes: Unlike colloquial 外边 (*wàibian*) or 外面 (*wàimiàn*) ('outdoors / outside the room'), *wàibù* belongs to formal and organizational register (e.g., 外部环境 'external environment', 外部资金 'outside funding', 外部人员 'external personnel'), always paired with its antonym 内部 (*nèibù*).

外面.etymology: Locative compound noun of 外 ('outside, exterior') + 面 ('face, surface, side'): 'outside, outdoors, the exterior surface'.

history.stage: Classical & Vernacular Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: outside; exterior surface

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 外面 (via 萌典)

多.etymology: Ideogram (会意字) attested on Shang oracle bones doubling 夕 (originally depicting two pieces of meat 肉/夕 stacked one atop another): 'many, much, plenty, more (opposite of 少 'few/little'); how…! (in exclamations and degree questions like 多大); odd/over (after round numbers: 十多个)'.

history.meaning: doubled pieces of meat = many, much, abundant
many; much; more; how (degree); over/plus

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 多 (via 萌典)

多久.etymology: An interrogative modifier-head compound combining 多 (duō, grammaticalized from 'many, much' into an interrogative degree adverb meaning 'how, to what extent') with the temporal adjective 久 (jiǔ, Old Chinese *\*[k]ʷəʔ*, 'long in time, enduring, of long duration'). In Classical Chinese, 'how long' was expressed by 何久 or 幾時; during the Tang–Song vernacular development, 多 came to precede positive-pole dimensional adjectives (多大 'how big/old', 多远 'how far', 多久 'how long') to question extent along a scale.

history.meaning: many/much + long duration of time (used separately in Classical Chinese)
how long (in time), what duration (interrogative and indefinite temporal pronoun/adverb)

morphemes.meaning: how, to what degree or extent (from 'many/much')

多久.notes: Functions both in direct questions (还要等多久？ 'How much longer do we have to wait?') and in negative/indefinite time expressions like 没多久 (*méi duōjiǔ*, 'not long after / before long').

多亏.etymology: Adverb and verb compound of 多 ('greatly, much') + 亏 (虧, 'owe to, thanks to someone's effort/favor'): 'thanks to, luckily because of'.

history.meaning: thanks to; fortunately owing to

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 多亏 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: superfluous, redundant (Sino-Vietnamese reading of 多餘)

多余.etymology: A coordinative and resultative-like compound of 多 (duō, 'many, much, in excess of what is needed') and 余 (yú, traditional 餘, Old Chinese *\*la*, written with the food radical 食 plus 余 phonetic, originally meaning 'food left over after a meal, surplus, remainder'). Attested in vernacular and literary Chinese from the Song and Ming periods onward, it evolved from a literal quantitative sense ('remaining left over, surplus beyond a quota') to a subjective, evaluative adjective meaning 'superfluous, redundant, uncalled-for, unnecessary'.

history.meaning: abundant / leftover provisions or remainder
left over in excess of requirement; surplus
unnecessary, superfluous, uncalled-for, redundant

多余.notes: Beyond describing unnecessary words or actions (多余的话 'unnecessary remarks'), in relationship and workplace dramas feeling like a 'third wheel' or an unwanted outsider is poignantly expressed as 觉得自己很多余 ('feeling completely superfluous').

rootFamily.gloss: be left over, remain; remainder, surplus

多加.etymology: An adverbial-verb compound formed from 多 (duō, 'more, to a greater degree, generously') modifying the light verb 加 (jiā, Old Chinese *\*kˤraiy*, composed of 力 'strength/effort' and 口 'mouth', meaning 'to add, increase, apply effort to'). In Literary Chinese and polite modern prose, 加 (alongside 加以 *jiāyǐ*) grammaticalized into a formal transitive verb-frame taking two-character verbal nouns of care, attention, or critique as its object; prefixing 多 yielded *duōjiā* ('to apply extra/more of [an action]').

history.meaning: greatly / to add or apply upon
to take extra care to, to apply increased effort toward (polite/formal preverbal construction)

morphemes.meaning: more, to a greater extent, generously

多加.notes: In modern grammar, *duōjiā* functions like an adverbial intensifier that MUST be followed by a two-syllable verb of mental attention, care, or guidance—classic collocations include 多加小心 ('take extra care'), 多加注意 ('pay extra attention'), and polite workplace requests like 请多加指教 ('please give me your generous guidance').

rootFamily.gloss: apply, carry out (formal light verb before disyllabic verbs)

多半.etymology: Compound quantifier and epistemic adverb of 多 ('more than') + 半 ('half'): 'more than half, the majority; most likely, probably'. Attested from Tang–Song poetry.

history.meaning: more than half; most likely, probably

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 多半 (via 萌典)

多媒体.etymology: A three-character compound combining 多 (duō, 'many, multiple', translating English prefix *multi-* or functioning as quantifier 'many') with 媒体 (méitǐ, traditional 媒體, 'medium, media'—itself a 20th-century compound of 媒 'marriage go-between, intermediary' + 體 'body, substance, carrier'). In digital and broadcasting contexts, *duōméitǐ* was coined in the late 20th century as a direct calque of English *multimedia* (integrating text, audio, and video); in spoken showbiz dialogue (and subtitle segmentation of 许多媒体 *xǔduō méitǐ* or 诸多媒体 *zhūduō méitǐ*), the sequence *duō méitǐ* also arises literally as 'many media outlets'.

history.meaning: marriage matchmaker or intermediary / physical body or form
communication medium, the press and broadcast media (translating English 'medium / media')
multimedia (calque of English 'multimedia'); or 'many media outlets' in phrases like [许]多媒体

多媒体.notes: Watch for two distinct contexts in media dramas like *Behind the Scenes*: as a single technical compound, 多媒体 means 'multimedia' (e.g., 多媒体制作 'multimedia production'); when preceded by 许 in 许多媒体 (*xǔduō méitǐ*), automatic word-splitters sometimes slice it as 许 + 多媒体, where it simply means 'many media outlets / journalists'.

rootFamily.gloss: media, news outlets, medium of communication

sources.title: Wiktionary: 多媒體 / 多媒体

多少.etymology: Antonymic compound combining 多 ('many, much') + 少 ('few, little', neutral tone shao when asking quantity): originally a Classical abstract noun meaning 'relative quantity (how much or how little)', which evolved into the standard interrogative numeral 'how many?, how much?' and indefinite 'somewhat, to some extent'.

history.meaning: amount; whether many or few
how many?; how much?; more or less

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 多少 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: many years, perennial (as in 多年草 'perennial plant')

多年.etymology: A modifier-head quantifier-noun compound of 多 (duō, 'many, numerous') directly modifying 年 (nián, Old Chinese *\*C.nˤi[ŋ]*, originally a bone-and-bronze-script graph showing a person 人 carrying ripe grain 禾, meaning 'annual harvest' and by extension 'a full seasonal cycle, year'). Because 年 in Chinese grammar is an autonomous measure noun (autonomous classifier), 多 combines directly with 年 without an intervening classifier, a pattern attested continuously from Tang poetry (e.g., Du Fu) to modern Mandarin.

history.meaning: harvest of grain crops; an agricultural year
many years, for a period of many years
history.stage: Tang–Song Literary Chinese to Modern Mandarin

多年.notes: Frequently paired with directional or localizer suffixes to anchor time relative to the present: 多年来 (*duōnián lái*, 'over the past many years') and 多年以前 (*duōnián yǐqián*, 'many years ago').

rootFamily.gloss: in recent years, over the past few years
all year round, year in year out
that year, back in those days

多着呢.etymology: An idiomatic Northern Mandarin predicate phrase built from the stative adjective 多 (duō, 'many, plentiful, abundant') + the aspectual suffix 着 (zhe, traditional 著, grammaticalized from Middle Chinese *drjak* 'to adhere, attach, touch' into a durative/intensive state marker) + the sentence-final modal particle 呢 (ne, expressing lively assertion and counter-expectation). Emerging in Qing-dynasty Beijing vernacular fiction (such as *Dream of the Red Chamber*), the frame *[Adj] + zhe + ne* intensifies the adjective to mean 'in a very high degree indeed—there is plenty of it!'.

history.meaning: being in an abundant state indeed (colloquial intensive adjectival predicate)
there is plenty of it; there are lots and lots of them; far more than you think!

多着呢.notes: A lively spoken pattern: you can swap 多 for almost any monosyllabic adjective in the *Adj + zhe + ne* frame to sound like a native speaker—e.g., 早着呢 (*zǎozhene*, 'it's still way too early!'), 远着呢 (*yuǎnzhene*, 'it's still a long way off!'), 忙着呢 (*mángzhene*, 'super busy right now!').

rootFamily.gloss: still way too early; far from done!
still a very long way off!
a great deal, very much (synonymous intensifier)

sources.title: Wiktionary: 多著呢 / 多着呢

多管闲事.etymology: A four-character adverbial + verb-object idiom: 多 (duō, used adverbially as 'excessively, unnecessarily, where uncalled-for') modifies the verb 管 (guǎn, originally 'bamboo wind-pipe or key to a lock', extended to 'to hold the keys to, manage, take charge of, meddle in'), which governs the modifier-head object 闲事 (xiánshì, traditional 閒事, from 閒 'idle, spare, unrelated to duty' + 事 'affair, matter'). Popularized in Ming and Qing vernacular novels (*Water Margin*, *Dream of the Red Chamber*), it literally means 'to overly manage affairs that do not concern oneself'.

history.meaning: to involve oneself in other people's private or non-official affairs

history.form: 多管閒事 / 多管闲事 (duōguǎnxiánshì)
history.meaning: to meddle, be nosy, poke one's nose into other people's business

morphemes.meaning: manage, take charge of, interfere in
idle, spare, unrelated to oneself (trad. 閒)

多管闲事.notes: In spoken Mandarin, 'Mind your own business! / Don't be nosy!' is most commonly barked as 少管闲事！ (*shǎo guǎn xiánshì*, replacing 多 'more' with 少 'less') or 别多管闲事！ (*bié duōguǎnxiánshì*).

rootFamily.gloss: mind your own business! (lit. meddle less in idle affairs)

sources.title: Wiktionary: 多管閒事 / 多管闲事

夜.etymology: Phono-semantic/ideographic character attested in bronze script combining 夕 ('crescent moon, dusk') + 亦 (yì phonetic, originally a standing person with dots under the arms): 'night, nighttime, darkness'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: night; nighttime

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 夜 (via 萌典)

夜空.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 夜 ('night') + 空 ('sky, air'): 'the night sky'.

history.meaning: night sky

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 夜空 (via 萌典)

夜里.etymology: A noun-plus-localizer temporal compound joining 夜 (yè, Old Chinese *\*[ɢ]Ak-s*, 'night, hours of darkness from dusk to dawn') with the postpositional localizer 里 (lǐ, traditional 裏 or 裡, Old Chinese *\*rəʔ*, written with the garment radical 衣 plus 里 phonetic, originally meaning 'the inner lining of a garment' as opposed to 表 'outer coat'). During the Tang and Song dynasties, 裏 grammaticalized from 'garment lining / interior' into the general spatial and temporal enclitic *-lǐ* ('inside, within, during'), yielding *yèlǐ* ('in the night, at night').

history.meaning: nighttime + inner lining of a robe / interior space
during the night, at night, late at night

morphemes.meaning: inside, within, during (trad. 裏/裡, 'garment lining')

夜里.notes: Compared with 晚上 (*wǎnshang*, 'in the evening / at night', which covers early evening socializing), *yèlǐ* specifically evokes the late, dark hours after people have gone to bed ('in the middle of the night / overnight').

rootFamily.gloss: late at night, in the dead of night
stay up all night, pull an all-nighter

够.etymology: A monomorphemic word whose modern character 够 (gòu, variant 夠, a phono-semantic compound combining 多 'many, abundant' with 句 *gōu* as phonetic) superseded the older classical graph 彀 (gòu, Old Chinese *\*[k]ˤok-s*, 'to draw a bow to its full limit'). From the core image of stretching a bowstring until it reaches full capacity, the word evolved in Song–Yuan–Ming vernacular Chinese to mean 'to reach a required standard or quantity, suffice, be enough', and further grammaticalized into a pre-adjectival degree adverb meaning 'quite, plenty, sufficiently'.

history.meaning: to draw a bow to its full extent; within bowshot or full capacity
to reach the required amount; to suffice, be enough; (adverb) quite, plenty

morphemes.meaning: to reach full capacity, suffice; enough, quite

够.notes: When used as an adverb before an adjective in spoken Mandarin, *gòu* typically takes the emphatic particle 的 (*de*) at the end of the clause—e.g., 够累的 (*gòu lèi de*, 'exhausting enough / plenty tired!') or 够呛 (*gòuqiàng*, 'rough going / barely tolerable').

rootFamily.gloss: be capable of, can; enough (formal disyllabic compound)

够到.etymology: Resultative verb compound combining 够 (夠, 'reach by stretching out the hand or body') + 到 ('attain, reach'): 'reach (an object high up or far away)'.

history.meaning: reach by stretching; get hold of

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 够到 (via 萌典)

够意思.etymology: A colloquial verb-object idiom functioning as an adjectival predicate, composed of 够 (gòu, 'to reach the standard of, measure up to, have enough of') and 意思 (yìsi, 'meaning, thought, sentiment, token of goodwill or fellowship'—from 意 'intent, heart's thought' + 思 'reflection, feeling'). In late imperial and modern Beijing/Northern vernacular, *yìsi* extended from 'meaning' to 'social warmth, generosity, or personal loyalty (*yìqi* 義氣) shown to friends'; hence *gòu yìsi* literally means 'measuring up to the standard of true fellowship'.

history.meaning: to reach the standard of + friendly sentiment, generosity, or fellowship
true-blue, loyal and generous as a friend; (of things/performances) really up to scratch, impressive

morphemes.meaning: measure up to, reach the standard of, suffice

够意思.notes: High-frequency praise in colloquial camaraderie: telling a friend 你真够意思！ (*Nǐ zhēn gòuyìsi!*) means 'You're a real pal / You really came through for me!', whereas its negative 不够意思 (*bù gòuyìsi*) chides someone for being stingy, disloyal, or letting friends down.

rootFamily.gloss: interesting, fun; meaning, token of appreciation
be a real friend, loyal and solid (synonymous Beijing slang)

sources.title: Wiktionary: 夠意思 / 够意思

大.etymology: Foundational pictograph (象形字) attested from Shang oracle bones showing a front-facing human figure standing with arms and legs stretched wide: 'big, large, great, wide, loud, strong, eldest, adult, very'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: person standing with arms and legs spread = big, great, large

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 大 (via 萌典)

大不了.etymology: A three-character potential-complement idiom formed from the adjective 大 (dà, 'big, grave, serious') + the negative infix 不 (bù, 'not, cannot') + the phase/completive verb 了 (liǎo, Middle Chinese *lewX*, 'to finish, bring to completion, reach the ultimate limit'). Originating in Yuan–Ming–Qing vernacular Mandarin, *dà-bu-liǎo* developed two complementary senses from the literal meaning 'to be unable to exceed a certain gravity': as a predicate (often negated in 没什么大不了), 'to be an overwhelmingly grave matter / a big deal'; and as a sentence-initial adverb, 'at the very worst, it cannot get any more serious than...'.

history.meaning: to be a matter of utmost gravity (usually in negation: nothing extraordinarily serious)
(adj) big deal, serious (in 没什么大不了); (adv) at worst, if the worst comes to the worst

morphemes.meaning: finish, reach the limit, resolve (read liǎo)

大不了.notes: Pay close attention to its two everyday patterns: (1) 没什么大不了的 (*méi shénme dàbuliǎo de*, 'It's no big deal / Nothing serious'), and (2) clause-initial 大不了我辞职！ (*Dàbuliǎo wǒ cízhí!*, 'At worst, I'll just quit!'). Do not confuse with 了不起 (*liǎobuqǐ*, 'amazing, extraordinary').

cognates.meaning: important matter, valuable thing (daiji); serious affair, crisis (ōgoto)
great affair, major matter of state

大事.etymology: A classical modifier-head compound uniting 大 (dà, Old Chinese *\*[d]ˤa[t]-s*, 'great, major, important') and 事 (shì, Old Chinese *\*[m-s-]rəʔ-s*, 'official duty, ritual service, affair, event'). Famously defined in the *Zuo Zhuan* (Duke Cheng, Year 13: 國之大事，在祀與戎 'The great affairs of a state lie in sacrifice and warfare'), *dàshì* in Classical Chinese denoted supreme matters of statecraft, ritual, or dynastic succession, before broadening in vernacular Chinese to any major historical event, life milestone, or serious crisis.

history.meaning: supreme affairs of state, specifically royal ancestral sacrifices and military campaigns
major event, important matter, milestone (or a serious crisis in 出了大事)

大事.notes: Beware the false friend with Japanese 大事 (*daiji*, which usually means 'precious, important, take care'); in Mandarin, *dàshì* is strictly a noun meaning 'major event / big matter' (e.g., 做大事 'accomplish great things', 终身大事 'the great matter of a lifetime = marriage', or 出大事了 'something huge/terrible has happened').

rootFamily.gloss: overall situation, general trend of events

cognates.meaning: great figure, person of great caliber, big shot

大人物.etymology: A left-branching modifier-head compound in which 大 (dà, 'big, great, prominent') modifies 人物 (rénwù, 'personage, figure of note, character'). In early Classical Chinese, 人 ('human') and 物 ('living creature / thing') formed a coordinative phrase meaning 'people and things'; during the Han and Six Dynasties period of character appraisal (epitomized by Liu Shao's 3rd-century treatise *Renwu Zhi* 人物志), *rénwù* narrowed to 'a person of notable talent or stature', and prefixing *dà* produced *dàrénwù* ('great personage, VIP, big shot').

history.meaning: a person of notable talent, character, or public standing
great figure, VIP, big shot, influential personage (often used with a touch of irony in spoken Mandarin)

morphemes.meaning: thing, creature (with 人 forming 人物 'figure/personage')

大人物.notes: While *dàrénwù* can genuinely honor a historical giant, in everyday workplace and media banter it translates English 'big shot / VIP / heavyweight' and contrasts directly with 小人物 (*xiǎorénwù*, 'an ordinary nobody / little guy').

rootFamily.gloss: figure, personage; character in a play/novel
big shot, industry tycoon/boss (colloquial showbiz/tech slang)

cognates.meaning: the general public, the masses, popular (as in 大衆文化 'pop culture')
the general public, the masses (as in 대중문화 'pop culture')

大众.etymology: A modifier-head compound of 大 (dà, 'great, vast, broad') and 众 (zhòng, traditional 眾, Old Chinese *\*tiuŋ-s*, an oracle-bone pictograph of three people 众 working under an eye/sun, meaning 'multitude, crowd, the many'). First attested in pre-Qin texts (*Xunzi*, *Zhuangzi*) for a large multitude, it became a key Buddhist term translating Sanskrit *mahāsaṅgha* ('the great assembly of monks'). In the 20th century, reinforced by Japanese 大衆 (*taishū*, translating English *the masses / popular*), it became the standard sociological and media term for 'the general public, the broad masses'.

history.meaning: a large multitude of people; the great monastic assembly (Sanskrit mahāsaṅgha)
the general public, the broad masses (in sociology and mass media)

大众.notes: A cornerstone of media studies and showbiz vocabulary: 大众传媒 (*dàzhòng chuánméi*, 'mass media'), 大众文化 (*dàzhòng wénhuà*, 'popular/mass culture'), and 大众审美 (*dàzhòng shěnměi*, 'mainstream public taste', contrasted with 小众 *xiǎozhòng*, 'niche'). (Also the Chinese brand name for Volkswagen, 'people's car'.)

rootFamily.gloss: niche, appealing to a small/specialized audience (antonym)

大伙.etymology: A modifier-head colloquial compound pronoun combining 大 (dà, 'big, whole, collective') with 伙 (huǒ, historically written 火 'campfire' and later 夥 'numerous' or 伙 'mess-group, band of companions'). Under the Northern Dynasties and Tang *fǔbīng* (府兵) militia system (famous from the *Ballad of Mulan*: 出門看火伴 'stepping out to see my messmates'), ten soldiers sharing one cooking fire (火) and mess kettle formed a *huǒ*; from 'mess-group / band of companions', prefixing *dà* ('the whole') in Ming–Qing vernacular created *dàhuǒ* ('the whole gang, everybody together').

history.meaning: a squad of ten soldiers sharing a cooking fire and mess kit; band of companions
the whole group of companions; everyone, all of us together

morphemes.meaning: mess-group, band of companions, crowd (from 火/夥)

大伙.notes: Warmer, more informal, and more solidarity-building than the neutral standard pronoun 大家 (*dàjiā*, 'everyone'); team leaders and directors on a film set often use *dàhuǒ* (or *dàhuǒr*) to rally the crew as 'the whole gang'.

rootFamily.gloss: partner, companion, mate (originally military messmate 火伴)

大伙儿.etymology: The rhotacized (*érhuà*) Northern Mandarin form of 大伙 (*dàhuǒ*), composed of 大 (dà, 'big, whole, collective') + 伙 (huǒ, from Tang military 火 'a squad sharing a cooking fire', hence 'band of companions, crowd') + the diminutive/colloquial retroflex suffix 儿 (ér / *-r*, grammaticalized from 兒 'child, small thing' into a sub-syllabic rhotic codal colouring `[dàhuǒr]`). In Beijing and northern vernacular speech from the Qing dynasty onward, attaching *-r* to collective nouns marks solidarity, familiarity, and casual spoken register.

history.meaning: the whole band of companions, everyone
everybody, the whole gang, all of us (colloquial Northern Mandarin rhotacized pronoun)
history.stage: Qing Beijing Vernacular to Modern Mandarin

大伙儿.notes: Pronounced as two syllables (*dà-huǒr*), not three! In spoken Northern Mandarin dialogue, *dàhuǒr* is the natural everyday way to say 'everybody / the whole gang' (e.g., 大伙儿都辛苦了 'Thanks, everybody, for your hard work!').

rootFamily.gloss: everyone, the whole gang (non-rhotacized written form)
together, in the same place (colloquial rhotacized adverb)

sources.title: Wiktionary: 大夥兒 / 大伙儿

大会.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 大 (dà, 'great, general, plenary') + 会 (huì, Traditional 會, 'assembly, meeting, gathering'). Originally attested in Classical Chinese for grand royal or ritual assemblies and Buddhist Dharma gatherings (法會), it was revitalized in late nineteenth-century Sino-Japanese institutional vocabulary to denote a plenary assembly, general congress, or company-wide convention.

history.meaning: grand state assembly or Buddhist congregational convocation
plenary meeting, general assembly, convention

大会.notes: Used for formal company-wide town halls (全员大会), shareholder assemblies (股东大会), or industry conventions; contrasts with 小会 (small breakout or committee meeting).

cognates.meaning: elder brother; boss, triad leader, big shot

大佬.etymology: Borrowed into Standard Mandarin from Cantonese 大佬 (daai6 lou2), a modifier-head compound of 大 ('big, eldest, chief') + 佬 (lou2, Middle Chinese *lɑuX, 'fellow, chap, grown man'). Originally a Cantonese kinship term for 'older brother', it expanded in Hong Kong vernacular and cinema to denote a triad boss or gang leader before entering pan-Chinese media and corporate slang for an industry mogul, tycoon, or authoritative heavyweight.

history.meaning: elder brother; chief of a brotherhood or gang
industry mogul, bigwig, boss, top expert

大佬.notes: In entertainment and tech circles, refers to a powerful investor, studio head, or revered veteran; also used playfully in internet slang to flatter someone skilled ('boss').

大使馆.etymology: Left-branching modifier-head compound of 大使 (dàshǐ, 'ambassador', literally 'grand envoy') + 馆 (guǎn, Traditional 館, 'official residence, lodge, hall'). While 大使 denoted imperial commissioners or envoys in Tang–Song administration, the modern diplomatic sense of 'embassy' crystalized in late nineteenth-century Meiji Japanese (大使館, taishikan) to translate Western diplomatic missions and was re-adopted into Chinese diplomatic terminology.

history.meaning: imperial grand commissioner + official state guest-house or hall
diplomatic embassy headed by an ambassador
embassy

大使馆.notes: Often abbreviated to 使馆 in formal news and conversation; distinguish from 领事馆 (lǐngshìguǎn, 'consulate'), which handles regional visas and citizen services outside the capital.

大做文章.etymology: Four-character verb-object phrase built from adverbial 大 (dà, 'on a grand scale, extensively') modifying the verb-object core 做文章 (zuò wénzhāng, literally 'to compose an essay/literary piece'). Originating in late imperial civil-service examination culture where candidates elaborated prolifically on a set theme, it shifted metaphorically in modern Mandarin to mean seizing upon an incident or pretext to stir up publicity, controversy, or calculated drama.

history.meaning: compose a formal literary essay on an assigned examination topic
make a huge fuss over an issue, exploit a topic for publicity or intrigue

morphemes.meaning: essay, literary composition; figurative pretext or drama

大做文章.notes: Commonly framed with 在...上大做文章 or 借题大做文章 ('use X as a pretext to make a big splash'); frequent in PR and media contexts for hyping a minor detail into a major storyline.

rootFamily.gloss: article, essay; hidden agenda or subtext
seize on a pretext to make a fuss
make a mountain out of a molehill

大力.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 大 (dà, 'great, mighty') + 力 (lì, 'physical strength, force, effort'). In Classical Chinese and Buddhist translations (such as 大力菩薩, bodhisattvas of great might), it functioned as a noun meaning 'great physical strength'; in modern Mandarin, it grammaticalized primarily into a high-register adverbial modifier meaning 'vigorously,energeticly, with full institutional backing'.

history.meaning: great physical strength or martial force
vigorously, strongly, sparing no effort (adverbial)

大力.notes: Typically precedes two-syllable verbs in corporate and media discourse, such as 大力支持 (strongly support), 大力宣传 (heavily promote), and 大力发展 (vigorously develop).

大动干戈.etymology: Classical four-character idiom (成语) composed of adverbial 大 ('on a grand scale'), verb 动 (dòng, Traditional 動, 'to mobilize, brandish'), and coordinative noun object 干戈 (gāngē, 'shields and dagger-axes', the standard Classical Chinese metonym for warfare and military weaponry attested in the *Analects* and *Book of Documents*). From its literal sense of waging full-scale war, it generalized to mobilizing massive resources or making an excessive production over a matter.

history.meaning: take up shields and halberds; launch military hostilities within or beyond the state
go to extraordinary lengths, mobilize a massive effort over something minor

大动干戈.notes: Often used in the negative (不必大动干戈, 'no need to make such a huge production out of it') when someone deploys excessive manpower or escalation for a manageable task.

rootFamily.gloss: turn hostility into friendship (bury the hatchet)
mobilize troops, deploy a huge crowd of people

大半年.etymology: Modifier-head temporal phrase formed from 大半 (dàbàn, 'the greater half, more than half', itself a modifier-head compound of 大 'large' + 半 'half') modifying 年 (nián, 'year'). Attested in Literary and vernacular Chinese since the Tang–Song period, the prefixing of 大 to 半 specifies the larger portion of a bisected whole—hence 'well over half a year, the better part of a year'.

history.meaning: the greater half + year (more than half of a year)
over half a year, the better part of a year

大半年.notes: Emphasizes subjective length of time spent waiting or working on a project (e.g., 忙活了大半年, 'toiled away for well over half a year'); parallel to 大半天 (most of the day) and 大半夜 (the dead of night).

rootFamily.gloss: more than half, for the most part
more than half the day; a very long time

大单.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 大 (dà, 'large, major, high-value') + 单 (dān, Traditional 單, 'single sheet, bill, commercial order, contract list'). In Ming–Qing commercial vernacular, 单 referred to invoices, manifests, and transaction slips; in contemporary business and media production Mandarin, 大单 denotes a lucrative contract, major sponsorship deal, or high-value client order.

history.meaning: recorded slip, commercial bill, inventory list
major contract, big commercial order, lucrative deal

大单.notes: Frequent in sales, advertising, and production agencies with verbs like 签下大单 (sign a major deal) or 接大单 (land a big contract).

rootFamily.gloss: close a deal, sign an order

大厅.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 大 ('large, main') + 厅 (廳, 'hall, reception room'): 'main hall, lobby, concourse, grand hall'.

history.meaning: main hall; lobby; lounge

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 大厅 (via 萌典)

大厨.etymology: Affectionate and respectful title combining 大 ('great; senior; head') + 厨 ('kitchen; cook', shelter radical 广 + 尌). Used in everyday Mandarin since the Song and Ming dynasties both to refer to a master chef and to address the person running a kitchen.

history.meaning: master cook of a banquet or inn kitchen
chef; head cook

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 大厨

大反转.etymology: Modifier-head compound consisting of intensifier 大 (dà, 'big, dramatic') + 反转 (fǎnzhuǎn, Traditional 反轉, a coordinative/directional compound of 反 'reverse, turn against' + 转 'turn, shift'). While 反轉 denoted physical rotation in the opposite direction in pre-modern texts, its narrative sense of a sudden dramatic reversal of fortune or public opinion gained currency via film/drama dramaturgy and internet news culture.

history.meaning: turn back, rotate in the opposite direction
dramatic plot twist, sudden reversal of a situation or public opinion

大反转.notes: A staple buzzword in entertainment PR, screenwriting, and social media commentary (剧情大反转, 'a huge plot twist' in a scandal or drama).

rootFamily.gloss: turn around a losing situation, reverse course

大叔.etymology: Modifier-head kinship compound of 大 (dà, 'eldest among a subset, senior') + 叔 (shū, Old Chinese *hljuk, 'father's younger brother'). Originally denoting the eldest among one's father's younger brothers in the traditional Chinese agnatic kinship system, it broadened into a polite form of address for any man of one's father's generation, and in contemporary pop culture (influenced by Korean 아저씨 *ajeossi* and Japanese おじさん *ojisan* tropes) came to describe a mature, charismatic older man—or teasingly, any man past his twenties.

history.meaning: father's younger brother (specifically the eldest among younger paternal uncles)
polite address for a middle-aged man; mature older guy (pop-culture archetype)

morphemes.meaning: father's younger brother, uncle, middle-aged man

大叔.notes: In modern drama and romance tropes, 大叔控 refers to an attraction to charming, dependable older men; when used by Gen Z toward someone in their late 20s or 30s, it can be playfully teasing about age.

rootFamily.gloss: uncle (father's younger brother; polite address for a man)

cognates.meaning: great renown; castle town name; daimyo (historically distinct reading)

大名.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 大 (dà, 'great, illustrious, esteemed') + 名 (míng, 'personal name, reputation, renown'). In Classical Chinese (e.g., *Zuozhuan*, *Shiji*), 大名 meant 'great fame or renown'; in Ming–Qing epistolary and conversational etiquette, it became an honorific second-person term meaning 'your illustrious name', while in vernacular usage it also denotes a person's formal registered name as opposed to a childhood nickname (小名/乳名).

history.meaning: great fame, illustrious reputation in the realm
your esteemed name (honorific); formal given name (vs. childhood nickname)

大名.notes: Most frequently heard in polite or mildly ironic social introductions such as 久仰大名 ('I have long admired your famous name') or 请问尊姓大名 ('May I ask your honorable surname and given name?').

大吵.etymology: Adverb-verb compound of 大 (dà, 'loudly, fiercely, on a large scale') + 吵 (chǎo, 'make noise, clamor, quarrel'). The character 吵 emerged in Song–Yuan vernacular with the mouth radical 口 plus 少 as phonetic to represent loud vocal clamor; modified by 大, it denotes having a heated, full-blown verbal row.

history.meaning: clamor, make a din, wrangle vocally
quarrel fiercely, have a huge shouting match

morphemes.meaning: fiercely, loudly, on a big scale

大吵.notes: Frequently appears with अएक架 as 大吵一架 ('have a massive fight/row') or in the four-character intensifier 大吵大闹 ('make a huge scene shouting and carrying on').

cognates.meaning: big role, major figure, A-lister (from 跤 kha 'foot, role')

大咖.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 大 (dà, 'big, major') + 咖 (kā), borrowed into Mandarin via Taiwanese entertainment media from Taiwanese Hokkien 大跤 (tuā-kha, literally 'big foot/leg', where 跤 kha denotes a 'member, player, or theatrical role' in a troupe or game, analogous to Mandarin 角儿 juér). Because Hokkien *kha* lacked a familiar Mandarin character in variety shows, Taiwanese TV subtitles wrote it phonetically with 咖 (originally a phonetic character coined for 咖啡 kāfēi 'coffee'), which Mainland speakers subsequently pronounced with its Mandarin reading *kā*.

history.meaning: major player in an opera troupe or gambling table; key figure
A-list celebrity, industry heavyweight, big shot

morphemes.meaning: role, player, celebrity figure (orthographic adaptation of Hokkien 跤 kha)

大咖.notes: Ubiquitous in Chinese variety shows, film production, and PR (e.g., 邀请大咖加盟, 'invite A-list stars to join the cast'); gave rise to derivative showbiz terms like 咖位 (celebrity tier/status) and 小咖 (minor celebrity).

rootFamily.gloss: status or billing tier of a celebrity in showbiz
leading actor, big star (Northern Mandarin equivalent)

大哥.etymology: Compound kinship and social title of 大 ('eldest') + 哥 ('elder brother'): 'eldest brother' (and used respectfully or colloquially to address an older man or friend of one's own generation).

history.meaning: eldest brother; friendly/respectful address for an older man

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 大哥 (via 萌典)

大堂.etymology: Compound noun of 大 ('main, grand') + 堂 ('elevated main hall of a palace, yamen court, or residence'). Historically the central courtroom of a magistrate's yamen or the main hall of a mansion; in modern Mandarin, the 'main lobby' of a hotel, bank, or commercial building.

history.meaning: main hall of a residence or magistrate's court
hotel or bank lobby; main hall

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 大堂 (via 萌典)

大声.etymology: Modifier-head compound from 大 ('big; loud; great') + 声 (simplified from 聲, originally depicting a stone chime 殸 and an ear 耳). Attested since the Six Dynasties and Tang period both as an attribute ('a loud voice') and adverbially ('aloud; at the top of one's voice').

history.meaning: loud sound or voice
loudly; in a loud voice

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 大声

大大.etymology: Reduplication of the core adjective 大 ('big; wide; great', oracle-bone pictograph of a person standing with arms and legs stretched wide). Doubling the syllable to 大大 intensifies the scale or openness of an action, as in 大大地打开 ('open wide').

history.meaning: greatly; on a large scale; wide
wide; greatly; big

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 大大

大学.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 大 (dà, 'great, higher, adult') + 学 (xué, Traditional 學, 'learning, school, academy'). Originally the title of a foundational Confucian classic (《大學》, *The Great Learning*, a chapter of the *Book of Rites*) and the name of the imperial institution of higher learning for nobles and officials, it was repurposed in Meiji Japan (大学, *daigaku*) to translate the modern Western 'university' and reintroduced into late Qing Chinese with this modern institutional sense.

history.meaning: education for adults in moral and statecraft governance; the Imperial Academy; *The Great Learning*
modern Western-style university (re-coined translation in Meiji Japan)
university, college

大学.notes: Wait—in classical citation (the Confucian text 《大学》) the traditional literati reading was *Dàxué*, and in modern Mandarin 大学 means both 'university' and 'college' (e.g., 上大学 'go to college').

rootFamily.gloss: college, institute, faculty within a university

大学生.etymology: Left-branching modifier-head compound composed of 大学 (dàxué, 'university') + 生 (shēng, 'scholar, student, apprentice', derived from Classical Chinese 生徒 / 儒生). Modeled in the late nineteenth century alongside Sino-Japanese educational terminology (大学生, *daigakusei*) to designate an undergraduate or tertiary student enrolled at a modern university.

history.meaning: student enrolled at the Imperial Academy (Taixue)
modern university or college student

大学生.notes: In workplace dramas, 大学生 or 应届大学生 ('fresh college graduate') often carries the nuance of being idealistic, energetic, and book-smart but inexperienced in office politics.

大家.etymology: Compound of 大 ('great, all') + 家 ('household, clan, people'). In Classical Chinese (Zuozhuan, Mencius), 大家 meant 'a great noble clan or household' (or a great master); from the Six Dynasties and Tang–Song vernacular onward, it grammaticalized into the inclusive collective pronoun 'everyone, everybody, all of us'.

history.meaning: great noble house; renowned master
everyone; everybody

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 大家 (via 萌典)

大小.etymology: Antonymic compound juxtaposing 大 ('large; big', frontal pictograph of a person with arms outstretched) + 小 ('small; tiny', three tiny grains or dots). In Chinese word-formation, pairing opposite poles of a scale creates the abstract noun for that dimension ('size; magnitude').

history.meaning: large and small; relative size
size; dimensions

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 大小

cognates.meaning: general situation, overall perspective (especially in Go/Shogi and politics)

大局.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 大 (dà, 'overall, macro-level, grand') + 局 (jú, 'board game layout, configuration, state of affairs'). Originating in Chinese board games—especially *weiqi* (Go, 围棋), where 局 refers to the whole board configuration as opposed to a local skirmish (局部)—it entered statecraft and modern organizational discourse to denote the overarching strategic situation or 'the big picture'.

history.meaning: whole-board configuration in Go (weiqi); overall strategic affairs of state
overall situation, big picture, broader institutional interest

morphemes.meaning: board layout, situation, state of affairs

大局.notes: Frequently appears in leadership and workplace collocations like 顾全大局 ('prioritize the big picture'), 大局观 ('sense of the big picture'), and 大局已定 ('the overall outcome is already decided').

rootFamily.gloss: sense of the big picture, strategic vision

大山.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 大 ('big, great, high') + 山 ('mountain'): 'large mountain, high mountains, mountain range'.

history.stage: Old & Classical Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: great mountain; high mountains

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 大山 (via 萌典)

大巴.etymology: Hybrid modifier-head compound of native Chinese 大 (dà, 'large') + 巴 (bā), clip of 巴士 (bāshì), which was borrowed via Hong Kong Cantonese (baa1 si2) from English *bus*. Coined in Cantonese to distinguish a full-sized motor coach or public transit bus (大巴) from a minibus (小巴, *siu2 baa1*), the term spread throughout Mainland Mandarin in the late twentieth century.

history.form: 巴士 (baa1 si2) → 大巴 (daai6 baa1)
history.meaning: full-sized bus or coach (contrasted with minibus)
long-distance coach, tour bus, charter bus

morphemes.meaning: bus (clipped phonetic loan from English 'bus' via Cantonese 巴士)

大巴.notes: In Mainland Mandarin, 大巴 (or 大巴车) usually refers to a chartered coach, tour bus, or airport shuttle rather than a regular municipal city bus (公交车).

大师.etymology: Compound noun of 大 ('great') + 师 (師, 'master, teacher'). Used in Classical and Buddhist texts for a revered spiritual teacher or monk, and in modern Mandarin for a 'grandmaster, great master (of art, music, craft, or scholarship)'.

history.meaning: great teacher; revered Buddhist master
great master; virtuoso; maestro

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 大师 (via 萌典)

大师兄.etymology: Left-branching modifier-head compound of 大 (dà, 'eldest, most senior') + 师兄 (shīxiōng, Traditional 師兄, literally 'master-elder brother', composed of 师 'teacher, master' + 兄 'elder brother'). Rooted in medieval Buddhist monastic lineages and traditional martial arts / opera guilds where disciples of the same master formed a pseudo-kinship hierarchy, 大师兄 designated the senior-most male disciple and now extends affectionately to a senior male alumnus of the same academic advisor, department, or mentor.

history.meaning: senior-most fellow disciple under the same Buddhist master or martial arts teacher
senior male disciple; senior alumnus or mentor-group upperclassman

大师兄.notes: Popularly associated in Chinese pop culture with Sun Wukong (the eldest disciple in *Journey to the West*), and widely used in universities and creative industries for a respected senior protégé of one's mentor.

rootFamily.gloss: senior male fellow student or apprentice
junior male fellow student or apprentice
senior female fellow student or apprentice

cognates.meaning: full width; large margin, drastically, sharply

大幅.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 大 (dà, 'large, wide') + 幅 (fú, 'width of woven cloth, breadth, margin'). In Classical and Literary Chinese, 幅 denoted the measured breadth of a bolt of silk or cloth (with cloth radical 巾); in modern economic, statistical, and media Mandarin (reinforced by Japanese 大幅 *ōhaba* 'full-width; by a large margin'), 大幅 functions as an adverb meaning 'by a wide margin, sharply, substantially'.

history.meaning: broad width of woven fabric or scroll; wide expanse
by a large margin, sharply, substantially (adverbial)

morphemes.meaning: width of cloth, breadth, margin or range of change

大幅.notes: Frequently paired with verbs of quantitative change in ratings, budgets, or market metrics: 大幅提升 (increase sharply), 大幅下滑 (drop steeply), or expanded as 大幅度 (by a large margin).

rootFamily.gloss: range, margin, extent of change or oscillation

cognates.meaning: strict taboo, something strictly to be avoided; imperial mourning period

大忌.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 大 (dà, 'grave, supreme, cardinal') + 忌 (jì, Old Chinese *gɯs, composed of 己 phonetic and 心 'heart', meaning 'dread, ritual abstinence, prohibition, taboo'). Attested in classical military, medical, and almanac texts, 大忌 denoted a fatal strategic blunder, an inauspicious day, or a strict medical contraindication; in modern usage it means a cardinal rule never to be broken in a profession or relationship.

history.meaning: supreme ritual prohibition; fatal strategic or medical error to be shunned
grave taboo, cardinal mistake, strict no-no in a profession

morphemes.meaning: taboo, dread, prohibition, thing to be avoided

大忌.notes: Common in workplace and industry advice: 职场大忌 ('a cardinal sin in the workplace') or 犯了行业大忌 ('committed a grave industry taboo').

rootFamily.gloss: be jealous or fearful of; scruple, avoid
harbor resentment or jealousy toward talent

大忙人.etymology: Three-character modifier-head compound structured as 大 (dà, 'big, extreme') + 忙人 (mángrén, 'busy person', from 忙 'hurried, occupied' + 人 'person'). Formed in colloquial modern Mandarin on the productive pattern `大 + [adjective/noun] + 人` (compare 大好人 'total sweetheart', 大红人 'hot favorite'), it designates someone whose schedule is perpetually packed.

history.meaning: person occupied with worldly affairs (contrasted with 閒人 'person of leisure')
super-busy person (often used playfully or teasingly)

大忙人.notes: Almost always used with affectionate or gently teasing irony when greeting a friend, colleague, or boss who is hard to book time with: 哟，大忙人怎么有空来啦？ ('Well, how does a super-busy person like you have time to drop by?').

rootFamily.gloss: exceptionally kind or overly accommodating person

大意.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 大 (dà, 'broad, general, rough') + 意 (yì, 'thought, meaning, attention, mindfulness'). In Classical and Literary Chinese, 大意 meant 'the overarching purport or general gist' of a text (a noun sense still preserved today, e.g., 段落大意 'paragraph summary'). From focusing only on 'the rough outline' rather than fine details, it developed a secondary verbal/adjectival sense in vernacular Mandarin (often pronounced with neutral-tone *dàyi* in speech, though indexed as *dàyì*) meaning 'inattentive, careless, caught off guard'.

history.meaning: general purport, main idea, overarching intention of a text or plan
1. general gist/main idea (noun); 2. careless, negligent, off guard (adjective/verb)

大意.notes: Famous in the idiom 粗心大意 ('careless and negligent') and the classical expression 大意失荆州 ('losing Jingzhou through carelessness', from Guan Yu's downfall in *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*).

cognates.meaning: great war, major battle, fierce contest

大战.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 大 (dà, 'great, major, fierce') + 战 (zhàn, Traditional 戰, 'battle, warfare, fight'). Attested across Classical Chinese military chronicles both as a noun ('a major battle') and as an adverb-verb construction ('to fight fiercely'), in modern Mandarin it extends metaphorically to commercial competition (e.g., 收视大战 'ratings war') and working flat out through a grueling session (e.g., 大战三天三夜 'battle/work flat out for three days and nights').

history.meaning: wage a major battle; a decisive military engagement
major battle or showdown; battle fiercely or work flat out through a grueling task

大战.notes: Versatile in media and workplace contexts: as a noun in 抢人大战 ('war for talent') or 公关大战 ('PR war'), and as a transitive/intransitive verb in 大战三百回合 ('fight 300 rounds') or 通宵大战 ('pull an all-nighter battling a deadline').

大批.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 大 (dà, 'large, massive') + 批 (pī, 'batch, lot, tranche'). The character 批 originally meant 'to strike or slap with the hand' (from 手 hand + 比 phonetic); in Tang–Song administrative usage it came to mean 'to endorse or comment officially on a document' (批示), and because goods or personnel were approved and dispatched on a single endorsed warrant, 批 grammaticalized into a classifier for a 'batch' or 'group', yielding 大批 ('a large batch of, in large numbers').

history.meaning: strike with the hand; write an official endorsement on a memorial or warrant
large batch of, huge number of, in droves

morphemes.meaning: batch, lot, group approved or arriving together

大批.notes: Used before countable or collective nouns (without needing 的) to indicate a large influx or wave, e.g., 大批粉丝 ('droves of fans'), 大批记者 ('a huge pack of reporters'), or 大批资金 ('massive tranches of capital').

rootFamily.gloss: in batches, in stages or tranches

大拇指.etymology: A vivid three-morpheme anatomical term combining 大 (dà, 'big'), 拇 (mǔ, 'thumb or big toe', formed with the hand radical 扌 and 母 'mother' as both phonetic and semantic 'chief/mother digit'), and 指 (zhǐ, 'finger, digit'). Classical Chinese called the thumb 巨指 ('giant finger') or 拇; vernacular Mandarin added 大 in front and 指 behind, literally 'the big mother-finger', and also uses 竖起大拇指 for praising someone with a thumbs-up.

history.meaning: thumb or big toe
thumb; thumbs-up gesture of praise

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 大拇指

大方.etymology: Compound of 大 ('great') + 方 ('method/principle; square earth'). In Classical Chinese (Zhuangzi's 吾长见笑于大方之家), 大方 meant 'great principles / experts of great learning'. In vernacular Mandarin (read dàfang with neutral tone), it means 'generous, ungrudging with money; natural, poised, and tasteful in manner or design'.

history.meaning: the great Way; great learning
generous; poised and natural; in good taste

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 大方 (via 萌典)

大早上.etymology: Colloquial modifier-head temporal expression formed from emphatic prefix 大 (dà, used before time nouns to stress 'right in the middle of' or 'so early/late in') + 早上 (zǎoshang, 'morning', from 早 'early' + locative/temporal suffix 上). In Mandarin colloquial grammar, prefixing 大 to a time word (compare 大晚上 'late at night', 大过年 'right during New Year's') highlights that an action is happening at an inconveniently or surprisingly early hour of the morning.

history.meaning: morning → first thing in the morning, at the crack of dawn (emphatic)

morphemes.meaning: emphatic temporal intensifier (right at, so early in)

大早上.notes: Often carries a mildly exasperated or emphatic tone about something happening too early: 大早上的吵什么？ ('Why are you making a racket at the crack of dawn?') or 大早上就赶飞机 ('rushing to catch a flight bright and early').

rootFamily.gloss: early morning, first thing in the morning

大暴雨.etymology: Left-branching modifier-head compound of 大 (dà, 'heavy, severe, major') + 暴雨 (bàoyǔ, 'violent rainstorm, torrential rain', itself a modifier-head compound attested since the *Warring States* period from 暴 'sudden, violent, fierce' + 雨 'rain'). In modern Chinese meteorology, 大暴雨 is also codified as a specific precipitation grade (100–249.9 mm of rainfall within 24 hours, one tier above 暴雨 and below 特大暴雨).

history.meaning: sudden violent downpour, torrential rain
heavy rainstorm, severe torrential downpour (100–250 mm/24h in meteorology)

大暴雨.notes: Used both literally in weather alerts and film shoot disruptions (遇上大暴雨, 'hit by a torrential downpour') and figuratively for a sudden storm of crisis or criticism.

rootFamily.gloss: heavy rainstorm with gale-force winds, tempest

大概.etymology: Compound noun, adjective, and epistemic adverb of 大 ('general, broad') + 概 ('leveling stick for a grain measure -> general outline, approximate'): 'general idea/outline; roughly, probably, most likely'. Attested since Tang–Song prose.

history.meaning: general outline; roughly; probably

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 大概 (via 萌典)

大牌.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 大 (dà, 'big, prominent') + 牌 (pái, 'wooden placard, signboard, brand, billing plaque'). Originating in late Qing and Republican-era traditional opera theaters (戏园子), where headlining stars had their names painted in oversized characters on prominent wooden billing plaques (水牌 / 挂牌) hung outside the venue, 大牌 came to denote a top-billed star or prestigious brand, and by extension an arrogant, diva-like attitude.

history.meaning: top-billed opera performer whose name appears on a large wooden signboard outside the theater
A-list celebrity, big-name luxury brand; famous, high-profile

morphemes.meaning: billing plaque, signboard, brand, status card

大牌.notes: Essential showbiz vocabulary: as an adjective/noun for an A-lister or luxury label (大牌明星 'A-list star'), and in the fixed verb-object phrase 耍大牌 (shuǎ dàpái, 'act like a diva, throw one's celebrity weight around').

rootFamily.gloss: act like a diva, pull rank as a celebrity
trump card, ace, flagship talent or show

大白话.etymology: Three-character compound of 大 ('plain, thorough') + 白话 ('vernacular, plain unadorned speech', 白 'plain/unvarnished' + 话 'spoken words'): 'plain everyday speech, straightforward vernacular (as opposed to jargon or literary flourishes)'.

history.meaning: plain, straightforward everyday talk

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 大白话 (via 萌典)

大红人.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 大 (dà, 'great, huge') + 红人 (hóngrén, Traditional 紅人, from 红 'red; auspicious, popular, in high favor' + 人 'person').
