In Chinese cultural symbolism, red (红) signifies celebration, prosperity, and imperial or theatrical favor—famous opera performers whose names were written in red ink on playbills were called 走红 ('turning red/popular'). Hence 红人 and its intensified form 大红人 denote either a trusted favorite of a powerful boss or the hottest celebrity of the moment.

history.meaning: trusted favorite of a high official or patron; rising star in opera troupes
huge star of the moment; hot favorite in high favor with leadership or the public

morphemes.meaning: red; popular, favored, in the limelight

大红人.notes: Has two main contexts: in showbiz, a breakout celebrity who is everywhere right now; in office politics, the boss's favored protégé (领导身边的大红人).

rootFamily.gloss: become popular, hit the big time, go viral
internet celebrity, influencer (short for 网络红人)

大结局.etymology: Left-branching modifier-head compound of 大 (dà, 'grand, final, ultimate') + 结局 (jiéjú, Traditional 結局, a verb-object/resultative compound from 结 'tie off, conclude' + 局 'game of Go/chess, state of affairs, plot structure'). Originally referring to the closing resolution of a board game or dramatic opera plot, 大结局 was popularized by Hong Kong and Mainland television broadcasting to designate the series finale of a serialized drama.

history.meaning: conclusion of a game of Go; final resolution of a literary plot or affair
grand finale, series finale of a television drama or saga

morphemes.meaning: board game, plot situation, episode arc

大结局.notes: Standard TV and streaming term for the final episode of a drama or variety season (收官大结局); also used metaphorically when a long-drawn-out real-life controversy or negotiation finally reaches its ultimate resolution.

rootFamily.gloss: finale, closing chapter (originally last step of a Go game)

大老爷们.etymology: Northern Mandarin colloquial compound formed from emphatic prefix 大 (dà, 'full-grown, burly') + 老爷们 (lǎoyémen, often pronounced with erhua as 老爷们儿 *lǎoyémenr*, from honorific prefix 老 + 爷 'master, adult male, gentleman' + plural collective suffix 们). In Qing-era Beijing vernacular, 老爷们儿 shifted from addressing male masters of a household to a hearty, rough-and-ready term for 'grown men, adult guys' (contrasted with 老娘们儿 'womenfolk').

history.meaning: masters of the house; adult menfolk in Northern vernacular
grown men, rugged guys (colloquial Northern Mandarin)

morphemes.meaning: human collective/plural suffix (used even for a single man as a class noun)

大老爷们.notes: Despite containing the plural suffix 们, 一个大老爷们 ('a grown man') frequently refers to a single male; evokes traditional Northern norms of being tough, straightforward, and not petty or overly emotional.

大胆.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正結構) formed from 大 (dà, 'big, great') and 膽 / 胆 (dǎn, 'gallbladder', the seat of courage and audacity in traditional Chinese physiological and psychological thought). Originally a literal description of someone possessing a 'large gallbladder'—an anatomical metaphor attested in Tang medical and historical texts (notably regarding the general Jiang Wei in the Records of the Three Kingdoms)—it lexicalized into an adjective meaning 'bold, fearless, or audacious' and an exclamation rebuking insolence toward a superior.

history.meaning: having a large gallbladder; fearless in battle
bold, daring; how dare you! (imperative rebuke in court drama)
bold, daring, audacious, boundary-pushing

大胆.notes: In creative and media contexts, 大胆 praises innovative risk-taking (e.g., 大胆尝试 'a bold attempt', 大胆创新 'bold innovation'), whereas in costume dramas a standalone shout of 大胆! means 'How dare you! / Insolent!'

大胖子.etymology: A colloquial modifier-head nominal compound combining the intensifier adjective 大 (dà, 'big, large') with the derived noun 胖子 (pàngzi, 'fat person, chubby person'), itself formed from 胖 (pàng, 'plump, stout', originally denoting half a sacrificial animal carcass in Old Chinese before shifting to bodily corpulence) plus the nominalizing diminutive suffix 子 (zi). The prefixed 大 amplifies both the physical size and the affectionate, teasing, or bantering tone of the appellation in spoken Mandarin.

history.meaning: half of a split sacrificial beast; broad, comfortable, corpulent
stout or portly person
big chubby person, big fatty (colloquial/joking)

morphemes.meaning: nominal suffix denoting a person or object

大胖子.notes: Used playfully among close friends or self-deprecatingly in casual speech (e.g., 吃成大胖子 'eat until turning into a big chubby person'), though addressing strangers this way is impolite.

大腕.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正結構) composed of 大 (dà, 'big, great') and 腕 (wàn, 'wrist'). Originating in Northern Mandarin and Beijing guild slang, 腕 (wrist) served as a metonym for manual skill, dexterity, and mastery of a craft—specifically how an opera performer, calligrapher, acrobat, or martial artist controls their instrument through wrist strength and finesse. In late 20th-century mainland entertainment jargon, 大腕 generalized from master Peking opera performers to top-tier, A-list celebrities and influential industry heavyweights.

history.meaning: wrist; by metonymy, manual skill, finesse, or tactical maneuver
master performer in traditional opera or folk arts with drawing power
big star, A-list celebrity, industry heavyweight

morphemes.meaning: wrist; metonymically, skill, mastery, or star performer

大腕.notes: Written and spoken across China without erhua as 大腕 (popularized nationwide by Feng Xiaogang's 2001 satirical comedy film 《大腕》, Big Shot's Funeral), referring to A-list stars who command top billing and clout.

rootFamily.gloss: wrist; finesse, political/managerial tact or trickery

大腕儿.etymology: The rhotacized (兒化 / erhua) Beijing and Northern Mandarin form of 大腕 (dàwàn), combining 大 (dà, 'big, great'), 腕 (wàn, 'wrist; metonym for consummate skill and drawing power in the performing arts'), and the diminutive/nominalizing retroflex suffix 兒 / 儿 (-r). In traditional Beijing梨園 (opera) and曲藝 (folk performing arts) argot, the erhua suffix marked 腕儿 as a concrete count noun denoting a headlining performer whose name alone could fill a theater; it subsequently entered mainstream showbiz vocabulary for an A-lister.

history.meaning: skilled practitioner or headliner in Beijing opera and folk arts
A-lister, superstar, entertainment heavyweight

morphemes.meaning: wrist; metonym for master performer or star
colloquial Northern Mandarin rhotic nominal suffix

大腕儿.notes: In spoken Northern Mandarin and showbiz banter, the erhua pronunciation dàwànr (often paired with 傍大腕儿 'latch onto a big star' or 耍大牌 'act like a diva') feels more natural and idiomatic than the un-rhotacized reading.

rootFamily.gloss: big star, A-list celebrity (standard un-rhotacized form)
famous opera actor or key role (Beijing argot with erhua)

sources.title: Wiktionary — 大腕兒 / 大腕儿

大致.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正結構) formed from 大 (dà, 'great, macro-level, general') and 致 (zhì, 'reach, bring about; trend, purport, fine detail or manner'). In Literary Chinese (attested from the Han–Six Dynasties onward), 大致 originally functioned as a noun meaning 'the overarching purport, general trend, or main gist' of an argument or situation. Through frequent adverbial placement before predicates, it grammaticalized into a degree and manner adverb meaning 'roughly, on the whole, or in broad outline'.

history.meaning: general purport, overarching trend, main outline (nominal)
roughly, generally, in broad strokes (adverbial and attributive)

大致.notes: Commonly collocates with 相同 (大致相同 'roughly the same'), 了解 (大致了解 'have a general understanding'), or nominal 情况 (大致情况 'the general situation'); slightly more formal than 大概 (dàgài) and focuses on 'in broad outline' rather than probability.

rootFamily.gloss: refined, exquisite; fine and close (of details)

大获全胜.etymology: A four-character idiom (成語) structured as two parallel verb-object / modifier-verb-object clauses: 大獲 / 大获 (dàhuò, 'greatly obtain / reap on a grand scale', with 大 functioning adverbially before 獲 'capture game in a hunt; obtain') and 全勝 / 全胜 (quánshèng, 'complete victory', from 全 'whole, intact, total' + 勝 'overcome, triumph').Syntactically, 全勝 also functions as the overarching object of 大獲 ('to reap a total victory on a grand scale'). Rooted in Classical Chinese military historiography (echoing Sunzi's ideal of 全勝 'triumphing intact/completely'), it describes a decisive, sweeping victory.

history.meaning: complete victory achieved with forces intact (Art of War)

history.form: 大獲全勝 (dà huò quán shèng)
history.meaning: win a decisive, sweeping military victory
history.stage: Late Imperial Literary Chinese & Military Chronicles

history.meaning: score a landslide victory (in ratings, competitions, elections, or sports)

大获全胜.notes: Frequently used in media and entertainment reporting when a show, film, or contestant sweeps ratings, box-office charts, or awards (e.g., 收视率大获全胜 'scored a landslide victory in ratings').

rootFamily.gloss: win a battle or competition; victory

sources.title: Wiktionary — 大獲全勝 / 大获全胜

大街.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 大 ('main, wide') + 街 ('street, thoroughfare', 行 + 圭): 'main street, avenue, the street'.

history.stage: Tang–Song urban vernacular to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: main street; avenue

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 大街 (via 萌典)

大衣.etymology: Modifier-head compound from 大 ('big; outer; full-length') + 衣 ('garment; coat', pictograph of a robe with overlapping collar). In classical ritual texts 大衣 denoted ceremonial outer robes; in modern Mandarin it specifically denotes a long overcoat or trench coat worn over indoor clothing.

history.meaning: full outer robe
overcoat; topcoat

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 大衣

大赛.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正結構) formed from 大 (dà, 'big, grand, major') and 賽 / 赛 (sài, 'compete, contest; ritual offering in gratitude to the gods'). In Classical and Middle Chinese, 賽 denoted a thanksgiving sacrifice to repay deities after a harvest or fulfilled prayer, which regularly featured competitive folk displays and theatrical performances; by the Song–Yuan period, 賽 had shifted to mean 'compete, rival, or contest'. In modern Mandarin, 大賽 functions as a compressed compound (alongside 大型比賽) for a major tournament, championship, or grand competition.

history.meaning: offer a thanksgiving sacrifice to repay the gods; rival in splendor
compete, contest, match
history.stage: Early Mandarin to Early Modern Chinese

history.meaning: major tournament, grand competition, championship

大赛.notes: A staple of talent-show and broadcast terminology (e.g., 歌唱大赛 'grand singing competition', 选秀大赛 'talent competition'), conveying prestige and large scale compared to an ordinary 比赛.

rootFamily.gloss: take part in a competition, compete

大都会.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正結構) combining 大 (dà, 'great, large') with 都會 / 都会 (dūhuì, 'capital city, major commercial hub, metropolis'). The base compound 都會 is attested in Han dynasty historiography (such as Sima Qian's Shiji, Biography of the Moneymakers) as a coordinative nominal compound of 都 (dū, 'imperial capital, walled city with an ancestral temple') and 會 / 会 (huì, 'convergence, gathering place of people and goods'). Modern usage of 大都会 as 'metropolis' was further reinforced in the Meiji/Republican era via Japanese 大都会 (daitokai) as a translation of English 'metropolis'.

history.meaning: great convergence hub of population and commerce; capital city (Shiji)
major imperial/commercial city; modern translation of 'metropolis'
cosmopolitan metropolis, megacity

大都会.notes: Must be pronounced dàdūhuì (with 都 as dū 'capital/city', never dōu 'all'); evokes a glamorous, cosmopolitan urban atmosphere (like Shanghai, New York, or Tokyo) more vividly than the administrative term 大城市.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 大都會 / 大都会

大门.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 大 ('main, front') + 门 (門, 'gate, door'): 'main entrance, front gate, front door'.

history.meaning: main gate; front door

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 大门 (via 萌典)

大门口.etymology: Three-character locative compound of 大门 ('main gate, front door') + 口 ('entranceway, opening'): 'at the main entrance, right by the front gate/door'.

history.meaning: main doorway; by the front gate

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 大门口 (via 萌典)

大雨.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 大 ('heavy, big') + 雨 ('rain'): 'heavy rain, downpour'. Attested from Shang oracle-bone weather divinations onward.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: heavy rain

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 大雨 (via 萌典)

大雨倾盆.etymology: Four-character vivid idiom (also 倾盆大雨) combining 大雨 ('heavy rain') + 倾盆 ('overturn a basin of water', 倾 'tilt/pour out' + 盆 'basin'), describing rain pouring down in torrents as if emptied from an overturned basin.

history.stage: Tang–Song poetry (e.g., Du Fu, Su Shi) to Modern Mandarin
history.form: 大雨傾盆 / 大雨倾盆
history.meaning: rain pouring down as if from an upturned basin; torrential downpour

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 大雨倾盆 (via 萌典)

天.etymology: Ancient character attested on Shang oracle bones depicting a front-facing human figure (大) with the head or the vault above the head emphasized by a round or horizontal mark: 'the top of the head -> the sky, heaven, nature, day, weather, season'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: crown of the head -> sky, heaven, day, weather, nature

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 天 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: the whole country, the world, realm under heaven; shogunal rule
the world, the realm under heaven

天下.etymology: A Classical Chinese locative-head compound (偏正結構) formed from 天 (tiān, 'Heaven, the sky') and 下 (xià, 'under, below'), literally 'that which lies beneath Heaven'. In Zhou dynasty bronze inscriptions and classical texts, 天下 denoted the entire civilized world centered around the Zhou Son of Heaven (天子), encompassing all lands, states, and subjects. Over millennia, its sense broadened from the political realm of the Chinese empire and the allegiance of its populace ('winning the hearts of the realm') to 'the whole world' or a specific domain dominated by someone.

history.meaning: all lands under Heaven; the civilized realm ruled by the Son of Heaven
imperial rule, state power, or the common people of the empire
the whole world; a domain or market dominated by a particular force or group

天下.notes: Beyond its grand historical sense ('the world'), modern Mandarin uses 是……的天下 to mean 'is the domain/monopoly of...' (e.g., 现在的市场是年轻人的天下 'the current market belongs to young people').

rootFamily.gloss: the world, human society (lit. under-sky between-people)
conquer or carve out a realm/career through hard struggle

cognates.meaning: peerless, best in the world, number one under heaven
number one in the world, peerless

天下第一.etymology: A four-character modifier-head phrase combining the classical locative noun 天下 (tiānxià, 'all under Heaven, the entire world') with the ordinal numeral compound 第一 (dì-yī, 'first, number one', composed of the ordinal prefix 第 dì—originally denoting the graded sequence of aristocratic residences—and 一 yī, 'one'). Attested in Han and Tang historical and literary texts to praise unmatched scholars, calligraphers, or scenic wonders, and later popularized in martial arts fiction (武俠) for the supreme warrior in the realm.

history.meaning: foremost in the empire (originally applied to officials' governance or supreme cultural works in Han–Tang texts)
peerless champion in the martial world (wuxia) or imperial examinations
number one in the world, second to none (often hyperbolic or humorous)

morphemes.meaning: under, realm beneath (together: the whole world)

天下第一.notes: In everyday and showbiz speech, often used hyperbolically or playfully (e.g., 天下第一好 'the best in the whole wide world', or teasing someone as 天下第一大傻瓜 'the biggest fool in the world').

rootFamily.gloss: the whole world, all under heaven

天亮.etymology: Subject-predicate compound of 天 ('the sky') + 亮 ('grow bright, become light'): 'daybreak, dawn, it gets light'.

history.meaning: the sky grows light = dawn, daybreak

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 天亮 (via 萌典)

天价.etymology: A modern figurative modifier-head compound (偏正結構) formed from 天 (tiān, 'the sky, heaven', used hyperbolically as 'sky-high, astronomical') and 價 / 价 (jià, 'price, value, monetary figure'). Just as 天文数字 ('astronomical figure') invokes the vastness of the heavens to describe an unfathomably large number, 天价 pairs 天 with 价 to denote an exorbitant, record-breaking, or astronomical price tag. Though built from classical roots, it crystallized in late 20th-century commercial and media journalism.

history.meaning: value, price of goods in market exchange
sky-high price, astronomical sum, exorbitant fee

天价.notes: Ubiquitous in Chinese entertainment industry headlines, especially in collocations like 天价片酬 ('astronomical acting fee/salary'), 天价违约金 ('sky-high contract penalty'), and 天价版权 ('astronomical copyright price').

cognates.meaning: Heavenly Empress (Mazu); pop diva, reigning female superstar

天后.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正結構) of 天 (tiān, 'Heaven, heavenly') and 后 (hòu, 'sovereign, empress, queen'). Historically, 天后 was a sacred imperial title: briefly adopted by Empress Wu Zetian in 674 CE Alongside Emperor Gaozong as 天皇 (Heavenly Emperor), and subsequently bestowed by Song, Yuan, and Qing emperors upon the sea goddess Mazu (媽祖, worshipped at 天后宮 temples across coastal China and Hong Kong). In late 20th-century Hong Kong Cantonese media (giving rise to the MTR station name Tin Hau and Cantopop press epithets), 天后 was secularized as the female counterpart to 天王 ('Heavenly King') to crown a reigning pop diva or female superstar.

history.meaning: Heavenly Empress (imperial title of Wu Zetian; honorific title of the goddess Mazu)
reigning queen of pop music or cinema, female superstar, pop diva
history.stage: Late 20th-Century Hong Kong Cantonese → Modern Mandarin Showbiz

天后.notes: In entertainment media, 天后 specifically designates an undisputed female superstar (especially in music, e.g., 乐坛天后 / 歌坛天后 'reigning diva of the music scene'), paired with 天王 ('male superstar / king of pop') and 影后 ('best actress / queen of cinema').

rootFamily.gloss: Heavenly King; reigning male pop/film superstar
best actress award winner, queen of cinema

天哪.etymology: Exclamatory phrase combining 天 ('Heaven!, the heavens') + emphatic modal particle 哪 (assimilation of 啊 after final -n of tiān): 'Good heavens!, Oh my God!, My goodness!'.

history.meaning: Good heavens!; Oh my gosh!

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 天哪 (via 萌典)

天壤之别.etymology: A classical four-character idiom (成語) structured as a modifier-head noun phrase linked by the genitive particle 之 (zhī): 天壤 (tiānrǎng, a coordinative compound of 天 'heaven, sky' and 壤 'cultivated earth, soft soil') + 之 ('of') + 別 / 别 (bié, 'separation, difference, distinction'). Literally 'the difference between heaven above and the earth below', the image derives from early Literary Chinese expressions such as 天壤之判 and poetry by Cao Zhi and Lu Ji contrasting the loftiest sky with the lowest soil to express a vast, unbridgeable disparity.

history.meaning: heaven and earth; the cosmos between sky and soil

history.form: 天壤之別 (tiān rǎng zhī bié)
history.meaning: a disparity as vast as that between heaven and earth
worlds apart, vast difference, poles apart

天壤之别.notes: Typically used as the object of 有 (有天壤之别 'there is a world of difference between them') or as a predicate; more elevated and emphatic than 差得很远.

sources.title: Wiktionary — 天壤之別 / 天壤之别

天天.etymology: A morphological reduplication (疊字) of the temporal noun and classifier 天 (tiān, 'day, 24-hour cycle; originally sky/Heaven'). In Mandarin grammar, reduplicating a classifier or temporal unit (such as 人人 'everyone', 年年 'every year', 次次 'every time') expresses universal distributive quantification ('every single X'). Once 天 supplanted Classical Chinese 日 (rì) as the primary vernacular word for 'day' during the Tang–Song transition, its reduplicated form 天天 emerged as the standard colloquial adverbial for 'every day, day in and day out'.

history.meaning: every day, day after day (Classical precursor)
every single day, daily, constantly
history.stage: Early Mandarin Vernacular to Modern Mandarin

天天.notes: More vivid and colloquial than 每天 (měitiān); often carries subjective emphasis on frequency or persistence (e.g., 天天向上 'make progress every single day', 天天加班 'work overtime every single day').

rootFamily.gloss: all day long, the whole day

天才.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正結構) formed from 天 (tiān, 'Heaven, nature; innate, heaven-bestowed') and 才 (cái, 'talent, ability, timber/aptitude'). Attested in Classical and Six Dynasties Chinese (e.g., Records of the Three Kingdoms and Wenxin Diaolong), 天才 originally denoted 'innate, heaven-endowed talent or natural aptitude' (a mass noun). During the Meiji era, Japanese scholars adopted the Sino-compound 天才 (tensai) to translate European Romantic concepts of 'genius' (an individual of transcendent creative intellect), and this person-denoting count-noun sense was re-imported into modern Mandarin.

history.meaning: heaven-endowed natural talent or innate aptitude (property, not person)
genius (both supreme creative intellect and the person possessing it, adapting European 'genius')
genius, prodigy; gifted, brilliant (noun and attributive adjective)

天才.notes: Functions both as a noun for a person (他是个音乐天才 'he is a musical genius') and as an attributive modifier (天才制作人 'genius producer'); compare 天赋 (tiānfù), which refers strictly to the abstract quality 'natural gift/talent' and never to a person.

天气.etymology: Compound noun of 天 ('sky, heaven') + 气 (氣, 'vapor, breath, atmosphere'): in Classical Chinese 'the vital breath/ether of heaven' or 'time of day', and in modern Mandarin the standard word for 'weather'.

history.meaning: the breath/atmosphere of the sky
weather

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 天气 (via 萌典)

天气预报.etymology: Four-character compound of 天气 ('weather', literally 'sky breath/atmosphere') + 预报 ('advance report', 预 'beforehand' + 报 'report/announce').

history.meaning: weather forecast

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 天气预报

天生.etymology: Subject-predicate/adverb-verb compound used as an adjective and adverb, combining 天 ('Heaven, nature') + 生 ('give birth to, produce, born'): 'born with, innate, by nature, natural'. Famously in Li Bai's 天生我材必有用 ('Heaven made my talents for a purpose').

history.stage: Classical & Tang poetry to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: endowed by nature; innate; born

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 天生 (via 萌典)

天真.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正結構) combining 天 (tiān, 'Heaven, nature; natural, uncarved') and 真 (zhēn, 'true, authentic, genuine, uncorrupted'). Coined in Daoist philosophy—specifically the Zhuangzi (〈漁父〉 'The Old Fisherman')—天真 originally denoted 'the authentic state of nature' or 'one's heaven-endowed, unspoiled true nature' prior to artificial social conditioning. Over time, its meaning shifted from Daoist spiritual authenticity to the charming, guileless innocence of children (天真爛漫) and, in adult contexts, to being naive, gullible, or overly idealistic.

history.meaning: uncorrupted natural authenticity; heaven-endowed true nature (Zhuangzi)
artless, guileless, candid, childlike in spirit (poetry and literati criticism)
innocent (of children); naive, unsophisticated, overly idealistic (of adults)

天真.notes: Context determines its connotation: praising a child as 天真活泼 means 'innocent and lively', whereas telling an adult or workplace newcomer 你太天真了 is a pointed critique meaning 'you're way too naive/idealistic'.

rootFamily.gloss: innocent and artless, bright and guileless (four-character idiom)

天空.etymology: Compound noun of 天 ('sky, heaven') + 空 ('open space, vault of the air'): 'the sky, the firmament'.

history.stage: Medieval Buddhist & poetic Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: the open sky

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 天空 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: the look of the sky, weather
color of the sky, weather, time of day

天色.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正結構) formed from 天 (tiān, 'the sky, heavens') and 色 (sè, 'color, hue, visible appearance'). Attested from Six Dynasties and Tang poetry onward, 天色 literally denotes the 'color and luminosity of the sky'. Because pre-modern Chinese society judged the progression of hours and approaching weather by observing the shifting brightness and hue of the heavens (dawn, dusk, gathering storm clouds), 天色 naturally extended to mean 'the time of day as indicated by daylight' and 'weather conditions'.

history.meaning: the hue and brightness of the sky; atmospheric appearance
sky light as an indicator of the hour of day or approaching weather

morphemes.meaning: color, hue, visible aspect or appearance

天色.notes: Most frequently appears in set phrases marking the passage of time at dawn or dusk, especially 天色不早了 ('it's getting late', lit. 'the sky-color is no longer early') and 天色渐暗 ('the sky is gradually darkening').

rootFamily.gloss: color, hue; facial expression or look
night scene, the dim light of night

天花板.etymology: Everyday word for 'ceiling', built from 天花 ('heavenly flowers') + 板 ('board'). 天花 first meant flowers falling from heaven in translated Buddhist texts; it was later applied to the decorated, painted panel ceilings of halls, and Ming–Qing builders called the grid of wooden panels 天花板. Modern Mandarin also uses it figuratively for an upper limit.

history.meaning: flowers raining from heaven
panelled decorative ceiling
ceiling; (figurative) upper limit

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 天花板 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: the Way of Heaven, natural law, Providence; the sun
the Way of Heaven, cosmic law, providence
the Way of Heaven, providence, natural justice

天道.etymology: A core philosophical modifier-head compound (偏正結構) formed from 天 (tiān, 'Heaven, the cosmos, nature') and 道 (dào, 'way, path, cosmic principle, governing law'). In early Classical Chinese texts (Zuo Zhuan, Laozi, Zhuangzi, Book of Changes), 天道 denoted both the regular astronomical cycles of the heavens and the impartial, self-operating moral and natural order of the universe, often contrasted with 人道 (réndào, 'the Way of human society'). In popular usage, it also came to mean cosmic justice, providence, or the principle that effort and virtue are ultimately rewarded.

history.meaning: astronomical cycles of the heavens; the impartial cosmic order and Way of Nature (Laozi, Zuo Zhuan)
providential justice, karmic retribution, moral law governing the universe
the Way of Heaven, natural law, cosmic fairness (as in 天道酬勤 'Heaven rewards diligence')

天道.notes: Often invoked in motivational contexts via the four-character maxim 天道酬勤 ('Heaven rewards the diligent / hard work pays off'), or in dramatic exclamations like 还有没有天道了 ('Is there any justice left in this world?!').

rootFamily.gloss: Heaven rewards diligence (hard work pays off)
reason, principle, sense; the way things work

太.etymology: Indicative character differentiated from 大 ('big, great') by adding a bottom dot (丶): originally interchangeable with 大 and 泰 ('supreme, extreme, highest'), and in Mandarin the primary degree adverb for 'too (excessively), extremely, so very (太好了!)'.

history.meaning: supreme; greatest; senior
too (excessively); extremely; very

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 太 (via 萌典)

太久.etymology: A degree-adverbial modifier-head phrase (偏正結構) combining the excessive degree adverb 太 (tài, 'excessively, too, extremely'—historically a graphic and phonological variant of 大/泰 denoting 'supreme, extreme') with the temporal adjective 久 (jiǔ, 'long in duration, a long time'). In Old Chinese, 久 originally meant 'to apply moxibustion over a prolonged period' (later written 灸) before specializing as the general word for temporal length; preceded by 太, it expresses that an elapsed or expected duration exceeds what is reasonable or bearable.

history.meaning: long in time, enduring, for a long duration
too long (in time), excessively long duration

太久.notes: Strictly refers to length of time (e.g., 等了太久 'waited too long', 耽误太久 'delayed too long'), never physical length in space (which is 太长 tàicháng).

rootFamily.gloss: for a long time; how long? / not long (after negator)
What took you so long! / I've been waiting ages (polite greeting)

太俗.etymology: A modifier-head adjectival phrase (偏正結構) formed from the excessive degree adverb 太 (tài, 'too, excessively') and the evaluative adjective 俗 (sú, 'common, vulgar, tacky, unrefined'). In Classical Chinese, 俗 (composed of 亻 'person' and 谷 'valley') originally denoted the local customs, habits, and mores of common folk living in a region (風俗), as well as the secular world in contrast to monastic life (世俗). In literati aesthetics (雅 vs. 俗, 'refined' vs. 'vulgar') and modern creative criticism, 俗 developed the pejorative sense of 'philistine, kitschy, hackneyed, or tacky'.

history.meaning: popular customs, local mores; common, ordinary, non-elite
unrefined, philistine, lacking literary or artistic elegance (contrasted with 雅 yǎ 'refined')
too tacky, overly cliché, vulgar, kitschy

太俗.notes: In television, film, and advertising critiques, 太俗 (or 太俗气 / 太俗套) is a frequent verdict dismissing a plotline, title, or design as 'too cheesy, tacky, or cliché'.

rootFamily.gloss: tacky, vulgar, kitschy, in poor taste
lowbrow, vulgar, trashy (of media or humor)

太多.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 太多. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 太多 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 太多 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 太多 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 太多. The etymology of 太多 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 太多
middle form of 太多
modern form of 太多

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 太多

太好了.etymology: High-frequency exclamatory phrase formed from degree adverb 太 ('exceedingly; so', derived from 大 with a distinguishing dot) + 好 ('good; wonderful') + modal particle 了 marking heightened emotion.

history.meaning: wonderful!; that's great!

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 太好了

太巧.etymology: A modifier-head adjectival phrase (偏正結構) combining the degree adverb 太 (tài, 'too, extremely, so') with the adjective 巧 (qiǎo, 'skillful, ingenious; by extension, fortuitous, opportune, coincidental'). In Classical Chinese, 巧 (written with 工 'carpenter's square / craft' and 丂, a phonetic element depicting breath) meant 'craftsmanship, dexterity, or clever artifice'. Because a timing or encounter that fits together as neatly as fine joinery feels almost crafted by fate (湊巧 / 恰巧), 巧 acquired the sense of 'coincidental or opportune', making 太巧(了) the standard exclamation for 'what a coincidence!' or 'far too coincidental'.

history.meaning: skillful, dexterous, ingeniously crafted; artful (of speech)
opportune, happening just at the right moment, coincidental
far too coincidental; what an amazing coincidence!

太巧.notes: With sentence-final 了 (太巧了!), it is a warm, everyday exclamation ('What a coincidence running into you!'); without 了 in analytical or skeptical contexts (这也太巧了吧), it implies suspicion ('That's way too coincidental to be an accident').

rootFamily.gloss: by coincidence, as luck would have it, fortuitously

太过火.etymology: A degree-modified adjectival compound consisting of the excessive degree adverb 太 (tài, 'too, way too') and the verb-object compound 過火 / 过火 (guòhuǒ, 'go beyond the proper heat/flame; go too far, overdo it'). The base word 過火 originates in traditional Chinese culinary, metallurgical, and alchemical practice (compare 火候 huǒhou, 'the precise degree and duration of heat in cooking or smelting'): when food or porcelain is exposed to heat beyond the optimal point (過 'exceed, pass beyond' + 火 'fire, heat'), it is scorched or ruined. Figuratively, 太过火 describes speech, pranks, or actions that cross the line of propriety.

history.meaning: exceed the proper degree of fire/heat in cooking, firing, or alchemy
go way too far, overstep boundaries, be excessive in speech or behavior

morphemes.meaning: fire, heat; figuratively the proper degree or limit

太过火.notes: Commonly used to criticize pranks, publicity stunts, or harsh remarks that cross the line (e.g., 玩笑开得太过火了 'the joke went way too far'); closely related to the culinary/figurative noun 火候 ('mastery of timing and degree').

rootFamily.gloss: go too far, overdo it, exceed proper limits
go too far, cross the line of one's role or duty (lit. exceed-part)
degree of heat and duration in cooking; mastery of timing and tact

太阳.etymology: Everyday spoken word for 'the sun': 太 ('great, utmost') + 阳 ('yang', the bright, warm principle opposed to 阴 yin). It is probably so named because the sun was seen as the utmost expression of yang. Classical Chinese usually said simply 日, which survives in words such as 日出 ('sunrise').

history.meaning: sun; day
the sun (the 'great yang')
sun; sunshine

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 太阳 (via 萌典)

夫妻.etymology: Coordinative kinship compound pairing 夫 ('husband, adult man', showing a man 大 with a hairpin 一 through his topknot marking adulthood) + 妻 ('wife', showing a woman 女 with hair held by a hand 又, denoting an equal partner in marriage): 'husband and wife, married couple'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Shijing, Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: husband and wife; married couple

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 夫妻 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: lapse, become invalid, expire (of a treaty, patent, or ticket)

失效.etymology: A verb-object compound (動賓結構) formed from 失 (shī, 'lose, forfeit, let slip') and 效 (xiào, 'effect, efficacy, validity, result'). In Classical Chinese, 效 meant 'to imitate, present results, or prove effective' (as in 成效, 效驗). In modern legal, medical, and administrative terminology—reinforced by Meiji-era Sino-Japanese legal vocabulary 失効 (shikkō, translating German/English concepts of a right, contract, or patent lapsing)—失效 denotes the loss of legal validity, contractual force, or medicinal/technical efficacy.

history.meaning: demonstrate results, prove efficacious, take effect
lose legal force or validity; lapse, expire (of contracts, laws, or patents)
history.stage: Meiji Sino-Japanese Legal Coinage → Early Modern Chinese

history.meaning: become invalid, expire (of contracts/links/documents); lose efficacy (of medicine/mechanisms)

失效.notes: Applies across three main domains: legal/administrative documents (合同失效 'the contract has become invalid/expired'), medicine (药物失效 'the medicine lost its efficacy'), and digital tech (链接失效 'the link has expired / is dead'). Antonym: 生效 (shēngxiào, 'take effect').

rootFamily.gloss: take effect, become valid, go into force (antonym of 失效)
effective, valid (of a ticket, contract, or method)
effect, result; sound/visual effects in media production

cognates.meaning: rudeness, breach of etiquette; goodbye / excuse me (sumo & Edo slang)
discourtesy, forgive my lack of respect

失敬.etymology: A verb-object compound (動賓結構) formed from 失 (shī, 'lose, fail in, neglect') and 敬 (jìng, 'reverence, respect, courteous deference'). Attested in Classical Chinese ritual and philosophical texts (such as the Xunzi and Book of Rites), 失敬 originally meant literally 'to fail in ritual reverence or proper deportment'. In Early Mandarin vernacular fiction and polite social intercourse, it specialized as a humble, self-deprecating apology formula ('forgive my lack of respect / I failed to recognize your stature'), often reduplicated as 失敬，失敬! upon learning a new acquaintance's distinguished identity.

history.meaning: fail to maintain ritual reverence or respectful deportment (Xunzi)
forgive my discourtesy / pardon me for not recognizing your eminent status (courtesy formula)
history.stage: Early Mandarin Vernacular (Ming–Qing) to Modern Mandarin

失敬.notes: Used almost exclusively as a polite, slightly old-fashioned or humorous social formula (often paired with 久仰 'I've long admired your name' when discovering someone is a big shot: 失敬失敬，原来您就是…… 'Forgive my discourtesy! So you are...').

rootFamily.gloss: pay tribute to, salute (also 'homage' in film/TV)
forgive my breach of etiquette, excuse my rudeness

失望.etymology: A verb-object compound (動賓結構) formed from 失 (shī, 'lose, forfeit') and 望 (wàng, 'gaze into the distance in anticipation; hope, expectation'). Attested in Classical Chinese historiography and philosophy (including the Mengzi and Shiji), 失望 originally meant literally 'to lose what one was hoping for' or 'to have one's expectations dashed'. Over time, it grammaticalized into a psychological state verb and adjective meaning 'disappointed' or 'let down', capable of taking degree adverbs (很失望 'very disappointed') while losing its ability to take a direct object.

history.meaning: have one's hopes or expectations thwarted; lose hope (Mengzi, Shiji)
disappointed, let down, disillusioned (stative verb / adjective)

失望.notes: Because 失望 is already a verb-object structure ('lose-hope'), it NEVER takes a direct object in Chinese: to say 'disappointed in someone/something', use the prepositional pattern 对……(感到/很)失望, and for 'disappoint someone', use 让/令某人失望.

rootFamily.gloss: despair, give up all hope (lit. sever-hope)
eagerly look forward to, yearn for

失物处.etymology: Three-character institutional compound combining 失物 ('lost property, lost items', 失 'lose' + 物 'object') + 处 (處, 'office, counter, department'): 'Lost and Found office/desk (short for 失物招领处)'.

history.meaning: Lost and Found desk/office

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 失物处 (via 萌典)

失眠.etymology: A verb-object compound (動賓結構) formed from 失 (shī, 'lose, fail to obtain') and 眠 (mián, 'close the eyes, sleep', composed of 目 'eye' and 民 as phonetic). First popularized in Tang and Song dynasty poetry (by poets such as Du Fu, Bai Juyi, and Su Shi reflecting on lying awake at night with anxious thoughts) and adopted into traditional Chinese medical texts alongside 不寐 (bùmèi), 失眠 literally means 'to lose sleep' and serves in modern Mandarin as both the everyday verb 'to lie awake unable to sleep' and the medical noun 'insomnia'.

history.meaning: lose sleep, lie awake through the night (poetic and literary usage in Tang–Song verse)
suffer from insomnia, be unable to sleep; clinical insomnia (as in 失眠症)

失眠.notes: As an intrinsic verb-object compound, 失眠 can refer either to a single sleepless night (昨晚我失眠了 'I couldn't sleep last night') or to chronic insomnia (严重失眠 'severe insomnia').

rootFamily.gloss: sleep, slumber (formal noun/verb, e.g., 睡眠质量 'sleep quality')

cognates.meaning: neglect of duty, malfeasance; loss of employment/office
neglect of duty; loss of office/job
dereliction of duty; lose one's post

失职.etymology: A verb-object compound (動賓結構) composed of 失 (shī, 'fail in, neglect, lose') and 職 / 职 (zhí, 'official duty, post, responsibility'). Attested in Classical Chinese administrative and historical texts (such as the Zuo Zhuan and Han Feizi), 失職 carried two closely linked meanings: 'to fail to fulfill the duties of one's office' (dereliction of duty) and 'to lose one's official post or livelihood'. In modern Mandarin, 失职 specializes strictly in the sense of 'fail in one's duty / dereliction of duty / malpractice' (whereas 'lose one's job' is expressed by 失业 shīyè).

history.meaning: fail to perform one's official duties; lose one's appointed post or station (Zuo Zhuan)
fail in one's duty, commit dereliction of duty or professional negligence

morphemes.meaning: fail in, neglect, fall short of

失职.notes: Beware the Sino-Japanese / Sino-Korean false friend: in Japanese (失職 shisshoku) and Korean (실직 siljik), the cognate primarily means 'lose one's job / become unemployed', whereas Mandarin 失职 strictly means 'fail in one's duty / professional negligence' (unemployment is 失业).

rootFamily.gloss: duty, responsibility, obligation of one's post
resign from a job, quit one's post
conscientious, fulfilling one's duty admirably (antonym of 失职)

失误.etymology: Coordinative verb and noun compound of 失 ('lose, slip up, miss') + 误 (誤, 'err, mistake'): 'make a mistake, slip up, lapse, fault, error'. Attested since Han historical texts.

history.stage: Han Classical Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: slip up; error; mistake; fault

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 失误 (via 萌典)

失败.etymology: A coordinative compound (並列結構) formed from two near-synonymous verbs of loss and ruin: 失 (shī, 'lose, miss, let slip, err') and 敗 / 败 (bài, 'destroy, ruin, suffer military defeat'—originally depicting a hand holding a club 攵 smashing a cowrie shell 貝 or cauldron). In Classical and Middle Chinese, 失敗 denoted military rout, ruin, or the spoiling of an enterprise. In modern Mandarin (and across the East Asian Sinosphere), it broadened into the universal verb and noun for 'fail; failure' in any endeavor, from projects and relationships to competitions.

history.meaning: suffer military defeat, be routed; fall into ruin or spoilation
fail in an endeavor, lose a match or competition; failure (antonym of 成功)

失败.notes: Functions flexibly as an intransitive verb (计划失败了 'the plan failed'), a noun (失败乃成功之母 'failure is the mother of success'), and in colloquial Mandarin even as a gradable adjective (我做人太失败了 'I'm such a failure as a person').

rootFamily.gloss: loser, person who has failed (composed with agentive suffix -者)

cognates.meaning: go missing, disappear without a trace

失踪.etymology: A verb-object compound (動賓結構) formed from 失 (shī, 'lose, lose sight of') and 蹤 / 踪 (zōng, 'footprint, track, trail, trace', composed of 足 'foot' and 從/宗 as phonetic). Attested in Tang and Song literary prose and vernacular tales (and alongside the fuller four-character phrase 失去蹤跡 'lose track/footprints of'), 失蹤 literally means 'to lose one's footprints or trail', hence 'to vanish without a trace' or 'become unaccounted for'. In modern legal and police usage, it is the standard term for a person, aircraft, or vessel going missing.

history.meaning: lose track of someone's footprints or whereabouts; vanish from sight
go missing, disappear, be unaccounted for (general and legal usage)

morphemes.meaning: lose, lose sight of, cease to show

失踪.notes: Unlike 消失 (xiāoshī, 'vanish/disappear', which applies to objects, feelings, or phenomena), 失踪 specifically implies that a person, animal, or vehicle's whereabouts are unknown and people are looking for them; in colloquial speech, 玩失踪 ('play at going missing') means 'ghosting someone / going MIA'.

失踪人士.etymology: A formal four-character modifier-head nominal compound (偏正結構) combining the verb-object compound 失蹤 / 失踪 (shīzōng, 'go missing, lose trace of whereabouts', from 失 'lose' + 蹤 'footprint, trace') with the collective honorific/formal noun 人士 (rénshì, 'personages, individuals, members of a category'). In Classical Chinese, 士 (shì) denoted an educated gentleman, officer, or retainer; paired coordinatively with 人 (rén, 'person'), 人士 evolved in modern journalistic, legal, and public-service registers (especially in Hong Kong, Taiwan, and formal mainland broadcasts) into a respectful plural/collective noun for 'persons' or 'individuals'.

history.meaning: men of standing, scholars and officials, notable personages

history.form: 失蹤人士 / 失踪人士 (shīzōng rénshì)
history.meaning: missing persons (formal police, legal, and news broadcasting register)

失踪人士.notes: Belongs to formal police, news broadcast, and public-notice register (e.g., 寻找失踪人士 'searching for missing persons', alongside mainland administrative 失踪人员); in everyday conversation one simply says 失踪的人.

rootFamily.gloss: go missing, disappear without a trace
successful figures / people who have achieved success (formal)

cognates.meaning: missing person, person whose whereabouts are unknown

失踪者.etymology: A modifier-head agentive compound formed from the verb-object compound 失踪 (shīzōng, Traditional 失蹤, 'to lose track of one's footprints; to disappear', from 失 'to lose' + 踪/蹤 'footprint, trace') and the Classical Chinese nominalizing agentive suffix 者 (zhě, 'one who'). While 失蹤 appeared in Tang–Song literature for losing a trail, the legal and journalistic agent noun 失踪者 crystallized in late 19th- and early 20th-century Sino-Japanese legal and news vocabulary (Japanese 失踪者 shissōsha).

history.meaning: to lose track of footprints or vanish without a trace
missing person (legal and journalistic designation)

morphemes.meaning: agentive nominalizer: one who, person who

失踪者.notes: Used in formal news broadcasts, police reports, and legal contexts; in everyday conversation, people usually say 走失的人 (zǒushī de rén) or 失联的人 (shīlián de rén, 'person out of contact').

rootFamily.gloss: to follow a trail, track down

失陪.etymology: Polite conversational formula combining 失 ('fail in, lose the chance to') + 陪 ('keep someone company'): literally 'fail to keep you company' -> 'excuse me for leaving first, I must be excusing myself'.

history.stage: Ming–Qing polite vernacular to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: excuse me for leaving your company

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 失陪 (via 萌典)

头.etymology: From Old Chinese *dô (Traditional 頭), a phono-semantic compound combining 豆 (dòu, originally a high-stemmed ritual vessel, serving as phonetic and suggesting a round elevated shape) and 頁 (xié, 'head', depicting a kneeling figure with a prominent head). In Classical Chinese, 首 (shǒu) was the primary literary word for 'head', while 頭 gained dominance in Han-era vernacular and expanded via metaphor to mean 'top, chief, first, leading endpoint' and later grammaticalized into a nominal suffix.

history.meaning: anatomical head; skull
head; top end; chief; nominal suffix
head; chief, leading; end/aspect; nominal suffix (-tou)

morphemes.meaning: head; top; chief; leading; nominal suffix

头.notes: Pronounced with full second tone (tóu) when meaning 'head' or 'leader/first' (as in 头号 'number one'), but neutralized to light tone (tou) when functioning as a dummy nominal suffix (as in 石头 'stone', 里头 'inside').

rootFamily.gloss: to take the lead, be the first to act

头上.etymology: Locative compound combining 头 (頭, 'head; top') + 上 ('on, above'): 'on one's head, overhead, on top'.

history.meaning: on the head; overhead

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 头上 (via 萌典)

头发.etymology: A modifier-head disyllabic compound formed from 头 (tóu, Traditional 頭, 'head') + 发 (fà, Traditional 髮, 'hair of the head', composed of 髟 'long flowing hair' and 犮 as phonetic). In Classical Chinese, monosyllabic 髮 (fà) alone meant 'scalp hair' (as opposed to 毛 máo, 'body hair, fur, feathers'). During the medieval vernacular disyllabification trend, 頭 was prefixed to specify and reinforce the meaning, and in 20th-century Mainland simplification both 發 ('to send forth') and 髮 ('hair') were merged into 发.

history.meaning: hair on the human head (monosyllabic root)
hair of the head (disyllabic vernacular compound)
hair on the head (simplified script, neutral-tone second syllable)

头发.notes: In Mainland China the second syllable is normally pronounced in the neutral tone (tóufa), whereas in Taiwan Mandarin it is pronounced in the fourth tone (tóufà, distinguishing 髮 fà from 發 fā). Never use 毛 (máo) for head hair.

头子.etymology: A colloquial suffixed noun formed from 头 (tóu, Traditional 頭, 'head, chief, leader') + the diminutive/nominalizing suffix 子 (zi). Attested in Tang–Song vernacular and Ming–Qing fiction (such as *Water Margin* / 水滸傳) initially for the leader of a band, guild, or military detachment, in modern Mandarin it took on a strongly pejorative or colloquial coloration referring to a ringleader, gang boss, or chieftain of an illicit faction.

history.meaning: chief of a band, military captain, or headman
ringleader, gang boss, chieftain (colloquial/pejorative)

头子.notes: Carries a derogatory or rough colloquial tone ('ringleader, gang boss'); for neutral or respectful 'leader/boss' in media or workplace contexts, use 领导 (lǐngdǎo), 负责人 (fùzérén), or colloquial 头儿 (tóur).

rootFamily.gloss: boss, chief (colloquial with erhua, often neutral/affectionate)

头条.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 头 (tóu, Traditional 頭, 'first, foremost, top') and 条 (tiáo, Traditional 條, 'strip, item, article, entry', originally 'slender tree branch'). Originally used in late imperial bureaucracy and commerce for the first item on a list or ledger (and in Northern slang for a sleek 'figure/strip'), in modern print and digital journalism it serves as an ellipsis of 头条新闻 (tóutiáo xīnwén, 'first-item news'), denoting the banner headline or lead story.

history.meaning: first item on a list or document; top strip
lead story, top headline in newspapers, broadcast, or trending media feeds

头条.notes: A staple of entertainment and showbiz vocabulary (as in *Behind the Scenes*): 上头条 (shàng tóutiáo, 'to make the headlines') and 抢头条 (qiǎng tóutiáo, 'to steal the headlines') are constant preoccupations of PR teams and producers.

rootFamily.gloss: entry, clause, item in a document or feed

头疼.etymology: Subject-predicate compound of 头 (頭, 'head') + 疼 ('ache, hurt'): literally 'have a headache' and figuratively 'find something a headache, feel troubled or exasperated by'.

history.meaning: headache; troublesome problem

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 头疼 (via 萌典)

头盔.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 头盔. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 头盔 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 头盔 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 头盔 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 头盔. The etymology of 头盔 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 头盔
middle form of 头盔
modern form of 头盔

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 头盔

cognates.meaning: clue, starting point, thread of a matter
clue, thread of a complex affair

头绪.etymology: A coordinative compound from sericulture (silk-reeling) imagery: 头 (tóu, Traditional 頭, 'end, tip') + 绪 (xù, Traditional 緒, 'the loose end of a silk thread on a cocoon', composed of the silk radical 糸/纟 and phonetic 者). When boiling cocoons to reel silk, finding the tip of the filament (緒) allows the entire skein to be unwound smoothly; by Tang–Song prose (e.g., Han Yu and Zhu Xi), 頭緒 had metaphorically generalized to 'the main thread, starting clue, or orderly arrangement of a complex problem'.

history.meaning: tip of a silk thread from a cocoon; lineage or succession
the loose end of a tangled skein; main thread or orderly clue to a complex matter
clue, inkling, mental thread or systematic order (second syllable often neutral tone)

morphemes.meaning: end of a silk thread; clue, order

头绪.notes: Almost always used with verbs of finding or lacking in crisis management and detective/production storylines: 理出头绪 (lǐchū tóuxù, 'to sort out a clue/thread'—literally 'comb out the silk end') or 毫无头绪 (háowú tóuxù, 'to have no clue where to start').

rootFamily.gloss: mood, emotional state (lit. threads of feeling)
clue, trail, storyline thread (lit. thread and rope)
ready, in order (lit. having reached its thread-order)

头衔.etymology: A modifier-head compound formed from 头 (tóu, Traditional 頭, 'top, foremost, heading') + 衔 (xián, Traditional 銜, originally 'metal bit in a horse's mouth', composed of 行 'marching/road' enclosing 金 'metal'). Because a horse's bit controls its rank in a procession—and because imperial officials had their full string of court ranks written at the very top (頭) of memorials and calling cards as if linked bit-to-bit (連銜)—头衔 came in Tang–Song bureaucratic usage to mean an official's formal rank and title, later generalizing to any professional or honorific title.

history.meaning: horse's metal bit; to hold in the mouth; official grade controlled by the court
full list of official court ranks inscribed at the head of a document or calling card
official title, professional rank, honorific designation

morphemes.meaning: horse's bit; official rank or title

头衔.notes: Common in corporate, academic, and entertainment contexts (e.g., a producer's or celebrity's impressive string of 头衔 on promotional posters), often contrasted with actual power (实权 shíquán).

rootFamily.gloss: to head a list, take lead billing (as lead actor/producer)
to link up, join seamlessly, transition (lit. bit-to-bit)

cognates.meaning: top of the head; overhead; to balance on the head

头顶.etymology: A modifier-head compound (also used as a subject-predicate verb phrase) composed of 头 (tóu, Traditional 頭, 'head') + 顶 (dǐng, Traditional 頂, 'crown of the head, summit, peak', from 頁 'head' + 丁 phonetic). While 頂 alone meant 'crown of the head' in the *Shuowen Jiezi* (顛也), combining 頭 and 頂 in medieval Chinese created both a concrete location noun ('the very top of the head; the space directly overhead') and a vivid verb ('to carry/bear atop one's head', e.g., 头顶蓝天 'with the blue sky overhead').

history.meaning: crown of the head, vertex
top of the head, crown; directly overhead; to bear on one's head

morphemes.meaning: crown of the head, peak, top; to carry on the head

头顶.notes: Functions both as a place word meaning 'on top of the head / directly overhead' (e.g., 头顶上的聚光灯 'the spotlight overhead') and as a literary/four-character-style verb meaning 'bearing upon one's head' (e.g., 头顶光环 'wearing a halo of fame').

rootFamily.gloss: peak, summit, pinnacle (of a mountain or career)
top-notch, cream of the crop, apex

夸.etymology: Phono-semantic character (traditional 誇, combining 言 'speech' + 夸 kuā 'spread wide, big'; simplified back to the base character 夸): originally 'speak big, boast, exaggerate' in Classical Chinese, and in everyday Mandarin 'praise, compliment, commend'.

history.meaning: big; boast; exaggerate
praise; compliment; boast

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 夸 (via 萌典)

夸夸.etymology: Reduplicated verb from 夸 ('praise, compliment'): 'praise a bit, give someone a compliment' (distinguished in tone and syntax from the literary bound root 夸夸 kuākuā in 夸夸其谈 'boastful talk').

history.meaning: give a compliment; praise a little

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 夸夸 (via 萌典)

夸奖.etymology: A coordinative verb/noun compound formed from 夸 (kuā, Traditional 誇, 'to speak grandly, boast, extol', from 言 'speech' + 夸 phonetic 'grand, expansive') + 奖 (jiǎng, Traditional 獎, 'to encourage, commend, reward', originally 'to urge on hunting dogs'). While 誇 in Classical Chinese often leaned toward 'boasting' or 'speaking extravagantly', pairing it with 獎 ('commend, encourage') in vernacular Ming–Qing Mandarin stabilized a positive transitive sense: 'to praise, compliment, commend'.

history.meaning: to speak grandly + to urge on, commend, reward (separate Classical roots)
to praise, commend; compliment, commendation

morphemes.meaning: to praise, speak grandly of (Traditional 誇)

夸奖.notes: Frequently used in polite self-deprecation when receiving a compliment: 过奖了，谢谢您的夸奖 (guòjiǎng le, xièxie nín de kuājiǎng, 'You flatter me, thank you for your kind praise'). Note that Simplified 夸 merges 誇 ('boast/praise') into 夸 ('grand').

夸张.etymology: A coordinative compound from 夸 (kuā, Traditional 誇, 'to speak extravagantly, magnify in speech') + 张 (zhāng, Traditional 張, 'to stretch a bowstring, expand, spread wide'). First attested in Six Dynasties literary criticism—most famously in Liu Xie's *Wenxin Diaolong* (文心雕龍·夸飾, c. 500 CE)—where 誇張 described magnifying and stretching imagery for rhetorical impact; in the 20th century, reinforced by Japanese 誇張 (kochō) as the translation of Western rhetorical 'hyperbole/exaggeration', it also became a high-frequency colloquial adjective meaning 'over the top, dramatic, ridiculous'.

history.meaning: to magnify and stretch in rhetoric or display; boastful expansion
hyperbole, exaggeration (noun/verb); exaggerated, over-the-top, dramatic (adjective)

morphemes.meaning: to boast, magnify in speech (Traditional 誇)
to stretch a bowstring, expand, spread wide (Traditional 張)

夸张.notes: In contemporary spoken Mandarin and entertainment circles, 夸张 is constantly used as a stative adjective (太夸张了吧! tài kuāzhāng le ba!, 'That's way over the top / insane!') to describe dramatic acting, lavish stage budgets, or outrageous rumors.

夹.etymology: Ancient ideogram (夾) attested on Shang oracle bones showing a central standing person (大) flanked under both arms by two smaller figures (二人): 'press from both sides, hold between, clip, pinch, carry under the arm, interleave' (read jiā), and 'double-layered/lined garment' (read jiá).

history.meaning: flank from both sides; press between; pincers/tongs
hold/press between; clip; folder (jiā); double-layered (jiá)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 夹 (via 萌典)

奇怪.etymology: Coordinative adjective and verb compound of 奇 ('unusual, rare, strange') + 怪 ('strange, odd, marvel at'): 'strange, odd, surprising; find something strange'. Attested since Han–Six Dynasties prose and poetry.

history.meaning: strange; unusual; odd; wonder at

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 奇怪 (via 萌典)

奇闻.etymology: A modifier-head compound composed of 奇 (qí, 'strange, rare, extraordinary, marvelous') + 闻 (wén, Traditional 聞, 'that which is heard; news, report, story', from 耳 'ear' inside 門 'gate' as phonetic). Attested in Classical and medieval Chinese prose for rare or marvelous accounts heard from afar, in modern media and tabloid journalism it denotes bizarre news stories, sensational anecdotes, or oddities (as in 千古奇闻 'an unheard-of oddity through the ages').

history.meaning: rare or marvelous account heard by ear; extraordinary tale
bizarre news story, strange anecdote, sensational oddity

morphemes.meaning: news, report, that which is heard (Traditional 聞)

奇闻.notes: Often paired in four-character media expressions like 奇闻轶事 (qíwén yìshì, 'bizarre news and curious anecdotes') or 天下奇闻 (tiānxià qíwén, 'the strangest news in the world', often used sarcastically when someone makes an absurd claim).

奉劝.etymology: A modifier-head honorific verb compound formed from the deferential prefixoid verb 奉 (fèng, originally depicting two hands 廾 offering up a lush plant 丰, hence 'to respectfully present with both hands') + 劝 (quàn, Traditional 勸, 'to urge, advise, exhort', with 力 'strength/effort'). Originating in epistolary and courtly Literary Chinese where 奉 served as a humble/respectful marker before verbs of communication (cf. 奉告 'to respectfully inform'), in modern usage 奉劝 has shifted via pragmatic irony into a stern, solemn warning ('I strongly advise you...').

history.meaning: to respectfully offer counsel or exhortation (epistolary/courtly deferential verb)
to earnestly advise, caution, or warn someone (often with a stern or admonitory edge)

morphemes.meaning: to offer respectfully with both hands (honorific/humble verb marker)

奉劝.notes: Despite containing the honorific morpheme 奉 ('respectfully'), in modern drama and negotiation dialogue 奉劝 is almost never deferential—saying 我奉劝你一句 (wǒ fèngquàn nǐ yí jù, 'Let me give you a piece of advice') is a veiled warning or ultimatum.

rootFamily.gloss: to respectfully inform (often in 无可奉告 'no comment')

cognates.meaning: acting by imperial or official command
receiving and carrying out an order

奉命.etymology: A Classical verb-object compound composed of 奉 (fèng, 'to receive or hold up respectfully with both hands') + 命 (mìng, 'imperial decree, mandate, command, order'). Attested across Warring States texts (*Zuo Zhuan*, *Shiji*) for an envoy or general receiving a sovereign's mandate with both hands and executing it, 奉命 survives in modern Mandarin as a crisp, formal verb phrase ('to act under orders') used in military, police, corporate, and playful everyday contexts.

history.meaning: to respectfully receive and carry out a ruler's or heaven's mandate
to act under orders, carry out instructions from a superior

morphemes.meaning: to receive respectfully with both hands, obey

奉命.notes: Grammatically precedes a second verb phrase specifying the mission (serial verb construction): e.g., 我奉命来接管这个项目 ('I am acting under orders to take over this project'). Can also be used humorously in domestic life (奉老婆之命 'acting under my wife's orders').

cognates.meaning: to keep someone company; to take on a challenge to the end

奉陪.etymology: A modifier-head honorific verb compound formed from 奉 (fèng, 'respectfully, with both hands') + 陪 (péi, 'to accompany, keep company, attend upon', originally 'mound added to a mound' from 阜/阝 + 咅). In Ming–Qing vernacular courtesy language, 奉陪 meant 'to have the honor of keeping a guest company' (and 恕不奉陪 meant 'forgive me for not keeping you company'); in modern usage, especially in 奉陪到底 ('keep you company to the very end'), it frequently expresses defiant readiness to accept a rival's challenge.

history.meaning: to respectfully keep a guest or superior company (courtesy formula)
to keep someone company (often negated in 恕不奉陪 or used defiantly in 奉陪到底 'take you on to the end')

奉陪.notes: Rarely used in simple affirmative sentences; learners will encounter it in two high-drama set phrases: 恕不奉陪 (shù bù fèngpéi, 'Excuse me for walking out / Count me out') and 奉陪到底 (fèngpéi dàodǐ, 'I'll take you on all the way to the end!').

rootFamily.gloss: to accompany a guest or VIP on an inspection/visit
to offer an apology, make amends

契约.etymology: A coordinative compound uniting two ancient technologies of binding agreements: 契 (qì, 'notched wooden or bamboo tally carved with a knife 刀 and split in two as proof of debt or pact', from 丰 'notches' + 刀 'knife' + 大) + 约 (yuē, Traditional 約, 'to bind with a silk cord; covenant, stipulation', with 糸/纟 'silk rope'). Attested since the *Zhan Guo Ce* and Han legal texts, 契约 was revitalized in the late 19th century via Meiji Japanese 契約 (keiyaku) to translate Western legal and philosophical 'contract / covenant' (such as Rousseau's *Social Contract*, 社会契约论).

history.meaning: notched tally-stick + silk-cord binding; solemn covenant or deed
written deed of sale, land title, or binding agreement
legal contract, solemn pact, covenant (as in 契约精神 'spirit of contract')

契约.notes: More elevated and abstract than 合同 (hétong, a standard commercial/employment contract). In Chinese workplace and media dramas, 契约精神 (qìyuē jīngshén, 'the spirit of contract / professional integrity in honoring agreements') is a key buzzword.

奖金.etymology: A modifier-head compound formed from 奖 (jiǎng, Traditional 獎, 'to commend, reward, prize') + 金 (jīn, 'metal, gold; money, cash, funds'). Formed in modern administrative and commercial Chinese (paralleling Japanese 賞金/奨金) on the productive pattern of [purpose + 金 'monetary fund'], it designates money awarded either as a performance bonus in a workplace or as prize money in a competition.

history.meaning: commendation/reward + gold/metal money (separate Classical morphemes)
monetary bonus, prize money, financial reward

奖金.notes: Covers both corporate bonuses (like 年终奖金 niánzhōng jiǎngjīn, 'year-end bonus') and contest prize money. Compare 奖学金 (jiǎngxuéjīn, 'scholarship', lit. 'study-encouragement money').

套.etymology: A compound ideograph/phono-semantic character composed of 大 (dà, 'big, wide') over 长/長 (cháng, 'long'), originally denoting something large and long that wraps or slips over an inner object ('outer casing, slipcover, harness'). Attested from the *Yupian* and Tang–Song vernacular, its core image of 'an outer sheath fitting over something' branched along three paths: (1) a matched 'set' or 'suite' of items (measure word/noun), (2) a 'formulaic convention' (客套, 老一套), and (3) a 'noose, snare, or setup/trap' slipped over an unsuspecting target (下套, 圈套).

history.meaning: wide, long outer wrapping or slipcover; to encase
outer case; harness; matched set/suite of books, clothes, or rooms; snare/noose
slipcover; matched set/suite (classifier/noun); formula/routine; trap/setup (as in 下套)

morphemes.meaning: outer cover, sheath; matched set; snare, trap, setup

套.notes: In business and showbiz dramas, 套 frequently means a 'trap, scheme, or setup': 给某人下套 (gěi mǒurén xiàtào, 'to set a trap for someone'), 钻进套里 ('walk right into the trap'), and 套路 (tàolù, 'calculated ploy/gimmick').

rootFamily.gloss: calculated routine, ploy, trope (originally martial arts sequence)
complete set, full package; to form a complete set

女.etymology: One of the oldest primary pictographs in Chinese writing: in Shang dynasty oracle bone script (甲骨文), 女 (Old Chinese *nraʔ) depicts a person kneeling gracefully with hands crossed softly at the front of the body. In Classical Chinese, 女 functioned as the free noun 'woman, maiden, daughter' (and with a falling-tone derivation *nras as the transitive verb 'to give one's daughter in marriage'). In modern Mandarin, standalone 女 primarily serves as a bound root or non-predicative adjective ('female', contrasted with 男 nán 'male').

history.meaning: woman, young unmarried woman, daughter (oracle bone pictograph of a kneeling figure)
woman, female; daughter
female (non-predicative adjective and bound morpheme); daughter (in compounds like 儿女)

女.notes: As an adjective meaning 'female', 女 modifies human nouns directly without 的 (e.g., 女导演 nǚ dǎoyǎn 'female director', 女主角 nǚ zhǔjué 'female lead'); when used as a standalone predicate ('She is female'), you must say 她是女的 (tā shì nǚ de).

女人.etymology: A modifier-head compound formed from 女 (nǚ, 'female') + 人 (rén, 'person, human being'). Already attested in Classical texts such as the *Zuo Zhuan* and *Mozi* to distinguish female persons from 男人 ('male persons'), 女人 became the standard everyday vernacular noun for an adult woman in Early Mandarin. Depending on stress on the second syllable, it distinguishes 'woman' (nǚrén) from older colloquial 'wife' (nǚren, neutral tone).

history.meaning: female person, woman (contrasted with 男人)
adult woman (full tone); wife (neutral-tone colloquialism in northern dialects)

女人.notes: Refers specifically to an adult woman with full feminine maturity (as in 女人味 nǚrénwèi, 'feminine charm/allure'); in formal or polite public contexts, 女性 (nǚxìng, 'females/women') or 女士 (nǚshì, 'Ms./lady') is preferred.

rootFamily.gloss: Ms., lady (polite title and formal noun)

女企业家.etymology: A layered modifier-head compound built from 女 (nǚ, 'female') + 企业家 (qǐyèjiā, Traditional 企業家, 'entrepreneur, industrialist'). Within 企业家, 企 (qǐ, originally 'to stand on tiptoe looking forward in anticipation', from 人 'person' over 止 'foot') + 业 (yè, Traditional 業, 'undertaking, business, enterprise') was coined/popularized in Meiji Japan (企業 kigyō, 'business enterprise') and combined with the specialist suffix 家 (jiā, 'expert, master of a field'). 女企业家 rose to prominence in Mainland Chinese media during the post-1978 economic reforms (改革开放).

history.meaning: entrepreneur, captain of industry (late 19th–early 20th c. Sino-Japanese compound)
female entrepreneur, businesswoman leading a major enterprise

morphemes.meaning: to stand on tiptoe anticipating; to initiate, plan

女企业家.notes: A high-prestige title reserved for founders or top executives of substantial companies (like media moguls or tech founders), not casual small-business owners. Often associated with the popular media label 女强人 (nǚqiángrén, 'career powerhouse woman').

女士.etymology: Compound of 女 ('woman, female') + 士 ('person of character/learning'). First attested in the Shijing (Book of Odes, 厘尔女士 'grant you a noble lady of virtue'), and standardized in modern Chinese as the polite formal title and noun for 'lady, Ms., madam, women (in public address)'.

history.meaning: woman of noble character
lady; Ms.; madam

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 女士 (via 萌典)

女孩.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 女 (nǚ, 'female') + 孩 (hái, 'child', originally 咳/孩 in the *Shuowen Jiezi* meaning 'a baby's giggle or smile', composed of 子 'child' + 亥 phonetic). While Classical Chinese used 孩 for any smiling infant (as in *Mencius* 孩提之童) and 少女 or 女子 for a young girl, vernacular Mandarin paired 女 with 孩 (and its suffixed/erhua forms 女孩子, 女孩儿) to create the standard warm everyday word for a girl or young unmarried woman.

history.meaning: smiling infant, young child (regardless of gender)
female child, girl; young unmarried woman

女孩.notes: In modern Chinese, 女孩 (and colloquial 女孩子 / 女孩儿) is routinely used not just for children, but affectionately for young women well into their twenties and early thirties (contrasting with the more mature 女人).

rootFamily.gloss: girl, young woman (colloquial with nominal suffix)

女性.etymology: A modifier-head compound composed of 女 (nǚ, 'female, woman') + 性 (xìng, 'inborn nature, character; biological sex/gender', from 心/忄 'heart-mind' + 生 'to be born, live', reflecting the ancient philosophical concept 生之謂性 'that which is inborn is called nature'). While 女性 appeared sporadically in Classical commentaries for 'feminine nature', its modern use as the standard formal noun for 'woman / the female sex' was popularized in the late 19th and early 20th centuries via Meiji Japanese 女性 (josei) translating English *female / womanhood*.

history.meaning: inborn feminine nature or disposition (rare philosophical collocation)
woman, female, women as a social/biological group (reinforced by Meiji Japanese 女性 josei)

morphemes.meaning: inborn nature, disposition; biological sex, gender

女性.notes: The most respectful, objective, and formal term for 'women / females' in media, sociology, marketing, and workplace discourse (e.g., 职场女性 'working women', 女性观众 'female audience'), avoiding the colloquial bluntness of 女人.

女朋友.etymology: A modifier-head calque compound formed from 女 (nǚ, 'female') + 朋友 (péngyou, 'friend'). The base compound 朋友 unites two ancient words for companionship: 朋 (péng, originally depicting two strings of cowrie shells hanging together, hence 'fellows studying under the same master') and 友 (yǒu, depicting two right hands 又 working together, hence 'comrade, friend'). In early 20th-century urban China, 女朋友 was coined as a structural calque of English *girlfriend* to express modern romantic courtship.

history.meaning: fellow disciples and comrades; friends (coordinative Classical compound)
girlfriend, female romantic partner (20th-century calque of English 'girlfriend')

morphemes.meaning: fellow, peer, companion (originally two strings of cowries)

女朋友.notes: Unambiguously means 'romantic girlfriend' in Mandarin (often shortened in casual speech to 女友 nǚyǒu). To refer to a platonic female friend without romantic ambiguity, say 女性朋友 (nǚxìng péngyou) or 女生朋友 (nǚshēng péngyou).

奶奶.etymology: Reduplicated kinship noun from 奶 ('breast; milk; nursemaid', woman 女 + phonetic 乃). Following the universal nursery-word pattern of reduplicating a labial/dental nasal syllable, 奶奶 shifted in Song-Yuan northern vernacular from 'wet nurse / lady' to the standard kinship term for paternal grandmother and a respectful address for elderly women.

history.meaning: lady of the house; paternal grandmother
paternal grandmother; grandma

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 奶奶

奶白色.etymology: Three-character descriptive color compound combining 奶 ('milk') + 白色 ('white color'): 'milky white, cream white, off-white'.

history.meaning: milky white; creamy white

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 奶白色 (via 萌典)

奶酪.etymology: Compound noun of 奶 ('milk') + 酪 ('fermented dairy curds/kumis/junket' in Classical and northern pastoral Chinese, 酉 'fermentation' + 各): standardized in modern Mandarin for 'cheese'.

history.meaning: fermented milk curd
cheese

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 奶酪 (via 萌典)

她.etymology: Third-person singular feminine pronoun ('she, her'), written with the woman component 女 beside 也 and pronounced tā identically to 他. Introduced into modern written Mandarin in the late 1910s (popularized by poet and linguist Liu Bannong) to distinguish 'she' visually on the page while preserving spoken tā.

history.meaning: third-person feminine pronoun 'she, her'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 她 (via 萌典)

她们.etymology: A plural personal pronoun formed from 她 (tā, 'she, her') + the human plural suffix 们 (men, Traditional 們, grammaticalized in Song–Yuan vernacular from 懣/門 'clan, group'). The character 她 was famously innovated and championed in the late 1910s by May Fourth linguist and poet Liu Bannong (劉半農, 1891–1934), who replaced the generic person radical 亻 of 他 (tā) with the female radical 女 to translate Western feminine third-person pronouns (*she/her*), while keeping the pronunciation identical to 他 (tā).

history.meaning: they, them (gender-neutral third-person plural in Song–Qing vernacular)
they, them (specifically referring to an all-female group; May Fourth orthographic innovation + plural suffix)

morphemes.meaning: plural marker for pronouns and human nouns (Traditional 們)

她们.notes: Pronounced identically to 他们 (tāmen, 'they [male or mixed]') and 它们 (tāmen, 'they [inanimate/animals]'). In written Chinese, 她们 is used ONLY when every single member of the group is female; if even one male is included, standard grammar requires 他们.

rootFamily.gloss: they, them (male or mixed gender group)

好.etymology: Core adjective 'good, fine, well' (hǎo), combining 女 ('woman') and 子 ('child'). Already among the earliest graphs on Shang oracle bones and ubiquitous in the Classic of Poetry, 好 expresses quality, readiness (修好了 'fixed and ready'), and greetings (你好 'hello').

history.meaning: good; fine; lovely (hǎo); to be fond of (hào)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 好 (via 萌典)

好不好.etymology: An A-not-A (正反问) interrogative construction formed by reduplicating the stative verb/adjective 好 (hǎo, 'good, fine, okay', originally a compound ideograph of 女 'woman' + 子 'child' representing affection and well-being) around the negative adverb 不 (bù, 'not'). Developed in medieval vernacular Chinese as the standard polar question pattern [V + 不 + V], 好不好 functions both as a literal question ('Is it good?') and as a pragmatic discourse tag seeking agreement, coaxing, or softening a request ('Alright? Okay?').

history.meaning: good, fine, pleasing; well-disposed
is it good or not?; alright?, okay?, how about it? (A-not-A polar question & pragmatic tag)

好不好.notes: At the end of a suggestion (我们休息一下，好不好？), it is a warm, cooperative tag ('shall we? / okay?'). However, when spoken with falling intonation after a statement of obvious fact (那只是演戏好不好！), it means 'Come on! / Give me a break!'.

rootFamily.gloss: depends on the situation, hard to say if it's appropriate
just right, happen to, by coincidence

cognates.meaning: with great difficulty, after much trouble
cognates.word: 好唔容易 (hou2 m4 jung4 ji6)

好不容易.etymology: An idiomatic degree-adverbial phrase composed of the intensifying adverb 好 (hǎo, grammaticalized in Tang–Song vernacular from 'good/well' into an emphatic intensifier meaning 'very, quite, so') + 不 (bù, 'not') + 容易 (róngyì, 'easy', a Classical coordinative compound from 容 'to allow, accommodate' + 易 'easy, effortless'). Literally 'very not-easy', it regularly co-occurs with the adverb 才 (cái, 'only then') to emphasize that an outcome was achieved only after immense effort.

history.meaning: easy, effortless; rash or casual (in Han–Tang prose)
with great difficulty, after a hard struggle (vernacular intensifying phrase)

好不容易.notes: A famous quirk of Mandarin syntax: because 不 here is a redundant/expletive negation in emphatic idioms, 好不容易 and 好容易 (hǎo róngyì) mean the EXACT same thing ('with great difficulty!') when followed by 才 (e.g., 好不容易才找到你 'I finally found you after so much trouble').

rootFamily.gloss: with great difficulty (synonymous emphatic variant without 不)

好主意.etymology: A modifier-head noun phrase combining 好 (hǎo, 'good, clever, fine') + 主意 (zhǔyi, 'idea, plan, definite view'). In Classical and medieval Chinese, 主意 (from 主 'master, host, main' + 意 'thought, intention, mind') meant 'the ruling intention or core purpose of a text or sovereign' (e.g., in Han Fei Zi and Song prose); in Ming–Qing vernacular Mandarin, the second syllable neutralized in tone (zhǔyi) and the meaning shifted to 'a practical plan, bright idea, or personal decision'.

history.meaning: governing intention, central thesis, or firm resolve
good idea, clever plan, bright suggestion (with neutral-tone final syllable)

好主意.notes: Be careful with pronunciation and look-alikes: 主意 ('idea/plan') is pronounced zhǔyi (neutral tone on 意), whereas 注意 ('to pay attention to') is pronounced zhùyì (fourth tone on both syllables). 出好主意 (chū hǎo zhǔyi) means 'to come up with a good idea'.

rootFamily.gloss: wicked scheme, bad idea, crooked plan

cognates.word: 好耐冇見 (hou2 noi6 mou5 gin3)

好久不见.etymology: A topic-comment vernacular greeting phrase composed of 好 (hǎo, emphatic degree adverb 'very, quite') + 久 (jiǔ, 'long time') + 不 (bù, 'not') + 见 (jiàn, Traditional 見, 'to see, meet'). Rooted in Tang–Song poetic and epistolary expressions such as 久不相見 ('long have we not seen each other'), 好久不见 crystallized in spoken Mandarin as the universal warm greeting when reuniting with an acquaintance, and was famously calqued into 19th-century Chinese Pidgin English and American English as *long time no see*.

history.meaning: have not seen one another for a long time (literary/epistolary clause)

history.form: 好久不見 / 好久不见 (hǎojiǔ bújiàn)
history.meaning: long time no see! (standard conversational greeting upon reunion)

好久不见.notes: Notice the tone sandhi: before the fourth-tone 见 (jiàn), 不 shifts to the second tone (hǎojiǔ bújiàn). This exact Chinese phrase is the historical source of the English idiom 'Long time no see!' via 19th-century contact English.

rootFamily.gloss: for a very long time, ages
to meet, see face to face
not for long; soon, before long

好事.etymology: A homographic compound with two distinct etymologies depending on the tone of 好: (1) As a modifier-head noun (hǎoshì, third tone on 好), it combines 好 (hǎo, 'good, auspicious') + 事 (shì, 'matter, affair, deed'), meaning 'a good thing, charitable deed (Buddhist punya), or joyous occasion (especially a wedding or romance)'. (2) As a Classical verb-object adjective/verb (hàoshì, fourth tone on 好, attested in *Mencius*), it combines 好 (hào, 'to be fond of') + 事 ('meddling/affairs'), meaning 'meddlesome, nosy, fond of stirring up trouble'.

history.meaning: fond of stirring up affairs; meddlesome or overly curious (*Mencius*)
good deed, Buddhist merit-making service; joyous event or auspicious affair
good thing, stroke of luck; happy event (especially marriage/engagement); ironic 'fine mess'
