好事.notes: Frequently used in three ways in modern dramas: literally ('a good thing/happy event'), euphemistically for romance or marriage (好事将近), and sarcastically when someone causes a disaster: 看你干的好事！(Kàn nǐ gàn de hǎoshì!, 'Look at the fine mess you've made!'). Compare fourth-tone 好事者 (hàoshìzhě, 'busybody/troll').

rootFamily.gloss: joyous occasion, wedding or birth celebration
good things never come easy; the course of true love never did run smooth

cognates.meaning: wedding bells are near, happy news is imminent
cognates.word: 好事將近 (hou2 si6 zoeng1 gan6)

好事将近.etymology: A four-character subject-predicate idiom (成语-style set phrase) composed of 好事 (hǎoshì, 'auspicious event, specifically marriage or betrothal') + 将 (jiāng, Traditional 將, Classical future/inchoative adverb 'about to, on the verge of') + 近 (jìn, 'near, approaching, imminent'). Preserving the Literary Chinese adverbial structure [將 + adjective/verb] ('about to draw near'), it serves in modern vernacular and entertainment journalism as the quintessential idiom for 'wedding bells are right around the corner'.

history.meaning: a joyous/auspicious event (especially a wedding) + is about to draw near (Literary Chinese syntax)
wedding bells are near; happy news (marriage, engagement, or major breakthrough) is imminent

morphemes.meaning: about to, soon, on the verge of (Traditional 將)

好事将近.notes: A staple of entertainment gossip headlines and workplace banter: whenever a celebrity couple is spotted ring-shopping or meeting parents, reporters ask 是不是好事将近了？ ('Are wedding bells right around the corner?').

rootFamily.gloss: about to, on the point of, soon (formal adverb)
approaching, drawing near (of a date or deadline)

好使.etymology: An early vernacular Mandarin compound formed on the evaluative-facilitative pattern 好 (hǎo, 'good; easy or pleasant to do') + 使 (shǐ, 'to use, employ, deploy'). In Classical Chinese, 使 meant 'to dispatch an envoy' or 'to command/employ', which broadened in Tang–Song vernacular into a general verb 'to use (a tool, method, or person)'. Combining facilitative 好 with 使 yielded 'easy to handle, obedient to command', which in northern Mandarin colloquially grammaticalized into 'effective, working well, handy'.

history.meaning: to send on a mission; to command or employ
easy to use; obedient or convenient to employ
effective; working well; handy (of tools, methods, or connections)

morphemes.meaning: to use; to employ; to make work

好使.notes: Primarily northern colloquial Mandarin; often used of gadgets, tricks, methods, or interpersonal leverage (e.g., 这一招真好使 'this move really works'). Synonymous with 好用 in standard registers.

好像.etymology: Compound adverb and verb of 好 ('quite, very', an intensifying adverb) + 像 ('resemble, be like'): 'seem, look like, as if'. Attested from Tang–Song poetry and vernacular.

history.meaning: very much resemble -> seem, look as if

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 好像 (via 萌典)

好几个.etymology: A modifier-quantifier-classifier construction composed of degree-intensifying adverbial 好 (hǎo, bleached from 'good' to an emphatic degree marker 'quite, full, a good many' in Song–Yuan vernacular), theapproximative numeral 几 (jǐ, Traditional 幾, originally 'subtle sign; how many'), and the general classifier 个 (gè, Traditional 個/箇, originally a tally of bamboo stalks). Together they form an emphatic paucal numeral phrase meaning 'a good several; quite a few'.

history.meaning: minute sign; nearly; how many
a good several; quite a few items or people
quite a few; several (emphatic)

好几个.notes: Unlike plain 几个 ('a few', neutral or small), adding 好 highlights that the speaker considers the count surprisingly large ('quite a few!'). Directly precedes nouns (好几个人, 好几个小时).

好几遍.etymology: A numeral-verbal-classifier phrase built from intensifying adverbial 好 (hǎo, 'quite, a good') + approximative numeral 几 (jǐ, Traditional 幾, 'several') + action-measure classifier 遍 (biàn, originally 'to go all around; everywhere' in Classical Chinese, written 徧/遍, which grammaticalized in Medieval Chinese into a verbal measure word for complete cycles of an action from start to finish). Literally 'a good several complete rounds/through-readings'.

history.meaning: all around; ubiquitous; to traverse completely
several complete times through
quite a few times (from start to finish)

morphemes.meaning: verbal classifier for complete occurrences from beginning to end

好几遍.notes: Contrast 遍 with 次 (cì): 好几遍 emphasizes going through the entire process from start to finish (e.g., reading a script, watching an episode, rehearsing a song), whereas 好几次 simply counts occurrences.

rootFamily.gloss: all over; everywhere; one time through

好吃.etymology: Evaluative compound adjective combining 好 ('good to…, pleasant to…', read hǎo) + 吃 ('eat'): 'good to eat -> delicious, tasty'.

history.meaning: good to eat; delicious; tasty

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 好吃 (via 萌典)

好吧.etymology: A discourse-pragmatic phrase combining the affirmative adjective 好 (hǎo, 'good, fine, agreed') with the sentence-final modal particle 吧 (ba, phonetic reduction of 罢/罷 bà, 'to cease, finish; let it be so' in late imperial vernacular). Because 吧 softens an assertion into a tentative suggestion or reluctant concession, 好吧 evolved as a marker of compromise, mild resignation, or concluding agreement ('all right then; okay, I suppose').

history.meaning: to stop, cease, dismiss; final particle of cessation ('let it end there')
all right then; okay (concessive or concluding)

morphemes.meaning: sentence-final modal particle expressing concession, suggestion, or mild reluctance

好吧.notes: Be careful not to confuse 好吧 with 好的: 好的 is brisk, willing compliance ('Sure! Got it!'), whereas 好吧 often carries a sigh of reluctance or concession ('Fine, okay then...') or wraps up a topic.

好听.etymology: Evaluative compound adjective combining 好 ('pleasant to…') + 听 (聽, 'listen to, hear'): 'pleasant to listen to -> nice-sounding, melodious, pleasing to the ear'.

history.meaning: pleasing to the ear; nice-sounding

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 好听 (via 萌典)

好喝.etymology: Evaluative compound adjective combining 好 ('pleasant to…') + 喝 ('drink'): 'good to drink -> tasty, delicious (of beverages or soup)'.

history.meaning: good to drink; delicious (of drinks/soup)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 好喝 (via 萌典)

好嘞.etymology: A colloquial northern Mandarin interjection composed of affirmative 好 (hǎo, 'good, agreed') + the fused energetic sentence-final particle 嘞 (lei, a northern colloquial contraction blending perfection/change-of-state 了 le with the demonstrative/response tone of 哩/呢, reinforced by theatrical and service-trade calls among Beijing peddlers and waiters in the Qing–Republican era). It conveys brisk, cheerful, enthusiastic readiness to comply.

history.meaning: very well! right away! (colloquial response cry)
sure thing!; coming right up!; you got it!

morphemes.meaning: sentence-final interjectional particle signaling upbeat, immediate compliance

好嘞.notes: Pronounced hǎolei (with a lively second or neutral tone on 嘞); ubiquitous in TV production sets, restaurants, and daily northern speech when cheerfully accepting an instruction ('You got it!').

好在.etymology: Modal adverb and verb phrase combining 好 ('what is good/fortunate is…') + 在 ('lie in, consist in'): literally 'the good thing lies in…' -> 'fortunately, luckily, thank goodness that'.

history.meaning: the good thing is that -> fortunately, luckily

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 好在 (via 萌典)

好处.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound combining 好 (hǎo, 'good, advantageous') and 处 (chù, Traditional 處, originally 'to dwell, stop, abide' in Classical Chinese, nominalized in the departing tone chù as 'place, point, aspect, locus'). In Tang–Song vernacular, 处 grammaticalized into an abstract nominalizer for points or qualities (compare 长处 'strong point', 难处 'difficulty'), so 好处 shifted from 'a good place' to 'a good point, merit, benefit, or personal gain'.

history.meaning: a good place or pleasant spot; a strong point or merit
advantage; benefit; illicit sweetener or kickback
benefit; advantage; gain (with neutral tone chù → chu)

好处.notes: In neutral contexts it means 'benefit, advantage' (对身体有好处), but in workplace and showbiz contexts (给点好处, 捞好处) it often implies a tangible perk, kickback, or personal inducement.

好多.etymology: An emphatic degree-adjective compound formed from intensifying adverbial 好 (hǎo, bleached from evaluative 'good' to degree intensifier 'very, quite, so' in Tang–Song vernacular poetry and prose) modifying the quantifier-adjective 多 (duō, 'many, much'). Originally an exclamatory predicate ('how numerous!'), it grammaticalized into a pre-nominal determiner-quantifier meaning 'a lot of, a great many'.

history.meaning: how many! very many; a great deal (also interrogative 'how much?' in some dialects)
so much; a lot of; very many

好多.notes: Colloquial and expressive equivalent of 很多; in Mandarin it can directly modify nouns without de (好多人 'so many people', 好多事 'so many things') or follow a verb comparatively (好多了 'much better').

好奇.etymology: Verb-object compound used as an adjective, combining 好 (here read hào in the fourth tone, the Classical verb meaning 'be fond of, love') + 奇 ('novelty, strange or unfamiliar things'): 'curious, inquisitive'. Attested since Han historical prose (e.g., Sima Qian's Shiji).

history.stage: Han Classical Chinese (Shiji, Hanshu) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: fond of the novel/unusual -> curious, inquisitive

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 好奇 (via 萌典)

好好.etymology: Reduplication of 好 ('good, well', read hǎohǎo or hǎohāor in northern speech): functions as an adverb meaning 'properly, carefully, thoroughly, to one's heart's content' (好好休息 'get a good rest') and as an adjective meaning 'perfectly fine, in good condition'.

history.meaning: properly; carefully; thoroughly; perfectly fine

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 好好 (via 萌典)

好客.etymology: Verb-object adjectival compound of 好 (read in the departing 4th tone *hào*, 'love; be fond of', Old Chinese *qʰˤuʔ-s*) + 客 ('guest; visitor', roof radical 宀 + 各 gè). Attested since the *Records of the Grand Historian* (*Shiji*) to praise hosts who delight in welcoming travellers and neighbours.

history.meaning: delight in welcoming guests and retainers
hospitable; welcoming

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 好客

好日子.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound composed of 好 (hǎo, 'good, auspicious, prosperous') + 日子 (rìzi, 'day; days; livelihood', itself formed from Classical Chinese 日 rì 'sun; day' plus the diminutive/nominalizing suffix 子 zi). In vernacular Mandarin, 日子 developed three layered senses—a specific calendar date, a span of days, and one's daily life or economic livelihood—giving 好日子 both the ritual sense 'auspicious date (for a wedding)' and the existential sense 'happy days, comfortable life'.

history.meaning: day; date; passage of daily life
auspicious calendar day (for marriage/ceremony); prosperous, happy life

好日子.notes: Has two common idioms: 过好日子 ('live a happy/prosperous life') and 挑个好日子 ('pick an auspicious date', e.g., for a wedding or show premiere), plus the ironic threat 没好日子过 ('won't have an easy time of it').

好歹.etymology: An antonymic coordinative compound pairing 好 (hǎo, 'good, fine') and 歹 (dǎi, 'bad, evil, vicious', graphically derived from 夕/歹 'remnant bones, death, misfortune' and popularized in Yuan-dynasty northern vernacular in opposition to 好). By juxtaposing the two poles 'good or bad', the compound evolved from the nominal sense 'good and bad; unforeseen mishap' into a modal adverb meaning 'whether for good or ill; anyhow; at least; no matter what'.

history.meaning: good and bad; right and wrong; unexpected mishap or danger
history.stage: Yuan–Ming Vernacular Mandarin (e.g., Water Margin, Dream of the Red Chamber)

history.meaning: anyhow; regardless; at least (modal adverb)

好歹.notes: As an adverb, 好歹 means 'at the very least / after all' when urging someone to compromise or show respect (好歹吃一口 'at least take a bite'; 他好歹是个导演 'he's a director after all'); as a noun in 不知好歹 it means 'unable to tell good from bad (ungrateful/foolish)'.

rootFamily.gloss: unable to tell good from bad; unappreciative

好玩.etymology: A facilitative-evaluative compound formed from 好 (hǎo, 'good to; pleasant to; enjoyable to') + 玩 (wán, originally 'to finger or admire jade ornaments' in Classical Chinese, from jade radical 王/玉 + 元 yuán, later broadened in Tang–Song vernacular to 'to play, amuse oneself, dally with'). Literally 'pleasant to play with', it lexicalized into a general adjective meaning 'fun, amusing, entertaining, interesting'.

history.meaning: to trifle with or admire jade curios; to dally with
enjoyable to play with; amusing; entertaining

morphemes.meaning: good to; pleasant or enjoyable to
to play; to amuse oneself; to have fun

好玩.notes: In northern Mandarin it often takes erhua as 好玩儿 (hǎowánr). Beyond games or places, media creatives frequently use 好玩 to praise a show concept, plot twist, or person as 'intriguing, fresh, and entertaining'.

rootFamily.gloss: to play; to have fun; to hang out (northern erhua)
to joke; to play a prank; kidding

好球.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound combining 好 (hǎo, 'good, fine, well-played') and 球 (qiú, originally a type of resonant fine jade 璆/球 in Classical Chinese, which shifted in Tang–Song times via 'jade-like sphere' to 'ball' used in polo 击鞠/打球 and kickball 蹴鞠). In modern sports and games, 好球 serves both as a live-action exclamation ('Nice shot! Great ball!') and, in baseball/softball, as the technical translation of a 'strike' (vs. 坏球 'ball').

history.meaning: fine resonant jade; spherical ball for polo or kickball
nice shot!; great play! (also baseball 'strike')

好球.notes: Shouted espontaneously by spectators or players in basketball, billiards, ping-pong, tennis, golf, or soccer immediately after an impressive shot or pass ('Nice shot!').

好的.etymology: A nominalized affirmative phrase formed from 好 (hǎo, 'good, fine, acceptable') + the structural nominalizer/affirmative particle 的 (de, evolved from Tang–Song vernacular 底 dǐ and written 的 from Yuan–Ming times onward). Elliptical for '(that is) a good/acceptable thing' or 'it is fine', 好的 lexicalized as a polite, crisp standalone response affirming agreement, comprehension, or compliance ('alright, okay, will do').

history.meaning: that which is good; of good quality
alright; okay; Roger that (affirmative response)

好的.notes: The go-to polite, professional affirmative in workplace and production teams ('Okay, got it!'). More cooperative and upbeat than 好吧 (which sounds reluctant) and slightly more formal than 好嘞.

好看.etymology: Evaluative compound adjective combining 好 ('pleasant to…') + 看 ('look at, watch'): 'pleasing to the eye -> good-looking, pretty, attractive; interesting (of a book, play, or film)'.

history.meaning: pleasing to look at; pretty; good-looking; interesting

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 好看 (via 萌典)

好笑.etymology: The adjective '好笑' (hǎoxiào, funny, laughable) joins '好' (good, easy, prone to) and '笑' (laugh). In early vernacular literature, the prefix '好-' frequently attached to verbs to indicate that an action was likely to happen or worth doing, such as '好看' (good-looking). '好笑' thus literally meant 'prone to causing laughter'. Over time, it solidified into a standard adjective describing something comical, ridiculous, or amusing. It is distinct from '可笑', which can sometimes carry a more mocking or derisive tone.

history.meaning: laughable

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 好笑

好让.etymology: Purposive conjunction combining modal/purposive 好 ('so as to, so that it is easy to…') + causative verb 让 (讓, 'let, allow'): 'so as to let, in order that'.

history.meaning: so as to let; so that

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 好让 (via 萌典)

好运.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 好 ('good') + 运 (運, 'revolving fortune, luck'): 'good luck, good fortune'.

history.meaning: good luck; good fortune

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 好运 (via 萌典)

好险.etymology: An exclamatory degree-adjective phrase combining the exclamatory degree adverb 好 (hǎo, 'how very! so!') with 险 (xiǎn, Traditional 險, from mound radical 阜/阝 + 僉 qiān, originally 'precipitous defile, steep mountain pass, perilous terrain' in Classical Chinese, later extended to 'dangerous, narrow escape'). Uttered after narrowly averting disaster, 好险 literally exclaims 'How perilous (that just was)!'—hence 'Close call! Phew!'.

history.meaning: precipitous terrain; narrow mountain pass; perilous
how dangerous!; what a narrow escape!; close call!
history.stage: Early Vernacular Mandarin to Modern Mandarin

好险.notes: Used right after dodging a crisis or near-miss (e.g., catching a broadcast error seconds before going live): 好险！(Hǎo xiǎn! 'Phew, that was close!').

如今.etymology: A Classical-to-vernacular temporal compound formed from 如 (rú, originally 'to resemble, be like' or 'to go to, reach' in Classical Chinese, functioning in temporal expressions as 'when it comes to / as for') + 今 (jīn, 'the present time, now'). Originally meaning 'as for the present' or 'compared to now' in early texts, 如今 fused in Han–Tang prose and poetry into a disyllabic temporal noun/adverb meaning 'nowadays, at present, as things stand today'.

history.meaning: as for the present; like the present time
now; nowadays; in these days (often contrasting with the past)

如今.notes: Slightly more reflective or narrative than 现在 (xiànzài); 如今 almost always evokes a contrast between past and present ('back then..., whereas nowadays...'). Very common in commentary and storytelling.

cognates.word: 如何 (いかん / ikan, いかに / ikani)

如何.etymology: A Classical Chinese interrogative verb-object compound of 如 (rú, 'to be like; to deal with') + interrogative pronoun 何 (hé, 'what; how'). In Archaic Chinese, 如…何 (with an object inserted between them, e.g., 如之何 'what can be done about it?') asked how to handle something, while contiguous 如何 meant 'like what? how is it? in what way?'. It survived intact into modern written and elevated spoken Mandarin as a concise synonym for 怎么样.

history.meaning: like what?; what to do about it?; how?
how; in what way; what do you think? (elevated or concise register)

morphemes.meaning: to be like; to deal with

如何.notes: Functions both pre-verbally as a formal equivalent of 怎么 ('how to...', e.g., 如何解决问题) and clause-finally as a brisk equivalent of 怎么样 ('how about it? how did it go?', e.g., 收视率如何？).

rootFamily.gloss: so; like this; to such a degree

如意算盘.etymology: A four-character modifier-head idiom combining 如意 (rúyì, Classical verb-object compound 'to accord with one's wishes', literally 如 'match/follow' + 意 'intent/desire', also the name of an S-shaped auspicious scepter) with 算盘 (suànpán, 'abacus; calculation', from 算 'to reckon with counting rods' + 盘 'tray/frame'). Coined in Ming–Qing vernacular fiction, an 'abacus that only clicks in accordance with one's own desires' is a metaphor for wishful thinking that counts only potential gains while ignoring obstacles or other people's reactions.

history.meaning: according to one's wishes; auspicious S-shaped scepter/back-scratcher
reckoning that assumes everything will go one's way; wishful calculation
history.stage: Ming–Qing Vernacular Mandarin (e.g., Guanchang Xianxing Ji)

history.meaning: wishful thinking; smug, one-sided scheme or calculation

如意算盘.notes: Typically collocated with the verb 打 (dǎ, 'to work an abacus'): 打如意算盘 ('to make wishful calculations / hatch a smug scheme'), often followed by 落空 ('fall through') when reality ruins the plan.

rootFamily.gloss: as one wishes; auspicious scepter;称心如意

如果.etymology: Conditional conjunction combining two Classical conditional markers: 如 ('if, suppose') + 果 ('if indeed, really, as expected'): 'if, in case, supposing that'. Attested from Tang–Song poetry and prose.

history.meaning: if indeed -> if, in case

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 如果 (via 萌典)

cognates.word: 如此 (かくのごとし / kaku no gotoshi, にょぜ / nyoze)

如此.etymology: A Classical Chinese verb-object demonstrative compound composed of 如 (rú, 'to resemble, be like') + 此 (cǐ, proximal demonstrative pronoun 'this'). Meaning 'to be like this; in this manner; to such an extent' throughout Classical and Literary Chinese, it remains active in modern Mandarin as a concise, slightly elevated demonstrative pronoun and degree adverb equivalent to 这样 or 这么.

history.meaning: to be like this; thus; to such a degree
so; like this; to such a degree (literary and formal-conversational)

如此.notes: Very common in fixed four-character frames and conversational set phrases: 原来如此 ('so that's how it is!'), 不仅如此 ('not only that'), 既然如此 ('since that is the case'), and before adjectives for emphasis (如此重要 'so very important').

rootFamily.gloss: so that's how it is!; I see!

妈.etymology: A phono-semantic character formed from the female radical 女 (nǚ, 'woman') and the phonetic component 马 (mǎ, Traditional 馬, Middle Chinese *mæX), first recorded in the 3rd-century dictionary *Guangya* (广雅: 妈，母也 'mā means mother'). Ultimately rooted in universal bilabial nursery vocalizations (*ma-ma*) cross-linguistically associated with nursing infants, standardized in Chinese with a level first tone (mā) as the everyday kinship root for 'mother, mum' and elder maternal figures.

history.meaning: mother (colloquial kinship term); mare
mum; mother; middle-aged or older female relative/servant title

morphemes.meaning: mother; mum; senior female kinship root

妈.notes: In direct address or casual speech, monosyllabic 妈 ('Mum') feels slightly more grown-up, intimate, or brisk than reduplicated 妈妈 ('Mommy/Mum'), and also forms titles like 大妈 ('auntie') or 姑妈 ('paternal aunt').

妈呀.etymology: An exclamatory kinship vocative composed of 妈 (mā, 'mother, mum') + the emphatic exclamation particle 呀 (ya, a phonological variant of 啊 a conditioned by preceding open vowels). Calling out to one's mother in moments of sudden fright, shock, exhaustion, or amusement is an old vernacular reflex (often expanded as 我的妈呀 'oh my mother!'), functioning identically to English 'Mamma mia!' or 'Oh my goodness!'.

history.form: 阿媽 / 娘呀 / 媽呀
history.meaning: cry to one's mother in shock or distress; oh my goodness!
oh my goodness!; good grief!; boy oh boy!

morphemes.meaning: sentence-final exclamatory particle (phonetic variant of 啊)

妈呀.notes: Extremely frequent in informal speech and variety shows (often as 哎呀妈呀 or 我的妈呀) to express surprise, relief, comedic overwhelm, or awe without any religious connotation.

rootFamily.gloss: goodness gracious!; oh my! (variant with 娘 'mother')

妈妈.etymology: Intimate reduplication of 妈 (woman classifier 女 + phonetic 马 mǎ), part of the near-universal bilabial nasal nursery pattern for 'mother' while anchored in Chinese script since the Guangyun dictionary (Middle Chinese).

history.meaning: mother
mother; mum

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 妈妈 (via 萌典)

妙.etymology: Ideographic/phono-semantic character combining 女 ('woman/maiden') + 少 ('young/subtle', also written 玅 with 玄 'mysterious'): in Classical Chinese (Laozi's 众妙之门) 'subtle, mysterious, wondrous', and in everyday Mandarin 'wonderful, clever, ingenious, fine'.

history.meaning: subtle; wondrous; youthful beauty
wonderful; clever; ingenious

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 妙 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: person who sets a bad precedent; originator of an evil practice

始作俑者.etymology: A Classical Chinese four-character idiom (成语) from *Mencius* (孟子·梁惠王上), where Confucius says: 「始作俑者，其无后乎！」 ('Was he who first made tomb figurines not destined to have no posterity?'). Structurally a nominalized verb phrase: 始 (shǐ, 'first, initially') + 作 (zuò, 'to make, craft') + 俑 (yǒng, 'wooden or clay human effigies buried with the dead') + 者 (zhě, agentive nominalizer 'the one who'). Confucius condemned inventing human-like burial figurines because it led to burying live people; hence the phrase came to mean 'the originator of a pernicious practice; the chief instigator or culprit'.

history.meaning: the person who first crafted human-shaped burial figurines (condemned by Confucius)
originator of a wicked custom or bad precedent; chief instigator or culprit behind a mess

morphemes.meaning: to make; to create; to initiate
wooden or terracotta funerary figurine buried with the dead

始作俑者.notes: Strictly derogatory or playfully accusatory: never use 始作俑者 to praise a pioneer or innovator (use 开创者 or 创始人 instead); in media/drama contexts it points to the mastermind who started a rumor, crisis, or scandal.

cognates.meaning: from beginning to end; always; constantly

始终.etymology: An antonymic coordinative compound from Classical Chinese pairing 始 (shǐ, 'beginning, inception', from 女 + 台) and 终 (zhōng, Traditional 終, 'end, completion', originally the knotted end of a silk thread from 糸 + 冬). In Pre-Qin texts (*Book of Documents*, *Analects*), 始终 functioned as a noun meaning 'the beginning and the end; the whole course of an affair', which subsequently grammaticalized into a temporal adverb meaning 'from start to finish; throughout; all along'.

history.meaning: beginning and end; the entirety of a process from inception to completion
from beginning to end; throughout; all along (adverb)

始终.notes: As an adverb, 始终 emphasizes unwavering consistency across an entire span of time (他始终没有放弃 'he never gave up from start to finish'), whereas 一直 focuses on continuous linear duration.

rootFamily.gloss: finally; in the end; at last

姐.etymology: A phono-semantic character composed of the female radical 女 (nǚ, 'woman') and the phonetic 且 (qiě / jiě, Old Chinese *tsjaːʔ). Recorded in the Han-dynasty *Shuowen Jiezi* (说文解字) as the Sichuanese (蜀) dialect word for 'mother' (蜀谓母曰姐), during the Northern and Southern Dynasties and Tang era 姐 shifted across northern and central vernaculars to replace Classical 姊 (zǐ) as the standard kinship term for 'older sister' and a respectful or familiar title for slightly older women.

history.meaning: mother (regional Shu/Sichuan word); elder female relative
older sister (supplanting Classical 姊); respectful term for young women
older sister; respectful/affectionate title ('Sis') for a female senior or peer

morphemes.meaning: older sister; senior female peer title

姐.notes: In Chinese workplaces and the entertainment industry (娱乐圈), attaching 姐 after a surname or given name (e.g., 王姐, 心遥姐) or calling a senior female colleague 姐 is the standard warm yet respectful way to address any woman with more seniority or experience.

rootFamily.gloss: young lady; Miss; eldest daughter in a traditional household

姐俩.etymology: A northern Mandarin collective kinship compound combining 姐 (jiě, elliptical here for 姐妹 jiěmèi 'older and younger sisters' or close female friends) with the fused numeral-classifier 俩 (liǎ, a phonological fusion in northern Mandarin of 两 liǎng 'two' + 个 gè 'individual classifier'). Parallel to 哥俩 ('two brothers/buddies') and 爷俩 ('father and child'), 姐俩 means 'the two sisters' or 'the two of us/them (female friends)'.

history.meaning: the two sisters; two close female companions
two sisters; a pair of close female friends or colleagues

morphemes.meaning: sister(s) (short for 姐妹 'older and younger sisters')
both; two of (fused form of 两个 'two + classifier')

姐俩.notes: Because 俩 already incorporates the classifier 个 (俩 = 两个), never add 个 or another classifier after it (*姐俩个 is ungrammatical). Frequently pronounced with erhua in Beijing/northern speech as 姐儿俩 (jiěrliǎ).

rootFamily.gloss: two brothers; two close male buddies
we two; the two of us

姐姐.etymology: A morphological reduplication of the kinship root 姐 (jiě, 'older sister', originally a regional Han-era word for 'mother' that displaced Classical Chinese 姊 zǐ during the Tang–Song period). Reduplicating monosyllabic kinship stems with a neutral tone on the second syllable (姐姐 jiějie, 妹妹 mèimei, 哥哥 gēge) became the canonical disyllabic kinship template in northern vernacular Mandarin from the Song–Yuan period onward.

history.meaning: older sister (transition from Classical 姊 to vernacular 姐)
older sister; polite address for a young woman slightly older than the speaker

姐姐.notes: Besides a biological older sister or female cousin, 姐姐 has become a trendy pop-culture term in modern Chinese variety shows (popularized by *Sisters Who Make Waves* 乘风破浪的姐姐) for confident, accomplished women in their 30s and beyond.

rootFamily.gloss: older and younger sisters; close female friends

姑姑.etymology: Affectionate kinship reduplication of 姑 (woman classifier 女 + phonetic 古 gǔ), attested since the Erya and Book of Odes specifically for one's father's sister—reflecting Chinese kinship's precise distinction between paternal (姑姑) and maternal (姨妈/阿姨) aunts.

history.meaning: father's sister; husband's mother
paternal aunt

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 姑姑 (via 萌典)

姑娘.etymology: Compound noun combining 姑 ('father's sister; young unmarried woman') + 娘 ('mother; young woman', neutral tone niang in this word): 'unmarried young woman, girl; daughter; (historically) paternal aunt'.

history.meaning: young woman; girl; daughter

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 姑娘 (via 萌典)

姓.etymology: Ancient ideogram/phono-semantic character attested on Shang oracle bones combining 女 ('woman') + 生 ('be born, give birth'): originally denoted a matriarchal clan lineage name shared by those born of the same ancestral mother (such as the ancient 姬, 姜, 嬴, 姒 clan names containing 女), now the general noun and verb for 'family name, surname; be surnamed'.

history.meaning: born of the same clan mother = ancestral clan surname
surname; family name; be surnamed

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 姓 (via 萌典)

委屈.etymology: A synonymous coordinative compound uniting 委 (wěi, originally 'to bend, droop, curve, entrust' from 禾 'grain bending' + 女) and 屈 (qū, 'to bend, crook, bow down; to suffer injustice', from 尸 + 出). In Classical and Han texts (*Xunzi*, *Hanshu*), 委屈 meant literally 'winding, sinuous, crooked (of paths or posture)', which evolved metaphorically in Tang–Song vernacular into 'bent under unfair pressure'—hence 'feeling wronged, aggrieved, shortchanged, or put in an unfairly subordinate position'.

history.meaning: bending and winding; sinuous; yielding or accommodating
to suffer unfair treatment; to feel wronged or aggrieved; to put someone out

morphemes.meaning: to bend; to droop; to yield under pressure
to bend; to crook; to suffer wrong or injustice

委屈.notes: Works as an adjective ('aggrieved, feeling wronged', 觉得很委屈), a noun ('grievance', 受委屈), and a causative verb ('to shortchange or put someone in a beneath-their-worth spot', 委屈你了 'sorry to put you through this / underutilize you'). Pronounced wěiqu with a neutral second syllable.

rootFamily.gloss: to entrust; to commission; to delegate

威胁.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative/means-action compound pairing 威 (wēi, 'awe-inspiring power, might, dominance, intimidation') and 胁 (xié, Traditional 脅/脇, originally 'the ribs, flank, underarm' from meat radical 月/肉 + 劦 'combined strength', extended verbally to 'to press against someone's ribs; to coerce, flank, or force by intimidation'). Attested in historical chronicles (*Book of Later Han*, *Book of Jin*), 威胁 literally means 'to coerce by awe and flank-pressure', hence 'to threaten, menace, or intimidate; a threat'.

history.meaning: to coerce by awe-inspiring force and physical pressure; to intimidate into submission
history.stage: Han to Six Dynasties Literary Chinese (Hou Hanshu, Jinshu)

history.meaning: to threaten; to menace; a threat (both interpersonal coercion and abstract danger)

morphemes.meaning: ribs/flank; to press against the side; to coerce or force

威胁.notes: Functions equally well as a transitive verb (拿合同威胁我 'threaten me with the contract') and as a countable noun (构成威胁 'pose a threat', 受到威胁 'come under threat').

rootFamily.gloss: to coerce; to force against one's will; to take hostage

娱乐.etymology: A Classical Chinese synonymous coordinative compound combining 娱 (yú, 'to amuse, delight, give pleasure', from 女 + 吴 wú) and 乐 (lè, Traditional 樂, 'joy, delight, pleasure; to rejoice'). Already attested in Han–Six Dynasties literature (e.g., Yang Yun's *Letter to Sun Huizong* 报孙会宗书 and Cao Zhi's prose) in the verbal sense 'to amuse oneself, rejoice together', 娱乐 (Japanese 娯楽 *goraku*) was revitalized in the Meiji–Republican era as the standard modern Sino-Japanese and Mandarin noun/verb for public 'recreation, amusement, and commercial entertainment'.

history.meaning: to delight and rejoice; to amuse oneself or guests
history.stage: Han to Six Dynasties Literary Chinese

history.meaning: recreation; pastime; public amusement (modernized via Meiji Japanese usage)
history.stage: Late 19th–Early 20th Century Sino-Japanese & Early Modern Mandarin

history.meaning: entertainment; showbiz; recreation; to entertain

morphemes.meaning: joy; happiness; to take pleasure in

娱乐.notes: Note the pronunciation of 乐 here is lè ('joy/pleasure', yúlè), not yuè ('music', yīnyuè). Forms the core root of modern media and showbiz terminology (娱乐节目 'variety/entertainment show', 娱乐新闻 'entertainment news').

娱乐圈.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound combining 娱乐 (yúlè, 'entertainment, amusement') with 圈 (quān, originally 'curved bamboo/wooden enclosure or pen' in Classical Chinese, written 棬/圈, which evolved via 'circle, ring' into the modern sociological metaphor 'professional or social circle, sphere, industry ecosystem'). Popularized in late-20th-century Hong Kong, Taiwan, and Mainland Chinese media discourse, 娱乐圈 literally denotes 'the entertainment circle'—i.e., show business.

history.meaning: enclosure; circular ring; bounded sphere or coterie
the entertainment circle; show business; celebrity and media industry

morphemes.meaning: circle; sphere; professional or social community

娱乐圈.notes: In industry slang, 娱乐圈 is often abbreviated simply to 圈里 or 圈内 ('inside the industry/circle', vs. 圈外人 'non-celebrity / industry outsider'), and entering or leaving showbiz is called 进圈 / 退圈.

娱乐精神.etymology: A modern four-character modifier-head nominal compound joining 娱乐 (yúlè, 'entertainment, amusement') with 精神 (jīngshén, originally Daoist/Classical Chinese 'refined vital essence 精 and numinous spirit 神' in *Zhuangzi* and *Huainanzi*, later borrowed via Meiji Japanese 精神 *seishin* to translate Western 'spirit, ethos, mindset'). Coined in contemporary Chinese media and pop culture, 娱乐精神 means 'the spirit of entertainment'—specifically a good-humored, sporting willingness in showbiz to poke fun at oneself, play along with gags, and keep things light for the audience's enjoyment.

history.meaning: vital essence and numinous spirit (*Zhuangzi*); later 'spirit, ethos, mentality'
history.stage: Classical Chinese to Modern Sino-Japanese Return Loan

history.meaning: spirit of entertainment; good-natured willingness to be a good sport and self-deprecate in media/showbiz

娱乐精神.notes: In Chinese TV production and variety shows, praising a celebrity or guest for having 娱乐精神 means they aren't a diva—they can take a joke, embrace self-deprecation (自黑), and play along to make good television.

娱记.etymology: A modern disyllabic syllabic-abbreviation compound (缩略词) contracted from the four-character phrase 娱乐记者 (yúlè jìzhě, 'entertainment journalist/reporter') by extracting the first morpheme of each constituent word: 娱 (yú, from 娱乐 'entertainment') + 记 (jì, from 记者 'reporter/journalist', originally a Meiji Japanese kanji coinage 記者 *kisha* from 記 'to record/chronicle' + agentive 者 'one who'). This 1+1 clipping pattern is a highly productive morphological mechanism in modern Chinese media vocabulary.

history.meaning: reporter; journalist (literally 'one who records events')
history.stage: Late 19th-Century Sino-Japanese Coinage to Modern Mandarin

history.meaning: entertainment reporter; showbiz/celebrity beat journalist (clipped compound)

娱记.notes: Neutral-to-colloquial industry shorthand for celebrity-beat and showbiz reporters; unlike 狗仔 (gǒuzǎi, 'paparazzi', which implies covert stalking), 娱记 covers accredited entertainment press at red carpets, press conferences, and studio interviews as well as gossip reporters.

婚姻.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative compound of 婚 (hūn, 'to take a wife; bride's family', originally written 昏 'dusk' because ancient betrothal and wedding rites were conducted at twilight, later augmented with the semantic radical 女 'woman') and 姻 (yīn, 'groom's family; marriage connection', phono-semantic compound with 女 and phonetic 因 yīn 'to rely on, follow', as the bride follows the groom). Attested in the Er Ya (爾雅·釋親), where the bride's father is called 婚 and the groom's father is called 姻; together they came to denote the institution of marriage itself.

history.meaning: affinal kin; the families of the bride and groom joined by dusk wedding rites
history.stage: Old Chinese (Classic of Poetry / Book of Rites)

history.meaning: matrimonial alliance between two clans; marriage
marriage as a legal and social institution or personal marital state

morphemes.meaning: to wed a wife; bride's side of a marriage (originally 'dusk ceremony')
marriage connection; groom's side of a marriage

婚姻.notes: Refers to the state or institution of marriage (e.g., 婚姻状况 'marital status', 步入婚姻 'enter into marriage'), whereas 结婚 (jiéhūn) is the verb/event of getting married and 婚礼 (hūnlǐ) is the wedding ceremony.

媒体.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-compound composed of 媒 (méi, 'matchmaker, go-between, intermediary', from 女 'woman' and phonetic 某 mǒu) and 体 (tǐ, traditional 體, 'body, substance, form, carrier'). Originally coined in the modern Sino-Japanese lexicon (Japanese 媒体 baitai) and twentieth-century Chinese scientific prose to translate English 'medium' (a physical or communicative substance through which something is transmitted), it later became the standard translation for mass 'media' (broadcasting, press, and digital platforms).

history.meaning: matchmaker or intermediary (媒) and physical body or vessel (體) as separate classical morphemes
physical or communicative medium of transmission (calquing English 'medium')
mass media, news organizations, and digital communication platforms

媒体.notes: Used both for 'the media' as press/news outlets (e.g., 主流媒体 'mainstream media', 新媒体 'new media', 自媒体 'self-media/independent creators') and in technical contexts for transmission media (多媒体 'multimedia').

媒体人.etymology: A contemporary Mandarin modifier-head compound combining 媒体 (méitǐ, 'mass media') with the agentive suffixal noun 人 (rén, 'person, professional'). Modelled on productive late-20th-century occupational formations with -人 (such as 制作人 'producer', 经纪人 'agent', 音乐人 'musician'), it emerged in the television, journalism, and entertainment industries to designate anyone whose vocation and public identity revolve around producing, editing, or broadcasting media content.

history.meaning: newspaper professional or journalist (precursor occupational formations with -人)
media professional, broadcaster, journalist, or content producer across print, TV, and digital platforms

媒体人.notes: In *Behind the Scenes* (*幕后之王*) and Chinese industry discourse, 媒体人 carries a sense of professional calling and public responsibility (e.g., 资深媒体人 'senior media professional'), broader and more prestigious than 记者 ('reporter').

媒体席.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound formed from 媒体 (méitǐ, 'media, press') and 席 (xí, 'woven mat; seat, seating area, place at an assembly'). In Classical Chinese, 席 denoted a woven reed mat on which people sat on the floor before chairs became widespread in China during the Tang–Song transition; by extension it came to mean a designated seat or section at banquets, courts, or auditoriums, yielding modern compounds like 媒体席 for the press gallery or media seating section at live broadcasts and press conferences.

history.meaning: woven floor mat for sitting; seat of honor at a banquet or court
press seating area or media gallery at live shows, press conferences, and competitions

媒体席.notes: In Chinese variety shows and singing competitions, the 媒体席 is often not merely passive seating for journalists but an active voting panel of media representatives alongside the 评委席 ('judges' panel') and 观众席 ('audience seating').

rootFamily.gloss: to attend, be present at a meeting/event

cognates.meaning: bride, daughter-in-law; to marry (of a woman)
to marry off (a daughter), transfer blame

嫁.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形聲字) attested from the Warring States and Han periods, composed of the semantic radical 女 (nǚ, 'woman') and the phonetic-semantic component 家 (jiā, Old Chinese *kˤra, 'household, family'). Literally signifying a woman's relocation into a new household (家), it originally denoted a woman marrying into her husband's family (as opposed to 娶 qǔ, a man taking a wife into his household), and by figurative extension 'to shift or transfer onto another' (as in 转嫁 zhuǎnjià).

history.meaning: (of a woman) to leave her natal clan and marry into a husband's household; (of parents) to give a daughter in marriage
to marry (of a woman); to shift or impute (blame, cost) onto someone else

morphemes.meaning: to marry (of a woman entering a household); to marry off; to transfer

嫁.notes: Traditionally directional: 嫁 is used when a woman is the subject ('to marry [a man]', or transitive 嫁女儿 'marry off a daughter'), whereas 娶 (qǔ) is used when a man takes a wife. In modern progressive usage, 结婚 (jiéhūn) is gender-neutral.

rootFamily.gloss: to shift, transfer (crisis, blame, cost) onto others

嫁给.etymology: A verb-complement compound combining the verb 嫁 (jià, 'for a woman to marry') with the dative/recipient prepositional complement 给 (gěi, 'to, for; to give'). In Classical Chinese, the recipient husband or family of 嫁 was introduced either directly as an object or via the preposition 於/于 (yú, as in 嫁於某人); in early modern and contemporary Mandarin, 给 grammaticalized from a verb meaning 'to supply/give' into the standard recipient marker attached directly to verbs of transfer (comparable to 送给, 交给).

history.meaning: to be married to (a husband or clan) (classical verb + locative/dative preposition)
to marry (a husband or partner; figuratively, to dedicate one's life to a career)

嫁给.notes: Requires a grammatical object directly after 给 (e.g., 她嫁给了他 'She married him'). Often used figuratively in workplace dramas for workaholics: 嫁给工作 ('married to one's job') or 嫁给舞台 ('married to the stage').

rootFamily.gloss: to marry into a wealthy/elite family

嫌.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形聲字) formed with the semantic radical 女 (nǚ, 'woman', often used in early graphs for emotional attitudes and interpersonal tensions) and the phonetic component 兼 (jiān, Old Chinese *kˤem, 'to hold two things together simultaneously'). In the Shuowen Jiezi (說文解字), 嫌 is glossed as 不平於心也 ('unease or dissatisfaction in the mind') and 一曰疑也 ('suspicion, doubt'). Being of two minds (兼) breeds both suspicion ('suspect') and critical dissatisfaction ('to dislike, find fault with').

history.meaning: mental doubt, suspicion of impropriety; to harbor resentment or unease
history.stage: Old Chinese (Book of Rites / Shuowen Jiezi)

history.meaning: suspicion, ill-will; to dislike, find fault with, or consider inadequate/excessive
to dislike, complain about, or find something too [adjective] (e.g., 嫌贵 'find it too expensive')

morphemes.meaning: to dislike, find fault with; suspicion, ill-will

嫌.notes: As a standalone verb in spoken Mandarin, 嫌 is frequently followed by a noun + adjective/clause to mean 'find X too Y / complain that X is Y' (e.g., 嫌他啰嗦 'find him too naggy', 不嫌麻烦 'not mind the trouble').

rootFamily.gloss: to disdain, look down on, shun
suspicion (of a crime or conflict of interest)
to avoid arousing suspicion (of conflict of interest)

嫌弃.etymology: A coordinative/resultative verbal compound joining 嫌 (xián, 'to dislike, find fault with, disdain') and 弃 (qì, traditional 棄, 'to cast aside, abandon, reject', originally depicting a newborn child 𠫓 being thrown away with a winnowing basket 箕 by two hands 廾). Attested in vernacular fiction from the Ming and Qing dynasties (such as Dream of the Red Chamber 紅樓夢), it combines the inner attitude of finding something beneath one's standards (嫌) with the outward act of shunning or rejecting it (弃).

history.meaning: to spurn, disdain, and cast aside someone or something as inferior or undesirable
to look down on, turn up one's nose at, mind, or express playful disgust toward

morphemes.meaning: to dislike, find fault with, consider inferior

嫌弃.notes: Ranges from polite self-deprecation (如果您不嫌弃 'if you don't mind my humble offering') to colloquial banter (一脸嫌弃 'a look of utter disdain/disgust' on someone's face).

cognates.meaning: suspect (usually 容疑者 yōgisha, with 嫌疑 kengi for suspicion)

嫌疑人.etymology: A modifier-head compound built from the Classical Chinese coordinative noun 嫌疑 (xiányí, 'suspicion, doubt', combining 嫌 'mental unease, suspicion' and 疑 'to doubt, suspect', attested as a binome in the Book of Rites 禮記·坊記 and Records of the Grand Historian 史記) plus the human head noun 人 (rén, 'person'). In modern Chinese criminal procedure law (especially following the 1996 revision of the Criminal Procedure Law of the PRC), 犯罪嫌疑人 (shortened to 嫌疑人) officially replaced 加上人犯 ('offender') to uphold the presumption of innocence prior to conviction.

history.meaning: suspicion of impropriety, doubt, or ambiguity between right and wrong
suspected offender or criminal suspect
suspect (neutral legal and journalistic designation for a person under suspicion)

嫌疑人.notes: 嫌疑人 is the standard formal/journalistic and legal term (often in full as 犯罪嫌疑人), whereas 嫌犯 (xiánfàn) is a brisker headline abbreviation used in news broadcasts.

嫩.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 女 ('delicate') + 敕 (shù/nèn): 'tender, soft, delicate (of young shoots, meat, or skin); inexperienced; light/pale (of colors)'.

history.stage: Classical & Medieval Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: tender; delicate; soft; young

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 嫩 (via 萌典)

子.etymology: Originally an oracle-bone pictograph of a swaddled infant with outstretched arms ('child; son; seed; small round thing', full tone zǐ). In medieval and modern northern Mandarin, unstressed neutral-tone -zi (子) grammaticalized from a diminutive suffix into a productive nominal marker attached to everyday count nouns (桌子 'table', 椅子 'chair', 盘子 'plate').

history.meaning: child; master; small object
diminutive and general noun suffix
neutral-tone nominal suffix

孔.etymology: Combines 子 ('child') + 乙 (depicting a swallow or curved opening; in early bronze inscriptions, an aperture or cavity, Middle Chinese *khungX*). From antiquity it has meant a small, neat hole or opening, such as a keyhole (钥匙孔) or screw hole (螺丝孔).

history.meaning: aperture; small hole; thorough
hole; small opening

字.etymology: Ancient ideogram attested on bronze vessels showing a child (子) under a house roof (宀): originally 'give birth to, rear and nurture a child' (and 'a woman's betrothal', 待字闺中). Because characters proliferated by compounding radicals and phonetics like offspring, since the Qin dynasty 字 has meant 'written Chinese character, word, script, handwriting' (as well as an adult courtesy name).

history.meaning: child under a roof = bear/rear offspring; adult courtesy name
written character; word; script

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 字 (via 萌典)

字母.etymology: Compound noun of 字 ('written word/character') + 母 ('mother, generative root'). Originally coined by Tang–Song Chinese phonologists (after Buddhist Sanskrit models) for the 36 initial consonant exemplars (三十六字母) from which syllables were generated, and adopted in modern Mandarin for an 'alphabetic letter, alphabet'.

history.meaning: consonant-initial mother characters
letter of an alphabet; alphabet

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 字母 (via 萌典)

字迹.etymology: Compound noun of 字 ('written characters') + 迹 (跡, 'footprints, traces, marks'): 'handwriting, written characters/script left on a surface'.

history.meaning: handwriting; written traces

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 字迹 (via 萌典)

存在.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative compound composed of 存 (cún, 'to survive, remain, preserve, be alive') and 在 (zài, 'to be present at, abide, live'). Attested in classical texts such as the Mencius and Xunzi in the sense of remaining alive or intact, the binome was repurposed in Meiji-era Japan (存在 sonzai) to translate Western philosophical concepts of 'existence' and 'Dasein/being' (Latin existentia), and subsequently re-entered modern Mandarin as both a verb ('to exist, be present') and an abstract noun ('existence').

history.meaning: to remain alive, survive, or be preserved intact
philosophical and ontological existence; to exist objectively
to exist, be present (often followed by an issue/risk); existence or presence

存在.notes: Functions both intransitively (这个问题一直存在 'this problem has always existed') and transitively with an indefinite post-verbal object introducing an issue (节目方案还存在一些漏洞 'the show proposal still has some loopholes'). Also popular in slang: 刷存在感 ('fish for attention / assert one's presence').

孙子.etymology: Kinship noun formed from 孙 (孫, combining 子 'child' + 系 'thread of descent/continuation': 'child's child, descendant') + nominal suffix 子 (neutral tone zi): 'grandson (specifically son's son)' (contrast классический 孫子 Sūnzǐ with full third tone on 子, 'Master Sun', author of The Art of War).

history.meaning: child's son; descendant
grandson

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 孙子 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: season, quarter of a year; youngest sibling

季.etymology: An ancient ideogrammic compound (會意字) attested on Shang oracle bone and Zhou bronze inscriptions, combining 禾 (hé, 'ripe grain stalk') and 子 (zǐ, 'child, young offspring'). Originally denoting 'young grain' and hence the youngest of brothers in the Zhou birth-order system—伯 (bó, eldest), 仲 (zhòng, second), 叔 (shū, third), 季 (jì, youngest)—it came to designate the final month of each three-month division of the year (季春, 季夏, 季秋, 季冬) and then a 'three-month quarter' or 'season' as a whole. In 21st-century Chinese television and streaming, 季 was adopted as a semantic calque of English television 'season' (e.g., 第一季 'Season 1').

history.meaning: youngest sibling in birth order; the last month of a three-month season
season of the year; three-month fiscal or calendar quarter
production/broadcast season of a television series or variety show (calquing English 'season')

morphemes.meaning: season (of the year or of a broadcast series); quarter; youngest in sequence

季.notes: In Chinese TV production (*幕后之王*), 季 refers to a full multi-episode run ('season', e.g., 第一季 'Season 1', 季播节目 'seasonal show'), whereas 期 (qī) is a single installment/episode of a variety show and 集 (jí) is an episode of a scripted drama.

rootFamily.gloss: third place / bronze medalist (from the birth-order sequence 伯仲叔季)

孤岛.etymology: A Classical Chinese modifier-head nominal compound uniting 孤 (gū, originally 'fatherless child, orphan', composed of 子 'child' and phonetic 瓜 guā, extended to mean 'solitary, isolated, standing alone') and 岛 (dǎo, traditional 島, 'island', an ideophonetic compound of 山 'mountain' rising from the waters where birds 鳥 roost). Used literally in Tang and Song poetry for a lone island in vast waters, it acquired powerful metaphorical senses in modern Chinese (notably the 'Isolated Island Period' 孤岛时期 of Shanghai between 1937 and 1941, and psychological or informational isolation).

history.meaning: a solitary island standing alone in the sea or river
an isolated enclave cut off from its surroundings (e.g., wartime Shanghai 1937–1941)
isolated island; metaphor for emotional alienation or an information silo (信息孤岛)

morphemes.meaning: island (mountain in water where birds perch)

孤岛.notes: Frequently used metaphorically in media, tech, and psychology: 信息孤岛 ('information silo / data island'), 社交孤岛 ('social island'), or quoting John Donne's 'No man is an island' (没有人是一座孤岛).

孤岛式.etymology: A contemporary Mandarin adjectival derivative formed by attaching the productive attributive suffix -式 (shì, 'style, pattern, mode, -esque', originally meaning 'ritual model, rule, chariot crossbar' in Classical Chinese) to the compound noun 孤岛 (gūdǎo, 'isolated island'). It functions as a non-predicative modifier (区别词) describing systems, lifestyles, or creative workflows that operate in self-contained isolation without communication or integration with the outside world.

history.meaning: 'isolated island' + 'model, pattern, style' as separate lexical items
isolated-island-style, siloed, self-enclosed, or cut off from external collaboration

孤岛式.notes: Used as an attributive modifier before nouns (often with 的): e.g., 孤岛式的生活 ('an insular, cut-off lifestyle') or 孤岛式研发 ('siloed R&D / closed-door production').

学.etymology: One of the foundational verbs of Chinese civilization, traditionally written 學 (simplified to 学 from its cursive form). In Shang oracle bone and Zhou bronze inscriptions (𢻻/斆), the graph depicts two hands (𦥑) manipulating counting rods or structural crossbeams (爻 yáo, 'interlocking tally sticks / hexagram lines') above a roof/building (冖) housing a child (子), representing the initiation and instruction of youth under a roof. Reconstructed in Old Chinese as *m-kˤruk ('to learn, imitate')—morphologically paired with the causative *s-kˤruk > *kˤraw-s (斆/教 jiào, 'to cause to learn, teach')—it denotes acquiring skill or knowledge through emulation and instruction.

history.meaning: to become aware through imitation and instruction; to study ritual, texts, and arts under a master
to study, learn; a school of thought or branch of learning
to learn, study, imitate; suffix for academic disciplines (-ology, -ics)

morphemes.meaning: to learn, study, imitate; school, branch of knowledge

学.notes: As a standalone transitive verb, 学 is more colloquial and direct than 学习 (e.g., 学开车 'learn to drive', 跟他学 'learn from him / imitate him'), and also serves as the productive bound suffix for academic fields (文学 'literature', 传播学 'communication studies').

学业.etymology: A Classical Chinese modifier-head nominal compound combining 学 (xué, traditional 學, 'learning, scholarship') and 业 (yè, traditional 業, originally depicting the notched wooden crossbar of a bell- or chime-stand, extended to mean 'assigned work, enterprise, calling, course of study'). Attested in the Book of Rites (禮記) and Han histories, 学业 denotes the formal body of coursework and scholarly enterprise undertaken by a student.

history.meaning: scholarly pursuits, mastery of classical texts, and academic cultivation
formal studies, schooling, or an academic program toward a diploma or degree

学业.notes: Belongs to a formal register referring to one's overall academic trajectory (e.g., 完成学业 'complete one's studies', 学业有成 'achieve success in one's studies', 荒废学业 'neglect one's studies'), rather than a single day's homework (作业).

学习.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound formed from 学 (xué, traditional 學, 'to learn, receive instruction, acquire knowledge') and 习 (xí, traditional 習, 'to practice repeatedly', originally depicting feathers/wings 羽 above the sun/white 白, representing a fledgling bird flapping its wings repeatedly to learn to fly). The pairing derives directly from the famous opening line of the Analects of Confucius (論語·學而): 學而時習之，不亦說乎 ('To learn and in due season to practice what one has learned—is that not a pleasure?'), later lexicalizing into a single disyllabic verb.

history.form: 學而時習 (xué ér shí xí)
history.meaning: to learn (from a teacher/tradition) and repeatedly practice/apply it (separate coordinated verbs)
history.stage: Old Chinese (Analects of Confucius, c. 5th c. BCE)

history.meaning: to study and practice; scholarly cultivation and training
to study, learn, or emulate (a skill, subject, or role model)

morphemes.meaning: to learn, acquire knowledge through instruction or imitation
to practice repeatedly (originally 'bird flapping its wings to fly')

学习.notes: Unlike single-character 学 (which typically requires an object), 学习 can be used both transitively (学习新技能 'learn new skills') and intransitively (好好学习 'study hard', 向您学习 'learn from your example').

rootFamily.gloss: to review, revise what one has learned

学会.etymology: A verb-resultative compound (动补结构) composed of the action verb 学 (xué, 'to learn, study') and the resultative complement 会 (huì, traditional 會, originally 'to meet, assemble, converge', which evolved in medieval and modern vernacular Chinese into 'to comprehend mentally, master a skill, know how to'). Whereas 学 denotes the process or attempt of learning, the resultative complement 会 signals that the learner has successfully mastered the skill and can now perform it.

history.meaning: to come together, meet; by extension, for the mind to grasp or understand (領會)
to learn and master a skill; (as a homographic noun, xuéhuì also means 'learned society/academic association')

morphemes.meaning: to master, grasp, know how to do

学会.notes: Crucial learner distinction: 学 means 'to study/try to learn' (process), whereas 学会 means 'to succeed in learning / master how to' (result): 我学了三年游泳，终于学会了 ('I took swimming lessons for three years and finally learned how to swim'). Note that 学会 as a noun also means 'academic society/association'.

rootFamily.gloss: to learn / acquire (knowledge or a lesson)
to grasp through experience, realize, appreciate

学位.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-compound composed of 学 (xué, traditional 學, 'learning, scholarship') and 位 (wèi, 'rank, seat, official standing', originally depicting a person 人 standing 立 at their assigned place at court). Used occasionally in Literary Chinese for a scholar's standing in learning, it was standardized in Meiji Japan (学位 gakui) and modern Chinese educational law (such as the 1935 and 1980 Academic Degrees Regulations) to translate Western university 'academic degrees' (学士 bachelor's, 硕士 master's, 博士 doctor's).

history.meaning: a scholar's status, seat, or attainment in classical learning
formal university academic degree (bachelor's, master's, doctorate) conferred upon graduation

morphemes.meaning: rank, title, official standing or seat

学位.notes: In China's higher education system, 学位 ('academic degree', attested by a 学位证) is distinct from 学历 ('educational record/diploma', attested by a 毕业证); in real-estate contexts, 学位 can also mean an 'enrollment slot' at a public school tied to a school-district home (学区房).

学到.etymology: A verb-resultative compound (动补结构) formed from the verb 学 (xué, 'to learn, study') and the resultative complement 到 (dào, originally 'to arrive at, reach', composed of 至 'arrive' and phonetic 刀 dāo, grammaticalized after perception and acquisition verbs to mark successful attainment or receipt of the object). Parallel to 看到 ('see'), 听到 ('hear'), and 得到 ('obtain'), 学到 emphasizes successfully acquiring specific knowledge, insights, or life lessons from an experience or mentor.

history.meaning: 'to learn' + 'to reach/attain' as verb and directional/attainment complement in vernacular Chinese
to learn, acquire, or gain (knowledge, experience, or a lesson) from a source or experience

学到.notes: Compare 学会 vs. 学到: 学会 takes a performative skill or verb phrase (学会游泳 'learn how to swim', 学会剪辑 'learn how to edit'), whereas 学到 takes a noun object representing knowledge, experience, or lessons gained (从她身上学到了很多东西 'learned a lot from her').

rootFamily.gloss: to learn how to (master a skill)

cognates.meaning: student or member of an academy/institute
cognates.word: 学園/学院員 (cognate morphemes 学 + 員)

cognates.meaning: trainee, student at a training institute
trainee, cadet, adult student at an academy

学员.etymology: A modern Mandarin modifier-head compound joining 学 (xué, 'to study, train') and 员 (yuán, traditional 員, originally a round ding cauldron 鼎 with a circle 〇 above it signifying 'round object, count, number', later extended to 'official, member of an organization or group'). Originally created in the 20th century for adult trainees at military academies, driving schools, or professional training institutes (as opposed to regular school 学生), 学员 was popularized across Chinese entertainment in the 2010s (starting with *The Voice of China* 中国好声音) to refer to reality-show contestants mentored by celebrity coaches (导师).

history.meaning: cadet, adult trainee, or participant enrolled in a military, cadre, or vocational training institute
trainee or team contestant mentored by a coach on a television talent/variety competition, as well as adult trainees in professional courses

学员.notes: In Chinese singing and talent shows (*幕后之王*), contestants are called 学员 ('trainees/mentees') and judges are called 导师 ('mentors') to frame the competition as an artistic masterclass rather than a harsh elimination game (where contestants are called 选手 xuǎnshǒu).

学校.etymology: Coordinative noun compound pairing two ancient Zhou-era educational institutions mentioned in Mencius (设痒序学校以教之): 学 (學, 'institution of higher learning; study') + 校 (xiào, 'community school and military training enclosure'). Standardized across modern East Asia for any 'school, educational institution'.

history.meaning: ancient state and local academies
school; educational institution

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 学校 (via 萌典)

学生.etymology: A modifier-head compound attested since the Jin and Tang dynasties (e.g., History of the Southern Dynasties 南史 and Bai Juyi's poetry), composed of 学 (xué, traditional 學, 'learning, school') and 生 (shēng, 'one who is born; scholar, youth, disciple', compare 先生 xiānsheng 'master, teacher [earlier-born]' and 书生 shūshēng 'scholar'). Originally designating scholars studying at state academies or under a master, it became the universal modern East Asian term for 'student' or 'pupil' from primary school through university.

history.meaning: scholar-disciple studying at an imperial or local academy or under a master
student or pupil at any educational level, or a follower/disciple of a mentor

学生.notes: Pronounced with a neutral tone on the second syllable (xuésheng) in standard Mainland Mandarin. Applies to all grade levels (小学生 'elementary pupil', 大学生 'college student') as well as personal mentorship (他是我的学生 'He is my student/protege').

cognates.word: hội sinh viên (calque) / học sinh hội

学生会.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound combining 学生 (xuésheng, 'student') and 会 (huì, traditional 會, 'assembly, association, union, society'). Emerging in early 20th-century Chinese and Japanese universities (and playing a famous historical role during the May Fourth Movement of 1919), 学生会 denotes the official student-run representative council or union responsible for campus activities, student welfare, and liaison with university administration.

history.meaning: student self-governing association or patriotic student union in Republican-era schools and universities
campus student union or student council organizing events and student governance in high schools and universities

学生会.notes: In Chinese university dramas and campus life, serving as 学生会主席 ('Student Union President') or head of its 文艺部 ('Arts & Entertainment Department') or 外联部 ('External Relations Department') is a classic stepping stone into media and event production.

学问.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative compound uniting 学 (xué, traditional 學, 'to study, learn') and 问 (wèn, traditional 問, 'to ask, inquire, question'). Drawn from the Confucian Doctrine of the Mean (中庸: 博學之，審問之，慎思之，明辨之，篤行之 'Study it extensively, inquire into it accurately, think it over carefully, sift it clearly, and practice it earnestly') and the Mencius, the compound encapsulates the classical Chinese ideal that true erudition requires both receptive study (学) and critical inquiry (问).

history.meaning: to study and to inquire; the twin processes of Confucian self-cultivation and scholarship
history.stage: Old & Middle Chinese (Mencius / Doctrine of the Mean)

history.meaning: deep scholarship, erudition, learning; (colloquially) intricate know-how or hidden art behind a skill

学问.notes: Pronounced with a neutral second syllable (xuéwen) in everyday speech. Beyond formal 'scholarship' (做学问 'engage in academic research', 有学问 'be learned/erudite'), it is frequently used colloquially for 'hidden intricacy / art / knack': 这里面大有学问 ('There is a whole art/science to this').

学院.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound composed of 学 (xué, traditional 學, 'learning, study') and 院 (yuàn, 'courtyard surrounded by walls; official compound or institution', with the mound/wall radical 阝 and 完 wán 'complete enclosure'). Originally used in Tang and Song China for imperial scholarly academies (such as 翰林學士院 and 书院 shūyuàn), 学院 became the standard modern term for a specialized higher-education 'college', 'academy', or 'conservatory' (e.g., 电影学院 'Film Academy', 传媒学院 'Media College') as well as a constituent school within a comprehensive university.

history.meaning: walled courtyard academy or hall of scholars in imperial China
specialized college, conservatory, or constituent school/faculty within a university

morphemes.meaning: walled courtyard; institutional compound, college, academy

学院.notes: In Chinese higher education, 学院 can refer either to an independent specialized institution (often prestigious in arts and media, like 北京电影学院 'Beijing Film Academy' or 中央戏剧学院 'Central Academy of Drama') or to a constituent school within a 大学 ('university', e.g., 新闻传播学院 'School of Journalism and Communication'). Also used in 学院派 ('academic/conservatory school of style').

rootFamily.gloss: dean / president of a college or academy

孩子.etymology: Compound noun of 孩 ('laughing infant, young child', from 子 'child' + phonetic 亥 hài, originally 咳 'infant's giggle' in Laozi and Mencius) + nominal suffix 子 (neutral tone zi): 'child, kid; one's son or daughter'.

history.meaning: smiling infant; young child
child; kid; son or daughter

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 孩子 (via 萌典)

孪生弟弟.etymology: A modifier-head compound phrase combining the attributive compound 孪生 (luánshēng, 'twin, born as twins') and the kinship noun 弟弟 (dìdi, 'younger brother'). The character 孪 (luán, traditional 攣, attested in the Shuowen Jiezi as 一乳兩子也 'two children born of one nursing/birth') combines 子 ('child') with the phonetic 䜌 (luán, 'entwined, linked silk threads', signifying two beings bound together from birth), paired with 生 ('born'). 弟弟 is a reduplicated vernacular kinship noun from Classical Chinese 弟 (dì, originally depicting leather thongs wrapped in sequential order around a stake, hence 'next in sequence, younger brother').

history.meaning: 'born as twins from a single birth' (Shuowen Jiezi) + 'younger brother in birth sequence'
twin younger brother (the younger-born of male twins, or a twin brother younger than oneself)

morphemes.meaning: twinned, two children born of one birth

孪生弟弟.notes: Even with twins, Chinese kinship terminology always distinguishes birth order down to the minute: the first-born is 孪生哥哥/姐姐 ('twin older brother/sister') and the second-born is 孪生弟弟/妹妹 ('twin younger brother/sister'). 孪生 is slightly more literary/formal than colloquial 双胞胎 (shuāngbāotāi).

cognates.meaning: would rather (literary kanbun reading of 寧)

宁可.etymology: A disyllabic modal conjunction/adverb formed from Classical Chinese 宁 (nìng, traditional 寧, originally 'peaceful, settled at heart', composed of a roof 宀, a heart 心, a dish 皿, and 丂, which already in Old Chinese functioned as a rhetorical optative particle meaning 'it would be better to; would rather') and 可 (kě, 'may, permit, approve, be acceptable'). Together, 宁可 literally means 'one would rather deem it acceptable to [do A than B]', expressing a reluctant or resolute preference between two suboptimal or demanding choices.

history.meaning: peaceful; optative/rhetorical particle: 'would rather, better that' (e.g., 寧為雞口，無為牛後)
would rather, prefer to (reinforced disyllabic conjunction in vernacular prose)
would rather, better to (typically paired with 也不 'than to...' or 也要 'even if it means...')

morphemes.meaning: would rather, better that (fourth tone nìng; distinct from níng 'peaceful')

宁可.notes: Always pronounced nìngkě (fourth tone on 宁, not second tone níng as in 安宁). It typically pairs with two correlative patterns: 宁可 A，也不 B ('would rather do A than ever do B') or 宁可 A，也要 B ('would rather endure A in order to achieve B').

rootFamily.gloss: would rather surrender one's life than yield (idiom)

宁静.etymology: Coordinative adjective compound of 宁 (寧, 'peaceful, settled at heart under a roof with a dish of food') + 静 (靜, 'quiet, still, calm'): 'peaceful and quiet, tranquil, serene'. Famously in Zhuge Liang's 夫君子之行，静以修身…非淡泊无以明志，非宁静无以致远.

history.stage: Classical Chinese (Chuci, Huainanzi, Zhuge Liang) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: tranquil; peaceful and quiet; serene

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 宁静 (via 萌典)

它.etymology: Non-human third-person singular pronoun ('it'). In Shang oracle-bone script, 它 was the original pictograph of a cobra/snake (written 蛇 shé after the insect/reptile radical 虫 was added), borrowed in Classical Chinese to mean 'other, another' (later written 他 with 亻). During the early 20th-century vernacular movement, 它 (alongside 牠 for animals) was standardized with the pronunciation tā for inanimate 'it', contrasting graphically with 他 ('he') and 她 ('she').

morphemes.meaning: classical 'other' standardized in modern Chinese for inanimate 'it' (tā)

history.meaning: snake pictograph -> other, another
third-person inanimate pronoun 'it'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 它 (via 萌典)

它们.etymology: Non-human third-person plural pronoun ('they, them [for things, plants, and animals]'), formed by adding the plural suffix 们 (-men) to the inanimate pronoun 它 ('it').

history.meaning: they/them (for non-human referents)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 它们 (via 萌典)

守.etymology: Ancient ideogram attested on bronze inscriptions combining 宀 ('roof, building, court') + 寸 ('hand; law/measure'): 'guard, defend, keep watch over, abide by (rules/promises), stay close by'.

history.meaning: guard a territory/post; abide by; keep
guard; defend; observe/abide by; stay close to

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 守 (via 萌典)

守住.etymology: A verb-resultative compound (动补结构) combining the verb 守 (shǒu, 'to guard, defend, keep watch over, abide by', an ideogrammic graph with a roof 宀 and a hand/thumb 寸, representing holding fast to an enclosure or post) and the resultative complement 住 (zhù, originally 'to stop, halt, reside firmly', grammaticalized after verbs to indicate holding something securely in place without losing or yielding it). Together, 守住 means to successfully defend, hold onto, or keep intact against pressure.

history.meaning: to guard a territory or city wall, keep watch, maintain a principle or post
to hold fast to, defend successfully, keep from slipping away (verb + firmness resultative complement)

morphemes.meaning: firmly in place, securely, without yielding or losing

守住.notes: Commonly used both for concrete defense and for abstract moral or professional resolve: 守住底线 ('hold the bottom line / never compromise one's core principles'), 守住初心 ('stay true to one's original aspiration'), or 守住秘密 ('keep a secret'). Has potential forms 守得住 ('able to hold onto') and 守不住 ('unable to hold onto').

rootFamily.gloss: to Persist in / stick to one's post or principle

cognates.meaning: code of conduct, rules to be observed
rules to be observed, code of conduct, safety regulations
code of rules, regulations to observe

守则.etymology: A Classical Chinese compound composed of 守 (shǒu, 'to abide by, observe, keep') and 则 (zé, traditional 則, 'rule, regulation, standard, law', originally depicting a knife 刀 carving inscriptions onto a bronze cauldron 鼎/貝 to fix legal statutes permanently). In Literary Chinese, 守則 could function as a verb-object phrase ('to abide by the rules'); in modern Mandarin and Sino-Japanese/Sino-Korean administrative usage, it functions as a modifier-head noun meaning 'rules to be observed' or a formal 'code of conduct'.

history.meaning: to observe laws and standards; principles to be upheld
code of conduct, handbook of rules, or professional guidelines for a specific group

morphemes.meaning: rule, standard, regulation, code (originally 'statute carved on bronze')

守则.notes: Typically placed after a noun naming a profession or role to title an official code of conduct: e.g., 员工守则 ('employee handbook/code of conduct'), 学生守则 ('student code of conduct'), or 职业守则 ('professional code of ethics').

rootFamily.gloss: rule, regulation (of a game or system)

cognates.meaning: security treaty/guarantee (Specifically Nichi-Bei Anpo; security guards are 警備 keibi)
national security (short for 안전보장 anjeon bojang)

安保.etymology: A modern syllabic abbreviation (缩略词) of the four-character phrase 安全保卫 (ānquán bǎowèi, 'safety and security protection') or 安全保障 (ānquán bǎozhàng, 'security guarantee'). It combines the initial morphemes 安 (ān, 'safe, secure, peaceful', originally a woman 女 settled beneath a roof 宀) and 保 (bǎo, 'to protect, guard, defend', originally depicting an adult 人 carrying a swaddled child 子 on their back). In contemporary Mainland Mandarin, 安保 refers both to security operations/measures at events and venues and to the security personnel carrying them out.

history.form: 安全保衛 / 安全保障 (ānquán bǎowèi / ānquán bǎozhàng)
history.meaning: public safety defense and security protection (full four-character administrative compounds)
event/venue security operations, safety protection, or security staff/personnel

安保.notes: Compare 安保 (ānbǎo) and 保安 (bǎo'ān): 保安 usually refers to an individual uniformed security guard (一名保安), whereas 安保 refers more broadly to the security system, event security team, or security operations (加强现场安保 'strengthen on-site security', 安保人员 'security staff') at concerts, broadcasts, and airports.

rootFamily.gloss: security check (at airports/venues, short for 安全检查)

安全.etymology: Coordinative adjective and noun compound of 安 ('peaceful, settled, safe', a woman 女 settled indoors under a roof 宀) + 全 ('whole, intact, unharmed'): 'safe and sound, secure; safety, security'. Attested since Classical prose (Xunzi, Hanshu).

history.stage: Classical Chinese (Xunzi, Hanshu) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: safe and intact; safety; security

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 安全 (via 萌典)

安安全全.etymology: AABB expressive reduplication of 安全 ('safe and secure', from 安 'peaceful/settled under a roof 宀' + 全 'whole/intact'). In Mandarin grammar, reduplicating a disyllabic adjective into AABB pattern intensifies it with a warm, reassuring nuance ('completely safe and sound').

history.meaning: completely safe and sound

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 安安全全

安慰.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative verbal compound joining 安 (ān, 'to calm, pacify, settle, make peaceful', depicting a woman 女 restful beneath a roof 宀) and 慰 (wèi, 'to soothe, console, comfort', formed from 心 'heart' and 尉 wèi, which originally depicted applying a heated flatiron 火 + 尸 + 寸 to smooth out wrinkles in cloth or soothe aching flesh, extended to smoothing out emotional distress in the heart). Attested in Han dynasty texts such as the Book of Han (漢書) and Records of the Three Kingdoms (三國志), it denotes soothing someone's grief or anxiety with kind words or care.

history.meaning: to pacify, reassure, and soothe subjects, soldiers, or grieving kin
to comfort, console, or reassure someone who is sad, anxious, or disappointed; consolation/solace

morphemes.meaning: to soothe, console, iron out distress in the heart

安慰.notes: Used both as a transitive verb (安慰朋友 'comfort a friend', 自我安慰 'console oneself / rationalize') and as a noun (这对我来说是很大的安慰 'This is a great comfort to me'). Also seen in 安慰奖 ('consolation prize') and 安慰剂 ('placebo').

安排.etymology: Coordinative verb and noun compound of 安 ('settle, place securely') + 排 ('set in order, line up'): 'arrange, plan, set up, schedule; arrangement'. First attested in Zhuangzi and popularized from Tang–Song poetry and vernacular onward.

history.meaning: settle and put in order -> arrange, plan, schedule

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 安排 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to place; to assign; to plant (someone)

安插.etymology: A coordinative-serial verbal compound formed from 安 (ān, 'to settle, to place securely') and 插 (chā, 'to insert, to stick in, to plant'). Attested in Tang and Song dynasty literary and vernacular prose (such as Bai Juyi's poetry and Song administrative writing) originally meaning 'to arrange a place for someone to stay or work', it later developed a covert or strategic connotation: 'to plant an agent, informant, or crony into a rival organization or faction'.

history.meaning: to settle someone in a place or post; to arrange placement
to assign to a position; to plant (an insider, spy, or protégé)

morphemes.meaning: to insert; to stick in; to plant

安插.notes: Frequently takes objects like 眼线 (yǎnxiàn, 'informant/mole'), 亲信 (qīnxìn, 'crony/trusted aide'), or 人手 (rénshǒu, 'personnel'); in workplace and media dramas it often carries a slightly scheming or strategic nuance.

rootFamily.gloss: to place; to find a spot for (personnel or displaced people)
interlude; episode inserted into a larger story

安静.etymology: Coordinative adjective and verb compound of 安 ('peaceful, settled, calm', woman 女 under a roof 宀) + 静 (靜, 'quiet, still, free of noise'): 'quiet, peaceful, calm; quiet down'. Attested since Classical prose (Xunzi, Shiji).

history.meaning: calm and still; quiet; peaceful

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 安静 (via 萌典)

宋.etymology: Ancient character combining 宀 ('roof, ancestral temple') + 木 ('tree/wood'): originally the name of the Zhou-era feudal state of Song (founded in eastern Henan by descendants of the Shang royal house), later the prestigious Song Dynasty (960–1279 CE), and a major Chinese surname.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Bronze inscriptions & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: State of Song; Song Dynasty; surname Song

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 宋 (via 萌典)

完.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 宀 ('roof, house') + 元 (yuán/wán phonetic, 'head/primary'): originally 'an intact, completed building without damage', hence 'whole, intact, complete; finish, run out of, come to an end' and Mandarin's primary completive verb complement (-wán).

history.meaning: intact; whole; repair/complete
finish; complete; run out of

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 完 (via 萌典)

完了.etymology: Verb/adjective + aspectual/modal particle 了 (le) from 完 ('finish, come to an end'): means literally 'be finished / done / over', and as a colloquial exclamation 'it's all over!, we're done for!, uh-oh!'.

history.meaning: finished; over; 'done for! / oh no!'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 完了 (via 萌典)
