完全.etymology: Coordinative adjective and adverb compound of 完 ('intact, complete') + 全 ('whole, entire'): 'complete, whole; completely, entirely, totally'. Attested since Han historical prose (Shiji).

history.stage: Han Classical Chinese (Shiji) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: intact and whole; complete; completely

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 完全 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to perfect; to improve and complete

完善.etymology: A coordinative compound uniting 完 (wán, 'whole, intact, complete', originally depicting a roof 宀 over 元 indicating structural wholeness) and 善 (shàn, 'good, fine, well-executed'). Used in Classical and Literary Chinese as a stative verb or adjective meaning 'intact and fine; thorough and faultless', in Modern Mandarin it functions both as an adjective ('comprehensive and well-developed') and causatively as a transitive verb ('to refine, to improve and make complete').

history.meaning: intact and good; thorough and well-prepared
well-developed, sound (adj.); to refine, to improve to perfection (verb)

完善.notes: As a transitive verb in professional and media contexts, 完善 often pairs with abstract nouns like 方案 (fāng'àn, 'proposal/plan'), 制度 (zhìdù, 'system'), or 剧本 (jùběn, 'script') to mean 'polishing and rounding out gaps'.

完好.etymology: Coordinative adjective compound of 完 ('intact, undamaged') + 好 ('good, sound'): 'intact, in good condition, undamaged'.

history.meaning: intact and in good condition

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 完好 (via 萌典)

完好无损.etymology: Four-character idiom combining 完好 ('intact and in good condition') + 无损 ('without damage or loss', 无 'without' + 损 'damage'): 'completely intact and undamaged, in mint/unscathed condition'.

history.form: 完好無損 / 完好无损
history.meaning: completely intact without the slightest damage

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 完好无损 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: completion; to complete; to bring to fruition

完成.etymology: A coordinative-resultative compound combining 完 (wán, 'to finish, to make whole') and 成 (chéng, 'to accomplish, to become complete'). Attested in Classical texts (such as *Zhouli* commentary and historical chronicles) in the sense of 'bringing a structure or undertaking to full realization', and reinforced in late-19th-century pan-East Asian modern vocabulary alongside Japanese *kansei* (完成).

history.meaning: to bring to full structural or functional realization
to complete; to accomplish (a task, project, or quota)

morphemes.meaning: to accomplish; to succeed; to form

完成.notes: The standard transitive verb for finishing tasks (完成任务), production targets, or creative works; compare 完毕 (wánbì), which is intransitive and marks the formal conclusion of a process.

rootFamily.gloss: completeness; degree of completion (e.g., of a performance)

完整.etymology: Coordinative adjective compound of 完 ('whole, intact') + 整 ('orderly, whole, complete'): 'complete, intact, integrated, undivided'.

history.meaning: whole and complete; intact

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 完整 (via 萌典)

完毕.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound of two near-synonyms: 完 (wán, 'to finish, to exhaust') and 毕 (bì, traditional 畢, originally a pictograph of a long-handled hunting net, extended in Old Chinese to mean 'to catch all, to end completely'). Used since the Song–Yuan vernacular period to mark the full termination of an action or ceremony.

history.meaning: to come to a complete end; to finish entirely
to be completed; 'over' (in radio/military or formal announcements)

完毕.notes: Strictly intransitive—it never takes a direct object. It typically follows a two-syllable action verb (e.g., 准备完毕 'preparations complete', 录制完毕 'recording finished', 汇报完毕 'report concluded').

rootFamily.gloss: to graduate; to complete one's studies
after all; when all is said and done

完美.etymology: Coordinative adjective compound of 完 ('complete, flawless') + 美 ('beautiful, fine, admirable'): 'perfect, flawless, consummate'.

history.meaning: complete and beautiful -> perfect, flawless

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 完美 (via 萌典)

宏图壮志.etymology: A four-character parallel idiom (*chéngyǔ*, structure A1-N1 + A2-N2) pairing 宏图 (hóngtú, 'vast plan, grand blueprint', from 宏 'spacious, grand' + 图 'map, chart, scheme') with 壮志 (zhuàngzhì, 'heroic/vigorous aspiration', from 壮 'robust, magnificent' + 志 'will, ambition'). Both two-character halves are deeply rooted in Han–Tang poetic diction (compare 壮志凌云 and 大展宏图) and combine symmetrically to praise visionary career or artistic ambitions.

history.meaning: grand design (宏圖) and heroic resolve (壯志) as classical poetic compounds
grand plans and lofty aspirations; visionary ambition

宏图壮志.notes: Also frequently appears in the reversed order 壮志宏图 (zhuàngzhì-hóngtú) or with 雄心 (xióngxīn-zhuàngzhì); often collocated with 怀揣 ('to harbor in one's heart') or 施展 ('to unfold/realize').

rootFamily.gloss: to unfold a grand plan; to realize one's ambition

cognates.meaning: bureaucracy / bureaucrats (官僚) + style of conduct (作風)
cognates.word: 官僚 (かんりょう, kanryō) + 作風 (さくふう, sakufū)

官僚作风.etymology: A four-character modifier-head nominal phrase joining 官僚 (guānliáo, originally a Classical Chinese coordinative compound of 官 'official' + 僚 'colleague in office, bureaucrat', later used in Meiji Japan and modern Chinese to translate European 'bureaucracy/bureaucrat') and 作风 (zuòfēng, 'style of work or conduct', from 作 'doing, work' + 风 'ethos, manner, custom'). Popularized in 20th-century Chinese administrative and workplace critique to denote rigid, aloof, red-tape-heavy behavior.

history.meaning: fellow government officials; members of the imperial administration
bureaucratic work style; pompous, rigid, or buck-passing organizational habits

官僚作风.notes: Used not only for government agencies but very commonly in corporate and television production settings to criticize executives who pull rank, obsess over hierarchy, or ignore practical creative realities.

rootFamily.gloss: style of work; attitude and conduct

官方.etymology: A modifier-head compound composed of 官 (guān, 'government, public authority, official') and 方 (fāng, 'side, party, direction, prescription/method'). In Song–Ming administrative texts, 官方 referred either to 'the moral and institutional norms of officialdom' or to 'the government side (as opposed to private citizens 民方)'. In contemporary media and internet usage, it has broadened from 'state authorities' to mean any 'official organization, brand, or verified production account' (as opposed to fan-made or third-party channels).

history.meaning: standards of officialdom; the government side or state authorities
official (attributive); the official side, verified account, or organizing body

官方.notes: In modern entertainment and social media, 官方 (and its slang abbreviation 官博 guānbó 'official Weibo account' or 官宣 guānxuān 'official announcement') refers to a show's or company's authorized voice rather than the state government.

定.etymology: Ancient ideogram combining 宀 ('roof, house') + 正 ('upright; foot 止 settled at a line'): 'settle down indoors -> fix, settle, decide, calm, book/reserve/order in advance, surely'.

history.meaning: settle; fix; calm; establish
decide; fix; book/order; surely

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 定 (via 萌典)

定好.etymology: Resultative verb compound combining 定 ('decide, fix, arrange') + 好 (resultative complement of satisfactory completion): 'settle upon, agree on, fix (a date, plan, or price) satisfactorily'.

history.meaning: settle on; fix and finalize

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 定好 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: treasured book or manual; precious volume

宝书.etymology: A transparent modifier-head nominal compound combining 宝 (bǎo, traditional 寶, depicting jade 玉, shell currency 貝, and pottery 缶 beneath a roof 宀: 'treasure, precious object') and 书 (shū, traditional 書, 'writing, book, manual'). Historically used in Literary Chinese for imperial edicts, Daoist/Buddhist scriptures, or rare calligraphies; in modern colloquial and workplace usage, it is often used playfully or figuratively for an indispensable guidebook, secret manual, or prized reference binder.

history.meaning: imperial document, sacred scripture, or treasured classic volume
treasured book; prized manual or 'bible' of a craft

宝书.notes: In contemporary dialogue (such as *Behind the Scenes*), calling someone's notebook or reference guide a 宝书 carries an affectionate, slightly humorous tone—akin to calling a producer's handbook their 'sacred playbook' or 'treasure tome'.

rootFamily.gloss: treasure trove; hidden gem (also used as slang for a talented person)
secret manual; martial arts or career guidebook

宝石.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound of 宝 (bǎo, traditional 寶, 'treasure, precious') and 石 (shí, 'stone, mineral'). Attested since Tang and Ming dynasty sources (including accounts of Maritime Silk Road trade when Zheng He's voyages brought rubies, sapphires, and spinels from South and Southeast Asia, recorded as 宝石 in Ming histories) to designate precious and semi-precious mineral stones.

history.meaning: precious mineral stone; imported ruby, sapphire, or jewel
gemstone; jewel

宝石.notes: Takes the classifiers 颗 (kē, for small round/faceted items) or 块 (kuài); distinguishes mineral gems from 珍珠 (zhēnzhū, 'pearl') and 钻石 (zuànshí, specifically 'diamond').

宝藏.etymology: Formed from 宝 (bǎo, simplified from 寶, depicting jade 玉, cowries 貝, and pottery 缶 stored safely beneath a roof 宀—hence 'precious treasure') and 藏 (zàng, 'storehouse, vault, hidden repository', distinct in tone from the verb cáng 'to hide'). In Tang–Song Buddhist and secular texts 宝藏 denoted both a royal treasury and a hidden cache of valuables underground, giving rise to modern literal 'buried treasure' and figurative 'cultural treasure trove'.

history.meaning: treasury vault; hidden cache of jewels
buried treasure; treasure trove

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 宝藏

实不相瞒.etymology: A four-character vernacular conversational formula (*guànyòngyǔ* / *chéngyǔ*) dating back to Yuan *zájù* plays and Ming–Qing vernacular novels (such as *Water Margin* 水浒传 and *Dream of the Red Chamber* 红楼梦). Structurally composed of 实 (shí, 'in truth, honestly') + 不 (bù, 'not') + 相 (xiāng, originally 'mutually', here grammaticalized as a directional pronominal adverb meaning 'toward you / to you') + 瞒 (mán, 'to conceal the truth, to deceive'). Literally: 'In truth, I do not conceal from you.'

history.meaning: in truth I do not hide it from you (stock candid confession formula in vernacular fiction and drama)
truth be told; to be completely frank with you

morphemes.meaning: to hide the truth; to conceal from

实不相瞒.notes: Used at the start of a sentence when the speaker is about to admit an awkward, confidential, or embarrassing fact; notice how 相 (xiāng) here does not mean 'each other' but points to the listener ('from you'), just as in 实话相告 ('to tell you the truth').

rootFamily.gloss: to conceal; to hide the truth; to keep someone in the dark
to deceive above and hide from below (idiom)

实习.etymology: A modifier-head verbal/nominal compound formed from 实 (shí, traditional 實, 'real, actual, hands-on') and 习 (xí, traditional 習, originally depicting wings 羽 over white/sun 白/日: 'repeated flight practice by a young bird; to practice, to train'). Popularized in late-19th and early-20th-century modern East Asian educational terminology alongside Japanese *jisshū* (実習) to denote applying classroom theory in real-world clinical, industrial, or media workplaces.

history.meaning: hands-on practical training; field practicum for students
history.stage: Late Qing / Meiji Sino-Japanese educational term

history.meaning: to intern; internship; field practice

morphemes.meaning: to practice; to train; to learn by doing

实习.notes: Functions both as an intransitive verb (在电视台实习 'to intern at a TV station') and a noun (实习期 'internship/probationary training period').

rootFamily.gloss: practical application; to put into practice

cognates.meaning: trainee; student in practical training; apprentice
cognates.word: 実習生 (じっしゅうせい, jisshūsei)

实习生.etymology: A three-character derived agent noun formed by suffixing 生 (shēng, 'student, scholar, trainee', a productive human-status suffix derived from Classical Chinese 先生/学生) to the compound 实习 (shíxí, 'hands-on practice, internship'). Shared across modern Chinese, Japanese (*jisshūsei*), and Korean (*silseupsaeng*) for university students or entry-level newcomers undergoing practical workplace training.

history.meaning: student trainee; workplace intern

morphemes.meaning: student; trainee; person learning a craft

实习生.notes: In Chinese entertainment and media workplaces, differentiate 实习生 (shíxíshēng, a corporate/production 'intern' like Chunyu Qiao's assistants) from 练习生 (liànxíshēng, an idol 'trainee' training in singing and dancing before debut).

cognates.meaning: real ability; actual strength or force
real capability; true skill; actual power

实力.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound uniting 实 (shí, traditional 實, 'solid, substantive, actual', originally strings of shells 貫 under a roof 宀 signifying a house full of wealth) and 力 (lì, 'strength, power, capability', originally a pictograph of a sinew or plow). Already attested in Classical Chinese texts (such as Han Fei's legalist writings and historical chronicles) in the sense of 'substantive military or economic power as opposed to empty reputation (虚名)', and widely used in modern Chinese for both geopolitical power and personal/professional competence.

history.meaning: substantive force or resources (contrasted with mere title or reputation)
actual strength; proven competence or skill

实力.notes: In Chinese showbiz, 实力派 (shílìpài, 'talent-driven actor/singer') is the classic contrast to 偶像派 (ǒuxiàngpài, 'idol/looks-driven star') or 流量明星 (liúliàng míngxīng, 'traffic/hype star').

rootFamily.gloss: skill-based performer; actor/singer who relies on real talent rather than hype

实在.etymology: Compound of 实 (實, 'real, solid, true') + 在 ('exist, be present'). Functions both as an adjective ('honest, dependable, solid, real') and as an adverb ('really, truly, honestly, indeed').

history.stage: Tang–Song Buddhist & vernacular Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: real, solid, dependable; really, truly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 实在 (via 萌典)

实心.etymology: A descriptive bahuvrihi-style compound joining 实 (shí, simplified from 實, originally cowrie wealth 貫 filling a house 宀, hence 'full, solid, substantial') and 心 (xīn, 'heart, core, interior'). Literally 'full-cored', 实心 describes timber, brass, brick, or pastry that has no hollow cavity inside (contrasting with 空心 'hollow-cored'), and in colloquial speech 实心眼儿 also describes an honest, guileless person.

history.meaning: solid-cored (of metal/wood); sincere at heart
solid (not hollow)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 实心

实情.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 实 (實, 'true, actual') + 情 ('situation, facts, circumstances'): 'the true situation, the actual facts, the truth of the matter'.

history.meaning: the actual facts; the truth of a matter

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 实情 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to implement; to enforce; to execute

实施.etymology: A modifier-head / coordinative verbal compound formed from 实 (shí, traditional 實, 'actually, concretely, in reality') and 施 (shī, 'to carry out, to bestow, to put into effect, to execute'). While 实 and 施 co-occurred in Literary Chinese prose meaning 'to genuinely bestow or apply', the tightly bound modern administrative term 实施 was reinforced via Meiji Japanese *jisshi* (実施) as the formal verb for putting laws, policies, or operational blueprints into concrete effect.

history.meaning: to put a law, decree, or plan into concrete operation
to implement; to carry out; to enforce (a plan, regulation, or project)

morphemes.meaning: to carry out; to apply; to execute

实施.notes: Compare 实施 (shíshī) and 实行 (shíxíng): 实施 focuses on the concrete operational execution of a specific plan, scheme, or law (实施方案 'implement a plan'), whereas 实行 focuses on adopting and practicing a broader system, policy, or principle (实行改革 'carry out reforms').

rootFamily.gloss: measure; step taken to address an issue
to construct; construction work in progress
to implement; to put into practice (a policy or system)

实现.etymology: A resultative-style modern compound uniting 实 (shí, 'real, actual, concrete') and 现 (xiàn, 'to appear, manifest visibly', originally the luster of jade 見 + 王). Adopted widely in late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century East Asian prose (alongside Japanese 実現 jitsugen) to translate 'realize' or 'bring into reality', 实现 means turning an abstract plan, dream, or prophecy into tangible fact.

history.meaning: bring an ideal or plan into reality
fulfil; come true; realize

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 实现

cognates.meaning: to practice; to carry out; to put into action

实行.etymology: A modifier-head verbal compound combining 实 (shí, traditional 實, 'truly, in deed, substantively') and 行 (xíng, 'to walk, to act, to practice, to carry out'). Found in Classical Chinese texts (such as *Guoyu* and Song Neo-Confucian philosophy) in the sense of 'practicing moral principles in actual conduct (rather than mere talk)', and later standardized across modern East Asian languages to mean putting policies, systems, or principles into practice.

history.meaning: to practice in actual conduct; genuine action (as opposed to empty words)
to implement; to put into practice (a policy, system, or rule)

morphemes.meaning: to act; to practice; to carry out

实行.notes: Typically takes macroscopic or institutional objects such as 制度 (zhìdù, 'system'), 政策 (zhèngcè, 'policy'), or 责任制 (zérènzhì, 'responsibility system').

rootFamily.gloss: to execute; to carry out (orders, a plan, or a contract); executive
to implement; to put into concrete operation

实话.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 实 (實, 'true, honest') + 话 (話, 'spoken words'): 'truth, honest words'.

history.meaning: truthful words; the truth

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 实话 (via 萌典)

实话实说.etymology: Four-character idiomatic phrase built on the repetition of 实 ('true, honestly'): 实话 ('true words') + 实说 ('speak frankly/truthfully') = 'tell the plain truth, speak frankly and honestly'.

history.form: 實話實說 / 实话实说
history.meaning: speak the plain truth; be completely frank

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 实话实说 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: actuality; reality; practical state; in fact

实际.etymology: Originally a Chinese Buddhist translation compound (translating Sanskrit *bhūta-koṭi*, 'the limit of reality / ultimate truth', in Kumārajīva's and Xuanzang's sutra translations), formed from 实 (shí, traditional 實, 'real, true') and 际 (jì, traditional 際, 'border, boundary, juncture, realm'). Secularized in Song–Ming philosophical prose and re-energized via Meiji Japanese *jissai* (実際) to denote concrete, real-world conditions in contrast to abstract theory or imagination.

history.meaning: the boundary of ultimate reality; true nature of dharma
actual, practical, real-world (adj.); reality, concrete circumstances (noun)

实际.notes: Can describe both objective conditions (实际情况 'actual situation', 实际操作 'hands-on/practical operation') and a person's mindset (这个人很实际 'this person is very pragmatic/down-to-earth' or sometimes 'materialistic').

cognates.meaning: in reality; in terms of actual practice

实际上.etymology: A disyllabic-plus-clitic discourse adverbial formed by attaching the locative/scope enclitic 上 (shàng, 'on the plane of, in the domain of, in terms of') to the noun 实际 (shíjì, 'actuality, reality'). Literally 'on the plane of reality', it grammaticalized in modern Mandarin into a high-frequency sentence adverb meaning 'in fact, actually, as a matter of fact', introducing a contrast between surface appearance and underlying truth.

history.meaning: in the realm of reality; in fact; actually

morphemes.meaning: on the level of; in terms of (scope marker)

实际上.notes: Slightly more formal and analytical than 其实 (qíshí, 'actually'); 实际上 shares the productive `-上` adverbial pattern seen in 事实上 (shìshíshàng, 'in fact'), 理论上 (lǐlùnshàng, 'in theory'), and 原则上 (yuánzéshàng, 'in principle').

rootFamily.gloss: as a matter of fact; in fact

实验.etymology: A modifier-head / resultative compound combining 实 (shí, traditional 實, 'actual, empirical, real') and 验 (yàn, traditional 驗, 'to test, to verify, to examine by proof'). Found in Literary Chinese in the sense of 'actual verification or proven effect', it was repurposed in Meiji Japan as *jikken* (実験) to translate European scientific 'experiment' (as opposed to passive observation), and entered modern Mandarin as the standard term for both laboratory experiments and bold artistic/media trials.

history.meaning: actual verification; proven efficacy in practice
scientific experiment; empirical trial; experimental work

morphemes.meaning: to test; to verify; to examine

实验.notes: Distinguish 实验 (shíyàn) from 试验 (shìyàn): 实验 tests a scientific hypothesis or explores a new creative concept (做实验 'run an experiment', 实验戏剧 'experimental theater'), whereas 试验 tests whether a specific device, product, or pilot scheme works as intended ('trial run / field test').

rootFamily.gloss: trial run; test; to test out (a product or scheme)

cognates.meaning: favored object; prized possession or pet (literary)

宠物.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound composed of 宠 (chǒng, traditional 寵, depicting a dragon 龍 under a roof 宀: 'imperial favor, doting affection, to pamper') and 物 (wù, 'creature, living thing, object'). In Tang–Song literary prose, 宠物 meant 'a prized possession or favored gift'; in modern Mandarin, it specialized (often translating English 'pet') to mean a domesticated companion animal kept for affection rather than labor.

history.meaning: a favored thing; prized object or creature doted upon by its owner
pet; companion animal (also figuratively 'darling/favorite')

morphemes.meaning: to dote on; to pamper; favor

宠物.notes: The root 宠 (chǒng, 'to dote on/spoil') is extremely active in modern media and fandom slang: 团宠 (tuánchǒng) is the 'group darling' whom everyone in a cast or team pampers, and 宠粉 (chǒngfěn) means 'spoiling one's fans'.

rootFamily.gloss: to dote on; to spoil with affection
to fall out of favor (historically in a palace; jokingly of pets or employees)

cognates.meaning: to examine closely; to judge; to audit
to examine; to judge; to vet
to examine; to investigate; to judge

审.etymology: A single-character verb (simplified 审 from traditional 審, originally depicting 采 'animal tracks / discerning details' inside 宀 'a house/roof': 'to examine closely inside, to investigate thoroughly'). In Old and Middle Chinese, 审 meant 'to scrutinize in detail, to ascertain the truth, to try a judicial case'. In contemporary Chinese media and broadcasting, it is the core monosyllabic verb for vetting, reviewing, and clearing content (审片 'reviewing a cut/episode', 审稿 'vetting a script/article').

history.meaning: to examine closely; to discern clearly; in detail
to interrogate or try a case; to audit, vet, and review (documents or media)

morphemes.meaning: to examine closely; to vet; to review; to try (a case)

审.notes: In television and film production (*Behind the Scenes*), 审 is ubiquitous in VO compounds like 审片 (shěnpiàn, 'reviewing a rough or final cut'), 送审 (sòngshěn, 'submitting for regulatory or executive review'), and 过审 (guòshěn, 'passing review/censorship').

rootFamily.gloss: to review and approve; to vet (a program, budget, or broadcast)
to examine; regulatory or editorial review

审核.etymology: Coordinate administrative compound of 审 ('examine thoroughly; investigate', originally inspecting tracks or details inside a house 宀 + 番) + 核 ('verify; check the core truth', wood radical 木 + phonetic 亥 hài, 'fruit pit/kernel'). Used in public administration and accounting for examining and approving applications or permits.

history.meaning: audit and review official documents or permits
official review; audit; inspection

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 审核

客人.etymology: Compound noun of 客 ('guest, visitor, traveler', roof 宀 + 各 'arrive at a lodging') + 人 ('person'): 'guest, visitor, customer/client'. Attested since Han–Tang poetry and prose.

history.meaning: guest; visitor; customer

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 客人 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: guest seat; visiting (professor, conductor, or speaker)
cognates.word: 客座 (きゃくざ, kyakuza) / 客員 (きゃくいん, kakuin)

客座.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound formed from 客 (kè, 'guest, visitor', depicting 宀 'roof' over 各 'arriving from outside') and 座 (zuò, 'seat, throne, position'). Originally denoting 'the seat of honor reserved for a guest' in Tang–Song literary Chinese, in modern Mandarin it functions primarily as an attributive noun meaning 'visiting, guest-appointed' for prestigious academic or media roles (such as 客座教授 'visiting professor' or 客座主持 'guest host').

history.meaning: the seat reserved for a guest; a visitor's place in a hall
visiting; guest (attributive modifier for professors, conductors, or hosts)

客座.notes: Rarely used alone as a standalone noun for 'a guest' (use 客人 kèrén or 嘉宾 jiābīn for that); instead, 客座 almost always modifies a professional title to indicate a distinguished outsider invited in temporarily.

rootFamily.gloss: guest host (of a TV or radio show)
to make a cameo or guest appearance (originally in Peking opera)

客座主持.etymology: A four-character modifier-head professional title combining 客座 (kèzuò, literally 'guest-seat', hence 'visiting / guest-appointed') and 主持 (zhǔchí, originally a Buddhist monastic term from Kumārajīva's translations meaning 'to preside over and uphold the Dharma', formed from 主 'to preside, direct' + 持 'to hold, maintain', now the standard Mandarin word for a TV/radio 'host, anchor, or emcee'). Together it designates a celebrity or specialist invited to host a program temporarily.

history.meaning: to uphold and preside over (a monastery, ritual, or affair)
guest host; celebrity or visiting emcee on a broadcast program

morphemes.meaning: to preside over; to direct; host
to hold; to maintain; to run

客座主持.notes: In variety shows and talk shows, a 客座主持 steps in for one or several episodes to bring fresh chemistry or star power, whereas a one-time interviewee or panelist is called a 飞行嘉宾 (fēixíng jiābīn, 'flying/one-episode guest') or 特邀嘉宾 (tèyāo jiābīn, 'special guest').

rootFamily.gloss: host; presenter; emcee; to preside over (a meeting or show)
honored guest; panelist on a TV show

客房.etymology: Compound noun of 客 ('guest') + 房 ('room'): 'guest room (in a house or hotel)'.

history.meaning: guest room; hotel room

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 客房 (via 萌典)

客服.etymology: A modern syllabic abbreviation (*suōlüèyǔ*) formed by extracting the first character of each half of the four-character phrase 客户服务 (kèhù fúwù, 'customer service', calqued from English *customer service*): 客 (kè, from 客户 'client, customer') + 服 (fú, from 服务 'service, to serve'). Coined in the late 20th century with the rise of call centers and e-commerce, it denotes both the 'customer service department/system' and an individual 'customer service representative'.

history.form: 客戶服務 / 客户服务
history.meaning: customer service (full four-character compound)
customer service; customer support agent (two-syllable blend)

morphemes.meaning: service; to serve (short for 服务)

客服.notes: Don't confuse the homophones 客服 (kèfú, 'customer service') and 克服 (kèfú, 'to overcome [a difficulty]'), which have identical pronunciation and tones!

客栈.etymology: Traditional courtyard inn or boutique guesthouse (counted with 家: 一家客栈), combining 客 ('traveler, guest') with 栈 ('wooden gallery, storehouse, wayside lodge'). Historic 客棧 served merchants and travelers along imperial post roads and remain iconic in preserved old quarters of Chengdu and Southwest China.

history.meaning: travelers' courtyard inn

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 客棧 (via 萌典)

客气.etymology: Compound noun, adjective, and verb of 客 ('guest') + 气 (氣, 'manner, air, demeanor', neutral tone qi in this word): literally 'the polite, deferential manner of a guest', hence 'polite, courteous, modest; stand on ceremony (别客气 don't be polite / you're welcome)'.

history.meaning: transient or artificial demeanor
polite; courteous; stand on ceremony

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 客气 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: objective; impartial; external to the mind

客观.etymology: A modifier-head philosophical compound coined in Meiji Japan as *kyakkan* (客観, paired with *shukan* 主観 'subjective') by Nishi Amane and fellow scholars to translate German *objektiv* / English *objective*, and rapidly borrowed into late-Qing Chinese. It combines 客 (kè, 'guest, outside observer, external object' as opposed to 主 'host, self, subject') and 观 (guān, traditional 觀, 'view, observation, perspective'): literally 'viewing from the standpoint of an outside observer'.

history.meaning: existing independently of the perceiving subject; philosophical objectivity
history.stage: Meiji Japanese / Late Qing return loan (late 19th c.)

history.meaning: objective (conditions); impartial, unbiased (judgment or assessment)

morphemes.meaning: guest; outside observer; external object (contrasted with 主 'subject/host')

客观.notes: Always paired with its antonym 主观 (zhǔguān, 'subjective, biased by personal feelings'): 客(guest/outside) vs. 主(host/inside) makes the pair effortless to remember.

cognates.meaning: publicity; promotion; propaganda; making a strong showing

宣传.etymology: A coordinative-serial verbal compound uniting 宣 (xuān, 'to proclaim publicly, to spread abroad', originally referring to a spacious royal hall where imperial decrees were announced) and 传 (chuán, traditional 傳, 'to transmit, to pass on, to circulate'). Attested in *Sanguozhi* (Records of the Three Kingdoms) and Tang administrative prose meaning 'to proclaim and transmit imperial orders', it was repurposed in modern Sino-Japanese (*senden* 宣伝) and 20th-century Chinese to cover both political 'propaganda' and commercial/entertainment 'publicity, promotion, and marketing'.

history.meaning: to proclaim and transmit (imperial decrees or teachings) to the public
to publicize, to promote; publicity, marketing, or public relations campaign

morphemes.meaning: to proclaim; to declare publicly; to spread
to transmit; to circulate; to pass on

宣传.notes: Unlike English 'propaganda' (which is strongly pejorative), 宣传 in Chinese is completely neutral and is the everyday industry word for film/TV marketing, PR, and promotional trailers (宣传片 xuānchuánpiàn 'promo video/trailer', 宣发 xuānfā 'publicity and distribution').

rootFamily.gloss: publicity and distribution (film/TV industry blend of 宣传 + 发行)

宣布.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound joining 宣 (xuān, 'to proclaim aloud, to make known') and 布 (bù, originally 'hemp cloth', extended by metaphor to 'to unfold, to spread out widely, to promulgate'). Attested as early as the *Book of Han* (汉书) and *Records of the Grand Historian* (史记) in the sense of 'promulgating sovereign decrees and spreading virtue across the realm', and used in Modern Mandarin as the standard verb for publicly announcing a decision, result, or official news.

history.meaning: to promulgate and spread (imperial decrees or benevolence) throughout the realm
to announce publicly; to declare (a decision, winner, or launch)

morphemes.meaning: to spread out; to promulgate; to publish

宣布.notes: Often used in broadcast and corporate settings for formal declarations (宣布结果 'announce the results', 宣布开机 'announce the start of filming'); compare 发布 (fābù), which emphasizes 'releasing/publishing' a press release, product, or data report.

rootFamily.gloss: to make public; to publish (a list, ranking, or truth)
to release; to issue (a product, news release, or video)

室内.etymology: Locative compound of 室 ('room; inner chamber', roof radical 宀 + 至 'arrive/stop') + 内 ('inside; within', depicting entry into an enclosure 冂 + 入). Contrasting with 室外 ('outdoors'), it is the standard architectural and everyday word for indoor spaces.

history.meaning: within the inner chamber of a house
indoors; indoor

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 室内

宫斗剧.etymology: A contemporary Chinese television genre compound formed from 宫斗 (gōngdòu, a modifier-head compression of 后宫争斗 hòugōng zhēngdòu, 'imperial harem/palace infighting', from 宫 'imperial palace, inner court' + 斗 'to struggle, to scheme and vie against one another') plus the head noun 剧 (jù, traditional 劇, 'drama, theatrical series'). Coined in the mid-2000s following the runaway success of TVB's *War and Beauty* (金枝欲孽, 2004) and cemented by mainland blockbusters like *Empresses in the Palace* (甄嬛传, 2011).

history.meaning: imperial court drama (broader late-20th-century genre term)
palace intrigue drama (specifically centering on scheming and rivalry in the imperial harem)

morphemes.meaning: imperial palace; inner court / harem (short for 后宫)
to fight; to scheme and vie for power (short for 争斗)

宫斗剧.notes: The `X + 斗 (+ 剧)` pattern became so iconic that Chinese viewers and workplace speakers now use 宫斗 figuratively for cutthroat office politics, alongside sister compounds like 宅斗剧 (zháidòujù, 'aristocratic household intrigue drama') and 职场宫斗 ('office palace intrigue').

rootFamily.gloss: costume / period drama (set in ancient times)

害.etymology: An ancient single-character root (Old Chinese *N-kˤat-s, attested in Shang oracle bone and Western Zhou bronze inscriptions depicting 宀 'a roof/house' over 丰/口 suggesting 'speaking or cutting/blocking inside a dwelling'). In Pre-Qin Classical Chinese it functioned as both noun ('calamity, injury, detriment', the antonym of 利 lì 'benefit') and transitive verb ('to harm, to injure, to murder'). In colloquial Modern Mandarin, besides meaning 'to harm', it frequently acts as a causative verb ('to cause someone trouble / to make someone suffer an unintended consequence').

history.meaning: harm, calamity, detriment; to injure or destroy
to harm or frame someone; (colloquial causative) to cause someone to end up in a bad spot (害得...)

morphemes.meaning: to harm; to hurt; to cause trouble for; detriment

害.notes: In everyday spoken dialogue, 害 (especially with 得: 害得我... or 都是你害的!) often translates not as 'maliciously injure', but as 'It's your fault that...' or 'You made me [miss the bus / stay up all night]!'.

rootFamily.gloss: to hurt; to injure; emotional or physical harm
to frame; to entrap; to set someone up
pros and cons; gains and losses; crucial point (literally 'benefit and harm')

家.etymology: Ancient character attested on Shang oracle bones showing a pig/boar (豕) beneath a roof (宀)—as domestic pig-rearing and ancestral offerings under a roof defined a settled household: 'home, family, household; specialist (-ist, as in 画家, 作家); classifier for families, shops, or companies'.

history.meaning: roof over a domesticated pig = household, family, home
home; family; specialist suffix; classifier for businesses/households

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 家 (via 萌典)

家人.etymology: Compound noun of 家 ('family, household') + 人 ('person, members'): 'family members, one's family, household'. Attested since the Yijing (Hexagram 37 家人) and Mencius.

history.stage: Old & Classical Chinese (Yijing, Mencius) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: members of the household; family

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 家人 (via 萌典)

家具.etymology: Compound noun of 家 ('home, household') + 具 ('utensils, implements, furnishings', originally two hands holding a vessel/shell): 'household furniture'. Attested from Tang–Song texts onward.

history.meaning: household furnishings; furniture

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 家具 (via 萌典)

家境.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound combining 家 (jiā, 'family, household') and 境 (jìng, 'boundary, territory, circumstances, condition', originally an earthen border marker 土 + 竟). Attested in Song–Qing literary and vernacular writings to denote the material and social conditions of a household, especially its level of wealth or poverty.

history.meaning: the material condition or economic circumstances of a household
family financial background; socioeconomic circumstances of one's family

morphemes.meaning: circumstances; condition; situation (as in 处境)

家境.notes: Specifically refers to a family's economic/material standing (commonly collocated with 富裕 fùyù 'well-off', 优渥 yōuwò 'privileged/affluent', or 贫寒 pínhán 'impoverished'), whereas 家教 (jiājiào) refers to 'family upbringing/manners' and 家世 (jiāshì) refers to 'family lineage/pedigree'.

rootFamily.gloss: family lineage; ancestral pedigree and social standing

家希.etymology: A two-character Chinese personal given name (名, míng) combining 家 (jiā, 'family, home, clan; specialist') and 希 (xī, 'to hope, to aspire to; rare and precious', from Old Chinese *qʰəj). Together, 家希 evokes 'the hope and precious treasure of the family'. In the television drama *Behind the Scenes* (幕后之王), it is the given name of the character 律家希 (Lǜ Jiāxī).

history.meaning: classical characters meaning 'family/household' (家) and 'to hope for; rare' (希)
modern Chinese personal given name evoking 'the hope/treasure of the family'

家希.notes: In Chinese two-character given names, the first character (like 家) often serves either as a generational poem character (字辈 zìbèi) shared by cousins or as a warm familial anchor, while the second character (希 'hope') expresses the parents' personal wish for the child.

家庭.etymology: A coordinative compound (並立式) combining 家 (jiā, 'house, clan, household', graphically a roof 宀 over a sacrificial pig 豕) and 庭 (tíng, 'courtyard, hall', originally the open court before a main hall). Attested in Classical and Six Dynasties texts (such as the Book of Han and Tang poetry) in the literal spatial sense of 'house and courtyard' or 'domestic quarters', and later reinforced via Meiji Japanese 家庭 (katei, translating English 'home' and 'family') to denote the modern nuclear family unit and domestic environment.

history.meaning: the house and courtyard; domestic quarters of an estate
home, household, family unit (translating Western 'home/family')
family, household, domestic sphere

家庭.notes: Unlike 家人 (family members), 家庭 refers to the family as a social unit, institution, or domestic environment (e.g., 原生家庭 'family of origin', 家庭背景 'family background').

家里.etymology: Locative compound combining 家 ('home, family') + 里 (裡, 'inside', neutral tone li): 'at home, in the family, home'.

history.meaning: at home; inside the house; one's family

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 家里 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: gate of one's house; one's family or clan

家门.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正式) compound formed from 家 (jiā, 'house, family estate') modifying 門 / 门 (mén, 'double-leaf gate, doorway'). In Classical Chinese (attested from the Zhou and Han periods, e.g., Kongzi Jiayu and Records of the Grand Historian), 家門 denoted both the physical outer gate of a residence and, by metonymy, the lineage, social standing, and reputation of an entire clan (as in 光耀家門 'bring glory to the family gate/name'). In modern colloquial Mandarin, it retains both the physical doorstep sense and the figurative clan/school sense (as in 自报家门 'announce one's lineage or background').

history.meaning: outer gate of a family residence; by extension, a family clan and its reputation
front gate of home, doorstep; family background or professional affiliation

家门.notes: Often appears in the idiom 自报家门 (zì bào jiāmén, originally a martial arts or opera trope of announcing one's master and clan, now used in workplaces when introducing one's department or company).

rootFamily.gloss: front entrance of home, right outside one's door
family ethos, clan tradition and upbringing
prominent aristocratic clan or prestigious family

家门口.etymology: A three-character nested modifier-head (偏正式) compound built by affixing 口 (kǒu, literally 'mouth', used spatially for an opening, aperture, or entranceway) to 家门 (jiāmén, 'home gate/door'). Emerging in early Mandarin vernacular (白话), the spatial suffix 口 shifts the focus from the physical door leaves (门) to the immediate threshold area and vicinity right outside one's residence.

history.meaning: threshold area and immediate space outside the home gate
front entrance of home; figuratively, one's own neighborhood or home turf

家门口.notes: Frequently used both literally ('waiting at the front entrance') and figuratively to mean 'right in one's own backyard/hometown' (e.g., 在家门口办比赛 'hosting a competition on home turf').

rootFamily.gloss: front gate of home, family lineage

容.etymology: Graphically a roof radical (宀, mián) over 谷 (gǔ, 'valley'), originally depicting a cavernous structure or spacious valley capable of holding and receiving contents (Old Chinese *loŋ, Middle Chinese yowng). From its primary verbal sense 'to contain, hold, accommodate', it developed the nominal sense of 'that which holds or manifests inner spirit'—hence 'carriage, demeanor, countenance, facial appearance' (already well attested in the Classic of Poetry and Book of Rites, e.g., 容貌 róngmào). In contemporary entertainment and beauty contexts, 容 acts as a bound or semi-free nominal morpheme referring specifically to facial features and cosmetic appearance (as in 整容 zhěngróng 'plastic surgery' and 毁容 huǐróng 'disfigurement').

history.meaning: to contain, accommodate; ceremonial bearing and deportment
facial countenance, visage, physical appearance
facial appearance, cosmetic look (especially in compounds like 整容, 美容)

容.notes: In showbiz and everyday speech, 容 as 'face/visage' is frequently detached in separable verb-object constructions like 整了个容 ('had some cosmetic work done').

rootFamily.gloss: cosmetic surgery, plastic surgery (literally 'adjust the visage')

容不下.etymology: A negative potential verb-complement (动补式可能补语) construction composed of the verb root 容 (róng, 'to contain, hold, tolerate, accommodate'), the negative infix 不 (bù, 'not, unable to'), and the directional/resultative complement 下 (xià, indicating sufficient capacity to fit or settle something down inside a space). Literally 'unable to fit [someone/something] inside', it evolved in vernacular Mandarin to express emotional, social, or institutional intolerance—having no room to brook a rival, dissent, or flaw.

history.meaning: physically unable to hold or fit within a space; unable to tolerate or accommodate
history.stage: Early Mandarin Vernacular to Modern Mandarin

morphemes.meaning: resultative complement of spatial capacity (fit down in)

容不下.notes: Common in dramatic and workplace dialogue in the pattern 眼里容不下沙子 ('cannot tolerate a single grain of sand in one's eye'—i.e., uncompromising toward flaws or betrayal) or 一山容不下二虎 ('one mountain cannot hold two tigers').

rootFamily.gloss: to tolerate, forgive, be lenient toward

容易.etymology: Coordinative adjective compound of 容 ('allow, accommodate, leisurely') + 易 (yì, 'easy, effortless'). Attested since Han texts (such as Dongfang Shuo's 谈何容易 'how could it be so easy to speak of?').

history.stage: Han Classical Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: easy; not difficult; likely/apt to

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 容易 (via 萌典)

宽.etymology: Phono-semantic/ideographic character (traditional 寬, combining roof 宀 + 萈 huán, a wild goat with wide-curving horns): 'wide, broad (opposite of 窄 'narrow'); spacious; lenient, relax/relieve (宽心)'.

history.meaning: spacious house; broad; lenient; generous
wide; broad; spacious; lenient

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 宽 (via 萌典)

宽度.etymology: Abstract measurement noun combining 宽 ('wide, broad') + 度 ('measure, degree, dimension'): 'width, breadth'.

history.meaning: width; breadth

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 宽度 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: extension of a deadline, grace period (literary)
to extend a deadline, grant grace time

宽限.etymology: A verb-object or causative-modifier compound formed from 寬 / 宽 (kuān, 'wide, broad, lenient; to relax or widen') and 限 (xiàn, 'threshold, boundary, time limit, deadline'). Attested in Tang, Song, and Yuan administrative and vernacular texts, it literally means 'to widen or relax the boundary/deadline'—hence granting a debtor or subordinate an extension of time to fulfill an obligation.

history.meaning: to relax a statutory deadline or grant administrative leniency on a time limit
to grant an extension, allow extra grace time (for payment or delivery)

morphemes.meaning: wide, lenient; to broaden or relax

宽限.notes: Typically used in polite pleas followed by a duration complement, e.g., 请再宽限几天 ('Please grant me a few more days' grace').

寄.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 宀 ('house, lodging') + 奇 (qí/jì phonetic): originally 'lodge temporarily at another's house, entrust to someone's care', and by extension 'send, mail, post (letters or parcels); depend on'.

history.meaning: lodge temporarily; entrust; transmit
mail; send by post; entrust

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 寄 (via 萌典)

寄件人.etymology: '寄件人' (jìjiànrén, sender) is a compound formed by '寄' (to send, to entrust), '件' (item, mail), and '人' (person). '寄' originally meant to entrust something to a temporary residence or to rely on someone, evolving in the postal context to mean sending goods or letters via a courier. The classifier '件' became associated with discrete items of mail or parcels. This standardized term emerged with the establishment of modern postal systems in China during the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It remains the formal designation on all mail and packages.

history.meaning: recipient

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 寄件人

密码.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正式) compound combining 密 (mì, 'dense, covert, secret, confidential') and 碼 / 码 (mǎ, originally 'agate stone' 瑪瑙, later adopted in Ming–Qing commercial vernacular for counting tallies and numerical symbols, 號碼). Coined in late Qing and Republican China during the adoption of telegraphy and cryptography to mean 'secret telegraph/cipher code', it subsequently became the standard term for numeric PINs, digital passwords, and figuratively the 'secret key' to success (e.g., 流量密码 'the secret code to web traffic/ratings').

history.meaning: secret cipher or telegraphic codeBook symbols
password, access code, PIN; figurative key or formula for success

密码.notes: In media and TV production (like Behind the Scenes), 流量密码 ('traffic password') and 收视密码 ('ratings password') are ubiquitous industry buzzwords for a guaranteed hit formula.

cognates.meaning: wealthy second-generation youth in China (borrowed from Mandarin)

富二代.etymology: A modern modifier-head (偏正式) neologism formed by prefixing 富 (fù, 'wealthy, affluent') to 二代 (èrdài, 'second generation'). Popularized in mainland Chinese media around 2007–2008 as the children of the first wave of post-1978 Reform and Opening-Up (改革开放) private entrepreneurs came of age, the term designates the privileged heirs of nouveau-riche family fortunes, and quickly spawned a productive morphological template X二代 (such as 星二代 'celebrity offspring' and 官二代 'children of officials').

history.meaning: second-generation heirs of China's post-reform private entrepreneurs; privileged wealthy youth

富二代.notes: Carries strong cultural connotations in Chinese dramas and public discourse—often stereotyping spoiled, flashy heirs, unless explicitly contrasted with a hardworking heir who tries to prove themselves independently.

富人.etymology: A transparent modifier-head (偏正式) compound combining 富 (fù, 'abundant, wealthy', graphically a roof 宀 over 畐, depicting a full wine jar signifying material abundance) and 人 (rén, 'person'). Attested in Classical Chinese philosophical and historical texts (such as the Guanzi and Records of the Grand Historian) in direct contrast to 貧人 / 穷人 (pínrén / qióngrén, 'poor person'), it has remained the unmarked everyday noun for a wealthy person across two millennia.

history.meaning: person of abundant wealth and property
wealthy person, rich people (as a socioeconomic class)

富人.notes: Neutral and everyday in register; unlike 富豪 (tycoon/magnate) or the slang 土豪 (nouveau riche spender), 富人 simply refers to wealthy people in general (e.g., 富人区 'wealthy neighborhood').

富豪.etymology: A coordinative compound (並立式) uniting 富 (fù, 'wealthy, affluent') and 豪 (háo, originally 'porcupine with long quills', extended in Classical Chinese to mean 'outstanding, heroic, powerful, or domineering clan'). First attested in Six Dynasties and Tang histories (such as the Book of Jin) to describe powerful local magnates who combined vast wealth (富) with formidable clan clout (豪), it now denotes ultra-wealthy tycoons and billionaires (e.g., 亿万富豪).

history.meaning: wealthy and powerful local clan leader or magnate
wealthy tycoon, magnate, multimillionaire or billionaire

morphemes.meaning: powerful, heroic, eminent person or clan leader

富豪.notes: Denotes top-tier elite wealth (often paired with 榜 as in 富豪榜 'rich list / Forbes billionaire ranking'), whereas 富人 is the ordinary word for rich people.

rootFamily.gloss: powerful and influential elite clan or family

cognates.meaning: cold study window; hardship of scholarly study

寒窗.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正式) compound combining 寒 (hán, 'cold, freezing, impoverished') and 窗 (chuāng, 'window'). Originally depicting the chilly, unheated study window by which an impoverished scholar read day and night, it was immortalized by the Yuan dynasty playwright Gao Ming in The Lute (琵琶記, Pípá Jì): 十年寒窗無人問，一舉成名天下知 ('For ten years by the cold window no one asks after you; once you win fame in the imperial exams, the whole world knows your name'). By metonymy, 寒窗 came to mean years of arduous, solitary study.

history.meaning: chilly window of a humble room (in Tang poetry)
the arduous, impoverished years spent studying for the imperial examinations
years of diligent, painstaking study (especially preparing for high-stakes exams or a career)

寒窗.notes: Almost always used in literary or emphatic collocations like 十年寒窗 ('ten years of arduous study') or 寒窗苦读 ('studying bitterly by the cold window'); fellow students who endured this together are called 同窗 ('window-mates / classmates').

rootFamily.gloss: humble or impoverished family background (literally 'cold gate')

寸.etymology: An ancient indicative character 寸 (cùn) created in Warring States and Qin–Han script by adding a single marker stroke just below the wrist of the hand graph 又, pointing to the pulse point roughly one thumb-width (~3.3 cm) from the palm—where traditional physicians felt the 寸口 pulse! Ten 分 made one 寸, and ten 寸 made one 尺 ('foot'). Beyond traditional carpentry and tailoring, 一寸 ('a single inch') thrives in idioms for tiny distances.

morphemes.meaning: one thumb-width / pulse-point distance from the hand 又 = Chinese inch

history.meaning: pulse-point unit: one-tenth of a foot (尺)
Chinese inch (~3.33 cm); tiny distance

寸步不离.etymology: A four-character Classical idiom (成语) structured as a topic/measure-modified negated verb phrase: 寸步 (cùnbù, 'an inch-long step, the tiniest step', where 寸 'inch' modifies 步 'pace/step') + 不离 / 不離 (bù lí, 'not depart from, not leave'). Attested from Tang-dynasty Buddhist Chan records and Ming–Qing vernacular novels (such as Water Margin and Dream of the Red Chamber), it literally means 'not departing by even a single inch of a step', describing unwavering physical proximity or protective shadowing.

history.meaning: not moving even a tiny step away; staying constantly by someone's side
history.stage: Medieval and Early Modern Vernacular Chinese

history.meaning: never leave someone's side, follow or guard closely without a moment's separation

寸步不离.notes: Often modifies verbs like 守着 ('guarding') or 跟着 ('following'), e.g., 保镖寸步不离地跟着他 ('The bodyguard followed him without leaving his side for a second').

rootFamily.gloss: unable to move a single step (due to obstacles or difficulty)

对.etymology: Originally 對 (showing a hand 寸 holding a lush upright stand/chisel 丵): in Classical Chinese 'respond/reply to a superior, face toward, match as a pair'. In Mandarin it means 'correct, right!; pair/couple (classifier); treat/face; preposition toward/to'.

history.meaning: answer; face toward; matched pair
right/correct; pair; toward/to; match/check

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 对 (via 萌典)

对不上.etymology: A negative potential verb-complement (动补式可能补语) construction composed of 对 / 對 (duì, 'to match, align, check one thing against another'), the negative potential infix 不 (bù, 'cannot, fail to'), and the resultative complement 上 (shàng, indicating successful contact, alignment, or connection). Literally 'unable to align into contact', it describes two accounts, schedules, lip movements/audio tracks, or ledger figures failing to match up.

history.meaning: unable to align, match, or fit together properly

morphemes.meaning: resultative complement of successful contact or alignment

对不上.notes: In TV/film production and detective plots alike, 对不上 is heavily used for accounts/alibis that don't add up (口供对不上), schedules that don't align (时间对不上), or audio/lip-sync mismatch (口型对不上).

rootFamily.gloss: to verify, check and compare (accounts, scripts, texts)

对不起.etymology: Sincere everyday apology ('I'm sorry'), a potential-complement phrase literally meaning 'unable to face (you) squarely / let you down': 对 ('face, treat rightly') + 不 ('not') + 起 ('measure up'). Standardized in Qing and modern Mandarin alongside its classic reassuring reply 没关系 ('it doesn't matter').

history.meaning: have let someone down; 'I am sorry'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 對不起 (via 萌典)

对了.etymology: A lexicalized discourse marker (话语标记) formed from 对 / 對 (duì, 'correct, right, aligned with reality') plus the sentence-final change-of-state particle 了 (le, signaling a sudden realization or new cognitive state). Originally a full predicate meaning '[Now] that is right / I have just remembered rightly', it grammaticalized in spoken Mandarin into an interjection ('Oh, right!', 'By the way!') used when a speaker suddenly recalls a pertinent point or pivots to a new topic in conversation.

history.meaning: that is correct now; you have got it right
by the way, oh right (discourse marker introducing a newly remembered topic); correct!

对了.notes: Sentence-initially (对了，明天开会...), it always means 'By the way / Oh, right, I just remembered...'; standalone as a response to a guess, it means 'Spot on / That's right!'.

rootFamily.gloss: to apologize, excuse me (literally 'unable to face uprightly')

对事不对人.etymology: A symmetric four-syllable antithesis (对举结构) contrasting two prepositional/verbal phrases: 对事 (duì shì, 'directed at the matter/issue') and 不对人 (bù duì rén, 'not directed at the person'). Built on the Classical and Mandarin directional/relational sense of 对 / 對 ('to face, be directed toward'), this modern workplace and civic maxim encapsulates professional objectivity—evaluating or criticizing the work or problem itself rather than harboring personal animus against the individual involved.

history.meaning: addressing the objective matter rather than targeting the individual personally

morphemes.meaning: face toward, target, be directed at

对事不对人.notes: A staple phrase in Chinese workplace dramas: executives and directors often say 我是对事不对人 ('It's nothing personal, I'm only addressing the work issue') before or after delivering harsh criticism.

rootFamily.gloss: to treat, handle, adopt an attitude toward
regarding, as for, with respect to

cognates.meaning: toward, regarding (equivalent Sino-Japanese root 対する taisuru)

对于.etymology: A compound preposition (介词) formed by combining 对 / 對 (duì, 'to face, answer, be directed toward') with the Classical locative/relational preposition 於 / 于 (yú, 'in, at, to, with regard to'). While 對 alone functioned as a verb and preposition ('facing, toward') in Classical and vernacular Chinese, the disyllabic compound 對於 crystallized in late Qing and May Fourth movement prose—heavily influenced by translations of Japanese に於いて / に対して and European 'as for / regarding / with respect to'—to mark the topic or target of an attitude, evaluation, or situation.

history.meaning: facing toward; standing in relation to (separate verb + preposition in Literary Chinese)
regarding, with respect to, as for (compound topic-marking preposition)

morphemes.meaning: face, be directed toward, correspond to

对于.notes: Unlike 关于 ('concerning/about', which introduces a broad subject matter), 对于 pinpoints the specific entity or target toward which an attitude, effect, or action is directed (often paired with 来说: 对于我们来说 'as far as we are concerned').

rootFamily.gloss: due to, owing to, because of

对付.etymology: A compound verb combining 对 / 對 (duì, 'to match, correspond, face') and 付 (fù, 'to hand over, entrust, bestow'). First attested in Song and Yuan dynasty vernacular texts (such as the Zhuzi Yulei and Yuan zaju plays) in the sense of 'matching together' or 'handing over to meet a need / making do with', it evolved in Ming–Qing vernacular into two main modern senses: (1) 'to cope with, tackle, or counter an adversary or thorny problem' (pronounced duìfu), and (2) 'to make do, get by passably' (in northern colloquial speech).

history.meaning: to match up; to hand over or supply in order to meet a situation
to deal with, counter, or target an opponent/problem; to make do with

对付.notes: When applied to a person (e.g., 他联手外人来对付我 'He teamed up with outsiders to target/deal with me'), 对付 carries an adversarial nuance of 'scheming against, countering, or handling an opponent'; for neutral 'treating' someone, use 对待.

rootFamily.gloss: to cope with, handle perfunctorily or respond to পরিস্থিতি
to treat, adopt a manner toward

对头.etymology: A vernacular compound combining 对 / 對 (duì, 'facing, opposing, matching') and 头 / 頭 (tóu, 'head, chief, end; nominal suffix denoting a person or side'). Emerging in Song, Yuan, and Ming vernacular literature, 对头 originally denoted 'the party standing directly opposite' (whether a marriage match, a partner in a transaction, or an opposing litigant), before specializing into 'adversary, nemesis, arch-rival' (often intensified as 死对头 'mortal enemy / arch-rival'). Note that with a full tone on tóu (duìtóu), it also functions as an adjective meaning 'on the right track, normal, or getting along'.

history.meaning: the party directly opposite in a match, dispute, or transaction; an opponent
rival, adversary, nemesis (duìtou); correct, normal, on good terms (duìtóu)

对头.notes: Pay close attention to tone and stress: with neutral tone (duìtou, often in 死对头), it is a noun meaning 'rival/nemesis'; with second tone (duìtóu, often negated as 不对头), it is an adjective meaning 'right/normal/amiss'.

rootFamily.gloss: wrong, amiss, fishy (literally 'not aligned at the head')

cognates.meaning: playing a board game (Go or shogi) face-to-face; a match
playing a game of Go/chess; a match of strategy

对局.etymology: A verb-object / modifier-head compound formed from 对 / 對 (duì, 'to face each other across') and 局 (jú, originally 'chessboard, game board layout', and by extension 'a match, game of strategy, or structured situation'). Attested in Tang and Song dynasty prose and poetry describing two players sitting opposite each other over a Go (围棋) or Xiangqi board, it denotes both a formal board-game match and, metaphorically in business and politics, a high-stakes strategic face-off.

history.meaning: to sit opposite an opponent playing Go or chess; a board-game match
match, game of strategy; strategic face-off or round of competition

morphemes.meaning: chessboard, game of strategy, overall situation

对局.notes: Originated in Go (围棋) and chess terminology, so when used in business or showbiz dramas it evokes a calculated battle of wits between master strategists.

rootFamily.gloss: overall situation, big picture, strategic scale
situation, state of affairs, aspect of a game/struggle
ending, outcome, finale (of a drama or match)

cognates.meaning: to face and receive; to treat (literary)
to treat, deal with; relative opposition

对待.etymology: A coordinative verb compound (並立式) combining 对 / 對 (duì, 'to face, respond to, stand in relation to') and 待 (dài, 'to wait upon, receive, treat, behave toward'). In Classical and Medieval Buddhist and philosophical texts, 對待 denoted 'correlative opposition' (how complementary concepts like light and dark stand in relation to each other), while in vernacular Chinese the sense of 待 ('to treat or receive a person') predominated, yielding the modern meaning 'to treat, handle, or adopt a particular attitude toward someone or something'.

history.meaning: to stand as correlative opposites; to face and receive someone
to treat, behave toward, approach (a person, work, or problem) with a certain attitude

对待.notes: Frequently modified by manner expressions like 认真对待 ('treat seriously/conscientiously'), 公平对待 ('treat fairly'), or 区别对待 ('treat differently / discriminate').

rootFamily.gloss: treatment, pay and benefits, social standing accorded to someone
to receive and attend to (guests, clients, delegations)
to look forward to, anticipate eagerly

对手.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正式) compound combining 对 / 對 (duì, 'opposing, matching, facing across') and 手 (shǒu, 'hand', extended metonymically in Classical and Medieval Chinese to mean 'person of skill, player, practitioner', as in 高手 'master hand' or 棋手 'chess player'). Already attested in the Book of Jin (晋书) and Tang poetry, 對手 originally meant 'a player of equal skill matched against another' (especially in board games or martial arts), and broadened to mean any competitor, rival, or worthy opponent.

history.meaning: an opponent of equal skill in a game or martial contest; a worthy match
rival, competitor, opponent; someone on par with one's abilities

对手.notes: In film and television acting, 对手戏 (duìshǒuxì) specifically refers to a 'one-on-one dramatic scene between two co-stars' where both actors play off each other's energy.

rootFamily.gloss: dramatic scene shared between two interacting actors

对接.etymology: A coordinative / resultative verb compound formed from 对 / 對 (duì, 'to align, point face-to-face, match up') and 接 (jiē, 'to connect, join, link, receive'). Originally used in carpentry, rail/bridge engineering, and later aerospace (such as spacecraft orbital docking, 空间对接) to mean 'joining two ends directly together in precise alignment', it underwent rapid semantic extension in 21st-century Chinese corporate, media, and administrative jargon to mean 'interfacing directly, coordinating workflows, or linking up designated points of contact between two teams'.

history.meaning: to join or couple two mechanical ends face-to-face; spacecraft docking
to coordinate directly with, interface between teams, align resources or contacts

对接.notes: A quintessential Chinese workplace and media-production verb: 跟你对接的人 ('your point of contact / the person interfacing with you') and 对接资源 ('matching up/integrating resources').

rootFamily.gloss: to hand over and take over duties or assets

cognates.meaning: the opposite side, the other party (archaic/legal; modern 相手 aite)
the other party, the opposite side (compare 상대방 sangdaebang)

对方.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正式) compound combining 对 / 對 (duì, 'opposite, facing across') and 方 (fāng, 'direction, side, party'). In Classical Chinese (such as the Zhuangzi and medical classics), 對方 meant 'the opposite direction' or 'matching a medical prescription (方) to an illness'. In modern Mandarin—reinforced by legal, diplomatic, and sports usage—it denotes 'the other side/party' in any bilateral interaction, conversation, contract, or competition.

history.meaning: the opposite direction; matching a medicinal formula to symptoms
the other party, the opposing side, one's interlocutor or counterpart

morphemes.meaning: direction, side, party in an interaction

对方.notes: Serves as a versatile, gender-neutral third-person reference for 'the other person/side' in negotiations, phone prompts (对方正在通话中 'the other party is on another call'), and sports/business rivalries.

rootFamily.gloss: both sides, both parties (in a contract or dispute)
party A / the client commissioning a project (crucial in media/agency work)

cognates.meaning: target, object (of study, action, or interest)
target, object, subject of interest or action

对象.etymology: A compound combining 对 / 對 (duì, 'facing, standing opposite, corresponding to') and 象 (xiàng, 'image, form, phenomenon, manifestation'). In medieval Chinese Buddhist epistemology and classical prose, 對象 referred to the 'external form or sensory phenomenon standing opposite consciousness'. During the Meiji era, Japanese scholars repurposed 対象 (taishō) to translate German Gegenstand / Objekt ('philosophical or scientific object of cognition or action'). Re-imported into modern Mandarin as a return graphic loan, 对象 came to mean both 'target, recipient, or subject (of an interview, service, or policy)' and, colloquially in mainland China since the mid-20th century, 'target of courtship—i.e., a romantic partner, boyfriend, or girlfriend'.

history.meaning: sensory form or phenomenon standing opposite the mind; matched manifestation
object of cognition, investigation, or action (translating German Objekt / Gegenstand)
target, recipient, interviewee (formal); romantic partner, date, boy/girlfriend (colloquial)

对象.notes: Has a famous register split: in professional/media contexts, 采访对象 is 'interviewee' and 服务对象 is 'target clientele'; in everyday life, 找对象 ('looking for a partner') and 有对象了 ('taken / in a relationship') refer to romance.

rootFamily.gloss: impression, mental image left by someone or something

cognates.meaning: mutual confrontation and cross-examination of witnesses; hostage (historical)
face-to-face confrontation and questioning of parties

对质.etymology: A Classical verb-object / coordinative legal compound formed from 对 / 對 (duì, 'to face each other directly') and 质 / 質 (zhì, 'to question, verify, substantiate, pledge as testimony'). First attested in Han and Six Dynasties historical and judicial records (where opposing plaintiffs, defendants, or witnesses were brought face-to-face before a magistrate to verify conflicting statements), it remains the standard term in law and high-drama confrontations for cross-examining or confronting someone face-to-face with evidence.

history.meaning: to bring opposing parties or witnesses face-to-face in court to verify testimony
to confront face-to-face, cross-examine conflicting accounts in person

morphemes.meaning: face each other directly, match accounts

对质.notes: Frequently used in the phrase 当面对质 ('confront and verify accounts face-to-face') when someone is suspected of lying or spreading rumors behind another's back.

rootFamily.gloss: to call into question, challenge the truth or validity of
to interrogate, question sternly, demand an explanation

对面.etymology: Locative and relational noun combining 对 ('face directly across') + 面 ('face, side'): 'opposite, across from, right in front, the other side'.

history.stage: Tang–Song poetry & vernacular to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: face-to-face; across the way; opposite side

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 对面 (via 萌典)

寻宝.etymology: A compact verb-object compound pairing 寻 (xún, simplified from 尋, originally an arm-span measure that evolved into 'to trace along, search for, seek') and 宝 (bǎo, 'treasure'). Modeled on classical verb-object patterns like 寻访 ('seek out and visit') and 寻根 ('search for one's roots'), 寻宝 became the standard lively Mandarin expression for treasure hunting in stories, games, and neighborhood clue walks.

history.meaning: search for + precious object
hunt for treasure; go on a treasure hunt

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 寻宝

cognates.meaning: guiding teacher, spiritual mentor, officiating Buddhist priest
guiding master, mentor, officiating Buddhist monk

导师.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正式) compound combining 導 / 导 (dǎo, 'to lead, guide along a path', formed from 道 'way/path' + 寸 'hand/thumb') and 師 / 师 (shī, 'master, teacher, exemplar'). Originally coined in early Chinese Buddhist translations (such as the Lotus Sutra and Vimalakirti Sutra, translating Sanskrit nāyaka or śāstṛ) to denote a 'guiding master who leads sentient beings onto the path of enlightenment', it was secularized in modern Chinese universities for 'graduate thesis advisor' (博士生导师) and later popularized across television talent competition shows (such as The Voice of China) to translate English 'celebrity mentor / coach'.

history.meaning: spiritual master who guides beings onto the Buddhist path (translating Sanskrit nāyaka)
academic research advisor; visionary leader or ideological guide
academic supervisor, career mentor, or celebrity coach/judge on a TV talent show

morphemes.meaning: lead, guide, direct along a way

导师.notes: In contemporary Chinese variety and music reality shows, 导师 is the universal title for the celebrity panelist/coach who selects and trains contestants.

rootFamily.gloss: director (of a film, drama, or broadcast)

导播室.etymology: A three-character modifier-head (偏正式) media compound formed by suffixing 室 (shì, 'room, chamber, studio office') to 导播 (dǎobō, 'broadcast director / live television switching', itself a compression of 指导广播 / 导演播出 'directing the broadcast'). Coined with the rise of modern radio and multi-camera live television broadcasting in the 20th century, 导播室 designates the broadcast control room (PCR/MCR) where the broadcast director monitors camera feeds, cues graphics and audio, and switches live signals.

history.meaning: broadcast control room / production control gallery in radio and television studios

导播室.notes: In television production dramas like Behind the Scenes (幕后之王), the 导播室 is the nerve center of every live show, distinct from the 演播室 / 演播厅 (the studio stage floor where hosts and performers appear).

rootFamily.gloss: broadcast director; to direct and switch a live broadcast

cognates.meaning: film or stage director; to direct a performance

导演.etymology: Originally a verb-object / coordinative compound combining 導 / 导 (dǎo, 'to guide, direct, instruct') and 演 (yǎn, originally 'water flowing out far', extended in Classical Chinese to 'expound, elaborate, practice exercises', and since Tang–Song theater to 'perform, act out on stage'). Adopted in early 20th-century Chinese spoken drama (话剧) and silent cinema circles (pioneered by figures like Hong Shen and Zheng Zhengqiu in the 1920s) to translate Western 'stage/film director', it functions both as a verb ('to direct a performance') and as a noun ('director').

history.meaning: to guide and rehearse a theatrical or cinematic performance; stage/film director
director (of film, television, stage, or variety shows); to direct (a production or figuratively a staged scheme)

morphemes.meaning: perform, act out, stage a production

导演.notes: On set and in production offices, a director is addressed by surname + 导 (e.g., 张导 'Director Zhang'), and the chief showrunner/director of a large TV variety show is the 总导演 ('Chief Director').

rootFamily.gloss: to perform, act; performance, acting skill

导演组.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正式) compound formed by attaching the organizational collective noun 组 / 組 (zǔ, originally 'woven silk cord or ribbon', extended in modern Chinese to 'organized group, section, crew, or team') to 导演 (dǎoyǎn, 'director'). In modern Chinese film and especially large-scale television variety production, 导演组 denotes the entire directing department—comprising the chief director (总导演), executive directors (执行导演), segment/field directors, and assistant directors—who plan, script, and execute the show.

history.meaning: the directing team or crew unit responsible for directing a film, drama, or broadcast program

morphemes.meaning: group, team, crew section (originally 'braided silk cord')

导演组.notes: In Chinese variety and reality TV production, 导演组 is a massive behind-the-scenes team that handles everything from guest briefing and game design to cueing storylines on set—often contrasted with 制片组 (production/logistics management) and 摄像组 (camera crew).

rootFamily.gloss: director; to direct a show or film
film or drama cast and crew unit

cognates.meaning: to guide and bring to; to induce (literary)
to lead to, result in, cause

导致.etymology: A verb-complement / coordinative compound combining 導 / 导 (dǎo, 'to channel, guide, lead along a path') and 致 (zhì, 'to cause to arrive, bring about, deliver to a destination'). In Classical and Medieval Chinese (such as the Book of Jin and Song dynasty essays), 導致 had a positive or neutral literal meaning of 'guiding and bringing [people, tribute, or vital qi] to a desired state or place'. In modern Mandarin, it grammaticalized into a formal causative verb meaning 'to lead to, result in, precipitate', most commonly introducing an unfavorable or unintended outcome.

history.meaning: to guide and bring someone or something to a destination or desired condition
to lead to, result in, bring about (predominantly negative or problematic consequences)

morphemes.meaning: channel, lead, guide along a pathway
cause to arrive, bring about, result in

导致.notes: In contemporary usage, 导致 usually introduces negative or problematic consequences (e.g., 导致节目停播 'led to the show being taken off the air', 导致误会 'caused a misunderstanding'); for positive outcomes, prefer 促成 ('help bring about') or 带来 ('bring').

rootFamily.gloss: to cause, result in (formal/written, often in 以致 'so much so that')
to devote oneself to, dedicate efforts toward
trigger, fuse, immediate cause of an incident (literally 'fire-guiding cord')

封.etymology: Ancient ideogram attested on Shang oracle bones showing a hand/measure (寸) planting trees (丰/木) on an earthen mound (土) to mark a fief boundary: 'enfeoff, confer a title; seal up, close securely; envelope' and the standard classifier for letters (一封信).

history.meaning: mound with boundary trees = fief, boundary, seal up
seal; close; envelope; classifier for letters

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 封 (via 萌典)

封杀.etymology: Coordinative-resultative compound of 封 (fēng, Old Chinese *poŋ, originally to heap earth and plant trees on a boundary mound, hence to seal off or blockade) and 杀 (殺, shā, OC *srad, to kill, extinguish, or put out). First coined in Japanese baseball jargon as 封殺 (fūsatsu, translating English "force out", where a baserunner is cut off from a base and put out) and board-game terminology (sealing off an opponent's move), it entered Mandarin sports vocabulary in the 20th century and was metaphorically extended in Hong Kong, Taiwanese, and Mainland entertainment media to mean blacklisting or banning a public figure from broadcast and commercial work.

history.meaning: to seal off boundaries (fēng) and to slay or extinguish (shā) as separate Classical Chinese verbs
to force out a baserunner in baseball or seal off an opponent's piece in board games
to blacklist, ban from broadcasts, or shut an artist out of the entertainment industry

封杀.notes: High-frequency showbiz and media term (e.g., 遭封杀 "to get blacklisted", 全面封杀 "a total ban"); stronger and more institutional than 拉黑 (to block on social media).

rootFamily.gloss: to seal and lock down, to blockade
to close down (a newspaper or venue); to block (a shot)
to wipe out, to obliterate (credit or talent)

封皮.etymology: Combines 封 (fēng, originally planting boundary trees on an earthen mound to seal off a fief, hence 'to seal, enclose, wrap') and 皮 (pí, 'skin, hide, outer layer'). Originally denoting the paper wrapper or sealing strip pasted over an official parcel or book bundle in Ming–Qing administration, 封皮 came to mean the protective outer cover or binding of any book, ledger, or notebook.

history.meaning: sealing strip or outer paper wrapper on a packet
book cover; notebook jacket

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 封皮

封面.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 封 (fēng, to seal, wrap, or bind a document or volume) and 面 (miàn, face, outer surface, front side). In Ming and Qing bookbinding and official chancellery practice, 封面 referred either to the outer sealing wrapper of an envelope or to the protective paper sheet pasted over the front face of a thread-bound volume (线装书) bearing the title slip. With the rise of modern printing and periodical publishing in the late 19th and 20th centuries, the term shifted to denote the front cover of a book, magazine, or album, as well as a digital cover image or thumbnail.

history.meaning: outer face of a sealed official envelope or protective front wrapper of a thread-bound book
front cover of a book or magazine; cover image or video thumbnail in modern media

morphemes.meaning: to seal, wrap, bind a volume

封面.notes: In media and entertainment, commonly appears in 封面人物 (cover star/feature subject), 上封面 (to make the front cover), and video-platform 封面图 (thumbnail image).

rootFamily.gloss: back cover of a book or magazine
page layout or newspaper page surface

将.etymology: Phono-semantic character (將, combining 爿 qiáng phonetic + 肉/夕 'meat' + 寸 'hand'): originally 'take/offer meat in hand -> escort, support, lead'. Read jiāng as an adverb ('be about to, will soon'), pre-verbal disposal/instrument marker (like 把), and verb ('take'); read jiàng as 'military general; check in chess'.

history.meaning: escort, hold, about to (jiāng); military commander (jiàng)
will/about to; formal disposal preposition (jiāng); general (jiàng)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 将 (via 萌典)

将功折罪.etymology: Four-character serial-verb idiom (成语) structured as an instrumental phrase 将功 (jiāng gōng, "taking/by means of meritorious service") followed by a verb-object phrase 折罪 (zhé zuì, "to offset or commute a crime/fault"). Here 将 (將, jiāng) functions in its medieval vernacular instrumental sense ("with, using"), while 折 (zhé) carries its legal-commercial sense of "to balance against, discount, commute". Originating in Song–Ming military and judicial discourse (attested in *Water Margin* 水浒传 and Ming official memorials alongside variants like 将功赎罪 and 将功补过), it described allowing a disgraced official or condemned soldier to cancel out prior punishment through subsequent valor.

history.form: 將功折罪 / 將功贖罪
history.meaning: to commute a legal sentence or military offense by rendering meritorious battle service
to make amends or atone for a mistake by performing good service

将功折罪.notes: Interchangeable in workplace and drama dialogue with 将功补过 (make up for a fault with good deeds) and 将功赎罪 (redeem a crime through merit); often used semi-jokingly when someone messes up a project and offers to fix it.

rootFamily.gloss: to make up for a fault through subsequent merit
to atone for a crime by meritorious service
achievement and fault, merits and demerits

将就.etymology: Coordinative verbal compound of 将 (將, jiāng, originally to escort, support, or bring along) and 就 (jiù, to approach, move toward, accommodate oneself to).
