Emerging in Tang and Song vernacular and literary prose (e.g., Bai Juyi's poetry, Zhu Xi's *Zhuzi Yulei*, and Yuan *zájù* dramas), 将就 originally meant to move partway toward someone or adapt oneself to existing conditions. Over time, the second syllable weakened to a neutral tone in Mandarin (jiāngjiu), and the meaning specialized into "making do with", "putting up with something less than ideal", or "settling for a compromise".

history.meaning: to accommodate oneself to, yield toward, or adapt to circumstances
to make do with, put up with, settle for what is available

morphemes.meaning: to approach, move toward, adapt to

将就.notes: Often used with 着 (将就着吃/用 "make do with eating/using it for now") or negated in romance/career contexts as 不将就 ("refuse to settle for second best").

rootFamily.gloss: to yield to, to accommodate someone's wishes
to make do with, to pass muster (colloquial northern Mandarin)
to take care of, to nurse or humor someone

将来.etymology: Modifier-head verbal phrase lexicalized into a temporal noun, composed of 将 (將, jiāng, prospective adverb "about to, going to", grammaticalized from the verb "to advance/bring") and 来 (來, lái, Old Chinese *m-rˤək, to come, arrive). Literally "that which is about to come". Attested as a two-character sequence in Classical and Six Dynasties texts (such as *Zhuangzi*, *Xunzi*, and Tao Yuanming's prose) referring to events or times about to arrive, it solidified across East Asian Sinographic languages (compare Japanese *shōrai*, Korean *jangnae*) as the standard noun and adverb for "the future".

history.meaning: about to come; times or events that are approaching hereafter
the future (noun); in the future (temporal adverb)

将来.notes: Unlike 未来 (wèilái, "the future" as an abstract or philosophical realm, which can modify nouns like 未来世界), 将来 is most often used adverbially before a verb or subject ("in the future, someday") or as a standalone time noun.

rootFamily.gloss: originally, at first; as it turns out

尊严.etymology: Coordinative compound of 尊 (zūn, originally a ritual bronze wine vessel 樽 held aloft in both hands, extended to lofty, noble, revered) and 严 (嚴, yán, stern, solemn, awe-inspiring). In Classical Chinese (attested in *Xunzi*, *Records of the Grand Historian*, and Han prose), 尊严 served primarily as a stative verb or adjective describing the imposing majesty and solemn authority of monarchs, ritual law, or elders. During the late 19th and early 20th centuries—reinforced by Meiji Japanese 尊厳 (songen) translating Western philosophical and legal concepts of Latin *dignitas* and German *Würde*—it acquired its modern nominal sense of personal dignity, self-respect, and inviolable human worth.

history.meaning: majestic, solemn, awe-inspiring, lofty in rank or authority
dignity, sanctity, self-respect (abstract noun)

尊严.notes: Commonly collocates with 维护 (uphold dignity), 伤自尊/伤尊严 (wound one's dignity), and 有尊严地活着 (live with dignity).

尊敬.etymology: Coordinate honorific compound of 尊 ('revere; honour', originally two hands 廾 offering a ceremonial wine vessel 酋) + 敬 ('respect; be reverent and attentive'). Used since classical antiquity both as a transitive verb ('respect') and as the standard formal salutation before titles in letters and speeches.

history.meaning: honour and respect elders or worthy persons
esteemed; respected; respect

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 尊敬

尊重.etymology: Coordinative verbal compound of 尊 (zūn, to honor, revere, hold in high position) and 重 (zhòng, heavy, weighty; used putatively in Classical Chinese to mean "to regard as weighty, attach great value to"). Attested in Warring States and Han texts (*Zhan Guo Ce*, *Hanfeizi*, *Book of the Later Han*), where it meant both "eminent and weighty in status" and "to treat someone with high regard". In modern Mandarin (and parallel Japanese 尊重 *sonchō*), it functions as the standard transitive verb and noun for respecting people, choices, creative work, or rights.

history.meaning: noble and weighty in status; to honor and attach great weight to someone
to respect, value, honor (a person, opinion, or right)

morphemes.meaning: weighty; to value highly, attach weight to

尊重.notes: Unlike 尊敬 (zūnjìng, which implies looking up to elders, teachers, or superiors with reverence), 尊重 applies equally across peers, subordinates, and abstract concepts (e.g., 尊重你的选择 "respect your choice", 互相尊重 "mutual respect").

rootFamily.gloss: to revere and respect (elders or superiors)
to value highly, to treasure; self-care
to attach importance to, take seriously

小.etymology: Ancient indicative/pictographic character attested on Shang oracle bones written with three tiny dots or grains of sand (小): 'small, little, young, minor, brief' and an affectionate/humble prefix before names or kinship terms (小晴, 小张).

morphemes.meaning: three small dots = small, little, young

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: three tiny specks = small, little, young

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 小 (via 萌典)

小事.etymology: Modifier-head nominal compound of 小 (xiǎo, Old Chinese *slep / *sjewX, small, minor, petty, depicted in oracle bones as three tiny dots of sand or grain) and 事 (shì, OC *m-s-rəʔ-s, affair, business, service, depicted in oracle bones as a hand holding a court banner or hunting/writing implement). Attested throughout Classical Chinese from the *Book of Documents* (*Shangshu*), *Analects*, and *Zuo Zhuan*—where it was systematically contrasted with 大事 (dàshì, "great affairs of state: sacrifice and warfare")—it has remained the everyday term for a minor matter or trifling issue.

history.meaning: minor administrative or ritual affair (as opposed to great affairs of state)
small matter, trivial issue, piece of cake (often 儿-suffixed as 小事儿 in northern speech)

小事.notes: Often heard in the reassuring phrase 小事一桩 (xiǎoshì yī zhuāng, "just a small matter / no big deal") or the proverb 小事化了 (turn a small matter into nothing).

rootFamily.gloss: major event, great affair; overall situation
minor details, non-essentials (as in 不拘小节)

小伙子.etymology: Colloquial compound of diminutive prefix 小 ('young') + 伙 ('companion; messmate; band', originally 'ten soldiers sharing a cooking fire 火') + nominal suffix 子 (-zi). It became the warm, everyday northern and standard Mandarin term for a lively young man.

history.meaning: energetic young man; young fellow
young fellow; lad

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 小伙子

小声.etymology: An intuitive modifier-noun phrase joining 小 (xiǎo, 'small, low in volume') and 声 (shēng, simplified from 聲, originally depicting a hand striking a suspended stone chime 磬 perceived by the ear 耳, hence 'sound, voice'). Whereas English uses a dedicated verb 'whisper', everyday Mandarin contrasts 小声 ('in a small voice') directly with 大声 ('in a big voice / aloud').

history.meaning: low voice; quietly
in a whisper; quietly (adverbial)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 小声

小姑娘.etymology: Modifier-head compound formed by prefixing the age/size adjective 小 (xiǎo, little, young) to the vernacular compound noun 姑娘 (gūniang, young woman, girl). 姑娘 itself arose in Song–Ming vernacular Chinese from 姑 (gū, originally father's sister or husband's mother/sister, also used politely for young women) + 娘 (niáng, mother or young lady). Adding 小 emphasizes youth, innocence, or seniority perspective, yielding an affectionate or mildly patronizing term for a young girl or young woman in her teens or early twenties.

history.meaning: paternal aunt; polite title for an unmarried daughter of a household or female immortal
young girl, lass, young woman (especially when referred to by someone older)

morphemes.meaning: mother; young lady (neutral tone in compound)

小姑娘.notes: In workplace dramas like *Behind the Scenes*, veterans often call twenty-something female interns or rookies 小姑娘—affectionate from a mentor, though it can sound dismissive if used to question someone's professional experience.

rootFamily.gloss: girl, young unmarried woman; daughter (northern colloquial)

小子.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 小 (xiǎo, small, young, humble) and 子 (zǐ / neutral-tone -zi, child, son, young person, nominal suffix). One of the oldest compounds in the Chinese lexicon, 小子 is attested in Western Zhou bronze inscriptions and the *Book of Documents* (*Shangshu*) as xiǎozǐ (with full third tone on both syllables), where Zhou kings referred to themselves humbly before Heaven and ancestral spirits as 予小子 ("I, the little child"), and in the *Analects* where Confucius addressed his disciples as 小子 ("my young fellows"). In Vernacular Mandarin, with phonological reduction of the second syllable to a neutral tone (xiǎozi), it became a casual, familiar, or slightly rough word for a young guy, boy, or fellow.

history.meaning: humble royal self-appellation ("I, the young child"); disciples, young men, or commoners
boy, son; casual, teasing, or gruff term for a young fellow or kid

morphemes.meaning: child, son, fellow (neutral tone in modern colloquial usage)

小子.notes: Commonly used after a pronoun in casual or bantering speech: 你小子 ("you rascal / you lucky guy") or 那小子 ("that guy/kid"); avoid using it toward superiors or in polite formal speech.

rootFamily.gloss: brat, stinky kid (often used affectionately or scoldingly)

小孩.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 小 (xiǎo, small, young) and 孩 (hái, Old Chinese *gˤə, child, infant). In the *Shuowen Jiezi* (100 CE) and *Laozi* (Chapter 20, 如婴儿之未孩), 孩 (originally written 咳 with 口 "mouth" before shifting to the 子 "child" radical) specifically denoted an infant old enough to smile or giggle, as seen in the Mencian compound 孩提 (háití, a Laughing-and-Carried toddler). During the Tang–Song vernacular transition, 小 + 孩 replaced monosyllabic 儿/子 as the primary colloquial noun for a child, frequently taking the diminutive retroflex suffix -r (小孩儿, xiǎoháir) in northern Mandarin.

history.meaning: infant old enough to laugh; young toddler carried in arms
young child, kid; son or daughter

小孩.notes: In spoken northern Mandarin, almost always pronounced with erhua as 小孩儿 (xiǎoháir) or expanded to 小孩子 (xiǎoháizi); calling an adult 小孩 implies they are acting childishly or naively.

rootFamily.gloss: child, children; one's own son or daughter
infancy and early childhood (from "laughing and carried in arms")

小小.etymology: Vivid AA reduplication of 小 ('small; tiny', oracle-bone script showing three tiny grains or specks of sand). Reduplicating 小 to 小小 adds an affectionate, diminutive colouring ('tiny little').

history.meaning: tiny; petite; very small
tiny; little

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 小小

小心.etymology: Compound verb and adjective of 小 ('make small, cautious,細緻') + 心 ('heart, mind'). In the Shijing (小心翼翼), 小心 meant 'reverent, circumspect, and scrupulously attentive in heart'; in everyday Mandarin it means 'be careful, watch out!, cautious'.

history.meaning: reverent and scrupulously cautious in mind
be careful; watch out; careful

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 小心 (via 萌典)

小提琴.etymology: Three-morpheme musical compound of 小 ('small; treble-register', contrasting with 大提琴 'cello' and 中提琴 'viola') + 提 ('carry or hold by hand', hand radical 扌 + 是) + 琴 ('stringed musical instrument'). Coined in modern Chinese to name the Western violin held on the shoulder and bowed by hand.

history.meaning: violin
violin

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 小提琴

小时.etymology: Compound time noun of 小 ('small, halved') + 时 (時, 'traditional double-hour 时辰'). Because the traditional Chinese day was divided into 12 时辰 (each equal to two modern hours), when the Western 24-hour clock was adopted in late Qing China, each 60-minute unit (half of a 大时/时辰) was named 小时 ('small hour' = 'hour').

history.meaning: half of a traditional two-hour 时辰 = 60-minute hour

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 小时 (via 萌典)

小时候.etymology: Three-character temporal noun phrase combining 小 ('young, little in age') + 时候 ('time, period'): 'in one's childhood, when one was little/young'.

history.meaning: when one was young; in childhood

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 小时候 (via 萌典)

小晴.etymology: Affectionate/familiar personal name formed with the endearing prefix 小 ('little, young', placed before a given name or surname among friends, family, and coworkers) + given name 晴 ('clear, sunny sky').

history.meaning: familiar address/given name 'Xiaoqing' (Little Qing)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 小晴 (via 萌典)

小有名气.etymology: Four-character adverbial-verb-object phrase composed of 小 (xiǎo, functioning adverbially as in Classical Chinese to mean "slightly, modestly, to a small extent") + 有 (yǒu, to possess, have) + 名气 (名氣, míngqì, reputation, renown, literally "name-aura/vitality"). The adverbial use of 小 before a verb is a classic literary pattern (compare 小康, 小成, 小有成就), while 名气 emerged in Ming–Qing vernacular prose to describe a person's public standing or fame. Combined, the four-character idiom means "to enjoy modest fame" or "to be somewhat well-known".

history.meaning: combination of Classical adverbial 小有 ("to possess to a modest degree") with Ming–Qing vernacular 名氣 ("reputation, fame")
to enjoy modest fame, be somewhat well-known in a field or locality

morphemes.meaning: modestly, slightly, to a small degree
vital energy, aura, standing (neutral tone in 名气)

小有名气.notes: A staple expression in entertainment and career contexts for describing rising talent or niche industry figures (e.g., 在业内小有名气 "somewhat well-known within the industry") without overstating their stardom.

rootFamily.gloss: to be renowned far and wide, famous (idiom)

小朋友.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 小 (xiǎo, young, little) and 朋友 (péngyou, friend; itself an ancient Classical coordinative compound of 朋 "peer/fellow disciple, originally two strings of cowrie shells" and 友 "companion/ally, originally two right hands working together"). While 朋友 dates back to Western Zhou bronze inscriptions and the *Analects*, the compound 小朋友 was coined and popularized in early-20th-century vernacular Mandarin during the May Fourth New Culture movement—most notably through Chung Hwa Book Company's landmark children's magazine 《小朋友》 (founded in 1922) and writer Bing Xin's (冰心) warm literary addresses to children—reflecting modern pedagogical ideals of treating children as respected "little friends".

history.meaning: peers and companions, fellow students and sworn friends
youngster, child, "little friend" (polite, warm address or reference to children)

小朋友.notes: The standard polite form of address used by teachers, TV hosts, and adults when speaking directly to children; in adult banter, calling a colleague or romantic partner 小朋友 is a playful, teasing way to call them cute or inexperienced.

rootFamily.word: 男朋友 / 女朋友 (nánpéngyou / nǚpéngyou)

rootFamily.gloss: old friend; playful term for a senior citizen

小粉红.etymology: Modifier-head compound formed from the diminutive prefix 小 (xiǎo, little, small) and the color compound 粉红 (粉紅, fěnhóng, pink; literally "powder-red", originally referring in Tang–Song cosmetics and painting to white lead face powder 粉 blended with red rouge 红 to produce a pale rose hue). By a productive colloquial Mandarin pattern where 小 + Color designates a small, endearing object or pet of that color (compare 小白, 小黄, 小黑), 小粉红 literally denotes a cute pink object (such as a cherished pink notebook in *Behind the Scenes*). Separately, in 2010s Chinese internet culture, the term was coined from the pink color scheme of the Jinjiang Literature City (晋江文学城) forum to refer to young cyber-nationalists.

history.meaning: pale rose/pink color made by mixing white cosmetic powder (粉) with red rouge (紅)
affectionate nickname for a small pink item (e.g., a pink notebook); in 2010s internet slang, a young nationalist netizen

小粉红.notes: Context is crucial: in daily life and in *Behind the Scenes* (*幕后之王*), it is a literal, affectionate nickname for a pink notebook or accessory, whereas in political/social media discussions it refers to young patriotic/nationalist netizens ("Little Pinks").

rootFamily.gloss: pink color; romantic or amorous aura (as in 粉红泡泡)
popular, in high demand; internet celebrity (网红)

小红花.etymology: Modifier-head nominal compound of 小 (xiǎo, small, little) + 红 (紅, hóng, red, traditionally the color of celebration, honor, and revolution in China) + 花 (huā, flower, blossom). While transparently meaning "little red flower", the compound became culturally institutionalized in mid-20th-century Mainland China as a miniature counterpart to the large red silk rosette (大红花, dàhónghuā) pinned onto the chests of combat heroes and model workers. In kindergartens and primary schools across China, teachers award paper cutouts or stickers of a "little red flower" (小红花) on wall charts to praise good behavior—making it the universal Chinese cultural equivalent of a "gold star".

history.meaning: red blossom; auspicious crimson silk flower worn by newlyweds, top imperial examinees (狀元), and later model workers
little red paper/sticker flower awarded to kindergarten children as a merit star; figurative token of praise

小红花.notes: Adults in Chinese workplaces frequently joke about "deserving a little red flower" (奖励一朵小红花) when asking for praise or recognition after finishing a tough task—just like getting a gold star in kindergarten.

rootFamily.gloss: large red silk rosette worn by honored heroes or model workers
brocade; used in 锦上添花 ("adding flowers to brocade")

小美.etymology: Affectionate/familiar personal name formed with the endearing prefix 小 ('little, young') + given name 美 ('beautiful, fine'): 'Xiaomei'.

history.meaning: familiar address/given name 'Xiaomei'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 小美 (via 萌典)

小节.etymology: Compound noun of 小 ('small, minor') + 节 (節, 'bamboo node, section, division'). In Classical prose it meant 'minor details of conduct or etiquette' (不拘小节); in modern music it is the standard term for a 'musical measure, bar'.

history.meaning: minor points of conduct
musical measure/bar; minor detail

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 小节 (via 萌典)

小诗.etymology: The word '小诗' (xiǎoshī, short poem) is a straightforward combination of '小' (small, brief) and '诗' (poem). Historically, Chinese poetic forms were heavily structured, but '小诗' was often used informally by literati to describe a casual, impromptu verse, sometimes written as a gift or observation. In the early 20th century, during the New Culture Movement, '小诗' gained prominence as a specific genre of modern, short-form free verse inspired by Japanese haiku and Western epigrams. Bing Xin (冰心) was particularly famous for popularizing this genre.

history.meaning: poetry

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 小诗

小谷.etymology: Hypocoristic (familiar/diminutive) personal name formed from the vocative prefix 小 (xiǎo, "Little / Young") + the personal name character or surname 谷 (gǔ, Old Chinese *kˤok, "valley, gorge, mountain stream"; in simplified Chinese also merging 穀, "grain, cereal"). In Mandarin social and workplace address, attaching 小 to a monosyllabic surname or to one syllable of a given name is the standard way for seniors, mentors, or peers to address a younger colleague with warmth and informality.

history.meaning: mountain valley or gorge; Chinese surname attested since the Spring and Autumn period
"Little Gu / Young Gu", familiar workplace or personal nickname

morphemes.meaning: Little, Young (familiar prefix for younger colleagues or friends)
valley, gorge (or grain 穀); surname/given-name character Gu

小谷.notes: In Chinese offices and TV production crews, pairing 小 (for juniors) or 老 (for seniors) with a surname or name character (e.g., 小谷, 老王) signals everyday camaraderie without the stiffness of full names or titles.

rootFamily.gloss: trough, low point (e.g., in ratings or career)

小路.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 小 ('small, narrow') + 路 ('road, path'): 'narrow path, lane, trail, footpath'.

history.meaning: path; lane; trail

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 小路 (via 萌典)

小队.etymology: Formed from 小 (xiǎo, 'small') and 队 (duì, simplified from 隊, originally 'a file or detachment of soldiers descending from a terrace mound 阝'). While 队 alone denotes any team, queue, or squad, prefixing affectionate 小 turns 小队 into a friendly everyday word for a small crew of coworkers, hikers, or tea regulars sharing an outing.

history.meaning: small detachment or work team
small team; friendly crew

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 小队

小院.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 小 ('small, cozy') + 院 ('walled courtyard, compound'): 'small courtyard'.

history.meaning: small courtyard

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 小院 (via 萌典)

小院客栈.etymology: Four-character compound combining 小院 ('small courtyard') + 客栈 ('traditional inn, guesthouse', 客 'traveler/guest' + 栈 'wooden lodge/storehouse'): 'Courtyard Inn, small courtyard guesthouse'.

history.form: 小院客棧 / 小院客栈
history.meaning: Courtyard Inn; courtyard guesthouse

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 小院客栈 (via 萌典)

小鸟.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 小 ('small, little') + 鸟 (鳥, 'bird', a pictograph of a Perched bird with feathers and claws): 'little bird, small bird'.

history.meaning: small bird; little bird

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 小鸟 (via 萌典)

少.etymology: Monomorphemic root written in Shang oracle bone inscriptions as four tiny dots (a graphic variant of 小 xiǎo, which had three dots) and later differentiated by an added diagonal stroke (丿) beneath 小. Derived from Old Chinese *s-tems / *hmjewʔ ("few, small in number"), it split by tone derivation into Middle Chinese rising tone *sjewX* (Mandarin shǎo, "few, little in quantity, lacking, to lessen") and departing tone *sjewH* (Mandarin shào, "young in age, junior", literally "having few years"). Here used in the rising-tone adjectival and adverbial sense "few, less, little".

history.meaning: few in number, scarce, a little; (in departing tone) young, junior
few, less, little; to lack, be short of; (adverbially) do less of something!

少.notes: Before a verb in spoken Mandarin, 少 often forms a blunt imperative meaning "cut it out / stop doing so much of..." (e.g., 少来这套! "Cut the act!", 少废话! "Save the chatter!"). Also watch the tone pair 少 (shǎo, few) vs. 少 (shào, young, as in 少年, 少爷).

尖.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 尖. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 尖 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 尖 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 尖 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 尖. The etymology of 尖 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 尖
middle form of 尖
modern form of 尖

尖端.etymology: '尖端' (jiānduān, peak, cutting-edge) is formed by '尖' (sharp, pointed) and '端' (end, extremity). The character '尖' is a classic ideogram, consisting of '小' (small) on top of '大' (large), visually representing a wedge or point. In classical texts, '尖端' literally referred to the physical sharp point of a needle, sword, or peak. In the mid-20th century, the term underwent a metaphorical shift to denote the most advanced or developed stage of something. It is now most frequently paired with '科技' (technology) to mean 'cutting-edge'.

history.meaning: sharp

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 尖端

cognates.meaning: this mortal world, the mundane world
the mundane world, this dusty world

尘世.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 尘 (塵, chén, Old Chinese *drin, dust, dirt; the traditional character 塵 depicts a herd of deer 鹿 kicking up clouds of earth 土 as they run) and 世 (shì, OC *hljaps, generation of thirty years, epoch, the human world). Coined and popularized during the Six Dynasties and Tang periods through the confluence of native Daoist poetry (compare Tao Yuanming's 尘网 "dusty net of the world") and Chinese Buddhist translations (where 尘 renders Sanskrit *guṇa* or *viṣaya*, the six sensory "dusts" 六尘 that defile the mind), 尘世 contrasts the transient, careworn mortal world with spiritual transcendence.

history.meaning: the dusty, defiled world of mortal attachments (in contrast to Buddhist nirvana or Daoist仙境 immortality)
this mortal world, the mundane everyday world (poetic and literary register)

尘世.notes: Belongs to a poetic/literary register (often seen in drama OST lyrics, period dramas, or philosophical dialogue as 远离尘世 "far from the madding crowd / mortal world"); close synonym of 红尘 (hóngchén, "the red dust of mortal life").

rootFamily.gloss: the world of mortals, earthly life ("red dust")
worldly, secular, bound by mundane conventions

尚.etymology: Monomorphemic Classical Chinese particle and verb (Old Chinese *djaŋs, Middle Chinese *dzyangH). In oracle bone and Western Zhou bronze inscriptions, the graph depicts a roofed building (向/冂) with strokes rising above the ridgepole (八), originally meaning "high above, to place on top, to add to, to esteem highly" (etymologically cognate with 上 shàng, "up, above"). Already in early Classical Chinese (*Book of Documents*, *Book of Odes*, *Analects*), the sense of "adding on / continuing further" grammaticalized into a temporal and modal adverb meaning "still, yet, even now".

history.meaning: to esteem, place above, surpass; (adverb) still, yet, even; (optative particle) would that, may...!
still, yet (literary adverb retained in formal Mandarin and four-character phrases)

morphemes.meaning: still, yet; to esteem, value highly

尚.notes: A concise literary replacement for 还 (hái, "still") in formal writing, news headlines, and set phrases such as 尚未 (shàngwèi, "not yet"), 尚可 (shàngkě, "still passable/feasible"), and 尚且 (shàngqiě, "even... let alone").

rootFamily.gloss: not yet (formal/written equivalent of 还没有)
to uphold, esteem, advocate; fashionable (时尚)

尚可一战.etymology: Four-character literary verbal phrase structured as 尚 (shàng, adverb "still, yet") + 可 (kě, modal auxiliary "can, be able to") + 一 (yī, numeral "one, once", quantifying a single decisive engagement) + 战 (戰, zhàn, "to fight, wage battle"). Modeled directly on Classical Chinese military chronicles—most famously Cao Gui's assessment before the Battle of Changshao in the *Zuo Zhuan* (左传·庄公十年: 可以一战 "we may fight a battle") and the *Records of the Grand Historian* (史记, where aging general Lian Po's readiness is tested: 尚能饭否)—it originally meant "our forces are still capable of fighting a battle". In modern Mandarin media, gaming, and workplace drama, it is used with heroic or self-deprecating flair to declare that an older veteran, underdog, or battered team "still has a fight left in them".

history.form: 可以一戰 / 尚可一戰
history.meaning: (of troops or a general) still capable of engaging the enemy in battle despite setbacks or age
still ready to fight and compete; still got what it takes in a tough rivalry

morphemes.meaning: can, be able to, worthy of

尚可一战.notes: Carries a mock-epic, wuxia/historical-drama ring when used in modern office or entertainment settings—perfect for a seasoned producer or ratings contender refusing to be written off as washed up.

rootFamily.gloss: to fight a decisive battle to the end (idiom)
still passable, fairly good, still feasible
challenge; to challenge to a contest

尝.etymology: Phono-semantic character (traditional 嘗, combining 尚 shàng/cháng phonetic + 旨 'delicious taste/spoon and sweet mouth'): originally 'taste food, sample a flavor; autumn harvest sacrifice', and in Classical Chinese an experiential past adverb ('once, formerly'); in Mandarin, 'taste, try the flavor of, experience'.

history.meaning: taste food; autumn offering; once in the past
taste; try (food); experience

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 尝 (via 萌典)

尝尝.etymology: Reduplicated verb from 尝 ('taste, try the flavor of'): 'have a taste, try a bite' (verb reduplication indicates a light, inviting, or brief sampling action).

history.meaning: have a taste; sample a little

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 尝尝 (via 萌典)

尝试.etymology: Coordinative verbal compound of 尝 (嘗/嚐, cháng, Old Chinese *djaŋ, originally to taste food or sacrificial offerings, hence to sample or test) and 试 (試, shì, OC *hljəks, to test, examine, put to use). Attested in Warring States philosophical prose (*Mencius* 孟子·梁惠王上: 我虽不敏，请尝试之 "Though I am not clever, please let me try it"; also *Xunzi* and *Lüshi Chunqiu*), the compound pairs the concrete sensory metaphor of tasting a sample (尝) with testing in action (试). It has remained in continuous use for over two millennia as both a verb and noun meaning "to try out, attempt".

history.meaning: to taste and test; to make a trial or attempt at an undertaking
to try out, attempt, experiment with; an attempt or venture (noun)

尝试.notes: More formal and deliberate than colloquial 试试 (shìshi): you say 试试看 for casual everyday things ("give it a try"), but 尝试新风格 / 勇敢尝试 when speaking about artistic experimentation, career pivots, or creative ventures.

rootFamily.gloss: to test, try out; exam, test (考试)
to taste, savor (food, wine, or life experiences)
to try, give it a shot (colloquial reduplication)

尤其.etymology: Lexicalized disyllabic degree/focus adverb formed through syntactic reanalysis of Classical Chinese 尤 (yóu, Old Chinese *ɢʷə, originally "anomalous, outstanding, fault", used adverbially to mean "surpassingly, especially, all the more") + 其 (qí, OC *gə, third-person/demonstrative pronoun "its, among them, that"). In Classical Chinese clauses such as 尤其甚者 ("among them, that which is especially extreme") or 尤其難者, 尤 modified the predicate while 其 belonged to the following nominalized phrase. By the Song and Ming periods, the two adjacent characters were rebracketed as a single compound adverb 尤其 meaning "especially, particularly".

history.meaning: "especially [among them / its]...", where 尤 ("particularly") and pronoun 其 ("its/among them") belonged to separate syntactic constituents
especially, particularly (fused disyllabic focus/degree adverb, often paired with 是 as 尤其是)

morphemes.meaning: outstanding, surpassing; especially, all the more
its, among them (reanalyzed into a compound adverb suffix)

尤其.notes: Used in two main patterns: 尤其 + adjective/stative verb (今天尤其冷 "especially cold today") or 尤其是 + noun/clause to single out a standout example ("especially...").

rootFamily.gloss: to harbor resentment and blame others (idiom, where 尤 = blame)

就.etymology: Ideogram combining 京 ('high mound/tower in the capital') + 尤 ('outstanding/reach'): originally 'move toward a high place, approach, take up (a post), accomplish'. In vernacular Mandarin it became one of the language's core adverbs and connectives: 'then, right away, as early as, precisely/just, even if'.

history.meaning: go toward; approach; accomplish; take office
then; immediately; right away; precisely/just

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 就 (via 萌典)

就事论事.etymology: Four-character serial prepositional-verbal idiom (成语) structured as 就事 (jiù shì, "approaching / sticking strictly to the matter at hand") + 论事 (lùn shì, "to discuss or judge the matter"). Here 就 (jiù) preserves its Classical Chinese prepositional-verbal sense of "moving toward, cleaving to, confining oneself to the scope of", while 论 (論, lùn) means "to analyze, evaluate, discourse upon". Attested in Qing-dynasty official memorials, scholarship, and vernacular novels such as *Ernü Yingxiong Zhuan* (儿女英雄传), it expresses the principle of judging an issue strictly on its objective merits without bringing in personal grudges, favoritism, or extraneous politics.

history.meaning: to discuss or adjudicate a case strictly within the bounds of the facts of the matter itself
to judge a matter purely on its own merits; to keep things strictly professional and objective

morphemes.meaning: sticking to, on the basis of, within the scope of

就事论事.notes: A quintessential workplace and negotiation phrase used to defuse defensiveness during a critique: 我是就事论事，不是针对你 ("I'm talking strictly about the issue itself, not attacking you personally"). Often contrasted with 对人不对事 (targeting the person rather than the issue).

rootFamily.gloss: to seek truth from facts, be practical and realistic (idiom)
to adapt measures to local conditions (idiom with prepositional 就/因)

cognates.meaning: accession to the throne; taking one's position
accession to the throne; taking one's post

就位.etymology: Verb-object compound of 就 (jiù, Old Chinese *dzuks, to approach, proceed to, assume, originally depicting moving toward a high tower 京) and 位 (wèi, OC *ɢʷrəps, assigned court rank, station, or seat, originally 𠈌 depicting a person 人 standing 立 at their ritual place in the courtyard). Directly inherited from Classical Chinese ritual classics—including the *Book of Etiquette and Ceremonial* (仪礼), *Book of Rites* (礼记), and *Zuo Zhuan*—where officials and nobles "proceeded to their designated stations" (就位) during court audiences and sacrifices. In modern Mandarin, it applies to officials taking office, athletes on the starting line (各就位 "On your marks!"), and film/TV crews taking their posts on set.

history.meaning: to step into one's assigned ritual station in court ceremonies; to ascend the throne
to take one's post, be in position (on a stage, film set, starting line, or job role)

就位.notes: Heard constantly on TV and film sets (各部门就位! "All departments in position!") and at track-and-field starts (各就各位，预备，跑! "On your marks, get set, go!"); compare 到位 (dàowèi, which also means "executed thoroughly/on point").

rootFamily.gloss: to be in place; thorough, spot-on in execution
to assume a high office or presidency; to take one's seat

就像.etymology: Simile verb/preposition compound combining emphatic adverb 就 ('just, right, exactly') + 像 ('resemble, be like'): 'just like, exactly as if'.

history.meaning: just like; just as if

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 就像 (via 萌典)

就是.etymology: Emphatic compound combining 就 ('precisely, just') + 是 ('be; right'): functions as an emphatic affirmation ('that's right!, precisely!'), a restrictive focus marker ('only, simply'), and a concessive/adversative connector ('even if; except that').

history.meaning: precisely is; that's right; simply; even if

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 就是 (via 萌典)

就是因为.etymology: Emphatic causal connective phrase composed of two disyllabic Mandarin words: 就是 (jiùshì, emphatic focus copula meaning "is precisely, is simply", formed from the focus adverb 就 "right then, precisely" + the copula 是 "to be", which itself grammaticalized in Han Chinese from the demonstrative pronoun "this") and 因为 (因為, yīnwèi, causal preposition/conjunction "because of, on account of", formed from Classical 因 "to rely on, follow from, cause" + 为 "for the sake of, on account of"). Together, 就是因为 highlights and pinpoints the exact cause of a situation: "it is precisely because..." or "just because...".

history.meaning: Classical Chinese prepositions "relying upon / owing to" (因) and "for the sake of / because of" (為), which combined into medieval vernacular 因為 ("because")
precisely because, just because (emphatic causal phrase combining focus copula 就是 + causal conjunction 因为)

morphemes.meaning: cause, reason; to rely on, follow from
for the sake of, on account of

就是因为.notes: Often paired with 才 (cái) in the second clause to form the high-frequency emphatic frame 就是因为 A，才 B ("It is precisely because of A that B happened").

rootFamily.gloss: precisely is; even if; quite right!

就算.etymology: Concessive conjunction combining 就 ('even if') + 算 ('count as, reckon, suppose'): 'even if, granted that, even supposing' (typically paired with 也 in the main clause: 就算…也…).

history.meaning: even if; granted that

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 就算 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: getting ready, completion of preparations; starting work
being in readiness, getting into order

就绪.etymology: Verb-object compound of 就 (jiù, to enter upon, settle into, accomplish) and 绪 (緒, xù, Old Chinese *s-ljaʔ, originally the loose end of a silk thread on a cocoon that must be found before reeling silk, hence beginning, sequence, order, or ongoing enterprise). In the *Book of Odes* (*Shijing*, 鲁颂·閟宫: 缵禹之绪 "continuing the enterprise/thread of Yu") and medieval literary Chinese, 就绪 originally meant to carry forward an enterprise or find the proper thread of order. From the sericultural metaphor of having all silk thread-ends sorted and aligned on the reel, it came to mean "all in order, completely ready to begin".

history.meaning: to carry on an ancestral undertaking; to sort out the silk thread-ends so work is in proper order
to be in readiness, all set and in order (especially of complex preparations)

morphemes.meaning: to enter into, attain, settle into
end of a silk thread; order, sequence, readiness

就绪.notes: Almost always used with pre-modifiers such as 准备就绪 ("preparations are all set") or 一切就绪 ("everything is in readiness")—standard broadcast/stage-management language right before a live show goes on air.

rootFamily.gloss: clue, thread of a story or investigation ("thread-end")

就要.etymology: Compound prospective adverbial auxiliary formed in Vernacular Mandarin from 就 (jiù, adverb of immediacy "soon, right away, immediately", grammaticalized from the Classical verb "to approach, move toward") and 要 (yào, prospective modal auxiliary "going to, about to, will", grammaticalized from the Classical verb yāo "to seek, demand, invite", originally depicting two hands 臼 at the waist 腰). By combining the temporal immediacy of 就 with the future modality of 要, 就要 (typically paired with sentence-final change-of-state particle 了 le) marks an imminent future event: "be about to, going to very soon".

history.meaning: Classical verbs "to approach" (就) and "to seek/demand" (要), which grammaticalized separately in Tang–Song vernacular into an immediacy adverb and a future/volitional auxiliary
be about to, on the verge of (imminent future marker, usually in the frame 就要……了)

就要.notes: Key grammar point for learners: unlike 快要……了 (kuàiyào...le), 就要……了 CAN be preceded by a specific time word (e.g., 节目下周就要播出了 "The show is going to air next week", where *下周快要播出了 is ungrammatical). Also note that with stress on 要, 就要 can mean "insist on wanting" (我就要这个 "I want this very one!").

rootFamily.gloss: about to, nearly, very soon (cannot follow a specific time noun)
about to, on the point of (formal/written register)

尴尬.etymology: Alliterative disyllabic binome (双声联绵词) in which neither character carries independent meaning alone; both are written with the semantic radical 尢 (wāng, variant of 尣, depicting a person 大 with a bent or crippled leg, signifying lameness or crooked gait) combined with the velar phonetics 监 (監, jiān, Old Chinese *kˤram) and 介 (jiè, OC *kˤrads). Recorded in Xu Shen's *Shuowen Jiezi* (说文解字, 100 CE) as 𡯂𡯃, it originally meant "walking irregularly, limping, unable to move forward smoothly". In Song, Yuan, and Ming vernacular literature, this physical image of halting or being stuck mid-stride metaphorically shifted to social and psychological predicaments ("neither here nor there, in a tight spot, awkward, embarrassed"). Although the historical Northern Mandarin reading was jiānjiè, the modern standard pronunciation gāngà was adopted in the 20th century from Wu (Shanghainese/Suzhou) dialectal readings where velar initials before Division II finals remained unpalatalized (*k- > g-).

history.meaning: limping, walking crookedly or haltingly (recorded under the lame-leg radical 尢 in the *Shuowen Jiezi*)
in a tight spot, caught between a rock and a hard place, shady ordubious (in Song–Ming vernacular fiction)
awkward, embarrassed, ill at ease, cringe-worthy (with standard reading adopted from unpalatalized Wu pronunciation)

morphemes.meaning: First syllable of the alliterative binome 尴尬 (radical 尢 "lame leg" + phonetic 监)
Second syllable of the alliterative binome 尴尬 (radical 尢 "lame leg" + phonetic 介)

尴尬.notes: In contemporary Mandarin and youth slang, 尬 (gà) has been liberated as a productive bound prefix meaning "awkwardly / cringe-inducingly", spawning words like 尬聊 (gàliáo, "awkward small talk"), 尬笑 (gàxiào, "awkward laugh"), and 尬舞 (gàwǔ, "awkward dance-off").

rootFamily.gloss: to make awkward small talk, force a conversation (modern coinage from 尴尬 + 聊)
hard to take, embarrassed, in a difficult position
ill at ease, awkward, unnatural (of manner or relationship)

尹家希.etymology: Three-character Chinese personal name consisting of the ancient surname 尹 (Yǐn, Old Chinese *m-qʷərʔ) and the two-character given name 家希 (Jiāxī). In Shang oracle bone and Western Zhou bronze inscriptions, 尹 depicts a right hand (又) grasping a vertical staff or brush of authority (丿), originally denoting a royal administrator, chief minister, or governor (as in 令尹, Prime Minister of Chu, and Yin Jifu 尹吉甫 of the Western Zhou), from which the hereditary surname arose. The given name combines 家 (jiā, "family, household, lineage") with 希 (xī, "rare, precious; to hope, aspire to"), forming a warm modern character name in *Behind the Scenes* (*幕后之王*).

history.meaning: to govern, administer; royal chief officer or governor (subsequently adopted as a lineage surname)
Yin Jiaxi (personal/character name combining surname 尹 with given name 家希 "family-hope/precious")

morphemes.meaning: Yin (ancient official title meaning governor/administrator, used as a surname)

尹家希.notes: Follows standard Chinese personal name structure (Surname + Two-character Given Name); 希 (xī, "hope / rare") is a popular unisex-to-feminine given-name character in contemporary Chinese naming.

rootFamily.gloss: Prime Minister of the ancient state of Chu; prefect/governor (as in 京兆尹)

尹正宇.etymology: Three-character Chinese personal name composed of the bureaucratic-origin surname 尹 (Yǐn, Old Chinese *m-qʷərʔ, originally depicting a hand 又 wielding a baton or brush of office to govern) and the masculine two-character given name 正宇 (Zhèngyǔ). Within the given name, 正 (zhèng, OC *tjeŋs, "upright, just, orthodox, proper") pairs as a modifier or coordinate element with 宇 (yǔ, OC *ɢʷ(r)aʔ, originally "the overhanging eaves of a roof", extended in Classical Chinese to "boundless space, the universe" and "personal bearing/demeanor", as in 器宇 qìyǔ), evoking a person of upright moral character and expansive, dignified bearing.

history.meaning: Classical administrative surname 尹 ("governor") + 正 ("upright, just") + 宇 ("roof eaves, cosmos, personal bearing")
Yin Zhengyu (personal name evoking uprightness and noble bearing)

morphemes.meaning: Yin (ancient official title meaning governor/director, used as a surname)
eaves, boundless space, universe, personal demeanor

尹正宇.notes: 宇 (yǔ) is one of the most popular characters in modern Chinese masculine given names because it sounds resonant and evokes both cosmic breadth (宇宙 "universe") and distinguished poise (器宇轩昂 "dignified and high-spirited bearing").

rootFamily.gloss: the universe, cosmos (literally "boundless space and eternal time")
having a dignified, spirited, and imposing bearing (idiom)

尺子.etymology: Derived noun from 尺 ('Chinese foot; measuring rule', originally depicting a hand span measured from wrist pulse to thumb tip) + nominal suffix 子. While bare 尺 functions as the traditional unit of length (roughly one-third of a meter), 尺子 designates the physical ruler or straightedge tool.

history.meaning: measuring stick; ruler
ruler; straightedge

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 尺子

尺寸.etymology: Coordinative noun compound pairing two traditional Chinese length units: 尺 ('Chinese foot', originally a hand span from thumb to forefinger below 尸, equal to 10 寸) + 寸 ('Chinese inch', a mark 一 one inch below the wrist on a hand 又, where the pulse is felt). Together they mean 'dimensions, measurements, size' (and figuratively 'proper measure/tact', read chǐcun).

history.stage: Classical Chinese (Guanzi, Hanshu) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: feet and inches -> dimensions, size, measurements

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 尺寸 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to exhaust, fulfill, devote oneself (尽くす)

尽.etymology: Simplified from 盡 (jìn, "to exhaust, use up, fulfill completely"), whose oracle bone and bronze script forms depict a hand (又/聿) holding a brush or scrubber cleaning out the inside of an empty vessel (皿), symbolizing a container scrubbed clean with nothing left behind. Note that modern simplified 尽 merges two distinct traditional characters: 盡 (jìn, "to exhaust, to fulfill to the utmost", Middle Chinese *dzinX) and 儘 (jǐn, "to the greatest extent, let/allow", Middle Chinese *tsinX). In the verbal sense "give to the utmost, exhaust", it continues traditional 盡.

history.meaning: vessel emptied or scrubbed clean; to use up completely
to exhaust, deplete, fulfill a duty or capacity completely
to give to the utmost, exhaust, fulfill

morphemes.meaning: to exhaust, use up, fulfill to the utmost (trad. 盡)

尽.notes: In Mandarin, 尽 is pronounced jìn (4th tone, from trad. 盡) when meaning "to exhaust" or "to fulfill" (as in 尽力, 尽职), vs. jǐn (3rd tone, from trad. 儘) when meaning "to the greatest possible extent" (as in 尽快, 尽量, 尽管).

rootFamily.gloss: to do one's utmost, spare no effort

尽义务.etymology: A verb-object (VO) syntactic phrase combining the verb 尽 (trad. 盡, jìn, "to fulfill completely, carry out to the utmost") with the nominal object 义务 (trad. 義務, yìwù, "duty, moral or legal obligation"). While 尽 + [duty noun] is a classical Chinese verb-object pattern (cf. 尽忠 "exhaust loyalty", 尽孝 "fulfill filial duty"), the compound noun 义务 was popularized in late 19th-century Meiji Japan (義務, gimu) to translate Western legal/philosophical concepts of "obligation" and "duty" (from 義 "righteousness/principle" + 務 "task/affair"), and subsequently re-borrowed into modern Chinese.

history.meaning: to carry out one's moral responsibility to the utmost (Classical VO schema)
legal or moral obligation (Meiji Japanese neoclassical coinage adopted into late Qing Chinese)
to fulfill an obligation or duty

morphemes.meaning: to fulfill, carry out to the utmost (trad. 盡)
affair, task, duty to attend to (trad. 務)

尽义务.notes: A separable verb-object (离合词) construction: aspect markers and modifiers are inserted between 尽 and 义务, e.g., 尽了应尽的义务 ("fulfilled the obligation one ought to fulfill").

rootFamily.gloss: to fulfill one's duty or responsibility

cognates.meaning: doing one's utmost, exertion of effort
to do one's utmost, exert all strength

尽力.etymology: A classical verb-object (VO) compound formed from 尽 (trad. 盡, jìn, "to exhaust, expend completely") and 力 (lì, "strength, physical or mental power", originally depicting a sinew or plowshare). Attested across Warring States and Han texts (such as the *Zuo Zhuan* and *Records of the Grand Historian*), 盡力 literally means "to exhaust one's strength" or "to pour all one's capability into a task", remaining unchanged in structure and sense from Classical Chinese to modern Mandarin.

history.meaning: to expend all of one's physical or mental strength in service
to exert oneself to the utmost, spare no effort
to do one's utmost, try one's best

morphemes.meaning: to exhaust, use up completely (trad. 盡)

尽力.notes: Functions as a separable verb-object compound (e.g., 尽了最大的力 "tried one's absolute best") and frequently appears in the four-character idiom 尽力而为 ("do one's utmost and leave the rest to fate"). In workplace dramas like *Behind the Scenes*, saying 我尽力了 ("I did my best") often signals a polite admission that a task could not be fully salvaged.

rootFamily.gloss: to do one's best, exert all effort (chengyu)
to exhaust one's heart and mind, devote oneself全心全意

尽快.etymology: A modifier-head adverbial compound formed from 尽 (trad. 儘, jǐn, "to the greatest extent, reaching the outer limit") and 快 (kuài, "fast, rapid, prompt"). Here 尽 represents traditional 儘 (derived from 盡 with the person radical 亻, emphasizing letting someone/something go all the way to a limit), which underwent grammaticalization into a degree/superlative prefix meaning "as ... as possible" before adjectives or verbs of scale. Combined with 快 (originally "pleased, gratifying" in Classical Chinese, shifting in vernacular Tang–Song Chinese to "sharp, quick, fast"), 尽快 means "at the fastest possible speed; as soon as possible".

history.meaning: 儘 ("to the utmost limit") and 快 ("gratifying > swift") develop as separate vernacular morphemes
as quickly as possible, at the earliest opportunity

morphemes.meaning: to the greatest extent possible (trad. 儘)

尽快.notes: In mainland China's standard pronunciation (*Putonghua*), 尽 in 尽快 and 尽量 is prescriptively pronounced in the 3rd tone (jǐn, corresponding to trad. 儘), though many native speakers colloquially pronounce it in the 4th tone (jìn) by analogy with 尽力. Essential in fast-paced media production for urgent deadlines (尽快落实 "implement ASAP").

rootFamily.gloss: as much as possible, to the greatest extent
feel free to, even though (trad. 儘管)

尽管.etymology: Compound of 尽 (儘, jǐn, 'to the utmost, freely let') + 管 ('attend to, concern oneself with'). Functions both as a permissive adverb before verbs ('feel free to…, go right ahead without hesitation') and as a concessive conjunction ('even though, despite, although').

history.meaning: feel free to (adverb); despite, even though (conjunction)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 尽管 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: as much as possible, to the fullest extent

尽量.etymology: Originally a verb-object compound 盡量 (jìnliàng) in Literary and early vernacular Chinese meaning "to exhaust one's capacity (especially drinking capacity)"—from 盡 ("exhaust") + 量 (liàng, "measured capacity, tolerance, limit"). Over time, a second sense crystalized as a modifier-head adverbial written 儘量 (jǐnliàng), combining 儘 ("to the greatest possible limit") + 量 ("extent, measure, scope"), meaning "to the fullest extent possible; as much as one can". In simplified characters both are written 尽量, and mainland standard Mandarin distinguishes adverbial jǐnliàng ("as much as possible") from verbal jìnliàng ("reach full capacity").

history.meaning: to reach the full limit of one's capacity (especially in drinking wine)
within the maximum possible measure; trying one's best within limits
as much as possible, to the greatest extent

morphemes.meaning: to the greatest possible extent, within the furthest limit (trad. 儘)

尽量.notes: Unlike 尽力 ("exert every ounce of strength"), 尽量 ("as much as possible / try to") is an adverb that precedes a verb (e.g., 我尽量赶过去 "I'll try my best to make it over there") and carries a pragmatic hedge—signaling willingness without guaranteeing 100% success.

cognates.meaning: bureau, department, board game match, situation
bureau, office, board game round, situation

局.etymology: In Old Chinese, 局 (*N-k<r>ok) meant "bent, curved, cramped, confined" (cf. /曲 *kʰ<r>ok "bent, crooked"), depicting a crouched body (尸) over a mouth/compartment. From "confined space / compartment", its meaning evolved in Han and Six Dynasties Chinese into two major branches: (1) a gridded board for games like *weiqi* (Go) or *liubo*, and by extension a single "game, match, round" played on that board, and metaphorically a "setup, trap, or strategic situation" (as in 设局 "set a trap/scheme", 饭局 "arranged dinner gathering"); and (2) an "office, bureau, or administrative division".

history.meaning: bent, curved, cramped; confined compartment
chess/game board; a round of a game; government office or workshop division
game, match, round (noun/classifier); social gathering or scheme; administrative bureau

morphemes.meaning: compartment, game board, round of a match, strategic setup, bureau

局.notes: Beyond being the standard classifier for matches/games (一局棋 "a game of chess", 赢了一局 "won a round"), in modern business and entertainment circles 局 frequently refers to an orchestrated social gathering (饭局, 酒局) or a calculated strategic scheme (做局 "rig a situation", 破局 "break a deadlock").

cognates.meaning: board surface; aspect or phase of a situation, stage of a game

局面.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound combining 局 (jú, "game board, strategic configuration") and 面 (miàn, "face, surface, aspect"). Originally a concrete term in Classical/Middle Chinese board games (especially *weiqi* / Go) referring to the physical "surface of the game board" and the arrangement of stones upon it at a given stage of play. By metaphorical extension from board-game strategy, it came to denote the "overall configuration of forces, state of affairs, or political/organizational situation" facing decision-makers.

history.meaning: surface of a Go/chess board and the layout of pieces during a match; exterior aspect/scale of a building
overall situation, configuration of events, state of affairs

morphemes.meaning: game board, strategic setup, overall configuration

局面.notes: Commonly collocates with dynamic verbs of control or transformation derived from the Go metaphor: 打开局面 ("open up the situation / achieve a breakthrough"), 控制局面 ("control the situation"), 挽回局面 ("salvage the situation"), and 僵局 ("stalemate").

rootFamily.gloss: overall situation, current trend/state of affairs
outsider, someone not involved in the game/situation

层.etymology: Phono-semantic character (traditional 層, combining 尸 'house/roof' + 曾 céng 'tiered steamer pot, add upon'): 'story, floor (of a building); layer, tier, stratum, level'.

history.meaning: multi-story building; tier; layer
floor/story; layer; tier; classifier for levels

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 层 (via 萌典)

层面.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 层 (trad. 層, céng, "story of a building, tier, stratum, layer", from 尸 "building/body" + 曾 phonetic, "piled up") and 面 (miàn, "surface, plane, facet"). Originally used in geological, architectural, or anatomical contexts for a physical "bedding plane" or "stratum surface", in 20th-century analytical and sociological Chinese it became a productive abstract noun meaning a conceptual "level, plane, tier, or dimension" of analysis (e.g., 精神层面 "spiritual/psychological dimension", 操作层面 "operational level").

history.meaning: separate morphemes for "story/tier" and "face/surface" in Medieval Chinese
physical stratum surface > abstract level, plane, or dimension of an issue or organization

层面.notes: Very frequent in corporate, academic, and media-production discourse in the frame 在…层面上 ("on the ... level / from the ... dimension"), such as 技术层面 ("technical level"), 商业层面 ("commercial dimension"), or 战略层面 ("strategic level").

rootFamily.gloss: hierarchy, level, gradation; sense of depth/structure in art or media

居然.etymology: Formed from 居 (jū, "to sit, dwell, remain in place, occupy") + the adverbial/stative suffix 然 (rán, "thus, in such a state"). In Classical Chinese (attested in the *Book of Odes* 詩經·大雅·生民: 居然生子 "she stayed at home and gave birth to a son safely"), 居然 meant "sitting calmly in place, securely, naturally, without commotion". Through pragmatic irony in Tang–Song–Ming vernacular—observing someone acting "calmly/brazenly as if nothing were amiss" in an outrageous situation—it underwent subjectification and counter-expectation shift to mean "unexpectedly, contrary to all expectations, to one's surprise, actually".

history.meaning: dwelling peacefully in place; calmly, naturally, effortlessly
brazenly, nonchalantly; easily, without ado > unexpectedly, surprisingly
actually, unexpectedly, to one's surprise (expressing disbelief or astonishment)

morphemes.meaning: to dwell, sit still, remain in place
-ly, in such a manner or state (stative/adverbial formative)

居然.notes: A near-synonym of 竟然 (jìngrán), both expressing counter-expectation ("actually / to one's surprise!"), though 居然 often carries a slightly stronger tone of incredulity or reproach at someone's audacity (e.g., 他居然敢迟到 "He actually dared to show up late!").

rootFamily.gloss: harbor evil intentions, have ulterior motives

屈尊.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound formed from 屈 (qū, "to bend, bow, stoop, humble", originally depicting a tail/body bent inside an enclosure) and 尊 (zūn, "noble status, exalted position, honor", originally depicting two hands offering a ritual wine vessel 酋). Literally meaning "to bend/lower one's exalted status", 屈尊 originated in Literary Chinese court and epistolary etiquette as a deferential expression asking or thanking a person of high rank for "condescending / graciously humbling themselves" to visit a lowly place or accept a modest role.

history.meaning: to bend/humble (屈) and noble/exalted status (尊) as classical roots
to lower one's lofty status, graciously condescend to visit or associate with a humble person
to condescend, humble oneself to accept a lower position or visit someone of lower rank (courteous or ironic)

morphemes.meaning: exalted status, noble rank, honor, dignity

屈尊.notes: Used either with genuine politeness (e.g., 屈尊光临 "graciously condescend to honor us with your presence") or with biting irony when an arrogant celebrity or executive is asked to take a smaller role or desk (e.g., 委屈您屈尊一下 "Sorry to make you stoop so low").

rootFamily.gloss: underusing someone's talent, doing a job beneath one's skill
to feel wronged, nurse a grievance; to put someone at a disadvantage

cognates.meaning: to waste talent, underuse someone's abilities

屈才.etymology: A classical verb-object (VO) compound functioning as a stative verb/adjective in Mandarin, composed of 屈 (qū, "to bend, cramp, stifle, wrong, suppress") and 才 (cái, "natural talent, ability, capability", originally a pictogram of a sprouting plant shoot pushing through the soil). Literally "to cramp/stifle talent", 屈才 describes placing a gifted person in a lowly or menial position where their abilities cannot be stretched out and exercised.

history.meaning: to suppress or fail to employ a person of talent in an appropriate official post
to waste or underuse someone's talent; (politely) a position is beneath someone's abilities

morphemes.meaning: to bend, cramp, stifle, do wrong to

屈才.notes: Often used in workplace diplomacy: when hiring or assigning an overqualified veteran to a junior post (as happens frequently in *Behind the Scenes*), a manager will say 让你做这个真是屈才了 ("Having you do this really underuses your talent").

rootFamily.gloss: to condescend, humble one's lofty status
a great talent used for a petty purpose (idiom)

屋子.etymology: Colloquial noun formed from 屋 ('house, room, roof', combining 尸 'roof/shelter' + 至 'where people arrive and rest') + nominal suffix 子 (neutral tone zi): 'room; house'.

history.meaning: room; house

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 屋子 (via 萌典)

屋檐.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound combining 屋 (wū, "house, room, roofed dwelling") and 檐 (yán, also written 簷 with the bamboo radical, "eaves, overhanging edge of a roof", from 木 "wood" + 詹 phonetic, denoting the projecting wooden rafters along the perimeter of a roof). While literal 屋檐 refers to the overhanging eaves that shelter a building's walls from rain, it acquired deep proverbial resonance in vernacular Chinese through the saying 在人屋檐下，不得不低头 ("Standing under someone else's low eaves, one has no choice but to bow one's head")—meaning that when dependent on another's shelter or authority, one must swallow one's pride.

history.meaning: house/roof (屋) and projecting wooden eaves of a roof (檐)
the overhanging eaves of a house roof; shelter provided by a household
eaves, roof overhang (literal and figurative for someone's domain or shelter)

morphemes.meaning: eaves, overhanging border of a roof (variant 簷)

屋檐.notes: In workplace and showbiz dramas, 屋檐 almost always evokes the proverb 人在屋檐下，不得不低头 ("When under someone else's roof/eaves, you have to bow your head"), used when an employee, artist, or agency must compromise before a powerful platform or boss.

rootFamily.gloss: flying eaves (upturned roof corners in traditional Chinese architecture)

屋里.etymology: Locative compound combining 屋 ('room, house') + 里 (裡, 'inside'): 'inside the room, indoors, in the house'.

history.meaning: inside the room; indoors

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 屋里 (via 萌典)

屋顶.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 屋 ('house') + 顶 (頂, 'crown of the head, top'): 'roof, housetop'.

history.meaning: roof of a house; rooftop

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 屋顶 (via 萌典)

屏幕.etymology: Coordinative noun compound of 屏 ('folding or standing screen that shields a view', 尸 + 并) + 幕 ('hanging tent or curtain cloth', 莫 + 巾). Originally named traditional decorative screens and stage curtains, then standardized in modern Chinese for a television, computer, phone, or cinema 'screen'.

history.meaning: partition screen and hanging curtain
display screen (TV, monitor, phone, cinema)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 屏幕 (via 萌典)

展开.etymology: A resultative verb compound pairing 展 (zhǎn, 'to unroll, stretch out flat, spread open') with the directional/resultative complement 开 (kāi, 'open, apart, outward'). In Classical Chinese 展 alone meant 'to unroll a scroll or extend one's limbs'; Mandarin added 开 to highlight the visible result of a folded sheet, map, or scroll opening out flat, and also extended 展开 figuratively to 'launching' a discussion or search.

history.meaning: unroll a scroll; spread flat
unfold; spread open; launch

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 展开

cognates.meaning: to belong to, be affiliated with (属する)
to belong to, be affiliated with

属于.etymology: A verb + prepositional-complement compound combining 属 (trad. 屬, shǔ, "to be attached to, be subordinate to, belong to a category", originally from 尾 "tail" + 蜀 phonetic, depicting one thing connected behind another like a tail) and 于 (trad. 於, yú, "to, in, at", the classical locative/dative preposition). In Classical Chinese, 屬於 (read zhǔ yú when meaning "connect/entrust to", or shǔ yú when meaning "be subordinate to / fall under the jurisdiction of") linked a verb to its prepositional phrase; in modern Mandarin, 属于 lexicalized into a single transitive verb meaning "to belong to, be part of, fall into the category of".

history.meaning: to be attached to, fall under the jurisdiction or category of (verb + preposition)
to be subordinate to, belong to, pertain to
to belong to, be part of, be classified as

morphemes.meaning: to be subordinate to, belong to, fall under a category (trad. 屬)
to, in, at (classical dative/locative preposition, trad. 於)

属于.notes: Unlike English "belong to", Mandarin 属于 is used not only for ownership/affiliation (这属于公司财产 "this belongs to company property", 舞台属于你 "the stage belongs to you") but also colloquially as a classificatory copula ("is considered / counts as", e.g., 这属于正常现象 "this counts as a normal phenomenon").

rootFamily.gloss: subordinate, underling; to be subordinate to

山.etymology: Foundational pictograph (象形字) attested from Shang oracle bones depicting three mountain peaks rising side by side: 'mountain, hill, peak'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: three peaks = mountain, hill

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 山 (via 萌典)

山丘.etymology: Compound noun of 山 ('mountain, hill') + 丘 ('earthen hillock, mound', originally two peaks standing on the ground 一): 'hill, hillock, knoll'. Attested since the Shijing and Chuci.

history.stage: Old & Classical Chinese (Shijing, Chuci) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: hill; mound; knoll

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 山丘 (via 萌典)

山毛榉木.etymology: Four-character botanical timber compound combining 山毛榉 ('beech tree, Fagus', literally 'mountain hairy zelkova-like tree', named for its hairy leaf margins and triangular nuts) + 木 ('wood, timber'): 'beechwood'.

history.form: 山毛櫸木 / 山毛榉木
history.meaning: beechwood (timber of the Fagus beech tree)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 山毛榉木 (via 萌典)

岁.etymology: Ancient character (traditional 歲) combining 步 ('step, planetary march across the sky') + 戌 ('axe', phonetic and graphic). In early Chinese astronomy, 歲 was the planet Jupiter (岁星), whose 12-year orbital cycle through the 12 ecliptic stations marked one 'year' per station; hence 'year (of harvest or time)' and the standard classifier for 'years of age'.

history.meaning: Jupiter's annual station -> year, harvest
year; years old (classifier for age)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 岁 (via 萌典)

岁数.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound composed of 岁 (trad. 歲, suì, "year, year of age", originally from 步 "step/planet's transit" + 戌 "battle-axe", denoting the 12-year orbital cycle of Jupiter, the "Year Star" 歲星, and hence a solar year) and 数 (trad. 數, shù, neutrally toned to shu in spoken Mandarin, "number, count, tally"). Literally "the count of one's years", 岁数 emerged in Tang–Song vernacular Chinese as an everyday spoken word for a person's age in years.

history.meaning: solar/Jupiter year (歲) and number/count (數) as Classical Chinese roots
number of years; a person's age in years (attested in Tang poetry and Song vernacular)
age, years of age (colloquial, especially of middle-aged or older adults)

岁数.notes: Spoken with a neutral tone on the second syllable (suìshu). Compared to the formal 年龄 (niánlíng, "age") and polite 年纪 (niánjì), 岁数 is warm and colloquial, and in phrases like 上了岁数 ("getting on in years") or 岁数大了 ("old in years") specifically refers to middle-aged or elderly people.

rootFamily.gloss: years, time, the passage of life (poetic/literary)
year of age (classifier); New Year's Eve (守岁)

崇拜.etymology: A subordinative/coordinative verbal compound combining 崇 (chóng, "lofty, high; to revere, exalt, hold in high esteem", from 山 "mountain" + 宗 phonetic/semantic "ancestral temple") and 拜 (bài, "to bow with clasped hands, doobeisance, worship", depicting two hands lowered in ritual salutation). Literally "to hold on high and bow down to", 崇拜 originally denoted religious or ritual veneration, was reinforced in late 19th-century Sino-Japanese (崇拝, sūhai) to translate Western "worship / cult" (e.g., 个人崇拜 "cult of personality", 偶像崇拜 "idolatry"), and broadened in everyday Mandarin to mean "to idolize, look up to, or deeply admire" a mentor or star.

history.meaning: to exalt/revere (崇) and to bow in ritual salutation (拜)
to revere and bow before; religious worship, veneration of ancestors or deities
to worship, idolize, admire greatly, look up to

morphemes.meaning: lofty, high; to revere, esteem, exalt
to bow in obeisance, pay homage, worship

崇拜.notes: Ranges from serious sociological contexts (个人崇拜 "cult of personality") to everyday fan/workplace enthusiasm (我是看着您的节目长大的，特别崇拜您 "I grew up watching your shows and really idolize you").

rootFamily.gloss: lofty, sublime, noble (of ideals or character)
to esteem, advocate, uphold (a value or style)
to pay a visit, call on (polite)

cognates.meaning: concert or theatrical tour (巡業 / 巡演)

巡演.etymology: A modern telescopic abbreviation (紧缩词) of the four-character phrase 巡回演出 (xúnhuí yǎnchū, "touring performance"), formed as a modifier-head compound from 巡 (xún, "to patrol, make a circuit, travel around inspecting", from 巛 "streams/paths" + 辶 "walk") and 演 (yǎn, "to perform, act out, stage", originally "water flowing out far and wide" > "to elaborate, deduce, perform"). As a noun it means "concert/theatrical tour"; as a verb, "to go on tour performing across multiple cities".

history.meaning: to make an inspection tour (巡) and to flow out / elaborate (演) in Classical Chinese
itinerant or circuit theatrical/musical performance across cities
concert tour, theatrical tour; to go on tour (abbreviated disyllabic compound)

morphemes.meaning: to tour, make a circuit, travel from place to place (from 巡回)
to perform, stage a show (from 演出)

巡演.notes: Standard showbiz term in music and theater production: 全国巡演 ("national tour"), 世界巡演 ("world tour"), 巡演首站 ("first stop of the tour"). Always expand mentally to 巡回演出 to understand its internal syntax.

rootFamily.gloss: performance, show; to perform, put on a show
to tour, go the rounds (of exhibitions, lectures, or shows)

工位.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound combining 工 (gōng, "work, labor, craft", abbreviated from 工作 "work" or 工人 "worker", originally a pictogram of a carpenter's square or rammed-earth tool) and 位 (wèi, "seat, place, station, position", depicting a person 亻 standing 立 at their assigned spot at court). Originally an industrial engineering and factory manufacturing term denoting an assembly-line "workstation" or "operation station", in contemporary white-collar office culture 工位 became the universal word for an employee's individual "office cubicle, desk, or workstation".

history.meaning: craft/work (工) and standing place/seat of rank (位) in Classical Chinese
industrial workstation on a factory floor or production line
office desk, cubicle, individual employee workstation in an open-plan office

工位.notes: Whereas 办公桌 (bàngōngzhuō) refers strictly to the physical piece of furniture ("office desk"), 工位 refers to the assigned cubicle or workspace unit (desk, chair, partition, and power outlet) belonging to an employee in a modern company. In workplace dramas, packing up one's 工位 (收拾工位) is the visual shorthand for resigning or being fired.

rootFamily.gloss: job post, position, station of duty

工作.etymology: Coordinative verb and noun compound of 工 ('artisan's square/rammer -> craft, labor, work') + 作 ('make, do, toil'). Attested since the Classic of Poetry and Han texts for 'physical labor, craftwork', and standardized in modern Chinese as the universal noun and verb for 'work, job, employment'.

history.meaning: manual labor; craftwork
work; job; employment

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 工作 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: work/construction + personnel (compounds 工作 and 人員 exist with distinct senses)

cognates.word: nhân viên công tác (人員工作)

工作人员.etymology: A four-character modifier-head nominal compound formed from 工作 (gōngzuò, "work, job, operation", a classical coordinative compound of 工 "craft/labor" + 作 "make/do" that acquired its modern noun/verb sense "work" via Meiji Japanese 工作 and early 20th-century Mandarin) modifying 人员 (rényuán, "personnel, staff", from 人 "person" + 员 "member/official tally"). Together, 工作人员 literally means "working personnel" and serves as the standard collective or individual term for "staff member(s), crew member(s), or event personnel".

history.form: 工作 (kuwng tsak) + 人員 (nyin hjwen)
history.meaning: craftsmanship/construction (工作) and headcount of officials/personnel (人員) in Literary Chinese

history.form: 工作人員 / 工作人员 (gōngzuò rényuán)
history.meaning: working personnel, staff member, production crew member

morphemes.meaning: personnel, staff member (from 人 'person' + 员 'member', trad. 員)

工作人员.notes: In film, television, and live events (*Behind the Scenes*), 工作人员 refers to the entire on-site production, stage, and logistical crew (as printed on lanyard badges: 工作人员证 "staff pass"), in contrast to 艺人/嘉宾 ("artists/guests") and 观众 ("audience").

工作室.etymology: Three-character compound of 工作 ('work') + 室 ('room'): 'studio, workshop, atelier, small professional office'.

history.meaning: studio; workshop; atelier

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 工作室 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: enthusiast, maniac, -aholic (as a productive suffix, e.g. 仕事狂 shigoto-kyō 'workaholic')

工作狂.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound and semantic calque of English *workaholic* (coined in 1968 by Wayne Oates), formed from 工作 (gōngzuò, "work, job") + the productive agentive/behavioral suffix 狂 (kuáng, "madman, fanatic, maniac, someone obsessively devoted to X"). In Classical Chinese, 狂 (*[g]ʷraŋ, from 犭 "dog" + 王 phonetic) meant "rabid dog > madness, frenzy, unbridled extravagance"; in modern Mandarin (paralleling Sino-Japanese -狂 *-kyō*), 狂 attaches to nouns or verbs to denote an obsessive enthusiast or addict (e.g., 购物狂 "shopaholic", 控制狂 "control freak", 工作狂 "workaholic").

history.meaning: rabid; madness, manic frenzy, unrestrained eccentricity
workaholic, person compulsively obsessed with working (late 20th-century calque of English 'workaholic')

morphemes.meaning: maniac, fanatic, -aholic (person obsessively addicted to an activity)

工作狂.notes: Both the protagonist Chunyu Qiao and布小谷 (Bu Xiaogu) in *Behind the Scenes* (幕后之王) are archetypal 工作狂. The suffix -狂 is highly productive in modern Mandarin for behavioral obsessions: 细节狂 ("detail freak"), 控制狂 ("control freak"), 购物狂 ("shopaholic").

cognates.word: 工作簡報 (gung1 zok3 gaan2 bou3)

工作简报.etymology: A four-character modifier-head nominal compound combining 工作 (gōngzuò, "work, operational") and 简报 (trad. 簡報, jiǎnbào, "brief report, bulletin, briefing"). Within 简报, 简 (trad. 簡, jiǎn) originally meant a "bamboo slip for writing" in Classical Chinese and by extension "concise, abridged, brief" (since a single slip held only a few lines), while 报 (trad. 報, bào) meant "to respond, report back to a superior" and in modern Chinese "report, bulletin, newspaper". Thus 工作简报 means a "concise work report" or "operational status briefing".

history.meaning: bamboo writing slip > concise/brief (簡) and to report/reply (報) in Classical Chinese
concise summary report, news bulletin, or briefing presentation
work brief, operational status briefing or summary bulletin

morphemes.meaning: brief, concise, summarized (trad. 簡, orig. 'bamboo slip')

工作简报.notes: Note a regional nuance: in mainland China, 简报 (and 工作简报) usually refers to a written concise status bulletin or executive summary document; in Taiwan, 简报 specifically means a slide presentation / briefing (such as a PowerPoint deck, 做简报 "give a presentation").

rootFamily.gloss: report; to report (formally to superiors or the public)

cognates.meaning: operative, agent (note false friend: Japanese 工作者 kōsakusha means 'spy/political operative')
operative (in Korean 공작원; Chinese 工作者 corresponds to 종사자 'practitioner')

工作者.etymology: Formed from the disyllabic root 工作 (gōngzuò, "work, professional activity") + the classical agentive/nominalizing suffix 者 (zhě, "one who does / person characterized by"). In Classical Chinese, 者 (*tAʔ) was a bound pronominal head meaning "that which / the one who" attached to verb phrases; in modern Mandarin (influenced by European *-er / -ist* translations via Sino-Japanese -者 *-sha*), 者 functions as a dignified agent suffix denoting a professional practitioner or intellectual worker in a specialized field (e.g., 医务工作者 "medical worker", 文艺工作者 "arts and culture practitioner").

history.meaning: nominalizing particle: 'the one who, that which' in Classical and Middle Chinese
worker, professional practitioner in an intellectual, artistic, or public-service domain

morphemes.meaning: -er, -ist, practitioner, one who engages in (classical agentive nominalizer)

工作者.notes: Crucial distinction between 工人 (gōngrén) and 工作者 (gōngzuòzhě): 工人 refers specifically to blue-collar industrial or manual laborers, whereas 工作者 is an elevated, respectful term used with a field modifier for professionals in media, arts, healthcare, science, or education—e.g., 电视工作者 ("television professional"), 新闻工作者 ("journalist / media worker"), 文艺工作者 ("arts practitioner"). Beware the Japanese false friend 工作者 (*kōsakusha*), which means "spy / covert operative"!

工作餐.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound combining 工作 (gōngzuò, "work, on-duty") and 餐 (cān, "meal, food; to eat", originally from 𣦼 "broken bones/food scraps" + 食 "eat"). Coined in modern institutional and corporate Mandarin to designate a "working meal" provided to staff on duty or eaten during a business meeting, as opposed to a formal banquet (宴请 / 应酬) or private dining. In film and TV production, 工作餐 specifically denotes the boxed crew meals (盒饭) distributed on set during a shoot.

history.meaning: to eat, swallow; a prepared meal or food ration in Classical Chinese
working meal, staff cafeteria meal, or production crew box lunch provided on duty

工作餐.notes: In Chinese television and film production (*Behind the Scenes*), ordering, distributing, and eating 工作餐 (typically 盒饭 "boxed meals") on set is a central ritual of crew logistics (场务) and a frequent symbol of the egalitarian grind shared by directors, producers, and crew alike.

rootFamily.gloss: boxed meal, bento (standard crew meal on a film/TV set)

工具.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound formed from 工 (gōng, "artisan, craft, work", originally a carpenter's square) and 具 (jù, "utensil, implement, apparatus; to prepare", originally depicting two hands 廾 holding a鼎/貝 vessel to set out utensils or provisions). Attested since the *Guanzi* and Han dynasty texts for an artisan's "craft implements / tools of a trade", 工具 broadened in modern Chinese to denote both physical hardware tools and abstract "instruments, vehicles, or means to an end" (e.g., 交通工具 "means of transport", 宣传工具 "propaganda instrument").

history.meaning: artisan's implements, carpenter's or craftsman's tools
implements of a trade or craft; utensils
tool, implement, instrument (literal hardware and figurative means to an end)

工具.notes: Used both literally and figuratively. In modern internet and workplace slang, 工具人 (gōngjùrén, "tool person") is a ubiquitous term for someone who is used purely as an instrument to get tasks done without receiving credit or genuine emotional reciprocation.

rootFamily.gloss: props, stage property (in theater/TV); item in a game

工具房.etymology: Three-character compound of 工具 ('tools, implements', 工 'work/craft' + 具 'utensil') + 房 ('room, shed'): 'tool room, toolshed'.

工具箱.etymology: Three-character compound of 工具 ('tools') + 箱 ('box, chest, case'): 'toolbox, toolkit'.
