工夫.etymology: Originally a compound of 工 (gōng, "work, craft, labor") and 夫 (fū, "adult male laborer, corvée worker"), attested in Three Kingdoms and Six Dynasties texts (such as the *Records of the Three Kingdoms*) meaning "laborers engaged in construction / corvée labor force". Because large-scale labor was measured in man-days of time and skill, 工夫 shifted metonymically in Tang–Song vernacular to mean "the time and effort expended on a task", and from there split into two senses: (1) "skill, mastery achieved through long practice" (increasingly written 功夫 in modern Chinese), and (2) "time, free time, spare moment, leisure" (preferentially written 工夫 and pronounced gōngfu with a neutral second syllable).

history.meaning: male corvée laborers; man-hours of labor > time and effort devoted to a task
time required for an activity; spare time, free moment; cultivated skill or workmanship
time (duration), free time, spare moment (distinguished orthographically from 功夫 'martial arts / deep skill')

morphemes.meaning: laborer, adult man > man-hour of time/effort (neutral tone in Mandarin)

工夫.notes: Modern prescriptive orthography differentiates 工夫 (time, free time, duration: 没工夫搭理你 "I don't have the spare time to deal with you", 一会儿工夫 "in just a moment's time") from 功夫 (deeply cultivated skill, effort, or martial arts: 下功夫 "put in hard effort", 真功夫 "real skill"), though both are pronounced gōngfu with a neutral second tone.

rootFamily.gloss: effort, skill, workmanship, kung fu (orthographic doublet)
to put in time and effort, apply oneself દિલથી

工工整整.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 工工整整. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 工工整整 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 工工整整 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 工工整整 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 工工整整. The etymology of 工工整整 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 工工整整
middle form of 工工整整
modern form of 工工整整

工整.etymology: A coordinate adjective compound uniting 工 (gōng, originally a carpenter's square 工, hence 'skilful, finely crafted, exact in workmanship') and 整 (zhěng, 'orderly, aligned, complete'). Praised since Tang–Song calligraphy and poetry criticism (as in 工整对仗 'neatly balanced couplets'), 工整 in everyday Mandarin especially commends handwriting whose strokes sit balanced and legible on the page.

morphemes.meaning: finely crafted; exact (from carpenter's square 工)

history.meaning: finely proportioned and balanced (of verse or brushwork)
neat and tidy (especially of handwriting)

工资.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound combining 工 (gōng, "work, labor") and 资 (trad. 資, zī, "wealth, money, allowance, resources, fee", from 貝 "cowrie shell / money" + 次 phonetic). Literally "labor remuneration / money paid for work", 工资 emerged in early modern Chinese administrative and economic usage to denote monetary wages or salary paid to workers and employees, eventually becoming the standard everyday word across mainland China for both monthly salary and hourly/daily wages.

history.meaning: work/craft (工) and money/resources/allowance (資) in Classical Chinese
wages, salary, monetary compensation paid for labor

morphemes.meaning: money, fee, allowance, capital (trad. 資, from 貝 'shell/money')

工资.notes: In everyday mainland Mandarin, 工资 covers both white-collar "salary" and blue-collar "wages" (发工资 "pay out salaries", 涨工资 "get a raise", 扣工资 "dock pay"), whereas 薪水 (xīnshuǐ) or 薪资 (xīnzī) sounds slightly more formal or white-collar/HR-oriented.

左.etymology: Ancient graph attested on Shang oracle bones as 𠂇 (pictograph of a left hand), to which 工 ('carpenter's square / tool', suggesting the left hand holding a tool to assist) was later added to distinguish 'left (side/hand)' (左) from the verb 'assist' (佐, which added 亻).

左手.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 左 ('left') + 手 ('hand'): 'left hand, left-hand side'. Attested since the Shijing and Classics.

巨大.etymology: A parallel/coordinative adjectival compound uniting two near-synonymous roots: 巨 (jù, "great, huge, chief, gigantic", originally depicting a large carpenter's square held by a hand, symbolizing a master builder's great measure) and 大 (dà, "big, large, great", a frontal pictogram of a person standing with arms and legs stretched wide). Pairing two synonyms of size creates an intensive disyllabic adjective meaning "immense, enormous, colossal, tremendous" in both physical scale and abstract magnitude.

history.meaning: great/large (巨, orig. carpenter's square) and big/vast (大) in Classical Chinese
vast, immense, of extraordinary size or scale (attested in Han–Tang prose)
huge, immense, enormous, tremendous (physical or abstract)

morphemes.meaning: huge, gigantic, great (orig. a large carpenter's square)

巨大.notes: Unlike 大, which is a general-purpose adjective ("big"), 巨大 is a non-gradable or high-intensity adjective meaning "immense / enormous" and frequently modifies abstract nouns in media and business contexts: 巨大的压力 ("immense pressure"), 巨大的成功 ("tremendous success"), 巨大的潜力 ("enormous potential").

rootFamily.gloss: arduous, monumental (of a task: 艰巨)

差.etymology: Ancient graph showing grain/hemp stalks of uneven length above a hand/tool (左/工): read chà 'differ, fall short of, lack (five minutes to…), poor/substandard in quality'; read chā 'difference, discrepancy, error'; read chāi 'send on an official errand (出差)'.

差不多.etymology: Idiomatic verb/adjective/adverb phrase combining 差 ('differ by, fall short by') + 不多 ('not much'): literally 'differs by not much' -> 'almost the same, nearly, just about, good enough'.

差点儿.etymology: Colloquial Beijing and standard Mandarin adverbial phrase combining 差 ('fall short by; miss by a margin') + 点儿 ('a tiny dot/bit', with diminutive retroflex suffix 儿 -r). It expresses that an event missed happening by only the narrowest margin ('nearly; almost').

history.meaning: miss by a hair; almost
nearly; almost

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 差点儿

差评.etymology: Compound noun and verb combining 差 (chà, 'poor, substandard, bad') + 评 (評, 'evaluation, review, rating'): 'negative review, bad rating'.

差距.etymology: A modifier-head or coordinative nominal compound combining 差 (chā, "divergence, difference, discrepancy, falling short", originally depicting a hand holding a grain stalk that diverges or hangs unevenly) and 距 (jù, "distance apart, separation", originally from 足 "foot" + 巨 phonetic, denoting a rooster's spur and by extension "to stand apart, distance between two points"). Literally "the distance of divergence", 差距 denotes the measurable or qualitative "gap, disparity, or shortfall" between two standards, competitors, or expectations.

history.meaning: to diverge/differ (差) and spur / distance apart (距) in Classical Chinese
gap, disparity, difference in level, quality, or distance between two things or people

差距.notes: Unlike 区别 (qūbié, neutral "difference/distinction in kind"), 差距 specifically implies a vertical or scalar "gap/disparity" where one side is ahead or superior and the other lags behind—e.g., 缩小差距 ("narrow the gap"), 拉开差距 ("widen the lead/gap"), 理想和现实的差距 ("the gap between ideals and reality").

rootFamily.gloss: error, mistake, slip-up (in work: 出差错)

cognates.meaning: already (すでに / 既に); to stop, finish (やむ)

已.etymology: A primary Classical Chinese character (已, yǐ, Old Chinese *ɢ(r)əʔ), graphically interrelated in early script with 巳 (sì, a fetus/serpent, the 6th earthly branch) and 己 (jǐ, a winding cord / oneself). Its core verbal meaning in Old Chinese was "to stop, cease, come to an end, finish" (as in 死而后已 "only in death does one stop"). By universal cross-linguistic grammaticalization (completion verb "to finish" > anterior/perfective aspect adverb "already"), 已 became the standard Classical Chinese adverb meaning "already", preserved in modern Mandarin both in formal/concise prose and as the first morpheme of disyllabic words like 已经 ("already"), 已婚 ("married"), and 已有 ("already existing").

history.meaning: to cease, stop, finish; (adverb) already, having completed an action
already; to come to an end; final particle (而已 'and that is all')
already (concise/formal counterpart of 已经; bound prefix in状态 compounds like 已婚, 已知)

已.notes: In spoken Mandarin, the disyllabic 已经 (yǐjīng) is preferred, whereas monosyllabic 已 is heavily used in headlines, status labels (已读 "read", 已发送 "sent", 已婚 "married"), and concise written or four-character expressions (木已成舟 "the wood has already become a boat / what's done is done", 赞叹不已 "praise without stopping"). Visually distinguish 已 (half-open on the left) from 己 (jǐ, fully open, "self") and 巳 (sì, fully closed).

rootFamily.gloss: and that is all, nothing more (classical final phrase common in speech)
cannot help oneself, have no choice (迫不得已)

cognates.meaning: married (Japanese uses 既婚 kikon with the synonymous classical prefix 既)

已婚.etymology: A modifier-head stative/adjectival compound formed from the classical aspectual adverbial prefix 已 (yǐ, "already, having completed") and 婚 (hūn, "to marry, marriage", originally from 女 "woman" + 昏 "dusk", because ancient Zhou dynasty wedding ceremonies—as recorded in the *Book of Etiquette and Ceremonial* 儀禮·士昏禮—took place at twilight/dusk when the groom fetched the bride). Coined as a concise administrative and legal category meaning "already married" in direct opposition to 未婚 (wèihūn, "not yet married / single").

history.meaning: dusk, twilight > wedding ceremony held at dusk; to take a wife in Classical Chinese
married (as an official civil, demographic, or personal status, contrasted with 未婚 'unmarried')

morphemes.meaning: marriage, to wed (orig. wedding ceremony held at dusk 昏)

已婚.notes: Functions as a non-gradable classification adjective (区别词): it modifies nouns directly (已婚人士 "married person", 已婚状态 "married status") or follows 是 (他是已婚的), and in entertainment/celebrity PR (*Behind the Scenes*), whether an idol is 未婚 ("single") or secretly 已婚 ("married", 隐婚 "secretly married") is a major career plot point.

rootFamily.gloss: secretly married (concealing one's marriage from the public/fans)

已有.etymology: A modifier-head verbal/attributive compound formed from the classical aspectual adverb 已 (yǐ, "already") modifying the existential/possessive verb 有 (yǒu, "to have, possess; there is/are", originally depicting a hand 又 holding meat 月/肉). Used continuously since Classical Chinese as a compact two-syllable predicate ("already has / there already are") and in modern Mandarin also as a pre-nominal attributive modifier meaning "existing, previously established, already in hand" (e.g., 已有经验 "existing experience", 已有成果 "already achieved results").

history.meaning: already has, there already exists (adverb + verb in Classical Chinese prose)
already possesses; there are already (followed by time duration or quantity)
there already are, already have; (attributive) existing, established

morphemes.meaning: to have, possess; there is/are (existential verb)

已有.notes: Used in two primary patterns: (1) as a verbal predicate before a number or duration in written/broadcast register (入行已有十年 "has already been in the industry for ten years"), and (2) as an attributive modifier before a noun meaning "existing / already on hand" (在已有的基础上 "on the existing foundation", alongside 现有 "currently available").

rootFamily.gloss: possess, own, command (a large audience or resource)

已经.etymology: Temporal aspect adverb combining two Classical completion words: 已 ('stop, finish, already') + 经 (經, 'pass through, experience, already'): 'already'. Attested from the Six Dynasties and Tang period onward.

history.meaning: already (having passed through or completed)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 已经 (via 萌典)

巴巴地.etymology: Formed by reduplicating the verb-root 巴 (bā, 'to hope earnestly; to cling to; to gaze expectantly', as in 巴望 and 眼巴巴) followed by the adverbial manner marker 地 (de). In Ming–Qing vernacular fiction, 巴巴 (often suffixed with 儿 or 地) described clinging or gazing with intense, almost pathetic anticipation, shifting into a vivid adverb for doing something eagerly yet often in vain.

history.meaning: to cling to; to wait or long for earnestly
anxiously, clings expectantly, earnestly (in Ming–Qing vernacular novels)
eagerly, earnestly, going out of one's way (often with a tinge of futility)

morphemes.meaning: to long for earnestly, to gaze expectantly

巴巴地.notes: Frequently takes the retroflex suffix in spoken northern Mandarin (巴巴儿地, bābārde) and implies pathetic or unrewarded eagerness, as when an intern waits anxiously for a producer's approval.

rootFamily.gloss: to look forward to earnestly, to gaze anxiously
hoping against hope, gazing helplessly or expectantly
cannot wait to, only too anxious to

巷子.etymology: Colloquial noun formed from 巷 (read xiàng, 'narrow street or residential lane between walls', 共 + 邑/巳) + nominal suffix 子 (neutral tone zi): 'lane, alley'.

history.meaning: alley; narrow residential lane

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 巷子 (via 萌典)

市.etymology: Ancient character attested on bronze inscriptions showing an enclosed ground with a signpost/banner at the top: originally 'walled marketplace where goods are bought and sold' (and verbally 'buy/trade'), extended in modern administration to 'city, municipality'.

market; city; municipality

市场.etymology: Compound noun of 市 ('trade, market') + 场 (場, 'open ground, square, venue'): 'marketplace, bazaar, economic market'. Attested since Han–Tang texts.

市里.etymology: Locative compound combining 市 ('city, municipality') + 里 (裡, 'inside'): 'in the city, downtown; the municipal authorities'.

布.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining 父 (fù/bù phonetic, reduced to 𠂇 at the top) + 巾 ('woven cloth'): originally 'woven hemp or ramie cloth' in Classical Chinese (contrasting with 帛 'silk'), and since the Yuan–Ming introduction of cotton, the general word for 'cotton or woven cloth, fabric; spread/declare/arrange (公布, 布置)'.

cloth; fabric; spread/arrange

布小谷.etymology: A modern Chinese personal name created for the female protagonist of the 2019 television drama 'Behind the Scenes' (幕后之王). It combines the rare surname 布 (Bù, originally meaning 'hemp cloth' or 'to spread', attested as an ancient surname in the Han dynasty) with the given name 小谷 (Xiǎogǔ, modifier-head: 小 'small, young' + 谷 'valley' or 'grain/millet'), evoking humble resilience, pastoral freshness, and capacity for growth.

history.meaning: personal name composed of classical surname 布 and diminutive nature-themed given name 小谷
Bu Xiaogu, fictional aspiring television producer in Behind the Scenes (幕后之王)

morphemes.meaning: small, little, young (endearing prefix in given names)

布小谷.notes: In Chinese screenwriting, pairing an uncommon surname like 布 with an unpretentious nature name (小谷, 'little valley') signals an earnest, grounded underdog heroine rising from intern to top variety-show producer.

rootFamily.gloss: low valley; career or emotional trough

cognates.meaning: opening strategy in Go/shogi; composition, layout
board positioning in baduk; strategic layout
composition, layout of a literary or artistic work

布局.etymology: Originally a verb-object compound (布 bù 'to spread out, deploy' + 局 jú 'chessboard, game situation') originating in classical Chinese board games, specifically Go (围棋), where it denoted placing stones across the board in the opening phase to establish strategic territory. By the Tang and Song dynasties, literati extended the term metaphorically to the structural composition of essays, calligraphy, and landscape painting, before it generalized in modern Mandarin into a noun and verb meaning overall layout, spatial arrangement, or strategic market planning.

history.meaning: to deploy stones across the Go board in the opening stage
structural composition of poetry, prose, or painting
spatial layout; strategic planning or industry positioning; to lay out

morphemes.meaning: to spread out, to deploy, to arrange

布局.notes: Used both as a concrete noun ('stage layout', 舞台布局) and as a high-register corporate or media verb ('to strategically position oneself in a sector', 布局海外市场).

rootFamily.gloss: overall situation, big picture, breadth of vision

布置.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound formed from 布 (bù, 'to spread out, to distribute, to display') and 置 (zhì, 'to set up, to place, to establish'). Attested since the Han dynasty (e.g., in the *Book of Han* 汉书), it originally meant deploying troops, officials, or ritual vessels in their proper positions. In modern Mandarin, its scope encompasses both physical decoration/staging (such as dressing a studio set or room) and assigning tasks or homework.

history.meaning: to deploy, position, or establish in order (troops, laws, or officials)
to arrange, decorate, or rig up a venue; to assign (work or tasks)

morphemes.meaning: to spread out, to arrange, to display
to place, to set up, to install

布置.notes: In film and TV production, 布置现场 means 'setting up/dressing the set or location', whereas 布置任务 means 'assigning production tasks'.

rootFamily.gloss: to set up, to install; settings
to place, to dispose; to purchase assets

布面.etymology: The noun '布面' (bùmiàn, cloth surface) consists of '布' (cloth) and '面' (surface, face). '布' originally referred to woven textiles made of hemp or cotton, contrasting with '帛' (silk). In pre-modern craftsmanship, '布面' described the fabric covering of items like shoes, umbrellas, or furniture. In modern contexts, it is widely used in publishing to describe clothbound books, as well as in manufacturing to describe the textural finish of various products. It distinguishes a textile finish from leather, plastic, or paper.

history.meaning: cloth surface

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 布面

cognates.meaning: commander; handsome (in soái ca, borrowed from 帅哥)

帅.etymology: In Old and Middle Chinese, 帥 (shuài, MC *srwijH*) meant 'commander-in-chief' or 'military leader' (and *srwit* 'to lead troops'). Because a supreme commander on the parade ground or opera stage was marked by a dashing, dignified, and commanding bearing (帅气), northern Mandarin colloquially shifted the noun into a vivid adjective meaning 'impressive, sharp, graceful' and eventually 'handsome, stylish, cool'.

history.meaning: commander-in-chief, general; to lead troops into battle
dashing, commanding, deft and impressive in posture (as in Beijing opera and martial arts)
handsome, dashing, stylish, sharp, cool (of appearance or actions)

帅.notes: While primarily used for male attractiveness (帅哥, 'handsome guy'), 帅 also praises anyone—male or female—whose actions, outfit, or professional execution look effortlessly cool and sharp (太帅了).

rootFamily.gloss: handsome guy (also used as a casual form of address for men)

cognates.meaning: senior male apprentice, upperclassman, or senior colleague

师兄.etymology: A modifier-head kinship-metaphor compound combining 师 (shī, 'master, teacher') and 兄 (xiōng, 'elder brother'). Originating in Chinese Buddhist monasticism, Daoist lineages, and traditional martial arts or craft guilds, it designated a male fellow disciple who entered under the same master (同门) earlier than oneself. In modern China, it expanded into universities and creative industries (like television and film schools) for a male upperclassman or senior alumnus from the same school, department, or mentor.

history.meaning: senior male fellow monk or disciple under the same master
history.stage: Middle Chinese / Tang–Song Monastic & Guild Usage

history.meaning: senior male classmate, upperclassman, or alumnus from the same school or mentor

师兄.notes: In Chinese media and entertainment circles, addressing an industry veteran who graduated from your university (e.g., Communication University of China) as 师兄 instantly invokes warm alumni mentorship and network solidarity.

rootFamily.gloss: junior male fellow student or apprentice
junior female fellow student or alumna
senior female fellow student or alumna

希望.etymology: Coordinative verb and noun compound of 希 ('look forward to, long for, rare') + 望 ('gaze into the distance, look toward, hope', showing a person 臣 standing on earth 壬 gazing at the distant moon 月). Attested since Classical and Tang prose.

history.stage: Classical & Tang Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: gaze forward in expectation -> hope, wish

cognates.meaning: writing or calligraphy copybook; placard, notice
calligraphy album, invitation card, prescription packet

帖.etymology: Derived from 巾 (jīn, 'cloth') + 占 (zhān, phonetic *tjem*), 帖 (tiě) originally referred in the Han and Six Dynasties periods to a strip of silk or bamboo inscribed with a label, official notice, or calligraphy model. In Ming–Qing social life it came to mean a written card, invitation (请帖), or public placard/bill posted on a wall (揭帖). With the rise of Chinese bulletin board systems (BBS) and web forums in the late 1990s, 帖 (and 帖子 tiězi) was naturally adopted as the standard term for an online forum post or thread.

history.meaning: inscribed silk strip, label, or calligraphy model album (tiè)

morphemes.meaning: inscribed slip, card, notice; online forum post or thread

帖.notes: Pronunciation depends on sense: tiě (3rd tone) for cards, invitations, and internet posts (发帖, 转帖), tiē (1st tone) for 'snug/submissive' (妥帖, 服帖), and tiè (4th tone) for calligraphy model books (字帖).

rootFamily.gloss: to post a thread online, to publish a forum post
to repost, to forward an online thread or post
printed invitation card; online forum post (tiězi)

带.etymology: Pictograph (traditional 帶) depicting a woven belt or girdle around the waist with hanging sash ornaments above a cloth (巾): originally 'belt, sash, girdle, ribbon, tire, zone/region', and verbally 'wear at the waist -> carry with one, bring, take along, lead, look after'.

belt/band/ribbon; bring; carry; lead

带到.etymology: A verb-complement (resultative/directional) compound formed from the action verb 带 (dài, originally 'waistband, girdle' in Old Chinese, verbalized as 'to carry on one's person, to lead, to bring along') and the resultative complement 到 (dào, 'to arrive at, to reach'). Together, 带到 expresses carrying, leading, or transmitting a person, object, or emotional state all the way to a specified destination or stage.

to bring to, to lead to, to carry over into (a place or state)

to arrive at, to reach (indicating attainment of destination)

rootFamily.gloss: to bring along, to usher in, to bring about
to take away, to carry off
to lead, to guide (a group or team)

带给.etymology: A verb-complement compound combining 带 (dài, 'to carry, to bring') with the dative/recipient complement 给 (gěi, originally 'to supply amply', grammaticalized in Mandarin as 'to give, to, for'). Unlike 带到 (which emphasizes reaching a spatial or conceptual destination), 带给 profiles transferring or imparting something—often intangible, such as joy, inspiration, or pressure—to a recipient person or audience.

history.meaning: to carry/bring + to supply or bestow upon a recipient
to bring to (someone), to give or impart to a recipient

morphemes.meaning: to give to, for the benefit/receipt of

带给.notes: While both 带给 and 带到 can translate as 'bring to', 带给 must be followed by a person or animate recipient (e.g., 带给观众欢乐 'bring joy to the audience'), whereas 带到 is followed by a place.

rootFamily.gloss: to bring, to bring about (without specifying a recipient immediately after)
to pass on to, to transmit to someone
to hand over to, to entrust to someone

带路.etymology: Verb-object compound of 带 ('lead, guide') + 路 ('the way, road'): 'lead the way, act as a guide'.

history.meaning: lead the way; show the way

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 带路 (via 萌典)

带队.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound consisting of 带 (dài, 'to lead, to guide, to take charge of') and 队 (duì, 'squad, troop, team, crew'). Originally military and athletic in flavor—referring to an officer marching at the head of a formation or a team captain leading a delegation—it is widely used in modern workplace and television production Chinese for heading a production unit, location crew, or project taskforce.

history.meaning: to march at the head of a military troop or expeditionary group
to lead a team, delegation, or production crew on location

morphemes.meaning: to lead, to guide, to take along

带队.notes: Because 带队 is a separable verb-object (离合词) construction, it does not take a direct object directly after 队; instead say 亲自带队去拍外景 ('personally lead the crew to shoot on location').

rootFamily.gloss: team leader, captain (of a sports team or production unit)

帮.etymology: Phono-semantic character (traditional 幫, combining 封/邦 bāng phonetic + 巾/帛 'cloth/shoe upper'): originally 'the side or upper lining of a shoe sewn on to reinforce it', hence metaphorically 'support from the side -> help, assist' and 'group, gang, band, outer leaves of cabbage'.

history.meaning: side lining reinforcing a shoe; edge
assist; help; group/band

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 帮 (via 萌典)

帮上.etymology: Resultative verb phrase from 帮 (simplified from 幫, 'assist; help', originally the side-lining of a shoe that supports the foot) + resultative complement 上 ('attain; succeed in reaching a goal'). Used especially with 忙 ('help') or in potential constructions (帮得上 / 帮不上) to mean successfully rendering assistance.

history.meaning: manage to help; be of actual assistance

帮个忙.etymology: An expanded verb-object (离合词) phrase built by inserting the general classifier 个 (ge, reduced from 一个 'one') inside the verb-object compound 帮忙 (bāngmáng, 帮 'to assist, to shore up' + 忙 'busyness, urgent work'). Literally 'to help with a bout of busyness', the insertion of 个 softens the request and makes the favor feel bounded, casual, and manageable in spoken Mandarin.

history.meaning: to assist someone when they are busy with urgent tasks (originally agricultural or artisanal)
to do a favor, to lend a quick hand

morphemes.meaning: a, one (softening and bounding the action)

帮个忙.notes: Because 忙 is already the grammatical object of 帮, you can never say *帮个忙我; instead place the beneficiary inside (帮我个忙, 'do me a favor') or before with 给.

rootFamily.gloss: to help, to do a favor (base verb-object compound)
to help out, to pitch in when things are hectic

帮助.etymology: A coordinative compound uniting vernacular 帮 (bāng, originally 'shoe-upper' or 'wrapping edge' that reinforces the sole, hence metaphorically 'to shore up, to support from the side') with classical 助 (zhù, 'to aid, to add strength to', written with 且 + 力 'strength'). Combining the concrete, vernacular root 帮 with the literary root 助 yielded the standard modern disyllabic verb and noun for 'to help; assistance'.

history.meaning: to assist, to lend strength or mutual aid (in Classical Chinese)
to help, to assist; help, assistance (coordinative compound)

morphemes.meaning: to support from the side, to help
to aid, to lend strength to

帮助.notes: Unlike 帮忙 (which is a separable verb-object word used mainly in speech and cannot take a direct object), 帮助 is a transitive verb and abstract noun that directly takes an object (帮助新人 'help newcomers') or modifies nouns (提供帮助 'provide assistance').

rootFamily.gloss: to assist, to provide coordinated support
to sponsor, to support financially (e.g., show sponsorship)

帮忙.etymology: Separable verb-object compound (离合词) of 帮 ('help, assist') + 忙 ('busy work, pressing tasks'): literally 'help with someone's busy work' -> 'help, lend a hand, do a favor' (e.g., 帮个忙 'do a favor').

history.meaning: help with busy tasks; lend a hand

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 帮忙 (via 萌典)

帮把手.etymology: A colloquial verb-object phrase built on the verb-object compound 帮手 (bāngshǒu, literally 'to help with a hand') with the classifier 把 (bǎ, originally 'to grasp with the hand', used as the measure word for hand-actions,一把) inserted between verb and object (帮[一]把手). It vividly portrays reaching out a hand to grip and lift a heavy load alongside someone else.

history.meaning: to lend a helping hand; helper

history.form: 帮一把手 → 帮把手 (bāng bǎ shǒu)
history.meaning: to lend a hand, to pitch in with practical effort

morphemes.meaning: measure word for a hand-action or grip (short for 一把)

帮把手.notes: Warm, informal, and physical in tone—ideal when a crew is swamped moving studio gear or rushing a cut and asks a colleague to 'pitch in and lend a hand' (过来帮把手).

rootFamily.gloss: to give a hand, to pull someone up (lit. pull a grip)
to pitch in, to set to work with one's hands

常事.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound composed of 常 (cháng, 'constant, invariable, ordinary, frequent', originally a banner or long lower garment in Old Chinese) and 事 (shì, 'affair, matter, event'). Attested in Classical Chinese (e.g., *Records of the Grand Historian* 史记 and Tang prose), it denotes an everyday occurrence or routine event that should occasion no surprise.

history.meaning: constant rule, regular affair, ordinary occurrence
common occurrence, routine matter, everyday thing

常事.notes: Often appears in the four-character idiom 家常便饭 ('homestyle meal' = routine thing) or the proverb 胜败乃兵家常事 ('victory and defeat are common occurrences for a strategist') to console someone after a setback.

cognates.meaning: always kept on hand, standing preparation (as in 常備薬 / 常備軍)

常备.etymology: A modifier-head verbal/attributive compound formed from 常 (cháng, 'constantly, at all times') and 备 (bèi, 'to prepare, to equip, to keep in readiness'). Used in classical statecraft for maintaining constant vigilance (常备不懈) and reinforced in the late 19th century via Meiji Japanese *jōbi* (常備, as in 常備軍 'standing army' and 常備薬 'household medicine kept on hand'), it describes supplies or forces kept permanently in stock for immediate use.

history.meaning: to maintain constant readiness or preparedness
standing (of armies); permanently stocked or kept on hand (of medicines, equipment, or backup plans)
history.stage: Modern Mandarin (reinforced by Japanese 漢語 jōbi)

morphemes.meaning: to prepare, to provide, to keep on hand

常备.notes: Functions mainly as a non-predicative adjective (区别词) before nouns (e.g., 常备药 'household standby medicine', 剧组常备物资 'supplies always kept on hand by the crew') or in the idiom 常备不懈 ('always on guard / prepared without slackening').

rootFamily.gloss: to prepare, to get ready; preparation
to keep on hand for contingency, backup, spare

常春藤.etymology: Botanical compound of 常 ('ever, constant') + 春 ('springtime greenness') + 藤 ('climbing vine', grass/plant crown 艹 + 滕), literally 'ever-spring vine' because its leaves stay glossy green through winter.

history.meaning: evergreen climbing ivy (Hedera)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 常春藤

常规.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 常 (cháng, 'constant, invariable, standard') and 规 (guī, originally 'carpenter's compass for drawing circles', extended in Classical Chinese to 'rule, regulation, standard norm'). Attested in Six Dynasties and Tang texts for established institutional rules, in modern Mandarin 常规 serves as both a noun ('convention, standard practice') and an attributive adjective ('routine, conventional').

history.meaning: invariable rule, established institutional standard
convention, routine practice; conventional, standard (e.g., 常规操作)

常规.notes: In creative media and showbiz, 打破常规 ('breaking convention / thinking outside the box') is a staple phrase for innovating a show format, while 常规操作 ('standard operating procedure') is also used ironically in slang for someone pulling off an impressive feat effortlessly.

rootFamily.gloss: rule, regulation, ground rules (e.g., of a competition show)
extraordinary, unconventional, emergency (lit. beyond the norm)

cognates.meaning: common sense, general knowledge (Meiji coinage translating English 'common sense')

常识.etymology: A modifier-head compound of 常 (cháng, 'ordinary, common, constant') and 识 (shí, 'knowledge, cognition, understanding'). While the character sequence appeared occasionally in classical Buddhist and philosophical texts for 'ordinary perception', its modern sense of 'common sense, general knowledge every member of society should possess' is a late 19th-century Japanese *wasei-kango* (常識 *jōshiki*) coined in Meiji Japan to translate English *common sense* (and Latin *sensus communis*), then borrowed into Mandarin at the turn of the 20th century.

history.meaning: Meiji Japanese Sino-compound coined to translate English 'common sense' and 'general knowledge'
common sense, elementary or general knowledge

常识.notes: Covers both practical judgment ('common sense', 没有常识) and basic factual literacy in a domain (生活常识 'everyday life know-how', 行业常识 'basic industry knowledge').

rootFamily.gloss: insight, breadth of knowledge and experience (jiànshi)

cognates.meaning: permanently stationed, resident (e.g., 常駐記者 'resident correspondent')

常驻.etymology: A modifier-head verbal compound combining 常 (cháng, 'permanently, long-term, constantly') and 驻 (zhù, written with 马 'horse' + 主 phonetic, originally meaning 'to halt a horse or carriage', extended to 'to garrison troops, to be stationed at a post'). Used in diplomatic, journalistic, and entertainment contexts, it describes personnel stationed long-term at a location or a regular panelist on a television program.

history.meaning: to halt a horse; to station troops or reside temporarily at an official post
to be permanently or long-term stationed (of diplomats, correspondents, or regular variety-show cast members)

morphemes.meaning: to halt a horse; to be stationed, to reside at a post

常驻.notes: In contemporary Chinese variety shows (综艺节目), 常驻嘉宾 ('regular/resident cast member', as opposed to 飞行嘉宾 'flying/guest star for a single episode') is a key industry term. Also beware the homophone 常住 (chángzhù, 'long-term residential registration').

rootFamily.gloss: to be stationed at, to garrison (e.g., 驻扎剧组)
to enter and station oneself (e.g., creators or brands joining a platform)
stationed at, accredited to (e.g., 驻京记者 'Beijing-based correspondent')

帽子.etymology: Derived from 帽 ('hat; headgear', cloth radical 巾 + phonetic 冒 mào, originally 'cover the head downward') + nominal suffix 子 (-zi). In classical Chinese 冠 designated formal ceremonial crowns while 帽 denoted soft everyday caps; 帽子 is now the universal Mandarin word for any hat.

history.meaning: cloth cap or head covering
hat; cap

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 帽子

幅.etymology: Written 幅 (fú) with the cloth radical 巾 ('woven textile') and phonetic 畐 (fú, 'full jar'). In Han and Tang textiles, 幅 denoted the full loom-width of a bolt of silk or hemp cloth. Because traditional Chinese paintings, maps, and calligraphy were mounted on full widths of silk or paper scrolls, 幅 grammaticalized into the standard classifier for paintings, sketches, maps, and banners.

morphemes.meaning: full width of cloth (巾 radical) -> measure word for paintings, sketches, and maps

history.meaning: loom-width of woven silk or cloth
classifier for paintings, drawings, maps, and textiles

cognates.meaning: behind the scenes, backstage; hidden mastermind (also 舞台裏)
behind the curtain, behind the scenes, secret manipulator

幕后.etymology: A modifier-head spatial compound formed from 幕 (mù, 'tent, canopy, stage curtain') and 后 (hòu, 'behind, rear, back'). In Classical Chinese, 幕 denoted a military commander's field tent (hence 幕府 *mùfǔ* and 幕僚 'tent aides/advisors'). With the rise of modern theater and cinema, 幕 came to mean the stage curtain; 幕后 ('behind the curtain') thus literally means 'backstage / off-camera' (contrasting with 台前 'on stage / in front of the camera') and figuratively 'behind the scenes' where producers, directors, and strategists operate.

history.meaning: inside or behind the commander's tent (where advisors plan strategy)
behind the stage curtain, backstage; behind the scenes (in production or covert manipulation)

幕后.notes: Central to the drama title 幕后之王 (*Behind the Scenes* / literally 'King of Behind-the-Scenes'): pairs with 台前幕后 ('in front of and behind the camera'), 幕后制作 ('behind-the-scenes production'), or 幕后推手 ('the driving force / mastermind behind the scenes').

rootFamily.gloss: to open the curtain; opening ceremony or start of a show/event

干.etymology: Simplified character merging three historical words: (1) 乾 (read gān, 'dry, moisture-free, empty, in vain'), (2) 幹 (read gàn, 'tree trunk -> main body, do, work, capable'), and (3) ancient 干 (pictograph of a forked weapon or shield, read gān: 'shield, offend, have to do with').

morphemes.meaning: dry (乾 gān); do, work (幹 gàn); shield/concern (干 gān)

history.form: 乾 (dry, gān) / 幹 (trunk, do, gàn) / 干 (shield, concern, gān)
history.meaning: three distinct classical words merged in simplified script
dry, empty (gān); do, work, trunk (gàn)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 干 (via 萌典)

干上.etymology: A verb-complement compound combining 干 (gàn, simplified from 幹, originally 'tree trunk' or 'main frame of wall-building boards', extended in Classical Chinese to 'capability, backbone' and in vernacular Mandarin to 'to do, to work at') with the directional/aspectual complement 上 (shàng, 'up; onto', indicating the inception or engagement of an action). Together, 干上 means to throw oneself into doing a job, get started on a line of work, or clash head-on with someone.

history.meaning: tree trunk, structural frame; capability, to manage affairs
to start working at a job; to become engaged in action or conflict

morphemes.meaning: to do, to work at, to engage in (trad. 幹)
up, onto (marking the start or locking-in of an action)

干上.notes: Colloquial and energetic: 干上这一行 means 'once you get started in / take up this profession (e.g., TV production)', while 干上一架 means 'get into a fight'.

rootFamily.gloss: capable, competent, good at getting work done
backbone, core member of a team or crew
to work hard, to go all out on a task

干什么.etymology: A verb-object interrogative phrase combining 干 (gàn, trad. 幹, 'to do, to work at') and the interrogative pronoun 什么 (shénme, evolved in Tang–Song vernacular from 甚么 / 拾没 < *shíwù* 什物 'what thing, miscellaneous thing'). Literally 'to do what?', it functions in Mandarin both as a direct question about someone's activity ('What are you doing?') and as a rhetorical challenge ('What for? Why on earth?').

history.meaning: to do what? for what purpose? (in Song–Yuan vernacular texts)
to do what; what are you doing; why / what for

morphemes.meaning: to do, to engage in (trad. 幹)

干什么.notes: Depending on intonation and position, 你干什么？ asks 'What are you doing?' (or 'What do you think you're doing?!'), while placed after a verb phrase (e.g., 你找他干什么？) it means 'What do you want him for? / Why look for him?'.

rootFamily.gloss: why, for what reason (lit. for what)
to do what (more colloquial northern contraction)
to do one's proper job, to get down to business (干正事)

干净.etymology: Coordinative adjective compound of 干 (乾, gān, 'dry, free of mud or moisture') + 净 (淨, 'clean, pure, clear', neutral tone jing in everyday speech): 'clean, neat and tidy; completely'.

history.meaning: dry and clean -> clean, neat, spotless

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 干净 (via 萌典)

干劲.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound formed from 干 (gàn, trad. 幹, 'to work, to do') and 劲 (jìn, 'muscular strength, vigor, spirit, enthusiasm', with 力 'strength' radical). Literally 'working strength / energy for doing things', it arose in northern Mandarin (often pronounced with erhua as 干劲儿 *gànjìnr*) to describe inner drive, gusto, and enthusiasm for tackling work.

history.meaning: to work + vigorous strength or spirit
drive, enthusiasm, vigor and motivation for work

干劲.notes: Note that 劲 has two pronunciations in Mandarin: jìn for 'energy, enthusiasm, drive' (干劲 gànjìn, 冲劲 chòngjìn, 起劲 qǐjìn) and jìng in literary compounds meaning 'strong, forceful' (强劲 qiángjìng, 劲敌 jìngdí). Often takes erhua in speech (干劲儿十足, 'brimming with drive').

rootFamily.gloss: enthusiastic, energetic, getting into the spirit of things (qǐjìn)

干吗.etymology: A northern Mandarin colloquial verb-object contraction of 干什么 (gàn shénme, 'to do what?'), combining 干 (gàn, trad. 幹, 'to do') with 吗 (má, here representing the phonological fusion of 什么 *shénme* / *shénma* into a single rising-tone syllable *má*, prevalent in Beijing and Tianjin vernacular). It functions both literally ('what are you doing?') and adverbially ('why? for what purpose?').

history.meaning: phonological contraction of 干什么 in Beijing/Northern Mandarin ('to do what / why')
what are you doing; why, what for (standard dictionary spelling alongside 干嘛)

morphemes.meaning: to do, to engage in (trad. 幹)
what (phonological fusion of 什么, pronounced má in 2nd tone)

干吗.notes: Here 吗 is pronounced má (2nd tone, meaning 'what', a fusion of 什么), NOT the neutral-tone yes/no sentence-final particle ma! *Contemporary Chinese Dictionary* (现代汉语词典) treats 干吗 as the normative form and 干嘛 as its informal variant.

rootFamily.gloss: to do what, why (uncontracted standard form)
why, what for (popular informal variant spelling of 干吗)
what's up? what is it? (Northern dialectal 嘛 má = 'what')

干嘛.etymology: An orthographically specialized variant of 干吗 (gànmá), combining 干 (gàn, trad. 幹, 'to do') with 嘛 (má, written with 口 'mouth' + 麻 phonetic to explicitly represent the 2nd-tone colloquial pronoun *má* < contraction of 什么 'what', avoiding confusion with the neutral-tone question particle 吗 *ma*). In spoken dialogue and scripts, 干嘛 is ubiquitous for 'why? what for?' or 'what are you up to?'.

history.form: 幹甚麽 → 幹嗎 / 幹嘛 (gànmá)
history.meaning: colloquial northern contraction of 干什么 ('to do what; why')
why, what for; what are you doing (preferred in screenplays and informal writing to distinguish má from neutral-tone 吗)

morphemes.meaning: to do, to work at (trad. 幹)
what (colloquial fusion of 什么, spelled with 嘛 to signal 2nd tone má)

干嘛.notes: In screenplays like *幕后之王*, writers strongly prefer 干嘛 over 干吗 so actors immediately read it as gànmá ('what for / why') rather than misreading 吗 as a yes/no particle. Standalone, "干嘛？" means "What do you want?" or "What are you doing?!".

rootFamily.gloss: to do what, why (normative dictionary spelling)
to do what, for what purpose (full uncontracted form)
to do what (Northeastern/northern colloquial equivalent using 啥 shá < 甚)

干得.etymology: A verb + structural particle/complement sequence composed of 干 (gàn, trad. 幹, 'to do, to execute, to perform work') and 得 (de / dé, originally 'to obtain, to succeed in' in Old Chinese, grammaticalized in Middle and Early Mandarin into a post-verbal particle introducing a complement of degree/evaluation or potential). It either links the verb 'do' to an evaluation (as in 干得漂亮 'beautifully done!') or, as 干得 (gànde), expresses potential ('can be done').

history.meaning: to perform/manage + to achieve or reach a degree of execution
to do (to a certain degree, e.g., 干得好 'well done!'); capable of being done

morphemes.meaning: to do, to work, to execute (trad. 幹)
particle introducing a degree/manner complement (de) or potential suffix 'able to' (de)

干得.notes: Most famously heard in workplace praise like 干得好！ ('Good job! / Well done!') and 干得漂亮！ ('Nicely done! / Brilliant work!'), or in potential constructions like 干得来 ('able to get along with / handle the work') and 干得过 ('able to outperform').

rootFamily.gloss: to remember, to bear in mind (verb + 得)
to understand, to know how (verb + 得)

干扰.etymology: A coordinative transitive compound uniting 干 (gān, here the original unmerged character 干 meaning 'to offend against, to intrude upon, to trespass', originally depicting a forked weapon or pestle in oracle bone script—NOT 幹 'trunk/do') and 扰 (rǎo, trad. 擾, 'to disturb, to throw into confusion, to harass'). Together, 干扰 means to intrude upon and disrupt a process, person's concentration, or broadcast signal.

history.form: 干 (*kan, 'to intrude upon, offend') + 擾 (*njewX, 'to disturb, trouble')
history.meaning: to encroach upon and throw into disorder
to interfere with, to disturb, to distract; radio/signal interference

morphemes.meaning: to intrude upon, to encroach, to offend (gān, trad. 干)
to disturb, to harass, to throw into confusion (rǎo, trad. 擾)

干扰.notes: Crucial false-friend alert: 干 in 干扰 is pronounced gān (1st tone, traditional 干 'to intrude/encroach', as in 干涉 gānshè), NOT gàn (4th tone, traditional 幹 'to work'). In broadcast television, 信号干扰 means 'signal interference'.

rootFamily.gloss: to interfere in, to meddle, to intervene (gānshè)
to disturb, to bother, to interrupt someone (dǎrǎo)
to perplex, to trouble, to plague (kùnrǎo)

干木头.etymology: Three-character modifier-head noun phrase combining 干 (乾, gān, 'dry, seasoned') + 木头 ('wood, timber'): 'dry wood, seasoned timber'.

history.meaning: dry wood; seasoned timber

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 干木头 (via 萌典)

干杯.etymology: Verb-object compound of 干 (乾, gān, 'empty, drain dry') + 杯 ('cup, glass'): literally 'drain the glass dry' -> 'cheers!, bottoms up!, drink a toast'.

history.meaning: drain one's cup = cheers!, bottoms up!

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 干杯 (via 萌典)

干活.etymology: A verb-object (离合词) compound combining 干 (gàn, trad. 幹, 'to do, to work at') and 活 (huó, originally 'to live, alive', nominalized in Ming–Qing vernacular via 活计 *huójì* 'means of livelihood' into 'work, manual labor, job task'). Often pronounced with erhua in northern Mandarin (干活儿 *gànhuór*), it is the everyday spoken verb for doing hands-on work or labor.

history.meaning: means of living → manual work, craft job, or task
to work, to do manual or practical work on the job

morphemes.meaning: to do, to perform, to work at (trad. 幹)

干活.notes: Compared to the formal 工作 (gōngzuò), 干活 (or 干活儿) is earthy, practical, and hands-on—what a TV director shouts on set ("开始干活！" = "Let's get to work!") or what crew members call real, sleeves-rolled-up labor. Because it is verb-object, modifiers go inside: 干点儿活 ('do a bit of work').

rootFamily.gloss: handiwork, job, work task (colloquial noun, huór)
hard physical labor, thankless heavy work (kǔhuó)

干燥.etymology: Coordinative adjective compound of 干 (乾, gān, 'dry') + 燥 ('parched, arid, dry', fire 火 + 喿): 'dry, arid, lacking moisture'. Attested since the Huainanzi and medical classics.

history.meaning: dry; arid; parched

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 干燥 (via 萌典)

干爽.etymology: Coordinative adjective compound of 干 (乾, gān, 'dry') + 爽 ('refreshing, crisp, clear'): 'dry and refreshing, pleasantly dry and crisp (of weather, air, or clothing)'.

history.meaning: dry and crisp/refreshing

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 干爽 (via 萌典)

干脆.etymology: Compound adjective and adverb of 干 (乾, gān, 'dry, clean-cut') + 脆 ('crisp, brittle, clear-cut'): describes speech or action that is 'straightforward, clean-cut, decisive', and as a modal adverb 'simply, might as well just…'.

history.meaning: clean-cut and straightforward (adj.); simply, might as well (adv.)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 干脆 (via 萌典)

干透.etymology: Resultative verb/adjective compound combining 干 (乾, gān, 'dry') + 透 ('penetrate all the way through, thoroughly'): 'dry all the way through, completely dry'.

history.meaning: thoroughly dry; dry right through

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 干透 (via 萌典)

平.etymology: Ancient character showing breath or water spreading evenly around a balance bar (于 + 八): 'flat, level, even, smooth; calm, peaceful; equal/draw; ordinary; level tone (平声)'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Bronze inscriptions & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: level; flat; even; calm; equal

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 平 (via 萌典)

平台.etymology: Compound noun of 平 ('flat, level') + 台 (臺, 'raised terrace, stage'): originally 'a flat-topped viewing terrace or roof terrace' in Classical architecture, and extended in modern Mandarin to a station 'platform' or a technical/digital/business 'platform'.

history.meaning: flat-topped raised terrace
terrace; balcony; platform (physical or digital/institutional)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 平台 (via 萌典)

平平.etymology: Reduplication of the stative adjective 平 ('level; flat; even', Old Chinese *bˤreng*). While classical prose used 平平 for 'orderly' or 'ordinary', vernacular Mandarin after resultative 得 (熨得平平的) uses the reduplicated form to vividly picture a surface pressed completely smooth and flat.

history.meaning: level; even; flat
nice and flat; evenly smooth

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 平平

平手.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 平 (píng, 'level, even, equal, balanced') and 手 (shǒu, 'hand; skill, bout, contestant's move', as in 高手 'master hand' and 对手 'opponent'). Originating in martial arts, board games, and wagering, an 'even hand' (平手) meant two contenders whose skill or score was perfectly balanced, hence a draw, tie, or dead heat.

history.meaning: equal skill or even outcome in a bout, game, or wager
draw, tie, even score (in sports, ratings battles, or competitions)

平手.notes: Commonly collocated with 打成 (打成平手, 'to fight/play to a draw; to tie'), often used in media when two rival variety shows or producers tie in viewership ratings or voting.

rootFamily.gloss: tied game, draw, stalemate (lit. even board)

平时.etymology: Temporal noun combining 平 ('ordinary, normal, peacetime') + 时 (時, 'time'): 'in normal times, ordinarily, usually'. Attested since Han–Tang historical prose.

history.meaning: in ordinary times; usually; normally

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 平时 (via 萌典)

平板.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 平 ('flat, level') + 板 ('board, plank, slab, panel'): 'flat board, wooden plank; flat panel' (and in contemporary Mandarin short for 平板电脑 'tablet computer').

history.meaning: flat board/plank; flat panel; tablet computer

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 平板 (via 萌典)

平级.etymology: A modifier-head compound formed from 平 (píng, 'equal, level, on the same plane') and 级 (jí, originally 'order of silk threads', extended in Qin–Han bureaucracy to 'steps of a staircase' and 'official rank, grade, administrative level'). It describes colleagues, departments, or organizational units that hold the exact same hierarchical rank.

history.meaning: of equal administrative grade or rank
of equal rank, peer-level (in corporate, civil service, or organizational hierarchies)

morphemes.meaning: step, grade, administrative or corporate rank

平级.notes: Frequently used in corporate and media-company politics: 平级调动 ('lateral transfer at the same rank', often a disguised demotion or sidelining) and 平级部门 ('peer-level departments' that cannot directly order each other around).

cognates.meaning: parallel (in geometry); running concurrently or abreast

平行.etymology: A modifier-head verbal/attributive compound from 平 (píng, 'level, even, side by side at equal height') and 行 (xíng, 'to walk, to move, to proceed'). In Classical Chinese it meant 'walking abreast as equals' or 'proceeding evenly'. In 1607, Matteo Ricci and Xu Guangqi adopted 平行線 in their Chinese translation of Euclid's *Elements* (几何原本) to render Greek *parallēlos* ('beside one another', parallel lines), establishing its modern mathematical, spatial, and structural senses.

history.meaning: to walk abreast at equal rank; to proceed evenly

history.form: 平行 (geometric calque in 幾何原本, 1607)
history.meaning: parallel (of lines or planes that never intersect, translating Greek parallēlos)
parallel (in space, rank, or concurrent execution, e.g., 平行剪辑 'parallel editing')

morphemes.meaning: level, even, abreast, of equal standing
to walk, to go, to proceed (xíng)

平行.notes: In film and television editing, 平行剪辑 / 平行蒙太奇 ('parallel editing / cross-cutting') cuts back and forth between two simultaneous storylines; in organizational structure, 平行项目组 refers to parallel project teams operating at the same level.

rootFamily.gloss: parallel world, multiverse (popular sci-fi and media trope)
plane, flat surface; print/graphic media (平面媒体)

平面图.etymology: Three-character architectural and cartographic compound from 平面 ('flat plane; horizontal surface') + 图 (simplified from 圖, 'diagram; drawing; map'). Adopted in modern engineering and architectural Chinese for a two-dimensional floor plan or layout diagram viewed from above.

history.meaning: floor plan; layout diagram

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 平面图

年.etymology: Ancient character (originally 秊 in oracle-bone and bronze scripts) showing a person (人) carrying a ripe stalk of grain (禾) on their back: originally 'harvest of grain' (which occurred once a year in northern China), hence 'year, annual, age, New Year'.

history.meaning: person carrying harvested grain = annual harvest -> year
year; New Year

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 年 (via 萌典)

年假.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正结构) combining 年 (nián, "year", originally Old Chinese *C.nˤi[ŋ] denoting the annual grain harvest, depicting a person carrying grain 禾) and 假 (jià, "leave of absence, furlough, holiday", originally "to borrow, temporary respite from official duty" in Han administrative usage). Historically referring to the traditional New Year administrative recess (年节休假), in modern labor terminology it functions as an ellipsis of 带薪年休假 ("paid annual leave").

history.meaning: annual harvest cycle + official furlough or temporary leave of absence
lunar New Year recess for officials, schools, and merchants
statutory paid annual vacation leave in corporate employment

年假.notes: In workplace contexts (*幕后之王*), 年假 specifically means statutory paid annual leave (请年假 / 休年假, "to take annual leave"), though in school contexts it can occasionally refer to the winter/New Year break.

rootFamily.gloss: take leave, ask for time off

年级.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正结构) formed from 年 (nián, "year, academic year") and 级 (traditional 級, jí, "step, rank, grade", originally silk threads arranged in order of quality, extended in Qin-Han law to administrative and military ranks and Stone steps). Adopted in late Qing and Meiji-era educational reforms (alongside Japanese 学年 gakunen and 年級 nenkyū) to classify students by chronological cohort in Western-style graded schooling.

history.meaning: year + rank or graded step in a hierarchy
academic year cohort or grade level in modern graded schools and universities

年级.notes: Used with ordinal numbers or stage prefixes for school cohorts: 一年级 (first grade / freshman year), 高年级 (upperclassmen / senior grades), 同年级 (same year/grade).

年轻.etymology: A subject-predicate compound (主谓结构) combining 年 (nián, "years of age, lifespan") and 轻 (traditional 輕, qīng, "light in weight, small in number, slight", originally a light war chariot). Literally "one's years are light/few" (contrast 年纪大 or Literary Chinese 年高 "advanced in years"). Attested in Tang-Song poetry and vernacular fiction (e.g., Du Fu's 子章髑髅血模糊，手提掷还崔大夫；眼枯即见骨，天地终无情... and Yuan-Ming vernacular narratives) as the standard everyday adjective for youthfulness.

history.meaning: few in years, young in age (standard Classical expressions)
light in years; young, youthful in age and vigor
young, youthful; comparatively junior in age or mindset

morphemes.meaning: light in weight, small in quantity, youthful

年轻.notes: Combines readily with 人 to form 年轻人 ("young people, youth") and can be used predicatively or attributively, including for mental state (心态年轻, "young at heart").

年轻人.etymology: Three-character compound combining 年轻 ('young in years', literally 'years light in weight': 年 'years of age' + 轻 'light/few') + 人 ('person'): 'young person, youth, young people'.

history.meaning: young person; young people

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 年轻人 (via 萌典)

年轻版.etymology: A three-character modifier-head compound (偏正结构) built from the disyllabic adjective 年轻 (niánqīng, "young, youthful", literally "light in years") modifying the head noun 版 (bǎn, "edition, version", originally wooden printing blocks 版籍/雕版 used in Tang-Song xylography). In contemporary media, television production, and marketing, this productive `X + 版` pattern designates a youth-oriented adaptation, a recast younger iteration of a character, or a person who resembles a younger incarnation of a veteran figure.

history.meaning: wooden boards for rammed-earth walls; register tablet; woodblock printing plate
printed edition or textual recension
younger version (of a person, character, or media format geared toward youth)

年轻版.notes: Frequently used in entertainment and showbiz (*幕后之王*) either to compare an up-and-coming protégé to a senior mentor ("a younger version of X") or to describe a youth-targeted spin-off of a show.

年龄.etymology: A coordinative compound (联合/并列结构) pairing 年 (nián, "years lived") with 龄 (traditional 齡, líng, "age, years of life", a phono-semantic character combining the tooth radical 齒 chǐ with phonetic 令 lìng, because the age of humans and horses was anciently gauged by examining the growth and wear of their teeth). Attested in Classical texts such as the *Book of Rites* (礼记·文王世子: "梦帝与我九龄") and standard throughout Sinitic languages for chronological age.

history.meaning: front teeth; years of life or longevity (inferred from dentition)
chronological age, lifespan (formal and general register)

morphemes.meaning: age, duration in years (originally judged by teeth 齒)

年龄.notes: More formal and technical than colloquial 年纪 (niánjì) or 岁数 (suìshu); used in demographics, broadcasting target-audience metrics (年龄层, "age bracket"), and official forms.

并.etymology: Merged simplified graph representing: (1) 並/竝 (two people 立 standing side by side: 'side by side, together, combine, and/moreover') and (2) 并 (two干 joined together: 'merge, annex, combine'). In Mandarin, 并 also serves as an emphatic adverb before negatives (并不 'not at all', 并非 'by no means').

morphemes.meaning: two figures side by side = together, combine, and

history.form: 並 (side by side, together) / 并 (combine, merge)
history.meaning: stand side by side; combine
combine; side by side; and; (before negation) at all

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 并 (via 萌典)

并且.etymology: A compound conjunction (连词) formed by combining 并 (traditional 並/竝, bìng, depicting two people 立 standing side by side: "side by side, together, simultaneously, moreover") and the Classical coordinative/progressive particle 且 (qiě, "moreover, furthermore, and also"). Both characters functioned independently as adverbials and conjunctions in Classical Chinese; their disyllabic fusion stabilized in Early Mandarin vernacular to mark additive progression across clauses or verb phrases.

history.meaning: side by side / simultaneously + moreover / furthermore (used as separate particles)
and furthermore, moreover, in addition (linking parallel actions or clauses)

并且.notes: Typically connects two verbs, verb phrases, or clauses where the second adds a further action or deeper degree (often paired with 不但... 并且..., "not only... but also..."). Unlike 和, it never joins simple nouns.

rootFamily.gloss: not at all, by no means (before negation)

并排.etymology: The adverb '并排' (bìngpái, side by side) combines '并' (to combine, side by side) and '排' (to align, row). '并' is an ancient character originally depicting two people standing together side by side. '排' typically refers to arranging things in a line or sequence. The combination '并排' emerged in vernacular Chinese to describe the physical state of two or more entities positioned laterally adjacent to each other. It is frequently used to describe spatial orientation in everyday actions like walking or sitting.

history.meaning: side by side

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 并排

cognates.word: sáp nhập và mua lại (semantic equivalent; Sino-Viet: bính cấu)

并购.etymology: A modern coordinative verbal-noun compound (联合结构) telescoped from 兼并 (jiānbìng, "to annex, absorb, merge", using 併/并 "to combine two into one") and 收购 (shōugòu, "to purchase, acquire, buy out", using 购/購 "to buy with cowries 貝"). Coined in late 20th-century Chinese financial and corporate law as a concise two-character rendering of English "mergers and acquisitions" (M&A).

history.meaning: annexation/absorption of territory or estates + purchasing in bulk with shell money
corporate mergers and acquisitions (M&A)

morphemes.meaning: purchase, acquire, buy out (from 收购)

并购.notes: A staple of corporate drama in *幕后之王* (e.g., studio and media-conglomerate takeovers: 企业并购, 并购案 "M&A deal", 恶意并购 "hostile takeover").

幸亏.etymology: An expressive sentence adverb combining 幸 (xìng, 'good fortune, lucky escape from danger') and 亏 (kuī, simplified from 虧, literally 'lack, deficit', which in Ming–Qing vernacular acquired the idiomatic sense 'owing to, thanks to the timely intervention of', as in 多亏). Together 幸亏 means 'fortunately, thanks to a lucky turn', introducing the factor that saved the situation.

morphemes.meaning: thanks to; owing to (idiomatic vernacular sense of 虧)

history.stage: Ming–Qing Vernacular Novels (e.g. Dream of the Red Chamber)
history.meaning: fortunately; thank goodness
fortunately; luckily

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 幸亏

cognates.meaning: fortunate meeting, pleasure to meet you (literary)

幸会.etymology: A modifier-head polite formulaic compound (偏正结构) combining 幸 (xìng, "fortunate, favored by luck, honored") and 会 (traditional 會, huì, "to meet, assemble, encounter", depicting a lidded vessel symbolizing gathering together). Literally "a fortunate meeting" or "I am favored by fortune to meet you," functioning since Ming-Qing epistolary and conversational etiquette as a deferential greeting upon a first acquaintance.

history.meaning: by good fortune + to meet or assemble together
it is an honor/pleasure to meet you (polite greeting on first introduction)

幸会.notes: Often reduplicated as 幸会，幸会 ("Charmed! Pleasure to meet you!") in professional, business, or formal social introductions alongside 久仰 ("I have long admired your reputation").

幸好.etymology: A compound modal adverb formed from 幸 (xìng, "by good fortune, undeservedly escaping harm", attested in Classical Chinese as an adverbial "fortunately") and 好 (hǎo, "good, well, advantageously"). Literally "fortunately it turned out well that...", grammaticalized in Early Modern Mandarin alongside 幸亏 (xìngkuī) and 幸而 (xìng'ér) to introduce a fortunate circumstance that averted an otherwise bad outcome.

history.meaning: by good fortune, luckily (avoiding calamity or receiving favor)
luckily, fortunately, it is a good thing that...

幸好.notes: Interchangeable in most spoken contexts with 幸亏 (xìngkuī) and 还好 (háihǎo); typically precedes the subject or verb of the rescuing clause (e.g., 幸好你来了, "Good thing you came!").

幸灾乐祸.etymology: A four-character Classical idiom (成语) with symmetric parallel verb-object halves (联合动宾结构): 幸灾 ("to rejoice at [another's] disaster 灾/災") and 乐祸 ("to take pleasure in [another's] calamity 祸/禍"). Here both 幸 and 乐 (lè) function in the Classical putative/attitudinal sense ("to consider fortunate / to delight in"). Directly derived from the *Zuo Zhuan* (左传·庄公二十年, 4th c. BCE): "背施幸灾，凶也" ("To turn one's back on kindness and rejoice in disaster isinauspicious") and *Zuo Zhuan* (僖公十四年): "背施无亲，幸灾不仁."

history.meaning: to treat a neighboring state's famine or calamity as one's own good fortune (in Warring States diplomacy)

history.form: 幸災樂禍 / 幸灾乐祸
history.meaning: to take malicious pleasure in others' misfortune; schadenfreude, gloating

幸灾乐祸.notes: The exact Chinese equivalent of German/English *schadenfreude*. Strongly pejorative; often used adverbially with 地 (幸灾乐祸地笑, "to smile gloatingly").

幸福.etymology: A coordinative compound (联合结构) uniting 幸 (xìng, "good fortune, imperial favor, escaping misfortune") and 福 (fú, "heavenly blessing, prosperity, sacrificial bounty", showing an altar 示 and a jar of ritual wine 畐). While attested in pre-modern Chinese texts (e.g., *Xunzi*, Song-Ming prose) in the sense of "good fortune and blessings," its modern psychological and philosophical sense of deep life satisfaction and eudaimonia ("happiness, well-being") was reinforced in the late 19th century via Meiji Japanese 幸福 (kōfuku), used to translate English *happiness* and German *Glückseligkeit*.

history.meaning: undeserved good luck + ritual blessing and material prosperity from ancestors/Heaven
Meiji philosophical translation of Western 'happiness, felicity, well-being'
deep happiness, blessedness, fulfilling life well-being (as adjective and noun)

幸福.notes: Unlike 快乐 (kuàilè, "cheerful, joyful") or 高兴 (gāoxìng, "glad in the moment"), 幸福 denotes deep, enduring emotional fulfillment and life satisfaction (幸福感, "sense of well-being").

幸运.etymology: A modifier-head or coordinative compound combining 幸 (xìng, "good fortune, favorable") and 运 (traditional 運, yùn, "revolving movement, cycle of fate, destiny, luck", originally to transport troops/chariots 軍 in motion 辶). Literally "favorable turn of fate" or "fortunate destiny," popularized across the East Asian Sinosphere (compare Japanese 幸運 kōun) for both the noun "good luck" and the adjective "lucky, fortunate."

history.meaning: fortunate favor + revolving cycle of heaven and destiny
good fortune, lucky, fortunate (person, event, or turn of fate)

幸运.notes: Functions as both an adjective (很幸运, "very lucky") and a noun; combines with 儿 to form 幸运儿 ("fortune's favorite, lucky person"). Contrast 运气好 (having good luck in a specific instance).

幻想.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正结构) joining 幻 (huàn, "magical illusion, sleight of hand, unreal appearance", heavily used in Chinese Buddhist translations for Sanskrit *māyā* "cosmic illusion") and 想 (xiǎng, "thought, mental image, conception", corresponding to Buddhist *saṃjñā* "perception/ideation"). Originally denoting illusory mental projections in Buddhist philosophy, it was adapted in modern East Asian lexicon (alongside Japanese 幻想 gensō) to render Western concepts of "fantasy, reverie, and unrealistic illusion."

history.meaning: conjurer's trick / Buddhist māyā (illusion) + mental conception or ideation
unrealistic illusion, daydream, or imaginative fantasy (noun and verb)

幻想.notes: Used both as a noun (抱有幻想, "harbor illusions"; 科学幻想 / 科幻, "science fiction") and as a verb ("to fantasize"). Often implies detachment from reality (不切实际的幻想).

幼稚.etymology: A coordinative compound (联合结构) combining two synonymous roots: 幼 (yòu, "young, tender, minor in age", from threads 幺 and strength 力, denoting small/slender strength) and 稚 (zhì, "late-planted young grain 禾; young child, fledgling, immature"). Attested in Han and Six Dynasties texts (e.g., *Records of the Grand Historian* 史记, *Book of Han* 汉书: "年齿幼稚") in the literal sense of "young in age, in early childhood," and later extended metaphorically to "childish, naive, or immature" in thought or behavior.

history.meaning: young in years, of tender childhood age (literal chronological youth)
childish, naive, unsophisticated, or emotionally immature (metaphorical)

幼稚.notes: When applied to adults or their ideas/behavior, 幼稚 is distinctly critical ("childish, immature, naive"), whereas的天真 (tiānzhēn) can be either endearing ("innocent") or mildly naive. Note that 幼稚园 ("kindergarten", from Japanese 幼稚園) is standard in Taiwan/HK, while Mainland China prefers 幼儿园.

幽默.etymology: A dual-origin phono-semantic loan (音义兼译). In Classical Chinese, 幽默 originally occurred in Qu Yuan's *Chu Ci* (楚辞·九章·怀沙: "孔静幽默", 3rd c. BCE) as a coordinative compound of 幽 (yōu, "secluded, dim, deep") and 默 (mò, "silent, still"), meaning "hushed and quiet." In May 1924, the bilingual essayist and philologist Lin Yutang (林语堂) published essays in the Beijing *Morning Post Supplement* (晨报副刊) repurposing 幽默 as a phonetic and aesthetic transcreation of English *humor* (from Latin *humor* "bodily fluid, temperament"), arguing that true wit is subtle and understated rather than loud buffoonery (滑稽).

history.meaning: deeply hushed, secluded, and silent (in Chu Ci poetry)
humorous, witty, possessing gentle and thoughtful comedic wit (coined by Lin Yutang, 1924)

幽默.notes: One of the most celebrated phono-semantic transcreations in modern Chinese. Collocates frequently with 感 in 幽默感 ("sense of humor") and 黑色幽默 ("black/dark humor").

广.etymology: From Old Chinese *kʷˤaŋʔ (Middle Chinese *kwangX), written in traditional script as 廣, a phono-semantic compound combining the shelter/roof radical 广 (yǎn, depicting a cliff-side or open-walled pavilion) with the phonetic 黄 (huáng, OC *N-kʷˤaŋ). Originally denoting a lofty, spacious hall under a wide roof ("殿之大屋也" in *Shuowen Jiezi*), it generalized in early Classical Chinese to mean "wide in breadth (east-west span), broad, vast, extensive" and verbally "to broaden, expand." The simplified form 广 reuses the ancient cliff-shelter radical graph.

history.meaning: a spacious, wide-roofed great hall; east-west breadth (paired with 輪 'north-south length')
wide, broad, extensive, vast; to propagate or expand widely

广.notes: Used standalone as a predicate adjective (见识很广, "having broad experience/knowledge"; 人脉广, "having a wide network of contacts") and as a prolific prefixoid in media terms (广播 "broadcast", 广告 "advertising", 推广 "promotion").

广告.etymology: A modifier-head / adverb-verb compound (偏正结构) combining 广 (traditional 廣, guǎng, "widely, broadly") and 告 (gào, "to announce, proclaim, inform"). While 广告 appears in Classical Chinese (e.g., *Book of Jin* 晋书: "广告四方", meaning "to proclaim widely to all quarters"), its modern commercial sense of "advertisement, commercial notice" was standardized in Meiji Japan (広告 kōkoku, attested in the 1870s press to translate English *advertisement*) and re-imported into late Qing and Republican Chinese.

history.meaning: to proclaim or announce widely across the realm
newspaper public notice, commercial advertisement (Meiji graphic loan)
commercial advertisement, ad spot, or brand sponsorship placement in media

广告.notes: In Chinese television production (*幕后之王*), 广告 covers both commercial break spots (插播广告) and integrated product placement / title sponsorship (植入广告 / 冠名广告), using the classifier 条 or 则.

广告商.etymology: A three-character modifier-head compound (偏正结构) formed by attaching the agentive/commercial head noun 商 (shāng, "merchant, trader, commercial enterprise", originally from the Shang dynasty people who became synonymous with trade after the Zhou conquest) to 广告 (guǎnggào, "advertisement, commercial sponsorship"). Literally "advertising merchant/business," designating corporate clients who buy ad time or sponsor television programs.

history.meaning: the Shang people; itinerant merchant or trader; commerce
corporate advertiser, commercial sponsor, or advertising agency/client

广告商.notes: In TV and variété production (*幕后之王*), 广告商 (alongside 金主 "financial backer/sponsor" and 客户 "client") refers to the brand sponsors whose funding drives show budgets and product placements.

广场.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 广 (廣, 'wide, broad, spacious') + 场 (場, 'open ground, square'): 'public square, plaza, piazza'.

history.meaning: broad open square; public plaza

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 广场 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: wide dissemination (archaic; modern radio uses 放送 hōsō)
wide propagation (modern radio uses 방송 放送)

广播.etymology: A modifier-head / adverb-verb compound (偏正结构) from 广 (traditional 廣, guǎng, "widely, broadly") and 播 (bō, "to sow seeds by hand 扌, scatter, disseminate, spread"). Attested in Classical Chinese (e.g., *Guanzi* 管子 and Three Kingdoms prose: "广播恩泽", "to scatter imperial grace widely"), it was selected in 1920s Republican China as a transparent structural calque of English *broadcast* (literally *broad* 广 + *cast/sow seeds* 播) for radio transmission.

history.meaning: to sow or scatter (seeds, virtue, or favor) widely across the land

history.form: 廣播 / 广播 (calque of English 'broadcast')
history.meaning: radio broadcasting, public-address transmission, or audio broadcast (adopted 1920s)

广播.notes: A textbook calque of English *broadcast* (which itself originally meant scattering seeds by hand). In modern media, 广播 specifically means audio/radio broadcasting or PA announcements (广播电台 "radio station", 广播体操 "calisthenics set to broadcast music"), while 播 alone forms 直播 ("live stream/broadcast") and 播出 ("to air").

rootFamily.gloss: air, broadcast a show on TV/radio

庆功宴.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正结构) in which the verb-object phrase 庆功 (traditional 慶功, qìnggōng, "to celebrate 庆 meritorious achievement/success 功") modifies the head noun 宴 (yàn, "banquet, feast", originally "peaceful rest indoors 宀 under the sun 日 with a woman 女", extended in Classical Chinese to festive wine banquets 宴饮). Originating in imperial military traditions of feasting victorious generals upon their return (饮至庆功), in modern film and television it denotes the celebratory banquet or wrap party held after a hit broadcast or completed production.

history.meaning: to celebrate military merit/victory + court or aristocratic feast
victory banquet, celebratory dinner, or showbiz wrap/ratings-success party

庆功宴.notes: In the film and TV industry (*幕后之王*), a 庆功宴 is thrown when a show achieves high ratings or wraps up triumphantly (compare 杀青宴, specifically the filming wrap banquet).

庆祝会.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正结构) combining the coordinative verb 庆祝 (traditional 慶祝, qìngzhù, from 庆 "to congratulate with a deer skin gift 鹿 and heart 心" + 祝 "to invoke blessings at an ancestral altar 示") with the nominal suffixoid 会 (traditional 會, huì, "gathering, assembly, party"). Formed productively in modern Mandarin to denote an organized party, reception, or assembly held to celebrate a milestone or victory.

history.meaning: to congratulate with gifts + ritual invocation of blessings + assembly/gathering
celebration party, celebratory reception or gathering

庆祝会.notes: More general and less alcohol/feast-centered than 庆功宴; a 庆祝会 can be an office reception, auditorium gathering, or party for an anniversary, award, or project launch.

床.etymology: Phono-semantic/ideographic character (originally 牀, combining 爿 qiáng 'wooden frame/plank set on legs' + 木 'wood'; variant 床 places 木 under 广 'house shelter'): 'bed, couch' (and a bed-like frame or river bed).

history.meaning: wooden sitting/sleeping platform; bed
bed; classifier for blankets/sheets

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 床 (via 萌典)

床上.etymology: A locative noun phrase (方位短语) combining 床 (chuáng, variant graphic form 牀, Old Chinese *dzraŋ, originally a phono-semantic character with phonetic 爿/丬 depicting a wooden frame or bench for sitting and sleeping) with the postpositional localizer 上 (shàng, "on, upon, on top of"). Attested since Han-Six Dynasties poetry (such as the famous Tang quatrain *Quiet Night Thought* 静夜思 by Li Bai: "床前明月光") and vernacular narratives to turn the concrete noun 床 ("bed") into a grammaticalized place expression ("in bed, on the bed").

history.meaning: wooden sitting/sleeping couch or platform + upper surface / upon
on the bed, in bed (locative noun used after 在, 到, 躺在, etc.)

床上.notes: In Chinese grammar, 床上 is a place word (处所词) required after prepositions like 在 or verbs like 躺 (躺在床上 "lying in bed", never *躺床). Also used attributively in 床上用品 ("bedding, bed linens").

rootFamily.gloss: get out of bed, wake up
go to bed, get into bed

床单.etymology: Compound noun of 床 ('bed') + 单 (單, 'single cloth sheet'): 'bedsheet'.

history.meaning: bedsheet

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 床单 (via 萌典)

床头.etymology: Locative compound noun of 床 ('bed') + 头 (頭, 'head/end'): 'head of the bed, bedside'. Famously in Li Bai's 床前明月光 / 床头.

history.meaning: head of the bed; bedside

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 床头 (via 萌典)

应付.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound (联合结构) combining 应 (traditional 應, yìng, fourth tone, "to respond to, answer, deal with, adapt to circumstances") and 付 (fù, "to hand over, entreg/deliver with the hand 寸 to a person 亻, bestow, pay"). Attested in Song–Yuan administrative and vernacular texts (e.g., *Water Margin* 水浒传, *History of Song* 宋史) originally meaning "to supply what is needed in response to a demand" or "to deal with external contingencies," later bifurcating into a neutral sense ("to cope with, handle") and a pejorative sense ("to do something perfunctorily just to get by").

history.meaning: to respond/correspond to + to hand over or supply
to supply provisions; to deal with or manage social and practical situations
(1) to cope with, handle, manage a challenge; (2) to go through the motions perfunctorily

morphemes.meaning: respond to, deal with, meet (a situation)
hand over, deliver, pay out, attend to

应付.notes: Has two distinct tonalities in context: 应付危机 / 应付裕如 ("to handle a crisis / cope effortlessly", neutral-positive) versus 应付差事 / 应付了事 ("to do a half-hearted job just to get people off one's back", negative). Note that in accounting, 应付账款 means "accounts payable" (from 应 yīng "ought to" + 付 "pay").

rootFamily.gloss: adapt to, get used to, fit in
pay, make a payment; devote effort

应急.etymology: Verb-object compound used as a verb and modifier, combining 应 (應, read yìng, 'respond to, deal with, meet') + 急 ('urgent need, emergency'): 'respond to an emergency, meet an urgent need; emergency (modifier, e.g., 应急灯 emergency light)'.

history.stage: Classical Chinese (Hou Hanshu) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: meet an urgent need; emergency

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 应急 (via 萌典)

应急方案.etymology: A four-character modifier-head compound (偏正结构) pairing the verb-object modifier 应急 (traditional 應急, yìngjí, "to respond to 应 an urgent crisis/emergency 急", attested in Ming-Qing governance for emergency relief measures) with the head noun 方案 (fāng'àn, "plan, scheme, proposal", from 方 "method, prescription, direction" + 案 "official desk/dossier, drafted plan"). Together they denote an actionable plan formulated to respond to an unexpected crisis or production breakdown.

history.meaning: to meet an urgent need + official desk dossier / prescribed method
emergency action plan, crisis response plan

应急方案.notes: Essential live-broadcasting and PR vocabulary in *幕后之王*: when a live show or celebrity scandal erupts, the producer immediately calls for the 应急方案 ("emergency response plan"). Compare 应急预案, which emphasizes a contingency protocol prepared *in advance*.

应急预案.etymology: A four-character modifier-head compound (偏正结构) combining the verb-object modifier 应急 (traditional 應急, yìngjí, "to respond to 应 an emergency 急") with the head noun 预案 (traditional 預案, yù'àn, "contingency plan drafted in advance", from 预 "beforehand, in advance" + 案 "official plan/dossier", a blend of 预先方案). Standardized in modern Chinese public administration, broadcasting, and corporate risk management for a pre-established contingency protocol.

history.meaning: to meet an urgent crisis + beforehand/in advance + official dossier or plan
pre-established emergency contingency plan or crisis protocol (SOP)
