应急预案.notes: While 应急方案 can be improvised on the spot during an emergency, 应急预案 specifically stresses the *pre-planned* nature (预 "in advance") of a backup protocol (e.g., 启动应急预案, "activate the emergency contingency plan").

cognates.meaning: application + procedure/program (Japanese computing prefers アプリ / 応用プログラム)

应用程序.etymology: A four-character modifier-head technical compound (偏正结构) combining 应用 (traditional 應用, yìngyòng, "practical application, applied use", from 应 "to suit/respond to practical needs" + 用 "to use", attested since Song dynasty prose and reinforced via Meiji Japanese 応用 ōyō) with 程序 (chéngxù, "orderly sequence, procedure, computer program", from 程 "measured standard/stage, grain measure 禾" + 序 "sequence, order"). Coined in late 20th-century Mainland Chinese computing as the formal translation of English *application program* (or *software application* / *mobile app*).

history.meaning: to put to practical use + measured sequence or administrative procedure
software application or mobile app (often shortened in speech to 应用 or App)

应用程序.notes: The formal Mainland term for a software or mobile application (often abbreviated to 应用, as in 应用商店 "App Store", or spoken simply as App). Note that Taiwan/HK Mandarin uses 应用程式 (yìngyòng chéngshì) for "application program."

cognates.meaning: accepting an official invitation or recruitment offer
accepting an invitation to a post (응빙)

应聘.etymology: A verb-object compound (动宾结构) formed from 应 (traditional 應, yìng, "to respond to, answer, accept") and 聘 (pìn, "to visit with ritual gifts and invite a worthy scholar or official to take office; to engage, betroth"). In Classical and Imperial Chinese (e.g., *Book of Later Han* 后汉书), 应聘 meant "to accept an emperor's or lord's formal invitation to take up a post." In modern HR usage, the perspective shifted to the job-seeker responding to a company's recruitment notice (招聘): "to apply for a job."

history.meaning: (of a recluse scholar) to accept a ruler's formal summons and gifts to enter official service
to apply for a job in response to a recruitment posting (paired with 招聘 'to recruit/hire')

morphemes.meaning: invite to office, engage services, recruit

应聘.notes: Always keep the directional pair straight in workplace Mandarin: the company does 招聘 (zhāopìn, "recruiting/hiring") and 聘用 (pìnyòng, "employing"), while the candidate does 应聘 (yìngpìn, "applying for the job"; 应聘者 = "job applicant").

rootFamily.gloss: recruit, hire, invite applications for a job

应该.etymology: Compound modal verb combining two necessity/obligation roots: 应 (應, yīng, 'ought to, fitting') + 该 (該, 'ought to, due'): 'should, ought to, must (epistemic)'.

history.meaning: should; ought to

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 应该 (via 萌典)

底.etymology: From Old Chinese *tˤijʔ (Middle Chinese *tejX), a phono-semantic character combining the shelter/building radical 广 (yǎn) with phonetic 氐 (dī, OC *tˤij, depicting the root of a plant or foundation touching the ground 一, cognate with 低 "low" and 根柢 "root"). Originally meaning "the lowest part, base, or underside of a dwelling or vessel" (*Shuowen Jiezi*: "山居也，一曰下也"), it developed rich metaphorical extensions in vernacular Mandarin: "the end of a period" (年底), "minimum baseline/reserve" (底线), "rough draft/master copy" (底稿), and "hidden truth or inside background" (底细 / 交底).

history.meaning: base, foundation, or bottom of a vessel or structure
underside; rough draft; inner details or hidden truth beneath the surface
bottom, base; end of a month/year; inside story, background, or confidence/ace in the hole (心里有底)

morphemes.meaning: bottom, base, foundation; inside story or confidence

底.notes: In *幕后之王* and negotiations, 底 frequently means "inside story, hidden background, or trump card": 摸底 ("sound out the real situation"), 交底 ("lay one's cards on the table / tell the inside truth"), and 心里有底 ("feel confident because one knows what to expect").

rootFamily.gloss: bottom line, minimum threshold or principle
after all, in the end, what on earth (in questions)

底下.etymology: Locative compound combining 底 ('bottom, base, underside', shelter 广 + 氐 'lowest root') + 下 ('below, under', neutral tone xia): 'underneath, below, at the bottom'.

history.meaning: underneath; below; at the bottom

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 底下 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: bottom layer, lower stratum of society

底层.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正结构) combining 底 (dǐ, "bottom, base, lowest part") and 层 (traditional 層, céng, "story of a building, tier, stratum, layer", from 尸 roof/body and 曾 "to add/pile up"). Literally "the bottom layer/tier," operating across three domains in modern Mandarin: (1) the ground floor of a building, (2) the lowest socioeconomic stratum of society (社会底层, "grassroots/underclass"), and (3) in software engineering and systems architecture, "low-level, underlying" (底层逻辑 "underlying logic", 底层架构 "low-level architecture").

history.meaning: bottom/base + piled-up story of a building or geological/social tier
ground floor; lowest social stratum (grassroots); underlying/low-level (in tech and business logic)

底层.notes: Watch the dual metaphorical usage in modern media and tech dramas: 底层员工 / 社会底层 means "entry-level/grassroots workers" or "the bottom of the social ladder," whereas in tech/business, 底层代码 ("low-level code") and 底层逻辑 ("fundamental underlying logic") mean "foundational."

底座.etymology: The noun '底座' (dǐzuò, base, pedestal) consists of '底' (bottom) and '座' (seat, pedestal). '底' refers to the lowest part of something, while '座' originally meant a place to sit, later expanding to refer to a supportive foundation or mount for an object. In pre-modern times, '底座' was commonly used in reference to religious statues or decorative vases mounted on wooden stands. In modern contexts, it applies broadly to the foundational component of any device or structure, such as a lamp or a monument.

history.meaning: bottom

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 底座

店.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 广 ('building/roof') + 占 (zhàn/diàn phonetic): originally 'a roadside stand or storehouse for displaying goods', then 'inn, tavern, shop, store'.

history.meaning: merchant storehouse; roadside inn; shop
shop; store; inn/hotel

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 店 (via 萌典)

店主.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 店 ('shop, inn') + 主 ('owner, proprietor, host'): 'shopkeeper, store owner, innkeeper'. Attested since Tang–Song tales and histories.

history.meaning: shop owner; shopkeeper; innkeeper

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 店主 (via 萌典)

店员.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 店 ('shop, store') + 员 (員, 'staff member, clerk'): 'shop assistant, store clerk, salesclerk'.

history.meaning: shop assistant; store clerk

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 店员 (via 萌典)

店长.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 店 ('shop, store') + 长 (長, read zhǎng, 'head, chief, manager'): 'store manager, shop manager'.

history.meaning: store manager

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 店长 (via 萌典)

店门.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 店 ('shop, store') + 门 (門, 'door, entrance'): 'shop door, storefront entrance'.

history.meaning: shop door; store entrance

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 店门 (via 萌典)

庞大.etymology: A coordinative compound (联合结构) combining 庞 (traditional 龐, páng, Old Chinese *bˤroŋ, from a shelter 广 and dragon 龍, originally meaning "a lofty, grand house" as glossed in *Shuowen Jiezi*: "高屋也", closely allied with 厖 "huge rock, bulky, abundant") and 大 (dà, "great, large, vast"). Literally "lofty/bulky and great," used to describe entities of immense, sprawling scale, volume, or organizational complexity.

history.meaning: a lofty, grand hall or massive rock + large in size
huge, vast, colossal, sprawling (of organizations, budgets, datasets, or physical bulk)

庞大.notes: Unlike 巨大 (jùdà, which emphasizes impressive magnitude or impact, like 巨大成功 "huge success"), 庞大 emphasizes sprawling volume, bulk, or structural complexity (庞大的机构 "a sprawling bureaucracy/organization", 庞大的开支 "enormous expenses", 庞大的数据库 "massive database"), sometimes hinting at unwieldiness.

rootFamily.gloss: huge, tremendous, immense (in scale or impact)

废话.etymology: Modifier-head compound (偏正結構) formed from 廢 (fèi, simplified 废, Middle Chinese *pjwojH, originally "to collapse" of a roof 广 with phonetic 發, hence "discarded, useless, superfluous") modifying 話 (huà, simplified 话, MC *hwaejH, "spoken words, talk, discourse"). Literally "discarded or superfluous speech", attested in Ming–Qing vernacular fiction (such as Hongloumeng) for pointless or redundant talk.

history.meaning: (Classical Chinese) 廢: to abandon, abolish, useless; 話: speech, words, maxim
superfluous remarks, idle talk, nonsense (attested in Qing vernacular novels)
nonsense, rubbish; also used as a colloquial verb-object compound (废什么话) meaning to waste one's breath

废话.notes: Extremely common in spoken Mandarin both as a noun (别说废话 "stop talking nonsense") and as a sarcastic interjection meaning "obviously! / no kidding!" (废话，我当然知道); in separable verb usage, elements can be inserted (少废话 "cut the chatter").

rootFamily.gloss: to abolish, abrogate, repeal (a law or treaty)
topic of conversation; discussion topic (e.g. trending topic)

度.etymology: Phono-semantic/ideographic character combining 庶 (shù/dù phonetic, reduced at top) + 又 ('hand', measuring by the span of the hand/arm): read dù as a noun and classifier meaning 'measure, degree (of temperature, angle, latitude, or electricity kWh), limit, tolerance, occasion/time'; read duó as a verb meaning 'surmise, estimate (揣度)'.

history.meaning: measure by hand; standard; degree (dù); estimate (duó)
degree; measure; limit; spend/pass (time)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 度 (via 萌典)

座.etymology: Phono-semantic/ideographic character formed by adding the building/shelter radical 广 to 坐 (zuò, 'sit'): 'seat, throne, pedestal/stand/base' and the standard classifier for large stationary objects that 'sit' firmly in place (mountains, bridges, buildings, cities, statues: 一座山, 一座桥).

history.meaning: seat; throne; pedestal
seat; stand; classifier for mountains, bridges, buildings

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 座 (via 萌典)

座位.etymology: Compound noun of 座 ('seat; pedestal; stand', shelter radical 广 + 坐 'sit') + 位 ('place; position; seat of honour', person radical 亻 + 立 'stand'). Together they form the standard countable noun for a seat in a café, theatre, train, or classroom.

history.meaning: assigned seat or sitting place
seat; seating

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 座位

座板.etymology: Compound noun of 座 ('seat') + 板 ('wooden board, flat panel'): 'seat board (of a chair, bench, or toilet seat)'.

history.meaning: seat board; flat seat panel

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 座板 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: settlement, reconciliation; compare Japanese 示談 (jidan) for out-of-court settlement

庭外和解.etymology: Four-character modifier-head legal phrase (偏正短語) combining 庭外 (tíngwài, "outside the courtroom", from 庭 tíng, MC *deng, "courtyard, royal court, law court [法庭]" + locative enclitic 外 wài, MC *ngwajH, "outside") with 和解 (héjiě, coordinative-resultative compound from 和 hé, MC *hwa, "harmonious, peace, reconcile" + 解 jiě, MC *kaejX, "to untie, resolve, settle"). Modeled in modern Chinese jurisprudence to translate English "out-of-court settlement".

history.meaning: to reconcile, make peace, resolve a dispute amicably (attested in Shiji and Han histories)
outside the law court (modern legal terminology calqued via Meiji/Republican legal codes)
out-of-court settlement between litigants prior to a judicial verdict

庭外和解.notes: Standard legal and entertainment-media term (frequent in contract or defamation disputes involving celebrities and studios); typically collocates with the verb 达成 (dáchéng tíngwài héjiě, "to reach an out-of-court settlement").

rootFamily.gloss: to reconcile, settle a dispute amicably
to mediate, act as peacemaker in a dispute

庭院.etymology: Coordinative noun compound pairing 庭 ('open courtyard in front of the main hall', shelter 广 + 廷) + 院 ('walled courtyard compound', mound/wall 阝 + 完): 'courtyard, yard, garden court'. Famously in Ouyang Xiu's 庭院深深深几许.

history.meaning: courtyard; walled garden court

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 庭院 (via 萌典)

康复.etymology: Coordinative/resultative compound (聯合/動補結構) composed of 康 (kāng, MC *khang, "husk-free grain; ease, well-being, vigour, health") and 復 (fù, simplified 复, MC *bjuwk, "to return, turn back, restore to a former state"). Originally used in Classical Chinese for restoring social peace and stability to a state or populace, it narrowed in modern medical and everyday usage to "restoring health; recuperating from illness or injury".

history.meaning: to restore peace, prosperity, and order (e.g., to a country or people)
to recover full health, convalesce; medical rehabilitation (translating English "rehabilitation")

康复.notes: More formal and medical in register than 好起来 or 恢复健康; frequently used in hospital contexts (康复中心 "rehabilitation center") and polite well-wishing formulas (祝您早日康复 "wishing you a speedy recovery").

rootFamily.gloss: to restore, resume, recover (general or functional)
relapse, recurrence of an old illness

延播.etymology: Modern television and radio industry compound (偏正/緊縮動賓結構, telescoped abbreviation of 延遲播出 or 延期播放) formed from 延 (yán, MC *jen, "to lengthen, stretch out, postpone, defer") and 播 (bō, MC *paH, originally "to sow seeds by hand 扌", extended in the 20th century via 廣播 "broadcasting" to transmitting audio/video signals). Literally "to postpone broadcasting".

history.meaning: (Classical Chinese) 延: to prolong, delay, invite; 播: to sow, scatter, disseminate
to broadcast (calque of English "broadcast", scattering signals like seeds)
to postpone or delay the scheduled broadcast of a television show or live transmission

morphemes.meaning: to postpone, delay, defer (short for 延迟/延期)
to broadcast, air (short for 播出/播放)

延播.notes: High-frequency television production jargon in *Behind the Scenes* (*幕后之王*); also refers specifically to "time-delayed broadcasting" (延时播出, tape delay) implemented by networks to prevent live broadcast accidents. Contrasts with 停播 ("suspend airing") and 开播 ("begin airing").

rootFamily.gloss: to broadcast, put on the air (TV/radio program)
to postpone, defer to a later date

延迟.etymology: Coordinative compound (聯合結構) pairing two synonymous verbal/adjectival roots: 延 (yán, MC *jen, "to draw out, prolong, protract, postpone") and 遲 (chí, simplified 迟, MC *drjij, "to walk slowly [辶 + 犀], tardy, late, sluggish"). Already attested in Literary Chinese (e.g., *History of the Northern Dynasties* 北史) for dawdling or delaying action, and reinforced in modern Mandarin for scheduling delays and technical latency.

history.meaning: to dawdle, procrastinate, delay execution of an order or journey
to postpone, defer, delay; also used as a noun for technical network/audio latency

延迟.notes: Functions both as a transitive/intransitive verb ("to postpone [an event], be delayed") and as a technical noun in broadcasting and computing meaning "latency / lag" (e.g., 直播信号有两秒延迟 "the live feed has a two-second delay").

rootFamily.gloss: to arrive late (for work, school, an appointment)
to postpone, push back (a deadline or schedule)
to extend, lengthen, prolong (time or distance)

cognates.meaning: to build, establish (on'yomi ken/kon; kun'yomi tateru)

建.etymology: From Old Chinese *kalls > Middle Chinese *kjonH. In the *Shuowen Jiezi* (說文解字), analyzed as an ideogrammic compound combining 聿 (yù, a hand holding a writing brush or stylus, symbolizing inscribing laws and statutes) and 廴 (yǐn, "long stride, measured movement"), originally glossed as 立朝律也 ("to establish court statutes and institutions"). From "setting up dynastic rules, standards, and capitals", the sense generalized in pre-Qin Classical Chinese to erecting poles, founding states, and constructing physical structures.

history.meaning: to establish court statutes; to set upright (a banner or pole), found (a state or feudal fief)
to build, construct, erect (buildings, bridges, public works); to propose (a plan)
to build, construct, establish, create (including digital folders, groups, or projects)

建.notes: While disyllabic compounds like 建设 or 建造 are preferred in formal prose, monosyllabic 建 remains highly active in everyday and media Mandarin with concrete or digital objects: 建群 ("create a group chat"), 建档 ("create a file/profile"), 建组 ("set up a film/production crew").

rootFamily.gloss: to build up, develop (infrastructure, organization, or society)
to construct, build, manufacture (large structures or vessels)

建成.etymology: Resultative verb compound (動補結構) formed from the action verb 建 (jiàn, MC *kjonH, "to build, construct, erect") and the resultative complement 成 (chéng, MC *dzyeng, "to complete, accomplish, bring to fruition"). Literally "to build to completion", regularly used with passive or unaccusative syntax (e.g., 大楼已经建成 "the building has been completed").

history.meaning: syntactic verb + resultative verb sequence in Literary Chinese: to build and complete
lexicalized resultative verb: to finish building, complete construction (of infrastructure or institutions)

建成.notes: Cannot be split into a potential form with 得/不 in formal prose (instead use 建得成 in spoken Mandarin); commonly followed by 投产 ("put into production") or 投入使用 ("put into service") in news reports on studios, venues, or public projects.

rootFamily.gloss: to accomplish, complete, fulfill (a task or project)
to be established, founded; to hold water (of an argument)

cognates.meaning: erection, construction (especially of temples, monuments, or institutions)
establishment, founding (of an institution, monument, or state)

建立.etymology: Coordinative compound (聯合結構) uniting two near-synonymous Classical Chinese verbs: 建 (jiàn, MC *kjonH, "to set upright, institute, found") and 立 (lì, MC *lip, pictograph of a person 大 standing on the ground 一, "to stand upright, set up, establish"). Attested in pre-Qin and Han texts (such as *Zhan Guo Ce* 戰國策 and *Shiji* 史記) for founding regimes, laws, or meritorious achievements, and broadened in modern Mandarin to abstract systems and relationships.

history.meaning: to set up, institute, found (dynasties, legal codes, feudal states, or military merit)
to establish, build up, set up (organizations, diplomatic ties, trust, or databases)

建立.notes: Used primarily for abstract or organizational objects (建立关系 "establish a relationship", 建立制度 "set up a system", 建立信任 "build trust") rather than physical buildings (where 建造 or 兴建 is preferred).

rootFamily.gloss: to found, establish (an organization), hold water
to set up, establish (an institution, prize, or department)
to set up an image, establish (a model, reputation, or brand)

建筑.etymology: Coordinative verb and noun compound of 建 ('establish, set up upright', 聿 + 廴) + 筑 (築, 'ram earth with a wooden杵 pestle to build walls', 竹 + 巩 + 木): 'build, construct; building, architecture'.

history.meaning: set up and ram earth to construct
build/construct; building; architecture

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 建筑 (via 萌典)

建筑师.etymology: Three-character occupational noun combining 建筑 ('architecture, building') + 师 (師, 'master, professional specialist'): 'architect'.

history.meaning: architect

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 建筑师 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: proposal, suggestion, motion (especially in deliberative assemblies)
proposal, suggestion, recommendation to an authority

建议.etymology: Originally a Classical Chinese verb-object compound (動賓結構) composed of 建 (jiàn, MC *kjonH, in the sense of "to set forth, put forward, propose [a policy]") and 議 (yì, simplified 议, MC *ngjeH, from 言 "speech" + 義 "proper/right", meaning "deliberation, counsel, opinion on what is right"). Attested in the *Book of Han* (漢書) for submitting a policy deliberation at court; in modern Mandarin it functions seamlessly as both a transitive verb ("to suggest, advise") and a countable noun ("a suggestion").

history.meaning: to put forward a policy deliberation or formal counsel at court (attested in Hanshu)
to suggest, advise, recommend; a suggestion, proposal, or recommendation (in general or professional life)

morphemes.meaning: to put forward, set up, propose

建议.notes: Unlike 劝 ("to urge/try to persuade personally"), 建议 is objective and consultative; as a verb it takes a clause directly (我建议先延播 "I suggest postponing the broadcast first"), and as a noun it pairs with 提出 ("put forward a suggestion") or 采纳 ("adopt a suggestion").

rootFamily.gloss: to propose, initiate, motion; a formal proposal
agreement, pact, protocol; to agree on

开.etymology: Ancient ideogram (traditional 開) showing two hands (廾) lifting away the horizontal bolt (一) that bars a pair of double doors (門): 'unbolt and open a door -> open, unfold, start/begin, turn on/switch on, drive/operate a vehicle, boil (of water), hold (a meeting), write out (a receipt/prescription)'.

morphemes.meaning: two hands removing the door bar

history.meaning: two hands unbolting double doors = open, begin
open; turn on; start; drive; boil

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 开 (via 萌典)

开业.etymology: Verb-object compound of 开 ('open; initiate', originally two hands lifting a bar from double doors 门) + 业 ('enterprise; trade; profession', originally the notched crossbeam of a bell-stand). Used for a shop, café, or practice officially opening its doors for business.

history.meaning: open a shop or enterprise for business
open for business; grand opening

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 开业

cognates.meaning: opening a meeting or assembly session
opening of a meeting or assembly session
to open a meeting or conference

开会.etymology: Separable verb-object compound (動賓結構 / 離合詞) formed from 開 (kāi, simplified 开, MC *khoj, "to unbar a door 門, open, initiate, convene") and 會 (huì, simplified 会, MC *hwajH, "to gather, assemble; an assembly, meeting, guild"). Originally used in Buddhist and Tang–Song texts for convening a grand Dharma assembly or festival, and reinforced in the late 19th/early 20th century (alongside Japanese 開会 *kaikai* "opening a parliamentary/committee session") to mean holding or attending a meeting.

history.meaning: to convene a Buddhist Dharma assembly or seasonal public gathering
to hold, convene, or attend a meeting or conference (both presiding over and participating in a meeting)

morphemes.meaning: meeting, assembly, gathering (short for 会议)

开会.notes: A classic separable verb (离合词): modifiers and aspect markers go between the characters (开了三个小时的会 "had a three-hour meeting", 开完会 "finish the meeting"). Note that Chinese 开会 covers both "holding/chairing a meeting" and simply "attending a meeting".

rootFamily.gloss: gathering, party, get-together; to get together
general assembly, plenary congress, mass rally

开关.etymology: Antonymic verb-pair compound turned noun: 开 ('open / switch on', originally two hands lifting a bar from门 gate leaves) + 关 ('shut / switch off', a crossbar latching门 shut). By pairing opposite actions, 开关 names an electrical switch or valve.

history.meaning: opening and closing a gate or pass
electrical switch; on-off control

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 开关 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: development, exploitation (of resources, real estate, products, or software)
development (of resources, land, technology, or programs)

开发.etymology: Coordinative compound (聯合結構) composed of 開 (kāi, simplified 开, MC *khoj, "to open up, unbar, clear") and 發 (fā, simplified 发, MC *pjot, "to shoot forth an arrow, send forth, uncover, bring out"). In Classical and Medieval Chinese, 開發 meant "to open up and reveal; to enlighten one's mind or unpack texts". In Meiji Japan, 開発 (*kaihatsu*) was repurposed to translate English "development / exploitation" (of land, resources, and industry), and this modern economic and technological sense returned to Mandarin as a graphic return loan.

history.meaning: to open up, unseal; to enlighten or awaken understanding; to clear wasteland for cultivation
economic, industrial, or resource development (Meiji–Shōwa Japanese semantic adaptation)
to develop (real estate, natural resources, software, IP, or new television formats); development

morphemes.meaning: to send forth, bring out, develop

开发.notes: Whereas 发展 (fāzhǎn) means organic growth or macro-level development ("develop the economy"), 开发 means actively unlocking or creating value from something previously untapped (开发新节目 "develop a new show format", 开发市场 "develop a market", 软件开发 "software development").

rootFamily.gloss: research and development (R&D), abbreviated from 研究开发
to pioneer, open up new territory or markets

cognates.meaning: opening one's mouth, beginning to speak; an aperture or opening
opening one's mouth to speak; an opening/aperture

开口.etymology: Separable verb-object compound (動賓結構) formed from 開 (kāi, simplified 开, MC *khoj, "to open, part") and 口 (kǒu, MC *khuwX, pictograph of an open mouth, "mouth, orifice"). Attested since the Warring States period (*Zhuangzi* 莊子: 開口而笑 "to open one's mouth and laugh"), it evolved by metonymy into "to break silence, start speaking, or bring oneself to make a difficult request or offer".

history.meaning: to open the mouth physically (to laugh, eat, or speak; attested in Zhuangzi and Han texts)
to begin speaking, speak up; to bring oneself to ask for a favor or name a price
to open one's mouth to speak, ask a favor, or quote terms; (technical noun) aperture/slit

开口.notes: In interpersonal and negotiation contexts, 开口 often implies overcoming hesitation to ask for help, money, or a concession (不好意思开口 "too embarrassed to ask", 狮子大开口 "demand an exorbitant price").

rootFamily.gloss: spoken language; colloquial speech; excuse/pretext (借口)
tone of voice, manner of speaking, implication
living expenses, mouths to feed; (media) audience/word-of-mouth (口碑)

开头.etymology: Verb-object/noun compound of 开 ('open, begin') + 头 (頭, 'head, beginning, first end'): 'begin, start; the beginning, opening (of a story, speech, or event)'.

history.meaning: beginning; start; open up

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 开头 (via 萌典)

开始.etymology: Coordinative verb and noun compound of 开 ('open, initiate') + 始 ('begin, start', woman 女 + 台): 'begin, start; beginning'.

history.stage: Classical & Buddhist Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: begin; start; beginning

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 开始 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: development, unfolding, expansion (note reversed morpheme order 展開 tenkai in Japanese)

开展.etymology: Coordinative/resultative compound (聯合/動補結構) combining 開 (kāi, simplified 开, MC *khoj, "to open, unfold") and 展 (zhǎn, MC *trjenX, "to roll over, unroll a scroll or garment, spread out, extend"). In Classical Chinese poets (e.g., Du Fu 杜甫), 開展 described clouds clearing or brow wrinkles smoothing out ("unfolding and spreading open"). In modern Mandarin, it became the standard transitive verb for launching and carrying out organized campaigns, projects, or partnerships (and also serves as an abbreviation of 开始展览 "to open an exhibition").

history.meaning: to unfold, spread open, clear up (of clouds, landscapes, or one's expression in Tang poetry)
to launch, carry out, develop (activities, work, or cooperation); open-minded; (abbr.) to open an exhibition

开展.notes: Takes abstract institutional or project nouns as objects: 开展工作 ("carry out work"), 开展合作 ("launch cooperation"), 开展调查 ("conduct an investigation"). Learners often confuse it with 展开 ("unfold/launch"), which can also be used post-verbally or with concrete/dramatic actions (展开讨论).

rootFamily.gloss: to unfold, spread out; to launch into (a discussion, competition, or investigation)
progress, headway (in a project, negotiation, or investigation)

开工.etymology: Separable verb-object compound (動賓結構 / 離合詞) formed from 開 (kāi, simplified 开, MC *khoj, "to open, start, commence") and 工 (gōng, MC *kuwng, pictograph of a carpenter's square or rammer, "craftsman's work, labor, engineering project, production shift"). Originating in pre-modern artisan and construction guilds for starting a building project or daily shift, it expanded in modern industrial and film/TV usage to mean starting factory operations, resuming work after the Lunar New Year (开工大吉), or beginning a day's shoot on set.

history.meaning: to break ground on a construction project or begin artisan/workshop labor
to start construction, begin factory operations, resume work after holidays, or start filming on a production set

morphemes.meaning: work, labor, construction project, production shift

开工.notes: In film and television production (as in *幕后之王*), 开工 specifically means "to start the day's work/shoot on set" (opposite of 收工 "wrap up for the day"), whereas 开机 means the formal launch/camera-roll of the entire production. Also used in Lunar New Year greetings: 开工大吉 ("auspicious start back to work").

rootFamily.gloss: to wrap up work for the day, call it a day (especially on a film set or construction site)
to go on strike, cease work in protest

开幕.etymology: Verb-object compound of 开 ('open, draw back') + 幕 ('stage curtain'): literally 'raise/open the stage curtain', and by extension 'open (of a performance, exhibition, festival, or conference)'.

history.meaning: raise the curtain -> open (of a show, exhibition, or event)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 开幕 (via 萌典)

开张.etymology: Separable verb-object compound of 开 ('open; unbar') + 张 ('draw a bowstring; spread out a canopy or shop display', bow radical 弓 + 长 cháng). Originally describing merchants unrolling their awning and spreading out wares at dawn, it became the classic word for a shop or café opening for business.

morphemes.meaning: spread out wares; set up shop

history.meaning: spread out shop stalls and open for trade
open for business; grand opening

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 开张

开心.etymology: Verb-object compound used as an adjective and verb, combining 开 ('open up, unfold') + 心 ('heart, mind'). In Tang poetry (Du Fu's 开心胸) it meant 'open one's heart frankly or relieve sorrow'; in modern Mandarin (reinforced by Cantonese and southern Mandarin usage) it is the everyday word for 'happy, joyful, glad, have fun'.

history.meaning: open one's heart; feel relieved and gladdened
happy; joyful; glad

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 开心 (via 萌典)

开播.etymology: Modern media compound (偏正/動賓緊縮結構, contracted from 開始播出 or 開始廣播) formed from 開 (kāi, simplified 开, MC *khoj, "to open, start, initiate") and 播 (bō, MC *paH, "to sow, disseminate, broadcast"). Literally "to begin broadcasting", coined in 20th-century radio and television Mandarin for the premiere of a program, the launch of a new broadcast channel, or the start of a livestream.

history.form: 開始廣播 / 開始播出
history.meaning: to commence radio or television broadcasting
to start airing, premiere on television/streaming, or launch a broadcast channel/livestream

morphemes.meaning: to broadcast, air, stream (short for 播出/直播)

开播.notes: Essential television and streaming vocabulary: used both for a series premiering (新剧今晚八点开播 "the new series premieres tonight at 8") and for a livestreamer going live (主播刚开播 "the streamer just went live").

rootFamily.gloss: to broadcast, air (a show or episode)
first broadcast, series or season premiere
news anchor, host, or livestreamer (short for 主要播音员 / 网络主播)

开放.etymology: Coordinative verb and adjective compound of 开 ('open') + 放 ('release, let go, blossom'): '(of flowers) bloom, blossom; open to the public; lift restrictions; open-minded'.

history.stage: Tang–Song poetry (blossoming flowers) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: bloom; open to the public; open-minded

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 开放 (via 萌典)

开机.etymology: Separable verb-object compound (動賓結構) composed of 開 (kāi, simplified 开, MC *khoj, "to open, switch on, start up") and 機 (jī, simplified 机, MC *kj+j, originally the trigger mechanism of a crossbow, extended in modern Chinese via 機器/機械 to "machine, engine, aircraft, camera, telephone, computer"). Originally meaning "to start up an industrial machine or engine", it acquired three specialized modern senses: switching on an electronic device (phone/TV/computer), a plane taking off, and—in film/TV production—uncovering the camera at the traditional开机仪式 ("camera-rolling ceremony") to mark the start of principal photography.

history.meaning: to trigger a mechanism; to enlighten or unlock spiritual insight (in Buddhist texts)
to start up a factory machine, loom, or engine
(1) to power on a phone, computer, or TV; (2) to begin principal photography on a film/TV show; (3) (of a plane) to take off

morphemes.meaning: to switch on, start up, open
machine, device, phone, or motion-picture camera (short for 机器/手机/摄影机)

开机.notes: Polysemous in *幕后之王*: in everyday dialogue 保持开机 means "keep your phone switched on" (opposite of 关机 "power off"), while in studio production 新节目下周开机 means "the new show starts filming / rolls cameras next week" (opposite of 杀青 "wrap filming").

rootFamily.gloss: to switch off a phone, computer, or machine; to stop factory operations
standby mode (of an electronic device or crew waiting on set)

开机率.etymology: Modifier-head technical compound (偏正結構) formed by attaching the statistical suffix 率 (lǜ, MC *srjwijH, originally "measuring net/rope", hence "ratio, rate, proportion") to the verb-object compound 開機 (kāijī, "to turn on a television set or machine"). Coined in television audience measurement (paralleling English "HUT: Homes Using Television" or "PUT: People Using Television") to denote the percentage of all households with television sets that have their sets switched on during a given time slot.

history.meaning: ratio of machines switched on (originally industrial equipment utilization rate, later television audience metric)
television turn-on rate (percentage of total TV households actively watching television at a given time)

morphemes.meaning: television set or machine (short for 电视机/机器)

开机率.notes: In TV industry analytics (a central plot point in *幕后之王*), distinguish three key metrics: 开机率 ("TV turn-on rate / HUT", how many TVs are turned on overall), 收视率 ("ratings", percentage of all TV households watching a specific show), and 市场份额 ("market share", percentage of *turned-on* TVs watching that show).

rootFamily.gloss: click-through rate, hit rate (for online video or articles)

开涮.etymology: Beijing dialect colloquial compound (動賓/動補結構) composed of 開 (kāi, simplified 开, MC *khoj, "to start, initiate an action") and 涮 (shuàn, MC *srwanH, onomatopoeic/action verb meaning "to rinse by swirling in water", and specifically in northern Chinese cuisine "to dip thin slices of meat briefly in boiling hotpot broth", as in 涮羊肉). From the vivid culinary metaphor of dipping and swirling someone around in boiling water like a slice of mutton, 拿某人开涮 ("take someone to dip in the hotpot") came to mean teasing, stringing someone along, or making sport of them.

history.meaning: to rinse out a vessel or swirl thinly sliced meat in a boiling hotpot (Yuan–Qing northern vernacular)
Beijing slang: to make sport of someone, play a trick on, tease, or string someone along

morphemes.meaning: to swirl/scald in boiling water; (figuratively) to toy with or make sport of

开涮.notes: Colloquial, lively northern Mandarin expression almost always used in the prepositional frame 拿 + [person] + 开涮 (e.g., 别拿我开涮了 "stop ribbing me / stop pulling my leg!"). Related to Beijing slang 涮 ("to stand someone up / trick someone", e.g., 被他涮了).

rootFamily.gloss: instant-boiled mutton hotpot (classic Beijing dish that gave rise to the metaphor)
hotpot pan; to eat hotpot by dipping ingredients in boiling broth
to tease, poke fun at, ridicule playfully (similar register)

开玩笑.etymology: Separable verb-object compound (動賓結構 / 離合詞) formed from the light/inchoative verb 開 (kāi, simplified 开, MC *khoj, "to initiate, engage in, make") and the nominalized compound 玩笑 (wánxiào, from 玩 wán, MC *ngwan, "to play with, trifle, jest" + 笑 xiào, MC *sjewH, "to laugh, smile, jest"). Attested in Qing dynasty vernacular novels (such as *Ernü Yingxiong Zhuan* 兒女英雄傳), where 玩笑 ("playful laughing, jesting") was paired with 開 to mean cracking a joke, kidding around, or playing a prank.

history.meaning: to jest and laugh playfully; a jest or joke (Ming–Qing vernacular fiction)
to crack a joke, kid around, tease; to treat a serious matter lightly

开玩笑.notes: Separable verb: the target of the joke is introduced with 跟 or 和 (跟他开了一个玩笑 "played a joke on him"), or inserted as a possessive modifier (别开我的玩笑 "don't make fun of me"). Used alone as an exclamation (开什么玩笑！), it means "You've got to be kidding! / No way!".

开篇.etymology: Verb-object compound (動賓結構) that also functions as a noun, composed of 開 (kāi, simplified 开, MC *khoj, "to open, begin, initiate") and 篇 (piān, MC *phjen, with bamboo radical 竹 because ancient writings were bound bundles of bamboo slips, meaning "a bound section of bamboo slips, chapter, essay, poem, or complete literary piece"). Literally "to open the bamboo-slip scroll / begin a composition", used in classical literary criticism (e.g., discussing how Du Fu or Li Bai opens a poem) and extended in modern media to the opening sequence of a book, script, or TV series.

history.meaning: to begin a poem or prose essay; the opening lines of a literary work (Song–Qing literary criticism)
the opening section or chapter of a book, essay, screenplay, or television series; to open a work

morphemes.meaning: bamboo-slip scroll, chapter, essay, literary piece

开篇.notes: More literary and structural than 开头 ("beginning"); in screenwriting and television production, 开篇 refers to the opening hook or pilot sequence of a work (e.g., 开篇立意 "establish the central theme right from the opening"). Also denotes the introductory ballad sung before the main story in Suzhou *pingtan* (评弹).

rootFamily.gloss: length of a piece of writing, space allotted in a publication or program
chapter, section, or movement of a grand literary or musical work
full-length work (e.g., 长篇小说 full-length novel, 长篇电视剧 long-form TV series)

开衫.etymology: Compound garment noun of 开 ('open down the front') + 衫 ('unlined upper garment, shirt/sweater',衣 + 彡): 'cardigan, front-buttoning or front-opening sweater'.

history.meaning: front-opening sweater; cardigan

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 开衫 (via 萌典)

开过.etymology: Verb + complement/aspect compound of 开 ('open, drive, bloom') + 过 (過, 'pass by; experiential aspect marker -guo'): either 'drive past / pass by' or 'have opened / have driven before'.

history.meaning: drive past; have opened/driven

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 开过 (via 萌典)

开锁.etymology: Verb-object compound of 开 ('open, unlock') + 锁 (鎖, 'metal lock', metal 钅 + 贝): 'unlock a lock, pick or open a lock'.

history.meaning: unlock; open a lock

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 开锁 (via 萌典)

开门.etymology: Verb-object compound of 开 ('open') + 门 (門, 'door, gate'): literally 'open the door' and commercially 'open for business (for the day)'.

history.stage: Old & Classical Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: open the door; open for business

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 开门 (via 萌典)

开门见山.etymology: Four-character serial-verb idiom (連謂結構成語) meaning literally "open the door (開門 kāimén) and immediately see the mountain (見山 jiànshān)". It originates in the Song dynasty poetry criticism treatise *Canglang Shihua* (滄浪詩話, "Canglang's Remarks on Poetry") by Yan Yu (嚴羽, c. 1191–1241), who praised Tang poet Du Fu with the words: 太白發句，謂之開門見山 ("Li Bai's opening lines may be called opening the door and seeing the mountain right in front of you")—inspired in turn by Tang poet Meng Jiao's verse 開門見青山. It shifted from praising direct poetic openings to general rhetoric: coming straight to the point without circumlocution.

history.form: 開門見青山 / 開門見山
history.meaning: literary critical metaphor in Yan Yu's Canglang Shihua (Song dynasty) for a poem that states its theme or imagery directly in the opening line
to come straight to the point in speech or writing without beating around the bush

开门见山.notes: Frequently used adverbially with 地 before a verb of speaking (开门见山地说 "to speak straight to the point") or as a predicate (咱们就开门见山吧 "let's cut straight to the chase"). Antonym: 拐弯抹角 ("beat around the bush").

rootFamily.gloss: to state one's main point right at the start of a speech or essay (literary synonym)
to beat around the bush, speak indirect or evasive words

cognates.meaning: to expel, dismiss from an organization or party

开除.etymology: Coordinative/resultative verb compound (聯合/動補結構) composed of 開 (kāi, simplified 开, MC *khoj, here in the sense of "to separate, clear away, strike off a register") and 除 (chú, MC *drjo, originally "steps to a palace hall 阜", extended in Classical Chinese to "to sweep away, remove, eliminate, strike off"). In Ming–Qing fiscal accounting (the Four-Column Ledger 四柱清冊: 舊管、新收、開除、實在), 開除 meant "expenditures / items struck off the account balance". From striking an entry or name off an official roster, it evolved into dismissing or expelling someone from employment, school, or party membership.

history.meaning: to deduct or strike off an item from an account book; outgoing expenditures (Ming–Qing bookkeeping)
to strike a person's name from the roster; to expel (from school/organization) or fire/dismiss (from a job)

morphemes.meaning: to clear away, separate, strike off a list

开除.notes: Stronger and more punitive than 解雇 ("lay off / terminate employment") or 辞退 ("let go"): 开除 implies disciplinary dismissal or expulsion for a serious rule violation (e.g., 开除学籍 "expel from school", 被公司开除 "get fired by the company"). In colloquial slang, often shortened to monomorphemic 开 (老板把他开了 "the boss fired him").

rootFamily.gloss: to abolish, repeal, abrogate (laws, treaties, or customs)
to eliminate, clear away, remove (obstacles or misunderstandings)
to remove a name from an official roll or roster; to strike off

开饭.etymology: Separable verb-object compound (動賓結構 / 離合詞) formed from 開 (kāi, simplified 开, MC *khoj, "to set out, lay out on the table, start") and 飯 (fàn, simplified 饭, MC *bjonH, "cooked grain/rice; a meal"). Originally used in households, inns, and canteens for setting out dishes and serving a meal (related to 開伙 / 開席), and used both transitively ("serve the meal") and intransitively ("dinner is served / start eating").

history.meaning: to set out food and serve a meal (attested in Qing vernacular fiction such as Hongloumeng and Rulin Waishi)
to serve a meal (in a home, canteen, or film set); to start eating

开饭.notes: Common everyday and institutional announcement (开饭了！ "Dinner's ready! / Come and get it!"). On Chinese film and television sets, 开饭 refers to distributing crew boxed meals (盒饭) during a break in shooting. Separable: 几点开饭？ / 开了饭再说.

rootFamily.gloss: boxed meal (ubiquitous caterer meal on Chinese film and TV production sets)
to eat a meal; (figuratively) to make a living

cognates.meaning: saying the same thing in unison, unanimous agreement
cognates.word: 異口同音 (ikudōon, variant with 音) / 異口同声 (ikudōsei)

异口同声.etymology: Four-character parallel/antithetical idiom (聯合結構四字格) contrasting 異口 (yìkǒu, "different mouths", from 異 yì, MC *jiH, "different, separate" + 口 kǒu, MC *khuwX, "mouth") with 同聲 (tóngshēng, "the same voice", from 同 tóng, MC *duwng, "same, together" + 聲 shēng, simplified 声, MC *syeng, "voice, sound"). Literally "different mouths, the same voice". Evolved from early fourth-century variants such as 異人同辭 (in Pan Yue's writings) and 異口同音 (in *Songshu* 宋書), stabilizing as 異口同聲 in Tang–Song prose to describe multiple people speaking out simultaneously or expressing the exact same opinion.

history.form: 異口同音 / 異口同聲
history.meaning: different mouths uttering the exact same sound or opinion (attested in Northern & Southern Dynasties and Tang histories)
to speak in unison or express unanimous agreement simultaneously

异口同声.notes: Most frequently used as an adverbial modifier before verbs of speaking (大家异口同声地回答 "everyone answered in one voice / in unison"). Note the balanced four-character structure where 异 ("different") and 同 ("same") form an exact semantic antithesis.

rootFamily.gloss: unanimous; without prior consultation yet acting in complete agreement
largely identical with minor differences; virtually the same
simultaneous interpretation (short for 同声传译, literally "same-voice interpreting")

弄.etymology: Ancient ideogram attested on bronze inscriptions showing two hands (廾) holding and playing with a piece of jade (王/玉): originally 'play with, handle,fondle (and play music)', and in colloquial Mandarin a versatile general action verb (read nòng, or literary lòng) meaning 'do, make, handle, fix, get, mess with'.

history.meaning: two hands handling jade = play with, handle, perform
do; make; handle; fix; cause to become

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 弄 (via 萌典)

弄坏.etymology: Resultative verb compound combining the general causative verb 弄 ('handle, do, make') + 坏 (壞, 'broken, ruined'): 'break, ruin, damage, mess up'.

history.meaning: break; damage; ruin

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 弄坏 (via 萌典)

弄清楚.etymology: Resultative verb-complement compound (動補結構) composed of the generalized causative verb 弄 (nòng, MC *luwngH, originally a pictophonetic/ideogrammic character showing two hands 廾 playing with jade 玉, meaning "to handle, play with, manipulate", which bleached in vernacular Mandarin into a general causative verb "to make, get, do") followed by the disyllabic adjectival resultative complement 清楚 (qīngchu, from 清 qīng, MC *tshjeng, "clear, pure water" + 楚 chǔ, MC *tsrhjoX, "neatly arranged thicket, distinct, orderly"). Literally "to handle/investigate until clear and distinct".

history.meaning: (Classical/Middle Chinese) 弄: tofondle jade, play with, handle; 清楚: clear and distinct, neatly ordered
to figure out clearly, ascertain, get to the bottom of, clarify (a fact or situation)

morphemes.kind: resultative root (2nd element, neutral tone in compound)

弄清楚.notes: Supports potential infixes 得 and 不 (弄得清楚 "can figure out", 弄不清楚 "cannot figure out / be confused about"), and frequently shortened to 弄清 in slightly tighter prose (弄清真相 "get to the bottom of the truth"). Colloquial Northern Mandarin often substitutes 搞清楚 with identical syntax.

rootFamily.gloss: to figure out, understand thoroughly (synonymous causative-resultative with 明白)
to clarify, clear up (a rumour, misconception, or muddy liquid)

弄脏.etymology: Resultative verb-complement compound (動補結構) combining the colloquial causative verb 弄 (nòng, MC *luwngH, "to handle, make, cause to become") with the adjectival resultative complement 髒 (zāng, simplified 脏, MC *tsang, "dirty, soiled, filthy"). Note that Simplified Chinese 脏 merges two distinct traditional characters and Middle Chinese words: 髒 (zāng, "dirty, filthy", written with the bone/skeleton radical 骨) and 臟 (zàng, "internal bodily organs, viscera", written with the flesh radical 肉/月). Literally "to handle or act so as to make dirty".

history.meaning: to soil, befoul, make dirty by handling or carelessness (Early Modern/Modern vernacular Mandarin)
to get dirty, soil, stain, or sully (clothing, hands, surfaces, or figuratively a reputation)

morphemes.meaning: to make, cause to become, handle

弄脏.notes: Frequently appears in the 把 disposal construction (别把衣服弄脏了 "don't get your clothes dirty") or passive 被 construction (地毯被弄脏了 "the carpet got soiled"). Remember the tonal and etymological split of 脏: first tone zāng ("dirty", trad. 髒) vs. fourth tone zàng ("internal organ", trad. 臟, as in 心脏 "heart").

rootFamily.gloss: stolen goods or illicitly obtained money/booty (homophonous cognate written with 贝 shell/money radical)

弄裂.etymology: Resultative verb compound combining 弄 ('handle, cause to become') + 裂 ('split, crack', 列 + 衣 'tear cloth'): 'crack, cause to split or crack'.

history.meaning: cause to crack or split

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 弄裂 (via 萌典)

弄错.etymology: Resultative verb-complement compound (動補結構) composed of the causative verb 弄 (nòng, MC *luwngH, "to handle, do, make") and the resultative complement 錯 (cuò, simplified 错, MC *tshwak / *tshwaH, originally "to inlay gold or silver on bronze [金 + 昔]; grindstone", extended in Classical Chinese to "crisscrossed, mixed up, disordered", and hence "mistaken, wrong, erroneous"). Literally "to handle or do something so that it turns out wrong or mixed up".

history.meaning: gold inlay on metal; grindstone; intersecting, mixed up, awry, mistaken (Classical Chinese)
to make a mistake, get something wrong, mix up, or misunderstand

弄错.notes: Covers both cognitive misunderstandings (你弄错了 "you've got it wrong / you're mistaken") and practical mix-ups (把播出时间弄错了 "mixed up the broadcast time"). Compare 看错 ("misread / misidentify visually"), 听错 ("mishear"), and 搞错 ("mess up / get wrong").

rootFamily.gloss: to miss (an opportunity, train, or person); to brush past each other

cognates.meaning: introduction, bringing in, adoption (of capital, systems, or technology)
cognates.word: 導入 (dōnyū) / 引入 (innyū, technical: leading-in wire)

cognates.meaning: drawing in, pulling in, leading in

引入.etymology: Verb-complement directional/resultative compound (動補結構) composed of 引 (yǐn, MC *jinX, pictograph of drawing a bow 弓 with a bowstring 丨, "to draw a bow, pull, draw toward, lead, guide") and 入 (rù, MC *nyip, "to enter, bring inside"). In Classical Chinese, 引入 meant physically ushering a guest into a hall or chamber, or drawing an enemy into a trap. In modern Mandarin, it shifted primarily to abstract and institutional objects: introducing foreign capital, new broadcasting formats, advanced technology, or external mechanisms into a system.

history.meaning: to usher or lead someone inside a hall/palace; to lure into an area (attested in Shiji and Tang prose)
to introduce from outside, bring in, adopt (capital, competition mechanisms, IP formats, or variables)

引入.notes: Slightly more abstract and systemic than 引进 (yǐnjìn, which emphasizes importing tangible talent, foreign equipment, or copyrighted shows); for instance, one says 引入竞争机制 ("introduce a competition mechanism") or 引入战略投资 ("bring in strategic investment"), as well as the four-character idiom 引人入胜 ("lead people into scenic wonders; captivating").

rootFamily.gloss: to import or bring in from abroad/outside (talent, technology, or foreign TV formats)
to guide, lead, channel (public opinion or an audience)
to attract, draw, fascinate (viewers, attention, or investment)

cognates.meaning: triggering, causing, inducing (a secondary explosion or event: 誘発 yūhatsu)

引发.etymology: Verb-resultative/coordinative compound (動補/聯合結構) formed from two archery metaphors in Classical Chinese: 引 (yǐn, MC *jinX, "to draw a bowstring back") and 發 (fā, simplified 发, MC *pjot, "to release the bowstring and shoot forth an arrow; to erupt, break out"). In Classical Chinese (*Mencius* 孟子: 引而不發 "drawing the bow without releasing the arrow"), 引 and 發 denoted the two sequential stages of shooting; compounded as 引發, "drawing and releasing/detonating" evolved into "to trigger, touch off, or spark" a chain reaction, public controversy, or medical symptom.

history.meaning: to draw a bow and shoot forth an arrow (classical archery metaphor in Mencius)
to trigger, touch off, spark, or set off (a debate, crisis, chain reaction, or ailment)

morphemes.meaning: to draw (a bow), pull, lead to
to shoot forth, discharge, break out, erupt

引发.notes: High-frequency journalistic and media verb used when an incident or broadcast sparks widespread public reaction (引发热议 "spark heated discussion", 引发关注 "draw widespread attention", 引发危机 "trigger a crisis"). Slightly more immediate and explosive in nuance than 引起 ("cause / give rise to").

rootFamily.gloss: to give rise to, cause, arouse (attention, suspicion, or discussion)
to detonate, touch off (an explosive or a viral media sensation: 引爆全场)
to erupt, break out suddenly (of war, applause, scandal, or a volcano)

引开.etymology: Resultative/directional verb-complement compound (動補結構) composed of 引 (yǐn, MC *jinX, "to draw, pull, lead, lure") and the directional/separative complement 開 (kāi, simplified 开, MC *khoj, "to open, part, move away from a point"). Literally "to draw or lure away from a spot", used in tactical, narrative, and everyday contexts for diverting guards, pursuers, crowds, or someone's attention away from a target.

history.meaning: to draw apart, pull open, or lead someone away from a location (Early Modern vernacular Mandarin)
to lure away, draw off (pursuers, reporters, or attention) from a person or place

引开.notes: Common in drama and entertainment scenes (e.g., 把狗仔队引开 "lure the paparazzi away", 引开他的注意力 "divert his attention"). Like other directional/resultative compounds with 开 ("away"), it takes potential infixes (引得开 / 引不开) and frequently occurs in the 把 construction.

rootFamily.gloss: to draw someone away from their post by a ruse (as in 调虎离山 "lure the tiger from the mountain")
to leave, depart from, separate from

cognates.meaning: to recommend a person for a post

引荐.etymology: A coordinative verb compound (引薦 in traditional script) pairing 引 (yǐn, originally depicting drawing a bowstring, hence 'to draw forth, lead, guide') with 荐/薦 (jiàn, originally fodder or a woven grass mat offered up, extended in Classical Chinese to 'to present, offer, recommend to a superior'). In imperial officialdom, it denoted formally presenting a worthy talent to court or a patron; in modern professional and media contexts, it refers to introducing someone to an influential decision-maker.

history.meaning: to lead forward and recommend a scholar or candidate to the imperial court or a high official
to recommend or personally introduce someone to an influential contact or mentor

引荐.notes: Higher in register than 介绍 (jièshào); 引荐 implies vouching for someone's talent when connecting them with a senior figure, investor, or producer.

引起.etymology: A resultative verb compound formed from 引 (yǐn, 'to draw, pull, lead out') and 起 (qǐ, 'to rise, get up, begin'). Literally 'to pull forth so that something rises up', it originated in Literary Chinese to describe drawing out latent phenomena or setting events in motion, and grammaticalized into the standard modern transitive verb meaning 'to give rise to, spark, or arouse' abstract reactions.

history.meaning: to draw upward, pull up, or set in motion
to give rise to, trigger, or arouse (attention, controversy, resonance)

引起.notes: Takes abstract nouns as objects—such as 引起注意 (attract attention), 引起共鸣 (strike a chord/resonate), or 引起争议 (spark controversy)—never concrete physical objects.

rootFamily.gloss: to trigger, touch off (a major event or debate)

引进.etymology: A directional-resultative verb compound combining 引 (yǐn, 'to draw, lead, guide') and 进/進 (jìn, originally depicting a bird advancing upward, 'to advance, enter'). In pre-modern usage it meant leading a person into a court or chamber; in twentieth-century Mandarin it specialized to mean 'leading across a boundary from the outside', denoting the strategic importation of foreign technology, capital, talent, or intellectual property formats.

history.meaning: to lead forward into court; to usher or recommend someone into office
to introduce from abroad or outside (technology, investment, talent, or media formats)

引进.notes: Unlike 进口 (jìnkǒu, commercial import of physical goods), 引进 is used for high-value intangibles or strategic assets: 引进人才 (recruit top talent), 引进技术 (introduce technology), or 引进节目模式 (import a TV show format).

rootFamily.gloss: to draw in, attract (investment or talent)

引进版.etymology: A modern modifier-head nominal compound formed by attaching the nominal suffix 版 (bǎn, originally 'wooden printing block or register plank', hence 'edition, version') to the verb compound 引进/引進 (yǐnjìn, 'to introduce from abroad'). Coined in modern publishing and television production, it designates an officially licensed domestic version or remake adapted from an overseas book, album, or broadcast format.

history.meaning: wooden plank used for rammed-earth walls or official population registers; later woodblock printing plate
licensed domestic edition or imported format adaptation of foreign media IP

morphemes.meaning: to lead in, draw from outside

引进版.notes: Crucial television industry term in *Behind the Scenes* (*幕后之王*), contrasting an 引进版 (licensed foreign format adaptation) with an 原创节目 (original homegrown show).

弟弟.etymology: Reduplicated kinship noun from 弟 (originally leather thongs wrapped in sequential order around a spear shaft, hence 'junior in sequence -> younger brother'). In Mandarin, 弟弟 (dìdi) is the standard everyday word for 'younger brother'.

history.meaning: younger brother
younger brother

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 弟弟 (via 萌典)

张.etymology: Measure word for flat, spread-out surfaces and paper items (一张桌子 'a table', 一张纸 'a sheet of paper', 一张床 'a bed'). Formed from 弓 ('bow') + 长 (cháng phonetic), 張 originally meant 'string and draw a bow open' in the Shijing, extending naturally to things spread flat.

history.meaning: draw or stretch a bow
classifier for flat sheets, tables, beds

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 張 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to mend, patch up, compensate for a deficiency

弥补.etymology: A coordinative verb compound (彌補 in traditional script) combining 弥/彌 (mí, originally 'to relax a bow', extended via 彌縫 to 'to fill up, seal cracks, span completely') and 补/補 (bǔ, composed of 衣 'garment' and 甫 phonetic, literally 'to patch torn clothing, mend, repair'). Attested in Literary Chinese for patching administrative or moral flaws, the compound evolved to mean making up for a deficit, loss, or regret.

history.meaning: to patch up gaps, mend torn places, and remedy deficiencies in governance or conduct
to make up for, compensate for, or remedy (a loss, flaw, or regret)

morphemes.meaning: to fill completely, close up gaps
to patch a garment, mend, supplement

弥补.notes: Commonly collocates with abstract deficits: 弥补损失 (make up for losses), 弥补不足 (remedy a shortcoming), or 弥补遗憾 (make up for a regret).

rootFamily.gloss: to subsidize, allowance; to patch up

弯.etymology: Simplified from 彎 (wān), originally depicting drawing a bow (弓) taut beneath silk/cord threads (絭), hence 'to draw a bow into an arc'. From the curved profile of a drawn bow, Classical Chinese generalized 彎 both as a verb ('to curve, bend') and as an adjective ('curved, winding, crooked'), contrasting directly with 直 ('straight').

morphemes.meaning: curved like a drawn bow 弓; bent (simplified from 彎)

history.meaning: draw a bow; curve into an arc
bent; curved; winding; turn a corner

弱.etymology: An ancient ideographic character (Old Chinese *njawk) depicting two adorned or pliable bows (弓 with decorative plumes or curving strokes) placed side by side, evoking something supple, tender, and unhardened. In Classical Chinese it meant 'young, tender, not yet robust' (as in 弱冠, age twenty when a youth was capped), before generalizing to 'physically weak, feeble, or inferior in strength'.

history.meaning: pliable, tender, young (especially of a youth reaching twenty); lacking physical force
weak, feeble, inferior in capability or competitive standing

弱.notes: In contemporary workplace and media slang, 弱 often means 'underwhelming in skill or competitiveness' (e.g., 实力太弱 'skill level is too weak').

弱势群体.etymology: A four-character modifier-head nominal compound structured as [弱势 + 群体]. The modifier 弱势/弱勢 (ruòshì) combines 弱 ('weak') + 势/勢 ('power, momentum, positional advantage') to mean 'a position of weakness or disadvantage'; the head 群体/群體 (qúntǐ) combines 群 ('flock, crowd') + 体/體 ('body, collective entity') to mean 'social group or collective'. Coined in late twentieth-century sociological and journalistic discourse, it translates the concept of socially or economically vulnerable populations.

history.meaning: weak momentum or inferior strategic position in military or political affairs
vulnerable groups; socially or economically disadvantaged members of society

弱势群体.notes: Used both earnestly in public-interest journalism and humorously in workplace banter when employees or creatives claim to be the 'underdog' (弱势群体) against powerful executives or investors.

弹.etymology: Phono-semantic character (彈) combining 弓 ('bow') + 单 (單, dān/tán phonetic): originally 'shoot pellets with a crossbow/slingshot'. Read tán as a verb meaning 'pluck or play a stringed/keyboard instrument (guitar, piano, zither), flick with the fingers, spring/bounce back'; read dàn as a noun meaning 'pellet, bullet, bomb (子弹, 炸弹)'.

history.meaning: shoot a pellet bow; flick/pluck strings (tán); pellet/ball (dàn)
pluck/play (an instrument), bounce (tán); bullet/pellet (dàn)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 弹 (via 萌典)

弹琴.etymology: Verb-object compound of 弹 (tán, 'pluck or strike musical strings/keys with the fingers') + 琴 ('ancient Chinese seven-stringed zither guqin -> stringed or keyboard instruments generally, especially the piano 钢琴'): 'play the zither, piano, or a keyboard/stringed instrument'. Attested since the Shijing.

history.meaning: play the zither -> play the piano or musical instrument

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 弹琴 (via 萌典)

强.etymology: Originally a phono-semantic character denoting a rice weevil or beetle (虫 radical with 弘 phonetic), 强 (and its graphic variant 強/彊, combining 弓 'bow' and 畺 phonetic, Old Chinese *gjang) was borrowed early in Old Chinese for the homophonous word meaning 'stiff, unyielding, powerful bow', hence 'strong, vigorous, forceful, superior'. Note that the character also carries two related readings: qiáng ('strong, powerful') and qiǎng ('to force, compel').

history.meaning: stiff and powerful (of a bow); physically strong, formidable, unyielding
strong, powerful, high-performing, superior in capability

强.notes: Watch the pronunciation split: qiáng means 'strong/powerful' (强大, 能力很强), qiǎng means 'by force/reluctantly' (勉强, 强迫), and jiàng means 'stubborn/unyielding' (倔强).

强推.etymology: A modifier-head verb compound combining adverbial 强/強 (qiáng / qiǎng, 'forcefully, aggressively, by sheer power') with the verb head 推 (tuī, composed of 扌 'hand' and 隹 phonetic, 'to push forward, advance, promote, recommend'). In contemporary corporate, media, and internet usage, it means either 'to ram through a proposal or project against resistance' or 'to heavily promote/recommend an artist, show, or product'.

history.meaning: to push or press forward by force
to push a project or candidate through forcefully; in media/fan slang, to heavily promote or strongly recommend

强推.notes: Has two distinct modern senses depending on context: in executive boardrooms, 'ramming a decision/artist through despite objections'; in fan and marketing culture, 'heavily promoting (a resource-backed star) or enthusiastically recommending'.

cognates.meaning: to turn round, return, revolve (Sino-Tibetan cognate)
to return, come back, belong to

归.etymology: The traditional form 歸 (simplified 归, Old Chinese *kwjəj) combines 止 ('foot, to step'), 婦省 ('broom/woman'), and 追省 (phonetic/mound), originally designating a bride's ceremonial 'returning home' (or entering her husband's household as her true home, as in *Shijing* 之子于歸), and more broadly 'to return to one's rightful place'. From 'returning to a rightful master or origin', it developed the institutional sense 'to revert to, belong under the jurisdiction of, or report to'.

history.meaning: to return home; to marry (of a woman); to give allegiance to a ruler
to revert to, be restored to, or fall under the jurisdiction of
to return; to belong to, fall under the authority of, or report to (a department/leader)

morphemes.meaning: to return; to belong to or fall under the jurisdiction of

归.notes: In workplace and corporate dialogue, 归 expresses lines of authority or ownership: 这件事归你管 ('This matter falls under your charge') or 这个部门归他带 ('This department reports to him').

rootFamily.gloss: to belong to, fall under the jurisdiction of
to return something to its rightful owner

当.etymology: Merged simplified graph (mainly from 當, combining 尚 shàng/dāng phonetic + 田 'fields of matching value'; also 噹): read dāng 'match, face, serve as / work as (当老师), ought to, just at (a time or place)'; read dàng 'treat as, consider right/proper, pawn (at a pawnshop)'.

history.meaning: fields of equal value -> match, face, ought to, act as (dāng); proper, fit (dàng)
work/serve as, when/at, ought (dāng); regard as, appropriate (dàng)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 当 (via 萌典)

当上.etymology: Resultative verb compound combining 当 (dāng, 'serve as, hold the role/post of') + 上 (complement of attainment 'successfully reach/assume'): 'become, land the role or post of'.

history.meaning: succeed in becoming; take up the role of

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 当上 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: at present, right now; Zen 'the here and now'
right now, at the very moment

当下.etymology: A temporal compound (當下 in traditional script) combining 当/當 (dāng, 'to face, match, be right at a point in time or space') and 下 (xià, 'beneath, under, the immediate point of time'). Popularized in Tang–Song Chan (Zen) Buddhist recorded sayings (語錄), where 當下 meant 'at the very instant of perception, right here and now' (as in 當下即是), it entered vernacular Chinese as an adverb ('instantly, on the spot') and modern Mandarin as a noun meaning 'the present moment'.

history.meaning: in that very instant of awakening; directly at the present moment (Chan Buddhist usage)
thereupon, immediately, on the spot (in vernacular fiction)
the present moment, right now, the current era or situation

morphemes.meaning: to face, be right at (a time or place)

当下.notes: Frequently used as a noun in reflective or media prose—e.g., 活在当下 ('live in the present moment') or 立足当下 ('ground oneself in the current reality').

当中.etymology: A locative compound (當中 in traditional script) composed of 当/當 (dāng, 'to be situated right at, directly facing') and 中 (zhōng, pictograph of a flagpole through the center, 'center, middle, interior'). Originally meaning 'right in the dead center' of a space, it broadened in vernacular Mandarin into a postpositional locative noun meaning 'in the midst of (a group or process), among'.

history.meaning: directly in the center or middle of a physical space
among (a group of people or things); in the middle or course of (an activity)

当中.notes: More conversational and rhythmic than single-character 中; placed after a noun or pronoun phrase: 在我们当中 ('among us') or 在节目制作当中 ('in the middle of show production').

rootFamily.gloss: on the spot, at the scene

cognates.meaning: that era; the current reign or generation
the present age; that historical period

当代.etymology: A modifier-head temporal compound (當代 in traditional script) combining 当/當 (dāng, 'the very, current, matching') and 代 (dài, originally 'to replace, succeed in turn', hence 'generation, dynasty, historical era'). In Classical and Imperial histories, 當代 meant 'the reigning dynasty or one's own generation'; in modern historiography and cultural criticism, it specifically designates the 'contemporary era' (as distinct from 近代 'early modern' and 现代 'modern').

history.meaning: that very dynasty or reign; one's own generation in imperial history
the contemporary era, present-day, living generation (especially in arts, literature, and society)

当代.notes: In Chinese cultural categorization, 当代 refers to the contemporary living era (e.g., 当代青年 'contemporary youth', 当代艺术 'contemporary art'), carrying a more immediate present-day sense than 现代 (modern).

rootFamily.gloss: back in those years, in that era

当众.etymology: A verb-object / prepositional compound functioning as an adverb (當眾 in traditional script), formed from 当/當 (dāng, 'to face directly, in the presence of') and 众/眾 (zhòng, originally three people 人 beneath an eye 目 or sun, 'a multitude, crowd, the public'). Literally 'facing the multitude', it has been used since Classical and vernacular Chinese to describe actions performed openly before everyone's eyes.

history.meaning: facing the crowd; openly before a gathering of people
in public, before everyone, in front of a crowd

morphemes.meaning: to face, in the presence of

当众.notes: Always functions adverbially before a verb: 当众道歉 ('apologize in public'), 当众宣布 ('announce before everyone'), or 当众出丑 ('make a fool of oneself in public').

rootFamily.gloss: face to face, to someone's face
the public, general audience, mass market

当初.etymology: A temporal compound (當初 in traditional script) combining 当/當 (dāng, 'right at the time of') and 初 (chū, an associative compound of 刀 'knife' and 衣 'garment', as cutting cloth is the first step in making clothes, hence 'beginning, outset'). Attested from Tang–Song poetry and vernacular narratives, it points back nostalgically or regretfully to 'that very beginning' when a relationship, venture, or decision first started.

history.meaning: at the very beginning of an affair or era; in former times
back at the start, originally, in the first place

morphemes.meaning: right at the time of, back at
beginning, outset (cutting cloth with a knife)

当初.notes: Famous in the set phrase 早知今日，何必当初 ('If I had known how things are today, why have acted that way in the first place?'), often used when reflecting on early career or personal choices.

cognates.meaning: right in front; for the time being, present

当前.etymology: A spatial-turned-temporal compound (當前 in traditional script) uniting 当/當 (dāng, 'to face directly, be situated at') and 前 (qián, originally 歬, depicting a foot止 on a boat舟 moving forward, hence 'in front, ahead, present'). Originally spatial ('directly before one's eyes'), it extended metaphorically to the temporal domain as 'the situation confronting us right now, at present'.

history.meaning: directly in front of one's eyes or person; in the immediate presence
at hand, before one; currently, in the present situation

当前.notes: Used both spatially in idioms like 大敌当前 ('with a formidable enemy right before us') and temporally in formal analysis like 当前形势 ('the current situation').

cognates.meaning: most pressing task of the moment

当务之急.etymology: A Classical Chinese four-character idiom (chengyu, 當務之急 in traditional script) originating in *Mencius* (*Mengzi*, Jinxin I: 知者無不知也，當務之為急 'The wise know all things, yet they treat what ought to be attended to right now as their urgent priority'). Structured as [当务 (what must currently be striven for) + 之 (genitive subordinator) + 急 (urgent matter)], it combines 当 ('ought, current'), 务/務 ('to devote effort to, task, affair'), 之 ('of'), and 急 ('urgent priority').

history.meaning: treating what ought to be attended to at present as the most urgent priority (*Mencius*)
the most urgent priority or pressing task of the moment

morphemes.meaning: ought to, at the present time

当务之急.notes: Typically serves as the subject or predicate nominal in strategic crisis discussions: 当务之急是稳住节目播出 ('The most urgent priority right now is to stabilize the show's broadcast').

rootFamily.gloss: pragmatic, practical, dealing with concrete matters

当回事.etymology: A colloquial Mandarin verb-object phrase (當回事 in traditional script) combining 当/當 (dāng / dàng, 'to treat as, regard as, count as'), the classifier 回 (huí, originally a spiral whirlpool, grammaticalized in vernacular Chinese as a measure word for occurrences, matters, or affairs), and 事 (shì, 'matter, affair, thing of consequence'), with ellipsis of the numeral 一 (yī, 'one'). Literally 'to treat [something] as a real matter', it means taking someone or something seriously.

history.meaning: to count or regard something as an affair worth heeding
to take seriously, treat as important (often used with 把 or in the negative 不当回事)

morphemes.meaning: piece, instance (of an affair or matter)

当回事.notes: Used overwhelmingly in the negative or with the disposal marker 把: 别太把自己当回事 ('Don't take yourself too seriously') or 他根本没把这规定当回事 ('He didn't take this rule seriously at all').

rootFamily.gloss: to treat as, regard as (slightly more formal)
how is it that...?, what's going on? (literally 'what affair')

cognates.meaning: on the spot, at the scene, immediately
on the spot, immediately at the scene
on the spot, right at the scene

当场.etymology: A prepositional-locative compound functioning as an adverb (當場 in traditional script), formed from 当/當 (dāng, 'right at, facing directly') and 场/場 (chǎng, composed of 土 'earth' and 易 phonetic, originally a leveled earthen clearing for sacrifices or threshing, hence 'arena, stage, scene of action'). Literally 'right at the scene or stage', it denotes doing something immediately on the spot without delay.

history.meaning: upon the performance stage or right at the arena of an event
on the spot, right then and there, at the scene

morphemes.meaning: arena, stage, site, scene of action

当场.notes: Highlights both spatial immediacy ('at the scene') and temporal immediacy ('without a moment's delay'): 当场拍板 ('make the final call on the spot') or 当场抓获 ('catch red-handed at the scene').

rootFamily.gloss: to wrap filming/taping, finish a shoot

cognates.meaning: to serve as a mandarin or official

当官.etymology: A verb-object compound (當官 in traditional script) pairing 当/當 (dāng, 'to bear, undertake, serve in the role of') with 官 (guān, originally depicting a roof 宀 over stacked mounds 㠯 representing an official hostel or government bureau, hence 'government official, magistrate, officeholder'). In imperial China it meant holding a state magistracy; in contemporary colloquial speech it extends to holding any managerial or executive title with authority over others.

history.meaning: to assume or hold an imperial government office or magistracy
to be a government official; colloquially, to hold a boss or executive title in an organization

morphemes.meaning: to serve as, act as, hold the post of

当官.notes: Separable verb-object (VO) compound (e.g., 当了三年官 'served as an official/boss for three years'). In corporate workplaces, teasing someone about 当官 means they have been promoted into management and out of hands-on creative work.

rootFamily.gloss: to be in charge, call the shots

cognates.meaning: in those years; that very year
that year; back in those days

当年.etymology: A modifier-head temporal compound (當年 in traditional script) combining 当/當 (dāng, 'that very, matching') and 年 (nián, originally 秊, depicting a person carrying harvested grain 禾, hence 'harvest cycle, year'). Depending on tone and context, dāngnián points back to 'those bygone years' (often one's prime or formative era), whereas dàngnián refers to 'that very same year'.

history.meaning: in one's prime years; in that very year or era of the past
back in those years, in the old days (dāngnián); that very same year (dàngnián)

当年.notes: Common in the nostalgic phrase 想当年 ('thinking back to those years') or 好汉不提当年勇 ('a true hero doesn't boast about past glories').

当心.etymology: Verb-object compound of 当 ('place right at, bear in') + 心 ('heart, mind'): originally 'keep at the center of one's mind/attention', and in Mandarin 'be careful, watch out!, take care'.

history.meaning: pay heed -> be careful, watch out

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 当心 (via 萌典)

当成.etymology: A verb-complement compound (當成 in traditional script) combining 当/當 (dāng / dàng, 'to match, equate, treat as') with the resultative complement 成 (chéng, 'to become, turn into, form'). By fusing the equative sense of 当 with the transformative resultative 成, the compound grammaticalized in vernacular Mandarin to mean 'to treat, regard, or mistakenly take X as Y'.

history.meaning: to equate with, count as, or take to be
to treat as, regard as, or mistake for (typically used in the 把...当成... construction)

morphemes.meaning: to equate, treat as, regard as
to become, form into, count as

当成.notes: Almost always appears in the disposal pattern 把 A 当成 B ('treat A as B', e.g., 把工作当成全部 'treat work as one's whole life') or passive 被当成 B ('be treated/mistaken as B').

rootFamily.gloss: to take seriously, treat as a real matter

cognates.meaning: at that time, in those days

当时.etymology: A modifier-head temporal noun (當時 in traditional script) composed of 当/當 (dāng, 'right at, matching, that very') and 时/時 (shí, combining 日 'sun/day' and 寺 phonetic, 'season, time, hour, moment'). Attested since the *Shijing* and *Shiji*, it anchors an event at the exact moment it occurred in the past ('at that time, back then'); with fourth tone on the first syllable (dàngshí), it means 'immediately, right at that very instant'.

history.meaning: at that time; during one's prime or when holding power in an era
at that moment, back then (dāngshí); right then and there (dàngshí)

当时.notes: Contrast 当时 ('at that specific time in the past') with 现在/当下 ('right now'); in storytelling and interviews, 当时 is the standard narrative anchor for recalling what happened at a key moment.

当枪使.etymology: A vivid colloquial serial verb / pivotal idiom (當槍使 in traditional script) structured as [当 (treat as) + 枪/槍 (spear/gun, weapon) + 使 (wield, deploy, use)]. Literally 'to use [someone] as a spear or gun', it draws on martial imagery where a hidden manipulator stays safe behind the scenes while provoking ahot-headed or naive front person to fire the shots and take the fallout—equivalent to the English 'use as a pawn, cat's-paw, or hired gun'.

history.meaning: to wield someone as a spear or gun; to manipulate someone into acting as one's front or cat's-paw in a conflict

morphemes.meaning: to wield, employ, make use of

当枪使.notes: Essential office-politics and media-drama idiom: 别被人当枪使了 ('Don't let yourself be used as someone else's pawn/hired gun') or 把媒体当枪使 ('use the media as a weapon to attack rivals').

rootFamily.gloss: manipulator who uses someone as a gun/front; ghostwriter/proxy
to walk right into the line of fire / become a target

当然.etymology: Compound adjective and modal adverb of 当 (dāng, 'ought to be, fitting') + 然 ('so, thus'): in Classical prose 'rightly so, as it ought to be', and in modern Mandarin the everyday word for 'of course, naturally, certainly'.

history.meaning: what is naturally right and fitting
of course; naturally; certainly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 当然 (via 萌典)

当着.etymology: A compound preposition (當著 in traditional script) formed from the spatial-relational verb 当/當 (dāng, 'to face directly, be in the presence of') suffixed with the continuous aspect marker 着/著 (zhe, originally 'to adhere, attach', grammaticalized in Middle and Early Mandarin to mark an ongoing posture or state). Together, 当着 means 'while facing / right in the presence of [someone]', typically followed by '...的面' ('someone's face').

history.meaning: facing directly toward; while in the immediate presence of
in front of, in the presence of, to someone's face (preposition)

morphemes.meaning: to face, confront, be in the presence of

当着.notes: Almost always frames a noun phrase ending in 的面 or 的人: 当着大家的面 ('in front of everyone') or 当着台长的面 ('right to the station director's face').
