感到.etymology: A resultative verb-complement compound (动补结构) composed of 感 (gǎn, 'to feel, to be affected internally', from phonetic 咸 xián over semantic 心 'heart-mind') and the resultative complement 到 (dào, 'to reach, to register'). Literally 'to feel and register [a sensation or emotion]', marking the onset or conscious registration of an inner emotional or physical state.

history.meaning: to be moved, to feel or respond to an external stimulus (*Book of Changes*, Classical Chinese)
to feel, to sense, to experience (a psychological or physical state)

morphemes.meaning: to feel, to sense, to be affected (咸 + 心)
to reach, to attain, to register consciously

感到.notes: More formal and strictly verbal than 感觉 or 觉得: 感到 is usually followed directly by a two-character emotional/mental adjective (感到骄傲 'feel proud', 感到抱歉 'feel sorry', 感到欣慰 'feel gratified') rather than a full opinion clause.

rootFamily.gloss: to feel, to sense; feeling, impression

感动.etymology: A classical compound (originally resultative/coordinative: 'to affect and stir into motion') combining 感 (gǎn, 'to touch/move the heart', composed of 咸 'all/bite' and 心 'heart') and 动/動 (dòng, 'to move, to stir'). Already attested in the *Book of Changes* (易经·咸卦: 圣人感人心而天下和平) and explicitly compounded as 感动 in Han-dynasty texts (*Liuxiang's Xinxu*, *Book of Han*), where sincerity in one's heart 'stirs and moves' Heaven or other people.

history.meaning: to stir and move (Heaven, spirits, or human hearts) through moral sincerity (*Book of Han*, Han Dynasty prose)
to move or touch emotionally (verb); emotionally moved or touched (adjective)

morphemes.meaning: to affect, to touch the heart (咸 + 心)
to move, to stir, to shake

感动.notes: Functions both as an adjective (我很感动, 'I am very touched') and as a transitive verb (他的故事感动了观众, 'His story moved the audience').

rootFamily.gloss: moving, touching (of a story or scene)
deeply moved, touched to the core
to be emotionally stirred, to have deep feelings

cognates.meaning: reception, sensitivity (as in 感受性 kanjusei, Sino-Japanese)

感受.etymology: A coordinative compound (联合式合成词) uniting 感 (gǎn, 'to sense, to be affected in the heart') and 受 (shòu, 'to receive, to take in, to undergo', originally a pictograph of two hands passing a boat/vessel 舟 between them). Literally 'to sense and take in internally', emphasizing the subjective, lived emotional experience or personal reception of an event, atmosphere, or work of art.

history.meaning: to be affected by and receive (physical/pathogenic influences in traditional medicine, or karmic sensations in Buddhist texts)
subjective emotional experience, personal feelings (noun); to experience deeply or take in with one's heart (verb)

morphemes.meaning: to feel, to be affected emotionally
to receive, to accept, to undergo

感受.notes: Unlike 感觉 (which can be a fleeting sensory impression or a casual 'I feel that...'), 感受 refers to deeper, internalized personal feelings and lived experience—e.g., 考虑别人的感受 ('consider other people's feelings') or 分享你的感受 ('share how you felt').

rootFamily.gloss: deep emotional stirring, reflections triggered by an experience

感怀.etymology: A classical poetic compound combining 感 (gǎn, 'to be stirred by emotion') and 怀/懷 (huái, 'bosom, inner heart, to cherish or recall in one's heart', originally depicting clothing 衣 enclosing a weeping eye 𥄉 over 心 'heart'). Famous as a genre title in Tang poetry (such as Li Bai's and Du Fu's *Ganhuai* 感怀 poems), it means either 'stirred emotions within one's bosom' or 'to recall and reflect upon past events with deep emotion'.

history.meaning: to have one's bosom stirred by circumstances; poetic reflections on life, history, or parting (Six Dynasties–Tang poetry, e.g., Li Bai, Zhang Jiuling)
to recall with deep emotion, to cherish fondly, or to reflect sentimentally on the past

morphemes.meaning: to be moved, to feel deeply
bosom, heart; to cherish in mind, to yearn for

感怀.notes: A high-register literary word (书面语) frequently used in tribute broadcasts, memoirs, and commemorative speeches (e.g., 感怀过去, 'recalling the past with deep emotion'). Everyday conversation uses 怀念 (huáiniàn, 'to miss/cherish the memory of').

rootFamily.gloss: to cherish the memory of, to miss fondly
feelings, lofty sentiment, ethos (a favorite buzzword in media/creative industries)
to sigh with emotion, to reflect wistfully

感情.etymology: A classical compound combining 感 (gǎn, 'emotional response to external things') and 情 (qíng, 'innate emotional disposition, affection, genuine feeling', from semantic 忄 'heart-mind' and phonetic 青 qīng). First attested in Six Dynasties and Tang texts (e.g., Zhang Yanyuan's *Lidai Minghua Ji* 历代名画记) for 'stirred emotional states', and later reinforced via Meiji Japanese 感情 (kanjō) as the general psychological noun for 'emotion', while also developing the distinctively Chinese relational sense of 'mutual affection, bond, or goodwill between people'.

history.meaning: stirring of the emotions or passions (Six Dynasties–Tang prose and Buddhist commentary)
(1) psychological emotion/sentiment; (2) interpersonal affection, attachment, or relational bond (Modern Mandarin)

morphemes.meaning: to feel, emotional response (咸 + 心)
emotion, affection, sentiment, bond (忄 + 青)

感情.notes: Unlike English 'emotion' (which in Mandarin psychology is 情绪 qíngxù), 感情 in everyday Chinese most often refers to the relational bond or affection between people—e.g., 培养感情 ('cultivate affection/rapport'), 伤感情 ('hurt a relationship/goodwill'), or 谈感情 ('talk about romance/personal loyalty').

cognates.meaning: to act on emotion rather than reason, to let personal feelings cloud judgment
cognates.word: 感情用事 (gam2 cing4 jung6 si6)

感情用事.etymology: A four-character idiom (成语) modeled on the classical construction 意气用事 (yìqì yòngshì, 'to handle affairs based on personal impulse/temper', attested in the *Book of Song* 宋书), substituting modern 感情 (gǎnqíng, 'personal emotions, sentimental attachment') as the adverbial instrument before 用事 (yòngshì, a Classical Chinese phrase meaning 'to manage affairs, to exercise authority, to act'). Literally 'to handle affairs by means of personal feelings [rather than objective reason or professional rules]'.

history.meaning: to govern or handle affairs driven by personal temper and pride (*Book of Song*, Southern Dynasties)
to let personal emotions or sentimental bias cloud one's professional judgment; to act on impulse/feelings

morphemes.meaning: to use, to employ, to exercise (authority/judgment)

感情用事.notes: A staple expression in workplace dramas like 幕后之王 when reminding executives or producers to stay objective and professional: 在工作上不能感情用事 ('You can't let personal feelings dictate your decisions at work').

rootFamily.gloss: to act on personal impulse or wounded pride (classical synonym)

感觉.etymology: A coordinative compound (联合式合成词) pairing 感 (gǎn, 'to sense, to be stimulated') and 觉/覺 (jué, 'to perceive, to awaken to, to become aware of'). First attested in Medieval Chinese philosophical essays (such as Fan Zhen's 范缜 5th-century *Shenmielun* 神灭论, contrasting sentient organisms that possess 感觉 with plants that lack it), and systematically re-employed in the late 19th century via Meiji Japanese 感覚 (kankaku) to translate Western psychological 'sensation / sense perception'. In contemporary spoken Mandarin, it also functions as an epistemic verb ('to feel that, to get the impression that').

history.meaning: sentient perception and awareness (Six Dynasties philosophy, Fan Zhen's *Shenmielun*)
sense perception, physical or psychological sensation (Meiji Japanese psychological loan into Early Modern Chinese)
sensation, feeling, vibe (noun); to feel, to have the impression that (verb)

morphemes.meaning: to feel, to respond to a stimulus (咸 + 心)
to perceive, to become aware, to sense

感觉.notes: Unique among the 感- family for functioning equally naturally as a countable noun (有一种奇怪的感觉, 'have a strange feeling'; 很有感觉, 'has a great vibe/chemistry') and as a casual verb interchangeable with 觉得 (我感觉他会来, 'I feel like he'll come').

rootFamily.gloss: to think, to feel that (subjective opinion/sensation)

感谢.etymology: A classical compound (sequential/coordinative: 'to feel moved inside and express thanks in words') combining 感 (gǎn, 'to feel moved by kindness in one's heart', compare 感恩) and 谢/謝 (xiè, 'to express in words, to acknowledge, to thank', composed of semantic 言 'speech' and phonetic 射 shè). Attested as early as the *Strategies of the Warring States* (战国策) and *Book of the Later Han* (后汉书), uniting inner gratitude (感) with verbal acknowledgment (谢).

history.meaning: to be moved by grace and express verbal acknowledgment (*Zhan Guo Ce*, *Book of the Later Han*)
to thank, to be grateful to (verb); gratitude, appreciation (noun)

morphemes.meaning: to feel moved, to appreciate inwardly (咸 + 心)
to thank, to acknowledge in words (言 speech + 射 phonetic)

感谢.notes: More formal and versatile than 谢谢 (xièxie): unlike 谢谢, 感谢 can be modified by degree adverbs (非常感谢 'thank you very much', 十分感谢) and can act as a noun (表示感谢 'express gratitude'). In showbiz and award speeches, 感谢 followed by a list of mentors and crew is standard protocol.

rootFamily.gloss: to feel grateful for kindness, thanksgiving/gratitude
to express thanks (especially with a gift or formal gesture)

cognates.meaning: to wish, to be willing; vow, wish

愿.etymology: In Simplified Chinese, 愿 merges two historically distinct characters: (1) 願 (yuàn, Old Chinese *ŋon-s, composed of semantic 页 'head' and phonetic 原 yuán 'spring/source'), originally meaning 'big head' in *Shuowen Jiezi* and universally used in Classical Chinese for 'to wish, to desire, to be willing, a solemn vow'; and (2) 愿 (yuàn, composed of 原 over 心 'heart-mind'), which in Classical Chinese meant 'sincere, honest, conscientious' (as in 恭敬忠愿). Modern simplified 愿 adopts the graphic form with 心 ('heart') to represent the meaning of 願 ('wish, be willing').

history.meaning: to wish, to hope, to be willing (Classical Chinese optative and volitional verb, e.g., 臣願 'Your servant wishes/is willing...')
solemn vow or aspiration (e.g., 许愿 'make a wish/vow', 心愿 'heart's desire')
to be willing (short for 愿意), to wish/hope (especially in optative blessings like 愿你平安 'May you be safe')

morphemes.meaning: heart, mind, inner wish (replacing traditional 页 'head' in simplified script)

愿.notes: As a standalone monosyllabic word in modern Chinese, 愿 either introduces an elevated blessing/toast ('May...': 愿我们合作成功, 'May our collaboration succeed!') or appears in negated/fixed expressions like 不愿 ('unwilling') and 宁愿 ('would rather'); in ordinary speech, 'willing' is disyllabic 愿意 (yuànyì).

rootFamily.gloss: to be willing, to wish to

愿意.etymology: Verb-object/coordinative compound of 愿 (願, 'wish, desire sincerely') + 意 ('wish, intention'): 'be willing to, wish, want, ready to'.

history.stage: Han–Six Dynasties Buddhist & vernacular Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: be willing to; wish

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 愿意 (via 萌典)

慈善.etymology: A coordinative compound (联合式合成词) combining 慈 (cí, 'tender love, maternal compassion, kindness toward the vulnerable', from 兹 zī phonetic over 心 'heart-mind', paired in Buddhism with 悲 as *maitrī* 'loving-kindness') and 善 (shàn, 'virtuous, good, charitable deeds', originally depicting sheep 羊 and speech 誩, denoting auspiciousness and moral goodness). Attested in the *Book of魏* (魏书) for 'compassionate and virtuous character', it shifted in the late 19th and 20th centuries (alongside Japanese 慈善 jizen) to denote organized 'charity, philanthropy, and public welfare'.

history.meaning: compassionate and kindhearted in character (*Book of Wei*, Tang–Song biographical prose)
charity, philanthropy, organized relief for the needy (e.g., 慈善机构 'charitable organization', 慈善晚会 'charity gala')

morphemes.meaning: compassionate, tender, loving (especially toward those in need)

慈善.notes: In contemporary media and entertainment circles (like 幕后之王), 慈善 constantly appears in collocations such as 慈善晚宴 ('charity gala dinner'), 慈善演出 ('benefit concert/show'), and 做慈善 ('do charity work'). For a person's kind facial expression, use 慈祥 (cíxiáng) or 和善 (héshàn) rather than 慈善.

rootFamily.gloss: compassion, mercy (originally Buddhist loving-kindness and compassion)

慌.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 忄 (心, 'heart, mind') + 荒 (huāng, 'barren, overgrown, confused'): 'flustered, panicked, nervous, in a flurry; (as a post-verbal complement with 得) unbearable (累得慌)'.

history.meaning: flustered; panicked; nervous; (with 得) awfully

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 慌 (via 萌典)

慎重.etymology: A classical coordinative adjective (联合式形容词) combining 慎 (shèn, 'careful, circumspect, heedful', composed of semantic 忄 'heart-mind' and phonetic 真 zhēn) and 重 (zhòng, 'weighty, serious, grave, not frivolous', as in 庄重 'solemn' and 稳重 'steady'). Already attested in the *Zuo Zhuan* (左传·襄公二十五年) and *Book of the Later Han* (后汉书), where acting with 慎重 means treating decisions with serious weight and circumspection rather than rashness.

history.meaning: circumspect and grave in conduct or statecraft (*Zuo Zhuan*, *Book of the Later Han*)
cautious, prudent, deliberate (especially when making major decisions or public statements)

morphemes.meaning: careful, heedful, circumspect (忄 heart + 真 phonetic)

慎重.notes: Unlike 小心 (xiǎoxīn, 'watch out / be careful' against physical accidents like slipping or breaking a glass), 慎重 refers to solemn prudence in high-stakes choices, contracts, or personnel decisions—most famously in the set phrase 慎重考虑 ('give prudent/serious consideration').

rootFamily.gloss: steady, staid, composed and reliable in manner

慢.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 忄 (心, 'heart, attitude') + 曼 (màn, 'drawn out, long'). In Classical Chinese, 慢 meant 'negligent, remiss, disrespectful, haughty' (怠慢, 傲慢); from the Six Dynasties and Tang period onward, 'unhurried/lax' became the primary Mandarin word for 'slow (opposite of 快 'fast'); wait/hold on'.

history.meaning: remiss; negligent; arrogant
slow; unhurried

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 慢 (via 萌典)

慢慢.etymology: Reduplication of the adjective/adverb 慢 ('slow'): 'slowly, unhurriedly, take one's time, gradually'.

history.stage: Tang–Song poetry & vernacular to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: slowly; unhurriedly; gradually

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 慢慢 (via 萌典)

慢点.etymology: A colloquial Mandarin modifier-complement phrase composed of 慢 (màn, originally 'remiss, negligent, arrogant' in Classical Chinese from heart radical 忄 + phonetic 曼 màn 'extended, drawn out', evolving in Middle Chinese to 'unhurried, slow') followed by the diminutive quantifier 點 / 点 (diǎn, 'a dot, a little bit', often pronounced with erhua as diǎnr). Literally 'a bit slower', it grammaticalized in spoken Mandarin into a polite imperative urging caution or unhurried action ('slow down; be careful; take your time').

history.meaning: negligent, remiss, haughty; unhurried
a little slower; take your time, be careful

morphemes.meaning: a little bit, somewhat (diminutive degree marker)

慢点.notes: Often pronounced with retroflex erhua as màndiǎnr (慢点儿) in northern Mandarin; used both literally ('walk/drive more slowly') and as a warm parting or cautionary phrase ('take care').

rootFamily.gloss: arrogant, haughty (retaining the Classical sense of 慢)

慢用.etymology: Polite dining formula combining 慢 ('slowly, take your time') + 用 ('partake of food/drink', polite verb for 'eat/drink'): 'please enjoy your meal, take your time eating'.

history.stage: Ming–Qing polite vernacular to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: take your time enjoying your meal; bon appétit

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 慢用 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: take care on your way out; goodbye (said by host)

慢走.etymology: An adverbial-verb (modifier-head) polite farewell formula combining 慢 (màn, 'slowly, unhurriedly', from Classical Chinese 'lax, unhurried') and 走 (zǒu, which in Old and Classical Chinese meant 'to run, to flee', before shifting in medieval vernacular Chinese to 'to walk, to leave, to depart', displacing 行 xíng). Literally 'walk slowly as you leave', it encodes traditional Chinese hospitality etiquette: the host wishes that the departing guest is reluctant to leave and watches their step on the road.

history.meaning: walk slowly; travel safely (literary and southern Sinitic host's farewell)
walk slowly; take care on your way out (host to departing guest)

慢走.notes: Strictly asymmetrical in etiquette: 慢走 is only ever said by the person staying behind (a host, receptionist, or restaurant staff) to someone who is leaving, often paired with 不送 ('please excuse me for not seeing you all the way out').

rootFamily.gloss: take one's time savoring food/drink ('eat/drink slowly')

cognates.meaning: to bend, to yield; humiliation, grievance (cognate of 屈)

憋屈.etymology: A colloquial northern Mandarin coordinative/resultative compound uniting 憋 (biē, 'to suppress, to hold back breath or emotion, to stifle', phono-semantic compound with 敝 bì as phonetic and 心/火 in variant developments) and 屈 (qū, 'bent, crooked; wronged, unjustly treated', from 尸 'body' + 出, originally depicting a crouched body or tail). Together they vividize the psychological and somatic sensation of having one's anger, talent, or grievance bottled up in the chest with no outlet for redress.

history.meaning: to bend, crouch; to suffer wrong or injustice
stifled and wronged; pent-up, aggrieved, frustrated

morphemes.meaning: to hold back, stifle, suppress, suffocate

憋屈.notes: Pronounced with a neutral tone on the second syllable (biēqu); frequently used in workplace and drama contexts when an employee or producer has to swallow an unfair blame or compromise without being able to speak out (受憋屈).

懂.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 忄 (心, 'heart, mind') + 董 (dǒng, 'supervise, set straight'): originally 'confused in mind (懵懂)', then in Song–Ming vernacular inverted/stabilized as the primary everyday verb for 'understand, comprehend, know'.

history.meaning: understand in mind; comprehend; know

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 懂 (via 萌典)

懂行.etymology: Verb-object compound used as an adjective and verb, combining 懂 ('understand, know inside out') + 行 (read háng, 'trade, profession, line of business'): 'know the ropes, be an expert/insider in the trade'.

history.meaning: know the trade; be knowledgeable in a field

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 懂行 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: dim, dull, confused (kanji reading of 懵)

懵.etymology: A phono-semantic character (懵, mēng, also mǒng in literary readings) formed from the heart radical 忄 (xīn, 'mind, cognition') and the phonetic-semantic component  / 蒙 (méng, 'covered, shrouded, overgrown, dark'). Attested in the *Erya* and *Guangyun* (Middle Chinese *muwngX* / *muwngH*), it originally meant 'mentally darkened, ignorant, muddled' (as in 懵懂懵懂). In modern colloquial Mandarin (pronounced first tone mēng), it evolved into a dynamic state verb meaning 'to be momentarily stunned, dazed, or blank-minded from shock'.

history.meaning: darkened in mind, ignorant, bewildered (attested in Erya & Guangyun)
naive, muddle-headed, half-comprehending
to be stunned, dazed, or mentally blank from surprise

morphemes.meaning: dazed, stunned, mentally blank or bewildered

懵.notes: In spoken Mandarin, the single verb takes first tone mēng (e.g., 我看懵了 'I watched it and was left totally baffled', 一脸懵逼 'a completely blank/stunned expression'), whereas in the literary compound 懵懂 ('naive, muddle-headed') it is pronounced third tone měng.

戏.etymology: Simplified as 戏 from traditional  / 戲 (xì, Old Chinese *ŋ̊rals*, Middle Chinese *xjeH*), a compound ideogram-phonetic graph combining 䖍 / 虍 (hū, tiger stripes / ritual stand phonetic) and 戈 (gē, 'halberd, weapon'). In pre-Qin Classical Chinese, 戲 denoted mock martial combat, weapon-play, or jesting sport, before broadening in Han–Tang times to acrobatic spectacles (百戲 bǎixì), theatrical performances, opera (戲曲), and in modern film/TV industry parlance, any dramatic production, scene, or acting performance.

history.meaning: martial sport, mock combat; jest, play, frolic
theatrical spectacle, stage play, traditional Chinese opera
drama, film/TV production, acting scene, dramatic tension

morphemes.meaning: play, drama, theatrical performance, scene; to jest

戏.notes: In Chinese film and television production (such as *Behind the Scenes*), 戏 means not just 'a play/show' as a whole, but also 'a specific scene' (一场戏), 'acting skill' (有戏 / 没戏), or 'dramatic conflict' (加戏 'add scenes/embellish drama').

rootFamily.gloss: screen time, share of scenes in a script

cognates.meaning: actor's share of scenes, screen time, role weight

戏份.etymology: A modern Sinitic modifier-head compound originating in Cantonese and Mandarin theatrical/cinematic jargon, combining 戲 / 戏 (xì, 'play, drama, dramatic scenes') and 份 (fèn, 'allotted share, portion, quota', a differentiated graph of 分 fēn 'to divide' with the person radical 亻). Literally 'one's allotted portion of the drama', it originally referred to the weight and number of scenes assigned to an opera or film actor, and now denotes both screen time in a production and figurative 'importance/weight' in a plot or project.

history.meaning: an actor's allotted scenes and role weight in an opera or screenplay
screen time, share of scenes; narrative weight or prominence in an event

戏份.notes: A quintessential showbiz term in Chinese entertainment circles: 抢戏 ('scene-stealing'), 加戏 ('padding one's screen time'), and 戏份很重 ('having a heavy/pivotal role in the script').

戏剧性.etymology: A modern polymorphemic noun/adjective formed from the coordinative compound 戲劇 / 戏剧 (xìjù, 'drama, theater', joining 戲 xì 'stage play, performance' and 劇 jù 'intense, severe; theatrical play', originally with the knife radical 刂 indicating sharpness/intensity) plus the abstract nominalizing/adjectival suffix -性 (xìng, 'nature, quality, -ness, -ity', productively expanded in late 19th–20th century Sino-Japanese translation vocabulary to render European '-tic / -ity' derivatives such as English *dramatic*).

history.meaning: theatrical play, stage drama (attested from Tang–Song vernacular literature)
dramatic nature, theatricality; dramatic, full of sudden twists

戏剧性.notes: In Mandarin grammar, nouns ending in -性 often modify other nouns with 的 (e.g., 戏剧性的转折 'a dramatic plot twist') or follow 具有 / 富有 ('possess dramatic tension': 很有戏剧性).

成.etymology: Ancient character attested on Shang oracle bones and Zhou bronzes combining 戊/戈 ('halberd/axe') + 丁 (dīng/chéng phonetic, 'nail/completeness'): 'accomplish, complete, succeed; become, turn into; established/ready-made; one-tenth (10%); okay/all right!'.

history.meaning: pacify/complete -> accomplish, succeed, become
succeed; become; complete; one-tenth; okay!

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 成 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to become, to constitute (kanji reading of 成為)

成为.etymology: A disyllabic verb-complement / serial verb compound formed from 成 (chéng, Old Chinese *deŋ*, 'to complete, accomplish, take shape', originally depicting a weapon/axe 戊 with phonetic 丁) and 為 / 为 (wéi, Old Chinese *ɢʷaj*, 'to make, to act as, to become, to be'). In Classical Chinese, 成 and 為 frequently occurred adjacent to each other as separate verbs ('to develop and become X'), before lexicalizing into the modern Mandarin disyllabic copular verb 成为 ('to become, to turn into').

history.meaning: to take shape and act as / become (two adjacent monosyllabic verbs)
to become, to turn into, to grow into

morphemes.meaning: to be, to act as, to become

成为.notes: Unlike simple 成 (which often acts as a resultative complement, e.g., 变成), 成为 is a formal disyllabic transitive verb that directly takes a noun phrase object (e.g., 成为一名制作人 'become a producer') and never takes 了 between its two characters.

cognates.meaning: to close a deal, clinch a transaction

成交.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound combining 成 (chéng, 'to complete, finalize, bring to fruition') and 交 (jiāo, 'to cross, exchange, hand over, trade', originally an oracle-bone pictograph of a person with crossed legs). Literally 'to complete an exchange or handover', it arose in traditional Chinese mercantile language to denote closing a commercial transaction or finalizing a contract, and is also used as a standalone interjection ('Deal!').

history.meaning: to cross legs; to exchange, associate, hand over mutually
to conclude a trade or business transaction; 'Deal!'

成交.notes: Used both as an intransitive verb in business/negotiation contexts (成交量 'trading volume', 成交价 'closing price') and as a crisp spoken exclamation when shaking hands on an agreement ('成交！' — 'Deal! / Sold!').

成功.etymology: Originally a Classical Chinese verb-object (VO) compound composed of 成 (chéng, 'to complete, bring to fulfillment') and 功 (gōng, 'meritorious work, labour, achievement', from 工 gōng 'work, tool' + 力 lì 'strength'). Attested in the *Book of Documents* (*Shangshu*) and *Analects* in the literal sense 'to bring a public work or meritorious task to completion', it gradually lexicalized across East Asian Sinitic languages into an intransitive verb, noun, and adjective meaning 'to succeed; success; successful'.

history.meaning: to complete a public work or meritorious task (attested in Shangshu)
to achieve success, succeed; success; successful

morphemes.meaning: to complete, accomplish, bring to fruition

成功.notes: Unusually flexible in part of speech in modern Mandarin: it functions as a verb (节目成功了 'the show succeeded'), a noun (取得成功 'achieve success'), and an attributive/predicative adjective (非常成功的制作人 'a very successful producer').

成就.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative compound uniting 成 (chéng, 'to complete, perfect, bring into being') and 就 (jiù, 'to approach, reach, accomplish, consummate', originally depicting approaching a high tower 京 + 尤). Attested from Han-dynasty histories (*Shiji*, *Hanshu*) onward, it meant both 'to bring something/someone to fulfillment' (transitive verb) and 'that which is accomplished' (noun: 'major achievement, attainment').

history.meaning: to bring to completion, cultivate, fulfill (attested in Han texts)
major achievement, accomplishment (noun); to help fulfill or make someone great (verb)

成就.notes: Besides its common noun sense ('achievement', as in 成就感 'sense of accomplishment'), 成就 remains active in elevated prose and media dialogue as a transitive verb meaning 'to make [someone/something] what they are' (e.g., 这部戏成就了他 'This drama made his career').

rootFamily.gloss: take up a post; attain a position

成熟.etymology: A coordinative/sequential compound joining 成 (chéng, 'to reach full form, complete growth') and 熟 (shú, colloquially shóu, 'cooked through; ripe, fully grown', originally written 孰 depicting a person offering a sacrificial lamb 享, later acquiring the fire radical 灬 to distinguish 'cooked/ripe' from the interrogative pronoun 'who/which'). Originally an agricultural term in Han–Tang texts for crops and fruits ripening to harvest, it extended metaphorically to human psychological maturity, seasoned professional skill, and well-developed plans.

history.meaning: (of grain or fruit) to grow to full ripeness and be ready for harvest
ripe; psychologically mature, seasoned, fully developed (of people, plans, or markets)

morphemes.meaning: to complete growth, reach full form

成熟.notes: While 熟 alone has a colloquial reading shóu when talking about ripe fruit or cooked food, in the disyllabic compound 成熟 ('mature, seasoned, well-developed') standard Mainland pronunciation strictly requires shú (chéngshú).

cognates.meaning: finished film/video cut; developed photographic slide/reel

成片.etymology: A modern modifier-head compound formed from 成 (chéng, here functioning as an attributive participle 'completed, finished, ready-made', as in 成品 chéngpǐn 'finished product') and 片 (piàn, originally 'a split wood plank or flat slice' from half of the tree graph 木, extended in 20th-century photography, cinema, and television to mean 'photographic negative, film reel, video programme'). In film and TV production, 成片 designates the final edited, color-graded, and sound-mixed master cut ready for broadcast, contrasted with 样片 (dailies/rough cut) or 素材 (raw footage).

history.meaning: forming a continuous expanse or stretch (VO: 成 + 片 'flat stretch')
finished film/video master cut ready for release (modifier-head: 'completed + film/programme')

成片.notes: Watch out for a homographic structure split: in media production (as in *Behind the Scenes*), 成片 is a noun meaning 'the finished master cut' (often pronounced chéngpiān or chéngpiàn), whereas in general descriptions (成片的森林), 成片 is a verb-object modifier meaning 'in contiguous stretches / by the sheet'.

rootFamily.gloss: sample reel, rough cut, pilot episode
film/TV producer (literally 'person who makes the film/programme')

cognates.meaning: establishment, formation, coming into existence; holding true

成立.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative compound combining 成 (chéng, 'to complete, form, come to fruition') and 立 (lì, 'to stand upright, set up, establish', an oracle-bone ideogram of a person 大 standing firmly on the ground 一). In pre-modern Chinese (*Analects*, *Book of Rites*), 成立 referred to a person reaching adulthood and establishing their moral character or career; in modern East Asian usage (reinforced by Meiji-era Sino-Japanese legal and logical terminology), it denotes both 'to found/establish an organization' and '(of a theory, contract, or argument) to hold water / be valid'.

history.meaning: to reach personal maturity and establish oneself in society (Classical Chinese)
to found or establish (an organization); to be valid or tenable (of an argument or contract)

morphemes.meaning: to form, complete, bring into being
to stand, set up, establish, found

成立.notes: Has two distinct modern syntactic uses: transitive/unaccusative for organizations (成立新部门 'establish a new department'; 公司成立于2015年 'the company was founded in 2015') and intransitive for logical/legal validity (这个理由不成立 'this excuse/argument does not hold water').

rootFamily.gloss: establish, set up (a system, diplomatic ties, or trust)
establish, set up (an institution, prize, or post)
stand on one's own feet; independent

成败.etymology: An antonymic coordinative compound (反义并列复合词) pairing 成 (chéng, 'to succeed, accomplish, bring to completion') and 败 / 敗 (bài, 'to ruin, be defeated, fail', originally depicting striking 攵 a cowrie vessel/cauldron 貝/鼎 to smash it). Attested in Warring States and Han historical and military texts (such as Zhuge Liang's *Chu Shi Biao*: 成敗利鈍 'success or failure, advantage or setback'), the juxtaposition of opposite poles creates an abstract noun meaning 'the outcome of success versus failure'.

history.meaning: success and/or failure; victory or defeat (attested in Warring States & Han prose)
success or failure, the decisive outcome of an endeavor

成败.notes: Frequently appears in aphorisms and high-stakes business/production idioms such as 细节决定成败 ('details determine success or failure') and 不以成败论英雄 ('do not judge heroes solely by whether they succeeded or failed'). Note the Japanese false friend 成敗 (*seibai*), which shifted in samurai usage to mean 'punishment/execution'.

成都.etymology: Historic capital of Sichuan province, named in the Warring States period (after the phrase in the records of King Tai of Zhou: 一年成聚，二年成邑，三年成都 'in one year it became a settlement, in two years a town, in three years a capital'): 成 ('become, form into') + 都 ('capital city').

history.meaning: Chengdu (capital of Shu / Sichuan, kept the same name for over 2,300 years)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 成都 (via 萌典)

成长.etymology: A coordinative developmental compound uniting 成 (chéng, 'to form, develop toward completion') and 長 / 长 (zhǎng, rising tone, Old Chinese *traŋʔ*, 'to grow, increase, mature; elder', originally a pictograph of a person with long hair holding a walking staff). Attested in Classical Chinese (*Guanzi*, *Book of Rites*) for the biological growth of plants and living beings to maturity, it expanded in modern Mandarin and Sino-Japanese to encompass psychological, professional, and corporate growth ('personal growth; career development').

history.meaning: (of crops, animals, or youths) to grow up toward full size and maturity
to grow up, mature; personal, artistic, or organizational growth and development

成长.notes: Always pronounced chéngzhǎng (with the third-tone verbal reading zhǎng 'to grow', never cháng 'long'). Unlike 生长 (biological growth of plants/organisms), 成长 emphasizes developmental maturation of people, characters, teams, or enterprises.

rootFamily.gloss: increase, grow (of economy, data, or metrics)

我.etymology: First-person singular pronoun ('I, me'), attested since Late Shang oracle-bone inscriptions, where the graph depicted a notched polearm before being borrowed phonetically for the first-person pronoun. In Classical Chinese texts such as the Classic of Poetry (Shijing) and Analects, 我 already serves unchanged as both subject 'I' and object 'me'.

history.meaning: first-person pronoun 'I, we, me'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 我 (via 萌典)

我们.etymology: First-person plural pronoun ('we, us'), combining 我 ('I') with the human plural suffix 们 (men). Plural markers written 弭, 伟, 懣, and finally 們 appear in Song and Yuan vernacular literature to form collective personal pronouns.

history.meaning: first-person plural 'we, us'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 我們 (via 萌典)

我的.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 我的. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 我的 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 我的 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 我的 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 我的. The etymology of 我的 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 我的
middle form of 我的
modern form of 我的

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 我的

cognates.meaning: acting strictly as one pleases, sticking to one's old ways
doing things one's own way regardless of others

我行我素.etymology: A four-character Classical Chinese idiom (*chengyu*) condensed from the *Doctrine of the Mean* (*Zhongyong* 《中庸》, chapter 14): 「君子素其位而行，不願乎其外」 ('The noble person acts in accordance with their present station [素, 'what is plain, original, or habitual to oneself'] and does not covet what lies outside it'). In late imperial and modern usage, this was recast into the parallel subject-verb-object pattern 我行我素 ('I practice my own habitual way') to describe someone who persists in doing things strictly their own way, impervious to outside criticism or convention.

history.form: 素其位而行 (sù qí wèi ér xíng)
history.meaning: to act in accordance with one's present/plain station without ambition beyond it (Zhongyong)

history.form: 我行我素 (wǒ xíng wǒ sù)
history.meaning: to follow one's own accustomed way regardless of what others say or do

morphemes.meaning: to practice, carry out, act upon
one's habitual, plain, or original way (originally 'undyed raw silk')

我行我素.notes: Can carry either a mildly critical nuance ('stubbornly aloof, ignoring team rules') or an admiring one ('uncompromisingly authentic, refusing to pander'), which is how maverick creative directors like Chun Yu are often described in *Behind the Scenes*.

rootFamily.gloss: act arbitrarily, go one's own way (stronger pejorative synonym)

戒指.etymology: Originally a verb-object compound turning into a noun, combining 戒 (jiè, 'to warn, guard against, abstain, observe a precept', an ideogram of two hands 廾 holding a halberd 戈 on guard) and 指 (zhǐ, 'finger', from 手 'hand' + phonetic 旨). In ancient court and domestic custom (recorded in Han–Tang notes and poetry as 指環 or 戒止), women and officials wore small bands on their fingers as tactile reminders (戒) regarding palace scheduling, pregnancy/menstruation taboos, or personal conduct; the term subsequently generalized to any ornamental or betrothal finger ring.

history.meaning: finger-ring worn as a token or courtly reminder/restraint
finger ring (originally a 'finger-reminder', later any jewellery or wedding ring)

morphemes.meaning: to warn, guard against, remind, observe a vow

戒指.notes: Pronounced with a neutral tone on the second syllable in standard Mandarin (jièzhi) and takes the classifier 枚 (méi, formal/romantic, e.g., 一枚钻戒 'a diamond ring') or 个 (gè, colloquial).鑽戒 (zuànjiè) is its common blend with 钻石 ('diamond').

rootFamily.gloss: diamond ring (blend of 钻石 + 戒指)

或者.etymology: Disjunctive conjunction and adverb originally formed in Classical Chinese (Mencius, Zuozhuan) from indefinite pronoun 或 ('someone, some') + nominalizer 者 ('one who') = 'someone, perhaps'. In Medieval and Modern Mandarin it evolved into the conjunction 'or (in declarative statements and possibilities)' and adverb 'perhaps, maybe'.

history.meaning: someone; perhaps
or (in statements); perhaps

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 或者 (via 萌典)

或许.etymology: A modal adverbial compound joining 或 (huò, Old Chinese *ɡʷɯːɡ*, originally the graph for 'walled state' 國 before acquiring the indefinite pronoun and epistemic sense 'someone; perhaps, it may be that') and 許 / 许 (xǔ, 'to allow, grant, admit as possible; approximately'). Combining the classical epistemic particle 或 ('perchance') with 許 ('granting the possibility'), 或許 crystallized in post-classical and modern Chinese as a slightly more literary counterpart to 也许 ('perhaps, maybe, possibly').

history.meaning: someone; perhaps, perchance, it may be that (Classical epistemic particle)
perhaps, maybe, quite possibly

morphemes.meaning: to allow, grant as possible, estimate

或许.notes: Synonymous with 也许 (yěxǔ) and 可能 (kěnéng), but 或许 carries a slightly more reflective, narrative, or written register — very common in script voiceovers, subtitles, and thoughtful dialogue.

cognates.meaning: war potential, fighting strength, valuable asset to a team
fighting power, combat capability, team strength

战力.etymology: A modifier-head compound and contraction of 戰鬥力 / 战斗力 (zhàndòulì), combining 戰 / 战 (zhàn, 'battle, warfare, to fight', from phonetic 單 dān 'hunting weapon/shield' + 戈 gē 'halberd') and 力 (lì, 'strength, power, capability', an oracle-bone pictograph of a sinew or plowshare). Reinforced in modern Mandarin by Japanese *senryoku* (戦力) and gaming/esports culture, it denotes both literal military combat power and the execution capacity or competitive strength of a workplace team or individual.

history.meaning: military combat strength, fighting capacity of troops
combat power; competitive execution power of a team or professional

战力.notes: In contemporary Chinese workplace, variety-show, and gaming slang, 战力 (or 战斗力) is constantly used metaphorically for how much high-pressure work a person or production crew can crank out (e.g., 战力爆表 'execution power off the charts').

战功赫赫.etymology: A four-character subject-predicate idiom (*chengyu*) composed of the modifier-head noun 戰功 / 战功 (zhàngōng, 'military merit, battle achievements', from 戰 'war, battle' + 功 'meritorious service') followed by the reduplicated ideophonic adjective 赫赫 (hèhè, 'fiery red, radiant, illustrious, awe-inspiring', where 赫 doubles the graph 赤 chì 'fiery red' to intensify brilliance and renown, attested in the *Book of Odes* 《詩經·大雅》: 赫赫師尹). Literally 'one's battle merits shine radiantly', it describes someone with a dazzling track record of victories or career triumphs.

history.meaning: blazing, radiant, illustrious, awe-inspiring (attested in Shijing)

history.form: 戰功赫赫 / 战功赫赫 (zhàngōng hèhè)
history.meaning: covered in battle glory; boasting an illustrious record of achievements

战功赫赫.notes: In modern corporate and media storytelling, 战功赫赫 is frequently applied to veteran executives, star producers, or sales directors who have a long list of blockbuster projects or market victories under their belt.

rootFamily.gloss: illustrious, prestigious, grand (of fame or family background)

战场.etymology: A modifier-head locative compound formed from 戰 / 战 (zhàn, 'battle, warfare, combat') and 場 / 场 (chǎng, 'flat open ground, ceremonial arena, site', from 土 tǔ 'earth, ground' + phonetic 易 yáng). Attested in Tang frontier poetry and historical chronicles (such as Li Hua's famous prose piece 《弔古戰場文》 'Lament for an Ancient Battlefield'), it denotes a literal military battleground and, by pervasive modern metaphor, any fiercely competitive arena such as a live broadcast control room, ratings war, or business market.

history.meaning: open ground where armies clash; military battlefield (attested in Tang literature)
battlefield; fiercely competitive arena (commerce, media ratings, exams)

战场.notes: Very frequently used metaphorically in Chinese workplace dramas (e.g., 商场如战场 'the business world is a battlefield'; 主战场 'the main arena of competition'). Note that 场 is pronounced third tone chǎng here.

rootFamily.gloss: on-site, live scene, filming set or studio floor

战略.etymology: A modifier-head compound joining 戰 / 战 (zhàn, 'war, campaign') and 略 (lüè, 'boundary line, territorial plan, stratagem, outline', originally 田 'field' + phonetic 各 gè 'to mark out land boundaries', whence 'to plan out, overarching scheme'). First attested in third-century Chinese historical texts (such as司馬彪 Sima Biao's prose title 《戰略》 cited in the *三国志* commentaries) for military grand strategy, it was revitalized in the late 19th century via Meiji Japanese *senryaku* (戦略, translating English/German *strategy* / *Strategie*) to cover military, national, and corporate strategy.

history.meaning: military grand stratagem and campaign planning (attested in 3rd c. Jin dynasty)

history.form: 戦略 (senryaku) → 戰略 / 战略 (zhànlüè)
history.meaning: overarching military, political, or corporate strategy (contrasted with 戰術 'tactics')

战略.notes: Always contrasted with 战术 (zhànshù, 'tactics'): 战略 refers to long-term, big-picture positioning (e.g., 战略合作伙伴 'strategic partner', 战略布局 'strategic layout'), while 战术 refers to concrete operational maneuvers.

cognates.meaning: combat unit, squadron, task force (popularized in Sentai genres)

战队.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 戰 / 战 (zhàn, 'battle, competition, combat') and 隊 / 队 (duì, 'military squad, file of soldiers, team', originally 阜 'mound/rampart' + 队 'group of people marching'). Historically a military term for a combat detachment or air/naval squadron (analogous to Japanese *sentai* 戦隊), 战队 surged in 21st-century Mainland Chinese media via esports and televised reality/singing competitions (such as *The Voice of China* and *Behind the Scenes*) to mean a mentor-led 'competition team' or 'squad'.

history.meaning: military combat detachment; air or naval squadron
esports roster; competition team led by a mentor/producer on a reality or talent show

战队.notes: Do not confuse with its exact homophone 站队 (zhànduì, 'to line up behind a faction / pick sides in office politics'), which is also ubiquitous in workplace dramas! In variety show contexts, 战队 (with 战 'battle') means a mentor's 'competition squad'.

rootFamily.gloss: team, collective group (in business or production)
troops, army unit,隊伍; rank and file

cognates.meaning: to cut, sever, intercept (kanji reading of 截)

截.etymology: A phono-semantic compound (截, jié, Old Chinese *dzeːd*, Middle Chinese *dzet*) combining 戈 ('halberd, cutting weapon', embedded in the 哉 component) and 隹 ('short-tailed bird'). Attested in the *Book of Odes* (*Shijing*) and *Zuo Zhuan*, its core meaning is 'to cut off neatly, sever cleanly (like slicing a bird or timber)'. From 'cutting across a path or stream', it developed the dynamic verbal senses 'to intercept, block midway, capture (a signal, ball, or fleeing target)' and 'a severed section/chunk' (as a classifier).

history.meaning: to cut off neatly, sever; neatly arranged (attested in Shijing)
to intercept, stop midway, cut off; a section or length (classifier)

morphemes.meaning: to cut off, sever, intercept, capture midway; a section

截.notes: Extremely productive in modern media and tech compounds: 截图 (jiétú, 'take a screenshot' — literally 'cut/capture an image'), 截稿 (jiégǎo, 'copy deadline'), 截止 (jiézhǐ, 'cut-off deadline'), and 截留 ('intercept and retain funds/resources').

rootFamily.gloss: close off, deadline, up to (a time)

cognates.meaning: to intercept someone else's winning tile in mahjong; to poach a deal/partner

截胡.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound originating in Chinese mahjong terminology, combining 截 (jié, 'to intercept, cut off midway') and 胡 / 和 (hú, 'to complete a winning hand in mahjong', a vernacular graphical substitution for 和 hé/hú 'harmonious completion of sets'). In mahjong, when two players are waiting on the same discarded tile, the player seated earlier in turn order can declare a win first and 'intercept the winning hand' (截胡) before the downstream player can claim it. In modern business, entertainment, and romance slang, it means to swoop in at the eleventh hour and snatch away a deal, IP, celebrity talent, or partner that a rival had nearly secured.

history.meaning: (in mahjong) to claim a discarded tile for a win ahead of another waiting player downstream
to poach or snatch away a nearly finalized deal, project, role, or talent at the last moment

morphemes.meaning: a winning hand in mahjong (metaphorically: a prize, deal, or target about to be won)

截胡.notes: A vivid, high-frequency showbiz and corporate idiom in modern China: if Studio A spends months negotiating with a star or buying a novel's IP, and Studio B swoops in with a higher offer right before signing, Studio A's deal has been 被截胡了 ('poached at the finish line').

rootFamily.gloss: win a hand in mahjong (胡牌)

戴.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining 異 ('raise both hands to place something on the head') + 戈 (𢦏 zāi/dài phonetic): in Classical Chinese 'carry on top of the head, respect/support (拥戴)', and in Mandarin the specific verb for 'wear or put on accessories on the head, face, neck, hands, or body (hat, glasses, watch, scarf, gloves, ring, badge)'.

morphemes.meaning: hands placing an item on the head

history.meaning: bear on the head; honor and support
wear (hats, glasses, watches, jewelry, gloves)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 戴 (via 萌典)

房.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 户 ('single-leaf door, household') + 方 (fāng, 'side, quarter'): originally 'a side room flanking the central hall (堂) of a traditional courtyard house', and from the Han–Tang period onward the general noun for 'house, building, room, chamber'.

history.meaning: side chamber flanking a main hall
house; building; room

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 房 (via 萌典)

房东.etymology: Compound noun of 房 ('house, property') + 东 (東, short for 东家/主人 'host, master, owner', because in traditional Chinese etiquette the host sat on the eastern side 东阶 while the guest sat on the west): 'landlord, landlady, homeowner'.

history.meaning: master/owner of the house = landlord, landlady

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 房东 (via 萌典)

房产.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 房 ('house, building') + 产 (產, 'property, estate, asset'): 'real estate, house property, residential or commercial buildings owned'.

history.meaning: house property; real estate

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 房产 (via 萌典)

房号.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 房 ('room') + 号 (號, 'number'): 'room number (in a hotel, apartment, or office building)'.

history.meaning: room number

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 房号 (via 萌典)

房子.etymology: Colloquial noun formed from 房 ('house, building, room') + nominal suffix 子 (neutral tone zi): 'house, apartment, building, room'.

history.meaning: house; building; apartment; room

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 房子 (via 萌典)

房梁.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 房 ('house, roof') + 梁 ('horizontal wooden bridge or roof beam', 水 + 刃 + 木): 'roof beam, main crossbeam of a house'.

history.meaning: roof beam; house crossbeam

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 房梁 (via 萌典)

房租.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 房 ('house, room') + 租 ('rent, tax', grain 禾 + 且): 'rent for a house or room'.

history.stage: Song–Ming commercial vernacular to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: house rent; room rent

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 房租 (via 萌典)

房间.etymology: Everyday two-syllable noun for 'room' (counted with 间: 一间房间), pairing 房 ('side house, chamber', attested in the Shijing) with 间 ('architectural bay, room space').

history.meaning: disyllabic noun 'room'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 房間 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: place; that which (nominalizer in漢文 kundoku: するところ)

所.etymology: A phono-semantic character (所, suǒ, Old Chinese *s-qʰraʔ*, Middle Chinese *srjoX*) combining 戶 (hù, 'single-leaf door') and 斤 (jīn, 'axe'). Originally depicting the sound of chopping wood or a specific dwelling/place by a doorway ('place, location, premises'), it grammaticalized already in Early Archaic Chinese (bronze inscriptions and *Shijing*) into an object-relative nominalizing particle placed before a transitive verb: 所 + V means 'the place where one V-s' and hence 'that which is V-ed / what one V-s'.

history.meaning: sound of chopping wood; a place, abode, location
that which is [verb]-ed; what one [verb]s (object nominalizer); passive marker with 為...所...
that which (literary nominalizer in compounds/idioms); bureau/institute; classifier for buildings

morphemes.meaning: that which, what is [verb]-ed (object nominalizer); place, institution

所.notes: Survives from Classical Chinese as a fossilized prefix in dozens of high-register modern Mandarin words and constructions: 所谓 ('what is called / so-called'), 所得 ('what is gained / earnings'), 所指 ('what is pointed to'), and the passive frame 为...所... ('be [verb]-ed by...').

rootFamily.gloss: place, venue, premises (retaining the original spatial noun sense)

所以.etymology: Originally a Classical Chinese relative phrase combining 所 (object nominalizer 'that which') + 以 ('by means of, because of') = 'that by which, the reason why' (e.g., 所以然). Because 'the reason why [result happens]' introduced the consequence clause after a cause, it grammaticalized into the conjunction 'therefore, so, as a result'.

history.meaning: that by which; the reason why
therefore; so; as a result

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 所以 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: income, earnings, revenue (source of 所得税 shotokuzei)

所得.etymology: A Classical Chinese pronominal nominalization combining the object-relative particle 所 (suǒ, 'that which is [verb]-ed') and the transitive verb 得 (dé, Old Chinese *tɯːɡ*, 'to obtain, acquire, gain', originally an oracle-bone graph showing a hand 寸/又 picking up a cowrie shell 貝 on the road 彳). Literally 'that which one obtains', it meant 'what is gained or learned' in Classical prose, and was adapted in modern East Asian fiscal and legal terminology (alongside Meiji Japanese *shotoku* 所得) to mean 'financial income, earnings, proceeds'.

history.meaning: that which one obtains, gains, or comprehends (Classical nominalized phrase)
financial income, earnings, proceeds (as in 所得税 'income tax'); personal gains/takeaways

所得.notes: Used both in formal economic/legal terms (个人所得税 'personal income tax', 非法所得 'ill-gotten gains / illegal proceeds') and in literary idioms like 劳有所得 ('to be rewarded for one's labor') or 一无所得 ('to come away empty-handed').

rootFamily.gloss: personal takeaway, insight gained from experience or study

cognates.meaning: the signified (in Saussurean linguistics: シニフィエ), what is pointed to

所指.etymology: A Classical Chinese nominalized construction formed from the object-relative particle 所 (suǒ, 'that which is [verb]-ed') and the verb 指 (zhǐ, 'to point at, indicate, refer to', originally 'finger' from 手 'hand' + 旨). Literally 'that which is pointed at or alluded to', it appears in classical commentary and idioms (such as 千夫所指 'pointed at in accusation by a thousand people') and was adopted in 20th-century Chinese linguistics to translate Ferdinand de Saussure's *signifié* ('the signified', paired with 能指 néngzhǐ 'the signifier').

history.meaning: that which is pointed at; the target of pointing or allusion (Classical Chinese)
what is alluded to or meant (as in 意有所指); the signified (in semiotics)

morphemes.meaning: to point at, indicate, allude to, refer to

所指.notes: In everyday and dramatic dialogue, 所指 most commonly occurs after 有 in phrases like 话里有话，意有所指 ('there is a hidden message in their words; they are alluding to someone/something specific') or 不知所指 ('not knowing what is being referred to').

rootFamily.gloss: allude to something, have a hidden point or target in one's words
the signifier (paired with 所指 'the signified' in linguistics)

所有.etymology: Originally a Classical Chinese relative phrase of 所 ('that which') + 有 ('possess, have') = 'what one possesses, one's possessions' (retained in 所有权 'ownership'). By extension ('everything that exists/is had'), it became the universal quantifier determiner 'all, every'.

history.meaning: that which one possesses; everything there is
all; every; possessions

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 所有 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: ownership, possession (retaining the older sense of 所有: shoyū)
ownership, possession (retaining the older sense of 所有: soyu)

所有人.etymology: A modifier-head noun phrase combining 所有 (suǒyǒu, originally a Classical Chinese nominalized phrase 所 + 有 meaning 'that which one possesses / everything that exists', which grammaticalized into a universal quantifier meaning 'all, every') and 人 (rén, 'person, people', an oracle-bone pictograph of a standing human figure in profile). Together, 所有人 means 'all people, everyone', though in strictly legal contexts it can also retain the older compositional sense 'owner, proprietor' (the person who possesses [something], i.e., 所有 + 人).

history.meaning: that which one has/possesses; all that exists in a place (Classical Chinese)
all people, everyone, everybody (universal quantifier + noun); also legal 'owner/proprietor'

morphemes.meaning: that which (nominalizer forming 所有 'all / what is possessed')
to have, possess, exist (forming 所有 'all, every')

所有人.notes: A fascinating ambiguity across registers: in 99% of spoken Mandarin and TV dialogue, 所有人 means 'everyone / everybody' (所有的人); however, in Chinese property law (such as 房屋所有人), 所有人 retains the literal classical sense of 所有 ('ownership/possession') and means 'the property owner'!

rootFamily.gloss: ownership, title to property (retaining the 'possess' sense of 所有)

所有者.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound formed from 所有 (suǒyǒu, "that which one possesses; property", itself a Classical Chinese pronominal-object construction combining the patient nominalizer 所 suǒ with 有 yǒu "to have, possess") and the agentive suffix 者 (zhě, "one who; person"). While 所有 and 者 both have deep Classical Chinese roots, the compound 所有者 was systematized in late 19th- and early 20th-century legal terminology (alongside Meiji Japanese 所有者 shoyūsha, translating German Eigentümer / English owner) to denote the legal holder of property or intellectual rights.

history.meaning: that which one has; possessions, holdings
legal owner, proprietor (modern civil-law term)
owner, proprietor, rights holder

所有者.notes: Primarily used in formal, legal, and contractual registers (such as 版权所有者 "copyright holder" or 商标所有者 "trademark owner"); in everyday spoken Mandarin, 主人 (zhǔrén) or 房东/车主 is preferred.

所谓.etymology: A Classical Chinese grammaticalized construction composed of the patient-relativizing particle 所 (suǒ, "that which") and the verb 谓 (繁體 謂, wèi, "to call, name, say of"). Literally meaning "that which is called [by people]", it appears frequently in Warring States philosophical prose (such as Mencius and Xunzi) to introduce an established term or quotation. In Modern Mandarin, it functions as a non-predicative adjective or discourse marker meaning "so-called", often carrying a skeptical or distancing tone toward a label.

history.meaning: that which is called; what people refer to as
what is known as; the aforementioned term
so-called (often skeptical); (in 无所谓) mattering, of consequence

morphemes.meaning: to call, to name, to speak of

所谓.notes: Frequently paired with 的 as 所谓的 ("so-called") to cast doubt on a hyped title or claim (e.g., 所谓的行业专家 "so-called industry experts"); also central to the high-frequency idiom 无所谓 (wúsuǒwèi, "cannot be called anything -> it doesn't matter / indifferent").

rootFamily.gloss: to not matter, to be indifferent
what is meant by; meaning, significance

扁.etymology: Written 扁 (biǎn), combining 户 ('door leaf') above 册 ('bamboo slips strung flat side by side'), originally depicting a flat wooden inscribed tablet hung above a doorway (later written 匾 when read biǎn 'horizontal plaque'). Because bamboo slips and door plaques are broad and thin rather than round, 扁 became the core Chinese adjective for flat, thin shapes (扁担 'flat carrying pole', 扁豆 'hyacinth bean').

morphemes.meaning: broad and thin like strung bamboo slips 册 beneath a doorway 户

history.meaning: inscribed flat door tablet; thin and flat
flat (thin in cross-section, not round)

扁豆.etymology: Descriptive botanical compound of 扁 ('flat, compressed') + 豆 ('bean, legume', originally a pictograph of a footed food vessel in oracle-bone script, transferred to pulses served in it), naming flat-seeded lentils and hyacinth beans.

history.meaning: flat-podded bean; lentil
lentil; flat bean

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 扁豆

扇.etymology: Ideogram combining 户 ('door') + 羽 ('bird wings/feathers'): originally 'woven bamboo or wooden door leaf' (because paired door leaves swing open like wings), then 'hand fan' (made of feathers, silk, or bamboo) and the standard classifier for doors and windows (一扇门, 一扇窗); read shān as the verb 'fan, flap, slap'.

history.meaning: swinging door leaf; fan
fan; classifier for doors/windows (shàn); fan with a hand/fan (shān)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 扇 (via 萌典)

手.etymology: Foundational pictograph (象形字) attested from Shang oracle bones depicting a human hand with five fingers and wrist: 'hand; hold in hand; person skilled in a craft or activity (-er, as in 歌手, 新手); personally; convenient'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: pictograph of a five-fingered hand = hand; skill; specialist

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 手 (via 萌典)

手上.etymology: A locative noun phrase formed from the body-part noun 手 (shǒu, "hand", Old Chinese *n̥jup) followed by the postpositional localizer 上 (shàng, "on, upon, within the sphere of"). Originally denoting physical placement on the palm or in the grasp of the hand, the compound underwent metonymic extension in vernacular Mandarin to signify resources, tasks, projects, or authority currently under a person's immediate disposal or active handling.

history.meaning: physically on or in the hand
in one's hands, at one's disposal, currently under one's handling

morphemes.meaning: on, upon, within the scope of

手上.notes: In workplace and production contexts, 手上 often refers to ongoing work or liquid assets currently in someone's possession (e.g., 手上的项目 "the project currently on one's plate", 手上没钱 "having no cash on hand").

rootFamily.gloss: in one's hands, under one's control
on hand, at hand (especially finances or current work)
in one's grasp or possession (more formal)

手下.etymology: A modifier-head locative compound combining 手 (shǒu, "hand", representing personal agency and command) and 下 (xià, "under, beneath"). Originally a spatial expression meaning "beneath the hand" (and hence "within reach, at the moment of action", or "under someone's authority"), it was nominalized in Tang–Song vernacular and military usage (cf. 手下人) to denote a person operating under a leader's direct command, i.e., a subordinate, retainer, or underling.

history.meaning: beneath the hand; under one's command or jurisdiction
subordinate, underling, staff member under a boss; (also) at the hands of

手下.notes: Used both as a count noun for a subordinate (他是我的手下 "he is my subordinate") and as a locative in idioms like 手下留情 (shǒuxià liúqíng, "show mercy beneath your hand / go easy on someone").

rootFamily.gloss: to show mercy, to go easy on someone
a defeated opponent (literally "defeated general under one's hand")

cognates.meaning: in the hand; within one's control or sphere
in the hand, in one's possession

手中.etymology: A Classical Chinese locative compound formed from 手 (shǒu, "hand") and the interior localizer 中 (zhōng, "inside, within, center"). Attested in early texts for holding an object in the hollow of the palm, it developed a regular metaphorical sense of holding power, fate, or assets within one's grasp or control, retaining a slightly more literary and elevated register than its colloquial counterparts 手里 and 手上.

history.meaning: in the hollow of the hand; held in the hand
in one's grasp, under one's control or possession

morphemes.meaning: inside, within, in the midst of

手中.notes: More literary and written in register than 手里 or 手上; commonly found in media narratives and dramatic dialogue (e.g., 把命运掌握在自己手中 "hold fate in one's own hands").

rootFamily.gloss: in the palm of one's hand (often in 玩弄于股掌/手掌之中)
to hold in one's hands, to command

手写.etymology: Noun-verb compound used as a verb and modifier, combining 手 ('by hand') + 写 (寫, 'write'): 'write by hand; handwritten'.

history.meaning: write by hand; handwritten

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 手写 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: at hand, in one's possession, money on hand

手头.etymology: A vernacular Mandarin noun formed from 手 (shǒu, "hand") and 头 (繁體 頭, tóu, originally "head, end, extremity", grammaticalized in Tang–Song vernacular as a locative and nominal suffix indicating proximity or an immediate area, as in 里头, 外头). Literally "at the tip/vicinity of one's hand", it came to mean both what is immediately at hand (tasks, tools) and one's immediate financial liquidity at a given moment.

history.meaning: right by one's hand; at hand; one's immediate personal funds
on hand, at hand (current work or resources); financial situation at the moment

手头.notes: Particularly idiomatic when describing temporary cash flow (手头紧 shǒutóu jǐn "short on cash right now" vs. 手头宽裕 shǒutóu kuānyù "flush with cash") or immediate workload (手头的工作 "the work currently on one's desk").

rootFamily.gloss: on one's hands, in one's current possession
at hand, right beside one's hand (conveniently reachable)

手套.etymology: Determinative compound of 手 ('hand', pictograph of a five-fingered hand) + 套 ('outer sheath; protective cover; case',的大 + 长). Used for winter gloves, work gloves, and padded kitchen oven mitts (烤箱手套).

history.meaning: hand covering; gloves or mitts
gloves; mitts

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 手套

手指.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 手 ('hand') + 指 ('finger, digit, point'): 'finger' (disambiguating fingers of the hand from toes 脚趾).

history.meaning: finger of the hand

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 手指 (via 萌典)

手掌.etymology: Anatomical compound of 手 ('hand') + 掌 ('palm of the hand; flat sole or pad', phonetic 尚 shàng above 手 'hand'). In bread-making and martial arts alike, 手掌 and 手掌根 ('heel of the palm') specify the broad, flat pad of the hand used to press and knead.

history.meaning: palm of the hand
palm of the hand

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 手掌

手握.etymology: A compact Classical-style noun-verb (instrument-action) compound combining 手 (shǒu, "hand", functioning adverbially as "with the hand / in one's hand") and 握 (wò, "to grasp, clench, hold fast", Old Chinese *qˤruk). Originally describing a warrior or ruler physically gripping a weapon, tally, or seal of office (e.g., 手握重兵 "holding command of massive troops"), it is widely used in modern media and business prose to mean commanding strategic resources, copyrights, or decision-making power.

history.meaning: to grasp in the hand (weapons, tallies, or state authority)
to hold in one's hands, to command (rights, capital, or leverage)

morphemes.meaning: hand; with the hand, in one's hands
to grasp, to clench, to hold control of

手握.notes: High-frequency in entertainment and business journalism to describe executives or studios that control key assets (e.g., 手握大IP "holding major intellectual-property rights", 手握实权 "wielding real power").

rootFamily.gloss: to grasp, to master, to have under control
to hold, to seize; assurance, certainty

手术.etymology: A modifier-head compound of 手 (shǒu, "hand") and 术 (繁體 術, shù, "art, skill, technique, method"). In traditional Chinese texts, 手术 occasionally referred to manual craft or sleight of hand; however, its modern medical sense ("surgical operation") was established in Meiji Japan (手術 shujutsu) as a literal translation of Dutch heelkunde / German Chirurgie (which itself derives via Latin chirurgia from Ancient Greek χειρουργία kheirourgía, from χείρ "hand" + ἔργον "work"), and was subsequently re-borrowed into Modern Mandarin.

history.meaning: manual skill, handiwork, craft
surgical operation (calros/semantic loan translating Western chirurgia "hand-work")
surgery, surgical operation; (figuratively) radical overhaul

手术.notes: Takes the verbs 做 (zuò) or 动 (dòng) ("to perform/undergo surgery"); in media editing and corporate restructuring, 动大手术 ("perform major surgery") is a common metaphor for drastically cutting or overhauling a script, program, or department.

手机.etymology: A modern modifier-head nominal compound combining 手 (shǒu, "hand; handheld") and 机 (繁體 機, jī, originally "trigger of a crossbow; loom; pivotal mechanism", generalized in modern Chinese as "machine, apparatus, device", and specifically clipped from 电话机 diànhuàjī "telephone set" or 无线电收发机). Coined in the late 20th century as cellular phones shrank from bulky portable transceivers (大哥大) into handheld sets (手提电话机 -> 手机).

history.meaning: hand-carried telephone apparatus (early portable cell phone)
mobile phone, cellphone, smartphone

手机.notes: The universal everyday word for "mobile phone / smartphone" across Mainland China and Taiwan; takes the classifier 部 (bù) or 台 (tái), or 个 (gè) in casual speech.

rootFamily.gloss: to turn off a phone or computer; to wrap filming (of a movie/show)

手柄.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 手 (shǒu, "hand") and 柄 (bǐng, "handle, haft of an axe or tool, stem", Old Chinese *praŋʔ). Originally denoting the wooden haft or grip of a hand tool, crank, or ceremonial fly-whisk Held in the hand, in Modern Mandarin it extends to mechanical control levers, camera pan-bars, foosball rod grips, and video-game controllers.

history.meaning: handgrip or haft of an implement, lever, or utensil
handle, grip, control lever, game controller

手柄.notes: Used for physical grips on machinery, table-soccer (foosball) rods, and studio equipment, as well as the standard term for a console gamepad (游戏手柄 yóuxì shǒubǐng). Compare 把手 (bǎshou), which usually refers to a door or drawer handle.

rootFamily.gloss: handle, grip, knob (on a door, drawer, or cup)
handle (used metaphorically for a vulnerability or dirt someone holds over you)

手电筒.etymology: Three-character compound combining 手 ('hand-held') + 电 ('electric') + 筒 ('tubular bamboo cylinder'): 'flashlight, electric torch' (named for its cylindrical battery tube held in the hand).

history.meaning: hand-held electric cylinder = flashlight, torch

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 手电筒 (via 萌典)

手续.etymology: A Sino-Japanese orthographic loan (wasei-kango) adopted into late Qing and Republican Chinese from Japanese 手続 / 手続き (tetsuzuki, "procedure, administrative formalities"), a compound of 手 (te / shǒu, "hand; step, measure, move") and 続 (tsuzuki / 续 xù, "continuation, sequence, succession"). Re-read in Mandarin pronunciation as shǒuxù, it denotes the sequential administrative steps, paperwork, or clearance procedures required to complete an official, legal, or financial transaction.

history.meaning: sequence of steps, administrative or legal procedure
formalities, paperwork, official clearance procedures

morphemes.meaning: hand; practical step or handling measure

手续.notes: Most commonly collocated with 办 or 办理 (bànlǐ shǒuxù, "to go through the formalities / process the paperwork"), such as 办入职手续 ("complete onboarding paperwork") or 办离职手续 ("complete exit clearance").

rootFamily.gloss: to continue, to carry on; continuation

手脚.etymology: Coordinative noun compound pairing 手 ('hands') + 脚 ('feet'): means literally 'hands and feet, limbs', and figuratively 'movements/motions (手脚快 nimble)', 'chore effort (费手脚)', or 'secret underhanded tricks (做手脚)'.

history.meaning: hands and feet; movements; secret tampering

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 手脚 (via 萌典)

手表.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 手 ('hand, wrist') + 表 (錶, 'timepiece, watch'): 'wristwatch'.

history.meaning: wristwatch

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 手表 (via 萌典)

手边.etymology: Locative compound from 手 ('hand', pictograph of a five-fingered hand) + 边 (simplified from 邊, 'side; margin; proximity'). Literally 'by one's hand', it refers to tools, materials, or tasks that are right within arm's reach or currently being handled.

history.meaning: close at hand; in one's possession
at hand; within easy reach

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 手边

手里.etymology: A vernacular locative compound formed from 手 (shǒu, "hand") and the interior localizer 里 (繁體 裏/裡, lǐ, originally "lining of a garment; inside"). Replacing Classical 手中 in everyday spoken Mandarin, it literally means "inside one's hand" and by extension refers to whatever money, resources, power, or tasks are currently held in a person's possession or control.

history.meaning: in the hand; in one's possession or custody
in one's hands, in one's possession, under one's control

手里.notes: The most conversational of the three "in one's hand" locatives (手里, 手上, 手中): 手里 emphasizes possession or control (钱在他手里 "the money is in his hands"), 手上 emphasizes active handling at the moment, and 手中 is more literary/formal.

rootFamily.gloss: in one's hands, currently being handled
inside the heart, in one's mind (parallel locative formation)

手镯.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound combining 手 (shǒu, "hand, wrist, arm") and 镯 (繁體 鐲, zhuó, Old Chinese *dˤrok). In Classical Chinese, 镯 originally denoted a small military bell used to regulate marching troops (as recorded in the Zhouli and Shuowen Jiezi); by the Tang and Song dynasties, because of the circular metallic ring shape and jingling sound of wrist ornaments, 镯 shifted semantically to denote a rigid circular bangle or bracelet worn around the wrist (手镯, contrasting with 脚镯 "anklet").

history.meaning: small military hand-bell used in ancient armies; later, circular metallic arm/wrist ring
bracelet, bangle (especially a rigid ring of jade, gold, or silver worn on the wrist)

morphemes.meaning: bangle, circular wrist ornament (originally a small bell)

手镯.notes: Specifically refers to a rigid ring-shaped bangle (such as a jade bangle 玉手镯 or gold bangle 金手镯), whereas a flexible chain bracelet made of links or beads is called 手链 (shǒuliàn).

才.etymology: Pictograph in Shang oracle-bone script of a sprouting plant shoot pushing through the soil with roots below: originally 'natural endowment, talent, timber/ability (人才, 才能)'. Also used (merging 纔 cái) as the restrictive temporal and focus adverb 'just now; only then (after a condition or late time); only'.

morphemes.meaning: plant shoot = talent, ability; (for 纔) just, only then

history.form: 才 (talent, ability) / 纔 (just, only then)
history.meaning: sprouting shoot = innate talent; adverb 'only then, just'
only then; just now; only; talent/ability

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 才 (via 萌典)

才华.etymology: A Classical Chinese modifier-head (or coordinative) compound composed of 才 (cái, "natural endowment, timber, innate ability") and 华 (繁體 華, huá, "blossom, flowering, outward splendor, luster"). First prominent in Six Dynasties aesthetic and literary criticism (such as Liu Xie's Wenxin Diaolong and the Nan Shi), 才华 literally meant "the flowering or outward radiance of innate talent", specifically denoting creative, literary, or artistic brilliance that manifests visibly in one's works.

history.meaning: the outward flowering of innate talent; literary and poetic brilliance
literary, artistic, or creative talent and brilliance

才华.notes: Unlike 才能 or 才干 (which emphasize practical or managerial competence), 才华 specifically highlights creative, artistic, musical, or literary flair (often in the chengyu 才华横溢 cáihuá héngyì, "brimming with artistic talent").

才能.etymology: In its adverbial/modal use ("only then can"), 才能 (cái néng) is a syntactic juxtaposition in vernacular Mandarin of the restrictive focus adverb 才 (cái, "only then, just now", grammaticalized from 財/才 "material, scarcely, barely" in Tang–Song vernacular) and the modal auxiliary verb 能 (néng, "can, be able to"). It also exists as an older Classical coordinative noun 才能 (cáinéng, from 才 "innate endowment" + 能 "capability, competence") meaning "talent and ability". In conditional sentences (especially after 只有 zhǐyǒu "only if"), the adverb+modal sequence 才能 marks a necessary precondition.

history.meaning: talent and capability (coordinative noun)
only then be able to; only under such conditions can (adverb + modal verb)

morphemes.meaning: only then, under no other condition (or as noun: innate talent)
can, to be able to (or as noun: capability)

才能.notes: Watch the two distinct functions: as a verb-phrase modifier (often paired with 只有...才能..., "only by... can one..."), 才 is a conditional adverb followed by modal 能; as a standalone noun (展示才能 "display one's talent"), it is a coordinative compound meaning "ability/talent".

rootFamily.gloss: only then will / only then can

扎.etymology: Originally written /扎, combining the semantic hand radical 扌 (shǒu) with the phonetic-semantic component 乚 (yà / zhá, depicting asprouting plant pushing through soil or a curved hook). In Classical Chinese (Shuowen Jiezi), 扎 meant "to pluck or pull out", while in vernacular Mandarin it developed three pronunciations and core senses around piercing and fixing in place: zhā ("to prick, stab; to plunge into; to pitch [a tent] or strike [roots]"), zhá ("to struggle", as in 挣扎), and zā ("to bind, tie in a bundle", alternating with 紮). The sense "to pitch (camp) / strike (roots)" derives from driving stakes or roots deep into the ground.

history.meaning: to pull out; to pierce, prick, or drive a stake into the ground
(zhā) to prick, plunge into, pitch (camp), strike (roots); (zā) to bind; (zhá) to struggle

morphemes.meaning: to prick, pierce, plunge into, pitch (stakes/camp), strike (roots)

扎.notes: A classic polyphonic character (多音字): read zhā for piercing, plunging in, or pitching/rooting (扎针 "acupuncture/injection", 扎根 "take root", 扎营 "pitch camp", 一头扎进工作 "plunge headfirst into work"); zā for tying/binding (包扎 "bandage"); and zhá in 挣扎 (zhēngzhá, "struggle").

rootFamily.gloss: to take root, to establish a solid base (literally "strike roots")
sturdy, solid, grounded (of skills or work)
to pitch camp, to station troops

扑上来.etymology: A verb-complement construction formed from the action verb 扑 (繁體 撲, pū, "to strike, pounce on, throw oneself forward, rush at", composed of the hand radical 扌 and phonetic 菐 pú) followed by the compound directional complement 上来 (shànglái, from 上 "up, forward, onto a target" + deictic 来 "hither, toward the speaker or focal point"). Literally "to pounce forward/upward toward the subject", it vividly depicts people, fans, reporters, or animals lunging or swarming eagerly toward someone.

history.meaning: to strike, beat; to pounce upon, throw oneself at
to pounce forward, rush up, or swarm eagerly toward someone

morphemes.meaning: to pounce on, rush at, throw oneself forward
up, forward, onto (indicating contact or approach)
hither, toward the speaker or narrative focus

扑上来.notes: Frequently used in showbiz and dramatic scenes to describe crowds of fans, paparazzi, or opportunistic suitors rushing toward a celebrity or resource all at once.

rootFamily.gloss: to pounce on, to rush toward (away from the speaker)
to throw oneself into someone's arms; to devote oneself completely to
to extinguish, to stamp out (a fire or crisis)

扒.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 扌 (手, 'hand') + 八 (bā/pá phonetic, 'part/divide'): read bā 'strip off, peel, pull down, cling to, push aside/dig up'; read pá 'rake together,扒饭 (shovel rice into the mouth), braise/stew, pickpocket'.

history.meaning: pull apart, cling to, dig/push aside (bā); rake, scoop, braise (pá)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 扒 (via 萌典)

打.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 扌 (手, 'hand') + 丁 (dīng/dǎ phonetic, originally a nail head). Originally 'strike, hit, beat', and from the Tang–Song vernacular onward bleached into Mandarin's most prolific light verb across dozens of everyday actions ('make a phone call, take a taxi, fetch water, open, sweep, give a discount, play ball, knit'); also read dá for 'a dozen (12)'.

history.meaning: strike; hit; forge
hit; light verb for everyday actions (dǎ); dozen (dá)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 打 (via 萌典)

打九折.etymology: Commercial verb-object phrase combining 打 ('give/apply a discount') + 九折 ('nine-tenths of the original price'): 'give a 10% discount (charge 90% of the list price)'.

history.meaning: charge 9/10 of original price = 10% off

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 打九折 (via 萌典)

打交道.etymology: A three-character separable verb-object (离合词) construction composed of the bleached light verb 打 (dǎ, originally "to strike", grammaticalized since the Tang–Song period as a general action verb meaning "to engage in, conduct, carry out") and the nominal object 交道 (jiāodào, from 交 "mutual contact, association, exchange" + 道 "way, path, channel of interaction"). Coined in early modern vernacular Mandarin, it literally means "to engage in the path of mutual association", i.e., to have dealings with, socialize with, or work alongside someone.

history.meaning: path of mutual intercourse; social or commercial dealings
to deal with, interact with, have professional or social dealings with

morphemes.meaning: to engage in, to carry out, to make (light verb)

打交道.notes: Because 打交道 is an intransitive verb-object phrase, the person or group one deals with must be introduced beforehand with the preposition 跟, 和, or 与 (e.g., 经常跟媒体打交道 "frequently deal with the media", never *打交道媒体).

rootFamily.gloss: to associate with, to socialize; interpersonal contact
to negotiate, to make representations with another party

cognates.meaning: blow, strike, shock, setback; batting (in baseball)
