打击.etymology: A coordinative disyllabic compound combining two synonymous transitive verbs of striking: 打 (dǎ, Middle Chinese *tæŋX / *tɛk, "to strike, hit, beat") and 击 (繁體 擊, jī, Old Chinese *kˤek, "to strike, attack, knock"). Attested in Medieval Chinese for physical beating or military assault, it expanded in modern East Asian usage (reinforced by Japanese 打撃 dageki) to function both as a transitive verb ("to strike, crack down on, demoralize") and as a noun meaning a severe emotional, career, or financial blow or setback.

history.meaning: to strike physically, beat, or attack militarily
(verb) to strike, crack down on, dampen morale; (noun) psychological, career, or financial blow, setback

morphemes.meaning: to strike, to hit, to beat
to strike, to attack, to knock

打击.notes: As a noun, it frequently collocates with 受到 (shòudào dǎjī, "suffer a blow/setback") or 沉重的打击 ("a heavy blow"); as a verb, it means either cracking down on illegal activity (打击盗版 "crack down on piracy") or crushing someone's confidence (打击积极性 "dampen enthusiasm").

rootFamily.gloss: to attack, to assault, to accuse

打动.etymology: A verb-resultative (动补) compound composed of the action verb 打 (dǎ, "to strike, knock, touch upon") and the resultative complement 动 (繁體 動, dòng, "to move, stir, budge"). Originally describing physically knocking an object so that it shifts position (as seen in Yuan–Ming vernacular plays and fiction), it underwent metaphorical internalization to mean "stirring or moving someone's heart", i.e., touching someone emotionally or winning them over with sincerity, talent, or persuasion.

history.meaning: to strike so as to move; to stir or move someone's heart/feelings
to move emotionally, to touch the heart of, to win over

morphemes.meaning: to strike, to touch upon, to act on
to move, to stir, to be emotionally affected (resultative)

打动.notes: Unlike 感动 (gǎndòng, which focuses on inspiring gratitude or deep moral emotion), 打动 emphasizes breaking through someone's initial reserve or skepticism to win their approval or emotional resonance (e.g., 用诚意打动投资人 "win over investors with sincerity").

rootFamily.gloss: to move emotionally, to touch; moved, touched
to move, to arouse, to sway (someone's mind or stance)

打印.etymology: Modern compound of轻-verb 打 ('strike; type; produce mechanically') + 印 ('seal; stamp; print', depicting a hand pressing down a seal). Formed by combining traditional woodblock printing (印) with mechanical striking (打字 'typewriting').

history.meaning: print out on paper

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 打印

打压.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound joining 打 (dǎ, "to strike, beat down, hit") and 压 (繁體 壓, yā, "to press down, crush, hold down, suppress"). Combining the metaphors of striking from above and pinning beneath weight, the compound gained prominence in modern political, economic, and workplace Mandarin (initially popular in Taiwan and Hong Kong journalism before spreading throughout Mainland media) to describe deliberately suppressing, stifling, or undercutting a rival, newcomer, or market price.

history.meaning: to beat down and press upon; to suppress or hold down by force or authority
to suppress, stifle, hold back (competitors or talent), or drive down (prices)

morphemes.meaning: to press down, to weigh upon, to suppress

打压.notes: Very common in entertainment-industry and corporate contexts for entrenched figures or rivals stifling rising talent or competing studios (e.g., 打压新人 "stifle newcomers", 恶意打压竞争对手 "maliciously undercut competitors").

rootFamily.gloss: to suppress, to inhibit, to stifle; oppressive
to force down (prices, costs, or arrogance)

打官司.etymology: A separable verb-object (离合词) construction formed from the generalized action verb 打 (dǎ, "to engage in, contest, conduct") and the noun 官司 (guānsi, originally a Classical/Middle Chinese compound meaning "government office, official post, or magistrate's department" from 官 "official" + 司 "to administer, bureau"). In Song–Yuan vernacular, because ordinary citizens went to the magistrate's bureau (官司) only when embroiled in litigation, 官司 shifted metonymically from "magistrate's office" to "lawsuit, legal dispute", yielding 打官司 ("to fight a lawsuit / go to court").

history.meaning: government office, official bureau, administrative duty
magistrate's court case -> to engage in a lawsuit, litigate
to fight a lawsuit, to go to court, to engage in litigation

morphemes.meaning: to engage in, to fight, to conduct (light verb)
to administer, bureau, department (together 官司: lawsuit)

打官司.notes: The standard conversational way to say "sue / go to court / fight a lawsuit" (e.g., 跟前东家打官司 "fight a lawsuit against one's former agency"); its formal legal equivalents are 提起诉讼 (tíqǐ sùsòng) or 进行诉讼.

rootFamily.gloss: lawsuit, legal case (often in 吃官司 "get sued / go to jail")
verbal battle, war of words, public dispute (literally "pen-and-ink lawsuit")

打开.etymology: Resultative verb compound combining 打 ('strike, act upon') + 开 (開, 'open'): 'open up (a door, window, box, book, or file); turn on / switch on (a light, TV, computer, or faucet)'.

history.meaning: open up; unfold; turn on / switch on

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 打开 (via 萌典)

打打.etymology: The AA verbal reduplication (动词重叠) of the polysemous verb 打 (dǎ, originally "to strike, hit", and by vernacular grammaticalization a versatile light verb for playing games/sports, making phone calls, doing odd jobs, or engaging in an activity). In Mandarin grammar, reduplicating a monosyllabic action verb into the AA pattern (often derived from 打一打 dǎ yī dǎ by dropping 一) adds a delimitative aspect, indicating that the action is performed briefly, casually, playfully, or "a little bit" (e.g., 打打球 "play a bit of ball", 打打下手 "help out a bit as an assistant").

history.meaning: to strike a few times; to engage in an activity briefly or casually (delimitative aspect)

morphemes.meaning: to strike, play, make, or engage in an activity
delimitative aspect marker (doing an action briefly, casually, or a bit)

打打.notes: Always takes an object that normally collocates with 打 to soften the tone and make the activity sound casual or low-stakes (e.g., 打打球 "play a little ball", 打打杂 "do a bit of odd jobs", 打打招呼 "say a quick hello"). In pronunciation, the second 打 is read in the neutral tone (dǎda).

rootFamily.gloss: to play ball, to play a ball game
to do odd jobs, to work as a general handyman or gopher
to act as an assistant, to lend a hand

打扫.etymology: Compound verb of 打 (light verb marking deliberate action) + 扫 (掃, 'sweep with a broom'): 'sweep, clean up, tidy (a room or courtyard)'. Attested since Song–Yuan vernacular.

history.meaning: sweep and clean

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 打扫 (via 萌典)

打扰.etymology: Polite compound verb of 打 (light verb) + 扰 (擾, 'disturb, trouble, throw into disorder'): 'disturb, bother, trouble, interrupt someone' (often used politely as 'sorry to bother you / excuse me for intruding').

history.meaning: disturb; trouble; bother

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 打扰 (via 萌典)

打抱不平.etymology: A four-character vernacular idiom constructed from the light/action verb 打 (dǎ, "to strike at, take action against") and the three-character verb-object phrase 抱不平 (bào bùpíng, from 抱 "to harbor in one's bosom, feel, cherish" + 不平 "unevenness, unfairness, injustice", a Classical Chinese term already used in Han–Tang texts like 路见不平 "seeing injustice on the road"). Popularized in Yuan drama and Ming–Qing chivalric (武侠) fiction such as Water Margin (水浒传), 打抱不平 means stepping forward to champion a wronged party and redress an injustice.

history.meaning: injustice, grievance; to harbor indignation at an injustice
to take action against an injustice on someone else's behalf; to champion the wronged
history.stage: Ming–Qing Vernacular Fiction to Modern Mandarin

morphemes.meaning: to strike against, to take action to redress
to harbor in one's chest, to feel (indignation)
level, fair, just (together 不平: injustice, unfairness)

打抱不平.notes: The beneficiary on whose behalf one speaks or acts is introduced with 为 (wèi) or 替 (tì), e.g., 替朋友打抱不平 ("stand up against an injustice for a friend"). Often linked with the chivalric proverb 路见不平，拔刀相助 ("see injustice on the road and draw one's sword to help").

rootFamily.gloss: to feel indignant about an injustice; to defend someone wronged
to cry out against an injustice (usually on someone else's behalf)

打招呼.etymology: Separable verb-object phrase combining 打 (light verb) + 招呼 ('call out and beckon with the hand', 招 'beckon with hand' + 呼 'call with voice'): 'greet someone, say hello, give advance notice'.

history.meaning: greet; say hello; give a heads-up

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 打招呼 (via 萌典)

打断.etymology: A verb-resultative (动补) compound formed from the transitive action verb 打 (dǎ, "to strike, hit") and the resultative complement 断 (繁體 斷, duàn, "to sever, snap, break in two, cut off", whose ancient graph 㡭 depicts silk threads being cut with a blade). Originally meaning to snap a bone, stick, or rope in two by striking it, it extended metaphorically in vernacular Mandarin to mean cutting off or interrupting a continuous flow of speech, thought, or action.

history.meaning: to break or snap in two by striking (e.g., legs, bones, or branches)
to break/fracture by hitting; (figuratively) to interrupt, cut short (speech, a train of thought, or plans)

morphemes.meaning: to strike, to hit, to intervene in
to sever, to snap, to cut off (resultative)

打断.notes: In workplace and media dialogues, almost always used for interrupting someone speaking or thinking (e.g., 打断一下 "let me interrupt for a second", 打断他的话 "cut off his words", 打断思路 "break someone's train of thought"). Can take potential infixes: 打得断 / 打不断.

rootFamily.gloss: to suspend, to interrupt, to break off midway
to sever, to cut off (supply, contact, or a path)

打架.etymology: A separable verb-object (离合词) compound combining the verb 打 (dǎ, "to strike, fight, engage in") with 架 (jià, originally "wooden frame, rack, prop", which in Ming–Qing vernacular developed the sense of a "quarrel, brawl, or physical confrontation", likely from the posture of propping up / parrying blows, cf. 招架 zhāojià "to ward off blows"). Hence 打架 literally means "to engage in a brawl/scuffle", denoting an interpersonal physical fight (as opposed to organized warfare 打仗 or verbal arguing 吵架).

history.meaning: to come to blows, brawl, engage in a street or interpersonal fight
to get into a physical fight, scuffle, brawl; (humorously) to clash or conflict

morphemes.meaning: to strike, to fight, to engage in

打架.notes: A separable verb-object word (离合词), so aspect markers and duration complements go between the two characters (e.g., 打了一架 "had a fight", 打过架 "have fought before"). Contrast 打架 (physical fight) with 吵架 (chǎojià, verbal argument/quarrel).

rootFamily.gloss: to quarrel, to have a verbal argument or row
to step in to break up a fight or mediate a quarrel
to kidnap, to abduct; to hold hostage

cognates.meaning: batted ball, hitting a ball (in baseball/sports)

打球.etymology: A separable verb-object (动宾) construction composed of the verb 打 (dǎ, "to strike, hit, play with the hands") and the noun 球 (qiú, originally "fine jade" in Classical Chinese, which since the Tang dynasty became the standard character for a round ball, first in polo 击球 / 打球 and kickball 蹴鞠). In Tang–Song court culture, 打球 specifically referred to playing polo on horseback or stick-ball (捶丸); in Modern Mandarin, it refers to playing any ball sport in which the ball is struck or handled with the hands, a racket, a bat, or a rod (basketball, volleyball, badminton, table tennis, tennis, golf, billiards, or foosball).

history.meaning: to play polo or ancient stick-ball by striking a ball with a mallet
to play a ball game (with hands, racket, bat, club, cue, or table rods)

morphemes.meaning: to strike, to hit, to play (with the hands or an implement)

打球.notes: Mandarin distinguishes ball sports by the body part used: sports using hands, rackets, cues, or table-soccer rods use 打 (打篮球 "play basketball", 打网球 "play tennis", 打桌球/打球 "play billiards or foosball"), whereas foot-based ball sports like soccer use 踢 (tī, "to kick": 踢足球).

rootFamily.gloss: fans of a ball sport (basketball, soccer, etc.)
sports court, field, or stadium for ball games

打电话.etymology: Separable verb-object phrase combining 打 (light verb, originally from cranking/ringing early magneto telephones) + 电话 ('telephone', 电 'electric' + 话 'speech'): 'make a phone call'.

history.meaning: make a telephone call

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 打电话 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: breaking down (a deadlock or convention), overthrow
breaking down, overthrowing (a convention or deadlock)

打破.etymology: A verb-resultative (动补) compound formed from the action verb 打 (dǎ, "to strike, hit") and the resultative complement 破 (pò, "to break, split open, cleave, rupture", Old Chinese *pʰˤals). Attested since the Tang–Song period both literally for smashing a vessel or breaching a city wall and figuratively in Chan (Zen) Buddhist koans for shattering mental illusions or conventions, 打破 is widely used in Modern Mandarin for breaking abstract boundaries, records, deadlocks, monopolies, or silence.

history.meaning: to smash open by striking; (in Chan Buddhism) to shatter delusion or convention
to break, shatter (both physical objects and abstract things like records, silence, rules, or deadlocks)

morphemes.meaning: to strike, to hit, to act forcefully upon

打破.notes: While it can describe breaking a physical object (打破杯子), it is the standard verb for abstract "breaking" collocations: 打破纪录 ("break a record"), 打破沉默 ("break the silence"), 打破常规 ("break convention"), and 打破僵局 ("break a deadlock").

rootFamily.gloss: to break through, to make a breakthrough; breakthrough
to damage, to destroy, to wreck
to burst, to rupture, to break down (of negotiations or relationships)

打碎.etymology: A verb-resultative (动补) compound combining the transitive action verb 打 (dǎ, "to strike, hit, knock") and the resultative complement 碎 (suì, "to smash into small fragments, pulverize, shatter", composed of the stone radical 石 and 卒 zú). More specific than 打破 ("to crack or break open"), 打碎 denotes striking or dropping a brittle object (such as glass, porcelain, jade, or figuratively a dream or illusion) so that it shatters into pieces.

history.meaning: to smash or shatter into fragments by striking or dropping
to shatter, smash to pieces (physical vessels, glass, or figuratively dreams/illusions)

morphemes.meaning: to strike, to hit, to knock

打碎.notes: Compared with 打破 (which can mean merely cracking something or breaking an abstract rule/record), 打碎 emphasizes reducing something brittle to fragments (e.g., 打碎花瓶 "shatter a vase", or figuratively 打碎幻想 "shatter an illusion").

rootFamily.gloss: to crush, to smash, to shatter; crushed, broken to pieces

打磨.etymology: Compound verb of 打 ('work on, strike') + 磨 ('grind, polish, rub smooth on a whetstone'): 'sand, polish, buff, grind smooth (wood, metal, jade, or figuratively a piece of writing)'.

history.stage: Song–Ming craft vocabulary to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: grind and polish smooth; sand; refine

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 打磨 (via 萌典)

打算.etymology: Compound verb and noun of 打 (light verb) + 算 ('calculate, reckon, plan'): 'plan, intend (to do); plan, intention'. Attested from Song–Ming vernacular.

history.meaning: reckon and plan; intend to; plan

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 打算 (via 萌典)

打进.etymology: A verb-directional/resultative compound formed from the verb 打 (dǎ, "to strike, fight one's way, drive, shoot") and the directional complement 进 (繁體 進, jìn, "to advance, enter, penetrate into", originally depicting a bird moving forward/upward). Originating in military and sports contexts for fighting one's way into a fortified position, scoring a ball into a goal, or advancing into a tournament round (e.g., 打进决赛 "advance to the finals"), it is widely used in commercial and media Mandarin for breaking into a competitive market or industry tier.

history.meaning: to fight or force one's way inside; to drive or strike (something) into
to score (a goal), advance into (finals), or break into / penetrate (a market or circle)

morphemes.meaning: to strike, to fight one's way, to shoot (a ball)

打进.notes: Versatile across three key domains: sports (打进一球 "score a goal", 打进总决赛 "make it into the finals"), business/media (打进国际市场 "break into the international market"), and telecommunications (电话打进来 "a phone call comes through").

rootFamily.gloss: to enter, to go into, to move into (a stage or market)
to march into, to make inroads into (a new market or field)
to open up, to forge ahead, to pioneer (a market)

cognates.meaning: to forge; to build; to fashion

打造.etymology: A coordinative-manner compound combining 打 (dǎ, Middle Chinese *tæŋX, 'to strike, hammer, beat metal') and 造 (zào, Middle Chinese *dzawX, 'to construct, fabricate, create'). Originally a literal metallurgical and artisanal term in Tang–Song vernacular Chinese referring to hammering and forging gold, silver, or iron implements on an anvil, it underwent semantic extension in late 20th-century Hong Kong and Taiwan media discourse to mean meticulously crafting a brand, star persona, or flagship television program.

history.meaning: to strike/hammer (打) + to construct/make (造)
to forge metalware, jewelry, or weapons by hammering; to fashion furniture
to craft, cultivate, or build into a premier brand, show, or talent

打造.notes: Ubiquitous in entertainment and marketing prose (e.g., 倾力打造 'spare no effort to craft', 打造爆款 'forge a blockbuster hit'); carries a more deliberate, artisanal nuance than simple 制作 (produce).

cognates.meaning: to forge and bring out; to successfully create

打造出.etymology: A resultative-directional verb compound formed by attaching the directional complement 出 (chū, Middle Chinese *tshwit, 'to emerge, come forth, produce as an outcome') to the disyllabic verb 打造 (dǎzào, 'to forge, craft'). While 打造 focuses on the deliberate process of hammering and fashioning raw material or talent, the complement 出 focalizes the successful emergence and completion of the finished product or flagship creation.

history.meaning: to forge metalware + to come out / emerge
to successfully forge, fashion, or bring into existence a finished work or brand

morphemes.meaning: out, forth (indicating emergence of a product)

打造出.notes: Requires a concrete or abstract resulting object immediately following it (e.g., 打造出一流节目 'forge a first-class program'); cannot stand at the end of a clause without an object.

扔.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 扌 (手, 'hand') + 乃 (nǎi/rēng phonetic): originally 'pull, draw near' in Classical dictionaries, and in northern Mandarin the everyday verb for 'throw, toss; throw away, discard'.

history.stage: Ming–Qing northern vernacular to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: throw; toss; throw away

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 扔 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to throw down; to leave behind

扔下.etymology: A verb-directional/resultative compound uniting 扔 (rēng, from Middle Chinese *nying, 'to pull, draw, throw, cast away', written with the hand radical 扌 and phonetic 乃) and the directional complement 下 (xià, Middle Chinese *hæX, 'downward, down into a settled state'). From the physical act of flinging an object downward to the ground, the compound developed the figurative sense of abruptly forsaking responsibilities, work, or companions.

history.meaning: to draw/throw + downward
to toss down an object; to leave behind or desert someone
to abandon, toss aside, or walk away from a person or duty

扔下.notes: Often appears in the disposal construction 把…扔下 (e.g., 把烂摊子扔下 'walk away and leave a mess behind') to emphasize irresponsible abandonment under pressure.

rootFamily.gloss: to lay down, let go of

扔掉.etymology: Resultative verb-complement compound from 扔 ('throw; toss; cast aside', hand 扌 + phonetic 乃) + phase/disposal complement 掉 ('fall off; get rid of; dispose'). Adding 掉 emphasizes that the discarded object is permanently thrown away and removed.

history.meaning: throw away; discard
throw away; toss out

cognates.meaning: to ask someone for a favor; to entrust someone

托人.etymology: A verb-object (VO) syntactic compound combining 托 (tuō, simplified from Traditional 託, Middle Chinese *thak, 'to entrust with words, commission, rely upon', composed of 言 'speech' and phonetic 乇) with the generic object 人 (rén, Middle Chinese *nyin, 'person, someone'). Note that simplified 托 merged two distinct classical characters: 托 ('to support on the palm') and 託 ('to entrust verbally'); here the underlying etymon is 託.

history.meaning: to entrust through speech + a person
to commission an intermediary to handle a matter or deliver a message
to ask someone to pull strings or handle an errand on one's behalf

托人.notes: Functions as a pivotal verb phrase (托人 + VP, e.g., 托人打听 'ask someone to inquire around') and frequently implies using personal connections (关系) behind the scenes.

cognates.meaning: to lift or carry with both hands/shoulders
to lift up, carry on shoulders

扛.etymology: A phono-semantic compound (形声) composed of the semantic hand radical 扌 (shǒu, 'hand, manual action') and the phonetic component 工 (gōng, Old Chinese *kˤoŋ, Middle Chinese *kuwŋ). In Classical Chinese, 扛 was read gāng (from *kuwŋ) and meant 'to lift a heavy object (such as a tripod cauldron) with both hands' (as in 力能扛鼎 'strength enough to lift a cauldron'). In Northern Mandarin, a voiced/aspirated colloquial reading káng emerged for carrying loads on a single shoulder, which later extended metaphorically to bearing heavy pressure or responsibility.

history.meaning: to lift a heavy vessel or crossbar with both hands (read gāng)
to carry a heavy load or pole on one's shoulder
to carry on the shoulder; to bear responsibility, withstand pressure, or carry box-office/ratings

扛.notes: In contemporary film and television jargon, 扛收视 (káng shōushì) or 扛票房 (káng piàofáng) means 'to carry the ratings/box office on one's shoulders' as a lead star or producer.

rootFamily.gloss: shoulder a burden and see it through

cognates.meaning: to shoulder and endure to the end

扛下来.etymology: A verb-directional-resultative phrase built from the verb 扛 (káng, 'to carry on one's shoulder, bear a heavy load') and the compound directional complement 下来 (xiàlái, 'down toward the speaker; continuing from a past challenge through to completion'). Here 下来 does not denote physical downward motion, but rather the aspectual-resultative sense of enduring an ordeal all the way through and successfully taking ownership of the burden.

history.meaning: to carry on the shoulder + downward toward the speaker
to take a heavy burden or crisis onto one's shoulders and endure it to completion

morphemes.meaning: hither, sustaining through to the present/end

扛下来.notes: Splits around an object (扛下这个责任来) or follows 把 (把所有压力都扛下来); signals grit and personal accountability when a project is in crisis.

扣.etymology: A phono-semantic compound combining the hand radical 扌 (shǒu, 'manual action') and phonetic 口 (kǒu, Old Chinese *kʰˤ(r)oʔ, Middle Chinese *khuwX / *khuwH). In the *Shuowen Jiezi* and Classical texts, 扣 originally meant 'to rein in or pull back a horse' (牵马也), while also serving as a graphic variant of 叩 ('to strike, knock, tap'). From the core sense of 'holding back a horse by the reins' evolved the meanings 'to fasten/hook together', 'to detain', and 'to hold back or deduct a portion of wages or points'.

history.meaning: to pull back or rein in a horse; to strike or knock (variant of 叩)
to hook, button, or fasten tightly; to hold back or detain
to deduct or dock (pay, points, budget); to fasten; to place upside down

扣.notes: Highly polysemous in workplace and media contexts: 扣工资 ('dock wages'), 扣分 ('deduct points'), 扣帽子 ('slap a political/negative label on someone'), and 环环相扣 ('closely linked like interlocking rings').

rootFamily.gloss: deduct, subtract from pay or score

扣留.etymology: A coordinative-resultative verb compound uniting 扣 (kòu, Middle Chinese *khuwX, 'to rein in, hold back, restrain forcibly') and 留 (liú, Middle Chinese *ljuw, 'to keep, cause to stay, detain'). Attested in Song–Yuan legal and vernacular administrative prose and reinforced in modern East Asian legal terminology, the compound literally means 'to restrain and keep from departing', applying both to persons held in custody and to goods or equipment impounded by authorities.

history.meaning: to rein in/restrain + to keep/cause to remain
to hold back goods, envoys, or suspects from leaving
to detain a person in custody or impound passports, vehicles, or equipment

扣留.notes: Used for both people (被警方扣留 'detained by police') and documents/cargo (扣留护照 'impound a passport', 扣留器材 'hold production gear'); less formal than 拘留 (jūliú, statutory administrative/criminal detention).

cognates.meaning: to be on duty (police, military, security)

执勤.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound formed from 执 (zhí, Traditional 執, Middle Chinese *tsyip, depicting hands in manacles/grasping tightly, hence 'to hold, grasp, perform') and 勤 (qín, Middle Chinese *gjin, 'toil, diligent service, official duty'). Coined in modern administrative and military Mandarin on the classical pattern of 执事 ('to hold charge of affairs'), it denotes actively performing scheduled guard, patrol, or security duty on site.

history.meaning: to grasp/undertake + diligent labor/service
to be on active guard, patrol, or security duty

执勤.notes: Specifically used for uniformed personnel—police, soldiers, or event security guards—stationed at a post (e.g., 保安在现场执勤 'security guards are on duty at the venue'), whereas office or studio staff use 值班 (zhíbān).

执行.etymology: A coordinative verb compound combining 执 (zhí, Traditional 執, Middle Chinese *tsyip, 'to grasp, hold in hand, maintain') and 行 (xíng, Middle Chinese *hæŋ, 'to walk, act, put into practice'). Already attested in Classical and Han-era texts (where 執法行令 meant 'to hold fast to the law and put orders into practice'), the compound was revitalized in Meiji Japan as 執行 (shikkō) to translate Western legal and administrative 'execution/enforcement' and re-entered modern Mandarin across legal, corporate, and media production spheres.

history.meaning: to hold fast to + to put into practice/action
to enforce laws or court judgments; to administer rites or duties
to carry out, implement, or execute a plan, order, or production schedule

执行.notes: In television and event production, 执行力 (zhíxínglì, 'execution capability / ability to get things done on the ground') is prized as the core trait of an effective production team.

rootFamily.gloss: executive director (of a board or show)

cognates.word: 執行監製 (zap1 hang4 gaam1 zai3)

执行监制.etymology: A four-character modifier-head nominal compound calqued on English 'executive producer', joining 执行 (zhíxíng, Traditional 執行, 'executing, operational, executive') with 监制 (jiānzhì, Traditional 監製, from 監 'to oversee, inspect from above' + 製 'to manufacture, produce'). While 監製 originally denoted an imperial official supervising court workshops (such as porcelain or weaponry manufacture) in Ming–Qing China, Hong Kong cinema and television adapted it for film/TV 'producer', and prefixing 执行 specifies the hands-on executive overseeing day-to-day production.

history.meaning: imperial official supervising state manufacturing workshops
film or television producer/supervisor
executive producer responsible for hands-on project execution and line supervision

执行监制.notes: In Mainland Chinese TV industry credits, 总监制 is often a senior network executive, whereas 执行监制 (or 执行制片人) is the hands-on producer running daily studio budgets, schedules, and crises.

cognates.meaning: to expand and replenish; to augment

扩充.etymology: A coordinative-resultative verb compound combining 扩 (kuò, Traditional 擴, Middle Chinese *khwak, 'to stretch out, broaden, extend outward') and 充 (chōng, Middle Chinese *tsyhuwŋ, 'to fill up, make full, replenish'). This pair traces directly to Mencius (*Mengzi*, 2A:6), who wrote of the 'four moral sprouts' (四端) in human nature: 知皆擴而充之矣 ('to know how to broaden and fill them out to their full capacity'). In modern East Asian usage, the classical phrase contracted into the disyllabic compound 扩充, meaning to expand and enrich equipment, staff, or capacity.

history.meaning: to broaden (moral sprouts) and fill them to full capacity (Mencius)
to expand and substantiate military forces, institutions, or faculties
to expand, augment, or build up (staff, equipment, memory, or content)

扩充.notes: Unlike 扩大 (which merely increases size or scale), 扩充 emphasizes adding substantive new content, personnel, or resources to fill out an organization (e.g., 扩充团队 'augment the team', 扩充设备 'expand equipment inventory').

rootFamily.gloss: escalate, expand in scale or scope

扩大.etymology: A verb-resultative / coordinative compound joining 扩 (kuò, Traditional 擴, Middle Chinese *khwak, composed of 扌 'hand' and phonetic 廣 guǎng 'wide', meaning 'to stretch wide, extend') and 大 (dà, Middle Chinese *dajH, 'large, great'). Standardized in modern Sino-Japanese (拡大 kakudai) and modern Mandarin, it describes stretching the boundaries of an area, market, influence, or conflict so that it becomes larger in scale or scope.

history.meaning: to stretch wide + large/great
to magnify optically; to enlarge the scope or scale of an organization or issue
to expand (influence, market, scale) or escalate (a conflict or crisis)

扩大.notes: Collates naturally with abstract nouns of scope or impact: 扩大影响 ('expand influence'), 扩大规模 ('expand scale'), or negatively, 事态扩大 ('the situation/crisis escalated').

cognates.meaning: diffusion, dispersion, spreading (also viral sharing online)

扩散.etymology: A coordinative verb compound pairing 扩 (kuò, Traditional 擴, Middle Chinese *khwak, 'to extend outward, widen') and 散 (sàn, Middle Chinese *sanH, 'to scatter, disperse, dissipate'). Originally popularized in modern scientific translation (via Japanese 拡散 kakusan for physical 'diffusion' of gases, light, or molecules), it broadened in general Mandarin to describe the outward spread of rumors, public opinion, disease, or viral media content.

history.meaning: to stretch outward + to scatter/disperse
physical diffusion of particles, heat, or light
to diffuse, spread, or go viral (of news, rumors, crises, or pollutants)

扩散.notes: In PR and showbiz crisis management, 防止消息扩散 ('prevent the news/leak from spreading') and 舆论扩散 ('spread of public opinion') are standard expressions.

扫.etymology: Ideogram (traditional 掃) combining 扌 (手, 'hand') + 帚 ('broom', depicting a bundle of twigs tied to a handle): 'sweep with a broom, clear away; sweep across (with the eyes or a scanner)'. Read sǎo as a verb ('sweep') and sào in nouns like 扫帚 ('broom').

history.meaning: hand holding a broom = sweep, clear away
sweep; clear; scan (sǎo)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 扫 (via 萌典)

扫描.etymology: A modern technical coordinative compound combining 扫 (sǎo, Traditional 掃, Middle Chinese *sawX, 'to sweep across with a broom') and 描 (miáo, Middle Chinese *mjew, 'to trace, delineate, copy lines with a brush'). Coined in the 20th century as an ingenious semantic translation of English 'scan' in cathode-ray television broadcasting and radar engineering—where an electron beam 'sweeps across' (扫) a screen to 'trace and render' (描) an image line by line—it subsequently came to mean digitizing paper documents with an optical scanner.

history.meaning: to sweep across + to trace/delineate lines
raster scanning of an electron beam in television CRT displays and radar systems
to scan a document, QR code, or medical image; to survey a topic rapidly

扫描.notes: Used both for office hardware (扫描文件 'scan a document', 扫描仪 'scanner') and in media headlines as a noun meaning 'panoramic overview' (e.g., 焦点扫描 'focus scan/roundup').

rootFamily.gloss: sweep one's eyes over; scan a QR code

扭.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining the hand radical 扌 with phonetic 丑 (*chǒu*, originally a hand twisting or gripping, Middle Chinese *nrjuwX*). From the core action of twisting or wrenching with the hand, it extended to spraining a joint (扭伤) or turning one's head or body around.

history.meaning: twist or wrench with the hand
twist; sprain (an ankle); turn around

cognates.meaning: to get mixed up with; to drag into

扯上.etymology: A verb-resultative compound formed from 扯 (chě, a vulgar/vernacular graphic variant of 撦 attested from Yuan–Ming times, meaning 'to pull, tug, tear, chat idly') and the resultative complement 上 (shàng, Middle Chinese *dzyangX, 'onto, into contact or attachment'). From the literal physical act of pulling two threads or garments until they snag on one another, 扯上 evolved metaphorically to mean getting entangled, implicated, or associated with a person, scandal, or topic.

history.meaning: to pull/tug + onto/into contact
to pull someone or something into a connection; to become entangled with

扯上.notes: Almost always collocates with 关系 (扯上关系 'get tangled up with / become implicated in') or 边 (扯不上边 'have nothing whatsoever to do with'), usually with an undertone of unwanted complication or gossip.

扳手.etymology: Compound tool noun combining 扳 (bān, 'pull or turn a lever/handle by hand', 扌 + 反) + 手 ('hand / tool handle'): 'wrench, spanner'.

history.meaning: levering hand tool = wrench, spanner

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 扳手 (via 萌典)

扶住.etymology: Resultative verb compound from 扶 ('support with the hand; steady', hand 扌 + phonetic 夫) + resultative complement 住 ('hold fast; stay firm'). Together they express catching or holding onto someone or something so that it stays upright and does not fall.

morphemes.meaning: support with the hand; prop up

history.meaning: hold steady with the hand
hold steady; support firmly

cognates.meaning: batch, lot; to comment on or approve officially; to wholesale
to strike; to critique or endorse officially (as in 批判, 批准)

批.etymology: A phono-semantic character composed of 扌 (shǒu, 'hand') and phonetic 比 (bǐ, Old Chinese *piʔ, Middle Chinese *phjej). In Classical Chinese, 批 meant 'to strike or slap with the hand' (as in *Zuo Zhuan*). During the Tang and Song dynasties, imperial and bureaucratic practice used 批 for writing vermilion rescripts or marginal decisions on submitted memorials ('to endorse/annotate an official document'). Because official rescripts authorized releases of goods or groups of candidates at one time, commercial and administrative Mandarin developed the measure-word and noun sense of 'a batch, lot, or shipment processed together'.

history.meaning: to strike with the hand; to push aside or pare
to write an official endorsement, judgment, or critical note on a document
batch, lot, or group of people/goods; to approve officially; to wholesale

批.notes: Extremely versatile: as a classifier/noun (一批新人 'a batch of newcomers', 分批 'in batches') and as a verb in studio management (批预算 'approve a budget').

批准.etymology: A verb-resultative administrative compound combining 批 (pī, Middle Chinese *phjej, 'to write an official rescript or endorsement on a petition') and 准 (zhǔn, Middle Chinese *tsywinX, 'to grant, permit, allow', specialized in bureaucratic usage from 準 'level, standard'). Originating in Song–Yuan–Ming memorial bureaucracy, where a magistrate or emperor wrote 批 ('endorsed') with the verdict 准 ('granted') at the end of a petition, it grammaticalized into a single verb meaning 'to officially approve or ratify'.

history.meaning: to annotate/endorse a petition + to grant/permit
to grant official sanction to a memorial; in international law, to ratify a treaty
to approve, sanction, or authorize a request, budget, or broadcast license

morphemes.meaning: endorse or respond to a written submission

批准.notes: Denotes top-down authorization from a superior or regulatory body (e.g., 广电总局批准 'approved by the broadcast regulator', 批准立项 'approve project greenlighting').

rootFamily.gloss: written instruction or approval from a superior

找.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 扌 (手, 'hand') + 戈 (gē). A vernacular character that emerged in Medieval–Ming Chinese (linked to 爪 zhǎo 'claw/grope for' and 划 huá 'row') as the everyday verb for 'look for, search for, seek; call on someone; give change (找钱)'.

history.meaning: look for; seek; give change

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 找 (via 萌典)

找不着.etymology: A negative potential verb-complement construction formed from 找 (zhǎo, originally a vernacular graph related to 爪/划 meaning 'to paddle, scratch', which replaced 尋 xún in Ming–Qing Mandarin as the primary verb for 'to look for, seek'), the negative potential infix 不 (bù, 'not / cannot'), and the resultative attainment particle 着 (zháo, Traditional 著, Middle Chinese *drjak, 'to touch, make contact with, attain a goal'). Literally 'to seek but fail to make contact with'.

history.meaning: to seek + not + to touch/attain
unable to find, locate, or get hold of someone or something

morphemes.meaning: make contact with, succeed in reaching (read zháo)

找不着.notes: More colloquial and vivid than 找不到 (zhǎobudào), especially in Northern Mandarin and idioms like 找不着北 ('lose one's bearings completely / be utterly confused'). Be careful to pronounce 着 as zháo, not zhe or zhuó.

找出.etymology: A verb-resultative/directional compound combining 找 (zhǎo, Ming–Qing vernacular verb meaning 'to look for, search') and the directional-resultative complement 出 (chū, Middle Chinese *tshwit, 'out, forth, into visibility'). Whereas 找到 (zhǎodào) simply records successful location, 找出 highlights extracting, uncovering, or singling out a hidden item, culprit, or root cause from among a larger group or complex situation.

history.meaning: to search for + to bring out into the open
to find out, uncover, or identify a hidden flaw, reason, or person

找出.notes: Frequently used in troubleshooting and investigation: 找出原因 ('uncover the cause'), 找出漏洞 ('find the loophole/flaw'), or 找出幕后黑手 ('uncover the mastermind behind the scenes').

找到.etymology: Resultative verb compound combining the search verb 找 ('look for') + the attainment complement 到 ('reach, succeed in finding'): 'find (succeed in locating what one was looking for)'.

history.meaning: search and reach = find

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 找到 (via 萌典)

找回.etymology: Resultative verb compound combining 找 ('look for') + 回 ('return, get back'): 'find and get back, recover, retrieve'.

history.meaning: find and recover; retrieve

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 找回 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to bear, endure, withstand; to inherit
to inherit, succeed to; to receive
to receive and inherit; to bear

承受.etymology: A coordinative verb compound uniting 承 (chéng, Old Chinese *djang, Middle Chinese *dzying, depicting two hands lifting or receiving an object from below, hence 'to hold up from beneath, receive respectfully') and 受 (shòu, Old Chinese *duʔ, Middle Chinese *dzyuwX, depicting a boat/vessel passed from one hand to another, hence 'to receive, accept, undergo'). In Classical and Buddhist Chinese, 承受 meant 'to receive and carry on a legacy, mandate, or teaching'; in modern Mandarin, it focuses on passively absorbing or withstanding heavy weight, pressure, or emotional blows from above.

history.meaning: to hold up from below + to receive/accept (a mandate, estate, or teaching)
to inherit property or legal rights; to bear physical weight
to bear, withstand, or endure psychological pressure, loss, or physical load

承受.notes: Contrast with 承担: 承受 emphasizes enduring impact or pressure exerted on oneself (承受压力 'withstand pressure', 承受打击 'endure a blow'), whereas 承担 emphasizes actively taking on a duty or cost.

cognates.meaning: to undertake, shoulder responsibility or expenses

承担.etymology: A coordinative verb compound joining 承 (chéng, Middle Chinese *dzying, 'to hold up from below, receive and undertake') and 担 (dān, Traditional 擔, Middle Chinese *tam, 'to carry on the shoulders with a carrying pole'). Combining the gesture of receiving a charge with lifting a shoulder pole, 承担 developed in Song–Ming vernacular and administrative prose to mean voluntarily or legally taking upon oneself a duty, risk, liability, or financial expense.

history.meaning: to receive from above + to carry on a shoulder pole
to undertake an official obligation, tax burden, or guarantee
to shoulder or bear responsibility, legal liability, risk, or expenses

承担.notes: Standard collocations are active and agentive: 承担责任 ('shoulder responsibility'), 承担后果 ('bear the consequences'), 承担费用 ('cover the expenses').

承认.etymology: A coordinative verb compound combining 承 (chéng, Middle Chinese *dzying, 'to receive, accept') and 认 (rèn, Traditional 認, Middle Chinese *nyinH, 'to recognize, identify, acknowledge as true'). Attested in Tang–Song vernacular and legal texts for confessing or acknowledging a claim, and later reinforced by Meiji Sino-Japanese 承認 (shōnin) in diplomatic and legal contexts (translating 'recognition' of a state or right), it means both 'to admit a fault/fact personally' and 'to grant official recognition'.

history.meaning: to accept/undertake + to recognize/acknowledge
diplomatic or legal recognition; to confess or acknowledge a fact
to admit (a mistake, feeling, or fact); to officially recognize (a status or government)

承认.notes: Covers both reluctant personal admission (承认错误 'admit a mistake', 不得不承认 'have to admit') and formal institutional recognition (获得国际承认 'gain international recognition').

技战术.etymology: A modern syllabic contraction (缩略语) of the coordinative phrase 技术和战术 (jìshù hé zhànshù, 'technical skills and battle tactics'). It pairs the first morpheme of 技术 (jìshù, Traditional 技術, from 技 *gjeX 'craft, manual skill' + 術 *zywit 'method, art') with the full disyllabic noun 战术 (zhànshù, Traditional 戰術, from 戰 *tsyenH 'warfare, combat' + 術 *zywit 'art, tactic'). Coined in 20th-century Chinese military training and sports broadcasting, it frequently extends to competitive television reality shows and business rivalries.

history.meaning: skill/craft + warfare/contest + method/art
individual technique + operational tactics
combined skills and tactics in sports, e-sports, military drills, or competitive shows

技战术.notes: Follows the typical Chinese [1 + 2]prosodic abbreviation pattern (like 科教片 from 科学 + 教育片); very common in sports commentary, e-sports, and competitive stage shows (技战术水平 'level of skills and tactics').

cognates.word: 技術人員 (gei6 seot6 jan4 jyun4)

cognates.meaning: technical personnel (cf. 技術者 gijutsusha / 技術要員)

技术人员.etymology: A four-character modifier-head nominal compound combining 技术 (jìshù, Traditional 技術, attested in *Shiji* and *Hanshu* for 'skill and artifice' and popularized in Meiji Japan as 技術 gijutsu to render Western 'technology/technique') with 人员 (rényuán, Traditional 人員, from 人 'person' + 員 'member of a roster, official personnel'). Together they designate specialized engineering or technical staff operating behind the scenes.

history.meaning: craft/skill (Classical) > technology (modern) + roster personnel
history.stage: Classical Roots to Early Modern Mandarin

history.meaning: technical staff, engineers, or technicians in a studio, factory, or organization

morphemes.meaning: member, personnel on a roster (Trad. 員)

技术人员.notes: A collective or individual occupational term in broadcast and film studios (e.g., 后台技术人员 'backstage technical crew' handling audio, lighting, and broadcast feeds); more formal than the slangy 理工男 or title 技师.

cognates.word: 技術犯規 (gei6 seot6 faan6 kwai1)

cognates.meaning: technical foul (often テクニカルファウル)
cognates.word: 技術犯規 / テクニカルファウル

技术犯规.etymology: A four-character modifier-head compound calqued on English 'technical foul' in basketball and competitive sports rules. It modifies the verb-object compound 犯规 (fànguī, Traditional 犯規, from 犯 *bjamX 'to violate, offend against' + 規 *kjwie 'carpenter's compass, rule, regulation') with the noun adjunct 技术 (jìshù, Traditional 技術, 'technical, procedural'). Beyond sports, colloquial Mandarin uses it metaphorically for breaking procedural rules or losing one's temper professionally.

history.meaning: to transgress established rules or monastic/administrative regulations
technical foul (non-contact unsportsmanlike or procedural infraction in sports); procedural slip-up

技术犯规.notes: Abbreviated in sports commentary as 技犯 (jìfàn) or 'T' (吃了一个T 'got hit with a T'); used humorously in workplace banter when someone commits a procedural blunder or outburst.

抄.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 抄. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 抄 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 抄 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 抄 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 抄. The etymology of 抄 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 抄
middle form of 抄
modern form of 抄

把.etymology: Measure word for objects you grip by a handle or back (一把钥匙 'a key', 一把椅子 'a chair') AND disposal coverb fronting a definite object before an action verb (把门打开). Both functions grew directly out of the Classical Chinese verb 把 ('grasp, hold in the hand', combining 扌 'hand' + 巴 phonetic).

history.meaning: hold or grasp in the hand
classifier for handled items; object-fronting marker

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 把 (via 萌典)

把手.etymology: Compound noun of 把 ('grasp, hold, handle', 扌 + 巴) + 手 ('hand', neutral tone shou when meaning 'handle/knob'): 'handle, grip, knob, pull (of a door, drawer, or tool)' (read bǎshou; contrast bǎshǒu 'person who guards a pass or skilled hand').

history.meaning: handle; knob; grip

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 把手 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: grasp, comprehension, command of a situation

把握.etymology: A coordinative verb-and-noun compound uniting two synonymous manual verbs: 把 (bǎ, Middle Chinese *pæX, 'to hold in the hand, grip') and 握 (wò, Middle Chinese *'æwk, 'to clench the fist around, grasp firmly'). Attested in Han–Tang texts (such as the *Book of Han* and Buddhist translations) in the literal sense of 'holding in one's grip', it evolved metaphorically along two paths: as a verb meaning 'to seize (an opportunity) or master (a rhythm/tone)', and as a noun meaning 'firm mental grip, certainty, or assurance of success'.

history.meaning: to hold in the hand + to clench/grasp firmly
to grasp the essence of a matter; to have firm control over
(noun) confidence, certainty of success; (verb) to seize an opportunity or control pacing/tone

把握.notes: As a noun, it almost always pairs with 有/没有 and takes a degree modifier (有十足的把握 'have 100% confidence/certainty'); as a verb, it collocates with 机会 ('seize an opportunity') or 节奏 ('control the pacing of a show').

cognates.meaning: handle; leverage or dirt on someone
handle, grip; point to seize upon in an argument

把柄.etymology: A coordinative/modifier-head nominal compound combining 把 (bǎ, Middle Chinese *pæX / *pæH, 'to grip in the hand; a grip') and 柄 (bǐng, Middle Chinese *pjængH, 'wooden handle or shaft of an axe, sword, or ladle; figuratively, authority or leverage', as in classical 國柄 'handle of state power'). Originally referring to the physical handle by which a tool or weapon is gripped, it shifted metaphorically in Tang–Song vernacular to mean a 'handle' or incriminating weakness that allows an adversary to control, blackmail, or attack someone.

history.meaning: hand-grip + wooden handle/shaft of an implement or authority
physical handle of a vessel or blade; a pretext or leverage in a dispute
incriminating proof, dirt, or leverage held over someone

morphemes.meaning: grip, part held by the hand

把柄.notes: Typically used with verbs of seizing: 抓到把柄 or 落下把柄 ('let someone catch incriminating dirt/leverage on you'), a staple trope in media and corporate intrigue dramas.

抓.etymology: A phono-semantic and associative compound (形声兼会意) formed by adding the semantic hand radical 扌 (shǒu, 'hand') to 爪 (zhǎo/zhuǎ, Old Chinese *tsˤruʔ, Middle Chinese *tsræwX, pictograph of a hand or bird's talon reaching downward to clutch). Originally meaning 'to scratch or claw with the fingernails' (synonymous with 搔), 抓 broadened in post-Tang vernacular Chinese to mean 'to clutch, grab tightly, arrest (a suspect), or take firm charge of (key tasks)'.

history.meaning: to scratch or claw with nails or talons
to clutch, snatch, or seize with the hand; to arrest
to grab, scratch, arrest; to take firm charge of (production, quality, ratings)

抓.notes: In management and media production, 抓 means 'to focus intensely on and oversee' (e.g., 抓质量 'focus on quality', 抓收视率 'drive ratings', 两手抓 'tackle two priorities simultaneously').

rootFamily.gloss: seize firmly, pay close attention to time/work

抓住.etymology: Resultative verb compound combining 抓 ('grab, clutch, seize with the hand/claws', 扌 + 爪) + 住 ('hold fast, firmly'): 'grab hold of, catch, grip tightly, seize (an opportunity or person)'.

history.meaning: grab and hold fast; catch; seize

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 抓住 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to catch, succeed in grabbing or arresting

抓到.etymology: A verb-resultative compound combining the action verb 抓 (zhuā, from Middle Chinese *tsræwX, 'to claw, clutch, seize, arrest') with the resultative complement 到 (dào, Middle Chinese *tawH, 'to arrive at, reach, attain'). While 抓 alone expresses the attempt or action of grabbing or hunting for something (such as a suspect, an opportunity, or a camera shot), adding 到 confirms that the target has been successfully captured or obtained.

history.meaning: to clutch/seize + to reach/attain
to succeed in catching, arresting, or obtaining (a person, flaw, or opportunity)

抓到.notes: Used both physically (抓到小偷 'caught the thief') and figuratively in media work (抓到观众痛点 'hit upon the audience's pain point', 抓到把柄 'get hold of incriminating leverage').

rootFamily.gloss: capture, catch hold of (a moment or suspect)
grab and hold fast, catch red-handed

抓紧.etymology: A resultative verb-complement compound (动补结构) formed from 抓 (zhuā, Middle Chinese *tsrwae*, a hand-radical derivative of 爪 zhuǎ 'claw, talon', meaning 'to clutch, scratch, or seize with the hand') and 紧 (jǐn, Trad. 緊, 'tightly bound, taut, firm', from 糸 'silk cord' + 臤 qiān 'firm, solid'). Literally 'to grasp until tight', it underwent metaphorical extension in modern Mandarin from gripping a physical object to seizing fleeing time or pressing forward urgently with a task.

history.meaning: to scratch, clutch, or seize with claws or hands
to grip tightly with the hand; figuratively to seize time or attend closely to a matter

morphemes.meaning: clutch, grab, seize with the hand

抓紧.notes: Frequently takes 时间 (shíjiān, 'time') as its object (抓紧时间 'make every second count') or stands alone in imperative exhortations ('Hurry up!'). In production and workplace settings, 抓紧办 means to fast-track a task.

rootFamily.gloss: seize firmly, take charge of (work or production)

cognates.meaning: throwing in, investment, commitment of resources

投入.etymology: A verb-complement directional compound combining 投 (tóu, Old Chinese *\*do*, 'to cast, throw, fling', composed of 扌 'hand' + 殳 shū 'striking weapon/pole') and 入 (rù, Old Chinese *\*njup*, 'to enter, go into'). In Classical Chinese (e.g., *Zuo Zhuan*, *Shiji*), 投入 meant literally 'to throw something into (a river, vessel, or fire)' or 'to go into for shelter'. In modern Mandarin—reinforced by Meiji-era Japanese *tōnyū* (投入)—it developed abstract senses: pouring capital or labor into a venture, putting a system into operation, or immersing oneself emotionally in a creative role.

history.meaning: to cast or fling an object into; to enter into a place for refuge
to commit resources or capital; to throw oneself wholeheartedly into an activity or role
history.stage: Modern Mandarin (reinforced by Japanese 投入 tōnyū)

投入.notes: Used both transitively for committing resources (投入资金 'put in funds', 投入使用 'put into service') and adjectivally/intransitively in showbiz and everyday speech for being deeply absorbed (演得很投入 'acting with total immersion').

rootFamily.gloss: devote oneself to, throw oneself into

投资.etymology: A verb-object compound (动宾结构) uniting 投 (tóu, 'to cast, put in, commit') and 资 (zī, Trad. 資, Old Chinese *\*tsij*, from 貝 'cowrie/money' + phonetic 次 cì, meaning 'property, wealth, goods, capital'). Although both morphemes are ancient in Classical Chinese, the compound 投資 was synthesized in Meiji Japan as a *wasei-kango* (*tōshi* 投資) to render English *investment* / *to invest*, and was borrowed back into late Qing and Republican Chinese as the standard financial and commercial term.

history.meaning: separate Classical roots: 投 'to cast/present' and 資 'wealth, provisions, material resources'
commitment of capital for financial return (translation of English 'invest / investment')
to invest capital; financial investment in a business, film, or project

投资.notes: Functions as both a noun ('an investment') and a separable or transitive verb ('to invest in'). In media and film production, 投资方 (tóuzīfāng) or 资方 refers to the financial backers/investors behind a show.

投资界.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正结构) formed by suffixing 界 (jiè, Old Chinese *\*kˤrerts*, 'boundary, border, realm', composed of 田 'field' + phonetic 介 jiè 'dividing line') to 投资 (tóuzī, Trad. 投資, 'investment'). In Classical Chinese, 界 denoted physical borders between fields or territories; through Buddhist Sanskrit translations (*dhātu* / *loka* = 界 'realm, world') and modern Sino-Japanese usage, -界 became a productive suffix denoting a professional sphere or community ('the world of...', 'circles').

history.meaning: boundary between agricultural fields; territorial border; Buddhist realm (dhātu)
the investment community, venture capital and financial circles

morphemes.meaning: boundary, realm, professional circle or community

投资界.notes: The suffix -界 (jiè) productively forms nouns for entire industries or public spheres, such as 娱乐界 (yúlèjiè, 'entertainment world'), 演艺界 (yǎnyìjiè, 'show business'), and 传媒界 (chuánméijiè, 'media circles').

rootFamily.gloss: outside world, public outside a given sector

抗议.etymology: A compound of 抗 (kàng, Old Chinese *\*kʰˤaŋs*, 'to lift up, withstand, oppose as an equal', from 扌 'hand' + phonetic 亢 kàng 'neck, high') and 议 (yì, Trad. 議, Old Chinese *\*ŋ(r)aj-s*, 'to deliberate, discuss, critique', from 言 'speech' + 義 yì 'rightness'). In Literary Chinese (e.g., *Hou Hanshu* and Tang memorials), 抗議 meant 'to speak out frankly to a ruler or superior, offering unyielding counsel'. In the Meiji era, Japanese repurposed 抗議 (*kōgi*) to translate Western legal and diplomatic *protest*, which then re-entered modern Mandarin.

history.meaning: to debate frankly with a superior; to submit forthright remonstrance at court
formal diplomatic, legal, or political protest (calque of Western 'protest')
to protest, object formally or collectively; a protest

morphemes.meaning: discuss, express opinion or criticism (Trad. 議)

抗议.notes: Used both formally in diplomacy and politics (提出强烈抗议 'lodge a strong protest') and semi-jokingly in workplace or team dialogue when staff object to grueling overtime or unfair decisions.

折.etymology: Ancient ideogram attested on Shang oracle bones and Zhou bronzes showing an axe (斤) cutting a tree branch in two (斷/艸, later written as 扌): 'snap, break, bend, fold, turn back, convert/discount (at tenths of full price)'. Read zhé ('fold, break, discount'), shé ('snap in two, lose money'), and zhē ('turn over, pour back and forth').

history.meaning: axe snapping a bough = break, bend, fold
fold, break, discount (zhé); snap/lose (shé)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 折 (via 萌典)

折叠.etymology: Coordinative verb compound of 折 ('bend, fold over') + 叠 (疊, 'pile up in layers, fold'): 'fold up, fold over'. Attested since Tang–Song poetry and prose.

history.meaning: fold up; collapsible

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 折叠 (via 萌典)

折叠椅.etymology: Three-character compound combining 折叠 ('folding, collapsible') + 椅 ('chair'): 'folding chair'.

history.meaning: folding chair

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 折叠椅 (via 萌典)

折扣.etymology: Merchant accounting compound of 折 ('break off, reduce proportionally') + 扣 ('hold back, deduct from a sum'). In Chinese shopkeeper usage, 打九折 states the fraction retained (9/10 = 90%), whereas 折扣 names the price reduction itself.

history.meaning: percentage deduction on list price
retail discount

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 折扣 (via 萌典)

折痕.etymology: A determinative compound combining 折 (zhé, depicting an axe 斤 severing or bending timber 木/艸 with the hand 扌, hence 'to fold, crease, snap') and 痕 (hén, 'visible trace, scar, mark'). Just as 刮痕 names a scratch mark and 泪痕 a tearstain, 折痕 names the crisp line impressed into paper, card, or linen where it has been folded.

history.meaning: fold + physical trace
paper or fabric crease; fold line

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 折痕

cognates.meaning: to break, snap; to grind, polish (constituent kanji)

折磨.etymology: A coordinative verb compound (联合结构) pairing 折 (zhé, Old Chinese *\*tet*, 'to snap, break in two, bend, humble', originally depicting an axe 斤 chopping a tree/plant 艸) with 磨 (mó, Middle Chinese *mwa*, 'to grind on a millstone, rub, wear down', from 石 'stone' + phonetic 麻 má). Attested in Tang poetry (e.g., Bai Juyi) and Yuan *zaju* drama (sometimes written 折挫), the pairing combines the violent snapping of wood with the slow grinding of stone to express relentless physical or mental torment and affliction.

history.meaning: to wear down, buffet, or exhaust through misfortune and hardship
to torment, subject to an ordeal; physical or psychological torture/affliction

折磨.notes: Note the second-tone reading zhé here (unlike first-tone zhē in 折腾). Commonly used both as a verb (折磨人 'to torture people') and as a noun for a grueling creative or emotional ordeal (受折磨 'suffer torment').

rootFamily.gloss: go back and forth exhaustingly; put someone through trouble

折纸.etymology: Verb-object compound and noun of 折 ('fold') + 纸 (紙, 'paper'): 'fold paper; paper folding, origami'.

history.meaning: fold paper; paper-folding craft (origami)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 折纸 (via 萌典)

折腾.etymology: A colloquial Northern Mandarin compound combining 折 (read in the first tone zhē, a vernacular vocalic divergence of 折 zhé meaning 'to flip over, turn back and forth, pour from one vessel to another') and 腾 (téng, neutralized to轻声 *teng*, Trad. 騰, Old Chinese *\*lˤəŋ*, 'to gallop, leap, rear up, stir about', from 馬 'horse' + phonetic 朕 zhèn). Recorded in Qing dynasty Beijing vernacular novels (such as *Hongloumeng* and *Ernü Yingxiong Zhuan*), it evolved from 'tossing and turning sleeplessly' to doing things over and over in an exhausting, chaotic, or restless way.

history.meaning: to toss and turn in bed; to turn things over repeatedly or squander wealth
to go back and forth exhaustingly; to put someone through repeated revisions or trouble; to bustle about

morphemes.meaning: flip over, turn back and forth (zhē)
leap, stir up, toss about (Trad. 騰, read neutral tone)

折腾.notes: One of the most expressive words in Mandarin workplace and TV-production slang: endless script rewrites, last-minute edits, or indecisive bosses 'tossing the team around' are all described as 折腾 (别折腾了 'stop making us jump through hoops').

rootFamily.gloss: flip over, do a somersault (read zhē跟头)
bustle about, stir up commotion; make room (腾出)

抛.etymology: A monomorphemic verb (Trad. 拋, pʰau in the *Guangyun* rime dictionary) formed from 扌 ('hand'), 尤 (yóu), and 力 (lì, 'muscular force'), arising in Six Dynasties and Tang vernacular Chinese as a graphic specialization of /摽 ('to fling with force'). Originally denoting the physical act of hurling a stone or ball through the air in an arc, it broadened in modern Mandarin to pitching ideas, unveiling plans, casting glances, or dumping goods on the market.

history.meaning: to fling, hurl, or cast away with the hand; to leave behind
to toss out, pitch (an idea or question), unveil, or dump (assets)

morphemes.meaning: toss, fling, cast out with the hand (Trad. 拋)

抛.notes: In media, variety shows, and business meetings, 抛 (often 抛出 pāochū) means to 'pitch' or 'put on the table'—e.g., 抛出一个问题 ('toss out a question'), 抛梗 (pāogěng, 'drop a punchline/setup'), or 抛砖引玉 ('offer a modest idea to elicit better ones').

rootFamily.gloss: sell off in large quantities, dump (stock/goods)
toss out a brick to attract jade; offer a preliminary idea

抛头露面.etymology: A symmetrical four-character verb-object idiom (成语) composed of two parallel V-O pairs: 抛头 (pāotóu, Trad. 拋頭, 'to thrust out or expose one's head') and 露面 (lùmiàn, 'to uncover or show one's face'). Coined in Song–Yuan–Ming vernacular drama and fiction, it originally reflected strict Confucian seclusion norms (*neiwai youbie*), under which women of respectable households were expected to stay indoors; showing one's face in public streets was censured as 抛头露面. In modern Mandarin, it describes appearing in the public eye or on camera, often in contrast to working behind the scenes (幕后).

history.meaning: (of women in traditional society) to appear unveiled in public view, considered undignified
to appear in public, go on camera, or make public appearances (often used playfully or self-deprecatingly)

抛头露面.notes: In *Behind the Scenes* (幕后之王) and media contexts, 抛头露面 contrasts directly with 幕后工作 ('behind-the-scenes work'): producers often joke that they prefer staying off-camera rather than 'showing their faces in public' (抛头露面).

rootFamily.gloss: show one's face, make an appearance
stand out, show off one's abilities in public

抛弃.etymology: A coordinative synonymous compound (联合结构) joining 抛 (pāo, Trad. 拋, 'to fling away, cast off') and 弃 (qì, Trad. 棄, Old Chinese *\*kʰi[t]-s*, 'to discard, abandon'). In oracle bone and bronze inscriptions, 棄 graphically depicts two hands (廾) holding a winnowing basket/scoop (畢) to cast away a newborn infant (子, written inverted as 𠫓). Combined in Tang–Song poetry and prose, 拋棄 reinforced the concrete act of throwing away with the emotional sense of forsaking a person, duty, or principle.

history.meaning: to cast away (originally an infant), abandon, reject
to fling away, forsake, abandon a person, belief, or possession

抛弃.notes: Stronger and more emotional than 放弃 (fàngqì, 'give up a goal/right'). While 放弃 takes abstract goals or rights as objects, 抛弃 typically takes people, loyalties, or old traditions that are callously cast aside.

rootFamily.gloss: give up, renounce, abandon (a goal or right)

抢.etymology: Phono-semantic character (traditional 搶, combining 扌 'hand' + 倉 cāng/qiǎng phonetic): 'snatch, grab by force, rob; vie/scramble to be first (抢着做); rush against time (抢修)'.

history.meaning: push against; snatch; vie for
snatch; grab; rush/vie for

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 抢 (via 萌典)

抢戏.etymology: A verb-object compound (动宾结构) formed from 抢 (qiǎng, Trad. 搶, Middle Chinese *tsʰjangX*, 'to snatch, vie for, grab by force', from 扌 'hand' + phonetic 倉 cāng) and 戏 (xì, Trad. 戲, Old Chinese *\*hŋ(r)aj-s*, 'play, theatrical performance, dramatic scene'). Originating in traditional Chinese opera (*xiqu*) and modern film/television jargon, it describes a supporting actor, extra, or even a prop 'snatching the dramatic focus' (戏) away from the lead performer, hence 'stealing the scene' or 'upstaging'.

history.meaning: separate roots: 搶 'to snatch, vie for' and 戲 'theatrical play, stage performance'
to steal a scene, upstage the lead actor; figuratively to draw attention away from the main focus

morphemes.meaning: theatrical scene, dramatic focus, performance (Trad. 戲)

抢戏.notes: Originally theater/TV slang for an actor overacting or outshining the protagonist, now widely used in everyday Mandarin and social media when a background detail, pet, or outfit steals all the attention (太抢戏了!).

rootFamily.gloss: steal the spotlight, steal the show
share of screen time or dramatic weight in a script

抢救.etymology: A modifier-head / serial verb compound combining 抢 (qiǎng, Trad. 搶, here used in its derived adverbial/verbal sense 'to rush against time, act urgently before it is too late', from 'vie/contend for') and 救 (jiù, Old Chinese *\*kuks*, 'to stop harm, rescue, save, relieve', from 攴 'strike/action' + phonetic 求 qiú). Rather than 'snatching by force', 抢 here marks a race against imminent loss (parallel to 抢修 'rush-repair'), yielding 'to rush to rescue'—whether resuscitating a critically ill patient or salvaging endangered cultural relics or a failing broadcast.

history.meaning: to rescue from danger, relieve distress, stop harm
to rush to rescue life, property, or a critical situation against urgent time pressure; to administer emergency medical treatment

morphemes.meaning: rush against time, act urgently (Trad. 搶)

抢救.notes: Used primarily for emergency medical resuscitation (送医院抢救 'rush to the hospital for emergency treatment'), disaster relief, and metaphorically in media production for 'rescuing' corrupted footage or a PR crisis at the eleventh hour.

rootFamily.gloss: do rush repairs (on infrastructure or equipment)
save, rescue from danger or ruin

抢滩登陆.etymology: A four-character serial verb-object phrase (连动结构) uniting 抢滩 (qiǎngtān, Trad. 搶灘, 'to rush a river shoal or storm a beach') and 登陆 (dēnglù, Trad. 登陸, 'to ascend the shore, make landfall', from 登 'ascend' + 陸 'high dry land'). Historically, 抢滩 referred to boatmen hauling vessels rapidly across treacherous river rapids (滩) before water levels shifted, and later to amphibious troops storming an enemy beachhead. In late 20th- and 21st-century business and media Mandarin, the military phrase was metaphorically extended to aggressively entering and capturing a new market or broadcasting platform ahead of rivals.

history.meaning: (of boats) to rush across shallow river rapids; (military) to storm a beachhead
to storm a beachhead and make an amphibious landing; figuratively to seize a foothold in a competitive market

morphemes.meaning: rush/seize the beach or shoal (Trad. 搶灘)
ascend/land on the shore (Trad. 登陸)

抢滩登陆.notes: A favorite idiom in media industry and venture-capital reporting: when streaming platforms or production houses race to launch in a new sector (e.g., short-video or overseas markets), headlines describe them as 抢滩登陆.

rootFamily.gloss: seize a beachhead; enter a market ahead of rivals
make landfall; log in / launch in a market
seize the initiative or commanding heights

报.etymology: A foundational monomorphemic root (Trad. 報, Old Chinese *\*pˤuks*). In Shang oracle bone and Western Zhou bronze inscriptions, 報 depicts a hand (又) gripping manacles (幸/𡴘) behind a kneeling person (卩), originally meaning 'to pass legal judgment on a convict commensurate with the crime' (*Shuowen Jiezi*: 報，當罪人也). From 'exact legal requital', its sense evolved in Classical Chinese to 'repay (kindness or vengeance)', then 'reply or report back to a superior', and finally in modern Mandarin to 'announce, report, register/sign up for (short for 报名), or newspaper'.

history.meaning: to adjudicate and sentence a criminal; to requite or repay (favor or grievance) in kind
to reply, report back to a superior; official gazette or bulletin (邸報)
to report, announce; to sign up / enroll in (as in 报名/报考); newspaper or periodical

morphemes.meaning: requite, report, announce, register for (Trad. 報)

报.notes: When followed by a course, competition, or audition (e.g., 报了个培训班 'signed up for a training class', 报节目 'submit a show entry'), 报 acts as a concise verb meaning 'to register/enroll in' (short for 报名 or 申报).

rootFamily.gloss: apply/submit for official approval (e.g., a project or budget)

报告.etymology: A coordinative compound (联合结构) pairing two Classical Chinese verbs of upward communication: 报 (bào, Trad. 報, 'to reply, report back to an authority') and 告 (gào, Old Chinese *\*kˤuk-s*, originally depicting an ox 牛 approaching a ritual vessel/mouth 口 to announce a sacrifice to the ancestors, meaning 'to proclaim, inform, report respectfully'). While attested in Literary Chinese for 'informing and reporting', 報告 was standardized in Meiji Japan (*hōkoku*) and modern Mandarin as the formal verb and noun for submitting an official report, briefing, or academic lecture.

history.meaning: to inform, announce, and report back to a superior or deity
to report formally (verb); a written or oral report, briefing, or public lecture (noun)
history.stage: Modern Mandarin (reinforced by Japanese 報告 hōkoku)

报告.notes: Unlike 报道 (bàodào, journalistic media coverage for the public), 报告 refers to reporting to a superior, boss, or institution (向总监报告 'report to the director'), or a formal document/talk (收视率报告 'ratings report').

rootFamily.gloss: inform, notify; official notice or call sheet (in film/TV: 通告)

报废.etymology: A verb-object / verb-complement compound combining 报 (bào, Trad. 報, 'to report officially to authorities or accounting') and 废 (fèi, Trad. 廢, Old Chinese *\*p(r)ats*, originally 'a collapsed roof/house' from 广 'shelter' + 發 fā, hence 'abandoned, ruined, out of service, obsolete'). Coined in modern administrative and industrial management for formally reporting equipment or vehicles as broken beyond repair so they can be written off and scrapped, it quickly entered colloquial Mandarin to mean 'completely ruined, wrecked, or exhausted'.

history.meaning: (of a building) to collapse; to abolish, discard, fall into disuse
to officially declare equipment obsolete and scrap it; colloquially, to be ruined, wrecked, or rendered useless

morphemes.meaning: ruined, discarded, out of commission (Trad. 廢)

报废.notes: In TV production and everyday speech, 报废 is used both literally for ruined broadcasting gear or footage and hyperbolically for human exhaustion (连轴转三天，人都快报废了 'After three days of non-stop shifts, I am practically ready for the scrapyard').

rootFamily.gloss: cast aside as useless; waste, scrap material
abolish, annul, cancel (a treaty or rule)
reimburse expenses; (slang) be wiped out or ruined

cognates.meaning: to report a case to the police

报案.etymology: A verb-object compound (动宾结构) formed from 报 (bào, Trad. 報, 'to report to authorities') and 案 (àn, Old Chinese *\*ʔˤans*, from 木 'wood' + phonetic 安 ān). In Classical Chinese, 案 denoted a short-legged wooden tray or magistrate's writing desk; during the Han–Tang periods, by metonymy from the official's desk to the documents placed upon it (案牘), 案 came to mean 'an official legal record or judicial case'. Thus 报案 literally means 'to report an incident so it is entered on the magistrate's/police docket'.

history.meaning: wooden serving tray or official's writing desk; by metonymy, official dossier or legal case on the desk
to formally report a crime or legal case to judicial or police authorities

morphemes.meaning: legal case, official dossier (originally 'magistrate's wooden desk')

报案.notes: Compare 报案 with 报警 (bàojǐng): 报警 focuses on calling the police or sounding an immediate emergency alarm (e.g., dialing 110), whereas 报案 emphasizes formally filing a criminal complaint or case report at the police station.

rootFamily.gloss: register and open an official legal case; project approval
solve a criminal case; proposal/plan (方案)

报纸.etymology: Compound of 报 ('report, gazette, bulletin', as in imperial 邸报 court gazettes) + 纸 ('paper', silk/fibre radical 纟 + 氏, perfected during the Eastern Han).

history.meaning: printed newspaper
newspaper; newsprint

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 报纸 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to call the police; to sound an alarm

报警.etymology: A verb-object compound (动宾结构) joining 报 (bào, Trad. 報, 'to report, announce') and 警 (jǐng, Old Chinese *\*kreŋʔ*, 'to warn, be on guard, alert', from 言 'speech' + 敬 jìng 'respectful vigilance'). In Ming–Qing military prose, 報警 meant 'to report an urgent border alert or enemy incursion'. After modern Chinese adopted 警察 (jǐngchá, from Meiji Japanese *keisatsu*) for 'police', 警 acquired the bound meaning 'police force', giving 报警 its dual modern senses: 'to call the police' and 'to sound an emergency alarm'.

history.meaning: to report an urgent military threat or sound a border defense alert
to call or report an emergency to the police; (of a device) to sound a warning alarm

morphemes.meaning: warning alert, emergency; police (short for 警察)

报警.notes: Separable verb (报了警 'called the police'). Also used in technical and studio settings for equipment alarms (烟雾报警器 'smoke detector', 系统报警 'system warning alert').

rootFamily.gloss: be on the alert, vigilant against danger

报道.etymology: A coordinative compound uniting 报 (bào, Trad. 報, 'to report, announce') and 道 (dào, Old Chinese *\*kə.lˤuʔ*, originally 'road, way', extended in Classical Chinese to 'to speak, recount, tell'). Attested in Tang–Song poetry and vernacular literature (e.g., Su Shi's *ci* lyrics) with the general sense 'to announce, pass word along', 報道 was specialized in modern journalism—reinforced by Japanese *hōdō* (報道)—to denote mass-media news reporting and coverage. (In Taiwan and Hong Kong, it is frequently written 報導 with 導 'to guide/convey'.)

history.meaning: to inform, pass word along, announce news orally
to cover or report news through mass media (verb); a news report or journalistic story (noun)
history.stage: Modern Mandarin (reinforced by Japanese 報道 hōdō)

报道.notes: Do not confuse 报道 ('news report / media coverage') with the homophonous 报到 (bàodào, with 到 'arrive', meaning 'to check in / register arrival at work, school, or a film set').

rootFamily.gloss: check in, report for duty or registration (homophone contrast)
newspaper and periodical press; media coverage
track and report a developing story (跟踪报道)

cognates.meaning: to claim reimbursement; to write off

报销.etymology: A serial verb compound (连动结构) combining 报 (bào, Trad. 報, 'to submit an official statement or account') and 销 (xiāo, Trad. 銷, Old Chinese *\*s.ew*, 'to melt down metal', from 金 'metal' + phonetic 肖 xiào, extended to 'cancel, annul, clear from a ledger'). Originating in Ming and Qing dynasty fiscal bureaucracy (報銷錢糧), officials had to submit an itemized report (報) to the Ministry of Revenue so that state funds advanced for public projects could be canceled/cleared (銷) from the imperial account books. In modern Mandarin, it means to submit receipts for expense reimbursement.

history.meaning: (of imperial officials) to submit final accounts of state expenditures to clear an advance from the treasury ledger
to submit an expense account for reimbursement; colloquially, to write off as destroyed or dead

morphemes.meaning: submit an account or report (Trad. 報)
melt metal; cancel, clear from an account book (Trad. 銷)

报销.notes: Essential workplace vocabulary: 开发票报销 ('get an official tax receipt for reimbursement'). In colloquial slang, 报销 can also mean 'wiped out' or 'totaled' (那辆车彻底报销了 'That car is a total write-off').

rootFamily.gloss: write off, cancel (an account, permit, or registration)

cognates.meaning: to open, spread out, disclose; to drape over shoulders
to drape over the shoulders; cape

披.etymology: A monomorphemic verb (Old Chinese *\*pʰ(r)aj*) formed from 扌 ('hand') and the phonetic-semantic component 皮 (pí, 'skin, hide, outer pelt'). Etymologically part of the Old Chinese word family including 皮 ('outer skin/fur') and 被 (bèi/pī, 'blanket, wear on the back'), 披 in Classical Chinese meant both 'to spread open with the hands, split apart' (as in opening a scroll, 披閱) and 'to drape a cloak, pelt, or armor over one's shoulders without putting the arms into sleeves' (披衣, 披甲). Both senses survive in modern Mandarin.

history.meaning: to spread open, divide; to drape a garment or armor loosely over the shoulders
to drape over one's shoulders (a coat, shawl, or loose hair); in compounds, to disclose or open (披露)

morphemes.meaning: drape over the shoulders; spread open, disclose

披.notes: Contrast 披 ('drape loosely over the shoulders', e.g., 披着外套, 披头散发 'with hair hanging loose over the shoulders') with 穿 (chuān, 'put on clothing by inserting arms/legs through sleeves/openings').

rootFamily.gloss: shawl, cape, poncho draped over the shoulders
open up and reveal; publicly disclose information
cleave through thorns and brambles; overcome obstacles on a pioneering path

抬.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 扌 (手, 'hand') + 台 (tái phonetic; also written 擡 with 臺): 'lift up, raise (one's head, hand, or eyes); carry a heavy object together between two or more people'.

history.meaning: lift; raise; carry together

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 抬 (via 萌典)

抬头.etymology: Verb-object compound of 抬 ('lift, raise') + 头 (頭, 'head'): 'raise one's head, look up' (and on invoices or receipts, the 'payee/header line').

history.meaning: raise one's head; look up; invoice header

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 抬头 (via 萌典)

抱.etymology: Phono-semantic/ideographic character of 扌 (手, 'hand/arms') + 包 (bāo, 'wrap, enfold'): 'hold in one's arms, embrace, hug; cherish/harbor (hope or an attitude); classifier for armfuls'.

history.stage: Old & Classical Chinese (Shijing, Laozi) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: enfold in the arms; hug; hold; cherish

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 抱 (via 萌典)

抱歉.etymology: A verb-object compound (动宾结构) functioning as a stative verb/adjective, composed of 抱 (bào, Old Chinese *\*m-pˤuʔ*, 'to hold in the arms, embrace, cherish or harbor in one's bosom') and 歉 (qiàn, Middle Chinese *kʰemX*, 'crop failure, dearth of grain; deficiency, regret', from 欠 'yawn/lack' + phonetic 兼 jiān). In *Shuowen Jiezi*, 歉 is glossed as 'not eating one's fill' (食不滿也) due to a poor harvest; by extension it came to mean 'falling short of what is due'. Literally 'to harbor a sense of deficiency/regret in one's heart', 抱歉 became a polite expression for feeling apologetic.

history.meaning: crop failure, dearth of grain; feeling of inadequacy or falling short
to harbor regret or a sense of falling short in one's bosom; to feel apologetic or sorry

morphemes.meaning: embrace, hold in the bosom, harbor in mind

抱歉.notes: More formal and courteous than 对不起 (duìbuqǐ). Unlike 对不起, 抱歉 can be modified by degree adverbs like 很 or 非常 (非常抱歉 'terribly sorry', 心怀抱歉 'feel apologetic at heart').

rootFamily.gloss: apologetic feeling, sense of regret or guilt

抵制.etymology: A coordinative / verb-resultative compound combining 抵 (dǐ, Old Chinese *\*tˤijʔ*, 'to push back, butt against, withstand, resist', from 扌 'hand' + phonetic 氐 dī) and 制 (zhì, Old Chinese *\*tets*, originally depicting a knife 刀 cutting branches off a tree 未, meaning 'to cut to measure, regulate, curb, hold in check'). While both roots are Classical, the compound 抵制 gained prominence in late Qing political movements (notably the 1905 anti-American boycott, 抵制美貨) as the standard Chinese rendering for English *boycott* and active resistance against harmful practices.
