history.meaning: Classical roots: 抵 'push against, withstand' and 制 'curb, restrain, regulate'
to hold in check and oppose; to boycott foreign goods or refuse participation in a practice or event

抵制.notes: In media and entertainment culture, 抵制 frequently refers to public or industry boycotts—e.g., 抵制劣迹艺人 ('boycott scandal-tainted celebrities') or 抵制盗版 ('boycott piracy').

rootFamily.gloss: conflict with, feel averse or resistant to
resist, stand up to (an aggressor or temptation)

抵触.etymology: A coordinative compound (Trad. 牴觸 or 抵觸) originally formed from two vivid pastoral verbs containing the 'horn' (角) or 'ox' (牛) radical: 牴 (dǐ, later simplified/merged into 抵, 'to butt or gore with horns') and 触 (chù, Trad. 觸, Old Chinese *\*tʰok*, from 角 'horn' + phonetic 蜀 shǔ, 'to ram, butt, or prod with horns', *Shuowen*: 觸，牴也). In Classical texts (*Hanshu*, *Huainanzi*), 牴觸 literally depicted two horned animals locking horns; it evolved metaphorically to mean 'to clash, contradict (of laws or arguments)' and in modern Mandarin 'to feel psychologically averse or resistant to'.

history.meaning: (of horned cattle or rams) to butt and gore each other with their horns; to clash violently
to conflict or contradict (of rules or statements); to feel psychological aversion or resistance toward (抵触情绪)

morphemes.meaning: butt with horns, push against (classically 牴)
gore, ram with horns; touch, clash (Trad. 觸)

抵触.notes: Often used in the collocation 产生抵触情绪 (chǎnshēng dǐchù qíxù, 'develop a resistant/hostile attitude') when team members or audiences push back against a new policy or creative direction, or 与…相抵触 ('be in conflict with [a regulation]').

rootFamily.gloss: touch, come into contact with; trigger emotions (触动)
clash, conflict, collision (of forces or ideas)

cognates.meaning: to wipe, erase, smear (e.g., 抹殺 massatsu)

抹.etymology: A monomorphemic hand-action verb composed of 扌 ('hand') and the phonetic-semantic element 末 (mò, Old Chinese *\*mˤat*, 'treetop, tip, fine powder'). Arising in post-Han and Six Dynasties Chinese, 抹 originally meant 'to rub powder or ointment onto a surface with the hand' or 'to wipe across'. In modern Mandarin it split into three readings by tone and vowel: mǒ ('to smear, apply cosmetics or salve, wipe away'), mò ('to plaster a wall, slip past'), and mā ('to wipe down with a cloth').

history.meaning: to rub, smear powder or salve with the hand; to wipe or stroke across
to apply, smear, or slick on (makeup, gel, ointment); to blot out or smear (figuratively, as in 抹黑)

morphemes.meaning: smear, apply, spread on, wipe (read mǒ)

抹.notes: In the reading mǒ, it is the everyday verb for putting on lipstick, face cream, hair gel, or ointment (抹口红, 抹发胶), as well as figurative idioms like 抹黑 (mǒhēi, 'smear someone's reputation') and 抹杀 (mǒshā, 'write off / obliterate').

rootFamily.gloss: blot out, erase, write off achievements or facts
apply makeup or paint thickly; doodle, scribble

押宝.etymology: A verb-object compound (动宾结构) formed from 押 (yā, Middle Chinese *ʔaep*, 'to press down, sign, pawn, place a wager on', from 扌 'hand' + phonetic 甲 jiǎ) and 宝 (bǎo, Trad. 寶, 'treasure; specifically the directional gaming die hidden inside a brass box in the traditional *yabao* gambling game'). In late imperial Chinese casinos, players in the game of 押寶 placed stakes (押) on which side of the covered 'treasure block' (寶) was facing which direction. Modern Mandarin generalized the gambling term into a vivid metaphor for backing a side or betting heavily on a person, project, or show.

history.meaning: to place a wager on the orientation of the hidden 'treasure' die in a traditional Chinese gambling game
to place one's bet, stake everything on a single person, project, or outcome

morphemes.meaning: pledge, pawn, place a wager on
treasure; the covered gaming die in the yabao game (Trad. 寶)

押宝.notes: Takes the preposition 在 (zài) to mark the target of the bet: 把全部希望都押宝在这部新剧上 ('stake all hopes on this new drama series'). Often used in investment and showbiz contexts when a studio bets big on an unproven talent or format.

rootFamily.gloss: place a bet, wager (in gambling or business)
mortgage, put up collateral for a loan

押韵.etymology: A traditional poetic verb-object compound joining 押 (yā, originally 'to sign a pledge or press down on a matching tally', in poetics 'to place a matching rhyme word at the end of a verse line') and 韵 (yùn, simplified from 韻, 'harmonious final syllable or rime'). Codified in Tang–Song regulated verse manuals, 押韵 passed into everyday Mandarin both as a verb ('to rhyme') and as a modifier (押韵的句子 'rhyming lines').

history.meaning: place matching rime syllables at verse endings
rhyme; be in rhyme

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 押韵

抽.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 扌 (手, 'hand') + 由 (yóu/chōu phonetic): 'pull out, draw out (a thread, lot, or drawer), pump/extract, whip/lash, shrink, smoke (inhale a cigarette)'.

history.meaning: draw out; pull forth; sprout
pull out; extract; find (time); smoke

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 抽 (via 萌典)

抽不出.etymology: A negative potential verb-complement construction (可能补语否定式) built from the root verb 抽 (chōu, Old Chinese *\*l̥u*, 'to pull out, draw forth', from 扌 'hand' + phonetic 由 yóu), the negative potential infix 不 (bù, 'unable to'), and the directional complement 出 (chū, 'out'). Originally denoting the physical pulling out of silk filaments or a blade, 抽出 (chōuchū) was metaphorically extended to 'extracting or freeing up' time, hands, or oneself from a tightly packed schedule; inserting 不 yields 抽不出 ('unable to pull out / spare').

history.meaning: to draw or pull out from inside (e.g., silk threads, a lot, or a weapon)
unable to draw out; figuratively unable to spare time (抽不出时间), hands (抽不出手), or oneself (抽不出身)

抽不出.notes: Almost always followed by an object indicating what cannot be spared: 抽不出时间 / 抽不出空 ('can't spare the time'), 抽不出手 ('have one's hands full'), or 抽不出身 ('can't get away from current duties'). Its affirmative counterpart is 抽得出.

rootFamily.gloss: find spare time, squeeze in free time
get away from duties, free oneself from an entanglement

抽屉.etymology: Compound furniture noun of 抽 ('pull out, draw forth') + 屉 (屜, originally a removable bamboo/wooden tray, pad, or tier inside a container, neutral tone ti): 'pull-out compartment -> drawer (of a desk or cabinet)'.

history.meaning: sliding drawer of a table or cabinet

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 抽屉 (via 萌典)

抽空.etymology: A separable verb-object compound (离合词 / 动宾结构) combining 抽 (chōu, 'to draw out, extract, pull from a tight bundle') and 空 (read in the departing fourth tone kòng, 'an empty space, gap, or unoccupied interval of time', derived by Old Chinese *-s* nominalizing suffixation from level-tone 空 kōng 'hollow, empty', from 穴 'cave' + phonetic 工 gōng). Literally 'to pull an empty slot out of a packed schedule', it vividly conceptualizes leisure time as something that must be extracted from busyness.

history.meaning: unoccupied space, gap, or interval of leisure (departing-tone derivation of 空 kōng 'empty')
to squeeze out or find spare time amidst busy work

morphemes.meaning: draw out, pull out, squeeze out
free interval, spare time, gap (read kòng)

抽空.notes: Note the fourth-tone pronunciation kòng (meaning 'spare time/space', often with erhua in Northern Mandarin: 抽空儿 chōukòngr), never first-tone kōng. Because it is a V-O separable verb, modifiers go in the middle: 抽个空 ('find a quick moment'), 抽点空 ('spare a little time').

rootFamily.gloss: have free time, be available (read yǒukòng)
get away from work or commitments

cognates.meaning: being in charge of (a class or duty)
being in charge of (esp. a homeroom class)
to undertake, hold the post of

担任.etymology: A coordinative verb compound (联合结构) uniting two Classical verbs grounded in the physical metaphor of carrying a load: 担 (dān, Trad. 擔, Old Chinese *\*tˤam*, 'to carry on the shoulders with a carrying pole', from 扌 'hand' + 詹 zhān) and 任 (rèn, Old Chinese *\*nəms*, 'to bear a burden, shoulder an office or responsibility', from 人 'person' + phonetic 壬 rén, which originally depicted a carrying pole). Consolidated in late imperial and modern usage (and parallel to Japanese *tannin* 担任), 'shouldering a burden' specialized into formally serving in an official post or professional role.

history.meaning: Classical roots: 擔 'to carry on one's shoulders' and 任 'to bear a load, hold an appointed office or trust'
to shoulder a responsibility; to serve as or hold the post of (an official, producer, director, or host)

morphemes.meaning: carry on the shoulders, undertake (Trad. 擔)
bear a burden, hold an office or duty

担任.notes: Always read with first-tone dān (verbal 'shoulder/undertake'), not fourth-tone dàn ('a physical load', as in 重担 zhòngdàn). It is the standard formal verb in media credits and résumés for holding a title: 担任总制片人 ('serve as executive producer').

rootFamily.gloss: take responsibility for, take charge of; homeroom teacher (班主任)

担心.etymology: Separable verb-object compound of 担 (擔, dān, 'carry on the shoulders, bear a load') + 心 ('heart, mind'): literally 'carry a burden on one's heart' -> 'worry, feel anxious, be concerned about'.

history.meaning: bear anxiety in one's heart = worry, be concerned

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 担心 (via 萌典)

拆.etymology: Phono-semantic/ideographic character combining 扌 (手, 'hand') + 斥 (chì, originally a cracked house/clod): 'split open, tear open (a letter or package), take apart, dismantle, demolish (a wall or old building)'.

history.meaning: crack open; split apart
open (mail/packages); dismantle; tear down

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 拆 (via 萌典)

拆信刀.etymology: A transparent three-part instrument compound formed from the verb-object phrase 拆信 (chāi xìn, 'to unseal/open a letter': 拆 'take apart, unseal' + 信 'letter') plus the head noun 刀 (dāo, 'knife, blade'). Coined in modern Chinese stationery usage alongside Western gummed and wax-sealed envelopes, 拆信刀 names the slender blunt-edged blade kept on a desk to slit envelopes cleanly.

history.stage: Late Qing / Early Modern Stationery Chinese
history.meaning: desk blade for opening sealed envelopes
letter opener; paper knife

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 拆信刀

拆开.etymology: A resultative verb-complement compound (动补结构) composed of 拆 (chāi, Middle Chinese *trhaek*, 'to split apart, tear open, unseal, demolish', from 扌 'hand' + 斥 chì, cognate with Classical 坼 chè 'fissure in parched earth, split open') and 开 (kāi, Trad. 開, Old Chinese *\*kʰˤəj*, 'to open', originally depicting two hands 廾 lifting a bar 一 from double doors 門). Here 开 functions as a resultative complement indicating separation achieved: 'to tear or take apart until open or separated'.

history.meaning: (of earth or plant husks) to split open; to unseal, tear apart, or dismantle by hand
to tear open (a letter or package), unpack, disassemble, or separate into parts

拆开.notes: Used both for physical unsealing/unpacking (拆开快递 'open a delivery package', 拆开信封 'slit open an envelope') and for breaking up a combined unit, script segment, or duo into separate pieces (把这两个部门拆开 'split these two departments apart').

rootFamily.gloss: demolish, tear down (a building or stage set)
disassemble, take apart (machinery or a structure)
expose a lie or scheme, unmask (拆穿)

拉.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 扌 (手, 'hand') + 立 (lì/lā phonetic). In Classical Chinese (Mengzi, Shiji), 拉 meant 'snap, break, crush by pulling'; from the Tang–Song vernacular onward it became the primary verb for 'pull, drag, draw, haul; play a bowed string instrument (violin, erhu); chat; help along'.

history.meaning: pull and break; crush
pull; draw; drag; play a bowed instrument

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 拉 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to pull, abduct (Sino-Japanese reading of 拉)

拉不开.etymology: A negative potential verb-complement construction (V-不-R) formed from 拉 (lā, Middle Chinese *lɑp, originally 'to break, crush, pull' in the Shuowen Jiezi, phono-semantic with 扌 'hand' and 立) + the negative potential infix 不 (bù, 'not / unable to') + the directional/resultative complement 开 (kāi, Middle Chinese *kʰʌi, 'to open, separate, part'). Literally 'unable to pull open or apart', it developed both physical senses (unable to slide open a door) and figurative senses in competition, social embarrassment (拉不开面子, unable to set aside pride/save face), and ratings gaps.

history.meaning: to pull apart, draw open physically
unable to pull open; unable to widen a gap or set aside face/inhibitions

拉不开.notes: Often used with abstract objects like 差距 (gap/lead, e.g., in TV ratings or scores: 拉不开差距 'unable to widen the lead') or 面子 (face/pride: 拉不开面子 'too embarrassed to refuse or be blunt').

rootFamily.gloss: able to pull open or widen
to pull and tug, drag along

拉倒.etymology: A resultative verb-complement compound (动补结构) composed of 拉 (lā, Middle Chinese *lɑp, 'to pull, drag') + 倒 (dǎo, Middle Chinese *tɑuX, 'to fall over, topple, collapse'). Originally meaning literally 'to pull down or pull until something collapses' (e.g., pulling down a wall or an opponent), in Northern Mandarin vernacular during the late Qing Dynasty it underwent colloquial semantic bleaching and idiomatization to mean 'to call something off, drop a matter, or leave it at that'—as if pulling down the framework of a dispute or plan so nothing remains standing.

history.meaning: to pull down, drag to the ground
to drop a matter, forget about it, call it quits (colloquial)
history.stage: Late Qing Vernacular to Modern Mandarin

拉倒.notes: Informal and slightly impatient in tone, frequently used at the end of a conditional clause (e.g., 不去就拉倒 'if you're not going, then forget it!') when abandoning a negotiation or argument.

拉开.etymology: A resultative verb-complement compound (动补结构) combining 拉 (lā, Middle Chinese *lɑp, 'to pull, draw, stretch', phono-semantic character with 扌 'hand' and 立) and 开 (kāi, traditional 開, Middle Chinese *kʰʌi, 'to open, unlatch, spread apart', depicting two hands removing a bar from a double door 門). From the literal physical action of pulling open a curtain, door, or bowstring, it extended metaphorically to 'initiating a grand event' (拉开序幕, pulling open the prologue curtain) and 'widening a spatial or competitive distance' (拉开距离/差距).

history.meaning: to pull open (a door, curtain, or bow) or draw apart physically
to pull open; to widen (a gap/lead); to kick off (an event)

拉开.notes: Essential in media and broadcasting collocations: 拉开序幕 ('pull back the curtain / kick off an event or series') and 拉开差距 ('widen the gap' in viewership ratings or rankings).

rootFamily.gloss: unable to pull open or widen

拉链.etymology: Compound noun combining 拉 ('pull') + 链 (鏈, 'interlocking metal chain'): 'zipper, slide fastener' (a descriptive calque of a chain fastened by pulling a slider).

history.meaning: pull-chain fastener = zipper

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 拉链 (via 萌典)

拉黑.etymology: A 21st-century Mainland Chinese internet and telecommunications neologism formed by telescoping the verb-object phrase 拉入黑名单 (lārù hēimíngdān, 'to pull/drag into a blacklist'). Here 拉 (lā, 'to pull, drag', representing the GUI action of dragging a contact or moving a record) combines with 黑 (hēi, Old Chinese *hmlɯːɡ, 'black', serving as a clipped morpheme for 黑名单 'blacklist', itself a calque of English 'blacklist'). Grammatically, it functions as a compact resultative-like verb compound where 黑 denotes the resulting status ('blacklisted/blocked').

history.meaning: blacklist (20th-century calque of English 'blacklist')
to drag into a blacklist; to block a user on phone or social media

拉黑.notes: Because 拉黑 originates as a contraction of a verb-object phrase, it can still take an aspect particle or object, or be split in playful colloquial speech, and pairs with 屏蔽 ('to mute/shield a feed').

rootFamily.gloss: to pull into a group chat

拌.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 拌. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 拌 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 拌 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 拌 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 拌. The etymology of 拌 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 拌
middle form of 拌
modern form of 拌

拍.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 扌 (手, 'hand') + 白 (bái/pāi phonetic): 'pat, clap, slap with the flat of the hand; swat; musical beat/meter; racket/bat; take (a photograph or film, from clicking the shutter); auction (from banging the gavel)'.

history.meaning: clap; pat; musical beat
pat; clap; beat; take (a photo/video)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 拍 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: photography, filming, shooting (related Sino-Japanese compound with 撮)

拍摄.etymology: A coordinative verb compound (并列结构) formed in modern Chinese photography and cinema terminology from 拍 (pāi, Middle Chinese *pʰˠæk, 'to clap, pat, strike, beat time') + 摄 (shè, traditional 攝, Middle Chinese *ɕiɛp, 'to grasp, gather, absorb, capture an image'). In late 19th and early 20th-century photography, 摄 was used in 摄影 (shèyǐng, 'to capture a shadow/image', attested in classical Daoist texts for 'gathering reflections' and repurposed for photography), while 拍 referred to snapping the shutter or clapping the slate on a film set. Combining 拍 and 摄 created the standard disyllabic verb for shooting photos, film, or television.

history.meaning: 拍: to strike, clap; 攝: to hold up, gather, absorb (qi or reflections)
to take photographs; to shoot film, video, or television scenes

拍摄.notes: In TV and film production (*幕后之王*), 拍摄 is the formal, professional verb for shooting scenes or programmes, whereas colloquial speech often uses 拍 alone (e.g., 拍戏 'shoot a drama', 拍片 'shoot a film').

拍摄组.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正结构) consisting of the disyllabic verbal noun 拍摄 (pāishè, 'filming, shooting', itself a coordinative compound of 拍 'to snap/shoot' and 摄 'to capture images') modifying the head noun 组 (zǔ, traditional 組, Middle Chinese *tsuoX, originally 'silk cord, ribbon, braid' with the silk radical 纟/糸 and phonetic 且, extended in Classical Chinese to 'to weave together, organize' and in modern Chinese to 'team, unit, crew, section'). Literally 'filming-unit', designating the on-location or studio production crew responsible for camera and shooting operations.

history.meaning: woven silk cord or ribbon; to braid or organize
filming unit, camera crew, production shooting team

拍摄组.notes: In television and film production, a large 剧组 (production crew) is often divided into specialized units such as 拍摄组 (filming crew/unit, sometimes split into A组 and B组) and 导演组 (directing team).

拐.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 扌 (手, 'hand') + 另 (lìng/guǎi, originally depicting a horned/forked walking staff): 'turn a corner, change direction; limp/hobble; walking stick (拐杖); abduct/swindle'.

history.meaning: turn a corner; crutch/walking stick; limp; swindle

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 拐 (via 萌典)

拐弯.etymology: Separable verb-object compound of 拐 ('turn') + 弯 (彎, 'curve, bend, corner'): 'turn a corner, make a turn, go around a bend'.

history.meaning: turn a corner; go around a bend

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 拐弯 (via 萌典)

cognates.word: 拒む (こばむ / kobamu; on'yomi きょ / kyo)

拒.etymology: From Classical Chinese 拒 (jù, Middle Chinese *ɡɨoX, Old Chinese *ɡaʔ), a phono-semantic character combining the hand radical 扌 (手, 'hand') with the phonetic component 巨 (jù, 'carpenter's square; great'). In early texts such as the *Lunyu* (Analects) and *Mencius*, 拒 is often interchangeable with 距 ('spur of a fighting cock; to stand against, resist') and means 'to ward off with the hands, hold at bay, defend against an advancing force', later generalizing to 'to refuse, reject, turn down' an offer, request, or entry.

history.meaning: to ward off, resist militarily, stop from advancing (attested in Analects: 其不可者拒之)
to repel, refuse, decline, turn down

morphemes.meaning: to ward off, resist, refuse, reject

拒.notes: As a monosyllabic verb, 拒 belongs to a terse, elevated, or journalistic register (e.g., 拒收 'refuse to accept', 拒签 'refuse a visa/signature'), though in modern workplace slang 被拒 ('got rejected') is ubiquitous.

拒不配合.etymology: A four-character semi-literary verbal phrase structured as 拒 (jù, Middle Chinese *ɡɨoX, 'to refuse, resist') + the negative adverb 不 (bù, 'not') + the coordinative disyllabic verb 配合 (pèihé, 'to coordinate, cooperate, match up', from 配 'to mate, match, pair' + 合 'to join, fit together'). The construction `拒不 + [Verb]` ('stubbornly refuse to [Verb]') uses 拒 adverbially/serially before a negated verb to emphasize deliberate, obstinate defiance (compare 拒不认罪 'refuse to plead guilty', 拒不执行 'refuse to execute an order').

history.meaning: to refuse and not [do something]; to obstinately defy an order
to flatly refuse to cooperate or coordinate

拒不配合.notes: Carries an official, legal, or journalistic tone often used in PR statements, police reports, or tense workplace disputes when a party stonewalls an investigation or production schedule.

rootFamily.gloss: to flatly refuse to admit guilt/fault

拒绝.etymology: Coordinative verb compound of 拒 ('ward off, resist, fend off with the hand', 扌 + 巨) + 绝 (絕, 'sever a silk thread -> cut off completely'): 'refuse, reject, decline, turn down'. Attested since the的后汉书 Book of the Later Han.

history.stage: Han Classical Chinese (Hou Hanshu) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: fend off and cut off -> refuse, reject, decline

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 拒绝 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to pull out, extract, surpass (Sino-Japanese ばつ / batsu; kun'yomi ぬく / nuku)

拔.etymology: From Old Chinese 拔 (bá, Old Chinese *bˤrat, Middle Chinese *bˠɛt), a phono-semantic character formed with the hand radical 扌 (手, 'hand') and the phonetic 犮 (bá, 'to pull by the roots; a dog running with its legs tied'). Glossing it as 擢也 ('to pull up, extract') in the *Shuowen Jiezi*, Classical Chinese used 拔 for pulling up plants by the roots (as in Mencius's famous parable 揠苗助长 / 拔苗助长), drawing a sword from its scabbard, capturing a fortified city, and elevating talent above the crowd (选拔, 提拔).

history.meaning: to pull up by the roots; to draw out; to storm and capture a walled city; to promote above others
to pull out, yank out, unplug, extract; to select or promote

拔.notes: Used across physical actions (拔草 'pull weeds', 拔牙 'pull a tooth', 拔插头 'unplug a cord/plug') and figurative elevation (提拔 'promote a subordinate').

rootFamily.gloss: to pull out, unplug, remove completely

拔掉.etymology: A resultative verb-complement compound (动补结构) combining 拔 (bá, Middle Chinese *bˠɛt, 'to pull out, uproot, extract') + the phase/resultative complement 掉 (diào, Middle Chinese *dieuH, originally 'to shake, wag', which grammaticalized in vernacular Mandarin into a completive resultative complement meaning 'off, away, completely removed'). Together, 拔掉 emphasizes the successful completion and disposal of the extraction—pulling a plug, tooth, weed, or obstacle all the way out.

history.meaning: to pull up by the roots, extract
to pull out completely, yank off, unplug, uproot

morphemes.meaning: off, away, out (indicating removal or completion)

拔掉.notes: More colloquial than 拔除; in broadcasting and studio settings, 拔掉 commonly refers to unplugging cables, microphones, or power cords (拔掉电源/插头).

拔腿就跑.etymology: Vivid four-character colloquial idiom from 拔 ('pull up; lift out') + 腿 ('leg') + 就 ('immediately; right away') + 跑 ('run; dash off'). Literally 'pull up one's legs and run at once', it depicts someone breaking into a run on the spot without a moment's hesitation.

history.meaning: take to one's heels immediately
take off running at once; bolt

拔除.etymology: A Literary Chinese coordinative/resultative verb compound composed of 拔 (bá, Middle Chinese *bˠɛt, 'to pull up by the roots, extract') + 除 (chú, Middle Chinese *ɖɨo, originally 'steps to a palace hall', extended in Old Chinese to 'to sweep away, clear out, eliminate, remove'). First attested in Han and Six Dynasties historical prose for 'uprooting and eliminating' weeds, evil factions, or deeply entrenched ailments, it retains a formal, surgical, or strategic register in modern Mandarin.

history.meaning: to uproot and sweep away (weeds, rebels, or spiritual impurities)
to root out, eradicate, surgically remove or extract (tubes, weeds, or factions)

morphemes.meaning: to pull up by the roots, extract

拔除.notes: Significantly more formal and written than 拔掉; used in medical contexts (拔除智齿 'extract a wisdom tooth') or metaphorically for rooting out rivals, strongholds, or systemic problems.

rootFamily.gloss: to eliminate, get rid of, clear away

拖慢.etymology: A resultative verb-complement compound (动补结构) formed from 拖 (tuō, Middle Chinese *tʰɑ, 'to drag, trail, haul behind, delay', with the hand radical 扌) + the adjectival resultative complement 慢 (màn, Middle Chinese *mˠanH, originally 'arrogant, negligent, lax' in Classical Chinese, shifting in Medieval Chinese to 'slow, unhurried'). Literally 'to drag (until) slow', describing how foot-dragging, bureaucracy, or technical glitches retard the pace of a project or production schedule.

history.meaning: 拖: to drag, trail behind; 慢: lax, negligent, slow
to slow down, retard, drag down the pace or progress of something

拖慢.notes: Commonly collocates with 进度 ('progress/schedule', e.g., 拖慢拍摄进度 'slow down the filming schedule') or 节奏 ('pace/rhythm').

rootFamily.gloss: to be in arrears, withhold pay
to drag down, encumber, be a burden on

拖欠.etymology: A modifier-head or serial verb compound (偏正/连动结构) combining 拖 (tuō, Middle Chinese *tʰɑ, 'to drag, trail behind, protract over time') + 欠 (qiàn, Middle Chinese *kʰɨɐmH, originally a pictograph of a person 儿/人 opening their mouth wide to yawn, lacking breath, hence 'to lack, be deficient, owe money or debt'). Attested in Ming and Qing dynasty administrative and vernacular texts for taxes or debts that are 'dragged out and owed' past their due date, it now specifically denotes defaulting on or withholding wages, rent, or contract payments.

history.meaning: to be in arrears on imperial taxes or private debts by dragging out payment
to be behind in payment, default on debts, withhold wages (e.g., 拖欠工资)

morphemes.meaning: to owe, be deficient, be in debt

拖欠.notes: Frequently appears in labor and contract disputes within the entertainment industry (e.g., 拖欠工资 'withhold wages', 拖欠片酬/尾款 'be in arrears on talent fees or final payments').

rootFamily.gloss: to owe money, be in debt; debt/arrears

cognates.meaning: to adhere rigidly to, be overly fastidious about
cognates.word: 拘泥 (こうでい / kōdei; こだわる / kodawaru)

cognates.meaning: to cling to, be bound by (hanja 拘泥)

拘泥.etymology: A Literary Chinese coordinative compound composed of 拘 (jū, Middle Chinese *kɨo, 'to seize, detain, restrain, bind', from 扌 'hand' + 句) + 泥 (nì, Middle Chinese *nieiH, in the departing tone meaning 'to be bogged down in mud, obstructed, inflexible, bigoted', derived by tone-derivation from 泥 ní 'mud, mire'). Notice the classical reading of 泥 in the sense of 'bogged down / obstinately attached' (originally attested in the *Analects* Zizhang chapter: 致远恐泥 'pursuing it too far, one fears becoming bogged down'). Together, 拘泥 literally means 'restrained and bogged down in mire', hence 'to cling rigidly to conventions or rules'.

history.meaning: to become bogged down in mud; to be held back by petty details or rigid doctrines (attested in Analects and Song Neo-Confucian texts)
to be rigidly confined to, stick stiffly to formalities or conventions

morphemes.meaning: to be bogged down in mud; inflexible, stubbornly attached

拘泥.notes: Almost always used in the negative with the preposition 于 (e.g., 不拘泥于形式 'not rigidly confined to formalities' or 别拘泥于传统套路 'don't cling stiffly to traditional formulas'). Note that standard Mainland Mandarin pronounces it *jūní* (second tone), while traditional/literary pronunciation preserves *jūnì* (fourth tone).

cognates.meaning: to beckon, invite, summon (Sino-Japanese しょう / shō; kun'yomi まねく / maneku)

招.etymology: From Old Chinese 招 (zhāo, Old Chinese *tjaw, Middle Chinese *tɕiɛu), a phono-semantic character combining the hand radical 扌 (手, 'hand') with the phonetic 召 (zhào, 'to summon by voice'). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as 手呼也 ('to summon by waving the hand, beckon'), contrasting 召 (calling with the mouth) and 招 (beckoning with the hand). From 'beckoning someone to come', it developed the senses 'to attract, invite, recruit (soldiers, students, or employees)', 'to provoke/incur (trouble)', and as a noun 'move, trick, strategy' (from martial arts hand movements).

history.meaning: to beckon with the hand; to summon, invite, attract
to recruit, enlist (soldiers/talent); to confess; a move or trick in martial arts
to recruit, hire (staff), admit (students); to beckon; trick/move

招.notes: In everyday workplace Mandarin, 招 is the go-to conversational verb for hiring or recruiting (e.g., 招人 'hire people', 招实习生 'recruit interns', 招生 'admit students').

rootFamily.gloss: greeting, hello; to notify or take care of

招呼.etymology: A coordinative compound (并列结构) uniting the two Classical Chinese synonyms for summoning: 招 (zhāo, Middle Chinese *tɕiɛu, 'to beckon with the hand', 手呼也) + 呼 (hū, Middle Chinese *huo, 'to call out with the voice, shout'). Originally a Literary Chinese verb meaning 'to beckon and call out to someone from afar', in Song–Yuan–Ming vernacular Mandarin (where 呼 undergoes tonal neutralization to *zhaohu*) it broadened into 'to greet someone verbally or with a wave', 'to give advance notice', and 'to look after or attend to guests'.

history.meaning: to beckon with the hand and call out with the voice; to summon
to greet, say hello (especially in 打招呼); to notify in advance; to look after guests

morphemes.meaning: to call out with the voice

招呼.notes: Most frequently encountered in the verb-object collocation 打招呼 (dǎ zhāohu), which means both 'to say hello / greet someone' and, in workplace/showbiz contexts, 'to give someone a heads-up or pull strings behind the scenes'.

rootFamily.gloss: to say hello; to give advance notice or pull strings
to call out to, appeal; to take care of

招待.etymology: Coordinate verb compound of 招 ('beckon with the hand; invite in', hand radical 扌 + 召 zhào) + 待 ('wait upon; treat; host', step radical 彳 + 寺). Together they express welcoming guests in and looking after them with tea, food, and courtesy.

history.meaning: receive and look after guests
receive; entertain; show hospitality to

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 招待

招手.etymology: Verb-object compound of 招 ('beckon with the hand') + 手 ('hand'): 'wave one's hand, beckon with the hand'. Attested since Classical prose and Tang poetry.

history.stage: Classical & Tang Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: beckon with the hand; wave

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 招手 (via 萌典)

招牌.etymology: Compound noun of 招 ('beckon, attract customers') + 牌 ('wooden or painted signboard, plaque'): originally the hanging wooden or cloth shop sign outside Song–Ming taverns and stores, and figuratively 'trademark, signature specialty, reputation'.

history.stage: Song–Ming urban commerce to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: shop signboard; signature specialty or reputation

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 招牌 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to invite and engage an expert or VIP with courtesy

招聘.etymology: A coordinative verb/noun compound (并列结构) formed from 招 (zhāo, Middle Chinese *tɕiɛu, 'to beckon, summon, invite') + 聘 (pìn, Middle Chinese *pʰiɛnH, 'to visit and inquire with ceremonial gifts; to engage a worthy scholar or betroth a bride with gifts'). In Classical Chinese statecraft, rulers 'summoned' (招) and 'sent ritual gifts of silk and jade to engage' (聘)贤士 (worthy scholars and advisors). In modern Mandarin, this classical courtly expression became the standard formal term for corporate recruitment and job hiring.

history.meaning: to summon and formally engage worthy scholars or officials with ceremonial gifts
to recruit, hire employees publicly; recruitment, hiring, job opening

morphemes.meaning: to engage with gifts, employ formally, hire

招聘.notes: Functions as both a verb ('to hire/recruit') and a noun ('hiring/recruitment', e.g., 校园招聘 'campus recruitment', 招聘会 'job fair'); contrasts with 应聘 (yìngpìn, 'to apply for a job').

rootFamily.gloss: to apply for a job (lit. respond to a recruitment call)

拜你所赐.etymology: A four-character semi-classical idiom (四字格) structured as 拜 (bài, Middle Chinese *pˠɛiH, 'to bow reverently in gratitude to receive') + 你 (nǐ, modern vernacular second-person pronoun 'you', replacing Classical 君/公) + 所 (suǒ, Classical Chinese object-relativizing particle turning the following verb into a nominalized patient, 'that which is...') + 赐 (cì, Middle Chinese *siᴇH, 'to bestow, grant from a superior to an inferior'). Literally 'I bow to receive that which you have graciously bestowed', originally a humble courtly expression of gratitude that is now used almost exclusively with biting irony and sarcasm ('all thanks to you!').

history.form: 拜君之賜 / 拜公所賜
history.meaning: to bow in gratitude for what Your Lordship has bestowed (sincere ceremonial expression in Zuozhuan and classical letters)

history.form: 拜你所賜 / 拜你所赐
history.meaning: all 'thanks' to you (ironic/sarcastic attribution of blame for a disaster or predicament)

morphemes.meaning: that which (marks the object of the following verb)

拜你所赐.notes: Despite its elevated, classical syntax (所赐), in modern dialogue it is virtually 100% sarcastic—used when confronting someone whose meddling or mistake caused a mess (e.g., 这全都是拜你所赐 'this mess is all thanks to you!').

rootFamily.gloss: to ask a favor, count on
to pay a formal visit; to worship/bow

cognates.meaning: to humbly request or entrust (Sino-Japanese はいたく / haitaku)

拜托.etymology: A sequential/coordinative polite verb compound formed from 拜 (bài, Middle Chinese *pˠɛiH, originally depicting two hands clasped and lowered in ritual obeisance, 'to bow in respect, salute') + 托 (tuō, traditional 託/托, Middle Chinese *tʰɑk, 'to entrust with the hand or in words, commission, rely upon'). Attested since the Tang and Song dynasties in epistolary and vernacular Chinese, 拜托 literally means 'to bow with clasped hands and entrust a matter to someone', evolving into both a polite verb ('to ask a favor of, entrust to') and a conversational interjection ('please! / come on!').

history.meaning: to bow respectfully and entrust a commission or request to someone (attested in Song–Yuan texts)
to ask a favor, count on someone; (colloquial interjection) please!, come on!

morphemes.meaning: to bow respectfully with clasped hands

拜托.notes: Has two distinct pragmatic uses in modern TV dramas: sincere entrustment (这件事就拜托你了 'I'm counting on you for this matter') and exasperated colloquial disbelief (拜托，你清醒一点！ 'Come on / Please, wake up!').

rootFamily.gloss: to pay a formal visit to
to ask a favor of someone (through connections)

cognates.meaning: colloquial farewell ('bye-bye', shortened from 'God be with ye')

拜拜.etymology: A 20th-century phonetic loanword (音译词) from English *bye-bye* (itself a reduplicated hypocoristic shortening of *goodbye*, from early modern English *God be with ye*). Written by repeating the character 拜 (bài, 'to bow with clasped hands'), which was chosen both for its close phonetic match to English *bye* and for its fortuitous graphic/semantic resonance with traditional Chinese parting bows and the folk gesture of waving or clasping hands at farewell.

history.meaning: colloquial reduplicated farewell in English
history.stage: Early Modern to Modern English Source

history.meaning: bye-bye, goodbye; (figuratively) to be finished, break up, or part ways with something

拜拜.notes: In casual spoken Mainland Mandarin, farewell 拜拜 is very often pronounced with rising second tones (*báibái*) rather than fourth tones (*bàibài*), which helps distinguish it from the ritual verb 拜拜 (bàibai, 'to worship deities at a temple with incense').

cognates.meaning: to imitate, model on, compare, plan (Sino-Japanese ぎ / gi; kun'yomi なぞらえる / nazoraeru)

拟.etymology: Simplified as 拟 from traditional 擬 (nǐ, Middle Chinese *ŋɨX, Old Chinese *ŋrəʔ), a phono-semantic character with the hand radical 扌 (手, 'hand') and the phonetic 疑 (yí, Middle Chinese *ŋɨ, 'to doubt, hesitate, deliberate'; the simplified form 拟 uses 以 as a cursive graphic reduction of 疑). Originally meaning 'to measure or estimate with the hand, compare, model upon' (*Shuowen Jiezi*: 度也), in Classical Chinese administrative and literary prose it developed the senses 'to deliberate and intend to do' and 'to draw up a tentative draft (of a decree, contract, or plan)'.

history.meaning: to estimate, measure against, compare; to imitate or simulate (attested in Yijing Xici: 擬諸其形容)
to draft (a document, proposal, or contract); to intend or plan to do (in official/journalistic prose)

morphemes.meaning: to draft, draw up; to intend; to simulate

拟.notes: Frequently used in corporate, legal, and media production contexts for drawing up contracts or proposals (e.g., 拟合同 'draft a contract', 拟定方案 'draw up a plan'), and in news headlines as a concise auxiliary meaning 'plan/intend to' (e.g., 公司拟收购... 'the company plans to acquire...').

rootFamily.gloss: to draft and finalize (a plan, list, or contract)
to draft a document or manuscript

拥堵.etymology: A coordinative verb/adjective compound (并列结构) composed of 拥 (yōng, traditional 擁, Middle Chinese *ʔɨoŋX, 'to embrace, throng, crowd around, surge together', from 扌 'hand' + 雍 'to dam up, obstruct') + 堵 (dǔ, Middle Chinese *tuoX, 'a low earthen wall; to wall up, block, stop up, clog', from 土 'earth' + 者). Notice that 雍 (the phonetic and etymonic core of 擁/壅) already carried the root sense of 'blocking a watercourse'. Combining 'crowding together' (拥) and 'blocking up' (堵) yields the vivid image of vehicles or crowds packing an artery until movement is choked off.

history.meaning: 擁: to throng, crowd together; 堵: earthen wall, to block or stop up
congested, gridlocked, bottlenecked (especially of urban road traffic or data networks)

拥堵.notes: More formal than colloquial 堵车 (dǔchē, 'traffic jam'); 拥堵 is the standard term used by GPS navigation apps, traffic broadcasts, and urban planners (e.g., 交通拥堵 'traffic congestion', 拥堵路段 'congested road section').

rootFamily.gloss: to be stuck in a traffic jam (colloquial VO)

cognates.meaning: to hold, possess (Sino-Japanese ようゆう / yōyū)

拥有.etymology: A coordinative/serial verb compound formed from 拥 (yōng, traditional 擁, Middle Chinese *ʔɨoŋX, 'to hold in one's arms, embrace, gather around oneself') + 有 (yǒu, Middle Chinese *ɦɨuX, Old Chinese *ɢʷəʔ, 'to have, possess, hold'). Originally attested in Han and Six Dynasties historical prose (such as the *Shiji* and *Hanshu*) in phrases describing warlords or monarchs 'holding in their embrace and possessing' vast territories, armies, or wealth (e.g., 拥有山河, 拥有重兵), in modern Mandarin it became the standard disyllabic transitive verb for 'to possess, own, enjoy (resources, rights, talent, or audiences)'.

history.meaning: to embrace and hold under one's command (territory, troops, or retainers)
to possess, have, own (property, rights, talent, or fanbases)

morphemes.meaning: to hold in one's arms, embrace, command

拥有.notes: Unlike simple 有, 拥有 carries a slightly elevated or emphatic nuance and typically takes valuable, sizable, or abstract objects (e.g., 拥有版权 'own the copyright', 拥有千万粉丝 'have tens of millions of fans', 拥有话语权 'hold the right to speak/authority').

rootFamily.gloss: to support, rally around (a leader or policy)

拦.etymology: Simplified as 拦 from traditional 攔 (lán, Middle Chinese *lɑn), a phono-semantic character combining the hand radical 扌 (手, 'hand') with the phonetic 闌 (lán, simplified 兰, Middle Chinese *lɑn, 'a gate-screen or railing blocking an entrance', itself from 門 'gate' + 柬). Thus 攔/拦 is literally the verbalization of 闌 ('railing/barrier'): 'to stretch out the arm like a gate-bar to block, intercept, or hold back someone's path'. Attested from the Tang and Song dynasties onward in vernacular and poetic texts.

history.meaning: a gate-railing; to bar a doorway or intercept with the hands (attested in Tang–Song vernacular)
to block, bar, hold back, stop someone in their tracks, intercept

morphemes.meaning: to block, bar, intercept, hold back

拦.notes: A high-frequency physical and figurative verb in spoken Mandarin: you can 拦 a person from leaving or making a rash decision (别拦我 'don't stop me!'), or 拦 a passing vehicle on the street.

rootFamily.gloss: to hail a cab or passing car
to block and obstruct, dissuade from doing something

拦住.etymology: A resultative verb-complement compound (动补结构) formed from 拦 (lán, traditional 攔, Middle Chinese *lɑn, 'to bar, block, intercept with the hands') + the resultative complement 住 (zhù, Middle Chinese *ɖɨoH, originally 'to halt, stop walking, abide, dwell', grammaticalized in vernacular Mandarin as a resultative marker of firm fixation or cessation of motion). While 拦 denotes the attempt or action of blocking, 拦住 expresses the successful outcome: 'to block and bring to a halt; to stop someone or something in its tracks'.

history.meaning: to intercept and halt someone's movement (attested in Yuan–Ming vernacular fiction such as Water Margin)
to stop successfully, hold back, block from passing or acting

morphemes.meaning: firmly, to a halt (indicating successful stopping or holding)

拦住.notes: In Mandarin, action verbs like 拦 ('try to block') vs. 拦住 ('succeed in stopping') distinguish effort from result; security guards or assistants on set are often told 把记者拦住 ('hold back the reporters!').

rootFamily.gloss: able to stop or hold back
unable to stop or hold back

拦得住.etymology: An affirmative potential verb-complement construction (V-得-R) derived by inserting the potential infix 得 (de, from Middle Chinese *tək 'to obtain, succeed, be able to') between the root verb 拦 (lán, traditional 攔, 'to block, bar, hold back') and the resultative complement 住 (zhù, 'firmly, to a halt'). Literally 'able to block to a halt', it tests or questions whether any force is sufficient to restrain a determined person or trend.

history.meaning: capable of intercepting and stopping someone (vernacular potential construction)
able to stop, hold back, or restrain

morphemes.meaning: to a halt, firmly in place

拦得住.notes: In natural speech, affirmative potential forms like 拦得住 appear overwhelmingly in rhetorical questions (他决定的事，谁拦得住？ 'Once he's made up his mind, who can stop him?') or replies, whereas simple affirmative statements usually use 能拦住.

rootFamily.gloss: unable to stop or hold back

拦车.etymology: A verb-object compound (动宾结构 / 离合词) composed of the transitive verb 拦 (lán, traditional 攔, Middle Chinese *lɑn, 'to block, intercept, flag down along a road') + the object noun 车 (chē, traditional 車, Middle Chinese *tɕʰia, Old Chinese *k-hlja, a pictograph of a wheeled carriage seen from above, 'wheeled vehicle, cart, car, taxi'). Originally meaning either 'to block a passing carriage' or 'to flag down a cart/ride by stepping out or raising a hand by the roadside', in modern urban Mandarin it commonly means 'to hail a taxi or passing car on the street'.

history.meaning: to intercept a carriage on the road (e.g., to present a petition or demand a halt)
to hail a cab or flag down a passing car on the street; to stop a vehicle

拦车.notes: Functions as a separable verb-object phrase (离合词), e.g., 在路边拦了一辆车 ('flagged down a car/taxi by the roadside'); compare 打车 (dǎchē, 'to take/get a taxi') and 叫车 (jiàochē, 'to call/book a ride via app').

拧.etymology: Phono-semantic character (traditional 擰, combining 扌 'hand' + 寧 níng phonetic): read拧 nǐng ('twist, turn a knob/cap/screw, wring out a wet towel'), níng ('pinch and twist skin'), and nìng ('stubborn, cross-grained').

history.meaning: twist, turn, wring out (nǐng); pinch (níng); stubborn (nìng)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 拧 (via 萌典)

拭目以待.etymology: A classical four-character idiom (成语) structured as a serial verb phrase linked by the subordinating conjunction 以 (yǐ, 'in order to, and thereby'): 拭 (shì, Middle Chinese *ɕɨk, 'to wipe clean with a cloth', from 扌 'hand' + 式) + 目 (mù, Middle Chinese *mɨuk, 'eye') + 以 (yǐ, 'in order to / and') + 待 (dài, Middle Chinese *dʌiX, 'to wait for, await'). First attested in the *Gongyang Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals* (公羊传·襄公二十七年: 诸侯莫不拭目而视 'none of the feudal lords failed to wipe their eyes and look') and the *History of the Later Han* (后汉书: 天下拭目以观), wiping one's eyes clear signifies keen anticipation so as not to miss the unfolding spectacle.

history.form: 拭目而視 / 拭目以觀 / 拭目以待
history.meaning: to wipe one's eyes clear in order to watch or await a momentous development (attested in Gongyang Zhuan and Hou Hanshu)
to wait and see eagerly how things turn out; to watch with keen anticipation

拭目以待.notes: A staple of television hosts, trailers, and competitive reality shows (让我们拭目以待！ 'Let us wait and see!'), as well as confident challenges between rivals in workplace dramas.

rootFamily.gloss: to look at someone with new eyes / heightened respect (lit. scrape one's eyes and look)
to wait for, look forward to

cognates.meaning: to rescue, save from distress (Sino-Japanese しょうきゅう / shōkyū)
cognates.word: 拯救 (しょうきゅう / shōkyū)

cognates.meaning: to rescue, save from peril (hanja 拯救)

拯救.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative verb compound (并列结构) uniting two near-synonyms: 拯 (zhěng, Middle Chinese *tɕɨŋX, Old Chinese *tjaŋʔ, originally written 拼/抍, glossed in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as 上举也 'to lift upward out of a pit or drowning water', with 扌 'hand' and 丞 'to assist/lift up with two hands from a pit') + 救 (jiù, Middle Chinese *kɨuH, 'to stop harm, come to the aid of, rescue, relieve'). Attested in early historical and philosophical texts for lifting the populace out of 'fire and water' (拯民于水火), in modern Mandarin it carries an elevated, dramatic register ('to save from ruin, crisis, or decline').

history.meaning: to lift up from drowning or danger and come to the rescue of (people in distress)
to rescue, save from crisis, ruin, or decline (both solemn and dramatic/hyperbolic uses)

morphemes.meaning: to lift up from drowning or peril, succor

拯救.notes: Carries a grander, more dramatic tone than simple 救; used both seriously (拯救生命 'save lives') and hyperbolically in entertainment industry talk (e.g., 拯救收视率 'save the tanking TV ratings', 拯救银河系 'saved the galaxy in a past life').

rootFamily.gloss: to save from extinction or grave danger; to remediate
to relieve disaster victims, provide charity relief

拱窗.etymology: Architectural compound noun combining 拱 ('arch, cup the hands together in an arch', 扌 + 共) + 窗 ('window'): 'arched window'.

history.meaning: arched window

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 拱窗 (via 萌典)

拱门.etymology: Compound of 拱 ('join hands in a curved bow; arch', hand classifier 扌 + phonetic 共 gǒng) + 门 ('gate, doorway', pictograph of double swinging gate leaves), naming a curved stone or brick archway.

history.meaning: arched stone or brick doorway

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 拱门 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: a reproduction, transcript, or duplicate (from Old French copie < Latin cōpia 'abundance, transcript')

拷贝.etymology: A early 20th-century phonetic loanword (音译词) borrowed—initially via Shanghainese and early Chinese cinema/publishing circles—from English *copy* (ultimately from Medieval Latin *copia* 'transcript, duplicate', from Classical Latin *cōpia* 'abundance, plenty', from *co-* + *ops* 'wealth, resources'). The characters 拷 (kǎo, Middle Chinese *kʰɑuX, 'to strike, beat') and 贝 (bèi, traditional 貝, 'cowrie shell, treasure') were selected purely for their phonetic approximation to English *co-py* (especially in Wu/Shanghainese and Mandarin). Originally denoting a positive film print struck from a negative for distribution to cinemas, it later expanded to computing ('copy files') and figurative cloning ('replicate a show format').

history.meaning: abundance (Latin) → transcript, duplicate, positive film print (English)
a positive motion-picture film print for screening; to strike a print (Republican-era Shanghai film industry)
to copy digital files or data; to clone, replicate, or imitate a program format; a copy/print

morphemes.meaning: co- (phonetic rendering of first syllable of English 'copy')
-py (phonetic rendering of second syllable of English 'copy')

拷贝.notes: In film and TV production (*幕后之王*), 拷贝 means both a physical/digital master print of a film/episode and the act of copying data onto a hard drive or cloning another show's concept; contrasts with native 复制 (fùzhì, the standard UI menu term for 'Copy').

rootFamily.gloss: to burn/record onto an optical disc or drive
to copy files onto a USB flash drive (colloquial clipped verb 拷)

cognates.meaning: to piece together; to go all out
to risk; to work hard at

拼.etymology: A phono-semantic compound (形聲) combining the hand radical 扌 (手, 'hand, manual action') with the phonetic component 并 (bìng, 'to combine, join together'). Originally recorded in Middle Chinese rime dictionaries with the sense of 'to follow' or 'to piece together', in vernacular Mandarin it converged functionally with 拚 (pàn/pīn, 'to cast aside, risk, stake everything'). From the verb 'to stake one's all', contemporary colloquial Chinese derived the stative/adjectival usage meaning 'hard-driving, fiercely dedicated, going all-out'.

history.meaning: to join together; to follow along
to disregard one's safety; to stake everything in a contest
hard-charging, all-out, fiercely competitive (predicative adjective)

拼.notes: Frequently used predicatively with 很 or 太 in workplace and showbiz contexts (e.g., 她工作太拼了, 'She works way too hard / is super driven').

rootFamily.gloss: to work with all one's might; to risk one's life
to struggle and fight hard for success

拼不过.etymology: A potential resultative verb compound (可能補語結構) formed from the verb 拼 (pīn, 'to compete fiercely, pit oneself against, stake everything') + the negative potential infix 不 (bù, 'cannot') + the directional/resultative complement 过 (過, guò, originally 'to pass, cross over', grammaticalized as a comparative/surpassing marker meaning 'to surpass, outdo'). Literally 'to pit oneself against [someone] and be unable to surpass [them]', hence 'unable to outmatch or outlast in a head-to-head struggle'.

history.meaning: unable to surpass or defeat in a direct contest of strength or endurance

morphemes.meaning: to compete all-out, pit oneself against

拼不过.notes: Commonly used when comparing stamina, resources, or youth in high-pressure industries (e.g., 拼不过年轻人, 'can't out-hustle the younger generation').

rootFamily.gloss: unable to beat in a fight or competition

cognates.meaning: strenuous, for dear life (cf. 一生懸命)

拼命.etymology: A verb-object (動賓) compound historically written 拚命 or 拼命, composed of 拼/拚 (pīn/pàn, 'to cast aside, wager, risk utterly') + 命 (mìng, 'life, fate, vital existence'). Originating in Song–Yuan vernacular literature with the literal sense 'to stake or forfeit one's life in combat', it underwent semantic bleaching and grammaticalization in Modern Mandarin to function both as a separable verb-object phrase ('to work oneself to the bone') and as an adverbial modifier ('desperately, with all one's might').

history.meaning: to disregard or wager one's life in battle or defiance
to exert every ounce of strength; desperately, at all costs (adverbial)

拼命.notes: As a separable verb (離合詞), it can take aspect particles or modifiers between the characters (as in 拼着命 or 拼了命), whereas directly before a verb (拼命工作) it acts as an intensifier adverb.

rootFamily.gloss: workaholic, someone who risks everything for their goal (lit. 'Desperate Saburo')

拼着命.etymology: An inflected separable verb-object construction (動賓離合結構) formed by inserting the continuous/durative aspect particle 着 (zhe, derived from Middle Chinese 著 *ɖjak, 'to attach, adhere to, keep in a state') inside the verb-object compound 拼命 (pīn-mìng, 'to risk one's life, stake everything'). The internal particle 着 highlights the sustained, deliberate posture of someone actively putting their life or health on the line while performing another action.

history.meaning: keeping one's life on the line; in a state of risking everything

拼着命.notes: Typically precedes a main action clause to emphasize self-sacrificing determination (e.g., 拼着命也要把节目做完, 'even at the risk of my life/health, I'll finish producing the show').

rootFamily.gloss: with all one's might; to risk one's life
to risk death, brave mortal danger

拿.etymology: Ideogram (会意字, variant of 拏) combining 合 ('join together, close') + 手 ('hand'): literally 'close the hand upon something' = 'take, hold, carry in the hand, fetch, seize', and in spoken Mandarin also an instrumental preposition ('with, using').

history.stage: Han–Tang Chinese (拏 / 拿) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: grasp with the hand; take; hold; fetch

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 拿 (via 萌典)

拿个.etymology: A colloquial verb-classifier sequence (動量/動名縮略結構) consisting of the transitive verb 拿 (ná, orthographic variant of 拏, 'to grasp with the hand, seize, take hold of', combining 合 'join' and 手 'hand') followed by the unstressed general classifier 个 (個/箇, ge, with the numeral 一 yī 'one' elided in post-verbal position). In spoken Mandarin, post-verbal 一 (yī) before a classifier regularly drops when the object is indefinite and casual, yielding the brisk, informal pattern '拿个 + Noun' ('grab a [noun], fetch a [noun], win a [prize]').

history.meaning: to seize/hold + single bamboo stalk / individual unit
to grab/take/win a (casual verb + elided 'one' + classifier)

拿个.notes: Always requires a following noun object in actual speech (e.g., 拿个奖 'grab/win an award', 拿个主意 'make a decision', 拿个快递 'pick up a package').

rootFamily.gloss: expert at, confident in (lit. 'steady in hand')

拿出.etymology: A directional verb-complement compound (動趨複合詞) formed from the action verb 拿 (ná, 'to grasp, hold, take in the hand', variant of 拏) + the directional verb/complement 出 (chū, 'to exit, go or come out', originally depicting a foot 止 stepping out of an enclosure 凵). Literally 'to take in hand and move outward', it extended from physical extraction ('take out of a pocket/bag') to abstract presentation in discourse ('put forward a plan, muster up courage, produce evidence').

history.meaning: to take out or bring forth from inside
to bring out; to put forward (proposals, proof, attitude, capital)

拿出.notes: In professional and media settings, 拿出 frequently collocates with abstract nouns of capability or resolution: 拿出方案 ('present a proposal'), 拿出诚意 ('show sincerity'), or 拿出实力 ('show one's true strength').

拿到.etymology: A resultative verb compound (動結式複合詞) combining the transitive verb 拿 (ná, 'to take, seize, hold', from 拏) with the resultative complement 到 (dào, originally 'to arrive at, reach a destination', grammaticalized as an attainment marker indicating successful completion of the verb's action). While 拿 alone expresses the attempt or action of taking, 拿到 explicitly encodes the successful acquisition or securing of the target object ('to get one's hands on, obtain, secure').

history.meaning: to seize and bring to a place; to succeed in grasping
to obtain, acquire, secure (rights, contracts, awards, objects)

morphemes.meaning: attainment marker: reach, succeed in getting

拿到.notes: Contrast 拿 ('to take/hold', action) with 拿到 ('to obtain/get', successful result)—e.g., 拿到版权 ('secure the broadcasting rights'), 拿到批文 ('obtain official approval').

rootFamily.gloss: to win/capture smoothly, lock down (a project or client)

拿手.etymology: Idiomatic compound of 拿 ('grasp firmly in the hand', 合 + 手) + 手 ('hand'). Originally describing a tool or technique held with sure, practiced grip, it lexicalized into an adjective meaning 'effortlessly skilled at; one's signature specialty' (拿手菜 'signature dish', 最拿手的事 'what one does best').

history.meaning: confident and practiced in hand; adept at
adept at; signature specialty

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 拿手

拿走.etymology: Resultative/directional verb compound combining 拿 ('take in the hand') + 走 ('walk away, leave'): 'take away, carry off'.

history.meaning: take away

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 拿走 (via 萌典)

cognates.word: 持久戦 (じきゅうせん, jikyūsen)

持久战.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) compound consisting of the disyllabic verbal modifier 持久 (chíjiǔ, 'to sustain for a long time, endure', itself a verb-complement/coordinative compound from Classical Chinese 持 'to hold fast, maintain' + 久 'long duration') modifying the head noun 战 (戰, zhàn, 'war, battle, campaign'). The compound 持久 originates in Classical texts such as the *Daodejing* (長生久視) and *Hanfeizi*, while 持久戰 (Japanese *jikyūsen*) crystallized in modern East Asian military terminology in contrast to 速決戰 ('war of quick decision') and became iconic in Chinese through Mao Zedong's 1938 treatise *On Protracted War* (《論持久戰》).

history.meaning: to hold fast and endure over a long period of time
protracted war; strategic military campaign of endurance (famous from 1938 《論持久戰》)
long-drawn-out struggle, marathon campaign (in business, media production, or negotiation)

持久战.notes: Frequently used metaphorically in workplace and entertainment contexts with the verb 打: 打一场持久战 ('fight a protracted campaign / prepare for a long haul').

rootFamily.gloss: to persist, insist on, hold fast

挂.etymology: Phono-semantic character (掛) combining 扌 (手, 'hand') + 圭 (guī/guà phonetic): originally 'suspend or divide counting stalks in Yijing divination', hence 'hang, hang up (a coat, picture, or phone), hook, register (a letter or hospital appointment), worry about (挂念)'.

history.meaning: set aside/suspend divination stalks -> hang up, suspend
hang; hang up (the phone); register

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 挂 (via 萌典)

挂不住.etymology: Potential verb-complement compound combining 挂 ('hang') + 不 ('not') + 住 ('hold fast'): means literally 'cannot hang/stay on firmly (keeps slipping off)', and figuratively in 脸上挂不住 'unable to save face, feel embarrassed'.

history.meaning: cannot stay hung on; feel embarrassed / lose face

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 挂不住 (via 萌典)

挂号信.etymology: Three-character postal compound combining 挂号 ('register a serial number in an official ledger', 挂 'enter/list' + 号 'number') + 信 ('letter'): 'registered letter, registered mail'.

history.meaning: registered letter

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 挂号信 (via 萌典)

挂断.etymology: Resultative verb compound combining 挂 ('hang up a telephone receiver') + 断 (斷, 'cut off, disconnect'): 'hang up the phone, disconnect a call'.

history.meaning: hang up the telephone; end a call

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 挂断 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to be on an IV drip (lit. 'hang salt water')
cognates.word: 掛鹽水 (kua平 ye平 sy上)

挂水.etymology: A colloquial verb-object (動賓) compound formed from 挂 (掛, guà, 'to hang, suspend from a hook or stand') + 水 (shuǐ, 'water, liquid', here clipping 盐水 yánshuǐ 'saline solution' or 药水 yàoshuǐ 'medicinal fluid'). The expression originated in the Yangtze Delta / Jianghuai and Wu dialect regions—vividly describing the suspended intravenous infusion bag or bottle hanging above a patient—and spread widely into everyday colloquial Mandarin across China alongside synonyms like 输液 (formal medical term) and 打点滴.

history.meaning: to suspend (hang) + water/liquid
to receive an intravenous (IV) infusion; to be on a drip

morphemes.meaning: to hang, suspend; to register/hook up
liquid, saline/medicinal solution (short for 盐水/药水)

挂水.notes: Colloquial register; in formal medical contexts use 输液 (shūyè, 'intravenous infusion'), while in northern or Taiwanese Mandarin 打点滴 (dǎ diǎndī) or 打吊瓶 (dǎ diàopíng) are also common.

rootFamily.gloss: to register at a hospital clinic; to send by registered mail
to hang up the phone; (slang) to die/fail
saline solution (often used in 挂盐水)

挂钟.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 挂 ('hang on a wall') + 钟 (鐘, 'clock'): 'wall clock'.

history.meaning: wall-mounted clock; wall clock

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 挂钟 (via 萌典)

挂钩.etymology: Compound of 挂 ('hang; suspend', hand radical 扌 + 圭 guī) + 钩 ('hook; curved metal catch', metal radical 钅 + 勾 gōu). Denotes a wall hook or peg on which keys, coats, or kitchen utensils are hung.

history.meaning: hanging hook; wall peg

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 挂钩

指.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 扌 (手, 'hand') + 旨 (zhǐ phonetic): 'finger, digit' and verbally 'point at, point out, indicate, direct, count on (指望)'.

history.stage: Old & Classical Chinese (Shijing, Mencius) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: finger; point at; indicate; refer to

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 指 (via 萌典)

指令.etymology: Historically a coordinative/verb-object compound from 指 (zhǐ, 'to point out, indicate, direct with the finger') + 令 (lìng, 'to command, order; an official decree'). In Literary Chinese (attested in tang-song administrative prose), 指令 meant 'to point out and command' or 'to direct orders'. In the late 19th and 20th centuries, reinforced by Sino-Japanese administrative and military usage (指令 *shirei*), it stabilized as a noun meaning an authoritative 'directive, operational order', and later in computing and broadcasting as a 'system instruction' or 'control command'.

history.meaning: to point out and order; to direct subordinates by decree
official military or administrative directive, operational order
history.stage: Early Modern East Asian Administrative Lexicon

history.meaning: directive, executive order; control room or computer instruction

指令.notes: Commonly paired with verbs like 下达 (xiàdá, 'issue [a directive]'), 听从 (tīngcóng, 'obey'), or 执行 (zhíxíng, 'execute'), both in live TV control rooms and in software engineering.

rootFamily.gloss: to direct, command (an orchestra, operation, or crew)
to indicate, point out; instructions from superiors

指南.etymology: Verb-object compound of 指 ('point toward') + 南 ('south'). Originated in ancient Chinese magnetic south-pointing instruments (指南车 'south-pointing chariot' and 指南针 'magnetic compass', which in Chinese tradition is described as pointing south rather than north), and broadened metaphorically to mean 'guide, guidebook, handbook'.

history.meaning: point south (of a compass or chariot)
guide; guidebook; directory

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 指南 (via 萌典)

指南针.etymology: A transparent three-morpheme compound combining 指 (zhǐ, 'to point'), 南 (nán, 'south'), and 针 (zhēn, 'needle'), literally 'south-pointing needle'. Traditional Chinese magnetic instruments—beginning with Han-dynasty lodestone spoons (司南) and Song-dynasty magnetized steel needles described by Shen Kuo in his Dream Pool Essays (1088)—treated south rather than north as the primary cardinal reference. In Modern Mandarin 指南针 denotes any magnetic compass.

history.meaning: magnetized south-pointing steel needle for navigation
magnetic compass

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 指南针

指导.etymology: A coordinative verbal/nominal compound (並列結構) composed of 指 (zhǐ, 'to point with the finger, indicate direction') + 导 (導, dǎo, 'to lead along a path, guide, conduct', formed from 道 'way/path' + 寸 'hand/measure'). Attested in early medieval historical texts such as the *Sanguozhi* (《三國志》, 3rd century CE) in the sense of 'pointing out the way and leading', it gained broad institutional currency in modern Chinese (reinforced by Japanese 指導 *shidō*) for professional mentoring, artistic/stage direction (e.g., 武术指导 'martial arts choreographer'), and official supervision.

history.meaning: to point the way and lead; to instruct and guide
history.stage: Late Han to Six Dynasties Literary Chinese (e.g., 《三國志》)

history.meaning: to guide, coach, supervise; guidance, advisor/director in a specialized field

morphemes.meaning: to lead, guide, conduct along a path

指导.notes: In film and television credits, 指导 is a title for specialist directors/coordinators (e.g., 艺术指导 'art director', 动作指导 'action director'), distinct from the overall 导演 ('director').

rootFamily.gloss: director (of a film, TV show, or stage play)
to guide, lead, channel (a conversation or trend)

指挥.etymology: A coordinative compound (並列結構) uniting 指 (zhǐ, 'to point with the finger, indicate a target') + 挥 (揮, huī, 'to wave the hand, brandish a signal flag, motion to troops'). Both characters share the semantic domain of manual signaling in military command. Attested in Tang–Song literature (and earlier as 指麾, where 麾 huī means a commander's signal pennon), it originally denoted directing troop movements by pointing and waving banners, later broadening to mean 'to command, direct, orchestrate' as a verb and 'commander; orchestra conductor' as a noun.

history.meaning: to point and wave signal banners to direct troops; to motion with the hands
Military Commander / Commissioner (official title in Tang–Ming dynasties)
to command, direct, dispatch (operations/crews); conductor (of music)

morphemes.meaning: to wave, motion, wield a signal banner (cf. 麾)

指挥.notes: Functions both as a transitive verb (指挥现场 'direct the live set') and as a noun (总指挥 'chief commander/director', 乐队指挥 'orchestra conductor').

rootFamily.gloss: command post, headquarters; to command an operation
to display, bring into play, give free rein to

cognates.word: 指揮系統 (しきけいとう, shiki keitō)

指挥系统.etymology: A four-character modifier-head nominal compound (偏正複合名詞) combining 指挥 (zhǐhuī, 'command, direction, dispatch', from 指 'point' + 挥 'wave/signal') with 系统 (xìtǒng, 'system, interconnected network', a coordinative/modifier-head compound from 系 'to tie, link, lineage' + 统 'interconnected main thread of silk, unified whole'). While 系 and 统 both have ancient roots in silk-thread metaphors for lineage and governance, 系统 in its modern scientific sense of 'system' was popularized via Meiji Sino-Japanese (系統 *keitō*), yielding 指挥系统 for a military 'chain of command' or a broadcast/emergency 'central dispatch and control system'.

history.meaning: command/direction + interconnected lineage/network
history.stage: Literary Chinese Roots & Meiji Sino-Japanese Synthesis

history.meaning: command system, chain of command, central dispatch and control architecture

morphemes.meaning: to point and wave; command, direction, dispatch
main silk thread, unified governance, system

指挥系统.notes: Used both for organizational hierarchies ('chain of command') and technical infrastructure ('central command/dispatch system' in live broadcasting, aviation, or military ops).

指教.etymology: A coordinative verb compound (並列結構) composed of 指 (zhǐ, 'to point out flaws or directions') + 教 (jiào, 'to teach, instruct, enlighten'). Attested in Classical Chinese as early as the *Zhan Guo Ce* (《戰國策》, *Strategies of the Warring States*) and Han-era histories, it originally meant 'to point out and instruct'. In Imperial and Modern Chinese epistolary and conversational etiquette, it specialized into a deferential, honorific verb used when asking someone for their critique, opinion, or advice.

history.meaning: to point out and instruct; to teach directly
to offer pointers, give advice or critique (polite/deferential expression)

指教.notes: Almost always used self-deprecatingly when requesting feedback from others (e.g., 请多指教 'Please give me your guidance/pointers', or 有何指教？ 'What advice/business do you have for me?'). Never say 我来指教你 unless being deliberately arrogant or ironic.

rootFamily.gloss: to give pointers, show someone how to do something
to teach and guide, instruct earnestly

指望.etymology: A compound formed from 指 (zhǐ, 'to point toward, fix a target upon') + 望 (wàng, 'to gaze into the distance, look toward with expectation, hope'). Originating in Song–Yuan vernacular Chinese (attested in *Zhuzi Yulei* 《朱子語類》 and *Water Margin* 《水滸傳》), the two morphemes combine the physical act of pointing at a specific target (指) with gazing expectantly toward it (望), yielding the sense 'to pin one's hopes on, count on, rely upon' as a verb, and 'prospect, hope, something to count on' as a noun.

history.meaning: to fix one's eyes and hopes upon a specific person or outcome; expectation
to count on, rely on; hope, prospect (often in negative or skeptical contexts)

morphemes.meaning: to point at, fix upon a specific target
to gaze afar, look forward to, hope

指望.notes: In spoken Mandarin, the second syllable is often pronounced in the neutral tone (zhǐwang), and it frequently appears in skeptical or negative statements (e.g., 别指望他了 'Don't count on him', 没指望了 'There's no hope left').

rootFamily.gloss: to look forward to, expect eagerly

cognates.meaning: to give pointers; to point out
to point out, guide, give directions

指点.etymology: A coordinative verb compound (並列結構) combining 指 (zhǐ, 'to point with the finger') + 点 (點, diǎn, originally 'a small black dot/fleck', extended verbally to 'to dab with a brush, mark key points, tap/indicate'). Attested in Tang poetry and Song prose, 指點 originally described physically pointing at features in a landscape (or pointing and gossiping behind someone's back, as in 指指點點), and evolved metaphorically into 'to highlight key points, give practical tips or expert pointers to help someone break through a difficulty'.

history.meaning: to point at with the finger; to indicate specific spots or criticize
to give pointers, offer expert tips or direction; (reduplicated 指指点点) to point and gossip

morphemes.meaning: to point with the finger, indicate
to dot, tap, mark key points, give a hint

指点.notes: More informal and practical than 指导 ('formal guidance') or 指教 ('polite request for advice'); e.g., 多亏前辈指点 ('Thanks to the senior colleague's pointers'). Be careful with the reduplicated form 指指点点 (zhǐzhidiǎndiǎn), which is negative ('to point fingers and gossip').

rootFamily.gloss: to give a crucial hint or enlightening tip (lit. 'touch and撥 open')
to point fingers and gossip critically behind someone's back

指责.etymology: A coordinative/serial verb compound (並列/連謂結構) formed from 指 (zhǐ, 'to point at, single out, expose') + 责 (責, zé, originally 'to demand payment of a debt', extended in Classical Chinese to 'to call to account, reprove, censure, blame'). Attested in Han and Six Dynasties historical prose, 指責 literally means 'to point the finger at a fault and hold someone accountable', whence modern Mandarin 'to criticize harshly, accuse, censure, blame'.

history.meaning: to point out faults and reprove; to call to account
to criticize, censure, accuse, blame publicly or directly

morphemes.meaning: to point at, single out, expose

指责.notes: Stronger and more adversarial than 批评 (pīpíng, 'to criticize constructively'); 指责 implies fault-finding or public accusation (e.g., 互相指责 'trade blame / point fingers at each other').

rootFamily.gloss: to blame, reproach (often gentler or reflexive, as in 自责)

指针.etymology: Formed from 指 (zhǐ, 'to point out, indicate with a finger') and 针 (zhēn, simplified from 針, 'metal needle', with the metal radical 钅 and 十). Created in early modern horology and instrument making, 指针 names any slender pivoting needle or hand that indicates a reading—whether the magnetized steel needle of a pocket compass, the hands of a clock tower, or the dial of a kitchen scale.

history.meaning: indicating hand of a clock or dial needle
clock hand; compass or gauge needle

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 指针

按.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 扌 (手, 'hand') + 安 (ān/àn, 'settle down'): 'press down with the hand or finger (a button, key, or doorbell); hold back/restrain; check; according to (preposition, short for 按照)'.

history.meaning: press down with the hand; halt; examine
press/push (a button); according to

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 按 (via 萌典)

按摩.etymology: An ancient coordinative compound (並列複合詞) combining two foundational manual therapy verbs: 按 (àn, 'to press down firmly with the hand') + 摩 (mó, 'to rub, stroke, chafe with the hand', formed from 麻 phonetic and 手 'hand'). Attested over two millennia ago in China's earliest medical canon, the *Huangdi Neijing* (《黃帝內經·素問》, *Yellow Emperor's Inner Canon*), 按摩 named the classical medical branch of therapeutic pressing and rubbing, which was also borrowed into Japanese as *anma* (按摩, the etymological ancestor of the Western term *ampuku* and precursor to *shiatsu*).

history.meaning: to press down and rub the body to regulate qi and blood (medical therapy)
history.stage: Classical Chinese (Warring States–Han Medical Texts, 《黃帝內經》)

history.meaning: massage; to give or receive a massage

morphemes.meaning: to press down with the hand, apply pressure
to rub, stroke, apply friction with the hand

按摩.notes: In contemporary China, 按摩 is the general everyday word for massage, whereas 推拿 (tuīná, 'pushing and grasping') refers specifically to clinical Traditional Chinese Medicine orthopedic/meridian therapy.

rootFamily.gloss: friction; conflict or rubbing between parties
to press, push down (a button or key)

按摩师.etymology: A modifier-head occupational noun (偏正結構) formed by attaching the agentive professional suffix 师 (師, shī, 'master, teacher, skilled specialist in a craft or profession') to the disyllabic root 按摩 (ànmó, 'massage, therapeutic pressing and rubbing'). In Classical Chinese, 師 designated a military host or an official master/specialist (such as 醫師 'physician' or 樂師 'court musician'); in Modern Mandarin, -师 productively forms respectful occupational titles for certified professionals and skilled practitioners.

history.meaning: therapeutic pressing/rubbing + master/specialist practitioner
history.stage: Classical & Imperial Chinese Roots (e.g., 唐代太醫署按摩師)

history.meaning: professional massage therapist, masseur / masseuse

按摩师.notes: Historically, 按摩師 was already an official medical rank in the Tang Dynasty Imperial Medical Bureau (太醫署); today it is the standard polite occupational title for a massage therapist.

按时.etymology: A verb-object / prepositional-object compound (動賓/介賓結構) formed from 按 (àn, originally 'to press down with the hand, check', which evolved in Classical Chinese via the sense 'to examine/verify against a standard' into the preposition 'according to, in accordance with') + 时 (時, shí, 'time, appointed season or hour'). Literally 'in accordance with the appointed time', it lexicalized as an adverb meaning 'on time, on schedule, at regular intervals'.

history.meaning: in accordance with the season or appointed hour; at the proper time
on time, on schedule, punctually (adverb)

按时.notes: Compare 按时 ('on schedule / according to the planned or regular time', e.g., 按时吃药 'take medicine on schedule', 按时交稿 'submit a script on time') with 准时 (zhǔnshí, 'precisely at the clock time, punctual').

rootFamily.gloss: on schedule, by the agreed deadline (more formal)

按照.etymology: A coordinative compound preposition (並列複合介詞) combining two characters that underwent parallel semantic pathways from concrete verification to prepositional 'according to': 按 (àn, 'to press down, examine, verify against a record') + 照 (zhào, 'to shine upon, reflect in a mirror', extended in Song–Yuan administrative documents to 'to compare against an official reference, in light of'). By the Ming–Qing bureaucratic and vernacular language, 按照 fused into a disyllabic preposition meaning 'according to, in accordance with, following'.

history.meaning: to check/verify against + to illuminate/compare with a reference document
according to, in accordance with, on the basis of (preposition)

morphemes.meaning: to check against, follow, according to
to reflect, compare against a standard, in light of

按照.notes: More formal and rhythmically versatile than single-syllable 按; typically introduces multi-syllable noun phrases (e.g., 按照合同规定 'in accordance with contract provisions', 按照导演的要求 'according to the director's requirements').

rootFamily.gloss: to follow, abide by (a precedent or rule)

按规定.etymology: A prepositional phrase (介詞短語) composed of the preposition 按 (àn, 'according to, in compliance with', from 'to check/verify with the hand') governing the disyllabic noun 规定 (guīdìng, 'regulation, stipulation, rule'). 规定 itself is a compound of 规 (規, guī, originally 'carpenter's compasses for drawing circles', extended in Classical Chinese to 'standard, rule, norm') + 定 (dìng, 'to fix, settle, establish'). Together, 按规定 means 'in accordance with the established rules or regulations'.

history.meaning: according to + rules fixed as by a compass/standard

按规定.notes: Standard bureaucratic and workplace collocation used to cite institutional policy or broadcast standards (e.g., 按规定办事 'do things by the book / follow protocol').

cognates.meaning: push-button (colloquial Cantonese also uses 掣 zai3)

按钮.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正複合名詞) formed from the verbal modifier 按 (àn, 'to press down with the finger') + the head noun 钮 (鈕, niǔ, 'metal knob on a seal or bronze bell, button, pivot', a phono-semantic character with 钅/金 'metal' and 丑 phonetic). In Classical Chinese, 鈕 referred to the raised grip or knob on top of an imperial seal (印鈕) or bronze vessel; in the 20th century, combined with 按 ('to press'), it was coined to denote a mechanical or electronic 'push button' (and later a GUI button on a screen).

history.meaning: metal knob on a seal or bell; clasp or button on clothing
push button (on a machine, control panel, or digital interface)

morphemes.meaning: to press down with the finger

按钮.notes: Don't confuse 按钮 ('push button / switch' on a mixing console, elevator, or computer screen) with 纽扣 (niǔkòu, 'clothing button' sewn onto a shirt or coat).

rootFamily.gloss: key on a keyboard or piano (lit. 'press-key')
rotary knob or dial (on an audio mixer or radio)

cognates.meaning: to carry on a shoulder pole; to pick/choose
to pick, select; to carry on a pole

挑.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形聲) combining the hand radical 扌 (手, 'hand') with the phonetic 兆 (zhào, Old Chinese *l'ewʔ). Its primary sense in Han–Tang Chinese was 'to carry loads suspended from both ends of a shoulder pole' (tiāo, level tone) or 'to lift, poke up,挑撥/provoke' (tiǎo, rising tone). From the concrete action of 'poking out or lifting up specific items from a pile with the hand or an implement' (and selecting which load to shoulder), 挑 (tiāo) developed the everyday transitive verb sense 'to pick out, select, choose, be picky about'.

history.meaning: to stir, provoke, lift up; to carry on a shoulder pole
to pick out, select carefully, choose; to find fault with (挑剔)

挑.notes: A heteronym (多音字): pronounced first tone tiāo when meaning 'to pick, choose' (挑剧本 'pick a script', 挑选 'select') or 'to carry on a shoulder pole' (挑担子), but third tone tiǎo when meaning 'to provoke, stir up, challenge' (挑战 tiǎozhàn, 挑衅 tiǎoxìn).

cognates.meaning: challenge, defiance, taking on a difficult task
