挑战.etymology: Originally a verb-object compound (動賓結構) in Classical Chinese composed of 挑 (tiǎo, rising tone, 'to provoke, stir up, entice out') + 战 (戰, zhàn, 'battle, combat'). Attested in *Zuo Zhuan* (《左傳》) and *Shiji* (《史記·項羽本紀》: 漢欲挑戰, 'Han wished to provoke a battle'), it meant 'to ride out before enemy lines to taunt and provoke them into battle'. In the 20th century, influenced by Japanese 挑戦 (*chōsen*), which translated English *challenge*, 挑战 expanded semantically from a separable military verb-object phrase into a general transitive verb and abstract noun ('a demanding test or challenge; to challenge a record or oneself').

history.meaning: to provoke or entice the enemy into coming out to fight a battle

history.form: 挑战 (tiǎozhàn, reinforced by Japanese 挑戦 chōsen and English 'challenge')
history.meaning: challenge (difficult task or test); to challenge (an opponent, limit, or authority)

morphemes.meaning: to provoke, stir up, call out (pronounced tiǎo)

挑战.notes: Always pronounced tiǎozhàn (third tone on 挑). Under English influence, modern Chinese uses 挑战 both as a countable noun (面对新的挑战 'face new challenges') and directly with an object (挑战自我 'challenge oneself').

rootFamily.gloss: to provoke, stir up trouble deliberately
to accept a challenge / engage the enemy in battle

挖.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形聲) combining the hand radical 扌 (手, 'hand, manual action') with 窔 (yào/wā, itself formed from 穴 'cave, hollow pit' + 乙, depicting digging deep into a recess or hollow). Emerging in Tang–Song texts as a vernacular graphic specialization of earlier  / 抉 / 掘, 挖 literally means 'to dig, excavate, hollow out with the hand or a tool'. In modern media and corporate Mandarin, it developed rich metaphorical extensions: 'to dig up or scoop an exclusive story' (挖新闻/挖黑料) and 'to poach talent from a rival' (挖人/挖墙脚).

history.meaning: to hollow out, dig into a pit or cavity with the hands or tools
to dig, excavate; (figuratively) to unearth secrets, scoop stories, or poach talent

morphemes.meaning: deep recess of a cave (穴 'cave' + 乙, phonetic wā)

挖.notes: In entertainment and business contexts, 挖 is heavily used for headhunting/poaching (挖人 'poach talent', 挖角 'poach a star/key player') and investigative reporting (深挖 'dig deep into a story').

rootFamily.gloss: to excavate, unearth; to discover and cultivate (talent/potential)
to poach talent or undermine a rival's foundation (lit. 'dig the foot of a wall')
to speak sarcastically, dig at someone verbally

挞底.etymology: Culinary compound combining 挞 (撻, tà, phonetic loan for Western pastry 'tart') + 底 ('bottom, base'): 'tart shell, pastry crust base'.

history.meaning: tart crust; pastry base

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 挞底 (via 萌典)

挞皮.etymology: Modern baking compound from 挞 (simplified from 撻, phonetic loan for English *tart* as in 蛋挞 'egg tart') + 皮 ('skin; outer crust; pastry shell'). Used in bakeries and kitchens for the shortcrust or puff-pastry shell of a tart before or after filling.

history.meaning: tart shell; pastry crust

挡.etymology: Phono-semantic character (traditional 擋, combining 扌 'hand' + 當 dāng/dǎng phonetic): 'block, bar, keep out (wind, rain, or light), get in the way of; gear of a vehicle (read dǎng or dàng)'.

history.meaning: block; shield; keep out; gear

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 挡 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to take a bullet for someone, act as a human shield

挡枪.etymology: A verb-object (動賓) compound formed from 挡 (擋, dǎng, 'to block, ward off, shield against', combining 扌 'hand' and 當 'to face, match, withstand') + 枪 (槍, qiāng, originally 'wooden spear', in modern times 'gun, firearm, bullet'). Literally 'to block a spear or take a bullet with one's own body to shield another', in contemporary workplace, PR, and entertainment slang it is used metaphorically for 'acting as a scapegoat, deflecting media fire or public criticism on behalf of a boss, celebrity, or colleague'.

history.meaning: to parry a spear or take a bullet for someone in combat
to take the heat/fall for someone; to act as a PR shield or decoy in a crisis

挡枪.notes: Almost always paired with the preposition 替 (tì) or 给 (gěi): 替老板挡枪 ('take a bullet / take the PR heat for the boss'). A related noun is 挡箭牌 (dǎngjiànpái, 'shield against arrows; pretext/foil').

rootFamily.gloss: to block toasts / drink alcohol on someone's behalf
shield; pretext, excuse, or person used as a buffer (lit. 'arrow-blocking shield')
to get in the way, block someone's path or career

cognates.meaning: to intercept toasts and drink on someone's behalf

挡酒.etymology: A verb-object (動賓) compound parallel in structure to 挡枪, composed of 挡 (擋, dǎng, 'to block, intercept, fend off') + 酒 (jiǔ, 'alcoholic drink, wine/liquor'). Rooted in Chinese banquet and business-drinking culture (酒桌文化), 挡酒 literally means 'to intercept incoming toasts', referring to an assistant, subordinate, or friend who steps in at a banquet to politely deflect a toast or drink the alcohol on behalf of a boss, VIP, or celebrity who cannot or does not wish to drink.

history.meaning: to fend off toasts or drink alcohol in someone else's stead at a banquet

挡酒.notes: An essential survival term in Chinese business and entertainment banquets (应酬 yìngchou), where assistants or PR managers are often expected to 替艺人/领导挡酒 ('block toasts for the artist/leader') when guests press them to drink (劝酒 quànjiǔ).

rootFamily.gloss: to take a bullet / deflect criticism for someone
to propose a toast, offer alcohol respectfully
to urge or pressure someone to drink at a banquet

挣.etymology: A phono-semantic compound (形聲) combining the hand radical 扌 (手, 'hand, manual effort') with 争 (爭, zhēng, 'to tug, contend, strive', itself originally depicting two hands pulling on an object). Emerging in Tang–Song vernacular Chinese as an action-specific derivative of 爭, 挣 originally meant 'to exert strength to push away or break free' (preserved in first-tone zhēng in 挣扎 zhēngzhá and fourth-tone zhèng in 挣脱 zhèngtuō). From 'striving hard with one's hands and labor', early Mandarin developed the fourth-tone sense zhèng meaning 'to earn through effort (money, a living, or reputation)'.

history.meaning: to exert force with the hands; to strain to break free or prop up
to earn (money, property, or a living) through hard work and striving

morphemes.meaning: to contend, strive, pull (爭, phonetic zhēng/zhèng)

挣.notes: Pronounced fourth tone zhèng when meaning 'to earn' (挣钱 'earn money', 挣表现 'strive to make a good impression') or 'to break free' (挣脱), but first tone zhēng in the compound 挣扎 (zhēngzhá, 'to struggle'). Compared to 赚 (zhuàn, 'to make a profit/earn'), 挣 emphasizes the sweat and toil required.

rootFamily.gloss: to earn money, make a living
to struggle, writhe, put up resistance (pronounced zhēngzhá)
to break free, shake off bonds (pronounced zhèngtuō)

挣扎.etymology: A coordinative/alliterative vernacular verb compound (雙聲並列複合詞) combining 挣 (zhēng, 'to strain, exert force to break free') + 扎 (zhá, 'to prick, pitch, strain the body to hold on or push upward'). Attested consistently in Yuan Dynasty *zaju* dramas (元雜劇) and Ming vernacular novels (such as *Water Margin* and *Journey to the West*, often written 掙揣 or 掙扎), it originally meant 'to summon up one's strength to prop oneself up or break free from physical bonds', later extending to psychological agony ('inner struggle') and desperate, futile resistance (垂死挣扎).

history.meaning: to strain every muscle to prop oneself up, push forward, or break free from restraints
to struggle physically or mentally; to put up desperate or futile resistance

morphemes.meaning: to strain, exert strength to break free (pronounced zhēng)
to strain, writhe, battle against resistance (pronounced zhá)

挣扎.notes: Watch the pronunciation of both characters, as both are heteronyms: in 挣扎 it is strictly zhēngzhá (first tone + second tone), unlike 挣钱 (zhèngqián) or 包扎 (bāozā) / 扎针 (zhāzhēn). Often used for inner conflict (内心很挣扎 'feeling very torn/conflicted inside').

rootFamily.gloss: to break free from restraints (pronounced zhèngtuō)
to put up a last-ditch, dying struggle

挣钱.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound formed from 挣 (zhèng, tradicional 掙, "to struggle for, to earn by exertion", composed of the hand radical 扌 and phonetic 争 zhēng) and 钱 (qián, traditional 錢, originally an ancient bronze farming implement and spade-shaped coin, later "copper cash, money"). In early vernacular Chinese (Yuan–Ming dynasties), 挣 shifted from physical straining or propping up to acquiring income through strenuous labor, yielding 挣钱 for earning wages through hard work.

history.meaning: bronze agricultural spade; ancient bronze coinage
to acquire copper cash through physical toil or trade
to earn money, to make a living

morphemes.meaning: to struggle to earn, to win by effort

挣钱.notes: More colloquial and physical in tone than 赚钱 (zhuànqián, "to make a profit/earn money"); 挣钱 emphasizes trading one's sweat or labor for wages.

rootFamily.gloss: to earn a living, to work for wages

挤爆.etymology: A resultative verb compound (动补结构) combining the action verb 挤 (jǐ, traditional 擠, "to push, press, crowd together") with the resultative complement 爆 (bào, "to crack in fire, burst, explode"). Originally referring to physical venues packed until the walls or doors figuratively burst open, it expanded in late 20th-century Hong Kong and Mainland media slang to describe servers, phone lines, or broadcast platforms crashing under overwhelming user traffic.

history.meaning: to push or thrust (擠); to crackle or burst in fire (爆)
to pack a venue to bursting capacity; to overload servers or lines with traffic

morphemes.meaning: to crowd, to squeeze, to press
to burst, to explode, to overload

挤爆.notes: Frequently used in entertainment and tech journalism when a celebrity scandal or hit show causes a website or ticketing platform to crash (e.g., 服务器被挤爆).

rootFamily.gloss: to pack a venue to full capacity

挤破头.etymology: An idiomatic resultative verb-object phrase structured as 挤破 ("to squeeze until broken/split open", resultative compound of 挤 jǐ "crowd, press" + 破 pò "break, split") taking the body-part object 头 (tóu, traditional 頭, "head"). Literally depicting a mob of people pressing forward so fiercely at a narrow doorway that their heads are bruised or split open, it grammaticalized in modern vernacular Mandarin as a vivid hyperbole for cutthroat competition over scarce positions.

history.meaning: to push forward in a crowd until one's head is bruised or bloodied
to scramble desperately for admission or a coveted spot

morphemes.meaning: to squeeze, to crowd, to push

挤破头.notes: Commonly paired with 往里钻 ("to bore one's way inside") when describing aspiring actors, interns, or applicants fighting for entry into elite entertainment agencies or civil service posts.

rootFamily.gloss: to rack one's brains; to scheme desperately for gain

挤进来.etymology: A directional verb compound (趋向动词短语) formed from the main action verb 挤 (jǐ, traditional 擠, "to squeeze, press, push through a crowd") followed by the compound directional complement 进来 (jìnlái, "inward toward the speaker", from 进 jìn "enter, advance" + 来 lái "come"). In Mandarin syntax, 进来 marks both spatial trajectory into an enclosed space and deictic orientation toward the speaker's vantage point.

history.meaning: to force or press one's way into an enclosed space toward the observer
to squeeze in (physically into a room/train or figuratively into a competitive market)

morphemes.meaning: to squeeze, to push through a crowd

挤进来.notes: Can be split around an object or potential marker: 挤得进来 ("able to squeeze in") or 挤不进来 ("unable to squeeze in"). Often used figuratively for breaking into a saturated industry.

rootFamily.gloss: to squeeze in (away from the speaker)

挥挥手.etymology: Reduplicated verb-object phrase from 挥手 (挥 'wave, brandish with the hand', 扌 + 军 + 手 'hand'): 'give a wave of the hand, wave goodbye or hello'.

history.meaning: wave one's hand (brief/friendly reduplication)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 挥挥手 (via 萌典)

挨个.etymology: An adverbial compound formed from 挨 (āi, in level tone: "to press close to, to be next to in sequence") and the general classifier 个 (gè, traditional 個/箇, originally "bamboo stalk", later a universal measure word for individuals). Because 挨 denotes contiguous spatial adjacency ("touching shoulder to shoulder"), 挨个 developed in Northern Mandarin vernacular to mean proceeding through items or people one after another without skipping any.

history.meaning: touching one bamboo tally or individual after the next in sequence
one by one, in turn, successively

morphemes.meaning: to lean close to, to follow in sequence (read āi)

挨个.notes: Note the pronunciation: 挨 is read in the first tone (āigè, often pronounced āigèr with erhua in Beijing Mandarin) when meaning "in sequence/close to", contrasting with second tone ái for "suffering" (as in 挨骂).

rootFamily.gloss: side by side, next to each other
from door to door, household by household

cognates.meaning: to get scolded, to be berated

挨骂.etymology: A passive-sense verb-object compound combining 挨 (ái, rising tone: "to suffer, endure, be subjected to", often historically written 捱 in Southern varieties) and 骂 (mà, traditional 罵, "to curse, scold, berate", composed of the net graphic 罒 and phonetic 马 mǎ). In vernacular Chinese, 挨 + verbal noun functions as a grammaticalized adversative passive construction comparable to English "get [verb]ed" or "take a [noun]-ing".

history.meaning: to revile, to insult verbally
to endure verbal abuse or scolding from a superior
to get scolded, to receive a tongue-lashing or public criticism

morphemes.meaning: to suffer, to endure, to be subjected to (read ái)

挨骂.notes: Always read with 挨 in the second tone (áimà). In TV production and workplace contexts, 挨骂 refers both to being chewed out by a director/boss and to getting flamed by netizens online.

rootFamily.gloss: to take a beating, to get hit

挪动.etymology: A verb-complement compound joining 挪 (nuó, 'to shift, rub, edge aside', written with the hand radical 扌 and phonetic 那) and 动 (dòng, simplified from 動, 'to move, stir'). Whereas 搬 means carrying heavy items to a new room, 挪动 specifically denotes shifting furniture, flagstones, or one's seat slightly from its spot—and under negation (一寸都不挪动) expresses stubbornly staying put.

history.meaning: shift or transfer slightly by hand
shift position; budge

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 挪动

cognates.meaning: to be roused, inspired (rare literary Sino-Japanese)

振奋.etymology: A coordinative (parallel) compound of two near-synonymous Classical Chinese verbs: 振 (zhèn, "to shake, flap, rouse, stir into motion") and 奋 (fèn, traditional 奮, pictographically a bird 隹 spreading its wings over a field 田 to take flight, hence "to spread wings, exert oneself, rise up vigorously"). Originally depicting a bird shaking its feathers and rising into flight, it came in Literary Chinese to describe rousing morale or feeling emotionally invigorated.

history.meaning: (of birds/beasts) to shake the body and spread wings; to rouse one's courage and energy
inspired, thrilled, galvanized; to boost morale or spirits

morphemes.meaning: to shake, to rouse, to stir up
to spread wings, to exert oneself vigorously

振奋.notes: Functions both as an adjective ("inspired, energized") and a causative verb ("to inspire"), frequently collocating with 人心 in 振奋人心 ("inspiring, heartening") or 精神 in 振奋精神 ("to rally one's spirits").

rootFamily.gloss: to revitalize, to rejuvenate (a nation or industry)
to struggle onward, to strive hard

振振有词.etymology: A four-character literary idiom (成语) composed of the reduplicated state adjective 振振 (zhènzhèn, from Classical Chinese "abundant, vigorous, forceful, plausible") and the verb-object predicate 有词 (yǒucí, traditional 有詞, "to have words/arguments"). While 振振 in the *Book of Odes* (*Shijing*) meant "noble, numerous, or harmonious", in late imperial vernacular fiction it combined with 有词 to portray someone speaking with high-sounding, self-assured fluency—typically defending a questionable position.

history.meaning: numerous, majestic, or vigorous (as in Shijing 振振公子)
speaking volubly and self-assuredly with seemingly weighty arguments
to speak plausibly and self-righteously (often when actually in the wrong)

振振有词.notes: Carries a distinctly skeptical or mildly derogatory nuance in modern usage: it implies the speaker feels completely justified and argues forcefully, even though their excuse is specious or self-serving.

rootFamily.gloss: eloquent and forceful on just grounds (positive counterpart)
deafening, rousing even the deaf (of forceful words)

挺.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 扌 (手, 'hand') + 廷 (tíng, 'stand upright at court'): originally 'pull out, stand straight and upright, stick out (one's chest), hold out/endure', and in colloquial Mandarin a common degree adverb meaning 'quite, rather, pretty (挺好的)'.

history.meaning: stand straight; draw forth; outstanding
stand straight; endure; quite/pretty (degree adverb)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 挺 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: recovery, restoration, making up for a loss
to retrieve, to salvage, to restore

挽回.etymology: A resultative verb compound formed from 挽 (wǎn, "to pull, draw back a carriage or bow, tug toward oneself") and 回 (huí, "to turn back, return, revolve"). Literally meaning "to pull back by force something that is slipping away", it is attested in Classical and Tang-Song poetic prose (e.g., pulling back departing springtime or declining imperial fortune) before becoming the standard pan-East Asian Sino-compound for salvaging a damaged reputation, lost market share, or failing relationship.

history.meaning: to pull back a departing carriage or reverse a declining trend/fortune
to redeem, to salvage, to retrieve or undo damage/loss

morphemes.meaning: to pull, to draw back, to haul

挽回.notes: Standard collocations in PR and showbiz crises include 挽回形象 ("salvage one's public image"), 挽回损失 ("recuperate losses"), and 无可挽回 ("irretrievable, beyond redemption").

rootFamily.gloss: to save from ruin, to rescue (a desperate situation)
to detain, to persuade someone to stay
to turn back the狂澜 (raging tide); to save a desperate situation

捅出来.etymology: A directional-resultative verb phrase built from the action verb 捅 (tǒng, "to poke, stab, jab through a paper window or membrane") and the compound directional complement 出来 (chūlái, "outward toward the speaker; into public view"). Derived from the physical imagery of poking a hole in a wasp's nest (捅马蜂窝) or piercing a paper window (捅破窗户纸) so that what was concealed spills out, it means to leak or blow open a scandal or secret.

history.meaning: to poke or pierce a container so that its contents spill out
to expose publicly, to leak or blow open a secret or scandal

morphemes.meaning: to poke, to jab, to pierce through
to come (into view / toward the speaker)

捅出来.notes: Informal and vivid; in media and office politics, 把事情捅出来 implies deliberately or recklessly leaking a cover-up to the press or higher-ups, causing an immediate uproar.

rootFamily.gloss: to stir up a hornet's nest; to court disaster
to pierce the paper window; to speak the unspoken truth openly

捉襟见肘.etymology: A four-character Classical Chinese idiom (成语) abridged from an anecdote about the impoverished Confucian disciple Zengzi (曾子) in the *Zhuangzi* (庄子·让王): "When he pulled together his lapel, his elbow showed through" (捉襟而肘见). Structurally a serial verb-clause construction: 捉襟 (zhuōjīn, VO: "grasp/pull together the front lapel of a ragged robe") + 见肘 (jiànzhǒu, where 见 is earlier read xiàn = 现 "to appear, be exposed", and 肘 zhǒu is "elbow"). It evolved from ragged poverty to any situation where resources are so scarce that covering one gap exposes another.

history.meaning: to pull one's tattered robe lapel closed only for one's bare elbow to poke through (of extreme poverty)
ragged and impoverished; unable to cover all needs at once
strapped for cash or resources, stretched painfully thin, unable to cope

morphemes.meaning: to show, to become visible (classical variant of 现)

捉襟见肘.notes: Note that in modern standard Mandarin mainland pronunciation, 见 here is usually read jiàn (捉襟见肘 zhuōjīn-jiànzhǒu), though etymologically it represents 现 (xiàn, "to show/be exposed"). Ideal for describing an underfunded film crew or overextended budget.

rootFamily.gloss: bosom, mind, breadth of vision (lit. chest and lapel)
to hold back by the elbow; to impede or hamstring someone
unable to attend to everything at once; stretched thin

捏.etymology: Phono-semantic character with the hand radical 扌 and phonetic Niè / 涅 ('black mud at the bottom of water', Middle Chinese *net*). From the original image of moulding soft clay between thumb and fingers, 捏 came to mean pinching, kneading dough, pressing pastry edges, or sculpting clay figurines.

history.meaning: press or pinch with the fingers; mold clay
pinch; crimp (pastry); mold with fingers

cognates.meaning: to abandon; to contribute/donate (in compounds like 義捐)

捐.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形声字) composed of the hand radical (扌, "hand action") and the phonetic component /연 (yuān, "little worm; empty/round"). In Classical Chinese, 捐 originally meant "to cast away, discard, abandon, or relinquish" (as in 捐弃 "to cast aside" or 捐躯 "to lay down one's life"). During the Han through Ming-Qing dynasties, the state system of 捐纳 (juānnà, relinquishing private grain or silver to the treasury in exchange for official rank or famine relief) shifted the core meaning from "relinquishing/giving up" to "contributing financially or donating to a public cause".

history.meaning: to discard, to cast away, to relinquish or sacrifice
to contribute wealth to the state treasury or public relief; to pay a tax/levy
to donate, to contribute (money, goods, organs) philanthropically

morphemes.meaning: to relinquish, to donate, to contribute

捐.notes: While modern standalone 捐 always means "to donate" (money, clothes, blood), its classical sense of "to abandon/sacrifice" survives in literary idioms like 捐弃前嫌 ("cast aside past grudges") and 為国捐躯 ("lay down one's life for the country").

rootFamily.gloss: to donate, to present as a gift to an institution
to sacrifice one's life for a cause (retaining classical sense "relinquish")

捐款.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound (also used nominalized as a modifier-head noun) combining 捐 (juān, "to relinquish, contribute, donate") and 款 (kuǎn, originally "sincerity; carved inscription; clause/item", which in late imperial fiscal terminology came to mean "a sum of money, fund, or financial allocation"). Coined in late Qing administrative and philanthropic prose, 捐款 serves as the standard formal term for making a monetary donation or the donated funds themselves.

history.meaning: sincere; clause or item in a document; later a sum of silver or treasury fund
to contribute funds for public relief or charity; donated sum of money

morphemes.meaning: sum of money, fund, financial item

捐款.notes: More formal than 捐钱; 捐款 works both as a separable VO verb (e.g., 捐了一笔款 "donated a sum of money") and as a noun ("charitable funds/donations", e.g., 慈善捐款).

rootFamily.gloss: to raise funds, to collect money
to donate money or goods for disaster relief

捐钱.etymology: A transparent verb-object (VO) compound pairing 捐 (juān, "to relinquish, contribute, donate") with the everyday noun 钱 (qián, traditional 錢, "copper coin, money"). Formed in vernacular Chinese as the colloquial counterpart to 捐款, it directly expresses handing over personal money to charity, temples, or relief efforts.

history.meaning: to contribute copper cash or silver to a temple, relief fund, or public work
to donate money (colloquial)

捐钱.notes: Strictly a separable verb-object phrase (e.g., 捐了多少钱 "how much money was donated?"), never used as a noun (unlike 捐款, which can mean "a donation"). Preferred in spoken dialogue over 捐款.

rootFamily.gloss: to donate materials or goods (paired in 捐钱捐物)
to spend money, to pay out cash

cognates.word: 損人利己 (そんじんりこ, sonjin riko)

损人利己.etymology: A symmetrical four-character Classical Chinese idiom (成语) juxtaposing two contrasting verb-object (VO) clauses: 损人 (sǔnrén, traditional 損人, "to diminish or harm others") and 利己 (lìjǐ, "to benefit or profit oneself", where 利 functions as a causative/putative verb "to bring profit to"). Rooted in Neo-Confucian moral discourse and classical historiography (cf. *Book of Wei* / *Zhuangzi* discussions on 损人益己), it condemns zero-sum egoism.

history.form: 損人益己 / 損人利己
history.meaning: to diminish others in order to enrich or advantage oneself
to harm others for personal gain; selfish and unscrupulous behavior

morphemes.meaning: to diminish, to harm, to damage

损人利己.notes: Often extended in conversation to the eight-character saying 损人不利己 ("harming others without even benefiting oneself"), used to criticize petty sabotage or malicious gossip in competitive workplaces.

rootFamily.gloss: harming others without even benefiting oneself
to sacrifice one's own interests for the sake of others (antonym)

损失.etymology: A coordinative compound of two Classical Chinese verbs/nouns: 损 (sǔn, traditional 損, "to decrease, diminish, reduce", also the name of Hexagram 41 in the *Yijing*) and 失 (shī, "to let slip from the hand, lose, miss"). Attested already in Han-dynasty historiography (*Shiji*, *Hanshu*) for the depletion of troops, territory, or wealth, it acts in modern Mandarin both as a noun ("financial/material loss") and a verb ("to lose, forfeit").

history.meaning: to diminish and lose (troops, wealth, or prestige); depletion
loss (financial, material, or personnel); to lose or suffer a loss

morphemes.meaning: to lose, to let slip away

损失.notes: Unlike 损害 (which emphasizes the act of injuring or harming an object/reputation), 损失 focuses on the quantifiable forfeiture or depletion of money, time, or talent (e.g., 弥补损失 "make up for a loss").

rootFamily.gloss: damage, harm; to injure or impair
wear and tear, depletion; to consume
gain and loss; pros and cons

损害.etymology: A coordinative verb/noun compound uniting 损 (sǔn, traditional 損, "to diminish, impair, injure") and 害 (hài, "to injure, harm, bring calamity upon"). Attested in Warring States and Han legal and philosophical texts (*Hanfeizi*, *Hanshu*) in the sense of impairing state order or injuring someone's wellbeing, it was also reinforced in modern legal Mandarin via shared Sino-Japanese legal terminology (損害賠償, "damages/compensation for injury").

history.meaning: to impair, injure, or bring harm upon (health, virtue, or the state)
to damage, harm, or infringe upon (interests, reputation, health); harm/damage

morphemes.meaning: to impair, to diminish, to damage

损害.notes: Typically takes abstract objects such as reputation, legal rights, interests, or health (e.g., 损害公司形象 "damage the company's image", 损害利益 "harm interests"), whereas 损坏 is used for physical objects breaking.

rootFamily.gloss: to damage or break (physical objects or equipment)
to injure, to hurt emotionally or physically

换.etymology: Phono-semantic character (換) of 扌 (手, 'hand') + 奂 (奐, huàn phonetic, originally two hands passing something through an opening): 'exchange, swap, trade, change (clothes, money, trains, or parts), replace'.

history.stage: Old & Classical Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: exchange with the hands; replace; change

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 换 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to substitute a player or replace personnel

换人.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound formed from 换 (huàn, traditional 換, "to exchange, barter, replace with one's hands", composed of 扌 "hand" + phonetic 奂 huàn) and 人 (rén, "person, personnel"). In vernacular Mandarin, it functions as a compact, versatile VO construction for substituting players in sports or replacing cast/crew members in media production.

history.meaning: to exchange, to swap or replace with the hands
to replace someone, to switch personnel or substitute a player/performer

morphemes.meaning: to exchange, to replace, to switch

换人.notes: In television and film production (like *Behind the Scenes*), 临时换人 ("replacing a cast/crew member at the last minute") is a major crisis trigger; as a separable VO verb, modifiers go in the middle (e.g., 换了一个人).

rootFamily.gloss: change of leadership or personnel; to change hands

换作.etymology: A compound verb/prepositional counterfactual marker formed from 换 (huàn, traditional 換, "to exchange, switch, substitute") and the literary/semi-literary copular complement 作 (zuò, "to act as, become, be taken as"). Originally meaning "to exchange A to serve as B", in early modern vernacular and modern Mandarin it grammaticalized at the start of a conditional clause to mean "if it were switched to [someone else] instead" ("put in the shoes of...").

history.meaning: to exchange or convert one thing into another; if replaced by (another person)
if it were (someone else instead); put in the place of

morphemes.meaning: to switch, to substitute, to exchange
to be, to act as, to become

换作.notes: Used almost exclusively to introduce a counterfactual comparison of people's reactions: e.g., 换作是我 ("If it were me instead...") or 换作别人早就放弃了 ("Anyone else in that position would have given up long ago"). Interchangeable with 换做.

rootFamily.gloss: to put oneself in another's shoes (empathy)
to treat as, to regard as
to be called, to be known as

换衣服.etymology: A verb-object (VO) phrase consisting of the transitive verb 换 (huàn, traditional 換, "to change, swap, replace") and the coordinative compound noun 衣服 (yīfu, "clothes, attire", formed from Classical Chinese 衣 yī "upper garment, robe" + 服 fú "garment, dress, worn attire"). In Mandarin, 衣 and 服 fused into a disyllabic noun whose second syllable takes a neutral tone (yīfu).

history.meaning: upper robes (衣) and lower garments/attire (服); clothing in general
to change one's garments or attire
to change clothes, to get changed (into a costume or fresh outfit)

morphemes.meaning: garment, attire, dress (neutral tone in 衣服)

换衣服.notes: Whereas 穿衣服 means "to put on clothes / get dressed", 换衣服 specifically means changing out of one outfit into another (such as performers changing costumes backstage or changing into home clothes).

rootFamily.gloss: to put on clothes, to get dressed

据悉.etymology: A concise literary compound formed from the preposition/verb 据 (jù, traditional 據, originally "to lean on, rely upon", hence "according to, on the basis of") and the classical cognitive verb 悉 (xī, composed of 采 biàn "to distinguish/sort out" + 心 xīn "heart/mind", meaning "to know thoroughly, learn in detail"). Solidified in late 19th- and 20th-century Chinese journalism (报刊文体) as a compact sentence-initial evidential marker meaning "according to what has been learned / it is reported that".

history.meaning: to lean on or rely upon (據); to know exhaustively or understand in full (悉)
according to information received; it is learned/reported that (journalistic evidential)

morphemes.meaning: to know thoroughly, to learn of

据悉.notes: A hallmark of news broadcasts, entertainment press releases, and formal briefings; almost never used in casual everyday chat (where 听说 "I heard that" is used instead). Often paired with 据了解 ("according to what is understood").

rootFamily.gloss: to learn of, to be informed of (formal)

据我所知.etymology: A four-character semi-literary epistemic phrase combining the preposition 据 (jù, traditional 據, "according to, based on") with the Classical Chinese pronominal relative clause 我所知 (wǒ suǒ zhī, "that which I know"). In Classical Chinese grammar, the particle 所 (suǒ) placed before a transitive verb (知 zhī, "to know") nominalizes the verb into an object relative ("what is [verb]ed"), so 据我所知 literally means "basing on that which I know".

history.meaning: that which one knows (Classical 所 + Verb nominalization)
according to that which I know; as far as my knowledge extends

morphemes.meaning: that which (object-nominalizing particle before a verb)
to know, to be aware of

据我所知.notes: Retains classical 所-nominalization syntax within everyday polite spoken and written Mandarin; useful for hedging statements in meetings or interviews without claiming absolute certainty.

rootFamily.gloss: all that one knows (as in 知无不言 "say all one knows")

cognates.meaning: base of operations, stronghold, foothold, hub

据点.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-compound combining 据 (jù, traditional 據, "to occupy, hold fast to, rely upon defensively") and 点 (diǎn, traditional 點, "spot, point, strategic location"). Popularized in modern East Asian military and geopolitical vocabulary via Japanese *wasei-kango* (拠点, *kyoten*, "strategic stronghold or base of operations"), it entered 20th-century Chinese war reporting before acquiring a playful colloquial sense in contemporary urban Mandarin for a group of friends' regular hangout spot or secret base.

history.meaning: fortified military stronghold or strategic base of operations
military stronghold; corporate hub; (colloquial) regular hangout spot or secret base

morphemes.meaning: to occupy, to rely upon as a foothold

据点.notes: In contemporary urban dialogue, calling a café, bar, or studio our 据点 ("our regular hangout / home base") is playful mock-military slang for a favorite gathering place.

rootFamily.gloss: to occupy, to hold (territory or market share)

掀开.etymology: A resultative compound uniting 掀 (xiān, 'to lift up by an edge, raise high', combining the hand radical 扌 with 欣 as phonetic) and 开 (kāi, 'open, apart'). Because 掀 specifically targets lifting a flat covering from one edge—a pot lid, curtain, quilt, or folded cloth flap—adding 开 highlights uncovering whatever was hidden beneath.

morphemes.meaning: lift up a lid, flap, or cover

history.meaning: lift up; raise a cover
lift open a lid; fold back a flap

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 掀开

掀起.etymology: A directional-resultative verb compound formed from 掀 (xiān, composed of the hand radical 扌 and 欣 xīn, meaning "to lift up, raise high, flip open a cover or curtain") and the directional complement 起 (qǐ, "to rise, upward"). Originally referring to physically lifting a heavy curtain, quilt, or lid, it was metaphorically extended to the wind lifting up towering ocean waves (掀起巨浪) and thence to sparking or setting off a massive social trend, media storm, or movement.

history.meaning: to lift up or raise high with the hands
to lift open (a curtain or cover); to stir up (waves, storms)
to lift open; to set off, spark, or unleash (a craze, wave, or uproar)

morphemes.meaning: to lift up, to flip open, to surge
up, upward, to rise or begin

掀起.notes: In media and entertainment contexts, 掀起 almost always collocates with wave/storm metaphors: 掀起热潮 ("spark a craze/boom"), 掀起轩然大波 ("stir up a massive uproar"), or 掀起讨论 ("touch off a wave of discussion").

rootFamily.gloss: to flip over (a table or page); to topple
to trigger, to set off (a reaction or discussion)
to surge up, to rise (of waves, movements, or trends)

授权.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound uniting 授 (shòu, "to hand over, confer, bestow", formed by adding the hand radical 扌 to 受 shòu "receive") and 权 (quán, traditional 權, originally "steelyard balance weight", by extension "political power, authority, legal right"). While conferring authority (授以权力) has classical roots, 授权 crystallized in modern legal and commercial Chinese for delegating official authority or licensing intellectual property (IP) rights.

history.meaning: to confer or hand over (授); balance weight, leverage, authority (權)
to delegate legal/administrative authority; to license copyright or IP rights

morphemes.meaning: to confer, to grant, to hand over

授权.notes: Crucial in television, music, and publishing industries, where 授权 specifically translates "to license (IP, broadcast rights, or adaptations)" as well as corporate "authorization".

rootFamily.gloss: copyright, intellectual property rights; rights to a work
to confer, to award (a title, degree, or prize)

授权书.etymology: A three-character modifier-head legal compound built by suffixing 书 (shū, traditional 書, originally "to write with a brush", hence "written document, letter, certificate") to the verb-object compound 授权 (shòuquán, traditional 授權, "to authorize, to grant legal or copyright authority"). Here 书 preserves its Classical and administrative Chinese meaning of an official legal instrument or charter (as in 契书, 证书, 委托书).

history.meaning: written document, official letter, charter, or edict
written instrument of authorization, power of attorney, or IP licensing certificate

授权书.notes: Notice that 书 in legal/business compounds like 授权书 ("letter of authorization"), 合同书 ("contract document"), or 起诉书 ("indictment") always means "official document/certificate", never "book".

rootFamily.gloss: power of attorney, letter of entrustment/proxy

掉.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 扌 (手, 'hand') + 卓 (zhuō/diào phonetic). In Classical Chinese, 掉 meant 'shake, wag, swing (as in 尾大不掉)' or 'turn around (掉头)'. From the Tang–Song vernacular onward it became the primary verb for 'fall, drop, lose, come off, fade' and a resultative complement of removal/disappearance (吃掉, 忘掉).

history.meaning: shake; wag; turn around
fall; drop; lose; resultative complement of removal

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 掉 (via 萌典)

掉以轻心.etymology: A four-character literary idiom (成语) traced to Tang-dynasty essayist Liu Zongyuan's (柳宗元) *Da Wei Zhongli Lun Shidao Shu* (答韦中立论师道书): "Therefore I never dare to approach it with a light/casual mind" (故吾每为文章，未尝敢以轻心掉之). In Classical Chinese, 掉 (diào) does not mean "to fall/drop" (a later vernacular shift), but "to shake, swing, agitate, or wield", and 以轻心 (yǐ qīngxīn) is an instrumental prepositional phrase ("with a light/frivolous mind"). Literally "to wield/approach a matter with a casual, unguarded mind", it means to let down one's guard or treat a serious risk lightly.

history.meaning: to wield or approach a weighty task with a casual, flippant attitude (where 掉 = shake/move)
to treat a serious matter with a careless, unguarded mind; to lower one's guard
history.stage: Late Imperial Literary Chinese to Modern Mandarin

morphemes.meaning: to shake, to wield, to move (classical sense, not "drop")

掉以轻心.notes: Almost always used in negative or warning sentences: 绝不能掉以轻心 ("we must never let down our guard / take this lightly"). Learners often misinterpret 掉 as "drop", whereas here it preserves its classical sense "to move/treat".

rootFamily.gloss: careless and negligent; to lower one's guard
to treat lightly, to underestimate (an opponent or problem)
too big to swing (classical idiom 尾大不掉, where 掉 also means "swing/wag")

掉色.etymology: Separable verb-object compound of 掉 ('drop; fall off; lose', hand radical 扌 + 卓 zhuō) + 色 ('colour; dye; pigment'). Literally 'to drop colour', used of fabrics that bleed dye in the wash or ink that fades over time; negated as 不掉色 ('colourfast; permanent ink').

history.meaning: lose dye or fade in colour
fade; lose colour

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 掉色

掌声.etymology: A modifier-head compound noun formed from 掌 (zhǎng, "palm of the hand", composed of phonetic 尚 shàng over 手 shǒu "hand", and by extension "clapping the palms") and 声 (shēng, traditional 聲, originally the sound of striking a stone chime 殸 perceived by the ear 耳, hence "sound, noise, voice"). Attested in Tang-Song poetry for the sound of clapping hands in delight or rhythm, it is the standard noun for audience applause.

history.meaning: the sound of clapping palms together in merriment or appreciation
applause, ovation (for a performance or speech)

morphemes.meaning: palm of the hand; clapping of palms

掌声.notes: Note the distinction: 掌声 is strictly the noun "applause" (e.g., 掌声雷动 "thunderous applause", 把掌声送给... "let's give a round of applause to..."), whereas the verb "to applaud / clap hands" is 鼓掌 (gǔzhǎng).

rootFamily.gloss: to applaud, to clap one's hands (verb)
palm of the hand; under one's control

cognates.meaning: taking command of, seizing control over (esp. troops/organization)
to grasp firmly, to master, to control

掌握.etymology: A coordinative compound derived from 掌 (zhǎng, "palm of the hand; to hold in the palm, take charge of") and 握 (wò, "to grasp firmly with the fingers closed, clench in the fist"). In Classical Chinese (*Hou Hanshu*, *Sanguozhi*), 掌握 originally functioned as a concrete noun meaning "the hollow of the palm and grasp of the hand" (e.g., 在掌握之中 "within the grasp of one's palm"), before verbalizing to mean holding firm control over power, information, or a skill.

history.meaning: the palm and the closed fist; within the physical grasp of one's hand
to hold in one's power; to command or control (authority, destiny)
to master (a skill, language, or technique); to have well in hand or control (information, a situation)

morphemes.meaning: palm of the hand; to hold in the palm, to control
to grasp firmly, to clench in the hand

掌握.notes: Covers two key English verbs: (1) "to master" a skill or body of knowledge (掌握技术, 掌握一门外语) and (2) "to have control/command of" a situation, evidence, or power (掌握主动权, 掌握情况).

rootFamily.gloss: to take control of, to steer (a ship, project, or situation)
to hold power, to be in authority

掐.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形声字) combining the hand radical (扌, "hand action") with the phonetic-ideographic component 臽 (xiàn, depicting a person falling into a pit, also seen in 陷 "trap/sink" and 掐's cognate graphic series denoting digging or pressing fingernails into flesh). Attested in Middle Chinese rime dictionaries (*Guangyun*) as pressing or digging into something with the fingernails, 掐 evolved in Northern Mandarin vernacular to mean "to pinch, nip off (a flower bud or stem), throttle, or count on the fingers", and in modern broadcasting/film jargon to mean "to cut off a feed or edit out a segment of footage".

history.meaning: to dig into or press with the fingernails; to nip off a stem or bud
to pinch, to choke/throttle; to measure on the fingers (掐算)
to pinch; to bicker (掐架); (broadcasting/film) to cut out footage or cut off a live signal

morphemes.meaning: to pinch with fingernails, to nip off, to cut out (broadcast/footage)

掐.notes: In TV and film production (*Behind the Scenes*), 把这段掐了 ("Cut this segment out!") or 掐掉直播信号 ("Cut the live broadcast feed!") comes directly from the physical metaphor of nipping off a plant stem with one's fingernails. Also used in 掐点 ("to time something to the exact second").

rootFamily.gloss: to cut off the head and tail; to quote out of context or trim beginning/end of a clip
to fight, to bicker fiercely (colloquial Beijing/Northern slang)
to count on one's fingers; to time or calculate precisely (as in 掐指一算)

排.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 扌 (手, 'hand') + 非 (fēi/pái phonetic, whose symmetrical wings also suggest two aligned rows): originally 'push open, push aside (排山倒海)', then 'arrange in order, line up, rehearse, drain/discharge' and the noun/classifier for 'a row, line, or platoon'.

history.meaning: push open; push aside; arrange in order
arrange in a line; row (noun/classifier); rehearse; drain

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 排 (via 萌典)

排名.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound that also functions as a noun, formed from 排 (pái, originally "to push aside," extended in Medieval Chinese to "to arrange in a row, line up") and 名 (míng, "name, reputation, rank"). Literally "to line up names in order," it evolved from arranging official rosters by seniority or merit into modern sports, academic, and entertainment chart rankings.

history.meaning: to arrange or list names in sequential order
ranking; to rank on a chart or leaderboard

morphemes.meaning: arrange in a row, line up

排名.notes: Functions both as a noun (排行榜上的排名, "place on the charts") and a separable verb-object compound in media and showbiz contexts (e.g., 排在第一名).

rootFamily.gloss: leaderboard, chart (e.g., music or ratings chart)

排挤.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound pairing 排 (pái, "to push, shove aside," phono-semantic with hand radical 扌 and phonetic 非 fēi) and 挤 (Traditional 擠, jǐ, "to crowd, squeeze, press against"). Both verbs originally denoted physical shoving in a crowd; together they lexicalized in vernacular Mandarin to mean "to elbow out" or "marginalize" rivals within a faction, workplace, or court.

history.meaning: to shove aside; to press or crowd out physically
to elbow out, ostracize, marginalize rivals

排挤.notes: Commonly used in workplace and entertainment-industry politics (职场排挤) for cliques freezing out a newcomer or rival producer; often appears in the passive 受到排挤 ("to be marginalized").

排斥.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative compound composed of 排 (pái, "to push away, thrust aside") and 斥 (chì, "to drive off, repulse, scold"). Attested in Han-era historiography (such as the *Book of Han*) for ousting political dissidents from court, it was later reinforced by Meiji Japanese 排斥 (haiseki) to translate Western scientific "repulsion" (in physics and immunology) as well as psychological or social rejection.

history.meaning: to oust, drive away, banish from court or office
repulsion (physics/biology); exclusion, boycott
to repel, reject coldly, be averse to

排斥.notes: In everyday conversation, 不排斥 ("not averse to / open to trying") is a very frequent litotes used when artists or executives express cautious willingness toward a new format or collaboration.

排除.etymology: A verb-complement (resultative) and coordinative compound combining 排 (pái, "to push aside, clear away") and 除 (chú, originally "palace steps," extended to "to sweep away, remove, eliminate"). Attested in Literary Chinese for clearing away physical obstacles or political opposition, and reinforced in modern East Asian legal and analytical usage (cf. Japanese 排除 haijo) for ruling out possibilities or eliminating interference.

history.meaning: to push open and clear away obstacles or opposition
to eliminate, rule out (a possibility), remove (a fault or obstacle)

排除.notes: Frequently used in analytical and production contexts: 排除故障 ("troubleshoot/clear a technical fault"), 排除万难 ("overcome all difficulties"), and 不排除…的可能 ("cannot rule out the possibility of...").

探.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形声字) combining the hand radical 扌 (shǒu, indicating manual action) with the phonetic-semantic component 㞥 (shēn, the archaic form of 深 "deep," depicting a hand reaching into a deep pit or hollow). Its core Old Chinese sense (*l̥ʰˁə[m], Baxter-Sagart) was "to reach deep into to feel for something unseen," which naturally evolved into "to probe, sound out, spy out, or discreetly inquire."

history.meaning: to reach deep into to fetch or feel out something hidden
to scout, spy out, sound out intentions; to visit
to stretch forward; to probe, sound out, visit

morphemes.meaning: reach deep to feel out, probe, scout

探.notes: In workplace and negotiation drama, 探 takes objects like 口风 or 底 (探口风, 探底, "to sound out someone's intentions or bottom line") to describe discreetly fishing for information.

rootFamily.gloss: to sound out someone's intentions or tone
to test the waters, sound out

探听.etymology: A coordinative/serial verbal compound formed from 探 (tàn, "to probe, reach out to scout") and 听 (Traditional 聽, tīng, "to listen, hear"). Attested in Tang-era poetry and vernacular fiction (such as *Water Margin* and *Dream of the Red Chamber*), it literally means "to feel out and listen in," capturing the covert act of gathering intelligence or prying into confidential news.

history.meaning: to scout out news, listen for tidings or military intelligence
to pry into, fish for information, gather intelligence discreetly

探听.notes: Carries a more covert, deliberate nuance ("snooping/intelligence-gathering") than the neutral everyday verb 打听 (dǎting, "to ask around"); often collocated with 消息 ("news") or 虚实 ("true situation").

rootFamily.gloss: to visit and inquire, seek out

探病.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound joining 探 (tàn, in its extended sense "to call upon, visit to check on someone's condition," from "to probe/inquire after") and 病 (bìng, "illness, a sick person"). Attested since the Tang dynasty (e.g., Bai Juyi's poetry), the compound compresses "to visit and inquire after an illness" into a compact social-etiquette verb.

history.meaning: to call upon an ailing friend or official to inquire after their health
to visit a sick person (at home or in hospital)

探病.notes: A separable verb-object compound (e.g., 去医院探病); in showbiz, compare the closely parallel VO compound 探班 (tànbān, "to visit cast/crew on set").

rootFamily.gloss: to visit someone (especially from afar or in hospital/prison)
to visit a crew working on set

探讨.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound combining 探 (tàn, "to probe deep, explore") and 讨 (Traditional 討, tǎo, originally "to govern, punish," extended in Literary Chinese to "to seek out, investigate, discuss thoroughly," as in 讨论). Attested in Song dynasty neo-Confucian and literary discourse for probing the deeper principles of texts, it now denotes collaborative, analytical exploration of professional or creative questions.

history.meaning: to probe into and investigate scholarly or philosophical principles
to discuss in depth, explore together (an issue, art, or strategy)

探讨.notes: More elevated and analytical than 讨论 (tǎolùn, "discuss"); favored by directors, producers, and academics when "exploring" creative direction or industry trends (深入探讨).

探险.etymology: The verb '探险' (tànxiǎn, to explore) is formed by '探' (to search, to probe) and '险' (danger, precipice). '探' originally referred to reaching into a hole to search for something, carrying a sense of probing the unknown. '险' denotes dangerous or treacherous terrain. '探险' traditionally meant venturing into perilous areas. By the late 19th century, it was adopted to translate Western concepts of geographic exploration and expeditions. Today, it encompasses both scientific expeditions and recreational adventure sports.

history.meaning: adventure

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 探险

接.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 扌 (手, 'hand') + 妾 (qiè/jiē phonetic): 'come into contact, join together, connect; receive/catch in the hand; answer (the phone); meet/pick up someone (at a station or school); take over/continue'.

history.meaning: come into contact; join; receive
connect; receive; answer (the phone); pick up (a person)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 接 (via 萌典)

接下来.etymology: A tri-morphemic verb-complement construction that grammaticalized into a discourse adverbial, built from the root verb 接 (jiē, "to connect, join, continue") plus the compound directional complement 下来 (xiàlái, literally "coming down [from past/present toward the speaker's timeline]"). Originally describing the physical or sequential handing down of an action, it evolved into a temporal transition marker meaning "next, following this."

history.meaning: to receive or continue an action downward in sequence
next, following this, from this point onward (discourse transition)

接下来.notes: A staple transition word for TV hosts and producers cueing the next segment or agenda item (e.g., 接下来请看…, "Next up, please watch..."), as well as a modifier before nouns (接下来的节目, "the upcoming show").

接任.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound formed from 接 (jiē, "to connect, take over in succession") and 任 (rèn, originally "to carry a load on a shoulder pole," extended in Classical Chinese to "burden, official post, duty"). Literally "to take up the official burden from a predecessor," it arose in Qing administrative and early modern bureaucratic prose to denote formal succession to an executive or official post.

history.meaning: to take over an official post or magistracy from a predecessor
to succeed to a post, take over an executive or leadership role

接任.notes: Unlike 接手 (which takes a project or task as object), 接任 takes either the title/post itself or the predecessor as its direct object (e.g., 接任总监一职, "succeed to the post of director").

rootFamily.gloss: to assume office, take up a post

接任者.etymology: A derived agentive noun combining the verb-object compound 接任 (jiērèn, "to succeed to a post," from 接 "take over" + 任 "official post/duty") with the Classical Chinese nominalizing agent suffix 者 (zhě, "one who does X"). This productive `[VO + 者]` pattern was heavily expanded in modern standard Chinese to translate formal administrative and corporate roles like "successor" or "incumbent replacement."

history.meaning: one who takes over an official appointment
successor, replacement in office or leadership

接任者.notes: Formal corporate and institutional register; in more idiomatic or dynastic/mentorship contexts, people often use 接班人 (jiēbānrén, "heir apparent / chosen successor").

接入.etymology: A verb-complement (directional/resultative) compound formed from 接 (jiē, "to join, connect, link") and 入 (rù, "to enter, feed into"). While attested in Literary Chinese in the literal sense of "receiving and bringing inside," it was revitalized in modern telecommunications, broadcasting, and computing to mean "to patch in (a live feed or phone line)" or "to connect into (a network or signal)."

history.meaning: to receive and bring inside; to join into
to patch in (audio/video feed), connect into (a network or circuit)

接入.notes: Essential control-room terminology in live broadcasting: 接入信号 ("patch in the signal"), 接入导播间 ("patch into the director's booth"), as well as telecom 互联网接入 ("Internet access").

rootFamily.gloss: to connect through (a phone line or circuit)
to cut in, switch to (a camera feed)

接受.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound uniting 接 (jiē, "to meet, come into contact with, receive in hand") and 受 (shòu, originally a pictograph of two hands passing a boat/vessel 舟 between them, meaning "to receive, accept"). Attested in Han and Six Dynasties texts (such as the *Book of Later Han*), the compound fused the physical act of taking delivery with mental or formal acceptance of offers, critiques, or interviews.

history.meaning: to take delivery of, receive (gifts, commands, or teachings)
to accept (an offer, condition, interview, or idea)

接受.notes: Distinguish from 接收 (jiēshōu, "to take over physical property / receive a broadcast signal"): 接受 is used for abstract things, offers, and media interactions like 接受采访 ("to give/accept an interview").

rootFamily.gloss: to receive (a broadcast signal); to expropriate/take over property

接口.etymology: Compound noun of 接 ('join, connect') + 口 ('opening, port, mouth'): literally 'joining opening/seam' (of pipes, carpentry joints, or clothing), and in modern technology 'interface, port, jack, connector'.

history.stage: Traditional craft to Modern technical Mandarin
history.meaning: joint seam; connector port; interface

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 接口 (via 萌典)

接待.etymology: Coordinative verb compound of 接 ('receive, welcome a guest') + 待 ('treat, entertain, wait upon'): 'receive and attend to (guests, visitors, or clients); reception'. Attested since the Book of Rites (Liji) and Han histories.

history.stage: Classical Chinese (Liji, Hanshu) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: receive and host guests; reception

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 接待 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to lend a hand; to take over

接手.etymology: Originally a verb-object (VO) compound from 接 (jiē, "to connect, catch, take over") and 手 (shǒu, "hand," metonymically "the person handling a task"). In Ming–Qing vernacular, 接手 meant literally "to take something from another's hand" or "to act as an intermediary handler," before lexicalizing into a transitive verb meaning "to take over responsibility for an ongoing job, project, or show."

history.meaning: to take an object from another's hand; an intermediary handler of goods
to take over (a job, project, show, or business) from someone else

接手.notes: Although historically a VO compound, in modern Mandarin 接手 routinely takes a direct object right after it (e.g., 接手这个节目, "take over this show"). Compare 交手 ("cross swords") and 插手 ("meddle in").

rootFamily.gloss: to meddle in, get one's hands into

接棒.etymology: A modern verb-object (VO) compound formed from 接 (jiē, "to receive, catch, take over") and 棒 (bàng, "club, stick, relay baton," here shortening 接力棒 jiēlìbàng, "relay baton"). Originating in twentieth-century track-and-field athletics for the baton pass in a relay race, it rapidly acquired a vivid metaphorical sense in broadcasting, corporate leadership, and entertainment for succeeding someone or taking the next time slot.

history.meaning: to take the baton in a track-and-field relay race (接力赛)
to take over the baton (succeed a leader, host, or preceding TV show in a time slot)

接棒.notes: Very common in TV scheduling and showbiz journalism: when Show B airs in the time slot just vacated by Show A, or Host B replaces Host A, media headlines say B接棒A. Its antonym is 交棒 ("pass the baton").

rootFamily.gloss: to hand over the baton, pass the torch
to take over a shift or succeed a leader

接洽.etymology: A verb-complement / coordinative compound combining 接 (jiē, "to meet, come into contact with, receive") and 洽 (qià, originally "to soak through, moisten thoroughly," extended in Classical Chinese to "to harmonize, be in accord, consult"). Coalescing in late imperial administrative and commercial correspondence, it means "to make contact so as to reach mutual accord"—hence "to liaise, coordinate, or take up business arrangements with another party."

history.meaning: to meet and converse in harmony; to consult thoroughly
to liaise with, coordinate, arrange business or official matters with

接洽.notes: Belongs to formal business and production register (e.g., 跟赞助商接洽, "liaise with sponsors"; 接洽业务, "negotiate business deals"). Do not confuse the pronunciation of 洽 (qià) with 恰 (qià, "just right").

rootFamily.gloss: to talk over business, negotiate terms

接着.etymology: Formed from the verbal root 接 (jiē, "to join, connect, follow closely upon") and the continuous/durative aspect suffix 着 (zhe, grammaticalized in Middle and Early Mandarin from 著 zhuó, "to attach, cleave to"). Literally "attaching/connecting continuously," it functions both as a verb ("to catch; to carry on speaking/acting") and as a temporal conjunction/adverb meaning "right after that, continuing on."

history.meaning: to catch hold of; to follow closely upon in sequence
continuing on, next, right after that; to keep on doing something

接着.notes: Can precede a verb directly to mean "keep on doing" (接着说, "keep talking"; 接着拍, "keep filming") or stand at the start of a clause as a narrative linker ("Next / Right after that..."). Pronounced jiēzhe.

rootFamily.gloss: closely following, right on the heels of

cognates.meaning: requisition, taking over control (postwar administrative term)

接管.etymology: A serial/coordinative verbal compound composed of 接 (jiē, "to receive, take over in succession") and 管 (guǎn, originally "bamboo key/pipe," extended in Classical and Middle Chinese to "to hold the keys to, govern, manage, control"). Meaning literally "to take over and manage," it became prominent in twentieth-century political, military, and corporate terminology for assuming full administrative control of an institution, company, or project.

history.meaning: to take over custody and management of an estate or office
to take over control, assume administrative or corporate management of

接管.notes: Stronger and more institutional than 接手: 接手 means taking over day-to-day handling of a project, whereas 接管 implies assuming comprehensive authority or ownership (e.g., 接管公司, "take over control of the company").

rootFamily.gloss: to take over control, be in charge of
to place under trusteeship or托管 care

cognates.meaning: to come into contact with, approach

接触.etymology: A coordinative compound uniting 接 (jiē, "to join, meet, touch") and 触 (Traditional 觸, chù, originally "to butt with horns," extended to "to touch, strike against"). While both characters co-occurred in Classical Chinese, the compound was popularized in Meiji Japan as 接触 (sesshoku) to translate Western physics/geometry "contact" (Latin *contactus*) and diplomatic/social interaction, before returning to modern Mandarin.

history.meaning: to meet and touch physically; to butt against
physical/electrical contact; diplomatic or interpersonal engagement
to come into contact with, engage with, approach (for a deal or role)

接触.notes: In entertainment and business, 跟某人接触 means "to make preliminary approaches / be in talks with someone" (e.g., casting directors approaching an actor or producers courting an investor).

rootFamily.gloss: close contact (also title of a famous novel)

接近.etymology: A verb-complement / coordinative compound formed from 接 (jiē, "to join, border on, come close") and 近 (jìn, "near, close in space or time"). Attested in the *Classic of History* (*Shangshu*, 五子之歌: 民可近，不可下) and Han commentaries in the sense of "to draw near to, be intimate with," it developed into a general verb and adjective meaning "to approach, near, or be close to (a target, number, or person)."

history.meaning: to be close to, consort with, draw near in space or intimacy
to approach, draw near to (a person, goal, or figure); close to

接近.notes: Used both for deliberate interpersonal approaches (故意接近他, "deliberately get close to him") and for numerical/qualitative approximation (收视率接近破二, "ratings are approaching 2%"). Easy to approach is 平易近人.

rootFamily.gloss: to draw near, move closer to

cognates.meaning: to control, dominate, hold in check

控制.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound combining 控 (kòng, originally "to draw a bowstring," extended to "to rein in a horse, hold back") and 制 (zhì, originally "to cut out, fashion," extended to "to regulate, restrain, govern"). In Six Dynasties and Tang texts, 控制 meant "to command a strategic choke point so as to hold territory in check"—a cavalry and military metaphor of reining in a steed that broadened in modern Chinese to translate English "control."

history.meaning: to rein in; to command a strategic position and hold surrounding territory in check
to control, dominate, regulate (emotions, budgets, or operations)

morphemes.meaning: draw a bow, rein in a horse, hold in check

控制.notes: Covers everything from emotional self-restraint (控制情绪) and budget management (控制成本) to broadcast engineering (总控制室 / 总控, "master control room"). Desire for control is 控制欲.

rootFamily.gloss: to go out of control, lose control
to restrain, hold in check, curb

cognates.meaning: filing a lawsuit, legal appeal, accusation
appeal to a higher court; accusation

控诉.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound formed from 控 (kòng, extended in Middle Chinese from "to pull/draw" to "to bring a charge before a higher authority," as in 控告) and 诉 (Traditional 訴, sù, "to tell, recount a grievance, accuse"). Used in Tang–Song legal petitions for lodging a complaint with a magistrate, it now carries strong emotional weight in public and media discourse for "publicly denouncing or pouring out grievances against an injustice."

history.meaning: to lodge a formal grievance or petition before a higher magistrate
to accuse, publicly denounce, pour out grievances against injustice or abuse

morphemes.meaning: bring a charge, appeal to authority

控诉.notes: Whereas 控告 (kònggào) is strictly legal ("to sue / press criminal charges"), 控诉 is often rhetorical and emotional (e.g., an artist or whistleblower denouncing industry exploitation in the press: 发文控诉). Beware false friend: Japanese 控訴 (kōso) means specifically "appealing a verdict to a higher court."

rootFamily.gloss: to sue, press legal charges against
to pour out one's woes, vent grievances

推.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 扌 (手, 'hand') + 隹 (zhuī/tuī phonetic): 'push forward with the hand (opposite of 拉 'pull'); shove; turn a millstone; infer/deduce (推理); recommend; postpone (推迟) or shirk'.

history.stage: Old & Classical Chinese (Shijing, Mencius) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: push with the hand; advance; infer; recommend; put off

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 推 (via 萌典)

推出.etymology: A verb-complement (directional) compound joining 推 (tuī, "to push forward with the hand," phono-semantic with 扌 and 隹) and the directional complement 出 (chū, "out, forth"). In Classical Chinese (e.g., *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*), 推出 meant literally "to push someone out (often to an execution ground)" or "to put forward a representative"; in modern commercial and media Mandarin, it developed the ubiquitous figurative sense "to roll out, launch, or release to the public."

history.meaning: to push forth physically; to put forward or nominate someone
to launch, roll out, release (a new show, album, product, or policy)

推出.notes: The standard verb in media, tech, and entertainment for releasing a new work: 推出新节目 ("launch a new show"), 推出新专辑 ("release a new album"), 隆重推出 ("proudly present").

rootFamily.gloss: to promote, popularize (a product or show)

cognates.meaning: impulsion, driving force (mostly in 推動力)

推动.etymology: A verb-complement (resultative) compound combining the action verb 推 (tuī, "to push, shove forward") and the resultative complement 动 (Traditional 動, dòng, "to move, stir, set in motion"). Literally "to push so that it moves," it is attested in Song–Yuan texts for physically budging heavy objects (like a millstone or door) and evolved in modern prose to mean "to propel, drive forward, or give momentum to (a plot, reform, or project)."

history.meaning: to push a physical object into motion
to push forward, drive, give impetus to (a project, industry, or storyline)

推动.notes: Very common in scriptwriting and production discussions: 推动剧情发展 ("drive the plot forward"), 推动项目落地 ("push a project through to execution"), and 推动力 ("driving force").

rootFamily.gloss: to advance, carry forward step by step

推开.etymology: Resultative verb compound from 推 ('push forward with the hand', hand 扌 + phonetic 隹) + directional/resultative complement 开 (simplified from 開, 'open; apart; away'). Used for pushing open a door or window as well as pushing objects or worries aside.

history.meaning: push open (a gate or door); push apart
push open; push aside

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 推开

推翻.etymology: A verb-complement (resultative) compound formed from 推 (tuī, "to push, shove") and 翻 (fān, originally "to fly back and forth," extended in Middle Chinese to "to turn over, capsize, invert"). Originally describing the physical act of tipping over a cart, table, or vessel in vernacular Mandarin, it developed powerful figurative extensions in modern Chinese: "to overthrow (a regime)" and "to overturn, refute, or completely scrap (a creative plan, verdict, or hypothesis)."

history.meaning: to push over, tip over, capsize a physical object or vessel
to overthrow (a regime); to overturn, scrap completely (a plan, script, or conclusion)

推翻.notes: In creative rooms, 推翻重来 ("scrap the whole thing and start over from scratch") and 推翻之前的方案 ("overturn the previous proposal") are everyday expressions when a producer rejects a draft.

rootFamily.gloss: to overturn a case or previous verdict/plan

推荐.etymology: A coordinative compound uniting 推 (tuī, extended from "to push forward" to "to put forward, exalt, nominate," as in 推举) and 荐 (Traditional 薦, jiàn, originally "fodder/grass mat presented as an offering," extended in Classical Chinese to "to present, offer up, recommend a worthy person to a ruler"). Attested in the *Records of the Grand Historian* (*Shiji*) and *Book of Han* for nominating talent to the imperial court, it functions today as both verb and noun for "recommendation."

history.meaning: to put forward and present a worthy candidate to the sovereign or court
to recommend, endorse; recommendation (of talent, content, or products)

推荐.notes: Note the Simplified character 荐 merges two distinct Traditional characters: 薦 ("recommend/straw mat," used here) and 荐 ("repeatedly"). In digital media, 首页推荐 ("homepage recommendation") and 算法推荐 ("algorithmic recommendation") drive viewership.

rootFamily.gloss: to recommend oneself (cf. 毛遂自荐)

推车.etymology: '推车' (tuīchē, cart, stroller) simply pairs '推' (to push) with '车' (vehicle). Historically, '推车' referred to a wheelbarrow, a vital tool for transporting goods and people in ancient rural China. These single-wheeled carts were often pushed by human labor. In modern urban settings, the term has expanded to cover any wheeled cart propelled by pushing, most notably shopping carts ('购物车') in supermarkets or baby strollers ('婴儿推车'). The core concept of a human-powered wheeled conveyance remains unchanged.

history.meaning: shopping cart

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 推车

cognates.meaning: propulsion, pushing ahead with a project

推进.etymology: A verb-complement / coordinative compound combining 推 (tuī, "to push forward, promote") and 进 (Traditional 進, jìn, originally "a bird/foot stepping forward," meaning "to advance, move ahead"). In Classical Chinese, 推进 meant "to nominate and advance talent at court"; in modern East Asian usage (reinforced by Japanese 推進 suishin in mechanical propulsion and project management), it means "to advance, carry forward step by step, or propel (a camera, campaign, or production schedule)."

history.meaning: to push forward and advance worthy officials at court
mechanical propulsion; advancing a military front or policy project
to advance, move forward, carry forward (a project, schedule, or camera shot)

推进.notes: Compared with 推动 (which emphasizes providing initial momentum or impetus), 推进 emphasizes steady, stage-by-stage progress along a timeline or spatial axis (e.g., 推进项目进度, "advance project progress"; 镜头推进, "camera push-in / dolly in").

rootFamily.gloss: progress, pace of advancement (on a schedule)

推迟.etymology: A verb-complement (resultative) compound formed from 推 (tuī, in its extended sense "to push away in time, put off, defer") and the adjectival resultative complement 迟 (Traditional 遲, chí, "slow, late, delayed," carrying the movement radical 辶). Literally "to push [a scheduled time] so that it becomes late," it stabilized in modern Mandarin as the standard verb for postponing or delaying an event, broadcast, or deadline.

history.meaning: to push back in time so as to make late or slow
to postpone, defer, delay (a meeting, broadcast, or schedule)

推迟.notes: The everyday standard word for postponing a scheduled event (e.g., 节目推迟播出, "the show's broadcast is postponed"); its antonym is 提前 (tíqián, "move up / ahead of schedule"). Compare formal 延后 / 延期.

rootFamily.gloss: to arrive late; to come late

推送.etymology: Originally a literal serial/coordinative compound of 推 (tuī, "to push") and 送 (sòng, "to send, deliver, escort"), used for physically pushing and delivering carts or materials. In the twenty-first-century mobile Internet era, it was repurposed as a semantic calque of English "push [notification / delivery]" (as in server push technology), denoting the automated pushing of news alerts, articles, or video streams to user devices.

history.meaning: to push and deliver (carts, goods, or materials); to escort forward
to push (notifications, articles, or live feeds to users' devices); a push post/notification

推送.notes: Ubiquitous in modern Chinese new-media and broadcast operations: 全网推送 ("push across the entire network"), 微信公众号推送 ("a WeChat Official Account post/push"), and 弹窗推送 ("pop-up push notification").

rootFamily.gloss: to send, transmit (a message or signal)
to promote, push out to a wider audience

掰.etymology: A remarkably expressive vernacular ideograph 掰 (bāi) composed of two hands (手 on the left and right) flanking 分 ('to divide, split apart') in the middle! Created in late imperial Northern vernacular script, the character visually depicts gripping an object with both hands to bend or snap it apart (掰面包 'break bread by hand', 掰弯 'bend out of shape').

morphemes.meaning: two hands dividing or bending something apart

history.meaning: split or bend apart with both hands
break apart or bend by hand

cognates.meaning: to rub, massage, crumple; to wrangle over

揉.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形声字) combining the hand radical 扌 (shǒu, indicating manual manipulation) with the phonetic-semantic component 柔 (róu, "soft, supple, pliable," Old Chinese *nu). Originally in Old Chinese (*nu / *nuʔ), 揉 meant "to bend or straighten wood by heating and working it by hand until pliable" (attested in the *Classic of Poetry* and *Book of Han*), before generalizing in Middle and Modern Chinese to "to rub, knead (dough), massage, or crumple."

history.meaning: to bend or make wood pliable by working it with hand and heat
history.stage: Old Chinese (Classic of Poetry / Han texts)

history.meaning: to rub with the hands, knead, massage, crumple
to rub (one's eyes), knead (dough); to work or tolerate (in idioms)

morphemes.meaning: rub, knead, work with the hands until pliable

揉.notes: Famous in the vivid idiom 眼里揉不进沙子 (literally "cannot rub/tolerate a single grain of sand in one's eye"), used in *Behind the Scenes* to describe a perfectionist producer or lover who has zero tolerance for flaws, deceit, or compromise.

rootFamily.gloss: to trample on, abuse, torment physically or emotionally

描写.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound (并列结构) uniting 描 (miáo, Middle Chinese *mjew, 'to trace, outline, copy by drawing', composed of the hand radical 扌 and phonetic 苗 'sprout') and 写 (Traditional 寫, xiě, Middle Chinese *sjaeX, originally 'to transfer items from one vessel to another, pour out, unburden', extended in Six Dynasties and Tang aesthetics to 'sketching out the spirit or form of an object'). Originally used in Tang–Song painting criticism for tracing and sketching visual forms, its modern literary and dramatic sense of 'verbal or cinematic depiction' was consolidated alongside Meiji Japanese 描写 (byōsha).

history.meaning: to trace lines by hand; to unburden or transfer onto silk and paper
to sketch, copy, and portray visual likenesses or scenes
to describe, depict, or portray in literature, scriptwriting, and film

描写.notes: Used for vivid, sensory, or psychological portrayal (e.g., 人物描写 'character portrayal', 细节描写 'detailed depiction' in scriptwriting), whereas 描述 focuses on a sequential or factual recounting of events.

rootFamily.gloss: to trace and paint; to portray vividly
touch-up, light sketching; understatement (as in 轻描淡写)
realistic portrayal, realism in art or drama

提.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 扌 (手, 'hand') + 是 (shì/tí phonetic): 'carry hanging from the hand (a bag, bucket, or kettle); lift up, raise, promote; bring up/mention (a topic); move earlier in time (提前)'.

history.stage: Old & Classical Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: carry by hand; lift; raise; mention

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 提 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to submit, to hand over formally

提交.etymology: A sequential/coordinative verbal compound (连动/并列结构) combining 提 (tí, Middle Chinese *dej, 'to lift by hand, carry suspended, bring forward', from 扌 'hand' + 是 phonetic) and 交 (jiāo, Middle Chinese *kaew, originally a pictograph of a person with crossed legs, meaning 'to cross, intersect, exchange, hand over'). Literally 'to bring forward and hand over', it evolved in Qing administrative prose and modern bureaucratic usage into the standard formal verb for submitting documents, proposals, or deliverables to a higher authority or committee.

history.meaning: to lift in the hand; to cross or exchange mutually
to bring forward a prisoner, dossier, or item and hand it over to an official body
to submit or hand in formally (a proposal, script, budget, or report)

提交.notes: High-register administrative and corporate verb; in television production (*幕后之王*), producers 提交方案 ('submit a program proposal') or 提交预算 ('submit a budget') to network executives, whereas的上交 emphasizes handing up to a superior and 递交 stresses formal delivery.

rootFamily.gloss: to hand over, transfer duties or assets
to present or submit formally (often in person or via courier)
to nominate, put forward a name for consideration

cognates.meaning: offer, supply, sponsorship (especially of a broadcast program)

提供.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound (并列结构) formed from 提 (tí, 'to lift, bring forward, present') and 供 (gōng, Middle Chinese *kjowng, 'to place offerings before ancestors or superiors, supply, furnish', from 亻 'person' + 共 'together/hold up with both hands'). While both characters co-occurred in Literary Chinese in the sense of presenting offerings or testimony, the modern transitive verb meaning 'to provide, supply, furnish (resources, venues, or sponsorship)' was popularized across East Asia through Meiji Japanese 提供 (teikyō) and re-entered late Qing and Republican Chinese as core commercial and media vocabulary.

history.meaning: to set forth sacrificial offerings; to supply respectfully
to offer, furnish, or tender in legal, commercial, and broadcasting contexts
to provide, supply, or furnish (support, funding, resources, or clues)

提供.notes: Takes abstract or concrete nouns as objects (提供资金 'provide funding', 提供场地 'provide a venue', 提供支持 'provide support'); in broadcasting, 节目由…提供 echoes Japanese TV sponsorship credit phrasing.

rootFamily.gloss: supply and demand; to provide for

cognates.word: 情報提供 (じょうほうていきょう, jōhō teikyō)
정보 제공 (情報提供, jeongbo jegong)

提供情报.etymology: A verb–object phrase (动宾短语) pairing the transitive verb 提供 (tígōng, 'to bring forward and supply') with the noun object 情报 (Traditional 情報, qíngbào, 'intelligence, inside information'). 情报 itself is a modifier–head Sino-compound combining 情 (qíng, Classical Chinese 'actual circumstances, true state of affairs', as in 敌情 'enemy situation') and 报 (Traditional 報, bào, 'report, dispatch, intelligence communiqué'), codified in modern military and journalistic usage via Meiji Japanese 情報 (jōhō, coined by Mori Ōgai to translate German 'Nachrichten' in Clausewitz's *Vom Kriege*).

history.meaning: actual conditions on the ground; an official reply or dispatch
military intelligence report on enemy conditions
history.stage: Meiji Japanese / Late Qing military loan

history.meaning: to supply intelligence; figuratively, to tip someone off with insider info in workplace drama

提供情报.notes: Originally espionage and military terminology, in modern workplace and media dramas (*幕后之王*) it is frequently used jocularly or metaphorically for feeding insider scoop, rival studio plans, or office gossip to an ally.

rootFamily.gloss: to report, cover in the news

cognates.meaning: presentation, filing, submission (of a thesis, bill, or document)

提出.etymology: A directional-resultative verbal compound (动趋/动结结构) formed from 提 (tí, Middle Chinese *dej, 'to lift by hand, draw up') and the directional complement 出 (chū, Middle Chinese *tshwij, 'to emerge, go out, bring forth into view'). Originally meaning physically lifting something out of a container or bringing a detainee out for trial in Vernacular Mandarin, it underwent metaphorical extension to mean 'to bring an idea out into open discussion—to put forward, raise, or propose'. Note a key Sino-Japanese divergence: Japanese 提出 (teishutsu) means 'to hand in/submit a document' (Chinese 提交), whereas Chinese 提出 means 'to raise/propose an idea, question, or demand'.
