history.meaning: to lift or draw something out physically; to bring a prisoner out from custody
history.stage: Early Mandarin (Ming–Qing vernacular fiction and legal records)

history.meaning: to put forward, raise, or articulate (a proposal, question, demand, or critique)

提出.notes: False friend alert with Japanese: Chinese 提出 takes abstract verbal/nominal objects of speech or thought (提出建议 'raise a suggestion', 提出问题 'pose a question', 提出要求 'make a demand'), whereas physical or digital documents take 提交.

rootFamily.gloss: to propose, put forward a motion

提到.etymology: A resultative verbal compound (动结结构) built from 提 (tí, 'to lift up, bring up in speech, mention') and the resultative phase/attainment complement 到 (dào, Middle Chinese *dawH, 'to arrive at, reach', grammaticalized in Vernacular Mandarin to mark that an action successfully reaches its target topic or object). Just as 看到 means 'to look and reach with the eyes (see)' and 想到 means 'to think of', 提到 means 'to bring up a topic in discourse so that one's speech touches upon it—to mention or refer to'.

history.meaning: to lift up; by extension in vernacular speech, to bring up a topic
to mention, touch upon, or refer to someone or something in conversation or writing

morphemes.meaning: raise, bring up in speech, mention

提到.notes: Unlike 提起 (which can mean actively initiating a topic or evoking a memory/emotion), 提到 simply states that a person or point was touched upon during speech or in a text (e.g., 他在会上提到了这个方案 'He mentioned this plan at the meeting').

rootFamily.gloss: to touch upon or mention in writing/formal speech

提前.etymology: A verb–complement / verb–locative compound (动补/动宾结构) composed of 提 (tí, 'to lift, shift, pull') and 前 (qián, Middle Chinese *dzen, 'front, forward, ahead in time or space', originally 歬 showing a foot 止 advancing on a boat 舟). Literally 'to pull or shift forward to an earlier position', it maps spatial advancement onto the timeline (where 'earlier' is 'in front' 前 in Chinese temporal metaphor), meaning either transitively 'to move an event/deadline to an earlier date' or adverbially 'in advance, ahead of schedule'.

history.meaning: to lift by hand; to advance forward in space or prior in time
to move a scheduled date, rank, or item forward; ahead of schedule

提前.notes: Functions both as a verb that can take an object or aspect particle (把播出时间提前了两天 'moved the broadcast date up by two days') and directly as a pre-verbal adverbial (提前准备 'prepare in advance'). Antonym: 推迟 ('push back, postpone').

提案.etymology: Originally a verb–object compound (动宾结构) reanalyzed as a noun, combining 提 (tí, 'to lift, bring forward, submit') and 案 (àn, Middle Chinese *'anH, originally 'a short-legged wooden tray or official desk', extended in Han–Tang legal and administrative usage to 'the official dossier, case file, or draft plan placed upon a magistrate's desk'). In Ming–Qing bureaucratic prose, 提案 meant calling up a legal case dossier; in the Meiji era, Japanese 提案 (teian) specialized into 'a formal parliamentary motion or business proposal', a sense re-imported into modern Chinese for parliamentary motions and creative media pitches.

history.meaning: wooden serving tray or magistrate's writing desk; official legal record or draft plan
to call up or bring forward a legal case file for review
a formal motion in an assembly; a creative or commercial pitch/proposal in media and business
history.stage: Modern Standard Chinese (influenced by Japanese teian)

morphemes.meaning: official desk; dossier, draft plan, proposal

提案.notes: Central showbiz and advertising term in *幕后之王*: a 提案 is a structured creative pitch (complete with deck, concept, and budget) presented to clients or network brass, more formal and actionable than a raw 想法 ('idea') or 创意 ('creative concept').

cognates.word: 提案会 (ていあんかい, teiankai)

提案会.etymology: A three-character modifier–head compound (偏正结构) formed by attaching the nominal head 会 (Traditional 會, huì, Middle Chinese *hwojH, 'to come together, assemble; a meeting, gathering, or assembly', originally depicting a lidded vessel with elements joined together) to the modifier 提案 (tí'àn, 'formal proposal, creative pitch'). Modeled on modern corporate and creative-industry terminology, it designates a formal session where producers, directors, or agencies pitch program concepts to decision-makers or sponsors.

history.meaning: to assemble, meet together; an assembly or ritual gathering
a formal pitch meeting or proposal review session in media, advertising, and corporate governance

提案会.notes: In television and advertising production (*幕后之王*), the 提案会 is the high-stakes pitch meeting where competing production teams present show formats (节目模式) to network executives or brand sponsors to win greenlight approval.

cognates.meaning: to propose, to suggest; a proposal

提议.etymology: A verb–object / coordinative compound (动宾/并列结构, Traditional 提議) composed of 提 (tí, 'to lift up, bring forward') and 议 (Traditional 議, yì, Middle Chinese *ngjeH, from 言 'speech/words' + 義 'what is right/proper', meaning 'to deliberate on what is right, discuss, voice an opinion or motion'). Originally meaning 'to bring a topic forward for deliberation', it functions in modern Chinese both as a verb ('to propose, move that...') and as a noun ('a proposal, motion, or suggestion').

history.meaning: to deliberate upon state affairs, discuss what is fitting; an official opinion
to put forward a motion for debate in a deliberative assembly
to propose or suggest a course of action; a proposal or motion

提议.notes: Unlike 提案 (which refers to a written or prepared pitch/motion document), 提议 can be a spontaneous verbal suggestion made during a meeting or conversation (e.g., 我提议大家先休息一下 'I propose we take a break first').

cognates.meaning: instituting a lawsuit, raising an issue or question

提起.etymology: A directional-resultative verbal compound (动趋/动结结构) combining 提 (tí, 'to lift by hand, carry suspended') and 起 (qǐ, Middle Chinese *khjijX, 'to rise from kneeling or sitting, stand up, raise up', from 走 'walk/run' + 己 phonetic). From its literal physical sense in Tang–Song vernacular ('to lift something up off the ground, hoist, or rouse one's spirits', as in 提起精神), it developed the conversational sense 'to raise or bring up a topic/person in speech' as well as the formal legal sense 'to institute or file (a lawsuit, 提起公诉)'.

history.meaning: to lift up physically with the hand; to rouse or muster (energy or attention)
history.stage: Late Tang–Song Vernacular Chinese (Chan Buddhist recorded sayings)

history.meaning: to bring up a past matter or person in conversation; to initiate legal proceedings
history.stage: Ming–Qing Mandarin to Modern Standard Chinese

morphemes.meaning: lift by hand, raise, bring up
rise, up, into action or awareness

提起.notes: Often used at the start of a clause to introduce a topic with emotional resonance (提起这件事 'Speaking of this matter...') or in negative sentences (别提起了 'Don't bring it up again'), as well as in idioms like 提起精神 ('perk up one's spirits').

rootFamily.gloss: to mention, touch upon in speech
to lift up, hoist; to pull up (e.g., 提起来)
to recall, call to mind, remember

提过.etymology: A verb–aspect construction (动+助结构, Traditional 提過) combining the monosyllabic verb 提 (tí, 'to lift up; by extension, to bring up in speech, mention') with the experiential aspect marker 过 (Traditional 過, guo/guò, Middle Chinese *kwaH, originally a motion verb meaning 'to pass by, cross over', from 辶 'walk' + 咼 phonetic). Through grammaticalization in Tang–Song vernacular Chinese, post-verbal 过 evolved from 'passing through a space' to marking that the subject has experienced or performed the action at least once at some indefinite time in the past ('to have mentioned before').

history.meaning: to lift by hand; to pass across a place or exceed a limit
to have lifted or carried past; to have brought up a matter previously
to have mentioned (at least once in the past)

morphemes.meaning: experiential marker (having occurred in the past)

提过.notes: Because 过 marks past experience rather than a current state, 提过 is negated with 没(有) rather than 不 (e.g., 他跟我提过这件事 'He has mentioned this to me before' vs. 他没提过 'He has never mentioned it').

rootFamily.gloss: to have spoken of, to have said before

cognates.meaning: to remind, to prompt to alertness (Sino-Vietnamese)

提醒.etymology: A causative-resultative verbal compound (动结结构) composed of 提 (tí, 'to lift up, tug, prompt') and the resultative complement 醒 (xǐng, Middle Chinese *sengX, from 酉 'fermented spirits/wine vessel' + 星 phonetic, originally meaning 'to sober up from drunkenness', extended to 'to wake from sleep or mental stupor, become clear-headed'). Literally 'to pull or prompt someone so that they wake up/sober up', it is attested in Tang–Song poetry and Chan Buddhist dialogues for rousing someone from delusion, and in modern Mandarin means 'to remind, warn, or call attention to'.

history.meaning: to recover sobriety after drinking wine; to awaken from sleep
to rouse from drowsiness, drunkenness, or spiritual delusion; to alert
to remind someone of a fact or task; to caution or tip off

morphemes.meaning: sober up, wake up, become alert

提醒.notes: Covers both English 'remind' (about a schedule or forgotten detail: 提醒我明天开会 'remind me about tomorrow's meeting') and 'caution/alert' (善意提醒 'a friendly heads-up / warning'); it never means 'remind X of Y by resemblance' (which is 让…想起).

rootFamily.gloss: to wake up, awaken (intransitive or figurative)
to awaken someone from sleep or illusion

提问.etymology: A compact verb–object or serial verbal compound (动宾/连动结构, Traditional 提問) formed from 提 (tí, 'to lift up, put forward, raise') and 问 (Traditional 問, wèn, Middle Chinese *mjunH, from 口 'mouth' + 門 phonetic, 'to inquire, ask a question, interrogate'). Contracted from the fuller phrase 提出问题 ('to put forward a question'), it functions as an intransitive verb (can take a prepositional target with 向: 向导演提问 'ask questions of the director') or as a verbal noun ('questioning, Q&A').

history.meaning: to inquire, ask respectfully, or interrogate
to raise a question formally in a classroom, press conference, or interrogation

提问.notes: Because 问 already occupies the internal object slot of 提, 提问 cannot take a direct person object (*提问他 is ungrammatical); instead use 向他提问 or 对他进行提问 ('put questions to him'), especially in press conferences, talk shows, or pitch meetings.

rootFamily.gloss: to question closely, interrogate; a question mark or doubt
to interview, gather news (as a journalist)

提高.etymology: A causative-resultative verbal compound (动结结构) uniting the action verb 提 (tí, 'to lift by hand, pull upward') with the stative adjectival complement 高 (gāo, Middle Chinese *kaw, originally a pictograph of a tall pavilion or lofty tower, meaning 'high, tall, elevated'). Literally 'to lift something so that it becomes higher', it extends from physical elevation (提高嗓门 'raise one's voice') to abstract enhancement of standards, quality, efficiency, ratings, or awareness.

history.meaning: to lift in the hand; lofty, high like a tower
to lift higher physically (such as raising a lantern, hem, or voice)
to raise, increase, improve, or enhance (levels, quality, consciousness, or ratings)

morphemes.meaning: high, elevated, at a higher level

提高.notes: Collocates typically with nouns denoting measurable levels, rates, skills, or awareness (提高收视率 'boost viewership ratings', 提高效率 'improve efficiency', 提高警惕 'heighten vigilance'), and can be used both transitively and intransitively.

rootFamily.gloss: to elevate, promote, upgrade (status, quality, or gear)
to promote in rank, pull up talent

插.etymology: Ideogram (会意字) showing a hand (扌) driving a pestle or pointed tool (千/干) into a mortar (臼): 'insert, stick in, plug in, plant (rice seedlings), interpose (a remark or episode)'.

history.stage: Old & Classical Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: pierce/insert into a socket = stick in, plug in, insert

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 插 (via 萌典)

插嘴.etymology: A colloquial separable verb–object compound (动宾离合词) formed from 插 (chā, Middle Chinese *tshreap, from 扌 'hand' + 𦥑 'mortar' pierced by 千/pestle, meaning 'to thrust in, insert, plant, interpose') and 嘴 (zuǐ, Middle Chinese *tsjweX, originally 觜 'horned owl's tuft / bird's beak', with 口 'mouth' added in Tang–Song vernacular to replace Classical 口 as the everyday word for 'mouth'). Literally 'to thrust one's mouth in between others' words', it vividly expresses butting in or chiming in uninvited while others are conversing.

history.meaning: to pierce or insert; a bird's beak or pointed spout
to thrust one's mouth into a conversation; to interrupt or chime in uninvited
history.stage: Early Mandarin (Ming–Qing vernacular novels such as *Dream of the Red Chamber*)

插嘴.notes: As a separable VO verb (离合词), aspect markers, modifiers, or negative complements are inserted between the two characters: 别插嘴 ('don't butt in'), 插不上嘴 ('unable to get a word in edgewise'), 插了一句嘴 ('chimed in with a remark'). A slightly more polite near-synonym is 插话.

rootFamily.gloss: to interject a remark into a conversation (more neutral than 插嘴)
to step in, meddle, get involved in an affair (literally 'insert a hand')
interlude, episode, or insert song in a film/TV drama

插销.etymology: Compound hardware noun combining 插 ('insert, slide in') + 销 (銷, 'metal pin, peg, bolt'): 'sliding door/window bolt, latch pin' (and in some dialects an electrical plug).

history.meaning: sliding bolt or latch on a door or window

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 插销 (via 萌典)

cognates.word: 握る (にぎる, nigiru) / 握 (あく, aku)

cognates.meaning: grasping, holding in the palm (Hanja root)

握.etymology: A monomorphemic phono-semantic character (形声字) composed of the semantic hand radical 扌 (手, 'hand') and the phonetic component 屋 (wū, Old Chinese *qˤok, 'house, roofed enclosure'). In Old Chinese (*qˤrok) and Middle Chinese (*'aewk), 握 meant specifically 'to close the fingers tightly around an object, grasp firmly in the fist or palm' (contrasting with 持 'to hold steady' and 执 'to seize'). By extension, it also denoted 'a handful' and metaphorically 'to hold power, control, or certainty in one's grasp'.

history.meaning: to clasp firmly in the closed palm; a handful; to hold authority
to grasp, clutch, or hold fast in the hand
to hold in the hand, grasp, clench, or wield (power/control)

握.notes: In modern Mandarin, single-character 握 often takes a resultative/directional complement (握紧 'grip tightly', 握住 'hold fast') or appears in key compounds like 握手 ('shake hands'), 掌握 ('grasp/master/control'), and 有把握 ('have confidence/certainty').

rootFamily.gloss: to grasp, master, have control over (a skill, situation, or power)
grasp, assurance, certainty of success (e.g., 有把握)

揣.etymology: When read chuāi in colloquial Northern and Southwestern Mandarin, 揣 (formed with the hand radical 扌 and phonetic 耑) means 'to tuck or nestle an object securely inside one's robe, bosom, or pocket'—originally slipping valuables into the folds of a traditional jacket (揣在怀里). Note that the same character read chuǎi is an older literary verb meaning 'to estimate or ponder' (揣摩).

morphemes.meaning: tuck securely into a garment fold or pocket (hand radical 扌)

history.meaning: measure by hand; estimate
tuck safely inside one's coat or pocket

揣摩.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative verbal compound (并列结构) pairing two tactile verbs with the hand radical 扌: 揣 (chuǎi, Old Chinese *t-hlˤorʔ, Middle Chinese *tshjweX, 'to measure height or depth by feeling with the hand, gauge, estimate') and 摩 (mó, Old Chinese *mˤaj, Middle Chinese *mwa, 'to rub, stroke, palpate, study closely by touch'). Famous from the Warring States diplomatic treatise *Guiguzi* (鬼谷子, which devotes an entire chapter titled 〈揣篇〉 and 〈摩篇〉 to gauging a ruler's hidden psychology and probing their reactions), it evolved to mean 'to fathom, puzzle out, or read between the lines of someone's intentions or a script/role'.

history.meaning: to gauge by hand and probe by touch; in Warring States rhetoric, to measure and test a ruler's hidden motives
to ponder deeply, study the nuances of classic texts or exam essays, and conjecture another's mind
history.stage: Middle Chinese to Late Imperial Literary Chinese

history.meaning: to try to figure out, fathom, or read between the lines (of a boss's intent, audience psychology, or a dramatic role)

揣摩.notes: A favorite word in acting, directing, and workplace contexts (*幕后之王*): actors 揣摩角色 ('fathom/internalize a character's psychology'), while subordinates 揣摩上意 ('try to read the boss's mind') or producers 揣摩观众心理 ('figure out audience psychology').

rootFamily.gloss: to speculate, guess, surmise (often with 揣测)
to rub, chafe; friction (physical or interpersonal)
to observe and emulate; to study a model closely

搅.etymology: Phono-semantic action verb combining the hand radical 扌 (semantic: manual action) with 觉 (phonetic *jiǎo* / Middle Chinese *kæwX*). Attested since medieval culinary and medical texts for stirring, whisking, or agitating a liquid in a pot or bowl.

history.meaning: stir or whisk a liquid mixture
stir; whisk

搅动.etymology: Resultative/coordinative verb compound from 搅 (simplified from 攪, hand 扌 + phonetic 覺 'stir; mix; agitate') + 动 (simplified from 動, 'move; set in motion'). Combines the circular motion of stirring with the resulting movement of the liquid or paint.

history.meaning: stir into motion; agitate
stir; swirl; agitate

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 搅动

搅匀.etymology: Resultative verb compound combining 搅 ('stir; whisk', hand radical 扌 + 觉) + 匀 ('even; uniform', pictograph of two equal marks 二 inside an embracing wrap 勹). In cooking and baking, it specifies stirring a sauce, batter, or curd until every ingredient is evenly blended.

history.meaning: stir until smooth and evenly blended

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 搅匀

cognates.meaning: to search, look for, investigate (sagasu / sō)
cognates.word: 捜 (そう, sō / 捜す, sagasu)

搜.etymology: A monomorphemic phono-semantic character (形声字, also historically written 廋) composed of the hand radical 扌 (手, 'hand') and the phonetic-ideographic component 叟 (sǒu, Old Chinese *sˤuʔ, which in bronze and seal script depicts a hand 又 holding a flaming torch 火 inside a house 宀 to look for something in the dark). In Old Chinese (*sru) and Middle Chinese (*srjuw), 搜 meant 'to rummage with the hands, search out hidden things, inspect thoroughly', extending in modern usage from physical frisking and rummaging to digital and online searching.

history.meaning: to search a dwelling with a torch or by hand; to seek out what is hidden
to rummage, inspect, or hunt for (fugitives, treasures, or poetic lines)
to search, rummage, or look up online (e.g., 热搜 'trending search')

morphemes.meaning: hand holding a torch indoors (*sˤuʔ, 叟)

搜.notes: In contemporary spoken Mandarin and media culture (*幕后之王*), standalone 搜 frequently means 'to search on the internet/search engine' (你在网上搜一下 'Search for it online'), alongside viral media terms like 热搜 ('hot/trending search list on Weibo').

rootFamily.gloss: to search for, look for; internet search
trending search topic (short for 热门搜索, vital in showbiz PR)
to search and seize, raid, frisk

cognates.meaning: collection, gathering (of data, evidence, or specimens)
cognates.word: 捜集 / 収集 (しゅうしゅう, shūshū)

搜集.etymology: A sequential-coordinative verbal compound (连动/并列结构) combining 搜 (sōu, Middle Chinese *srjuw, 'to seek out, search everywhere') and 集 (jí, Middle Chinese *dzip, originally 雧 depicting three birds 隹 perched together atop a tree 木, meaning 'to flock together, assemble, gather into one place'). Literally 'to search out from scattered places and gather together', it is attested from Tang–Song prose onward for compiling books, evidence, folklore, or intelligence.

history.meaning: to search out hidden things; birds flocking on a tree, to assemble
to seek out and compile scattered texts, poems, or historical records
history.stage: Middle Chinese to Early Mandarin (Song–Ming scholarship)

history.meaning: to collect, gather, and compile (materials, evidence, data, or story leads)

搜集.notes: Compare near-homophonous 收集 (shōují): 搜集 emphasizes the active effort of *searching out* hard-to-find or scattered items (搜集证据 'search for and gather evidence', 搜集素材 'gather creative source material'), whereas 收集 focuses simply on bringing items together into a collection.

rootFamily.gloss: to hunt for and collect (rare books, talent, or curiosities)

搞.etymology: A monomorphemic phono-semantic character (形声字) composed of the hand radical 扌 (手, 'hand') and the phonetic 高 (gāo, Middle Chinese *kaw; cf. 敲 *khaw 'to strike/knock' and 搅 *kaewX 'to stir/disturb'). Originally a regional verb in Southwest Mandarin and Xiang/Chu dialects (Hunan, Hubei, Sichuan) meaning 'to stir, beat, work with the hands', 搞 entered national general Mandarin in the mid-20th century (accelerated by Hunan/Hubei leaders and writers during the 1940s–1950s) as a highly versatile pro-verb ('to do, make, manage, work on, get, cause'), parallel to northern 弄 (nòng).

history.meaning: to beat, stir, or manipulate with the hand (regional Chu/Southwest vernacular)
history.stage: Late Imperial Regional Mandarin and Xiang/Gan dialects

history.meaning: generalized transitive verb: to do, carry out, engage in, produce, get, or cause
history.stage: Modern Standard Chinese (popularized nationwide from the 1940s–1950s)

搞.notes: The ultimate colloquial Swiss-army verb in spoken Mandarin: depending on its object or complement, 搞 can mean 'engage in' (搞创作 'do creative work'), 'set up' (搞活动 'organize an event'), 'secure/get' (搞到票 'get tickets'), or 'mess with' (搞心态 'mess with someone's mindset'). Avoid in stiff formal writing.

rootFamily.gloss: to make laugh, funny, comedic (literally 'stir up laughter')
to engage in spoofs or parody (from Japanese kuso culture via Taiwan/HK)
to settle, handle successfully, get it done

搞不定.etymology: A negative potential resultative construction (可能补语否定式) built from the generalized action verb 搞 (gǎo, 'to do, handle, manage'), the negative potential infix 不 (bù, 'cannot, unable to achieve'), and the resultative complement 定 (dìng, Middle Chinese *dengH, 'to settle, fix, stabilize, bring to order', from 宀 'roof' + 正 'upright/correct'). As the negative counterpart of 搞得定 / 搞定, it literally means 'unable to work on something until it is settled', i.e., 'unable to handle, cope with, or resolve (a difficult person, crisis, or task)'.

history.meaning: to settle, establish, make firm and orderly
unable to settle, fix, or handle a thorny task or person (colloquial potential construction)

morphemes.meaning: unable to, cannot achieve the result

搞不定.notes: Very common in fast-paced workplace dramas (*幕后之王*) for admitting or worrying that a crisis, temperamental celebrity, or technical glitch is beyond one's ability to resolve (e.g., 这个艺人太难缠，我搞不定 'This artist is too difficult; I can't handle them'). Affirmative potential: 搞得定.

rootFamily.gloss: able to handle, capable of resolving (affirmative potential form)

搞好.etymology: A resultative verbal compound (动结结构) combining the general transitive verb 搞 (gǎo, 'to do, carry out, manage') with the stative/completion complement 好 (hǎo, Middle Chinese *xawX, 'good, well, properly completed'). In Mandarin resultative grammar, post-verbal 好 marks both completion of an action and a satisfactory outcome; thus 搞好 means 'to do or manage something so that it turns out well—to build well, handle properly, or do a good job on'.

history.meaning: good, fine, pleasing; post-verbally in vernacular Chinese, 'to a proper completion'
to do a good job on, manage well, or put on a sound footing (relations, production, or work)

搞好.notes: Frequently used with interpersonal or organizational objects, most famously 搞好关系 ('build/maintain good relationships or rapport') and 把节目搞好 ('do a great job producing the show').

rootFamily.gloss: to do well, complete properly (more formal/standard equivalent of 搞好)
exactly right, just in time, happens that

cognates.meaning: to settle, finish, get it done (source of the modern pop-culture spread)

搞定.etymology: A resultative verbal compound (动结结构) pairing 搞 (gǎo, 'to do, handle, work on') with 定 (dìng, Middle Chinese *dengH, 'settled, fixed, resolved'). While 搞定 fits native Mandarin resultative syntax ('to work on something until it is settled') and existed in Southwest Mandarin, its explosive nationwide popularity in late-20th-century urban Mandarin was heavily reinforced by Hong Kong Cantonese 搞掂 (gaau2 dim6, literally 'handle until straight/settled'), adapted into Mandarin via the near-homophonous and semantically transparent complement 定.

history.meaning: to make straight, handle successfully, finish off a task
history.stage: Cantonese vernacular (spread via Hong Kong cinema and pop culture in the 1980s–1990s)

history.meaning: to settle a problem, win over a person, or finish a task completely ('Done! / Sorted!')

搞定.notes: Used both transitively for winning over people or solving problems (搞定客户 'win over the client', 搞定版权 'secure the copyright') and as a crisp standalone exclamation ('搞定！' = 'Done! / All set!').

rootFamily.gloss: unable to handle or resolve (negative potential form)

搞清楚.etymology: A resultative verbal compound (动结结构) formed from the causative/general verb 搞 (gǎo, 'to do, make, get') and the disyllabic adjectival complement 清楚 (qīngchu, 'clear, distinct'). 清楚 itself is a Classical Chinese coordinative compound uniting 清 (qīng, 'clear, limpid, pure water') and 楚 (chǔ, 'thorny brushwood neatly arrayed; distinct, sharp, orderly', as in 衣冠楚楚). Literally 'to work on a matter until it becomes clear and distinct', 搞清楚 means 'to figure out, find out for sure, clarify, or get straight'.

history.meaning: clear and distinct, neat and orderly
to clarify, figure out, or ascertain the truth of a situation

morphemes.meaning: distinct, sharp, orderly (neutral tone in compound)

搞清楚.notes: Equivalent to 弄清楚; often used in imperatives when confronting someone or demanding accountability in workplace drama (你先搞清楚状况！ 'Get the situation straight first!' / 把事情搞清楚 'Find out what really happened').

rootFamily.gloss: to figure out, clarify (northern/standard synonym of 搞清楚)
to clarify, explain clearly (a statement or rumour)

搞砸.etymology: A colloquial resultative verbal compound (动结结构) combining the general action verb 搞 (gǎo, 'to do, handle, manage') with the resultative complement 砸 (zá, from 石 'stone' + 匝 phonetic, originally meaning 'to pound, tamp, smash, or crush with a heavy weight'). In Beijing and northern Pear Garden (Peking Opera) theatrical slang of the late Qing and Republican eras, 演砸了 or 砸锅 ('smashing the cooking pot') meant a performance flopping disastrously; combined with 搞, 搞砸 means 'to bungle, botch, ruin, or screw up'.

history.meaning: to pound, smash, or shatter by striking heavily
to smash the pot; theatrical slang for a performance failing or ruining one's livelihood
to botch, bungle, ruin, or mess up (a project, pitch, broadcast, or relationship)

morphemes.meaning: smash, shatter; figuratively botched, ruined, flopped

搞砸.notes: Almost always appears with the perfective particle 了 (把事情搞砸了 'botched the whole thing', 直播搞砸了 'the live broadcast was ruined') or in potential forms (搞不砸 / 别搞砸了 'don't screw it up'). Near-synonym: 弄砸.

rootFamily.gloss: to mess up, bungle (synonym using 弄)
to fail disastrously, flop (literally 'smash the cooking pot')
to smash to pieces; to ruin someone's brand/reputation (砸招牌)

搬.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 扌 (手, 'hand') + 般 (bān, 'shift, transport by boat'): 'move, carry, shift (heavy objects or furniture from one place to another)'. Attested from Tang–Song vernacular onward.

history.meaning: move; shift; carry heavy items

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 搬 (via 萌典)

搬家.etymology: Separable verb-object compound of 搬 ('move, shift') + 家 ('home, household'): 'move house, relocate one's home'.

history.meaning: move house; change residence

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 搬家 (via 萌典)

搬家公司.etymology: Four-character compound combining 搬家 ('move house') + 公司 ('company'): 'moving company, household movers'.

history.meaning: moving company

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 搬家公司 (via 萌典)

搭把手.etymology: A colloquial verb–object idiom (动宾惯用语) with an elided numeral 一 (dā [yī] bǎ shǒu), composed of 搭 (dā, Middle Chinese *tap, 'to lay across, join together, put up, attach'), the classifier 把 (bǎ, originally 'to grasp in the hand', grammaticalized as the measure word for a handful, a grip, or a quick manual effort), and 手 (shǒu, 'hand'). Literally 'to lay on a hand-grip alongside someone else' (as when two people lift a heavy load together on a set or stage), it means 'to lend a hand, pitch in briefly to help out'.

history.meaning: to lay hands together on an object; to join hands or assist in lifting
to lend a quick hand, pitch in and help someone with a task

morphemes.meaning: place upon, join in, add to
measure word for a grasp, handful, or brief effort (with elided 一)

搭把手.notes: Warm, everyday colloquial phrasing (often heard when moving studio props or handling urgent backstage tasks: 快来搭把手 'Come lend a quick hand!'); the classifier 把 softens the request by implying the help needed is just a brief, easy effort.

rootFamily.gloss: partner, teammate, co-host (literally 'one who joins the same file/team')
to match, pair up, coordinate (outfits, cast members, or elements)

搭档.etymology: Compound verb and noun of 搭 ('join together, pair up', 扌 + 荅) + 档 (檔, 'group, team, stage/business slot'): originally from traditional Chinese opera and storytelling for two performers teaming up on stage, now the general word for 'team up, cooperate; partner, teammate'.

history.stage: Qing–Republican performing arts to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: pair up as partners; partner

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 搭档 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: capturing an image, imaging (cognate of the modifier 摄像)
capturing an image, video recording (cognate of 摄像)

摄像师.etymology: A three-character modifier–head compound (偏正结构, Traditional 攝像師) consisting of the VO modifier 摄像 (shèxiàng, 'to capture images / record video') and the occupational suffix 师 (Traditional 師, shī, Middle Chinese *srij, originally 'military division' or 'master teacher', productive in modern Chinese for skilled specialists). Within 摄像, 摄 (Traditional 攝, shè, Middle Chinese *sjep, from 扌 'hand' + 聶 'three ears', meaning 'to draw in, absorb, take hold of') combines with 像 (xiàng, 'likeness, image, figure') to mean optically capturing moving images.

history.meaning: to draw in or hold; a likeness or portrait; a master of a craft
photographer or cinematographer (literally 'master of capturing shadows/light')
videographer, television/broadcast camera operator
history.stage: Modern Standard Chinese (television and digital video era)

morphemes.meaning: draw in, capture optically, take (a picture/video)

摄像师.notes: Media industry distinction in Mainland China (*幕后之王*): 摄像师 specifically denotes a television, studio, or video camera operator (working with electronic video cameras, 摄像机), whereas 摄影师 refers either to a still photographer or a film cinematographer/director of photography (working on movies).

rootFamily.gloss: photographer; film cinematographer / director of photography
to record video, videotape; video recording

cognates.meaning: imaging tube / video camera tube (related technical root)
cognates.word: 撮像機 / 撮像管 (さつぞうかん, satsuzōkan)

摄像机.etymology: A three-character modifier–head compound (偏正结构, Traditional 攝像機) joining the verbal modifier 摄像 (shèxiàng, from 摄 'draw in, capture optically' + 像 'likeness, visual image') with the head noun 机 (Traditional 機, jī, Middle Chinese *kj+j, from 木 'wood' + 幾 'subtle/minute', originally 'the intricate trigger mechanism of a crossbow or the shuttle apparatus of a loom'). In modern scientific and technical Chinese, 机 serves as the productive head for mechanical or electronic apparatuses, yielding 'image-capturing machine—a video camera or broadcast camcorder'.

history.meaning: crossbow trigger mechanism or loom apparatus; subtle pivot of motion
motion-picture film camera (literally 'shadow-capturing machine')
electronic video camera, broadcast television camera, or camcorder

摄像机.notes: Contrast three camera terms: 照相机 (or 相机) is a still photo camera; 摄影机 is a cinema film camera; 摄像机 is a video/broadcast television camera (and 摄像头 is a small webcam or security camera lens). In TV studio slang, a camera position is called a 机位.

rootFamily.gloss: camera position or angle on a film/TV set (crucial director's term)
webcam, security camera, phone camera module
still camera; or 'wait for an opportunity' (classical sense)

摄像棚.etymology: A three-character modifier–head compound (偏正结构, Traditional 攝像棚) combining the modifier 摄像 (shèxiàng, 'video recording, television filming') with the head noun 棚 (péng, Middle Chinese *bong, from 木 'wood' + 朋 phonetic, originally 'a covered wooden framework, awning, mat-shed, or temporary pavilion'). When early-20th-century Chinese film studios erected large glass-roofed or enclosed soundstages, they adopted 棚 ('large covered shed/pavilion') to translate 'studio stage' (摄影棚), from which television production derived 摄像棚 (and 演播棚/演播室) for a video recording studio.

history.meaning: wooden trellis, canopy, or temporary mat-shed for shade, staging, or storage
enclosed film soundstage or photography studio
television/video recording studio or soundstage

摄像棚.notes: In television and film production (*幕后之王*), 棚 is used productively as a bound or free morpheme for studio work: 进棚 ('enter the studio to record/shoot'), 棚拍 ('studio shoot', as opposed to 外景 'location shoot'), 摄影棚 ('film/photo studio'), and 录音棚 ('recording studio').

rootFamily.gloss: audio recording studio (for voiceover, dubbing, or music)
to burst at the seams; overcrowded or wildly popular (literally 'burst the shed')

摆.etymology: Phono-semantic character (traditional 擺, combining 扌 'hand' + 罷 bà/bǎi phonetic): 'set out, arrange, display, place (furniture, dishes, or goods); wave/swing back and forth (like a pendulum 钟摆); put on airs'.

history.meaning: arrange; set out; display; swing back and forth

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 摆 (via 萌典)

摆放.etymology: A coordinative verb compound pairing 摆 (bǎi, trad. 擺, from 扌 'hand' + 罢 'cease/spread', originally 'to push aside, spread out, arrange') with 放 (fàng, 'to release, let go, put, place'). In Ming–Qing vernacular Mandarin, 摆 shifted from 'to wave, shake' to 'to lay out in order', combining with 放 to denote setting objects down in a deliberate spatial arrangement or display.

history.meaning: to drive away, release; to place or set down
to lay out and arrange items in order
to place, position, or arrange on display

摆放.notes: Unlike simple 放 ('to put'), 摆放 implies care, orderliness, or visual presentation—such as props arranged on a studio set or merchandise on shelves.

rootFamily.gloss: to set out, arrange in order
to place, put in a certain spot

摊.etymology: Phono-semantic character (traditional 攤, combining 扌 'hand' + 難 nán/tān phonetic): 'spread out flat on a surface; vendor's stall or booth (摆摊); fry a thin batter (pancake/omelet); share/divide costs equally; befall'.

history.meaning: spread out; vendor's stall; share a portion

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 摊 (via 萌典)

摔.etymology: A phono-semantic compound (摔, shuāi; Middle Chinese *srwit*) formed with the hand signific 扌 (shǒu) and the phonetic 率 (shuài/lǜ, Old Chinese *s-rut*). Attested in the *Shuowen Jiezi* area and Medieval rime books as 'to棄/throw to the ground' or 'to pluck', it developed in northern vernacular Mandarin into an ambitransitive verb meaning both 'to fling down and smash' (transitive) and 'to lose one's footing and tumble' (intransitive).

history.meaning: to hurl to the ground; to seize and throw down
to fall down; to drop and break; to fling down in anger

morphemes.meaning: to throw down, smash; to fall, tumble

摔.notes: Exhibits striking ambitransitivity in spoken Mandarin: 摔跤 ('to trip and fall', intransitive) vs. 摔杯子 ('to smash a cup by throwing it down', transitive) or 摔门 ('to slam a door').

rootFamily.gloss: to shatter by dropping or throwing
to temper oneself through hardships and setbacks

摔倒.etymology: A verb-resultative compound combining the action verb 摔 (shuāi, 'to stumble, lose balance, fall') with the resultative complement 倒 (dǎo, 'to topple over, fall prostrate'). While 摔 specifies the sudden loss of footing or impact with the ground, 倒 encodes the resulting state of having collapsed from an upright posture to a horizontal one.

history.meaning: to fall over, topple, invert
to lose one's footing and fall to the ground

摔倒.notes: Used for both people tripping on stage/set and objects being knocked flat; can accepts potential infixes like 摔不倒 ('cannot be knocked down').

摘.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 扌 (手, 'hand') + 啇 (dì/zhāi phonetic): 'pluck, pick (flowers, fruit, or tea leaves with the fingers); take off (glasses, a hat, or a hanging item); select/excerpt passages'.

history.stage: Old & Classical Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: pick/pluck with the hand; take off (glasses/hat); excerpt

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 摘 (via 萌典)

摸.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 扌 (手, 'hand') + 莫 (mò/mō phonetic, which also means 'dusk/dark'): 'feel, touch, stroke gently with the hand; grope in the dark for; figure out/sound out (摸清)'.

history.meaning: touch; feel; stroke; grope for

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 摸 (via 萌典)

摸摸.etymology: Reduplicated verb from 摸 ('touch, feel, stroke'): 'touch gently, give a pat or stroke, feel with one's hand'.

history.meaning: touch or stroke gently

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 摸摸 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to feel out and understand thoroughly

摸清.etymology: A metaphorical verb-resultative compound built from 摸 (mō, 'to grope, feel with the hand, stroke', a medieval vernacular graph replacing classical /捫) and 清 (qīng, originally 'clear, limpid water', used as a resultative complement meaning 'clearly, thoroughly'). The image is of groping in the dark or murky water until the contours of an object are completely clear—hence 'to fathom or ascertain the bottom-line reality'.

history.meaning: to grope with the hands / clear and limpid (separate lexemes)
to ascertain thoroughly; to figure out the ins and outs of

morphemes.meaning: to feel, grope for, sound out

摸清.notes: Frequently collocates with hidden or complex objects of inquiry such as 底细 ('inside story/background'), 门道 ('the ropes/tricks of the trade'), or 规律 ('underlying patterns').

rootFamily.gloss: to grope around; to figure out slowly by trial and error
to figure out thoroughly, get to the bottom of
to sort out, clarify (a mess or train of thought)

cognates.meaning: unable to hold up or endure

撑不住.etymology: A negative potential verb-complement construction formed from 撑 (chēng, trad. 撐/, 'to prop up with a pole, brace, support'), the negative potential infix 不 (bù, 'unable to'), and the resultative complement 住 (zhù, 'to hold fast, stay firm in place'). Literally 'unable to prop up so that it stays firm', it evolved from physical structural bracing to physical, emotional, or financial exhaustion under pressure.

history.meaning: to prop up a structure with a diagonal pole; to pole a boat
unable to bear the weight; unable to hold out under strain

撑不住.notes: Very common in high-pressure workplace and production settings when someone's stamina, composure, or cash flow is on the verge of collapsing (e.g., 身体撑不住了, 场面撑不住了).

rootFamily.gloss: to put on a brave front, tough it out

撒.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 扌 (手, 'hand') + 散 (sàn/sǎ phonetic, 'scatter'): read sǎ 'scatter, sprinkle, strew (seeds, salt, powder, or water), spill'; read sā 'let go, release, cast (a net), let oneself go (撒娇)'.

history.meaning: let go, cast (sā); scatter, sprinkle, spill (sǎ)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 撒 (via 萌典)

撕.etymology: A phono-semantic character 撕 (sī) pairing the hand radical 扌 ('manual action') with phonetic 斯 (sī, which in Old Chinese itself meant 'to cleave or split wood with an axe 斤'). Emergent in Tang–Yuan vernacular literature to replace classical 裂 ('rend'), 撕 specifically denotes gripping paper, cloth, or leaves with the fingers and ripping them apart.

history.meaning: rip or tear paper/cloth by hand
tear; rip

撕破.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 撕破. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 撕破 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 撕破 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 撕破 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 撕破. The etymology of 撕破 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 撕破
middle form of 撕破
modern form of 撕破

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 撕破

cognates.meaning: to drop all pretense of civility and have a falling-out

撕破脸.etymology: An idiomatic verb-object phrase built from the resultative verb 撕破 (sīpò, from 撕 'to rip, tear apart with the hands' + 破 'broken, torn through') and the direct object 脸 (liǎn, trad. 臉, 'face', functioning sociolinguistically as 脸面 'social face, polite facade'). Tearing through the 'face' vividly metaphors stripping away the veneer of mutual politeness to engage in open hostility.

history.meaning: to tear through the mask of politeness; to cast aside all courtesy
to have an acrimonious open falling-out, drop all pretense of amicability

morphemes.meaning: face; social facade and mutual respect (object)

撕破脸.notes: Often appears with 彻底 ('completely') or 跟/和…撕破脸 ('to have an open falling-out with someone'); reflects the centrality of 'face' (面子/脸面) in Chinese conflict management.

rootFamily.gloss: to turn hostile suddenly, fall out with someone
social prestige, sensibility about face; cheek
to tear to shreds (e.g., a contract or script)

撞.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 扌 (手, 'hand/strike') + 童 (tóng/zhuàng phonetic): originally 'strike a bell or drum with a wooden ram', hence 'bump into, knock against, collide with, run into by chance'.

history.stage: Classical Chinese (Zhuangzi, Shiji) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: strike against; bump into; collide; meet by chance

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 撞 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to be possessed, run into uncanny bad luck

撞邪.etymology: A verb-object compound uniting 撞 (zhuàng, 'to strike against, bump into, encounter unexpectedly') with 邪 (xié, 'awry, heterodox, noxious qi or demonic influence', in contrast to 正 'upright, orthodox'). Rooted in traditional Chinese folk religion and medicine—where sudden delirium or inexplicable misfortune was attributed to colliding with a wandering baleful spirit or noxious pneuma (邪气)—it now functions colloquially as 'to run into freakish, jinxed bad luck'.

history.meaning: noxious pathogen or malevolent spirit causing illness or misfortune
to encounter a haunting spirit; (colloquial) to hit a bizarre streak of bad luck or act possessed

morphemes.meaning: to bump into, collide with, run into
evil spirit, demonic influence, freakish anomaly (object)

撞邪.notes: Used hyperbolically on film/TV sets and in daily speech when everything goes wrong at once (e.g., 今儿真是撞邪了 'Today is seriously jinxed'), akin to 見鬼 (jiànguǐ).

rootFamily.gloss: demonic spirit, haunting influence; crooked ways
to ward off evil spirits or bad luck
to collide; to run into by chance

cognates.meaning: withdrawal, removal (in compounds like 撤退, 撤去)

撤.etymology: Written 撤 (chè; Middle Chinese *drjet*), a phono-semantic variant of classical 徹 (chè, 'to penetrate; to clear away dinner vessels after a banquet or ritual sacrifice') differentiated by adding the hand radical 扌 (shǒu) in place of 彳 (chì). From the ritual sense 'to remove food trays when a feast concludes' (recorded in the *Analects* and *Book of Rites* as 徹), it generalized to removing props/equipment, pulling back troops, and colloquially 'heading out / taking off'.

history.meaning: to clear away sacrificial vessels or banquet dishes after a meal
to remove, dismantle, or withdraw (troops, officials, or dishes)
to clear away, pull down, withdraw; (colloquial) to head out, leave

撤.notes: In casual spoken Mandarin (先撤了! 'I'm heading out first!'), 撤 has become a brisk, playful military metaphor for leaving a gathering or wrapping up at the office.

rootFamily.gloss: to retreat, pull back (troops or personnel)
to revoke, cancel, annul (an order or post)
to evacuate, withdraw from a site

cognates.meaning: withdrawal, pulling out (of a market or territory)

撤出.etymology: A verb-directional compound combining 撤 (chè, 'to remove, withdraw, pull back') with the directional complement 出 (chū, 'out, outward from an enclosed space or situation'). The compound emphasizes extracting personnel, capital, equipment, or programming out of a specific venue, market, or broadcast slot.

history.meaning: to clear away or pull back / to go or bring out (separate verbs)
to withdraw or pull out from a position, territory, or venture

撤出.notes: Frequently used in business and media contexts for pulling capital (撤出资金), exiting a market (撤出市场), or pulling a crew out of a location.

rootFamily.gloss: to withdraw from a location, evacuate
to withdraw from, quit (a competition or group)

cognates.meaning: revocation, withdrawal, retraction (of a statement or bill)

撤回.etymology: A verb-directional compound joining 撤 (chè, 'to withdraw, revoke') with 回 (huí, 'to return, turn back to the point of origin'). Shared across the modern East Asian Sinographic legal-administrative lexicon (cf. Japanese 撤回 *tekkai*), it denotes calling back something already dispatched—whether troops, a legal motion, a broadcast statement, or a sent chat message.

history.meaning: to recall deployed troops or officials back to base
to retract, revoke, or recall (a statement, complaint, proposal, or digital message)
history.stage: Modern Mandarin (reinforced by Sino-Japanese legal usage)

撤回.notes: In contemporary Chinese, 撤回 is both a formal term for retracting an official statement/lawsuit and the everyday WeChat button term for 'unsending' a message (撤回了一条消息).

rootFamily.gloss: to revoke, cancel officially (a decision or department)
to駁回/reject and send back (an appeal or proposal)

撤掉.etymology: A verb-resultative compound formed from 撤 (chè, 'to clear away, remove, pull') and the colloquial resultative complement 掉 (diào, originally 'to shake, fall off', grammaticalized in post-Tang vernacular into a completive/disposal marker meaning 'away, off, completely gone'). Together they denote completely taking down a show, advertisement, set piece, or personnel assignment.

history.meaning: to clear away, remove
to take down, remove completely, scrap (a program, banner, or post)

morphemes.meaning: to clear away, remove, pull down

撤掉.notes: In television and live production, 撤掉 is the standard colloquial verb for pulling a segment from the rundown, taking down trending search topics (撤掉热搜), or striking stage props.

rootFamily.gloss: to remove from shelves or streaming platforms, delist
to delete, cut out (footage or text)

撬.etymology: Written 撬 (qiào), combining the hand radical 扌 with 毳 ('fine animal down', serving here for sound analogy with 橇 qiāo 'wooden sled/lever'). Attested in Ming–Qing vernacular texts for inserting a crowbar, chisel, or flat iron bar beneath a heavy stone slab, nail, or tight lid to lever it upward.

morphemes.meaning: phonetic component in vernacular craft character

history.meaning: lever up or pry open with a bar or wedge
pry open; lever up

cognates.meaning: to sow, scatter, broadcast (in compounds like 播種, 伝播)

播.etymology: A phono-semantic graph (播, bō; Old Chinese *pˤar-s*, Middle Chinese *pwaH*) combining the hand signific 扌 (shǒu) with the phonetic 番 (fān/pān). Its primary sense in the *Classic of Poetry* (*Shijing*) and *Shuowen Jiezi* is 'to sow seeds by scattering with the hand' (播种). By exact semantic parallel with English *broadcast* (originally 'to cast seed broadly', extended to radio in the 1920s), 播 was adapted in 20th-century Mandarin (via 广播 'broad-sowing = broadcasting') to mean transmitting radio, television, or streaming programs.

history.meaning: to sow seed by scattering; to spread abroad, shake, or flee
to disseminate widely; (20th c.) radio/television broadcasting
to broadcast, air, stream (a program, drama, or live feed); to sow

morphemes.meaning: to sow, scatter; to broadcast, air

播.notes: A remarkable cross-linguistic semantic calque: both Chinese 播 (in 广播) and English *broadcast* began as agricultural terms for scattering seeds by hand before becoming the core verbs of electronic media transmission.

rootFamily.gloss: radio or television broadcasting; to broadcast widely
live stream, live broadcast; to air live

cognates.meaning: to broadcast, air on television or radio

播出.etymology: A verb-directional compound combining 播 (bō, 'to broadcast, transmit, air', originally 'to scatter seed') with the directional complement 出 (chū, 'out, forth to the public'). Formed in 20th-century media Chinese, it frames airing a program as sending the finished signal or recorded episode outward from the station or platform to the audience.

history.meaning: to scatter or spread abroad / to go or send forth (separate classical verbs)
to broadcast, transmit, put on the air (a radio or television program)

播出.notes: Works both transitively (播出新剧 'to air a new drama') and unaccusatively/passively (节目今晚播出 'the show airs tonight'), and frequently pairs with 时段 ('time slot') or 平台 ('platform').

rootFamily.gloss: to premiere, air for the first time

播放.etymology: Coordinative verb compound of 播 ('sow, spread abroad, broadcast', 扌 + 番) + 放 ('release, play back'): 'broadcast (over radio/TV) or play (recorded audio or video)'.

history.meaning: broadcast; play (audio or video)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 播放 (via 萌典)

播放量.etymology: A three-character modifier-head nominal compound structured as [播放 + 量]: 播放 (bōfàng, a coordinative verb compound of 播 'broadcast/transmit' + 放 'release/play back audio or film') modifies the head noun 量 (liàng, 'measured quantity, volume, count'). Coined in the digital video and streaming era by analogy with 收视率 ('TV viewership rating') and 点击量 ('click count'), it designates the total number of times a video or audio track has been streamed.

history.meaning: to broadcast or play back recorded audio/film through equipment
total play count or view count on digital streaming platforms

播放量.notes: In modern Chinese entertainment, 播放量 is the online streaming counterpart to traditional television's 收视率 ('viewership ratings'); hitting 破亿播放量 ('surpassing 100 million views') is a standard benchmark for a hit show.

rootFamily.gloss: to play back or broadcast video/audio; playback

撮.etymology: Phono-semantic character with hand radical 扌 ('pinch with the fingers') + phonetic 最 (*zuì* / Middle Chinese *tswat*). As a verb it means to gather up with thumb and two fingers; as a culinary measure word (一小撮盐 'a small pinch of salt'), it counts tiny pinches of salt, spices, or tea leaves.

history.meaning: a pinch or handful of earth
pinch (measure word for salt, herbs, or powder)

cognates.meaning: to be skilled at, excel in

擅长.etymology: A compound combining 擅 (shàn, originally 'to act on one's own authority, monopolize, lay exclusive claim to') with 长 (cháng, trad. 長, 'long; strong point, specialty, area in which one excels', as in 一技之长). In Literary Chinese, 擅场 (shànchǎng, 'to dominate the arena') and 擅长 originally meant 'to monopolize or surpass others in a forte'; over time the sense of 'monopolizing' softened into 'to possess special mastery or proficiency in'.

history.meaning: to monopolize or command exclusively / a forte or strong point
to surpass others in a particular skill; to be uniquely adept at
to be good at, excel at, specialize in (a skill or field)

擅长.notes: Beware the pronunciation of 长 here: it is always read *cháng* ('long / strong point', cf. 特长 *tècháng* 'specialty'), never *zhǎng*; 擅长 takes either a noun phrase or verb phrase object (擅长综艺制作 'excel at variety show production').

rootFamily.gloss: one's strengths and weaknesses; merits and demerits
to act on one's own authority without permission (preserves the older sense of 擅)

cognates.meaning: operation, handling, manipulation (of machinery, data, or markets)
to operate, perform technical steps; drill

操作.etymology: A coordinative compound of 操 (cāo, 'to grasp in the hand, hold, wield, practice') and 作 (zuò, 'to do, make, work, act'). In Classical Chinese (e.g., *Book of Rites*, *History of the Later Han*), 操作 denoted 'personal physical labor and industrious conduct'. In the late 19th and 20th centuries—reinforced by Japanese *sōsa* (操作) as a translation of English *operation* and *manipulation*—it specialized into operating machinery, executing technical procedures, or pulling strings behind the scenes.

history.meaning: to labor with one's hands; industrious toil and moral conduct
to operate machinery, instruments, or technical procedures; to handle or execute
history.stage: Modern Mandarin (reshaped by Sino-Japanese technical usage)

操作.notes: Beyond operating equipment or software, 操作 is ubiquitous in media and business slang for 'behind-the-scenes execution/maneuvering'—e.g., 暗箱操作 ('backroom dealing') or internet slang 神操作 ('a god-tier move') and 骚操作 ('a flashy/audacious move').

rootFamily.gloss: to drill, practice; to handle a matter

cognates.meaning: to worry about, take pains over

操心.etymology: A verb-object separable compound (离合词) formed from 操 (cāo, 'to grasp, hold firm, exercise, tax') and 心 (xīn, 'heart-mind'). In Classical Chinese (e.g., *Mencius*: 操心也危 'they keep their hearts-and-minds under anxious vigilance'), 操心 meant 'to hold fast to one's moral resolve under adversity'. In Ming–Qing vernacular Mandarin, it shifted into an everyday expression meaning 'to tax one's mind with worry and care over someone or something'.

history.meaning: to maintain steadfast mental resolve and vigilance under hardship (Mencius)
to take trouble and worry over someone's affairs; to fret and care for

morphemes.meaning: to exercise, tax, hold, busy oneself with

操心.notes: A classic separable verb (离合词): modifiers go inside between 操 and 心 (e.g., 操了不少心 'worried a great deal', 操碎了心 'worried one's heart to pieces'), while the person or matter worried about is introduced with 为 or 替 (替你操心).

rootFamily.gloss: to be free from worry; worry-free, reassuring
to rack one's brains, take pains over
to take charge of and arrange (a wedding, event, or project)

操控.etymology: A coordinative verb compound pairing 操 (cāo, 'to grasp in the hand, wield, steer') with 控 (kòng, originally in the *Shijing* 'to draw back a bowstring to rein in horses', hence 'to rein in, control, command'). Both characters evoke hands gripping reins or levers, combining in modern Mandarin to denote steering a vehicle/system or covertly manipulating people, public opinion, or events from behind the scenes.

history.meaning: to grasp in the hand / to rein in a horse or draw a bow (separate classical verbs)
to steer, control, or manipulate (machinery, markets, public opinion, or people)

操控.notes: Compared with 操纵 (cāozòng, 'to manipulate like a puppet master', which is strongly pejorative in interpersonal contexts), 操控 spans both neutral technical handling (操控无人机 'piloting a drone') and psychological/media manipulation (操控舆论 'manipulating public opinion').

rootFamily.gloss: to control, keep in check; control
to manipulate from behind the scenes (literally 'to hold tight and let loose' like puppet strings)
remote control; to control from afar

擦.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 扌 (手, 'hand') + 察 (chá/cā phonetic): 'rub, wipe clean (with a cloth or towel), scrub, erase, brush past closely, apply (ointment/lotion)'.

history.meaning: wipe; rub; scrub; brush past

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 擦 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to save up, hoard, gather together

攒.etymology: Written 攒 in simplified script (merging traditional 攢, a phono-semantic compound of 扌 'hand' + 贊 zàn 'assist/gather', and /儹). In Medieval Chinese, read *cuán* (Middle Chinese *dzwan*), it meant 'to gather together in a cluster, assemble'. In northern vernacular Mandarin from the Yuan–Ming period onward, a distinct colloquial reading *zǎn* emerged with the specialized sense 'to hoard bit by bit, save up money or resources over time'.

history.meaning: to collect, cluster together, assemble in one place
to save up bit by bit, accumulate money or goods over time

morphemes.meaning: to save up bit by bit, accumulate, hoard

攒.notes: A classic polyphone (多音字): read *zǎn* when meaning 'to save up money, vacation days, or goodwill bit by bit' (攒钱, 攒人品), but read *cuán* in literary compounds meaning 'to cluster or piece together' (万头攒动 'a sea of bobbing heads', 攒眉 'to knit one's brows').

rootFamily.gloss: to save up bit by bit, accumulate over time
to save up money, build a nest egg
to piece together; to assemble a custom PC or project team (colloquial *cuán*)

cognates.meaning: to have saved up and set aside

攒下.etymology: A verb-resultative/directional compound combining 攒 (zǎn, trad. 攢, 'to save up bit by bit, accumulate') with the directional/resultative complement 下 (xià, 'down', grammaticalized here to denote retention, fixation, and preservation for the future, as in 存下 or 留下). It emphasizes not merely the act of saving, but the resulting reserve of money, resources, or goodwill successfully set aside.

history.meaning: to accumulate and lay aside (savings, property, or merit) over time
to save up and keep; to have accumulated as a reserve

morphemes.meaning: to save up bit by bit, accumulate

攒下.notes: The complement 下 highlights the lasting outcome of patient accumulation—e.g., 攒下一笔钱 ('to have saved up a sum of money') or 攒下不少经验 ('to have accumulated a wealth of experience').

rootFamily.gloss: to save up bit by bit, hoard
to deposit and keep, save up (money or supplies)
to leave behind, retain, stay behind

cognates.meaning: branch, division, support; counter for long thin items or flutes

支.etymology: An ancient ideograph (支, zhī; Old Chinese *ke*, Middle Chinese *tsje*) depicting a hand (又) holding a bamboo sprig or branch cut from a plant; it is the original graph for 枝 ('tree branch'). From the concrete image of a slender bamboo stalk or offshoot branch, it grammaticalized along two paths: (1) as a verb 'to prop up, sustain, branch off' and (2) as a nominal classifier for rod-like objects (pens, flutes, arrows), organized detachments ('branches' of troops or bands), and by extension musical pieces, songs, and promotional trailers/commercials.

history.meaning: a bamboo twig or tree branch (ancestor of 枝); to prop up or divide into branches
history.stage: Old & Classical Chinese (Oracle Bone & Bronze Scripts)

history.meaning: classifier for slender rod-like objects (arrows, brushes, flutes), troop detachments, and melodies/songs
classifier for pens, cigarettes, songs, dances, bands/teams, and video trailers or commercials

morphemes.meaning: branch; classifier for slender objects, teams/bands, songs, and video trailers/ads

支.notes: In the entertainment and advertising industries, 支 is the standard professional classifier for songs/singles (一支单曲), bands/teams (一支乐队/团队), commercials (一支广告), and promotional trailers (一支预告片).

rootFamily.gloss: branch, offshoot (of a river, organization, or system)

支持.etymology: A coordinative compound uniting 支 (zhī, 'to prop up, sustain, bear weight') and 持 (chí, 'to grasp in the hand, hold fast, maintain'). In Classical and Literary Chinese, 支持 meant 'to prop up physically, hold an enterprise together, or hold out against pressure'. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries—influenced by Japanese *shiji* (支持) translating English *support* in political and civic discourse—it expanded to include moral, financial, political, and fan backing (both verb and noun).

history.meaning: to prop up physically; to sustain or hold a situation together under strain
to back, endorse, or stand behind (a person, project, or cause); support, backing
history.stage: Modern Mandarin (expanded via Sino-Japanese political/media usage)

支持.notes: Unlike 支撑 (which stresses bearing heavy physical or structural strain so something doesn't collapse), 支持 stresses endorsement, encouragement, or providing resources/backing to a person, show, or proposal.

rootFamily.gloss: approval rating, support rate (in polls or market research)
to prop up, sustain under pressure
to persist, hold fast to, insist on

收.etymology: Ancient character attested on Shang oracle bones combining 丩 ('bind/gather together') + 攵 ('hand holding a stick/implement'): originally 'arrest/gather in, harvest crops', and by extension 'receive, accept (a gift, letter, or payment); put away/collect; bring to a close; restrain'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: gather in; harvest; receive; collect; put away

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 收 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to rein in a bit, tone down slightly

收一收.etymology: A tentative/delimitative verb construction followed by the V-一-V pattern: 收 (shōu, 'to gather in, draw back, restrain, rein in') is reduplicated around the numeral 一 (yī, 'one'), which marks a brief, mild, or moderating action. Derived from the classical polarity of 放 ('letting loose, projecting outward') vs. 收 ('drawing back, restraining'), 收一收 instructs someone to dial back their emotional intensity, temper, or performance style just a notch.

history.meaning: to gather in, draw back, restrain one's expression or behavior
to tone down a bit, rein in one's temper or performance, pull back slightly (V-一-V delimitative)

morphemes.meaning: to draw in, restrain, tone down

收一收.notes: A classic director's note on set (这儿情绪收一收 'dial back the emotion a bit here') as well as everyday advice to rein in one's temper or arrogance (把你那脾气收一收); Chinese acting aesthetics prize 收放自如 ('effortlessly alternating between restraint [收] and full projection [放]').

rootFamily.gloss: to restrain oneself, tone down arrogance or intensity; to converge
able to restrain and project at will (masterful control in acting/writing)
to draw back, pull in, contract

收入.etymology: Originally a verb-directional/coordinative compound combining 收 (shōu, 'to gather in, harvest, collect, receive') and 入 (rù, 'to enter, take in, bring inside'). In Literary Chinese (e.g., *Zuo Zhuan*, Tang–Song histories), 收入 functioned primarily as a transitive verb meaning 'to take in, gather into storage, or annex'. In the modern era—reinforced by Japanese *shūnyū* (収入) as the standard economic term for *income / revenue*—it lexicalized primarily as a noun denoting money earned or received.

history.meaning: to gather in, receive into a storehouse or treasury (verb)
monetary income, revenue, earnings (noun); to take in or include (verb)
history.stage: Modern Mandarin (nominal sense consolidated via Sino-Japanese economics)

收入.notes: Compare 收入 ('total income/revenue coming in, whether wages or box-office receipts') with 收益 ('returns, yield, or net benefit generated from an investment or project').

rootFamily.gloss: income and expenditure; cash flow balance (收 + 支)
input, investment; to put into (an endeavor or production)

收到.etymology: A verb-resultative compound uniting 收 (shōu, 'to receive, accept, collect') with the resultative complement 到 (dào, 'to arrive, reach, attain'). While 收 alone expresses the action of collecting or receiving, the complement 到 confirms successful receipt at the destination ('to have received'). In 20th-century radio telephony and modern workplace/set culture, standalone 收到! became the standard equivalent of 'Copy that! / Roger that!'.

history.meaning: to gather or receive / to arrive at a destination (separate verbs)
to have received (a letter, payment, or parcel)
to receive; (standalone interjection) 'Copy that! / Got it!' in walkie-talkie and workplace communication

收到.notes: Ubiquitous on film/TV production walkie-talkies and in workplace WeChat/DingTalk groups: when a director or producer issues an instruction, crew members reply simply 收到! ('Copy that! / Understood!').

rootFamily.gloss: to accept, receive (an assignment, signal, or concept)
to sign for receipt of a delivery or document
receipt (written acknowledgment of payment or goods received)

cognates.meaning: recovery, retrieval (usually inverted as 回収 kaishū)

收回.etymology: A verb-directional compound formed from 收 (shōu, 'to gather in, take back, collect') and the directional/resultative complement 回 (huí, 'back, returning to the original holder or source'). Attested in vernacular and administrative Chinese for reclaiming land, authority, or loans, it extends metaphorically to taking back spoken words, revoking delegated rights, or recouping production costs.

history.meaning: to take back into one's possession; to reclaim territory or authority
to take back, reclaim, recoup (costs/sovereignty), or retract (a remark or order)

morphemes.meaning: to take in, collect, gather back

收回.notes: Often collocates with 成命 ('an issued order': 收回成命 'countermand an order'), 成本 ('production costs': 收回成本 'recoup costs'), or spoken words (我收回刚才的话 'I take back what I just said').

rootFamily.gloss: to recycle, recover, retrieve (note the inverted morpheme order 回 + 收)
to withdraw, retract (a formal motion, statement, or sent message)
to redeem, buy back (a pawned item, bond, or contract)

cognates.meaning: to wrap up, bring to a conclusion, finish off

收尾.etymology: A verb-object separable compound (also used nominally as 'the ending/finale') combining 收 (shōu, 'to gather in, draw to a close, wind up') with 尾 (wěi, 'tail; final section or concluding stage of an affair'). Drawing on the classical structural metaphor of 首尾 ('head and tail = beginning and end'), 收尾 literally means 'to gather in the tail end'—hence wrapping up the final tasks of a project, narrative, or broadcast.

history.meaning: the concluding section of a classical essay, poem, or musical piece; to bring a work to a close
to wrap up final details, wind up a project, or record the closing segment of a show

morphemes.meaning: to gather in, wind up, conclude

收尾.notes: In television and event production, 收尾 refers both to finishing the final stages of post-production (收尾工作 'wrap-up work') and to the host delivering the closing segment of a show; its opposite is 开场 ('opening') or 起头 ('starting off').

rootFamily.gloss: ending, conclusion; to conclude a story or show
from beginning to end ('head and tail'); coherent throughout (首尾呼应)
to wind up a performance, game, or tricky situation; finale

cognates.meaning: to knock off work for the day; (slang) to finish someone off

收工.etymology: A verb-object separable compound pairing 收 (shōu, 'to gather up tools, bring to a close, wind up') with 工 (gōng, 'work, labor, craft, shift'). Originating in traditional artisanal, agricultural, and opera troupe usage—where workers literally packed up their tools and instruments when the day's shift ended—it became the universal film, television, and stage production term for 'wrapping for the day' (opposite of 开工 'starting work / cameras rolling').

history.meaning: to pack up tools and cease manual or craft work at the end of a shift or project
history.stage: Late Imperial & Early Modern Chinese (especially Cantonese & Mandarin guild usage)

history.meaning: to wrap up work for the day (especially on film/TV sets, construction sites, and studios)

morphemes.meaning: to gather up, wind up, finish

收工.notes: On Chinese film and television sets, 收工! is the exact equivalent of the director calling 'That's a wrap (for today)!'—distinguished from 杀青 (shāqīng), which means wrapping principal photography on the entire season or movie.

rootFamily.gloss: to start work, begin shooting or construction (antonym of 收工)
to finish a project; completion of construction or production
to finish work hours and go off duty (white-collar equivalent)

cognates.meaning: to tidy up, pack; to fix or punish someone

收拾.etymology: A coordinative verb compound combining 收 (shōu, 'to gather in, collect, put away') and 拾 (shí, reading *shè* in some classical contexts, 'to pick up from the ground, glean, gather tenfold'). In Classical and Tang poetry (e.g., Du Fu), 收拾 meant literally 'to gather up scattered items or remnants'. By the Song–Yuan vernacular period, it expanded to 'putting things in order, tidying a room, packing luggage, repairing', and colloquially 'dealing with / teaching someone a lesson'.

history.meaning: to gather up scattered remnants; to collect and take in
to tidy up, pack (belongings), repair; (colloquial) to settle someone's hash, punish

morphemes.meaning: to gather in, put away, collect
to pick up, glean, arrange in order

收拾.notes: In spoken Mandarin the second syllable is always neutral tone (*shōushi*), and the verb has a sharp colloquial edge depending on its object: 收拾行李 means 'to pack luggage', 收拾屋子 means 'to tidy the room', and 看我怎么收拾你! means 'Just watch how I deal with you / teach you a lesson!'.

rootFamily.gloss: to sort out, organize, put in order (files, thoughts, or rooms)
to pick up, tidy, clean up (regional/colloquial synonym)
to sweep and clean; to clear away

收据.etymology: Compound noun of 收 ('receive payment or goods') + 据 (據, 'written proof, voucher, certificate'): 'written receipt'.

history.meaning: written voucher of receipt; receipt

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 收据 (via 萌典)

收益.etymology: A compound of 收 (shōu, 'to harvest, gather in, reap, receive') and 益 (yì, originally an ideograph of water overflowing a vessel, hence 'increase, benefit, profit, gain'). Originally a Literary Chinese verb-object phrase meaning 'to reap benefit or gain an increase', it was standardized across modern East Asian legal and economic terminology (alongside Japanese 収益 *shūeki*) as a noun denoting financial returns, investment yield, or the net payoff of a venture.

history.meaning: to reap the benefit or harvest the increase (verb-object phrase)
financial returns, investment yield, proceeds, or net payoff (noun)
history.stage: Modern Mandarin (reinforced by Sino-Japanese legal and financial usage)

收益.notes: Don't confuse 收益 (shōuyì, 'returns, profit yield, payoff', noun) with the near-homophone 受益 (shòuyì, 'to benefit from, be the beneficiary', verb, as in 受益匪浅 'to benefit immensely').

cognates.meaning: to watch a broadcast (shūshi is preferred, though shūkan appears in Sinitic contexts)

收看.etymology: A modern Mandarin serial-verb compound combining 收 (shōu, 'to receive, gather, take in', originally depicting a hand grasping twisted threads in oracle bone script) and 看 (kàn, 'to look at, watch', graphically a hand 手 shading the eye 目). Coined in the twentieth century on analogy with 收听 (shōutīng, 'to tune in and listen to radio') to denote receiving a television or video signal and watching the broadcast.

history.meaning: to gather in (harvest/items) + to shade the eyes and look
to tune in and watch a television or visual broadcast

morphemes.meaning: to receive, gather, take in (a signal)

收看.notes: Used specifically for broadcasts, television shows, or livestreams (e.g., 欢迎收看 'welcome to the show'); never used for watching films in a cinema (use 观看 or 看).

rootFamily.gloss: television viewership; to receive and view

cognates.meaning: reception and viewing of television broadcasts (shūshi)

收视.etymology: A literary-register serial-verb / coordinative compound (traditional 收視) formed from 收 (shōu, 'to draw back, gather, receive') and 视 (shì, traditional 視, 'to look at, inspect, regard'). In Classical Chinese (e.g., Lu Ji's *Wen Fu* 文赋: 收视反听), 收视 meant 'to withdraw one's gaze inward' in contemplation; in twentieth-century broadcasting terminology, 收 was reanalyzed as 'receiving a broadcast signal' and 视 as 'viewing television', shifting the compound to mean television reception and audience viewership.

history.meaning: to withdraw or turn inward one's external gaze (in meditation or literary composition)
to receive and watch television broadcasts; television viewership

morphemes.meaning: to view, look at, inspect (traditional 視)

收视.notes: In TV production dramas like *幕后之王*, 收视 functions as a clipped noun for viewership performance (e.g., 收视长虹 'may viewership soar like a rainbow').

cognates.meaning: audience rating, viewership percentage (shichōritsu, close broadcasting parallel)

收视率.etymology: A three-morpheme modifier-head compound (traditional 收視率) consisting of 收视 (shōushì, 'television broadcast reception and viewing', from 收 'receive' + 视 'view') plus the statistical suffix 率 (lǜ, 'rate, ratio, proportion', attested in Classical Chinese mathematical texts such as *Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art* 九章算术 in the sense of 'numerical ratio or standard'). It designates the percentage of television-owning households or viewers tuned in to a specific program during a given time slot.

history.meaning: standard ratio, numerical proportion, rate
television audience viewership rating (percentage of total viewers/households)

收视率.notes: The central metric of television industry dramas; collocations include 破一 ('surpass 1% rating'), 收视率造假 ('ratings fraud'), and 收视率保障 ('a guaranteed ratings draw').

rootFamily.gloss: viewership; to receive and watch TV

改.etymology: Ancient ideogram combining 己 ('self / coiled thread') + 攵 ('hand holding a rod'): 'correct faults -> change, alter, modify, revise, correct (homework/papers), switch to'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: correct; change; alter; revise

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 改 (via 萌典)

改则生.etymology: A concise Classical Chinese-style conditional aphorism (traditional 改則生) structured as [verb + conditional conjunction + verb]: 改 (gǎi, 'to alter, reform, correct', depicting a hand with a rod 攵 disciplining a kneeling figure or child 己) + 则 (zé, 'then, consequently', originally a bronze cauldron 鼎 incised with legal stipulations 刀) + 生 (shēng, 'to live, survive, thrive', depicting a plant sprouting from the earth). Modeled on classical maxims such as 变则通 ('change and you will succeed' from the *Book of Changes* 易经·系辞), it encapsulates the media-industry credo that only through innovation and reform can a program or enterprise survive.

history.meaning: when things change, they find a way through (classical syntactic template)
if one reforms/adapts, one survives; innovate or perish

改则生.notes: Often paired antithetically with 不改则亡 ('fail to reform and perish') or 守则死 ('cling to the old and die') in corporate and television production pitches.

rootFamily.gloss: to revamp or redesign a show/edition

cognates.meaning: to change, alter, modify (kaihen, often negatively as 'tampering')

改变.etymology: A coordinative disyllabic verb-noun compound (traditional 改變) uniting two near-synonymous Classical Chinese verbs: 改 (gǎi, 'to correct, replace, alter deliberately', from 己 + 攵) and 变 (biàn, traditional 變, 'to transform, undergo change', composed of phonetic 䜌 luan 'tangled threads/speech' and signific 攵 'tap/action'). Already attested as a binome in Han and Six Dynasties texts, it combines the intentional agency of 改 ('to modify') with the state transition of 变 ('to shift').

history.meaning: to alter an existing state, custom, or decree
to change, transform; a change or alteration (both transitive and intransitive)

改变.notes: Unlike 变化 (which is intransitive or nominal, describing natural shifts), 改变 can take a direct object (e.g., 改变命运 'change one's fate', 改变主意 'change one's mind').

改变主意.etymology: A verb-object phrase (traditional 改變主意) combining the transitive verb 改变 (gǎibiàn, 'to alter, change') with the nominal object 主意 (zhǔyi, 'definite view, decision, plan', composed of 主 'master, principal, core' + 意 'thought, intention, mind'). While 主意 emerged in Song–Yuan vernacular Chinese to mean one's settled intention or governing idea (with 意 weakening to neutral tone in Mandarin), the full phrase crystallized in modern Mandarin for reversing a prior decision.

history.meaning: to hold a firm intention; a principal idea or resolution

history.form: 改變主意 / 改变主意
history.meaning: to change one's mind, reverse a prior decision

morphemes.meaning: thought, intention, mind (neutral tone in 主意)

改变主意.notes: Note the mandatory neutral tone on the final syllable of 主意 (zhǔyi, 'idea/plan'), which distinguishes it from 主义 (zhǔyì, 'doctrine/-ism'). Collocates frequently with 临时 ('at the last minute').

rootFamily.gloss: to make up one's mind, decide
to come up with an idea or scheme

cognates.meaning: to retract one's words or change address (cải khẩu)

改口.etymology: A separable verb-object compound (VO) composed of 改 (gǎi, 'to alter, switch') and 口 (kǒu, 'mouth', by metonymy 'speech, wording, mode of address'). Attested from Tang–Song vernacular and Ming–Qing fiction (such as *Dream of the Red Chamber* 红楼梦), it operates along two metonymic paths: retracting or revising what one just said ('to change one's tune/statement'), and switching to a new kinship form of address upon marriage (e.g., calling one's in-laws 爸妈 'Mom and Dad').

history.meaning: to alter one's words; to switch to a new form of kinship address
to change one's tune, correct a slip of the tongue, or adopt married kinship terms

morphemes.meaning: mouth; speech, wording, form of address

改口.notes: Grammatically a separable verb (离合词): aspects and modifiers insert between the characters, e.g., 改了口 ('changed one's tune') or 改不了口 ('unable to get used to the new way of speaking').

rootFamily.gloss: to open one's mouth; to start speaking or ask a favor

cognates.meaning: to change only the surface appearance while keeping the substance (kaitō-kanmen)
repackaging or changing one's outward guise (gaeduhwanmyeon)

改头换面.etymology: A four-character parallel idiom (chengyu, traditional 改頭換面) structured as two symmetric verb-object pairs: 改头 (gǎitóu, 'to alter the head') + 换面 (huànmiàn, 'to swap the face'). Originally derived from Tang–Song Chan (Zen) Buddhist discourse records (such as *Wudeng Huiyuan* 五灯会元 and Hanshan's poems), where it described the Buddha-nature or karmic consciousness assuming different physical bodies across reincarnations; in later secular usage, it shifted to mean either a thorough outward makeover or a superficial repackaging of old content to deceive others.

history.meaning: to take on a new bodily form across rebirths while the inner mind remains unchanged

history.form: 改頭換面 / 改头换面
history.meaning: to undergo a complete outward transformation; to repackage old things under a new guise

改头换面.notes: Often carries a critical or ironic undertone in media criticism (e.g., an old, plagiarized, or banned show being 'repackaged' under a new title), though it can also describe a dramatic visual overhaul.

rootFamily.gloss: to be thoroughly reborn, turn over a new leaf (positive)
to take on an entirely new look (positive)
to revamp or redesign a program/edition
