改建.etymology: Compound verb of 改 ('change, alter, remodel') + 建 ('build, construct'): 'rebuild, remodel, reconstruct, convert (an existing building or structure)'.

history.meaning: rebuild; remodel; convert a structure

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 改建 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: revision of a printing plate or edition (gaepan)

改版.etymology: A verb-object compound (VO) combining 改 (gǎi, 'to alter, revise') and 版 (bǎn, 'wooden printing block, plate, edition', composed of signific 片 'split wood plank' and phonetic 反 fǎn). Originating in Song–Qing woodblock and movable-type publishing for engraving a revised printing block or issuing a new layout edition of a book or newspaper, it was extended in twentieth- and twenty-first-century broadcasting and digital media to mean revamping the format, segments, or visual design of a television show or website.

history.meaning: to re-engrave woodblocks or reset type for a revised printing edition
to redesign a newspaper layout; to revamp or reformat a TV program or website

morphemes.meaning: printing block, layout, edition, program format

改版.notes: A core television production term in *幕后之王*: when a show's ratings (收视率) slump, producers pitch a 节目改版 ('program format revamp').

rootFamily.gloss: copyright; rights to the printing plate
page layout, newspaper section, or forum board

cognates.meaning: to change one's trade or line of business (cải hàng)

改行.etymology: A separable verb-object compound combining 改 (gǎi, 'to change, switch') and 行 (háng, 'row, guild, trade, profession'). The character 行 (originally depicting a four-way crossroads in oracle bone script, OC *gˤraŋ) meant 'street, thoroughfare', then 'row of market stalls along a street' in Tang–Song urban commerce (giving rise to the reading háng as opposed to xíng 'to walk'), and by extension 'merchant guild or occupational trade' (as in 三百六十行 'the 360 trades'). Thus 改行 literally means 'to switch to another guild/trade row'.

history.meaning: row of market stalls; merchant guild or occupational trade
to switch trades, change one's profession or career path

改行.notes: Always pronounce 行 here as second tone háng ('trade/profession'), never xíng! Like 改口, it is a separable verb: 改了三次行 ('changed careers three times').

rootFamily.gloss: peer in the same trade or industry; colleague

cognates.meaning: to improve, make progressive changes (cải tiến)

改进.etymology: A serial-verb / resultative compound (traditional 改進) formed from 改 (gǎi, 'to alter, amend, correct') and 进 (jìn, traditional 進, 'to advance, move forward', composed of 隹 'short-tailed bird, which only hops forward' and 辶 'movement'). Popularized in late nineteenth-century Meiji Japan (as 改進 kaishin, e.g., Rikken Kaishintō 立憲改進党 'Constitutional Progressive Party' in 1882) and rapidly adopted into Late Qing and Republican Chinese, it denotes modifying an existing method, product, or work process so that it advances to a higher level.

history.meaning: to reform and advance politically or institutionally
to improve, enhance (methods, technology, work quality); improvement

morphemes.meaning: to advance, move forward, progress (traditional 進)

改进.notes: Differs from 改善 (gǎishàn): 改进 targets technical methods, workflows, or product performance ('improve a design/process'), whereas 改善 targets conditions, living standards, or relationships ('ameliorate/make better').

rootFamily.gloss: to ameliorate, improve conditions or relations

cognates.meaning: turning away from evil and returning to righteousness (gaesagwijeong)
to forsake evil and return to the right path (cải tà quy chính)

改邪归正.etymology: A four-character symmetrical verb-object idiom (chengyu, traditional 改邪歸正) contrasting two foundational ethical poles in Chinese thought: 改邪 (gǎixié, 'to correct/renounce crookedness and heterodoxy', where 邪 originally named the ancient place Langya before serving as a loan for 'awry, perverse, evil') and 归正 (guīzhèng, 'to return to uprightness and orthodoxy', where 归 歸 means 'to return home/allegiance' and 正 means 'straight, proper, orthodox'). Attested in Song–Yuan historical and religious texts (such as the *History of Song* 宋史), it describes forsaking immoral or heterodox ways to rejoin moral society.

history.meaning: to abandon heterodox/rebellious practices and return to orthodox allegiance

history.form: 改邪歸正 / 改邪归正
history.meaning: to turn over a new leaf, mend one's ways, go straight

morphemes.meaning: to return to, pledge allegiance to (traditional 歸)

改邪归正.notes: In everyday conversation, it is frequently used with playful irony toward friends who stop staying up late, quit a bad habit, or settle down in relationships.

rootFamily.gloss: evil does not prevail over the righteous
to wash one's heart and renew one's face; reform thoroughly

改革.etymology: A coordinative verb-noun compound formed from 改 (gǎi, 'to alter, amend') and 革 (gé, originally a pictograph of a flayed, stretched animal hide stripped of hair—hence 'raw hide, leather', and verbally 'to strip away, moult, remove the old, transform radically', as in the *Book of Changes* hexagram 革 'Revolution/Moulting'). First attested as a compound in the *Book of Later Han* (后汉书·黄琼传) for sweeping institutional changes, it was reinforced in the Meiji era as the standard Sino-Japanese translation for English 'reform' (kaikaku) and became a cornerstone term of modern Chinese governance (e.g., 改革开放 'Reform and Opening Up').

history.meaning: stripped animal hide; to moult, shed the old, transform fundamentally
to alter and abolish outdated laws or customs
systematic social, institutional, or organizational reform; to overhaul

morphemes.meaning: hide; to strip away the old, overhaul, transform

改革.notes: Carries weightier structural and institutional connotations than 改变 ('change') or 改进 ('improve'), applying to policies, corporate structures, or economic systems.

rootFamily.gloss: revolution (lit. stripping away the Mandate of Heaven)

攻击.etymology: A coordinative verb-noun compound (traditional 攻擊) uniting two Classical Chinese martial verbs: 攻 (gōng, 'to assault, besiege, work upon', composed of phonetic 工 gōng and signific 攵 'hand striking with a weapon/implement') and 击 (jī, traditional 擊, 'to strike, hit, beat', composed of 𣪠 'axe/chariot' + 手 'hand'). Attested in Warring States and Han military histories (such as *Zhan Guo Ce* 战国策 and *Shiji* 史记), it originally denoted armed military assault before extending metaphorically to verbal, media, or cyber attacks (such as 人身攻击 'personal attack').

history.meaning: to strike and besiege an enemy force in warfare
military, physical, cyber, or verbal attack/assault; to attack or vilify

攻击.notes: In media and PR contexts (*幕后之王*), frequently appears in 恶意攻击 ('malicious attacks'), 人身攻击 ('ad hominem/personal attacks'), and 网络攻击 ('online trolling/cyberattacks').

rootFamily.gloss: to strike, hit; a blow or setback
to break through, breach by attacking

cognates.meaning: to breach or break through an enemy fortification (công phá)

攻破.etymology: A resultative verb compound (动补结构) formed from the action verb 攻 (gōng, 'to attack, assault, work intensely at') and the resultative complement 破 (pò, 'to break, split, shatter, breach', composed of signific 石 'stone' and phonetic 皮 pí 'skin/peel'). Attested in Classical Chinese military narratives (e.g., *Shiji* 史记: 攻破城邑 'assaulted and breached the walled cities'), it literally means 'to breach by attacking' and extends metaphorically in modern Mandarin to overcoming a psychological defense, solving a technical bottleneck, or cracking a tough problem.

history.meaning: to assault and breach a fortified city or defensive line
to break through (defenses, bottlenecks, or someone's emotional guard)

攻破.notes: Because it is a resultative verb compound, potential infixes 得 ('can') and 不 ('cannot') can be inserted between the two characters: 攻得破 ('able to break through') and 攻不破 ('impregnable').

rootFamily.gloss: to break through, make a breakthrough
to capture and occupy (a city or market share)

放.etymology: Phono-semantic/ideographic character combining 方 (fāng phonetic, 'direction/outward') + 攵 ('hand with a stick driving or releasing'): originally 'drive out, banish, let go free', and from the Six Dynasties and Tang period onward also the primary Mandarin verb for 'put, place, set down; let out/turn on; blossom; have a holiday (放假)'.

history.meaning: let go; release; drive away; unrestrained
put/place; release; let off; bloom; play

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 放 (via 萌典)

放在心上.etymology: A four-character vernacular verb-locative phrase structured as 放 (fàng, 'to put, place, set down') + 在 (zài, 'at, in, upon', locative preposition derived from an existential verb) + 心 (xīn, 'heart-mind', the seat of both emotion and cognition in Chinese anthropology) + 上 (shàng, 'on, upon', postpositional localizer). Literally 'to place upon one's heart-mind', it developed in Ming–Qing vernacular fiction (such as *Dream of the Red Chamber* 红楼梦) as the standard idiom for taking a remark, slight, or responsibility seriously and holding it in active memory.

history.meaning: to lodge a matter or instruction upon one's heart-mind; to pay heed to
to take to heart, bear in mind, care deeply or harbor concern about

放在心上.notes: Most commonly appears in the negative: 别放在心上 ('don't take it to heart / don't mind it') or 没放在心上 ('didn't pay it any real mind').

rootFamily.gloss: to set one's mind at ease, feel relieved (lit. put down the heart)
to keep in mind, remember with concern
to take to heart, go to one's head (shorter variant)

cognates.meaning: abandonment, renunciation of a right or duty (hōki)
to abandon, renounce, give up (phóng khí)

放弃.etymology: A coordinative verb compound (traditional 放棄) joining 放 (fàng, 'to release, let go, drive away', composed of phonetic 方 fāng and signific 攵 'hand with stick driving livestock out') and 弃 (qì, traditional 棄, 'to cast away, abandon', originally an oracle-bone graph depicting two hands tossing a newborn infant 子 in a winnowing basket 箕). Attested in Classical Chinese (*Zhan Guo Ce* 战国策) for casting aside troops or duties, and reinforced in modern East Asian legal prose (Japanese 放棄 hōki) for waiving a right or claim, it denotes relinquishing a goal, effort, or entitlement.

history.meaning: to cast aside, dismiss, or abandon people or obligations
to give up (a goal or struggle), abandon, or legally waive/renounce (a right)

morphemes.meaning: to cast away, discard, abandon (traditional 棄)

放弃.notes: Unlike 抛弃 (pāoqì, which implies heartlessly deserting a person, pet, or moral duty), 放弃 is neutral to positive or melancholic, used for giving up a dream, project, or legal right.

rootFamily.gloss: to desert, cast off (a spouse, child, or principle)
to let go (literally of one's hand, or figuratively of control)
to abstain from voting or waive a right

放心.etymology: Separable verb-object compound of 放 ('set down, put at ease') + 心 ('heart, mind'): originally in Mencius (求其放心 'seek back one's lost/straying heart'), reinterpreted in Song–Ming vernacular as 'set one's heart at rest -> rest assured, stop worrying, feel at ease'.

history.meaning: a straying/unbridled mind
put one's mind at rest; rest assured; not worry

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 放心 (via 萌典)

放心大胆.etymology: A four-character coordinative idiomatic phrase (traditional 放心大膽) combining two somatic psychological compounds: 放心 (fàngxīn, 'to set one's heart-mind down, be at ease', originally from Mencius 孟子·告子上 where 求其放心 meant 'to seek one's lost/strayed moral mind', before reversing polarity in Song–Ming vernacular to mean 'to put down an anxious heart') and 大胆 (dàdǎn, traditional 大膽, 'having a large gallbladder, bold, courageous', rooted in Traditional Chinese Medicine where the gallbladder 胆 governs courage and decision-making). Together they mean acting with complete peace of mind and fearlessness.

history.form: 放心 (孟子 → 宋明白話)
history.meaning: from 'lost/strayed moral mind' (Classical) to 'putting down an anxious heart; feeling reassured' (Vernacular)

history.form: 放心大膽 / 放心大胆
history.meaning: with complete reassurance and boldness; without worry or hesitation

morphemes.meaning: to set down, put at ease
gallbladder; seat of courage and nerve (traditional 膽)

放心大胆.notes: Typically used adverbially with 地 before a verb phrase to encourage a subordinate or colleague: 放心大胆地去做 ('go ahead and do it boldly without worry').

rootFamily.gloss: to feel reassured, set one's mind at rest
timid, cowardly (lit. gallbladder small as a mouse)

cognates.meaning: releasing one's hold, parting with an item (tebanasu, native Japanese calque/parallel)
to let go of one's hand, give free rein (phóng thủ)

放手.etymology: A separable verb-object compound (VO) composed of 放 (fàng, 'to release, unclench, let go') and 手 (shǒu, 'hand'). Attested in Tang–Song poetry and Chan Buddhist texts (where 悬崖撒手 / 放手 'letting go of one's grip on a precipice' symbolized sudden enlightenment and total non-attachment), it evolved along three semantic paths in Mandarin: physically unclenching one's grip, delegating authority without micromanaging (e.g., 放手一搏 'go all out without holding back'), and emotionally letting go of a romantic partner.

history.meaning: to unclench one's hand and release one's physical grip
to let go physically or romantically; to relinquish micromanagement and act boldly

放手.notes: In workplace and romantic contexts alike, 学会放手 ('learn to let go') means either empowering a team without micromanaging or accepting the end of a relationship. Collocates strongly in 放手一搏 ('risk everything on a bold try').

rootFamily.gloss: to let go of someone's hand (more physical/literal)
to break up, part ways romantically
to begin, set one's hand to a task

放松.etymology: A resultative verb compound (traditional 放鬆) formed from the verb 放 (fàng, 'to release, let out') and the resultative adjective complement 松 (sōng, traditional 鬆, 'loose, slack, uncoiled', originally composed of signific 髟 'long hair' and phonetic 松 sōng 'pine tree', depicting hair unbound and hanging loosely). Note that in simplified Chinese, the characters 松 ('pine tree') and 鬆 ('loose/unbundled hair') were merged into 松. Literally 'to let loose/slacken', it shifted from loosening ropes or garments to relaxing physical tension, mental stress, or vigilance.

history.meaning: unbound, loose-hanging hair; slack, unfastened
to slacken a grip or rope; to relax physically or mentally; to let one's guard down

放松.notes: Can be positive ('relax and unwind', 放松心情) or cautionary when paired with vigilance ('let one's guard down', 放松警惕).

rootFamily.gloss: light and relaxed, effortless (traditional 輕鬆)
to breathe a sigh of relief (lit. let out a loose breath)
to relax, take it easy (colloquial three-syllable variant)

cognates.meaning: to indulge, be unbridled or dissolute (phóng túng)

放纵.etymology: A coordinative verb-adjective compound (traditional 放縱) combining 放 (fàng, 'to release, let run wild') and 纵 (zòng, traditional 縱, 'to slacken the reins, let fly, release a bowstring or tether', composed of signific 糸 'silk cord/reins' and phonetic 从 cóng). Attested in Classical Chinese philosophical and historical texts (such as *Xunzi* 荀子 and *Hanfeizi* 韩非子), it originally evoked the metaphor of dropping the reins on horses or loosing hunting hounds, and by extension giving free rein to one's desires, impulses, or someone else's misbehavior without moral restraint.

history.meaning: to slacken the reins; to act without ritual or legal restraint
to indulge oneself or coddle another unchecked; self-indulgent, unrestrained

morphemes.meaning: to slacken the reins, let loose (traditional 縱)

放纵.notes: Traditionally derogatory ('hedonistic, undisciplined'), though in contemporary pop culture and music it is sometimes used for 'cutting loose' for a night (放纵一下) after intense work pressure.

rootFamily.gloss: to connive at, indulge someone's wrongdoing
to control, manipulate (lit. hold and slacken the cords)

放肆.etymology: A coordinative adjective-verb compound formed from 放 (fàng, 'to release, cast off restraint') and 肆 (sì, 'to stretch out fully, act without scruple, display openly', originally depicting a hand 聿 holding a blade or implement beside a carcass or long hair 镸). Attested in the *Book of Rites* (礼记·表记) and *Zhuangzi* (庄子), it denotes throwing off hierarchical decorum and social propriety—acting or speaking with presumptuous insolence toward a superior, or (in modern poetic/youth usage) living with uninhibited abandon.

history.meaning: to cast off ritual restraint; unbridled, willful, violating propriety
presumptuous, insolent (especially toward superiors); uninhibited, wild

morphemes.meaning: unrestrained, wanton, to stretch out without scruple

放肆.notes: Famous in historical court dramas as a single-word bark from emperors or superiors (放肆! 'How dare you! / Insolence!'), while in modern youth slogans (e.g., 放肆青春) it is reclaimed positively as 'unapologetically bold'.

rootFamily.gloss: without the slightest scruple or fear; brazenly
to indulge, let oneself go unchecked

放轻松.etymology: A colloquial three-morpheme resultative verb-complement construction (traditional 放輕鬆) built from the causative/release verb 放 (fàng, 'to let go, put into a state of') and the disyllabic state adjective 轻松 (qīngsōng, traditional 輕鬆, 'light and loose, relaxed, stress-free', from 轻 'lightweight, originally a light fast war chariot 車+巠' + 松 鬆 'loose, uncoiled hair'). Particularly common in Taiwan Mandarin and contemporary conversational Mainland Mandarin, it translates English 'take it easy' or 'chill out' when reassuring a nervous performer or colleague.

history.meaning: light in weight and unburdened; carefree
to relax, take it easy, loosen up (especially before a performance or interview)

morphemes.meaning: to release, let go, put into a state of

放轻松.notes: More conversational and comforting than 放松; frequently used as a standalone imperative to calm someone on stage or before going live on camera: 放轻松，别紧张 ('Take it easy, don't be nervous').

rootFamily.gloss: to relax, slacken, let one's guard down
to lighten, alleviate (a burden or pressure)

放进去.etymology: Verb + complex directional complement combining 放 ('put, place') + 进去 ('go inside, away from the speaker'): 'put inside, place in'.

history.meaning: put in; place inside

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 放进去 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: political risk (seiji risuku, using the same Sino-Japanese compound 政治)

政治风险.etymology: A four-character modifier-head compound (traditional 政治風險) uniting 政治 (zhèngzhì, 'politics, governance', from 政 'rectifying governance' + 治 'regulating water/order', attested in the *Book of Documents* 尚书 and repurposed in Meiji Japan as seiji to translate 'politics') and 风险 (fēngxiǎn, traditional 風險, literally 'wind and perilous shoals/precipices', a nautical metaphor from river and maritime navigation for unpredictable hazards). In contemporary Chinese media and corporate contexts, it denotes regulatory, diplomatic, or public-affairs hazards that could lead to a broadcast or project being pulled.

history.form: 政治 (尚書 / 周禮 → 明治日本語)
history.meaning: from 'moral governance and state administration' (Classical) to modern 'politics' (Sino-Japanese)

history.form: 政治風險 / 政治风险
history.meaning: political, diplomatic, or regulatory risk affecting investments, broadcasts, or public affairs

政治风险.notes: In Chinese media production (*幕后之王*), 政治风险 encompasses not only international diplomacy during live foreign broadcasts but also regulatory compliance and sensitivity review.

政策.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-Japanese graphic loan (*wasei-kango*) composed of 政 (zhèng, 'governance, state administration', from 正 'straight/correct' + 攵 'action') and 策 (cè, 'bamboo slip for writing royal decrees; horsewhip; stratagem, plan', with signific 竹 'bamboo'). Coined in Meiji-period Japan (政策 seisaku) to translate English 'policy' and German *Politik/Maßnahme*, it was borrowed into Late Qing Chinese by reformist writers like Liang Qichao to denote an official course of action or regulatory guideline adopted by a government or institution.

history.meaning: bamboo writing strip for state edicts; tactical plan or stratagem
governmental, institutional, or corporate policy and guidelines
history.stage: Meiji Japanese to Late Qing & Modern Mandarin

morphemes.meaning: bamboo decree strip; plan, strategy, measure

政策.notes: Often paired with 对策 (duìcè, 'countermeasure') in the famous folk saying 上有政策，下有对策 ('those above have policies, while those below have ways of getting around them').

rootFamily.gloss: countermeasure, way to deal with a situation
to plan, mastermind, produce (a media event or show)

故事.etymology: Modifier-head noun compound of 故 ('old, former, past') + 事 ('affair, event, practice'). In Classical Chinese (Hanshu, Tang histories), 故事 meant 'past events, historical precedents, established routine'. In Tang–Song popular storytelling (说话) it came to mean 'narrative tale, story, plot' (read gùshi with neutral tone).

history.meaning: past events; historical precedent
story; tale; narrative

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 故事 (via 萌典)

故作潇洒.etymology: A four-character verb-object phrase (traditional 故作瀟灑) formed from the adverbial-verb unit 故作 (gùzuò, 'to deliberately put on an act of, feign', from 故 'on purpose' + 作 'to make, act as') and the disyllabic aesthetic adjective 潇洒 (xiāosǎ, traditional 瀟灑, originally an alliterative and rhyming nature binome in Tang–Song poetry describing clear, deep, wind-swept rain and water—both characters bearing the water radical 氵—before shifting metaphorically to describe a person's unrestrained, dashing, and carefree demeanor). Together they mean putting on a forced front of nonchalance to mask inner hurt or anxiety.

history.meaning: (of wind and rain) brisk and clear; (of a person's bearing) untrammeled, dashing, free of worldly dust

history.form: 故作瀟灑 / 故作潇洒
history.meaning: to feign nonchalance, put on a carefree or dashing front to hide distress

morphemes.meaning: clear and deep water; dashing, unrestrained (traditional 瀟)
to sprinkle water; free and easy,洒脱 (traditional 灑)

故作潇洒.notes: The frame 故作 + [two-syllable adjective] is highly productive in Mandarin for feigning an emotional state: compare 故作镇定 ('feign calmness'), 故作坚强 ('act tough'), and 故作神秘 ('act mysterious').

rootFamily.gloss: to feign composure, pretend to be calm

cognates.meaning: intentionality, mens rea (in law), on purpose (koi)

故意.etymology: A modifier-head compound formed from 故 (gù, 'cause, reason; old; by design, purposely', composed of phonetic 古 gǔ 'ancient/established' and signific 攵 'deliberate action') and 意 (yì, 'thought, intention, mind', from 音 'sound/voice in the heart' + 心 'heart-mind'). In Han–Tang texts (such as *Book of Han* 汉书 and Du Fu's poetry), 故意 originally meant 'old feelings of friendship' or 'established thoughts', while already in legal texts of the秦/Qin and Han dynasties 故 alone meant 'with criminal intent'; by the Song–Yuan vernacular period, 故意 had fully shifted to 'with deliberate intent, on purpose'.

history.meaning: old affection, long-standing feelings; or calculated intention in legal prose
deliberately, intentionally, on purpose (adverb and legal noun for mens rea)

故意.notes: In everyday speech, often nominalized with 是...的: 他是故意的 ('He did it on purpose') vs. 我不是故意的 ('I didn't mean to'). Contrasts with 特意 (tèyì, 'specially/going out of one's way for a positive gesture').

rootFamily.gloss: specially, going out of one's way to do something thoughtful
reason, cause; for no reason (in 无缘无故)

cognates.meaning: rendering service, exerting oneself for another (kōrō)
to render service, toil for someone (hiệu lao)

效劳.etymology: A verb-object compound (traditional 效勞) composed of 效 (xiào, 'to offer up, dedicate, exert to the utmost', originally 'to imitate, model after', from phonetic 交 jiāo and signific 攵) and 劳 (láo, traditional 勞, 'toil, physical exertion, meritorious labor', depicting 力 'strength' beneath 熒 'blazing torches/fire at night'). Attested in Classical and Literary Chinese (such as *Three Kingdoms* 三国志 and *Selections of Refined Literature* 文选), it literally means 'to offer up one's toil' in loyal service to a ruler or patron, surviving in modern Mandarin as a polite, slightly deferential expression for 'to be of service'.

history.meaning: to dedicate one's physical toil and loyal service to a lord or state
to be of service, lend a hand (polite or deferential register)

效劳.notes: A polite, somewhat formal or humorous phrase used with the preposition 为 (wèi, 'for'): 很荣幸为您效劳 ('It is an honor to be of service to you').

rootFamily.gloss: to pledge loyalty and devote one's service to (e.g., a team or country)

效果.etymology: A coordinative / modifier-head noun compound combining 效 (xiào, 'verified result, efficacy, outcome of an action', evolved from 'to imitate/verify against a model') and 果 (guǒ, 'fruit on a tree', pictograph of fruit 田 atop a tree 木, extended in Buddhist and philosophical Chinese to 'result, consequence, fruition', as in 因果 'cause and effect'). Popularized across East Asia via Meiji Japanese (効果 kōka), it denotes both the practical efficacy of a measure and, in broadcasting and film, aesthetic 'effects' (such as 节目效果 'show/comedic effect' and 视觉效果 'visual effects').

history.meaning: verified outcome, practical efficacy, or resultant effect of an action
effect, result, efficacy; audiovisual or stage effect in media production

效果.notes: In variety show and television production (*幕后之王*), 节目效果 ('program effect'—how entertaining, dramatic, or engaging a moment plays on screen) is a ubiquitous industry buzzword.

rootFamily.gloss: efficiency; rate of output per unit of input
special effects (SFX/VFX, clipped from 特殊效果)
result, outcome (neutral, whether good or bad)

cognates.meaning: efficiency, ratio of useful output to input (kōritsu)

效率.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-Japanese compound (*wasei-kango*) formed from 效 (xiào, 'useful effect, output, efficacy') and 率 (lǜ, 'rate, ratio, proportion'). Coined in late nineteenth-century Japan (効率 kōritsu) during the translation of Western thermodynamics, mechanics, and industrial management to express 'mechanical/work efficiency' (the ratio of useful work performed to total energy or time expended), it entered Chinese at the turn of the twentieth century and became standard for both physical and workplace productivity.

history.meaning: thermodynamic or mechanical efficiency (ratio of useful work output to energy input)
work, organizational, or operational efficiency (output per unit of time/effort)

效率.notes: Do not confuse 效率 (xiàolǜ, 'efficiency'—doing things fast with minimal wasted effort, collocating with 高/低) and 效果 (xiàoguǒ, 'effect/effectiveness'—achieving a good outcome, collocating with 好/差).

效益.etymology: A modern coordinative compound combining 效 (xiào, 'effect, result, efficacy', originally 'to imitate, to exert') and 益 (yì, 'benefit, profit, increase', originally a pictophonetic graph of water overflowing a vessel 皿). Literally 'efficacy and benefit', it emerged in twentieth-century economic and administrative discourse to denote the measurable return or positive outcome yielded by an investment of resources or labor.

history.meaning: to yield results (效) and to increase or benefit (益) as separate verbs/nouns
beneficial effect, economic return, or social yield of production and investment

效益.notes: Frequently paired with 经济 (jīngjì xiàoyì, 'economic returns') or 社会 (shèhuì xiàoyì, 'social benefit'); in television production (*幕后之王*), executives weigh ratings against commercial 效益.

敌.etymology: From Old Chinese *l'eːɡ (傳統漢字: 敵), a phono-semantic compound with phonetic 啇 (dī, *teːɡ) and semantic 攵 (pū, 'to strike, beat with a hand-held implement'). Originally meaning 'to match, be an equal counterpart to', it evolved by extension into 'to oppose, resist as an equal' and hence 'adversary, rival, enemy'. Simplified in modern PRC orthography by replacing 啇 with 舌 ('tongue').

history.meaning: counterpart, peer, equal match; to resist or oppose
hostile adversary, military enemy; to contend with
enemy, rival, opponent; to match or withstand (in idioms like 寡不敌众)

morphemes.meaning: enemy, rival; to match or oppose

敌.notes: As a standalone word in modern Mandarin, 敌 appears mostly in concise headlines, military contexts, or four-character idioms (如临大敌, 势均力敌), whereas everyday speech prefers the disyllabic 敌人 or 对手.

敌人.etymology: A modifier-head compound formed from 敌 (dí, Trad. 敵, 'opposing, hostile; adversary') modifying 人 (rén, 'person, human being'). While Classical Chinese regularly used monosyllabic 敵 for 'enemy', the disyllabic compound 敵人 is already attested in early texts (such as the *Guanzi* and Han histories) and became the standard vernacular noun as Mandarin disyllabification progressed to resolve homophony.

history.meaning: an opposing person or military adversary
enemy, foe, personal or political antagonist

敌人.notes: Carries a strong, serious tone ('foe/enemy'); in workplace or media competition, speakers use 敌人 hyperbolically (or quote the proverb 没有永远的敌人 'there are no permanent enemies'), preferring 竞争对手 for literal business rivals.

敏感.etymology: A modifier-head (or coordinative) Sino-compound combining 敏 (mǐn, 'quick, agile, keen, astute') and 感 (gǎn, 'to feel, perceive, respond emotionally'). Popularized in modern East Asian lexicon via Meiji Japanese *wasei-kango* 敏感 (binkan), which translated European physiological and psychological terms ('sensitive, susceptible') before re-entering early twentieth-century Mandarin to describe both keen perception and touchy topics.

history.meaning: quick/agile (敏) and to be moved/feel (感) as distinct Classical words
physiologically or psychologically responsive to stimuli ('sensitive')
perceptive, keen; emotionally touchy; politically or commercially delicate

敏感.notes: In media and broadcasting, 敏感 swings between praise (对市场很敏感, 'keenly attuned to the market') and caution (敏感话题 / 敏感词, 'sensitive topics / censored keywords').

救.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining 求 (qiú/jiù phonetic) + 攵 ('hand action'): originally 'stop/prevent evil', then 'succor, rescue, save (from danger, fire, or distress), relieve, help'.

history.stage: Old & Classical Chinese (Shijing, Analects) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: rescue; save; relieve; help

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 救 (via 萌典)

救下.etymology: Resultative verb compound combining 救 ('rescue, save') + 下 (complement indicating successfully taking/keeping someone out of danger): 'rescue, save (from harm or danger)'.

history.meaning: successfully rescue and save

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 救下 (via 萌典)

救助.etymology: A parallel coordinative verb-noun compound uniting 救 (jiù, 'to rescue, save from danger, relieve') and 助 (zhù, 'to assist, lend strength'). Attested since the Warring States and Han periods (e.g., *Mencius*, *Shiji*) for coming to a neighbor's or ally's aid in crisis, it remains the standard formal term for humanitarian relief, welfare assistance, and emergency rescue.

history.meaning: to succor and assist someone in peril or distress (e.g.,出入相友，守望相助，疾病相扶持)
to provide formal relief, financial/medical aid, or emergency rescue

救助.notes: More institutional and formal than 救命 ('save a life!') or 帮忙 ('help out'); commonly used in 社会救助 ('social welfare relief'), 医疗救助 ('medical aid'), and 流浪动物救助 ('stray animal rescue').

救护车.etymology: A three-character modifier-head noun phrase composed of the coordinative verb compound 救护 (jiùhù, Trad. 救護, 'to rescue [救] and protect/care for [護] the injured') modifying the head noun 车 (chē, Trad. 車, 'wheeled vehicle, car'). Coined in the modern era to translate Western medical 'ambulance' vehicles used in wartime and municipal emergency services.

history.meaning: to rescue and shelter/protect someone from harm
emergency medical ambulance vehicle

救护车.notes: Takes the classifier 辆 (yī liàng jiùhùchē); in Mainland China, calling an ambulance uses the emergency number 120 (打120叫救护车).

rootFamily.gloss: to rescue and give medical care

救星.etymology: Metaphorical compound noun of 救 ('rescue, save') + 星 ('auspicious star'): literally 'saving star' -> 'savior, deliverer, lifesaver (person or thing that comes to the rescue in a pinch)'. Attested from Song–Yuan drama and vernacular.

history.meaning: saving star -> lifesaver, savior

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 救星 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: firefighting (in historical Edo compounds like 火消し)

救火.etymology: An idiomatic verb-object (VO) compound of 救 (jiù, here in its older Classical sense 'to stop, check, relieve a calamity' rather than 'to save') and 火 (huǒ, 'fire, conflagration'). Literally 'to relieve/stop a fire', attested since the *Zuo Zhuan* and *Hanfeizi*. Because 救 ordinarily means 'save', learners often find 'save a fire' paradoxical until recognizing 救's ancient sense 'to arrest a disaster'. In modern workplace slang, it means 'troubleshooting an urgent crisis'.

history.meaning: to check or extinguish a conflagration (attested in Zuo Zhuan & Hanfeizi)
to put out a fire; figuratively, to step in as an emergency troubleshooter or PR crisis fixer

morphemes.meaning: to stop, relieve, rescue from calamity

救火.notes: Because it is a separable verb-object (离合词) in literal use, modifiers can intervene, but in TV/PR industry slang (*幕后之王*), 救火 (and 救火队长, 'crisis fixer') is ubiquitous for last-minute script, broadcast, or celebrity PR rescues.

rootFamily.gloss: to save a crisis/situation (lit. 'save the stage/scene')

教.etymology: Ancient ideogram attested on Shang oracle bones showing a hand holding a teaching rod (攵) beside a child (子) learning counting/imitation marks (爻, i.e., 孝): read jiāo in spoken Mandarin for 'teach, instruct (someone a skill or subject)', and read jiào in compounds and nouns for 'instruct, education, religion (教育, 教室, 宗教)'.

history.meaning: hand with rod guiding a child = teach, instruct, education
teach (jiāo); instruct, education, religion (jiào)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 教 (via 萌典)

教授.etymology: A coordinative compound of 教 (jiào, 'to teach, instruct') and 授 (shòu, 'to confer, transmit, hand down knowledge'). Originally a Classical verb meaning 'to instruct and transmit learning' (attested in *Shiji*), it became an official academic title in the Song dynasty for prefectural Confucian school instructors. In Meiji Japan, 教授 (kyōju) was repurposed to translate the modern Western university rank of 'professor', and this sense returned to modern Mandarin.

history.meaning: to teach and pass down texts or skills to disciples
state-appointed instructor in prefectural and military schools
university professor (noun); to instruct or teach formally (verb)
history.stage: Modern Mandarin (via Meiji Japanese return loan)

教授.notes: As a noun ('professor') and verb ('to instruct formally'), both syllables are pronounced in the fourth tone (jiàoshòu); contrast with單字 教 (jiāo, first tone) when used alone in colloquial speech for 'to teach'.

rootFamily.gloss: to give a lecture, teach a class

教练.etymology: A coordinative verb-derived compound combining 教 (jiào, 'to instruct, teach') and 练 (liàn, Trad. 練, originally 'to boil and soften raw silk', extended to 'to drill, practice, train repeatedly'). Used in Tang–Song military texts for drilling troops ('to instruct and drill'), it shifted in modern Mandarin into an agentive noun meaning 'coach, sports trainer, or driving instructor'.

history.meaning: to instruct and drill soldiers in martial skills
coach, athletic trainer, driving or vocal/stage instructor

教练.notes: Covers athletics, fitness, and practical skills (篮球教练, 健身教练, 驾校教练) as well as talent show performance mentors, whereas academic teachers are 老师 or 导师.

教训.etymology: A coordinative compound of 教 (jiào, 'to teach, guide') and 训 (xùn, Trad. 訓, 'to instruct, admonish, lecture', with semantic 言 'speech' and phonetic 川). Attested in the *Zuo Zhuan* ('十年生聚，十年教训') for moral and civic instruction of the populace. In modern vernacular Mandarin, it bifurcated into a noun ('a hard-won lesson learned from failure') and a colloquial verb ('to chide, rebuke, or teach someone a lesson').

history.meaning: to educate, instruct, and morally guide the people or juniors
(n.) moral or painful lesson from a mistake; (v.) to scold, lecture, or punish someone to teach them a lesson

教训.notes: Often pronounced with a neutral second syllable (jiàoxun) in speech; as a noun it pairs with 吸取 ('absorb a lesson': 吸取教训), while as a verb (我得好好教训他) it means 'to put someone in their place'.

敞开.etymology: Resultative verb compound of 敞 ('spacious, open wide, uncovered', 尚 + 攵) + 开 (開, 'open'): 'open wide (doors, windows, coats, or one's heart); unrestricted'.

history.meaning: open wide; throw open

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 敞开 (via 萌典)

敢.etymology: Ancient character attested on bronze inscriptions showing hands seizing a wild boar or obstacle with 攵: 'dare, have the courage or boldness to, venture to; (in questions/rhetorical phrases) how could one dare…'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: boldly confront = dare, venture to, courageous

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 敢 (via 萌典)

敢不敢.etymology: An A-not-A (正反问) interrogative construction built on the modal verb 敢 (gǎn, Old Chinese *kˁamʔ, 'to dare, have the courage or audacity to') separated by the negative adverb 不 (bù, 'not'). While Classical Chinese expressed 'dare or not?' with particles or 敢不 (which meant rhetorical 'how could one not dare?'), vernacular Mandarin developed the symmetrical V-不-V template 敢不敢 to issue direct challenges or test someone's nerve.

history.meaning: to dare, venture, have the courage or presumption to act
do you dare or not? (interrogative and provocative challenge construction)

敢不敢.notes: Beyond neutral questioning, 你敢不敢…? ('Do you dare to…?') is the classic Mandarin phrasing for a high-stakes bet, taunt, or pitch challenge in competitive workplaces and reality shows.

rootFamily.gloss: to dare say, venture to state; as it turns out

散伙.etymology: A vernacular verb-object (VO) compound combining 散 (sàn, 'to scatter, disperse, break up') and 伙 (huǒ, Trad. 夥/火, 'messmates, partnership, band of companions'). 伙 originally referred to soldiers sharing a cooking fire (火) in the Northern and Southern Dynasties, evolving into 'business or work partnership'. Thus 散伙 literally means 'to disperse the mess-group/partnership', i.e., to dissolve a team, band, or joint venture.

history.meaning: comrades sharing a camp stove; business or labor partners
history.stage: Middle Chinese to Early Vernacular Mandarin

history.meaning: to dissolve a partnership, disband a group, or split up a team

散伙.notes: Colloquial and lively—often heard in 散伙饭 (sànhuǒfàn, 'farewell dinner when a graduation class, project crew, or startup disbands') and takes erhua in northern speech (散伙儿).

rootFamily.gloss: to form a partnership, pool capital

散会.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound formed from 散 (sàn, 'to disperse, dismiss, break up') and 会 (huì, Trad. 會, 'assembly, meeting, gathering'). Originally used in Tang–Song literature for the dispersing of a banquet or religious assembly, it stabilized in modern administrative and corporate Mandarin as the direct antonym of 开会 (kāihuì, 'to hold/start a meeting').

history.meaning: the dispersal of a banquet, festival gathering, or assembly
to adjourn or conclude a formal meeting or conference

散会.notes: A separable verb-object (离合词); when an executive barks 「散会！」 at the end of a tense production briefing, it corresponds directly to English 'Meeting adjourned!' or 'Dismissed!'.

rootFamily.gloss: to hold or attend a meeting
to break up (after a show/market); to end a relationship

cognates.meaning: prose poem (calque of French poème en prose)

cognates.word: thơ văn xuôi (calque) / tản văn thi

散文诗.etymology: A three-character modifier-head compound combining 散文 (sǎnwén, 'prose, non-rhyming unmetrical writing', where 散 sǎn in the third tone means 'loose, unconstrained by strict meter') with the head noun 诗 (shī, Trad. 詩, 'poetry, verse'). Coined in late nineteenth-century Japan as 散文詩 (sanbunshi) to translate French *poème en prose* (popularized by Baudelaire and Turgenev) and adopted into Mandarin during the May Fourth literary movement by writers like Lu Xun (*Wild Grass* 野草).

history.meaning: unrhymed/unconstrained prose (散文) vs. regulated verse (詩) as contrasting genres
prose poem (calque of French poème en prose)
prose poem: lyrical composition written in prose paragraphs rather than verse lines

morphemes.meaning: writing, literary composition (together 散文 = prose)

散文诗.notes: Note the tone of 散: in 散文 and 散文诗 it is pronounced in the third tone (sǎn, 'loose, unrestrained state'), whereas in 散伙 and 散会 it is the fourth tone (sàn, 'to disperse actively').

散步.etymology: A leisurely verb-object phrase coined in Six Dynasties and Tang literati prose from 散 (sàn, 'to loosen, unbind, let wander freely without constraint') and 步 (bù, 'footsteps, paces'). Originally contrasting relaxed, unhurried pacing (散步庭院 'strolling freely in the courtyard') with formal court marches, 散步 remains the everyday Mandarin verb for taking a pleasant walk.

history.meaning: walk unhurriedly at ease in a garden or lane
take a walk; go for a stroll

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 散步

敬.etymology: Ancient ideogram combining 苟 (jí, showing a figure with horned/alert head Gear and mouth 口 speaking circumspectly, NOT the grass-radical 苟 gǒu) + 攵 ('hand action'): originally 'be reverently alert and circumspect', hence 'respect, revere, honor; offer politely (a toast, tea, or salute)'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: reverent alertness = respect, honor, offer respectfully

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 敬 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: reverence for one's work (Confucian classical term)
devotion to one's studies or profession

敬业.etymology: A Classical verb-object compound (used adjectivally in modern Mandarin) from 敬 (jìng, 'to revere, treat with solemn respect and single-minded care') and 业 (yè, Trad. 業, 'learning, study, calling, profession'). Originating in the *Book of Rites* (*Liji* 礼记·学记: 「敬业乐群」, 'to revere one's studies and find joy in fellowship'), it evolved from scholarly diligence into modern professional work ethic and devotion to one's craft.

history.meaning: to apply oneself with reverent single-mindedness to one's studies (Liji, Xueji)
dedicated to one's job, consummate in work ethic, professional

morphemes.meaning: to respect, revere, treat with earnest care

敬业.notes: In the entertainment and television industry, 敬业 is the highest praise for an actor or crew member who memorizes scripts, performs their own stunts, or works through illness without complaint.

rootFamily.gloss: professional, specialized; major field of study

敬重.etymology: Coordinative verb compound of 敬 ('respect, revere') + 重 ('value highly, attach great weight to'): 'respect deeply, hold in high esteem, revere'. Attested since the漢書 Book of Han.

history.stage: Han Classical Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: respect and esteem highly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 敬重 (via 萌典)

数.etymology: From Old Chinese *sroʔ (verb, 'to count') and *sros (exoactive s-suffix derivation -> noun, 'number, count, calculation, fate'), written 數 in Traditional script (phono-semantic with phonetic 娄 lóu and semantic 攵 'to tap/tally'). From 'numerical calculation' it developed the Classical sense of 'heavenly allotment, predictable regularity' and the colloquial Mandarin sense of 'a clear mental reckoning or certainty' (as in 心里有数).

history.meaning: to count, enumerate (shǔ); number, computation, fate, art/technique (shù)
number, figure; clear mental grasp, certainty, or limit (especially in 心里有数 / 有数)

数.notes: When meaning 'a clear idea/reckoning' in spoken idioms like 心里有数 ('to know the score / have a clear idea in mind') or 没数 ('clueless about limits'), it is pronounced shù (fourth tone) and often takes erhua (有数儿).

rootFamily.gloss: to have a clear idea of how things stand

数千年.etymology: A quantitative modifier-head noun phrase composed of 数 (shù, Trad. 數, used in its Literary Chineseapproximative sense 'several, a few', between two and nine), 千 (qiān, 'thousand'), and 年 (nián, 'year, harvest cycle'). Preserving the literary quantifier 数 ('several') rather than colloquial 几 (jǐ), it denotes a grand historical span of 'several thousand years' or 'millennia'.

history.meaning: several thousand years (literary quantifier phrase)
thousands of years, several millennia (formal/written register)

数千年.notes: Belongs to an elevated, documentary, or rhetorical register (often paired with 历史 or 文明: 数千年的文明); in casual speech, speakers say 几千年 instead.

rootFamily.gloss: hundreds of millions; tens of thousands (millions/billions)

数字.etymology: Compound noun of 数 (數, shù, 'number, count') + 字 ('written character, symbol'): 'numeral, digit, figure, number; digital'.

history.meaning: written numeral; figure; number; digital

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 数字 (via 萌典)

数据.etymology: A modern modifier-head (or coordinative) compound combining 数 (shù, Trad. 數, 'number, numerical value') and 据 (jù, Trad. 據, 'evidence, basis, proof, certificate', as in 凭据 and 证据). Literally 'numerical evidence' or 'quantitative basis for calculation and inference', it was coined in twentieth-century Chinese scientific and statistical terminology to render English/Latin *data* (whereas Japanese adopted the katakana loan データ *dēta*).

history.meaning: numbers/calculations (數) and documentary proof/basis (據) as separate morphemes
scientific, statistical, or digital data; streaming and ratings metrics in media

数据.notes: In contemporary Chinese entertainment (*幕后之王*), 数据 specifically refers to view counts, TV ratings (收视率), and social media engagement metrics—even spawning the fan-culture phrase 做数据 ('artificially boosting a celebrity's online engagement stats').

数据报告.etymology: A four-character modifier-head nominal compound uniting 数据 (shùjù, 'quantitative/digital data') with 报告 (bàogào, 'report, formal account', a coordinative compound of 报 'to report, announce' and 告 'to inform, declare'). It designates an analytical document or presentation summarizing empirical metrics, audience demographics, or market performance.

history.meaning: to report and inform superiors; a formal written or oral report (standardized via Meiji 報告 hōkoku)
data report, analytics study, or metrics briefing

morphemes.meaning: to inform, declare (together 报告 = report)

数据报告.notes: Takes the classifier 份 (yī fèn shùjù bàogào); a staple prop in Chinese corporate and media dramas where producers evaluate a show's viewer retention and commercial viability.

数量.etymology: A coordinative nominal compound joining 数 (shù, Trad. 數, 'number, discrete count') and 量 (liàng, 'capacity, measured volume, magnitude', originally measuring grain with a vessel). Together they synthesize discrete counting (数) and continuous measurement (量) to express 'quantity, numerical amount' in contrast to 质量 (zhìliàng, 'quality').

history.meaning: reckoned measure, capacity, or numerical allowance in administrative texts
quantity, numerical amount (often contrasted with 质量 'quality')

数量.notes: Note the fourth tone on 量 (liàng) when it means 'quantity/amount' as a noun (vs. second tone liáng 'to measure'); constantly paired with 质量 ('quality') in the maxim 重质量，不重数量 ('prioritize quality over quantity').

敲.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining 高 (gāo/qiāo phonetic) + 攴/攵 ('hand holding a striker'): 'knock on, tap, strike, rap (a door, drum, table, or keyboard)'.

history.stage: Old & Classical Chinese (Zuozhuan) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: strike sideways; tap; knock; beat

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 敲 (via 萌典)

敲中.etymology: Resultative verb compound combining 敲 ('knock, strike, tap') + 中 (read zhòng in the fourth tone, 'hit the target/mark'): 'strike right on target, hit the mark by tapping/knocking'.

history.meaning: strike and hit the exact spot/target

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 敲中 (via 萌典)

敲击.etymology: Coordinative verb compound of 敲 ('knock, tap') + 击 (擊, 'strike, beat, hit'): 'rap, tap, percuss, strike repeatedly'.

history.meaning: knock and strike; tap; percuss

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 敲击 (via 萌典)

敲定.etymology: A resultative verb compound (动补结构) formed from the action verb 敲 (qiāo, 'to knock, strike, tap') and the resultative complement 定 (dìng, 'settled, fixed, decided'). Metaphorically derived from either a carpenter driving a peg/nail firmly into place with a hammer strike or an auctioneer/judge striking a gavel (敲槌定音) to seal a transaction, it means 'to finalize, clinch, or lock in a deal, cast, or plan'.

history.meaning: literal action of striking/hammering (敲) until firmly fixed in place (定)
to finalize, lock in, or settle a contract, schedule, or decision

敲定.notes: Extremely common in media production and business negotiations (敲定档期 'lock in a broadcast slot', 敲定嘉宾 'lock in the guest lineup', 敲定方案 'finalize the proposal')—more vivid and brisk than 确定.

rootFamily.gloss: to set the final tone/decision (lit. 'one hammer strike fixes the sound')

敲敲.etymology: Formed by verbal reduplication (AA pattern) of 敲 (qiāo, 'to knock, rap, tap', composed of 高 'tall' as phonetic and 攴 'hand holding a striker'). In Mandarin grammar, doubling a monosyllabic action verb softens its force and bounds its duration ('give a quick, gentle tap or two'), fitting testing whether a courtyard stone sounds hollow or knocking politely on a guest's door.

morphemes.meaning: knock; tap with a stick or knuckle

history.meaning: strike or rap lightly with a rod
give a quick, gentle tap or knock

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 敲敲

敲门.etymology: Separable verb-object compound of 敲 ('knock on, rap') + 门 (門, 'door'): 'knock on the door' (famous from Jia Dao's Tang couplet 鸟宿池边树，僧敲月下门, the origin of 推敲 'weigh words carefully').

history.meaning: knock on a door

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 敲门 (via 萌典)

整.etymology: Ideogram/phono-semantic character combining 敕 (bundle of wood 束 beaten into order by a hand 攵) + 正 (zhèng, 'straight, upright, exact'): 'put in order, tidy up, repair; whole, entire, full/exact (of round numbers or hours on the clock); (colloquially) fix/do/tease'.

history.meaning: put ranks/items in neat order; whole
whole; entire; exact; tidy up; mend

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 整 (via 萌典)

整个.etymology: Modifier-classifier compound determiner and adjective of 整 ('whole, entire') + 个 (個, general unit classifier): 'the whole, the entire'.

history.meaning: the whole; the entire

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 整个 (via 萌典)

整合.etymology: A coordinative/resultative verb compound combining 整 (zhěng, 'to put in order, arrange neatly, make whole', composed of 束 + 攵 + 正) and 合 (hé, 'to join together, combine, unite'). Popularized in late twentieth-century business, technology, and media administration (initially via Taiwan and Hong Kong corporate usage translating English 'integrate / consolidate'), it denotes reorganizing scattered parts into a unified, synergistic system.

history.meaning: bringing parts into orderly alignment and coherence (logic, geology, systems)
to integrate, consolidate, or merge resources, teams, or media channels

morphemes.meaning: to put in order, arrange, make whole

整合.notes: A buzzword in corporate strategy and media production—especially in 资源整合 ('resource integration') and 整合营销 ('integrated marketing communications').

整团.etymology: A modifier-head quantitative compound composed of 整 (zhěng, 'whole, entire, complete, undivided') directly modifying the collective noun/classifier 团 (tuán, Trad. 團, 'round mass; organized group, troupe, regiment, or idol group'). In Mandarin syntax, 整 + classifier/group-noun expresses 'the entire [group] as a single undivided unit'.

history.meaning: a whole round mass or an entire military regiment/troupe
an entire troupe, tour group, or pop/idol group acting or contracted together

morphemes.meaning: group, troupe,团 (idol group / tour group / regiment)

整团.notes: In Chinese variety show and C-pop culture (*幕后之王*), 整团 refers to booking or showcasing 'the whole idol group together' (e.g. 整团出道 'debut as a full group', 整团签约 'sign the entire group') rather than solo members (单飞).

整圈.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 整 (zhěng, 'whole, complete, unbroken') with 圈 (quān, 'circle, ring, circuit, social/industry sphere', originally 'a curved wooden enclosure or pen'). Literally 'a full circle or complete lap', it is used both spatially (running or searching a full circuit) and socially (across an entire industry circle, such as 娱乐圈 'showbiz').

history.meaning: circle, ring, loop, or bounded sphere of activity
a full circle, complete lap, or the entirety of a professional/social circle

整圈.notes: Often appears with 绕 or 跑 (绕了一整圈 'went around in a huge full circle, coming back to square one') or to describe word spreading across an entire professional circle.

rootFamily.gloss: the whole night, all night long (parallel 整+N pattern)

整夜.etymology: Temporal compound of 整 ('whole, entire') + 夜 ('night'): 'the whole night, all night long'.

history.meaning: all night long; the entire night

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 整夜 (via 萌典)

整天.etymology: Temporal compound of 整 ('whole, entire') + 天 ('day'): 'all day long, the whole day'.

history.meaning: the whole day; all day long

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 整天 (via 萌典)

整排.etymology: Quantifier phrase combining 整 ('whole, entire') + 排 ('row, line'): 'the whole row, an entire row of'.

history.meaning: the entire row

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 整排 (via 萌典)

整改.etymology: A telescopic portmanteau and coordinative verb compound formed from 整顿 (zhěngdùn, 'to tidy up, reorganize, restore discipline') and 改革 / 改正 (gǎigé / gǎizhèng, 'to reform, correct, amend'). Originating in twentieth-century PRC administrative and regulatory vocabulary, it means 'to reorganize and rectify defects in compliance with official standards or inspection findings'.

history.meaning: to put in order (整頓) and to correct/reform (改正/改革) as paired directives
to rectify, overhaul, and correct compliance or quality problems (often by official mandate)

morphemes.meaning: to put in order, reorganize, discipline (from 整顿)
to correct, amend, reform (from 改正/改革)

整改.notes: Carries strong regulatory and institutional weight: in Chinese broadcasting and streaming, 停播整改 ('suspend broadcast for rectification/overhaul') or 限期整改 ('rectify within a deadline') signals mandatory compliance revisions.

整整.etymology: Reduplication of 整 ('whole, full'): used as an emphatic adverb before numeral-classifier phrases (整整三天 'a full three days') to mean 'a full, a whole, no less than'.

history.meaning: a full; a whole (before quantities/durations)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 整整 (via 萌典)

整整齐齐.etymology: AABB-pattern vivid reduplication of the disyllabic adjective 整齐 ('neat, tidy, even'): 'neat and tidy, in apple-pie order, nicely aligned'.

history.form: 整整齊齊 / 整整齐齐
history.meaning: very neat and tidy; in perfect order

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 整整齐齐 (via 萌典)

整理.etymology: Coordinative verb compound of 整 ('put in neat order') + 理 ('cut and polish jade along its natural veins -> put in order, arrange, manage'): 'put in order, tidy up, sort out, organize, collate'. Attested since Han texts.

history.stage: Han Classical Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: put in order; tidy up; sort out; organize

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 整理 (via 萌典)

整篇.etymology: A modifier-classifier compound combining 整 (zhěng, 'whole, entire, complete') with 篇 (piān, 'bound bamboo bundle of writing; sheet, chapter, complete piece of writing', with semantic 竹 'bamboo slips' and phonetic 扁 biǎn). Because ancient Chinese texts were written on bamboo slips tied into bundles (篇), 整篇 literally means 'the entire bound scroll/piece of writing from start to finish'.

history.meaning: a bundle of bamboo slips constituting a complete chapter, essay, or poem
the entire article, essay, script, or written piece

morphemes.meaning: piece of writing, article, sheet (classifier & bound noun)

整篇.notes: Can stand alone (整篇都很好 'the whole piece is great') or directly precede a noun without 的 (整篇文章 'the entire article', 整篇稿子 'the whole script/draft').

rootFamily.gloss: length of a piece of writing, space on a page/screen
chapter, section of a composition or work

整齐.etymology: Coordinative adjective and verb compound of 整 ('orderly, arranged') + 齐 (齊, 'even, uniform in height like ears of grain'): 'neat, tidy, even, well-ordered'. Attested since the Zuozhuan and Shiji.

history.stage: Classical Chinese (Zuozhuan, Shiji) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: even and orderly; neat; tidy

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 整齐 (via 萌典)

文件.etymology: Compound noun of 文 ('writing, text') + 件 ('individual item, document'): 'official document, paper, file (physical or computer file)'.

history.stage: Qing administrative Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: official document; paper; file

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 文件 (via 萌典)

文件夹.etymology: Modern office and computing compound from 文件 ('document; paper; file') + 夹 (simplified from 夾, 'press from both sides; clip; folder'). Used both for physical cardboard or plastic binders that hold loose sheets and, by calque of English *folder*, for digital directories.

history.meaning: file folder; binder

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 文件夹

文化.etymology: An ancient Classical Chinese compound of 文 (wén, 'pattern, literary refinement, civil virtue', contrasted with 武 wǔ 'martial force') and 化 (huà, 'to transform, educate, civilize'). First attested in Han dynasty texts such as Liu Xiang's *Shuiyuan* (说苑·指武: 「凡武之兴，为不服也；文化不改，然后加诛」, 'when civilizing transformation through moral/literary refinement fails to reform them, only then apply martial punishment'). In Meiji Japan, 文化 (bunka) was repurposed as a graphic loan to translate German *Kultur* and English *culture*, and this modern anthropological and artistic sense returned to Mandarin.

history.meaning: moral and civic transformation through literary/ritual refinement rather than military force (Shuiyuan, Han dynasty)
culture, civilization (translation of German Kultur / English culture)
culture, civilization, arts and heritage; also formal schooling/literacy level (as in 有文化)

文化.notes: Beyond 'culture' (传统文化, 企业文化), colloquial Mandarin uses 文化 to mean 'formal education or literacy': 有文化 means 'educated/literate' (not just 'cultured'), and 文化课 means 'academic subjects (as opposed to art/sports)'.

cognates.meaning: person of culture, intellectual, literary figure (bunkajin)

文化人.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 文化 (wénhuà, 'culture, literary education, scholarship') with the agentive head noun 人 (rén, 'person'). Coined in twentieth-century East Asian discourse (alongside Japanese 文化人 *bunkajin*), it denotes an educated intellectual, writer, artist, or someone working in cultural and publishing spheres.

history.meaning: man/woman of letters, intellectual engaged in cultural or artistic pursuits
person of culture, intellectual, educated person (used both sincerely and with light irony in speech)

文化人.notes: In everyday speech (frequently with erhua: 文化人儿), it can be a sincere compliment for a well-read creator or a playfully teasing remark when someone uses fancy idioms or wears scholarly glasses (装文化人 'acting like an intellectual').

文化大国.etymology: A four-character modifier-head nominal compound in which 文化 (wénhuà, 'culture, heritage') modifies 大国 (dàguó, 'great state, major country', a Classical phrase attested since the *Laozi* 「治大国若烹小鲜」 and *Mencius*). In contemporary Chinese public and media discourse, it designates a nation endowed with vast historical heritage and cultural resources.

history.meaning: a large, populous feudal state or major power (Laozi, Mencius)
major cultural nation; a country rich in cultural heritage and artistic output

文化大国.notes: In Chinese media policy and television speeches (*幕后之王*), 文化大国 ('a country big in cultural heritage/scale') is frequently paired with 文化强国 ('a country strong in global cultural soft power'), urging creators to turn heritage into world-class content.

rootFamily.gloss: cultural powerhouse, nation strong in soft power

文本.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 文 (wén, 'written characters, literary composition') and 本 (běn, originally 'tree root', extended to 'bound volume, manuscript edition, foundational script', as in 版本 and 剧本). Used in medieval Chinese philology for an original physical manuscript or edition, 文本 was revitalized in late twentieth-century literary theory, linguistics, and television production to translate English *text* (from Latin *textus*, 'woven fabric of words') and to denote a show's written script or treatment.

history.meaning: physical manuscript copy, authoritative written edition, or literary foundation
written text (in literary theory, computing, and law); finalized script or written proposal in film/TV production

morphemes.meaning: root, source edition, bound book, script

文本.notes: In film and TV production (*幕后之王*), producers distinguish between a raw idea (创意) and a solid 文本 ('written treatment / script text'); in computing and linguistics, it translates 'text' (纯文本 'plain text').

文章.etymology: Coordinative compound of 文 (wén, 'interlaced pattern,纹; written character, literary composition') and 章 (zhāng, 'colorful emblem, musical movement, structured stanza'). In Classical Chinese (e.g., Analects), 文章 originally denoted ornate ritual patterns, courtly insignia, and cultural refinement before narrowing in Six Dynasties and Tang literary criticism to structured prose essays and articles.

history.meaning: ornate ritual patterns, courtly emblems, and cultural accomplishment
belletristic prose composition, literary essay
article, essay, published piece; hidden subtext or fuss (as in 做文章)

文章.notes: Besides standard print or online articles (一篇文章), the idiom 做文章 (zuò wénzhāng, 'to make an issue out of something / spin a narrative around a detail') is ubiquitous in media and PR drama.

斗.etymology: In standard mainland simplification, 斗 merges two distinct historical graphs: 斗 (dǒu, a ten-liter grain-measuring dipper, pictograph of a ladle) and 鬥/鬭 (dòu, 'to grapple, contend, fight', oracle bone pictograph of two bare-handed figures facing each other in combat). In the verbal sense 'to contend with, vie against', it descends strictly from 鬥 (Old Chinese *tˤok-s).

history.meaning: to grapple hand-to-hand, clash in combat
to contest, pit animals against each other, vie in wit or skill
to contend with, fight against, outmaneuver in rivalry

斗.notes: Remember the tonal and graphic split: dǒu (third tone, trad. 斗) means 'peck/dipper' (as in 北斗星, Big Dipper), whereas dòu (fourth tone, trad. 鬥) means 'to fight or vie with' (as in 斗智斗勇, matching wits and courage).

rootFamily.gloss: to match wits, battle of brains
factional infighting (especially palace or office politics)

斗争.etymology: Coordinative compound uniting 斗 (trad. 鬥, dòu, 'to grapple, clash in combat') and 争 (trad. 爭, zhēng, 'to tug over an object, contest, vie for', depicting two hands pulling on an object). Attested in Classical Chinese for armed or factional contention, its modern abstract sense of ideological, political, or institutional 'struggle' was reinforced in the late 19th and 20th centuries alongside Japanese 闘争 (tōsō, rendering German Kampf).

history.meaning: physical clash, brawl, or factional contention
ideological, class, or political struggle; internal corporate or factional infighting

斗争.notes: While historically heavy with political connotations (阶级斗争, class struggle), in workplace and showbiz dramas 内部斗争 or 派系斗争 refers to boardroom turf wars and factional infighting.

料.etymology: Associative compound (会意) in the Shuowen Jiezi composed of 米 (mǐ, 'hulled grain, rice') inside 斗 (dǒu, 'measuring scoop/peck'), originally meaning 'to measure out grain' and hence 'to calculate, estimate, or provision'. From 'measured provisions and raw grain', the noun sense broadened to 'raw material, culinary ingredient, substance' and in modern media slang (often via Cantonese 爆料 bou6 liu2) to 'insider scoop, tabloid dirt, or dramatic substance'.

history.meaning: to measure grain with a scoop; to reckon, estimate; fodder/provisions
raw material, timber, culinary ingredient; innate talent or makings of a person
ingredient, material; juicy insider scoop, tabloid fodder, substance in a show

morphemes.meaning: measured grain; material, ingredient; insider scoop; to anticipate

料.notes: In entertainment and journalism, 猛料 (měngliào) means 'explosive scoop/bombshell', 爆料 (bàoliào) means 'to leak juicy gossip', and 笑料 (xiàoliào) means 'comedy fodder / laughingstock'.

rootFamily.gloss: to leak or drop an exclusive scoop/secret

斜.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining 余 (yú/xié phonetic) + 斗 ('ladle/scoop'): originally 'ladle out liquid' (by tilting a scoop), hence 'tilted, slanting, oblique, diagonal, leaning (opposite of 正 'straight/upright')'.

history.stage: Old & Classical Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: tilted like a scooping ladle = slanting, oblique, diagonal

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 斜 (via 萌典)

斜坡.etymology: The noun '斜坡' (xiépō, slope) joins '斜' (slanting, oblique) and '坡' (slope, bank). '斜' originally referred to something scooped out or not straight, later becoming a general term for an angle or incline. '坡' specifically refers to uneven or slanted ground. '斜坡' is a straightforward descriptive compound that has been used since classical times to describe non-level terrain. In modern usage, it applies equally to natural geographical features and artificial structures like ramps.

history.meaning: slope

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 斜坡

断.etymology: Ancient ideogram (traditional 斷) showing an axe (斤) cutting through skeins of silk thread (㡭): 'cut in two, sever, snap, break off; stop/abstain from; judge/decide (判断); (in negative sentences) absolutely'.

history.meaning: axe severing silk threads = cut off, break, decide
break; snap; cut off; interrupt; judge

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 断 (via 萌典)

新.etymology: Ancient phono-semantic/ideographic character attested on Shang oracle bones combining 亲/辛 ('chisel/hazel tree') + 木 ('wood') + 斤 ('axe'): originally 'chop fresh firewood from a tree', hence 'new, fresh, newly, renew (opposite of 旧/老)'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: axe cutting fresh wood = new, fresh, newly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 新 (via 萌典)

新一季.etymology: Modifier-head phrase formed from 新 (xīn, 'new, fresh', originally a phono-semantic graph of 亲/ces plus 斤 'axe', cutting fresh timber) modifying the numeral-classifier compound 一季 (yījì, 'one season'). 季 (jì) originally denoted the youngest of four brothers (禾 'grain' over 子 'child', the late-ripening crop) and hence the final month of a quarter or a three-month 'season'. In modern television production, 季 calques English broadcast 'season'.

history.meaning: youngest brother; final month of a three-month quarter; agricultural season
a brand-new quarterly season or broadcast television season

morphemes.meaning: season (of the year or of a serialized TV program)

新一季.notes: Chinese television traditionally aired continuous single-run serials, so counting variety shows and streaming dramas by 季 (新一季, 第一季) reflects modern seasonal production cycles modeled on international TV formats.

rootFamily.gloss: quarter of a financial or broadcast year
season finale,收官 of a season

新人.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 新 (xīn, 'new, newly arrived') and 人 (rén, 'person'). In Classical and Tang-Song Chinese (e.g., Du Fu's poem 新婚别: '新人虽言好，未若故人姝'), 新人 primarily meant a 'new bride' (and later 'bride and groom'). In modern Mandarin—reinforced by Japanese 新人 (shinjin) in entertainment and corporate parlance—it predominantly denotes a 'newcomer, rookie talent, or new hire'.

history.meaning: new bride; newlywed spouse (contrasted with 故人 'former spouse')
newlywed couple; newcomer to an organization, rookie artist or debutant in entertainment

新人.notes: Context determines which sense applies: at a wedding, 一对新人 means 'the happy newlywed couple'; in a TV production house or talent agency, 带新人 means 'to mentor rookie performers/new hires'.

cognates.meaning: newly appointed, newly assigned to a post

新任.etymology: Modifier-head compound combining 新 (xīn, 'newly, recently') and 任 (rèn, 'to bear a burden, hold official post, appoint to office', from 人 'person' + 壬 phonetic). First attested in medieval imperial bureaucracy (Tang–Song administrative records) for an official newly installed in a magistracy or ministry, it functions in modern Mandarin as a non-predicative adjective ('newly appointed') or noun ('the new appointee').

history.meaning: newly installed imperial magistrate or official post-holder
newly appointed, incoming (executive, director, or official)

morphemes.meaning: to assume office, official post, appointment

新任.notes: 新任 is a non-predicative attributive modifier placed directly before titles (often without 的), as in 新任总监 ('the newly appointed director') or 新任总裁 ('the incoming CEO').

rootFamily.gloss: to assume office, take up a post
to appoint, assign to a post

新剧.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 新 (xīn, 'new, newly produced') and 剧 (trad. 劇, jù, 'theatrical play, drama series'). The character 劇 (from 虍 'tiger' + 豕 'wild boar' = 豦 'fierce struggle between beasts', plus 刀 'knife') originally meant 'severe, intense, arduous' in Classical Chinese; by the Yuan, Ming, and Qing dynasties (via compounds like 杂剧 zájù and 戏剧 xìjù) it specialized as the generic head noun for staged theatrical works and modern scripted screen dramas.

history.meaning: severe, acute, arduous, intense (of illness, labor, or speed)
early 20th-century 'new drama' (spoken theater 文明戏/话剧 contrasted with traditional opera)
newly produced or upcoming television drama series or stage play

morphemes.meaning: theatrical play, scripted drama series (trad. 劇)

新剧.notes: In contemporary entertainment industry usage, 开新剧 means 'to launch a new drama series' and 宣传新剧 means 'to promote an upcoming show', whereas in theater history 新剧 referred specifically to early 1900s Western-inspired spoken drama.

rootFamily.gloss: crew and cast of a drama/film production

新意.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 新 (xīn, 'new, fresh, novel') and 意 (yì, 'thought, conception, artistic intent', composed of 音 'sound/voice' over 心 'heart-mind', i.e., recognizing the intent behind words). Attested in Tang and Song poetics and literary criticism (e.g., Su Shi and Ouyang Xiu) to praise a poem or essay that achieves fresh conceptual angles rather than recycling worn-out tropes.

history.meaning: fresh poetic conception, original literary or artistic thought
originality, creative freshness, novel angle (in media, design, or writing)

新意.notes: Frequently used in creative critiques and pitch meetings with verbs like 缺乏新意 ('lacking originality') or 毫无新意 ('completely unoriginal / derivative'), or positively as 颇有新意 ('quite original').

新手.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 新 ('new') + 手 ('hand -> person practicing a craft or skill'): 'new hand, novice, beginner, newcomer'. Attested since Tang–Song poetry and prose.

history.meaning: new hand; beginner; novice

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 新手 (via 萌典)

新来乍到.etymology: Four-character parallel (ABAC-style) vernacular idiom (成语) pairing 新来 (xīnlái, 'newly arrived') with 乍到 (zhàdào, 'just arrived for the very first time'). 乍 (zhà) is a Classical and vernacular adverb meaning 'suddenly, abruptly, for the first time', interlockingly synonymous with 新 ('newly'), while 来 ('come') and 到 ('arrive') form a synonymous verbal pair. Popularized in Yuan zaju drama and Ming-Qing vernacular fiction (such as Water Margin and Dream of the Red Chamber).

history.meaning: having just arrived at a new place or household for the first time
brand-new to a company, city, or social circle; unfamiliar with the ropes

morphemes.meaning: for the first time, just now

新来乍到.notes: A polite, self-deprecating stock phrase used by interns, new hires, or transfers introducing themselves to colleagues: 我新来乍到，请多关照 ('I've just arrived and am new here—please show me the ropes').

rootFamily.gloss: at first glance, upon first seeing
upon first arriving in a new place, unfamiliar with local ways

新歌.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 新 (xīn, 'new, newly composed') and 歌 (gē, 'song, chant', composed of 哥 phonetic—doubled 可 representing prolonged vocalization—and 欠 'open mouth / exhale'). Attested in Classical poetry (e.g., Tang verse contrasting 新歌 'newly composed lyrics/melodies' with 旧曲 'old tunes'), and used in modern Mandarin music and broadcasting for a singer's newly released single or track.

history.meaning: newly composed court or banquet song/ballad
newly written or newly released song/single in the music industry

新歌.notes: Takes the literary classifier 首 (一首新歌, 'a new song'). Common music-showbiz collocations include 发新歌 ('to drop/release a new song'), 打榜新歌 ('chart-competing new single'), and 新歌发布会 ('new single launch event').

新气象.etymology: Modifier-head compound combining 新 (xīn, 'new, revitalized') with the compound noun 气象 (qìxiàng, trad. 氣象). In Classical and Song-Ming Chinese, 气象 united 气 ('vital vapor, spirit, aura') and 象 ('visible configuration, phenomenon, image') to denote both 'atmospheric/celestial phenomena' and the 'prevailing aura, grandeur, or spirit of an age or place' (e.g., Fan Zhongyan's 岳阳楼记: 气象万千). 新气象 thus means a 'fresh, invigorated atmosphere or new outlook'.

history.meaning: atmospheric phenomena; grand aura, spirit, or prevailing aspect of a scene or dynasty
fresh new look, revitalized atmosphere, dynamic new ethos (in an organization or era)

新气象.notes: Anchored in the popular four-character proverb 新官上任三把火 ('a new official lights three fires upon taking office') and the New Year saying 新年新气象 ('New Year, fresh new atmosphere/look'), often used when a new executive shakes up a company.

新版.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 新 (xīn, 'new, revised') and 版 (bǎn, 'wooden printing block, register tablet, edition', from 片 'split wood plank' + 反 phonetic). In Song-Qing woodblock printing, 新版 denoted a newly carved woodblock printing plate or newly typeset edition of a book; in contemporary media, software, and television, it extends to any revamped edition, remake of a classic drama, or updated format of a show.

history.meaning: newly carved woodblock printing plate or newly printed book edition
new edition, revamped version, remake (of a TV series, program format, or software)

新版.notes: In television and publishing, 新版 contrasts with 旧版 or 老版 ('old/original version') and 原版 ('original unadapted edition'). Revamping a variety show's format is called 改版 (gǎibǎn), producing a 新版节目.

rootFamily.gloss: to revamp a show's format or redesign a publication layout

cognates.meaning: promising newcomer, rising star in a field

新秀.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 新 (xīn, 'newly emerged') and 秀 (xiù, 'flowering grain ear; flourishing, outstanding talent'). 秀 originally depicted a cereal plant (禾) bowing with fertile grain/blossom, extending in Classical Chinese to 'outstanding, refined, eminent person' (as in 秀才 xiùcái, 'flourishing talent'). Attested in Jin-dynasty literature (Book of Jin / 晋书) for a rising young scholar-official, 新秀 now denotes a 'rising star, rookie talent, or promising newcomer' in entertainment or sports.

history.meaning: newly risen young scholar or eminent talent of the generation
history.stage: Middle Chinese (Six Dynasties, e.g., Book of Jin)

history.meaning: rising star, promising rookie talent, breakout newcomer (in showbiz, arts, or sports)

morphemes.meaning: flowering grain; outstanding talent, standout performer

新秀.notes: Note the dual life of 秀 in modern Chinese: in 新秀 ('rising talent') and 优秀 ('excellent'), 秀 retains its native Classical meaning 'outstanding', whereas in 选秀 ('talent audition show') and 脱口秀 ('talk show') it blends with a phonetic loan from English 'show'.

rootFamily.gloss: talent competition / audition show (blending classical 秀 'talent' + English 'show')

cognates.meaning: new car, brand-new vehicle or train carriage

新车.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 新 (xīn, 'new') and 车 (trad. 車, chē, 'wheeled vehicle, chariot, car', an oracle-bone pictograph of a two-wheeled carriage with axle, yoke, and shaft). Attested in Classical Chinese for a newly built horse-drawn carriage or war chariot, in modern Mandarin 新车 refers to a brand-new automobile (as opposed to 二手车 'used car') or a newly launched vehicle model.

history.meaning: newly crafted horse-drawn chariot or carriage
brand-new automobile or newly launched car model

新车.notes: Takes the classifier 辆 (一辆新车, 'a new car'). In commercial media and sponsorship contexts, 新车发布会 ('new car model launch event') is a staple corporate PR assignment for production directors.

新闻.etymology: Modifier-head nominalized compound of 新 (xīn, 'newly') and 闻 (trad. 聞, wén, 'that which is heard; tidings, intelligence', from 耳 'ear' inside 門 'gate' phonetic). First attested in Tang-dynasty texts (and Song court gazettes / 小报) in the literal sense 'newly heard matters, fresh hearsay or tidings'. In the 19th century, Protestant missionaries in China (e.g., 遐迩贯珍) and Meiji Japanese translators adopted 新聞 to render Western 'news' and 'newspaper'.

history.meaning: newly heard tidings, fresh hearsay or novel anecdotes
journalistic news, press reports, broadcast news

morphemes.meaning: to hear; that which is heard, tidings, report (trad. 聞)

新闻.notes: Classic Sino-Japanese false friend: in Modern Chinese 新闻 means 'news' (a newspaper is 报纸 bàozhǐ), whereas in Japanese 新聞 (shinbun) and Korean 신문 (sinmun) the word means 'newspaper' (while broadcast 'news' is ニュース / 뉴스).

新闻学.etymology: Compound formed by affixing the disciplinary suffix -学 (trad. 學, xué, 'branch of learning, academic study, -ology') to 新闻 (xīnwén, 'journalistic news, the press'). Modeled on early 20th-century Sino-Japanese academic terminology (新聞学 shinbungaku, translating German Zeitungswissenschaft and English 'journalism studies'), it became an established university discipline in China following the founding of Peking University's Journalism Research Society in 1918.

history.meaning: academic discipline of journalism and press studies

新闻学.notes: In Chinese universities, 新闻学 ('journalism studies') is often paired with 传播学 (chuánbōxué, 'communication/media studies') inside a 新闻与传播学院 ('School of Journalism and Communication', abbreviated 新传).

新项目.etymology: Modifier-head phrase combining 新 (xīn, 'new') with 项目 (xiàngmù, trad. 項目, 'itemized entry, project').
