In 项目, 项 (trad. 項, 'nape of the neck', extended to 'category, clause, sum') and 目 ('eye', extended to 'index entry, heading, sub-item' as in 纲目) form a coordinative compound originally denoting 'specific clauses or entries in a catalog'. In 20th-century economic, engineering, and media management usage, 项目 specialized to render English 'project' (and sports 'event').

history.meaning: specific clauses, sub-headings, or itemized entries in an official ledger or treatise
new business venture, newly greenlit production project, or new athletic event

新项目.notes: In film, TV, and tech companies, 项目 is the everyday word for 'project': 立项 (lìxiàng) means 'to officially greenlight/register a project', and 接新项目 means 'to take on a new project'.

新鲜.etymology: Coordinative adjective compound of 新 ('new, fresh') + 鲜 (鮮, 'freshly caught fish/mutton -> fresh, bright, delicious', neutral tone xian in everyday speech): 'fresh (of food, flowers, or air); novel, new and unfamiliar'. Attested since Han–Six Dynasties prose.

history.meaning: fresh (not spoiled or stale); novel; new

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 新鲜 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: sense of freshness, feeling of novelty

新鲜感.etymology: Formed by attaching the productive abstract-noun suffix -感 (gǎn, 'feeling, sense, perception of', from 咸 phonetic + 心 'heart-mind') to the coordinative compound 新鲜 (xīnxiān, 'fresh, novel'). In 新鲜, 新 ('new') pairs with 鲜 (trad. 鮮, 'freshly caught fish', composed of 魚 'fish' + 羊 'mutton', prized for fresh flavor in antiquity). 新鲜感 thus shifts concrete sensory freshness into the psychological 'sense of novelty, excitement, or spark'.

history.meaning: fresh and unspoiled (of fish, meat, or newly picked produce); bright and vivid
psychological sense of novelty, fresh excitement, romantic or creative spark

morphemes.meaning: fresh (originally of fish/meat), vivid, rare (trad. 鮮)

新鲜感.notes: Used equally in media critique (观众失去了新鲜感, 'the audience has lost the sense of novelty') and in relationship talk (保持新鲜感, 'to keep the spark/novelty alive in a relationship').

方.etymology: In oracle bone and bronze inscriptions, 方 (fāng, Old Chinese *paŋ) depicted either a wooden plowshare blade breaking earth or two boats lashed side-by-side in parallel, from which derived the core senses 'parallel, four-cornered square, compass direction, region, and prescription/method'. As a prominent Chinese surname (方), genealogical traditions trace it to Fang Lei (方雷) in the legendary Yellow Emperor era and to the Western Zhou minister Fang Shu (方叔), whose descendants adopted his style name as a lineage surname.

history.meaning: side-by-side boats / square blade; four-cornered square; quarter of the compass; Zhou lineage surname (from Fang Shu)
square, direction, region, medical prescription, method; surname Fang

morphemes.meaning: square, direction, side, method; surname Fang

方.notes: When introducing the surname 方 in conversation, native speakers often disambiguate it from homophones (like 房 Fáng) with the phrase 方圆的方 ('the Fang of square-and-round') or 方向的方 ('the Fang of direction').

rootFamily.gloss: square and circle; circumference, surrounding area
party, side (in a contract or production, e.g., 甲方 client, 节目方 show producer)

方不方便.etymology: Interrogative A-not-AB (अधूरा/incomplete reduplication) construction derived from the disyllabic adjective 方便 (fāngbiàn, 'convenient'). In Mandarin morphosyntax, disyllabic adjectives and modal verbs form neutral yes-no questions by anticipating only the first syllable before the negator 不 (bù) followed by the full compound (AB -> A不AB: 方不方便), grammaticalizing a polite inquiry into whether circumstances, timing, or privacy permit an action.

history.form: 方便不方便 / 方不方便
history.meaning: is it convenient or not? would this be a good time/place to speak or act?

morphemes.meaning: method, convenient (first syllable of 方便)

方不方便.notes: In workplace and professional Chinese, 现在方不方便说话？ ('Is now a good time to talk?') or 方不方便加个微信？ ('Would you mind if we connected on WeChat?') is the go-to polite softener for checking someone's availability or boundaries.

rootFamily.gloss: convenient, handy; euphemism for using the restroom

cognates.meaning: expedient means (upāya), white lie or tactical device
means, medium, vehicle (shifted from Buddhist expedient means)

方便.etymology: Coordinative compound of 方 (fāng, 'method, proper technique') and 便 (biàn, 'advantageous, opportune, at ease'). During the Six Dynasties and Tang translations of Mahāyāna Buddhist texts (e.g., Kumārajīva's Lotus Sūtra), 方便 was chosen to translate Sanskrit upāya (or upāya-kauśalya)—the 'skilful, adaptable expedient means' a bodhisattva uses to guide sentient beings according to their capacity. From 'accommodating expedient means', it secularized into everyday Mandarin 'convenient, handy'.

history.meaning: opportune method; Buddhist upāya ('skilful expedient means' adapted to the listener)
to do a charitable favor for someone (行方便); convenient, accommodating, handy
convenient, easy; having spare cash (手头方便); polite euphemism for using the toilet

方便.notes: Watch out for a famous Sino-Xenic false friend and a euphemism: in Japanese 方便 (hōben, as in 嘘も方便 'even a lie can be a useful expedient') means 'ulterior expedient / white lie', not 'convenient' (which is 便利 benri); in Chinese, 我去方便一下 is a polite euphemism for 'I'm going to use the restroom'.

rootFamily.gloss: is it convenient? would now be a good time?
convenient, facile; taking the opportunity while at it (shùnbiàn)

方向.etymology: Coordinative/modifier-head compound combining 方 (fāng, 'compass quarter, side, orientation') and 向 (xiàng, 'north-facing window', extended in Classical Chinese to 'to face toward, direction of movement, bearing'). Attested in Tang poetry and Song prose for physical spatial bearing, and extended in modern Mandarin to strategic, creative, or career direction.

history.meaning: compass quarter and spatial bearing toward which one faces
physical direction, orientation; strategic, creative, or research course

方向.notes: Common collocations span literal navigation (方向盘 'steering wheel', 方向感 'sense of direction') and creative/corporate strategy (调整方向 'to pivot/adjust strategic direction', 大方向 'overall strategic direction').

方向感.etymology: '方向感' (fāngxiànggǎn, sense of direction) is a three-character compound formed by '方向' (direction) and the suffix '感' (sense, feeling). '方向' originally referred to spatial orientation, notably the cardinal points, while '感' means perception or sensory ability. The construction of psychological terms using the '-感' suffix became highly productive in early 20th-century Chinese, influenced by translations of Western psychology and physiology. '方向感' specifically denotes an individual's innate or learned ability to orient themselves spatially.

history.meaning: direction

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 方向感

cognates.meaning: mode, form, established method or system

方式.etymology: Coordinative compound of 方 (fāng, 'method, rule, squared standard') and 式 (shì, 'model, pattern, ritual standard, style', derived from 工 'carpenter's square/work' + 弋 phonetic). In Classical Chinese, 方 and 式 both denoted 'normative standards or models to emulate'; in modern Mandarin (reinforced by Meiji Japanese 方式 hōshiki rendering English 'mode' or 'manner'), 方式 denotes the characteristic pattern, style, or mode in which something is carried out.

history.meaning: normative model, standard rule, or prescribed pattern of conduct
way, manner, mode, style of operation or living (e.g., 生活方式)

方式.notes: Learner distinction: 方法 (fāngfǎ) emphasizes a concrete 'technique or method' for solving a problem, whereas 方式 (fāngshì) emphasizes the 'mode, style, or manner' of doing or organizing something (e.g., 生活方式 'lifestyle', 联系方式 'contact method/info', 合作方式 'mode of cooperation').

方格.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 方 ('square') + 格 ('grid, lattice, check'): 'square grid, check/plaid pattern, squared box on paper or fabric'.

history.meaning: square grid; check pattern

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 方格 (via 萌典)

方案.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 方 (fāng, 'method, prescription, strategic plan') and 案 (àn, 'wooden tray or magistrate's desk', composed of 安 phonetic + 木 'wood', which extended in imperial administration to 'official dossier, legal record, or drafted proposal laid on a magistrate's desk'). Popularized in modern administrative and corporate usage (alongside Japanese 方案 hōan) for an actionable plan, pitch proposal, or design scheme.

history.meaning: low wooden serving tray; magistrate's desk; official dossier or drafted proposal on the desk
formulated action plan, operational scheme, or creative pitch proposal

morphemes.meaning: official desk; dossier, drafted proposal, record

方案.notes: In media production, advertising, and corporate settings, 方案 is the core term for a 'project proposal' or 'pitch deck': 做方案 ('to draft a proposal'), 改方案 ('to revise a proposal'), and 备选方案 ('backup plan / Plan B').

方案会.etymology: Three-character modifier-head compound formed by attaching 会 (trad. 會, huì, 'assembly, meeting, conference', originally depicting a lidded vessel with people gathering) to 方案 (fāng'àn, 'action plan, creative proposal'). Coined in modern Chinese corporate, advertising, and television production workflows, 方案会 designates a formal meeting convened to pitch, critique, and sign off on production proposals.

history.meaning: proposal review meeting, creative pitch session, or planning meeting in corporate/media production

方案会.notes: In Chinese TV and agency culture (as seen throughout *Behind the Scenes*), 开方案会 ('holding a proposal/pitch meeting') and 过方案 ('getting a proposal approved in a review meeting') are high-stakes milestones before a show can enter production.

rootFamily.gloss: to hold or attend a meeting

方法.etymology: Coordinative compound of 方 (fāng, 'carpenter's square, medical prescription, technique') and 法 (fǎ, 'law, model, standard method', originally 灋 from 水 'level as water' + 廌 'mythical unicorn that gores the guilty' + 去 'cast out'). In Classical Chinese (e.g., Mozi, Mencius), 方法 meant 'standards of measurement (the square and the rule)' or 'prescribed techniques (especially medical prescriptions or Buddhist dharmas)', later generalizing to any systematic 'method or way'.

history.meaning: standards of square-and-rule measurement; medical prescription or technical recipe
systematic method, procedure, or concrete way of accomplishing a task or inquiry

方法.notes: Compare near-synonyms: 方法 (fāngfǎ) is a systematic 'method or technique' (often formal/written), 办法 (bànfǎ) is a practical 'way out or solution to a specific problem' (e.g., 想办法 'figure out a way'), and 方式 (fāngshì) is an overall 'mode or style'.

rootFamily.gloss: practical way of handling something, solution
methodology (the study or system of methods)
way of doing things, practice, approach

cognates.meaning: magnetic compass needle; guiding policy, course, principle
guiding policy, principle, course of action

方针.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 方 (fāng, 'compass direction, orientation') and 针 (trad. 針/鍼, zhēn, 'metal needle', from 金 'metal' + 十/咸 phonetic). Originally denoting the 'magnetic needle of a compass' (罗盘方针) that points the way for navigators, it was popularized in late 19th-century Meiji Japanese (方針 hōshin) and re-adopted into Modern Mandarin as a dead metaphor for an organization's or state's 'guiding policy, strategic principle, or overarching orientation'.

history.meaning: magnetic compass needle indicating directional bearing; Buddhist metaphor for a guiding pointer
guiding policy, overarching strategic principle or directive (of a company, project, or government)

方针.notes: Because 方针 retains its metaphor of a 'compass needle', it refers to high-level 'guiding principles or strategic directives' (制定方针 'to formulate a guiding policy'), whereas 政策 (zhèngcè) refers to concrete regulatory 'policies'.

rootFamily.gloss: directed at, targeted toward, in light of
to hit the nail on the head ('draw blood with a single needle-prick')

方面.etymology: Coordinative/modifier-head compound of 方 (fāng, 'compass quarter, region, side') and 面 (miàn, 'face, surface, side facing toward', originally an oracle-bone pictograph of an eye framed by facial contours). In Classical Chinese (e.g., Book of Han / 汉书), 方面 denoted a 'strategic frontier region or military commandery in one quarter of the empire' (as in 独当一面). In Modern Mandarin, it broadened to an abstract 'aspect, facet, respect, or party/side'.

history.meaning: one strategic quarter or regional military command of the realm
aspect, facet, respect (of an issue); party or side (e.g., 公司方面 'on the company's side')

方面.notes: Extremely versatile in discourse: use 在……方面 ('in terms of / in the area of...'), the correlative pair 一方面……另一方面…… ('on the one hand... on the other hand...'), or after a noun (节目组方面 'for the production team's part') to mean 'the X side'.

rootFamily.gloss: to take charge of an entire department or front on one's own

旁.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining 帝/凡 (broad/spread above) + 方 (fāng/páng phonetic): originally 'wide, spreading in all directions', then 'side, beside, nearby; other (旁人)'.

history.stage: Old & Classical Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: side; beside; other

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 旁 (via 萌典)

旁边.etymology: Locative compound noun combining 旁 ('side, beside') + 边 (邊, 'edge, side'): 'beside, next to, by the side of'.

history.meaning: side; beside; next to

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 旁边 (via 萌典)

旅游.etymology: Coordinative verb and noun compound of 旅 ('travel away from home; troop of 500 soldiers marching under a banner 㫃') + 游 (遊, 'wander, roam, sightsee'): 'travel for pleasure, tour, sightseeing, tourism'.

history.meaning: travel and roam
tour; travel for leisure; tourism

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 旅游 (via 萌典)

旅行.etymology: Coordinative verb and noun compound of 旅 ('travel away from home') + 行 ('walk, go on a journey'): 'travel, take a trip, journey'.

history.meaning: travel in a group or on a journey
travel; trip; journey

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 旅行 (via 萌典)

旋律.etymology: Sino-Japanese / literary Chinese musical compound combining 旋 ('revolve, return in phrases') + 律 ('pitch-pipe standard, musical law/temperament'). Standardized across modern East Asian musical terminology to render 'melody'.

history.meaning: twelve-tone pitch pipes and temperament
melody

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 旋律 (via 萌典)

cognates.word: 旋回 / 自転 (cf. 旋転 senten)

旋转.etymology: Coordinative verb compound uniting 旋 (xuán, 'to wheel around, pivot beneath a banner', composed of 方/㫃 'fluttering banner' + 疋 'foot', depicting troops wheeling around a standard) and 转 (trad. 轉, zhuǎn, 'to revolve, turn a wheel', composed of 車 'wheeled vehicle' + 專 'spindle' phonetic). Attested together since Han-Tang texts for the wheeling of celestial bodies, vortices, or wheels, 旋转 in Modern Mandarin means 'to spin, rotate, or revolve around an axis'.

history.meaning: to wheel around in formation; revolution of celestial spheres or turning of wheels
to spin, rotate, revolve around an axis (of stages, cameras, chairs, or dancers)

morphemes.meaning: to turn, revolve (like a wheel or spindle, trad. 轉)

旋转.notes: In stage and studio design (as well as everyday life), 旋转 appears in iconic compounds like 旋转舞台 ('revolving stage'), 旋转椅 ('swivel chair', famous on singing-competition shows), 旋转门 ('revolving door'), and 旋转木马 ('carousel / merry-go-round').

rootFamily.gloss: to turn, shift, transform; to broadcast/relay (转播)

无.etymology: Written as simplified 无 and traditional 無 (wú, Middle Chinese *mju, Old Chinese *ma). In Oracle Bone and Bronze inscriptions, 無 originally depicted a person dancing while holding luxuriant plumes or branches in both hands—the graph is the ancestral form of 舞 (wǔ, "to dance"). Already in early Zhou texts it was borrowed rebus-style for the homophonous existential negative verb "to not have, to lack" (the opposite of 有 yǒu), and later grammaticalized into a productive bound privative prefix ("-less, un-, non-") across Literary and modern Mandarin compounds.

history.meaning: to dance with plumes; borrowed phonetically for 'to not have, there is not'
to lack, to not exist; negative prohibitive 'do not' (equivalent to 毋)
to lack, have no (literary verb); productive privative prefix in disyllabic compounds

无.notes: In modern spoken Mandarin, standalone 无 is restricted to formal, written, or fixed idiomatic registers (where colloquial speech uses 没有 méiyǒu), but it remains wildly productive as a prefix equivalent to English "un-" or "-less".

rootFamily.gloss: unable to, have no way to

无不无聊.etymology: A colloquial Mandarin A-not-AB interrogative reduplication formed from the disyllabic adjective 无聊 (wúliáo, "bored, silly, pointless, having nothing better to do"). In the A-not-AB pattern (无 + 不 + 无聊), only the first syllable A (无 wú) is reduplicated before the negative particle 不 (bù) to create a rhetorical or pointed question ("Are you bored or what? / Don't you have anything better to do?"). The base word 无聊 originated in Classical Chinese as a verb-object compound (無聊, "to lack anything to rely on / to lack livelihood or emotional support") before shifting in vernacular Mandarin to mean "bored" or "tacky/senseless".

history.meaning: lacking anything to rely on; destitute and despondent (as in Chu Ci)
bored, listless; silly, pointless, tiresome
is that pointless or what?; have nothing better to do? (rhetorical A-not-AB question)

morphemes.meaning: reduplicated initial syllable of 无聊 for A-not-AB question formation
interrogative-negative pivot particle in A-not-AB construction
bored, silly, having nothing better to do (literally 'without reliance/pastime')

无不无聊.notes: Frequently used in drama dialogue with a finals particle like 啊 (a) or 呀 (ya)—e.g., "你无不无聊啊？" ("Don't you have anything better to do? / How childish can you get?")—to chide someone for petty pranks, gossip, or time-wasting antics.

rootFamily.gloss: idle chatter, to shoot the breeze

无偿.etymology: A verb-object Sino-compound 无偿 (traditional 無償, wúcháng), composed of the privative verb/prefix 无 (wú, "to lack, without") + 偿 (償 cháng, "to repay, to compensate, to indemnify", from 亻 "person" + 賞 shǎng as phonetic and semantic component "reward/recompense"). While both morphemes are ancient in Classical Chinese, the compact disyllabic legal and economic term 無償 ("without consideration / gratis") was standardized in Meiji-era Japanese legal translation (無償 mushō, translating German unentgeltlich / French à titre gratuit in civil law) and reinforced in modern Chinese legal and administrative prose.

history.meaning: to repay a debt, make restitution, fulfill an obligation
without legal consideration or compensation, gratuitous
history.stage: Modern Sino-Japanese & Late Qing Return Loan

history.meaning: free of charge, unpaid, pro bono (used adverbially or attributively)

无偿.notes: Higher and more institutional in register than 免费 (miǎnfèi, "free of charge" for consumer goods); 无偿 typically modifies transfers of rights, labor, or public service, such as 无偿献血 ("voluntary unpaid blood donation") or 无偿转让 ("royalty-free transfer of IP/rights").

rootFamily.gloss: paid, for a fee (antonym of 无偿)
to repay, pay back a debt

无奈之举.etymology: A four-character Literary Chinese modifier-head noun phrase (无奈之举, traditional 無奈之舉, wúnài zhī jǔ). The modifier 无奈 (wúnài, shortened from Classical 無奈之何, "to have no way to deal with it, to have no alternative") is linked via the classical associative/subordinating particle 之 (zhī, equivalent to modern 的) to the head noun 举 (舉 jǔ, originally a verb meaning "to lift up with two hands", extended in Classical Chinese to mean "an action, undertaking, move, or measure"). Literally, "an action taken out of having no alternative."

history.meaning: to be unable to do anything about a situation; helplessly
a measure or step taken out of sheer necessity or lack of options
a move made out of necessity, a last-resort measure

morphemes.meaning: way to cope with, remedy, alternative
literary attributive particle (linking modifier to head noun)

无奈之举.notes: Common in corporate, political, and entertainment-industry statements when justifying an unpopular decision (e.g., cutting a budget, canceling a show, or compromising with a rival): "这也是无奈之举" ("This too was a move made out of necessity").

rootFamily.gloss: wise move, brilliant stroke (parallel X之举 pattern)

无妨.etymology: A verb-object compound 无妨 (traditional 無妨, wúfáng), formed from the existential negative verb 无 (wú, "to have no, there is no") + 妨 (fáng, "hindrance, harm, obstruction, impediment", composed of 女 semantic + 方 fāng phonetic). Attested since Tang and Song dynasty literary and vernacular texts, it literally means "there is no hindrance" or "it causes no harm," functioning both as a reassuring reply ("no harm done, go right ahead") and in the concessive idiom 但说无妨 ("feel free to speak frankly, it does no harm to say it").

history.meaning: there is no hindrance; it does not interfere with anything
it does not matter, no harm done, might as well

无妨.notes: Carries a poised, courteous, slightly literary tone compared to colloquial 没关系 (méi guānxi); often heard in workplace dramas from senior executives granting permission, especially in "但说无妨" ("Speak freely, no harm done").

rootFamily.gloss: might as well, there is no harm in trying
harm, detriment (mostly in negative 没何妨害)

无所谓.etymology: Originating as a Classical Chinese verb-object phrase 無所謂 (simplified 无所谓, wúsuǒwèi), composed of 无 (wú, "to lack, there is not") + 所 (suǒ, a nominalizing pronominal particle turning the following verb into an object noun phrase, "that which is...") + 谓 (謂 wèi, "to call, to name, to designate, to speak of"). In Classical prose, 無所謂 X meant "there is nothing that can be called X" or "cannot be termed X." By the Ming–Qing vernacular period, when used intransitively without a following noun phrase, it shifted semantically to "there is nothing to be said about it / it makes no difference / to not care."

history.meaning: there is no such thing as...; cannot be called or spoken of as...
it cannot be helped; it makes no difference, to be indifferent
to not care, be indifferent; it doesn't matter; so-called X does not exist

morphemes.meaning: to call, to say, to matter/signify

无所谓.notes: Functions both as a standalone conversational response ("无所谓" = "Whatever / I don't care / Either way is fine") and as a stative verb taking a subject ("我无所谓" = "I don't mind"), while retaining its classical sense before nouns ("无所谓输赢" = "Winning or losing doesn't matter / There's no such thing as winning or losing").

rootFamily.gloss: meaningless, pointless (literally 'having nothing to say for itself')

无敌.etymology: Verb-object compound used as an adjective, combining 无 (無, 'have no, without') + 敌 (敵, 'match, rival, enemy'): 'have no match/equal -> invincible, unmatched, peerless' (from Mencius's 仁者无敌 'the benevolent person has no match in the world').

history.meaning: without match or rival; invincible; peerless

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 无敌 (via 萌典)

无比.etymology: A verb-object compound 无比 (traditional 無比, wúbǐ), composed of 无 (wú, "to have no") + 比 (bǐ, originally two people standing side by side in Oracle Bone script, meaning "to compare, to match, peer, equal"). Attested in Classical Chinese and early Buddhist translations (translating Sanskrit anupama / asama, "peerless, unequaled"), 無比 originally functioned as a predicate or post-nominal attribute meaning "having no equal, matchless" (e.g., 世間無比). In modern Mandarin it also grammaticalized into a high-degree intensifier adverb ("incomparably, supremely") preceding two-syllable adjectives or psychological verbs.

history.meaning: having no equal, peerless, matchless (translating Sanskrit anupama)
incomparably, beyond measure (both pre-verbal adverb and post-adjectival complement)

无比.notes: Unusually flexible syntactically: it can precede a disyllabic adjective/verb as an adverb (无比激动 "incomparably excited", 无比自豪 "immensely proud") or follow a disyllabic adjective as an intensive complement (美丽无比 "incomparably beautiful").

rootFamily.gloss: to be on a par with, rival, match

cognates.meaning: lawless, outrageous (muhō — false friend in modern sense)

无法.etymology: A verb-object compound 无法 (traditional 無法, wúfǎ), formed from 无 (wú, "to have no, to lack") + 法 (fǎ, "method, way, means, law"). In Classical Chinese, 無法 meant "without laws or standards, lawless" (a sense preserved in the idiom 無法無天 and in Japanese 無法 muhō). However, in Late Imperial vernacular Mandarin, 法 in this compound took on the everyday sense of 方法/法子 ("way, method, means"), so 无法 (parallel to colloquial 没法 méifǎ) grammaticalized into an auxiliary-like verb meaning "to have no way to, to be unable to" before a two-syllable verb phrase.

history.meaning: lacking laws, rules, or institutional standards; lawless
having no method or means to do something; unable to
unable to, have no way to (followed by a verb phrase)

无法.notes: Watch out for the Japanese false friend 無謀/無法 (muhō, "lawless, reckless"): in modern Mandarin, standalone 无法 before a verb (e.g., 无法接受 "unable to accept", 无法想象 "unimaginable") strictly means "unable to / have no way to", whereas the colloquial equivalent is 没法 (méifǎ).

rootFamily.gloss: lawless, reckless, defying human and divine law

无理取闹.etymology: A four-character serial verb/adverbial-head idiom (chengyu) 无理取闹 (traditional 無理取鬧, wúlǐ-qǔnào), attested in Tang–Song literary prose (such as Han Yu's and Zhu Xi's writings). The first half, 无理 (wúlǐ, VO compound: 无 "lacking" + 理 "reason, principle, justification"), acts as an adverbial modifier ("unreasonably, without justification") to the second half, 取闹 (qǔnào, VO compound: 取 qǔ "to seek, court, stir up" + 闹 nào "commotion, trouble, quarrel"). Together it denotes deliberately picking a fight or making a scene when one knows one is in the wrong.

history.form: 無理取鬧 (Song Neo-Confucian & vernacular texts)
history.meaning: to stir up trouble or noisy argumentation devoid of moral principle or reason
to make a scene unreasonably, throw a tantrum or pick a quarrel on purpose

无理取闹.notes: A staple phrase in modern relationship and workplace dramas when one character accuses another of acting out of jealousy, pettiness, or diva behavior rather than legitimate grievance ("你别在这里无理取闹！").

rootFamily.gloss: to make a fuss, cause a scene,闹事
self-inflicted humiliation, asking for trouble (parallel 取X pattern)

无盐.etymology: Verb-object/modifier phrase combining 无 (無, 'without, no') + 盐 (鹽, 'salt'): 'unsalted, salt-free (e.g., 无盐黄油 unsalted butter)'.

history.meaning: unsalted; salt-free

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 无盐 (via 萌典)

无耻.etymology: A Classical Chinese verb-object compound 无耻 (traditional 無恥, wúchǐ), formed from 无 (wú, "to lack, to have no") + 耻 (恥 chǐ, "sense of shame, disgrace, humiliation", composed of 耳 "ear" — from the reddening of the ears when blushing in shame — and 心 "heart/mind"). Deeply rooted in Confucian moral philosophy (such as the Mencius: 人不可以無恥 "A person must not be without a sense of shame" and the Zuo Zhuan), where 恥 was one of the foundational moral sentiments separating ethical conduct from brazen self-interest.

history.meaning: lacking a moral sense of shame or conscience
shameless, brazen, unscrupulous (strong pejorative adjective)

无耻.notes: A harsh moral condemnation in Mandarin; it frequently pairs with 卑鄙 (bēibǐ, "base, despicable") in the four-character denunciation 卑鄙无耻 ("base and shameless") or 无耻之徒 ("brazen scoundrel").

无聊.etymology: Verb-object compound used as an adjective, combining 无 (無, 'have nothing') + 聊 ('rely on, find sustenance or solace in'). In Chuci and Shiji (民不聊生 / 无聊), 无聊 meant 'having nothing to rely on, destitute and despondent'; in modern Mandarin it means 'bored, boring, dull, silly/senseless'.

history.meaning: lacking support or solace; dispirited
bored; boring; dull; senseless

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 无聊 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: of course, needless to say (mochiron — semantic shift)
cognates.word: 勿論 / 無論 (もちろん)

无论.etymology: Formed from the prohibitive/negative的无 (传统 無 wú, here functioning like prohibitive 毋 wú, "do not") + 论 (論 lùn, "to discuss, debate, consider, weigh"). In early medieval Chinese (such as Tao Yuanming's *Peach Blossom Spring*, "乃不知有漢，無論魏晉" — "They did not even know of the Han dynasty, let alone the Wei and Jin"), 無論 meant "not to mention, let alone." In Late Imperial and modern Mandarin, it grammaticalized into a universal concessive conjunction ("regardless of, no matter [who/what/how]"), typically paired with a question word or choice and echoed by 都 (dōu) or 也 (yě) in the main clause.

history.meaning: do not speak of; let alone, not to mention; without distinction
no matter (who, what, how), regardless of (paired with 都/也)

无论.notes: Beware the Japanese/Korean false friend: Japanese 勿論/無論 (mochiron) and Korean 물론 (mullon) mean "of course!", whereas Mandarin 无论 strictly means "no matter / regardless of" and requires an interrogative pronoun (谁, 什么, 怎么) or A/B choice followed by 都 or 也.

rootFamily.gloss: no matter what, by all means
no matter, regardless of (slightly less formal synonym)

无论如何.etymology: A four-character concessive idiom and adverbial phrase 无论如何 (traditional 無論如何, wúlùn-rúhé), combining the concessive conjunction 无论 (wúlùn, "regardless of, no matter") with the Classical Chinese interrogative compound 如何 (rúhé, contraction of 如之何, "like what? / how? / in what state?"). Literally meaning "no matter how [things stand]", it crystallized in Late Imperial and modern Mandarin as an emphatic sentence-level adverb meaning "no matter what, under any circumstances, come what may."

history.meaning: regardless of how the situation turns out; under any condition
history.stage: Late Imperial to Early Modern Mandarin

history.meaning: no matter what, whatever happens, at all costs

morphemes.meaning: be like, resemble (in 如何 'like what / how')

无论如何.notes: Just like standalone 无论, a clause introduced by 无论如何 almost always takes 都 (dōu) or 也 (yě) before the main verb (e.g., "无论如何我都要试试" — "No matter what, I'm going to try").

rootFamily.gloss: why, for what reason (parallel X何 classical interrogative)

无限量.etymology: A tri-morphemic modifier-head / verb-object formation 无限量 (traditional 無限量, wúxiànliàng), built from the privative prefix 无 (wú, "without, lacking") + 限量 (xiànliàng, "restricted quantity, quota, limit on amount", from 限 xiàn "boundary, threshold, limit" + 量 liàng "measured capacity, quantity"). While 無限 ("boundless, infinite") and 限量 ("to limit quantity; quota") both appear in medieval Chinese (often in Buddhist expressions like 不可限量 "immeasurable"), modern 无限量 functions both figuratively ("boundless prospects") and commercially ("unlimited quantity, all-you-can-use/eat").

history.form: 不可限量 / 無限量 (Medieval & vernacular texts)
history.meaning: beyond measurable bounds; immeasurable in capacity or future achievement
unlimited in quantity, boundless, uncapped

无限量.notes: Used in two distinct registers: in commercial/media contexts for uncapped supply (e.g., 无限量供应 "unlimited supply"), and in elevated praise of someone's career potential (前途无限量 "having boundless future prospects").

无非.etymology: A Classical Chinese double-negation compound 无非 (traditional 無非, wúfēi), combining the existential negative verb 无 (wú, "there is nothing that is...") with the negative copula/adjective 非 (fēi, originally a graph of two opposing wings, meaning "is not, contrary to"). Literally "there is nothing that is not [X]" -> "all of it is [X] / nothing other than [X]." Through pragmatic reanalysis in Tang–Song and Ming–Qing prose, this double negative shifted from universal affirmation ("every single one is...") to a downplaying restrictive adverb ("nothing more than, simply, merely"), usually followed by 是 (shì).

history.meaning: there is none that is not...; every single thing is... (as in Shijing & Han prose)
it is nothing other than...; merely, simply boils down to...
nothing more than, simply, only (often paired with 是 or 就是)

无非.notes: Often used when unmasking someone's true, simpler motive behind a complicated excuse: "他这么做，无非是想引起你的注意" ("His doing this is nothing more than wanting to get your attention").

rootFamily.gloss: could it be that...? (rhetorical question adverb)
really isn't, is by no means

既.etymology: In Oracle Bone script, 既 (jì, Middle Chinese *kjɨjH, Old Chinese *kəds) is a compound ideograph depicting a kneeling person (卩/旡) turning their head away with an open mouth from a food vessel (皀, a ceremonial bowl filled with fragrant grain) after finishing a meal. From its concrete primary meaning "to finish eating a meal; to exhaust/complete" (compare 朝食既 "after the morning meal"), it grammaticalized in early Old Chinese into the perfective aspectual adverb "already, having finished" and subsequently into the correlative conjunction "both... [and...]" (paired with 且 qiě in Classical Chinese, and with 又 yòu, 也 yě, or 且 qiě in modern Mandarin).

history.meaning: to finish eating a meal (kneeling person turning away from a food vessel); to exhaust completely (e.g., total solar eclipse 日有食之既)
already, after having done X; correlative 'not only / both... (paired with 且 or 又)'
both... (correlative conjunction paired with 又, 也, or 且); bound root 'already'

既.notes: In modern Mandarin, standalone 既 almost never appears alone; it operates in correlative frames like "既 A 又 B" ("both A and B", for two verbs or adjectives of similar positive/negative valence) or "既 A 也 B".

rootFamily.gloss: established, already existing, set (e.g., 既定事实)

cognates.meaning: since it is already so (giran, literary)

既然.etymology: A Classical Chinese compound conjunction 既然 (jìrán), composed of the perfective adverb 既 (jì, "already, having already") + the demonstrative pro-verb/pronoun 然 (rán, "to be so, thus, like this", originally a graph of roasting dog meat over fire, borrowed phonetically for "so/thus"). In Classical Chinese, 既然 meant "since it is already so / things having already come to this." Over time, 然 lost its independent pronominal weight and fused with 既 as a suffix forming a causal/premise conjunction ("since, now that, given that"), introducing an already-established fact as the premise for an inference or suggestion (usually marked by 就 jiù, 那 nà, or 也 yě in the main clause).

history.meaning: since it is already thus; things having already been so (two separable morphemes)
since, now that, given that (introducing a presupposed premise)

morphemes.meaning: so, thus (classical demonstrative predicate fused as conjunction suffix)

既然.notes: Key learner distinction vs. 因为 (yīnwèi, "because"): 既然 introduces a known, mutually agreed-upon fact ("Since you're already here...") and points toward a logical conclusion or deduction with 就, whereas 因为 supplies a new, unknown cause for an event.

rootFamily.gloss: as expected, sure enough (parallel X然 adverb)

日光.etymology: Compound noun from 日 ('sun', originally a circle with a central dot) + 光 ('light; radiance', fire 火 above a kneeling person 儿). Attested in classical prose and poetry for natural sunlight, and used in modern compounds such as 日光灯 ('daylight fluorescent lamp').

history.meaning: light of the sun; daylight
sunlight; daylight

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 日光

日子.etymology: Colloquial noun formed from 日 ('sun -> day') + nominal suffix 子 (neutral tone zi): means 'a specific day or date; days (count of time); everyday life or livelihood (过日子)'.

history.meaning: day; date; days; life/livelihood

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 日子 (via 萌典)

日期.etymology: Compound noun of 日 ('day') + 期 ('appointed time, date'): 'calendar date, appointed date'. Attested since the Zuozhuan and Shiji.

history.stage: Classical Chinese (Zuozhuan, Shiji) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: appointed day; calendar date

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 日期 (via 萌典)

日程.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-compound 日程 (rìchéng), formed from 日 (rì, "day, daily", originally a solar pictograph) + 程 (chéng, "measured stage of a journey, distance, quota, procedure", from 禾 "grain" + 呈 chéng phonetic, originally a unit of measurement). In Classical and Tang–Song Chinese, 日程 meant "the distance traveled in a single day's march or journey" (e.g., 計日程功, "to calculate the work accomplished by the daily stages"). In Meiji Japan, 日程 (nittei) was repurposed to translate Western parliamentary and administrative "agenda, order of the day, daily schedule," and this modern sense was re-adopted into 20th-century Mandarin alongside its classical roots.

history.meaning: distance covered in a single day's journey; daily work quota
parliamentary agenda, order of the day, daily schedule or itinerary
schedule, timetable, agenda, itinerary

morphemes.meaning: stage of a journey, itinerary, procedure, schedule

日程.notes: Very frequent in production, media, and corporate settings (e.g., 排日程 "to arrange a schedule", 提上日程 "to put on the agenda / move into active planning").

旧.etymology: Simplified form of 舊 (originally an owl-like horned bird 萑 above a mortar 臼, borrowed phonetically in Old Chinese *gʷids -> jiù for 'old, former, past, used/worn, old friend'). Contrasts with 老 ('aged in years') by meaning 'used, old (opposite of 新 new), former'.

history.meaning: old (not new); former; long-standing; old friend
old; used; worn; former

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 旧 (via 萌典)

旧事.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 旧 (舊, 'old, past, former') + 事 ('affair, event, matter'): 'past events, old matters, things of the past'.

history.meaning: past events; old stories/matters

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 旧事 (via 萌典)

cognates.word: 旧怨 / 舊怨 (きゅうえん)

旧怨.etymology: A Classical Chinese modifier-head noun compound 旧怨 (traditional 舊怨, jiùyuàn), composed of 旧 (舊 jiù, "old, former, long-standing", originally depicting an owl 萑 perched over a mortar 臼, borrowed phonetically for "old/former") + 怨 (yuàn, "resentment, grievance, grudge, enmity", composed of 夗 yuàn "to turn over/toss in bed" + 心 "heart/mind"). Attested in pre-Qin and Han historical chronicles (such as the *Zuo Zhuan* and *Shiji*: 修舊怨 "to revive an old feud" or 解舊怨 "to resolve an old grudge"), it denotes a deep-seated personal or factional grievance carried over from the past.

history.meaning: a long-standing feud, ancestral enmity, or past grievance between states or clans
old grudge, past feud, lingering resentment

旧怨.notes: Often paired with 新仇 ("new hatred") in the four-character phrase 新仇旧怨 (or 新仇旧恨, "new hatreds and old grudges") when describing rival executives, families, or factions in drama series.

旧物.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 旧 (舊, 'old, used, bygone') + 物 ('object, thing, article'): 'old object, keepsake from the past, secondhand/used item'.

history.stage: Classical & Tang–Song Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: old article; object from the past

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 旧物 (via 萌典)

旧账.etymology: A modifier-head noun compound 旧账 (traditional 舊賬 / 舊帳, jiùzhàng), composed of 旧 (舊 jiù, "old, past, former") + 账 (賬 zhàng, "account, debt, financial record"). The character 賬 (with the cowrie/money radical 貝) differentiated in medieval and vernacular Chinese from 帳 (originally "canopy, tent, curtain", because accounts were kept on hanging cloth or scrolls inside a tent). From its literal bookkeeping sense of "unsettled past debts or old ledgers," 旧账 acquired the vivid metaphorical meaning of "old scores, past mistakes, or old grievances," especially in the verb-object idiom 翻旧账 ("to dig up old scores / bring up past mistakes in an argument").

history.form: 舊帳 / 舊賬 (Medieval & vernacular bookkeeping)
history.meaning: old financial accounts or unpaid debts from previous years
old financial accounts; (figuratively) old scores, past grievances or missteps

旧账.notes: Almost always encountered in its figurative sense in everyday speech and TV dialogue via the collocations 翻旧账 (fān jiùzhàng, "to rake up the past / bring up old mistakes") or 算旧账 (suàn jiùzhàng, "to settle old scores").

rootFamily.gloss: to settle accounts; to get even with someone

早.etymology: Ideogram combining 日 ('sun') above 十/甲 ('first, armor/helm, or treetop'): 'the sun rising at the start of the day -> morning, early; long ago; (as a greeting) Good morning!'.

history.stage: Old & Classical Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: sun at first light = early, morning, 'Good morning!'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 早 (via 萌典)

早上.etymology: Everyday noun for 'morning' (early morning until around nine or ten o'clock), combining 早 ('early, dawn', attested throughout Classical Chinese) with the noun-forming time/location suffix 上. Pairs with 好 to form the warm greeting 早上好！ ('Good morning!').

history.meaning: vernacular disyllabic noun 'morning'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 早上 (via 萌典)

早就.etymology: A lexicalized disyllabic temporal adverb 早就 (zǎojiù), formed by fusing the temporal adverb 早 (zǎo, "early, long ago", in Small Seal script depicting the sun 日 rising above a helmet/plant 甲) with the emphatic temporal/consequential adverb 就 (jiù, "already, right away, as early as", originally a high mound京 + 尤 meaning "to approach, move toward"). In vernacular Mandarin, placing 早 before 就 reinforces the earliness or prior completion of a state or action ("long ago already, way back when"), or indicates doing something "first thing / right from the start."

history.meaning: early on + already / right then
long ago, already at an early point, right from the start

早就.notes: Very common in emphatic statements like "我早就知道了" ("I knew that a long time ago!") or "我早就跟你说过" ("I told you so ages ago!"), often paired with sentence-final 了 (le).

rootFamily.gloss: long since, already (formal/written equivalent of 早就)

早日.etymology: A modifier-head compound 早日 (zǎorì), composed of 早 (zǎo, "early, soon") + 日 (rì, "day, date, time"). In Tang–Song poetry and vernacular texts, 早日 could refer either to "former days, days gone by" or "early in the morning." In modern Mandarin, it stabilized as a forward-looking adverbial expression meaning "at an early date, soon, as soon as possible," functioning specifically in optative or hopeful clauses (expressing wishes, goals, or blessings before a two-syllable verb).

history.meaning: in former days; early in the morning; an early future day
at an early date, soon (adverb used in wishes and aspirations)

早日.notes: Restricted to hopeful or forward-looking contexts before disyllabic verbs (e.g., 祝你早日康复 "Wishing you a speedy recovery", 希望项目早日上线 "Hoping the project launches soon"); never used for simple past narrative ("he arrived early").

rootFamily.gloss: at an early stage, early period (noun)
in the early years, years ago
as early as possible, at the earliest opportunity

早晚.etymology: An antonymic coordinative compound (dvandva) 早晚 (zǎowǎn), pairing 早 (zǎo, "morning; early") with its opposite 晚 (wǎn, "evening; late", from 日 "sun" + 免 miǎn phonetic). In Classical and medieval Chinese, combining the two poles of the daily cycle ("morning and evening") naturally extended in three directions: (1) literally "in the morning and evening" (e.g., temperature differences), (2) an abstract degree/time question "when, at what time" (similar to 多会儿 in northern dialects), and (3) a disjunctive adverb "whether early or late — i.e., sooner or later, eventually" (synonymous with 迟早 chízǎo).

history.meaning: morning and evening; at all hours; when / how soon
sooner or later, eventually (adverb); morning and evening (noun)

早晚.notes: When pronounced with full tones on both syllables (zǎowǎn), it usually means the adverb "sooner or later" ("这件事早晚会被发现" — "This matter will be discovered sooner or later", interchangeable with 迟早 chízǎo) or the noun "morning and evening" ("早晚温差大" — "big temperature difference between morning and night").

rootFamily.gloss: sooner or later (exact synonym in the adverbial sense)
early in the morning, bright and early

早晨.etymology: Coordinative temporal noun compound of 早 ('early morning') + 晨 ('daybreak, morning', sun 日 + 辰 'time of morning fieldwork'): 'morning, early morning'. Attested since the爾雅 Erya and Six Dynasties poetry.

history.meaning: early morning; morning

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 早晨 (via 萌典)

早点.etymology: A disyllabic Mandarin formation 早点 (traditional 早點, zǎodiǎn) with two distinct etymological pathways depending on part of speech. As the adverb meaning "a bit earlier, soon" (often rhotacized in northern speech as 早点儿 zǎodiǎnr), it is an adjective + comparative/quantifier construction: 早 (zǎo, "early") + 点 (點 diǎn, shortened from 一点儿 yīdiǎnr, "a little bit, slightly"). As a homographic noun meaning "light breakfast", it is a modifier-head compound from 早 ("morning") + 点 (short for 点心 diǎnxin, "pastry, light refreshment"). In the target adverbial sense ("earlier, soon"), it urges someone to act ahead of time or without delay.

history.form: 早 + 一點(兒) (Vernacular comparative contraction)
history.meaning: a little bit earlier; slightly sooner
earlier, soon, a bit earlier (adverb); light breakfast (homographic noun)

morphemes.meaning: a bit, slightly (reduced from 一点儿 in comparative adverbial use)

早点.notes: Ubiquitous in warm everyday parting expressions like "早点休息" ("Get some rest early!") or "早点回来" ("Come back early/soon!"). Don't confuse this adverbial use with the noun 早点 ("breakfast snack", as in 吃早点).

rootFamily.gloss: a little bit faster, hurry up (parallel Adj+点 adverb)
early morning; breakfast (synonymous in noun sense)

早间.etymology: Temporal compound noun and modifier of 早 ('early morning') + 间 (間, 'time interval, period'): 'in the morning, morning hours (e.g., 早间新闻 morning news)'.

history.meaning: morning time; in the morning

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 早间 (via 萌典)

早餐.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 早 ('morning') + 餐 ('meal'): 'breakfast' (slightly more formal or written than 早饭).

history.meaning: morning meal; breakfast

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 早餐 (via 萌典)

早餐店.etymology: A tri-morphemic modifier-head compound noun 早餐店 (zǎocāndiàn), structured as [早 + 餐] + 店. The modifier 早餐 (zǎocān, "breakfast, morning meal") combines 早 (zǎo, "morning, early") + 餐 (cān, "meal, food; to eat", attested since the *Shijing*), while the head noun 店 (diàn, "shop, store, inn", originally a shelter under a cliff 广 with a raised stand 占 for displaying wares) productively forms commercial establishment nouns across Mandarin.

history.form: 朝食 / 早膳 -> 早餐 (Evolution of 'breakfast')
history.meaning: morning meal, breakfast (早餐 generalized in modern standard Chinese)
breakfast shop, morning eatery or diner

早餐店.notes: In contemporary urban dramas (especially across Taiwan and mainland cities), the neighborhood 早餐店 serving soy milk (豆浆), crullers (油条), or egg crepes (蛋饼) is a quintessential warm, grounded setting for morning conversations between leads.

早饭.etymology: Everyday compound noun of 早 ('morning') + 饭 (飯, 'cooked rice, meal'): 'breakfast'.

history.meaning: morning meal; breakfast

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 早饭 (via 萌典)

时.etymology: Ancient character (traditional 時) combining 日 ('sun') + 寺/之 (shí phonetic, originally a foot 止 stepping forward on the ground): 'the sun's movement through the year -> season (the four seasons 四时), time, hour (ancient double-hour 时辰 or modern o'clock), opportunity, when, from time to time'.

history.meaning: seasonal advance of the sun = season, time, hour
time; hour; o'clock; season; when

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 时 (via 萌典)

时候.etymology: Coordinative temporal noun compound pairing 时 (時, 'time, season') + 候 ('five-day micro-season or astronomical watch interval', neutral tone hou in this word). In Classical calendrical science, three 候 made one solar term (节气); in vernacular Mandarin 时候 fused into the general noun for 'time, moment, period, (when…的)时候'.

history.meaning: seasons and five-day phenological intervals
time; moment; period

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 时候 (via 萌典)

时刻.etymology: A coordinative time-measurement compound 时刻 (traditional 時刻, shíkè), uniting two ancient Chinese astronomical and clepsydra (water-clock) units: 时 (時 shí, "double-hour [one of the 12 辰 shíchén of a day], season, time") and 刻 (kè, "notch carved on a water-clock float rod", where one full day and night was divided into 100 刻 in traditional timekeeping, later adjusted to 96 刻 or 15-minute quarter-hours; from 亥 hài phonetic + 刂 "knife"). Combining the larger hour (時) and the finer water-clock notch (刻) yielded both the noun "specific moment, critical juncture" and the adverb "at every moment, constantly."

history.meaning: hours and water-clock notches; exact time of day
moment, critical hour, juncture (noun); constantly, always (adverb)

morphemes.meaning: water-clock notch, quarter-hour, brief moment (literally 'to carve')

时刻.notes: Serves a dual role in Mandarin: as an elevated noun for a pivotal juncture (关键时刻 "critical moment", 高光时刻 "highlight moment") and as a pre-verbal adverb meaning "constantly, at all times" (时刻准备着 "always be prepared", 时刻关注 "keep a constant eye on").

rootFamily.gloss: immediately, at once (literally 'standing for a water-clock notch')
at this very moment, right now

时刻表.etymology: Three-character compound combining 时刻 ('hour and quarter-hour -> exact time') + 表 ('table, chart, schedule'): 'timetable, schedule (of trains, buses, flights, or classes)'.

history.meaning: timetable; schedule

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 时刻表 (via 萌典)

时差.etymology: A modifier-head astronomical and geographical compound 时差 (traditional 時差, shíchā), formed from 时 (時 shí, "time, solar hour") + 差 (chā, "difference, discrepancy, divergence"). Originally coined in Ming–Qing astronomical treatises (such as the calendar reforms involving Jesuit astronomers) to denote the "equation of time" (the discrepancy between apparent solar time and mean solar time, 均時差), in the modern era of global time zones and commercial aviation (reinforced by Japanese 時差 jisa) it came to denote the "time difference between time zones" and, metonymically in everyday speech, "jet lag" (as in 倒时差 "to adjust to a time zone / get over jet lag").

history.meaning: equation of time (discrepancy between true solar time and mean solar time)
time difference between geographical longitudes/zones; physiological jet lag

时差.notes: To express "having or getting over jet lag" in Mandarin, speakers use the vivid verb-object collocation 倒时差 (dǎo shíchā, literally "to flip/shift the time difference"), as in "我还在倒时差" ("I'm still getting over jet lag").

rootFamily.gloss: gap, disparity, difference (in quality or level)

时期.etymology: A coordinative / modifier-head temporal compound 时期 (traditional 時期, shíqī), composed of 时 (時 shí, "time, season, era") + 期 (qī, "appointed time, cycle, fixed span or phase", from 其 qí phonetic + 月 "moon/month"). In Classical and medieval Chinese, 時期 referred to an "appointed time, deadline, or seasonal juncture." In modern historiography and standard Mandarin (reinforced by Meiji Japanese 時期 jiki), it specialized to mean a bounded "historical period, developmental phase, or stage" characterized by specific conditions (unlike 时代 shídài, which denotes a grand macro-historical epoch).

history.meaning: appointed time, scheduled date, or seasonal juncture
historical period, developmental phase, or specific stage of events

时期.notes: Compare 时期 (shíqī) and 时代 (shídài): 时期 refers to a specific, bounded phase of development or crisis (非常时期 "extraordinary/crisis period", 青春期/过渡时期 "transitional period"), whereas 时代 refers to a grand historical or cultural epoch (互联网时代 "the Internet age", 黄金时代 "golden age").

时机.etymology: A modifier-head compound 时机 (traditional 時機, shíjī), composed of 时 (時 shí, "time, season") + 机 (機 jī, originally the delicate trigger mechanism of a crossbow or the shuttle-release of a loom, extended in Classical Chinese philosophy and military strategy to mean "pivotal spring of action, decisive turning point, subtle opportunity"). Attested in Six Dynasties and Tang strategic and literary texts, 時機 literally means "the temporal trigger-point"—the exact moment when conditions align for decisive action.

history.meaning: the pivotal turning point of time; the subtle moment when action can succeed
timing, opportune moment, right occasion for action

morphemes.meaning: pivotal moment, opportunity (originally 'crossbow trigger / loom mechanism')

时机.notes: Unlike 机会 (jīhuì, "an opportunity/chance" in general), 时机 specifically means "timing / ripeness of the moment" and collocates with "ripeness" metaphors: 时机成熟 ("the timing is ripe") or 把握时机 ("seize the right moment").

rootFamily.gloss: favorable turn of events, silver lining

时至今日.etymology: A four-character Literary Chinese subject-predicate temporal phrase 时至今日 (traditional 時至今日, shí-zhì-jīnrì), structured as 时 (時 shí, "time, the course of time") + 至 (zhì, "to arrive at, to reach", in Oracle Bone script depicting an arrow hitting the ground target) + 今日 (jīnrì, modifier-head noun: 今 "present, current" + 日 "day", i.e. "today, the present day"). Literally "Time having arrived at the present day," it functions as a solemn sentence-initial discourse adverbial ("down to the present day, even now, after all this time"), typically introducing a reflection on something that has either persisted unexpectedly or still remains unresolved.

history.form: 時至今日 (Literary Chinese temporal clause)
history.meaning: with time having reached the present day; down to this day
history.stage: Late Imperial to Modern Literary Chinese

history.meaning: down to the present day, even now, at this late stage

morphemes.meaning: to reach, arrive at, come down to

时至今日.notes: Carries a reflective, weighty, or slightly rueful tone in speeches and dramatic monologues (e.g., "时至今日，我才明白他的苦心" — "Only now, after all this time, do I understand his painstaking intentions").

rootFamily.gloss: up to now, to this day (concise two-syllable equivalent)
matters having reached this stage, now that things have come to this (parallel X至此 idiom)

时间.etymology: Compound noun of 时 (時, 'time') + 间 (間, 'interval, span'): 'time (both duration of time and a point in time)'.

history.meaning: span or point of time; time

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 时间 (via 萌典)

时间胶囊.etymology: Modern compound of 时间 ('time', sun radical 日 in 时 + interval 间) + 胶囊 ('capsule', flesh/organic radical 月 in 胶 'gelatin/gum' + 囊 'bag; sack; pouch'). Adopted as a semantic calque of English 'time capsule' for a sealed container of keepsakes hidden for future discovery.

history.meaning: time capsule

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 时间胶囊

时间表.etymology: A tri-morphemic modifier-head compound noun 时间表 (traditional 時間表, shíjiānbiǎo), structured as [时间] + 表. The modifier 时间 (時間 shíjiān, originally "an interval of time", popularized in its modern general sense via Meiji Japanese 時間 jikan translating English "time") combines 时 ("time") + 间 ("interval, space"). The productive head morpheme 表 (biǎo, originally "outer fur garment", extended in Classical Chinese to "memorial presented to the throne" and "tabular chart, gauge, or schedule that displays information outwardly") turns it into a "timetable, schedule, or timeline."

history.meaning: tabular chronological chart (as in Sima Qian's 十表 'Ten Chronological Tables' in the Shiji)
timetable, schedule, project timeline, shift roster

时间表.notes: Used both for concrete daily/production schedules (e.g., 拍摄时间表 "shooting schedule", 值班时间表 "shift roster") and figuratively in negotiations or project management for a target deadline roadmap (e.g., 给出明确的时间表 "give a clear timeline/timetable").

cognates.meaning: neglecting one's official duties (kanji: 曠職)
absence from work or school without leave

旷工.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound formed from 旷 (trad. 曠, kuàng, 'vast, empty; to leave vacant, neglect') and 工 (gōng, 'work, labor, official duty'). In Classical Chinese (e.g., Book of Documents / 尚書), 曠官 and 曠工 referred to officials leaving their posts vacant or neglecting state duties; in modern Mandarin it narrowed to skipping work without leave.

history.meaning: to neglect official duties or leave a government post vacant
to be absent from work without leave; truancy from duty

旷工.notes: As a separable verb-object compound (离合词), it can take aspect particles or duration complements between the characters, e.g., 旷了三天工 ('skipped three days of work'). Parallel to 旷课 ('cut class').

rootFamily.gloss: long-drawn-out, protracted (wasting days and enduring long)

明亮.etymology: Coordinative adjective compound of 明 ('bright, luminous', sun 日 + moon 月 shining together) + 亮 ('bright, clear, shining'): 'bright, well-lit, luminous, shining'. Attested since Six Dynasties and Tang poetry.

history.meaning: bright; well-lit; clear and shining

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 明亮 (via 萌典)

明信片.etymology: Three-character postal compound combining 明信 ('open/unsealed letter', 明 'open to view, unsealed' + 信 'letter') + 片 ('flat card, slip'): 'postcard' (introduced in late Qing postal service alongside Japanese 葉書).

history.meaning: open unsealed letter-card = postcard

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 明信片 (via 萌典)

明天.etymology: Noun meaning 'tomorrow', combining 明 ('bright, next dawning', combining 日 'sun' + 月 'moon') with 天 ('day, sky'). Classical Chinese said 明日 ('next sun/day'); vernacular Mandarin replaced 日 with everyday 天 to form 明天.

history.meaning: tomorrow
tomorrow

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 明天 (via 萌典)

明天见.etymology: A colloquial Mandarin farewell phrase structured as a temporal topic/adverbial 明天 (míngtiān, 'tomorrow', literally 'bright/next day', from 明 'bright, next following' + 天 'day, sky') modifying the verb 见 (trad. 見, jiàn, 'to see, meet'). While Classical Chinese used 明日 (míngrì) for 'the next day', vernacular Mandarin replaced 日 with 天 and paired it with 见 on the pattern of 再见 ('see you again').

history.meaning: to meet or have an audience on the following day
see you tomorrow (standard parting greeting)

明天见.notes: Part of the productive '[Time] + 见' parting formula in spoken Mandarin, alongside 一会儿见 ('see you in a bit'), 回头见 ('see you later'), and 下周见 ('see you next week').

明年.etymology: Temporal compound of 明 ('next, following', literally 'when the next cycle dawns into light') + 年 ('year'): 'next year'. Attested since the Zuozhuan and Analects.

history.stage: Classical Chinese (Zuozhuan, Analects) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: the coming year; next year

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 明年 (via 萌典)

明早.etymology: Contracted temporal compound of 明天 ('tomorrow', 明 'next') + 早晨/早上 ('morning'): 'tomorrow morning'.

history.meaning: tomorrow morning

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 明早 (via 萌典)

明明.etymology: Reduplication of 明 ('bright, clear, evident'). In the Classic of Poetry (Shijing) and Great Learning (明明德), 明明 meant 'illustrious and bright'; in vernacular Mandarin it functions as an epistemic/adversative adverb meaning 'obviously, plainly, clearly (contrary to what someone says or does)'.

history.meaning: bright and illustrious
obviously; plainly; clearly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 明明 (via 萌典)

明明白白.etymology: An AABB state-adjective reduplication of the disyllabic coordinative compound 明白 (míngbai, 'bright and white; clear, plain, evident'). In Mandarin morphology, reduplicating a disyllabic adjective AB into AABB intensifies the descriptive vividness and thoroughness ('thoroughly clear, in full view, without a shadow of ambiguity'), functioning adverbially before a verb or as a vivid predicate.

history.meaning: bright and clear; unambiguous; upright
plainly and clearly; thoroughly understood or aboveboard

明明白白.notes: In AABB reduplications of neutral-tone words like 明白 (míngbai), the final syllable regains its full lexical tone (míngmíngbáibái) in standard pronunciation; often used with 得 as a resultative/descriptive complement (说得明明白白, 'explained crystal clearly').

cognates.meaning: Venus, morning star; rising star or celebrity in a field

明星.etymology: Originally a modifier-head compound from 明 (míng, 'bright, shining') + 星 (xīng, 'star, celestial body'). In Classical Chinese (attested in the Classic of Poetry / 詩經·鄭風·女曰雞鳴: 子興視夜，明星有爛), 明星 designated the bright morning star (Venus, 啟明星) or any luminous star. In the early 20th century, with the rise of cinema and mass media, it acquired the semantic calque of English 'star' (celebrity, entertainer).

history.meaning: the Morning Star (Venus); a brightly shining star in the night sky
celebrity, movie/pop star, prominent public figure (calque of English 'star')

明星.notes: Core entertainment-industry term in *Behind the Scenes* (幕后之王), combining productively into 超级明星 ('superstar'), 流量明星 ('traffic/trending idol star'), and 明星效应 ('star power/celebrity effect').

明显.etymology: A coordinative (synonym-parallel) compound uniting 明 (míng, 'bright, clear, luminous') and 显 (trad. 顯, xiǎn, 'manifest, visible, prominent', originally depicting silk threads seen in sunlight). In Classical Chinese (e.g., Book of Han / 漢書), 明顯 described things shining forth visibly or truths made manifest; in modern Mandarin it functions as the primary adjective and adverb for 'obvious, noticeable, clear'.

history.meaning: brightly visible, illustrious, manifest to the eye or mind
obvious, clear, evident, noticeable

明显.notes: Unlike 显然 (which is restricted to adverbial or sentence-initial modal use, 'evidently'), 明显 is primarily an adjective that can take degree adverbs (很明显, 非常明显), modify nouns (明显的优势), or modify verbs (明显改善, 'visibly improve').

明智.etymology: Coordinative adjective compound of 明 ('clear-sighted, discerning') + 智 ('wise, intelligent'): 'wise, sensible, sagacious'. Attested since the Hanshu and Three Kingdoms prose.

history.stage: Han Classical Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: clear-sighted and wise; sensible

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 明智 (via 萌典)

明智之举.etymology: A four-character semi-literary phrase (四字格) structured as a modifier-head construction linked by the Classical Chinese attributive particle 之 (zhī): 明智 (míngzhì, 'clear-sighted and wise', a coordinative compound of 明 'discerning' + 智 'wise') + 之 ('of, subordinating marker') + 举 (trad. 舉, jǔ, 'action, move, undertaking', originally 'to lift up with both hands'). Literally 'an action of clear wisdom'.

history.meaning: a wise undertaking or discerning course of action (literary syntactic pattern)
a wise move, a sensible decision or course of action

morphemes.meaning: literary attributive marker (equivalent to modern 的)

明智之举.notes: The frame '[Two-character modifier] + 之举' is highly productive in formal and media Mandarin for evaluating strategic decisions: 无奈之举 ('a move made out of helplessness/last resort'), 惊人之举 ('an astonishing move'), and 创新之举 ('an innovative step').

rootFamily.gloss: to make a move in chess; every action and movement (一举一动)

明白.etymology: A coordinative compound combining 明 (míng, 'bright, luminous, clear') and 白 (bái, 'white, plain, unstained'). Attested in Warring States texts (e.g., Guanzi / 管子 and Xunzi / 荀子) in the concrete and moral sense of 'bright and pure, clear and unambiguous'. In Tang–Song vernacular Chinese, it underwent semantic extension from an objective state ('clear, plain') to a cognitive verb ('to see clearly, understand, realize').

history.meaning: bright and white; clear, open, unambiguous; upright in conduct
to understand, realize, grasp; clear and sensible

明白.notes: Beware the Sino-Japanese false friend: in Japanese, 明白 (meihaku) is strictly a formal adjective meaning 'obvious, indisputable', whereas in Mandarin 明白 (míngbai, with a neutral tone on the second syllable) is an everyday verb ('to understand') and adjective ('clear, sensible'). Often used as a resultative complement: 听明白 ('hear and understand'), 弄明白 ('figure out').

rootFamily.gloss: to confess, speak frankly; frank and open

星.etymology: Ancient character attested on Shang oracle bones originally showing three/five twinkling stars (晶) above phonetic 生 (shēng/xīng), later simplified to a single 日 ('celestial orb') above 生: 'star, heavenly body, planet, satellite; tiny speck/spark'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: celestial lights + phonetic 生 = star, heavenly body, speck

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 星 (via 萌典)

星天.etymology: A modern proper-noun coinage (used in *幕后之王* / *Behind the Scenes* as the name of the premier television and media production company 星天娱乐, Xīngtiān Entertainment) combining 星 (xīng, 'star, celebrity, constellation') and 天 (tiān, 'sky, heaven, firmament'). Built on the classical poetic imagery of a star-filled firmament (星空 / 满天星斗), in Chinese showbiz naming conventions it evokes a 'firmament of stars' (celebrities) and boundless reach.

history.meaning: stars and the heavens / starry sky (poetic juxtaposition)
Xingtian (fictional flagship media production company in Behind the Scenes)

星天.notes: Chinese entertainment and media agencies frequently name themselves using auspicious celestial or grand characters like 星 ('star'), 天 ('sky/heaven'), 光 ('light'), or 华 ('splendor')—compare real-world studios such as 光线传媒 (Enlight Media) and 天娱传媒 (EE-Media).

星星.etymology: Formed by nominal reduplication of 星 (xīng, originally three small twinkling orbs 晶 above phonetic 生 in Shang–Zhou script, denoting celestial stars). In Classical Chinese single-syllable 星 sufficed, whereas spoken Mandarin reduplicated it as 星星 (with a light neutral second syllable xīngxing) for everyday warmth and rhythm—both for night-sky stars and small five- or eight-pointed star emblems.

history.meaning: celestial star
star; star-shaped mark

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 星星

星期.etymology: Compound noun of 星 ('star/heavenly body') + 期 ('cycle, appointed period'). In Classical poetry (such as the Seventh Night festival of the Cowherd and Weaver Girl), 星期 meant 'the appointed tryst of the stars'. In the late Qing dynasty (promoted by Yuan Jiasan and early modern calendars to replace the older Seven Luminaries 七曜 cycle), 星期 was adopted for the seven-day 'week' (because the 7 days of the week were traditionally named after the Sun, Moon, and five visible planets).

history.meaning: appointed meeting of stars

history.stage: Late Qing to Modern Standard Mandarin
history.meaning: seven-day week

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 星期 (via 萌典)

星期一.etymology: Calendar compound combining 星期 ('week') + 一 ('one, first day of the working week'): 'Monday'.

history.meaning: first day of the week = Monday

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 星期一 (via 萌典)

星期三.etymology: Calendar compound combining 星期 ('week') + 三 ('three, third day of the week'): 'Wednesday'.

history.meaning: third day of the week = Wednesday

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 星期三 (via 萌典)

星期二.etymology: Calendar compound combining 星期 ('week') + 二 ('two, second day of the week'): 'Tuesday'.

history.meaning: second day of the week = Tuesday

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 星期二 (via 萌典)

星期五.etymology: Calendar compound combining 星期 ('week') + 五 ('five, fifth day of the week'): 'Friday'.

history.meaning: fifth day of the week = Friday

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 星期五 (via 萌典)

星期六.etymology: Calendar compound combining 星期 ('week') + 六 ('six, sixth day of the week'): 'Saturday'.

history.meaning: sixth day of the week = Saturday

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 星期六 (via 萌典)

星期四.etymology: Calendar compound combining 星期 ('week') + 四 ('four, fourth day of the week'): 'Thursday'.

history.meaning: fourth day of the week = Thursday

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 星期四 (via 萌典)

星期天.etymology: Calendar compound combining 星期 ('week') + 天 ('day / Heaven', parallel to 星期日 and 礼拜天): 'Sunday'.

history.meaning: Sunday

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 星期天 (via 萌典)

星级.etymology: Compound noun of 星 ('star') + 级 (級, 'grade, rating tier'): 'star rating (of hotels, restaurants, or service quality)'.

history.meaning: star rating; star grade

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 星级 (via 萌典)

春天.etymology: Compound season noun of 春 ('spring', showing grass/plants 艸 sprouting under the warming sun 日 with phonetic 屯 chūn) + 天 ('season, sky, time of year'): 'spring, springtime'.

history.meaning: the spring season; springtime

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 春天 (via 萌典)

春风得意.etymology: A classical four-character idiom (成语) derived from the famous Tang dynasty poem 《登科后》(After Passing the Imperial Examination) by Meng Jiao (孟郊, 751–814): 春风得意马蹄疾，一日看尽长安花 ('Flush with success in the spring breeze, my horse's hooves fly fast; in a single day I view all the blossoms of Chang'an'). Structurally, 春风 ('spring breeze', referring both to the season of the Tang metropolitan examination and auspicious favor) acts as an adverbial/contextual setting for 得意 (déyì, VO compound 'to attain one's wish; proud and elated').

history.meaning: exultant in the spring breeze after passing the imperial examination, riding swiftly through the capital
riding high, flush with success, thriving smoothly in career or love

morphemes.meaning: spring breeze (symbol of good fortune and renewal)

春风得意.notes: Originally specifically about academic or civil-service triumph, 春风得意 now broadly describes anyone whose career or personal life is thriving; often paired in the saying 赌场失意，情场得意 / 官场春风得意 or used attributively for a beaming expression (一脸春风得意).

rootFamily.gloss: radiant with happiness, beaming like a spring breeze
carried away by success, forgetting oneself in excitement

昨天.etymology: Temporal compound of 昨 ('yesterday, the day just past', sun/day 日 + 乍 zhà) + 天 ('day'): 'yesterday'.

history.meaning: yesterday

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 昨天 (via 萌典)

昨晚.etymology: Contracted temporal compound of 昨天 ('yesterday') + 晚上 ('evening, night'): 'last night, yesterday evening'.

history.meaning: yesterday evening; last night

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 昨晚 (via 萌典)

是.etymology: Equative copula ('be: am, is, are') linking two nouns or noun phrases. In Classical Chinese (Analects, Mencius), 是 originally functioned as the proximal demonstrative 'this' and adjective 'right, correct'; in Han-dynasty prose its résumé position between topic and predicate ('X, this [is] Y') reanalyzed into the modern copula 'be'.

history.meaning: demonstrative 'this'; 'right, correct'
copula 'to be'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 是 (via 萌典)

是不是.etymology: A-not-A affirmative-negative question construction built on the copula 是 ('is') + 不 ('not') + 是 ('is'): literally 'is it or is it not?', used to form yes-no questions, tag questions ('…right?, isn't it?'), or express 'whether or not'.

history.meaning: is it or not?; right?; whether or not

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 是不是 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: whether or not; right and wrong; pros and cons
whether or not; right or wrong

是否.etymology: An antonymous coordinative compound formed from 是 (shì, originally a demonstrative 'this' and adjective 'right, correct, true', later the copula 'to be') and 否 (fǒu, 'not so, negative; or not'). In Classical Chinese (e.g., Shiji / 史記), 是非 and 是否 juxtaposed 'right and wrong' or 'affirmative and negative'. Through grammaticalization in Literary and Modern Chinese, 是否 came to function as a formal indirect question adverb meaning 'whether or not' (equivalent to colloquial 是不是).

history.meaning: what is right and what is wrong; whether a proposition holds true or not
whether or not (formal adverb introducing an embedded polar question)

morphemes.meaning: not to be so; negative, or not

是否.notes: Register marker: 是否 is the formal/written (书面语) counterpart of spoken 是不是 or ...没有. Note the sharp Japanese false friend: in Japanese, 是非 (zehi) means 'by all means / definitely', whereas in Mandarin 是否 always means 'whether or not' (and 是非 means 'right and wrong / gossip').

cognates.meaning: day and night, around the clock

昼夜.etymology: An antonymous coordinative compound pairing 昼 (trad. 晝, zhòu, 'daytime, daylight', composed of 聿 brush/boundary + 日 sun, 'the bounded period of sunlight') and 夜 (yè, 'night'). Famous from Confucius's exclamation by a river in the Analects (論語·子罕): 逝者如斯夫，不舍晝夜 ('That which passes away is like this flowing water, never ceasing day or night!'). Functions both as a noun ('day and night') and adverbially ('round the clock,ceaselessly').

history.meaning: daytime and nighttime; continuously through day and night
day and night, round the clock, 24-hour period

昼夜.notes: Belongs to elevated or written register (书面语) compared to everyday 白天和晚上 or 日夜; frequently precedes action verbs directly as an adverbial of continuous effort, e.g., 昼夜不停 ('nonstop day and night') or 昼夜赶工 ('work round the clock to meet a deadline').

rootFamily.gloss: day and night (more common colloquial/written synonym)
polar day / midnight sun; white night
late at night, in the dead of night

显得.etymology: Evaluative verb-complement compound combining 显 (顯, 'show, appear, manifest visibly') + structural particle 得 (de): 'appear, seem, look (followed by an adjective or verb phrase, e.g., 显得很年轻 'look very young')'.

history.meaning: appear; seem; look

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 显得 (via 萌典)

显然.etymology: Derived from Classical Chinese 显 (trad. 顯, xiǎn, 'visible, manifest, prominent') + the classical stative/adverbial suffix 然 (rán, 'to be like so, in such a manner', grammaticalized from 'to burn'). In Classical texts (e.g., Book of Han / 漢書 and Lunheng / 論衡), 顯然 was a descriptive stative predicate meaning 'plainly visible, manifest in appearance'; in modern Mandarin it functions primarily as an evaluative sentence adverb meaning 'obviously, evidently, clearly'.

history.meaning: manifestly visible, prominent, standing out clearly
obviously, evidently, clearly (modal adverb)

morphemes.meaning: -ly, in the manner of, so (classical adverbial/stative formative)

显然.notes: Frequently reinforced by 很 as 很显然 ('quite obviously'). Unlike 明显, 显然 cannot modify nouns with 的 (*显然的错误 is ungrammatical; use 明显的错误) and instead modifies whole clauses or verb phrases as a speaker's epistemic judgment.

rootFamily.gloss: self-evident, obvious at a glance (four-character idiom)

显示.etymology: A coordinative/causative compound combining 显 (trad. 顯, xiǎn, 'to appear, make manifest, reveal') and 示 (shì, 'to show, indicate, proclaim to others', originally depicting an altar table where signs from heaven were revealed). In Six Dynasties and Buddhist texts, 顯示 meant 'to reveal or make manifest (a truth or power)'. In modern Mandarin, it encompasses 'to show, demonstrate (data/qualities)' as well as technological 'to display (on a screen)'.

history.meaning: to make manifest, reveal, demonstrate openly (power, virtue, or Buddhist dharma)
to show, indicate (of data/results); to display (on a monitor); to show off

显示.notes: Extremely versatile across registers: in journalism and business, 数据显示 / 调查显示 ('data/surveys show that...'); in computing, 显示器 ('monitor/display'); in interpersonal contexts, 显示实力 ('demonstrate one's strength/capability').

rootFamily.gloss: to show off, flaunt (colloquial northern Mandarin)

晃.etymology: Phono-semantic compound combining 日 ('sun; bright light') + 光 ('radiance; gleam', fire above a kneeling figure). Its original sense is 'bright light flashing or dazzling the eyes' (pronounced huǎng, as in 晃眼 'dazzle/trick the eyes'); a secondary reading huàng means 'sway back and forth like flickering light'.

history.meaning: bright gleam; flash before the eyes
dazzle the eyes (huǎng); sway (huàng)

cognates.meaning: to be promoted, advance in rank

晋升.etymology: A coordinative verb compound composed of 晋 (trad. 晉, jìn, 'to advance, move forward as the sun rises; to promote', attested in the I Ching hexagram 晉 'Progress') and 升 (trad. 昇/陞, shēng, 'to ascend, rise in rank, mount steps'). Used in imperial Chinese bureaucracy for advancing an official to a higher court rank, it remains the standard formal term for career promotion in corporate, civil service, and military hierarchies, as well as advancing to the next round in competitions.

history.meaning: to ascend in court rank or official position
to be promoted (at work); to advance to the next round (in a tournament or show)

morphemes.meaning: to rise, ascend, go up in rank

晋升.notes: In talent shows and television production (*幕后之王*), 晋升 (alongside 晋级, 'advance to the next stage') is constantly used both for corporate promotions (晋升为总监, 'promoted to director') and contestants moving up in rankings. More formal than 升职 ('get a promotion').

rootFamily.gloss: to advance to the next round/level (in competitions or ranks)
to get promoted at work (colloquial VO compound)

晕倒.etymology: A resultative verb compound (动补结构) formed from 晕 (trad. 暈, yūn, originally yùn 'solar or lunar halo', extended in medical and vernacular Chinese to 'dizzy, giddy, to lose consciousness' as one's vision blurs like a halo) and the resultative complement 倒 (dǎo, 'to fall down, topple, collapse'). Together they mean 'to become dizzy/unconscious and collapse to the ground'.

history.meaning: halo around the sun or moon; dizziness, vertigo, blurring of vision
to faint and fall down, pass out, collapse from exhaustion or shock

morphemes.meaning: to be dizzy, giddy; to faint, pass out (yūn)

晕倒.notes: Pronunciation alert: 晕 is a polyphone (多音字)—pronounced first tone yūn when meaning 'to faint, pass out, feel dizzy immediately' (晕倒, 头晕), but fourth tone yùn in compounds referring to halos, motion sickness, or lingering vertigo (晕车 'carsick', 日晕 'solar halo', 眩晕 'vertigo'). In internet slang, 晕倒 (or just 晕) is used like 'I'm floored / fainting from disbelief'.

晕开.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 晕开. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 晕开 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 晕开 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 晕开 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 晕开. The etymology of 晕开 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 晕开
middle form of 晕开
modern form of 晕开

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 晕开

晚.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining 日 ('sun/day') + 免 (miǎn/wǎn phonetic, 'draw away'): 'the sun drawing down at the end of the day -> evening, night; late (opposite of 早 'early'); junior/later'.

history.meaning: sunset/dusk -> evening, night; late

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 晚 (via 萌典)

晚上.etymology: Temporal noun combining 晚 ('evening, night') + nominal locative/temporal suffix 上 (neutral tone shang): 'in the evening, at night'.

history.meaning: evening; night
