sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 晚上 (via 萌典)

晚上好.etymology: Polite evening salutation formed on the pattern of 早上好 ('good morning'), combining 晚上 ('evening', from 晚 'late sun setting' + 上) + 好 ('good; well'). Used warmly when welcoming guests or audiences to an evening gathering.

history.meaning: good evening

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 晚上好

晚安.etymology: Polite bedtime/parting greeting combining 晚 ('evening, night') + 安 ('peace, peaceful rest'): 'Good night!'.

history.meaning: evening peace = Good night!

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 晚安 (via 萌典)

晚茶.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 晚 ('evening; late-season') + 茶 ('tea'): 'evening tea (and dim sum snacks served in the evening); late-harvest tea'.

history.meaning: evening tea; late-season tea

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 晚茶 (via 萌典)

晚饭.etymology: Everyday compound noun of 晚 ('evening') + 饭 (飯, 'cooked rice, meal'): 'dinner, supper, evening meal'.

history.meaning: evening meal; dinner; supper

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 晚饭 (via 萌典)

普通.etymology: A coordinative compound from 普 (pǔ, 'universal, widespread, everywhere under the sun') and 通 (tōng, 'to pass through, reach everywhere, be common to all'). Attested in Classical and Medieval Buddhist texts (e.g., Lotus Sutra translations and Song histories) in the literal sense of 'universally reaching, shared across all places without restriction'. From 'universally shared / common to all', the meaning naturally evolved in modern East Asian languages to 'common, ordinary, average, unexceptional'.

history.meaning: universally penetrating, shared in common across all things or regions
ordinary, common, average, regular (as opposed to special or elite)

morphemes.meaning: to pass through, connect, be common to all

普通.notes: In 普通话 ('Mandarin / Standard Chinese', literally 'the commonly shared speech across the nation'), 普通 retains its older sense of 'universally shared/general', whereas in 普通人 ('ordinary person') it means 'average, unremarkable'.

rootFamily.gloss: to popularize, make universal; universal education/access

晴天.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 晴 ('clear, cloudless sky after rain', sun 日 + 青 'clear blue') + 天 ('sky, day, weather'): 'sunny day, clear day, fair weather'. Attested since Tang poetry.

history.meaning: clear, sunny sky; sunny day

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 晴天 (via 萌典)

晴朗.etymology: Coordinative adjective compound of 晴 ('clear and sunny', sun 日 + 青) + 朗 ('bright and clear', 良 + 月 'bright moonlight'): '(of the sky or weather) clear and bright, sunny and cloudless'.

history.stage: Classical & Tang–Song Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: clear, bright, and cloudless

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 晴朗 (via 萌典)

晶晶.etymology: A monosyllabic character reduplication (叠字) of 晶 (jīng, 'bright, sparkling, crystal-clear'). The character 晶 is an ancient graphic triplication (品字形会意字) of 日 (rì, 'sun'), originally depicting the glittering light of stars or sunbeams (explained in the Shuowen Jiezi / 說文解字 as 精光也 'pure essence of light'). Reduplicated as 晶晶, it vividly evokes twinkling, glistening, or sparkling light, and also frequently appears as a feminine given name in Chinese.

history.meaning: pure brilliance of stars/sunlight; rock crystal (水晶)
sparkling, glittering, gleaming; common Chinese given name (Jingjing)

morphemes.meaning: bright, luminous, crystal-clear (tripled sun radical 日)

晶晶.notes: In everyday Mandarin, 晶晶 is most commonly attached after the adjective 亮 ('bright') to form the ABB vivid adjective 亮晶晶 (liàngjīngjīng, 'shiny and sparkling, twinkling', e.g., 亮晶晶的眼睛 'sparkling eyes'), and is also a recurring character name in *幕后之王*.

cognates.meaning: intelligence quotient (IQ, formal term alongside知能指数)
cognates.word: 知能指数 (chinō shisū) / 智商

智商.etymology: A 20th-century compound abbreviation (缩略词) of 智力商数 (zhìlì shāngshù), calqued directly from English 'intelligence quotient' (IQ, itself coined from German Intelligenzquotient by psychologist William Stern in 1912). It combines 智 (zhì, 'wisdom, intellect', short for 智力 'intelligence') + 商 (shāng, 'mathematical quotient', originally the Shang dynasty and 'merchant/trade', extended in traditional Chinese mathematics to 'to reckon/divide' and thus 'quotient', 商数).

history.form: 智力商數 (calque of Intelligence Quotient)
history.meaning: psychometric ratio of mental age to chronological age multiplied by 100
IQ; colloquial metonym for intelligence, wits, or common sense

morphemes.meaning: quotient (short for 商数, result of division)

智商.notes: Extremely productive in modern Chinese slang and media: served as the model for 情商 ('EQ / emotional intelligence'), 财商 ('financial intelligence'), and viral expressions like 智商税 ('IQ tax'—money wasted on gullible scams or overhyped products) and 智商在线 ('having one's wits about one / acting smart').

rootFamily.gloss: IQ tax (slang for gullible consumer spending)

晾架.etymology: Compound noun of 晾 ('air-dry or cool in the open air', sun/air radical 日 + phonetic 京 *jīng*) + 架 ('supporting frame or rack', 加 + 木 'wood'). In a bakery kitchen, it denotes the raised wire rack that lets air circulate beneath warm loaves and tart shells so their crusts stay crisp.

morphemes.meaning: cool or dry in circulating air

history.meaning: cooling rack; drying rack

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 晾架

暂且.etymology: A coordinative compound of two temporal adverbs: 暂 (trad. 暫, zàn, 'for a short time, briefly, temporarily', from 斩 'to cut short' + 日 'time/sun') and 且 (qiě, 'for the time being, tentatively, just for now' in Classical Chinese). Already combined in Tang–Song poetry and vernacular narratives (e.g., Bai Juyi's poetry and Water Margin / 水滸傳), 暂且 expresses a deliberate decision to set something aside or adopt a provisional measure 'for the time being'.

history.meaning: briefly for the moment, tentatively for now (in Tang poetry and Song–Yuan vernacular)
for the time being, provisionally for now (before taking further action)

morphemes.meaning: temporarily, briefly, for a short time
for the time being, tentatively, for now

暂且.notes: Nuance vs. 暂时: 暂且 is strictly an adverb used before intentional verbs to mean 'let's provisionally do X (or leave X aside) for now' (e.g., 这事暂且不提, 'let's leave this matter aside for now'), whereas 暂时 can modify non-volitional states, adjectives, or nouns (暂时的困难, 'temporary difficulties').

rootFamily.gloss: for the time being, tentatively (literary synonym)

cognates.meaning: short time, a little while (usually read shibaraku)
temporary, provisional, for the time being

暂时.etymology: A modifier-head temporal compound composed of 暂 (trad. 暫, zàn, 'brief, short-lived, temporary', from 斬 'cut short' + 日 'sun/day') and 时 (trad. 時, shí, 'time, period'). In Classical and Middle Chinese, 暫時 meant 'a brief moment, an instant' (a sense preserved in Korean 잠시 jamsi 'for a moment' and Japanese 暫時 zanji). In Mandarin, it shifted from 'a brief instant' to 'temporarily, provisionally, for the present period (subject to future change)'.

history.meaning: a brief moment, a short span of time
temporarily, for the time being; provisional, temporary (non-predicate adjective)

暂时.notes: Watch out for the Korean/Japanese false friend: Korean 잠시만요 (暫時-) means 'just a moment / excuse me', whereas Mandarin 暂时 means 'temporarily / for the time being (until things change)', not 'wait a second' (which is 稍等 or 等一下).

rootFamily.gloss: to suspend, pause; timeout (in sports/media playback)

暖.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 日 ('warming sun', historically also written 煖 with 火 'fire') + 爰 (yuán/nuǎn phonetic): 'warm, genial (of weather, sunlight, or feelings); warm up'.

history.stage: Old & Classical Chinese (Mencius, Chuci) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: warm (from fire or sun); warm up

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 暖 (via 萌典)

暖和.etymology: Coordinative adjective and verb compound of 暖 ('warm') + 和 ('mild, gentle', pronounced neutral tone huo in this word): 'nice and warm, pleasantly warm; warm up'.

history.meaning: warm and mild (of spring weather)
pleasantly warm; warm up

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 暖和 (via 萌典)

暖暖.etymology: Vivid AA-reduplication of the adjective 暖 ('warm'): 'cosily warm, softly warm' (first attested in Laozi's 暧暧内含光 / 暖暖).

history.meaning: gently and cosily warm

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 暖暖 (via 萌典)

暖风.etymology: Modifier-head compound from 暖 ('warm; genial', sun 日 + phonetic 爰) + 风 (simplified from 風, 'wind; breeze'). Celebrated in Song-dynasty poetry (most famously Lin Sheng's 暖風熏得遊人醉 'the warm breeze lulls sightseers into drunkenness') and used today for both spring breezes and warm air blown from a heater or oven.

history.meaning: warm spring breeze
warm breeze; warm air current

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 暖风

暗.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 日 ('sun/light') + 音 (yīn/àn phonetic): 'lack of sunlight -> dark, dim, gloomy (opposite of 明/亮); hidden, secret, in the dark'.

history.stage: Old & Classical Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: dim; dark; secret; hidden

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 暗 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: hinting, implying (related compound 暗示 anji)

暗指.etymology: A modifier-head verb compound formed from the adverbial modifier 暗 (àn, 'dark, hidden, in secret, covertly', composed of 日 'sun' + 音 'sound', originally 'obscured from sunlight') and the head verb 指 (zhǐ, 'to point at, refer to, indicate with a finger'). Literally 'to covertly point at', hence 'to allude to, hint at, or insinuate without naming someone or something explicitly'.

history.meaning: to point to or refer to covertly (adverb + verb construction)
to hint at, imply, insinuate, allude to indirectly

morphemes.meaning: secretly, covertly, implicitly, in the dark
to point at, refer to, indicate

暗指.notes: Nuance vs. 暗示 (ànshì): while both mean 'to hint/imply', 暗指 specifically takes as its object the target person, rival, or issue being covertly referred to (e.g., 这番话暗指竞争对手, 'these remarks covertly pointed at the competitor'), whereas 暗示 means giving a subtle cue or psychological suggestion.

rootFamily.gloss: to hint, drop a hint; psychological suggestion
in secret, covertly, behind the scenes

暗门.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 暗 ('hidden, concealed, secret') + 门 (門, 'door'): 'hidden door, secret door, concealed doorway set flush with a wall'.

history.meaning: secret door; concealed door

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 暗门 (via 萌典)

暴躁.etymology: A coordinative adjective compound combining 暴 (bào, 'violent, sudden, fierce, scorching', originally depicting hands spreading grain out under the hot sun) and 躁 (zào, 'impetuous, restless, quick-tempered', with the foot radical 足 depicting stamping or pacing restlessly in agitation). Already paired in Warring States and Han texts (e.g., Xunzi / 荀子 and Book of the Later Han / 後漢書) to describe an explosive, volatile, and impatient temperament.

history.meaning: violent and impetuous in conduct; lacking composure and restraint
irritable, hot-tempered, explosive, easily angered

暴躁.notes: Orthographic trap: never confuse 躁 (zào, 'restless/impatient', with the foot radical 足, as in 暴躁, 急躁) with 燥 (zào, 'dry/parched', with the fire radical 火, as in 干燥 'dry', 口干舌燥) or 噪 (zào, 'chirping/noise', with the mouth radical 口, as in 噪音 'noise'). Collocates closely with 脾气 (脾气暴躁, 'have a fiery/explosive temper').

rootFamily.gloss: to fly into a thundering rage (idiom)

暴雨.etymology: A modifier-head noun compound formed from 暴 (bào, 'sudden, violent, fierce') modifying 雨 (yǔ, 'rain'). Attested in Classical Chinese philosophical and meteorological texts (such as the Laozi / 老子 Chapter 23: 飄風不終朝，驟雨不終日 and Lüshi Chunqiu / 呂氏春秋: 疾風暴雨), where 暴雨 denoted a sudden, violent cloudburst. In modern meteorology and everyday Mandarin, it is the standard term for a torrential rainstorm (officially >= 50 mm of rainfall in 24 hours).

history.meaning: sudden, violent downpour of rain
torrential rain, rainstorm; meteorological severe rain warning category

暴雨.notes: Frequently appears in weather warnings (暴雨预警) and in the classic four-character idiom 狂风暴雨 ('violent wind and torrential rain'), which is also used metaphorically in media dramas for a fierce crisis or public backlash.

rootFamily.gloss: violent storm, hurricane-force wind and rain (also metaphorical crisis)

暴风雨.etymology: Three-character weather compound combining 暴 ('sudden, fierce, violent', 日 'scorching sun' + 出 + 廾 + 米) + 风雨 ('wind and rain'): 'rainstorm, tempest, storm' (both meteorological and figurative).

history.meaning: violent wind and rain; rainstorm; tempest

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 暴风雨 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: photographic exposure (kanji: 露光 rokō; 曝 is used in 曝露 bakuro 'exposure')

曝光.etymology: Originally a verb-object compound from 曝 (pù or bào, 'to sun, expose to sunlight', which adds an extra 日 'sun' radical to 暴, the original graph for drying grain under the sun) + 光 (guāng, 'light'). Coined in modern photography as a calque of English 'exposure' (exposing photosensitive film to light), it rapidly expanded into journalism, entertainment, and PR to mean 'to expose a scandal/secret to the public eye' or 'to gain media publicity'.

history.meaning: photographic exposure: exposing light-sensitive film or plates to light
to expose (a scandal or secret) to the public; media exposure/publicity

morphemes.meaning: to expose to the sun/light, lay bare (pù / bào)

曝光.notes: Pronunciation & register split: in Mainland China, pùguāng is traditionally prescribed for technical photographic exposure, while bàoguāng has become the overwhelmingly dominant pronunciation (and was officially recognized in modern dictionaries) for media/publicity exposure and scandal revelations (e.g., 恋情曝光 'a celebrity romance is exposed'). In Taiwan, pùguāng is used for both senses.

rootFamily.gloss: to expose to scorching sunlight (pùshài / bàoshài)

曝光率.etymology: A three-character modifier-head noun compound formed by suffixing 率 (lǜ, 'rate, ratio, proportion') to 曝光 (bàoguāng / pùguāng, 'media exposure, public visibility'). Developed in late 20th-century advertising, television, and celebrity management to quantify how frequently a celebrity, brand, or program appears before the public across media channels.

history.meaning: rate or frequency of media appearances and public visibility

morphemes.meaning: to expose to light/public view; media publicity (曝 + 光)

曝光率.notes: Central showbiz metric in *幕后之王*: producers and talent agents constantly strategize to 提高曝光率 ('boost media exposure rate') or 保持曝光率 ('maintain public visibility') for artists and variety shows; closely parallel to 收视率 ('TV viewership ratings') and 点击率 ('click-through rate').

rootFamily.gloss: to expose to the public; photographic/media exposure

曲子.etymology: Colloquial noun formed from 曲 (read qǔ in the third tone, 'melody, tune, song, verse lyric', extended from 曲 qū 'bent, winding' -> 'winding melodic turns of a tune') + nominal suffix 子 (neutral tone zi): 'tune, melody, piece of music'.

history.stage: Tang–Song–Yuan music & drama to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: melody; tune; musical piece

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 曲子 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: musical selection, song title, program item, track
musical piece title, repertoire, program list

曲目.etymology: A modifier-head noun compound combining 曲 (qǔ, 'melody, tune, song, musical piece', originally qū 'bent, winding', extended to the winding modulations of a melody) and 目 (mù, 'eye; item, entry, catalog list'). Patterned on traditional Chinese bibliographic compounds like 书目 ('book catalog') and 剧目 ('theatrical repertoire'), 曲目 denotes either a catalog/repertoire of musical pieces or an individual song/track on a concert or show program.

history.meaning: catalog or list of musical and operatic pieces
musical repertoire, setlist, album tracklist, or a specific musical item/song on a program

曲目.notes: Pronunciation alert: 曲 is pronounced third tone qǔ whenever it relates to music, songs, or drama (曲目 qǔmù, 歌曲 gēqǔ, 作曲 zuòqǔ), and first tone qū when it means 'bent, curved, winding' (曲线 qūxiàn, 弯曲 wānqū). In music reality shows (*幕后之王*), 参赛曲目 means 'competition song selection' and 保留曲目 means 'signature/standby repertoire piece'.

曲线.etymology: A modifier-head noun compound formed from 曲 (qū, 'bent, curved, crooked', originally depicting a woven bamboo basket or bent carpenter's square, contrasted with 直 zhí 'straight') and 线 (trad. 線/綫, xiàn, 'thread, line'). Standardized in modern East Asian geometry and science (alongside Japanese 曲線 kyokusen) as the exact counterpart to 直线 ('straight line'), and extended to statistical chart curves (e.g., ratings curves) and bodily contours.

history.meaning: a curved line (as opposed to 直線, a straight line) in geometry and draughtsmanship
geometric curve; chart/trend line (e.g., 收视曲线); graceful body contours; indirect ('roundabout') approach

曲线.notes: Contrast 曲线 (qūxiàn, first tone qū 'curved') with 曲目 (qǔmù, third tone qǔ 'melody'). In television production (*幕后之王*), 收视率曲线 ('viewership ratings curve') tracks minute-by-minute audience retention, while colloquially 曲线救国 ('save the nation via an indirect curve') means achieving a goal through a clever, roundabout strategy.

更.etymology: Ancient character combining 丙 + 攵 ('strike/alter'): read gēng as a verb/noun meaning 'change, replace, alternate; night-watch period (one of the five two-hour night watches 五更 struck on a drum/gong)'; read gèng as Mandarin's primary comparative degree adverb meaning 'even more, still more, further'.

history.meaning: change, alternate, night watch (gēng); even more, further (gèng)
more; even more; still more

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 更 (via 萌典)

更为严重.etymology: A formal four-character comparative phrase (四字格) composed of the literary disyllabic degree adverb 更为 (gèngwéi, 'even more', formed from 更 gèng 'further, even more' + the classical copular/adverbial formative 为 wéi) modifying the coordinative adjective 严重 (trad. 嚴重, yánzhòng, 'grave, severe, serious', from 严 'strict, stern, acute' + 重 'heavy, weighty'). Literally 'to be even more grave and weighty'.

history.meaning: to be even more strict, weighty, or grave (literary comparative construction)
even more severe, far more serious or critical

morphemes.meaning: literary adverbial formative attached to degree adverbs (wéi)
severe, grave, critical, serious (严 + 重)

更为严重.notes: In formal written and broadcast Mandarin, attaching 为 (wéi) to monosyllabic degree adverbs creates a rhythmic two-syllable modifier that pairs naturally with two-syllable adjectives to form balanced four-character phrases: 更为严重 ('even more severe'), 尤为重要 ('especially important'), 极为罕见 ('extremely rare'), 最为关键 ('most crucial').

rootFamily.gloss: even more (colloquial/neutral counterpart of 更为)

更改.etymology: A synonym-coordinative verb compound uniting 更 (gēng, first tone, 'to change, alter, replace', originally depicting a hand striking to alter or renew, also used for the five night watches 五更 as the watchmen changed shifts) and 改 (gǎi, 'to change, correct, revise', depicting a hand holding a rod 攵 to correct a kneeling figure/self 己). Attested since the Qin–Han period (e.g., Shiji / 史記) for altering laws, plans, or names.

history.meaning: to alter, replace, or revise (laws, decrees, calendars, or official arrangements)
to change, modify, revise (plans, schedules, settings, or passwords)

morphemes.meaning: to change, alter, replace (first tone gēng)

更改.notes: Pronunciation alert: 更 is a high-frequency polyphone (多音字)—read first tone gēng when it is a verb meaning 'to change, replace, alternate' (更改 gēnggǎi, 更新 gēngxīn, 更换 gēnghuàn, 变更 biàngēng), and fourth tone gèng when it is an adverb meaning 'even more' (更为严重 gèngwéi yánzhòng, 更好 gènghǎo).

rootFamily.gloss: to revise, amend, edit (a text, script, or plan)

cognates.meaning: renewal, update, regeneration, breaking a record

更新.etymology: Originally a verb-complement / coordinative compound from 更 (gēng, first tone, 'to change, replace') and 新 (xīn, 'new, fresh; to make new'), meaning 'to replace the old and make new, to regenerate'. Attested in Classical Chinese (e.g., Huainanzi / 淮南子 and Book of the Later Han / 後漢書, and the idiom 万象更新 'all things take on a new aspect [in spring]'). In the digital and media era, it became the standard equivalent for English 'to update / refresh' (software, episodes, social media feeds).

history.meaning: to change for the new, rejuvenate, reform, or make a fresh start
to update, upgrade, renew (equipment/ideas); to release a new episode or post (media/software)

morphemes.meaning: to change, replace, alternate (first tone gēng)
new, fresh; to make new, renew

更新.notes: Pronounced gēngxīn (first tone on 更). In streaming television, web novels, and social media (*幕后之王*), 更新 (often abbreviated to 更, as in 日更 'daily update/episode', 停更 'suspend updates', 催更 'urge the creator to drop the next episode') refers to releasing new episodes or content.

rootFamily.gloss: to replace the old with the new (four-character idiom, esp. for tech/equipment)
all things take on a fresh new look (New Year idiom)

cognates.meaning: formerly, once (katsute, written with 嘗/曾)

曾经.etymology: Coordinative disyllabic adverbial compound formed from 曾 (céng, Middle Chinese *dzong, 'already; in the past; once', originally depicting a tiered steamer pot 甑 and loaned for temporal precedence) and 經/经 (jīng, MC *keng, originally 'warp threads of a loom', extended to 'pass through, experience, undergo'). In Classical Chinese, 曾 and 經 functioned independently as preverbal experiential aspect markers; their juxtaposition into 曾經 crystallized during the Six Dynasties and Tang vernacular to reinforce the experiential past ('having passed through before').

history.meaning: monosyllabic adverbs 'once before' (曾) and 'to pass through, undergo' (經)
to have experienced or undergone in the past; once formerly
once, formerly (preverbal experiential marker)

morphemes.meaning: to pass through, experience (lit. warp threads)

曾经.notes: Unlike the verbal suffix 过 (guò), 曾经 precedes the verb (often paired with 过 as 曾经…过) and emphasizes that a past state or action no longer holds true in the present.

rootFamily.gloss: as if one had experienced it before; déjà vu

替.etymology: Ideogram combining two standing figures (夫/立) side by side above 日/曰: originally 'one replacing or supplanting another', hence the verb 'replace, substitute for, take the place of' and the benefactive preposition 'for, on behalf of'.

history.meaning: replace; supersede; decline
take the place of; for / on behalf of

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 替 (via 萌典)

cognates.word: 代替 (だいたい) / 替代

cognates.meaning: substitution, replacement (usually ordered 대체 代替)

替代.etymology: Coordinative verbal compound uniting 替 (tì, Middle Chinese *thejH, 'to decline, supersede, replace', graphically depicting two figures 竝/立 over 曰/白 suggesting one displacing another) and 代 (dài, MC *dojH, 'to alternate, take the place of; generation, era', from person 亻 and stake 弋). In Classical Chinese, 替 meant 'to abolish or supplant' (as in 興替 'rise and fall') while 代 meant 'to succeed in turn'; their combination 替代 unites both synonymous roots into a transitive verb meaning 'to take the place of, supersede'.

history.meaning: 替 'to decline, discard, supplant' and 代 'to alternate, succeed'
to take the place of another person in office or duty; to substitute
to replace, substitute for; alternative (adj./noun modifier)

morphemes.meaning: to replace, supersede, act on behalf of

替代.notes: Often used in formal, technical, and industry contexts (e.g., 不可替代 'irreplaceable', 替代方案 'alternative plan'), whereas 代替 focuses more on acting in place of someone or using X instead of Y.

rootFamily.gloss: to replace, substitute for (often temporary or functional)

最.etymology: Ideogram combining 曰/冃 ('cap/cover') + 取 ('take by the ear, seize first prize in battle'): originally 'take the foremost/top share', grammaticalized since Han texts into Chinese's primary superlative degree adverb 'most, -est'.

history.meaning: foremost; first in merit; gather
superlative adverb 'most, -est'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 最 (via 萌典)

最严.etymology: Modifier-head superlative compound composed of the superlative prefix 最 (zuì, Middle Chinese *dzwajH, originally 'to amass, capture the top military merit', from 曰/冃 'cap' + 取 'take', hence 'foremost, most') and 嚴/严 (yán, MC *ngjaem, 'urgent, stern, strict, majestic', phonosemantic with 吅 'clamor/stern command' and phonetic 敢). Commonly used in modern administrative and media headlines to describe regulatory crackdowns or rigorous production standards.

history.meaning: urgent, stern, awe-inspiring, tightly guarded
most strict, most rigorous, tightest (of laws, standards, or security)

最严.notes: A staple of Chinese news and entertainment industry headlines (e.g., 史上最严限薪令 'the strictest salary cap in history'), functioning both predicatively and as a compact two-character attributive modifier.

rootFamily.gloss: tight,严密; closely sealed or organized

cognates.word: 最低価 (さいていか) / 最低価格

最低价.etymology: Trimorphemic modifier-head nominal compound structured as [[最 + 低] + 价]: superlative prefix 最 (zuì, 'most'), adjectival root 低 (dī, Middle Chinese *tej, 'low, to bow down', from 亻 'person' + 氐 'bottom, foundation'), and head noun 價/价 (jià, MC *kaeH, 'price, value', derived from 賈 'merchant, trade'). Literally 'the lowest price', widely used in commerce, bidding, and licensing negotiations.

history.meaning: low price, cheap valuation in market trade

history.form: 最低價 / 最低价 (Modern Mandarin)
history.meaning: lowest price, floor price, reserve price in bidding

最低价.notes: In media licensing and commercial negotiations, 最低价 can mean either the 'rock-bottom price' a seller can accept (底价) or the 'lowest price on the market'.

rootFamily.gloss: base price, reserve price, floor price

最佳.etymology: Modifier-head superlative compound combining the superlative prefix 最 (zuì, Middle Chinese *dzwajH, 'foremost, most') with the classical aesthetic adjective 佳 (jiā, MC *kwae, 'fine, beautiful, auspicious, excellent', composed of 亻 'person' and phonetic 圭 *kwej 'jade tablet'). Preserves the elevated literary register of 佳, making 最佳 the standard formal term for 'optimal' or 'Best [Award Category]'.

history.meaning: beautiful, fine, auspicious, distinguished
finest, optimal, best (in quality, timing, or award titles)

最佳.notes: Unlike 最好 (colloquial 'best'), 最佳 is an attributive adjective used before nouns in formal contexts and showbiz awards (e.g., 最佳导演 'Best Director', 最佳状态 'peak condition').

rootFamily.gloss: fine work, masterpiece (of art or literature)
good news, auspicious tidings (esp. award or wedding)

最后.etymology: Superlative temporal/spatial noun and adjective combining 最 ('most, -est') + 后 (後, 'after, behind, last'): 'the very last, final; finally, in the end, at last'.

history.stage: Han Classical Chinese (Shiji) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: the very last; final; finally

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 最后 (via 萌典)

最多.etymology: Superlative quantifier and adverb combining 最 ('most') + 多 ('many, much'): 'the most (in quantity); at most, at the outside'.

history.meaning: the largest amount; at most

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 最多 (via 萌典)

最大.etymology: Modifier-head superlative compound formed from the superlative prefix 最 (zuì, Middle Chinese *dzwajH, 'foremost, most', originally 'supreme military merit') and the core stative verb/adjective 大 (dà, MC *dajH / *daH, Old Chinese *lˤats, Oracle Bone Script depicting a frontal standing human figure with arms and legs outstretched to signify 'large, great, vast').

history.meaning: large, great, vast, noble (depicting an outstretched person)
largest, biggest, greatest, maximum

morphemes.meaning: most, supreme, to the highest degree

最大.notes: Frequently combines with abstract nouns in formal and media speech (e.g., 最大限度 'to the maximum extent', 最大看点 'biggest highlight/selling point of a show').

cognates.meaning: fastest (in kanji compounds; native hayai is used colloquially)
cognates.word: 最快 / 最速 (さいそく)

最快.etymology: Modifier-head superlative compound uniting the superlative prefix 最 (zuì, Middle Chinese *dzwajH, 'most') and 快 (kuài, MC *khwaejH, 'pleased, gratifying; sharp; swift', from 忄 'heart' + 夬 'to part, decide resolutely'). Note the classic semantic shift in Chinese history: in Classical Chinese, 快 meant 'cheerful, gratified' (still seen in 快乐, 痛快) and 'sharp', before shifting in Tang–Song vernacular to 'fast, rapid' (displacing Classical 疾 and 速).

history.meaning: pleased, gratified in heart; decisive, brisk
sharp (of blades); fast, rapid, quick
fastest, quickest; at the earliest/soonest

最快.notes: When placed before a time expression (e.g., 最快明天 'tomorrow at the earliest/soonest'), 最快 means 'at the soonest' rather than physical velocity.

rootFamily.gloss: joyful, happy (preserving the classical sense of 快)

最新.etymology: Modifier-head superlative compound formed from the superlative prefix 最 (zuì, Middle Chinese *dzwajH, 'most') and 新 (xīn, MC *sin, Old Chinese *s-tsʰi[n], 'new, fresh, recently harvested/cut', graphically composed of 斤 'axe' cutting wood 榛/辛 'freshly cut timber'). In modern media and broadcasting, 最新 is the standard modifier for breaking news, latest episodes, and up-to-the-minute updates.

history.meaning: freshly cut wood; new, fresh, newly established
newest, latest, most up-to-date

最新.notes: Ubiquitous in media and entertainment collocations such as 最新消息 ('latest/breaking news'), 最新一期 ('the latest episode/issue'), and 最新动态 ('latest updates').

rootFamily.gloss: to update, renew, refresh (e.g. a show episode)

最终.etymology: Modifier-head compound combining the superlative prefix 最 (zuì, Middle Chinese *dzwajH, 'most, extreme') and 終/终 (zhōng, MC *tsyuwng, Old Chinese *tuŋ, 'end, conclusion, completion', originally depicting the knotted end of a skein of silk threads 糸 + 冬, where 冬 itself was the ancient graph for knotted thread ends before being loaned for 'winter'). Functions both as an attributive adjective ('final, ultimate') and a sentence-level adverb ('ultimately, in the end').

history.meaning: knotted end of silk thread; conclusion, end of life or cycle; finally
final, ultimate (attributive); eventually, in the end (adverbial)

morphemes.meaning: end, completion, conclusion (lit. knotted thread end)

最终.notes: More formal and objective than 最后 (zuìhòu): 最终 emphasizes the ultimate outcome after a long process or struggle (e.g., 最终解释权 'right of final interpretation', 最终定稿 'finalized script/draft').

rootFamily.gloss: from beginning to end; always, all along
to terminate, bring to an end, stop
for life, lifelong (lit. until the end of one's body/life)

cognates.meaning: at the very least, minimum (jyutping: zeoi3 kei2 maa5)

最起码.etymology: Trimorphemic compound formed from the superlative prefix 最 (zuì, 'most') and 起碼/起码 (qǐmǎ, 'minimum, starting threshold'). 起码 originated in late imperial commercial and gaming slang: 起 ('to start, raise') + 码 ('counting rods or numeral tally counters', from 碼 'agate stone used as counter/weight'), referring to the minimum starting wager or initial tally required to open a transaction, hence 'at the bare minimum, at the very least'.

history.meaning: to begin tallying counters; minimum starting stake or batch size in trade

history.form: 最起碼 / 最起码 (Modern Mandarin)
history.meaning: at the very least, bare minimum (adverbial and attributive)

最起码.notes: Functions both as a sentence adverb ('at the very least, [clause]') and as an attributive modifier with 的 (e.g., 最起码的尊重 'the most basic/bare-minimum respect').

最近.etymology: Modifier-head superlative compound formed from the superlative prefix 最 (zuì, Middle Chinese *dzwajH, 'most') and 近 (jìn, MC *gjonX / *gjonH, Old Chinese *N-kərʔ, 'near, close in space or time', composed of 辶 'walking/road' + phonetic 斤). Originally spatial ('nearest, closest in distance'), its extension to temporal proximity ('most recent; lately, recently') became dominant in modern Mandarin and Sino-Japanese.

history.meaning: nearest in spatial distance or kinship; most closely approximating
recently, lately (past or near future); nearest (in space)

最近.notes: In Mandarin, temporal 最近 can refer not only to the recent past ('lately') but also to the immediate future when paired with upcoming plans (e.g., 我最近要出差 'I will be going on a business trip in the next few days').

rootFamily.gloss: in the near future, recently; near term

月.etymology: Foundational pictograph (象形字) attested from Shang oracle bones depicting a crescent moon: 'the moon; month (originally the lunar synodic month of ~29.5 days, now each of the 12 calendar months); monthly'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: crescent moon pictograph = moon, month

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 月 (via 萌典)

月底.etymology: Temporal compound of 月 ('month') + 底 ('bottom, end'): 'the end of the month'.

history.meaning: end of the month

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 月底 (via 萌典)

有.etymology: Verb of possession ('have') and existence ('there is, there are'), attested from Shang oracle bones and bronze inscriptions through Classical and modern Mandarin. Unlike every other Mandarin verb, 有 is always negated with 没 (没有), never 不.

history.meaning: have; possess; there is

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 有 (via 萌典)

有一天.etymology: Temporal phrase built from existential verb 有 ('there is / there was') + 一 ('one', pronounced yì by tone sandhi before 1st-tone tiān) + 天 ('day'). Used both to introduce a past narrative ('one day...') and in conditional clauses for a hypothetical future day ('if one day / if ever...').

history.meaning: one day (past or future)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 有一天

cognates.meaning: have a, there is a (jau5 go3)

有个.etymology: Verb-classifier contraction of 有一个 (yǒu yī gè), uniting the existential/possessive verb 有 (yǒu, Middle Chinese *hjuwX, Old Chinese *ɢʷəʔ, Oracle Bone and Bronze graphs depicting a hand 又 holding meat 月/肉, hence 'to hold, possess, exist') and the general classifier 個/个 (gè, MC *kaH, originally 'bamboo stalk' 竹 + 固, generalized in vernacular Chinese as the universal individual classifier). In spoken Mandarin, unstressed numeral 一 (yī) regularly elides between 有 and a classifier.

history.meaning: to possess, hold; there exists (hand holding meat)
to have one [item/person]; there is a certain... (with elision of 一)
have a; there is a (introducing an indefinite singular noun)

morphemes.meaning: general individual classifier (contracted from 一个 'one [unit]')

有个.notes: Extremely frequent in conversational Mandarin to introduce a new, indefinite topic or story (e.g., 我有个想法 'I have an idea', 有个人找你 'There is someone looking for you').

cognates.meaning: emergency, contingency (yusa, e.g. 유사시 有事時)

有事.etymology: Verb-object compound combining the existential/possessive verb 有 (yǒu, Middle Chinese *hjuwX, 'to have; there is') and 事 (shì, MC *dzriH, Old Chinese *m-s-rəʔ-s, Bronze script depicting a hand 又 holding up a hunting/official standard or brush史, meaning 'official business, affair, matter, incident'). In Classical Chinese, 有事 meant 'to have state business, sacrifice, or military conflict'; in modern vernacular, it means 'to be busy with something' or 'to have a problem/trouble'.

history.meaning: to perform state rituals/sacrifices; to have military hostilities or state affairs
to have matters to attend to (be busy); to have something wrong/an incident

有事.notes: Context determines whether 有事 is neutral ('busy / have something to discuss', e.g., 你找我有事吗？ 'Did you need me for something?') or grave ('in trouble / an accident happened', contrasting with 没事 'it's fine / nothing's wrong').

rootFamily.gloss: nothing wrong, never mind; free/not busy

有些.etymology: Compound determiner and degree adverb formed from the existential verb 有 (yǒu, Middle Chinese *hjuwX, 'to have; there is') and the plural/uncountable quantifier 些 (xiē, MC *sjae, originally a Chu dialect sentence-final modal particle in the *Chuci* 楚辭 before grammaticalizing in Tang–Song vernacular as an indefinite quantifier meaning 'a small amount, a few, some', often contracted from 有一些).

history.meaning: sentence-final incantatory particle in Chu poetry (e.g. 招魂)
a little bit, some, a few (indefinite quantifier and degree adverb)
some (determiner before nouns); somewhat, rather (adverb before stative verbs)

morphemes.meaning: some, a few, a little bit (indefinite plural/mass measure)

有些.notes: Functions both as a determiner before nouns (有些人 'some people') and as a slightly more formal degree adverb than 有点儿 before adjectives (有些担心 'somewhat worried').

cognates.meaning: manned, crewed (yūjin, e.g. 有人飛行 manned flight)

有人.etymology: Existential verb-object compound uniting 有 (yǒu, Middle Chinese *hjuwX, 'there is, to have') and 人 (rén, MC *nyin, Old Chinese *ni[ŋ], Oracle Bone pictograph of a side-profile standing human figure). In Mandarin syntax, 有人 functions both as an indefinite pronoun ('someone, somebody') and as an existential predicate ('there is someone present / occupied'). In technical compounds, it contrasts with 无人 ('unmanned').

history.meaning: there is a person; someone among the people
someone, somebody (indefinite pronoun); occupied/taken (of a seat or room)

有人.notes: On a knock at a restroom door or pointing to a seat, saying 有人 simply means 'Occupied!' or 'Taken!'.

rootFamily.gloss: no one; unmanned, automated (e.g. 无人机 drone)
talent, talented person (crucial in media/agency recruiting)

cognates.meaning: what advice/instructions do you have for me? (jau5 ho4 zi2 gaau3)

有何指教.etymology: Four-character semi-literary polite/idiomatic expression structured as [有 + 何 + 指教]: existential verb 有 ('to have'), Classical interrogative pronoun 何 (hé, Middle Chinese *ha, 'what'), and deferential verb-object/coordinative noun 指教 (zhǐjiào, from 指 'to point out with the finger' + 教 'to instruct, teach'). Literally 'What pointing-out and instruction do you have [for me]?', originating in epistolary and courteous Mandarin etiquette.

history.meaning: to point out flaws and offer instruction or guidance

history.form: 有何指教 (Late Imperial & Modern Mandarin)
history.meaning: what advice or instructions do you have for me? (courteous or guarded inquiry)

有何指教.notes: While originally a humble request for guidance ('How may you enlighten me?'), in modern workplace and drama dialogue (such as *Behind the Scenes*) it is often used with cool, polite distance or irony when a rival visits unexpectedly ('What can I do for you?').

rootFamily.gloss: to give advice or comments; please advise (polite)
to point out and guide, give directions/coaching

cognates.meaning: what is your honorable business here? (jau5 ho4 gwai3 gon3)

有何贵干.etymology: Four-character honorific/semi-literary formula structured as [有 + 何 + 贵 + 干]: existential verb 有 ('to have'), Classical interrogative pronoun 何 (hé, 'what'), honorific prefix 貴/贵 (guì, Middle Chinese *kjwijH, 'precious, noble, honorable [your]', originally depicting two hands 廾 holding earth/basket 臾 with cowrie shell 貝), and 幹/干 (gàn, MC *kanH, 'trunk; capability; business, affair to manage'). Literally 'What honorable business do you have?'

history.meaning: your honorable business or errand (polite deferential inquiry)

history.form: 有何貴幹 / 有何贵干 (Modern Mandarin)
history.meaning: what brings you here? what is your business? (formal or ironic)

morphemes.meaning: precious, noble, your honorable (deferential second-person modifier)
business, affair, matter to handle (trad. 幹)

有何贵干.notes: Note that 干 here represents traditional 幹 (gàn, 'business, work to do'), not 干 (gān). In modern conversation, asking 有何贵干 often sounds either old-fashionedly courteous or playfully/coldly sarcastic ('To what do I owe the pleasure?').

rootFamily.gloss: your honorable surname (polite inquiry: 免贵姓…)
capable, competent in handling work (trad. 能幹)
core staff, backbone personnel (trad. 骨幹)

cognates.word: 有關 / 有関 (ゆうかん)

cognates.meaning: related, relevant (yugwan, e.g. 유관 기관 related agencies)

有关.etymology: Verb-object compound formed from 有 (yǒu, Middle Chinese *hjuwX, 'to have') and 關/关 (guān, MC *kwaen, Old Chinese *kˤron, 'wooden crossbar of a gate; mountain pass; connection, bearing', depicting門 'gate' with thread/bolt 丗/絲 drawn across). From the physical crossbar locking two gate doors together evolved the sense of 'interlocking connection, relevance, concern', yielding 有关 ('to have a connection/bearing on').

history.meaning: wooden gate bolt; frontier pass; to bolt shut; to interconnect or involve

history.form: 有關 / 有关 (Literary & Modern Mandarin)
history.meaning: to have a bearing on, be related to (verb); relevant, concerned (attributive)

有关.notes: Operates in two distinct syntactic frames: as a predicate with 与/跟/和 (与…有关 'be related to...') and as a direct pre-nominal attributive without 的 (有关部门 'the relevant departments', 有关人员 'personnel concerned').

rootFamily.gloss: unrelated, having nothing to do with (与…无关)

有力.etymology: Verb-object compound used as an adjective, combining 有 ('have, possess') + 力 ('strength, force, power'): 'strong, forceful, powerful, vigorous'. Attested since the Shijing.

history.meaning: possessing strength; strong; forceful; powerful

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 有力 (via 萌典)

有劲.etymology: Verb-object adjectival compound from 有 ('have; possess') + 劲 (simplified from 勁, strength 力 + phonetic 巠 'muscular strength; vigour; spirit'). Literally 'possessing strength', it describes strong hands, energetic music or movement, or gripping activities.

history.meaning: strong; vigorous; spirited
strong; energetic; forceful

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 有劲

cognates.meaning: preparedness prevents disaster (yūbi-mukan, 備えあれば憂いなし)
cognates.word: 有備無患 (ゆうびむかん)
hữu bị vô hoạn (有備無患)

有备无患.etymology: Classical four-character idiom (chengyu) with parallel conditional VO+VO structure [有備 → 無患], attested in the *Book of Documents* (*Shangshu* 尚書·說命中) and *Zuo Zhuan* (左傳·襄公十一年): '惟事事，乃其有備，有備無患' ('Only by attending to every affair will there be preparedness; where there is preparedness, there is no calamity'). Composed of 有 ('have'), 備/备 (bèi, 'readiness, precaution', originally arrows in a quiver), 無/无 (wú, 'lack, have no'), and 患 (huàn, 'worry, calamity', from 串 'pierced/strung heart' 心).

history.form: 有備無患 (Classical Chinese — Shangshu / Zuo Zhuan)
history.meaning: where there is military and administrative preparedness, there will be no calamity or invasion
preparedness prevents calamity; better safe than sorry

morphemes.meaning: calamity, trouble, anxiety (heart pierced with worry)

有备无患.notes: A high-frequency proverb in crisis PR and live broadcasting management: preparing backup plans (B方案) ensures 有备无患 when live events go wrong.

rootFamily.gloss: to guard against, take precautions against

cognates.meaning: is there an end to this or not? (jau5 jyun4 mou5 jyun4)
cognates.word: 有完沒完 / 有完冇完

有完没完.etymology: Colloquial Northern Mandarin A-not-A rhetorical question idiom structured as [有完 + 没完], pairing positive existential 有 ('to have') and negative existential 没 ('not have') around the verbal/nominal complement 完 (wán, Middle Chinese *hwan, 'whole, intact; to finish, come to an end', from 宀 'roof' + 元 'head/origin'). Literally 'Does this have an end or not?', used as an exasperated rebuke meaning 'Will you ever stop? Enough already!'

history.meaning: endless, never-ending, dragging on interminably
will it never end?! enough already! (exasperated rhetorical question)

有完没完.notes: Strictly conversational and emotionally charged, expressing impatience when someone keeps nagging, arguing, or creating drama (e.g., 你到底有完没完？ 'Are you ever going to stop?!'). Compare the narrative form 没完没了 ('endless, drag on forever').

有幸.etymology: Verb-object / adverbial compound combining 有 (yǒu, Middle Chinese *hjuwX, 'to have') and 幸 (xìng, MC *hengX, Old Chinese *N-qʰˤreŋʔ, originally depicting manacles/shackles 𡴘 and hence 'narrowly escaping punishment or calamity by stroke of luck; good fortune, favor, imperial grace'). In Classical and modern formal Chinese, 有幸 means 'to have the good fortune or privilege to [do something]'.

history.meaning: to be fortunate enough to escape disaster or receive favor (contrasting with 不幸)
to have the good fortune, privilege, or honor to (polite preverbal modifier)

有幸.notes: A staple of polite speeches, interviews, and award shows (e.g., 我很有幸能参与这部作品 'I had the great fortune/privilege of participating in this production').

有意思.etymology: Verb-object adjectival compound formed from 有 (yǒu, 'to have') and the disyllabic noun 意思 (yìsi, 'meaning, thought, interest, appeal'). 意思 itself combines 意 (yì, Middle Chinese *'ijH, 'thought, intention, meaning', from 音 'sound/words' + 心 'heart/mind') and 思 (sī, MC *si, 'to think, ponder, longing', from 囟 'fontanelle/skull' + 心 'heart'). Thus 有意思 literally means 'having thought-content or significance', shifting in vernacular Mandarin to 'interesting, fun, intriguing'.

history.meaning: state of mind, intention, artistic conception or meaning
meaningful, interesting, amusing; having romantic interest in someone

morphemes.meaning: meaning, thought, intention (sound in the heart)
thought, reflection, sentiment (neutral tone in 意思)

有意思.notes: Besides 'interesting/fun', saying 对某人有意思 means 'to have a crush on / be romantically interested in someone', and in sarcastic contexts 你这人真有意思 means 'You're really something (ridiculous/unreasonable)!'.

rootFamily.gloss: meaning, idea; token of appreciation; hint
boring, dull, pointless (lit. having no meaning/interest)
embarrassed; excuse me / sorry to bother you

cognates.meaning: that which one has; reason/means (classical reading yūsho / tokoro ari)
to some extent (in Sino-Korean 4-character phrases, yuso-)

有所.etymology: Classical Chinese syntactic construction combining the existential verb 有 (yǒu, Middle Chinese *hjuwX, 'to have, there is') and the pronominal object-nominalizer 所 (suǒ, MC *srjoX, Old Chinese *s-qʰ<r>aʔ, originally 'sound of chopping wood' 戶 + 斤, extended to 'place, location' and grammaticalized as a relative particle nominalizing the object of the following verb: 'that which [one V-s]'). Thus 有所 + V literally means 'there is that which [one V-s]', yielding 'to V to some extent / in some respect'.

history.meaning: there is something that [subject] V-s; to have a place/object to V
to some extent, somewhat (formal adverbial modifier before disyllabic verbs)

morphemes.meaning: that which, the aspect/extent to which (orig. place)

有所.notes: In modern formal Mandarin, 有所 almost always precedes a two-character verb or verbal noun to form a four-character rhythmic phrase (e.g., 有所改善 'improve to some extent', 有所准备 'be somewhat prepared', 有所保留 'hold back to some degree').

rootFamily.gloss: to have nothing to [rely on/fear/gain] (in 无所畏惧, 一无所有)
the reason why, that by which (hence 'therefore')

cognates.meaning: to grasp, comprehend, have a handle on (haaku)

有把握.etymology: Verb-object phrase formed from 有 (yǒu, 'to have') and the coordinative compound 把握 (bǎwò, 'firm grasp, certainty'). 把握 unites two synonymous hand-action verbs: 把 (bǎ, Middle Chinese *paeX, 'to hold, grip in the hand', from 扌 'hand' + phonetic 巴) and 握 (wò, MC *'aewk, 'to clasp, clench in the palm', from 扌 'hand' + 屋). Literally 'to have a firm grip in one's hand', metaphorically meaning 'to have confidence or assurance of success'.

history.meaning: to grip or clench physically in the hand; a handful
to have a firm grasp of a situation; to be confident or sure of success

morphemes.meaning: to hold, grip, handle (with the hand 扌)
to grasp, clench in the palm; certainty, assurance

有把握.notes: Unlike 自信 (general self-confidence in personality), 有把握 specifically refers to objective confidence about the outcome of a particular task or venture (e.g., 我对这次提案很有把握 'I am very confident about this pitch').

rootFamily.gloss: to grasp, seize (an opportunity); assurance, certainty
to master, have command of, control

cognates.meaning: some days, quite a while (jau5 jat6 zi2)

有日子.etymology: Colloquial Northern Mandarin verb-object temporal idiom combining 有 (yǒu, 'to have, reach an amount of') and 日子 (rìzi, 'days, time, period of days'). 日子 is formed from 日 (rì, Middle Chinese *nyit, Old Chinese *C.nik, solar disc pictograph meaning 'sun, day') plus the nominalizing diminutive suffix 子 (zi, neutral tone, originally 'child'). Literally 'to have [quite a few] days', idiomatic for 'for quite some days now; for a long while'.

history.meaning: a specific date or day; a stretch of days; daily life/livelihood
for quite some days, for a good while (often followed by a negative verb or 了)

morphemes.meaning: noun suffix (neutral tone, forming disyllabic nouns)

有日子.notes: Typically used in colloquial speech with 了 or before 没 + Verb to mean 'for quite a while now' (e.g., 咱们有日子没见了 'We haven't seen each other for quite a while', 他来北京有日子了 'He's been in Beijing for some time now').

cognates.word: 有時 (ゆうじ) / 時有って

有时.etymology: Verb-object temporal adverbial compound formed from the existential verb 有 (yǒu, Middle Chinese *hjuwX, 'there is, to have') and 時/时 (shí, MC *dzyi, Old Chinese *də, 'season, time, hour, occasion', composed of 日 'sun' + phonetic 寺 *s-təʔ, which in Bronze script combines 止 'foot' and 寸 'hand/measure'). Literally 'there are times [when...]', attested since Classical Chinese (e.g. *Analects*, *Mencius*) and lexicalized as the standard adverb 'sometimes, at times'.

history.meaning: there is a time/season for it; at certain times
sometimes, at times, now and then (often alternating as 有时…有时…)

有时.notes: A slightly more compact, written/formal variant of 有时候 (yǒushíhou); frequently appears in correlative pairs 有时…有时… ('sometimes X, sometimes Y').

rootFamily.gloss: always, constantly; Moment, point in time

有时候.etymology: Temporal phrase combining 有 ('there are') + 时候 ('times, occasions'): 'there are times when… -> sometimes, at times, now and then'.

history.meaning: sometimes; at times

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 有时候 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: have or not? is there? (jau5 mou5)
have or not; did [you] or not? (ū-bô)

有没有.etymology: A-not-A affirmative-negative question construction combining the existential/possessive verb 有 (yǒu, Middle Chinese *hjuwX, 'to have; there is') and its negated form 没有 (méiyǒu, with the second syllable 有 elided in the A-not-A frame or viewed as 没 + 有). 没 (méi, MC *mwot, originally 'to dive, submerge in water' 氵 + 𠬛, grammaticalized in Tang–Song vernacular as the negative existential and perfective marker, replacing Classical 無 and 未). Literally 'have or not have'.

history.meaning: existence and non-existence; whether one has or lacks something

history.form: 有沒有 / 有没有 (Early & Modern Mandarin)
history.meaning: do you have or not? is there or not? did [action] happen or not?

morphemes.meaning: not (have); did not (orig. submerge in water)

有没有.notes: Besides asking about possession/existence ('Do you have any?'), influenced by Southern Mandarin, Taiwanese Mandarin, and Cantonese, 有没有 + Verb is widely used in modern showbiz and daily speech to ask 'Have you ever / Did you [Verb]?' (e.g., 你有没有看昨晚的节目？) or as an audience hype catchphrase ('有没有？！').

rootFamily.gloss: to not have; there is not; did not (past negation)
existence or non-existence; whether there is (formal)
nothing at all, not a single thing (idiom)

有点.etymology: Degree adverb and quantifier phrase contracted from 有一点 ('have a little bit of'): before adjectives or psychological verbs (有点累, 有点冷) it serves as a degree adverb meaning 'somewhat, a bit, rather'; before nouns it means 'have a little (of something)'.

morphemes.meaning: a little bit (short for 一点)

history.meaning: a little; somewhat; rather

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 有点 (via 萌典)

有用.etymology: Verb-object adjectival compound formed from 有 (yǒu, Middle Chinese *hjuwX, 'to have') and 用 (yòng, MC *juwngH, Old Chinese *loŋ-s, Oracle Bone graph depicting a bronze bell or wooden barrel/vessel pierced by a handle, signifying 'instrument, utility, to use, employ'). Already lexicalized in Classical Chinese (e.g. *Zhuangzi* 莊子·人間世 contrasting 無用之用 'the usefulness of the useless' with 有用 'having practical utility'), meaning 'useful, effective'.

history.meaning: possessing practical utility or serviceability to the state/craftsman
useful, helpful, effective (of tools, advice, methods, or people)

有用.notes: Covers both 'useful/handy' (of information or tools, e.g., 有用的建议 'useful advice') and 'effective/works' (e.g., 这个办法很有用 'This method really works'). Its colloquial antonym is 没用 ('useless'), while formal contexts use 无用.

rootFamily.gloss: use, function, effect, role; to act on

cognates.meaning: to have free time (related concept; Cantonese uses 得閒 dak1 haan4)

有空.etymology: Verb-object compound uniting 有 (yǒu, Middle Chinese *hjuwX, 'to have') and 空 (kòng, MC *khungH, 'empty space, gap, leisure time', departing-tone nominal/causative derivation of level-tone 空 kōng, MC *khung, 'hollow, empty, sky', from 穴 'cave/cavity' + phonetic 工 *kuwng). From 'unoccupied space or interval' evolved the temporal sense 'unoccupied time, spare time, availability'.

history.meaning: cavity, empty space (level tone kōng); gap, interval, leisure (departing tone kòng)
to have free time, be available, have leisure

morphemes.meaning: free time, leisure, unoccupied interval (pronounced fourth tone kòng)

有空.notes: Crucial pronunciation trap: 空 must be pronounced in the 4th tone (kòng, 'spare time/blank space'), never the 1st tone (kōng, 'empty/sky'). In Northern Mandarin, it is often erhua-ized as 有空儿 (yǒukòngr).

rootFamily.gloss: to find/make time in a busy schedule (kòng, 4th tone)
idle, free, unoccupied; leisure time (kòng, 4th tone)

cognates.meaning: having a karmic affinity or connection (yūen, contr. 無縁 muen)
cognates.word: 有縁 (ゆうえん / うえん)

有缘.etymology: Verb-object adjectival compound formed from 有 (yǒu, Middle Chinese *hjuwX, 'to have') and 緣/缘 (yuán, MC *ywen, originally 'decorative silk hem or border of a garment', from 糸 'silk' + phonetic 彖 *thwanH). During the Six Dynasties, Chinese Buddhist translators adopted 緣 (and 因緣) to render Sanskrit *pratyaya* ('conditioning cause, secondary causal link, karmic affinity'). From Buddhist karmic causality, 有緣 entered everyday Chinese for 'brought together by destiny, having a natural affinity'.

history.meaning: hem or decorative border of a robe; to climb or follow along
possessing karmic affinity (*pratyaya*) to encounter the Dharma or another person across lifetimes
brought together by fate/serendipity; clicking well, meant to be

morphemes.meaning: predestined affinity, karmic connection, serendipity (orig. garment hem)

有缘.notes: Used both for romantic/personal chemistry (咱们真有缘 'We were really meant to meet!') and for missing out on a professional opportunity or award (与冠军无缘 'fated not to win the championship', 有缘无分 'destined to meet but not to stay together').

rootFamily.gloss: predestined affinity, fate that brings people together, serendipity
having no affinity; failing to obtain/win (e.g. 无缘决赛)
cause, reason, origin (from Buddhist primary & secondary causes 因缘)

有说服力.etymology: A four-character verb-object phrase built from 有 (yǒu, 'to have, possess') governing the nominalized compound 说服力 (shuōfúlì, 'persuasive power'). Within 说服力, 说服 (Classical 說服, originally read shuìfú with 說 in the departing tone meaning 'to persuade by argument' + 服 'to submit, be convinced') is a resultative verb compound ('to speak until [the listener] submits'), to which the productive suffix -力 (lì, 'power, efficacy, force') is attached.

history.meaning: to persuade into submission through rhetoric (Classical Chinese)
power of persuasion, convincingness
possessing persuasive power; convincing, compelling

有说服力.notes: In Mainland Mandarin, 说 in 说服 is standardized to first tone (shuōfú), whereas Taiwan Mandarin preserves the historical persuasion reading shuìfú; in media pitches, 有说服力 describes proposals, data, or performances that win over skeptical producers.

有请.etymology: A deferential verb phrase composed of the existential/courtesy prefix 有 (yǒu, used before disyllabic or monosyllabic verbs in polite formulas like 有劳 'Excuse me for troubling you' or 有失远迎) and 请 (qǐng, Classical 請, 'to request, invite'). Originating in traditional Chinese theatrical, banquet, and court ushering announcements ('there is an invitation [for...]'), it became the standard broadcast and stage formula used by emcees to introduce a guest onto the stage.

history.meaning: to request respectfully, to invite a guest
ceremonial announcement inviting a guest into a hall or onto a stage
please welcome (stage/broadcast host cue)

morphemes.meaning: polite existential/courtesy marker before action verbs

有请.notes: A staple of variety shows and gala broadcasts (often paired as 下面有请... or 掌声有请... 'Please welcome with applause...'); it belongs strictly to formal hosting and stage announcements rather than casual conversation.

rootFamily.gloss: to trouble someone (polite formula with 有-)

有过.etymology: Formed from the existential and possessive verb 有 (yǒu, 'to have, there is') followed by the experiential aspect marker 过 (guò, Traditional 過, grammaticalized from the verb 'to pass across, traverse'). In Mandarin grammar, attaching -过 to 有 explicitly marks that a possession, relationship, or experience occurred at least once in the past without implying that it still holds in the present. In Classical Chinese, the same character sequence 有過 (yǒu guò) was a verb-object compound meaning 'to have a fault/transgression'.

history.meaning: to have a fault or transgression (Classical verb-object sense)
to have experienced or possessed once in the past (aspectual sense)
to have once had (an experience, collaboration, or feeling)

有过.notes: Frequently takes abstract object nouns in interviews and scripts (e.g., 有过合作 'have collaborated before', 有过怀疑 'have once doubted'), emphasizing a past episode that is now over or being reflected upon.

rootFamily.gloss: past experience, what one has been through

有过之而无不及.etymology: A Classical Chinese antithetical idiom (成语) attested in the *Zuo Zhuan* (左傳·昭公二十六年) and the *Book of Jin* (晉書). Literally structured as 有 (yǒu, 'there is') + 过之 (guò zhī, 'surpassing it') + 而 (ér, adversative/coordinating conjunction 'and moreover') + 无 (wú, 'there is no') + 不及 (bùjí, 'failing to reach / falling short'). It contrasts two extremes of comparison—exceeding a benchmark versus falling short of it—to assert that one thing goes even further than another.

history.form: 有過之矣，未之有不及也
history.meaning: it surpasses them indeed, and never falls short of them (early classical prototype)

history.form: 有過之而無不及 (yǒu guò zhī ér wú bùjí)
history.meaning: to exceed something and in no way fall short of it

history.form: 有过之而无不及 (yǒu guò zhī ér wú bùjí)
history.meaning: to match and even surpass (either in excellence or in severity)

有过之而无不及.notes: Typically introduced by the comparative frame 比起...来 (or 与...相比) and usable for both praise and criticism—whether describing a sequel's production scale or a rival's ruthlessness.

rootFamily.gloss: to fall short of, not as good as
to go too far, excessive (from 过 + 不及)

有限.etymology: A verb-object compound formed from 有 (yǒu, 'to have') + 限 (xiàn, 'boundary, threshold, restriction', originally containing 阜 'mound/terrace' + 艮 'to stop/gaze darkly', denoting a physical barrier or raised threshold). Literally 'having a boundary or limit', it is attested in Middle Chinese poetry and prose to describe finite quantities, lifespans, or resources, in direct structural opposition to 无限 (wúxiàn, 'boundless, infinite'). In modern legal and commercial usage, it also renders English 'limited' in 有限公司 ('limited company').

history.meaning: having a fixed boundary or finite measure (opposed to 無限)
limited in quantity, budget, time, or capacity; finite (mathematics/law)

有限.notes: In production and workplace dialogue, 预算有限 ('the budget is tight'), 时间有限 ('time is limited'), and 精力有限 ('energy is limited') are standard polite ways to decline scope creep.

朋友.etymology: Coordinative noun compound pairing two ancient relationship terms: 朋 (originally two strings of cowrie shells 玨 hung together -> 'fellow students who study under the same master') + 友 (two right hands 又 joined in mutual assistance -> 'comrades who share the same aspirations', neutral tone you in modern speech): 'friend'. Famously in the opening line of the Analects: 有朋自远方来，不亦乐乎.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones, Shijing, Analects) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: fellow students (朋) and helpful comrades (友) -> friend

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 朋友 (via 萌典)

朋友们.etymology: Formed from the coordinative compound 朋友 (péngyou, 'friend') plus the human collective/plural suffix -们 (men, Traditional 們). In Classical Chinese, 朋 (originally depicting two strings of cowrie shells hung together, hence 'peer, fellow student under the same master') and 友 (two right hands 廾/又 acting in concert, hence 'companion who helps') were distinct nuances summarized by commentators as 同师曰朋，同志曰友 ('sharing a teacher is called 朋; sharing aspirations is called 友'). Suffix -们 grammaticalized in Song–Yuan vernacular from 懣/門 to mark personal plurals.

history.meaning: peers and companions sharing study and principles (Classical coordinative compound)
friends (pluralized with vernacular human collective suffix -們)
friends; vocative address to an audience ('Friends!')

morphemes.meaning: peer, fellow cohort (originally two strings of cowries)
plural marker for human nouns and pronouns

朋友们.notes: In television and live broadcasts, 观众朋友们 ('dear viewers/audience friends') and 媒体朋友们 ('friends from the media') are warm, standard vocatives used by hosts to address the crowd.

朋友圈.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 朋友 (péngyou, 'friend') with 圈 (quān, 'circle, ring, enclosure; social sphere'). Originally used in twentieth-century sociology and everyday speech as a transparent equivalent to 'circle of friends' or 'social circle' (alongside 交际圈 and 娱乐圈), it underwent a major semantic shift in 2012 when Tencent's WeChat (微信) adopted 朋友圈 as the official Chinese name for its 'Moments' social feed, turning the word into the default term for a user's personal social media timeline.

history.meaning: interpersonal circle of friends, social milieu
WeChat Moments social feed (coined by Tencent in WeChat 4.0, April 2012); social circle

朋友圈.notes: Collocates with 发 ('post to Moments', 发朋友圈) and 刷 ('scroll through Moments', 刷朋友圈); in contemporary mainland usage, saying 发个朋友圈 almost exclusively means posting an update on WeChat Moments.

rootFamily.gloss: entertainment industry, showbiz circle (lit. entertainment circle)

服务.etymology: Verb-object/coordinative compound of 服 ('submit to, undertake duties, serve') + 务 (務, 'devote effort to, task, business'): 'serve, provide service; service'.

history.meaning: perform an assigned duty
serve; service

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 服务 (via 萌典)

服气.etymology: A verb-object compound (which functions as a separable verb, 离合词) formed from 服 (fú, 'to yield, submit, be convinced') + 气 (qì, Traditional 氣, 'breath, vital spirit, temper, pride'). Literally 'to make one's spirit/temper submit', it contrasts someone who merely complies outwardly with someone whose inner pride (气) genuinely acknowledges another's superiority or fairness.

history.meaning: to ingest vital breath/vapor (early Daoist cultivation sense); later, to subdue one's defiant spirit and accept defeat
to be genuinely convinced, accept defeat or someone's superiority without resentment

服气.notes: Most frequently encountered in the negative 不服气 ('refuse to accept defeat, feel indignant/unconvinced') or in the emphatic idiom 心服口服 ('convinced in both heart and mouth'). As a separable verb, modifiers go in the middle (e.g., 服了气).

rootFamily.gloss: wholeheartedly convinced (heart and mouth both submit)

服药.etymology: A Classical Chinese verb-object compound composed of 服 (fú, in its classical medical sense 'to ingest, take internally, administer', extended from 'to apply to the body / wear / submit to') and 药 (yào, Traditional 藥, 'medicinal herb, drug', formed with the grass radical 艸 over 樂). Already attested in the *Book of Documents* (*Shangshu*: 若藥弗瞑眩，厥疾弗瘳) and Han medical texts, 服藥 remained the formal medical and literary term for taking medication.

history.meaning: to ingest medicinal herbs or elixirs internally
to take medication (formal and medical register)

服药.notes: 服药 belongs to written, medical, or formal broadcast register (e.g., 按时服药 'take medication on schedule'), whereas everyday spoken Mandarin strongly prefers 吃药 (chīyào, literally 'eat medicine').

望.etymology: In oracle bone and bronze inscriptions, 望 (Old Chinese *maŋs) depicts a person (人/壬) standing upright with a prominent eye (臣) gazing into the distance toward the full moon (月), with 亡 serving as a phonetic component in the lineage of 朢/望. From the physical act of 'gazing afar on tiptoe', it evolved along two closely linked nominal pathways in Classical Chinese: (1) what one looks forward to from afar, hence 'hope, expectation' (as in 不负众望 / 不负所望), and (2) what others look up to from afar, hence 'prestige, renown, moral standing' (德高望重, 名望).

history.meaning: to gaze into the distance; the full moon on the 15th day of the lunar month
to look afar; expectation, hope; prestige or reputation looked up to by others
expectations, hopes; prestige (primarily bound in idioms like 不负所望 and compound nouns)

morphemes.meaning: to gaze afar; expectation, hope; prestige

望.notes: As a noun meaning 'expectations' or 'prestige', 望 is bound in elevated four-character idioms such as 不负众望 / 不负所望 ('live up to everyone's expectations') and 大失所望 ('be bitterly disappointed').

朝.etymology: Ancient character attested on Shang oracle bones showing the sun (日) rising among grass/trees (茻) while the pale moon/tide (月/舟) is still visible: read zhāo 'morning, dawn, day'; extended to morning royal audiences at court and read cháo 'imperial court, dynasty; face toward, look toward; preposition toward'.

history.meaning: morning dawn (zhāo); attend morning court, dynasty, face toward (cháo)
face toward, toward, dynasty (cháo); morning (zhāo)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 朝 (via 萌典)

期.etymology: Composed of 其 (qí, phonetic, originally depicting a winnowing basket) and 月 (yuè, 'moon, month', semantic indicator of cyclical time). In Old and Classical Chinese, 期 (*gɯ) meant an appointed time, a full cycle of a year or month (期年), or a covenanted meeting date. In modern publishing and broadcasting, this sense of a recurring cyclical appointment specialized into a classifier/measure word for serialized publications, training cohorts, and installments or episodes of a regularly scheduled program (such as a weekly variety show).

history.meaning: appointed time, covenanted date; a full cycle of months or a year
scheduled interval, phase, or stage
classifier for issues of periodicals, cohorts, or episodes of a regular television/variety program

morphemes.meaning: appointed time, period; classifier for serialized issues or show episodes

期.notes: In television production, 期 is the standard classifier for episodes of variety shows, reality competitions, and talk shows (e.g., 第一期节目 'Episode 1', 这一期 'this episode'), whereas 集 (jí) is used for scripted drama episodes. Also note that Mainland Mandarin pronounces 期 exclusively as first tone (qī), whereas Taiwan Mandarin often uses second tone (qí).

期待.etymology: A coordinative verb compound pairing 期 (qī, 'to stipulate a time, hope for, expect') and 待 (dài, 'to wait for, await', with the step radical 彳 and 寺 phonetic). Both components share the semantic field of awaiting an expected future event: literally 'to hope for and await'. While both characters co-occurred in Literary Chinese, the compound's modern transitive verbal and nominal usage ('to look forward to; anticipation, expectation') was reinforced across East Asia during the Meiji-era standardization of shared Sino-Japanese vocabulary.

history.meaning: to expect at an appointed time / to await (Classical verbal roots)
to await with hope, look forward to; expectation, anticipation

morphemes.meaning: to expect, hope for, appoint a time

期待.notes: A ubiquitous keyword in entertainment marketing—used both as a verb (敬请期待 'please stay tuned / look forward to it') and a noun (不负期待 'live up to expectations'). Unlike 等待 ('to wait'), 期待 always carries positive emotional anticipation.

rootFamily.gloss: to earnestly hope for, high expectations

期待值.etymology: A three-character modifier-head compound formed from 期待 (qīdài, 'expectation, anticipation') + 值 (zhí, 'numerical value, worth, index'). Originally coined in Japanese probability theory as 期待値 (*kitaichi*) to render mathematical 'expected value' (which Mainland Chinese mathematics usually calls 期望值), 期待值 entered popular Mandarin media, gaming, and entertainment discourse to quantify an audience's 'level of anticipation' or 'hype meter' as if it were a measurable stat.

history.meaning: expected value in probability theory; quantified degree of expectation (Japanese coinage)
level of anticipation, audience hype index (in media, fandom, and everyday speech)

期待值.notes: In entertainment publicity and social media, 期待值 constantly collocates with 拉满 (把期待值拉满 'max out the hype/anticipation level') or 降低期待值 ('lower one's expectations').

rootFamily.gloss: value, worth (also 'worth it' as an adjective)

期间.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 期 (qī, 'appointed time, fixed cycle') and 间 (jiān, Traditional 間, originally 閒 depicting moonlight 月 shining through the crevice of a double door 門, hence 'interval, space between'). Together, 期间 denotes the bounded temporal interval spanning a specific event, stage, or term. While rooted in Classical Chinese temporal expressions, its standardized modern legal and administrative usage as 'duration, period' was consolidated alongside Japanese 期間 (*kikan*).

history.meaning: within that appointed interval of time (Classical phrase)
period of time, duration, course of an event (e.g., 录制期间 'during the recording period')

morphemes.meaning: appointed time, scheduled cycle or phase

期间.notes: Almost always placed after a noun or verb phrase denoting an activity or event to mean 'during...' (e.g., 播出期间 'during the broadcast run', 比赛期间 'during the competition', 在此期间 'during this period').

cognates.meaning: term, time limit, deadline, expiration date

期限.etymology: A modifier-head or coordinative noun compound formed from 期 (qī, 'appointed date, fixed time') and 限 (xiàn, 'boundary, limit, threshold'). Already attested in Han and post-Han administrative prose (such as the *Book of Later Han* 後漢書) to denote an official time limit set by decree or law, it specifies the temporal boundary by which a task must be completed or a contract expires.

history.meaning: appointed time limit for official duties, tax delivery, or legal compliance
deadline, allotted term, expiration period

期限.notes: Used for contractual windows and final deadlines; common collocations in production management include 最后期限 ('final deadline'), 宽限期限 ('grace period'), and 超过期限 ('exceed the deadline / be overdue').

木.etymology: Foundational pictograph (象形字) attested from Shang oracle bones depicting a tree with branches above and roots below the ground line: 'tree (in Classical Chinese); wood, timber, lumber; wooden; numb/stiff'.

history.meaning: pictograph of a tree with crown and roots = tree, wood
wood; timber; wooden

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 木 (via 萌典)

木凳.etymology: Material-object compound from 木 ('wood; timber', pictograph of a tree with crown and roots) + 凳 ('backless stool or bench',登 + 几 'small table/seat'). Wooden stools joined with mortise-and-tenon stretchers have been a staple of Chinese workshops, teahouses, and courtyards for over a millennium.

history.meaning: wooden stool or bench
wooden stool

木匠.etymology: Compound occupational noun of 木 ('wood') + 匠 ('artisan, craftsman', showing an axe 斤 inside a tool box 匚, neutral tone jiang in everyday speech): 'carpenter, joiner, woodworker'. Attested since Han–Tang prose.

history.meaning: wood craftsman = carpenter

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 木匠 (via 萌典)

木头.etymology: Colloquial noun formed from 木 ('wood, tree') + nominal suffix 头 (頭, neutral tone tou, originally denoting a block/end of cut timber): 'wood, log, timber, piece of wood'.

history.meaning: wood; timber; log

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 木头 (via 萌典)

木屑.etymology: A classical material-noun compound pairing 木 (mù, 'tree, timber, wood') and 屑 (xiè, 'fine crumbs, filings, or shavings', written with 尸 and 肖). Attested already in historical anecdotes of the Jin dynasty—where thrifty officials saved bamboo and wood shavings (竹头木屑) from shipbuilding to strew over muddy paths—木屑 denotes fragrant wood curls or sawdust planed from timber such as cedar.

history.meaning: sawdust and wood shavings from carpentry
wood shavings; sawdust

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 木屑

木工.etymology: Compound noun of 木 ('wood') + 工 ('craftwork, artisan'): means both 'woodworking, carpentry' and 'carpenter, woodworker'. Attested since the Book of Rites (Liji: 考工记).

history.meaning: carpentry; woodworking; carpenter

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 木工 (via 萌典)

木工房.etymology: Three-character compound combining 木工 ('woodworking, carpentry') + 房 ('room, workshop'): 'woodworking shop, carpentry workshop'.

history.meaning: carpentry workshop; woodshop

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 木工房 (via 萌典)

木条.etymology: Compound noun from 木 ('wood; timber') + 条 (simplified from 條, originally 'slender tree branch', wood 木 + phonetic 攸). Denotes any narrow strip, slat, or batten of sawn wood used in carpentry, framing, and furniture making.

history.meaning: slender strip or batten of wood
wooden strip; wooden slat

木板.etymology: Determinative compound of 木 ('tree; wood; timber', oracle-bone pictograph of a tree with branches above and roots below) + 板 ('plank; flat board', wood radical 木 + phonetic 反 fǎn). Denotes any sawn wooden board, shelf plank, or key board.

history.meaning: wooden plank or printing block
wooden board; panel

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 木板

木桌.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 木 ('wooden') + 桌 ('table, desk'): 'wooden table'.

history.meaning: wooden table

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 木桌 (via 萌典)

木牌.etymology: Compound noun from 木 ('wood') + 牌 ('plaque; signboard; tally tablet', split-wood radical 片 + phonetic 卑). Wooden plaques hung outside shop doors or inns have been used across China since the Tang and Song dynasties to display shop names, open hours, or official notices.

history.meaning: wooden tally or notice board
wooden sign; wooden plaque

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 木牌

木窗.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 木 ('wooden') + 窗 ('window'): 'wooden-framed window, wooden window'.

history.meaning: wooden window

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 木窗 (via 萌典)

木箱.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 木 ('wooden') + 箱 ('box, chest, crate'): 'wooden box, wooden chest or crate'.

history.meaning: wooden box; wooden chest

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 木箱 (via 萌典)

木纹.etymology: Compound noun from 木 ('wood') + 纹 (simplified from 紋, silk radical 纟 + 文 'pattern; grain; lines'). Refers to the natural annual-ring figure and grain lines visible on planed or oiled timber.

history.meaning: natural grain pattern of wood
wood grain

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 木纹

木花架.etymology: Three-character compound combining 木 ('wooden') + 花架 ('flower stand, plant rack'): 'wooden flower stand, wooden plant shelf'.

history.meaning: wooden flower stand / plant rack

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 木花架 (via 萌典)

木门.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 木 ('wooden') + 门 (門, 'door'): 'wooden door'.

history.meaning: wooden door

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 木门 (via 萌典)

未.etymology: In oracle bone script, 未 (Old Chinese *mɯds) depicts a tree (木) with an extra upper layer of branches and dense foliage—contrasting with 末 (mò, a tree marked at the very tip, 'treetop, end') and 本 (běn, marked at the roots). Used early on as a phonetic loan for the eighth Earthly Branch (associated with 1–3 p.m. and the Goat/Sheep) and for the aspectual negative adverb 'not yet, not having [completed an action]', contrasting in Classical Chinese with 不 (general/habitual negation) and 弗. In modern Mandarin, 未 functions both as a concise literary adverb ('not yet') and as a highly productive privative prefix ('un-', as in 未知, 未成年, 未播).

history.meaning: 8th Earthly Branch; aspectual negative adverb 'not yet, have not'
not yet (contrasting with 已 'already')
not yet, without having (formal/literary adverb and productive prefix 'un-')

未.notes: In everyday conversation, speakers say 还没(有) ('not yet'); single-character 未 appears in headlines, contracts, stage captions (e.g., 未完待续 'to be continued'), and four-character idioms.

rootFamily.gloss: the future (lit. what has not yet come)

cognates.meaning: not necessarily, by no means certain

未必.etymology: A Classical Chinese compound adverb formed from the negative adverb 未 (wèi, 'not yet, not') negating the modal adverb 必 (bì, 'necessarily, certainly, inevitably'). This exemplifies partial negation (部分否定) in Chinese syntax: whereas 必不 means 'certainly not' (total negation), 未必 negates certainty itself, yielding 'not necessarily so, may not turn out to be'. It is attested across Warring States texts including the *Analects* (論語·憲問: 有德者必有言，有言者不必有德) and *Mencius*.

history.meaning: it is not necessarily the case that... (Classical modal negation)
not necessarily, maybe not (more concise and slightly more formal than 不一定)

未必.notes: More crisp and rhetorical than its colloquial synonym 不一定 (bùyīdìng); it can also stand alone as a one-word skeptical reply (未必吧 'Not necessarily / I wouldn't be so sure').

未播先火.etymology: A modern four-character entertainment-industry phrase molded on the classical template 未 X 先 Y ('before X has even happened, Y already occurs', compare 未老先衰 'grow decrepit before growing old' and 未卜先知 'know beforehand without divination'). Here, 未播 (wèibō, 'not yet broadcast/aired', from 播 'to sow, broadcast') is paired with 先火 (xiānhuǒ, 'already become fiery popular / go viral first', using the slang stative verb 火 'to be red-hot, trending'). It describes a television series or variety show that becomes a massive trending topic through trailers, casting, or leaks before its premiere episode even airs.

history.meaning: classical four-character correlative pattern 'before [X] has occurred, already [Y]' (e.g., 未老先衰)

history.form: 未播先火 (wèi bō xiān huǒ)
history.meaning: to become a viral hit before airing (television and streaming media idiom)

morphemes.meaning: to broadcast, air (originally to sow seeds)
