未播先火.notes: A quintessential Chinese showbiz buzzword used by PR teams and entertainment journalists when a show's trailers, IP adaptation announcement, or star lineup dominate Weibo hot searches months ahead of release.

rootFamily.gloss: grow old before one's time (structural model 未X先Y)

未来.etymology: Originally a Buddhist translation compound formed from 未 (wèi, 'not yet') + 来 (lái, Traditional 來, 'to come, arrive'), literally 'that which has not yet come'. In Six Dynasties and Tang Chinese translations of Sanskrit Buddhist scriptures, 未來世 (wèiláishì) was coined to render Sanskrit *anāgata* ('not-come, future'), forming one of the 'Three Times' (三世: 過去 'past, what has passed', 現在 'present, what is manifest now', and 未來 'future, what has not yet arrived'). From Buddhist cosmology, 未来 entered general secular Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and Vietnamese as the standard noun for 'the future'.

history.meaning: the future world/rebirth (calque of Sanskrit anāgata in the Buddhist triad 過去・現在・未來)
the future, time to come; future, upcoming (attributive)

未来.notes: Can be used both as a noun (展望未来 'look toward the future') and directly before another noun without 的 as an attributive modifier (未来发展 'future development', 未来趋势 'future trends'). Compare 将来, which focuses more on the near/personal future.

rootFamily.gloss: originally, from the beginning; supposed to

未知.etymology: A Classical Chinese verb phrase turned adjective/noun, composed of the negative aspectual adverb 未 (wèi, 'not yet') and 知 (zhī, 'to know, perceive, understand'). In Classical texts such as the *Analects* (論語·先進: 未知生，焉知死 'Not yet understanding life, how can one understand death?'), 未知 was a syntactic sequence meaning 'have not yet come to know'. In modern Mandarin (and across the Sinosphere via shared literary and mathematical terminology like 未知数 'unknown quantity/variable'), it lexicalized as a modifier and abstract noun meaning 'unknown, uncharted, the unknown'.

history.meaning: to not yet know, to have not yet learned (free syntactic phrase)
unknown, uncharted; the unknown (lexicalized adjective and noun)

未知.notes: Often used as an abstract noun after verbs like 探索未知 ('explore the unknown') or 面对未知 ('face the unknown'), or in the popular metaphor 未知数 (wèizhīshù, 'an unknown variable / anyone's guess').

rootFamily.gloss: unknown variable (in math); uncertain outcome, X-factor
known, already known (antonym of 未知)

本.etymology: Measure word for bound books, notebooks, and ledgers (一本书 'a book', 一本账本 'a ledger'). Formed by marking the lower root of 木 ('tree') with a stroke, 本 meant 'tree root, foundation, origin' in Classical Chinese, then 'bound volume' once bamboo slips were superseded by stitched codices.

history.meaning: root of a tree; foundation
bound volume; classifier for books

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 本 (via 萌典)

本事.etymology: A vernacular Mandarin noun derived from 本 (běn, 'root, foundation, one's own') + 事 (shì, 'matter, affair, duty, craft'). In Classical and Tang–Song administrative Chinese, 本事 meant 'the original matter/story' (as in Meng Qi's Tang anthology 本事诗 'Poems and the Original Stories Behind Them') or 'one's primary occupation/duty' (specifically agriculture or one's assigned craft). In Yuan drama and Ming–Qing vernacular fiction, 'one's own craft/stock-in-trade' shifted to mean 'personal capability, skill, prowess, or nerve' (written interchangeably with 本领), with the second syllable reduced to neutral tone (běnshi).

history.meaning: primary occupation (agriculture); the original story behind a poem; one's own assigned craft
martial or professional skill, personal capability, stock-in-trade (Yuan–Ming vernacular)
ability, skill, capability; nerve or guts (in challenges like 有本事你…!)

本事.notes: Always pronounced with a neutral tone on the second syllable (běnshi). Aside from meaning 'real skill' (真本事, 各凭本事 'each relying on their own ability'), 有本事你... ('If you've got what it takes / If you have the nerve, then...') is a classic conversational dare.

cognates.meaning: the person in question, the principal himself/herself
the person in question, oneself, I (formal)

本人.etymology: A modifier-head compound formed from 本 (běn, originally a tree 木 marked with a stroke at its base, 'tree root, origin', grammaticalized in Middle and administrative Chinese as a reflexive/demonstrative determiner meaning 'this very, the ~ in question, one's own') and 人 (rén, 'person'). Attested in Song–Yuan legal and official documents to designate 'the principal party in question' (as opposed to a proxy or family member), it functions in modern Mandarin both as an appositive pronoun ('oneself, in person') and as a formal first-person pronoun ('I, the undersigned').

history.meaning: the principal person concerned in a legal or administrative case (as opposed to an agent)
the person oneself, in the flesh; I / me (in formal statements or résumés)

morphemes.meaning: this very, the ~ in question (originally root of a tree)

本人.notes: In celebrity and showbiz culture, Noun + 本人 means 'the star in the flesh' (e.g., 他本人比电视上更帅 'He's even more handsome in person than on TV'), and internet slang uses X本人 to mean 'the quintessential embodiment of X'.

rootFamily.gloss: itself, in itself (used for things, concepts, or reflexively)
this company, our firm; the ~ in question
party directly involved in a case or event

本土.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 本 (běn, 'root, original, native, one's own') and 土 (tǔ, 'earth, soil, territory, land'). In medieval Chinese Buddhist texts and historical geographies, 本土 meant 'one's native land' or 'the original territory of a state/teaching' (as opposed to foreign lands, 他土/异域). In modern geopolitics, it denotes the metropolitan mainland of a country (as opposed to overseas territories), while in media, commerce, and cultural criticism it functions attributively to mean 'homegrown, domestic, local, indigenous'.

history.meaning: one's native soil or original territory (opposed to foreign lands in Buddhist and historical texts)
metropolitan mainland; local, domestic, homegrown (culture, brands, or talent)

本土.notes: In Chinese television and film industry discussions, 本土 contrasts homegrown domestic creations (本土综艺 'homegrown variety shows', 本土品牌 'domestic brands') with imported foreign formats (引进模式) or overseas productions.

rootFamily.gloss: local, native to this area (synonymous in local contexts)

cognates.word: 本土化 (hondoka) / ローカライズ
bản địa hóa / bản thổ hóa

本土化.etymology: Formed by attaching the productive deadjectival/denominal suffix -化 (huà, 'to transform into, -ize / -ization', popularized via Meiji Sino-Japanese translations of European *-ize/-ification* terms) to 本土 (běntǔ, 'native soil, local, domestic'). Literally 'making [something] native to the local soil', it denotes the process of adapting foreign ideas, business operations, or media formats to fit local cultural tastes, language, and audience habits.

history.meaning: combining classical 'native soil' with modern transformative suffix -化 ('-ize / -ization')
localization, indigenization, cultural adaptation of foreign formats or products

本土化.notes: In television production (*幕后之王*), 本土化 (or 本土化改造) is the central challenge when adapting an overseas show format—reworking foreign rules, humor, and pacing so domestic audiences connect with it. For software translation specifically, 本地化 (běndìhuà) is also common.

本地.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun and modifier of 本 ('root -> this, current, native') + 地 ('place, locality'): 'this locality, local, native'. Attested since Song–Ming texts.

history.meaning: this locality; local

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 本地 (via 萌典)

本场.etymology: A determiner-classifier compound composed of the proximal demonstrative determiner 本 (běn, 'this current, the ~ at hand', extended from 'root/origin' in administrative Chinese) and the classifier/noun 场 (chǎng, Traditional 場, originally 'leveled earthen altar or threshing ground' from 土 + 易, later 'stage, arena' and classifier for performances, matches, and events). Together, 本场 specifies 'this current match, round, or live performance session'.

history.meaning: leveled ground for sacrifices or threshing; later, arena or theatrical stage
this match, this round, this live performance session (determiner + classifier)

morphemes.meaning: classifier for matches, shows, and events; stage, arena

本场.notes: Standard broadcast and stage-hosting phrasing in sports and competitive variety shows: 本场比赛 ('this match/round of competition'), 本场竞演 ('this live performance round'), and 本场最佳 ('MVP / best performer of this round').

rootFamily.gloss: on the spot, live at the venue/set
to go on stage, enter the arena/court

本子.etymology: Colloquial noun formed from 本 (indicative character showing a mark 一 at the root of a tree 木: 'root, source -> bound volume, edition, notebook') + nominal suffix 子 (neutral tone zi): 'notebook, exercise book, pad, bound booklet'.

history.stage: Song–Ming book printing to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: bound volume; notebook; booklet

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 本子 (via 萌典)

本届.etymology: A determiner-classifier compound combining the proximal determiner 本 (běn, 'this current') with the classifier 届 (jiè, originally composed of 尸 'body' + 凷, meaning 'to reach, arrive at an appointed time or limit'). Because 届 came to denote a scheduled recurrence that arrives at regular intervals, it grammaticalized in modern Chinese as the dedicated classifier for periodic conferences, graduating classes, terms of office, film festivals, and recurring competitions; 本届 thus means 'this current edition/session'.

history.meaning: to reach, arrive at a limit or appointed time (as in 屆時 'when the time comes')
this current session, this year's edition, the current term or cohort

morphemes.meaning: classifier for regularly recurring sessions, editions, cohorts, or terms

本届.notes: Used only for events or bodies that happen in numbered editions or terms (e.g., 本届电影节 'this year's film festival', 本届大赛 'this edition of the competition', 上一届 'the previous edition', 往届 'past editions'); one-off events cannot take 届.

rootFamily.gloss: all previous editions or graduating classes
this year's graduating class / current cohort

本来.etymology: Compound adjective and adverb of 本 ('root, origin, original') + 来 ('come from the beginning'). Originated in Medieval Buddhist translations and Tang–Song prose for 'original nature', and in Mandarin means 'original, originally; of course, as a matter of fact'.

history.stage: Tang–Song Buddhist & vernacular Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: originally; at first; of course

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 本来 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: regular/main academic course (as opposed to preparatory 予科 or specialized 別科)
main/regular undergraduate course (opposed to preparatory 예과)

本科.etymology: A modifier-head compound formed from 本 (běn, 'main, foundational, principal, regular') and 科 (kē, originally from 禾 'grain' + 斗 'measuring scoop', meaning 'measurement, category, division, academic subject or examination stream'). In late imperial Chinese civil-service administration, 本科 referred to one's 'own examination category or administrative department'. During late Meiji Japan and late Qing educational reforms (such as the 1902–1904 imperial school regulations), 本科 (*honka*) was adopted to designate a university's 'regular/main degree program' in contrast to 预科 (yùkē, preparatory course) and 专科 (zhuānkē, specialized/vocational diploma), stabilizing in modern Mandarin as 'undergraduate bachelor's degree studies'.

history.meaning: one's own examination stream or administrative division (Imperial Chinese bureaucracy)
the main/regular university curriculum (contrasted with preparatory 豫科/予科 in Meiji & late Qing universities)
four-year undergraduate studies, bachelor's degree program

本科.notes: In Mainland China's higher education system, 本科 specifically refers to a standard four-year (or five-year medical/architecture) bachelor's program, sitting between 专科/大专 (two-to-three-year associate diploma) and 研究生 (postgraduate master's/doctoral studies).

rootFamily.gloss: academic discipline, subject, branch of learning
liberal arts / humanities vs. science streams

cognates.meaning: one's own body/person; originally (in medieval texts)

本身.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 本 (běn, 'root, original, one's own') and 身 (shēn, originally a pictograph of a torso with a prominent belly, meaning 'body, torso, self, person'). In medieval Chinese Buddhist translations and Daoist texts, 本身 referred to 'one's original/fundamental body' or a previous incarnation of the Buddha (rendering Sanskrit *jātaka*, 'birth-story of the Buddha himself', alongside 本生). By Song–Ming vernacular Chinese, it broadened into a reflexive and emphatic pronoun meaning 'one's own person' and subsequently 'itself, in itself' (applicable to abstract concepts, institutions, and objects as well as people).

history.meaning: one's original body or previous life-form (Buddhist translations); one's own physical person
oneself, itself, in and of itself (emphatic/reflexive pronoun for things or people)

本身.notes: Unlike 本人 (which can only refer to a human being), 本身 typically follows abstract nouns, objects, or issues to mean 'in itself / per se' (e.g., 节目本身没有问题 'There is nothing wrong with the show itself', 这件事本身 'this matter in itself').

rootFamily.gloss: the person oneself, in person (human only)
oneself, one's own (often before abstract nouns like 自身利益)

朵.etymology: Written 朵 (duǒ), depicting a drooping cluster or blossom (乃/几) atop a tree branch (木). In Tang poetry 朵 meant a flower bud or cluster swaying on a stem (花朵), and from Tang–Song vernacular onward it grammaticalized into the dedicated Mandarin classifier for flowers, clouds (一朵云), and flower-shaped motifs such as a compass rose.

morphemes.meaning: blossom on a tree 木 -> measure word for flowers and clouds

history.meaning: flower cluster swaying on a branch
measure word for flowers, blossoms, and clouds

机会.etymology: A classical compound uniting 机 (jī, Traditional 機, originally 'the trigger mechanism of a crossbow or loom', hence 'pivotal moment, subtle turning point, crucial juncture') and 会 (huì, Traditional 會, 'to meet, converge, come together at the right moment'). Already attested in Six Dynasties and Tang texts (such as the *Book of Sui* 隋書 and Bai Juyi's prose), 機會 literally denoted 'the convergence (會) of a pivotal trigger-moment (機)'—a fleeting alignment of circumstances when action can succeed. Its modern predominance as the standard equivalent of English 'opportunity, chance' was further reinforced via Meiji Japanese 機会 (*kikai*).

history.meaning: crossbow/loom trigger mechanism (pivotal juncture) + convergence of circumstances
favorable juncture, opportune convergence of timing and events
opportunity, chance, favorable occasion

morphemes.meaning: pivotal juncture, trigger mechanism, subtle turning point

机会.notes: Collocates with 抓住/把握 ('seize an opportunity'), 错过 ('miss an opportunity'), and 给...一个机会 ('give [someone] a chance'). Compare 机遇 (jīyù), which is more elevated and refers to major life or historical opportunities rather than everyday chances.

rootFamily.gloss: favorable turn of events,lucky break, major opportunity
crisis (lit. danger 危 + pivotal juncture/opportunity 机)

cognates.meaning: opportunity cost (Japanese uses 費用 'expense' for 'cost')

机会成本.etymology: A modern economic calque of English *opportunity cost* (a concept formulated by Austrian economist Friedrich von Wieser in 1914 as *Alternativkosten* / *opportunity cost*), constructed as a modifier-head compound from 机会 (jīhuì, 'opportunity') + 成本 (chéngběn, 'cost, capital outlay'). In traditional Chinese mercantile accounting, 成本 (from 成 'to complete, produce' + 本 'principal capital, root outlay') denoted the total capital required to produce or procure goods; combining 机会 with 成本 expresses the value of the best foregone alternative when a choice is made.

history.meaning: capital outlay required to produce or acquire goods (traditional commercial accounting)
opportunity cost (calque of English 'opportunity cost' in modern economics and decision-making)

morphemes.meaning: capital, principal outlay (with 成 = production cost)

机会成本.notes: Originally a technical economics term, 机会成本 is now widely used in business negotiations, career planning, and media production (e.g., choosing which project to greenlight or which show slot to commit an artist's schedule to). Note that Japanese and Korean use 機会費用 / 기회비용 (*비용* = 费用) rather than 成本.

rootFamily.gloss: sunk cost (parallel economic compound with 成本)

cognates.meaning: seat aboard an aircraft; camera or machine position

机位.etymology: A modern Mandarin modifier-head compound combining 机 (jī, Traditional 機, abridged from 摄像机 shèxiàngjī "video camera" or 照相机 zhàoxiàngjī "camera", originally meaning a loom or mechanical trigger in Classical Chinese) and 位 (wèi, "position, seat, station"). Coined in twentieth-century film, television, and aviation terminology to designate either the physical placement and angle of a camera on set or an assigned passenger seat aboard an aircraft.

history.meaning: mechanical apparatus or loom trigger + ranked standing place at court
camera setup position on a production floor; passenger seat on an airliner

机位.notes: In television and studio production (as in *Behind the Scenes*), 给机位 or 找机位 refers to blocking a shot or finding the active camera angle; in travel contexts, it means an airline seat assignment.

rootFamily.gloss: multi-camera setup (e.g., 双机位 two-camera shoot)

机制.etymology: A modifier-head compound of 机 (jī, Traditional 機, "mechanical device, pivotal spring, organic workings") and 制 (zhì, "system, regulation, institutional ordinance"). While 制 appears in Classical Chinese statecraft for laws and decrees, 机制 coalesced in modern Chinese academic and administrative prose (reinforcing translations of English "mechanism") to denote first the interacting parts of a machine or biological organism, and by extension an institutional workflow or governance framework.

history.meaning: pivotal trigger/spring + sovereign decree or institutional regulation
mechanical or physiological workings (translating European "mechanism")
institutional workflow, operating mechanism, or systemic protocol

机制.notes: Frequently paired with verbs like 建立 (establish) or 完善 (perfect) in corporate and media production settings (e.g., 评审机制 "evaluation mechanism", 应急机制 "emergency protocol").

机器.etymology: A coordinative/modifier-head compound formed from 机 (jī, Traditional 機, originally a wooden loom or crossbow trigger mechanism in Old and Middle Chinese) and 器 (qì, "vessel, implement, utensil, instrument"). Already attested in Tang–Song literary texts for ingenious mechanical contrivances, the compound was revitalized in the nineteenth century during industrial modernization to translate Western "machine" and "machinery".

history.meaning: crossbow/loom mechanism + ritual or practical vessel/implement
ingenious mechanical contrivance or crafted apparatus
power-driven machine, engine, or automated hardware

机器.notes: In film and broadcast studios, 机器 colloquially refers to the main recording cameras or editing rigs (e.g., 开机器 "roll the cameras"). Compare 机械 (jīxiè), which leans toward "mechanical" or "machinery" in the abstract.

rootFamily.gloss: equipment; props and gear (especially camera/lighting gear)

机场.etymology: A twentieth-century modifier-head compound contracting 飞机场 (fēijīchǎng, "flying-machine ground"): 机 (jī, Traditional 機, short for 飞机 fēijī "airplane") modifies 场 (chǎng, Traditional 場, originally a leveled earthen floor for threshing grain or sacrificial altars in Classical Chinese, later any open plaza or field). Coined with the rise of commercial and military aviation in Republican-era China.

history.meaning: leveled ritual ground or grain-threshing arena
airfield; aerodrome for landing aircraft
commercial airport or aviation terminal

机场.notes: In Chinese entertainment culture, 机场街拍 ("airport street photography") is a major celebrity publicity phenomenon where stars showcase fashion between flights.

机油.etymology: Compound noun of 机 (機, 'machine, engine', shortened from 机器) + 油 ('oil, lubricant'): 'engine oil, motor oil, machine lubricating oil'.

history.meaning: engine oil; machine oil

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 机油 (via 萌典)

机票.etymology: A modern modifier-head compound abbreviating 飞机票 (fēijīpiào, "airplane ticket"), combining 机 (jī, Traditional 機, clipped from 飞机 "aircraft") with 票 (piào, originally "spark, flame, nimble" in Classical Chinese, which in Song–Ming commercial vernacular shifted to mean a printed paper slip, bank draft, warrant, or voucher).

history.meaning: rising spark of fire; swift, nimble movement
printed paper voucher, remittance draft, or official warrant
airline passenger ticket (clipping of 飞机票)

机票.notes: Takes the classifier 张 (zhāng) because tickets are flat paper/digital slips: 一张机票. Common collocations include 订机票 (book a flight) and 改签机票 (rebook/change a flight ticket).

cognates.meaning: to kill; to slay; to dull or diminish

杀.etymology: From Old Chinese *srat (Middle Chinese *sˠɛt), written 殺 in Traditional script (depicting a hand 殳 striking a tree/creature 𣏟). Inherited from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *s-rjat ~ *g-sat ("to kill, extinguish"). Beyond literal slaying in Classical Chinese, it developed a secondary reading shài ("to pare down, reduce by hierarchy") and rich colloquial extensions in modern Mandarin including "to cut/wrap up a film shoot" (杀青), "to slash prices" (杀价), and "to sting/burn painfully".

history.meaning: to slay, execute, or put to death; to pare down or diminish by degree
to kill; to fight one's way into/out of; (as post-verbal intensifier) to an extreme degree (e.g., 笑殺)
to kill; to terminate/cut; to slash prices; to wrap production

morphemes.meaning: to kill; to slay; to cut off or terminate

杀.notes: In film and television production, 杀青 (shāqīng, literally "scorching the green bamboo" to prepare ancient writing strips) means to wrap filming! Also used figuratively for fierce competition (杀出重围 "fight one's way out of heavy encirclement").

rootFamily.gloss: to wrap filming; to finish a manuscript (lit. dry green bamboo)
to write off; to obliterate or negate

杀伐决断.etymology: A four-character Classical-style coordinative idiom (成语 chéngyǔ) pairing two disyllabic nominalized verb compounds: 杀伐 (shāfá, Traditional 殺伐, "slaying and launching punitive military expeditions", attested in the *Book of Rites* and *Zuo Zhuan* as a prerogative of sovereign power) and 决断 (juéduàn, Traditional 決斷, "breaching a dike and severing cleanly", hence "making resolute, unhesitating judgments"). Together they describe an executive leader who acts with iron-fisted, unflinching decisiveness.

history.meaning: sovereign authority to wage war and execute + decisive judicial/political resolution
ruthlessly decisive, iron-willed, and unhesitating in executive leadership

morphemes.meaning: to strike; to launch a punitive campaign
to breach; to decide; to resolve

杀伐决断.notes: A hallmark praise term in workplace and corporate dramas (*Behind the Scenes*) for a powerhouse producer or CEO who makes tough cuts and high-stakes decisions without sentimental hesitation. Often varied as 杀伐果断 (shāfá-guǒduàn).

杂事.etymology: A modifier-head compound attested since the Han and Six Dynasties periods, combining 杂 (zá, Traditional 雜, originally "to mix various colors of silk in garments", hence "variegated, mingled, sundry, miscellaneous") and 事 (shì, "affair, business, duty, service"). In Classical historical prose it denoted minor administrative duties outside core state rituals; in modern Mandarin it refers to everyday odd jobs and trivial errands.

history.meaning: minor court or administrative matters outside primary state affairs
everyday miscellaneous chores, trivial errands, and household/office odd jobs

杂事.notes: More colloquial and everyday than 杂务 (záwù). Often takes a retroflex suffix in northern speech (杂事儿 záshìr) when complaining about petty, time-consuming errands that distract from creative work.

cognates.meaning: miscellaneous duties; routine office chores; odd jobs
sundry duties; odd jobs in an organization

杂务.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 杂 (zá, Traditional 雜, "mixed, sundry, miscellaneous") with 务 (wù, Traditional 務, "to strive after; official duty, business, task"). Recorded in Tang–Song bureaucratic texts for ancillary administrative tasks, and reinforced in modern East Asian organizational usage (alongside Japanese 雑務 *zatsumu*) for routine operational duties done by interns, production assistants, or back-office staff.

history.meaning: ancillary bureaucratic duties outside a magistrate's primary portfolio
routine office chores, logistical odd jobs, and non-specialized workplace tasks

杂务.notes: Slightly more formal and workplace-oriented than 杂事: interns and junior production assistants on a film crew often start by 打杂 or 处理杂务 ("handling odd jobs and logistics").

杂音.etymology: Determinative acoustic compound of 杂 ('mixed; variegated; stray', originally multicoloured garments 衣 + 集) + 音 ('sound; musical tone'). Contrasting with pure musical pitch (乐音), it denotes unwanted mechanical buzz, static, or background noise.

history.meaning: unwanted noise; acoustic buzz or static
unwanted noise; squeak; buzz

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 杂音

权利.etymology: Originally a Classical Chinese coordinative compound 權利 (quánlì) pairing 权 (quán, Traditional 權, literally the sliding weight of a steelyard balance, hence "political leverage, authority, expediency") and 利 (lì, "sharpness, profit, material advantage"), used in *Xunzi* and *Records of the Grand Historian* to mean "power and wealth/gain". In 1864, American missionary William A. P. Martin (丁韪良) repurposed 權利 in his translation of Wheaton's *Elements of International Law* (*Wanguo Gongfa*) to render Western legal "right(s)", a semantic shift swiftly adopted in Meiji Japan (権利 *kenri*) and re-entrenched across modern Chinese law.

history.meaning: political authority and material profit/advantage (often viewed critically in Confucian texts)
legal and natural right; legitimate entitlement under law (calquing English "right" / Latin *ius*)
civil, contractual, or legal right (strictly contrasted with 权力 "power")

权利.notes: Crucial homophone distinction in Chinese law and media: 权利 (quánlì with 利 "benefit") means "legal right/entitlement" (e.g., 知识产权 "intellectual property rights"), whereas exact homophone 权力 (quánlì with 力 "force") means "political/executive power".

rootFamily.gloss: power; authority; clout (homophone of 权利!)

cognates.meaning: rights and interests; concessions (e.g., railway or mining rights)

权益.etymology: A modern coordinative compound compressing 权利 (quánlì, "legal rights") and 利益 (lìyì, "interests, benefits"): 权 (quán, Traditional 權, "right, entitlement, authority") + 益 (yì, originally a pictograph of water overflowing a vessel, hence "increase, benefit, profit"). Popularized in late nineteenth- and twentieth-century diplomatic, legal, and commercial discourse (shared with Japanese 権益 *ken'eki*) to denote the combined legal entitlements and material stakes held by an individual, creator, or state.

history.meaning: steelyard weight / authority + overflowing vessel / benefit, gain
treaty concessions, commercial stakes, and legal entitlements
legitimate rights and interests (of consumers, creators, or shareholders)

权益.notes: Standard in contract negotiations, copyright disputes, and consumer law: 维护合法权益 ("safeguard legitimate rights and interests"). In showbiz, VIP membership tiers are often called 会员权益 ("member perks/benefits").

权限.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-Japanese legal and bureaucratic compound (Japanese 権限 *kengen*, adopted into late Qing and Republican Chinese as 權限 quánxiàn), combining 权 (quán, Traditional 權, "authority, official power, right") and 限 (xiàn, "threshold, boundary, limit"). Literally "the boundary of authority", it originally defined the statutory jurisdiction of an official or court, and in the digital age expanded to mean software/system "access permissions".

history.meaning: official authority/leverage + physical threshold or boundary limit
statutory scope of official jurisdiction or administrative competence
history.stage: Meiji Japanese / Late Qing Administrative Loan

history.meaning: organizational decision-making authority; digital system/account access permissions

权限.notes: Used both in corporate hierarchy (越权 vs. 在我的权限之内 "within my authority to approve") and in IT/broadcasting workflows (开通权限 "grant access permissions").

杏仁.etymology: Compound of 杏 ('apricot/almond tree', wood 木 + 口) + 仁 ('edible seed kernel inside a pit', extended from 'humane heart/core' to the tender inner seed of stone fruits); used in Chinese baking and herbal cuisine for sweet almonds and apricot kernels.

history.meaning: apricot or almond kernel
almond; apricot kernel

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 杏仁

cognates.meaning: apricot; common female given name (Anzu / Kyōko)

杏子.etymology: As a common noun (xìngzi), formed from 杏 (xìng, "apricot tree/fruit", Old Chinese *C.qˤraŋʔ, depicting a tree 木 with a mouth/fruit 口 below) plus the diminutive nominal suffix 子 (zi, originally "child/seed"). As a personal name in *Behind the Scenes* (幕后之王) and modern Chinese media (pronounced Xìngzǐ), it also echoes the Japanese female given name 杏子 (Kyōko / Anzu), where 子 (-ko) functions as a classic aristocratic and modern feminine name suffix.

history.meaning: apricot tree/fruit + seed, kernel, or child
apricot fruit (with neutralized diminutive suffix -zi)
given name of the veteran producer/executive character in *Behind the Scenes* (also rendering Japanese 杏子 Kyōko/Anzu)

morphemes.meaning: diminutive noun suffix (-zi); feminine name suffix (-zǐ / Japanese -ko)

杏子.notes: Pay attention to tone! When meaning the fruit "apricot", 子 is neutral tone (xìngzi); when used as the character's given name "Xingzi" (as in 杏子姐 in *Behind the Scenes*), 子 keeps its full third tone (Xìngzǐ).

rootFamily.gloss: Sister Xingzi (respectful workplace form of address)

杏子姐.etymology: A vocative and titular compound combining the personal name 杏子 (Xìngzǐ) with the kinship honorific suffix 姐 (jiě, originally "mother" in ancient Chu dialect recorded in *Shuowen Jiezi*, shifting by the Tang–Song periods to mean "elder sister"). In contemporary Chinese media, entertainment, and corporate culture, appending 姐 (or 哥 "elder brother") to a colleague's or senior's given name expresses warm deference, professional respect, and camaraderie without the stiffness of bureaucratic titles.

history.meaning: mother (regional Chu dialect term recorded in Han lexicons)
elder sister; respectful address for a young or senior woman
"Sister Xingzi" — deferential yet approachable workplace address for a senior female mentor/executive

morphemes.meaning: elder sister; respectful title for a senior female colleague or mentor

杏子姐.notes: In Chinese film sets and television agencies, calling a senior female producer or star "[Name]+姐" (like 杏子姐) is the universal etiquette: it signals respect for her seniority and industry clout while keeping the relationship warm and collaborative.

rootFamily.gloss: young lady; Miss; eldest daughter of a prominent family (大小姐)

cognates.meaning: material; ingredients; data or factors (e.g., in market analysis)

材料.etymology: A coordinative compound uniting 材 (cái, originally "timber suitable for carpentry", hence "raw physical material, natural talent") and 料 (liào, phono-semantic graph of grain 米 in a measuring斗 dǒu, meaning "to measure grain, calculate, provision, stuff/ingredients"). Attested from Song–Ming vernacular and administrative prose for building supplies or culinary ingredients, it broadened in modern Mandarin to include written dossiers, archival evidence, and creative source material.

history.meaning: cut timber for construction + measured grain/provisions; to calculate
raw materials for crafting/building; culinary ingredients; personal aptitude/makings of a talent
raw materials; cooking ingredients; written dossier, application documents, or creative source files

材料.notes: Highly versatile across registers: in a kitchen it means "ingredients"; in an office or TV production room it means "dossier/reference documents" (交材料 "submit paperwork"); colloquially, 不是那块材料 means "not cut out for that job".

rootFamily.gloss: literary or creative subject matter / source material
theme; subject matter (of a film or show)

条.etymology: Measure word for long, narrow, or winding things: streets, lanes, rivers, towels, trousers, and legal clauses (一条老街 'an old street', 一条毛巾 'a towel'). In the Classic of Poetry, 條 originally named a long, slender tree branch, from which the long-strip classifier grew.

history.meaning: long slender branch
classifier for streets, rivers, ropes, clauses

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 條 (via 萌典)

条件.etymology: Originally a Tang–Song legal and bureaucratic compound 條件 (tiáojiàn) combining 条 (tiáo, Traditional 條, "slender branch", extended to "itemized clause or article of law") and 件 (jiàn, "to divide and enumerate cattle/items", hence "individual item or document"). In pre-modern Chinese it meant "itemized articles or clauses in an official document". In Meiji Japan, 条件 (*jōken*) was used to translate European philosophical and legal "condition" (*Bedingung* / *condicio*), and this sense returned to modern Chinese for contractual terms, prerequisites, and personal qualifications.

history.meaning: slender tree branch / statutory clause + enumerated item or document
itemized clauses, articles, or stipulations listed in an official memorial or contract
prerequisite, contractual term, logical condition, or personal/material qualification (reinforced via Japanese 条件 *jōken*)

条件.notes: In business negotiations (*Behind the Scenes*), 谈条件 or 讲条件 means "to negotiate terms" or "bargain"; when describing a person or studio (他自身条件很好), it means "qualifications, assets, or background advantages".

rootFamily.gloss: clause; article; provision in a contract

条例.etymology: Coordinative legal noun compound of 条 (條, 'branch -> numbered article or clause of a code') + 例 ('precedent, rule, regulation'): 'regulations, ordinances, bylaws, statutory rules'. Attested since Tang–Song administrative law.

history.stage: Tang–Song administrative law to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: codified articles and regulations; ordinance

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 条例 (via 萌典)

条文.etymology: Compound legal noun of 条 (條, 'numbered clause, article') + 文 ('written text, wording'): 'written clauses or provisions (of a law, contract, or regulation)'.

history.stage: Tang–Song legal Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: written articles or clauses of a law/contract

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 条文 (via 萌典)

来.etymology: Pictograph (來) in Shang oracle-bone script of a ripening wheat plant (麦) with awns, ears, and roots. Because wheat was traditionally seen as aheaven-sent grain that 'came' from afar, 來 was borrowed from the earliest inscriptions for the verb 'come (toward the speaker), arrive; next/future (来年); do (a colloquial pro-verb); approximate number suffix (十来个); since (三天来)'.

history.meaning: wheat plant graph borrowed for 'come, arrive'
come; arrive; pro-verb; directional complement toward speaker

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 来 (via 萌典)

来不了.etymology: A modern Mandarin negative potential verb-complement construction (V + 不 + 了 liǎo) composed of 来 (lái, Traditional 來, originally a pictograph of wheat *mˤrək, phonetically borrowed in Old Chinese for "to come, arrive"), the negative infix 不 (bù, "not"), and the phase/completion complement 了 (liǎo, originally "to finish, conclude, understand", functioning here as a modal marker of capability). Literally "to come—not—finish/manage", i.e., "unable to come or make it".

history.meaning: wheat / to come + negator + to finish or bring to completion
cannot manage to come; prevented by circumstances from arriving

morphemes.meaning: to come; to arrive; to attend
not; unable to (in V-不-C potential constructions)
to complete; to be able to carry through (pronounced liǎo)

来不了.notes: The complement 了 here is always pronounced liǎo (third tone), never neutral-tone le! Its affirmative counterpart is 来得了 (lái de liǎo, "able to come / can make it"). Very common when a guest or artist has a scheduling conflict.

rootFamily.gloss: able to come; can make it (affirmative counterpart)
have enough time to; can make it in time

来不及.etymology: Potential verb-complement compound combining 来 ('come, make it in time') + 不 ('not') + 及 ('reach, catch up with in time'): 'there's not enough time (to do something), too late to'.

history.meaning: cannot make it in time; too late

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 来不及 (via 萌典)

来信.etymology: Modifier-head / verb-object compound of 来 ('come toward the recipient, incoming') + 信 ('letter'): 'incoming letter, your letter; send a letter here'.

history.stage: Tang–Song epistolary Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: incoming letter; send a letter

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 来信 (via 萌典)

来到.etymology: A directional/resultative verb-complement compound combining 来 (lái, Traditional 來, "to come, move toward the speaker or focal point") and 到 (dào, "to arrive at, reach a destination"). Formed during the medieval vernacular grammaticalization of serial verbs into verb-resultative compounds, allowing 來 (which in strict Classical Chinese rarely took a direct locative object without a preposition or resultative) to directly govern a destination noun phrase.

history.meaning: serial verbs: to come toward + to arrive at a destination
to come to; to arrive at (a place, stage, or moment)

来到.notes: Unlike bare 来, 来到 is slightly more formal/narrative and requires a concrete or abstract location object immediately after it (e.g., 欢迎来到我们的节目 "Welcome to our show!"; 比赛来到了关键时刻 "The competition has reached a critical moment").

rootFamily.gloss: to arrive; to reach; to achieve
to come from; to hail from

来回.etymology: Antonymic directional compound pairing 来 ('come') + 回 ('return, go back'): 'go back and forth, round trip; a round trip (as a noun/classifier)'.

history.meaning: back and forth; round trip

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 来回 (via 萌典)

来得及.etymology: A positive potential verb-complement construction (V + 得 + 及) combining 来 (lái, Traditional 來, used here as a dummy/modal verb of action or temporal arrival), the structural potential infix 得 (de, originally "to obtain, succeed"), and the classical verb 及 (jí, oracle bone pictograph of a hand 又 catching up to a person 人 from behind, meaning "to overtake, reach in time"). Literally "able to come up and catch in time", hence having enough time before a deadline.

history.meaning: to catch up to a person from behind; to reach in time; to extend to
there is still enough time to act; able to make it before a deadline

morphemes.meaning: to come; to bring about an action in time
able to; obtains the possibility of (in V-得-C constructions)
to catch up with; to reach in time

来得及.notes: Always paired in learners' minds with its negative twin 来不及 (láibují, "too late / not enough time"). In live broadcast emergencies, 只要现在改还来得及 means "As long as we change it now, we can still make it in time!"

rootFamily.gloss: too late; not enough time to (negative counterpart)
cannot come; unable to make it

来日方长.etymology: A four-character Classical-style subject-predicate idiom (成语 chéngyǔ): 来日 (láirì, Traditional 來日, modifier-head compound meaning "coming days, the future", attested in the *Book of Odes* and Han poetry) serves as the subject, while 方长 (fāngcháng, adverb 方 "just now, right in the midst of, still" + stative verb 长 cháng, Traditional 長, "long, stretching far") serves as the predicate. Literally "the days to come are still stretching long ahead".

history.meaning: coming days (the future) + are just now beginning to stretch long ahead
there is plenty of time ahead for us to collaborate, settle scores, or see how things turn out

morphemes.meaning: just now; still; right in the process of

来日方长.notes: Pragmatically dual-edged in dramas like *Behind the Scenes*: said warmly to a friend or mentor, it means "we have plenty of time ahead to work together or repay your kindness"; said coolly to a rival after a setback, it is a veiled warning ("this isn't over yet—we'll see who wins in the long run").

rootFamily.gloss: over a long period; in the long run (日久天长)
just unfolding; in the ascendant (方兴未艾)

来自.etymology: A verb-preposition compound fusing the directional verb 来 (lái, Traditional 來, "to come") with the Classical Chinese ablative preposition 自 (zì, originally an oracle-bone pictograph of a human nose, extended in Old Chinese to mean "self" and prepositional "from, originating in"). In Classical syntax, 來自 [Place] was parsed as "[Subject] comes [from Place]"; in modern Mandarin it has lexicalized into a single transitive verb meaning "to come from, hail from, or originate in".

history.meaning: verb "to come" followed by ablative preposition "from [a source/origin]"
lexicalized transitive verb: to hail from, originate in, or stem from

来自.notes: A staple of broadcast introductions (e.g., 欢迎来自北京的选手 "Welcome the contestant from Beijing") as well as abstract sources (压力来自各方 "pressure comes from all sides"). Unlike 从...来, 来自 cannot be split and takes its source directly as an object.

rootFamily.gloss: to originate from; to stem from (more formal)
to come to; to arrive at

来讲.etymology: A discourse-marking particle phrase formed from the purposive/modal linker 来 (lái, Traditional 來, grammaticalized from "to come" into a prospective linker before a verb, akin to "to proceed to") and 讲 (jiǎng, Traditional 講, originally "to practice, expound, explain Classics", later "to speak, discuss"). Always closes a prepositional frame (对/从/按 X 来讲, literally "taking X to speak of it"), marking the perspective, standard, or experiencer of a judgment.

history.meaning: to expound, explain, or practice military/scholarly arts
clause-final perspective marker: speaking of; from the standpoint of (used with 对/从/按...)

morphemes.meaning: to speak; to explain; to discuss

来讲.notes: Nearly interchangeable with 来说 (láishuō) in frames like 对我来讲 ("as far as I'm concerned") or 从收视率来讲 ("in terms of ratings"), though 来讲 sounds slightly more analytical or southern/cantonese-influenced in spoken commentary.

rootFamily.gloss: as far as ... is concerned; speaking of (near-synonym)
to speak; to give a speech; remarks
to be particular about; to pay attention to nuance/craft

来说.etymology: A grammaticalized topic-perspective particle phrase combining the modal linker 来 (lái, Traditional 來, "to come / proceed to") with 说 (shuō, Traditional 說, originally "to explain, unpack in words, persuade"). Used at the end of a prepositional phrase headed by 对 (duì), 从 (cóng), or 一般 (yībān) to frame the topic or vantage point from which a statement holds true ("to speak of it from X's angle").

history.meaning: to explain, expound, or set forth an argument in speech
topic-framing particle: as far as [X] is concerned; speaking from the angle of [X]

morphemes.meaning: to say; to speak; to explain

来说.notes: Almost never stands alone at the start of a sentence without a preceding modifier or prepositional phrase: pair it as 对...来说 ("for / as far as ... is concerned"), 从...来说 ("from the perspective of..."), or 一般来说 ("generally speaking").

rootFamily.gloss: way of putting things; statement; explanation

杯.etymology: Noun 'cup' and measure word for cupfuls or glassfuls of drinks (一杯热茶 'a cup of hot tea', 一杯咖啡 'a cup of coffee'). Written with 木 ('wood', reflecting early lacquered wooden drinking vessels) and 不 phonetic, 杯 is attested in Classical banqueting scenes in the Shiji and Mencius.

history.meaning: drinking cup

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 杯 (via 萌典)

杯子.etymology: Formed from 杯 ('cup', phono-semantic character with 木 'wood'—reflecting early lacquered wooden drinking vessels—and phonetic 不) plus the nominalizing diminutive suffix 子 (neutral tone zi), which turns monosyllabic nouns into natural two-syllable spoken Mandarin words.

history.meaning: lacquered wooden or ceramic wine/soup cup
cup; mug; glass

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 杯子 (via 萌典)

松.etymology: Merged simplified graph representing two historical characters: (1) 松 (wood 木 + 公 gōng/sōng phonetic: 'pine tree', symbol of longevity and resilience in Chinese culture) and (2) 鬆 (hair 髟 + 松 sōng phonetic: 'loose, disheveled hair -> loose, slack, relax, loosen, soft and flaky').

history.form: 松 (pine tree) / 鬆 (loose, slack, relax)
history.meaning: pine tree vs. loose/unfastened
loose; relax; loosen; pine tree

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 松 (via 萌典)

极了.etymology: Post-adjectival degree intensifier combining 极 (極, 'ridgepole of a roof -> utmost point, extreme') + modal particle 了 (le): placed directly after an adjective or psychological verb (好极了 'wonderful!', 高兴极了 'extremely happy') to mean 'extremely, to the utmost'.

history.meaning: post-predicate superlative intensifier 'extremely, awfully'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 极了 (via 萌典)

极端.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 极 (jí, Traditional 極, originally the highest ridgepole of a roof in Old Chinese, hence "zenith, pole, utmost limit") and 端 (duān, "tip, extremity, starting point, end of a thread"). While both characters appear in Classical philosophy, 極端 was popularized in Meiji Japan (*kyokutan*) as a translation of English/French "extreme" (Latin *extremus*, "outermost end") and re-entered late Qing Chinese as both a noun ("an extreme") and an adjective ("radical, extreme").

history.meaning: roof ridgepole / utmost pole + tip, sprouting shoot, or end point
outermost boundary or opposite pole; extreme (translating Western "extreme")
history.stage: Meiji Japanese / Late Qing Return Loan

history.meaning: extreme, radical, or polarized (in behavior, weather, or ideology); an extreme (走极端)

极端.notes: Used both as an adjective/adverb (极端天气 "extreme weather", 想法太极端 "thinking is too extreme") and as a noun in the high-frequency verb-object phrase 走极端 (zǒu jíduān, "to go to extremes").

极端组织.etymology: A modern four-character modifier-head nominal compound uniting 极端 (jíduān, Traditional 極端, "extreme, radical, extremist") and 组织 (zǔzhī, Traditional 組織, originally a coordinative silk-weaving verb compound in Classical Chinese—组 "to braid silk cords/ribbons" + 织 "to weave cloth on a loom"—which in Meiji Japan 組織 *soshiki* was repurposed to translate biological "tissue" and sociological "organization"). In contemporary news and security broadcasts, it specifically designates an "extremist organization".

history.meaning: to braid silk cords + to weave textiles on a loom (figuratively, to structure literary or state patterns)
organic tissue; institutional or political organization (modern Sino-Japanese semantic loan)
extremist group or militant radical organization (standard journalistic/broadcast term)

morphemes.meaning: organization; organized group (lit. braiding cords and weaving cloth)

极端组织.notes: Standard broadcast journalism and newsroom terminology (relevant to crisis reporting segments in media dramas). Note how 组织 retains its textile metaphor in phrases like 严密的组织 ("a tightly woven/structured organization").

极限.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 极 (jí, Traditional 極, "roof ridgepole, utmost pole, highest degree") and 限 (xiàn, "threshold, boundary, limit"). Attested in late imperial prose for a final boundary or allotted lifespan, and formalized in modern Sino-Japanese scientific and mathematical terminology (Japanese 極限 *kyokugen*) to render calculus "limit" (*limes*) as well as the maximum physical or psychological endurance threshold.

history.meaning: highest ridgepole / zenith + physical threshold or barrier
mathematical limit in calculus; maximum physical boundary
utmost limit of human endurance, capacity, or time; extreme (as in 极限运动 "extreme sports")

极限.notes: Whereas 极端 (jíduān) means "polarized/radical", 极限 (jíxiàn) means the "maximum ceiling or breaking point" of capacity, stamina, or deadlines (e.g., 挑战极限 "challenge the limits", 突破极限 "break through one's limits", 极限运动 "extreme sports"). Also gave rise to the hit Chinese variety show 极限挑战 (*Go Fighting!*).

rootFamily.gloss: limited; finite (e.g., 有限公司 Ltd.)

cognates.meaning: to frame; to entrap by fabrication (literary)

构陷.etymology: A literary coordinative/manner-result verb compound attested in dynastic histories (*Book of Later Han*, *New Book of Tang*), uniting 构 (gòu, Traditional 構, originally "to interlock wooden beams in carpentry", extended to "fabricate, concoct a plot") and 陷 (xiàn, oracle bone/seal graph of a person 人 falling into a pit 臼 next to a mound 阜, meaning "to plunge into a pitfall, entrap, incriminate"). Literally "to build a fabrication so as to drop someone into a trap".

history.meaning: to interlock timber / concoct a scheme + to drop someone into a pitfall or snare
to weave false charges at court in order to bring about a rival's downfall
to frame; to maliciously fabricate evidence and falsely implicate someone

morphemes.meaning: to construct; to fabricate; to plot (from interlocking timber 構)
to entrap in a pitfall; to frame; to incriminate

构陷.notes: High-register literary verb favored in workplace thrillers, palace dramas, and media rivalries (*Behind the Scenes*) when a competitor fabricates a scandal or leaks doctored material to ruin someone's career. More formal than 陷害 (xiànhài) or 栽赃 (zāizāng).

rootFamily.gloss: to frame; to set up and harm someone (more common everyday synonym)
to fabricate; to make up out of thin air; fictional
to sink into; to fall into (a crisis or quagmire)

枉费.etymology: A modifier-head verb compound attested in Tang–Song poetry and Ming–Qing vernacular novels (*Dream of the Red Chamber*), combining 枉 (wǎng, originally "crooked or warped wood", extended in Classical Chinese to "unjustly, in vain, to no purpose") and 费 (fèi, Traditional 費, "to expend, squander, consume wealth or effort"). Literally "to expend in vain", i.e., to waste painstaking effort or resources for nothing.

history.meaning: crooked wood / unjustly, in vain + to expend or squander resources
to waste or expend (effort, thought, or words) to no avail
to waste in vain; to squander painstaking effort or goodwill

morphemes.meaning: in vain; futilely; to no purpose (orig. crooked timber)
to expend; to spend; to waste; to consume

枉费.notes: Almost always collocates with mental effort, devotion, or goodwill: 枉费心机 ("scheme in vain / waste one's cálculos"), 枉费心血 ("waste one's blood, sweat, and tears"), or 枉费一番苦心 ("waste someone's painstaking good intentions"). Compare 浪费 (làngfèi), which applies broadly to wasting money, food, or time.

rootFamily.gloss: to waste; to squander (time, money, resources)
to wrong someone; injustice; to do something in vain (冤枉路)
to expend; to cost; to consume (time/effort)

枕头.etymology: Colloquial noun formed from 枕 ('wooden headrest/pillow', wood 木 + 冘 yín, because ancient Chinese pillows were carved from wood, bamboo, or porcelain before cloth/filled pillows) + nominal suffix 头 (頭, neutral tone tou): 'pillow'.

history.meaning: pillow

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 枕头 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: counter for flat, thin objects (sheets of paper, plates, coins, shirts)
counter for flat sheets, medals, or leaves
classifier for coins, medals, or wooden gags; plum blossom (homograph)

枚.etymology: From Old Chinese *mˤə (Middle Chinese *muʌi), written with the wood radical 木 and phonetic 攵/卜. Originally in the *Book of Odes* and *Rites of Zhou*, 枚 meant a "tree trunk, stem, or slender wooden stick" (including the wooden gag 銜枚 held in soldiers' mouths during night marches to enforce silence). By the Han and Six Dynasties periods, counting sticks led 枚 to grammaticalize into a general classifier for countable objects, narrowing in modern Mandarin to small, finely crafted or disc-shaped items like rings, coins, medals, stamps, and missiles.

history.meaning: tree stem, slender wooden switch, or wooden gag held between a soldier's teeth during stealth marches
general measure word for countable items (statues, fruits, utensils, coins)
specialized classifier for small exquisite items (rings, coins, medals, badges, stamps) and projectiles (missiles, rockets); playful internet classifier for people (一枚小鲜肉)

morphemes.meaning: classifier for rings, coins, medals, stamps, and missiles (orig. tree stem / wooden tally stick)

枚.notes: A high-taste classifier! Use 一枚戒指 for a ring, 一枚奖章 for a medal, 一枚邮票 for a stamp, and (by shape/precision) 一枚火箭 for a rocket. In playful modern social media slang, young speakers also use 一枚 for people (e.g., 吃货一枚 "onecertified foodie", 美女一枚 "one total beauty"). Note the false friend with Japanese 枚 (*mai*), which counts flat sheets like paper or T-shirts (Mandarin uses 张 or 件 for those).

rootFamily.gloss: impossible to enumerate one by one; too numerous to count (idiom)
to march in silence with wooden gags in mouth; to advance stealthily (idiom)

cognates.meaning: fruit; nut; berry; legal fruits/proceeds of property
fruit (of a tree); figurative fruits of effort
fruit; botanical pericarp and seed; figurative fruit of labor

果实.etymology: A coordinative compound uniting 果 (guǒ, oracle bone pictograph of round fruits hanging atop a tree 木, meaning "tree fruit, result, outcome") and 实 (shí, Traditional 實, originally strings of cowrie shells 貫 under a roof 宀, meaning "full, solid, seed/fruit of a plant"). In Classical Chinese botanical glosses, 果 denoted tree fruit and 實 denoted grain/seed or flesh; combined as 果實, it signifies both literal botanical fruit and the hard-won "fruits of labor" or creative achievement.

history.meaning: tree-borne fruit + plant seed/grain (originally a house full of cowrie treasure)
ripened fruit and seeds of plants; harvest yield
botanical fruit (as opposed to grocery 水果); figurative fruits of labor, victory, or creative production

morphemes.meaning: fruit on a tree; outcome; result

果实.notes: Learner distinction: 水果 (shuǐguǒ, "watery fruit") is culinary fruit you buy at the supermarket to eat (apples, bananas); 果实 (guǒshí) is either botanical fruit on a plant (结出果实 "bear fruit") or metaphorical "fruits of labor/success" (胜利的果实 "fruits of victory", 劳动果实 "fruits of one's hard work"). In showbiz dramas, 窃取别人的劳动果实 means "stealing the fruits of someone else's creative labor".

rootFamily.gloss: achievement; positive result of work or research

果汁.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正结构) formed from 果 (guǒ, 'tree fruit', originally a pictograph of fruit atop a tree 木) and 汁 (zhī, 'liquid, sap, broth', phono-semantic compound with 氵 'water' and 十 phonetic). Attested in medieval Chinese medical and culinary texts for the pressed liquid of fruits, it now serves as the standard term for fruit juice.

history.meaning: tree fruit + pressed liquid, broth, or sap
extracted liquid or juice of fruits used in medicine and drink
fruit juice (commercial or freshly squeezed beverage)

果汁.notes: Often paired with 鲜榨 (xiānzhà, 'freshly squeezed') in cafe and catering contexts; Takes the classifiers 杯 (bēi, 'cup/glass') or 瓶 (píng, 'bottle').

果然.etymology: Derived from Classical Chinese 果 (guǒ, 'to come to fruition; in fact, really', extended from the sense of a tree bearing actual fruit rather than mere blossoms) suffixed with the adverbial/stative marker 然 (rán, 'to be so, thus'). Literally 'coming to fruition thus', it expresses that an outcome matches prior expectation or hypothesis.

history.meaning: to bear fruit / turn out in reality + to be thus, so
truly, really; as expected (also attested with the variant sense 'full-bellied' in Zhuangzi)
sure enough, just as expected

morphemes.meaning: actually, turning out in fact (from 'to bear fruit')

果然.notes: Used when an actual event confirms what the speaker or subject previously guessed (e.g., 果然不出所料, 'sure enough, just as predicted'); contrast with 果真 ('if indeed / really').

果酱.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 果 ('fruit') + 酱 (醬, 'thick fermented or cooked paste/sauce'): 'jam, fruit preserves, marmalade'.

history.meaning: fruit jam; preserves

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 果酱 (via 萌典)

枝.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining the wood radical 木 ('tree/plant') + phonetic 支 (*zhī*, itself originally a hand holding a bamboo sprig). Used since the *Classic of Poetry* both as a noun ('tree branch; twig') and as the graceful measure word for cut flower stems and herb sprigs (两小枝香草).

history.meaning: branch or twig of a tree
sprig; stem; branch (measure word)

枝条.etymology: Coordinative botanical noun compound pairing 枝 ('tree branch', wood 木 + 支) + 条 (條, 'slender twig, shoot'): 'branches and twigs, slender boughs'. Attested since the漢書 Book of Han and Six Dynasties poetry.

history.stage: Han–Six Dynasties Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: branches and slender twigs

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 枝条 (via 萌典)

架.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 加 (jiā, 'place one atop another') + 木 ('wood'): 'wooden frame, rack, stand, shelf, trestle; prop up, support; quarrel/fight (吵架, 打架); classifier for framed machines, aircraft, pianos, or cameras (一架飞机, 一架钢琴)'.

history.meaning: wooden frame; rack; prop up
shelf/frame; prop up; classifier for planes, pianos, machines

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 架 (via 萌典)

架势.etymology: A modifier-head vernacular compound combining 架 (jià, 'frame, rack, structural stance', especially the poised framework of the body in martial arts and opera) and 势 (shì, 'posture, momentum, configuration of force', Traditional 勢). Originally describing a martial artist's or performer's physical stance, it broadened in Mandarin to mean 'the look of things' or an imposing posture.

history.meaning: supporting frame/stance + strategic posture or momentum
physical stance in martial arts; outward posture, bearing, or the developing look of a situation
posture, stance, the look of things (often read with neutral tone jiàshi)

架势.notes: Frequently appears in the colloquial frame 看这架势 (kàn zhè jiàshi, 'looking at how things are shaping up') or 摆架势 ('to strike a pose / put on airs').

架子.etymology: Colloquial noun formed from 架 ('wooden frame, stand, rack') + nominal suffix 子 (neutral tone zi): means literally 'shelf, rack, stand, framework' and figuratively 'haughty airs, pretension (摆架子 put on airs)'.

history.meaning: shelf; rack; stand; framework; haughty airs

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 架子 (via 萌典)

架空.etymology: A verb-object / resultative compound from 架 (jià, 'to prop up on a frame, to elevate on trestles') and 空 (kōng, 'empty, in mid-air, hollowed out'). Literally 'to prop up into thin air' (attested in medieval poetry for spanning an abyss, e.g., high bridges), in modern political and corporate usage it means elevating or surrounding someone so their feet no longer touch the ground of real operational power—turning them into a figurehead.

history.meaning: built high in the air; spanning empty space (as of trestles or bridges)
unfounded, detached from reality; suspended overhead (e.g., power lines)
to strip of real authority, to sideline into a figurehead; (in fiction) alternate-universe/fictional setting

morphemes.meaning: to prop up, to elevate on a frame
empty, in mid-air, devoid of substance

架空.notes: In workplace and political dramas like *Behind the Scenes*, 被架空 (bèi jiàkōng) is the classic term for an executive whose subordinates bypass them, leaving them with a title but no real authority.

某.etymology: In Oracle Bone and Bronze inscriptions, 某 (mǒu) was a compound ideograph of 甘 ('sweet/mouth') atop 木 ('tree'), originally depicting the sour plum later written with the determinative 梅 (méi). Because of phonetic similarity in Old Chinese (*mɯːʔ), 某 was borrowed early in Classical ritual and legal texts (such as the *Yili*) as an indefinite placeholder pronoun ('so-and-so, a certain person or thing') when the specific name was unknown or intentionally withheld.

history.meaning: sour plum (original graph for 梅); borrowed as placeholder for an unspecified name in ritual templates
a certain (person, place, or time); humble first-person pronoun 'I, so-and-so' in vernacular fiction
a certain, some (unspecified determiner before nouns or surnames, e.g., 张某)

某.notes: Placed before a noun/measure word (某天 'a certain day', 某位 'a certain person') or after a surname in legal/news reporting (王某 'a certain Mr./Ms. Wang') to preserve anonymity.

某个人.etymology: A modern Mandarin determiner-classifier-noun phrase composed of the indefinite determiner 某 (mǒu, 'a certain'), the general individual classifier 个 (gè, Traditional 個), and 人 (rén, 'person'). Insertion of the classifier 个 individuates the referent more vividly and colloquially than the compact Literary-derived compound 某人.

history.meaning: a certain + individual classifier + person
a certain someone, some specific individual

某个人.notes: In conversation, 某个人 can either mean 'some specific person' generally or coyly hint at a particular person present in the room ('a certain someone').

cognates.meaning: a certain person; I (humble archaic, bōjin)

某人.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining the Classical indefinite determiner 某 (mǒu, 'a certain, unspecified') directly with 人 (rén, 'person') without an intervening classifier. Directly inherited from Literary Chinese, where it designated an unnamed or confidentially referenced individual ('so-and-so').

history.meaning: a certain unnamed person, so-and-so
someone, a certain person (often used playfully or pointedly for a known person left unnamed)

某人.notes: In teased or ironic dialogue, speakers often say 某人 ('a certain somebody') while looking directly at the person they are talking about.

柔化.etymology: Derived causative verb combining 柔 ('soft, gentle, supple', 矛 + 木 'pliable wood') + verbalizing suffix 化 ('transform into, -ize, -en'): 'soften (light, edges, tone, or contrast), make gentle'.

history.meaning: soften; make gentle or mellow

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 柔化 (via 萌典)

柔和.etymology: Coordinative adjective compound of 柔 ('soft, supple, gentle') + 和 ('mild, gentle, harmonious'): 'soft, gentle, mild (of light, colors, music, voice, or breeze)'. Attested since Classical prose and poetry.

history.meaning: soft and gentle; mild; mellow

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 柔和 (via 萌典)

柔软.etymology: Coordinate synonym compound of 柔 ('supple; pliant like young wood',矛 + 木) + 软 ('soft; yielding', cart radical 车 + 欠, originally 'spongy wheel spokes'). Together they describe pleasant softness and pliability in bread dough, cushions, fabrics, or gentle voices.

history.meaning: soft and supple
soft; supple

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 柔软

cognates.meaning: yuzu citrus (Citrus junos), borrowed from Chinese 柚子

柚子.etymology: Formed from 柚 (yòu, a phono-semantic character with 木 'tree' and 由 phonetic, attested as early as the *Shujing* and *Shan Hai Jing* for the pomelo, *Citrus maxima*) plus the nominal suffix 子 (zi). While in Chinese 柚子 refers primarily to the large thick-rinded pomelo, the compound was borrowed into Japanese as *yuzu* for *Citrus junos* (known in Chinese botanical terminology as 香橙).

history.meaning: pomelo tree and its fruit (Citrus maxima)
pomelo fruit (suffixed with nominal diminutive/noun formative 子)
pomelo (and by cross-cultural beverage/culinary influence, sometimes used in translating Japanese yuzu products)

柚子.notes: Beware the false friend between East Asian languages: in standard Mandarin 柚子 is the large sweet pomelo (*Citrus maxima*), whereas Korean *yuja* (유자茶 / 柚子茶) and Japanese *yuzu* refer to the smaller, tart *Citrus junos* (香橙).

柜台.etymology: Compound noun of 柜 (櫃, 'cabinet, chest') + 台 (臺, 'raised counter, platform'): 'shop counter, service desk/counter (in a store, hotel, bank, or airport)'.

history.stage: Ming–Qing commercial vernacular to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: shop counter; service counter

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 柜台 (via 萌典)

柜子.etymology: Colloquial noun formed from 柜 (櫃, combining 木 'wood' + 巨/匱 guì: 'wooden storage cabinet or chest') + nominal suffix 子 (neutral tone zi): 'cabinet, cupboard, wardrobe, chest'.

history.meaning: cabinet; cupboard; wardrobe

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 柜子 (via 萌典)

柠檬.etymology: Disyllabic phonetic loan for 'lemon' written with two tree-radical characters (木 + 宁 níng and 木 + 蒙 méng). Attested in Song–Yuan maritime and botanical records (such as Fan Chengda's Guihai Yuheng Zhi and southern trade glossaries) transcribing Indo-Iranian / Malay-Arabic citrus terms ultimately akin to Sanskrit nimbū and Persian līmūn.

morphemes.kind: phonetic loan syllable (with 木 tree radical)
phonetic loan syllable (with 木 tree radical)

history.meaning: tart citrus fruit cultivated in Lingnan
lemon

cognates.meaning: citrus fruit borrowed along the same Indo-Persian trade network

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 柠檬 (via 萌典)

柠檬塔.etymology: Three-character culinary compound combining 柠檬 ('lemon', a phonetic loan via Cantonese/Southeast Asian trade from Persian/Arabic līmūn / English lemon, written with the tree radical 木) + 塔 ('tart', phonetic loan from French tarte / English tart): 'lemon tart'.

history.meaning: lemon tart

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 柠檬塔 (via 萌典)

柠檬挞.etymology: Three-character culinary compound combining 柠檬 ('lemon') + 挞 (撻, tà, phonetic transcription of 'tart'): 'lemon tart' (orthographic variant of 柠檬塔 using 挞 specifically for Western pastry tarts).

history.meaning: lemon tart

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 柠檬挞 (via 萌典)

柠檬汁.etymology: Three-morpheme culinary noun combining 柠檬 ('lemon', a Song–Yuan phonetic loan via Cantonese/Persian *līmūn*, written with wood radical 木) + 汁 ('pressed liquid; juice', water radical 氵 + 十). It denotes freshly squeezed lemon juice used in tea and pastry making.

history.meaning: lemon fruit (loanword from Persian/Arabic līmūn)
lemon juice

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 柠檬汁

柠檬酱.etymology: Culinary compound of 柠檬 ('lemon') + 酱 ('thick cooked condiment, spread, or curd'). In pastry kitchens, 柠檬酱 refers specifically to glossy lemon curd cooked gently from fresh lemon juice, egg yolks, sugar, and butter to fill tart shells.

history.meaning: lemon curd; lemon spread

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 柠檬酱

查.etymology: Originally written  or 楂 and interchangeable with 槎 (chá, 'wooden raft; felled timber', combining 木 'tree/wood' and 且 phonetic). In medieval administrative and legal usage, 查 was adopted (replacing or converging with 察 chá, 'to examine closely') to mean 'to audit, inspect official records, or look up information'.

history.meaning: wooden raft in water; tree stump (variant of 槎)
to inspect official dossiers, audit, investigate (converging functionally with 察)
to check, look up (in a dictionary or database), investigate

morphemes.meaning: to check, examine, look up, investigate

查.notes: Covers both casual looking up of information (查字典 'look up in a dictionary', 查资料 'look up materials') and formal inspection or investigation (查案 'investigate a case'). When used as a surname, it is pronounced Zhā (as in Jin Yong's birth name, 查良镛 Zhā Liángyōng).

rootFamily.gloss: to look up and verify, consult

查出来.etymology: A verb-complement construction (动补结构) consisting of the action verb 查 (chá, 'to investigate, check, look into') and the complex directional-resultative complement 出来 (chūlái, literally 'to come out', figuratively 'to bring to light, uncover, or detect through an action').

history.meaning: to investigate + to emerge/exit + toward the speaker (directional/resultative serial construction)
to find out by investigation, to uncover or detect (truth, cause, or culprit)

morphemes.meaning: out into the open, uncovered (directional/resultative complement)

查出来.notes: Supports potential infixes: 查得出来 ('able to find out by investigating') and 查不出来 ('unable to uncover/detect').

rootFamily.gloss: to find out clearly, get to the bottom of

查无此人.etymology: A four-character semi-literary administrative formula (四字格) structured as two compressed clauses: 查 (chá, 'upon checking the register / investigation') + 无此人 (wú cǐ rén, 'there is no such person', using the Classical negative existential verb 无 and proximal demonstrative 此). Originating in postal, household registration (户籍), and bureaucratic endorsements, it passed into everyday speech.

history.meaning: upon checking the rolls, there is no such person (official endorsement on returned mail or registries)
no such person on record; 'return to sender: addressee unknown'

morphemes.meaning: to not have, there is not (literary existential negation)

查无此人.notes: Standard stamp on undeliverable mail in Chinese postal systems, and frequently used in drama scripts when a background check or database search turns up no trace of an alias.

rootFamily.gloss: unfounded, without factual basis upon checking

查查.etymology: Formed by full verbal reduplication (AA pattern) of 查 (chá, 'to check, look into, investigate'). In Mandarin grammar, reduplicating a volitional action verb marks delimitative aspect—indicating that the action is performed briefly, casually, or as a quick trial ('to have a look into, check a bit').

history.meaning: delimitative verbal reduplication: to check briefly or give something a quick look-up

morphemes.meaning: delimitative aspect marker (brief, informal, or tentative action)

查查.notes: The second syllable is pronounced in the neutral tone (chácha); softens commands or suggestions (e.g., 你帮我查查 'help me check real quick') compared to the bare verb 查.

rootFamily.gloss: to check a bit (expanded 查一查 variant)
to take a look (parallel AA verb reduplication)

栅栏.etymology: The noun '栅栏' (zhàlán, fence) consists of '栅' (palisade, fence) and '栏' (railing, pen). Both characters feature the wood radical, indicating their original construction materials. '栅' historically referred to a defensive wall made of wooden stakes, while '栏' was an enclosure for animals. In combination, '栅栏' refers to a barrier or fence, typically made of spaced wooden or metal posts, used to mark boundaries or prevent passage. The term retains its association with rural enclosures and boundary marking.

history.meaning: fence

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 栅栏

标.etymology: Simplified from 標 (biāo), composed of the tree/wood radical 木 and phonetic 票 (piào, originally sparks rising from fire). Its earliest sense in Han–Tang texts was the topmost slender branch of a tree—visible from afar—which extended naturally to wooden signposts, boundary markers, and banners, and as a verb to 'marking, numbering, or labeling' items.

morphemes.meaning: treetop marker 木 -> mark, number, or label (simplified from 標)

history.meaning: treetop; raised wooden marker post
mark; label; indicate with a sign or number

标准.etymology: A coordinative compound (联合结构) of two Classical measuring instruments: 标 (biāo, Traditional 標, 'treetop; uprightwooden sighting pole or gnomon used as a visible mark') and 准 (zhǔn, Traditional 準, 'water-level instrument used by carpenters and surveyors to establish horizontal levelness'). Already paired in Tang–Song prose (e.g., Du Fu) for a benchmark or model, it was reinforced in the late 19th and early 20th centuries via Japanese *hyōjun* (標準) as the translation of Western scientific and industrial 'standard' or 'criterion'.

history.meaning: upright sighting pole/mark + water-level gauge
model, benchmark, exemplar of measurement or conduct
standard, criterion (noun); standard, canonical, up to par (adjective, e.g., 标准普通话)

标准.notes: Note that Simplified Chinese merges 准 ('allow, approve') and 準 ('water level, accurate, standard') into 准; in 标准 it represents Traditional 準. Functions both as a noun ('a standard') and an adjective ('standard, textbook-quality').

标签.etymology: Compound of 标 ('treetop mark; sign; indicator', wood radical 木 + 票) + 签 ('inscribed bamboo slip or book tag', bamboo radical 竹 + 佥 *qiān*). Originally naming the titled paper or bamboo slips inserted into book scrolls, it is now the universal word for adhesive labels and tags.

history.meaning: inscribed title slip attached to a scroll or ledger
label; sticker; tag

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 标签

标题.etymology: Coordinative noun compound of 标 (標, 'treetop mark, signpost, label') + 题 (題, 'forehead -> inscription, title, heading'): 'title, heading, headline, caption'.

history.stage: Tang–Song literary & administrative Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: heading; title; headline

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 标题 (via 萌典)

栋.etymology: Phono-semantic character (棟) of 木 ('wood/tree') + 东 (東, dōng/dòng phonetic): in Classical architecture 'the main central ridgepole of a building' (preserved in 栋梁 'ridgepole and beam -> pillar of the state'). Because counting ridgepoles counted whole buildings, it became the standard classifier for 'a building, house, or apartment block (一栋楼)'.

history.meaning: central ridgepole of a roof
classifier for buildings and houses

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 栋 (via 萌典)

栏杆.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 栏杆. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 栏杆 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 栏杆 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 栏杆 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 栏杆. The etymology of 栏杆 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 栏杆
middle form of 栏杆
modern form of 栏杆

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 栏杆

树.etymology: Phono-semantic/ideographic character (traditional 樹, combining 木 'tree' + 尌 shù 'stand a drum upright with the hand'). In Classical Chinese, 'tree' as a noun was 木, while 樹 was the verb 'plant (trees), set up upright' (as in 百年树人). From the Six Dynasties and Tang period onward, 樹 replaced 木 as the everyday noun for a living 'tree'.

history.meaning: plant trees; set upright
tree; plant/establish

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 树 (via 萌典)

树下.etymology: Locative compound combining 树 ('tree') + 下 ('under, beneath'): 'under the tree, beneath the trees'.

history.stage: Six Dynasties–Tang poetry to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: under a tree

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 树下 (via 萌典)

树叶.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 树 ('tree') + 叶 (葉, 'leaf of a plant', originally depicting flat leaves growing on a tree 木, before葉 added the grass radical 艹 and simplified back to 叶): 'tree leaf, leaves, foliage'.

history.meaning: tree leaf; foliage

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 树叶 (via 萌典)

树荫.etymology: The noun '树荫' (shùyīn, shade of a tree) pairs '树' (tree) with '荫' (shade). In ancient texts, '荫' specifically denoted the protective cover provided by foliage, and by metaphorical extension, the protection or blessing bestowed by ancestors upon their descendants. '树荫' refers to the cool, dark area created by a tree blocking the sunlight. The term is evocative in Chinese literature, often associated with rest, summer heat relief, and idyllic rural scenes.

history.meaning: shady and cool

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 树荫

校际.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-compound combining 校 (xiào, 'school, college, academy', originally a wooden enclosure or military/educational stockade in Classical Chinese) and 际 (jì, Traditional 際, 'border, boundary, junction between two walls/realms', containing 阝 'mound/wall' and 祭 phonetic). Patterned on modern academic/diplomatic compounds in -际 (such as 国际 'international' and 人际 'interpersonal') to translate English *intercollegiate* or *interscholastic*.

history.meaning: school/enclosure + boundary, interval, or meeting point between two sides
intercollegiate, inter-school (between schools or universities)

校际.notes: A bound attributive adjective (非谓形容词) that modifies nouns directly without 的 in formal titles, such as 校际比赛 ('intercollegiate competition') or 校际交流 ('inter-university exchange').

校风.etymology: A modifier-head compound joining 校 (xiào, 'school, academy') and 风 (fēng, Traditional 風, 'wind', which already in the *Classic of Poetry* [Shijing] developed the metaphorical sense of 'prevailing moral influence, ethos, custom, or atmosphere', as winds sway grass). Together they denote the moral and intellectual ethos of an educational institution.

history.meaning: school + wind / prevailing moral custom and ethos
school ethos, campus spirit, institutional tradition and atmosphere

校风.notes: Often paired in Chinese school mottoes with 学风 (xuéfēng, 'academic ethos/study habits') and 教风 (jiàofēng, 'teaching ethos').

rootFamily.gloss: general mood, prevailing practice or custom

cognates.meaning: form, style, appearance; polite suffix (yō / sama)

样.etymology: Written 樣 in Traditional characters (simplified to 样), originally a phono-semantic compound with 木 ('tree') and 羕 (yàng, phonetic), denoting the oak tree or acorn (*Quercus acutissima*, cognate with 橡 xiàng). In Tang-dynasty vernacular and administrative texts, 樣 was borrowed phonetically for 'wooden pattern, mold, model, or shape', from which it grammaticalized into a noun and classifier meaning 'kind, sort, type, or appearance'.

history.meaning: acorn / oak tree (later differentiated as 橡)
pattern, model, mold, appearance, style
kind, sort, type (classifier); appearance, shape (noun)

样.notes: As a classifier, 样 (yàng) counts distinct 'kinds, sorts, or items' (e.g., 三样菜 'three kinds of dishes', 各种各样的 'all kinds and sorts of'). In Beijing speech, adding 儿 yields 样儿 (yàngr, 'look, air').

rootFamily.gloss: appearance, manner, the way things look
the same, alike, identical (lit. one pattern)

样子.etymology: Derived from 样 (yàng, Traditional 樣, 'pattern, model, shape, appearance') suffixed with the unstressed nominal formative 子 (zi). Attested since Tang and Song vernacular texts (such as Zen *yulu* dialogues and Song *huaben*) for a physical pattern or outward demeanor, it became the core Mandarin word for 'appearance, manner, or the state of things'.

history.meaning: model, pattern for shoes or garments; outward form or demeanor
appearance, look, manner, air; the way a situation looks

样子.notes: Extremely versatile: 看样子 (kàn yàngzi) means 'by the looks of it / it seems that', while 装样子 (zhuāng yàngzi) means 'to put on an act / go through the motions for show'.

核准.etymology: A verb-resultative / sequential administrative compound combining 核 (hé, 'to examine to the core, audit, verify', extended from 'fruit pit/stone' and graphic interchange with 覈 hé, 'to investigate rigorously') and 准 (zhǔn, 'to grant, permit, approve officially' in imperial and modern bureaucratic usage). Literally 'to audit and grant approval'.
