history.meaning: to examine facts strictly + to grant official permission
to examine and officially approve (a budget, application, or regulatory filing)

核准.notes: Belongs to formal bureaucratic, legal, and corporate register (e.g., 经有关部门核准 'upon examination and approval by the relevant authorities'); more formal than 批准 (pīzhǔn).

rootFamily.gloss: to examine and approve (synonymous official compound)
to audit, examine and verify (accounts or qualifications)

核对.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound formed from 核 (hé, 'to verify, audit, examine strictly', representing Classical 覈) and 对 (duì, Traditional 對, 'to match up, place face-to-face, compare against a counterpart'). Literally 'to audit and match side-by-side', used when cross-checking figures, tallies, or texts for discrepancies.

history.meaning: to investigate strictly + to match or compare side by side
to verify, check, cross-check (data, accounts, identity, or lists)

morphemes.meaning: to match, compare side by side, check against

核对.notes: Commonly collocated with data or records: 核对账目 ('verify accounts'), 核对名单 ('cross-check a roster'), or 核对身份 ('verify identity').

rootFamily.gloss: to compare, contrast against a standard

核心.etymology: A coordinative / modifier-head compound joining 核 (hé, 'hard pit or stone at the center of a fruit', phono-semantic with 木 'tree' and 亥 phonetic) and 心 (xīn, 'heart; central pith or inner core of a plant or organ'). Literally 'the heart of the fruit stone', it metaphorically denotes the indispensable central nucleus of an organization, theory, or system.

history.meaning: fruit stone/pit + heart or central pith
the innermost center, kernel, nucleus, core (of a group, issue, or technology)

核心.notes: Used both as a noun (团队的核心 'the core of the team') and an attributive modifier (核心竞争力 'core competitiveness', 核心人物 'key figure'). In fruit anatomy contexts, the literal pit is often pronounced hú (果核儿 guǒhúr) in colloquial northern Mandarin, but in 核心 it is always read hé.

rootFamily.gloss: atomic/nuclear energy (using 核 in its scientific sense 'nucleus')

核桃木.etymology: Three-character timber compound combining 核桃 ('walnut', originally 胡桃 'Central Asian peach/nut' introduced along the Silk Road during the Han dynasty, later written 核桃 'kernel peach') + 木 ('wood, timber'): 'walnut wood'.

history.meaning: walnut wood; walnut timber

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 核桃木 (via 萌典)

根.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 木 ('tree') + 艮 (gèn/gēn phonetic): 'root of a tree or plant; base, foot, foundation, cause/origin' and the standard classifier for long, slender objects (strings, wires, hairs, pillars, bananas, matches: 一根线).

history.meaning: root of a tree or plant; foundation
root; base; classifier for long slender objects

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 根 (via 萌典)

根据.etymology: Originally a Classical Chinese metaphor combining 根 (gēn, 'tree root', with 木 'tree' and 艮 phonetic) and 据 (jù, Traditional 據, 'to grasp with the hand, occupy, rely firmly upon', with 扌 'hand' and 豦 phonetic). First attested in historical prose (such as the *Records of the Three Kingdoms*) for 'taking root and occupying a stronghold', it evolved into a noun meaning 'foundation, grounds, basis' and grammaticalized in modern Mandarin into a preposition meaning 'according to, on the basis of'.

history.meaning: tree root + to hold fast, occupy, or rely upon
to take root firmly; an entrenched base or stronghold; foundational basis of an argument
basis, grounds, foundation (noun); according to, based on (preposition)

morphemes.meaning: root of a tree, foundation, origin

根据.notes: Functions both as a preposition (根据规定 'according to regulations') and as a noun (没有根据 'without foundation / baseless').

根本.etymology: Coordinative noun, adjective, and adverb compound pairing two Classical 'tree-root' words: 根 ('root') + 本 ('base/root of a trunk'). Means 'root, foundation, fundamental/essential', and before negatives (根本不/没) an emphatic adverb meaning 'at all, simply, from the ground up'.

history.meaning: roots and trunk base -> foundation, fundamental
fundamental; root; (with negation) at all, simply

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 根本 (via 萌典)

案例.etymology: A modifier-head legal and administrative compound from 案 (àn, originally 'short-legged wooden tray or magistrate's desk', hence by metonymy the official files, dossiers, and legal cases placed upon the magistrate's desk) and 例 (lì, 'precedent, established rule, illustrative instance', with 亻 'person' and 列 phonetic). Originally referring to judicial precedents in imperial law codes, it expanded in modern business, media, and academia to mean 'case study' or 'representative example case'.

history.meaning: magistrate's desk / official legal dossier + legal precedent or rule
established judicial precedent or recorded legal case
case study (in business, medicine, law, or media production), illustrative case

morphemes.meaning: legal or administrative case, file (originally 'magistrate's desk')

案例.notes: In media, PR, and business contexts, 经典案例 ('classic case study') and 案例分析 ('case analysis') refer to real-world projects analyzed as models, whereas 案件 (ànjiàn) is restricted to legal/criminal cases.

桌.etymology: Phono-semantic/ideographic character combining 卓 (zhuō, 'tall, elevated upright') + 木 ('wood'): 'high wooden table'. Emerged during the Tang–Song transition when high-legged tables and chairs (桌椅) replaced ancient low floor-sitting mats and low tables (几案).

history.stage: Tang–Song furniture evolution to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: high-legged wooden table; desk

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 桌 (via 萌典)

桌上.etymology: A locative noun phrase formed from 桌 (zhuō, 'table, desk', originally written 卓 'lofty, tall' before adding the wood determinative 木 in post-Tang vernacular script to distinguish elevated tables from low floor-mats 席 and short-legged trays 案) followed by the enclitic localizer 上 (shàng, 'on, upon, top surface').

history.meaning: elevated wooden table + upper surface / locative enclitic 'on'
on the table, on the desk (locative nominal)

桌上.notes: Because 桌上 is already a place word (处所词), it can directly follow verbs/prepositions like 在 (在桌上 'on the desk') or 放在 (放在桌上 'put on the desk') without needing another locative particle. Also used attributively in 桌上游戏 ('tabletop/board game', often shortened to 桌游).

rootFamily.gloss: board game, tabletop game (short for 桌上游戏)

桌子.etymology: Colloquial noun formed from 桌 ('high wooden table') + nominal suffix 子 (neutral tone zi): 'table, desk'.

history.meaning: table; desk

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 桌子 (via 萌典)

桌布.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 桌 ('table') + 布 ('cloth'): 'tablecloth'.

history.meaning: tablecloth

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 桌布 (via 萌典)

桌式.etymology: A modifier-head technical compound combining 桌 (zhuō, 'table, desk') and the suffixoid 式 (shì, 'style, model, type, pattern', originally a ritual rule or chariot crossbar in Classical Chinese). Formed in modern technical Mandarin to classify equipment or games designed in a 'table-style' or 'tabletop' configuration.

history.meaning: table/desk + style, model, or configuration

桌式.notes: Appears in compound nouns like 桌式足球 (zhuōshì zúqiú, 'foosball / table soccer'); for desktop computers, Mainland Mandarin prefers 台式 (táishì, e.g., 台式电脑), while Taiwanese Mandarin often uses 桌上型.

rootFamily.gloss: desktop / benchtop style (Mainland term for desktop PCs)

桌面.etymology: A modifier-head compound of 桌 (zhuō, 'table, desk') and 面 (miàn, 'face, surface, plane'). Originally denoting the physical flat surface of a table or desk, in the late 20th century it acquired a semantic loan (calque) from English *desktop* in graphical user interface (GUI) computing.

history.meaning: physical top surface of a table or desk; dishes spread on a banquet table
tabletop; metaphorically 'open, aboveboard arena' (as in 摆到桌面上 'put on the table for open discussion'); computer desktop interface

桌面.notes: In addition to 'tabletop' and 'computer desktop', the idiom 摆到桌面上 (bǎi dào zhuōmiàn shàng, 'to put out on the table') is common in workplace and negotiation dramas for bringing hidden agendas into open discussion, while 上不了台面/桌面 means 'not presentable in public'.

档.etymology: Written 檔 in Traditional characters (simplified to 档), a phono-semantic character combining 木 ('wood') and 當 (dāng, phonetic, 'to match, crosspiece'). Originally denoting wooden crossbars, shelves, or pigeonhole compartments in a cabinet for sorting documents, it extended by metonymy to the categorized files stored in those compartments, then to 'grades/tiers/gears', and finally to a classifier for scheduled events, affairs, or broadcast programs (一档节目 'a TV/radio program').

history.meaning: wooden crossbar, frame, or shelf compartment in a cabinet
pigeonhole compartment for official dossiers; categorized grade, tier, or group of items/events
file/archive; grade/level; mechanical gear; classifier for television/radio programs or affairs (e.g., 一档综艺节目)

morphemes.meaning: wooden shelf compartment; file; grade; classifier for broadcast shows/events (檔)

档.notes: In television and entertainment production (*Behind the Scenes*), 档 (dàng) is the signature classifier for shows: 一档节目 ('a program/show'), 黄金档 ('prime-time slot'), and 同档竞争 ('competing in the same broadcast slot').

rootFamily.gloss: schedule, time slot (for filming or broadcasting)
grade, tier, quality class (e.g., 高档 'high-end')

档期.etymology: A modifier-head compound from the Hong Kong and Mandarin film/broadcasting industry, combining 档 (dàng, Traditional 檔, 'slotted compartment; scheduled broadcast or screening slot') and 期 (qī, 'appointed time, period, dates'). Originally referring to the specific dates a cinema theater slotted a film for screening (上档), it broadened to mean the available schedule or booking dates of actors, directors, and television programs.

history.meaning: scheduled slot/compartment + appointed time period
screening or broadcast slot (e.g., 贺岁档期 'Lunar New Year slot'); an entertainer's or crew's available schedule dates

档期.notes: Essential showbiz vocabulary: 调档期 (tiáo dàngqī, 'adjust one's schedule'), 撞档期 ('have a scheduling conflict'), and 没档期 ('fully booked / no open dates'). Do not use 档期 for ordinary office meetings (use 日程 or 时间 instead).

rootFamily.gloss: to set a release or broadcast date

档案.etymology: A compound originating in early Qing-dynasty administrative terminology (attested in the 17th-century *柳边纪略* *Liubian Jilüe*), combining 档 (dàng, Traditional 檔, 'wooden shelf frames or pigeonhole compartments on which official records were hung or filed') and 案 (àn, 'official table/desk; government records and legal dossiers'). Together they denoted official records filed on archival shelves, later becoming the standard modern word for 'archive, dossier, or personnel file'.

history.meaning: official wooden shelf compartments and the government dossiers stored in them (Qing Manchu-Chinese administrative usage)
archives, official records, personal/personnel dossier; (in Taiwan/HK computing) computer file

morphemes.meaning: wooden shelving compartment for sorting records (檔)

档案.notes: In Mainland China, 人事档案 (rénshì dàng'àn) refers specifically to the official sealed personnel dossier that follows a citizen from school through employment; in Taiwan and Hong Kong, 档案 is also the standard word for a computer 'file' (called 文件 in Mainland Mandarin).

rootFamily.gloss: to place on file, file away in the archives

桥.etymology: Phono-semantic character (traditional 橋) of 木 ('wood', as early bridges were timber structures) + 乔 (喬, qiáo, 'tall and arched'): 'bridge'. Attested since the Shijing and Mencius.

history.stage: Old & Classical Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: high arched timber structure = bridge

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 桥 (via 萌典)

桩.etymology: Phono-semantic character (traditional 樁) of 木 ('wood') + 庄 (莊, zhuāng phonetic): 'wooden stake, post, or pile driven into the ground' and a classifier for matters, cases, or transactions (一桩事 'a matter').

history.meaning: wooden stake/pile; classifier for matters or deals

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 桩 (via 萌典)

桶.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 木 ('wood', from staved wooden pails) + 甬 (yǒng/tǒng, 'tubular vessel/measure'): 'bucket, pail, barrel, tub, bin' and classifier for buckets or barrels.

history.meaning: wooden bucket, pail, barrel, or tub

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 桶 (via 萌典)

梦寐以求.etymology: Four-character Classical idiom combining 梦寐 ('in dreams and sleep', 梦 'dream' + 寐 'sleep', echoing the opening ode of the Shijing: 窈窕淑女，寤寐求之 'waking and sleeping he sought her') + 以 ('therein / wherewith') + 求 ('seek'): 'long for even in one's dreams, crave/dream of attaining'.

history.stage: Classical Chinese (modeled on Shijing's 寤寐求之) to Modern Mandarin
history.form: 夢寐以求 / 梦寐以求
history.meaning: seek even in one's dreams; long-dreamed-of

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 梦寐以求 (via 萌典)

梦幻.etymology: A coordinative compound from 梦 (mèng, Traditional 夢, 'dream', originally depicting a person on a bed 爿 with indistinct vision 目/宀 at night 夕) and 幻 (huàn, 'magical illusion, conjuration, sleight of hand'). Popularized by Kumārajīva's famous 5th-century translation of the closing gāthā of the *Diamond Sūtra* (一切有为法，如梦幻泡影 — 'All conditioned phenomena are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows'), it shifted from a Buddhist term for the illusory impermanence of the world to a modern aesthetic adjective meaning 'dreamlike, magical, enchanting'.

history.meaning: sleep dream + conjurer's illusion or mirage
dreams and illusions (Buddhist metaphor for the unreality and transience of phenomena, translating Sanskrit svapna-māyā)
dreamlike, magical, fantastical, surreal (often with positive romantic or aesthetic connotations)

梦幻.notes: In classical idioms like 梦幻泡影 ('dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows'), it still means 'vain illusion', but in modern everyday Mandarin (e.g., 梦幻般的婚礼 'a dreamlike wedding', 梦幻联动 'a dream crossover collaboration') it is overwhelmingly positive and romantic.

rootFamily.gloss: fantastic, bizarre, magical (as in fantasy genres)

梦想.etymology: Modifier-head verb and noun compound of 梦 (夢, 'dream') + 想 ('think of, long for, aspiration'): originally 'think of in a dream, vain daydream' in Song prose, and in modern Mandarin 'cherished dream, aspiration; dream of'.

history.stage: Song dynasty prose to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: dream of; cherished dream or aspiration

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 梦想 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to see in a dream (yumemiru, calqued on 夢見る)
to see in a dream (mộng kiến)

梦见.etymology: A verb-resultative compound combining 梦 (mèng, Traditional 夢, used verbally as 'to dream') and the perceptual resultative complement 见 (jiàn, Traditional 見, 'to see, perceive'). Attested since Warring States and Han texts (such as the *Zhuangzi* and *Shiji*), where 梦见 introduces the person or event perceived inside a dream ('to dream of / see in a dream').

history.meaning: to see or encounter (someone or something) in a dream
to dream about, to see in a dream (transitive verb taking a noun or clause object)

morphemes.meaning: to see, perceive (perceptual resultative complement 見)

梦见.notes: Whereas 做梦 (zuòmèng, 'to have a dream') is a VO compound that cannot directly take an object (*做梦你 is ungrammatical), 梦见 (or 梦到) is transitive and directly takes the person or scene dreamed about: 我昨晚梦见你了 ('I dreamed about you last night').

rootFamily.gloss: to dream of, dream about (synonymous resultative with 到)
to have a dream, day-dream (VO compound)
to see, catch sight of (parallel perceptual -见 compound)

梧桐.etymology: Disyllabic botanical name combining 梧 (wood 木 + phonetic 吾) and 桐 (wood 木 + phonetic 同), both denoting the Chinese parasol tree (*Firmiana simplex*). Revered in classical Chinese lore as the noble tree on which the mythical phoenix (鳳凰) perches and prized for its resonant timber used to craft *guqin* zithers; in modern cities it also commonly refers to avenue plane trees (法国梧桐).

history.meaning: Chinese parasol tree (*Firmiana simplex*)
Chinese parasol tree; plane tree

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 梧桐

梧桐巷.etymology: Three-character street name combining 梧桐 ('Chinese parasol tree, Firmiana simplex', a poetic shade tree famous in Chinese literature and lane plantings) + 巷 ('lane, alley'): 'Wutong Lane (Parasol-Tree Alley)'.

history.meaning: Wutong Lane (lane lined with Chinese parasol trees)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 梧桐巷 (via 萌典)

梯子.etymology: Derived from 梯 ('wooden steps or ladder', wood radical 木 + phonetic 弟 dì, which also carries the sense 'ordered sequence/steps') + nominal suffix 子 (-zi).

history.meaning: wooden scaling or household ladder
ladder; stepladder

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 梯子

cognates.meaning: inspection and repair (especially of railway rolling stock)

检修.etymology: A serial and coordinative verbal compound (檢修, jiǎnxiū) combining 检 (trad. 檢, jiǎn, 'to check, examine, inspect', originally a wooden book-label or envelope seal) and 修 (xiū, 'to repair, mend, cultivate'). Formed in modern technical Mandarin (alongside Sino-Japanese 検修) to denote the sequential engineering process of first inspecting machinery or broadcasting equipment for faults and then repairing or servicing it.

history.meaning: to examine/verify and to mend/embellish (separate Classical Chinese verbs)
to inspect and overhaul machinery, vehicles, or technical facilities

检修.notes: Commonly used in industrial, aviation, and media production contexts (e.g., 检修设备 'overhaul the studio equipment' or 定期检修 'scheduled maintenance').

检查.etymology: Coordinative verb and noun compound of 检 (檢, 'inspect, verify, restrain') + 查 ('examine, investigate, look into'): 'inspect, check, examine; self-criticism/inspection'.

history.stage: Tang–Song administrative Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: inspect; check; examine

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 检查 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: inspection, checking item by item; scrutiny

检点.etymology: A coordinative compound (檢點, jiǎndiǎn) pairing 检 (trad. 檢, jiǎn, 'to examine, restrain, regulate') and 点 (trad. 點, diǎn, 'to mark with a dot, tally, check off item by item'). In Tang and Song dynasty vernacular and literary texts, it meant to tally inventory or inspect items one by one; by extension, it came to mean scrutinizing and restraining one's own words and conduct, yielding the modern adjectival sense 'discreet, proper, mindful of one's behavior'.

history.meaning: to check off item by item; to tally or inspect troops and supplies
to watch or restrain one's own speech and conduct
cautious and proper in behavior; discreet (especially in public life)

检点.notes: In modern Mandarin, it appears overwhelmingly in negative or admonitory contexts, such as 行为不检点 ('improper/indiscreet behavior', a stock phrase in celebrity scandal reporting) or 注意检点 ('watch your conduct').

棉纸.etymology: A craft-paper compound combining 棉 (mián, 'cotton plant or soft fibrous floss', formed with 木 and 帛 'fine silk') and 纸 (zhǐ, simplified from 紙, 'paper'). Historically in southwestern China and later in Western watercolour papermaking alike, 棉纸 refers to tough, long-fibered rag or bark/cotton paper prized by calligraphers and mapmakers because its fibers resist tearing and hold ink washes crisply.

history.meaning: tough long-fibered handmade paper
heavy cotton paper (for watercolour and archival art)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 棉纸

棋子.etymology: A subordinate noun compound (棋子, qízǐ) composed of 棋 (qí, 'board game Strategy game such as weiqi/Go or xiangqi/Chinese chess', phono-semantic character with wood radical 木 and phonetic 其 qí) and 子 (zǐ, 'small round object, seed, piece', here retaining its full lexical third tone zǐ rather than the neutral-tone nominal suffix -zi when denoting an individual game piece). Figuratively extended from board games to mean a 'pawn' manipulated by powerful players behind the scenes.

history.meaning: stone or wooden piece used in weiqi (Go) or liubo board games
chess piece or Go stone; figuratively, a pawn in a larger scheme or power struggle

棋子.notes: Pronounced qízǐ (with a full third tone on 子) in standard usage; in workplace and showbiz dramas, 一颗棋子 ('a mere pawn') is a frequent metaphor for artists or staff used as bargaining chips by executives.

rootFamily.gloss: situation on a chessboard; overall political/business situation

棒.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 木 ('wood') + 奉 (fèng/bàng phonetic): originally 'wooden club, stick, cudgel, baton'. In northern Mandarin vernacular, from 'sturdy/solid like a heavy stick', it developed the lively adjective sense 'great, awesome, excellent, strong, capable (真棒!)'.

history.meaning: wooden stick; club; baton

history.stage: Qing northern vernacular to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: stick/bat; great, awesome, first-rate

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 棒 (via 萌典)

棕色.etymology: Modifier-head color compound of 棕 ('coir palm fiber', stripped from the trunk of the windmill palm 棕榈, naturally dark reddish-brown) + 色 ('color'): 'brown'.

history.meaning: palm-fiber color = brown

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 棕色 (via 萌典)

棚.etymology: A single-morpheme noun 棚 (péng), formed as a phono-semantic graph with the wood radical 木 (mù, 'timber, wooden frame') and the phonetic component 朋 (péng, 'clustered strings of cowries; companion'). In Old and Middle Chinese it denoted a makeshift wooden or bamboo canopy, awning, or thatched shed; in 20th-century film and television vernacular, it underwent semantic specialization from 'large covered shed/hangar' to a 'soundstage' or 'recording studio' (as in 录影棚 and 录音棚).

history.meaning: wooden platform, canopy, or temporary bamboo/thatch shed
covered shed, awning, or shack (e.g., 茶棚 tea stall, 棚户 shack)
recording studio or production soundstage; shed or canopy

棚.notes: In television and music production slang, 棚 means 'the studio/soundstage': 进棚 ('go into the recording/filming studio'), 棚拍 ('studio shoot' vs. 外景 'location shoot'), and 棚里 ('on the soundstage').

森林.etymology: Ideographic-cumulative botanical compound from 森 (three trees 木 stacked together, 'dense, towering trees') + 林 (two trees 木 side by side, 'woods; grove'). Together the five tree graphs vividly evoke a vast, thick forest canopy.

morphemes.meaning: dense with trees; dark and lush

history.meaning: dense, expansive woods
forest; woodland

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 森林

棵.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining the wood/tree radical 木 with phonetic 果 (*guǒ*, Middle Chinese *khwaX*). Specialized in vernacular Mandarin since the Yuan and Ming dynasties as the dedicated measure word for individual trees, cabbages, and rooted plants.

morphemes.meaning: measure word for trees and individual plants

history.meaning: classifier for trees, stalks, and plants
measure word for trees and plants

椅.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 木 ('wood') + 奇 (qí/yǐ phonetic). In the Shijing, 椅 (read yī) named a catalpa-like tree; during the Tang–Song adoption of high-backed seating (originally called 绳床 or 倚床, from 倚 yǐ 'lean one's back against'), 椅 (read yǐ) was repurposed for a 'chair with a backrest'.

history.meaning: species of tree

history.stage: Tang–Song furniture evolution to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: chair (seat with a backrest)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 椅 (via 萌典)

椅子.etymology: Formed from 椅 (wood radical 木 + phonetic 奇 qí; originally a type of catalpa tree in Classical texts, reassigned during the Tang–Song transition from floor mats to high-seated backed chairs) + nominal suffix 子.

history.meaning: folding chair and backed wooden chair
chair

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 椅子 (via 萌典)

楼.etymology: Phono-semantic character (traditional 樓) of 木 ('wood/timber construction') + 娄 (婁, lóu, whose stacked components also evoke multiple stories piled up): 'multi-story building, tower, upper floor/story (二楼 second floor)'.

history.meaning: multi-story timber building; watchtower; upper floor
multi-story building; floor/story

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 楼 (via 萌典)

楼上.etymology: Locative compound combining 楼 ('storied building, floor') + 上 ('up, above'): 'upstairs, on an upper floor'.

history.meaning: upstairs; on the upper floor

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 楼上 (via 萌典)

楼下.etymology: Locative compound combining 楼 ('storied building, floor') + 下 ('down, below'): 'downstairs, below the building'.

history.meaning: downstairs

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 楼下 (via 萌典)

楼梯.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 楼 ('multi-story building, upper floor') + 梯 ('wooden ladder, steps', 木 + 弟 'sequential steps'): 'stairs, staircase, stairway'.

history.meaning: stairs; staircase

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 楼梯 (via 萌典)

楼梯口.etymology: Three-character locative compound combining 楼梯 ('staircase, stairs') + 口 ('opening, entrance'): 'stairway entrance, head or foot of the stairs, landing'.

history.meaning: head or foot of the stairs; stairwell entrance

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 楼梯口 (via 萌典)

概率.etymology: A modifier-head technical compound (概率, gàilǜ) combining 概 (gài, 'general, approximate, overarching tendency', originally a wooden striker used to level grain in a measuring斗) and 率 (lǜ, 'ratio, proportion, rate'). Coined in modern Chinese mathematical terminology (alongside the older synonym 几率 jīlǜ and Japanese 確率 kakuritsu) to translate mathematical 'probability'—the overarching ratio of favorable outcomes to total possible outcomes—before spreading into everyday speech as 'chance' or 'likelihood'.

history.meaning: general measure/approximation + numerical ratio/proportion (separate Classical terms)
mathematical probability; colloquial likelihood or chance of an event occurring

概率.notes: Note the pronunciation lǜ (fourth tone, 'rate/ratio'), not shuài ('to lead'); in contemporary colloquial Mandarin, 大概率 ('in all likelihood / high probability') is ubiquitous as an adverbial phrase.

模仿.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound (模仿, mófǎng; historically also written 摹倣) uniting 模 (mó, 'mold, pattern, model', or 摹 mó, 'to trace or copy a model by hand') and 仿 (trad. 倣/仿, fǎng, 'to imitate, resemble, copy'). Attested in Song-dynasty literary criticism for emulating the brushwork or poetic style of ancient masters, and used in modern Mandarin for imitating someone's voice, behavior, or artistic format.

history.meaning: to trace or emulate a calligraphic or literary model
to imitate, mimic, or copy behavior, style, or creative works

模仿.notes: Neutral in tone compared to 抄袭 (chāoxí, 'plagiarize') or 山寨 (shānzhài, 'knockoff'); in entertainment, 模仿秀 ('impersonation/impression show') is a popular variety television segment.

cognates.meaning: model, pattern, schematic type (as in 模式図 schematic diagram)

模式.etymology: A coordinative noun compound (模式, móshì) formed from 模 (mó, 'wooden mold, matrix, standard form') and 式 (shì, 'rule, pattern, standard, ceremony'). Attested in medieval Chinese histories (such as the *History of the Northern Dynasties*) in the sense of an exemplary behavioral standard or model, and revitalized in 20th-century social science, engineering, and media discourse (reinforced by Japanese 模式 moshiki) to render English 'model', 'pattern', 'paradigm', or television 'format'.

history.meaning: standard rule, exemplary model of conduct or craftsmanship
structural pattern, paradigm, business model, or TV program format

模式.notes: In television production (*幕后之王*), 节目模式 means a 'TV show format' (the licensed blueprint of a variety show), alongside 商业模式 ('business model') and 开启…模式 (slang for 'switching into [work/party] mode').

横档.etymology: Carpentry compound from 横 ('horizontal; crosswise') + 档 (simplified from 檔, wood 木 + phonetic 當 'wooden crosspiece; shelf; rung'). In traditional Chinese furniture joinery, the 横档 (or 棖) is the horizontal stretcher mortised between stool or table legs to brace the frame against racking.

history.meaning: horizontal wooden crossbar or rung on furniture
crossbar; horizontal rung or stretcher

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 横档

橄榄油.etymology: Compound of 橄榄 ('olive', originally naming native Chinese Canarium white/black olives with wood radical 木 on both characters, then applied to Mediterranean Olea europaea) + 油 ('pressed oil').

history.meaning: olive oil

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 橄榄油

橙子.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 橙子. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 橙子 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 橙子 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 橙子 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 橙子. The etymology of 橙子 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 橙子
middle form of 橙子
modern form of 橙子

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 橙子

橙汁.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 橙 ('sweet orange', wood 木 + 登) + 汁 ('juice, liquid', water 氵 + 十): 'orange juice'.

history.meaning: orange juice

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 橙汁 (via 萌典)

橙皮.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 橙皮. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 橙皮 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 橙皮 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 橙皮 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 橙皮. The etymology of 橙皮 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 橙皮
middle form of 橙皮
modern form of 橙皮

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 橙皮

橙色预警.etymology: A four-character modifier-head compound (橙色預警, chéngsè yùjǐng) combining 橙色 (chéngsè, 'orange color', from 橙 chéng 'sweet/bitter orange tree' + 色 sè 'color, hue') and 预警 (trad. 預警, yùjǐng, 'advance warning', from 预 yù 'in advance, beforehand' + 警 jǐng 'to warn, alert, guard'). Standardized in modern Chinese meteorological and emergency-management administration as the second-highest tier in China's four-tier color-coded warning system (blue 蓝色, yellow 黄色, orange 橙色, red 红色).

history.meaning: orange color + advance military/disaster warning (separate modern compounds)
orange alert (second-highest severity level in meteorological and public emergency warning systems; figuratively, a severe crisis alert)

橙色预警.notes: In China's official four-color weather alert scale (蓝-黄-橙-红), 橙色预警 is the second most severe level, often forcing outdoor filming crews and live events to halt operations; figuratively used in workplace slang for an impending major crisis.

橡木.etymology: Modifier-head timber compound of 橡 ('oak tree, acorn', wood 木 + 象) + 木 ('wood, timber'): 'oak wood, oak'.

history.meaning: oak wood; oak

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 橡木 (via 萌典)

次.etymology: Ideogram combining 二/冫 ('two, second in sequence') + 欠 ('person exhaling/pausing on the road'): originally 'halt for the night in sequence -> second in order, next, inferior/second-rate', and from the Han–Tang period onward the primary verbal/nominal classifier for 'time, occasion, occurrence (一次 once)'.

history.meaning: camping halt in sequence; order; second/next
classifier for times/occurrences; next; second-rate

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 次 (via 萌典)

欢快.etymology: Coordinative adjective compound of 欢 (歡, 'joyous, lively') + 快 ('cheerful, brisk'): 'lively and cheerful, joyous and upbeat (especially of music, rhythm, or mood)'.

history.meaning: cheerful and lively; upbeat

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 欢快 (via 萌典)

欢迎.etymology: Modifier-head verb and noun compound of 欢 (歡, 'gladly, joyfully') + 迎 ('go out to meet, welcome'): 'welcome, greet warmly'. Attested since Han–Tang historical prose.

history.meaning: joyfully go to meet = welcome

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 欢迎 (via 萌典)

欢迎词.etymology: Three-morpheme compound of 欢迎 ('warmly welcome', 欢 'joyful' + 迎 'go out to greet') + 词 ('spoken or written words; speech; address', speech radical 讠 + 司). It designates the welcoming remarks or formal speech delivered to greet arriving guests.

history.meaning: welcome speech; welcoming address

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 欢迎词

cognates.meaning: appreciation and enjoyment of art or beauty

欣赏.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound (欣賞, xīnshǎng) joining 欣 (xīn, 'joyful, delighted, glad', with the欠 yawn/exhale radical indicating an expression of delight) and 赏 (trad. 賞, shǎng, 'to reward; to take pleasure in viewing, savor'). First attested in Six Dynasties literary prose (such as Tao Yuanming's famous line 奇文共欣赏 'remarkable writings are enjoyed together' in *Moving House*), evolving from 'to savor aesthetic beauty with delight' to both 'to enjoy art/music' and 'to admire/think highly of a person's talent'.

history.meaning: to take joyful pleasure in contemplating literature, nature, or art (e.g., Tao Yuanming)
to appreciate (music, art, performance); to admire or recognize someone's talent and character

欣赏.notes: Used both for aesthetic enjoyment (欣赏音乐 'appreciate music') and interpersonal esteem (我很欣赏你的才华 'I really admire your talent', frequently used by mentors, producers, and bosses).

欧芹.etymology: Botanical compound of 欧 ('European', short for 欧洲) + 芹 ('aromatic umbellifer herb; Chinese celery', grass radical 艹 + phonetic 斤 *jīn*, attested since the *Shijing*). The prefix 欧 distinguishes Mediterranean garden parsley (*Petroselinum crispum*) from native Chinese celery (水芹/旱芹).

history.meaning: fragrant aquatic or garden celery herb
parsley (*Petroselinum crispum*)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 欧芹

欺负.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound (欺負, qīfu) combining 欺 (qī, 'to deceive, cheat, mistreat, insult') and 负 (trad. 負, fù, originally 'to carry on the back', extended in Classical Chinese to 'to rely on one's strength/backing' or 'to betray, wrong, slight'). Attested from the Han and Tang dynasties onward in the sense of 'to wrong, oppress, or take advantage of the weak by relying on superior power', with the second syllable reducing to a neutral tone (qīfu) in colloquial northern Mandarin.

history.meaning: to wrong, slight, or oppress someone by taking advantage of superior position
to bully, pick on, tease, or mistreat someone weaker

morphemes.meaning: rely on power; wrong, betray, slight (trad. 負)

欺负.notes: Pronounced with a neutral tone on the second syllable (qīfu); covers a spectrum from serious workplace hazing/bullying (欺负新人 'bullying newcomers') to playful teasing between intimates.

rootFamily.gloss: let down, fail to live up to

款.etymology: Ancient character combining 祟/奈 ('sacrificial altar') + 欠 ('person bowing/exhaling in sincerity'): originally 'sincere, cordial (款待 entertain cordially); knock slowly', then 'inscribed item/clause on a bronze vessel -> article, paragraph, sum of money/funds (付款), style/model (款式), and classifier for product models or designs'.

history.meaning: sincere; entertain cordially; inscribed clause
sum of money/payment; style/model; classifier for models

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 款 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to cease, exhaust, rest (as in 間歇 kanketsu 'intermittent')
to rest, cease, stop (as in 간헐 ganheol 'intermittent')

歇.etymology: A single-morpheme verb 歇 (xiē), constructed with the semantic radical 欠 (qiàn, 'open-mouthed exhalation, sighing, panting') and the phonetic component 曷 (hé, Old Chinese *gˤat; 歇 is Old Chinese *qʰat). In *Shuowen Jiezi* and Classical Chinese, it meant 'to exhale, catch one's breath, cease, or become exhausted'; by the Six Dynasties and Tang period, 'stopping to catch one's breath' generalized into the everyday vernacular verb for 'to rest, take a break, or knock off work'.

history.meaning: to cease, stop to catch one's breath; to be exhausted or depleted
to rest, lodge for the night, or pause from labor
to rest, take a breather, stop working or operating

歇.notes: More colloquial and conversational than 休息 (xiūxi); common in spoken phrases like 歇一会儿 ('rest a bit'), 歇歇脚 ('rest one's feet'), and 歇业 ('close down a business temporarily or permanently').

rootFamily.gloss: take a rest, knock off work

歇会儿.etymology: A colloquial verb-complement phrase (歇會兒, xiēhuìr, contraction of 歇一會兒 xiē yīhuìr) combining the verb 歇 (xiē, 'to cease labor, catch one's breath, rest') with the durational measure noun 会儿 (trad. 會兒, huìr, derived from 会 huì 'a junction of time, a brief moment' plus the diminutive retroflex suffix 儿 -r). The numeral 一 (yī, 'one') is elided in natural northern Mandarin speech when post-verbal, yielding a breezy conversational expression for 'taking a quick breather'.

history.meaning: to rest for a brief spell or moment of time
to rest for a bit, take a short breather (colloquial contraction with erhua)

morphemes.meaning: rest, take a break, catch one's breath
brief moment, spell of time (trad. 會)
diminutive retroflex noun suffix (erhua, trad. 兒)

歇会儿.notes: A warm, natural northern Mandarin spoken expression (often heard on busy production sets: 先歇会儿吧 'let's take a breather first'); being a verb-object/duration construction, particles or reduplication go inside (歇了一会儿, 歇歇).

歉.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining 兼 (jiān/qiàn phonetic) + 欠 ('lack, yawn/open mouth'): originally 'crop failure, dearth of grain -> lack, fall short', and by extension 'feel regretful and apologetic for falling short in courtesy (道歉 apologize, 抱歉 sorry)'.

history.meaning: poor harvest; deficiency
apologetic regret; sorry

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 歉 (via 萌典)

歌.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining 哥 (gē, the original graph for 'sing', doubling 可 'exhale/voice') + 欠 ('person opening the mouth to breathe/sing'): 'sing; song'. Attested since the Shijing and Shangshu.

history.stage: Old & Classical Chinese (Shijing) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: sing; song

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 歌 (via 萌典)

歌手.etymology: A modifier-head agentive compound (歌手, gēshǒu) composed of 歌 (gē, 'song, to sing', with 欠 'open mouth exhaling/chanting' and phonetic 哥 gē) and the agentive suffixal root 手 (shǒu, literally 'hand', used since Classical and Middle Chinese to denote a person skilled in a craft or activity, cf. 水手 'sailor', 棋手 'chess player'). Already attested in Tang poetry (e.g., Bai Juyi's 歌手春相续) for vocal performers, and reinforced in modern Mandarin by Sino-Japanese 歌手 (kashu) as the standard professional term for a singer or vocalist.

history.meaning: a vocal performer or songstress (attested in Tang poetry)
professional singer, recording artist, or vocalist

歌手.notes: The standard, neutral professional term for a popular or contemporary vocalist (e.g., 创作歌手 'singer-songwriter', 实力派歌手 ' powerhouse vocalist'), whereas 歌唱家 (gēchàngjiā) is reserved for classical, operatic, or folk virtuosos.

rootFamily.gloss: contestant, competitor in a show or sport

cognates.word: ngôi sao ca nhạc / ca tinh

歌星.etymology: A modifier-head noun compound (歌星, gēxīng) combining 歌 (gē, 'song, singing') and 星 (xīng, 'star, celestial body'). Formed in 20th-century Mandarin via semantic calquing of English 'star' (as in 'movie star' 影星 and 'pop/singing star' 歌星), where 星 serves as a productive root for a celebrity who shines in the public eye.

history.meaning: song/singing + celestial star (separate Classical roots)
famous singer, pop star, celebrity vocalist (calos-loan metaphor from English 'star')

歌星.notes: Highlights celebrity status and fame rather than just the profession (contrast 歌手 'singer'); slightly dated in casual youth slang compared to 偶像 (ǒuxiàng 'idol') or 顶流歌手 ('top-traffic singer'), but still standard in media reporting.

歌曲.etymology: A coordinative noun compound (歌曲, gēqǔ) uniting 歌 (gē, 'sung lyrics, vocal chanting') and 曲 (qǔ, 'melody, tune, musical inflection', originally 'bent or winding' like the twists and turns of a tune). In traditional Chinese poetics (*Yuefu* and *Han Shu*), 歌 originally denoted unaccompanied vocal singing while 曲 denoted the melodic tune; fused together since the Six Dynasties, 歌曲 designates a complete song comprising both lyrics and melody.

history.meaning: vocal chant/lyrics (歌) and winding musical melody/tune (曲)
a song (combining lyrics and melody)

歌曲.notes: More formal and collective than standalone 歌 (gē): used in written and broadcast contexts (e.g., 流行歌曲 'pop songs', 原创歌曲 'original songs', 主打歌曲 'title track'), whereas in casual speech one says 唱一首歌 ('sing a song').

cognates.meaning: King of Singers (popularized in music competition formats)

歌王.etymology: A modifier-head noun compound (歌王, gēwáng) formed from 歌 (gē, 'song, singing') and 王 (wáng, 'king, monarch; supreme champion in a domain'). Modeled on traditional Chinese titles of supremacy (such as 诗王 'king of poetry' or 戏王 'king of opera'), and popularized in Hong Kong, Taiwanese, and Mainland Chinese pop culture and televised singing competitions to crown the supreme male vocalist or grand champion ('King of Singers').

history.meaning: song/singing + king/monarch (separate Classical roots)
'King of Singers'; grand champion of a singing competition or legendary male vocalist

morphemes.meaning: king, monarch; supreme champion in a field

歌王.notes: A staple title in Chinese music variety shows (such as *Singer* / *我是歌手* and *蒙面唱将*): 歌王爭霸赛 ('Battle for the King of Singers'). Its female counterpart in award ceremonies is 歌后 (gēhòu, 'Queen of Singers').

rootFamily.gloss: Queen of Singers, best female vocalist
king of acting, Best Actor award winner

歌迷.etymology: A modifier-head noun compound (歌迷, gēmí) combining 歌 (gē, 'song, singing, singer') and 迷 (mí, originally 'to lose one's way, be bewildered', extended to 'to be infatuated with, obsessed with', and nominalized as 'enthusiast, devotee, fan'). Modeled on early 20th-century Chinese theater and sports compounds like 戏迷 (xìmí, 'opera buff') and 球迷 (qiúmí, 'ball-game/sports fan'), it serves as the native Chinese equivalent for a 'music fan' or 'fan of a singer'.

history.meaning: person infatuated with opera (戲迷), extended in the 20th century to devotees of popular music and singers (歌迷)

歌迷.notes: Unlike the phonetic loanword 粉丝 (fěnsī, 'fans' of any celebrity or idol), 歌迷 specifically emphasizes devotion to a singer's music and vocal artistry (e.g., 歌迷见面会 'fan meeting for a singer').

rootFamily.gloss: be fascinated by, be obsessed with

正.etymology: Ancient ideogram attested on Shang oracle bones showing a foot (止) marching toward or stopping squarely at a horizontal target line or walled settlement (一/囗): 'go straight to -> straight, upright, centered, right/correct, main/principal, positive, exact (on the hour), right in the middle of (progressive adverb)'.

history.meaning: foot stopping squarely at the mark = straight, upright, right, exact
straight; upright; main; right; just now / right in the middle of

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 正 (via 萌典)

正事.etymology: A modifier-head noun compound (正事, zhèngshì) combining 正 (zhèng, 'upright, proper, principal, main', originally depicting a foot 止 marching straight toward a walled settlement or target 一) and 事 (shì, 'affair, matter, occupation, business'). Attested in Classical and vernacular Chinese for official state duties or one's primary, legitimate occupation, as opposed to trivial distractions or idle pastimes (闲事 xiánshì).

history.meaning: official public duties or primary legitimate affairs (as opposed to private or trivial matters)
serious business, proper work, or the main matter at hand (often with erhua 正事儿 in northern speech)

正事.notes: Very often pronounced with erhua in spoken Mandarin (正事儿 zhèngshìr); common in workplace dialogue like 说正事 ('let's talk business / get to the point') and 不务正业 / 不干正事 ('not doing proper work').

正在.etymology: Progressive aspect adverb combining two markers of immediate presence: 正 ('right at this moment, just') + 在 ('at the point of doing'): placed before a verb to express an action 'in progress right now (be V-ing)'.

history.meaning: right in the middle of (doing); in progress

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 正在 (via 萌典)

正好.etymology: Compound adjective and adverb of 正 ('just, right on the mark') + 好 ('good, fitting'): 'just right (in size, temperature, or amount); happen to, by a happy coincidence, just in time'.

history.stage: Tang–Song poetry & vernacular to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: just right; happen to; just in time

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 正好 (via 萌典)

正常.etymology: Coordinative adjective compound of 正 ('proper, regular') + 常 ('constant, ordinary, normal'): 'normal, regular, ordinary'.

history.meaning: regular and ordinary; normal

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 正常 (via 萌典)

正式.etymology: Modifier-head adjective and adverb compound of 正 ('proper, standard, official') + 式 ('model, form, ceremony'): 'formal, official, regular'.

history.meaning: proper form -> formal, official

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 正式 (via 萌典)

正方形.etymology: The term '正方形' (zhèngfāngxíng, square) combines '正' (upright, exact, regular), '方' (square, four-sided), and '形' (shape). In ancient Chinese geometry, '方' was the fundamental concept of a four-sided shape, contrasting with '圆' (circle). The prefix '正' explicitly clarifies that the shape is regular, with all sides and angles equal, distinguishing it from '长方形' (rectangle). This terminology became standardized with the translation of Western mathematical texts into Chinese during the late Ming and early Qing dynasties.

history.meaning: rectangle

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 正方形

正是.etymology: A modifier-head emphatic copular compound (正是, zhèngshì) uniting the adverbial modifier 正 (zhèng, 'straight on target,恰好, right, precisely') with the copula 是 (shì, originally a demonstrative pronoun 'this' in Old Chinese meaning 'right/correct', which grammaticalized by the Han dynasty into the copular verb 'to be'). Literally 'is squarely/precisely [this]', used both to focus identification ('is none other than, is precisely') and as a traditional affirmative interjection ('Quite so! Exactly!').

history.meaning: rightly is this / is indeed so (adverb + demonstrative/copula)
is precisely, is none other than; 'Exactly so!' (in traditional vernacular opera and fiction)

正是.notes: Frequently used in cleft-like focus constructions such as 正是因为… ('It is precisely because...') or 这正是我们需要的 ('This is exact/precisely what we need').

rootFamily.gloss: just in the middle of (doing); right at (a time)

正确.etymology: Coordinative adjective compound of 正 ('right, straight, accurate') + 确 (確, 'solid, firm as rock, true'): 'correct, right, accurate, proper'.

history.meaning: right and true; correct; accurate

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 正确 (via 萌典)

正经.etymology: Originally a modifier-head noun compound (正經, zhèngjīng) combining 正 (zhèng, 'orthodox, standard, upright') and 经 (trad. 經, jīng, 'warp threads of a loom; canonical text, constant standard'). In Classical Chinese it denoted the orthodox Confucian classics (as opposed to apocrypha or heterodox writings); in Yuan, Ming, and Qing vernacular Mandarin, 'conforming to the orthodox canon' shifted into an everyday adjective meaning 'upstanding, decent, serious, or legitimate' (with the second syllable often taking a neutral tone zhèngjing in colloquial speech).

history.meaning: orthodox canonical texts (such as the Confucian classics) or constant moral principles
morally upright, respectable, legitimate, serious-minded
serious, earnest, decent, proper, or standard/legitimate

morphemes.meaning: warp threads; canonical classic, constant norm (trad. 經)

正经.notes: Watch the tonal and expressive range: 一本正经 (yīběn zhèngjīng) means 'deadpan / sanctimoniously serious', while 不正经 (bù zhèngjing) means either 'flippant/joking around' or 'morally improper/lewd' depending on context.

正要.etymology: Immediate-future aspect phrase combining 正 ('just at that moment') + 要 ('be about to, intend to'): 'be just about to (do something when…)'.

history.meaning: be just about to

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 正要 (via 萌典)

正途.etymology: A modifier-head noun compound (正途, zhèngtú) combining 正 (zhèng, 'straight, upright, legitimate, orthodox') and 途 (tú, 'road, way, pathway, career path'). In Ming and Qing dynasty bureaucracy, 正途 specifically designated the 'orthodox career path' into officialdom via the imperial civil service examinations (科举), as opposed to 异途 (yìtú, purchasing office or clerical promotion); in modern Mandarin it means 'the right/honest path in life or business'.

history.meaning: the main road; in Ming–Qing administration, appointment to office via the orthodox imperial examinations
the right path, legitimate avenue, or honorable course of action

正途.notes: More literary and elevated than its conversational synonym 正道 (zhèngdào) or 正路 (zhènglù); commonly appears in collocations like 走上正途 ('get onto the right path') or 步入正途 ('embark on a legitimate course').

正面.etymology: A modifier-head compound (正面, zhèngmiàn) composed of 正 (zhèng, 'straight, direct, main, upright') and 面 (miàn, 'face, surface, side, aspect'). Originally spatial and postural in Classical Chinese ('facing straight forward' or 'the front side of a building, coin, or object', opposite 反面 fǎnmiàn 'reverse side' and 侧面 cèmiàn 'side profile'), it expanded in modern Mandarin to mean 'head-on, direct' (e.g., 正面回应 'respond directly') and 'positive, constructive' (e.g., 正面形象 'positive public image').

history.meaning: to face straight ahead; the front face or obverse side of an object or structure
the front side; head-on/direct; positive or favorable (in media, PR, and psychology)

正面.notes: Crucial in public relations and media management: 正面报道 ('positive coverage'), 正面形象 ('positive public image'), and 正面回应 ('respond head-on to rumors'), contrasting with 负面 (fùmiàn, 'negative').

此事.etymology: A Classical Chinese demonstrative-noun phrase (此事, cǐshì) retained in formal modern Mandarin, composed of the proximal demonstrative pronoun 此 (cǐ, 'this, here', originally a compound graph of 止 'foot' and 匕 'person turning/standing right here') and 事 (shì, 'matter, affair, incident'). It functions as a compact, two-syllable formal equivalent of colloquial 这件事 (zhè jiàn shì, 'this matter').

history.meaning: this matter, this affair (standard Classical demonstrative phrase)
this matter, this incident (used in formal speech, news, legal notices, and PR statements)

此事.notes: Belongs to written and formal spoken register (e.g., 针对此事发表声明 'issue a statement regarding this matter' or 此事必有蹊跷 'there is surely something fishy about this'); in casual conversation, use 这件事.

cognates.meaning: this moment / time of day (shared Sinitic morphemes)

此刻.etymology: A modifier-head temporal compound (此刻, cǐkè) combining the proximal demonstrative 此 (cǐ, 'this') and 刻 (kè, originally 'to carve notches on a water clock [漏刻]', hence a short unit of time—historically 1/100 of a day or a quarter-hour—and by extension 'an instant, moment'). Together they mean 'this very notch of time, this exact moment'.

history.meaning: this + carved notch on a clepsydra (water clock) marking a brief interval of time
this very moment, right now (elevated/poetic temporal noun)

此刻.notes: Carries more emotional weight and dramatic immediacy than 现在 (xiànzài 'now'); often paired in the four-character phrase 此时此刻 ('at this very time and moment', a staple of stage hosts and dramatic monologues).

此前.etymology: A Classical Chinese demonstrative-locative compound (此前, cǐqián) formed from the proximal demonstrative 此 (cǐ, 'this [point in time or discourse]') and 前 (qián, 'before, prior to, in front of', originally 歬, depicting a foot 止 advancing on a boat 舟). Preserved in modern formal and journalistic Mandarin as a concise temporal noun/adverb meaning 'prior to this, previously, before now'.

history.meaning: before this place or prior to this point in time
previously, prior to this, earlier (formal and journalistic register)

此前.notes: Extremely common in news reports and corporate/entertainment briefings (e.g., 此前有媒体报道 'media previously reported...') as a sleek, two-syllable alternative to 在这之前 (zài zhè zhīqián).

cognates.meaning: besides this, in addition (parallel kanbun construction)

此外.etymology: A Classical Chinese demonstrative-locative phrase (此外, cǐwài) combining 此 (cǐ, 'this') and 外 (wài, 'outside, beyond, besides'). Literally 'outside of this [matter just mentioned]', it grammaticalized from a spatial/conceptual noun phrase into a cohesive discourse conjunction meaning 'besides, in addition, furthermore, moreover'.

history.meaning: outside of this; beyond the aforementioned scope or territory
besides, in addition, moreover (sentence-initial discourse connector)

此外.notes: A high-frequency formal transition word used at the start of a clause or sentence (followed by a comma: 此外，…) to introduce an additional point, equivalent to 除此之外 ('apart from this') or 另外 ('in addition').

cognates.meaning: this occasion / next time (shared Sinitic morpheme 次)

此次.etymology: A demonstrative-classifier compound (此次, cǐcì) composed of the Literary Chinese proximal demonstrative 此 (cǐ, 'this') and the verbal/nominal measure word 次 (cì, originally 'to camp in order, sequence, turn', grammaticalized by Middle Chinese into the standard classifier for occurrences, occasions, or events). It serves as the formal written counterpart of colloquial 这次 (zhècì, 'this time, this occasion').

history.meaning: this + sequence/halting-place/occasion
this time, this occasion, this particular event or incident (formal determiner)

此次.notes: Used directly before two-syllable nouns without 的 in formal announcements and press releases: 此次活动 ('this event'), 此次合作 ('this collaboration'), 此次事故 ('this incident').

步.etymology: Ancient ideogram (会意字) attested on Shang oracle bones depicting a left foot (止) and a right foot (𣥂) placed one ahead of the other in walking stride: 'step, pace; walk on foot; stage/step in a process; situation (地步)'.

morphemes.meaning: left and right feet walking = step, pace

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: left foot and right foot stepping in alternation = step, pace, walk

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 步 (via 萌典)

步入.etymology: A verb-complement compound (步入, bùrù) combining 步 (bù, 'a pace, step; to walk on foot, stride', originally an ideograph depicting two footprints 止 placed one above the other in walking sequence) and 入 (rù, 'to enter, go into'). Retained from Literary Chinese syntax (where 入 functions as a directional verb/complement taking a direct location object), it denotes either physically walking with measured steps into a hall/venue or figuratively entering a new stage of life, career, or history.

history.meaning: to walk on foot into a place (e.g., 步入庭中 'stepped into the courtyard')
to step ceremoniously into a venue; figuratively, to enter upon a new phase, era, or state (e.g., marriage, middle age, the right track)

morphemes.meaning: step, pace; walk with measured steps

步入.notes: More elevated and ceremonious than 走进 (zǒujìn); used for solemn physical entrances (步入红毯/殿堂 'walk onto the red carpet / into the hall of marriage') and abstract milestones (步入正轨 'get onto the right track', 步入中年 'enter middle age').

步子.etymology: The noun '步子' (bùzi, step, pace) is formed by '步' (step) and the nominal suffix '子'. '步' is a very ancient character; its oracle bone form shows two feet taking a stride. In classical Chinese, '步' functioned as both a verb and a noun for a step or a unit of distance. In modern vernacular Mandarin, the addition of the neutral-tone suffix '-子' makes it a concrete noun referring to the physical action or distance of a single stride. It is commonly used in spoken language.

history.meaning: pace

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 步子

cognates.meaning: step by step, with every step (literary)
step by step (as in bộ bộ kinh tâm)

步步.etymology: A reduplicated noun/classifier construction (步步, bùbù) formed by doubling 步 (bù, 'step, pace', originally two sequential footprints 止). In Classical and Middle Chinese, reduplicating a measure word or noun distributes its reference across every member of the set ('every single step, step after step'), which then functions adverbially before a predicate to mean 'at every step, progressively, or cautiously step by step'.

history.meaning: at every pace, step after step (e.g., 步步生蓮 'every step brings forth a lotus flower')
step by step, at every turn, progressively (adverbial modifier in idioms and four-character phrases)

morphemes.meaning: step, pace (reduplicated for distributive meaning 'every step')

步步.notes: Thrives in vivid four-character idioms central to workplace and palace/showbiz dramas: 步步惊心 ('startling at every step'), 步步为营 ('consolidate at every step / proceed with extreme caution'), and 步步高升 ('rise higher with every step / steady promotion').

rootFamily.gloss: one step at a time, step by step (colloquial)

cognates.meaning: viewing as divergent; discrimination (Sino-Japanese literary cognate)

歧视.etymology: A modifier-head verbal/nominal compound (歧視, qíshì) combining 歧 (qí, 'forked road, diverging branch, unequal, different', originally a variant of 岐 with 止 'foot' and 支 'branch') and 视 (trad. 視, shì, 'to look at, regard, treat'). Literally 'to look upon differently / treat as diverging from the norm' (opposite 一视同仁 yīshì tóngrén 'to regard everyone equally with the same benevolence'); attested in late imperial Chinese administrative prose for 'unequal treatment' and established in the 20th century as the standard term for social, racial, or gender 'discrimination'.

history.meaning: to regard differently or treat unequally (contrasted with 一視同仁 'regarding all equally')
discrimination, bias, prejudice; to discriminate against (based on gender, age, background, etc.)

morphemes.meaning: look at, regard, view, treat (trad. 視)

歧视.notes: Functions as both a transitive verb (歧视女性 'discriminate against women') and a noun (性别歧视 'gender discrimination', 年龄歧视 'ageism', 地域歧视 'regional bias'); its exact idiomatic antonym is 一视同仁 ('treat everyone equally').

歪.etymology: Compound ideogram (会意字) combining 不 ('not') atop 正 ('straight, upright'): literally 'not straight' = 'crooked, askew, tilted, slanting, devious'. Attested from Yuan–Ming vernacular onward.

history.meaning: not straight (不 + 正) = crooked, askew, tilted

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 歪 (via 萌典)

死.etymology: From Old Chinese *sijʔ (Baxter-Sagart), inherited from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *səj ("to die"; compare Written Tibetan འཆི་བ / ཤི་བ, Burmese သေ). In oracle bone script (甲骨文), the character 死 is an ideogrammic compound (会意) depicting a kneeling person (匕/人) bowing in mourning beside a skeletal bone fragment (歹/歺, representing stripped human remains). In Mandarin, besides the primary verbal meaning "to die" and adjectival sense "rigid, fixed, impassable," it grammaticalized from early vernacular Chinese onward into a post-verbal degree complement (e.g., 忙死了 "busy to death") functioning as an emphatic intensifier.

history.meaning: to die; death; lifeless remains (Oracle Bone & Classical Chinese)
to die; rigid, inflexible; willing to die for (Middle Chinese)
to die; impassable or fixed; extreme degree complement ("to death")

morphemes.meaning: to die; rigid; to an extreme degree

死.notes: Extremely productive in colloquial Mandarin as a post-verbal resultative/degree complement (Verb/Adj + 死了, e.g., 累死了 "exhausted to death", 气死了 "furious to death") to express hyperbolic intensity without any literal reference to mortality.

死党.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) compound formed from 死 (sǐ, "to the death; sworn to die for") and 党 (dǎng, traditional 黨, "faction, partisan group, clique"). Originally attested in Classical and Imperial historiography (such as the History of the Later Han, 后汉书) with a serious political sense denoting "sworn followers ready to die for their leader or faction" (效死之徒党). In modern colloquial Mandarin (especially mediated through Taiwan and Hong Kong youth slang), the term underwent amelioration and trivialization to mean an inseparable, ride-or-die best friend or close confidant.

history.meaning: sworn partisans or followers willing to die for a faction leader
diehard political clique; inseparable best friend, ride-or-die buddy

死党.notes: While 党 in formal political discourse means "political party," in colloquial compounds like 死党 or 狐朋狗党 it retains its classical sense of a tight-knit personal circle; 死党 is warm, informal, and affectionately used for one's closest friends.

死性不改.etymology: A four-character idiomatic subject-predicate phrase (主谓短语) structured around the subject 死性 (sǐxìng, "inflexible, stubborn, ingrained nature," from 死 "rigid, unchangeable" + 性 "inborn nature, temperament") and the negated verb phrase 不改 (bùgǎi, "does not change / refuses to mend," from 不 "not" + 改 "to alter, to correct"). Popularized in Ming and Qing vernacular fiction (白话小说) and Cantonese/Mandarin colloquial speech as a vivid, reproachful variant of the classical chengyu 本性难移 ("one's fundamental nature is hard to shift").

history.meaning: to stubbornly cling to one's ingrained bad habits without reforming
incorrigible, refusing to mend one's ways despite repeated lessons

morphemes.meaning: to change, to correct, to mend

死性不改.notes: Carries a distinctly exasperated, scolding tone—used either bitterly for someone who repeatedly commits the same mistake or playfully among close friends teasing someone about an unshakeable quirk.

rootFamily.gloss: to correct mistakes and turn over a new leaf

死磕.etymology: A modifier-head verbal compound originating in Northern Chinese (particularly Beijing Mandarin, 京片子) vernacular, combining the adverbial intensifier 死 (sǐ, "to the death, doggedly, relentlessly") with the action verb 磕 (kē, "to knock, strike, or bash against a hard surface," written with the stone radical 石 + phonetic 盍). Literally "to bash one's head against something to the bitter end," it metaphorically shifted from fighting an adversary tooth and nail to doggedly grinding away at a difficult task, project, or goal without backing down.

history.meaning: to fight someone tooth and nail; to lock horns uncompromisingly (Northern dialect)
to grind away relentlessly at a problem, project, or rival until the end

morphemes.meaning: to knock against, to collide, to battle head-on

死磕.notes: In contemporary workplace and media culture (such as television production in 幕后之王), 死磕 has shifted from a rough street-fighting word to an admired badge of craftsmanship—e.g., 死磕细节 ("obsessively perfecting every detail") or 跟自己死磕 ("pushing oneself to the limit").

rootFamily.gloss: to knock, bump against; stumbling blocks
to hold out to the bitter end, defend to the death

死路.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) nominal compound composed of 死 (sǐ, here functioning in its dual sense of "blocked, impassable" and "fatal, leading to death") and 路 (lù, "road, path, way"). In spatial usage, 死 contrasts with 活 ("live, open, passable") to denote a cul-de-sac or blind alley (compare 死胡同); in metaphorical usage attested since Song–Yuan vernacular texts, it denotes a suicidal course of action or a path leading to certain ruin.

history.meaning: a road leading to death; a blocked or impassable route (Song–Ming vernacular)
dead end, cul-de-sac; path to ruin or destruction

死路.notes: Frequently appears in the four-character set phrases 死路一条 ("nothing but a dead end / certain doom") and 自寻死路 ("to court one's own destruction"), contrasting directly with 生路 or 活路 ("a way out / path to survival").

rootFamily.gloss: way out, path to survival or livelihood

残疾人.etymology: A modifier-head noun phrase formed from the coordinative compound 残疾 (cánjí, "disability, impairment") + the head noun 人 (rén, "person"). Within 残疾, 残 (cán, traditional 殘, composed of 歹 "bones/death" + 戔 "to cut/destroy") means "damaged, incomplete, crippled," and 疾 (jí, sickness radical 疒 + 矢 "arrow," originally an acute illness striking swiftly like an arrow) means "disease, bodily defect, infirmity." Attested as a classical compound in Tang–Song legal and medical texts, 残疾人 was standardized in late 20th-century Mainland Chinese law (replacing older, more stigmatizing terms like 残废) as the respectful official designation for a person with a disability.

history.meaning: severe physical infirmity or bodily impairment (Tang legal code 唐律疏议)
person with a physical or mental disability (modern legal and respectful standard)

残疾人.notes: In Mainland China, 残疾人 is the standard respectful, legal, and media term (as in 中国残疾人联合会, China Disabled Persons' Federation), whereas Taiwan and Hong Kong often prefer 身障人士 (shēnzhàng rénshì, "person with a physical/mental barrier"); avoid the outdated and derogatory term 残废 (cánfèi, "crippled/useless").

段.etymology: Phono-semantic/ideographic character showing a hand with a hammer (殳) striking rock/metal fragments from a cliff face: originally 'hammer/forge metal' (later written 鍛 duàn), and from splitting something into pieces, the standard noun and classifier for 'a section, segment, stretch (of road, time, pipe, or wood), paragraph, or episode'.

history.meaning: split piece; section; stage
section; segment; paragraph; classifier for stretches of road, time, or text

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 段 (via 萌典)

段子手.etymology: A modern Mandarin derivative noun formed from 段子 (duànzi, "short comedic routine, joke, or witty anecdote") + the agentive suffix 手 (shǒu, literally "hand," extended since Classical Chinese to denote a skilled practitioner or specialist, as in 水手, 歌手, 高手). 段子 itself derives from 段 ("section, segment, passage of text or performance") + diminutive nominal suffix 子, originally a traditional northern storytelling and crosstalk (相声) term for a self-contained performance piece (一段相声). In the 2010s social media era (Weibo, variety shows), 段子手 was coined for sharp-witted writers and personalities who effortlessly craft viral jokes and punchlines.

history.meaning: a segment or routine in traditional storytelling (评书) and crosstalk (相声)
online joke writer, witty raconteur, variety-show quip master

段子手.notes: A staple buzzword in Chinese entertainment and variety-show culture: celebrities who win fans through quick-witted banter and self-deprecating humor rather than just scripted acting or singing are affectionately dubbed 被演艺事业耽误的段子手 ("a comedy writer held back by a showbiz career").

rootFamily.gloss: joke, short comedic routine or skit

cognates.meaning: palace hall, sanctuary, hall of fame (Sino-Japanese)

殿堂.etymology: A coordinative (并列) architectural compound combining 殿 (diàn, "grand lofty hall, palace hall, temple hall") and 堂 (táng, "elevated main hall or reception chamber built on a raised rammed-earth platform"). In pre-Qin Classical Chinese, 堂 referred broadly to any elevated main hall, whereas from the Qin and Han dynasties onward, 殿 became restricted to grand imperial palace halls and major religious sanctuaries. Joined together in Han–Tang prose and Buddhist translations, 殿堂 denoted magnificent palace or temple halls, later acquiring the elevated metaphorical sense of the "highest realm, pantheon, or sacred hall" of an art or discipline (e.g., 艺术殿堂, 音乐殿堂).

history.meaning: grand palace halls and elevated ceremonial chambers (Han–Tang literature)
magnificent hall or temple; figuratively, the highest pantheon or pinnacle of an art/field

殿堂.notes: In modern media, music, and cultural criticism, 殿堂 is frequently paired with the suffix 级 ("level/grade") to form 殿堂级 (diàntángjí, "Hall-of-Fame tier / legendary / pantheon-level"), used to praise iconic singers, producers, or masterpieces.

母亲.etymology: A modifier-head or appositional kinship compound formed from 母 (mǔ, Old Chinese *mˤəʔ, originally a pictograph in oracle bone script of a kneeling woman 女 with two dots highlighting her breasts to signify nursing and motherhood) and 亲 (qīn, traditional 親, "parent, blood relative, intimate kin"). In Classical Chinese, 母 and 亲 could each stand alone for "mother" or "parent"; during the disyllabification trend of Middle and Early Mandarin, 母亲 coalesced (parallel to 父亲 "father") as the standard dignified disyllabic noun for "mother."

history.meaning: mother; female parent or nursing female (Oracle Bone & Classical Chinese)
one's mother (attested in Tang–Song poetry and vernacular texts)
mother (formal and respectful standard register)

母亲.notes: 母亲 belongs to the formal, written, and respectful spoken register (used in narratives, speeches, or metaphors like 母亲河 "Mother River"), whereas in everyday family conversation speakers almost always say 妈妈 (māma) or 妈 (mā).

每.etymology: Ancient character attested on Shang oracle bones showing a woman/mother (母) with a sprouting hairpin or lush crest (屮) on her head: originally 'lush growth, fertile' (later written 莓/繁), borrowed since the earliest classics for the distributive determiner and adverb 'every, each'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: every; each; on every occasion

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 每 (via 萌典)

每个.etymology: A determiner-classifier compound combining the distributive pronoun 每 (měi, Old Chinese *mˤəʔ, originally an oracle-bone/bronze graph depicting a woman 女 wearing a lush hairpin or plumed headdress 屮, signifying flourishing growth of grass before grammaticalizing into "each, every") and the general classifier 个 (gè, traditional 個/箇, originally a classifier for bamboo stalks before becoming the universal Mandarin individual classifier). Together, 每个 functions as the standard distributive determiner phrase meaning "each and every single (one)."

history.meaning: each (used directly before nouns in Classical Chinese) + bamboo/individual counter
every single, each (grammaticalized determiner + general classifier unit)

每个.notes: In Mandarin grammar, distributive phrases with 每 (such as 每个, 每天, 每周) almost always co-occur with the universal quantifier 都 (dōu, "all") before the main verb—e.g., 每个人都有自己的梦想 ("Every single person has their own dream").

每周.etymology: A modifier-head temporal compound formed from the distributive determiner 每 (měi, "each, every") and 周 (zhōu, traditional 週/周, "cycle, circuit, revolution," and in modern usage "week"). In Classical Chinese, 周 meant a complete revolution or cycle (such as a full year or astronomical cycle). During the late Qing dynasty and Meiji Japan modernization period, when the seven-day Western calendar week was adopted across East Asia, 周/週 was assigned to the seven-day cycle (alongside 星期 and 礼拜), giving rise to 每周 ("every week, weekly").

history.meaning: every complete cycle or circuit (Classical Chinese); every seven-day week (Late Qing–Modern)
every week, weekly (standard formal and media temporal adverb/noun)

每周.notes: 每周 is more concise and formal than 每个星期 (měi gè xīngqī) or 每个礼拜 (měi gè lǐbài), making it the preferred choice in television broadcasting schedules (e.g., 每周六晚八点播出 "airs every Saturday at 8 PM") and workplace reporting (周报 "weekly report").

每天.etymology: A modifier-head temporal compound composed of the distributive determiner 每 (měi, "each, every") and 天 (tiān, Old Chinese *l̥ˤin, originally an anthropomorphic bronze/oracle-bone graph depicting the top of a standing figure's head and by extension the "sky, heaven" above). Over time, 天 extended from "sky/heaven" to the natural cycle of daylight ("a day, 24-hour period"), allowing 每天 to replace the more literary 每日 (měirì) in vernacular Mandarin as the standard everyday word for "every day, daily."

history.meaning: every day (每日 in Classical prose; 每天 emerging in Yuan–Ming vernacular)
every day, daily (standard modern temporal noun and adverb)

每天.notes: Because 天 functions as a quasi-classifier (like 年 "year" and 周 "week"), it never takes 个 between 每 and 天 (*每个天 is ungrammatical; always say 每天). In formal written titles, 每日 often substitutes for 每天 (e.g., 每日新闻 "Daily News").

rootFamily.gloss: day by day; every single day (reduplicated)

每日.etymology: Classical and formal time expression from 每 ('every; each', originally depicting a woman 女 wearing a fertile sprout/hairpin) + 日 ('day; sun'). Retained in modern Mandarin for schedules, newspapers, and shop specials such as 'daily menu' (每日菜单).

history.meaning: every day; daily
daily; every day

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 每日

每次.etymology: Distributive temporal/quantifier phrase combining 每 ('every, each') + 次 ('time, occasion'): 'every time, each time'.

history.meaning: every time; each occasion

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 每次 (via 萌典)

毒瘤.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) compound combining 毒 (dú, "poison, toxin, virulence, malignancy") and 瘤 (liú, formed from the sickness radical 疒 + phonetic 留 liú, "swelling, tumor, growth"). Originally a traditional Chinese medical term denoting a virulent or malignant swelling/tumor on the body, 毒瘤 developed a powerful sociopolitical metaphor in modern Chinese journalism and public discourse for a deep-seated "cancer, blight, or rot" corrupting an organization, industry, or society (such as 行业毒瘤 "an industry blight" or 社会毒瘤 "a cancer on society").

history.meaning: virulent or malignant swelling/tumor (Traditional Chinese medical texts)
malignant tumor; figuratively, a corrosive blight, cancer, or rot within a system

毒瘤.notes: In modern usage, literal medical contexts usually prefer 恶性肿瘤 (èxìng zhǒngliú) for "malignant tumor," whereas 毒瘤 is overwhelmingly used figuratively in strong polemical or media contexts (often collocating with 铲除 or 清除, "to eradicate a rot/blight").

比.etymology: Ancient ideogram (会意字) attested on Shang oracle bones showing two people (二人) standing closely side by side facing the same direction (the mirror image of 从): originally 'stand side by side, close together (比邻)', hence 'compare, match, emulate; ratio/score' and Mandarin's primary comparative preposition ('than': A 比 B 大).

morphemes.meaning: two people standing side by side to compare

history.meaning: two people side by side = close together, compare, match
compare; comparative marker 'than'; ratio/score

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 比 (via 萌典)

比例.etymology: Coordinative noun compound of 比 ('compare, ratio') + 例 ('standard, regular scale'): 'proportion, ratio, scale'.

history.meaning: proportion; ratio; scale

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 比例 (via 萌典)

比对.etymology: Coordinative verb compound of 比 ('compare side by side') + 对 (對, 'check, match, verify'): 'compare and check against each other, cross-check, match'.

history.stage: Song–Ming administrative Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: compare and check; cross-verify

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 比对 (via 萌典)

比方说.etymology: A three-character colloquial discourse marker composed of the noun/verb compound 比方 (bǐfāng, "analogy, comparison, example," from 比 "to compare, liken" + 方 "method, parallel, comparison") followed by the verb 说 (shuō, "to say, to speak"). In Classical and Tang–Song Chinese, 比方 meant "to compare alongside" or "an illustrative analogy" (打比方 "to draw an analogy"); in Mandarin vernacular, appending 说 grammaticalized the phrase into a conversational discourse opener meaning "for example, say for instance, suppose that."

history.meaning: to compare side by side; analogy, illustrative case (Tang–Ming vernacular)
for example, take for instance, suppose (colloquial discourse marker)

比方说.notes: Conversational and approachable in register—synonymous with 比如说 (bǐrú shuō) in spoken Mandarin, whereas formal essays and news broadcasts prefer 例如 (lìrú) or 譬如 (pìrú). You can also split it into the verb-object phrase 打个比方 ("let me give an analogy/example").

rootFamily.gloss: for example, for instance (slightly more general)

比赛.etymology: A coordinative (并列) verbal and nominal compound formed from 比 (bǐ, Old Chinese *pijʔ, originally an oracle-bone graph of two people standing closely side by side, hence "to line up, compare, match against") and 赛 (sài, traditional 賽, originally a ritual offering of thanksgiving to the gods after harvest, which evolved via competitive temple festivals into "to vie, rival, surpass, compete"). Attested from Song–Ming vernacular onward, 比赛 became the standard modern Mandarin word for both the verb "to compete" and the noun "competition, match, contest, tournament."

history.meaning: ritual offering to repay the gods; festival display vying in splendor (Han–Tang)
to compare skills and compete; athletic, artistic, or professional contest/match

morphemes.meaning: to compare, to match side by side

比赛.notes: Functions effortlessly as both a noun (一场精彩的比赛 "a thrilling competition/match") and a verb (我们比赛吧 "let's compete/race"), and in talent-show and television production contexts (like 幕后之王) its second character 赛 generates a whole family of showbiz terms: 赛制 (competition format), 赛区 (competition zone), 决赛 (finals), and 淘汰赛 (elimination round).

rootFamily.gloss: competition format or system (crucial in TV talent shows)

比赛规则.etymology: A four-character modifier-head (偏正) nominal compound combining 比赛 (bǐsài, "competition, contest," from 比 "to compare/match" + 赛 "to vie/compete") with 规则 (guīzé, "rules, regulations"). Within 规则, 规 (guī) originally denoted a carpenter's compass used to draw circles and 则 (zé) denoted a carved bronze standard or law; together in Classical Chinese (规矩法度之则), they meant "standards and principles." As a composite phrase, 比赛规则 denotes the official regulations and scoring criteria governing a tournament or contest.

history.meaning: standards measured by compass and law; established norms and regulations (Tang–Song)
competition rules, official regulations of a contest or game

比赛规则.notes: In television variety shows and competitive reality programs, 比赛规则 (often shortened to 赛制 "competition format/rules") is a central plot engine—commonly paired with verbs like 遵守 ("abide by"), 制定 ("formulate"), or 修改 ("modify the competition rules").

rootFamily.gloss: rules, established standards or etiquette (literally "compass and square")
rules of the game (often used figuratively for industry politics)

比起.etymology: A compound prepositional phrase (derived from a verb + directional complement construction) formed from 比 (bǐ, "to compare with") and the directional/inchoative complement 起 (qǐ, originally "to rise, to stand up," grammaticalized after verbs of evaluation or speech to mean "when starting to perform the action of V / when bringing up for comparison," often alternating with the fuller frame 比起……来).
