By setting up a topic of comparison at the start of a clause, 比起 functions as an emphatic comparative preposition meaning "compared with, in comparison to."

history.meaning: when one starts comparing X (with Y)... (Ming–Qing vernacular directional construction)
compared with, in comparison to (topicalizing comparative preposition)

morphemes.meaning: up; inchoative marker of evaluation ("when bringing into comparison")

比起.notes: Unlike the simple preposition 比 (which usually sits between Subject and Predicate: A 比 B 好), 比起 loves to sit at the very front of the sentence to topicalize the baseline of comparison: 比起台前的明星，幕后制作人更辛苦 ("Compared with the stars on stage, the producers behind the scenes work even harder").

rootFamily.gloss: compared with (often used interchangeably with 比起)
speaking of, when it comes to (parallel V+起 discourse marker)

比较.etymology: Coordinative verb and degree adverb compound of 比 ('compare') + 较 (較, 'compare carriages/measures, weigh against'). Functions both as a verb/noun ('compare; comparison') and as a very common degree adverb before adjectives ('comparatively, relatively, rather, quite').

history.meaning: compare and weigh
compare (verb); relatively, quite (adverb)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 比较 (via 萌典)

毕业.etymology: A verb-object (动宾) separable compound (离合词) formed from 毕 (bì, traditional 畢, originally a pictograph of a long-handled hunting net used to catch every last bird or animal, hence "to finish completely, to conclude") and 业 (yè, traditional 業, "course of study, enterprise, profession"). Attested in Classical Chinese educational texts (such as the Tang code and Song academies) in the sense of "completing one's prescribed studies of the classics," 毕业 was revitalized during late Qing educational reforms (alongside Japanese 卒業 sotsugyō) as the standard modern term for graduating from a school or university.

history.meaning: to complete one's prescribed classical studies or official task (Tang–Song prose)
to graduate from an educational institution (separable verb and noun)

morphemes.meaning: to finish, to complete, to conclude

毕业.notes: Grammar trap for learners: 毕业 is an intransitive verb-object compound (离合词), so you NEVER put the school name after it as a direct object (*毕业北电 is wrong); always use the preposition 从 ("from"): 从北京电影学院毕业 ("graduate from Beijing Film Academy").

毕竟.etymology: A coordinative (并列) disyllabic adverb composed of two synonymous classical verbs of completion: 毕 (bì, traditional 畢, "to finish completely, to end") and 竟 (jìng, composed of 音 "sound/music" + 人, originally meaning "to reach the end of a musical performance," hence "to finish, ultimately, to the end"). First popularized in Six Dynasties and Tang Buddhist translations (where 毕竟 translated Sanskrit *atyanta*, "ultimately, in the final analysis"), it grammaticalized into a concessive/explanatory adverb meaning "after all, when all is said and done."

history.meaning: to finish completely; ultimately, in the final analysis (Buddhist Chinese & Tang poetry)
after all, when all is said and done (explanatory/concessive adverb)

morphemes.meaning: to finish completely, in the end
to reach the end of a piece; ultimately, finally

毕竟.notes: Used to introduce an undeniable underlying fact that explains or tempers another statement—often paired with a preceding concession: 他虽然有缺点，但毕竟是个有才华的制作人 ("Although he has flaws, he is, after all, a talented producer"). Contrast with 究竟 (jiūjìng), which is used in questions ("what on earth / actually?"), whereas 毕竟 is used only in declarative explanations.

rootFamily.gloss: ultimately, after all (in questions: what on earth?)
throughout one's whole life (literally "finish one's life")

cognates.meaning: hair, fur; one-tenth of a rin/sen (Sino-Japanese)

毛.etymology: From Old Chinese *mˤaw (Baxter-Sagart), originally a pictograph in bronze and seal script depicting a tuft of fine animal fur, down, or bird feathers. Because fine hairs and feathers represented something tiny and lightweight, 毛 semanticized into a metaphor for minute quantities and small fractional units (alongside 毫). In late Qing and Republican currency usage, when decimal silver coins were minted alongside the main silver dollar (元/圆/块), the fractional 10-cent coin (formally 角 jiǎo, "one-tenth of a yuan") came to be called 毛 in spoken Mandarin (originally contrasting "fuzzy/fractional small silver coins" 毛钱 with whole silver dollars, before standardizing as the colloquial unit for 0.1 yuan).

history.meaning: hair, fur, feathers, down; fine vegetation on the earth (Classical Chinese)
fine hair; minute fraction, tiny amount (Middle Chinese)
hair/fur; colloquial monetary unit for one-tenth of a yuan (dime, 0.1 RMB, = 角)

morphemes.meaning: hair, fur; tiny fraction; one-tenth of a yuan (colloquial for 角)

毛.notes: Chinese currency has two parallel register systems: formal/written 元 (yuán) – 角 (jiǎo) – 分 (fēn) printed on banknotes and price tags, versus spoken/colloquial 块 (kuài) – 毛 (máo) – 分 (fēn) used in everyday speech (e.g., 五毛钱 "fifty cents / half a yuan"). In internet slang, 一毛钱关系都没有 means "doesn't have even a dime's worth of connection (nothing whatsoever to do with)."

rootFamily.gloss: flaw, defect, bad habit (originally a horse's coat blemish)

毛巾.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 毛 ('nap, terry loops, hair/fuzz') + 巾 ('woven cloth, towel'): 'towel (especially a cotton terrycloth face or bath towel)'.

history.meaning: terrycloth towel; towel

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 毛巾 (via 萌典)

毛毛雨.etymology: Vivid descriptive compound from 毛毛 (reduplication of 毛 'fine hair; down; fur') + 雨 ('rain', pictograph of raindrops falling from clouds under heaven). Compares mist-like, drifting drizzle to fine animal down floating in the air.

history.meaning: fine, misty drizzle
drizzle; fine misty rain

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 毛毛雨

毛毡.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 毛 ('animal hair, wool') + 毡 (氈, 'pressed wool felt', 毛 + 占): 'felt, woolen felt pad or mat'.

history.stage: Classical & Medieval Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: wool felt; felt pad

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 毛毡 (via 萌典)

毛衣.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 毛 ('wool, yarn') + 衣 ('upper garment, clothing'): 'woolen sweater, knit sweater'.

history.meaning: woolen sweater; jumper

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 毛衣 (via 萌典)

毫无关系.etymology: A four-character emphatic verb-object idiom composed of 毫 (háo, "fine autumn tip of an animal hair; a tiny fraction, the slightest bit," sharing its bottom graphic component with 毛), 无 (wú, traditional 無, classical existential negator "to lack, to not have"), and the object noun 关系 (guānxì, traditional 關係, "connection, relation, bearing," from 关 "wooden bolt of a gate; to link, involve" + 系 "to tie, bind together"). Together, 毫无 ("to not have a single hair's breadth of") + 关系 ("connection") means "to have nothing whatsoever to do with."

history.meaning: not having the slightest bit of, utterly devoid of (Song–Ming literary and vernacular prose)
to have nothing whatsoever to do with, completely unrelated

morphemes.meaning: fine hair; the slightest bit, at all
gate bolt; to involve, to connect
to tie, to link (forming 关系 "relationship/connection")

毫无关系.notes: Typically used in the frame A 跟/与 B 毫无关系 ("A has nothing whatsoever to do with B"); 毫无 is a highly productive semi-formal emphatic negator that pairs with two-syllable nouns across Mandarin (毫无意义 "utterly meaningless", 毫无根据 "completely groundless", 毫无疑问 "beyond a shadow of a doubt").

rootFamily.gloss: beyond a shadow of a doubt, unquestionably
not in the least, not a single bit

毫米.etymology: Metric length unit combining 毫 ('fine tip of a hair -> one-thousandth, milli-') + 米 ('meter', phonetic loan from French mètre): 'millimeter (mm, 1/1,000 of a meter)'.

history.meaning: one-thousandth of a meter = millimeter (mm)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 毫米 (via 萌典)

毯子.etymology: A suffixed nominal compound formed from the root 毯 (tǎn, a phono-semantic character combining the semantic radical 毛 "fur, wool, animal hair" with the phonetic 炎 yán, originally created during the Tang–Song period to denote woven woolen rugs, carpets, and felt mats imported via Inner Asian trade routes) plus the unstressed Mandarin nominal suffix 子 (zi). In modern Mandarin, 毯子 refers primarily to a soft blanket or throw (while 地毯 specifies a floor carpet).

history.meaning: woven woolen rug, felt mat, or heavy tapestry (Tang–Song texts)
blanket, throw rug, woolen or fleece covering

morphemes.meaning: woven woolen rug, blanket, felt covering

毯子.notes: Distinguish carefully between 毯子 / 毛毯 (a blanket or throw used to cover oneself on a sofa or bed, often seen in backstage studios when cast and crew work late) and 地毯 (dìtǎn, "carpet / rug" on the floor, as in 红地毯 "red carpet"). Use the classifier 条 (tiáo) or 张 (zhāng): 一条毯子.

民众.etymology: A coordinative/collective nominal compound combining 民 (mín, Old Chinese *miŋ, "the common people, subjects, folk") and 众 (zhòng, traditional 眾, originally an oracle-bone pictograph showing three people 乑 working beneath the sun 日, hence "a multitude, crowd, the many"). Attested in pre-Qin Classical Chinese texts (such as Mencius and Xunzi) in the literal sense of "the multitude of common people," 民众 was reinforced in late 19th- and early 20th-century East Asian civic discourse (alongside Japanese 民衆 minshū) as a modern journalistic and political term for "the general public, ordinary citizens, the populace."

history.meaning: the multitude of common subjects, the populace (Pre-Qin & Han Classical prose)
the general public, ordinary citizens, residents (modern civic and media register)

民众.notes: In news broadcasting and journalism, 民众 is the go-to neutral, civic-minded word for "the general public / ordinary citizens" (e.g., 引发民众热议 "sparked heated discussion among the public"), sitting in register between the loftier राजनीतिक term 人民 ("the People") and the colloquial 老百姓 ("ordinary folks").

cognates.meaning: public opinion, will of the people (Sino-Korean)
popular sentiment, will of the people (Sino-Vietnamese)

民意.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) compound formed from 民 (mín, "the people, citizens, the public") and 意 (yì, composed of 音 "sound/voice" + 心 "heart/mind," meaning "thought, will, sentiment, intention"). Already attested in Imperial Chinese political philosophy and memorials to the throne (such as 顺应民意 "to accord with the sentiments of the people"), 民意 transitioned smoothly into modern political science, journalism, and media polling to denote "public opinion, popular sentiment, the will of the public."

history.meaning: the sentiments, desires, and hearts of the common people (Han–Tang political prose)
public opinion, popular will, audience/voter sentiment (modern civic & media register)

民意.notes: Frequently appears in media and polling contexts such as 民意调查 (mínyì diàochá, often abbreviated as 民调 míndiào, "public opinion poll") and 违背民意 ("to go against public sentiment"—also used jokingly by viewers when a popular contestant is eliminated on a show!).

rootFamily.gloss: public opinion poll (often shortened to 民调)
popular support, the hearts of the people

气.etymology: Ancient pictograph (氣; in oracle-bone and bronze scripts written 气 with three horizontal cloud-vapor lines, before 米 'rice' was added to form 氣 for 'vital breath/energy' and then simplified back to 气): 'rising cloud vapor -> air, gas, breath, weather, smell/odor, vital energy (qi), spirit/tone, anger/annoy'.

morphemes.meaning: rising layers of vapor/air = breath, air, gas, anger

history.meaning: rising cloud/breath vapor = air, breath, vital energy
air; gas; breath; smell; anger

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 气 (via 萌典)

气味.etymology: A coordinative (并列) compound uniting 气 (qì, traditional 氣, originally "rising vapor, mist, breath, airborne exhalation," hence "smell, odor") and 味 (wèi, "taste, flavor, savor"). In pre-Qin and Han Classical Chinese (such as the Zuo Zhuan and Book of Rites), 气味 was a dual sensory term meaning "odor (气) and taste (味)," and by extension "shared temperament or affinity" (气味相投 "congenial in tastes and temperament"). In modern Mandarin, the compound underwent semantic narrowing (偏义复词 tendency) toward the olfactory pole of 气, meaning "smell, scent, odor" or a figurative "lingering aura/vibe."

history.meaning: odor and flavor; figuratively, moral character or congeniality of temperament (Classical Chinese)
smell, scent, odor (neutral olfactory noun); lingering atmosphere or flavor

气味.notes: 气味 is the neutral, objective word for any "smell or odor" (whether pleasant or unpleasant), whereas 香味 (xiāngwèi) is specifically a pleasant fragrance/aroma, 臭味 (chòuwèi) is a stench, and 味道 (wèidào) covers both food taste and everyday smell in casual speech.

rootFamily.gloss: breath, aura, flavor of life or art

气氛.etymology: A coordinative (并列) meteorological-turned-psychological compound formed from 气 (qì, traditional 氣, "vapor, air, vital energy, aura") and 氛 (fēn, composed of 气 "vapor" + phonetic 分 fēn, originally denoting "mist, fog, or auspicious/inauspicious atmospheric halo" observed in ancient sky-divination, as in 氛氲 "thick swirling mist"). In Classical Chinese, 气氛 referred to visible atmospheric vapors or portents in the sky; in modern Mandarin, it shifted metaphorically to the emotional or social "atmosphere, mood, or tension" palpable inside a room or gathering.

history.meaning: atmospheric vapor, mist, or portentous aura in the sky (Han–Tang literature)
emotional atmosphere, mood, or palpable tension in a room or event

气氛.notes: Compare 气氛 with 氛围 (fēnwéi): 气氛 focuses on the immediate, dynamic emotional mood of a specific scene or interaction (e.g., 现场气氛很热烈 "the live atmosphere is electric", 气氛突然变得很尴尬 "the mood in the room suddenly turned awkward"), and is the source of the showbiz slang 气氛组 ("hype crew / mood-makers").

气泡水.etymology: Three-character compound combining 气泡 ('air/gas bubbles', 气 'gas/air' + 泡 'bubble') + 水 ('water'): 'sparkling water, carbonated water, seltzer'.

history.meaning: sparkling water; carbonated water

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 气泡水 (via 萌典)

气窗.etymology: Architectural compound from 气 (simplified from 氣, 'air; vapour; breath') + 窗 ('window; skylight', originally a pictograph of a lattice opening under the cave/roof radical 穴). Denotes a small transom window or high vent window set above a door or high on a wall to let rising warm air and steam escape.

history.meaning: ventilation window; transom window
transom window; small vent window

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 气窗

气色.etymology: A coordinative/modifier-head compound rooted in Traditional Chinese Medicine (中医望诊, visual diagnosis) and classical physiognomy, combining 气 (qì, traditional 氣, "internal vital energy, breath, life force") and 色 (sè, "facial color, complexion, countenance"). According to classical medical texts like the Huangdi Neijing (黄帝内经), the vitality of one's internal organs and blood (气血) manifests outwardly in the luster and hue of the face (色); hence 气色 denotes a person's facial complexion and visible state of health and energy.

history.meaning: manifestation of vital qi in facial color; facial expression or atmospheric hue (Classical & Medical Chinese)
facial complexion, healthy color and vitality showing in one's face

气色.notes: A favorite everyday compliment or expression of concern in Mandarin: 你最近气色真好 ("You look so radiant/healthy lately!") vs. 你气色不太好，是不是没休息好？ ("You look pale/drawn—have you not been resting well?"). Contrast with 脸色 (liǎnsè), which can mean either physical paleness or an angry/displeased facial expression (看人脸色 "walk on eggshells around someone's mood").

rootFamily.gloss: vital energy and blood (traditional root of good complexion)
expression, look in one's eyes and face

气质.etymology: A Song-dynasty Neo-Confucian (理学) philosophical compound combining 气 (qì, traditional 氣, "vital breath, psychophysical energy") and 质 (zhì, traditional 質, "fundamental substance, material constitution, innate nature"). Coined and popularized by thinkers like Zhang Zai (张载) and Zhu Xi (朱熹) in the concept of 气质之性 ("the physical/temperamental nature endowed by one's qi and bodily constitution," which could be refined through moral self-cultivation, 变化气质), the word evolved in modern Mandarin into an aesthetic and psychological term for a person's "innate poise, cultivated aura, elegance, and temperament."

history.meaning: inborn psychophysical constitution and temperament (Song Neo-Confucian philosophy)
poise, cultivated aura, charisma, and refined personal temperament

气质.notes: In Chinese showbiz and everyday compliments, 有气质 ("to have poise/charisma") is higher praise than merely 漂亮 ("pretty"): 漂亮 praises surface facial features, whereas 气质 praises the deeper bearing, posture, artistic refinement, and presence that a performer or professional radiates.

rootFamily.gloss: charismatic presence, commanding aura (modern showbiz sister word)
innate talent, natural endowment or disposition

氛围.etymology: A compound combining 氛 (fēn, "mist, vapor, atmospheric aura") and 围 (wéi, traditional 圍, "to surround, encircle, perimeter, environment"), literally "the surrounding envelope of vapor/air." In the late 19th century, Japanese scholars coined 雰囲気 (fun'iki, "surrounding vapor-air") to translate the Dutch/English scientific term *atmosphere* (originally gaseous envelope around a planet, then figurative social/aesthetic ambiance); Chinese subsequently adopted the succinct two-character form 氛围 for the figurative sense of "surrounding ambiance, cultural climate, or aesthetic vibe."

history.meaning: gaseous envelope surrounding a body; surrounding social or aesthetic atmosphere (Meiji–Republican era)
ambiance, surrounding environment, overall vibe or aesthetic mood

氛围.notes: Slightly more literary and aesthetic than 气氛 (qìfēn): 氛围 emphasizes the broader, enveloping environment or aesthetic setting (e.g., 营造良好的工作氛围 "cultivate a great working environment", 学术氛围 "academic climate"), and has spawned the viral contemporary aesthetics term 氛围感 (fēnwéigǎn, "aesthetic vibe / atmospheric allure" in photography, lighting, and staging).

rootFamily.gloss: immediate mood or atmosphere in a room/event
to surround, to revolve around, to center on

水.etymology: Fundamental noun 'water' (shuǐ), descended from an oracle-bone pictograph of a flowing stream flanked by ripples and droplets. Serves both as an independent word (热水 'hot water', 喝水 'drink water') and as the left-hand component 氵 in hundreds of liquid-related characters.

history.meaning: water; river

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 水 (via 萌典)

水彩.etymology: A transparent compound joining 水 (shuǐ, 'water') and 彩 (cǎi, 'pigment, colour'), coined during late Qing and early Republican artistic exchanges (alongside Japanese 水彩 suisai) as an exact calque for Western 'watercolour'—pigments bound with water-soluble gum arabic rather than oil, building on China's own millennia-old tradition of water-based ink-and-colour wash.

history.meaning: water-soluble colour pigment; watercolour medium
watercolour (paint or painting)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 水彩

水性.etymology: Compound from 水 ('water') + 性 ('nature; property; disposition', heart 忄 + 生). In classical prose 水性 meant the natural flow of water or a swimmer's familiarity with water; in modern materials terminology it serves as a modifier meaning 'water-based' (as in 水性漆 'water-based paint' or 水性笔 'water-based pen').

history.meaning: the nature of water; swimming ability
water-based (paint/ink); water properties

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 水性

水杯.etymology: A straightforward modifier-head (偏正) nominal compound composed of 水 (shuǐ, Old Chinese *s.turʔ, originally an oracle-bone pictograph of flowing river currents, "water, liquid") and 杯 (bēi, variants 盃/桮, combining the wood radical 木 with phonetic 不, originally denoting an oval wooden or lacquered drinking vessel in pre-Qin and Han times). While Classical Chinese used 杯 primarily for wine or soup vessels (酒杯, 羹杯), modern Mandarin formed 水杯 to designate any everyday drinking cup, mug, tumbler, or portable water bottle.

history.meaning: wooden or lacquered cup for wine or broth (Warring States & Han texts)
water cup, drinking glass, mug, or insulated tumbler

水杯.notes: In contemporary Chinese daily life (and backstage on film/TV sets), 水杯 covers not only open glasses and mugs on a desk, but also screw-top portable water bottles and thermoses (保温杯 bǎowēnbēi, "insulated thermos mug," famously associated with keeping warm water or goji-berry tea on hand during long shoots). Use the classifier 个: 一个水杯 (whereas 一杯水 means "a cup of water").

rootFamily.gloss: wine glass, goblet; trophy cup (as in 奖杯)

水桶.etymology: Compound of 水 ('water') + 桶 ('staved wooden pail or tub', wood radical 木 + phonetic 甬 yǒng), preserved even when modern buckets are metal or plastic.

history.meaning: coopered wooden measure or water bucket
water bucket; pail

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 水桶

水池.etymology: The noun '水池' (shuǐchí, pool, sink) is composed of '水' (water) and '池' (pool, pond). In classical usage, '池' referred to a man-made body of water or a moat surrounding a city wall. '水池' thus referred to any constructed basin for holding water. In modern times, its meaning has broadened significantly. It can refer to large outdoor decorative pools in parks, as well as small indoor plumbing fixtures like kitchen sinks or bathroom washbasins, depending on the context.

history.meaning: swimming pool

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 水池

水痕.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 水 ('water') + 痕 ('scar, mark, trace', 疒 + 艮): 'water mark, water stain, high-water line'. Attested in Tang–Song poetry (e.g., Su Shi's 水痕收) and everyday descriptions.

history.meaning: water mark; water stain; trace left by water

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 水痕 (via 萌典)

水管.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 水 ('water') + 管 ('bamboo tube -> pipe, hose'): 'water pipe, water hose, plumbing pipe'.

history.meaning: water pipe; hose

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 水管 (via 萌典)

水阀.etymology: Modifier-head technical compound of 水 ('water') + 阀 (閥, 'gate leaf -> mechanical valve'): 'water valve, shut-off valve'.

history.meaning: water valve

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 水阀 (via 萌典)

水龙头.etymology: Three-character metaphorical compound of 水 ('water') + 龙头 ('dragon head', 龙 'dragon' + 头 'head'). Because traditional Chinese rain-god iconography and early public water spouts were cast in the shape of a dragon's head spouting water, 水龙头 became the everyday Mandarin word for a 'water faucet, tap'.

history.stage: Late Qing–early 20th c. urban waterworks to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: dragon-head water spout = faucet, tap

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 水龙头 (via 萌典)

永.etymology: Originally an oracle bone pictograph depicting the long, branching, and continuous flow of subterranean or surface water currents, explained in the Shuowen Jiezi as 'long' (水长也) in reference to the endless coursing of rivers; semantically extended in Old Chinese to temporal perpetuity ('forever, eternally') and related by derivation to 泳 (yǒng, 'to swim through water').

history.meaning: long-flowing (of rivers and streams); enduring, perpetual
eternally, forever; long-lasting
forever, perpetually (primarily bound or literary adverb)

永.notes: In modern Mandarin, 永 rarely stands alone as a free adverb outside of four-character idioms (such as 永垂不朽) or concise literary slogans (such as 永不放弃, 'never give up').

永久.etymology: A coordinative disyllabic compound formed from 永 (yǒng, 'long-flowing, perpetual') and 久 (jiǔ, 'long duration of time'). Attested in Literary Chinese from the Han and Six Dynasties onward, pairing spatial-fluvial continuity with temporal endurance to express unbroken permanence.

history.meaning: enduring for a long duration, long-lasting
permanent, permanently, everlasting

永久.notes: Compared with 永远 (which is primarily adverbial and emotionally expressive), 永久 often functions as an attributive modifier meaning 'permanent' in institutional, legal, or technical contexts (e.g., 永久居留, 'permanent residency'; 永久封禁, 'permanent ban').

永远.etymology: A coordinative compound uniting 永 (yǒng, 'endlessly flowing, perpetual') and 远 (Traditional 遠, yuǎn, 'far-reaching, distant'). Originally used in Classical and Literary Chinese to describe vast spatial and temporal reach ('far and long'), it grammaticalized into the standard modern Mandarin temporal adverb meaning 'forever' or, with negation, 'never'.

history.meaning: distant and long-lasting; extending far into the future
forever, always; never (when preceding negative adverbs)

永远.notes: Frequently pairs with negators like 不 or 别 to mean 'never' (e.g., 永远不会忘记, 'will never forget'), carrying stronger emotional resonance in spoken dialogue than 永久.

rootFamily.gloss: distant, remote in time or space

汁.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 汁. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 汁 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 汁 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 汁 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 汁. The etymology of 汁 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 汁
middle form of 汁
modern form of 汁

求.etymology: Ancient pictograph attested on Shang oracle bones depicting a fur garment with hairs along the pelt (later written 裘 qiú with the clothing radical 衣 when 求 was borrowed for 'seek'): 'seek, look for, strive for; beg, request, entreat, ask a favor of'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: borrowed from 'fur coat (裘)' for 'seek, request, beg'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 求 (via 萌典)

求求.etymology: Formed by verbal reduplication of 求 (qiú, 'to seek, entreat, beseech'), whose oracle bone and bronze script forms depict a hand grasping a fur pelt or garment (originally the graph for 裘 'fur coat', borrowed phonetically for 'seek, beg'). In vernacular Mandarin, doubling the verb softens the syntactic force while heightening the interpersonal urgency of the plea.

history.meaning: to seek, request, entreat
to beg earnestly, plead with someone

morphemes.meaning: iterative/intensifying verbal reduplication marking earnest pleading

求求.notes: Almost always followed directly by a personal pronoun (most commonly 求求你, 'I beg you / please!'), where the second syllable is pronounced in neutral tone in natural colloquial speech.

汇报.etymology: A serial-verb / modifier-head compound combining 汇 (Traditional 匯, huì, 'to converge, gather together, compile', originally describing whirling waters collecting in a vessel) and 报 (Traditional 報, bào, 'to report, respond, inform'). It denotes gathering dispersed information or progress metrics and presenting them systematically to a superior or collective body.

history.meaning: to gather accounts and submit an official report
history.stage: Late Imperial and Early Modern Chinese

history.meaning: to report back, brief a superior, present a work summary

汇报.notes: A staple of Chinese workplace and production-team discourse, typically used with the preposition 向 to mark the recipient superior (e.g., 向总监汇报工作, 'report on work to the director').

cognates.meaning: the world at large, society outside officialdom (kōko)
the martial arts world, underworld, wider society (giang hồ)

江湖.etymology: A coordinative nominal compound literally juxtaposing 江 (jiāng, 'the Yangtze / great river') and 湖 (hú, 'the lakes, especially Dongting Lake'). First attested with philosophical resonance in the *Zhuangzi* (庄子·大宗师: 相忘于江湖, 'forgetting each other in the rivers and lakes'), it came to signify the realm of hermitage outside imperial court control, later evolving in Song–Ming vernacular fiction into the marginal society of wanderers, entertainers, and martial artists, and in modern usage into any fiercely competitive professional arena.

history.meaning: rivers and lakes; the natural realm of recluses beyond the imperial court
the subculture of itinerant martial artists, outlaws, and street performers
the wider world, competitive professional arena, or showbiz/business fray

江湖.notes: In contemporary media and corporate drama (*幕后之王*), 江湖 metaphorically refers to the unwritten rules, rivalries, and shifting alliances of an industry (e.g., 职场江湖, 娱乐圈江湖).

rootFamily.gloss: the world out there is treacherous
seasoned veteran, old hand in the ways of the world
rivers and mountains; state power or territory

江湖险恶.etymology: A four-character subject-predicate idiom (成语) composed of the nominal subject 江湖 (jiānghú, 'the wider world / competitive arena, literally rivers and lakes') and the coordinative adjectival predicate 险恶 (xiǎn'è, from 险 'precipitous, perilous' + 恶 'malicious, treacherous'). Originally describing the hazards of traveling waterways and navigating outlaw society, it warns of hidden traps and cutthroat rivalry in society.

history.meaning: the realm of rivers, lakes, and outlaws is full of peril and malice
the wider world (or industry arena) is treacherous and cutthroat

morphemes.meaning: the wider world, competitive arena (literally rivers and lakes)

江湖险恶.notes: Often used either seriously to warn newcomers against workplace backstabbing or playfully among friends to tease someone about a minor scheme (e.g., 江湖险恶，人心叵测).

汤.etymology: Phono-semantic character (湯) of 氵 (水, 'water') + 昜 (yáng/tāng phonetic, 'sun rising/heat'): in Classical Chinese, 湯 meant 'hot or boiling water' (as in 赴汤蹈火 'tread boiling water and walk through fire', while meat broth was 羹 gēng). From the Tang–Song period onward, 汤 shifted to the everyday word for 'soup, broth, decoction'.

history.meaning: hot water; boiling water
soup; broth

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 汤 (via 萌典)

汤碗.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 汤 (湯, 'soup') + 碗 ('bowl', stone 石 + 宛): 'soup bowl'.

history.meaning: soup bowl

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 汤碗 (via 萌典)

汽车.etymology: Compound noun of 汽 ('steam, vapor', water 氵 + 气) + 车 (車, 'wheeled vehicle'). Originally coined in the 19th century for steam-powered vehicles (and in Japanese 汽車 kisha for a steam train), then standardized in early 20th-century Chinese for the 'automobile, motorcar, car, bus'.

history.meaning: steam/motor vehicle -> automobile, car

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 汽车 (via 萌典)

沁.etymology: A phono-semantic compound combining the water semantic radical 氵(水, shuǐ) with the phonetic component 心 (xīn, Old Chinese *[s]ə[m], 'heart'). Originally the proper name of the Qin River (沁水) in Shanxi and Henan recorded in the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it developed in medieval and vernacular Chinese the verbal sense of 'to fathom water', 'to seep into', and 'to permeate gently like cool spring water'.

history.meaning: name of the Qin River in northern China
to dip into water; to seep, ooze, or permeate gently
to seep into, permeate, soak gently or refreshingly into

morphemes.meaning: to seep into, permeate, infuse gently

沁.notes: Carries a poetic, sensory nuance of cool moisture or fragrance gently penetrating the skin or heart, most famously preserved in the idiom 沁人心脾 ('permeating and refreshing one's heart and spleen').

rootFamily.gloss: refreshing and gladdening the heart (of fragrance, music, or breeze)

沉不住气.etymology: A four-character negated potential verb-object construction built from 沉 (chén, 'to sink, settle down, keep steady'), the negative potential infixal sequence 不住 (bùzhù, 'unable to hold/keep in place'), and the grammatical object 气 (Traditional 氣, qì, 'vital breath, composure, temper'). It draws on traditional Chinese physiological imagery in which emotional poise requires keeping one's *qì* settled low in the abdomen rather than letting it rise agitatively.

history.form: 沉不住氣 / 沉不住气 (chénbuzhù qì)
history.meaning: unable to keep one's breath/temper settled; to lose one's cool or show impatience

morphemes.meaning: to sink, settle down, keep steady
firmly, in place (resultative complement of stability)

沉不住气.notes: Its positive counterpart is 沉得住气 ('able to stay calm and collected under pressure'); both are high-frequency expressions in high-stakes negotiation and media crisis scenes.

rootFamily.gloss: able to stay calm and patient under pressure

沉重.etymology: A coordinative adjectival compound joining 沉 (chén, originally written 沈, 'to sink in water; deep, heavy') and 重 (zhòng, 'heavy, weighty'). Attested in Han and Six Dynasties texts for severe illness or physical weight, it broadened to describe both literal physical heaviness (such as footsteps or burdens) and psychological or atmospheric solemnity (such as grief, mood, or responsibility).

history.meaning: weighty, severe (especially of illness or physical load); dignified
heavy (physically or emotionally), solemn, weighed down, critical

沉重.notes: Commonly modifies abstract nouns related to mood, blows, or costs (e.g., 心情沉重, 'with a heavy heart'; 沉重的代价, 'a heavy price'), whereas plain 重 is preferred for measuring concrete weight in kilograms.

沏.etymology: A phono-semantic character composed of the water radical 氵(水) and the phonetic element 切 (qiē, 'to cut'). In Classical Chinese (such as the *Chuci*), 沏 (then pronounced qì) was an onomatopoeic and descriptive verb for the rushing or dashing sound of water currents; during the Ming and Qing dynasties, following the shift from whisked powdered tea to loose-leaf infusion, it specialized in northern vernacular Mandarin to mean 'to steep or brew by pouring boiling water over leaves'.

history.meaning: sound of rushing or dashing water; water flowing swiftly
to infuse or brew (especially tea) by pouring boiling water

morphemes.meaning: to brew, steep, infuse with boiling water

沏.notes: Primarily collocates with 茶 (沏茶, 'to make/steep tea'); in northern Mandarin 沏茶 is the standard everyday expression alongside the more pan-Mandarin 泡茶.

沙子.etymology: A suffixed nominal compound formed from the root 沙 (shā, 'sand, fine gravel', a compound ideograph in the *Shuowen Jiezi* combining 水 'water' and 少 'few', depicting fine granules revealed when water recedes) and the diminutive nominal suffix 子 (zi, grammaticalized from 'child, seed'). It denotes either fine sand particles collectively or an irritating grain of grit.

history.meaning: sand, pebbles along a riverbed or shoal
sand, grit, small granules

morphemes.meaning: nominal suffix marking concrete nouns or small granules

沙子.notes: Appears in vivid idioms about intolerance for deceit or flaws, such as 眼里容不下沙子 ('unable to tolerate a single grain of sand in one's eye' — i.e., having zero tolerance for dishonesty or sloppiness).

沟通.etymology: A verb-complement (resultative) compound combining 沟 (Traditional 溝, gōu, 'irrigation ditch, channel, trench', used verbally as 'to dredge or dig a channel') and 通 (tōng, 'to pass through, connect without obstruction'). First attested in the *Zuo Zhuan* (左传·哀公九年: 秋，吴城邗，沟通江淮, 'In autumn, Wu fortified Han and dredged a canal connecting the Yangtze and Huai rivers'), its concrete hydraulic sense of linking waterways was metaphorically extended in modern Chinese to interpersonal and organizational communication.

history.meaning: to dig a canal connecting two bodies of water; to link waterways
to bridge differences, exchange ideas, communicate effectively

morphemes.meaning: ditch, channel; to channel or link

沟通.notes: Unlike 交流 (which emphasizes mutual exchange of ideas or culture), 沟通 highlights bridging a gap, resolving misunderstandings, or aligning expectations between parties (e.g., 跟客户沟通, 'communicate/align with the client').

rootFamily.gloss: ditch, trench; chasm, gap (as in 代沟 'generation gap')
to connect, link up; smooth and unobstructed

没.etymology: Existential and past-completion negator read méi ('not have; did not'), written with the water component 氵. Under its literary reading mò ('sink, submerge'), the graph appears in Classical Chinese; by late Tang and Song lyric poetry (such as Wei Zhuang's ci), 沒 had grammaticalized in spoken Chinese to negate 有 and completed events.

history.meaning: sink beneath water; disappear
not have; did not

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 沒 (via 萌典)

没事.etymology: A verb-object compound formed from the existential negator 没 (méi, 'not have, there is no', originally 'to dive or sink in water' 沒, mò, before grammaticalizing in late medieval vernacular Chinese as the colloquial replacement for 无) and the nominal object 事 (shì, 'affair, matter, trouble, business'). Literally 'to have no matter/trouble', it serves both to describe having free time and as a reassuring conversational formula meaning 'it's alright / never mind'.

history.meaning: to have no affairs, emergencies, or official business
it's nothing, never mind, I'm fine; to be free/unoccupied

没事.notes: Frequently pronounced with erhua in northern Mandarin (没事儿, méishìr) and used in two distinct ways: as a polite brush-off or reassurance ('No problem / I'm okay') and as an adverbial frame meaning 'when having nothing to do' (e.g., 没事别乱跑).

rootFamily.gloss: to have something come up; be in trouble
to have an accident or run into serious trouble

没什么.etymology: A verb-object phrase combining the existential negative verb 没 (méi, shortened from 没有, 'not have, be without') and the indefinite/interrogative pronoun 什么 (shénme, 'what, anything', which evolved during the Tang–Song period from the colloquial interrogative 什物 / 甚么, 'what thing'). In declarative contexts, the interrogative pronoun functions as an indefinite minimizer, yielding 'nothing much' or 'nothing to speak of'.

history.meaning: to have nothing in particular; nothing of consequence
nothing much, it's nothing serious, no big deal

没什么.notes: In addition to standing alone as a modest reply ('It's nothing much'), 没什么 can precede a noun or adjective to mean 'hardly any' or 'not very' (e.g., 没什么问题, 'hardly any problem').

没关系.etymology: Warm reassuring reply to an apology ('it doesn't matter; no problem'), combining 没 ('not have') with 关系 ('connection, bearing, consequence'—literally 'no bearing / nothing to worry over').

history.meaning: it doesn't matter; never mind

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 沒關係 (via 萌典)

没劲.etymology: A verb-object compound lexicalized as an adjective, consisting of 没 (méi, 'not have, lack') and 劲 (Traditional 勁, jìn, 'muscular strength, vigor, spiritedness, interest'). Literally 'lacking vigor or energy', it denotes either physical exhaustion or, very commonly in colloquial speech, the feeling that an activity, situation, or person is dull, uninspiring, and no fun.

history.meaning: lacking physical strength or energy; boring, flat, no fun

没劲.notes: Often pronounced 没劲儿 (méijìnr) in northern speech; its antonym 带劲 or 有劲 means 'exciting, energetic, full of punch'.

没商量.etymology: A negated verb-object phrase combining 没 (méi, 'there is no [room for]') with the coordinative verbal/nominal compound 商量 (shāngliang, 'to consult, discuss, negotiate', composed of 商 'to deliberate, reckon' + 量 'to measure, weigh'). Literally 'there is no negotiating', it expresses absolute finality and refusal to compromise.

history.meaning: leaving no room for negotiation; non-negotiable, categorical

morphemes.meaning: not have, there is no room for

没商量.notes: Popularized nationwide as an emphatic post-verbal tag by the 1992 Chinese television comedy *爱你没商量* (*Loving You Without Negotiation*), allowing structures like 加班没商量 ('overtime is non-negotiable').

没想到.etymology: A negated resultative verb construction formed from the perfective negator 没 (méi, 'did not, have not'), the cognitive verb 想 (xiǎng, 'to think, anticipate'), and the resultative complement 到 (dào, 'to arrive at, reach'). Here 到 marks successful mental attainment of a thought or foresight; negating it with 没 literally means 'one's thinking did not reach [that outcome]', hence 'never expected' or 'to one's surprise'.

history.meaning: did not anticipate, never expected, unexpectedly

没想到.notes: Frequently stands at the start of a clause as a discourse marker of surprise ('Little did I expect that...'), interchangeable in higher registers with 未曾料到 or 出乎意料.

没意思.etymology: A verb-object construction functioning as an adjectival predicate, composed of 没 (méi, 'not have, lack') and the compound noun 意思 (yìsi, 'meaning, significance, interest, appeal', from 意 'thought, intent' + 思 'reflection, sentiment'). As 意思 broadened in vernacular Mandarin from 'semantic meaning' to 'fun, charm, or point', 没意思 came to mean 'boring, pointless, or unappealing'.

history.meaning: lacking interest, charm, or point; boring, dull, awkward

没意思.notes: Beyond 'boring', 没意思 is often used in interpersonal dialogue to mean 'ungenerous, petty, or not being a good sport' (e.g., 你这样就没意思了, 'If you act like that, it takes all the fun/goodwill out of it').

没有.etymology: Negative counterpart of 有 ('do not have; there is no; did not'), combining the negative 没 with 有. Established in Song–Yuan vernacular texts, 没有 both negates possession/existence before nouns and negates completed actions before verbs.

history.meaning: not have; there is not

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 沒有 (via 萌典)

没法.etymology: A verb-object compound combining the existential negator 没 (méi, 'not have, there is no') and 法 (fǎ, 'method, way, standard', short for 方法 or 办法). Literally 'to have no method or way', it functions both as a predicate ('to be helpless') and, before another verb, as an adverbial marker of impossibility ('no way to [do something]').

history.meaning: having no method or recourse; unable to act
no way to, unable to; helpless

没法.notes: Usually followed directly by a verb (e.g., 没法交代, 'no way to explain oneself / account for it'; 没法比, 'incomparable') or expanded as 没法子 / 没办法 when standing alone at the end of a sentence.

rootFamily.gloss: there is no way, nothing can be done about it

没空.etymology: Verb-object phrase combining 没 ('not have') + 空 (read kòng in the fourth tone, 'free time, leisure, unoccupied space/time'): 'have no free time, be busy, be unavailable'.

history.meaning: have no free time; be busy

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 没空 (via 萌典)

没见.etymology: A negated perception verb phrase formed from the perfective negative adverb 没 (méi, 'did not, have not') and 见 (Traditional 見, jiàn, 'to see, catch sight of, meet', whose oracle bone graph depicts a kneeling person 人 topped by a prominent eye 目). It negates the occurrence of visual perception or an interpersonal encounter up to the reference time.

history.meaning: have not seen, did not meet or observe
have not seen, did not see or run into

没见.notes: Common in everyday greetings like 好久没见 ('long time no see', alongside 好久不见) and in rhetorical rebukes such as 没见过世面 ('never seen the world / unsophisticated').

rootFamily.gloss: to meet, see someone in person
have not seen for a long time; not necessarily

没错.etymology: Affirmative predicate phrase combining 没 ('not have, without') + 错 (錯, 'error, mistake'): 'that's right!, quite right!, no mistake, correct'.

history.meaning: no mistake -> that's right!, correct!

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 没错 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: ruin, fall into misery, sink low (rinraku)

沦落.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound uniting 沦 (Traditional 淪, lún, originally 'ripples on water', extended in Classical Chinese to 'to sink into water, be engulfed') and 落 (luò, 'to fall, shed leaves, drop down'). Combining the imagery of sinking beneath waves and falling from a height, it was immortalized in Bai Juyi's Tang-dynasty poem *Pipa Xing* (同是天涯沦落人, 'Both of us are people fallen into misfortune at the ends of the earth') to denote declining into poverty, obscurity, or an undignified station.

history.meaning: to sink into misfortune, wander in exile or poverty, fall from grace
history.stage: Middle Chinese / Tang Poetic Literary Chinese

history.meaning: to sink to, be reduced to an ignoble state or low station

morphemes.meaning: to sink into water, be engulfed, decline
to fall, drop down, decline in status

沦落.notes: Frequently takes the resultative prepositional complement 到 or 至 to introduce the undesirable state one has fallen into (e.g., 沦落到这个地步, 'reduced to such a state').

rootFamily.gloss: to fall into enemy hands or sink into depravity/ruin
down and out, in dire straits

河.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 氵 (水, 'water') + 可 (kě/hé phonetic). In Old and Classical Chinese, 河 was the proper name of the Yellow River (黄河, while the Yangtze was 江), before generalizing from the Han–Tang period onward into the common noun for any 'river, stream, waterway'.

history.meaning: the Yellow River
river; waterway

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 河 (via 萌典)

河水.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 河 ('river') + 水 ('water'): 'river water'. Attested since the Shijing (河水洋洋).

history.meaning: river water

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 河水 (via 萌典)

河沙.etymology: A modifier-head noun pairing 河 (hé, originally the Yellow River, generalized to any 'river') and 沙 (shā, 'sand', written with water 氵 beside 少 'few/tiny', i.e. fine mineral grains visible where water grows shallow). Builders and gardeners distinguish clean, rounded freshwater 河沙 from salt-laden sea sand (海沙) because river sand drains cleanly without corroding metal or brick.

morphemes.meaning: fine sand grains washed by water

history.meaning: grains of river sand (also Buddhist idiom 恒河沙 'sands of the Ganges')
clean freshwater river sand

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 河沙

沸沸扬扬.etymology: An AABB reduplicated four-character idiom derived from the disyllabic roots 沸 (fèi, 'to bubble up, boil over', originally 'spring water bubbling up') and 扬 (Traditional 揚, yáng, 'to toss upward, winnow, scatter in the air'). Literally depicting water boiling furiously and winnowed chaff flying everywhere, it is attested in Ming–Qing vernacular novels (such as *Shuihu Zhuan* and *Hongloumeng*) as a vivid metaphor for public commotion, gossip, or media scandals spreading wildly.

history.meaning: bubbling like boiling water and swirling like winnowed grain; in noisy commotion
in an uproar, buzzing everywhere with rumors or public controversy

morphemes.meaning: to boil, bubble up (reduplicated for intensity)
to rise, toss upward, spread widely (reduplicated)

沸沸扬扬.notes: A staple of entertainment journalism and PR crisis dialogue, almost always paired with verbs like 闹得 or 传得 (e.g., 网上闹得沸沸扬扬, 'causing a huge uproar all over the internet').

rootFamily.gloss: to boil; to seethe with excitement

油.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining the water/liquid radical 氵 with phonetic 由 (*yóu*, Middle Chinese *juw*). Originally naming the smooth, glossy flow of river water in the *Chuci*, it generalized by the Han dynasty to pressed plant oils, animal fats, and lubricating oils.

history.meaning: glossy flowing liquid; pressed vegetable or animal oil
cooking oil; lubricating oil

油漆.etymology: Coordinate craft compound of 油 ('drying tung oil', pressed from Aleurites fordii seeds to waterproof timber) + 漆 ('natural lacquer sap' from Toxicodendron vernicifluum trees, attested since Neolithic China); together naming protective architectural paint.

history.meaning: tung-oil and lacquer wood finish
paint; varnish

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 油漆

治病.etymology: A separable verb-object (离合词) compound combining 治 (zhì, 'to regulate, bring into order, heal', originally the name of the Chi River before extending to dredging floodwaters and governing disorder) and 病 (bìng, 'illness, disease, ailment'). Viewing disease as bodily disorder analogous to flood or social chaos, Classical medical and philosophical texts used 治病 for restoring physiological balance.

history.meaning: to regulate and cure bodily illness or disease
to treat an illness, provide medical treatment, cure disease

治病.notes: Because 治病 is a separable verb-object compound (离合词), aspect particles, modifiers, or complements are inserted between the two characters (e.g., 治好病, 'cure the illness'; 治不了病, 'unable to cure the illness').

沾.etymology: A phono-semantic character combining the water radical 氵(水) and the phonetic element 占 (zhān, 'to divine, occupy'). Originally the name of the Zhan River in Shanxi, it merged in medieval and vernacular script with 霑 (zhān, 'to moisten with rain, soak, wet'). From the physical sense of being lightly moistened or stained by contact with liquid, it extended metaphorically to 'touching upon', 'getting involved with', or 'benefiting from association with'.

history.meaning: to moisten, wet, dampen with rain or dew
to moisten, stain; to touch upon, have contact with, benefit from association with

morphemes.meaning: to moisten, lightly touch, get involved with, be tainted by

沾.notes: Often implies that even slight contact leaves a trace or consequence, whether positive (沾光, 'bask in someone's reflected glory') or negative (沾染恶习, 'pick up a bad habit'; 滴酒不沾, 'not touch a drop of alcohol').

rootFamily.gloss: to benefit from association with someone, bask in another's glory
to be contaminated by, pick up (a habit or taint)
to be relevant to, touch the edge of

沾地.etymology: Verb-object compound from 沾 ('touch lightly; moisten; wet', water 氵 + phonetic 占) + 地 ('ground; floor'). Almost always used in negative or potential constructions (脚不沾地, 敢沾地) to describe whether a foot touches or bears weight on the ground.

history.meaning: touch the ground
touch the ground (of one's foot)

沾过手.etymology: An experiential verb-object construction built from the separable compound 沾手 (zhānshǒu, literally 'to moisten or touch with the hand', from 沾 'to touch lightly, get on oneself' + 手 'hand') split by the experiential aspect marker 过 (guò, 'to have experienced doing'). It expresses having previously handled, touched, or participated in a project, transaction, or affair.

history.meaning: to touch with one's hand; to have a hand in handling an affair
to have had a hand in, to have previously handled or been involved in

morphemes.meaning: to touch, come into contact with, get involved in
experiential aspect suffix indicating past involvement

沾过手.notes: Frequently appears in workplace investigations or accountability discussions (especially in negated form 没沾过手, 'never had a hand in it') to establish whether someone ever touched a project or fund.

rootFamily.gloss: to touch with the hand; to handle or get involved in
to take over handling a task or case
to handle personally, pass through one's hands

cognates.meaning: leaking a secret, breach of confidentiality (semitsu)

泄密.etymology: A verb-object (separable) compound compressed from 泄露秘密 ('to leak a secret'), combining 泄 (also written 洩, xiè, 'to seep out, discharge, vent, leak', originally a tributary river name before extending to fluid seepage) and 密 (mì, 'secret, confidential matter', originally 'mountain shelter, dense, hidden'). It denotes the unauthorized disclosure of confidential state, corporate, or personal information.

history.meaning: to divulge confidential matters or state secrets
to leak secrets, breach confidentiality

泄密.notes: Functions as an intransitive verb-object compound (e.g., 防止泄密, 'prevent leaks'; 泄密者, 'leaker/whistleblower'); if a specific leaked object is named, use the transitive verb 泄露 instead (e.g., 泄露商业机密).

rootFamily.gloss: to keep a secret, maintain confidentiality

cognates.meaning: leaking, disclosure of secrets or data (rōei / seirō)

泄露.etymology: A coordinative transitive verbal compound combining 泄 (Traditional 洩, xiè, 'to ooze out, seep, discharge') and 露 (lù, 'to expose, become visible, reveal', originally 'morning dew' which appears openly on surfaces). Attested in Classical texts such as the *Zuo Zhuan* and *Hanfeizi*, it unites the metaphor of liquid seeping through a crack with that of hidden things becoming exposed to view.

history.meaning: to let slip or expose hidden plans, state affairs, or fluids
to leak, divulge (secrets, information, data, or gas/liquid)

morphemes.meaning: to seep out, discharge, let slip

泄露.notes: Note the orthographic distinction in modern Mainland standards: 泄露 (with 露 'expose') is preferred for leaking secrets, news, or data, whereas 泄漏 (with 漏 'drip through a hole') is often used for physical leaks of gas, oil, or radiation, though the two overlap in practice.

rootFamily.gloss: to expose, unmask, come to light

法.etymology: Ancient ideogram (originally 灋 in bronze and seal script) combining 氵 (水, 'water, which always finds a level surface, symbolizing fairness and evenness') + 廌 (zhì, a mythical one-horned beast that butts the guilty party in a trial) + 去 ('drive away/cast out wrongdoers'): 'law, statute; method, way; Buddhist Dharma; France (法国)'.

history.meaning: level as water + remove wrongdoers = law, standard, method
law; method; way

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 法 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: legal affairs, corporate legal department; Buddhist monastic service (hōmu)

法务.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound combining 法 (fǎ, 'law, statute, dharma') and 务 (Traditional 務, wù, 'affairs, duties, business'). Originally used in medieval Chinese Buddhism for monastic religious duties (佛法之事务), it was repurposed in Meiji Japan (法務, *hōmu*) as a modern institutional term for judicial and legal administration, and subsequently re-adopted into modern Mandarin to denote legal affairs, a company's legal department, or in-house legal counsel.

history.meaning: monastic affairs and religious duties relating to the Buddhist Dharma
judicial administration and state legal affairs (Sino-Japanese institutional revival)
history.stage: Early Modern East Asian Legal Terminology

history.meaning: corporate legal affairs, legal department, or in-house legal counsel

法务.notes: In modern corporate and media industry settings (*幕后之王*), 法务 refers both to the legal department (法务部) and metonymically to the in-house legal specialists who review contracts and issue cease-and-desist letters.

法庭.etymology: A modifier-head compound joining 法 (fǎ, 'law, judicial standard') and 庭 (tíng, 'courtyard, central hall where a magistrate or monarch hears cases'). In imperial China, judicial hearings took place in the open courtyard or hall (庭) before the magistrate's seat; in modern legal terminology (alongside the Japanese graphic variant 法廷), 法庭 specifically designates the physical courtroom or a specialized tribunal bench within a court of law.

history.meaning: hall of law or judicial courtyard where cases are heard
courtroom, judicial tribunal, court session

morphemes.meaning: courtyard, hall of audience or adjudication

法庭.notes: Distinguish 法庭 ('courtroom' or specific trial chamber, as in 上法庭 'go to court / take the stand' or 法庭见 'see you in court!') from 法院 ('court of law' as the overarching judicial institution, e.g., 最高人民法院).

rootFamily.gloss: to open a court session, hold a hearing

法律.etymology: Coordinative noun compound pairing 法 ('law, general legal principle') + 律 ('codified statute, penal code', originally pitch-pipes that set a uniform standard): 'law, statute, legislation'. Attested since the管子 Guanzi and Xunzi.

history.stage: Classical Chinese (Guanzi, Xunzi) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: laws and statutes; law

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 法律 (via 萌典)

法律效力.etymology: A four-character modifier-head nominal compound combining 法律 (fǎlǜ, 'law, statute', itself a Classical Chinese coordinative compound of 法 'standard, model, law' and 律 'pitch-pipe, regulation, statute') with 效力 (xiàolì, 'efficacy, binding force', originally a Classical verb-object phrase meaning 'to exert one's strength' that evolved via Meiji-era Sino-Japanese legal terminology into a modifier-head noun meaning 'effective force' or 'validity', translating German Rechtswirkung / Gültigkeit).

history.meaning: Classical Chinese: 法律 'legal statutes and penal codes' (attested in Guanzi and Shiji); 效力 'to render service by exerting strength'
Meiji Japanese / Late Qing legal calque: 'efficacy, binding legal effect' (translating European jurisprudence concepts)
Modern Standard Mandarin: 'legal validity, binding force in law'

morphemes.meaning: efficacy, binding force (originally VO: 效 'to render/effect' + 力 'strength/force')

法律效力.notes: Frequently used in entertainment and media contracts (e.g., 具有法律效力 'to be legally binding') when negotiating broadcast rights, non-disclosure agreements, or artist management terms.

法案.etymology: Compound legal noun of 法 ('law') + 案 ('official desk -> legal case, draft proposal, bill'): 'legislative bill, proposed law, act'.

history.meaning: legislative bill; act

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 法案 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: Courthouse (archaic or specific to Chinese/Taiwanese courts)

法院.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-compound composed of 法 (fǎ, Old Chinese *pqab, 'model, standard, law', originally written 灋 with 水 'water [level]', 廌 'mythical justice-dispensing beast', and 去 'cast out') modifying 院 (yuàn, 'walled courtyard, public institution'). In Tang–Song Buddhist usage, 法院 denoted a monastic hall of the Dharma; during the late Qing New Policies judicial reforms (1906–1910), it was repurposed as the modern institutional term for a judicial court of law.

history.meaning: Classical & Tang Chinese: 法 'law, Buddhist Dharma' + 院 'walled compound, monastery hall', forming 'hall of Dharma'
Late Qing judicial reform (1906): secularized institutional designation for a 'court of law' replacing imperial tribunals (衙门 / 大理寺)
Modern Standard Mandarin: 'court of law, judiciary tribunal'

法院.notes: Takes the classifier 家 (jiā) or 座 (zuò); in media dramas, 告上法院 ('to take someone to court') is a staple phrase in intellectual property and contract disputes.

泡.etymology: A phono-semantic character combining the semantic water radical 氵 (水, shuǐ, 'water, liquid') with the phonetic component 包 (bāo, Old Chinese *pˤru, 'to wrap, enclose'). Originally recorded in the Shuowen Jiezi as the name of a river and as 'water bubbles, foam, froth' (Old Chinese *pˤru-s > Middle Chinese phæwH); in vernacular Mandarin from the Yuan–Ming period onward, it underwent verbal derivation meaning 'to immerse in liquid, steep, infuse, or brew'.

history.meaning: Han Dynasty (Shuowen Jiezi): 'water bubble, froth, blister' (nominal)
Vernacular Early Mandarin: 'to soak, steep in hot water, infuse' (verbal extension from bubbling water)
Modern Mandarin: 'to brew (tea/coffee), soak, dawdle, or hang out'

泡.notes: As a transitive verb in production offices, 泡茶 ('brew tea') and 泡咖啡 ('make instant/pour-over coffee') are everyday collocations; figuratively, 泡在录音棚里 means 'to spend all one's time immersed in the recording studio'.

波.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 氵 (水, 'water') + 皮 (pí/bō, 'skin/surface'): literally 'rippling skin/surface of water' = 'wave, ripple, undulation, surge; physical wave (sound or electromagnetic wave)'.

history.stage: Old & Classical Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: undulating surface of water = wave, ripple

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 波 (via 萌典)

注意.etymology: Originally a Classical Chinese verb-object construction composed of 注 (zhù, 'to pour liquid into, channel, fix upon') and 意 (yì, 'thought, mind, intention'), literally meaning 'to pour or direct one's mind toward'. Attested in Han-era historical texts such as the Shiji and Hanshu; in the late 19th century, Meiji Japanese adopted 注意 (chūi) as the standard psychological and administrative term for 'attention, heed, caution', reinforcing its high-frequency usage in modern Mandarin.

history.meaning: Han Classical Chinese: 'to pour or direct one's thoughts toward a person or matter' (verb-object phrase)
Meiji Japanese: 'cognitive attention, caution, notice' (translating English 'attention' / German 'Aufmerksamkeit')
Modern Standard Mandarin: 'to pay attention to, take note of, watch out for'

morphemes.meaning: to pour into, concentrate, fix upon

注意.notes: Functions as a separable verb-object compound in some constructions (e.g., 多加注意) and takes direct clauses or nominal objects (e.g., 注意安全 'watch out for safety', 注意细节 'pay attention to details').

rootFamily.gloss: to gaze fixedly at, stare at

注意力.etymology: A three-character modifier-head nominal compound formed by suffixing 力 (lì, 'strength, faculty, capacity') to the verb-object compound 注意 (zhùyì, 'to direct one's mind toward, pay attention'). Coined in modern Sino-Japanese and early 20th-century Chinese psychological terminology to render the faculty of cognitive attention ('power of attention' or 'attention span').

history.meaning: Classical roots: 注意 ('direct one's mind') + 力 ('physical or mental faculty/strength')
Meiji–Taishō Japanese psychology: 'faculty of attention, concentration capacity'
Modern Mandarin: 'attention, focus, attention span'

morphemes.meaning: to pay attention, direct one's mind (VO: 注 'pour/focus' + 意 'mind')

注意力.notes: In media and television production (*Behind the Scenes*), 吸引观众的注意力 ('capture the audience's attention') and 分散注意力 ('distract attention') are core industry phrases; compare 注意力经济 ('the attention economy').

注解.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative compound (also written 註解 in traditional script) combining 注/註 (zhù, literally 'to channel water', extended in Han philology to mean 'exegetical gloss that channels the meaning of a classic') and 解 (jiě, 'to untie, dissect, explain, elucidate', originally depicting hands dividing a bull's horn). Attested from the Six Dynasties and Tang exegetical traditions onward as both a verb ('to annotate and explain') and a noun ('commentary, marginal notes').

history.meaning: Han philology: 注 'gloss that channels meaning' + 解 'analytical explanation (dissecting a knot)'
Six Dynasties & Tang scholarship: 'philological commentary and exegesis on classical canons'
Modern Mandarin: 'annotation, explanatory note, footnote; (figuratively) illustration'

注解.notes: Used both for written script notes (剧本注解 'script annotations') and metaphorically in journalism (做了一个生动的注解 'served as a vivid illustration/footnote to...').

cognates.meaning: to lay stress on, attach importance to

注重.etymology: A verb-complement / coordinative compound formed from 注 (zhù, 'to pour, direct one's gaze or focus upon') and 重 (zhòng, 'heavy; to regard as weighty, value highly, emphasize'). Emerging in late imperial and early modern Mandarin prose, it blends the directional focus of 注 (as in 注意 'pay attention') with the evaluative weight of 重 (as in 重视 'value highly'), yielding 'to direct emphasis toward, attach importance to'.

history.meaning: Classical Chinese roots: 注 ('to focus/channel upon') and 重 ('weighty; to esteem/value') used separately
Late Qing & Early Republican prose: 'to direct emphasis onto, lay stress on'
Modern Standard Mandarin: 'to attach importance to, emphasize, prioritize (quality, detail, substance)'

morphemes.meaning: to focus on, channel attention toward

注重.notes: Commonly collocates with abstract nouns denoting quality, craft, or aesthetics (e.g., 注重品质 'emphasize quality', 注重细节 'pay close attention to detail', 注重用户体验 'prioritize user experience').

rootFamily.gloss: to value highly, attach importance to

泪水.etymology: Determinative compound of 泪 ('tears', water radical 氵 + 目 'eye', literally 'water of the eye') + 水 ('water; liquid'). Adding 水 reinforces the liquid, brimming quality of tears welling up in the eyes.

history.meaning: teardrops; brimming tears
tears; teardrops

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 泪水

泰语.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound combining 泰 (tài, phonetic abbreviation of 泰国 Tàiguó 'Thailand', itself a 20th-century phono-semantic transcription of Thai ไทย *Thai* 'free', deliberately chosen for the auspicious Classical Chinese meaning of 泰 'great, peaceful, prosperous') and 语 (yǔ, simplified from 語, 'speech, language'). Replaced the older ethnonymic designation 暹罗语 (Xiānluóyǔ, 'Siamese language') after Siam officially renamed itself Thailand in 1939 (and permanently in 1949).

history.meaning: Ming–Qing & Early Republican era: 'Siamese language' (from 暹羅 Xiānluó 'Siam')
Mid-20th century onward: 'Thai language' (after Siam changed its official name to Prathet Thai / 泰国 in 1939–1949)

morphemes.meaning: Thai, Thailand (phono-semantic rendering of Thai 'ไทย' + auspicious sense 'peaceful/great')

泰语.notes: Follows the standard Mandarin pattern [Country/Ethnonym abbreviation] + 语 for languages (like 法语 'French', 德语 'German'); in Chinese media distribution, Thai-dubbed dramas (泰语配音) represent a major Southeast Asian export market.

洋甘菊.etymology: Three-character botanical name from 洋 ('foreign; Western; ocean') + 甘 ('sweet; pleasant') + 菊 ('chrysanthemum', grass 艹 + 匊). Coined in modern Chinese herbalism and tea culture as a calque and descriptive translation of European chamomile (*Matricaria chamomilla*), whose daisy-like blossoms resemble small sweet chrysanthemums.

history.meaning: chamomile

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 洋甘菊

洋葱.etymology: Botanical compound of 洋 ('ocean; introduced from overseas') + 葱 ('scallion; allium', grass radical 艹 + phonetic 匆 *cōng*). Just as 洋芋 and 洋白菜 marked crops introduced via maritime trade, 洋葱 named the bulb onion (*Allium cepa*) in contrast to native green scallions (大葱/小葱).

history.meaning: bulb onion (*Allium cepa*)
onion

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 洋葱

洒.etymology: Phono-semantic character (merging 灑 and 洒, combining 氵 'water' + 西/麗): originally 'sprinkle water on the ground before sweeping dust (洒扫)', hence 'sprinkle, splash, spill (liquid), scatter, shed; free and easy (潇洒)'.

history.stage: Old & Classical Chinese (Shijing, Analects) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: sprinkle water; spill; splash; scatter

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 洒 (via 萌典)

洒满.etymology: Resultative verb compound combining 洒 ('sprinkle, spill, cast [of liquid or sunlight]') + 满 (滿, 'full, covering the whole surface'): 'be sprinkled all over with, be bathed or flooded with (sunlight, moonlight, or water)'.

history.meaning: sprinkle or flood all over (with water or light)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 洒满 (via 萌典)

洗.etymology: A phono-semantic character formed from the water radical 氵 (水, shuǐ, 'water') and the phonetic component 先 (xiān, Old Chinese *sˤər, 'first, precede'). In the Shuowen Jiezi and Classical Chinese (pronounced xiǎn, Old Chinese *sˤərʔ), 洗 specifically meant 'to wash the feet', contrasting with 沫 ('wash the face'), 沐 ('wash the hair'), and 浴 ('bathe the body'). By the Middle Chinese period (with the readingMC sejX > Mandarin xǐ), it generalized to become the universal verb for 'to wash, cleanse, or rinse'.

history.meaning: Old Chinese (Oracle Bone & Bronze / Shuowen): 'to wash the feet' (specialized cleansing verb)
Middle Chinese (Six Dynasties–Tang): generalized to 'to wash, launder, rinse, cleanse' (displacing specialized verbs 沐, 沫, )
Modern Mandarin: 'to wash, bathe, develop (film), shuffle (cards), or launder (money/reputation)'

洗.notes: In showbiz PR slang, 洗 marks several vivid metaphors: 洗白 ('to whitewash or rehabilitate a celebrity's tarnished image'), 洗脑 ('brainwash' / earworm), and 洗牌 ('reshuffle the industry deck').

rootFamily.gloss: to take a bath or shower

洗手池.etymology: Three-character compound combining 洗手 ('wash hands') + 池 ('basin, pool, sink'): 'washbasin, bathroom sink'.

history.meaning: hand-washing sink; washbasin

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 洗手池 (via 萌典)

洗手间.etymology: Three-character polite euphemistic compound combining 洗手 ('wash hands') + 间 (間, 'room'): 'washroom, restroom, lavatory, bathroom'.

history.meaning: washroom; restroom; bathroom

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 洗手间 (via 萌典)

洗澡.etymology: Coordinative/verb-object compound of 洗 ('wash with water') + 澡 ('bathe, wash the body', water 氵 + 喿): 'take a bath or shower, bathe'. Attested since Han–Six Dynasties texts.

history.meaning: wash and bathe the body; take a bath or shower

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 洗澡 (via 萌典)

洗澡水.etymology: Three-character compound combining 洗澡 ('take a bath/shower') + 水 ('water'): 'bathwater, water for bathing'.

history.meaning: bathwater

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 洗澡水 (via 萌典)

洗胃.etymology: A modern medical verb-object compound combining 洗 (xǐ, 'to wash, flush, irrigate') with 胃 (wèi, 'stomach', originally an ideographic/pictographic character depicting a sac-like organ filled with rice grains 囟/田 above flesh 月/肉). Coined in modern clinical Chinese medicine to translate Western 'gastric lavage' (literally 'washing the stomach'), it behaves syntactically as a separable verb-object phrase.

history.meaning: Classical Chinese roots: 洗 ('to wash') + 胃 ('stomach, digestive organ' in Huangdi Neijing)
20th-century Modern Mandarin medical coinage: 'to perform gastric lavage, pump the stomach' (after acute poisoning or alcohol overdose)

morphemes.meaning: stomach (pictograph of a food sac + meat radical 月)

洗胃.notes: In Chinese workplace and entertainment dramas, 喝酒喝到去医院洗胃 ('drinking at business banquets until having to get one's stomach pumped at the hospital') is a recurring trope illustrating extreme client-entertainment pressure (应酬).

活.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 氵 (水, 'flowing water') + 舌 (shé/huó phonetic). In the Shijing (北流活活), 活 imitated the sound of rushing living water; because flowing water does not stagnate, it came to mean 'live, alive, living, survive; movable/flexible (灵活); vivid; work, manual job, product (干活)'.

history.meaning: flowing water -> live, alive, survive
alive; live; movable/flexible; manual work/job

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 活 (via 萌典)

活儿.etymology: A colloquial Northern Mandarin rhotacized (erhua) noun formed from 活 (huó, 'to live, survive; livelihood; work/labor') plus the diminutive nominalizing suffix 儿 (ér, reduced from 兒 'child' to a retroflex coda -r). In Classical Chinese, 活 meant 'alive, to live'; via compounds like 生活 ('livelihood') and 做活/干活 ('to work for a living'), 活 narrowed in vernacular Mandarin to mean 'manual or skilled work, job, task', with the erhua suffix 活儿 distinguishing the concrete noun ('a job/task/piece of craft') from the adjective 活 ('alive, flexible').

history.meaning: Classical Chinese: 'to live, survive, be alive' (verb/adjective)
Vernacular Song–Ming Mandarin: 'livelihood, labor, work done to earn a living'
Modern Colloquial Mandarin (with erhua suffix -儿): 'work, job, gig, task, or craftsmanship'

活儿.notes: The erhua suffix is essential here: without -儿, 活 usually means 'alive' or 'flexible', whereas 活儿 means 'job, gig, or handiwork' (e.g., 干活儿 'do work', 接活儿 'take on a freelance gig/project', 手艺活儿 'skilled craft').

rootFamily.gloss: to work, do manual or practical work

活动.etymology: Originally a Middle and Early Modern Chinese coordinative compound of 活 (huó, 'alive, mobile, unfixed') and 动 (dòng, simplified from 動, 'to move, stir'), meaning 'to move about freely, be mobile or loose'. During the Meiji period in Japan, 活動 (katsudō) was adopted as a calque of English 'activity' and German 'Tätigkeit' / 'Aktivität' in philosophy, biology, and commerce; this nominalized sense ('organized event, public activity, campaign') was re-imported into modern Mandarin in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

history.meaning: Song–Qing vernacular & literary Chinese: 'to move about, exercise one's limbs, be movable/unfixed' (verbal/adjectival)
Meiji Japanese return loan (wasei-kango semantic shift): 'activity, operation, organized social or commercial action'
Modern Standard Mandarin: 'event, promotional activity, campaign (noun); to move around, exercise (verb); shaky, movable (adj)'

活动.notes: In media, PR, and entertainment, 活动 specifically refers to a scheduled promotional event, gala, or roadshow (e.g., 办一场线下活动 'host an offline event', 出席商业活动 'attend a commercial promotional event').

cognates.meaning: faction, sect, school; to dispatch (in compounds)

派.etymology: Formed from the water radical 氵 (水, shuǐ, 'water') and 𠂢 (pài, Old Chinese *pʰˤres, an ancient pictograph of branching water channels, inverted from 永 'long flowing water'). In the Shuowen Jiezi, 派 means 'diverging tributaries or distributaries of a river'. From 'to branch off like a stream', it evolved along two semantic pathways in Middle Chinese: (1) nominal 'branch, sect, school of thought, faction' and (2) causative verbal 'to branch out personnel, assign, delegate, dispatch'.

history.meaning: Old Chinese (Shuowen Jiezi): 'diverging tributary, branching stream of water'
Middle Chinese (Six Dynasties–Song): nominal extension to 'artistic/philosophical school, clan branch, faction' and verbal 'to divide, allot, assign'
Modern Mandarin: 'to dispatch, send, assign (verb); school, faction, style/panache (noun)'

派.notes: Frequently used in pivotal (兼语) constructions where the object of 派 is the subject of the following verb: 派人去调查 ('send someone to investigate'), 派记者跟进 ('dispatch a reporter to follow up').

rootFamily.gloss: to send, deploy on a mission

cognates.meaning: to dispatch, send out; branch station (e.g., 派出所)

派出.etymology: A verb-complement (directional/resultative) compound combining the verb 派 (pài, 'to assign, send, dispatch', originally 'to branch off like a river tributary') with the directional complement 出 (chū, 'to go/come out, issue forth'). Reinforced in late 19th- and early 20th-century administrative usage alongside Sino-Japanese 派出 (hashutsu, as in 派出所 'local police substation, dispatch office'), it denotes formally sending personnel or teams out from a central headquarters.

history.meaning: Late Imperial Mandarin: verbal 派 ('assign, send') + directional complement 出 ('outward')
Meiji Japanese & Late Qing administrative usage: 'official dispatch of personnel or branch offices' (e.g. 派出所)
Modern Standard Mandarin: 'to dispatch, send out (representatives, teams, vehicles)'

派出.notes: More formal and institutional than bare 派; often takes a direct object referring to a team or representative (e.g., 派出精锐团队 'dispatch an elite team', 派出所 'local police station').

rootFamily.gloss: to dispatch on an official mission

cognates.meaning: part, match, social gathering (ultimate Romance source of English party)

派对.etymology: A 20th-century phonetic loanword (音译词) transcribing English 'party' (itself from Old French *partie* 'part, side, social entertainment', from Latin *partīta*, past participle of *partīre* 'to divide'). Originally popularized in Shanghai and Hong Kong cosmopolitan urban culture (where Cantonese 派對 *paai3 deoi3* closely approximates English /ˈpɑː(r)ti/), the character choice 派 ('style, flair, group') + 对 (對, 'pair, match, gathering') also lends a subtle folk-etymological resonance of a stylish social gathering.

history.meaning: Western donor stages: Old French 'divided part, hunting/social group' > Modern English 'social gathering for pleasure'

history.form: 派對 (Cantonese paai3 deoi3 / Shanghai Mandarin pàiduì)
history.meaning: 20th-century port-city phonetic borrowing: 'Western-style social party, cocktail or dance party'
Modern Standard Mandarin: 'party, celebratory social gathering'

morphemes.meaning: transcribes '-ty' of English 'party' via Cantonese deoi3 / Mandarin duì (literally 'pair/match')

派对.notes: Common in entertainment and lifestyle contexts (单身派对 'bachelor/bachelorette party', 庆功派对 'wrap/success party', 开派对 'throw a party'); in colloquial Northern student slang, English 'party' is also playfully rendered as 趴体 (pātǐ).

rootFamily.gloss: gathering, get-together, native synonym for party
celebratory banquet after a show wraps

流动.etymology: Coordinative verb compound from 流 ('flow; stream', water 氵 + phonetic 㐬) + 动 (simplified from 動, 'move; circulate'). Used since the Han and Six Dynasties for flowing water, drifting air currents, and circulating goods or people.

history.meaning: flow and move (of water or air)
flow; circulate

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 流动

流淌.etymology: Coordinate disyllabic verb combining 流 ('flow like a current', water radical 氵 + 旒) + 淌 ('stream; trickle; run', water radical 氵 + phonetic 尚 *shàng*). Used literally for brooks or teardrops and figuratively for a musical melody flowing seamlessly from phrase to phrase.

history.meaning: flow and stream smoothly
flow; stream (of water or music)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 流淌

流程.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound formed from 流 (liú, 'to flow, stream, circulate') and 程 (chéng, 'measure, journey stage, itinerary, procedure, order'). In Classical Chinese poetry and prose, 流程 literally denoted 'the flowing course or journey of a river stream'; in 20th-century industrial engineering, broadcasting, and management Mandarin, it was metaphorically extended to mean 'the sequential flow of operations, workflow, procedure, or stage rundown'.

history.meaning: Classical & Literary Chinese: 'the course of flowing water; distance traveled along a waterway' (e.g., Song–Ming travel writing)
20th-century Industrial & Media Mandarin: 'technological process (工艺流程), operational workflow, or live show stage rundown'

morphemes.meaning: stage of a journey, sequence, order, procedure

流程.notes: A high-frequency buzzword in TV production (*Behind the Scenes*) and corporate China: 走流程 ('go through the formal approval process/red tape'), 节目流程 ('show rundown/cue sheet'), and 对流程 ('go over the stage rundown before broadcast').

流行.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative verbal compound combining 流 (liú, 'to flow like water, spread') and 行 (xíng, 'to walk, move, circulate, prevail'). Famous from Mencius (孟子·公孙丑上: 德之流行，速于置邮而传命, 'The flowing spread of virtue is faster than relaying orders by post-stage'), where it meant 'to spread widely, circulate rapidly' (including of customs or epidemics). In the Meiji era and 20th century, it took on the modern cultural sense of 'popular, fashionable, in vogue, pop'.

history.meaning: Warring States Classical Chinese (Mencius): 'to flow and circulate widely, spread rapidly across the realm'
Meiji Japanese & Early Modern Chinese: 'social trend, fashion, vogue; epidemic spread (as in 流行病)'
Modern Standard Mandarin: 'popular, trendy, fashionable, pop (adj); to be in vogue, circulate (verb)'

流行.notes: Functions both as a stative verb/adjective ('popular, trendy', e.g., 最近很流行 'very trendy lately') and as a classifying modifier meaning 'pop' (流行文化 'pop culture', 流行音乐 'pop music'), while retaining its older medical sense in 流行性感冒 ('influenza, epidemic flu').

cognates.word: 流行音楽 / ポピュラー音楽 (ryūkō ongaku)

流行乐.etymology: A three-character modifier-head nominal compound abridged from 流行音乐 (liúxíng yīnyuè, 'popular music'), combining 流行 (liúxíng, 'popular, circulating widely, pop') with 乐 (yuè, simplified from 樂, Old Chinese *ŋˤrawk, 'music, musical instrument', originally depicting silk strings 幺 mounted on a wooden frame 木).
