Coined in 20th-century Sinophone music criticism and broadcasting to translate English 'pop music' (contrasting with 古典乐 'classical music' and 摇滚乐 'rock music').

history.meaning: Classical Chinese: 'ritual and court music, musical performance'
20th-century Modern Mandarin: 'popular music, commercial pop music' (calquing English 'popular/pop music')

morphemes.meaning: popular, pop, widely circulating (coordinative: 流 'flow' + 行 'circulate')

流行乐.notes: Watch the heteronym reading of 乐: here it MUST be pronounced yuè ('music'), never lè ('happy'). Parallel three-character genre terms include 摇滚乐 (yáogǔnyuè, 'rock music'), 爵士乐 (juéshìyuè, 'jazz'), and 交响乐 (jiāoxiǎngyuè, 'symphonic music').

cognates.meaning: to reveal, betray, show (feelings or thoughts)

流露.etymology: A verb-complement / coordinative compound combining 流 (liú, 'to flow out, trickle forth') and 露 (lù, 'dew; to uncover, expose, become visible'). In Six Dynasties and Tang–Song poetry, 流露 literally meant 'flowing or dripping morning dew'; by the Ming–Qing literary period, it was reanalyzed verbally as 'to flow out and become exposed', metaphorically describing inner emotions, true feelings, or artistic temperament naturally and unintentionally showing through.

history.meaning: Tang–Song poetic usage: 'flowing dew, trickling dewdrops' (modifier-head / verb-object imagery)
Ming–Qing literary criticism & prose: 'to flow forth and become visible; (of emotions or spirit) to manifest naturally'
Modern Standard Mandarin: 'to reveal unintentionally, betray, let show (emotions, expressions, affection)'

流露.notes: Almost always followed by the directional complement 出 (流露出...) and takes objects denoting genuine inner feelings or facial expressions (e.g., 眼神中流露出疲惫 'exhaustion showed in his eyes', 真情流露 'a natural outpouring of true emotion').

rootFamily.gloss: to reveal, show (a smile or expression)

浇.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 浇. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 浇 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 浇 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 浇 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 浇. The etymology of 浇 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 浇
middle form of 浇
modern form of 浇

测量.etymology: Coordinative verb-noun compound combining 测 (trad. 測, 'to fathom water depth, gauge', from 氵 'water' + 则 phonetic/standard) + 量 ('to measure volume or length with a vessel'). Attested since the Rites of Zhou and Han astronomy texts for surveying and measuring.

history.meaning: to fathom and measure; to survey

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 测量 (via 萌典)

浏览.etymology: A Classical Chinese modifier-head / coordinative verbal compound composed of 流 (liú, 'to flow swiftly, glide smoothly without stopping') and 览 (lǎn, simplified from 覽, 'to view, look over, inspect, read'). Attested as early as Cao Pi's *Dianlun* and the *Selections of Refined Literature* (文选, Six Dynasties), where 流览 meant 'to cast a sweeping, fluid gaze over scenery or books'. In the digital age, it was adopted as the standard term for 'browsing' the web (and in瀏覽器 'web browser').

history.meaning: Six Dynasties & Tang Classical Chinese: 'to sweep one's gaze fluidly over landscapes or texts; to read rapidly and broadly'
20th-century Modern Mandarin: 'to skim through (books/documents), glance over, browse (stores or exhibitions)'
Late 20th–21st century Internet Mandarin: 'to browse the web, view webpages (yielding 浏览器 browser and 浏览量 page views)'

morphemes.meaning: to flow swiftly, glide over without lingering
to look at, view, inspect, read

浏览.notes: In digital media and showbiz analytics, 浏览量 (liúlǎnliàng, 'page views / view count') and 浏览器 (liúlǎnqì, 'web browser') are ubiquitous derivatives.

浓.etymology: Phono-semantic character (trad. 濃) composed of semantic 氵 ('water, liquid') + phonetic 农 (農, Old Chinese *nuːŋ). Originally denoted heavy dew in the Classic of Poetry (《诗经·蓼萧》 '零露浓浓'), later generalized to thick liquids, strong tea, and deep colors or aromas.

history.meaning: thick with dew -> dense, concentrated, strong (of liquids, scents, colors)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 浓 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: concentration (of a solution/gas), density, thickness (of color/shadow)

浓度.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound formed from 浓 (nóng, simplified from 濃, 'thick, dense, heavy of dew or liquid, concentrated') and the abstract degree suffix 度 (dù, 'measure, degree, extent', originally 'to measure by hand-span'). Coined in Meiji-era Japanese scientific terminology (濃度 nōdo) to translate Western chemical 'concentration' and optical 'density', and subsequently borrowed into modern Mandarin for both scientific concentration and metaphorical intensity.

history.meaning: Classical Chinese roots: 濃 ('heavy dew, thick liquid, deep flavor/color') + 度 ('standard of measurement, degree')
Meiji Japanese scientific coinage: 'chemical concentration of a solute; optical density'
Modern Standard Mandarin: 'concentration (of liquid/gas/coffee/alcohol), strength, saturation'

morphemes.meaning: thick, dense, strong, concentrated (of liquids, scents, colors)

浓度.notes: Used literally for beverages and chemistry (咖啡浓度 'coffee strength', 酒精浓度 'blood/beverage alcohol concentration') and playfully in contemporary Chinese internet/media slang (e.g., 二次元浓度很高 'having a very high concentration of anime/subculture vibes').

rootFamily.gloss: to concentrate, condense; espresso (浓缩咖啡)

浓稠.etymology: Coordinate culinary adjective combining 浓 ('thick; concentrated; rich in flavour or dew', water radical 氵 + 农 *nóng*) + 稠 ('dense; closely packed; viscous', grain radical 禾 + 周 *zhōu*). Ideal for describing slow-cooked lemon curd, rich lentil soup, or thick congee.

history.meaning: thick, rich, and viscous
thick and rich (of sauces, curds, or soups)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 浓稠

浓缩.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 浓缩. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 浓缩 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 浓缩 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 浓缩 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 浓缩. The etymology of 浓缩 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 浓缩
middle form of 浓缩
modern form of 浓缩

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 浓缩

浓郁.etymology: Coordinative adjective compound joining 浓 (trad. 濃, 'thick, strong, concentrated') + 郁 (trad. 鬱, 'luxuriant, rich in fragrance'). Used especially of rich, full-bodied aromas, flavors, or atmosphere.

history.meaning: rich, strong, and full-bodied (of fragrance or flavor)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 浓郁 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: thick and heavy, rich, deep (of colors or makeup)

浓重.etymology: A coordinative adjectival compound combining 浓 (nóng, simplified from 濃, 'thick, dense, saturated', originally describing heavy dew in the *Book of Odes*) and 重 (zhòng, 'heavy, deep, weighty, intense'). Attested from Tang–Song literature onward, the pairing of 'saturation' (浓) and 'weight/depth' (重) describes sensory impressions—such as colors, ink brushstrokes, stage makeup, fragrances, accents, or emotional atmospheres—that are richly saturated and deeply pronounced.

history.meaning: Tang–Song poetic & artistic prose: 'thick and heavy (of clouds, mist, ink wash, or floral fragrance)'
Modern Standard Mandarin: 'rich, dense, heavy, vivid, pronounced (of colors, makeup, accents, or emotional atmosphere)'

浓重.notes: Frequently collocates with sensory or stylistic nouns in visual arts and broadcasting: 色彩浓重 ('rich and vivid colors'), 浓重的口音 ('a thick/heavy accent'), and the idiom 浓墨重彩 ('in thick ink and heavy colors' — describing a grand, vividly detailed portrayal).

rootFamily.gloss: in thick ink and heavy colors; vividly highlighted
thick, strong, deep (of interest or atmosphere)

cognates.meaning: romance, romanticism (Meiji phonetic rendering of French/English roman)

浪漫.etymology: A fascinating semantic fusion of a Classical Chinese poetic compound and a Meiji Japanese phonetic loan (*ateji*). In Tang–Song Chinese (e.g., Su Shi), 浪漫 (làngmàn, from 浪 'unrestrained waves' + 漫 'overflowing water, unbound') was a coordinative compound meaning 'unrestrained, dissolute, overflowing without bounds'. In Meiji Japan, the novelist Natsume Sōseki used the kanji 浪漫 (*rōman*) as a phono-semantic match for French *roman* / English *romantic* (as in 浪漫主義 *rōmanshugi* 'Romanticism'); this re-infused term returned to China during the May Fourth era meaning 'romantic'.

history.meaning: Tang–Song Classical Chinese: 'overflowing like waves; unrestrained, bohemian, dissolute' (coordinative compound of 浪 + 漫)
Meiji Japanese (Natsume Sōseki): phono-semantic kanji rendering (ateji) of French 'roman' / English 'romantic'
Modern Standard Mandarin: 'romantic, poetic, passionate and imaginative'

morphemes.meaning: wave, unrestrained; matches 'ro-' in Japanese rōman (roman)
overflowing, unbound; matches '-man' in Japanese rōman (roman)

浪漫.notes: A textbook example of a Sino-Japanese graphic return loan whose pre-existing Classical Chinese imagery ('unfettered waves') harmonized seamlessly with the Western phonetic loan ('romance'). Collocates with 浪漫主义 ('Romanticism') and 制造浪漫 ('create romance').

rootFamily.gloss: long, boundless, endless (of night or road)

浪费.etymology: A modifier-head verbal and nominal compound combining 浪 (làng, originally 'billowing waves', extended in Middle Chinese to mean 'unrestrained, reckless, in vain, without purpose') and 费 (fèi, simplified from 費, 'to expend, spend, consume', containing the cowrie-shell money radical 贝/貝). Attested in Song–Ming vernacular and administrative prose, 浪费 literally means 'to spend/consume recklessly like unbridled waves', hence 'to waste or squander'.

history.meaning: Middle Chinese: 浪 ('recklessly, in vain, unrestrained') modifying 費 ('to spend wealth, expend resources')
Modern Standard Mandarin: 'to waste, squander (time, money, talent); wasteful, extravagant'

浪费.notes: Takes concrete and abstract objects alike: 浪费时间 ('waste time'), 浪费资源 ('waste resources'), and 暴殄天物 / 浪费才华 ('waste natural gifts or talent').

浮夸.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative compound composed of 浮 (fú, 'to float on water; superficial, ungrounded, hollow') and 夸 (kuā, representing traditional 誇, 'to boast, exaggerate, speak extravagantly', combining 言 'speech' with 夸 'expansive'). Famous from Han Yu's Tang-dynasty essay *Jin Xue Jie* (进学解), where ancient texts are contrasted with writing that is 浮夸 ('superficial and boastful, flashy without substance'). In modern Mandarin (reinforced by Cantonese pop culture, notably Eason Chan's hit song 《浮夸》), it describes over-the-top acting, flashy styling, or exaggerated praise.

history.meaning: Tang Classical Chinese (Han Yu): 'superficial and boastful in rhetoric or conduct; lacking grounded substance'
Modern Mandarin & Cantonese showbiz usage: 'exaggerated, over-the-top, melodramatic, flashy, ostentatious'

浮夸.notes: A staple critique in acting and variety show reviews: 演技浮夸 ('over-the-top, hammy acting') and 造型浮夸 ('flashy, ostentatious styling'). Note that simplified 夸 merges two traditional characters: 誇 ('boast/exaggerate', used here) and /夸 ('grand').

海外.etymology: A Classical Chinese modifier-head locative compound combining 海 (hǎi, 'sea, ocean') and 外 (wài, 'outside, beyond'), literally 'beyond the seas'. In pre-Qin and Han cosmological geography (such as the *Classic of Mountains and Seas*, 山海经, which includes chapters titled 海外南经 'Classic of the Regions Beyond the Southern Sea'), the central states were imagined as surrounded by the Four Seas (四海), so 海外 designated distant, semi-mythical lands beyond the seas. In modern usage, it denotes foreign countries or international markets ('overseas, abroad').

history.meaning: Pre-Qin & Han Cosmology (Shanhaijing): 'distant lands lying beyond the Four Seas surrounding the central realm'
Tang–Ming Maritime Era: 'foreign lands reached by sea trade; islands beyond the coast'
Modern Standard Mandarin: 'overseas, abroad, international (used even for landlocked foreign countries)'

morphemes.meaning: sea, ocean (historically the 'Four Seas' bounding the known world)

海外.notes: Used as a general synonym for 国外 ('abroad') regardless of whether sea travel is involved; in media business (*Behind the Scenes*), 海外发行 ('overseas distribution') and 海外版权 ('international copyright sales') are key revenue streams. Compare 海归 ('sea turtle' — pun on 海外归来, an overseas-educated returnee).

海水.etymology: Determinative compound of 海 ('sea; ocean', water radical 氵 + 每 *měi*) + 水 ('water'). Attested since the *Zhuangzi* and *Mencius*, it is the everyday word for salty ocean water.

history.meaning: water of the sea
seawater

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 海水

海盐.etymology: Endocentric noun compound combining 海 ('sea, ocean') + 盐 (trad. 鹽, 'salt', originally picturing brine pan,卤, and vessel 皿). Refers to salt evaporated from seawater, documented in Chinese economic treatises since antiquity.

history.meaning: sea salt; salt produced from evaporated seawater

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 海盐 (via 萌典)

海绵.etymology: Compound of 海 ('sea') + 绵 ('soft silk floss', silk radical 纟 + 帛 'fine cloth'), originally describing natural marine sponges by likening their porous springiness to silk wadding, later extended to synthetic cleaning sponges.

history.meaning: marine sponge
sponge (natural or household)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 海绵

涂.etymology: Simplified from 塗 (tú), formed from the water radical 氵, phonetic 余, and earth 土 underneath—originally meaning 'mud, mire' and as a verb 'to plaster a wall with mud or lime'. From daubing plaster, Classical and vernacular Chinese broadened 涂 to brushing or spreading any smooth coat—beeswax onto linen, glaze onto pastry, or paint onto wood.

morphemes.meaning: plaster with mud/liquid (氵 + 土, simplified from 塗) -> coat, spread, brush on

history.meaning: mud; plaster a wall; coat a surface
spread on; brush a coat of wax, glaze, or paint

cognates.meaning: digestion; assimilation of knowledge or quotas
digestion; mastering a role or concept

消化.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative and resultative verbal compound composed of 消 (xiāo, 'to melt away, dissolve, dissipate') and 化 (huà, 'to transform, change state, transmute'). Attested in Han-dynasty medical and philosophical texts (such as Wang Chong's *Lunheng* and early materia medica) to describe food 'dissolving and transforming' into nourishment in the stomach. Extending naturally from physiological digestion, it also means 'to absorb, assimilate, or process (information, negative emotions, or market inventory)'.

history.meaning: Han–Tang Classical Chinese (Lunheng & medical texts): 'to dissolve and transform (food in the stomach, or ice/metals)'
Modern Standard Mandarin: 'physiological digestion; (figuratively) to absorb, process, or stomach new information, criticism, or stress'

消化.notes: Frequently used metaphorically in workplace and media contexts when someone needs time to mentally process shocking news, heavy feedback, or complex scripts (e.g., 让我先消化一下这个消息 'let me digest this news first', 消化不良 'indigestion').

消息.etymology: Originally an antonymic compound of 消 ('to vanish, wane, melt away') + 息 ('to grow, wax, breathe'), used in the I Ching (《易·丰》 '与时消息') for the cyclical waxing and waning of cosmic forces; by the Han–Tang period shifted to mean 'tidings, news, report of changes'.

history.stage: Classical Chinese (I Ching) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: waxing and waning -> news of how things stand; tidings, message

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 消息 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: news source, informant, source of information

消息源.etymology: A three-character modifier-head nominal compound combining 消息 (xiāoxī, 'news, tidings, information') with the head noun 源 (yuán, 'water spring, fountainhead, source'). Remarkably, 消息 began in the *I Ching* (易经·丰卦) as an antonymic coordinative compound of 消 ('to wane, diminish, melt away') and 息 ('to wax, grow, breathe/multiply'), denoting the cyclic waxing and waning of yin and yang; by the Six Dynasties and Tang period, asking after someone's 'waxing and waning' evolved into 'tidings, news, message', to which modern journalism suffixed 源 ('source') to calque English 'news source'.

history.meaning: Classical Chinese: 消息 'waxing and waning of cosmic forces, cyclic change'; 源 'mountain spring, river headwaters'
Six Dynasties–Tang semantic shift: 'tidings, news of how someone is faring, intelligence'
Modern Journalism Mandarin: 'news source, informant, origin of a media report' (calquing English 'news source')

morphemes.meaning: news, tidings, information (originally antonymic: 消 'wane' + 息 'wax')

消息源.notes: Essential journalism and entertainment PR vocabulary (*Behind the Scenes*): 保护消息源 ('protect a news source'), 可靠的消息源 ('a reliable source'), and 匿名消息源 ('anonymous source'). Often shortened to 信源 (xìnyuán).

消消气.etymology: A colloquial Mandarin reduplicated verb-object phrase (AAB pattern) formed by reduplicating the verb 消 (xiāo, 'to dissolve, dispel, subside, abate') before its nominal object 气 (qì, simplified from 氣, 'vital breath, pneuma; anger, temper'). In Traditional Chinese Medicine and everyday idiom, anger is conceptualized as rising or blocked *qì* (生气 'generate anger-qì', 怒气 'wrathful qì'); 消气 literally means 'to dissipate the pent-up气 of anger', and the verbal reduplication 消消 softens the imperative into a gentle, soothing coax: 'cool down a bit, don't be angry'.

history.meaning: Classical & Medical Chinese: 'to dispel stagnated vital breath (qì); to let wrath subside'
Modern Colloquial Mandarin: 'calm down a little, cool your temper, let your anger subside' (polite/soothing imperative)

morphemes.meaning: to dispel, abate, cool down a little bit

消消气.notes: exemplifies how Mandarin uses verb reduplication inside a separable verb-object compound (V-O -> V-V-O) to make commands sound warm and persuasive rather than abrupt (e.g., 您先喝口茶消消气 'Have a sip of tea and cool down a bit first').

rootFamily.gloss: to calm down, stop being angry (base VO form)
to get angry, take offense (lit. 'generate qì')

消肿.etymology: Separable verb-object medical compound of 消 ('dissolve; subside; cause to vanish', water radical 氵 + 肖 *xiāo*) + 肿 ('swelling; inflammation', flesh/body radical 月 + 重 *zhǒng*). Used since traditional medical manuals for reducing swelling in a sprained joint.

history.meaning: reduce bodily swelling or inflammation
go down in swelling; reduce swelling

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 消肿

cognates.word: 消費群体 / 消費者層 (shōhishasō)

消费群体.etymology: A four-character modifier-head nominal compound combining 消费 (xiāofèi, 'consumption, to consume/spend', a coordinative compound of 消 'dissipate, use up' and 费 'expend wealth' that was standardized via Meiji Japanese 消費 *shōhi* to translate economic 'consumption') with 群体 (qúntǐ, 'group, collective demographic', composed of 群 'flock, crowd, group' + 体 'body, entity'). Together they denote a 'consumer group, target market segment, or audience demographic'.

history.meaning: Classical & Early Modern roots: 消費 ('to expend and use up') + 群體 ('collective body, flock')
Late 20th–21st century Commercial & Media Mandarin: 'consumer group, target demographic, market segment'

morphemes.meaning: consumption, spending (coordinative: 消 'use up' + 费 'spend')
group, collective demographic (modifier-head: 群 'flock/group' + 体 'body/entity')

消费群体.notes: In television production, advertising, and media strategy (*Behind the Scenes*), identifying the 核心消费群体 ('core consumer demographic') or 年轻消费群体 ('young consumer demographic') drives sponsorship pitches and show positioning.

cognates.word: 嫌疑をかける (kengi o kakeru)

涉嫌.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound telescoping the phrase 涉及嫌疑 (shèjí xiányí, 'to touch upon suspicion'). 涉 (shè, Old Chinese *djap) originally depicted two feet (步) crossing a stream (水), meaning 'to wade across water' and by extension 'to be implicated in'; 嫌 (xián, OC *gˤem) combines 'woman' (女) with 'hold together' (兼), meaning 'to harbor resentment or suspicion'.

history.meaning: to wade across a river / to harbor doubt or discontent
suspicion, being subject to doubt or accusation
to be suspected of (an offense, crime, or violation)

morphemes.meaning: to wade into, touch upon, be involved in
suspicion, ill will (short for 嫌疑)

涉嫌.notes: Formal legal and journalistic verb taking a crime or violation as its object (e.g., 涉嫌抄袭 'suspected of plagiarism' in media scandals); never used for everyday personal doubts.

淋浴喷头.etymology: Four-character nominal phrase combining 淋浴 ('shower', from 淋 'to drench from above' + 浴 'to bathe') + 喷头 (trad. 噴頭, 'spray nozzle', from 喷 'to spurt, spray' + 头 'head, tip').

history.form: 淋浴噴頭 / 淋浴喷头
history.meaning: shower head; spray nozzle of a shower

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 淋浴喷头 (via 萌典)

淋湿.etymology: Resultative verb compound combining 淋 ('pour water upon; drench with rain', water radical 氵 + 林 lín 'forest', evoking water dripping continuously like rain through trees) + 湿 ('wet; soaked').

history.meaning: drench or get soaked by rain
get drenched by rain; soak

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 淋湿

淋透.etymology: Resultative verb compound formed from 淋 ('to pour down on, drench', originally continuous rain in Shuowen) + 透 ('to penetrate through, thoroughly').

history.meaning: drenched through; soaked to the skin

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 淋透 (via 萌典)

淘汰.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound formed from two synonymous hydro-metallurgical and grain-washing verbs: 淘 (táo, Middle Chinese *daw), 'to wash grain or pan for gold in a sieve by swirling water', and 汰 (tài, MC *thajH), 'to rinse away dregs or excess'. Originally describing physical panning and winnowing, it gained metaphorical force in Literary Chinese ('weeding out the inferior') and was reinforced in the late 19th century via Yan Fu's and Japanese translations of Darwinian 'natural selection' (自然淘汰).

history.meaning: to wash and rinse away husks, sand, or impurities with water
to weed out corrupt or incompetent officials and retain the worthy
to eliminate in competition or phase out through selection

morphemes.meaning: to wash in a pan or sieve, dredge, pan for gold
to rinse away, scour out excess or dregs

淘汰.notes: Ubiquitous in reality television and talent competitions (*幕后之王*) for eliminating contestants (被淘汰), as well as in tech/industry for obsolete products being phased out.

rootFamily.gloss: to pan for gold; (modern) hunt for bargains online
to prune, pare down冗余 personnel or text

淡.etymology: Phono-semantic character composed of semantic 氵 ('water, liquid') + phonetic 炎 (yán/dàn). Originally described thin, mild, tasteless broth or water low in salt (contrasting with 浓 'thick, strong' and 咸 'salty'), then extended to pale colors and indifferent attitudes.

history.meaning: thin or mild in flavor -> light, pale,淡泊 (unassuming)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 淡 (via 萌典)

淡淡.etymology: Reduplication (AA pattern) of 淡 (dàn, written with water 氵 beside stacked flames 炎: water tempering heat/saltiness, hence 'light in flavor, pale in tint, gentle'). Doubling 淡 into 淡淡 softens the adjective into an evocative sensory description—'faintly fragrant, delicately tinted, understated'—celebrated in Chinese aesthetics from Su Shi's poetry to everyday descriptions of tea and mint.

history.meaning: faintly tinted; gently scented; unassuming
faint; delicate; light (of scent, colour, or smile)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 淡淡

深.etymology: Phono-semantic character with semantic 氵 ('water') and a right-hand component depicting a hand holding a torch or probing inside a cave/pit (窅/𥥍) to gauge depth. Denotes deep water first, then spatial, chromatic, or intellectual depth.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Bronze & Seal script) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: deep (of water) -> profound, dark (of color), late (of time)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 深 (via 萌典)

深度.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound combining 深 (shēn, Old Chinese *hljəm), 'deep (of water)', and the abstract degree/measure suffix 度 (dù, OC *dˤak-s), originally meaning 'linear measurement' or 'standard'. While attested in Literary Chinese for physical depth, its widespread modern use for intellectual profundity and attributive 'in-depth' (深度报道 'in-depth reporting') was reinforced by modern Sino-Japanese scientific and journalistic usage (深度 shindo).

history.meaning: deep water / measured standard or extent
physical depth of water, valleys, or excavations
depth of thought/analysis; attributive 'in-depth'

深度.notes: In media and television production, 深度 functions both as a noun (有深度 'has depth') and directly before nouns as an uninflected modifier (深度访谈 'in-depth interview', 深度合作 'deep collaboration').

深有体会.etymology: A four-character adverbial-verb-object idiom (成語-style quadrisyllabic phrase) structured as [adverbial 深 'deeply' + verb 有 'possess' + nominalized object 体会 'embodied understanding']. 体会 (tǐhuì) itself is a Literary Chinese compound from Neo-Confucian self-cultivation discourse: 体 (tǐ, 'to embody personally, put oneself in something's place') + 会 (huì, 'to mentally grasp or synthesize').

history.meaning: to grasp a principle through personal embodiment and reflection
to possess a deep, firsthand experiential understanding of something

深有体会.notes: Often used with the preposition 对 (duì) to introduce the topic: 对此我深有体会 ('I know this all too well from personal experience').

rootFamily.gloss: to learn through personal experience; personal understanding
to experience for oneself; user experience
to have deep feelings or resonance about something

深色.etymology: Attributive compound combining 深 ('deep, dark in shade') + 色 ('color, hue'). Contrasts with 浅色 ('light color').

history.meaning: dark color; deep shade

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 深色 (via 萌典)

淳于.etymology: An ancient disyllabic Chinese surname (複姓 fùxìng) originating as a toponymic lineage name from the Spring and Autumn period state of Chunyu (淳于國, located in modern Anqiu, Shandong), later annexed by Qi. 淳 (chún, Old Chinese *djun) means 'pure, unadulterated, rich' and 于 (yú, OC *ɢʷ(r)a) is a locative preposition/particle in archaic state names. Famous historical bearers include the Warring States wit Chunyu Kun (淳于髠) and the early Han physician Chunyu Yi (淳于意).

history.meaning: name of an ancient polity in Shandong (Zhou–Spring and Autumn period)
hereditary two-character surname adopted by descendants of the state of Chunyu
two-character surname (borne by male lead Chunyu Qiao in Behind the Scenes)

淳于.notes: One of the classic two-character surnames (复姓) in the *Hundred Family Surnames* (百家姓); in Chinese dramas, rare disyllabic surnames like 淳于 are frequently chosen for protagonists to give their names an distinctive, memorable literary ring.

rootFamily.gloss: Chunyu Qiao (protagonist of Behind the Scenes)
rich, pure, and mellow (of wine or customs)

淳于乔.etymology: A full personal name consisting of the ancient two-character surname 淳于 (Chúnyú, from the Spring and Autumn state of Chunyu) followed by the given name 乔 (qiáo, Old Chinese *g(r)jaw), which originally meant 'tall and curving upward (especially of lofty trees)' as glossed in the *Shuowen Jiezi* (高而曲也). In *Behind the Scenes* (幕后之王), it is the name of the elite television producer played by Luo Jin.

history.meaning: Chunyu (toponymic surname) + Qiao ('lofty, towering like a tall tree')
Chunyu Qiao (full name of the male lead producer in Behind the Scenes)

morphemes.meaning: tall, lofty, towering (of trees or mountains)

淳于乔.notes: Note that the surname is the two-character 淳于 (Chúnyú) and the given name is the single character 乔 (Qiáo), NOT surname Chun + given name Yuqiao—hence colleagues address him as 淳于总 ('Director Chunyu').

rootFamily.gloss: Director Chunyu (workplace title for Chunyu Qiao)

淳于总.etymology: A workplace address form combining the two-character surname 淳于 (Chúnyú) with the postpositive professional title 总 (zǒng), clipped from 总经理 (zǒngjīnglǐ, 'general manager'), 总监 (zǒngjiān, 'chief director'), or 总裁 (zǒngcái, 'president/CEO'). 总 (Old Chinese *tsˤoŋʔ) originally meant 'to tie together in a bundle (as silk threads)' and evolved to mean 'overall, chief'.

history.meaning: to bind silk cords together; to gather and oversee as a whole
chief supervisor / general manager
Director Chunyu / Chief Chunyu (corporate honorific address)

morphemes.meaning: chief, director, general manager (short for 总监/总经理)

淳于总.notes: In contemporary Chinese corporate and media culture, [Surname] + 总 is the default respectful address for any executive, producer, or department head (e.g., 王总, 淳于总), regardless of whether they are the CEO or a division director.

混.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形聲字) combining the water radical 氵(水, 'water') with the phonetic-semantic component 昆 (kūn, Old Chinese *kˤun, 'together, numerous, swarming'). Originally denoting a 'vast, muddy, or turbulent torrent of water' (*gˤunʔ / *gˤun-s), it shifted in Classical and Middle Chinese to mean 'to mingle, blend indiscriminately, muddle through', and in colloquial Mandarin 'to get by, hang out, or scrape a living in a milieu'.

history.meaning: abundant, turbid, or surging flow of water; undifferentiated chaos (混沌)
to mix together, blend indiscriminately, confuse
to mix; (colloquial) to muddle along, make one's way in an industry or circle

morphemes.meaning: to mix, blend, muddle along (water radical 氵 + phonetic 昆)

混.notes: Beyond literal 'mixing', colloquial 混 is vital in showbiz and workplace speech for 'making it in a circle' or 'scraping by' (在娱乐圈混 'making one's way in the entertainment industry', 混日子 'drifting through life').

rootFamily.gloss: to muddle along, drift through life without ambition

混血儿.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound formed from the verb-object compound 混血 (hùnxuè, 'mixed blood': 混 'to mix, blend' + 血 'blood', calquing European expressions like English *mixed-blood* / German *Mischblut* via late 19th-century Sino-Japanese 混血児 *konketsuji*) plus the nominal suffix 儿 (ér, 'child, person').

history.meaning: to mix + blood + child (separate Classical morphemes)
child or person of mixed ethnic/racial parentage (shared with Japanese 混血児)

混血儿.notes: In contemporary Mandarin, 混血儿 (or simply 混血 as a predicate/modifier, e.g., 他是混血) applies to adults as well as children and frequently carries positive aesthetic connotations in Chinese pop culture and casting.

淹死.etymology: A resultative verb compound (動補結構) combining the action verb 淹 (yān, Old Chinese *ʔ(r)jam, water radical 氵 + phonetic 奄 yǎn 'to cover'), meaning 'to submerge, inundate, soak in water', with the resultative complement 死 (sǐ, OC *sijʔ), 'to die, to death'. The compound literally means 'to submerge with the result of dying'.

history.meaning: to submerge in water, inundate; to tarry or linger long
to drown to death, be drowned by submerging in water

淹死.notes: Can be used transitively ('drown someone/something') or ergatively/passively (差点被淹死 'nearly drowned'); occurs in the famous proverb 会水的淹死 ('it is the good swimmers who drown'—overconfidence leads to downfall).

rootFamily.gloss: to drown (formal/written equivalent of 淹死)
to starve to death (parallel resultative pattern)

添.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining semantic 氵 ('water, liquid') + 忝 (tiǎn, phonetic). Originally meant to add water or top up a vessel, then generalized to adding or increasing anything (添衣, 添茶).

history.meaning: to replenish liquid -> to add, increase, append

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 添 (via 萌典)

添乱.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound pairing 添 (tiān, Middle Chinese *them, water radical 氵 + 忝 tiǎn), meaning 'to add to, replenish, increase on top of what exists', with the nominalized object 乱 (luàn, Old Chinese *rˤon-s), originally depicting two hands untangling silk threads on a spool and meaning 'tangled disorder, chaos, trouble'. Literally 'to add disorder (to an already busy situation)'.

history.meaning: to replenish or add / disorder, entanglement, turmoil
to add to the chaos, make more trouble when people are already busy

添乱.notes: As a separable verb-object (离合词) compound, it takes a beneficiary with 给 (别给我添乱了 'Stop making more trouble for me!') and allows aspect particles or modifiers between the characters (添了不少乱).

rootFamily.gloss: to cause trouble for someone, inconvenience someone
to add bricks and tiles—to do one's part to help a project
to cause chaos, sabotage, make trouble

添麻烦.etymology: A verb-object (VO) phrase combining 添 (tiān, 'to add, increase') with the disyllabic noun 麻烦 (máfan, 'trouble, bother'). 麻烦 itself is a vernacular compound of 麻 (má, 'hemp fibers', metaphorically 'tangled and messy like uncombed hemp') and 烦 (fán, Old Chinese *ban, fire/heat radical 火 + head 页, 'feverish headache, vexation, annoyance'). Literally 'to add tangled vexation (onto someone)'.

history.meaning: to add + tangled hemp + mental vexation/heat in the head
to cause extra trouble or inconvenience for someone

添麻烦.notes: A staple of polite Chinese workplace and social etiquette, typically used with 给 (gěi): 不好意思，给您添麻烦了 ('Sorry to have put you to so much trouble').

rootFamily.gloss: to add to the chaos, make more trouble

清.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形聲字) combining the water radical 氵(水, 'water') with 青 (qīng, Old Chinese *s.r̥ˤeŋ, 'blue-green of sprouting plants; clear hue'). In Old Chinese (*tsʰeŋ), 清 denoted limpid, sediment-free water—contrasting directly with 浊 (zhuó, 'turbid, muddy water')—and expanded across Classical and Modern Chinese to mean 'morally pure', 'quiet', 'distinct', and as a verb/complement 'to settle or clear completely (as accounts or inventory)'.

history.meaning: limpid, transparent, unmuddied (of water); morally pure and incorruptible
clear, distinct; to tally, audit, or settle accounts completely
clear, clean, pure; settled or cleared out completely

morphemes.meaning: clear, limpid, pure; to clear or settle completely (氵water + 青 phonetic/semantic)

清.notes: Functions both as an adjective ('clear, pure') and as a potent resultative complement after verbs meaning 'distinctly' or 'completely settled' (说清 'explain clearly', 算清 'settle accounts', 撇清关系 'disavow any connection').

rootFamily.gloss: to clean up, sort out, audit

清亮.etymology: Coordinative adjective compound from 清 ('clear; pure; limpid', water 氵 + 青) + 亮 ('bright; resonant; shining'). Combines visual clarity with acoustic ring to describe crystal-clear eyes, limpid water, or a bright, ringing voice or guitar tone.

history.meaning: clear and resonant (of voice); bright and limpid
clear and bright; crisp and ringing

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 清亮

清凉.etymology: The adjective '清凉' (qīngliáng, refreshing and cool) combines '清' (clear, pure) and '凉' (cool). The term has deep roots in classical literature, often describing a pleasant, refreshing coolness that contrasts with oppressive summer heat. It was also used metaphorically in Buddhist texts to describe a state of spiritual peace, free from the 'heat' of earthly desires. In contemporary usage, it is a common descriptive word for weather, beverages, or clothing that provides a comfortable, cool sensation.

history.meaning: cool

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 清凉

清单.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound originating in Ming–Qing commercial and bureaucratic accounting: 清 (qīng, here in its verbal/resultative sense 'audited, tallied clearly, settled item by item') modifies 单 (dān, Old Chinese *tˤar, 'single sheet, slip of paper, bill, register'). Originally a 'clear itemized invoice or inventory', it now covers any checklist or roster.

history.meaning: single; a single slip of paper or recorded list of items
an audited, itemized statement of goods, gifts, or accounts
checklist, itemized list, inventory, roster

清单.notes: Used across corporate, production, and daily contexts for any structured list: 任务清单 ('task checklist'), 节目清单 ('program lineup'), or 拉清单 ('draw up an itemized reckoning / settle scores').

rootFamily.gloss: to take inventory, count item by item

清楚.etymology: Compound adjective from 清 ('clear, limpid water') + 楚 ('neat, distinct, orderly', originally thickets of vitex shrubs cleared into neat rows, as in 《诗经》 '言刈其楚' and 楚楚 'neat and vivid'). Together means clear and distinct.

history.meaning: clear, distinct, well-ordered; to understand clearly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 清楚 (via 萌典)

清淡.etymology: A coordinative adjectival compound joining two hydrological and gustatory roots: 清 (qīng, 'clear, unclouded, pure') and 淡 (dàn, Old Chinese *lˤamʔ, water radical 氵 + double fire 炎, originally 'thin, watery, not salty or strong in flavor', contrasting with 浓 nóng 'thick, rich'). In Six Dynasties aesthetics and Tang poetry it praised detached, unadorned literary style and character; it also describes lightly seasoned food and sluggish market volume.

history.meaning: clear and mild; detached from worldly ambition, tranquil and unadorned in poetic style
light and mildly seasoned (of food/broth); quiet or slack (of business/trade)
light/mild in flavor; understated; sluggish (of sales or market activity)

清淡.notes: Has three primary domains: culinary (饮食清淡 'eat light, non-greasy food'), aesthetic/stylistic ('understated, subtle'), and commercial (生意清淡 'business is slow/slack').

rootFamily.gloss: indifferent to fame and wealth, tranquil
clear and refreshing, clean and cool

清清楚楚.etymology: Four-syllable AABB reduplication of 清楚 ('clear; distinct', originally describing a grove where underbrush 楚 has been cleared away as limpidly as spring water 清). The AABB pattern intensifies clarity so that every detail is seen or heard unmistakably.

history.meaning: crystal clear; completely distinct
crystal clear; unmistakably

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 清清楚楚

清漆.etymology: Compound of 清 ('clear; transparent; unpigmented') + 漆 ('natural tree lacquer; varnish', water radical 氵 + 桼 depicting sap dripping from cuts in a lacquer tree *Toxicodendron vernicifluum*). Distinguishes transparent wood varnish that showcases natural wood grain from coloured paint (油漆).

history.meaning: transparent lacquer or varnish
clear varnish

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 清漆

清爽.etymology: Coordinate sensory adjective of 清 ('clear; pure; cool', water radical 氵 + 青 *qīng*) + 爽 ('brisk; bright; invigorating', depicting clear lattice light patterns 爻 beside 大). It describes crisp morning air, bright citrus aromas, and clean, ungreasy flavours.

history.meaning: clear, cool, and refreshing
bright and refreshing; crisp

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 清爽

清白.etymology: A coordinative compound of two metaphors of unblemished purity: 清 (qīng, 'limpid, unclouded water') and 白 (bái, Old Chinese *bˤrak, 'white, unstained silk or light'). Attested as early as the *Chu Ci* (楚辭, 'Songs of Chu': 清白以死直兮) and Han dynasty official biographies to mean 'morally untainted and incorruptible', it later developed the legal and personal sense of 'innocent of wrongdoing' or 'an unblemished reputation'.

history.meaning: pure and unstained; morally upright and incorruptible (of officials or scholars)
of respectable, untainted family lineage; free from scandal or illicit conduct
innocent, clean-handed; (noun) one's good name or innocence

清白.notes: Used both as an adjective (他是清白的 'he is innocent') and as a noun in high-stakes media or legal dramas: 还我清白 ('restore my good name / prove my innocence') and 证明自己的清白.

rootFamily.gloss: honest and upright, free from corruption (of officials)
clear and unambiguous; plain to see

清空.etymology: Resultative verb compound combining 清 ('to clear out, purge') + 空 ('empty, vacant'). Used both for physically emptying a container or room and digitally clearing a cache or list.

history.meaning: to clear out completely; to empty

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 清空 (via 萌典)

清脆.etymology: Coordinate sensory adjective of 清 ('clear; pure in tone') + 脆 ('crisp; resonant; brittle'). Applied both to acoustics—the bell-like ring of a well-tuned piano key or brass bell—and to crisp foods like fresh apples or pastries.

history.meaning: clear and ringing in tone (of instruments or birdsong)
clear and crisp

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 清脆

清茶.etymology: Modifier-head compound from 清 ('clear; plain; unadorned') + 茶 ('tea', grass 艹 + person 人 + tree 木). Refers to light, fragrant green or herbal tea served plain without milk, sugar, or heavy snacks.

history.meaning: plain, clear tea
light, plain tea; green or herbal tea

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 清茶

清除.etymology: A coordinative/resultative verbal compound combining 清 (qīng, 'to make clear, cleanse completely') with 除 (chú, Old Chinese *lra, mound/steps radical 阝 + phonetic 余 yú), which originally denoted the steps leading to a palace hall and by extension 'to sweep away dirt from the steps, remove, eradicate'. Attested in Han texts for clearing roads for an imperial procession, it now means 'to purge, clear away obstacles, or wipe data'.

history.meaning: to sweep clean and clear a thoroughfare for an imperial carriage
to eradicate, purge, clear out obstacles, pests, or corrupt elements

清除.notes: Stronger and more thorough than 清理 (qīnglǐ, 'tidy up/sort out'): 清除 implies total removal of something unwanted, such as 清除障碍 ('clear away obstacles'), 清除隐患 ('eliminate hidden dangers'), or clearing cache/data.

rootFamily.gloss: to clean up, sort out, put in order
to rule out, exclude, clear away (difficulty)

清静.etymology: A coordinative adjectival compound of 清 (qīng, 'clear, pure, untroubled') and 静 (jìng, Old Chinese *dzek-s / *dzeŋʔ, 'still, tranquil, free from agitation'). Originally a central philosophical term in Daoism (*Laozi* and *Zhuangzi*: 清靜無為 'purity, stillness, and non-action') for a mind unclouded by desires, it generalized in vernacular Mandarin to describe a peaceful, noise-free environment or being left undisturbed.

history.meaning: mental purity and stillness free from worldly agitation (Daoist ideal of governance and cultivation)
secluded, quiet, and peaceful (of a monastery, retreat, or lifestyle)
peaceful and quiet, undisturbed (of a place, atmosphere, or person's ears/mind)

清静.notes: Often pronounced with a neutral second syllable (qīngjing) in everyday speech; commonly used in the idiom 耳根清静 ('peace and quiet for one's ears'—free from nagging or media noise). Distinguish from homophonous 清净 (qīngjìng, 'clean and pure; Buddhist purity').

渗.etymology: Phono-semantic character (trad. 滲) formed from semantic 氵 ('water') + phonetic 参 (參, cān/shēn). Attested in Shuowen Jiezi as 'to leak downward' (下漉也), describing liquid seeping or oozing slowly through pores or cracks.

history.meaning: to seep through; to ooze or permeate slowly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 渗 (via 萌典)

渡过难关.etymology: A four-character verb-object phrase built on a vivid geographical metaphor: 渡过 (dùguò, verb + directional/resultative complement: 渡 'to ferry across a river' + 过 'across, past') + 难关 (nánguān, modifier-head noun: 难 'difficult, perilous' + 关 'mountain pass, fortified frontier gate'). Literally 'to ferry across a perilous mountain pass or river barrier', hence 'to pull through a crisis'.

history.meaning: to ferry across a waterway / a bolted frontier gate or mountain pass
a fortified pass hard to cross; a critical juncture or ordeal (especially settling debts at year-end)
to tide over a crisis, pull through a difficult period

morphemes.meaning: to ferry across water, cross over

渡过难关.notes: Standardly written with water-radical 渡 (dù, 'ferry across a perilous crossing') when paired with 难关 or 危机 ('crisis'), whereas 度过 (without water radical) is used for spending ordinary spans of time (度过周末 'spend the weekend').

rootFamily.gloss: to pass through or spend (a period of time)
critical juncture, decisive barrier or test

渣男.etymology: A 21st-century Mandarin internet slang compound (modifier-head structure) combining 渣 (zhā, Middle Chinese *tsra, originally the sediment of River Zha and by extension 'dregs, residue,滓 left after pressing oil, soy, or wine', clipped from 人渣 rénzhā 'human dregs/scum') with 男 (nán, 'man, male'). Literally 'dregs-man' or 'scumbag male', popularized on Chinese social media and relationship dramas in the 2010s.

history.meaning: sediment, dregs, solid residue left after extracting liquid
dregs of humanity, social scumbag
cad, two-timing jerk, emotionally manipulative or unfaithful man

渣男.notes: Specifically targets men who are unfaithful, two-timing, emotionally manipulative, or shirk responsibility in romantic relationships; 渣 has also become a productive slang adjective in Mandarin (他很渣 'he is trashy/a cad').

rootFamily.gloss: toxic or two-timing woman (female counterpart of 渣男)

温.etymology: Phono-semantic/associative character (trad. 溫) combining 氵 ('water') + 昷 (showing a vessel 皿 with an item inside, warming or feeding). Originally the name of a warm river in Shuowen, and generally 'lukewarm, mild, gentle' or 'to warm up, review'.

history.meaning: warm, lukewarm; mild, gentle; to warm up

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 温 (via 萌典)

温开水.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound composed of 温 (wēn, Old Chinese *ʔˤun, 'lukewarm, gently heated') + 开水 (kāishuǐ, literally 'opened water', where 开 kāi 'to open' developed the vernacular physical sense 'to bubble open, come to a rolling boil' in Ming–Qing Mandarin, replacing Literary 沸水 fèishuǐ). Thus 温开水 is 'water that has been boiled to sterilization and cooled to a lukewarm temperature'.

history.meaning: warm water, thermal spring water
water brought to a rolling boil ('opened water')
warm boiled drinking water

温开水.notes: A cornerstone of Chinese daily health habits (多喝温开水 'drink more warm boiled water'); also used figuratively in media/drama critiques for a plot, personality, or relationship that is bland, safe, and lacks dramatic spark (像一杯温开水).

rootFamily.gloss: plain boiled water (cooled or warm, without tea leaves)

温暖.etymology: Coordinative compound joining 温 (trad. 溫, 'warm, mild, lukewarm') + 暖 ('warm, genial sun-warmth'). Used both literally of pleasant physical warmth and figuratively of emotional kindness.

history.meaning: warm and genial (of weather, places, or feelings)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 温暖 (via 萌典)

温柔.etymology: Coordinative compound combining 温 (trad. 溫, 'warm, gentle, mild') + 柔 ('soft, pliant, yielding, tender', originally flexible wood). Classical ideal of character in the Book of Rites (温柔敦厚).

history.meaning: gentle, soft, and tender in manner

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 温柔 (via 萌典)

温水.etymology: Attributive noun compound combining 温 (trad. 溫, 'lukewarm, moderately warm') + 水 ('water').

history.meaning: lukewarm water; warm water

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 温水 (via 萌典)

温热.etymology: Coordinative adjective compound joining 温 (trad. 溫, 'lukewarm, mild') + 热 (trad. 熱, 'hot, heated'), describing something pleasantly warm to the touch or palate.

history.stage: Classical Chinese Medical Texts to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: moderately warm; tepid to warm

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 温热 (via 萌典)

温馨.etymology: Coordinative adjective combining 温 (trad. 溫, 'warm, genial') + 馨 ('fragrance spreading far'). Originally described warm, fragrant air in medieval poetry, now standard for a cozy, warm, and welcoming home atmosphere.

history.meaning: warm and fragrant -> cozy, heartwarming, welcoming

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 温馨 (via 萌典)

游戏性.etymology: A modern derivational compound attaching the abstract quality suffix -性 (-xìng, originally 'inborn nature' in Classical Chinese, revitalized via Japanese -性 *-sei* to translate English *-ness / -ity*) to the compound noun 游戏 (yóuxì, 'game, play', from Classical 游 'to roam, swim freely' + 戏 'to sport, jest, stage play'). Modeled partly on Japanese 遊戯性 (*yūgisei*) and ゲーム性 (*gēmu-sei*), it denotes 'gameplay appeal, playability, or playful interactivity'.

history.meaning: to roam and sport freely; playful recreation or theatrical diversion
playability, gameplay quality, or playful game-like engagement (in games and variety shows)

游戏性.notes: In television variety production (*幕后之王*) and game design, 游戏性 refers to how engaging, interactive, and fun a format or mechanic is for participants and viewers (增强节目的游戏性 'enhance the show's playful engagement').

rootFamily.gloss: watchability, visual appeal (of a show or performance)

湿.etymology: Phono-semantic character (trad. 濕) composed of semantic 氵 ('water') + 显/𤇾 (silk threads drying under the sun over fire, phonetic *qhliːb). Simplified 湿 merges with the ancient river name 湿 (Tà). Means 'wet, damp, moist'.

history.meaning: wet, damp, humid

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 湿 (via 萌典)

湿气.etymology: A classical natural-philosophy and everyday compound combining 湿 (shī, simplified from 濕, 'wet, damp') and 气 (qì, simplified from 氣, 'air, vapor, atmospheric breath'). Used in both traditional Chinese medicine and everyday Sichuanese/Mandarin household life—especially in humid river-basin cities like Chengdu—湿气 denotes ambient moisture or damp air that can seep into wood, paper, and stone.

history.meaning: damp vapor rising from earth or rain
dampness; moisture; humidity

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 湿气

湿透.etymology: Resultative verb compound combining 湿 (trad. 濕, 'wet, damp') + 透 ('through, thoroughly'), meaning 'soaked through'.

history.meaning: soaked through; completely wet

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 湿透 (via 萌典)

溅.etymology: Phono-semantic character (trad. 濺) combining semantic 氵 ('water') + phonetic 贱 (賤, jiàn). Describes liquid splashing or spattering outward on impact.

history.meaning: to splash; to spatter liquid

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 溅 (via 萌典)

滑.etymology: Phono-semantic character composed of semantic 氵 ('water') + phonetic 骨 (gǔ/huá). Originally denoted smooth, flowing water, then 'slippery, smooth, slick, cunning'.

history.meaning: smooth-flowing; slippery, slick; to slide

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 滑 (via 萌典)

滑出来.etymology: Directional verb compound combining 滑 ('to slide, slip, glide') + 出来 (trad. 出來, compound directional complement 'out toward the speaker').

history.meaning: to slide out; to slip out

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 滑出来 (via 萌典)

滚.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形聲字) combining the water radical 氵(水) with the phonetic 衮 (gǔn, Old Chinese *kˤunʔ, 'imperial ceremonial robe embroidered with curling dragons'). Originally denoting 'water surging, roiling, and bubbling up' (synonymous with 滾滾 gǔngǔn, 'rolling torrents'), it developed the physical sense 'to roll, tumble, trundle' in Middle Chinese and the blunt colloquial imperative sense 'roll away! / get out! / scram!' in vernacular Mandarin.

history.meaning: to surge, roil, or bubble vigorously (of flowing or boiling water)
to roll, trundle, turn over and over along a surface
to roll, boil; (blunt imperative) get out!, get lost!

morphemes.meaning: to roll, boil, surge; (slang) get out (氵water + 衮 phonetic)

滚.notes: As a standalone imperative (滚！'Get out! / Piss off!'), this is harsh and confrontational; in dramas, a boss or character shouting 滚 signals complete loss of temper. In culinary contexts, however, 滚水 simply means 'boiling water'.

rootFamily.gloss: to roll about, tumble; (coll.) get out of here!
get out!, roll out of here!

滚出去.etymology: A directional verb phrase combining the blunt verb 滚 (gǔn, 'to roll; [colloquial] get lost, clear out') with the complex directional complement 出去 (chūqù, 'out and away from the speaker': 出 'to exit, go out' + 去 'to go away from the deictic center'). Literally 'roll out away from here!'.

history.form: 滾 + 出 + 去 (gǔn + chū + qù)
history.meaning: to roll (physically) out and away from an enclosed space
Get out of here! (blunt command ejecting someone from a room or organization)

滚出去.notes: Whereas standalone 滚 means 'get lost / get out of my sight', 滚出去 specifically orders someone out of an enclosed space, office, studio, or company (给我滚出去！'Get the hell out of here!').

rootFamily.gloss: get out! (slightly less vulgar than 滚出去, using 走 'walk/leave')

滚蛋.etymology: A colloquial northern Mandarin verb-object (VO) slang compound combining 滚 (gǔn, 'to roll away, get out') with the dummy/pejorative nominal object 蛋 (dàn, 'egg', which functions in northern Mandarin vulgar and colloquial slang both as a pejorative person-suffix—as in 坏蛋 'bad egg/scoundrel', 笨蛋 'fool'—and as a round object that literally rolls away). Literally 'roll the egg away' -> 'pack off / beat it / scram'.

history.meaning: to roll + egg (pejorative colloquial nominal formative in northern Mandarin)
to get lost, scram, pack off, or be fired unceremoniously

滚蛋.notes: Used both as a direct barked command (滚蛋！'Beat it! / Scram!') and in declarative sentences meaning 'to be sacked/kicked out' (做不好就滚蛋 'If you can't do the job, pack your bags and get out').

满.etymology: Phono-semantic character (trad. 滿) composed of semantic 氵 ('water') + phonetic 㒼 (mǎn, 'even, level'). Originally described a vessel filled to the brim with liquid, extended to 'full, complete, satisfied, whole'.

history.meaning: filled to the brim -> full, complete, whole

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 满 (via 萌典)

满分.etymology: Attributive noun compound combining 满 (trad. 滿, 'full, maximum') + 分 ('score, mark, point, fraction'). Denotes a perfect score on an examination or evaluation.

history.meaning: full marks; a perfect score

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 满分 (via 萌典)

满嘴.etymology: A modifier-head nominal/adverbial compound combining 满 (mǎn, Old Chinese *mˤonʔ, water radical 氵 + 𣦼, originally 'filled to the brim with liquid') and 嘴 (zuǐ, Middle Chinese *tsjweX, mouth radical 口 + 觜 zī 'horn/beak', originally 'bird's beak' before replacing 口 kǒu as the everyday Mandarin word for 'mouth'). Literally 'the whole mouth full of', used both physically (mouthful of food) and metaphorically (mouthful of lies or jargon).

history.meaning: filling the whole mouth; speaking unreservedly or profusely
a mouthful of; (talking) full of (nonsense, lies, excuses, or oil/food)

满嘴.notes: In conversation and drama dialogue, 满嘴 most often introduces disapproving descriptions of someone's speech: 满嘴胡言 ('talking complete nonsense'), 满嘴跑火车 ('shooting one's mouth off with wild boasts/lies'), or 满嘴借口 ('full of excuses').

rootFamily.gloss: mouthful; profusely, unreservedly (more literary counterpart using 口)
all over the face (e.g., 满脸笑容 'all smiles')

满意.etymology: Verb-object compound used adjectivally, combining 满 (trad. 滿, 'to fill, fulfill') + 意 ('wish, intention, mind'). Literally 'to fulfill one's wishes', hence 'satisfied, pleased'.

history.meaning: fulfilling one's wishes -> satisfied, pleased

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 满意 (via 萌典)

满街.etymology: A quantifier-noun compound combining 满 (mǎn, 'full, the entirety of, all over') with 街 (jiē, Old Chinese *kˤre,行 'crossroads/thoroughfare' + phonetic 圭 guī, 'urban street or avenue'). Literally 'filling the entire street', functioning as a locative nominal and adverbial expression meaning 'all over the streets' or 'all over town'.

history.meaning: filling the streets (attested in Tang–Song poetry for blossoms, carriages, or crowds filling the avenues)
all over town, on every street, ubiquitous in public

满街.notes: Often followed by 都是 (dōu shì, 'are everywhere') or expanded into the four-character colloquialism 满大街 (mǎn dàjiē) to emphasize that a trend, rumor, or commodity has become ubiquitous across town.

rootFamily.gloss: all over the main streets, everywhere in town (colloquial expansion)
to stroll the streets, go window-shopping

滴.etymology: Phono-semantic character composed of semantic 氵 ('water') + phonetic 啇 (dī). Denotes both the action 'to drip, trickle' and a single 'drop' of liquid (also used as a classifier for drops).

history.meaning: to drip, trickle; a drop of liquid

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 滴 (via 萌典)

漂亮.etymology: Originally described fabrics rinsed in flowing water (漂, piǎo 'to bleach/rinse') until bright and lustrous (亮, liàng 'bright, shining'). By the Ming–Qing vernacular novels, generalized to 'handsome, pretty, bello/beautiful' and 'splendidly done'.

history.meaning: rinsed bright and lustrous -> pretty, handsome, splendid

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 漂亮 (via 萌典)

漆.etymology: Originally written 桼, a pictograph of a lacquer tree (木) with droplets of sap trickling down its trunk. Later 氵 ('liquid') was added on the left to form 漆, denoting raw tree lacquer and subsequently any paint or coating.

history.meaning: sap of the lacquer tree -> lacquer, paint, varnish

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 漆 (via 萌典)

漏.etymology: Phono-semantic/associative character with semantic 氵 ('water') + 屚 (depicting rain 雨 falling through a roof 尸). Originally meant a roof leaking rain indoors, extended to any fluid leak, water clock (铜漏), or accidental omission.

history.meaning: rain leaking through a roof -> to leak, drip through, omit

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 漏 (via 萌典)

漏水.etymology: Verb-object compound combining 漏 ('to leak, seep through') + 水 ('water').

history.meaning: to leak water; a water leak

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 漏水 (via 萌典)

漏洞.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound combining 漏 (lòu, Old Chinese *N-rˤok-s, water radical 氵 + 尸 'roof' + 雨 'rain falling indoors', originally 'a roof leaking rainwater' or 'water-clock drip') with 洞 (dòng, OC *lˤoŋ-s, 'swift stream; cave, cavity, hole'). Literally 'a leaking hole (in a roof, vessel, or dike)', which evolved metaphorically into a 'flaw in an argument, security vulnerability, or legal/contractual loophole'.

history.meaning: water leaking through a roof + cavity/hole; a physical leak or breach in a vessel or embankment
loophole (in a law or contract), logical flaw, or security vulnerability

漏洞.notes: Essential in corporate, legal, and tech contexts: 法律漏洞 ('legal loophole'), 合同漏洞 ('contractual loophole'), 系统漏洞 ('system vulnerability/bug'), and the idiom 漏洞百出 ('riddled with flaws/plot holes').

rootFamily.gloss: riddled with gaping flaws or loopholes
to leak out, divulge (a secret or information)
gap, opening; loophole to exploit (钻空子)

演.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形聲字) combining the water radical 氵(水) with 寅 (yín, Old Chinese *ɢ(r)jər, 'to stretch out, extend'). In Old Chinese (*N-q(r)janʔ), 演 originally meant 'water flowing far and wide in a long stream' (*Shuowen*: 長流也). From 'flowing out and extending', it shifted in Classical Chinese to 'expound, elaborate, or work out (as hexagrams or doctrines)', then to 'practice martial drills (演武)', and finally to 'perform on stage, act a role'.

history.meaning: (of water) to flow in a long, continuous stream; to extend and elaborate (principles or divination)
to drill, rehearse, or stage a narrative/dramatic performance (演義, 演戲)
to act (a role), perform (on stage or screen), play pretend

morphemes.meaning: to flow out, elaborate, perform, act a role (氵water + 寅 phonetic/semantic)

演.notes: In modern showbiz and everyday speech, 演 means both professional acting (演戏, 演男主角) and colloquially 'putting on an act / faking it' in real life (别演了 'Stop putting on an act!').

rootFamily.gloss: director (of a film, TV show, or stage play)

演出.etymology: A verb-complement compound combining 演 (yǎn, 'to elaborate, stage, perform') with the directional/manifestative complement 出 (chū, 'out, forth, into public view'). Originally meaning 'to deduce or manifest outward', in modern theatre and media it means 'to put on a show, perform publicly (as a verb)' or 'a live show/performance (as a noun)'.

history.meaning: to evolve, deduce, or bring forth into manifestation
to stage a public performance, put on a show; a performance or concert (noun)

演出.notes: Major Sino-Japanese false friend for media professionals: in Mandarin, 演出 means 'to perform on stage / a live performance' (measure word: 一场演出), whereas in Japanese 演出 (*enshutsu*) and Korean 연출 (*yeonchul*) it means 'stage/screen directing and production' (which is 导演 or 执导 in Mandarin).

rootFamily.gloss: to perform, put on a show or demonstration
to play a role, appear in a production (especially in credits)

演变成.etymology: A verb-complement compound combining 演变 (yǎnbiàn, 'to evolve, develop gradually') with the resultative complement 成 (chéng, 'to become, turn into'). 演变 itself is a coordinative compound of 演 (yǎn, originally 'water flowing far and wide', extended in Classical Chinese to 'unfold, deduce, develop over time') and 变 (biàn, 'to change, transform'). Together with 成, the trisyllabic structure expresses how a situation or phenomenon gradually unfolds and transforms into a new state.

history.meaning: to flow out at length and undergo transformation
to evolve or develop gradually over time
to evolve into, to turn gradually into (a resulting state)

演变成.notes: Takes the resulting state or noun phrase directly as its object (e.g., 演变成一场危机, 'evolve into a crisis'), emphasizing a gradual, often unintended escalation.

演员.etymology: A modifier-head compound formed from 演 (yǎn, 'to perform, act out, stage', extended from its earlier sense of 'to practice martial arts or unfold a text') and the personal agentive suffix 员 (yuán, originally a round cauldron in Shang oracle bone script, extended to 'round number, quota', and later 'official, member, personnel'). Coined in the modern era to replace older, often socially disparaging terms for stage performers such as 戏子 (xìzi) or 优伶 (yōulíng) with a neutral professional designation.

history.meaning: to practice/perform + official/member of a roster
stage, film, or television actor; professional performer

morphemes.meaning: person engaged in a profession or member of a group

演员.notes: The standard, respectful umbrella term for actors across theater, film, and television; in colloquial internet slang, calling someone an 演员 ('actor') in daily life or gaming means they are faking or intentionally throwing a match.

rootFamily.gloss: director (of a film or stage play)
cast and crew, performers and staff

演唱.etymology: A coordinative verb compound pairing 演 (yǎn, 'to perform before an audience, enact') and 唱 (chàng, 'to sing, chant, lead in singing'). While 唱 alone refers to the vocal act of singing in any setting, prefixing 演 frames the vocalization specifically as a staged artistic performance delivering both music and dramatic expression to an audience.

history.meaning: to expound/perform and chant aloud (as in Buddhist vernacular storytelling)
to sing in a formal concert or broadcast performance

演唱.notes: Used in formal and showbiz contexts (e.g., 演唱歌曲, 'to perform a song'; 领衔演唱, 'lead vocals'), whereas casual singing is simply 唱歌 (chànggē).

演唱权.etymology: A modifier-head legal and entertainment compound combining 演唱 (yǎnchàng, 'vocal performance, singing in public') with 权 (quán, simplified from 權, originally the yellow-flowered *Mallotus* tree, loaned in Classical Chinese for 'sliding scale weight', whence 'balance, authority, power', and in late nineteenth-century Sino-Japanese legal translations, 'legal right'). It denotes the specific licensed right to perform or record a musical composition vocally.

history.meaning: steelyard weight; leverage, authority, power
legal right or entitlement (via Meiji Japanese 権利)
vocal performance right; legal license to sing a copyrighted song commercially

演唱权.notes: A key music-industry term in television talent shows and pop production, where securing a song's 演唱权 (or 翻唱权, cover rights) is mandatory before broadcast.

演技.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-Japanese compound (wasei-kango 演技, *engi*, popularized in modern Chinese theatrical and cinematic discourse) combining 演 (yǎn, 'to act, perform a role') and 技 (jì, phono-semantic character with hand radical 扌 and phonetic 支, meaning 'manual dexterity, craft, artistry, skill'). It specifically denotes an actor's technical and emotional craft in portraying a character.

history.meaning: to practice/perform + skill, craft, martial or artistic feat
theatrical acting skill, dramatic performance technique
acting skill, dramatic craft (on stage or screen)

演技.notes: Frequently paired with evaluative adjectives like 演技精湛 ('consummately skilled acting') or 演技派 ('method/character actor Known for real acting chops' vs. 偶像派, 'idol star').

rootFamily.gloss: actor known for strong acting skills rather than just looks

演播厅.etymology: A trimorphemic modifier-head compound built from 演播 (yǎnbō, a coordinative compound of 演 'perform, stage' + 播 'broadcast, disseminate', originally 'sow seeds') and the architectural head noun 厅 (tīng, simplified from 廳, a phono-semantic character combining shelter 广 with phonetic 聽 tīng, meaning 'great hall, reception hall, auditorium'). Coined in the twentieth century with the rise of television broadcasting to designate a large studio auditorium capable of seating a live audience.

history.meaning: official hall for hearing cases; large reception hall
large broadcast performance hall or television auditorium

演播厅.notes: Distinguished by scale from 演播室 (yǎnbōshì): an 演播厅 is a spacious auditorium or soundstage used for variety shows, galas, and live audiences, whereas an 演播室 is a smaller enclosed studio room (such as a newsroom set).

演播室.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 演播 (yǎnbō, 'to perform and broadcast', from 演 'perform' + 播 'sow, disseminate, broadcast') with the head noun 室 (shì, 'room, inner chamber', depicting a roof 宀 over the phonetic/semantic component 至 'arrive, reach the innermost point'). Created in modern radio and television terminology to denote an enclosed room acoustically treated and equipped for recording or transmitting broadcasts.

history.meaning: inner chamber of a house; room
radio or television broadcast studio room

演播室.notes: The standard term for a TV news anchor's studio or a talk-show recording room (e.g., 欢迎回到演播室, 'Welcome back to the studio').

rootFamily.gloss: large broadcast hall or soundstage auditorium

演示稿.etymology: A modern modifier-head compound joining 演示 (yǎnshì, a coordinative verb compound of 演 'demonstrate, enact' + 示 'show, display, reveal', originally an altar showing omens from heaven) and 稿 (gǎo, 'grain stalks', extended in Literary Chinese to 'rough draft, manuscript, script'). Formed in the digital office era (often as a clipped form of 演示文稿, the standard Chinese translation for Microsoft PowerPoint 'presentation') to denote a slide deck or presentation script.

history.meaning: dried grain stalks, straw; rough literary draft or manuscript
presentation draft, slide deck, or pitch script

演示稿.notes: Common in corporate and media pitch meetings as the native Chinese equivalent of 'PPT' or 'slide deck', alongside the slightly more formal full term 演示文稿 (yǎnshì wéngǎo).

rootFamily.gloss: demonstrate, give a presentation or demo

演讲稿.etymology: Attributive compound combining 演讲 (trad. 演講, 'public speech, lecture', from 演 'to expound, perform' + 讲 'to speak, explain') + 稿 ('draft, manuscript', originally grain stalks 禾).

history.meaning: written speech draft; lecture manuscript

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 演讲稿 (via 萌典)

漫长.etymology: A coordinative (or descriptive modifier-head) adjective compound combining 漫 (màn, phono-semantic with water radical 氵 and phonetic 曼 màn 'drawn out, extended', originally meaning 'overflowing water spreading boundlessly without banks') and 长 (cháng, 'long in space or time'). The watery boundlessness of 漫 intensifies 长, evoking a spatial expanse or temporal duration that stretches out endlessly without a visible boundary.

history.meaning: overflowing/boundless + long in distance or duration
vast and stretching far (of roads/rivers); long and drawn-out (of time)

morphemes.meaning: boundless, overflowing, stretching far and wide

漫长.notes: Used overwhelmingly for subjective or objective lengths of time and processes (e.g., 漫长的等待, 'an agonizingly long wait'; 漫长的岁月, 'long drawn-out years') rather than physical objects like ropes or sticks.

rootFamily.gloss: boundless, vast and indistinct (of water, night, or snow)

漱.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形声字) combining the semantic water radical 氵 (shuǐ) with the phonetic and co-semantic component 欶 (shuò, Old Chinese *s-rˤok, formed from 束 'bind' and 欠 'open mouth/exhale', meaning 'to suck in, sip'). Attested in the *Shuowen Jiezi* (说文解字) as 盪口也 ('to swish water in the mouth'), it has denoted rinsing out the oral cavity since Warring States and Han ritual texts such as the *Liji* (礼记).

history.meaning: to swish water in the mouth, rinse the mouth; to wash or scour (of streams)
to rinse the mouth, gargle (also poetic: to wash against rocks, as in 漱石)
to rinse out, gargle (chiefly bound in 漱口 or separable 漱漱口)

morphemes.meaning: rinse the mouth, swish liquid, gargle

漱.notes: Most commonly encountered in the separable verb-object compound 漱口 (shùkǒu, 'to rinse one's mouth'), which can be reduplicated or expanded in speech (e.g., 漱一下口 or 漱漱口).

rootFamily.gloss: to wash one's face and rinse one's mouth (morning ablutions)

潜力股.etymology: A modern metaphorical modifier-head compound joining 潜力 (qiánlì, 'latent power, hidden potential', from 潜 'submerged, hidden underwater' + 力 'strength, force') with 股 (gǔ, originally 'thigh, haunch' in Classical Chinese, extended to 'one strand of a rope' or 'one portion/share of a joint enterprise', and in modern finance 'stock share'). Originating on the stock market for an undervalued stock with strong growth prospects, it passed into popular and showbiz slang for an up-and-coming talent or promising romantic partner.

history.meaning: thigh; strand of twisted cord; share in a commercial partnership
stock with high growth potential on the equity market
rising star, promising newcomer, or partner with great future prospects

潜力股.notes: Widely used in both entertainment scouting (describing a rookie actor or trainee bound for stardom) and dating culture (a humble partner who is likely to become successful).

潜水.etymology: A verb-object (or verb-locative) compound formed from 潜 (qián, simplified from 潛, phono-semantic with water radical 氵, originally meaning 'to wade across deep water, to hide beneath the surface, submerge') and 水 (shuǐ, 'water'). Attested in Classical Chinese for swimming or hiding underwater (like fish or dragons), in modern Mandarin it denotes both recreational/technical scuba diving and, in internet slang, 'lurking' silently in group chats or forums without posting.

history.meaning: to swim or conceal oneself beneath the water's surface
underwater diving, scuba diving, or submarine submerging
to lurk in an online forum or chat group without speaking

morphemes.meaning: submerge, dive, hide beneath the surface

潜水.notes: In contemporary Chinese media and workplace group chats, 潜水 ('diving') is the everyday verb for 'lurking' silently while reading messages, contrasted with 冒泡 (màopào, 'bubbling up', i.e., posting a message).

rootFamily.gloss: professional or recreational diver; forum lurker
submerge, hide under cover, go undercover

潜能.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 潜 (qián, 'submerged, hidden beneath the surface, latent') and 能 (néng, originally a pictograph of a bear-like beast in Shang/Zhou bronze inscriptions, loaned early for 'ability, capability, talent, energy'). Originally used in modern scientific translations for 'potential energy' (later standardized in physics as 势能 or 位能), it became established in psychology and everyday usage for untapped human capability.

history.meaning: hidden beneath the surface + ability/capacity
latent energy (physics); untapped innate human capability or potential

潜能.notes: Frequently collocates with verbs of awakening or unlocking, such as 激发潜能 ('spark/stimulate latent potential') or 挖掘潜能 ('tap into hidden potential'); slightly more internal/innate in nuance than 潜力 (qiánlì).

潮湿.etymology: Coordinative adjective compound joining 潮 ('morning tide; dampness rising from the ground') + 湿 (trad. 濕, 'wet, moist').

history.meaning: damp, moist, humid

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 潮湿 (via 萌典)

澄不澄清.etymology: An A-not-AB (A不AB) affirmative-negative interrogative construction built on the disyllabic verb 澄清 (chéngqīng, 'to clarify, clear up', literally 'to settle until clear and pure'). In Mandarin morphosyntax, disyllabic verbs undergoing A-not-A question formation frequently apocopate the first affirmative syllable to avoid repeating the entire word (*澄清不澄清 → 澄不澄清), meaning 'whether or not to clarify' or 'clarify or not?'.

history.meaning: full reduplicated affirmative-negative question: 'to clarify or not to clarify'
contracted A-not-AB interrogative phrase: 'whether (or not) to clarify / clear up'

morphemes.meaning: settle (liquid) until clear (reduplicated first syllable of 澄清)

澄不澄清.notes: Illustrates the productive Mandarin A不AB question pattern (like 喜不喜欢 from 喜欢, or 解不解释 from 解释); in celebrity PR crises, 澄不澄清 ('whether or not to issue a clarification') is a classic strategic dilemma.

rootFamily.gloss: to clarify (facts/rumors); to settle until clear (of water)

cognates.meaning: clarification; purifying turbulent waters or politics
to purify, clarify, settle until clear

澄清.etymology: Originally a verb-resultative (or coordinative) compound combining 澄 (chéng / dèng, phono-semantic with water radical 氵 and phonetic 登, meaning 'still, settled, limpid water') and 清 (qīng, 'clear, pure, unclouded water'). In the *Book of the Later Han* (后汉书·范滂传), Fan Pang famously mounted his carriage grasping the reins with the ambition of 澄清天下 ('settling the muddy waters of the empire until pure'). From restoring political clarity, the metaphor shifted in modern Mandarin to dispelling rumors, misunderstandings, or false accusations.

history.meaning: to cause muddy water to settle and become limpid; figuratively, to purge corruption and bring order to the realm
to allow sediment in liquid to settle until the liquid is clear
to clarify facts, dispel rumors, or clear up a misunderstanding

澄清.notes: Has a literary-colloquial pronunciation split (文白异读): pronounced chéngqīng when meaning 'to clarify a rumor/fact' (e.g., 澄清事实, 发声明澄清), but pronounced dèngqīng when referring literally to letting muddy water or limewater settle.

rootFamily.gloss: whether or not to clarify (A-not-AB interrogative)
crystal clear, limpid (of water or sky)
to clear oneself of suspicion or blame

激动.etymology: Originally a verb-resultative compound combining 激 (jī, phono-semantic with water radical 氵 and 敫, originally 'water dashing violently against rocks or a weir and surging upward', whence 'to stir up, provoke, surge') and 动 (dòng, simplified from 動, 'to move, stir, shake'). In Classical Chinese (such as Wang Chong's *Lunheng*), 激动 literally described wind or water violently buffeting things into motion, before shifting to emotional arousal—having one's feelings surged and stirred up by an external stimulus.

history.meaning: to dash against and set in motion (of surging water, wind, or sound); to stir someone's resolve
emotionally stirred up, agitated, worked up, or deeply excited

morphemes.meaning: surge, dash against, stimulate, stir up (originally: rushing water blocked by rocks)

激动.notes: Unlike English 'excited' (which is almost always positive and maps closer to 兴奋 xīngfèn), 激动 covers any intense emotional surge where composure is lost—whether from joy, gratitude, anger, or agitation (e.g., 你先别激动, 'Calm down / Don't get worked up first').

rootFamily.gloss: fierce, intense, heated (of competition or debate)

激烈.etymology: A coordinative adjective compound uniting two high-intensity hydrodynamic and pyrodynamic metaphors: 激 (jī, 'rushing water dashing violently against an obstruction, surging, vehement') and 烈 (liè, featuring the four-dot fire radical 灬 at the base, originally 'raging fire, blazing heat', extended to 'fierce, vehement, heroic'). Together, water surging over rocks and fire blazing at full force depict acute, uncompromising intensity in conflict, debate, or competition.

history.meaning: vehement,upright and unyielding in speech or temperament; surging and blazing (of wind/water/music)
fierce, intense, acute, heated (of competition, combat, or argument)

morphemes.meaning: surging, dashing violently (like blocked water), vehement

激烈.notes: The standard collocate for high-stakes rivalry or conflict: 竞争激烈 ('fierce competition'), 争论激烈 ('heated debate'), or 战况激烈 ('intense fighting').

rootFamily.gloss: intense, strong, violent (of light, pain, or desire)

灌.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形声字) combining the water radical 氵 (shuǐ) with the phonetic component 雚 (guàn, Old Chinese *kʷˤar-s, depicting a horned owl or heron). Originally referring to the Guan river and the pouring of ceremonial wine libations (cognate with 裸 guàn) or channeling water to irrigate fields, its meaning generalized to pouring liquid forcefully or copiously into a narrow opening, and colloquially to plying someone with alcohol until drunk.

history.meaning: to pour water; to irrigate fields; to pour ritual wine libations
to pour liquid into a vessel or throat; to force-feed liquid; to cast molten metal into a mold
to pour into, irrigate; to ply someone with drinks; to record/burnonto media (as in 灌录)

morphemes.meaning: pour into, irrigate, fill with liquid, ply with alcohol

灌.notes: At Chinese business banquets and entertainment industry dinners, 灌 (or 灌酒, guànjiǔ, 灌醉, guànzuì) specifically means pressuring or tricking someone into drinking heavily; in media production, 灌唱片 means to cut/record an album.

rootFamily.gloss: to ply someone with alcohol, force someone to drink
to instill, indoctrinate, funnel ideas into someone's mind

火.etymology: Pictograph in oracle-bone and bronze inscriptions showing rising flames and sparks. One of the fundamental radicals and Five Phases (五行) of Chinese cosmology.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: fire, flame; heat, anger

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 火 (via 萌典)

火漆.etymology: Literally 'fire-lacquer', combining 火 (huǒ, 'fire, flame') and 漆 (qī, 'natural tree lacquer, resinous varnish'). When shellac-and-rosin sealing wax sticks became widespread in Ming–Qing postal and diplomatic correspondence—replacing ancient clay seals (封泥)—Chinese speakers named the red resinous stick 火漆 because it had to be melted over a candle flame before stamping with a brass signet.

history.meaning: flame-melted resinous sealing wax
