sealing wax (for envelopes and documents)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 火漆

火苗.etymology: Endocentric compound combining 火 ('fire') + 苗 ('young shoot, sprout', picturing grass 艹 growing over a field 田). Likens a flickering tongue of flame to a sprouting shoot.

history.meaning: tongue of flame; flickering small flame

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 火苗 (via 萌典)

火车.etymology: Calque/neologism coined in the 19th century from 火 ('fire, steam-boiler fire') + 车 (trad. 車, 'wheeled vehicle, carriage') to translate the steam-powered railway train (originally 火轮车).

history.stage: Late Qing (19th c.) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: fire/steam vehicle -> railway train

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 火车 (via 萌典)

火车头.etymology: Attributive compound combining 火车 (trad. 火車, 'train') + 头 (trad. 頭, 'head, front, leader'), denoting the railway locomotive that pulls the train.

history.meaning: train head -> railway locomotive

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 火车头 (via 萌典)

火车站.etymology: Compound noun formed from 火车 (trad. 火車, 'train') + 站 ('station, post-horse relay stop').

history.meaning: train station; railway station

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 火车站 (via 萌典)

火锅.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 火 (huǒ, 'fire, live coals') and 锅 (guō, simplified from 鍋, phono-semantic with metal radical 钅/金 and phonetic 咼, meaning 'cooking pot, cauldron, boiler'). Known in earlier classical culinary texts as 古董羹 (gǔdǒnggēng, onomatopoeic for food splashing into boiling broth) or 暖锅 (nuǎnguō, 'warming pot'), 火锅 literally describes a cooking pot kept simmering right at the dining table over an active heat source.

history.meaning: metal pot heated over a charcoal brazier at the table for simmering meats and vegetables in broth
history.stage: Song to Qing Dynasty Vernacular Chinese

history.meaning: hotpot (both the communal simmering pot apparatus and the meal itself); figuratively, a volatile situation

火锅.notes: Beyond being the quintessential Chinese communal meal (commonly eaten by film and TV crews to celebrate wrapping a shoot or welcoming cast members), 吃火锅 is a staple social bonding ritual in contemporary urban culture.

rootFamily.gloss: cooking pot, wok, pan; figuratively 'blame' (in 背锅)
to take the blame for someone else, be a scapegoat (literally: carry the black pot)

灯.etymology: Phono-semantic character (trad. 燈) combining semantic 火 ('fire, flame') + phonetic 登 (dēng, simplified with 丁 dīng). Originally referred to an oil lamp on a stemmed pedestal (豆/登), later generalized to any lamp or electric light.

morphemes.meaning: phonetic component in simplified 灯 (trad. 登)

history.meaning: pedestal oil lamp -> lamp, lantern, light fixture

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 灯 (via 萌典)

灯光.etymology: Attributive noun compound combining 灯 (trad. 燈, 'lamp, light') + 光 ('light, radiance, glow').

history.meaning: lamplight; artificial lighting

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 灯光 (via 萌典)

灯泡.etymology: Metaphorical compound combining 灯 (trad. 燈, 'lamp, electric light') + 泡 ('bubble, blister, bulb-shaped globe'), coined for the glass incandescent light bulb.

history.meaning: light bulb

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 灯泡 (via 萌典)

灯笼.etymology: Attributive compound combining 灯 (trad. 燈, 'lamp') + 笼 (trad. 籠, 'bamboo cage or basket'), originally a bamboo-framed paper or silk enclosure shielding a candle or oil flame from the wind.

history.meaning: lantern (originally bamboo-and-paper enclosed lamp)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 灯笼 (via 萌典)

灯罩.etymology: Attributive compound combining 灯 (trad. 燈, 'lamp') + 罩 ('cover, shade, fish-trap hood'). Refers to a lampshade or glass chimney over a lamp.

history.meaning: lampshade; lamp cover

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 灯罩 (via 萌典)

灰.etymology: Associative compound in oracle-bone and seal script combining 又/𠂇 ('hand') + 火 ('fire'): ash or embers cool enough to be handled or raked by hand. Extended from 'ash, dust, lime' to the color 'gray' and 'disheartened'.

history.meaning: wood ash; dust, lime; gray

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 灰 (via 萌典)

灰尘.etymology: Coordinative noun compound combining 灰 ('ash, fine powder') + 尘 (trad. 塵, 'dust stirred up by running deer 鹿 over earth 土', simplified as 小 + 土 'tiny earth particles').

history.meaning: dust and dirt

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 灰尘 (via 萌典)

灰度.etymology: A modifier-head technical and metaphorical compound formed from 灰 (huī, originally a compound ideograph of a hand 又/𠂇 holding or raking fire 火, meaning 'cold ashes, cinders', whence the color 'ash-grey') and the abstract suffix 度 (dù, 'linear measure, degree, gradation, scale'). Coined in modern optics, photography, and digital imaging to translate 'grayscale' (the graduated luminance steps between pure black and pure white), and subsequently extended to moral ambiguity and phased software rollouts.

history.meaning: wood ash (grey color) + measure/degree
grayscale, luminance gradation between black and white in photography and television engineering
moral/psychological shades of grey (in storytelling/management); canary/phased release (in tech: 灰度测试)

灰度.notes: Used in three distinct modern contexts: (1) visual/broadcast engineering ('grayscale'), (2) drama writing and Huawei-style management philosophy ('shades of grey / moral complexity' vs. black-and-white extremes), and (3) internet product launches (灰度发布, 'canary/phased rollout').

rootFamily.gloss: phased rollout, canary testing (software/media product release)

灰心.etymology: Metaphorical verb-object compound from 灰 ('cold ashes') + 心 ('heart, mind'), alluding to莊子 (Zhuangzi, 《齐物论》 '心固可使如死灰乎' — 'heart like dead ashes'). Shifted from detached equanimity to 'discouraged, disheartened'.

history.meaning: heart like dead ashes -> to lose heart, be discouraged

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 灰心 (via 萌典)

灰浆.etymology: A masonry compound uniting 灰 (huī, 'ash; slaked lime 石灰') and 浆 (jiāng, simplified from 漿, 'thick liquid paste or slurry'). For over two millennia traditional Chinese bricklayers bedded courtyard flagstones and grey bricks in lime mortar (石灰浆, often strengthened with sticky-rice paste), shortened in everyday building craft to 灰浆.

history.meaning: lime-and-sand masonry mortar
mortar (between stones or bricks)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 灰浆

灰色.etymology: Attributive compound combining 灰 ('ash; gray') + 色 ('color').

history.meaning: the color gray; ash-gray

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 灰色 (via 萌典)

灵.etymology: Simplified from 靈, which originally depicted shamans (巫) offering prayers with three mouths (口) beneath falling rain (雨) to summon spirit power (Middle Chinese *leng*). From 'numinous; efficacious (of prayers or medicine)', 灵 developed the everyday vernacular senses of 'nimble, responsive, quick-witted, and working smoothly'.

history.meaning: numinous spirit; efficacious
clever; nimble; effective (of medicine or tools)
nimble; flexible; working well

灾害.etymology: A coordinative noun compound pairing 灾 (zāi, simplified from 災/烖, a classical ideograph placing a roof 宀 or blocked river 巛 over fire 火, representing a house fire or flood—nature's primary calamities) and 害 (hài, 'harm, injury, damage, affliction'). Attested since the *Xunzi* (荀子) and *Rites of Zhou* (周礼), it specifically links a natural or external catastrophe (灾) with the tangible harm and destruction (害) it inflicts on human livelihoods.

history.meaning: calamity sent by heaven/nature (flood, drought, fire, pestilence) and the resulting harm to crops and people
disaster, calamity (especially natural, meteorological, or geological hazards)

morphemes.meaning: calamity, natural disaster (originally: fire under a roof or blocked floodwater)

灾害.notes: More formal and administrative than 灾难 (zāinàn), 灾害 is the standard term in meteorology, insurance, and government relief (e.g., 自然灾害, 'natural disasters'; 次生灾害, 'secondary disasters').

rootFamily.gloss: disaster conditions, extent of a calamity
people affected by a disaster, disaster victims

cognates.meaning: disaster situation, conditions in a disaster area

灾情.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 灾 (zāi, 'disaster, calamity, flood or fire') with 情 (qíng, phono-semantic with heart radical 忄 and phonetic 青, originally 'genuine inner feelings', extended in administrative and military prose since the Classical era to 'the actual facts, circumstances, or conditions of a situation', as in 敌情 'enemy situation' or 病情 'patient's condition'). It denotes the real-time severity, scope, and unfolding conditions of a disaster.

history.meaning: disaster/famine + actual circumstances on the ground (in imperial famine-relief memorials)
disaster conditions, severity and status of an emergency situation

morphemes.meaning: situation, actual conditions, state of affairs

灾情.notes: A staple of news broadcasting and emergency management (e.g., 汇报灾情, 'report on the disaster conditions'; 灾情严重, 'the disaster situation is severe').

灾难.etymology: A coordinative noun compound uniting 灾 (zāi, 'natural calamity, conflagration, flood') and 难 (nàn, in the falling tone *nàn*, meaning 'distress, tribulation, adversity, catastrophe', derived from the level-tone adjective nán 'difficult, hard to endure'). Attested in early Buddhist translations and Six Dynasties histories, the compound pairs external catastrophe (灾) with human suffering and tribulation (难).

history.meaning: karmic or worldly tribulations, calamities, and suffering (in early Buddhist scriptures and dynastic histories)
history.stage: Middle Chinese / Six Dynasties to Tang

history.meaning: catastrophe, major disaster (natural, historical, or figurative)

灾难.notes: Note the fourth-tone pronunciation of the second character (zāinàn, not *zāinán): whenever 难 means 'disaster/suffering/refugee' (as in 灾难, 遇难, 难民), it is read in the falling tone nàn. Unlike 灾害, 灾难 is freely used figuratively in media for a 'total fiasco' or 'trainwreck' (e.g., 这场演出简直是一场灾难).

灾难性.etymology: A derived attributive adjective/noun formed by affixing the nature/quality suffix -性 (-xìng, originally 'innate human nature, disposition', repurposed in late nineteenth- and twentieth-century Sino-Japanese and Mandarin translation as an equivalent to English '-ic', '-ous', '-ive', or '-ity') to the noun 灾难 (zāinàn, 'catastrophe, disaster'). It functions as a non-gradable modifier meaning 'catastrophic in nature' or 'having the proportions of a disaster'.

history.meaning: inborn nature, inherent disposition (from 心 'heart' + 生 'born/grow')
suffix forming abstract nouns and attributive modifiers denoting a property or quality
disastrous, catastrophic (in scale or consequence)

灾难性.notes: Used primarily as an attributive modifier before a noun (with or without 的), especially in phrases like 灾难性的后果 ('catastrophic consequences') or 灾难性的失误 ('a disastrous blunder').

炉子.etymology: Derived from 炉 ('brazier; stove; hearth; furnace', fire radical 火 + 卢 lú 'vessel') + nominal suffix 子 (zi). In modern households and cafés, 炉子 refers to the kitchen cooking stove or range.

history.meaning: brazier; stove; censer
kitchen stove; burner

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 炉子

炉架.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 炉架. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 炉架 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 炉架 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 炉架 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 炉架. The etymology of 炉架 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 炉架
middle form of 炉架
modern form of 炉架

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 炉架

cognates.meaning: to stir-fry, sauté (also native loan xào)

炒.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形声字) combining the semantic fire radical 火 (huǒ) with the phonetic 少 (shǎo, Old Chinese *s-tʰewʔ); attested in earlier orthography in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as 𦏁 (with 刍). Originally meaning 'to dry-roast or parch grain in a pan while stirring continuously', it became the core verb for Chinese wok stir-frying. In late twentieth-century Cantonese and Mandarin, the image of tossing ingredients rapidly over high heat to inflate volume and aroma gave rise to the vivid metaphors of 'speculating to drive up prices' (炒股, 炒房) and 'whipping up media hype' (炒新闻, 炒热度).

history.meaning: to parch or roast grain over fire; to stir-fry rapidly in a heated cauldron or wok
to speculate on assets by rapid buying and selling (炒卖); to fire an employee ('stir-fry squid', 炒鱿鱼)
to hype up, stir publicity, manufacture buzz around a topic or celebrity

morphemes.meaning: stir-fry over high heat; speculate financially; whip up publicity/hype

炒.notes: One of modern Mandarin's most versatile culinary metaphors: besides cooking (炒菜, 'stir-fry dishes'), it gives 炒股 ('trade/speculate in stocks'), 炒鱿鱼 ('fire someone', because squid curls up when stir-fried like a worker rolling up their bedding to leave), and 炒话题 / 炒CP ('hype up a trending topic or celebrity couple').

rootFamily.gloss: to rehash old news or stale topics (literally: stir-fry leftover cold rice)

炒作.etymology: A verb-verb / verbal-noun compound formed from the metaphorical sense of 炒 (chǎo, literally 'to toss and stir-fry over a high flame', extended to 'artificially heating up attention or prices') and 作 (zuò, 'to make, do, contrive, stage', as in 操作 'manipulate/operate' or 做作 'put on an act'). Emerging in Hong Kong, Taiwan, and Mainland financial and entertainment journalism in the late 1980s and 1990s, it shifted from market speculation ('manipulating prices upward') to showbiz PR ('manufacturing media hype or sensationalism').

history.meaning: to stir-fry over high heat + to contrive/operate
to drive up asset or stock prices through coordinated speculative trading and rumor-mongering
media hype, publicity stunt, artificially engineered buzz or sensationalism

morphemes.meaning: stir-fry over high heat; whip up attention or prices

炒作.notes: Carries a distinctly cynical or critical undertone in Chinese entertainment circles, implying that a scandal, romance rumor, or trending hashtag was deliberately staged or inflated for traffic (e.g., 恶意炒作, 'malicious hype'; 自我炒作, 'self-promotion stunt').

炒蛋.etymology: Verb-object/attributive culinary term combining 炒 ('to stir-fry, sauté in a pan', from 火 'fire' + 少 phonetic) + 蛋 ('egg').

history.meaning: scrambled eggs; stir-fried eggs

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 炒蛋 (via 萌典)

炭笔.etymology: A determinative art-supply compound pairing 炭 (tàn, 'charcoal', depicting mountain cliff/kiln timber 山/厂 burned over fire 火) and 笔 (bǐ, simplified from 筆, 'writing brush, pen, drawing stick', crowned with bamboo 竹). Made by charring slender willow or vine twigs without oxygen, 炭笔 is the classic medium for quick portrait sketches (炭笔素描).

history.meaning: vine or willow charcoal stick/pencil for sketching
charcoal pencil; drawing charcoal

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 炭笔

炮灰.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 炮 (pào, originally written 礮 with the stone radical 石 for ancient trebuchets/catapults, rewritten with the fire radical 火 after the invention of gunpowder artillery for 'cannon, artillery piece') and 灰 (huī, 'ashes, cinders'). Coined in modern Chinese military and political discourse as a semantic translation and adaptation of the European idiom 'cannon fodder' (German *Kanonenfutter*, French *chair à canon*, coined by Chateaubriand in 1814), replacing 'flesh/fodder' with the vivid Chinese image of soldiers reduced to ashes by artillery fire.

history.meaning: artillery cannon + ashes left by fire
cannon fodder; rank-and-file soldiers sacrificed as expendable pawns in war (adapting European 'cannon fodder')
expendable pawn, sacrificial lamb, or minor contestant/character eliminated early to prop up the stars

炮灰.notes: Ubiquitous in television reality shows, office politics, and drama tropes (where 炮灰角色 or 炮灰女配 refers to a disposable supporting character or contestant used purely as a stepping stone or ratings foil for the protagonist).

rootFamily.gloss: artillery fire, gunfire; figuratively 'fierce public criticism'
to bombard, verbally attack or roast someone publicly
ashes, dust; completely wiped out (in 灰飞烟灭)

炸毛.etymology: A colloquial verb-object compound (V-O structure) combining 炸 (zhà, 'to explode, burst out, puff up or flare outward', originally a vernacular graphic derivative of 煠 meaning 'deep-fry in boiling oil' before acquiring the sense of 'explode/burst') and 毛 (máo, 'fur, hair, feathers'). Literally describing how a startled or furious cat, dog, or bird makes its fur or feathers puff straight out in every direction to appear larger, it passed from northern Mandarin dialect into nationwide slang for 'bristling with sudden anger or panic' and 'freaking out'.

history.meaning: to burst/flare outward + animal fur or bird feathers (when startled or defensive)
to bristle, fly into a tizzy, freak out, or lose one's cool when provoked or teased

morphemes.meaning: explode, burst outward, puff up, flare up

炸毛.notes: Because it evokes the image of a puffed-up kitten, 炸毛 usually describes a sudden, flustered, slightly reactive or endearing outburst (e.g., being teased on a variety show or caught off guard) rather than terrifying, cold rage; can also literally describe frizzy, static-blown hair.

rootFamily.gloss: explode, blow up (literally or in temper); go viral
fly into a rage, blow one's top (harsher than 炸毛)
anxious, flustered, impatient (literally: hair on fire)

点.etymology: Phono-semantic character (trad. 點) combining semantic 黑 ('black soot/ink') + phonetic 占 (zhān/diǎn). Originally a small black fleck or ink dot, extended to 'drop, spot, o'clock, to kindle, to nod, and a little bit (classifier)'.

history.meaning: black dot, speck -> point, drop, a bit, to light/tap

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 点 (via 萌典)

点儿.etymology: Rhotacized colloquial form of 点 (trad. 點兒, diǎnr), combining 点 ('dot, small amount') + diminutive suffix 儿 (兒). Used after 一 or verbs/adjectives to mean 'a little bit'.

history.stage: Ming–Qing Beijing Mandarin to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: a little bit; a tiny amount

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 点儿 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to call the roll, call by name

点名.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound formed from 点 (diǎn, simplified from 點, phono-semantic with黑 'black' and 占 zhān, originally 'a small black ink dot', whence the verb 'to mark with a brush dot on a register, to check off one by one, to single out') and 名 (míng, 'personal name'). Originating in imperial military and bureaucratic administration, where an officer checked off soldiers' or corvée laborers' names on a roster with a dab of vermilion ink, it evolved to mean both 'taking roll call' and 'singling someone out by name for praise, criticism, or a task'.

history.meaning: to check off names on a muster roll with an ink dot; to call the roll
history.stage: Tang-Song to Ming-Qing Vernacular & Administrative Chinese

history.meaning: to take attendance; to single someone out by name (for a task, praise, or public criticism)

morphemes.meaning: dot with ink, check off on a list, single out, designate
name, personal appellation on a roster

点名.notes: functions both as a separable verb-object compound (e.g., 点了他的名, 'called his name specifically') and directly before a verb phrase as an adverbial meaning 'by specific request' (e.g., 导演点名要他出演, 'the director specifically asked for him by name to star in it'; 被点名批评, 'be singled out by name for criticism').

rootFamily.gloss: critique, comment on key points (by a judge or mentor)
count and check items one by one, take inventory

点头.etymology: Verb-object compound combining 点 (trad. 點, 'to dip downward lightly like dotting with a brush') + 头 (trad. 頭, 'head'), meaning 'to nod one's head' in greeting or agreement.

history.meaning: to nod one's head (in assent or greeting)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 点头 (via 萌典)

点心.etymology: Idiomatic culinary compound literally meaning 'touch (点) the heart (心) lightly'. Attested since the Tang dynasty (*Nenggaizhai Manlu*), where a small morning or afternoon pastry was said to 'lightly touch the heart' before a full meal; the neutral tone on *xin* marks its lexicalized everyday noun status.

history.meaning: light cakes or pastries taken with tea to 'touch the heart'
pastry; light refreshment; dim sum

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 点心

cognates.meaning: commentary, critical review of specific points

点评.etymology: A coordinative compound derived from the traditional Chinese philological and literary practice of 评点 (píngdiǎn): combining 点 (diǎn, 'to mark key passages of a text with brush dots and circles—圈点—to highlight structural or stylistic merits') and 评 (píng, 'to evaluate, judge, write marginal critical commentary—批注'). Popularized by Song, Ming, and Qing literary critics (such as Jin Shengtan's famous annotated editions of classic novels and drama), 点评 shifted in modern media and television talent shows to mean an expert's or judge's focused, point-by-point critique of a performance.

history.form: 評點 / 點評 (点评) — literary criticism
history.meaning: to punctuate a text with brush dots (点) and write marginal critical evaluations (评) on its artistry
history.stage: Song to Qing Dynasty Literary Criticism

history.meaning: incisive commentary, review, or judge's critique on a performance, work, or event (noun and verb)

morphemes.meaning: mark with brush dots, pinpoint key details, highlight

点评.notes: An essential term in Chinese talent competitions, variety shows, and film/food reviews (e.g., 导师点评, 'mentor's critique'; 精彩点评, 'incisive commentary'), where judges pinpoint specific strengths and flaws immediately after a stage performance.

rootFamily.gloss: put the finishing touch on; get right to the heart of the matter (literally: dot the painted dragon's eyes)

点酒.etymology: Verb-object (VO) compound formed from 点 (trad. 點, diǎn, originally "black speck, dot", later "to mark with a dot on a register or menu" and hence "to select, order") and 酒 (jiǔ, "fermented grain beverage, alcohol", depicting a jar 酉 with liquid 氵). Beginning in Tang–Song urban tavern culture, patrons or waiters ticked items on a menu board or tally with a brush dot, giving rise to the commercial sense "to order drinks."

history.meaning: to place a brush dot; fermented millet or rice liquor
to select or prepare tea and wine in taverns and teahouses
to order alcoholic beverages at a bar, club, or restaurant

morphemes.meaning: to dot, check off, select, order (from a menu)

点酒.notes: Separable verb-object (离合词) compound: modifiers and aspect markers insert between the characters, e.g., 点了三瓶酒 ("ordered three bottles of alcohol").

rootFamily.gloss: to order food from a menu
to order tea; light refreshments, dim sum

点钟.etymology: Time-telling compound of 点 ('point on a clock dial; stroke on a gong marking the hour') + 钟 ('bell; mechanical clock', metal radical 钅 + 中 zhōng). Placed after a number (六点钟 'six o'clock'), it is the full spoken form corresponding to shorter 点.

history.meaning: o'clock (hour struck on a clock)
o'clock

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 点钟

烂.etymology: Phono-semantic compound (形聲): semantic 火 ("fire") + phonetic 蘭 (trad. 蘭, lán, OC *g·raːn). In the *Shuowen Jiezi*, 爛 (originally also written 燘) meant "cooked thoroughly over fire until tender or mushy" (熟也). From overcooked food softening and disintegrating, the sense extended in Middle and early Mandarin to organic decay ("rotten, putrid"), physical ragging ("tattered, smashed"), and colloquial evaluative senses ("lousy, chaotic, messy").

history.meaning: thoroughly cooked over fire; brightly gleaming, resplendent
overripe, decayed, tattered, decomposed into pulp
rotten, mushy; messy, chaotic, of abysmal quality

烂.notes: Highly productive in colloquial and entertainment slang as an evaluative adjective or prefix meaning "trashy, botched, chaotic" (e.g., 烂片 "terrible movie", 烂摊子 "unholy mess").

rootFamily.gloss: resplendent, brilliant (preserving the ancient 'bright fire' sense)

烂事.etymology: Modifier-head (偏正) compound combining the colloquial evaluative adjective 烂 (trad. 爛, làn, "rotten, botched, sordid, messy", evolved from "overcooked until falling apart") and the head noun 事 (shì, "affair, matter, business", originally a hand holding a hunting or scribal tally in oracle bone script). Coalesced in vernacular Mandarin to denote a sordid, tangled, or thankless predicament.

history.meaning: thoroughly cooked / decayed + court or public affair
trivial, botched, or disreputable trouble
rotten mess, sordid drama, thankless hassle

烂事.notes: Often takes the retroflex diminutive suffix 儿 in Northern Mandarin (烂事儿 lànshìr) and frequently collocates with 摊上 ("to get saddled with") or 一堆 ("a whole pile of").

rootFamily.gloss: shambles, unholy mess left behind to clean up

烈酒.etymology: Modifier-head (偏正) compound formed from 烈 (liè, "blazing, fierce, intense", containing the fire bottom radical 灬/火 and phonetic 列 liè, originally describing roaring flames) modifying 酒 (jiǔ, "alcoholic beverage"). Originally used in Tang–Song poetry to describe potent fermented or newly distilled beverages that burn the throat like fire, and standardized in modern Chinese for high-proof distilled spirits.

history.meaning: blazing fire, fierce intensity + grain wine
potent, fiery wine or distilled liquor
hard liquor, high-proof distilled spirits (whisky, baijiu, vodka)

烈酒.notes: Contrasts with 低度酒 (low-alcohol drinks) or 甜酒 (sweet liqueurs); in drama scripts, ordering 烈酒 at a bar typically signals a character's emotional turmoil or recklessness.

烘烤.etymology: A coordinate dual-verb culinary compound uniting 烘 (hōng, 'to warm or dry gently by radiant heat', fire radical 火 + phonetic 共) and 烤 (kǎo, 'to roast or bake at high heat', fire radical 火 + phonetic 考). While 烤 alone is the everyday spoken verb, disyllabic 烘烤 specifically evokes even, enclosed oven heat for breads, cakes, and roasted nuts.

morphemes.meaning: warm or dry with radiant heat

history.meaning: dry-warm + roast by fire
bake evenly in an oven; roast

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 烘烤

烤.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining semantic 火 ('fire') + phonetic 考 (kǎo). Appears in Ming–Qing vernacular for roasting, baking, or toasting food (or warming oneself) beside a fire.

history.meaning: to roast, bake, toast, or warm by fire

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 烤 (via 萌典)

烤盘.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 烤盘. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 烤盘 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 烤盘 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 烤盘 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 烤盘. The etymology of 烤盘 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 烤盘
middle form of 烤盘
modern form of 烤盘

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 烤盘

烤箱.etymology: Attributive compound combining 烤 ('to bake, roast') + 箱 ('box, chest, cabinet'), coined in modern Mandarin for a kitchen baking oven.

history.meaning: oven; baking oven

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 烤箱 (via 萌典)

烦.etymology: Ideogrammic and phono-semantic compound (會意兼形聲): 火 ("fire, feverish heat") + 頁 (trad. 頁, yè, originally depicting a human head 首 atop a kneeling body). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines 煩 (OC *[b]ar) as 熱頭痛也 ("feverish headache"). From the physical sensation of a hot, throbbing head, its meaning shifted already in Warring States and Han prose to mental agitation, vexation, overcomplication, and feeling bothered or fed up.

history.meaning: feverish headache; heat pain in the head
mentally agitated, vexed, overburdened with numerous details
annoyed, bothered, sick and tired of; to pester or trouble someone

morphemes.meaning: human head (classical sense of 页/頁)

烦.notes: Functions both as a stative verb/adjective ("I'm annoyed": 我很烦) and a transitive verb ("Stop bugging me": 别烦我), as well as in the polite formula 麻烦你 ("sorry to trouble you").

rootFamily.gloss: troublesome, inconvenient; to bother someone politely
fed up with, sick and tired of

烦心事.etymology: Three-character nominal compound from 烦心 (trad. 煩心, 'to vex or trouble the mind', from 烦 'feverish headache, vexed' + 心 'heart/mind') + 事 ('matter, affair').

history.meaning: worrisome matter; something that troubles the mind

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 烦心事 (via 萌典)

烦恼.etymology: Coordinative (聯合) compound of two near-synonyms: 烦 (trad. 煩, fán, "feverish headache, mental agitation") and 恼 (trad. 惱, nǎo, "vexed, distressed", composed of the heart radical 忄 and phonetic 𡿺, cognate with 腦 "brain/head"). While both characters existed in native Chinese, the compound 煩惱 was popularized through Six Dynasties and Tang Buddhist translations (such as Kumārajīva's works) as the standard rendering of Sanskrit *kleśa* ("mental afflictions or defilements that cloud the mind"), before secularizing into everyday worries and troubles.

history.meaning: mental defilements and passions (greed, anger, delusion) that bind beings to samsara
emotional distress, heartache, vexation in vernacular fiction and poetry
everyday worries, anxieties, troubles; to feel worried or troubled

烦恼.notes: Retains a slightly more reflective or emotional register than plain 烦; commonly used as a countable noun with 自寻烦恼 ("to bring troubles upon oneself").

烦死.etymology: Resultative / degree-complement (述補) compound combining the verb/adjective 烦 (trad. 煩, fán, "to annoy, pester; annoyed") with the extreme degree complement 死 (sǐ, literally "to die", attested since Tang–Song vernacular as a hyperbole marker meaning "to death, to the extreme"). The construction expresses either that an external nuisance pesters someone beyond endurance or that the speaker is exasperated to the limit.

history.meaning: to vex / feel feverish + to die literally
to vex someone to death (colloquial hyperbole in drama and fiction)
to pester to death, annoy no end; exasperated beyond belief

morphemes.meaning: to annoy, pester; annoyed, fed up
to death (hyperbolic complement of extreme degree)

烦死.notes: Almost always followed by the modal particle 了 and/or an object pronoun: 烦死了 ("So annoying!") or 烦死人了 ("It drives people crazy!").

烧.etymology: Phono-semantic character (trad. 燒) composed of semantic 火 ('fire') + phonetic 尧 (堯, yáo/shāo). Originally meant to burn wild grass or timber, then generalized to burning, cooking/braising, and running a fever.

history.meaning: to burn; to roast/braise/boil; to run a fever

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 烧 (via 萌典)

烫.etymology: Associative/phono-semantic character (trad. 燙) composed of 汤 (湯, 'boiling water', serving as both meaning and phonetic tàng) + 火 ('fire'). Means 'scalding hot to the touch' or 'to scald, iron clothes, perm hair'.

history.meaning: scalding hot; to scald, heat in hot water, or iron

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 烫 (via 萌典)

热.etymology: Phono-semantic/associative character (trad. 熱) combining semantic 灬 (火, 'fire') + 埶 (yì, a kneeling person planting a seedling, phonetic *ŋjed). Denotes high temperature, heat, fervor, or to heat up.

history.meaning: hot; heat; fervent; to heat up

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 热 (via 萌典)

热乎乎.etymology: ABB-pattern vivid adjective formed from 热 (trad. 熱, 'warm, hot') + reduplicated suffix 乎乎, expressing a comforting, freshly heated warmth to the touch.

history.meaning: nice and warm; piping warm

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 热乎乎 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to warm up the venue or audience

热场.etymology: Verb-object (VO) compound formed from 热 (trad. 熱, rè, "hot; to heat up", with the fire radical 灬 at the base) used causatively ("to warm up, liven up") and 场 (trad. 場, chǎng, "ritual clearing, stage, performance venue, atmosphere", composed of earth 土 and phonetic 昜 yáng). Emerging from modern live theater, variety television, and concert production jargon, it parallels English "warm up the crowd/house" by treating audience energy as ambient temperature.

history.meaning: hot, to heat + leveled earthen altar or threshing ground
to liven up a theatrical stage or banquet gathering
to warm up the audience or atmosphere ahead of a live broadcast or show

morphemes.meaning: to heat up, warm up, make lively (causative use of 'hot')

热场.notes: Core TV-production vocabulary in *Behind the Scenes* (*幕后之王*): synonymous with 暖场 (nuǎnchǎng) and directly opposite to 冷场 (lěngchǎng, "awkward silence, dead air on stage").

rootFamily.gloss: to warm up a crowd or event; opening act
awkward silence, dead air at a show or party
to wrap up or salvage a situation/show

cognates.meaning: degree of heat, temperature; enthusiasm, feverishness

热度.etymology: Modifier-head (偏正) Sino-compound combining 热 (trad. 熱, rè, "heat, hot") and the abstract measure suffix 度 (dù, "degree, extent, standard of measurement", originally depicting a hand 又 measuring across a span). Coined in late 19th- and early 20th-century scientific terminology (alongside Japanese *netsudo*) to mean physical temperature or thermal intensity, and metaphorically extended in digital-era Chinese media to quantify viral buzz, search volume, and public attention.

history.meaning: physical heat + linear measurement or legal standard
degree of physical heat, temperature; level of emotional fervor
media buzz, viral popularity index, public attention level (as well as physical heat)

热度.notes: In entertainment PR and social media, 蹭热度 (cèng rèdù, literally "rub against the heat") is the standard idiom for "clout-chasing" or piggybacking on a trending topic or celebrity.

rootFamily.gloss: to clout-chase, piggyback on trending buzz

热情.etymology: Modifier-head (偏正) compound joining 热 (trad. 熱, rè, "hot, fervent, ardent") and 情 (qíng, "innate feeling, emotion, disposition", phono-semantic with heart 忄 and phonetic 青 qīng). Popularized across the East Asian Sinosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries (reinforced by Japanese *netsujō*, translating Western "enthusiasm" and "ardor") to conceptualise emotional warmth and hospitable zeal via the universal metaphor of internal heat.

history.meaning: hot, burning + genuine human emotion or disposition

history.form: 熱情 (Japanese netsujō / early modern Chinese)
history.meaning: passionate sentiment, ardent zeal (translating Western 'enthusiasm / passion')
enthusiastic, warm, hospitable (adjective); enthusiasm, passion (noun)

热情.notes: Unlike English "passionate" (which often implies romantic or erotic intensity, 激情), 热情 frequently describes everyday social warmth, hospitality toward guests, or civic enthusiasm.

热搜榜.etymology: Three-morpheme nested modifier-head (偏正) compound coined in 21st-century Chinese internet culture: 热搜 (rèsōu, contraction of 热门搜索 "hot/trending search", from 热 "hot/popular" + 搜 "to search, seek out") modifying the head noun 榜 (bǎng, "public placard, roll of successful imperial examination candidates, leaderboard", composed of wood 木 and phonetic 旁 páng). It bridges imperial-era public honor rolls (金榜) with real-time algorithmic social-media rankings.

history.meaning: wooden placard posted publicly to announce imperial exam graduates or edicts
ranking chart (music/box office) +热门搜索 (popular internet search queries)
real-time trending-search chart on platforms like Weibo or Baidu

morphemes.meaning: public roll, placard, ranking chart, leaderboard

热搜榜.notes: In Chinese entertainment PR, 上热搜 ("make the trending chart"), 买热搜 ("buy a trending slot"), and 撤热搜 ("pull/suppress a trending topic") are central plot devices in showbiz dramas.

rootFamily.gloss: imperial exam honor roll; prestigious list

热文.etymology: Modifier-head (偏正) compound formed in the mobile-internet era by contracting 热门文章 (rèmén wénzhāng, "popular/trending article") into 热 (trad. 熱, rè, "hot, viral, trending") + 文 (wén, "written text, essay, article", originally a pictograph of a standing figure with tattooed or painted chest markings). Popularized via WeChat Official Accounts (微信公众号) and Weibo feeds for articles achieving massive readership and shares.

history.meaning: criss-cross pattern, tattoo, ornate refinement; written graph or text
popular or widely read newspaper/magazine article
viral online article, trending blog or social-media post (often 100k+ views)

morphemes.meaning: writing, article, essay, post (short for 文章)

热文.notes: Often contrasted with 爽文 ("feel-good wish-fulfillment fiction") or 软文 ("soft-sell advertorial article") in digital publishing and PR agencies.

热水.etymology: Attributive compound combining 热 (trad. 熱, 'hot') + 水 ('water').

history.meaning: hot water

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 热水 (via 萌典)

热水器.etymology: Three-character compound combining 热水 (trad. 熱水, 'hot water') + 器 ('appliance, vessel, apparatus'), referring to a domestic water heater.

history.meaning: water heater

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 热水器 (via 萌典)

热水管.etymology: Three-character compound combining 热水 (trad. 熱水, 'hot water') + 管 ('pipe, tube, originally bamboo pipe').

history.meaning: hot-water pipe

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 热水管 (via 萌典)

热汤.etymology: Attributive phrase combining 热 (trad. 熱, 'hot') + 汤 (trad. 湯, 'soup, broth', originally 'hot/boiling water' in Classical Chinese).

history.meaning: hot soup; hot broth

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 热汤 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: hot topic, Wi-Fi hotspot, focal point

热点.etymology: Modifier-head (偏正) compound of 热 (trad. 熱, rè, "hot, intense") + 点 (trad. 點, diǎn, "point, spot, locus"), functioning in modern Mandarin partly as a semantic loan (calque) of English "hot spot." Initially used in physics and geology (a localized point of intense heat or volcanic activity) and Cold War journalism (geopolitical flashpoint), it expanded in media and tech to mean both a "trending news topic / focal point of public interest" and a "Wi-Fi hotspot."

history.meaning: heat / hot + black dot or point
localized point of thermal concentration; geopolitical conflict zone or focal issue
trending news story, hot topic of public debate; mobile Wi-Fi hotspot

热点.notes: Dual modern usage worth remembering: in journalism/PR, 追热点 means "chasing trending news cycles," whereas on a smartphone, 开热点 means "turning on a personal Wi-Fi hotspot."

rootFamily.gloss: focal point, center of attention, focus
bright spot, highlight (of a show or report)

热烈.etymology: Coordinative (聯合) compound uniting two characters sharing the four-dot fire radical (灬, derived from 火): 热 (trad. 熱, rè, "hot, fervent") and 烈 (liè, "blazing, fierce, intense"). Attested in Classical Chinese (e.g., *Zhuangzi* and Han dynasty texts) in the literal sense of "scorching, fiercely blazing fire or sunlight," before shifting in modern Sino-Japanese and Mandarin into an adjective for exuberant, demonstratively warm public atmosphere or applause.

history.meaning: scorching hot, fiercely blazing (of fire, drought, or summer heat)
ardent, vehement, emotionally fervent in public speech and ceremony
warm, enthusiastic, exuberant, spirited (of applause, welcome, or discussion)

热烈.notes: Key distinction from 热情: 热情 describes a person's inner disposition or hospitality toward others (他很热情), whereas 热烈 describes the external atmosphere, applause, or collective response (掌声热烈, 热烈欢迎).

rootFamily.gloss: intense, fierce, violent (of motion or conflict)
warm and lively, bustling with noise and excitement
strong, intense, powerful (of feelings or light)

cognates.meaning: to love ardently, be devoted to

热爱.etymology: Modifier-head (偏正) verbal compound combining 热 (trad. 熱, rè, "hot, ardent, fervent", functioning adverbially as "ardently, passionately") with the head verb 爱 (trad. 愛, ài, "to love, cherish", originally written in bronze and seal script with a heart 心 inside a figure looking back 旡 and walking 夊, conveying lingering affection). Shared across modern East Asian languages to express wholehearted devotion to a calling, art, life, or country.

history.meaning: burning heat + lingering heart-affection, fondness
passionate love or ardent devotion (to ideals, nation, or a partner)
to love deeply, have ardent passion for (a profession, art, life, or homeland)

热爱.notes: False-friend alert inside the Sinosphere: in Japanese (熱愛) and Korean (열애), this compound usually means a celebrity's steamy romantic affair, whereas in Mandarin 热爱 takes abstract or noble objects like 舞台 ("the stage"), 音乐 ("music"), or 生活 ("life").

rootFamily.gloss: to adore, dote on, love fondly

热腾腾.etymology: Vivid ABB adjective formed from 热 ('hot', fire radical 灬 at the base) + reduplicated 腾腾 ('rising upwards like galloping vapour or steam', horse radical 马 + 朕). It evokes the visible clouds of fragrant steam rising from freshly baked bread or hot soup.

history.meaning: steaming hot; piping hot
piping hot; steaming hot

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 热腾腾

热身.etymology: Verb-object compound combining 热 (trad. 熱, 'to warm up') + 身 ('body'), a modern athletic term (calqued in part alongside English 'warm up') for limbering up the body before exercise or performance.

history.meaning: to warm up (before exercise or an event)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 热身 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: popular, in high demand, odds-on favorite

热门.etymology: Modifier-head (偏正) compound from 热 (trad. 熱, rè, "hot, bustling with visitors") and 门 (trad. 門, mén, originally "double-leaf gate of a household", extended to "noble house, school of thought, specialty, category"). Derived from traditional Chinese idioms contrasting a powerful household whose gate is crowded with visitors (门庭若市, 炙手可热) against a neglected gate where one can net sparrows (门可罗雀), 热门 lexicalized to mean any field, commodity, or candidate attracting intense public demand.

history.form: 熱 + 門 (cf. 門庭若市)
history.meaning: hot, bustling + household gate crowded with petitioners and guests
influential, much-frequented household or trade vs. neglected specialty
popular, trending, in high demand; front-runner or favorite in a competition

热门.notes: Directly paired with its antonym 冷门 (lěngmén, "niche, obscure, dark-horse"): e.g., 热门话题 ("trending topic"), 夺冠大热门 ("heavy favorite to win the title"), vs. 爆冷门 ("pull off an upset").

rootFamily.gloss: way in, knack, trick of the trade

热闹.etymology: Coordinative compound combining 热 (trad. 熱, 'fervent, bustling with warmth') + 闹 (trad. 鬧, 'noisy, bustling marketplace', from 鬥 'quarrel' + 市 'market'). Attested since Tang poetry (e.g., Bai Juyi) for lively, crowded scenes.

history.meaning: bustling with noise and excitement; lively

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 热闹 (via 萌典)

然后.etymology: Classical connective phrase (trad. 然後) formed from 然 ('so, thus, being like this') + 后 (後, 'afterward, after'). Literally 'it being so, afterward...', attested in Mencius and Xunzi, now the standard conjunction 'then, after that'.

history.stage: Classical Chinese (Warring States) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: that being so, afterward -> then, after that

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 然后 (via 萌典)

照.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining semantic 灬 (火, 'fire, light') + 昭 (zhāo, 'bright sunlight', serving as both phonetic and co-semantic). Means 'to shine upon, illuminate, reflect in a mirror, take a photograph, or act according to'.

history.meaning: to shine upon, illuminate; to reflect; according to

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 照 (via 萌典)

照应.etymology: Coordinative (聯合) compound combining 照 (zhào, "to shine upon, illuminate, reflect; to watch over", with the fire base 灬 and phonetic 昭 zhāo "bright") and 应 (trad. 應, yìng, "to respond, echo, correspond to", with heart 心 and phonetic 䧹). Originally used in classical literary criticism and martial strategy for elements that "illuminate and respond to one another" (首尾照应, structural foreshadowing and callback), it broadened in vernacular Mandarin to mean "to look after, attend to, or keep an eye on someone."

history.meaning: to shine light upon + to answer or correspond in heart

history.form: 照應 (in poetics and narrative criticism)
history.meaning: mutual echo and structural correspondence between earlier and later passages
to look after, take care of (often 照应 yīng in speech); literary correspondence or coordination

morphemes.meaning: to shine upon, watch over, look after
to respond to, attend to, coordinate with

照应.notes: In everyday speech meaning "to look after / help each other out" (互相照应), the second syllable is routinely pronounced in the neutral tone (zhàoyìng -> zhàoying), and carries a warmer, more reciprocal nuance than 照顾 (zhàogù).

rootFamily.gloss: to take care of, look after, attend to
to look after, keep an eye on (property or people)
to echo, correspond to, coordinate with

cognates.meaning: after the pattern; all the same, as usual

照样.etymology: Verb-object / prepositional (動賓/介賓) compound formed from 照 (zhào, originally "to shine upon, mirror", grammaticalized into a preposition meaning "according to, by mirroring") and 样 (trad. 樣, yàng, "wooden pattern, mold, model, manner", originally the acorn of the 橡 oak tree before being borrowed for 羕/式 "pattern, style"). Literally "following the existing pattern," it evolved into an adverb meaning "in the same manner" and concessively "all the same, regardless."

history.meaning: to mirror/reflect + wooden mold or pattern
in exact accordance with the model or previous practice
all the same, just as well, still (despite obstacles or changes)

照样.notes: Frequently pairs with concessive conjunctions like 即使 / 就算 ("even if...") to emphasize that an outcome holds true regardless: 就算没有预算，我们照样能把节目做好 ("Even without a budget, we can pull off the show all the same").

rootFamily.gloss: as usual, as before, per routine

照片.etymology: Word for 'photo', built from 照 ('shine on, reflect; take a picture', as in 照相 'take a photo') + 片 ('thin flat piece, card'). The second character names the flat print, just as in 名片 ('business card') and 明信片 ('postcard'). A near synonym is 相片.

history.meaning: photograph

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 照片 (via 萌典)

照顾.etymology: Coordinative verb compound combining 照 ('to shine upon, look after') + 顾 (trad. 顧, 'to turn the head to look back at, attend to, patronize'). Means 'to look after, care for, show consideration to'.

morphemes.meaning: to look back at; attend to

history.meaning: to look after, take care of, attend to

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 照顾 (via 萌典)

煮.etymology: Phono-semantic culinary character combining phonetic 者 (*zhě*, Old Chinese *taʔ*) above the four-dot fire radical 灬 ('cooking fire beneath a vessel',Middle Chinese *tsyoX*). Attested since the *Rites of Zhou* for boiling water, simmering soup, or evaporating brine into salt.

morphemes.meaning: boil; simmer; cook in liquid over fire

history.meaning: boil or simmer in a cauldron over fire
boil; cook; simmer

煮开.etymology: Resultative verb compound combining 煮 ('boil; heat over fire') + 开 ('open out; break into a rolling boil'). In Mandarin culinary usage, 开 serves as the standard resultative complement for liquid reaching the boiling point (烧开, 煮开).

history.meaning: boil; bring to a boil

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 煮开

熟.etymology: Ideogrammic and phono-semantic character (會意兼形聲): originally written 孰 (shú, OC *duk), depicting a hand (丮) offering a sacrificial lamb (羊) at an ancestral shrine (享) — i.e., a cooked offering. When 孰 was borrowed as the interrogative pronoun "who/which," the four-dot fire radical (灬, from 火) was added at the bottom to disambiguate the original culinary sense "cooked through." From "cooked food," the meaning extended naturally to "ripened grain/fruit," "deep (sleep)," "practiced/skilled," and "well-acquainted, familiar."

history.meaning: cooked sacrificial meat; thoroughly cooked food (as opposed to 生 'raw')
ripened (of crops); deeply practiced; intimately acquainted with
cooked, ripe; familiar with, close to (a person or place); skilled, fluent

熟.notes: Has a well-known literary vs. colloquial reading split (文白异读): pronounced shóu in everyday spoken Mandarin for cooked food, ripe fruit, or personal familiarity (我们很熟), and shú in two-character compounds like 熟悉 (shúxī) and 成熟 (chéngshú).

熟人.etymology: Determinative compound of 熟 ('cooked through; ripe; familiar by long acquaintance', phonetic 孰 *shú* above fire radical 灬) + 人 ('person'). By metaphorical extension from food cooked until tender to relationships mellowed by time, 熟人 denotes a familiar neighbour, acquaintance, or regular guest.

history.meaning: familiar person; acquaintance
acquaintance; regular; familiar face

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 熟人

熟悉.etymology: Coordinative / modifier-head compound combining 熟 (shú, "thoroughly cooked, ripe, well-practiced, intimate") and 悉 (xī, "to know exhaustively, understand in every detail; all", formed from 采 biàn, originally depicting animal tracks that one distinguishes carefully, over 心 "heart/mind"). Attested in Han–Six Dynasties historical prose (such as *Book of Han* and *Records of the Three Kingdoms*) in the sense of "knowing every detail of a matter through long acquaintance."

history.meaning: thoroughly cooked/practiced + to discern exhaustively in the mind
to know intimately and exhaustively (terrain, military affairs, or customs)
familiar with, well-acquainted with ( adjective ); to familiarize oneself with ( verb )

morphemes.meaning: to know exhaustively, discern in full detail

熟悉.notes: Standard pronunciation in Mainland Putonghua is shúxī (not shóuxī); functions both as an adjective (熟悉的声音 "a familiar voice") and as a transitive verb (先熟悉一下流程 "first familiarize yourself with the workflow").

rootFamily.gloss: to be informed of, learn of (formal correspondence)

熨.etymology: Compound ideograph and phono-semantic character combining 尉 ('hold down flat from above', phonetic *wèi/yù*) over 火 ('fire'). Originally naming a bronze pan filled with glowing charcoal used to press silk smooth in the Han dynasty, it remains the standard verb for ironing cloth flat.

morphemes.meaning: press cloth smooth with heat; iron

history.meaning: smooth silk or linen with a heated charcoal pan
iron; press flat

cognates.meaning: to stay up all night, pull an all-nighter

熬夜.etymology: Verb-object (VO) compound of 熬 (áo, composed of phonetic 敖 áo above the fire radical 灬/火, originally meaning "to dry-roast grain or decoct medicine over a slow fire for hours", and by extension "to endure, hold out through protracted hardship") and 夜 (yè, "night", depicting a human figure 亻 under the moon 夕). Literally "to slow-boil or endure the night," it vividly captures the physical attrition of staying awake through the night.

history.meaning: to dry-roast or decoct over slow heat + nighttime
to endure the long hours of the night awake; to tough out hardship
to stay up late, pull an all-nighter (working, editing, or studying)

morphemes.meaning: to simmer slowly over fire; to endure, hold out through

熬夜.notes: Separable verb-object (离合词) compound: "stayed up all night three times" is 熬了三次夜, and "staying up all night until dawn" is 熬通宵.Ubiquitous in TV production rooms where editors and producers pull all-nighters.

rootFamily.gloss: to boil porridge or decoct herbal medicine slowly

cognates.meaning: to burst, explode, leak news, go viral

爆.etymology: Phono-semantic compound (形聲): semantic 火 ("fire") + phonetic 暴 (bào, OC *bˤawk-s, originally "to expose to scorching sun, sudden, violent"). In early texts, 爆 (and its precursor 灼/暴) described bamboo joints or tortoise shells crackling and bursting open when heated in fire (as in New Year firecrackers 爆竹). In modern media and internet Mandarin, the core sense of "sudden violent bursting" extended both to "going explosively viral" (Weibo's dark-red 爆 tag) and, often interchangeably with 曝 (pù/bào, "to expose to light"), to "breaking or leaking bombshell news."

history.meaning: to crackle and pop in fire (of heated bamboo or divination shells)
to burst open, detonate (gunpowder, firecrackers); to quick-fry in hot oil
to explode; to break/leak explosive news (cf. 爆料); to go viral or overflow capacity

morphemes.meaning: phonetic and semantic component bào ('sudden, violent, expose')

爆.notes: In showbiz journalism, 爆 ("to burst out news") frequently overlaps with 曝 (pù / colloquially bào, "to expose to sunlight"), as in 爆料 ("to drop insider gossip") and 曝光 ("to expose to the public/camera"). On Weibo's 热搜榜, a dark-red 爆 icon is the highest tier of viral traffic above 沸 ("boiling"), 热 ("hot"), and 新 ("new").

rootFamily.gloss: to drop insider info, leak a scoop or scandal
to burst at the seams, sell out completely (venue or box office)

爆发.etymology: Coordinative / sequential verbal compound of 爆 (bào, "to crackle and burst open from intense heat") and 发 (trad. 發, fā, "to shoot forth an arrow from a bow 弓, to emit, break out, erupt"). Popularized across the modern Sinosphere (alongside Japanese *bakuhatsu*) initially for volcanic eruptions and artillery detonations, and specialized in Mandarin for the sudden eruption of volcanoes, wars, epidemics, applause, or latent talent/emotion.

history.meaning: to crackle/burst in fire + to release an arrow or send forth

history.form: 爆發 (Japanese bakuhatsu / early modern Chinese)
history.meaning: detonation of explosives; volcanic eruption; sudden outbreak of war or revolution
to break out, erupt suddenly (of applause, crises, conflicts, or pent-up emotion)

morphemes.meaning: to shoot forth, issue, break out

爆发.notes: Compare 爆发 (used for abstract forces, wars, applause, volcanoes, or sudden bursts of power: 爆发力 "explosive power", 爆发出热烈掌声 "erupted into warm applause") with 爆炸 (used for physical bombs, gas, or metaphorical mind-blowing shocks). Also note the homophone 暴发 (bàofā, written without 火), used in 暴发户 ("nouveau riche, parvenu") and 山洪暴发 ("flash flood").

rootFamily.gloss: explosive power, burst strength (in sports or acting)
nouveau riche, upstart (written with 暴 'sudden' rather than 爆)

爆款.etymology: Modifier-head (偏正) compound coined in early 21st-century Chinese e-commerce (originally on Taobao and Tmall around the late 2000s) from 爆 (bào, "explosively popular, selling like wildfire", short for 火爆/卖爆) and 款 (kuǎn, "model, style, product design, item", originally meaning "sincere, inscribed pattern on ritual bronzes", hence "clause, style, model" as in 款式). From online retail ("runaway best-selling product style"), it crossed over into television, film, and music production to mean a "smash hit" or "viral blockbuster."

history.meaning: carved inscription or clause on bronze vessels; sincere; pattern or item
fashion/product style + selling explosively in commercial retail
runaway e-commerce best-seller; smash-hit TV drama, variety show, or viral song

morphemes.meaning: style, model, product line, show/work (short for 款式)

爆款.notes: In Chinese media and e-commerce, 打造爆款 ("engineering a smash hit / viral best-seller") is the holy grail of producers and marketers alike.

rootFamily.gloss: style, design, model, cut (of clothing or products)
the exact same style (e.g., celebrity-worn item: 明星同款)
smash-hit drama or film; box-office sensation

爆炸.etymology: Coordinative (聯合) compound uniting two synonyms carrying the fire radical 火: 爆 (bào, "to crackle and burst open from intense heat") and 炸 (zhà, originally a graphic variant of 煠 meaning "to deep-fry in boiling oil," which acquired the falling-tone reading zhà in Ming–Qing vernacular when gunpowder shells and firecrackers shattered outward). Together they reinforce the violent physical detonation and shattering of an explosive body.

history.meaning: to pop in fire + to scald or cook in boiling fat/water

history.form: 爆炸 (with gunpowder weaponry and mines)
history.meaning: to burst and shatter violently from internal explosive pressure
to explode, detonate; explosion (literal or figuratively 'mind-blowing / overwhelming')

morphemes.meaning: to burst open, detonate from heat or pressure
to shatter outward, blow up, explode (zhà; cf. zhá 'deep-fry')

爆炸.notes: Watch the tonal minimal pair on 炸: fourth tone zhà means "to explode, blow up" (爆炸 bàozhà, 炸弹 zhàdàn "bomb"), whereas second tone zhá means "to deep-fry in oil" (炸鸡 zhájī "fried chicken"). Colloquially, 心态爆炸 ("my mental state just exploded") means tilting or losing one's cool under pressure.

rootFamily.gloss: to bombard, bomb; to blitz with media or messages

爆炸性.etymology: Derived attributive (附加式) three-character word formed by suffixing the abstract quality/property marker -性 (xìng, originally "innate human nature, disposition", from heart 忄 and phonetic 生 shēng "birth/life", grammaticalized in modern Sino-Japanese and Mandarin to translate English "-ive, -ic, -ity") onto the verbal noun 爆炸 (bàozhà, "explosion"). Used both in chemistry ("explosive property") and journalism ("bombshell, sensational").

history.meaning: physical detonation + inborn nature or quality
having the chemical property of exploding; sensational or shocking in impact
explosive, bombshell, earth-shattering (especially modifying 新闻 'news' or 增长 'growth')

爆炸性.notes: Functions as a non-predicative adjective (区别词) that directly modifies nouns like 爆炸性新闻 ("bombshell news") or 爆炸性消息 ("explosive scoop"), or follows 有 ("possess"): 很有爆炸性 ("packs a real bombshell punch").

rootFamily.gloss: sensational,轰动性 stirring up a huge commotion

爬.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining semantic 爪 ('claw, hand') + phonetic 巴 (bā/pá). Originally meant 'to scratch or claw', then shifted in medieval vernacular to 'to crawl on hands and knees, climb, clamber'.

history.meaning: to scratch with claws -> to crawl, creep, climb

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 爬 (via 萌典)

爬过.etymology: Verb-complement compound combining 爬 ('to crawl, climb') + 过 (trad. 過, directional/experiential complement 'across, over').

history.meaning: to crawl across; to climb over

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 爬过 (via 萌典)

爱.etymology: Phono-semantic/associative character (trad. 愛) originally written 𢖻 (semantic 心 'heart' + phonetic 旡 'figure looking back with open mouth/breath'), to which 夊 ('dragging foot, reluctant to part') was added below. Simplified 爱 replaces 心 with 友 ('friend').

morphemes.meaning: heart (in trad. 愛; replaced by 友 in 爱)

history.meaning: to cherish, be reluctant to part with -> to love, be fond of

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 爱 (via 萌典)

爱上.etymology: Verb-complement (動補 / 述補) compound joining the stative verb 爱 (trad. 愛, ài, "to love, feel affection for") with the directional/inchoative resultative complement 上 (shàng, originally "up, to ascend", grammaticalized after verbs of emotion and perception to mark the inception and attachment of a new state, i.e., "to come to love, become attached to"). This converts the static state 爱 ("to love") into a dynamic, punctual transition ("to fall in love with").

history.meaning: to cherish/love in the heart + to ascend or mount

history.form: V + 上 (e.g. 看上, 愛上)
history.meaning: grammaticalization of 上 as an inchoative/attachment complement after psychological verbs
to fall in love with (a person, place, or calling)

morphemes.meaning: to love, feel deep affection for
inchoative complement indicating entering into a state and fixing upon a target

爱上.notes: Crucial aspectual distinction for learners: 我爱你 (wǒ ài nǐ) describes an ongoing state ("I love you"), whereas 我爱上你了 (wǒ àishàng nǐ le) expresses the transition ("I have fallen in love with you"). Parallel formations include 喜欢上 ("come to like") and 看上 ("take a fancy to").

rootFamily.gloss: to take a fancy to, set one's heart on
to become obsessed with, get hooked on
to be in love, romantic relationship

cognates.meaning: fondness for, love of; amateur/enthusiast (in 愛好家 aikōka)

爱好.etymology: Coordinative (聯合) compound combining two classical synonyms of affection and inclination: 爱 (trad. 愛, ài, "to love, cherish") and 好 (in its departing-tone verbal reading hào, OC *qʰˤuʔ-s, "to be fond of, take delight in", derived from the adjective hǎo "good", depicting a woman 女 and child 子). Already paired in Han–Tang texts (such as Wang Chong's *Lunheng*) as a verb meaning "to take delight in, be fond of," it nominalized in modern Mandarin into the standard noun for "hobby, avocation, special interest."

history.meaning: to cherish + to be fond of, take pleasure in (as in 知之者不如好之者)

history.form: 愛好 (in Han–Tang prose, e.g., 論衡)
history.meaning: to be fond of, have a predilection for; personal inclination or taste
hobby, pastime, special interest (noun); to be fond of, keen on (verb)

morphemes.meaning: to be fond of, take delight in (pronounced hào in the 4th tone!)

爱好.notes: Pronunciation trap: the second character MUST be read in the fourth tone (hào, "to be fond of"), never the third tone (hǎo, "good"). Adding the agent suffix -者 creates 爱好者 (àihàozhě, "enthusiast, aficionado, amateur fan", e.g., 音乐爱好者 "music lover").

rootFamily.gloss: hobby, special interest, inclination (slightly more formal)

cognates.meaning: to begrudge parting with, cherish, hold dear
to cherish, prize, grieve over losing

爱惜.etymology: Coordinative (聯合) compound uniting 爱 (trad. 愛, ài, which in Classical Chinese frequently meant not just "to love" but specifically "to begrudge spending, be sparing with, treasure", as in *Mencius* 百姓皆以王為愛也) and 惜 (xī, "to pity, begrudge losing, cherish, spare", composed of heart 忄 and phonetic 昔 xī). Attested since Han and Three Kingdoms literature, the compound preserves the classical nuance of valuing something so dearly that one guards it against waste, wear, or harm.

history.meaning: to hold dear and begrudge wasting or losing

history.form: 愛惜 (in Han–Tang poetry and prose)
history.meaning: to treasure and spare from harm (time, reputation, life, or talented people)
to cherish, take good care of, use sparingly (one's health, feathers/reputation, time, or property)

morphemes.meaning: to love, treasure, begrudge wasting (classical sense)

爱惜.notes: Often confused with 珍惜 (zhēnxī): 珍惜 emphasizes valuing something precious or fleeting (珍惜机会 "cherish an opportunity", 珍惜感情), whereas 爱惜 emphasizes practical care and avoiding damage or waste (爱惜身体 "take care of one's health", 爱惜公物 "take care of public property", 爱惜羽毛 "protect one's reputation").

rootFamily.gloss: to treasure, value highly, cherish (abstract or emotional)
to feel heartache over, dote on, begrudge spending
it is a pity, regrettable, too bad

父亲.etymology: Modifier-head / appositional kinship compound formed from 父 (fù, OC *baʔ, originally depicting in oracle bone and bronze script a hand 又 holding a stone axe or rod of household authority 丨) and 亲 (trad. 親, qīn, "intimate, blood relative, parent", composed of 見 "to see closely" and phonetic 亲 shēn/qīn). While Classical Chinese used monosyllabic 父 for "father" and 親 for "parents," disyllabic 父親 became established in Tang–Song vernacular and formal prose to distinguish "father" unambiguously from 母親 ("mother") and 父母 ("parents").

history.meaning: male head of household holding a rod/axe + blood relative or parent

history.form: 父親 (paired symmetrically with 母親)
history.meaning: one's father (disyllabic kinship term in vernacular and formal writing)
father (formal or respectful term of reference, contrasting with colloquial 爸爸)

morphemes.meaning: father, male elder of the family

父亲.notes: Register distinction: 父亲 (often pronounced fùqin with a neutral second syllable in speech) is used in formal speech, writing, or when referring respectfully to one's or another's father in the third person, whereas 爸爸 (bàba) or 爸 (bà) is used in direct family address.

父母.etymology: A classical coordinative (dvandva) compound pairing 父 (fù, 'father', originally an ideograph of a hand holding a stone axe or symbol of authority) and 母 (mǔ, 'mother', an oracle-bone pictograph of a kneeling woman with prominent breasts). Attested continuously since the Book of Odes (詩經), the compound fuses the two primary parental poles into a single collective noun for 'parents'.

history.meaning: father and mother; one's parents; metaphorically the ruler as protector of the people
parents; also used in 父母官 for a local magistrate
parents (standard formal and neutral register)

父母.notes: More formal and written than 爸妈 (bàmā); frequently appears in legal, educational, and serious dramatic dialogue (e.g., 赡养父母, 'to support one's parents').

爷爷.etymology: Reduplicated kinship noun from 爷 (trad. 爺, phono-semantic from 父 'father' + 耶 phonetic). Originally meant 'father' in Northern Dynasties and Tang ballads (such as 《木兰诗》 '阿爷无大儿'), later shifted in Mandarin to 'paternal grandfather' and a respectful address for elderly men.

history.meaning: father -> paternal grandfather; respectful term for an old man

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 爷爷 (via 萌典)

爸爸.etymology: A reduplicated kinship term built on 爸 (bà, 'father'), itself a phono-semantic compound with 父 ('father') as semantic signific and 巴 (bā) as phonetic indicator. First recorded in the Three Kingdoms-era dictionary Guangya (廣雅: 「爸，父也」), it originates in the universal nursery labial syllable *pa/*ba and became the standard colloquial word for 'dad' across Mandarin dialects via kinship reduplication.

history.meaning: father (regional and colloquial monosyllabic kinship term)
dad, papa (reduplicated affectionate kinship address)
dad, father; also slang 'benefactor/sponsor' (as in 金主爸爸)

morphemes.meaning: diminutive/intimate kinship reduplication with neutral tone

爸爸.notes: In modern television and advertising industry slang, 爸爸 is playfully appended to clients or sponsors (甲方爸爸, 金主爸爸) to joke about their absolute authority over a production's budget.

爽朗.etymology: Coordinative adjective combining 爽 ('bright, clear, brisk, refreshing', originally daylight shining through lattice windows 爻 around 大) + 朗 ('bright, clear, resonant', originally clear moonlight). Describes clear weather or a hearty, open-hearted personality.

history.stage: Six Dynasties (Shishuo Xinyu) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: clear and bright (of weather); hearty, frank, and cheerful

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 爽朗 (via 萌典)

片.etymology: Pictograph derived from splitting the tree character 木 vertically in half (the right half is 片, the left half is 爿). Originally meant 'split wood plank', then generalized to any flat, thin slice, flake, stretch of land, or classifier for flat/expansive things.

morphemes.meaning: half of a split tree (木) -> flat slice

history.meaning: split wood plank -> thin slice, flat piece, expanse (classifier)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 片 (via 萌典)

片子.etymology: A noun-suffix derivative formed from 片 (piàn, originally half of a split tree trunk 爿, hence a flat, thin slice, strip, or reel frame) plus the nominalizing diminutive suffix 子 (-zi). Originally denoting any flat strip or card (such as calling cards or photographic plates in late Qing), it shifted via celluloid film strips and reels to mean 'motion picture', 'edited broadcast footage', or 'recorded programme' (frequently pronounced piānzi with retroflexion piānr in Beijing and showbiz speech).

history.meaning: flat slice, wood chip, thin slab
flat slip of paper, calling card, photographic plate, phonograph record
film, movie, television programme, edited video cut

片子.notes: In television and film production rooms, 片子 (often spoken as piānzi or piānr) refers concretely to the edited video package or rough cut ready for review or broadcast (e.g., 审片子, 剪片子).

片酬.etymology: A modern modifier-head (endocentric) compound combining 片 (piàn, abridged from 影片 'film, television programme') and 酬 (chóu, 'reward, remuneration', originally a host toasting a guest a second time with wine, 酉, hence 'to reciprocate, repay'). Coined in the twentieth-century Hong Kong and Shanghai film industries, it denotes the contractual compensation paid to actors or guests for appearing in a film or television project.

history.meaning: to toast a guest in return; to requite, reward
remuneration paid to an actor per motion picture
appearance fee or star salary for films, dramas, or variety shows

morphemes.meaning: film, show, production (short for 影片/节目片)
remuneration, fee, reward (short for 酬劳)

片酬.notes: A core showbiz budget term; often collocated with 天价片酬 ('astronomical appearance fees') or 友情片酬 ('friend-rate/token fee').

版本.etymology: A Song-dynasty bibliographic modifier-head compound pairing 版 (bǎn, 'wooden printing block', from 片 'wood slice' + 反 phonetic) and 本 (běn, 'bound book, codex, root text'). With the rise of woodblock printing (雕版印刷) during the Tang and Song dynasties, 版本 distinguished texts printed from carved woodblocks from hand-copied manuscripts (写本), later generalizing to any 'edition' of a book and, in modern media and software, any 'version' or 'cut' of a programme.

history.meaning: woodblock-printed book edition (as opposed to hand-copied scroll)
specific printing or textual edition of a work
version, edition, or edit cut of a text, software, or broadcast show

版本.notes: In television production, 版本 refers to distinct edit cuts or format adaptations (e.g., 粗剪版本 'rough-cut version', 国际版本 'international format version').

rootFamily.gloss: to publish, come off the press

版权.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-Japanese legal coinage (wasei-kango 版権, hanken) created in Meiji Japan (attributed to Fukuzawa Yukichi around 1873 to translate English 'copyright') and borrowed into late-Qing Chinese. It combines 版 (bǎn, 'printing plate, publication') and 权 (quán, originally a scale weight of yellow-berry wood, extended in classical philosophy to 'authority' and in modern translation to legal 'right').

history.meaning: exclusive right to print and publish a book (translation of 'copyright')
publishing copyright over books and printed works
copyright and intellectual property licensing rights across print, music, TV formats, and streaming

版权.notes: In the entertainment industry, 版权 covers not just written works but show formats (节目模式版权), broadcast rights, and music licensing; more colloquial and commercial than the strictly statutory term 著作权.

版权库.etymology: A contemporary three-character modifier-head nominal compound formed by attaching 库 (kù, originally an arsenal or storehouse for military chariots 车 under a roof 广, modernized as 'repository, database') to the disyllabic base 版权 (bǎnquán, 'copyright'). Coined in the digital media and television production era, it denotes a company's curated catalog or database of licensed intellectual properties, show formats, and scripts held for development.

history.meaning: chariot storehouse, armory, treasury
database, resource repository
copyright library, IP catalog/repository held by a media studio or platform

版权库.notes: In *Behind the Scenes* (幕后之王) and Chinese studio operations, a rich 版权库 (IP library of original formats, novels, and music catalogs) is a production company's core strategic moat.

牌.etymology: A phono-semantic character composed of 片 (piàn, 'flat wooden tablet or split bamboo') as semantic radical and 卑 (bēi) as phonetic. In Middle Chinese it denoted wooden placards, tally passes, and official signboards; from the Tang and Song dynasties onward, with the invention of叶子戏 (leaf-card games) and bone dominoes/mahjong tiles, it came to mean 'playing card, tile' and metaphorically a strategic 'card' or leverage played in negotiations.

history.meaning: wooden placard, official tally tablet, shield board
playing card, domino/mahjong tile; commercial shop signboard (招牌)
playing card, brand, badge; figuratively a strategic card or trump card in business/politics

morphemes.meaning: wooden tablet, placard, playing card, brand

牌.notes: Figurative expressions from card games saturate corporate and media negotiations: 打感情牌 ('play the emotion card'), 王牌 ('trump card / flagship show'), and 底牌 ('hole card / hidden leverage').

rootFamily.gloss: trump card, ace; flagship talent or programme
hole card, hidden reserve or bottom line in negotiations

牌子.etymology: Noun formed from 牌 ('flat wooden placard, tablet, signboard, or tally', with semantic 片 'flat board' + 卑 phonetic) + nominal suffix 子. Extended from shop signboards to 'brand, trademark, label, or badge'.

history.meaning: signboard, placard, tally -> brand, trademark

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 牌子 (via 萌典)

牙齿.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 牙齿. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 牙齿 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 牙齿 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 牙齿 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 牙齿. The etymology of 牙齿 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 牙齿
middle form of 牙齿
modern form of 牙齿

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 牙齿

牛奶.etymology: Attributive compound combining 牛 ('cow, cattle', an ancient pictograph of a horned bovine head) + 奶 ('milk, breast').

history.meaning: cow's milk

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 牛奶 (via 萌典)

牛排.etymology: A hybrid modifier-head compound combining 牛 (niú, 'cattle, beef') with 排 (pái, originally 'to arrange in a row', later used for 'rib/chop' as in 排骨 because ribs align in rows, and simultaneously serving in late-19th/early-20th-century Shanghai treaty-port Mandarin as a phono-semantic adaptation of English 'pie' / 'steak' alongside Cantonese 牛扒). It designates a pan-seared or grilled slab of beef steak in Western cuisine.

history.meaning: row of ribs, pork/beef rib chop
Western-style beef steak (coined in Shanghai Haipai Western restaurants)
beef steak

牛排.notes: Steak doneness in Mandarin uses odd numbers of tenths (几分熟): 三分熟 (medium-rare), 五分熟 (medium), 七分熟 (medium-well), and 全熟 (well-done).

牛皮纸.etymology: Three-character compound from 牛皮 ('oxhide; cowhide') + 纸 (simplified from 紙, silk 纟 + 氏 'paper'). Named because unbleached kraft wood-pulp paper shares the tough tear-resistance and warm tan-brown color of tanned cowhide.

history.meaning: kraft paper; brown wrapping paper

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 牛皮纸

物理.etymology: Compound of 物 ('thing; matter; phenomenon', ox radical 牛 + 勿 *wù*) + 理 ('inner pattern or vein in jade; natural principle', jade radical 王 + 里 *lǐ*). Used in classical Chinese philosophy for the inherent principles of all things, and standardized in late 19th-century East Asia as the translation for 'physics'.

history.meaning: inherent principles governing things
physics; physical laws

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 物理

牵扯.etymology: A coordinative (synonym-compounded) verb combining 牵 (qiān, 'to lead an ox by a rope', depicting an ox 牛 beneath a halter 冖 and 玄 phonetic) and 扯 (chě, vernacular variant of 撦, 'to pull, tug, tear apart by hand'). Both verbs share the physical image of tugging on a tether or garment; joined together in Ming–Qing vernacular fiction, they developed the figurative sense of 'pulling into an affair, entangling, or dragging others into a complex situation'.

history.meaning: to lead an animal by a halter rope; to pull along
to tug and pull back and forth; to entangle in a dispute or lawsuit
to involve, implicate, entangle (interests, personnel, or complicated subplots)

morphemes.meaning: to lead by a rope, pull, draw in

牵扯.notes: Unlike 牵连 (which strongly implies dragging someone into guilt or punishment), 牵扯 is often used more broadly for entangling multiple parties, budgets, or interests (e.g., 牵扯太多利益, 牵扯精力).

rootFamily.gloss: to implicate, drag into trouble alongside
to hold back, tie down,牵制 check and balance
to pull, tug; to chat idly or ramble

cognates.meaning: implication, entanglement in a crime or affair

牵连.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound joining 牵 (qiān, 'to pull by a halter rope, draw along') and 连 (lián, 'to link in a train of carts, connect continuously'). Attested from Han and Six Dynasties histories onward, the metaphor is that of animals or prisoners tethered together on a single rope: when one falls or commits an offense, the others bound to the line are dragged down alongside.

history.meaning: to be linked together; to implicate associates in a legal investigation or punishment
to implicate, embroil, drag innocent or associated parties into trouble
to implicate, involve in scandal, liability, or fallout

morphemes.meaning: to lead by a tether, pull along
to link, join, connect in a chain

牵连.notes: Almost always carries negative prosody (bad consequences, scandals, legal/PR fallout), commonly in the passive pattern 受…牵连 or 被…牵连 ('to be implicated by...').

特.etymology: Originally a phono-semantic character (牛 'ox' + 寺 'temple/hall' phonetic, Old Chinese *dɯːɡ) meaning a single bull selected for sacrifice, and by extension 'a solitary beast standing apart from the herd'. In Classical Chinese it evolved through 'standing alone, exceptional, single' to 'specially, on purpose'; in modern Northern (especially Beijing) colloquial Mandarin, it functions as a high-frequency degree adverb meaning 'especially, super, extraordinarily' (an apocopated/shortened use of 特别).

history.meaning: sacrificial bull; a single mount or beast standing apart from the herd; exceptional
specially, on purpose; only, merely (adverbial particle in Literary Chinese)
especially, super, extremely (colloquial degree adverb before adjectives/stative verbs)

特.notes: As a standalone degree adverb directly before an adjective (e.g., 特好 'super good', 特牛 'super awesome', 特有戏 'super dramatic'), 特 has a lively, brisk Northern Mandarin flavor very common in spoken TV dialogue.

特价.etymology: Commercial compound of 特 ('special; exceptional') + 价 ('price; value', person radical 亻 + 介 jiè). Denotes a special promotional price or bargain discount.

history.meaning: special price; bargain offer

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 特价

特别.etymology: Compound adjective/adverb combining 特 ('bull singled out as an offering; outstanding, special', from 牛 'ox' + 寺 phonetic) + 别 (trad. 別, 'to divide, distinguish, different'). Means 'distinct from others, special, especially'.

history.meaning: singled out and distinct -> special, particular; especially

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 特别 (via 萌典)

特意.etymology: Attributive adverbial compound combining 特 ('special, singled out') + 意 ('intention, purpose'). Means 'with special intent, purposely, going out of one's way'.

history.meaning: with special purpose; специально, on purpose

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 特意 (via 萌典)
