由头.notes: Pronounced yóutou with a neutral tone on 头; in workplace and media contexts, 找个由头 ("find an excuse/angle") is less morally condemning than 借口 ("alibi/excuse") and often means finding a convenient peg or pretext to initiate a meeting, visit, or PR event.

cognates.meaning: from this, thereby (in kanbun reading: kore yori)

由此.etymology: A lexicalized Classical Chinese prepositional phrase composed of the preposition 由 (yóu, "from, out of, proceeding from") and the proximal demonstrative pronoun 此 (cǐ, "this, here"). Used continuously since Warring States prose (such as Mencius 《孟子》: 由此觀之, "viewed from this standpoint"), it functions in modern formal and journalistic Mandarin as a conjunctive adverb meaning "from this, thereby, hence, consequently".

history.form: 由此 (Classical Chinese, e.g.,《孟子》由此觀之)
history.meaning: from this place, starting from this premise or fact
from this, thereby, hence, as a result of this

morphemes.meaning: from, proceeding out of, by way of

由此.notes: A staple transition word in formal narration, documentary voiceovers, and contracts, frequently collocating in set frames like 由此可见 ("from this it can be seen that...") and 由此产生 ("arising therefrom").

rootFamily.gloss: from this it can be seen that..., thus it is evident
because of this, for this purpose, to this end

cognates.meaning: appeal, lodging a formal complaint or petition

申诉.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound pairing 申 (shēn, originally "to stretch, extend", hence in Classical Chinese "to state, set forth, explain clearly to a superior") with 诉 (sù, Simplified; 訴 Traditional, "to recount, tell, accuse, appeal a grievance"). Used in imperial legal and administrative petitions for stating one's grievance to a higher tribunal, it is now the standard institutional and legal verb for lodging a formal appeal, grievance, or representation (against a verdict, penalty, or platform takedown).

history.meaning: to set forth and recount a grievance to a magistrate or higher authority
history.stage: Middle to Late Imperial Literary Chinese

history.meaning: to appeal (a ruling or disciplinary action), lodge a formal representation or complaint

morphemes.meaning: to state, express, set forth formally
to tell, recount, accuse, appeal a grievance

申诉.notes: Distinguish 申诉 from 上诉 (shàngsù): 上诉 is strictly appealing a court judgment to a higher court before it takes effect, whereas 申诉 applies broadly to petitioning for review of an already effective ruling, workplace decision, copyright strike, or industry dispute.

rootFamily.gloss: to appeal to a higher court; judicial appeal
to file a lawsuit, litigate; litigation
to lodge a consumer or service complaint

申请.etymology: A coordinative/sequential verbal compound formed from 申 (shēn, "to state, report, set forth to a superior") and 请 (qǐng, Simplified; 請 Traditional, "to request respectfully, petition, ask for"). In Tang–Ming bureaucratic correspondence, 申請 meant presenting a formal report to a superior authority to request approval or instructions; reinforced in the late 19th and early 20th centuries by Japanese administrative usage (申請 shinsei), it became the universal modern Mandarin verb and noun for "to apply for / application" (visas, budgets, patents, broadcasting permits).

history.meaning: to report upwards to a superior official and request instructions or authorization
history.stage: Middle to Late Imperial Literary Chinese

history.meaning: to apply for, file a formal application or request; an application

morphemes.meaning: to state, report, set forth formally
to request respectfully, ask for, petition

申请.notes: Functions both as a transitive verb taking the desired item as object (申请预算, "apply for a budget"; 申请专利, "apply for a patent") and as a noun (提交申请, "submit an application").

rootFamily.gloss: to ask for instructions from a superior

电工.etymology: Attributive compound combining 电 (trad. 電, 'lightning -> electricity') + 工 ('artisan, skilled worker'). Denotes an electrician or electrical engineering work.

history.meaning: electrician; electrical work

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 电工 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: elevator, lift (Sino-Vietnamese reading, alongside thang máy)

电梯.etymology: A modern modifier-head nominal compound combining 电 (diàn, Simplified; 電 Traditional, originally "lightning flash", repurposed in the 19th century to translate "electricity, electric") and 梯 (tī, "wooden ladder, staircase, steps"). Coined in the late 19th / early 20th century as electric elevators were introduced to treaty-port cities like Shanghai, 电梯 literally means "electric ladder/staircase".

history.meaning: classical roots for lightning and wooden ladder
elevator, lift (and in broad or regional usage, escalator)

电梯.notes: In Mainland Mandarin, 电梯 usually defaults to a vertical enclosed elevator (sometimes specified as 直梯), while an escalator is specified as 扶梯 (fútī) or 自动扶梯; in Hong Kong Cantonese, 电梯 often refers to an escalator while 升降机 refers to an elevator.

rootFamily.gloss: freight elevator, service lift (used for stage/studio gear)

电灯.etymology: Modern compound noun from 电 (simplified from 電, originally 'lightning flash' under rain 雨, adopted in the 19th century for electricity) + 灯 (simplified from 燈, fire 火 + 登 'oil lamp; lantern'). Coined in late-Qing coastal cities when incandescent electric lighting replaced kerosene and oil lamps.

history.meaning: electric lamp
electric light; electric lamp

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 电灯

电盒.etymology: Attributive noun compound combining 电 (trad. 電, 'electricity') + 盒 ('small box, case'), referring colloquially to an electrical junction box, fuse box, or power box.

history.meaning: electrical box; junction or breaker box

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 电盒 (via 萌典)

电线.etymology: Modern compound combining 电 ('electricity', originally 'lightning' flashing under rain 雨 in oracle-bone and bronze script) + 线 ('thread, wire', silk radical 纟 + phonetic 戋).

history.meaning: 'lightning' and 'silk/hemp thread'
electrical wire

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 电线 (via 萌典)

电脑.etymology: Metaphorical compound combining 电 (trad. 電, 'electric, electronic') + 脑 (trad. 腦, 'brain'), coined in the mid-20th century as a vivid calque of 'electronic brain' for the electronic computer.

history.meaning: electronic brain -> computer

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 电脑 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: television (early Sino-Japanese rendering before テレビ became dominant)

电视.etymology: A modern modifier-head / instrumental-verbal neologism combining 电 (diàn, Simplified; 電 Traditional, "electricity, electromagnetic") and 视 (shì, Simplified; 視 Traditional, "to look at, view, vision"). Coined in the 1920s–1930s (alongside Japanese 電視 denshi and competing early Chinese translations like 无线电传视) as a semantic calque of Greek-Latin "tele-vision" (adapting 电 from Telegraph/Telephone 电报/电话 to render tele- "far/electric transmission" + 视 for -vision "sight"), it became the standard Chinese word for both the medium of television and (colloquially, short for 电视机) a TV set.

history.meaning: electrical transmission of visual images; television
television (the broadcasting medium, programming, or television receiver)

morphemes.meaning: to look at, view, vision, visual

电视.notes: Notice how early modern Chinese systematically used 电 ("electric") to render Greek tele- ("far") across communication technologies: 电报 (telegraph), 电话 (telephone), and 电视 (television); for the physical appliance, 电视机 is formal while 电视 is used in everyday speech.

电视台.etymology: A left-branching modifier-head nominal compound ((电 + 视) + 台) formed by affixing 台 (tái, Simplified; 臺 Traditional, originally "a raised earthen viewing platform, terrace, or watchtower" in Old Chinese, extended in modern times to "broadcasting station, transmitter platform, or institutional desk") to 电视 (diànshì, "television"). Following the earlier pattern of 电台 (diàntái, "radio/telegraph station"), 电视台 denotes a television broadcasting station or network.

history.meaning: elevated earthen terrace, observation tower, or high governmental secretariat
television station, TV broadcasting network

morphemes.meaning: raised platform, stage; broadcasting station or channel

电视台.notes: In industry and everyday speech, 台 alone frequently acts as a bound or semi-free word for both a "broadcasting network" (台里, "at the station/network"; 卫视, "satellite TV network") and a "TV channel" (换台, "change the channel").

rootFamily.gloss: backstage, behind the scenes; backstage supporter/backing

电视史.etymology: A left-branching modifier-head nominal compound ((电 + 视) + 史) combining 电视 (diànshì, "television") with the bound nominal head 史 (shǐ, in oracle bone script a hand holding a writing brush or tally tablet to record court events, originally "court archivist, scribe", and since Sima Qian's Shiji 《史記》 "history, historical annals"). It means "the history of television" as a medium and industry.

history.meaning: court scribe/archivist; historical records and annals
history of television, annals of television broadcasting

电视史.notes: In Mandarin, the monosyllabic bound root 史 (shǐ) attaches directly to nouns to form disciplinary or medium histories—such as 电视史 ("history of television"), 电影史 ("film history"), and 文学史 ("literary history")—where using two-character 历史 would sound less compact.

电视圈.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound formed from 电视 (diànshì, 'television', itself a 20th-century neologism combining 电 'electricity, lightning' + 视 'to look at, view' as a calque of Greek-derived 'tele-vision') and the quasi-suffix 圈 (quān, 'circle, enclosure, social sphere', originally meaning a livestock pen or curved wooden vessel in Classical Chinese). Together they denote the professional and social milieu of the television industry.

history.meaning: livestock pen; circular enclosure; circumference
electrical transmission of visual images; television
the television industry and its professional social circle

电视圈.notes: Compared to the more formal 电视界, 电视圈 is more conversational and emphasizes the insider social network, interpersonal politics, and cliques within the TV business.

电视机.etymology: A modifier-head compound built from 电视 (diànshì, 'television', literally 'electric vision') and the instrumental head noun 机 (jī, traditional 機, 'machine, apparatus, device'). In Classical Chinese, 機 originally denoted the trigger mechanism of a crossbow or the complex wooden frame of a weaving loom, before generalizing in the 19th and 20th centuries to render Western mechanical and electronic appliances.

history.meaning: loom; crossbow trigger mechanism; pivotal device
television receiving apparatus; television set
television set (physical appliance)

电视机.notes: Refers strictly to the physical hardware appliance (measured with classifier 台 tái), whereas 电视 alone can refer either to the medium/programming or the appliance.

电视界.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 电视 (diànshì, 'television') with the productive bound morpheme 界 (jiè, 'boundary, realm, domain, professional sector'). In Classical Chinese, 界 denoted a territorial border between fields (composed of 田 'field' over phonetic 介 'border, armor'); through Meiji-era Sino-Japanese translation usage and Buddhist cosmology (where 界 rendered Sanskrit dhātu 'realm'), -界 evolved into a formal suffix designating an entire professional field or sector of society.

history.meaning: border between fields; territorial boundary; realm (Buddhist dhātu)
professional sector; public sphere (influenced by Japanese -kai)
the television industry; the world of television broadcasting

电视界.notes: Higher in register than 电视圈; 电视界 is favored in award ceremonies, press releases, and formal journalism to refer respectfully to the television broadcasting profession as a whole.

电话.etymology: Attributive compound combining 电 (trad. 電, 'electric') + 话 (trad. 話, 'spoken words, speech'), coined in the late 19th century for the telephone (alongside early transliteration 德律风).

history.stage: Late Qing / 20th c. to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: electric speech -> telephone, phone call

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 电话 (via 萌典)

电话会议.etymology: A four-character modifier-head compound composed of two Meiji-era Sino-Japanese *wasei-kango* return loans: 电话 (diànhuà, traditional 電話, literally 'electric speech', coined in Japan as *denwa* to translate 'telephone') modifying 会议 (huìyì, traditional 會議, 'meeting, conference', a classical coordinative compound of 会 'assemble' + 议 'deliberate, discuss' repurposed in Meiji Japan as *kaigi* for formal parliamentary and business assemblies). Together they calque English 'telephone conference' or 'conference call'.

history.meaning: to assemble and deliberate on state affairs
telephone / formal conference (adopted via Meiji Japanese)
conference call; teleconference

电话会议.notes: In corporate and media production settings, this pairs with the verb 召开 (zhàokāi, 'convene') or the colloquial 开电话会议 ('have a conference call'); contrast with 视频会议 ('video conference').

男.etymology: An ancient associative compound ideogram (会意文字) attested on Shang dynasty oracle bone inscriptions, combining 田 (tián, 'cultivated field', depicting a grid of irrigated plots) on top and 力 (lì, 'arduous physical strength; wooden plowshare') on the bottom. As explained in Xu Shen's *Shuowen Jiezi* (100 CE), '男，丈夫也。从田从力，言男用力於田也' ('Man, an adult male; composed of field and strength, signifying that a man exerts strength in the fields'). From Old Chinese *nˁə[m] (Middle Chinese *nom), it functions in Modern Mandarin both as a bound nominal root ('man') and a non-predicative adjective ('male').

history.meaning: adult male agricultural laborer; son; baron (fifth rank of nobility)
male person; son; masculine
male (attributive adjective); man; son

morphemes.meaning: field (graphic component 田) + strength/plow (graphic component 力) → male; man

男.notes: As an adjective meaning 'male' for humans, 男 is non-predicative: it attaches directly before nouns without 的 (e.g., 男演员 'male actor', 男导演 'male director'), whereas animal sex uses 公 (gōng) or 雄 (xióng).

rootFamily.gloss: men and women; male and female

男一号.etymology: A modern theatrical and film-industry compound formed from 男 (nán, 'male [character/actor]') + 一 (yī, 'number one, primary') + 号 (hào, traditional 號, 'number, designation, role rank'). Originally derived from stage blocking and call-sheet numbering in 20th-century Chinese drama and film studios, where principal characters were ranked numerically by billing and screen time, 男一号 designates the top-billed male protagonist.

history.meaning: to cry out; command; identifying mark or title
number one; primary unit or designation
male lead; top-billed leading man in a film or television drama

男一号.notes: In Chinese film and TV production slang, 男一号 is frequently clipped to 男一 (nányī) and contrasts with 女一号 (nǚyīhào, 'female lead') and 男二号 (nán'èrhào, 'second male lead').

rootFamily.gloss: second male lead; supporting male lead

男人.etymology: Attributive noun compound combining 男 ('male, man', an ancient associative compound of 田 'field' + 力 'plow/strength', i.e., one who expends strength working the fields) + 人 ('person').

history.meaning: man; adult male person

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 男人 (via 萌典)

男友.etymology: A disyllabic modifier-head contraction of 男朋友 (nánpéngyou, 'boyfriend'), combining 男 (nán, 'male') and 友 (yǒu, 'friend, companion'). In oracle bone and bronze inscriptions, 友 depicted two right hands (又 + 又) reaching in the same direction to assist one another, signifying mutual aid and comradeship; in modern media and journalism, 男友 serves as the compact two-syllable equivalent of 男朋友.

history.meaning: two hands joined in mutual assistance; comrade; friend
boyfriend; male romantic partner (calqued from English)
boyfriend (concise disyllabic form)

男友.notes: Because Chinese prosody strongly prefers two-syllable roots in compounds and headlines, 男友 (rather than 男朋友) is mandatory in derivatives like 前男友 ('ex-boyfriend') and 绯闻男友 ('rumored boyfriend').

男孩子.etymology: A modifier-head compound consisting of 男 (nán, 'male') + 孩 (hái, 'child') + the diminutive nominal suffix 子 (zi, neutral tone, originally meaning 'offspring, child'). In Classical Chinese, 孩 (composed of 子 'child' + phonetic 亥 *gˁəʔ) meant a 'laughing infant' or toddler (*Shuowen*: '小兒笑也'). Together, 男孩子 literally means 'male child/boy', though in contemporary spoken Mandarin it routinely extends to unmarried young men in their twenties.

history.meaning: smiling infant; young child
child; youth (with diminutive suffix -子)
boy; young man; guy (especially in dating or social contexts)

男孩子.notes: In adult conversation and romance/workplace dramas, 男孩子 often means 'young guy / bachelor' rather than a literal child, especially when discussing dating habits or personality traits (e.g., 那个男孩子很体贴 'that guy is very considerate').

男星.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 男 (nán, 'male') with 星 (xīng, 'star; celebrity', clipped from 明星 míngxīng 'bright star; celebrity'). In Classical Chinese, 星 (originally 晶 'three twinkling celestial bodies' above phonetic 生) denoted astronomical stars and planets; in the early 20th century, under the semantic influence of English 'movie star', 明星 and the bound root -星 acquired the sense of a famous entertainment figure.

history.meaning: celestial body; star; planet
bright star (Venus); film or theatrical celebrity (semantic loan from English 'star')
male celebrity; male film or television star

男星.notes: Primarily used in entertainment journalism, gossip columns, and industry talk as a punchy disyllabic counterpart to 女星 (nǚxīng, 'female star/actress').

男朋友.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound calqued in the 20th century from English 'boyfriend', combining 男 (nán, 'male') with 朋友 (péngyou, 'friend'). In Classical Chinese, 朋 (originally depicting two strings of cowrie shells, designating 'peer group, fellow') and 友 ('companion who lends a hand') formed a coordinative compound denoting platonic comrades or fellow disciples of a master; only in modern urban Chinese did prefixing 男/女 specialize the term into an exclusive romantic partner.

history.meaning: fellow disciples; peers and companions (coordinative compound)
male friend; romantic boyfriend (calque of English 'boyfriend')
boyfriend (romantic partner)

男朋友.notes: Unlike English 'male friend', 男朋友 by itself almost exclusively means romantic 'boyfriend'; to say 'a platonic male friend' without ambiguity, Mandarin speakers say 男性朋友 (nánxìng péngyou) or 男生朋友.

男神.etymology: A 21st-century Chinese internet and pop-culture neologism patterned by analogy on 女神 (nǚshén, 'goddess; idealized female crush'), combining 男 (nán, 'male') and 神 (shén, 'deity, god, divine spirit'). In Classical Chinese, 神 denoted celestial spirits and numinous powers; in contemporary youth and entertainment slang, 男神 elevates an exceptionally handsome, charismatic, or accomplished man into an object of quasi-religious admiration.

history.meaning: celestial spirit; deity; numinous vitality
goddess (mythological); idealized dream woman (slang extension)
male idol; dream guy; charismatic male celebrity or crush

男神.notes: Widely used both for A-list male celebrities and for an unattainable personal crush in everyday life; its humorous opposite in internet slang is 屌丝 (diǎosī, 'loser') or 渣男 (zhānán, 'scumbag/player').

rootFamily.gloss: expressions; look in one's eyes; charisma

男鞋.etymology: Attributive compound combining 男 ('men's, male') + 鞋 ('shoes').

history.meaning: men's shoes

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 男鞋 (via 萌典)

画.etymology: Associative compound (trad. 畫) combining 聿 ('writing/drawing brush held in hand') + 田/界 ('delineated field boundaries'). Originally meant 'to demarcate boundaries, draw lines', hence 'to paint, draw' and 'a painting, picture'.

morphemes.meaning: brush held in hand (in trad. 畫)

history.stage: Old Chinese (Bronze inscriptions) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: to delineate boundaries with a brush -> to draw, paint; painting

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 画 (via 萌典)

画框.etymology: A transparent compound joining 画 (huà, simplified from 畫, 'painting, drawing, picture') and 框 (kuàng, 'wooden frame', composed of the wood radical 木 and 匡 'rectangular basket/straight border'). Whereas traditional Chinese hanging scrolls were mounted on silk rollers (画轴), wooden 画框 became standard for displaying charcoal sketches, watercolours, and maps under glass.

history.meaning: wooden frame around a mounted picture
picture frame

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 画框

cognates.meaning: painting surface; screen; television image; frame
surface of a painting; screen image

画面.etymology: A modifier-head compound of 画 (huà, traditional 畫, 'painting, drawing, delineated image', originally depicting a brush 聿 tracing boundary lines around a field 田) and 面 (miàn, 'face, surface, plane'). Originally used in traditional Chinese art criticism to denote the physical surface and compositional plane of a scroll painting, it was extended in modern visual media (reinforced by Japanese *gamen*) to mean a film frame, camera shot, or television screen image.

history.meaning: the surface plane and visual composition of a painting
projected motion-picture image; photographic frame (reinforced by Japanese 画面 gamen)
screen image; camera shot; video feed; mental picture or tableau

画面.notes: In TV production, 画面 refers to the video feed or visual shot (as opposed to 声音/音频 'audio'), while in everyday speech 画面感 (huàmiàngǎn) describes how vividly a story or song evokes a mental movie.

界限.etymology: A classical coordinative compound (并列结构) pairing two near-synonyms: 界 (jiè, 'border between fields, boundary line') and 限 (xiàn, 'threshold, raised barrier, limit', composed of 阜 'mound/terraced steps' + phonetic 艮 'obstinate, stopping'). Attested from the Six Dynasties and Tang periods for physical and administrative borders, it later broadened to abstract moral, interpersonal, and conceptual boundaries.

history.meaning: field boundary + raised earthen threshold or barrier
territorial demarcation; administrative border between jurisdictions
boundary; dividing line; interpersonal or conceptual limit

界限.notes: Frequently collocated with 划清 (huàqīng jièxiàn, 'draw a clear line of demarcation / dissociate oneself from') or 模糊 (móhu jièxiàn, 'blur the boundaries'). Distinguish from 界线 (jièxiàn), which prefers physical border lines on maps or sports courts.

留.etymology: Phono-semantic/associative character combining 卯 (phonetic *ru) + 田 ('field'). Means 'to stay, remain behind, keep, detain, or leave something behind'.

history.meaning: to stay, remain; to keep, retain, leave behind

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 留 (via 萌典)

留下.etymology: A verb-directional/resultative compound (动趋结构) combining 留 (liú, 'to stay, remain, detain, keep behind', from Old Chinese *ru, graphically composed of phonetic 丣 above 田 'field', denoting halting and remaining in a cultivated settlement) with the directional complement 下 (xià, 'down; to settle into a fixed state'). Here 下 loses its literal vertical sense and grammaticalizes into a resultative marker indicating that a person or object remains behind in a stable position after others depart.

history.meaning: to halt; remain in place; detain; keep behind
to leave behind; to stay behind (verb + directional/resultative complement)
to stay on; remain behind; to leave (something/someone) behind

morphemes.meaning: down; resultative marker of settling or remaining in place

留下.notes: Ambitransitive: intransitively it means 'to stay behind / stay on at a company' (我决定留下 'I decided to stay'), and transitively it means 'to leave something behind' (留下深刻印象 'leave a deep impression').

rootFamily.gloss: to stay on; remain here (with speaker-oriented 来)
to keep a souvenir; take a commemorative photo

留下来.etymology: A verb with a complex directional complement (复合趋向补语) formed from the root verb 留 (liú, 'to stay, remain') + the compound directional suffix 下来 (xiàlái, literally 'down-come'). In Mandarin aspectual grammar, 下来 grammaticalizes from spatial downward motion toward the speaker into a resultative-continuative marker indicating that the subject settles into a state of remaining at the current deictic location ('here with us') continuing from the past into the present or future.

history.meaning: to stay; halt; remain behind
to remain behind at the speaker's location or persist down to the present
to stay on (here); remain behind; be preserved down through time

morphemes.meaning: down; settling into a fixed state
hither; deictic orientation toward the speaker or present moment

留下来.notes: Adding 来 to 留下 anchors the viewpoint at the current place or group ('stay here with us / stay on at this company'), making 留下来 warmer and more conversational when persuading a colleague or loved one not to leave.

rootFamily.gloss: to persist;persevere through to the present

留在.etymology: A verb-complement construction (动补结构) combining 留 (liú, 'to stay, remain, keep') with the locative prepositional/resultative complement 在 (zài, 'to be located at, reside in'). In Classical Chinese, 留 was followed by the locative preposition 於/于 (liú yú...); during the medieval vernacular transition, 在 replaced 於 as the post-verbal locative complement, fusing prosodically with 留 to introduce the exact place where someone or something remains.

history.meaning: to remain at; be detained in (a place)
to stay at; remain in (locative complement replacing 於)
to stay at; remain in; keep (something) in a place

留在.notes: 留在 must always be followed by a location or abstract domain (e.g., 留在北京 'stay in Beijing', 留在公司 'stay at the company', 留在记忆里 'remain in one's memory'); it cannot stand at the end of a sentence without an object.

cognates.meaning: studying abroad (historically coined in Tang relations)

留学.etymology: A classical Sino-Japanese-Chinese compound of 留 (liú, 'to stay behind, remain') and 学 (xué, traditional 學, 'to study, pursue learning'). First attested in Tang dynasty historical records and Japanese Nara/Heian court documents (such as *Shoku Nihongi*) referring to Japanese envoys who remained behind in Chang'an to continue their studies after diplomatic missions returned home (留学生, *ryūgakusei*), the term was revitalized in late 19th-century Meiji Japan and re-adopted in China for modern overseas education.

history.meaning: (of foreign envoys/monks) to remain behind in the Tang capital to study after a mission departs
to travel to and reside in a foreign country for modern academic study
to study abroad (separable verb: 留过学)

留学.notes: Grammatically a separable verb (离合词): aspect particles and durations go between the two characters (e.g., 留了三年学 'studied abroad for three years'), and the destination is introduced with 去 or 到 before the verb (去英国留学 'go to the UK to study abroad').

rootFamily.gloss: to visit for academic exchange; visiting scholar

cognates.meaning: staying behind to watch the house; absence from home (rusu)
staying behind to guard the capital or home

留守.etymology: A classical coordinative/serial-verb compound combining 留 (liú, 'to remain behind') and 守 (shǒu, 'to guard, defend, keep watch over', composed of 宀 'roof' over 寸 'hand/law'). Attested in the *Shiji* (*Records of the Grand Historian*) and Han-Tang administrative usage for garrison commanders or regents who remained behind to guard the capital while the emperor was away on campaign, it now refers both to staff staying behind to mind an office during holidays and to rural children or elders left behind by migrant workers.

history.meaning: to remain behind to guard the capital or garrison while the ruler is on campaign; viceroy title (Tang–Song)
to stay behind to mind headquarters, an office, or a home
to stay behind to hold the fort (at work); left-behind (rural children/elderly)

morphemes.meaning: to stay behind; remain in place

留守.notes: In workplace dramas, 留守 means staying at the office or studio to handle emergencies while the main team travels on location; note the false friend in Japanese, where 留守 (rusu) shifted to mean 'being away from home'.

rootFamily.gloss: left-behind children (in rural areas while parents work in cities)
to guard; defend; hold fast to

cognates.meaning: paying attention; keeping in mind; taking heed

留意.etymology: A classical verb-object compound (动宾结构) formed from 留 (liú, 'to keep, detain, fix in place') and 意 (yì, 'thought, mind, attention, intention', composed of 音 'sound/voice' over 心 'heart-mind'). First attested in Han dynasty texts such as the *Book of Han* (*Hanshu*), literally meaning 'to detain or rest one's mind upon something', hence to take heed, pay careful attention, or keep a watchful eye out for something.

history.meaning: to fix one's thoughts upon; give careful consideration to (verb-object)
to be mindful of; keep an eye out for
to pay close attention to; look out for; take note of

morphemes.meaning: to keep; hold; fix in place

留意.notes: Slightly softer and more observational than 注意 (zhùyì, 'pay attention / watch out'): 留意 often implies keeping an eye or ear open for subtle clues, opportunities, or someone's wellbeing (帮我留意一下 'keep an eye out for me').

rootFamily.gloss: to take care; be careful; pay attention (similar VO structure)
to pay attention to; take note of
to care about; mind; take to heart

留着.etymology: A verb-aspect combination consisting of 留 (liú, 'to keep, retain, save, let grow') followed by the durative/continuous aspect particle 着 (zhe, historically grammaticalized in Tang-Song vernacular Chinese from the verb 著 zhuó 'to attach, adhere, remain in contact'). The suffix 着 marks the enduring resultant state of keeping something on hand or reserving it for future use.

history.meaning: to keep + to attach/adhere (serial verbs in medieval vernacular)
keeping in a continuous state; saving on hand
to keep on hand; save for later; continue wearing (hair/beard)

morphemes.meaning: to keep; save; retain; let grow (hair)
durative aspect marker indicating a maintained state

留着.notes: Used both for saving physical/digital items or energy for later (留着以后用 'save it for later use') and for maintaining a hairstyle or facial hair (留着长发 'wearing one's hair long').

rootFamily.gloss: to keep on hand; hold in reserve

留给.etymology: Verb-complement compound combining 留 ('to keep, save, leave behind') + 给 (trad. 給, recipient marker 'for, to').

history.meaning: to leave for; to save or bequeath to someone

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 留给 (via 萌典)

留言.etymology: Verb-object/noun compound combining 留 ('to leave behind') + 言 ('words, spoken or written message'). Attested in Tang–Song literature for parting words or inscriptions, now also a written note or voice/text message left for someone.

history.meaning: words left behind; to leave a message

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 留言 (via 萌典)

略显.etymology: A literary modifier-head verbal compound combining the degree adverb 略 (lüè, 'slightly, briefly, somewhat', originally meaning to trace land boundaries around a field 田 + phonetic 各, later extending to 'outline, summary, slightly') with the copular/manifestative verb 显 (xiǎn, traditional 顯, 'to appear, manifest, look visibly', originally depicting silk threads illuminated in sunlight 日 + 丝 + 页). Together they form a concise disyllabic verb meaning 'to appear slightly' or 'to look somewhat'.

history.meaning: to trace field boundaries → briefly, slightly / to be manifest in sunlight → appear visibly
to appear somewhat; show slight signs of (literary adverb + verb)
history.stage: Late Imperial and Modern Literary Chinese

history.meaning: appear slightly; seem somewhat (followed by two-syllable adjectives)

略显.notes: Belongs to a polished written or journalistic register (书面语) and almost always takes a disyllabic adjective expressing a subtle flaw, fatigue, or emotion as its complement (e.g., 略显疲惫 'appear slightly exhausted', 略显尴尬 'seem somewhat awkward').

番茄.etymology: Botanical naming compound of 番 ('foreign, introduced from overseas', originally referring to non-Han borderlands and maritime trade) + 茄 ('eggplant/nightshade fruit', plant radical 艹 + 加), literally 'foreign eggplant' after tomatoes arrived via maritime trade in the Ming dynasty.

history.meaning: tomato (Solanum lycopersicum)
tomato

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 番茄

疏忽.etymology: A classical coordinative compound (并列结构) uniting 疏 (shū, 'wide-meshed, sparse, lax, inattentive', originally depicting a foot 疋 emerging smoothly at birth 㐬, hence 'unobstructed, widely spaced, lax') and 忽 (hū, 'to disregard, overlook, suddenly forget', composed of 勿 'do not / banner fluttering away' over 心 'heart-mind'). Attested in Han-Tang prose (such as the *Shiji* and *Book of Han*), it describes mental laxity where details slip through wide gaps in one's attention.

history.meaning: wide-meshed, lax + to disregard in the heart-mind
careless; lax and neglectful in official duties
to neglect; overlook; negligence or oversight (verb and noun)

疏忽.notes: Functions both as a verb ('to neglect/overlook through carelessness', e.g., 疏忽了一个细节) and as a noun ('an oversight/lapse', e.g., 这是我的疏忽 'this was my oversight'); often paired in the four-character idiom 疏忽大意.

疏远.etymology: A classical coordinative compound combining 疏 (shū, 'sparse, dispersed, relationally distant', in contrast to 亲 qīn 'intimate, close kin') and 远 (yuǎn, traditional 遠, 'far away, distant, to keep at a distance'). Attested in Warring States and Han texts (such as *Xunzi* and *Shiji*), where 远 was frequently used causatively ('to treat as distant, keep away from'), 疏远 describes both the state of an estranged relationship and the active verb of distancing oneself from someone.

history.meaning: genealogically or politically distant from the ruler; to keep advisers at a distance
estranged in friendship or family ties; to drift apart
to distance oneself from; shun; drift apart; estranged (verb and adjective)

morphemes.meaning: sparse; not close; estranged (opposite of 亲)
far; distant; to keep at a distance

疏远.notes: Can be used transitively for deliberately shunning someone (他开始疏远我 'he started distancing himself from me') or intransitively/adjectivally for mutual drifting apart over time (关系变得疏远了 'the relationship grew distant').

rootFamily.gloss: to stay away from; keep far from
degrees of kinship/intimacy; close and distant

疯.etymology: A phono-semantic compound (形声字) composed of the sickness radical 疒 (nè, depicting a person lying on a sickbed) and the phonetic component 风 (fēng, traditional 風, 'wind', Old Chinese *pəŋ, Middle Chinese *pjuwng). In traditional Chinese medicine, 'head wind' (頭風) and internal wind pathogens were believed to cause paralysis, convulsions, leprosy (麻疯), and erratic mental derangement; by the Song-Yuan vernacular period, 疯 had specialized from neurological 'wind-illness' into the primary word for madness, insanity, and wild frenzy.

history.meaning: head-wind illness (頭病); chronic headache, paralysis, or leprosy caused by wind pathogens
mental derangement; madness; insanity
to go crazy; insane; mad; wild or frenzied (with work or excitement)

morphemes.meaning: illness radical (疒) + wind phonetic/pathogen (风) → madness; go crazy

疯.notes: In everyday speech and workplace dramas, 疯 is constantly used hyperbolically for working or acting with frantic intensity: 快忙疯了 ('nearly driven crazy with busyness'), 想疯了 ('miss someone like crazy'), or 疯抢 ('snap up in a frenzy').

rootFamily.gloss: to go mad; lose one's temper or mind (VO compound)

疯婆子.etymology: A colloquial modifier-head compound combining 疯 (fēng, 'crazy, mad, deranged') + 婆 (pó, 'old woman, married woman, matron', originally a phono-semantic character with 女 'woman' and phonetic 波 bō) + the nominal suffix 子 (zi, neutral tone). In Ming-Qing vernacular fiction, 婆子 denoted an older female servant or formidable matron; prefixed with 疯, it became a vivid derogatory term for an unhinged, hysterical, or fiercely erratic woman.

history.meaning: elderly woman; grandmother; matron
older woman; female servant or matron (often mildly colloquial or rough)
crazy woman; madwoman; hysterical or frantic woman (derogatory/jocular)

疯婆子.notes: Either a harsh insult toward an erratic woman or used in self-deprecating humor by women describing themselves when disheveled, sleep-deprived, or stressed out (e.g., 忙得像个疯婆子 'so busy I look like a madwoman').

疼.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形声字) composed of the sickness radical 疒 (nè, 'sickbed, illness') and the phonetic component 冬 (dōng, 'winter', Old Chinese *tˁuŋ, Middle Chinese *tuwng; compare 疼 Middle Chinese *duwng). Emerging in medieval Chinese (attested in the *Guangyun* rime dictionary with the gloss '痛也', 'to ache, hurt'), 疼 gradually became the primary northern Mandarin verb for physical pain, aching, and—by emotional extension from 'one's heart aching for a child'—tender doting affection.

history.meaning: to ache; hurt physically (glossed as 痛也 in Guangyun)
to ache; feel physical pain; to dote on tenderly (as if feeling their pain)
to hurt; ache; to love dearly / dote on

morphemes.meaning: sickness radical (疒) + phonetic 冬 (dōng/téng) → to hurt; ache; dote on

疼.notes: Has two distinct everyday uses: intransitive 'to ache/hurt' (头疼 'have a headache', favored in northern spoken Mandarin over 痛 tòng) and transitive 'to dote on / cherish tenderly' (他很疼老婆 'he dotes on his wife').

rootFamily.gloss: to feel heartache for someone; love dearly; begrudge spending
to love dearly; dote on (a child or partner)

病.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形声字) combining the sickness radical 疒 (nè, depicting a person lying prostrate on a bed) with the phonetic component 丙 (bǐng, Old Chinese *praŋʔ; compare 病 Old Chinese *[b]raŋ-s, Middle Chinese *bjaengH). In Classical Chinese (as noted in the *Analects* and *Shuowen Jiezi*: '疾加也'), 疾 (jí) denoted an ordinary or sudden illness, whereas 病 specifically meant a *severe* or worsening illness; by the Han-Six Dynasties period, 病 generalized to become the standard word for any illness or disease.

history.meaning: severe or critical illness (specifically a worsening of 疾 jí); exhaustion; fault
illness; disease in general (replacing 疾 in vernacular usage); to fall ill
illness; ailment; disease; defect; to fall sick

morphemes.meaning: sickbed radical (疒) + phonetic 丙 (bǐng) → illness; disease; fall ill

病.notes: In Classical Chinese idioms, remember that 病 originally meant 'critically ill' or 'flaw/fault' (as in 语病 'grammatical flaw' or 诟病 'criticize as a fault'), whereas in modern speech 生病 (shēngbìng) is the standard verb-object phrase for 'getting sick'.

rootFamily.gloss: to fall ill; get sick (VO compound)

病人.etymology: A transparent modifier-head compound combining 病 (bìng, 'illness; sick') and 人 (rén, 'person, human being'). Attested since the Six Dynasties and Tang periods (e.g., in medical treatises and Buddhist scriptures translating Sanskrit *glāna* 'sick person'), it serves in Modern Mandarin as the standard everyday word for both a 'sick person' at home and a 'medical patient' under hospital care.

history.meaning: person suffering from an illness; invalid
medical patient; sick person under treatment

病人.notes: 病人 is the universal spoken and written term for 'patient'; in formal hospital signage or clinical reports, 患者 (huànzhě, 'sufferer of a condition') is often used as a more technical and respectful synonym.

病危.etymology: A classical subject-predicate (主谓结构) compound formed from 病 (bìng, 'illness, medical condition') as the topic/subject and 危 (wēi, 'precarious, perilous, in mortal danger', originally depicting a person 人 crouching atop a steep cliff 厂 above a kneeling figure 卩) as the predicate. Literally 'one's illness is precarious/life-threatening', it has been used in medical and biographical writing since imperial times to indicate that a patient is near death.

history.meaning: precipitous; lofty and precarious; in mortal danger
one's illness becomes life-threatening; critically ill (subject-predicate)
to be critically ill; in critical condition (hospital prognosis)

病危.notes: A high-stakes dramatic term in television series, frequently appearing in the hospital phrase 下达病危通知书 (xiàdá bìngwēi tōngzhīshū, 'issue a critical condition notice to the family').

rootFamily.gloss: serious illness; to be gravely ill

cognates.meaning: nature or condition of an illness; patient's condition
patient's condition; state of an illness
state or progression of an illness

病情.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 病 (bìng, 'illness, disease') and 情 (qíng, 'actual state of affairs, circumstances, condition'). While 情 (composed of 心 'heart' + phonetic 青 qīng) meant 'innate feelings, passions' in philosophical Classical Chinese, in legal, military, and medical prose it developed the crucial secondary sense of 'objective reality, actual circumstances' (as in 军情 'military situation' or 实情 'true facts'); thus 病情 means 'the actual state and clinical progression of an illness'.

history.meaning: innate emotions; genuine reality; actual state of affairs (情况)
manifestations and actual state of a patient's disease
history.stage: Medieval and Late Imperial Chinese medical prose

history.meaning: patient's condition; clinical course or severity of an illness

morphemes.meaning: condition; state of affairs; circumstances (clipped from 情况)

病情.notes: Note that 情 here means 'condition/situation' (情况), not 'emotion' (感情)! Common medical collocations include 病情稳定 ('condition is stable'), 病情恶化 ('condition worsened'), and 隐瞒病情 ('conceal the diagnosis/condition').

cognates.word: 病室 (びょうしつ) / 病房 (びょうぼう)

病房.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正结构) combining 病 (bìng, 'illness, disease, sick person', Old Chinese *N-praŋ-s, phono-semantic with 疒 'sickness' radical and 丙 phonetic) and 房 (fáng, 'side-room, chamber, house', Old Chinese *Cə-baŋ). Originally in Tang and Song dynasty monastic and residential architecture, 病房 denoted a quiet side-chamber or infirmary room reserved for nursing the sick; in modern medical terminology, it became the standard term for a hospital inpatient room or ward.

history.meaning: monastic infirmary chamber or private sickroom in a residence
hospital inpatient room or clinical ward

病房.notes: Standard hospital term; distinguish from 病床 (sickbed/hospital bed) and 诊室 (consultation room). Common collocations include 住院病房 (inpatient ward) and 重症监护病房 (ICU).

痒.etymology: Simplified from 癢, a phono-semantic character combining the sickness/symptom radical 疒 with phonetic 養 (*yǎng*, Middle Chinese *yangX*). Denotes both a skin itch and, by playful figurative extension (手痒, 心里痒痒), an eager restlessness to try one's hand at something.

history.meaning: itch; irritation of the skin
itchy; itching to do something

痕迹.etymology: A coordinative synonym compound (并列结构) uniting 痕 (hén, 'scar, welt, mark left by a wound', phono-semantic with 疒 'sickness' and 艮 phonetic, Old Chinese *gˤən) and 迹 (jì, traditional 跡/蹟, 'footprint, track, vestige', with 辶 'walk' and 亦/責 phonetic, Old Chinese *tsjek). Both characters denote physical impressions left behind—one on the skin, the other on the ground—which fused in post-Han literary prose to signify any physical or metaphorical trace, clue, or digital/documentary footprint.

history.meaning: physical scar on skin (痕) and footprint on the ground (跡)
visible mark, impression, or vestige left behind by an object or event
physical trace, artistic brushwork sign, or audit/digital footprint in records

痕迹.notes: Frequently pairs with 留 (leave behind) or 抹去 (erase), as in 不留痕迹 ('leave no trace', used both for seamless acting/production editing and for covering up wrongdoing).

痛下杀手.etymology: A four-character adverbial-verb-object idiom (偏正+动宾结构) composed of 痛 (tòng, 'painfully, bitterly, thoroughly, ruthlessly'), 下 (xià, 'to apply, to strike, to deliver [a blow or move]'), and 杀手 (shāshǒu, originally 'a lethal move or killing blow' in martial arts and board games, from 杀 'to kill' + 手 'hand/move/technique', distinct from its modern homograph meaning 'assassin'). Literally 'to ruthlessly deliver a lethal hand/move', it evolved from late imperial vernacular fiction into a vivid idiom for taking merciless, decisive action against a rival.

history.meaning: to deliver a fatal martial blow or treacherous strike
to strike a ruthless blow; to mercilessly cut, eliminate, or crush a competitor

痛下杀手.notes: In corporate and media drama (*Behind the Scenes*), it is used figuratively for ruthlessly axing a program, firing staff, or crushing a business competitor. Compare 杀手锏 (trump card / lethal weapon).

rootFamily.gloss: to start, to put one's hand to

痛快.etymology: A compound combining 痛 (tòng, originally 'physical pain', Old Chinese *l̥ˤoŋ-s, which grammaticalized in Han–Six Dynasties Chinese into an intensive degree adverb meaning 'to an extreme, thoroughly, keenly') and 快 (kuài, 'cheerful, brisk, gratified, sharp'). Rather than meaning 'painful and happy', the structure is adverbial-head or intensive coordinative: 'keenly gratifying, thoroughly brisk and uninhibited'. In vernacular Mandarin, its pronunciation softened to neutral tone on the second syllable (tòngkuai) with the sense of 'cathartic, forthright, without hesitation'.

history.meaning: intensely gratifying, incisive and exhilarating (especially of speech or writing)
joyful to one's heart's content; straightforward, forthright, brisk

痛快.notes: Notice how 痛 acts as an intensifier ('keenly/thoroughly'), not literal 'pain'. Used both for emotional catharsis (哭个痛快 'have a good cry') and personality/dealing (说话很痛快 'speak forthrightly without beating around the bush').

rootFamily.gloss: to drink to one's heart's content

痛恨.etymology: A modifier-head verbal compound (偏正结构) formed from 痛 (tòng, 'painfully, bitterly, deeply, to the bone') modifying 恨 (hèn, 'to resent, to regret, to hate', Old Chinese *gˤəns, phono-semantic with 忄 'heart' and 艮 phonetic). In Classical Chinese, 恨 primarily meant 'bitter regret or remorse' before shifting in post-Han and vernacular Chinese toward 'hatred, detestation'; hence 痛恨 evolved from 'to bitterly lament/regret' in Han historiography to 'to detest, abhor, and hate bitterly' in modern Mandarin.

history.meaning: to feel bitter remorse, deep regret, or grieving resentment
history.stage: Classical / Han Literary Chinese (e.g., Chu Shi Biao)

history.meaning: to detest, abhor, and hate bitterly

痛恨.notes: A famous Classical false friend appears in Zhuge Liang's *Chu Shi Biao* (未尝不叹息痛恨于桓、灵也), where 痛恨 meant 'bitterly regret/lament', whereas in modern Chinese 痛恨 strictly means 'bitterly detest/abhor' (often in 深恶痛绝 / 令人痛恨).

瘦.etymology: A monomorphemic phono-semantic character (形声字) combining the sickness radical 疒 (nè, indicating a bodily condition) with the phonetic component 叟 (sǒu, 'old man', Old Chinese *s-ruʔ), reconstructing to Old Chinese *s-ru-s and Middle Chinese *srjuwH. As recorded in *Shuowen Jiezi* (瘦，臞也), it originally denoted pathological emaciation or wasting away from illness (implied by 疒), before generalizing to describe any slender body build, tight-fitting clothing, or lean meat (瘦肉).

history.meaning: emaciated, wasted, gaunt from illness or hunger
thin, slim, slender (of people); lean (of meat); tight-fitting (of clothes)

瘦.notes: Antonym of 胖 (pàng, fat/plump for people) and 肥 (féi, fatty for meat/animals, or loose for clothes). In showbiz contexts, 上镜显胖 ('the camera adds pounds') makes 瘦身 (slimming down) a constant preoccupation for on-screen talent.

瘫痪.etymology: A coordinative medical compound (并列结构) uniting 瘫 (tān, traditional 癱, 'numbing palsy, paralysis', phono-semantic with 疒 'sickness' and 难/難 phonetic) and 痪 (huàn, 'weakness or paralysis of the limbs', phono-semantic with 疒 and 奂/奐 phonetic, which is etymologically tied to 涣 'dispersed, slackened, dissolved'). Coined in Song–Ming traditional Chinese medicine for motor paralysis caused by wind-stroke (中风), it expanded metaphorically in the 20th century to describe the complete breakdown or freeze of traffic, institutions, or computer servers.

history.meaning: motor paralysis or palsy of the limbs in traditional medicine
to be medically paralyzed; (figuratively) to grind to a halt, crash, or collapse (of traffic, networks, or organizations)

瘫痪.notes: In media and tech contexts, 系统瘫痪 or 网络瘫痪 describes a server crash or network outage caused by a sudden surge in traffic (e.g., when a celebrity scandal or live broadcast overwhelms a platform).

rootFamily.gloss: hemiplegia, paralysis of one side of the body
to slump down, collapse limp on the ground

登入.etymology: A verb-complement compound (动补结构) formed from 登 (dēng, 'to ascend, mount, or enter into an official register', Old Chinese *tˤəŋ) and the directional complement 入 (rù, 'to enter into', Old Chinese *njup). In Literary Chinese, 登入 meant literally 'to ascend and enter (a hall or carriage)' or 'to record into a ledger'; in late 20th-century computing, it was adopted as a calque for English 'log in / sign in', conceptualizing user authentication as registering and stepping inside a digital system.

history.meaning: to ascend and enter a chamber; to enter items into an official register
to log in or sign in to a computer system, account, or website

登入.notes: Near-synonymous with 登录 (dēnglù) in computing; 登入 is default in Taiwan, Hong Kong, and macOS/iOS localization, while 登录 is preferred in Mainland China UI standards, though both are universally understood. Antonym: 登出 (log out).

cognates.meaning: to go on stage, mount the podium
to take the stage, mount the platform

登台.etymology: A verb-object compound (动宾结构) combining 登 (dēng, 'to step up, ascend, mount', Old Chinese *tˤəŋ, pictographically footsteps 癶 stepping up onto a sacrificial vessel 豆) and 台 (tái, traditional 臺, 'raised earthen terrace, viewing platform, theatrical stage'). In Classical Chinese poetry and history, 登臺 meant climbing a high terrace to gaze afar; with the rise of elevated opera stages in Song–Yuan–Ming China, it specialized into 'mounting the stage to perform or speak'.

history.meaning: to ascend a raised earthen terrace or observation tower
to go on stage to perform (in opera/theater) or step onto a podium in public life

登台.notes: Focuses on the physical act of going up onto a stage or podium to perform or speak (e.g., 登台演出 'perform on stage', 登台亮相 'make a stage appearance'). Antonym: 下台 (step down from the stage / leave office).

rootFamily.gloss: to step down from the stage; to fall from power

cognates.meaning: to enter the stage, make an appearance (of a character)
to appear on stage, enter the scene

登场.etymology: A verb-object compound (动宾结构) formed from 登 (dēng, 'to ascend, step onto') and 场 (chǎng, traditional 場, 'leveled ceremonial ground, threshing floor, arena, performance venue', phono-semantic with 土 'earth' and 易/ phonetic). Originally denoting stepping into an imperial examination hall or theatrical arena in Tang–Ming Chinese, it was also reinforced in modern Chinese by Japanese theatrical and literary usage (登場 *tōjō*) to mean a character, performer, or new product making its entrance onto the scene.

history.meaning: to enter the threshing ground, examination hall, or performance arena
to take the stage; to make an entrance in a show, narrative, or market (e.g., 闪亮登场)

登场.notes: Broader and more dramatic than 登台: while 登台 refers literally to walking onto a physical stage, 登场 is used for TV/film entrances, characters appearing in a script, or products launching (often in 闪亮登场 / 隆重登场 'make a grand entrance'). Antonym: 退场 (exit the stage).

rootFamily.gloss: to come on stage, appear on the scene

cognates.meaning: registration, entry in a record; login

登录.etymology: A coordinative / verb-object compound (并列/动宾结构) combining 登 (dēng, 'to ascend; by extension, to enter or post an item onto an official roll', as in 登载) and 录 (lù, traditional 錄, 'to copy down, inscribe, record in a register', Old Chinese *p.rok). In Tang–Song administrative Chinese, 登录 meant 'to inscribe names or deeds into an imperial register'. Re-popularized via Japanese *tōroku* (登録, 'registration') in modern legal/commercial administration, it later became Mainland China's standard term for 'logging in' to a digital network or 'landing on' a broadcast platform.

history.meaning: to record or enroll candidates and officials into an official register
to register officially; to log in to a computer/account; (media) to debut or air on a broadcast channel

morphemes.meaning: post, enter onto a roll, mount

登录.notes: Do not confuse with its homophone 登陆 (dēnglù, 'to make landfall / land on shore'). Note that in Mainland entertainment news, 登陆某卫视 ('land on X satellite TV') uses 陆, whereas 登录网站 ('log in to a website') uses 录!

rootFamily.gloss: to record (audio/video), take down in writing

登记.etymology: Coordinative verb compound combining 登 ('to ascend; to enter/record in an official register') + 记 (trad. 記, 'to record in writing'). Used for officially registering a name, item, or check-in.

history.meaning: to enter in a register; to register, check in

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 登记 (via 萌典)

登记本.etymology: Compound of 登记 ('enter in a register', 登 'ascend/enter on an official roll' + 记 'write down/record') + 本 ('bound notebook or volume', originally a mark at the base of 木 'tree', extended via bamboo/paper bindings to books).

history.meaning: registration ledger
guest book; register ledger

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 登记本

白.etymology: Ancient character in oracle-bone script (variously analyzed as a pictograph of a thumb nail, a whiterice/acorn kernel, or the rising sun's bright rays). Denotes the color 'white', 'bright/clear', 'plain/blank', and 'in vain'.

morphemes.meaning: bright ray / white kernel -> white, clear, plain

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: white; bright, clear; blank, plain; in vain

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 白 (via 萌典)

白天.etymology: Compound of 白 ('white; bright daylight', depicting a bright ray of sunlight or candle flame) + 天 ('sky; day'). Literally 'the bright part of the day', contrasting with 晚上 ('evening') and 夜里 ('nighttime').

history.meaning: daylight hours; daytime
daytime; by day

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 白天

白板.etymology: Attributive compound combining 白 ('white, blank') + 板 ('board, plank'). Historically denoted an uncarved blank tablet (or the blank white tile in Mahjong); in modern offices and classrooms, a dry-erase 'whiteboard'.

history.meaning: blank board -> dry-erase whiteboard

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 白板 (via 萌典)

白水.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正结构) combining 白 (bái, 'white, clear, unadorned, plain', Old Chinese *bˤrak) and 水 (shuǐ, 'water', Old Chinese *s.turʔ). In Classical Chinese (e.g., *Zuo Zhuan*), 白水 denoted 'clear, limpid river water'; in vernacular Mandarin, 白 acquired the sense of 'unflavored, without additives' (as in 白饭 'plain rice' or 白味 'plain taste'), making 白水 (often expanded as 白开水) the everyday word for plain drinking water as opposed to tea, broth, or alcohol.

history.meaning: clear, limpid, unmuddied stream water
plain water (especially boiled drinking water without tea leaves or flavoring)

白水.notes: In everyday speech, 白水 and 白开水 both mean plain (usually boiled) drinking water, contrasting with 茶水 (tea) or 饮料 (beverages). To cook meat or vegetables in plain water without soy sauce is called 白水煮.

rootFamily.gloss: plain, insipid, lacking flavor or excitement

白痴.etymology: A modifier-head or descriptive compound (偏正结构) joining 白 (bái, 'blank, empty, uncomprehending, pure') and 痴 (chī, traditional 癡, 'foolish, witless, mentally dull', phono-semantic with 疒 'sickness' and 疑 'doubt/hesitate'). Attested in Six Dynasties and Tang texts (and Buddhist translations comparing spiritual ignorance to a blank folly), it was adopted in Meiji Japan (白痴 *hakuchi*) as the clinical psychiatric translation for severe intellectual disability ('idiocy'), then re-entered modern Mandarin where it now functions primarily as a colloquial insult ('idiot') or self-deprecating suffix ('hopeless novice at X', e.g., 路痴).

history.meaning: blank-minded folly; congenital dullness of wit
clinical idiocy (via Meiji Japanese medical usage); colloquial 'idiot' or 'person clueless about a domain'

白痴.notes: Used both as a sharp insult ('idiot!') and productively as a playful suffix for someone hopeless at a specific skill: 路痴 (no sense of direction), 音痴 (tone-deaf), 电脑白痴 (computer-illiterate).

rootFamily.gloss: person with no sense of direction

白白.etymology: An AA-pattern reduplicated adverb (叠音词) formed from 白 (bái, Old Chinese *bˤrak). From its primary sense of 'white, unadorned, blank', 白 underwent semantic extension in post-Tang vernacular Chinese to mean 'empty-handed, without return or compensation, in vain' (compare English 'blank' in 'draw a blank'). Reduplicating 白 into 白白 intensifies the adverbial force: 'completely in vain, for no reason at all, with zero gain'.

history.meaning: white, plain, empty, unrewarded
in vain, to no purpose, for nothing (adverbial reduplication)

白白.notes: Almost always precedes a verb of loss, expenditure, or suffering: 白白浪费 (waste in vain), 白白错过 (miss out for nothing), 白白辛苦一场 (work hard all for naught).

rootFamily.gloss: for nothing, in vain; plain and clear
for free, without paying; in vain (adv.)

白砂糖.etymology: Three-character culinary compound from 白 ('white; refined') + 砂 ('granules like fine sand', stone 石 + 少) + 糖 ('sugar', grain 米 + phonetic 唐). Named for its sparkling, sand-like crystalline grains refined from sugarcane or sugar beet juice.

history.meaning: refined white granulated sugar
white granulated sugar; caster sugar

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 白砂糖

白纸包.etymology: Three-character nominal phrase combining 白纸 (trad. 白紙, 'white paper') + 包 ('wrapped bundle, packet'). Literally 'a packet wrapped in white paper'.

history.meaning: white-paper packet; bundle wrapped in white paper

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 白纸包 (via 萌典)

白费.etymology: An adverbial-verb compound (偏正结构) combining the vernacular adverb 白 (bái, 'in vain, fruitlessly, without result', evolved from 'blank/empty') with the verb 费 (fèi, 'to expend, consume, squander, waste', Old Chinese *pʰəs, phono-semantic with 贝 'cowrie/money' and 弗 phonetic). Attested in Ming–Qing vernacular novels (such as *Dream of the Red Chamber*), it literally means 'to expend (effort, resources, or words) for zero return'.

history.meaning: to expend money, energy, or speech fruitlessly
to go to waste, be in vain, squander effort for nothing

白费.notes: Frequently takes abstract nouns of effort or speech as objects: 白费力气 / 白费劲 (waste one's energy), 白费苦心 (waste one's painstaking efforts), 白费口舌 (waste one's breath talking).

rootFamily.gloss: to take great pains, rack one's brains in vain

白跑一趟.etymology: A four-character vernacular verbal phrase structured as adverbial + verb + verbal-classifier complement (状语+动词+动量补语): 白 (bái, 'in vain, fruitlessly') + 跑 (pǎo, 'to run, to travel on an errand') + 一 (yī, 'one') + 趟 (tàng, verbal measure word for a round trip or journey). In colloquial Mandarin, 跑一趟 means 'to make a trip somewhere (often to handle business)'; prefixing 白 yields 'to make the whole trip for nothing'.

history.meaning: to make a journey or errand in vain without accomplishing one's purpose

白跑一趟.notes: A classic everyday conversational phrase: e.g., 幸好先打了电话，不然又白跑一趟 ('Good thing I called ahead, otherwise I would have made a trip in vain'). Note that 趟 (tàng) is the specific classifier for trips.

rootFamily.gloss: to work hard in vain, busy oneself for nothing
to run errands, work as a field reporter/courier

百.etymology: Phono-semantic character in oracle-bone and bronze inscriptions formed from 一 ('one') + 白 (phonetic *pˁrak). Represents the numeral 'hundred' (100) and figuratively 'all kinds of, numerous' (百花, 百姓).

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: one hundred; numerous, all kinds of

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 百 (via 萌典)

百万.etymology: A multiplicative numeral compound (偏正数词结构) combining 百 (bǎi, 'hundred', 10², Old Chinese *pˤrak) and 万 (wàn, traditional 萬, originally a pictograph of a scorpion borrowed phonetically in Shang oracle bones for the myriad unit 10⁴, 'ten thousand', Old Chinese *maŋ-s). Because the Chinese numeral system groups large numbers by myriads (万进, powers of 10⁴) rather than thousands (10³), 'one million' (10⁶) is expressed as 'one hundred myriads' (100 × 10,000 = 百万).

history.meaning: one hundred myriads (1,000,000); figuratively an immense army or vast multitude
one million (1,000,000); used attributively for 'million-level' (e.g., 百万富翁 millionaire)

百万.notes: When translating quickly between English and Chinese numbers, remember the benchmark: 1 万 = 10 thousand, 10 万 = 100 thousand, and 100 万 (百万) = 1 million. In showbiz, 百万调音师 ('million-yuan audio engineer') is slang for heavy autotune!

rootFamily.gloss: tens of millions; by all means /千萬 be sure to

百亿.etymology: A multiplicative numeral compound (偏正数词结构) combining 百 (bǎi, 'one hundred', 10²) and 亿 (yì, traditional 億, 'one hundred million', 10⁸). In early Classical Chinese, 億 originally meant 10⁵ ('ten myriads') under the lower-scale system (下数), before standardizing under the myriad-myriad system (万万为亿, 10⁴ × 10⁴ = 10⁸). Multiplying 百 (10²) by 亿 (10⁸) yields 10¹⁰, i.e., 'ten billion' in short-scale English.

history.meaning: countless multitudes; in Buddhist cosmology, 'a hundred亿 worlds' (百亿日月)

百亿.notes: Mental conversion tip: since 1 亿 = 100 million (0.1 billion), 10 亿 = 1 billion, and 百亿 (100 亿) = 10 billion. Common in entertainment industry headlines like 百亿票房先生 ('ten-billion-yuan box-office actor') or 百亿估值 ('ten-billion valuation').

百分之.etymology: A Classical fractional prefix construction (分数结构: Denominator + 分 + 之 + Numerator) composed of 百 (bǎi, 'one hundred'), 分 (fēn, 'equal part, share, division', from 八 'divide' + 刀 'knife'), and the Classical genitive/attributive particle 之 (zhī, 'of, ’s', Old Chinese *tə). Literally meaning 'out of one hundred equal parts, [numerator] of them', this ancient fractional template (attested in *The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art*, 九章算术) was standardized in modern Chinese to express Western percentages (%).

history.meaning: [X] parts out of one hundred parts (Classical Chinese fractional syntax)
percent (%) — standard prefix placed before a number to read percentages

百分之.notes: Crucial word-order rule: Chinese states the denominator BEFORE the numerator! Whereas English says '50 percent (50 per 100)', Chinese says 百分之五十 ('of 100 parts, 50'). The same pattern builds all fractions: 三分之一 ('one-third').

百分之九十九.etymology: A phrasal numeral compound built on the Classical Chinese fractional frame 百分之 (bǎi fēn zhī, 'out of one hundred parts') followed by the numerator 九十九 (jiǔshíjiǔ, 'ninety-nine', literally 9 × 10 + 9). Retaining the ancient *Nine Chapters* denominator-first syntax (母先子后), it denotes the exact ratio 99/100 (99%) as well as the hyperbolic rhetorical sense of 'virtually certain, ninety-nine times out of a hundred'.

history.meaning: ninety-nine parts out of a hundred; 99 percent (99%) or near-total certainty

百分之九十九.notes: Often used hyperbolically in speech for near-certainty (我百分之九十九确定 'I'm 99% sure') or in the famous translation of Edison's quote: 天才是百分之一的灵感加上百分之九十九的汗水 ('Genius is 1% inspiration and 99% perspiration').

百分之五十.etymology: A phrasal numeral compound combining the Classical fractional prefix 百分之 (bǎi fēn zhī, 'out of one hundred equal parts', with 百 '100' + 分 'part' + 之 'of') and the numerator 五十 (wǔshí, 'fifty', 5 × 10). Following the indigenous Chinese denominator-before-numerator order, it expresses the mathematical percentage 50% (one half), often used in business equity, television ratings share, or probability contexts ('a 50-50 chance').

history.meaning: fifty parts out of a hundred; fifty percent (50%)

百分之五十.notes: Equivalent in quantity to 一半 (half) or 二分之一 (1/2), but 百分之五十 sounds more precise and analytical—frequently used for probability (百分之五十的把握 'a 50% chance') or shareholding/royalty splits.

百叶窗.etymology: Three-character compound combining 百叶 (trad. 百葉, 'hundred leaves/slats') + 窗 ('window'). Likens the numerous overlapping slats of a louvered shutter or Venetian blind to a hundred leaves.

history.meaning: louvered window shutter; Venetian blind

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 百叶窗 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: amidst a very busy schedule (polite epistolary phrase)
cognates.word: ご多忙中 (ごたぼうちゅう) / 百忙中

百忙之中.etymology: A four-character literary locative phrase (偏正结构) built from 百忙 (bǎimáng, 'a hundred pressing affairs, extreme busyness', where 百 'hundred' means 'manifold, all kinds of' and 忙 'hurried, busy', phono-semantic with 忄 'heart' and 亡 phonetic) linked by the Classical associative particle 之 (zhī, 'of') to the locative noun 中 (zhōng, 'the midst, inside'). Literally 'in the midst of a hundred pressing affairs', it crystallized in Ming–Qing epistolary and polite vernacular usage as a courteous formula thanking guests or VIPs for making time despite a packed schedule.

history.meaning: manifold pressing affairs, extreme hustle and bustle
amidst a myriad of pressing duties; despite a packed schedule (polite formula)

morphemes.meaning: a hundred, manifold, all kinds of

百忙之中.notes: A staple of polite hosting, gala introductions, and business emails: 感谢您在百忙之中抽空出席 ('Thank you for taking time out of your packed schedule to attend'). Also used ironical-humorously: 百忙之中敷衍一下 ('squeezing in a half-hearted reply amidst a busy schedule').

rootFamily.gloss: to take time out (from a busy schedule)

百花.etymology: Attributive poetic compound combining 百 ('a hundred -> all kinds of, myriad') + 花 ('flowers, blossoms'), meaning 'all sorts of flowers' (as in 百花齐放).

history.stage: Six Dynasties–Tang Poetry to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: a hundred flowers; all kinds of blossoms

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 百花 (via 萌典)

百里香.etymology: Descriptive botanical name literally meaning 'fragrant (香) for a hundred (百) *li* (里)'. Originally applied to wild creeping thyme (*Thymus quinquecostatus*) carpeting northern Chinese hillsides whose herbal scent carries on the wind, and extended to Mediterranean culinary thyme (*Thymus vulgaris*).

history.meaning: aromatic wild thyme (*Thymus* spp.)
thyme

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 百里香

的.etymology: Structural particle de linking an owner, noun, adjective, or clause to a following noun (我的书 'my book', 安静的院子 'quiet courtyard'), or forming a headless possessive ('mine, Teacher Song's'). In Tang–Song vernacular texts this linker was often written 底 (dǐ) before standardizing on 的 in Yuan–Ming prose.

history.meaning: attributive and possessive linker
possessive and descriptive particle

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 的 (via 萌典)

的时候.etymology: High-frequency temporal enclitic phrase formed from structural particle 的 (linking a modifying clause to a head noun) + 时候 (simplified from 時候, 'time; moment; season', originally astronomical timekeeping periods). Placed at the end of a verb or clause (`V/Clause + 的时候`), it functions as the standard Mandarin equivalent of English 'when...' or 'at the time of...'.

morphemes.meaning: links modifying clause to head noun

history.meaning: at the time when...
when...; at the time of...

的话.etymology: A grammaticalized enclitic conditional marker (助词) originally formed as a noun phrase combining the attributive particle 的 (de) and the head noun 话 (huà, traditional 話, 'spoken words, speech, statement, matter'). In late Ming–Qing vernacular Mandarin, clauses ending in …的话 literally meant '[assuming] the words/statement that…' or '[speaking of] the matter of…'. Through high-frequency topic-comment usage, the lexical meaning of 话 ('words') bleached away, turning clause-final 的话 into a pure enclitic conditional and topic marker meaning 'if / in the event that'.

history.meaning: the words/saying that…; speaking of the matter of… (literal noun phrase)
clause-final conditional particle ('if…') or contrastive topic marker ('as for…')

的话.notes: Placed at the END of the 'if' clause, either alone (你去的话，我也去 'If you go, I'll go too') or paired as a bracket with 如果 / 要是 / 假如 at the start (如果明天不下雨的话… 'If it doesn't rain tomorrow…'). Also marks topics: 周末的话，我一般在家 ('As for weekends, I'm usually at home').

皮.etymology: Associative compound in bronze and seal script showing a hand (又) stripping the hide or pelt off an animal carcass. Extended from 'animal hide, leather' to human skin, tree bark, fruit peel, and outer wrappers.

morphemes.meaning: hand flaying an animal hide -> skin, peel, leather

history.stage: Old Chinese (Bronze inscriptions) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: animal hide, leather; skin, bark, peel, outer cover

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 皮 (via 萌典)

皮鞋.etymology: Attributive compound combining 皮 ('leather, hide') + 鞋 ('shoes'), referring to leather shoes.

history.meaning: leather shoes

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 皮鞋 (via 萌典)

皱.etymology: Phono-semantic character (trad. 皺) combining semantic 皮 ('skin, hide') + phonetic 刍 (芻, chú/zhòu, 'bundled dried grass'). Describes skin, cloth, or paper creasing and puckering into wrinkles (as in 皱眉 'to furrow one's brow').

history.meaning: to wrinkle, crease, furrow; wrinkles

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 皱 (via 萌典)

盏.etymology: Phono-semantic character (trad. 盞) combining semantic 皿 ('shallow dish or cup') + phonetic 戋 (戔, jiān/zhǎn, 'small, shallow'). Originally a small shallow wine cup or oil-lamp saucer, whence its modern use as the standard classifier for lamps (一盏灯).

history.meaning: small shallow cup -> oil-lamp dish -> classifier for lamps

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 盏 (via 萌典)

盐.etymology: Simplified from traditional 鹽 (combining 臣 'official supervision', 人, 卤 'natural salt crystal/brine', and 皿 'vessel'), simplified in modern script to 土 ('earth'), 卜 (phonetic cue), and 皿 ('dish/pan'). One of the oldest core nouns in Sino-Tibetan, denoting culinary sea salt or rock salt.

history.meaning: brine salt crystallized in vessels
salt

cognates.meaning: executive producer, film producer (especially in Hong Kong cinema)

监制.etymology: A modifier-head / verb-object compound (偏正/动宾结构) combining 监 (jiān, traditional 監, 'to look down upon, inspect, supervise', originally an oracle-bone pictograph of a person bending over a basin 皿 of water to see their reflection, Old Chinese *kˤram) and 制 (zhì, traditional 製, 'to cut out garments, manufacture, produce', with 衣 'clothing' and 制 'cut'). In imperial China, 监制 denoted an official overseeing the court manufacture of porcelain, weaponry, or ritual goods; in 20th-century Hong Kong and Mainland film/TV studios, it became the standard title for an 'executive producer' or 'supervising producer'.

history.meaning: imperial official supervising the manufacture of court porcelain, books, or armaments
to supervise film/TV/music production; executive producer or supervising producer

监制.notes: Essential *Behind the Scenes* (*幕后之王*) showbiz term! In Chinese film and television credits, 监制 (executive/supervising producer) often oversees creative and budgetary quality on behalf of the studio or platform, sitting alongside 制片人 (line/managing producer) and 出品人 (financier/studio head).

监控.etymology: A coordinative verbal/nominal compound (并列结构) uniting 监 (jiān, traditional 監, 'to inspect, watch over, monitor', originally gazing into a water vessel 皿) and 控 (kòng, 'to draw a bowstring; by extension, to rein in, control, regulate', Old Chinese *kʰˤoŋ-s). Formed in 20th-century technical and administrative Chinese as a condensation of 监视 ('to watch over / surveil') and 控制 ('to control'), it denotes both the act of electronic/institutional monitoring and, by metonymy in everyday speech, security cameras (CCTV) or their recorded footage.

history.meaning: to monitor and control industrial systems, finances, or public security
surveillance; (colloquial noun) security camera (CCTV) or security footage (e.g., 调监控)

监控.notes: In contemporary spoken Mandarin and drama scripts, 监控 is used directly as a concrete noun for 'security camera' or 'CCTV footage': 查监控 / 调监控 ('check/pull the security camera footage') and 监控摄像头 ('surveillance camera').

rootFamily.gloss: to watch closely, keep under surveillance
to control, master; control room (控台)

cognates.meaning: supervision, direction; film director / sports manager
supervision, oversee; film director / team manager

监督.etymology: A coordinative verbal/nominal compound (并列结构) combining 监 (jiān, traditional 監, 'to inspect from above, watch over') and 督 (dū, 'to examine closely, superintend, urge on', Old Chinese *tuk, composed of 目 'eye' and 叔 phonetic, originally meaning 'the center seam of the back' and hence 'to oversee with a sharp eye'). First attested in Han dynasty histories (*Book of Later Han*) for military and administrative oversight, it means 'to supervise and hold accountable'.

history.meaning: to inspect and command troops or local administration; an imperial inspector
to supervise, oversee, and monitor compliance (e.g., 舆论监督 public/media oversight)

morphemes.meaning: superintend, examine with the eye, urge

监督.notes: Watch out for the Japanese/Korean false friend: in Japanese (監督 *kantoku*) and Korean (감독 *gamdok*), this word means 'film director' or 'sports coach', whereas in Mandarin a film director is 导演 (dǎoyǎn) and 监督 strictly means 'to supervise / oversight' (except in anime credits borrowed from Japanese).

rootFamily.gloss: to urge, supervise and press for completion

盒.etymology: Phono-semantic/associative character combining 合 ('to join together, close a lid', serving as both phonetic hé and meaning) + 皿 ('vessel, container'). Denotes a small lidded box or case.

history.meaning: small lidded box or case; classifier for boxed items

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 盒 (via 萌典)

盒子.etymology: Suffixed noun formed from 盒 ('small lidded container') + nominal suffix 子.

history.meaning: box, case, casket

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 盒子 (via 萌典)

盖.etymology: Phono-semantic character (trad. 蓋) combining semantic 艹 ('thatch grass') + phonetic 盍 (hé/gài, itself 'to cover a vessel'). Originally meant thatch for roofing a house or a woven mat cover, then generalized to 'lid, cover' and 'to cover, build (a house), stamp (a seal)'.

history.meaning: thatch roof cover -> lid, cover; to cover, build, stamp

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 盖 (via 萌典)

盖子.etymology: Suffixed noun combining 盖 (trad. 蓋, 'lid, cover, cap') + nominal suffix 子.

history.meaning: lid, cover, cap, top

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 盖子 (via 萌典)

盖章.etymology: Separable verb-object compound of 盖 ('cover from above; press down a seal', grass radical 艹 + 盍 *hé*) + 章 ('official emblem, seal, or chop', 音 + 十). In Chinese administrative culture, stamping a vermilion or blue seal (盖章) authenticates an official letter or permit.

history.meaning: affix an official seal or chop
stamp; affix a seal

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 盖章

盘.etymology: Originally a broad, shallow bronze ritual basin for washing hands (written 盤 in traditional script: 般 bān 'turn/carry round' + 皿 mǐn 'vessel', Middle Chinese *ban*). From a flat serving dish or baking tray, it grammaticalized as the standard classifier for trays of baked goods or plates of food (一盘柠檬挞).

history.meaning: shallow bronze basin or tray
serving plate; classifier for dishes of food
tray; plate (measure word)

盘子.etymology: Everyday count noun formed from 盘 ('shallow dish; plate; tray', from 般 + vessel radical 皿) + neutral-tone nominal suffix 子 (zi). While bare 盘 acts as the measure word ('four trays of tart'), 盘子 is the full noun for a dinner or dessert plate.

history.meaning: plate; platter; dish
plate; dish

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 盘子

盛典.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正结构) combining 盛 (shèng, 'flourishing, abundant, grand, magnificent', Old Chinese *djeŋ-s, originally grain mounded high inside a ritual vessel 皿) and 典 (diǎn, 'canon, statute, solemn ceremony', Old Chinese *tˤenʔ, pictographically sacred bamboo tablets 冊 elevated on a stand 丌). In Tang–Ming court prose, 盛典 denoted a grand state ritual or imperial anniversary ceremony; in contemporary media and entertainment, it is the go-to word for televised award galas, anniversary celebrations, and red-carpet extravaganzas.

history.meaning: magnificent imperial rite or solemn state ceremony
grand ceremony, awards gala, or televised media extravaganza

盛典.notes: Ubiquitous in Chinese showbiz and live broadcasting: 颁奖盛典 ('awards gala'), 年度盛典 ('annual gala ceremony'), 跨年盛典 ('New Year's Eve gala'). Compare 典礼 (formal ceremony, such as a graduation or wedding).

rootFamily.gloss: ceremony, celebration rite (e.g., 毕业典礼)

盛宴.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正结构) joining 盛 (shèng, 'abundant, sumptuous, grand', depicting an overflowing ritual vessel 皿) and 宴 (yàn, 'repose, banquet, feast', Old Chinese *ʔˤen-s, composed of 宀 'roof', 日 'sun/day', and 女 'woman', originally signifying peaceful indoor leisure and feasting). Attested since Tang poetry (such as Wang Bo's *Preface to the Pavilion of Prince Teng*: 盛宴难再 'a grand banquet is hard to repeat'), it denotes a lavish feast and, metaphorically in modern media, a 'visual or auditory feast' (视觉盛宴 / 听觉盛宴).

history.meaning: sumptuous court or literary banquet; grand feast
lavish banquet, gala dinner; figuratively a 'sensory feast' (e.g., 视听盛宴)

盛宴.notes: In television and stage production (*Behind the Scenes*), 视听盛宴 ('an audiovisual feast') and 音乐盛宴 ('a musical feast') are classic promotional collocations praising high-production-value concerts or variety shows. Also watch the character: 宴 (banquet) vs. 燕 (swallow bird).

盛情.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正结构) combining 盛 (shèng, 'abundant, profuse, ardent, generous') and 情 (qíng, 'feeling, sentiment, affection, goodwill', Old Chinese *dzjeŋ, phono-semantic with 忄 'heart' and 青 phonetic). In Classical and Tang–Song poetry, 盛情 meant 'intense emotion or abundant literary feeling'; in polite social and epistolary Chinese, it specialized to mean 'overflowing goodwill, gracious kindness, and warm hospitality' shown by a host or inviter.

history.meaning: ardent feeling, abundant sentiment or enthusiasm
boundless kindness, warm hospitality, or gracious invitation from a host

盛情.notes: Most famously used in the four-character set phrase 盛情难却 (shèngqíng nán què, 'such warm hospitality is hard to decline') and the polite collocation 盛情邀请 ('a gracious/warm invitation') or 盛情款待 ('lavish and warm hospitality').

rootFamily.gloss: deep affection, profound kindness or friendship
such warm hospitality is hard to refuse (idiom)

目前.etymology: Spatial-to-temporal compound combining 目 ('eye', an ancient pictograph of a human eye) + 前 ('in front'). Literally 'before one's eyes', shifted metaphorically to 'at present, currently'.

history.meaning: before one's eyes -> at present, currently

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 目前 (via 萌典)
