目标.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正结构) uniting 目 (mù, 'eye, gaze, visual focus', Old Chinese *mruk, a pictograph of a human eye) and 标 (biāo, traditional 標, 'topmost branch of a tree; raised wooden post, beacon, or target marker', Old Chinese *pjew). Literally 'a visual marker or post that catches the eye', it appeared in medieval Chinese (e.g., Song dynasty prose) for a conspicuous landmark, was standardized in Meiji Japan (目標 *mokuhyō*) to translate Western military/philosophical 'target, objective, goal' (cf. German *Ziel*), and became core vocabulary in modern Mandarin.

history.meaning: a conspicuous visual marker, signpost, or landmark that guides the eye
shooting target, military objective, or abstract life/project goal (reinforced via Meiji Japanese 目標)

morphemes.meaning: topmost branch, marker post, target, sign

目标.notes: Covers both concrete targets (击中目标 'hit the target') and abstract goals or demographics (实现目标 'achieve a goal', 目标受众 'target audience', 目标收视率 'target ratings'). Distinguish from 目的 (mùdì, 'purpose / motive / end').

rootFamily.gloss: gaze, line of sight, vision (lit. eye-light)

目的.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 目 (mù, 'eye; to look at') and 的 (dì, 'bright center of an archery target'). Originally a metaphor from archery denoting the bullseye on which an archer fixes their gaze, it was popularized in its abstract modern sense ('objective, purpose, goal') via Meiji-era Japanese 目的 (mokuteki), which translated German Zweck and English purpose, before re-entering late Qing Mandarin as a graphic return loan.

history.meaning: white center or bullseye of an archery target
target of the eye; abstract aim or objective (Meiji translation of German Zweck)
purpose, goal, objective

morphemes.meaning: bullseye of an archery target (read dì)

目的.notes: Note the literary pronunciation dì for 的 ('target', as in 众矢之的 'target of all arrows'), preserved in dictionary standards as mùdì. Commonly collocates with 达到目的 ('achieve a goal') and 明确目的 ('clarify an objective').

rootFamily.gloss: target of a multitude of arrows; object of public criticism

盯.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining semantic 目 ('eye') + phonetic 丁 (dīng). Means 'to fix one's gaze upon, stare intently at, keep a close watch on'.

history.meaning: to stare at; to fix one's eyes on; to watch closely

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 盯 (via 萌典)

盯住.etymology: A verb-resultative (动补) compound formed from the action verb 盯 (dīng, 'to fix one's gaze on, stare intently', phono-semantic compound with eye radical 目 and phonetic 丁 dīng) and the resultative complement 住 (zhù, 'to stop, stay fast, hold firmly in place'). The complement 住 indicates that the visual focus locks onto the target and does not let it escape sight or control.

history.meaning: to stare straight ahead, gaze fixedly
to fix one's eyes firmly on; keep a close watch on without losing sight

morphemes.meaning: to stare at, fix one's eyes on

盯住.notes: Frequently used in television production, sports, and security contexts for tracking a subject, camera angle, or competitor without letting them slip away (e.g., 盯住镜头 'keep eyes locked on the camera' or 盯住进度 'keep a firm watch on the schedule').

rootFamily.gloss: watch closely, keep a tight eye on
follow and watch someone closely, shadow
keep an eye on a person (in sports defense or supervision)

盯紧.etymology: A verb-resultative (动补) compound uniting 盯 (dīng, 'to gaze fixedly, watch intently') with the adjectival resultative complement 紧 (jǐn, 'tight, taut, close, strict'). Literally 'to stare tightly', the construction expresses maintaining unremitting, high-alert surveillance or supervision so that no detail or movement is missed.

history.meaning: tightly bound string; taut, urgent, strict
to watch closely, keep under tight observation or supervision

morphemes.meaning: to fix one's gaze on, watch intently

盯紧.notes: Whereas 盯住 emphasizes locking onto a target so it does not slip away, 盯紧 stresses the intensity and zero-slack vigilance of the monitoring—often used by directors and producers urging staff to stay on top of a crisis or key guest.

rootFamily.gloss: keep a firm eye on, lock one's gaze onto
follow closely at someone's heels; monitor closely

直.etymology: Ideographic compound in oracle-bone script showing an eye (目) looking straight along a vertical plumb line (十/丨), later augmented with an L-shaped carpenter's square (乚). Means 'straight, vertical, direct, candid, continuously'.

morphemes.meaning: eye sighting straight along a line

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: sighted straight -> straight, vertical, direct, frank

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 直 (via 萌典)

直击.etymology: A modifier-head verbal compound composed of the adverbial modifier 直 (zhí, 'straight, directly, without intermediary') and the verb head 击 (擊, jī, 'to strike, hit, attack'). Originally a martial and physical term meaning 'to strike directly', in modern broadcast journalism and television production (reinforced by Japanese media usage 直撃 chokugeki) it shifted metaphorically to 'hitting the scene directly'—reporting live from the front line or witnessing events firsthand.

history.meaning: to strike or attack directly without detour
to strike directly; to cover live on the scene, witness firsthand in broadcast media

直击.notes: A staple headline and broadcast buzzword in Chinese television news and entertainment shows (e.g., 直击现场 'live on the scene', 直击幕后 'a direct look behind the scenes', 直击痛点 'hit the pain point directly').

rootFamily.gloss: witness with one's own eyes, see firsthand

直到.etymology: Compound preposition/verb combining 直 ('straight, continuously without interruption') + 到 ('to arrive at, reach, until'). Means 'all the way until, right up to'.

history.meaning: straight until; right up to

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 直到 (via 萌典)

直奔主题.etymology: A four-character verb-object phrase built from the modifier-head verb 直奔 (zhíbèn, 'to rush or head straight toward', from 直 'straight, directly' + 奔 bèn 'to head directly toward a destination') governing the noun phrase object 主题 (zhǔtí, 'main topic, central theme', from 主 'main, principal' + 题 'topic, thesis'). Originally describing physical movement straight toward a destination, it is used figuratively in rhetoric, meetings, and media scripting for skipping pleasantries and cutting straight to the core issue.

history.meaning: to run or head straight toward a physical destination

history.form: 直奔主題 / 直奔主题 (zhíbèn zhǔtí)
history.meaning: to cut straight to the main topic or central point without digression

morphemes.meaning: to head toward, rush toward (read bèn)

直奔主题.notes: In this sense of heading toward a specific goal, 奔 is often pronounced in the fourth tone (bèn) in spoken northern Mandarin, though standard dictionary readings also accept first tone (bēn). Contrast with 拐弯抹角 ('beat around the bush').

rootFamily.gloss: head toward, strive for; run quickly

直接.etymology: Compound adjective/adverb combining 直 ('straight, unmediated') + 接 ('to connect, touch, meet'). Means 'direct, immediate, without an intermediary'.

history.meaning: direct, immediate; directly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 直接 (via 萌典)

直播.etymology: A modern telescopic modifier-head compound abbreviating 直接广播 (zhíjiē guǎngbō) or 现场直接播送 (xiànchǎng zhíjiē bōsòng, 'direct on-site broadcasting'). It combines 直 (zhí, 'direct, unmediated, real-time') with 播 (bō, originally 'to sow seeds by scattering' in Classical Chinese, extended in the 20th century to 'to broadcast, transmit signals or programs'). From traditional radio and television live transmissions, it expanded in the 2010s to become the standard term for internet livestreaming.

history.meaning: to sow seeds; to spread, disseminate
live radio or television broadcast (contrasted with pre-recorded 录播)
live broadcast; interactive internet or mobile livestreaming

morphemes.meaning: to broadcast, transmit (originally: to sow, spread)

直播.notes: In television production (*幕后之王*), 直播 ('live broadcast') is constantly contrasted with 录播 (lùbō, 'recorded broadcast') and 重播 (chóngbō, 'rerun/rebroadcast'), carrying high stakes because live errors cannot be edited out.

直播平台.etymology: A doubly compounded modifier-head noun phrase joining 直播 (zhíbō, 'live broadcast, livestreaming', from 直 'direct/live' + 播 'broadcast') with 平台 (píngtái, originally 'flat raised terrace or stage' in Classical architecture, from 平 'flat, level' + 台 'terrace, platform', later calqued onto English 'platform' in computing and media). It denotes the digital infrastructure, website, or mobile app ecosystem hosting real-time video streams.

history.meaning: flat architectural terrace or viewing pavilion
technological, institutional, or media platform (semantic loan from English platform)
online livestreaming platform or service

直播平台.notes: Central to modern Chinese media industry discourse, where traditional TV networks (电视台) compete or partner with digital 直播平台 for audience traffic (流量) and real-time interactivity.

直播车.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound combining 直播 (zhíbō, 'live broadcast', from 直 'direct, real-time' + 播 'broadcast') with the head noun 车 (車, chē, 'wheeled vehicle, van, truck'). Coined in modern television engineering to designate a mobile production control room mounted inside a van or truck—known in English broadcast terminology as an Outside Broadcast (OB) van—used for on-location live switching, audio mixing, and satellite/cellular transmission.

history.meaning: wheeled carriage, chariot, cart
mobile television broadcast vehicle (outside broadcast van)

直播车.notes: In television drama production settings like *幕后之王*, the 直播车 (often also called 转播车 zhuǎnbōchē) serves as the high-pressure mobile nerve center where the director (导播) calls camera switches during outdoor or concert live events.

rootFamily.gloss: outside broadcast relay vehicle, OB van
live broadcast studio or online room

直播间.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound pairing 直播 (zhíbō, 'live broadcast, livestream') with the spatial head noun 间 (間, jiān, originally depicting moonlight shining through a doorway, meaning 'space between; room, compartment, studio'). First used in radio and television for a physical on-air broadcast studio, it underwent digital semantic extension in the 2010s to denote an anchor's virtual livestream room on mobile apps where viewers watch, comment, and purchase goods.

history.meaning: interval, space between; room or chamber in a building
physical radio or television live broadcast studio
physical live studio; virtual online livestream room or channel

直播间.notes: Covers both physical acoustic studios in a TV station and virtual chat/video rooms on streaming platforms (e.g., 欢迎来到直播间 'Welcome to the livestream room'). Compare 演播室 (yǎnbōshì), which refers strictly to a physical broadcast studio.

rootFamily.gloss: physical television or radio broadcast studio

直男.etymology: A modern modifier-head nominal calque combining 直 (zhí, 'straight, direct, unbending') and 男 (nán, 'man, male'). Initially coined in the 2000s as a direct loan-translation of English 'straight man' (heterosexual male, contrasting with 同志/弯 'gay/bent'), it quickly underwent a secondary culturally specific semantic shift in Chinese internet and pop-culture slang—overlapping with the native sense of 直 ('blunt, literal-minded, inflexible')—to stereotype an unromantic, emotionally oblivious, or aesthetically clunky man.

history.meaning: heterosexual man (calque of English straight man)
heterosexual man; (slang) literal-minded, unromantic, or emotionally insensitive guy

直男.notes: Frequently appears in humorous compounds like 钢铁直男 ('steel straight guy', a man completely impervious to romantic hints) and 直男审美 ('straight-guy aesthetics'). Used playfully or critically in modern workplace and romance dramas.

直话直说.etymology: A four-character parallel idiom (ABAC/AABB-like correlative pattern) juxtaposing the nominal modifier-head phrase 直话 (zhíhuà, 'straight talk, candid words') with the adverb-verb phrase 直说 (zhíshuō, 'to speak directly/frankly'). Repeating the morpheme 直 (zhí, 'straight, candid, without evasion') in both the object and the manner slot creates a rhetorical symmetry meaning 'to speak candid words in a candid manner'—i.e., to lay all cards on the table without euphemism.

history.form: 直話直說 / 直话直说 (zhíhuà zhíshuō)
history.meaning: to speak frank words frankly; to call a spade a spade without mincing words

直话直说.notes: Often used as a conversational preface to soften an upcoming blunt critique in workplace or production meetings: 我就直话直说了 ('I'll just be completely frank with you'). Synonymous in higher register with 直言不讳 (zhíyán-bùhuì).

rootFamily.gloss: speak bluntly without taboo or concealment (literary idiom)

直说.etymology: A modifier-head verbal compound formed from the adverbial modifier 直 (zhí, 'straight, directly, candidly, without circumlocution') and the verb head 说 (說, shuō, 'to speak, say, explain'). In Classical Chinese, the equivalent expression was 直言 (zhíyán, 'to speak frankly/remonstrate candidly'); as 说 replaced 言 as the primary vernacular verb of speaking from the Tang–Song transition onward, 直说 became the standard spoken form for speaking plainly without beating around the bush.

history.meaning: to speak candidly or remonstrate forthrightly
to say directly, speak frankly without roundabout politeness

直说.notes: Very common in everyday dialogue structures such as 有话直说 ('if you have something to say, say it straight') and 打开天窗说亮话 ('open the skylight and speak bright words—speak frankly').

rootFamily.gloss: speak frankly, call a spade a spade

相互.etymology: A coordinative compound uniting two synonymous Classical Chinese reciprocity morphemes: 相 (xiāng, originally 'to inspect closely', early grammaticalized into a reciprocal adverb 'mutually, each other') and 互 (hù, originally depicting a bamboo reel or interlocking meat hooks, meaning 'interlocking, alternating, mutually'). Paired together, the two characters reinforce the symmetrical, two-way nature of an action or relationship between parties.

history.meaning: mutually, reciprocally; interlocking with one another
mutually, reciprocally, each other (adverbial and attributive)

相互.notes: 相互 and its reversed twin 互相 (hùxiāng) are largely interchangeable as adverbs before two-syllable verbs (相互支持 / 互相支持 'support each other'), but 相互 is strongly preferred as an attributive modifier before nouns (e.g., 相互关系 'mutual relationship').

相亲.etymology: A verb-object (动宾) compound where 相 retains its original Classical Chinese fourth-tone verbal sense (xiàng, 'to examine by looking, appraise appearance and physiognomy', composed of 目 'eye' + 木 'tree') and 亲 (親, qīn, 'marriage alliance, betrothed relative, prospective spouse'). Historically referring to families formally inspecting a prospective bride or groom's appearance and demeanor before betrothal, it evolved in modern society to mean going on an arranged blind date with marriage in mind.

history.meaning: to inspect visually, appraise a person's appearance or fortune
for families to visually appraise a prospective marriage partner before betrothal
to go on a matchmaking blind date arranged by family, friends, or a service

morphemes.meaning: to look over, appraise visually (historically xiàng, now read xiāng)
marriage match, prospective spouse or in-law

相亲.notes: Although etymologically derived from fourth-tone 相 (xiàng, 'to appraise visually', as in 看相 'physiognomy'), modern Mainland standard pronunciation (Putonghua) has shifted it to first tone xiāngqīn by analogy with reciprocal 相 ('each other'). Dating reality shows (相亲节目) are a major television genre in China.

rootFamily.gloss: get married, form a marriage alliance

相信.etymology: Compound verb from 相 ('mutually; toward an object') + 信 ('to trust, believe in', from 人 'person' + 言 'word'). Originally 'to trust one another' in classical texts, now the transitive verb 'to believe, trust in'.

history.meaning: to trust one another -> to believe, trust

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 相信 (via 萌典)

相关.etymology: A modifier-head verbal and adjectival compound combining the reciprocal adverb 相 (xiāng, 'mutually, with one another') and the verb 关 (關, guān, originally 'wooden crossbar or bolt of a gate', extended to 'to interlock, connect, involve, concern'). Literally 'to bolt or interlock with one another', in Literary Chinese it denoted mutual sympathy or involvement, and in modern Mandarin it serves as a high-frequency adjective and attributive modifier meaning 'relevant, related, correlated'.

history.meaning: gate bolt; to close, connect, mechanically interlock
to be mutually connected or concerned with one another (e.g., 痛痒相关)
relevant, related, Pertinent; statistically correlated

morphemes.meaning: to connect, interlock, concern (originally: gate bolt)

相关.notes: Used primarily as a non-predicative adjective before nouns without 的 (e.g., 相关部门 'relevant departments', 相关人员 'personnel concerned', 相关报道 'related media coverage') or in the frame 与……相关 ('be related to...').

相同.etymology: Compound adjective combining 相 ('mutually, with each other') + 同 ('same, alike'). Means 'identical, the same as one another'.

history.meaning: mutually the same; identical, alike

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 相同 (via 萌典)

相处.etymology: A modifier-head verbal compound formed from the reciprocal adverb 相 (xiāng, 'mutually, together, with one another') and the Classical verb 处 (處, chǔ, third tone, 'to dwell, reside, stay in a place; to conduct oneself among others'). Attested since the *Zuo Zhuan* and *Xunzi*, it originally meant 'to dwell together in the same space' and naturally evolved to mean 'to interact and get along with one another over time'.

history.meaning: to dwell together, coexist in the same place or society
to get along with one another, interact in personal or professional relationships

morphemes.meaning: to dwell, coexist, deal with (read chǔ)

相处.notes: Always pronounced with the verbal third tone chǔ (not fourth tone chù 'place'). Common collocations include 和睦相处 ('get along harmoniously') and 好相处 / 难相处 ('easy / difficult to get along with'). In Mandarin grammar, do not put the person as a direct object after 相处; use 跟/与……相处 instead.

相当于.etymology: A trisyllabic verbal compound combining 相当 (xiāngdāng, 'to match one another, correspond, be commensurate', from reciprocal 相 'mutually' + 当 dāng 'to match, equal, face') with the Classical prepositional/transitive marker 于 (於, yú, 'to, with respect to'). The resulting structure 相当于 functions as a transitive relational verb introducing the standard of equivalence ('to be equivalent to, amount to, correspond to').

history.meaning: to match each other in strength, rank, or value; to correspond
to be equivalent to, amount to, correspond to (introducing a comparative equivalent)

morphemes.meaning: to match, equal, correspond to (read dāng)
to, in relation to, with respect to

相当于.notes: An indispensable explanatory connector in media pitches and explanations, used to equate an unfamiliar technical concept or scale to something concrete (e.g., 这场直播的流量相当于三个卫视跨年晚会 'the traffic of this livestream is equivalent to three satellite TV New Year galas').

rootFamily.gloss: act as, serve as, play the role of
be equal to, equal (mathematical or exact equivalence)

相比.etymology: A modifier-head verbal compound joining the reciprocal adverb 相 (xiāng, 'mutually, with each other') and the verb 比 (bǐ, originally depicting two people standing side by side, meaning 'to line up side by side, compare, match'). Attested in Classical texts, it literally means 'to place side by side with one another for comparison' and is widely used in modern Mandarin comparative frames.

history.meaning: to stand side by side; to compare or match two things
to compare with one another; in comparison with

morphemes.meaning: to compare, place side by side

相比.notes: Typically used in the frame 与/跟 X 相比 ('compared with X') or 相比之下 ('by comparison, in contrast'). Unlike 比较, 相比 rarely takes a direct noun object after it.

rootFamily.gloss: contrast, compare side by side; ratio

cognates.meaning: look attentively; hope for, long for (literary)

盼.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形声字) combining the semantic eye radical 目 (mù, 'eye, vision') with the phonetic-semantic component 分 (fēn, Old Chinese *pən / *pˁrəns, 'to divide, clearly separate'). In the *Shijing* (*Book of Songs*, 巧笑倩兮，美目盼兮), 盼 originally meant 'having clearly divided black and white in the eyes; beautiful, bright-eyed gaze'. From 'gazing intently into the distance', it shifted by the Tang–Song vernacular period to 'looking forward eagerly, longing for, hoping'.

history.meaning: having a clear division of black pupil and white sclera; bright-eyed gaze (*Shijing*)
to look around or gaze into the distance (as in 左顾右盼)
to look forward eagerly to, long for, hope earnestly

morphemes.meaning: to divide clearly (phonetic *pˁrəns, distinct black and white of the eye)

盼.notes: Do not confuse 盼 (pàn, with the 5-stroke eye radical 目, 'gaze/long for') with /盼 lookalikes or 扮 (bàn, with hand radical 扌, 'dress up/play a role'). Preserves its ancient sense 'look around' in the idiom 左顾右盼 ('glance left and right').

rootFamily.gloss: hope for, look forward to eagerly
thing hoped for, prospect, bright hope

盼着.etymology: A verb-aspect combination pairing the verb 盼 (pàn, 'to gaze with longing, look forward eagerly to') with the continuous/durative aspect particle 着 (zhe, grammaticalized in Medieval Vernacular Chinese from 著 zhuó 'to attach, adhere, stay put'). The suffix 着 profiles the psychological state of yearning or anticipation as an ongoing, sustained posture of waiting for a desired outcome.

history.meaning: to remain in an ongoing state of gazing/longing for something
to be looking forward eagerly to, keep hoping for

morphemes.meaning: to long for, look forward eagerly to

盼着.notes: Characteristic of warm, colloquial spoken Mandarin (e.g., 盼着节目早点开播 'eagerly counting the days until the show premieres', 盼着你回来 'longing for your return'). More conversational and emotionally immediate than 期盼.

rootFamily.gloss: good prospect, something to look forward to (colloquial)

省.etymology: An ancient compound ideogram/phono-semantic graph combining 少 (shǎo, 'few, little, to lessen') and 目 (mù, 'eye'). In Oracle Bone and Bronze Inscriptions, it splits into two cognate etymological readings: xǐng ('to narrow the eyes to inspect closely; examine oneself') and shěng ('to reduce, diminish, pare down'). From 'reducing official expenditures and paperwork' in Classical Chinese, the reading shěng developed the everyday verbal sense 'to save, economize, spare (money, time, effort, or trouble)'.

history.meaning: to reduce, curtail, diminish (expenses, punishments, or duties)
to save, economize, omit, spare (money, time, or trouble); administrative province (from 元行中书省)

morphemes.meaning: small, few, to lessen or reduce

省.notes: A classic heteronym (多音字): read shěng when meaning 'save, omit, spare' (省钱 'save money', 省心 'save worry', 省略 'omit') or 'province' (浙江省), and read xǐng when meaning 'examine, reflect upon, become conscious' (反省 'self-reflect', 省亲 'visit parents').

rootFamily.gloss: save worry, be trouble-free and reassuring

省得.etymology: A lively colloquial conjunction grammaticalized from the verb 省 (shěng, 'to save, spare, economize on trouble or effort') plus the complement marker 得 (de). Literally meaning 'saving oneself the trouble of...', 省得 emerged in Yuan–Ming spoken drama and novels to introduce an undesirable consequence that a sensible precaution avoids ('so nobody ends up tripping').

history.meaning: sparing the trouble of; lest
so as to avoid; lest

cognates.meaning: lest; to save the bother of (functional equivalent)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 省得

省心.etymology: Verb-object adjective compound combining 省 ('to save, economize, spare', originally 'to inspect, reduce') + 心 ('mental effort, worry'). Literally 'to save worry', hence 'worry-free, trouble-saving'.

history.meaning: saving mental effort -> worry-free, trouble-saving

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 省心 (via 萌典)

省钱.etymology: Verb-object compound combining 省 ('to save, economize, cut down on') + 钱 (trad. 錢, 'money, coins').

history.meaning: to save money; economical

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 省钱 (via 萌典)

眉头.etymology: Suffixed noun combining 眉 ('eyebrow', an oracle-bone pictograph of an eye 目 with hairs arched above it) + 头 (trad. 頭, locative/nominal suffix 'brow area, tip of the brows').

history.meaning: eyebrows; the brow (especially as a seat of worry)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 眉头 (via 萌典)

眉毛.etymology: An everyday anatomical compound combining 眉 (méi, an ancient Shang oracle-bone pictograph showing curved brow hairs arched directly above an eye 目!) and 毛 (máo, 'hair, fur, fine down'). Classical Chinese used monosyllabic 眉 (as in 眉头 'brow'), while spoken Mandarin added neutral-toned 毛 to form disyllabic 眉毛.

morphemes.meaning: brow arch above the eye 目

history.meaning: eyebrow (pictograph over eye 目)
eyebrow

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 眉毛

看.etymology: Associative compound formed from 手 (龵, a hand shaded over the brow) placed above 目 ('eye'): shielding the eyes with one's hand to look into the distance. The standard Mandarin verb for 'to look at, see, read, watch, visit'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Seal script) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: shading the eyes with a hand to peer -> to look, see, read

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 看 (via 萌典)

看一看.etymology: A tentative/delimitative verbal reduplication following the A一A pattern, where the action verb 看 (kàn, originally an ideogram of a hand 手/龵 shading the eye 目 to look into the distance) is reduplicated around the numeral 一 (yī, 'one'). Emerging in Vernacular Chinese from the Tang–Song period onward, the A一A construction iconically frames the action as 'one brief instance of looking'—hence 'to take a quick, casual, or trial look'.

history.meaning: to shade the eyes with the hand to look; to view, observe
to take a brief or casual look, have a look-see (delimitative aspect)

morphemes.meaning: one (marking a single, brief, tentative instance)
to look (reduplicated stem softening the action)

看一看.notes: In natural speech, 一 is pronounced in the neutral tone (kànyikàn). Like 看看, it softens imperatives and invitations in polite workplace or social conversation (e.g., 大家先看一看这份策划案 'Everyone, take a quick look at this proposal first').

rootFamily.gloss: set one's sights on, value and choose
way of looking at a thing, view, opinion

看上.etymology: A verb-directional/resultative (动趋/动补) compound combining 看 (kàn, 'to look at, observe') with the directional complement 上 (shàng, originally 'upward; onto a surface', grammaticalized as a resultative marker of contact, attainment, and attachment). Literally 'for one's gaze to land and stick upon something', it metaphorically expresses taking a fancy to a person or object, falling for someone romantically, or setting one's sights on a talent or project.

history.meaning: for one's eyes to settle favorably upon; to take a liking to or fancy (a person, match, or item)

morphemes.meaning: onto, reaching and fixing upon a target

看上.notes: Read with neutral tone kànshang in colloquial speech. Can be converted into potential forms 看得上 ('deem worthy of one's liking') and 看不上 ('look down on, consider beneath one's standards'). In entertainment dramas, producers 'set their sights on' (看上) a script or artist, while in romance it means 'fall for'.

rootFamily.gloss: look down upon, find not good enough for one's standards
set one's sights on and select (more deliberative)
take a liking to, fall in love with

看不出来.etymology: A negative potential directional-complement construction (V + 不 + 出来) composed of the perception verb 看 (kàn, 'to look, observe'), the negative potential interfix 不 (bù, 'unable to, cannot'), and the compound directional complement 出来 (chūlái, 'outward toward the speaker', grammaticalized to express cognitive discernment, detection, or emergence from concealment). Literally 'by looking, unable to make [a hidden quality or truth] come out into view', hence 'unable to tell, fail to discern'.

history.meaning: to discern or detect something so that it becomes manifest to the observer

history.form: 看不出來 / 看不出来 (kànbuchūlái)
history.meaning: unable to tell by looking; fail to notice or discern; (idiomatic) 'who would have thought!'

morphemes.meaning: cannot, unable to achieve the result
outward into view; discerning hidden information

看不出来.notes: Used both literally ('I can't tell the difference', 真看不出来有什么区别) and as an exclamation of pleasant surprise when someone reveals an unexpected talent or age (真看不出来你还会编曲! 'I never would have guessed just by looking at you that you can also arrange music!'). Affirmative form: 看得出来.

rootFamily.gloss: discern, make out, tell by looking
able to tell or discern by looking (affirmative potential)

看不着.etymology: A negative potential verb-complement construction (V + 不 + 着) combining 看 (kàn, 'to look'), the negative potential marker 不 (bù, 'unable to'), and the resultative complement 着 (zháo, second tone, derived from Middle Chinese 著 djak 'to touch, make contact with, hit the mark'). Because 着 (zháo) marks successful sensory or physical contact with a target, 看不着 means 'looking without succeeding in making visual contact'—i.e., 'unable to see, out of sight'.

history.meaning: to make contact with, touch, hit upon, attain
unable to catch sight of, cannot see (due to obstruction, distance, or absence)

morphemes.meaning: making contact, reaching the target (read zháo)

看不着.notes: Here 着 MUST be pronounced zháo (second tone, indicating attainment of result, as in 睡不着 'can't fall asleep' or 找不着 'can't find'), never neutral tone zhe. More colloquial and northern in flavor than its near-synonym 看不见 (kànbujiàn). Affirmative form: 看得着 (as in 看得见摸得着 'visible and tangible').

rootFamily.gloss: unable to see, out of sight (standard equivalent)

看不见.etymology: Potential resultative verb phrase combining 看 ('to look') + 不 ('not, cannot') + 见 (trad. 見, perceptual resultative complement 'to perceive, see'). Literally 'to look but be unable to see'.

history.meaning: unable to see; invisible

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 看不见 (via 萌典)

看不顺眼.etymology: A four-character negative potential verb-complement phrase built from 看 (kàn, 'to look at'), the negative potential marker 不 (bù), and the verb-object adjectival compound 顺眼 (shùnyǎn, literally 'flowing smoothly with the eye', from 顺 'following the grain, smooth, agreeable' + 眼 'eye'). Literally 'looking at [someone/something] without it feeling agreeable to the eye', it denotes finding a person's behavior, style, or presence irritating or offensive to one's sensibilities.

history.meaning: pleasing to the eye, harmonious or agreeable to look at

history.form: 看不順眼 / 看不顺眼 (kànbushùnyǎn)
history.meaning: to find displeasing to the eye; to harbor an instinctive dislike or irritation toward someone or something

morphemes.meaning: smooth, agreeable, rubbing the right way

看不顺眼.notes: Often used with the disposal marker 把 or by splitting the object in between: 看他不顺眼 or 把某人看不顺眼 ('can't stand the sight of him / find everything he does irritating'). Common in workplace rivalry tropes where two strong-willed colleagues clash at first sight.

rootFamily.gloss: pleasing to the eye, easy on the eyes
pleasing to the ear, agreeable to hear
displeasing to the eye, unsightly, grates on the nerves

看中.etymology: A verb-resultative (动补) compound uniting 看 (kàn, 'to look at, inspect, evaluate') with the resultative complement 中 (zhòng, fourth tone, a Classical archery verb meaning 'to hit the center of the target'). Literally 'to look at and hit the bullseye with one's judgment', it expresses evaluating options and deliberately singling out a person, script, talent, or item as the exact one that meets one's criteria.

history.meaning: for an arrow to hit the center of the target
to set one's sights on, single out favorably after inspection, value and choose

看中.notes: Here 中 MUST be read in the fourth tone zhòng ('hit the mark', as in 打中 'hit a target' and 中奖 'win a prize'), not first tone zhōng ('middle'). Also do not confuse with its homophone 看重 (kànzhòng, 'to value highly, attach importance to'): 看中 is about *selecting/choosing* a specific candidate or item, whereas 看重 is about *respecting/prizing* a quality or person.

rootFamily.gloss: value highly, attach great importance to (homophonous contrast)
select and hit upon; be chosen/selected
take a liking to, fancy (more emotional/spontaneous)

看准.etymology: A verb-resultative (动补) compound combining 看 (kàn, 'to look, observe, gauge') with the adjectival resultative complement 准 (準, zhǔn, originally 'a water level used by carpenters to determine flatness', hence 'level, accurate, exact, unerring'). Literally 'to gauge with the eye until the aim is level and exact', it means to spot a trend, opportunity, or target with pinpoint accuracy before acting.

history.meaning: water-level instrument; standard, accurate, exact
to sight accurately, gauge with certainty, time or spot a target precisely

看准.notes: Frequently collocates with strategic business and production objects: 看准时机 ('time the opportunity right'), 看准方向 ('spot the right direction'), 看准市场 ('accurately read the market'). Implies sharp foresight followed by decisive action.

rootFamily.gloss: take aim at, sight a target
determine, be certain of after observation

看出.etymology: A verb-directional/resultative (动趋/动补) compound pairing 看 (kàn, 'to look at, examine') with the directional complement 出 (chū, originally depicting a foot stepping out of an enclosure, meaning 'to come or go out; to emerge into view'). By metaphorical extension from physical emergence ('looking until something comes out of hiding'), 出 marks cognitive detection: discerning, making out, or realizing an underlying truth, flaw, or emotion from outward signs.

history.meaning: to go out, emerge, become visible or manifest
to discern, detect, make out, perceive through observation

morphemes.meaning: out, forth (indicating cognitive detection or discovery)

看出.notes: Slightly more concise and written-register friendly than 看出来 (kànchūlái). Commonly takes abstract nouns or whole clauses as its object: 看出破绽 ('spot a flaw/giveaway'), 看出端倪 ('discern a clue/inklings'), 从他的表情可以看出…… ('from his expression one can tell that...').

rootFamily.gloss: unable to tell or discern by looking
make out by listening, tell from someone's voice/words

看到.etymology: A verb-resultative (动补) compound combining the active perception verb 看 (kàn, 'to look, direct one's gaze') with the resultative complement 到 (dào, originally 'to arrive at, reach a destination'). In Mandarin grammar, bare 看 denotes the volitional act of looking without guaranteeing visual capture, whereas adding the attainment complement 到 ('reach, achieve') converts it into a telic achievement verb meaning 'to catch sight of, see, witness'.

history.meaning: for one's gaze to reach and successfully perceive an object; to see
to see, catch sight of, witness (both physical sight and intellectual realization)

看到.notes: Crucial Mandarin distinction: 看 alone means 'to look at / watch / read' (an action), while 看到 (or 看见) means 'to see' (the successful perceptual result). Compared to 看见 (which focuses purely on visual sensory registration), 看到 can also take abstract objects and clauses (e.g., 看到希望 'see hope', 看到节目的潜力 'see the show's potential').

rootFamily.gloss: think of, call to mind, anticipate

看得出来.etymology: A potential directional-resultative verb construction formed from 看 (kàn, "to look at, to examine", originally an ideogrammic compound of 手 "hand" shading 目 "eye") + the potential infix 得 (de, "able to, obtain") + the compound directional complement 出来 (chūlái, "come out, emerge into view"). Literally "by looking, able to make [something] emerge toward the observer," it grammaticalized in vernacular Mandarin to express discerning an underlying truth or hidden emotion from outward signs.

history.meaning: to shade the eyes with the hand to peer into the distance; to observe
to discern or detect by looking
to be able to tell; to be discernible from appearances

看得出来.notes: Its negative counterpart is 看不出来 (kànbuchūlái, "cannot tell / wouldn't have guessed"), frequently used in showbiz dialogues when someone's hidden talent or true personality surprises observers.

rootFamily.gloss: to see clearly, to see someone's true colors

看懂.etymology: A verb-resultative compound combining 看 (kàn, "to look at, read, watch") with the resultative complement 懂 (dǒng, "to understand, comprehend", written with 忄 "heart-mind" and phonetic 董 dǒng). While Classical Chinese expressed reading comprehension through 知 (zhī) or 解 (jiě), 懂 emerged in late imperial vernacular Mandarin and paired with perceptual verbs like 看 and 听 (tīng) to separate the sensory action from its cognitive outcome.

history.meaning: to look/watch + to be muddled or later to comprehend mentally
to understand through reading or watching

看懂.notes: Takes potential infixes readily: 看得懂 ("able to understand what one reads/watches") and 看不懂 ("unable to make sense of a script, film, or person's behavior").

cognates.meaning: from the look of things (cognate Kanji roots)

看来.etymology: Originally a directional verb phrase composed of 看 (kàn, "to look at, assess") + 来 (lái, "to come [toward the speaker's perspective]"). In Song–Yuan vernacular texts, 看来 functioned at the end of a clause (e.g., 依我看来 "judging from how it comes to my view") before undergoing discourse grammaticalization into a sentence-initial epistemic adverb meaning "as it appears" or "it seems."

history.meaning: looking from here; as it comes into view
it seems, apparently (epistemic discourse marker)

morphemes.meaning: hither, toward the speaker's viewpoint (directional particle)

看来.notes: Often paired with prepositional frames like 在我看来 (zài wǒ kànlái, "in my view") or used clause-initially to draw an inference from evidence just witnessed.

rootFamily.gloss: at first glance, in the final analysis
rootFamily.word: 归根结底看来 / 照此看来

cognates.meaning: way of looking at things, viewpoint (parallel formation)

看法.etymology: A modifier-head (nominalized verb + method) compound combining 看 (kàn, "to look at, regard, evaluate") + 法 (fǎ, "method, way, principle; Buddhist dharma"). Literally "way of looking at [a matter]," the suffix -法 productively attaches to action verbs in Mandarin to denote the manner or subjective approach of doing something, shifting here from visual angle to intellectual opinion or perspective.

history.meaning: law, standard, model, method
way of viewing a matter; opinion, perspective

看法.notes: To "have an opinion about someone" expressed as 对某人有看法 (duì mǒurén yǒu kànfǎ) is a polite euphemism in workplace and production-team contexts for harboring a complaint or disapproval toward them.

rootFamily.gloss: way of speaking, phrasing, version of events

看清.etymology: Resultative verb compound from 看 ('look; see', hand 手 shading the eye 目 to gaze into the distance) + 清 ('clear; distinct'). Used directly or in potential form (看得清 / 看不清) to express making out visual details clearly.

history.meaning: see clearly; discern
see clearly; make out distinctly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 看清

看看.etymology: Reduplicated tentative verb from 看 ('to look, see, read'), softening the action to 'take a look, have a look, see how things go'.

history.meaning: to take a brief look; have a look

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 看看 (via 萌典)

看管.etymology: Coordinative verb compound combining 看 (pronounced kān, 'to watch over, guard') + 管 ('to manage, be in charge of'). Means 'to look after, guard, tend, supervise'.

history.meaning: to watch over and guard; to look after

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 看管 (via 萌典)

看花.etymology: Verb-object phrase combining 看 ('to look at, view, admire') + 花 ('flowers, blossoms'), or resultative 'to look until one's eyes blur (眼花)'.

history.meaning: to view flowers; to look until one's eyes blur

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 看花 (via 萌典)

看见.etymology: Resultative verb compound combining 看 ('to look') + 见 (trad. 見, resultative complement 'to perceive, catch sight of'). Distinguishes the completed perception ('to see, catch sight of') from the intentional action 看 ('to look').

history.meaning: to see; to catch sight of

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 看见 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: when looked at, it appears that
cognates.word: 睇起上嚟 (tai2 hei2 soeng5 lai4)

看起来.etymology: Formed from the perceptual verb 看 (kàn, "to look") + the inchoative/evaluative directional complement 起来 (qǐlái, literally "rise and come," grammaticalized as "when one starts to [V] / evaluated in terms of [V]-ing"). Originally meaning "when one begins to look at it," it evolved into a topic-comment evaluative phrase indicating how someone or something appears on the surface.

history.meaning: to begin looking; when viewed and assessed
to look like, to appear on the surface

morphemes.meaning: inchoative and evaluative directional marker (when assessed by V-ing)

看起来.notes: Unlike 看来 (which draws a logical inference from a situation, "so it seems"), 看起来 focuses directly on visual impression or outward demeanor ("he looks tired / this stage set looks grand").

rootFamily.gloss: speak of, when it comes to talking about it

cognates.meaning: to make light of, despise (classical Sino-Japanese parallel)

看轻.etymology: A verb-resultative / putative compound uniting 看 (kàn, "to look upon, regard") + 轻 (trad. 輕, qīng, "light in weight, trifling, unimportant", from 車 "chariot" + phonetic 巠 jīng). Reflecting the ancient Chinese conceptual metaphor where importance is weight (重 zhòng vs. 轻 qīng, already attested in Classical Chinese 轻视 qīngshì), 看轻 means "to regard as light in weight," hence to underestimate or belittle.

history.meaning: to treat as light in weight; to disdain or belittle
to look down on, underestimate, think little of

morphemes.meaning: light in weight, trivial, of little value

看轻.notes: Directly contrasts with 看重 (kànzhòng, "to value highly"); in workplace dramas, characters often warn rivals 别看轻了新人 ("don't underestimate the newcomers").

看过.etymology: A verb + experiential aspect construction composed of 看 (kàn, "to look at, watch, read") + 过 (trad. 過, guò / guo, originally a full movement verb meaning "to pass by, cross over," written with 辶 "walk" + phonetic 咼 guā). In Tang–Song vernacular Chinese, 过 after a verb grammaticalized from a spatial directional complement ("pass through") into an experiential aspect marker indicating that an event has been experienced at least once in the past.

history.meaning: to pass by, cross over, exceed
to look over; to have seen or read at least once before
have watched, have read, have seen (experiential)

morphemes.meaning: experiential aspect marker (have experienced V-ing) / resultative 'over'

看过.notes: When pronounced with neutral tone (kànguo), it is purely experiential ("I have read the proposal"); with full fourth tone (kànguò) followed by 了, it can mean "finished looking over/reviewing."

rootFamily.gloss: have been to, have gone before

看重.etymology: A verb-complement compound joining 看 (kàn, "to look upon, regard") + 重 (zhòng, "heavy, weighty, important"). Built on the pervasive Chinese metaphor EQUATING WEIGHT WITH IMPORTANCE (cf. Classical Chinese 重视 zhòngshì "to view as heavy/important" and 举足轻重 "a move of the foot tips the balance between light and heavy"), 看重 literally means "to view as weighty," i.e., to prize, value highly, or attach great importance to someone's talent or a quality.

history.meaning: to regard as weighty; to attach high importance to
to value highly, to think highly of (a person, ability, or outcome)

看重.notes: Whereas 重视 (zhòngshì) is more formal and institutional ("the company attaches importance to safety"), 看重 is personal and evaluative ("what the producer values most in you is your creativity").

rootFamily.gloss: think highly of, favor and mentor (a junior)

cognates.meaning: to mistake by looking, misread, misjudge

看错.etymology: A verb-resultative compound consisting of 看 (kàn, "to look at, read, judge") + 错 (trad. 錯, cuò, "wrong, mistaken"). In Old and Middle Chinese, 錯 originally meant "to inlay metal with gold or silver" and "grindstone" (from 金 "metal" + phonetic 昔 xī), then extended to "crisscrossed, mixed up, disordered," and finally in vernacular Mandarin to "erroneous, wrong." Thus 看错 means to look and arrive at a mistaken visual identification or personal judgment.

history.meaning: to inlay metal; intersecting, disorderly, awry
to misread, misidentify visually, or misjudge someone's character

看错.notes: Frequently used with 人 as 看错人 (kàncuò rén, "to misjudge a person"), either in regret after betrayal ("I misjudged him") or relief ("I knew I didn't misjudge you!").

rootFamily.gloss: walk the wrong way, take a wrong turn in life/strategy

真.etymology: Originally a Taoist and classical character (seal script combining 匕 'transformation' + 目/鼎 + 兀 'pedestal') denoting an authentic, perfected immortal (真人) or genuine inner reality, later the general word for 'true, real, genuine, really'.

history.meaning: authentic, genuine, true; really, indeed

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 真 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: source expression for the partial calque/loanblend

真人秀.etymology: A modern hybrid loan-translation (calque + phonetic loanblend) coined in the late 1990s–2000s Chinese television industry to render English "reality show." It combines 真人 (zhēnrén, "real/actual people," ironically an ancient Daoist term from the *Zhuangzi* for a "Perfected Person" or spiritual transcendent, repurposed in modern Mandarin for "real-life non-fictional person") + 秀 (xiù, originally "grain coming into ear / flowering / elegant," phonetically borrowed via Taiwanese/Hong Kong media Mandarin to transliterate English "show").

history.meaning: Daoist 'Perfected Person' + grain flowering / elegant display
reality television show featuring unscripted real people

morphemes.meaning: show, broadcast performance (phonetic loan from English 'show')

真人秀.notes: Essential television production terminology in *Behind the Scenes* (*幕后之王*); note how 秀 (xiù) now acts as a productive media morpheme in 脱口秀 (tuōkǒuxiù, "talk show"), 选秀 (xuǎnxiù, "talent show"), and 作秀 (zuòxiù, "put on a publicity stunt").

rootFamily.gloss: put on a show, stage a publicity stunt

真名.etymology: Attributive noun compound combining 真 ('true, real') + 名 ('name, given name'). Contrasts with a pseudonym, pen name, or nickname.

history.meaning: real name; true legal name

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 真名 (via 萌典)

真实.etymology: A coordinative (synonymous) compound pairing 真 (zhēn, "true, genuine, unadorned," first prominent in Daoist philosophy for authentic nature) + 实 (trad. 實, shí, "full, solid, substantial, factual," written with 宀 "roof" over 貫 "strings of cowries/wealth," meaning a house full of real goods as opposed to empty虛 xū). Attested since Han–Six Dynasties literature and Buddhist translations, the pairing unites "unfeigned/genuine" with "substantive/factual."

history.meaning: sincere, substantial, not illusory (also Buddhist tattva / ultimate reality)
real, genuine, authentic, true to life

真实.notes: In television production and film criticism, 真实 praises performances or reality programs that feel unscripted and emotionally grounded rather than contrived (虚假 xūjiǎ).

真实性.etymology: Formed by attaching the abstract nominalizing suffix -性 (xìng, originally "inborn nature, disposition," from 忄 "heart" + 生 "birth/life") to the disyllabic adjective 真实 (zhēnshí, "real, authentic"). During the Meiji era, Japanese scholars used -性 (-sei) to translate European abstract noun suffixes (-ity, -ness, -tät); this productive morphological pattern was absorbed into modern Mandarin to form abstract analytical nouns like 真实性 ("authenticity, veracity").

history.meaning: inborn human nature, inherent disposition
authenticity, veracity, quality of being real (modern academic/media coinage)

真实性.notes: A high-register analytical noun frequently used in journalism, documentary production, and legal vetting (e.g., 核实新闻的真实性 "verify the authenticity of the news").

真心.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 真 (zhēn, "true, genuine, unadulterated") + 心 (xīn, "heart, mind, intention"). Originally used in Six Dynasties and Tang Buddhist scriptures (such as the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*) to denote the "True Mind" (pure, original enlightened consciousness, Sanskrit *bhūtatathatā-citta*) as opposed to 妄心 (wàngxīn, "deluded mind"), it secularized in everyday language to mean "sincere heart, genuine goodwill," and adverbially/adjectivally "sincere, heartfelt."

history.meaning: the pure, unclouded True Mind (Buddhist philosophy); an unfeigned heart
sincere intention, heartfelt goodwill; sincerely, truly

真心.notes: Functions as a noun ("exchange sincere hearts" 以真心换真心), an attributive modifier ("sincere words" 真心话), and in contemporary colloquial Mandarin even as an emphatic degree adverb ("this show is genuinely great" 这节目真心不错).

rootFamily.gloss: honest truth, words from the heart

真心话.etymology: A left-branching modifier-head compound [[真 + 心] + 话] composed of 真心 (zhēnxīn, "sincere heart, genuine feeling") + 话 (trad. 話, huà, "spoken words, speech, talk," from 言 "speech" + 舌 "tongue"). Whereas 真话 (zhēnhuà) denotes factually true statements (the opposite of a lie), 真心话 specifically highlights words arising from one's innermost emotional sincerity and vulnerability.

history.meaning: speech, spoken words, conversation
heartfelt words, honest confession from the heart

真心话.notes: Culturally iconic in the party and variety-show game 真心话大冒险 (zhēnxīnhuà dà màoxiǎn, "Truth or Dare"), a staple segment in Chinese celebrity reality shows.

rootFamily.gloss: words from the bottom of one's heart

真是.etymology: A lexicalized adverbial-copular compound formed from 真 (zhēn, "truly, really, indeed") + 是 (shì, originally a demonstrative pronoun meaning "this" and an adjective meaning "right, correct" in Old Chinese, which evolved by the late Han dynasty into the copula "to be"). Combined as 真是, it affirms that a state or evaluation is genuinely the case, and with final 的 (真是的) grammaticalized into a standalone exclamation of mild exasperation ("Honestly! / Really now!").

history.meaning: this; right, correct (contrasted with 非 'wrong/not')
truly is, indeed is (emphatic copular phrase)
truly, really (emphatic adverb and exclamatory marker)

morphemes.meaning: to be, indeed (copula and affirmation marker)

真是.notes: Used before predicates for emotional emphasis (真是太好了 "that's truly wonderful!") or elliptically on its own (你真是(的)! "You really are something! / Come on!").

真正.etymology: Coordinative adjective/adverb combining 真 ('true, genuine') + 正 ('upright, authentic, proper'). Means 'genuine, true, veritable'.

history.meaning: genuine, true, real; truly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 真正 (via 萌典)

真的.etymology: Adverbial/adjectival phrase combining 真 ('true, real') + structural particle 的. Used both as 'really, truly' and as an exclamation or confirmation ('Really? / For real!').

history.meaning: really, truly; for real

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 真的 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: the real facts, truth of a situation
the truth, real facts of a case

真相.etymology: A modifier-head compound uniting 真 (zhēn, "true, real") + 相 (xiàng, "outward appearance, form, physiognomy, characteristic mark," written with 目 "eye" inspecting 木 "tree"). In Medieval Chinese Buddhist texts, 真相 rendered Sanskrit *bhūta-lakṣaṇa* or *tattva-lakṣaṇa* ("the true mark/nature of reality" behind illusory phenomena), and in Song–Ming portraiture it also meant a "true-to-life portrait." In modern Mandarin and Sino-Japanese, it shifted to mean the hidden factual reality behind a mystery or scandal.

history.meaning: ultimate reality / true mark of dharmas (Buddhism); lifelike portrait
the actual facts, the underlying truth of an event or case

morphemes.meaning: appearance, form, aspect, state of affairs

真相.notes: Commonly collocates with 查明 (chámíng, "investigate and clarify") or the four-character idiom 真相大白 (zhēnxiàng dàbái, "the whole truth has come out into the open"), a frequent dramatic climax in media scandals.

rootFamily.gloss: the whole truth comes to light

真行.etymology: A colloquial northern Mandarin degree-adverb + adjective phrase formed from 真 (zhēn, "truly, really") + 行 (xíng, "capable, competent, alright"). The character 行 originally depicted a four-way crossroads in oracle bone script and meant "to walk, to move, to work/function." From the sense "a road is passable / a method works," vernacular Beijing and northern Mandarin developed the adjectival sense 行 (xíng, "capable, up to the mark"), making 真行 an exclamation of admiration—or ironic disbelief—at someone's skill or audacity.

history.meaning: crossroads; to walk, to go, to put into practice, to work
really capable, quite impressive (or ironically: 'what a piece of work!')

真行.notes: Highly tone- and context-dependent: said warmly (你真行! "You're amazing!"), it praises resourcefulness; said with a sigh or cold smile ("Well, aren't you something!"), it chides someone for making a mess. Do not confuse with the classical reading zhēnháng/zhēnxìng ("virtuous conduct").

rootFamily.gloss: won't do, no good, out of the question

真诚.etymology: Coordinative adjective combining 真 ('true, genuine, unfeigned') + 诚 (trad. 誠, 'sincere, honest', from 言 'words' + 成 'complete, fulfilled'). Means 'sincere, genuine, heartfelt'.

history.meaning: sincere, genuine, heartfelt

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 真诚 (via 萌典)

真话.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 真 (zhēn, "true, factual, genuine") + 话 (trad. 話, huà, "spoken words, statement"). Emerging in vernacular Mandarin alongside its antonym 假话 (jiǎhuà, "false words, lies"), it denotes speech that corresponds to objective fact or honest belief, contrasting with literary 真言 (zhēnyán, "true words / Buddhist mantra").

history.meaning: truthful words; esoteric mantra (dhāraṇī)
truthful speech, the truth (as spoken)

真话.notes: The standard collocation is 说真话 (shuō zhēnhuà, "tell the truth"); compare 真心话 (zhēnxīnhuà, "words from the heart / emotional confession") and 真相 (zhēnxiàng, "the objective factual truth of a case").

眯.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining the eye radical 目 with phonetic 米 (*mǐ*, 'tiny grain of rice', Middle Chinese *mej*). Originally meaning 'a speck of dust or chaff getting into the eye', it naturally extended to narrowing the eyes into a squint or taking a brief catnap.

morphemes.meaning: narrow the eyes; squint; take a nap

history.meaning: speck getting into the eye; narrow the eyes
squint; narrow one's eyes

眼.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining semantic 目 ('eye') + phonetic 艮 (gěn/yǎn). Originally meant 'eyeball' in classical Chinese (where 目 was the whole eye), before replacing 目 as the everyday Mandarin noun for 'eye, small hole/aperture' and classifier for glances or wells.

history.stage: Old Chinese ('eyeball') to Modern Mandarin ('eye; glance classifier')
history.meaning: eyeball -> eye, aperture; classifier for glances

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 眼 (via 萌典)

眼前.etymology: Locative-temporal compound from 眼 ('eye', eye 目 + phonetic 艮) + 前 ('in front; before'). Used since Tang-dynasty poetry both literally for what lies directly before one's eyes and temporally for the immediate present.

history.meaning: before one's eyes; at present
right before one's eyes; at the present moment

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 眼前

眼泪.etymology: Determinative anatomical compound of 眼 ('eye', eye radical 目 + phonetic 艮 *gèn*) + 泪 ('tears', water 氵 + eye 目). Forming the standard everyday Mandarin word for tears, it pairs naturally with 掉 ('shed tears') or 擦 ('wipe tears').

history.meaning: tears from the eyes
tears

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 眼泪

眼熟.etymology: Subject-predicate adjective compound combining 眼 ('eye, sight') + 熟 ('cooked -> familiar, well-acquainted'). Literally 'familiar to the eye', i.e., 'looking familiar'.

history.meaning: looking familiar; familiar-looking

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 眼熟 (via 萌典)

眼球.etymology: A modifier-head compound joining 眼 (yǎn, "eye," written with 目 "eye" + phonetic 艮 gěn) + 球 (qiú, originally "fine jade," later "sphere, ball, globe"). First used as an anatomical term for the physical "eyeball" (alongside Japanese *gankyū*), in late-1990s and 2000s media and internet Chinese it underwent a semantic loan from English "eyeballs" (in marketing jargon like "eyeball economy" 眼球经济) to mean "public attention, viewership, or audience gaze."

history.meaning: eyeball (traditional native terms using 珠 'pearl/bead')
anatomical eyeball (modern medical term)
eyeballs; public attention, media viewership (semantic loan from English)

眼球.notes: A signature showbiz and marketing buzzword in phrases like 吸引眼球 (xīyǐn yǎnqiú, "catch the public's eye") and 博眼球 (bó yǎnqiú, "pull stunts to grab attention/clicks").

rootFamily.gloss: right in front of one's eyes, at present

cognates.meaning: field of vision; mental horizon, experience (Buddhism & general)
field of vision, mental horizon, perspective
field of vision, breadth of outlook

眼界.etymology: A modifier-head compound composed of 眼 (yǎn, "eye, faculty of sight") + 界 (jiè, "boundary, realm, sphere, world"). Originating in Chinese Buddhist translations of Sanskrit *cakṣur-dhātu* ("the realm/element of the eye," the first of the eighteen realms of perception or 十八界 *aṣṭādaśa dhātavaḥ*), it passed into Tang–Song poetry to mean "the expanse visible to the eye," and from there into general Mandarin for one's intellectual or experiential "horizons" and breadth of outlook.

history.meaning: cakṣur-dhātu, the sensory realm/faculty of the eye in Buddhist Abhidharma
physical field of view; breadth of knowledge and worldly experience
history.stage: Song–Ming Literary & Vernacular Chinese to Modern Mandarin

眼界.notes: Almost always appears in verbs of expansion: 开阔眼界 (kāikuò yǎnjiè, "broaden one's horizons") or 大开眼界 (dà kāi yǎnjiè, "be a real eye-opener").

rootFamily.gloss: be a real eye-opener, broaden one's horizons greatly
field of vision, breadth of view/perspective

眼眶.etymology: Anatomical compound of 眼 ('eye') + 眶 ('socket or rim of the eye', eye radical 目 + phonetic 匡 *kuāng*, which itself means 'square basket or frame'). It names the bony rim around the eye where tears gather when someone is deeply moved.

morphemes.meaning: eye socket; rim of the eye

history.meaning: rim or socket of the eye
eye socket; rim of the eyes

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 眼眶

眼睛.etymology: Compound noun combining 眼 ('eye') + 睛 ('eyeball, pupil', from 目 'eye' + 青 'clear/dark pupil'). Together forms the standard disyllabic Mandarin noun for 'eye(s)'.

history.meaning: eye; eyes

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 眼睛 (via 萌典)

眼线.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 眼 (yǎn, "eye, watcher") + 线 (trad. 線, xiàn, "thread, line, wire,线索 clue/lead"). In Ming–Qing vernacular detective and bandit fiction (such as *Water Margin* / *Shuihuzhuan*), an 眼线 was a planted scout or informant who acted as the "eyes" (watching the target) and the "thread" (feeding a line of intelligence back to the handler). In the 20th century, it independently acquired a second sense as a calque of cosmetic "eyeliner."

history.meaning: planted lookout, secret informant, guide who tracks targets
(1) informant, mole, plant; (2) cosmetic eyeliner

眼线.notes: In corporate and entertainment-industry dramas (*Behind the Scenes*), 安插眼线 (ānchā yǎnxiàn) means "to plant a mole/informant" inside a rival team; in a dressing room, 画眼线 (huà yǎnxiàn) means "to apply eyeliner."

rootFamily.gloss: clue, lead, thread of a story

cognates.meaning: in one's eyes, in one's estimation
cognates.word: 眼裡 / 眼內 (ngaan5 leoi5 / ngaan5 noi6)

眼里.etymology: A noun + localizer compound formed from 眼 (yǎn, "eye") + 里 (trad. 裏 or 裡, lǐ, originally "lining of a garment," written with 衣 "clothing" + phonetic 里 lǐ, which grammaticalized into the general spatial postposition "inside, within"). Beyond literal location inside the physical eye (e.g., sand in one's eye), 眼里 metaphorically conceptualizes the field of visual attention as a container: to be "in someone's eyes" means to be noticed, valued, or respected by them.

history.meaning: inner lining of a robe; inside, interior
inside the eye; within one's field of regard, estimation, or respect

眼里.notes: Crucial in the idiom 不放在眼里 (bù fàng zài yǎnlǐ, literally "not place inside one's eyes," meaning "to pay no heed to / treat with disdain") and 看在眼里 (kàn zài yǎnlǐ, "to observe silently and take note of everything").

rootFamily.gloss: in one's eyes (slightly more formal variant)
right before one's eyes, the present moment

眼镜.etymology: Attributive compound combining 眼 ('eye') + 镜 (trad. 鏡, 'mirror, optical lens'), coined during the Ming dynasty when optical spectacles were introduced and crafted.

history.meaning: eyeglasses; spectacles

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 眼镜 (via 萌典)

着.etymology: Graphic divergence of 著 (originally 'to adhere to, touch, apply'). In medieval vernacular, a post-verbal verb meaning 'to touch/stay attached' grammaticalized into the continuous/durative aspect particle zhe (看着 'looking'), while retaining verbal readings zháo ('touch, catch fire, fall asleep') and zhuó ('wear, touch').

morphemes.meaning: variant of 著: to adhere -> durative aspect particle (zhe) / resultative (zháo)

history.meaning: to adhere/touch -> durative aspect marker (-ing) / to catch, feel

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 着 (via 萌典)

着凉.etymology: A verb-object compound combining 着 (trad. 著, zháo, originally "to adhere to, come into contact with, be affected by, suffer") + 凉 (trad. 涼, liáng, "cool, cold air, chill"). In Middle and Early Mandarin medical and everyday parlance, 着 (zháo) functioned as a transitive verb meaning "to be touched/struck by [an external pathogen or element]"; thus 着凉 literally means "to be touched/afflicted by cold air," i.e., to catch a chill or cold.

history.meaning: to come into contact with, be affected by + cool/cold air
to catch a chill, catch a cold from exposure to coolness

morphemes.meaning: to touch, come into contact with, suffer from (read zháo)

着凉.notes: Always pronounced zháoliáng (second tone on 着); takes a separable structure in warnings like 小心别着了凉 ("Be careful not to catch a chill") and is virtually synonymous with 受凉 (shòuliáng).

rootFamily.gloss: cool down, become desolate (or slang: 'be doomed/flop')

着急.etymology: Verb-object adjective compound combining 着 (zháo, 'to touch, be affected by, catch') + 急 ('urgent, anxious, impatient'). Means 'to feel anxious, worry, be in a hurry'.

history.meaning: to feel anxious; to worry or be in a rush

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 着急 (via 萌典)

着迷.etymology: A verb-object compound formed from 着 (trad. 著, zháo, "to touch, come under the influence of, be struck by") + 迷 (mí, originally "to lose one's way, go astray," written with 辶 "walk" + phonetic 米 mǐ, extended to "bewilderment, enchantment, obsession"). Literally "to be struck by enchantment / fall into a spell," it describes becoming deeply captivated or infatuated by an art form, idol, or pursuit.

history.meaning: to go astray, lose one's way; to be deluded or enchanted
to fall under a spell; to be fascinated, captivated, or obsessed

morphemes.meaning: to be affected by, fall into,succumb to (read zháo)

着迷.notes: Pronounced zháomí; typically used with the preposition 对 or 为 to mark the source of fascination (e.g., 对音乐着迷 "be fascinated by music" or 令人着迷 "spellbinding, captivating").

rootFamily.gloss: be obsessed with, indulge in, be engrossed in
fan, enthusiast (e.g., 歌迷 music fan, 影迷 film fan)

睡.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining semantic 目 ('eye, eyelid') + phonetic 垂 (chuí, 'to droop, hang down', which is also co-semantic). Originally meant 'to nod off with drooping eyelids while sitting', later replacing classical 寝/眠 as the general verb 'to sleep'.

history.stage: Old Chinese ('doze with drooping eyelids') to Modern Mandarin ('to sleep')
history.meaning: drooping eyelids, dozing -> to sleep

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 睡 (via 萌典)

睡着.etymology: A verb-resultative compound combining 睡 (shuì, originally in Old Chinese "to nod off while sitting," written with 目 "eye" + phonetic 垂 chuí "droop," which replaced Classical 寝 qǐn and 眠 mián as the general verb "to sleep" in Tang–Song vernacular) + the resultative complement 着 (trad. 著, zháo, "to touch, reach, attain a target state"). While 睡 alone denotes the action of trying to sleep or lying in bed, 睡着 indicates successfully "attaining" the state of sleep, i.e., falling asleep.

history.meaning: to droop the eyelids and doze off while sitting
to succeed in falling asleep (verb + attainment complement)

morphemes.meaning: attainment of state (resultative complement, read zháo)

睡着.notes: Be careful with pronunciation and grammar: 睡着了 is read shuìzháole ("fell asleep"), whereas 睡着 with neutral tone zhe (shuìzhe) is the durative aspect ("while sleeping"). Its negative potential form is 睡不着 (shuìbuzháo, "cannot fall asleep / have insomnia").

rootFamily.gloss: unable to fall asleep, suffer from insomnia

睡觉.etymology: Separable verb-object compound of 睡 ('doze; sleep', eye radical 目 + 垂 'droop', originally 'drooping eyelids') + 觉 (read *jiào* in the departing tone, 'a sleep; nap', derived from the noun nominalization of 觉 *jué* 'wake from sleep'). In modern Mandarin it is the universal everyday verb for sleeping or going to bed.

history.meaning: sleep; take a rest
sleep; go to bed

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 睡觉

睡醒.etymology: A verb-resultative compound formed from 睡 (shuì, "to sleep") + 醒 (xǐng, originally "to sober up from alcohol," written with 酉 "fermented spirits/wine vessel" + phonetic 星 xīng, later broadened to "awaken from sleep or illusion"). Literally "to sleep until one awakens," Chinese resultative syntax allows the initial state verb (睡 "sleep") to take its terminating transition (醒 "wake up") as a resultative complement, expressing waking up naturally after sleeping.

history.meaning: to recover sobriety after drunkenness; to awaken from sleep
to wake up from sleep (after having slept)

睡醒.notes: Contrasts with 叫醒 (jiàoxǐng, "wake someone up by calling") and 吵醒 (chǎoxǐng, "wake someone up by noise"): 睡醒 is intransitive and implies waking up on one's own after a period of sleep (e.g., 还没睡醒 "still groggy / not fully awake yet").

cognates.meaning: to urge, press, demand action (cognate Kanji compound)
to urge, press for completion or payment

督促.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound combining 督 (dū, "to oversee, inspect, superintend," written with 目 "eye" watching from above + phonetic 叔 shū, originally meaning "to examine closely") + 促 (cù, "to press, urge, hasten," written with 亻 "person" + 足 "foot," originally "to step closely / press near"). Attested in post-Han administrative and historical prose, the two roots unite "supervising from above" (督) with "pressing for timely execution" (促).

history.meaning: to inspect/oversee closely + to press near, hasten
to supervise and urge to complete a duty or task

督促.notes: A constructive, semi-formal verb used for parents, mentors, or producers keeping a team on schedule (e.g., 互相督促 "hold each other accountable / keep each other on track"); unlike 催促 (cuīcù, "badger/rush"), 督促 emphasizes oversight and responsibility.

cognates.meaning: blind; blindly,recklessly (cognate character used in loans)

瞎.etymology: A phono-semantic character composed of 目 ("eye") + phonetic 害 (hài, "to injure, harm"; Old Chinese *ɦaːds / *qʰrˤat). In Classical and Middle Chinese, 瞎 originally meant "blind in one eye" or "having a damaged eye" (contrasted with 盲 máng, "completely blind"), before becoming the standard vernacular Mandarin adjective for "blind." Placed directly before an action verb (瞎 + V), it grammaticalized into a vivid colloquial adverb meaning "blindly, recklessly, without rhyme or reason, or to no avail."

history.meaning: blind in one eye; physically blind
(adj.) blind, tangled; (adv.) blindly, wildly, groundlessly, in vain

瞎.notes: Extremely productive as a colloquial prefixal adverb in northern Mandarin: 瞎忙 ("busy oneself in vain"), 瞎猜 ("guess wildly"), 瞎操心 ("worry needlessly"), and 瞎编 ("make things up out of thin air").

rootFamily.gloss: busy oneself for nothing, run around in circles

cognates.word: 亂噏 (lyun6 ngap1) / 瞎扯 (hat6 ce2)

瞎扯.etymology: A modifier-head verbal compound formed from the adverbial 瞎 (xiā, "blindly, aimlessly, without basis") + 扯 (chě, originally written 撦, from 扌 "hand" + 止/奢, meaning "to pull, tug, tear apart"). In Ming–Qing vernacular Mandarin, 扯 developed a metaphorical sense from "pulling out a long thread" (as in 扯闲话 "spin idle yarns" or 拉扯 "drag into conversation") to mean "chat, ramble, drag irrelevancies into talk." Combined as 瞎扯, it means "to pull yarns blindly," i.e., to talk nonsense or BS.

history.meaning: to pull, tear, tug; (metaphorically) to spin out talk or gossip
to ramble aimlessly, talk nonsense, bullsh*t

morphemes.meaning: to pull, tug; to spin out talk or ramble

瞎扯.notes: Colloquial and lively: 瞎扯 can mean either "spouting absurd nonsense" (别听他瞎扯 "don't listen to his BS") or more casually "shooting the breeze / bantering about random things" (闲聊瞎扯).

rootFamily.gloss: talk nonsense, spout absurdities (even more colloquial)

瞎说.etymology: A modifier-head verbal compound joining the adverbial modifier 瞎 (xiā, "blindly, groundlessly, irresponsibly") + 说 (trad. 說, shuō, originally "to explain, expound, persuade" in Old Chinese, written with 言 "speech" + 兌 duì, which replaced 言 yán and 曰 yuē as the general vernacular verb "to speak, say"). Literally "to speak blindly without seeing the facts," it denotes making unfounded assertions or speaking irresponsibly.

history.meaning: to explain, elucidate; to speak, say
to speak blindly without factual basis, talk nonsense

瞎说.notes: Slightly more direct and serious about factual falsity than 瞎扯: telling someone 别瞎说! ("Don't say things like that without proof! / Don't jinx it!") warns them against spreading false rumors or tempting fate.

rootFamily.gloss: talk nonsense, speak wildly (synonymous with 胡 'recklessly')

瞒.etymology: Phono-semantic character (trad. 瞞) combining semantic 目 ('eye') + phonetic 㒼 (mán, 'level, covered over'). Originally meant 'half-closed or平-lidded eyes', whence 'to pull the wool over someone's eyes, conceal the truth from, hide'.

history.meaning: obscured eyes -> to hide the truth from, conceal

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 瞒 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: deceive, hoodwink (in compounds like 欺瞞 giman)

瞒不过.etymology: A negative potential verb-complement construction formed from 瞒 (mán, traditional 瞞, phono-semantic compound with 目 'eye' and phonetic /满, originally meaning 'half-closed eyes' or 'blinded view' in the *Shuowen Jiezi*, later extended to 'conceal the truth from, hoodwink'), the negative potential infix 不 (bù, 'cannot'), and the directional/resultative complement 过 (guò, 'pass by, surpass, get past'). Literally 'cannot deceive past [someone's eyes]', it developed in Ming–Qing vernacular fiction to express that a deception cannot get past a perceptive observer.

history.meaning: to have drooping or obscured eyes; to hoodwink or conceal truth from
unable to deceive or hide the truth from someone

瞒不过.notes: Often takes a person or their 'eyes' as the direct object (e.g., 瞒不过你的眼睛, 'nothing gets past your eyes'); its affirmative counterpart is 瞒得过.

rootFamily.gloss: to conceal, hide from view or knowledge
to deceive above and bully below (idiom)
to successfully keep in the dark

瞒住.etymology: A resultative verb-complement compound combining 瞒 (mán, traditional 瞞, 'to obscure vision, conceal the truth from, deceive') with the resultative complement 住 (zhù, originally 'to halt, reside, stay firm', functioning grammatically as a complement of fixation or successful containment). Literally 'to conceal and hold fast', it signifies keeping a secret tightly contained so that the target remains unaware.

history.meaning: conceal (verb) + hold fast / fix in place (resultative complement)
successfully keep a secret from someone; keep under wraps

morphemes.meaning: hold fast, keep securely in place

瞒住.notes: Frequently appears in potential constructions (瞒不住, 'cannot keep it under wraps any longer') or with the disposal marker 把 (把事情瞒住, 'keep the matter hushed up').

rootFamily.gloss: to conceal or cover up the truth

瞒着.etymology: Formed from the transitive verb 瞒 (mán, traditional 瞞, 'to conceal the truth from, pull the wool over someone's eyes', from 目 'eye' + phonetic 满/㒼) suffixed with the durative/imperfective aspect particle 着 (zhe, grammaticalized in Medieval Vernacular Chinese from 著 'to attach, adhere, remain'). It describes an ongoing state of keeping someone in the dark while doing something else behind their back.

history.meaning: to obscure the eyes; to deceive or keep uninformed
keeping (someone) in the dark; behind someone's back

morphemes.meaning: durative aspect marker (in an ongoing state of)

瞒着.notes: Typically used in serial verb constructions as '瞒着 + [Person] + [Verb Phrase]' (e.g., 瞒着大家签合同, 'sign a contract behind everyone's back').

瞧.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining semantic 目 ('eye') + phonetic 焦 (jiāo/qiáo). Emerged in Yuan–Ming northern vernacular Mandarin as a lively colloquial verb meaning 'to look, glance, see'.

history.stage: Yuan–Ming Northern Mandarin to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: to look; to take a glance; see

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 瞧 (via 萌典)

瞧瞧.etymology: Tentative verb reduplication (VV pattern) of 瞧 ('look; glance at', eye 目 + phonetic 焦). Common in northern Mandarin colloquial speech, reduplicating 瞧 invites someone in a warm, casual tone to 'come take a quick look'.

morphemes.meaning: take a quick or casual look

history.meaning: take a look; have a glance
take a look; see for oneself

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 瞧瞧

cognates.meaning: looking ahead and behind; being overly cautious and indecisive

瞻前顾后.etymology: A four-character Classical Chinese parallel idiom (*chengyu*) with an interleaved Verb–Object + Verb–Object structure: 瞻 (zhān, 'to look up at, gaze ahead') + 前 (qián, 'what is in front') and 顾 (gù, traditional 顧, 'to turn the head to look back') + 后 (hòu, traditional 後, 'what is behind'). Attested in Qu Yuan's *Li Sao* (离骚, *Chuci*, Warring States period): '瞻前而顾后兮，相观民之计极' ('Gazing ahead and looking back, I survey the ultimate state of the people's counsels'), where it originally praised thorough circumspection before later shifting in Song Neo-Confucian prose (such as *Zhuzi Yulei*) to criticize overcautious hesitation.

history.form: 瞻前而顧後 (zhān qián ér gù hòu)
history.meaning: to gaze ahead and look behind; to examine a situation thoroughly from all angles

history.form: 瞻前顧後 / 瞻前顾后 (zhānqián-gùhòu)
history.meaning: to hesitate and overthink every step; to be overly cautious and indecisive

morphemes.meaning: turn the head to look back at

瞻前顾后.notes: In modern Mandarin this idiom is almost always mildly pejorative, describing someone who is paralyzed by worry over consequences rather than acting decisively.

rootFamily.gloss: to look up to with reverence; to view
to look forward to the future and back at the past
to take into consideration, attend to

cognates.word: 知唔知道 (zi1 m4 zi1 dou3)

知不知道.etymology: An A-not-AB (affirmative–negative) interrogative construction formed by reduplicating the initial syllable of the disyllabic compound verb 知道 (zhīdào, 'to know, be aware of', originally a Classical verb–object phrase meaning 'to know the Way/principle') around the negator 不 (bù). This clipped A-not-AB pattern (知不知道 rather than full 知道不知道) became standard in early modern northern vernacular Mandarin as a direct, high-frequency way to ask for confirmation or emphasize a point.

history.meaning: to understand the Way or moral principle; later grammaticalized to 'to know'
do (you) know or not?; are (you) aware of whether...

morphemes.meaning: know, be aware of (lit. know the way)

知不知道.notes: At the end of a declarative sentence (e.g., 这很重要，知不知道？), it functions rhetorically like 'got it?' or 'you know?', often carrying an urgent or lecturing tone.

cognates.meaning: acquaintance; appreciative friend who truly understands one
intimate friend who knows one's heart

知己.etymology: A Classical Chinese verb–object compound nominalized through metonymy: 知 (zhī, 'to know deeply, appreciate, understand') + 己 (jǐ, reflexive pronoun 'oneself'). Literally 'one who knows me', it is famously immortalized in Sima Qian's *Shiji* (史记·刺客列传, 'Biographies of the Assassins', c. 91 BCE): '士为知己者死，女为悦己者容' ('A man of honor dies for one who truly understands him; a woman adorns herself for one who delights in her'), as well as Wang Bo's Tang poem: '海内存知己，天涯若比邻' ('So long as a bosom friend remains within the four seas, the farthest corners of the earth are like next-door neighbors').

history.meaning: to understand oneself (as in 知己知彼); or one who understands and appreciates oneself
intimate friend, kindred spirit, soulmate

知己.notes: Pairs famously in two contrasting proverbs: 知己知彼 ('know yourself and know your enemy', where 己 is truly reflexive) versus 人生得一知己足矣 ('in life, having one true kindred spirit is enough').

rootFamily.gloss: intimate friend who appreciates one's music/talent (lit. know the tone)
know yourself and know your adversary

cognates.meaning: knowing the circumstances or true facts (legal/literary)
knowing the facts or circumstances (especially in law)

知情.etymology: A Classical Chinese verb–object compound composed of 知 (zhī, 'to know, be aware of') + 情 (qíng, 'the actual facts, underlying circumstances, true state of affairs'—the classical sense of 情 as 'reality/circumstances', rather than modern 'emotion'). Attested in early legal and historical texts, where 知情 denoted having prior knowledge of a crime or hidden state of affairs.

history.meaning: to know the true facts or inner workings of a matter (especially in legal contexts)
to be informed, be privy to the facts of a situation

morphemes.meaning: actual facts, circumstances, state of affairs

知情.notes: Because 知情 is an intransitive verb–object compound, it cannot take a direct object; to say 'privy to this matter', use 对此事知情 or 知情人 ('an insider / person in the know').

rootFamily.gloss: right to know, right to be informed
person in the know, insider, witness

cognates.meaning: right to know (conceptual parallel using 権 ken)
