知情权.etymology: A modern legal and journalistic neologism formed as a modifier–head compound: 知情 (zhīqíng, verb–object compound 'to know the facts/circumstances') + the suffixoid 权 (quán, traditional 權, originally 'steelyard weight, balance of power', adopted in late 19th-century Sino-Japanese legal translations for Western 'right' or *ius*). It calques the modern English journalistic and legal concept 'right to know' (coined in the mid-20th century by Kent Cooper regarding freedom of information and later extended to consumer and patient informed consent).

history.meaning: being informed of the facts + legal/civil right
the right to know; right to be informed (in media, law, and medicine)

知情权.notes: Heavily used in media, PR, and medical dramas (e.g., 尊重公众的知情权, 'respect the public's right to know').

rootFamily.gloss: to be informed, know the facts

知识.etymology: A coordinative compound of two near-synonymous cognitive verbs: 知 (zhī, 'to know, perceive, comprehend', from 矢 'arrow' + 口 'mouth', suggesting speech hitting the mark rapidly) and 识 (shí, traditional 識, neutralized to轻声 *shi* in modern Mandarin, 'to recognize, discern, remember'). In Classical Chinese and Medieval Chinese Buddhist translations (where 善知识 translated Sanskrit *kalyāṇa-mitra*, 'good spiritual friend/acquaintance'), it meant 'acquaintance' or 'discernment/consciousness'. During the Meiji period in Japan, 知識 (*chishiki*) was repurposed to translate English 'knowledge' and German *Wissen*, and this philosophical/scientific sense was re-imported into modern Mandarin.

history.meaning: perception and discernment; an acquaintance or learned friend (especially in Buddhist texts)
knowledge, learning, expertise (reinforced via Meiji Japanese 知識)

知识.notes: Note that 识 is pronounced with a neutral tone (*zhīshi*) in Mainland standard Mandarin; it takes the classifier 门 (for a branch of knowledge) or 点 (for a bit of knowledge), never 个.

知道.etymology: Originally a classical verb-object phrase 知 ('to know, understand', from 矢 'arrow hitting the mark' + 口 'words') + 道 ('the Way, moral/cosmic principle'). By the Tang–Song period, 道 bleached into a disyllabic verbal suffix, yielding the everyday verb 'to know, be aware of'.

history.stage: Classical ('to know the Way') to Tang–Modern Mandarin ('to know')
history.meaning: to know the Way -> to know, be aware of

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 知道 (via 萌典)

短.etymology: An ancient Associative/Ideographic compound (*huiyi*) combining 矢 (shǐ, 'arrow') and 豆 (dòu, 'stemmed ritual vessel'). As explained in Xu Shen's *Shuowen Jiezi* (说文解字, 100 CE), '有所长短，以矢为正'—arrows and ritual vessels served as standardized implements for measuring length: 长 (long) vs. 短 (short, measured by the shorter vessel 豆 alongside the measuring arrow 矢). From Old Chinese *\*toːnʔ*, it has denoted spatial shortness, temporal brevity, and figurative deficiency or fault since pre-Qin antiquity.

history.meaning: short in length (measured by arrow and vessel); brief in time; lacking or deficient
short, brief; shortcoming or weak point; to lack or owe

短.notes: Alongside its everyday adjectival use ('short' in length or time, contrasting with 长 *cháng*), 短 also functions as a noun meaning 'fault/shortcoming' (as in 说人长短 or 揭短, 'expose someone's faults').

cognates.meaning: short term, short period of time

短期.etymology: A modifier–head compound formed from 短 (duǎn, 'short, brief') modifying 期 (qī, 'appointed time, fixed period, cycle, deadline'). While both characters are ancient, the compact compound 短期 gained widespread currency in late 19th- and early 20th-century East Asian administrative, financial, and educational vocabulary (reinforced by Japanese 短期 *tanki*) to contrast with 长期 (chángqī, 'long-term').

history.meaning: brief + appointed period or fixed span of time
short-term, brief duration (in finance, planning, and scheduling)

短期.notes: Functions primarily as a non-predicative adjective (attributive modifier, e.g., 短期目标 'short-term goal') or time noun (在短期内 'in the short run').

cognates.meaning: short-term training program (structural parallel sharing 短期)

短期培训.etymology: A four-character modifier–head compound combining 短期 (duǎnqī, 'short-term', itself a modifier–head compound of 短 'brief' + 期 'time period') with 培训 (péixùn, 'to cultivate and train', a coordinative compound of 培 'to bank up earth around roots, nurture, foster' + 训 'to instruct, drill, guide'). It arose in modern Mandarin institutional, corporate, and educational discourse to designate intensive skills-training courses or bootcamps lasting from a few days to several months.

history.meaning: to earth up / nurture plants + to instruct or lecture
short-term training program or intensive course

短期培训.notes: Often abbreviated in speech and job advertisements as 短训 (duǎnxùn) or 培训班 (péixùnbān, 'training class').

rootFamily.gloss: to train, cultivate personnel; training program

短板.etymology: A modifier–head compound composed of 短 (duǎn, 'short') + 板 (bǎn, 'wooden plank, stave'). Literally 'the short stave (of a wooden bucket)', its modern figurative meaning ('weak spot, bottleneck, Achilles' heel') derives from management economist Laurence J. Peter's 'Cannikin Law' / 'Wooden Bucket Theory' (木桶理论 / 短板效应, inspired by Justus von Liebig's Law of the Minimum): a wooden bucket's capacity to hold water is determined not by its longest stave (长板), but by its shortest stave (短板).

history.meaning: a short wooden board or stave
limiting factor, bottleneck, weak spot, Achilles' heel (from Wooden Bucket Theory)

短板.notes: A favorite buzzword in Chinese business, media production, and politics, most commonly paired with the verb 补齐 or 补上 (补齐短板, 'to shore up one's weak spots').

rootFamily.gloss: strong point, core advantage (lit. long stave)
rigid, inflexible; printing plate or board

短话.etymology: Attributive noun compound combining 短 ('short, brief', from 矢 'arrow used as a short measure' + 豆 phonetic) + 话 (trad. 話, 'spoken words, message'). Means 'a brief message, short remarks' (as in 长话短说).

history.meaning: short message; brief words

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 短话 (via 萌典)

矮凳.etymology: Modifier-head compound from 矮 ('short in stature; low', arrow 矢 + phonetic 委) + 凳 ('backless stool; bench'). Refers to a low wooden or bamboo stool used when sitting near the floor, washing, or resting an injured foot.

history.meaning: low stool
low stool; footstool

石墙.etymology: Attributive compound combining 石 ('stone, rock', an ancient pictograph of a rock beneath a cliff 厂) + 墙 (trad. 牆, 'wall').

history.meaning: stone wall

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 石墙 (via 萌典)

石头.etymology: Suffixed noun combining 石 ('stone, rock') + nominal suffix 头 (trad. 頭, toneless -tou used on concrete nouns since the Six Dynasties–Tang period).

history.meaning: stone; rock; pebble

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 石头 (via 萌典)

石板.etymology: Compound of 石 ('stone; rock', pictograph of a cliff overhang with a boulder beneath) + 板 ('flat slab; plank'). Denotes flat-cut paving stones or flagstones used in traditional Chinese courtyards and alleyways.

history.meaning: flat paving stone; flagstone
flagstone; stone slab

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 石板

石板路.etymology: Three-character compound combining 石板 ('flagstone, stone slab', from 石 'stone' + 板 'flat slab') + 路 ('road, path'). Denotes a flagstone-paved street or path.

history.meaning: flagstone path; stone-paved street

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 石板路 (via 萌典)

石桥.etymology: Attributive compound combining 石 ('stone') + 桥 (trad. 橋, 'bridge', originally a tall arched wooden footbridge). Denotes a stone bridge.

history.meaning: stone bridge

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 石桥 (via 萌典)

码.etymology: Phono-semantic character (trad. 碼) combining semantic 石 ('stone, agate pebble') + phonetic 马 (馬, mǎ). Used historically for agate counting tokens (筹码), hence 'number, code, stack of goods', and since the 19th century as the phonetic loan/translation for the English length unit 'yard' and shoe/clothing 'size'.

history.stage: Ming–Qing ('counting token') to Modern Mandarin ('number, size, yard')
history.meaning: agate counter -> number, code, size, yard

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 码 (via 萌典)

砂纸.etymology: Compound of 砂 ('coarse mineral grit, quartz/emery sand', stone radical 石 + 少) + 纸 ('paper'), naming abrasive grit bonded onto heavy paper backing for carpentry smoothing.

history.meaning: abrasive sandpaper

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 砂纸

砌.etymology: Phono-semantic architectural character combining the stone radical 石 ('stone/brickwork') + phonetic 切 (*qiè/qì*, 'cut neatly in courses'). Originally denoting paved stone steps in Han rhyme dictionaries, it became the standard verb for laying bricks or stones with mortar to build a wall (砌墙).

morphemes.meaning: lay bricks or stones in courses; build masonry

history.meaning: stone-paved steps; lay stone courses
build a brick or stone wall

研一.etymology: A contemporary Mainland Chinese campus abbreviation coined by clipping 研究生一年级 (yánjiūshēng yī niánjí, 'graduate student, first academic year') to its initial morphemes: 研 (yán, originally 'to grind fine on a stone', standing for 研究生 'graduate student / postgraduate school') + 一 (yī, 'one, first year'). It follows the productive university year-level paradigm modeled on 大一 (dàyī, 'freshman in college') through 大四 (dàsì, 'senior').

history.form: 研究生一年級 (yánjiūshēng yī niánjí)
history.meaning: first-year student in a postgraduate degree program
first year of graduate school (usually master's year 1)

morphemes.meaning: graduate school / postgraduate student (clipped from 研究生)

研一.notes: Parallel campus abbreviations include 大一 to 大四 (undergraduate years 1–4), 研一 to 研三 (master's years 1–3), and 博一 to 博四 (doctoral years 1–4).

rootFamily.gloss: to take the graduate school entrance exam (考研)

研究.etymology: Coordinative verb-noun compound combining 研 ('to grind ink or stone fine; to examine minutely') + 究 ('to probe to the end of a cave 穴; to investigate thoroughly'). Used since Han–Six Dynasties scholarship for deep inquiry and in modern Mandarin for academic or practical 'research, study'.

morphemes.meaning: to probe to the bottom; investigate

history.meaning: to grind fine and probe deeply -> to research, study, examine

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 研究 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: research student (non-degree auditing researcher in Japan; false friend!)

研究生.etymology: A modifier–head compound formed from 研究 (yánjiū, a Classical Chinese coordinative verb compound of 研 'to grind fine, rub, examine thoroughly' + 究 'to probe to the bottom of a cave/matter, investigate', attested since the Han–Tang eras) + the agentive/status suffix 生 (shēng, 'scholar, student, pupil'). Adopted in modern East Asian higher education systems to designate a student pursuing advanced academic research beyond a bachelor's degree.

history.meaning: to grind fine and probe thoroughly; to investigate deeply
graduate student (master's or doctoral candidate in Chinese universities)

研究生.notes: Watch out for the Japanese false friend: in Chinese, 研究生 means a degree-seeking graduate student (Master's 硕士生 or PhD 博士生, often specifically Master's in casual speech), whereas in Japanese 研究生 (*kenkyūsei*) means a non-degree preparatory research student (a degree-seeking grad student in Japan is 大学院生 *daigakuinsei*).

砖.etymology: Phono-semantic character (trad. 磚, also 甎) combining semantic 石 ('stone, masonry') or 瓦 ('fired clay') + phonetic 专 (專, zhuān). Denotes a kiln-fired clay or stone building brick.

history.meaning: fired clay or stone building brick

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 砖 (via 萌典)

砖墙.etymology: Attributive compound combining 砖 (trad. 磚, 'kiln-fired brick') + 墙 (trad. 牆, 'wall').

history.meaning: brick wall

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 砖墙 (via 萌典)

砖头.etymology: Suffixed noun combining 砖 (trad. 磚, 'brick') + nominal suffix 头 (trad. 頭, -tou). Denotes a building brick or a broken piece of brick.

history.meaning: brick; piece of brick

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 砖头 (via 萌典)

砖房.etymology: Attributive compound combining 砖 (trad. 磚, 'brick') + 房 ('house, building'). Denotes a brick-built house.

history.meaning: brick house

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 砖房 (via 萌典)

破.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining semantic 石 ('stone') + phonetic 皮 (pí/pò, 'skin, hide'). Originally meant 'stone splitting or cracking apart', extended to 'broken, torn, worn-out, damaged' and 'to break, defeat, expose'.

history.meaning: stone cracking -> broken, torn, worn-out; to break

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 破 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: exceptional, unprecedented, outside normal standards or grammar

破格.etymology: A Classical Chinese verb–object compound composed of 破 (pò, 'to break, smash, breach') + 格 (gé, originally 'tall tree branches', extended in imperial administrative and poetic usage to mean 'standard, lattice framework, official rank qualification, or metrical rule'). Attested in Tang dynasty poetry and civil service administration (e.g., Du Fu and imperial edicts) to describe either breaking poetic meter or promoting a talented candidate outside the rigid bureaucratic seniority rules.

history.meaning: to break poetic meter; or to bypass standard bureaucratic rank requirements in promoting officials
making an exception to the rules (especially in hiring, admission, or promotion)

破格.notes: Almost always used adverbially before verbs of hiring, admission, or promotion: 破格录取 ('admit by waiving normal requirements') or 破格提拔 ('promote ahead of standard seniority').

破费.etymology: A verb–object or coordinative compound formed from 破 (pò, 'to break into, split open, expend/consume', as in 破财 'lose money') + 费 (fèi, 'expenditure, expenses, to spend'). Emerging in Song–Yuan and Ming–Qing vernacular literature (such as *Water Margin* and *Dream of the Red Chamber*), it literally meant 'to break into one's funds and spend', evolving into a polite conversational formula used by a guest or gift recipient to thank a host for going to financial trouble.

history.meaning: to expend money, incur expenses or waste wealth
(polite) to go to great expense; to put someone to the trouble of spending money

破费.notes: Used almost exclusively as a polite social courtesy directed at someone who is treating you or giving you a gift (e.g., 又让您破费了！ 'You shouldn't have gone to such expense again!').

rootFamily.gloss: to suffer unexpected financial loss (lit. break wealth)

cognates.meaning: great scholar; master's degree (used in China/Korea; Japan uses 修士 shūshi)

硕士.etymology: A Classical Chinese modifier–head compound combining 硕 (shuò, traditional 碩, from 页 'head' + 石 'stone/great', originally meaning 'large-headed, great, eminent, abundant') + 士 (shì, 'scholar, gentleman, cultivated official'). In the *Book of Changes* (易经) and Tang–Song prose (such as Han Yu), 硕士 meant 'a scholar of great virtue and erudition'. In the early 20th century, Chinese and Korean educational reformers adopted 硕士 as the official translation for the Western academic 'Master's degree' (ranked between 学士 Bachelor and 博士 Doctor).

history.meaning: a scholar of great learning and high moral stature
master's degree; holder of a master's degree

硕士.notes: Forms the standard Chinese academic degree triad: 学士 (Bachelor's), 硕士 (Master's), and 博士 (Doctorate/PhD); note that standard Mainland pronunciation is *shuòshì* (not *shíshì*).

rootFamily.gloss: doctorate, PhD; court erudite in antiquity
great achievements or abundant fruits (lit. huge fruits)

cognates.meaning: hard, stiff, firm (in compounds like 강경)

硬.etymology: A phono-semantic compound (*xingsheng*) composed of semantic radical 石 (shí, 'stone, rock', indicating physical hardness) and phonetic 更 (gēng, Old Chinese *\*kraːŋs*). Emerging in post-Han and Six Dynasties Chinese (partially replacing earlier Classical 坚 *jiān* and 刚 *gāng* in vernacular speech), 硬 originally meant 'physically hard or solid like stone', then extended metaphorically to 'stiff, tough, uncompromising, high-capability' and adverbially to 'by force, stubbornly, doggedly'.

history.meaning: hard like stone, solid, firm, stiff
hard, tough, strong in quality; (adverb) stubbornly, forcing oneself to do something against the odds

硬.notes: As an adverb (often followed by 是, as in 硬是 or 硬着头皮), 硬 means 'by sheer willpower, doggedly, or forcing something through despite resistance' (e.g., 他硬把任务完成了, 'he powered through and finished the task anyway').

rootFamily.gloss: to brace oneself and force one's way through (lit. stiffen one's scalp)

硬币.etymology: Compound of 硬 ('hard, rigid', stone radical 石 + 更) + 币 ('currency', originally ritual silk offerings in Classical Chinese, later generalized to money), contrasting metal coins with paper 纸币.

history.meaning: ritual silk gift; medium of exchange
metal coin

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 硬币 (via 萌典)

硬盘.etymology: A modern Mainland Chinese computing calque of English *hard disk* / *hard drive*, constructed as a modifier–head compound: 硬 (yìng, 'hard, rigid') + 盘 (pán, traditional 盤, originally 'wooden or bronze basin/tray', extended to any flat round platter or rotating magnetic disk). It was coined in the late 20th century in direct opposition to 软盘 (ruǎnpán, 'floppy disk', lit. 'soft platter').

history.meaning: hard/rigid + round tray or rotating platter
computer hard disk drive (HDD) or solid-state storage drive

硬盘.notes: Mainland China uses 硬盘 (yìngpán), whereas Taiwan Mandarin calls a hard drive 硬碟 (yìngdié, using 碟 'small saucer/disc'); common subtypes are 移动硬盘 ('external portable hard drive') and 固态硬盘 ('SSD').

确保.etymology: A modifier–head or coordinative verbal compound formed from 确 (què, traditional 確/皵, from 石 'stone' + 寉, meaning 'rock-solid, firm, certain, reliably') + 保 (bǎo, 'to protect, safeguard, guarantee, maintain', originally an ideograph of an adult carrying a child on their back). Popularized across modern East Asian administrative and legal prose via Japanese 確保 (*kakuho*), it means 'to firmly guarantee or secure'.

history.meaning: firmly / certainly + safeguard or guarantee
to ensure, make sure, guarantee, secure (reinforced via Meiji Japanese 確保)

确保.notes: More formal than 保证 (bǎozhèng); 确保 can take either a noun phrase (确保安全, 'ensure safety') or a full clause (确保节目按时播出, 'make sure the show airs on time').

确切.etymology: A coordinative adjectival compound joining 确 (què, traditional 確, 'rock-solid, firm, authentic, true') and 切 (qiè, originally 'to cut close with a knife', extended in Classical Chinese to 'pressing close to reality, exact, right to the point', from the pulse-taking sense of pressing down directly on the vessel). Attested in Tang–Song literary criticism and official memorials to describe arguments or facts that are both rock-solid (确) and right on the mark (切).

history.meaning: firmly grounded and hitting close to the mark (of prose, evidence, or judgments)
exact, definite, precise, accurate (of news, dates, meanings, or figures)

morphemes.meaning: cut close, correspond closely to reality, precise

确切.notes: Commonly modifies words like 消息 ('news'), 时间 ('time'), 数字 ('figure'), or 意思 ('meaning'), and often appears in the conversational hedge 确切地说 ('to be exact / more precisely').

rootFamily.gloss: realistic, feasible, practical (lit. close to reality)
accurate, precise (lit. hit the mark firmly)

确定.etymology: A coordinative/resultative compound combining 确 (què, traditional 確, 'firm, solid like stone, unmistakable') and 定 (dìng, 'to settle, fix in place, decide', from 宀 'roof/house' + 正 'upright/correct'). Found in medieval Chinese prose in the sense of 'firmly settled or resolved', its modern verbal and adjectival senses ('to determine, settle on, confirm; definite') were standardized across East Asia during the late 19th and early 20th centuries alongside Japanese 確定 (*kakutei*).

history.meaning: firmly settled, fixed and unwavering (of plans, principles, or mind)
to decide firmly, settle on, determine, confirm; definite, fixed (also used as 'OK' button in UIs)

确定.notes: Learner distinction: 确定 means 'to settle on / decide / make definite' (fixing something previously undecided, or being sure in one's mind, e.g., 你确定吗？ 'Are you sure?'), whereas 确认 means 'to verify/acknowledge something that already exists'.

cognates.meaning: certain, reliable, sound, sure (adjective/adverb; partial semantic shift from Mandarin adverb 'indeed')

确实.etymology: A coordinative compound composed of 确 (què, traditional 確, 'rock-solid, firm, true') + 实 (shí, traditional 實, from 宀 'roof' + 贯 'strings of cowries/wealth', meaning 'full, solid, substantial, true to fact'). Attested in Qing dynasty official and vernacular prose to mean 'solid, authentic, and verifiable', it developed in modern Mandarin both into an adjective ('reliable, authentic') and a high-frequency sentence adverb ('indeed, truly, really').

history.meaning: solid, substantial, true to the facts, verifiable
(adverb) indeed, really, truly; (adjective) reliable, authentic, certain

morphemes.meaning: full, substantial, actual, true to fact

确实.notes: In spoken Mandarin, 确实 is frequently used by itself as a one-word reply ('Indeed!' / 'True that!') to validate what someone else just said.

确认.etymology: A modifier–head or coordinative compound formed from 确 (què, traditional 確, 'firmly, definitely, unmistakably') + 认 (rèn, traditional 認, 'to recognize, identify, acknowledge'). Originally coined or popularized in Meiji Japan as 確認 (*kakunin*) in legal terminology to translate German *Anerkennung* / *Feststellung* and English *confirmation* / *acknowledgment*, it entered modern Mandarin as a return loan (*wasei-kango*) and became ubiquitous in law, business, and computing.

history.meaning: legal acknowledgment, verification, or confirmation of an existing fact or right
to confirm, verify, double-check, or formally acknowledge

确认.notes: Unlike 确定 ('to decide on / fix something not yet settled'), 确认 means 'to verify, check, or officially acknowledge an existing fact, identity, or order' (e.g., 确认身份 'verify identity', 请确认收货 'please confirm receipt of goods').

碎.etymology: A phono-semantic compound (*xingsheng*) combining the semantic radical 石 (shí, 'stone, rock') with the phonetic component 卒 (zú / cuì, Old Chinese *\*sˤut* / *\*[ts]ʰˤut-s*). Recorded in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as '䃺也' ('to grind/crush stone into small bits'), it has been used since the Warring States and Han periods both as a verb ('to shatter, smash to smithereens') and as an adjective ('fragmented, broken into tiny pieces,琐碎/petty').

history.meaning: to crush or smash stone into small fragments; shattered
to shatter, break to pieces; fragmented, broken; chatterbox/trivial (colloquial)

morphemes.meaning: shatter, break into small pieces; fragmented

碎.notes: Functions both as an independent verb/adjective (心碎 'heartbroken', 碎玻璃 'broken glass') and as a high-frequency resultative complement after action verbs (打碎 'smash to pieces', 摔碎 'drop and shatter').

rootFamily.gloss: to smash to pieces, shatter; crushed
trivial, petty, fragmented (of chores or details)

碎玻璃.etymology: A modifier–head compound combining 碎 (suì, 'shattered, broken into fragments') with 玻璃 (bōli, 'glass'). Notably, 玻璃 (attested in medieval Chinese texts as 颇黎 *pōlí* or 玻瓈) is an ancient Buddhist loanword from Sanskrit *sphaṭika* (स्फटिक) / Prakrit *phaḷika*, which originally designated 'rock crystal' or 'quartz' before shifting in the Ming–Qing periods to denote manufactured silica glass. Thus 碎玻璃 joins a native Old Chinese stone-shattering root with an Indo-Aryan crystal loanword.

history.form: 頗黎 / 玻瓈 (pōlí < Sanskrit sphaṭika)
history.meaning: rock crystal, quartz, or translucent gem; later blown glass
broken glass, shattered glass shards

morphemes.meaning: glass (originally Sanskrit loanword for rock crystal)

碎玻璃.notes: In Mandarin word order, 碎玻璃 (Adjective + Noun) is a noun phrase meaning 'broken glass / glass shards', whereas 玻璃碎了 (Subject + Predicate Verb) is a clause meaning 'the glass shattered'.

rootFamily.gloss: fragile, oversensitive heart (lit. glass heart, internet slang)

碗.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining semantic 石 ('stone/ceramic ware', variants 椀 with 木 'wood' or 盌 with 皿 'vessel') + phonetic 宛 (wǎn, also suggesting a curved concavity). Denotes a hemispherical eating or drinking bowl.

history.stage: Old Chinese (盌/椀) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: bowl; classifier for bowls of food or drink

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 碗 (via 萌典)

碰.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining semantic 石 ('stone') + phonetic 并/𡘋 (pèng). Emerged in vernacular Mandarin for 'to bump into, knock against, meet by chance, touch'.

history.meaning: to bump into, collide, touch; to meet by chance

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 碰 (via 萌典)

碰上.etymology: A verb–complement compound formed from 碰 (pèng, traditional 掽/碰, from 石 'stone' + phonetic 并 *bìng*, emerging in Yuan–Ming vernacular Chinese with the meaning 'to collide, bump into, strike against') + the directional/resultative complement 上 (shàng, 'up, onto', grammaticalized to express making contact or successfully encountering a target). Literally 'to bump onto', it shifted from physical collision to unexpectedly running into a person, event, or situation.

history.meaning: to collide, knock against, bump into
to run into by chance, cross paths with, happen to encounter (a person or situation)

morphemes.meaning: bump into, collide, meet by chance

碰上.notes: Can take either a person (我在电梯里碰上他了, 'I bumped into him in the elevator') or an unfavorable/lucky circumstance (碰上堵车, 'get caught in a traffic jam'). Near-synonyms include 碰到 and 碰见.

rootFamily.gloss: to bump into, run into, encounter
to meet by chance, run into (a person)
to try one's luck (lit. bump into luck)

碰到.etymology: Resultative verb compound from 碰 ('bump into; touch; meet by chance') + resultative complement 到 ('reach; make contact with'). Expresses either physical contact ('touch / brush against') or running into a person or problem unexpectedly.

history.meaning: bump into; touch; come across
touch; bump into; run into

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 碰到

碰头.etymology: Verb-object compound combining 碰 ('to bump together, meet') + 头 (trad. 頭, 'head'). Literally 'to bring heads together', used colloquially for meeting up briefly to confer or compare notes.

history.meaning: to meet up; to get together to discuss

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 碰头 (via 萌典)

磕破.etymology: Resultative verb compound combining 磕 ('to knock or strike against a hard surface', from 石 'stone' + 盍 phonetic) + 破 ('broken, skinned, split open').

morphemes.meaning: to knock against a hard surface

history.meaning: to knock and break/scrape open

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 磕破 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: grind, polish, rub (in compounds like 연마)

磨.etymology: A phono-semantic/associative compound (*xingsheng*/*huiyi*) composed of 麻 (má, 'hemp', serving as phonetic, Old Chinese *\*mˤaj*) and 石 (shí, 'stone', indicating grinding with stone). Derived from the earlier Classical graph 摩 (mó, 'to rub with the hand', which uses 手 'hand' instead of 石 'stone'), 磨 is famously attested in the *Classic of Poetry* (诗经·卫风·淇奥, '如琢如磨', 'like carving and polishing stone/jade'). Note its tonal split by transitivity/nominalization: level tone *mó* ('to rub, grind, polish, wear down, pester/dawdle') vs. departing tone *mò* (Old Chinese *-s* nominalizing suffix, 'millstone, grindstone; to grind grain in a mill').

history.meaning: to polish or abrade stone and jade (*mó*); a stone mill (*mò*)
to rub, sharpen, polish; to wear down over time; to dawdle or pester

morphemes.meaning: rub, grind, polish, wear down; dawdle

磨.notes: Pay close attention to the two readings of 磨: *mó* (2nd tone) means 'to rub, polish, wear down, or dawdle' (磨刀 'sharpen a knife', 折磨 'torment', 磨蹭 'dawdle'), whereas *mò* (4th tone) refers to a 'millstone' or 'grinding grain into flour/paste' (石磨 'stone mill', 磨豆腐 'grind soy for tofu').

rootFamily.gloss: to dawdle, drag one's feet; rub lightly against
to torment, put through an ordeal (lit. break and grind)
to polish, refine (a script, artwork, or skill) over time

磨砂.etymology: Verb-object compound used adjectivally, combining 磨 ('to grind, abrade, polish') + 砂 ('coarse sand, grit, abrasive'). Describes glass, metal, or leather given a matte, frosted finish by sandblasting or grinding.

history.meaning: frosted (of glass); matte-ground

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 磨砂 (via 萌典)

磨蹭.etymology: A colloquial northern Mandarin coordinative compound combining 磨 (mó, 'to rub, abrade, wear down slowly') and 蹭 (cèng, neutralized to *ceng*, from 足 'foot' + phonetic 曾, originally meaning 'to shuffle the feet, graze, rub lightly against in passing'). From the physical image of rubbing and shuffling one's feet with high friction and minimal forward movement, it developed the vivid metaphorical sense of 'dawdling, dilly-dallying, dragging one's feet, or moving at a snail's pace'.

history.meaning: to rub against + to shuffle or graze with the feet
to dawdle, dilly-dally, drag one's feet, waste time moving slowly

morphemes.meaning: rub, grind, move slowly with friction
shuffle the feet, rub lightly against, loiter

磨蹭.notes: Pronounced with a neutral second syllable (*móceng*); very common in everyday spoken reprimands like 别磨蹭了，快走吧！ ('Stop dawdling, let's get going!'). Near-synonym in northern speech: 磨叽 (móji).

rootFamily.gloss: to rub, grind, wear down, polish
to dawdle or chatter repetitively (colloquial northern variant)
to freeload or hitch a ride/meal (lit. rub against for free)

cognates.meaning: to bow in worship, religious service

礼拜.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound (Traditional: 禮拜, lǐbài) composed of 禮 (lǐ, 'ritual propriety, reverent ceremony') and 拜 (bài, 'to bow in obeisance, pay homage'). Originally attested in medieval Buddhist and classical texts for bowing in religious veneration, it was adopted by Chinese Muslims (for Jumu'ah Friday congregational prayer) and later by Christian missionaries for Sunday church worship, from which the cycle of weekly worship services generalized by metonymy in vernacular Mandarin and southern dialects to mean 'week' or 'Sunday'.

history.meaning: to bow in ceremonial reverence; religious worship (esp. Buddhist veneration)
weekly congregational worship service (Islamic Friday prayer and Christian Sunday service)
week; Sunday (by metonymy from the weekly worship cycle)

礼拜.notes: Colloquial and conversational compared to 星期 (xīngqī) or 周 (zhōu); precedes numerals for days Monday–Saturday (礼拜一 to 礼拜六) and takes 天 or 日 for Sunday (礼拜天/礼拜日), while standing alone after measure words to mean 'week' (一个礼拜, 'one week').

礼物.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 礼物. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 礼物 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 礼物 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 礼物 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 礼物. The etymology of 礼物 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 礼物
middle form of 礼物
modern form of 礼物

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 礼物

礼貌.etymology: Attributive/coordinative noun compound combining 礼 (trad. 禮, 'ritual propriety, courtesy', from 示 'altar' + 豊 'ritual vessel') + 貌 ('outward demeanor, countenance, deportment'). Attested in Mencius (《孟子·离娄下》 '礼貌衰') for respectful deportment and polite manners.

history.meaning: courteous deportment -> politeness, good manners

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 礼貌 (via 萌典)

社交.etymology: A modifier-head or telescopic compound (shèjiāo) combining 社 (shè, clipped from 社會 shèhuì 'society', originally 'altar to the god of the soil; local community association') and 交 (jiāo, clipped from 交際 jiāojì 'intercourse, mutual exchange', originally 'to cross legs; intersect, associate with'). Popularized in late Qing and Republican Chinese alongside Meiji Japanese 社交 (shakō) as an orthographic loan to render Western concepts of 'social intercourse' and 'socializing' in public life.

history.meaning: local community association + mutual association/exchange
social intercourse, polite society interaction (coined/standardized in Meiji Japan)
history.stage: Meiji Japanese / Late Qing Return Loan

history.meaning: social interaction, socializing, networking (including digital social media)

morphemes.meaning: to associate, exchange, interact (from 交际)

社交.notes: Highly productive as an attributive noun in modern media and workplace discourse, appearing in compounds like 社交媒体 (shèjiāo méitǐ, 'social media'), 社交软件 ('social networking apps'), and 社交恐惧症 (shèkǒng, 'social anxiety').

社会.etymology: Originally a Tang–Song dynasty Literary Chinese compound (Traditional: 社會, shèhuì) constructed as a modifier-head or coordinative noun from 社 (shè, 'god of the soil; village shrine community of twenty-five households') and 會 (huì, 'festive gathering, assembly'). In pre-modern China it denoted a seasonal village festival or guild assembly around the local earth deity's shrine; in Meiji Japan (1870s, notably by Fukuchi Gen'ichirō), 社會 (shakai) was repurposed as a graphic translation for English 'society' and re-borrowed into late Qing Chinese with its modern sociological sense.

history.meaning: village gathering at the local earth-god shrine; guild or community association
human society, civil body politic (repurposed to translate English 'society')
society at large, the real world outside school or family

morphemes.meaning: altar to the soil deity; community group

社会.notes: In entertainment and workplace contexts, 社会 often contrasts the tough 'real world' with campus life (进入社会, 'enter the real world') or refers to public opinion at large (社会舆论, 'public sentiment').

祝.etymology: Associative compound in oracle-bone script depicting a priest kneeling (兄, person 儿 with open mouth 口) before an ancestral altar (示) to offer prayers. Evolved from 'invoker priest, to pray to the spirits' to 'to express good wishes, congratulate'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: to pray at an altar -> to wish well, express good wishes

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 祝 (via 萌典)

祝你好运.etymology: A four-character double-object or pivotal benedictory phrase (Traditional: 祝你好運, zhù nǐ hǎoyùn) composed of the verb 祝 (zhù, originally a kneeling priest 兄 before an ancestral altar 示 praying to the spirits, hence 'to invoke blessings, wish'), the second-person pronoun 你 (nǐ, 'you'), and the modifier-head noun phrase 好運 (hǎoyùn, 'good fortune, favorable destiny', from 好 'good' + 運 'revolving cycle of fate'). While rooted in native Chinese syntax, its high frequency as a standalone farewell calques and parallels English 'good luck (to you)' in modern vernacular and media dialogue.

history.meaning: shaman/priest invoking ancestral spirits at the altar; to pray for blessings
to express good wishes that someone enjoy auspicious fortune
good luck to you! (idiomatic conversational encouragement or ironic parting shot)

祝你好运.notes: Used both sincerely before auditions, broadcasts, or high-stakes pitches and sarcastically in workplace drama when leaving a rival to handle an impossible crisis on their own.

祝福.etymology: A verb-object and coordinative compound (zhùfú) formed from 祝 (zhù, 'to pray to the gods at an altar, invoke blessings') and 福 (fú, showing an altar 示 beside a jar of sacrificial wine 畐, 'heavenly blessing, auspicious prosperity'). Attested in Classical and Literary Chinese for ritual prayers requesting divine favor, it later absorbed Christian translations of 'benediction/blessing' and generalized in modern Mandarin into an everyday verb or noun meaning 'to wish someone happiness' or 'warm wishes'.

history.meaning: to pray to deities for auspicious fortune; New Year ritual sacrifice (esp. in Jiangnan)
religious benediction; to bless
blessing, good wishes; to wish someone well (in romance, career, or life)

morphemes.meaning: to pray for, invoke, express wishes

祝福.notes: In entertainment and celebrity culture, 送上祝福 ('to send one's blessings') is the standard phrase used by fans, colleagues, or ex-partners when a public figure announces a relationship, marriage, or career milestone.

神奇.etymology: Coordinative adjective compound combining 神 ('divine, spirit-like, unfathomable') + 奇 ('extraordinary, wondrous, rare'). Famous from Zhuangzi (《庄子·知北游》 '臭腐复化为神奇') and now standard for 'magical, miraculous, wondrous'.

history.meaning: miraculous, magical, wondrous

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 神奇 (via 萌典)

神秘.etymology: Coordinative adjective compound combining 神 ('divine, unfathomable') + 秘 ('secret, arcane, hidden', also with 礻 'altar/numinous' + 必 phonetic). Means 'mysterious, enigmatic, mystical'.

history.meaning: mysterious, mystical, enigmatic

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 神秘 (via 萌典)

票.etymology: Originally a phono-semantic character (piào, Old Chinese *pʰew-s) depicting fire (火/灬) rising lightly, meaning 'sparks flying upward; swift, nimble,飘忽'. Beginning in the Song and Ming dynasties, because paper slips were light and fluttery, 票 was loaned/extended to denote official paper warrants, merchant promissory notes (銀票), pawn tickets, and theater admission slips, and in the late 19th and 20th centuries further extended to election or competition 'ballots/votes' (選票, 投票).

history.meaning: flying sparks of fire; light, swift, fluttering
printed paper warrant, receipt, banknote, or admission slip
ticket (for transit/shows); ballot or vote (in elections and showbiz competitions)

票.notes: In television production and variety shows, 票 constantly shifts between 'vote/ballot' in live audience rankings (投票 'to vote', 拉票 'to canvass for votes', 票数 'vote count') and 'ticket/box office' (门票 'admission ticket', 票房 'box office').

禁止.etymology: Coordinative verb compound combining 禁 ('to forbid, restrain, taboo', from 林 'trees/grove' + 示 'sacred omen/altar') + 止 ('to stop, halt', originally a pictograph of a foot). Attested since pre-Qin legal and historical texts for 'to prohibit, ban'.

history.meaning: to prohibit, forbid, ban

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 禁止 (via 萌典)

福利.etymology: A coordinative compound (fúlì) joining 福 (fú, 'auspicious fortune, heavenly blessing') and 利 (lì, showing grain 禾 cut with a sharp knife 刀, hence 'sharp; benefit, advantage, profit'). First attested in Han dynasty philosophical and historical texts (such as Jia Yi's *Xinshu* and *Hou Hanshu*) meaning 'good fortune and material benefit (as opposed to calamity 禍害)', it was revitalized in the 20th century (alongside Japanese 福利 fukuri) to translate 'social welfare' and 'employee benefits/perks'.

history.meaning: auspicious fortune and material advantage (contrasted with disaster and harm)
social welfare, public well-being; institutional employee benefits (modern socio-economic sense)
employee perks; fan-service bonus or giveaway in media and livestreaming

福利.notes: Beyond HR compensation (公司福利, 'company perks/benefits'), entertainment and social media use 福利 for 'fan perks/giveaways'—such as exclusive selfies, gifts, or behind-the-scenes clips released when a celebrity hits a follower milestone (发福利, 粉丝福利).

离.etymology: Originally 離, a phono-semantic character with semantic 隹 ('short-tailed bird') + phonetic 离 (chī, depicting a bird caught in a net or a mountain beast). Used from early antiquity as a loan/extended word for 'to part from, leave, be separated from (in space or time)'.

morphemes.meaning: to part from; be away from (trad. 離)

history.meaning: to part from, leave; away from (preposition of distance)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 离 (via 萌典)

离不了.etymology: A negative potential verb-complement construction (Traditional: 離不了, líbuliǎo) formed from the verb 離 (lí, originally a mountain bird caught in a net 离 + 隹, early extended to 'to part from, separate from, leave'), the negative infix 不 (bù, 'not'), and the potential/completive complement 了 (liǎo, originally 'to finish, complete, manage', grammaticalized as a marker of capability). Literally 'unable to complete the act of separating from', it evolved in vernacular Mandarin to mean 'cannot do without, cannot leave, inextricably tied to'.

history.meaning: to separate from, depart, be parted from
unable to leave or get away from; cannot dispense with (potential complement construction)
cannot leave (a job, place, or partner); cannot do without; inextricably bound to

离不了.notes: Be careful to pronounce 了 as liǎo (not le); in spoken Mandarin, 离不了 is slightly more colloquial and emotionally immediate than 离不开 (líbukāi, 'inseparable from'), often used when someone is tied down by work obligations or unable to go through with a divorce/departure.

离开.etymology: Resultative verb compound combining 离 (trad. 離, 'to part from, depart') + 开 (trad. 開, directional/resultative complement indicating separation 'apart, away').

history.meaning: to leave; to depart from

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 离开 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: leaving one's job, separation from employment
to leave office, step down from a post

离职.etymology: A verb-object compound (Traditional: 離職, lízhí) composed of 離 (lí, 'to leave, depart from') and 職 (zhí, showing an ear 耳 and phonetic 戠, 'official duty, post, employment'). Attested in Literary Chinese administrative texts for an official stepping away from his appointed post (either temporarily or permanently), it became the standard modern HR and workplace term for leaving a company's employment or resigning.

history.meaning: to leave or be absent from one's official post or appointed duty
to resign, leave one's job, terminate employment at an organization

离职.notes: A separable verb (离合词) in formal workplace Chinese: while 办理离职 ('process job separation') is standard, slightly broader than 辞职 (cízhí, 'voluntarily resign'), as 离职 covers the entire departure process from a company.

cognates.meaning: private affairs, selfishness; I (first-person pronoun watakushi)

私.etymology: A phono-semantic or ideogrammic character (sī, Old Chinese *səj) combining 禾 (hé, 'standing grain, millet') and 厶 (sī, an ancient graph depicting a bent arm or cocoon, originally the graph for 'self/private' before being loaned for 某). In *Han Feizi* and *Shuowen Jiezi*, Cangjie is said to have formed 私 as 'one's own grain crop' in direct opposition to 公 (gōng, 'public, shared equally'); from 'personally owned grain' it generalized in Classical Chinese to 'personal matters, private interest, selfish partiality, and secret dealings'.

history.meaning: one's own grain harvest; private property (contrasted with 公 'public/ducal')
personal affairs, private interest, selfish bias; secretly, illicitly
personal matters, private interest (often paired with 公 in idioms and workplace expressions)

私.notes: As a standalone noun in modern Mandarin, 私 most often appears in contrast with 公 ('public/company business'), as in 公私分明 ('keep public/work duties and personal matters strictly separate') or 以权谋私 ('abuse power for personal gain').

私下.etymology: A modifier-head or localizer compound (sīxià) combining 私 (sī, 'private, personal, secret') and the spatial/relational localizer 下 (xià, 'under, beneath, in the sphere/condition of'). Emerging in late imperial vernacular fiction and administrative prose (Ming–Qing *baihua*), it conceptualizes private dealings as taking place 'under cover of personal space'—away from the public eye or official record—meaning 'in private, privately, off the record'.

history.meaning: in secret, privately, outside official channels or public view
in private, privately, off the record, behind the scenes in personal life

私下.notes: Frequently used in media and workplace settings to contrast a celebrity's or colleague's public persona with how they behave or communicate off-camera (私下关系很好, 'have a great relationship in private'; 私下沟通, 'communicate privately').

私下里.etymology: An extended spatial-adverbial compound (Traditional: 私下裡/私下裏, sīxiàlǐ) formed by suffixing the interior localizer 裡/里 (lǐ, originally 'lining of a garment', grammaticalized as 'inside, within') to 私下 (sīxià, 'in private, under personal circumstances'). Attested in Qing vernacular novels such as *Dream of the Red Chamber* (*Hongloumeng*), the added localizer 裡 reinforces the sense of an enclosed, intimate, or off-the-record sphere ('in the interior of private space').

history.meaning: in private, behind closed doors, away from public scrutiny
privately, in private life, off the record

私下里.notes: Slightly more conversational and narrative in rhythm than two-syllable 私下; preferred before full clauses describing someone's true personality off-stage (e.g., 他私下里其实很害羞, 'He is actually very shy in private').

私事.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (sīshì) combining 私 (sī, 'private, personal') and 事 (shì, originally a hand holding a hunting net or writing brush/banner for court service, meaning 'affair, matter, business'). Attested in Classical Chinese (including the *Analects* and *Book of Rites*) in direct structural opposition to 公事 (gōngshì, 'official state business'), denoting matters belonging to an individual's household or personal life rather than public duty.

history.meaning: personal or household affairs (as opposed to court or state duty 公事)
private affair, personal matter (contrasted with company work or public business)

私事.notes: Commonly paired with 公事 ('work/official business') in workplace dramas when characters draw boundaries between professional duty and personal drama (这是我的私事, 'This is my personal business').

私人.etymology: Attributive compound combining 私 ('private, personal, self-owned', originally 'one's own grain crop 禾') + 人 ('person'). Attested in the Classic of Poetry (《诗经·大雅·崧高》 '迁其私人') for personal retainers, now 'private, personal' or 'private individual'.

history.meaning: personal retainer -> private individual; private, personal

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 私人 (via 萌典)

私人照.etymology: A three-character modifier-head nominal compound (sīrénzhào) combining 私人 (sīrén, 'private individual; personal, private', attested since the *Book of Odes* and *Zuo Zhuan* for personal retainers or private persons) and 照 (zhào, clipped from 照片 zhàopiàn 'photograph', originally 'to shine, illuminate, reflect in a mirror', adapted in the 19th century for optical photography). It denotes candid, non-public photographs taken in one's personal life rather than official publicity stills.

history.meaning: private person/personal + optical photograph
private photo, candid personal snapshot (distinct from commercial or studio publicity photos)

私人照.notes: In entertainment and PR crises, leaked 私人照 ('private photos') contrast with 官方照 ('official photos') or 宣传照 ('promotional stills'), often triggering privacy and image-management storylines.

私家.etymology: A modifier-head compound (sījiā) formed from 私 (sī, 'private, personal, non-state') and 家 (jiā, showing a pig 豕 under a roof 宀, 'household, family, noble clan estate'). Attested in Han and Six Dynasties historical prose (such as *Hanshu*) to distinguish private family estates, scholarship, or collections (私家藏書) from imperial or state-owned institutions (官家, 公家); in modern Mandarin (reinforced by Cantonese usage), it functions as an attributive adjective meaning 'privately owned, personal, exclusive'.

history.meaning: private household or clan estate (as opposed to the imperial court or state 官家/公家)
private, personally owned, exclusive to an individual or family

私家.notes: Used almost exclusively as an attributive modifier before nouns in fixed collocations like 私家车 (sījiāchē, 'private car'), 私家侦探 ('private detective'), and 私家珍藏 ('personal collection/stash'), rather than as a predicate adjective.

私密性.etymology: A three-character derived abstract noun (sīmìxìng) built from the coordinative adjectival compound 私密 (sīmì, 'private and confidential/intimate', from 私 'private, personal' + 密 'dense, hidden, secret, intimate') plus the nominalizing suffix -性 (-xìng, originally 'inborn nature, disposition', popularized in modern Chinese and Sino-Japanese to form abstract quality nouns equivalent to English '-ness' or '-ity'). It denotes the quality or degree of privacy, confidentiality, and discreet seclusion.

history.meaning: secret and personal; confidential, intimate
privacy, confidentiality, degree of discreet seclusion (abstract quality noun with -性)

私密性.notes: Unlike 隐私 (yǐnsī, 'personal privacy/secrets as a right or possession'), 私密性 describes the *attribute* of a space, VIP venue, residential compound, or communication channel (e.g., 这家餐厅私密性很好, 'This restaurant has great privacy/seclusion'—a key concern for celebrities).

私照.etymology: A disyllabic modifier-head compound (sīzhào) formed by rhythmic contraction (双音节化 abbreviation) of 私人照片 (sīrén zhàopiàn, 'private/personal photograph'), combining 私 (sī, 'private, personal, off-duty') and 照 (zhào, 'photograph, snapshot'). Coined in modern media, tabloid journalism, and internet fan culture, it refers specifically to non-commercial, off-stage, or personal photographs of a celebrity or individual.

history.meaning: abbreviated compound for 'personal photograph / off-camera snapshot'

私照.notes: A staple of entertainment news headlines (e.g., 曝光私照, 'expose/release private photos'), referring either to casual everyday photos shared by stars themselves or to intimate snapshots leaked to paparazzi.

cognates.meaning: child born out of wedlock, illegitimate child
cognates.word: 私生児 / 私生子 (shiseiji / shiseishi)
con tư sinh / tư sinh tử

私生子.etymology: A three-character modifier-head compound (sīshēngzǐ) consisting of the modifier-head verbal phrase 私生 (sīshēng, 'born privately/illicitly outside formal marriage rites', from 私 'private, illicit, unacknowledged' + 生 'to give birth to, be born') modifying the head noun 子 (zǐ, 'child, son, offspring'). Attested in vernacular and legal-historical texts and standardized in modern East Asian civil law terminology to denote a child born out of wedlock.

history.meaning: offspring born outside recognized marriage rites or clan registry
child born out of wedlock (colloquial/narrative counterpart to legal 非婚生子女)

morphemes.meaning: to bear, give birth to, be born

私生子.notes: Carries a dramatic or tabloid connotation in television scripts and gossip columns (with 私生女 used specifically for a daughter); modern Chinese civil law replaces it in formal statutes with the neutral term 非婚生子女 ('non-marital child'). Also note that in idol fandoms, 私生 (short for 私生饭, from Korean 사생팬 *sasaeng fan*) refers to obsessive stalker fans, a distinct modern homographic usage.

rootFamily.gloss: biological child, one's own flesh and blood

私聊.etymology: A modifier-head verbal compound (sīliáo) combining the adverbial modifier 私 (sī, 'privately, one-on-one, off the public channel', clipped from 私下) with the verb 聊 (liáo, originally 'ringing in the ears; to rely on momentarily', which evolved in Ming–Qing Beijing vernacular via 聊天 liáotiān to mean 'to chat, converse casually'). Popularized in the late 20th and early 21st centuries through online chatrooms, instant messaging (QQ, WeChat), and workplace communication, it denotes talking one-on-one in private or via direct message rather than in a group setting.

history.meaning: privately + to chat casually
to message privately (in a chatroom/WeChat vs. 群聊 'group chat'); to talk one-on-one behind closed doors

morphemes.meaning: to chat, converse, talk (from 聊天)

私聊.notes: Originating in internet chatrooms as the opposite of 群聊 (qúnliáo, 'group chat') or 公屏 ('public screen'), 私聊 is now ubiquitous both online ('DM me') and offline in offices ('let's talk one-on-one in private').

rootFamily.gloss: group chat, chat in a group

cognates.meaning: privately, on one's own without authorization

私自.etymology: A coordinative adverbial compound (sīzì) combining 私 (sī, 'privately, in one's personal capacity, without public sanction') and 自 (zì, originally a pictograph of a nose, hence 'oneself, on one's own initiative'). Attested since Han and Six Dynasties histories (such as *Shiji* and *Hou Hanshu*), it describes acting purely on one's own personal authority while bypassing proper hierarchy, law, or institutional approval.

history.meaning: privately and on one's own initiative (without imperial or official authorization)
without authorization, behind the backs of superiors or rules, on one's own initiative

私自.notes: Always carries a critical or rule-breaking nuance in organizational contexts (e.g., 私自决定 'decide without authorization', 私自行动 'act on one's own behind management's back'), closely synonymous with 擅自 (shànzì).

cognates.meaning: private collection, keeping in one's personal possession
to hoard privately, keep in a personal collection

私藏.etymology: A modifier-head verbal compound (sīcáng) composed of the adverbial modifier 私 (sī, 'privately, secretly, unlawfully') and the verb 藏 (cáng, 'to hide, conceal, store away, collect'). In Classical and Imperial legal Chinese, 私藏 meant illicitly concealing prohibited items (such as weapons, salt, or fugitives); in modern lifestyle and media Mandarin, alongside its legal sense, it has softened playfully to mean 'to keep in one's personal stash or secret collection' (e.g., favorite cafés, songs, or unshared photos).

history.meaning: to secretly conceal or hoard contraband, weapons, or state property
to harbor illicitly; (colloquial/lifestyle) to keep in one's personal stash or private collection without sharing

私藏.notes: Used seriously in crime/legal contexts (私藏枪支, 'illegally possess firearms') and playfully in everyday conversation and social media for gatekeeping or sharing one's favorite hidden gems (私藏歌单, 'my secret personal playlist'; 私藏好店, 'favorite hidden-gem shop').

rootFamily.gloss: to collect, keep in a collection

秋天.etymology: Compound of 秋 ('autumn, harvest', combining 禾 'ripening grain stalk' + 火 'fire', originally depicting harvest grain and hearth/field fire in oracle-bone script) + 天 ('season, sky').

history.meaning: grain-harvest season; autumn
autumn; fall

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 秋天 (via 萌典)

种.etymology: Phono-semantic character (trad. 種) combining semantic 禾 ('grain plant') + phonetic 重 (zhòng/chóng). As a noun/classifier (zhǒng), originally 'plant seed', extended to 'breed, species, kind, sort, type'; as a verb (zhòng), 'to sow, plant'.

morphemes.meaning: phonetic in simplified 种 (trad. 重)

history.meaning: seed -> kind, sort, type (classifier); to plant

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 种 (via 萌典)

种类.etymology: A coordinative nominal compound (Traditional: 種類, zhǒnglèi) uniting 種 (zhǒng, showing grain 禾 and phonetic 重, 'plant seed; biological lineage, breed, sort') and 類 (lèi, originally 'dog-like species that resemble one another', hence 'category, class, kind'). Attested in Warring States and Han texts (such as *Xunzi*, *Zhuangzi*, and *Shiji*) for biological breeds, clans, and natural categories of things, it remains the standard Mandarin noun for 'kind, variety, or category'.

history.meaning: biological seed/lineage and natural category; breed, sort, class of things or beings
kind, variety, type, category (of goods, programs, or phenomena)

种类.notes: Remember the third-tone pronunciation zhǒnglèi (meaning 'seed/kind', as opposed to fourth-tone zhòng 'to plant'); frequently paired with 繁多 or 丰富 (种类繁多, 'a wide variety of kinds').

种花种草.etymology: A four-character parallel verb-object idiom (Traditional: 種花種草, zhònghuā-zhòngcǎo) structured on the A-B-A-C reduplicative pattern, repeating the transitive verb 種 (zhòng, fourth tone, Old Chinese *tjoŋ-s, a departative tone derivation from zhǒng 'seed' meaning 'to sow seeds, plant, cultivate') before two coordinated botanical objects: 花 (huā, 'flowers, blossoms') and 草 (cǎo, 'grasses, herbaceous plants'). Literally 'to plant flowers and cultivate plants', it serves as an idiomatic expression for tending a garden or enjoying a quiet, leisurely domestic lifestyle.

history.meaning: to plant flowers and cultivate ornamental herbs/grasses
to grow flowers and plants, do gardening (often evoking a peaceful, retired, or leisurely lifestyle)

种花种草.notes: Here 种 is read in the fourth tone (zhòng, 'to plant'); in fast-paced workplace dramas, 种花种草 often symbolizes a peaceful retirement or escape from high-pressure corporate life (note also that standalone 种草 on social media is modern slang for 'planting the desire to buy a product').

科.etymology: Associative compound formed from 禾 ('grain') + 斗 ('measuring scoop'): measuring and grading grain into categories. Extended to 'class, department, academic discipline, administrative section, biological family'.

history.meaning: measuring grain into grades -> branch of study, department, category

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 科 (via 萌典)

科学.etymology: Originally a Song–Ming Literary Chinese modifier-head compound (Traditional: 科學, kēxué) shortened from 科舉之學 ('learning for the imperial civil-service examinations', from 科 'subject division, exam category' + 學 'learning, study'). In the 1870s, Meiji Japanese scholars (such as Nishi Amane) reanalyzed 科學 (kagaku) as 'specialized branch-by-branch learning' (分科之學) to translate Western 'science' (Latin *scientia*); re-imported into late Qing China by Kang Youwei and Yan Fu, it also developed a colloquial Mandarin adjectival usage meaning 'scientific, rational, well-designed, sensible'.

history.meaning: studies preparing for the imperial civil service examinations (科舉之學)
systematic, specialized empirical discipline; 'science' (Meiji semantic coinage)
history.stage: Meiji Japanese / Late Qing Return Loan

history.meaning: science (noun); scientific, rational, well-designed, reasonable (adjective)

科学.notes: In everyday spoken Mandarin, 科学 is very frequently used as a predicate adjective meaning 'reasonable, sensible, well-planned, or making sense'—especially in the negative: 这不科学! (Zhè bù kēxué!, 'That makes no sense! / That's irrational!').

科技.etymology: A modern syllabic contraction (缩略词, kējì) formed in 20th-century Mandarin by taking the first morpheme of 科學 (kēxué, 'science') and the first morpheme of 技術 (jìshù, 'technology, technical craft, skill'). While coordinative in underlying structure ('science and technology'), in contemporary business, media, and everyday usage it frequently functions as a unified noun or modifier equivalent to English 'technology' or 'tech'.

history.meaning: science and technology (telescoped coordinative compound)
science and technology; high-tech industry or technological innovation ('tech')

morphemes.meaning: technology, craft, skill (clipped from 技术)

科技.notes: While 科技 literally combines 'science and technology', in business and media contexts (科技公司 'tech company', 高科技 'high-tech', 黑科技 'cutting-edge/futuristic tech') it translates English 'tech' or 'technology'.

秒.etymology: Phono-semantic/associative character combining 禾 ('grain ear') + 少 ('small, fine', also phonetic miǎo). Originally denoted the tiny hair-like awn (芒) at the tip of a grain husk; used by Song–Ming astronomers and Jesuits for 1/60 of a minute ('second' of arc or time).

morphemes.meaning: tiny awn at the tip of grain (miǎo)

history.stage: Old Chinese ('grain awn') to Ming–Modern Mandarin ('second of time')
history.meaning: tiny beard on a grain husk -> minute fraction -> second (of time)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 秒 (via 萌典)

秒钟.etymology: Attributive noun compound combining 秒 ('second') + 钟 (trad. 鐘, 'clock, bell, time'), forming the disyllabic noun for a 'second' of time.

history.meaning: second (unit of time)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 秒钟 (via 萌典)

秘不发丧.etymology: A four-character Classical Chinese historical idiom (Traditional: 秘不發喪, mì bù fāsāng) composed of the adverbial/verbal 秘 (mì, 'to keep secret, conceal'), the negative adverb 不 (bù, 'not'), and the verb-object phrase 發喪 (fāsāng, 'to publicly announce a death and commence mourning rites', from 發 'to issue, announce' + 喪 'funeral, mourning'). Famous from Sima Qian's *Records of the Grand Historian* (*Shiji*)—where Chancellor Li Si and Zhao Gao concealed the death of Qin Shi Huang during an imperial tour in 210 BCE to prevent rebellion until they returned to the capital—it is used metaphorically in modern corporate and political drama for keeping a leader's departure, illness, or crisis strictly under wraps to maintain stability.

history.meaning: to keep a monarch's or general's death secret and delay announcing mourning rites to prevent mutiny or succession chaos
(figurative) to keep an executive's resignation, incapacitation, or major institutional blow secret to preserve market or organizational stability

秘不发丧.notes: In boardroom and media dramas, 秘不发丧 is used figuratively (and often with dark humor) when a company withholds news that a key producer, star, or executive is leaving or sidelined until a replacement or transition plan is locked in.

秘密.etymology: Word for 'secret', a compound of two near synonyms: 秘 ('hidden, secret'; variant 祕 with the spirit/altar component) and 密 ('dense, close, concealed'). 秘 was historically read bì and still has a b- initial in most other Chinese varieties; Mandarin mì comes from its conflation with 密 in this very compound.

history.meaning: secret / dense, close
secret

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 秘密 (via 萌典)

秘诀.etymology: Compound of 秘 ('secret; confidential; rare', grain/sacred radical 禾/示 + 必 bì) + 诀 ('rhymed mnemonic formula; craft secret handed down by a master', speech radical 讠 + 夬 guài). Originally a master's oral formula in traditional crafts or medicine, it now means any key secret to success—especially in cooking.

history.meaning: confidential formula or master's knack
secret trick; key to success

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 秘诀

租.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining semantic 禾 ('grain') + phonetic 且 (qiě/zū). Originally meant 'land tax paid in grain', then shifted to 'land rent' and the general verb 'to rent, lease, hire'.

history.stage: Old Chinese ('grain tax') to Modern Mandarin ('to rent, lease')
history.meaning: grain tax -> rent; to rent, lease, hire

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 租 (via 萌典)

租房.etymology: A separable verb-object compound (zūfáng) combining 租 (zū, showing grain 禾 and phonetic 且, originally 'land tax paid in grain' in Classical Chinese, which evolved by the Tang–Song period into 'to lease, rent') and 房 (fáng, originally 'side room flanking a central hall', generalized in vernacular Mandarin to 'house, apartment, room'). It means either to rent an apartment as a tenant or, depending on context, to lease out housing.

history.meaning: grain land-tax / to lease + side-room / house
to rent a house or room (as tenant or landlord)
to rent an apartment or house (a central rite of passage for young urban professionals)

租房.notes: A classic separable verb (离合词): you say 租了一套房 ('rented an apartment') or 租不起房 ('cannot afford to rent an apartment'), and pair it with 房租 (fángzū, 'rent money') and 房东 (fángdōng, 'landlord').

租约.etymology: Attributive noun compound combining 租 ('rent, lease') + 约 (trad. 約, 'binding agreement, contract'). Denotes a lease agreement or rental contract.

history.meaning: lease; rental contract

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 租约 (via 萌典)

秦箫.etymology: A two-character Chinese personal name (Traditional: 秦簫, Qín Xiāo) composed of the ancient toponymic surname 秦 (Qín, originally depicting two hands pounding millet 禾 with a pestle, the name of the ancestral Zhou-era polity in modern Gansu/Shaanxi that unified China as the Qin dynasty) and the given name 簫 (xiāo, combining bamboo 竹 and phonetic 肅, denoting the vertical notched bamboo flute or panpipes). Together, 秦簫 evokes classical poetic imagery—such as the legend of Nong玉 and Xiao Shi playing the *xiao* flute in the state of Qin (秦臺吹簫)—combining a major historical surname with a refined musical instrument.

history.meaning: State/Surname Qin + vertical bamboo flute or panpipes (classical poetic motif of Qin flute music)
Qin Xiao (contemporary Chinese personal name, a character in *Behind the Scenes* / *幕后之王*)

morphemes.meaning: Qin (Chinese surname; historic state and dynasty)

秦箫.notes: Illustrates a classic Chinese naming pattern where a historical surname (秦) is paired with an elegant literary or musical noun (箫, the vertical bamboo flute) to give a character an artistic, cultured resonance.

rootFamily.gloss: flute music, sound of the xiao

积极性.etymology: A three-character abstract noun (Traditional: 積極性, jījíxìng) derived from 積極 (jījí, 'positive, proactive, energetic') + the nominalizing suffix -性 (-xìng, 'nature, quality'). In Meiji Japan, philosopher Nishi Amane coined 積極 (sekkyoku, literally 'accumulating/charging pole', from 積 'to accumulate' + 極 'magnetic/electrical pole') vs. 消極 (shōkyoku, 'discharging/negative pole') to translate Western 'positive' vs. 'negative'; borrowed into 20th-century Chinese with the suffix -性, 積極性 became the core workplace and organizational term for 'enthusiasm, proactiveness, and initiative'.

history.meaning: positive pole (in electricity/philosophy); active, positive (as opposed to 消極 'negative/passive')
history.stage: Meiji Japanese Coinage / Late Qing Loan

history.meaning: proactive drive, enthusiasm, personal initiative in work or collective action

morphemes.meaning: to accumulate, build up (part of 积极 'positive/active')
pole, extreme, utmost point (part of 积极)

积极性.notes: A cornerstone of Chinese management and workplace vocabulary, typically collocating with verbs of motivation or discouragement: 调动积极性 ('mobilize/inspire enthusiasm and initiative') or 打击积极性 ('dampen someone's enthusiasm/morale').

cognates.meaning: to call, name, style, claim; symmetry, proportion
to call, name, style oneself, weigh up to

称.etymology: A character (Traditional: 稱, chēng / chèn) whose orthodox form combines 禾 (hé, 'grain') with 爯 (chēng, a claw/hand 爪 lifting an object to weigh its heft, Old Chinese *tʰəŋ). Its primary sense in Old Chinese was 'to lift and weigh grain on a steelyard'; from 'measuring weight accurately' it branched along two paths: (1) level tone chēng, 'to appraise, praise, call by a name or title, style, claim'; and (2) departing tone chèn (*tʰəŋ-s), 'to match in weight, fit, measure up to (a title, role, or garment)'.

history.meaning: to lift by hand and weigh grain; to measure weight and balance
(chēng) to call, style, praise, declare; (chèn) to match, fit, measure up to an office or title (稱職)
to call, address as, state/claim (chēng); to fit or measure up to a standard/role (chèn)

morphemes.meaning: to weigh; to call, style, praise (chēng); to fit, measure up to (chèn)

称.notes: A polyphonic character (多音字): read chēng when meaning 'to call, address, or claim' (被称为 'be called/hailed as', 自称 'claim to be', 称赞 'praise'), and read chèn when meaning 'to fit or measure up to a role/standard' (称职 chènzhí 'competent, measuring up to one's job', 对称 duìchèn 'symmetrical').

称呼.etymology: A coordinative verbal-nominal compound (並立式) formed from 稱 (chēng, Traditional 稱/称, originally 'to weigh on a steelyard', hence 'to evaluate, style, or name') and 呼 (hū, 'to exhale, shout, call out'). In Literary Chinese the two verbs were paired to mean 'to call or style someone by a title', later grammaticalizing in vernacular Mandarin with a neutral-tone second syllable (chēnghu) as both the verb 'to address (someone as)' and the noun 'form of address'.

history.meaning: to weigh and style; to cry out or summon
to call by name or title; mode of address
to address as; term of address

morphemes.meaning: to weigh; to name, style, call
to breathe out; to call out, summon

称呼.notes: Functions as both a verb (怎么称呼您？ 'How should I address you?') and a noun (礼貌的称呼 'a polite form of address'); pronounced with a neutral tone on the second syllable (chēnghu).

稀.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 稀. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 稀 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 稀 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 稀 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 稀. The etymology of 稀 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 稀
middle form of 稀
modern form of 稀

程序.etymology: A coordinative nominal compound (並立式) combining 程 (chéng, originally a grain measure from 禾 'grain' + 呈 phonetic, extended to 'standard, rule, stage of a journey') and 序 (xù, originally 'east-west side walls of a courtyard school', extended to 'order, sequence, arrangement'). Attested in Classical texts such as the *Xunzi* for established rules and sequential order, it was adopted in 20th-century technical Mandarin to translate English 'procedure' and computing 'program'.

history.meaning: fixed standard and sequential order; established regulation
administrative or legal procedure; computer program or routine

程序.notes: In Mainland Mandarin, 程序 means both 'formal procedure' (走程序 'go through the formal process') and 'computer program' (程序员 'programmer'), whereas Taiwan Mandarin prefers 程式 (chéngshì) for software programs.

程度.etymology: A coordinative compound (並立式) joining 程 (chéng, 'measure, standard, capacity, regulated stage') and 度 (dù, 'linear measure, standard, degree, limit'). In Literary Chinese both characters denoted standards of measurement; in Meiji Japan 程度 (teido) was standardized to render Western concepts of 'degree, extent, or grade', a sense reinforced across modern East Asian languages including Mandarin.

history.meaning: regulations, standards of measurement, and quantitative limits
degree, grade, standard, extent (translating English 'degree')
degree, extent, level of attainment or severity

程度.notes: Often pairs with 达到 ('reach a level of') or 某种程度上 ('to a certain extent'); in everyday speech, 到了这种程度 ('reached this point/degree') emphasizes how extreme a situation has become.

稍微.etymology: A synonymous coordinative adverbial compound (並立式) combining 稍 (shāo, from 禾 'grain' + 肖 phonetic, originally 'gradually budding grain', hence 'gradually, somewhat, a little') and 微 (wēi, 'minute, tiny, subtle, slight'). While 稍 in Classical Chinese often meant 'gradually' (漸), its pairing with 微 in post-classical vernacular solidified the sense 'slightly, to a small degree'.

history.meaning: gradually, bit by bit (稍); minute, subtle, hidden (微)
slightly, a little bit, to a minor extent
slightly, a little, briefly

稍微.notes: As an adverb of small degree, 稍微 must be accompanied by a tentative or quantitative complement on the verb or adjective (e.g., 稍微等一下 'wait a little bit', 稍微好一点 'slightly better') rather than modifying a bare verb alone.

rootFamily.gloss: wait a moment, hold on briefly

稍等.etymology: A modifier-head verbal compound (偏正式) in which the adverbial morpheme 稍 (shāo, 'briefly, slightly, a little') modifies the verb 等 (děng, originally 'neat rows of bamboo slips, rank, grade' in Classical Chinese, which evolved in medieval vernacular Chinese into the primary verb 'to wait, await'). Together they form a concise, polite imperative or deferential verb phrase meaning 'to wait briefly'.

history.meaning: a little, gradually (稍); rank, equal grade (等)
to wait, await (vernacular semantic shift from 'to rank/align')
to wait a moment, hold on briefly

稍等.notes: A polite, semi-formal everyday expression used frequently in customer service, phone calls, and office interactions (请稍等 'Please hold on a moment').

rootFamily.gloss: later on, in a little while

稍等一下.etymology: A four-character vernacular verb-complement phrase built from the modifier-head verb 稍等 (shāoděng, 'to wait briefly') followed by the verbal classifier construction 一下 (yīxià, literally 'one stroke/time'). In Mandarin grammar, post-verbal 一下 functions as a delimitative aspect marker softening the action and indicating brief duration ('for a moment, quickly').

history.meaning: wait briefly + one time/stroke (delimitative verbal complement)

稍等一下.notes: Adding 一下 softens the tone of 稍等, making it sound warmer and less abrupt in spoken interaction; in Northern Mandarin it is often rhotacized as 稍等一下儿 (shāoděng yīxiàr).

rootFamily.gloss: all at once, in a single stroke

税务.etymology: Administrative compound of 税 ('grain tithe; tax', grain radical 禾 + 兑 *duì*) + 务 ('public affairs; administrative business'). Used for fiscal administration, tax regulations, and accounting.

history.meaning: tax collection and revenue affairs
taxation; tax affairs

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 税务

稳.etymology: Phono-semantic character (trad. 穩) combining semantic 禾 ('grain') + phonetic 隐省/急 (originally 㥯 'careful'). Originally meant 'to tread and gather grain evenly', evolving to 'steady, stable, firm, sure'.

history.meaning: steady, stable, firm, sure

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 稳 (via 萌典)

稳住.etymology: A resultative verb-complement compound (動補式) combining 稳 (wěn, Traditional 穩, from 禾 'grain' + 隱 phonetic, 'stable, firm, settled, steady') with the resultative complement 住 (zhù, 'to stop, hold fast, stay firmly in place'). Literally 'to steady so that it stays fixed', it is used both intransitively ('keep one's composure, hold firm') and transitively ('keep someone calm or stalled so they don't act rashly').

history.meaning: firm, settled (穩); to halt, reside, stay fixed (住)
to hold steady, keep calm; to stall or pacify someone temporarily

morphemes.meaning: firmly in place, fast, halted (resultative marker)

稳住.notes: In workplace and crisis-management contexts (such as live broadcasting or PR crises in *Behind the Scenes*), 稳住他 means 'keep him calm / stall him for time', while 稳住阵脚 means 'hold the line / keep one's footing'.

rootFamily.gloss: to hold fast, Persist; to grasp firmly

稳妥.etymology: A coordinative adjectival compound (並立式) pairing 稳 (wěn, Traditional 穩, 'steady, firm, secure, free from oscillation') and 妥 (tuǒ, an ideogram of a hand 爪 gently settling a woman 女, 'secure, settled, appropriate, proper'). Together they describe a plan, arrangement, or manner of handling affairs that is both rock-solid and free of risk.

history.meaning: stable, firm (穩); settled, peaceful, proper (妥)
safe and reliable, sound, free from risk or slip-ups

稳妥.notes: Frequently modifies plans, solutions, or actions (稳妥起见 'to be on the safe side'; 办得很稳妥 'handled very reliably and safely').

稳定.etymology: Coordinative adjective/verb compound combining 稳 (trad. 穩, 'steady, firm') + 定 ('settled, fixed, calm'). Means 'stable, steady' or 'to stabilize'.

history.meaning: stable, steady; to stabilize

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 稳定 (via 萌典)

稳稳.etymology: Reduplicated adverb/adjective from 稳 (trad. 穩, 'steady, firm, sure'), meaning 'steadily, firmly, securely'.

history.meaning: steadily; firmly; securely

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 稳稳 (via 萌典)

稳重.etymology: Coordinative adjective compound combining 稳 (trad. 穩, 'steady, composed') + 重 ('weighty, dignified, serious'). Describes a person's manner as staid, composed, and dependable.

history.meaning: steady and dignified; composed, dependable

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 稳重 (via 萌典)

稿.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形聲) composed of the semantic radical 禾 (hé, 'cereal grain, stalk') and the phonetic component 高 (gāo, Old Chinese *kˤawʔ; variant graphical form 稿/藁 with 木). Originally denoting dry cereal stalks or straw, it was extended in Han–Tang literati usage to mean a rough, unpolished 'straw draft' of a composition (草稿), and later any manuscript, script, or article contribution.

history.meaning: dried stalks of grain, straw; rough preliminary draft of writing
literary draft, sketch, manuscript, speech script, press release

morphemes.meaning: stalk of grain; rough draft, manuscript, script

稿.notes: Notice how both 草 ('grass') and 稿 ('grain straw') came to mean 'rough draft' (草稿): ancient writers likened a hasty, unpolished first version to humble, unrefined straw before it is polished into final text. In media and TV production, 审稿 ('review a script/copy'), 撰稿 ('write copy'), and 通稿 ('syndicated press release') are core industry terms.

rootFamily.gloss: original manuscript; copy for publication or broadcast

稿子.etymology: A derived nominal compound (附加式/派生詞) formed from the root noun 稿 (gǎo, originally 'grain stalk, straw', by extension 'rough literary draft, manuscript') plus the nominalizing diminutive suffix 子 (zi, neutral tone). The suffix 子 allows the monosyllabic classical root 稿 to function as an independent, prosodically balanced disyllabic noun in spoken Mandarin.

history.meaning: straw; rough draft of a document or poem
written draft, manuscript, speech text, or mental plan/outline

稿子.notes: The everyday spoken counterpart of 稿件; used both for physical/digital scripts and articles (写稿子 'write an article/script', 背稿子 'memorize one's script') and figuratively for a mental plan (心里没稿子 'have no plan in mind').

cognates.meaning: ultimate, final, after all, in the end
ultimately, after all, in the end
ultimately, in the end; final goal

究竟.etymology: A coordinative compound (並立式) combining 究 (jiū, from 穴 'cave/hole' + 九 phonetic, 'to probe to the very end of a cavity, investigate thoroughly') and 竟 (jìng, related to 音 'music/sound', 'the end of a musical piece, border, to finish, ultimately'). Prominent in medieval Buddhist translations (rendering Sanskrit *uttara* or *niṣṭhā*, 'ultimate consummation or final truth'), it evolved into a Mandarin noun ('ultimate outcome') and emphatic interrogative adverb ('after all, what on earth').

history.meaning: to probe to the bottom (究); to finish, reach the end (竟)
ultimate truth or final stage (Buddhist technical term); to investigate thoroughly
after all, when all is said and done; (in questions) what on earth, actually; (noun) the actual outcome

morphemes.meaning: to examine thoroughly, probe to the end
to finish, complete; finally, in the end

究竟.notes: Used primarily in questions to press for the underlying truth (究竟发生了什么？ 'What on earth happened?'), synonymous with 到底; it can also act as a noun in the fixed phrase 看个究竟 ('go see what is really going on').

rootFamily.gloss: after all, when all is said and done

穷人.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正式) formed from 穷 (qióng, Traditional 窮, from 穴 'cave/tunnel' + 躬 'bent body' phonetic/semantic, originally 'to reach the end of a tunnel, blocked, exhausted, in dire straits') modifying 人 (rén, 'person, human being'). In Classical Chinese, 窮 contrasted with 達 ('career success') to mean 'blocked in official advancement or trapped in extremity', whereas in vernacular Mandarin it narrowed primarily to material poverty ('impoverished, poor').
