history.meaning: a person in dire straits, trapped at an impasse, or blocked from official advancement
an impoverished or destitute person; the poor

穷人.notes: Note the semantic shift of 穷 from Classical Chinese ('exhausted, at the end of a path', still preserved in 穷途末路 'at a dead end' and 层出不穷 'emerging endlessly') to Modern Mandarin ('financially poor', opposite of 富人 'rich person').

rootFamily.gloss: at the end of one's rope, at a dead end

空.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining semantic 穴 ('cave, cavity, hole') + phonetic 工 (gōng/kōng, also associated with boring a hole). Evolved from 'hollow cavity, hole' to 'empty, vacant, the sky/air, in vain'.

history.meaning: cavity, hollow -> empty, vacant; sky, air

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 空 (via 萌典)

空城.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正式) combining 空 (kōng, from 穴 'cave/cavity' + 工 phonetic, 'hollow, empty, vacant, devoid of') and 城 (chéng, from 土 'rammed earth' + 成 phonetic, 'defensive city wall, citadel, walled town'). Literally 'an unguarded or deserted walled city', it became famous through military lore and the *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* (三國演義), and is used figuratively in modern workplaces for an office or company left without its core leaders or staff.

history.meaning: an unguarded or deserted walled city or citadel
deserted city (as during holidays); figuratively, an office or organization left empty or leaderless

空城.notes: Beyond historical warfare, modern Chinese media uses 空城 both for major cities emptied out during Spring Festival migration and for a department or company hollowed out when key personnel leave or are absent.

空城计.etymology: A modifier-head three-character idiom (偏正式) composed of 空城 (kōngchéng, 'empty, unguarded walled city') modifying 计 (jì, Traditional 計, from 言 'speech/plan' + 十 'ten/complete', 'calculation, ruse, military stratagem'). Listed as the 32nd of the *Thirty-Six Stratagems* (三十六計) and immortalized in Chapter 95 of *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* (where Zhuge Liang sits calmly playing the guqin atop an unguarded city gate to trick Sima Yi into retreating), it denotes bluffing confidence to conceal vulnerability.

history.meaning: the military ruse of leaving a fort's gates wide open to deceive a superior enemy into suspecting an ambush
history.stage: Ming–Qing Literary & Vernacular Chinese (三十六計 / 三國演義)

history.meaning: bluffing strength while short-handed; leaving a post or venue empty/unguarded; figuratively, an empty stomach

空城计.notes: Frequently used with 唱 ('sing', from Peking Opera's famous aria *Empty Fort Strategy*): 唱空城计 means either 'pull off a bold bluff when lacking resources/staff' or 'leave an office completely deserted'.

空子.etymology: A derived nominal formation (附加式) combining 空 (kòng, fourth-tone departing-tone derivation of 空 kōng, meaning 'to leave vacant; an empty space, gap, or interval') with the diminutive nominal suffix 子 (zi, neutral tone). Literally 'a small gap in space or time', it developed the figurative sense of an overlooked vulnerability, blind spot, or legal/procedural loophole that an opportunist can exploit.

history.meaning: vacant space, gap, interval of leisure (departing-tone nominal/causative derivation)
unoccupied gap in space or time; exploitable loophole or weakness in rules or defenses

morphemes.meaning: vacant space, gap, interval, opening (pronounced kòng)

空子.notes: Pronounced with the fourth tone on the first syllable (kòngzi, not kōngzi!); almost always appears in the verb-object collocation 钻空子 (zuān kòngzi, 'to worm one's way through a loophole / exploit a gap in the rules').

rootFamily.gloss: gap, crack, rift between people or things

空气.etymology: Attributive compound combining 空 ('sky, empty space') + 气 (trad. 氣, 'air, vapor, breath'). Used in medieval texts for atmospheric vapor and standardized in modern science for 'air, atmosphere'.

history.meaning: air; atmosphere

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 空气 (via 萌典)

空白.etymology: Coordinative compound combining 空 ('empty, unoccupied') + 白 ('white, unprinted, blank'). Refers to blank space on paper or an unfilled gap.

history.meaning: blank space; blank, unfilled

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 空白 (via 萌典)

空空.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 空空. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 空空 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 空空 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 空空 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 空空. The etymology of 空空 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 空空
middle form of 空空
modern form of 空空

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 空空

空荡荡.etymology: ABB-pattern vivid adjective formed from 空 ('empty, vacant') + reduplicated suffix 荡荡 (trad. 蕩蕩, 'vast, wide open, bare'). Describes a room, street, or building that feels hollow and deserted.

history.meaning: empty and deserted; hollow and bare

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 空荡荡 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: air conditioning, climate control (source of the compound)
cognates.word: 空調 (kūchō, short for 空気調節 kūki chōsetsu)

空调.etymology: A syllabic abbreviation (縮略語) of 空气调节 (kōngqì tiáojié, 'air regulation/conditioning') or 空气调节器 ('air-conditioning apparatus'), modeled on the Japanese Sino-compound abbreviation 空調 (kūchō, short for 空気調節 kūki chōsetsu), which was coined to translate English 'air conditioning'. It combines 空 (kōng, representing 空气 'air') and 调 (tiáo, representing 调节 'to regulate, adjust, condition').

history.meaning: air conditioning (Japanese syllabic contraction of translation of English 'air conditioning')
air conditioning system or air conditioner unit

morphemes.meaning: to regulate, adjust (short for 调节 tiáojié)

空调.notes: In Mainland China 空调 is the universal everyday word for an air conditioner (开空调 'turn on the AC', 中央空调 'central air'); in Taiwan Mandarin, 冷气 (lěngqì, 'cold air') is more common in casual speech.

空闲.etymology: A coordinative adjectival and nominal compound (並立式) combining 空 (kòng/kōng, 'vacant, unoccupied, free of tasks') and 闲 (xián, Traditional 閒/閑, originally 'moonlight shining through a doorway crevice' or 'a wooden bar across a gate', extended to 'tranquil, unhurried, at leisure, idle'). Attested in medieval poetry and prose for quiet, unoccupied space or time, it denotes being free and unscheduled in modern Mandarin.

history.meaning: unoccupied, tranquil, free from official duties or commotion
free, unscheduled, idle; leisure time, spare time

空闲.notes: Standard Mainland pronunciation is kòngxián (fourth tone on 空, matching 有空 yǒukòng 'to have free time'), though kōngxián is also heard; functions both as an adjective (空闲时间 'free/unscheduled time') and a noun ('spare time').

rootFamily.gloss: to have free time, be available
idle talk, chat; to chat casually

cognates.meaning: space, room, expanse (wasei-kango source of modern physical/abstract sense)

空间.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正式) composed of 空 (kōng, 'empty, open, void, sky') modifying 间 (jiān, Traditional 間, 'interval, gap between two doors, room, space'). While attested in Tang poetry (such as Bai Juyi) for an 'empty gap or room', it was repurposed in Meiji Japan as 空間 (kūkan, paired with 時間 jikan 'time') to translate the Western philosophical and physical concept of 'space', and re-entered Mandarin as a graphic return loan.

history.meaning: an empty interval, open gap, or vacant room
physical, geometric, or philosophical space (contrasted with 時間 'time')
physical or abstract space; room for growth, maneuver, or development

空间.notes: Beyond physical or cosmic space, 空间 is heavily used in professional and media contexts for abstract 'room/margin': 发展空间 ('room for career growth'), 提升空间 ('room for improvement'), and 利润空间 ('profit margin').

穿.etymology: Associative compound formed from 穴 ('hole, burrow') + 牙 ('tooth'): boring or gnawing a hole through something (as in 'rat boring through a wall' in the Classic of Poetry, 《诗经·召南·行露》 '谁谓鼠无牙，何以穿我墉'). Extended to 'to pierce through, thread, pass through' and 'to put on, wear (clothes/shoes)'.

history.meaning: to bore through -> to pass through, thread -> to wear clothes/shoes

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 穿 (via 萌典)

穿小鞋.etymology: A three-character colloquial verb-object idiom (動賓慣用語) literally meaning 'to wear small/tight shoes', composed of the verb 穿 (chuān, originally 'to bore through, pierce', hence 'to thread one's limbs through clothing or footwear, to put on') and the modified object 小鞋 (xiǎoxié, 'undersized shoes'). Alluding to the painful, unseen constriction of bound feet or ill-fitting shoes that look normal from the outside while torturing the wearer with every step, it usually appears in the causative frame 给某人穿小鞋 ('make someone wear tight shoes'), meaning to covertly harass, sabotage, or make life difficult for a subordinate or rival through petty abuse of power.

history.meaning: literally to put on undersized shoes; metaphorically to subject someone to covert, pinching workplace harassment or retaliation

morphemes.meaning: to pierce through; to put on, wear

穿小鞋.notes: Almost always used with 给 ('give/make'): 领导给他穿小鞋 ('the boss is covertly making life hard for him'). The brilliance of the metaphor lies in the fact that only the person wearing the tight shoes feels the constant pain, while outsiders see nothing overtly illegal.

rootFamily.gloss: to dress, wear clothes; clothing style
to expose, see through a lie or trick

穿过.etymology: The verb '穿过' (chuānguò, to pass through) pairs '穿' (to pierce, to wear) and '过' (to pass). The original meaning of '穿' involved boring a hole, such as stringing a thread through a needle, leading to its extended meaning of passing through a space or putting on clothes. '过' acts as a directional complement indicating the completion of the crossing. '穿过' vividly describes movement that intersects a barrier or space, such as a forest, a tunnel, or a crowd. It is widely used in both literal and figurative contexts.

history.meaning: pass by

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 穿过

突兀.etymology: A Classical Chinese rhyming/ideophonic binome (疊韻聯綿詞 / 並立式) combining 突 (tū, from 穴 'cave' + 犬 'dog', 'a dog lunging suddenly out of a cave; to jut out, rush forth abruptly') and 兀 (wù, an ideogram of a flat-topped high plateau or bald head above legs, Old Chinese *ŋʷˤət, 'towering high and bare, jutting up steeply'). Originally describing craggy peaks or towers rising sheer and isolated (as in Du Mu's *Epang Palace Rhapsody*: 蜀山兀，阿房出), it shifted metaphorically to describe remarks, plot twists, or designs that stick out jarsingly or happen abruptly out of nowhere.

history.meaning: towering steeply, jutting up bare and craggy above the surroundings
abrupt, unexpected, out of the blue; jarring, out of place in a composition or scene

morphemes.meaning: to rush out suddenly, jut out, protrude
towering high and bare, rising steeply and alone

突兀.notes: Unlike 突然 (which simply means 'suddenly' in time), 突兀 carries an aesthetic or social judgment: it means something feels 'jarring, unmotivated, or awkwardly out of place' (e.g., 这句台词很突兀 'this line of dialogue feels jarring/forced'; 这么问可能有点突兀 'asking this might seem a bit out of the blue').

rootFamily.gloss: to protrude, stand out prominently; prominent

cognates.meaning: breaking out of an encirclement; making it into the finals/next round
breaking through a siege or encirclement

突围.etymology: A verb-object compound (動賓式) formed from the verb 突 (tū, 'to charge forth, dash violently, break through') and its object 围 (wéi, Traditional 圍, from 囗 'enclosure' + 韋 'guards marching around a perimeter', 'military encirclement, siege, surrounding ring'). Attested in dynastic histories (such as the *Book of Han* and *Records of the Three Kingdoms*) for besieged troops charging out of an enemy ring, it is widely used in modern media and business for breaking out of a fierce competitive bottleneck or crisis.

history.meaning: to charge through and break out of a military siege or encirclement
to break out of an encirclement; figuratively, to break through fierce competition or a crisis

morphemes.meaning: to dash forward, charge, break through

突围.notes: Because 突围 is an inherent verb-object compound (突 + 围), modifiers are inserted between the two characters (e.g., 突出重围 'break out of a heavy encirclement', 成功突围 'successfully break through the pack'). In TV and film marketing, 票房突围 means a dark-horse show or movie breaking out amid heavy competition.

rootFamily.gloss: predicament, tight spot; to rescue from a siege/crisis (解围)

cognates.meaning: suddenly, abruptly, all of a suđen

突然.etymology: A derived descriptive adjectival/adverbial compound (附加式) composed of the verbal root 突 (tū, 'a dog rushing out of a cave; to lunge forth, dash abruptly') plus the Classical Chinese manner-adverbial and adjectival suffix 然 (rán, originally 'to burn', grammaticalized in Old Chinese as a demonstrative and stative suffix meaning 'in such a manner, -ly, like so'). Literally 'in a rushing-out manner', it has been the standard word for 'sudden(ly)' since medieval Chinese.

history.meaning: in an abrupt, rushing-forth manner; all of a sudden
sudden, unexpected; suddenly, abruptly

morphemes.meaning: to rush out abruptly, charge forth, sudden

突然.notes: Unlike 忽然 (hūrán), which is strictly an adverb ('suddenly'), 突然 functions as both an adverb (突然下雨了 'it suddenly rained') and an adjective that can take degree adverbs or function as a predicate (太突然了 'that was way too sudden'; 事情很突然 'the matter was very unexpected').

rootFamily.gloss: suddenly, all of a sudden (adverb only)

突然袭击.etymology: A four-character modifier-head phrase (偏正式短語) in which 突然 (tūrán, 'sudden, unexpected') modifies the coordinative military verb/noun 袭击 (xíjī, Traditional 襲擊, combining 襲 xí 'to march covertly in double garments to catch an enemy unprepared, sneak-attack' and 擊 jī 'to strike, hit, assault'). Originating in modern military terminology for a surprise tactical strike, it passed into everyday speech for blindsiding someone with an unannounced inspection, question, or crisis.

history.meaning: to launch a covert raid (襲); to strike or attack (擊)
to launch a surprise attack or ambush; figuratively, to blindside someone with an unannounced demand or check
history.stage: Modern Mandarin (often abbreviated 突袭 tūxí)

morphemes.meaning: to raid covertly, catch by surprise

突然袭击.notes: Often contracted to the two-syllable verb 突袭 (tūxí, 'to raid / launch a surprise attack'); in workplace and media contexts, 搞突然袭击 means springing a major question, audit, or announcement on colleagues without warning.

cognates.meaning: breakthrough, breaking through, surpassing a limit or figure

突破.etymology: A resultative verb-complement compound (動補式) combining the action verb 突 (tū, 'to charge forward, dash, ram') with the resultative verb 破 (pò, from 石 'stone' + 皮 'skin/split', 'to shatter, split open, breach, defeat'). Originally used in medieval military narratives for charging and breaching enemy defensive lines or city walls, its modern usage—reinforced by Japanese 突破 (toppa)—extends to achieving a creative or scientific breakthrough and surpassing a numerical milestone (such as ratings or box-office records).

history.meaning: to charge and breach an enemy fortification or battle line
to break through a bottleneck; a major breakthrough; to surpass or top a numerical record
history.stage: Modern Mandarin (reinforced by Japanese 突破 toppa)

morphemes.meaning: to charge forth, dash, rush against
to break open, shatter, breach, surpass

突破.notes: In media and business reporting, 突破 frequently takes a numerical object to mean 'surpass/top a milestone' (收视率突破百分之二 'ratings topped 2%', 销量突破百万 'sales surpassed one million'), alongside its noun/verb sense of 'making a creative breakthrough' (取得新突破).

rootFamily.gloss: to break out of an encirclement
to smash, break, destroy (a record or rule)

cognates.meaning: breakthrough opening, way out of a deadlock

突破口.etymology: A three-character modifier-head nominal compound (偏正式) formed from 突破 (tūpò, 'to charge and breach; a breakthrough') modifying 口 (kǒu, 'mouth, opening, gap, breach'). Originating in military tactics for the specific gap blasted open in an enemy's defensive line through which attacking forces pour in, it is universally used in negotiations, investigations, and project management for the initial weak spot or strategic opening that unlocks a complex problem.

history.meaning: the physical breach or gap opened in an enemy defensive line during an assault
history.stage: Modern Military Sinitic (shared with Japanese 突破口 toppakō)

history.meaning: strategic opening, entry point, or key angle that unlocks a deadlock or tough problem

突破口.notes: Commonly paired with 找 ('find') or 打开 ('open up'): 找到突破口 ('find the strategic opening / key angle to crack the problem'). In media production or negotiations, a 突破口 is the one persuasive hook or vulnerable detail that makes a stubborn party agree.

窄.etymology: Phono-semantic/associative character combining 穴 ('cave, cramped space') + 乍 (zhà/zhǎi, phonetic). Originally 'cramped, confined', becoming the standard everyday antonym of 宽 ('wide') for 'narrow'.

history.meaning: cramped -> narrow (antonym of 宽)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 窄 (via 萌典)

窄窄.etymology: Reduplicated vivid adjective from 窄 ('narrow'), meaning 'quite narrow, slender and cramped'.

history.meaning: narrow; quite narrow

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 窄窄 (via 萌典)

窗.etymology: Originally 囱, a pictograph of a latticed skylight or smoke vent in a roof or wall; later augmented with semantic 穴 ('opening/cavity in a building') above and 心/囱 below to form 窗. Means 'window'.

history.meaning: latticed vent/skylight -> window

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 窗 (via 萌典)

窗台.etymology: The noun '窗台' (chuāngtái, windowsill) is formed by '窗' (window) and '台' (platform, terrace). Historically, '窗' featured a radical for a hole or opening in a wall, reflecting early architectural designs. '台' referred to an elevated, flat structure. '窗台' describes the flat ledge at the bottom of a window frame. The term became prevalent as architectural styles evolved to include wider, functional window ledges. It is commonly associated with placing small objects or plants near a window.

history.meaning: window

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 窗台

窗外.etymology: Locative noun compound combining 窗 ('window') + 外 ('outside').

history.meaning: outside the window

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 窗外 (via 萌典)

窗帘.etymology: Attributive compound combining 窗 ('window') + 帘 (trad. 簾, 'hanging bamboo or fabric screen/curtain').

history.meaning: window curtain; drapery

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 窗帘 (via 萌典)

窗户.etymology: Coordinate architectural compound of 窗 ('window opening, lattice skylight', cave/roof opening radical 穴 + phonetic 囱 'chimney/vent') + 户 ('single-leaf casement or shuttered opening', pictograph of half a double gate 门). The neutral-tone second syllable marks lexicalized everyday Mandarin.

history.meaning: skylight lattice (窗) and casement door/shutter (户)
window

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 窗户

窗板.etymology: Attributive compound combining 窗 ('window') + 板 ('wooden board, shutter'), referring to wooden window shutters or a windowsill board.

history.meaning: wooden window shutter; window board

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 窗板 (via 萌典)

窗边.etymology: Locative noun compound combining 窗 ('window') + 边 (trad. 邊, 'side, edge, by').

history.meaning: by the window; windowside

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 窗边 (via 萌典)

立.etymology: Pictograph in oracle-bone and bronze inscriptions showing a person (大) standing planted firmly on the ground (一). Classical verb for 'to stand, erect, set up, establish', preserved in compounds and idioms.

morphemes.meaning: person standing on the ground -> to stand, establish

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: to stand upright; to erect, establish, set up

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 立 (via 萌典)

立了项.etymology: An aspectual realization of the separable verb-object compound 立项 (lìxiàng, 'to establish/greenlight a project'), formed from the verb 立 (lì, originally an ideogram of a person 大 standing firmly on the ground 一, 'to stand, set up, establish formally') + the perfective aspect particle 了 (le, grammaticalized from the verb 了 liǎo 'to finish, complete') + the object noun 项 (xiàng, Traditional 項, originally 'nape of the neck', extended to 'item, clause, project'). Because 立项 is a separable verb (离合词), the aspect marker 了 must be infixed between the verb 立 and its internal object 项.

history.meaning: established/set up + [completed aspect] + item/project (separable verb-object construction)

morphemes.meaning: to stand, set up, formally establish
perfective aspect marker (indicating completion of the action)
nape of the neck; item, entry, project

立了项.notes: Illustrates how Mandarin separable verbs (离合词) like 立项 work: to say 'the project has already been officially greenlit', speakers insert 了 inside the compound (节目已经立了项) rather than saying *立项了项目.

rootFamily.gloss: officially greenlight or register a project

立刻.etymology: Compound adverb combining 立 ('standing on the spot, immediately', as in classical 立待) + 刻 ('a notch on a water clock; a brief moment'). Means 'immediately, at once, right away'.

history.meaning: at this very moment -> immediately, right away

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 立刻 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: on the spot, immediately, at once
cognates.word: 立処に (tachidokoro ni) / 即座に (sokuza ni)

cognates.meaning: immediately, at once, on the spot

立即.etymology: A classical compound adverb combining 立 (lì, 'standing upright in place; while still standing, without even sitting down or moving away') and 即 (jí, originally an ideogram of a kneeling person 卩 approaching a vessel of food 皀 to eat, 'to approach closely, thereupon, right then and there'). In Classical Chinese (such as the *Records of the Grand Historian*), 立 alone functioned adverbially as 'on the spot, before one has time to sit', and combining it with 即 reinforced the sense of zero delay ('immediately, at once').

history.meaning: while still standing, on the spot (立); approaching the seat, right then and there (即)
immediately, forthwith, at once without delay

morphemes.meaning: standing in place, on the spot, immediately
to approach; right then, at once, promptly

立即.notes: Slightly more formal and written in register than 马上 (mǎshàng) or 立刻 (lìkè); frequently used in official directives, news broadcasts, and urgent workplace orders (立即执行 'execute immediately', 立即停止 'cease at once').

rootFamily.gloss: about to, on the verge of, soon

cognates.meaning: standpoint, position, situation, footing (source of the Sino-compound)

立场.etymology: An orthographic return loan from Japanese *wasei-kango* (和製漢語): originally an indigenous Japanese compound noun 立場 (tachiba, combining native Japanese *tachi-* from *tatsu* 立 'to stand' + *ba* 場 'place, ground'), literally 'standing ground, footing, or roadside stopping place for palanquin bearers', which evolved in Meiji Japan to mean 'one's social, ideological, or argumentative standpoint' (translating German *Standpunkt* / English *standpoint*). Adopted into early 20th-century Chinese with Sinitic readings as 立场 (lìchǎng), it denotes both ideological stance and one's rightful ground or authority to speak.

history.meaning: literal place where one stands or stops; figuratively, one's standpoint, footing, or perspective (rendering German Standpunkt)
political, moral, or personal standpoint; legitimate ground or status to speak or intervene
history.stage: Modern Mandarin (20th-century orthographic loan from Japanese)

立场.notes: Beyond politics or negotiation (坚定立场 'hold firm to one's stance', 换位思考/站在你的立场 'stand in your shoes'), interpersonal Mandarin frequently uses 有/没有立场 to mean 'having (or lacking) the right/ground to meddle or criticize' (你有什么立场管我？ 'What ground/right do you have to boss me around?').

rootFamily.gloss: to have a foothold, establish oneself in society or an industry
on the spot, live, production set or site

cognates.meaning: to render distinguished service, achieve a great feat
cognates.word: 立功 (rikkō) / 大功を立てる (taikō o tateru)

cognates.meaning: to establish great merit or achievement

立大功.etymology: An expanded verb-object phrase (動賓短語) built from the classical verb-object compound 立功 (lìgōng, attested in the *Zuo Zhuan* as one of the 'Three Immortalities' 三不朽: 太上立德，其次立功，其次立言, 'to establish enduring meritorious deeds') with the adjective 大 (dà, 'great, major, huge') inserted before the object 功 (gōng, from 工 'work/skill' + 力 'strength', 'meritorious service, achievement, credit'). Literally 'to establish a great merit', it denotes performing a major service or saving the day for one's team or organization.

history.meaning: to establish great military or state merit worthy of reward and historical record
to perform a huge service, score a major achievement, or save the day for a team/project

立大功.notes: Because 立功 is a separable verb-object compound (离合词), modifiers like 大 ('huge') or 头 ('first/top') go right between 立 and 功: 立大功 ('perform a huge service'), 立了大功 ('performed a huge service'), 立头功 ('earn top credit'). In everyday workplace speech, it is often used warmly or playfully when someone's quick thinking saves a project.

rootFamily.gloss: to render meritorious service, win credit
merit, contribution, credit for an achievement

立式.etymology: Attributive compound combining 立 ('standing upright, vertical') + 式 ('type, style, model'). Used of upright pianos (立式钢琴), floor lamps, or vertical appliances.

history.meaning: upright model; vertical type (e.g., upright piano)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 立式 (via 萌典)

立项.etymology: A modern bureaucratic and corporate verb-object compound (動賓式 / 離合詞) formed from the verb 立 (lì, 'to set up, formally establish, put on the official register', as in 立案 'to register a legal case') and the object 项 (xiàng, Traditional 項, 'item, entry, project', short for 项目 xiàngmù 'project, program'). Originating in late 20th-century Chinese administrative, academic, and corporate planning vocabulary, it denotes the formal institutional approval, registration, and budget allocation that officially launches a project or TV/film production.

history.meaning: to formally register, approve, and establish a project on the official plan and budget roster
history.stage: Contemporary Mainland Mandarin (Reform-era administrative & corporate coinage)

morphemes.meaning: to set up, establish, formally register
project, item (short for 项目 xiàngmù)

立项.notes: A crucial milestone term in Chinese media production, tech, and academia (Equivalent to Hollywood's 'greenlight'): until a show, film, or R&D initiative completes 立项, it has no official budget, team code, or regulatory filing. Works as a separable verb (立了项 'got greenlit', 立不上项 'unable to get greenlit') and as a noun modifier (立项报告 'project proposal/approval report').

rootFamily.gloss: got officially greenlit as a project
to register and open a legal/official case file

立马.etymology: Originally a Classical Chinese verb-object compound (立馬, lìmǎ) composed of 立 (lì, 'to stand; to halt') and 馬 (mǎ, 'horse'), literally meaning 'to halt one's horse' or 'to stand by one's horse ready to mount'. In Tang and Song dynasty military and poetic contexts, writing a dispatch or composing a poem 'while halting one's horse' (立馬待發) denoted extreme urgency without dismounting. Through metaphorical extension in Northern Mandarin vernacular, it grammaticalized into a high-frequency colloquial adverb meaning 'on the spot' or 'immediately'.

history.meaning: to rein in and halt one's horse; to stand ready by a horse
in the time it takes to halt a horse; without delay; on the spot
right away; immediately; instantaneously

立马.notes: More colloquial and punchier than 立刻 (lìkè) or 马上 (mǎshàng); ubiquitous in fast-paced television production rooms when directors demand instant adjustments.

rootFamily.gloss: on the spot; then and there

站.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining semantic 立 ('to stand') + phonetic 占 (zhàn). Originally meant 'to stand upright, stand still'; under Liao–Yuan Mongol administration it also translated Mongol jam ('postal relay station', 驿站), giving both modern senses: 'to stand' and 'station, stop'.

history.meaning: to stand on one's feet; relay post -> station, stop

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 站 (via 萌典)

站台.etymology: Attributive compound combining 站 ('railway or transit station') + 台 (trad. 臺, 'raised platform, terrace'). Denotes a railway or subway boarding platform.

history.meaning: station platform; railway platform

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 站台 (via 萌典)

站好岗.etymology: A separable verb-complement-object phrase (站好崗, zhànhǎo gǎng) built from the verb 站 (zhàn, 'to stand at a post'), the resultative complement 好 (hǎo, 'properly; to satisfactory completion'), and the nominal object 崗 (gǎng, originally 'hillock' or 'ridge', extended in late imperial and modern military usage to a raised sentry post or duty station). The phrase originated in military guard duty ('to stand one's sentry watch properly') before broadening in modern Mainland Chinese institutional and workplace discourse to mean fulfilling one's professional responsibilities faithfully until the very end.

history.meaning: to stand sentry duty at a lookout post or guard station
to perform one's sentry or professional duty conscientiously to completion

morphemes.meaning: to stand; to occupy a station
resultative complement indicating thoroughness or proper completion

站好岗.notes: Often appears in the collocation 站好最后一班岗 ('stand one's last shift faithfully'), used when an employee or producer is about to leave a project or retire.

rootFamily.gloss: to stand sentry; to be on guard duty
to report for duty; to take up one's post

站直.etymology: Resultative verb compound combining 站 ('to stand') + 直 ('straight, upright').

history.meaning: to stand up straight

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 站直 (via 萌典)

站队.etymology: A verb-object compound (站隊, zhànduì) combining 站 (zhàn, 'to stand', borrowed in Middle Chinese from Old Turkic / Mongolic *jam* 'post station' via 'to stop at a relay station') and 隊 (duì, originally 'a squad or file of soldiers'). Literally meaning 'to line up in formation' or 'to fall into rank', the word underwent metaphorical shift in mid-20th-century political campaigns and contemporary corporate and entertainment slang to mean aligning oneself with a faction, declaring allegiance, or taking sides in a dispute.

history.meaning: to fall in line; to stand in military or physical queue formation
to align with a faction; to take sides publicly in a conflict

morphemes.meaning: to stand; to take a position

站队.notes: In Chinese office politics and showbiz fandoms, 被迫站队 ('being forced to take sides') describes the pressure on staff or celebrities when two powerful executives or stars clash.

竞争.etymology: A coordinative compound (競爭, jìngzhēng) uniting 競 (jìng, 'to contend; to vie; to race', graphically depicting two figures speaking/striving against each other) and 爭 (zhēng, 'to struggle for; to dispute', depicting two hands pulling on an object). Attested in Classical Chinese texts such as the *Zhuangzi* (*Qi물lun*: 有競有爭 'there is vying and there is striving'), the compound was revitalized in the late 19th century via Meiji Japanese *kyōsō* (競争), where Fukuzawa Yukichi coined/repurposed the Sino-compound to translate English 'competition' in political economy and evolutionary theory.

history.meaning: to vie and contend; to strive against one another
economic, social, or evolutionary competition (translation of English 'competition')
competition; to compete (in business, sports, or ratings)

morphemes.meaning: to vie; to contend; to race
to strive; to contend for; to dispute

竞争.notes: Functions as both a verb and a noun; common media collocations include 恶性竞争 ('cutthroat/malignant competition') and 公平竞争 ('fair competition').

rootFamily.gloss: to fight for; to vie for

竞争对手.etymology: A four-character modifier-head nominal compound (競爭對手, jìngzhēng duìshǒu) formed from 競爭 (jìngzhēng, 'competition; competing') modifying 對手 (duìshǒu, 'opponent; match'). 對手 literally means 'opposing hand' (對 'facing/opposing' + 手 'hand/adept person'), originating in board games like Go (weiqi) and martial arts in Tang–Song literature to denote a worthy adversary of equal skill before broadening to business and industry rivals.

history.meaning: an opponent or equal match in chess (weiqi) or martial combat
competitor; rival firm, program, or contender

竞争对手.notes: The standard professional term in television production and corporate strategy for a rival network, competing show in the same timeslot, or business adversary.

竞唱.etymology: A modern modifier-head compound (競唱, jìngchàng) combining the bound morpheme 競 (jìng, 'to compete; competitively') with 唱 (chàng, 'to sing; vocal performance'). Modeled by analogy on established Sino-Japanese/Mandarin compounds like 競演 (jìngyǎn, 'competitive performance') and 競標 (jìngbiāo, 'competitive bidding'), it emerged in 21st-century Chinese reality television and music variety shows (such as *Singer* / 歌手) to denote live vocal competition rounds where singers perform sequentially for audience or judge rankings.

history.meaning: to vie; to contend in a contest
to compete in singing; vocal competition round in a music television show

竞唱.notes: A signature variety-show term (综艺词汇) used specifically for televised music shows where professional or contestant singers battle via stage performances, such as 竞唱歌手 ('competing singers').

竞演.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-compound (競演, jìngyǎn) composed of 競 (jìng, 'to compete; to vie') and 演 (yǎn, originally 'water flowing far', extended in Classical and Literary Chinese to 'to elaborate; to practice; to perform'). First popularized in Japanese (*kyōen*) and Korean (*gyeong-yeon*, notably through the Korean music variety format *I Am a Singer* / 나는 가수다), the term was adopted into contemporary Mainland Chinese television production jargon to describe high-stakes competitive stage performances.

history.meaning: artists or actors competing in skill on the same stage
competitive stage performance in reality TV and music variety shows

morphemes.meaning: to perform; to act; to stage

竞演.notes: Unlike a generic 比赛 (bǐsài, 'match/contest'), 竞演 emphasizes artistic stagecraft and production value alongside rankings, making it the preferred industry term in idol and music survival shows.

竟.etymology: In oracle bone and bronze inscriptions, 竟 (jìng) combines 音 (yīn, 'musical sound/melody') atop 人 (rén, 'person'), originally denoting the completion or end of a musical piece (*Shuowen Jiezi*: 樂曲盡為竟 'when a musical composition finishes, it is 竟'). From 'end of a song', its meaning broadened in Classical Chinese to spatial boundaries ('border/frontier', later written 境) and temporal completion ('to finish; throughout; in the end'). Through pragmatic shift from 'in the end / after all that', it grammaticalized into a counter-expectation adverb meaning 'unexpectedly; contrary to all expectations; actually'.

history.meaning: the conclusion of a musical piece; to finish; border/boundary
ultimately; in the end; from start to finish (e.g. 竟日 'the whole day')
unexpectedly; to one's surprise; actually (short for 竟然)

竟.notes: Used as a monosyllabic, slightly more concise and dramatic variant of 竟然 (jìngrán) in scripts, headlines, and emphatic speech to express shock or disbelief.

rootFamily.gloss: after all; when all is said and done
what on earth; after all; outcome

竟然.etymology: Adverb formed from 竟 ('to reach the end, finally -> unexpectedly, contrary to expectation') + adverbial suffix 然 ('so, thus'). Expresses surprise that something happened against expectations ('unexpectedly, actually, to one's surprise').

history.meaning: unexpectedly; to one's surprise; actually

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 竟然 (via 萌典)

章.etymology: Composed in early Chinese paleography of 音 (yīn, 'musical sound') and 十 (shí, 'ten; a complete cycle'), 章 (zhāng) originally meant a complete movement of music (*Shuowen Jiezi*: 樂竟為一章 'the completion of a piece of music is one 章'). Because ancient poetry and music were inseparable, 章 came to denote a stanza of verse (as in the *Shijing*), and subsequently a structured chapter or section of prose, legal statutes (約法三章), patterned brilliance (文章), and an official seal or badge.

history.meaning: a complete musical movement; a stanza of song; patterned design
a chapter of a text; a memorial to the throne; an official seal or statute
chapter (classifier for book/script sections); regulation; stamp/seal

章.notes: As a classifier and bound noun, 章 divides books, treaties, or major narrative arcs (e.g., 第一章 'Chapter One'), whereas 集 (jí) and 期 (qī) are used for TV episodes.

rootFamily.gloss: chapter and verse; logical order; method in work

童年.etymology: Attributive noun compound combining 童 ('child, youth') + 年 ('years, age'). Attested since Six Dynasties and Tang poetry for 'childhood, juvenile years'.

history.meaning: childhood; early years of life

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 童年 (via 萌典)

端.etymology: Phono-semantic/associative character combining 立 ('standing upright') + 耑 (zhuān/duān, depicting a plant sprouting upward above ground and roots below). Means 'upright, proper', 'tip, extremity, beginning', and as a verb, 'to hold or carry level with both hands (as a tray or bowl)'.

history.meaning: upright, proper; end/tip; to carry level in the hands

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 端 (via 萌典)

端庄.etymology: Coordinative adjective compound combining 端 ('upright, proper, regular') + 庄 (trad. 莊, 'dignified, grave, sedate'). Describes a person's bearing or appearance as dignified, poised, and graceful.

history.meaning: dignified, poised, and graceful

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 端庄 (via 萌典)

竹篮.etymology: Material-object compound from 竹 ('bamboo', pictograph of drooping bamboo leaves) + 篮 (simplified from 籃, bamboo 竹 + phonetic 監 'basket with handle'). Split-bamboo baskets woven in herringbone or hexagonal plaiting have been everyday market and kitchen containers in China since antiquity.

history.meaning: woven bamboo basket
bamboo basket

笑.etymology: Written with the bamboo radical 竹 (zhú) atop 夭 (yāo, 'to bend gracefully; swaying figure'), 笑 (xiào) has long fascinated Chinese philologists. Early glosses starting with Xu Xuan's Song-era annotation to the *Shuowen Jiezi* proposed that when bamboo is blown by the wind, it bends like a person doubled over in laughter. Phonological and paleographical evidence indicates an Old Chinese root *slew-s* meaning 'to smile; to laugh' (and by extension 'to mock or laugh at'), covering both quiet smiling and audible laughter in Chinese across three millennia.

history.meaning: to smile; to laugh; to laugh at (deride)
to smile; to laugh; to ridicule

morphemes.meaning: to smile; to laugh; to mock

笑.notes: Unlike English, which lexically separates 'smile' and 'laugh', Mandarin 笑 covers both; add modifiers like 微笑 (wēixiào, 'smile faintly') or 大笑 (dàxiào, 'laugh out loud') to disambiguate.

笑话.etymology: A modifier-head compound (笑話, xiàohuà; realized with neutral tone *xiàohua* in Standard Mandarin) combining 笑 (xiào, 'laughing; laughable') and 話 (huà, 'speech; story; talk'). In Song and Yuan dynasty storytelling (*huaben*), 笑話 originally designated a humorous oral tale or jest meant to provoke laughter. In Ming–Qing vernacular fiction, it also developed a transitive verb usage ('to laugh at; to mock someone') and a second nominal sense ('a laughingstock; an object of ridicule').

history.meaning: a humorous tale or jest told by professional storytellers; to mock
joke (verbal jest); laughingstock/travesty; to laugh at someone

笑话.notes: Watch the two distinct collocations: 讲笑话 (jiǎng xiàohua) means 'to tell a joke', whereas 看笑话 (kàn xiàohua) or 闹笑话 (nào xiàohua) means 'to watch someone make a fool of themselves' or 'to become a laughingstock'.

rootFamily.gloss: punchline; comedic gimmick; source of laughter
comedy point; trigger for laughter in a script

笔.etymology: Associative compound (trad. 筆) originally formed from 竹 ('bamboo shaft') + 聿 ('hand holding a brush', replaced in simplified 笔 by 毛 'animal hair'). Directly reflects the construction of a traditional Chinese writing brush with a bamboo handle and hair tip; generalized to pens, pencils, and strokes.

morphemes.meaning: hair tip of brush (in 笔; trad. 聿 'brush')

history.meaning: bamboo-and-hair writing brush -> pen, pencil, writing implement

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 笔 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: written record; note taken by brush/pen

笔录.etymology: A modifier-head or instrument-verb compound (筆錄, bǐlù) formed from 筆 (bǐ, 'writing brush; pen; by means of a brush') and 錄 (lù, originally 'metallic luster', extended in Han bureaucracy to 'to inscribe; to copy down; a register'). Attested in Six Dynasties and Tang texts as an adverbial-verb construction meaning 'to record in writing with a brush' (as opposed to oral transmission 口傳), it nominalized into a term for verbatim written notes, meeting minutes, or police/legal interrogation transcripts.

history.meaning: to write down with a brush; a written transcription of oral remarks
history.stage: Middle Chinese / Literary Chinese (Six Dynasties – Tang)

history.meaning: written record; meeting minutes; official interrogation transcript; to take down in writing

morphemes.meaning: to record; to transcribe; written register

笔录.notes: In workplace dramas, 会议笔录 refers to written meeting minutes, while in legal or police contexts 做笔录 means 'to take/give a formal written statement'.

rootFamily.gloss: notes; written jottings; to take notes

笔挺.etymology: Metaphorical adjective combining 笔 (trad. 筆, 'writing brush stem, straight as a brush shaft') + 挺 ('standing straight, stiff, erect'). Describes posture or ironed clothing as 'ramrod-straight, trim and well-pressed'.

history.meaning: straight as a brush -> ramrod-straight, crisp and well-pressed

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 笔挺 (via 萌典)

笔直.etymology: The adjective '笔直' (bǐzhí, perfectly straight) is a vivid compound combining '笔' (brush, pen) and '直' (straight). The writing brush, made with a straight bamboo or wooden shaft, was a ubiquitous tool in ancient China. By using '笔' as a metaphor for straightness, '笔直' describes something that is as straight as a writing brush shaft. It can be applied to physical objects like a road or a posture, and occasionally in a figurative sense to describe someone's uncompromising character.

history.meaning: straight

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 笔直

笔记本.etymology: Three-character compound combining 笔记 (trad. 筆記, 'written notes, jottings', from 笔 'pen/brush' + 记 'to record') + 本 ('bound book, pad'). Refers to a paper notebook (and by extension a laptop computer, 笔记本电脑).

history.meaning: notebook (pad for writing notes, or laptop)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 笔记本 (via 萌典)

笔迹.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (筆跡 / 筆蹟, bǐjì) combining 筆 (bǐ, 'writing brush; pen') and 跡 (jì, 'footprint; trace; track', composed of 足 'foot' and phonetic 亦/責). First attested in Six Dynasties and Tang calligraphy criticism and historical biographies (such as the *Book of Jin*), it literally denotes the 'physical traces left by a brush', referring both to an individual's distinctive handwriting style and to authentic surviving manuscripts by a past writer.

history.meaning: traces of the calligrapher's brush; authentic handwritten work
person's handwriting; chirography (often as an identifier)

笔迹.notes: Refers to handwriting as an identifiable personal trait or physical trace (e.g., 认出他的笔迹 'recognize his handwriting'), whereas 字迹 (zìjì) focuses on the legibility or neatness of written characters.

rootFamily.gloss: handwriting; written characters and their neatness
handwritten work; authentic calligraphy of a notable person

cognates.meaning: to conform to; to match; suitable

符合.etymology: Derived from an ancient administrative and military verification practice (符合, fúhé). In Warring States and Han China, a 符 (fú, 'bamboo or bronze tally', written with 竹 'bamboo' + 付 'to hand over') was inscribed with text and split into two halves: one kept by the court and one given to an envoy or general. When issuing orders, the two halves were brought together—合 (hé, 'to join; to match')—to verify authenticity (*Mengzi*: 若合符節 'like joining the halves of a bamboo tally'). From 'the two halves of a tally matching perfectly', it evolved into the general verb meaning 'to accord with; to conform to; to meet (standards or criteria)'.

history.meaning: the two halves of a bamboo or bronze credential tally matching together
to correspond exactly; to tally with facts or prophecies
to conform to; to match; to meet (requirements, standards, or expectations)

morphemes.meaning: bamboo tally; symbol; to tally with
to join; to fit together; to match

符合.notes: A staple of professional and broadcast evaluation: 符合要求 ('meet requirements'), 符合节目定位 ('fit the show's positioning'), and 不符合规定 ('violate/fail to conform to regulations').

rootFamily.gloss: to tally with; to match; consistent (negated as 不符)
qualified; meeting standards; up to par

笨.etymology: A phono-semantic compound (笨, bèn) composed of the bamboo radical 竹 (zhú) and the phonetic component 本 (běn, Old Chinese *pˤənʔ*). In the *Shuowen Jiezi* (100 CE), 笨 is defined strictly as 竹裏也 ('the coarse inner white pith/membrane of bamboo'), which lacked the flexibility and strength of the outer green skin (竹青). Because bamboo pith is thick, rigid, and unusable for fine weaving, the character was metaphorically extended during the魏晉南北朝 (Six Dynasties) and Tang periods to mean 'thick, unwieldy, clumsy', and then to 'slow-witted, dull, or foolish'.

history.meaning: the coarse inner white pith of a bamboo stalk
bulky; rough; clumsy; lacking agility or cleverness
slow-witted; stupid; clumsy; awkward

笨.notes: Covers both mental slowness (脑子笨 'slow-witted') and physical awkwardness (笨手笨脚 'all thumbs/clumsy'); often used affectionately or self-deprecatingly in colloquial speech.

第.etymology: Phono-semantic character (also written 弟 in early manuscripts) combining semantic 竹 ('bamboo slips tied in sequence') + phonetic 弟 (dì, 'leather cord wrapped in order around a shaft; younger brother in birth order'). Used since the Warring States and Han as the prefix for ordinal numbers ('first, second...').

history.meaning: graded sequence -> ordinal number prefix (-st, -nd, -th)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 第 (via 萌典)

第一.etymology: An ordinal numeral compound (第一, dì-yī) formed by prefixing 第 (dì, originally written 弟 for a graded sequence of bamboo slips bound by leather thongs, hence 'order; rank; Imperial examination grade') to the cardinal numeral 一 (yī, 'one'). Established during the Han dynasty to rank court officials, aristocratic estates, and imperial examination candidates (such as 治平為天下第一 'ranked first in the empire for governance'), it became the universal pan-Sinitic ordinal for 'first' and an adjective meaning 'foremost' or 'primary'.

history.meaning: rank one in official imperial assessment or peerage order
first (ordinal number); foremost; supreme in a category (天下第一)
first; number one; primary; most important

第一.notes: Can modify nouns directly without a classifier when meaning 'first-rate / foremost' (e.g., 第一手资料 'firsthand data', 安全第一 'safety first'), or precede a classifier for countable ordinal sequences.

第一支.etymology: An ordinal numeral-classifier phrase (第一支, dì-yī zhī) combining the ordinal 第一 (dì-yī, 'first') with the classifier 支 (zhī). In Old Chinese, 支 depicted a hand (又) holding a bamboo branch (竹), meaning 'branch; offshoot; to support'. In Classical and Literary Chinese poetic traditions (such as 竹枝詞 'Bamboo Branch Songs', where songs were metaphorically counted as 'branches/sprigs' of melody), 支/枝 grammaticalized into the specialized measure word for musical compositions, songs, dances, and teams/troops, alongside rod-shaped objects.

history.meaning: bamboo branch; offshoot; classifier for songs/melodies and troop detachments
the very first (song, single, music video, dance piece, or team)

morphemes.meaning: classifier for songs, musical works, teams, and rod-like objects

第一支.notes: In the music and television industry, 支 (zhī) and 首 (shǒu) both count songs, but 支 feels slightly more literary or professional and is also used for music videos (第一支MV), promotional trailers (第一支预告片), and bands/teams (第一支乐队).

第一时间.etymology: A four-character nominal and adverbial compound (第一時間, dì-yī shíjiān) combining the ordinal 第一 (dì-yī, 'first') with 時間 (shíjiān, 'time', itself a Meiji Japanese graphic loan *jikan* translating philosophical and physical 'time' from 時 'season/hour' + 間 'interval'). Originally a late-20th-century journalism and emergency-response term in Hong Kong and Taiwan media referring to the critical 'first window of time' immediately after a breaking event (like English 'at the earliest possible moment'), it spread across Mainland Mandarin as an emphatic adverbial phrase meaning 'immediately; the very instant something happens'.

history.meaning: time; temporal interval (coined/standardized in Meiji Japan)
the earliest moment after an incident; immediately; right away; firsthand

第一时间.notes: Ubiquitous in newsrooms, PR crisis management, and live broadcasting: 第一时间赶到现场 ('rush to the scene at the very first moment') or 第一时间通知我 ('notify me the instant you know').

rootFamily.gloss: at that very moment; right away

第一期.etymology: An ordinal numeral-classifier compound (第一期, dì-yī qī) combining 第一 (dì-yī, 'first') with 期 (qī, composed of 其 phonetic and 月 'moon/month', originally meaning 'an appointed time; a full cycle of time'). In late Qing and Republican publishing, 期 was adopted as the standard classifier for periodic issues of magazines, journals, and training cohorts. With the rise of modern television, Chinese broadcasting established a strict lexical division: scripted narrative dramas are counted in 集 (jí, 'collections/episodes'), whereas periodic non-scripted variety shows, talk shows, and reality programs are counted in 期 ('issues/installments/episodes').

history.meaning: appointed time; fixed cycle of a month or year; deadline
Issue No. 1 of a periodical journal or first cohort of an academy (e.g., Whampoa)
Episode One (of a variety/reality TV program); Phase One (of a project); Issue One

morphemes.meaning: scheduled cycle; issue (of a periodical); episode (of a variety show); phase

第一期.notes: Crucial showbiz distinction: use 第一期 for Episode One of a variety or reality show (综艺节目), but 第一集 (dì-yī jí) for Episode One of a scripted drama series (电视剧).

rootFamily.gloss: Episode Two / Issue Two / Phase Two

第一次.etymology: An ordinal verbal-classifier compound (第一次, dì-yī cì) combining 第一 (dì-yī, 'first') with 次 (cì). In Old Chinese, 次 (composed of 二 'two/sequence' and 欠 'yawning/halting person') meant 'to camp in sequence; a resting stage on a march; second in order'. Because military halts occurred in sequential order, 次 evolved in Middle and Early Modern Chinese into a noun meaning 'order/sequence' (次序) and then grammaticalized into the core verbal classifier for occurrences or instances ('time; occasion').

history.meaning: to pitch camp on a march; sequential order; second in rank
classifier for occurrences, turns, or instances of an action
the first time; for the first time; maiden occurrence

morphemes.meaning: verbal classifier for occurrences or times; sequence

第一次.notes: Functions both as a time adverbial ('for the first time', e.g., 第一次上台 'go on stage for the first time') and as a noun ('one's first time/debut experience').

rootFamily.gloss: next time; on the next occasion

第三.etymology: An ordinal numeral compound (第三, dì-sān) formed from the ordinal prefix 第 (dì, originally 'sequence of bamboo slips; rank; grade') and the cardinal numeral 三 (sān, 'three', represented since oracle bone script by three horizontal tally strokes). Used since the Han dynasty to designate the third rank in official hierarchies, legal codes, or sequential enumerations, it also serves in modern compounds to denote an external or neutral party outside a binary pair (as in 第三方 'third party' or 第三者 'third party in a relationship').

history.meaning: third in official rank, grade, or sequential order
third (ordinal numeral); third-ranked; external/neutral (in compounds)

第三.notes: Frequently forms institutional and legal compounds in media production, notably 第三方平台 ('third-party platform') and 第三方数据 ('third-party ratings/data').

rootFamily.gloss: third party (in contracts, data verification, or law)

第三季.etymology: An ordinal numeral-classifier phrase (第三季, dì-sān jì) combining 第三 (dì-sān, 'third') with 季 (jì). In Old Chinese, 季 (composed of 禾 'grain' and 子 'child') meant 'the youngest of brothers' (孟仲叔季) and, by extension, the final month of a three-month astronomical season, eventually shifting to mean 'a three-month season of the year' (四季 'the four seasons') or a quarterly period. In late-20th and 21st-century Chinese media, 季 was calqued on English television 'season' (originally because US/UK television broadcast cycles aligned with quarterly seasons) to denote a full annual production run of a show.

history.meaning: youngest brother; the last month of a season; a three-month season of the year
the third season of the year; the third fiscal quarter (Q3)
Season Three (of a television series, variety show, or web series)

morphemes.meaning: season (of the year or of a television program); fiscal quarter

第三季.notes: In Chinese TV hierarchy, a multi-year franchise is divided into 季 (jì, 'seasons', e.g., 第三季 'Season 3'), and each season is subdivided into 期 (qī, for variety show episodes) or 集 (jí, for drama episodes).

rootFamily.gloss: quarter of a year (e.g., Q1–Q4 in business/broadcasting)

第二.etymology: An ordinal numeral compound (第二, dì-èr) combining the ordinal prefix 第 (dì, 'sequence; grade; rank') with the cardinal numeral 二 (èr, 'two', written since oracle bone inscriptions as two parallel horizontal strokes). Attested from the Han dynasty onward (e.g., *Shiji* and *Hanshu*, where officials or scholars are praised as 無出其右 'none surpassing him' or ranked 第二 'second in the empire'), it functions both as the ordinal number 'second' and as a modifier meaning 'secondary, next in importance, or alternative'.

history.meaning: second in imperial rank, merit assessment, or sequence
second (ordinal number); runner-up; secondary in priority

第二.notes: When used without a classifier before a noun (e.g., 第二天), note that 第二天 means 'the next day / the following day' in a narrative, whereas 'Day Two' of a schedule is often clarified as 第二日 or 活动第二天.

rootFamily.gloss: the next day; the following day
unique; unmatched (lit. 'having no equal or second')

第二名.etymology: An ordinal numeral-classifier compound (第二名, dì-èr míng) combining 第二 (dì-èr, 'second') with 名 (míng, 'name; reputation; roster entry'). In Tang–Song civil service examinations (科舉), successful candidates' names were inscribed in ranked order on a public placard (金榜題名), causing 名 ('a name on an official roster') to grammaticalize into the classifier for ranked positions in a competition and for persons holding a status or role. Thus 第二名 literally means 'the second name on the honor roll', i.e., 'second place' or 'runner-up'.

history.meaning: the candidate whose name is listed second on an examination roster
history.stage: Middle & Early Modern Chinese (Song–Ming examination usage)

history.meaning: second place; runner-up in a competition or ranking

morphemes.meaning: name; rank position on a roster; classifier for ranked places

第二名.notes: The standard everyday term for 'second place / runner-up', whereas formal award ceremonies and press releases often use the literary synonym 亚军 (yàjūn).

第二届.etymology: An ordinal numeral-classifier phrase (第二屆, dì-èr jiè) combining 第二 (dì-èr, 'second') with the classifier 屆 (jiè, originally composed of 尸 'body' and 凷/由, meaning 'to reach an extremity; to arrive at an appointed time'). In Ming and Qing civil service examinations and modern institutional governance,因为 examinations and congresses convened at fixed periodic intervals ('arriving at the appointed term'), 屆 grammaticalized into the specialized classifier for recurring institutional sessions, graduating classes, festivals, and periodic awards or competitions.

history.meaning: to reach a limit; to arrive at an appointed time or juncture (屆時)
the second periodic session, cohort, or edition of a recurring conference, festival, or competition

morphemes.meaning: classifier for regular conferences, graduating classes, tournaments, and annual editions

第二届.notes: Used for major recurring events, award shows, and annual festivals (e.g., 第二届音乐节 'the 2nd Annual Music Festival' or 第二届毕业生 'the second graduating class'), whereas multi-year seasons of a TV show use 季 (jì).

rootFamily.gloss: at the appointed time; when the time comes

第二快.etymology: An ordinal superlative adjectival construction (第二快, dì-èr kuài) formed by placing the ordinal numeral 第二 (dì-èr, 'second') directly before the gradable adjective 快 (kuài, originally 'cheerful; gratified' from 心 'heart' + 夬, which shifted in Tang–Song vernacular to 'sharp' and then 'fast; rapid', replacing Classical 疾 and 速). In Modern Mandarin grammar, attaching an ordinal numeral `第 + N` directly before a monosyllabic adjective (`第 + N + Adj`) productively encodes ranked superlatives ('the N-th most [Adj]'), hence 'second fastest'.

history.meaning: pleased; cheerful; gratified in heart (e.g. 快意)
sharp-edged; fast; rapid; quick
second fastest (in speed or reaction time)

第二快.notes: Exemplifies the productive Mandarin pattern `第 + Number + Adjective` (like 第二大 'second largest', 第二高 'second highest'), which needs no word for 'most' (最).

rootFamily.gloss: joyful; cheerful (preserving the ancient sense of 快)

第二把交椅.etymology: An idiomatic phrase (第二把交椅, dì-èr bǎ jiāoyǐ) centered on 交椅 (jiāoyǐ, 'folding armchair'), literally 'chair with crossed legs' (交 'crossed/intersecting' + 椅 'chair'). Introduced from Central Asian folding stools (胡床) and fitted with a curved back and armrests during the Northern Song dynasty, the 交椅 became the seat of honor for generals, dignitaries, and outlaw chieftains. Popularized by the Ming dynasty classic *Water Margin* (*Shuihu Zhuan*, 水滸傳), where the Liangshan marsh heroes ranked their leadership hierarchy by who sat in the first, second, or third folding armchair in the hall, 'sitting in the second armchair' (坐第二把交椅) became the quintessential idiom for being second-in-command or number two in an organization or industry.

history.meaning: a folding wooden armchair with a curved back used by Song-era elites and commanders
to occupy the second seat of chieftainship in a stronghold (*Water Margin*)
second-in-command; the number-two position of power or industry dominance

morphemes.meaning: classifier for chairs and objects with handles
crossed; intersecting (legs of a folding frame)

第二把交椅.notes: Usually collocates with the verb 坐 (zuò, 'to sit in'): 坐上行业第二把交椅 ('take the #2 spot in the industry') or 稳坐第二把交椅 ('firmly hold the second-in-command seat').

rootFamily.gloss: the #1 seat of authority; top leader (from *Water Margin*)

第二期.etymology: An ordinal numeral-classifier phrase (第二期, dì-èr qī) combining 第二 (dì-èr, 'second') with 期 (qī, originally 'an appointed cycle of time', written with 其 phonetic and 月 'moon/month'). Following the evolution of 期 in modern print and broadcast media to denote a scheduled installment of a periodical, training program, construction project, or non-scripted television program, 第二期 designates 'Issue Two', 'Phase Two', or 'Episode Two' of a variety/reality show.

history.meaning: appointed time; fixed monthly or yearly cycle
Issue Two of a periodical; Phase Two of a project; Episode Two of a variety television show

morphemes.meaning: classifier for scheduled installments, variety show episodes, magazine issues, and project phases

第二期.notes: In television production (*Behind the Scenes* / *幕后之王*), 第二期节目 specifically refers to the second broadcast installment of a variety or competition show, often when ratings stabilize after the premiere (第一期).

rootFamily.gloss: Episode One / Issue One / Phase One
next episode / next issue (of a variety show or magazine)
later stage; post-production (in film and television)

第十四.etymology: Ordinal number phrase combining ordinal prefix 第 + 十四 ('fourteen', from 十 'ten' + 四 'four'), meaning 'the fourteenth'.

history.meaning: the fourteenth (14th)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 第十四 (via 萌典)

第四.etymology: Ordinal number formed with ordinal prefix 第 ('sequence; Bamboo-slip order', bamboo radical 竹 + 弟) + cardinal numeral 四 ('four').

history.meaning: fourth in order
fourth; number four

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 第四

等.etymology: Associative/phono-semantic character combining 竹 ('bamboo slips') + 寺 ('government hall/court', also phonetic děng): aligning bamboo legal documents evenly in court. Extended from 'equal rank, grade, class' and 'et cetera' to the vernacular verb 'to wait (for)'.

history.stage: Old Chinese ('rank, equal') to Tang–Modern Mandarin ('to wait; etc.')
history.meaning: equal rank/grade -> et cetera; to wait

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 等 (via 萌典)

等等.etymology: Reduplicated form of 等: as a verb, tentative reduplication meaning 'wait a moment, hold on'; at the end of a list, 'and so on, et cetera'.

history.meaning: wait a moment; and so forth, et cetera

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 等等 (via 萌典)

答.etymology: Originally written with the bamboo radical 竹 (zhú) atop 合 (hé, 'to join; to match', Old Chinese *kˤəp*), 答 (dá) is defined in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as 'small beans' (小菽也), while the Classical verb 'to reciprocate; to reply' was originally written 荅 (with the grass radical 艸). In Han and Six Dynasties clerical script, 答 (bamboo + 合, evoking bamboo tallies fitting together in response) replaced 荅 for the verbal sense 'to reciprocate a courtesy or gift' (報答) and 'to answer a question' (回答), becoming the standard character for 'answer; reply to'.

history.meaning: to reciprocate (a gift, salute, or action); to respond in kind; to answer
to answer; to reply to a question or letter; solution

morphemes.meaning: to answer; to reply; to reciprocate

答.notes: Often used as a bound root in compounds (回答, 答案), or as a concise transitive verb before objects like 题 (答题 'answer test/quiz questions') or in Q&A headers (问/答 'Q/A').

rootFamily.gloss: answer; solution (to a question or problem)
to promise; to agree; to respond

答不上来.etymology: A negative potential directional verb-complement construction (答不上來, dá bu shànglái) composed of the verb 答 (dá, 'to answer'), the negative potential infix 不 (bu, 'cannot'), and the compound directional-resultative complement 上來 (shànglái, literally 'come up'). In Mandarin spatial metaphor, retrieving words, memories, or answers from the mind to the mouth is conceptualized as bringing them 'upward into view/speech' (as in 说不上来 'cannot put into words' and 想不起来 'cannot recall'); thus 答不上来 vividly expresses being unable to come up with an answer when questioned.

history.meaning: potential directional complement construction indicating inability to bring something up or summon a mental/verbal response
unable to answer; stumped for a reply; at a loss for an answer

morphemes.meaning: upward directional/resultative complement ('up to the surface/speech')

答不上来.notes: The affirmative counterpart is 答得上来 (dá de shànglái, 'able to come up with the answer'); closely parallels 说不上来 ('can't quite say/put one's finger on it') and 背不上来 ('can't recite it from memory').

rootFamily.gloss: unable to say; can't quite put into words
to reply regarding; to account for; to give an explanation

答复.etymology: A coordinative verbal and nominal compound (并列结构) formed from 答 (dá, 'to answer, reply', originally written 荅 'small beans' and borrowed phonetically for 'to match, respond') + 复 (fù, traditionally written 覆 or 復 in this sense, 'to return, reciprocate, reply'). In Literary Chinese administrative and epistolary usage, the two synonymous morphemes combined to mean returning a formal answer to an inquiry or petition.

history.meaning: to match and respond; to return or report back (Classical Chinese)
to reply to a letter, petition, or inquiry (Literary Chinese)
to reply; a formal answer or response (Modern Mandarin)

morphemes.meaning: to return, reply, reciprocate (trad. 覆/復)

答复.notes: More formal and interactive than 回答; frequently used in business, legal, and media production contexts for giving an official response to a proposal or offer (e.g., 给你一个明确的答复).

答应.etymology: Coordinative/resultative verb compound combining 答 ('to reply, answer') + 应 (trad. 應, 'to respond, consent, promise'). Means 'to answer, reply' and 'to agree, promise, consent'.

history.meaning: to reply, answer; to agree, promise

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 答应 (via 萌典)

答案.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正结构) composed of 答 (dá, 'to reply, answer') + 案 (àn, originally 'a wooden serving tray or low table', extended in imperial bureaucracy to 'official desk -> dossier, legal case file, or proposed plan'). Historically denoting a drafted official reply or examination script, it was reinforced in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries alongside Japanese 答案 (tōan) to mean the solution to a question, test, or mystery.

history.meaning: wooden tray or official desk; administrative dossier or verdict (Classical & Literary Chinese)
written examination script or drafted official response (Late Imperial / Meiji Wasei-kango influence)
answer, solution to a problem or question (Modern Mandarin)

答案.notes: Unlike 答复 (a communicative reply to a person), 答案 refers to the objective solution to a question, riddle, test, or existential dilemma (e.g., 寻找答案 'searching for the answer').

策划.etymology: A coordinative compound (并列结构) uniting 策 (cè, originally 'bamboo horse-whip' or 'inscribed bamboo slip', extended in Classical Chinese to 'military stratagem, policy, plan') + 划 (huà, traditionally 劃, 'to incise or score with a blade', hence 'to delineate, mark out, plan'). Attested in Literary Chinese for devising political or military strategies, it has expanded in contemporary Mandarin media into both a verb ('to plan, mastermind') and a noun ('programme proposal' or 'creative planner/producer').

history.meaning: bamboo slip or stratagem; to score with a knife or delineate boundaries (Classical Chinese)
to devise strategies and lay out plans (Literary Chinese)
to plan and produce; programme proposal; creative planner (Modern Mandarin)

morphemes.meaning: to carve, delineate, map out, plan (trad. 劃)

策划.notes: In television and entertainment (*幕后之王*), 策划 refers both to the creative proposal/concept of a show and to the job title of the creative planner (策划人).

cognates.meaning: project proposal, planning document (kikakuan, parallel formation)

策划案.etymology: A modifier-head tri-character compound (偏正结构) formed from the disyllabic modifier 策划 (cèhuà, trad. 策劃, 'strategic planning, creative concept') + the nominal head 案 (àn, originally a wooden table or tray, extended in bureaucratic Chinese to a 'formal dossier, case document, or written proposal'). Coined in modern corporate, advertising, and broadcast production usage to designate a comprehensive written pitch or programme proposal.

history.meaning: to devise a plan + official dossier or written proposal (Literary Chinese components)
written project or programme proposal detailing concept, budget, and execution (Modern Mandarin)

策划案.notes: While 策划 can refer abstractly to planning or a person's role, 策划案 specifically denotes the tangible written pitch deck or proposal document submitted for approval.

cognates.meaning: bamboo tally; to plan, raise funds

筹.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形声字, trad. 籌) composed of the semantic bamboo radical 竹 (zhú) and the phonetic component 壽 (shòu, Old Chinese *du, Middle Chinese dzyuw). Originally denoting small bamboo tally sticks used in antiquity for counting, arithmetic, and pitch-pot games (投壶), it underwent verbal extension in Classical Chinese to mean 'to reckon with tallies -> to calculate, devise strategies' (as in 运筹帷幄), and in modern Mandarin 'to gather or raise funds and resources'.

history.meaning: bamboo counting tally or pitch-pot arrow; to reckon, calculate, strategize (Classical Chinese)
to plan, arrange, or raise funds and supplies (Late Imperial Literary Chinese)
to raise (funds), plan, prepare; chip or token (Modern Mandarin)

morphemes.meaning: bamboo counting tally; to reckon, plan, raise resources (trad. 籌)

筹.notes: In media and business contexts, 筹 as a verb most often collocates with money or resources (筹钱, 筹资 'to raise capital'), while in idioms like 拔得头筹 ('win the first tally') it retains its ancient 'tally/prize token' sense.

rootFamily.gloss: to plan as a whole, coordinate

cognates.meaning: to prepare and plan in advance

筹备.etymology: A coordinative/sequential compound verb (并列结构, trad. 籌備) formed from 筹 (chóu, trad. 籌, 'to reckon with bamboo tallies, plan, raise resources') + 备 (bèi, trad. 備, originally 'a quiver full of arrows', hence 'to make ready, prepare completely, equip'). Emerging in late Qing administrative prose and early modern Mandarin, it combines strategic calculation with practical readiness to mean planning and preparing a major undertaking in advance.

history.meaning: to calculate with tallies + to make fully ready (Classical Chinese roots)
to plan and make preliminary arrangements for an institution or event (Late Imperial / Early Republican Chinese)
to prepare and plan a project, event, or production (Modern Mandarin)

morphemes.meaning: to reckon, plan, raise resources (trad. 籌)
to prepare, make ready, equip (trad. 備)

筹备.notes: Unlike 准备 (general everyday preparation), 筹备 implies large-scale, multi-stage logistical and financial preparation for major events, weddings, companies, or television shows (e.g., 筹备新节目).

筹备期.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正结构, trad. 籌備期) built from the disyllabic verbal modifier 筹备 (chóubèi, 'to plan and prepare') + the bound nominal head 期 (qī, originally 'an appointed time or cycle of the moon', hence 'period, phase, stage'). A standard modern administrative and film/television production term denoting the pre-production phase prior to filming or launch.

history.meaning: appointed time, stipulated cycle, fixed date (Classical Chinese)
preparatory or pre-production phase of a project or show (Modern Mandarin)

morphemes.meaning: to calculate, plan, raise resources (trad. 籌)

筹备期.notes: In film and television production, 筹备期 specifically refers to the pre-production stage (script development, casting, budgeting, set building) before 开机 (start of principal photography) and 制作期 (production).

签.etymology: Phono-semantic character (trad. 籤 / 簽) combining semantic 竹 ('pointed bamboo slip') + phonetic 佥 (僉, qiān). Originally a thin bamboo tally or divination lot inscribed with a name or mark, whence the verb 'to sign one's name, endorse'.

history.stage: Han–Tang ('bamboo slip/label') to Modern Mandarin ('to sign, label')
history.meaning: inscribed bamboo slip -> label, lot; to sign one's name

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 签 (via 萌典)

签个字.etymology: A separable verb-object construction (离合词扩展式, trad. 簽個字) expanding the verb-object compound 签字 (qiānzì, 'to sign one's name') by inserting the unstressed general classifier 个 (ge, trad. 個, originally 'a single stalk of bamboo', grammaticalized into a universal individual classifier) before the nominal object 字 (zì, 'written character, name'). In Mandarin grammar, inserting 个 between verb and object bounds the action as a quick, single, casual event ('put down a quick signature').

history.meaning: to inscribe one's name on an official slip or document (Song–Ming Vernacular & Administrative Chinese)
to jot down a signature, sign one's name quickly or casually (Modern Mandarin)

morphemes.meaning: to sign, inscribe on a slip (trad. 簽)
single unit; casual/bounded action marker (trad. 個)

签个字.notes: Adding 个 softens imperatives in workplace interactions: asking a director or executive 请您签个字 ('Could you just give this a quick signature?') sounds much more polite and less abrupt than 请签字.

rootFamily.gloss: to sign one's name; signature, autograph

签名.etymology: Verb-object compound combining 签 (trad. 簽, 'to sign, inscribe on a slip or document') + 名 ('one's name'). Means 'to sign one's name' or 'a signature, autograph'.

history.meaning: to sign one's name; signature, autograph

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 签名 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to sign one's name (ký tự / ký tên)

签字.etymology: A verb-object compound (动宾结构, trad. 簽字) composed of 签 (qiān, trad. 簽, originally 'sharp bamboo slips or labels inserted into bundles of scrolls for identification', extended in Song–Ming bureaucracy to 'to write one's name or endorsement on a label/document') + 字 (zì, 'written character, personal name'). Because 签字 is structurally a separable verb-object phrase, aspect particles and modifiers are placed between the two characters (e.g., 签了字, 签完字).

history.meaning: bamboo slip, label, or tag attached to documents (Middle & Literary Chinese)
to inscribe one's name or cipher on official files (Song–Qing Administrative Chinese)
to sign one's name on a contract, bill, or treaty (Modern Mandarin)

morphemes.meaning: bamboo label; to sign, endorse (trad. 簽)

签字.notes: Compare 签字 and 签名: 签字 emphasizes the legal or administrative act of signing to authorize a contract or bill, whereas 签名 can refer either to the act of signing or to a celebrity's autograph (索要签名).

rootFamily.gloss: signature, autograph; to sign one's name

签字函.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正结构, trad. 簽字函) combining the verb-object compound 签字 (qiānzì, 'to sign one's name; signed') as an attributive modifier with the classical nominal head 函 (hán, originally an ideogram depicting an arrow or object inside a receptacle, meaning 'case, wooden envelope', and by extension in Literary Chinese 'formal letter, epistle, official correspondence'). Used in modern corporate, legal, and media administration for a signed letter of confirmation or authorization.

history.meaning: box, envelope, or formal epistle enclosed in a case (Classical & Literary Chinese)
signed letter of authorization, confirmation, or intent (Modern Mandarin)

morphemes.meaning: envelope; formal letter or official correspondence

签字函.notes: The classical morpheme 函 survives in modern business and entertainment law as a productive suffix for formal correspondence, alongside 邀请函 (invitation letter) and 律师函 (lawyer's cease-and-desist letter).

签收.etymology: Serial verb compound combining 签 (trad. 簽, 'to sign one's name') + 收 ('to receive, accept delivery'). Means 'to sign for the receipt of a package or letter'.

history.meaning: to sign for receipt (of mail or goods)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 签收 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to sign a contract or treaty

签约.etymology: A verb-object compound (动宾结构, trad. 簽約) formed from 签 (qiān, trad. 簽, 'to sign one's name') + 约 (yuē, trad. 約, originally 'to bind with silk cords', extended in Classical Chinese to 'a binding covenant, treaty, or contract', here serving as a bound compression of 合约 or 契约). It functions both as a separable verb ('to sign a contract', e.g., 签了约) and as an attributive modifier ('contracted, under contract').

history.meaning: to bind with cord; covenant, alliance, sworn agreement (Classical Chinese)
to sign a treaty or commercial/employment contract (Modern Mandarin)

morphemes.meaning: to sign, inscribe one's name (trad. 簽)
to bind; covenant, contract, agreement (trad. 約)

签约.notes: In the entertainment industry, 签约 often refers specifically to signing a talent management or recording contract (e.g., 跟经纪公司签约), and its antonym for terminating a contract is 解约.

签约歌手.etymology: A four-character modifier-head nominal compound (偏正结构, trad. 簽約歌手) composed of 签约 (qiānyuē, 'having signed a contract; under contract') modifying 歌手 (gēshǒu, 'singer, vocalist'). 歌手 itself is formed from 歌 (gē, 'song; to sing') + the agentive suffix 手 (shǒu, literally 'hand', used since Tang–Song Chinese to denote a person skilled in a craft or activity, reinforced by Japanese 歌手 kashu).

history.meaning: to chant or sing + hand or specialist practitioner (Classical & Medieval Chinese)
recording artist or vocalist officially signed to a record label or agency (Modern Mandarin)

morphemes.meaning: hand; agentive suffix for a skilled practitioner

签约歌手.notes: Contrasts in the music industry with 独立音乐人 (indie musician) or amateur contestants; becoming a 签约歌手 is the primary prize of many television singing competitions.

签约艺人.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正结构, trad. 簽約藝人) combining the attributive modifier 签约 (qiānyuē, 'under contract') with 艺人 (yìrén, trad. 藝人, 'performing artist, entertainer'). 艺 (trad. 藝, originally 'to plant', extended in Classical Chinese to the Six Arts 六艺 or refined skills) + 人 ('person') meant a skilled artisan or scholar in pre-modern texts, before narrowing in modern Chinese (alongside Japanese 芸能人/芸人) to actors, singers, and media personalities.

history.meaning: person accomplished in the Six Arts, divination, or technical crafts (Classical Chinese)
stage performer, folk artist, or entertainer (Early Modern Chinese)
entertainer or celebrity under an agency management contract (Modern Mandarin)

签约艺人.notes: In Chinese showbiz, 艺人 is the umbrella industry term covering actors, idols, singers, and variety personalities managed by a talent agency (经纪公司).

cognates.meaning: to sign and conclude a treaty (seitei, rare Sino-compound)
to sign and conclude (a treaty or agreement)

签订.etymology: A coordinative/resultative verbal compound (并列/动结结构, trad. 簽訂) formed from 签 (qiān, trad. 簽, 'to sign one's name') + 订 (dìng, trad. 訂, originally 'to deliberate upon,议定, or collate and fix a text', extended to 'to agree upon, conclude, draw up'). While 签 denotes the physical act of signing, 订 expresses the binding legal result of settling and finalizing the terms of a contract or treaty.

history.meaning: to deliberate and settle; to revise and fix a text (Classical & Literary Chinese)
to sign and officially conclude a treaty, contract, or agreement (Modern Mandarin)

morphemes.meaning: to settle, agree upon, conclude (trad. 訂)
