组织.notes: Notice the striking parallel between East Asian and European metaphor: just as French/English 'tissue' and 'text' come from Latin texere ('to weave'), 组织 originally meant 'braiding and weaving' before becoming both 'biological tissue' and 'institutional organization'.

rootFamily.gloss: to form, to make up, to compose

cognates.meaning: gentleman, man of high social standing and polite manners

绅士.etymology: A coordinative/modifier-head compound of 绅 (shēn, trad. 紳, 'the wide ceremonial silk sash worn around the waist by scholar-officials, with hanging ends upon which tablets or notes were inscribed') and 士 (shì, 'scholar, retainer, cultivated man of status'). In Ming and Qing China, 紳士 referred to the local landed gentry and retired degree-holding officials; during the Meiji era in Japan and late Qing in China, the term was adopted to translate the English social ideal of 'gentleman'.

history.meaning: ceremonial silk sash of an official (紳) and cultivated scholar-retainer (士)
local degree-holding gentry and retired officials (the shenshi class)
gentleman; chivalrous, well-mannered (via Meiji Japanese 紳士 shinshi alignment with English 'gentleman')

morphemes.meaning: ceremonial silk girdle/sash worn by officials; gentry (trad. 紳)

绅士.notes: In colloquial modern Mandarin, 绅士 is often used predicatively with 很 (hěn) as an adjective meaning 'chivalrous, gentlemanly, gallant' (e.g., 他表现得很绅士 'he acted very much like a gentleman', 绅士风度 'gentlemanly demeanor').

细.etymology: Phono-semantic character 细 (細), combining the silk radical 纟 (糸, 'fine silk filaments') + phonetic 田 (tián / Old Chinese *lˤiŋ), meaning 'fine, thin, slender, minute, careful'.

history.meaning: fine silk thread -> thin, minute, detailed
thin, slender, fine, meticulous

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 细 (via 萌典)

细小.etymology: Coordinate compound adjective joining 细 (細, 'thin, fine, minute') + 小 ('small, tiny').

history.meaning: tiny, fine and small, trivial

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 细小 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: minor details, particulars; small points of conduct

细节.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound composed of 细 (xì, trad. 細, originally 'fine silk thread', hence 'minute, small, subtle') and 节 (jié, trad. 節, 'knot or node of bamboo', which divides a bamboo stalk into segments; hence 'joint, section, item, moral principle'). In Han dynasty histories (such as the Shiji and Book of Han), 細節 meant 'minor points of etiquette or trivial scruples' (contrasted with 大節 'fundamental moral integrity'); in modern Mandarin, it shifted to the neutral analytical sense of 'specific details or particulars'.

history.meaning: minor points of etiquette or petty matters of conduct (vs. 大節 major moral principle)
small divisions, intricate parts of a narrative or artwork
details, particulars, fine points (of a plan, production, or story)

morphemes.meaning: fine silk thread; thin, minute, tiny (trad. 細)
bamboo node; joint, segment, item (trad. 節)

细节.notes: Commonly appears in idioms and professional production expressions such as 细节决定成败 ('the details determine success or failure') and 抠细节 (kōu xìjié, 'obsess over / nitpick and polish every tiny detail').

终于.etymology: Disyllabic adverb grammaticalized from Classical Chinese 終於 ('to end at, culminate in'), combining 终 (終, 'end of a skein of thread, conclusion, finally') + 于 (於, 'at, in').

history.meaning: to come to an end in
at last, finally, in the end

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 终于 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: conclusion, termination, bringing to an end
to conclude, to terminate, final end

终结.etymology: A coordinative compound uniting two silk-knotting metaphors: 终 (zhōng, trad. 終, whose Oracle Bone and Bronze script forms depict a skein of thread with knotted ends to prevent unraveling, later reinforced with the silk radical 糸 and phonetic 冬; 'the end of a thread, conclusion, death') and 结 (jié, trad. 結, 'to tie a knot, to finish off'). Attested in Han through Tang Literary Chinese for bringing an affair or cycle to a definitive close.

history.meaning: the knotted end of a silk skein (終) and to tie a knot (結)
to come to a close, to conclude a text, karmic cycle, or historical affair
to bring to a permanent end, to terminate; conclusion

morphemes.meaning: knotted end of a thread; end, finish, conclusion (trad. 終)
to tie a knot; to conclude, to settle (trad. 結)

终结.notes: Carries a dramatic, definitive register ('to terminate, put an end to once and for all') compared to the everyday 结束 (jiéshù); it is also used for the series finale of a show or novel (大终结) and in 终结者 ('The Terminator').

rootFamily.gloss: from beginning to end, all along, throughout
to end, to finish, to conclude

绊倒.etymology: A verb-complement phrase combining 绊 (bàn, 'to stumble, to entangle', written with the silk radical 纟 and 半 originally for animal hobbles) and 倒 (dǎo, 'to fall over'). It vividly describes tripping over an obstacle and falling.

history.meaning: to trip and fall

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 绊倒

cognates.meaning: past experience, career history; to go through

经历.etymology: A coordinative verbal/nominal compound combining 经 (jīng, trad. 經, from 糸 'silk' + 巠 phonetic 'underground water currents', originally 'the longitudinal warp threads on a loom', hence 'to pass through lengthwise, to traverse') and 历 (lì, trad. 歷, depicting feet 止 passing through a row of grain/trees 麻, 'to pass one by one through space or time'). Attested since the Pre-Qin and Han periods for passing through places or events, and later used both as a verb ('to go through') and a noun ('what one has lived through').

history.meaning: to pass through places, seasons, or celestial positions one by one
to experience personally; also an administrative title ('Registrar') in Yuan–Qing government offices
to go through, to undergo; personal experience or life/career history

morphemes.meaning: warp threads; to pass through, to undergo (trad. 經)
to pass through one by one, to traverse in time or space (trad. 歷)

经历.notes: Crucial learner distinction: 经历 refers to the specific events, trials, or career stages one has lived through (and functions as both a verb and a noun: 经历了很多困难 'went through many hardships'), whereas 经验 (jīngyàn) is a noun meaning the practical skill or know-how gained from those events.

rootFamily.gloss: to pass by, to go through; process; by way of

cognates.meaning: ordinary, regular, recurring (as in 経常利益 'ordinary profit')

经常.etymology: A coordinative compound of two Classical Chinese synonyms for invariable constancy: 经 (jīng, trad. 經, 'the lengthwise warp threads on a loom', which remain fixed and taut while the shuttle moves back and forth, hence 'constant rule, invariable norm') and 常 (cháng, originally 'lower skirt or ceremonial banner', extended in Pre-Qin philosophy to 'eternal, unchanging principle'). In Literary Chinese, 經常 meant 'unchanging standard' or 'regular operating expenses'; in modern Mandarin, it grammaticalized into a high-frequency temporal adverb meaning 'often, frequently'.

history.meaning: invariable norm, constant moral or institutional principle (warp and constant)
routine, regular, ongoing (especially of fiscal revenues and expenditures)
often, frequently, regularly; day-to-day, routine

morphemes.meaning: warp threads; constant rule, regular norm (trad. 經)

经常.notes: Primarily used as an adverb before verbs ('often, frequently': 他经常加班 'he often works overtime'), it retains its older adjectival sense ('regular, routine, day-to-day') in formal expressions like 经常性开支 ('recurring/routine expenses').

经济.etymology: An ancient contraction of the four-character Confucian political maxim 经世济民 (jīng shì jì mín, trad. 經世濟民) or 经邦济世: 经 (jīng, trad. 經, 'to arrange the warp threads on a loom; to order and govern the state') and 济 (jì, trad. 濟, 'to ford a river; to relieve, to aid the people'). Attested from the Jin and Sui–Tang dynasties (e.g., Wang Tong's Wenzhongzi) in the sense of 'statecraft and public administration', it was adopted by Meiji Japanese thinkers (経済 keizai) to translate English 'economy' and 'political economy', and re-entered late Qing Mandarin as a graphic return loan.

history.form: 經濟 (jīngjì, short for 經世濟民)
history.meaning: ordering the realm and relieving the people; statecraft and governance
political economy, economic system, finances (calquing English 'economy')
economy, financial dealings, personal finances; economical, thrifty

morphemes.meaning: to set warp threads; to govern, to manage the world (trad. 經)
to cross a river; to aid, to relieve the people (trad. 濟)

经济.notes: A prime homophone trap in media and business Chinese: 经济 (jīngjì, with water radical 氵 in 济) means 'economy, finances, financial dealings' (经济条件 'financial standing', 经济纠纷 'financial dispute'), whereas 经纪 (jīngjì, with silk radical 纟 in both characters) means 'brokerage, talent management'.

rootFamily.gloss: to manage, to operate a business
to relieve, to provide financial aid or succor

经理.etymology: Compound originally meaning 'to manage and put in order' (as warp threads on a loom and veins in jade), combining 经 (經, 'warp threads of a loom, to govern, manage') + 理 ('to polish jade along its natural grain, administer'); used in modern Chinese as a noun for 'manager, director'.

history.meaning: to govern, administer, put in order
manager, director; to manage

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 经理 (via 萌典)

morphemes.meaning: jade grain, to put in order

经纪.etymology: A coordinative compound drawn directly from ancient silk-weaving technology: 经 (jīng, trad. 經, 'the main lengthwise warp threads on a loom') and 纪 (jì, trad. 紀, 'the leading end or tie-thread that separates, counts, and keeps silk skeins from tangling'). In Pre-Qin classics (such as the Guoyu and Book of Rites), 經紀 meant 'the warp and guide-threads of order; to regulate and manage affairs'. During the Tang–Song commercial revolution, 'managing affairs between parties' specialized into commercial brokerage, and in modern entertainment Chinese it denotes 'talent management and agency representation'.

history.meaning: warp threads and silk-sorting guide threads; guiding principles of order; to manage affairs
to act as a commercial middleman; market broker or trade agent
brokerage (finance/real estate); talent management and artist representation in showbiz

morphemes.meaning: warp threads on a loom; to manage, to regulate (trad. 經)
silk thread-end that orders strands; rule, to put in order (trad. 紀)

经纪.notes: Notice that both characters have the silk radical 纟 (经纪): the metaphor is that an agent or broker organizes complex human and commercial threads like the warp (经) and sorting-thread (纪) on a loom. Always distinguish it in writing from its exact homophone 经济 ('economy/finances').

经纪人.etymology: A modifier-head agentive noun formed by attaching the personal suffix 人 (rén, 'person, agent') to 经纪 (jīngjì, trad. 經紀, originally 'warp and guide-threads on a loom; to manage affairs', and from the Tang–Song era onward 'commercial middleman or broker'). Attested in Ming and Qing commercial vernacular alongside 牙人 (yárén, 'licensed market broker'), 經紀人 was modernized in the twentieth century to translate 'commission broker' (in real estate, insurance, and securities) and 'talent manager / artist's agent' in entertainment and sports.

history.meaning: market middleman or trade broker who negotiates transactions for a commission
commercial broker (stocks, insurance, real estate) or theatrical agent
talent manager, artist's agent; licensed commercial broker

morphemes.meaning: brokerage, talent management (lit. 'warp and guide-threads', trad. 經紀)

经纪人.notes: In the Chinese entertainment industry, a 经纪人 combines the roles of what Hollywood separates into a 'talent agent' (who procures deals and auditions) and a 'personal manager' (who oversees daily scheduling, PR, and image), whereas day-to-day on-set errands are handled by an 艺人助理 ('artist's assistant').

经纪公司.etymology: A modern modifier-head nominal compound joining 经纪 (jīngjì, trad. 經紀, 'brokerage, talent management', from the classical silk-weaving metaphor of warp 經 and strand-ordering thread 紀) with 公司 (gōngsī, originally 'public office' in Classical Chinese, used in the Qing dynasty Canton trade for the British East India Company as a 'joint/publicly managed firm', and generalized for 'corporation, company'). Coined in late twentieth-century Greater China media and commercial usage to designate a talent agency or brokerage firm.

history.meaning: commercial brokerage (經紀) and chartered trading company or corporation (公司)
talent agency, artist management company; brokerage firm

经纪公司.notes: In Chinese showbiz, signing with a talent agency is expressed as 签约经纪公司 (qiānyuē jīngjì gōngsī), while terminating one's agency representation—often a major plot point in industry dramas—is 解约 (jiěyuē).

经纪合同.etymology: A modifier-head legal and entertainment compound combining 经纪 (jīngjì, trad. 經紀, 'talent management, brokerage', from classical loom warp 經 and guide-thread 紀) and 合同 (hétong, literally 'joined together as one', which originated in Tang–Yuan commercial practice where a contract was written across two halves of paper stamped at the seam so the two tallies could be matched together to verify authenticity). Together they denote a binding agency or talent-management contract.

history.meaning: commercial brokerage (經紀) and tally-matched written contract (合同)
brokerage contract; talent-agency representation contract (演艺经纪合同)

morphemes.meaning: contract, written agreement (originally tally halves matched together)

经纪合同.notes: Takes the classifier 份 (fèn, for documents/contracts in duplicate): 签一份经纪合同 ('sign a talent-agency contract'). In Taiwan and Hong Kong, 经纪合约 (jīngjì héyuē) or 经理人合约 is also frequently used.

经纪方.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound formed from 经纪 (jīngjì, trad. 經紀, 'talent management, brokerage', from classical warp 經 and guide-thread 紀) and the productive legal/organizational suffix 方 (fāng, originally 'two boats lashed side by side; direction, side, party'). Patterned on contractual terms such as 甲方 ('Party A') and 制作方 ('the production side'), it designates the talent agency or management team as a negotiating party in industry dealings.

history.meaning: brokerage/management (經紀) and side, direction, or party (方)
the management side, the artist's agency (as a contracting or negotiating party)

morphemes.meaning: side, party (in a negotiation, contract, or production)

经纪方.notes: In television and film negotiations, 经纪方 ('the artist's management side') is typically juxtaposed with 制作方 or 剧方 ('the production side'), 平台方 ('the streaming platform side'), and 品牌方 ('the brand/sponsor side').

经纪部.etymology: A modifier-head organizational compound combining 经纪 (jīngjì, trad. 經紀, 'talent management, brokerage', from classical loom warp 經 and sorting thread 紀) with 部 (bù, with the city/territory radical 阝, originally 'administrative subdivision, military cohort, or government ministry' in Han imperial governance, and in modern corporate structure 'department, division'). It denotes the in-house talent-management department of an entertainment conglomerate or production company.

history.meaning: brokerage/management (經紀) and administrative division or cohort (部)
talent-management department (or brokerage division in a financial firm)

经纪部.notes: Many large Chinese entertainment companies house both a 制作部 ('production department', which makes shows) and a 经纪部 ('talent-management department' or 艺人经纪部, which signs and manages actors and singers), often creating internal negotiations over casting.

经过.etymology: Compound verb and noun combining 经 (經, 'to pass through like warp threads, undergo') + 过 (過, 'to pass by, cross over').

history.meaning: to travel or pass through
to pass by, go through; process, course of events; through (prep.)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 经过 (via 萌典)

经验.etymology: A coordinative compound of 经 (jīng, trad. 經, 'warp threads; to pass through, to undergo') and 验 (yàn, trad. 驗, from 馬 'horse' + 僉 phonetic, used in Han Chinese for 'to examine, to verify by practical effect or proof'). Attested in Eastern Han philosophical and medical prose (such as Wang Chong's Lunheng) meaning 'practical verification or tested efficacy', 経験 (keiken) was chosen by Meiji Japanese philosophers to translate Western philosophical and empirical 'experience' (German Erfahrung / English experience) and re-entered modern Mandarin as a return loan.

history.meaning: to verify through personal observation; tested efficacy (especially of medical remedies)
empirical or practical experience (translating English 'experience' / German 'Erfahrung')
experience, practical know-how, lessons learned from practice

morphemes.meaning: warp threads; to pass through, to undergo (trad. 經)
to test, to verify, to examine by effect (trad. 驗)

经验.notes: Unlike Japanese 経験 (which can be used as a verb with する), Mandarin 经验 is strictly a noun meaning 'practical know-how or accumulated wisdom' (工作经验 'work experience', 经验丰富 'richly experienced'); to express the verb 'to experience/go through', use 经历 (jīnglì) or 体验 (tǐyàn).

rootFamily.gloss: to go through, to experience; past experience
to experience for oneself, personal taste/trial

绑.etymology: Phono-semantic verb combining the silk/cord radical 纟 (semantic: tying with thread or rope) + phonetic 邦 (*bāng*). It is the everyday Mandarin verb for tying herbs into a bundle, fastening parcels with twine, or binding sticks together.

morphemes.meaning: tie; bind with cord or string

history.meaning: tie or bind with rope or string
tie; bind

绑架.etymology: A coordinative/serial verbal compound formed from 绑 (bǎng, trad. 綁, from 糸 'silk/rope' + 邦 bāng phonetic, emerging in Song–Yuan vernacular for 'to tie up with ropes, to truss behind the back') and 架 (jià, originally 'wooden frame or rack', extended in vernacular Chinese to 'to prop up under the arms and carry off forcibly', as in 架走). Coalescing in late Qing and Republican Chinese alongside 绑票 ('to seize a hostage as a ransom ticket'), it means 'to kidnap, to abduct by force'.

history.meaning: to tie up with cords (綁) and to prop up or carry off forcibly on a frame/under the arms (架)
to seize and truss up a hostage for ransom or coercion; to abduct
to kidnap, to abduct; figuratively, to hold hostage (e.g., moral or emotional blackmail)

morphemes.meaning: to tie up with ropes, to bind (trad. 綁)
wooden frame; to prop up and carry off by force

绑架.notes: Beyond literal criminal abduction, 绑架 is widely used metaphorically in contemporary media and public discourse for coercion or blackmail, especially in 道德绑架 (dàodé bǎngjià, 'moral kidnapping / guilt-tripping') and 舆论绑架 ('trial or coercion by public opinion').

rootFamily.gloss: to kidnap for ransom (lit. 'tie up as a pawn ticket')
to tie up, to bundle together (also 'bundled sale')

绒布.etymology: Composed of 绒 (róng, 'fluff, down, fine hair') and 布 (bù, 'cloth'). 绒 features the silk radical 纟 and historically referred to fine, downy fabrics like wool or velvet pile. The term perfectly describes the plush lining used in antique jewelry boxes.

history.meaning: flannel; velvet cloth

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 绒布

cognates.meaning: to tie a knot, to bind, to conclude, to settle accounts
to tie a knot, to form, to conclude or settle
to tie a knot, to unite, to conclude or settle

结.etymology: A monomorphemic phono-semantic character (trad. 結) composed of 糸 ('silk thread') and 吉 (jí, Old Chinese *klliɡ, phonetic). Its primary sense in Oracle Bone and Classical Chinese is 'to tie a knot in silk or cord'. Because early Chinese record-keeping and tallies relied on knotted cords (結繩記事) and stringing coins together in tied bundles, 'tying off the knot' naturally evolved in Ming–Qing commercial vernacular into 'to close out an account, to settle a bill'.

history.meaning: to tie a knot in silk or cord; to bind together; to congeal
to tie off; to conclude a legal case or close out a commercial ledger
to tie, knot; to conclude; to settle (a bill, account, or wages)

morphemes.meaning: to tie a knot; to conclude, to settle a bill or account (trad. 結)

结.notes: In everyday commercial and hospitality contexts, 结 is used transitively for paying a bill or settling wages (e.g., 把账结了 'settle the bill', 结工资 'settle/pay out wages', 日结 'paid daily'). Note that when meaning 'to bear fruit' (开花结果), it is pronounced first tone jiē in standard Mainland Mandarin.

rootFamily.gloss: to pay the bill, to settle accounts
to end, to finish, to conclude

cognates.meaning: to combine, to unite, to integrate

结合.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound joining 结 (jié, trad. 結, 'to tie together in a knot, to bind') and 合 (hé, originally depicting a lid fitting over the mouth of a vessel, hence 'to close together, to join, to unite'). In Classical Chinese (such as the Guoyu and Shiji), 結合 meant 'to form a political/military alliance, to join forces, or to unite in marriage'; in modern Mandarin, reinforced by Sino-Japanese scientific and philosophical usage (結合 ketsugō), it means 'to combine, to integrate, or to link together'.

history.meaning: to bind together in alliance, friendship, or marriage; to join military forces
chemical bonding, structural union, or conceptual integration
to combine, to unite, to integrate (e.g., theory with practice); romantic/marital union

morphemes.meaning: to tie a knot, to bind together (trad. 結)
to fit together, to join, to unite

结合.notes: Frequently used in structured patterns like 把 A 和 B 结合起来 ('combine A and B together') or 结合实际情况 ('taking actual circumstances into account / combining with reality'), as well as as a literary euphemism for romantic or marital union.

rootFamily.gloss: to settle; to tie a knot

结婚.etymology: A verb-object compound composed of 结 (jié, trad. 結, 'to tie a knot, to contract a bond') and 婚 (hūn, from 女 'woman' + 昏 hūn 'dusk, twilight', because according to the Shuowen Jiezi and Book of Rites, ancient wedding processions fetched the bride at dusk; hence 'marriage, matrimonial alliance'). Literally 'to tie the matrimonial knot', it is attested in Classical Chinese histories (such as the Book of Han) for forming a marriage alliance between families and became the standard modern verb/noun for getting married across East Asia.

history.meaning: to form a matrimonial bond or marriage alliance between two families
civil and personal marriage (standardized in Meiji Japan and Republican China)
to get married, to marry; marriage

morphemes.meaning: to tie a knot, to form a bond (trad. 結)
marriage, matrimony (from 昏 'dusk', when brides were traditionally welcomed)

结婚.notes: Grammar trap for English speakers: 结婚 is a separable verb-object compound (VO), so it CANNOT take a direct object after it (*结婚他 is ungrammatical). Always use 跟/和 (gēn/hé) before the partner: 跟他结婚 ('marry him') or 他们结婚了 ('they got married').

rootFamily.gloss: marriage, matrimony (as an institution or state)

结实.etymology: Originally a verb-object phrase 結實 ('of a plant: to set fruit, bear solid seed/grain', from 结 'to tie, form fruit' + 实 'fruit, solid, full'); with neutral-tone second syllable (jiēshi), lexicalized as an adjective meaning 'sturdy, solid, durable, robust'.

history.meaning: to bear fruit or grain
sturdy, solid, strong, rugged

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 结实 (via 萌典)

结尾.etymology: Compound noun and verb combining 结 (結, 'to tie off a knot, conclude') + 尾 ('tail, end, final section').

history.meaning: ending, conclusion, final part

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 结尾 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: conclusion, finale, after all, in the end
ending, final outcome; after all, ultimately

结局.etymology: Originally a verb-object compound from board games: 结 (jié, trad. 結, 'to tie off, to bring to a close') and 局 (jú, originally 'bent, cramped', extended in Han–Six Dynasties Chinese to 'a game board and the configuration of pieces in weiqi/Go or chess', and hence 'situation, match, dramatic setup'). In Song through Qing weiqi manuals and drama/fiction criticism (such as Jin Shengtan's commentaries), 結局 meant 'closing out the game board' or 'the concluding act of a play', lexicalizing as a noun meaning 'ending, final outcome'.

history.meaning: to bring a game of weiqi (Go) or chess to its endgame conclusion
the structural resolution or final act of a drama, novel, or affair
ending (of a story, drama, or film), final outcome, denouement

morphemes.meaning: to tie off, to conclude, to finish (trad. 結)
game board position; situation, phase, dramatic setup

结局.notes: False-friend alert for learners of Japanese or Korean: whereas Japanese 結局 (kekkyoku) and Korean 결국 (gyeolguk) are used mainly as adverbs meaning 'after all / in the end', Mandarin 结局 is strictly a noun meaning 'ending, finale, final outcome' (e.g., 大结局 'series grand finale', 圆满的结局 'happy ending').

rootFamily.gloss: opening phase (of a game, show, or situation)

结束.etymology: Coordinate verb compound combining 结 (結, 'to tie a knot, wind up') + 束 ('to bind a bundle of wood with cord, tie up'); originally meant 'to tie up one's attire or baggage ready for departure', then 'to conclude, finish, end'.

history.meaning: to bind up garments or luggage
to wind up, finish, conclude, end

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 结束 (via 萌典)

结构.etymology: Coordinative compound (并列结构) of 结 (jié, Traditional 結, Middle Chinese *ket, 'to tie, knot, join together') and 构 (gòu, Traditional 構, Middle Chinese *kuwH, 'to interlock timbers, frame a building'). In Classical Chinese architectural and literary criticism, 結構 originally denoted the physical mortise-and-tenon framing of a timber building and, by extension, the compositional layout of calligraphy or prose; in modern Chinese it broadened to denote abstract system or narrative structure.

history.meaning: to join timbers together; architectural framework (Han–Six Dynasties)
compositional layout of an essay, poem, or calligraphic work (Tang–Qing)
structure, internal setup, or organizational framework

morphemes.meaning: to frame with interlocking timbers, construct

结构.notes: In television and screenwriting (*幕后之王*), frequently collocated as 节目结构 (program structure) or 叙事结构 (narrative structure).

rootFamily.gloss: to conceive a plot or artistic design

结果.etymology: Originally a botanical verb-object phrase 結果 ('to bear fruit', from 结 'to form' + 果 'tree fruit'), reinforced by Buddhist usage (फल phala 'karmic fruit/consequence') to mean 'outcome, result; as a result, in the end'.

history.meaning: to bear fruit -> karmic consequence, outcome
result, outcome (noun); as a result, ended up (conj.)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 结果 (via 萌典)

结论.etymology: Modifier-head or verb-object Sino-Japanese return loan (和制汉语 *wasei-kango* via Japanese 結論 *ketsuron*, coined in the Meiji era to translate English 'conclusion' in logic and law, while building on Classical Chinese roots), composed of 结 (jié, Traditional 結, 'to tie off, bring to a close, settle') and 论 (lùn, Traditional 論, 'discourse, thesis, judgment'). Literally 'the closing thesis that ties up an argument'.

history.meaning: 結 'to tie a knot, conclude a case' and 論 'to discourse, deliberate' as separate Classical lexemes
logical proposition reached at the end of a syllogism or debate (Meiji Japanese)
conclusion, final verdict, official finding

结论.notes: Standardly takes verbs 下 (xià, 'to hand down/reach') or 得出 (déchū, 'to arrive at'), as in 下结论 ('jump to or issue a conclusion').

结过婚.etymology: Separable verb-object compound (离合词,動賓結構) 结婚 (jiéhūn, Traditional 結婚, 'to tie the matrimonial bond') infixed with the experiential aspect marker 过 (guò, Traditional 過, grammaticalized from the verb 'to pass through'). 结 ('to tie, form a bond') governs 婚 (Old Chinese *hmuːn, originally 昏 'dusk', when ancient wedding ceremonies were conducted, later written with the woman radical 女). Because 结婚 is syntactically verb + object, aspect particles must be inserted between 结 and 婚.

history.meaning: to form a marriage alliance between two families
grammaticalization of 過 as an experiential aspect marker between verb and object (Tang–Song vernacular)
to have been married (at least once in one's life)

morphemes.meaning: to tie, contract, form a bond

结过婚.notes: A classic separable verb (离合词): never say *结婚过; aspect markers (过, 了) and complements always split 结 and 婚. In showbiz dramas, ocultar or revealing that an idol 结过婚 is a recurring PR crisis trope.

绕.etymology: From Traditional 繞 (also variant 遶), Middle Chinese *nyewX / *nyewH, Old Chinese *nˤewʔ. A phono-semantic compound (形声) combining the silk radical 纟/糸 (mì, 'thread, cord') with the phonetic 尧 (yáo, Traditional 堯, 'high, mound'). Originally denoting the winding of silk thread around a spool or coiling around an object, it extended in Classical Chinese to moving in a circle, detouring around obstacles, or speaking circuitously.

history.meaning: to wind silk thread around; to coil, twine around (Warring States–Han)
to circle around, make a detour, linger around (as sound in rafters 餘音繞樑)
to circle around, wind, detour; to confuse or speak in circles

morphemes.meaning: to wind thread around, circle, detour

绕.notes: Used both physically (绕路 'take a detour') and figuratively in workplace dialogue (绕弯子 'beat around the bush', 把人绕进去 'confuse someone with convoluted talk').

rootFamily.gloss: to go on a detour, beat around the bush

绕开.etymology: Resultative verb-complement compound (动补结构) formed from the action verb 绕 (rào, Traditional 繞, 'to wind, circle, detour') and the directional/resultative complement 开 (kāi, Traditional 開, 'to open, separate, move away from'). Literally 'to circle so as to move away from', hence to skirt around an obstacle, avoid a sensitive topic, or sidestep a person.

history.meaning: separate verbs 'to detour' and 'to open/part' in Classical Chinese
grammaticalization of 開 as a resultative complement indicating separation or avoidance
to bypass, skirt around, avoid (a topic, obstacle, or person)

morphemes.meaning: resultative complement of separation or moving away

绕开.notes: Compared with 绕过, 绕开 emphasizes steering clear of or avoiding contact with something altogether (e.g., 绕开敏感话题 'steer clear of sensitive topics').

rootFamily.gloss: to bypass, go past an obstacle or authority

绕过.etymology: Resultative/directional verb-complement compound (动补结构) combining 绕 (rào, Traditional 繞, 'to circle, detour') with the directional complement 过 (guò, Traditional 過, Middle Chinese *kwaH, 'to pass across, get past'). Literally 'to detour and pass beyond', evolving from physical navigation around a barrier into a vivid institutional metaphor for going over someone's head or bypassing a gatekeeper in a corporate hierarchy.

history.meaning: to make a detour past a geographical obstacle or city wall
to bypass, go around an obstacle, regulation, or person in the chain of command

绕过.notes: In corporate and media workplace dramas (*幕后之王*), 绕过 + [person/department] specifically means going over someone's head in the reporting chain (e.g., 绕过制作部直接向台长汇报).

rootFamily.gloss: to skirt around, avoid contact with

给.etymology: Phono-semantic character 给 (給), combining silk radical 纟 (糸) + phonetic 合 (hé / *kˤop); in Classical Chinese read jǐ ('to supply, provide amply, suffice'), and in Mandarin vernacular read gěi ('to give; for, to; passive marker').

history.meaning: to supply, furnish, be well-provided
to give, grant; to/for (benefactive); by (passive)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 给 (via 萌典)

给面子.etymology: Verb-object idiomatic phrase (动宾短语) consisting of 给 (gěi, Traditional 給, 'to give, grant') and 面子 (miànzi, 'social face, prestige, standing'). 面 (Middle Chinese *mjienH, 'face, surface') acquired the sociological sense of public prestige and relational respect in Tang–Song vernacular (originally alongside 體面), affixed with the nominalizer 子 (zi). Literally 'to give someone face', i.e., to show deference that upholds another person's social prestige in public.

history.meaning: physical face, countenance, or sense of shame in facing others (Classical Chinese)
social prestige and the vernacular idiom of granting deference to preserve another's standing (Song–Qing vernacular)
to show respect, do someone the honour, accommodate someone out of deference

给面子.notes: Allows pronouns or modifiers to be inserted between 给 and 面子 (e.g., 给足他面子 'give him plenty of face', 不给面子 'snub someone publicly'). Central to Chinese entertainment-industry negotiation.

绝.etymology: From Traditional 絕 (Middle Chinese *dzjwet, Old Chinese *dzot), originally a compound ideograph showing silk threads (糸) being severed by a knife (刀) held by a kneeling person (卩). From its core verbal sense 'to sever, cut off completely', it developed in Classical Chinese into an adjective ('cut off, extreme, unsurpassed') and an emphatic adverb ('utterly, categorically, under any circumstances'), especially before negatives (不, 无, 非).

history.meaning: to sever silk threads; to cut off, terminate, break off relations (Warring States–Han)
unsurpassed, matchless; adverbially 'utterly, categorically' before negation (Han–Tang)
absolutely, by any means (before negation); matchless, brilliant (colloquial predicate)

morphemes.meaning: to sever, cut off; extreme, absolute

绝.notes: As an adverb, 绝 is almost always followed by a negative morpheme (绝不, 绝非, 绝无); in colloquial speech, 绝了! as a standalone predicate means 'that's brilliant / unbelievable!'.

rootFamily.gloss: to refuse, reject (sever and ward off)
to break off relations, sever ties

cognates.meaning: never, by no means (in Sino-Korean expressions)

绝不.etymology: Modifier-head adverbial compound (偏正结构) combining the emphatic degree adverb 绝 (jué, Traditional 絕, Middle Chinese *dzjwet, 'categorically, utterly, with all possibilities severed') and the general negator 不 (bù, Middle Chinese *pjuw, Old Chinese *pə, 'not'). Literally 'severed-ly not', expressing an uncompromising categorical refusal or impossibility.

history.meaning: categorically not, never under any circumstances (attested from Han–Six Dynasties prose onward)
never, under no circumstances, by no means

绝不.notes: Often confused in writing with 决不 (from 决定 'resolutely not'): 绝不 stresses objective or categorical impossibility ('under no circumstances'), while 决不 stresses subjective determination, though modern usage frequently overlaps.

rootFamily.gloss: by no means, anything but (before nouns)

绝对.etymology: Compound originally meaning 'without a matching pair, incomparable, cut off from comparison' (and in Buddhist philosophy translating Sanskrit paramārtha / absolute), from 绝 (絕, 'to sever silk thread, cut off, extreme') + 对 (對, 'paired opposite, counterpart').

history.meaning: beyond comparison, unconditional
absolute; absolutely, definitely

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 绝对 (via 萌典)

绝望.etymology: Verb-object compound (动宾结构) formed from 绝 (jué, Traditional 絕, Middle Chinese *dzjwet, 'to sever, cut off, exhaust') and 望 (wàng, Middle Chinese *mjangH, originally 'to gaze into the distance toward the full moon', hence 'to look forward to, hope'). Literally 'to sever all hope'. Already attested in Classical Chinese texts (*Zhuangzi*, *Shiji*) in the literal verbal sense 'to abandon hope', and reinforced in modern Mandarin as both a stative adjective ('despairing, hopeless') and a noun ('despair').

history.meaning: to cut off or abandon hope of something (attested in *Shiji* and *Hanshu*)
despairing, hopeless; despair (used both as stative verb/adjective and abstract noun)

绝望.notes: To say 'despair of X' or 'lose all hope in X', Mandarin uses the prepositional frame 对……感到绝望 rather than a direct object after 绝望.

统一.etymology: Verb-complement or verb-object compound (动补/动宾结构) of 统 (tǒng, Traditional 統, Middle Chinese *thwongX, 'main silk thread that gathers all strands together; to gather, govern as a whole') and 一 (yī, Middle Chinese *'jit, 'one; into one'). Originally a Classical political term meaning 'to gather the realm into a single polity' (cf. *Gongyang Zhuan* 大一統), it functions in modern Mandarin as a transitive verb ('to unify, standardize'), adjective ('unified'), and adverb ('uniformly, altogether as one').

history.meaning: to gather all feudal states or threads of governance into one sovereign order
to unify, standardize; unified; uniformly, together as a single unit

morphemes.meaning: main silk thread; to gather, unite, govern as a whole

统一.notes: Used adverbially before a verb (e.g., 统一安排 'arrange uniformly/centrally', 统一回复 'give a single collective reply') to indicate centralized action rather than individual handling.

统一口径.etymology: Verb-object four-character collocation (动宾短语) combining the transitive verb 统一 (tǒngyī, Traditional 統一, 'to unify, standardize') with the noun object 口径 (kǒujìng, Traditional 口徑, compounded from 口 'mouth, opening, bore' + 径 'diameter, path'). 口径 was coined in modern technical Chinese to translate 'caliber / bore diameter' of a gun barrel or pipe; by mid-20th-century bureaucratic and media metaphor, 'having the same barrel caliber' came to mean maintaining the exact same official stance, figures, or talking points when speaking to outsiders.

history.meaning: inner diameter or caliber of a cannon barrel, firearm, or vessel opening (late Qing–Republican technical term)
to align talking points, coordinate a single unified story or public statement

统一口径.notes: A staple of PR crisis management, entertainment publicity (*幕后之王*), and corporate communications: 對外統一ロ徑 means ensuring everyone on a team gives reporters the exact same version of events.

rootFamily.gloss: caliber; official stance or line of speech
tone of voice, official narrative tone

统辖.etymology: Coordinative verbal compound (并列结构) uniting two Classical Chinese metaphors of control: 统 (tǒng, Traditional 統, Middle Chinese *thwongX, 'to gather the main silk cord that controls all threads') and 辖 (xiá, Traditional 轄, Middle Chinese *hæwk, originally the iron linchpin inserted into the end of a chariot axle to keep the wheel from coming off, hence 'to secure, govern, hold jurisdiction over'). Together, 'to hold the master cord and the axle linchpin' over subordinate units.

history.meaning: 統 'to gather threads/command' and 轄 'chariot axle linchpin; to control' in Han administrative prose
to exercise imperial, military, or provincial jurisdiction over multiple subordinate commands (Tang–Qing)
to govern, exercise direct authority over multiple departments or units

morphemes.meaning: main cord; to gather, command as a whole
axle linchpin; to control, have jurisdiction over

统辖.notes: High-register administrative verb; in corporate or television network hierarchy, used when an executive producer or vice-president takes direct command over several subordinate divisions.

继续.etymology: Coordinate verb compound combining 继 (繼, 'to splice or connect silk threads end to end, succeed, carry on') + 续 (續, 'to join threads, continue without interruption').

history.meaning: to join threads continuously -> to carry on
to continue, go on, proceed

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 继续 (via 萌典)

续住.etymology: Hospitality verb compound combining 续 ('continue; join a thread; renew', silk radical 纟 + 卖 mài) + 住 ('stay; reside; lodge', person radical 亻 + 主). Literally 'to continue staying', it is the standard inn and hotel term for extending a guest's reservation.

history.meaning: extend one's stay at an inn or hotel

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 续住

cognates.meaning: contract renewal (related Sino-morphemes 続 + 約)

续约.etymology: Verb-object compound (动宾结构) formed from 续 (xù, Traditional 續, Middle Chinese *zjuwk, 'to join silk threads end-to-end, continue, extend') and 约 (yuē, Traditional 約, Middle Chinese *'jak, originally 'to bind with cord', hence 'covenant, pact, contract', here short for 合约 héyuē or 契约 qìyuē). Literally 'to splice/extend a binding pact', i.e., to renew an expiring contract.

history.meaning: 續 'to splice thread, continue' and 約 'to bind with rope; covenant, treaty' in Classical Chinese
to extend or renew a diplomatic treaty or commercial contract (late Qing–modern legal/commercial usage)
to renew a contract (especially in entertainment, sports, or employment)

续约.notes: Core showbiz and talent-agency vocabulary (*幕后之王*): pairs with 签约 (qiānyuē, 'sign a contract'), 解约 (jiěyuē, 'terminate a contract'), and 违约 (wéiyuē, 'breach a contract').

绯闻.etymology: Modifier-head compound (偏正结构) combining 绯 (fēi, Traditional 緋, Middle Chinese *phj+j, 'crimson, bright pink/scarlet silk', formed with the silk radical 纟/糸 and phonetic 非) and 闻 (wén, Traditional 聞, Middle Chinese *mjun, 'that which is heard; news, rumor'). Modeled on English 'scarlet' or 'pink' news (compare 桃色新闻 'peach-colored news') and popularized via Hong Kong, Taiwanese, and Japanese media usage, where crimson/pink evokes blush, romance, and illicit passion.

history.meaning: crimson or dark-red silk worn by Tang-dynasty officials above the fifth rank
romantic or sexual rumor/scandal involving public figures (20th-century media coinage)

绯闻.notes: First syllable is pronounced *fēi* (1st tone, 'crimson'), though many native speakers colloquially pronounce it *fěi*; specifically denotes romantic/dating rumors (e.g., 传绯闻 'be the subject of dating rumors', 绯闻男友 'rumored boyfriend'), whereas 丑闻 (chǒuwén) means a serious moral or criminal scandal.

绳.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining the silk/cord radical 纟 ('twisted fiber') + 黾 (*mǐn/shéng*). Attested since the *Classic of Poetry* and *Book of Changes* for twisted hemp cord, plumb lines, and kitchen twine.

history.meaning: twisted hemp cord; carpenter's chalk line
string; cord; rope

绳子.etymology: Formed by 绳 (shéng, 'rope, cord') and the nominal suffix 子 (zi). 绳 uses the silk radical 纟, indicating early cordage made from twisted plant fibers or silk. The suffix 子 grounds it as a commonplace, everyday noun.

history.meaning: rope
rope; string

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 绳子

维持.etymology: Coordinative compound (并列结构) of 维 (wéi, Traditional 維, Middle Chinese *jwij, 'heavy corner-rope of a net or carriage canopy; to tie, hold together') and 持 (chí, Middle Chinese *drj+j, 'to grasp with the hand, uphold, sustain'). Attested in Classical Chinese (*Hanfeizi*, *Hanshu*) in the sense of 'holding together and supporting the state or moral order', and reinforced in modern Mandarin to mean preserving a state, relationship, or operation from collapsing.

history.meaning: to tie together and uphold; to support and protect the state or social order (Warring States–Han)
to maintain, keep going, preserve an existing state or order

morphemes.meaning: staying rope; to tie, hold together
to grasp in the hand, hold up, sustain

维持.notes: Unlike 保持 (bǎochí, keeping a desirable quality like vitality or a high rating), 维持 often implies keeping something going at a baseline level or under strain (e.g., 维持秩序 'maintain order', 维持生计 'make ends meet', 维持现状 'maintain the status quo').

综艺.etymology: Modifier-head portmanteau compound (偏正缩略词) abridged from 综合艺术 (zōnghé yìshù, 'synthetic/composite arts') or 综合游艺 (zōnghé yóuyì, 'variety entertainment'). 综 (zōng, Traditional 綜, Middle Chinese *tsowngH, originally the heddle of a loom that gathers warp threads up and down, hence 'to gather together, synthesize') modifies 艺 (yì, Traditional 藝, Middle Chinese *ngjejH, originally 'to plant crops', extended in Classical Chinese to 'cultivated skill, art'). Coined in 20th-century Chinese broadcasting to translate English 'variety show'.

history.meaning: 綜 'loom heddle; to gather threads' and 藝 'to plant; six noble arts (六藝)' in Classical Chinese

history.form: 綜合藝術 / 綜藝節目
history.meaning: composite stage/broadcast entertainment blending comedy, music, games, and talk (mid-20th century Taiwan/Hong Kong/Mainland television)

morphemes.meaning: to gather warp threads on a loom; comprehensive, composite (short for 综合)
skill, performance art, entertainment (short for 艺术/游艺)

综艺.notes: The central genre of *幕后之王*: 综艺 can refer either to the genre itself or to an individual variety show (一档综艺 'a variety program', 真人秀综艺 'reality variety show', 综艺感 'a celebrity's knack for being funny and engaging on variety TV').

绿.etymology: Phono-semantic character 绿 (綠), combining silk radical 纟 (糸, 'dyed silk') + phonetic 录 (彔 lù), originally denoting 'greenish-yellow dyed silk' and since antiquity the standard word for 'green'.

history.meaning: green-dyed silk, green
green

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 绿 (via 萌典)

绿叶.etymology: Determinative botanical compound of 绿 ('green', silk radical 纟 + phonetic 录 *lù*, originally 'green-dyed silk') + 叶 ('leaf', grass radical 艹 + 枼, pictograph of flat leaves on a branch). Used both literally for fresh green foliage and proverbially in 红花配绿叶 ('red flowers set off by green leaves').

history.meaning: fresh green leaves
green leaf

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 绿叶

绿色.etymology: Compound noun combining 绿 (綠, 'green') + 色 ('color, hue').

history.meaning: the color green; eco-friendly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 绿色 (via 萌典)

缓慢.etymology: Coordinate compound adjective joining 缓 (緩, 'slack thread, unhurried, gentle, slow') + 慢 ('unhurried, leisurely, slow').

history.meaning: slow, unhurried, gradual

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 缓慢 (via 萌典)

缓解.etymology: Coordinative verbal compound (并列结构) of 缓 (huǎn, Traditional 緩, Middle Chinese *hwanX, formed with the silk radical 纟/糸, 'slack or loose cord; slow, to relax tension') and 解 (jiě, Middle Chinese *kæjX, originally 'to separate an ox's horn with a knife', hence 'to untie a knot, loosen, relieve'). Literally 'to slacken a taut cord and untie a knot', metaphorically easing pressure, pain, or a crisis.

history.meaning: 緩 'slack silk cord; to loosen, delay' and 解 'to untie a knot, dissect' in Classical Chinese
to relieve, ease, alleviate (pressure, conflict, symptoms, or crisis)

morphemes.meaning: slack cord; to loosen, relax, slow down

缓解.notes: Frequently collocates with abstract nouns of tension: 缓解压力 ('relieve stress/pressure'), 缓解矛盾 ('ease a conflict'), or 缓解危机 ('alleviate a crisis').

rootFamily.gloss: to relax, ease tension,缓和气氛 (ease the atmosphere)
to解除, remove, lift (a ban or crisis)

编.etymology: From Traditional 編 (Middle Chinese *pen, Old Chinese *pˤen), a phono-semantic character combining the silk radical 纟/糸 (mì, 'cord') and phonetic 扁 (biǎn, 'flat bamboo slips'). Originally referring to binding split bamboo slips (简牍) together in sequence with silk or hemp cords to form a book roll (cf. 韋編三絕), it naturally extended to 'weaving/braiding', then to 'compiling, editing, writing a script', and colloquially to 'fabricating or making up a story out of whole cloth'.

history.meaning: to bind bamboo writing slips in order with silk cords; to plait or weave (Warring States–Han)
to compile, edit, compose literary works or annals (Han–Qing)
to weave; to edit, compile, write (scripts); colloquially, to make up or fabricate (a story or excuse)

morphemes.meaning: to bind bamboo slips with cord; to weave, edit, fabricate

编.notes: In television production (*幕后之王*), 编 spans both formal professional titles (编导 'writer-director', 编剧 'screenwriter', 主编 'chief editor') and punchy colloquial speech (瞎编 'make things up', 编故事 'spin a yarn').

缘由.etymology: Coordinative compound (并列结构) of 缘 (yuán, Traditional 緣, Middle Chinese *jwen, originally 'decorative silk hem along the edge of a garment', extended under Buddhist and Classical influence to *pratyaya* 'karmic condition, causal link, along/by reason of') and 由 (yóu, Middle Chinese *juw, 'from, starting point, cause, origin'). Together, the two roots reinforce each other to mean the underlying causal chain or story behind an event.

history.meaning: 緣 'garment hem; to follow along' and 由 'origin, path from which something arises' in Classical Chinese
causal condition, underlying reason or full backstory of an affair (Tang–Song vernacular and Buddhist prose)
cause, reason, underlying story behind something

morphemes.meaning: origin, source, cause from which something stems

缘由.notes: Slightly more literary and narrative in flavor than 原因 (yuányīn): 缘由 often refers to the human backstory or sequence of circumstances behind why someone acted a certain way (e.g., 追问事情的缘由).

rootFamily.gloss: cause, reason, reason for an action

缠.etymology: A verb featuring the silk radical 纟 and the phonetic 廛 (chán). It originally denoted winding threads onto a spool or silk from a cocoon. It metaphorically and literally describes anything tightly wound, bound, or entangled.

history.meaning: to wind; to spool
to wrap; to entangle

缩写.etymology: Compound verb and noun combining 缩 (縮, 'to draw back, shrink, contract, abridge') + 写 (寫, 'to write').

history.meaning: to abbreviate, abridge; abbreviation, acronym

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 缩写 (via 萌典)

缺.etymology: Phono-semantic/associative character 缺, combining the earthen-vessel radical 缶 ('pottery jar') + 夬 (guài, 'to break, notch'), originally meaning 'a cracked or chipped earthenware vessel', hence 'to lack, be short of, be missing; gap'.

history.meaning: chipped pottery vessel -> flaw, gap, deficiency
to lack, be short of, be absent

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 缺 (via 萌典)

缺乏.etymology: Coordinative compound (并列结构) of 缺 (quē, Middle Chinese *khjwet, composed of 缶 'earthenware jar' + 夬 'to break open', originally 'a chipped or cracked pottery vessel', hence 'incomplete, deficient, lacking') and 乏 (fá, Middle Chinese *bjop, 'exhausted, in want, short of supplies', graphically an inverted的正 in oracle/bronze script). Together they form a transitive verb meaning to lack or be deficient in an essential quality or resource.

history.meaning: 缺 'broken earthenware vessel; gap, defect' and 乏 'destitute, exhausted of supplies' in Classical Chinese
to be short of provisions, funds, or talent (post-Han literary and administrative prose)
to lack, be short of, be deficient in (abstract qualities, experience, or resources)

缺乏.notes: Prefers abstract two-character objects such as 缺乏经验 ('lack experience'), 缺乏创意 ('lack creativity'), or 缺乏诚意 ('lack sincerity'), whereas 缺 alone is common with concrete everyday items (缺钱, 缺人).

rootFamily.gloss: to be short of,缺少 (lack in quantity)

缺少.etymology: Coordinate verb compound combining 缺 ('to lack, be deficient') + 少 ('to be few, be short of').

history.meaning: to lack, be short of, miss

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 缺少 (via 萌典)

缺德.etymology: Verb-object compound (动宾结构) functioning as a stative adjective: 缺 (quē, Middle Chinese *khjwet, 'to lack, be deficient in') governing 德 (dé, Middle Chinese *tok, Old Chinese *tˤək, 'moral virtue, inner rectitude, karmic merit'). Originating in late imperial popular morality and karmic beliefs—where cruel or deceitful acts were thought to deplete one's store of moral merit (損德 / 缺德) and harm one's descendants—it became a vivid colloquial adjective meaning 'mean-spirited, unscrupulous, lacking basic human decency'.

history.meaning: 缺 'deficient' and 德 'virtue, moral power' as separate Classical concepts
to be deficient in moral merit; wicked, unscrupulous, mean-spirited (Ming–Qing vernacular)
lacking basic morals or decency, mean-spirited, unethical

缺德.notes: Colloquial and strongly evaluative: often appears in 缺德事 ('a scummy/unethical deed') or 干这种事太缺德了 ('doing something like that is really low/mean-spirited'). In media controversies, yellow-press paparazzi or cyberbullies are often condemned as 缺德.

rootFamily.gloss: character, moral standing (of a person or artist)

罐.etymology: Phono-semantic character 罐, combining the earthen-vessel radical 缶 ('pottery jar') + phonetic 雚 (guàn), denoting a 'jar, jug, pot, tin can' and used as a classifier for canned or jarred goods.

history.meaning: earthenware water jar, pitcher
jar, pot, tin/can; classifier for cans or jars

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 罐 (via 萌典)

罐子.etymology: Derived from 罐 ('earthenware or ceramic jar', fired-clay radical 缶 + phonetic 雚 *guàn*) + nominal suffix 子 (-zi). Used for kitchen storage crocks, ceramic canisters for sugar and salt, and glass jars.

history.meaning: pottery or porcelain storage jar
jar; canister

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 罐子

网.etymology: From Traditional 網 (Middle Chinese *mjwangX, Old Chinese *maŋʔ). The earliest form 罔 in oracle bone script was a direct pictograph of a knotted hunting or fishing net; when 罔 was borrowed for the negative 'not, none', the phonetic 亡 was added, and subsequently the silk radical 糸 was added to create 網. In modern Mandarin, the ancient simplified variant 网 (recovering the pictographic criss-cross mesh inside a frame) was standardized, and its meaning expanded from fishing/hunting nets to broadcasting networks and the internet.

history.meaning: knotted cord net for catching fish, birds, or game (*Shijing*, *Yijing*)
web, mesh, imperial dragnet of law (法網) or interpersonal connections (Han–Qing)
net, web; broadcasting network, computer network, the internet

网.notes: Productive hub morpheme for virtually all digital-age compounds in Mandarin (上网 'go online', 全网 'across the entire internet', 官网 'official website').

rootFamily.gloss: to go online, surf the internet

网上.etymology: Noun-postposition locative compound (方位短语/处所词) combining 网 (wǎng, Traditional 網, 'net, network, the internet') with the bound localizer 上 (shàng, Middle Chinese *dzyangX, 'on, upon, within the sphere of'). Modeled on spatial expressions like 街上 ('on the street') or 报上 ('in the newspaper') and calquing the English spatial metaphor 'on the net / online' in the 1990s.

history.meaning: literally 'upon a fishing net or spiderweb' in pre-modern Chinese
online, on the internet (late 20th-century digital coinage)

morphemes.meaning: locative postposition meaning 'on, in the medium of'

网上.notes: Functions both as a place noun (在网上看到 'see on the internet') and as an attributive modifier before nouns or verbs (网上购物 'online shopping', 网上热议 'heatedly discussed online').

rootFamily.gloss: to go online, access the internet

cognates.word: vọng hữu (rare; usually cư dân mạng)

网友.etymology: Modifier-head nominal compound (偏正结构) combining 网 (wǎng, Traditional 網, short for 网络 'the internet') and 友 (yǒu, Middle Chinese *hjuwX, originally two hands 又 clasping together in oracle bone script, 'friend, fellow, associate'). Coined in the late 1990s alongside the rise of Chinese bulletin boards (BBS) and chatrooms on the model of 笔友 (bǐyǒu, 'pen pal') and 书友 (shūyǒu, 'book-lover/fellow reader').

history.meaning: friend, companion, associate sharing a common pursuit (Classical Chinese)
online friend or acquaintance met in a chatroom; general internet user / netizen commenting online (1990s–present)

morphemes.meaning: net, the internet (short for 网络)

网友.notes: Has two distinct senses depending on context: (1) a personal friend met online (见网友 'meet an online friend in person'), and (2) the collective 'netizens / online commenters' in media reporting (广大网友纷纷表示... 'netizens everywhere commented...').

cognates.meaning: netizen (often 네티즌 or 누리꾼, Sino-Korean 망민 rare)

网民.etymology: Modifier-head nominal compound (偏正结构) formed from 网 (wǎng, Traditional 網, short for 互联网 'the internet') and 民 (mín, Middle Chinese *mjin, 'the people, citizenry, populace'). Coined in the late 1990s as a direct morphological calque of English *netizen* (*net* + *citizen*), on the analogy of 公民 (gōngmín, 'citizen') and 市民 (shìmín, 'urban resident').

history.meaning: the common people, subjects, populace (Classical Chinese)
internet users as a demographic or online public (late 1990s calque of 'netizen')

网民.notes: More sociological and statistical in register than 网友: official reports and ratings analyses say 中国网民规模 ('the scale of China's internet population'), whereas entertainment news about social-media reactions prefers 网友.

网站.etymology: Modifier-head nominal compound (偏正结构) combining 网 (wǎng, Traditional 網, short for 网络 'network, internet') and 站 (zhàn, Middle Chinese *dræmH, originally 'to stand upright', extended during the Mongol Yuan dynasty via Mongolian *jam* to mean a postal relay station 驛站, and in modern times a transit station or operational hub). Coined in the 1990s to render English *website* (literally 'network station/site').

history.meaning: to stand; postal relay station (驛站) along imperial highways (Yuan–Qing dynasties)
website, internet portal or site (1990s digital coinage)

网站.notes: In Chinese media and television (*幕后之王*), 视频网站 ('video-streaming websites/platforms' like iQIYI, Youku, Tencent Video) are the major rivals and partners of traditional satellite TV stations (电视台).

cognates.word: 網羅 / ネットワーク (kanji roots 網 + 絡)

网络.etymology: Coordinative nominal compound (并列结构) of 网 (wǎng, Traditional 網, 'knotted fishing or hunting net') and 络 (luò, Traditional 絡, Middle Chinese *lak, 'unreeled silk fibers, net-like mesh, or branching collateral vessels 經絡 in traditional Chinese medicine'). Originally a Classical verb-noun compound meaning 'tocrisscross or encompass like a mesh of cords and vessels', it was adopted in modern Chinese to translate English *network* (telecommunications, television broadcasting, and computer networks) and, by metonymy, the internet itself.

history.meaning: tocrisscross, intertwine, or encompass like a net of cords (*Hou Hanshu*, Buddhist scriptures)
telecommunications/broadcasting network; computer network; the internet (20th–21st century)

morphemes.meaning: silk fiber mesh, branching vessels, to connect

网络.notes: Note the Mainland standard pronunciation *wǎngluò* (4th tone on 络); in Taiwan, 網路 (*wǎnglù*, literally 'net-paths') is the standard term for the internet. Used extensively as a modifier: 网络综艺 (简称网综, 'online streaming variety show').

rootFamily.gloss: to contact, get in touch with
arteries and veins; thread of thought or plotline (脉络)

罗盘.etymology: A compound of 罗 (luó, 'to gather, net') and 盘 (pán, 'plate, tray'). Originally referencing the complex geomantic compasses of Feng Shui that 'gathered' directional energies on a dial, it became the standard term for a navigational compass.

history.meaning: geomantic compass
compass

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 罗盘

罪责.etymology: Coordinative nominal compound (并列结构) of 罪 (zuì, Middle Chinese *dzwojX, replacing the older Qin character 辠 because 辠 resembled 皇 'emperor'; composed of 罒 'net' + 非 'wrong', i.e., 'caught in the net of the law for wrongdoing, crime, offense') and 责 (zé, Traditional 責, Middle Chinese *tsæk, originally 'debt, obligation', hence 'responsibility, accountability, blame'). Together they denote moral or legal culpability for a fault.

history.meaning: 罪 'offense, crime' and 責 'debt, duty, reproof' in Classical legal and philosophical texts
culpability, blame, or punishment for an administrative or legal fault (Tang–Qing legal/official prose)
blame, culpability, responsibility for a fault or wrongdoing

罪责.notes: Formal register; commonly appears in expressions about accountability during workplace or legal fallout, such as 难辞其咎/难逃罪责 ('hard to escape blame') or 推卸罪责 ('shirk culpability').

署名.etymology: Verb-object compound (动宾结构) formed from 署 (shǔ, Middle Chinese *dzyoX, originally 'to arrange, place in position, inscribe officially on a tablet or document') and 名 (míng, Middle Chinese *mjeng, 'personal name'). Already attested in Han–Six Dynasties bureaucratic practice for an official inscribing his name on a memorial or register, and reinforced in modern legal, publishing, and media usage for signing a document or receiving formal byline/screen credit.

history.meaning: to inscribe one's official name on a bamboo/wooden tablet or state memorial (Han–Tang bureaucracy)
to sign one's name to a treaty, petition, or published article; authorial byline or screen credit

morphemes.meaning: to write down officially, inscribe, sign; public office

署名.notes: In film, television, and publishing (*幕后之王*), 署名权 (shǔmíngquán, 'right of attribution / screen credit') is a fiercely contested copyright issue for screenwriters and producers. Also a separable verb (署上自己的名字).

羊毛.etymology: Nominal compound combining 羊 ('sheep, goat', oracle-bone pictograph of a horned ram's head) + 毛 ('hair, fur, fleece, wool').

history.meaning: sheep's wool, fleece

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 羊毛 (via 萌典)

羊毛毡.etymology: Three-character compound combining 羊毛 ('sheep's wool') + 毡 (氈 / 毡, 'felted wool fabric, felt rug', formed from 毛 'hair/wool' + phonetic 占 zhān).

history.meaning: wool felt

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 羊毛毡 (via 萌典)

美.etymology: Ancient graph attested on oracle bones showing a person (大) wearing a tall ram-horn or feathered headdress (羊), signifying 'fine, handsome, stately' (later explained in Shuowen Jiezi as 羊 + 大 'a big fat sheep is delicious/good').

history.meaning: adorned, fine, beautiful, good
beautiful, pretty, good; the Americas (short for 美洲/美国)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 美 (via 萌典)

美好.etymology: The adjective '美好' (měihǎo, beautiful, fine) simply pairs two positive characters: '美' (beautiful, pleasing) and '好' (good, well). While '美' often refers to aesthetic beauty and '好' to functional or moral goodness, their combination creates a comprehensive term for something that is both visually pleasing and emotionally uplifting. It is frequently used to describe abstract concepts like memories, futures, or ideals, emphasizing a sense of perfection and harmony. The word has deep roots in classical poetry and literature.

history.meaning: pretty

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 美好

美妙.etymology: Coordinate compound adjective joining 美 ('beautiful, fine') + 妙 ('wonderful, subtle, exquisite').

history.meaning: exquisitely fine, wonderful
wonderful, splendid, melodious, lovely

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 美妙 (via 萌典)

美式.etymology: A modern modifier-head nominal and adjectival compound formed from 美 (měi, abbreviation of 美国 Měiguó, 'the United States of America', itself a phonetic-semantic rendering of 'America' where 美 means 'beautiful') and 式 (shì, 'style, pattern, model, standard', from Old Chinese *hljək, originally a carpenter's rule or ritual standard). Literally 'American pattern/style'.

history.meaning: model, rule, ritual pattern, standard
America; the United States of America (phonetic transcription)
American-style, in the American manner (also short for Americano coffee)

美式.notes: In contemporary urban and media speech, 美式 used alone as a noun almost universally refers to an Americano coffee (美式咖啡), while as an attributive modifier it pairs directly with nouns like 美式英语 (American English) or 美式幽默 (American humor).

美誉.etymology: A Classical Chinese modifier-head nominal compound combining 美 (měi, 'fine, admirable, noble, beautiful', written with 羊 'sheep' above 大 'large') and 誉 (yù, simplified from 譽, 'fame, praise, renown', a phono-semantic character with 言 'speech/words' and phonetic 與 yǔ). Attested in Han and Six Dynasties prose for an honorable name praised by others.

history.meaning: noble renown, admirable reputation praised in speech
high praise, fine reputation, honorary title

美誉.notes: Typical of formal journalism, PR announcements, and entertainment awards commentary; it almost always appears in the frame 享有……的美誉 ('to enjoy the fine reputation of being...').

群.etymology: From Old Chinese *gʷən (Middle Chinese *gjun), a phono-semantic graph combining semantic 羊 (yáng, 'sheep') with phonetic 君 (jūn, *kʷən, 'lord'). Originally denoting a flock of sheep (typically three or more in the Shuowen Jiezi), it generalized in Classical Chinese to any herd, crowd, or social multitude, and subsequently grammaticalized into a collective classifier for groups of people or animals.

history.meaning: flock of sheep; herd; multitude of peers
group, crowd (collective classifier); online chat group

群.notes: Beyond its standard role as a classifier (一群人, 'a crowd of people'), 群 functions as a standalone noun in modern workplace and media Chinese for a WeChat or messaging group chat (e.g., 拉个群 'start a group chat', 群发 'mass-message a group').

rootFamily.gloss: background actor, extra (short for 群众演员)

群策群力.etymology: A four-character Classical Chinese parallel coordinative idiom (ABAC pattern: 群策 + 群力) attested in Yang Xiong's Han-dynasty philosophical treatise Fayan (法言·重黎): '群策屈群力' ('collective counsel bends collective strength'). Here 群 (qún, 'the multitude, everyone') modifies both 策 (cè, 'bamboo slip, stratagem, plan') and 力 (lì, 'physical or organizational strength'), meaning to unite the counsel and effort of the entire team.

history.meaning: collective strategy commands collective strength (Yang Xiong, Fayan)
to pool everyone's wisdom and efforts toward a common goal

群策群力.notes: Frequently invoked by producers, directors, and executives in production meetings to rally a team around a difficult project; near-synonymous with 集思广益, which emphasizes gathering ideas, whereas 群策群力 covers both brainstorming (策) and execution (力).

翻.etymology: Phono-semantic character 翻, combining 羽 ('feathers, wings') + phonetic 番 (fān), originally meaning 'to fly back and forth, wheel in flight', hence 'to turn over, flip, rummage through, translate'.

history.meaning: to wheel in flight -> to turn over, reverse
to turn over, flip (pages), cross over, translate

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 翻 (via 萌典)

翻来覆去.etymology: A vernacular four-character directional-oppositional idiom structured as V1-来-V2-去, combining near-synonyms 翻 (fān, 'to turn over, flip, flutter') and 覆 (fù, 'to overturn, capsize, invert') with complementary deictic directional complements 来 (lái, 'hither, this way') and 去 (qù, 'thither, that way'). Attested in Song–Yuan vernacular texts (such as Zhuzi Yulei) for tossing and turning in bed or repeating an action endlessly.

history.meaning: turning over this way and that; tossing and turning repeatedly
over and over again; tossing and turning; saying or doing the same thing repeatedly

翻来覆去.notes: Used both physically for insomnia (翻来覆去睡不着, 'tossing and turning unable to sleep') and figuratively for rehashing the same few points or revising a script/proposal endlessly. Note that 覆 retains its traditional character here rather than merging into 复 in standard idiom orthography, though both are seen.

cognates.meaning: churning rivers and overturning seas; great upheaval

翻江倒海.etymology: A parallel verb-object four-character idiom (VO1 + VO2: 翻江 + 倒海) combining 翻 (fān, 'to turn upside down, churn') + 江 (jiāng, 'great river, specifically the Yangtze') and 倒 (dǎo, 'to topple, pour out, upend') + 海 (hǎi, 'the sea'). Originating in Tang–Song literary and Daoist/supernatural narratives describing dragons or immortals stirring up cosmic waters, it evolved in Ming vernacular fiction to describe overwhelming physical, emotional, or social turbulence.

history.form: 翻江攪海 / 翻江倒海
history.meaning: to churn the rivers and upend the seas (of dragons or supernatural powers)
churning violently; in great turmoil (of emotions, nausea, or dramatic upheaval)

翻江倒海.notes: In modern drama and conversation, 翻江倒海 frequently modifies 心里 ('in one's heart', for surging inner turmoil) or 胃里 ('in one's stomach', for violent nausea).

rootFamily.gloss: make a comeback, turn the tables

翻译.etymology: A coordinative and metaphorical compound of 翻 (fān, 'to turn over, flip') and 译 (yì, simplified from 譯, 'to interpret, decode foreign speech', from 言 'speech' + 睪 phonetic). Coined in Six Dynasties and Tang Buddhist sutra-translation circles: as the Song monk Zanning explained in Song Gaoseng Zhuan (宋高僧传), translating Sanskrit into Chinese is like turning over (翻) a piece of brocade—the pattern on both sides is the same, only the orientation of the threads reverses.

history.meaning: to interpret the speech of border peoples (Liji / Zhouli)
to turn over and render Buddhist scriptures from Sanskrit into Chinese
to translate or interpret; translator, interpreter; translation

翻译.notes: Functions as both a verb ('to translate') and a noun meaning either the translated text or the person doing the interpreting (e.g., 请个翻译 'hire an interpreter'). For specifically written vs. oral work, formal contexts distinguish 笔译 (written translation) and 口译 (oral interpretation).

rootFamily.gloss: translated version or film dub/subtitled release

老.etymology: Oracle-bone and bronze ideograph depicting a bent-over elder with long hair leaning on a walking staff, meaning 'old, aged, venerable, experienced, long-standing'.

history.meaning: aged person leaning on a staff -> old, venerable
old, experienced, tough/overcooked; always; friendly prefix

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 老 (via 萌典)

morphemes.meaning: elder with long hair and cane

老东家.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound composed of prefixal modifier 老 (lǎo, 'old, former, previous') and the compound noun 东家 (dōngjia, 'master, host, employer, proprietor'). 东家 derives from Classical Chinese 东道主 ('host on the eastern road', because in traditional courtyard architecture the host's chambers stood on the eastern side while guests stayed on the west). Adding 老 shifts the sense from 'current boss/proprietor' to 'one's former employer, studio, or agency'.

history.meaning: eastern neighbor; household host or master (vis-à-vis western guest/tutor)
shop proprietor, landlord, or master; one's longtime or former master
former employer, previous company, record label, or talent agency

老东家.notes: Ubiquitous in the entertainment, music, and sports industries to refer to an artist's, producer's, or athlete's former agency, TV network, or record label (e.g., 回老东家 'return to one's former studio').

老交情.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 老 (lǎo, 'old, long-standing, time-tested') with 交情 (jiāoqíng, 'friendship, mutual affection formed through association'). Within 交情, 交 (jiāo, originally a pictograph of a person with crossed legs, meaning 'to cross, associate, exchange') modifies or coordinates with 情 (qíng, 'feelings, sentiment, bond'). Thus 老交情 denotes a personal bond built up over many years of acquaintance.

history.meaning: sentiment and bond of mutual acquaintance (attested in Shiji)
long-standing friendship or personal connection

老交情.notes: Often used in professional networking and negotiations (讲老交情, 'appeal to old friendship/ties') when asking a favor or smoothing over business friction in media production.

老人.etymology: Modifier-head noun compound combining 老 ('old, aged') + 人 ('person').

history.meaning: elderly person, aged parents/grandparents

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 老人 (via 萌典)

老地方.etymology: A colloquial modifier-head nominal phrase formed from 老 (lǎo, 'old, habitual, familiar, unchanged') and 地方 (dìfang, 'place, locality', originally a Classical compound meaning 'the square earth' in contrast to round heaven 天圆地方, which shifted in Tang–Song vernacular to 'local region' and then 'spot/place' with neutral-tone second syllable). Literally 'the familiar/usual spot'.

history.meaning: the earth as square (cosmology); local administrative area or region
the usual place, the old familiar haunt or meeting spot

morphemes.meaning: direction, region, place (neutral tone in compound)

老地方.notes: In spoken Mandarin, 老地方见 ('See you at the usual place') is a staple shorthand between close colleagues, friends, or romantic partners who share a regular café, bar, or meeting spot.

老城区.etymology: Three-character compound combining 老 ('old, historic') + 城区 (城區, 'urban district, city area', from 城 'walled city' + 区 'district, area').

history.meaning: old town, historic city district

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 老城区 (via 萌典)

老大.etymology: Formed from the kinship/status prefix 老 (lǎo, an affectionate or respectful prefix used before birth-order ranks since the Tang–Song period) and 大 (dà, 'big, eldest, foremost'). Originally denoting the eldest sibling in a family (ranked before 老二, 老三), it extended via sworn brotherhoods, guild hierarchies, and underworld triads in late imperial China to mean the top leader, chief, or boss of a group.

history.meaning: old and grown up (as in 少壯不努力，老大徒傷悲, 'when old and grown')
eldest child/sibling; guild master, boat captain, or gang leader
eldest sibling; boss, chief, number one in a team or industry

老大.notes: In modern media agencies and startup teams, subordinates often call their team lead or department head 老大 as a warm, informal, loyal form of address ('Boss' / 'Chief'), distinct from the formal 老板 (company owner) or 领导 (institutional superior).

rootFamily.gloss: big brother; gang leader; industry leader

老天.etymology: A vernacular modifier-head compound combining the honorific/familiar prefix 老 (lǎo, 'venerable, ancient') with 天 (tiān, Old Chinese *l'iːn, originally an anthropomorphic pictograph of a great figure with a prominent head/sky above, meaning 'heaven, sky, supreme deity'). By adding 老 (and often 爷 yé, 'grandpa/lord'), popular Chinese religion and everyday speech personified supreme Heaven as a venerable, watchful sky-deity.

history.meaning: the sky; Heaven as supreme cosmic and moral authority
Good Heaven, Old Man Heaven (personified providence and exclamation)
Heaven, providence; 'good heavens!', 'my goodness!'

老天.notes: Used both as a subject in fate expressions (老天不公, 'Heaven is unfair'; 老天眷顾, 'blessed by Heaven') and as a standalone interjection of shock, relief, or exasperation ('My goodness!'). Often expanded to 老天爷 in colloquial speech.

老头.etymology: A vernacular derivative formed from the lexical root 老 (lǎo, 'old, aged', from an ideogram of an elderly person with long hair leaning on a cane) and the nominal suffix 头 (tóu, simplified from 頭, originally 'head', which bleached in Tang–Song vernacular into a noun suffix marking persons or objects with a salient trait, often pronounced in the neutral tone or with erhua 老头儿).

history.meaning: old man, old fellow (colloquial nominalization with -頭 suffix)
old man, old guy (colloquial; often pronounced lǎotóur in northern speech)

morphemes.meaning: nominal suffix for a person or thing (originally 'head')

老头.notes: Colloquial and informal; calling someone 老头 directly to their face can sound disrespectful unless used affectionately for a crusty mentor, father, or husband. For polite reference, use 老人家 or 老先生 instead.

老师.etymology: Compound combining 老 ('venerable, experienced') + 师 (師, 'master, preceptor, model'); attested in Tang–Song times for revered scholars or Zen masters, and in modern Mandarin the standard respectful word for 'teacher'.

history.meaning: venerable scholar, master, examination mentor
teacher, instructor

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 老师 (via 萌典)

老弟.etymology: Affectionate colloquial address formed from the familiar prefix 老 + 弟 ('younger brother').

history.meaning: younger brother; friendly address to a younger man ('my young friend, bro')

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 老弟 (via 萌典)

老方.etymology: A productive Mandarin vocative and referential compound combining the social prefix 老 (lǎo, 'familiar, senior, old') with the Chinese surname 方 (Fāng, originally denoting a square, region, or side, and borne as a lineage surname since the Zhou dynasty). Attested from the Tang dynasty onward (as when poets addressed Bai Juyi or Yuan Zhen with 老 + surname), the pattern [老 + monosyllabic surname] signals collegial familiarity and warmth among peers or toward a senior colleague.

history.form: 老 + 姓 (e.g. 老杜 / 老白)
history.meaning: affectionate or familiar address for a peer or elder by surname
Old Fang (familiar, collegial way to address or refer to someone surnamed Fang)

morphemes.meaning: familiar/senior social prefix before a surname

老方.notes: In Chinese workplaces, addressing a colleague as 老 + Surname (like 老方, 老王, 老张) conveys camaraderie and seniority without the stiff hierarchy of titles, whereas 小 + Surname (小方) is used for younger colleagues.

rootFamily.gloss: Young Fang (address for a junior colleague surnamed Fang)

老板.etymology: Originally written 老版 in southern river-port and theatrical guilds (老 respectful prefix + 板/版 'wooden printing block, shop counter, or rhythmic clapper'), addressing the proprietor or master of an inn, workshop, or troupe; now standard relaxed Mandarin for 'boss' or 'shopkeeper'.

history.meaning: shop owner; troupe master
boss; shopkeeper; innkeeper

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 老板 (via 萌典)

老毛病.etymology: A modifier-head compound of 老 (lǎo, 'old, chronic, recurrent') and 毛病 (máobìng, 'flaw, defect, illness, bad habit'). Significantly, 毛病 originated in Song–Yuan horse-judging jargon: 毛 referred to a horse's coat of hair and 病 to a defect—specifically, swirled or discolored patches of hair (毛旋) believed to betray a horse's hidden physical ailment or temperamental vice, before generalizing to any human illness, technical glitch, or behavioral flaw.

history.meaning: blemish in a horse's coat indicating a hidden defect; flaw or illness
chronic ailment; persistent bad habit or recurring technical glitch

morphemes.meaning: coat hair (originally of a horse, site of a blemish)

老毛病.notes: Commonly paired with the verb 犯 (fàn, 'to have a recurrence of'): 老毛病又犯了 ('The old ailment/bad habit is acting up again'), applicable equally to a stomach ulcer, a machine malfunctioning, or a coworker's habitual lateness.

rootFamily.gloss: have a relapse of an illness; act up again (of a habit)
failing, bad habit, flaw in character

老牌.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 老 (lǎo, 'old, long-standing, time-honored') and 牌 (pái, 'wooden placard, shop signboard, trademark, brand', from semantic 片 'split wood plank' + phonetic 卑). Originating in late Qing and Republican commercial culture (alongside 老字号), where established merchant houses hung carved wooden shop-signs (招牌), 老牌 came to describe a long-established brand and, by extension, any veteran institution, company, or performer.

history.meaning: wooden tablet, official tally, or shop signboard
time-honored commercial brand; veteran, long-established (attributive)

老牌.notes: Functions primarily as a non-predicative adjective (attributive modifier) before nouns in media and business discourse: 老牌制作公司 ('a veteran production company'), 老牌歌手 ('a veteran singer'), or 老牌劲旅 ('a long-established powerhouse team').

老老实实.etymology: An AABB reduplicated intensive adverbial/adjectival form derived from the disyllabic adjective 老实 (lǎoshi, 'honest, guileless, well-behaved, docile'). In 老实, 老 ('seasoned, steady') coordinates with 实 (shí, simplified from 實, 'full, solid, genuine, sincere', originally a roof 宀 filled with cowries and goods 貫). Reduplicating AB to AABB (老老实实) intensifies the sense to 'thoroughly honest, obediently, without any tricks or fuss'.

history.meaning: steady and genuine; honest, guileless (attested in Song–Yuan vernacular)

history.form: 老老實實 / 老老实实
history.meaning: strictly honestly, obediently, staying in line without tricks or complaint

老老实实.notes: As an adverb before a verb (e.g., 老老实实待着 'stay put obediently without causing trouble'; 老老实实交代 'confess honestly'), it often carries a warning or pragmatic tone: 'do it properly and don't try anything clever'. Note that in the AABB form, the final 实 regains its full second tone (lǎolǎoshíshí) in standard reading.
