老花镜.etymology: Three-morpheme compound of 老花 ('presbyopia; age-related farsightedness', literally 老 'advancing years' + 眼花 'blurred close vision') + 镜 ('optical lens; spectacles', metal radical 钅 + 竟 *jìng*). It is the warm everyday term for reading glasses.

history.meaning: convex spectacles for reading; reading glasses
reading glasses

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 老花镜

老街.etymology: Modifier-head noun compound combining 老 ('old, historic, long-established') + 街 ('street, thoroughfare').

history.meaning: old street, historic commercial lane

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 老街 (via 萌典)

老规矩.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound pairing 老 (lǎo, 'old, established, customary') with 规矩 (guīju, 'rules, established custom, etiquette'). 规矩 is a classic coordinative metonymy from Warring States texts (such as Mencius: '不以规矩，不能成方圆'): 规 (guī) is the carpenter's compass used to draw circles, and 矩 (jǔ) is the carpenter's L-square used to draw right angles. Together they lexicalized as 'standards and rules', and with 老 as 'the usual practice'.

history.meaning: carpenter's compass and square; moral or institutional standard (Mencius)
established custom, the old rule, the usual practice or arrangement

morphemes.meaning: carpenter's square (for right angles); standard (neutral tone in compound)

老规矩.notes: Frequently used as a standalone conversational phrase—按老规矩办 ('Let's do it according to the usual rule') or 老规矩，我请客 ('Usual rule—my treat')—to invoke an unspoken agreement or industry convention.

老远.etymology: Colloquial intensive compound combining intensifying prefix 老 ('very, quite') + 远 (遠, 'far, distant').

history.meaning: very far away, from a long way off

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 老远 (via 萌典)

老陈.etymology: Colloquial form of address combining the familiar prefix 老 ('old, familiar') + the Chinese surname 陈 (陳, originally the name of the ancient Zhou-era state of Chen in modern Henan).

history.meaning: Old Chen (friendly address to someone surnamed Chen)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 老陈 (via 萌典)

考核.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative verb/noun compound combining 考 (kǎo, originally 'aged/deceased father', extended in Zhou–Han administrative texts to 'examine, inspect, verify') and 核 (hé, originally 'fruit pit/stone', hence 'to get to the core, verify facts rigorously', historically interchangeable with 覈). In imperial civil service administration (考课/考核), it denoted the periodic audit of officials' actual achievements against their titles.

history.meaning: to audit and verify the administrative performance of imperial officials
performance evaluation, assessment, examination; to evaluate (staff or trainees)

考核.notes: A core workplace and media-industry term for KPI reviews, probation evaluations, and trainee assessments (e.g., 绩效考核 'performance evaluation', 年终考核 'year-end review', 考核期 'probation/evaluation period'). Unlike 考试 (an academic test), 考核 evaluates practical competence and job results.

rootFamily.gloss: audit, examine and approve (a budget or program)
inspect, make an on-site investigation or study tour

考虑.etymology: A coordinative mental-verb compound uniting 考 (kǎo, 'to examine, probe, inquire into') and 虑 (lǜ, simplified from 慮, 'to ponder, deliberate, plan carefully', a phono-semantic character with 思 'thought/heart' below phonetic 虍 hū). Attested in Han and Tang historical prose for carefully examining circumstances and weighing future consequences before making a decision.

history.meaning: to examine and ponder carefully; thoughtful deliberation
to consider, think over, weigh (an offer, proposal, or option)

考虑.notes: In business and showbiz negotiations, 我再考虑考虑 ('Let me think it over some more') is frequently a polite, face-saving way to stall or softly decline an offer without saying 'no' outright.

考进.etymology: A productive Mandarin verb-resultative compound formed from the action verb 考 (kǎo, 'to take an examination, be tested') and the directional/resultative complement 进 (jìn, simplified from 進, 'to advance, enter into', originally depicting a bird 隹 stepping forward 辶). Literally 'to enter (an institution) by passing an entrance examination'.

history.meaning: to gain admission into an academy or official rank via examination
to pass the entrance exam and be admitted into (a school, conservatory, or company)

考进.notes: Takes the institution directly as its object (e.g., 考进传媒大学 'test into Communication University', 考进电视台 'pass the exam to join the TV station'), and accepts potential infixes: 考得进 ('able to test in') and 考不进 ('unable to pass the exam to get in'). Near-synonymous with 考上 and 考入.

rootFamily.gloss: pass an exam to enter (a school or post)

考量.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative compound of 考 (kǎo, 'to examine, inspect, verify') and 量 (liáng, 'to measure with a vessel, weigh, estimate, gauge'). Attested in Six Dynasties and Tang administrative and Buddhist texts (such as the Book of Sui 隋书) for measuring officials' merits or weighing pros and cons, it remained common in Taiwanese, Hong Kong, and literary Mandarin before surging across Mainland professional and media discourse.

history.meaning: to examine and measure; to assess merits or weigh factors (Sui Shu)
to weigh carefully, evaluate; strategic consideration or factor (noun/verb)

考量.notes: More formal and analytical than 考虑: whereas 考虑 is everyday 'thinking something over', 考量 implies weighing strategic trade-offs (e.g., 出于商业考量 'out of commercial considerations', 综合考量 'weigh comprehensively') and is used heavily by executives and producers.

cognates.meaning: to test, put to the test; ordeal

考验.etymology: A coordinative compound of 考 (kǎo, 'to examine, inspect, test') and 验 (yàn, simplified from 驗, originally 'a fine horse' from 馬 + 僉 phonetic, which in Han legal and medical texts came to mean 'to verify by concrete proof, inspect, prove effective'). Attested in Tang–Song administrative prose for verifying credentials and testing officials, it broadened in modern Mandarin (reinforced by Japanese 考験) to mean a severe trial or test of character, loyalty, or durability.

history.meaning: to inspect and verify official credentials or factual evidence (New Book of Tang)
trial, ordeal, test of mettle or quality; to put to the test

考验.notes: Applies to testing people, relationships, or capabilities through real-world hardship or crisis rather than paper exams—commonly collocating with 经受住考验 ('withstand the test/ordeal') or 时间会考验一切 ('time will test everything').

rootFamily.gloss: experiment, test; to conduct an experiment

而.etymology: Originally an oracle-bone and bronze pictograph of facial whiskers/beard on the chin and cheeks, borrowed very early by rebus for the grammatical conjunction 而 ('and, yet, but, while').

history.meaning: whiskers (pictograph) -> conjunction 'and, yet, while'
and, yet, whereas, in order to

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 而 (via 萌典)

而且.etymology: Compound coordinating/progressive conjunction joining 而 ('and, furthermore') + 且 ('moreover, besides, also').

history.meaning: and moreover, furthermore, not only ... but also

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 而且 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: nothing more, merely (literary kanbun particle: nomi)

而已.etymology: A Classical Chinese sentence-final compound particle lexicalized from the conjunction 而 (ér, 'and then, and at that point', originally a pictograph of whiskers/beard used as a phonetic loan for *njə) followed by the verb 已 (yǐ, 'to stop, cease, come to an end'). Literally 'and there it stops'—hence 'and nothing more, that is all, merely'. Heavily attested in the Analects and Mencius (e.g., '夫子之道，忠恕而已矣').

history.meaning: and there it stops; that is all, nothing more (Analects, Mencius)
that's all, nothing more, merely (sentence-final limiting particle)

而已.notes: Placed at the very end of a clause, often paired with an earlier 只是, 不过, or 仅仅 ('merely... and nothing more'): 我只是随便问问而已 ('I was just asking casually, that's all'). It downplays the stakes or scale of an action.

rootFamily.gloss: have no choice, cannot help it (cannot stop)

而是.etymology: A compound adversative-affirmative conjunction formed from the Classical connective 而 (ér, 'and yet, but rather') and the copula 是 (shì, originally a demonstrative 'this' and adjective 'right/correct' in Old Chinese *djek, which grammaticalized into the copula 'to be' during the Han dynasty). Together, 而是 literally means 'but rather it is [the case that]...', correcting a negated premise.

history.meaning: and this is / and is right (two separate grammatical words in Classical prose)
rather, but instead (compound conjunction in correlative 'not A, but B' constructions)

而是.notes: Almost always paired with a preceding negation in the correlative frame 不是 A，而是 B ('not A, but rather B'). Learners should avoid using 而是 after a positive clause (where 而且 'moreover' or 反而 'on the contrary' is needed instead).

耐心.etymology: The noun '耐心' (nàixīn, patience) combines '耐' (to endure, to bear) and '心' (heart, mind). '耐' features the '寸' (inch) radical, historically related to enduring rules or punishments, while '心' represents the inner psychological state. '耐心' refers to the mental capacity to endure difficulties, delays, or annoyance without complaining. It became a standardized psychological term in modern Chinese to describe the virtue of patience. It is commonly used both as a noun and as an adjective in daily life.

history.meaning: impatient

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 耐心

耳朵.etymology: Derived anatomical noun from 耳 ('ear', oracle-bone pictograph of the outer pinna) + 朵 (originally a drooping flower bud on a tree 木, added as a noun suffix by visual analogy with the hanging earlobe). In Mandarin, disyllabic 耳朵 replaced monosyllabic 耳 in nearly all everyday spoken contexts.

history.meaning: earlobe; outer ear
ear

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 耳朵

耳机.etymology: A modern 20th-century modifier-head nominal neologism combining 耳 (ěr, Old Chinese *njəʔ, originally a pictograph of a human ear) and 机 (jī, simplified from 機, originally 'crossbow trigger mechanism' or 'loom', which became the productive modern suffix for mechanical and electronic devices). Coined in early telecommunications and radio broadcasting for a telephone/radio earpiece, and later applied to studio headphones and wireless earbuds.

history.meaning: ear + mechanical trigger/loom (separate Classical morphemes)
telephone or telegraph receiver earpiece; headphones, earphones, in-ear monitors

耳机.notes: In television and live music production (*Behind the Scenes*), 耳机 covers both studio monitoring headphones (监听耳机) worn by sound engineers and producers, and in-ear monitors (耳返) worn by singers and hosts on stage. Takes the classifier 副 (一双/一副耳机) for a pair, or 只 for a single earbud.

rootFamily.gloss: in-ear monitor (stage earpiece returning audio feed)

耽误.etymology: A coordinative-causative verbal compound combining 耽 (dān, from 耳 'ear' + 冘 phonetic; originally 'large drooping ears', extended in Classical Chinese to 'indulge in pleasure, linger, delay', often interchangeable with 耽/𠄢) and 误 (wù, simplified from 誤, from 言 'speech' + 吳 phonetic; 'to err, miss, bungle, impede'). Attested in Yuan–Ming drama and vernacular fiction for lingering and thereby causing a delay or missing an opportunity.

history.meaning: to linger and miss an opportunity; to hold up or botch an affair (Yuan zaju drama)
to delay, hold up, take up (someone's time or progress) (dānwu)

morphemes.meaning: err, miss, impede, bungle (neutral tone in compound)

耽误.notes: Pronounced with a neutral tone on the second syllable (dānwu) in everyday speech. Frequently used in polite apologies when interrupting a busy colleague (耽误您几分钟, 'sorry to take up a few minutes of your time') or when warning that a delay will hurt a project (别耽误了进度, 'don't hold up the schedule'). Near-synonymous with 耽搁, though 耽误 emphasizes the negative consequence or loss caused by the delay.

rootFamily.gloss: miss (a train, flight, or opportunity); hold back
lapse, mistake, fault; miss out on

聊.etymology: Phono-semantic character 聊, combining the ear radical 耳 + phonetic 卯 (mǎo / Old Chinese *mˤruʔ), originally meaning 'ringing in the ears' and in Classical Chinese 'to rely on, makeshift, slightly', then in vernacular Mandarin 'to chat, talk idly'.

history.meaning: ringing in the ears; to rely on; slightly/just
to chat, talk

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 聊 (via 萌典)

聊一聊.etymology: A tentative/delimitative verbal construction formed by reduplicating the verb 聊 (liáo) with the numeral infix 一 (yī, 'one'): V-一-V. The character 聊 (from 耳 'ear' + 卯 phonetic) originally meant 'ringing in the ears' in the Shuowen Jiezi, functioned in Classical Chinese as an adverb ('tentatively, for a moment') or noun ('reliance, livelihood', as in 民不聊生, 无聊), and evolved in late imperial Beijing vernacular into a verb meaning 'to chat, talk casually' (as in 聊天).插入 一 marks the chat as brief, casual, and low-pressure.

history.meaning: ringing in the ears; to rely on; tentatively, for the nonce (Shijing / Chuci)
to chat idly; to have a quick or casual talk about something

聊一聊.notes: Unlike 聊天 (which is a separable verb-object compound meaning 'to make small talk' and cannot take a direct object), 聊一聊 is transitive and can take a topic directly: 我们聊一聊这个方案 ('Let's have a chat about this proposal'). In workplace settings, 'Let's 聊一聊' from a boss often signals a serious one-on-one talk softened by casual phrasing.

rootFamily.gloss: chat, make small talk (separable VO verb)
bored, boring, senseless (originally 'having nothing to rely on')

聊天.etymology: Northern Mandarin verb-object compound combining 聊 ('to chat idly') + 天 ('sky, weather, the world at large', i.e. talking about anything under the sky).

history.meaning: to chat, make small talk

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 聊天 (via 萌典)

聊聊.etymology: Tentative/casual verb reduplication (AA pattern) of 聊 ('to chat'), meaning 'to have a little chat, talk for a bit'.

history.meaning: to chat a bit, talk things over casually

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 聊聊 (via 萌典)

职.etymology: From Old Chinese *tjək (Middle Chinese *tɕɨk), written in traditional script as 職: a phono-semantic character combining semantic 耳 (ěr, 'ear') with phonetic 戠 (zhí, *tjək). In the Shuowen Jiezi ('職，記微也'), it originally meant to listen attentively and record subtle administrative details—the core duty of Zhou court scribes and officials—whence it came to denote an official's specific charge, duty, or post.

history.meaning: to attend to and record official matters; official charge, tribute, or post (Zhouli / Zuozhuan)
official post, job position, duty (bound root and object of verbs like 辞职/就职)

职.notes: In modern Mandarin, 职 rarely stands alone as a free noun except in set bureaucratic phrases (如：官复原职, 身兼数职) or when split out of separable verb-object compounds like 辞职 ('resign from a post' -> 辞了职) and 升职 ('get promoted').

职业.etymology: A coordinative nominal compound joining 职 (zhí, 'official duty, post') and 业 (yè, simplified from 業, originally a pictograph of a jagged wooden rack for hanging bells and drums in court music, hence 'musical performance, scholarly study, livelihood, enterprise'). While 職業 appeared in Classical Chinese (such as Ban Gu's Book of Han 汉书) for one's proper duties and livelihood, its modern sense of 'profession, career, occupation' (translating English 'profession' / 'vocation') was reshaped in Meiji Japan and re-entered modern Mandarin as a return graphic loan.

history.meaning: official duties and agricultural/scholarly livelihood (Book of Han)
modern translation of Western 'occupation, profession, vocation'
career, profession, occupation; professional (attributive, e.g. 职业制作人)

职业.notes: Functions both as a noun ('profession/occupation', e.g., 填职业 'fill in one's occupation') and as an attributive modifier meaning 'professional' (as opposed to amateur 业余): 职业经理人 ('professional manager'), 职业素养 ('professionalism'). Contrast with 事业, which refers to a grand cause, life's work, or public-sector undertaking.

rootFamily.gloss: undertaking, cause, career (with a sense of mission)

职位.etymology: A modifier-head compound formed from 职 (zhí, trad. 職, 'official duty, post, office', originally phono-semantic from 耳 'ear' and 音/戠 indicating attentive listening to and recording of official duties) and 位 (wèi, 'standing place, rank, seat of office', ideogrammic compound of 人 'person' standing at 立 'court position'). Attested in Literary Chinese (e.g., History of the Northern Dynasties) for bureaucratic rank and post, and adapted in modern Mandarin for corporate and institutional job positions.

history.meaning: court rank and official seat in the imperial bureaucracy
job position, professional post, or organizational role

职位.notes: Refers to a specific slot or title in an organizational hierarchy (e.g., 申请职位 'apply for a position', 职位空缺 'job vacancy'), whereas 职务 emphasizes the duties and authority attached to that post.

职务.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 职 (zhí, trad. 職, 'official post, stewardship') and 务 (wù, trad. 務, 'affairs, task, business to which one applies effort'). First attested in Classical and Literary Chinese statecraft texts to denote the concrete administrative affairs belonging to an official's appointment, later reinforced in modern legal and bureaucratic usage via Sino-Japanese 職務 (shokumu) to mean both an official title/function and its attendant responsibilities.

history.meaning: administrative affairs and tasks assigned to a state official
official post, managerial title, or functional job duties

职务.notes: Often used in formal corporate, legal, and media administration contexts (e.g., 担任…职务 'hold the post of...', 解除职务 'relieve someone of their post/duties', 职务犯罪 'white-collar/official crime').

职场.etymology: A modifier-head compound of 职 (zhí, trad. 職, 'employment, profession, office') and 场 (chǎng, trad. 場, 'open ground, arena, sphere of activity'). Initially popularized in East Asia via Japanese 職場 (shokuba, a hybrid kanji reading meaning physical place of employment), and subsequently adopted and broadened in late 20th-century Mandarin on the analogy of 官场 ('officialdom') and 商场 ('business world') to denote the entire professional arena and corporate career sphere.

history.meaning: physical site of work or employment
the professional world, corporate arena, or workplace environment

职场.notes: Unlike English 'workplace' (which can mean a physical office building), 职场 usually refers abstractly to the competitive world of white-collar work (e.g., 职场新人 'workplace newcomer', 职场剧 'workplace drama' like Behind the Scenes).

职权.etymology: A modifier-head compound joining 职 (zhí, trad. 職, 'official post, function') and 权 (quán, trad. 權, 'steelyard weight, balance, leverage, authority'). While 职 and 权 co-occurred in Literary Chinese discussions of bureaucratic delegation, the tight compound 職權 was standardized in late Qing and Republican legal-administrative terminology (alongside Japanese 職権 shokken) to designate the specific scope of authority vested in an office.

history.meaning: delegated bureaucratic power attached to a state office
official authority, executive powers of a post or role

职权.notes: Frequently appears in executive and corporate governance contexts with verbs like 行使职权 ('exercise official authority'), 滥用职权 ('abuse one's power'), or 超出职权范围 ('exceed one's authority').

cognates.meaning: duty of one's post, official responsibility

职责.etymology: A coordinative / modifier-head compound of 职 (zhí, trad. 職, 'official charge, post') and 责 (zé, trad. 責, 'obligation, accountability, demand', originally from 朿 'thorn' and 貝 'cowrie/money', meaning to demand repayment of a debt). Attested in Song–Ming bureaucratic prose (such as Zhuzi Yulei) for the accountability inherent in holding public office, and retained in modern Mandarin for role-specific job duties.

history.meaning: accountability and charge incumbent upon an officeholder
job responsibility, professional duty of a position

职责.notes: More specific than 责任 ('responsibility in general'): 职责 refers strictly to the duties required by one's job or role (e.g., 履行职责 'fulfill one's duties', 职责所在 'where one's duty lies').

rootFamily.gloss: be in charge of, be responsible for

联合.etymology: A coordinative verbal and attributive compound formed from 联 (lián, trad. 聯, 'to connect in a continuous string', from 耳 'ear' and 絲 'silk threads') and 合 (hé, 'to close together, join, combine'). Used in Literary Chinese for joining forces or linking elements together, and widely deployed in modern Mandarin both as a verb ('to unite, ally') and an attributive modifier ('joint, combined, co-produced').

history.meaning: to join together, connect in sequence or alliance
to unite; joint, combined, co- (in institutional and media titles)

联合.notes: In television and film production (*Behind the Scenes*), 联合出品 ('jointly presented/produced by') and 联合制作 ('co-production') are standard industry credits, alongside institutional names like 联合国 ('United Nations').

联系.etymology: A coordinative compound of 联 (lián, trad. 聯, 'to string together, link') and 系 (xì, trad. 繫, 'to tie, fasten, bind with a cord', distinct in traditional script from 係 'to belong/relate' and 系 'lineage', all merged into simplified 系). Originally denoting physical or structural linkage ('to tie together'), it evolved in modern Mandarin to mean abstract interrelatedness ('connection') as well as interpersonal communication ('to get in touch with, contact').

history.meaning: to bind or tie together; structural linkage
to contact, get in touch with; connection or correlation

联系.notes: Functions both as a verb (联系我 'contact me', 跟他联系 'get in touch with him') and as a noun (保持联系 'keep in touch', 有密切联系 'have a close connection'). Note that simplified 系 merges three traditional characters: 系, 係, and 繫.

联赛.etymology: A modern telescoped modifier-head compound contracting 联合比赛 (liánhé bǐsài, 'combined/league competition') or 联欢/联盟比赛, composed of 联 (lián, trad. 聯, 'linked, allied, multi-team league') and 赛 (sài, trad. 賽, 'competition, match', originally a ritual offering in thanksgiving to the gods to compete in lavishness, from 貝 'cowrie wealth' and 塞 phonetic). Coined in 20th-century sports and broadcast terminology as a calque for Western 'league tournament'.

history.meaning: to make a ritual thanksgiving offering; to vie or compete in display
league tournament or multi-club championship series

联赛.notes: Used for season-long round-robin competitions (e.g., 超级联赛 'Super League', 职业联赛 'professional league'), in contrast to 杯赛 ('cup tournament') or 锦标赛 ('championship').

聘用.etymology: Compound verb combining 聘 ('to visit with ceremonial gifts to invite a worthy person to office, engage') + 用 ('to employ, use').

history.meaning: to engage by formal invitation -> to hire, employ, appoint

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 聘用 (via 萌典)

聚会.etymology: A coordinative compound of 聚 (jù, 'to assemble, flock together', from 取 phonetic and 乑 'crowd of people') and 会 (huì, trad. 會, 'to meet, converge, assemble'). Attested since Han and Six Dynasties texts (e.g., History of the Three Kingdoms) for people coming together in assembly, and used in modern Mandarin as the standard everyday word for a social gathering, get-together, or party.

history.meaning: to converge and assemble; a formal or communal gathering of people
social gathering, party, reunion, or get-together

聚会.notes: Covers everything from casual friend get-togethers (朋友聚会) and class reunions (同学聚会) to house parties and company socials, whereas 派对 (pàiduì, loanword from English 'party') specifically implies a Western-style party.

rootFamily.gloss: have a communal meal / dinner gathering

聚集.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound pairing two near-synonyms: 聚 (jù, 'to congregate, amass', with the crowd component 乑) and 集 (jí, 'to flock together, assemble', originally an ideogram 雥 of birds 隹 perching together on a tree 木). Attested in Classical Chinese (including the Zuo Zhuan and Han histories) to describe troops, people, or resources converging in one place.

history.meaning: to flock together, mass troops, or collect resources in one place
to gather, assemble, congregate (of crowds, fans, or things)

聚集.notes: Unlike 聚会 (which is a social event), 聚集 describes the physical action of people or things collecting in a spot (e.g., 门口聚集了很多记者 'many reporters gathered at the entrance').

聪明.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative compound uniting 聪 (cōng, trad. 聰, 'acute of hearing', from 耳 'ear' and /匆 phonetic) and 明 (míng, 'clear of sight, bright', from 日 'sun' and 月 'moon' or 囧 'window' and 月). In Classical texts such as the Book of Documents (Shangshu) and Xunzi, 耳聪目明 ('ears acute and eyes clear') described a ruler whose sensory channels were unobstructed and who therefore possessed keen perception; by metaphorical extension, 聪明 came to mean 'mentally sharp, intelligent, clever'.

history.meaning: acute of hearing (聰) and clear of sight (明); keen-sensed and perceptive
intelligent, smart, clever, quick-witted

聪明.notes: In modern Mandarin the second syllable is pronounced in the neutral tone (cōngming). Compare the classical four-character idiom 耳聪目明 ('sharp-eared and clear-eyed') and the cautionary proverb 聪明反被聪明误 ('too clever for one's own good').

肆虐.etymology: A Literary Chinese verb-object or adverbial-verbal compound composed of 肆 (sì, 'to let loose without restraint, indulge callously') and 虐 (nüè, 'cruelty, savagery, calamity', originally depicting a tiger 虍 clawing a person or爪). Attested in the Book of Documents (Shangshu, 'Tang Gao': 尔万方百姓，罹其凶害，弗忍荼毒... 肆虐 'unleashing ruthless cruelty'), originally describing tyrants or bandits acting with unchecked brutality, and later extended metaphorically to natural disasters, storms, or epidemics raging unchecked.

history.meaning: to indulge in unbridled cruelty or tyranny without restraint
to rage, rampage, or wreak havoc (of typhoons, floods, viruses, or villains)

肆虐.notes: A high-register literary verb very common in news broadcasts and dramatic narration for severe weather or crises (e.g., 狂风肆虐 'gale-force winds raged', 暴雨肆虐 'torrential rain wreaked havoc').

肉.etymology: Originally a pictograph (肉, ròu; Old Chinese *njuɡ) depicting a cut slice of animal flesh with visible ribs or marbling streaks. In the spoken dialog of *Behind the Scenes* (and modern colloquial Mandarin), when 肉 appears as the first syllable of the A-not-A question pattern 肉不肉麻 (ròu bu ròumá, 'is that cheesy/mushy or what?'), it is a syntactic clipping of the disyllabic adjective 肉麻 (ròumá, 'giving one goosebumps; cloyingly sentimental, cheesy') under Mandarin's AB-not-AB → A-not-AB reduplication rule.

history.meaning: animal flesh, meat, bodily tissue
clipped first morpheme of 肉麻 ('mushy, cheesy') in A-not-A interrogatives; also dialectally 'slow-moving, sluggish, or doughy'

morphemes.meaning: flesh, meat; clipped first syllable of 肉麻 (cheesy, mushy) in A-not-A constructions

肉.notes: In Mandarin disyllabic A-not-A questions (AB不AB), the first word is routinely truncated to its first character: 肉不肉麻 ('isn't that cheesy/mushy?'), just like 高不高兴 ('happy or not?'). Standalone northern colloquial 肉 can also mean 'slow-poke / sluggish' or 'pulpy/mealy (of fruit)'.

肉桂.etymology: Compound noun combining 肉 ('fleshy, thick') + 桂 ('cassia/cinnamon tree', wood radical 木 + phonetic 圭 guī), naming the thick, aromatic inner bark of the cassia/cinnamon tree.

history.stage: Han–Tang Materia Medica to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: fleshy cassia bark -> cinnamon

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 肉桂 (via 萌典)

肉桂卷.etymology: Three-character culinary compound combining 肉桂 ('cinnamon') + 卷 (捲, 'roll, rolled pastry').

history.meaning: cinnamon roll, cinnamon bun

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 肉桂卷 (via 萌典)

肉麻.etymology: A subject-predicate descriptive compound composed of 肉 (ròu, 'flesh, skin') and 麻 (má, 'numb, tingling, prickly', derived from麻 'hemp fibers' via the sensation of pins-and-needles). Literally meaning 'making one's flesh tingle or creep (with goosebumps)', it emerged in Ming–Qing vernacular literature to describe physical revulsion or cringing embarrassment, and specialized in modern Mandarin to describe overly sentimental, sappy, or 'cheesy' flattery and romance.

history.meaning: causing one's flesh to tingle or creep from shock, disgust, or awkwardness
cringeworthy, overly sentimental, mushy, corny, or cheesy (of words or behavior)

肉麻.notes: Used when someone says overly sappy, romantic, or flattering things that make listeners cringe (e.g., 别说这么肉麻的话 'stop saying such cheesy/mushy things!'). Closely related in bodily metaphor to 起鸡皮疙瘩 ('get goosebumps').

rootFamily.gloss: flesh, meat; cheesy (in 肉不肉麻)

肚子.etymology: Nominal compound formed from 肚 ('stomach, belly, abdomen', flesh radical 月/肉 + phonetic 土 tǔ) + nominal suffix 子.

history.meaning: belly, abdomen (dùzi); tripe/stomach as food (dǔzi)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 肚子 (via 萌典)

股.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining flesh/body radical 月 + phonetic 殳 (*shū/gǔ*), originally meaning 'thigh' or 'one strand twisted into a rope'. From 'single strand of a braided cord' it grammaticalized into a vivid measure word for wafts of fragrance, puffs of steam, or currents of air (这股清爽的柠檬热气).

history.meaning: thigh; strand of a twisted cord
measure word for wafts of scent, steam, or currents

股东.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 股 (gǔ, originally 'thigh, haunch', from 月/肉 'flesh' and 殳 phonetic; extended in Ming–Qing commercial usage to 'a limb/branch or proportional share of a joint venture') and 东 (dōng, trad. 東, short for 东家 dōngjiā 'master, proprietor, host', because in ancient Chinese architecture the host or master of the house occupied the eastern steps 东阶 while guests stood on the west). Hence 股东 literally means 'proprietor/owner of a capital share'.

history.meaning: master of the house (standing on the eastern steps); proprietor or employer
partner holding a capital share in a merchant house; modern corporate shareholder or stockholder

股东.notes: The morpheme 东 ('east') means 'owner/boss' in several traditional commercial compounds: 股东 ('shareholder'), 房东 ('landlord'), and 做东 ('act as host / pay the bill'). Key collocations in corporate dramas include 大股东 ('majority/major shareholder') and 股东大会 ('shareholders' meeting').

cognates.meaning: share, stock portion in a company

股份.etymology: A coordinative / modifier-head commercial compound of 股 (gǔ, originally 'thigh', extended to 'one strand of a rope' or 'one part of a divided whole, capital share') and 份 (fèn, 'allotted portion, share, quota', differentiated from 分 fèn by the person radical 亻). Originating in Ming–Qing merchant partnerships (合股) where capital and profits were divided into proportional lots, it became the standard modern term for corporate shares and stock holdings.

history.meaning: proportional capital lot or profit share in a traditional merchant partnership
corporate shares, stock ownership portions in a joint-stock company

morphemes.meaning: capital share, divided strand or portion

股份.notes: Used for the concrete portions of ownership in a company (e.g., 持有百分之十的股份 'hold 10% of the shares', 股份有限公司 'joint-stock limited company'). Compare 股权, which emphasizes the legal rights and control conferred by those shares.

股权.etymology: A modifier-head legal-financial compound combining 股 (gǔ, 'capital share, stock') and 权 (quán, trad. 權, 'legal right, claim, authority, ownership interest'). Coined in modern Chinese corporate law to denote the bundle of proprietary, voting, and dividend rights attached to share ownership ('shareholder equity / equity stake').

history.meaning: legal ownership rights and claims attached to company stock
history.stage: Early Modern Chinese (20th c. commercial law)

history.meaning: equity shares, equity stake, or shareholder voting/ownership rights

股权.notes: Central to corporate M&A and boardroom plots in *Behind the Scenes*: common collocations include 股权转让 ('equity transfer'), 股权激励 ('equity incentive / stock options'), and 私募股权 ('private equity').

肥皂.etymology: Compound of 肥 ('plump, rich, fatty') + 皂 ('black soap-pod cleanser', from 皂荚 Gleditsia sinensis pods traditionally boiled or pounded into washing cakes in China before tallow/oil bar soaps arrived).

history.meaning: plump soap-bean pods pounded into washing balls
bar of soap

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 肥皂

肥皂水.etymology: Three-character compound combining 肥皂 ('soap', originally plump black soap-pods of the Gleditsia tree 皂荚) + 水 ('water').

history.meaning: soapy water, suds

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 肥皂水 (via 萌典)

肩膀.etymology: Coordinate anatomical compound joining 肩 ('shoulder', pictograph of the shoulder joint above flesh 月) + 膀 ('upper arm, shoulder, wing', flesh radical 月 + phonetic 旁 páng).

history.meaning: shoulder

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 肩膀 (via 萌典)

cognates.word: 긍 (geung, as in 긍정 肯定)
khẳng (as in khẳng định 肯定)

肯.etymology: Originally an anatomical ideogrammic compound (肯, kěn; Old Chinese *kʰˤəŋʔ, from 冎 'stripped bone' and 月/肉 'flesh') defined in the Shuowen Jiezi as 'the flesh clinging directly to the bone; the Tendon-bone junction'. Made famous by Cook Ding's speech in the Zhuangzi (技经肯綮之未尝, 'the critical junctions where flesh adheres to bone'), where hitting the exact spot meant 'fitting the mark / hitting the point'. From 'fitting the mark / reasonable' in Six Dynasties and Tang vernacular, it grammaticalized into a modal auxiliary verb meaning 'to assent, consent, be willing to'.

history.meaning: flesh attached to bone; the crucial joint or tendon-bone nexus (as in 肯綮)
fitting the mark; to nod assent, deign, or consent to do something
to be willing to, agree to, consent to (modal auxiliary verb)

morphemes.meaning: be willing to, consent to (originally: flesh adhering to bone, critical point)

肯.notes: Most frequently used in negative, interrogative, or conditional contexts to highlight someone's willingness or stubbornness (e.g., 他死活不肯答应 'he refused to agree no matter what', 你肯帮我吗？ 'are you willing to help me?'). Its original anatomical sense survives in 中肯 (zhòngkěn, 'hitting the bone-joint → pertinent, to the point').

rootFamily.gloss: pertinent, to the point, sound (of advice/criticism)

肯定.etymology: Compound combining 肯 ('meat clinging to bone' -> 'to consent, be willing, affirm') + 定 ('to settle, fix, determine'); expanded in modern Chinese (partly via Japanese kōtei 肯定) to mean 'affirmative; to affirm; definitely, for sure'.

history.meaning: to affirm, approve; positive, definite; certainly (adv.)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 肯定 (via 萌典)

育儿室.etymology: A trimorphemic [VO + head] compound consisting of the verb-object phrase 育儿 (yù'ér, trad. 育兒, 'to rear/nurture infants', from 育 'give birth to and raise' + 儿 'child, infant') modifying the head noun 室 (shì, 'room, chamber'). Modeled in modern East Asian institutional terminology (parallel to Japanese 育児室 ikujishitsu) for a dedicated nursery room in hospitals, workplaces, or homes.

history.meaning: to nurture and raise young children
nursery, infant care room, or workplace mother-and-baby room

育儿室.notes: Refers to an infant care room or nursery in a home, maternity hospital, or public/corporate facility (distinct from 幼儿园 yòu'éryuán, 'kindergarten/preschool'). Productive with the room suffix -室 (e.g., 会议室 'conference room', 办公室 'office').

肺炎.etymology: A modifier-head medical compound formed from 肺 (fèi, 'lungs', from 月/肉 'flesh' and 巿 phonetic) and 炎 (yán, 'blazing flame, scorching heat', an ideogram of stacked fire 火 over 火, adapted in 19th-century Meiji Japanese and late Qing medical translations to render the Greek-derived clinical suffix '-itis' = inflammation). Originally coined in Sino-Japanese medicine (肺炎 haien) to translate Western 'pneumonia' ('inflammation of the lungs') and rapidly adopted into modern Chinese medicine.

history.meaning: inflammation of the lungs, pneumonia (calque of Western medical 'pneumonia / pneumonitis')
pneumonia, pulmonary inflammation

肺炎.notes: The morpheme 炎 ('flame') productively translates English '-itis' ('inflammation') across modern Chinese anatomy: 肺炎 ('pneumonia'), 胃炎 ('gastritis'), 肝炎 ('hepatitis'), and 发炎 ('become inflamed').

肿.etymology: Simplified from 腫, a phono-semantic character combining the flesh/body radical 月 (肉) with phonetic 重 (*zhòng*, 'heavy; thick', Middle Chinese *tsyowngX*). Denotes swelling or inflammation of body tissue after a sprain, bruise, or insect bite.

history.meaning: swelling; bodily tumefaction
swell; swollen

胃.etymology: An ancient compound ideogram (胃, wèi; Old Chinese *ɢʷəts) attested in bronze inscriptions and analyzed in the Shuowen Jiezi: the upper component ⽥ (originally a pouch-like pictograph 囗 containing rice grains 米 or digested matter, later regularized to 田) depicts the stomach sac filled with food, while the lower component 月 (肉, 'flesh') marks it as an internal bodily organ. Throughout Classical and Modern Chinese, it has continuously denoted the anatomical stomach.

history.meaning: the stomach sac (granary organ receiving food, paired with the spleen 脾 in classical medicine)
stomach (anatomical organ of digestion)

morphemes.meaning: stomach (from pictograph of a food-filled sac over 肉 flesh)

胃.notes: Be careful not to confuse 胃 ('stomach', the digestive organ) with 肚子 (dùzi, 'belly, abdomen, tummy'): in casual speech 'stomachache' is often 肚子疼, whereas 胃疼/胃病 specifically points to gastric pain (often associated with overwork, skipping meals, or stress in workplace dramas).

胃出血.etymology: A trimorphemic subject-predicate / modifier-head clinical compound combining 胃 (wèi, 'stomach') with the verb-object compound 出血 (chūxiě / chūxuè, 'to bleed, hemorrhage', literally 'emit blood', from 出 'go out, emit' + 血 'blood'). Used in modern medical and everyday Mandarin for acute gastric hemorrhage.

history.meaning: to bleed, shed blood
gastric hemorrhage, stomach bleeding

胃出血.notes: In Chinese television dramas like *Behind the Scenes*, 胃出血 is a classic narrative trope illustrating an overworked producer or executive pushing themselves to exhaustion through skipped meals, coffee, and alcohol at business banquets. Pronounced wèichūxiě in everyday speech or wèichūxuè in formal medical readings.

胃口.etymology: Originally a Classical Chinese anatomical term (attested in the Huangdi Neijing / Yellow Emperor's Inner Canon) composed of 胃 (wèi, 'stomach') and 口 (kǒu, 'opening, orifice'), denoting the cardiac and pyloric orifices where food enters and exits the stomach. Because Traditional Chinese Medicine linked the functioning of the stomach's entrance to one's desire for food, by the Ming–Qing vernacular period 胃口 shifted semantically to mean 'appetite for food' and figuratively 'one's personal taste, liking, or craving'.

history.meaning: the anatomical orifice/entrance of the stomach (cardia/pylorus)
desire for food, appetite; figurative taste, interest, or curiosity

胃口.notes: Extremely versatile in figurative idioms crucial to media and showbiz: 吊胃口 (diào wèikǒu, 'dangle before the appetite → whet the audience's appetite, keep people in suspense with a teaser'), 合胃口 ('suit someone's taste'), and 倒胃口 ('spoil one's appetite / be a turn-off').

胃病.etymology: A transparent modifier-head compound combining 胃 (wèi, 'stomach') and 病 (bìng, 'illness, disease, ailment', from 疒 'sickbed radical' and 丙 phonetic). Used since traditional Chinese medical treatises and everyday vernacular as the general umbrella term for chronic or acute stomach ailments (such as gastritis or ulcers).

history.meaning: disorder or disharmony of the stomach organ
stomach ailment, gastric trouble (e.g., chronic gastritis or ulcers)

胃病.notes: Follows the productive `[organ] + 病` pattern (心脏病 'heart disease', 肝病 'liver disease'). In modern urban China, 犯胃病 ('have a flare-up of one's stomach trouble') is a quintessential occupational complaint of high-stress professionals.

胃药.etymology: A modifier-head compound formed from 胃 (wèi, 'stomach') and 药 (yào, trad. 藥, 'medicinal herb, medicine, remedy', from 艸 'grass/herb' and 樂 phonetic). Built on the productive Mandarin pattern `[target organ/symptom] + 药` to denote any medication taken to treat gastric pain, indigestion, or ulcers.

history.meaning: herbal or medicinal preparation for regulating the stomach
stomach medicine, antacid, or gastric remedy

胃药.notes: Takes the verb 吃 ('eat/take'): 吃胃药 ('take stomach medicine'). Compare parallel formations like 感冒药 ('cold medicine'), 止痛药 ('painkiller'), and 眼药水 ('eye drops').

胃镜.etymology: A modern modifier-head medical compound clipped from 胃部内窥镜 (wèibù nèikuījíng, 'gastric endoscope'), combining 胃 (wèi, 'stomach') and 镜 (jìng, trad. 鏡, originally 'cast bronze mirror', from 金 'metal' and 竟 phonetic; extended in modern optics to 'lens, optical scope, instrument'). Refers both to the gastroscope instrument itself and metonymically to a gastroscopy examination.

history.meaning: polished bronze mirror; later glass lens or optical viewing instrument
gastroscope (stomach endoscope) or gastroscopy examination

胃镜.notes: In everyday clinical usage, 做胃镜 or 照胃镜 means 'to have a gastroscopy / upper endoscopy done' (including 无痛胃镜 'painless/sedated gastroscopy'). The optical suffix -镜 also forms 肠镜 ('colonoscopy/colonoscope'), 显微镜 ('microscope'), and 望远镜 ('telescope').

胆小.etymology: Subject-predicate compound adjective combining 胆 (膽, 'gallbladder', traditional seat of courage in Chinese medicine and idiom) + 小 ('small'), literally 'small-gallbladdered' = 'timid, cowardly'.

history.meaning: small of gall -> timid, faint-hearted

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 胆小 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: back; to turn one's back on
back; to turn away, recite from memory (배송 背誦)
back; to turn away, recite from memory

背.etymology: Originally a phono-semantic compound (背, bèi; Old Chinese *pˤəks / *bˤəks): the top component 北 (běi, originally a pictograph of two people standing back-to-back, hence 'to turn one's back on' and 'north') serves as both semantic and phonetic root, while the bottom component 月 (肉, 'flesh') specifies the anatomical 'back of the body'. From the verbal sense 'to turn one's back toward (the teacher or the book scroll)', attested in Medieval Chinese schooling (背书 / 背诵, facing away from the text while reciting aloud), 背 developed the transitive sense 'to recite from memory, learn by heart'.

history.meaning: the anatomical back of the body; to turn one's back on, face away from
to face away from a written text and recite it aloud from memory
to memorize, learn by heart, or recite from memory (scripts, lines, vocabulary)

morphemes.meaning: recite from memory, learn by heart (originally: anatomical back; turn one's back to a text)

背.notes: Note the two tones of 背: fourth tone bèi means 'the back', 'to turn away from / betray' (背叛), or 'to memorize/recite' (背台词 'memorize lines', 背单词 'memorize vocabulary', 背书 'recite a text'); first tone bēi means 'to carry on one's back' (背书包 'carry a backpack', 背黑锅 'carry a black pot → take the blame as a scapegoat').

rootFamily.gloss: recite from memory, learn by heart

背叛.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative verbal compound joining 背 (bèi, 'to turn one's back on, forsake an allegiance or covenant') and 叛 (pàn, 'to split away in rebellion, defect to the other side', from 半 'half, split in two' and 反 'turn against'). Attested since the Zuo Zhuan and Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji, e.g., 群臣背叛 'the ministers turned their backs in rebellion'), it originally described political or military defection and broadened in modern Mandarin to cover any personal, romantic, or professional betrayal.

history.meaning: to turn one's back on a ruler or alliance and defect in rebellion
to betray, double-cross, or forsake (a friend, partner, company, or principle)

morphemes.meaning: turn one's back on, forsake, violate

背叛.notes: Used for high-stakes personal, romantic, or corporate betrayal (e.g., 背叛朋友 'betray a friend', 遭到背叛 'suffer betrayal'). Compare 出卖 (chūmài, 'sell out / rat out someone for gain').

rootFamily.gloss: recite from memory; turn one's back on

背景调查.etymology: A four-character modifier-head compound uniting two Sino-Japanese return loans (wasei-kango): 背景 (bèijǐng, 'background, backdrop', coined in Meiji Japan as haikei from 背 'rear, behind' + 景 'scenery, stage view' to translate Western theatrical and artistic 'background') and 调查 (diàochá, trad. 調查, 'investigation, survey, inquiry', standardized via Japanese chōsa from 調 'examine, verify' + 査 'inspect'). Together they calque English 'background check / background investigation'.

history.meaning: stage/pictorial background + official inquiry or investigation
pre-employment background check, corporate vetting, or due diligence investigation into someone's history

背景调查.notes: In modern HR and corporate workplace speech (including *Behind the Scenes*), 背景调查 ('background check / vetting') is very frequently abbreviated to the two-character disyllable 背调 (bèidiào, e.g., 做背调 'run a background check').

背面.etymology: Compound noun combining 背 ('the back of the body, rear side', north/turned-away 北 + flesh 月) + 面 ('face, surface, side').

history.meaning: the back side, reverse side, rear

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 背面 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: being equal to a task or office (literary)
being equal to a duty or office
to be equal to a task, qualified for a role

胜任.etymology: A Classical Chinese verb-object compound composed of 胜 (shèng, trad. 勝, originally in the first tone shēng in Old and Middle Chinese, meaning 'to be able to bear the weight of, sustain, be equal to', from 力 'strength' and 朕 phonetic) and 任 (rèn, 'a burden carried on a shoulder pole; by extension, an official charge, trust, or responsibility'). Attested in the Zuo Zhuan and the Mencius, where 胜任 literally meant 'to have the strength to bear the burden of an office', and preserved in modern Mandarin as 'to be fully qualified or competent for a post'.

history.meaning: to possess the strength to bear a heavy load or sustain the charge of an office
to be competent for, equal to, or fully qualified for a job or responsibility

morphemes.meaning: be able to bear, sustain, be equal to (older reading shēng, modern shèng)

胜任.notes: Notice that 胜 here preserves its classical meaning 'able to bear / sustain' (as in 不胜枚举 'too numerous to list' or 弱不胜衣 'too frail to bear the weight of clothes'), NOT its common modern sense 'win / defeat'. Standard collocations include 完全胜任 ('fully qualified for') and 胜任这份工作 ('be equal to this job').

rootFamily.gloss: appoint to an office, take up a post
more than one can bear (e.g., 喜不自胜)

cognates.meaning: famous scenic spot; place of interest

胜地.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正结构) attested in Literary Chinese (traditionally written 勝地, shèngdì), combining 胜 (勝, shèng, originally "to bear, sustain" and by extension "to surpass, excel; superb, scenic") and 地 (dì, "earth, land, place, locality"). In classical landscape poetry and travel writing from the Six Dynasties and Tang onward, 胜 denoted scenery that "surpasses" the ordinary; in modern usage, 胜地 designates both renowned scenic resorts (旅游胜地) and figuratively any premier "go-to spot" or mecca for a particular activity.

history.meaning: to surpass / excel + earth / territory
locality of surpassing scenic beauty; celebrated site
renowned tourist resort; premier go-to spot or hub

胜地.notes: Do not confuse 胜地 (shèngdì, famed scenic or go-to spot, with 胜 "superb") with homophonous 圣地 (shèngdì, sacred ground or pilgrimage site, with 圣 "holy"), though both are used metaphorically in entertainment media for industry hubs.

胡乱.etymology: A coordinative / modifier-head compound formed in Medieval vernacular Chinese (Tang–Song dynasties), combining 胡 (hú, originally an ethnonym for non-Sinitic northern and western steppe peoples, which underwent pejorative semantic bleaching in Tang–Song vernacular to mean "wild, reckless, unrestrained, at random") and 乱 (亂, luàn, originally "to untangle silk threads", hence "tangled, chaotic, disorderly, indiscriminately"). Together they form an adverb and adjective describing action done without rule, care, or method.

history.meaning: non-Sinitic northern peoples + disorder, chaos, rebellion
recklessly, wildly, without regard to order or propriety
carelessly, casually, indiscriminately, at random

morphemes.meaning: recklessly, wildly, at random (originally "northern steppe peoples")

胡乱.notes: Typically precedes a verb as an adverbial modifier (e.g., 胡乱猜测 "guess wildly", 胡乱应付 "handle perfunctorily") to emphasize a lack of serious thought or standards.

cognates.meaning: to let one's imagination run wild; overthink
cognates.word: 胡思亂想 (wu4 si1 lyun6 soeng2)

胡思乱想.etymology: A four-character interlocking parallel idiom (四字格并列结构, ABAC/A1B1A2B2 pattern) built by splitting the compound 胡乱 ("wildly, indiscriminately") across two synonymous verbs of cognition: 思 (sī, "to ponder, reflect") and 想 (xiǎng, "to think, imagine"). Attested in Song–Ming vernacular literature (such as *Zhuzi Yulei* 朱子语类), it literally means "to ponder wildly and imagine chaotically," describing ungrounded, anxious, or fanciful overthinking.

history.meaning: to ponder deeply + to visualize / call to mind
to indulge in wild, undisciplined thoughts (Neo-Confucian & Ming vernacular texts)
to let one's imagination run wild; to overthink anxiously

胡思乱想.notes: Very common in conversational reassurance—别胡思乱想 ("don't overthink it / don't let your imagination run wild")—when someone jumps to worst-case conclusions about relationships or workplace politics.

胡萝卜.etymology: Botanical compound of 胡 ('introduced from Central/Western Asia along the Silk Road') + 萝卜 ('radish; taproot vegetable'). Carrots (*Daucus carota*) reached China from Iran via Central Asia during the Yuan dynasty and were named 胡萝卜 ('Silk-Road radish') after their crisp taproot.

history.meaning: cultivated carrot introduced via Central Asia
carrot

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 胡萝卜

胡说.etymology: A modifier-head verbal compound (偏正结构) attested from the Song dynasty onward, combining the adverbial prefix 胡 (hú, "wildly, recklessly, groundlessly", evolved from the ethnonym for non-Sinitic steppe peoples via medieval semantic extension to "unruly, nonsensical") and the verb 说 (說, shuō, "to speak, explain, say"). Originally meaning "to speak without basis or propriety," it became the standard everyday verb for talking nonsense or making baseless claims.

history.meaning: foreign / wild + to explain, speak, persuade
to speak groundlessly or improperly (attested in Song *Jingde Chuandeng Lu* & *Zhuzi Yulei*)
to talk nonsense; to make baseless claims; "rubbish!"

胡说.notes: Used both as a verb in sentences (别听他胡说 "don't listen to his nonsense") and as a sharp standalone interjection ("Nonsense! / Rubbish!") to immediately refute an accusation or rumor.

cognates.word: 胡說八道 (wu4 syut3 baat3 dou6)

胡说八道.etymology: A four-character coordinative idiom expanding 胡说 ("to talk nonsense") with 八道 (bādào, "eight paths/ways"). Historically, 八道 referred to the Eightfold Path of Buddhism (八正道) or the eight stages of Daoist alchemy/cultivation; when paired with 胡说 ("wildly expounding"), it originally mocked charlatans or itinerant monks "wildly preaching the Eight Paths" without genuine comprehension, before grammaticalizing into an emphatic idiom meaning "to spout utter nonsense in every direction."

history.meaning: to speak wildly + the Eight Paths (of Buddhist/Daoist doctrine)
to preach or babble wildly without rhyme or reason (Ming–Qing vernacular novels)
to talk utter nonsense; to spout complete rubbish

胡说八道.notes: Stronger and more emphatic than plain 胡说; frequently used in workplace dramas and media contexts to dismiss tabloid rumors, slander, or absurd excuses.

cognates.meaning: to fool around, make a scene, act recklessly

胡闹.etymology: A modifier-head verbal compound (偏正结构) formed in Ming–Qing vernacular Mandarin, combining the adverbial prefix 胡 (hú, "wildly, recklessly, without restraint", from the medieval semantic extension of the ethnonym 胡) and 闹 (鬧, nào, originally depicting noisy contention in a market 巿/門, meaning "noisy, boisterous; to make a scene, stir up trouble"). It denotes acting up, fooling around, or behaving recklessly in defiance of sensible limits.

history.meaning: wild / unruly + noisy disturbance, commotion
to cause an unruly commotion; to act mischievously or unreasonably (Ming–Qing vernacular)
to fool around, horse around, act recklessly or absurdly

morphemes.meaning: to make noise, stir up trouble, fool around (trad. 鬧)

胡闹.notes: Depending on tone of voice, 胡闹 ranges from affectionate scolding of playful behavior ("stop horsing around") to a stern reprimand of unprofessional or reckless conduct in a high-stakes project ("this is sheer recklessness!").

rootFamily.gloss: lively, bustling with noise and excitement
make a scene, throw a tantrum without reason

胳膊.etymology: Disyllabic anatomical noun combining 胳 ('armpit, upper arm', flesh radical 月 + phonetic 各 gè) + 膊 ('upper arm, shoulder', flesh radical 月 + phonetic 尃 fū).

history.meaning: arm

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 胳膊 (via 萌典)

胶带.etymology: Descriptive compound of 胶 ('glue, gum, rubber', flesh/organic radical 月 + phonetic 交) + 带 ('belt, ribbon, strip', pictograph of a waist sash with hanging cloth).

history.meaning: adhesive tape; electrical/packing tape

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 胶带 (via 萌典)

胶水.etymology: Compound of 胶 ('animal hide glue, plant resin, adhesive', flesh/organic radical 月 + phonetic 交 jiāo 'join together') + 水 ('liquid, water'), naming liquid glue in contrast to solid glue sticks or tape.

history.meaning: joinery glue used in bows, wheels, and instruments
liquid glue

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 胶水

能.etymology: Originally an oracle-bone and bronze pictograph of a clawed, thick-bodied bear (related to 熊 xióng), borrowed early in Old Chinese for 'ability, talent, capable; can, be able to'.

history.meaning: three-legged/clawed bear -> strength, ability, can
can, be able to, capable; energy

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 能 (via 萌典)

能力.etymology: A coordinative / modifier-head Sino-compound combining 能 (néng, originally a pictograph of a bear-like beast in Old Chinese *nˤə, early borrowed for "able, capable; talent, skill") and 力 (lì, "sinew, physical strength, power, force"). While 能 and 力 frequently co-occurred in Classical Chinese (e.g., *Xunzi*, *Hanshu*) to mean "talent and strength," the modern abstract sense of "capacity, faculty, competence" (translating English *ability* / *capacity* and German *Fähigkeit*) was standardized in Meiji Japan (能力, *nōryoku*) and re-entered late Qing Mandarin as a pan-East Asian modern lexical item.

history.meaning: talent / capability + physical strength / power
faculty, legal/mental capacity, competence (Meiji Japanese translation of Western "ability/faculty")
history.stage: Meiji Japanese / Late Qing return loan

history.meaning: ability, capability, competence (in work, cognition, or action)

能力.notes: The standard noun for professional competence; in workplace contexts it commonly pairs with 强/弱 (能力很强 "highly capable") or specific domains like 业务能力 ("professional/technical chops").

cognates.meaning: to be able to, can, capable of

能够.etymology: A disyllabic modal verb compound formed in Medieval and Early Mandarin by combining 能 (néng, "to be able to, capable of") with 够 (夠/勾, gòu, originally "to reach, stretch to, suffice, be enough"). In Yuan–Ming vernacular texts, it was frequently written 能勾 (nénggōu, "able to reach / manage to accomplish"), before standardizing with the character 够 ("to suffice, reach the requisite threshold"). The compound reinforces monosyllabic 能 with a sense of reaching sufficient conditions to achieve an action.

history.meaning: to be able, capable of
to manage to reach; to be in a position to accomplish (Yuan *zaju* plays & Ming vernacular novels)
to be able to, can, be capable of (modal auxiliary verb)

morphemes.meaning: to reach, suffice, be enough (trad. 夠)

能够.notes: More formal and rhythmically weightier than monosyllabic 能; preferred in two-syllable prosodic slots (e.g., 希望能够合作 "hope to be able to collaborate"), though in negative form people usually say 不能 rather than 不能够.

能干.etymology: A verb-object / modifier-head compound attested from the Tang and Song dynasties (traditionally written 能幹, nénggàn), combining 能 (néng, "skilled, capable, adept") and 干 (幹, gàn, originally the wooden trunk or frame used in rammed-earth construction, extended in Classical Chinese to "mainstay, backbone, practical affairs, to manage or execute business"). Notice that 干 here represents traditional 幹 (gàn, "to do, manage affairs"), not 乾 ("dry") or 干 ("shield"). Literally "capable in handling practical affairs," it describes a person who gets things done efficiently.

history.meaning: capable, skilled + tree trunk / backbone / practical administration
competent in official or practical administration (Song histories & vernacular)
capable, competent, efficient, street-smart at work or household affairs

morphemes.meaning: to do, manage affairs; practical ability (trad. 幹)

能干.notes: A high-praise adjective for hands-on competence and execution (精明能干 "shrewd and capable"); remember the second syllable is fourth tone gàn (trad. 幹 "to do"), never first tone gān.

rootFamily.gloss: backbone, core member of an organization

能量.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 能 (néng, "ability, capacity; energy in physics") and 量 (liàng, "measure, capacity, tolerance, magnitude"). In Classical and Imperial Chinese (e.g., *Book of Jin* 晋书), 能量 meant "one's capacity of talent and moral measure." In modern Chinese, it was repurposed to translate physical *energy* (combining 能 "energy/work capacity" + 量 "quantity/measure"), and subsequently gained two vivid figurative extensions in contemporary Mandarin: social/institutional "clout, pull, influence" (as in 很有能量 "having huge clout behind the scenes") and emotional "vibes" (正能量 "positive energy").

history.meaning: measure of a person's talent and capability (attested in Six Dynasties & Tang texts)
physical energy (quantitative capacity to perform work in modern physics)
physical energy; personal clout/influence; emotional aura (e.g., 正能量)

能量.notes: In media, business, and showbiz contexts (like *Behind the Scenes*), 说一个人很有能量 usually means they wield impressive behind-the-scenes clout, resources, and influence rather than physical stamina.

脆.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 脆. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 脆 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 脆 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 脆 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 脆. The etymology of 脆 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 脆
middle form of 脆
modern form of 脆

脆皮.etymology: Modifier-head culinary compound combining 脆 ('crisp, brittle, crunchy', flesh radical 月 + 危 wēi) + 皮 ('skin, crust, outer layer').

history.meaning: crispy skin, crispy crust

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 脆皮 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: dirty, filthy; internal organs (in zong6 reading)

脏.etymology: In simplified Chinese, 脏 merges two distinct traditional characters: 髒 (zāng, "dirty, filthy, soiled") and 臟 (zàng, "internal organs, viscera", as in 心脏 "heart"). In the sense "dirty" (zāng), the traditional form 髒 is composed of 骨 ("bone/skeleton") and 葬 (zàng, "to bury a corpse"), originally extracted from the medieval binome 骯髒 (kǎngzǎng / āngzāng, which meant "fat/bulky" or "upright/unyielding" in Six Dynasties poetry before shifting in Yuan–Ming vernacular to "filthy, squalid, unclean"). Monosyllabic 脏 (zāng) is the clipped vernacular core of 肮脏 (骯髒).

history.meaning: bulky of body; stiff, unbending against corruption (Six Dynasties–Tang poetry)
filthy, soiled, squalid (Yuan–Ming vernacular semantic shift)
dirty, filthy, soiled; morally foul or underhanded (simplified merger with 臟)

morphemes.meaning: dirty, filthy, soiled (trad. 髒; simplified form merges with 臟 zàng "viscera")

脏.notes: Watch the heteronym: first tone zāng (trad. 髒) means "dirty" (脏衣服, 脏话), whereas fourth tone zàng (trad. 臟) means "internal organ" (心脏 "heart", 内脏 "viscera").

脏水.etymology: A transparent modifier-head compound (偏正结构) combining 脏 (髒, zāng, "dirty, filthy, sullied") and 水 (shuǐ, "water, liquid"). Beyond its literal household sense of wastewater or slops, 脏水 developed a vivid metaphorical sense in modern Mandarin via the verbal idiom 泼脏水 (pō zāngshuǐ, literally "to splash dirty water on someone"), referring to malicious slander, mudslinging, or framing someone to ruin their reputation.

history.meaning: filthy / soiled + water / liquid
dirty water, slops; (figuratively) malicious slander or smear campaigns

脏水.notes: In entertainment and PR crisis dialogues, 脏水 almost always appears in the collocation 往…身上泼脏水 ("to throw mud at / smear someone").

脑子.etymology: Nominal compound formed from 脑 (腦 / 匘, 'brain, marrow of the head', showing hair 巛 and skull 囟 with flesh 月) + nominal suffix 子.

history.meaning: brain, mind, head

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 脑子 (via 萌典)

脚.etymology: A phono-semantic character (traditionally 腳, variant 脚) composed of the semantic radical 肉 (⺼, "flesh, body part") and the phonetic 卻 (què, Old Chinese *kʰak, alongside 腳 OC *kak). In Pre-Qin and Han Classical Chinese, 足 (zú) denoted the "foot" while 腳 (jiǎo) meant the "calf, shank, lower leg" (as defined in *Shuowen Jiezi*: 脛也 "the shin/shank"). During the Six Dynasties and Tang period, 脚 underwent a downward anatomical shift (metonymic extension from lower leg to foot), replacing classical 足 as the everyday vernacular word for "foot" across Mandarin and most Sinitic varieties.

history.meaning: calf, shin, lower leg (distinct from 足 "foot")
lower leg and foot; base or support of an object
foot; base/leg of furniture; role/actor (variant for 角 jué)

脚.notes: Plays a huge role in vivid Chinese idioms about work and movement: 手脚麻利 ("nimble-handed / quick and efficient"), 站稳脚跟 ("gain a firm foothold"), and 抱佛脚 ("cram at the last minute").

rootFamily.gloss: hands and feet; secret tampering (as in 动手动脚/做手脚)

脚下.etymology: Locative compound combining 脚 (腳, 'foot', originally 'calf/lower leg') + 下 ('underneath, below').

history.meaning: under one's feet, where one steps; at present

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 脚下 (via 萌典)

脚后跟.etymology: Three-character anatomical compound from 脚 ('foot') + 后 ('back; rear') + 跟 ('heel of the foot', foot 足 + phonetic 艮). Unambiguously specifies the back heel of the foot or of a shoe.

history.meaning: heel of the foot
heel

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 脚后跟

脚步声.etymology: Three-character compound combining 脚步 (腳步, 'footstep, pace', from 脚 'foot' + 步 'step') + 声 (聲, 'sound').

history.meaning: sound of footsteps

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 脚步声 (via 萌典)

脚趾.etymology: Anatomical compound from 脚 ('foot') + 趾 ('toe; foot', foot radical 足 + phonetic 止, which was itself the original pictograph of a three-toed footprint). Adding 脚 distinguishes toes (脚趾) from fingers (手指) in spoken Mandarin.

history.meaning: toe of the foot
toe

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 脚趾

脚踝.etymology: Anatomical compound of 脚 ('foot', flesh radical 月 + 却) + 踝 ('anklebone; malleolus', foot radical 足 + phonetic 果 *guǒ*, Old Chinese *gˤrʷajʔ*). Combining the general word for foot with the classical term for the ankle joint yields the clear disyllabic modern noun 脚踝.

history.meaning: anklebone
ankle

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 脚踝

脱.etymology: Phono-semantic character 脱 (脫), combining flesh radical 月 (肉) + phonetic 兑 (duì / *lˤot-s), originally meaning 'for flesh to fall away from bones, shed skin, peel off', hence 'to take off (clothes), shed, escape from'.

history.meaning: to strip off, shed, cast off
to take off (clothing/shoes), shed, come off, escape

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 脱 (via 萌典)

脸.etymology: Phono-semantic character 脸 (臉), combining flesh radical 月 (肉) + phonetic 佥 (僉 qiān), attested since the Six Dynasties and Tang for 'cheeks, upper face where rouge is applied', later displacing 面 in northern Mandarin as the general word for 'face'.

history.meaning: cheeks, facial area under the eyes
face, countenance, prestige/reputation

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 脸 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: on the face; facial expression or prestige

脸上.etymology: A noun-postposition localizer phrase combining 脸 (臉, liǎn, originally a Middle Chinese word meaning "cheeks"—specifically the part of the face where rouge was applied—which broadened by the Yuan–Ming era to replace classical 面 miàn as the primary vernacular word for the whole "face") and the enclitic spatial localizer 上 (shàng, "on, upon, on the surface of"). Beyond physical location ("on one's face"), 脸上 frequently carries the sociological sense of visible pride, prestige, or embarrassment (as in 脸上无光 "to lose face / feel ashamed" or 脸上贴金 "to put a feather in one's cap").

history.meaning: cheek / upper cheek + above, upon
on the face; in one's facial expression or social standing (Yuan–Ming vernacular)
on the face (literal surface, visible expression, or social prestige)

morphemes.meaning: on, upon, on the surface of (pronounced neutral tone shang)

脸上.notes: Notice how 脸上 bridges physical expression and social "face" (面子): 脸上挂不住 means both "unable to keep a straight/composed face" and "feeling publicly humiliated."

rootFamily.gloss: facial expression, complexion, mood shown on face

脸色.etymology: Compound noun combining 脸 (臉, 'face') + 色 ('color, complexion, facial expression').

history.meaning: complexion, facial expression

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 脸色 (via 萌典)

脾气.etymology: Compound originating in traditional Chinese medicine, combining 脾 ('spleen', flesh radical 月 + phonetic 卑 bēi, associated with the Earth element and digestive/emotional regulation) + 气 (氣, 'vital breath, disposition'), shifting in vernacular Mandarin to 'temperament, disposition, bad temper'.

history.meaning: vital qi of the spleen
temperament, disposition, temper

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 脾气 (via 萌典)

腻.etymology: Phono-semantic character 腻 (膩), combining flesh/fat radical 月 (肉) + phonetic 贰 (貳 èr / *ni[t]-s), originally meaning 'sleek, rich, fatty, greasy', extended to 'cloying, tired of, fed up with; meticulously smooth'.

history.meaning: fat, greasy, smooth
greasy, oily; cloying, bored/fed up with

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 腻 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: unable to clear out or free up (time/space/hands)
cognates.word: 騰唔出來 (tang4 m4 ceot1 loi4)

腾不出来.etymology: A negative potential directional verb construction (V-不-出来) built on the verb 腾 (騰, téng). In Classical Chinese, 腾 (from 马 "horse" + 朕 phonetic) meant "to gallop, leap up, soar." In Ming–Qing vernacular Mandarin, 腾 developed the causative spatial sense "to clear out, vacate, move things aside to make room" (as in 腾地方 "clear space", 腾出手 "free up one's hands", 腾出时间 "free up time"). Combined with the negative potential infix 不 (bù, "cannot") and the compound directional complement 出来 (chūlái, "outward / into availability"), 腾不出来 means "unable to free up or spare (time, personnel, space, or hands)."

history.meaning: (of a horse) to leap, gallop, soar upward
to vacate, empty out, clear room or resources for another use (Ming–Qing vernacular)
unable to free up or spare (time, hands, staff, funds, or space)

morphemes.meaning: to vacate, clear out, free up (trad. 騰, originally "to leap/gallop")
out, forth (indicating emergence into availability, trad. 出來)

腾不出来.notes: Extremely idiomatic in busy production or office settings: commonly takes objects like 空儿/时间 ("time"), 手 ("hands"), 人手 ("staff"), or 地方 ("space"), e.g., 我实在腾不出手来 ("I really can't free up my hands right now").

rootFamily.gloss: free up, vacate, clear out (space, time, hands)
move around, toss about, put through the wringer
soar, rise rapidly (e.g., economy or career)

腿.etymology: Phono-semantic character 腿, combining flesh radical 月 (肉) + phonetic 退 (tuì), originally denoting the 'lower leg or thigh' and in Mandarin the general word for 'leg' (human, animal, or furniture).

history.meaning: lower leg, thigh
leg; ham

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 腿 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: ever since (a past point in time)

自从.etymology: A synonym-compound preposition (同义复词) grammaticalized during the Six Dynasties and Tang period by fusing two Classical Chinese ablative prepositions meaning "from": 自 (zì, originally a pictograph of a nose, used in Oracle Bone and Classical Chinese as both "self" and the ablative preposition "from [a point in space or time]") and 从 (從, cóng, originally two figures walking one behind another, "to follow" -> ablative preposition "from, by way of"). Combining them created a prosodically stable disyllabic temporal preposition marking the starting point of a past event ("ever since").

history.meaning: from (spatial/temporal origin) + to follow / from
ever since, from the time that (attested in Tang poetry, e.g., Du Fu & Bai Juyi)
ever since (introducing a past temporal clause, often paired with 以后/之后)

自从.notes: Unlike English "since," 自从 only marks a starting point in time (never "since = because"), and usually pairs with a closing localizer like 以后, 之后, or 以来 (自从他来了以后… "Ever since he arrived…").

rootFamily.gloss: since, ever since (placed after the time phrase)
formerly, in the past, once upon a time

cognates.meaning: to flatter oneself; unrequitedly imagine someone likes you
cognates.word: 自作多情 (zi6 zok3 do1 cing4)

自作多情.etymology: A four-character verbal idiom structured as reflexively modified verb + object (自 + 作 + 多情): 自 (zì, "oneself, on one's own"), 作 (zuò, "to make, act as, play the role of"), and 多情 (duōqíng, a classical poetic compound meaning "abounding in sentiment/affection, passionate, romantic"). Formed in late imperial and modern vernacular, it literally means "to unilaterally play the passionate lover on one's own"—hence to flatter oneself by imagining that one's romantic or personal feelings are reciprocated when the other party has no such intention.

history.meaning: full of deep sentiment or romantic sensitivity (Tang–Song lyric poetry)
to unilaterally indulge in romantic sentiment; to flatter oneself that affection is mutual

自作多情.notes: A staple expression in romance and workplace dramas (别自作多情了! "Stop flattering yourself!") used to deflate someone who misinterprets polite professional kindness as romantic interest or special favor.

rootFamily.gloss: reap what one has sown, bring trouble on oneself

自制.etymology: In simplified Chinese, 自制 merges two distinct traditional compounds that share identical pronunciation (zìzhì): (1) 自製 ("self-made, homemade, produced in-house"), combining 自 ("self, one's own") and 製 (zhì, from 衣 "garment" + 制, originally "to cut and tailor clothes", hence "to manufacture, produce, make"); and (2) 自制 ("self-control, self-restraint"), combining 自 ("oneself") and 制 (zhì, "to regulate, restrain, govern", attested in *Xunzi*). In media and broadcasting (*Behind the Scenes*), 自制 primarily represents traditional 自製 ("produced in-house", as in 自制剧 "in-house original drama" or 自制综艺 "platform-produced variety show").

history.form: 自制 (OC *dzits *krets) / 自製 (MC dzijH tsyejH)
history.meaning: to restrain oneself (*Xunzi*) vs. to tailor/make by oneself (Six Dynasties–Tang)
homemade, manufactured in-house (自製) / self-control (自制)
self-made, homemade, in-house produced (merged in Simplified Chinese with 自制 "self-control")

morphemes.meaning: to manufacture, produce (trad. 製); or to restrain, control (trad. 制)

自制.notes: In streaming and TV production, 自制 (trad. 自製) means "original in-house production" (e.g., 平台自制节目 "platform-produced original show", contrasting with licensed/purchased shows 外购剧), whereas in 自制力 it means "self-control" (trad. 自制).

cognates.meaning: spontaneous, voluntary, of one's own accord

自发.etymology: A subject-predicate / reflexive-verb compound (traditionally 自發, zìfā) combining 自 (zì, "from oneself, of its own accord") and 发 (發, fā, originally "to shoot an arrow", hence "to issue forth, arise, initiate, manifest"). In Classical and Buddhist Chinese (e.g., *Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* 圆觉经), 自发 meant "arising from within oneself." During the Meiji period in Japan, 自発 (*jihatsu*) was standardized as the philosophical and scientific translation for English *spontaneous* / *voluntary* (contrasting with 誘発 "induced"), and reinforced this modern sense across East Asia.

history.meaning: to arise or issue forth from oneself (Classical & Tang Buddhist texts)
spontaneous, voluntary, unprompted (Meiji Japanese philosophical & scientific usage)
history.stage: Meiji Japanese / Late Qing return reinforcement

history.meaning: spontaneously, voluntarily, of one's own accord (without external directive)

morphemes.meaning: by oneself, from within, of its own accord
to issue forth, arise, initiate (trad. 發)

自发.notes: Frequently modifies actions taken by fans, netizens, or employees without top-down organization or payment (e.g., 粉丝自发宣传 "fans spontaneously promoting the show of their own accord").

rootFamily.gloss: initiative, autonomy, act on one's own
voluntary, of one's own free will

自大.etymology: A classical reflexive-putative compound attested since the Pre-Qin and Han eras (e.g., *Laozi*, *Zhuangzi*, *Records of the Grand Historian*), combining 自 (zì, "oneself") and 大 (dà, used putatively/causatively as "to regard as great, to aggrandize, to magnify"). Literally "to consider oneself great" or "to magnify oneself," it has continuously denoted arrogance, conceit, and megalomania for over two millennia.

history.meaning: to consider oneself great; to aggrandize oneself (attested in *Zhuangzi* & *Shiji*)
arrogant, conceited, full of oneself, megalomaniacal

morphemes.meaning: great; to regard as great, magnify

自大.notes: Often paired with its antonym 自卑 ("inferiority complex") in psychological observations (既自卑又自大 "simultaneously insecure and arrogant") or expanded into the four-character idiom 狂妄自大 ("wildly arrogant and conceited").

rootFamily.gloss: parochial arrogance, delusions of grandeur (lit. Yelang thinks itself huge)

自家.etymology: Compound pronoun and noun combining 自 ('self, own') + 家 ('family, household'), meaning 'one's own family/home' and in colloquial or regional Mandarin 'oneself'.

history.meaning: one's own family/home; oneself

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 自家 (via 萌典)

自己.etymology: Reflexive pronoun combining two synonymous Classical Chinese roots: 自 ('nose' -> 'self, personally') + 己 ('oneself', 6th heavenly stem).

history.meaning: oneself, one's own
oneself, one's own

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 自己 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: one of us, insider, trusted ally

自己人.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound formed in Early Modern vernacular Mandarin by attaching 人 (rén, "person, people") to the disyllabic reflexive pronoun 自己 (zìjǐ, "oneself, one's own", itself a fusion of two Classical Chinese reflexives: 自 "self" and 己 "self, one's own person"). Reflecting the relational sociology of Chinese in-group vs. out-group circles (差序格局), 自己人 literally means "one's own people"—denoting a family member, trusted insider, or loyal member of the same camp, in direct contrast to 外人 (wàirén, "outsider").

history.form: 自己 (MC dzijH kijX) + 人 (MC nyin)
history.meaning: oneself / one's own + person / people
member of one's own family, faction, or trusted inner circle (Ming–Qing vernacular novels)
one of us; trusted insider, ally, or team member

自己人.notes: Calling someone 自己人 ("you're one of us / we're all family here") is a classic social lubricant in Chinese workplace and negotiation culture to signal trust, drop formalities, or ask for a favor; its direct opposite is 外人 ("outsider").

rootFamily.gloss: one of us, family/insider (colloquial northern variant)

cognates.meaning: to ask for trouble, bring trouble upon oneself
cognates.word: 自找麻煩 (zi6 zaau2 maa4 faan4)

自找麻烦.etymology: A four-character vernacular verb-object phrase structured as 自 ("by oneself") + 找 (zhǎo, "to seek, look for") + 麻烦 (麻煩, máfan, "trouble, nuisance, hassle"). The object 麻烦 combines 麻 ("hemp fibers", connoting something tangled, messy, and tedious to sort out) and 烦 (煩, from 火 "fire" + 页 "head", originally "feverish headache", hence "vexed, bothered, troublesome"). Together, 自找麻烦 literally means "to go looking for tangled trouble on one's own," i.e., to ask for trouble or bring a headache upon oneself through needless meddling or poor choices.

history.meaning: to seek for oneself + tangled/vexing trouble (Qing–Modern vernacular)
to ask for trouble; to bring unnecessary hassle or difficulty upon oneself

自找麻烦.notes: Often shortened to the predicate 自找的 ("you asked for it / brought it on yourself", e.g., 这是他自找的) when someone suffers the predictable consequences of meddling.

rootFamily.gloss: trouble, hassle, inconvenient; to bother someone
bring humiliation or rebuff upon oneself
bring destruction upon oneself, court disaster

自有.etymology: A disyllabic compound combining 自 (zì, both the adverb "naturally, of course, inherently" and the reflexive pronoun "one's own") and 有 (yǒu, "to have, possess, exist"). Attested in Classical and Literary Chinese (e.g., famous proverbs like 书中自有黄金屋 "within books there naturally are houses of gold"), 自有 operates in two closely related ways in modern Mandarin: (1) adverb + verb ("naturally has / there is bound to be", e.g., 自有办法 "naturally have a way", 自有分寸 "naturally know the proper limits"), and (2) modifier + verb in business/legal contexts ("self-owned, proprietary", e.g., 自有品牌 "in-house/private-label brand", 自有资金 "proprietary capital").

history.meaning: naturally possesses; inherently has of itself (Classical Chinese prose & poetry)
(1) naturally have (one's own way/reason); (2) self-owned, proprietary (in commerce/law)

自有.notes: Pay attention to context: in idiomatic speech (我自有安排 "I naturally have my own arrangements"), 自 means "naturally / of course"; in business terms (自有版权 "proprietary copyright"), 自 means "self-owned."

rootFamily.gloss: know the proper limits, have a sense of measure

自然.etymology: Coinage of early Daoist philosophy (*Laozi* / *Daodejing* ch. 25: 道法自然 "The Way models itself on that which is so of itself"), combining 自 (zì, "of itself, from itself") and the stative demonstrative suffix 然 (rán, "to be so, thus"). In Classical Chinese, 自然 meant "self-so, spontaneous, occurring without external coercion or artifice"—hence also the adverb "naturally, of course."
