In the Meiji era, Japanese scholars selected 自然 (*shizen*) to translate the Western noun *Nature* (the physical universe and natural world), and this nominal sense was re-borrowed into modern Chinese alongside the native classical adverbial ("naturally, of course") and adjectival ("natural, unforced") senses.

history.meaning: being so of itself; spontaneous, uncontrived (*Laozi*, *Zhuangzi*)
spontaneous, unforced; naturally, as a matter of course
(adv.) naturally, of course; (adj.) natural, unforced; (n.) nature (via Meiji Japanese *shizen*)

morphemes.meaning: so, thus, in such a state

自然.notes: As an adverb (他自然会明白 "he will naturally understand"), 自然 retains its ancient Daoist sense of "as a natural consequence / of course," whereas as a noun (大自然 "Mother Nature") it reflects the modern Meiji translation of *nature*.

rootFamily.gloss: let things take their natural course
naturally, as a matter of course, needless to say
of course, certainly (lit. ought to be so)

自由.etymology: A reflexive-verbal compound attested since the Han dynasty (*Book of Later Han* 后汉书 and the Han narrative poem *The Peacock Flies Southeast* 孔雀东南飞: 吾意久怀忿，汝岂得自由), combining 自 (zì, "from oneself, on one's own") and 由 (yóu, "to follow, proceed from, depend upon"). In Han–Tang vernaculari, 自由 meant "acting on one's own impulse, unrestrained, at one's own disposal" (and in Chan Buddhism, spiritual liberation from worldly fetters). In the 1860s–1870s (notably Nakamura Masanao's 1872 Japanese translation of J.S. Mill's *On Liberty*, 自由之理), 自由 (*jiyū*) was repurposed to translate Western political and philosophical *liberty / freedom*, returning to late Qing Chinese with its modern civic and existential meanings.

history.meaning: to act according to one's own wishes; unrestrained by others (Han–Six Dynasties)
at ease, unrestrained; spiritual liberation (Tang Chan Buddhism & poetry)
free; freedom, liberty (political/personal right, reinforced via Meiji Japanese *jiyū*)

morphemes.meaning: to follow, proceed from, depend upon

自由.notes: Used both as an adjective (很自由 "very free", 自由职业者 "freelancer") and as an abstract noun (财务自由 "financial freedom", 言论自由 "freedom of speech").

自私.etymology: A reflexive-verbal/adjectival compound attested in Classical Chinese since the Warring States and Han periods (e.g., *Hanfeizi* 韩非子 and *Huainanzi* 淮南子), combining 自 (zì, "for oneself") and 私 (sī, from 禾 "grain" + 厶 "private/enclosed", originally denoting "one's own private grain field" in contrast to 公 gōng "the duke's/communal field", hence "private, personal, partial, self-serving"). In Legalist and Confucian political thought, 自私 meant "seeking private advantage for oneself at the expense of the public good (公)," which evolved directly into the modern adjective "selfish, self-centered."

history.meaning: to pursue private advantage for oneself (*Hanfeizi*, *Huainanzi*)
selfish, self-centered, concerned only with one's own interests

自私.notes: Often intensified in the four-character coordinative idiom 自私自利 ("selfish and self-seeking"); its classical and modern moral opposite is 无私 ("selfless, altruistic", lit. "without private bias").

rootFamily.gloss: selfish and self-serving, out only for one's own gain

自虐.etymology: A reflexive-verb compound combining 自 (zì, "oneself") and 虐 (nüè, originally an oracle-bone graph depicting a tiger's claws 虍 mauling a person, meaning "cruel, tyrannical; to torment, abuse, maltreat"). While 自虐 occasionally appeared in Literary Chinese to mean "bringing ruin or harm upon oneself," its modern psychological sense ("masochism, self-torture, self-torment") was coined in Japanese (自虐, *jigyaku*, alongside 自虐症 for Krafft-Ebing's *masochism*) and entered 20th-century Mandarin. In contemporary colloquial Chinese, it is very frequently used hyperbolically for grueling workouts, punishing work schedules, or emotional self-punishment ("torturing oneself").

history.meaning: oneself + cruel / to maltreat, ravage
masochism, self-torment (modern Japanese psychological coinage borrowed into Chinese)
to torture oneself (psychologically, physically, or hyperbolically through grueling effort)

自虐.notes: In everyday speech and workplace dramas, 简直是在自虐 ("practically torturing oneself") is used humorously or sympathetically for taking on brutal workloads, dieting, or re-watching sad memories.

rootFamily.gloss: torture, torment, put someone through an ordeal
self-mutilation, self-harm (more severe/clinical than 自虐)

自觉.etymology: Formed by 自 (zì, 'self') and 觉 (jué, 'to feel, to realize'). From its philosophical roots in self-awareness and enlightenment, it has evolved in modern Mandarin to describe acting proactively and conscientiously without needing external reminders.

history.meaning: self-aware
conscious; proactive

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 自觉

自豪.etymology: Compound of reflexive pronoun 自 ('oneself') + 豪 ('heroic; spirited; proud', phonetic 高 above 豕). In modern Mandarin, 自豪 expresses warm, positive pride in honorable craftsmanship, community, or shared accomplishment, without the negative arrogance of 骄傲.

history.meaning: proud; full of wholesome pride

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 自豪

自身.etymology: A reflexive compound pronoun attested in Classical Chinese since the Warring States and Han periods (e.g., *Zhuangzi*, *Classic of Filial Piety* 孝经), combining 自 (zì, "self, one's own") and 身 (shēn, originally a pictograph of a torso/pregnant body, meaning "body, torso, person, self"). In Classical Chinese, 身 itself regularly functioned as a reflexive pronoun ("one's own person / oneself"); compounding it with 自 created 自身 ("one's own person, oneself, in itself"), which serves in modern Mandarin as a formal reflexive pronoun applicable to both people and abstract entities (such as companies, projects, or systems).

history.meaning: one's own body or person; oneself (*Zhuangzi*, Han prose)
oneself, one's own (formal reflexive pronoun for persons, organizations, or things)

自身.notes: More formal than 自己, and frequently used as an attributive modifier before abstract nouns (自身利益 "one's own interests", 自身价值 "one's own value", 从自身找原因 "look within oneself for the cause") or in the idiom 自身难保 ("unable even to save oneself").

rootFamily.gloss: unable even to protect/save oneself (let alone help others)
oneself, in person, personally (focusing on the agent's identity)

cognates.meaning: surrender oneself to the authorities, turn oneself in
surrender to authorities, turn oneself in
turn oneself in, confess to authorities

自首.etymology: An ancient Chinese legal term attested since the Qin–Han legal codes and the *Records of the Grand Historian* (史记), combining 自 (zì, "by oneself, voluntarily") and 首 (shǒu, originally "head", used verbally in Qin–Han legal language—traditionally read fourth tone shòu in classical glosses, though pronounced third tone shǒu in modern Mainland standard—to mean "to bow one's head and confess guilt, to report a crime to the authorities", cf. 首告, 出首). Codified explicitly in the *Tang Code* (唐律疏议: 诸犯罪未发而自首者，原其罪 "Whoever voluntarily confesses a crime before it is discovered shall have the punishment remitted"), 自首 has remained the exact statutory term in Chinese criminal law for over two thousand years for voluntarily turning oneself in.

history.meaning: to voluntarily report and confess one's offense to the magistrate (Qin–Han legal strips & *Shiji*)
statutory voluntary surrender before an offense is exposed (*Tang Code* 唐律疏議)
to turn oneself in to the police/authorities; (humorously) to own up to a mistake

morphemes.meaning: to confess guilt to authorities, turn in (originally "head")

自首.notes: Strictly a legal term for surrendering to police or prosecutors (投案自首), though speakers also use it playfully in everyday life ("I'm here to turn myself in—I ate your cake").

rootFamily.gloss: surrender and turn oneself in to the authorities
first of all, above all, to begin with

cognates.meaning: as for, when it comes to; to reach the point of (至る)

至于.etymology: A verb-preposition compound attested since the Pre-Qin classics (*Book of Documents* 尚书, *Analects* 论语, *Mencius* 孟子, traditionally written 至於), combining 至 (zhì, originally a pictograph of an arrow hitting the ground, meaning "to arrive at, reach, go so far as") and the classical locative/allative preposition 于 (於/于, yú, "at, in, to"). In Classical Chinese, 至於 literally meant "arriving at / reaching to [a place, degree, or new subject]"; through discourse topic-shifting ("coming now to the topic of X..."), it grammaticalized into a topic-introducing conjunction/preposition meaning "as for, when it comes to," while also retaining its degree sense in constructions like 不至于 ("not go so far as to").

history.meaning: to arrive at, reach; coming to the subject of (*Shangshu*, *Lunyu*, *Mengzi*)
to go so far as; as for, with regard to (introducing a new or secondary topic)
(prep./conj.) as for, when it comes to; (verb in 不至于/至于吗) to go so far as to

morphemes.meaning: to arrive at, reach, go so far as
to, at, with regard to (trad. 於)

至于.notes: Has two high-frequency uses: (1) sentence-initially to pivot to a new topic (至于那件事… "As for that matter…"), and (2) as a predicate verb questioning or denying an extreme reaction: 至于吗？ ("Is it really that serious / worth going that far?") and 不至于 ("it won't go that far").

rootFamily.gloss: so much so that, to the extent that (introducing a result)
even, so far as to (emphatic focus particle)
not go so far as to, hardly that bad

至关重要.etymology: Four-character degree-modified predicate phrase (Traditional: 至關重要) composed of 至 (zhì, 'to the utmost degree, supremely', originally an ideograph of an arrow striking the ground to signify reaching a terminus), 关 (guān, Trad. 關, 'to concern, hinge upon, bear upon', from the wooden crossbar of a frontier pass), and the coordinative adjective 重要 (zhòngyào, 'weighty and essential, important'). Literally 'to the utmost degree hinging upon what is weighty and essential'.

history.meaning: Classical Chinese elements meaning 'reaching the ultimate limit' and 'frontier pass; to pivot or bear upon'

history.form: 至關重要 / 至关重要 (zhìguānzhòngyào)
history.meaning: of supreme importance, crucially vital to an outcome

至关重要.notes: High-register expression common in news, business briefings, and formal drama dialogue; typically functions as a predicate (e.g., 这一点至关重要) or attributive modifier with 的.

至极.etymology: Coordinative compound (Traditional: 至極) uniting two synonymous morphemes of terminal limit: 至 (zhì, 'to arrive at the furthest point, utmost') and 极 (jí, Trad. 極, 'ridgepole at the highest peak of a roof; ultimate extremity, pole'). In Warring States philosophical prose (such as *Zhuangzi* and *Xunzi*), 至極 functioned as a noun or predicate meaning 'the ultimate apex or supreme limit'; in modern Mandarin, it grammaticalized primarily into a post-adjectival or post-verbal degree complement meaning 'to the utmost degree'.

history.meaning: the highest pinnacle, ultimate limit, or supreme principle
to the utmost degree, extremely (used post-verbally or post-adjectivally)

morphemes.meaning: arrive at the limit, utmost, supreme

至极.notes: Unlike pre-adjectival intensifiers such as 非常 or 极其, 至极 almost always follows the two-syllable adjective or psychological verb it intensifies without 得 (e.g., 感激至极 'grateful beyond measure', 荒谬至极 'utterly absurd').

舍不得.etymology: Potential verb complement construction formed from 舍 (捨, 'to give up, part with, abandon') + 不得 ('cannot, unable to bear'), meaning 'cannot bear to part with, begrudge spending or leaving'.

history.meaning: unable to bear parting with or using

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 舍不得 (via 萌典)

舍得.etymology: Verb-complement potential compound (Traditional: 捨得) formed from the transitive verb 舍 (shě, Trad. 捨, 'to let go, abandon, part with, give alms') followed by the modal/potential complement particle 得 (de, derived from the verb 得 dé 'to obtain, succeed in', marking feasibility or psychological willingness). Emerging in Song–Yuan vernacular Chinese alongside its negative counterpart 捨不得 (shěbude), it expresses having the emotional readiness to part with money, possessions, or attachments, and was further popularized as a philosophical noun compound ('giving up and gaining') in modern Buddhist-inflected proverbs.

history.meaning: to release from the hand, set aside, relinquish, give alms
able or willing in one's heart to part with or expend something
to be willing to part with, not begrudge spending or giving up

morphemes.meaning: to abandon, part with, give up (Trad. 捨)
potential/modal marker indicating willingness or ability

舍得.notes: Note the character merger and heteronym: 舍 as shě ('abandon, part with', Trad. 捨) must be distinguished from 舍 as shè ('dwelling, hostel', as in 宿舍). Its negative form 舍不得 ('cannot bear to part with') is even more frequent in everyday speech.

rootFamily.gloss: unable to bear parting with or leaving
to give up, abandon, cast aside
to sacrifice one's life for righteousness

cognates.meaning: to give up life and choose righteousness

舍生取义.etymology: Classical four-character idiom (成语, Traditional: 捨生取義) structured as two antithetical verb-object clauses in parallel coordination: 舍生 (shě shēng, 'relinquish life') + 取义 (qǔ yì, 'choose moral righteousness'). Directly condensed from *Mencius* (*Mengzi*, Book 6A *Gaozi I*): 「生，亦我所欲也；義，亦我所欲也。二者不可得兼，舍生而取義者也」 ('Life is what I desire, and righteousness is also what I desire; if I cannot have both, I will let go of life and choose righteousness'). In the received classical text, 舍 was already used as a phonetic loan for 捨.

history.form: 舍生而取義 (OC *l̥jAʔ sreng nji tshjoʔ ng(r)aj-s)
history.meaning: to let go of life and choose moral duty when the two conflict (*Mencius*)

history.form: 捨生取義 / 舍生取义 (shěshēngqǔyì)
history.meaning: to lay down one's life for a noble cause or moral principle

舍生取义.notes: A foundational Confucian ethical idiom learned by every Chinese student from Mencius's 'Fish and Bear's Paw' (鱼与熊掌) passage; used in elevated prose for heroic self-sacrifice.

rootFamily.gloss: to risk or sacrifice one's own life to save others
unflinching devotion to righteousness in the face of death

舒服.etymology: Compound adjective combining 舒 ('to unroll, stretch out, relax, ease') + 服 ('to submit, adapt, be accustomed to', neutral tone fú -> fu in Mandarin).

history.meaning: relaxed and at ease -> comfortable, feeling well

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 舒服 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: stage, theatrical setting, sphere of activity

舞台.etymology: Modifier-head noun compound (Traditional: 舞臺) combining 舞 (wǔ, 'to dance, posture with sleeves or plumes', originally a bronze-script pictograph of a person holding ox-tails or feathers in both hands) and 台 (tái, Trad. 臺, 'elevated earthen terrace or viewing platform'). First attested in Six Dynasties and Tang literary texts (such as Cao Zhi's prose and Tang court poetry) for a raised terrace built for ceremonial dances; in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, reinforced by Meiji Japanese *butai* (舞台), it broadened to mean any theatrical stage and metaphorically a public arena of action.

history.meaning: elevated open-air terrace constructed for court or ritual dance performances
theatrical performance stage; metaphorical arena for displaying talent or influence

舞台.notes: Used both literally for a physical theater or concert stage (走上舞台 'step onto the stage') and figuratively for a sphere of action (政治舞台 'the political arena', 人生舞台 'the stage of life').

舞台恐惧症.etymology: Modern compound noun (Traditional: 舞臺恐懼症) formed as a right-branching modifier-head calque of English *stage fright* integrated into modern Sino-medical nosology: 舞台 (wǔtái, 'performance stage') modifies 恐惧症 (kǒngjùzhèng, 'phobia, anxiety syndrome'). Within 恐惧症, the classical coordinative compound 恐惧 (kǒngjù, Trad. 恐懼, 'terror and dread') is nominalized by the medical suffix 症 (zhèng, 'pathological condition, syndrome', bearing the illness radical 疒 and phonetic 正, historically specialized from 證 'clinical symptom').

history.meaning: to fear and tremble with dread (classical coordinative verb)

history.form: 舞臺恐懼症 / 舞台恐惧症 (wǔtái kǒngjùzhèng)
history.meaning: stage fright, acute performance anxiety before an audience or camera

舞台恐惧症.notes: While 舞台恐惧症 sounds clinical or psychological (matching the `-症` phobia pattern like 幽闭恐惧症 'claustrophobia'), in everyday showbiz and rehearsal conversation people often use the punchy two-syllable VO verb 怯场 (qièchǎng, 'to get stage fright').

rootFamily.gloss: to have stage fright, be nervous on stage

cognates.meaning: class, sort, group; general (in 一般)

般.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining 舟 (zhōu, 'boat') and 殳 (shū, 'hand wielding a pole or implement to turn a vessel'). In Old and Middle Chinese, 般 (originally read pān/bān, cognate with 盤 'to turn round, transport') meant 'to pivot a boat, shift, distribute into classes'. During the Tang and Song dynasties, its vernacular classifier sense 'sort, category, manner' (as in 一般 'the same sort', 這般 'this manner') grammaticalized into a postnominal similative particle (`Noun + 般`) meaning 'like, -like, after the manner of'.

history.meaning: to turn round, transport by boat; to cycle or distribute
sort, kind, manner, way (classifier in Tang–Song vernacular)
postnominal particle meaning 'like, -like, sort of' (often paired with 像 or 如)

morphemes.meaning: sort, kind, manner; postnominal similative marker '-like, as if'

般.notes: As a similative enclitic, 般 attaches directly after a noun phrase (often introduced by 像 or 如) to form vivid imagery: 像梦一般 ('like a dream'), 钢铁般的意志 ('an iron-like will'), 闪电般的速度 ('lightning-like speed').

rootFamily.gloss: ordinary, general; the same as (literally 'one sort')
in this way, such, to this extent
in a hundred ways, by every possible means

cognates.meaning: performer, entertainer, accomplished artist in traditional arts

艺人.etymology: Modifier-head compound (Traditional: 藝人) composed of 艺 (yì, Trad. 藝, 'cultivated skill, craft, performance art', evolving from the oracle-bone and bronze-script graph 埶 depicting a kneeling person planting a sapling with both hands, later augmented with 艸 'plant' and 云) and 人 (rén, 'person'). In Classical Chinese (*Book of Documents*, *Mencius*), 藝人 denoted persons accomplished in the Six Arts (六藝) or skilled craftsmen; from the Song–Yuan urban theater era through modern media, it specialized to refer to stage performers, actors, singers, and agency-managed entertainment talent.

history.meaning: person accomplished in the Six Arts, ritual skills, or specialized crafts
professional storyteller, opera actor, or folk performer in urban entertainment quarters (瓦舍)
performing artist, celebrity, or entertainment-industry talent (actor, singer, idol)

艺人.notes: In contemporary Mandarin media and showbiz, 艺人 specifically means an entertainer or celebrity talent (actors, pop singers, variety stars) signed to an agency, whereas a fine artist (painter, sculptor) is called 艺术家 (yìshùjiā).

rootFamily.gloss: entertainment and performing arts; show business
outstanding maestro or fine artist (painter, musician, sculptor)
folk craftsman or traditional master performer

艺人总监.etymology: Modern entertainment-industry modifier-head title (Traditional: 藝人總監) combining 艺人 (yìrén, 'performing artist, managed entertainment talent') with 总监 (zǒngjiān, Trad. 總監, 'chief director, head supervisor'). The title 總監 originated in Sui, Tang, and Ming imperial bureaucracy—formed from 总 (zǒng, 'to gather together, overall, chief') modifying 监 (jiān, 'to oversee, inspect; royal directorate', originally depicting a person bending over a basin of water to examine their reflection)—and was revived in late 20th-century corporate Chinese to translate English *director* (as in *creative director*, *talent director*).

history.meaning: imperial chief overseer of a military campaign or court directorate (Sui–Tang–Ming)

history.form: 藝人總監 / 艺人总监 (yìrén zǒngjiān)
history.meaning: head of artist management or talent director in a media company or television production

morphemes.meaning: performing artist, entertainment talent (Trad. 藝人)

艺人总监.notes: A signature corporate title in Chinese entertainment agencies and variety-show studios (like in *Behind the Scenes* / 《幕后之王》), responsible for booking, negotiating with, and managing celebrity talent (艺人统筹/艺人经纪).

rootFamily.gloss: executive producer, chief supervisor of a film/show

艺术.etymology: Coordinative compound (Traditional: 藝術) joining 艺 (yì, Trad. 藝, 'horticultural planting skill; cultivated accomplishment, liberal art') and 术 (shù, Trad. 術, 'avenue inside a settlement [行 + phonetic 朮]; method, technique, specialized discipline'). First attested in the *Book of Later Han* (《後漢書·伏湛傳》) for scholarly erudition, technical crafts, medicine, and divination; during the Meiji period, Japanese scholars repurposed 芸術 (*geijutsu*) to translate Western aesthetic *art* / *fine arts*, and this modern sense was re-imported into Chinese as an orthographic return loan in the late 19th century.

history.meaning: cultivated scholarly disciplines, practical crafts, and technical methods (*Book of Later Han*)

history.form: 芸術 (Japanese geijutsu) → 藝術 / 艺术 (yìshù)
history.meaning: aesthetic fine arts and creative expression (semantic return loan via Meiji Japanese)

艺术.notes: Functions both as a noun ('art, the arts', e.g., 行为艺术 'performance art') and as an adjective meaning 'artistic, tastefully designed, or tactful' (e.g., 他说话很艺术 'he speaks very tactfully').

节外生枝.etymology: Four-character botanical metaphor (成语, Traditional: 節外生枝) structured as a locative-verb-object clause: 节外 (jié wài, 'outside the natural node/joint of a bamboo stalk or tree trunk') + 生 (shēng, 'sprouts, gives rise to') + 枝 (zhī, 'side branches or twigs'). Because bamboo and timber normally branch only at their nodes (節), sprouting twigs outside a joint represents an abnormal, superfluous offshoot. Popularized in Song dynasty Neo-Confucian and Chan Buddhist discourse (notably Zhu Xi's *Zhuzi Yulei* 《朱子語類》) to criticize proliferating side-arguments, and later generalized to mean causing unnecessary new complications.

history.meaning: sprouting side-branches outside a node; generating superfluous doctrinal offshoots (*Zhuzi Yulei*)

history.form: 節外生枝 / 节外生枝 (jiéwàishēngzhī)
history.meaning: to deliberately raise new obstacles or have unexpected complications arise when a matter is nearly settled

morphemes.meaning: bamboo joint, node, regular division (Trad. 節)
to grow, sprout, give rise to

节外生枝.notes: Frequently used in warnings or workplace strategy (e.g., 免得节外生枝 'lest extra complications arise', 不要节外生枝 'don't complicate matters further') when a deal or production plan is close to completion.

rootFamily.gloss: minor details, side issues (literally 'branch tips and bamboo joints')
critical juncture, decisive link or stage
complex and tangled (like twisted roots and gnarled joints)

节奏.etymology: Classical musical compound of 节 ('bamboo node; regular metrical division', bamboo radical 竹 + 即, because bamboo joints divide a stalk into measured intervals) + 奏 ('perform music, advance in time').

morphemes.meaning: bamboo joint; regular beat or measure

history.meaning: measured pauses and movement in music and ritual
musical rhythm; tempo; pace

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 节奏

cognates.meaning: constancy, chastity, moral integrity, fidelity to principle

节操.etymology: Coordinative compound (Traditional: 節操) combining 节 (jié, Trad. 節, 'bamboo node; moral restraint and unwavering integrity', metaphorically drawn from the rigid structural joints that keep bamboo upright in winter) and 操 (cāo, 'that which the hand grasps firmly; personal conduct, steadfast principle'). Attested since the Han dynasty (e.g., Ban Gu's *Book of Han* 《漢書》) for uncompromising moral rectitude. In 21st-century Chinese internet and ACG subculture, influenced by ironic Japanese slang usage of *sessō*, it underwent playful semantic amelioration/inversion to mean 'one's filter, sense of shame, or dignified restraint'.

history.meaning: unwavering moral integrity, chastity of principle, and ethical constancy (*Book of Han*)
high moral integrity (formal); playful dignity, personal filter, or sense of shame (colloquial/internet)

morphemes.meaning: bamboo joint; moral restraint, integrity (Trad. 節)
what one holds fast to; personal conduct, principle

节操.notes: Exhibits a striking register split: in formal prose it means 'sterling moral integrity' (高尚的节操), whereas in colloquial media and youth slang it is used humorously for losing one's dignity or filter for laughs or ratings (掉节操 'lose one's shame', 节操碎了一地 'dignity shattered all over the floor').

rootFamily.gloss: high moral integrity and unyielding courage

节日.etymology: Combines 节 (jié, 'joint, node') and 日 (rì, 'day'). 节 originally denoted the nodes of a bamboo stalk, extending metaphorically to significant temporal nodes or divisions in the calendar. A 节日 is a nodal point of celebration in the rhythmic cycle of the year.

history.meaning: festival day
holiday; festival

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 节日

cognates.meaning: item on a performance bill, act, program

节目.etymology: Coordinative compound (Traditional: 節目) uniting 节 (jié, Trad. 節, 'bamboo joint, section, segment') and 目 (mù, 'eye; mesh of a net; item, entry, or sub-heading on a list'). In Six Dynasties and Song Literary Chinese (e.g., *Book of Southern Qi* and Zhu Xi's writings, where 綱領 'main headrope' contrasts with 節目 'individual knots and meshes'), it meant 'specific clauses, subdivisions, or itemized entries'. In the 20th century, this 'item on a list/bill' sense was applied to theatrical playbills and broadcasting schedules, yielding 'stage act' and 'radio/television program or show'.

history.meaning: knots of a net or joints of timber; itemized clauses, subdivisions, or detailed particulars
individual performance act on a bill; radio, television, or streaming program/show

morphemes.meaning: eye; itemized entry, heading, list item

节目.notes: Covers both an entire broadcast show (一档电视节目 'a TV show', 综艺节目 'variety show') and a single performance number within an event (演出节目 'a performance item on the program'). In colloquial idiom, 很有节目 can also mean 'full of antics/entertainment'.

rootFamily.gloss: catalog, table of contents, directory list
repertoire of plays or performance programs

cognates.meaning: to host a program (chủ trì tiết mục)

节目主持.etymology: Modifier-head / OV compound (Traditional: 節目主持) formed from 节目 (jiémù, 'stage, radio, or television program') and 主持 (zhǔchí, 'to preside over, take charge of; host'). The word 主持 is itself a coordinative verbal compound (主 zhǔ 'to be master of, lead' + 持 chí 'to hold up, maintain, manage') that originated in Tang–Song Chinese Buddhism as a monastic title and verb for an abbot presiding over a temple and upholding the Dharma, before secularizing in modern Chinese to mean chairing a meeting or hosting a broadcast program.

history.meaning: to uphold the Buddhist Dharma and preside as head abbot of a monastery (Tang–Song)

history.form: 節目主持 / 节目主持 (jiémù zhǔchí)
history.meaning: hosting a broadcast or stage show; a show host or television presenter (short for 节目主持人)

morphemes.meaning: broadcast or stage program (Trad. 節目)

节目主持.notes: Can refer either to the profession/discipline of hosting (学习节目主持 'study program hosting') or directly to the host as a person (担任节目主持 'serve as the show host'), alongside the fuller agentive form 节目主持人.

rootFamily.gloss: to preside over, take charge of, chair; host

节目组.etymology: Modifier-head institutional compound (Traditional: 節目組) combining 节目 (jiémù, 'television, radio, or streaming program') with the organizational suffix 组 (zǔ, Trad. 組, 'team, unit, crew, section'). In Old and Middle Chinese, 組 (combining the silk radical 糸 with phonetic 且 qiě) denoted a woven silk cord or ribbon used to bind hair or jade pendants; from the semantic extension 'to weave together, organize' (组织), 组 developed in 20th-century administrative and media Mandarin into a productive bound noun for a specialized working group or production unit.

history.meaning: woven silk cord or sash; to braid or bind together
the dedicated production team or crew behind a specific television or variety show

morphemes.meaning: team, crew, unit, working group (Trad. 組)

节目组.notes: In Chinese variety shows and reality TV, 节目组 is constantly referenced on-screen (often personified as an adversary or prankster to the cast) to distinguish a variety/reality show's crew from a scripted drama or film crew, which is called 剧组 (jùzǔ).

rootFamily.gloss: cast and crew of a scripted drama, film, or play
directorial team (chief director and assistant directors)

cognates.meaning: flower; to spend (in 화비 花費)

花.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining the grass/plant radical 艹 (艸, cǎo) with the phonetic component 化 (huà, OC *qʷʰˤrar-s, 'to transform'). In pre-Qin Old Chinese, 'flower, blossom' was written  or 華 (OC *N-qʷʰˤra); during the Han and Six Dynasties periods, 花 was coined to represent the colloquial pronunciation specifically for 'blossom', leaving 華 (huá) for 'splendor, China'. From the visual imagery of multi-colored petals scattering in the wind, Ming–Qing vernacular Chinese developed the transitive verb sense 'to scatter, expend, spend (money, time, or energy)'.

history.meaning: blossom, flower of a plant; variegated pattern or ornament
to scatter, dissipate, expend (money, time, or effort); blurred (of vision)
noun: flower, blossom; verb: to spend or expend (money, time, effort)

morphemes.meaning: flower, blossom; variegated; to spend (money or time)

花.notes: A high-frequency polysemous word: as a noun it means 'flower/blossom' (鲜花), as an adjective 'multicolored/patterned, blurred, or playboy-ish' (眼花了, 花心), and as a transitive verb 'to spend money or time' (花时间, 花了不少心血).

rootFamily.gloss: to spend money, expend; expenses, costs

花园.etymology: Modifier-head noun compound combining 花 ('flower, blossom') + 园 (園, 'walled garden, orchard, park').

history.meaning: flower garden, garden

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 花园 (via 萌典)

花摊.etymology: Modifier-head noun compound combining 花 ('flower') + 摊 (攤, 'spread-out market stall, vendor stand').

history.meaning: flower stall, florist stand

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 花摊 (via 萌典)

花瓶.etymology: Determinative compound of 花 ('flower; blossom', grass radical 艹 + phonetic 化 *huà*) + 瓶 ('vase; narrow-necked vessel', phonetic 并 *bìng* + tile/pottery radical 瓦). Used since Song and Ming interior aesthetics for porcelain or glass vessels holding cut flowers or green leaves.

history.meaning: porcelain or bronze flower vase
flower vase

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 花瓶

花盆.etymology: Compound of 花 ('blossom, flower', grass/plant radical 艹 + phonetic 化) + 盆 ('basin, pot', phonetic 分 atop 皿 'vessel/dish').

history.meaning: ceramic or terracotta flowerpot
flowerpot

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 花盆 (via 萌典)

花絮.etymology: Metaphorical compound noun (Traditional: 花絮) composed of 花 (huā, 'blossoms, flowering plants') and 絮 (xù, originally 'coarse silk wadding or raw cotton batting' from 如 + 糸, extended in Six Dynasties and Tang poetry to fluffy airborne plant catkins, especially willow catkins 柳絮). In Tang–Song verse (e.g., Su Shi's poetry), 花絮 literally described drifting spring blossoms and willow fluff. In early 20th-century Chinese journalism, columns of light, colourful side-notes floating around major news stories were christened 花絮, which then specialized in film and television for 'behind-the-scenes clips, outtakes, and making-of highlights'.

history.meaning: drifting flower petals and fluffy willow catkins in spring (Tang–Song poetry)
light, colourful journalistic sidelights and miscellaneous tidbits accompanying a major event (Republican press)
behind-the-scenes footage, making-of clips, bloopers, and outtakes in media production

morphemes.meaning: silk wadding; fluffy willow catkins drifting in the air

花絮.notes: Essential media and showbiz vocabulary: 幕后花絮 (mùhòu huāxù) is the standard term for 'behind-the-scenes featurettes / making-of clips', while 搞笑花絮 or NG花絮 refers specifically to 'blooper reels / outtakes'.

rootFamily.gloss: willow catkins drifting in spring wind
verbose, long-winded and repetitive in speech (like endless cotton fibers)

花草.etymology: Coordinate collective noun combining 花 ('flowers, blossoms') + 草 ('grasses, herbaceous plants').

history.meaning: flowers and plants, garden flora

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 花草 (via 萌典)

花钱.etymology: Verb-object (VO) separable compound (Traditional: 花錢) formed from the vernacular verb 花 (huā, 'to spend, expend, scatter') and its direct object 钱 (qián, Trad. 錢, 'money, coin'). In Old Chinese, 錢 (combining the metal radical 金 with phonetic 戔 jiān 'small, thin') originally denoted an agricultural digging spade; because miniature bronze spades (布幣) and later round bronze cash coins served as currency in the Zhou and Qin–Han periods, 錢 became the standard generic word for 'copper coin, money'. Combined with 花 in Ming–Qing vernacular, 花錢 became the everyday expression for spending money.

history.meaning: bronze agricultural spade; cast bronze coin currency
to spend money, disburse funds (separable verb-object compound)

花钱.notes: Grammatically a classic separable verb (离合词): aspect markers, modifiers, and amounts are inserted between 花 and 钱 rather than after the compound (e.g., 花了很多钱 'spent a lot of money', 钱花光了 'the money is all spent').

rootFamily.gloss: daily expenses, outlay; to spend money

cognates.meaning: carbonated water, club soda (source of phonetic loan + calque)

苏打水.etymology: Hybrid phonetic-loan and semantic-head compound (Traditional: 蘇打水) combining 苏打 (sūdǎ, Trad. 蘇打, a late Qing / early Republican phonetic transcription of English *soda*, ultimately from Medieval Latin and Italian *soda* 'glasswort/saltwort plant burned for sodium carbonate ash', likely from Arabic *suwwād*) with the native head noun 水 (shuǐ, 'water, liquid beverage'). Constructed on the exact structural model of English *soda water* (and parallel to Meiji Japanese 曹達水 / ソーダ水 *sōdasui*).

history.meaning: effervescent water charged with carbon dioxide or sodium bicarbonate (late 19th–early 20th c. port-city loan)
soda water, club soda, sparkling water, or weakly alkaline bicarbonate water

morphemes.meaning: soda, sodium carbonate/bicarbonate (from English 'soda', Trad. 蘇打)

苏打水.notes: In contemporary mainland China, 苏打水 often refers specifically to unflavored or lightly flavored weakly alkaline sodium bicarbonate water (which may even be non-carbonated 无气苏打水), whereas fizzy carbonated water is increasingly called 气泡水 (qìpàoshuǐ, 'sparkling water').

rootFamily.gloss: sparkling water, fizzy drink, soda pop

苦.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining the grass/plant radical 艹 (艸, cǎo) with the phonetic component 古 (gǔ, OC *kˤaʔ). Inherited from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *k(r)a-n ('bitter; liver/gall', cognate with Tibetan *kha-ba* 'bitter'). In the *Shuowen Jiezi* and early Zhou texts (*Classic of Poetry* 《詩經》), 苦 specifically named a bitter-tasting wild herb (sow thistle, *Sonchus oleraceus*, glossed as 大苦) as well as the basic gustatory quality 'bitter' (one of the Five Flavors 五味). Already in Old Chinese, it extended metaphorically to 'painful, grueling, suffering' and adverbially to 'painstakingly, to the point of hardship' ( further reinforced by Buddhist translations where 苦 rendered Sanskrit *duḥkha* 'suffering').

history.meaning: sow thistle (a bitter herb); bitter in taste; coarse or defective (of crafted goods)
bitter; physical or existential suffering (translating Sanskrit duḥkha); painstakingly, earnestly
bitter in taste; tough, arduous, painful; to suffer from or agonize over

morphemes.meaning: bitter; painful, tough, arduous; hardship; painstakingly

苦.notes: Bridges sensory taste and emotional/physical endurance: 吃苦 (chīkǔ, literally 'eat bitterness') is a core cultural concept praising the ability to endure hardship and grueling work without complaint.

rootFamily.gloss: to endure hardship, bear tough conditions ('eat bitterness')

苦心人.etymology: Modifier-head noun compound formed from 苦心 (kǔxīn, 'a heart-mind taxed with painstaking care and arduous devotion', itself a modifier-head/psych-predicate compound from 苦 'bitter, painstakingly taxed' + 心 'heart-mind') modifying 人 (rén, 'person'). While 苦心 appears in Tang poetry and Ming prose for 'painstaking effort or well-meaning intent', the three-character noun 苦心人 was immortalized in Chinese cultural memory by the Qing dynasty author Pu Songling (蒲松齡, 1640–1715) in his self-encouragement couplet: 「苦心人、天不負，臥薪嘗膽，三千越甲可吞吳」 ('Heaven never disappoints a person of painstaking devotion...').

history.meaning: a mind taxed with painstaking effort or earnest, well-meaning care
a person who pours painstaking effort and perseverance into a goal (immortalized by Pu Songling's couplet)
history.stage: Early Mandarin (Qing Dynasty) to Modern Mandarin

morphemes.meaning: heart, mind, mental effort and intention

苦心人.notes: Almost always evokes the famous proverb 皇天不负苦心人 or 天不负苦心人 ('Heaven never lets down a person who pours painstaking effort into their goal'), used to comfort or praise someone whose long backstage grind finally pays off.

rootFamily.gloss: painstaking effort, earnest and well-meaning intent (as in 一片苦心)
to take great pains, rack one's brains with painstaking care
earnestly and with painstaking solicitude (of advice)

苦情.etymology: Modifier-head noun/attributive compound (Traditional: 苦情) combining 苦 (kǔ, 'bitter, sorrowful, agonizing') and 情 (qíng, 'emotion, feeling, romantic attachment; plight, circumstances'). In traditional Literary Chinese, 苦情 meant 'bitter plight, distressing circumstances, or aggrieved feelings' (a sense preserved in Japanese *kujō* 苦情 'customer complaint, grievance'). In 20th-century Taiwanese Hokkien pop culture (*khó͘-chêng*) and Mandarin film, television, and music criticism, it specialized to denote tear-jerking, melodramatically sorrowful, or star-crossed emotional narratives and personas.

history.meaning: bitter plight, distressing personal circumstances, or aggrieved feelings
tearful heartbreak, melodramatic sorrow, or tragic emotional narrative (in TV dramas, songs, and character tropes)

苦情.notes: Beware the false friend with Japanese: in Japanese, 苦情 (*kujō*) means a formal 'complaint or grievance', whereas in modern Mandarin media and showbiz, 苦情 means 'tear-jerking, melodramatic heartbreak' (e.g., 苦情戏 'tearjerker melodrama', 苦情歌 'sad heartbreak ballad', 卖苦情 'play the sob-story card on a reality show').

英式.etymology: Modifier-head attributive compound composed of 英 (Yīng, clipped exonym for 英国 Yīngguó 'Britain, England', which is itself shortened from the Qing-dynasty phonetic transcription 英吉利 Yīngjílì for *English* / *England*, selecting the character 英 'flower blossom; outstanding hero') and the bound nominal/attributive root 式 (shì, 'model, pattern, style, ceremony, formula', originally a carpenter's rule or ritual standard in Old Chinese). Literally 'patterned after the British model; British-style'.

history.meaning: phonetic transcription of 'English/England' shortened to the country prefix 英- (18th–19th c.)
British-style, following British standards, customs, or pronunciation

morphemes.meaning: Britain, England, British (short for 英国)

英式.notes: A non-predicative adjective (区别词) that modifies nouns directly without 的 in fixed collocations: 英式英语 ('British English'), 英式下午茶 ('British afternoon tea'), 英式摇滚 ('Britpop / British rock'), contrasting with 美式 (měishì, 'American-style').

rootFamily.gloss: American-style (as in 美式咖啡 'Americano', 美式英语 'American English')

cognates.meaning: English writing, English text or sentence

英文.etymology: Modifier-head noun compound combining 英 (Yīng, abbreviation of 英国 Yīngguó / 英吉利 Yīngjílì 'England, Britain', originally a character meaning 'flower blossom; outstanding talent' adopted in the Qing dynasty to transcribe the first syllable of *Eng-land*) and 文 (wén, 'written graph, script, language, literary text', originally an oracle-bone pictograph of a standing figure with a tattooed or painted pattern on the chest). While 文 originally contrasted written script with 語 (yǔ, 'spoken language'), in modern Chinese 英文 encompasses the English language in both written and spoken mediums.

history.meaning: written English script and texts (contrasting with 英語 for spoken English)
the English language (written or spoken), English text

morphemes.meaning: Britain, England, English (short for 英国/英吉利)

英文.notes: In everyday speech (especially in Taiwan, Hong Kong, and casual mainland conversation), 英文 and 英语 (Yīngyǔ) are largely interchangeable for 'the English language' (e.g., 说英文 'speak English'), though 英文 is mandatory when referring specifically to written letters or text (英文字母 'English alphabet', 英文歌 'song in English').

rootFamily.gloss: the English language (especially spoken or as an academic subject)

苹果.etymology: Compound noun combining 苹 (蘋, 'apple', adapted in Ming dynasty from Buddhist Sanskrit transcription 頻婆 / 蘋婆 bimbā 'bright red fruit', reapplied to Malus pumila) + 果 ('fruit').

history.meaning: apple

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 苹果 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: bimba fruit, Momordica monadelpha (source of 頻婆/蘋果 via Buddhist translation)
apple juice (using Sino-Korean 과즙 果汁)

苹果汁.etymology: Left-branching modifier-head noun compound (Traditional: 蘋果汁) composed of 苹果 (píngguǒ, Trad. 蘋果, 'apple') + 汁 (zhī, 'juice, expressed liquid, broth', formed from the water radical 氵 and phonetic 十 shí). The word 蘋果 itself has a remarkable Buddhist Silk Road etymology: whereas ancient indigenous Chinese crabapples were called 柰 (nài) or 林檎 (línqín), Ming-dynasty speakers adapted 頻婆果 (pínpóguǒ)—a Tang Buddhist transcription of Sanskrit *bimba(phala)* ('bright red *Momordica monadelpha* fruit', famous from the idiom *bimba-like red lips*)—and reshaped it with the plant radical into 蘋果 for the large sweet apple.

history.form: 頻婆 (MC bjin bwa ← Sanskrit bimba) → 蘋果 (Ming Mandarin píngguǒ)
history.meaning: red bimba fruit in Buddhist sutras, transferred and graphically reshaped in the Ming dynasty to denote the sweet orchard apple
history.stage: Middle Chinese to Early Mandarin (Ming Dynasty)

history.meaning: apple juice (pressed liquid from apples)

morphemes.meaning: apple (Trad. 蘋果, from Buddhist Sanskrit transcription 頻婆 + 果 'fruit')

苹果汁.notes: The productive suffix 汁 (zhī) forms any fruit or vegetable juice (`Fruit + 汁`): 橙汁 (chéngzhī, 'orange juice'), 芒果汁 (mángguǒzhī, 'mango juice'), 果汁 (guǒzhī, 'fruit juice').

rootFamily.gloss: apple (the fruit or the tech brand Apple)

范围.etymology: Coordinative compound (Traditional: 範圍) combining 范 (fàn, Trad. 範, 'bamboo or clay outer mold used for casting bronze; model, rule, to cast or bound', distinct from the surname 范 which was merged into it in simplification) and 围 (wéi, Trad. 圍, 'to surround, enclose, measure the circumference of'). Originating in the *Book of Changes* (《易經·繫辭上》: 「範圍天地之化而不過」—'molding and encompassing the transformations of Heaven and Earth without excess'), where it functioned as a transitive coordinative verb ('to cast in a mold and circumscribe'); in the late 19th century, reinforced by Meiji Japanese *han'i* (範囲), it crystallized into the standard modern noun for 'scope, range, or bounds'.

history.form: 範圍 (OC *bomʔ ɢʷəj / MC bjomX hjwij)
history.meaning: to mold and encompass, to circumscribe within a model or boundary (*Yijing*, *Xici I*)

history.form: 範囲 (Japanese han'i) → 範圍 / 范围 (fànwéi)
history.meaning: noun: scope, range, extent, sphere, or limits within which something operates or applies

morphemes.meaning: casting mold, model, boundary; to mold or limit (Trad. 範)
to surround, enclose; circumference, perimeter (Trad. 圍)

范围.notes: Frequently framed by spatial postpositions like 在……范围之内 ('within the scope of...') or 超出……范围 ('exceed the scope/bounds of...'), e.g., 业务范围 ('business scope'), 职权范围 ('scope of authority').

rootFamily.gloss: category, conceptual domain or sphere (also from the *Shujing*)

茶.etymology: Mandarin word for 'tea' (chá), written with 艹 ('plant'), 人, and 木 ('tree'). Prior to the Mid-Tang dynasty, tea was written with the shared bitter-herb graph 荼 (tú); tea master Lu Yu's Classic of Tea (Cha Jing, c. 760) popularized removing one horizontal stroke to establish 茶—the ancestor of English 'tea' (via Hokkien tê) and 'chai' (via northern chá).

history.meaning: bitter herb; tea plant

history.stage: Tang dynasty (Lu Yu, Cha Jing, c. 760)
history.meaning: tea

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 茶 (via 萌典)

茶叙.etymology: Refined compound noun/verb from 茶 ('tea') + 叙 (simplified from 敘, 'chat; recount; converse in order'). Originating in literary and diplomatic gatherings where hosts and guests converse informally over tea and light pastries rather than a formal banquet.

history.meaning: converse with guests over tea
tea gathering; tea social; chat over tea

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 茶叙

茶壶.etymology: Modifier-head noun compound combining 茶 ('tea', differentiated in Tang dynasty from 荼 tú 'bitter herb') + 壶 (壺, 'pot, kettle, lidded vessel with a spout').

history.meaning: teapot

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 茶壶 (via 萌典)

茶室.etymology: Modifier-head noun compound combining 茶 ('tea') + 室 ('room, chamber, house').

history.meaning: tearoom, teahouse

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 茶室 (via 萌典)

茶杯.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 茶 ('tea', graphically split from 荼 tú during the Tang dynasty around Lu Yu's Classic of Tea) + 杯 ('cup'), naming a vessel dedicated to hot tea.

history.form: 茶瓯 / 茶盏 / 茶杯
history.meaning: tea bowl or teacup
teacup

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 茶杯 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: tea and water; liquid tea served to guests

茶水.etymology: Dual-structure compound noun composed of 茶 (chá, 'tea plant and leaf', graphically created in the mid-Tang dynasty around Lu Yu's *Classic of Tea* 《茶經》 by removing one horizontal stroke from 荼 tú 'bitter herb') and 水 (shuǐ, 'water, liquid beverage'). Structurally, 茶水 operates both as a modifier-head compound ('tea-water, brewed liquid tea') and as a coordinative compound ('tea and boiled water; basic drinks and hospitality refreshments provided to guests, performers, or workers').

history.meaning: tea plant and brewed infusion (orthographically distinguished from 荼 in the Tang dynasty)
brewed liquid tea; tea and hot water served as hospitality refreshments or workplace provisions

茶水.notes: In hospitality, film sets, and offices, 准备茶水 means 'prepare tea, water, and light beverages for guests/crew'. Historically, 茶水费 ('tea-and-water fee') was a cover fee at teahouses, and colloquially a euphemism for a small tip or kickback.

rootFamily.gloss: tea leaves (dry tea prior to brewing)
refreshments, tea and pastries served at a conference or reception

茶水间.etymology: Modifier-head spatial compound (Traditional: 茶水間) combining 茶水 (cháshuǐ, 'tea and boiled water, beverages and refreshments') with the locative room-noun 间 (jiān, Trad. 間, 'space between, room, compartment', originally an ideograph of moonlight ⽉/日 shining through the gap of a double door 門). Originally designating the service room or boiler pantry in traditional government offices, theaters, and railway cars where attendants boiled water and brewed tea, it evolved in modern corporate architecture into the standard term for an office pantry or employee break room.

history.meaning: crevice between doors; interval, bay between pillars, room or compartment
pantry for boiling water and brewing tea; modern corporate office pantry or break room equipped with coffee, tea, and snacks

morphemes.meaning: tea and water, beverages and refreshments

茶水间.notes: In Chinese workplace dramas (like *Behind the Scenes* / 《幕后之王》), the 茶水间 is the archetypal water-cooler setting where colleagues bump into each other, vent, or overhear office gossip. Note how `-间` forms compact functional rooms: 洗手间 ('restroom'), 更衣间 ('changing room'), 直播间 ('livestream studio').

茶碟.etymology: Modifier-head noun compound combining 茶 ('tea') + 碟 ('small shallow plate, saucer', stone/ceramic radical 石 + phonetic 枼 yè).

history.meaning: tea saucer

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 茶碟 (via 萌典)

茶艺师.etymology: Modifier-head occupational compound (Traditional: 茶藝師) composed of 茶艺 (cháyì, Trad. 茶藝, 'the art and aesthetic ritual of tea brewing and appreciation') and the professional agentive suffix 师 (shī, Trad. 師, 'master, teacher, certified specialist', originally a military garrison or court tutor in Old Chinese). The term 茶藝 was coined in Taiwan in the late 1970s (popularized by folklorist Lou Tsu-k'uang and tea scholars) to revive Chinese tea culture with a less rigid, more accessible native term than Japanese-associated 茶道 (*chadō*), and 茶艺师 was subsequently standardized in mainland China in 1999 as an officially certified national profession.

history.meaning: the aesthetic art, technique, and cultural appreciation of preparing and serving tea
certified tea master or tea-ceremony specialist skilled in tea selection, brewing aesthetics, and tea culture

morphemes.meaning: master, teacher, certified professional specialist (Trad. 師)

茶艺师.notes: Parallels other modern lifestyle and culinary specialist titles built with `-师`: 咖啡师 (kāfēishī, 'barista'), 调酒师 (tiáojiǔshī, 'bartender/mixologist'), 侍酒师 (shìjiǔshī, 'sommelier').

rootFamily.gloss: the art of tea brewing and appreciation, tea ceremony
the Way of Tea, traditional tea ceremony philosophy

茶艺社.etymology: Modifier-head institutional compound (Traditional: 茶藝社) combining 茶艺 (cháyì, Trad. 茶藝, 'art of tea, tea-ceremony aesthetics') with 社 (shè, 'association, society, club, cultural establishment'). In Old Chinese, 社 (composed of the altar radical 示 shì and 土 tǔ 'earth') denoted the communal altar to the god of the soil and the local village community gathered around it; by the Tang–Song era, 社 had broadened to mean guilds, literary societies (詩社), and specialized cultural establishments. Thus 茶艺社 denotes either a refined traditional teahouse dedicated to tea-art appreciation or a tea-ceremony club/society.

history.meaning: altar of the god of the soil; local community, guild, or literary society (詩社, 茶社)
traditional-style teahouse specializing in the art of tea, or a tea-ceremony club/society

morphemes.meaning: society, club, guild, cultural establishment (originally 'altar of the soil god')

茶艺社.notes: Unlike a noisy neighborhood mahjong/chatting teahouse (茶馆 cháguǎn) or a Cantonese dim-sum restaurant (茶楼 chálóu), a 茶艺社 (or 茶艺馆) emphasizes quiet ambience, gongfu tea ceremonies, and private rooms for quiet conversation or business meetings—or, on university campuses, a student tea-art club.

rootFamily.gloss: the art of tea, tea ceremony aesthetics
traditional teahouse (for socializing, storytelling, or drinking tea)

荆棘.etymology: A coordinative compound (联合式) pairing 荆 (jīng, chaste tree or vitex shrub used for switches) and 棘 (jí, sour jujube bush or thorny bramble, pictogram of doubled thorn-trees 朿). Attested in Classical Chinese (e.g., *Zuo Zhuan* and *Mengzi*) for dense, spiky undergrowth blocking untamed land, it evolved metaphorically to denote formidable obstacles and trials along a career or life path.

history.meaning: thorny shrubs, vitex and jujube brambles overgrowing wasteland
besetting obstacles, hardships, and perilous circumstances
thorns, brambles; figurative trials and tribulations

荆棘.notes: Commonly appears in the four-character idiom 披荆斩棘 (pī jīng zhǎn jí, 'to hack through thorns and brambles'), a staple metaphor in media and drama for overcoming career adversity.

rootFamily.gloss: to hack through thorns and brambles; to overcome obstacles
proffering a birch switch to ask forgiveness; humble apology

cognates.meaning: panicking at every shadow; extreme paranoia
fearing every blade of grass and tree as an enemy soldier

草木皆兵.etymology: A four-character historical idiom (成语) structured as a subject-predicate clause: 草木 ('grass and trees', coordinative noun phrase) + 皆 ('all', adverb) + 兵 ('soldiers/weapons', predicate noun). Originating in the *Book of Jin* (*晋书·苻坚载记*), after Former Qin ruler Fu Jian's rout at the Battle of Fei River (383 CE), he looked up at Mount Bagong and mistook the swaying vegetation for pursuing Jin troops.

history.meaning: every grass and tree on Mount Bagong appears to be an enemy soldier
state of extreme paranoia and panic in which harmless signs seem threatening

草木皆兵.notes: Frequently paired with 风声鹤唳 (fēngshēng hèlì, 'the whistling wind and crying cranes') to describe PR crises or workplace paranoia when rumors sweep through a production team.

rootFamily.gloss: panicked by the sound of wind and cranes; jittery with fear
military troops and horses; armed forces

草本.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 草本. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 草本 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 草本 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 草本 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 草本. The etymology of 草本 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 草本
middle form of 草本
modern form of 草本

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 草本

草率.etymology: A coordinative compound (联合式) combining 草 (cǎo, 'grass', extended to 'rough, coarse, unrefined', as in cursive script 草书) and 率 (shuài/lǜ, 'rash, hasty, unceremonious', as in 轻率). Used in Literary Chinese to describe actions or writings executed hurriedly without proper care or polish, it remains standard in modern Mandarin for sloppy decision-making.

history.meaning: coarse and unceremonious; executed without proper deliberation
hasty, careless, slapdash, perfunctory

草率.notes: Often modifies verbs of decision or closure as an adverbial phrase, e.g., 草率决定 (decide hastily) or 草率收场 (wind up a project or show sloppily).

草稿.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正式) in which 草 (cǎo, originally 'grass', extended in Han-Tang scribal usage to 'rough, preliminary, drafted in rapid cursive') modifies 稿 (gǎo, variant 藁, originally 'grain stalks/straw', metaphorically extended to an unpolished literary manuscript or sketch). Together they denote an initial, unedited draft of a text or design.

history.meaning: preliminary literary composition written in rapid draft script
rough draft, preliminary manuscript, sketch, or script outline

morphemes.meaning: stalks of grain; manuscript, draft, sketch

草稿.notes: In spoken Mandarin and media banter, 打草稿 (dǎ cǎogǎo, 'to make a rough draft') appears in the teasing idiom 吹牛不打草稿 ('boasting without even writing a draft', i.e., lying effortlessly on the spot).

rootFamily.gloss: initial draft, first version of a script or plan
to finalize a manuscript or design; final draft

草莓.etymology: Compound noun combining 草 ('herbaceous plant, grass', distinguishing low-growing Fragaria from woody berry shrubs) + 莓 ('berry, bramble fruit', grass radical 艹 + phonetic 每 měi).

history.meaning: herbaceous berry -> strawberry

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 草莓 (via 萌典)

荒谬.etymology: A coordinative compound (联合式) joining 荒 (huāng, 'barren wasteland, overgrown', extended in Classical Chinese to 'wild, ungrounded, excessive') and 谬 (miù, Traditional 謬, 'wild speech, error, falsehood', composed of speech radical 言 and phonetic 翏). Together they describe claims, plots, or logic that are utterly baseless and contrary to reason.

history.meaning: wild, uncultivated, and erroneous in speech or doctrine
absurd, preposterous, ridiculous, wildly illogical

荒谬.notes: Higher and more formal in register than 荒唐 (huāngtáng); while 荒唐 often criticizes dissolute behavior or silly antics, 荒谬 targets logical, intellectual, or situational absurdity (e.g., 荒谬的借口 'an absurd excuse').

荣幸.etymology: A coordinative compound (联合式) pairing 荣 (róng, Traditional 榮, 'blossoming of Paulownia flowers', extended in Classical Chinese to 'glory, splendor, high honor') and 幸 (xìng, 'good fortune, imperial favor, lucky privilege'). Originally denoting glory and imperial grace in Literary Chinese, it grammaticalized into a polite predicate adjective meaning 'honored and privileged'.

history.meaning: high glory and fortunate favor (especially from a ruler)
honored, privileged, flattered (in polite social formulas)

荣幸.notes: Essential in formal interviews, award speeches, and business meetings: 很荣幸能参与这个项目 ('I am deeply honored to participate in this project') or 三生有幸 ('blessed across three lifetimes').

药.etymology: A phono-semantic compound (形声) in Traditional 藥 (Simplified 药): the grass/plant semantic radical 艹 (艸) tops the phonetic 樂 (yuè/lè, Old Chinese *rˤawk, simplified to 约 by graphic analogy in cursive script). Because ancient Chinese materia medica consisted overwhelmingly of botanical herbs, the plant determinative marked healing substances that restore harmony and well-being.

history.meaning: medicinal herbs and botanical remedies for curing illness
any medicinal preparation, potion, chemical powder (including gunpowder 火藥)
medicine, pharmaceutical drug, remedy, chemical agent

morphemes.meaning: medicinal herb, medicine, drug, curative substance

药.notes: Takes different measure words depending on form: 一片药 (a tablet/pill), 一粒药 (a capsule/granule), 一副中药 (a dose/packet of traditional herbal medicine), and 吃药 ('take medicine', literally 'eat medicine').

药剂师.etymology: Professional title formed from 药剂 ('compounded medicine; pharmaceutical preparation', from 药 'medicinal herb' + 剂 'measured dose', knife 刂 cutting an even portion 齐) + 师 ('master; licensed specialist').

history.meaning: pharmacist; chemist

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 药剂师

药店.etymology: Modifier-head noun compound combining 药 (藥, 'medicinal herb, medicine, drug') + 店 ('shop, store').

history.meaning: pharmacy, drugstore, apothecary

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 药店 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: household medicine chest or first-aid box

药箱.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正式) combining 药 (yào, 'medicine, pharmaceuticals') and 箱 (xiāng, 'woven bamboo chest, box, case', bearing the bamboo radical 竹 and phonetic 相). In pre-modern China it referred to the portable wooden or bamboo medicine cabinet carried by itinerant physicians (走方医); in modern usage it denotes a household or on-set first-aid kit.

history.meaning: portable wooden or bamboo chest used by physicians to store herbs and needles
medicine chest, first-aid kit, emergency medical box

药箱.notes: Often specified as 医药箱 (yīyàoxiāng) or 急救药箱 (jíjiù yàoxiāng, 'emergency first-aid kit'), a frequent prop in drama scenes when an overworked producer or actor collapses on set.

莓果.etymology: A botanical compound of 莓 (méi, 'berry') and 果 (guǒ, 'fruit'). 莓 bears the grass radical 艹 above the phonetic 每, pointing to small, fleshy fruits growing on low herbaceous plants or shrubs. It serves as a general classification for various culinary berries.

history.meaning: berry (general term)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 莓果

莫不是.etymology: A rhetorical modal adverbial phrase formed by combining the Classical Chinese negative/indefinite pronoun 莫 (mò, 'none, nothing, do not', here functioning as a conjectural particle 'could it be that not...') with the negated copula 不是 (bùshì, 'is not'). Attested profusely in Song–Ming vernacular fiction (*话本* and *水浒传*), the double negation softens an inference into a surprised rhetorical question ('could it be that...?').

history.meaning: could it be that...?; surely it must be that... (colloquial conjectural marker)
could it be that...; don't tell me that... (rhetorical or slightly literary adverb)

morphemes.meaning: none; conjectural modal marker ('could it be')

莫不是.notes: Functions synonymously with 莫非 (mòfēi) and 难道 (nándào), lending a slightly dramatic, incredulous, or bantering tone when guessing someone's hidden motive or secret.

rootFamily.gloss: could it be that...?; lest, unless
baffled, utterly unable to make head or tail of something
isn't it the case that...; rhetorical tag

cognates.meaning: acquisition, obtaining, winning (a prize or rights)
to obtain, to acquire, to gain

获得.etymology: A verb-complement / coordinative compound combining 获 (huò, Traditional 獲, originally 'to capture game in a hunt', showing the dog radical 犭 and a hand grasping a bird 隻) and 得 (dé, 'to obtain, acquire', originally a hand holding a cowrie shell 貝 along a road 彳). Over time 獲 lost its literal hunting restriction and merged with 得 to denote formally acquiring awards, rights, approval, or resources.

history.meaning: to capture wild game in hunting; to seize in battle
to obtain, to come into possession of, to succeed in getting
to obtain, acquire, win, or garner (support, awards, rights)

获得.notes: Prefers abstract or formal objects in media and professional contexts—such as 获得版权 (acquire broadcasting rights), 获得好评 (garner critical acclaim), or 获得投资 (secure investment)—whereas 得到 (dédào) is more conversational.

rootFamily.gloss: to reap, harvest; gains, rewarding takeaway
to win a prize or award

cognates.meaning: edible greens, side dish, rape blossom

菜.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形声) combining the plant radical 艹 (艸) with phonetic 采 (cǎi, 'to pluck/gather with the hand 爪 from a tree 木', also etymologically cognate: 'that which is gathered for food'). Originally denoting wild and cultivated edible greens in Classical Chinese, it broadened in Tang–Song times to any prepared dish accompanying grain, and in contemporary slang to 'one's romantic type' or 'weak/noob skill level'.

history.meaning: edible herbs and vegetables gathered as supplemental food alongside grain (穀)
any cooked dish (vegetable or meat) served with rice; cuisine
vegetable; prepared dish; (slang) one's romantic type; (gaming/slang) weak, unskilled

morphemes.meaning: edible greens, vegetable; cooked dish; (slang) one's type or weak skill

菜.notes: In modern urban drama dialogue, 是我的菜 (shì wǒ de cài, literally 'is my dish') is the standard idiomatic way to say 'is my type / my cup of tea' (e.g., 他不是我的菜 'He's not my type').

rootFamily.gloss: side dish; piece of cake, something trivial (小菜一碟)

菜单.etymology: Compound of 菜 ('cooked dish, vegetable/course', plant crown 艹 + 采 'pluck/gather') + 单 ('single sheet, itemized list'), naming a written restaurant or café bill of fare.

history.meaning: written list of dishes for a banquet or tavern
menu

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 菜单

菜单卡.etymology: Three-character compound from 菜单 (simplified from 菜單, 'dish list; menu') + 卡 ('card', phonetic loan from English *card*). Refers to a printed or handwritten tabletop card listing daily dishes or afternoon-tea selections.

history.meaning: menu card

菜板.etymology: Determinative kitchen compound of 菜 ('vegetables; food ingredients') + 板 ('flat wooden board; plank', wood radical 木 + phonetic 反 *fǎn*). It is the everyday spoken word for a wooden chopping board.

history.meaning: wooden chopping board; cutting board

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 菜板

菜谱.etymology: Combines 菜 (cài, 'vegetable, dish') and 谱 (pǔ, 'register, manual'). 谱 contains the speech radical 讠 and historically referred to systematic records or musical scores. Applied to food, it elevated culinary instructions into a structured, formal manual.

history.meaning: cookbook; recipe
recipe; menu

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 菜谱

菜鸟.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正式) pairing 菜 (cài, 'vegetable; weak, inferior, easily preyed upon, or unseasoned') with 鸟 (niǎo, 'bird', a colloquial Taiwanese and Southern Min/Mandarin slang suffix for a person or guy, parallel to 老鸟 lǎoniǎo 'veteran'). Coined in 20th-century Taiwanese military and campus slang for a slow, fledgling bird raised for meat or recién hatched, it spread across Mainland China during the 1990s internet boom to mean 'rookie, newbie, novice'.

history.meaning: fledgling bird; raw recruit in military training (Taiwanese Mandarin slang)
rookie, novice, workplace newcomer, or inexperienced player

morphemes.meaning: bird; colloquial figurative suffix for a person or fellow

菜鸟.notes: Its direct antonym in workplace and showbiz slang is 老鸟 (lǎoniǎo, 'old bird / seasoned veteran') or 大神 (dàshén, 'master/guru'); calling oneself a 小菜鸟 is a common self-deprecating icebreaker for interns.

rootFamily.gloss: seasoned veteran, old hand (direct antonym of 菜鸟)

营业.etymology: Verb-object compound from 营 (simplified from 營, originally 'lay out a ringed camp', hence 'manage; operate; run') + 业 (simplified from 業, 'occupation; business; trade'). Standard commercial term for a shop, inn, or restaurant conducting business or being open for customers.

history.meaning: pursue a trade or livelihood
be open for business; operate commercially

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 营业

营养师.etymology: A three-morpheme compound formed by suffixing the professional agentive noun 师 (shī, 'master, specialist, licensed expert') to the coordinative verb-noun compound 营养 (yíngyǎng, 'nutrition, nourishment', from 营 'to manage, build up, sustain' + 养 'to nourish, nurture'). While 營養 appeared in Literary Chinese for 'nurturing life', modern scientific 营养 and the occupational title 营养师 crystalized in the 20th century alongside Japanese *wasei-kango* 栄養 (eiyō) / 栄養士.

history.meaning: to nurture and sustain life or health

history.form: 營養 (influenced by Japanese 栄養)
history.meaning: biological nutrition, dietary nourishment
certified nutritionist or dietitian managing health and meal plans

营养师.notes: In the entertainment industry, top celebrities and vocalists frequently employ a personal 营养师 to manage strict body-fat or throat-care diets during filming and concert tours.

营销.etymology: A modern telescopic coordinative compound (联合式/缩略词) blending 经营 (jīngyíng, 'to manage, operate a business') and 销售 (xiāoshòu, 'to sell, distribute goods'). Literally combining 营 ('to operate, plan, manage') and 销 ('to melt metal', extended to 'to sell off, distribute on the market'), it became the standard Mainland Mandarin equivalent for 'marketing' (often abbreviated from 市场营销) during post-1980s economic reforms.

history.meaning: business management and commercial sales distribution
marketing, brand promotion, and audience engagement strategy

营销.notes: In Chinese entertainment and social media, 营销 also carries a cynical edge when referring to 炒作营销 (hype marketing) or 营销号 (yíngxiāohào, clickbait/gossip marketing accounts on Weibo and Douyin).

rootFamily.gloss: clickbait or promotional social media account ('marketing account')
to manage and operate (a business or project)

营销单.etymology: A three-character modifier-head compound (偏正式) attaching the head noun 单 (dān, Traditional 單, originally a forked hunting weapon, extended in commercial Chinese to 'single sheet, bill, invoice, order, or contract ticket') to the modifier 营销 (yíngxiāo, 'marketing'). In modern Chinese media and advertising agencies, it denotes a commercial marketing order, sponsored campaign brief, or promotional contract.

history.meaning: commercial bill, invoice, or itemized list written on a single slip of paper
marketing order, promotional campaign contract, or ad-sales work order

morphemes.meaning: sheet, bill, commercial order, contract ticket

营销单.notes: In agency and showbiz jargon, 接单 (jiēdān, 'take an order/client brief') and 签营销单 ('sign a marketing order') refer to securing commercial sponsorship deals that fund a variety show or agency.

rootFamily.gloss: order form, commercial order (for goods or services)

落.etymology: Phono-semantic character 落, combining grass radical 艹 + phonetic 洛 (luò), originally meaning 'for leaves of plants and trees to wither and fall', extended to 'to fall, drop, set (of the sun), lag behind, settle'.

history.meaning: falling of autumn leaves -> to drop, fall, settle
to fall, drop, set; to leave behind (là)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 落 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: falling to the ground, touching down

落地.etymology: A verb-object / verb-complement compound combining 落 (luò, 'for leaves to fall, to drop, to descend') and 地 (dì, 'the earth, ground, local soil'). Originally meaning literally 'to fall to the ground' (including a newborn infant's birth, 呱呱坠地/落地), it extended to an aircraft 'touching down' and, in 21st-century Chinese corporate and TV production jargon, to a concept, policy, or foreign format being 'executed on the ground' or 'localized into concrete practice'.

history.meaning: to fall or drop onto the ground (of leaves, fruit, or a newborn baby at birth)
to touch down (of an aircraft); floor-to-ceiling (e.g., 落地窗)
to be put into concrete execution on the ground; to materialize locally (of a project or IP)

morphemes.meaning: to fall, drop, descend, settle down
ground, earth, local site or reality

落地.notes: A ubiquitous buzzword in contemporary Chinese business and TV production: 项目落地 means turning a pitch deck or overseas show format into an actual, localized, operating production.

rootFamily.gloss: to take root where one lands; to settle down permanently in a new place

cognates.meaning: to settle, put into practice, confirm

落实.etymology: A verb-complement (动补式 / 结果补语) compound in which 落 (luò, 'to fall, come to rest, settle') is followed by the resultative complement 实 (shí, Traditional 實, originally 'wealth/goods 貫 under a roof 宀', hence 'full, solid, real, concrete'). In early vernacular Chinese it meant 'to feel settled or assured in heart'; in modern administrative and business Mandarin it means 'to make solid—to implement, follow through on, or verify'.

history.meaning: to come to rest on solid ground; to feel assured and settled in mind
to put into concrete practice, implement, fulfill, or verify (a plan, budget, or detail)

morphemes.meaning: to fall, settle, come down to

落实.notes: Compare 落地 and 落实: 落地 emphasizes a high-level creative concept or policy 'touching the ground' in real-world execution, whereas 落实 focuses on pinning down specific responsibilities, budgets, or action items (e.g., 落实细节 'nail down/confirm the details').

rootFamily.gloss: to verify, check and confirm the facts
dependable, steady; feeling at ease and secure in mind

著名.etymology: Historically a verb-object compound (动宾式) in Classical Chinese—著 (zhù, 'to become manifest, prominent, clearly displayed') + 名 (míng, 'name, reputation'), literally 'to make one's name manifest' (attested in *Xunzi* and *Records of the Grand Historian*). Over time it lexicalized into an attributive adjective meaning 'renowned, celebrated, prominent in reputation'.

history.meaning: to make one's name prominent and widely known; to establish a reputation
famous, renowned, celebrated, eminent (attributive modifier)

著名.notes: Primarily used as a formal attributive modifier before prestigious nouns and titles (e.g., 著名制作人 'renowned producer', 著名导演 'celebrated director') rather than as a casual conversational predicate (where 有名 yǒumíng or 出名 chūmíng is preferred).

rootFamily.gloss: remarkable, notable, significant (of results or achievements)
well-known, famous (slightly less formal than 著名)

cognates.meaning: member of a board of directors

董事.etymology: Originally a verb-object compound (动宾式) in Classical and Imperial Chinese: 董 (dǒng, 'to supervise, direct, regulate, oversee uprightly', attested in the *Book of Documents* 董之用威) + 事 (shì, 'affairs, business, official matters'), literally 'to supervise affairs'. By the late Qing dynasty, it shifted from a verb phrase to a noun designating a local civic trustee or a member of a modern corporate board of directors.

history.meaning: to supervise and direct official or public affairs (verb-object phrase)
local gentry trustee or manager overseeing community institutions
corporate director, member of a company's board of directors

董事.notes: Often placed directly after a surname as a high-status corporate form of address in workplace dramas: 张董 (Zhāng Dǒng, 'Director Zhang'), outranking 经理 (jīnglǐ, 'manager') and 总裁 (zǒngcái, 'CEO/president').

rootFamily.gloss: chairperson of the board of directors

cognates.meaning: board of directors, board of trustees

董事会.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正式) formed by adding the collective institutional noun 会 (huì, Traditional 會, 'assembly, council, committee, association') to 董事 (dǒngshì, 'board director'). Modelled during late Qing and early Republican corporate law reforms to translate Western 'board of directors' or 'board of trustees', it denotes the supreme governing council elected by shareholders.

history.meaning: governing council of trustees or corporate directors in modern joint-stock companies
board of directors of a corporation or media group

董事会.notes: In corporate drama plotlines, 召开董事会 ('convene a board meeting') is the classic high-stakes showdown scene where executives vote on budgets, mergers, or ousting a leader.

cognates.meaning: chairperson of the board of directors

董事长.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正式) suffixing 长 (zhǎng, 'elder, chief, head, presiding leader') to 董事 (dǒngshì, 'corporate director', functioning as a shorthand for 董事会 'board of directors'). Coined in modern Chinese corporate governance terminology, it designates the presiding head of the board of directors and legal representative of a corporation.

history.meaning: chief presiding officer of a board of directors or trustees
chairperson of the board of directors (in Mainland and Taiwan corporate law)

董事长.notes: Note the mandatory reading zhǎng ('chief/head') for 长 here, never cháng; in Hong Kong corporate usage, the equivalent role is more commonly called 董事局主席 (dǒngshìjú zhǔxí).

cognates.meaning: harboring a scheme or plot for a long time

蓄谋已久.etymology: A four-character idiom (成语) structured as a subject-predicate or verb-complement sequence: 蓄谋 (xùmóu, 'to harbor/store up a plot', from 蓄 'to accumulate, store up herbs/provisions, harbor inwardly' + 谋 'to scheme, plan') followed by 已久 (yǐjiǔ, 'already for a long time'). It denotes an action or trap that was not impulsive, but deliberately premeditated over a long period.

history.meaning: having secretly harbored and cultivated a scheme for a long time
premeditated long ago, long-plotted, calculated well in advance

morphemes.meaning: to store up, accumulate, harbor inwardly
long in time, for a long duration

蓄谋已久.notes: Usually carries a negative or suspicious connotation (corporate sabotage, PR ambushes, or crimes), though in romance subplots it is sometimes used playfully for a long-planned confession or courtship.

rootFamily.gloss: to harbor a premeditated scheme; premeditation

蓝.etymology: Phono-semantic character 蓝 (藍), combining grass radical 艹 + phonetic 监 (監 jiān / Old Chinese *kˤram), originally naming the polygonum indigo plant (蓼蓝) used to dye cloth blue, hence the color 'blue'.

history.meaning: indigo dyer's plant
indigo blue, blue

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 蓝 (via 萌典)

蓝天.etymology: Modifier-head noun compound combining 蓝 (藍, 'blue') + 天 ('sky, heaven').

history.meaning: blue sky

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 蓝天 (via 萌典)

cognates.word: 藍海 (rankai) / ブルーオーシャン

蓝海.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正式) combining 蓝 (lán, Traditional 藍, originally the indigo plant *Persicaria tinctoria*, hence 'deep blue') and 海 (hǎi, 'sea, ocean'). While literally denoting the deep blue sea in Chinese poetry, its dominant modern business and media sense is a 2005 loan translation (calque) of English *blue ocean* from W. Chan Kim and Renée Mauborgne's *Blue Ocean Strategy* (*蓝海战略*), designating an untapped, uncontested market space.

history.meaning: the deep blue sea, azure ocean waters (literal poetic description)
uncontested, high-growth new market space free of cutthroat competition

morphemes.meaning: sea, ocean; vast domain or market

蓝海.notes: Always contrasted in business and media pitch meetings with 红海 (hónghǎi, 'red ocean'—a saturated market bloodied by cutthroat competition among rivals).

rootFamily.gloss: blue ocean strategy (creating uncontested market space)

蓝色.etymology: Compound noun combining 蓝 (藍, 'indigo, blue') + 色 ('color, hue').

history.meaning: the color blue

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 蓝色 (via 萌典)

蓝色预警.etymology: A two-part modifier-head noun phrase (偏正式): 蓝色 (lánsè, 'blue color', from indigo 蓝 + color 色) modifies 预警 (yùjǐng, 'early warning, advance alert', from 预 'beforehand, in advance' + 警 'to warn, guard against danger'). Standardized in China's national four-tier meteorological and emergency alert system (蓝 'blue' Level IV, 黄 'yellow' Level III, 橙 'orange' Level II, 红 'red' Level I), it denotes the lowest-tier official warning for severe weather.

history.meaning: advance military or civil warning of approaching danger
Level IV (lowest-tier) official meteorological or emergency warning; figurative early warning sign

morphemes.meaning: to warn, alert, guard against danger

蓝色预警.notes: China's weather alerts escalate from 蓝 (blue, lowest) → 黄 (yellow) → 橙 (orange) → 红 (red, highest); outdoor film and variety crews closely monitor these alerts because a higher tier forces production shutdowns.

rootFamily.gloss: red alert (highest-tier emergency or weather warning)

蔬菜.etymology: Coordinate collective noun combining 蔬 ('edible greens, cultivated vegetable crops', grass radical 艹 + 疏 shū) + 菜 ('edible wild or garden greens, vegetable dish').

history.meaning: edible greens and herbs
vegetables, greens

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 蔬菜 (via 萌典)

薄.etymology: Phono-semantic character 薄, combining grass radical 艹 + phonetic 溥 (pǔ / Old Chinese *pˤak), originally referring to dense or spreading vegetation and thickets, early used for 'thin, flimsy, weak, meagre, ungenerous'.

history.meaning: thin, slight, dilute, ungenerous
thin, flimsy, weak, light

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 薄 (via 萌典)

薄荷.etymology: A botanical name characterized by a unique pronunciation (bò he) distinct from its constituent characters (bó 'thin' and hé 'lotus'). Featuring the grass radical 艹, this phonetic loanword traces back to early transcriptions of the aromatic cooling herb.

history.meaning: mint
mint (bò he)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 薄荷

薄荷茶.etymology: Compound of 薄荷 ('mint, Mentha', plant crown 艹 on both characters; note colloquial reading bò he preserving an older disyllabic herbal name) + 茶 ('tea, herbal infusion').

history.meaning: aromatic cooling mint herb
mint tea

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 薄荷茶

薄薄.etymology: Reduplicated state adjective from 薄 ('thin; fine; delicate', grass 艹 + 溥). In Mandarin, reduplicating 薄 as 薄薄 (typically followed by 的) creates a vivid sensory modifier meaning 'delicately thin, sheer, or light', used for pastry crusts, coats of paint, or morning mist.

history.meaning: thin; light and delicate
nicely thin; light and sheer
