薪水.etymology: A coordinative compound (联合式) literally meaning 'firewood (薪 xīn, grass radical 艹 + axe 斤 cutting wood 新) and water (水 shuǐ)'—the two most basic daily necessities for cooking and survival. In the Six Dynasties (*Book of Southern Qi* and Tao Yuanming's letters, where Tao sent a servant to help his son with '薪水之劳', the chores of gathering firewood and drawing water), officials began receiving stipends to cover firewood and water expenses, which metonymically became the general word for 'salary, wages'.

history.meaning: firewood and water; the daily manual labor of gathering fuel and drawing water
history.stage: Six Dynasties Literary Chinese (Tao Yuanming / Nan Qi Shu)

history.meaning: official stipend or allowance granted to cover household fuel and water costs
salary, white-collar pay, wages, remuneration

薪水.notes: More conversational than 薪酬 (xīnchóu, 'compensation package') and slightly more white-collar in feel than 工资 (gōngzī, 'wages/pay'); compounds like 加薪 (pay raise) and 年薪 (annual salary) drop the 水.

rootFamily.gloss: adding fuel to a cauldron to stop it boiling; counterproductive measure (preserves literal 'firewood' sense)
rootFamily.word: 扬汤止沸，不如釜底抽薪 (釜底抽薪)

藏.etymology: Phono-semantic character 藏, created by adding the grass radical 艹 ('concealing reeds/brush') to 臧 (zāng, 'good; to store away'); read cáng as a verb ('to hide, conceal, store up') and zàng as a noun ('storehouse, Buddhist canon; Tibet').

history.meaning: to conceal in vegetation, store up
to hide, conceal, store (cáng); storehouse, Tibet (zàng)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 藏 (via 萌典)

藏宝图.etymology: A compound uniting 藏 (cáng, 'to hide'), 宝 (bǎo, 'treasure'), and 图 (tú, 'map, drawing'). Evocative of adventure and piracy lore, this term describes any drawn chart or sketch used to conceal and rediscover valuable items.

history.meaning: treasure map

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 藏宝图

藤条.etymology: Compound noun combining 藤 ('climbing vine, rattan, cane', grass radical 艹 + phonetic 滕 téng) + 条 (條, 'long slender stem, rod, strip').

history.meaning: rattan cane, pliable vine stem

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 藤条 (via 萌典)

蘸.etymology: Phono-semantic character 蘸, combining grass radical 艹 + 醮 (jiào, 'libation of wine; to dip briefly'), meaning 'to dip food into sauce or a brush into ink'.

history.meaning: to dip briefly in liquid, sauce, or ink

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 蘸 (via 萌典)

虐死.etymology: A verb-resultative complement compound (动补式) combining 虐 (nüè, 'to tyrannize, mistreat, torment cruelly', an ideogram showing a tiger's head 虍 and claws 爪 attacking a person) with the extreme resultative complement 死 (sǐ, 'to die; to death, to an extreme degree'). Used literally for 'to abuse or torture to death', in contemporary Chinese media and fandom slang it functions hyperbolically for being 'emotionally devastated' by a tragic plot or 'brutally crushed' by an exhausting workload.

history.meaning: to tyrannize, torture, or mistreat someone to death (literal)
to abuse to death; (colloquial hyperbole) to torment or emotionally wreck to the extreme

morphemes.meaning: to die; resultative intensifier ('to death / to the extreme')

虐死.notes: In drama fandom and workplace banter, 虐死我了 (nüèsǐ wǒ le) rarely means physical abuse—it means a tear-jerker script (虐恋) or a ruthless producer/mentor has emotionally or workloads-wise 'tortured me to death'.

rootFamily.gloss: heart-wrenching, emotionally torturous (of a drama plot)
self-abuse; masochistic self-torment (often humorous for overworking)

虐残.etymology: A verb-resultative complement compound (动补式) pairing the verb 虐 (nüè, 'to abuse, torment, subject to brutal treatment or grueling training') with the resultative complement 残 (cán, Traditional 殘, composed of the bone/death radical 歹 and doubled halberds 戋, 'to maim, cripple, leave disabled or wrecked'). Literally meaning 'to abuse into disability', in colloquial workplace and gaming slang it also hyperbolically describes exhausting or crushing someone until they are 'wrecked/incapacitated'.

history.meaning: to mistreat cruelly and maim or cripple physically
to abuse to disability; (colloquial hyperbole) to work or crush someone until they are completely wrecked

morphemes.meaning: to mistreat, abuse, torment, put through grueling ordeal

虐残.notes: Often used alongside 虐死 and 虐跑 in three-part parallel workplace exaggerations (e.g., describing how a notoriously demanding chief producer 'breaks' interns and writers).

虐跑.etymology: A verb-resultative complement compound (动补式) combining the transitive action verb 虐 (nüè, 'to mistreat, torment, subject to harsh critique or grueling demands') with the directional/resultative verb 跑 (pǎo, 'to run away, flee, quit'). As a productive Mandarin resultative pattern (parallel to 吓跑 'scare away' or 气跑 'anger into leaving'), 虐跑 means 'to torment or overwork someone so severely that they run away / quit the job'.

history.form: V + 跑 (e.g., 嚇跑 / 趕跑)
history.meaning: productive Mandarin resultative construction meaning 'to drive/cause to flee by V-ing'
to abuse, torment, or overwork someone until they flee or quit

morphemes.meaning: to mistreat, torment, put through grueling demands
to run away, flee, quit as a result

虐跑.notes: In *Behind the Scenes* (*幕后之王*) and similar workplace dramas, 把实习生虐跑了 ('tormented the interns until they ran away/quit') vividly captures a devil-boss mentor's terrifying reputation.

rootFamily.gloss: to torture one's heart; emotionally grueling

cognates.meaning: empty, void, hollow; deficiency in Sino-Japanese medicine

虚.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形声) combining phonetic 虍 (hū, tiger stripes) and semantic 丘 (qiū, 'large mound or hill', modified in modern script to 业). Its original Classical Chinese sense was 'great deserted mound' or 'abandoned ruins' (later written with the earth radical as 墟 xū). From 'deserted, empty, hollow', it evolved in classical philosophy and Traditional Chinese Medicine (*Huangdi Neijing*) to denote depletion of vital qi or blood—hence 'physically weak, run-down, diffident'.

history.meaning: great mound; deserted ruins; empty, vacant, void
depleted of vital qi, yin, or yang; constitutionally weak or exhausted
empty, hollow; physically weak, run-down, depleted; diffident or guilty (心虚)

morphemes.meaning: empty, void, hollow; physically depleted, weak, diffident

虚.notes: In everyday Chinese health talk, saying someone's body is 很虚 (hěn xū) or 气虚/肾虚 draws directly on Traditional Chinese Medicine—meaning 'run-down, depleted of vital energy, needing nourishment (补 bǔ)', not merely 'muscularly weak'.

rootFamily.gloss: lacking confidence, diffident, having a guilty conscience

虚假.etymology: A coordinative compound (联合式) uniting 虚 (xū, 'empty, hollow, unsubstantiated, devoid of real substance') and 假 (jiǎ, originally 'to borrow temporarily', extended in Classical Chinese to 'artificial, simulated, false, not genuine', contrasted with 真 zhēn). Together they describe information, data, feelings, or publicity that is hollow and fabricated.

history.meaning: empty of substance and unauthentic; illusory (often in Buddhist and philosophical texts)
false, fabricated, sham, fraudulent, insincere

虚假.notes: Common in media, legal, and regulatory contexts such as 虚假宣传 (false advertising), 虚假数据 (fabricated viewership/streaming data), and 虚假繁荣 (false/hollow prosperity).

rootFamily.gloss: to practice fraud, falsify data or results

虚假广告.etymology: A four-character modifier-head nominal phrase combining two coordinative compounds: 虚假 (xūjiǎ, 'empty and false, fabricated', attested in Classical and Tang-Song prose from 虚 'empty, hollow' + 假 'borrowed, artificial, false') modifying 广告 (guǎnggào, literally 'widely announce', a Classical Chinese verb-object phrase repurposed in Meiji Japan as 広告 to translate English 'advertisement' and re-imported into modern Mandarin).

history.meaning: empty and unreal; feigned or illusory (in Classical and Buddhist texts)
public notice; commercial advertisement (via Meiji Japanese 広告)
false advertising, fraudulent commercial claims

虚假广告.notes: A legal and media-regulatory term (codified in China's Advertising Law) frequently invoked in entertainment industry dramas when celebrity endorsements or sponsor integrations face public backlash.

虫.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 虫. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 虫 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 虫 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 虫 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 虫. The etymology of 虫 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 虫
middle form of 虫
modern form of 虫

虽然.etymology: Lexicalized from a Classical Chinese two-word concessive clause 雖然 (suī rán), literally 'even if [it be] so', where 雖 (suī, Old Chinese *s-luj, 'even though, granting that') is a concessive conjunction and 然 (rán, 'to be thus, so') is an anaphoric demonstrative verb-pronoun referring back to a preceding statement. In Classical prose it functioned as a standalone sentence-initial transition ('Even so, ...'); from the Tang-Song period onward it coalesced into a single disyllabic conjunction meaning 'although'.

history.meaning: even if it is so; granting that to be true (standalone clause)
although, even though (disyllabic subordinating conjunction)
although, though (typically paired with 但是 or 可是)

morphemes.meaning: to be so, thus, like that

虽然.notes: In Mandarin discourse, 虽然 almost always anticipates a correlative adversative marker (但是, 可是, or 却) in the main clause; omitting the second half sounds unfinished in spoken Chinese.

rootFamily.gloss: although it is said that, even though
naturally, of course, as it should be

蚂蚁.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 蚂蚁. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 蚂蚁 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 蚂蚁 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 蚂蚁 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 蚂蚁. The etymology of 蚂蚁 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 蚂蚁
middle form of 蚂蚁
modern form of 蚂蚁

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 蚂蚁

蛋糕.etymology: Modifier-head culinary compound combining 蛋 ('bird's egg') + 糕 ('steamed or baked rice/flour cake', rice radical 米 + phonetic 羔 gāo).

history.meaning: egg cake, sponge cake, Western-style cake

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 蛋糕 (via 萌典)

蛋黄.etymology: Compound of 蛋 ('egg', originally written 蜑 and generalized in Tang–Song vernacular to bird and hen eggs) + 黄 ('yellow', depicting a jade pendant or field glow). Literally 'the yellow of the egg', it names the rich egg yolk used in custards and lemon curd.

history.meaning: egg yolk
egg yolk

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 蛋黄

蜂.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 蜂. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 蜂 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 蜂 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 蜂 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 蜂. The etymology of 蜂 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 蜂
middle form of 蜂
modern form of 蜂

蜂蜜.etymology: Transparent compound of 蜂 ('bee', combining the insect classifier 虫 with phonetic 夆 fēng) + 蜜 ('honey', combining 虫 at the base with phonetic 宓 mì). Notably, Old Chinese *mit (蜜) is widely recognized as an ancient Silk Road / Central Asian loanword cognate with Tocharian B mit ('honey, mead') and Proto-Indo-European *médʰu.

history.meaning: honey
bee honey

rootFamily.gloss: hundred flowers (as in 百花蜂蜜)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 蜂蜜 (via 萌典)

蜂蜡.etymology: A straightforward pairing of 蜂 (fēng, 'bee') and 蜡 (là, 'wax'). The term explicitly links the raw material to its entomological source. Long valued for sealing, waterproofing, and polishing, it evokes historical authenticity and tactile antiquity.

history.meaning: beeswax
beeswax

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 蜂蜡

蜡.etymology: Featuring the insect radical 虫 and the phonetic 昔 (xī), this character originally denoted beeswax, humanity's oldest waxy substance. While the word's meaning expanded to include plant and synthetic waxes, its ancient insectile origin remains visible in the script.

history.meaning: beeswax
wax

蜡布.etymology: Combines 蜡 (là, 'wax') and 布 (bù, 'cloth'). Before the invention of modern polymers, soaking heavy fabric in melted wax or oil was the standard for waterproofing. It implies durability, weathering, and robust protection.

history.meaning: wax cloth; oilcloth

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 蜡布

融入.etymology: A verb-complement (resultative/directional) compound formed from 融 (róng, Old Chinese *luŋ, originally 'steam rising from cooking; to melt, thaw, fuse together') + 入 (rù, Old Chinese *njup, 'to enter, go into'). Originally describing physical melting or diffusion of one substance into another in Literary Chinese, it underwent metaphorical extension to describe social assimilation, artistic synthesis, or blending an element seamlessly into a larger whole.

history.meaning: to thaw, melt and flow into; to fuse physically
to integrate into, blend into (a team, culture, or creative work)

融入.notes: Very common in workplace and creative production contexts: 融入团队 ('integrate into the team') or 把传统文化融入节目 ('blend traditional culture into the program').

螺丝.etymology: Compound of 螺 ('spiral snail/conch shell', insect/mollusc classifier 虫 + 累) + 丝 ('fine thread'), vividly likening the helical threading on a metal screw to the spiral whorls of a snail shell.

history.meaning: threaded screw
screw

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 螺丝 (via 萌典)

螺丝刀.etymology: Three-character tool compound combining 螺丝 (螺絲, 'screw', literally 'spiral-shell thread', from 螺 'spiral snail shell' + 丝 'fine thread') + 刀 ('knife, blade, tool').

history.meaning: screwdriver

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 螺丝刀 (via 萌典)

螺纹.etymology: Modifier-head compound combining 螺 ('spiral snail/conch shell') + 纹 (紋, 'pattern, line, ridge, grain'), naming the helical ridges on a shell, fingertip whorl, or machine screw.

history.meaning: spiral whorl; screw thread

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 螺纹 (via 萌典)

血压.etymology: Modern medical compound (via Meiji Japanese ketsuatsu 血圧) combining 血 ('blood') + 压 (壓, 'pressure, to press down').

history.meaning: blood pressure

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 血压 (via 萌典)

行.etymology: Originally an oracle-bone pictograph of a four-way crossroads (行), whence two pronunciation lineages diverged: (1) xíng ('to walk, go, travel, act, be all right/okay'); (2) háng ('row, column, line of march, trade guild, business firm/bank').

history.meaning: crossroads -> road, row (háng); to walk, act (xíng)
to walk, do, be okay (xíng); row, line, profession, bank (háng)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 行 (via 萌典)

行不通.etymology: A negative potential verb-complement construction formed from 行 (xíng, 'to walk, travel, proceed, carry out') + 不 (bù, negative potential infix 'cannot') + 通 (tōng, 'to pass through, reach unimpeded, succeed'). Literally 'to walk and not get through [a blocked road]', a spatial metaphor rooted in Classical expressions such as 行道不通 that grammaticalized in vernacular Mandarin into an idiomatic predicate meaning a plan, method, or proposal is unworkable.

history.meaning: impassable by road; unable to travel through
unworkable, impracticable, won't work (of a scheme or idea)

行不通.notes: Its positive counterpart is 行得通 ('viable, workable'); in script meetings and production rooms, 这个方案行不通 ('this proposal won't work') is a standard way to reject an unfeasible idea.

rootFamily.gloss: cannot figure out, unable to accept emotionally

行业.etymology: A modifier-head or coordinative compound combining 行 (háng, Middle Chinese *ɣɑŋ, originally 'column of marching troops, row, line', which by the Tang dynasty came to denote a 'street of merchants of the same trade' and hence a 'trade guild' or 'line of business') + 業 (yè, 'occupation, livelihood, estate'). Notice the reading háng (from the noun sense 'row, guild') rather than xíng ('to walk').

history.meaning: row, file; Tang-Song merchant guild street or trade association
line of trade, occupation, industry, profession

morphemes.meaning: row, guild, line of trade (read háng)

行业.notes: Always pronounced hángyè (never *xíngyè); central to phrases like 娱乐行业 ('entertainment industry') and 行业潜规则 ('unwritten industry rules').

rootFamily.gloss: person in the same trade, peer, rival in the industry

行事.etymology: A Classical Chinese verb-object compound (attestations in the *Zuo Zhuan* and *Analects*) composed of 行 (xíng, 'to carry out, practice, perform') + 事 (shì, 'affair, matter, duty'). Literally 'to carry out affairs', it evolved from managing official state duties to a general verb meaning 'to act, conduct oneself, handle matters'.

history.meaning: to execute official duties, carry out affairs of state
history.stage: Classical Chinese (Spring and Autumn / Warring States)

history.meaning: to act, behave, conduct oneself; mode of action

morphemes.meaning: to carry out, execute, practice (read xíng)

行事.notes: Frequently used in four-character idioms describing workplace or personal style, such as 低调行事 ('keep a low profile'), 便宜行事 ('act at one's discretion'), and 看眼色行事 ('take cues from others' expressions').

rootFamily.gloss: manner of handling affairs, style of work
to handle affairs, work, manage matters

行动.etymology: A coordinative compound from Classical Chinese combining 行 (xíng, 'to walk, go, act') + 動 (dòng, 'to move, stir, set in motion'). In pre-Qin and Han texts (such as *Xunzi* and *Hanshu*), 行動 described physical bodily movement ('walking and moving about'); in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, reinforced by Meiji Japanese 行動 (kōdō), it broadened to translate Western philosophical, military, and everyday concepts of purposeful 'action' or 'operation'.

history.meaning: walking and moving; bodily movement or travel
purposeful action, operation, deed; to take action

行动.notes: Functions as both a noun (采取行动 'take action') and an intransitive verb (马上行动 'act immediately'), as well as retaining its literal physical sense in 行动不便 ('having limited mobility').

rootFamily.gloss: capacity for action, drive, execution power

行动力.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound formed by suffixing 力 (lì, 'strength, power, capability, capacity') to 行动 (xíngdòng, 'action, taking action'). Shaped in the modern East Asian lexicon alongside Japanese 行動力 (kōdōryoku), where -力 productively derives abstract nouns of personal or organizational competence ('the capacity to turn ideas into concrete action').

history.meaning: capacity for action, initiative, dynamism (Sino-Japanese and modern Chinese coinage)
action power, execution drive, proactivity in workplace and personal goals

行动力.notes: A staple buzzword in modern corporate and media-production culture (alongside 执行力 'execution power'), praising producers or assistants who immediately turn a creative pitch into reality: 行动力超强 ('super high drive/initiative').

rootFamily.gloss: execution ability, ability to get things done

行政.etymology: Originally a Classical Chinese verb-object phrase 行政 (xíng zhèng, attested in the *Zuo Zhuan* and *Shiji*), composed of 行 (xíng, 'to carry out, exercise') + 政 (zhèng, 'governance, state affairs'), meaning 'to exercise governance'. In the 19th century, Meiji Japanese scholars adopted 行政 (gyōsei) as a noun to translate Western legal-political 'administration' (the executive branch as opposed to legislation and judiciary), and the nominalized sense returned to Chinese, later extending to corporate office administration.

history.meaning: to carry out governance, administer state affairs (verb-object phrase)
executive administration, public administration (via Meiji Japanese 行政)
public administration; corporate office operations and back-office management

行政.notes: In contemporary Chinese companies (including TV networks and production houses), 行政 colloquially refers to back-office operations (facilities, supplies, reception, scheduling) or the staff who run them (e.g., 找行政领工牌 'get your badge from Admin').

rootFamily.gloss: governing, being in power; politics, government affairs

行政处.etymology: A modifier-head institutional compound combining 行政 (xíngzhèng, 'administration, administrative affairs') + 处 (chù, falling tone, Middle Chinese *tɕʰjwoH, originally 'place, dwelling, spot', which in Tang–Song and modern bureaucratic nomenclature became an official designation for a 'division, bureau, or office' within an institution).

history.meaning: place, location; administrative bureau or office in imperial and modern bureaucracy
history.stage: Middle Chinese to Late Imperial Chinese

history.meaning: administrative office or division (in universities, state organs, or broadcasters)

行政处.notes: In organizational hierarchies, 处 (division/office, headed by a 处长) typically belongs to government agencies, universities, hospitals, or state-owned broadcasters, whereas private companies prefer 部 (department, as in 行政部).

行政部.etymology: A modifier-head organizational compound formed from 行政 (xíngzhèng, 'administration, office operations') + 部 (bù, Old Chinese *bˤoʔ, originally 'section, tribe, division, command', used since the Sui–Tang Six Ministries 六部 to denote a 'ministry' or corporate 'department'). Literally 'the department in charge of administrative operations'.

history.meaning: military or administrative division; imperial ministry (since Sui–Tang)
administrative department or general affairs division in a company or studio

行政部.notes: Standard corporate name for the General Affairs / Admin Department in Chinese media companies, handling everything from conference rooms and office supplies to travel logistics.

行李.etymology: A fascinating Classical Chinese survival with a folk-etymological graph. In the *Zuo Zhuan* (左傳·僖公三十年, 7th c. BCE), 行李 (xínglǐ) meant 'traveling diplomatic envoy, messenger'—originally written 行理 ('one who manages [理] affairs on a journey [行]', or的行吏 'traveling official'), with 李 ('plum') serving as a phonetic loan character (假借) for 理/吏 (Old Chinese *rəʔ). From 'diplomatic envoy and their traveling retinue', the meaning shifted by the Tang dynasty to 'the provisions and gear required for a journey', i.e., 'luggage, baggage'.

history.form: 行李 (var. 行理 / 行吏)
history.meaning: diplomatic envoy, traveling messenger (phonetic loan for 理/吏)
history.stage: Classical Chinese (Spring and Autumn period, Zuo Zhuan)

history.meaning: traveling gear, baggage, provisions for a journey
luggage, baggage (often pronounced with neutral tone xíngli)

morphemes.meaning: to travel, journey, go on the road
phonetic loan for 理/吏 (originally envoy/steward; later travel gear)

行李.notes: The second character 李 ('plum') has nothing to do with fruit here—it is an ancient phonetic loan from the *Zuo Zhuan*! In modern Mandarin,李 is usually pronounced in the neutral tone (xíngli), as in 收拾行李 ('pack one's bags') and 行李箱 ('suitcase').

行李牌.etymology: Three-character compound combining 行李 ('traveler's baggage, luggage', originally 'envoy or provisions for a journey') + 牌 ('tag, label, plaque').

history.meaning: luggage tag, baggage label

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 行李牌 (via 萌典)

行李箱.etymology: Three-character compound combining 行李 ('luggage, travel baggage') + 箱 ('box, trunk, case').

history.meaning: suitcase, travel trunk; car trunk/boot

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 行李箱 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: itinerary, journey, stage of a trip (haengjeong)

行程.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound from Classical and Medieval Chinese combining 行 (xíng, 'travel, journey, marching') + 程 (chéng, Old Chinese *lreŋ, originally 'unit of measurement, standard measure', extended to 'stage of a journey, distance traveled, schedule'). Attested in Tang poetry and prose for the distance or stages of a journey, and used in modern Mandarin for a planned travel route or daily schedule.

history.meaning: stages or distance of a journey; route of travel
travel itinerary, daily schedule of appearances and flights

morphemes.meaning: measure, stage of a journey, schedule, procedure

行程.notes: In Chinese showbiz and fandom culture, 行程 specifically refers to a celebrity's or executive's appearance and flight schedule (艺人行程 'artist schedule', 排行程 'book/arrange the schedule').

行行好.etymology: A colloquial verb-object phrase built by reduplicating the verb in 行好 (xíng hǎo, 'to perform a good deed, practice charity', where 行 xíng means 'to perform, practice' and 好 hǎo functions as a nominalized object 'goodness, mercy', parallel to Buddhist-influenced vernacular 行善 'do good deeds'). The AAB verb-reduplication pattern (行行好, xíngxhíng hǎo) softens and intensifies the imperative into an urgent, pleading, or exasperated entreaty: 'do a little good, have a heart, do me a favor'.

history.meaning: to perform charitable deeds, accumulate merit through kindness
have a heart! do me a favor! give me a break! (pleading or exasperated)

morphemes.meaning: to perform, carry out, practice (reduplicated for entreaty)

行行好.notes: Originally the cry of beggars asking for alms ('Kind sir/madam, have mercy!'), in modern office or drama dialogue it is used jokingly or in exasperated pleading with a colleague or boss ('Have a heart / Give me a break!').

rootFamily.gloss: to practice charity, do good deeds
to do a favor, show kindness (dialectal/colloquial)

街.etymology: Phono-semantic character 街, combining the crossroads/road radical 行 + phonetic 圭 (guī / Old Chinese *kˤre), originally meaning 'a four-way thoroughfare inside a city' -> 'street, market street'.

history.meaning: four-way urban thoroughfare
street, avenue, market town

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 街 (via 萌典)

街上.etymology: Locative compound combining 街 ('street') + localizer 上 ('on, in').

history.meaning: on the street, in town, out in the streets

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 街上 (via 萌典)

街口.etymology: Compound noun combining 街 ('street') + 口 ('mouth, entrance, intersection opening').

history.meaning: street entrance, street intersection

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 街口 (via 萌典)

街坊.etymology: Compound noun combining 街 ('street') + 坊 ('walled urban ward, neighborhood lane'); originally 'urban streets and wards', then with neutral-tone second syllable (jiēfang) 'neighbors, neighborhood'.

history.meaning: city streets and residential wards
neighbors, neighborhood

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 街坊 (via 萌典)

街角.etymology: Modifier-head noun compound combining 街 ('street') + 角 ('corner, angle').

history.meaning: street corner

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 街角 (via 萌典)

街边.etymology: Locative compound combining 街 ('street') + 边 (邊, 'side, edge, roadside').

history.meaning: roadside, street side, curb

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 街边 (via 萌典)

街道.etymology: Coordinate noun compound combining 街 ('urban street') + 道 ('road, way, thoroughfare').

history.meaning: street, avenue, urban subdistrict

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 街道 (via 萌典)

街门.etymology: Compound noun from 街 ('street; thoroughfare', step 彳/行 + phonetic 圭) + 门 (simplified from 門, 'gate; door'). In traditional northern courtyard architecture (四合院) and town inns, the 街门 is the outer gate that opens directly onto the public street.

history.meaning: outer courtyard gate facing the street
street gate; front street door

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 街门

衣服.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative compound (attested in the *Book of Odes* 詩經 and *Zuo Zhuan*) combining 衣 (yī, Old Chinese *ʔ(r)əj, pictograph of a upper-body robe with collar and sleeves, specifically 'upper garment' in antiquity) + 服 (fú, Old Chinese *bək, 'to wear, submit to; garments, attire in general'). Over time the two near-synonyms fused into the standard everyday disyllabic word for 'clothing, clothes', with 服 losing its tone in spoken Mandarin (yīfu).

history.meaning: upper garments (衣) and general attire/robes of rank (服)
clothes, clothing, garment (general everyday noun)

morphemes.meaning: attire, dress; to wear (neutral tone in modern speech)

衣服.notes: Counted with the classifier 件 (一件事/一件衣服) for individual garments or 套 (一套衣服) for a full outfit; in formal or costume contexts, 服装 (fúzhuāng) is preferred over conversational 衣服.

补写.etymology: Compound verb combining 补 (補, 'to mend clothes, patch, fill in a gap, supplement') + 写 (寫, 'to write').

history.meaning: to write in later, fill in omitted text, add in writing

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 补写 (via 萌典)

补齐.etymology: A resultative verb-complement compound formed from 补 (bǔ, Traditional 補, Old Chinese *pˤaʔ, composed of semantic 衣 'clothing' + phonetic 甫, originally 'to patch or mend torn clothes', extended to 'to supplement, make up a deficiency') + 齐 (qí, Traditional 齊, Old Chinese *dzˤej, pictograph of even heads of grain, 'even, uniform, complete, all present'). Literally 'to mend/supplement until complete and even'.

history.meaning: to patch/replenish (補) until even and complete (齊)
to make up a shortfall in full, supply all missing items or documents

morphemes.meaning: to mend, patch, supplement, make up for
even, complete, all present without omission

补齐.notes: Essential in administrative, financial, and production workflows: 把材料补齐 ('submit all the missing documents'), 补齐差价 ('make up the price difference'), or 补齐镜头 ('shoot the missing pick-up shots').

rootFamily.gloss: to remedy, make up for a deficiency or mistake

cognates.meaning: surface, outside, chart, to express (hyō / omote)

表.etymology: Originally a compound ideograph (會意) in Seal Script showing 毛 ('fur, hair') on top of 衣 ('garment'): ancient fur coats were worn with the fur on the outside, so 表 (biǎo, Old Chinese *p(r)jawʔ) meant 'outer garment' (as opposed to 裏 lǐ, 'inner lining'). From 'outer coat', it developed the noun sense 'exterior, surface, chart/memorial to the throne' and the transitive verb sense 'to put on the outside, make visible, manifest, express, state'. Note that simplified Chinese merged 錶 ('watch, meter') into 表, though the verbal sense 'to express' comes directly from ancient 'to manifest outwardly'.

history.meaning: outer fur garment; exterior surface (contrasted with 裏 'lining')
history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle Bone / Seal / Warring States)

history.meaning: to manifest outwardly, display, mark; formal memorial presented to the emperor
to express, state, show (bound or semi-free verb in 表态, 表示, 表明); chart, form; watch

morphemes.meaning: outer garment, exterior; to make outwardly visible, express, state

表.notes: Understanding the original meaning of 表 ('fur worn on the outside of a coat') unlocks the entire family of compounds: 表面 ('outer surface'), 表现/表示/表达 ('bring inner thoughts to the outside'), and 表白 ('make one's heart outwardly clear').

rootFamily.gloss: to declare one's position, take a stand
to make clear, state clearly, indicate

表哥.etymology: Kinship compound combining 表 ('outer, outside the patrilineal clan', i.e. related through one's mother or father's sister) + 哥 ('older brother').

history.meaning: older male cousin (on the mother's or aunt's side)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 表哥 (via 萌典)

表弟.etymology: Kinship compound of 表 ('outer; related through one's mother, father's sister, or mother's brother', originally the outer fur of a garment) + 弟 ('younger brother'). Traditional Chinese kinship distinguishes paternal parallel cousins (堂弟, sharing the same family surname within the hall 堂) from cousins through female lines (表弟 'outer younger male cousin').

morphemes.meaning: cousin related through a female line ('outer kin')

history.meaning: younger male cousin on the maternal or aunt's side
younger male cousin

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 表弟

表情.etymology: Compound combining 表 ('outer surface; to show, express') + 情 ('inner feeling, emotion, sentiment'), meaning 'facial expression; to express emotion'.

history.meaning: to express feelings -> facial expression, look
facial expression; emoji/sticker

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 表情 (via 萌典)

表演.etymology: A coordinative verb/noun compound formed from 表 (biǎo, 'to manifest outwardly, display, show') + 演 (yǎn, Old Chinese *N-q(r)anʔ, originally 'water flowing far and wide', extended in Classical Chinese to 'to draw out, elaborate, practice, rehearse, act out on stage'). Combining 'outward display' with 'elaborating/acting out', 表演 emerged in late imperial and modern Chinese as the standard term for theatrical, musical, or artistic performance.

history.meaning: to display outwardly (表) and elaborate/practice/enact (演)
to perform on stage, act, demonstrate; a theatrical or artistic performance

morphemes.meaning: to evolve, practice, act out, perform

表演.notes: Can be used both literally for stage/screen acting (表演节目 'perform a program/number') and sarcastically in workplace settings for someone putting on a dramatic show (看你表演 'watching you put on an act').

rootFamily.gloss: performance, show, concert; to put on a show
director (of a film, TV show, or stage play)

表现.etymology: A coordinative/resultative compound combining 表 (biǎo, 'to manifest on the outside, show') + 现 (xiàn, Traditional 現, originally the intransitive reading xian of 見 'to appear, become visible, manifest'). Attested in medieval Buddhist and Tang–Song texts in the sense of 'to become outwardly visible, manifest', and reinforced in the 20th century via Sino-Japanese 表現 (hyōgen) to denote both 'manifestation/display' and 'how one performs or conducts oneself'.

history.meaning: to manifest outwardly, become visible, reveal
to show off, display one's capability, perform; behavior or performance record

表现.notes: Unlike 表演 (stage/artistic acting), 表现 refers to how someone conducts themselves or performs in a job, exam, or competition (今天表现不错 'you did well today'), or trying to impress superiors (爱表现 'loves showing off').

rootFamily.gloss: to appear, emerge, come into view

表白.etymology: A verb-complement (resultative) compound from Literary Chinese combining 表 (biǎo, 'to manifest outwardly, state') + 白 (bái, Old Chinese *bˤrak, 'white, clear, plain; to make clear, state plainly, vindicate'). In Tang–Ming texts (and Buddhist liturgical declarations), 表白 meant 'to clear one's name, vindicate oneself, or state one's true intentions plainly'. In contemporary Mandarin, under the influence of modern romance media (and parallel to 告白 gàobái), it specialized into 'to confess romantic feelings, declare one's love'.

history.meaning: to state plainly, explain and vindicate one's innocence or true intentions
history.stage: Middle Chinese to Ming–Qing Literary Chinese

history.meaning: to confess one's romantic love, declare one's feelings to a crush

morphemes.meaning: white, clear, plain; to make clear or state openly

表白.notes: While older dictionaries still list the literary sense 'to vindicate oneself', in modern everyday speech and dramas 向某人表白 almost exclusively means 'to confess one's crush/love to someone'.

rootFamily.gloss: to confess love, make a public declaration (via Japanese 告白)
frank, candid, to confess (a secret or wrongdoing)

表示.etymology: A coordinative compound from Classical and Han-era Chinese (attested in the *Hou Hanshu* 後漢書) composed of 表 (biǎo, 'to manifest on the outside, mark') + 示 (shì, Old Chinese *g-dar-s, originally an altar pictograph for divine portents revealed from heaven, hence 'to show, reveal, indicate to others'). Literally 'to display outwardly and show'.

history.meaning: to display visibly, set up a marker to show others, signify
to express, indicate, state (an attitude or opinion); token of appreciation (noun)

表示.notes: Extremely versatile: in news and workplace registers it introduces indirect speech or attitudes (他表示支持 'he expressed support'), while colloquially 有所表示 means 'give a tangible token of appreciation/gift'.

rootFamily.gloss: to indicate, point out; instructions, directive

表达.etymology: A verb-complement (resultative) compound combining 表 (biǎo, 'to manifest outwardly, bring to the surface') + 达 (dá, Traditional 達, Old Chinese *lˤat, 'to pass through unhindered, reach, arrive at, communicate thoroughly'). Literally 'to manifest inner thoughts so that they reach [the listener]'.

history.meaning: to manifest outwardly (表) and reach/communicate through (達)
to express, convey, articulate (ideas, feelings, or artistic meaning)

morphemes.meaning: to display outwardly, bring to the surface
to reach, pass through, communicate thoroughly

表达.notes: Compared to 表示 (which often takes simple attitudes or clauses, e.g. 表示同意), 表达 takes abstract nouns of inner emotion, thought, or meaning (表达感情 'express feelings', 表达能力 'ability to articulate oneself').

rootFamily.gloss: to pass on, convey, transmit (a message or spirit)
to express, state (an opinion or attitude)

表面.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound combining 表 (biǎo, 'outer garment, exterior, outside') + 面 (miàn, Old Chinese *mjan-s, pictograph of a human face enclosed in a frame, extended to 'face, front, surface, side'). Literally 'the outer face/surface', contrasting with 内里 (nèilǐ, 'the inside/lining') or 本质 (běnzhì, 'essence').

history.meaning: outer surface of an object; outward facial or physical appearance
physical surface; superficial appearance, facade (as noun or attributive modifier)

表面.notes: Frequently used metaphorically in workplace and drama contexts for superficial politeness or keeping up appearances: 表面工夫 ('window dressing / lip service'), 表面上 ('on the surface / outwardly').

rootFamily.gloss: facial expression, look on one's face

衬衫.etymology: Modifier-head garment compound combining 衬 (襯, 'inner garment worn next to the skin, lining') + 衫 ('unlined upper garment, robe, shirt').

history.meaning: undergarment robe -> shirt, blouse

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 衬衫 (via 萌典)

袋.etymology: A phono-semantic compound (形聲) combining semantic 衣 (yī, 'cloth, garment') with phonetic 代 (dài, Old Chinese *lˤək-s). Originally written  (with 巾 'cloth' as the semantic determinative) in the *Shuowen Jiezi*, denoting a cloth sack or pouch for holding items. By regular classifier grammaticalization in Mandarin, the noun meaning 'bag, sack, pouch, pocket' also functions as a container measure word (classifier) for bagfuls of items.

history.meaning: cloth sack, pouch, bag for carrying goods or garments
bag, sack, pocket (noun); bagful, sackful, pack (classifier)

morphemes.meaning: bag, sack, pouch, pocket (composed of phonetic 代 + semantic 衣)

袋.notes: As a classifier (measure word), 一袋 measures anything packaged in a bag or pouch (一袋零食 'a bag of snacks', 一袋面粉 'a sack of flour'); as a bound noun root it forms 口袋 ('pocket') and 袋子 ('bag').

rootFamily.gloss: bag, sack, pouch (free noun with nominal suffix -子)

袋子.etymology: Nominal compound formed from 袋 ('bag, sack, pouch, pocket', clothing radical 衣 + phonetic 代 dài) + nominal suffix 子.

history.meaning: bag, sack, pouch

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 袋子 (via 萌典)

袖子.etymology: Nominal compound formed from 袖 ('sleeve of a garment', clothing radical 衤/衣 + phonetic 由 yóu) + nominal suffix 子.

history.meaning: sleeve

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 袖子 (via 萌典)

被.etymology: A textbook example of grammaticalization in Chinese historical syntax. Formed as a phono-semantic character from semantic 衣 (衤, 'garment, bedding') + phonetic 皮 (pí, Old Chinese *b(r)aj), 被 (bèi, Old Chinese *b(r)ajʔ) originally meant 'sleeping quilt, blanket' (still preserved in 被子 bèizi). From 'bedding', it developed the transitive verb sense 'to cover, drape over oneself' and thence 'to be covered by, suffer, undergo, incur [an affliction or action]' in Warring States and Han Chinese (e.g. 被災 'suffer disaster'). By the Late Han and Six Dynasties, when followed by a verb or Agent + Verb, it grammaticalized into the canonical passive voice marker ('by').

history.meaning: sleeping quilt, blanket; to drape over or cover the body

history.form: 被 + V / 被 + Agent + V
history.meaning: to suffer, undergo, be subjected to (adversative passive marker)
by (general passive preposition/auxiliary, with or without an explicit agent)

morphemes.meaning: passive marker ('by / be V-ed'); originally 'quilt; to be covered by, undergo'

被.notes: Traditionally carried an adversative nuance (something unfortunate happening to the subject, like 被骂 'get scolded' or 被骗 'get cheated'), though under modern Europeanized grammar and expressions like 被誉为 ('be hailed as') it now also marks positive passives; in internet slang, 被 + intransitive/active verb (e.g. 被自愿 'be \"volunteered\" against one's will') mocks forced compliance.

rootFamily.gloss: quilt, comforter, blanket (retaining the original noun meaning!)

被子.etymology: Nominal compound formed from 被 ('bedding quilt, coverlet', clothing radical 衤/衣 + phonetic 皮 pí) + nominal suffix 子.

history.meaning: quilt, comforter, blanket

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 被子 (via 萌典)

被打脸.etymology: A passive verb-object phrase combining the passive marker 被 (bèi, 'be [subjected to]') + 打脸 (dǎ liǎn, literally 'to slap [someone's] face', from 打 'to strike, hit' + 脸 'face, prestige, social standing'). Because 脸 (liǎn) in Chinese sociolinguistics embodies public dignity and credibility, 'getting slapped in the face' evolved in contemporary Mandarin and internet slang into a vivid metaphor for having one's boast, prediction, or public persona swiftly and publicly contradicted by reality.

history.meaning: to slap someone in the face; to humiliate someone and make them lose face
to get publicly contradicted, have one's claims debunked, eat one's words

被打脸.notes: A ubiquitous showbiz and social-media expression (often paired with 光速被打脸 'contradicted at the speed of light') when a celebrity, PR team, or character makes a bold denial or promise that is immediately disproven.

rootFamily.gloss: to slap in the face; to debunk or prove someone wrong publicly
to lose face, bring shame on oneself
to turn hostile suddenly, fall out with someone

被毙.etymology: A colloquial passive phrase formed from the passive marker 被 (bèi, 'to get, be') + 毙 (bì, Traditional 斃, Old Chinese *bet-s, composed of 敝 'tattered, worn out' + 死 'die', originally meaning 'to fall down dead, perish', and in modern legal/military Mandarin short for 枪毙 qiāngbì, 'to execute by shooting'). In Chinese media, publishing, and TV/film production jargon, 毙 ('shoot dead / execute') is used metaphorically for a superior 'killing' or rejecting a creative pitch, script, or budget proposal, so 被毙 means 'to get shot down / axed'.

history.meaning: to fall prostrate, collapse dead; to kill or execute
to get shot down, be axed or rejected (of a proposal, script, or program pitch)

morphemes.meaning: to die violently, execute by shooting; metaphorically to kill/reject a proposal

被毙.notes: Essential Chinese TV/film industry slang: 方案又被毙了 ('the proposal got shot down again') or 选题被总监毙掉 ('the topic pitch was killed by the director') parallels English 'killed' or 'shot down'.

rootFamily.gloss: to execute by shooting; colloquially to reject/kill a draft or proposal
to kill off, shoot down, reject (with resultative complement 掉)
to die violently, perish on the spot

被誉为.etymology: A semi-literary passive construction combining 被 (bèi, passive marker 'be') + 誉 (yù, Traditional 譽, Old Chinese *la-s, from 言 'speech' + 與 phonetic, 'to praise, eulogize, acclaim') + 为 (wéi, Traditional 為, Classical copular complement 'as, to be'). While Classical Chinese expressed this with 譽之為 ('praise him/it as...'), modern journalistic and biographical prose fused the passive marker 被 with the Literary verb-complement 誉为 to match English 'be hailed as / be acclaimed as'.

history.meaning: to praise, eulogize; to acclaim as (Classical active construction)
to be hailed as, be acclaimed as, be renowned as

被誉为.notes: A signature high-register phrase in award introductions, press releases, and showbiz bios (e.g., 他被誉为幕后之王 'He is hailed as the King Behind the Scenes').

被骗.etymology: A passive verb phrase combining the adversative passive marker 被 (bèi, 'to suffer, be subjected to') + 骗 (piàn, Traditional 騙, Middle Chinese *pʰjɛnH, composed of 馬 'horse' + 扁 phonetic, originally a Tang-dynasty vernacular word meaning 'to leap or vault onto a horse's back from the side', which by the Song–Yuan period shifted via 'sleight of movement / agile trick' to 'to swindle, hoodwink, deceive').

history.meaning: to vault or leap onto a horse; later to trick, swindle, deceive (Song–Yuan)
to be deceived, get cheated, be duped or scammed

morphemes.meaning: to deceive, cheat, swindle, dupe (originally 'leap onto a horse')

被骗.notes: Can stand alone without an explicit agent (我被骗了 'I got scammed/duped') or take an agent between 被 and 骗 (被他骗了 'was deceived by him'). Its horse radical 馬 is a relic of its medieval meaning 'vault onto a horse'!

cognates.meaning: to raid, ambuscade, launch a surprise attack

袭击.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative/modifier-head military compound combining 袭 (xí, Traditional 襲, Old Chinese *s-lup, originally 'a double robe for dressing a corpse; to wear layered garments', which in the *Zuo Zhuan* acquired the specific military definition 'to march covertly without drums and catch the enemy unawares, launch a surprise raid') + 击 (jī, Traditional 擊, Old Chinese *kˤek, 'to strike, hit, attack'). Literally 'to raid by surprise and strike'.

history.meaning: to launch a covert surprise raid without war-drums (襲) and strike (擊)
to launch a surprise attack, raid, or assault; an attack or strike (military, physical, or metaphorical)

morphemes.meaning: to launch a covert surprise raid, catch unawares

袭击.notes: Used both for physical or military assaults (恐怖袭击 'terrorist attack') and metaphorically for sudden storms, crises, or media waves hitting a person or company (受到舆论袭击 'hit by a wave of public criticism').

rootFamily.gloss: sneak attack, ambush; to do something on short notice
to strike, hit, blow; to dishearten or打击
to attack, assault, accuse (militarily or verbally)

裂.etymology: Phono-semantic character 裂, combining clothing radical 衣 ('leftover scraps of cloth when cutting a garment') + phonetic 列 (liè, 'to divide, split'), meaning 'to tear cloth, split open, crack, rend'.

history.meaning: to tear silk or cloth -> to split, crack
to crack, split open, tear

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 裂 (via 萌典)

裂开.etymology: Resultative verb compound combining 裂 ('to crack, split') + directional/resultative complement 开 (開, 'open, apart').

history.meaning: to split open, crack apart

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 裂开 (via 萌典)

装.etymology: Phono-semantic character 装 (裝), combining clothing radical 衣 + phonetic 壮 (壯 zhuàng), originally meaning 'travel attire, to wrap and pack baggage for a journey', extended to 'to load, pack, install, assemble; to dress up, pretend'.

history.meaning: travel kit, to pack -> attire, adorn
to pack, hold, install/assemble; clothing; to pretend

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 装 (via 萌典)

装回.etymology: Resultative verb-complement compound combining 装 (裝, 'to pack, load, install, fit') + 回 ('back to its original place').

history.meaning: to put back inside, reinstall, reassemble

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 装回 (via 萌典)

装满.etymology: Resultative verb compound from 装 (simplified from 裝, 'pack; load; fill into a container') + 满 (simplified from 滿, 'full to the brim'). Combines the action of packing or pouring into a vessel with the result that the container is completely full.

history.meaning: fill a container or vehicle to capacity
fill to the brim; pack full

裙子.etymology: Nominal compound formed from 裙 ('lower garment, skirt, petticoat', clothing radical 衤/衣 + phonetic 君 jūn) + nominal suffix 子.

history.meaning: skirt, dress

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 裙子 (via 萌典)

裸辞.etymology: A 21st-century Chinese internet and workplace neologism formed as a modifier-head compound: 裸 (luǒ, 'naked, bare, without backing or preparation') modifies 辞 (cí, shortened from 辞职 cízhí, 'to resign from office'). The metaphor of 'nakedness' (裸-) became a productive prefix in contemporary Mainland Mandarin for undertaking major life steps without material security or a fallback plan (cf. 裸婚 'marrying without property', 裸考 'taking an exam without studying').

history.meaning: to take leave of one's official post or ministerial duty
to quit a job without having secured a new position first

morphemes.meaning: naked, bare, without preparation or safety net
to resign, take leave of office (short for 辞职)

裸辞.notes: Functions as a separable verb-object or modifier-verb construction in casual speech (e.g., 裸辞了三次), though usually used intransitively; very common in modern white-collar and media industry discourse.

rootFamily.gloss: to marry without buying a house, car, or wedding ring
to sit an exam without prior preparation

褪色.etymology: A verb combining 褪 (tuì, 'to slip off, shed', with the clothing radical 衤) and 色 (sè, 'color'). Metaphorically, a pigment 'sheds' its vividness just as an animal sheds skin or a person removes a garment, elegantly capturing the slow decay of colors in sunlight.

history.meaning: to fade (colors)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 褪色

西北.etymology: The directional noun '西北' (xīběi, northwest) is a direct combination of '西' (west) and '北' (north). In traditional Chinese geography and meteorology, intermediate directions are always formed by placing east or west before north or south (unlike English, which places north/south first). The Northwest region of China, known as '大西北', is culturally and geographically significant, historically associated with the Silk Road, arid climates, and vast expanses. The term is fundamental in geographical descriptions.

history.meaning: southeast

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 西北

西方.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 西 (xī, 'west', originally a pictograph of a bird's nest at dusk when birds return to roost) and 方 (fāng, 'direction, region, quarter'). In pre-Qin Classical Chinese it denoted the western cardinal direction or western borderlands; during the Six Dynasties and Tang period it acquired the Buddhist cosmological sense of Amitābha's Western Pure Land (西方极乐世界); from the late Ming and Qing Jesuit encounters onward, it shifted to designate Europe and the Euro-American geopolitical cultural sphere ('the Occident / the West').

history.meaning: the western cardinal direction; western lands
the Western Pure Land of Sukhāvatī in Buddhist cosmology
the Western world (Europe and North America)

西方.notes: Used both as a noun ('the West') and attributively before nouns without 的 (e.g., 西方国家 'Western countries', 西方文化 'Western culture').

西装.etymology: Determinative clothing compound of 西 ('Western', originally a bird nesting at dusk) + 装 ('attire; dress; outfit', 壮 + 衣 'garment'). Coined in the late 19th and early 20th centuries to designate a tailored Western-style jacket-and-trousers suit.

history.meaning: tailored Western-style suit
suit; Western suit

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 西装

西餐厅.etymology: A right-branching modifier-head compound built from 西餐 (xīcān, 'Western meal/cuisine', itself a late Qing / Republican-era compound of 西 'Western' + 餐 'food, meal') plus the suffixing architectural noun 厅 (tīng, 'hall, salon, dining room', simplified from 廳). 餐厅 ('dining hall, restaurant') emerged in modern urban Chinese to denote an indoor dining establishment, replacing older tavern terms like 酒楼 or 饭庄 for modern or foreign-style venues.

history.meaning: European-style food and table service in treaty-port China
Western-style restaurant or dining room

西餐厅.notes: In TV dramas and urban life, 西餐厅 typically evokes an upscale setting for formal dates or business negotiations (cutting steak, drinking red wine), contrasting with casual 快餐店 ('fast-food joints').

要.etymology: High-frequency verb and modal ('want, need, will / be going to'). Originally depicting two hands at the waist (later clarified as 腰 'waist'), 要 in Classical Chinese meant 'seek, invite, essential' (yāo / yào), from which vernacular Mandarin developed 'need, want' and imminent future 'be about to'.

history.meaning: seek; essential; important
want; need; be going to

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 要 (via 萌典)

要不.etymology: An elliptical colloquial conditional compound formed from 要 (yào, 'if; suppose', grammaticalized from the modal verb 'to want, require' in early vernacular Mandarin) and the negator 不 (bù, 'not'). It originated as a phonetic and syntactic truncation of 要不然 (yàobùrán, 'if it is not so; otherwise') or 要不是 (yàobùshì, 'if not for'), and further developed a pragmatic discourse function for floating tentative suggestions ('how about... / or else we could...').

history.meaning: if not; otherwise (elliptical conditional)
otherwise; or how about (proposing an alternative)

要不.notes: Extremely frequent in conversational dialogue to soften a suggestion or pivot to Plan B (e.g., 要不咱们改天再聊？ 'How about we chat another day?'). Pronounced with a neutral tone on 不 (yàobu) when introducing a suggestion.

要不是.etymology: A vernacular counterfactual conditional conjunction composed of 要 (yào, 'if', grammaticalized from 'want/need'), 不 (bù, 'not'), and the copula 是 (shì, 'to be; to be the case'). Literally 'if it were not the case that...', it crystallized in vernacular northern Mandarin during the late imperial period to introduce a real condition that prevented a hypothetical (usually negative) consequence.

history.meaning: if it were not for (literary counterfactual)
if it were not for; had it not been for

morphemes.meaning: to be, to be the case

要不是.notes: Typically paired with a result clause containing 就 ('then') or 早就 ('long ago would have'), e.g., 要不是你帮忙，我早就放弃了 ('If it hadn't been for your help, I would have given up long ago').

要不然.etymology: A hybrid literary-vernacular conditional conjunction combining the colloquial conditional marker 要 (yào, 'if') with the Classical Chinese negative anaphoric phrase 不然 (bùrán, 'not so; not like this', where 然 means 'thus, so'). Literally 'if it is not so', it bridges Classical 不然 ('otherwise') and spoken Mandarin conditional syntax, serving both as a warning of consequences ('otherwise / or else') and a conversational pivot to an alternative option ('or how about').

history.meaning: it is not so; if not so, otherwise
if not so; otherwise; or else how about

要不然.notes: Interchangeable with 要不 in both 'otherwise' and 'how about' senses, though 要不然 has slightly more rhythmic weight and emphasis when warning of an undesirable alternative.

要么.etymology: Formed from the modal/conditional root 要 (yào, 'to want, choose; if') and the vernacular suffix 么 (me, written 麼/末 in older texts, a grammaticalized interrogative and pause particle). Used correlatively as 要么……要么…… ('either... or...'), it grammaticalized in modern Mandarin from the rhetorical presentation of mutually exclusive choices ('if you want this... or if you want that...').

history.meaning: or else; either ... or ... (presenting alternatives)

morphemes.meaning: vernacular modal/topic particle marking an option

要么.notes: Almost always appears in pairs (要么 A，要么 B 'either A or B') to frame a sharp, exhaustive dilemma with no middle ground, or singly at the start of a clause as a synonym for 要不 ('or else how about...').

rootFamily.gloss: so, in that case; that much

要回.etymology: Resultative verb-complement compound combining 要 (yào, 'to ask for, demand') + 回 ('back').

history.meaning: to ask for something back, reclaim, get back

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 要回 (via 萌典)

要是.etymology: Conditional conjunction combining 要 ('if, suppose', grammaticalized from modal 'will, want') + copula 是 ('is, be the case').

history.meaning: if, suppose, in case

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 要是 (via 萌典)

要求.etymology: A coordinative verbal and nominal compound uniting 要 (yāo in Classical Chinese, 'to seek, press for, intercept, coerce', shifting to yào in modern Mandarin) and 求 (qiú, 'to seek, request, beseech'). Attested in Classical Chinese (e.g., *Mencius*, *Book of Han*) in the sense of seeking or soliciting something, it was reinforced in the late 19th and early 20th centuries via Meiji Japanese 要求 (*yōkyū*) as the standard legal, diplomatic, and professional translation for 'demand, requirement, claim'.

history.meaning: to seek after, solicit, ask for (favour or advantage)
to demand, require; requirement, stipulation (n./v.)

morphemes.meaning: to demand, press for, need (orig. yāo 'seek')

要求.notes: Functions smoothly as both a transitive verb (要求他重做 'demand that he redo it') and a countable noun (提出严格的要求 'put forward strict requirements').

要紧.etymology: A coordinative/modifier-head vernacular compound composed of 要 (yào, 'essential, pivotal, vital', derived from its original pictographic sense of the 'waist' 腰, the central pivot of the body) and 紧 (jǐn, 'taut, urgent, pressing, strict'). While Literary Chinese preferred the order 紧要 (jǐnyào), northern vernacular Mandarin from the Yuan and Ming dynasties onward favored 要紧 (yàojǐn) for 'critical, urgent, serious'.

history.meaning: urgent, critical, of vital importance
important, critical, serious (often in negative 不要紧)

要紧.notes: Often used in the predicate pattern 身体要紧 ('health comes first!') in workplace dramas, as well as in the ubiquitous polite reassurance 不要紧 ('never mind / it's nothing serious').

见.etymology: Oracle-bone and bronze ideograph 见 (見) depicting a large eye (目) atop a kneeling or standing person (儿/人), emphasizing visual perception: 'to see, catch sight of, meet, appear'.

history.meaning: person with prominent eye -> to see, behold, meet
to see, meet, catch sight of; view/opinion

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 见 (via 萌典)

见到.etymology: A resultative verb-complement compound formed from the perception verb 见 (jiàn, 'to see, perceive, meet', originally a kneeling person 人 topped by a prominent eye 目) and the phase/resultative complement 到 (dào, 'to arrive at, reach, succeed in'). While 见 alone serves as a bound resultative complement after sensory verbs (看见, 听见), attaching 到 after 见 creates a transitive verb meaning 'to succeed in seeing or meeting someone/something in person'.

history.meaning: to see, catch sight of, have an audience with
to see, catch sight of, meet in person

见到.notes: Unlike 见面 (which is a separable VO compound requiring 跟/和 before the person: 跟他见面), 见到 takes a direct object directly (见到他 'see/meet him').

rootFamily.gloss: to meet face to face (separable VO)

见得多了.etymology: An idiomatic verb-complement construction consisting of 见 (jiàn, 'to see, witness, experience'), the structural complement marker 得 (de, linking a verb to a descriptive/degree complement), the adjective 多 (duō, 'many, much, frequent'), and the aspectual/change-of-state particle 了 (le). Literally 'to have seen [to the extent of being] plenty now', it grammaticalized in spoken Mandarin as an expression of seasoned, worldly-wise familiarity.

history.meaning: to have seen a great deal of; to be thoroughly accustomed to seeing

见得多了.notes: Typically used with a fronted topic (这种场面我见得多了 'I've seen plenty of scenes like this') to project veteran composure and dismiss something as unremarkable. Can also be shortened to 见多了.

rootFamily.gloss: what one has seen and heard, firsthand experience

cognates.meaning: knowledge, experience, what one has seen and heard
knowledge gained by seeing and hearing

见闻.etymology: A coordinative nominalized compound uniting the two primary Classical Chinese sensory verbs: 见 (jiàn, Traditional 見, 'to see with the eyes') and 闻 (wén, Traditional 聞, 'to hear with the ears', showing an ear 耳 inside a doorway 門). Attested since the Han dynasty (*Book of Han*, *Lunheng*), the juxtaposition of 'seeing and hearing' underwent nominalization to denote the totality of one's firsthand observations, lived knowledge, and empirical awareness.

history.meaning: to see and hear; what one sees and hears firsthand
firsthand experience, observations, general knowledge of the world

morphemes.meaning: to hear, learn of; auditory report

见闻.notes: Frequently collocated with verbs of broadening or enriching, such as 增长见闻 ('broaden one's horizons/experience') or 旅途见闻 ('things seen and heard on a journey').

见面.etymology: Verb-object compound combining 见 (見, 'to see, meet') + 面 ('face'), literally 'to see each other face to face'.

history.meaning: to meet in person, see each other

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 见面 (via 萌典)

观众.etymology: A modifier-head compound composed of 观 (guān, Traditional 觀, 'to watch, view, observe intently') and 众 (zhòng, Traditional 衆, 'multitude, crowd, the many', originally three people 人 under an eye 目 or sun). While both characters are ancient, the specific compound 观众 gained currency in modern Chinese alongside Japanese 観衆 (*kanshū*) to designate a collective theatrical, cinematic, or broadcast 'audience / spectators', contrasting with 听众 ('listeners / radio audience').

history.meaning: to observe the multitude (verb-object phrase in Classical texts)
spectators, viewers, audience (modifier-head noun)

观众.notes: A core term in *Behind the Scenes* (*幕后之王*): in Chinese television production, 观众 refers both to home viewers (电视机前的观众朋友) and the live studio audience (现场观众).

rootFamily.gloss: to watch, view (a performance or match)

观察.etymology: A coordinative compound uniting two near-synonymous verbs of visual and cognitive scrutiny: 观 (guān, Traditional 觀, 'to look at carefully, survey, contemplate') and 察 (chá, 'to examine closely, inspect, discern'). Attested in Classical Chinese (*Zuo Zhuan*, *Liji*) for inspecting someone's conduct or political conditions, and used in Tang–Qing administration for the post of Surveillance Commissioner (观察使); in the late 19th century it also absorbed the modern scientific and clinical sense of 'observation' via Japanese 観察 (*kansatsu*).

history.meaning: to scrutinize, inspect, examine carefully (conduct or omens)
Imperial Surveillance / Circuit Intendant Commissioner
to observe scientifically, monitor clinically, or watch closely

观察.notes: Used both for sharp psychological or professional scrutiny (观察她的反应 'observe her reaction') and for medical monitoring in a hospital (留院观察 'keep in the hospital for observation').

rootFamily.gloss: to inspect, investigate on the spot

规划.etymology: A coordinative compound combining 规 (guī, Traditional 規, 'carpenter's compass for drawing circles; to map out, regulate') and 划 (huà, Traditional 畫/劃, 'to delineate, draw boundary lines, carve out a plan'). Originally evoking the draftsman's act of using a compass and marking lines to lay out land or architecture (attested in Medieval Chinese texts such as *Wen Xuan* and Tang histories), it developed in modern Mandarin into the standard term for macro-level 'strategic planning' or a 'long-term roadmap'.

history.meaning: to lay out with compass and lines; to devise a scheme or strategy
long-term strategic plan, urban/career roadmap; to plan strategically

morphemes.meaning: compass; to regulate, map out standards
to delineate, draw lines, plan out

规划.notes: Connotes a macro-level, long-term, systematic roadmap (e.g., 职业规划 'career planning', 城市规划 'urban planning'), whereas 计划 (jìhuà) can refer to routine, short-term schedules or everyday plans.

rootFamily.gloss: to plot, scheme, mastermind (a show or campaign)

规则.etymology: A coordinative nominal compound pairing 规 (guī, Traditional 規, 'carpenter's compass; standard, norm') with 则 (zé, Traditional 則, 'law, pattern, rule', originally a bronze cauldron 鼎 beside a knife 刀, signifying legal statutes inscribed into ritual bronzes). Attested from the Tang dynasty onward for institutional standards and literary models, and reinforced in modern East Asian legal/administrative lexicon alongside Japanese 規則 (*kisoku*).

history.meaning: standard model, institutional norm, established statute
rule, regulation (noun); regular, symmetrical (adjective)

规则.notes: In workplace and entertainment industry dramas, 行业规则 ('industry rules') and 潜规则 (qiánguīzé, 'unwritten/hidden rules') are central concepts.

rootFamily.gloss: unwritten rules, hidden rules (esp. in showbiz/workplace)

规定.etymology: Compound verb and noun combining 规 (規, 'drafting compass, standard, rule') + 定 ('to fix, settle, establish').

history.meaning: to stipulate, prescribe; rule, regulation, provision

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 规定 (via 萌典)

规矩.etymology: Metaphorical coordinate compound joining 规 (規, 'carpenter's compass for drawing circles') + 矩 ('carpenter's square for drawing right angles'); since Mencius and pre-Qin texts used figuratively for 'standards, rules, proper etiquette, well-behaved'.

history.meaning: compass and square -> moral or technical standard
rule, custom, manners; well-behaved, proper

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 规矩 (via 萌典)

视线.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-Japanese graphic loan (*wasei-kango*, Japanese 視線 *shisen*) coined in Meiji Japan to translate European optical and anatomical terms ('line of vision / visual axis', German *Sehlinie*), combining 视 (shì, Traditional 視, 'to look at, vision') and 线 (xiàn, Traditional 線, 'thread, line, ray'). Adopted into Mandarin in the early 20th century, it quickly expanded from physical optics to the metaphorical 'gaze' of a person or 'the public eye' in media culture.

history.meaning: optical line of vision, direction of gaze (Meiji coinage)
line of sight, gaze; public attention / media spotlight

视线.notes: Used both physically (挡住视线 'block the line of sight', 移开视线 'look away') and in PR/media contexts (转移公众视线 'divert public attention', 淡出公众视线 'fade from the public eye').

视频.etymology: A modern Mainland Chinese technical neologism formed as a modifier-head compound: 视 (shì, Traditional 視, 'visual, television/video') modifies 频 (pín, Traditional 頻, shortened from 频率 pínlǜ, 'frequency'). Coined in the mid-20th century in telecommunications engineering as a direct calque of English 'video frequency' (parallel to 音频 yīnpín 'audio frequency' and 射频 shèpín 'radio frequency'), it generalized during the digital and internet era to replace 录像 (lùxiàng, 'videotape recording') as the everyday Mainland word for 'video'.

history.meaning: video frequency (telecommunications signal band)
digital video clip, video stream, video call

morphemes.meaning: frequency (short for 频率); signal channel

视频.notes: Standard in Mainland China for 'video' (看视频 'watch a video', 发视频 'post a video', 视频会议 'video conference'), whereas Taiwan and Hong Kong use 影片 (yǐngpiàn) or 视讯 (shìxùn, for video calls/feeds).

觉.etymology: Phono-semantic/associative character 觉 (覺), combining 见 (見, 'to see, perceive') with phonetic 學省; split into two readings: (1) jué ('to wake up to, sense, feel, become aware'); (2) jiào ('a sleep, nap', originally 'waking from sleep', as in 睡觉).

history.meaning: to awaken from sleep -> to perceive, realize
to feel, sense, wake up (jué); sleep, nap (jiào)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 觉 (via 萌典)

觉得.etymology: Compound cognitive/sensory verb formed from 觉 (覺 jué, 'to sense, perceive, feel') + verbal suffix 得 (neutral tone de, originally 'to obtain, register').

history.meaning: to feel, sense, think (that)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 觉得 (via 萌典)

觉着.etymology: A northern colloquial Mandarin verb-particle formation combining 觉 (jué, Traditional 覺, 'to sense, feel, perceive') with the unstressed durative/experiential suffix 着 (zhe, originally a Classical verb meaning 'to attach, cleave to', grammaticalized in Middle and Early Modern Chinese into a continuous marker). It is the colloquial northern counterpart of 觉得 (juéde, 'to feel, think'), preserving the older vernacular suffix 着 after verbs of sensation and cognition.

history.meaning: to sense, feel in body or mind; to reckon
history.stage: Ming–Qing Northern Vernacular Mandarin (e.g., Dream of the Red Chamber)

history.meaning: to feel, think, reckon (colloquial northern register)

morphemes.meaning: colloquial suffix marking ongoing feeling or cognitive state

觉着.notes: Semantically identical to 觉得 (juéde), both meaning 'to feel (physically)' or 'to think/feel (an opinion)', but 觉着 carries a warm, folksy Beijing/northern conversational flavor frequently heard in spoken dialogue.

角.etymology: Oracle-bone and bronze pictograph of a ridged, pointed animal horn (角), extended since antiquity to 'corner, angle (jiǎo); ancient wine vessel; one-tenth of a yuan / dime; role/character in drama (jué)'.

history.meaning: animal horn -> corner, angle
horn, corner, angle, 10-cent unit (jiǎo); actor's role (jué)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 角 (via 萌典)

角上.etymology: Locative compound combining 角 ('corner, horn') + localizer 上 ('on, at').

history.meaning: at the corner, on the corner

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 角上 (via 萌典)

角度.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 角 (jiǎo, 'horn, corner, geometric angle') and 度 (dù, 'measure, degree, extent'). Originally a mathematical and astronomical term measuring the degree of an angle between two intersecting lines (crystallized in modern scientific usage alongside Meiji Japanese 角度 *kakudo*), it underwent metaphorical extension in the 20th century—strongly reinforced by camera work, journalism, and photography—to mean a cognitive 'perspective, standpoint, or angle of approach'.

history.meaning: measurement of a geometric angle in degrees
geometric angle; camera angle; conceptual perspective or viewpoint

角度.notes: Crucial in media and debate: key collocations include 从……的角度来看 ('from the perspective of...'), 换个角度想 ('think about it from another angle'), and 拍摄角度 ('camera angle').

角落.etymology: Compound noun combining 角 ('corner, angle') + 落 ('nook, settlement, place where things gather/settle').

history.meaning: corner, nook, out-of-the-way spot

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 角落 (via 萌典)

解.etymology: Compound ideograph combining 角 ('horn') + 刀 ('knife') + 牛 ('ox'), originally depicting a butcher or craftsman using a knife to separate an ox's horn and joints (Middle Chinese *kæX*, famous from the *Zhuangzi* parable of Cook Ding). From 'unjoint; separate cleanly', it generalized to 'untie a knot or apron string' (解下围裙) and 'solve a riddle or problem' (解开谜团).

history.meaning: separate joints; untie a knot
untie; unfasten; solve

解决.etymology: A coordinative/resultative compound uniting two vivid Classical Chinese metaphors for clearing an impasse: 解 (jiě, 'to untie a knot, dissect an ox at the joints', composed of a knife 刀, cow 牛, and horn 角) and 决 (jué, 'to breach a dike so pent-up water flows through; to decide definitively'). Attested in Literary Chinese for untangling a dispute or clearing up a stalemate, and standardized in modern Chinese alongside Japanese 解決 (*kaiketsu*) for 'to solve, resolve, settle'.

history.meaning: to untangle and breach an obstruction; to settle a dispute
to solve (a problem), resolve (a crisis), dispose of / take care of

morphemes.meaning: to breach a channel, decide, settle definitively

解决.notes: Beyond standard collocations like 解决问题 ('solve a problem'), in colloquial and dramatic speech 解决 can mean 'to take care of / finish off' a meal, a troublesome task, or even an opponent (把午饭解决了 'polish off lunch').

解开.etymology: A resultative verb-complement compound combining 解 (jiě, 'to untie, unfasten, dissect, loosen') with the directional/resultative complement 开 (kāi, Traditional 開, 'to open, spread apart, come undone'). Whereas Classical Chinese used bare 解 for untying a cord or emotional knot, vernacular Mandarin added 开 to explicitly mark the successful result of parting or opening what was bound.

history.meaning: to untie a knot, unfasten garments, dispel sorrow
to untie, unfasten; to clear up (a mystery or emotional knot)

解开.notes: Used both for physical fasteners (解开安全带 'unfasten a seatbelt', 解开绳子 'untie a rope') and figuratively for emotional burdens or mysteries (解开心结 'untie an emotional knot / let go of a grudge', 解开谜团 'unravel a mystery').

rootFamily.gloss: emotional knot, lingering resentment or worry in the heart
to untie, dissolve, lift (a ban or contract)

解放.etymology: A coordinative verb compound pairing 解 (jiě, 'to untie, unbind, release from fetters') and 放 (fàng, 'to let go, set free, release'). Attested in Medieval Chinese (e.g., *History of the Northern Dynasties* and Buddhist texts) in the literal sense of untying captives or releasing animals, it was repurposed in Meiji Japan (解放 *kaihō*) to translate Western political concepts of 'emancipation' and 'liberation', then re-entered China to become a foundational political term as well as a colloquial verb for freeing up one's hands, mind, or time.

history.meaning: to unbind and release (prisoners or captive creatures)
social/political emancipation, liberation (calque of European terms)
political liberation; to free up, unburden, emancipate (hands, mind, time)

morphemes.meaning: to untie, unbind, release from restraint
to let go, release, set free

解放.notes: While historically weighty (解放军 'People's Liberation Army'), in everyday modern speech it is very often used lightly and colloquially for being freed from a grueling workload or chore (这周末终于解放了！ 'I'm finally free this weekend!', 解放双手 'free up one's hands').

rootFamily.gloss: to release, set free (prisoners or energy/emotions)
open, liberal; to open up to the outside world
to relieve, extricate oneself from predicament

cognates.meaning: cancellation of a contract, termination of agreement

解约.etymology: A verb-object compound (functioning as a separable verb in Mandarin) contracted from 解除合约 / 解除契约 ('to dissolve a contract'), combining 解 (jiě, 'to untie, dissolve, annul') and 约 (yuē, Traditional 約, 'knot of silk rope; binding agreement, covenant, contract'). In ancient China, covenants were metaphorically 'tied' with silk cords (约) and 'untied' (解) when terminated; in modern commercial and entertainment law (reinforced by Japanese 解約 *kaiyaku*), it denotes the formal termination of a binding contract.

history.meaning: to break off an alliance or release a covenant
to terminate or cancel a legal/agency contract

解约.notes: A high-stakes showbiz term in *Behind the Scenes*: when artists or producers clash with a talent agency (经纪公司), unilateral contract termination (单方面解约) triggers massive liquidated damages (违约金). Because it is a VO compound, say 跟公司解约 (never *解约公司).

rootFamily.gloss: to sign a contract (with an agency or client)
to breach a contract; breach of contract

解释.etymology: Coordinate verb compound combining 解 ('to untie a knot, dissect an ox at the joints, analyze', horn 角 + knife 刀 + ox 牛) + 释 (釋, 'to untangle, loosen, explain, release').

history.meaning: to untie and loosen -> to expound, explain
to explain, interpret; explanation

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 解释 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: cancellation, lifting (of a ban/alarm), termination, disarmament

解除.etymology: A coordinative/resultative verb compound uniting 解 (jiě, 'to untie, dissolve, dispel') and 除 (chú, 'to remove, eliminate, clear away', originally steps of a palace mound, extended to sweeping away or deducting). Attested in Han dynasty texts (*Shiji*, *Book of Han*) for dispelling curses, removing danger, or relieving official duties; in modern Mandarin (reinforced by Japanese legal terminology 解除 *kaijo*), it means to formally lift, revoke, or dissolve a restriction, state of alert, or legal relationship.

history.meaning: to dispel misfortune, remove guilt or official obligations
to lift (a ban/alert), dissolve (a contract/marriage), eliminate (a threat)

解除.notes: Takes abstract institutional or state nouns as objects: 解除危机 ('defuse/lift a crisis'), 解除合同 ('terminate a contract'), 解除警报 ('sound the all-clear / lift an alert'), 解除误会 ('clear up a misunderstanding').

rootFamily.gloss: to dissolve, disband (an organization or team)

言论.etymology: A coordinative compound combining 言 (yán, 'spoken words, speech, statement') and 论 (lùn, Traditional 論, 'to discourse upon, debate, reasoned argument'). Attested since the *Book of Han* and *Selections of Refined Literature* (*Wen Xuan*) to denote someone's spoken discourse and reasoned arguments; in the late 19th century, influenced by Meiji Japanese 言論 (*genron*), it also acquired the modern civic and media sense of 'public speech, commentary, expression' (as in 言论自由 'freedom of speech').

history.meaning: spoken discourse, debate, verbal arguments
public remarks, statements, political/media speech and opinion

言论.notes: Belongs to a formal or journalistic register: in media and PR crises, characters worry about 不当言论 ('inappropriate remarks'), 发表言论 ('making public statements'), or 网上言论 ('online commentary').

警察.etymology: A coordinative compound composed of 警 (jǐng, 'to warn, guard against, stay vigilant') and 察 (chá, 'to inspect, examine, investigate'). First attested in Tang dynasty historical texts (*Old Book of Tang*) as a verbal phrase meaning 'to stay on guard and inspect closely'. In the 1870s, Meiji Japan repurposed 警察 (*keisatsu*) as an institutional noun to translate the Western concept of a modern 'police force / policing system', which was borrowed back into late Qing China during the New Policies reforms around 1901.

history.meaning: to exercise vigilance and inspect closely (verbal phrase)
modern civil police administration and force (institutional noun)
police force; individual police officer

morphemes.meaning: to guard against, warn, keep watch

警察.notes: Unlike English 'the police' (collective) vs. 'police officer' (individual), Chinese 警察 refers to both the institution and an individual officer (一位警察 'a police officer').

rootFamily.gloss: to call the police; report an emergency to police

警局.etymology: A disyllabic modifier-head contraction of 警察局 (jǐngchájú, 'police bureau / station'), combining 警 (jǐng, 'police', abbreviated from 警察) and 局 (jú, 'bureau, office, department', originally a game board with compartments, extended in Tang–Song administration to a government agency or bureau). Chinese prosody strongly favors two-syllable institutional compounds in brisk narrative and media speech, yielding 警局 from 警察局.

history.meaning: municipal police bureau or station (Republican era onward)
police station, police department (contracted form)
