警局.notes: Very common in TV dramas, news headlines, and Hong Kong/Taiwan/Mainland urban speech (e.g., 带回警局调查 'bring back to the police station for questioning'); in everyday Mainland administrative usage, local neighborhood precincts are officially called 派出所 (pàichūsuǒ) or 公安局 (gōng'ānjú).

警方.etymology: A modifier-head institutional compound combining 警 (jǐng, 'police', shortened from 警察) and 方 (fāng, 'side, party, institutional actor', derived from 'direction/quarter'). In modern journalistic and legal Mandarin, -方 serves as a productive bound morpheme designating an official party or institutional actor in an event or dispute (cf. 官方 'officialdom/authorities', 校方 'the school administration', 院方 'the hospital authorities', 主办方 'the organizers').

history.meaning: the police authorities, the police as an institutional party in news/law

警方.notes: Strictly a collective noun used in news reports, public relations statements, and formal narratives (e.g., 警方表示 'the police stated', 配合警方调查 'cooperate with the police investigation'); you can never say *一个警方 for an individual officer.

rootFamily.gloss: the organizer, host party (of a show or event)
the opposing side, the other party

计划.etymology: Compound verb and noun combining 计 (計, 'to calculate, reckon, devise a plan', speech 訁 + ten 十) + 划 (劃, 'to mark off with a blade, delineate, plan out').

history.meaning: plan, project, schedule; to plan, map out

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 计划 (via 萌典)

计时器.etymology: Three-morpheme instrument compound of 计 ('calculate; count', speech radical 讠 + 十) + 时 ('time', sun 日 + 寺) + 器 ('implement; device', four vessel mouths 口 around 犬). It designates any mechanical or digital timer used in baking, sports, or laboratories.

history.meaning: timer; timekeeping device

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 计时器

订.etymology: Phono-semantic character 订 (訂), combining the speech radical 訁 (言) + phonetic 丁 (dīng), originally meaning 'to deliberate, appraise, revise a text', extended to 'to agree upon, conclude (a treaty), reserve/book, subscribe, staple/bind pages'.

history.meaning: to weigh words, deliberate, revise
to book/reserve, subscribe, draw up an agreement, bind

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 订 (via 萌典)

认.etymology: Phono-semantic character 认 (認), combining the speech radical 訁 (言) + phonetic 忍 (rěn), meaning 'to distinguish, recognize, identify, admit, acknowledge'.

history.meaning: to recognize, identify, admit
to recognize, know, admit, accept

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 认 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to recognize as, deem, consider to be

认为.etymology: A verb-complement cognitive compound formed from 认 (rèn, Traditional 認, 'to recognize, identify, acknowledge') and the Classical copular/transformative verb 为 (wéi, Traditional 為, 'to be, to act as, to take as'). Modeled on the ancient Classical Chinese cognitive pattern 以为 (yǐwéi, 'to take [X] to be [Y]'), 认为 emerged in vernacular and modern standard Mandarin to express a reasoned judgment or held opinion ('to recognize/deem to be; to hold that...').

history.meaning: to recognize or identify [someone/something] as [a role or status]
to believe, hold the opinion that, consider that (taking a clause object)

morphemes.meaning: to be, to deem as, to hold that

认为.notes: Key learner distinction: 认为 expresses a considered opinion or judgment (我认为这个方案可行 'I believe this plan is feasible'), whereas 以为 (yǐwéi) in modern Mandarin usually implies a mistaken prior assumption ('I mistakenly thought...'), and 觉得 (juéde) is a softer, more casual 'feel/think'.

rootFamily.gloss: to think (often implying a mistaken assumption)
to recognize, know, be acquainted with

认可.etymology: A resultative-coordinative compound (认可 / 認可, rènkě) combining 认 (認, rèn, 'to recognize, acknowledge', phono-semantic character with 言 speech radical and 忍 phonetic) and 可 (kě, 'to approve, permit, deem acceptable'). Originally a Tang–Song Chan Buddhist term denoting a master's formal certification of a disciple's awakening, later generalized in administrative and modern usage (reinforced by Meiji Japanese legal usage 認可) to mean 'to acknowledge and approve as valid'.

history.meaning: to certify a disciple's spiritual attainment in Chan Buddhism; to acknowledge as valid
to approve, recognize officially or socially, endorse

认可.notes: Frequently used as both a transitive verb and an abstract noun in professional and media contexts (e.g., 得到观众的认可, 'to win the audience's approval / recognition').

认命.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound (认命 / 認命, rènmìng) formed from 认 (認, rèn, 'to acknowledge, accept, submit to') and 命 (mìng, originally 'royal decree, command of Heaven', extended in Classical Chinese to 'fate, destiny, allotted lifespan'). Attested in vernacular fiction and drama from the Yuan–Ming period onward, it expresses the act of bowing to one's preordained lot after exhausting resistance.

history.meaning: Heaven's mandate; allotted fate or destiny
to accept one's destined lot without further struggle
to resign oneself to fate (often used wryly or playfully in everyday speech)

认命.notes: As a separable VO verb, modifiers can be inserted between the two characters (e.g., 认了命, 'accepted one's fate'); in workplace and drama dialogue, it often carries a humorous, self-deprecating tone ('I give up, I'll just deal with it').

rootFamily.gloss: to admit defeat, throw in the towel

认得.etymology: A verb phrase formed by 认 (rèn, 'to recognize', using the speech radical 讠) and the complement 得 (de). It implies not just visual perception, but the mental acknowledgement and spoken confirmation of a familiar face, handwriting, or symbol.

history.meaning: to recognize

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 认得

认清.etymology: A verb-resultative compound (认清 / 認清, rènqīng) pairing the action verb 认 (認, rèn, 'to recognize, discern, identify') with the adjectival resultative complement 清 (qīng, literally 'clear, limpid of water', extended metaphorically to 'distinct, unambiguous'). The compound structure denotes discerning the true nature of a situation or person with complete clarity.

history.meaning: to discern, identify / clear, limpid, distinct
to recognize clearly, see through to the true nature of

认清.notes: Commonly collocates with abstract nouns denoting reality, direction, or true colors (e.g., 认清形势 'recognize the situation clearly', 认清现实 'face up to reality', 认清真面目 'see someone's true colors').

rootFamily.gloss: to recognize, know, be acquainted with

cognates.meaning: taking seriously, earnestness (in expressions like 認真的)

认真.etymology: Originally a verb-object (VO) compound (认真 / 認真, rènzhēn) composed of 认 (認, rèn, 'to recognize, take as') and 真 (zhēn, Daoist/Buddhist term for 'the authentic, true reality, genuine'). First prominent in Tang–Song poetry and Chan Buddhist discourse meaning literally 'to mistake the illusory for the real' or 'to take something as real/serious', it grammaticalized in Ming–Qing vernacular into an adjective and adverb meaning 'earnest, conscientious, taking matters seriously'.

history.meaning: to take as real; to treat something as genuine or serious
earnest, conscientious, serious, no-nonsense

morphemes.meaning: to recognize, treat as, take as

认真.notes: Although fully adjectival in modern Mandarin (很认真 'very conscientious'), its historical VO structure survives in colloquial phrases like 认起真来 ('when one starts getting serious').

rootFamily.gloss: to take seriously, be pedantic about

认识.etymology: Coordinate cognitive verb compound combining 认 (認, 'to recognize, identify') + 识 (識, 'to know, discern, remember', neutral tone shí -> shi in Mandarin).

history.meaning: to discern, cognize, recognize
to know (a person or character), be acquainted with; understanding

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 认识 (via 萌典)

认输.etymology: Verb-object compound combining 认 (認, 'to admit, acknowledge') + 输 (輸, 'to lose a wager or contest, be defeated').

history.meaning: to admit defeat, concede, give up

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 认输 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to bargain, haggle over prices or terms
cognates.word: 討價還價 (tou2 gaa3 waan4 gaa3)

讨价还价.etymology: A four-character parallel verb-object idiom (讨价还价 / 討價還價, tǎojià-huánjià) juxtaposing two commercial actions: 讨价 (討價, 'to ask/demand a price', from 讨 'to demand, request' + 价 'price') and 还价 (還價, 'to counter-offer a price', from 还 'to return, counter' + 价 'price'). Originating in Ming–Qing merchant vernacular, it vividly depicts the back-and-forth negotiation between seller and buyer, and extends figuratively to haggling over conditions or contracts.

history.meaning: for seller to name an asking price and buyer to make a counter-offer in marketplace trade
to bargain, haggle over prices or negotiate terms stubbornly

讨价还价.notes: Used both literally in shopping and figuratively in business/media negotiations (e.g., 在合同条款上讨价还价, 'haggling over contract terms').

rootFamily.gloss: to ask for a debt, demand payment
to cut the price, bargain down

讨厌.etymology: Originally a verb-object compound (讨厌 / 討厭, tǎoyàn) combining 讨 (討, tǎo, in its vernacular sense 'to incur, invite, provoke, elicit', cf. 讨喜, 讨打) and 厌 (厭, yàn, 'satiety, revulsion, loathing, dislike'). Attested in Ming–Qing colloquial literature (such as *Dream of the Red Chamber*), its literal sense 'to incur disgust / provoke annoyance' evolved into both a stative transitive verb ('to dislike, loathe') and an adjective ('annoying, disagreeable, repulsive').

history.meaning: to be satiated with, loathe / to seek, incur, provoke
to incur dislike; to be annoying or loathsome; to detest
to dislike, hate; annoying, obnoxious, troublesome

morphemes.meaning: to loathe, detest, be fed up with

讨厌.notes: Unusually versatile in syntax: it can be a transitive verb (我讨厌他 'I dislike him'), a predicative adjective (这人真讨厌 'this person is really annoying'), or a playful interjection ('Stop it! / You're awful!').

rootFamily.gloss: to loathe, detest, feel revulsion toward
to be sick of, weary of, bored with

讨论.etymology: A coordinative verb compound (讨论 / 討論, tǎolùn) formed from 讨 (討, tǎo, 'to investigate, probe into, examine thoroughly') and 论 (論, lùn, 'to discourse upon, analyze, debate'). Already attested in the *Analects* (《论语·宪问》: 世叔讨论之, 'Shishu investigated and discussed/edited them'), where it meant examining texts and deliberating on their principles; in modern Chinese it is the standard verb and noun for 'to discuss; discussion'.

history.meaning: to investigate, examine critically, and deliberate upon texts or affairs of state
to discuss, talk over; discussion, deliberation

讨论.notes: Neutral and collaborative in register (unlike 争论 'to argue/dispute' or 辩论 'to formally debate'); ubiquitous in production meetings and academic settings (e.g., 展开热烈讨论, 'engage in lively discussion').

cognates.word: 討論会 (とうろんかい, tōronkai)

讨论会.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (讨论会 / 討論會, tǎolùnhuì) built from the disyllabic verbal noun 讨论 (討論, tǎolùn, 'discussion, deliberation') and the nominal head 会 (會, huì, originally 'to assemble, converge', extended to 'meeting, assembly, conference'). Popularized across East Asia in the late 19th and 20th centuries for structured group deliberations, colloquia, and panel discussions.

history.meaning: to investigate and discuss + assembly, gathering
discussion meeting, symposium, forum, panel session

讨论会.notes: Productive pattern with -会 (huì) for institutional gatherings; in TV production and corporate contexts, compare 研讨会 (seminar/symposium) and 座谈会 (informal panel/roundtable).

让.etymology: Phono-semantic character 让 (讓), combining the speech radical 訁 (言) + phonetic 襄 (xiāng / Old Chinese *njang-s), evolving from 'to reprove politely, yield ceremoniously, give way' to the primary Mandarin causative verb ('to let, allow, make, have someone do') and passive marker.

history.meaning: to yield politely, cede, defer
to yield, give way; to let, allow, make

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 让 (via 萌典)

让开.etymology: A verb-resultative / directional compound (让开 / 讓開, ràngkāi) combining 让 (讓, ràng, Classical 'to yield modestly, give way, cede') with the directional-resultative complement 开 (開, kāi, 'to open, move apart, clear away from'). As a compound, it expresses yielding space so as to open a clear path.

history.meaning: to yield, defer courteously, give way on a road or position
to step aside, move out of the way, clear a path

morphemes.meaning: apart, away, open (directional/resultative complement of separation)

让开.notes: Used frequently as an urgent imperative on busy film sets or streets (请让开! 'Please step aside!' or 让开一下 'Make way for a moment'); takes the potential infixes 得/不 (让得开 / 让不开).

rootFamily.gloss: to give way, yield the road or right of way
to walk away, step aside, leave

让步.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound (让步 / 讓步, ràngbù) composed of 让 (讓, ràng, 'to yield, cede, defer') and 步 (bù, 'step, pace'). In Literary Chinese (e.g., Tang–Song prose), it meant literally 'to yield a step on the path' out of deference or in martial/chess maneuvers; in modern Mandarin (reinforced by Sino-Japanese diplomatic usage 譲歩), it means figuratively 'to make concessions, compromise, give ground in a dispute or negotiation'.

history.meaning: to yield a physical step on a path out of courtesy or deference
to make a concession, yield ground, compromise in negotiations

让步.notes: A separable VO compound that often takes 作出 (作出让步, 'to make concessions') or the preposition 向/对 (向对方让步, 'to yield ground to the other party').

rootFamily.gloss: to step back, leave room for maneuver
to transfer, assign rights or property

cognates.meaning: to discuss, comment on; argumentative prose

议论.etymology: A coordinative compound (议论 / 議論, yìlùn) uniting two synonymous Classical speech verbs: 议 (議, yì, 'to deliberate upon what is right, appraise, critique') and 论 (論, lùn, 'to discourse, analyze systematically'). Attested since the Han dynasty (*Shiji*, *Hanshu*) for political deliberation and critical commentary, in modern Mandarin it shifted slightly toward informal or behind-the-scenes commentary, gossiping, or public talk about someone or something.

history.meaning: to deliberate on state affairs; critical discourse or appraisal in prose
to comment on, talk about, gossip over; public remarks or commentary

morphemes.meaning: to discourse upon, comment on, analyze

议论.notes: Unlike 讨论 (collaborative discussion to solve a problem), 议论 often implies bystanders talking about or evaluating someone behind their back (e.g., 议论纷纷 'everyone is talking/buzzing about it', 背后议论人 'gossiping about people behind their backs').

记.etymology: Phono-semantic character 记 (記), combining the speech radical 訁 (言) + phonetic 己 (jǐ), meaning 'to keep in mind, remember, write down, record; birthmark, sign'.

history.meaning: to commit to memory, record in writing
to remember, write down, record; mark, birthmark

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 记 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to write down, note down, record
cognates.word: 記低 (gei3 dai1) [structural parallel] / 記下來 (gei3 haa6 loi4)

记下来.etymology: A verb plus complex directional-resultative complement (记下来 / 記下來, jìxiàlái), formed from 记 (記, jì, 'to record in writing, commit to memory') + 下 (xià, 'down', indicating fixation onto a surface or medium) + 来 (來, lái, directional deictic marker indicating completion of fixing information into the speaker's accessible state). In Mandarin grammar, -下来 regularly marks the transition from ephemeral speech or thought into a preserved record.

history.meaning: to record on bamboo/silk, inscribe, remember
to write down, jot down, record for future reference or commit to memory

morphemes.meaning: down, into a fixed state (directional-resultative complement)
hither, into current retention (deictic directional complement)

记下来.notes: When taking a direct object, the object usually precedes 把 (把电话号码记下来) or splits the directional complement (记下重点来, 'jot down the key points').

cognates.meaning: to remember firmly, keep in mind

记住.etymology: A verb-resultative compound (记住 / 記住, jìzhù) combining the cognitive verb 记 (記, jì, 'to remember, keep in mind') with the resultative complement 住 (zhù, originally 'to halt, dwell, stay fast', grammaticalized in Middle/Early Mandarin as an aspectual-resultative marker of firm retention or immobility, cf. 抓住 'grab hold of', 站住 'stand still'). Together they mean 'to lock into memory, remember firmly'.

history.meaning: to remember + to hold fast, remain fixed (post-verbal resultative)
to remember firmly, keep in mind, not forget

morphemes.meaning: to remember, commit to memory, record
firmly, fast, securely (resultative complement of retention)

记住.notes: Whereas 记得 describes the existing state of remembering ('I recall'), 记住 focuses on the deliberate action or successful result of fixing something into memory (请记住这句话! 'Please keep these words in mind!').

rootFamily.gloss: to bear firmly in mind, never forget

记号.etymology: Composed of 记 (jì, 'to record', with the speech radical 讠) and 号 (hào, 'symbol, cry'). Together, they denote any deliberately left mark or symbol meant to aid memory or serve as an identifying signpost for others to follow.

history.meaning: mark; sign

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 记号

记录.etymology: Coordinate verb and noun compound combining 记 (記, 'to write down, note') + 录 (錄, 'to copy, inscribe, register').

history.meaning: to record, take notes; written record, minutes, sports record

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 记录 (via 萌典)

记得.etymology: Compound cognitive verb formed from 记 (記, 'to remember, retain in memory') + verbal suffix 得 (neutral tone de, marking retention/capability).

history.meaning: to remember, recall

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 记得 (via 萌典)

记得清.etymology: A potential/descriptive complement phrase (记得清 / 記得清, jìdeqīng) composed of 记 (記, jì, 'to remember, recall'), the structural/potential particle 得 (de, grammaticalized from Middle Chinese 得 'to obtain, manage to'), and the adjectival complement 清 (qīng, 'clear, distinct'). Depending on context, it functions either as a potential complement ('capable of remembering clearly', contrasting with 记不清 'unable to recall clearly') or a descriptive degree construction ('remembers with great clarity').

history.meaning: to remember + modal/complement linker + clear, distinct
to remember clearly; able to recall distinctly

morphemes.meaning: structural/potential complement marker (able to / to the extent of)

记得清.notes: Its negative counterpart is 记不清 ('cannot remember clearly, hazy in memory'), NOT *不记得清; frequently reduplicated for emphasis as 记得清清楚楚 ('remember crystal-clearly').

rootFamily.gloss: to see clearly / able to see clearly

记忆.etymology: Coordinate compound combining 记 (記, 'to remember, retain') + 忆 (憶, 'to recall, recollect, ponder in the heart').

history.meaning: memory, recollection; to remember

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 记忆 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to bear a grudge, harbor resentment

记恨.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound (记恨 / 記恨, jìhèn) formed from 记 (記, jì, 'to keep in memory, hold in mind') and 恨 (hèn, in Classical Chinese 'regret, remorse, vexation', later shifting in vernacular Chinese to 'hatred, resentment, grudge'). Attested in Ming–Qing vernacular novels, it denotes nursing resentment in one's heart rather than letting a past slight go.

history.meaning: to keep in mind + regret, resentment, hatred
to bear a grudge, harbor resentment against someone

morphemes.meaning: to remember, keep in mind, hold onto

记恨.notes: Can be used intransitively (他这人不记恨, 'he's not one to hold grudges') or transitively taking a person as direct object (别记恨我, 'don't hold a grudge against me'), closely synonymous with 记仇.

rootFamily.gloss: to bear a grudge, seek payback for a slight

记者.etymology: An agentive compound (记者 / 記者, jìzhě) combining 记 (記, jì, 'to record, write down, chronicle') and the Classical agentive nominalizer 者 (zhě, 'one who does'). While 记者 appeared occasionally in Literary Chinese with the literal sense 'one who records an account or inscription', its modern sense 'newspaper/broadcast journalist, reporter' was coined/repurposed in Meiji Japan (記者, kisha) in the 1870s and borrowed back into late Qing Chinese with the rise of modern journalism.

history.meaning: one who writes down an account or commemorative record
newspaper reporter, press correspondent (Meiji Japanese lexical innovation)
journalist, news reporter, correspondent

morphemes.meaning: to record, chronicle, report in writing
agentive suffix (-er, one who performs the action)

记者.notes: Core media-industry vocabulary in *Behind the Scenes* (*幕后之王*); collocates with 采访 (记者采访 'press interview'), 发布会 / 记者会 ('press conference'), and 特派记者 ('special correspondent').

讲.etymology: Phono-semantic character 讲 (講), combining the speech radical 訁 (言) + phonetic 冓 (gòu / Old Chinese *kˤroŋʔ, 'interlocking timber framework'), originally meaning 'to reconcile, discuss, expound Classics', and in Mandarin 'to speak, tell, explain, negotiate, stress'.

history.meaning: to reconcile, discuss, practice/expound
to speak, tell, explain, lecture, care about

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 讲 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: studying and devising a method or solution
to study carefully, pay fastidious attention to

讲究.etymology: A coordinative verb compound (讲究 / 講究, jiǎngjiu / jiǎngjiū) pairing 讲 (講, jiǎng, 'to expound, discuss, cultivate') and 究 (jiū, 'to probe to the bottom, investigate thoroughly'). In Song–Ming Neo-Confucian and scholarly prose, 講究 (jiǎngjiū) meant 'to investigate and deliberate thoroughly upon scholarly or practical principles'; in modern Mandarin (with neutral tone on the second syllable, jiǎngjiu), it evolved to mean 'to pay particular attention to, be fastidious about', as well as an adjective ('exquisite, tasteful') and noun ('subtlety, fine point of etiquette or craft').

history.meaning: to investigate, study, and deliberate thoroughly upon principles or policies
to be particular about, stress; exquisite, refined; intricate detail or rule of craft

morphemes.meaning: to expound, discuss, pay attention to, stress
to investigate thoroughly, probe into, study

讲究.notes: A classic three-way polyseme in Mandarin: 1) verb 'to care about / stress' (讲究效率 'stress efficiency'), 2) adjective 'refined / particular' (穿得很讲究 'dressed very exquisitely'), 3) noun 'fine point / art to something' (这里面大有讲究 'there's a whole art/science to this').

rootFamily.gloss: to probe to the bottom, after all, ultimately
to make do, not be fussy (antonym of 讲究)

cognates.meaning: explaining, expounding a text or doctrine

讲解.etymology: A coordinative/resultative verb compound (讲解 / 講解, jiǎngjiě) combining 讲 (講, jiǎng, 'to lecture, discourse upon, speak') and 解 (jiě, originally 'to untie a knot / butcher an ox along its joints', extended in Classical Chinese to 'to analyze, unravel, explain'). Attested from the Six Dynasties and Tang period for Buddhist and Confucian masters expounding scriptures sentence by sentence, in modern Mandarin it means 'to explain in detail, walk someone through how something works'.

history.meaning: to expound and interpret canonical scriptures or philosophical texts
to explain, give an explanatory presentation or guided commentary

讲解.notes: More structured and instructional than 解释 ('to explain a reason/excuse'); 讲解 implies breaking down a topic, project plan, or exhibit for an audience (hence 讲解员, 'docent / tour guide').

讲讲.etymology: Tentative/casual verb reduplication (AA pattern) of 讲 (講, 'to speak, tell, explain'), meaning 'to talk a bit about, explain briefly'.

history.meaning: to tell a bit, talk over, explain briefly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 讲讲 (via 萌典)

讲话.etymology: Formed from 讲 (講, jiǎng, 'to speak, lecture, discourse') and 话 (話, huà, 'spoken words, speech, talk'). In Literary Chinese (Song–Ming), 講話 referred to oral storytelling or public lecturing on history and scriptures; in modern Mandarin it operates along two distinct tracks: 1) as a separable verb-object (VO) compound meaning 'to speak, talk' (synonymous with 说话), and 2) as a nominal compound meaning 'a formal public address or leader's remarks' (发表讲话 'deliver an address').

history.meaning: to expound stories or lectures orally (Song–Ming vernacular storytelling)
to speak, talk (VO verb); formal speech, public address, remarks (noun)

讲话.notes: Notice the dual grammar: as 'to speak/talk', it is a separable VO verb (讲了一会儿话 'talked for a while'); as 'a formal speech/address', it is an inseparable noun (重要讲话 'important address').

rootFamily.gloss: to give a speech, public lecture

许.etymology: Phono-semantic character 许 (許), combining the speech radical 訁 (言) + phonetic 午 (wǔ / Old Chinese *qʰˤaʔ), originally meaning 'to listen to and grant a request, assent, promise, allow; perhaps; approximately'.

history.meaning: to assent, permit, promise; place/degree
to allow, promise, praise; perhaps, somewhat; surname Xu

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 许 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: a long time, quite a while

许久.etymology: A modifier-head temporal expression (许久 / 許久, xǔjiǔ) combining 许 (許, xǔ, used in Six Dynasties and Tang vernacular/literary Chinese as a degree or approximative modifier meaning 'so, such, quite, to a considerable extent', cf. 许多, 少许, 几何许) and 久 (jiǔ, 'long in time, enduring'). Literally 'so long / quite a long duration', it has served since Middle Chinese as a refined literary and narrative word for 'a long time, ages'.

history.meaning: so long a time, quite a long while
a long time, for ages (literary and narrative register)

morphemes.meaning: so, quite, to a considerable degree (degree modifier)
long in duration, a long time

许久.notes: More literary in flavor than 很久 or 好久; typically placed either after the verb as a duration complement (等了许久 'waited for a long time') or before a negative verb (许久不见 'long time no see').

rootFamily.gloss: a little, a small amount, slightly

cognates.word: 許許多多 (heoi2 heoi2 do1 do1)

许许多多.etymology: An AABB-pattern expressive reduplication (许许多多 / 許許多多, xǔxǔduōduō) derived from the disyllabic quantifier/adjective 许多 (許多, xǔduō, 'many, a great deal of', itself composed of degree modifier 许 'so, quite' + 多 'many, numerous'). In Mandarin morphology, AABB reduplication of disyllabic adjectives intensifies quantity and distributive vividness, yielding 'countless, myriad, a vast multitude of'.

history.meaning: so much, a great many, numerous

history.form: 許許多多 / 许许多多
history.meaning: countless, very many, all sorts and kinds of (intensified AABB reduplication)

morphemes.meaning: so, quite, to a large extent (reduplicated)

许许多多.notes: Used almost exclusively as an attributive modifier before a noun (usually followed by 的, e.g., 许许多多的幕后工作者 'countless behind-the-scenes workers'), never after degree adverbs like *很许许多多.

rootFamily.gloss: how much, how many; more or less (AABB parallel)

许诺.etymology: A coordinative verb/noun compound (许诺 / 許諾, xǔnuò) combining two Classical speech verbs of assent: 许 (許, xǔ, 'to grant, agree to, pledge') and 诺 (諾, nuò, 'to answer in the affirmative, give one's word of honor', as in 一诺千金 'a single promise is worth a thousand pieces of gold'). Attested since the Warring States and Han periods (*Xunzi*, *Shiji*), it means 'to make a solemn promise or pledge; a commitment'.

history.meaning: to assent to a request, pledge one's word, grant consent
to promise, pledge; a promise, commitment

morphemes.meaning: to assent, give one's word, promise

许诺.notes: Watch the East Asian false friend: in Japanese (許諾 kyodaku, e.g., 著作権許諾 'copyright licensing') and Korean (허락 heorak), the compound means 'permission / authorization', whereas in Mandarin 许诺 means 'to make a promise / pledge' (synonymous with 承诺).

rootFamily.gloss: promise, pledge, one's word of honor

论文.etymology: Historically a dual-origin compound (论文 / 論文, lùnwén): in Classical Chinese (most famously Cao Pi's 3rd-century *Dianlun: Lunwen* 《典论·论文》), it was a verb-object phrase meaning 'to discourse upon literature / critique writing'. In the late 19th century, Meiji Japanese re-analyzed 論文 (ronbun) as a modifier-head noun ('argumentative/analytical text') to translate Western 'academic paper, treatise, thesis, dissertation', which was then re-borrowed into modern Chinese.

history.meaning: to discuss or evaluate literary composition and style
academic paper, treatise, dissertation, thesis (Meiji Japanese semantic realignment)
academic paper, thesis, dissertation, scholarly article

morphemes.meaning: to discourse upon, argue, analyze; treatise

论文.notes: Takes the classifier 篇 (一篇论文, 'a thesis / academic paper'); common compounds include 毕业论文 ('graduation thesis') and 发表论文 ('to publish a research paper').

论断.etymology: A coordinative/resultative compound (论断 / 論斷, lùnduàn) combining 论 (論, lùn, 'to deliberate, analyze, weigh arguments') and 断 (斷, duàn, originally 'to sever with an axe', extended in Classical legal and philosophical prose to 'to adjudicate, decide, reach a definitive judgment'). Attested in Han–Tang historical and legal texts (*Hanshu*, *Hou Hanshu*) for passing judgment after deliberation, in modern Chinese it functions as both a formal verb ('to conclude, judge definitively') and a noun ('inference, proposition, judgment').

history.meaning: to deliberate upon and adjudicate a legal case or historical question
to conclude, judge; a definitive judgment, thesis, or conclusion

论断.notes: High-register word used both as a noun (作出科学的论断 'make a scientific judgment/conclusion') and in Christian biblical Chinese where 论断 translates Greek *krinō* ('Judge not, that ye be not judged' — 你们不要论断人).

rootFamily.gloss: conclusion (reached at the end of reasoning)

设备.etymology: A coordinative compound (设备 / 設備, shèbèi) composed of 设 (設, shè, 'to set up, establish, arrange, install') and 备 (備, bèi, 'to prepare, provide against need, make ready in full'). In Classical Chinese (*Hanshu*), 設備 was a verbal expression meaning 'to set up and prepare (defenses or provisions)'; in the Meiji era, Japanese repurposed 設備 (setsubi) as a noun for modern industrial/technical 'equipment, facilities, installations', which returned to modern Mandarin as the standard term for gear, apparatus, and equipment.

history.meaning: to set up and prepare military defenses or provisions in advance
industrial facilities, technical installations, equipment (Meiji Japanese lexical shift)
equipment, gear, apparatus, facilities, hardware devices

morphemes.meaning: to set up, install, arrange, establish
to prepare, equip, make ready, provide

设备.notes: Essential broadcast and film-production term (音响设备 'audio equipment', 摄影设备 'camera gear', 移动设备 'mobile devices'); usually uncountable or measured with 套 ('set') or 台 ('unit/machine').

rootFamily.gloss: equipment, outfit, gear (military, sports, or gaming)

设计.etymology: Compound originally meaning 'to lay out a stratagem or plan' (from 设 設 'to set up, arrange, establish' + 计 計 'plan, calculation'), broadened in modern Chinese (reinforced by Japanese sekkei 設計) to 'to design, plan; design'.

history.meaning: to devise a plan or stratagem
to design, plan; design

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 设计 (via 萌典)

访谈.etymology: A coordinative verb/noun compound (访谈 / 訪談, fǎngtán) uniting 访 (訪, fǎng, Classical 'to inquire広く, seek counsel from, visit in person') and 谈 (談, tán, 'to converse, talk, discuss'). While attested in Literary Chinese for visiting someone to converse, in contemporary media Chinese (initially prominent in Taiwan and Hong Kong broadcast journalism before spreading across Mainland TV) it specifically designates a structured, conversational 'talk-show interview' or 'in-depth sit-down interview'.

history.meaning: to visit and inquire + to converse, talk
in-depth interview, talk-show conversation; to interview conversationally

morphemes.meaning: to visit, inquire, interview, seek out

访谈.notes: Unlike 采访 (general news reporting/newsgathering, including street vox-pops), 访谈 refers specifically to an extended, conversational sit-down interview (e.g., 访谈节目 'talk show / interview program', 人物访谈 'celebrity/profile interview').

rootFamily.gloss: to interview (for news), gather news stories
conversation, talk; to have a formal talk with

cognates.meaning: access volume / page views (conceptual parallel to 访问量)
cognates.word: アクセス数 / 訪問数 (hōmonsū)

访问量.etymology: A modern digital-era modifier-head compound (访问量 / 訪問量, fǎngwènliàng) combining 访问 (訪問, fǎngwèn, 'to visit, call upon', extended as a computing calque of English 'to access / visit a website or server') with the productive quantitative head suffix 量 (liàng, 'measured quantity, volume, traffic'). Literally 'visit-volume', it denotes web traffic, page views, or server hit counts.

history.meaning: to inquire and visit in person; official diplomatic visit
web traffic, number of site visits or page views (Internet/media metric)

morphemes.meaning: to visit, call on, seek out
to inquire, ask after (with 访 forming 'to visit / access')

访问量.notes: Part of a core family of media-analytics compounds ending in -量 (liàng) central to digital showbiz: 访问量 ('site visits/web traffic'), 点击量 ('click volume'), 播放量 ('stream/play count'), and 收视率 ('TV viewership rating').

rootFamily.gloss: to visit (diplomatically or socially); to access (a website/data)
traffic, data flow, viewership/celebrity clout metric

cognates.word: 実証 (じっしょう, jisshō) [reversed morphemes] / 証実

证实.etymology: A verb-resultative compound (证实 / 證實, zhèngshí) formed from 证 (證, zhèng, 'to testify, verify, demonstrate by evidence'; simplified 证 merges Classical 證 'testify/prove' and 諫-related 證 'remonstrate') and the resultative complement 实 (實, shí, 'solid, real, true, factual'). Literally 'to verify as true/factual', it was used in Tang–Song Buddhist texts for realizing ultimate truth and in legal/historical prose for corroborating a report or suspicion with solid facts.

history.meaning: to realize ultimate reality (Buddhist); to verify an allegation or report as factual
to confirm, verify, corroborate, substantiate (a rumor, hypothesis, or report)

morphemes.meaning: to testify, prove, verify with evidence

证实.notes: Whereas 证明 ('to prove') builds a logical or evidentiary case from scratch, 证实 ('to confirm / corroborate') specifically means verifying that a previously existing rumor, report, or hypothesis is indeed true (e.g., 消息已得到证实, 'the news has been confirmed').

rootFamily.gloss: to verify, check and confirm accuracy

证据.etymology: A coordinative nominal/verbal compound (证据 / 證據, zhèngjù) combining 证 (證, zhèng, 'testimony, proof, verification') and 据 (據, jù, originally 'to lean upon, occupy a stronghold', extended in Classical Chinese to 'basis, documentary ground, voucher'). Attested since the Six Dynasties and Tang period (e.g., Yan Zhitui's *Yanshi Jiaxun* and Kong Yingda's commentaries) for textual or legal grounds that substantiate a claim.

history.meaning: textual citation or legal testimony serving as the basis for a claim
evidence, proof, exhibit (in law, journalism, or investigation)

证据.notes: Strictly a noun in modern Mandarin (never a verb); collocates with 确凿 (证据确凿 'the evidence is ironclad/irrefutable'), 搜集证据 ('gather evidence'), and 毁灭证据 ('destroy evidence').

rootFamily.gloss: argumentative evidence, supporting data (in an essay)
witness, testimony; to bear witness to

证明.etymology: A verb-resultative compound (证明 / 證明, zhèngmíng) pairing 证 (證, zhèng, 'to testify, verify by evidence') with the resultative complement 明 (míng, 'bright, clear, manifest'). Attested in Han–Tang texts (and Buddhist translations of Sanskrit *pramāṇa* / *vyākaraṇa*) with the literal sense 'to make clear and manifest through testimony or evidence'; in modern Chinese (reinforced by Meiji Japanese 証明 in logic, law, and mathematics) it serves as both the verb 'to prove, demonstrate' and the noun 'proof, certificate, identification document'.

history.meaning: to make clear through testimony; to bear witness and illuminate the truth
to prove, demonstrate; proof, certificate, testimonial document

morphemes.meaning: to testify, verify, demonstrate by evidence
clear, manifest, evident (resultative complement of clarity)

证明.notes: Functions both as a verb ('to prove': 事实证明 'facts prove that...') and as a concrete noun meaning an official 'certificate / written attestation' (e.g., 开具工作证明 'issue a proof-of-employment certificate', 身份证明 'ID proof').

rootFamily.gloss: certificate, credential, license (ID card, diploma, etc.)
to show clearly, indicate, make known

评价.etymology: Verb-object and coordinate compound of 评 ('weigh in words; comment fairly', speech radical 讠 + 平 'even/fair') + 价 ('value; worth; price', person radical 亻 + 介). Originally 'assess the fair price or worth of goods', it broadened to evaluating quality, work, or performance.

history.meaning: appraise the worth of something
evaluate; comment on; assessment

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 评价

cognates.meaning: evaluation, assessment (hyōka, a close structural parallel)

评估.etymology: A coordinative verbal-nominal compound (並立式) formed from 評 (Trad. 評, píng, Middle Chinese *bjaeng, 'to weigh words, adjudicate, critique', from 言 'speech' + 平 'level, balanced') and 估 (gū, MC *kuX, 'to estimate market value or tax price', from 人 'person' + 古 phonetic). Originally uniting verbal critique with commercial appraisal, it crystallized in modern administrative and media Mandarin for formal professional assessment of project viability, ratings, or risk.

history.meaning: to weigh merits in speech (評) and to estimate commercial price or tax value (估) as separate Classical and Tang-Song mercantile verbs
to appraise property value or audit financial worth
to evaluate or assess systematically (projects, broadcast performance, or risk)

评估.notes: Higher in register than 评价 (general evaluation/opinion); 评估 implies a structured, data-driven, or institutional assessment (e.g., 风险评估 'risk assessment', 节目评估 'show evaluation').

评分.etymology: A verb-object compound (動賓式) that also functions as a deverbal noun, combining 評 (Trad. 評, píng, 'to judge, adjudicate') with 分 (fēn, Middle Chinese *pjun, 'allotted share, fractional point, grade', originally depicting a knife 刀 cleaving something 八 in two). As modern numerical grading systems entered Chinese education, arts competitions, and media ratings in the 20th century, 評分 lexicalized both the act of assigning points and the resulting numerical score.

history.meaning: to adjudicate merits (評) and to divide or allot shares/measures (分)
to assign numerical marks; a rating score or grade in competitions and media reviews

评分.notes: Used both as a separable verb-object (给节目评个分 'give the show a score') and as an unseparable noun (豆瓣评分 'Douban rating', 观众评分 'audience score').

评委.etymology: A modern telescopic abbreviation (縮略語) of 評審委員 (píngshěn wěiyuán, 'review/judging committee member') or 評判委員 ('adjudicating committee member'). It pairs 評 (Trad. 評, píng, 'to judge, critique') with 委 (wěi, MC *'jweX, 'to entrust, delegate, commission', from 禾 'grain' + 女 'woman', denoting bowing under entrusted weight). In contemporary Chinese talent shows and broadcast competitions, 評委 denotes an individual panel judge.

history.form: 評審委員 / 評判委員
history.meaning: appointed member of an adjudication or examination committee
panel judge, competition adjudicator, or talent-show juror

morphemes.meaning: adjudicate, evaluate (short for 评审/评判)

评委.notes: A staple of music and variety show vocabulary (e.g., 评委席 'judges' panel', 专业评委 'professional judge'); refers strictly to the person, whereas 评审 can mean either the judge or the review process.

cognates.meaning: council, deliberation (hyōgi, sharing the root 評)

评审.etymology: A coordinative compound (並立式) uniting 評 (Trad. 評, píng, 'to weigh merits, critique') and 審 (Trad. 審, shěn, Middle Chinese *syimX, 'to examine thoroughly, investigate, try a case', originally depicting inspecting animal tracks 釆 inside a roofed dwelling 宀). Initially a verbal compound meaning to deliberate and examine closely, it also functions nominally for an adjudication process or—especially in Taiwan, Hong Kong, and entertainment broadcasts—a competition juror.

history.meaning: to critique fairly (評) and to investigate or try a legal/scholarly matter thoroughly (審)
to review and adjudicate entries; a jury panel or competition judge

评审.notes: In Mainland administrative contexts 评审 is primarily the review process (项目评审 'project review'), while in entertainment television (influenced by Taiwan/HK usage) 评审老師 is a frequent title for a showbiz judge alongside 评委.

评审员.etymology: Three-character agent noun combining 评审 (評審, 'to evaluate and adjudicate', from 评 'to comment, appraise' + 审 'to examine carefully') + agent suffix 员 (員, 'member, person').

history.meaning: judge, panelist, evaluator, reviewer

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 评审员 (via 萌典)

评断.etymology: A coordinative or sequential verbal compound (並立/連謂式) combining 評 (Trad. 評, píng, 'to weigh and discuss') with 斷 (Trad. 斷, duàn, Middle Chinese *twanH, 'to sever with an axe 斤, decide conclusively, render a verdict'). Attested in Tang and Song prose (such as poetry criticism and administrative memorials), the compound traces the movement from balanced verbal deliberation (評) to a decisive, cutting judgment (斷).

history.meaning: to deliberate upon and render a decisive verdict in legal, literary, or moral matters
to judge fairly, weigh the merits and decide conclusively

评断.notes: Carries a slightly elevated or earnest tone compared to 判断 ('determine/judge'); often used in the phrase 自有公论/由观众评断 ('let the public/audience be the judge').

rootFamily.gloss: make a resolute decision, sever ties

评论.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative compound (並立式) joining 評 (Trad. 評, píng, 'to appraise, weigh fairly') and 論 (Trad. 論, lùn, Middle Chinese *lwijH / *lwon, 'to discourse systematically, debate, arrange arguments in order', from 言 'speech' + 侖 'orderly bundle of bamboo slips'). Attested since the Later Han and Six Dynasties period for character appraisal (月旦評) and literary critique, it later absorbed modern journalistic senses (via Meiji Japanese 評論) for media commentary and online comments.

history.meaning: to appraise historical figures, officials, or literary works through reasoned discourse
history.stage: Late Han & Six Dynasties Literary Chinese

history.meaning: to comment on or critique; a critical essay, media editorial, or digital user comment

评论.notes: seamlessly bridges high-register media critique (发表评论 'publish an editorial/commentary') and everyday social-media usage (评论区 'comment section', 刷评论 'scroll/spam comments').

评论员.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正式) formed by attaching the agentive suffix 員 (Trad. 員, yuán, Middle Chinese *hjwien, originally a round cauldron 鼎 with a circle 〇 above, extended to 'headcount, official personnel, professional member') to the compound stem 評論 (pínglùn, 'commentary, critique'). Patterned on 20th-century institutional and journalistic terminology, it designates a professional broadcast, sports, or political commentator.

history.meaning: editorial or broadcast staff member assigned to write or deliver commentary
professional commentator, pundit, or colour analyst in news, music, and sports broadcasts

评论员.notes: Distinguish 评论员 (a broadcast/news commentator or panel pundit, e.g., 特约评论员 'special guest commentator') from 评论家 (an accomplished literary, music, or art critic).

cognates.meaning: commentary box/desk (kaisetsuseki, using the same head morpheme 席)

评论席.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正式) combining 評論 (Trad. 評論, pínglùn, 'commentary, critique') with 席 (xí, Middle Chinese *zjek, 'woven straw mat for sitting', hence 'seat, place at a banquet or assembly, designated booth'). InClassical Chinese, 席 denoted the floor mat where scholars or officials sat during debates; in modern studio production, 評論席 designates the physical commentary desk or pundits' box.

history.meaning: woven sitting mat; designated seat of honour or scholarly lecture mat (講座/席)
commentary desk, commentators' booth, or critics' panel seating in live broadcasts and shows

morphemes.meaning: seat, mat, designated station or desk

评论席.notes: Common in live television, award ceremonies, and music competition broadcasts alongside 评委席 ('judges' table') and 嘉宾席 ('VIP guest seating').

rootFamily.gloss: attend a meeting or event (lit. enter one's seat)

cognates.meaning: curse, malediction, incantation (juso, preserving an older ritual compound)

诅咒.etymology: A coordinative compound (並立式) uniting two near-synonymous ritual speech roots: 詛 (zǔ, Middle Chinese *tsjoX, 'to call down divine punishment upon someone, imprecate', from 言 'speech' + 且 phonetic, originally an ancestral altar stand) and 咒 (zhòu, MC *tsjuwH, variant 呪, 'to chant an incantation or malediction', from 口 'mouth' + 兄 'invoker/elder kneeling in prayer'). In Old and Middle Chinese ritual and Buddhist texts, it denoted formal imprecations or dhāraṇī spells before narrowing to 'curse, hex'.

history.meaning: to invoke ancestral spirits or deities to witness an oath or strike down an oath-breaker
to utter ritual maledictions, hexes, or binding incantations against an enemy
to curse, wish ill upon someone, or figuratively 'jinx' in everyday or dramatic speech

诅咒.notes: Functions as both a verb (诅咒别人 'curse others') and a noun (打破诅咒 'break a curse/jinx'); do not confuse with 骂 (scold/swear verbally without the supernatural or fateful implication of 诅咒).

rootFamily.gloss: scold and curse angrily in speech

cognates.meaning: a person who understands the needs of the times is a great talent (siksimumuja wihunjun)
to know the affairs of the times, be pragmatic (thức thời vụ)

识时务.etymology: A verb-object phrase (動賓短語) drawn directly from the celebrated aphorism 識時務者為俊傑 ('He who recognizes the imperatives of the times is a true hero'), recorded in the *Records of the Three Kingdoms* (三國志·蜀書·諸葛亮傳) quoting the recluse Sima Hui (司馬徽). 識 (Trad. 識, shí, MC *syik, 'to discern, recognize') governs 時務 (shíwù, modifier-head: 時 'era, opportune season' + 務 'urgent affairs, pressing duties').

history.form: 識時務 (識時務者為俊傑)
history.meaning: to discern the grand historical currents and pressing political imperatives of one's era
history.stage: Late Han / Three Kingdoms Literary Chinese

history.meaning: to know which way the wind blows, read the room pragmatically, and adapt wisely to circumstances or power dynamics

识时务.notes: In workplace and showbiz dramas, 算你识时务 ('Good thing you know which way the wind blows') or 识时务者为俊杰 is often used ironically or pragmatically when someone yields to a stronger party or industry reality.

rootFamily.gloss: sensible, tactful, knowing how to act in a situation

cognates.meaning: deceit, fraud (sa, as in sagi 詐欺)

诈.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形聲字): 言 (Trad. 言, yán, 'words, speech') serves as the semantic determinative, while 乍 (zhà, Old Chinese *dzraːs, Middle Chinese *dzraeH, 'suddenly, abruptly, catches off guard') provides both the phonology and the core etymological image of springing a sudden verbal trap. From Classical military deception (兵不厭詐 'warfare never tires of deception'), colloquial Mandarin developed the specific transitive sense 'to bluff someone into revealing the truth by pretending one already knows'.

history.meaning: to deceive, feign, use artifice or stratagem in diplomacy and warfare (e.g. 爾虞我詐)
to defraud financially (诈骗); colloquially, to bluff or startle someone into confessing hidden information (拿话诈他)

morphemes.meaning: deceive with words, feign; bluff information out of someone

诈.notes: In spoken dialogue (e.g., 他是在诈你 'He's just bluffing you to see how you react!'), 诈 specifically means pretending to know a secret so the other person panics and spills the beans.

诉讼.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative compound (並立式) combining 訴 (Trad. 訴, sù, Middle Chinese *suH, 'to lay a grievance before a superior, accuse, recount', from 言 'speech' + 斥 'drive away/point out') and 訟 (Trad. 訟, sòng, MC *zjungH, 'to dispute in public court, litigate', from 言 'speech' + 公 'public, open court, duke'). Already attested in the *Book of Changes* (易經) and Han legal codes, it was reinforced in modern East Asian jurisprudence (alongside Japanese 訴訟) for civil or criminal litigation.

history.meaning: to present a plaint of grievance (訴) and argue a dispute before a magistrate's public court (訟)
lawsuit, legal action, formal litigation (e.g. 民事诉讼 'civil lawsuit')

诉讼.notes: Formal legal register (提起诉讼 'file a lawsuit', 法律诉讼 'legal proceedings'); in everyday conversation, speakers often say 打官司 ('fight a lawsuit') or 告 ('sue').

rootFamily.gloss: prosecute, sue, bring a lawsuit against
appeal a court verdict to a higher court
win a lawsuit, prevail in court

cognates.meaning: writer, author (sakka, source of the modern compound suffix 作家)

词曲作家.etymology: A modern four-character modifier-head compound (偏正式) built from the coordinative stem 詞曲 (Trad. 詞曲, cíqǔ: 詞 'song lyrics, poetic words' + 曲 'musical melody, tune') and the professional title 作家 (zuòjiā, 'creative writer, author', a classical Tang–Song term for a literary master that was revitalized via Meiji Japanese *sakka*). In the contemporary Mandarin music industry, 詞曲作家 denotes a professional songwriter who writes lyrics and/or melodies.

history.meaning: vernacular lyric genres of the Song (詞) and Yuan (曲) dynasties; words and music together
professional songwriter, lyricist-composer in the modern recording and broadcast industry

morphemes.meaning: song lyrics, words (short for 歌词)
melody, musical composition (short for 乐曲/作曲)

词曲作家.notes: Carries more professional prestige and career weight than 词曲作者: a 词曲作家 is a recognized songwriter by profession, whereas 词曲作者 often refers to the credited writer(s) of a specific track.

词曲作者.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正式) pairing the coordinative musical stem 詞曲 (Trad. 詞曲, cíqǔ, 'lyrics 詞 and melody 曲') with 作者 (zuòzhě, 'maker, creator, author', from 作 'to make, compose, originate' + the Classical nominalizing particle 者 'the one who'). While 作者 in Classical Chinese (*Analects*, *Liji*) meant a sage creator or literary author, 詞曲作者 in modern music publishing specifically identifies the credited lyricist and composer of a song.

history.meaning: one who originates rites/music or composes literary works (e.g. 作者七人矣 in the Analects)
the credited lyricist and composer of a musical work (in copyright, liner notes, and royalties)

词曲作者.notes: Standard legal and broadcast credit term (e.g., 尊重词曲作者的版权 'respect the copyright of the songwriters/lyricist-composers'); on screen credits, often split into 作词 ('lyrics by') and 作曲 ('music by').

试.etymology: Phono-semantic character 试 (試), combining the speech radical 訁 (言) + phonetic 式 (shì, 'model, standard, use'), meaning 'to put to use, test, try out, examine'.

history.meaning: to test, try out, examine
to try, test, examination

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 试 (via 萌典)

试吃员.etymology: Three-character agent compound combining 试吃 (試吃, 'to sample food, taste-test', from 试 'to try, test' + 吃 'to eat') + agent suffix 员 (員, 'person, staff member').

history.meaning: food taster, taste-tester

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 试吃员 (via 萌典)

试用期.etymology: Three-character compound combining 试用 (試用, 'to use on a trial basis, place on probation') + 期 ('period of time, term').

history.meaning: probationary period, trial period

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 试用期 (via 萌典)

试试.etymology: Tentative verb reduplication (AA pattern) of 试 (試, 'to try, test'), meaning 'to give it a try, try out for a moment'.

history.meaning: to have a try, test out

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 试试 (via 萌典)

诚实.etymology: Coordinate adjective compound combining 诚 (誠, 'sincere, genuine, truthful', speech 訁 + 成 chéng) + 实 (實, 'solid, true, real, honest').

history.meaning: sincere and true
honest, truthful, sincere

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 诚实 (via 萌典)

诚恳.etymology: Coordinate adjective compound combining 诚 (誠, 'sincere, genuine') + 恳 (懇, 'earnest, heartfelt', heart 心 + 豸 + 艮).

history.meaning: sincere and earnest, heartfelt

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 诚恳 (via 萌典)

诚意.etymology: Originates as a Classical Chinese verb-object phrase (動賓式) in the Confucian classic *Great Learning* (大學): 欲正其心者，先誠其意 ('Those who wished to rectify their hearts first made their intentions sincere/authentic'). Here 誠 (Trad. 誠, chéng, MC *dzyeng, 'true, unfeigned, to make authentic', from 言 'speech' + 成 'complete/realize') governed 意 (yì, MC *'jiH, 'thought, intention of the heart-mind', from 音 'sound/voice' + 心 'heart'). Over time it reanalyzed into a modifier-head noun (偏正式) meaning 'sincere intention, good faith'.

history.meaning: to make one's inner intentions wholly authentic and free of self-deception (a core step of Confucian self-cultivation)
sincerity, earnestness, or tangible good faith in personal relations and business negotiations

诚意.notes: In business and entertainment negotiations (e.g., 拿出一点诚意来 'show some real good faith'), 诚意 often implies backing up polite words with concrete terms, concessions, or compensation.

话.etymology: Phono-semantic/associative character 话 (話), combining the speech radical 訁 (言) + 舌 ('tongue', phonetic in Old Chinese *gˤrats), meaning 'spoken words, speech, talk, dialect/language'.

history.meaning: spoken words, good speech, talk
words, speech, talk, language/dialect

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 话 (via 萌典)

话筒.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正式) coined during the late Qing and early Republican adoption of telecommunications and audio technology. It combines 話 (Trad. 話, huà, Middle Chinese *hwaeH, 'spoken words, speech') with 筒 (tǒng, MC *duwngX, 'thick section of bamboo tube', from 竹 'bamboo' + 同 phonetic). Originally denoting the cylindrical speaking tube or telephone transmitter handset (傳話筒), it shifted to become the standard everyday noun for a stage or studio microphone.

history.meaning: acoustic speaking tube or early telephone transmitter mouthpiece shaped like a bamboo cylinder
microphone (handheld, podium, or broadcast mic) in everyday and television production usage

话筒.notes: Coexists with the English loanword 麦克风 (màikèfēng, often shortened to 麦, as in 开麦 'turn on the mic', 抢麦 'grab the mic'); 话筒 emphasizes the physical handheld or desk object (递话筒 'hand over the microphone').

话说回来.etymology: An idiomatic subject-predicate discourse clause (主謂短語) built from 話 (Trad. 話, huà, 'the words, the line of talk') + 說 (Trad. 說, shuō, 'to speak') + the directional-resultative complement 回來 (huílái: 回 'turn back, return' + 來 'hither, toward the speaker's vantage point'). Literally 'steering the talk back to the starting point', it arose in Ming–Qing vernacular storytelling (章回小說) to pivot back from a digression, and now serves in conversation to introduce a qualifying counter-perspective ('that said, then again').

history.meaning: narrator's formula returning from a side plot to the main thread ('turning our story back...') in vernacular fiction
conversational discourse marker: 'then again', 'come to think of it', 'on the other hand'

morphemes.meaning: the talk, the subject of speech
turn back hither, return to the baseline

话说回来.notes: Frequently paired with 不过 ('However...') as 不过话说回来 ('Still, come to think of it / that being said...') to soften a criticism or look at the flip side of a situation.

rootFamily.gloss: traditional storyteller's opening ('The story goes that...') / by the way

话里.etymology: A noun-postposition locative phrase (方位短語) combining 話 (Trad. 話, huà, Middle Chinese *hwaeH, 'spoken words, utterance') with the enclitic locative particle 裏/裡 (Simplified 里, lǐ, MC *liX, originally 'inner lining of a garment', composed of 衣 'clothing' + 里 phonetic, later merged graphically in Simplified Chinese with 里 'village/mile'). Literally 'inside the lining of one's words', it conceptualizes speech as a container holding subtext or hidden intent.

history.meaning: within one's spoken remarks; the subtext or implication beneath the surface of an utterance
in one's words, between the lines of what someone says

话里.notes: Most famously used in the idiom 话里有话 ('there is a hidden meaning behind those words / reading between the lines') and 话里话外 ('both inside and outside one's words, in every hint').

rootFamily.gloss: there is more to the words than meets the ear; implied subtext
in one's heart of hearts, inwardly
implication beyond the words, unspoken subtext

话题.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (偏正式) joining 話 (Trad. 話, huà, 'speech, talk, story') and 題 (Trad. 題, tí, Middle Chinese *dej, 'forehead', from 頁 'head' + 是 phonetic, extended in Classical Chinese to the 'frontispiece, title, or theme inscribed at the head of a text or poetry examination'). Popularized across modern East Asia (reinforced by Japanese 話題 *wadai*), it evolved from 'subject of a conversation' into the modern media and social-network sense of 'trending topic, media buzz, hashtag'.

history.meaning: the heading or theme of a poetic/storytelling discourse; subject of conversation
topic of conversation; in showbiz and social media, a trending subject, hashtag, or publicity buzz (话题度)

话题.notes: In *Behind the Scenes* and contemporary media Mandarin, 话题 often means 'media buzz / talking point' (制造话题 'manufacture buzz', 话题人物 'controversial/buzzworthy figure', 微博话题 'Weibo hashtag topic').

该.etymology: Phono-semantic character 该 (該), combining the speech radical 訁 (言) + phonetic 亥 (hài / Old Chinese *kˤə), originally meaning 'military code/preparation; complete, all-inclusive', then grammaticalized into a modal verb ('ought to, should; to be someone's turn; to owe') and demonstrative ('the said, that').

history.meaning: code, complete, ought to include
should, ought to; to be one's turn; to owe; the said

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 该 (via 萌典)

详细.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative adjectival compound (並立式) pairing 詳 (Trad. 詳, xiáng, Middle Chinese *zjang, 'to scrutinize and state fully in words, complete, exhaustive', from 言 'speech' + 羊 phonetic) with 細 (Trad. 細, xì, MC *sejH, 'fine silk thread, minute, delicate, meticulous', from 糸 'silk'). Attested since Han histories (*Shiji*, *Hanshu*), it unites verbal exhaustiveness (詳, opposed to 略 'brief/sketchy') with fine-grained precision (細, opposed to 粗 'coarse').

history.meaning: exhaustive in verbal account (詳) and fine-grained in detail (細) in historical chronicles and memorials
detailed, thorough, meticulous (of plans, explanations, or reports)

详细.notes: Used to describe information, plans, or explanations (详细说明 'explain in detail'); for people's personalities or habits, use 仔细 ('careful/attentive') or 细心 ('meticulous/considerate') instead.

rootFamily.gloss: know clearly and in full detail (formal)

语音.etymology: Compound noun combining 语 (語, 'language, speech') + 音 ('sound, tone, pronunciation').

history.meaning: speech sounds, pronunciation; voice message

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 语音 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: misunderstanding (gokai, rarely used compared to 誤解)

误会.etymology: A modifier-head verbal and nominal compound (偏正式) combining the adverbial-adjectival root 誤 (Trad. 誤, wù, Middle Chinese *nguH, 'erroneously, by mistake, to err', from 言 'speech' + 吳 phonetic) with 會 (Trad. 會, huì, MC *hwajH, originally 'to meet, assemble', extended in Six Dynasties and Tang Chinese—as in 會意 or 體會—to 'mentally grasp, comprehend where meanings converge'). Thus 誤會 literally means 'to grasp someone's intention erroneously'.

history.meaning: to misconstrue a text's purport or misread another person's intention
to misunderstand personally; an interpersonal misunderstanding or mix-up (noun and transitive verb)

误会.notes: Compared to 误解, 误会 focuses on interpersonal mix-ups over intentions or feelings (你误会我了 'You've got me wrong!', 消除误会 'clear up a misunderstanding') and is very common in spoken dialogue.

rootFamily.gloss: understand tacitly without words (lit. heart grasps and spirit comprehends)

误解.etymology: A modifier-head compound (偏正式) pairing 誤 (Trad. 誤, wù, 'erroneously, amiss') with 解 (jiě, Middle Chinese *kaeX, originally 'to unfasten and separate an ox's horn 牛 with a knife 刀', metaphorically extended in Classical Chinese to 'untangle a knotty problem, analyze, interpret, understand'). Literally 'to untangle or interpret wrongly', it denotes misinterpreting facts, concepts, policies, or motives.

history.meaning: to explicate or interpret a classical text, doctrine, or statement erroneously
to misinterpret or misunderstand; a misconception or misinterpretation (both noun and verb)

误解.notes: More analytical and objective than 误会: one can 误解 a policy, an artistic concept, or a person's character (对行业有误解 'have misconceptions about the industry'), whereas 误会 is usually an accidental interpersonal mix-up.

说.etymology: Phono-semantic character 说 (說), combining the speech radical 訁 (言) + phonetic 兑 (duì / Old Chinese *lhot), originally meaning 'to explain, untangle in words, delight' (cf. 悦 yuè) and in vernacular Mandarin the primary verb for 'to speak, say, talk'.

history.meaning: to explain, persuade; pleased (yuè)
to say, speak, talk, explain, scold

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 说 (via 萌典)

说一不二.etymology: A four-character vernacular idiom (成語) structured by parallel negation: 說一 (Trad. 說一, shuō yī, 'to say one') + 不二 (bù èr, 'not [change it to] two'). It draws on the Classical Chinese moral trope 言不二價 ('not quoting two prices') and 一言九鼎 ('one word carries the weight of nine bronze tripods'), crystallizing in Yuan–Ming–Qing vernacular fiction (such as *Water Margin* and *Dream of the Red Chamber*) to describe a leader or person of integrity whose word is final and unshakeable.

history.meaning: speaking one word and never altering it to a second; possessing absolute authority or unyielding credibility
to mean every word one says, keep one's word without fail, or command unquestioned authority in decision-making

morphemes.meaning: never alter to 'two' (no wavering or duplicity)

说一不二.notes: Can praise someone's rock-solid trustworthiness (说话算数，说一不二) or describe an executive's commanding, non-negotiable authority in the workplace (在公司里说一不二).

rootFamily.gloss: unique, one and only (lit. sole one without a second)
count for what one says, keep one's word
a promise is worth a thousand pieces of gold

说一套做一套.etymology: A juxtaposed six-character colloquial idiom (熟語/慣用語) built from two parallel verb-object clauses: 說一套 (Trad. 說一套, shuō yī tào, 'to speak one set [of fine words]') and 做一套 (zuò yī tào, 'to enact a [different] set [of deeds]'). Here 套 (tào, originally a 'leather cover or harness wrapper', grammaticalized as a classifier for a complete set, routine, or repertoire of tricks) highlights the theatrical disconnect between someone's public rhetoric and their actual behind-the-scenes behavior.

history.meaning: to recite one repertoire of principles in public while practicing another in private
to say one thing and do another; to be two-faced or hypocritical

说一套做一套.notes: The classifier 套 often carries a skeptical nuance of 'canned routine, PR spin, or act' (as in 少来这一套 'drop the act!'). Its classical four-character equivalent is 言行不一 ('words and deeds do not match').

rootFamily.gloss: words and actions do not match (formal idiom)

说不定.etymology: Originates as a verb-complement construction (動補式) combining 說 (Trad. 說, shuō, 'to state, predict, declare') with the negative potential complement 不定 (bùdìng: 不 'not' + 定 'fixed, settled, certain'). Literally 'cannot state with certainty [how things will turn out]', it underwent syntactic reanalysis and grammaticalization in Ming–Qing vernacular Mandarin from a predicate ('is impossible to say for sure') into a sentence-level epistemic modal adverb meaning 'maybe, perhaps, for all one knows'.

history.meaning: cannot be stated or predicted with certainty (e.g. 這事還說不定 'This matter cannot be settled/predicted yet')
maybe, perhaps, quite possibly (often introducing an unexpected or hopeful turn of events)

说不定.notes: Unlike 也许 or 可能 (neutral 'perhaps'), 说不定 often hints at a surprising, ironic, or newly realized possibility ('Who knows, maybe he actually likes the idea!'). It can still occasionally stand at the end of a clause (也说不定 '...or maybe so').

rootFamily.gloss: unable to get a firm grasp on; unsure (colloquial)
rootFamily.word: 拿不定 (主意) / 说不准

说不通.etymology: A negative potential verb-complement construction (動補式可能補語) formed from 說 (Trad. 說, shuō, 'to explain, argue, talk through') + the negative potential marker 不 (bù, 'cannot') + the resultative complement 通 (tōng, Middle Chinese *thuwng, 'to pass all the way through without obstruction, penetrate, make logical sense'). Literally 'talking it through hits a dead end', it means either that an argument is logically incoherent or that persuasion fails to get through to someone.

history.meaning: able (說得通) or unable (說不通) to carry an argument through unobstructed or persuade someone to agree
to make no logical sense, fail to hold water; or to fail to talk someone around

说不通.notes: Its affirmative counterpart is 说得通 ('makes sense, is tenable', e.g., 这个逻辑说不通 'This logic doesn't hold water'), while the non-potential resultative 说通了 means 'succeeded in talking someone around' (我已经把他思想工作做通/说通了).

rootFamily.gloss: figure out, come around mentally to accepting something
impassable, dead end (of a road or method)

说到底.etymology: A verb-complement discourse phrase (動補短語) combining 說 (Trad. 說, shuō, 'to speak, trace an argument') with the resultative prepositional complement 到底 (dàodǐ: 到 'arrive at, reach' + 底 'the bottom of a vessel or body of water', from 广 'shelter/slope' + 氐 'root, lowest foundation'). Literally 'speaking all the way down to the very bottom', it strips away surface complexities or excuses to expose the fundamental truth of a matter.

history.meaning: to carry an explanation or inquiry all the way to its foundational bottom
at bottom, when all is said and done, in the final analysis (discourse marker)

说到底.notes: Used at the start of a clause to sum up the core issue after weighing various details (说到底，还是预算不够 'When all is said and done, it boils down to insufficient budget'); compare 归根结底 (higher, more formal register).

rootFamily.gloss: to the end; (in questions) after all, on earth
in the final analysis (formal idiom: return to root and tie the bottom)
confidence, trump card, or reserve strength (lit. bottom qi)

说实话.etymology: A verb-object phrase (動賓短語) composed of 說 (Trad. 說, shuō, 'to speak, utter') and the modifier-head noun 實話 (Trad. 實話, shíhuà: 實 'solid, full, true', originally depicting a house 宀 filled with cowrie shells and goods 貫, as opposed to 虛 'empty/false' + 話 'spoken words'). Literally 'to speak solid, unvarnished words', it serves both as a literal verb phrase ('tell the truth') and as a pragmatic conversational hedge ('frankly speaking, to be honest').

history.meaning: to speak truthful, unfabricated words (contrasted with 說假話 or 說空話)
to tell the truth; as a discourse marker, 'honestly speaking, to tell you the truth'

说实话.notes: As a sentence-initial discourse marker, 说实话 signals candor or softens an awkward admission (说实话，我对这个方案不太满意 'To be honest, I'm not very satisfied with this proposal'); synonymous with 老实说 and 说真的.

rootFamily.gloss: fact, reality (lit. matters that are solid/real)

说明.etymology: A verb-complement compound (動補式) that dates back to Han–Tang exegetical prose, formed from 說 (Trad. 說, shuō, Middle Chinese *sywet, 'to explain, expound in words') and the resultative complement 明 (míng, MC *mjaeng, 'bright, clear, illuminated', combining 日 'sun' and 月 'moon'). Literally 'to expound something until it becomes bright and clear', it was also adopted in Meiji Japan (説明 *setsumei*) and reinforced in modern Mandarin as both a verb ('explain, show/prove') and a noun ('explanation, manual').

history.meaning: to expound and clarify the meaning of a classical text or principle until it is luminous
to explain, illustrate, or demonstrate (that...); an explanation, caption, or user manual (说明书)

说明.notes: Has two distinct modern verbal uses: (1) human agent explaining something (向大家说明情况 'explain the situation to everyone'), and (2) non-human evidence demonstrating a point (这说明他很专业 'This shows/proves that he is very professional').

cognates.meaning: persuasion (settoku, a structural parallel using 得 instead of 服)
to persuade, win over by argument (seolbok)

说服.etymology: A verb-resultative compound (動補式) originating in Warring States and Han rhetorical traditions (such as the diplomat-persuaders 縱橫家), combining 說 (Trad. 說, classically read *shuì* in the departing tone, MC *sywejH*, 'to lobby, counsel, persuade a ruler with strategic arguments', now pronounced *shuō* in Mainland standard and *shuì* in Taiwan/traditional literary readings) with 服 (fú, MC *bjuwk, 'to submit, yield, be won over in heart'). Literally 'to win someone's compliance through speech'.

history.meaning: to counsel a ruler or rival and win their submission through persuasive rhetoric (contrasted with 征服 'conquer by force')
to persuade, convince, talk someone into accepting an idea or course of action

morphemes.meaning: persuade, counsel, argue (classically shuì, modern shuō)

说服.notes: Note the famous pronunciation split: Mainland China standardized the reading to *shuōfú* (treating 说 as 'talk until convinced'), whereas Taiwan and classical purists preserve the historical departing-tone reading *shuìfú* (as in 游说 *yóushuì* 'to lobby').

rootFamily.gloss: lobby, go around campaigning to persuade decision-makers
be genuinely convinced in heart and mind (idiom)

说法.etymology: Originally a Medieval Chinese Buddhist verb-object compound (說法, shuōfǎ) translating Sanskrit धर्मदेशना (dharmadeśanā, "preaching the Dharma"), formed from 說 (shuō, "to explain, expound") and 法 (fǎ, "law, method, Buddhist Dharma"). In vernacular Mandarin, the compound underwent prosodic and semantic shift: read with a neutral tone on the second syllable (shuōfa), it reanalyzed as a modifier-head noun meaning "way of speaking, wording, version of events," and by extension an "official explanation or satisfactory account" given to resolve a dispute.

history.meaning: to expound the Buddhist Dharma or doctrines
way of phrasing a matter; argument or version of events
statement, version, or accountable explanation demanded in a dispute

说法.notes: Pronounced with a neutral tone (shuōfa) when meaning "explanation, wording, or satisfactory account" (e.g., 给个说法, "give an explanation/accountability" in PR crises), whereas full-toned shuōfǎ retains the religious sense of "preaching the Dharma."

说话.etymology: Verb-object compound combining 说 (說, 'to speak, say') + 话 (話, 'spoken words, speech'); in Tang–Song times also a noun for vernacular storytelling.

history.meaning: to speak, talk, say words; vernacular storytelling (hist.)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 说话 (via 萌典)

说说.etymology: Formed by full verbal reduplication (AA pattern) of 说 (trad. 說, shuō, Old Chinese *ljud, "to explain, speak, persuasion"). In Old Chinese, 說 was a phono-semantic compound combining 言 ("speech") and 兌 (*lˤot-s, phonetic and semantic "to please, clear"). In Mandarin grammar, reduplicating an action verb into the AA pattern softens the imperative mood and adds a tentative, delimitatieve aspect ("to say a little, talk briefly, give one's take").

history.meaning: to explain, elucidate, or set forth in speech
to talk briefly, chat, or casually express one's view
to talk briefly; go ahead and say; mildly reprimand

morphemes.meaning: delimitatieve aspect marker indicating brief, casual, or tentative action

说说.notes: With a neutral tone on the second syllable (shuōshuo), it lowers interpersonal pressure in meetings or conversations (e.g., 你说说看, "go ahead and share what you think"), though in familial or workplace contexts it can also mean "to gently scold or talk some sense into someone."

说起.etymology: A verb-complement compound combining the speech verb 说 (trad. 說, shuō, "to speak, talk") with the directional-inchoative complement 起 (qǐ, "to rise, get up, initiate"). Literally meaning "to raise up in speech," 起 functions aspectually to mark the initiation of a topic or the mental retrieval of a subject in discourse ("to bring up, broach, or speaking of...").

history.meaning: to raise or initiate a point in speech
to mention, bring up a topic, or speak of

morphemes.meaning: upward directional and inchoative complement (to start, bring up)

说起.notes: Frequently used at the start of a clause as a topic-shifting discourse marker (说起这件事..., "Speaking of this matter..."), often expanded to 说起来 ("when you come to talk about it / actually").

rootFamily.gloss: to start talking about; speaking of

请.etymology: Polite request marker ('please') and hospitality verb ('invite; treat someone to a meal'), combining 讠 ('words') with 青 (qīng phonetic). In Classical Chinese etiquette (Analects, Liji), 請 meant 'respectfully request permission or invite', which remains the heart of modern 请进 ('please come in') and 请坐 ('please sit').

history.meaning: request respectfully; invite

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 請 (via 萌典)

请假.etymology: A verb-object compound (請假) attested since the Tang and Song dynasties in official bureaucratic usage, composed of 请 (trad. 請, qǐng, "to request respectfully, petition") and 假 (jià, "furlough, official leave, borrowed time"). The second element 假 originally meant "to borrow, lend, grant temporarily," which in imperial civil service administration specialized in the fourth tone (jià, Middle Chinese *kæH) to denote an authorized leave of absence granted to an official.

history.meaning: for a court official to petition the throne or ministry for a temporary furlough
to ask for leave or take approved time off from work or school

morphemes.meaning: leave of absence, furlough, holiday (fourth tone jià)

请假.notes: Because 请假 is a separable verb-object (离合词, líhécí) in Mandarin, modifiers for duration or frequency must be inserted between the two characters: e.g., 请三天假 ("ask for three days of leave") or 请了个假 ("took a leave").

rootFamily.gloss: leave note, written request for time off
to go on vacation, take a holiday

请客.etymology: Verb-object compound combining 请 (請, 'to invite politely') + 客 ('guest'), meaning 'to invite guests to dinner, stand treat, pick up the bill'.

history.meaning: to host guests, treat someone to a meal

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 请客 (via 萌典)

请教.etymology: A Classical Chinese verb-object compound (請教) formed from 请 (trad. 請, qǐng, "to request respectfully, invite") and 教 (jiào, "instruction, teaching, guidance"). Attested in pre-Qin and Han texts (such as Mencius and the Book of Rites) where disciples or envoys formally requested moral or strategic instruction from a master, it evolved into a standard deferential expression for asking someone's advice or expertise.

history.meaning: to respectfully request moral or scholarly instruction from a master
to ask for advice, consult an expert or senior colleague politely

请教.notes: A polite, deferential verb used in professional and creative settings when consulting someone with more expertise (e.g., 向您请教一个问题, "May I ask your advice on a question?").

rootFamily.gloss: to give advice or comments (polite: 'please enlighten me')

请示.etymology: A formal verb-object compound (請示) originating in imperial administrative and epistolary Literary Chinese, combining 请 (trad. 請, qǐng, "to petition, request respectfully") and 示 (shì, "to show, manifest, issue a directive or sign"). Originally meaning "to ask a superior to manifest their will or issue a written directive (批示)," it became entrenched in modern organizational and media production hierarchies for seeking greenlight or instructions from upper management.

history.meaning: to petition a higher authority to reveal a decision or issue a directive
to ask for instructions or authorization from a superior; a written request for instructions

请示.notes: Strictly upward-directed in workplace hierarchy: subordinates 请示 (ask for instructions from) executives or producers, whereas executives 批示 or 指示 (issue directives to) subordinates.

rootFamily.gloss: written comment or approval from a superior

请进.etymology: A polite imperative verb phrase (請進) structured from the deferential invitation verb 请 (trad. 請, qǐng, "to invite, request; please") followed by the directional verb 进 (trad. 進, jìn, "to advance, enter"). In Classical Chinese, 請 functioned as a performative verb ("I beg leave to... / I invite you to..."), which grammaticalized into the standard Mandarin politeness marker before an action verb, while 進 originally depicted a bird advancing upward (隹 + 辵).

history.meaning: to invite a guest to step forward and advance into a hall
"please come in" (standard polite response to a knock at the door)

请进.notes: The quintessential two-syllable office response in Chinese dramas when an assistant or producer knocks on an executive's door; parallel polite formulas include 请坐 ("please have a seat") and 请讲 ("please speak / go ahead").

rootFamily.gloss: please sit down, have a seat

请问.etymology: Polite question opener ('excuse me, may I ask…'), pairing 请 ('respectfully request') with 问 ('ask'). Already attested as a courteous formula in Classical dialogues in Mencius ('Dare I respectfully ask…'), it remains Standard Mandarin's everyday way to approach a front desk or stranger.

history.meaning: respectfully ask a question

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 請問 (via 萌典)

读.etymology: Phono-semantic character 读 (讀), combining the speech radical 訁 (言) + phonetic 卖 (賣/𧶠 yù / Old Chinese *C.lˤok), originally meaning 'to recite aloud from bamboo slips, chant and expound a text', then 'to read, attend school'.

history.meaning: to recite a text aloud, study
to read, read aloud, attend school/university

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 读 (via 萌典)

读书.etymology: Verb-object compound combining 读 (讀, 'to read aloud, study') + 书 (書, 'book, written text'), meaning both literally 'to read a book' and generally 'to study, attend school'.

history.meaning: to read books; to study, go to school

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 读书 (via 萌典)

读书会.etymology: A three-character modifier-head compound (讀書會) consisting of the classical verb-object compound 读书 (trad. 讀書, dúshū, "to read books, study," from 讀 "to chant/read aloud" + 書 "writings, book") modifying the head noun 会 (trad. 會, huì, "gathering, association, club"). While scholarly reading societies existed in late imperial China, the modern institutional sense of a public or media-sponsored "book club / reading salon" was reinforced by Meiji-era Japanese 読書会 (dokushokai).

history.meaning: a gathering of literati for reading and discussing texts
history.stage: Late Imperial Literary Chinese / Meiji Japanese 読書会

history.meaning: book club, reading group, or literary salon event
