读书会.notes: In contemporary Chinese media and cultural industries, a 读书会 can be either a private reading group or a live-streamed/televised cultural salon used to promote intellectual IP and authors.

rootFamily.gloss: to read books; to study, attend school

读书角.etymology: Modern compound noun from 读书 (simplified from 讀書, 'read books; study') + 角 ('corner; nook'). Built on the same productive `X + 角` pattern as 咖啡角 ('coffee corner'), it designates a quiet corner furnished with shelves and seating for reading.

history.meaning: reading corner; book nook

读读.etymology: Tentative/delimitative reduplication of 读 ('read; read aloud', speech radical 讠 + phonetic 卖 *mài/dòu*). In Mandarin grammar, doubling a monosyllabic action verb (AA pattern with neutral tone on the second syllable) gives a warm, invitational nuance: 'have a quick read; read a little'.

morphemes.meaning: delimitative 'a bit / have a read' (neutral tone)

history.meaning: have a read; read over briefly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 读读

诽谤.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative compound (誹謗) pairing two synonymous phono-semantic speech verbs: 诽 (trad. 誹, fěi, Old Chinese *pʰəjʔ, from 言 "speech" + 非 "wrong, negate", meaning "to criticize behind someone's back, disparage") and 谤 (trad. 謗, bàng, Old Chinese *pˤaŋ-s, from 言 "speech" + 旁 "side, broad", meaning "to speak ill of openly, denounce"). In Han dynasty governance (e.g., 誹謗之木, boards erected for public criticism of the ruler), it could mean public remonstrance, before narrowing exclusively to malicious slander and legal defamation.

history.meaning: to criticize or speak ill of (originally including public criticism of rulers)
to maliciously slander, calumniate, or defame someone's reputation
to slander, defame, libel (both general and statutory legal term)

morphemes.meaning: to disparage, speak ill of behind one's back

诽谤.notes: A high-register and formal legal term in media/showbiz PR disputes (e.g., 恶意诽谤, "malicious defamation", or 造谣诽谤, "fabricating rumors and defaming"), often cited in celebrity studio cease-and-desist statements (律师函).

rootFamily.gloss: to frame, make false accusations against

课本.etymology: Determinative educational compound of 课 ('assigned lesson; course of study', speech radical 讠 + 果 *guǒ*) + 本 ('bound book; volume'). It is the universal Mandarin word for a school or professional textbook.

history.meaning: course textbook
textbook

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 课本

谁.etymology: Interrogative pronoun 'who, whom' (shuí or shéi), combining 言/讠 ('speech, ask') with 隹 (zhuī phonetic). Already standard across Classical Chinese (Shijing, Analects), 谁 stays in place in Mandarin questions and takes 的 to form 谁的 ('whose?').

history.meaning: interrogative pronoun 'who?'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 誰 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: tone, tune; to investigate; to adjust, harmonize

调.etymology: A phono-semantic character (trad. 調) combining the semantic radical 言 (yán, "speech, words, musical sound") with the phonetic component 周 (zhōu, Old Chinese *tiw, meaning "all around, complete, well-fitted"). In Old Chinese, the rising/level-tone reading (tiáo < *lˤiw) meant "to harmonize, blend flavors or musical strings, regulate," whereas the departing-tone derivation (diào < *lˤiw-s) nominalized into "musical mode, melody, levy" and verbalized into "to transfer, shift, deploy personnel or resources."

history.meaning: to harmonize musical notes, blend seasonings, or bring into balance
musical mode; imperial tax levy; to transfer or dispatch troops and officials
to adjust, regulate, tune (tiáo); to transfer, move, call up (diào)

morphemes.meaning: to adjust, harmonize, regulate (tiáo); to transfer, shift, tune (diào)

调.notes: A crucial polyphone (多音字): read tiáo when meaning "to adjust, fine-tune, mediate" (调整, 调节, 调音), and read diào when meaning "to transfer personnel, dispatch, investigate, or musical tone" (调动, 调职, 调查, 声调). In studio production, both readings occur constantly (e.g., 调音 tiáoyīn "mix audio" vs. 调人 diàorén "transfer staff").

调令.etymology: A modifier-head administrative compound (調令, diàolìng) formed from 调 (trad. 調, diào, in its departing-tone bureaucratic sense "to transfer, reassign, deploy") modifying 令 (lìng, "command, decree, official order," originally depicting a kneeling figure beneath an authority cover 亼 + 卩). Originating in imperial military and civil service administration for troop or magistrate reassignments, it remains the standard term in modern corporate and institutional HR for a formal transfer directive.

history.meaning: imperial or ministerial decree ordering the transfer of officials or troops
official written order reassigning an employee or cadre to another post or department

调令.notes: Always pronounced diàolìng (never tiáolìng); typically collocates with verbs like 下达 ("issue") or 收到 ("receive"), e.g., 一纸调令 ("a single sheet of transfer orders") in workplace dramas.

rootFamily.gloss: to transfer to a new post (diàozhí)

调到.etymology: A verb-resultative compound (調到, diàodào) combining the action verb 调 (trad. 調, diào, "to transfer, reassign, shift") with the resultative complement of arrival 到 (dào, "to arrive at, reach"). Unlike the bare verb 调, which focuses on the act of moving or reassigning, the addition of 到 grammaticalizes the destination or new department as the direct post-verbal argument.

history.meaning: to transfer someone or something so that it arrives at a specified place
to transfer or be reassigned to (a department, position, or location); to tune/set a dial to

morphemes.meaning: to transfer, shift (diào); or to adjust, tune (tiáo)
resultative complement marking arrival at a location, post, or level

调到.notes: Usually read diàodào when referring to personnel or file transfers (e.g., 把他调到总编室, "transfer him to the chief editor's office"), though it can be read tiáodào when adjusting a setting or dial to a level (e.g., 把音量调到最大).

rootFamily.gloss: to transfer away / out of a unit (diàozǒu)

调动.etymology: A verb-resultative / coordinative compound (調動, diàodòng) formed from 调 (trad. 調, diào, "to transfer, deploy, marshal") and 动 (trad. 動, dòng, "to move, stir, set in motion"). First attested in Tang–Song military and administrative prose for moving troops or shifting officials between posts, it later developed a metaphorical sense in modern Chinese: "to mobilize, arouse, or stir up" abstract resources such as audience emotion (调动气氛) or team enthusiasm (调动积极性).

history.meaning: to move troops or reassign officials from one post to another
to reassign staff/resources; to mobilize, arouse, or stir up (energy, atmosphere, enthusiasm)

调动.notes: Always pronounced diàodòng; in TV production and workplace contexts it has two high-frequency uses: HR personnel transfers (人事调动) and a director/host "stirring up" the live studio mood or audience energy (调动现场气氛 / 调动情绪).

rootFamily.gloss: to transfer to a new post (diàozhí)

调性.etymology: Modern musical compound combining 调 (調 diào, 'musical mode, key, tune, melody') + abstract noun suffix 性 ('nature, property, quality').

history.meaning: musical tonality, key; stylistic tone

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 调性 (via 萌典)

调整.etymology: A coordinative/resultative compound (調整, tiáozhěng) combining 调 (trad. 調, tiáo, "to harmonize, regulate, adjust") and 整 (zhěng, "to put in order, make neat, arrange," composed of 束 + 攵 + 正). Attested in Han and Six Dynasties texts (such as the Book of Han) in the sense of "putting troops, horses, or state affairs into harmonious order," its modern usage for calibrating schedules, strategies, or broadcast parameters was further reinforced by shared Sino-Japanese technical usage (調整, chōsei).

history.meaning: to put into proper order and balance (e.g., steeds, carriages, or music)
to adjust, revise, realign, or fine-tune (plans, mindset, schedules, or equipment)

morphemes.meaning: to put in order, arrange, rectify

调整.notes: Always pronounced tiáozhěng (second tone + third tone); versatile across both technical contexts (调整方案, "adjust the proposal/plan") and personal psychological ones (调整心态 / 调整状态, "adjust one's mindset / get back into form").

rootFamily.gloss: to sort out, put in order, organize (zhěnglǐ)

调查.etymology: A coordinative verb compound (調查, diàochá) composed of 调 (trad. 調, diào, "to call up records, calculate, examine") and 查 (chá, "to inspect, examine, look into"). Popularized in late Qing and Republican Chinese as an orthographic return loan from Meiji Japanese 調査 (chōsa), which was coined to translate Western administrative and legal terms such as English "investigation," "inquiry," and "survey." In Mandarin, the first character took the departing-tone administrative reading diào ("to requisition/examine files").

history.meaning: official inquiry, fact-finding survey, or legal investigation
to investigate, look into, conduct a survey or fact-finding inquiry into

调查.notes: Always pronounced diàochá; used both as a verb ("to investigate a leak or incident") and as a noun ("survey, investigation," e.g., 市场调查 "market research" or 背景调查 "background check").

cognates.meaning: to dispatch, assign personnel to a task

调派.etymology: A coordinative verb compound (調派, diàopài) combining 调 (trad. 調, diào, "to transfer, requisition, muster") and 派 (pài, originally "branching water currents," extended to "to branch out, assign, dispatch, delegate"). Developed in Ming–Qing officialdom to describe transferring and dispatching officials or troops to a specific mission, it is used in modern organizational management for deploying staff or production crews to a project.

history.meaning: to muster and dispatch officials or military forces to an assignment
to dispatch, deploy, or assign personnel and resources to a task

调派.notes: Always read diàopài; emphasizes managerial authority in reallocating human resources from one place and sending them to another (e.g., 调派人手, "dispatch extra hands/staff").

rootFamily.gloss: to dispatch, send on a mission

cognates.meaning: transferring and utilizing personnel or funds

调用.etymology: A serial verb / coordinative compound (調用, diàoyòng) formed from 调 (trad. 調, diào, "to transfer, requisition, call up") followed by 用 (yòng, "to use, employ, put to service"). Attested in imperial administrative texts (such as the History of Song and History of Ming) for requisitioning grain, funds, troops, or officials from one jurisdiction for use in another, it has expanded in modern Mandarin to include both deploying studio/corporate resources and, in computing, "calling/invoking" a function or archive.

history.meaning: to transfer officials, troops, or tax supplies for deployment elsewhere
history.stage: Middle and Early Modern Literary Chinese (Song–Ming)

history.meaning: to transfer and deploy (funds, equipment, staff, or archival footage); to call/invoke (a routine)

调用.notes: Always pronounced diàoyòng; in television and media production, it frequently describes requisitioning shared company resources—such as camera crews, studios, budgets, or archival footage (调用资金 / 调用素材 / 调用设备)—across departments.

rootFamily.gloss: to requisition, expropriate for public/official use

调职.etymology: A verb-object compound (調職, diàozhí) composed of the administrative verb 调 (trad. 調, diào, "to transfer, reassign") and the noun object 职 (trad. 職, zhí, "official post, duty, position," originally from 耳 "ear" + 音/戠 phonetic, referring to recording and attending to official duties). Patterned on classical bureaucratic compounds such as 調任 (diàorèn, "to transfer to a new appointment") and 升職 (shēngzhí, "to be promoted"), it denotes a lateral or vertical job reassignment within an organization.

history.meaning: to transfer an official's post or duties within the bureaucracy
to transfer or be reassigned to a new job position or branch

调职.notes: Always pronounced diàozhí; belongs to a core set of Mandarin V-O career-change compounds with 职: 入职 (join a company), 升职 (get promoted), 调职 (transfer posts), 降职 (be demoted), and 辞职/离职 (resign/leave).

rootFamily.gloss: to get promoted, advance in rank

调音.etymology: Verb-object compound combining 调 (調 tiáo, 'to harmonize, adjust, regulate') + 音 ('musical pitch, sound, tone').

history.meaning: to tune a musical instrument, adjust sound

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 调音 (via 萌典)

调音扳手.etymology: Four-character compound combining 调音 (調音, 'tuning an instrument') + 扳手 ('wrench, spanner', from 扳 bān 'to pull/turn a lever' + 手 'handle, tool').

history.form: 調音扳手 / 调音扳手
history.meaning: tuning wrench, tuning hammer (for pianos, harps, or drums)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 调音扳手 (via 萌典)

谈.etymology: A phono-semantic character (trad. 談, tán) combining the semantic radical 言 (yán, "speech, words") with the phonetic component 炎 (yán, Old Chinese *ɢʷram / *lˤam, "blazing fire"). In Old Chinese (*lˤam) and Middle Chinese (*dam), 談 denoted engaged, expansive conversation or discourse—often contrasted with 言 (direct assertion) and 語 (dialogic reply)—and gained prominence during the Wei–Jin period in 清談 (qīngtán, "pure conversation" philosophical debates).

history.meaning: to converse, discourse upon, speak at length
to engage in philosophical discourse, chat, or recount stories
to talk, discuss, chat, or negotiate (a project, contract, or relationship)

谈.notes: Unlike 说 (which can be a one-way statement), 谈 inherently implies interactive exchange, discussion, or negotiation between parties—hence its use in business (谈合作 "discuss collaboration", 谈合同 "negotiate a contract") and romance (谈恋爱).

谈一谈.etymology: Formed via the Mandarin V-一-V tentative/delimitatieve construction (談一談) around the root verb 谈 (trad. 談, tán, "to talk, discuss, converse"), inserting the numeral 一 (yī, "one") between the reduplicated verb stems. Developing in vernacular Mandarin from a literal verb-cognate object structure ("to talk one bout of talking"), the V-一-V pattern grammaticalized to express a bounded, polite, and non-threatening invitation or intention to have a brief discussion.

history.meaning: to engage in a single brief round of conversation
to have a talk, chat briefly, or talk things over

morphemes.meaning: tentative/delimitatieve marker ('one / a bit') softening the verb action
reduplicated verb stem completing the delimitatieve frame

谈一谈.notes: In the spoken rhythm of tányitán, 一 is usually reduced to a neutral tone; when a boss or partner says 我们谈一谈吧 ("Let's have a talk"), the polite grammatical softening often masks a serious or consequential conversation.

rootFamily.gloss: to talk briefly, have a chat (AA reduplication)
to talk briefly, say a few words
to chat, have a casual conversation

谈判.etymology: A serial/resultative Sino-Japanese compound (談判, tánpàn) combining 谈 (trad. 談, tán, "to discuss, confer, converse") and 判 (pàn, "to divide, judge, decide, settle," composed of 半 "half" + 刀 "knife," literally cutting in two to render a verdict). Popularized in late nineteenth-century diplomacy via Meiji Japanese 談判 (danpan, "discussing in order to reach a settlement; diplomatic parley") and adopted into Mandarin for formal diplomatic, legal, and commercial negotiations.

history.meaning: diplomatic parley or formal deliberation to settle a dispute
to negotiate; formal negotiations or bargaining talks (diplomatic, commercial, or contractual)

谈判.notes: Functions as both a noun (商业谈判 "business negotiations", 谈判桌 "negotiating table") and an intransitive verb (跟对方谈判 "negotiate with the other party").

谈到.etymology: A verb-resultative compound (談到, tándào) formed from the speech verb 谈 (trad. 談, tán, "to talk, converse, discuss") followed by the resultative complement 到 (dào, "to reach, arrive at"). Literally meaning "to talk until reaching (a specific point or topic)," 到 marks that the flow of conversation has touched upon or arrived at a given subject ("to speak of, touch upon, refer to").

history.meaning: to converse up to a certain point, time, or subject
to speak of, touch upon, or mention in the course of conversation

morphemes.meaning: resultative complement indicating arrival at a topic or point in time

谈到.notes: More formal than 说起 or 提到; frequently used in media interviews, press releases, and meetings when introducing a speaker's remarks on a specific topic (e.g., 谈到这次节目改版..., "Speaking of this show's revamp...").

cognates.meaning: to have a heart-to-heart talk, confide in one another

谈心.etymology: A verb-object / idiomatic compound (談心, tánxīn) composed of 谈 (trad. 談, tán, "to talk, converse") and 心 (xīn, "heart, mind, inner thoughts and feelings"). First attested in Tang dynasty poetry (such as Bai Juyi's verse) to describe intimate friends sharing their innermost thoughts without reserve, it remains a warm, idiomatic separable verb in modern Mandarin for having a candid heart-to-heart conversation.

history.meaning: for close companions to converse intimately about their inner thoughts and aspirations
to have a heart-to-heart talk, share inner feelings candidly

morphemes.meaning: to talk, converse, share in speech
heart, mind, innermost feelings and thoughts

谈心.notes: A separable verb-object compound (离合词): to say "talk heart-to-heart with someone," use the prepositional frame 跟/和某人谈心, and to soften it, reduplicate the verb stem to 谈谈心.

rootFamily.gloss: innermost thoughts, words from the heart (zhīxīnhuà)
what is on one's mind, unspoken thoughts (xīnshì)
to open one's heart, pour out one's feelings (jiāoxīn)

谈恋爱.etymology: A modern verb-object compound (談戀愛, tán liàn'ài) combining the interactive verb 谈 (trad. 談, tán, "to talk, engage in, court through conversation") with the disyllabic noun 恋爱 (trad. 戀愛, liàn'ài, "romantic love"). The object 戀愛 gained currency in early twentieth-century China via Meiji Japanese 恋愛 (ren'ai, coined to translate English "romantic love" as distinct from familial oruniversal affection), while Chinese prefixed 谈 ("to converse/conduct") because modern courtship centered on free romantic dialogue and dating rather than arranged marriage.

history.meaning: romantic love and courtship between individuals
history.stage: Meiji Japanese / May Fourth Era Chinese (early 20th c.)

history.meaning: to be in a romantic relationship, court, or date someone

morphemes.meaning: to yearn for, be deeply attached to

谈恋爱.notes: Because 谈恋爱 is a verb-object construction (literally "to talk/conduct romantic love"), modifiers go between 谈 and 恋爱 (e.g., 谈了一场恋爱, "had a romantic relationship"), and the person one dates is introduced with 跟/和 (跟她谈恋爱).

rootFamily.gloss: to suffer a breakup, be lovelorn (shīliàn)

cognates.meaning: conversation, talk; informal official statement to the press

谈话.etymology: A compound (談話, tánhuà) formed from 谈 (trad. 談, tán, "to converse, discuss") and 话 (trad. 話, huà, "spoken words, speech, talk"). Attested in Six Dynasties and Tang vernacular/literary texts as a coordinative or verb-object compound meaning "to converse, chat," it also absorbed the modern Sino-Japanese journalistic sense of 談話 (danwa, "a formal statement or remarks issued in an interview") alongside its everyday Mandarin use as "a serious talk or conversation."

history.meaning: to converse, chat, or exchange spoken stories
to speak or converse with someone; a formal talk, interview, or public statement

谈话.notes: More formal than 说话 or 聊天: in a workplace or institutional setting, 找你谈话 ("ask to have a talk with you") typically refers to a serious one-on-one conversation initiated by a manager, producer, or HR director.

谈谈心.etymology: An AAB verb-object reduplication (談談心, tántanxīn) derived from the separable compound 谈心 (trad. 談心, tánxīn, "to have a heart-to-heart talk," from 談 "to converse" + 心 "heart, inner mind"). Because 谈心 has an internal verb-object structure, Mandarin morphology reduplicates only the verbal first syllable (谈 → 谈谈) while keeping the nominal object (心) intact, adding a relaxed, congenial, and tentative aspect ("to have a nice little heart-to-heart chat").

history.meaning: to converse intimately about inner thoughts and feelings
to have a casual, warm heart-to-heart chat

morphemes.meaning: delimitatieve verbal reduplication marking a relaxed, brief, or friendly action

谈谈心.notes: Exemplifies the classic AAB reduplication rule for Mandarin separable verbs (离合词): just as 散步 becomes 散散步 and 聊天 becomes 聊聊天, 谈心 reduplicates as 谈谈心 (never *谈心谈心).

rootFamily.gloss: to have a heart-to-heart talk (base form)
to have a casual chat (AAB reduplication)
to take a leisurely walk (AAB reduplication)

谎话.etymology: A modifier-head noun compound (謊話, huǎnghuà) composed of 谎 (trad. 謊, huǎng, "lie, falsehood, wild unverified talk") modifying the head noun 话 (trad. 話, huà, "spoken words, speech"). The character 謊 is a phono-semantic compound combining 言 ("speech") with 荒 (huāng, Old Chinese *hmlˤaŋ, "wasteland, overgrown, wild, unsubstantiated"), originally referring to delirious sleep-talking or baseless claims before specializing in Yuan–Ming vernacular Mandarin as deliberate "lies, falsehoods."

history.meaning: wild, unsubstantiated, or delirious speech
history.stage: Middle Chinese to Early Vernacular Mandarin

history.meaning: lie, falsehood, deliberate fabrication in speech
history.stage: Early Modern and Modern Standard Mandarin

谎话.notes: The standard everyday noun for a "lie" (collocates with 说 or 讲: 说谎话, "to tell lies", or 撒谎), whereas 谎言 (huǎngyán) is its more literary, dramatic counterpart.

rootFamily.gloss: to tell a lie, lie (sāhuǎng / shuōhuǎng)

谜团.etymology: Metaphorical compound of 谜 ('riddle; enigma', speech radical 讠 + 迷 mí 'lost; bewildered') + 团 ('round ball; tangled cluster', enclosure 囗 + 专). Pictures an unsolved mystery as a tightly wound ball of thread waiting to be untangled (解开谜团).

history.meaning: mystery; cluster of riddles

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 谜团

cognates.meaning: to thank, apologize, decline; surname Sa
to thank, express gratitude, apologize; surname Tạ

谢.etymology: A phono-semantic character (trad. 謝, xiè) combining the semantic radical 言 (yán, "speech, words") with the phonetic component 射 (shè, Old Chinese *Cə.lAk-s, "to shoot an arrow, let go"). In Old Chinese (*s-lak-s), 謝 originally meant "to take leave in words, decline an offer or office, renounce," from which two core social meanings branched out: "to acknowledge a fault, apologize" (as preserved in 谢罪 and Japanese 謝る ayamaru) and "to express gratitude, thank" (via polite ritual acknowledgment upon receiving a gift), alongside its status as an ancient surname originating in the Western Zhou state of Shen at Xie (謝).

history.meaning: to decline politely, take one's leave, or acknowledge a fault in words; ancient surname
to express gratitude, thank; to apologize; (of flowers) to wither and fall away
to thank; to apologize or decline (in compounds); surname Xie

morphemes.meaning: to thank, express gratitude; to apologize or decline; surname Xie

谢.notes: While standalone 谢 and 谢谢 mean "thank" in modern Mandarin, 谢 retains its classical senses of "apologize" (谢罪), "decline/refuse" (婉谢, 谢绝), and "wither/fade" (凋谢, 花谢了) in compounds, and is also a major Chinese surname (as in 谢总).

谢天谢地.etymology: Four-character idiomatic exclamation (ABCD / A-B-A-C pattern) combining 谢 (謝, 'to thank') + 天 ('Heaven') + 谢 ('to thank') + 地 ('Earth').

history.form: 謝天謝地 / 谢天谢地
history.meaning: thank Heaven and Earth! -> thank goodness!

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 谢天谢地 (via 萌典)

谢总.etymology: A modern Chinese workplace honorific title (謝總, Xiè Zǒng) combining the surname 谢 (trad. 謝, Xiè, an ancient toponymic surname granted to Yin Jifu's relative Shen Bo at the fief of Xie in modern Henan during the Western Zhou dynasty) with the postposed executive title 总 (trad. 總, zǒng, clipped from 总经理 zǒngjīnglǐ "general manager," 总裁 zǒngcái "president/CEO," or 总监 zǒngjiān "chief director"). The [Surname] + 总 pattern arose in post-1980s corporate Mandarin as the universal form of address for senior executives and chief producers.

history.meaning: surname Xie + prefix denoting 'general / chief' in administrative titles
Director Xie / President Xie / General Manager Xie (workplace honorific)

morphemes.meaning: surname Xie (originally an ancient Zhou fiefdom name)
executive honorific clipped from 总经理 (general manager), 总裁 (president), or 总监 (chief director)

谢总.notes: In Chinese corporate and entertainment industry settings (such as *Behind the Scenes* / *幕后之王*), [Surname] + 总 is used for virtually anyone at the director (总监), producer (总制片人), or C-suite level, always placing the surname first.

cognates.meaning: gratitude, appreciation; intention to resign or apologize

谢意.etymology: A modifier-head noun compound (謝意, xièyì) composed of 谢 (trad. 謝, xiè, "to thank, express gratitude") modifying 意 (yì, "thought, mind, feeling, sentiment," formed from 音 "sound/voice" + 心 "heart," meaning the intent within the heart). Attested in Tang–Song literary prose and reinforced in modern formal correspondence alongside Sino-Japanese 謝意 (shai), it literally denotes "feelings or sentiments of gratitude."

history.meaning: sentiment of gratitude or polite acknowledgment expressed in letters or gifts
gratitude, appreciation, thankful sentiment (formal noun)

谢意.notes: A formal, written-register noun that never functions as a verb; it almost always appears as the object of verbs of expression such as 表达 ("express") or 表示 ("show"): 表达谢意 / 表示谢意 ("to express one's gratitude").

谢谢.etymology: Everyday expression of gratitude ('thank you'), formed by reduplicating 谢 ('thank, express gratitude; decline politely', written with 讠 'speech' + 射 phonetic). Single 謝 for thanking someone appears in Han-dynasty historical records (Shiji), while reduplicated 謝謝 became standard in Ming–Qing spoken Mandarin.

history.meaning: express thanks or apology
thank you

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 謝謝 (via 萌典)

谣言.etymology: Modifier-head compound (偏正结构) formed from 谣 (trad. 謠, yáo, 'unaccompanied folk song, popular ditty; unverified street talk') + 言 (yán, 'speech, words'). In Classical Chinese statecraft, rulers collected street ballads (歌謠) to gauge public sentiment, as folk rhymes often encoded political satire or ominous prophecies; from 'anonymous street verse' the compound narrowed to 'unfounded rumor, baseless talk'.

history.meaning: popular ballad, folk rhyme, or prophetic street talk
unfounded rumor, baseless hearsay, fabricated report

谣言.notes: Commonly takes the classifier 条 (tiáo) or 阵 (zhèn) and collocates with 散布 (sànbù, 'spread rumors'), 造谣 (zàoyáo, 'fabricate rumors'), and 辟谣 (pìyáo, 'debunk a rumor')—essential PR crisis vocabulary in media and entertainment dramas.

rootFamily.gloss: to refute or debunk a rumor

谱架.etymology: Modifier-head noun compound combining 谱 (譜, 'musical score, sheet music') + 架 ('supporting frame, stand, rack').

history.meaning: music stand

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 谱架 (via 萌典)

豪华.etymology: Coordinative compound (联合结构) combining 豪 (háo, 'preeminent, heroic, powerful, unrestrained; wealthy clan') and 华 (trad. 華, huá, 'blossom; splendid,magnificent, ornate'). Attested in Literary Chinese to describe the ostentatious lifestyle of aristocratic clans (豪族), and reinforced in modern Mandarin alongside Japanese kanji usage (豪華, gōka) to denote lavish material luxury or an all-star lineup.

history.meaning: powerful and ostentatious; the extravagant splendor of aristocratic families
luxurious, deluxe, sumptuous; star-studded (of a cast or lineup)

豪华.notes: Beyond physical luxury (豪华酒店 'deluxe hotel', 豪华游轮 'luxury cruise'), showbiz and TV production frequently use 豪华阵容 (háohuá zhènróng, 'all-star/blockbuster lineup or cast').

cognates.meaning: to bear, carry on the back; to be defeated; negative
to carry on the back, bear; to owe; negative

负.etymology: From Old Chinese *bəʔ (traditional 負), an ideogrammic compound combining 人 (rén, 'person', bent over at top) + 貝 (bèi, 'cowrie shell, valuables, wealth'), originally depicting a person carrying a load or treasure on their back. From the physical sense 'to carry on the back, shoulder a burden', it extended across Classical Chinese to 'bear a duty', 'owe a debt', 'turn one's back on / betray / fail someone' (as in 辜负), 'suffer defeat', and in mathematics 'negative'.

history.meaning: to carry on the back; to rely on; to owe; to turn one's back on
to bear responsibility; to suffer defeat; to betray or let down; minus/negative
to shoulder (a duty/load); to fail or let down (someone); to lose; negative

morphemes.meaning: to carry on the back; to bear; to betray/fail; negative

负.notes: As a free verb in modern speech, 负 most often means 'to shoulder/bear' (负全责 'bear full responsibility') or, in elevated emotional phrasing, 'to let someone down / betray their devotion' (如：不负众望 'not fail everyone's expectations', 宁教我负天下人).

rootFamily.gloss: burden, load; to bear a burden
to let down, fail to live up to
victory or defeat, outcome of a contest

cognates.meaning: load, burden; electrical or mechanical load

负荷.etymology: Coordinative compound (联合结构) of two synonymous Classical Chinese verbs: 负 (trad. 負, fù, 'to carry on the back') + 荷 (hè, fourth tone in this sense, originally 'lotus leaf' but loaned since the *Shijing* and *Zuo Zhuan* for 'to carry on the shoulder'). In Literary Chinese (e.g. *Zuo Zhuan*: 其父析薪，其子弗克負荷 'the father splits firewood, the son is unable to carry the load'), it meant shouldered weight or ancestral duty; in the modern era it also absorbed the technical Japanese *wasei-kango* sense of mechanical, electrical, or psychological load/capacity.

history.meaning: to carry on the back and shoulders; to inherit and sustain an onerous duty
physical, electrical, or mental load, workload, operating capacity
history.stage: Modern Mandarin (reinforced via Japanese 負荷)

morphemes.meaning: to carry on the back, bear
to carry on the shoulder, bear a load (pronounced hè)

负荷.notes: Note the pronunciation of 荷 here is fourth tone (hè, 'to shoulder a load'), not second tone (hé, 'lotus'). Frequently used in high-pressure workplace contexts like 超负荷工作 (chāofùhè gōngzuò, 'working beyond capacity / overworking').

cognates.meaning: to be in charge of, be responsible for

负责.etymology: Verb-object compound (动宾结构) formed from 负 (trad. 負, fù, 'to carry on the back, shoulder, bear') + 责 (trad. 責, zé, 'duty, obligation, accountability; originally to demand payment of a debt'). Literally 'to shoulder an obligation or accountability', it lexicalized in late imperial and modern Chinese into both a transitive/prepositional verb ('to be in charge of [a project/department]') and an adjective ('conscientious, responsible').

history.meaning: to shoulder accountability or official obligation
to be in charge of (a task/domain); to be held accountable; conscientious

morphemes.meaning: to bear, shoulder, carry on the back

负责.notes: Functions both transitively with a direct object of the domain managed (我负责后期制作 'I am in charge of post-production') and with 对...负责 ('be accountable to someone/something', e.g., 对观众负责 'be responsible to the audience').

rootFamily.gloss: person in charge, head of a project/unit

负责人.etymology: Modifier-head trisyllabic compound (偏正结构) built from the verb-object stem 负责 (trad. 負責, fùzé, 'to bear responsibility / be in charge') modifying the head noun 人 (rén, 'person'). Coined in modern administrative and institutional Mandarin to designate the individual holding formal operational authority and accountability over a project, department, or organization.

history.meaning: person in charge, director, project or department head

负责人.notes: In TV production and corporate settings, 项目负责人 (xiàngmù fùzérén, 'project lead / showrunner') and 部门负责人 ('department head') are standard titles used when asking 'who has final sign-off here?'.

rootFamily.gloss: to be in charge of; responsible

负责任.etymology: Verb-object phrase/compound (动宾结构) consisting of 负 (trad. 負, fù, 'to bear, shoulder') + 责任 (trad. 責任, zérèn, 'duty, responsibility, obligation'). While 负责 can govern a work domain (负责宣传 'in charge of publicity'), 负责任 explicitly incorporates the full disyllabic noun 责任 to emphasize moral or legal accountability ('to take responsibility for consequences') or the character trait of being trustworthy and conscientious.

history.form: 負責任 / 负责任 (fù zérèn)
history.meaning: to bear moral or legal responsibility; conscientious and accountable

负责任.notes: Unlike 负责, 负责任 cannot take a direct object (you cannot say *负责任这个项目); instead use 对...负责任 or use it attributively/predicatively (不负责任的言论 'irresponsible remarks'). In speech, 负着责任 or 负起责任 splits the verb from its object.

rootFamily.gloss: to be in charge of; responsible

负面.etymology: Modifier-head compound (偏正结构) formed from 负 (trad. 負, fù, in its mathematical/polar sense of 'negative, minus', extended from 'turning one's back / deficit') + 面 (miàn, 'face, surface, aspect, side'). Popularized in late 20th-century Mandarin (initially common in Taiwan and Hong Kong media before becoming ubiquitous across Mainland China) as a semantic calque and counterpart to 正面 (zhèngmiàn, 'front side; positive'), referring to adverse sides, unfavorable publicity, or detrimental effects.

history.meaning: negative side, adverse aspect, unfavorable (news, impact, or emotion)

负面.notes: A staple of entertainment PR and media discourse: 负面新闻 (fùmiàn xīnwén, 'negative press / scandal'), 负面影响 ('adverse impact'), and 负面情绪 ('negative emotions'). Its exact antonym is 正面 (zhèngmiàn, 'positive').

财务.etymology: Modifier-head compound (偏正结构) combining 财 (trad. 財, cái, 'wealth, money, property', with 貝 'cowrie/money' radical + 才 phonetic) + 务 (trad. 務, wù, 'affairs, business, task, duty'). Literally 'wealth-related affairs', it became standardized in late Qing and Republican administrative Chinese (alongside Japanese *wasei-kango* 財務, zaimu) for corporate or institutional financial management, and by metonymy in everyday workplace speech for the accounting department or finance officer.

history.meaning: institutional financial administration and fiscal management
history.stage: Meiji Japanese (財務) & Late Qing/Republican Chinese

history.meaning: financial affairs; accounting department or finance staff

财务.notes: In workplace conversation, 财务 frequently refers metonymically to the finance department or accountant (把发票交给财务报销 'hand the invoice to Finance/the accountant for reimbursement'). Do not confuse with its homophone 财物 (cáiwù, 'property and belongings').

责任.etymology: Coordinative compound (联合结构) uniting 责 (trad. 責, zé, 'to demand fulfillment, hold accountable; duty', containing 貝 'cowrie/debt') + 任 (rèn, 'to carry on a shoulder-pole; burden, official post, trust'). Although both characters appear closely linked in Classical Chinese discussions of official accountability (责 vs. 任), the fixed noun compound 責任 was crystallized in Meiji Japan (sekinin) to translate European legal and ethical concepts of 'responsibility/liability' and rapidly re-entered Chinese in the late 19th century.

history.meaning: official accountability and appointed burden/charge (used in parallel)
legal, moral, or administrative responsibility and liability
history.stage: Meiji Japanese return loan to Late Qing Chinese

history.meaning: responsibility, duty, obligation; blame/liability (in an accident)

morphemes.meaning: burden, trust, appointed charge or office

责任.notes: Takes verbs like 承担 (chéngdān, 'shoulder/assume'), 推卸 (tuīxiè, 'shirk/shift'), and 追究 (zhuījiū, 'investigate/hold liable for'): 追究法律责任 ('pursue legal liability').

rootFamily.gloss: to be in charge of; responsible

责无旁贷.etymology: Four-character classical idiom (成语, chéngyǔ) structured as a subject-predicate clause: 责 (trad. 責, zé, 'one's duty/responsibility') + 无 (trad. 無, wú, 'there is no [room to]') + 旁 (páng, 'to the side, onto others') + 贷 (trad. 貸, dài, 'to shift, loan, or pardon/shirk'). Literally 'a responsibility that cannot be shifted onto others on the side', emphasizing an inescapable personal or institutional obligation.

history.form: 責無旁貸 (zé wú páng dài)
history.meaning: one's official or moral duty admits of no shifting onto others
duty-bound, having an unshirkable obligation

morphemes.meaning: to shift onto others, excuse, loan

责无旁贷.notes: Here 贷 (dài) does not mean 'bank loan' (贷款), but retains its classical sense of 'to shift/pass off or pardon' (as in 严惩不贷 'punish severely without leniency'). Used in formal speeches or crisis pledges to declare that one is duty-bound to step up.

账.etymology: Phono-semantic character (形声字) with 贝 (trad. 貝, bèi, 'cowrie shell, money') as semantic radical and 长 (trad. 長, zhǎng/cháng) as phonetic. Originally written 帳 (zhàng, 'fabric canopy, curtain, scroll') with the cloth radical 巾, because Han and Tang officials recorded inventories and taxes on hanging cloth or paper scrolls (計帳); later scribes replaced 巾 with 貝 to create the dedicated financial character 賬 (simplified to 账) for 'account ledger, monetary record, bill, debt'.

history.meaning: curtain, canopy; scroll register used for household and tax records (計帳)
financial ledger, monetary account, debt, or bill (differentiated with 貝 radical)
account, bill, tab, debt, financial record

账.notes: Rich in idiomatic verb-object collocations: 结账/买单 ('pay the bill'), 算账 ('settle accounts / get even with someone'), 记账 ('keep books / put on a tab'), and 买账 ('buy into / show respect for someone's authority', e.g., 观众不买账 'the audience isn't buying it').

rootFamily.gloss: to pay the bill, settle an account
to settle accounts; to get even with someone

账户.etymology: Modifier-head compound (偏正结构) combining 账 (trad. 賬/帳戶, zhàng, 'financial record, monetary ledger') + 户 (hù, 'door; household, registered unit or client in an official register'). Originally denoting a household or merchant unit holding a separate page in a bank or treasury ledger, it expanded in the digital age to cover both bank accounts (银行账户) and online user accounts.

history.meaning: named client entry or unit in a banking or commercial ledger
bank account, financial account; digital user account

账户.notes: Compare 账户 (zhànghù) and 账号 (zhànghào): 账户 refers to the account itself as a repository of funds or user data (冻结银行账户 'freeze a bank account'), whereas 账号 refers specifically to the account number, handle, or login ID (社交媒体账号 'social media handle/account').

rootFamily.gloss: account number, login ID, social media handle
to open an account (at a bank or brokerage)

账本.etymology: Modifier-head noun compound combining 账 (賬/帳, 'financial account, credit/debt record', originally recorded on canopy/curtain scrolls 帳 and later differentiated with the shell/money radical 贝) + 本 ('bound notebook, register, volume').

history.meaning: account book, ledger

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 账本 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: items of an account, bookkeeping entries

账目.etymology: Modifier-head compound (偏正结构) formed from 账 (trad. 賬/帳, zhàng, 'financial ledger, monetary record') + 目 (mù, 'eye; itemized entry, category, list heading', by metaphorical extension from the meshes of a net or divisions on a list). Attested in imperial fiscal administration (originally written 帳目) for the itemized entries in an accounting book.

history.meaning: itemized entries in an official or commercial account register
itemized accounts, financial books and ledgers

morphemes.meaning: eye; itemized entry, heading, list item

账目.notes: Refers to the detailed entries inside accounting books rather than a single restaurant bill: 核对账目 ('audit/check the accounts'), 账目清楚 ('the books are in clear order'), 做假账 ('cook the books').

货车.etymology: Modifier-head noun compound combining 货 (貨, 'goods, commodities, freight') + 车 (車, 'wheeled vehicle, cart, wagon').

history.meaning: freight cart -> freight train car, goods truck/lorry, van

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 货车 (via 萌典)

质疑.etymology: Verb-object compound (动宾结构) from 质 (trad. 質, zhì, 'to confront, verify, put a question to, call to account'—derived from presenting a pawn/pledge for verification) + 疑 (yí, 'doubt, suspicion, unresolved question'). Attested in Classical Chinese (e.g., *Book of Han* 《漢書·陳遵傳》 and Tao Yuanming's 《移居》: 奇文共欣賞，疑義相與析 'appreciate rare writings together and resolve doubtful meanings') in the sense of 'to ask questions in order to resolve doubts'; in modern Mandarin it shifted toward a more confrontational sense: 'to call into question, challenge the validity or credibility of'.

history.meaning: to pose questions to an authority or peer in order to resolve doubts
to call into question, challenge, cast doubt on (someone's motives, ability, or authenticity)

质疑.notes: Stronger and more public than 怀疑 (huáiyí, 'to suspect/doubt inwardly'): 质疑 means overtly challenging or calling into question (网友质疑节目组黑幕 'netizens called into question shady dealings by the show's production team'). Often used as a noun in 提出质疑 ('raise a challenge/question').

rootFamily.gloss: to question closely, interrogate, demand an explanation

质量.etymology: Compound formed from 质 (trad. 質, zhì, 'fundamental substance, nature, inherent character') + 量 (liàng, 'measure, quantity, capacity, degree'). In physics, 質量 was coined in Meiji Japan (shitsuryō) to translate 'mass' (quantity of matter). In 20th-century Mainland Chinese, however, 质量 also developed as a modifier-head/coordinative compound meaning 'level or measure of inherent quality' (corresponding to 品質 pǐnzhì in Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Japanese).

history.meaning: physical mass (quantity of matter in a body)
history.stage: Meiji Japanese scientific coinage & Early Modern Chinese

history.meaning: quality (of a product, broadcast, or work); mass (in physics)

质量.notes: In Mainland Mandarin, 质量 means both 'quality' (节目质量很高 'the show's quality is very high', 睡眠质量 'sleep quality') and scientific 'mass'. Note the false friend with Japanese 質量 (shitsuryō), which ONLY means physical 'mass' (Japanese uses 品質 hinshitsu for 'quality').

贩子.etymology: Suffixed noun (附加式合成词) formed from the root 贩 (trad. 販, fàn, 'to buy cheap and sell dear; peddler, trader', composed of semantic 貝 'cowrie/money' + phonetic 反 fǎn) + the nominalizing suffix 子 (zi, neutral tone, marking an agent or occupational category, often with a colloquial or pejorative nuance). While 販 in Classical Chinese was neutral for a merchant who buys and resells (as in 商販), 贩子 in vernacular Mandarin took on a derogatory tone for hawkers, scalpers, or illicit traffickers.

history.meaning: to buy and resell goods; itinerant trader or peddler (as in 販夫)
peddler, hawker; (pejorative) illicit dealer, monger, trafficker

morphemes.meaning: to buy and resell, peddle, traffic in

贩子.notes: Almost always carries a negative or low-status connotation in modern compounds: 票贩子 ('ticket scalper', also called 黄牛), 人贩子 ('human trafficker'), 毒贩子 ('drug dealer'), and 战争贩子 ('warmonger'). For neutral 'small vendor', use 小商贩 or 摊贩.

贪小便宜.etymology: Verb-object idiomatic phrase (动宾短语) composed of 贪 (trad. 貪, tān, 'to covet, be greedy for', with 貝 'money/valuables' + 今 phonetic) + 小 (xiǎo, 'small, petty') + 便宜 (piányi, originally biànyí 'that which is convenient and advantageous', which shifted in vernacular Mandarin with neutral-tone yi to 'cheap price; petty unearned advantage'). Literally 'to covet small advantages or petty bargains'.

history.meaning: convenient and fitting action -> petty advantage or bargain price

history.form: 貪小便宜 / 贪小便宜 (tān xiǎopiányi)
history.meaning: to chase petty gains, seek small unearned perks, or cut corners for trivial savings

贪小便宜.notes: Pronounced tān xiǎopiányi (never biànyí here). Often paired in the cautionary proverb 贪小便宜吃大亏 (tān xiǎopiányi chī dàkuī, 'chasing petty gains leads to huge losses'—i.e., penny wise and pound foolish). In production or procurement, it describes cutting corners with cheap suppliers.

rootFamily.gloss: to take advantage of (someone); to get a bargain

贬低.etymology: Resultative/coordinative verb compound (动补/联合结构) combining 贬 (trad. 貶, biǎn, 'to diminish, demote in rank, censure', formed from 貝 'value/wealth' + 乏 fá 'lack, deficiency') + 低 (dī, 'low; to lower'). Literally 'to reduce in value/status so as to make low', extending the classical bureaucratic practice of demoting officials (貶官) and historiographical censure (褒貶 'praise and blame') to everyday psychological and rhetorical disparagement.

history.meaning: to diminish in value; to demote an official in rank; to censure in historiography
to belittle, disparage, devalue, or put down

morphemes.meaning: to diminish in value, demote, censure, disparage

贬低.notes: Its direct antonym is 抬高 (táigāo, 'to elevate/inflate') or 夸大 ('exaggerate'), and they frequently appear together in 抬高自己，贬低别人 ('build oneself up by putting others down'). Also compare 贬义 (biǎnyì, 'pejorative meaning') vs. 褒义 (bāoyì, 'approbative meaning').

rootFamily.gloss: to lose value, depreciate, devalue (of currency or assets)

购物清单.etymology: Modifier-head four-character compound (偏正结构) combining the verb-object compound 购物 (trad. 購物, gòuwù, 'to purchase goods', from 購 'to buy with cowries/money' + 物 'things, merchandise') + the modifier-head noun 清单 (trad. 清單, qīngdān, 'clear itemized list', originally a Qing dynasty bureaucratic and commercial term for an audited inventory or manifest). Literally 'an itemized list for purchasing goods'.

history.meaning: clear itemized inventory of goods, tax items, or gifts

history.form: 購物清單 / 购物清单 (gòuwù qīngdān)
history.meaning: shopping list, procurement checklist

购物清单.notes: While 购物清单 is the standard term for a consumer 'shopping list', 清单 alone is productive across corporate and media production settings: 任务清单 ('to-do/task list'), 设备清单 ('equipment manifest'), and 问题清单 ('list of issues to rectify').

贴.etymology: Phono-semantic character 贴 (貼), combining the cowrie/money radical 贝 (貝) + phonetic 占 (zhān / *tʰˤep), originally meaning 'to pledge as collateral, make up a deficit, subsidize', then 'to press close against, stick on, paste, glue'.

history.meaning: to pledge, compensate; to stick close, paste
to paste, stick on, press close to, subsidize; allowance

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 贴 (via 萌典)

贵.etymology: Ancient character 贵 (貴) showing two hands (臾) holding earth/basket or cowrie shells (貝, added in Zhou–Qin script), meaning 'of high value, costly, precious, noble; respectful prefix for your'.

history.meaning: high in rank or price, precious, noble
expensive, costly, precious; honorable (your)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 贵 (via 萌典)

贵姓.etymology: Polite honorific compound combining 贵 (貴, 'noble, honorable, your') + 姓 ('family name, surname'), used in the courteous inquiry 您贵姓？ ('What is your honorable surname?').

history.meaning: your honorable surname

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 贵姓 (via 萌典)

贵宾.etymology: Modifier-head compound (偏正结构) composed of 贵 (trad. 貴, guì, 'precious, high-ranking, noble', containing 貝 'cowrie/valuables') + 宾 (trad. 賓, bīn, 'honored guest, visitor', originally depicting a visitor under a roof 宀 receiving or presenting cowrie gifts 貝). Attested in Classical Chinese (e.g., *Book of Han*) for aristocratic or diplomatic visitors, and used in modern Mandarin as the standard equivalent of English 'VIP'.

history.meaning: high-ranking noble guest or diplomatic envoy
distinguished guest, VIP (in hospitality, aviation, and events)

贵宾.notes: Compare 贵宾 (guìbīn) and 嘉宾 (jiābīn): 贵宾 means 'VIP / dignitary' in hospitality and service (贵宾室 'VIP lounge', 贵宾卡 'VIP card'), whereas 嘉宾 ('honored guest') is the standard term for a guest star on a TV variety show or talk show (特邀嘉宾 'special guest star', 飞行嘉宾 'episode guest').

rootFamily.gloss: honored guest; guest star on a TV show or ceremony

费用.etymology: Coordinative compound (联合结构) formed from 费 (trad. 費, fèi, 'to expend, squander, consume wealth', with semantic 貝 'cowrie/money' + phonetic 弗 fú) + 用 (yòng, 'to use, employ; expenditure, outlay'). Attested in Classical Chinese (e.g., *Book of Han*, *Zizhi Tongjian*) both as a verb ('to expend resources') and as a noun ('expenditures, operating outlays'), and reinforced in modern accounting and legal usage for 'cost, fee, expenses'.

history.meaning: to expend wealth; material expenditures and fiscal outlays
cost, fee, expenses, charges (in budgeting and everyday life)

morphemes.meaning: to expend, spend; fee, cost, expense

费用.notes: More formal and comprehensive than the single character 费 (which attaches as a suffix to specific charges like 制作费 'production fee', 版权费 'copyright fee', 出场费 'appearance fee'). In production budgeting, 承担一切费用 ('cover all expenses') and 报销费用 ('reimburse expenses') are standard collocations.

cognates.meaning: rebel, traitor, bandit, pirate (as in 海賊 kaizoku)

贼.etymology: From Old Chinese *dzək (trad. 賊), an ideogrammic/phono-semantic compound combining 戈 (gē, 'dagger-axe, weapon') + 則 (zé, originally combining 貝 'cowrie/valuables' and 刀 'knife'). In Old Chinese (*Shijing*, *Zuo Zhuan*, *Mencius*), 賊 meant 'to injure, assassinate, destroy' or 'traitor, usurper, violent outlaw who harms the state or righteousness' (whereas 盜 dào meant 'stealer of property'). From the Six Dynasties through vernacular Mandarin, 賊 semantically shifted and merged with 盜 to become the everyday word for 'thief, burglar, sneak'.

history.meaning: to mutilate, assassinate, or ruin; violent traitor, rebel, or destroyer of virtue
bandit, rebel insurgent; thief or burglar
thief, burglar; (colloquial adjective)furtive, sly; (dialectal intensifier) extremely

morphemes.meaning: thief, burglar; traitor; sly, furtive; (colloquial) extremely

贼.notes: In modern colloquial Mandarin, beyond 'thief' (做贼心虚 'have a guilty conscience like a thief'), 贼 is used as an adjective meaning 'sly/shifty' (贼眉鼠眼) and in northern/colloquial speech as an adverbial intensifier meaning 'ridiculously / super' (贼好看 'super good-looking', 贼贵 'crazy expensive').

rootFamily.gloss: to have a guilty conscience (lit. act as a thief and feel weak at heart)
traitor to one's country (retaining the classical sense of 賊)

资助.etymology: Modifier-head / coordinative verb compound combining 资 (trad. 資, zī, 'wealth, provisions, material resources; to supply with funds', containing 貝 'cowrie/money' + 次 phonetic) + 助 (zhù, 'to assist, aid, lend strength'). Attested in Literary Chinese (e.g., *Book of Wei*, Tang–Song prose) for supplying someone with money or provisions to help them succeed, and used today for charitable funding, fellowships, or patronage.

history.meaning: to supply with provisions or funds in support of an endeavor
to fund, subsidize, or sponsor financially (especially students, scholars, or公益 causes)

资助.notes: Carefully distinguish 资助 (zīzhù) from 赞助 (zànzhù): 资助 implies charitable, educational, or philanthropic financial aid without expecting commercial publicity (资助贫困学生 'fund underprivileged students'), whereas 赞助 refers to commercial sponsorship in media and events (冠名赞助商 'title sponsor' of a TV show).

rootFamily.gloss: to subsidize, grant financial aid (especially to students)

资料.etymology: Compound of 资 (trad. 資, zī, 'resources, supplies, that on which one relies') + 料 (liào, 'measured grain; materials, ingredients, stuff'). In Tang–Song Literary Chinese, 資糧 / 資料 referred to material provisions, travel expenses, or raw supplies needed for daily life; in Meiji Japan, 資料 (shiryō) was repurposed for 'research materials, documentation, reference data', a sense re-borrowed into modern Chinese and extended in media production to archival footage and background files.

history.meaning: material provisions, livelihood supplies, or raw ingredients
reference materials, research data, dossier, archival footage (素材/资料片)
history.stage: Meiji Japanese return loan to Modern Mandarin

morphemes.meaning: resources, supplies, basis to rely upon

资料.notes: In television and film production (*Behind the Scenes*), 资料 refers both to background dossiers/research files (背景资料 'background dossier', 个人资料 'personal profile') and to archival video footage (资料片 'archival footage clip', 历史资料 'historical footage').

rootFamily.gloss: raw material; unedited footage or source material (in media)

资本.etymology: Modifier-head compound (偏正结构) combining 资 (trad. 資, zī, 'wealth, money, resources') + 本 (běn, 'tree root; foundation, principal sum of money'). Already used in Song–Ming mercantile Chinese (e.g., 資本/本錢) for a merchant's principal investment fund, it was adopted in Meiji Japan (資本, shihon) to translate European political economy's 'capital' (German *Kapital*, English *capital*, ultimately from Latin *caput* 'head') and returned to modern Chinese with full macroeconomic and figurative force.

history.meaning: merchant's principal sum of money or starting trade fund (本錢)
economic capital (as a factor of production); leverage or advantage one can trade on
history.stage: Meiji Japanese return loan to Modern Mandarin

资本.notes: In contemporary Mainland entertainment industry jargon, 资本 is constantly used as a personified collective noun for 'big financial backers / venture capital / media conglomerates' (资本进场 'big capital enters the market', 被资本裹挟 'hijacked by corporate backers'), as well as figuratively for personal leverage (年轻就是最大的资本 'youth is the greatest asset/capital').

cognates.meaning: qualifications, eligibility, legal capacity or status

资格.etymology: Coordinative/modifier-head compound formed from 资 (trad. 資, zī, 'natural endowment; accumulated seniority and service record, 資歷') + 格 (gé, 'wooden lattice/standard; official rank, statutory category, or qualifying standard'). Originating in Tang–Song civil service administration (資格) for the statutory seniority and rank thresholds required for promotion, it was broadened via Meiji Japanese (資格, shikaku) to cover formal qualifications, credentials, and the moral or legal right to do something.

history.meaning: statutory seniority and rank threshold required for official appointment or promotion
formal qualification, credential, eligibility; right or standing to speak/act

资格.notes: Used both for formal credentials/eligibility (取消参赛资格 'disqualify from a competition', 资格证书 'qualification certificate') and in heated interpersonal drama to challenge someone's standing: 你有什么资格批评我？ ('What right/standing do you have to criticize me?'). Also note 摆老资格 ('pull rank / flaunt one's seniority').

rootFamily.gloss: qualifications and record of service, seniority
exceptionally, bypassing normal rank/seniority rules (as in 破格录用)

资深.etymology: Subject-predicate compound (主谓结构) used attributively, composed of 资 (trad. 資, zī, 'accumulated seniority, length of service, 資歷') + 深 (shēn, 'deep, profound, long-standing'). Attested in imperial personnel evaluations (e.g., 資深望重 'deep in seniority and weighty in prestige') for officials with long service records, and revived in late 20th-century professional Mandarin (initially in Hong Kong and Taiwan corporate/media circles) as the polished equivalent of English 'senior, veteran, seasoned'.

history.meaning: possessing a long record of official service and seniority
senior, veteran, seasoned, experienced (of professionals or enthusiasts)

资深.notes: Primarily an attributive adjective placed before professional titles without needing 的: 资深制作人 ('veteran producer'), 资深媒体人 ('seasoned media professional'), or playfully 资深吃货 ('veteran foodie'). Its classical opposite in bureaucratic jargon is 资浅 (zīqiǎn, 'junior in seniority').

rootFamily.gloss: qualifications and record of service, seniority

资源.etymology: Modifier-head compound (偏正结构) combining 资 (trad. 資, zī, 'wealth, material supplies, that upon which production relies') + 源 (yuán, 'water spring, fountainhead, source'). Molded in modern East Asian economic vocabulary (alongside Japanese 資源, shigen) as a semantic counterpart to English *resources* (which itself comes from Old French *resourdre* 'to spring up again'), literally 'the fountainhead of productive wealth'.

history.meaning: natural, mineral, or economic resources of a nation
natural or human resources; (showbiz slang) industry connections, casting opportunities, and endorsements

资源.notes: In Chinese entertainment and media circles (*幕后之王*), 资源 has a specialized, high-frequency meaning: 'industry backing, casting opportunities, brand endorsements, and media slots'—hence 抢资源 ('fight over casting/sponsorship opportunities'), 顶级资源 ('top-tier industry backing'), and 资源咖 ('an actor pushed by powerful industry connections rather than popularity').

资讯.etymology: Coordinative compound (联合结构) formed from 资 (trad. 資, zī, 'reference data, materials', abbreviated from 資料 zīliào) + 讯 (trad. 訊, xùn, 'news, message, rapid dispatch', abbreviated from 訊息 xùnxī / 通訊 tōngxùn). Coined in late 20th-century Hong Kong and Taiwan Chinese to render English *information* (as in 資訊科技 'information technology, IT'), it subsequently entered Mainland Mandarin with a more specialized media nuance: 'curated news, industry updates, and actionable information'.

history.meaning: information, data (standard translation of 'information' in HK/Taiwan, e.g. IT)
news updates, media/industry briefings, and timely information (in Mainland Mandarin)

morphemes.meaning: message, news dispatch, rapid communication (from 讯息)

资讯.notes: Regional nuance: in Taiwan and Hong Kong, 资讯 is the general word for 'information / IT' (where Mainland China uses 信息, xìnxī, as in 信息技术). In Mainland media and showbiz, however, 资讯 specifically means 'timely news updates, industry feeds, or lifestyle/entertainment briefings' (娱乐资讯 'entertainment news updates', 时尚资讯 'fashion updates').

资质.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative nominal compound (資質) uniting 资 (trad. 資, zī, 'endowment, resources, innate capability', originally cowrie shells 貝 with phonetic 次 cì) and 质 (trad. 質, zhì, 'substance, basic nature, disposition'). Attested since the Han and Six Dynasties periods (e.g., *Book of Han* and *Records of the Three Kingdoms*) in the sense of 'innate constitution and character', it later broadened in modern administrative and commercial usage to include formal 'corporate qualifications and credentials'.

history.meaning: innate disposition, natural endowment, and physical or moral character
natural caliber or talent; institutional or professional qualifications and credentials

资质.notes: Has two distinct register uses in modern Mandarin: describing a person's innate talent/aptitude (e.g. 资质平平 'of mediocre talent') and describing a company's or practitioner's official licensing/credentials (e.g. 营业资质 'operating qualifications').

赐给.etymology: A verb-complement compound formed from the Classical Chinese verb 赐 (trad. 賜, cì, 'to bestow, confer from a superior to an inferior', composed of the cowrie/wealth radical 貝 and phonetic 易 yì) followed by the dative/recipient complement 给 (trad. 給, gěi, 'to give, to/for', originally 'to supply amply' in Silk 糸 + 合 hé). As vernacular Mandarin replaced classical monosyllabic verbs with disyllabic verb-recipient structures, 赐给 became the standard elevated form for a sovereign, deity, or revered figure granting something to a recipient.

history.meaning: (of a ruler, elder, or heaven) to bestow a gift, favor, or reward upon an inferior
to bestow upon, grant to (used in religious, ceremonial, or ironic elevated contexts)

morphemes.meaning: to, unto (recipient marker / verb of giving)

赐给.notes: Strictly downward in social or cosmic hierarchy (Heaven/God bestowing blessings, or a monarch granting titles); in everyday speech it is used either poetically (上天赐给的礼物 'a gift bestowed by Heaven') or with playful irony.

rootFamily.gloss: to graciously bestow; a favor from above
please instruct me (humble request for advice)

赔偿.etymology: A coordinative verbal and nominal compound (賠償) pairing 赔 (trad. 賠, péi, 'to make good a loss, stand a financial loss', formed from the wealth radical 貝 and phonetic 咅 pǒu) with 偿 (trad. 償, cháng, 'to repay, restore, make restitution', formed from the person radical 亻 and phonetic 賞 shǎng). While 償 is ancient in Classical Chinese legal and moral texts, 賠 emerged in Tang–Song vernacular legal and commercial language, and the disyllabic compound 賠償 stabilized in late imperial law before also serving as the equivalent of Western legal 'damages/indemnity' in the 19th century.

history.meaning: to repay a debt, make restitution, requite value for value
to make good a loss, restore damaged property or money
to compensate, indemnify, pay legal or contractual damages

morphemes.meaning: make good a loss, compensate financially

赔偿.notes: Standard legal and contractual term for financial restitution when one party causes loss or breaches a contract (e.g. 要求赔偿 'demand compensation', 违约赔偿 'breach-of-contract damages').

rootFamily.gloss: to lose money in business; to apologize/compensate
to compensate, reimburse (often state or institutional)

赔偿金.etymology: A modifier-head trimorphemic legal compound (賠償金) consisting of the coordinative verb-noun stem 赔偿 (trad. 賠償, péicháng, 'compensation, indemnification') modifying the head noun 金 (jīn, 'metal, gold; monetary sum, fund'). This formation `[Disyllabic Action/Legal Concept] + 金` was popularized during the late Qing and Meiji modernization of East Asian civil and international law (cf. Japanese *baishōkin* 賠償金) to denote a specific monetary sum awarded or paid as damages.

history.meaning: monetary sum paid as legal damages, contractual indemnity, or war reparations
history.stage: Late Qing / Modern Legal Mandarin (19th–20th c.)

赔偿金.notes: In media and entertainment contracts (as in *Behind the Scenes*), 赔偿金 often appears alongside 违约金 ('liquidated damages for breach of contract') when talent or production companies break agreements.

rootFamily.gloss: liquidated damages for breach of contract

cognates.meaning: to apologize, make amends for an offense

赔罪.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound (賠罪) formed from 赔 (trad. 賠, péi, 'to make amends for, offer restitution') and 罪 (zuì, 'offense, fault, blame, transgression'). Originating in Song–Yuan–Ming vernacular literature (such as *Water Margin* and *Dream of the Red Chamber*), the metaphor extends financial restitution (賠, making good a deficit) into interpersonal etiquette: one 'pays back' or 'makes restitution for' the offense (罪) one has committed by offering an apology, gift, or toast.

history.meaning: to make amends for an offense, offer a formal apology to appease someone wronged
to apologize, make amends (often accompanied by a gesture like a meal, drink, or gift)

赔罪.notes: As a separable verb-object (离合词) compound, modifiers are frequently inserted between the two characters, as in 赔个罪 ('offer a quick apology') or 向你赔罪 ('apologize to you'), often while treating someone to dinner or drinks to smooth things over.

rootFamily.gloss: to apologize with a smile or polite deference
to offer an apology, make amends (variant: 赔礼)

赚.etymology: A phono-semantic compound (trad. 賺, zhuàn; also read zuàn in the sense 'to deceive/hoax') composed of the semantic radical 貝 (bèi, 'cowrie shell, money, trade') and the phonetic component 兼 (jiān). Emerging in post-classical vernacular Chinese (Tang–Song–Yuan mercantile and theatrical texts), the character initially meant 'to sell at an advantage or trick in a transaction' before bifurcating into two pronunciations and senses: *zhuàn* ('to earn a profit, make money', replacing classical 獲利/贏利 in spoken Mandarin) and *zuàn* ('to gull, trick').

history.meaning: to gain profit in trade; (read zuàn) to trick or inveigle in a transaction
to earn (money), make a profit, gain

morphemes.meaning: earn, profit, gain financially (semantic 貝 wealth + phonetic 兼)

赚.notes: Its direct antonym in business and everyday speech is 赔 (péi) or 亏 (kuī, 'to lose money'); in colloquial speech, 赚了! means 'What a bargain! / Came out ahead!'.

rootFamily.gloss: to make money, earn a living
to earn a great deal (of money, ratings, or tears); to make a killing
to earn (audience tears, profit); to pull in

cognates.meaning: to earn money, make a profit

赚钱.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound (賺錢) combining the vernacular commercial verb 赚 (trad. 賺, zhuàn, 'to earn, gain profit') with the object noun 钱 (trad. 錢, qián, originally an ancient agricultural spade implement cast in bronze with radical 金 and phonetic 戔 jiān, which became early Chinese spade coinage and subsequently the general word for 'copper cash, money'). Attested from Ming–Qing vernacular fiction onward, it is the primary spoken Mandarin expression for generating income or commercial profit.

history.meaning: to gain copper cash or silver profit through trade or labor
to make money, earn an income, be profitable

赚钱.notes: Functions both as a separable verb-object phrase (e.g. 赚大钱 'make big money', 赚了不少钱 'earned quite a bit of money') and as an adjectival predicate meaning 'profitable, lucrative' (这个项目很赚钱 'this project is very lucrative').

赞.etymology: In simplified Chinese, 赞 merges two related Classical characters: 贊 (zàn, originally 'to come forward with tribute/gifts 貝 to assist or introduce someone before a ruler', from 兟 'to advance' + 貝 'valuables') and 讚 (zàn, with the speech radical 言 added to specify 'to praise, eulogize in words'). From 'verbal praise and commendation', it developed into a colloquial southern/Taiwanese and pan-Chinese stative adjective ('awesome, praiseworthy') in the late 20th century, and in the 2000s–2010s was adopted by Chinese social media platforms (Facebook, Weibo, WeChat) as the standard noun and verb for an online 'like' or 'thumbs-up'.

history.meaning: to assist at court ceremonies; to praise, commend, compose a eulogy
to praise, approve; (colloquial adjective) great, awesome
(noun/verb) a 'like' or 'thumbs-up' on social media; praise, approval

morphemes.meaning: praise, commend; social-media 'like' (merging 贊 assist/present and 讚 eulogize)

赞.notes: In social media and showbiz contexts, 赞 as a countable noun takes the classifier 个 and routinely collocates with 点 ('click/tap'): 点赞 ('to give a like') or 集赞 ('to collect likes').

rootFamily.gloss: to give a like (on social media); to express approval
to sponsor financially (e.g. a TV show); commercial sponsorship

cognates.meaning: to present a gift, confer, bestow
to present as a gift, dedicate

赠给.etymology: A verb-complement compound (贈給) built from the Classical Chinese verb 赠 (trad. 贈, zèng, 'to present a parting gift, bestow a valuable present', composed of the wealth/cowrie radical 貝 and phonetic 曾 zēng) followed by the recipient marker/complement 给 (trad. 給, gěi, 'to give to, unto'). In Old and Middle Chinese (e.g., *Book of Odes*), 贈 denoted presenting jade, horses, or poems to a departing friend or dignitary; adding the vernacular complement 给 creates a formal modern transitive verb taking a direct recipient.

history.meaning: to present valuables or verses as a gift (especially upon parting) or posthumous honorific title
to present as a gift to, donate or dedicate to (a person or institution)

morphemes.meaning: to, unto (recipient marker / verb of giving)

赠给.notes: More formal and respectful than 送给 (sònggěi), making it common in ceremonial presentations, book dedications, and high-level corporate or diplomatic gift-giving.

rootFamily.gloss: to present as a gift, give formally
complimentary gift, freebie included with purchase

赢.etymology: Complex character 赢 (贏), built with the cowrie/wealth radical 贝 (貝, amid 亡, 口, 月, 凡), originally meaning 'to have a surplus of profit in trade', hence 'to win, triumph, beat'.

history.meaning: mercantile profit, surplus -> to win
to win, beat, triumph

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 赢 (via 萌典)

走.etymology: Oracle-bone and bronze ideograph 走 depicting a person swinging their arms above a foot (止), originally meaning 'to run, flee swiftly' in Classical Chinese, before shifting in Tang–Modern Mandarin to 'to walk, go, leave, move'.

history.meaning: to run, hurry, flee
to walk, go, leave, move

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 走 (via 萌典)

走不了路.etymology: Four-character separable verb potential phrase formed by inserting the negative potential infix 不了 (*bùliǎo*, 'unable to carry out') inside the verb-object compound 走路 ('walk on a road; walk'). Expresses physical inability to walk, as after spraining an ankle.

history.meaning: unable to walk

走台.etymology: A verb-object (VO) theatrical and production compound (走台, trad. 走臺) combining 走 (zǒu, 'to walk, pace through', which shifted from Old Chinese 'to run' to Middle/Modern Chinese 'to walk, move along a course') and 台 (trad. 臺, tái, 'raised platform, theatrical stage'). Originating in traditional Chinese opera (戏曲) jargon—where actors paced out their stage entrances, movements, and positions—it was adopted into modern television, concert, and fashion-show production to mean 'blocking rehearsal / stage walkthrough'.

history.meaning: (in traditional Chinese opera) for actors to walk through their stage movements and positions
to rehearse stage blocking, lighting marks, and camera positions (or walk a fashion runway)

走台.notes: Essential TV and live-event production jargon in *Behind the Scenes* (幕后之王): before a full dress rehearsal (彩排), performers and directors do a 走台 to check stage marks, camera angles, mic cues, and lighting transitions.

rootFamily.gloss: to step onto the stage, appear in a performance

走向.etymology: A verb-complement (and nominalized) compound (走向) formed from 走 (zǒu, 'to walk, move, proceed', from Old Chinese 'to run') and the directional/prepositional complement 向 (xiàng, 'facing, toward, direction', originally depicting a north-facing window in a house 宀 + 口). As a verbal phrase it means 'to walk/move toward' (both physically and figuratively, as in 'moving toward maturity/internationalization'); as a derived noun it means 'trajectory, trend, or narrative direction'.

history.meaning: to walk toward, head in the direction of (a physical place)
(verb) to head toward, advance into (a state or stage); (noun) trend, trajectory, plot direction

走向.notes: Used both as a transitive verb taking abstract goals (走向世界 'go global', 走向成功 'head toward success') and as a noun in media/finance (剧情走向 'plot trajectory', 市场走向 'market trend').

走廊.etymology: Modifier-head architectural compound combining 走 ('to walk') + 廊 ('roofed veranda, colonnade, gallery flanking a courtyard', shelter radical 广 + phonetic 郎 láng).

history.meaning: covered walkway, veranda, corridor, hallway

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 走廊 (via 萌典)

走心.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound turned stative adjective (走心) composed of 走 (zǒu, 'to pass through, travel via, engage') and 心 (xīn, 'heart, mind, emotional core'). Historically in northern Mandarin dialects, 走心 could mean 'for the mind to wander, be absent-minded'; however, in 21st-century media, advertising, and artistic criticism, it underwent a semantic reanalysis based on the conduit sense of 走 ('to pass through/enter into', cf. 走脑子 'use one's brain'): something that 'passes right into the heart' or is created by 'channeling one's genuine heart and soul'.

history.meaning: (regional/older) to let one's mind wander, lose focus; to take something to heart
heartfelt, emotionally resonant, thoughtfully crafted with genuine care and emotional investment

走心.notes: A ubiquitous praise word in contemporary Chinese TV, music, and advertising (e.g. 走心的表演 'a heartfelt performance', 走心的设计 'a thoughtful, emotionally resonant design'), contrasting with 敷衍 ('perfunctory, phoning it in').

rootFamily.gloss: attentive, diligent, putting one's mind to something
heart-piercing, deeply moving or emotionally devastating

走漏.etymology: A coordinative/resultative verbal compound (走漏) combining 走 (zǒu, 'to escape, let slip, leak out', derived from its ancient sense 'to run away, flee', as in 走气 'lose gas/flavor') and 漏 (lòu, 'to drip through, seep, leak', formed from the water radical 氵 and 屚, depicting rainwater dripping through a roof 尸 + 雨). Attested in Song–Yuan–Ming vernacular novels and official dispatches, it describes confidential news, secrets, or fugitives slipping through containment.

history.meaning: to let a secret, rumor, or fugitive slip out and escape containment
to leak out inadvertently, divulge (confidential news or plans)

走漏.notes: Almost always collocates with 風聲 / 风声 ('wind-sound', i.e. rumor/wind of a plan) or 消息 ('news/information'), as in 走漏风声 ('let wind of a secret leak out').

rootFamily.gloss: to accidentally let slip in speech (a Freudian slip or secret)

走着.etymology: A verb-aspect construction consisting of the verb 走 (zǒu, 'to walk, go on foot; to move along', which evolved from Old Chinese 'to run/flee' to Middle and Modern Mandarin 'to walk') followed by the durative/progressive aspect particle 着 (zhe, grammatically bleached from Middle Chinese 著 zhuó/zháo, 'to attach, adhere, remain in contact'). Together, 走着 expresses an ongoing manner or continuous state of walking ('on foot / while walking') or continuing along a path ('as we go along').

history.meaning: walking continuously; proceeding on foot
walking, on foot (as manner modifier: 走着去 'go on foot'); continuing to move along

morphemes.meaning: walk, go on foot, move along
durative aspect marker (indicating an ongoing action or manner)

走着.notes: Commonly used before another motion verb to specify going on foot (e.g. 我们走着去吧 'Let's walk there'), or in the famous colloquial idiom 走着瞧 ('We'll see as we go along / Wait and see!').

rootFamily.gloss: wait and see! (lit. 'look as we walk along')

走路.etymology: Verb-object compound combining 走 ('to walk') + 路 ('road, way'), functioning as the standard intransitive verb phrase for 'to walk, go on foot'.

history.meaning: to walk, travel on foot

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 走路 (via 萌典)

走过.etymology: Verb-complement compound combining 走 ('to walk') + directional/experiential complement 过 (過, 'past, across, through').

history.meaning: to walk past, walk through

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 走过 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to proceed to, go to (a post or place) + promise/appointment
to go to keep an appointment or treaty

赴约.etymology: A Literary Chinese verb-object (VO) compound (赴約) composed of 赴 (fù, 'to go toward, attend, hurry to a destination', formed from the running/walking radical 走 and phonetic 卜 bǔ, originally meaning 'to hasten to report or attend') and 约 (trad. 約, yuē, 'appointment, pact, prior agreement', originally 'to bind with cord 糸'). Retaining an elevated, slightly literary flavor in modern Mandarin, it specifically denotes going to a pre-arranged meeting, romantic date, or formal engagement.

history.meaning: to proceed to a pledged meeting, covenant, or rendezvous at the appointed time
to keep an appointment, show up for a scheduled meeting or date

morphemes.meaning: go to attend, repair to, betake oneself to

赴约.notes: More formal and stylistically polished than 去约会; frequently used in written narratives and polite speech (e.g. 准时赴约 'arrive on time for the appointment', 爽约 'fail to show up for an appointment').

rootFamily.gloss: appointment, date; to make or go on a date
to attend a banquet or formal dinner
to go all out, spare no effort (lit. 'go with all one's strength')

cognates.meaning: to rush, hurry, drive away, catch in time

赶.etymology: A phono-semantic character (trad. 趕, simplified 赶, gǎn) combining the semantic radical 走 (zǒu, 'to run, pursue swiftly') with the phonetic 旱 (hàn; simplified to 干 gān). In early lexicography (*Shuowen Jiezi*), 趕 meant 'to run with a raised tail', which developed in Middle and Early Mandarin into 'to pursue, chase after, drive (livestock or people) away', and by further extension 'to hurry toward a target, rush against time, or try to catch (a vehicle, deadline, or occasion)'.

history.meaning: to run swiftly; to chase, pursue, or drive away
to chase after; to hurry toward, rush to meet a time or event
to rush to catch (transport/deadlines), hurry; (adj.) pressed for time; to drive away

morphemes.meaning: rush, hurry, chase after, catch in time (semantic 走 run + phonetic 干/旱)

赶.notes: Extremely versatile in modern Mandarin: as a transitive verb it takes vehicles, schedules, or deadlines (赶时间 'rush against the clock', 赶进度 'rush to meet project progress'); as a stative adjective it means 'in a rush / pressed for time' (时间很赶 'the schedule is very tight').

rootFamily.gloss: to catch up with, make it in time for
to rush work against a deadline

赶上.etymology: A verb-resultative complement (动补) compound (趕上) combining the verb 赶 (trad. 趕, gǎn, 'to chase after, hurry toward') with the directional/resultative complement 上 (shàng, 'up to, reaching contact or completion of a goal'). The complement 上 indicates that the pursuit has successfully reached its moving target—hence its three interconnected senses: (1) physically or competitively catching up with someone ahead, (2) making it in time for a scheduled event or vehicle, and (3) happening to coincide with a particular era or situation.

history.meaning: to overtake or catch up with someone or something moving ahead
to catch up with; to make it in time for (a train, event); to happen to encounter (an occasion or circumstance)

morphemes.meaning: pursue, hurry toward, rush to catch
up to, reaching successful contact or attainment

赶上.notes: Frequently takes the potential infixes 得 (gǎndeshàng 'able to make it in time / catch up') and 不 (gǎnbushàng 'unable to make it in time / can't keep up with').

rootFamily.gloss: to catch up with, overtake (by chasing)
to keep up with (a pace, trend, or person)

赶出来.etymology: A verb plus compound directional/resultative complement construction (趕出來) built from 赶 (trad. 趕, gǎn, in two distinct senses: 'to rush to produce against a deadline' or 'to drive out/expel') and the directional-resultative complement 出来 (trad. 出來, chūlái, literally 'come out', grammaticalized to mean 'into existence / to completion through effort'). In media, writing, and production contexts, 赶出来 means 'to rush-produce or crank out a finished work (a script, cut, or proposal) before a deadline'.

history.meaning: to drive or expel someone/something out; to rush to produce something into finished existence

morphemes.meaning: rush to produce against time (or drive out)

赶出来.notes: In workplace and TV production dialogue (e.g. 今晚必须把方案赶出来 'We must rush this proposal out tonight'), 出来 marks the successful creation of a tangible output under time pressure; note that in another context 把他赶出来 means 'kick/drive him out'.

rootFamily.gloss: to rush work against a deadline
to rush to produce or manufacture (goods, episodes)
to produce, make, work out (a finished product)

cognates.meaning: to rush work against a deadline
to rush work against a deadline

赶工.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound (趕工) pairing 赶 (trad. 趕, gǎn, 'to hurry, rush against a schedule') with 工 (gōng, originally depicting a carpenter's square or rammer tool, meaning 'craftsman's work, labor, project schedule'). Developed in modern industrial, construction, and media-production vocabulary, it denotes accelerating labor or working overtime to meet a tight project deadline.

history.meaning: to rush work, accelerate production or labor to meet a deadline

赶工.notes: A staple term in film/TV post-production, construction, and manufacturing when teams pull all-nighters to meet a broadcast or delivery date (e.g. 连夜赶工 'rush work through the night').

rootFamily.gloss: to rush to manufacture or produce (e.g. props, edits)
to work overtime, pull extra hours
to start work or filming; construction/production begins
