赶快.etymology: A verb-complement / coordinative adverbial compound (趕快) composed of 赶 (trad. 趕, gǎn, 'to hurry, hasten') and 快 (kuài, 'fast, quick, rapid', originally 'pleased/gratified in heart 忄' in Classical Chinese before shifting in Tang–Song vernacular to 'sharp' and then 'quick, speedy'). By combining the action of hastening (赶) with the state of speed (快), the compound grammaticalized in Mandarin into a high-frequency adverb meaning 'quickly, right away, without delay'.

history.meaning: to hasten one's pace, hurry up; (adverb) quickly, forthwith
(adverb) quickly, right away, hurry up and (do something)

赶快.notes: Nearly synonymous with 赶紧 (gǎnjǐn), mostly used in imperative or urgent suggestions (e.g. 赶快走吧! 'Let's hurry up and go!'); unlike 快, 赶快 cannot be modified by degree adverbs like 很 (*很赶快 is ungrammatical).

rootFamily.gloss: hurry up and, right away, lose no time in
hastily, in a hurry, right away

赶着.etymology: A verb-aspect construction (趕著, simplified 赶着) formed from the verb 赶 (trad. 趕, gǎn, 'to hurry, rush to do, or avail oneself of a timely moment') and the durative/accompanying aspect marker 着 (zhe). In Mandarin syntax, `赶着 + VP` means 'to be in the midst of hurrying to do [VP]' (e.g., 赶着去开会 'hurrying off to a meeting'), or before a time/condition phrase, 'taking advantage of while a condition holds' (similar to 趁着).

history.meaning: driving (livestock/carts); hurrying along or rushing to do something; availing oneself of a time window
to be in a hurry to (do something); rushing to

morphemes.meaning: hurry, rush to catch or accomplish
durative/accompanying aspect marker (in the state of rushing)

赶着.notes: Typically followed immediately by another verb phrase indicating the urgent destination or task: 我正赶着写稿子呢 ('I'm right in the middle of rushing to finish a script/draft') or 赶着去机场 ('hurrying to the airport').

rootFamily.gloss: in a rush, pressed for time

赶紧.etymology: A verb-complement / coordinative adverbial compound (趕緊) combining 赶 (trad. 趕, gǎn, 'to hurry, hasten, press forward') and 紧 (trad. 緊, jǐn, 'taut, tight, urgent, pressing', originally 'tightly spun or bound silk cord' with 糸 and 臤). Literally 'to press urgently / pull tight the pace', 赶紧 grammaticalized in Mandarin into an urgent pre-verbal adverb meaning 'lose no time in, hurry up and, right away'.

history.meaning: to press on urgently without slackening; (adverb) hurriedly, at once
(adverb) hurry up and, right away, without delay

赶紧.notes: Very close to 赶快, but 赶紧 carries a slightly stronger nuance of 'seizing the moment before it's too late / without any slack' (e.g. 趁热赶紧吃 'Hurry and eat it while it's hot') and can be used both in imperatives and in past-tense narratives ('he hurriedly did X').

rootFamily.gloss: to seize the time/opportunity, step up efforts without slacking off

赶飞机.etymology: A modern verb-object (VO) phrase (趕飛機) uniting the verb 赶 (trad. 趕, gǎn, 'to rush to catch a scheduled transport') with the disyllabic noun 飞机 (trad. 飛機, fēijī, 'airplane, aircraft', a late-19th/early-20th-century Sino-Japanese compound from 飛 fēi 'to fly' + 機 jī 'machine, mechanism, contrivance'). It exemplifies the productive Mandarin pattern `赶 + [scheduled vehicle]` (cf. 赶火车 'catch a train', 赶末班车 'catch the last bus').

history.meaning: to hurry to the airport to catch a scheduled flight

赶飞机.notes: Contrast 坐飞机 ('to travel by plane / take a flight' neutrally) with 赶飞机 ('to rush to catch a flight', emphasizing the time pressure of getting to the airport before boarding closes).

rootFamily.gloss: to rush to catch a train
to catch the last bus/train (or figuratively, the last chance)

起.etymology: Phono-semantic/associative character 起, combining 走 ('to walk, move') + phonetic 己 (jǐ / 巳), meaning 'to rise from a kneeling or seated position, stand up, get up, start, originate; upward directional complement'.

history.meaning: to rise up, stand up, begin
to get up, rise, start; upward/inchoative complement

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 起 (via 萌典)

起到.etymology: A verb-resultative complement (动补) compound formed from 起 (qǐ, 'to rise, initiate, generate, exert [an effect]', originally composed of 走 'to run/move' and 己 jǐ, meaning 'to rise from a seated or kneeling posture') and the resultative attainment complement 到 (dào, 'to arrive at, reach, achieve'). While monosyllabic 起 can govern abstract nouns like 作用 ('role/effect') or 效果 ('result'), adding the resultative 到 specifies that the action or factor successfully achieves and delivers that effect.

history.meaning: to successfully exert (an influence), play (a role), or achieve (an effect)
history.stage: Modern Mandarin (20th–21st c. formal & media prose)

morphemes.meaning: rise, generate, exert (an effect or function)

起到.notes: Almost exclusively takes abstract nouns denoting function, role, or impact as its object—most famously 起到…的作用 ('play the role of...') and 起到…的效果 ('achieve the effect of...').

rootFamily.gloss: to play a role, have an effect, take effect
to reach, achieve, attain (a goal or standard)
to trigger, give rise to, cause

起哄.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound (起鬨, simplified 起哄) composed of the inchoative verb 起 (qǐ, 'to raise, stir up, start') and the noun 哄 (trad. 鬨, hòng, 'clamor, uproar, boisterous crowd noise', originally depicting two men or crowds contending 鬥 with phonetic 共 gòng). Originating in Beijing and northern Mandarin colloquial speech during the Qing dynasty, it describes a crowd stirring up noisy commotion, jeering, or playfully egging people on for amusement.

history.meaning: to stir up a noisy crowd commotion, jeer, or create an uproar together
to egg someone on noisily (e.g. chanting for a couple to kiss or a performer to do an encore), heckle, or join in a boisterous commotion

morphemes.meaning: crowd clamor, uproar, boisterous jeering (trad. 鬨)

起哄.notes: Read *qǐhòng* (fourth tone on 哄, representing traditional 鬨 'crowd uproar', distinct from *hǒng* 'to coax' and *hōng* 'roar of laughter'); very common at parties, live shows, and studio tapings when onlookers chant 在一起! ('Get together!') or 亲一个! ('Kiss!') to tease people, e.g. 别跟着起哄 ('Don't join in egging them on').

rootFamily.gloss: a whole crowd roaring with laughter together (hōng堂大笑)
to disperse in an uproar (of a crowd) (一hòng而散)
to coax, appease, or trick someone (hǒng)

cognates.meaning: getting out of bed, rising from sleep (also historical geological 'upheaval of strata')
getting out of bed, reveille, rising

起床.etymology: A verb-location/source compound (起床) formed from 起 (qǐ, 'to rise, get up from a lying or seated posture') and 床 (chuáng, variant 牀, 'bed, couch', originally depicting a wooden frame 爿/片 on which a person rests). Attested in medieval Chinese poetry and vernacular texts (Tang–Song onwards, where classical 夙興/起身 were joined by 起床), it functions in modern Mandarin as the standard separable verb (离合词) for getting out of bed after sleeping.

history.meaning: to rise from one's bed or couch after sleep or illness
to get out of bed, get up in the morning

起床.notes: Because 起床 is a separable verb-object construction (离合词), aspect markers and complements go between the two characters (e.g. 起不了床 'can't get out of bed', 起了床 'got out of bed'); also spawns the popular modern slang 起床气 ('grumpiness upon waking up').

rootFamily.gloss: grumpiness or irritability right after waking up
to get into bed, go to bed
to get up, rise (from sitting/lying), or set out on a journey

起来.etymology: Compound directional and aspectual verb (and post-verbal complement) combining 起 ('to rise, start') + 来 (來, 'hither, toward the speaker'), meaning 'to stand/get up' and, after verbs or adjectives, marking upward motion or the beginning of a state/action.

history.meaning: to get up, stand up; inchoative/upward complement

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 起来 (via 萌典)

起色.etymology: Originally a verb-object compound turned abstract noun (起色) combining 起 (qǐ, 'to rise, revive, begin to appear') and 色 (sè, 'facial complexion, color, visible vitality'). In traditional Chinese medical and physiognomic contexts, when a patient recovering from illness regained healthy color and vitality in their face (氣色/面色), their complexion 'rose/revived' (起色); by the Ming–Qing period, this nominalized to mean 'visible signs of recovery, improvement, or upturn' in health, business, ratings, or career.

history.meaning: recovery of healthy facial complexion and vitality after illness or distress; initial sign of improvement
signs of improvement, recovery, or positive turnaround (in health, work, ratings, or business)

起色.notes: Almost always used with 有 ('have') or 没有/毫无 ('lack') to describe whether a struggling project, show's ratings, or patient's condition is turning around: 节目收视率终于有了起色 ('The show's ratings are finally showing signs of improvement').

rootFamily.gloss: facial complexion and vitality; look of health or fortune
color, hue; facial expression or quality
outstanding, remarkable, splendid (lit. 'standing out in color')

cognates.meaning: to draft (a bill, constitution, contract, or document)
drafting a document or bill; to draft
to draft, draw up a preliminary text

起草.etymology: A Classical Chinese verb-object (VO) compound (起草) composed of 起 (qǐ, 'to initiate, start, originate') and 草 (cǎo, originally 'grass, plants', which in Han–Jin chancellery and calligraphic usage came to mean 'cursive script 草書' written rapidly and hence a 'rough preliminary draft 草稿' of an imperial edict or memorial). Attested since the Six Dynasties and Tang imperial secretariat, 起草 literally means 'to initiate the rough draft' and remains the standard formal term for drafting laws, contracts, speeches, or proposals.

history.meaning: to write up the preliminary draft of an imperial edict, memorial, or literary composition
to draft, draw up (a contract, law, treaty, speech, or official document)
history.stage: Modern Mandarin (shared across Sino-Japanese legal/administrative usage)

起草.notes: Used specifically for formal or official texts such as contracts (起草合同), legislation (起草法案), and official statements (起草声明), rather than casual creative writing.

rootFamily.gloss: rough draft, preliminary manuscript or sketch
draft bill, draft contract, or draft resolution
to draft, draw up (an official document or plan)

cognates.meaning: indictment, prosecution, bringing a legal action
to prosecute, indict, institute legal proceedings

起诉.etymology: A verb-object (VO) legal compound (起訴) composed of 起 (qǐ, 'to initiate, raise, institute') and 诉 (trad. 訴, sù, 'to accuse, lay a complaint, appeal to a magistrate', formed from the speech radical 言 and phonetic 斥 chì). While both characters are ancient in Chinese legal history, the compound 起訴 was standardized in late-19th-century Meiji Japanese jurisprudence (translating German *Anklage erheben* / *Klage erheben*, 'to institute legal proceedings') and adopted into modern Chinese civil and criminal procedure law.

history.meaning: to lodge a grievance or accusation before a magistrate or sovereign
to file a lawsuit (in civil court) or bring an indictment/prosecution (in criminal court)
history.stage: Late Qing / Modern East Asian Legal Mandarin

起诉.notes: In mainland Chinese usage, 起诉 covers both civil lawsuits ('to sue someone', e.g. 起诉违约方 'sue the breaching party') and criminal prosecution by the procuratorate (提起公诉); its antonym when dropping a case is 撤诉 ('withdraw a lawsuit').

rootFamily.gloss: to appeal a court verdict to a higher court
to withdraw a lawsuit; to lose/win a lawsuit (败诉/胜诉)

起雾.etymology: Separable verb-object compound of 起 ('rise; form; spring up') + 雾 ('fog; mist', rain radical 雨 + phonetic 务 wù). Used both for morning mist rising over a river or courtyard and for eyeglasses or windowpanes steaming up from warm tea.

history.meaning: fog rises; mist forms
fog up; mist over

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 起雾

趁.etymology: Phono-semantic character 趁, combining 走 ('to run, pursue') + phonetic 㐱 (zhěn), shifting from 'to chase after, follow closely' to 'to avail oneself of an opportunity, while (a condition holds)'.

history.meaning: to pursue, follow upon -> to take advantage of
while, taking advantage of (an opportunity or time)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 趁 (via 萌典)

趁热.etymology: Prepositional/adverbial phrase combining 趁 ('while, taking advantage of') + 热 (熱, 'hot, warm'), as in eating food or striking iron while it is still hot.

history.meaning: while it is still hot

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 趁热 (via 萌典)

趁着.etymology: A prepositional/conjunctive compound formed from 趁 (chèn, 'to avail oneself of an opportunity, take advantage of a favorable time or condition', originally a phono-semantic character with the running radical 走 and phonetic 㐱 zhěn meaning 'to follow closely behind, pursue') plus the durative aspect particle 着 (zhe, indicating that the favorable state or time window is currently ongoing). By Middle and Early Mandarin, 趁 shifted from 'following in someone's footsteps' to 'riding on the momentum of an occasion', and 趁着 became the standard marker for 'while [a condition still lasts], taking advantage of'.

history.meaning: to follow behind, pursue; (Tang–Song) to avail oneself of an opportunity or go to a periodic market (趁墟)
taking advantage of (an ongoing condition or time window), while...

morphemes.meaning: avail oneself of, take advantage of (an opportunity or time)
durative aspect marker (while the state or window holds)

趁着.notes: Introduces a temporary condition or opportunity before the main clause—often paired with 赶紧 or 赶快 in the main clause, e.g. 趁着年轻多学点东西 ('While you're still young, learn as much as you can') or 趁着大家都在 ('While everyone is here...').

rootFamily.gloss: to seize an opportunity, take advantage of a chance
while it is still early / before it is too late
to strike while the iron is hot (idiom)

超.etymology: A phono-semantic compound (形聲): semantic 走 (zǒu, 'to run, walk swiftly') + phonetic 召 (zhào, Old Chinese *drcaw). In the Shuowen Jiezi (《說文解字》), 超 is glossed as 跳也 ('to leap over, bound across'). From the concrete physical motion of vaulting over an obstacle in Classical Chinese, it developed the abstract transitive sense 'to surpass, transcend, exceed' and in modern Mandarin also functions as a productive prefix calquing English 'super-' or 'ultra-' and as a colloquial degree adverb ('super, extremely').

history.meaning: to leap over, bound across an obstacle
to surpass, transcend, excel beyond normal limits
to exceed; prefix 'super-'; colloquial intensifier 'super'

morphemes.meaning: to leap over, surpass, exceed; super-

超.notes: In contemporary spoken Mandarin and media dialogue, 超 is heavily used before adjectives and psychological verbs as a casual intensifier (e.g., 超好看 'super good-looking', 超喜欢 'like it so much'), alongside its formal verbal and prefixal uses.

超出.etymology: A verb-complement (resultative/directional) compound formed from 超 (chāo, 'to leap over, surpass') + 出 (chū, 'to go out, emerge beyond a boundary'). Literally 'to leap past and emerge outside (a limit)', it grammaticalized in Literary and vernacular Chinese to express exceeding a quantitative threshold, budget, scope, or expectation.

history.meaning: to rise above and stand out from the crowd; to step beyond a boundary
to exceed, surpass a limit, quota, or expectation

morphemes.meaning: out, beyond a boundary or limit

超出.notes: Takes abstract nouns of limit or scope as its object—most commonly 超出预算 (exceed the budget), 超出范围 (go beyond the scope), and 超出想象 (exceed imagination).

rootFamily.gloss: to exceed the standard or target

超市.etymology: A modern Mandarin syllabic abbreviation (缩略语) of 超级市场 (chāojí shìchǎng), itself a mid-20th-century loan translation (calque) of English 'supermarket': 超 (chāo, shortened from 超级 'super-grade, super-') + 市 (shì, shortened from 市场 'market, marketplace'). In Classical Chinese, 市 originally denoted an enclosed trading plaza or fixed daily market.

history.meaning: supermarket (full loan translation of English 'supermarket')
supermarket, grocery store (disyllabic abbreviation)

超市.notes: While 超级市场 is still understood and occasionally heard in older Hong Kong or Taiwan usage, 超市 is the universal everyday term across Mainland China for both large supermarkets and small neighborhood convenience-style grocers.

超级.etymology: Originally a verb-object or modifier-head Sino-compound composed of 超 (chāo, 'to surpass, transcend') + 级 (jí, traditional 級, originally 'order of silk threads', extended in Qin legal rankings to 'steps, grades, or official ranks'). Literally 'transcending normal grades/ranks', it was popularized in the 20th century (reinforced by Japanese 超級 chōkyū, e.g. 超弩級 'super-dreadnought class') as the standard translation equivalent of English 'super-'.

history.meaning: to skip ranks in official promotion; transcending ordinary grades
super-, ultra-grade; colloquial adverb 'extremely, super'

超级.notes: In entertainment and media contexts (such as talent shows and television production), 超级 forms high-profile titles like 超级女声 (Super Girl) and 超级IP (mega-IP), and also modifies adjectives directly in speech (超级棒 'super great').

超越.etymology: A coordinative (synonymous parallel) verbal compound uniting 超 (chāo, 'to leap over, bound past') + 越 (yuè, 'to cross over, step across a boundary'). Both constituents share the semantic radical 走 ('to run/walk') and originally denoted physical vaulting over barriers in Classical Chinese before converging on the abstract sense of surpassing rivals, predecessors, or one's own prior achievements.

history.meaning: to leap across; to skip over ranks or physical barriers
to surpass, transcend, outperform (a competitor, era, or oneself)

超越.notes: Unlike 超出 (which takes a quantitative limit or scope as its object), 超越 takes a competitor, benchmark, or person as its object—most famously in the idiom 超越自我 ('to surpass oneself').

超过.etymology: Verb-complement compound combining 超 ('to leap over, surpass, exceed', walk/run 走 + 召 zhào) + 过 (過, 'to pass beyond, surpass').

history.meaning: to overtake, surpass, exceed

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 超过 (via 萌典)

越.etymology: A phono-semantic compound (形聲): semantic 走 (zǒu, 'to walk, run') + phonetic 戉 (yuè, Old Chinese *ɢʷat, 'broad battle-axe'). In the Shuowen Jiezi, 越 is defined as 度也 ('to cross over, pass beyond'). From the verbal sense 'to step further across a threshold', Late Tang and Song vernacular Chinese grammaticalized the correlative adverbial pattern 越 A 越 B ('the more A, the more B'), replacing the earlier Literary Chinese 愈…愈… (yù... yù...).

history.meaning: to cross over, transgress a boundary; name of the southern Yue peoples
to pass beyond; emerging degree adverb 'increasingly'
correlative adverb 'the more ... the more'; bound verb 'to cross, overstep'

morphemes.meaning: to cross over, exceed; correlative adverb 'the more...'

越.notes: The correlative structure 越 A 越 B (or 越来越 A 'more and more A') is one of Mandarin's core grammatical frames; never combine 越 with 很 or 最 in the same predicate (*越很好 is ungrammatical).

越发.etymology: An early vernacular Mandarin compound adverb formed from 越 (yuè, degree adverb 'all the more, increasingly', from the verb 'to cross beyond') + 发 (fā, traditional 發, originally 'to shoot forth an arrow, put forth, manifest', bleached in Song–Yuan vernacular into an adverbial suffix marking progressive intensification). Literally 'stepping beyond and manifesting even further', it means 'even more, all the more'.

history.meaning: all the more, increasingly (vernacular adverb in Yuan drama and Ming fiction)
even more, all the more (often after a stated condition or cause)

越发.notes: Slightly more literary or expressive in register than 更加 or 越来越, 越发 typically appears after a reason or change of circumstance (e.g., 听了这话，他越发着急了 'hearing this, he grew all the more anxious').

越大.etymology: A productive adverb-adjective syntagm combining the correlative degree adverb 越 (yuè, 'the more, increasingly', grammaticalized from Classical 越 'to cross over') with the stative verb/adjective 大 (dà, 'big, large, great', originally an oracle-bone pictograph of a standing person with arms and legs outstretched). It functions as either the protasis or apodosis of a 越…越… correlative construction ('the bigger...').

history.meaning: the larger / grows ever greater (vernacular correlative degree phrase)
the bigger, the greater (in correlative clauses like 压力越大，动力越大)

morphemes.meaning: big, large, great in scale or intensity

越大.notes: Frequently paired in workplace and drama aphorisms such as 能力越大，责任越大 ('the greater the ability, the greater the responsibility') or 希望越大，失望越大 ('the greater the hope, the greater the disappointment').

越来越.etymology: Correlative degree construction formed by repeating 越 ('to cross over, exceed; the more ...') around 来 (來, marking ongoing progression over time), meaning 'more and more ... as time goes on'.

history.meaning: more and more, increasingly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 越来越 (via 萌典)

越界.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound from Literary Chinese: 越 (yuè, 'to cross over, transgress') + 界 (jiè, 'boundary, border between fields', composed of 田 'field' + 介 'dividing line'). Originally denoting physically crossing a territorial border or property line, it extended metaphorically to overstepping professional authority, personal boundaries, or ethical norms.

history.meaning: to step across a territorial border or administrative boundary
to overstep bounds (professional, interpersonal, or jurisdictional)

morphemes.meaning: to cross over, transgress, step beyond

越界.notes: In corporate and showbiz dramas like 《幕后之王》, 越界 is a sharp reprimand used when a subordinate, partner, or rival interferes in someone else's jurisdiction or private affairs (你越界了 'You've overstepped your bounds').

越过.etymology: A verb-complement (directional/phase) compound formed from 越 (yuè, 'to cross over, step across') + 过 (guò, traditional 過, 'to pass by, traverse across'). Literally 'to step over and pass across', it combines both physical traversal (crossing a mountain ridge, barrier, or obstacle) and figurative workplace usage ('to bypass a person in the chain of command, go over someone's head').

history.meaning: to climb or pass across a physical barrier, mountain, or river
to cross over (an obstacle); to bypass or go over someone's head

越过.notes: In organizational settings, 越过 (e.g., 越过总监直接向董事长汇报 'bypass the director and report directly to the chairperson') is a transparent verbal counterpart to the formal four-character idiom 越级汇报.

趟.etymology: Phono-semantic character 趟, combining 走 ('to walk, travel') + phonetic 尚 (shàng / tàng), used in Mandarin as a verbal and nominal classifier for 'a round trip, journey, time, row, or scheduled train/bus run'.

history.meaning: classifier for trips, journeys, or scheduled runs

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 趟 (via 萌典)

足.etymology: An ancient pictograph-ideograph (象形/指事) in oracle bone and bronze script depicting a human leg/foot below a knee or calf circle (口 above 止 'foot'). Its primary meaning in Old Chinese (*tsjok) was 'foot, lower leg'. Already in pre-Qin Classical Chinese (such as the Analects and Mencius), it developed the secondary stative/adjectival sense 'complete, ample, sufficient, worthy of', likely via the semantic shift from 'standing firmly on both feet / full measure' to 'having enough'.

history.meaning: human foot or lower leg; extended to 'sufficient, ample, enough to'
foot (literary); sufficient, abundant, complete
full, ample, strong enough; bound root 'foot' (as in 足球 'soccer')

足.notes: As a standalone word in modern Mandarin, 足 means 'ample, sufficient, strong enough' (e.g., 底气很足 'have plenty of confidence/backing', 创意十足 'full of creativity'), whereas 'foot' in everyday speech is 脚 (jiǎo), with 足 surviving in compounds like 足球 (football/soccer) and 立足 (gain a foothold).

cognates.meaning: be sufficient to (classical kanbun訓読: motte ... ni taru)

足以.etymology: A disyllabic lexicalization from a Classical Chinese syntactic phrase: 足 (zú, auxiliary/stative verb 'to be sufficient, ample enough') + 以 (yǐ, instrumental preposition/conjunction 'thereby, with which to, in order to'). In pre-Qin texts (e.g., Mencius 《孟子》: 足以王矣 'is sufficient thereby to become a true king'), 足 and 以 were two separate words that fused through high-frequency collocation into a compound modal adverb meaning 'sufficient to, quite enough to'.

history.meaning: sufficient thereby to (syntactic sequence of adjective 足 + instrumental particle 以)
sufficient to, quite enough to (lexicalized modal adverb taking a verbal phrase)

morphemes.meaning: thereby, wherewith to, so as to

足以.notes: Always followed by a two-syllable or longer verb phrase (e.g., 足以证明 'quite enough to prove', 足以改变一切 'sufficient to change everything'); it lends a crisp, persuasive register to professional arguments and scripts.

足够.etymology: A coordinative (synonymous) compound combining the Classical root 足 (zú, 'sufficient, ample, full') with the vernacular root 够 (gòu, traditional 夠/彀, originally 'to draw a bow to its full extent' in Classical Chinese, whence 'reaching the required mark, enough'). By pairing the literary morpheme 足 with the spoken morpheme 够, Mandarin created a versatile disyllabic word that functions as an adjective, verb, or adverb ('enough, sufficient').

history.meaning: ample and drawn to full measure (pairing of literary 足 and vernacular 夠)
enough, sufficient, amply

足够.notes: Unlike單syllabic 够 (which rarely modifies nouns directly without 的), 足够 can precede nouns (足够的时间 'enough time'), follow subjects as a predicate (时间足够 'time is sufficient'), or modify adjectives/verbs (足够好 'good enough').

cognates.meaning: football/soccer match (蹴球試合 is older; 試合 shiai is cognate with 比赛's competitive sense)

足球比赛.etymology: A four-character modifier-head compound phrase composed of 足球 (zúqiú, 'football, soccer', literally 足 'foot' + 球 'ball', coined in the late 19th/early 20th century as a loan translation of English 'football', echoing the ancient Chinese sport 蹴鞠 cùjū 'kick-ball') + 比赛 (bǐsài, 'competition, match', a coordinative compound of 比 'to compare, compete side-by-side' + 赛 'to contend, rival, originally a thanksgiving ritual competition'). In office recreation contexts, it can also refer playfully to a table-soccer (foosball) match.

history.meaning: ancient military and court kick-ball game; ritual competition

history.form: 足球比賽 / 足球比赛 (zúqiú bǐsài)
history.meaning: football / soccer match (or table-soccer match in indoor settings)

足球比赛.notes: In casual speech, 足球比赛 is often shortened to 球赛 (qiúsài, 'ball game/match') when the sport is clear from context; table soccer (foosball), popular in media production offices, is specifically 桌上足球比赛.

跑.etymology: Phono-semantic character 跑, combining the foot radical 足 + phonetic 包 (bāo / páo), originally meaning 'of a horse or beast: to paw the ground with its hooves' (read páo), then in medieval and modern vernacular Mandarin (read pǎo) 'to run, flee, run errands', displacing Classical 走.

history.meaning: to paw the earth -> to gallop, run
to run, dash, escape, run errands for

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 跑 (via 萌典)

距离.etymology: A coordinative compound combining 距 (jù, originally 'cock's spur' from 足 'foot' + 巨 phonetic, extended in Classical Chinese to 'to stand opposite, be separated from') + 离 (lí, traditional 離, 'to part from, be separated from'). While both characters individually meant 'separated from' in Classical Chinese, the compound 距離 (kyori) was standardized in Meiji-era Japanese to translate Western scientific and spatial 'distance' and re-entered modern Mandarin as both a noun ('distance, gap, lead') and a preposition ('apart from, until').

history.meaning: to stand at a remove from; to part or be separated from
spatial or temporal distance (Meiji Sino-Japanese standardization adopted into Mandarin)
distance, gap (in score, skill, or emotional closeness); preposition 'from/until'

morphemes.meaning: to be apart from, distance between
to separate, leave, be away from

距离.notes: Functions both as a noun—spanning physical distance, a competitive gap in ratings/scores (拉开距离 'widen the lead/gap'), and interpersonal aloofness (保持距离 'keep one's distance')—and as a formal preposition before places or times (距离播出还有三天 'three days left until broadcast').

跟.etymology: Phono-semantic character 跟, combining the foot radical 足 + phonetic 艮 (gēn), originally naming the 'heel of the foot', hence 'to follow closely at someone's heels', and grammaticalized in Mandarin into a comitative preposition ('with') and conjunction ('and').

history.meaning: heel of the foot -> to follow closely behind
heel; to follow; with (prep.); and (conj.)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 跟 (via 萌典)

跟我走.etymology: A three-syllable serial/prepositional verb phrase in vernacular Mandarin: 跟 (gēn, originally 'heel of the foot', grammaticalized into the verb 'to follow at someone's heels' and comitative preposition 'with') + 我 (wǒ, first-person pronoun 'I, me') + 走 (zǒu, 'to walk, go, leave'). Note the dramatic semantic shift of 走: in Old Chinese, 走 meant 'to run, flee' (while 行 meant 'walk'), whereas by Tang–Song vernacular Mandarin 走 shifted to the general verb 'to walk, go, depart'. Literally 'follow me and walk/go' or 'come along with me'.

history.form: 跟 (heel → follow) + 我 (me) + 走 (run → walk/go)
history.meaning: emergence of comitative/serial phrase 'follow me and go' in vernacular Chinese
come with me, follow me (physically or in joining a team/venture)

跟我走.notes: Depending on context and tone, 跟我走 ranges from a literal directive ('follow me this way') to a high-stakes workplace invitation when a senior producer or executive leaves a firm and asks a trusted protégé to come along.

rootFamily.gloss: to follow closely, keep up with

跟拍.etymology: A modern modifier-head / serial-verb compound forged in television, documentary, and film production terminology: 跟 (gēn, 'to follow closely at someone's heels, shadow') + 拍 (pāi, originally 'to clap, strike with the palm', extended via 拍照/拍摄 'to snap a camera shutter, film, shoot'). Literally 'to follow and film', it denotes shadowing a subject continuously with a camera in reality TV, documentaries, or entertainment journalism.

history.meaning: compound coined in late-20th-century film, news, and reality television production

morphemes.meaning: to shoot, film, photograph (short for 拍摄)

跟拍.notes: Essential reality-TV and showbiz jargon: in variety show production (such as in 《幕后之王》), each celebrity guest typically has a dedicated 跟拍导演 (follow-cam director/PD) and 跟拍摄影师 (follow-cam operator) who shadow them 24/7.

rootFamily.gloss: to secretly photograph or film (paparazzi style)

跟着.etymology: A verb + aspect-particle formation composed of 跟 (gēn, originally 'heel of the foot' from 足 'foot' + 艮 phonetic, verbalized in post-Han vernacular as 'to step right behind someone's heels, follow') + 着 (zhe, continuous/durative aspect particle, grammaticalized from Middle Chinese 著 djak 'to attach, adhere to'). Literally 'following and staying attached to', it means both 'to follow along behind' and, in professional/apprenticeship contexts, 'to work or study under (a mentor or boss)'.

history.meaning: following closely behind; durative aspect marker grammaticalized from 'adhere to'
to follow along; to work under or apprentice with a senior figure

morphemes.meaning: to follow at the heels of
durative aspect marker (ongoing state or accompaniment)

跟着.notes: In Chinese workplace and media culture, 跟着 + [Person] (e.g., 跟着淳于乔干 'working under Chunyu Qiao') implies more than formal reporting—it conveys a mentor-protégé bond of learning a master's craft and advancing together.

跟踪.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound formed from 跟 (gēn, 'to follow closely at the heels') + 踪 (zōng, traditional 蹤, 'footprint, track, trace', a phono-semantic character of 足 'foot' + 從 'to follow'). Literally 'to follow someone's footprints', it originated in vernacular detective and martial stories for tailing a person and expanded in modern professional Mandarin to mean 'to conduct continuous follow-up monitoring (of a project, story, or data)'.

history.meaning: to follow someone's footprints, shadow or tail a suspect
to tail/stalk a person; to track continuously or conduct follow-up monitoring

跟踪.notes: Be aware of its dual register: alone with a person as object (跟踪某人), it means 'to tail or stalk someone', whereas in journalism, medicine, and project management (跟踪报道 'follow-up reporting', 全程跟踪 'full-process tracking'), it is completely positive and professional.

跟风.etymology: A metaphorical verb-object (VO) compound combining 跟 (gēn, 'to follow closely') + 风 (fēng, traditional 風, 'wind', which already in Classical Chinese—such as the Preface to the Book of Odes 《詩大序》 and Analects—carried the metaphorical sense of 'prevailing social custom, trend, or influence that sways people like wind over grass'). Literally 'to follow the wind', it means to jump on the bandwagon or uncritically copy market trends.

history.meaning: 'wind' extended to 'social trend/fashion'; vernacular VO compound 'to follow prevailing trends'
to jump on the bandwagon, copy trends uncritically

跟风.notes: Almost always carries a mildly critical or cautionary tone in media and business (e.g., 盲目跟风 'blindly jumping on the bandwagon' by cloning a hit TV show format instead of innovating).

cognates.meaning: to kneel down (quỳ is an early loan from Middle Chinese *gjojX)

跪.etymology: A phono-semantic compound (形聲): semantic 足 (zú, 'foot, leg posture') + phonetic 危 (wēi, Old Chinese *ŋʷral, indicating a high, precarious, upright posture). In ancient China (prior to the Tang–Song introduction of high chairs), people sat on floor mats with knees bent and weight resting on their heels (坐 zuò); 跪 (guì) specifically meant rising up on the knees with the torso erect as a gesture of formal respect, apology, or submission.

history.meaning: to kneel upright on floor mats with torso erect (as a formal posture of respect or plea)
to kneel down in reverence, submission, or supplication
to kneel down; internet slang 'to bow down in awe / admit defeat' (给…跪了)

morphemes.meaning: to kneel down on one's knees

跪.notes: Beyond literal kneeling, modern Mandarin internet and youth slang uses 给…跪了 ('I kneel to...') and 跪求 ('begging on my knees for...') as humorous hyperbole expressing awe at someone's skill or desperate pleading.

rootFamily.gloss: to kneel down, drop to one's knees
to drop to one's knees before someone
to kowtow and kneel in worship/submission

跪下.etymology: A verb-complement (directional) compound formed from 跪 (guì, 'to kneel on one's knees') + 下 (xià, directional complement 'down, downward into a fixed posture'). While Classical 跪 could denote straightening the torso up from a heel-sitting position on a floor mat, once chair-sitting became universal in Song–Yuan China, kneeling required dropping downward from a standing posture, giving rise to 跪下 ('to drop to one's knees').

history.meaning: to drop down onto one's knees from a standing position
to kneel down, drop to one's knees

跪下.notes: Compare 跪下 and 下跪: 跪下 is a verb-complement action often used in direct commands or vivid narrative ('kneel down!'), whereas 下跪 functions as an intransitive verb focusing on the act or gesture of kneeling in submission (向某人下跪 'to kneel before someone').

rootFamily.gloss: to kneel in submission (act of kneeling)

路.etymology: Phono-semantic character 路, combining the foot radical 足 + phonetic 各 (gè / Old Chinese *C-rˤak-s), originally meaning 'a thoroughfare passable by foot and carriage', extended to 'road, path, journey, route, bus line, way/sort'.

history.meaning: road, highway, path, journey
road, street, route, bus line, way

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 路 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: on the road, on the street

路上.etymology: A noun + localizer compound combining 路 (lù, 'road, path, way, journey', a phono-semantic character of 足 'foot' + 各 phonetic) + 上 (shàng, enclitic localizer 'on, upon, in the course of'). Literally 'upon the road', it denotes both physical location on a street and the dynamic state of being en route ('on the way, in transit').

history.meaning: on the road, during a journey or travel
on the road; on the way, in transit (pronounced with neutral-tone localizer -shang)

路上.notes: In everyday communication, 我在路上 ('I'm on my way') and 路上小心 / 一路平安 ('be careful on the way / have a safe trip') are among the most frequent conversational phrases; note that 上 is pronounced in the neutral tone (lùshang).

rootFamily.gloss: halfway, midway through a journey or project

路人.etymology: Compound of 路 ('road; street; lane', foot radical 足 + 各 gè) + 人 ('person'). Attested since Tang poetry (such as Du Mu's famous Qingming quatrain 路上行人欲断魂) for pedestrians and passers-by walking along a street.

history.meaning: traveler or passer-by on the road
passer-by; pedestrian

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 路人

路口.etymology: Modifier-head noun compound combining 路 ('road, street') + 口 ('mouth, opening, crossing').

history.meaning: road intersection, crossing, entrance to a road

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 路口 (via 萌典)

路子.etymology: A vernacular Mandarin noun formed by suffixing the nominalizer 子 (zi, neutral tone, originally 'child/seed' in Old Chinese, bleached into a noun suffix) to 路 (lù, 'road, path, way'). By adding the diminutive/concrete suffix -zi, Mandarin differentiated the literal highway (道路/马路) from the figurative sense of 'operational approach, method, style, or back-channel connections'.

history.meaning: path, method of operating, style, or social connections (vernacular derivation)

morphemes.meaning: road, path, way of doing things
nominal suffix forming concrete or idiomatic nouns

路子.notes: Very common in creative industries and business talk: 野路子 ('wild approach') describes an unorthodox, self-taught style outside formal academy training, while 路子广/路子野 means having wide connections or bold, unconventional ways of getting things done.

路数.etymology: A modifier-head compound originating in traditional Chinese martial arts (武术) and opera terminology: 路 (lù, 'set sequence of movements, routine, path', as in 拳路 'boxing form') + 数 (shù, traditional 數, 'number, count, technique/art'). Originally denoting the numbered sequences and tactical patterns of a martial artist's routine, it entered general colloquial Mandarin (with 数 pronounced in the neutral tone, lùshu) to mean 'style, approach, playbook, or underlying method'.

history.meaning: sequence of moves and techniques in martial arts or Chinese opera
approach, style, playbook, or pattern of behavior in business and art

morphemes.meaning: count, technique, tactical pattern (neutral tone in compound)

路数.notes: Often used when sizing up a rival or newcomer in competitive workplaces: 摸清他的路数 ('figure out his playbook/style') or 不按常理出牌，看不懂他的路数 ('can't read his game plan').

rootFamily.gloss: moves, trick, tactical play in martial arts or business

路灯.etymology: The noun '路灯' (lùdēng, streetlight) simply pairs '路' (road) and '灯' (lamp). Historically, Chinese cities did not have extensive public street lighting, relying instead on lanterns carried by individuals or hung by wealthy households. With the introduction of gas and later electric lighting in treaty ports like Shanghai in the late 19th century, the term '路灯' was coined to describe these permanent, public fixtures illuminating the thoroughfares. It is now a ubiquitous feature of modern urban infrastructure.

history.meaning: lamplight

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 路灯

路线.etymology: A Sino-compound combining 路 (lù, 'road, way, path') + 线 (xiàn, traditional 線/綫, 'thread, line', from 糸 'silk' + 戋/泉 phonetic). Standardized in late-19th and early-20th-century Sino-Japanese (路線 rosen) for railway/transit 'routes, lines' and subsequently extended in 20th-century political and media discourse to mean 'strategic direction, ideological line, or artistic/brand positioning'.

history.meaning: transport line, railway or shipping route
physical route; strategic direction, policy line, or celebrity/brand positioning

路线.notes: In entertainment and media industries, 走…路线 ('to pursue a ... persona/strategy', e.g., 走实力派路线 'take the serious-talent route' vs. 走流量路线 'take the traffic/idol route') is the standard expression for artist or show positioning.

路边.etymology: Locative noun compound combining 路 ('road') + 边 (邊, 'side, edge, margin').

history.meaning: roadside, wayside, curb

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 路边 (via 萌典)

路过.etymology: A subject-predicate or adverbial-verb compound formed from 路 (lù, 'by way of the road, en route') + 过 (guò, traditional 過, 'to pass by, traverse'). Literally 'to pass by along one's route', it grammaticalized as a transitive and intransitive verb meaning 'to walk past, pass through a place incidentally while heading somewhere else'.

history.meaning: to pass through or by a place along one's journey
to pass by, walk past incidentally

morphemes.meaning: along the road, on the way

路过.notes: Can take a location directly as an object (路过你的办公室 'passed by your office') and emphasizes that passing by was incidental rather than a planned destination (我只是路过 'I was just passing by').

rootFamily.gloss: on the way, on the road
to pass by, go through (a place or process)

跳.etymology: Phono-semantic character 跳, combining the foot radical 足 + phonetic 兆 (zhào / Old Chinese *lˤew), meaning 'to leap, jump, bounce, skip, beat/palpitate'.

history.meaning: to leap, jump up
to jump, leap, bounce, dance, skip, beat (of heart)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 跳 (via 萌典)

跳槽.etymology: A vivid metaphorical verb-object (VO) compound from vernacular Mandarin: 跳 (tiào, 'to jump, leap') + 槽 (cáo, 'wooden feeding trough or manger for livestock', composed of 木 'wood' + 曹 phonetic). Originally an agricultural image of a horse or mule abandoning one feeding trough to eat from another, it was used in Ming–Qing vernacular literature for shifting allegiances in pleasure quarters or guilds, and in modern Mandarin became the universal idiom for leaving one employer to join another firm (often a competitor).

history.meaning: (of livestock) to leave one feeding trough for another; (in Ming–Qing vernacular) to switch patrons or partners
to switch jobs to another company or rival firm

跳槽.notes: Because 跳槽 is grammatically a separable verb-object compound (离合词), it cannot take a destination company directly as its object (*跳槽同心文化); instead, use the preposition 到 or 去 (跳槽到另一家公司 'jump ship to another company').

rootFamily.gloss: to complain, roast, vent (slang: 'spit into the trough')
to poach talent (literally 'dig the corner of a wall')

跳跃.etymology: Coordinate verb compound combining 跳 ('to jump, leap') + 跃 (躍, 'to bound, spring upward').

history.meaning: to jump, leap, bound

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 跳跃 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to step into, enter upon (fumikomu is the native equivalent)

踏入.etymology: A verb-complement (directional) compound in Literary Chinese style: 踏 (tà, 'to step on, tread upon', a phono-semantic character of 足 'foot' + 沓 phonetic) + 入 (rù, 'to enter, go inside'). Literally 'to set foot into', it preserves the elevated literary register of both constituents and is used for crossing an important threshold—stepping into a building, entering a profession, or embarking on a new life stage.

history.meaning: to set foot inside a gate, hall, or territory
to step into, enter (a prestigious venue, industry, or stage of life)

踏入.notes: More formal and weighty than everyday 走进 (zǒujìn): 踏入 frequently collocates with career or life milestones such as 踏入社会 ('enter society / start working life'), 踏入职场 ('step into the workplace'), or 踏入演艺圈 ('enter showbiz').

踏板.etymology: Compound noun from 踏 ('step on; tread', foot 足 + phonetic 沓) + 板 ('board; plank; flat plate'). Originally the wooden footboard of a carriage, bed, or loom treadle, it now also refers to a low step-stool, a bicycle pedal, or a piano foot pedal.

history.meaning: wooden footboard or treadle
footboard; step; pedal; footrest

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 踏板

踏破.etymology: A verb-resultative compound formed from 踏 (tà, 'to tread upon, trample with the feet') + 破 (pò, 'to break, wear through, shatter'). Literally 'to tread upon until worn through', it is immortalized in Classical poetry and proverbs—most famously the Song-dynasty couplet 踏破铁鞋无觅处，得来全不费工夫 ('having worn through iron shoes treading everywhere in vain search, it comes to hand with no effort at all') and the hyperbolic image 踏破门槛 ('to wear down the threshold by a constant stream of visitors').

history.meaning: to wear through (shoes, thresholds, or mountain paths) by incessant treading; to trample down in battle
to wear down or break through by constant treading (especially in 踏破门槛 and 踏破铁鞋)

踏破.notes: In drama and business dialogue, 门槛都要被踏破了 ('the threshold is about to be worn through by visitors' footsteps') is a classic, vivid hyperbole describing how sought-after a hit producer, celebrity, or company has become.

rootFamily.gloss: to break through, make a breakthrough

踏踏实实.etymology: An AABB emphatic state-adjective reduplication of the disyllabic compound 踏实 (tāshi, traditional 踏實, "planted on solid ground; dependable; free from anxiety"). Structurally a verb-complement / coordinative compound uniting 踏 (tà/tā, "to step on, tread firmly upon the earth") and 实 (shí, traditional 實, "solid, full, substantial, real"). The AABB reduplication intensifies the image of having both feet planted squarely on firm ground, shifting metaphorically from physical footing to psychological composure and unpretentious, step-by-step diligence.

history.meaning: to tread with the foot (踏) + full, solid, substantial (實) as independent Classical Chinese lexemes
having firm footing; dependable, practical, and free from anxiety
in a thoroughly grounded, steady, down-to-earth manner; with complete peace of mind

morphemes.meaning: step firmly, plant one's feet on the ground

踏踏实实.notes: In spoken Mandarin, the base word 踏实 is pronounced tāshi (first tone + neutral tone), whereas in the AABB form 踏踏实实, the final two syllables commonly take full second tone (tātàshíshí) or neutral-full cadence; it frequently modifies 做人 (conduct oneself) or 做事 (handle work).

rootFamily.gloss: to step into, set foot in

踢.etymology: A phono-semantic compound character (形声字) combining the semantic foot radical 足 (zú, written ⻊ on the left, indicating an action performed with the foot) with the phonetic component 易 (yì, Old Chinese *lek, Middle Chinese *thjek > Mandarin tī). In Classical Chinese texts, 蹴 (cù) and 躢 were initially more common for kicking, while 踢 emerged in Han-to-Tang vernacular and lexicographical sources (such as *Guangyun*) as the primary everyday verb for striking outward with the foot, later developing figurative senses of ousting or eliminating someone from a team or competition.

history.meaning: to kick, strike or propel with the foot
to kick; to play (ball games with the feet); to expel or boot out (figurative)

踢.notes: Beyond literal uses like 踢球 (play soccer), workplace and entertainment slang uses 踢出局 (kick out of the game/project) or 把某人踢走 (boot someone out) for cutting someone from a roster or production team.

rootFamily.gloss: to play football / soccer; to pass the buck (figurative)
to kick out of a competition or group

踩.etymology: Phono-semantic character 踩, combining the foot radical 足 + phonetic 采 (cǎi), attested in vernacular Mandarin for 'to step on, tread on, press a pedal'.

history.meaning: to step on, tread on, trample, press a pedal

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 踩 (via 萌典)

踱步.etymology: A verb joining 踱 (duó, 'to pace', bearing the foot radical ⻊) and 步 (bù, 'step'). It denotes a deliberate, measured, rhythmic walking back and forth, closely associated with deep thinking, anticipation, or anxiety.

history.meaning: to pace

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 踱步

蹭.etymology: An expressive verb featuring the foot radical ⻊. Originally depicting a scraping or dragging motion of the feet, its usage expanded to cover any gentle, frictional contact or brushing against a surface, vividly portraying a cat rubbing against a leg.

history.meaning: to scrape; to rub

身上.etymology: Locative compound combining 身 ('body, torso, person', originally an oracle-bone pictograph of a person in profile with a prominent belly) + localizer 上 ('on').

history.meaning: on one's body; with oneself (of money/belongings)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 身上 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: social status, one's station or identity

身份.etymology: A modifier-head compound originally written 身分 and later differentiated graphics-wise in Mainland standard orthography as 身份. It joins 身 (shēn, "body, person, self") with 份 / 分 (fèn, "allotted share, social station, role, duty"). In imperial and Literary Chinese, 身分 denoted a person's hierarchical rank, social standing, or moral allotment in society. In modern Mandarin, while retaining the sense of social prestige or dignity (as in 有身份, "of high status"), it broadened into the standard legal and sociological term for personal "identity" or role capacity.

history.meaning: one's social rank, station, or allotted status within a hierarchy
personal or legal identity; role capacity; social standing or prestige

morphemes.meaning: allotted share, social role, status, capacity

身份.notes: Frequently appears in the frame 以……的身份 ("in the capacity/role of...", e.g., 以制作人的身份, "in the capacity of producer"), as well as in 身份证 (identity card) and 掉身份 (beneath one's dignity).

身体.etymology: A classic coordinative (synonymous) compound (联合式合成词) pairing 身 (shēn, Traditional/Simplified, originally a pictograph of a torso with a prominent abdomen, meaning "trunk of the body, torso, person") and 体 (tǐ, traditional 體, "skeletal frame, limbs, organic whole"). Attested in pre-Qin classics including the *Classic of Filial Piety* (*Xiaojing*: 身体发肤，受之父母, "One's torso, limbs, hair, and skin are received from one's parents"), where 身 specifically referred to the trunk and 体 to the four limbs; fused together, they denote the entire physical organism and, by extension, one's state of physical health.

history.meaning: the torso (身) and the limbs/frame (體); the physical human body as a whole
human body, physique; state of physical health and well-being

morphemes.meaning: torso, trunk of the body, self

身体.notes: In everyday conversation, 身体 often translates better as "health" rather than anatomical "body" (e.g., 注意身体 means "take care of your health", and 身体不舒服 means "feeling unwell").

身后.etymology: Locative compound combining 身 ('body, person') + 后 (後, 'behind, after'); means both literally 'behind one's body/back' and figuratively 'after one's death'.

history.meaning: behind someone; posthumously

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 身后 (via 萌典)

身处.etymology: A subject-predicate / adverbial-verb literary compound combining 身 (shēn, "one's own body/person; personally") with 处 (chǔ, traditional 處, third tone, "to dwell, reside, be situated in"). In Classical Chinese, 身 often functioned adverbially before a verb to mean "in person, with one's own self," while 处 meant to occupy a place or circumstance. Together, 身处 literally means "one's person dwells within [a given environment or predicament]," surviving in modern Mandarin as an elevated transitive verb phrase that takes a two-syllable or four-syllable object describing a milieu or crisis.

history.meaning: to dwell or be situated personally in a place or station
to find oneself in, be situated within (an environment, industry, or predicament)

morphemes.meaning: to dwell, reside, be situated in (pronounced chǔ)

身处.notes: Always remember the third-tone reading chǔ (verbal "to be situated in"), not fourth-tone chù ("place"); it is slightly formal and pairs naturally with abstract environments like 身处娱乐圈 (in the entertainment industry) or 身处逆境 (in adversity).

rootFamily.gloss: to put oneself in someone else's shoes
to get along with one another

cognates.meaning: body and mind, soma and psyche

身心.etymology: A coordinative (parallel) compound (联合式合成词) pairing 身 (shēn, "physical body, corporeal self") and 心 (xīn, originally a pictograph of the heart organ, denoting "heart, mind, affective and cognitive faculties"). While both characters appear together in early philosophical texts, 身心 gained special prominence through Chinese Buddhist translations (rendering Sanskrit *kāya-citta* or *nāma-rūpa*, the physical and mental aggregates of sentient existence) and Neo-Confucian self-cultivation discourse (身心修养). In modern usage it compactly denotes holistic physical and psychological well-being.

history.meaning: the corporeal body (身) and the heart-mind (心), especially in Buddhist and Confucian self-cultivation
body and mind; physical and mental well-being as an integrated whole

身心.notes: Commonly used in four-character collocations such as 身心俱疲 (exhausted in both body and mind—a staple description of overworked TV production crews) and 身心健康 (physically and mentally healthy).

rootFamily.gloss: exhausted in both body and mind

身段.etymology: A modifier-head compound joining 身 (shēn, "human body, torso") with 段 (duàn, "section, segment, proportion, technical measure or artistry"). Originating in vernacular Chinese and traditional Chinese戲曲 (opera) and dance terminology, 身段 first denoted the proportional contours of a woman's figure and the stylized physical postures, movements, and stage bearing of an opera performer. From "graceful stage posture held aloft," it underwent a vivid metaphorical shift in modern Mandarin to mean "aloof social posture, pride, or airs," especially in the phrase 放下身段 ("to drop one's airs / humble oneself").

history.meaning: physical build, bodily proportions, and graceful posture (especially of a dancer or woman)
stylized stage movement in Chinese opera; a woman's figure; social airs, pride, or high-and-mighty posture

morphemes.meaning: section, proportion, stylized movement or routine

身段.notes: In workplace and entertainment dramas, 身段 almost always appears in 放低身段 or 放下身段 ("lower/drop one's airs, swallow one's pride") or 摆身段 ("put on airs"), describing whether a star or executive is willing to humble themselves.

身经百战.etymology: A four-character set idiom (成语) with a subject-predicate internal structure: 身 (shēn, "one's own body/person, personally") serves as the topic/subject, followed by the verb-object predicate 经百战 (jīng bǎi zhàn, traditional 經百戰, "to pass through / experience a hundred battles," where 百 "hundred" is a classical numerical hyperbole for "countless"). Drawn from medieval military biographies and histories (such as accounts of Tang and Song generals who personally fought in scores of campaigns), it transitioned from literal battlefield veterans to anyone deeply seasoned by high-stakes professional crises.

history.form: 身經百戰 (shēn jīng bǎi zhàn)
history.meaning: having personally fought through countless military engagements and campaigns
battle-hardened; thoroughly seasoned and experienced through countless trials or high-pressure projects

身经百战.notes: In modern media and corporate contexts, it praises veteran producers, PR directors, or crisis managers who have survived countless live-broadcast emergencies without panicking.

rootFamily.gloss: to pass through, experience; one's past experience
to personally experience on the spot

cognates.meaning: around oneself, one's immediate surroundings or close associates

身边.etymology: A modifier-head place noun (方位合成词) composed of 身 (shēn, "one's body, person, self") and the localizer/noun 边 (biān, traditional 邊, "side, margin, proximity"). Attested from Tang-Song poetry and vernacular prose onward, it literally designates the spatial zone immediately adjacent to one's body. Over time, its meaning extended along three axes: physical proximity ("right beside me"), relational closeness ("the people in one's inner circle, such as assistants, family, or partners"), and immediate possession ("on one's person," as in having cash or documents with one).

history.meaning: by the side of one's body; on one's person
at one's side; in one's immediate social circle or entourage; on one's person

身边.notes: Functions grammatically as a place word, so it can directly follow 在, 到, or 离开 without needing 那里 (e.g., 留在他身边, "stay by his side", or 身边的人, "the people around one").

躬.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining 身 ('body; torso') + 吕/弓 ('curved spine or bow', Middle Chinese *kjung*). Literally 'the body bent forward like a bow', it survives in modern Mandarin primarily as the bound noun object of the separable verb 鞠躬 ('to bow', 鞠个躬 'take a bow').

history.meaning: body; bend the body respectfully
bow of the body (in 鞠躬)

躲.etymology: Phono-semantic character 躲, combining the body radical 身 + phonetic 朵 (duǒ), literally 'to move one's body out of the way', hence 'to hide oneself, dodge, avoid, take shelter from'.

history.meaning: to hide, dodge, avoid, take cover

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 躲 (via 萌典)

躺.etymology: Phono-semantic character 躺, combining the body radical 身 + phonetic 尚 (shàng / tǎng), created in vernacular Mandarin to mean 'to lie down flat, recline'.

history.meaning: to lie down, recline

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 躺 (via 萌典)

车.etymology: Oracle-bone and bronze pictograph 车 (車) depicting a two-wheeled chariot with axle, linchpins, draught pole, and yoke viewed from above; evolved from 'wheeled cart/chariot' to any 'wheeled vehicle, car, train, machine/lathe'.

history.meaning: wheeled chariot, carriage, cart
vehicle, car, bus, train, bike; lathe; chariot in chess (jū)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 车 (via 萌典)

车上.etymology: Locative compound combining 车 (車, 'vehicle, car, bus, train') + localizer 上 ('on, in, aboard').

history.meaning: in the car, on the bus/train, aboard the vehicle

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 车上 (via 萌典)

车票.etymology: Modifier-head noun compound combining 车 (車, 'train, bus, vehicle') + 票 ('printed slip, ticket, banknote').

history.meaning: train or bus ticket, transit fare ticket

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 车票 (via 萌典)

车站.etymology: Modifier-head noun compound combining 车 (車, 'train, bus, vehicle') + 站 ('relay post, station, stop', originally from Middle Mongolian jam 'postal relay station' blended with Chinese 站 'to stand').

history.meaning: railway station, bus stop, transit station

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 车站 (via 萌典)

车身.etymology: Modifier-head noun compound combining 车 (車, 'vehicle, car') + 身 ('body, main frame').

history.meaning: body of a vehicle, car body

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 车身 (via 萌典)

车轮.etymology: Modifier-head noun compound combining 车 (車, 'wheeled vehicle, cart, car') + 轮 (輪, 'spoked wheel').

history.meaning: wheel of a cart or vehicle

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 车轮 (via 萌典)

转.etymology: Phono-semantic character 转 (轉), combining the vehicle/wheel radical 车 (車) + phonetic 专 (專 zhuān), split by tone in Mandarin: (1) zhuǎn ('to turn, shift direction, transfer, pass on'); (2) zhuàn ('to revolve, spin, rotate around an axis').

history.meaning: to revolve like a wheel, turn around, convey
to turn, change direction, forward (zhuǎn); to spin, rotate (zhuàn)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 转 (via 萌典)

转一转.etymology: A tentative/delimitative verbal construction following the productive Mandarin `V + 一 + V` pattern, built on the verb 转 (zhuàn, traditional 轉, fourth tone, "to turn in a circle, revolve; by extension, to stroll around or make a circuit of a place"). In Classical Chinese, 轉 originally denoted the revolution of a chariot wheel (车 + 专). In Northern Mandarin vernacular, the fourth-tone reading zhuàn developed the colloquial spatial sense of walking around a neighborhood or venue; inserting 一 (yī, "one") between reduplicated tokens of the verb softens the action into a casual, brief, low-stakes stroll or look-around.

history.meaning: to revolve like a wheel; to turn around or make a circuit
to take a casual stroll around, walk around for a bit, look around a place

morphemes.meaning: to walk around in a circuit, stroll around (pronounced zhuàn)
to stroll around, look around (pronounced zhuàn)

转一转.notes: Be careful with the tone: in the sense of "stroll around / look around a venue," 转 is pronounced in the fourth tone (zhuàn, often with兒化 zhuànyizhuànr in northern speech), not third tone zhuǎn; it is synonymous with 逛一逛 or 转悠.

rootFamily.gloss: to stroll around aimlessly, pace about (colloquial)
to revolve, rotate, spin (fourth tone zhuàn)
to turn around, pivot (third tone zhuǎn)

转发.etymology: A serial verb / modifier-verb compound (连动/偏正式合成词) combining 转 (zhuǎn, traditional 轉, "to pass on, relay, transfer from one point to another") and 发 (fā, traditional 發, "to send out, dispatch, issue"). Originally coined in modern administrative, postal, and telecommunications usage to mean "to forward a dispatch, circular, or piece of mail received from a higher or outside office," it underwent explosive semantic rejuvenation in the internet and social-media era (especially on Weibo and WeChat) as the standard verb for "reposting, retweeting, or forwarding" digital content.

history.meaning: to relay or forward an official directive, letter, or telegram to subsequent recipients
to repost, share, or forward a social-media post, message, or broadcast signal

morphemes.meaning: to relay, pass on, transfer onward
to send out, dispatch, publish, post

转发.notes: Along with 点赞 (like) and 评论 (comment), 转发 forms the core triad of Chinese social-media engagement metrics that TV producers and PR teams track obsessively in *Behind the Scenes*.

rootFamily.gloss: to relay a broadcast; live relay

转发量.etymology: A three-character right-branching modifier-head compound `[转发 + 量]` formed by suffixing the productive quantitative head noun 量 (liàng, "measured quantity, volume, capacity," originally a weight/volume measure in Classical Chinese) to the verbal compound 转发 (zhuǎnfā, traditional 轉發, "to forward, repost, share"). Coined in the 21st-century Chinese social-media ecosystem (particularly Sina Weibo and WeChat Official Accounts), it quantifies viral reach by measuring how many times a post, promotional trailer, or PR statement has been shared onward by users.

history.meaning: to relay/forward (轉發) + measured volume or capacity (量) as separate administrative and metrological terms
repost count; total volume of shares or retweets on a digital platform

转发量.notes: The suffix -量 (liàng) is highly productive in media analytics: compare 播放量 (play/view count), 阅读量 (read count), 点击量 (click-through volume), and 流量 (traffic/star buzz).

rootFamily.gloss: to repost, forward (a post or message)
view count, number of video plays/streams
data traffic; internet/celebrity buzz and popularity

转变.etymology: A coordinative / serial-verb compound (联合式合成词) uniting 转 (zhuǎn, traditional 轉, "to turn, shift direction, pivot") and 变 (biàn, traditional 變, "to change, alter, transform"). In Buddhist and medieval Literary Chinese texts, 轉變 denoted the ceaseless flux, transformation, or evolution of phenomena (for instance, the transformation of consciousness *vijñāna-pariṇāma* in Yogācāra Buddhism). In modern Mandarin, it functions both as an ambitransitive verb ("to shift, transform") and as an abstract noun meaning a directional shift in attitude, strategy, style, or circumstances.

history.meaning: evolution, flux, or transformation of phenomena and consciousness; cyclic change of fortunes
to change or shift from one state, stance, or direction to another; a turnaround or transformation

转变.notes: Often used when someone's mindset, role, or public opinion undergoes a directional pivot, as in 转变观念 (shift one's mindset), 转变态度 (change one's attitude), or 发生转变 (undergo a shift).

rootFamily.gloss: turning point, plot twist, shift in course
structural transition, transformation (e.g., of a business or career)

cognates.meaning: passing on a message (archaic/literary kanji compound)
to pass on a message, convey word

转告.etymology: A modifier-head verbal compound (偏正式合成词) in which 转 (zhuǎn, traditional 轉, "indirectly, through an intermediary, by relaying") adverbially modifies 告 (gào, "to tell, inform, report"). Attested in Tang-Song prose and vernacular fiction, 转告 literally means "to inform by relaying through a third party." Unlike 直接告诉 (tell directly), 转告 presupposes a three-party communication chain (Speaker A -> Intermediary B -> Recipient C) and remains the standard polite everyday verb for asking someone to pass along word.

history.meaning: to report or convey word indirectly through an intermediary
to pass on a message, communicate word to someone through a third person

转告.notes: Syntactically, 转告 takes the final recipient directly as its object (e.g., 请帮我转告他, "Please pass the message on to him for me"), or precedes a clause specifying the message.

rootFamily.gloss: to pass on, convey, transmit (orders or feelings)

转播车.etymology: A three-character compound noun `[转播 + 车]` built from the modern broadcasting verb 转播 (zhuǎnbō, traditional 轉播, "to relay a broadcast; to transmit live audio/video signals from a field venue to a station," combining 转 "relay, transfer" + 播 "sow, broadcast, disseminate") and the head noun 车 (chē, traditional 車, "wheeled vehicle, truck, van"). Coined in 20th-century television engineering to translate English "outside broadcast (OB) van / mobile production truck," it designates the mobile control-room vehicle parked outside stadiums or concert halls to direct and transmit live television programs.

history.meaning: to relay a radio/television broadcast (轉播) + wheeled vehicle (車)
outside broadcast (OB) truck; mobile television production and transmission van

morphemes.meaning: to broadcast, disseminate (originally to sow seeds)

转播车.notes: In television production dramas like *Behind the Scenes* (*幕后之王*), the 转播车 is the nerve center of live outdoor or arena shoots, where the chief director calls camera cuts and manages emergencies in real time.

rootFamily.gloss: to relay a broadcast; live or delayed broadcast relay

转正.etymology: A verb-complement / abbreviated verb-object compound (动补/紧缩合成词) combining 转 (zhuǎn, traditional 轉, "to convert, transition, shift status") with 正 (zhèng, "formal, regular, full-status, official," abbreviating 正式员工 "regular employee" or 正职 "full post"). Historically, in late imperial bureaucracy, passing from an acting or expectant appointment (候补 / 署理) to a substantive post was called 实授 or 转正; in 20th-century Chinese organizational and HR usage, 转正 became the standard term for converting from a probationary intern/trial worker (试用期) or party candidate into a permanent, full-status employee or member.

history.meaning: to convert from an acting, deputy, or probationary status to a full, regular official position
to pass probation and become a permanent full-time employee; (slang) to become an official romantic partner

morphemes.meaning: official, regular, full-status (short for 正式)

转正.notes: A crucial milestone for newcomers in Chinese workplace dramas (passing the 试用期 "probation period" to 转正); colloquially, it is also used humorously when an unofficial admirer or backup suitor becomes the official romantic partner.

rootFamily.gloss: formal, official, regular (e.g., 正式员工 regular staff)
to change jobs or transfer to another profession/post

转移.etymology: A coordinative (synonymous) verbal compound (联合式合成词) pairing 转 (zhuǎn, traditional 轉, "to turn, shift, convey from one place to another") and 移 (yí, originally meaning to transplant rice seedlings, hence "to move, relocate, shift"). Already attested in Han-Tang historical texts for relocating populations, supplies, or official posts, and reinforced in modern Sino-Japanese scientific/legal terminology (Japanese 転移 *ten'i*), 转移 covers both concrete spatial relocation (moving troops, evacuating people, transferring assets) and abstract redirection (diverting attention, shifting a crisis, or changing a topic).

history.meaning: to move, relocate, or shift from one position or state to another
to shift, transfer, divert (attention, assets, personnel), or evacuate; (medicine) to metastasize

转移.notes: Highly versatile across registers: it collocates with concrete nouns (转移阵地 "shift base/location", 转移资金 "transfer funds") and psychological/media nouns (转移注意力 "divert public attention", 转移视线 "deflect scrutiny").

rootFamily.gloss: to change the subject, deflect the topic
firm and unshakeable (literally "cannot be shifted or turned")

转移话题.etymology: A four-character verb-object phrase (动宾短语) combining the transitive verb 转移 (zhuǎnyí, traditional 轉移, "to shift, divert, redirect") with the nominal object 话题 (huàtí, traditional 話題, "topic of conversation, subject of discourse," composed of 话 "speech, talk" + 题 "forehead; heading, subject, theme"). While 转移 is classical in origin, 话题 gained currency in modern East Asian print and broadcast culture (alongside Japanese 話題 *wadai*). Together, 转移话题 literally means "to shift the topic of conversation away from an uncomfortable or sensitive point."

history.meaning: to shift or relocate (轉移) + topic or theme of conversation (話題)
to change the subject; to deflect or steer a conversation away from a sensitive issue

morphemes.meaning: topic of conversation, subject under discussion (话 speech + 题 theme)

转移话题.notes: A frequent conversational and PR maneuver: in dialogue, speakers often call someone out directly with 你别转移话题！ ("Don't change the subject!"). Compare 岔开话题 (interrupt and sidetrack the topic).

rootFamily.gloss: topic of conversation; media buzz/talking point
to sidetrack or change the subject of conversation

转角.etymology: Compound noun combining 转 (轉 zhuǎn, 'to turn a corner') + 角 ('corner, bend').

history.meaning: street corner, bend, turning

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 转角 (via 萌典)

转让.etymology: Compound verb combining 转 (轉, 'to transfer, shift') + 让 (讓, 'to yield, cede, make over to another').

history.meaning: to transfer ownership, assign, make over

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 转让 (via 萌典)

转身.etymology: Verb-object compound combining 转 (轉, 'to turn') + 身 ('body'), meaning 'to turn one's body around; in the blink of an eye'.

history.meaning: to turn around

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 转身 (via 萌典)

转轮.etymology: Compound noun combining 转 (轉, 'revolving, rotating') + 轮 (輪, 'wheel, rotor').

history.stage: Buddhist & Medieval Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: revolving wheel, rotor, potter's or mechanical wheel

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 转轮 (via 萌典)

转达.etymology: Serial verb compound combining 转 (轉, 'to pass on, relay') + 达 (達, 'to reach, convey, communicate').

history.meaning: to pass on a message, convey

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 转达 (via 萌典)

轮.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形声字, traditional 輪) combining the semantic chariot/vehicle radical 车 (chē, traditional 車) with the phonetic component 仑 (lún, traditional 侖, Old Chinese *run, "ordered, arranged in sequence"). Its primary sense in pre-Qin Classical Chinese is a spoked chariot wheel; because a wheel rotates in full 360-degree cycles and resembles a disk, 轮 extended naturally into a classifier (measure word) for disk-like celestial bodies (一轮明月 "a bright full moon"), a verb meaning "to take turns in rotation," and a classifier for sequential "rounds" of competitions, auditions, bidding, or negotiations.

history.meaning: spoked wheel of a chariot or carriage
wheel; disk; to rotate or take turns; classifier for full moons or cyclic series
round (classifier for stages of competition, talks, or financing); wheel; to take turns

morphemes.meaning: phonetic indicator (*run) also suggesting ordered rotation

轮.notes: In talent shows, media production, and business (all central to *Behind the Scenes*), 轮 is the essential classifier for stages of elimination or negotiation: 第一轮海选 (first audition round), 新一轮谈判 (a new round of talks), or A轮融资 (Series A funding round).

rootFamily.gloss: by turns, in rotation, one after another

轮休.etymology: A modifier-head verbal compound (偏正式合成词) compressed from 轮流休息 (lúnliú xiūxi, "to rest in rotation / take turns resting"). The first morpheme 轮 (lún, traditional 輪, literally "wheel," used adverbially to mean "by turns, in rotation, on a staggered schedule") modifies the verbal head 休 (xiū, originally an ideogram of a person 亻 leaning against a tree 木, meaning "to rest, cease work, take leave"). It arose in modern industrial, media, and public-service scheduling where operations run continuously 24/7 and staff must rotate their days off rather than all resting on weekends.

history.meaning: to rotate in turn (輪) + to rest beneath a tree / cease labor (休)
to take staggered or rotating days off on a shift schedule

morphemes.meaning: in rotation, by turns, on a staggered cycle (short for 轮流)
to rest, take time off work (short for 休息)

轮休.notes: Common in industries that never shut down on weekends—such as TV broadcasting stations, hospitals, and film crews—contrasting with 双休 (having both Saturday and Sunday off) and 调休 (compensatory time off).

rootFamily.gloss: to rest, take a break; to take vacation/leave
to take turns, do something in rotation; shift work
to adjust working days / take compensatory leave

轮到.etymology: Verb-complement compound combining 轮 (輪, 'to revolve in order, take turns like a wheel') + resultative complement 到 ('to reach, arrive at').

history.meaning: to be someone's turn

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 轮到 (via 萌典)

软.etymology: Phono-semantic character 软 (軟, variant 輭), combining the wheel/carriage radical 车 (車, originally referring to wrapping rush padding around chariot wheels to cushion the ride) + 欠 / 耎 (ruǎn), meaning 'soft, pliable, gentle, weak'.

history.meaning: padded wheel -> soft, pliant, yielding
soft, flexible, gentle, weak

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 软 (via 萌典)

软垫.etymology: Modifier-head compound from 软 (simplified from 軟, cart 車 + 欠, originally wheels wrapped in rushes to soften the ride, hence 'soft;pliable') + 垫 (simplified from 墊, 'pad; mat; cushion'). Denotes any padded seat cushion or upholstered mat placed on a wooden chair or bench.

history.meaning: soft padded cushion or mat
soft cushion; padded mat

轴.etymology: Phono-semantic character 轴 (軸), combining the vehicle radical 车 (車) + phonetic 由 (yóu / Old Chinese *lruk), originally naming the 'axle-tree on which chariot wheels turn', extended to 'roller for a scroll, spool of thread, pivot, axis'.

history.meaning: wheel axle; scroll roller
axle, shaft, spindle, scroll, axis

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 轴 (via 萌典)

轴套.etymology: Modifier-head mechanical compound combining 轴 (軸, 'axle, rotating shaft') + 套 ('sheath, sleeve, casing').

history.meaning: axle sleeve, bushing, bearing bush

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 轴套 (via 萌典)

轴销.etymology: Modifier-head mechanical compound combining 轴 (軸, 'axle, pivot shaft') + 销 (銷, 'metal pin, peg, linchpin, bolt').

history.meaning: axle pin, pivot pin, clevis pin

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 轴销 (via 萌典)

轻.etymology: Phono-semantic character 轻 (輕), combining the vehicle radical 车 (車, originally denoting a light, fast two-wheeled war chariot) + phonetic 巠 (jīng), meaning 'light in weight, agile, gentle, slight, to treat lightly'.

history.meaning: light fast chariot -> light in weight, nimble, slight
light, gentle, soft, minor, young

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 轻 (via 萌典)

轻快.etymology: Coordinate adjective compound combining 轻 (輕, 'light in weight or step') + 快 ('fast, brisk, cheerful').

history.meaning: light and brisk, lively, sprightly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 轻快 (via 萌典)

轻拿轻放.etymology: Four-character handling instruction (A-B-A-C pattern) combining 轻 (輕, 'gently, lightly') + 拿 ('to pick up, hold') + 轻 ('gently') + 放 ('to set down, place').

history.form: 輕拿輕放 / 轻拿轻放
history.meaning: pick up and set down gently -> handle with care

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 轻拿轻放 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: light and easy; rash, hasty, careless
light and easy; frivolous or rash

轻易.etymology: A coordinative (synonymous) compound (联合式合成词) pairing 轻 (qīng, traditional 輕, "light in weight; slight, frivolously, without due gravity") and 易 (yì, "easy, effortless; lightly, casually"). Attested in pre-Qin and Han historical classics (such as *Zuo Zhuan* and *Records of the Grand Historian*), 輕易 originally functioned both as an adjective meaning "simple and undemanding" and as an adverb meaning "rashly, lightly, without serious deliberation." In modern Mandarin, both senses survive, most frequently in negative or cautionary contexts warning against acting rashly or giving up too easily.

history.meaning: light and easy; acting lightly, rashly, or without due caution and gravity
easily, lightly, rashly (especially in negative predicates like 不轻易放弃 "not give up easily")

morphemes.meaning: light in weight; lightly, without solemnity, rashly

轻易.notes: Unlike 容易 (róngyì, neutral "easy"), 轻易 carries a strong modal nuance of "lightly / rashly / without much resistance" and overwhelmingly appears with negation: 别轻易相信 (don't trust too easily/rashly), 绝不轻易放弃 (never give up easily).

rootFamily.gloss: to treat lightly, underestimate (an opponent or problem)
rash, indiscreet, hasty (in speech or action)
easy to do; easily accomplished at a single stroke

轻松.etymology: A coordinative compound (联合式合成词) combining 轻 (qīng, traditional 輕, "light in weight, unburdened") and 松 (sōng, traditional 鬆, with the hair radical 髟 + 松, meaning "loose, untied, slackened, relaxed," as opposed to 緊 jǐn "tight, tense"). Originating in vernacular Chinese descriptions of untying a tight load or loosening tense muscles, 轻松 bridges the physical domain ("lightweight and untightened") and the psychological domain ("free from pressure, relaxed, effortless"). Note that simplified Chinese merged 鬆 ("loose") into 松 ("pine tree"), whereas traditional script keeps 輕鬆 distinct.

history.meaning: physically light in weight and loose/unconstrained; free of heavy burdens
relaxed, at ease, light-hearted; effortless or low-stress (of work or atmosphere)

轻松.notes: Can describe a person's mood (心情很轻松 "feeling relaxed"), a work atmosphere (工作氛围轻松 "relaxed work vibe"), or how easily a task is handled; it can also take a reduplicated adverbial form 轻轻松松 or verb-object 轻松一下 ("relax for a bit").

rootFamily.gloss: a sigh of relief; to breathe easier (松一口气)

轻装上阵.etymology: A four-character serial-verb idiom (成语) structured as `[轻装] + [上阵]`. The first half, 轻装 (qīngzhuāng, traditional 輕裝, "light equipment/attire," from 轻 "lightweight" + 装 "baggage, military gear, outfit"), acts as an adverbial state describing how one performs the second half, 上阵 (shàngzhèn, traditional 上陣, "to step onto the battle formation / go into combat," from 上 "go up to, enter" + 阵 "battle array, front line").
