Rooted in classical military strategy where shedding heavy armor and supply baggage allowed cavalry or infantry to strike swiftly, it is used figuratively in modern Mandarin for entering a major project, competition, or life stage free of psychological baggage or bureaucratic encumbrances.

history.meaning: attired in light gear without heavy baggage (輕裝) + to advance into battle formation (上陣)
to march into battle travelling light; to tackle a challenge unburdened by mental pressure or excess baggage

morphemes.meaning: to go up to, enter, step onto
battle formation, front line, arena of action

轻装上阵.notes: Frequently used in sports, exams, and showbiz production when a team sheds past failures, ego, or overcomplicated plans to enter a live broadcast or pitch with a clear, unburdened mindset.

rootFamily.gloss: light gear, travelling light (e.g., 轻装简从)
to go into battle; to take the stage or field in person (e.g., 亲自上阵)

轻轻.etymology: Reduplicated adverb and adjective (AA pattern) of 轻 (輕, 'light, soft, gentle').

history.meaning: lightly, gently, softly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 轻轻 (via 萌典)

轻轻松松.etymology: An AABB vivid state-adjective reduplication of the disyllabic coordinative compound 轻松 (qīngsōng, traditional 輕鬆, "light and loose; relaxed, effortless," from 轻 "light in weight" + 松/鬆 "loose, untensed"). In Mandarin morphology, expanding a two-syllable adjective `AB` into `AABB` (轻轻松松) shifts the word from a simple gradable quality to a vivid, emphatic depiction of manner or state—portraying an action accomplished "without breaking a sweat, with complete ease and zero tension," or a lifestyle enjoyed in total leisure.

history.meaning: light in weight and unrestrained; relaxed and free from tension
effortlessly, with complete ease, in a thoroughly relaxed and unhurried manner

轻轻松松.notes: In spoken Beijing and standard Mandarin, the second syllable is often neutral-toned while the third and fourth take high level tones (`qīngqing-sōngsōng`), and it commonly precedes 地 (de) before a verb phrase (e.g., 轻轻松松地搞定 "pull it off effortlessly").

rootFamily.gloss: gently, softly, lightly (reduplication of 轻 alone)

较真.etymology: A Northern Mandarin (especially Beijing dialect) verb-object / verb-complement colloquial compound combining 较 (jiào, traditional 較, "to compare, contend, dispute, measure up against," as in 计较 "to haggle or fuss over") with 真 (zhēn, "what is true, authentic, literal, real"). Originally pronounced with erhua as 较真儿 (jiàozhēnr), it literally means "to contend or insist to the bitter end over whether something is strictly true or exact." From northern vernacular speech, it entered standard Mandarin to describe taking a casual remark too literally, splitting hairs, or refusing to compromise on technicalities.

history.meaning: to compare, contend, or measure against (較) + truth, reality, genuineness (真)
to be dead serious, take things too literally, split hairs, or insist uncompromisingly on exactness

morphemes.meaning: to contend over, measure strictly, fuss over (cf. 计较)

较真.notes: Can be used negatively ("stop being so pedantic / taking a joke so seriously": 别跟喝醉的人较真) or admiringly for a perfectionist producer/craftsman who refuses to cut corners on quality (对作品特别较真).

rootFamily.gloss: to haggle over, fuss about, hold a grudge over trivialities
to pit one's strength or skill against; a showdown

辆.etymology: Phono-semantic character 辆 (輛), combining the vehicle radical 车 (車) + 两 (兩 liǎng, 'a pair'), originally referring to the pair of wheels on a single chariot/cart, hence the standard classifier for wheeled vehicles.

history.meaning: pair of wheels on a cart -> counter for carriages
classifier for cars, buses, bicycles, and wheeled vehicles

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 辆 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to transport, send, convey (retains the original Classical Chinese sense!)
cognates.word: 輸 (shu / yu - e.g., 輸送 yusō)

cognates.meaning: to transport; to lose, be defeated (also loaned as thua)

输.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形声字, traditional 輸) combining the semantic chariot/vehicle radical 车 (chē, traditional 車) with the phonetic 俞 (yú, Old Chinese *lo, Middle Chinese *syu > Mandarin shū). In Classical Chinese, 輸 meant exclusively "to transport, haul by cart, deliver tribute or supplies to another state." The remarkable semantic shift from "transport/deliver goods" to "lose, be defeated (opposite of 赢 yíng)" arose in Han-to-Tang historical and gambling contexts:when a defeated state had to cart and hand over tribute to the victor (or a gambler had to hand over their stakes), "paying over / delivering up" (输) came to mean "losing a match or wager."

history.meaning: to transport by cart; to convey goods, taxes, or tribute to another place
to hand over stakes in a wager; to suffer defeat or lose in a game or contest; to transport
to lose, be defeated (as an independent verb); to transport, input, or transfuse (in compounds like 运输, 输入, 输血)

morphemes.meaning: wheeled cart, carriage, vehicle for hauling

输.notes: Fascinatingly, 输 keeps both its ancient and modern meanings in contemporary Mandarin: standing alone as a verb, 输 always means "to lose (a game/bet)" (opposite of 赢 yíng), whereas inside two-character compounds like 运输 (transport), 输入 (input/import), and 输送 (convey), it retains its ancient sense of "transport/convey"!

rootFamily.gloss: win or lose; victory or defeat (composed of 输 lose + 赢 win)
to transport, haul, carry (retaining the Classical sense of 输)
to admit defeat, concede (服输 / 认输)

辛苦.etymology: A coordinative (parallel) compound (联合式合成词) pairing two of the classical "Five Flavors" (五味): 辛 (xīn, "acrid, pungent, biting, hot," originally a pictograph of a sharp tattooing/punishment chisel, hence stinging pain) and 苦 (kǔ, "bitter," originally the bitter sow-thistle plant). Attested together as early as the *Zuo Zhuan* and Han poetry, the two sharpest, most unpleasant gustatory sensations—"biting/acrid" and "bitter"—were fused metaphorically to describe the physical exhaustion, privation, and arduous toil of soldiers, travelers, and laborers, later also evolving into a polite formula of appreciation for someone's hard work.

history.meaning: acrid/pungent in flavor (辛) and bitter in taste (苦)
subject to biting hardship, physical exhaustion, and arduous toil
hard-working, exhausting, arduous; to work hard / go to great trouble (often used in polite thanks: 辛苦了)

morphemes.meaning: bitter in taste; painful, hard, toilsome

辛苦.notes: In Chinese workplace and production-crew etiquette, 辛苦了！ or 大家辛苦了！ ("You've worked hard! / Thank you for all your hard work!") is the universal warm salutation said by a director or boss when wrapping a shoot or checking in on staff.

rootFamily.gloss: to work industriously and tirelessly through hardship
hardship, suffering, misery; to endure hardship (吃苦)

cognates.meaning: to betray trust, fail to live up to kindness
to betray or be ungrateful for someone's kindness/expectations

辜负.etymology: A coordinative / modifier-head verbal compound originally written 孤负 (gūfù, traditional 孤負) in Han and Six Dynasties texts (such as Li Ling's *Letter in Reply to Su Wu*: 陵虽孤恩, and *Book of Han*), before later orthographic standardization replaced 孤 ("alone, orphaned; to isolate or leave unreciprocated") with the homophonous 辜 (gū, "crime, guilt, fault"). The second morpheme 负 (fù, traditional 負, depicting a person 亻 carrying cowrie shells 贝 on their back) means "to turn one's back on, betray, fail to uphold (a debt of gratitude or trust)." Together, 辜负 means to turn one's back on someone's kindness, trust, or high expectations, leaving their goodwill unrequited.

history.meaning: to leave kindness unreciprocated (孤) and turn one's back on an obligation or trust (負)
to let down, disappoint, fail to live up to (someone's trust, expectations, or nurturing); to waste (good times or talent)

morphemes.meaning: to wrong, leave unrequited (historically written 孤, phonetically replaced by 辜 fault/guilt)
to turn one's back on, betray, fail to live up to (traditional 負)

辜负.notes: Takes positive abstract nouns or people as its object—such as 辜负大家的期望 (fail to live up to everyone's expectations), 辜负好意 (let down someone's kindness), or 不辜负青春 (make the most of / not waste one's youth). Never used for letting down a negative expectation.

rootFamily.gloss: to betray, turn one's back on faith or kindness (忘恩负义)
to bear responsibility; to be in charge of

cognates.meaning: resignation from a post or job
to resign from office or a job

辞职.etymology: A separable verb-object compound (动宾式离合词) uniting 辞 (cí, traditional 辭, originally meaning to untangle a legal dispute or speak eloquent words, extended in Classical Chinese to "take leave of, decline politely, bid farewell to") with the nominal object 职 (zhí, traditional 職, "official duty, post, employment, office"). In imperial Chinese historiography, officials submitted memorials to 辭職 or 辭官 ("decline/relinquish office"); in modern East Asian usage (reinforced across Chinese, Japanese 辞職, and Korean 사직), it is the universal standard verb for resigning from a job or stepping down from a position.

history.meaning: to request permission to relinquish an official court post or public duty
to resign from a job, quit one's position or employment

morphemes.meaning: to decline, take leave of, relinquish, bid farewell to (traditional 辭)
post, office, job, official duty (traditional 職)

辞职.notes: Because 辞职 has an internal verb-object structure, it cannot take a direct object (say 向公司辞职 "resign from the company," never *辞职公司), and aspect particles or modifiers can be inserted between the two characters (e.g., 辞了职 "resigned", 辞过一次职 "resigned once before").

rootFamily.gloss: resignation letter / written notice of resignation
to dismiss, fire, terminate an employee's contract

辞职信.etymology: A three-character right-branching modifier-head compound noun `[辞职 + 信]` formed by attaching the head noun 信 (xìn, originally "trustworthiness, reliable envoy," extended since the Six Dynasties and Tang to mean "letter, written epistle, missive") to the verb-object compound 辞职 (cízhí, traditional 辭職, "to resign from one's post or job"). Replacing the more formal bureaucratic term 辞呈 (cíchéng, "memorial/petition of resignation submitted to a superior"), 辞职信 is the everyday modern Mandarin term for a written or emailed letter of resignation handed to a manager or HR department.

history.meaning: to relinquish office (辭職) + written letter or epistle (信)
letter of resignation; written notice quitting a job

morphemes.meaning: to decline, relinquish, take leave of (traditional 辭)

辞职信.notes: Typical workplace collocations include 写辞职信 (write a resignation letter), 递交辞职信 / 交辞职信 (submit/hand in a resignation letter), and 批辞职信 (approve a resignation letter); its higher-register bureaucratic counterpart is 辞呈 (cíchéng) or 辞职报告.

rootFamily.gloss: formal written resignation submitted to a superior
letter of recommendation; thank-you letter (productive -信 compounds)

辩解.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound (传统作「辯解」, biànjiě) combining 辩 (biàn, 'to dispute, argue, distinguish verbally', graph showing speech 言 between two criminals/knives 辛) and 解 (jiě, 'to untie, loosen, explain', picturing hands removing a horn 角 from an ox 牛 with a knife 刀). In Classical Chinese, it meant to untangle a dispute or explicate a point through argument; in modern Mandarin it shifted slightly toward offering self-justifications or excuses under criticism.

history.meaning: to explicate a dispute; to resolve an accusation through argument
to defend oneself verbally; to offer explanations or excuses

辩解.notes: Often carries a slightly defensive nuance ('make excuses for oneself'), frequently used in negated structures like 无可辩解 (irrefutable, leaving no room for excuses) or 不作辩解.

辩证.etymology: A coordinative compound (传统作「辯證」, biànzhèng) pairing 辩 (biàn, 'to discriminate, argue critically') with 证 (zhèng, 'to verify, demonstrate, prove'). Originally used in medieval Chinese texts and traditional medicine (Often written 辨证) to mean investigating and verifying symptoms or evidence. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, it was adopted via Meiji Japanese philosophical terminology (弁証法, benshōhō) to translate German 'dialektisch' / Greek 'dialektikē' (Hegelian and Marxist dialectics).

history.meaning: to discriminate and verify evidence or clinical symptoms
philosophical translation of German Dialektik / English dialectic
dialectical; examining both sides of a contradiction holistically

辩证.notes: In everyday professional and media discourse, 看问题要辩证 ('one must look at issues dialectically') simply means weighing both pros and cons rather than taking a one-sided view.

边.etymology: Phono-semantic character 边 (邊, simplified via handwritten cursive of 邊), combining the walking/road radical 辶 + 臱 (biān), originally meaning 'walking along the edge of a cliff or borderland', hence 'edge, side, margin, border; localizer suffix; while doing'.

history.meaning: edge, margin, borderland
side, edge, border; locative suffix (-biān/-bian)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 边 (via 萌典)

边框.etymology: A compound of 边 (biān, 'edge') and 框 (kuàng, 'frame', with the wood radical 木). Originally denoting actual wooden frames around structural openings or paintings, it now applies to any distinct border framing an object or image.

history.meaning: border; frame

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 边框

边缘.etymology: Merges 边 (biān, 'edge') and 缘 (yuán, 'hem, fringe', with the silk radical 纟). 缘 originally referred to the reinforced hem woven into a garment's edge. This textile origin evolved into a universal spatial concept for the periphery of any object.

history.meaning: hem of a garment
edge; periphery

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 边缘

边角.etymology: Coordinate noun compound combining 边 (邊, 'edge, side') + 角 ('corner, angle').

history.meaning: edges and corners, leftover trimmings, rim

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 边角 (via 萌典)

达成.etymology: A resultative verb compound (传统作「達成」, dáchéng) formed from 达 (dá, 'to arrive at, reach, penetrate through', containing the walking radical 辶) and 成 (chéng, 'to complete, accomplish, become'). Literally 'to reach and bring to completion', it crystallized in modern administrative, diplomatic, and commercial prose (reinforced by shared Sino-Japanese usage 達成) to denote successfully concluding an agreement, consensus, or target.

history.meaning: to reach unhindered (達); to bring to completion (成)
to reach (an agreement, consensus, deal) or achieve (a goal)

达成.notes: A high-frequency formal transitive verb in business and showbiz negotiations; standard collocations include 达成协议 (reach an agreement), 达成共识 (reach a consensus), and 达成目标 (achieve a goal).

rootFamily.gloss: reach, arrive at (a metric or destination)

迁就.etymology: A serial/coordinative verb compound (传统作「遷就」, qiānjiù) composed of 迁 (qiān, 'to move, shift, relocate one's position') and 就 (jiù, 'to approach, go toward, accommodate oneself to'). Attested in Han and Song dynasty historical prose, it literally means 'to shift one's own stance in order to move toward another', hence yielding to, humoring, or making concessions to someone's wishes or flaws.

history.meaning: to shift one's position to approach or adapt to another circumstance or person
to accommodate, yield to, indulge or humor someone uncritically

morphemes.meaning: approach, draw near to, adapt to

迁就.notes: Often implies compromising one's own principles or standards to humor someone else (e.g., 一味迁就, 'blindly accommodating/indulging someone').

rootFamily.gloss: make do with, put up with

过.etymology: Phono-semantic character 过 (過), combining the movement radical 辶 + phonetic 咼 (guō / Old Chinese *kʷˤaj-s), meaning 'to pass by, cross over, spend (time/holidays), exceed, fault' and, when unstressed (guo), the experiential aspect particle ('have ever done').

history.meaning: to pass by, cross over, exceed; transgression
to cross, pass, spend time (guò); experiential aspect marker (guo)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 过 (via 萌典)

过不过激.etymology: An A-not-A (正反问) interrogative construction formed by reduplicating the initial morpheme of the disyllabic adjective 过激 (guòjī, 传统作「過激」, 'excessively radical or aggressive') around the negator 不 (bù): 过 + 不 + 过激. In Mandarin morphosyntax, disyllabic adjectives XY regularly form polar questions via the X-不-XY pattern ('is it XY or not?'), testing whether an action or statement crosses the threshold into extremity.

history.meaning: excessively fierce, extreme, or radical
whether or not something is overly aggressive/extreme (A-not-A question form)

过不过激.notes: Demonstrates Mandarin's productive 'X-不-XY' A-not-A question pattern for two-syllable adjectives; used either as a direct question ('Is that too extreme?') or embedded after verbs like 看/觉得 ('see whether it is too aggressive').

过于.etymology: A verb-preposition lexicalization (传统作「過於」, guòyú) combining 过 (guò, 'to pass beyond, exceed') and the Classical Chinese locative/comparative preposition 于 (yú, 'in, at, than, with respect to'). In Classical Chinese, 过于 X meant 'to surpass X' (e.g., 苛政猛于虎 / 莫过于此, 'nothing surpasses this'). When followed by a stative verb or adjective, it grammaticalized into a degree adverb meaning 'to an extent surpassing the norm; overly, excessively'.

history.meaning: to surpass or exceed (someone/something) in degree
overly, excessively, too (degree adverb)

过于.notes: More formal and written in register than 太 (tài); unlike 太, 过于 cannot take sentence-final 了 and almost always precedes two-syllable adjectives or psychological verbs (e.g., 过于敏感, 过于担心).

rootFamily.gloss: nothing surpasses this; couldn't be more...

cognates.meaning: to pass through customs or a checkpoint

过关.etymology: A separable verb-object (VO) compound (传统作「過關」, guòguān) joining 过 (guò, 'to cross, pass through') and 关 (guān, 'mountain pass, frontier checkpoint, bolted gate', originally picturing a wooden crossbar 𢇇 inside gates 門). Literally 'to pass through a guarded frontier checkpoint', it underwent metaphorical extension in vernacular Chinese (such as the idiom 过五关斩六将) to mean passing a test, clearing a review hurdle, or meeting quality standards.

history.meaning: to pass through a frontier gate, toll barrier, or mountain pass
to pass a test, clear an inspection hurdle, or meet required standards

过关.notes: In media production and workplace settings, 过关 means getting a proposal/edit approved by higher-ups or meeting quality standards (e.g., 质量过关, 技术过关). Because it is a VO compound, modifiers can be inserted (过不了关, 'cannot pass muster').

过分.etymology: Originally a verb-object compound (传统作「過分」or「過份」, guòfèn) formed from 过 (guò, 'to exceed, overstep') and 分 (fèn, fourth tone, 'one's allotted portion, proper duty, social station, or moral bounds', as in 本分 běnfèn). In Classical Chinese, 过分 meant 'to step beyond one's proper allotment or bounds of propriety'. Over time it grammaticalized into a stative adjective and degree adverb meaning 'excessive, unreasonable, going too far'.

history.meaning: to exceed one's proper lot, station, or bounds of propriety
excessive, crossing the line (adj.); overly (adv.)

过分.notes: Notice that 分 here is underlyingly fourth tone (fèn, 'proper bounds/lot', often neutralized to guòfen in speech), not first tone (fēn, 'divide'). Calling someone's behavior 太过分了 means 'that's crossing the line / going way too far'.

rootFamily.gloss: one's proper duty or role; well-behaved

过半.etymology: A verb-object compound (传统作「過半」, guòbàn) combining 过 (guò, 'to surpass, exceed, pass beyond') and 半 (bàn, 'half', originally depicting an ox 牛 split in two by eight 八, 'to divide'). Attested in Classical Chinese historiography (such as *Shiji* and *Zizhi Tongjian*), it concisely expresses that a quantity, vote share, or time duration has crossed the fifty-percent mark.

history.meaning: to exceed half; more than half (of troops, casualties, or time)
to pass the halfway mark (of a schedule, project, or majority vote)

过半.notes: Concise, slightly formal verb used in project management, voting, and scheduling (e.g., 赛程已经过半, 'the competition is already past the halfway point'; 人数过半, 'quorum/majority reached').

过去.etymology: Compound directional verb and time noun combining 过 (過, 'to cross over, pass by') + 去 ('to go away from the speaker'); as a noun/adverb means 'in the past, formerly', and as a verb/complement (guòqu) 'to go over, pass away/faint'.

history.meaning: to go over, pass by; the past, formerly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 过去 (via 萌典)

过大.etymology: A modifier-head stative compound (传统作「過大」, guòdà) composed of the adverbial prefixoid 过 (guò, 'exceedingly, overly, surpassing the proper norm') and the stative verb/adjective 大 (dà, 'large, great, intense'). Following a productive Classical-to-Modern Mandarin pattern (過 + monosyllabic adjective, such as 过高, 过小, 过快), it denotes size, scale, pressure, or risk that exceeds acceptable or safe parameters.

history.meaning: exceedingly large; surpassing proper scale or magnitude
excessively large, oversized, too great (of pressure, gap, or volume)

过大.notes: Belongs to a formal/written register compared to 太大; commonly collocates with abstract nouns in professional contexts, such as 压力过大 (excessive stress/pressure), 风险过大 (excessive risk), or 差距过大 (too large a gap).

过奖.etymology: A modifier-head verbal compound (传统作「過獎」, guòjiǎng) formed from 过 (guò, 'excessively, beyond what is deserved') and 奖 (jiǎng, 'to praise, commend, encourage, reward'). Literally 'to praise beyond one's actual merit', it became conventionalized in polite Chinese social etiquette as a self-deprecating response to compliments ('you praise me too highly' / 'you flatter me').

history.meaning: to commend or praise someone beyond their due merit
you flatter me; to overpraise (polite formulaic response to a compliment)

过奖.notes: Used almost exclusively as a polite, modest formula when accepting a compliment (您过奖了, 'You flatter me / You're too kind'), parallel to 哪里哪里 or 谬赞.

过家家.etymology: A colloquial verb-object phrase (传统作「過家家」, guòjiājiā) combining 过 (guò, 'to pass time, live a life, manage a household', as in 过日子 guò rìzi, 'to live day-to-day domestic life') with the reduplicated noun 家家 (jiājiā, 'little family/household', using child-directed diminutive reduplication). Literally 'playing at running a little household', it refers to the children's make-believe game of playing house.

history.meaning: to manage household affairs and live everyday domestic life
to play house (children's role-playing game); figuratively, to treat serious work like child's play

过家家.notes: In workplace and showbiz dramas, 过家家 is frequently used sarcastically to scold amateurs or unprofessional behavior: 你以为这是小孩子过家家吗？ ('Do you think this is kids playing house?!').

rootFamily.gloss: live one's life, get by day-to-day

过度.etymology: Originally a verb-object compound (传统作「過度」, guòdù) joining 过 (guò, 'to exceed, surpass') and 度 (dù, 'measure, standard, proper limit', originally picturing a hand 又 measuring length). Attested in Warring States and Han philosophical texts, 过度 literally meant 'to transgress the proper measure or norm'. It subsequently lexicalized as an adjective and adverb meaning 'excessive(ly), over-'. Do not confuse with its homophone 过渡 (guòdù, 'to ferry across; transition').

history.meaning: to exceed the proper standard, measure, or legal/moral limit
excessive, immoderate; excessively, over- (modifier of verbs/nouns)

过度.notes: Watch out for the exact homophone 过渡 (with 氵, meaning 'transition / interim', as in 过渡期 'transition period'). 过度 (without 氵) means 'excessive / over-' (e.g., 过度劳累 'overworked', 过度解读 'over-interpret').

过得.etymology: A verb + structural particle sequence (传统作「過得」, guòde) composed of the verb 过 (guò, 'to pass time, spend one's days, live through') and the post-verbal complement marker 得 (de, derived by grammaticalization from the Classical verb 得 dé, 'to obtain, manage to'). This frame introduces either a descriptive complement of manner/state (e.g., 过得很好, 'living very well') or a potential complement (e.g., 过得去, 'able to pass muster / get by').

history.meaning: to pass through and attain/manage (serial verb construction)
to live/fare (in a certain state, taking a descriptive or potential complement)

morphemes.meaning: structural particle linking a verb to a state or potential complement

过得.notes: Essential in everyday greetings and reflections on life: 你最近过得怎么样？ ('How have you been doing lately?') or 日子过得很充实 ('leading a very fulfilling life').

rootFamily.gloss: passable, can get by; feel okay about
spend (a holiday or period of time)

过意不去.etymology: An idiomatic four-character vernacular construction (传统作「過意不去」, guòyìbùqù) built from 过意 (guòyì, 'to let something pass through one's mind/conscience comfortably') and the negative potential directional complement 不去 (bùqù, 'cannot go through / cannot pass'). Originating in Ming–Qing vernacular fiction (such as *Hongloumeng*), it literally means 'one's mind/conscience cannot get past it', hence feeling apologetic, uneasy, or guilty about troubling someone or receiving an undeserved favor.

history.form: 過意不去 / 心裡過不去
history.meaning: one's heart/mind cannot move past a matter; feeling uneasy in conscience
to feel apologetic, feel bad or embarrassed about troubling someone

过意不去.notes: More heartfelt and personal than the routine apology 不好意思; often paired with 让您破费/麻烦您，真过意不去 ('I feel really bad about putting you to such expense/trouble'). Its positive counterpart 过意得去 is rare; people usually say 心里过得去.

rootFamily.gloss: cannot get over it; make things hard for someone

过敏.etymology: A modifier-head compound (传统作「過敏」, guòmǐn) combining 过 (guò, 'excessively, overly') and 敏 (mǐn, 'quick, acute, sensitive, reactive'). Coined in modern East Asian medical terminology (alongside Japanese 過敏 kabin, 'hypersensitivity') to translate Western clinical concepts of 'hyperesthesia / hypersensitivity' and immunological 'allergy' (Greek *allos* + *ergon*), literally 'to be overly reactive/sensitive'. It later broadened back into everyday figurative speech for emotional touchiness.

history.meaning: nervous or physiological hypersensitivity (calque of Western medical 'hypersensitivity')
to have an allergic reaction; figuratively, to be overly touchy or hypersensitive

过敏.notes: To state what you are allergic to, Mandarin uses the preposition 对 before the verb: 我对花生/花粉过敏 ('I am allergic to peanuts/pollen'). Also used figuratively: 政治过敏 or 神经太过敏 ('too touchy/paranoid').

rootFamily.gloss: keen, sharp, acute (of senses or insight)

过来.etymology: Compound directional verb and post-verbal complement combining 过 (過, 'to cross over, pass') + 来 (來, 'to come toward the speaker').

history.meaning: to come over, come here; directional/restorative complement

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 过来 (via 萌典)

过渡.etymology: Compound of 过 ('pass across') + 渡 ('ferry across a river', water radical 氵 + 度 *dù*). Originally literal ('cross a river at a ferry'), it developed a rich figurative sense in literature and music for a connecting bridge or transition passage (过渡段) linking two sections.

history.meaning: cross a river by ferry
transition; musical bridge

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 过渡

过激.etymology: A modifier-head stative compound (传统作「過激」, guòjī) composed of 过 (guò, 'excessively, beyond bounds') and 激 (jī, 'water surging violently against an obstacle; fierce, vehement, aroused'). Attested in Song–Ming literary criticism for overly vehement rhetoric, its modern political and psychological sense ('radical, extremist, overly aggressive') was strongly reinforced by Meiji Japanese 過激 (kageki, used to translate 'radical/extremist', as in 過激派).

history.meaning: overly vehement or fierce in tone or argument (derived from rushing water 激)
political radicalism or extremism (translation of Western 'radical')
too aggressive, extreme, or radical (of words, reactions, or behavior)

过激.notes: Frequently modifies nouns like 言论 (remarks), 行为 (behavior), or 反应 (reaction) in media and PR crises—e.g., 情绪过激，做出了过激行为 ('became overly emotional and acted too aggressively').

过生日.etymology: A verb-object (VO) phrase (传统作「過生日」, guò shēngrì) pairing the transitive verb 过 (guò, 'to pass through, observe, celebrate a temporal milestone or festival', as in 过年, 过节) with the compound noun 生日 (shēngrì, 'birth-day', from 生 'to give birth / be born' + 日 'day'). In Chinese temporal metaphors, one 'passes through' or 'crosses' (过) an annual festival or birthday by observing its rituals.

history.meaning: day of birth (生日, attested since Tang); to observe a seasonal festival (過節)
to celebrate or observe one's birthday

morphemes.meaning: pass, observe, celebrate (a holiday or milestone)

过生日.notes: To say 'celebrate someone's birthday for them', use 给/替 someone 过生日 (e.g., 今晚大家给你过生日). For respected elders, the more formal VO phrase 祝寿 (zhùshòu) or 过寿 is often preferred.

过目.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound (传统作「過目」, guòmù) combining 过 (guò, 'to pass before, cause to pass across') and the Classical Chinese word 目 (mù, 'eye', pictograph of a human eye). Attested in Six Dynasties and Tang texts (e.g., 过目不忘, 'never forgetting what has passed before one's eyes'), it literally means 'to let a document or object pass before the eyes'—used both for rapid perusal and as an honorific verb inviting a superior or client to review something.

history.meaning: to pass before one's eyes; to scan or read through once (e.g., 過目不忘)
to look over, inspect, or review (polite/deferential usage in business and officialdom)

morphemes.meaning: pass across, cause to pass through

过目.notes: A staple of polite workplace and media-production etiquette when handing a script, contract, or cut to a director or boss: 请您过目 ('Please look this over / For your review'). Also appears in the famous chengyu 过目不忘 ('photographic memory').

rootFamily.gloss: have a photographic memory (lit. pass the eyes and never forget)
witness firsthand, see with one's own eyes

过程.etymology: Originally a verb-object or coordinative spatial compound (传统作「過程」, guòchéng) combining 过 (guò, 'to pass through, traverse') and 程 (chéng, 'a unit of measurement, a stage of a journey, a road or itinerary'). In pre-modern Chinese, 程 denoted stages along a post-road; in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, via Meiji Japanese 過程 (katei), it was standardized as a noun translating English/German 'process'—the temporal sequence of stages through which a phenomenon develops.

history.meaning: stages traversed along a journey or itinerary
scientific and philosophical translation of Western 'process'
process, course of events, progression over time

morphemes.meaning: stage of a journey, route, procedure, measure

过程.notes: Frequently appears in the frame 在……(的)过程中 ('in the process/course of...'), contrasting the ongoing journey (过程) with the final outcome (结果).

过量.etymology: Originally a verb-object compound (传统作「過量」, guòliàng) joining 过 (guò, 'to exceed, surpass') and 量 (liàng, fourth tone, 'capacity, measured quantity, allowance, tolerance', especially for food, drink, or medicine). Attested in Tang–Song poetry and medical writings (where 过量 meant 'to drink beyond one's capacity' or 'exceed the prescribed dosage'), it functions in modern Mandarin as an adjective or adverb meaning 'excessive in quantity; overdosed'.

history.meaning: to exceed one's drinking capacity or a measured allowance
excessive in dosage or quantity; to take an overdose (of medicine, alcohol, or additives)

过量.notes: Whereas 过度 applies to abstract intensity or behavior ('overly tired'), 过量 specifically targets measurable physical quantities, dosages, or intake (e.g., 饮酒过量 'excessive drinking', 服药过量 'drug overdose').

cognates.meaning: to inquire into, concern oneself with

过问.etymology: A serial/coordinative verb compound (传统作「過問」, guòwèn) combining 过 (guò, 'to come over, pay a visit, pass by') and 问 (wèn, 'to ask after, inquire into'). In Classical and vernacular Chinese, it originally meant 'to stop by and inquire after someone's well-being'. By the Ming–Qing period, it shifted toward 'to look into, take an active hand in, or concern oneself with (an affair)', frequently used in the negative to mean staying out of a matter.

history.meaning: to pass by to visit and ask after someone
to inquire into, concern oneself with, or intervene in administrative/personal matters

过问.notes: Most commonly used in negative or restrictive contexts (如 不予过问, 从不过问, 无权过问) to mean 'stay out of it / not micromanage or meddle in someone else's domain'.

迈.etymology: Simplified from 邁, combining the walking radical 辶 with phonetic 萬 (*wàn*, Middle Chinese *maejH*). In Classical Chinese it meant 'travel far; advance boldly'; in modern Mandarin it specifically denotes lifting the foot and taking a stride (迈步).

history.meaning: march forward; travel far
take a step; stride

迎.etymology: Phono-semantic character 迎, combining the movement radical 辶 + phonetic 卬 (áng / yíng, 'to look up to, face'), meaning 'to go out to meet, face toward, welcome, receive'.

history.meaning: to go out to meet and receive a guest
to welcome, greet, go to meet, face directly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 迎 (via 萌典)

迎接.etymology: Coordinate verb compound combining 迎 ('to go out to meet, welcome') + 接 ('to receive, meet, connect').

history.meaning: to go out to meet, welcome, greet

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 迎接 (via 萌典)

迎来.etymology: A verb-directional compound (传统作「迎來」, yínglái) formed from 迎 (yíng, 'to go out to meet, face, welcome, receive') and the directional complement 来 (lái, 'hither, toward the speaker/present moment'). Literally 'to welcome as it arrives here', it evolved from physical reception of guests (as in 迎来送往, 'welcoming arrivals and seeing off departures') into a transitive verb meaning to usher in or greet a new era, opportunity, guest, or climax.

history.meaning: to go out to greet arriving guests (paired with seeing off departing ones)
to usher in, greet, or welcome (a milestone, turning point, or guest)

morphemes.meaning: go to meet, greet, receive, welcome
come hither, arrive toward the vantage point

迎来.notes: A favorite verb in journalism, broadcasting, and showbiz hosting to build anticipation: 节目迎来了高潮 ('the show ushered in its climax') or 迎来转机 ('usher in a turning point').

rootFamily.gloss: meet, greet, embrace (a challenge or occasion)

运作.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound (传统作「運作」, yùnzuò) joining 运 (yùn, 'to revolve, transport, wield, move strategically') and 作 (zuò, 'to act, work, make, operate'). In medieval Chinese texts, 运作 described the dynamic movement of cosmic forces (qi) or physical labor. In late 20th-century Mandarin (initially popularized in Taiwan and Hong Kong business/media usage), it acquired the modern sense of how an organization, capital market, or behind-the-scenes campaign operates or is strategically maneuvered.

history.meaning: cyclical movement and activity of natural forces; physical labor or exertion
to operate, function (of a system/team); to maneuver or manage behind the scenes (of capital, PR, or projects)

运作.notes: In the entertainment and corporate world (*幕后之王*), 运作 often carries a savvy behind-the-scenes nuance: 资本运作 (capital maneuvering), 暗箱运作 (backroom maneuvering), or 幕后运作 (behind-the-scenes orchestration).

rootFamily.gloss: run, operate (of machinery, software, or celestial bodies)

运动.etymology: A coordinative compound (传统作「運動」, yùndòng) combining 运 (yùn, 'to revolve, circulate, transport') and 动 (dòng, 'to move, stir, act'). In Classical Chinese, it meant the revolving motion of celestial bodies or the deployment of troops. During the Meiji era in Japan, 運動 (undō) was repurposed to translate English 'motion' (physics), 'physical exercise / athletics', and 'social/political movement'—senses that were re-borrowed wholesale into modern Chinese at the turn of the 20th century.

history.meaning: revolving motion of celestial bodies, seasons, or military forces
calque of Western 'motion' (physics), 'athletic exercise', and 'political/social movement'
sports, physical exercise; physical motion; organized campaign or movement; (neutral tone yùndong) to pull strings

morphemes.meaning: revolve, circulate, move in an orbit

运动.notes: Beyond 'sports/exercise' and 'social movement', note an older colloquial Mandarin usage with a neutral-toned second syllable (yùndong): 'to lobby or pull strings behind the scenes'.

运气.etymology: Compound originating in ancient Chinese cosmology and medicine (運氣, 'the revolving movement of the five phases and six atmospheric qi'), which shifted in vernacular Mandarin (yùnqi) to 'luck, fortune, destiny' (while retaining yùnqì for 'directing vital breath in martial arts/singing').

history.meaning: revolving cycle of cosmic qi
luck, fortune

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 运气 (via 萌典)

运营.etymology: A coordinative compound (传统作「運營」, yùnyíng) pairing 运 (yùn, 'to revolve, deploy, put into motion') with 营 (yíng, 'to lay out a camp, plan, manage, conduct business'). While both morphemes are ancient Chinese, the compound 运营 crystallized in modern commercial and institutional Chinese (alongside Sino-Japanese 運営 un'ei) to denote the ongoing day-to-day management, monetization, and audience cultivation of an enterprise, media channel, or digital platform.

history.meaning: to deploy/move (運) and to lay out/manage (營, originally military encampments)
institutional administration and commercial operations management
operations (business, media, or internet user/content operations); to run operations

运营.notes: In modern Chinese tech, television, and entertainment industries, 运营 is a core job function and department (e.g., 内容运营 'content operations', 用户运营 'user operations', 节目运营 'show operations'), distinct from pure production (制作).

rootFamily.gloss: do business, open hours (营业时间)

cognates.meaning: operation, movement (of vehicles, ships, or celestial bodies)

运行.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound (传统作「運行」, yùnháng) formed from 运 (yùn, 'to revolve, move in a cycle') and 行 (xíng, 'to walk, travel, move along a course'). Attested as early as the *Yijing* (Book of Changes: 日月运行, 'the sun and moon move in their courses'), it originally described celestial orbits and seasonal cycles. In modern Mandarin, it extended naturally to the smooth, regular execution of trains, machinery, institutional mechanisms, and computer software.

history.meaning: cyclical movement of the sun, moon, stars, and cosmic qi along their courses
to run, operate, or execute along a regular track or protocol (of celestial bodies, transit, systems, or software)

morphemes.meaning: revolve, circulate, move in an orbit
move, travel, proceed along a course (xíng)

运行.notes: Compare the "运-" quartet: 运动 = physical motion/exercise; 运行 = systematic/mechanical/software execution along set rules; 运作 = strategic/organizational working; 运营 = commercial/platform operations and management.

rootFamily.gloss: revolve, turn round, operate (of machines or capital)

近.etymology: Phono-semantic character 近, combining the movement/distance radical 辶 + phonetic 斤 (jīn / Old Chinese *N-kərʔ), meaning 'near in space or time, close, intimate, approximately'.

history.meaning: near, close, approach
near, close, recent, intimate

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 近 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: recent state, how someone has been lately

近况.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (传统作「近況」, jìnkuàng) combining 近 (jìn, 'near in space or time, recent') and 况 (kuàng, 'circumstance, condition, state of affairs', originally meaning cold water or comparison). Emerging in late imperial epistolary Chinese and reinforced by shared Sino-Japanese usage (近況 kinkyō), it means 'the state of affairs in recent times'—specifically how a person or enterprise has been doing lately.

history.meaning: recent circumstances or personal state (used in letter-writing and inquiries)
recent condition, current situation, how someone has been lately

近况.notes: Slightly formal and concise; often used when catching up with acquaintances or reporting on celebrity updates in entertainment news (e.g., 透露近况 'reveal how one has been lately', 近况如何 'how have things been recently?').

近路.etymology: The noun '近路' (jìnlù, shortcut) combines '近' (near, close) and '路' (road, path). The concept of finding a more direct route is universal. '近路' literally means 'a nearer road'. It is a common vernacular term in spoken Mandarin, contrasting with '远路' (a roundabout or longer route). The act of taking a shortcut is frequently expressed with the verb '抄' (to take a shortcut, to transcribe), forming the very common phrase '抄近路'.

history.meaning: shortcut

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 近路

还.etymology: Phono-semantic character 还 (還), combining the movement radical 辶 + phonetic 睘 (qióng / huán), originally meaning 'to turn around and return, give back' (retained in the verbal reading huán), and grammaticalized in vernacular Mandarin under the reading hái ('still, yet, also, even more').

history.meaning: to return, turn back, give back
still, yet, also, even (hái); to return, give back (huán)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 还 (via 萌典)

还好.etymology: Adverbial and predicative compound combining 还 (還 hái, 'still, passably, fortunately') + 好 ('good, well, fine').

history.meaning: fortunately, luckily; not bad, passable

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 还好 (via 萌典)

还是.etymology: Compound adverb and disjunctive conjunction combining 还 (還 hái, 'still, after all') + copula/focus marker 是 ('is, indeed'); used both for 'still, all the same, had better' and in alternative questions ('or').

history.meaning: still, nevertheless, had better; or (in questions)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 还是 (via 萌典)

还有.etymology: Additive verbal and conjunctional compound combining 还 (還 hái, 'still, also, in addition') + 有 ('there is, have').

history.meaning: still have; furthermore, in addition, and also

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 还有 (via 萌典)

还要.etymology: A disyllabic adverbial-modal sequence (传统作「還要」, háiyào) combining the additive/continuative adverb 还 (hái, 'still, even more, in addition', grammaticalized from the verb huán 'to return, come back around') and the modal verb 要 (yào, 'to want to, need to, be going to', originally 'waist' 腰, then 'to seek/demand' yāo). Together they express either an additional desire/requirement ('also want/need to') or a comparative intensification ('even more than...').

history.meaning: furthermore/still (還) + to demand, need, or intend (要)
also want/need to; still going to; even more (in comparisons: 比 X 还要 + Adj)

morphemes.meaning: still, also, in addition, even more (hái)
want to, need to, be going to

还要.notes: Has two primary syntactic functions: (1) before a verb phrase: 'also want/need to do X' (我还要再改一版, 'I still need to revise one more draft'); (2) in comparisons after 比: 比昨天还要忙 ('even busier than yesterday').

rootFamily.gloss: still is; or (in questions); had better

这.etymology: Proximal demonstrative ('this'), pairing with a measure word before nouns (这个 'this one', 这间房 'this room'). Written with the movement component 辶 plus 言, 這 emerged in Tang–Song vernacular Chinese (alongside earlier 者) to replace Classical 此 ('this').

history.meaning: demonstrative 'this'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 這 (via 萌典)

这一首.etymology: A demonstrative-numeral-classifier phrase (这 + 一 + 首, 传统作「這一首」, zhè yī shǒu) composed of the proximal demonstrative 这 (zhè, 'this', evolved in Tang–Song vernacular from 之/者), the numeral 一 (yī, 'one, single'), and the measure word 首 (shǒu, originally 'head', pictograph of a head with hair). Because Classical Chinese poems and songs were indexed by their 'heading' or opening line (詩一首), 首 grammaticalized by the Six Dynasties and Tang period into the standard classifier for poems and songs.

history.meaning: one poem or song (counted by its 'head' or opening title/stanza)
this single song or poem (proximal demonstrative + numeral + classifier)

morphemes.meaning: measure word for songs and poems (originally 'head')

这一首.notes: In music production and variety shows, the head noun 歌 ('song') is frequently omitted after 这一首 when context is clear (e.g., 这一首编曲太棒了, 'The arrangement on this one [song] is fantastic'). In rapid speech, 一 is often dropped (这首歌).

rootFamily.gloss: premiere, debut broadcast (of a song or show)

这个.etymology: Demonstrative-classifier compound combining proximal demonstrative 这 (這 zhè / zhèi, 'this', emerging in Tang–Song vernacular from 遮/者) + general classifier 个 (個/箇, 'unit, individual').

history.meaning: this one, this; conversational filler ('uh, well')

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 这个 (via 萌典)

这么.etymology: Demonstrative manner/degree adverb combining proximal 这 (這, 'this') + suffix 么 (麼, 'way, degree', descended from medieval 沒/摩), meaning 'so, such, in this way'.

history.meaning: so, such, like this, this way

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 这么 (via 萌典)

这么久.etymology: A modifier-head temporal phrase combining the colloquial degree demonstrative 这么 (zhème, 'so, to this degree', formed from proximal demonstrative 这 [trad. 這] + vernacular suffix 么 [trad. 麼]) and the stative temporal adjective 久 (jiǔ, Old Chinese *kʷjəʔ, 'long in duration'). Emerging in Early Mandarin vernacular, it intensifies temporal duration ('for such a long time').

history.meaning: long in time, enduring
to this extent of duration, so long
for such a long time

这么久.notes: Commonly placed after a verb as a duration complement (e.g., 等了这么久 'waited for so long') or before a verb phrase to emphasize elapsed time.

这事.etymology: A determiner-noun compound with classifier ellipsis, pairing the proximal demonstrative 这 (zhè, trad. 這, emerging in Tang–Song vernacular from earlier 遮/者, 'this') directly with 事 (shì, Old Chinese *dzrəʔ-s, 'affair, matter, business'). Omitting the classifier 件 (jiàn) yields a brisk, conversational reference to an immediate affair or issue.

history.meaning: this affair, this matter
this matter (colloquial demonstrative without classifier)
this matter, this business

这事.notes: Frequently spoken with erhua in northern Mandarin (这事儿 zhèshìr) in casual dialogue when referring to a tricky situation or workplace development.

这些.etymology: Plural proximal demonstrative combining 这 (這, 'this') + plural/indefinite quantifier 些 ('a small amount, some, several').

history.meaning: these

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 这些 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: matter, case, item (Sino-Japanese cognate of 件)

这件.etymology: A demonstrative-classifier construction combining the proximal demonstrative 这 (zhè, trad. 這, 'this') with the nominal classifier 件 (jiàn, Middle Chinese *gjenX, originally 'to divide, itemize', graphically 亻 'person' + 牛 'ox', referencing partitioning livestock). By Tang–Song times, 件 grammaticalized into the standard classifier for discrete matters, garments, and items.

history.meaning: to divide, separate item, article
this item, this matter
this (matter, piece of clothing, or item)

这件.notes: Pairs most frequently with abstract affairs (这件事 'this matter'), clothing (这件衣服 'this garment'), or luggage/gifts; can stand alone anaphorically when the noun is understood.

cognates.meaning: part, portion, share (Sino-Vietnamese cognate of 分/份)

这份.etymology: A demonstrative-classifier compound composed of the proximal demonstrative 这 (zhè, trad. 這, 'this') and the classifier 份 (fèn, Middle Chinese *bjunH, derived by adding the person radical 亻 to 分 'to divide', denoting an allotted share, portion, or copy). In modern usage it classifies documents, contracts, jobs, and abstract emotional commitments.

history.meaning: allotted share, portion, lot
this share, this copy/portion
this (document, contract, job, or sentiment)

这份.notes: Essential in media and corporate contexts for contracts, proposals, and scripts (这份合同 'this contract', 这份策划案 'this proposal'), as well as abstract feelings (这份心意 'this kindness').

这会儿.etymology: Colloquial northern Mandarin time expression combining 这 (這, 'this') + 会儿 (會兒 huìr, erhua diminutive of 会 'moment, brief interval of time').

history.meaning: at this moment, right now

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 这会儿 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: rank, position, counter for ghosts/persons (Sino-Japanese cognate of 位)

这位.etymology: A polite demonstrative-classifier compound joining 这 (zhè, trad. 這, 'this') and 位 (wèi, Old Chinese *ɢʷrəp-s, graphically 亻 'person' + 立 'to stand', originally 'court standing place, official rank, seat'). Through metonymy—addressing a person by their honorable seat or rank rather than directly—位 grammaticalized into the deferential classifier for people.

history.meaning: place of standing at court, official rank, throne, seat
this honorable person / gentleman / lady
this (polite determiner/pronoun for a person)

这位.notes: Used both before a human noun (这位老师 'this teacher/mentor') and standalone as a polite pronoun when introducing someone on stage or in meetings (这位是... 'This is...').

这儿.etymology: Northern Mandarin locative pronoun combining proximal demonstrative 这 (這, 'this') + erhua locative/diminutive suffix 儿 (兒 -r, often contracted from 这里).

history.meaning: here, this place

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 这儿 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: house, family, establishment (Sino-Japanese cognate of 家)

这家.etymology: A demonstrative-classifier compound formed from 这 (zhè, trad. 這, 'this') and 家 (jiā, Old Chinese *kˤra, graphically 宀 'roof' + 豕 'pig', originally 'household, family, clan estate'). Because traditional Chinese commercial enterprises were family-operated establishments, 家 extended naturally into the standard classifier for businesses, companies, studios, and institutions.

history.meaning: household, clan estate, school of thought
this household, this shop/establishment
this (company, firm, shop, or media outlet)

这家.notes: Standard determiner for companies, agencies, TV networks, restaurants, and hospitals (这家公司 'this company', 这家媒体 'this media outlet').

这是.etymology: A subject-copula phrase combining the proximal demonstrative pronoun 这 (zhè, trad. 這, 'this') with the copular verb 是 (shì, Old Chinese *djeʔ). In Old Chinese, 是 was a demonstrative pronoun ('this') and an adjective ('right, correct'); through topic-comment reanalysis in Late Han and Medieval Chinese, 是 grammaticalized into the equational copula ('to be').

history.meaning: this; right, correct (pre-copular demonstrative)
this is (demonstrative + equational copula)
this is

这是.notes: Used to introduce people, present documents or props, or open explanatory/rhetorical clauses (这是什么意思？ 'What is the meaning of this?').

cognates.meaning: period, term, issue (Sino-Japanese cognate of 期)

这期.etymology: A demonstrative-classifier compound uniting 这 (zhè, trad. 這, 'this') and 期 (qī, Old Chinese *g(r)ə, graphically 其 phonetic + 月 'moon/month' semantic, originally 'appointed time, full cycle of time'). In modern publishing and broadcasting, 期 classifies serialized installments positioned at regular intervals, such as magazine issues, training cohorts, and television episodes.

history.meaning: appointed time, stipulated date, cycle
this scheduled period or issue (of a periodical)
this episode (of a show), this issue (of a publication)

这期.notes: In television production (*幕后之王*), 期 specifically refers to an episode or installment of a variety/reality show (这期节目 'this episode of the program'), whereas 集 (jí) is used for scripted drama episodes.

这样.etymology: Demonstrative pronoun, adjective, and adverb combining 这 (這, 'this') + 样 (樣, 'pattern, kind, appearance, manner').

history.meaning: like this, this kind, so, thus

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 这样 (via 萌典)

这样吧.etymology: A pragmatic discourse phrase formed from the demonstrative manner pro-form 这样 (zhèyàng, trad. 這樣, 'this manner/way', where 样 originally denoted an oak-acorn pattern or mold) plus the sentence-final modal particle 吧 (ba, grammaticalized via phonetic reduction of 罢 bà, 'to cease, finish'). Together they signal a negotiative proposal: 'let us settle on doing it this way'.

history.meaning: this pattern, this manner or way
let it be this way then; how about this

这样吧.notes: A classic workplace and negotiation pivot used when floating a compromise or practical solution after a stalemate ('Tell you what / How about this...').

cognates.meaning: order, sequence, time (Sino-Japanese cognate of 次)

这次.etymology: A demonstrative-classifier compound combining 这 (zhè, trad. 這, 'this') and 次 (cì, Old Chinese *s-nhi[t]-s, originally 'temporary encampment in sequence, order of lodging', hence 'sequence, turn, occurrence'). As a verbal and nominal classifier, 次 enumerates discrete occurrences or instances ('this time, this occasion').

history.meaning: halting place on a march, sequence, second in order
this turn, this occasion
this time, this occasion

这次.notes: Functions both as a standalone temporal noun ('this time around') and as a determiner modifying an event noun (这次合作 'this collaboration', 这次录影 'this recording session').

这歌.etymology: A demonstrative-noun phrase with classifier ellipsis, pairing the proximal demonstrative 这 (zhè, trad. 這, 'this') directly with 歌 (gē, Old Chinese *kˤaj, graphically 哥 phonetic + 欠 'open mouth/exhale' semantic, 'to chant, sing; song'). Omitting the formal classifier 首 (shǒu) imparts a direct, conversational rhythm typical of studio and music-industry speech.

history.meaning: to sing in drawn-out voice; song, ballad
this song (colloquial demonstrative-noun construction)
this song

这歌.notes: Common in informal critique among music producers and singers (这歌不好唱 'this song is hard to sing'), equivalent to the slightly more formal 这首歌.

cognates.meaning: time, interval (Sino-Japanese cognate of 時間)

这段时间.etymology: A modifier-head noun phrase combining the demonstrative-classifier unit 这段 (zhè duàn, 'this segment/stretch', where 段 originally meant 'to hammer/break into sections') with 时间 (shíjiān, trad. 時間, 'time, temporal interval', from 时 'season/time' + 间 'interval/space between'). Together they conceptualize a recent or current span of time as a bounded linear segment.

history.meaning: section, segment / interval of time

history.form: 這段時間 / 这段时间
history.meaning: this stretch of time, this recent period

morphemes.meaning: section, stretch, segment (of time or distance)

这段时间.notes: Can refer to the recent past ('lately, over this past period') or the immediate present/near future ('during this current period'), depending on context and aspect markers.

cognates.meaning: seed, species, kind (Sino-Japanese cognate of 種)

这种.etymology: A demonstrative-classifier compound combining 这 (zhè, trad. 這, 'this') and 种 (zhǒng, trad. 種, Old Chinese *toŋʔ, graphically 禾 'grain' + 重 phonetic, originally 'cereal seed for planting', extended in Classical Chinese to 'biological breed, lineage, category, kind'). It functions as the primary taxonomic determiner meaning 'this kind/type of'.

history.meaning: seed of grain; breed, race, kind, category
this sort, this category of
this kind of, this type of

这种.notes: Modifies both concrete and abstract nouns (这种事 'this kind of thing', 这种风格 'this kind of style'); can carry a critical or dismissive tone when paired with personal pronouns (你这种人 'people like you').

cognates.meaning: body, person, status (Sino-Japanese cognate of 身)

这身.etymology: A demonstrative-classifier construction joining 这 (zhè, trad. 這, 'this') with 身 (shēn, Old Chinese *hljigin, originally a pictograph of a torso in profile, 'body, trunk, person'). Through metonymy, 身 grammaticalized into a measure word for what covers or embodies the whole person—either a complete outfit of clothing or a pervasive personal attribute/skill.

history.meaning: human body, torso, oneself
this full outfit (on the body); this bodyful of (attributes/skills)
this whole outfit of; this bodyful of (skills, debt, sweat, etc.)

这身.notes: Used either for a head-to-toe ensemble (这身衣服/打扮 'this outfit/look') or figuratively for qualities pervading a person (这身本事 'this whole set of skills', 这身脾气 'this temper of yours').

这边.etymology: Proximal locative pronoun combining 这 (這, 'this') + 边 (邊, 'side, direction, area').

history.meaning: this side, over here, this way

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 这边 (via 萌典)

这里.etymology: Location pronoun meaning 'here' ('this place'), formed strictly parallel to 那里 ('there') and 哪里 ('where'). Placed right after 在 to anchor where someone or something is.

history.meaning: here; this place

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 這裡 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: head, counter for poems and songs (Sino-Japanese cognate of 首)

这首.etymology: A demonstrative-classifier compound combining 这 (zhè, trad. 這, 'this') with 首 (shǒu, Old Chinese *hljuʔ, originally a pictograph of a human head with hair, meaning 'head, chief, beginning'). Because classical poems and songs were indexed by their opening heading or stanza, 首 became the dedicated literary classifier for poems and musical compositions by the Six Dynasties and Tang era.

history.meaning: head, leader, beginning; classifier for poems and songs
this (poem or song)
this (song or poem)

morphemes.meaning: classifier for songs and poems (originally: head)

这首.notes: The standard classifier for songs and poems (这首歌 'this song', 这首曲子 'this musical piece'); often used without the noun when the song is already the topic of conversation.

进.etymology: Oracle-bone and bronze ideograph 进 (進) depicting a bird (隹) and a foot/road (止/辶)—birds walk only forward without stepping backward—hence 'to advance, move forward, enter, come/go in'. (Simplified 进 replaces 隹 with phonetic 井 jǐng.)

history.meaning: to advance forward, enter, present
to enter, come/go in, advance; directional complement

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 进 (via 萌典)

进不去.etymology: A negative potential directional verb construction formed by inserting the negator 不 (bù, 'not, unable') between the verb 进 (jìn, trad. 進, Old Chinese *tsin-s, 'to advance, enter') and the directional complement 去 (qù, 'to go away from the speaker'). Literally 'enter-not-go', it denotes physical, institutional, or figurative inability to gain entry into a space or circle away from the speaker's current vantage point.

history.meaning: to advance, enter / to depart, go
unable to enter or get in (potential complement construction)

进不去.notes: Contrasts in deictic perspective with 进不来 (jìnbulái, 'unable to come in [toward the speaker]') and in affirmative potential with 进得去 (jìndeqù, 'able to get in'). Also used figuratively for exclusive industries or someone's heart.

cognates.meaning: march, advance; (modern Chinese sense of further study is distinct)

进修.etymology: A serial/coordinative verbal compound combining 进 (jìn, trad. 進, Old Chinese *tsin-s, 'to advance, move forward') and 修 (xiū, Old Chinese *s-lju, 'to adorn, cultivate, study, practice'). Attested in Classical Chinese (e.g., *Book of Changes* 進德修業 'to advance in virtue and cultivate one's work'), it specialized in modern Mandarin to mean pursuing advanced academic study or professional refresher training.

history.meaning: to advance in moral virtue and cultivate learning/conduct
to engage in advanced studies or professional training (often away or abroad)

进修.notes: Typically refers to mid-career professionals, artists, or teachers taking specialized courses or going abroad (出国进修) to upgrade their credentials without necessarily pursuing a full degree.

进入.etymology: A coordinative/directional verb compound pairing 进 (jìn, trad. 進, Old Chinese *tsin-s, graphically 辶 'walk' + 隹 'short-tailed bird', which only hops forward, hence 'to advance') with 入 (rù, Old Chinese *njup, 'to enter, go inside'). In Classical Chinese 進 meant 'move forward' and 入 meant 'go inside'; combined as 進入, they form a disyllabic transitive verb meaning 'to enter' both physical spaces and abstract states or phases.

history.meaning: to advance forward / to enter inside
to advance and enter into (court, territory, or realm)
to enter (a place, stage, market, or state of mind)

进入.notes: More formal than 进 or 进去; strongly favored when taking a direct abstract object (进入状态 'get into the zone/character', 进入市场 'enter the market', 进入倒计时 'enter the countdown').

进去.etymology: Compound directional verb and post-verbal complement combining 进 (進, 'to enter, go in') + 去 ('away from the speaker').

history.meaning: to go in, enter (away from speaker)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 进去 (via 萌典)

进展.etymology: A coordinative compound combining 进 (jìn, trad. 進, Old Chinese *tsin-s, 'to advance forward') and 展 (zhǎn, Old Chinese *trjanʔ, 'to unroll, unfold, expand'). Popularized in modern East Asian lexicon alongside Japanese 進展 (shinten), it conceptualizes headway in a project, negotiation, or investigation as both forward motion (进) and unfolding expansion (展).

history.meaning: to advance / to unroll, spread out, extend
(verb/noun) to make headway; progress, development in an undertaking

进展.notes: Functions as both a noun (取得进展 'make progress', 有新进展 'have new developments') and an intransitive verb paired with 顺利 (进展顺利 'progress smoothly'). Compare 进步 (personal improvement or societal advancement).

进来.etymology: Compound directional verb and post-verbal complement combining 进 (進, 'to enter, come in') + 来 (來, 'toward the speaker').

history.meaning: to come in, enter (toward speaker)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 进来 (via 萌典)

进步.etymology: Originally a literal verb-object phrase 進步 ('to take a step forward', from 进 'to advance' + 步 'step, pace'), generalized in modern Chinese for 'progress, improvement; to make progress, improve'.

history.meaning: to step forward, advance
progress, improvement; to make progress, improve

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 进步 (via 萌典)

进程.etymology: A modifier-head compound joining 进 (jìn, trad. 進, Old Chinese *tsin-s, 'advancing, forward movement') and 程 (chéng, Old Chinese *lriŋ, graphically 禾 'grain' + 呈 phonetic, originally 'measure of grain', extended to 'measured stage of a journey, itinerary, road'). Literally 'course of advancement', it denotes the overarching trajectory, process, or timetable of a project or historical development.

history.meaning: measured stage of travel, itinerary; forward march of a journey
process, course of development, project timeline/progression

进程.notes: Used for macro-level historical processes (历史进程 'course of history'), computing processes, or production schedules/timelines (加快项目进程 'accelerate the project timeline'). Compare 过程 (any general process from start to finish).

进行.etymology: A coordinative compound uniting 进 (jìn, trad. 進, Old Chinese *tsin-s, 'to advance') and 行 (xíng, Old Chinese *gˤraŋ, 'to walk, march, carry out'). In Classical Chinese (e.g., *Rites of Zhou*, military treatises), 進行 meant literally 'to march forward'. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, reinforced by Meiji Japanese 進行 (shinkō), it grammaticalized in Mandarin into a formal "light/dummy verb" used to nominalize and govern disyllabic action nouns ('to conduct, carry out').

history.meaning: to advance on foot, march forward (especially of troops)
to be underway; to conduct, carry out (formal light verb governing nominalized actions)
history.stage: Late Qing / Republican to Modern Mandarin

进行.notes: Acts either as an intransitive verb meaning 'to be in progress' (正在进行中 'currently underway') or as a formal transitive light verb before two-syllable action nouns (进行讨论 'conduct discussions', 进行彩排 'carry out a rehearsal').

进门.etymology: Verb-object compound combining 进 (進, 'to enter') + 门 (門, 'door, gate, household, craft').

history.meaning: to enter the door, come inside; to marry into a family or begin learning a craft

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 进门 (via 萌典)

远.etymology: Phono-semantic character 远 (遠), combining the road/movement radical 辶 + phonetic 袁 (yuán / 元), meaning 'far in space or time, distant, remote, by far'.

history.meaning: far, distant, remote
far, distant, remote

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 远 (via 萌典)

远远.etymology: Reduplicated adverbial/attributive form of 远 (simplified from 遠, walking radical 辶 + phonetic 袁 'far; distant'). Reduplicating 远 into 远远 emphasizes viewing, hearing, or smelling something from a considerable distance away.

history.meaning: far away in the distance
from afar; far away

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 远远

违反.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound combining 违 (wéi, trad. 違, Old Chinese *ɢʷjəj, graphically 辶 'walk' + 韋 'opposing feet around an enclosure', originally 'to walk away in opposite directions, go against, disobey') and 反 (fǎn, Old Chinese *panʔ, graphically 又 'hand' turning over a cliff 厂, 'to turn back, reverse, rebel against'). Attested in Classical Chinese, it gained modern legal precision via Sino-Japanese 違反 (ihan, 'violation of rules/laws').

history.meaning: to go against, diverge from, oppose, disobey
to violate, contravene, infringe (laws, regulations, or principles)

违反.notes: Takes formal objects such as rules, regulations, contracts, or objective laws (违反规定 'violate regulations', 违反合同 'violate a contract'). Compare 违背 (violate morals, promises, or personal wishes).

违约.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound pairing 违 (wéi, trad. 違, Old Chinese *ɢʷjəj, 'to go against, contravene') with 约 (yuē, trad. 約, Old Chinese *ʔewk, graphically 糸 'silk cord' + 勺 phonetic, originally 'to bind with a cord', extended to 'binding covenant, treaty, contract, appointment'). Attested in Classical historiography for breaking a treaty or appointment, in modern law it denotes 'breach of contract' or 'default'.

history.meaning: to break a covenant, treaty, or appointed meeting
to breach a contract, default on an agreement or debt

违约.notes: Because 违约 is an internal verb-object (VO) compound, it is intransitive and does not take a direct noun object (*违约合同 is ungrammatical; say 违反合同 or 构成违约 'constitute a breach of contract').

cognates.meaning: penalty for breach of contract, liquidated damages (Sino-Japanese cognate)
penalty for breach of contract (Sino-Korean cognate)

违约金.etymology: A modifier-head legal-financial compound combining the VO compound 违约 (wéiyuē, trad. 違約, 'breach of contract') with the head noun 金 (jīn, Old Chinese *kəm, originally 'metal, bronze, gold', extended in financial terminology to 'money, monetary sum, fee'). Standardized in modern East Asian civil law alongside Japanese 違約金 (iyakukin), it denotes 'liquidated damages' or a 'contractual penalty fee'.

history.meaning: breach of covenant + metal/monetary sum (classical roots)
liquidated damages, contractual penalty fee for breach of contract
history.stage: Late Qing / Republican to Modern Mandarin (civil law)

违约金.notes: A staple plot device in Chinese entertainment dramas (*幕后之王*), where talent agencies and broadcasters leverage天价违约金 ('astronomical penalty fees') over artists or producers seeking to break exclusive contracts.

连.etymology: Associative/phono-semantic character 连 (連), combining the movement radical 辶 + 车 (車, 'wheeled cart'), originally meaning 'carts linked or pulled in a continuous train', hence 'to link, join, connect, in succession; military company; even (focal preposition, paired with 都/也)'.

history.meaning: linked carts -> to join, connect, continuous
to link, join; continuously; even (連...都/也)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 连 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: collective responsibility, guilt by association (Sino-Japanese cognate)

连坐.etymology: A modifier-head verbal compound from ancient Chinese legal terminology, combining 连 (lián, trad. 連, Old Chinese *ran, 'to link together, connect in a row') and 坐 (zuò, Old Chinese *dzˤojʔ, 'to kneel/sit', which in Qin–Han legal codes meant 'to be knelt at trial, be adjudicated guilty of a crime'). Introduced systematically by Legalist reformer Shang Yang (4th c. BCE), 连坐 denoted collective criminal liability across families or five-/ten-household units.

history.meaning: to be adjudicated and punished collectively under Qin–Han mutual-responsibility laws
to punish by association; collective punishment in organizations or groups

morphemes.meaning: to be convicted/punished for a crime (originally: to kneel/sit)

连坐.notes: In modern corporate and media settings, 连坐 is used figuratively and often critically for collective workplace punishment (e.g., docking an entire production team's bonus because of one member's mistake).

rootFamily.gloss: sit still and wait for death/ruin

cognates.meaning: night after night, consecutive nights (Sino-Japanese cognate)

连夜.etymology: A verb-object / adverbial compound combining 连 (lián, trad. 連, Old Chinese *ran, graphically 辶 'walk' + 車 'chariot', originally 'chariots linked in a train; to join continuously without break') and 夜 (yè, Old Chinese *N-rAk-s, 'night'). In Classical poetry and prose, 連夜 meant either 'consecutive nights' or 'spanning continuously through that very night'; in modern Mandarin it functions adverbially as 'overnight, right through the night without waiting for morning'.

history.meaning: night after night; continuously throughout the night
through the night, overnight (acting urgently without waiting for daybreak)

morphemes.meaning: to link continuously, span without pause

连夜.notes: Always placed directly before an action verb to emphasize urgency and crisis management (连夜赶工 'work through the night to meet a deadline', 连夜开会 'hold an emergency overnight meeting', 连夜剪辑 'edit footage overnight'). Compare Japanese 連夜 (ren'ya), which means 'night after night'.

rootFamily.gloss: stay up all night, pull an all-nighter

cognates.meaning: chain-link stratagem (Sino-Japanese borrowing from Chinese military classics)

连环计.etymology: A modifier-head three-character compound formed from 连环 (liánhuán, trad. 連環, 'interlocking jade/metal rings', from 连 'linked' + 环 'annular ring') modifying 计 (jì, trad. 計, Old Chinese *kˤij-s, originally 'to calculate, reckon', hence 'calculated stratagem, ruse'). Immortalized as the Thirty-Fifth of the *Thirty-Six Stratagems* (三十六计) and in *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* (where Wang Yun and Diaochan ensnare Dong Zhuo and Lü Bu, and Pang Tong chains Cao Cao's warships at Red Cliffs), it denotes a multi-stage scheme where each plot triggers the next.

history.meaning: interlinked rings + calculated military stratagem
interlocking stratagem (famous in Yuan dramas and Romance of the Three Kingdoms)
interlocking stratagem, multi-part scheme or PR/business maneuver

连环计.notes: Frequently invoked in corporate, PR, and palace-intrigue dramas when a strategist executes a multi-step maneuver where the opponent's reaction to Step A traps them in Step B.

cognates.meaning: being implicated or entangled in another's trouble (Sino-Japanese cognate)

连累.etymology: A coordinative/resultative verbal compound combining 连 (lián, trad. 連, Old Chinese *ran, 'to link, connect') and 累 (lěi, Old Chinese *rujʔ, graphically 糸 'silk thread' + 田, originally 'to bind with rope, entangle, implicate'; carefully distinguished in traditional script from 纍 'to bind/entangle' though merged in simplified 累). Together they mean 'to entangle someone else by association, dragging an innocent party into trouble'.

history.meaning: to bind together and entangle; to implicate others in one's misfortune or offense
to implicate, drag into trouble through no fault of theirs

连累.notes: Note the pronunciation lěi (3rd tone, or neutral tone in speech liánlei) when meaning 'to implicate/burden', distinct from lèi ('tired') and léi ('accumulate'). Common in apologetic speech: 对不起，连累你了 ('Sorry for dragging you into this').

迟到.etymology: Modifier-verb compound combining 迟 (遲, 'slow, late, tardy') + 到 ('to arrive').

history.meaning: to arrive late, be late

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 迟到 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to lose one's way, be perplexed, be infatuated with (Sino-Japanese cognate)

迷.etymology: A monomorphemic root written 迷 (mí, Old Chinese *mˤij, a phono-semantic compound combining semantic 辶 'to walk, travel' + phonetic 米 *mˤijʔ 'rice'). Originally meaning 'to lose one's way while walking, go astray', it extended metaphorically in Classical Chinese to 'mental confusion, bewilderment', and subsequently to 'being spellbound, enchanted, or infatuated with'—which also yielded the modern agentive noun sense 'enthusiast, fan' (e.g., 歌迷 'music fan').

history.meaning: to lose one's way on a path, go astray; to be confused or deluded
to enchant, fascinate; to be infatuated with; enthusiast/fan

morphemes.meaning: to lose one's way; be infatuated with; fan/enthusiast

迷.notes: Highly versatile in entertainment contexts: as a verb (迷上某人 'become infatuated with someone'), as a stative verb (着迷 'be fascinated'), and as a productive suffix for fans (歌迷 'music fan', 影迷 'movie fan', 粉丝迷).

迷人.etymology: An adjective pairing 迷 (mí, 'to bewilder, to enchant') with 人 (rén, 'person'). 迷 combines the walking radical 辶 and 米, evoking the confusion of losing one's way. Thus, a 'bewitching' thing causes one to lose oneself entirely in its charm.

history.meaning: charming; fascinating

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 迷人

追.etymology: A monomorphemic verb root written 追 (zhuī, Old Chinese *truj, combining semantic 辶 'to walk/run in pursuit' + 𠂤 duī, originally depicting troop encampments or terraced mounds). Attested on Shang oracle bone inscriptions for pursuing fleeing enemies or game, it broadened from physical chasing to 'seeking after (ideals/goals)', 'courting (a romantic partner)', and in modern pop culture 'following serialized shows or idols'.

history.meaning: to chase after fleeing enemies or game, pursue on foot
history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle Bone & Bronze Inscriptions / Classical Chinese)

history.meaning: to pursue, seek after, trace back; to court romantically
to chase, pursue; to court; to follow (a TV series, celebrity, or trend)

追.notes: Beyond physical chasing and romantic courtship (追女孩 'pursue a girl'), 追 is central to modern media fandom: 追星 ('follow celebrities/stan idols'), 追剧 ('binge-watch/follow an ongoing drama series'), and 追热点 ('chase trending topics').

追上.etymology: A verb-resultative/directional compound formed from 追 (zhuī, 'to chase, pursue', composed of the walking radical 辶 and phonetic/semantic 𠂤 'troop/mound') and the directional-resultative complement 上 (shàng, 'up; onto; reaching contact/attainment'). Originally denoting physical pursuit until overtaking a target in Early Mandarin, the resultative sense of 上 ('successfully reaching a goal') extended metaphorically in modern colloquial Mandarin to mean winning someone over romantically.

history.meaning: to chase after and physically overtake a moving target
to catch up with (in pace or ability); to successfully court or win someone's heart

morphemes.meaning: up to, reaching attainment or contact

追上.notes: Functions as a separable resultative verb: potential forms insert 得 or 不 between the elements (追得上 'able to catch up / win over', 追不上 'unable to catch up / out of one's league').

rootFamily.gloss: to fall in love with, set one's heart on

追寻.etymology: A coordinative (parallel) verbal compound uniting 追 (zhuī, 'to chase after, track') and 尋/寻 (xún, originally a measure of eight尺 equal to outstretched arms in Old Chinese, early extended to 'to grope for, seek, search out'). Attested in Literary Chinese from the Tang and Song dynasties onward for tracking down lost traces or persons, it shifted in modern literary Mandarin toward elevated, abstract quests for ideals, truth, or artistic inspiration.

history.meaning: to track down, search for physical traces or a missing person
to quest after, pursue (dreams, truth, memories, or artistic ideals)

追寻.notes: More literary and poetic than 追求; typically takes abstract or evocative objects such as 梦想 (dreams), 真相 (truth), or 足迹 (footsteps/traces), whereas 追求 can also take a romantic partner.

rootFamily.gloss: to trace back to the origin

追求.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound pairing 追 (zhuī, 'to chase, pursue') with 求 (qiú, 'to seek, request, strive for', originally an oracle-bone pictograph of a fur pelt Coat 裘 borrowed phonetically for 'to seek'). Attested already in Warring States and Han texts (such as the *Hanfeizi* and *Strategies of the Warring States*) for actively seeking advantage or office, it now covers both striving after abstract goals (artistic perfection, career success) and courting a romantic partner.

history.meaning: to press after, actively seek (profit, office, or fleeing targets)
to pursue or strive after (ideals, quality, truth); to court romantically; (noun) aspiration

追求.notes: Can act as both a transitive verb (追求卓越 'pursue excellence'; 追求她 'court her') and a noun meaning 'personal standards/ambition' (e.g., 他是一个很有追求的制作人 'He is a producer with high artistic standards').

cognates.meaning: following closely in someone's footsteps, emulation

追随.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound formed from 追 (zhuī, 'to follow closely behind, pursue') and 隨/随 (suí, 'to follow, accompany, attend upon', composed of 辶 'walk' and phonetic 隋). Attested in Classical Chinese (*Zhuangzi*, *Shiji*) for physically walking behind a carriage or retinue, it evolved to signify loyal adherence to a mentor, artistic pioneer, or leader.

history.meaning: to follow closely behind in a retinue or procession
to follow loyally, stand behind (a mentor, leader, or movement)

追随.notes: Carries a respectful tone of devotion or allegiance; in workplace and entertainment contexts, 追随一位前辈 describes apprenticing oneself loyally to a senior figure.

rootFamily.gloss: to follow closely (a person or trend)

退.etymology: Ancient character 退 (oracle-bone and bronze forms show a foot 止/夂 moving away from a building or sun 皀/日, later written with 辶 + 艮), meaning 'to step back, retreat, withdraw, return/refund, fade'.

history.meaning: to step backward, withdraw, yield
to move back, retreat, return/cancel, fade

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 退 (via 萌典)

退休.etymology: Combines 退 (tuì, 'to withdraw') and 休 (xiū, 'to rest'). 休 visually depicts a person (亻) leaning against a tree (木). It formally denotes withdrawing from one's career duties to enter a prolonged, well-earned period of rest.

history.meaning: to retire from office
to retire

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 退休

cognates.meaning: withdrawal, exit, leaving a room or stage

退出.etymology: A verb-directional/resultative compound combining 退 (tuì, 'to step back, retreat, withdraw', composed of walking radical 辶 and 艮 'to turn back/resist') with 出 (chū, 'to go out, emerge'). In Classical and Literary Chinese, 退出 described retiring backward from a royal court or ceremonial hall; in modern Mandarin, it extends from physical exit to formally withdrawing from a competition, project, market, or digital platform/account.

history.meaning: to retire from a hall or court presence; to retreat outward
to withdraw from (a contest, show, or organization); to log out or exit (software)
