退出.notes: In talent shows and television production, 宣布退出比赛 ('announce one's withdrawal from the competition') is the standard formal phrasing for a contestant stepping down, while on phones/computers 退出 means 'Quit / Log out'.

rootFamily.gloss: to step back, leave the stage/venue
to retire from the entertainment industry or public life

退后.etymology: Verb-complement compound combining 退 ('to step back, retreat') + 后 (後, 'backward, behind').

history.meaning: to step back, move backward, fall back

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 退后 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: withdrawal or expulsion from school, dropping out
to drop out or be expelled from school

退学.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound pairing 退 (tuì, 'to withdraw from, relinquish') with 學/学 (xué, 'school, formal study'). While attested in Song–Ming Neo-Confucian records for leaving an academy, its modern institutional sense ('to terminate enrollment in a school or university, either voluntarily or by administrative dismissal') was reinforced across East Asia during late 19th-century Meiji educational reforms (Japanese *taigaku*).

history.meaning: to withdraw from a Confucian academy or abandon one's studies
to withdraw from school, drop out, or be dismissed from enrollment
history.stage: Modern Mandarin (reinforced via Japanese 退学)

退学.notes: Because 退学 is a separable verb-object (VO) compound, modifiers go between the characters: 办了退学手续 ('completed withdrawal procedures') or 退了学 ('dropped out of school'). Compare 休学 ('take a temporary leave of absence from school').

rootFamily.gloss: to take a temporary leave of absence from school
to enroll in or start school
to drop out of school (often due to hardship)

退步.etymology: Originally a verb-object compound from 退 (tuì, 'to move backward') and 步 (bù, 'a pace, step', originally an oracle-bone depiction of two footprints striding), literally 'to take a step backward'. Attested in Literary Chinese in the literal physical sense and in Chan Buddhist aphorisms (such as 退步原来是向前 'stepping back is actually moving forward'), it developed its modern abstract sense of 'regression in skill, academic standing, or civilization' as the antonym of 进步 (jìnbù, 'progress').

history.meaning: to step backward physically; to yield ground or leave leeway
to regress, fall behind, decline in proficiency or quality

退步.notes: Direct antonym of 进步 (jìnbù, 'to make progress / improve'). As a VO compound, degree or measure complements often follow or split it (e.g., 退步了很多 'regressed a lot').

cognates.meaning: to withdraw from an agreement or treaty

退约.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound formed from 退 (tuì, 'to withdraw from, cancel, return') and 約/约 (yuē, originally 'to bind with cord' via the silk radical 糸, extended in Classical Chinese to 'covenant, pact, contract, appointment'). Modeled on commercial-legal VO compounds such as 签约 (qiānyuē, 'sign a contract') and 解约 (jiěyuē, 'terminate a contract'), 退约 specifically denotes pulling out of a binding agreement, booking, or treaty.

history.meaning: to withdraw from a covenant or cancel a pledged agreement
to withdraw from a contract, pull out of a commercial or talent agreement

morphemes.meaning: to withdraw from, cancel, back out of

退约.notes: In the entertainment and media industry, compare 签约 ('sign a contract'), 续约 ('renew a contract'), 解约 ('terminate a contract'), 违约 ('breach a contract'), and 退约 ('pull out of / cancel a contract').

rootFamily.gloss: to terminate or dissolve a contract
to breach a contract; breach of contract

送.etymology: Ancient character 送 combining the road/movement radical 辶 + 朕/关, originally meaning 'to escort a departing guest or bride along the road', extended to 'to see someone off, deliver, carry, give as a gift'.

history.meaning: to escort on departure, see off, send
to deliver, send, see off, give as a present

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 送 (via 萌典)

送上去.etymology: A trimorphemic verb-directional construction combining the action verb 送 (sòng, 'to escort, send, deliver', attested in *Shijing* for seeing off a bride or guest) with the compound directional complement 上去 (shàngqù, composed of 上 'ascend, go up' + 去 'move away from the speaker's deictic center'). This serial verb-directional pattern crystallized in Vernacular Chinese (Early Mandarin) to specify both the trajectory of delivery (upward, e.g., upstairs or onto a stage/desk) and deictic perspective (away from the speaker).

history.meaning: to escort, see off, present or send an item
to deliver or send something up (upstairs, onstage, or to higher-ups) away from the speaker

morphemes.meaning: up, upward, upstairs, onto a higher surface/level

送上去.notes: When taking a direct object without 把, a noun object typically goes between 上 and 去 (把文件送上去 or 送文件上去 'deliver the documents upstairs'). Contrast with 送上来 ('deliver upstairs toward the speaker').

rootFamily.gloss: to deliver up toward the speaker

送到.etymology: A verb-resultative compound uniting 送 (sòng, 'to send, escort, deliver') with the resultative/prepositional complement 到 (dào, 'to arrive at, reach a destination', from 至 'arrive' + phonetic 刀). In Middle and Early Mandarin Chinese, 到 grammaticalized after motion and transfer verbs to mark the successful arrival of the theme at a goal location or recipient.

history.meaning: to escort someone or convey an item until arriving at a place
to deliver to (a location, person, or point in time/extent)

morphemes.meaning: to reach, arrive at (a destination or recipient)

送到.notes: Must be followed immediately by a place or recipient object (e.g., 把合同送到总监办公室 'deliver the contract to the director's office'); in formal legal/postal contexts, compare the inverted literary compound 送达 (sòngdá, 'to serve/deliver officially').

送来.etymology: Verb-complement compound combining 送 ('to send, deliver, bring') + directional complement 来 (來, 'hither, toward the speaker').

history.meaning: to deliver here, send over, bring

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 送来 (via 萌典)

送货车.etymology: Three-character compound combining 送货 (送貨, 'to deliver goods', from 送 'to deliver' + 货 'goods') + 车 (車, 'vehicle, van, truck').

history.meaning: delivery van, delivery truck

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 送货车 (via 萌典)

适合.etymology: Coordinate verb and adjective compound combining 适 (適 shì, 'to go toward, fit, suit, comfortable') + 合 ('to match, join together, conform').

history.meaning: to suit, fit, be suitable for

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 适合 (via 萌典)

适应.etymology: A coordinative verb compound pairing 適/适 (shì, 'to go toward; to fit, suit, match', composed of 辶 'walk' and phonetic 啇) with 應/应 (yìng, 'to respond to, correspond to, answer'). While 適應 occurred in Classical and Medieval Chinese for 'suiting and responding to circumstances', its modern biological, psychological, and sociological sense ('to adapt to an environment or condition') was popularized via Meiji-era Japanese *tekiō* (適応), rendering English *adaptation*.

history.meaning: to conform and respond appropriately to circumstances
to adapt to, adjust to, get used to (a new environment, role, or pace)
history.stage: Modern Mandarin (reinforced via Japanese 適応)

适应.notes: Unlike English 'adapt to', 适应 is directly transitive and takes no preposition before its object: 适应新环境 ('adapt to the new environment') or 适应高强度的工作节奏 ('get used to a high-intensity work pace'). Compare 适合 ('to suit / be suitable for').

rootFamily.gloss: to suit, fit, be suitable for
to respond to, cope with, deal with

逃.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形聲字) attested from Warring States bamboo slips and the *Shuowen Jiezi*, composed of the semantic walking radical 辶 (辵, 'stepping/running movement') and the phonetic component 兆 (zhào, Old Chinese *l'ewʔ, originally cracking lines on divination tortoise shells, which also carries a connotative image of splitting apart or diverging). Throughout Classical and Modern Chinese, 逃 has continuously denoted fleeing danger, captivity, or obligation.

history.meaning: to flee, desert, run away from battle or captivity
to escape, flee, sneak away; to evade or skip (classes, fare, taxes)

逃.notes: As a monosyllabic verb, 逃 is vivid in narrative prose and combines productively with objects to mean 'skip/evade' (e.g., 逃课 'skip class', 逃单 'walk out on a bill', 逃票 'dodge a ticket fare', 逃税 'evade taxes').

rootFamily.gloss: to evade, shirk, avoid (responsibility or reality)

cognates.meaning: flight, being a fugitive, going into exile
flight, running away, being a fugitive
to flee into exile, go on the run

逃亡.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound formed from 逃 (táo, 'to flee, run away') and 亡 (wáng, whose primary sense in Old Chinese and the *Zuo Zhuan* / *Shiji* was 'to flee, go into exile, abscond', before narrowing in later vernacular to 'to perish, die'). Because both roots meant 'to flee/abscond' in Classical Chinese, 逃亡 denotes going on the run as a fugitive or refugee, not dying while fleeing.

history.meaning: to desert, abscond from one's state or military post, go into exile
to flee, be on the run (as a fugitive or displaced person)

morphemes.meaning: to flee into exile, abscond (archaic sense of 亡)

逃亡.notes: A classic etymological trap for learners: 亡 here preserves its Classical Chinese meaning 'to flee/go into exile' (as in 流亡 'live in exile'), NOT its modern meaning 'to die' (死亡). Thus 逃亡 means 'to be on the run', not 'to die escaping'.

rootFamily.gloss: to go into exile, be displaced

逃离.etymology: A verb-complement / coordinative compound combining 逃 (táo, 'to flee, escape') with 離/离 (lí, 'to leave, depart from, separate from', originally a net for catching orioles/birds 離, early borrowed for 'to part from'). While 逃 specifies the urgent act of flight, 离 introduces the ablative relation ('away from a source or confining place'), allowing the compound to take a direct spatial or psychological object.

history.meaning: to flee and depart from a place of danger or siege
to escape from, break away from (a physical site, toxic environment, or high-pressure city life)

morphemes.meaning: to leave, depart from, separate from

逃离.notes: Directly takes the place or situation being left behind as its object without needing 从 (e.g., 逃离现场 'flee the scene', or the famous urban media catchphrase 逃离北上广 'escape Beijing, Shanghai, and Guangzhou').

rootFamily.gloss: to break away from, cast off, lose contact with
to evacuate, withdraw from a site

逃脱.etymology: A verb-resultative compound uniting 逃 (táo, 'to flee, run away') with 脫/脱 (tuō, originally 'to peel off flesh from bone' via radical 肉/月 and phonetic 兌, extended in Classical Chinese to 'to shed, cast off restraints, slip free'). Attested in vernacular narratives since the Song and Ming dynasties, 脱 expresses the successful result of slipping out of a trap, custody, or binding obligation.

history.meaning: to slip free and escape from capture, fetters, or encirclement
to escape from (danger or custody); to shirk or evade (blame, punishment, or responsibility)

morphemes.meaning: to shed, slip free from, cast off restraints

逃脱.notes: Emphasizes successfully breaking free from a trap or obligation (e.g., 逃脱责任 'shirk responsibility', 逃脱惩罚 'escape punishment'). Also seen in the popular entertainment term 密室逃脱 ('escape room game').

rootFamily.gloss: to cast off, break free from (control or a predicament)
to shirk, shift blame away from oneself
to break away from, detach from

逃走.etymology: Originally a coordinative compound in Classical Chinese (*Shiji*, *Hanshu*) pairing 逃 (táo, 'to flee') with 走 (zǒu, which in Old and Middle Chinese meant 'to run swiftly, sprint, flee', as depicted by the oracle-bone figure of a swinging-armed runner above a foot 止). In Modern Mandarin, where 走 shifted to 'walk; leave/go away', 走 in 逃走 is reanalyzed as a directional/resultative complement meaning 'away' ('flee away').

history.meaning: to flee at a run, bolt from a battlefield or pursuer
to flee away, run off, make one's getaway (intransitive)

morphemes.meaning: to run (Classical); to go away, leave (Modern complement)

逃走.notes: Strictly intransitive in Modern Mandarin (unlike 逃离 or 逃脱, which can take an object): one says 从后门逃走了 ('fled out the back door'), never *逃走现场. Compare 拿走 ('take away') and 帶走 ('bring away').

rootFamily.gloss: to leave, walk away; to pass away

选.etymology: Phono-semantic character 选 (選), combining the movement radical 辶 + phonetic 巽 / 先 (xuǎn / xiān), meaning 'to select, choose, pick out, elect'.

history.meaning: to choose, select, appoint
to choose, select, pick, elect

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 选 (via 萌典)

选定.etymology: A verb-resultative compound combining 選/选 (xuǎn, 'to choose, select, pick out', composed of 辶 and phonetic 巽) with the resultative complement 定 (dìng, 'to settle, fix, establish firmly', showing a roof 宀 over 正 'proper/straight'). While 选 expresses the process of screening candidates or options, 定 marks the finalization of that choice ('select and lock in').

history.meaning: to select officials or texts and officially ratify the appointment
to select and settle on (a finalist, broadcast slot, venue, or proposal)

选定.notes: Unlike 选择 ('to choose / be choosing'), 选定 is telic and resultative—it emphasizes that the decision is final and locked in (e.g., 节目组已经选定了总决赛场地 'The production team has finalized the venue for the grand finale').

rootFamily.gloss: to confirm, fix upon, make sure

cognates.meaning: selected player, representative athlete or competitor

选手.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound composed of 選/选 (xuǎn, 'chosen, selected') and 手 (shǒu, literally 'hand', productively used since Six Dynasties and Tang Chinese as an agentive suffix for a person skilled in an activity, as in 高手 'master' or 歌手 'singer'). Although *Zhaoming Wenxuan* (6th c.) was abbreviated as 選 and its copyists called 選手, the modern sense ('selected competitor, athlete, or show contestant') is an early 20th-century return graphic loan from Meiji Japanese *senshu* (選手, abbreviated from 選抜手 'selected hand/player').

history.meaning: a representative athlete or player chosen to compete in a tournament
competitive athlete; contestant in a talent show, singing competition, or esports tournament

morphemes.meaning: person skilled or engaged in an activity (lit. 'hand')

选手.notes: Originally used for sports athletes (运动选手), 选手 is now ubiquitous in Chinese reality TV, singing competitions, and variety shows for 'contestant' (参赛选手). In contemporary slang, X型选手 ('type-X player') playfully describes someone's personality style (e.g., 天赋型选手 'naturally gifted type').

选手村.etymology: A three-character modifier-head nominal compound formed by affixing 村 (cūn, 'village, residential compound', graph Variant of 邨) to 選手/选手 (xuǎnshǒu, 'selected athlete, contestant'). Originally calqued in East Asia on the Olympic *Athletes' Village* (Japanese 選手村 *senshumura*, Korean 선수촌 *seonsuchon*), in contemporary Chinese television production it was adopted for the closed dormitory/studio complex where reality-show or singing-competition contestants live and rehearse during filming.

history.meaning: residential village housing athletes during the Olympic or Asian Games
athletes' village; contestants' living and rehearsal quarters in a reality/talent show production

选手村.notes: In mainland Chinese sports journalism, 奥运村 ('Olympic Village') or 运动员村 ('Athletes' Village') is also common, whereas 选手村 is especially favored in variety/talent show production (*幕后之王* style) and Taiwan/Korean/Japanese-influenced broadcasts for the contestants' residential quarters.

rootFamily.gloss: eliminated or auditioning contestants' holding area; village

选择.etymology: A classic coordinative compound uniting two near-synonymous Old Chinese verbs: 選/选 (xuǎn, 'to select, pick out') and 擇/择 (zé, 'to pick out with the hand, sort and choose', composed of the hand radical 扌 and phonetic 睪). Attested together already in the *Mencius*, *Mozi*, and *Shiji*, 选择 has remained the core pan-stylistic word for 'to choose' and 'choice' across more than two millennia of Chinese.

history.meaning: to sort through and select worthy persons, courses of action, or territories
to choose, select (verb); choice, option, alternative (noun)

morphemes.meaning: to sort out, choose by hand

选择.notes: Functions seamlessly as both a verb (选择放弃 'choose to give up') and a noun (尊重你的选择 'respect your choice'). For picking out concrete everyday items by hand, spoken Mandarin often prefers 挑 (tiāo) or 挑选 (tiāoxuǎn), while 选择 is used for decisions, paths, and options.

cognates.meaning: to cast actors for roles (often pronounced syun2 gok3)

选角.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound formed from 選/选 (xuǎn, 'to select, audition') and 角 (jué / jiǎo, short for 角色 juésè 'dramatic role, character'). In traditional Chinese theater (since Yuan *zaju* and Ming–Qing opera), 角 (originally 'animal horn; musical note; to contend/wrestle') came to denote the specialized role-type or lead performer on stage; combining it with 选 created the modern film and television term for 'casting'.

history.meaning: role category or actor's persona in traditional Chinese opera and drama
to cast roles, hold casting auditions (verb); casting (noun/attributive)

morphemes.meaning: dramatic role, character (short for 角色)

选角.notes: Pronunciation note: in mainland standard dictionaries (《现代汉语词典》), 角 in the sense of 'dramatic role' is prescribed as jué (选角 xuǎnjué, 角色 juésè, 主角 zhǔjué), though xuǎnjiǎo is widely heard in colloquial industry speech and Taiwan Mandarin. Common collocation: 选角导演 ('casting director').

rootFamily.gloss: character, role, part (in a play or film)

选题.etymology: Originally a verb-object (VO) compound pairing 選/选 (xuǎn, 'to select, choose') with 題/题 (tí, originally 'forehead' via page/head radical 頁, extended in Six Dynasties and Tang literary culture to 'inscribed title, poetry/examination topic, subject'). Through frequent nominalization in academic, publishing, and broadcasting contexts, 选题 came to mean not only the act of 'selecting a topic' but also the resulting 'chosen topic, story angle, or show pitch' itself.

history.meaning: to select a composition or examination topic
to select a research or media topic (VO verb); show topic, story angle, or editorial pitch (noun)

选题.notes: A core newsroom and TV production term: in *Behind the Scenes* (*幕后之王*), producers hold 选题会 ('topic-pitching / story-selection meetings') to evaluate which 选题 ('show concept / episode angle') has the strongest audience appeal.

rootFamily.gloss: discussion topic, conversation piece, trending hashtag

透.etymology: Phono-semantic character 透, combining the movement radical 辶 + phonetic 秀 (xiù / Old Chinese *l̥ˤok-s), originally meaning 'to leap or pass right through', hence 'to penetrate, seep through, show through, transparent; thoroughly (as a degree complement)'.

history.meaning: to leap over, pass right through
to penetrate, let light/air through, reveal; thoroughly

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 透 (via 萌典)

透过.etymology: Compound verb and preposition combining 透 ('to penetrate, pass through') + 过 (過, 'through, across').

history.meaning: to penetrate, shine/show through; through, by means of (prep.)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 透过 (via 萌典)

透露.etymology: Coordinate verb compound combining 透 ('to pass through, let out') + 露 ('to expose, show, reveal, leak').

history.meaning: to divulge, disclose, leak, reveal

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 透露 (via 萌典)

递.etymology: Phono-semantic character 递 (遞), combining the road/movement radical 辶 + phonetic 弟 / 乕 (dì, 'in turn, successively'), originally meaning 'to relay by post-horse in turns', hence 'to hand over, pass something to someone, deliver'.

history.meaning: to alternate, relay by courier
to hand over, pass, deliver; successively

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 递 (via 萌典)

递到.etymology: A verb-resultative compound formed from 遞/递 (dì, 'to pass in turn, hand over, transmit', originally 'to alternate, relay via post-stations' with walking radical 辶 and phonetic /虎) and the resultative complement 到 (dào, 'to reach, arrive at'). While 递 depicts the short-range manual action of passing an object from hand to hand, 到 specifies the endpoint where the object arrives (commonly X的手里 'into X's hands' or X面前 'in front of X').

history.meaning: to relay in succession, transmit by courier; (Vernacular Chinese) to pass by hand
to hand over to, pass directly into someone's hands or reach

morphemes.meaning: to pass, hand over, deliver by hand
to reach, arrive at (a recipient or location)

递到.notes: Unlike 送到 (which can involve transporting something across town or upstairs), 递到 specifically describes an arm's-reach gesture of handing an object directly to someone (e.g., 把麦克风递到她手里 'handed the microphone right into her hand').

rootFamily.gloss: to hand over, submit formally (a application or resignation)
to pass on, transmit, convey (a message, baton, or emotion)

逗.etymology: A phono-semantic character (辶 'walk/halt' + phonetic 豆 dòu) attested in the *Shuowen Jiezi* and Han texts with the original meaning 'to halt, linger, stay' (preserved in modern 逗留 dòuliú, 'to stay/sojourn'). In Tang–Song vernacular and Yuan drama, the sense of 'lingering around someone to provoke a reaction' shifted to 'to entice, play with, amuse, tease, or kid'—whether coaxing a child or pet to laugh or playfully bantering with an adult.

history.meaning: to halt on a march, linger, delay, tarry (attested in *Hanshu*)
to entice, stir up, play with, tease playfully
to tease, kid, amuse (verb); funny, hilarious (colloquial Northern Mandarin adjective)

morphemes.meaning: to tease, kid, amuse; funny (archaic: to linger)

逗.notes: In everyday speech, 逗你玩的 ('I'm just kidding/teasing you!') and 你真逗 ('You're so funny!') are high-frequency expressions. In traditional crosstalk comedy (相声), the lead comedian who delivers the punchlines is called the 逗哏 (dòugén, 'joke-teaser'), paired with the straight man 捧哏 (pěnggén).

rootFamily.gloss: to stay temporarily, linger, stop over (preserves original Classical sense)
comma (punctuation mark marking a brief pause, from 'halt')

通.etymology: A phono-semantic character composed of the walking radical 辶 (辵) and phonetic 甬 (yǒng, Old Chinese *loŋʔ, originally depicting a tubular bell or open pathway/corridor, cf. 甬道). From its core Classical Chinese sense of 'to pass through without obstruction' (opposed to 塞 sāi / 堵 dǔ 'blocked'), 通 extended systematically to physical routes ('open, connected'), bodily qi/circulation, logical or grammatical coherence ('making sense'), and intellectual mastery ('thoroughly conversant with').

history.meaning: to penetrate, pass all the way through; unobstructed, open (opposed to 塞 'blocked')
unobstructed, connected (of roads/calls); coherent, making sense (of logic/phrasing); thoroughly versed in

通.notes: Extremely versatile predicative and resultative root: 电话打通了 ('the phone call went through'), 这句话讲不通 ('this sentence/argument doesn't make sense'), 想通了 ('figured it out / made peace with it'). As a suffix, X通 means an 'expert on X' (e.g., 中国通 'China hand/expert').

rootFamily.gloss: proficient in, well-versed in, master of

通告.etymology: A modifier-head / coordinative compound combining 通 (tōng, 'all-around, universally, throughout') and 告 (gào, 'to announce, notify, proclaim'). Attested since the *Book of Han* (*Hanshu*) for notifying all relevant parties or issuing a general proclamation, it acquired a specialized entertainment-industry meaning in Taiwan Mandarin—and subsequently across Mainland Chinese television and showbiz—where 通告 denotes a 'call sheet, scheduled media appearance, or guest booking on a variety show'.

history.meaning: to notify universally; a public proclamation or circular notice issued by authorities
history.stage: Classical to Early Modern Chinese (Han–20th c.)

history.meaning: 1. official public notice; 2. (showbiz/TV) call sheet, show booking, scheduled guest appearance
history.stage: Contemporary Mandarin (Showbiz sense popularized via Taiwan TV)

morphemes.meaning: to announce, notify; notice, schedule call

通告.notes: Essential showbiz vocabulary in *Behind the Scenes* (*幕后之王*): 赶通告 ('rush from one show booking/appearance to another'), 发通告 ('issue the daily production call sheet'), 通告费 ('appearance fee paid to a celebrity guest'), and 通告艺人 ('variety-show regular who makes a living from guest bookings').

通报.etymology: A compound verb/noun formed from 通 (tōng, 'to convey through, circulate universally') and 報/报 (bào, originally 'to requite, respond to a judgment', extended in Tang–Song officialdom to 'to report, announce, Gazette'). In late imperial vernacular and formal etiquette, 通报 meant having a doorkeeper or attendant go inside to announce a visitor's arrival; in modern institutional Chinese, it also means to circulate an official briefing, commendation, or reprimand across an organization.

history.meaning: to convey a message inward to announce a guest's arrival; to exchange intelligence
to announce a visitor's arrival; to circulate an official briefing or notice; official bulletin

通报.notes: Has two distinct register contexts: (1) polite interpersonal/office reception: 请帮我通报一声 ('Please let them know / announce that I'm here'); (2) administrative broadcasting: 通报批评 ('circulate a formal notice of criticism') or 情况通报 ('situation briefing').

rootFamily.gloss: to report back (to a superior); debriefing report
forecast, advance notice (e.g., weather or show preview)

通知.etymology: Verb-complement/coordinate compound combining 通 ('to pass through, communicate, convey') + 知 ('to know, cause to know, inform').

history.meaning: to notify, inform; notice, notification, circular

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 通知 (via 萌典)

通讯.etymology: A compound formed from 通 (tōng, 'to connect, transmit across distance') and 訊/讯 (xùn, 'to inquire; message, Tidings, signal, dispatch', composed of speech radical 言 and phonetic 卂 'swift flight'). Originally denoting the exchange of letters or inquiries in Literary Chinese, 通讯 expanded in the 19th and 20th centuries to cover both technological telecommunications (frequently interchanging with 通信 tōngxìn) and journalistic news dispatches or newsletters.

history.meaning: to exchange letters, inquiries, or messages across a distance
telecommunications, communications; journalistic news dispatch or feature report

通讯.notes: Productive in media and tech compounds: 通讯录 ('contacts list / address book'), 通讯社 ('news agency', e.g., Xinhua), 通讯员 ('correspondent / stringer'), and 即时通讯 ('instant messaging'). Technical regulations often prefer 通信 for engineering 'telecommunications' and 通讯 for media/messaging, though everyday usage overlaps heavily.

cognates.meaning: passing through; approval/passage of a bill or exam
passage through; passing an exam, audition, or bill
to pass through; to adopt/approve; by means of

通过.etymology: A coordinative / verb-complement compound combining 通 (tōng, 'to pass all the way through without blockage') and 過/过 (guò, 'to cross, pass by, traverse'). Attested in Classical Chinese (*Xunzi*, *Hanshu*) for physically traversing a pass or territory, 通过 acquired two major modern extensions in the 20th century (partly reinforced by Japanese *tsūka* 通過): (1) passing an audition, inspection, or legislative vote; and (2) grammaticalizing into a preposition meaning 'by means of, through, via'.

history.meaning: to pass unimpeded through a gate, road, or territory
1. (verb) to pass through; to pass/approve (an audition, review, or bill); 2. (prep.) through, by means of, via

通过.notes: Dual grammatical role: as a verb in media/showbiz, 恭喜你通过海选 ('Congratulations on passing the open audition!') or 方案通过了 ('The proposal was approved'); as a preposition, 通过这次合作 ('through/by means of this collaboration').

rootFamily.gloss: to pass by, go through (a place or process); process
to pass an exam or test, meet the standard

通道.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound formed from 通 (tōng, 'unobstructed, leading through, connecting') and 道 (dào, 'way, road, path, channel', originally depicting a head 首 moving along a crossroads 彳/辶). In Classical Chinese (*Shiji*, *Hanshu*), 通道 meant 'to open up a road/diplomatic route' (VO) or 'an open thoroughfare'; in Modern Mandarin, it denotes a physical corridor, aisle, or gateway (such as a backstage VIP accessway or emergency exit) as well as an abstract channel or pipeline.

history.meaning: an open thoroughfare or trade route; (VO) to open up roads or diplomatic relations
corridor, passageway, access lane (e.g., backstage or airport lane); abstract channel or audio/data track

通道.notes: Very common in studio, concert, and public-venue signage: 安全通道 ('emergency exit passageway'), 员工通道 ('staff-only entrance/corridor'), VIP通道 ('VIP access lane'), and 绿色通道 ('fast-track / priority channel').

rootFamily.gloss: broadcast channel, TV channel; frequency band
pipeline, conduit; channel or means (of communication)

逛.etymology: A phono-semantic compound (形聲) combining the walking radical 辶 (辵, 'to walk slowly and stop') as semantic indicator with 狂 (kuáng, 'mad, wild, unrestrained', Old Chinese *ɡʷaŋ) as phonetic and semantic co-indicator, originally signifying 'to run about wildly or erratically' in Middle Chinese before softening in Ming–Qing vernacular into 'to stroll leisurely, wander for pleasure, or browse'.

history.meaning: to run wildly, dart about erratically
to roam, wander leisurely, visit sights
to stroll around, window-shop, browse

morphemes.meaning: to walk, movement along a road

逛.notes: Extremely common in spoken Mandarin as a transitive verb taking places or venues as direct objects (逛商场 'browse the mall', 逛夜市 'stroll the night market', 逛淘宝 'browse Taobao').

rootFamily.gloss: to go shopping, stroll the streets
to stroll about, potter around (colloquial northern Mandarin)

cognates.meaning: to go window-shopping, stroll the streets (often行街 in vernacular)

逛街.etymology: A verb-object (動賓) compound formed from 逛 (guàng, 'to stroll, wander leisurely') and 街 (jiē, 'street, thoroughfare, market avenue'). Arising in late imperial urban vernacular as commercial street culture flourished, it shifted from literally walking along city avenues to the modern sense of going out shopping or window-shopping with friends.

history.meaning: to stroll through city streets and market lanes
to go shopping, window-shop along commercial streets

逛街.notes: Because 逛街 is an inseparable verb-object (离合词) construction, aspect markers and durations go between the two characters (e.g., 逛了三个小时的街 'shopped for three hours').

速度.etymology: Compound noun of 速 ('fast, rapid', walking radical 辶 + 束) + 度 ('measure, rate, degree'): 'speed, velocity, pace, rate'.

history.meaning: rate of movement; speed; velocity

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 速度 (via 萌典)

造反.etymology: A verb-object (動賓) compound composed of 造 (zào, 'to make, initiate, stir up, contrive') and 反 (fǎn, 'to turn over, revolt, rebel against authority'). Already attested in Han dynasty historiography (such as the Book of Han) for plotting treason or armed insurrection against the throne, it is frequently used hyperbolically and humorously in modern workplace and domestic banter for 'staging a mutiny'.

history.meaning: to instigate treason or armed rebellion against the sovereign
to rebel, revolt; (colloquial/jocular) to act up, stage a mutiny against a boss or parent

造反.notes: In contemporary workplace and family settings, 要造反啊？ ('Are you staging a mutiny?') is a lighthearted, teasing reprimand when subordinates, interns, or children talk back.

造成.etymology: A resultative verb-complement (動補) compound uniting 造 (zào, 'to make, construct, fashion') and 成 (chéng, 'to complete, become, accomplish'). In Classical Chinese (attested in the Rites of Zhou and Tang poetry), it meant 'to construct to completion' or 'to train into maturity', before grammaticalizing in modern prose into a causative transitive verb meaning 'to bring about, give rise to, or cause' (typically undesirable outcomes).

history.meaning: to build to completion, fashion, cultivate into form
to cause, bring about, result in (often negative consequences)

造成.notes: In modern Mandarin, 造成 exhibits strong negative prosody, almost always collocating with unfavorable nouns like 损失 ('loss'), 误会 ('misunderstanding'), 困扰 ('trouble'), or 事故 ('accident').

造谣.etymology: A verb-object (動賓) compound formed from 造 (zào, 'to fabricate, concoct, invent') and 谣 (傳統字 謠, yáo, 'unaccompanied folksong, ballad; popular hearsay, unfounded rumor'). In ancient China, 謠 referred to street ballads that often carried political satire or unverified gossip; combining it with 造 yielded 'to fabricate rumors out of thin air'.

history.meaning: to invent popular ditties or concoct false hearsay
to fabricate and spread false rumors, start a smear campaign

造谣.notes: Essential showbiz and PR vocabulary: entertainment studios regularly issue legal statements condemning 造谣抹黑 ('fabricating rumors and smearing') and 造谣传谣 ('inventing and spreading rumors').

rootFamily.gloss: to refute a rumor, debunk false news

逻辑.etymology: A phonetic loanword (音譯詞) coined in 1902 by the translator and enlightenment thinker Yan Fu (嚴復) in his translation of John Stuart Mill's 'A System of Logic' (*穆勒名學*) to render English 'logic' (ultimately from Ancient Greek λογική, logikḗ, from λόγος, lógos, 'reason, discourse, word'). Remarkably, the compound 邏輯 already existed in Literary Chinese with the unrelated meaning 'to patrol and inspect', which Yan Fu repurposed for its close phonetic match to 'logic'.

history.meaning: to patrol, rove and keep watch (indigenous Literary Chinese compound)
the formal discipline of logic (Yan Fu's 1902 phonetic borrowing from English 'logic')
logic, objective regularity, line of reasoning

morphemes.meaning: to patrol; phonetic syllable luó rendering English 'lo-'
to compile, gather; phonetic syllable jí rendering English '-gic'

逻辑.notes: Pronounced with a neutral tone on the second syllable in everyday speech (luóji), it commonly collocates with 符合 ('conform to'), 毫无 ('utterly lack'), and 强盗逻辑 ('bandit logic').

rootFamily.gloss: to patrol, make the rounds (preserves original sense of 逻)

cognates.meaning: to press upon, draw near, compel

逼.etymology: A phono-semantic compound (形聲) combining the walking radical 辶 (辵, 'step, movement') with the phonetic component 畐 (fú / bī, Old Chinese *pɯk, originally depicting a full jar, hence 'full, pressing tightly'). In Classical Chinese (often written interchangeably with 偪), it meant 'to draw close, crowd, press tightly upon', whence 'to drive into a corner, coerce, or compel'.

history.meaning: to crowd closely, press near, encroach upon
to hem in, pressure, coerce, approach closely
to force, compel, drive into a corner, extort

逼.notes: Frequently enters pivotal constructions (逼某人做某事 'force someone to do something') and high-register four-character idioms like 形势所逼 ('compelled by circumstances') or 咄咄逼人 ('overbearing and aggressive').

rootFamily.gloss: lifelike, true to life (literally 'pressing close to reality')

遍.etymology: Phono-semantic character (徧/遍) combining 辶 ('walk, go through') + 扁 (biǎn/biàn phonetic): originally 'go all around, everywhere, universal, all over', and from the Tang–Song period onward the primary verbal classifier for 'a complete time through from start to finish (reading a book, listening to a song, or checking something once through: 看一遍)'.

history.meaning: go all around; everywhere; throughout
all over; verbal classifier for one complete pass from beginning to end

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 遍 (via 萌典)

遍地.etymology: A modifier-head or verb-object compound formed from 遍 (biàn, variant 徧, 'all over, everywhere, throughout, to pervade') and 地 (dì, 'earth, ground, land'). Attested since Six Dynasties and Tang Buddhist narratives (where 遍地黄金 described ground covered in gold), it describes something blanketing the entire surface of the ground or existing everywhere.

history.meaning: covering the whole ground, throughout the land
all over the ground, everywhere, ubiquitous

遍地.notes: Often paired with four-character idioms such as 遍地开花 ('blossoming everywhere' — used in media production when a project or trend succeeds across multiple platforms simultaneously).

rootFamily.gloss: all over the body, covered in

道.etymology: Ancient ideogram attested on Zhou bronzes combining 辶 ('road, walk') + 首 ('head', leading the way): 'road, path, way, channel/course; the Way/Dao (universal principle, morality, or method); speak/say (说道); classifier for courses of food, doors/walls, streaks/lines, questions, or orders'.

history.meaning: road; path; the Way; principle; speak
road; way/method; say; classifier for doors, dishes, lines, questions

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 道 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: the Way that can be told (opening of the Tao Te Ching)
cognates.word: 道可道 (michi no michi to subeki wa)

cognates.meaning: the Way that can be spoken of
the Way that can be spoken of

道可道.etymology: The celebrated opening clause of Chapter 1 of the *Laozi* (*Daodejing*, 老子·道德經): 道可道，非常道 ('The Way that can be spoken of is not the constant Way'). It exploits Classical Chinese polysemy through antanaclasis: the first 道 is a noun ('the cosmic Way, ultimate principle, Dao'),的可 (kě) is the modal auxiliary ('can be, is able to be'), and the second 道 functions as a passive verb ('to speak of, articulate, tread/follow').

history.meaning: the Way (principle) that can be articulated or guided by words
the Way that can be spoken of (quoted philosophically or playfully in modern discourse)

morphemes.meaning: can be, may be (modal marker of possibility)

道可道.notes: Every educated Chinese speaker knows the full couplet 道可道，非常道; in modern TV dramas and witty conversation, quoting 道可道 signals philosophical depth or playful mystique when explaining an ineffable creative concept.

rootFamily.gloss: Taoism, philosophy of the Way; morality and ethics
to explain, state clearly (verb sense of 道)

道歉.etymology: A verb-object (動賓) compound joining 道 (dào, here in its transitive verbal sense 'to speak, express, state', as in 道谢 'to express thanks') with 歉 (qiàn, originally 'crop failure, dearth, deficiency', extended in Literary Chinese to 'feeling of inadequacy, regret, remorse'). Thus 道歉 literally means 'to voice one's sense of inadequacy or regret'.

history.meaning: to express regret or remorse for a shortcoming
to apologize formally or personally

道歉.notes: Like other verb-object compounds, it takes a recipient via the preposition 向 or 跟 (向某人道歉 'apologize to someone') and can be split to insert modifiers (道个歉 'offer an apology').

rootFamily.gloss: feeling of guilt or apologetic regret
to express thanks (parallel verb-object with 道)

道理.etymology: Coordinative noun compound pairing two central concepts of Chinese philosophy: 道 ('the Way, guiding principle') + 理 ('natural pattern or veins in jade -> reason, order', neutral tone li in everyday speech): 'reason, principle, sense, justification, the right way'.

history.meaning: universal principle and order
reason; sense; principle; argument

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 道理 (via 萌典)

道路.etymology: A coordinative (聯合/並列) disyllabic compound pairing two near-synonyms from Classical Chinese: 道 (dào, 'thoroughfare, broad way, path') and 路 (lù, 'road, route, path for travel'). Attested in pre-Qin classics including the *Book of Rites* (*Liji*) and *Zuo Zhuan*, it encompasses both physical highways and figurative life or career paths.

history.meaning: roads and pathways, public thoroughfares
road, street, thoroughfare; figurative path or course of development

道路.notes: While 路 alone is preferred in casual speech for physical streets, 道路 is slightly more formal and frequently used metaphorically for career or artistic journeys (人生道路 'path in life', 创作道路 'creative path').

避避.etymology: Reduplicated verb from 避 ('avoid, step aside from, take shelter from', 辶 + 辟, as in 避雨 'take shelter from the rain'): 'take shelter for a bit, step aside briefly to avoid (rain, wind, heat, or someone)'.

history.meaning: take brief shelter; avoid for a moment

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 避避 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: taking shelter from the rain (literary; vernacular is 雨宿り amayadori)
to take shelter from the rain

避雨.etymology: A transparent verb-object (動賓) compound formed from 避 (bì, 'to avoid, shun, take refuge from') and 雨 (yǔ, 'rain'). Attested in Tang and Song dynasty prose and poetry, it follows the productive Classical pattern 避 + natural hazard (compare 避暑 'escape the summer heat', 避风 'take shelter from the wind').

history.meaning: to seek cover or shelter from falling rain
to take shelter from the rain

morphemes.meaning: to avoid, evade, take shelter from

避雨.notes: A classic romance-drama trope in Chinese film and television (*幕后之王* included), where two characters forced to 避雨 under the same eaves share an intimate conversation.

rootFamily.gloss: to escape summer heat, go to a summer resort

邀.etymology: A phono-semantic compound (形聲) combining the walking radical 辶 (辵, 'movement along a path') with 敫 (jiǎo / yāo, Old Chinese *kewk, 'bright, to call out'). Originally in Classical Chinese (where it was often written 徼), it meant 'to go out to meet, intercept on the road, or seek to obtain', which naturally evolved in Six Dynasties poetry (such as Li Bai's 举杯邀明月 'raising my cup to invite the bright moon') into 'to invite or summon as a guest'.

history.meaning: to intercept along the way, go out to meet, seek after
to welcome, summon, invite as a guest
to invite, request the presence of (literary or succinct register)

morphemes.meaning: to walk, go out to meet along a path

邀.notes: As a monosyllabic verb, 邀 belongs to a refined or journalistic register (e.g., 应邀出席 'attend upon invitation', 特邀嘉宾 'specially invited guest' on variety shows).

rootFamily.gloss: to seek credit or reward for oneself (preserves older sense 'to seek')

cognates.meaning: to invite and make an appointment; invitation

邀约.etymology: A coordinative (聯合) compound uniting 邀 (yāo, 'to invite, bid') and 约 (傳統字 約, yuē, 'to bind by agreement, arrange an appointment, invite beforehand'). Used as a literary verb in late imperial Chinese ('to invite by prior arrangement'), it has surged in modern Mandarin media and entertainment industry usage as a noun meaning a formal 'booking offer, appearance invitation, or social engagement'.

history.meaning: to invite and arrange to meet together
(verb) to invite to an appointment; (noun) formal invitation, showbiz booking offer

morphemes.meaning: to make an appointment, agree upon, pact

邀约.notes: In television and talent agency parlance, 收到节目组的邀约 ('receive a booking offer/invitation from the production team') and 发出邀约 ('extend an offer') are standard industry collocations.

rootFamily.gloss: to make an appointment, arrange to meet; date

邀请.etymology: A coordinative (聯合) compound pairing two courteous verbs of bidding: 邀 (yāo, 'to go out to meet, invite') and 请 (傳統字 請, qǐng, 'to request respectfully, ask the favor of someone's presence'). Attested since the Six Dynasties and Tang period, the combination reinforces the deferential act of inviting an esteemed guest or participant.

history.meaning: to respectfully bid and request a guest's presence
to invite (verb); invitation (noun)

邀请.notes: The standard, versatile word for 'invite' across both spoken and written Mandarin; compare 请客 ('treat someone to a meal') where 请 implies paying the bill, whereas 邀请 focuses on requesting attendance.

那.etymology: Distal demonstrative ('that'), pairing with a measure word before nouns (那个 'that one', 那条街 'that street') or opening a clause with 'well then'. Attested as a demonstrative in Han–Six Dynasties colloquial texts, contrasting directly with proximal 这.

history.meaning: that; over there

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 那 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: that one (Mandarin borrowing alongside native 嗰個)

那个.etymology: A demonstrative-classifier compound formed from the distal demonstrative pronoun 那 (nà, colloquial reading nèi, attested as a distal demonstrative since the Tang–Song vernacular transformation from Classical 爾/若) and the general classifier 个 (傳統字 個/箇, gè, originally 'bamboo stalk', grammaticalized by the Six Dynasties into the universal individual classifier). Together they form the standard distal determiner 'that (one)' and a ubiquitous conversational discourse filler.

history.meaning: that one, that person or thing
that (determiner/pronoun); um, well, you know (hesitation marker)

morphemes.meaning: general classifier for individuals or items

那个.notes: In spoken northern Mandarin, 那個 is often pronounced nèige (a historical contraction of 那 nà + 一 yī + 个 ge) and serves as the most common verbal filler ('um, uh, well') when pausing for thought.

rootFamily.gloss: like that, in that way; then

那么.etymology: Distal demonstrative adverb and conjunction combining 那 ('that') + manner/degree suffix 么 (麼, me): 'like that, so (before adjectives: 那么大 'that big'); then, in that case (as a discourse conjunction)'.

history.meaning: like that; so (degree); then / in that case

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 那么 (via 萌典)

那些.etymology: Plural distal demonstrative determiner and pronoun combining 那 ('that') + plural/indefinite quantifier 些 ('some, a number of'): 'those'.

history.meaning: those

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 那些 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: at that moment (northern Mandarin loan; native is 嗰陣時)

那会儿.etymology: A demonstrative temporal phrase combining the distal demonstrative 那 (nà / nèi, 'that') with 会儿 (傳統字 會兒, huìr, the rhotacized diminutive of 会 huì, 'junction, meeting, brief moment or interval of time'). Originating in northern Mandarin (especially Beijing vernacular) during the Qing dynasty, it refers either to a brief moment ('at that exact moment') or nostalgically to an entire past era ('back in those days').

history.meaning: that brief moment, that juncture in time
at that time, back then, that moment (past or future)

morphemes.meaning: diminutive rhotic suffix (-r) marking colloquial temporal nouns

那会儿.notes: Warm, conversational, and slightly nostalgic compared to the neutral 那时候; e.g., 我刚入行那会儿 ('Back when I first entered the industry...').

rootFamily.gloss: right now, at this moment (proximal counterpart)

那儿.etymology: Spoken northern Mandarin rhotacized (儿化 érhuà) distal locative pronoun combining 那 ('that') + retroflex locative suffix 儿 (-r, corresponding to 那里): 'there, that place'.

history.stage: Qing Beijing vernacular to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: there (spoken equivalent of 那里)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 那儿 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: that day (standard written form; spoken 嗰日)

那天.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) temporal compound combining the distal demonstrative 那 (nà, 'that') directly with 天 (tiān, originally 'sky, heaven' in Old Chinese *qʰl'iːn, extended in vernacular Mandarin to mean 'day, 24-hour cycle', largely replacing Classical 日 rì in speech). Because 天 functions as a quasi-measure word of time, it attaches directly to 那 without an intervening classifier.

history.meaning: that day (past or future)
that day, the other day

那天.notes: When used at the start of a story without prior context, 那天 often translates naturally into English as 'the other day' (e.g., 那天我在电梯里碰到他 'I ran into him in the elevator the other day').

那头.etymology: Colloquial distal locative noun combining 那 ('that') + nominal locative suffix 头 (頭, 'end, side'): 'that end (of a rope, bridge, room, or phone line), over there'.

history.meaning: that end; the other end; over there

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 那头 (via 萌典)

那就.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 那就. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 那就 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 那就 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 那就 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 那就. The etymology of 那就 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 那就
middle form of 那就
modern form of 那就

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 那就

那帮人.etymology: A demonstrative noun phrase structured as demonstrative 那 (nà, 'that') + collective classifier 帮 (傳統字 幫, bāng, originally 'shoe upper or side reinforcement', extended in Ming–Qing vernacular to 'guild, faction, boatmen's gang', and grammaticalized into a collective measure word for a crowd or clique) + head noun 人 (rén, 'person, people'). Literally 'that gang or clique of people'.

history.meaning: that guild, gang, or band of people
that crowd of people, that bunch, that crew

那帮人.notes: Carries an informal, lively, and sometimes mildly dismissive or exasperated tone ('that bunch / that crew'), unlike the polite and formal 那批人 or 那些人.

rootFamily.gloss: to help, assist (verbal sense of 帮)

那时.etymology: Deictic time compound of distal demonstrative 那 ('that') + 时 ('time; moment'). Points back to a specific period in a story ('back then; at that time'), contrasting with 这时 ('at this moment').

history.meaning: at that time; back then
back then; at that time

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 那时

那样.etymology: A demonstrative pro-form combining the distal stem 那 (nà, 'that') with 样 (傳統字 樣, yàng, originally the 'acorn of the Oriental oak', loaned in Tang–Song vernacular for 'wooden pattern, mold, model, appearance, manner'). Thus 那样 literally means 'of that pattern or manner', serving as a demonstrative of manner, degree, or quality ('like that, in that way').

history.meaning: of that pattern, in that fashion or appearance
like that, in that way, of that kind, so

那样.notes: Frequently paired with 像...那样 ('like / in the way that...') or contrasted in the idiom 这样那样 ('this and that; all sorts of', as in 遇到这样那样的问题 'encounter all sorts of problems').

cognates.word: 那段時間 (naa5 dyun6 si4 gaan3)

那段时间.etymology: A four-syllable modifier-head temporal phrase composed of the distal demonstrative 那 (nà, 'that'), the section classifier 段 (duàn, 'segment, length, stretch of something long'), and the disyllabic noun 时间 (傳統字 時間, shíjiān, 'time, temporal interval', from 时 'season, time' + 间 'interval, space between'). Together they conceptualize a past timeframe spatially as a 'cut segment of time'.

history.form: 那段時間 / 那段时间 (nà duàn shíjiān)
history.meaning: that stretch or period of time

morphemes.meaning: segment, section, stretch (of road, text, or time)

那段时间.notes: Unlike 那天 (a single day) or 那会儿 (a moment or general era), 那段时间 specifically frames a bounded, continuous stretch of weeks or months (e.g., 节目筹备那段时间 'during that period when the show was in preparation').

rootFamily.gloss: recently, this recent period of time (proximal counterpart)

那边.etymology: Distal locative compound noun combining 那 ('that') + 边 (邊, 'side', often neutral tone bian): 'that side, over there, beyond'.

history.meaning: that side; over there

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 那边 (via 萌典)

那里.etymology: Standard distal locative pronoun combining 那 ('that') + 里 (裡, 'place, inside', neutral tone li): 'there, that place'.

history.meaning: there; that place

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 那里 (via 萌典)

邮件.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) compound combining 邮 (傳統字 郵, yóu, in Classical Chinese 'a border relay station or posthouse for transmitting official dispatches on foot or horseback') and 件 (jiàn, 'individual item, document, parcel'). Coined in modern postal administration for 'postal matter, letters and parcels', it was seamlessly extended in the digital era as the standard ellipsis for 电子邮件 ('electronic mail, email').

history.meaning: imperial relay posthouse for official dispatches
postal items, letters and parcels sent by mail
mail piece; email (short for 电子邮件)

邮件.notes: In contemporary workplace dialogue (such as media agencies in *幕后之王*), 发邮件 ('send an email') and 查收邮件 ('check and receive one's email') almost always refer to electronic mail rather than physical post; the classifier is 封 (一封邮件).

邮戳.etymology: Compound of 邮 ('postal relay station; mail',垂/由 + city radical 阝) + 戳 ('jab; stamp; official seal mark',羽 + 戈 'halberd'). Denotes the dated ink postmark stamped by a post office across a postage stamp and postcard.

history.meaning: postal cancellation stamp; postmark

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 邮戳

邮箱.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) compound formed from 邮 (傳統字 郵, yóu, 'posthouse, postal mail') and 箱 (xiāng, originally 'bamboo carriage box or granary chest' with the bamboo radical 竹, hence 'box, chest, receptacle'). Originally denoting a street pillar box or household letterbox for physical mail, it underwent semantic extension in the 1990s to mean an 'email inbox or email address' (short for 电子邮箱).

history.meaning: physical postbox, street pillar box, household letterbox
physical mailbox; email account, email inbox, email address

邮箱.notes: When a colleague asks 你的邮箱是多少？ ('What is your email address?'), they are asking for your email address string, not your physical postal box!

邮递员.etymology: Three-character occupational compound combining 邮递 ('postal delivery', 邮 'post-station relay' + 递 'hand over in turn, deliver') + 员 (員, 'staff member, worker'): 'postal carrier, mailman, postman'.

history.meaning: mailman; postal carrier

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 邮递员 (via 萌典)

邻居.etymology: Coordinative/modifier-head compound noun of 邻 (鄰, 'neighbor, five-household neighborhood unit in Zhou times', 令 + 阝) + 居 ('dwell, residence'): 'neighbor'. Attested since Tang–Song poetry and vernacular.

history.meaning: neighboring household; neighbor

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 邻居 (via 萌典)

cognates.word: 鄭重 (teichō, often written 丁重)

郑重.etymology: Originally a rhyming binome (疊韻連綿詞) in Han dynasty Chinese (both 鄭 *drengH and 重 *drjowngX had retroflex dental-stop initials in Middle Chinese). In Han–Tang texts (such as the *Book of Han* biography of Wang Mang), 鄭重 meant 'frequent, repeated, solicitous, or painstakingly attentive'. Over time, through folk-etymological reinforcement by 重 (zhòng, 'weighty, serious, grave'), its core sense shifted to 'solemn, earnest, formal, and serious'.

history.meaning: frequent, repeated; solicitous and attentive in parting or courtesy
solemn, earnest, formal, serious in manner or declaration

morphemes.meaning: solicitous, earnest (originally first syllable of rhyming binome; also state surname Zhèng)

郑重.notes: Often used adverbially in formal announcements, apologies, or promises, especially in the four-character intensifier 郑重其事 ('treating a matter with utmost solemnity') or 郑重声明 ('solemnly declare').

cognates.meaning: section, department, club; counter for copies of books/newspapers
part, division, ministry; classifier for books/films
ministry, department, part; classifier for works/machines

部.etymology: A phono-semantic compound (形聲) combining phonetic 咅 (pǒu / bù, Old Chinese *bˤəʔ) with the right-hand city/territory radical 阝 (邑 yì, 'settlement, administrative district'). In Han dynasty administration, 部 meant 'an administrative jurisdiction, military command division, or tribal group', then 'a category or multi-volume literary compilation' (such as the Four Categories 四部), whence its modern usage both as a noun ('ministry, department, unit') and as a classifier for complete literary/cinematic works (一部电影) and complex machines/vehicles/phones (一部手机).

history.meaning: administrative division, military command unit, territorial tribe
government ministry (e.g., Six Ministries 六部); category of books; classifier for multi-volume works
department, ministry, unit; classifier for films, novels, vehicles, and phones

部.notes: Essential in film and television production as the standard classifier for movies, TV drama series, and books (拍一部剧 'shoot a drama series', 一部大片 'a blockbuster film').

部分.etymology: Coordinative noun compound of 部 ('section, division, part') + 分 (fèn, 'allotted share, component part'): 'part, section, portion, share'.

history.meaning: divide into sections and shares
part; portion; section

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 部分 (via 萌典)

部门.etymology: A coordinative (聯合) compound uniting 部 (bù, 'administrative division, category, bureau') and 门 (傳統字 門, mén, originally 'double-leaf gate', extended in Classical Chinese to 'school of thought, lineage, classification category, or administrative branch'). Already attested in Song–Ming texts for 'categories and branches', it was reinforced in modern organizational terminology (alongside Japanese 部門 bumon) to denote a functional 'department, division, or sector' within a company or government.

history.meaning: classified categories and branches of learning or affairs
organizational department, government agency, corporate division

部门.notes: Core corporate vocabulary: in television networks and production companies, workflows constantly cross between 节目部门 ('programming department'), 宣发部门 ('publicity and distribution department'), and 有关部门 ('relevant authorities').

rootFamily.gloss: internal, inside a department or organization
head of a department or government minister

都.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 者 (zhě/dū phonetic) + 邑 (阝, 'walled city'). In Classical Chinese, read dū, it meant 'great walled city with an ancestral temple -> capital city, metropolis' (as in 首都, 成都) and 'refined, all/gather'. From the Tang–Song vernacular onward, read dōu, its sense of 'gather together' grammaticalized into Mandarin's universal inclusive adverb 'all, both; even; already'.

history.meaning: capital city; gather; refined
all, both, even, already (dōu); capital city, metropolis (dū)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 都 (via 萌典)

配.etymology: Ideogram combining 酉 ('wine vessel') + 己 (' kneeling person'): originally 'blend and match wine colors/flavors at a feast', hence 'match, mate, marry (配偶); mix/compound (medicine or paint); cut/make a matching key (配钥匙); go together with; deserve/be worthy of'.

history.meaning: blend wine; match as a pair; spouse; worthy of
match; go with; mix/prepare; make a matching key/part; deserve

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 配 (via 萌典)

配合.etymology: A coordinative (聯合) compound combining 配 (pèi, originally 'color of wine', early used in the *Book of Odes* for 'to match, be a worthy mate or counterpart to, pair up') and 合 (hé, 'to join together, close, harmonize, fit'). Attested in the *Book of Odes* (*Shijing*) and Han texts for 'matching and uniting harmoniously' (originally of cosmic forces or marriage partners), it broadened in modern Mandarin into 'to coordinate, work in sync, cooperate with someone's lead'.

history.meaning: to pair with, match harmoniously as counterparts
to coordinate, cooperate, act in concert with, support someone's work

morphemes.meaning: to join, combine, harmonize, fit together

配合.notes: Unlike 合作 ('collaborate as equal partners'), 配合 often implies one party adapting to, supporting, or syncing with another's lead or schedule (e.g., 感谢大家的配合 'Thank you all for your cooperation', 配合宣传 'cooperate with the promotional campaign').

rootFamily.gloss: to collaborate, work together as partners (shares 合)
to match, pair up (clothing, colors, roles)
to dub a film/show, voice acting (shares 配 'to match voice to picture')

配套.etymology: Verb-object compound used as a verb and modifier, combining 配 ('match together, fit') + 套 ('complete set'): 'form a complete matching set, complement each other; supporting/matching (facilities or equipment)'.

history.meaning: form a complete set; matching; complementary

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 配套 (via 萌典)

配方.etymology: Originally a verb-object (動賓) compound in traditional Chinese medicine and pharmacy combining 配 (pèi, 'to compound, proportion, blend ingredients according to rules') and 方 (fāng, 'medical prescription, formula, method'). Over time it lexicalized into a noun denoting any 'formula, recipe, or proprietary blend' of ingredients in medicine, food, cosmetics, or metaphorically in creative production.

history.meaning: to compound a medicinal prescription; a pharmaceutical formula
formula, recipe, blend of ingredients; metaphorical creative formula

配方.notes: Popularized in modern pop-culture banter by the viral phrase 原来的配方，熟悉的味道 ('the original formula, the familiar taste'), often used jokingly when a TV show or producer relies on classic, predictable tropes.

rootFamily.gloss: side dish, garnish; supporting ingredients (shares 配)

酒.etymology: A phono-semantic and ideographic compound (會意兼形聲) combining the water/liquid radical 氵 (水 shuǐ, 'liquid') with 酉 (yǒu, Old Chinese *ljuʔ, an ancient oracle-bone pictograph of a narrow-necked ceramic amphora or fermenting jar used for brewing millet beer). In Old and Classical Chinese, 酒 denoted fermented grain beverages (millet or rice wine/beer), later expanding after the Yuan dynasty to cover all fermented and distilled alcoholic drinks.

history.meaning: fermented millet or rice beverage used in rituals and banquets
fermented wine, ale, and early fruit/herbal liquors
any alcoholic beverage (wine, beer, spirits, liquor)

morphemes.meaning: fermenting jar or amphora (co-semantic and phonetic *ljuʔ)

酒.notes: Unlike English 'wine' (made specifically from grapes), 酒 is the superordinate term for all alcoholic drinks: 啤酒 ('beer'), 红酒/葡萄酒 ('grape wine'), and 白酒 ('clear distilled sorghum liquor'). Socializing over drinks to close deals is known as 酒局 ('drinking banquet').

酒店.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 酒 ('wine, alcoholic drink') + 店 ('shop, inn, tavern'). In Tang–Song–Ming China (famously Du Mu's 借问酒家何处有 and vernacular tales), 酒店 meant 'wine shop, tavern, inn'; in modern Mandarin it refers both to a 'wineshop/restaurant' and a large 'hotel'.

history.meaning: tavern; wineshop and inn
hotel; restaurant/tavern

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 酒店 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: ethyl alcohol, spirit of wine (older scientific term)

酒精.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) compound combining 酒 (jiǔ, 'alcoholic beverage, wine, liquor') and 精 (jīng, originally 'finely milled choice rice', extended in Daoist alchemy and classical philosophy to 'pure essence, vital spirit, refined extract'). Coined in early modern East Asian chemistry as a calque of European 'spirit of wine' (Latin *spiritus vini*, the volatile essence distilled from wine), it denotes pure chemical 'alcohol / ethanol' as well as alcoholic content in beverages.

history.meaning: the refined essence or spirit of wine (early chemical translation of 'spirit of wine')
alcohol, ethanol (both medical/chemical rubbing alcohol and beverage alcohol content)

酒精.notes: Crucial distinction: you drink 酒 ('alcoholic drinks'), NEVER 酒精 ('pure ethanol / rubbing alcohol'), which is used only for medical disinfection (医用酒精), chemical contexts, or describing physiological reactions like 酒精过敏 ('alcohol allergy') and 酒精中毒 ('alcohol poisoning').

rootFamily.gloss: spirit, vigor, mental state; energetic (shares 精)

酒量.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) compound formed from 酒 (jiǔ, 'fermented beverage, wine, alcohol', graphically derived from the vessel radical 酉 depicting an amphora for fermenting millet must) and 量 (liàng, 'measured capacity, volume, tolerance'). Attested in Literary Chinese from the Song dynasty onward (e.g., Su Shi's prose and poetry), it originally denoted the physical volume of wine a person could consume before intoxication, and in modern business and entertainment culture often figures in social networking at banquets.

history.meaning: fermented grain liquor + measured vessel capacity
personal capacity for drinking wine without becoming drunk
tolerance or capacity for alcohol

酒量.notes: Commonly collocated with 大/好 ('high tolerance') or 小/浅 ('low tolerance'), e.g., 酒量不错; a staple topic at Chinese media industry dinners and client banquets (应酬).

酝酿.etymology: A coordinative (并列) verbal compound combining two characters that both share the fermentation-vessel radical 酉 (yǒu): 酝 (traditional 醞, yùn, 'to ferment grain must incrementally by adding yeast and mash') and 酿 (traditional 釀, niàng, 'to brew wine by fermenting grain'). Already used figuratively in Han and Six Dynasties texts (such as the History of the Later Han and Zuo Si's Shu Du Fu) to describe the slow, organic cultivation of literary atmosphere, scholarly refinement, or emotional depth, before broadening in modern Mandarin to mean preparing plans, emotions, or creative projects gradually behind the scenes.

history.meaning: to ferment and brew alcoholic liquor through gradual stages
to cultivate or steep in literary, artistic, or emotional atmosphere
to brew; to mull over, deliberate, or get into an emotional state gradually

酝酿.notes: In film and television production, 酝酿情绪 ('to build up or get into the right emotional state before a take') is standard on-set terminology for actors and directors.

rootFamily.gloss: to ferment, cause to happen, brew (a disaster)
warm, gentle, and refined (like aged wine)

酥皮.etymology: Modifier-head culinary noun of 酥 ('flaky, crisp and melting in the mouth', originally clarified butter/curd from milk 酉 + 禾) + 皮 ('outer crust, pastry skin'): 'flaky pastry crust, puff pastry'.

history.meaning: flaky pastry; puff pastry crust

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 酥皮 (via 萌典)

酥脆.etymology: Coordinate culinary texture adjective combining 酥 ('flaky; short; tender-crisp', fermentation/dairy radical 酉 + 禾, originally 'clarified butter pastry') + 脆 ('crisp; snapping cleanly'). In Chinese baking, 酥脆 praises pastry crusts and tart shells that are both delicately flaky and crisp.

history.meaning: flaky and crisp (of baked pastries)
crisp and flaky

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 酥脆

酸.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 酸. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 酸 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 酸 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 酸 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 酸. The etymology of 酸 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 酸
middle form of 酸
modern form of 酸

酸梅汤.etymology: A three-character modifier-head (偏正) culinary compound composed of 酸梅 (suānméi, 'sour smoked plum, dark plum', itself a modifier-head compound of 酸 'sour, acidic' + 梅 'Prunus mume, Chinese plum') modifying the head noun 汤 (traditional 湯, tāng, 'hot decoction, herbal infusion, broth'). Originating in imperial palace kitchens (notably refined by the Qing imperial pharmacy 御茶膳房 using smoked烏梅 wūméi, osmanthus, hawthorn, and rock sugar) and traditional Beijing street stalls, the word preserves the older sense of 汤 as a brewed medicinal or refreshing decoction served chilled in summer.

history.meaning: decoction boiled from smoked sour plums and sweetener
traditional chilled sweet-and-sour smoked plum beverage

酸梅汤.notes: Notice that 汤 here retains its classical meaning of 'herbal decoction / infused drink' (as in 绿豆汤) rather than a savory meal soup; it is a classic summer refreshment for cooling down (解暑).

rootFamily.gloss: smoked dark plum used in decoctions

醋.etymology: Originally borrowed from a homophonous Classical graph meaning 'guest toasting the host' (wine/fermentation radical 酉 + phonetic 昔 xī), adopted to replace the older Classical word 酢/醯 ('sour fermented grain vinegar') so host-and-guest ritual toasts would not be confused with sourness.

history.meaning: fermented grain vinegar
vinegar

醒.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 酉 ('fermented wine jar') + 星 (xīng/xǐng phonetic): originally 'recover sobriety after drunkenness, sober up' (as in Qu Yuan's 众人皆醉我独醒 'all the world is drunk and I alone am sober'), and extended to 'wake up from sleep, awaken, become clear-headed, be striking to the eye (醒目)'.

history.meaning: sober up from wine -> regain clear awareness
wake up from sleep; sober up; awaken

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 醒 (via 萌典)

醒悟.etymology: A coordinative-resultative (并列/动补) compound uniting 醒 (xǐng, 'to sober up from alcohol; to wake from sleep', bearing the wine-vessel radical 酉) and 悟 (wù, 'to awaken mentally, comprehend, realize', bearing the heart-mind radical 忄). By mapping physical sobering/waking (醒) onto spiritual and cognitive awakening (悟, heavily reinforced by Buddhist translations of Sanskrit bodhi / prabodha), the compound evolved in Tang–Song vernacular and Chan (Zen) discourse to mean snapping out of delusion or error and coming to a sudden realization of truth.

history.meaning: to sober up from wine + to comprehend in one's heart-mind
to awaken from spiritual delusion or cognitive error
to come to realize, wake up to reality or one's mistake

醒悟.notes: Often paired with directional or adverbial phrases like 幡然醒悟 ('to realize one's error suddenly and completely') or 醒悟过来 ('to come to one's senses').

rootFamily.gloss: to come to a sudden realization, dawn on one

醒过来.etymology: A verb-directional-complement (动趋) construction formed from the action verb 醒 (xǐng, Originally 'to recover from drunkenness', early extended to 'to wake from sleep or unconsciousness') followed by the compound directional complement 过来 (traditional 過來, guòlái, 'across toward the speaker / back to the normal state of consciousness'). In Mandarin aspectual grammar, 过来 grammaticalized from physical movement ('cross over here') into a restorative state-change marker indicating recovery from fainting, coma, sleep, or bewilderment back to normal awareness.

history.meaning: to sober up from intoxication; to awake from sleep
to transition back into waking consciousness from sleep or fainting
to wake up, regain consciousness, come to one's senses

醒过来.notes: Can be used both literally for someone waking from sleep/unconsciousness (他终于醒过来了) and figuratively for snapping out of an emotional stupor or obsession.

rootFamily.gloss: to wake from a dream; as if waking from a dream
to recover consciousness, come to (from a faint)

醒醒.etymology: A verbal reduplication (重叠式, AA pattern) of the monosyllabic root verb 醒 (xǐng, 'to sober up; to wake up, be awake'), pronounced with a neutral tone on the second syllable (xǐngxing). In Mandarin morphology, reduplicating a state-change or cognitive verb softens or intensifies an imperative call to action—either urging someone who is asleep or drowsy to rouse themselves physically, or exhorting someone who is daydreaming, naive, or self-deceived to snap back to reality.

history.meaning: to sober up; to wake from sleep
wake up! rouse yourself! freshen up your mind!

morphemes.meaning: delimitative/imperative reduplication ('wake up a bit / snap out of it!')

醒醒.notes: In spoken drama and everyday dialogue, 醒醒吧！ ('Wake up!') is the quintessential colloquial interjection to tell someone to stop fantasizing or being naive; also used in 醒醒神 / 醒醒脑 ('freshen up one's mind').

rootFamily.gloss: to remind, call attention to, warn

cognates.meaning: adoption, acceptance (of a proposal or petition)

采纳.etymology: A sequential coordinative (并列/连动) compound joining 采 (traditional 採, cǎi, 'to pluck with the hand, gather, select', originally 采 depicting a hand 爪 picking fruit or leaves from a tree 木) and 纳 (traditional 納, nà, 'to bring inside, receive into storage, admit'). Attested in Han dynasty historiography (such as Ban Gu's Book of Han), where a ruler 'selects and takes in' (采纳) the remonstrances or counsel of his ministers, the compound generalized in modern standard Mandarin to accepting proposals, suggestions, or creative pitches.

history.meaning: to select (as if plucking fruit) and receive (counsel or tribute) into court
to adopt, accept, and act upon (advice, opinions, or proposals)

采纳.notes: Takes abstract objects like 意见 ('opinion'), 建议 ('suggestion'), or 方案 ('proposal/plan'); in workplace and production meetings, 采纳方案 means greenlighting a pitched idea.

rootFamily.gloss: to adopt, employ (a method, technology, or material)
to collect, gather (samples, data, folk songs)

采访.etymology: A coordinative (并列) compound formed from 采 (traditional 採, cǎi, 'to gather, collect, select') and 访 (traditional 訪, fǎng, 'to inquire widely, seek out, visit in order to ask'). In Tang dynasty administrative history, the 采访使 (Cǎifǎngshǐ, 'Imperial Commissioner for Inquiring and Gathering') was an inspector dispatched to investigate local governance and gather intelligence across provinces; in the late 19th and early 20th centuries (reinforced by modern journalistic usage shared with Japanese 採訪), it specialized into journalistic news-gathering and interviewing a subject.

history.meaning: to seek out and gather (rare books, local customs, or administrative intelligence)
to gather news; to interview a person; a journalistic interview

采访.notes: Functions as both verb and noun in media contexts: 接受采访 ('to give an interview'), 独家采访 ('exclusive interview'), 现场采访 ('on-the-spot coverage/interview').

rootFamily.gloss: to visit and interview; talk show / in-depth interview
to pay a visit to, call on

里.etymology: Merged simplified graph representing three related characters: (1) 里 (combining 田 'farmland' + 土 'earth': 'village settlement, neighborhood lane; traditional Chinese mile of ~500 meters'), (2) 裡/裏 (combining 衣 'garment' + 里 lǐ phonetic: 'inner lining of a garment -> inside, interior, within'), and (3) 哩.

morphemes.meaning: fields and earth = village/mile; merged with 裡 'inside'

history.form: 里 (village, Chinese mile) / 裡, 裏 (garment lining -> inside)
history.meaning: settlement/mile vs. inner lining/interior
inside, within, interior; neighborhood lane; Chinese mile (0.5 km)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 里 (via 萌典)

里头.etymology: A suffixed localizer noun (方位词) consisting of the spatial root 里 (traditional 裏/裡, lǐ, originally meaning 'the inner lining of a garment', framed by the clothing radical 衣 around phonetic 里, hence 'interior, inside') plus the bleached nominal/locative suffix 头 (traditional 頭, tou, originally 'head, end, extremity'). During the Tang–Song vernacular transition, 头 grammaticalized into an unstressed locative suffix attached to spatial roots (上头, 下头, 外头, 里头) to form disyllabic place words in colloquial northern Mandarin.

history.meaning: inner lining of a garment; interior space
the inside, interior part of a place or object
inside, within (colloquial localizer)

里头.notes: More colloquial and conversational than 里面 (lǐmiàn); very natural in spoken northern Mandarin for both physical interiors (屋里头 'inside the room') and social circles or organizations.

里子.etymology: A suffixed noun formed from 里 (traditional 裏/裡, lǐ, 'inner lining of a garment', contrasting with 表 biǎo 'outer fur/cloth surface') and the diminutive nominal suffix 子 (zi). While retaining its concrete tailoring sense ('garment lining'), in Ming–Qing vernacular and modern Chinese sociology it developed a crucial metaphorical pairing with 面子 (miànzi, 'outer surface / public prestige'): 面子 is the public reputation shown to outsiders, whereas 里子 is the actual inner substance, private integrity, or tangible benefit behind the scenes.

history.meaning: inner lining of clothing (contrasted with 表 'outer garment surface')
cloth lining of a coat or robe; inner substance
garment lining; inner substance, real benefit, or private dignity (vs. 面子)

里子.notes: Almost always contrasted with 面子 ('face, public prestige') in negotiations and showbiz politics, e.g., 既要面子，也要里子 ('wanting both public prestige and real underlying substance').

rootFamily.gloss: outer surface; public prestige, 'face' (antonym of 里子)
inside and outside; through and through

里边.etymology: A disyllabic compound localizer (方位词) combining the spatial root 里 (traditional 裏/裡, lǐ, 'inner lining; interior, inside') with the directional/locative element 边 (traditional 邊, biān, 'border, side, margin', pronounced in a neutral tone biān/bian in localizers). Like 里头 and 里面, it arose in vernacular Mandarin as a prosodically balanced disyllabic spatial noun meaning 'the inside part, within', frequently taking retroflex erhua (里边儿 lǐbiānr) in northern speech.

history.meaning: interior + side/margin
the inside, interior side or area
inside, within

里边.notes: Interchangeable with 里面 and 里头 in everyday speech, though 里面 is preferred in formal written prose while 里边 and 里头 sound warmer and more conversational.

rootFamily.gloss: beside, next to, by one's side

里面.etymology: Locative compound noun combining 里 (裡, 'inside, inner lining') + 面 ('side, surface, interior'): 'inside, within, the interior'.

history.meaning: inside; interior

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 里面 (via 萌典)

重.etymology: Ancient character attested on Zhou bronzes showing a person (人) standing on the earth (土) carrying a heavy bundled sack (東): read zhòng 'heavy (opposite of 轻 'light'), weight, weighty, important, serious, value highly'; read chóng 'layer upon layer, repeat, again, double'.

morphemes.meaning: person carrying a heavy load on the ground

history.meaning: person bearing a heavy pack = heavy, important (zhòng); layered, repeat, again (chóng)
heavy, weighty, serious (zhòng); repeat, again, layer (chóng)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 重 (via 萌典)

重出江湖.etymology: A four-character idiomatic verb-object phrase (四字格短语) structured as 重出 (chóngchū, 'to come out again, re-emerge', with adverbial 重 chóng 'again, anew' modifying verb 出 chū 'go/come out') + 江湖 (jiānghú, literally 'rivers and lakes'). First coined in Zhuangzi (庄子·大宗师) as the natural realm of free-swimming fish ('forget each other in the rivers and lakes', 相忘于江湖), 江湖 evolved across Tang poetry and Song–Ming martial-arts/underworld vernacular to mean the tumultuous world of itinerant knights-errant, entertainers, and society outside officialdom; hence 重出江湖 means a retired master or veteran returning to the arena.

history.meaning: the rivers and lakes; life of recluse freedom outside the imperial court (Zhuangzi)
to roam or re-enter the pugilistic/itinerant world after seclusion (secular & wuxia fiction)
to come out of retirement and return to competitive action or the public eye

morphemes.meaning: rivers (Yangtze); part of 'rivers and lakes' (the public arena)
lakes; part of 'rivers and lakes' (the public arena)

重出江湖.notes: Borrowed from wuxia (martial arts) lore into showbiz and business journalism to describe a legendary producer, director, or star making a high-profile comeback after years away.

rootFamily.gloss: to retire from the public arena / wash one's hands of the game (antonym)
veteran of the world, streetwise old hand
to make a comeback after defeat (related idiom)

重回.etymology: An adverb-verb modifier-head (状中偏正) compound formed from 重 (chóng, 'in layers, doubled; again, once more', preserving the Middle Chinese voiced level-tone reading *drjowng distinct from departing-tone *drjowngH 'heavy') modifying the motion verb 回 (huí, 'to revolve, turn back, return').
