Used in literary and journalistic Mandarin, it denotes returning once again to a former place, stage, peak status, or career role after an absence.

history.meaning: again, anew + to turn back, return
to return once more to (a place, position, or state)

重回.notes: Always pronounced chónghuí (second tone on 重); in Mandarin syntax it directly takes a destination object without a preposition, e.g., 重回舞台 ('return to the stage') or 重回巅峰 ('return to the peak').

rootFamily.gloss: to revisit an old haunt (idiom: 旧地重游)
to return to, go back to (more formal synonym)

重复.etymology: Coordinative verb and adjective compound of 重 (read chóng, 'repeat, layer again') + 复 (複/復, 'repeat, duplicate, return again'): 'repeat, duplicate, do or say over again; repetitive'.

history.meaning: repeat; duplicate; over again

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 重复 (via 萌典)

重大.etymology: A coordinative (并列) adjectival compound uniting 重 (zhòng, 'heavy in weight; weighty, serious, grave') and 大 (dà, 'large in scale, great, major'). Attested in Han dynasty legal and political memorials (such as the Book of Han and History of the Later Han, e.g., 事体重大 'the matter is weighty and great'), the compound pairs weight (重) and magnitude (大) to qualify decisions, crises, projects, or breakthroughs of far-reaching consequence.

history.meaning: heavy in weight and large in size; weighty and momentous (of state affairs or legal offenses)
major, grave, significant, of great consequence

重大.notes: Pronounced zhòngdà (fourth tone on 重); collocates with high-register nouns like 重大决定 ('major decision'), 重大突破 ('major breakthrough'), and 事关重大 ('the matter is of vital importance').

rootFamily.gloss: solemn, serious, grave (of atmosphere or occasion)
severe, grave, critical (of a problem or crisis)

重审.etymology: An adverb-verb modifier-head (状中偏正) compound combining 重 (chóng, 'again, anew, a second time') with 审 (traditional 審, shěn, 'to examine thoroughly, investigate, adjudicate', originally depicting inspecting animal tracks 釆 inside a roof 宀). Originating in imperial judicial administration (where higher tribunals ordered a case to be re-tried or re-investigated from scratch), in modern media and regulatory contexts it also refers to re-reviewing or re-auditing a broadcast program, script, or contract.

history.meaning: to re-examine or retry a legal case in court
to retry (a legal case); to re-examine, review anew (a project, script, or broadcast)

morphemes.meaning: examine, review, try in court, audit

重审.notes: Pronounced chóngshěn (second tone on 重); in Chinese television and film production, having a cut or proposal sent back for 重审 means undergoing a second round of content or executive review (审查/审核).

rootFamily.gloss: to examine, audit, review (a budget, script, or application)
to try a legal case, bring to trial

重担.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) nominal compound composed of the adjective 重 (zhòng, 'heavy, weighty') modifying the deverbal noun 担 (traditional 擔, dàn, 'a shoulder-pole load, burden carried on a carrying pole', fourth tone dàn as a noun derived from first-tone verb dān 'to carry on a shoulder pole'). From the literal physical load borne across a porter's shoulders (attested in pre-Qin and Han texts like Guoyu and Lunheng), it metaphorized into an onerous duty, executive mission, or weighty responsibility entrusted to a leader.

history.meaning: a heavy physical load carried on a shoulder pole
a heavy burden; a weighty responsibility or difficult mission

morphemes.meaning: load carried on a shoulder pole, burden (dàn)

重担.notes: Both characters are fourth tone (zhòngdàn); typically used with shoulder-carrying verbs like 挑起重担 ('to shoulder a heavy responsibility') or 卸下重担 ('to lay down a heavy burden').

rootFamily.gloss: load on a shoulder pole; responsibility (dànzi)

重新.etymology: Adverbial compound combining 重 (read chóng, 'again, anew') + 新 ('new, freshly'): 'anew, all over again, afresh'. Attested from Tang–Song poetry (e.g., Du Fu, Lu You).

history.meaning: afresh; anew; all over again

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 重新 (via 萌典)

重新开业.etymology: Four-character verb phrase combining 重新 ('anew, all over again') + 开业 ('open for business', 开 'open' + 业 'business/enterprise'): 'reopen for business'.

history.form: 重新開業 / 重新开业
history.meaning: reopen for business

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 重新开业 (via 萌典)

重来.etymology: An adverb-verb modifier-head (状中偏正) compound formed from 重 (chóng, 'again, afresh, from the beginning') and the pro-verb 来 (traditional 來, lái, originally 'wheat' and loaned for 'to come', which in vernacular Mandarin developed a broad pro-verbal sense 'to do, perform an action'). Literally 'to come at it again', 重来 grammaticalized in colloquial Mandarin to mean scrapping a flawed attempt and starting all over again from scratch.

history.meaning: to come back again to a place (e.g., Du Mu's poem 重來已是十年事)
to redo an action, start all over again from scratch

morphemes.meaning: come; pro-verb for performing an action

重来.notes: Pronounced chónglái (second tone on 重); in studio recording and filming, 重来一遍 ('let's do another take / take it from the top') and 推倒重来 ('scrap everything and start from scratch') are heard daily.

rootFamily.gloss: afresh, anew, all over again (adverbial synonym)
to make a comeback (idiom: 卷土重来)

重活.etymology: Modifier-head compound from 重 (*zhòng*, 'heavy; strenuous') + 活 ('work; manual labor; livelihood'). Contrasted with 轻活 ('light work'), it refers to heavy physical chores such as lifting crates, moving furniture, or hauling timber.

history.meaning: heavy manual labor
heavy work; strenuous chores

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 重活

cognates.meaning: important point, emphasis, priority, center of gravity

重点.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) Sino-compound combining 重 (zhòng, 'heavy, weighty, important') and 点 (traditional 點, diǎn, 'dot, spot, geometric point'). Originally coined in Meiji-era Japanese (重点 jūten) in physics and geometry to translate 'center of gravity / weighted point' (alongside 重心 jūshin) and extended to strategic or administrative 'focal point, main priority', it entered 20th-century Chinese as a return graphic loan and became indispensable in modern Chinese for the crux of an argument or top priority of a plan.

history.meaning: weighted point; focal point of emphasis or strategic priority (Meiji Japanese kanji compound)
key point, main focus, top priority; focal (used attributively)

重点.notes: Pronounced zhòngdiǎn (fourth tone on 重); used both as a noun (讲重点 'get to the point!', 划重点 'highlight the key points') and as an uninflected modifier (重点项目 'key priority project').

rootFamily.gloss: center of gravity; core focus, heart of a matter

cognates.meaning: appointing to a position of trust and responsibility; prizing highly
to entrust with an important position, value highly

重用.etymology: An adverb-verb modifier-head (状中偏正) compound formed from 重 (zhòng, 'heavily, in a weighty and prestigious manner') modifying 用 (yòng, 'to employ, appoint to office, make use of'). Attested in Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian (史记) and the Book of Han, where emperors 'heavily employ' (重用) capable statesmen or generals by entrusting them with high office and real authority, it remains the standard corporate and institutional verb for promoting or placing talent in a key role.

history.meaning: to appoint a minister or general to a high, trusted office in statecraft
to put someone in a key position, entrust with major responsibility

morphemes.meaning: heavily, in a weighty or trusted capacity (zhòng)

重用.notes: Pronounced zhòngyòng (fourth tone on 重); frequently appears in passive or receiving constructions in workplace contexts, such as 得到重用 / 受到重用 ('to be entrusted with a key role by management').

rootFamily.gloss: to appoint to an important post (especially overcoming convention, 破格任用)
important official duty or key post (zhòngrèn)

重要.etymology: Coordinative adjective compound of 重 (read zhòng, 'weighty, of great weight') + 要 ('essential, pivotal, key'): 'important, significant, major, vital'. Attested since the漢書 Book of Han and的后汉书 Book of the Later Han.

history.stage: Han Classical Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: weighty and essential = important, vital

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 重要 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: attaching importance to, taking seriously, valuing highly
to attach importance to, treat with high regard

重视.etymology: An adverb-verb modifier-head (状中偏正) compound combining 重 (zhòng, 'heavily, as weighty and important') with 视 (traditional 視, shì, 'to look upon, regard, view', bearing the altar/sign radical 示 and phonetic 见 'see'). Already attested in Classical and Han texts (such as Xunzi and the Book of Han) in contrast with 轻视 (qīngshì, 'to look upon lightly, disdain'), and reinforced in modern standard usage alongside Japanese 重視 (jūshi), it literally means 'to look upon as heavy/weighty'—hence to value highly or take seriously.

history.meaning: to regard with great weight or seriousness (contrasted with 輕視 'to look down upon lightly')
to attach great importance to, value highly, take seriously

重视.notes: Pronounced zhòngshì (fourth tone on 重); its direct structural and semantic antonym is 轻视 ('to slight, underestimate, treat lightly') or 忽视 ('to overlook, neglect').

rootFamily.gloss: to look down on, slight, underestimate (direct antonym)
to inspect, examine closely; to view as (shìwéi)

重逢.etymology: Modifier-head verb compound of 重 (read chóng, 'again, once more') + 逢 ('meet, come across on the road', 辶 + 夆): 'meet again after a separation, reunite'. Attested across Tang–Song poetry.

history.meaning: meet again after parting; reunite

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 重逢 (via 萌典)

重量级.etymology: A three-character suffixed nominal/attributive compound built from 重量 (zhòngliàng, 'physical weight, mass', a modifier-head compound of 重 'heavy' + 量 'measured quantity') plus the taxonomic suffix 级 (traditional 級, jí, originally 'order of silk threads; steps of a staircase; rank or class'). Coined in modern East Asian sports terminology (alongside Japanese 重量級 jūryōkyū) as a calque of English 'heavyweight (division)' in boxing and weightlifting, it quickly metaphorized to describe top-calibre stars, executives, or projects of massive industry clout.

history.meaning: physical weight + rank/grade (originally silk quality or step-rank)
heavyweight division in combat sports; top-calibre, A-list, or highly influential person/project

重量级.notes: In entertainment and media, 重量级嘉宾 ('heavyweight / A-list guest') and 重量级人物 ('heavyweight figure, industry titan') are ubiquitous, contrasting with 轻量级 ('lightweight').

cognates.meaning: open country, uncultivated field; out of office; rustic, wild

野.etymology: A monosyllabic phono-semantic character (形声字) composed of the semantic radical 里 (lǐ, 'settled village/hamlet grid of tilled fields') and the phonetic element 予 (yǔ, Old Chinese *laʔ > Middle Chinese *jaX > Mandarin yě; early oracle-bone and bronze script forms 埜 combined double trees 林 'forest' over 土 'earth'). Originally denoting the uncultivated open countryside beyond the city walls and suburban settlements (郊外为野), it developed a rich contrast with 朝 (cháo, 'the royal court') and 文 (wén, 'cultured refinement'), evolving to mean 'unofficial', 'untamed, wild', and in contemporary Mandarin creative slang, 'boldly unconventional, edgy, and unbridled'.

history.meaning: open, uncultivated countryside beyond the suburbs; rustic, unpolished (as in Analects 质胜文则野)
outside the imperial court (在野); untamed, feral, unruly
wild, untamed; boldly unconventional, edgy, out-of-the-box (of creative ideas or style)

morphemes.meaning: open country; wild, untamed, boldly unconventional

野.notes: In contemporary media and creative industries, praising a proposal or style as 路子很野 ('having a wildly unconventional approach') or 脑洞很野 ('boldly out-of-the-box') can be a high compliment for edgy originality.

rootFamily.gloss: field of vision, horizon, breadth of perspective (shìyě)
unconventional, unorthodox approach or self-taught method (yělùzi)

野花.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 野花. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 野花 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 野花 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 野花 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 野花. The etymology of 野花 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 野花
middle form of 野花
modern form of 野花

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 野花

量.etymology: Originally an oracle-bone and bronze-script compound of 日/口 over 重 ('weight; measure'), depicting grain measured out in a vessel under daylight. Read in the rising second tone (*liáng*, Middle Chinese *ljang*) when used as a verb meaning 'to measure with a ruler, scale, or vessel', and in the falling fourth tone (*liàng*) as a noun meaning 'quantity or capacity'.

history.meaning: measure out grain or length with a standard vessel or rule
measure (liáng); quantity (liàng)

金.etymology: Ancient character attested on Zhou bronzes showing metal nuggets/ore dots buried under a covering shelter/crucible (亼) in the earth (土) with phonetic 今 (jīn): in Pre-Qin Chinese 'metal in general (especially bronze)', and from the Han dynasty onward specifically 'gold; metal; money; golden; metal percussion instruments; surname Jin'.

morphemes.meaning: metal ore in earth + phonetic 今 (jīn)

history.meaning: metal (especially bronze); gold; metal bells
gold; metal; money; golden

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 金 (via 萌典)

金光闪闪.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 金光闪闪. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 金光闪闪 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 金光闪闪 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 金光闪闪 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 金光闪闪. The etymology of 金光闪闪 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 金光闪闪
middle form of 金光闪闪
modern form of 金光闪闪

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 金光闪闪

金子.etymology: A suffixed noun formed from the root noun 金 (jīn, Old Chinese *kəm, originally referring to cast metal in general—especially bronze in Shang and Zhou bronze inscriptions—before narrowing by the Han–Six Dynasties period primarily to yellow gold) and the nominalizing suffix 子 (zi, bleached from 'child/seed' into a bound noun marker). As Mandarin shifted toward disyllabic nouns in the Tang–Song vernacular period, monosyllabic 金 acquired the suffix 子 in spoken usage to denote physical gold metal or bullion, while bare 金 remained productive in compounds.

history.meaning: metal in general (especially bronze); yellow gold (黄金)
gold (as a precious metal or bullion)
gold (colloquial noun for the precious metal)

金子.notes: Famous in the proverb 是金子总会发光 ('True gold will always shine'—meaning genuine talent will eventually be recognized even if initially hidden behind the scenes).

rootFamily.gloss: to guild or plate with gold; to get prestigious credentials (dùjīn)

金属.etymology: Compound noun of 金 ('metal') + 属 (屬, 'category, class, genus'): literally 'the category of metals' -> 'metal (as a material or chemical class)'.

history.meaning: things of the metal class = metal

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 金属 (via 萌典)

金币.etymology: Pairs 金 (jīn, 'gold') with 币 (bì, 'currency'). 币 originally referenced bolts of silk used as high-value currency before coinage. This term carries strong associations with antiquity, treasure hoards, and historical commemorative tokens.

history.meaning: gold coin

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 金币

金牌.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) compound combining 金 (jīn, 'gold') and 牌 (pái, 'flat wooden or metal tablet, tally, plaque, badge'). In Song, Yuan, and Ming imperial administration, a 金牌 was an inscribed gold-plated tally or tablet bestowed by the emperor on elite envoys or generals to command urgent post-horse relays (such as the twelve gold tallies召回 Yue Fei) or confer special immunity; in the 20th century it came to translate 'gold medal' in sports and subsequently developed a vibrant attributive sense in Hong Kong and Mainland media meaning 'ace, top-tier, gold-standard' (e.g., 金牌制作人 'ace producer').

history.meaning: imperial gold-inscribed tally or tablet granting supreme authority or urgent dispatch
gold medal in athletics; ace, top-tier, premier (used attributively of professionals)

金牌.notes: Extremely productive in showbiz and media as a pre-nominal modifier meaning 'ace / star / top-ranked': 金牌制作人 ('ace producer'), 金牌编剧 ('star screenwriter'), 金牌主持 ('top host').

金色.etymology: Modifier-head color compound of 金 ('gold') + 色 ('color'): 'golden color, gold, golden'.

history.stage: Medieval Buddhist & poetic Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: gold color; golden

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 金色 (via 萌典)

金额.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) compound formed from 金 (jīn, 'gold; money, currency, funds') modifying 额 (traditional 額, é, originally 'forehead', extended via the inscribed plaque hung over a doorway 匾额 to mean 'fixed quota, stipulated number, or total sum'). Standardized in modern East Asian financial and legal vocabulary (reinforced by Japanese 金額 kingaku), it denotes the exact numerical sum of money involved in a transaction, contract, or budget.

history.meaning: gold/money + forehead / inscribed quota or fixed quantity
monetary amount, sum of money (in finance, contracts, and commerce)

金额.notes: Formal financial and contractual register (e.g., 合同金额 'contract sum', 投资金额 'investment amount', 金额巨大 'a huge sum of money'); always written with an apostrophe in Pinyin (jīn'é) to separate the syllables.

rootFamily.gloss: quota, allotted share or number of places (míng'é)

金饭碗.etymology: A three-character modifier-head (偏正) metaphorical compound combining 金 (jīn, 'gold') with 饭碗 (traditional 飯碗, fànwǎn, 'rice bowl', itself a modifier-head compound of 饭 'cooked grain, rice' + 碗 'bowl'). In vernacular Chinese, one's 'rice bowl' (饭碗) is the classic metonym for one's livelihood or job; modeled alongside 铁饭碗 (tiěfànwǎn, 'iron rice bowl'—an unbreakable, secure state job) and 泥饭碗 ('clay rice bowl'—a precarious job), 金饭碗 ('golden rice bowl') denotes a job or position that is not only prestigious but exceptionally lucrative.

history.meaning: bowl for eating cooked rice; by metonymy, one's means of livelihood or employment
a 'golden rice bowl': a highly lucrative, enviable, and prestigious job or career position

morphemes.meaning: bowl; metonym for job or position

金饭碗.notes: Contrast the three classic 'rice bowls' of Chinese career talk: 铁饭碗 ('iron rice bowl' = rock-solid job security, like civil service), 金饭碗 ('golden rice bowl' = high pay and high prestige), and 端稳饭碗 ('to hold onto one's job securely').

rootFamily.gloss: rice bowl; one's job or livelihood (fànwǎn)
'iron rice bowl': a guaranteed, lifetime-secure job

金黄.etymology: Modifier-head color adjective compound of 金 ('gold') + 黄 ('yellow'): 'golden yellow'.

history.meaning: golden yellow

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 金黄 (via 萌典)

针.etymology: A monosyllabic phono-semantic character (形声字) with two historical graphic variants: 鍼 (composed of semantic 金 'metal' and phonetic 咸 *ɡrəm) and 針 (simplified to 针, composed of 金 'metal' and 十 *ɡjɯb, originally depicting a thread or vertical stitch marker; Old Chinese *t.kəm > Middle Chinese *tsjim > Mandarin zhēn). Attested from Warring States texts (such as Xunzi, Hanfeizi, and the Huangdi Neijing) for both sewing needles (preceded in the Neolithic by bone needles 骨针) and medical acupuncture/lancing needles, it also serves as a metaphor for sharp, pinpoint precision.

history.meaning: metal sewing needle; medical lancing or acupuncture needle
needle, pin, pointer (as on a compass or dial)
needle, pin, injection/acupuncture shot, clock hand

针.notes: Appears in vivid idioms frequently used in workplace and script critiques, such as 一针见血 ('to draw blood with a single needle prick' = to hit the nail on the head with a piercing remark) and 大海捞针 ('fishing for a needle in the ocean').

rootFamily.gloss: to draw blood with one prick: to hit the nail on the head (idiom)
pointer, clock hand, compass needle; guiding principle (zhēnzhēn / fāngzhēn)
tit for tat, needle point against wheat awn (idiom)

针对.etymology: Originally a noun-verb or adverb-verb compound formed from 针 (traditional 針, zhēn, 'needle, pointer, acupuncture needle') and 对 (traditional 對, duì, 'to face directly, point toward, answer to'). Derived from the image of a needle tip or compass pointer aimed squarely at a target (compare the idiom 针锋相对 'needle points facing each other directly'), it evolved in 20th-century Mandarin from a lexical verb meaning 'to aim straight at, direct toward' into a high-frequency preposition meaning 'aimed at, tailored to, or in view of (a specific problem, audience, or person)'.

history.meaning: needle/pointer + to face or aim directly at
to aim directly at, target; (preposition) in view of, tailored to, directed against

morphemes.meaning: needle point, pointer (aiming with pinpoint precision)
face toward, aim at, direct at

针对.notes: Has two distinct nuances depending on syntax: as a prepositional frame (针对这个问题... 'In view of / addressing this issue...') it is neutral and analytical, whereas as a transitive verb taking a person (他故意针对我 'He's deliberately targeting/picking on me') it implies hostility.

rootFamily.gloss: to be diametrically opposed, go tit for tat (idiom)
guiding policy, general direction (literally 'compass needle', fāngzhēn)

针眼.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) compound combining 针 (traditional 針, zhēn, 'needle') and 眼 (yǎn, 'eye; small aperture, hole, or puncture'). Because 眼 in Chinese regularly extends by metaphor to small round openings or marks (as in 锁眼 'keyhole', 泉眼 'spring orifice'), 针眼 developed three closely linked senses in vernacular Mandarin: (1) the tiny aperture at the blunt end of a sewing needle through which thread passes ('eye of a needle'), (2) the tiny puncture mark left by a needle or injection ('pinprick'), and (3) a folk medical term for hordeolum ('stye' on the eyelid).

history.meaning: the eye (thread-hole) of a sewing needle; a tiny hole or puncture left by a needle
eye of a needle; needle prick / injection mark; stye on the eyelid

morphemes.meaning: eye; small hole, aperture, or puncture mark

针眼.notes: In hospital or medical drama scenes, 针眼 usually refers to the tiny puncture mark left on the skin by an IV drip or syringe; in colloquial speech, 心眼比针眼还小 ('having a heart-aperture smaller than the eye of a needle') describes someone petty and jealous.

rootFamily.gloss: literally 'heart's aperture': mindfulness, cleverness, or pettiness (xīnyǎn)

钟.etymology: Merged simplified graph representing two historical bronze characters: (1) 鐘 (metal 钅 + 童 tóng/zhōng phonetic: 'suspended chime bell without an internal clapper, struck from the outside -> mechanical clock, hour/time on the clock') and (2) 鍾 (metal 钅 + 重 zhòng/zhōng phonetic: 'ancient wine vessel/measure; concentrate affection upon, as in 钟情/一见钟情').

history.form: 鐘 (bell, clock) / 鍾 (wine goblet; concentrate feelings)
history.meaning: chime bell vs. wine vessel/concentrate
bell; clock; time in hours/minutes; concentrate affection

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 钟 (via 萌典)

钟声.etymology: The noun '钟声' (zhōngshēng, sound of a bell) pairs '钟' (bell, clock) and '声' (sound). '钟' initially referred exclusively to large bronze bells used in ancient Chinese ceremonial music and Buddhist temples. The '声' (sound) of these bells was culturally significant, often marking the time of day or religious events. When Western mechanical clocks were introduced, they were also called '钟', and their chimes were similarly termed '钟声'. Today, the word evokes both traditional temple bells and modern clock chimes.

history.meaning: clock

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 钟声

钟头.etymology: A suffixed nominal compound formed from 钟 (traditional 鐘, zhōng, originally 'cast bronze bell' used in chime sets and time-striking towers, and applied from the late Ming–Qing Jesuit introduction of European mechanical striking clocks 自鸣钟 to mean 'clock, hour struck by a clock') plus the nominal suffix 头 (traditional 頭, tóu, marking a discrete unit or interval, widely used in southern and Jianghuai/Wu/Cantonese vernaculars before spreading into general Mandarin). Unlike 点钟 (diǎnzhōng, which marks a point on the clock face, e.g., 三点钟 'three o'clock'), 钟头 exclusively denotes a sixty-minute duration ('an hour').

In Classical texts 鑰 named the metal bolt of a gate lock while 匙 named the key inserted to open it; vernacular Mandarin joined the pair into one disyllabic noun.

钦点.etymology: Adverbial-verb compound (偏正结构) formed from 钦 (qīn, trad. 欽, 'respectfully; by the emperor himself', originally 'to yawn / gape in awe' from 欠 + 金 phonetic) and 点 (diǎn, trad. 點, 'to mark with a dot, check off, select'). In late imperial China (Ming and Qing dynasties), during the palace examination (殿试), the emperor personally ticked the names of top candidates or officials with a vermilion brush (朱笔钦点). In modern Mandarin and media parlance, it is used figuratively—often with a humorous or mildly ironic tone—to mean 'personally handpicked by the top boss, director, or investor'.

to handpick or designate personally from a position of supreme authority (such as an executive producer or CEO)

钩子.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 钩子. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 钩子 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 钩子 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 钩子 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 钩子. The etymology of 钩子 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

钱.etymology: Phono-semantic character (traditional 錢) of 钅 (金, 'metal') + 戋 (戔, jiān/qián phonetic). In the Shijing (庤乃钱镈), 錢 originally named an ancient bronze agricultural spade or hoe; because miniature bronze spades were cast as currency in Warring States China, 钱 became the universal word for 'copper coin, money, wealth, cash, and a weight unit (1/10 of a tael 两)'.

钱包.etymology: The noun '钱包' (qiánbāo, wallet, purse) combines '钱' (money) and '包' (bag, pouch). Historically, '钱' referred to metal coins, notably copper cash, and '包' referred to any wrapped bundle or cloth pouch. Before modern wallets, people carried coins in pouches or strung them on strings. As paper currency became dominant and Western-style billfolds were introduced, the term '钱包' adapted to refer to modern wallets and small purses. It is the standard everyday term for a money container.

history.meaning: coin purse

钻.etymology: Single-character verb 钻 (zuān, trad. 鑽; Middle Chinese *tswan*), a phono-semantic compound composed of the metal radical 金 (钅, indicating a metal tool) and phonetic 赞 (trad. 贊, *tsanH*). Originally denoting an awl or auger used to bore through wood or metal (as in《论语》钻燧改火, 'drilling flint/wood to renew fire'), the verb developed the spatial sense 'to squeeze or worm one's way through a narrow opening' and then the figurative social sense 'to exploit loopholes, curry favor, orwheeler-deal one's way into an opportunity'.

铁.etymology: Phono-semantic character (traditional 鐵, combining 金 'metal' + 呈/𢧤 tiě phonetic; simplified 铁 uses 钅 + 失 shī): 'iron (metal); iron-hard, unshakable, indisputable (铁证); railway/subway (地铁); weapons'.

铁三角.etymology: Modifier-head nominal compound (偏正结构) combining 铁 (tiě, trad. 鐵, 'iron', used metaphorically for 'unbreakable, rock-solid') with 三角 (sānjiǎo, 'triangle', literally 'three corners/angles'). Taking inspiration from both structural mechanics—where a triangle of iron struts forms the most rigid geometric frame—and 20th-century geopolitical/political-science usage ('iron triangle'), contemporary Mandarin popularized 铁三角 in film, television, and business to describe an inseparable, complementary trio of partners whose collaboration guarantees success.

history.meaning: rigid triangular military formation or geopolitical 'iron triangle' stronghold
an inseparable, rock-solid trio of creative partners, executives, or friends

morphemes.meaning: angle, corner; vertex of a triangle

铁三角.notes: A favorite showbiz and workplace idiom in Mainland China (famously applied to the TV trio Zhang Guoli, Wang Gang, and Zhang Tielin) to describe three collaborators whose complementary skills make them invincible together.

铁杆.etymology: Modifier-head compound (偏正结构) originally functioning as a noun meaning 'iron rod, iron pole, or rifle barrel', formed from 铁 (tiě, trad. 鐵, 'iron') and 杆 (gǎn, 'pole, shaft, rod', trad. 桿). In late Qing military and agrarian terminology, 铁杆庄稼 ('iron-stalk crops') referred to the guaranteed hereditary stipends of Eight Banners soldiers that never failed like ordinary crops. From the unbending rigidity of an iron bar, Northern Mandarin extended 铁杆 (often with erhua as 铁杆儿) into an adjective meaning 'staunch, die-hard, unwaveringly loyal'.

history.meaning: solid iron rod or shaft; unfailing hereditary bannerman stipend (鐵桿莊稼)
die-hard, staunch, unwaveringly devoted (especially of fans, allies, or supporters)

铁杆.notes: In entertainment and fan culture, 铁杆粉丝 (often shortened to 铁粉) is the standard term for a 'die-hard fan' who supports an artist or program through thick and thin.

Originally denoted the ornamental bronze boss/plate holding a door-knocker ring (铺首); extended to two tonal readings in Mandarin: pū as a verb meaning 'spread out, lay flat, pave (a road), make (a bed)', and pù as a noun meaning 'shop, store (also written 舖); sleeping berth/bed'.

铺垫.etymology: Coordinative compound (并列结构) uniting two synonymous verbs/nouns of spreading and cushioning: 铺 (pū, trad. 鋪, 'to spread out, lay down flat') and 垫 (diàn, trad. 墊, 'to pad, prop up, or place a cushion underneath'). Literally referring to laying down bedding, straw, or stone foundations to level an uneven surface, classical Chinese rhetoric and traditional drama/fiction criticism (such as Jin Shengtan's and Mao Zonggang's Ming–Qing novel commentaries) adopted 铺垫 for narrative foreshadowing and scene-setting that prepares the audience for a climax.

铺满.etymology: Resultative verb compound (动补结构 / 述补结构) composed of the action verb 铺 (pū, trad. 鋪, 'to spread out, unfold, lay across a surface') and the resultative complement 满 (mǎn, trad. 滿, 'full, completely covered'). As the resultative construction grammaticalized in Medieval and Early Mandarin, attaching 满 directly after verbs of placement or spreading (铺满, 摆满, 充满) came to express exhaustive spatial coverage across an entire surface or venue.

销毁.etymology: Coordinative verb compound (并列结构) pairing 销 (xiāo, trad. 銷, Middle Chinese *sjew*, 'to melt down metal, fuse, dissolve') and 毁 (huǐ, trad. 毀, Middle Chinese *xjwéX*, 'to smash, break down, demolish, ruin'). In Classical Chinese (such as贾谊《过秦论》销锋镝, 'melting down arrowheads and blades'), 销 specifically meant melting metal weapons in a furnace so they could never be reused, while 毁 meant smashing earthen or wooden structures. morphemes.meaning: to blame, reproach, find fault with

错怪.notes: Very common in interpersonal apologies in drama and daily life (e.g., 对不起，我错怪你了, 'I'm sorry, I blamed you wrongly'); softer and more conversational than 冤枉 ('to wrong/frame unjustly').

错误.etymology: Coordinative compound (并列结构) combining two classical morphemes of deviation and miscalculation: 错 (cuò, trad. 錯, Middle Chinese *tshwak*, originally 'crossed, interlocking, mixed up', whence 'deviating from the right order, wrong') and 误 (wù, trad. 誤, Middle Chinese *nguH*, from 言 'speech/thought' + 吳 phonetic, 'to go astray mentally, miscalculate, err'). Attested since the Han and Six Dynasties histories (e.g.,《后汉书》), 错误 functions in modern Mandarin both as an adjective ('wrong, erroneous') and as a noun ('mistake, error').

history.meaning: disordered and mistaken; a clerical, tactical, or moral misstep
wrong, incorrect (adj.); mistake, error, blunder (noun)

morphemes.meaning: to err, miscalculate, miss, go astray (trad. 誤)

错误.notes: Functions both as an attributive/predicative adjective (错误的决定, 'a wrong decision') and a countable noun (犯了一个错误, 'made a mistake'); in everyday speech, single-character 错 is more colloquial while 错误 sounds slightly more formal.

rootFamily.gloss: to blame wrongly out of misunderstanding
to miss an opportunity or pass by each other

cognates.meaning: forging metal; training, discipline, tempering oneself
forging; physical or mental training and discipline
to forge; to train and temper oneself

锻炼.etymology: Coordinative verb compound (并列结构) drawn directly from ancient metallurgy: 锻 (duàn, trad. 鍛, with the metal radical 钅/金, 'to hammer and forge heated metal on an anvil') and 炼 (liàn, trad. 煉, with the fire radical 火, 'to smelt and refine ore or metal in a furnace'). Already used metaphorically in漢–Tang literary criticism for 'polishing poetic diction' and in Daoist/Buddhist cultivation for 'tempering body and mind', 锻炼 expanded in modern Chinese (reinforced by Japanese 鍛錬 *tanren*) to mean both 'to toughen and hone one's skills through real-world trials' and 'to do physical exercise'.

history.meaning: to smelt metal in fire and hammer it on the anvil; by extension, to fabricate a tight legal case or polish verse
to temper and hone one's character or professional ability through practice; to work out physically

morphemes.meaning: to forge and hammer metal (trad. 鍛)
to smelt and refine with fire (trad. 煉)

锻炼.notes: In workplace and showbiz contexts (such as sending a young producer or intern to a tough live show 去基层锻炼一下), it means 'to cut one's teeth / get toughened up through practical experience', alongside its everyday meaning of 'working out' (锻炼身体).

rootFamily.gloss: to temper through hardship; slow, grueling trial
to refine and purify; concise and polished

镇台之宝.etymology: Four-character modifier-head idiom (偏正四字格) modeled on the traditional commercial and folkloric phrase 镇店之宝 ('the talismanic treasure that anchors and protects a shop') or 镇山之宝 ('treasure that guards a mountain monastery'). Here, 镇 (zhèn, trad. 鎮, 'to press down with a heavy weight, pacify, anchor, guard') takes 台 (tái, trad. 臺, 'broadcasting station / television network') as its object, linked by the classical genitive particle 之 (zhī, 'of') to the head noun 宝 (bǎo, trad. 寶, 'treasure'). It designates a TV network's flagship host, star producer, or marquee program that guarantees ratings and prestige.

history.form: 鎮山之寶 / 鎮店之寶
history.meaning: talismanic heirloom or priceless masterpiece that anchors the fortune and prestige of a temple or merchant house
the crown-jewel star, anchor host, or flagship show of a television or radio network

morphemes.meaning: to weight down, anchor, guard, hold the fort (trad. 鎮)
platform, stage; broadcasting station or TV network (trad. 臺)

镇台之宝.notes: A vivid broadcasting industry idiom: just as a traditional merchant shop relies on its 镇店之宝 to draw customers, a TV station relies on its 镇台之宝 (its top anchor or signature variety show) to anchor its brand and ratings.

rootFamily.gloss: flagship treasure of a store or restaurant
to hold the fort; for a senior figure to be personally present in command

sources.title: Wiktionary: 鎮店之寶 / 镇店之宝

镇定.etymology: Coordinative adjective and verb compound of 镇 (鎮, 'press down with a heavy bronze weight -> calm, pacify') + 定 ('settled, steady, calm'): 'calm, composed, collected, unruffled; calm down'. Attested since Six Dynasties and Tang histories.

history.meaning: calm and composed; steady; cool-headed

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 镇定 (via 萌典)

镊子.etymology: Derived from 镊 ('pinch or pluck with small metal tongs', metal radical 钅 + phonetic 聂 niè) + nominal suffix 子 (-zi), attested since medical and goldsmithing treatises for fine precision tweezers.

history.meaning: small metal pincers; hair or splinter tweezers
tweezers; forceps

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 镊子

cognates.meaning: camera lens; film shot or take

镜头.etymology: Suffixed/modifier-head noun compound formed from 镜 (jìng, trad. 鏡, originally 'bronze mirror', extended in the Ming–Qing periods when Western glass optics arrived to 'optical lens, glass') and 头 (tóu, trad. 頭, 'head, end, tip', serving here both in its concrete sense 'the front optical assembly/end of a camera' and as a nominal suffix). With the rise of photography and cinema in late 19th- and early 20th-century China, 镜头 came to mean first the physical 'camera lens' and then, by metonymy, the 'camera shot, take, or on-screen moment' captured through that lens.

history.meaning: the optical glass lens assembly mounted at the front of a telescope, microscope, or photographic camera
camera lens; by metonymy, a film/TV shot, take, scene, or on-screen appearance

镜头.notes: In film and TV production, 镜头 means both the physical 'camera lens' (换个广角镜头, 'switch to a wide-angle lens') and 'screen time / shot' (抢镜头 'hog the camera', 给个特写镜头 'give a close-up shot'). Note that 镜 is always pronounced jìng.

rootFamily.gloss: sense of the camera; photogenic presence and instinct before the lens
to appear on camera; to go on screen
shot breakdown; storyboard in film/TV directing

镜子.etymology: Colloquial noun formed from 镜 (鏡, combining 钅 'metal' + 竟 jìng phonetic, because ancient Chinese mirrors from the Shang through the Ming dynasties were cast of polished bronze before silvered glass mirrors) + nominal suffix 子 (neutral tone zi): 'mirror, looking glass'.

history.meaning: mirror; looking glass

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 镜子 (via 萌典)

镜片.etymology: Compound noun from 镜 (simplified from 鏡, metal 钅 + phonetic 竟 'mirror; optical lens') + 片 ('thin flat slice or disc'). Used since optical spectacles and magnifying glasses spread in Ming-Qing China for the ground glass or resin lens of eyeglasses, magnifiers, and cameras.

history.meaning: glass lens of spectacles
eyeglass lens; optical lens

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 镜片

长.etymology: Ancient pictograph (長) attested on Shang oracle bones depicting an elder figure with long flowing hair walking with a staff: read cháng as an adjective/noun meaning 'long (in space or time, opposite of 短 'short'), length, lasting, strong point/forte'; read zhǎng as a verb/noun meaning 'grow up, increase; elder, senior, chief/head (店长, 校长)'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: long, length, lasting (cháng); grow up, elder, head/chief (zhǎng)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 长 (via 萌典)

长大.etymology: Resultative verb compound combining 长 (read zhǎng, 'grow') + 大 ('big, adult'): 'grow up (from childhood to adulthood), grow big'.

history.meaning: grow up; reach adulthood

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 长大 (via 萌典)

长学问.etymology: Verb-object compound (动宾结构) in which 长 is read in its rising-tone verbal reading zhǎng (trad. 長, Middle Chinese *trjangX*, 'to grow, increase, foster') governing the disyllabic noun object 学问 (xuéwen, trad. 學問, 'learning and inquiry; knowledge, scholarship', a coordinative compound from《易经》and《中庸》博学之，审问之). Literally 'to grow one's learning', 长学问 is an idiomatic spoken Mandarin expression meaning to broaden one's horizons and gain practical or scholarly knowledge from an experience.

history.meaning: to increase one's learning and cultivation through study and worldly experience
to broaden one's knowledge; to learn something new and valuable

morphemes.meaning: to grow, increase, develop (read zhǎng; trad. 長)
inquiry, questioning; together 学问 = knowledge, scholarship (trad. 問)

长学问.notes: Be careful with the polyphonic character 长: here it is a verb meaning 'to grow/increase' and MUST be pronounced zhǎng (third tone, zhǎng xuéwen), just like 长见识 ('broaden one's horizons') and 长本事 ('grow in skill'), never cháng.

rootFamily.gloss: to broaden one's horizons and experience; to learn the ropes
progress, improvement in skill or maturity (also read zhǎngjìn)

长时间.etymology: Modifier-head nominal compound (偏正结构) combining the adjective 长 (cháng, trad. 長, Middle Chinese *drjang*, 'long in space or time') with the temporal noun 时间 (shíjiān, trad. 時間, 'time, interval of time', formed from 时 'time/season' + 间 'interval/space between', popularized in modern East Asia via Meiji Japanese 時間 *jikan* translating English 'time'). Together, 长时间 denotes a prolonged continuous duration of time, typically measured in hours or days rather than years.

history.meaning: an extended continuous interval of time (adopted into modern Chinese alongside Meiji-era temporal vocabulary)
a long time; for a prolonged stretch of hours or days

morphemes.meaning: interval, space between; together 时间 = time, duration (trad. 間)

长时间.notes: Contrast 长时间 with 长期: 长时间 refers to a long continuous stretch within a single activity or day (e.g., 长时间工作 'working for many hours straight'), whereas 长期 refers to long-term duration over months, years, or eras (e.g., 长期合作 'long-term cooperation').

rootFamily.gloss: over the long term, long-standing (months or years)
length of time, duration (especially of a video or audio clip)

sources.title: Wiktionary: 長時間 / 长时间

长期.etymology: Modifier-head compound (偏正结构) formed from 长 (cháng, trad. 長, 'long, extended') modifying 期 (qī, Middle Chinese *gji*, 'appointed time, fixed cycle, period, phase'). While classical Chinese already combined 長 with temporal nouns, 长期 crystallized in late 19th- and early 20th-century Sino-Japanese administrative, financial, and military prose (cf. Japanese 長期 *chōki*, as in 長期戦 'protracted war' or 長期公債 'long-term bonds') to designate a multi-month or multi-year horizon in contrast to 短期 ('short-term').

history.meaning: an extended period or long-term cycle in finance, strategy, or administration
history.stage: Late Qing–Republican Mandarin (reinforced by Japanese 長期)

history.meaning: long-term, over a long period; chronic or long-standing

长期.notes: Often used adverbially directly before a verb without 的 (e.g., 长期从事幕后工作, 'engaged in behind-the-scenes work for a long time') or attributively before a noun (长期合同, 'long-term contract'). Antonym: 短期 (duǎnqī).

长椅.etymology: The noun '长椅' (chángyǐ, bench) joins '长' (long) and '椅' (chair). '椅' originally referred to a specific type of wood, but by the Tang dynasty, it evolved to mean a seat with a backrest, influenced by Buddhist folding stools. '长椅' simply describes a chair that has been elongated to accommodate multiple people. While benches existed in ancient China (often called '凳', which usually lack backrests), '长椅' specifically conjures the image of a long seat with a back, typical of modern parks and waiting areas.

history.meaning: chair

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 长椅

长篇大论.etymology: Four-character coordinative idiom (并列四字成语) interleaving two parallel modifier-head pairs: 长篇 (chángpiān, trad. 長篇, 'a long written scroll or composition', where 篇 originally meant a bundle of bamboo slips) and 大论 (dàlùn, trad. 大論, 'a grand or lengthy discourse/argument'). Originating in Literary Chinese appreciation of monumental essays and treatises, in vernacular Mandarin (such as曹雪芹《红楼梦》) it shifted toward a mildly critical or ironic sense: a long-winded, rambling lecture or verbose speech.

history.meaning: a monumental essay and grand disquisition on statecraft or scholarship

history.form: 長篇大論 / 长篇大论
history.meaning: a lengthy, often tedious or pompous speech, lecture, or treatise

morphemes.meaning: bamboo-slip scroll; essay, article, piece of writing

长篇大论.notes: In modern conversation, 长篇大论 almost always carries a slightly impatient or critical undertone ('going on and on in a long-winded lecture'), e.g., 别跟我发表长篇大论了 ('stop giving me a long-winded lecture').

rootFamily.gloss: full-length novel (as opposed to a short story)
make a long story short (the direct rhetorical opposite)
to comment on, discuss; public opinion or commentary

sources.title: Wiktionary: 長篇大論 / 长篇大论

长话短说.etymology: Compressed four-character topic-comment / object-fronted verbal phrase (主谓/宾语前置四字格): 长话 (chánghuà, trad. 長話, 'a long story / lengthy matter to tell') serves as the topicalized patient, and 短说 (duǎnshuō, trad. 短說, 'to speak briefly / tell in short') is the adverbial-verb predicate. Built on the classical and vernacular Chinese fondness for antithetical pairing of antonyms (长 'long' vs. 短 'short') at positions 1 and 3, the phrase arose in Ming–Qing storytelling and opera dialogue as a brisk transition meaning 'to make a long story short'.

history.meaning: to sum up a complicated story in a few brief words (used by storytellers and characters in vernacular fiction)
history.stage: Early Vernacular Mandarin (Ming–Qing fiction and drama)

history.meaning: to make a long story short; to get straight to the point when pressed for time

长话短说.notes: Frequently used as a discourse marker at the start of an urgent briefing or phone call: 时间紧迫，咱们长话短说 ('Time is tight, so let's make a long story short').

rootFamily.gloss: to explain in simple, concise terms; in a nutshell
topic of conversation; talking point or trending subject

sources.title: Wiktionary: 長話短說 / 长话短说

长进.etymology: Coordinative verbal/nominal compound (并列结构) uniting 长 in its rising-tone verbal reading (zhǎng, trad. 長, Middle Chinese *trjangX*, 'to grow, mature, increase') with 进 (jìn, trad. 進, Middle Chinese *tsjinH*, 'to advance, move forward, improve'). Attested in Song–Ming philosophical and vernacular texts (such as《朱子语类》and Ming novels), 长进 blends biological growth with forward movement along a path of study or craftsmanship, yielding the noun/verb 'progress, improvement in skill, character, or professional competence'.

history.meaning: to advance in moral cultivation, scholarship, or martial skill; growth and progress
progress, improvement, or headway in one's ability, maturity, or career

morphemes.meaning: to grow, develop, increase (read zhǎng; trad. 長)
to advance, move forward, improve (trad. 進)

长进.notes: Read zhǎngjìn (with 长 in the third tone, 'grow'). Most frequently used in the negative or evaluative pattern 有/没有长进 (e.g., 一点长进都没有, 'hasn't made a bit of progress / hasn't grown up at all') when a mentor or boss critiques someone's development.

rootFamily.gloss: to broaden one's knowledge (also read zhǎng)
to grow up, come of age (read zhǎngdà)

长远.etymology: Coordinative adjectival compound (并列结构) pairing temporal/spatial length 长 (cháng, trad. 長, Middle Chinese *drjang*, 'long') with spatial/temporal distance 远 (yuǎn, trad. 遠, Middle Chinese *hjwonX*, 'far, distant, remote'). Used in Classical and Literary Chinese since the Han and Tang dynasties to describe vast geographical distances or enduring historical legacies, 长远 in modern Mandarin primarily modifies abstract nouns of vision, planning, or interest (长远目光, 长远利益) to mean 'long-range, far-sighted, looking far into the future'.

history.meaning: stretching far in space or enduring across distant ages
long-term, long-range, far-sighted (especially regarding strategy, vision, or interests)

morphemes.meaning: long in time or space (read cháng; trad. 長)

长远.notes: While 长期 focuses on the objective duration of a state or contract ('long-term cooperation'), 长远 emphasizes strategic foresight and future consequences (e.g., 从长远来看 'in the long run / taking the long view', 长远规划 'long-range planning').

长长的.etymology: Reduplicated state adjective (AA的形容词重叠式) formed by reduplicating the monosyllabic adjective 长 (cháng, trad. 長, 'long') into 长长 (chángcháng) and attaching the descriptive attributive/predicative particle 的 (de). In Mandarin morphosyntax, AA的 reduplication shifts a bare scalar adjective ('long' as a neutral measurement) into a vivid, sensory, or affective state adjective ('stretching out long, nice and long, lengthy'), often carrying a visual or emotional impression.

history.meaning: long and drawn-out; stretching far in space or time (poetic reduplication in Tang–Song verse)
long, lengthy (vivid descriptive modifier or predicate, e.g., a long corridor, a long sigh)

morphemes.meaning: vivid/affective reduplication intensifying the visual or temporal impression of length

长长的.notes: Used for vivid visual or sensory description—such as 长长的走廊 ('a long, stretching corridor'), 长长的睫毛 ('long eyelashes'), or 长长地叹了一口气 ('heaved a long sigh')—rather than dry numerical measurements. Do not confuse with 常常 (chángcháng, 'often').

rootFamily.gloss: length (abstract noun formed from long + short)

门.etymology: Core noun 'door, gate', descended directly from a Shang oracle-bone pictograph of two swinging wooden gate leaves under a lintel. Counted with the measure word 扇 (一扇门 'a door') and productive in compounds like 开门 ('open the door'), 门口 ('doorway'), and 大门 ('front gate').

history.meaning: gate; door; entrance

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 門 (via 萌典)

门口.etymology: Locative compound noun combining 门 (門, 'door, gate', a pictograph of twin swinging gate leaves) + 口 ('opening, entranceway'): 'doorway, entrance, right outside or by the door'.

history.meaning: doorway; entrance; by the door

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 门口 (via 萌典)

门户网站.etymology: Four-character modifier-head nominal compound (偏正结构) combining the classical metaphor 门户 (ménhù, trad. 門戶, 'gateway, main entrance to a household') with the late-20th-century digital neologism 网站 (wǎngzhàn, trad. 網站, literally 'net-station', i.e., 'website'). In Classical Chinese, 门 (two-leaf outer gate) and 户 (single-leaf inner door) together meant a household's entrance, faction, or strategic gateway. In the late 1990s dot-com boom, Chinese tech media calqued English 'web portal' as 门户网站 to describe comprehensive gateway sites (like Sina, Sohu, NetEase, and Tencent) that serve as a user's starting point on the internet.

history.meaning: outer gate and inner door; a household, family lineage, or strategic gateway
web portal; major comprehensive news and media gateway website (calque of English 'portal site')

morphemes.meaning: single-leaf door; household; together 门户 = gateway, portal (trad. 戶)
station, stop, hub; together 网站 = website (trad. 站)

门户网站.notes: In Mainland Chinese media history, the 'Four Major Portals' (四大门户网站: Sina, Sohu, NetEase, Tencent) dominated online news and entertainment coverage before the shift to mobile apps and short-video platforms.

rootFamily.gloss: threshold, doorsill; entry barrier or qualification bar

sources.title: Wiktionary: 門戶網站 / 门户网站

门槛.etymology: Modifier-head nominal compound (偏正结构) formed from 门 (mén, trad. 門, 'door, gate') and 槛 (kǎn, trad. 檻, Middle Chinese *hramX*, with the wood radical 木, 'wooden railing, cage bar, or raised wooden sill at the bottom of a doorway'). In traditional Chinese timber architecture, the 门槛 was a removable wooden beam across the bottom of the main gate that kept out rainwater, drafts, and pests while symbolizing the boundary and status of the household. By metaphor, crossing the sill means gaining admission, so 门槛 in modern Mandarin universally denotes an 'entry barrier, minimum qualification, or prerequisite bar'.

history.meaning: raised wooden doorsill or threshold beam at the foot of a traditional gate
physical doorsill; figuratively, the entry bar, minimum requirement, or barrier to entry into an industry or club

morphemes.meaning: wooden sill, threshold beam (read kǎn; trad. 檻)

门槛.notes: Notice the pronunciation: 槛 is read kǎn in 门槛 ('threshold / entry bar', e.g., 准入门槛高 'high barrier to entry', 零门槛 'zero barrier to entry'), whereas in classical expressions like 槛车 ('prisoner's cage-cart') it is read jiàn. In Wu/Shanghainese-influenced Mandarin, 门槛精 also means 'street-smart, savvy'.

rootFamily.gloss: way in, knack, insider connections or know-how
outsider, layperson who hasn't crossed the threshold of a trade

门牌.etymology: Determinative compound of 门 ('door; gate', pictograph of double swinging gates) + 牌 ('inscribed wooden or metal plaque',片 + 卑). Originally a household registration plaque hung beside the front gate in Song–Ming towns, it is today the standard word for a street-number doorplate.

history.meaning: household registration plaque at a doorway
street number; doorplate

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 门牌

门禁系统.etymology: Four-character modifier-head compound (偏正结构) joining 门禁 (ménjìn, trad. 門禁, 'gate restriction / entrance guard') with 系统 (xìtǒng, trad. 系統, 'system', a modern Sino-Japanese term from 系 'connected thread/lineage' + 统 'governing main thread'). In Classical and Imperial Chinese (attested from the Han and Tang codes onward), 门禁 referred to palace or city-gate curfews and guard regulations controlling who could pass through a gate. In late-20th-century building security, 门禁 was repurposed for electronic access control (keycards, turnstiles, biometrics), forming 门禁系统 ('door access-control system').

history.meaning: imperial palace or city-gate guard regulations and night curfew restrictions
electronic door access-control system (badge readers, turnstiles, intercoms, or biometric locks)

morphemes.meaning: prohibition, restriction, guard control; together 门禁 = access control / curfew
series, linked thread, connection (trad. 系/繫)
main governing thread, interconnected whole; together 系统 = system (trad. 統)

门禁系统.notes: In modern corporate and TV-station settings, 门禁卡 is your 'access badge/keycard' and 门禁系统 is the security turnstile or card-reader system; in campus or dorm contexts, 门禁 still retains its older sense of 'night curfew'.

rootFamily.gloss: curfew, prohibition on going out at night

门边.etymology: Locative compound from 门 (simplified from 門, 'door; doorway') + 边 (simplified from 邊, 'side; edge; beside'). Transparently denotes the space immediately beside a door or doorway.

history.meaning: beside the door
by the door; doorway side

门铃.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 门 (門, 'door') + 铃 (鈴, 'bell'): 'doorbell'.

history.meaning: doorbell

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 门铃 (via 萌典)

门锁.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 门 (門, 'door') + 锁 (鎖, 'lock'): 'door lock'.

history.meaning: door lock

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 门锁 (via 萌典)

门面.etymology: Modifier-head nominal compound (偏正结构) composed of 门 (mén, trad. 門, 'gate, door, shop entrance') and 面 (miàn, 'face, front surface, facade'). In Song–Yuan urban commerce, 门面 designated the street-facing facade of a shop or residence—the visible front where goods were displayed and customers judged the proprietor's wealth. Because a grand storefront projected prestige, 门面 naturally extended to mean 'public appearances, social face, or the flagship representative (a star, product, or lobby) that serves as an organization's showcase'.

history.meaning: the street-facing facade of a house or commercial shopfront in urban marketplaces
storefront; outward appearances, prestige, or flagship showcase/representative of a company or network

morphemes.meaning: face, front surface, facade; social prestige

门面.notes: Used both for a physical retail storefront (门面房) and metaphorically in media/business for a 'flagship showcase' or 'star who keeps up appearances' (e.g., 撑门面 'keep up appearances / carry the prestige of the house', 门面担当 'the visual/face of an idol group or company').

rootFamily.gloss: to prop up appearances; to act as the prestigious showcase for an organization

闪.etymology: Vivid ideogram (閃) showing a person (人) ducking quickly inside or through a doorway (門): 'dodge, step aside quickly (闪开); twist/sprain (闪腰); flash, sparkle, gleam, lightning (闪电), flash past'.

history.meaning: person darting in a doorway = dodge, flash, gleam, lightning

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 闪 (via 萌典)

闪电.etymology: Compound of 闪 ('flash, dart suddenly', pictograph of a person 人 dodging swiftly through a doorway 门) + 电 ('lightning', rain cloud 雨 above a jagged flash 申 in bronze/oracle script, before 电 was extended to modern electricity).

history.meaning: flash of atmospheric lightning
lightning

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 闪电

闪耀.etymology: Coordinative verb compound (并列结构) uniting two vivid light-emission morphemes: 闪 (shǎn, trad. 閃, an associatively formed character showing a person 人 darting inside a doorway 門, hence 'to flash, glint, dart suddenly') and 耀 (yào, Middle Chinese *jewH*, composed of 光 'light' + 翟 'pheasant plumes', meaning 'to shine brilliantly, dazzle, illuminate'). While 闪 captures the dynamic, sparkling flicker of light, 耀 expresses steady, radiant brilliance; together, 闪耀 means 'to shine brightly, glitter, or radiate star power'.

history.meaning: to glint and shine with dazzling light (of stars, blades, or jewels)
to shine brightly, glitter, sparkle; figuratively, to shine on stage or in the public eye

morphemes.meaning: to flash, glint, sparkle suddenly (trad. 閃)
to shine brightly, dazzle, radiate light

闪耀.notes: Commonly used both for literal light (群星闪耀, 'stars shining brightly') and in entertainment/showbiz prose for star power or dazzling talent on stage (闪耀全场, 'dazzling the entire venue').

rootFamily.gloss: to flicker, twinkle, glimmer; evasive (of speech)

闭.etymology: Ancient ideogram (閉) attested on Shang oracle bones showing a timber crossbeam and upright prop (才) barring a pair of double doors (門): 'shut, close (doors, eyes, or mouth), block, stop up, conclude (闭幕)'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: timber bar across double doors = close, shut

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 闭 (via 萌典)

闭上.etymology: Resultative verb compound combining 闭 ('close, shut') + 上 (directional/resultative complement of bringing two edges together): 'close, shut (especially one's eyes 闭上眼睛 or mouth 闭上嘴)'.

history.meaning: close; shut (eyes or mouth)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 闭上 (via 萌典)

闭嘴.etymology: Verb-object compound (动宾结构) formed from the transitive verb 闭 (bì, trad. 閉, showing a bolt 才/材 barring a double gate 門, 'to shut, close, bolt') and the colloquial noun object 嘴 (zuǐ, originally a bird's beak 觜 + 口, which replaced classical 口/唇 in vernacular Mandarin as the everyday word for 'mouth'). Literally 'to shut one's mouth', 闭嘴 serves in modern Mandarin both as a descriptive verb phrase ('keep silent') and, in the imperative, as the blunt command 'Shut up!'.

history.meaning: to close one's mouth and refrain from speaking (the classical equivalent)
to keep one's mouth shut; imperative 'Shut up!' (replacing classical 口 with vernacular 嘴)
history.stage: Early Vernacular Mandarin (Ming–Qing) to Modern Mandarin

闭嘴.notes: As an imperative (你给我闭嘴！), 闭嘴 is blunt and confrontational, equivalent to English 'Shut up!'; in polite or formal contexts, speakers use 请保持安静 ('please keep quiet') instead. Separable in grammar (闭上嘴, 'shut one's mouth').

rootFamily.gloss: a slammed door, cold refusal to meet someone
to talk back, argue; to interrupt

闭门羹.etymology: Three-character modifier-head idiom (偏正结构) where the verb-object phrase 闭门 (bìmén, trad. 閉門, 'to shut the door') modifies the head noun 羹 (gēng, Middle Chinese *kang*, 'thick meat or vegetable soup/broth'). The allusion goes back to the Tang dynasty anecdote recorded in Feng Yan's《封氏闻见记》(and linked to the courtesan Shi Feng 史凤 of Xuancheng): when an unwelcome or lower-ranking suitor called at her residence, she refused to receive him inside and instead had a bowl of soup (羹) served to him outside the closed door to send him away. From this ironic 'closed-door soup', 闭门羹 (almost always used with the verb 吃, 'to eat') came to mean 'a cold refusal to meet, having the door slammed in one's face'.

history.meaning: a bowl of soup served outside a barred door to turn away an unwelcome caller without granting an audience (Tang anecdote)
a flat refusal to see a visitor; having the door shut in one's face (collocated with 吃 or 给)

morphemes.meaning: thick soup, broth (ironically 'served' as a dismissal)

闭门羹.notes: Almost always used with the verbs 吃 ('eat/suffer') or 给 ('give/serve'): 吃了个闭门羹 means 'got the door slammed in one's face / was refused a meeting', while 给某人吃闭门羹 means 'to turn someone away at the door'.

rootFamily.gloss: to shut up, keep one's mouth shut
to work behind closed doors in isolation from reality (literally 'build a cart behind closed doors')
to shut oneself indoors and reflect on one's mistakes

sources.title: Wiktionary: 閉門羹 / 闭门羹

问.etymology: Phono-semantic/ideographic character (問) attested on Shang oracle bones combining 门 (門, 'door', phonetic mèn/wèn and suggesting calling at a gate) + 口 ('mouth'): 'ask, inquire, question; ask after someone's well-being (问好); hold responsible'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: ask; inquire; question

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 问 (via 萌典)

问一问.etymology: Tentative verb-reduplication construction (V一V动词重叠式) built on the monosyllabic root verb 问 (wèn, trad. 問, Middle Chinese *mjunH*, composed of 門 'gate' phonetic + 口 'mouth', 'to ask, inquire') with the numeral 一 (yī, 'one') infixed between the base and its reduplicant. Developing in Early Mandarin from a verb + cognate-object counting phrase ('ask one asking' -> 'ask once'), the V一V pattern grammaticalized into the delimiter/tentative aspect, softening the force of the action to mean 'ask briefly, make a quick inquiry, ask around a bit'.

history.meaning: to inquire, ask a question, or send polite greetings
to ask briefly, make a quick or casual inquiry (tentative/delimitative aspect)
history.stage: Early Vernacular Mandarin (Yuan–Ming) to Modern Mandarin

morphemes.meaning: one; marks brief duration or tentative, polite softening of the action
repeated verb root expressing a casual or brief attempt (trad. 問)

问一问.notes: Equivalent in tone to 问问 or 问一下: using 问一问 instead of bare 问 makes a request or suggestion sound much gentler, less confrontational, and more conversational (e.g., 我去问一问导演的意思, 'Let me go ask the director what he thinks').

rootFamily.gloss: to ask about, touch upon in questioning; manage to ask
to denounce, condemn and demand accountability

问到.etymology: Resultative verb compound (动补结构 / 述补结构) formed from the verb 问 (wèn, trad. 問, 'to ask, inquire') and the directional/resultative complement 到 (dào, originally 'to arrive at, reach a destination'). When 到 grammaticalized as a post-verbal resultative marker in Medieval and Early Vernacular Chinese, attaching it to verbs of speech or perception (问到, 说到, 提到, 看到) came to express that the inquiry successfully reached a particular topic or person ('asked about / touched upon X in questioning' or 'managed to track down and ask X').

history.meaning: to direct a question to a specific person or reach a specific point in an interrogation or conversation
to ask about, touch upon in questioning; to reach someone with a question

morphemes.meaning: to reach, arrive at; indicates that the question touches upon a specific topic or person

问到.notes: Distinguish 问到 ('to touch upon a topic in questioning / ask someone about X', e.g., 记者问到了新节目的预算, 'the reporter asked about the budget for the new show') from 问道 ('asked, saying:', which introduces a direct quote in written narrative).

rootFamily.gloss: to mention, bring up a topic in speech
to stump someone with a question; ask right to the heart of the matter
to ask briefly, make a quick inquiry

cognates.meaning: to accuse of a crime, denounce, call to account
to denounce an offense and hold someone accountable
to interrogate and condemn for an offense

问罪.etymology: Verb-object compound (动宾结构) directly inherited from Classical Chinese military and legal terminology: 问 (wèn, trad. 問, Middle Chinese *mjunH*, here in its classical forensic sense 'to interrogate, call to account, demand an explanation for') governs the noun object 罪 (zuì, Middle Chinese *dzwojX*, 'crime, guilt, transgression'). In the Zuozhuan (《左传》) and classical histories, a punitive military expedition was justified as 兴师问罪 ('raising an army to call a transgressor to account for their crimes'). In modern Mandarin, 问罪 means to confront, denounce, or demand accountability for a blunder or offense.

history.meaning: to call a vassal state or offender to account for a transgression; to interrogate and pronounce guilt
to denounce, condemn, or angrily demand accountability for a mistake or wrongdoing

morphemes.meaning: to interrogate, call to account, demand an explanation (trad. 問)

问罪.notes: Frequently appears in the four-character idioms 兴师问罪 ('to march in angrily and confront someone over a fault') and 负荆请罪 / 登门问罪; in workplace or media dramas, 找某人问罪 means 'to come after someone to hold them accountable for a fiasco'.

rootFamily.gloss: to muster forces to denounce someone; to confront someone angrily over a fault
to hold someone accountable for negligence or failure (modern institutional term)
to offend someone, get on someone's bad side

cognates.meaning: demand for an explanation; censure; reproof

问责.etymology: A verb-object (VO) or coordinative Sino-compound composed of 问 (wèn, Middle Chinese *mjunH*, "to inquire, interrogate, call to account") and 责 (zé, Middle Chinese *tsrek*, "duty, responsibility; to reprove, demand fulfillment of an obligation"). In Classical Chinese legal and administrative prose, 问 already carried the judicial sense of "to interrogate or investigate an offense" (as in 问罪), while 责 denoted exacting payment or holding an official to their charge. Combined as 问责, the compound gained prominence in modern administrative, corporate, and media governance (reinforced by Japanese 問責 monseki) to mean investigating negligence and enforcing institutional accountability.

history.meaning: to interrogate judicially / to exact an obligation or reprove for a fault
to censure for negligence; to investigate and hold an official or executive accountable

问责.notes: Common in corporate and media crisis dramas in collocations like 问责制 ("accountability system") and 启动问责 ("launch an accountability investigation") after a broadcast or PR failure.

问起.etymology: A verb-directional/inchoative compound formed from the verb 问 (wèn, Old Chinese *muns*, Middle Chinese *mjunH*, phono-semantic graph with 门 "gate" as phonetic and 口 "mouth" as semantic, "to ask, inquire") and the directional complement 起 (qǐ, Middle Chinese *khj+X*, "to rise, raise, initiate"). In Early Mandarin vernacular, 起 grammaticalized as a post-verbal aspectual/directional marker indicating the initiation of an action or the bringing of a topic into active discourse ("to bring up by asking").

history.meaning: to ask, inquire after, interrogate
to begin asking about; to bring up a person or matter in questioning

morphemes.meaning: up; initiating or bringing a topic to the surface

问起.notes: Frequently used in narrative dialogue (e.g., 有人问起这件事, "if someone asks about this matter"); takes its object after 起 rather than splitting, unlike 想起…来.

问问.etymology: Reduplicated verb from 问 ('ask, inquire'): 'ask around, make a quick inquiry, ask someone a bit'.

history.meaning: ask a little; make an inquiry

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 问问 (via 萌典)

问题.etymology: Compound noun of 问 (問, 'ask, examine') + 题 (題, 'topic, subject, examination item'): originally 'question on an examination or topic for discussion', and in modern Mandarin the standard word for both 'question (to be answered)' and 'problem, issue, trouble (to be solved)'.

history.meaning: question posed on a topic
question; problem; issue

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 问题 (via 萌典)

闯过来.etymology: A verb-complement construction combining the action verb 闯 (chuǎng, traditional 闖, Middle Chinese *tsrhjangX*, an ideogrammic compound showing a horse 马 bursting violently through a doorway 门, originally meaning "to bolt out, charge in suddenly") with the compound directional complement 过来 (guòlái, "across and hither"). Metaphorically extended from physically charging across a barrier toward the speaker's vantage point to surviving and fighting one's way through a grueling ordeal or career crisis into the present.

history.meaning: of a horse, to bolt through a gate; to rush in suddenly and forcefully

history.form: 闖過來 / 闯过来 (chuǎng guòlái)
history.meaning: to charge across to this side; figuratively, to fight one's way through hardship and survive

morphemes.meaning: hither, toward the speaker's present vantage point

闯过来.notes: Typically takes 一路 ("all the way") or 难关 ("crisis/hurdle") in showbiz and entrepreneurial contexts (e.g., 一路闯过来, "having fought one's way through all the way to now").

rootFamily.gloss: venture into the world to make a living; weather storms
cause trouble, bring about a disaster
endure and pull through a painful ordeal

闲.etymology: Represented in simplified script by 闲 (originally the graph 閑, an ideogrammic compound of 门 "gate" and 木 "wooden crossbar", Old Chinese *gˤran*, Middle Chinese *hean*, meaning "wooden barrier, fence; to bar, defend"), which became graphically and phonetically merged with 閒 (gate 门 with moon 月 shining through the crevice, meaning "interval, gap, leisure"). From the spatial sense of an open interval or unoccupied gap between duties, 闲 developed the adjectival sense of "unoccupied, at leisure, idle, not in use."

history.meaning: wooden gate-bar (閑); gap or crevice between doors, temporal interval (閒)
unoccupied time, leisure, tranquil, free from official duties
idle, free, having nothing to do; unoccupied

闲.notes: Contrasts with 忙 ("busy"); as a verb or adjective it can be benevolent (清闲, "peacefully unoccupied") or critical (吃闲饭, "freeloader"), depending on context.

rootFamily.gloss: idle time, leisure; to sit around doing nothing

闲得慌.etymology: A colloquial degree-complement construction composed of the stative verb/adjective 闲 (xián, "idle, having nothing to do"), the structural particle 得 (de, reduced from Middle Chinese 得 *tok* "to obtain, attain", marking the extent or result of a state), and the expressive complement 慌 (huāng, Middle Chinese *xwang*, originally "dim, flustered, agitated", grammaticalized after 得 to indicate an unbearable or restless extreme of a state). Literally "so idle that one feels flustered and restless."

history.meaning: idle to the point of mental restlessness or agitation
bored out of one's mind; having way too much idle time on one's hands

morphemes.meaning: structural marker introducing a degree or result complement
flustered, unbearably so, to an extreme degree

闲得慌.notes: Often used sarcastically in spoken Mandarin to chide someone for meddling or creating drama out of boredom (e.g., 你是不是闲得慌？ "Do you have nothing better to do?").

rootFamily.gloss: bored out of one's mind, unbearably闷/stifled
exhausted to the point of misery

间.etymology: Measure word for rooms of every kind (一间客房 'a guest room', 一间书房 'a study'), combining 门 ('doorway, gate') with 日 ('sunlight'). Depicting light peeking through a doorway gap, 間 in Classical Chinese meant 'interval, space between' and the bay between building pillars—hence one room.

history.meaning: space between; structural room bay

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 間 (via 萌典)

间谍.etymology: A coordinative Sino-compound of 间 (jiàn, traditional 間, Middle Chinese *keanH*, "crevice, interval; to sow discord, infiltrate between enemies") and 谍 (dié, Middle Chinese *dep*, phono-semantic graph with 言 "speech" and 枼 phonetic, meaning "military intelligence, espionage; to spy"). In Classical Chinese military treatises such as the *Sunzi Bingfa* (《孙子兵法·用间》), 间 alone denoted a spy who exploits gaps in the enemy camp, while 谍 denoted gathering covert intelligence; their pairing 间谍 is attested since the Wei-Jin and Tang periods.

history.meaning: to infiltrate a gap or sow discord among enemies (間); to gather military intelligence covertly (諜)
military scout or secret agent sent into enemy territory
spy, espionage agent (military, political, or corporate)

morphemes.meaning: gap, crevice; infiltrate, spy, sow discord

间谍.notes: In workplace and entertainment industry dramas like *Behind the Scenes*, 间谍 or 商业间谍 ("corporate spy") is frequently used for moles leaking project proposals to rival studios.

rootFamily.gloss: traitor, mole, insider working for the enemy

闹.etymology: Originally written 鬧 (and in orthodox seal/clerical tradition 閙), an associative compound combining 鬥 ("to fight, brawl, contend") and 市 ("marketplace"), vividly depicting the clamorous din and brawling of a crowded market. In Middle Chinese (*nraewH*) and Early Mandarin vernacular, it functioned both as an adjective ("noisy, bustling") and as an active verb meaning "to make a clamor, stir up trouble, kick up a fuss, or suffer from an outbreak of something."

history.meaning: clamor and contention in a marketplace; noisy, turbulent
to make a scene, stir up trouble, quarrel, or vent emotions noisily

morphemes.meaning: make noise, stir up trouble, create a scene, act up

闹.notes: Extremely productive verb in spoken Mandarin: it can mean throwing a tantrum (闹脾气), creating a public scandal (闹事), or experiencing a comical/awkward mishap (闹笑话).

rootFamily.gloss: lively, bustling with noise and excitement
make a fool of oneself, make an embarrassing blunder

闹掰.etymology: A verb-resultative (VR) colloquial compound composed of 闹 (nào, "to quarrel, make a fuss, have a conflict") and the resultative complement 掰 (bāi, an ideogrammic compound of 分 "divide/split" between two hands 手, originally meaning "to break or snap apart with both hands"). By metaphor, quarreling (闹) until the relationship is snapped in two (掰) yields the vivid colloquial sense "to fall out completely, break off relations, or split up acrimoniously."

history.meaning: to break or pry apart with both hands
to quarrel to the point of breaking off a friendship, partnership, or romance

morphemes.meaning: break apart with two hands; split completely, sever ties

闹掰.notes: Informal, northern-flavored spoken Mandarin; roughly synonymous with 闹翻 ("fall out") or 决裂 ("break off relations", which is much more formal). Can take 了 (闹掰了).

rootFamily.gloss: fall out, quarrel until things overturn
have an awkward rift or disagreement in a relationship
break apart by hand; sever ties (colloquial)

闹钟.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 闹 (鬧, 'noisy, make a racket / sound an alarm') + 钟 (鐘, 'clock'): 'alarm clock'.

history.meaning: alarm clock

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 闹钟 (via 萌典)

闺女.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 闺 (guī, traditional 閨, Middle Chinese *kwej*, a small arched inner doorway 圭 inside a gate 门 leading to the women's quarters of a traditional household, hence "boudoir, inner women's chambers") and 女 (nǚ, Middle Chinese *nrjoX*, "unmarried girl, daughter, woman"). Originally in Tang–Song literature 闺女 denoted a young, unmarried maiden residing in the inner family chambers; in Northern Mandarin vernacular it warmed into the affectionate everyday word for "daughter" (or an endearing form of address from an elder to a young woman).

history.meaning: young unmarried woman living in the inner family quarters (boudoir)
unmarried girl; (warm colloquial) one's own daughter or a young woman of the next generation

闺女.notes: Pronounced with a neutral tone on the second syllable (*guīnü*); carries warm, folksy, parental affection compared to the standard register 女儿 (*nǚ'ér*).

rootFamily.gloss: well-bred young lady from an eminent family

闺蜜.etymology: A late-20th/early-21st-century Mandarin blend (clipped from 闺中密友, guīzhōng mìyǒu, "intimate friend of the inner women's chambers") combining 闺 (guī, traditional 閨, "women's boudoir, female sphere") and 蜜 (mì, Middle Chinese *mjit*, "honey, sweet", functioning both as a phonetic pun on 密 mì "intimate, close, secret" and as a semantic intensifier evoking sweetness and affection). It rapidly lexicalized in urban Chinese media and everyday speech as the standard term for a woman's closest friend.

history.meaning: intimate female confidante admitted to one's private inner chambers
best female friend, female confidante, bestie

morphemes.meaning: honey-sweet / intimate confidante (pun on 密友)

闺蜜.notes: Ubiquitous in modern C-dramas and lifestyle media; also spawns sub-terms like 男闺蜜 ("male bestie") and 塑料闺蜜 ("plastic/fake bestie").

闻.etymology: Ancient ideogram/phono-semantic character (聞) attested on Shang oracle bones showing a kneeling person with a prominent ear (耳) listening at a doorway (門, phonetic wén). In Classical Chinese, 聞 meant 'hear (with the ears)' and 'news/reputation' (retained in 新闻 'news' and 见闻). From the Tang–Song period onward, in everyday spoken Mandarin 听 took over 'hear', while 闻 shifted to 'smell, sniff (with the nose)'.

history.meaning: perceive with the ear = hear; news; famous
smell, sniff (with the nose); hear/news (in compounds)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 闻 (via 萌典)

闻闻.etymology: Reduplicated verb from 闻 ('smell, sniff'): 'take a sniff, smell a bit'.

history.meaning: take a sniff; smell a little

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 闻闻 (via 萌典)

阀门.etymology: Coordinative/modifier-head mechanical compound of 阀 (閥, originally a great family's inscribed gate pillar, adopted in modern engineering for a 'valve') + 门 (門, 'gate, shut-off door'): 'valve (controlling flow in a pipe)'.

history.meaning: mechanical valve

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 阀门 (via 萌典)

阁楼.etymology: Architectural compound of 阁 ('elevated timber pavilion or upper chamber', gate radical 门 + phonetic 各 gè) + 楼 ('multi-storey timber building', wood radical 木 + phonetic 娄 lóu), naming a tucked upper loft or attic beneath a pitched roof.

history.meaning: multi-storeyed pavilions and galleries
attic; garret loft

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 阁楼

队.etymology: Utilizes the mound/ear radical 阝 alongside 人 (rén, 'person'). Classically describing a descending formation of soldiers, it serves in modern Chinese as an inclusive term for any organized column, row, or team of people.

history.meaning: column of soldiers
team; row

队伍.etymology: A coordinative Sino-compound derived from ancient Chinese military organization, combining 队 (duì, traditional 隊, Middle Chinese *dwojH*, originally "to fall from a height", early extended to a squad or detachment of soldiers) and 伍 (wǔ, Middle Chinese *nguX*, the basic five-man infantry file in Zhou and Qin military administration, from 人 "person" + 五 "five"). Together, 队伍 originally denoted ordered military ranks and files, and broadened in modern Mandarin to mean any organized contingent, professional workforce, or production team.

history.meaning: military detachment or company (隊) and five-man infantry file (伍)
ordered military troops and formations; an organized line or procession
