troops; organized contingent, professional team, or ranks of personnel

队伍.notes: Often pronounced with a neutral second syllable (*duìwu*); used for everything from a physical queue/parade to a talent pool or production crew (e.g., 壮大我们的队伍, "expand our ranks/team").

cognates.meaning: member of a squad, party, or team

队员.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-compound formed from 队 (duì, traditional 隊, Middle Chinese *dwojH*, "military squad, detachment, team") and 员 (yuán, traditional 員, Middle Chinese *hjwien*, originally a round bronze ding-vessel, extended in Classical Chinese to "count, quota of personnel, official or member"). Modeled on modern institutional compounds in late Qing/early Republican Mandarin and Japanese (隊員 taiin), it designates an individual member belonging to an organized team, squad, or competitive group.

history.meaning: squad/detachment + counted personnel or official
member of a team, squad, expedition, or competitive contingent

morphemes.meaning: member, personnel, individual belonging to a group

队员.notes: Common in sports, reality competition shows, and task-force settings (e.g., 老队员 "veteran team member", 主力队员 "key/starting team member").

队长.etymology: The noun '队长' (duìzhǎng, captain, team leader) consists of '队' (team, line) and '长' (leader, head). '队' historically referred to a military formation or a group of people falling into line. '长' is a common suffix denoting the head or senior member of a designated group. Originally a military term for the commander of a small unit, '队长' expanded in modern times to cover civilian contexts, including sports teams, work crews, and expedition groups. It conveys both authority and responsibility.

history.meaning: team

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 队长

阳光.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 阳 (陽, 'the sun, sunny south side of a hill', mound 阝 + 昜 'rising sun casting bright rays') + 光 ('light, rays'): 'sunlight, sunshine' (and figuratively 'sunny, upbeat, transparent'). Attested since Pre-Qin and Han prose.

history.meaning: sunlight; sunshine; sunny

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 阳光 (via 萌典)

阳光房.etymology: Three-character architectural compound combining 阳光 ('sunlight, sunshine') + 房 ('room'): 'sunroom, conservatory, glass-enclosed veranda'.

history.meaning: sunroom; glass conservatory

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 阳光房 (via 萌典)

阳台.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 阳台. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 阳台 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 阳台 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 阳台 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 阳台. The etymology of 阳台 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 阳台
middle form of 阳台
modern form of 阳台

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 阳台

阴影.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 阴影. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 阴影 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 阴影 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 阴影 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 阴影. The etymology of 阴影 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 阴影
middle form of 阴影
modern form of 阴影

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 阴影

cognates.meaning: yin and yang; shade and light; astronomy/divination
cognates.word: 陰陽 (いんよう / おんみょう, in'yō / onmyō)

cognates.meaning: yin and yang; the worlds of the dead and the living

阴阳.etymology: An ancient coordinative compound of 阴 (yīn, traditional 陰, Old Chinese *q(r)əm*, Middle Chinese *'jim*, with semantic 阜 "mound/hill" and 侌 "cloud shade", originally the dark, north-facing slope of a hill or south bank of a river) and 阳 (yáng, traditional 陽, Old Chinese *laŋ*, Middle Chinese *yjang*, with 阜 "hill" and 昜 "sunlight shining", originally the sunny, south-facing slope of a hill or north bank of a river). In Warring States natural philosophy (*Yijing*, *Zhuangzi*), 阴阳 became the foundational cosmological polarity of shade/sunlight, passive/active, covert/overt. In contemporary colloquial and internet Mandarin, 阴阳 is also used as a verb or adjective (clipped from 阴阳怪气) meaning "to be passive-aggressive, snarky, or backhanded."

history.meaning: the shaded (north) slope and sunlit (south) slope of a mountain; cosmic duality of dark/light and receptive/active forces
dual cosmic principles governing medicine, divination, and the realms of the dead and living
yin and yang; (modern slang/showbiz) dual/fraudulent (as in 阴阳合同) or passive-aggressive/snarky (clipped from 阴阳怪气)

morphemes.meaning: shaded north slope; dark, covert, lunar, passive principle (yin)
sunlit south slope; bright, overt, solar, active principle (yang)

阴阳.notes: Beyond philosophy, media and entertainment contexts use 阴阳合同 ("yin-yang contracts", i.e. a fake low-pay contract for tax authorities and a secret real one) and 阴阳怪气 ("speaking in a snide, passive-aggressive tone").

阴魂不散.etymology: A four-character subject-predicate idiom (chengyu) structured as 阴魂 ("dark/netherworld spirit", from 阴 "shade, realm of the dead" + 魂 "ethereal soul") + 不散 ("does not disperse/dissipate"). Rooted in traditional Chinese beliefs that the aggrieved or unappeased spirit (魂) of a deceased person clings to the living world rather than dispersing, the phrase is attested in Ming–Qing vernacular fiction (such as *Xingshi Hengyan*) and is used figuratively in modern Mandarin for a bothersome person, rival, scandal, or trouble that refuses to go away.

history.meaning: an unappeased ghost or dark spirit clings to a place and refuses to disperse
to linger like a haunting ghost; of an annoying person, rival, or problem, to keep showing up and refuse to go away

阴魂不散.notes: Frequently used with exasperation or dark humor in dramas when a persistent ex-partner, paparazzo, or workplace nemesis keeps turning up unexpectedly.

rootFamily.gloss: frightened out of one's wits (lit. soul flies and scatters)

cognates.meaning: lineup, cast, team roster, personnel structure
battle array; lineup, roster, team structure

阵容.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-compound composed of 阵 (zhèn, traditional 陣, Middle Chinese *drjinH*, "battle array, military formation, troop disposition") and 容 (róng, Middle Chinese *yjwong*, "appearance, bearing, configuration"). In Classical and Imperial Chinese military prose (e.g., *Records of the Three Kingdoms*, Tang histories), 阵容 denoted the outward configuration, discipline, and imposing appearance of an army drawn up for battle. In modern Mandarin (and parallel Japanese 陣容 jin'yō), it shifted into entertainment, sports, and politics to mean the "lineup, cast, or roster of talent" assembled for a production or match.

history.meaning: the physical configuration, order, and imposing bearing of troops in battle array
the assembled lineup, cast of performers, or roster of a team or production

阵容.notes: A core showbiz term in *Behind the Scenes*: collocations like 明星阵容 ("star-studded lineup"), 豪华阵容 ("all-star/deluxe cast"), and 主创阵容 ("core creative team") appear constantly in TV/film production.

rootFamily.gloss: disposition, deployment, battle formation; grand scene

阶层.etymology: A coordinative architectural metaphor composed of 阶 (jiē, traditional 階, Middle Chinese *keaj*, with semantic 阜 "mound/steps" and phonetic 皆, meaning "flight of stairs, earthen or stone steps leading up to a hall, rank") and 层 (céng, traditional 層, Middle Chinese *dzong*, "story of a multi-tiered building, layer, stratum"). Originally denoting physical steps and stories of a structure, 阶层 was popularized in modern East Asian social science (alongside Japanese 階層 kaisō, translating German *Schicht* / English *stratum*) to denote a socioeconomic stratum or group within a hierarchy.

history.meaning: steps/stairs leading to a hall (階) and stories/tiers of a building (層)
social stratum, socioeconomic tier, or occupational sub-class

阶层.notes: Often paired with modifiers like 中产阶层 ("middle stratum/class") or 社会各个阶层 ("all strata of society"); slightly more neutral and sociological than 阶级 ("political/economic class" in Marxist usage).

rootFamily.gloss: level, tier, hierarchy, depth of thought

cognates.meaning: stage, phase, grade, step in a process

阶段.etymology: A Sino-compound combining 阶 (jiē, traditional 階, Middle Chinese *keaj*, "steps, stairs, graduated rank") and 段 (duàn, Middle Chinese *dwanH*, "a cut section, segment, piece"). In classical and vernacular architecture, 阶段 (or 段阶) referred literally to a flight or section of stone steps. In modern Mandarin (paralleling Japanese 段階 dankai, with the morphemes in reverse order in standard modern Japanese, though 階段 kaidan retained the literal sense "staircase" in Japanese), 阶段 specialized metaphorically to mean a distinct temporal "segment or step" in a process—hence "phase, stage."

history.meaning: a flight or section of stairs/steps leading up a platform
a distinct phase, stage, or period in the progression of a project or historical process

morphemes.meaning: section, segment, stretch of time or space

阶段.notes: Essential in project management and TV production workflows: 筹备阶段 ("preparation phase"), 宣传阶段 ("promotional phase"), and 阶段性成果 ("phased/interim results").

rootFamily.gloss: flight of steps; figurative way out of an awkward spot (下台阶)
time period, segment of time, slot

cognates.meaning: resistance, drag (less common than 抵抗力)

阻力.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-compound composed of 阻 (zǔ, Middle Chinese *tsrjoX*, with semantic 阜 "mound/terrain barrier" and phonetic 且, originally "steep,險/impassable terrain; to obstruct, hinder, block") and 力 (lì, Middle Chinese *lik*, a pictograph of a sinew or plowshare, meaning "physical strength, force, power"). Coinage in modern scientific and socio-political Mandarin (initially translating physical "drag/resistance" in mechanics and fluid dynamics, such as 空气阻力 "air resistance") quickly extended metaphorically to institutional pushback, obstacles, or opposition against a plan.

history.meaning: to obstruct/hinder by terrain barriers (阻) + physical force or strength (力)
physical drag or resistance in mechanics; figuratively, opposition, pushback, or headwind against an initiative

阻力.notes: Frequently paired withits antonym 动力 ("driving force, motivation"), as in 化阻力为动力 ("turn resistance/pushback into motivation").

rootFamily.gloss: obstruct, stand in the way, impede

cognates.meaning: prevention, obstruction, stopping, holding in check

阻止.etymology: A coordinative/resultative Sino-compound uniting 阻 (zǔ, Middle Chinese *tsrjoX*, "to obstruct, block with a barrier") and 止 (zhǐ, Middle Chinese *tsyiX*, originally a pictograph of a foot, meaning "to halt, stop, cease"). Attested in Classical and Medieval Chinese historical texts (where 阻止 could mean "to be blocked and halted by terrain or an enemy"), it functions in modern Mandarin (and parallel Japanese 阻止 soshi / Korean 저지 jeoji) as an active transitive verb meaning "to stop, prevent, or block someone/something from proceeding."

history.meaning: to be obstructed and brought to a halt by barriers or opposing forces
to actively stop, prevent, or block an action or person from proceeding

阻止.notes: More forceful and direct than 劝阻 ("dissuade, talk someone out of"); 阻止 implies actively intervening to prevent an action (e.g., 没人能阻止我, "no one can stop me").

rootFamily.gloss: block, intercept, stop someone in their tracks

cognates.meaning: attached table, appended schedule or chart
cognates.word: 付表 / 附表 (ふひょう, fuhyō)

附表.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-compound composed of 附 (fù, Middle Chinese *bjuH*, with semantic 阜 "mound" and phonetic 付 "hand over", meaning "to adhere to, attach, append") and 表 (biǎo, Middle Chinese *pjewX*, originally "outer fur garment", extended in Han historiography—most famously Sima Qian's *Shiji*—to mean "chronological chart, tabular schedule, or memorial"). Combined as 附表, it designates a supplementary table, schedule, or appendix attached to a main contract, report, or regulatory document.

history.meaning: to attach/append (附) + tabular chart or schedule (表, as in historical tables)
attached table, appended schedule, or supplementary chart in a contract or report

附表.notes: Standard legal and administrative term in media production contracts (e.g., 详见合同附表, "see the attached schedule to the contract for details" covering shooting dates or payment tranches).

rootFamily.gloss: attachment, annex, email attachment or spare part
appendix, addendum to a book or contract

附近.etymology: Coordinative locative noun and adjective compound of 附 ('adhere to, be close to', mound 阝 + 付) + 近 ('near, close'): 'nearby, in the vicinity, neighborhood'. Attested since the史记 Shiji and Hanshu.

history.stage: Han Classical Chinese (Shiji, Hanshu) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: close by; in the vicinity; nearby

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 附近 (via 萌典)

陈年.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 陈 (chén, traditional 陳, Middle Chinese *drjin*, originally the name of an ancient state and "to lay out, display in battle array", which evolved the sense "laid out for a long time, old, aged, stale") and 年 (nián, Middle Chinese *nen*, originally "grain harvest", hence "year"). Literally "of old/aged years", 陈年 has long been used positively for aged wine, vinegar, or tea (陈年老酒), and figuratively—often with a touch of irony—for bygone, stale, or long-past grievances and gossip (陈年旧事).

history.meaning: stored for a long time, aged (陳) + years (年)
aged over many years (of wine/grain); bygone, stale, from years ago (of past events or accounts)

morphemes.meaning: aged, stored for a long time, old, stale

陈年.notes: Dual-register nuance: prized when modifying wine or tea (陈年佳酿, "fine aged vintage"), but dismissive when modifying old drama or grudges (陈年旧账, "stale old scores").

rootFamily.gloss: outdated, obsolete, old-fashioned (of equipment or ideas)
display, exhibit, lay out (preserving the earlier sense of 陈)
trivial, stale matters (lit. stale sesame and rotten millet)

陌生.etymology: Compound adjective of 陌 ('raised footpath running east–west between fields -> unfamiliar passerby on the road', as in the Han ballad 陌上桑 and 陌路人) + 生 ('unripe, unfamiliar, unacquainted'): 'unfamiliar, strange, unknown'. Attested from Tang–Song poetry and vernacular.

history.meaning: unfamiliar; strange

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 陌生 (via 萌典)

陌生人.etymology: Three-morpheme compound of 陌生 ('unfamiliar; strange', from 陌 'raised east-west field path' + 生 'unripe/unfamiliar', literally someone met on a country road whom one does not know) + 人 ('person'). Contrasts directly with 熟人 ('acquaintance; familiar face').

history.meaning: unfamiliar passerby; stranger
stranger

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 陌生人

降低.etymology: A verb-resultative (VR) compound formed from the verb 降 (jiàng, Old Chinese *kˤruŋ-s*, Middle Chinese *kaewngH*, originally an ideogrammic graph showing two footprints 夂 descending a terraced mound 阜, meaning "to descend, step down, send down") and the adjectival resultative complement 低 (dī, Middle Chinese *tej*, "low, bowed down"). Together, "to bring down so that it becomes low" lexicalized in Early and Modern Mandarin as the standard transitive and intransitive verb meaning "to lower, reduce, or cut down (costs, standards, volume, risk)."

history.meaning: to descend a hill; to step down, fall, or send down from above
to lower, reduce, bring down to a lower level (of height, cost, standard, or intensity)

降低.notes: Takes abstract or measurable nouns such as 成本 ("costs"), 标准 ("standards"), 要求 ("requirements"), or 姿态 ("posture/pride", i.e. humble oneself). Do not confuse with the homograph reading *xiáng* ("to surrender/subdue", as in 投降).

rootFamily.gloss: decline, drop, fall (intransitive, of ratings or temperature)

院.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 阝 (阜, 'earthen mound/wall') + 完 (wán/yuàn, 'complete enclosure'): originally 'a continuous surrounding wall around a residence -> courtyard', and extended to major public or scholarly institutions enclosed by courtyards ('academy, hospital 医院, theater/cinema 剧院, court 法院').

history.meaning: walled courtyard; compound
courtyard; institutional compound (hospital, academy, theater, court)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 院 (via 萌典)

院子.etymology: Colloquial noun formed from 院 ('walled courtyard') + nominal suffix 子 (neutral tone zi): 'courtyard, yard'.

history.meaning: courtyard; yard

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 院子 (via 萌典)

院门.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 院 ('courtyard') + 门 (門, 'gate, door'): 'courtyard gate'.

history.meaning: courtyard gate

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 院门 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to remove, exclude, except (as 除く nozoku)
cognates.word: 除 (じょ / のぞく, jo / nozoku)

除.etymology: A phono-semantic character (Old Chinese *lra*, Middle Chinese *drjo*) combining semantic 阜 (阝, "mound, terraced steps") with phonetic 余 (yú). Its primary concrete sense in Classical Chinese was "the steps leading up to a palace hall", from which it developed the verbal sense "to sweep clean the palace steps, clear away, remove, eradicate" (and in mathematics, "to divide"). From "removing or setting aside X from the count", 除 grammaticalized in Medieval and Literary Chinese into a preposition meaning "setting aside, except for, apart from, besides"—most commonly in the circumpositional frame 除…之外 / 除…以外.

history.meaning: palace steps; to sweep away, clear out, remove, or appoint to office (clearing away the old title)
setting aside, excluding; apart from, besides (usually paired with 外 or 了)

除.notes: As a standalone monosyllabic preposition, 除 belongs to a slightly more concise or formal register than 除了, and almost always requires a closing spatial/scope particle like 之外 or 以外 (e.g., 除你之外, "apart from you").

rootFamily.gloss: exclude, rule out, remove an obstacle
New Year's Eve (lit. the evening of sweeping away the old year)

除了.etymology: Formed in Early Mandarin vernacular by univerbating the verb/preposition 除 (chú, Middle Chinese *drjo*, "to remove, set aside, exclude") with the perfective/completion particle 了 (le, grammaticalized from Middle Chinese 了 *leawX* "to finish, complete"). Literally "having set aside / once X is excluded", it became the standard spoken and written Mandarin preposition meaning "except for, apart from, besides." Depending on the correlative adverb in the main clause (都 "all" vs. 还/也 "also"), it expresses either exclusion ("except for X") or additive inclusion ("besides X, also...").

history.meaning: having removed or set aside; excluding, apart from
besides, apart from, except for (functioning as a preposition of exclusion or addition)

morphemes.meaning: completion marker fused into a compound preposition

除了.notes: Watch the correlative adverb in the second clause: 除了…都… means "except for X, everyone/everything..." (exclusive), whereas 除了…还/也… means "in addition to X, also..." (inclusive).

rootFamily.gloss: unless, only if (lit. excluding that it is not...)

除此之外.etymology: A four-character literary-style discourse connector built on a Classical Chinese circumpositional frame: 除 (chú, "setting aside, excluding") + 此 (cǐ, Middle Chinese *tshjeX*, proximal demonstrative pronoun "this") + 之 (zhī, Middle Chinese *tsyi*, attributive/genitive marker linking modifier to head) + 外 (wài, Middle Chinese *ngwajH*, "outside, beyond"). Literally "outside of setting this aside", it serves as a cohesive transition phrase in modern spoken and written Mandarin meaning "besides that, apart from this, in addition."

history.form: 除此以外 / 除此之外
history.meaning: beyond the exclusion of this matter; outside of this
besides that, apart from this, in addition to what was just mentioned

除此之外.notes: Very common at the beginning of a sentence in pitches, reports, and negotiations to introduce an additional point or condition ("On top of that... / Apart from this...").

rootFamily.gloss: because of this, therefore, thus (parallel classical 此 pattern)

除非.etymology: Exclusive conditional conjunction combining 除 ('exclude, except for') + 非 ('is not'): literally 'excluding the case where it is not…' -> 'only if, unless'. Attested from Tang–Song poetry and vernacular.

history.meaning: only if; unless

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 除非 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: treacherous, perilous,险悪/hostile, grim (of atmosphere or relations)

险恶.etymology: A coordinative Sino-compound combining 险 (xiǎn, traditional 險, Middle Chinese *xjemX*, with semantic 阜 "steep mound/precipice" and phonetic 僉, originally "precipitous, narrow mountain defile, perilous terrain") and 恶 (è, traditional 惡, Middle Chinese *'ak*, with 心 "heart" and 亞, meaning "foul,noxious, harsh, wicked, malevolent"). In Classical and Medieval Chinese (e.g., *Hanshu*, *Zizhi Tongjian*), 险恶 described both rugged, life-threatening topography and treacherous human character; in modern Mandarin it applies to perilous environments, cutthroat industry politics, or sinister motives (用心险恶).

history.meaning: precipitous and harsh (of mountain terrain or waterways); treacherous and malevolent (of character)
treacherous, perilous, hostile (of social/workplace conditions, illness, or malicious intentions)

险恶.notes: Classic collocations in drama dialogue include 江湖险恶 / 人心险恶 ("the world / human hearts are treacherous") and 用心险恶 ("harboring sinister/malicious motives").

cognates.meaning: to attend on, accompany a superior (as in 陪席 baiseki)
to accompany, attend upon (as in 배석 陪席)

陪.etymology: A phono-semantic character (Old Chinese *bˤə*, Middle Chinese *bwoj*) combining semantic 阜 (阝, "terraced mound, layered earth") with phonetic 咅 (pǒu). Originally meaning "to pile up earth in layers, to add dirt to a mound", it extended in Classical Chinese to "to augment, assist as a subordinate, attend upon a superior at court or at a banquet" (as in 陪臣 "vassal of a vassal"). By the Tang–Song period, the hierarchical sense generalized into the everyday transitive verb "to accompany, keep someone company, or stay by someone's side."

history.meaning: to heap up layered earth; to attend upon a noble or act as a subordinate companion at a banquet or ritual
to accompany, keep someone company, or go along with someone

陪.notes: Do not confuse with its homophone 赔 (péi, with 贝 "cowrie/money" radical, meaning "to compensate, indemnify, or lose money",though the two share the same phonetic series and historically overlapped in phrases like 陪笑/赔笑).

rootFamily.gloss: accompany, keep warm and supportive company
accompany (often an official, guest, or VIP); entourage
apologize, offer an apology (historically linked with 赔不是)

陪床.etymology: A modern verb-object (VO) compound formed from 陪 (péi, "to accompany, stay by someone's side in attendance") and 床 (chuáng, Middle Chinese *dzrjang*, "bed", here specifically a hospital inpatient bed, 病床). Created in modern Chinese healthcare and everyday hospital usage, 陪床 denotes the practice of a family member, partner, or hired caregiver staying overnight beside a hospitalized patient's bed to tend to their needs,and by extension the cot/extra bed rented for that companion.

history.meaning: to keep company / attend upon (陪) + bed/couch (床)
to stay overnight by a hospital bed to care for an inpatient; a folding cot for a hospital companion

陪床.notes: Important cultural and false-friend note: despite literally containing "accompany + bed", 陪床 in standard mainland Mandarin strictly means tending to a sick person overnight in a hospital (hospital bedside care), never anything romantic or sexual!

rootFamily.gloss: accompany a patient for medical care or hospitalization
get out of bed; wake up in the morning

陪陪.etymology: Formed by AA verb reduplication of 陪 (péi, Middle Chinese *bwoj*, "to accompany, keep someone company"). In Mandarin morphosyntax (developing from Song–Yuan vernacular constructions like 陪一陪), reduplicating a volitional action verb adds a delimitative, tentative, and affectionate aspectual nuance—softening the tone and indicating "to spend a little time keeping someone company" in a warm, unhurried, and considerate way.

history.meaning: to accompany or keep someone company for a while
to spend some quality time with someone; to keep someone company for a bit

陪陪.notes: The second syllable takes a neutral tone (*péipei*); very common in family and relationship scenes in C-dramas when busy professionals promise to make time for loved ones (e.g., 多陪陪家人, "spend more time with family").

rootFamily.gloss: chat for a bit, have a casual conversation (parallel AA verb)
take a look, see for a bit (parallel AA verb)

陶土.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 陶 ('pottery, earthenware', mound 阝 + 匋 'kiln cradling clay vessels') + 土 ('clay, earth'): 'potter's clay, ceramic clay, terracotta clay'.

history.meaning: pottery clay; ceramic clay

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 陶土 (via 萌典)

陶瓷.etymology: Coordinative compound uniting China's two great fired-clay traditions: 陶 ('earthenware/stoneware', combining 阝 mound with 匋 depicting a kiln wrapping fired vessels) and 瓷 ('high-fired glazed porcelain', combining phonetic 次 cì with 瓦 'tile/ceramic ware').

history.meaning: kiln-fired pottery
vitrified glazed porcelain
ceramics; pottery and porcelain

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 陶瓷 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to fall into, plunge into, be bogged down in (a crisis or state)
cognates.word: 陥入 (かんにゅう, kannyū / おちいる, ochiiru)

cognates.meaning: to fall into, sink into, be bogged down in

陷入.etymology: A verb-resultative/directional Sino-compound combining 陷 (xiàn, Old Chinese *gˤrom-s*, Middle Chinese *heamH*, an ideogrammic compound with 阜 "earthen wall/mound" and 臽 showing a person 人 falling into a pit 臼, originally meaning "pitfall, trap; to fall or sink into a pit") and 入 (rù, Middle Chinese *nyip*, "to enter, go into"). Attested from Classical and Han prose onward for physically sinking into mud, a pitfall, or enemy hands, 陷入 is used in modern Mandarin primarily in the figurative sense of being plunged or bogged down into an adverse state, crisis, or deep emotion.

history.meaning: to fall into a pitfall or earthen trap (陷) + to enter inside (入)
to sink physically into mud or a pit; of a city or army, to fall into enemy hands
to sink into, be plunged into, or become mired in (a predicament, crisis, silence, or deep thought)

morphemes.meaning: fall into a pit, sink, get bogged down

陷入.notes: Takes abstract nouns representing states that are hard to extricate oneself from: 陷入困境 ("sink into a predicament"), 陷入危机 ("be plunged into crisis"), 陷入沉思 ("fall into deep thought"), or 陷入僵局 ("reach a deadlock").

rootFamily.gloss: frame someone, set up a false accusation against someone
sink deeply into (an addiction, obsession, or quagmire)

cognates.meaning: to frame; to entice into a trap

陷害.etymology: A coordinative-resultative verbal compound formed from 陷 (xiàn, Middle Chinese *ɣɛmH*, 'to fall into a pit; to plunge; to entrap') and 害 (hài, Middle Chinese *ɣɑiH*, 'to injure; to harm; to murder'). Literally 'to drop someone into a pit and harm them,' the metaphor derives from ancient hunting traps (陷穽) and was lexicalized in Han-era legal and historical prose to denote maliciously framing an innocent person through false accusations or engineered evidence.

history.meaning: to cause to fall into a pit and suffer injury
to ensnare and ruin through slander or fabricated charges
to frame, set up, or maliciously incriminate someone

morphemes.meaning: to sink; to trap in a pit; to frame
to harm; to injure; to ruin

陷害.notes: Frequently collocates with 设计 (shèjì, 'by design/scheme') or 栽赃 (zāizāng, 'to plant stolen goods/evidence') in workplace and media dramas when rivals sabotage a producer or celebrity.

rootFamily.gloss: to trump up charges, frame falsely

陷阱.etymology: A coordinative nominal compound uniting 陷 (xiàn, 'pitfall; to sink into a pit,' showing 阜 'mound/earthwork' beside 臽, a pictograph of a person falling into a hole) and 阱 (jǐng, also written 穽 in Classical texts, 'pit dug to catch wild beasts'). Attested in pre-Qin military and ritual classics, the compound originally denoted concealed stake-lined pits for trapping tigers or enemy cavalry before broadening into a figurative term for any deceptive scheme or snare.

history.meaning: concealed pit dug in the earth to capture wild animals or advancing troops
political or moral snare; hidden danger
trap, pitfall, or deceptive scheme (such as a contract trap)

morphemes.meaning: to fall into a pit; pitfall
well; covered pit for catching beasts

陷阱.notes: Commonly used with verbs like 掉进 (diàojìn, 'fall into') or 设下 (shèxià, 'lay/set up'), and in entertainment industry contexts such as 合同陷阱 ('contractual trap').

rootFamily.gloss: to sink into, become bogged down in

隆重.etymology: A coordinative adjectival and adverbial compound joining 隆 (lóng, Middle Chinese *ljuwng*, 'lofty, flourishing, abundant, eminent') and 重 (zhòng, Middle Chinese *drjowngH*, 'weighty, solemn, dignified'). In Han and Six Dynasties prose, 隆重 described the exalted status of state rituals or deep reverence accorded to scholars and ministers; in modern Mandarin it characterizes grand-scale, formal ceremonies, galas, and stage introductions.

history.meaning: exalted and weighty in dignity, status, or ritual observance
grand, solemn, and richly appointed (of ceremonies or receptions)
grandly, formally, on a magnificent scale

隆重.notes: A staple of television hosting and event production, especially in the stock MC formula 隆重推出 ('to grandly present/launch') or 隆重介绍 ('to formally introduce with fanfare').

rootFamily.gloss: grand, prosperous, booming (of business or events)
grand, magnificent (of a pageant or event)

随便.etymology: Originally a verb-object construction combining 随 (suí, Middle Chinese *zwje*, 'to follow; to comply with; to go along with') and 便 (biàn, Middle Chinese *bjenH*, 'convenience; advantageous occasion; ease'), literally 'to follow what is convenient.' In Tang–Song vernacular and Ming–Qing fiction, it grammaticalized from 'acting at one's convenience' into an adjective and conversational adverb meaning 'casual, unceremonious, or whichever one likes.'

history.meaning: to act according to convenience or suitable circumstances
at one's pleasure; without strict restriction or formality
as one pleases; casual; indiscriminate; careless

morphemes.meaning: to follow; to comply with; to let

随便.notes: As a standalone reply ('Whatever / Up to you'), it is neutral, but describing a person as 太随便 ('too casual/indiscriminate') carries strong disapproval regarding lax work ethic or boundaries.

随口.etymology: A verb-object adverbial compound formed from 随 (suí, 'to follow; to let go along effortlessly with') and 口 (kǒu, 'mouth; spoken words'), literally 'following the movement of the mouth.' Built on the productive vernacular pattern 随 + body part (compare 随手 'with a casual flick of the hand,' 随眼 'with a casual glance'), it emerged in Song–Yuan vernacular narratives to describe uttering remarks spontaneously without prior deliberation.

history.meaning: speaking immediately in response or following one's vocal impulse
offhandedly, casually, without forethought or verification

随口.notes: Always functions adverbially before a verb of speaking or asking, such as 随口问一句 ('ask casually in passing') or 随口答应 ('agree offhandedly without thinking it through').

rootFamily.gloss: say casually off the cuff, mention in passing
without extra effort, while one's hand is at it

随口一说.etymology: A four-character vernacular verb phrase structured as an adverbial modifier 随口 (suíkǒu, 'following the mouth; offhandedly') plus the punctual verbal construction 一说 (yī shuō, 'one utterance; to give a quick mention'). Here 一 functions as an aspectual marker of brevity and tentativeness ('just once / casually'), yielding the idiomatic sense of making an off-the-cuff remark with no serious commitment behind it.

history.meaning: to utter a single remark offhandedly without deliberation
to say casually off the cuff; to mention in passing (often used to walk back a statement)

随口一说.notes: Frequently used defensively in dialogue—如：我就是随口一说，你别当真 ('I was just saying it off the cuff, don't take it seriously')—to defuse tension after floating a risky idea.

rootFamily.gloss: to blurt out, speak without thinking

随手.etymology: Adverbial compound combining 随 (隨, 'follow along smoothly without extra effort') + 手 ('hand'): 'conveniently while one's hand is at it, without extra trouble (e.g., 随手关门 close the door behind you); casually'. Attested since Tang–Song prose.

history.meaning: conveniently in passing; without extra effort; right at hand

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 随手 (via 萌典)

随时.etymology: Temporal adverb combining 随 (隨, 'follow according to') + 时 (時, 'the time or moment'): in Classical Chinese (Yijing: 随时之义大矣哉) 'adapt to the times', and in modern Mandarin 'at any time, whenever needed'.

history.meaning: adapt to the season/occasion
at any time; whenever necessary

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 随时 (via 萌典)

随身.etymology: Adverbial and modifier compound combining 随 (隨, 'accompany, stay with') + 身 ('one's body, person'): '(carry) on one's person, with one'. Attested since Han–Tang prose.

history.meaning: on one's person; carried with oneself

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 随身 (via 萌典)

随随便便.etymology: The AABB state-intensifying reduplication of the disyllabic compound 随便 (suíbiàn, from 随 'to follow' + 便 'convenience'). In Mandarin morphosyntax, reduplicating a disyllabic adjective AB into AABB heightens its descriptive vividness and subjective evaluation, shifting 'casual / at one's convenience' into 'effortlessly, nonchalantly, or in an overly slipshod, devil-may-care manner.'

history.meaning: acting in an unrestrained, informal, or thoroughly casual manner
casually, effortlessly, without any fuss; carelessly or perfunctorily

随随便便.notes: Echoes the famous lyric from the classic song 《真心英雄》 (没有人能随随便便成功, 'No one can succeed casually without effort'), making it a favorite phrase among demanding TV directors and mentors.

隐婚.etymology: A modern Mandarin compression blend (portmanteau) of the four-character phrase 隐瞒婚姻 (yǐnmán hūnyīn, 'to conceal one's marriage'), structured on a modifier-head / verb-object pattern combining 隐 (yǐn, Middle Chinese *ʔjɨnX*, 'to hide; secret; concealed') and 婚 (hūn, Middle Chinese *xwon*, 'marriage; wedlock'). Coined in mainland Chinese and Hong Kong entertainment and workplace journalism in the early 2000s, it originally described white-collar workers hiding marital status to avoid career bias and idols hiding spouses to retain fan appeal.

history.meaning: classical roots for 'to hide/keep secret' and 'matrimony'
to be secretly married; to conceal one's marital status from the public or employer

隐婚.notes: A core showbiz trope in Chinese idol culture: when an idol's 隐婚 ('secret marriage') is exposed by paparazzi, it often triggers a major PR crisis over 'fan deception' (欺骗粉丝).

rootFamily.gloss: to conceal, hide from view or knowledge

隐私.etymology: A coordinative and modifier-head compound joining 隐 (yǐn, 'hidden, concealed, unrevealed') and 私 (sī, 'private, personal, self-regarding,' originally denoting private grain plots as opposed to 公 'public/communal'). In traditional Literary Chinese, 隐私 referred to concealed personal secrets or illicit private affairs that one wished to keep hidden; in the 20th century, it was semantically recalibrated as the standard legal and sociological equivalent of English 'privacy.'

history.meaning: hidden personal faults, ulterior motives, or secret private matters
personal privacy; protected private life and confidential personal information

隐私.notes: In media and entertainment law, frequently appears in 个人隐私 ('personal privacy'), 侵犯隐私 ('invade privacy'), and 隐私权 ('right to privacy').

隔.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 阝 (阜, 'mound/partition wall') + 鬲 (lì/gé phonetic, a three-legged cauldron): 'separate, partition, divide, stand between; at an interval of (time or space: 隔一天 every other day)'.

history.stage: Old & Classical Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: partition; separate; stand between; at an interval of

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 隔 (via 萌典)

隔壁.etymology: Verb-object/modifier-head locative compound of 隔 ('separated by') + 壁 ('partition wall'): 'separated by a single wall -> next door, the room or house next door'. Attested since Six Dynasties and Tang texts.

history.meaning: on the other side of the wall = next door

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 隔壁 (via 萌典)

隔音.etymology: Modern architectural and acoustic compound of 隔 ('partition; separate; block off', mound radical 阝 + 鬲 lì) + 音 ('sound; tone'). Literally 'to block sound from passing through', used both as a verb-object compound and as an attributive modifier (隔音木板 'acoustic / sound-insulating wooden panels').

history.meaning: soundproofing; acoustic insulation

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 隔音

障碍.etymology: A coordinative compound uniting 障 (zhàng, Middle Chinese *tɕjangH*, 'to Partition off; screen; defensive dike or barricade') and 碍 (ài, traditional 礙, Middle Chinese *ŋojH*, 'to obstruct; to block; to hinder with a boulder'). Heavily popularized in Medieval Chinese through Buddhist translations of Sanskrit *āvaraṇa* ('spiritual or karmic hindrance blocking enlightenment'), it subsequently generalized into everyday secular usage for physical, communicative, or institutional barriers.

history.meaning: karmic or cognitive hindrance (*āvaraṇa*) obstructing spiritual awakening; physical barrier
obstacle, barrier, impediment, or dysfunction (physical, technical, or psychological)

morphemes.meaning: to hinder; to obstruct; boulder in the way

障碍.notes: Used across concrete and abstract registers alike, from 扫除障碍 ('sweep away obstacles' in a project) to 沟通障碍 ('communication barrier').

rootFamily.gloss: to hinder, obstruct, get in the way of

难.etymology: From Old Chinese *nˤar* (level tone nán, 'difficult, arduous, hard to accomplish'; departing tone *nˤar-s* nàn, 'disaster, calamity, to rebuke'). The traditional graph 難 combines the semantic signific 隹 (zhuī, 'short-tailed bird') with the phonetic 堇 (jǐn, originally depicting scorched clay or drought). Productive throughout Chinese history both as an independent predicate adjective ('hard, difficult') and as a pre-verbal prefixoid ('hard to [verb]; unpleasant to [sense]').

history.meaning: arduous, troublesome, hard to manage; (in departing tone) calamity or distress
difficult; hard to accomplish; disagreeable to the senses (before perception verbs)
hard, difficult, tricky; bad/unpleasant to (look at, hear, taste)

难.notes: Keep the two tones distinct: second tone nán means 'difficult' (难办, 难度), whereas fourth tone nàn means 'disaster, adversity, or blame' (灾难 'catastrophe', 责难 'to censure').

rootFamily.gloss: hard to avoid, bound to happen

难不倒.etymology: A negative potential resultative construction (V + 不 + complement) composed of 难 (nán, used here as a causative verb: 'to stump, to baffle, to put in a difficult spot'), the negative potential infix 不 (bù, 'cannot'), and the resultative complement 倒 (dǎo, 'to topple, knock down, defeat'). Literally 'cannot be toppled by difficulty,' it crystallized in modern colloquial Mandarin to express confidence that a challenge cannot stump a resourceful person.

history.meaning: unable to topple or defeat someone with a difficult problem or test

morphemes.meaning: to stump; to baffle with difficulty
to topple; to defeat; to bowl over

难不倒.notes: Takes the person as its direct object and the problem as its subject: 这点小事难不倒他 ('A little thing like this can't stump him'), whereas its affirmative counterpart is 难得倒 or the resultative 难倒 ('to stump').

rootFamily.gloss: to stump, baffle, overwhelm with difficulty

难不成.etymology: A rhetorical modal adverbial phrase grammaticalized in Song–Yuan–Ming vernacular Chinese from 难 (nán, 'hard, difficult'), 不 (bù, 'not'), and 成 (chéng, 'to become; to turn out to be; to succeed'). Originally a compressed rhetorical predicate asking 'is it hard not to turn out that...?' or 'if not this, what else could it become?', it evolved alongside 难道 (nándào) into a sentence-initial marker of incredulous conjecture ('could it really be that...?; surely not...').

history.meaning: rhetorical formula in vernacular drama and fiction: 'can it be that...?; surely it doesn't mean...?'
could it be that...; surely not... (expressing disbelief, irony, or reluctant realization)

morphemes.meaning: to become; to turn out to be; accomplished

难不成.notes: Slightly more colloquial and punchy than 难道 (nándào); can stand at the start of a clause or even at the very end of a rhetorical question (e.g., 你还想辞职难不成？ 'Don't tell me you're thinking of quitting?').

rootFamily.gloss: could it be that..., don't tell me... (rhetorical adverb)

难免.etymology: A Classical Chinese modifier-head / auxiliary-verb compound formed from 难 (nán, 'difficult, hard to') and 免 (miǎn, Middle Chinese *mjenX*, 'to escape, evade, be spared from'). Attested in pre-Qin and Han historical texts in the literal sense 'hard to escape (punishment or disaster),' it later grammaticalized in Literary and Modern Mandarin into a modal adjective/adverb meaning 'inevitably; bound to happen; humanly unavoidable.'

history.meaning: difficult to escape or be exempted from (harm, blame, or death)
unavoidable; hard to keep from happening
hard to avoid, bound to happen, naturally prone to (used to soften criticism)

morphemes.meaning: to avoid; to escape; to be spared

难免.notes: Often used empathetically to excuse minor flaws or mistakes—e.g., 第一次上台，难免紧张 ('Going on stage for the first time, it's only natural/hard to avoid being nervous').

难办.etymology: A modifier-head adjectival compound formed from the pre-verbal difficulty element 难 (nán, 'hard to') and the verb 办 (bàn, Middle Chinese *bɛnH*, 'to manage, handle, transact, tackle'). Literally 'hard to handle or administer,' it developed in late imperial administrative and vernacular Mandarin to describe a delicate, thorny situation where every course of action carries practical or interpersonal complications.

history.meaning: difficult to administer, execute, or settle (of official or practical affairs)
hard to handle, tricky, awkward to fix or arrange

morphemes.meaning: to handle; to manage; to attend to

难办.notes: In workplace diplomacy, saying 这事儿有点难办 ('This matter is a bit tricky to handle') is frequently a polite indirect refusal or a cue that extra concessions are needed.

rootFamily.gloss: means, method, way of handling something

难受.etymology: A modifier-head compound joining 难 (nán, 'hard to; unpleasant to') and 受 (shòu, Middle Chinese *dʑjuwX*, 'to receive; to endure; to bear; to feel'). Originally meaning 'hard to endure or stomach,' it underwent subjectification in Ming–Qing vernacular Mandarin to denote both physical malaise ('feeling unwell, aching, nauseous') and emotional distress ('feeling hurt, heavy-hearted, or miserable').

history.meaning: hard to endure, bear, or accept
physically uncomfortable or unwell; emotionally distressed or pained

morphemes.meaning: to bear; to endure; to feel

难受.notes: Covers both bodily discomfort (浑身难受 'aching/uncomfortable all over') and emotional heartache (心里难受 'feeling awful/sad inside'), contrasting with 舒服 (shūfu, 'comfortable').

rootFamily.gloss: feeling awful or unwell inside, hard to pass (of days)
to endure, bear, put up with

难堪.etymology: A Classical Chinese compound combining 难 (nán, 'hard to') and 堪 (kān, Middle Chinese *khom*, 'to bear, endure, withstand; to be equal to'). In Tang poetry and Song prose, 难堪 meant 'utterly unbearable' (of grief, cold, or hardship). In modern Mandarin, its center of gravity shifted toward social and psychological intolerability: being placed in a mortifying, awkward, or face-losing position.

history.meaning: intolerable; impossible to endure (of sorrow, pain, or harsh conditions)
painfully embarrassing, awkward, mortifying; hard to bear socially

morphemes.meaning: to bear; to endure; to withstand

难堪.notes: Often used in causative social contexts like 让人难堪 ('put someone on the spot / make someone feel mortified') or 一脸难堪 ('wearing a pained, embarrassed expression').

rootFamily.gloss: cannot bear, utterly (used before negative adjectives: 疲惫不堪)

难度.etymology: A modern modifier-head abstract nominal compound formed from 难 (nán, 'difficult') and the mensural/abstract suffixoid 度 (dù, Middle Chinese *duH*, 'degree, measure, extent,' originally 'to measure length'). Built on the productive modern Sino-Japanese and Mandarin scientific pattern [Adjective + 度] (compare 强度 'intensity,' 速度 'speed'), it calibrates how challenging a technical feat, performance, or task is.

history.meaning: classical roots for 'difficulty' and 'graduated measure'
degree of difficulty; technical or operational challenge level

难度.notes: Collocates with 高 ('high') or 大 ('great') rather than 多: 高难度动作 ('a high-difficulty stunt/move') or 有一定难度 ('has a certain degree of difficulty').

cognates.meaning: rare, precious; (as ありがたい arigatai) grateful, welcome

难得.etymology: A Classical Chinese modifier-head compound joining 难 (nán, 'hard to') and 得 (dé, Old Chinese *tˤək*, 'to obtain, acquire, get hold of'). Famous since the *Laozi* (不贵难得之货, 'do not prize goods that are hard to obtain') and Buddhist scriptures (人身难得, 'a human rebirth is hard to attain'), it evolved from describing scarce material treasures to characterizing rare opportunities or uncharacteristic behavior.

history.meaning: hard to obtain or capture (of rare treasures, talent, or auspicious timing)
precious and rare; on a rare occasion
rare, hard to come by; uncharacteristically (as an adverb: 'for once')

morphemes.meaning: to obtain; to get; to achieve

难得.notes: Functions both as an adjective (难得的机会 'a rare opportunity') and as a wry conversational adverb meaning 'for once!' (你今天难得这么早来 'You've come early for once today!').

难怪.etymology: Modal verb/adverb compound combining 难 (難, nán, 'hard to, difficult to') + 怪 ('blame, wonder at'): literally 'hard to blame / hard to find strange' -> 'no wonder!, little wonder that'.

history.stage: Tang–Song poetry & vernacular to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: hard to blame -> no wonder!

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 难怪 (via 萌典)

难搞.etymology: A modern colloquial compound pairing 难 (nán, 'hard to') with the generalized Southwest/Central Mandarin verb 搞 (gǎo, 'to do, make, deal with, mess with, sort out'), which entered standard Mandarin in the 20th century. Modeled on older 难办 ('hard to handle') and 难弄 ('hard to work with'), 难搞 specifically highlights how fussy, high-maintenance, or uncooperative a client, celebrity, or technical problem is.

history.meaning: regional southwestern/central Mandarin colloquialism for 'troublesome to deal with'
hard to deal with, demanding, high-maintenance, finicky (of people or tasks)

morphemes.meaning: to deal with; to handle; to work on (colloquial)

难搞.notes: In media production and agency slang, calling an artist or sponsor 难搞 means they are a diva or notoriously fussy—pair it with 搞定 (gǎodìng, 'to settle/win over/sort out').

rootFamily.gloss: to settle, sort out, wrap up successfully (colloquial)
hard to handle, tricky, awkward to fix
hard to deal with or serve, high-maintenance

难看.etymology: A modifier-head adjectival compound formed from the evaluative prefixoid 难 (nán, here meaning 'unpleasant or disagreeable to,' as in 难听 'unpleasant to hear' and 难吃 'unpleasant to eat') and 看 (kàn, 'to look at, view, behold'). Literally 'unpleasant to look at,' it developed two parallel senses in vernacular Mandarin: aesthetically ugly, and socially unseemly, disgraceful, or embarrassing to witness.

history.meaning: unpleasant to behold; unsightly in appearance
ugly, unsightly; unseemly, embarrassing, or hostile (of a facial expression or scandal)

morphemes.meaning: to look at; to see; to behold

难看.notes: Beyond physical ugliness, watch for its idiomatic uses in 脸色很难看 ('looking grim/furious') and 吃相太难看 ('having ugly table manners,' used figuratively in showbiz for greedy or ungraceful behavior).

难过.etymology: Compound verb and adjective of 难 (難, 'hard, difficult') + 过 (過, 'pass through, get by'). Originally meant 'hard to cross (a pass) or hard to get by in life', then specialized in vernacular Mandarin for 'feel sad, sorry, grieved, or physically unwell'.

history.meaning: hard to bear -> feel sad, upset, or unwell

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 难过 (via 萌典)

难道.etymology: Rhetorical question adverb combining 难 (難, 'hard to') + 道 ('say'): originally in Tang–Song poetry and vernacular 'it is hard to say…', which grammaticalized into the emphatic rhetorical question marker 'could it really be that…?, don't tell me that…!'.

history.meaning: hard to say/state
rhetorical question adverb 'could it possibly be that…?'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 难道 (via 萌典)

集体待命.etymology: A four-character modifier-head verbal phrase combining 集体 (jítǐ, 'collective; as a whole body or group,' from 集 'gather' + 体 'body') with 待命 (dàimìng, a Classical verb-object compound from 待 'to await' + 命 'command, orders'). While 待命 is attested in pre-Qin and Han military/official chronicles for troops or envoys awaiting imperial instructions, 集体待命 crystallized in modern military, emergency, and television production jargon for an entire crew remaining on standby at once.

history.meaning: to await imperial decree, military orders, or fate

history.form: 集体 (collective) + 待命 (stand by for orders)
history.meaning: for an entire unit, crew, or team to remain on standby together awaiting instructions

集体待命.notes: In live TV broadcasting and film sets, 全组集体待命 ('the whole crew is standing by together') captures high-alert production crunches when a director or crisis response team may call action at any minute.

集合.etymology: A coordinative verbal and nominal compound uniting 集 (jí, Old Chinese *dzup*, 'to flock together; to gather,' originally depicting birds 隹 perching together on a tree 木) and 合 (hé, Old Chinese *ɡˤop*, 'to join, close together, unite'). Attested in Han and Six Dynasties prose for assembling troops or compiling texts, it was reinforced in the Meiji/late-Qing era via Sino-Japanese 集合 (*shūgō*) to serve as the standard command for mustering a group and as the mathematical term for 'set.'

history.meaning: to gather together in one place; to compile or unite scattered elements
to muster/fall in (of troops or students); mathematical set
to assemble, gather round, muster; assembly or mathematical set

morphemes.meaning: to flock together; to gather; to collect

集合.notes: Frequently barked as a one-word imperative by directors, stage managers, and tour leaders—集合了！ ('Gather round / Fall in!')—to call cast and crew to a meeting point.

rootFamily.gloss: collective, group; together as a group
to assemble, rally, muster (often troops or elite teams)

集市.etymology: Compound of 集 ('gather together', originally depicting birds 隹 perched together on a tree 木) + 市 ('market', attested from bronze inscriptions for a walled trading precinct). Together 集市 names a periodic or open-air neighbourhood market where farmers and craftspeople gather.

history.meaning: 'walled marketplace' and 'gathering'
open-air street market; country fair

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 集市 (via 萌典)

雕.etymology: Merged graph representing 彫 ('carve, engrave patterns in jade, wood, or stone', 周 + 彡 'decorative strokes'), 雕 (周 + 隹 'short-tailed bird': 'large eagle/hawk'), and 凋 ('wither'). In everyday Mandarin, 雕 primarily means 'carve, engrave, sculpt; sculpture; eagle'.

history.meaning: carve patterns in wood/stone/jade
carve; engrave; sculpt; eagle

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 雕 (via 萌典)

雨.etymology: Foundational pictograph (象形字) attested from Shang oracle bones depicting raindrops falling from a cloud beneath the arch of the sky (一 + 冂): 'rain'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: pictograph of drops falling from heaven = rain

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 雨 (via 萌典)

雨后.etymology: Temporal phrase combining 雨 ('rain') + 后 (後, 'after'): 'after the rain' (familiar from the idiom 雨后春笋 'like bamboo shoots springing up after a spring rain').

history.meaning: after the rain

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 雨后 (via 萌典)

雨声.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 雨 ('rain') + 声 (聲, 'sound'): 'the sound of rain, patter of rain'.

history.meaning: sound of falling rain

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 雨声 (via 萌典)

雨夜.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 雨 ('rainy') + 夜 ('night'): 'rainy night'.

history.meaning: rainy night

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 雨夜 (via 萌典)

雨水.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 雨 ('rain') + 水 ('water'): 'rainwater' (and the name of the second of the 24 solar terms 二十四节气 in early spring).

history.stage: Han calendrical texts & Classical Chinese to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: rainwater; 'Rain Water' solar term

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 雨水 (via 萌典)

雨点.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 雨 ('rain') + 点 (點, 'dot, drop'): 'raindrop' (often rhotacized in northern speech as 雨点儿 yǔdiǎnr).

history.meaning: raindrop

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 雨点 (via 萌典)

雪松.etymology: Modifier-head botanical compound of 雪 ('snow', evoking the snow-capped Himalayas where the deodar cedar grows) + 松 ('pine/conifer'): 'cedar, deodar cedar (Cedrus)'.

history.meaning: cedar tree; cedarwood

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 雪松 (via 萌典)

雪白.etymology: Simile-based adjective compound from 雪 ('snow', rain 雨 over broom/hand 彐) + 白 ('white'). Built on the productive Mandarin pattern `Noun + Color Adjective` (like 金黄 'golden yellow' or 碧绿 'jade green'), it means 'white as fresh snow'.

history.meaning: pure white like snow
snow-white; gleaming white

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 雪白

cognates.meaning: to freeze out or shelve an artist; to refrigerate

雪藏.etymology: A modifier-head verbal compound composed of 雪 (xuě, 'snow; ice-cold') and 藏 (cáng, 'to store away, hide, conceal'), literally 'to store in snow.' In Song–Ming literary Chinese, it described preserving perishable delicacies or fruits in snow or ice cellars. In late 20th-century Hong Kong Cantonese media jargon, where 雪藏 means 'to refrigerate/put in the freezer,' it was metaphorically extended—and rapidly borrowed into Mainland entertainment Mandarin—to mean 'freezing out' or shelving a contracted celebrity by denying them public work.

history.meaning: stored in snow or covered over by snowfalls (of foods, plants, or secluded objects)
to refrigerate in a fridge/freezer; metaphorically to bench a player or shelve a talent under contract
to freeze out, shelve, or sideline an entertainer, athlete, or project while keeping them bound by contract

morphemes.meaning: to store away; to hide; to conceal

雪藏.notes: Unlike 封杀 (fēngshā, an industry-wide blacklist or ban), 雪藏 specifically means an artist's own agency or network puts them 'on ice'—keeping them under exclusive contract while refusing to give them projects or exposure.

rootFamily.gloss: to blacklist, ban from the industry

零.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 雨 ('rain') + 令 (lìng/líng phonetic): originally 'gentle raindrops falling sparsely, scattered', hence 'fractional remainder after a round number, odd/spare, wither and fall (凋零)', and in mathematics the number 'zero (0)'.

history.meaning: softly falling rain; scattered drops; remainder
zero (0); fractional remainder; odd/small change

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 零 (via 萌典)

零钱.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 零 ('odd, fractional, small-denomination') + 钱 (錢, 'money, cash'): 'small change, loose change, pocket money'.

history.stage: Ming–Qing commercial vernacular to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: small change; loose coins/bills

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 零钱 (via 萌典)

零钱袋.etymology: Three-character compound combining 零钱 ('small change, coins') + 袋 ('pouch, bag'): 'coin purse, change pouch'.

history.meaning: coin purse; change pouch

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 零钱袋 (via 萌典)

零食.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound formed from 零 (líng, Middle Chinese *leng*, originally 'light, scattered raindrops,' extended to 'fractional, odd, piecemeal, outside the main count') and 食 (shí, Middle Chinese *zyik*, 'food, meal, provisions'). Literally 'scattered/fractional food,' it arose in late imperial and modern vernacular Chinese to designate small nibbles eaten piecemeal between regular meals (正餐), parallel to 零钱 ('small change') and 零件 ('spare parts').

history.meaning: classical roots for 'scattered drops/remnants' and 'edible provisions'
snacks, nibbles, or light refreshments eaten between main meals

morphemes.meaning: scattered; fractional; odd; outside the main whole

零食.notes: Refers specifically to packaged or casual nibbles (chips, nuts, candy, dried fruit) eaten for pleasure between meals, whereas 点心 (diǎnxin) refers to pastries or light dim-sum courses and 小吃 (xiǎochī) to local street-food specialties.

需求.etymology: A coordinative compound uniting 需 (xū, Middle Chinese *sju*, 'to need, require; necessary provisions') and 求 (qiú, Middle Chinese *gjuw*, 'to seek, request, strive for'). Attested in Literary Chinese in the verbal sense 'to require and seek out,' it was nominalized in modern East Asian economic and administrative vocabulary to translate economic 'demand' (paired with 供给 'supply') as well as client or user requirements in business and media production.

history.meaning: to require and seek after; to demand provisions or tribute
economic demand; user/client needs, specifications, or requirements

morphemes.meaning: to seek; to request; to demand

需求.notes: In agency, tech, and TV production workplaces, 提需求 ('submit requirements') and 满足客户需求 ('meet client needs') are everyday buzzwords, whereas 需要 (xūyào) is preferred when used as a verb ('to need').

需要.etymology: Compound verb and noun meaning 'need, require', pairing 需 ('await, require', attested in the Yijing) with 要 ('essential, need'). Used in polite requests and everyday explanations of what a task calls for.

history.stage: Classical roots in Yijing (需) & Mencius (要)
history.meaning: require + essential -> modern compound 需要 'need'

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 需要 (via 萌典)

露.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 雨 ('rain/moisture from the sky') + 路 (lù phonetic): originally 'morning dew' (which condenses openly in the night air). Because dew lies uncovered in the open, it developed the verbal meaning 'uncover, reveal, show, expose' (read lù in literary compounds like 暴露 and colloquial lòu in 露面 'show one's face').

history.meaning: dew; uncovered, exposed to the sky
dew, syrup, reveal/expose (lù); show, leak out (lòu)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 露 (via 萌典)

露出.etymology: A directional-resultative verb compound combining 露 (lù / lòu, Middle Chinese *luH*, originally 'dew,' extended by metaphor to 'to lie bare in the open air; to uncover, reveal, show') and the directional complement 出 (chū, 'out, forth'). Literally 'to uncover so as to come out into view,' it is used in Mandarin to describe a hitherto hidden object, emotion, smile, or flaw becoming visible on the surface.

history.meaning: to emerge into the open air; to become uncovered and visible
to reveal, show, or let appear (a smile, expression, clue, or physical part)

morphemes.meaning: to uncover; to reveal; to show

露出.notes: In standard Mainland Mandarin, 露出 is pronounced *lùchū* in literary/standard reading (especially in 露出笑容 'reveal a smile' or 露出马脚 'give the game away'), while standalone colloquial verbs like 露面 or 露一手 take the colloquial reading *lòu*.

rootFamily.gloss: to reveal, let slip (information or feelings)

cognates.meaning: showing one's face; appearing in public (archaic/literary)

露面.etymology: A separable verb-object compound (离合词) formed from 露 (lòu, colloquial Mandarin reading of Middle Chinese *luH*, 'to show, reveal, uncover') and 面 (miàn, 'face; public presence'). Originally meaning 'to uncover one's face' (for instance, removing a veil or stepping out from seclusion in Song–Ming vernacular literature), it idiomatized into 'to make a public appearance' or 'to show up in person.'

history.meaning: to uncover one's face to others; to step out of seclusion into public view
to show one's face; to make a public or social appearance

morphemes.meaning: to show; to reveal; to let be seen

露面.notes: Always pronounced *lòumiàn* (not *lùmiàn*) and behaves as a separable verb-object word (离合词): 'make a brief appearance' is 露个面 or 露一面, never *露面一下.

rootFamily.gloss: to show off a skill or trick (colloquial: lòu yīshǒu)
to appear on stage or in public view, make a public appearance

青春.etymology: A Classical Chinese modifier-head nominal compound uniting 青 (qīng, Old Chinese *s.rˤeŋ*, 'verdant green/blue-green,' the color of sprouting vegetation and the East in Five-Phase *Wuxing* cosmology) and 春 (chūn, 'springtime,' the season correlated with Wood and East). Originally denoting the verdant spring season in *Chuci* and Han poetry, it was metaphorically extended via traditional longevity and life-cycle correlations to the 'green springtime of human life'—youth and young adulthood.

history.meaning: the verdant season of spring (associated with the East and sprouting foliage)
history.stage: Old & Early Middle Chinese (Chuci / Han Poetry)

history.meaning: prime of youth; springtime of one's years (contrasted with 白日 or 秋霜 'autumn frost of old age')
youth, young adulthood, adolescence (and as a modifier: 'youthful, teen/young-adult')

青春.notes: In entertainment and media, 青春 is also a major genre label—as in 青春剧 ('youth/coming-of-age drama') and 吃青春饭 ('making a living off one's youth and looks,' said of idols and models).

静静地.etymology: An adverbial construction formed by reduplicating the stative root 静 (jìng, Middle Chinese *dzjengX*, 'still, quiet, tranquil, unagitated') into the vivid AA pattern 静静 (jìngjìng, 'quietly and calmly') and attaching the structural adverbial particle 地 (de, grammaticalized from Tang–Song vernacular 底/地 'manner/ground'). The AA reduplication softens the tone and emphasizes a continuous, unhurried state of quietude accompanying an action.

history.meaning: in a serene, hushed, and undisturbed state
quietly, silently, calmly (modifying a following verb phrase)

morphemes.meaning: -ly (marks preceding phrase as an adverbial modifier before a verb)

静静地.notes: Always precedes a verb (e.g., 静静地看着 'watching quietly', 静静地等待 'waiting quietly'); note also the viral humorous internet pun 我想静静 ('I want some peace and quiet' vs. 'I miss [a girl named] Jingjing').

非.etymology: Originally an oracle bone pictograph of two bird wings facing in opposite directions (Old Chinese *pəj, Middle Chinese pj+j), signifying 'contrary to' or 'at variance with'. In Classical Chinese it functioned as the negative copula ('is not') and verb ('to go against, blame'). The modern adverbial sense 'insist on, simply must' developed through the grammaticalization and ellipsis of the double-negative frame 非…不可 (fēi... bùkě, 'if not [doing X], it will not do'), where the initial negator came to carry the modal force of stubborn necessity on its own.

history.meaning: contrary to; is not (negative copula); to reproach
cannot do without; must inevitably (double-negative construction)
insist on, simply must (with optional 不可)

非.notes: In spoken Mandarin, adverbial 非 (fēi) often retains the closing 不可 (bùkě) at the end of the clause (e.g., 他非去不可), though in colloquial dialogue the 不可 is frequently dropped while keeping the emphatic tone of willful insistence.

非常.etymology: Modifier-head compound of 非 ('not') + 常 ('ordinary, usual, constant'). In Classical Chinese (Laozi's 道可道，非常道 'the Way that can be spoken of is not the constant/ordinary Way', and Shiji), 非常 meant 'extraordinary, unusual, emergency'. In modern Mandarin it grammaticalized into a high-frequency degree adverb meaning 'very, extremely, extraordinarily'.

history.meaning: not ordinary; extraordinary; unusual
very; extremely; extraordinary

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 非常 (via 萌典)

非要.etymology: A Mandarin modal compound combining the emphatic adverbial negator 非 (fēi, 'contrary to; nothing less than', derived by ellipsis from the double-negative construction 非…不可) with the volitional auxiliary verb 要 (yào, 'to want, demand, insist on', originally a pictograph of a person with hands on the waist, Old Chinese *ʔrew). Structurally a modifier-head modal cluster, it intensifies volition into obstinate determination ('insist on, stubbornly must'), whether or not the clause concludes with 不可.

history.meaning: not (other than) + to demand or require
stubbornly insist on, simply must

morphemes.meaning: simply must, nothing short of (from 非…不可)

非要.notes: Stronger and more subjective than 一定要 (yīdìng yào); 非要 implies that the subject is being headstrong or unreasonable in pushing their way against advice or obstacles.

非议.etymology: A Classical Chinese compound attested in Han-dynasty historical texts (such as the Shiji and Hanshu), formed from 非 (fēi, here in its classical verbal/adverbial sense 'to consider wrong, find fault with, reproach') and 議/议 (yì, 'to deliberate, discuss critically, pass judgment on', phono-semantic with 言 'speech' and 義 'right conduct/phonetic'). Originally a modifier-head or coordinative verbal compound meaning 'to criticize as improper', it functions in modern prose both as a noun ('reproach, critical gossip') and in formal idioms like 无可非议 ('beyond reproach').

history.meaning: to censure, criticize policies or conduct as improper
reproach, critical gossip, public censure

非议.notes: Belongs to a formal or journalistic register; in media and showbiz contexts it frequently appears in 遭受非议 (zāoshòu fēiyì, 'incur public reproach') or the set phrase 无可非议 (wúkě fēiyì, 'blameless, beyond reproach').

靠.etymology: Phono-semantic character of 告 (gào/kào phonetic) + 非 ('two sides pressing against each other'): originally 'press against each other', hence in Mandarin 'lean against, rest on (a backrest or wall); draw near to/pull alongside (靠岸); rely on, depend on'.

history.meaning: lean against; come alongside; rely/depend on

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 靠 (via 萌典)

靠垫.etymology: Compound noun of 靠 ('lean against; rest one's back or limb on', 告 + 非) + 垫 ('cushion; pad'). It names a soft throw pillow or back cushion placed on a wooden chair or sofa for support.

history.meaning: backrest cushion on a chair or couch
cushion; throw pillow

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 靠垫

靠谱.etymology: Originally a northern Mandarin (Beijing and Tianjin) vernacular verb-object (VO) compound from traditional Chinese opera, music, and artisanal trades: 靠 (kào, 'to lean on, adhere to, rely upon') + 谱 (pǔ, 'musical score, manual, standard chart, or established template', oftenpronounced with erhua as 靠谱儿 kàopǔr). A performer who stayed close to the score or a craftsman following the manual was 'adhering to the standard'; by metaphorical extension, the compound grammaticalized into an adjective meaning 'reliable, dependable, plausible, on the mark'.

history.meaning: following the musical score or established manual; close to the mark
history.stage: Late Imperial / Early Republican Beijing Vernacular

history.meaning: reliable, dependable, trustworthy, sensible (of people, plans, or news)

morphemes.meaning: lean on, adhere to, rely on

靠谱.notes: Because 靠谱 originated as a verb-object construction (靠 + 谱), its negation uses 不靠谱 (bù kàopǔ, 'unreliable, flaky') and degree modifiers can either precede the whole word (很靠谱) or split it in colloquial northern speech (靠点儿谱, 'be a bit more sensible/reliable').

靠近.etymology: A verb-complement / coordinative compound formed from 靠 (kào, 'to lean against, press near to', composed of 非 'opposing' and 告 phonetic, originally meaning 'to lean against each other') and 近 (jìn, 'near, to approach', from 辵 'walk' and 斤 phonetic). In Vernacular Mandarin since the Ming–Qing novels, 靠 shifted from 'lean against' to 'move alongside', and 靠近 combines the action of drawing alongside with the resultative state of proximity ('draw near, step closer to').

history.meaning: to lean against + near, to approach
to draw near to, move closer to; near, close by

靠近.notes: Unlike 接近 (jiējìn), which can describe abstract closeness (such as nearing a target number or a similar style), 靠近 primarily describes physical, spatial movement toward a person or object (or emotional intimacy by metaphor).

面.etymology: Merged simplified graph representing two ancient characters: (1) 面 (pictograph in oracle-bone script of a human face framing an eye 目: 'face, surface, side, aspect, in person, classifier for flat surfaces like mirrors/walls/flags') and (2) 麵/麪 (combining 麥 'wheat' + 丏/面 miàn phonetic: 'wheat flour; noodles, dough').

morphemes.meaning: human face framing an eye = face, surface, side; merged with 麵 'flour, noodles'

history.form: 面 (face, surface, side) / 麵, 麪 (wheat flour, noodles)
history.meaning: face/surface vs. wheat flour/noodles
face; surface; side; flour; noodles

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 面 (via 萌典)

面临.etymology: A Literary Chinese modifier-head / coordinative verbal compound formed from 面 (miàn, 'face; with one's face turned toward', an ancient pictograph of a human face framing an eye 目) and 臨/临 (lín, 'to look down upon from above, approach, arrive at, confront', Old Chinese *rəm). Originally describing a building or person physically overlooking or standing directly before water or a precipice in medieval poetry, it evolved in modern formal Mandarin to mean 'to be confronted with, to face (a crisis, choice, or turning point)'.

history.meaning: to face and overlook (a river, valley, or frontier)
to face, be confronted with (challenges, pressure, or opportunities)

面临.notes: 面临 describes an objective situation that looms before someone (e.g., 面临淘汰 'facing elimination', 面临危机 'facing a crisis') and cannot be used in the imperative; compare 面对 (miànduì), which emphasizes a person's active attitude in confronting something.

rootFamily.gloss: temporary, provisional; at the time when
come in person, grace with one's presence

cognates.meaning: in one's presence, before one's face; honor/face
in front of one's face, in one's presence

面前.etymology: A Classical Chinese modifier-head spatial noun (attested in the Shiji and Han texts) combining 面 (miàn, 'face, countenance', Old Chinese *C.men-s) and 前 (qián, 'front, before', originally 歬, showing a foot 止 advancing above a boat 舟). Literally 'before the face', it denotes the space immediately in front of a person (or metaphorically before a judge, audience, or abstract force like truth or difficulty).

history.meaning: directly before someone's face; in a person's presence
in front of (a person or personified entity); in the face of

面前.notes: 面前 is almost exclusively used after nouns referring to people, animals, or abstract concepts treated as witnesses/judges (e.g., 在观众面前 'in front of the audience', 在事实面前 'in the face of facts'); for inanimate buildings or vehicles, use 前面 (qiánmiàn) or 跟前 (gēnqián) instead.

面包.etymology: Modifier-head culinary compound combining 面 (麵, 'wheat flour, dough') + 包 ('baked or steamed bun/loaf'): 'bread'.

history.meaning: wheat-flour loaf = bread

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 面包 (via 萌典)

面包卷.etymology: Three-character culinary compound combining 面包 ('bread') + 卷 (捲, 'roll'): 'bread roll, dinner roll'.

history.meaning: bread roll

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 面包卷 (via 萌典)

面包师.etymology: Three-character occupational noun combining 面包 ('bread, baking') + 师 (師, 'master craftsman, specialist'): 'baker'.

history.meaning: baker

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 面包师 (via 萌典)

面包店.etymology: The noun '面包店' (miànbāodiàn, bakery) is composed of '面包' (bread) and '店' (shop). '面' refers to wheat flour, and '包' means a bun or wrapped item. '面包' originally referred to baked, yeast-leavened bread introduced by Westerners, distinguishing it from traditional Chinese steamed buns ('馒头' or '包子'). '面包店' thus describes a commercial establishment specializing in baking and selling Western-style bread and pastries. It reflects the globalized culinary landscape of modern Chinese cities.

history.meaning: bread

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 面包店

面包房.etymology: Three-morpheme compound of 面包 ('bread', literally 面 'wheat flour' + 包 'baked loaf/bun') + 房 ('house; workshop; room', 户 + 方). It designates either a dedicated artisan bakery shop or the baking kitchen of an inn.

history.meaning: bakery; bakehouse

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 面包房

面团.etymology: Modifier-head culinary compound of 面 (麵, 'flour') + 团 (團, 'kneaded ball, lump'): 'dough, ball of kneaded dough'.

history.meaning: kneaded dough

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 面团 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: face, honor, prestige (borrowed from Mandarin miànzi)
social prestige, dignity (calqued from Chinese 面子)

面子.etymology: A vernacular noun formed from 面 (miàn, 'face, outer surface, social front') and the nominalizing suffix 子 (zi, neutral tone, grammaticalized from 'child'). Attested by the Tang–Song period first for the 'outer surface or lining of a garment' and 'physical facial appearance', it developed its sociological sense of 'social standing, prestige, public pride, personal dignity in the eyes of peers' in Yuan–Ming vernacular literature. This Chinese term is the direct source of the English calques 'to save face' and 'to lose face' as well as Japanese メンツ (mentsu).

history.meaning: outer surface of an object; facial appearance; social standing
social prestige, public pride, personal dignity, favors granted out of respect

面子.notes: Key collocations in workplace and entertainment contexts include 给面子 (gěi miànzi, 'show respect / do someone a favor out of deference'), 留面子 (liú miànzi, 'spare someone's pride'), and 丢面子 / 没面子 (diū/méi miànzi, 'lose face').

rootFamily.gloss: to love showing off, be keen on saving face
courtesy,情面 sensibility to others' feelings/pride

面孔.etymology: A disyllabic noun attested since Six Dynasties and Tang-dynasty vernacular texts, combining 面 (miàn, 'face, visage') and 孔 (kǒng, 'aperture, facial orifices, features'). In Classical medical and physiognomic texts, 孔 referred to the seven orifices of the head (七孔: eyes, ears, nostrils, mouth) that define a person's facial features; paired with 面, 面孔 came to denote the physical countenance, facial expression, or a person's recognizable visage (as in 'a new face' 新面孔).

history.meaning: facial features and orifices; physical visage
face, countenance, facial expression; recognizable figure/person in a group

面孔.notes: While 脸 (liǎn) is the everyday word for the anatomical face, 面孔 focuses on a person's recognizable identity or demeanor—commonly used in media and casting for 生面孔 (shēng miànkǒng, 'unfamiliar face'), 新面孔 (xīn miànkǒng, 'fresh talent/newcomer'), or 板着面孔 (bǎnzhe miànkǒng, 'wearing a stern expression').

cognates.meaning: to face each other, interview, meet face-to-face

面对.etymology: A compound verb combining 面 (miàn, 'face; with one's face turned toward') and 對/对 (duì, 'to answer, face directly, stand opposite', Old Chinese *tˤəp-s). In Classical Chinese, 面 and 對 frequently co-occurred in the phrase 面對而語 ('to speak face-to-face') or 對面 ('facing each other'). In modern Mandarin, the modifier-head verb 面对 ('to face, confront directly') denotes both physical orientation toward something and psychological readiness to confront reality, pressure, or an audience.

history.meaning: to stand face-to-face with; to reply in person
to face, confront (a person, camera, audience, or difficulty)

morphemes.meaning: face directly, stand opposite, respond to

面对.notes: Unlike 面临 (miànlín), which passively describes a situation looming ahead, 面对 emphasizes subjective agency and courage (e.g., 勇敢面对镜头 'bravely face the camera', 面对现实 'face reality') and can be reduplicated as 面对面对 (miànduìmiàn, 'face-to-face').

面对面.etymology: Three-character phrase combining 面 ('face') + 对 ('face toward') + 面 ('face'): 'face to face, in person'. Attested from Tang–Song poetry and Chan Buddhist dialogues.

history.meaning: face to face; in person

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 面对面 (via 萌典)

面板.etymology: Compound noun with two meanings corresponding to the two roots of 面: (1) from 面 ('face, front surface') + 板 ('board, panel'): 'front panel, control panel, tabletop surface board'; (2) from 麵 ('flour, dough') + 板 ('board'): 'pastry board, kneading board'.

history.meaning: tabletop/control panel (面 'surface'); pastry/dough board (麵 'flour')

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 面板 (via 萌典)

面目全非.etymology: A four-character chengyu (idiom) crystallized from Tang–Song literary prose (echoing lines such as Han Yu's and Liuhua's descriptions of devastated landscapes or altered visages). Structurally a subject-predicate clause: 面目 (miànmù, a coordinative compound of 'face' + 'eyes', meaning 'visage, original appearance') serves as the topic/subject, modified by the adverb 全 (quán, 'completely, wholly') and predicated by 非 (fēi, in its classical verbal sense 'is no longer what it was, contrary to its former state')—literally 'its visage and eyes are wholly not what they were'.

history.meaning: visage/appearance + is completely no longer as before
changed beyond recognition, mangled or altered out of all likeness

面目全非.notes: In television and creative production, a classic complaint by screenwriters and directors is that a script or cut has been 被改得面目全非 (bèi gǎi de miànmù quánfēi, 'edited/rewritten beyond recognition'), carrying a strong negative connotation of distortion.

rootFamily.gloss: people and things have changed with time

面糊.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 面糊. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 面糊 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 面糊 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 面糊 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 面糊. The etymology of 面糊 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 面糊
middle form of 面糊
modern form of 面糊

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 面糊
