面试.etymology: A Classical Chinese modifier-head compound attested in Song-dynasty administrative records (such as the Songshi examination statutes), combining 面 (miàn, 'face-to-face, in person') and 試/试 (shì, 'to test, examine, try out', from 言 'speech/inquiry' + 式 phonetic). Originally denoting an in-person imperial or bureaucratic examination conducted directly before the examiner to prevent ghostwriting, it transitioned in modern human resources and showbiz usage to mean 'job interview' or 'in-person audition/screening'.

history.meaning: to examine candidates face-to-face in imperial or official selection
to interview for a job or role; job/casting interview

面试.notes: Functions seamlessly as both a noun (参加面试 'attend an interview') and a transitive verb (面试新人 'interview newcomers'); in film/TV casting, a screen test or acting audition is more specifically called 试镜 (shìjìng) or 试戏 (shìxì).

革新.etymology: Derived from the Classic of Changes (Yijing, Hexagram 49 革 Gé and Hexagram 50 鼎 Dǐng: 革，去故也；鼎，取新也 'Ge means stripping away the old; Ding means taking up the new'). 革 (gé, Old Chinese *kˤrək) originally depicted a stretched animal hide stripped of its hair ('raw leather; to peel off, abolish, transform'), while 新 (xīn, Old Chinese *s-tsʰi[n]) means 'new, to renew'. Consolidated as a two-character verb/noun in medieval Chinese and reinforced in the late 19th century via Meiji Japanese 革新 (kakushin) as a translation for Western 'innovation, thorough reform, overhaul'.

history.meaning: to strip away the old and institute the new; moral or institutional renewal
systemic reform, technological or creative innovation, overhaul

morphemes.meaning: strip away the old, transform, reform (originally 'animal hide')

革新.notes: 革新 (géxīn) occupies a middle ground between 创新 (chuàngxīn, 'creative innovation, originality') and 革命 (gémìng, 'revolution'): it stresses boldly discarding outdated methods or formats to overhaul an existing system or show.

鞋.etymology: Phono-semantic character (originally 鞵) of 革 ('tanned leather/hide') + 圭 (guī/xié phonetic): 'shoe, footwear' (replacing Classical 履 lǚ and 屦 jù in vernacular Chinese from the Tang–Song period onward).

history.stage: Tang–Song vernacular (鞵 -> 鞋) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: shoe; footwear

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 鞋 (via 萌典)

鞋子.etymology: Derived noun from 鞋 ('shoe; footwear', leather 革 + phonetic 圭, originally leather-soled shoes) + nominal suffix 子. The standard disyllabic Mandarin word for shoes of any material.

history.meaning: shoe; footwear
shoe; shoes

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 鞋子

鞠.etymology: Written with the leather radical 革 + 匊 ('two hands cupped around grain', Middle Chinese *kjuk*), 鞠 originally meant 'to curve or cup respectfully' (as well as a stitched leather ball). In the ancient compound 鞠躬 (attested in the *Analects* of Confucius, 乡党 chapter), 鞠 means 'to bend and curve the upper body in respect'.

history.meaning: bend the body in respectful salutation
bow (verb component of 鞠躬)

rootFamily.gloss: bow of the body (in 鞠躬)

音.etymology: Ancient indicative character attested on Zhou bronzes formed by adding an inner mark (一) inside 言 ('speech/flute mouth'): 'voiced musical tone, note, sound, pronunciation/reading of a character, news/tidings (佳音)'.

morphemes.meaning: modulated tone emerging from the mouth = sound, musical note

history.stage: Old Chinese (Bronze inscriptions & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: tone; musical note; sound; pronunciation

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 音 (via 萌典)

音乐.etymology: Word for 'music', joining 音 ('sound, tone') and 乐 (yuè, 'music'; the same character read lè means 'joy'). The compound 音樂 is attested in Classical Chinese for musical sound and ritual music; in the late 19th century it was standardized (in Japanese 音楽 ongaku as well) as the general term for music as an art, and that modern sense became standard in Chinese.

history.meaning: musical sound; ritual music
music (general term)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 音乐 (via 萌典)

音乐厅.etymology: Three-character compound combining 音乐 ('music') + 厅 (廳, 'auditorium, concert hall'): 'concert hall, music hall'.

history.meaning: concert hall

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 音乐厅 (via 萌典)

音乐组.etymology: A modern modifier-head nominal compound formed from 音乐 (yīnyuè, 'music', a classical coordinative compound attested in the Record of Music 樂記 combining 音 'cultured tone, note' and 樂/乐 'musical performance, instrumental ensemble') + the productive organizational suffix 组 (zǔ, originally 'woven silk cord or ribbon', from 糸 'silk' and 且 phonetic, extended to mean 'to organize, weave together' and hence 'working group, crew, department'). In television and film production, 音乐组 designates the specialized music crew or audio-musical department responsible for scoring, cue selection, and live musical direction.

history.meaning: music (tones and melodies) + woven silk cord / organized group
music department, music production crew (on a film/TV set)

音乐组.notes: In Chinese TV and variety production (such as in *Behind the Scenes* / 幕后之王), production crews are divided into functional 组 (zǔ): 导演组 (director's team), 摄像组 (camera crew), 灯光组 (lighting crew), and 音乐组 (music crew).

音符.etymology: Modifier-head musical compound of 音 ('musical tone, pitch') + 符 ('written tally, symbol, mark'): 'musical note (written symbol on a staff)'.

history.meaning: musical note (symbol)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 音符 (via 萌典)

音阶.etymology: Modifier-head musical compound of 音 ('musical pitch, tone') + 阶 (階, 'steps, ascending/descending stairs'): 'musical scale' (imagining notes ascending and descending like steps on a staircase).

history.meaning: steps of pitch = musical scale

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 音阶 (via 萌典)

音频.etymology: A modern scientific and broadcasting neologism coined as a modifier-head compound calquing English 'audio frequency' (and by extension 'audio signal/feed/track'): 音 (yīn, 'sound, acoustic tone', Old Chinese *ʔ(r)əm) + 频 (pín, abbreviated from 频率 pínlǜ 'frequency', where 頻 originally meant 'repeatedly, in rapid succession', from 步 'step' and 頁 'head'). First used in telecommunications to mean 'audio frequency (AF, 20 Hz–20 kHz)' in contrast to 视频 (shìpín, 'video frequency / video'), it broadened in digital media to mean any 'audio feed, sound clip, or audio track'.

history.meaning: audio frequency (acoustic wave range in electronics and radio)
audio feed, audio track, recorded sound file or broadcast signal

morphemes.meaning: frequency, signal band (short for 频率)

音频.notes: Always paired with 视频 (shìpín, 'video') in broadcasting and post-production; in control rooms, engineers monitor 音频信号 (yīnpín xìnhào, 'audio feed/signal') and 音视频同步 (yīn-shìpín tóngbù, 'audio-video sync').

页.etymology: Foundational pictograph (traditional 頁) attested on Shang oracle bones depicting a kneeling figure with a large, prominent head at the top: in Old Chinese (and as a radical in 头, 顶, 额, 颜), 頁 meant 'head' (read xié). Later borrowed for 葉 (yè, 'leaf -> leaf/page of a book') and standardized as the noun and classifier for 'page, sheet (of a book, document, or webpage)', read yè.

morphemes.meaning: human head -> leaf/page of a book (yè)

history.meaning: pictograph of a human head
leaf/page of a book; classifier for pages

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 页 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: crown of the head, summit, top (Sino-Japanese)
crown of the head, peak, top

顶.etymology: A phono-semantic character (頂/顶, Old Chinese *tˤeŋʔ, Middle Chinese tengX) combining semantic 頁/页 (yè, pictograph of a prominent human head) and phonetic 丁 (dīng, *tˤeŋ, 'nail/peg'). Its primary sense in the Shuowen Jiezi is 'the crown of the head' (顛也). From the noun 'crown of the head, summit', it developed verbal meanings in medieval and early Mandarin: 'to carry on the head', 'to prop up from underneath with the head/shoulders', 'to push back against head-on', and by workplace extension 'to step in and hold up a post, fill in for someone'.

history.meaning: crown of the head; mountain peak, summit
to carry on the head; to prop up, withstand; to substitute for, replace
to hold up, fill in for someone, push back against; (slang) to upvote/bump a post

morphemes.meaning: crown of head; prop up, withstand, fill in for

顶.notes: Extremely versatile in workplace dialogue: 先顶一下 (xiān dǐng yīxià) or 顶上去 (dǐng shàngqù) means 'step in to cover/hold the fort for now', while 顶嘴 (dǐngzuǐ) means 'talk back' (literally 'butt against with the mouth').

rootFamily.gloss: replace, substitute for someone in a role/shift

顶上.etymology: Locative compound combining 顶 (頂, 'crown of the head -> top, peak') + 上 ('on, above'): 'on top, at the very top'.

history.meaning: on the top; at the summit

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 顶上 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: substitute stealthily; take the rap for someone

顶包.etymology: A verb-object (VO) compound originating in Yuan–Ming–Qing vernacular commerce and criminal slang, combining 顶 (dǐng, 'to substitute for, replace') and 包 (bāo, 'wrapped parcel, bundle of goods'). Originally, 顶包 referred to a fraudulent sleight-of-hand by merchants or porters who swapped a package of genuine silver or high-grade goods with a dummy parcel of inferior items ('parcel-swapping', similar to 掉包 diàobāo). By extension into judicial and modern colloquial usage, substituting an innocent or subordinate person for the real culprit in court or a scandal came to be called 顶包 ('to take the rap/fall for someone else').

history.meaning: to secretly swap a wrapped parcel of goods with a counterfeit or inferior bundle
to act as an impostor or scapegoat; to take the fall/rap for the real culprit

顶包.notes: Often used alongside 背锅 (bēiguō, 'carry the black pot / be a scapegoat') and 顶罪 (dǐngzuì, 'take the blame for a crime'); because 顶包 is a separable verb-object (VO) word, you can say 替人顶包 ('take the fall for someone') or 顶了个包.

rootFamily.gloss: take the blame for someone else's crime/fault

cognates.meaning: at most, at the very most

顶多.etymology: A colloquial Mandarin adverbial compound formed from 顶 (dǐng, grammaticalized from the noun 'summit, uppermost limit, ceiling' into the superlative degree adverb 'to the highest point, utmost') and 多 (duō, 'many, much', Old Chinese *tˤaj). Literally 'reaching the ceiling of muchness', 顶多 parallels 最多 (zuìduō) and 至多 (zhìduō), setting an upper boundary on an estimate, concession, or worst-case scenario ('at most, at best').

history.form: 頂 (uppermost limit / most) + 多 (much, many)
history.meaning: at the highest limit of quantity or degree
at most, at best, no more than

morphemes.meaning: to the top limit, utmost, most (from 'crown/summit')

顶多.notes: More colloquial and conversational than 至多 (zhìduō); frequently used to downplay a risk or limit a concession (e.g., 顶多挨顿骂 'at worst/most we'll get scolded once').

cognates.meaning: able to hold up, able to withstand

顶得住.etymology: A Mandarin potential verb-complement construction (V-得-R) built on the verb root 顶 (dǐng, 'to prop up from beneath with the head/shoulders, push back against pressure'), the potential infix 得 (de, 'able to achieve', grammaticalized from 'to obtain'), and the resultative complement 住 (zhù, 'to halt, stand firm, hold fast in place', from 人 'person' and 主 phonetic). Literally 'able to prop up and hold firm', it expresses the capacity to withstand heavy physical, financial, or psychological pressure.

history.meaning: prop up / resist + able to + hold firm in place
able to withstand, hold up against pressure or adversity

morphemes.meaning: prop up, push back against, bear
firmly, fixed in place, holding fast

顶得住.notes: Its negative counterpart is 顶不住 (dǐngbuzhù, 'unable to hold out, caving under pressure'); in high-stakes workplace dramas, 顶得住压力 ('can withstand the pressure') is a stock phrase for testing a producer's or director's grit.

rootFamily.gloss: unable to hold up, cannot withstand
hold out, brace oneself against pressure

顶楼.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 顶 (頂, 'top, topmost') + 楼 (樓, 'floor, story of a building'): 'top floor, penthouse floor, roof deck'.

history.meaning: top floor; rooftop level

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 顶楼 (via 萌典)

顶灯.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 顶 (頂, 'ceiling, roof of a room or car') + 灯 (燈, 'lamp, light'): 'ceiling light, overhead dome light'.

history.meaning: ceiling light; overhead light

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 顶灯 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: clause, item, nape of the neck (Sino-Japanese)
item, clause, nape of the neck

项.etymology: A phono-semantic character (項/项, Old Chinese *gˤroŋʔ, Middle Chinese haewngX) combining semantic 頁/页 (yè, 'head/neck region') and phonetic 工 (gōng, *kˤoŋ). In the Shuowen Jiezi, its primary anatomical meaning is 'the nape or back of the neck' (頭後也). Because the cervical vertebrae and ledger entries are arranged as distinct, countable segments supporting a larger whole, 項 developed by the Tang–Song fiscal and legal administration into a noun meaning 'category, budgetary entry, clause' and a measure word (classifier) for itemized tasks, projects, clauses, records, and athletic events.

history.meaning: nape of the neck, back of the neck
itemized category in tax/accounting ledgers; classifier for funds or clauses
classifier for tasks, projects, policies, awards, and sports events; item/neck

morphemes.meaning: nape of neck; item, clause; classifier for tasks/projects

项.notes: The original anatomical sense 'neck' survives in compounds like 项链 (xiàngliàn, 'necklace') and 望其项背 (wàng qí xiàngbèi, 'catch sight of someone's neck and back = approach their level'), while in standalone modern usage 项 is primarily a formal classifier (一项任务 'a task', 立项 'approve a project').

rootFamily.gloss: set up or approve a project (literally 'establish an item')

项目.etymology: A coordinative compound of two bodily metaphors turned administrative terms: 項/项 (xiàng, 'nape of the neck' -> 'category, clause') and 目 (mù, 'eye' -> 'mesh hole of a net, sub-heading, itemized entry', as in 綱舉目張 'when the headrope is lifted, the meshes open'). Reinforced via Meiji Japanese 項目 (kōmoku, 'item, heading, category in a list or budget'), it entered 20th-century Mandarin first as 'itemized entry, sports event' and subsequently expanded under modern management terminology to translate English 'project' (as in 项目管理 'project management').

history.meaning: heading and sub-entry in a document, ledger, or classification table; athletic event
business/creative project, engineering venture, or sports/test item

项目.notes: In Mainland Mandarin, 项目 is the standard word for a business, tech, or television 'project' (e.g., 综艺项目 'variety show project', 项目负责人 'project lead'); in Taiwan Mandarin, a business project is more often called 专案 (zhuān'àn), while 项目 retains the narrower sense of 'item, category, event'.

顺位.etymology: A modifier-head Sino-Japanese and Literary Chinese compound combining 順/顺 (shùn, 'following in sequence, in accordance with', originally picturing a river 川 flowing smoothly along the contours of a head 頁) and 位 (wèi, 'rank, seat, position', originally a person 人 standing 立 at their assigned court place). Popularized in modern East Asian legal, sports, and entertainment usage via Japanese 順位 (jun'i, 'order of rank, priority precedence'), it denotes a numbered slot in a succession, draft, competition, or showbiz billing order.

history.meaning: order of rank, line of succession or legal precedence (e.g., inheritance rank)
priority rank, draft pick order, billing or performance slot in competitions/shows

顺位.notes: Originally restricted to legal inheritance (第一顺位继承人 'first-in-line heir') and sports drafts (选秀顺位 'draft pick rank'), 顺位 has become ubiquitous in Chinese reality and music competition shows for contestant ranking and performance order.

rootFamily.gloss: in sequence, one after another in order

顺便.etymology: Adverbial compound combining 顺 (順, 'follow along in the same direction, smoothly') + 便 ('convenience, handy occasion'): 'conveniently in passing, while one is at it, on the way'. Attested from Song–Ming vernacular.

history.meaning: conveniently in passing; while one is at it

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 顺便 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: smooth, favorable, without a hitch (literary Sino-Japanese)

顺利.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative compound attested since the Han–Six Dynasties period (e.g., in the Book of Song and Buddhist translations), combining 順/顺 (shùn, 'flowing with the current, compliant, unobstructed', from 川 'river' + 頁 'head') and 利 (lì, 'sharp, cutting smoothly, advantageous, favorable', originally depicting a blade 刀 harvesting grain 禾). Both morphemes share the core image of unimpeded motion—water flowing downstream and a sharp sickle slicing grain—yielding the meaning 'smoothly, favorably, without a hitch'.

history.meaning: favorable and unobstructed (of winds, voyages, or governance)
smoothly, successfully, without a hitch (of work, filming, or negotiations)

顺利.notes: Used both as a predicate adjective (拍摄很顺利 'filming went very smoothly') and as an adverbial modifier before verbs of completion (顺利完成 'complete without a hitch', 顺利通过 'pass smoothly').

rootFamily.gloss: follow the trend;順勢 take advantage of an opportunity
convenient; by the way, in passing

顺序.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative compound attested in Han-dynasty commentaries and histories, combining 順/顺 (shùn, 'following along in natural succession') and 序 (xù, 'east-west side galleries of a courtyard school; chronological or hierarchical arrangement, sequence', from 广 'building' and 予 phonetic). Originally verbal or adjectival ('to arrange in proper sequence; orderly'), its modern usage as the standard noun for 'chronological or spatial order, sequence' was strongly reinforced by Meiji Japanese 順序 (junjo).

history.meaning: harmonious and orderly; to arrange in proper succession
order, sequence (spatial, temporal, or procedural)

morphemes.meaning: following in natural succession, along with

顺序.notes: In broadcasting and live events, 出场顺序 (chūchǎng shùnxù, 'order of appearance/performance') and 播放顺序 (bōfàng shùnxù, 'playback order') are critical production terms; compare 次序 (cìxù), which is a near-synonym, and 秩序 (zhìxù), which means 'public/social order' rather than a sequential list.

顺着.etymology: Prepositional compound from 顺 (simplified from 順, river stream 川 + head 頁 'follow the current; go along with') + continuous aspect marker 着 (*zhe*). Literally 'following along in the direction of', it governs nouns like wood grain, a path, a wall, or a breeze.

morphemes.meaning: follow along; go with the grain or current

history.meaning: following along; in the direction of
along; following (the grain, path, or direction)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 顺着

cognates.meaning: to look back, reflect on, care for, patronize (Sino-Japanese)
to look back, care for, regard

顾.etymology: A phono-semantic character (顧/顾, Old Chinese *kˤaʔ-s, Middle Chinese kuH) combining semantic 頁/页 (yè, 'head') and phonetic 雇 (gù, *kˤaʔ-s, a bird 隹 under a door 戶). Its primary meaning in the Shuowen Jiezi and Classical Chinese is 'to turn the head to look back or around' (還視也, as in 三顧茅廬 'three visits/turning one's gaze to the thatched cottage'). From 'turning one's gaze toward', it naturally extended to 'to pay heed to, attend to, look after, take into consideration', and in commercial contexts 'to patronize (as a customer)'.

history.meaning: to turn the head and look back; to gaze upon, visit out of respect
to attend to, look after, take into consideration; however/on the contrary (particle)
to look after, attend to, take into account (often in compounds or negative constructions)

morphemes.meaning: turn head to look; attend to, look after, consider

顾.notes: As a standalone verb in modern Mandarin, 顾 most often appears in negative or potential patterns such as 顾不上 (gùbushàng, 'too busy to attend to'), 不顾一切 (bùgù yīqiè, 'recklessly, regardless of everything'), or 只顾 (zhǐgù, 'merely focus on, be absorbed in').

rootFamily.gloss: look after, care for, show consideration to
customer, client (literally 'honored visitor who turns their gaze here')

顾忌.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative compound attested in Han–Three Kingdoms historical texts (such as the Hanshu and Sanguozhi), combining 顧/顾 (gù, 'to look back in caution, take into consideration, have regard for') and 忌 (jì, 'to dread, shun, hold as taboo or scruple', composed of 心 'heart' and 己 phonetic, Old Chinese *g(r)ə-s). Together they depict the mental state of 'looking over one's shoulder in apprehension and holding back out of fear of consequences or offending someone'—hence 'hesitation, misgiving, scruple, qualm'.

history.meaning: to look back in apprehension and abstain from acting; scruples or dread of authority/taboo
hesitation, misgiving, scruple; to hold back out of concern for consequences or others' reactions

morphemes.meaning: look back cautiously, have regard for

顾忌.notes: Compared with 顾虑 (gùlǜ, 'worry, practical concern'), 顾忌 specifically implies holding back because of a taboo, someone's power/feelings, or fear of crossing a line—famously seen in the idiom 肆无忌惮 (sìwújìdàn) and 无所顾忌 (wúsuǒ gùjì, 'acting without any scruples or restraint').

顿.etymology: Phono-semantic character (頓) combining 屯 (tún/dùn phonetic) + 页 (頁, 'head'): originally 'bow the head to the ground in salute (顿首)', hence 'tap the ground, pause briefly (停顿), arrange, suddenly (顿时)' and the standard classifier for 'meals, beatings, or scoldings (一顿饭 a meal)'.

history.meaning: bow the head to the ground; pause; settle
pause; suddenly; classifier for meals (一顿饭) or spells

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 顿 (via 萌典)

预告片.etymology: A modern cinema and television compound formed from 预告 (yùgào, 'advance notice, preview announcement', a modifier-head Sino-compound reinforced via Meiji Japanese 予告 yokoku, from 預/预 'beforehand, in advance' + 告 'to announce, proclaim') and the head noun 片 (piàn, colloquially pronounced piānr in northern Mandarin for films, originally 'flat slice or strip of wood', extended in the 20th century to 'photographic negative, celluloid film strip, motion picture'). Literally 'advance-announcement film strip', it designates a promotional trailer, teaser, or preview clip.

history.form: 預告 (yùgào, advance notice) + 片 (piàn, celluloid film reel)
history.meaning: promotional film reel shown in theaters ahead of a feature release
trailer, teaser, preview clip (for films, TV dramas, or variety episodes)

morphemes.meaning: film strip, clip, motion picture (originally 'flat slice')

预告片.notes: In Mainland standard pronunciation, 片 is read fourth tone (yùgàopiàn), though in northern colloquial speech and industry chatter the retroflex first-tone 预告片儿 (yùgàopiānr) is also heard; shorter early-stage teasers are often called 先导片 (xiāndǎopiàn, 'pilot/teaser clip').

rootFamily.gloss: feature film, main episode (as opposed to trailer/extras)

预定.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 預/预 (yù, 'in advance, beforehand', originally written 豫 in Classical Chinese for the sense 'to prepare beforehand, be at ease', later merged with 預 'to participate in') and 定 (dìng, 'to fix, settle, decide', showing a foot/step 𤴓 settled under a roof 宀). Attested in medieval Chinese and heavily standardized in modern administrative and commercial Mandarin via Meiji Japanese 予定 (yotei, 'prearranged schedule, fixed plan'), it means both 'scheduled, predetermined' (attributive adjective) and 'to pre-book, reserve in advance' (verb).

history.meaning: to settle or decide upon beforehand
scheduled, predetermined (plan, time, or target); to reserve or pre-book in advance

预定.notes: Carefully distinguish 预定 (yùdìng, with 定 'fix/settle': 'scheduled, predetermined' as in 预定时间 'scheduled time', or 'reserve a room/seat') from its homophone 预订 (yùdìng, with 订 'order/subscribe': exclusively 'pre-order goods, tickets, or subscriptions').

预期.etymology: A modifier-head compound formed from 預/预 (yù, 'in advance, beforehand', from classical 豫/預) and 期 (qī, 'appointed time; to await, look forward to, expect', Old Chinese *g(r)ə, phono-semantic with 月 'moon/month' and 其 phonetic). Already occurring in Ming–Qing literary prose in the sense of 'to anticipate beforehand' and reinforced by Japanese 予期 (yoki), it functions in modern Mandarin both as a transitive verb ('to predict, foresee, expect') and as a noun ('expectations, projected outcome').

history.meaning: beforehand + to await an appointed time or outcome
to foresee, anticipate, expect; projected expectation or target
history.stage: Early Modern East Asian / Modern Mandarin

morphemes.meaning: expect, look forward to; appointed time/phase

预期.notes: Very common in media ratings, economics, and project management as a noun in phrases like 超出预期 (chāochū yùqī, 'exceed expectations'), 达到预期 (dádào yùqī, 'meet expectations'), and 预期效果 (yùqī xiàoguǒ, 'expected effect/ratings').

预算.etymology: Compound of 预 ('beforehand, in advance') + 算 ('calculate with counting rods', bamboo 竹 + 具 + 廾 two hands).

history.meaning: financial budget calculated in advance

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 预算 (via 萌典)

预言.etymology: A verb and noun consisting of 预 (yù, 'in advance') and 言 (yán, 'words, to speak'). Combining foresight with the act of speaking, it carries a more mystical, authoritative, or formal weight than simple guessing, denoting a true prophecy.

history.meaning: to predict
prophecy; prediction

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 预言

预警.etymology: A modern modifier-head compound combining 預/预 (yù, 'in advance, beforehand') and 警 (jǐng, 'to warn, guard against, sound an alarm', Old Chinese *keŋʔ, composed of 言 'speech/command' and 敬 'reverent/attentive, phonetic'). Coined in 20th-century military defense as a translation of English 'early warning' (as in 预警机 yùjǐngjī 'early-warning aircraft, AWACS' and 雷达预警 'radar early warning'), it expanded into meteorology, disaster prevention, public safety, and corporate PR crisis management to mean 'early warning, weather/safety alert, or risk alert'.

history.meaning: military radar or aerial early warning against incoming attack
early warning, weather/safety alert, crisis or risk alert; to issue an advance warning

预警.notes: Used across official meteorology (黄色/红色预警 'yellow/red weather alert'), broadcast crisis management (公关预警 'PR crisis alert'), and internet slang (前方高能预警 'high-energy alert ahead = spoiler/intensity warning for an upcoming scene').

预订.etymology: Modifier-head verb compound of 预 (預, 'in advance, beforehand') + 订 (訂, 'agree upon, book, subscribe', speech 讠 + 丁): 'book in advance, reserve (a room, table, or ticket), pre-order'.

history.meaning: book in advance; reserve; pre-order

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 预订 (via 萌典)

领先.etymology: A verb-complement / verb-object compound formed from 领 (lǐng, Traditional 領, Old Chinese *reŋʔ, originally 'neck' or 'collar of a garment', extended by metonymy to 'to lead by the collar, guide') and 先 (xiān, Old Chinese *sˤər, 'front, before, ahead'). Structurally, 领 acts as the verbal head ('to lead') and 先 specifies the positional outcome ('at the front, ahead of others'), yielding 'to hold the lead' or 'to stay in first place'.

history.meaning: neck/collar (n.) -> to lead (v.); to go before, precede
to lead in rank, score, or progress; to stay ahead of competitors

领先.notes: Frequently used in broadcast ratings, box-office charts, and competitive rankings (e.g., 收视率遥遥领先 'ratings are far ahead'); takes the preposition 于 (yú) when followed by the surpassed party.

cognates.meaning: to adopt a child or pet

领养.etymology: A serial verb / coordinative verbal compound combining 领 (lǐng, Traditional 領, from the sense 'to receive, take into one's charge, claim') and 养 (yǎng, Traditional 養, Old Chinese *jaŋʔ, 'to rear, nourish, raise'). Literally 'to take into custody and raise', it coalesced in early modern legal and vernacular usage to denote the formal or household adoption of a child not born to oneself, and later extended to adopting pets.

history.meaning: to receive/take charge of; to nourish, rear, support
to claim and raise an orphan or child from another family
to legally adopt a child or rescue/adopt a pet

morphemes.meaning: to receive, claim, take into one's care

领养.notes: Applies to both legal child adoption (办理领养手续 'process adoption paperwork') and pet adoption (领养代替购买 'adopt, don't shop'); contrast with 收养 (shōuyǎng), which is more formal/legal and restricted to human children.

rootFamily.gloss: to collect, claim (an item or award)
to adopt and raise (formal/legal, for children)

领地.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound composed of 领 (lǐng, Traditional 領, 'to govern, exercise jurisdiction over, possess') and 地 (dì, 'land, territory, ground'). Attested in medieval Chinese historical texts (such as the *Book of Han* and Tang-Song administrative records) for land under a lord's or state's jurisdiction, and reinforced in modern East Asian usage via Japanese 領地 (ryōchi), where it translated European feudal 'fief' or 'domain'. In contemporary Mandarin it also carries the figurative sense of personal 'turf' or exclusive sphere of control.

history.meaning: land governed or held in fief by a noble or state
feudal domain, territory under sovereign or lordly control
territory, animal habitat, or personal turf/domain in a workplace

morphemes.meaning: to govern, possess, have jurisdiction over

领地.notes: Often used metaphorically in workplace and showbiz dramas for someone's guarded 'turf' or department (e.g., 踏入他的领地 'step onto his turf'), alongside its literal senses in history and zoology.

领域.etymology: A modifier-head compound of 领 (lǐng, Traditional 領, 'to govern, hold under jurisdiction') and 域 (yù, Old Chinese *ɢʷrək, 'bounded land, frontier, region', originally written 或 before the 囗 enclosure and 土 radical were added). While both morphemes are native Chinese, the compound gained prominence in modern Mandarin via Meiji Japanese 領域 (ryōiki), which first denoted sovereign state bounds and was soon extended to translate English 'domain', 'sphere', or academic/professional 'field'.

history.meaning: to govern/rule; bounded state or frontier region
sovereign territory; abstract sphere, domain, or academic field
professional field, branch of study, or sphere of activity

领域.notes: The standard high-register word for an industry sector or academic discipline (e.g., 传媒领域 'the media sector', 专业领域 'professional field').

cognates.meaning: guidance, leadership (less common than 指導)

领导.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound pairing 领 (lǐng, Traditional 領, 'to lead by the collar, head, command') and 导 (dǎo, Traditional 導, Old Chinese *lˤuʔ-s, composed of 道 'way/path' and 寸 'hand/thumb', meaning 'to guide along a path, direct'). Both verbs reinforce the sense of 'leading and guiding'. In twentieth-century Chinese, the verb compound also underwent zero-derivation into a count noun meaning 'leader, executive, boss'.

history.meaning: to lead/command; to guide along the way
to lead, direct (v.); institutional leader, superior, boss (n.)

领导.notes: Functions both as a verb ('to lead a team') and as the everyday workplace noun and title for one's superiors or executives (e.g., 台里领导 'the network executives', 王领导 'Leader/Director Wang').

rootFamily.gloss: to lead, stay ahead in first place
director (of a film or TV show)

领带.etymology: Modifier-head garment compound of 领 (領, 'neck, collar', 令 + 页 'head/neck') + 带 (帶, 'band, ribbon, tie'): 'necktie, tie'.

history.meaning: collar band = necktie

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 领带 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to ask for advice; to experience someone's skill or temper firsthand
to receive instruction; to experience firsthand

领教.etymology: A verb-object compound formed from 领 (lǐng, Traditional 領, 'to receive humbly, accept') and 教 (jiào, Old Chinese *kˤraw-s, 'instruction, teaching, guidance'). Originating in late imperial epistolary and courteous speech as a deferential formula ('to receive your esteemed instruction'), it developed an ironic or tough-minded secondary sense in martial arts and workplace parlance: 'to get a firsthand taste of someone's formidable skills, temper, or methods'.

history.meaning: to humbly receive another's teaching or advice (polite formula)
to ask advice (polite); to experience firsthand someone's tough methods or prowess (often ironic)

领教.notes: In modern drama dialogue, 领教了 ('I've seen what you're capable of') is frequently used with dry irony after witnessing a rival's or boss's ruthless competence (e.g., 领教了魔鬼制作人的手段 'experienced the demon producer's methods firsthand').

rootFamily.gloss: to consult, ask for advice humbly
lesson learned (from a mistake or setback)

颇深.etymology: A modifier-head adjectival phrase combining the classical degree adverb 颇 (pō, Traditional 頗, Old Chinese *pʰˤaj, composed of 皮 phonetic and 页 'head', originally 'tilted of the head, leaning to one side', hence 'inclined, considerably, quite') and 深 (shēn, Old Chinese *hljəm, 'deep, profound'). Retaining a refined Literary Chinese flavor, it describes impressions, affections, accomplishments, or misunderstandings that run 'quite deep'.

history.meaning: tilted/leaning -> somewhat, quite, considerably; deep of water -> profound
quite deep, considerable (of impressions, friendship, resentment, or mastery)

morphemes.meaning: quite, rather, considerably (originally: leaning to one side)

颇深.notes: A polished, semi-literary predicate typically paired with abstract two-syllable subjects in four-character rhythms: 印象颇深 ('left a quite deep impression'), 交情颇深 ('have deep ties'), 成见颇深 ('hold deep prejudices'), or 造诣颇深 ('possess profound attainment').

rootFamily.gloss: biased, partial (retaining the original sense of 颇 'leaning')

频繁.etymology: A coordinative adjectival compound uniting 频 (pín, Traditional 頻, Old Chinese *bin, depicting a person 步/涉 knitting their brow 页 at a river bank, extended to 'urgent, contiguous, repeatedly') and 繁 (fán, Old Chinese *ban, originally a horse's ornate head-plume, extended to 'luxuriant, numerous, manifold'). Already attested in Tang and Song literary prose (first often written 频烦 'repeated and bothersome/numerous'), it means 'occurring at short intervals and in great number'.

history.meaning: repeated and numerous, incessant (of official duties, courier dispatches, or visits)
frequent, occurring repeatedly at close intervals

频繁.notes: Functions both as an attributive/predicative adjective (接触频繁 'frequent contact') and adverbially before verbs (频繁出现 'appear frequently', 频繁跳槽 'job-hop frequently').

频频.etymology: A full reduplication of the classical morpheme 频 (pín, Traditional 頻, Old Chinese *bin, 'urgent, contiguous, time after time'). Reduplicating the syllable iconically conveys continuous, back-to-back recurrence. Attested since the *Classic of Poetry* (*Shijing*, Daya, *Sang Rou*: 国步斯频 'the state's plight comes thicker and faster') and Han-Tang poetry (e.g., Du Fu's 频频 in verse), it serves in modern Mandarin as a brisk adverb meaning 'time and again, repeatedly'.

history.meaning: urgently, in rapid succession, continuously
repeatedly, again and again (modifying two-syllable or monosyllabic actions)

频频.notes: Strictly an adverb placed directly before verbs, especially gestures and news headlines: 频频点头 ('nod repeatedly'), 频频频出状况 / 频出状况 ('incidents keep cropping up'), 频频示好 ('repeatedly make friendly overtures').

颗.etymology: Phono-semantic character (顆) combining 果 (guǒ/kē phonetic, which also depicts round fruit on a tree) + 页 (頁, 'head'): originally 'a small head or round clod of earth', and from the Han–Tang period onward the standard classifier for 'small, round, bead-like or grain-like objects (pearls, stars, teeth, buttons, pills, seeds, hearts: 一颗星, 一颗心)'.

history.meaning: small head; round clod or grain
classifier for small round objects (stars, pearls, beans, teeth, hearts)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 颗 (via 萌典)

题目.etymology: A coordinative nominal compound joining 题 (tí, Traditional 題, Old Chinese *dˤe, composed of 是 phonetic and 页 'head', originally 'forehead', extended to 'frontispiece inscription, heading, to inscribe') and 目 (mù, Old Chinese *mruk, 'eye', extended to 'index entry, item, catalogue heading'). In Tang-Song imperial examination culture, 题目 referred to the set essay prompt or poetic theme; from there it broadened to mean any article/show title, discussion topic, or test question.

history.meaning: forehead -> heading/inscription; eye -> catalogue item or heading
imperial examination prompt, poetic theme, or book/essay title
title (of a work or program), discussion topic, or exam question/problem

题目.notes: Covers both 'title/topic' (节目题目 'program title', 演讲题目 'speech topic') and 'exam question' (这道题目很难 'this test question is hard'); contrast with 主题 (zhǔtí, 'central theme/motif') and 标题 (biāotí, 'written headline/caption').

rootFamily.gloss: topic of conversation; trending hashtag topic

cognates.meaning: face value / facial attractiveness score (source expression 顔面偏差値)

颜值.etymology: A contemporary modifier-head compound combining 颜 (yán, Traditional 顏, Old Chinese *C.ŋˤrar, originally 'space between the eyebrows, forehead', broadened to 'face, countenance, complexion') and 值 (zhí, 'numerical value, score, worth'). Coined in 21st-century Chinese internet and entertainment culture by condensing Japanese ACG/variety-show slang 顔面偏差値 (ganmen hensachi, 'facial standard-deviation score'), it treats physical attractiveness as a quantifiable 'stat' or 'face value'.

history.meaning: brow/countenance; price, numerical value
jocular 'facial attractiveness deviation score' in Japanese pop culture
physical attractiveness, screen good looks ('face value')

颜值.notes: Ubiquitous in entertainment, casting, and idol-show discourse; collocates with 高/低 ('high/low'), 爆表 (yánzhí bàobiǎo, 'looks off the charts'), 在线 (yánzhí zàixiàn, 'looking on point'), and 颜值担当 ('the visual/heartthrob of a group').

颜色.etymology: Coordinative compound from 颜 (simplified from 顏, 'brow; facial expression') + 色 ('complexion; facial hue; color'). In Classical Chinese 颜色 meant 'countenance and facial expression'; by the Tang dynasty it had shifted in vernacular usage to become the general noun for 'color, hue, or pigment'.

history.meaning: facial expression and complexion
color; hue; pigment
color

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 颜色

额头.etymology: Compound anatomical noun of 额 (額, 'forehead; fixed quota/plaque above a door', 客 + 页 'head') + nominal suffix 头 (頭, 'head'): 'forehead, brow'.

history.meaning: forehead; brow

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 额头 (via 萌典)

颠覆.etymology: A coordinative verbal compound uniting 颠 (diān, Traditional 顛, Old Chinese *tˤin, composed of 真 phonetic and 页 'head', originally 'crown of the head', hence 'to fall headlong, turn upside down, topple') and 覆 (fù, Old Chinese *pʰuk, 'to capsize, overturn, cover over'). Attested in the *Classic of Poetry* (*Shijing*, Daya, *Yi*: 颠覆厥德 'overturning his own virtue') and *Zuo Zhuan*, it originally meant to topple a carriage or dynasty and in modern usage extends to 'radically subverting' conventions or expectations.

history.meaning: to fall headlong and capsize; to topple a state or ruin virtue
to overthrow politically; to subvert, revolutionize, or upend expectations/traditions

morphemes.meaning: to fall headlong, topple, invert (originally: crown of the head)

颠覆.notes: Beyond its grave political sense ('subvert state power'), it is a favorite buzzword in creative industries for 'radically reinventing' a genre, image, or concept: 颠覆传统 ('upend tradition'), 颠覆性创新 ('disruptive innovation'), 颠覆认知 ('blow away one's assumptions').

rootFamily.gloss: to invert, turn upside down, confuse (right and wrong)
summit, peak (preserving the original sense of 颠 'crown/top')
to be annihilated, capsize completely (lit. 'whole army overturned')

风.etymology: Ancient phono-semantic character (traditional 風). In Shang oracle-bone script, the graph for 'wind' was borrowed from the magnificent crested Phoenix (鳳), seen as the mythical bird whose wings stirred the winds of the four quarters; later written with 凡 (fán/fēng phonetic) enclosing 虫 ('living creatures stirred by seasonal winds'): 'wind, breeze; air, style, custom, manner; news/rumor'.

history.meaning: wind; air; custom; ballad/style (as in 国风)
wind; breeze; style; custom

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 风 (via 萌典)

风味.etymology: A coordinative / modifier-head nominal compound combining 风 (fēng, Traditional 風, 'wind', extended in Six Dynasties aesthetics to 'air, style, bearing, local custom') and 味 (wèi, Old Chinese *mət-s, 'taste, flavor, aesthetic relish'). In Tang-Song literati writing, 风味 denoted a person's refined bearing or the poetic 'savor' of a scene; it concurrently developed its culinary sense of a region's or dish's 'signature local flavor'.

history.meaning: refined personal bearing, aesthetic charm, or poetic savor
distinctive local culinary flavor; special aesthetic charm or style

风味.notes: Used both for regional cuisine (地方风味小吃 'local-style snacks') and in the set phrase 别有一番风味 (bié yǒu yī fān fēngwèi, 'to have a distinctive charm/appeal all its own').

cognates.meaning: sound of wind; rumor, leaked news, wind of trouble

风声.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound of 风 (fēng, Traditional 風, 'wind') and 声 (shēng, Traditional 聲, 'sound, voice, news'). Literally 'the sound of the wind rustling', it was already used in the *Book of Documents* (*Shangshu*: 树之风声 'establish their reputation/moral influence') for reputation carried afar, and in Yuan-Ming vernacular fiction came to mean 'whispers carried on the wind—rumored news, leaked word, or signs of impending inspection/trouble'.

history.meaning: literal sound of the wind; far-reaching moral reputation or renown
rumored word, leaked tip-off, or tense atmosphere during a crackdown

morphemes.meaning: wind; rumor carried on the air

风声.notes: Commonly appears in media and workplace intrigue collocations: 走漏风声 ('leak wind of a plan/secret'), 听到一点风声 ('catch wind of a rumor'), and 风声很紧 ('the heat is on / scrutiny is tight').

rootFamily.gloss: jittery and paranoid at the slightest sign of trouble (lit. 'wind's sound and cranes' cry')

风扇.etymology: Compound noun from 风 (simplified from 風, 'wind; air current') + 扇 ('fan; swinging leaf of a door', wings 羽 under a door 户). Originally referring to hand-operated or water-wheel rotary fans used to cool halls in imperial China, it now primarily denotes an electric fan or ventilation fan.

history.meaning: rotary or hanging cooling fan
fan; electric or exhaust fan

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 风扇

风景.etymology: Coordinative noun compound pairing 风 (風, 'wind, atmosphere, natural air') + 景 ('sunlight, bright view, scenery'): 'scenery, landscape, view'. Famously attested in the Jin dynasty chronicle Shishuo Xinyu (风景不殊，正自有山河之异).

history.meaning: wind and light -> scenery, landscape, view

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 风景 (via 萌典)

风景区.etymology: A three-character compound formed by adding the locative head noun 区 (qū, Traditional 區, 'district, zone, area') to the classical disyllabic noun 风景 (fēngjǐng, Traditional 風景, attested since the Eastern Jin dynasty in *Shishuo Xinyu*: 风景不殊 'the scenery is no different'). Within 风景, 风 ('wind, breeze, atmosphere') and 景 ('sunlight, view, vista') coordinate to mean 'scenic landscape'; adding 区 designates a demarcated 'scenic area' or 'tourist resort zone'.

history.meaning: breeze and sunlight; natural scenery, landscape vista
designated scenic area, natural park, or tourist resort district

风景区.notes: Often shortened to 景区 (jǐngqū) in everyday tourism, location scouting, and administrative usage (e.g., 国家5A级风景区 'National 5A-level Scenic Area').

风暴.etymology: Originated in Classical Chinese as a subject-predicate phrase (风暴, 'the wind is fierce/violent', where 暴 bào means 'sudden, violent, scorching'), alongside its inverted modifier-head counterpart 暴风 ('violent wind'). In modern Mandarin, 风暴 solidified as a noun meaning 'tempest, gale-force storm', and by metaphor under the influence of European expressions (such as 'brainstorming' and 'financial storm'), a sudden, turbulent crisis or upheaval.

history.meaning: the wind is fierce and sudden (clausal); fierce gale
meteorological storm/tempest; sudden public, financial, or emotional crisis/upheaval

风暴.notes: Widely used figuratively in media and corporate contexts: 头脑风暴 (tóunǎo fēngbào, calque of 'brainstorming'), 舆论风暴 ('public opinion firestorm'), and 金融风暴 ('financial crisis/storm').

rootFamily.gloss: violent wind and torrential rain, tempest
public controversy, scandal, mini-crisis (lighter than 风暴)

风格.etymology: A compound of 风 (fēng, 'wind, custom') and 格 (gé, 'pattern, standard'). The 'wind' of a region describes its prevailing artistic atmosphere, which, when paired with a rigid 'pattern', perfectly defines a consistent, recognizable architectural or aesthetic style.

history.meaning: style; character

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 风格

风气.etymology: A coordinative nominal compound uniting 风 (fēng, Traditional 風, 'wind; social custom, moral influence, prevailing practice') and 气 (qì, Traditional 氣, 'air, breath, vital atmosphere, spirit'). In Han-Six Dynasties texts, 风气 first denoted regional climatic conditions ('wind and air') and was soon extended to the intangible moral or cultural 'climate' and prevailing habits of an era, region, or institution.

history.meaning: regional climate and weather; prevailing social customs and cultural atmosphere
prevailing social climate, workplace ethos, or collective habit/culture

风气.notes: Refers to the moral or behavioral culture of a group or industry (e.g., 行业风气 'industry ethos', 不良风气 'unhealthy practices', 整顿职场风气 'rectify workplace culture').

rootFamily.gloss: atmosphere, ambiance (of a room or meeting)
aura, commanding presence (of a star or executive)

cognates.meaning: wind and tide; current trend, fashion, zeitgeist
trend, tendency, current of the times

风潮.etymology: A coordinative metaphorical compound combining 风 (fēng, Traditional 風, 'wind; fashion, trend') and 潮 (cháo, 'ocean tide, surging wave'). Literally 'wind and tide' in Song-Yuan poetry, it acquired its modern sociological meaning—'a sweeping social trend, craze, or wave of agitation'—in late Qing and Republican Chinese alongside Meiji Japanese 風潮 (fūchō). In early 20th-century texts it also specifically denoted student or labor strikes ('agitation waves').

history.meaning: literal wind and ocean tide in nature poetry
sweeping social trend, current of the times; mass agitation or strike wave
prevailing trend, craze, wave of fashion or industry movement

风潮.notes: Used in media and marketing for a sweeping industry or pop-culture craze: 掀起一股复古风潮 ('set off a retro craze'), 引领时尚风潮 ('lead the fashion wave').

rootFamily.gloss: trend, historical tide, fashion (also yields 潮 'trendy')
upsurge, craze, boom (e.g., a ratings or investment boom)

cognates.word: 風生水起 (fung1 saang1 seoi2 hei2)

风生水起.etymology: A four-character parallel subject-predicate idiom (风生 'the wind rises' + 水起 'the waters surge'). Its imagery goes back to Song dynasty literary writing—notably Su Shi's preface to the *Classic of Changes* (*Dongpo Zhuan*), which describes wind stirring over water to create natural ripples—and entered traditional Chinese geomancy (*fengshui*) and Cantonese mercantile usage to signify 'vital energy (气) flowing dynamically so that a venture or career booms with unstoppable momentum'.

history.form: 風生水起 / 風起水湧
history.meaning: wind rising and water surging—vivid natural dynamism in prose and geomancy
thriving with flair, booming, going from strength to strength in business or career
history.stage: Modern Mandarin (popularized via Cantonese business/media usage)

morphemes.meaning: water (associated with wealth and flow in fengshui)

风生水起.notes: Frequently used as a complement after 混得 (hùn de) or 做得 (zuò de) to describe someone's career or company booming: 在娱乐圈混得风生水起 ('thriving with flair in showbiz') or 把节目做得风生水起 ('making the show a roaring success').

rootFamily.gloss: talking with wit and animation (lit. 'talking so that wind rises')
rising Clouds and surging wind; turbulent and dramatic

风险.etymology: A coordinative nominal compound pairing 风 (fēng, Traditional 風, 'wind, storm at sea') and 险 (xiǎn, Traditional 險, Old Chinese *qʰrəmʔ, 'steep precipice, perilous pass, danger'). Originating in maritime and riverine navigation for 'the perils of wind and waves on the water', it was adopted in modern commercial and financial Chinese as the standard equivalent of English 'risk'—the probability of loss or unforeseen hazard in an enterprise.

history.meaning: perilous winds and waves encountered by boats; concrete physical danger
financial, legal, or operational risk; uncertainty of loss or failure

风险.notes: Collocates with 承担/冒 (chéngdān/mào, 'bear/take a risk'), 规避 (guībì, 'avert/mitigate risk'), 评估 ('assess'), and forms 风险投资 (fēngxiǎn tóuzī, shortened to 风投 fēngtóu, 'venture capital / VC').

rootFamily.gloss: to take a risk, venture into danger; adventure

cognates.meaning: wind and rain; storm; trials and hardships

风雨.etymology: An ancient coordinative nominal compound uniting 风 (fēng, Traditional 風, 'wind') and 雨 (yǔ, Old Chinese *C.ɢʷ(r)aʔ, 'rain'). Famous since the *Classic of Poetry* (*Shijing*, Zhengfeng, *Feng Yu*: 风雨如晦，鸡鸣不已 'Through wind and rain dark as night, the cock crows without ceasing'—already an allegory for steadfastness amid dark times), it denotes both literal inclement weather and metaphorical 'storms, trials, and shared hardships'.

history.meaning: wind and rain; stormy weather (and early poetic symbol of troubled times)
wind and rain; life's trials, career hardships, and political/industry storms

风雨.notes: Pervasive in inspirational and workplace idioms: 风雨同舟 (fēngyǔ-tóngzhōu, 'stand together in the same boat through thick and thin'), 经历风雨 ('weather trials and hardships'), and 风雨无阻 ('rain or shine, stopped by nothing').

rootFamily.gloss: to share the same boat through wind and rain; stand together through thick and thin
precarious, tottering in the storm (of a company or regime)

cognates.meaning: to sweep over, overwhelm, take by storm (for 風靡)
to sweep over, dominate an era (for 風靡)

风靡全球.etymology: A four-character verb-object phrase combining the classical verb风靡 (fēngmǐ, 'to sweep over like wind flattening grass') with the modern object 全球 (quánqiú, 'the whole globe/world'). 风靡 originates in the *Book of Han* (汉书: 望风靡 'seeing the wind, they bend low like grass', where 靡 mǐ, Old Chinese *majʔ, means 'to bend down, fall flat, yield'); 全球 ('whole sphere/globe') was coined in 19th-century missionary-Chinese geography. Together they mean 'to take the entire world by storm'.

history.meaning: grass bending flat before the wind; to sweep over or overwhelm
to sweep the globe, become a worldwide hit or sensation

morphemes.meaning: to bend down flat, sweep over, carry away (pronounced mǐ)

风靡全球.notes: Pronunciation trap: 靡 here must be read in the third tone mǐ ('to bend flat'), not mí (as in 奢靡 shēmí, 'extravagant'). A closely related idiom is 风靡一时 (fēngmǐ-yīshí, 'be all the rage for a time').

rootFamily.gloss: to be all the rage for a period, sweep an era
to bend in submission at the mere sight of someone's power

飘.etymology: Phono-semantic character combining phonetic 票 (*piào/piāo*, 'light spark rising') with the wind radical 风 ('wind/breeze'). Attested since classical poetry for petals, snow, musical notes, or cooking aromas floating and drifting lightly on the air.

morphemes.meaning: float; drift lightly on the breeze

history.meaning: whirl or float lightly in the wind
float; drift in the air (of music, scent, or leaves)

飙升.etymology: A modifier-head verbal compound combining 飙 (biāo, Traditional 飆/颷, Old Chinese *pjew, composed of 猋 'three dogs running swiftly' and 风 'wind', meaning 'whirlwind, upward-spiraling gale') and 升 (shēng, Old Chinese *s-təŋ, originally a scoop/dry measure, extended to 'to rise, ascend'). Popularized in late 20th-century Hong Kong and mainland journalism, it vividly pictures numbers, ratings, or prices 'shooting upward like a whirlwind'.

history.meaning: whirlwind, violent gale spiraling upward (*erya*, *Chuci*); to ascend, rise
to skyrocket, soar, surge dramatically (of ratings, prices, or adrenaline)
history.stage: Modern Mandarin (via Hong Kong/Cantonese media register)

morphemes.meaning: whirlwind, violent upward gust; rapidly, at breakneck speed

飙升.notes: A staple of entertainment and financial headlines: 收视率飙升 ('TV ratings skyrocketed'), 人气飙升 ('popularity soared'), 肾上腺素飙升 ('adrenaline surged'). Note that 飙 also appears in 飙戏 (biāoxì, 'actors going head-to-head in an intense acting duel').

rootFamily.gloss: to race cars at breakneck speed; street racing
actors competing intensely in a scene ('dueling acting skills')

飞.etymology: A primary monosyllabic root (Traditional 飛, Old Chinese *C.pə[r], Middle Chinese *pjɨj) originating as an oracle-bone and bronze-script pictograph of a bird soaring upward with outspread wings. From its core meaning 'to fly through the air', it developed extended verbal and adverbial senses across Chinese history: 'to flutter, hover, move at lightning speed, vanish into thin air, or spread unfoundedly'.

history.meaning: (of a bird) to fly with outspread wings; to soar aloft
to fly (of birds, aircraft, or air passengers); to move swiftly or evaporate

morphemes.meaning: to fly, soar, travel by air; swiftly

飞.notes: In modern spoken Mandarin, 飞 is used transitively with a destination to mean 'fly to (a city) on a trip': 我今晚飞北京 ('I'm flying to Beijing tonight'), and in showbiz slang 空中飞人 ('airborne flyer') describes a celebrity or producer constantly living on planes.

rootFamily.gloss: to take off (of an aircraft or a career/economy)

飞机.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound combining 飞 (fēi, Traditional 飛, 'flying') and 机 (jī, Traditional 機, Old Chinese *kəj, originally the trigger mechanism of a crossbow or the shuttle apparatus of a loom, extended in modern times to 'mechanical contrivance, machine, engine'). Formed in the early 20th century (alongside the fuller 飞行机, compare Japanese 飛行機 hikōki) as a transparent calque for 'flying machine / aeroplane'.

history.meaning: to fly; crossbow trigger or loom mechanism -> ingenious mechanical device
powered heavier-than-air flying machine, airplane

飞机.notes: Takes the classifier 架 (jià, 一架飞机) or 班 (bān, for scheduled flights); also appears in the indispensable colloquial idiom 放鸽子 / 放飞机 (Cantonese-influenced slang for 'standing someone up / breaking an appointment').

食品.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound uniting 食 (shí, Old Chinese *mə-lək, depicting a covered vessel of cooked grain, meaning 'food, to eat') and 品 (pǐn, Old Chinese *pʰrəmʔ, originally 'articles of various kinds, grade, category'). In classical ritual texts (such as the *Rites of Zhou*), 食品 meant 'the graded varieties or courses of food allotted by rank'; in modern East Asian usage (reinforced by Japanese 食品 shokuhin), it denotes processed, packaged, or commercial 'foodstuffs and food products'.

history.meaning: varieties or graded courses of food in ritual and courtly dining
manufactured, packaged, or commercial foodstuffs and groceries

食品.notes: Refers specifically to commercial, processed, or retail food products and snacks (e.g., 食品安全 'food safety', 垃圾食品 'junk food', 绿色食品 'organic/green food products'); unlike 食物, you would not call raw prey in nature 食品.

食物.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound composed of 食 (shí, Old Chinese *mə-lək, 'to eat; edible nourishment') and 物 (wù, Old Chinese *C.mut, originally 'multicolored ox', generalized to 'thing, creature, substance, matter'). Attested since the Warring States period (*Zhuangzi*, *Hanfeizi*, and *Strategies of the Warring States*), 食物 literally means 'edible things / substances for eating' and serves as the broadest, most neutral term for 'food'.

history.meaning: things to eat, sustenance, provisions
food, edible sustenance (for humans or animals)

食物.notes: The most general word for 'food' as physical nourishment (e.g., 食物中毒 'food poisoning', 食物链 'food chain', 消化食物 'digest food'); compare 食品 (commercial/packaged food products) and 饭 (a prepared meal or cooked rice).

rootFamily.gloss: vegetarian food; to eat a vegetarian diet
food and clothing; basic necessities of life

cognates.meaning: meal ticket, food voucher (comparable formation 食券)

餐券.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound joining 餐 (cān, Old Chinese *tsʰˤan, 'to eat a meal; a prepared meal') and 券 (quàn, Old Chinese *kʰʷran-s, written with 刀 'knife' at the bottom—distinct from 力 'strength' in 倦—originally a notched wooden tally split in two with a knife as a binding contract, later 'ticket, voucher, certificate'). Together they denote a 'meal voucher' or 'canteen coupon' issued to staff, crew, or guests.

history.meaning: to eat / a meal; notched wooden contract tally (split with a knife 刀)
printed or digital meal voucher, staff canteen coupon, or dining certificate

morphemes.meaning: ticket, voucher, coupon (originally: notched wooden tally)

餐券.notes: Pronunciation and orthography alert: 券 is pronounced quàn (never juàn) and has 刀 ('knife', for cutting a tally) at the bottom, not 力; common in studio production and corporate settings where crews receive 员工餐券 ('staff meal vouchers').

rootFamily.gloss: boxed meal (staple of film/TV crews on set)

餐巾.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 餐 ('meal, dining') + 巾 ('cloth, towel, napkin'): 'table napkin, serviette'.

history.meaning: table napkin

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 餐巾 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: cooked rice; meal (esp. in ご飯 gohan)

饭.etymology: A core Sinitic phono-semantic character (Traditional 飯, Old Chinese *banʔ-s) composed of the semantic radical 食 (shí, 'food, eating') and the phonetic component 反 (fǎn, *Cə.panʔ). In Old Chinese, the rising-tone reading (*banʔ) was a verb meaning 'to eat grain, feed', while the departing-tone nominal derivation (*banʔ-s > fàn) meant 'cooked grain (originally millet or rice)' and by synecdoche 'a meal' or 'one's livelihood'.

history.meaning: to eat grain, feed (v.); cooked grain—millet, sorghum, or rice (n.)
cooked rice; a meal in general; livelihood ('rice bowl'); phonetic loan for English 'fan' (follower)

morphemes.meaning: cooked rice; meal; livelihood (also modern phonetic loan for 'fan')

饭.notes: Dual role in showbiz Mandarin: besides 'cooked rice / meal' (吃饭 'have a meal', 铁饭碗 'iron rice bowl / secure job'), 饭 is a ubiquitous phonetic loan from English 'fan' (via Japanese ファン fan), yielding 饭圈 (fànquān, 'fandom circle').

rootFamily.gloss: boxed meal (standard meal on film/TV production sets)
fandom circle, idol fan culture (loan blend from English 'fan')

cognates.meaning: wooden tub for serving cooked rice (literal sense only)

饭桶.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound combining 饭 (fàn, Traditional 飯, 'cooked rice') and 桶 (tǒng, 'wooden bucket, tub, cask'). Literally the wooden tub used to hold steamed rice in traditional kitchens, it was already turned into a vivid metaphor by Song-Yuan Chan Buddhist masters and vernacular storytellers (and famously attributed to the Three Kingdoms wit禰衡 Mi Heng: 苟彧可使吊丧问疾，其余皆衣架、饭桶、酒囊、肉袋耳 'the rest are mere clothes-racks, rice-buckets, wine-sacks, and meat-bags') to mock someone who only consumes food without accomplishing anything—a 'good-for-nothing'.

history.meaning: wooden tub or bucket for holding steamed rice
colloquial/derogatory or self-deprecating term for an incompetent person, freeloader, or slouch (lit. 'rice bucket')

饭桶.notes: Used either as a sharp scolding insult by an angry boss ('A bunch of good-for-nothings!') or in humorous self-deprecation; parallels the four-character idiom 酒囊饭袋 (jiǔnáng-fàndài, 'wine-sack and rice-bag—useless glutton').

rootFamily.gloss: good-for-nothing glutton (lit. 'wine sack and rice bag')

饭点.etymology: A modern colloquial Mandarin modifier-head (偏正) compound combining 饭 (fàn, Traditional 飯, "cooked grain, meal", phono-semantic graph with semantic 食 "food" and phonetic 反 *pjanʔ) and 点 (diǎn, Traditional 點, "point, dot; chime of a water clock, hour on the clock"). As 点 shifted in late imperial and modern vernacular from a strike on a clepsydra or bronze bell marking night watches (更点) to a specific hour of the clock (钟点), 饭点 emerged in northern colloquial speech to denote the customary clock-hour for taking meals.

history.meaning: cooked grain/meal + strike marking time on a water clock or bell
customary clock time for eating a meal; rush hour at eateries

饭点.notes: Colloquial and everyday in register; commonly used with 赶上 ("catch mealtime") or 错过 ("miss mealtime"), especially on busy film sets and production crews where meals depend on shooting breaks.

cognates.meaning: beverage, drink (especially in cafes and menus)

饮品.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) Sino-compound formed from 饮 (yǐn, Traditional 飲, Old Chinese *qɯmʔ, "to drink; liquid nourishment") and 品 (pǐn, "article, commodity, grade, class of goods"). While Classical Chinese used 饮 alone as a noun for beverages (as in 《周礼》 浆人 steering six kinds of drinks), modern commercial and culinary Chinese paired 饮 with the categorical noun suffix 品 (modeled after 食品 "foodstuff" and 商品 "commodity"), popularized heavily through Cantonese catering terminology and commercial café menus across Greater China.

history.meaning: to drink; potable liquid or湯飲 in ritual and medical texts
commercial beverage item, prepared drink product

饮品.notes: Slightly more commercial, menu-oriented, and upscale in register than 饮料; café menus, tea shops, and craft beverage sponsors on variety shows almost always label their offerings 饮品.

饮料.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) compound combining 饮 (yǐn, Traditional 飲, "to drink") and 料 (liào, originally "to measure grain in a斗 scoop", extended in Middle Chinese to "material, ingredient, provision, stuff"). Popularized in the late 19th and early 20th centuries alongside Meiji-era Japanese Sino-compound usage (飲料, inryō, translating Western "beverage" and "drinkable provision" in hygiene, military, and commercial contexts), it became the standard everyday Mandarin term for any prepared non-alcoholic (especially bottled or canned) drink.

history.meaning: to drink + measured grain/material provision
potable liquid, manufactured beverage (Sino-Japanese lexical standardization)
history.stage: Meiji Japanese / Late Qing Return Loan

history.meaning: beverage, soft drink, bottled drink

饮料.notes: In everyday mainland Mandarin, 饮料 defaults to sweet bottled/canned soft drinks, juices, or tea drinks rather than plain water (白开水) or alcohol (酒).

cognates.meaning: eating and drinking, food and drink (inshoku)

饮食.etymology: An ancient Classical Chinese coordinative (并列) compound uniting 饮 (yǐn, Traditional 飲, Old Chinese *qɯmʔ, "to drink; liquids") and 食 (shí, Old Chinese *ɦljɯɡ, "to eat; solid grain food"). Attested in the earliest pre-Qin classics including the *Book of Changes* (《易经·需卦》: "君子以饮食宴乐") and *Mencius*, the pair originally functioned both verbally ("to drink and eat") and nominally ("drink and food"). Over two millennia it grammaticalized into a single collective noun meaning "diet, nutrition, or culinary habits".

history.meaning: to drink and to eat; beverages and solid food
diet, daily food and drink, culinary culture

饮食.notes: Formal and written in tone compared to 吃喝; frequently used in health, lifestyle, and celebrity fitness contexts such as 控制饮食 ("control one's diet") or 饮食习惯 ("dietary habits").

饱.etymology: A native Sinitic phono-semantic character (形声字): the semantic radical 饣 (Traditional 食, "food, eating") combines with the phonetic component 包 (bāo, Old Chinese *pˤ<r>u, "to wrap, enclose, swell"), yielding Old Chinese *pˤruʔ > Middle Chinese *pæwX > Mandarin bǎo. Its core etymological image is a stomach "wrapped/swollen full" with food, attested since the *Classic of Poetry* (《诗经·周颂》: "既醉既饱", "having drunk to the full and eaten to satiety"). Metaphorically extended in Literary and modern Chinese to mean "fully imbued with" or "plump/saturated" (as in 饱满, 饱和).

history.meaning: satiated with food, having eaten one's fill (contrasted with 飢 "hungry")
full from eating; plump, saturated, to the full (as a resultative complement)

饱.notes: Extremely productive as a resultative verb complement: 吃饱 ("eat until full"), 看饱眼福 ("feast one's eyes"), or the ironic slang 撑饱了没事干 ("having nothing better to do").

rootFamily.gloss: plump, full and energetic (of spirit or form)
to feast one's eyes on, enjoy to the fullest

饼干.etymology: Compound of 饼 ('flat round grain cake or pastry', food radical 饣 + phonetic 并 bìng) + 干 (gān, 'baked dry, moisture-free'), originally naming dry travel rations and adopted in modern Mandarin for crisp biscuits and cookies.

history.meaning: crisp dry-baked biscuit or cookie

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 饼干

饿.etymology: Phono-semantic character (餓) combining 饣 (食, 'food, eat') + 我 (wǒ/è phonetic). In Classical Chinese (Mencius, Hanfeizi), 飢 (jī) meant ordinary hunger while 餓 meant 'severe hunger, starve'; in vernacular Mandarin 饿 became the everyday adjective and verb for 'hungry, starve'.

history.meaning: suffer severe hunger; starve
hungry; starve

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 饿 (via 萌典)

馋.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 馋. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 馋 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 馋 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 馋 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 馋. The etymology of 馋 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 馋
middle form of 馋
modern form of 馋

首.etymology: Foundational pictograph (象形字) attested on Shang oracle bones depicting a human or animal head topped by tufts of hair (巛) above a face/eye (自): in Classical Chinese 'head', hence 'first, foremost, chief, leader (首都 capital); poem/song classifier (一首歌 a song)'.

morphemes.meaning: head with hair = head, first, classifier for songs/poems

history.meaning: pictograph of a haired head = head, chief, first, beginning
first/chief; classifier for songs and poems

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 首 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: first of all, above all (useon / suseon)

首先.etymology: A Classical Chinese coordinative (并列) disyllabic compound uniting 首 (shǒu, Old Chinese *l̥uʔ, originally a pictograph of a human head with hair, extended to "head, chief, beginning, first") and 先 (xiān, Old Chinese *sˤər, "to go forward in front, precede, earlier"). Originally used in漢-Tang prose as a verbal or adverbial phrase meaning "to take the lead in front of others" (e.g., 《汉书》), it grammaticalized into a discourse-structuring adverb ("first of all, in the first place") introducing the primary point in an argument or sequence.

history.meaning: at the very head and front; to take the lead before others
first of all, firstly (sentence-initial discourse marker or adverb)

首先.notes: In structured speech, presentations, and executive meetings, 首先 ("firstly") almost always pairs with 其次 ("secondly") and 最后 ("finally").

rootFamily.gloss: to take the lead, be the first to do something

首字母.etymology: Three-character compound combining 首 ('first, initial') + 字母 ('alphabetic letter'): 'initial letter, first letter (of a word or name); acronym initials'.

history.meaning: initial letter; initials

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 首字母 (via 萌典)

首席内容官.etymology: A modern corporate multi-tiered modifier-head (偏正) calque of English *Chief Content Officer (CCO)*, modeled on the earlier calque 首席执行官 (*Chief Executive Officer, CEO*). It combines 首席 (shǒuxí, "head mat/seat", from Classical banquet seating order where the guest of honor or highest official sat at the first mat, later used for "chief/principal"), 内容 (nèiróng, "inner capacity -> content", standardized via Meiji Japanese 内容 nairyō), and the classical bureaucratic suffix 官 (guān, "official, officer").

history.meaning: seat of honor (Classical) + inner substance/content (modern Sino-Japanese) + government official
Chief Content Officer (CCO), executive in charge of media/entertainment IP and programming

首席内容官.notes: A signature C-suite title in Chinese streaming platforms (iQIYI, Tencent Video, Youku) and production houses like the one depicted in *Behind the Scenes* (*幕后之王*), where the CCO greenlights variety shows and drama IPs.

rootFamily.gloss: chief, principal (e.g., first chair in an orchestra)

首席娱记.etymology: A contemporary media modifier-head (偏正) compound combining 首席 (shǒuxí, literally "first sitting-mat" at a formal banquet in Classical Chinese, now "chief, lead, principal") with the syllabic portmanteau 娱记 (yújì, an abbreviation of 娱乐记者 yúlè jìzhě, "entertainment journalist/reporter"). Within Chinese entertainment journalism, 娱记 emerged in tabloid and portal newsroom slang in the late 1990s and 2000s by taking the first morpheme of 娱乐 ("amusement, entertainment") and the first morpheme of 记者 ("one who records -> reporter").

history.meaning: chief seat + entertainment reporter (full compound phrase)
chief entertainment reporter, lead showbiz correspondent

首席娱记.notes: Unlike 狗仔 (paparazzi, which carries a sneaky, derogatory tone), 首席娱记 is an official, prestigious newsroom title used by entertainment portals to signal insider access and exclusive celebrity interviews.

首秀.etymology: A modern hybrid Sino-English modifier-head (偏正) compound combining the native Classical morpheme 首 (shǒu, "head, first, inaugural") with 秀 (xiù, originally a pictograph of flowering grain ears in Old Chinese meaning "luxuriant, elegant, outstanding", repurposed in late 20th-century Taiwanese and Mainland media Mandarin as a phono-semantic loanword from English *show*). Thus 首秀 literally means "first show" — a calque/hybrid equivalent to French-derived English *debut*.

history.form: 首 + 秀 (phonetic-semantic loan for English 'show')
history.meaning: first/inaugural + stage performance or broadcast show
debut performance, inaugural public appearance or broadcast

首秀.notes: Ubiquitous in entertainment, sports, and livestreaming: e.g., 荧幕首秀 ("screen debut"), 综艺首秀 ("variety show debut"), or 直播首秀 ("livestreaming debut").

rootFamily.gloss: premiere screening (of a film or drama)

首选.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) compound combining 首 (shǒu, Old Chinese *l̥uʔ, "head, chief, first in rank") and 选 (xuǎn, Traditional 選, Old Chinese *s-qʷʰarʔ, "to select, choose, appoint"). In imperial civil service and official appointment contexts, 首选 referred to the top-ranked candidate selected in an examination or roster; in modern Mandarin it functions as a compact noun or attributive modifier meaning "first choice, top pick, or default preference".

history.meaning: first-ranked selection among candidates or appointees
first choice, top preference, number-one pick

首选.notes: Frequently used in advertising, casting, and business strategy (e.g., 居家旅行首选, "the top choice for home and travel", or 品牌代言人首选, "first choice for brand ambassador").

rootFamily.gloss: candidate, person under consideration for a role

首页.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) compound formed from 首 (shǒu, "head, first, beginning") and 页 (yè, Traditional 頁, originally a pictograph of a human head with a prominent skull atop a kneeling body, archaic variant of 首/颉, later borrowed in medieval Chinese bookbinding for a "leaf" or "page" of a codex/book). Originally denoting the title page or front page of a printed book or newspaper, in the 1990s internet era 首页 was adopted as the standard translation for a website's or app's "home page" or "landing page".

history.meaning: first leaf/page of a bound book, manuscript, or newspaper
history.stage: Late Imperial & Early Modern Print Chinese

history.meaning: front page (of a publication); home page or main feed (of a website or app)

首页.notes: In social media and entertainment marketing (such as Weibo or video apps), 登上首页 ("making it onto the home page/main feed") is a major visibility metric for a trending show or celebrity topic.

rootFamily.gloss: title page, flyleaf of a book

香.etymology: Ancient ideogram (会意字) attested on oracle bones and bronzes showing millet grain (黍, later shortened to 禾) above a mouth/sweetness (甘, shortened to 日): originally 'the sweet, fragrant aroma of cooked millet and fermented grain wine', hence 'fragrant, sweet-smelling, aromatic; delicious/savory; sleep soundly (睡得香); incense or spice'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: grain (黍/禾) + sweet (甘/日) = fragrant, aromatic, tasty, incense

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 香 (via 萌典)

香味.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 香 ('fragrant, savory') + 味 ('smell, scent, flavor'): 'fragrance, pleasant scent, savory aroma'.

history.meaning: fragrant scent; savory aroma

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 香味 (via 萌典)

香柏木.etymology: Three-character timber compound combining 香 ('fragrant, aromatic') + 柏 ('cypress/cedar tree') + 木 ('wood, timber'): 'aromatic cedarwood, cypress wood (prized for its natural scent and resistance to moths and moisture)'.

history.meaning: aromatic cedarwood / cypress wood

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 香柏木 (via 萌典)

香甜.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 香甜. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 香甜 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 香甜 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 香甜 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 香甜. The etymology of 香甜 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 香甜
middle form of 香甜
modern form of 香甜

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 香甜

香草.etymology: Modifier-head botanical and culinary compound of 香 ('fragrant, aromatic') + 草 ('herb, grass, plant'). In Classical Chinese (especially Qu Yuan's Chuci), 香草 meant 'fragrant herbs' symbolizing noble virtue; in modern culinary Mandarin it means 'culinary herbs' and specifically 'vanilla'.

history.meaning: fragrant plants and aromatic herbs
vanilla; culinary aromatic herb

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 香草 (via 萌典)

马上.etymology: Metaphorical temporal adverb originally meaning literally 'on horseback' (马 'horse' + 上 'on', as in the Han saying 居马上得之 'won the empire on horseback'). In Yuan–Ming vernacular drama and fiction, 'as fast as a mounted rider / without even dismounting' grammaticalized into the everyday adverb for 'right away, immediately, at once'.

history.meaning: on horseback
immediately; right away; at once

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 马上 (via 萌典)

cognates.meaning: to curse, revile, abuse verbally (ba / nonoshiru)
to curse, revile (ma, in 욕설매도 罵倒)

骂.etymology: A Classical Chinese phono-semantic character (形声字) combining the net radical 罒 (wǎng, Traditional 网, signifying "to snare, implicate, or cast over someone") with the phonetic component 马 (mǎ, Traditional 馬, Old Chinese *mˤraʔ), yielding Old Chinese *mˤras > Middle Chinese *mæH > Mandarin mà. Defined in the Han-dynasty *Shuowen Jiezi* (《说文解字》) as "詈也" ("to revile/curse to someone's face"). In modern Mandarin, its range spans from fierce cursing to parental scolding and online roasting.

history.meaning: to revile, hurl verbal abuse, curse openly
to scold, berate, curse out, flame/roast online

morphemes.meaning: net (罒/网, to ensnare or cast verbal blame upon)

骂.notes: In showbiz and social media, 挨骂 ("get scolded/flamed") and 被骂上热搜 ("get roasted onto the trending list") are everyday hazards for producers, directors, and celebrities.

rootFamily.gloss: to scold and lecture; a tongue-lashing
street-style cursing; to shrewishly berate in public

cognates.meaning: to deceive, swindle (hen, as in 詐欺騙取)

骗.etymology: A phono-semantic character (形声字) with semantic 马 (mǎ, Traditional 馬, "horse") and phonetic 扁 (biǎn/piān, Middle Chinese *pjenX). Originally attested in Middle Chinese (such as the Tang-dynasty *Yupian* and martial narratives) with the concrete equestrian meaning "to leap agilely onto a horse's back from the side" (跃上马). By the Song and Yuan dynasties, the image of vaulting nimble-footedly onto a horse by sleight of body shifted metaphorically in vernacular Chinese to "hoodwink, pull a fast one, trick, or defraud".

history.meaning: to vault or leap agilely onto a horse's back
to trick by sleight or cunning, deceive, cheat, swindle
history.stage: Early Mandarin (Song–Yuan Vernacular) to Modern Mandarin

morphemes.meaning: horse (馬/马, originally referring to vaulting onto horseback)

骗.notes: Look out for the horse radical 马: people often expect "deceive" to have the speech radical 讠(like 诈 or 诳), but 骗 started out as a horse-vaulting stunt before coming to mean "pulling a stunt on someone".

骗人.etymology: A transparent verb-object (动宾) compound uniting 骗 (piàn, Traditional 騙, originally "to vault onto a horse", shifted in Song–Yuan vernacular to "to trick, deceive, cheat") with the generic human object 人 (rén, "person, people, others"). Adding the dummy/generic object 人 allows the transitive verb 骗 to function intransitively as a general predicate meaning "to tell a lie, fool people, or be deceptive/bogus".

history.meaning: to deceive or swindle other people
to lie, fool people; (adjectivally with 的) fake, deceptive, bogus

骗人.notes: In spoken Mandarin, 骗人! ("You're lying! / No way!") is a common exclamation of disbelief, and 骗人的 ("fake/deceptive") is used as an everyday adjective (e.g., 都是骗人的, "it's all a lie").

rootFamily.gloss: to deceive oneself as well as others
to trick or coax (often children or gullible people)

骤然.etymology: A Literary and formal Mandarin adverbial compound formed from 骤 (zhòu, Traditional 驟, phono-semantic with 馬 "horse" and 聚 jù, Old Chinese *dzˤros, originally meaning "a horse galloping at full speed", extended in pre-Qin prose to "swiftly, frequently, suddenly") and the Classical adverbial/stative suffix 然 (rán, "in such a manner, -ly"). The image of a steed charging forward without warning gave 骤然 its vivid sense of an abrupt, dramatic change in weather, mood, or circumstance.

history.meaning: a horse galloping swiftly + adverbial suffix ("in the manner of")
suddenly, abruptly, all of a sudden

骤然.notes: More literary and dramatic than 突然 or 忽然; frequently collocates with rapid shifts in temperature, atmosphere, or ratings — e.g., 气氛骤然紧张 ("the atmosphere suddenly grew tense") or 骤然降温 ("temperature plunged abruptly").
