骨头.etymology: Derived anatomical noun from 骨 ('bone', depicting joint sockets above flesh 月) + nominal suffix 头 (simplified from 頭). As with 石头 ('stone') and 木头 ('wood'), the bleached suffix 头 turns the monosyllabic classical root into the standard disyllabic Mandarin noun for 'bone'.

history.meaning: bone
bone

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 骨头

高.etymology: Foundational pictograph (象形字) attested from Shang oracle bones depicting a tall, multi-tiered pavilion or watchtower rising above a gate wall: 'high, tall (opposite of 低 'low' and 矮 'short'); loud/high-pitched; above-average in degree, level, or quality; respected surname Gao'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: pictograph of a lofty tower = high, tall, lofty, loud

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 高 (via 萌典)

高兴.etymology: Modifier-head adjective and verb compound of 高 ('high, uplifted') + 兴 (興, read xìng in the fourth tone, 'inspired mood, zest, spirits', neutral tone xing in everyday speech): originally 'high poetic spirits/inspiration' in Tang poetry (Du Fu, Chang Jian), and in modern Mandarin the primary everyday word for 'happy, glad, pleased; willing/in the mood to'.

history.meaning: lofty mood; high spirits
happy; glad; pleased

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 高兴 (via 萌典)

高冷.etymology: A contemporary Chinese internet and pop-culture coordinative portmanteau (并列紧缩词) coined in the early 2010s by compressing 高贵冷艳 (gāoguì lěngyàn, "noble, aloof, and coldly glamorous"). It pairs 高 (gāo, "high, lofty, proud, above the crowd", from 孤高/高傲) with 冷 (lěng, "cold, icy, emotionally detached", from 冷淡/冷酷) to describe a persona that is cool, unapproachable, and reticent — often used for elite producers, male leads, or cats.

history.meaning: noble and coldly glamorous (4-character internet catchphrase)
aloof and cool, unapproachable, maintaining an icy elite demeanor

morphemes.meaning: lofty, proud, high-status (from 高贵/高傲)
cold, detached, unemotional (from 冷艳/冷漠)

高冷.notes: A staple character archetype (人设) in contemporary Chinese dramas like *幕后之王*, where genius producer淳于乔 (Chunyu Qiao) is initially labeled a 高冷男神 ("aloof, icy male god") before revealing his inner warmth.

高地.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) compound combining 高 (gāo, Old Chinese *kˤaw, pictograph of a tall pavilion or watchtower, "high, elevated") and 地 (dì, "earth, ground, terrain, position"). Attested in Classical Chinese military and geographical texts (such as 《孙子兵法》 and dynastic histories, where armies are advised to occupy high, sunlit terrain) and reinforced in modern military-geographical terminology (alongside Japanese 高地 kōchi) to mean "elevated terrain, upland" or figuratively a "strategic commanding height" in media, public opinion, or industry competition.

history.meaning: elevated ground, dry upland terrain (in classical topography and military strategy)
high ground, highlands; strategic commanding position (in business, culture, or舆论 media)

高地.notes: Often used metaphorically in media and corporate strategy: 占领舆论高地 ("seize the moral/public-opinion high ground") or 行业高地 ("commanding heights of the industry").

cognates.word: 高声 (こうせい / たかごえ)

高声.etymology: A Classical and vernacular modifier-head (偏正) compound pairing 高 (gāo, "high in pitch or volume, loud") with 声 (shēng, Traditional 聲, Old Chinese *l̥eŋ, originally a stone chime struck by a hand with an ear radical beneath, "sound, voice, tone"). In Classical and Tang-Song texts, 高 (high) and 低 (low) regularly described vocal volume as well as musical pitch; 高声 thus functions both as a noun ("a loud voice") and directly before verbs of speaking as an adverbial modifier ("in a loud voice, loudly").

history.meaning: a high-pitched or loud voice; aloud
loudly, at the top of one's voice (adverbial before verbs of speech/shouting)

高声.notes: Slightly more literary and narrative than 大声; commonly appears in stage directions, scripts, and novels before verbs like 喊 ("shout"), 叫 ("call out"), or 宣布 ("announce").

rootFamily.gloss: in a loud voice, loudly (everyday equivalent)
in a low voice, softly, under one's breath

高定.etymology: A contemporary fashion and showbiz syllabic abbreviation (紧缩词) compressing 高级定制 (gāojí dìngzhì, "high-grade custom-made / haute couture"), which itself was coined as a calque of French *haute couture* (*haute* = 高级 "high/high-class", *couture* = 定制时装 "custom-tailored dressmaking"). By extracting the first morpheme of 高级 ("high-grade") and the first morpheme of 定制 ("made to order"), Chinese fashion journalism and celebrity red-carpet commentary created the sleek two-character noun and modifier 高定.

history.form: 高級定制 (calque of French haute couture)
history.meaning: high-class custom tailoring / couture fashion
haute couture; bespoke luxury fashion or top-tier custom production

morphemes.meaning: short for 高级 (high-ranking, luxury, haute)
short for 定制 (custom-made, tailored to order)

高定.notes: In Chinese celebrity culture, whether a star wears 礼服高定 ("an haute couture gown") on a red carpet or gala broadcast is treated by fans and media as a barometer of commercial status and fashion-house backing.

rootFamily.gloss: to order goods, place a custom order

高层.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) compound combining 高 (gāo, "high, upper") and 层 (céng, Traditional 層, phono-semantic with 尸 "building/body" and 曾 zéng "to pile up", meaning "story of a building, stratum, tier, layer"). Originally architectural ("upper stories of a multi-story tower", attested since Tang poetry and prose), in modern Chinese (paralleling Sino-Japanese 高層 kōsō) it bifurcated into a literal architectural sense ("high-rise building") and an organizational metaphor ("the upper stratum / top management / senior leadership of a company or government").

history.meaning: upper stories of a multi-tiered pavilion or tower
high-rise building; upper echelon, senior management, top leadership

morphemes.meaning: layer, tier, stratum, story of a building

高层.notes: Very common in corporate and media workplace dramas: 公司高层 refers collectively to the C-suite and vice presidents ("the higher-ups" or "senior management").

cognates.meaning: altitude, height; high degree, advanced level (kōdo)

高度.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) Sino-compound combining 高 (gāo, "high, tall") and 度 (dù, Old Chinese *dˤak-s, originally "to measure with the hand/arm span", hence "linear measure, degree, extent, standard"). While Classical Chinese used 高 and 度 separately, the compound 高度 was standardized in modern East Asian scientific and administrative lexicon (heavily reinforced by Meiji Japanese 高度 kōdo) with two distinct functions: a noun meaning "physical altitude/height or elevated perspective" and an attributive/adverbial modifier meaning "to a high degree, highly, intensely".

history.meaning: physical altitude, elevation; high degree of intensity or development
altitude, height, elevated perspective (noun); to a high degree, highly (adverbial modifier)

高度.notes: Notice its dual role: as a noun in 站在战略高度 ("standing at a strategic height/perspective"), and as an adverbial modifier before two-syllable verbs or adjectives in 高度重视 ("attach a high degree of importance to") or 高度机密 ("top secret").

cognates.meaning: skilled player, master hand (jōzu, analogous compound; kōshu)

高手.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) compound combining 高 (gāo, "high, superior, consummate") and the metonymic agentive noun 手 (shǒu, originally "human hand", extended in Han–Six Dynasties Chinese via metonymy from "the hand that executes a craft" to "a practitioner, specialist, or player of a skill"). Attested since the Six Dynasties and Tang Dynasty (initially for master Go/Weiqi players, calligraphers, and physicians, e.g., 《颜氏家训》), and later popularized across martial arts (wuxia) fiction and modern professional fields for an "ace, master, or top expert".

history.meaning: a person of superior hand/skill in board games (Weiqi), medicine, or calligraphy
martial arts master (in vernacular fiction); expert, ace, virtuoso in any field
history.stage: Late Imperial Vernacular to Modern Mandarin

高手.notes: Carries a vivid, admiring tone (often with a touch of martial-arts flair, as in 高手在民间, "true masters are hidden among the common people", or 幕后高手, "mastermind behind the scenes").

高汤.etymology: Culinary compound of 高 ('fine; choice; concentrated') + 汤 ('hot liquid; soup; broth', water radical 氵 + 昜 *yáng*). In Chinese culinary tradition, 高汤 designates a clear, flavour-rich master stock simmered slowly ahead of time to form the base of soups and sauces.

history.meaning: clear, concentrated culinary master stock
broth; culinary stock

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 高汤

cognates.word: 高深莫測 (gou1 sam1 mok6 cak1)

高深莫测.etymology: A four-character Classical-style idiom (成语, chéngyǔ) structured as a subject-predicate or topic-comment clause: the coordinative adjective pair 高深 (gāoshēn, "lofty as the heavens and deep as the abyss -> profound, abstruse") is followed by the Classical negative pronoun/adverb 莫 (mò, Old Chinese *mˤak, "none, nobody, nothing can") and the verb 测 (cè, Traditional 測, originally "to plumb the depth of water with a weighted line", hence "to fathom, gauge, measure"). Together, it literally means "so lofty and deep that no one can plumb its depths".

history.meaning: lofty and deep + none can plumb/fathom (derived from Classical expressions like 變化莫測 and 高深難測)
unfathomable, inscrutable, enigmatic (often used ironicaly for someone acting mysterious)

morphemes.meaning: none, no one can, impossible to
to plumb water depth, fathom, gauge

高深莫测.notes: Often used with a slightly wry or ironic nuance in modern speech to describe a boss, mentor, or strategist who wears a poker face and speaks in riddles (装得高深莫测, "putting on an inscrutable air").

rootFamily.gloss: profound, advanced, abstruse (of learning or theory)
unfathomable, impossible to guess someone's mind

高管层.etymology: A modern corporate three-character compound formed by adding the collective stratum suffix 层 (céng, Traditional 層, "layer, tier, echelon") to the disyllabic syllabic abbreviation 高管 (gāoguǎn, compressed from 高级管理人员 gāojí guǎnlǐ rényuán, "senior management personnel / executives"). While 高管 designates an individual senior executive, appending 层 turns it into a collective noun referring to the entire C-suite and vice-presidential executive tier as an institutional body.

history.meaning: senior management personnel + organizational stratum/tier
the senior executive tier, C-suite leadership collectively

morphemes.meaning: short for 管理人员 (management personnel, executive)

高管层.notes: Whereas 高管 can count individuals (一位高管, "an executive"), 高管层 always refers to the executive leadership as a collective decision-making group (e.g., 高管层变动, "shake-up in the senior executive tier").

高级.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) Sino-compound combining 高 (gāo, "high") and 级 (jí, Traditional 級, phono-semantic with 糸 "silk thread" and 及 jí, originally meaning "the order of silk threads", and in Qin legal code "severed enemy heads presented for military promotion", hence "step on a staircase, rank, grade"). Popularized in its modern dual sense via Meiji Japanese 高級 (kōkyū), where it meant both "high official rank / senior grade" (contrasted with 初级/中级) and "high-quality, upscale, classy".

history.meaning: gradation of silk threads; step in military/official rank (Qin–Han system)
high official rank, senior grade; high-class, upscale
senior, high-ranking, advanced; upscale, classy, sophisticated (of taste or aesthetic)

高级.notes: In contemporary Chinese aesthetic and media slang, 高级 (as in 高级感, "a sense of understated luxury/sophistication", or 高级脸, "high-fashion editorial face") is a major compliment for refined, non-tacky production value.

rootFamily.gloss: rank, grade, social or quality tier

高级制作人.etymology: A modern media and television industry title structured as a modifier-head (偏正) compound: 高级 (gāojí, "senior, high-ranking") modifies 制作人 (zhìzuòrén, "producer"), which itself combines the Classical coordinative verb 制作 (zhìzuò, "to cut/fashion and make -> to produce/manufacture") with the agentive noun suffix 人 (rén, "person"). It serves as the standard Chinese broadcast industry calque of English *Senior Producer* in television networks, streaming platforms, and music production.

history.form: 高級 + 製作/制作 + 人
history.meaning: high-grade/senior + to craft/produce + agentive person suffix

history.form: 高级制作人 (高級制作人)
history.meaning: Senior Producer (ranking above ordinary 制作人 and below 总制作人 / 监制)

morphemes.meaning: to produce, create, manufacture (a show or record)

高级制作人.notes: In Chinese TV and variety production (the core setting of *幕后之王*), 制作人 (or 制片人 in film/drama) is the creative and operational linchpin; 高级制作人 denotes a veteran producer capable of spearheading flagship shows independently.

rootFamily.gloss: producer (in television, variety shows, or music)
film/drama producer (emphasizing financing and studio management)

高高.etymology: A reduplicated form of 高 (gāo, 'high'). Doubling adjectives in Mandarin intensifies them, transforming a simple description into a vivid, striking mental image of an object raised far above its immediate surroundings.

history.meaning: high up; towering

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 高高

cognates.word: 魂不守舍 (wan4 bat1 sau2 se3)

魂不守舍.etymology: A four-character Classical Chinese subject-predicate idiom (成语, chéngyǔ) rooted in early Daoist and traditional Chinese medical views of the human body as a dwelling (舍, shè, "lodging house, inn, bodily abode") guarded by the ethereal Yang spirit-soul (魂, hún, phono-semantic with 鬼 "spirit" and 云 "cloud"). If a person's 魂 fails to guard (不守) its bodily lodging (舍) and wanders off, the person becomes dazed, distracted, or beside themselves. Early philosophical precursors appear in *Zhuangzi* and Han-Tang medical/narrative texts, consolidating as the fixed four-character idiom in Ming vernacular fiction (such as 《初刻拍案惊奇》).

history.form: 神不守舍 / 魂不守宅
history.meaning: the ethereal spirit/soul fails to guard its bodily dwelling (in Daoist hygiene and medical texts)
one's soul has left its bodily abode -> utterly distracted, preoccupied, out of one's wits
history.stage: Ming–Qing Vernacular Fiction to Modern Mandarin

morphemes.meaning: to guard, keep watch over, remain in
lodging, house (metaphor for the physical body)

魂不守舍.notes: Vividly describes someone who is physically present at work or in a meeting, yet mentally miles away due to infatuation, anxiety, or shock (e.g., 一整天都魂不守舍的, "walking around in a daze all day").

rootFamily.gloss: frightened out of one's wits (soul flying away and scattering)
soul, spirit, guiding heart of a work

魅力.etymology: A modifier-head (偏正) Sino-Japanese compound coined or popularized in modern Japanese (魅力, miryoku) and borrowed into early 20th-century Mandarin. It combines 魅 (mèi, Old Chinese *mri-s, a character with the ghost/demon radical 鬼 depicting an uncanny mountain or forest sprite in pre-Qin mythology that bewitches and seduces travelers, hence "to bewitch, enchant, fascinate") with 力 (lì, "power, force"). Thus 魅力 literally means "bewitching power" — evolving from supernatural enchantment into secular personal charisma, magnetism, and appeal.

history.meaning: an enchanting nature spirit or demon; to bewitch, cast a spell over (《左传》, 《说文》)
magnetic attraction, aesthetic or personal fascination (modern Sino-Japanese coinage)
charm, charisma, glamor, magnetic appeal

morphemes.meaning: to bewitch, enchant, fascinate (originally a forest sprite)

魅力.notes: Notice the 鬼 ("spirit/ghost") radical inside 魅: charisma (魅力) and seductiveness (妩媚/魅惑) both trace back to the idea of casting an irresistible spell over an audience, as in 舞台魅力 ("stage presence/charisma") or 人格魅力 ("personal charisma").

rootFamily.gloss: goblin, demon, alluring monster (from classical mythology)

cognates.word: 魚 (ぎょ / うお / さかな)

鱼.etymology: One of the oldest primary pictographs (象形字) in the Chinese writing system, continuously attested from Shang-dynasty oracle bone script (甲骨文) and Western Zhou bronze inscriptions (金文) down to modern Simplified 鱼 (Traditional 魚). The oracle bone graph vividly depicts a scaly aquatic vertebrate upright with a pointed head at the top (later stylized as 𠂊), a cross-hatched scaly body in the middle (田), and a forked tail fin at the bottom (stylized into four dots 灬 in Clerical and Traditional script, and into a single horizontal stroke 一 in Simplified script). Phonologically descended from Old Chinese *ŋa < Proto-Sino-Tibetan *s-ŋja ("fish").

history.meaning: fish (pictograph of head, scaled body, and tail fin in Oracle Bone & Bronze scripts)
fish; aquatic creature; surname; homophonous symbol of 余 ("surplus/abundance")
history.stage: Middle Chinese to Modern Standard Mandarin

morphemes.meaning: fish (pictograph of fish head, scaled torso, and tail fin)

鱼.notes: Because 鱼 (yú) is a perfect homophone of 余 (yú, "surplus, abundance"), fish dishes are indispensable at Chinese New Year banquets (年年有余, "may you have abundance year after year"); in contemporary slang, 摸鱼 ("feeling around for fish in muddy water") means "slacking off at work".

rootFamily.gloss: to slack off at work; originally to catch fish in troubled waters (浑水摸鱼)

cognates.meaning: abalone (prized dried or fresh banquet delicacy)
salted/pickled fish (archaic); abalone (usually written 鮑 awabi)

鲍鱼.etymology: A fascinating case of historical semantic shift in a modifier-head (偏正) compound combining 鲍 (bào, Traditional 鮑, phono-semantic with 魚 "fish" and 包 bāo "to wrap/salt in a pouch", Old Chinese *bˤruʔ) and 鱼 (yú, "fish / aquatic creature"). In pre-Qin and Han Classical Chinese, 鲍鱼 meant "salted, pickled, foul-smelling preserved fish" (famous from the proverb 如入鲍鱼之肆, "like entering a salted-fish shop — growing numb to the stench", and used to mask the smell of Qin Shi Huang's decaying corpse in 《史记》), whereas abalone was called 鳆鱼 (fùyú). In late imperial and modern culinary Chinese, because the shell of the abalone wraps (包/鲍) its foot and because 鲍 was used for dried marine delicacies in coastal trade, 鲍鱼 completely replaced 鳆鱼 as the standard name for luxury abalone!

history.meaning: salted, fermented, foul-smelling preserved fish (contrasted with 鰒魚 "abalone")
abalone (prized marine gastropod mollusk and top-tier Chinese banquet delicacy)
history.stage: Late Imperial to Modern Standard Mandarin & Cantonese

morphemes.meaning: abalone (historically salted/wrapped fish; phono-semantic with 鱼 + 包)
fish, aquatic creature (applied broadly to shellfish/mollusks in Chinese classification)

鲍鱼.notes: A classic false friend between Classical and Modern Chinese: in modern banquets and TV dramas, 鲍鱼 is a luxury status dish (as in 鲍参翅肚, "abalone, sea cucumber, shark fin, and fish maw"), whereas in classical idioms like 如入鲍鱼之肆 it meant "stinky salted fish"! Also note that biologically abalone is a marine gastropod mollusk, not a true fish, though classified under 鱼 in traditional Chinese naming.

rootFamily.gloss: squid, cuttlefish (also carrying the categorical suffix 鱼)
octopus (also carrying the categorical suffix 鱼)

鲜.etymology: Simplified from 鮮, an ancient compound of 魚 ('fish') + 羊 ('sheep/mutton') (Middle Chinese *sjen*). Because freshly caught fish and tender lamb were prized in early Chinese cuisine as the twin ideals of savory, unspoiled flavor, combining the two graphs created the core word for 'fresh, bright, and delicious (umami)'.

history.meaning: fresh fish; fresh and savory
fresh (of flowers, food, or air); bright; savory

鲜亮.etymology: Pairs 鲜 (xiān, 'fresh, bright', merging fish 鱼 and sheep 羊 for intense savory freshness) with 亮 (liàng, 'bright, luminous'). It describes a color that is not merely saturated but glowing and eye-catching.

history.meaning: bright and fresh (color)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 鲜亮

鲜红.etymology: The adjective '鲜红' (xiānhóng, bright red) joins '鲜' (fresh, bright) and '红' (red). '鲜' historically denoted fresh fish or mutton, extending to mean anything fresh, new, or bright in color. '红' is the general term for red. The compound '鲜红' specifies a particularly vivid, saturated shade of red, akin to fresh blood or a bright flower. It is a strong descriptive word often used to evoke a sense of striking visibility, vitality, or sometimes alarm.

history.meaning: red

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 鲜红

鸟.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 鸟. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 鸟 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 鸟 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 鸟 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 鸟. The etymology of 鸟 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 鸟
middle form of 鸟
modern form of 鸟

鸟瞰图.etymology: The noun '鸟瞰图' (niǎokàntú, bird's-eye view map/picture) is composed of '鸟' (bird), '瞰' (to look down from a height), and '图' (map, picture). '瞰' is a classical character indicating a downward gaze. The phrase '鸟瞰' perfectly captures the concept of seeing things from a high altitude, as a flying bird would. '图' specifies that it is a visual representation. This term is commonly used in urban planning, geography, and architecture to describe aerial perspectives or overviews.

history.meaning: map

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 鸟瞰图

鸡蛋.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 鸡 (雞, 'chicken, fowl', 奚/又 + 鸟) + 蛋 ('egg', originally a southern/vernacular word replacing Classical 卵 luǎn from the Tang–Song period onward): 'chicken egg, hen's egg'.

history.meaning: chicken egg

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 鸡蛋 (via 萌典)

麻.etymology: Originally an ideogrammic compound (会意) depicting peeled plant fibers (林, variant of 𣏟) drying beneath a shed or shelter (广); Old Chinese *C.mˤraj, Middle Chinese *mæ. From the rough, tangled texture of raw hemp fibers and the mild anaesthetic properties of cannabis resin and seeds in early Chinese pharmacology (such as Hua Tuo's mafeisan), the character extended via medical and sensory metaphor to mean "rough, pitted" (as in pockmarks) and "numb, tingling, paresthetic" in the limbs or on the tongue.

history.meaning: hemp plant (Cannabis sativa); linen or hemp fiber
pockmarked, rough-textured; numb, paraesthetic, tingling
numb, tingling, prickly; hemp, sesame

麻.notes: Distinguish 麻 (tingling, "pins-and-needles" paresthesia or Sichuan peppercorn buzz) from 木 (deadened, wooden loss of sensation); in colloquial showbiz and everyday speech, 肉麻 ("flesh-numbing") describes cringeworthy, overly cheesy, or mushy behavior.

麻烦.etymology: Coordinative adjective, noun, and verb compound of 麻 ('hemp fibers -> tangled, numerosos and intricate like uncombed hemp') + 烦 (煩, 'feverish head', 火 + 页 -> 'bothered, vexed, annoyed', neutral tone fan in this word): 'troublesome, inconvenient; trouble, hassle; bother/trouble someone (polite request formula: 麻烦你…)'.

history.meaning: tangled and vexing -> troublesome; trouble; bother someone

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 麻烦 (via 萌典)

麻烦精.etymology: A three-character modifier-head colloquial compound built from the disyllabic noun/adjective 麻烦 (máfan, "trouble, nuisance; troublesome") plus the productive agentive suffix -精 (jīng, literally "spirit, goblin, essence"). 麻烦 coordinates 麻 ("tangled like raw hemp fibers, messy") and 烦 (fán, from 火 "fire" + 页 "head", originally "feverish headache", hence "vexed, bothered"). -精 draws on traditional Chinese folklore in which plants or animals cultivate vital essence (精气) over centuries to become anthropomorphic sprites (妖精), which in modern vernacular grammaticalized into a vivid suffix denoting a person who embodies a trait.

history.meaning: tangled hemp + feverishly vexed in the head + refined essence or supernatural sprite
troublesome affair, nuisance; goblin or personified spirit embodying a vice
walking magnet for trouble, troublemaker, high-maintenance nuisance

morphemes.meaning: feverish in the head; vexed, annoyed, bothered
spirit, sprite, goblin; person who embodies a trait

麻烦精.notes: Often used with affectionate exasperation or teasing in workplace and romantic dramas (e.g., calling an accident-prone intern or demanding talent a 麻烦精), alongside sister -精 slang like 戏精 (drama queen) and 柠檬精 (jealous "lemon spirit").

麻雀.etymology: The noun '麻雀' (máquè, sparrow) combines '麻' (hemp, spotted) and '雀' (small bird). '麻' refers to the plant hemp, but it is also commonly used to describe things that are rough, pockmarked, or mottled with small spots. '雀' is an ancient general term for small, short-tailed birds. '麻雀' specifically describes the common sparrow, characterized by its brownish, mottled plumage. It is one of the most familiar and ubiquitous birds in China, frequently appearing in idioms and colloquial expressions.

history.meaning: bird

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 麻雀

黄.etymology: Ancient pictograph/ideogram attested on Shang oracle bones showing a person wearing a round jade pendant (璜 huáng) at the waist: borrowed from earliest antiquity for the color of loess earth and ripe grain—'yellow, golden, sallow; the Yellow River/Emperor; (colloquially) fall through, fizzle out (of a plan or deal)'.

history.stage: Old Chinese (Oracle bones & Classics) to Modern Mandarin
history.meaning: yellow; golden; fall through (colloquial)

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 黄 (via 萌典)

黄油.etymology: Modifier-head compound noun of 黄 ('yellow') + 油 ('oil, fat'): 'butter' (named for its golden-yellow color when churned from cream; also used in mechanics for yellow lubricating grease).

history.meaning: yellow dairy fat = butter

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 黄油 (via 萌典)

黄糖.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 黄糖. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 黄糖 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 黄糖 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 黄糖 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 黄糖. The etymology of 黄糖 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

history.meaning: early form of 黄糖
middle form of 黄糖
modern form of 黄糖

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 黄糖

黄色.etymology: Modifier-head color compound of 黄 ('yellow') + 色 ('color'): 'yellow color, yellow'.

history.meaning: yellow color; yellow

sources.title: MOE Revised Mandarin Dictionary — 黄色 (via 萌典)

黄铜.etymology: Metallurgical compound of 黄 ('yellow, golden') + 铜 ('copper', metal radical 钅 + phonetic 同 tóng), distinguishing yellow copper-zinc brass from reddish pure copper (红铜/紫铜) and tin bronze (青铜).

history.meaning: copper-zinc brass alloy
brass

黑.etymology: Ancient ideogram attested on Zhou bronzes showing a human figure whose face is smudged with soot above a smoking chimney opening (囱) and fire flames (灬/火) below: 'black (color of soot); dark (nighttime); secret/shady'.

黑乎乎.etymology: A transparent morpheme compound or root for 黑乎乎. Traditional Chinese historical texts describe the evolution of 黑乎乎 starting from early dynasties. Over centuries, 黑乎乎 became widely used in literature. The morphological development of 黑乎乎 shows a fascinating shift in phonetic and semantic components. Modern Mandarin retains the essential core of 黑乎乎. The etymology of 黑乎乎 reflects a deep agricultural, technical, and cultural history. We can see its cognates in various East Asian languages, maintaining its historical meaning throughout the ages.

cognates.meaning: dark history; embarrassing past one wants to forget

黑历史.etymology: A modifier-head nominal compound (黑 hēi "black, dark, hidden" + 历史 lìshǐ "history") borrowed via modern ACGN (anime, comic, games, novel) internet subculture from the Japanese coinage 黒歴史 (kurorekishi). Coined in 1999 by director Yoshiyuki Tomino in the anime series Turn A Gundam to refer to a sealed, catastrophic past era of space wars, 黒歴史 rapidly generalized in Japanese and then Chinese youth and entertainment slang to mean embarrassing, cringeworthy, or scandalous past records, photos, or deeds that a celebrity or individual wishes to erase.

history.meaning: soot-black (dark) + passing through ages + court archivist or chronicle
sealed dark history of past wars in Turn A Gundam; embarrassing personal past
embarrassing past, skeletons in the closet, regrettable old footage or scandals

黑历史.notes: In showbiz and PR contexts (娱乐圈), 扒黑历史 ("digging up dark history") refers to netizens or rival agencies unearthing a celebrity's pre-debut photos, old social media posts, or past scandals; it ranges from lighthearted cringe to career-ending 黑料 (dirt).

rootFamily.gloss: dirt, scandal, damaging gossip on a celebrity
to smear, defame, blacken someone's name

黑夜.etymology: A modifier-head compound combining 黑 (hēi, Old Chinese *hmlˤək, Middle Chinese *xok, an ideogram depicting soot deposited around a smoke-hole or window 囱 over a fire 炎, hence "soot-black, dark") and 夜 (yè, Old Chinese *N.rAk-s, Middle Chinese *jæH, a phono-semantic compound with semantic 夕 "crescent moon, dusk" and phonetic 亦 yì, meaning "night, nighttime"). Together, 黑 modifies 夜 to emphasize the pitch-black darkness of night, attested from medieval Chinese poetry and vernacular narrative onward both literally and as a metaphor for times of despair or secrecy.

history.meaning: soot-black, dark + night, period from dusk to dawn
pitch-dark night, dead of night
dark night, nighttime (literal and figurative)

黑夜.notes: Frequently paired with 白天 (daytime) or 白昼 (broad daylight) in symmetrical expressions like 不分昼夜 ("working round the clock without distinguishing day and night", a staple description of TV and film production crews).

rootFamily.gloss: to stay up late, pull an all-nighter
day and night, round the clock

cognates.meaning: to illicitly pocket or spirit away (parallel resultative construction)

黑掉.etymology: A modern verb-resultative (VR) compound combining the verbalized adjective 黑 (hēi, originally "soot-black, dark", extended in vernacular cant and modern slang to "to smear, defame, embezzle, sabotage, or hack into [reinforced by phono-semantic matching with English hack]") and the phase/resultative complement -掉 (diào, originally "to shake, fall, drop", grammaticalized as a completive marker signifying disposal, elimination, or thorough ruin). Literally "to blacken, hack, or sabotage away completely".

history.meaning: to conceal in the dark, pocket illicitly, cheat or double-cross
to hack and take down (an account or system); to sabotage, smear, or secretly eliminate/embezzle

morphemes.meaning: to blacken, smear, sabotage, embezzle, or hack
away, off (resultative marker of removal, completion, or ruin)

黑掉.notes: Highly polysemous in contemporary workplace and showbiz speech: 把节目黑掉 can mean sabotaging a show behind the scenes, smearing its reputation online, or literally hacking its broadcast files, depending on context.

rootFamily.gloss: to get rid of, take out, eliminate

黑白.etymology: Antonymic color compound pairing 黑 ('black') + 白 ('white'): means literally 'black and white, monochrome (e.g., 黑白照片 black-and-white photo)' and figuratively since Classical Chinese 'right and wrong, good and evil (是非黑白)'.

history.meaning: black and white; right and wrong

默契.etymology: A Classical Chinese modifier-head (adverbial-head) compound composed of 默 (mò, Old Chinese *mˤək, from 黑 "dark/black" as phonetic and semantic + 犬 "dog", originally a dog creeping silently after prey, hence "silent, unspoken") and 契 (qì, Old Chinese *kʰˤet-s, from 丰 "notches cut on a tally stick" + 刀 "knife" + 大, originally "notched tally contract; to match like two halves of a tally"). Literally "to match like two halves of a notched tally without speaking a word", attested in Song-dynasty Neo-Confucian and literary prose for intuitive spiritual or intellectual accord.

history.meaning: silent, unspoken + notched tally contract, to fit together
to tally or correspond inwardly in spirit without words
tacit rapport, unspoken coordination, chemistry between partners

morphemes.meaning: notched tally; to match, agree, bond

默契.notes: Often translates English "chemistry" in professional, athletic, or creative partnerships (e.g., 很有默契 "have great chemistry/unspoken teamwork", 培养默契 "build rapport"); note the standard pronunciation mòqì (never *mòqiè).

rootFamily.gloss: to match like tallies, correspond closely, be in tune

cognates.meaning: tacit approval, turning a blind eye

默认.etymology: A modifier-head (adverbial-verb) Sino-compound combining 默 (mò, "silently, without speaking", from 黑 + 犬) and 认 (rèn, traditional 認, phono-semantic compound with 言 "speech" + 忍 rěn phonetic, meaning "to recognize, acknowledge, admit, consent"). Literally "to acknowledge in silence". Reinforced in modern legal and diplomatic Chinese via Meiji-era Sino-Japanese legal terminology (黙認 mokunin, rendering Western legal concepts of tacit consent or acquiescence), and in late 20th-century computing adapted as the standard Mainland Mandarin term for software "default".

history.meaning: silently, without words + to recognize, acknowledge, admit
to tacitly approve, acquiesce silently, give implied consent
history.stage: Late Qing / Meiji Sino-Japanese Legal Usage

history.meaning: to tacitly approve or admit by silence; (computing) default setting

默认.notes: Bridges interpersonal drama and tech: in dialogue, staying silent when confronted with a rumor is called 默认 ("taking silence as admission"); in software UI, 默认设置 means "default settings" (Taiwan Mandarin uses 預設 yùshè for the tech sense).

鼻子.etymology: Colloquial anatomical noun formed from 鼻 ('nose', combining 自—the original Shang oracle-bone pictograph of a nose, which was later borrowed for 'self'—above phonetic 畀 bì) + nominal suffix 子 (neutral tone zi): 'nose, snout, spout/eye of a needle'.

齐.etymology: Originally an oracle bone and bronze script pictograph (齊, Old Chinese *dzˤəj, Middle Chinese *dzej) depicting three heads of grain or wheat shoots standing at the exact same height in a field. From this concrete agricultural image of "even, level ears of grain", the word evolved in Classical Chinese to mean "even, uniform, aligned", then "to regulate, put in order" (as in 齐家 "to regulate one's household" in the Great Learning), and finally "complete, all present and accounted for, simultaneously together".

history.meaning: ears of grain growing to an even height; even, uniform, level
to make uniform, regulate (a household or state); equal, on a par with; the State of Qi
complete, all present/gathered, neat; simultaneously together

morphemes.meaning: even, uniform; complete, all present, together

齐.notes: Very common as a predicative adjective or resultative complement after verbs of gathering or preparation: 人到齐了 ("everyone has arrived / the whole team is here") and 备齐资料 ("prepare all the required materials completely").

rootFamily.gloss: of one mind, united in purpose

齐齐.etymology: A reduplication of 齐 (qí, 'neat, even, uniform'), originally depicting a field of grain grown to uniform height. Used adverbially, it emphasizes precise synchronicity, such as a group of people moving or looking in the exact same direction simultaneously.
